units.tr: To the most distinguished and magnificent men, the Consuls and the whole Senate of the illustrious Republic of Zurich, my most honoured lords and fathers: Rudolph Gwalther of Zurich wishes grace and peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: ETVS haec consuetudo est, & sanctorum patrum exemplis confirmata, quòd bonarum artium & literarum sectatores, studiorum suorum fructus uel amicis uel principibus uiris, authoritate & honore eximiis, dedicare solent, ut uel illos aliquo amoris officio demereantur, uel idoneos laborum suorum patronos sibi parent. Quòd autem ego meas in apostolorum Acta lucubrationes, uobis potissimum (amplißi uiri, Domini & patres summa fide mihi obseruandi) nuncupandas esse putauerim, multae me & graues causae mouerunt. Priuatim enim uestra in me beneficentia, publicè uerò assidua cura, qua patriae simul & communi religionis causae consultum cupiatis, exigebat, ut & ego aliquo gratitudinis officio meam erga uos voluntatem fidemque testarer, & ardens illud uestrae pietatis studium publico ecclesiae nostrae testimonio commendaretur: cuius exemplum iam annis aliquot permultos non obscuros rerumpub. proceres imitari minimè puduit. Vt tamen ingenuè quod res est fatear, haec mihi potissima mei consilii ratio fuit, quòd libri huius argumentum eiusque consyderationem ad uos omnino pertinere uiderem. Hoc enim uniuersa Ecclesiae Christi ratio absolutiss. continetur, quam omnibus qui in magistratu versantur, cumprimis cognitam & perspectam esse conuenit. Nec enim illi audiendi sunt qui politicos magistratus prophana tantum curare, à sacris autem in uniuersum abstinere uolunt. Qui mihi in ea omnino sententia esse uidentur, ut respub. à Dei prouidentia eximant, quas ne Ethnici quidem sine hac coseruari posse senserunt. Et nota est diuini illius & regij Psalmis sententia: Nisi Dominus custodiat ciuitatem, frustra uigilat custos. Qui idem reges & principes hortatur, ut Dei uerbo sese erudiri patiantur, & filium Dei, Iesum Christum, exosculentur atque obseruent. At quorsum reges Dei uerbo erudiri opus est, si nullus uerbi huius in reipub. administratione usus esse debet? Aut quomodo Christum exosculabuntur, & reuerenter obseruabunt, si ecclesiam, quam ille pupilla oculi sui, imò uita sua chariorem habet, neglexerint? Quomodo item corpus illud negliget, cuius nisi membra fuerint sub Christo capite, salui esse non poterunt? Potius ergo Isaias audiendus erit, qui de Christi Ecclesia uaticinans, inter alia ait: Erunt reges nutritij tui, & reginae eorum nutrices tuae. Quo oraculo non tam Ecclesiam consolari uidetur, quàm regum & magistratuum officium atque dignitatem commendare, quæ in eo præcipuè elucent, quòd illis Deus curæ Ecclesiæ suæ committe‑re dignatur, quàm filij sui sanguine redemptam voluit. Fatemur quidem Deum in hac re hominum opera nequaquam opus habere, siquidem ab‑soluta sua potestate uti uelit. Nec etiam negamus, Ecclesias plerunque oc‑culta potius Dei virtute & ineffabili consilio, quàm hominum industria, propagari atq; defendi, Id uerò non ideo fieri dicimus, quòd magistratuū curam & officium Deus improbet, sed ut omnem Ecclesiæ conseruatæ lau‑dem & gloriam ipsi uni acceptam ferri debere constet, neue quis religio‑nem ab hominum potius arbitrio, quàm Dei prouidentia pendere arbi‑tretur. Interim ea est Dei bonitas, ut homines cooperarios habere digne‑tur, quorum ministerio electos suos per verbum regenerat, & eosdem sub piis magistratibus inter undiq; imminentia pericula aduersus mūdi huius furores tuetur: ut quatenus fidei & salutis ipsorum ratio exigit, pace frui posint. Atque hanc Dei voluntatem esse, non scripturæ modò testantur, sed unanimis omnium gentium consensus probat. Certè aureo illo patri‑archarum seculo, penes unum & eundem & regni & sacerdotij functio‑nem fuisse legimus. Postquam verò in lege Deus hæc officia distincta esse voluit, idem tamen summam inter reges & sacerdotes coniunctionem in‑stituit: ne vel illi absq; religione regnarent, vel hi ab illorum cura atq; pro‑tectione exempti, impiorum libidini & tyrannidi paterent. Quo cum pri‑mis referri debet, quòd cum Iudæorum gentem primum lege sua instrue‑ret, Mosem & Aaronem, fratres germanos delegit, & huic quidem tabers‑naculi & totius cultus diuini curam, illi uerò reipub. administrationem con‑credidit: ita docens, tunc demum respub. simul & Ecclesias saluas fore, si fraterna sit inter duos hosce ordines coniunctio. Viderunt hoc quotquot uel ex Iudicum uel Regum numero ob rectam reipub. administrationem in sacris literis commendantur: quales cum primis Gedeonem, Samuelem, Dauidem, Iosaphan, Ezechiā & Iosiam fuisse legimus. Quibus si reliquos conferas, quos nigro calculo spiritus sanctus notauit, hanc unam illis priuatim & publicè omnis mali causam fuisse comperies, quòd uel Dei uer‑bum & religionis curam nihil ad se pertinere putarunt, uel in his pro suo arbitrio ludere ausi sunt. Quòd si gentium historias legamus, illas quidem in ueri Dei cognitione hallucinatas esse, & proinde Dei cultum horren‑dis erroribus polluisse constat. At eædem commune illud principium si‑ue axioma firmiter retinuerunt, quo admonebantur, respub. absque uero Dei cultu & diuinæ uoluntatis cognitione feliciter administrari non pos‑se. Quæ causa fuit, quòd & philosophos, sapientiæ haud uulgaris profes‑fores, in pretio habuerunt, & Deorum oracula in rebus dubijs quæsiue‑runt, & in extruendis Deorum templis, aris atq; imaginibus immodicos & insanos sumptus fecerunt. Athenienses certè, quorum ciuitas uniuersa‑lis & publica sapientiæ schola habita fuit, religionem adeò sibi curandam putarunt, ut inter publici iurisiurandi articulos, quibus ciues obstringe‑bantur, bantur, hic non postremus esset, ἀμωῶ δὲ καὶ ὑπὲρ ἱερῶν καὶ ὑπὲρ ὁσίων, καὶ μόνος καὶ μετὰ πολλῶν, id est pugnabo pro templis & sacris solus & cum aliis. Senserunt ergo isti homines, de Dei cultu cum primis oportere solicitos esse, quicunque vel publicam pacem retinere, vel priuatim feliciter agere cupiunt. Nemo igitur me temeritatis accusauerit, si & communi sensu carere, & profanis gentibus caeciores esse dixero eos, qui ecclesiae & religionis curam a politicis magistratibus alienam esse clamant. Nec me aberraturum putauero, si eosdem, ut publicos humani generis hostes cauedos esse dicam.
units.tr: Such is the custom, confirmed by the examples of the holy Fathers, that devotees of the liberal arts and letters are wont to dedicate the fruits of their studies to friends or to princes and men distinguished by authority and honour, either to win their favour by some service of affection or to secure for themselves fit patrons for their labours. Why I thought fit to dedicate my commentaries on the Acts of the Apostles chiefly to you, most distinguished men, my lords and fathers whom I am bound to honour with the utmost loyalty, several weighty reasons moved me. For your kindness towards me in private, and your constant care in public, by which you seek the welfare of our homeland and at the same time of the common cause of religion, demanded that I too should bear witness to my goodwill and loyalty towards you by some duty of gratitude, and that your ardent zeal for piety be commended by the public testimony of our Church. Many distinguished leaders of the commonwealth have for several years not been ashamed to imitate this example. But to confess frankly how things stand, the chief reason for my plan was that I saw the subject of this book and its consideration to pertain wholly to you. For the entire system of Christ's Church is most completely contained in it, and it is fitting that it be known and understood especially by all who hold office in government. Those should not be listened to who want the civil magistrates to attend only to profane matters and to keep entirely away from sacred ones. They seem to me to hold the view that commonwealths are removed from God's providence, though not even the heathens thought they could be preserved without it. The saying of that divine and royal Psalm is well known: "Unless the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh in vain." The same Psalm exhorts kings and princes to allow themselves to be taught by the word of God, and to kiss and honour the Son of God, Jesus Christ. But why must kings be taught by God's word, if no use of this word is to be made in the administration of the commonwealth? Or how will they kiss Christ and reverently honour him, if they neglect the Church, which he holds dearer than the apple of his eye, indeed dearer than his own life? Likewise, how will they neglect that body, without whose members under Christ the head they cannot be saved? Rather, Isaiah should be heeded, who, prophesying about Christ's Church, says among other things: "Kings shall be your nursing fathers, and their queens your nurses." In this oracle he seems less to console the Church than to commend the office and dignity of kings and magistrates, which shine out especially in this, that God deigns to entrust to them the care of his Church, which he willed to be redeemed by the blood of his Son. We admit indeed that in this matter God has by no means need of human work, if he chose to use his absolute power. Nor do we deny that Churches are for the most part propagated and defended by the hidden power of God and his ineffable counsel rather than by human industry. But we do not say this because God disapproves of the care and office of magistrates, but so that it is plain that all praise and glory for the preservation of the Church must be ascribed to him alone, and lest anyone think religion depends on human judgment rather than on God's providence. Meanwhile God's goodness is such that he deigns to have men as co-workers, through whose ministry he regenerates his elect by the word, and under pious magistrates he protects them on every side against the dangers threatening them and the rages of this world, so that, as far as the reason of their faith and salvation requires, they may enjoy peace. Not only do the Scriptures attest that this is God's will, but the unanimous consensus of all nations proves it. Certainly in that golden age of the patriarchs we read that the function of kingship and priesthood was in one and the same person. But after God willed these offices to be distinct under the law, he nonetheless established the closest union between kings and priests, so that the former should not reign without religion, nor the latter, freed from their care and protection, be exposed to the lust and tyranny of the wicked. To this must first be referred the fact that when he instructed the Jewish nation by his law, he chose Moses and Aaron, full brothers, and entrusted to the one the care of the tabernacle and of the whole divine worship, and to the other the administration of the commonwealth, thereby teaching that the commonwealth and the Churches would be safe only if there were a brotherly union between these two orders. All who are commended in Holy Scripture for the right administration of the commonwealth, whether among the Judges or the Kings, saw this. Such men especially were Gideon, Samuel, David, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah, as we read. If you compare with them the rest, whom the Holy Spirit has marked with a black stone, you will find that for them, both privately and publicly, the one cause of every evil was that either they thought God's word and the care of religion did not pertain to them, or they dared to trifle with these things at their own pleasure. And if we read the histories of the nations, it is clear that they went astray in the knowledge of the true God, and therefore polluted the worship of God with dreadful errors. Yet they firmly retained that common principle or axiom, by which they were reminded that a commonwealth cannot be happily administered without the true worship of God and knowledge of the divine will. This was why they both held philosophers, professors of no common wisdom, in high esteem, and sought the oracles of the gods in doubtful matters, and spent immoderate and mad sums on building temples, altars and images of the gods. The Athenians certainly, whose city was regarded as the universal and public school of wisdom, thought religion so much their concern that among the articles of the public oath by which citizens were bound, this was not the least: "I will defend the temples and the sacred things and the holy things, alone and with many" [ἀμυνῶ δὲ καὶ ὑπὲρ ἱερῶν καὶ ὑπὲρ ὁσίων, καὶ μόνος καὶ μετὰ πολλῶν], that is, I will fight for temples and sacred rites, alone or with others. These men therefore felt that all who wish either to keep public peace or to live happily in private must be especially concerned about the worship of God. No one, then, will accuse me of rashness if I say that those who cry out that the care of the Church and of religion is foreign to political magistrates lack common sense and are blinder than the profane nations. Nor do I think I would be mistaken if I said that they should be avoided as public enemies of the human race.

units.la: Nam si religionem homini auferamus, quid reliquum erit, quo ille a brutis differat? Eosdem certe in hominibus affectuum motus, qui in feris sunt, cernimus; qui nisi religionis sensu coerceantur, mox quauis occasione erumpunt, eoque nocentius grassantur, si publica authoritate & ciuilis gladij iure armati fuerint. Ne quid tamen audaci & praepostero carnis consilio peccetur, multum proderit ueram & germanam Ecclesiae formam habere, quam in suis consilijs sibi imitandam proponant, quicunque illam uel tueri uel collapsam instaurare studuerunt. Hanc nobis passim sacrae literae exhibent: & in lege quidem omnes illius partes sub Tabernaculi typo, in prophetis uero sub sponsae, gregis, uineae, templi & urbis Hierosolymae allegoria inspiciendas proponunt. Exemplum autem illius absolutum & euidens hic liber comprehendit, & Ecclesia ita aliquando enatam esse, talemque fuisse docet, qualem nobis olim prophetae descripserunt; ne quis nos Ecclesiam in ore habere dicat, quae nec unquam in terris fuerit, nec unquam futura sit, quod olim de Platonis repub. sapientes & acuti homines dixerunt. Etsi enim complementum Ecclesiae olim in coelis demum uisuri simus, eam tamen illius formam liber hic exhibet, cui quicunque se accommodauerint, ij coelestis illius & omnibus numeris absolutae Ecclesiae membra erunt, simulque intelligent, quam uiam ipsi quoque in reformandis & conseruandis ecclesijs tenere debeant, nec ullis persecutionum & aduersae fortunae casibus offendentur, nec illorum somnia admittent, qui nouam nobis Ecclesiae formam obtrudunt, dum ueteribus multa defuisse dicunt, quae postea demum a sanctis patribus constituta, & publica Conciliorum authoritate recepta atque stabilita sint. Cum enim liber hic annorum circiter XXVIII. historiam comprehendat, & ecclesiae per totum orbem propagatae res gestas, adhaec apostolorum conciones, consilia, dicta factaque tum publica tum priuata, sufficienti & dilucida narratione exponat; quis non impudentem dixerit esse eum, qui alia nonnulla ad salutem necessaria esse contendat, quibus ueterem illam Ecclesiam uere Christianam & apostolicam caruisse sciamus? Cuius item arrogantiae fuerit cum apostolis, quos Dei filius orbis totius doctores rerumque suarum testes esse voluit, certamen suscipere? Quae uero a nobis perfectius quiddam excogitari & fingi possit? Porro non parum proderit, ueterem illam Ecclesiae formam, & praecipuas illius partes, quasi per transennam inspicere. Quam primo quidem ex Dei uerbo enatam esse Lucas docet, quando & Christum in coelos conscendisse, & inde spiritum suum misisse scribit, quo instructi apostoli euangelium mundo praedicare, & Christo discipulos adducere coeperunt. Unde colligimus a sana verbi Dei doctrina illis incipiendum esse, quicunque vel ipsi Ecclesiae Christi membra fieri, vel alios ad huius communionem adducere instituerunt. Quia enim irae filii nascimur, coelitus regeneremur oportet, ut Dei filii reddamur. Regenerationis vero huius semen est aeternum illud Dei Verbum, quod hominum quidem ministerio praedicatum, sed spiritus virtute in auditorum animis uiuificatum, totam hominis naturam innouat, ut mortificato carnis ingenio, uni Deo per Christum viuant, qui paulo ante a Deo alieni, peccato viuebant. Caeterum verbi doctrinam unam & eandem passim apostoli tradiderunt, quam suis partibus Christus ipse distinxerat, quando in suo nomine primo poenitentiam, deinde peccatorum remissionem praedicare iussit. Et quamuis non idem semper auditores darentur, imo illos tum conditione tum moribus & ingenio multum discrepare viderent: nihil tamen propterea in euangelii doctrina vel mutandum vel omittendum esse putarunt, in hoc unum intenti, ut recte secando verbum quam plurimos Christo adducerent. Verbi doctrinae Sacramentorum usum coniunxerunt, & quos credidisse viderant, eos una cum suis omnibus per baptismum in Ecclesiae consortium receperunt, & ipsdem Eucharistiae ritum, ab ipso Christo praescriptum, tradiderunt, cuius exercitio redemptionis beneficium obsignatur, & grata peragitur mortis Domini commemoratio, & firmiori charitatis nexu totum Ecclesiae corpus coalescit. Atqui istis rationibus intra annos uiginti octo totum terrarum orbe Christo subiectum fuisse constat, & quidem illorum ministerio, quos nec generis nobilitas, nec pristinae conditionis dignitas, nec eruditionis existimatio commendabat. Diuinum ergo & coeleste hoc opus fuit, in quo & Dei potentiam reuereri, & eiusdem bonitatem exoculari debemus, qui mundo sub diaboli tyrannide laboranti tam benigne consultum voluit. Ecclesiae vero primitiuae studia idem hic liber diligentissime exponit. Audiuerunt euangelii doctrinam peccatores insignes & palam scelerati, imo illi ipsi, qui paucis diebus ante unigeniti filii Dei sanguinem nefario ausu effuderat. At idem in peccatorum cognitionem adducti, illa ingenue confessi sunt, & sola Dei misericordia per Christum freti, remissionis gratiam impetrarunt. Inde vero omissis peccatorum studiis uitam in melius commutarunt, & ab illis secessionem fecerunt, quorum conuersatione se polui posse uidebant. Innocentiae studio preces coniunxerunt, in quibus assiduos fuisse multa exempla docent, cum & propriae infirmitatis sensu, & quotidianis periculis excitarentur. Ne vero vel doctrinae vel Sacramentorum salutari exercitio quicquam decederet, potissima illis cura fuit, ut ministri & presbyteri passim haberentur, quos & oppidatim ordinandos, & diligenti cura in officio retinendos esse censuerunt. Tandem ne in inani dunni duntaxat speculatione Christianismus cõsistere uideretur, tantum apud istos homines beneficentiæ & charitatis studium fuit, ut illud hodie admirari facilius sit quàm imitari. Nam & suis pauperibus singulæ ecclesiæ fide liter prospexerunt, & si quæ opulentiores erat, exterorum quoq; inopiam missis eleemosynis subleuarunt: nimirum Christi memores, qui è terris di scessurus, pauperes in suum locum substituit, secþ in suas rationes ascriptu rum pollicetur, quicquid beneficij in illos collatum fuerit. At cum tam san-ctis studiis occupati, ab omnibus amari & coli mererentur, undiq; hostes infensissimi exorti sunt. Contradixerunt illis ludæorum scribæ & gentium philosophi: quare cum illis perpetuo pugnandum fuit, qui inter ludæos simul & gentes præcipuam sapientiæ & eruditionis laudem sustinebant. Adhæc in ipsa Ecclesia falsi fratres exorti sunt, qui & tristibus exemplis primùm nascentis fidei progressus interruperunt, & fraudulentis conatibus multos offenderunt; qualis ex ludæis Ananias, ex Samaritanis verò Simon Magus fuere. Sed & nepharij quidã & illicitis artibusediti, apostolis & psijs negotium fecerunt, in Cypro quidem Bariehu, siue Elymas Magus, Philippis autem Pythonis spiritu afflata puella, & ludæi quidam exorcistæ apud Ephesios. At quia omnibus hisce nihil se profecturum uidebat satan, ipsos magistratus excitare cœpit, qui nascentem veræ & salutaris fidei segetem publica authoritate reprimerent. Et huius quidem rei initium ludæi fecerunt, ut eo magis suspecta esset Christiana religio, quando necab ea gente admitteretur, unde primùm exorta fuerat. Hierosolymis ergo in Senatum uocatur apostoli, silentium illis indicitur, uirgis cæsi cum minacibus electis dimittuntur. Tandem lapidatur Stephanus, psij urbe fugantur, longè lateq; grassatur persecutio, neque ipsis apostolis parcitur, quando Iacobum Herodes obtruncat, idem Petro quoq; in ludæorum gratiam facturus, nisi illum Dominus præsenti periculo miraculose subduxisset. Necid ludæis satis esse uisum fuit, quòd ipsi Christum regem & salutarem agnoscere dedignarentur, sed eundem ne inter gentes quidem regnare uoluerunt. Idem ergo passim apostolis turbarum authores sunt, ut exijs patet, quæ Antiochiæ, Iconij, Lystris, Corinthi, Thessalonicæ, & in finitis aliis locis euenerunt. Horum denique opera effectum est, ut apostoli ac Christianæ fidei professores, non modò circa religionem peccare, ueru-metiam in Romanorum leges audacter delinquere, & orbem uniuersum turbare dicerentur. Quare eò usque tandem res deducta fuit, ut Romani quoque imperatores, quorum potentia illo tempore per omnes mundi partes extendebatur, in Christianos gladium stringerent. In tantis uerò tamq; uarijs periculis, & hostium uaferrimis simul atque immaniss. conatibus, admiranda apostolorum & reliquorum credentium constantia eluxit, qua & fidem in Christum ingenuè professi sunt, & ueritatis doctrinâ fideliter asseruerunt, nec ullis uel blanditiis uel minis sese adduci passi sunt, ut à statione, in quam à Domino collocati erant, discederent. Non defuit ergo sanctæ constantiæ fidelis Deus, sed ecclesiam suam sibi curæ esse, multis ijsdemque luculentissimis argumentis testatus est. Nam & angelorum ministerio vinctos liberat, visionibus lætis consolatur, patientiæ & constantiæ spiritu armat, os & linguam largitur cui nemo resistere potest, miraculis doctrinam & fidem suorum confirmat, hominum mentes ut illis credant efficaciter trahit, facit denique ut vel invito mundo & mundi principe evangelii doctrina per tela, per ignes, felicibus auspiciis in toto orbe propagetur. Et in his quidem perfecta & omnibus numeris absoluta Ecclesiæ forma continetur, sub cuius partes omnia ea referri possunt, quæ de illa in scripturis passim traduntur. Hanc vero vos quoque viri amplissimi observuaasse res ipsa testatur. Cum enim annis ab hinc retro triginta novem, Helvetiam nostram verbi sui fulgore Deus illustrare, & ex superstitionum tenebris in evangelii lucem revocare dignaretur, nullam amplius moram ad mittendam esse arbitrati, de Christi regno in vestra Repub. instaurando mature & serio cogitare coepistis. Mox ergo Episcopos, & inter hos Constantiensem in primis, ad cuius curam ditio vestra tota pertinebat, solicitare voluistis, ut illi in tollendis abusibus & superstitionibus operam suam vobis locare, & Ecclesiæ reformationem ipsi vobis adiuvatibus instituere vellent. At cum illi suæ vocationis & officii parum memores cunctarentur, iniquissimum & indignissimum vobis facinus esse videbatur, illorum negligentiam publicæ saluti & gloriæ Dei diutius obstare, & vosipsos (ne vestro officio deesse tis) pulcherrimi sanctissimique facti duces & authores præbuistis: nimirum Ezechiæ, Iosiæ, Constantini & aliorum exemplum imitati, quos olim cessantibus ecclesiarum ministris sive præsulibus idem magna cum laude facti tavisse legimus. Nam indicto omnium, qui in urbe & agro vestro ecclesiis ministrabant, publico & generali conventu, de præcipuis fidei & religionis capitibus illos ex Dei verbo inter se conferre iussistis. Nec deerant, qui huic instituto sese acriter opponerent, qui huius causæ determinationem, non in unius Reipub, aut Principis arbitrio consistere, sed ad generalis & Oecumenici Concilii authoritatem pertinere clamabant. Non tamen apud vos tanta fuit illorum authoritas, ut a tergo respicere velletis, postquam iam manum aratro admoveratis. Feliciter ergo successit pie sancteque inceptum negotium. Vicit enim in disputatione illa Veritas, & ita vicit, ut maxima eorum pars, qui illam oppugnaturi venerant, illi sponte colla submitterent, & ex eo sibi præcipuam laudem & gloriam venarentur, quod feliciter devictis Christi triumphantis currum sequi datum esset. Ab eo tempore nunquam destitistis ea consultare simul & facere, quæ ad regni Christi gloriam pertinere videbatis. Nam & templa ab imaginum altariumque sordibus, & doctrinam ab humanarum traditionum perniciosis figmentis repurgavistis, publica authoritate cavent es, ne quis vel superstitiones abolitas reduceret, vel Christi ovibus aliquid ab evangelii doctrina alienum inter docendum propinaret. Sacramentorum vero usum & administrationem ad primæ institutionis formam reuocari, præ‐ces tum publicè tum priuatim ritè instituti, & quæcunque alia sunt ueræ fi‐dei officia secundum apostolicæ doctrinæ præscriptum exerceri, imò publi‐cas quoque leges & morum disciplinam iuxta euangelij normam reforma‐ri curauistis. Et ne quis hæc à uobis uel priuati commodi, uel nouarum re‐rum studio fieri putaret, diligenter cauistis, ut ad uos nihil feré quàm refor‐mandi molestia, ad alios autem lætissimus reformationis fructus rediret. Nec enim Ecclesiarū bonis temerarias & rapaces manus iniecistis, nec quen‐quam inter uestræ ditionis homines, siue nobilem siue ecclesiasticum, suo iure depulistis. Eos enim quos commune illud ignorantiæ malum decep‐perat, non inhumaniter eiicere, sed amica & fraterna institutione lucrifa‐cere studuistis. Quo factum est, ut qui inter illos ingenio ualebant, egre‐giam postea operam Christo & Ecclesiæ ipsius nauarent, reliqui uero quos uel senium uel ingenij tarditas impediebat, bonis suis & redditibus pacifi‐ce fruerentur, nec aliquam uel quiritandi uel tumultuandi causam habe‐rent. Quicquid uero bonorum uestræ administrationi cessit, illud omne partim scholis, partim pauperum subuentioni destinatum est. Nec enim artium modo & linguarum professores, uerumetiam illarum candidatos iuuenes non minus octoginta continuo stipendio liberaliter alere consue‐uistis: adeo ut plerique illorum, qui hodie in urbe & agro uestro (qui paro‐chias circiter centum quadraginta continet) Christum prædicant, aut bo‐nas literas profitentur, uestræ illud liberalitati debeant, quòd in eo gradu constituti sunt. Tanta uero fuit uestra in his omnibus instituendis dexte‐ritas, tanta consulendi prudentia & agendi modestia, ut quod impossibile factu uidebatur, facilliùs successerit: adeo ut in gente libera, absque ullo se ditionis publicæ metu, hæc quæ diximus omnia, magno cum populi ap‐plausu, breui admodum temporis spacio, & instituta & ad suum finem per ducta sint. Etsi enim multa sæpe tentarint, qui Papatum sibi quæstuosum putabant, & proinde illius ruinam æquo animo ferre non poterant, singu‐lari tamen Dei beneficio factum est, ut illorum conatus semper irriti fue‐rint, & per hos excitatæ tempestates cœlestis numinis salutari aura discu‐terentur. Qua in re iuxta Christi præceptum & columbina simplicitas, & prudentia serpentina in uestris consiliis eluxit. Quoties enim aduersarij uos uel blandis & amicis promissionibus uel terrificis minis ab instituto reuocare, uel saltem persuadere conati sunt, ut totam religionis causam Episcoporū & Præsulum iudicio subiicere dignaremini, prudenter simul & simpliciter hoc unum respondistis: Vos nec posse nec uelle ea negare & reiicere, quæ ex Dei uerbo uera esse didiceritis, paratos autem esse ad reddendam rationem cuiuis petenti, imò libenter cuiuis esse cessuros, qui uos per scripturæ sacræ oracula erroris conuincere, & meliorem salutis ra‐tionem edocere posit. Extant eius generis responsiones permultæ, qui‐bus multorum ora obturauistis, & in quibus plane illud apostolicum au‐ ditur: An iustum sit in conspectu Dei uos potius audire quàm Deum, iudicate. Non enim possumus, quæ uidimus & audiuimus, non loqui. Item: Oportet Deo obedire magis quàm hominibus. Fauit ergo tam prss conatibus cœlestis & æterni numinis gratia, qua factum est, ut Respub. uestra infinita omnis generis tribulationum pericula feliciter euaserit, & hodie inter dubios & horribiles totius orbis Christiani motus, non ipsa modo pace fruatur, uerumetiam exteris hinc inde ad uos confluentibus tutum asylum præbeat. Magnis ergo & grauibus causis me moueri sentio, amplissimi uiri & Domini mihi unicè obseruandi, ut uestræ Amplitudini hunc meum laborem dedicem, quo pro gratia mihi diuinitus concessa, eum liberum illustrare conatus sum, qui primam nascentis in hoc orbe terrarum Ecclesiæ faciem, progressus, incrementa & conditionem omnem describit, cuius exemplar uos non minori studio & labore quàm felici successu imitatos esse uideo. Quem si familiarem sibi habeant qui uobis in Reipub. administratione succedent, & uos nihil temerè fecisse uidebunt, & haud leuibus stimulis sese excitari sentient, ut eam restitutæ Ecclesiæ & religionis formam, quam à uobis acceperunt, totis uiribus retinere conentur. Et sane multum refert crebrò meditari, quibus initiis & rationibus maiores nostri tum Reipub. tum Ecclesiæ formam constituerint. Ita enim nec calumniatores audient, qui piè & sanctè facta maligne carpunt, nec insurgentibus persecutionum procellis & minacibus mundi studiis sese à uero reuocari patientur. Prodest item apud populum de his non raro uerba facere, qui ut plerunque præsentibus ducitur: ita & præteritorum obliuione faci le capi, & raram de futuris cogitationem habere solet. Quare magistratuum consilia tunc demum probat, quando illa uel cum præsenti aliquo commodo coniuncta, uel tuta & ἀxινδωx esse uidet. Vt primum uero periculi metus & terror oboritur, mox & prudentiam & integritatem in iis desiderat, quorum consilia iuuare, & isdem fideliter obedire debebat. Quòd si uero idem intelligat, magistratum suorum consiliorum ducem & authorem habuisse Deum, & ex officio fecisse quæcunque fecit, certè religiosius multò de illis iudicare discit & isdem facilius obtemperat, nec temerè ad quosuis imminentium periculorum rumores offenditur. Mihi certè hæc potissimum ratio ob oculos uersata est, cum librum hunc Ecclesiæ Christi, quæ apud uos est, publicè interpretari, & quæ publicè dixeram scriptis mandare & in uulgus edere instituissem. Videbam enim eam esse seculi nostri subinde in deterius ruentis conditionem, ut necesse omnino sit sacræ scripturæ libros indesinenti studio euoluere, & quæ in illis exstant Ecclesiæ ueteris exempla populo spectanda proponere, ne illorum commentis se decipi patiatur, qui sub falso uetustatis nomine nouos errores obtrudunt, & quæ graues & sancti uiri nobis ex Dei uerbo restitue-rūt, nouitatis accusant. Excipietis ergo meas hæce lucubrationes, amplissimi & magnifici uiri, eo fauore, quo pietatis uerae studiū iam multis annis, meq mecū una cum multis æqualibus meis iam inde à puero prosecuti estis. Pergite autem ea, qua coepistis uia, uerum Dei cultum prouehere. Pergite studiis sacris fauere. Pergite peregrinos & Christi exules solita humanitate excipere. Pergite legum disciplinam tueri, populi mores corrigere, uirtutum studia propagare, & scelera sancto iustitiæ freno cohercere. Regnat multis in locis horribilis Dei contemptus. Multi salutare uerbi Dei & cognitionis Christi beneficium improbè fastidiunt. Refrigescit multorum charitas, & fides paulatim emoritur. Abundat iniquitas, & noua indies scelerum genera pullulant. Minatur ergo pœnas iratus Deus, & orbem terrarum prodigiis, portentis, & horrendis regnorum motibus territat. Idem tamen ils nunquam deerit, qui gloriam ipsius prouehere, Ecclesiam Christi sui tueri, & pro suæ uocationis modulo officium facere perrexerint. Benedicet illê laboribus uestris, & consilia uestra suo spiritu diriget. Benedicet populo uestro uniuerso, ut & sanctis legibus sponte pareat, & læto euangelicæ pacis beneficio felicis, fruatur. Benedicet ecclesiæ uestræ toti, ut in pietatis doctrina simul & exercitio maiores indies progressus faciat. Ipsi, qui solus est, Dominus dominantium, immortalis & æternus Deus, debetur benedictio, honor gloria, & potestas in æternum. Amen. Datæ Tiguri, in uestra ciuitate, inclyta Heluetiorum metropoli, Cal. Augusti, anno salutis humanæ M. D. LVII.
units.tr: If we take religion away from man, what will remain by which he differs from the brutes? We certainly see in men the same surges of passion that are in wild beasts, and unless these are restrained by a sense of religion, they break out on any occasion, and rage all the more harmfully when they are armed with public authority and the power of the civil sword. Still, so that nothing is done through a rash and foolish fleshly plan, it will greatly help to have the true and genuine form of the Church before one's eyes, and to propose it for imitation in one's counsels, whoever has tried either to defend it or to restore it when it has fallen. Holy Scripture sets this form before us everywhere: in the Law, all its parts are to be seen under the type of the Tabernacle, and in the Prophets under the allegory of the bride, the flock, the vineyard, the temple and the city of Jerusalem. This book contains a complete and clear example of it, and it teaches that the Church once arose and was such as the prophets earlier described it to us. Let no one say that we have in our mouth a Church which has never existed on earth and never will exist, as wise and shrewd men once said of Plato's commonwealth. For although we shall see the fulfilment of the Church only in heaven, this book sets forth that form of it, and whoever conform themselves to it will be members of that heavenly Church, absolute in every respect. At the same time they will understand what way they too ought to follow in reforming and preserving churches, and they will not be offended by any cases of persecution or adverse fortune, nor will they admit the dreams of those who thrust upon us a new form of the Church, saying that the early Church lacked many things which were only afterwards established by the holy Fathers and received and confirmed by the public authority of the Councils. For since this book covers a history of about twenty-eight years, and sets out with sufficient and clear narrative the deeds of the Church spread through the whole world, as well as the sermons, counsels, and words and deeds of the apostles, both public and private, who could fairly call impudent the man who insists that some other things are necessary for salvation, without which we know that the ancient Church, truly Christian and apostolic, lacked? And whose arrogance would it be to take on a contest with the apostles, whom the Son of God wished to be teachers of the whole world and witnesses of his deeds? Or what more perfect thing could be devised and invented by us? Moreover, it will be of no small benefit to look, as it were through a window, at that ancient form of the Church and its chief parts. Luke teaches that it first arose from the Word of God, when he writes both that Christ ascended into heaven and from there sent his Spirit, by whom the apostles, equipped, began to preach the gospel to the world and to bring disciples to Christ. From this we gather that those who undertake either to become members of the Church of Christ themselves, or to bring others into its fellowship, must begin with the sound doctrine of the Word of God. For since we are born children of wrath, we must be regenerated from heaven, so that we may become children of God. The seed of this regeneration is that eternal Word of God, which, though it is preached through the ministry of men, is made alive in the minds of the hearers by the power of the Spirit, and renews the whole nature of man, so that, with the nature of the flesh put to death, they may live to God alone through Christ, who a little before lived alien from God, in sin. Moreover, the apostles everywhere handed down one and the same teaching of the Word, which Christ himself had divided into its parts, when he commanded that in his name repentance should be preached first, and then the forgiveness of sins. And although the hearers were not always the same, but they saw that they differed greatly in condition, morals and temperament, they nevertheless thought that nothing in the doctrine of the gospel should be changed or omitted on that account, intent on this one thing alone, that by rightly handling the word they might bring as many as possible to Christ. They joined the use of the sacraments to the doctrine of the Word, and those whom they saw to have believed, together with all their household, they received into the fellowship of the Church through baptism; and they handed down to them the rite of the Eucharist, prescribed by Christ himself, by the practice of which the benefit of redemption is sealed, the grateful remembrance of the Lord's death is performed, and the whole body of the Church is joined together by a firmer bond of love. And indeed it is well known that by these means the whole world was subjected to Christ within twenty-eight years, and this by the ministry of men whom neither nobility of birth, nor the dignity of their former station, nor the reputation for learning commended. This work was therefore divine and heavenly, in which we ought both to revere the power of God and to admire his goodness, who was pleased to provide so kindly for a world labouring under the tyranny of the devil. This same book sets out most diligently the zeal of the primitive Church. Notorious sinners and open criminals heard the doctrine of the gospel, indeed even those very men who had a few days before wickedly shed the blood of the only-begotten Son of God. But these same men, brought to the knowledge of their sins, openly confessed them, and, relying on God's mercy alone through Christ, obtained the grace of forgiveness. Then, giving up their sinful pursuits, they changed their life for the better, and withdrew from those whose company they saw could defile them. They joined prayers to their zeal for innocence, and many examples teach that they were constant in these, since they were stirred both by a sense of their own weakness and by daily dangers. And so that nothing should be lacking to the doctrine or to the saving exercise of the sacraments, their chief care was that ministers and elders should be appointed everywhere, and they judged that these should be ordained town by town and kept diligently to their duty. Finally, lest Christianity seem to consist in an empty speculation of mere opinion, there was among those people such zeal for beneficence and charity that it is now easier to admire it than to imitate it. For each church faithfully provided for its own poor, and if any were richer, they also relieved the want of strangers by sending alms, mindful of Christ, who, about to depart from the earth, substituted the poor in his own place, and promised that whatever kindness was shown to them would be credited to his own account. But while they were occupied with such holy pursuits, and deserved to be loved and honoured by all, most hostile enemies arose on every side. The scribes of the Jews and the philosophers of the Gentiles spoke against them; hence they had to fight constantly against those who, among Jews and Gentiles alike, held the chief reputation for wisdom and learning. Besides this, false brothers arose within the Church itself, who by sad examples interrupted the early progress of the nascent faith, and by fraudulent attempts offended many: such were Ananias from among the Jews, and from the Samaritans Simon Magus. But also certain sorcerers, given to unlawful arts, made trouble for the apostles and the godly: in Cyprus Bar-Jesus, or Elymas the magician; at Philippi a girl possessed by the spirit of Python; and certain Jewish exorcists at Ephesus. But since Satan saw that he would gain nothing by all these means, he began to stir up the magistrates themselves, who were to suppress by public authority the young crop of the true and saving faith. And the Jews made a beginning of this business, so that the Christian religion might be the more suspected, since it was not admitted by that nation from which it had first arisen. So at Jerusalem the apostles were summoned before the Senate, silence was ordered for them, and after being beaten with rods, they were dismissed with threats. Then Stephen was stoned, the godly were driven out of the city, and persecution raged far and wide, nor were the apostles themselves spared, since Herod put James to death, intending to do the same to Peter also to please the Jews, had not the Lord miraculously rescued him from the imminent danger. Nor did it seem enough to the Jews that they themselves refused to acknowledge Christ as king and saviour; they did not even want him to reign among the Gentiles. So they were everywhere the authors of tumults against the apostles, as appears from what happened at Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Corinth, Thessalonica, and in other places without number. Finally, through their work it came about that the apostles and professors of the Christian faith were called not only sinners in religion, but also bold transgressors of the laws of the Romans, and disturbers of the whole world. Hence matters were at last brought to such a pass that the Roman emperors also, whose power at that time extended through all parts of the world, drew the sword against the Christians. But amid such great and varied dangers, and the most crafty and at the same time most savage attempts of enemies, the admirable constancy of the apostles and of the other believers shone forth. They openly professed their faith in Christ and faithfully defended the doctrine of the truth, and they allowed themselves to be moved neither by flattery nor by threats from the post in which the Lord had placed them. God, then, was not wanting to his faithful saints in constancy, but has testified by many and most striking proofs that he cared for his Church. For through the ministry of angels he frees the bound, comforts them with joyful visions, arms them with the spirit of patience and constancy, gives a mouth and a tongue which no one can resist, confirms the teaching and faith of his people by miracles, draws the minds of men effectively to believe them, and finally brings it about that the doctrine of the gospel, through swords and through fires, is spread abroad with prosperous auspices throughout the whole world, even though the world and the prince of the world are opposed. In these things is contained the perfect form of the Church, complete in every respect, and under its parts can be referred all those things which are passed down about the Church everywhere in the Scriptures. And that you too, most distinguished men, have observed this form, the fact itself bears witness. For when, thirty-nine years ago, God deigned to illuminate our Helvetia with the brightness of his Word and to call it back from the darkness of superstitions into the light of the gospel, you, thinking that no further delay was to be made, began to consider maturely and seriously the restoration of Christ's kingdom in your commonwealth. Immediately, therefore, you wished to press the bishops, and among them especially the Bishop of Constance, to whose care your whole territory belonged, that they should be willing to devote their work to you in removing abuses and superstitions, and to undertake the reform of the Church with your help. But since they, rather unmindful of their calling and office, delayed, it seemed to you a most unjust and unworthy wrong that their negligence should any longer stand in the way of public welfare and the glory of God. So, lest you fail in your own duty, you yourselves became the leaders and authors of a most beautiful and holy deed, imitating, no doubt, the example of Hezekiah, Josiah, Constantine and others, of whom we read that, when the ministers or prelates of the churches were idle, they did the same with great praise. For, having summoned by public and general assembly all who served the churches in the city and in your countryside, you ordered them to confer with one another from the Word of God on the chief heads of faith and religion. Nor were there lacking men who opposed this undertaking vigorously, who cried out that the decision of this matter did not rest with the judgment of one commonwealth or prince, but belonged to the authority of a general and ecumenical Council. Yet their authority did not weigh so much with you that you wished to look back, now that you had already put your hand to the plough. So the pious and holy undertaking succeeded happily. For in that disputation Truth prevailed, and prevailed so completely that the greatest part of those who had come to oppose it submitted their necks of their own accord, and they sought for themselves especial praise and glory in this, that they were granted the privilege of following the chariot of triumphant Christ, now that they had been happily conquered. From that time you never ceased to deliberate and to do those things which you saw to pertain to the glory of Christ's kingdom. For you cleansed the churches of the filth of images and altars, and the doctrine of the pernicious inventions of human traditions, and by public authority you took care that no one should restore the abolished superstitions, or offer anything foreign to the doctrine of the gospel to the sheep of Christ in teaching. You also saw to it that the use and administration of the sacraments were brought back to the form of their first institution, that prayers, both public and private, were duly ordered, and that whatever other duties of true faith there are should be performed according to the rule of apostolic doctrine; indeed, you also took care that the public laws and the discipline of morals should be reformed according to the norm of the gospel. And lest anyone think that these things were done by you from private advantage or a love of novelties, you took care that for yourselves there should come almost nothing but the trouble of reforming, while the most joyful fruits of the reformation should return to others. For you did not lay rash and greedy hands on the goods of the churches, nor did you drive out anyone among the men of your domain, whether noble or ecclesiastical, from his right. Those whom that common evil of ignorance had deceived, you did not expel inhumanly, but you sought to win them back by friendly and brotherly instruction. The result was that those among them who were gifted in mind afterwards devoted their excellent labour to Christ and to his Church, while the rest, whom old age or slowness of mind hindered, enjoyed their goods and revenues in peace, and had no cause either to complain or to make an uproar. Moreover, whatever of the goods came into your administration was all set aside partly for the schools, partly for the relief of the poor. For you have been accustomed to support liberally not only the teachers of the arts and languages, but also not fewer than eighty young men who were candidates for these, with a constant stipend; so that most of those who today preach Christ or profess sound learning in your city and countryside (which contains about one hundred and forty parishes) owe to your liberality the fact that they stand in this rank. Such was your skill in establishing all these things, such your prudence in deliberating and your moderation in acting, that what seemed impossible to do was accomplished more easily; so that among a free people, without any fear of public power, all these things which we have mentioned were established, and were carried through to their end, in a very short space of time and with great applause of the people. For although those who thought the Papacy profitable to themselves, and therefore could not bear its ruin with calm mind, often made many attempts, yet by a singular blessing of God it came about that their efforts were always in vain, and the storms raised by them were dispersed by the healthy breeze of the heavenly divine power. In this matter, according to the precept of Christ, both the simplicity of the dove and the serpent's prudence shone forth in your counsels. For as often as the adversaries tried, either with friendly and flattering promises or with terrifying threats, to call you back from your undertaking, or at least to persuade you to submit the whole cause of religion to the judgment of bishops and prelates, you wisely and at the same time simply gave this one answer: that you could neither deny nor reject those things which you had learned from the Word of God to be true, but that you were ready to give an account of your faith to anyone who asked it, and indeed would gladly yield to anyone who could convict you of error from the oracles of Holy Scripture and teach you a better way of salvation. There are very many replies of this kind extant, by which you stopped the mouths of many, and in which that apostolic voice is plainly heard: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard." Likewise: "We ought to obey God rather than men." So the grace of the eternal and heavenly divine power favoured these undertakings, by which it came about that your commonwealth escaped happily from the infinite dangers of every kind of tribulation, and today, amid the doubtful and terrible movements of the whole Christian world, not only enjoys peace itself, but also offers a safe refuge to strangers flocking to you from every side. I therefore feel that I am moved by great and weighty reasons, most distinguished men and lords whom I alone am bound to honour, to dedicate to your Eminence this my labour, in which, by the grace granted me from God, I have tried to set forth freely that book which describes the first face of the Church arising in this world, its progress, growth and every condition; and I see that you have imitated its pattern with no less zeal and labour than happy success. If those who will succeed you in the administration of the commonwealth hold this book as familiar to themselves, they will see that you have done nothing rashly, and they will feel that they are roused by no slight incentives to try with all their strength to keep that form of the restored Church and religion which they have received from you. And indeed it matters much to meditate often on the beginnings and principles by which our forefathers established the form both of the commonwealth and of the Church. For thus they will neither listen to the slanderers who maliciously pick apart what has been done piously and holily, nor will they allow themselves to be called back from the truth by the storms of persecution rising against them or by the threatening pursuits of the world. It is also useful to speak of these matters often before the people, who, as is usually the case, are led by the present, and so are easily caught by forgetfulness of the past, and are accustomed to have little thought for the future. Therefore they approve the counsels of magistrates only when they see them joined to some present advantage, or safe and ἀκίνδυνος [without danger]. But as soon as the fear and terror of danger arises, they then begin to miss prudence and integrity in those whose counsels they ought to help and faithfully obey. But if the people understand that God was the guide and author of their magistrates' counsels, and that the magistrates did whatever they did from a sense of duty, they learn to judge of them far more reverently, and obey them more readily, and are not hastily offended at every rumour of impending dangers. For my own part, this consideration above all has been before my eyes, when I resolved to expound publicly this book of the Church of Christ which is among you, and to commit to writing and publish what I had already said in public. For I saw that it is the condition of our age, which is constantly sinking into worse, that it is necessary to read through the books of Holy Scripture with unceasing zeal, and to set before the people for their contemplation the examples of the ancient Church found in them, lest they allow themselves to be deceived by the inventions of those who, under the false name of antiquity, thrust upon us new errors, and accuse of novelty those things which grave and holy men have restored to us from the Word of God. Therefore, most distinguished and magnificent men, receive these my labours with that favour with which you have for many years, from my boyhood, cherished the true zeal for piety, both toward me and toward many of my contemporaries. Continue, moreover, in the way you have begun, to advance the true worship of God. Continue to favour sacred studies. Continue to receive foreigners and exiles of Christ with your accustomed kindness. Continue to uphold the discipline of the laws, to correct the morals of the people, to spread the pursuit of virtues, and to restrain crimes with the holy bridle of justice. The horrible contempt of God reigns in many places. Many shamefully despise the saving Word of God and the benefit of the knowledge of Christ. The love of many grows cold, and faith gradually dies. Iniquity abounds, and new kinds of crimes spring up every day. Therefore angry God threatens punishments, and terrifies the world with prodigies, portents, and dreadful upheavals of kingdoms. Yet he will never be wanting to those who have gone on to advance his glory, to defend his Church, and to perform their duty according to the measure of their calling. He will bless your labours, and direct your counsels by his Spirit. He will bless your whole people, so that they may willingly obey the holy laws, and may enjoy happily the joyful benefit of the gospel's peace. He will bless your whole Church, so that it may make ever greater progress in the doctrine and practice of piety. To him who alone is the Lord of lords, the immortal and eternal God, belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. Given at Zurich, in your city, the famous metropolis of the Helvetians, on the first day of August, in the year of human salvation 1557.

units.la: Multa relucenti debent hæc tempora Lucæ, Et debet Lucas multa Rodolphe tibi. Lux Lucæ luxit totum diffusa per orbem, Lux Lucæ lucet nunc magè luce tua. Ergo tibi Lucæ tantum qui luminis adfers, Christus cum Lucæ lucida regna dabit.
units.tr: These times owe much to the shining Luke, and Luke owes much to you, Rudolph. The light of Luke shone, spread through the whole world; the light of Luke now shines even more brightly through your light. Therefore to you, who bring the light of Luke, Christ will give the bright kingdoms of Luke.

units.la: Quæ πράξεις fuerint Apostolorum, Qui ritus veteres apudá Patres, Et quot: discere Lector est ne cordi? Huc adsis, avido legantur ore Hæc quæ scripta videspererudita, Sacris eruta scripta quæq; libris, Aut è Patribus eruta Orthodoxis. Quæ multo peperit tibi labore Gualtherus, pietate clarus atq; Doctrina, patriæ decus suæq; Præfulgens, celebres habendus inter Scriptores: potes id negare Liuor? Laudes quid memorare pergo plures? Vino vendibili haud opus virente Est suspensa hedera: Liber loquatur.
units.tr: What were the Acts [πράξεις] of the Apostles, what were the ancient rites among the Fathers, and how many were there? Does not the learning of these things, reader, appeal to your heart? Come here and let these writings be read with eager mouth, the learned writings drawn from the sacred books or from the orthodox Fathers. Gwalther, famous for his piety and learning, the glory and light of his homeland, has produced these with great labour for you, and deserves to be counted among celebrated writers. Can envy deny this? Why do I go on recounting more praises? Ivy hung out does not need wine to sell. Let the book speak for itself.

units.la: IN ACTA APOSTOLORVM PER DIVVM LVCAM DESCRIPTA, RODOLPHI GVALTHERI Tigurini Homiliæ. HOMILIA I.
units.tr: IN THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, DESCRIBED BY THE DIVINE LUKE: HOMILIES OF RUDOLPH GWALTHER OF ZURICH. HOMILY I.

units.la: PRIOREM quidem sermonem fecimus, ô Theophile, de omnibus, quæ coepit Iesus facere & docere ad eum vsq; diem, quo postquam mandata per Spiritum sanctum dedisset apostolis, sursum assumptus est.
units.tr: The former discourse I made, O Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began to do and teach, up to the day on which, after he had given commands to the apostles through the Holy Spirit, he was taken up.

units.la: MAGNA historia, etiam prophanæ, laus est, quod eam sapientissimi quiq; teste tem porum, lucem veritatis, vitam memoriæ, magistram vitæ & nuntiá vetustatis dixerunt. Nulli tamen titulos hosce merito & verius tribui, certũ est, quàm ei, quà veteris & noui Testamenti libris comprehensam Spiritus sanctus ecclesiæ tradidit. Ea enim temporũ exactam & infallibilem supputationem à prima mundi origine ad Christi Iesu vsq; natales ducit, quæ apud omnes alios incerta & fallax habetur. Eadem veritatis historicæ non modo lux est, sed etiam index, ad quem reliquorũ historicorum scripta & fides examinari debent. Hæc rerum & verè gestarum & ad nostram salutem verè pertinen tium memoriâ nobis conseruat, & quæ in abditissimis sacrosanctæ vetustatis penetrabilibus habentur, nobis fidelissimè nuntiat. Vitæ verò magistra vnica & sola dici meretur. Quia non exempla tan tum vitiorũ & virtutum proponit, variosq; rerum euentus, ex quibus quæ ad præsentis vitæ institu tionem spectant, discamus: sed altiori volatu se extollens, de æterna animarum salute præcepta tra dit, dei voluntatè sanctam reuelat, promissionum & minarũ Dei exempla proponit, iudicia dei con tra immorigeros describit, & eiusdem patrocinium, quo cultoribus suis fideliter adest, commemorat. De niq; vniuersum Dei ingenium, ceu in speculo contemplandũ proponit, vt quiuis videre possit, qualis er ga nos deus esse dignetur, & quales nos vicissim exigat. Quæ nisi animo coprehendamus, frustra in o mnibus aliarũ gentium historijs versabimur, quæ animum quidem inani voluptate demulcere pos sunt, eundem verò virtutis veræ amore & sanctæ religionis studio inflammare non possunt.
units.tr: Great history, even profane history, is praised because the wisest men of every age have called it the witness of times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, and the messenger of antiquity. Yet it is certain that none of these titles is rightly and more truly given to any history than to that which the Holy Spirit has handed down to the Church, contained in the books of the Old and New Testaments. For it traces an exact and infallible reckoning of times from the very origin of the world to the birth of Christ Jesus, whereas elsewhere such reckoning is held to be uncertain and deceptive. This same history is not only the light of historical truth but also the standard by which the writings and credibility of all other historians must be tested. It preserves for us the memory of events that truly happened and truly pertain to our salvation, and it faithfully reports to us what lies in the most hidden recesses of sacred antiquity. It deserves to be called the one and only teacher of life. It does not merely set before us examples of vices and virtues or various outcomes of events, from which we may learn what concerns the ordering of present life. Rising on a higher flight, it hands down precepts concerning the eternal salvation of souls, reveals the holy will of God, sets forth examples of God's promises and threats, describes God's judgments against the disobedient, and recalls his protection, by which he faithfully stands by his worshippers. Finally, it presents the whole character of God as if to be contemplated in a mirror, so that anyone can see what kind of God he deigns to be toward us and what kind of people he in turn requires us to be. Unless we grasp these things in our minds, we shall labour in vain over all the histories of other nations, which may indeed soothe the mind with empty pleasure but cannot kindle it with a love of true virtue and a zeal for holy religion.

units.la: Cæterum inter sacræ scripturæ libros, qui historicas rerũ gestarũ narrationes continent, nullum extare puto, cuius lectio & cognicio & vtilior sit & magis necessaria hoc ipso, qui de apostolorũ actis inscribitur: cuius explicationem, diuinæ gratiæ auxilio freti suscepimus. Nam vt de authore Luca ni hil dicam, cuius laus est in euangelio Christi, quiq; omniũ fere oculatus testis fuit (nec enim diuinæ literæ, cum diuinitus inspiratæ sint, hominum authoritate comendari debent) tanta est rerum quæ in hoc tractantur, dignitas & maiestas, vt si quem illa in huius libri admirationem & amorem abri pere nequit, illum frustra humanis rationibus persuadere coneris. Ex illis ergo eas in præsenti com memorabimus, quæ totius narrationis argumentum & summam comprehendere videntur.
units.tr: Moreover, among the books of Sacred Scripture that contain historical narratives of events, I think there is none whose reading and knowledge is more useful and more necessary than this one, which is entitled the Acts of the Apostles. Trusting in the help of divine grace, we have undertaken its explanation. For, to say nothing of the author Luke, who is praised in the Gospel of Christ and who was almost an eyewitness of everything (for divine writings, since they are inspired by God, ought not to be commended by human authority), the dignity and majesty of the things treated in this book are so great that if anyone cannot be drawn by them to admiration and love of this book, you will try in vain to persuade him by human arguments. So from these matters we shall now recall those that seem to comprehend the subject and summary of the whole narrative.

units.la: Et primo quidem describitur à Luca regni Christi, quod in hoc mundo habet, initium, progressus & incrementũ, de quo multa à prophetis prædicta extant. Dauid enim Christum à deo patre regem declaratum esse testatur, cuius hereditas sint omnes gentes terræ, & eundem insulis quoq; imperitatu rum dicit. Psa. 2. & 72. Zacharias regni ipsius limites à mari ad mare extendendos esse, vaticinatur. Zach. 9. Apud Danielè vero mons dicitur, qui totum orbem impleat. Dan. 2. Quò etiam referri de bent, quæ apud alios prophetas in hac verba legûtur: Temporibus postremis erit mons domus domi ni præparatus in vertice montiũ, & editior erit collibus, confluentq; ad eum omnes gentes, &c. Isa. 2. Mich. 4. &c. Præterea multa, ne prolixior sim, quæ in hanc sententiam produci poterant. As si hæc in Christi Iesu historia, quæ ab Euangelistis descripta est, requiras, nihil aut parum inuenies, quod oraculis tam magnificis respondeat. Illi enim Christum describunt humilem, egenũ, iniurijs & contu meliis quorumuis obnoxium, quiq; post infinitas calamitates in Cruce infamem mortem sustinuerit. Adhæc regni ipsius terminos perquàm angustos indicant, eò quòd huius mysteria à paucissimis tantum modò agnoscerentur. Quod si verò hunc librū inspicias, mox patebit verissima esse, quæcunq; de Christi regno prophetæ prædixerūt. Qui enim contemptus & nullius precij homo videbatur, gloriosa ascensione in cælos de Satana & omni aduersaria potestate triumphans, ad dexterā patris consīdet, inde promissum ante spiritum apostolis demisit, quo illi inflammati Christum prædicare incipiunt, nec Iudææ finibus contenti, in gentes disperguntur, & inter has regnū Christi simplici euangelij prædicatione longè latéq; propagant. Ita Christus à mari ad mare regnum extendit. Ita insulæ maris regem hunc agnoscere cœperunt, & apostolorū ministerio factum est, vt ad montem hunc, super omnes colles exaltatum, imò in cælis regnantē, omnes gentes & populi confluxerint, quod fore ipse Christus paucis ante mortem suam diebus, his verbis prædixerat: Vbi exaltatus fuero à terra, omnes traham ad meipsum. Ioban.12. Tamq; euidens est istud regni Christi & diuinæ in Christo potentiæ argumentum, vt nullum hoc euidentius inueniri possit. Nec enim vllus principū, quantumuis potens, vniuersam orbis terrarū faciem innouare tam citò potuisset, quàm paucis annis apostoli, viles & contempti homines, Christi spiritu in ipsis operante, animis hominū nouum & incognitum antea fidei & religionis Christianæ studium inseruerunt. Nisi ergo hic liber extaret, regni Christi veritas & maiestas, vel nulla omnino appareret, vel saltem obscura & incerta videri poterat.
units.tr: First, Luke describes the beginning, progress and growth of the kingdom of Christ in this world, of which many things were foretold by the prophets. For David testifies that Christ was declared King by God the Father, whose inheritance are all the nations of the earth, and he also says that Christ will rule over the islands (Ps. 2 and 72). Zechariah prophesies that the boundaries of his kingdom are to extend from sea to sea (Zech. 9). In Daniel a mountain is spoken of that fills the whole world (Dan. 2). To this also should be referred what is read in other prophets in these words: "In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord will be established on the top of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills, and all nations will flow to it," etc. (Isa. 2; Mic. 4, etc.). Besides these, there are many other passages that could be brought forward to this effect, but I shall not be longer. Now if you look for these things in the history of Christ Jesus, as described by the Evangelists, you will find little or nothing that answers to such magnificent oracles. For they depict Christ as humble, needy, and exposed to insults and reproaches of every kind, and as one who, after countless calamities, suffered an infamous death on the cross. Moreover, they indicate that the limits of his kingdom were very narrow, because its mysteries were recognised by only a very few. But if you examine this book, it will soon be plain that all the things the prophets foretold about the kingdom of Christ are most true. He who seemed a despised man of no account, triumphing over Satan and every hostile power by his glorious ascension into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and from there sent the promised Spirit upon the apostles. Kindled by him, they began to preach Christ, and, not content with the bounds of Judea, they were scattered among the nations, and among these they spread the kingdom of Christ far and wide by the simple preaching of the gospel. Thus Christ extended his kingdom from sea to sea. Thus the islands of the sea began to acknowledge this King, and by the ministry of the apostles it came about that all nations and peoples flowed together to this mountain, exalted above all the hills, indeed reigning in heaven. Christ himself had foretold this, a few days before his death, in these words: "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men to myself" (John 12). This is as clear a proof of the kingdom of Christ and of divine power in Christ as any that could be found. For no ruler, however powerful, could have changed the whole face of the earth as quickly as the apostles did in a few years: they were base and despised men, yet, with the Spirit of Christ working in them, they implanted in the minds of men a new zeal for faith and the Christian religion, previously unknown. Therefore, if this book did not exist, the truth and majesty of Christ's kingdom would either appear not at all, or at least would seem obscure and uncertain.

units.la: Accedit his aliud, cuius cognitio non minus vtilis & necessaria est, quæ nimirū primitiuæ ecclesiæ, per apostolos fundatæ, forma & facies fuerit, secundum quam omnibus seculis ecclesia, si qui erroribus & abusus incidunt, reformari debeat. De qua re vt hodie passim ab omnibus disputatur: ita pauci inuenias, qui recta via, & per apostolos olim aperta, velint ingredi. Quo fit, vt veterib. erroribus nouos surrogemus, & veteres superstitiones nouis non minus ineptis & noxijs propulsemus. Quòd si verò quæ à Luca scribuntur obseruare libeat, tam Doctrinæ quàm Ceremoniarū, quas olim apostoli ecclesijs tradiderunt, certa & infallibilis ratio constabit. Docuerunt illi vnum Iesum Christum, qui vnicus & solus nostræ salutis author sit: ac homines, qui natura peccatores & damnationi obnoxij sunt, non alia ratione quàm fide in Iesum Christum iustificari & saluari cōtendunt. Imò scatet liber hic exemplis illustrißimis, quibus principalis & summus, quem modò diximus, fidei Christianæ articulus contra omnes Sophistarum & Pharisæorū cauillationes confirmatur. Quid enim ab impuris gentibus, & à repub. populi Dei alienis, vnquà aliud requisiuerunt apostoli, quàm vt veteri superstitione abiecta, in Christum crederent? Nonne ex aperta idololatria conuersis salutē & peccatorum remissionē prædicarunt? Nōme tenebrionibus istis sese opposuerunt valdissimē, qui legis opera gentibus obtrudere conabantur, quasi Christus nō nisi illis salutifer esset, qui per legis opera sese ad hunc præparauissent? Quòd si ergo gentibus olim fides in Iesum Christum sufficere potuit, nec legis diuinæ latæ operibus & ceremonijs aggrauari debuerunt: quid obsecro obstabit, quò minus hæc ipsa fides nobis hodie sufficiat? Vel num hominum traditiones ad iustificationem & salutem consequendam magis vtiles & necessarias dicemus, quàm quæ à Deo olim ad tēpus correctionis vsq; instituta fuerunt? Quoad verò ceremonias & externos ritus nefas duxerūt apostoli, quicquā priuata authoritate ecclesijs obtrudere. Baptismū, cuius formā à Christo domino acceperant, simplicißimē tradiderūt: Cœnae dominicae vsum & formam, qualem Christus instituerat, retinendā esse putauerunt. In reliqua verò ecclesiæ œconomia hoc illis potißimū curæ fuit, vt salua & integra esset disciplina, qua improbos & falsos fratres coerceri Christus voluit, & vt pauperibus digne prospiceretur, quorum causam & curam dominus tanto studio nobis commendare dignatus est. Quæ præter hæc hodie ecclesijs sub apostolorum nomine & Canonum apostolicorū prætextu obtruduntur, pro apostolicis agnoscere nō possumus: nec id nobis aliquis bonus vitio vertet, quando nullam horum mentionē Lucas facit, cuius opera & studio spiritus sanctus in apostolorū concionibus & actis consignandis vti voluit. Ego certè spiritum sanctum nunquam vel tam imprudentē putabo, vt negligentem scriptorem tantis rebus adhibuerit: vel tam obliuiosum, vt illi quicquam eorum, quorū cognitio & obseruatio in ecclesijs necessaria est, excidere potuerit. Dicerē de singulis copiosius, nisi in historiæ tractatione recurrerent, vbi cōmodius de illis agi potérit. Sufficiat modò eximiam huius libri vtilitatem monstrauisse, quòd verā & infallibilem ecclesiæ reformandæ regulam exhibet, quam nisi obseruent, qui reformatores dici & haberi volunt, reformationibus quidē carnis iudicio gloriari poterunt, ecclesias verò nunquam dabunt, quas omni ex parte fynceras & vere apostolicas quisquam in sacris literis mediocriter versatus, agnoscere possit.
units.tr: To this is added another matter, whose knowledge is no less useful and necessary: namely, what the form and appearance of the primitive Church, founded by the apostles, was, according to which the Church ought to be reformed in every age whenever errors and abuses creep in. Although everyone now debates this matter everywhere, you will find few who want to walk the straight path that was once opened by the apostles. The result is that we substitute new errors for old ones, and drive out old superstitions with new ones no less foolish and harmful. But if we are willing to observe what Luke writes, both as to the doctrine and the ceremonies that the apostles once handed down to the churches, a certain and infallible rule will be established. They taught one Jesus Christ, who alone is the unique author of our salvation, and they maintained that men, who by nature are sinners and liable to damnation, are justified and saved by faith in Jesus Christ and by no other means. Indeed, this book abounds in most illustrious examples by which the principal article of the Christian faith, which I have just mentioned, is confirmed against all the sophistries of the Sophists and Pharisees. For what else did the apostles ever require of the impure nations, who were alien to the commonwealth of the people of God, than that, having cast aside their old superstition, they should believe in Christ? Did they not preach salvation and the forgiveness of sins to those converted from open idolatry? Did they not most vigorously oppose those wretches who tried to force the works of the law upon the Gentiles, as if Christ were saving only those who had prepared themselves for him by the works of the law? If, then, faith in Jesus Christ was once sufficient for the Gentiles, and they ought not to be burdened with the works and ceremonies of the divine law, what, I ask you, will prevent this same faith from being sufficient for us today? Or shall we say that human traditions are more useful and necessary for obtaining justification and salvation than those things which God once instituted for a time of correction? As for ceremonies and external rites, the apostles thought it wrong to impose anything on the churches by private authority. They faithfully handed down the baptism whose form they had received from the Lord Christ. They judged that the use and form of the Lord's Supper should be retained as Christ had instituted it. In the rest of the economy of the Church, their chief concern was that the discipline by which Christ willed that wicked and false brethren be restrained should be kept safe and whole, and that the poor should be properly cared for, whose cause and care the Lord has deigned to commend to us with such zeal. As for the things that are today imposed on the churches under the name of the apostles and on the pretext of the Apostolic Canons, besides these, we cannot acknowledge them as apostolic. Nor will any good man find fault with us for this, since Luke, through whose work and study the Holy Spirit wished to use the sermons and acts of the apostles to be recorded, makes no mention of them. For my part, I shall never think the Holy Spirit so imprudent as to employ a careless writer for such great matters, nor so forgetful as to let slip from Luke anything whose knowledge and observance is necessary in the churches. I would speak of each point more fully, were it not that they will recur in the treatment of the history, where it can be discussed more conveniently. It is enough for now to have shown the outstanding usefulness of this book, in that it sets forth the true and infallible rule for reforming the Church. Unless those who wish to be called and considered reformers observe this rule, they may indeed boast of reforms of the flesh by human judgment, but they will never produce churches that anyone moderately versed in the sacred letters could acknowledge as pure in every respect and truly apostolic.

units.la: Atqui non formam modò & exemplar ecclesiæ Christi liber hic exhibet, verumetiâ quæ illius in terris hisce conditio sit, disserte docet: quam cognouisse cum primis vtile & necessarium est, cùm propter doctrinam & institutionem, tum propter consolationem, quæ inde ad nos redit. Videbimus enim apostolos vbiq; terrarum expertos esse, quod de cruce & persecutionibus sustinendis Christus prædixerat. Nec enim ita per ipsos operari voluit dominus, vt sponte illorum prædicationi cederent quæ super stitiosè & impiè eòusq; in mundo obseruata erant. Sed laboribus & contentionibus illos exercuit. Et vbiuis locorum inuenti sunt, qui ipsorum doctrinæ contradicerent, ijsq; non vulgares homines & obscuri, sed qui illo seculo eruditionis & pietatis nomine à plerisque suspiciebantur, quales inter Israelitas scribæ & sacerdotes erant, & inter gentes philosophi. Nec verbum modò actum est. Sed tantum authoritate valuerunt veritatis hostes, vt magistratus in suas partes pertraherent. Coram his ergo causam dicere, & illorum mandatis cum aperto capitis discrimine sese opponere coacti sunt. Profligati ergo è natali solo, exilij molestias sustinuere, terra mariq; periclitati sunt, carcerũ squalore & vinculorum molestijs sunt exerciti, omnium petiti odijs & conuitijs, tandemq; morte & sanguine impositam sibi euangelizandi functionem finiuere. Hæc si expendamus, videbimus quid nobis hodie sperandum sit, nec offendemur vlla hominum vel authoritate vel potentia, qui simili furore & conatu euangelij doctrinæ reluctantur. Rursum verò mirificè nos consolabitur Christi fides, quam in promissis suis apostolis sanctissimam & inuiolabilem experti sunt. Promiserat enim sui spiritus suggestionem, præsens in aduersis consilium, patrocinium & defensionem contra quosuis. Quæ omnia sic præstitit, vt omni fortuna superiores, inuito mundo & mundi principe, causam suam obtinere, & comisso sibi munere feliciter omnino defungi potuerint. Nemo igitur hodie tyrannorum minis concutiatur, neminem Satanæ conatus perterreant, nemo mudi procellis frangatur. Viuit enim adhuc Christus, & inuiolata est pro missionum ipsius veritas: quæ vt apostolis olim facta sunt, ita ad omnes extenduntur, qui in Christũ iuxta ipsorum doctrinã credunt. Ioan. 17. Et sane, si nulla alia esset huius libri vtilitas, quàm vnâ hæc, nemo non videt quàm necessaria sit hodie eius cognitio, quando & mundi contra Christi ecclesiã horribiles conatus, & infelices ecclesiæ motus passim oculis nostris incurrunt.
units.tr: Yet this book does not merely set out the form and pattern of Christ's Church; it also clearly teaches what condition the Church is in on earth. Knowing this is especially useful and necessary, both for teaching and instruction and for the consolation that comes to us from it. For we will see that the apostles everywhere experienced what Christ had foretold concerning the cross and the endurance of persecutions. The Lord did not intend to work through them so that the superstitious and impious practices observed in the world up to that time would yield willingly to their preaching. Instead he exercised them with labours and conflicts. Everywhere they found men who contradicted their teaching: not ordinary or obscure men, but those who in that age were esteemed by most for their learning and piety, such as the scribes and priests among the Israelites and the philosophers among the Gentiles. Nor was it only words. The enemies of the truth had such authority that they drew magistrates to their side. So the apostles were compelled to make their case before these men and to oppose their commands at the risk of their very lives. Driven from their native soil, they bore the troubles of exile, were endangered on land and sea, were worn down by the squalor of prisons and the hardships of chains, were targets of hatred and abuse from all, and at last brought to an end the office of preaching the gospel laid upon them by death and bloodshed. If we weigh these things, we will see what we ought to expect today, and we will not be dismayed by any authority or power of men who resist the doctrine of the gospel with similar rage and effort. Again, Christ's faithfulness will wonderfully comfort us, which the apostles found to be most holy and inviolable in his promises to them. For he had promised the prompting of his Spirit, present counsel in adversity, and protection and defence against all comers. He fulfilled all these things, so that, superior to every fortune, they won their cause against the will of the world and the prince of the world, and were able to discharge the office entrusted to them happily and fully. Let no one therefore today be shaken by the threats of tyrants; let no attempts of Satan terrify anyone; let no one be broken by the storms of the world. For Christ still lives, and the truth of his promises is unviolated: what was done for the apostles once is extended to all who believe in Christ according to their teaching. John 17.
