And indeed, if this book had no other usefulness than this one, no one would fail to see how necessary its knowledge is today, when on every side we encounter with our own eyes the terrible attempts of the world against the Church of Christ and the unhappy disturbances within the Church.

units.la: Præter hæc tamen omnia non exiguum eruditionis & pietatis fructum exempla nobis præbent, quibus historia hæc refertissima est. Conspiciuntur enim in hoc quasi theatro ecclesiæ apostoli viri, apostolici, quorum exemplo ecclesiæ Christi ministri omnes discunt qua fide & prudentia Christi causam agere, qua constantia in veritate defendenda vti, qua morũ integritate reliquis præire, qua item fortitudine & patientia aduersam fortunam omne superare debeant. Producuntur hic magistratus boni & mali, ex quorum consilijs & factis, qui in magistratu versantur, sui munéris formâ sumere possunt. Non desunt diuitũ exempla, non pauperum. Habent viri à quibus discant, & cumprimis illustria mulierum quarundam acta commemorantur, ex quibus totus ille sexus viuendi regulam sumere potuerit. Deniq; nullus in repub. & ecclesia hominũ ordo est, quem non infinitis, & illis quidem proprijssimis, exemplis liber hic instituat. Et licet pauca sint, quæ in eius commendatione dixi, constare tamen ex his puto, deum singulari quodã & pretiosissimo thesauro ecclesiam suã, in hoc mundo militantem, donare voluisse, quando per Diui Lucæ ministerium apostolica & primitiuæ ecclesiæ hi storiam conscribi voluit. Huius bonitate nos agnoscere, & spiritus sancti diligentiam imitari decet in ijs cognoscendis, quæ scripto hoc tam salutari comprehensa sunt, quod his verbis Lucas orditur.
units.tr: Besides all these things, however, the examples with which this history is very richly filled offer us no small fruit of learning and piety. For in this, as it were, theatre of the Church we behold apostolic men, the apostles, by whose example all the ministers of Christ's Church learn with what faith and prudence they ought to conduct Christ's cause, with what constancy they ought to defend the truth, with what integrity of life they ought to go before the rest, and likewise with what courage and patience they ought to overcome every adverse fortune. Here are presented good and bad magistrates, from whose counsels and deeds those who hold office can take the pattern of their duty. Examples are not lacking for the rich or for the poor. Men have models to learn from, and in particular the notable deeds of certain women are recorded, from which that whole sex can take a rule of living. Finally, there is no order of men in the commonwealth and the Church that this book does not instruct with countless examples, and those very fitting to them. And although the points I have made in its commendation are few, I think it is clear from them that God wished to give his Church, militant in this world, a singular and most precious treasure, when through the ministry of St Luke he willed the history of the apostolic and primitive Church to be written down. It is fitting for us to acknowledge his goodness and to imitate the diligence of the Holy Spirit in coming to know those things that are contained in this most salutary writing, which Luke begins with these words.

units.la: Priore quidem sermone fecimus, ô Theophile, de omnibus, quæ coepit Iesus facere & docere, &c. Priusquam rerum per apostolos gestarum narratione incipiat, ea quæ Christus à resurrectione sua cum apostolis paulo ante ascensionem egit, commemorat. Præfatiuncula verò vtitur breui & perspicua, qua per Anacephalæosim hunc librũ cum priori, qui euangelium Iesu Christi secundum Lucam inscribitur, coniungit, simulq; innuit, quid altero hoc suo libro tractare instituat. Sensus enim verborum hic esse videtur: Priori libro de omnibus ijs sermone feci, quæ Dei filius Iesus Christus, dum in terris hisce versatus est, nostræ salutis ergò egit: Nunc verò eorũ narratione institui, quæ postquam corpore suo è mundo hoc sese subduxit, apostolorũ suorum ministerio perfici voluit. Et librum quidem hunc Theophilo inscribit, quem singulare aliquem Lucæ amicum, & fide insignem fuisse, pleriq; ar-
units.tr: "The former account I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began to do and teach," and so on. Before he begins the narrative of the things done by the apostles, he recalls what Christ did with the apostles after his resurrection, shortly before the ascension. He uses a brief and clear little preface, by which, through a recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις], he joins this book to the former one, which is entitled the Gospel of Jesus Christ according to Luke, and at the same time indicates what he intends to treat in this second book. The sense of the words seems to be this: "In the former book I gave an account of all those things which the Son of God, Jesus Christ, did for our salvation while he dwelt in this earth. Now I have undertaken to narrate those things which, after he withdrew himself from this world in his body, he willed to be carried out through the ministry of his apostles." He addresses this book to Theophilus, whom many suppose to have been a particular friend of Luke's and distinguished in faith. The epithet, at any rate, with which he honours him in the inscription of his Gospel, most excellent [κράτιστος], that is, "most outstanding," belongs only to men of rank. Indeed, just below we will hear that the same title is given to Felix and Festus, governors of Judea. So there was some pious prince, of the sort God always gives to his Church, to help and protect her as she struggles in the arena of this world. Yet no one should conclude from this that the book does not pertain to all of us. Rather, let each one strive to show himself also a Theophilus, that is, a lover of God, and let him think that Luke speaks to him no less than to that ancient Theophilus. And indeed, all who believe in Christ, reconciled to God through him, love him from the heart and with all their strength. But however these things stand, it matters little, since it is quite certain that the whole doctrine of both the Old and the New Testament pertains above all to all who love God, so that they may have instruction and consolation from it. Romans 15. It is useful, moreover, to examine these few words of the evangelist more carefully.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiæ conditio in hoc mundo. birantur. Epitheton certè, quo illũ in operis sui Euangelici inscriptione ornat, κράτισ‑ τος, id est præ‑ stantissimum vocando, non nisi principibus viris convenit. Et infra hoc ipsum Felici & Festo, præ‑ fidibus Iudæa tribui audiemus. Fuit ergo princeps aliquis pius, quales semper Deus ecclesiæ suæ dare solet, qui illam in huius mundi palæstra certantem iuvent & protegant. Nec tamen inde quisquam colligat, librum hunc non ad omnes nos pertinere. Quin potius singuli studeant se quoq; ipsos Theo‑ philos, idest, Dei amantes præbere, & Lucam sibi non minus quàm veteri illi Theophilo loqui co‑ gitent. Et sanè quotquot Christo credunt, per hunc Deo reconciliati, eundem ex animo & totis viri‑ bus suis diligunt. Sed ut hæc sese habeant, non multum interest, quando satis constat, omnem tam veteris quàm novi Testamenti doctrinam cum primis ad omnes Dei amantes pertinere, ut inde doctri‑ nâ & consolatione habeant. Rom. 15. Prodest autem pauca hæc Euangelistæ verba diligentius excutere.
units.tr: 3. The condition of the Church in this world. ...are praised. The epithet, at any rate, with which he adorns Theophilus in the inscription of his Gospel, κράτιστος [kratistos], that is, most excellent, belongs only to men of rank. Below, we shall hear that this same title is given to Felix and Festus, governors of Judea. So there was some pious ruler, such as God is always accustomed to give to his Church, to help and protect it as it struggles in the arena of this world. Yet no one should infer from this that the book does not concern all of us. Rather, let each of us strive to show himself also a Theophilus, that is, a lover of God, and let us consider that Luke speaks to us no less than to that ancient Theophilus. Indeed, all who believe in Christ, reconciled to God through him, love him from the heart and with all their strength. But however these things stand, it matters little, since it is quite certain that the whole doctrine of both the Old and New Testament pertains above all to all lovers of God, so that they may have from it teaching and consolation. Rom. 15. It is useful to examine these few words of the Evangelist more carefully.

units.la: Ubi primo occurrit, quod se de omnibus scripsisse profitetur. Potest enim videri Lucas Iohanni contradicere, qui circa finem euangelij, abs se conscripti, ait: Sunt & alia multa quæ fecit Iesus, quæ si singula scribantur, nec ipse opinor mundus caperet eos, qui scriberentur, libros. Sed facilis est locorum conciliatio. Nec enim Lucas omnia abs se singulatim scripta esse gloriatur, sed de omnibus abs se dictum esse testatur: iis nimirum, quorum cognitio ad salutem aliquendam nobis necessaria est, & quæ sufficienti Christi Iesu cognitione nos instruere possunt. Nam licet non omnia Christi tum dicta tum facta Euangelistæ commemorent, nihil tamen fidei in Christum decedit, nec ut omnia exponeren‑ tur, opus fuit. Constat equidem Christum, qui ipsa veritas est, sibi ipsi nusquam contradixisse, sed unum & eundem in omnibus sermonibus suis finem observauisse. Constat ad eundem scopum omnia Christi opera tendere. Quare etsi nihil ex omnibus illis reticuissent apostoli, non tamen aliam habere possemus Christi cognitionem, non aliam fidem, quàm quæ ex iis quæ scripta extant, discitur. Testatur hoc Iohannes, quando inquit: Multa quidem alia signa fecit Iesus in conspectu discipulorum suorum, quæ non sunt scripta in libro hoc: Hæc autem scripta sunt, ut credatis, quòd Iesus est Christus ille filius Dei, & ut credentes vitam habeatis per nomen eius. Iohan. 20. Fide in Christum nos vitam consequi Iohannes fatetur. Quia verò fides illa ex iis, quæ de Christo scripta sunt, plenè disci & percipi potest, nemo opinor, nisi planè imprudens, negare poterit, in scripturis euangelicis perfectâ salutis nostræ & fidei Christianæ doctrinam comprehendi. Arguit igitur hisce verbis Lucas Sophistarũ nostri seculi arrogantem impudentiam, qui cum ecclesiæ absque scripturæ sacræ authoritate multâ obtrusisse conuin‑ cuntur, hoc effugio se se subducere conantur, quòd non omnia scripturis comprehensa sint, quæ credi & observari necesse sit. Quod si admittamus, vel fidem in Christum ab apostolis & prophetis imper‑ sectè tradi, vel hanc ad salutem non sufficere, fatendum erit. At neutrum ex his Christianis auribus tolerabile esse poterit.
units.tr: Here we first meet the claim that he has written about everything. For Luke may seem to contradict John, who at the end of his Gospel says: "There are also many other things which Jesus did, which, if they were written every one, I suppose the world itself could not contain the books that would be written." But the passages are easily reconciled. Luke does not boast that he has written down everything individually, but testifies that he has spoken of everything that is necessary for us to know for our salvation, and that can instruct us in a sufficient knowledge of Christ Jesus. For although the Evangelists do not record all the words and deeds of Christ, nothing is taken away from faith in Christ, nor was it necessary that everything be set out. It is certain that Christ, who is truth itself, never contradicted himself, but kept one and the same aim in all his discourses. It is certain that all the works of Christ tend to the same goal. Therefore, even if the apostles had passed over nothing of all those things, we could still not have any other knowledge of Christ, or any other faith, than what is learned from those things that are extant in writing. John bears witness to this when he says: "Many other signs truly Jesus did in the sight of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life through his name." John 20. John confesses that we obtain life through faith in Christ. Since that faith can be fully learned and grasped from those things which have been written about Christ, no one, I suppose, unless he is quite foolish, could deny that the full doctrine of our salvation and of the Christian faith is comprehended in the Gospel Scriptures. Luke, therefore, by these words rebukes the arrogant impudence of the Sophists of our age, who, when they are convicted of having imposed many things on the Church without the authority of Holy Scripture, try to escape by this subterfuge: that not everything which must be believed and observed is contained in the Scriptures. But if we were to admit this, we would have to concede either that faith in Christ was handed down imperfectly by the apostles and prophets, or that it is not sufficient for salvation. Yet neither of these can be tolerated by Christian ears.

units.la: Porrò vniuersum Iesu Christi ministerium, siue munus, quod in terris gessit, duobus terminis com‑ prehendit Lucas, Factis nimirum siue operibus, & Doctrina. Nolumus hic de doctoris officio loqui, quæ operum exemplo præire debere, bene dicitur. Nõ enim hoc loco doctoris partes tradere vult Euan‑ gelista, sed ea proponere, quæ in Christo consyderari debent. Primum verò locũ Operibus tribuit, quo‑ rum nomine non miracula modò intelligi debent, sed quacunq; nostræ salutis causa, tanquam Rex & Sacerdos, egit. Regem enim & Sacerdotẽ ecclesiæ dei datum fuisse, passim scriptura docet, in primis verò Dauid, cui peculiaris de hoc promissio facta fuit, Psal. 2. 110. Itaq; pro Regis officio leges tulit vitæ æternæ, & in mundum hunc quasi expeditione facta, aduersus Satanam communé nostri generis hostẽ bellum gessit, eundem deuicit, & nos qui peccatorũ laqueis constricti tenebamur, in libertatem asseruit. Adhæc plusquàm regia liberalitate regni cœlorum thesauris omnes in se credentes abundè ditauit. Rursum verò Sacerdotis munere defungens docuit, orauit pro omnibus, tum pro iis quoq;, à quibus in crucem agebatur, & corpus suum atq; sanguinẽ, quæ à nobis sumpserat, pro peccatis nostris hostiam sufficientè & deo gratissimâ obtulit. His accesserunt miracula, quibus sensus quoq; hominũ in fidei obedientiâ capere, & quantumuis rudibus sui cognitionẽ persuadere voluit. Alterũ locũ Doctrinæ tribuit, qua omniũ, quæ per Christum gesta sunt, ratio exponitur. Interim nõ temere factũ putabimus, quòd Opera & Doctrinâ coniungens Lucas, duobus hisce terminis omnia, quæ Christũ spe‑ ctant, comprehendit. Docet enim, in Christi consyderatione duo hæc necessario coiungi debere. Nisi enim doctrinã consyderemus cũ operibus, hæc nõ plus ad salutis cognitionẽ nobis cõferent, quàm alte‑ rius rius cuiusdam, qui annis mille quingentis aut amplius nos praecesserit, res gestae conferre possent. At si do Etrina consyderemus, omnia haec propter nos facta esse intelligemus, ut Christi redemptoris beneficio salus nobis obtingeret. Simul etiam operum consyderatio doctrinae authoritatem & fidem concilia-bit, eo quod haec de divina Christi virtute, adeoq; ipsa divinitate, luculentissimum testimonium ferunt: quod ipse Christus admonet, dicens: Opera quae dedit mihi pater, ut perficiam ea, ipsa inquam opera quae ego facio, testificantur de me, quod pater miserit me. Ioan. 5. Et rursum: Si non facio opera patris mei, nolite credere mihi. Sin vero facio, etsi mihi non creditis, operibus credite, ut cognoscatis & credatis, quod pater in me est, & ego in eo. Ioan. 10. Arguuntur hic nostri saeculi pseudochristiani, qui opera quidem Christi fatentur omnia, et historica fide instructi, quaecunque ille vnquam vel fecit vel passus est, magnifice commemorare solent: ubi vero de fide in unum Christum collocanda & salute in unius Christi merito quaerenda agitur, mox quasi prioris Confessionis obliti, alio convertuntur, & extra Christum infinita salutis consequendae media confingunt. Perinde autem faciunt isti homines, quod ij, qui vel communis famae testimonio vel amicitiae & familiaritatis vinculo compulsi, medico rum artem splendide praedicant, ubi vero ipsi laborare coeperunt, illa uti detrectant, ea re abunde declarantes, se illorum arti & peritiae profusus diffidere. Ita isti quod ore de Christo confitentur, factis negant. Causa vero huius tam noxiae tergiversationis non alia est, quam quod nuda Christi opera consyderant, quibus in aliquam eius admirationem rapiuntur, quae tamen stabilis & firma esse non potest, quia doctrinae fulcro destituitur, & operum finem ignorat. Quod si vero Christum docentem audirent, opera haec ideo & facta & descripta esse intelligerent, ut in uno hoc omnem salutis spem repositam habeamus. Huius enim vox est: Ego sum via, lux & veritas. Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Ioan. 14. Quisquis bibit ex aqua elementali, vel proprijs viribus hausta, iterum sitiet; qui autem biberit ex aqua, quam ego do, non sitiet in aeternum. Ioan. 4. Venite ad me, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis praestabo. Matth. 11. & c.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke sums up the whole ministry or office that Jesus Christ performed on earth under two heads, namely his deeds or works, and his teaching. I do not want to speak here about the teacher's office, which, as is rightly said, ought to go before by the example of works. For the Evangelist does not intend to set out the teacher's part in this passage, but to present those things which must be considered in Christ. He assigns the first place to works, under which we must understand not only miracles but everything he did for our salvation, as King and Priest. Scripture teaches throughout that the King and Priest was given to the Church of God, above all David, to whom a special promise about this was made (Ps. 2, 110). Accordingly, in the office of King he enacted the laws of eternal life, and, as if on a campaign into this world, he waged war against Satan, the common enemy of our race, defeated him, and set free us who were held bound in the snares of sinners. Besides this, with more than royal generosity he enriched all who believe in him from the treasures of the kingdom of heaven. In turn, discharging the office of Priest, he taught, he prayed for all, even for those by whom he was being led to the cross, and he offered his body and blood, which he had taken from us, as a sufficient sacrifice for our sins, and one most pleasing to God. To these were added the miracles, by which he willed to win over even the senses of men to obedience of faith, and to persuade even the rudest of the knowledge of himself. The second place he assigns to teaching, by which the meaning of all that was done through Christ is set out. Meanwhile we shall not think it was by chance that Luke, joining works with teaching, embraces in these two heads everything that concerns Christ. For he teaches that these two must necessarily be joined in our consideration of Christ. For unless we consider the teaching together with the works, these would contribute no more to our knowledge of salvation than the deeds of some other person who had gone before us a thousand five hundred or more years ago could do. But if we consider the teaching, we shall understand that all these things were done on our account, so that salvation might come to us through the benefit of Christ the Redeemer. At the same time, consideration of the works will also win authority and credibility for the teaching, because these bear the clearest witness to the divine power of Christ, and so to his very divinity; as Christ himself reminds us, saying: "The works which the Father has given me to finish, these very works which I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me" (John 5). And again: "If I do not the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do, though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in him" (John 10). Here are rebuked the false Christians of our age, who indeed acknowledge all the works of Christ, and, being instructed in historical faith, are accustomed to recount magnificently whatever he ever did or suffered; but when it comes to placing faith in Christ alone and seeking salvation in the merit of Christ alone, they straightway turn aside, as if they had forgotten their earlier confession, and invent for themselves endless means of obtaining salvation outside Christ. These people act just as those do who, moved either by the testimony of common report or by the bond of friendship and familiarity, praise the art of physicians in fine terms, but when they themselves fall ill, refuse to use that art, thereby making it abundantly clear that they utterly distrust the skill and expertise of those men. So these people deny by their deeds what they confess with their mouths about Christ. The cause of this harmful evasion is nothing else than that they consider the bare works of Christ, by which they are carried away into some admiration of him, which yet cannot be stable and firm, because it lacks the support of doctrine and does not know the purpose of the works. But if they heard Christ teaching, they would understand that these works were both done and written down so that we might place all our hope of salvation in this one person. For this is his voice: "I am the way, the light and the truth. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14). "Whoever drinks of the elemental water, or water drawn by his own strength, will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I give will never thirst" (John 4). "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11), etc.

units.la: Praeterea non negligendum est, quod euangelica historiae terminum fiue limitem Christi ascensionem Lucas constituit. Dicit enim se priori libro de omnibus dixisse, quae Christus tum fecit tum docuit, usq; ad illum diem, quo postquam Apostolis, quos elegerat, mandata dedisset, assumptus est in caelos. Hinc colligimus, Christum gloriosa in caelos ascensione omnes nostrae redemptionis & salutis partes impleuisse. Nam supra docuimus, euangelio perfectè tradi, quae saluti nostrae seruiunt. Quia ergo in hoc postremo locum ascensio Christi obtinet, eandem omnium, quae ad nos salvandos necessaria erant, Colophonem fuisse certum est. Hoc si teneamus, luce clarius patebit, nos corporali Iesu Christi in terris praesentia posthac non opus habere. Quid enim in terris ageret, qui ita olim quae agenda erant, fideliter simul & plene praestitit? Spiritu, gratia, merito, doctrina, consilijs & protectione Christi nobis opus est, quae ille nunquam a suis aufert, & ea ratione sicut promisit, cum illis est usq; ad consummationem saeculi. Matth. 28. Idem vero fidem illis adhibere probibet, qui ipsum corporaliter praesentem alicubi monstrare audent. Matth. 24. Sed quia de his paulo post comodior erit differendi locus, ubi Ascensionis historia tractabitur, paucula haec in praesenti sufficiant.
units.tr: Besides, it should not be overlooked that Luke sets the ascension of Christ as the end or limit of the gospel history. For he says that in his former book he had spoken of all that Christ both did and taught, up to the day on which, after giving commands to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up into heaven. From this we gather that Christ, by his glorious ascension into heaven, fulfilled all the parts of our redemption and salvation. For we have shown above that the gospel fully sets forth all that serves our salvation. Since, therefore, the ascension of Christ holds the final place in this history, it is certain that it was the crowning point of everything that was necessary for our salvation. If we hold to this, it will be clearer than light that we have no need of the bodily presence of Jesus Christ on earth from now on. For what would he do on earth, who once so fully and faithfully accomplished in one act all that had to be done? We need the Spirit, grace, merit, teaching, counsel and protection of Christ, which he never takes away from his own, and in the manner he promised, he is with them even to the end of the age (Matt. 28). The same Christ forbids us to give credence to those who dare to show him somewhere bodily present (Matt. 24). But since a more suitable place for discussing these matters will come a little later, when the history of the Ascension is treated, these few points will suffice for the present.

units.la: Illud nunc observandum venit, quod non antea terras hasce deserere voluit Christus, quam manda tis suos instruxisset apostolos. Neq; enim de vnito illo mandato hunc locum intelligo, quo ne ab Hierò solymis discederet praecepit, priusquam spiritum promissum accepissent. Sed vniuersaliter de omnibus illis mihi Lucas dicere videtur, de quibus Christus suos admonere voluit, & in primis quidem ijs, quae ad apostolici muneris functionem pertinebant, de qua infra plura adhuc sequentur. Est autem hoc consolatione plenum, quod Christum, licet corpore absentem, ecclesiae suae cura minime depositte constat. Boni enim & fidi patrisfamilias officio in praesenti fungitur, qui peregre profecturus, familiae suae curam amicis, quorum fides ipsi perspectissima est, committit, simulq; quid singuli domesticorum interea dum ipse abest faciant, praecipit. Ita Christus in caelos ascensurus, ecclesiae suae curam apostolis commendauit, quos amicorum loco se habuisse in euangelio testatur. Eosdem vero mandatis instituit, ne vel temeritate vel insciti peccare possent. Faciunt ad huius loci expositionem parabolae, quae Matth. 24. & 25. habentur. Nemo itaq; sese tyrannis & seductoribus ita praeda expositu putet, ut nullo Christi praesidio munitus, illorum crudelitati & libidini per omnia subiaceat. Qui enim oves suas proprij sanguinis precio redemit, & earundem curam, e mundo discessurus, apostolis comisit, eas haud dubie nunc quoq; videt, nec illas è manu sua eripi patietur. Ioan.10. Interim & institutioni hoc ipsum seruire debet. Qui enim discessurus mandata dedit, ea re se aliquando rediturum non obscurè testatur. Praeparemur ergo ad ipsius aduentum, semper verborum Christi memores, quibus ait: Sint lumbi vestri praecincti, & lucernae accensae, & vos similes hominibus expectantibus dominum suum, quando reuertatur à nuptijs, vt cùm venerit ac pulsauerit, confestim aperiant ei. Beati serui illi, quos cùm venerit dominus, inuenerit vigilantes, &c. Luc.12.
units.tr: It remains now to observe that Christ did not wish to leave this earth before he had instructed his apostles in their commands. For I do not understand this passage to refer to that one command by which he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem until they had received the promised Spirit. Rather, Luke seems to me to speak in general about all those things on which Christ wished to admonish his people, and especially those which pertained to the discharge of the apostolic office, of which more will follow below. Now this is full of comfort: that Christ, although absent in body, is clearly not to be thought to have abandoned the care of his Church at all. For he acts as a good and faithful householder does who, about to go abroad, entrusts the care of his household to friends whose faithfulness is best known to him, and at the same time instructs each of the household what to do in the meantime while he is away. So Christ, about to ascend into heaven, committed the care of his Church to the apostles, whom in the gospel he declares to have been in the place of friends. And he instructed them by commands, so that they might not sin either through rashness or through ignorance. The parables which are found in Matthew 24 and 25 help in the exposition of this passage. Let no one therefore think himself so exposed to tyrants and seducers that, being protected by no defence of Christ, he is in every way subject to their cruelty and lust. For he who redeemed his sheep at the price of his own blood, and who, about to depart from the world, committed their care to the apostles, undoubtedly sees them even now, and will not allow them to be snatched out of his hand (John 10). Meanwhile this very fact ought also to serve for our instruction. For he who gave commands on departing has clearly testified that he will someday return. Let us therefore prepare for his coming, always mindful of the words of Christ, in which he says: "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may immediately open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watching, etc." (Luke 12).

units.la: Priusquam verò sermoni finem imponamus, quaedam in his excutienda restant, quae apostolicae doctrinae dignitatem authoritatemq; nobis commendant. Primum in his est, quòd illos à Christo electos dicit. Loquitur autem de speciali electione, qua non modò in saluandorum numerum cooptati, sed in eum quoq; finem & vsum destinati fuerunt, vt diuinae gratiae, per Christum collatae, praecones, & (vt Paulus nominat) mysteriorum Dei dispensatores essent. 1. Cor. 4. Deinde hos à Christo mandata quae accepisse dicit. Vt enim principes legatis literas mandatorias (quas nostrates Instructiones vocant) expediunt, quibus non modo rerum agendarum memoria conseruatur, verumetiam legatis fides & authoritas conciliari solet: Ita Iesus Christus suos legatos mandatis instruere voluit, vt quid illi agere deberent omnibus compertum esset. At quia multi Christum Iesum, vt nudum hominem, consyderant, nec in Apostolis quicquam vulgari hominum conditione excellentius obseruant, addit Lucas, mandata haec per spiritum sanctum data esse. Haec si omnia in vnum conferamus, diuinum, non humanum, patebit negotium esse, cuius executio Apostolis commissa fuit. Patebit item, doctrinam ipsorum ad Christum authorem debere referri. Nam Christi nomine legatione funguntur, vt Paulus monet. 2. Cor. 5. Et Christi testimonio commendantur, dicentis: Qui recipit quemcunq; misero, me recipit. Ioan.13. Item: Qui recipit vos, me recipit: & qui me recipit, recipit eum qui misit me. Matt.10. Nostrum ergo est fratres, vt de Apostolorum functione & doctrina recte indicemus, & ineffabile Dei beneficium, quod horum praedicatione nobis offert, gratis animis agnoscamus, ac fide vera amplectamur. Sic enim fiet, vt immortali illo diuini verbi semine regenerati, vitam filijs Dei dignam degamus, & illius praesidio ex mundi huius immanibus procellis erepti, aeternum in coelis viuamus cum filio Dei, domino nostro & saluatore vnico, Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Before I bring this sermon to an end, there are some points still to be examined which commend to us the dignity and authority of the apostolic teaching. The first is that Luke says they were chosen by Christ. He is speaking of a special election, by which they were not only enrolled in the number of those to be saved, but were also appointed to this end and purpose: that they should be heralds of the grace of God, offered through Christ, and (as Paul calls them) stewards of the mysteries of God. 1 Cor. 4. Next, he says they received commands from Christ. For just as princes send their envoys letters of instruction (which our people call instructions), by which not only is the memory of the business to be done preserved, but trust and authority are usually won for the envoys, so Jesus Christ wished to equip his envoys with commands, so that what they ought to do was known to everyone. But because many look upon Christ Jesus as a mere man and see nothing in the apostles more excellent than the common condition of men, Luke adds that these commands were given through the Holy Spirit. If we put all of these things together, it will be clear that the business whose carrying out was entrusted to the apostles is divine, not human. It will also be clear that their teaching must be referred to Christ as its author. For they act as envoys in Christ's name, as Paul reminds us. 2 Cor. 5. And they are commended by Christ's own testimony, when he says: "He who receives whoever I send receives me." John 13. Likewise: "He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me." Matt. 10. It is our task, therefore, brothers, to judge rightly concerning the office and teaching of the apostles, and with grateful hearts to acknowledge the inexpressible benefit of God which he offers us through their preaching, and to embrace it with true faith. For in this way it will come about that, reborn by that immortal seed of the divine word, we shall live a life worthy of the children of God, and, snatched by his protection from the savage storms of this world, we shall live eternally in heaven with the Son of God, our Lord and the only Saviour, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA II.
units.tr: HOMILY II.

units.la: Quibus [apostolis Iesus] etiam seipsum exhibuit viuentem, postquam passus erat, idq; compluribus argumentis, dum per dies quadraginta ab illis conspicitur, & disserit de regno Dei.
units.tr: To [the apostles, Jesus] also showed himself alive after he had suffered, and by many proofs, appearing to them over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God.

units.la: Dluus Lucas de Apostolorum actis scripturus, eam narrationem cum euangelica historia, vt heri diximus, connectit. Facit hoc non temere, sed spiritus sancti consilio, & suggestione admonitus, qui sublimius quiddam hac connexione nos docere voluit. Hinc enim patet, apostolicam historiam ab euangelica nullo modo separari vel disjungi debere, & quacunq; per apostolos in euangelij ac regni Iesu Christi propagatione facta sunt, nò minus ad Christi authorem esse referenda, quam ea, quae is in propria persona gessit, cù corpore adhuc in terris ageret. Constat enim apostolos nihil priuato consilio vel proprijs viribus egisse, sed vt electa Christi organa, illius spiritu ad quaeuis agenda fuisse impulsos. Docet hoc ipsias Christi verba, dicētis: Nō vos estis loquentes, sed spiritus patris mei, qui in vobis est. Matt.10. Et alibi spiritū pollicetur, qui omne veritatem, adeoq; rerū agendarū consilia suggerat. Ioan.14. Quò Paulus respiciens Corinthijs ait: Nū experimentū quaritis loquentis in me Christi? 2. Cor.13. Non inanis autem est horum cognitio, eo quòd institutioni & consolationi multū seruiunt. His enim testimonijs docemur, apostolorum doctrinae & scriptis nos tuto credere posse, nō modo quia Iesu Christi legati sunt (Nā legatos aliquādo παρεπιδημεῖν videmus) sed quia Christi spiritu instructi, illo suggerente & mouente sua functione obierunt. Consolatio verò nō vulgaris est, quòd ecclesia Christi curae esse cernimus. Qui enim olim corpore discessurus apostolos reliquit, quorū ministerio illa congregaretur, idem omnibus seculis spiritus sui dona distribuens, ecclesiae suae dat alios quidè apostolos, alios verò prophetas, alios autē euangelistas, alios autē pastores ac doctores ad instaurationē sanctorū in opus opus administrationis, in edificationem corporis sui, &c. Ephes. 4. Caeterum quia in hesternis Lucas ascensionis Christi in caelos meminerat, inde occasione sumpta, ultimum Christi actum, quem paulo ante ascensionem habuit, commemorat: eo quod is institutae narrationi plurimum serviebat. Et in praesenti quidem duo proponuntur, de quibus Christus cum discipulis suis tractavit, quorum alterum est, Resurrectionis assertio diligens, alterum Institutio sive doctrina de regno Dei. Nos de utroq;, quantum dominus dederit, dicemus.
units.tr: Blessed Luke, writing the Acts of the Apostles, connects that narrative with the gospel history, as we said yesterday. He does this not rashly but by the counsel and prompting of the Holy Spirit, who wished to teach us something more elevated through this connection. For it is plain from this that the apostolic history can in no way be separated or divided from the gospel, and that whatever was done through the apostles in spreading the gospel and the kingdom of Jesus Christ must be referred to Christ the author no less than what he did in his own person while still living on earth in the body. For it is certain that the apostles did nothing by private counsel or their own strength, but as chosen instruments of Christ they were driven by his Spirit to do whatever they did. Christ's own words teach this, saying: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of my Father who is in you." Matt. 10. And elsewhere he promises the Spirit, who will teach all truth and so suggest the plans of action. John 14. Looking at the Corinthians, Paul says to them: "Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?" 2 Cor. 13. The knowledge of these things is not empty, since they greatly serve instruction and consolation. For by these testimonies we are taught that we can safely trust the teaching and writings of the apostles, not only because they are legates of Jesus Christ (for we sometimes see legates staying abroad [παρεπιδημεῖν]), but because, instructed by the Spirit of Christ, they discharged their office at his prompting and under his motion. The consolation is no small one, that we see the Church of Christ is his care. For he who once left the apostles when he was about to depart in body, through whose ministry that church was gathered, the same, distributing the gifts of his Spirit through all ages, gives to his church some apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of his body, etc. Eph. 4. But since yesterday Luke had mentioned Christ's ascension into heaven, taking occasion from that, he recounts the last act of Christ, which he performed shortly before the ascension, because it greatly served the narrative he had undertaken. And at present two things are set forth, about which Christ dealt with his disciples: one is the careful assertion of the resurrection, the other the teaching or doctrine concerning the kingdom of God. We shall speak about each, as much as the Lord grants.

units.la: Atqui in resurrectionis veritate asserenda paucis quidem sed iis gravissimis verbis utitur. Ille enim Iesus (inquit) qui antequam moreretur multa in terris fecerat & docuerat, ut inquit, postquam passus fuit & mortuus, sese viventem denuo exhibuit discipulis, & seipsum quidem, non alium, nec alio assumpto corpore, sed hoc ipso, in quo passus erat. Nec obiter tantum, et quasi aliud agens, se illis exhibuit, sed se re vera vivere, ac vero suo corpore, quo antea in terris usus erat, vere resurrexisse, multis argumentis & infallibilibus demonstrationibus comprobavit. Loquitur autem de illis Lucas, quae in Evangelii historia de rebus Christi post resurrectionem gestis copiosius describuntur. Primum inter illa loca apparitiones tenet, ut quod Mariae Magdalenae in horto prope sepulchri locum hortulani habitu visus, et ab illa agnitus est. Ioan. 20. Et paulo post reliquis etiam mulieribus a sepulchro redeuntibus occurrens, illis & salutem dicit, & suam resurrectionem fratribus suis, ac in primis quidem Petro, annunciare iussit. Matt. 28. Mar. 16. Rursum duobus discipulis Emauntem proficiscentibus sese comitem itinere adiunxit, & post longam disputationem, cum iam mensae accubuissent, se illis agnoscendum praebuit. Luc. 24. Et post multas eius generis apparitiones, unde plus quingentis fratribus (ut Paulus testatur) apparuit. 1. Cor. 15. Caeterum quia oculorum sensus ut plurimum fallit, & notae sunt daemonum praestigiae, quibus incautos apparitionibus falsis saepe dementavit, non videndum modo, verumetiam contrectandum suis sese praebuit dominus. Timentibus enim, ne satanica aliqua illusione aut spectro fallerentur, ait: Videte manus meas, & pedes meos, quia ego ipse sum. Contrectate me et videte, quia spiritus carnem & ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Luc. 24. Non ergo formam modo pristini corporis, verumetiam substantiam & partes, adeo carnem et ossa, Christus a mortuis resurgens assumpsit. Et ut certius esset eius rei argumentum, non tantum contrectari sese passus est, sed etiam nequid superesset dubij, cibum petijt, & spectantibus discipulis manducavit. Non quidem ea ratione, quod corpora, quae in resurrectione clarificata sunt, cibo et potu refici, & alii opus habeant (quia enim ab omni corruptione libera sunt, generatione etiam nulla indigent) sed ut omnibus testatum faceret, se omnes organici corporis partes retinere. Clarificatio enim nec substantiam nec partes corporis tollit, sed corruptionem et affectiones, quae ex peccato in corporibus obortae sunt, aufert, ut iuxta Pauli sententiam, quod corruptibile fuerat & mortale, incorruptibile, immortale, gloriosum & caelestis vitae capax resurgat. 1. Cor. 15. Facit vero ad resurrectionis Christi assertionem & temporis circumstantia. Nec enim uno aut altero die haec inter discipulos egit, sed quadraginta diebus continuis cum illis conversatus est, & singulis quidem diebus eiusmodi resurrectionis suae argumenta praebuit.
units.tr: Indeed, in asserting the truth of the resurrection he uses few words, but very weighty ones. For that Jesus (he says), who before he died had done and taught many things on earth, as he says, after he had suffered and died, showed himself alive again to his disciples, and showed himself indeed, not another, nor with another body assumed, but this very one in which he had suffered. Nor did he show himself only in passing, as if doing something else, but he proved, by many arguments and infallible demonstrations, that he truly lives and truly rose again in the very body with which he had lived on earth before. Luke speaks of those things which are described more fully in the gospel history concerning the events of Christ after the resurrection. Among those places, he first records the appearances, such as to Mary Magdalene in the garden near the sepulchre, when he appeared to her in the guise of a gardener and was recognized by her. John 20. And shortly after, meeting the other women also as they returned from the sepulchre, he greeted them and ordered them to announce his resurrection to his brothers, and especially to Peter. Matt. 28. Mark 16. Again, he joined himself as a companion to two disciples going to Emmaus, and after a long discussion, when they had already reclined at table, he presented himself to be recognized by them. Luke 24. And after many appearances of that kind, he appeared to more than five hundred brothers (as Paul testifies). 1 Cor. 15. Moreover, since the sense of sight for the most part deceives, and the tricks of demons are well known, by which they have often driven the incautious mad with false appearances, the Lord presented himself to be not only seen but also handled. For fearing lest they be deceived by some satanic illusion or ghost, he says: "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Handle me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have." Luke 24. Therefore Christ, rising from the dead, assumed not merely the form of his former body, but its substance and parts, indeed flesh and bones. And so that the proof of this might be more certain, he not only allowed himself to be handled, but, lest any doubt remain, he asked for food and ate in the sight of the disciples. Not indeed for this reason, that bodies which have been glorified in the resurrection are refreshed by food and drink and need them (for since they are free from all corruption, they need no generation either), but to make it attested to all that he retained all the parts of an organic body. For glorification does not remove the substance or parts of the body, but takes away the corruption and affections which arose in bodies from sin, so that, according to Paul's judgment, what was corruptible and mortal rises incorruptible, immortal, glorious, and capable of heavenly life. 1 Cor. 15. The circumstance of time also serves to assert the resurrection of Christ. For he did not carry on these things among the disciples on one or two days, but conversed with them for forty continuous days, and on each day gave such proofs of his resurrection.

units.la: Fuerunt haec copiosius Paulo et diligentius recensenda, fratres in Christo dilecti, eo quod omnibus seculis reperti sunt, qui vel resurrectionem Christi in dubium vocare, vel corporis refusicitati veritatem aliquo modo exinanire conati sunt. Nec desunt hodie, qui Christi corpus clarificatione ita mutatum et conversum esse contendunt, ut ita nullo loco certo contineri opus sit, sed ubiq; praesens esse queat. Nec aliam habent sui illius dogmatis causam, quam quod corporale Christi in Caena praesentia tuebantur. Non autem vident interea contentiosi homines, se dum corporalem praesentiam statuunt, corporis Christi veritatem negare, & ita sponte abijcere id, pro quo ardentissime tanquam pro focis & aris depugnant. Si enim corporaliter in Caena Christus praesens est, aut corpus eius loco contineri oportet, aut non magis in Caena quam ubiuis alibi a nobis reperiri et percipi poterit. Qua autem ratione fieri poterit, ut certo loco coineatur, quod multis in locis simul est? Rectius ergo hac D. Augustinus perspexit, qui locorum spatia a corporibus adeo non separari posse vidit, ut si illa auferas, corpora amplius non dici merentur. Spatia locorum (inquit) tolle corporibus, nusquam erunt: et quia nusquam erunt, nec erunt. Tolle ipsa corpora qualitatibus corporum, non erit ubi sint, & ideo necesse est, ut non sint. Idem Augustinus in hac causa ad Christi divinitatem & omnipotentiam confugientibus, egregie respondet, cum ait: Caendum est, ne ita divinitatem astruamus hominis, ut veritate corporis auferamus.
units.tr: These things, beloved brothers in Christ, must be recounted a little more fully and carefully, because in every age there have been those who either called the resurrection of Christ into doubt or tried in some way to empty the truth of the raised body. Nor are there lacking today those who contend that the body of Christ has been so changed and transformed by glorification that it need not be contained in any certain place, but can be present everywhere. And they have no other cause for this opinion than that they defend the corporeal presence of Christ in the Supper. But these contentious men do not see that, while they assert a bodily presence, they deny the truth of Christ's body, and so of their own accord cast away that for which they fight most ardently, as for hearth and altar. For if Christ is present bodily in the Supper, either his body must be contained in a place, or he can be found and perceived by us in the Supper no more than anywhere else. But how can it come about that what is in many places at once be contained in a certain place? Augustine saw this more rightly, who perceived that the spaces of places cannot be separated from bodies to such an extent that, if you take them away, bodies no longer deserve to be called bodies. "Take away space from bodies (he says), and they will be nowhere; and because they will be nowhere, they will not be." "Take away the bodies themselves from the qualities of bodies, and there will be no place where they may be, and so they must necessarily not be." The same Augustine, in this matter, answers admirably those who take refuge in the divinity and omnipotence of Christ, when he says: "We must take care not so to assert the divinity of the man that we take away the truth of the body."

units.la: Sed de his alibi plura dicentur. Nunc ad eas causas explicandas transeamus quae Christum, ut sui corporis resurrectionem tam multis asseret, moverunt.
units.tr: But more will be said about these things elsewhere. Now let us pass on to explain the causes which moved Christ to assert the resurrection of his body by so many proofs.

units.la: Prima hic mihi esse videtur, regni Christi maiestas & certitudo, quam resurrectione comprobari oportuit. Quia enim Christum Iesum vere mortuum & sepultum esse constat, quod & Iudaei fatentur, nisi eundem vere a mortuis resurrexisse constaret, vanissima haberentur quaecunque de illius regno extant testimonia. Quis enim hunc super montem Sion, id est, ecclesiam dei regem constitutum crederet, quem mortuum esse certo sciret, resuscitatum vero esse nesciret? Quis ad dextram patris illum sedere, & hostibus suis tanquam pedum scabello uti confidat, de cuius vita incertus est? Nisi ergo Christi Iesu resurrectio nobis perfectissima sit, illum nec regem agnoscere, nec in illius regno quicquam praesidij vel auxilij sperare poterimus. Nec dubium est, Apostolos hac fiducia omnes mundi minas contempsisse, & impositio munere tanta constantia fuisse defunctos, quod illum mortis victore agnoscebant, & in coelis regnare noverant, qui ipsos sui Evangelij ministros fecerat.
units.tr: The first reason, it seems to me, is the majesty and certainty of Christ's kingdom, which had to be proved by the resurrection. For since it is agreed that Christ Jesus truly died and was buried, as the Jews also admit, unless it were established that he truly rose from the dead, all the testimonies that exist about his kingdom would be held to be most empty. For who would believe that he has been set up as king upon Mount Zion, that is, the Church of God, if he knew for certain that he had died but did not know that he had been raised? Who would trust that he sits at the right hand of the Father and uses his enemies as a footstool, if he were uncertain whether he is alive? Unless, then, the resurrection of Christ Jesus is wholly certain to us, we shall be able neither to acknowledge him as king nor to hope for any protection or help in his kingdom. And there is no doubt that the Apostles, relying on this confidence, despised all the threats of the world, and they discharged so great an office with such constancy, because they knew that he who had made them ministers of his Gospel had conquered death and reigns in heaven.

units.la: Secundam assertionis huius tam diligentis causam arbitror Apostolorum doctrinam atq; functionem, cuius certitudinem contra mundi iudicia fortiter asserri oportebat. Quod vero illius efficacius argumentum inveniri potuit, quam gloriosa ac omnibus nota Christi, quem illi praedicabant, resurrectio? Quod si obscurum aliquem & ignotum omnibus hominem praedicassent, non immerito suspecti esse poterant. Quis autem nunc de illorum doctrina dubitet, qui eum annuntiant atq; docent, qui potenti resurrectione mortis imperium contriuit, ac omni adversaria potestate superata regnum in coelis sempiternum obtinuit? Huius equidem consyderatio facile nobis fidem facit, ut Christum Iesum suo spiritu in Apostolis locutum esse credamus, & quae illi tradiderunt, totis animis amplectamur.
units.tr: I think the second reason for so careful an affirmation of this is the teaching and office of the Apostles, whose certainty had to be vigorously asserted against the judgements of the world. And what more effective proof could be found of it than the glorious and well-known resurrection of Christ, whom they preached? If they had preached some obscure man unknown to everyone, they could rightly have been suspected. But who now could doubt the teaching of those who announce and teach him who, by his mighty resurrection, broke the power of death, and, with every hostile power overcome, obtained an everlasting kingdom in heaven? Indeed, the consideration of this makes it easy for us to believe that Christ Jesus spoke through his Spirit in the Apostles, and to embrace with our whole hearts what they handed down to us.

units.la: Tertio, Christi resurrectionem testatissimam esse oportuit, eo quod in hac universus nostrae redemptionis & salutis cardo versetur. Illum enim in Evangelio frequenter resurrectione & vitam aeternam nobis polliceri legimus. Qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit a morte in vitam. Ioan. 5. Haec est voluntas eius, qui misit me, ut omnis qui videt filium & credit in eum, habeat vitam aeternam, & ego suscitabo eum in novissimo die. Ioan. 6. Et alibi dicit: Ego sum resurrectio & vita. Qui credit in me, etiamsi mortuus fuerit, vivet: & omnis qui vivit, & credit in me, non morietur in aeternum. Ioan. 11. Quid multis? Non alia nobis in Christum credendi causa est, quam quod tam corporum quam animarum vitam in illo nobis deus passim pollicetur. Quis vero vitam in eo inveniri putaret, qui seipsum in vitam asserere non posset? Ne ergo Christi morte offensi, de illius promissionibus dubitaremus, tertio statim post morte die reuixit, & vero corpore resuscitatus, se nostra quoq; corpora resuscitandi ius et potestatem habere declaravit. Qui enim cum iuxta humanam naturam vere mortuus & sepultus esset, seipsum excitare potuit, nonne multo magis iam viuens & regnans, nos e mortuis revocare, & in terra nerfis corporibus nostris vita restituere poterit? Eodem & aliae Christi promissiones pertinent, quae illius resurrectione flagitabant. Ait enim: Ubi ego sum, illic & minister meus erit. Ioan. 12. Et alibi: Iterum veniam & assumam vos ad meipsum, ut ubi ego sum & vos sitis. Ioan. 14. Item: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, ut videant gloriam meam. Ioan. 17. Quid vero promissiones istae tam magnificae aliud quam mortem nobis denuntiare poterant, nisi a morte Christus resuscitatus in coelis viueret? Sic enim necessario concludendum fuisset: Ubi Christus est, ibi erunt et ministri ipsius, qui in illum credunt. Atqui Christus mortuus & sepultus in morte mansit. Ergo & ministri ipsius in morte manere oportet. Argumentu vero hoc, desperationis plenum, Christi resurrectio validissime confutat, & contra mortis minas & inferorum terrores sic argumentari docet: Ubi Christus est, ibi & ministri eius erunt. Christus mortuus a morte resurrexit, & in coelos subuectus ad dextram dei patris confidet. Ergo & ministri Christi a mortuis resurgent, & in coelis cum Christo rege suo aeternum viuent. Quae si penitius inspecta animis suis recondat fideles, mox cum Paulo Apostolo Christi fiducia animati, tam morti quam omni adversariae potestati insultare audebut et dicere: Ubi tuus o mors aculeus? Ubi tua o inferna victoria? Si deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Persuasum sit, quod neq; mors neq; vita, ipsos separare possit a dilectione dei, quae est in Christo Iesu domino nostro. Vide locos 1. Cor. 15. & Rom. 8. cap. Accedit his, quod mors, quae peccati stipendium atq; poena est, non aliter quam resurrectione vinci poterat. Quoad enim illa mortuos detinebat, quos semel e vita sustulerat, vires illius nequaquam confracta et attrita videri poterant. Atqui illam vinci oportebat, siquidem humano generi libertas e peccatis & salus debebat obtingere. Quis enim de peccatorum remissione & reconciliatione cum Deo patre certus esset, regnante adhuc morte, quam deus ira sua peccati poenam constituerat? Christum Iesum igitur mortis iugum excutere, & e sepulchro suscitari necesse fuit, ut certo constaret & mortem deuictam, & peccatum (qui mortis aculeus erat. 1. Cor. 15.) sublatum, & humano generi salutem ex integro restitutam esse. Non temere ergo factum est, quod Christus suae resurrectionis veritatem tot tam quam euidentibus argumentis afferendam putauit. Et haec causa maxima est, quod eandem veteres prophetae, spiritu Christi instigati, praedixerunt ut cum alibi, tum Psal. 16. & Isa. 53. cernitur. Hanc certe piorum omnium spem praecipuam fuisse & summum Confessionis & fidei articulum, ex quo catholici & veri cultores Dei semper agniti & probati sunt, Iobi exemplo discimus, qui ab amicis nimium importunis violatae fidei & religionis accusatus, hoc uno se innocentem esse probat, quod radicem et fundamentum salutis firmum credat. Quod vero illud fundamentum, & quae illa radix est? Noui (inquit) & ego, quod vindex meus viuit, qui nouissimo tempore adhibebit vim suam pulueri. Postquam vero corpus hoc mea cute circumdederit, spectabo Deum e carne mea. Quem ego mihi contemplabor, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius: quod unicum meum est desyderium. Vide Iob. 19. cap.
units.tr: Thirdly, the resurrection of Christ had to be most fully attested, because on it hangs the whole hinge of our redemption and salvation. For we read in the Gospel that he often promises us resurrection and eternal life. "He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life" (John 5). "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day" (John 6). And elsewhere he says: "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me, even if he dies, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die" (John 11). What more need be said? We have no other reason to believe in Christ than that God promises us life, both of body and of soul, in him, on every side. Who indeed would think that life is to be found in one who could not assert life for himself? Lest therefore we be offended by the death of Christ and doubt his promises, he rose again the third day after his death, and, raised in a true body, he showed that he also has the right and power to raise up our bodies. For if he, who was truly dead and buried according to human nature, was able to raise himself, will he not much more, now living and reigning, be able to call us back from the dead and restore life to our bodies on earth? To the same end belong the other promises of Christ, which required his resurrection. For he says: "Where I am, there also my minister will be" (John 12). And elsewhere: "I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be also" (John 14). Likewise: "Father, those whom you have given me, I wish that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory" (John 17). But what could these so great promises announce to us, except death, unless Christ, raised from the dead, lived in heaven? For it would have been necessary to conclude thus: where Christ is, there his ministers also who believe in him will be. But Christ, dead and buried, remained in death. Therefore his ministers too must remain in death. This argument, full of despair, is most powerfully refuted by the resurrection of Christ, and it teaches us to argue against the threats of death and the terrors of the underworld in this way: where Christ is, there his ministers will also be. Christ died and rose from the dead, and, taken up into heaven, he sits at the right hand of God the Father. Therefore the ministers of Christ also will rise from the dead, and will live forever in heaven with Christ their king. If the faithful look into these things more deeply and store them in their minds, then, encouraged by the confidence in Christ, like the Apostle Paul they will dare to mock both death and every hostile power and to say: "O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory? If God is for us, who is against us?" Let it be settled that neither death nor life can separate them from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. See the passages 1 Cor. 15 and Rom. 8. To this is added that death, which is the wages and punishment of sin, could be overcome in no other way than by resurrection. For as long as death held those whom it had once taken from life, its powers could by no means seem broken and worn down. Yet it had to be overcome, since freedom from sins and salvation were to come to the human race. For who could be certain of the forgiveness of sins and of reconciliation with God the Father, while death still reigned, which God had appointed as the punishment of sin in his wrath? It was therefore necessary for Christ Jesus to shake off the yoke of death and to be raised from the sepulchre, so that it might be firmly established that death was conquered, that sin (which is the sting of death, 1 Cor. 15) was taken away, and that salvation had been fully restored to the human race. It was not without reason, then, that Christ thought fit to set forth the truth of his resurrection with so many and such clear proofs. And this is the chief reason why the ancient prophets, moved by the Spirit of Christ, foretold it, as is seen both elsewhere and in Psalm 16 and Isaiah 53. We learn from the example of Job that this was the chief hope of all the godly, and the highest article of confession and faith, by which the true and catholic worshippers of God have always been recognised and approved. Job, accused of violating faith and religion by his overly insistent friends, proves himself innocent by this alone, that he believes in a firm root and foundation of salvation. But what is that foundation, and what is that root? "I know," he says, "that my redeemer lives, who at the last time will bring his power to the dust. And after this body has been surrounded by my skin, I shall see God from my flesh. Whom I shall behold for myself, and my eyes shall see him, and no other; this is my one desire." See Job 19, ch.

units.la: Docet locus hic, quid de resurrectionis illusoribus iudicari debeat, quales omnibus seculis fuisse hi floriae probant, & nouissimo seculo regnaturos Apostoli praedixerunt. 2. Pet. 3. Et audiuntur passim hodie prophanae ac impiae voces eorum, qui tum demum se egregios congerrones & ciuiliter facetos censent, si quicquid de nouissimo Christi aduentu et corporum resurrectione creditur, scurrilibus iocis exagitent. At hi nullo alio argumento euidentius, quam vno hoc, se ab omni religione alienos esse, probare poterant. Ita enim in hoc articulo omnia fidei & religionis capita conueniunt, ut qui hunc negarint, omnem fidem & omnia humanae salutis mysteria semel subuluerint. Sensum hunc ex Pauli verbis accepimus, qui contra eos scribens, qui apud Corinthios resurrectionem negabant, inter alia inquit: Si Christus praedicatur a mortuis resurrexisse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos, non esse resurrectionem mortuorum? Equidem si mortui non resurgunt, ne Christus quidem resurrexit. Quod si Christus non resurrexit, superuacanea & inanis est fides vestra, adhuc estis in peccatis vestris. Igitur & qui in Christo obdormierunt, perierunt. Et si in hac vita spem in Christo tantum fixam habemus, maxime miserabiles omnium hominum sumus, &c. 1. Cor. 15. Procul ergo arcendi sunt impij isti illusores, & locus negandus talibus in bene ordinatis rebuspub. Quid enim intentatum relinquent, qui salutis nostrae fundamentum tam audacter euertere conantur, & quasi vno ictu, quantum in ipsis est, omnem fidem atq; religionem iugulant?
units.tr: This passage teaches how those who mock the resurrection ought to be judged. Such men, as the events show, have existed in every age, and the Apostles foretold that they would be rulers in the last age (2 Pet. 3). Everywhere today one hears the profane and impious words of those who think themselves fine companions and civilly witty only if they ridicule with scurrilous jokes whatever is believed about the last coming of Christ and the resurrection of bodies. Yet they could prove by no argument more clearly than this one that they are alien to all religion. For in this article all the heads of faith and religion so agree that whoever denies it has at once overthrown all faith and all the mysteries of human salvation. We take this sense from the words of Paul, who, writing against those among the Corinthians who denied the resurrection, says among other things: "If Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. And if Christ has not risen, your faith is empty and vain; you are still in your sins. Therefore those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. And if in this life we have only hope fixed in Christ, we are of all men most miserable," etc. (1 Cor. 15). Therefore these impious mockers must be kept far away, and no place must be given to such people in well-ordered commonwealths. For what will they leave untried, who so boldly attempt to overturn the foundation of our salvation, and, as it were with one blow, as far as lies in them, strangle all faith and religion?

units.la: Discamus autem in resurrectionis meditatione rite versari, ut ea & vitae gubernandae & consolationi seruiat. Efficacissimum enim hoc est contra carnis & mundi illecebras antidotum, si nouissimi iudicij simulachrum, in scripturis propositum, crebro ob oculos & in mentem renocemus. Rursum nulla Christiano homini efficacior consolatio obtingit, quam cum in resurrectione mortuorum, in hoc ipso corpore caelestis vitae gaudia sese percepturum cogitat, quod nunc infinitis molestijs, curis & doloribus conficitur. Paulus certe Christianos hortatur, ut ijs sese mutuo consolentur, quae de hoc articulo in scripturis tradita extant. 1. Thess. 4.
units.tr: Let us learn, then, to occupy ourselves rightly with the meditation on the resurrection, so that it may serve both to guide our life and to console us. For this is a most effective antidote against the allurements of the flesh and the world, if we often call to mind before our eyes and in our thoughts the image of the last judgement set forth in the Scriptures. Again, no consolation comes to a Christian more powerfully than when he reflects that in the resurrection of the dead he will receive in this very body the joys of the heavenly life, a body that now is worn down by endless troubles, cares and sorrows. Paul certainly exhorts Christians to console one another with those things which the Scriptures hand down concerning this article. 1 Thess. 4.

units.la: Restat, ut de altero illo dicamus, quod Christus in ultima illa cum discipulis conuersatione tractauit. Locutus est (inquit Lucas) de regno Dei. Visitatus vero ille scripturae mos est, ut nostrae redemptionis et salutis negotium regni Dei vel caelorum nomine appelletur: eo quod hic vnicus illius finis & scopus est, ut quoad hic viuimus dei spiritu regamur, et hac vita exempti, cum deo viuamus et regnemus in caelis. Quaecunque ergo ad huius rei mysteria pertinent, Christus diligenter & ordine certo exposuit. Huius vero initium a nobis sumitur. Ante omnia enim, quo nam in regno nascamur et versemur, antequam nobis Christus illucescit, nouisse oportet. Nisi enim peccatores nasceremur, et propter peccatum regno diaboli atq; inferorum effemus obnoxij, nulla in nobis regni dei instauratione opus esset. At quia tam misera est nostra conditio, filiu Dei dare oportuit, qui peccata nostra in se transferens, illa corporis & sanguinis sui sacrificio in ara crucis expiaret, & spiritus sui operatione nos per immortale verbi sui semen regeneraret in filios Dei. Quae regeneratio veteris hominis mortificationem & vitae totius innovationem gignit, & facit, ut qui antea Satanicis suggestionibus & corruptis affectibus regebantur, sub fidei obedientiam redacti, toti à deo et verbo ipsius pendeant. Et hoc illud Dei regnum est, quod per filium suum inter nos instauravit, & pro cuius instauratione, iubente Christo, oramus dicentes: Adveniat regnum tuum. Necesse vero fuit, huius regni mysteria Apostolis diligenter explicari, eò quòd communi Iudaeorum errore decepti, terrenum in Christo regnum imaginabantur, in quo honores, opes & victorias, & pacem huius seculi sperabant, quod crebrae illorum de primatu contentiones abundè docent. Matth. 18. & 20. Luc. 22. & c.
units.tr: There remains the other matter, which Christ treated in that last conversation with his disciples. He spoke, says Luke, of the kingdom of God. It is the customary usage of Scripture that the business of our redemption and salvation is called by the name of the kingdom of God or of heaven, because this is its sole end and goal: that, while we live here, we may be ruled by the Spirit of God, and, once freed from this life, we may live and reign with God in heaven. Christ therefore set out with care and in fixed order everything that pertains to the mysteries of this matter. We must take its beginning from ourselves. Before all else, before Christ shines upon us, we ought to know into what kingdom we are born and in which we live. For if we were not born sinners, and were not, because of sin, subject to the kingdom of the devil and of the lower world, there would be no need for any restoration of the kingdom of God in us. But because our condition is so wretched, it was necessary for the Son of God to be given, who, taking our sins upon himself, would expiate them by the sacrifice of his body and blood on the altar of the cross, and by the working of his Spirit would regenerate us through the immortal seed of his word into sons of God. This regeneration brings about the mortification of the old man and the renewal of the whole of life, and makes it so that those who were formerly governed by Satanic suggestions and corrupt affections, brought back under the obedience of faith, depend wholly on God and his word. And this is that kingdom of God which he restored among us through his Son, and for whose restoration, at Christ's command, we pray, saying: Thy kingdom come. It was necessary, however, that the mysteries of this kingdom be carefully explained to the apostles, since, deceived by the common error of the Jews, they imagined an earthly kingdom in Christ, in which they hoped for honours, wealth, victories and the peace of this age; their frequent contentions over primacy amply show this. Matt. 18 and 20; Luke 22, etc.

units.la: Porrò non ofcitanter Christi exemplum obseruare decet, qui apostolos, ad euangelij praedicationem & ecclesiae suae ministerium destinatos, tanta diligentia et studio in regni Dei cognitione erudire & docere voluit. Atqui hoc cum illo triennio fere toto versatos, concionibus ipsius interfuisse, & miraculorum omnium spectatores, ad praedicandum deniq; missos fuisse legimus. Voluit ergo admonere dominus, docendi prouinciam in ecclesia non temere à quouis suscipi, nec etiam cuiuis sine diligenti examine committi debere. Si enim res pretiosa, quarum custodia difficilis & periculosa est, nō cuiuis committuntur, nec illas, quicunq; sapit, apud se temere deponi patitur: quanto maiori cura & studio hic opus est, vbi de ecclesia Christi et animarum salute, quas proprio sanguine filius dei redimere dignatus est, agitur? Num vero aliquid his pretiosius inueniri poterit? Quàm difficilis autem et periculi plena sit harum conseruatio, non ignorare potest, qui nostrae carnis infirmitate, mundi illecebras & communis nostri hostis artes perspectas habet. Atqui dei vox est, quae Ezechieli olim denuntiata, ad omnes ecclesiae ministros pertinet: Sanguinem pereuntium de manu tua requiram. Ezech. 3. et 33. Huius frequenter meminisse debent, qui Theologiae candidati, munus hoc aliquando subituri sunt, ut ardentius sacrarum literarum lectioni incumbant, & in regni dei mysterijs inuestigandis indefesso studio desudent, ne forte ignorantia decepti in functione hac perperam aliquid committant. Paulus equidem periculi, quod hic maximum subest, non immemor, Timotheum, quem à puero sacras literas didicisse fatetur, graviter urget, ut lectioni sedulò incumbat. 2. Tim. 3. & 1. Tim. 4. Debent huius etiam meminisse, quorum ea est authoritas in ecclesia, ut ministros eligere et ordinare possint, ne ineptos eligendo ecclesiam dissipent, cuius cura ipsis maximè cordi esse debet. Nec enim leuis est error, qui hic committitur: quia & dissipationis in ecclesia authores sunt, et alienis peccatis communicant, ut Paulus non obscurè monet. 1. Tim. 5. Utinam observarent haec, qui ecclesiae ministerium pauperta-tis asylum fingentes, illud non nisi priuati commodi et ventris causa inuadunt, vel nullo maturo consilio adhibito, sed caecis affectibus ebrij, ecclesijs ineptissimos homines, et interdum palam improbos ac omnis disciplinae ofores obtrudunt.
units.tr: Moreover, it is fitting that we observe the example of Christ, who wished the apostles, destined for the preaching of the gospel and the ministry of his Church, to be instructed and taught in the knowledge of the kingdom of God with such great diligence and zeal. Indeed we read that they spent almost the whole of those three years in his company, were present at his sermons, were witnesses of all his miracles, and were at last sent out to preach. The Lord therefore wished to admonish us that the office of teaching in the Church ought not to be undertaken rashly by anyone, nor committed to anyone without careful examination. For if precious things, whose custody is difficult and dangerous, are not entrusted to just anyone, and no one who is wise allows them to be lightly placed in his keeping, how much greater care and zeal are needed here, where the Church of Christ and the salvation of souls, which the Son of God deigned to redeem with his own blood, are at stake? Indeed, can anything more precious be found? How difficult and full of danger the preservation of these is, he cannot fail to know who has a clear view of the weakness of our flesh, the allurements of the world and the arts of our common enemy. Yet it is the voice of God, once declared to Ezekiel, that pertains to all ministers of the Church: I will require the blood of the perishing at your hand. Ezek. 3 and 33. Those who are candidates for theology, and who will one day take up this office, ought often to remember this, so that they may apply themselves more ardently to the reading of the sacred letters and labour with unwearied zeal in investigating the mysteries of the kingdom of God, lest perhaps, deceived by ignorance, they commit something wrongly in this function. Paul, indeed, mindful of the danger which here lies greatest, earnestly urges Timothy, whom he confesses to have learned the sacred letters from childhood, to devote himself diligently to reading. 2 Tim. 3 and 1 Tim. 4. Those too ought to remember this who have the authority in the Church to elect and ordain ministers, lest by choosing unfit men they scatter the Church, whose care ought to lie especially close to their hearts. For the error committed here is no light one: they are both the authors of the scattering in the Church and share in the sins of others, as Paul plainly warns. 1 Tim. 5. Would that those who, feigning the ministry to be a refuge for the poor, take it up for no reason but private gain and the belly, or without any mature counsel, but drunk with blind affections, thrust upon the churches most unfit men, and sometimes openly wicked men, hostile to all discipline, would heed these things.

units.la: Postremò, Christi exemplo discimus, quae & qualia Christianorum colloquia esse debeant. Sancta nimirum, et quae morum emendationi pietatiq; seruiant. Christus enim de regno Dei cum apostolis colloquitur. Ad huius exemplum intenti, de regno Dei et salutis nostrae per Christum partae negotio frequenter differamus. Excutiamus diligenter naturae nostrae corruptionem, & ut hanc alij quoq; intelligant, elaboremus. Meditemur & praedicemus Christi in nos beneficia. Repetamus officium, quo is nos sibi totos obstrinxit. Fugiamus vicissim colloquia prava, quae bonos mores corrumpunt, Pauli ni dicti memores, qui turpiloquium inter ea recenset, propter quae venit ira Dei super omnes inobedientes. Col. 3. Et illud Christi nunquam non occurrat, qui de omni verbo otioso nos rationem reddituros esse dicit in die iudicij. Matth. 12. Faxit Deus, ut in regni sui meditatione crebrò versantes, terrena fastidire, caelestia amare, carne mori, & spiritu viuere discamus, ut olim in caelis viuere & regnare detur cum Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, from the example of Christ we learn what and of what kind the conversations of Christians ought to be: holy, certainly, and serving the amendment of morals and piety. For Christ conversed with the apostles about the kingdom of God. Following his example, let us frequently discuss, with attention, the kingdom of God and the business of our salvation obtained through Christ. Let us diligently examine the corruption of our nature, and labour to make others understand it too. Let us meditate upon and proclaim Christ's benefits toward us. Let us recall the duty by which he has bound us wholly to himself. Conversely, let us avoid evil talk, which corrupts good morals, mindful of Paul's words, who lists filthy talk among those things on account of which the wrath of God comes upon all the disobedient. Col. 3. And let that saying of Christ never escape us, who says that we shall give account of every idle word on the day of judgement. Matt. 12. May God grant that, while we dwell often in the meditation of his kingdom, we learn to loathe earthly things, to love heavenly things, to die to the flesh and live in the Spirit, so that one day it may be granted to us to live and reign in heaven with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA III.
units.tr: HOMILY III.

units.la: Et congregatis illis, praecepit, ne discederent Hierosolymis, sed expectarent promissum patris, De quo (inquit) audiuistis ex me: Quia Ioannes quidem baptizauit aqua: Vos autem baptizabimini spiritu sancto post dies hosce non multos.
units.tr: And when they were assembled, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, "which (said he) you have heard from me: for John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence."

units.la: Quoniam Apostolos in eum finem Christus delegerat, ut ipsorum ministerio salutis doctrina in omnes gentes disseminaretur, necesse fuit, ut ipsi priores probè instituerentur in omnibus ijs, quæ ad illorum munus spectabant. Qua in re vt nihil intermisit Christus, quem nostræ salutis sitien-tissimum esse constat: ita diuus Lucas postremam ipsius cum apostolis conuersationem magna diligen-tia describit, partim quidem vt Christi studium nobis innotescat, partim vero vt ostendat quæ nam verbi ministris maximè necessaria sint. Et primò quidem resurrectionis suæ veritatem multis argu-mentis per dies quadraginta asseruit. Quia enim hæc salutis nostræ fundamentum est, nihil in euan-gelij prædicatione profecerit, quicunq; illam non probè habuerit perspectam et cognitam. Secundo lo-co regni dei mysteria exposuit: tum vt opinionem ex communi errore de terreno Christi regno concep-tam, animis illorum eximeret: tum vt intelligerent, quo modo & ordine salutis & fidei negotium per euangelij prædicationem mundo prædicari debeat. Coharet duobus hisce tertium, promissio nimi-rum de spiritu sancto, quam & in præsenti repetit, & illius veritatem, ne subitò ipsius è terris discef-su toti consternarentur, graui testimonio confirmat, simulq; de loco & tempore, quæ hic illis obseruanda erant, admonet. Est autem insignis locus, cuius diligens consyderatio tam institutioni quàm conso-lationi plurimum seruit.
units.tr: Since Christ had chosen the apostles for this end, that the teaching of salvation should be spread among all nations through their ministry, it was necessary that they themselves first be thoroughly instructed in all those things that pertained to their office. In this matter Christ left nothing undone, as is well known to be most eager for our salvation. So the divine Luke describes his final conversation with the apostles with great care, partly so that Christ's concern for us may become known, and partly so that he may show which things are most necessary for the ministers of the Word. First, he asserted the truth of his resurrection by many proofs over forty days. For since this is the foundation of our salvation, whoever has not understood and known it properly will make no progress in preaching the gospel.
