Second, he explained the mysteries of the kingdom of God, both to free their minds from the opinion of an earthly kingdom of Christ, which they had formed from common error, and so that they might understand in what manner and order the business of salvation and faith ought to be proclaimed to the world through the preaching of the gospel. A third thing coheres with these two, namely the promise concerning the Holy Spirit, which he repeats at this point and confirms with weighty testimony, so that they would not be utterly dismayed by his sudden departure from the earth; at the same time he admonishes them about the place and time that they were to observe here. This is a notable passage, whose careful consideration serves both instruction and consolation greatly.

units.la: Principio de loco admonet, dum præcipit, ne ab Hierosolymis digrediantur, sed illic patris pro-missum expectent. Hierosolymorum ergo vrbs negotio omnium maximo destinatur, quo nullum vn-quam salutarius et excellentius in orbe terrarum contigit. Et vt in ea dei filius corporis & sangui-nis sui sacrificio humani generis salutem reparauit: ita ibidem apostolos spiritu suo illustrari et euan-gelicæ prædicationis initium fieri voluit. Erit hic quod cum stupore admiremur, si vrbis huius statū consyderes. Illa enim ipsa ciuitas est, de quatam dira & horrenda pronuntiauit Christus dominus. In illam dicitur quod extat Matth. 23. Hierusalem Hierusalem, quæ occidis prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te mittuntur: quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodū gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas, & tu noluisti? Et cùm in Galilæa agens de insidijs ab Herode sibi structis admoneretur, respondet, fieri non posse, vt propheta alibi pereat, quàm Hierosolymis. Luc. 13. Nec illa tantum de ciuitatis illius peccatis recenset, sed eidem interitum & excidium non semel denuntiat. Matt. 23. & 24. Luc. 19. Quam ergo causam fuisse putabimus, quæ Christum, vt sceleratam vrbem, & exitio proximam, tantæ rei & tam sanctæ destinaret, impulit? Non alia certè quàm irrefragabilis dei veritas, cuius promissiones fallere non possunt. A prophetis olim prædictum erat, salutis prædicationem hinc orituram. Temporibus nouissimis (aiunt prophetæ) erit mons domus domini præparatus in vertice montium, & editior erit collibus: confluentq; ad eum omnes gentes, & proficiscentur multi populi dicentes: Adeste, & ascendamus ad montem domini, ad domum Dei Iacob, & docebit nos de viis suis, ambulabimusq; in semitis eius: quoniam de Zion exibit lex, & verbum domini de Hierusalem. Isa. 2. Mich. 4. Vbi non prætermittendum mihi videtur, cuius Suetonius, quamuis ethnicus author & Christianis male propitius, in Vespasiano meminit, In toto Oriente veterem & constantem opinio-nem fuisse, in fatis esse, vt Iudæa profecti rerum potirentur. Quod oraculū ipse quidem, vtpote homo prophanus, de Vespasiano interpretatur, qui Iudaico bello strenuè res gerendo ad imperium sibi et fi-lijs aditum fecit. Rectius autem de apostolis exponemus, qui ex Iudæa oriundi, in Hierosolymorum vrbe euangelicam prædicationem exorsi, postea totam Iudæam doctrina sua repleuerunt, tandemq; ex Iudæa in omnes gentes dispersi, totum orbem Christo subiecerunt. Hæc quia à deo patre decreta esse, Christus ignorare non potuit, Apostolos Hierosolymis discedere vetat.
units.tr: First, he admonishes about the place, when he commands them not to depart from Jerusalem, but there to wait for the Father's promise. So the city of Jerusalem is designated for the greatest of all undertakings, in which nothing more saving and excellent has ever happened in the world. Just as in that city the Son of God restored the salvation of the human race by the sacrifice of his body and blood, so there he willed that the apostles be illumined by his Spirit and that the beginning of the evangelical preaching be made. Here there is something we should admire with amazement, if you consider the state of this city. For it is that very city of which Christ the Lord pronounced such dire and dreadful things. Concerning it stands what is written in Matthew 23: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you: how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not?" And when, while in Galilee, he was warned about the snares laid for him by Herod, he replied that it was not possible for a prophet to perish anywhere else than at Jerusalem (Luke 13). Nor does he recount only the sins of that city, but he also repeatedly announces to it ruin and destruction (Matt. 23 and 24; Luke 19). What cause, then, shall we think it was that impelled Christ to destine such a holy undertaking for a city that was wicked and close to destruction? Certainly none other than the unfailing truth of God, whose promises cannot deceive. It had been foretold long ago by the prophets that the preaching of salvation would arise from here. "In the last days" (say the prophets) "the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and it shall be higher than the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall go and say: Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths; for the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Isa. 2; Mic. 4). Here it seems to me not to be passed over that Suetonius, although a heathen author and ill-disposed toward Christians, mentions in his life of Vespasian that throughout the whole East there was an old and firm opinion that it was fated for men coming out of Judea to obtain dominion over the world. He himself, being a profane man, interprets this oracle of Vespasian, who by fighting the Jewish war vigorously opened the way to empire for himself and his sons. But we shall rightly expound it of the apostles, who, being natives of Judea, began the evangelical preaching in the city of Jerusalem, afterwards filled all of Judea with their teaching, and finally, scattered from Judea among all nations, subjected the whole world to Christ. Since Christ could not be ignorant that these things had been decreed by God the Father, he forbids the apostles to depart from Jerusalem.

units.la: Interim nostræ tam consolationi quàm institutioni plurimū seruit horū consyderatio. Hinc énim constat, dei promissiones aliquorū hominum improbitate & impietate non in vniuersum irritas fieri siue aboleri. Quid enim (inquit Paulus) si quidam fuerunt increduli? Num illorum incredulitas fidem Dei faciet irritam? Absit: imò sit Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Rom. 3. Debet hoc imis animis recondi, quia frequenter fieri videmus, vt vniuersali ferè omniū hominū impietate & incredulitate conspecta, ab omni nostræ salutis spe deijciamur, quasi aliorum impietas nobis etiam fraudi sit. Quæ tentatio grauissima est, & vt Deum vel nimiæ seueritatis, vel etiā iniustitiæ infimu-lat: itain pietatis cursu quàm maximè remoratur. Cur enim in illo pergat, qui semel in animum in-duxit, quod ipsi vnà cum maiori impiorum numero sit pereundum? Hic ergo nos contra armari ne-cesse est. Nullis autem armis validioribus poterimus instrui, quàm si cogitemus, Deum suos nouisse, vtut ingens impiorum turba sit. 2. Tim. 2. Et apud prophetam, si eo in nos affectu præditum esse sa-
units.tr: Meanwhile, consideration of these things serves our consolation and instruction greatly. For from this it is clear that God's promises are not utterly annulled or abolished by the wickedness and impiety of some men. For what, says Paul, if some were unbelieving? Will their unbelief make the faith of God void? God forbid; rather let God be true, but every man a liar (Rom. 3). This ought to be stored deep in our hearts, because we often see that, when the almost universal impiety and unbelief of all men is observed, we are cast down from every hope of our salvation, as if the impiety of others were a loss to us too. This is a most grievous temptation, and it accuses God of either excessive severity or even injustice, and so it greatly hinders the course of piety. For why would one persist in that course, who has once persuaded himself that he must perish together with the greater number of the impious? Here, therefore, we must arm ourselves against it. Yet we can be equipped with no weapons more powerful than if we consider that God knows his own, however vast the crowd of the impious may be (2 Tim. 2). And in the prophet, if he is shown to be endowed with such affection toward us

units.la: Hierosolymis euangelij prædicationis initium fit.
units.tr: In Jerusalem the beginning of the preaching of the gospel is made.

units.la: Multorum impietas dei promissa non facit irrita. tetur, quo matres ex vtero suo prognatos infantes prosequuntur. Ifa.49. Et quia iustus vniuerse terra iudex est, non perdit piu cum impio, id quod pater credentiu Abraham probe obseruauit. Gen.18. Rursum, quia & sapientissimus est & omnipotens, facile inter pios ac impios discernere, et his quide meritas poenas immittere, illos vero tueri potest. Quo referri debet, quod Baptista Christo ventilabrum tribuit, quo aream suam purgat, & paleas a tritico discernit. Matt.3. Extant huius rei exempla vndiq. Nouit Lotum in medijs Sodomis dominus. Idem patriarchar cura habet inter Chananaeos versantium, licet illi diuina sententia excidio iam effent destinati. Ita in praesenti apostolos suos nouit, & quoscunq; Hierosolymis ex electorum suorum numero habuit: nec illis fraudi est aliorum corruptio & impietas, qui numero et authoritate praualebat. Eade ergo ratione et nos hodie pro suis agnoscet et saluabit, modo ab iniquitate discedamus, et vita exprimamus Christiani nominis professione.
units.tr: The impiety of many does not make God's promises void. ... as mothers embrace the infants born from their womb (Isa. 49). And because he is the just judge of the whole earth, he does not destroy the righteous together with the wicked, which the father of the faithful, Abraham, well observed (Gen. 18). Again, because he is both most wise and almighty, he can easily distinguish between the pious and the impious, inflicting deserved punishments on the one and protecting the other. To this must be referred what the Baptist ascribes to Christ, the winnowing fan with which he cleans his threshing floor and separates the chaff from the wheat (Matt. 3). Examples of this fact exist everywhere. The Lord knew Lot in the midst of Sodom. The same God had care of the patriarchs who lived among the Canaanites, although those had already been destined for destruction by divine sentence. So now he knows his apostles and all those whom he had in Jerusalem from the number of his elect, and the corruption and impiety of others, who prevailed in number and authority, did them no harm. By the same reasoning he will also now acknowledge and save those of his own, provided that we depart from iniquity and express in our life the profession of the Christian name.

units.la: Ad vitae vero institutionem facit quod Hierosolymorum exemplo discimus, nulla vel maiorum gloria & authoritate, vel nominis praerogatiua, eos contra dei iudicium defendi posse, qui impij & deo ingrati esse pergunt. Si quae enim vnquam vrbes gloria & potentia insignes fuerunt, inter has facile sibi primatum Hierusalem vendicat. Nam vt omittam, quod per annos circiter quadringentos septuaginta septem in populo Dei regni simul & sacerdotij sedes fuit, quod regnum ad Euphraten vsq; extendit, quod fortissimos reges, sanctissimos sacerdotes, & prophetas diuinissimos peperit: vnu hoc omnem mundi gloriam longe superat, quod illam ecclesiae Christi Iesu typum & exemplar deus facere dignatus est. Eo enim nomine tot praeconijs apud prophetas & in Psalmis illustratur. Ideo in Zion Christus regnaturus dicitur. Psalm.2. Ideo ciuitatem magni regis illam scripturae appellant. Psal.48. Matth.5. Accedit vero ad gloriam hanc, quod in eadem & spiritum sanctum accipiunt apostoli, & diuinis auspicijs salutarem euangelij praedicationem primum aggrediuntur. Num vero omnis haec gloria illam ex manu irati dei & imminenti excidio liberare potuit, cum beneficiorum & praeceptorum Dei immemor, nec maiorum virtutibus responderet, nec deo sese gratam & obedientem exhiberet? Imo, quia eos potius ex patrum numero imitari placuit, qui diuina & humana iura violauerant & prophetarum sanguinem effuderant, non Dauidis (qui primus illic sedem regno & templo constituerat) pietas, non Solomonis sapientia, non Iosaphati integritas, non Ezechiae fortitudo, non Iosiae zelus, non prophetarum sermones quibus personuerat, non miracula per Christum & apostolos edita, non illic inchoatum euangelij praeconium, obstare potuit, quin intra quadraginta annos tota funditus excinderetur, & solo aequata vix aliquod vrbis tantae monumentum possit relinqueret. Et quod Hierosolymis contigisse dicimus, hoc ipsum & Capernaum (peculiaris illa ciuitas domini) & Corozain & Bethsaida apostolis alumnis praeclarae, senserunt. Vide Matth.11. Desinant ergo auitis maiorum virtutibus & antiquis Dei beneficijs gloriari, qui ingratitudine et inobedientia Dei iram provocare non desinunt. Nisi enim verbi Dei audientes, eiusdem beneficijs respondeant, eandem cum infaustis Iudaeae ciuitatibus fortem subibunt.
units.tr: What we learn from the example of Jerusalem also serves the institution of life: that neither the greater glory and authority of ancestors, nor any prerogative of name, can defend those against God's judgment who persist in impiety and ingratitude toward God. For if ever any cities were distinguished by glory and power, Jerusalem can easily claim first place among them. For, to omit that for about four hundred and seventy-seven years it was the seat of both kingdom and priesthood among the people of God, that its kingdom extended to the Euphrates, that it produced most valiant kings, most holy priests, and most divine prophets, this alone far surpasses all the glory of the world: that God deigned to make it a type and pattern of the church of Jesus Christ. For under this name it is so greatly extolled by so many proclamations among the prophets and in the Psalms. Therefore Christ is said to be going to reign in Zion (Ps. 2), and therefore the Scriptures call it the city of the great king (Ps. 48; Matt. 5). Moreover, to this glory is added that in that city the apostles also received the Holy Spirit and under divine auspices first undertook the saving preaching of the gospel. But could all this glory deliver it from the hand of an angry God and from impending destruction, when, forgetful of God's benefits and commands, it corresponded neither to the virtues of its ancestors nor showed itself grateful and obedient to God? Indeed, because it pleased them rather to imitate those of their fathers who had violated divine and human laws and shed the blood of the prophets, neither the piety of David (who first established there a seat for the kingdom and the temple), nor the wisdom of Solomon, nor the integrity of Jehoshaphat, nor the courage of Hezekiah, nor the zeal of Josiah, nor the sermons of the prophets with which it had resounded, nor the miracles performed by Christ and the apostles, nor the gospel proclamation begun there, could prevent it from being utterly uprooted within forty years and, levelled to the ground, leaving scarcely any monument of so great a city. And what we say happened to Jerusalem, the same Capernaum (that particular city of the Lord), Chorazin and Bethsaida, famous nurseries of apostles, also experienced (see Matt. 11). Let those therefore cease to glory in the old virtues of their ancestors and the ancient benefits of God, who do not cease to provoke God's wrath by ingratitude and disobedience. For unless they, hearing the Word of God, respond to its benefits, they will undergo the same fate as the unfortunate cities of Judea.

units.la: Porro vt ad Christi institutum reuertamur, quid apostoli in Hierosolymorum vrbe facere debuerint, videndum est. Iubet autem vt ibi expectent promissum patris. Quo nomine spiritum sanctum intelligit, quem patris promissum vocat, tum quod a solo deo patre & vere promittitur & datur, tum autem quod ille per prophetas non semel pollicitus erat, se in aduentu Messiae spiritu suum super homines liberaliter effundere velle, quemadmodum Petrus infra ex Ioele docebit. Interim suas quoque promissiones ipsis in animum reuocat, quae passim in euangelio extant. Si quis credit in me (inquit) sicut dicit scriptura: flumina de ventre eius fluent aquae viuae. Ioan.7. Quae verba de spiritu sancto, quem in Christum credentes accepturi erant, intelligi debere, Euangelista ibidem docet. Et alibi ait: Ego rogabo patrem, & alium consolatorem dabit vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in aeternum, spiritum veritatis, quem mundus non potest accipere. Ioan.14. Item: Paracletus ille, qui est spiritus sanctus, quem pater mittet nomine meo, ille vos docebit omnia, & suggeret vobis omnia quaecunq; dixi vobis. Et rursum Ioban.15. Cum venerit paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis a patre, spiritus veritatis qui a patre procedit, ille testimonium perhibebit de me. Et paulo post: Cum venerit ille, qui est spiritus veritatis, ducet vos in omnem veritatem. Ioban.16. Quia ergo & pater olim per prophetas spiritum hunc filij sui Iesu Christi cultoribus promisit, & eundem Christus pro mediatoris et intercessoris officio nobis a patre impetrauit, recte patris promissum dicitur.
units.tr: Now, to return to Christ's instruction: we must consider what the apostles ought to do in the city of Jerusalem. He orders them to wait there for the Father's promise. By this he means the Holy Spirit, whom he calls the Father's promise, both because it is the Father alone who truly promises and gives it, and because through the prophets he had more than once pledged that at the coming of the Messiah he would generously pour out his Spirit upon men, as Peter will later show from Joel. Meanwhile he also calls to their minds his own promises, which appear throughout the Gospel: "If anyone believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly" (John 7). The Evangelist himself teaches in that place that these words must be understood of the Holy Spirit, whom those who believe in Christ were to receive. And elsewhere he says: "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive" (John 14). Likewise: "That Paraclete, who is the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things, and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." And again, in John 15: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness of me." And shortly after: "When he comes, who is the Spirit of truth, he will lead you into all truth" (John 16). Therefore, since the Father long ago promised through the prophets this Spirit to the worshippers of his Son Jesus Christ, and Christ, in his office of Mediator and Intercessor, obtained him for us from the Father, it is rightly called the Father's promise.

units.la: Venis Venit autem hic obseruandum, quòd Christus Iesus discipulos suos iam olim ecclesiasticæ vel euan gelicæ functioni destinatos, & longo tempore abs se fidelissimè institutos, non illico ad muneris huius administrationem exilire paticur, sed obedientiam exigens, promissum à patre spiritum expectare iu- bet. Docemur hoc Christi exemplo, diuinorum præceptorum obedientiam cum primis à verbi ministris requiri. Æquum enim est, vt qui alios ad obedientiam fidei (qui euangelicæ prædicationis scopus est, 2. Cor.10. Rom.1. & 16.) adducere debent, ipsi priores obedientiæ assuescant, nec quicquam sine Christi imperatoris sui nutu atq; præcepto faciant. Ita enim non tam doctrina quàm proprio exemplo obedientiæ studium auditoribus persuadebunt.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that Christ Jesus, though he had long since faithfully trained his disciples, destined for ecclesiastical or evangelical service, does not allow them to rush straight into the exercise of this office, but, requiring obedience, orders them to wait for the Spirit promised by the Father. We are taught by this example of Christ that obedience to the divine precepts is above all required of ministers of the Word. For it is fitting that those who ought to bring others to the obedience of faith (which is the aim of evangelical preaching: 2 Cor. 10; Rom. 1 and 16) should themselves first become accustomed to obedience, and do nothing without the nod and command of Christ, their Commander. For in this way they will persuade their hearers of the zeal for obedience less by teaching than by their own example.

units.la: Præterea admonet locus hic, non sufficere ministris verbi, si rerum cognitione & eruditione instru & sint, nisi spiritus sancti donum accedat. Quia enim nemo venit ad Christum nisi à patre cœlesti tra- batur, frustra docendo & monendo instabunt qui ecclesiarum antistites sunt, nisi spiritum sanctum suis studijs & laboribus cooperantem habeant. Vidit hoc Paulus apostolus, qui ecclesiam Dei agricolatio- nem vocat, & nec eum qui plantat, nec eum qui rigat, quicquam esse fatetur, sed omnem huius functio-nis effectum & gloriam vni Deo transcribit, qui incrementum solus dare potest. Præparatione ergo per spiritum sanctum ministris opus est, ne dum sine huius auspicijs tatum onus suscipiunt, non sibijpsis modò, verumetiam toti ecclesiæ malum dent. Nec vnquam huic muneri idoneus erit, qui non efficaces intra animum suum spiritus sancti motus experitur. Hinc præparationes illæ prophetarum in scripturis leguntur, quales sunt, quæ Isaiæ, Ieremiæ, Ezechielis & aliorum prædicationem præcesserunt. Quæ causa videtur, quòd neophytos ad ecclesiæ ministerium admitti Paulus prohibet, eò quòd tales plerunque de spiritus sancti operatione & præsente auxilio non satis certi esse possunt. Caterum quod de verbi ministris dicitur, ad omnes quoque alios referri debet, qui rebus arduis & ad publicam multorum salutem pertinentibus destinati sunt. Quorum in numero non postremum locum obtinent, qui in magistratu versantur, & iudiciorum Dei interpretes, dij nominari in scripturis solent. Quid enim illi vel rectè prospicere vel iudicare poterunt, nisi spiritus sancti virtute prauì affectus, qui transfuersos abripiunt, coherceantur? Vel quæ nam rerumpublicarum incolumitas esse poterit, quæ non Dei spiritu, sed carnali prudentia reguntur, quando omnem felicitatem ab vno Deo dependere constat? Ob seruauit hoc sapientissimus mortalium Solomon, qui cùm optionem inter ea, quæ maximo in pretio inter homines habentur, sibi diuinitus offerri audiret, omnibus alijs contemptis, sapientiæ spiritum à Deo petijt, & verè quidem illius sapientiæ, quam in Proverbiorum libro describit, cuius initium & radix est timor Domini. Atqui vtinam in huius rei meditatione frequentes essent, qui hodie ecclesiarum & rerumpublicarum habenas moderantur. Ea enim ad preces ac pietatis studium ardens accenderet, & verbi Dei audientiores redderet, vnde non posset non vera & solida emanare populi, qui ipsorum fidei commissus est, incolumitas.
units.tr: Moreover, this passage shows that it is not enough for ministers of the Word to be equipped with knowledge of things and with learning, unless the gift of the Holy Spirit is added. For since no one comes to Christ unless he is drawn by the heavenly Father, those who are the leaders of the churches will labour in vain in teaching and admonishing, unless they have the Holy Spirit working together with their studies and labours. The apostle Paul saw this, who calls the Church of God a field under cultivation, and who confesses that neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but ascribes the whole effect and glory of this function to the one God, who alone can give the increase. Ministers therefore need preparation through the Holy Spirit, lest, undertaking so great a burden without his guidance, they bring harm not only to themselves but to the whole Church. Nor will anyone ever be fit for this office who does not experience the effective movements of the Holy Spirit within his own mind. Hence those preparations of the prophets are read of in the Scriptures, such as those which went before the preaching of Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the others. This seems to be the reason why Paul forbids neophytes to be admitted to the ministry of the Church, because such men can for the most part not be sufficiently certain of the working of the Holy Spirit and of his present help. But what is said of ministers of the Word must also be applied to all others who are appointed to difficult tasks that concern the public welfare of many. Among these no small place is held by those who hold office in the magistracy, and who are customarily called gods in the Scriptures, as interpreters of the judgements of God. For what could they rightly foresee or judge, unless the evil affections which drag men this way and that were restrained by the power of the Holy Spirit? Or what soundness of commonwealths could there be which are governed not by the Spirit of God but by carnal prudence, since it is agreed that all happiness depends upon the one God alone? Solomon, the wisest of mortals, observed this, who, when he heard that a choice was offered him by God among those things which are held in the highest esteem among men, having despised all the others, asked God for the spirit of wisdom: and truly of that wisdom which he describes in the book of Proverbs, whose beginning and root is the fear of the Lord. Would that those who today guide the reins of the churches and commonwealths were frequent in the meditation upon this matter! For it would kindle them to prayer and to an ardent zeal for piety, and would make them more attentive hearers of the Word of God, from which there could not but flow true and solid soundness for the people committed to their faith.

units.la: Priusquam verò ab hoc loco digrediamur, duo excutienda restant, quæ ex promissione spiritus san- cti, apostolis facta, non sine fructu elici possunt. Primò enim hinc constat, apostolicæ doctrinæ autho- rem esse spiritum sanctum, & proinde illam, non humanam, sed diuinam censeri debere. Quia enim do- cendi munus accepto demum spiritu sancto subierunt, qui iuxta Christi promissionem, omnem veritatem illis suggessit, ad eundem certè spiritum omnis illorum doctrina referri debet. Hinc tanta eius agnoscì debet dignitas & authoritas, quantam illi Christus tribuit, dum prædicatum discipulos emittens, ait: Qui vos audit, me audit: qui autem vos spernit, me spernit. Luc.10. Quo ipso argumento Paulus mihi animatus dixisse videtur: Si angelus è cœlo prædicauerit vobis euangelium præter id, quod prædicauimus vobis, anathema sit. Gal.1. Nam quantacunq; sit angelorum maiestas & gloria, ea tamen si cum spiritu sancto, per quem illi creati sunt, conferatur, nullius momenti fuerit. Habemus itaque hoc loco quod illis respondeamus, qui vbi humanas traditiones à nobis reijci & damnari audiunt, apostolos quoque homines fuisse clamant, & hoc vno euinci posse confidunt, vel apostolorum quo que doctrinam reijci debere, vel aliquem humanis traditionibus locum in ecclesia esse relinquendum. Atqui homines fuisse apostolos non ignoramus. Quia verò non vt homines locuti sunt, nec humanæ mentis cogitationes inter docendum exposuerunt, sed diuinatim cordibus ipsorum spiritu sancto salutis & regni cœlorum mysteria nunciarunt, illorum dogmata inter humanas traditiones nullo modo censeri merentur.
units.tr: Before we depart from this passage, two matters remain to be examined, which may be drawn with profit from the promise of the Holy Spirit made to the apostles. First, it is evident from this that the Holy Spirit is the author of the apostolic doctrine, and therefore that it ought to be judged not human but divine. For since they undertook the office of teaching only after receiving the Holy Spirit, who, according to Christ's promise, suggested to them all truth, all their teaching must certainly be referred to that same Spirit. Hence his dignity and authority must be acknowledged as great as Christ ascribed to it, when, sending out the disciples to preach, he said: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me" (Luke 10). By this very argument Paul seems to have spoken to me with spirit: "If an angel from heaven preaches to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1). For however great the majesty and glory of the angels may be, yet if it is compared with the Holy Spirit, by whom they were created, it would be of no weight. We have therefore here an answer for those who, when they hear that human traditions are rejected and condemned by us, cry out that the apostles too were men, and trust that this one point can be proven: either that the apostolic doctrine too must be rejected, or that some place must be left in the Church for human traditions. But we are not ignorant that the apostles were men. Yet since they did not speak as men, nor set out the thoughts of the human mind in their teaching, but by divine inspiration announced in their hearts, through the Holy Spirit, the mysteries of salvation and of the kingdom of heaven, their doctrines deserve by no means to be counted among human traditions.

units.la: Secundò admonet locus hic, nihil in ecclesia doceri & prædicari debere nisi à spiritu sancto traditum. Dei enim domus est ecclesia, in qua vnius patrisfamilias vox audiri, & ad huius præscriptum omnia institui debent. Et vt sponsa vnius sponsi iussis obtemperat, nec casta censebitur, si amatorum & impudentium procorum vel blanditiis vel promissis aures præbeat: ita cum fidelium ecclesiam Dei filius proprio sanguine ablutam sibi ipsi desponderit, nosq́ (qui coniugij proprissimus finis est) bonorum suorum omnium fecerit consortes, minimè admittendum erit, vt aliam vocem sequamur, quàm quæ sponsus Christus nos ad sese inuitat. Adhæc quia oues sui gregis nos fecit Christus, & salutem nostram proprij sanguinis dispendio redemit, illius vocem nos sequi, non alienam & mercenariam audire conuenit. Ioan. 10. Nec illorum opinio recipienda est, qui venia dignum errorem censent, si in salutis & fidei doctrina non malo instituto quicquam immutent, modò in omnibus vnius Dei cultum solicitè spectent. Nam vt concedamus tales habere zelum Dei, quia tamen scientia veritatis destituuntur, Deo non magis placere poterunt, quàm Iudæi olim, qui zelo Dei inflammati, propriam iustitiam stabilire nitebantur, eam verò reiiciebant, quam in filio suo nobis Deus per fidem amplectendam offert. Et sanè, si nostER zelus in tanta re sufficeret, superuacaneum erat, apostolos spiritus sancti missionem expectare. Quin ergo prorumpebant ad euangelizandum, & pio animi proposito tradebant quaecunque ad Dei cultum & Christi gloriam pertinere videbantur? Sed Christi præceptum obstabat, qui vt alibi abs se tradita prædicare iussit (Matth. 10. & 28.) ita non sine spiritu duce ipsos prædicandi munus subire vult, ne vel humanæ sapientiæ consilijs, vel corruptis carnis affectibus seducti exorbitarent. Atqui eodem præcepto veteres prophetas obstrictos fuisse legimus, in quibus spiritum Christi locutum esse Apostolus non obscurè testatur. 1. Pet. 1. Ieremiæ equidem dicitur: Ecce ego posui verba mea in os tuum. Ierem. 1. Et Ezechiel audit à Deo: Audies verbum ex ore meo, & diserte monebis eos ex me. Ezechiel. 3. & 33. Impia ergo & Cyclopæa illorum temeritas est, qui sibi permissum putant, nouos fidei articulos fingere, & humanæ rationis ductu inuentas traditiones ecclesijs obtrudere. Et quis obsecro fidelem paranymphum dixerit, quicunque sponsam, vt suis legibus & iussis obtemperet, solicitare non vereatur? Ex Dei igitur ore doctrinam suam omnem excerpant, qui in ecclesia docendi munere funguntur. Loquitur is nobis in scripturis per spiritum suum. Has ergo legant, & errare non poterunt.
units.tr: Second, this passage shows that nothing ought to be taught and preached in the Church except what has been handed down by the Holy Spirit. For the Church is the house of God, in which the voice of one Father of the household ought to be heard, and by his prescription everything ought to be ordered. And as a bride obeys the commands of her one bridegroom, and would not be counted chaste if she lent her ears to the flatteries or promises of lovers and shameless suitors, so, since the Son of God has betrothed to himself the Church of the faithful, washed with his own blood, and has made us, for whom marriage is the very purpose, partners of all his goods, it must by no means be allowed that we should follow any voice other than that of Christ the Bridegroom, who invites us to himself. Besides, since Christ has made us the sheep of his flock, and has redeemed our salvation at the cost of his own blood, it is fitting that we follow his voice and hear no strange or hireling voice (John 10). Nor is the opinion of those to be received who think that an error worthy of pardon is committed if they change anything in the teaching of salvation and faith from a bad institution, provided that in all things they carefully aim at the worship of the one God. For even if we grant that such men have zeal for God, yet because they lack the knowledge of the truth, they can no more please God than the Jews of old, who, inflamed with zeal for God, strove to establish their own righteousness, but rejected that which God offers us in his Son to be embraced through faith. And indeed, if our zeal were sufficient in so great a matter, it would have been superfluous for the apostles to await the mission of the Holy Spirit. Why, then, did they not rush forth to preach, and hand on with a pious purpose whatever seemed to pertain to the worship of God and the glory of Christ? But the command of Christ stood in the way, who, as he ordered them to preach what he had delivered elsewhere (Matt. 10 and 28), so also wills that they undertake the office of preaching not without the Spirit as guide, lest, led astray by the counsels of human wisdom or by corrupt affections of the flesh, they should go astray. Indeed we read that the ancient prophets were bound by the same command, in whom the apostle plainly testifies that the Spirit of Christ spoke (1 Pet. 1). Of Jeremiah it is indeed said: "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth" (Jer. 1). And Ezekiel hears from God: "You shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall warn them plainly from me" (Ezek. 3 and 33). Impious and Cyclopean, then, is the rashness of those who think it allowed to them to devise new articles of faith, and to thrust upon the churches traditions discovered by the guidance of human reason. And who, I ask, would call a faithful go-between one who does not hesitate to court the bride, so that she may obey his laws and commands? Let those who hold the office of teaching in the Church therefore draw all their doctrine from the mouth of God. He speaks to us in the Scriptures through his Spirit. Let them read these, and they will not be able to err.

units.la: Caeterum ad Christi verba, vnde digressi sumus, reuertamur. Is enim præcepti sui causam redditurus ait: De quo audiuistis ex me. Quia Ioannes quidem baptizauit aqua: vos autem baptizabimini spiritu sancto post dies hosce non multos. Habent verba hæc promissionis confirmationem & consolationem cumprimis necessariam. Vt enim multa erant alia, quæ apostolos in sui muneris consyderatione solicitos reddere poterant: ita non leuis timendi causa erat, ne ex mora & diuturniori spiritus sancti cunctatione aliquid incommodi oboriretur. Quapropter vt omnem metum eximat, promissiones suas repetit, non ijs quidem verbis, quibus apud Euangelistas comprehensæ sunt, sed talibus, quæ etiam Ioannis Baptistæ hac de re sententiam in animum reuocare poterant: id quod factu erat valde necessarium propter summam, qua apud omnes pollebat, Ioannis authoritatem. Nec absurdum videri debet, Christum Iesum (qui alibi ab homine testimonium non accipit, Ioan. 5.) promissioni suæ, argumento ab Ioannis & baptismi authoritate ducto, fidem facere voluisse: quando hic Dei mos est, vt nostri captus imbecillitati sese accommodet, & Ioannem ex spiritu sancto locutum esse constat. Hic ergo verborum Christi mihi sensus esse videtur: Si quæ & ipse non semel pollicitus sum, & quæ ex Ioanne præcursore meo audiuistis, memori mente reuoluatis, de spiritus sancti missione dubitare amplius non poteritis. Is enim cùm ad se venientes baptizaret in Iordane, non sibi, sed mihi populum colligebat, quem se præstantiorem esse ingenuè fatebatur, & quid ipse in me credentibus collaturus esset, monebat, spiritum videlicet sanctum, qui & adoptionis spiritus est ac salutis arrhabo, & credentes mirifico ardore regni mei prouebendi accendit. Huius beneficij per me olim conferendi symbolum erat aquæ baptismus, quem cùm non sine numinis ductu ab Ioanne acceperitis, nolite dubitare de ijs quæ idem vobis pollicitus est. Vt enim suo officio erga vos Ioannes defunctus est, & aqua tinctos in mei corporis, id est ecclesiæ, consortium assumpsit: ita ego quoque quod mearum est partium non minus fideliter exequar, ve spiritum meum liberalissimè in vos effundam, cuius signaculum iam olim accepistis. Hic sensus (inquam) Christi instituto pra aliis conuenire videtur. Nec Christus hoc loco inter suum & Ioannis baptismum externum distinguere voluit. Quia unum baptismum esse constat & Ioannis & Christi, cum hic ab illo baptizari voluerit. Potius ergo inter rem signam & signum distinguit, inter suum & Ioannis officium. Spiritus sancti vero missionem baptismi nomine appellat per allusionem & propter analogiam, quae in Sacramentis inter signa externa & res signatas cernitur. Caeterum habemus in his duo consyderatu dignissima.
units.tr: But let us return to Christ's words, from which we have digressed. For, about to give the reason for his command, he says: "Of which you have heard from me. For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence." These words contain a confirmation and consolation of the promise that is especially necessary. For just as there were many other things that could make the apostles anxious as they considered their office, so there was no slight cause for fear, lest some harm arise from the delay and the lengthy hesitation over the Holy Spirit. Therefore, to remove all fear, he repeats his promises, not in the words by which they are recorded in the Evangelists, but in words that could also call to mind John the Baptist's opinion on this matter. This was very necessary because of the great authority John had among all. Nor should it seem absurd that Christ Jesus, who elsewhere does not accept testimony from man (John 5), wished to give credence to his promise by an argument drawn from the authority of John and of baptism. For this is God's custom, to accommodate himself to the weakness of our understanding, and it is clear that John spoke by the Holy Spirit. Here, then, the sense of Christ's words seems to me to be this: "If you call back to mind, with a remembering mind, both the things I myself have promised more than once and the things you heard from John my forerunner, you will no longer be able to doubt concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit. For when he baptized in the Jordan those who came to him, he was gathering a people not for himself but for me. He frankly confessed that this people was superior to himself, and he warned them what he himself would bestow on those who believe in me, namely the Holy Spirit, who is both the Spirit of adoption and the pledge of salvation, and who kindles believers with a wonderful ardor to advance my kingdom. The sign of this benefit, to be conferred once through me, was the baptism of water. Since you received it from John not without divine guidance, do not hesitate concerning what he promised you. For just as John has discharged his office toward you, and has taken those washed with water into the fellowship of my body, that is, the Church, so I too will no less faithfully carry out what is my part, and pour out my Spirit most generously upon you, whose seal you have already received long ago." This sense (I say) seems to agree better with Christ's purpose than the others. Nor did Christ wish in this place to distinguish between his own baptism and John's external baptism. For it is established that there is one baptism of John and of Christ, since Christ wished to be baptized by John. Rather, he distinguishes between the thing signified and the sign, between his own office and John's office. But he calls the sending of the Holy Spirit by the name of baptism, through allusion and because of the analogy seen in the sacraments between external signs and the things signified. Moreover, we have two points here that are most worthy of consideration.

units.la: Primo, distinguendum esse inter ministros & Christum, cuius illi ministri sunt, ne his tribuatur quod solius Christi est. Ioannes aqua baptizat, Christus vero spiritum sanctum largitur. Minister er go circa externa occupatur, dum verbum praedicat, monet, hortatur, increpat, consolatur, dum pro ecclesia preces fundit, & sacramenta administrat. In animis vero hominum nihil illi iuris est, ut illos pro suo arbitrio formare sive flectere possit. Sed uni Christo subiacent, qui in illis per spiritum suum pro bona sua voluntate verbi semine vivificat, motus sanctos operatur, consolatione exhilarat, totos deniq; ad dei imaginem reformat. Nec obstat, quod omnia haec ministris interdum tribuuntur, & quod Paulus se Corinthios in Christo genuisse, & Galatas se denuo parturire dicit. Quia enim Deus, qui nostri minime indigebat, hominibus cooperarijs uti dignatur, ut maior sit minister abs se institutus authoritas illud eiusmodi titulis ornare consueuit. Quae causa est, quod ide Paulus Corinthijs, quos ministris nimium addictos esse videbat, ait: Quis est Paulus? quis Apollo? nisi ministri per quos credidistis, & ut cuiq; DOMINVS dedit. Ego plantavi, Apollo rigavit, sed DEVS dedit incrementum. Itaq; neq; qui plantat est aliquid, neq; qui rigat, sed qui dat incrementum, deus. Haec si observentur, & ecclesiae ministerium digne aestimabimus, & Christo tribuemus omnem nostrae salutis gloriam, pro qua spiritus ipsius passim in scripturis tam constanter dimicat.
units.tr: First, one must distinguish between the ministers and Christ, whose ministers they are, lest what belongs to Christ alone be attributed to them. John baptizes with water; Christ bestows the Holy Spirit. The minister, therefore, is occupied with external things when he preaches the Word, admonishes, exhorts, rebukes, and consoles, when he pours out prayers for the Church and administers the sacraments. But he has no right over men's minds, so that he could shape or bend them at his own discretion. Rather, they are subject to Christ alone, who in them, through his Spirit and by his good will, quickens them with the seed of the Word, works holy movements, cheers them with consolation, and finally reforms them wholly to the image of God. Nor is it an objection that all these things are sometimes attributed to ministers, or that Paul says he begot the Corinthians in Christ and that he is again in labor with the Galatians. For since God, who had no need of us, deigns to use men as co-workers, he is accustomed to adorn the authority of the minister he has appointed with such titles, so that it may be greater. This is why the same Paul, seeing that the Corinthians were too attached to the ministers, says to them: "What is Paul? What is Apollos? Only ministers through whom you believed, and as the Lord gave to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase." If these things are observed, we will both value the ministry of the Church rightly and ascribe to Christ all the glory of our salvation, for which his Spirit contends so constantly throughout the Scriptures.

units.la: Secundo cum primis memorabile est, quod Christus a baptismo argumentum ducit, quo apostolis suae promissionis fidem facit. Docemur hic, Sacramenta Dei promissiones & beneficia sic obsignare, ut nullus dubitationi locus superfit. Nec enim inanibus signis & promissionibus nos ludit Deus, sed quae cunq; verbo pollicetur, & sacramentis obsignat, vere nobis praestare solet. Promittit autem per evangelii praedicationem peccatorum remissionem in Iesu Christi nomine & adoptionis spiritum, quo in filios dei regeneremur. Promissioni baptismum signaculi instar addit, quo tincti visibiliter in externam ecclesiae Christi vel filiorum dei societatem cooptamur. Quisquis ergo evangelicae promissioni crediderit, de peccatorum suorum remissione & adoptione sua ac caelestis hereditatis possessione tam certus est, quam certo se baptismi lavacro tinctum esse novit.
units.tr: Second, what is especially memorable is that Christ draws an argument from baptism, by which he assures the apostles of his promise. We are taught here that God seals his promises and benefits with sacraments in such a way that no room for doubt remains. For God does not mock us with empty signs and promises. Whatever he promises by the word and seals by the sacraments, he is accustomed to truly give us. He promises, moreover, through the preaching of the gospel, the forgiveness of sins in the name of Jesus Christ and the spirit of adoption, by which we are regenerated as sons of God. To the promise he adds baptism, as a kind of seal, by which those who are washed are visibly admitted into the external fellowship of the Church of Christ, or of the sons of God. Whoever therefore believes the gospel promise is as certain of the forgiveness of his sins, of his adoption, and of possession of the heavenly inheritance, as he knows he has been washed in the bath of baptism.

units.la: Sacramentadei promissiones obsignant.
units.tr: Sacraments seal God's promises.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Postquam non sine magna diligentia Diuus Lucas exposuit, vt saluator noster Iesus Christus apostolos, quos totius orbis doctores esse volebat, omnibus illis instruxerit, quorum cognitio & vsus ipsis in muneris fui administratione necessarius erat, tandem ad gloriosam Ascensionis Christi historiam transitum parat. Praemittit vero illi narrationi postremum actum, qui Christo cum discipulis intercessit, in quo illos & consolatur, & de officio ipsorum, cuius rationem hucusque minus perspexisse videbantur, euidentius & plenius disserit. Occasionem vero de his differendi Christo ipsi discipuli praebuerunt, dum crassam regni Christi ignorantiam ineptissima & multis modis absurda quaestione produnt. Et quia locus hic multiplicem rerum cumprimis necessariarum cognitionem continet, neminem vel studij vel temporis pigere debet, quod in singularum partium consyderatione erit impendendum. Et primo quidem discipulorum quaestionem, deinde vero vt Christus illi responderit, videbimus.
units.tr: Having explained with great care how our Saviour Jesus Christ furnished the apostles, whom he wished to be teachers of the whole world, with all the knowledge and practice that their ministry required, Saint Luke at last prepares to pass to the glorious history of Christ's Ascension. He places before that narrative the final act that Christ performed with the disciples, in which he both comforts them and more clearly and fully discusses their office, the nature of which they seemed hitherto to have understood poorly. The disciples themselves gave the occasion for this discussion, when they revealed their gross ignorance of Christ's kingdom by a most foolish question, absurd in many ways. Since this passage contains a manifold knowledge of especially necessary things, no one should begrudge the study or time that must be spent on the consideration of its individual parts. First we shall look at the disciples' question, and then at how Christ answered it.

units.la: Quaestionem paucis verbis proponunt, sed quae multiplicem ignorantiam & ruditatem incredibilem arguant. Domine (inquiunt) an in tempore hoc restitues regnum Israeli? Quaerunt autem de terreno & carnali regno, quale commune Iudaeorum vulgus ex prophetarum oraculis finistre intellectis exoriturum sperabat. Nam Dauidi Dominus dixerat: Quum exacti fuerint dies tui, dormieris cum patribus tuis, excitabo semen tuum post te, quod egredietur de vtero tuo, regnum eius firmabo. Et firmabitur domus tua & regnum tuum perpetuo coram facie tua, firmumque erit solium tuum perpetuo, &c. 2. Sam 7. Item: Semel per sanctitatem meam iuraui, haudquaquam Dauidem fefellero. Semen eius in aeternum erit, solium eius coram me vt Sol perstabit. Firmum vt Luna manebit, quae est aeternus in aethere testis. Psal. 89. Et rursum: Ecce dies venient, dicit dominus, vt excitem germen iustum Dauidi, regnabit rex, & prudenter rem geret, & faciet iudicium & iustitiam in terra. In diebus eius saluabitur Iuda, & Israel habitabit tuto, &c. Ierem. 23. Omitto infinita alia, quae in hanc sententiam passim apud prophetas & in Psalmis extant. Haec vero cum secundum literam acciperent discipuli, terrenum regem ex Dauidis posteritate proditurum credebant, qui Israeliticam gentem, e Romanorum tyrannide liberatam, auita libertati restitueret, regnumque constitueret victoriis & triumphis clarum, quale olim Dauidis & Solomonis temporibus fuerat. Quo errore etiamnum hodie Iudaei fascinati, Iesum Christum, verum Dauidis filium, aspernantur, & Messiam, qualem modo descripsimus, vanissima spe expectant. Idem error, quia quasi per contagium, discipulorum quoque mentes obsederat, quaestionem hanc valde ineptam loco & tempore importunissimo proponunt, insigne documentum dantes, quid ijs eueniat, qui in scripturis oscitanter versantes, in solo cortice haerent, nec ad ipsam medullam vel nucleum sancto studio contendunt.
units.tr: They put the question in few words, but it reveals a manifold ignorance and an incredible crudeness. "Lord," they say, "will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" They are asking about an earthly and carnal kingdom, such as the common mass of the Jews hoped would arise from the oracles of the prophets, misunderstood as they were. For the Lord had said to David: "When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come out of your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. Your house and your kingdom shall be established for ever before your face, and your throne shall be firm for ever," etc. (2 Sam. 7.). Likewise: "Once I have sworn by my holiness; I will by no means deceive David. His seed shall be for ever, and his throne before me shall stand like the sun. It shall remain firm like the moon, which is the everlasting witness in the sky" (Ps. 89.). And again: "Behold, the days will come, says the Lord, when I will raise up for David a righteous branch; a king shall reign and act wisely, and shall execute judgment and justice in the land. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely," etc. (Jer. 23.). I pass over the countless other passages that occur everywhere in the prophets and the Psalms to this effect. But when the disciples took these words literally, they believed that an earthly king from the posterity of David would arise, who would restore the people of Israel, freed from Roman tyranny, to their ancestral liberty, and would establish a kingdom famous for victories and triumphs, such as had existed once in the times of David and Solomon. Even today the Jews, bewitched by this error, despise Jesus Christ, the true son of David, and look for a Messiah, such as we have just described, with the emptiest hope. The same error, spreading as if by contagion, had also taken possession of the minds of the disciples, and so they put forward this very foolish question at an extremely inopportune time and place, giving a notable lesson about what befalls those who, handling the Scriptures carelessly, cling only to the bark and do not strive with holy zeal toward the marrow and kernel itself.

units.la: Sed praestat circumstantias omnes excutere, vt videas tot fere in quaestione hac errores, quot verba continentur. Primo insignis error est, quod de regno terreno quaerunt, cum Christus toties illos de cruce ferenda admonuisset. Ipsum dicentem audiuerunt: Si quis vult post me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam, & sequatur me. Matth. 16. Ecce mitto vos vt oues in medium luporum. Tradent enim vos in concilia, & in conciliabulis suis flagris caedent vos: quin & ad principes ac reges ducemini, in testimonium ipsis ac gentibus. Matth. 10. Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequetur. Alienos a synagogis facient vos. Et veniet tempus, vt quisquis interficiat vos, videatur cultum praestare deo. Ioan. 15. & 16. Item: In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Luc. 21. Haec (inquam) & multa alia huius generis ex Christo audiuere. Nihilominus tamen omnium immemores, terrenum regnum somniant, in quo se quoque rerum dominos fore sperant. Arguit hoc in illis & ambitionis malum & ignauum timorem, quo periculi aduersa & crucem imminentem horrent, ac regnare cupiunt priusquam de regno, vt bonos milites decet, certauerint.
units.tr: But it is worth examining all the circumstances, so that you may see almost as many errors in this question as there are words in it. First, there is the striking error that they ask about an earthly kingdom, when Christ had so often warned them about bearing the cross. They heard him saying: "If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me" (Matt. 16.). "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. For they will hand you over to councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues; indeed you will be led before governors and kings, for a testimony to them and to the Gentiles" (Matt. 10.). "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you. They will put you out of the synagogues. And the time will come when whoever kills you will think he is offering worship to God" (John 15. and 16.). Likewise: "In your patience you will possess your souls" (Luke 21.). I say they heard these and many other things of this kind from Christ. Nevertheless, forgetful of them all, they dream of an earthly kingdom, in which they hope they too will be lords of affairs. This reveals in them both the evil of ambition and a cowardly fear, by which they dread the adversities of danger and the cross that hangs over them, and desire to reign before, as good soldiers should, they have fought for the kingdom.

units.la: Deinde in hoc quoque reprehendendi sunt, quod de Christi regno quaerentes, Israelis solius mentionem faciunt, nihil de aliarum gentium salute soliciti. Atqui veteres scripturae, Christum saluatorem non in Israele solo, sed in toto orbe regnaturum docet. Illi enim dicitur: Ego constitui regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum. Postula a me, dabo gentes vt sint haereditas tua, & terminos terrae vt sint possessio tua. Psal. 2. De eodem quoque intelligi debent quae Psal. 72. legimus: Imperitet a mari ad mare vsque, & a flumine vsque ad terminos terrae. Coram illo procumbant accolae deserti, & inimici eius puluerem lingant. Reges mediterranei maris & insularum munera adferant, reges Scheba & Seba honoraria. noraria adducant. Et adorent eum omnes reges, omnes gentes seruiant ei, &c. An non ergo notabilis discipulorum error est, quòd de solius Israelis regno scisciantur? Ita enim & Christo multum derogant, cuius regnum tam angustis terminis includunt: & in reliquas gentes vehementer iniurij sunt, quarum salus ipsis commendatissima esse debebat.
units.tr: Next, they must also be rebuked for this: in asking about Christ's kingdom they mention only Israel, and are not concerned at all for the salvation of the other nations. Yet the ancient Scriptures teach that Christ would reign not in Israel alone, but over the whole world. For it is said to him: "I have set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. Ask of me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession" (Ps. 2.). What we read in Psalm 72. must also be understood of him: "Let him rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Let the dwellers in the wilderness bow before him, and let his enemies lick the dust. Let the kings of the Mediterranean sea and the islands bring gifts, let the kings of Sheba and Seba bring presents. And let all kings adore him, and all nations serve him," etc. Is it not therefore a notable error of the disciples that they inquire about a kingdom of Israel alone? For in this way they greatly detract from Christ, confining his kingdom within such narrow limits, and they do great wrong to the other nations, whose salvation ought to have been most commended to them.

units.la: His si fontem mali omnis conferas, & quo affectu moti quaestionem hanc moueant, inquiras, grauissimam adhuc culpam deprehendes, cuius reos illos paulò post Christus facit: curiositatem velicet, quam nemo absq; graui numinis offensa sequi, & cui nemo absq; ingenti salutis iactura satisfacere potest. Nec enim de regni restitutione simpliciter quaerunt, sed temporis articulum scrutantur, quo regnum illud (quod fore nequaquam dubitabant) restitui debeat. At quàm multa alia reflabant, quorum inquisitio ipsis & vtilior erat & magis necessaria? Quin potius de suo officio interrogant, & quia Christum in terris principum more regnaturum confidunt, quae ipsis in regno illo munia obeunda sint, scisciscantur? Cur non suam industriam, sua studia, curas, vigilias & labores ad Christi regnū prouehendum alacriter offerunt? Sed est hoc curiositatis malum, vt de iis, quae nihil ad nos pertinent, vehementer soliciti, ea facile negligamus, in quibus omnis nostri officij ratio versatur.
units.tr: If you compare these things with the source of all evil, and inquire with what feeling they were moved to raise this question, you will discover a still more serious fault, of which Christ soon makes them guilty: namely curiosity, which no one can follow without grave offence to the divinity, and for which no one can make satisfaction without enormous loss of salvation. For they do not ask simply about the restoration of the kingdom, but they investigate the moment of time at which that kingdom (which they did not doubt would come) ought to be restored. But how many other things were there that would have been both more useful and more necessary for them to inquire about? Why do they not rather ask about their own office, and since they trust that Christ will reign on earth in the manner of princes, ask what duties they must perform in that kingdom? Why do they not eagerly offer their own industry, studies, cares, vigils and labours to advance Christ's kingdom? But this is the evil of curiosity: anxious about things that do not concern us at all, we easily neglect those things in which the whole reason of our office lies.

units.la: Diligentius autem & prolixius in Apostolorum errore inuestigando versamur, non quòd volupe sit illos cum contemptu traducere & diffamare, quorum labor & fides postea in salutis regno longè latè propagando clarissimè eluxit, & quibus gratias debent immortales quicunq; illorum doctrina Christi cognitionem adepti sunt. Sed in hoc sumus, vt nostrae carnis & corruptae naturae ingenium discamus agnoscere, qui primus salutifera illius & verae sapientiae gradus est. Et solet in eum vsum scriptura frequenter horribiles sanctissimorum hominum lapsus commemorare, vt in illis eluceat, quàm facilè omnibus nobis ad peccatum & damnationem ruina accidere possit, nisi fideli & continua Dei cura & spiritus ipsius manuductione sustentemur. Quid enim de se sperabit amplius, qui Dauidis, viri iuxta cor Dei, adulterium & atrox homicidium, Solomonis sapientissimi regum omnium polygamiam nimisq; vxorium animum, Petri fœdum lapsum, & hic omnium apostolorum simul collectorum tam multiplicem errorem viderit? Fatendum vtiq; erit, nos ex nobis ipsis non esse idoneos, vt vel cogitemus aliquid boni, nedum faciamus, sed omnes bene agendi facultates nobis ab vno Deo contingere, qui in nobis operatur & velle & facere pro bona sua voluntate. 2. Cor. 3. Phil. 2.
units.tr: We are dwelling more fully and at greater length on the error of the apostles, not because it is pleasing to disparage and defame them with contempt, whose labour and faith afterwards shone most brightly in spreading the kingdom of salvation far and wide, and to whom all those immortal men owe thanks who have gained the knowledge of Christ through their teaching. Rather, our aim is to learn to recognise the nature of our flesh and corrupted nature, which is the first step of that saving and true wisdom. Scripture is accustomed to recall for this purpose the dreadful falls of the most holy men, so that in them it may be seen how easily ruin can befall all of us toward sin and damnation, unless we are sustained by the faithful and continual care of God and by the guidance of his Spirit. For who will hope more of himself, when he has seen the adultery and atrocious murder of David, a man after God's own heart, the polygamy and excessive uxoriousness of Solomon, the most wise of all kings, the shameful fall of Peter, and here the manifold error of all the apostles gathered together? It must surely be admitted that we are not of ourselves fit even to think anything good, much less to do it, but that all our abilities to act well come to us from the one God, who works in us both to will and to do according to his good pleasure (2 Cor. 3.; Phil. 2.).

units.la: Praeterea, quo animo Christum & doctrinam ipsius amplectantur, qui spiritu Christi non ducuntur, praesenti hoc apostolorum exemplo patet. Quemadmodum enim isti de caelesti Christi regno parum soliciti, terrenum regnum expectant, & in hoc magnarum opum, potentiae, gloriae & voluptatum spem animo conceperunt: ita plerosque cùm Christi meritum, & in hoc libertas nobis restituta praedicatur, affectos videas hodie, vt in sola terrena bona intenti, sub Christi praetextu honores, opes, pacem publicam & alia eius generis quaerant, nulla interim coelestium & aeternorum bonorum ratione habita, quae sanguinis sui merito nobis Christus acquisiuit. Vt interim de impuris illis, Epicuri de grege porcis, nihil dicam, qui Christianam fidem professi hoc vnum agunt, vt omni sanctioris vitae disciplina abiecta effrenem peccandi licentiam sectentur. Certè qui nostro seculo inter optimos haberi possunt, sub plausibili pacis & concordiae praetextu non raro à fidei simplicitate discedunt, & in hominum gratiam multa & concedunt & faciunt, quae à Christi praeceptis alienissima sunt: quasi vero mundi studium cum Christi vero cultu coniungi possit, & non verius multò Iacobus pronunciet, amicitiam huius mundi esse inimicitiam cum deo. Iacob. 4. Est autem haec maxima fidei & religionis pestis, quae licet interdum egregio fuco & praetextu sese celet, tandem tamen horribili cum iactura salutis & multorum offendiculo erumpit. Ex hac enim σκόπαιροι, id est, praematuri & nimium praecoces enasci solent, quos Dominus apud Matthaeum per terram petricosam adumbrat. Nam vt haec semen quidem excipit & confestim in lucem profert, illud ipsum vero ad maturitatem & frugem aliquam proferre nequit, quia humoris expers est, quo illud contra torrentes Solis aestus defendat: ita isti homines, quum priuati alicuius comodi spem ex euangelio conceperunt, illius miro studio flagrare videntur, Christum nunquam non in ore habent, & pro illius gloria cum quouis pugnare paratos sese gloriantur. Ast vbi spes illa fallit, & praeter spem crucis aestus incumbit, atq; exilium, paupertas, periculaq; omnis generis sese offerunt, mox tanquam angue confecto resiliunt, atq; omni fide fideiq; simulatione abiecta, ne vocibus quidem temperant, quibus se improbè deceptos conqueruntur, & in apertos veritatis hostes degenerant, qui paulò
units.tr: Moreover, the spirit in which people embrace Christ and his teaching, when they are not led by the Spirit of Christ, is plain from this example of the apostles. For just as these men, little concerned with Christ's heavenly kingdom, looked for an earthly kingdom and conceived in their minds the hope of great wealth, power, glory and pleasures, so today you may see many people, when the merit of Christ is preached and liberty is restored to us through him, so intent on earthly goods only that under the pretext of Christ they seek honours, riches, public peace and other things of that kind, taking no account of the heavenly and eternal goods which Christ has won for us by the merit of his blood. I say nothing for now of those impure men, the swine of Epicurus' herd, who profess the Christian faith and do only this: casting off all discipline of a holier life, they pursue unbridled licence to sin. Certainly those who may be counted among the best in our age, under the plausible pretext of peace and concord, often depart from the simplicity of faith, and grant and do many things to win men's favour which are utterly alien to the precepts of Christ, as if the pursuit of the world could be joined with the true worship of Christ, and as if James did not declare far more truly that friendship with this world is enmity with God. James 4. This is the greatest plague of faith and religion. Although it sometimes hides behind an excellent disguise and pretext, in the end it breaks out with terrible loss of salvation and a stumbling block to many. For from this soil there usually spring up the [σκόπαιροι], that is, the premature and overly early ones, whom the Lord in Matthew shadows forth as the stony ground. For while that ground takes in the seed and at once brings it into the light, it cannot bring the same seed to maturity and some crop, because it lacks the moisture that would protect it against the scorching heat of the sun. So these men, when they have conceived some hope of private advantage from the gospel, seem to burn with wonderful zeal for it; they always have Christ on their lips and boast that they are ready to fight anyone for his glory. But when that hope fails, and beyond expectation the heat of the cross bears down, and exile, poverty and dangers of every kind present themselves, they at once recoil as if struck by a snake. With all faith and pretence of faith cast aside, they do not even hold back their words, by which they complain that they were shamefully deceived, and they degenerate into open enemies of the truth, who only a little before were thought to be champions of Christ.

units.la: Sanctorum lapsus nostram corruptionem arguunt.
units.tr: The falls of the saints prove our corruption.

units.la: Quid in Christo quaerant calamitates. ante illius propugnatores putabantur. Ne quid ergo tale & nobis contingat, Christum & doctrinam eius recte nos æstimare convenit. Quaeramus in illo cœlestia bona, quæ æternæ saluti serviunt. Quoad vero hic viximus, crucem & afflictiones omniunarias nos manere putemus. Ita fiet, ut nec sæpe frustremur, quæ nobis in cælo repostia est, nec cruce & afflictionibus offendamur, ad quas patienter ferendas nos iam olim præparauimus.
units.tr: What they seek in Christ are calamities... before they were thought to be his defenders. So that nothing of this kind happens to us as well, we ought to value Christ and his teaching rightly. Let us seek in him the heavenly goods which serve eternal salvation. As long as we live here, let us think that the cross and afflictions of every kind await us. In this way it will come about that we are neither often disappointed of what is laid up for us in heaven, nor offended by the cross and afflictions, for which we have long since prepared ourselves to bear patiently.

units.la: Accedit his alia adhuc ex Apostolorum errore utilitas. Docet enim horum exemplum, quam difficile & laboriosum sit inueteratos errores hominum animis eximere, in quibus & ipsi consenuerunt, & publico multorum exemplo confirmantur. Nam ut paulo ante dictum est, vetus & communis hic fuit de terreno Messiæ regno Iudæorum error, in quo corrigendo Christus Iesus plus fere quam vspiam alibi laborauisse legitur. Quoties enim hoc errore seducti de primatu contendunt apostoli, toties illos humilitatis admonet, & longe aliam sui regni, quam mundi huius, rationem esse testatur. Vide Matt. 18. & 20. Luc. 22. Nec semel à resurrectionis die in hanc disputationem incidit. Cum enim duobus Emauntem euntibus, erronea hæc opinio offendiculi occasionem præberet, & illum crucifixū ac mortuum esse quererentur, quem ipsi Israelis redemptorem fore sperauerant, Christus respondet: O stulti & tardi corde ad credendum omnibus, quæ locuti sunt prophetæ. Nonne hæc oportuit pati Christum, & intrare gloriam suam? Luc. 24. Adhæc supra Lucas monuit, Christum per quadraginta dies cum apostolis conuersatum esse, & cum illis de regno Dei, adeoq; de omnibus sui regni mysteriis disseruisse. Unde ergo hoc est, quod toties explosa & fortissimè confutata quæstio denuo profertur? Non aliunde profectò, quam ex corrupto nostræ naturæ ingenio, quæ ut errores facile imbibit, ita eosdem pertinacissimè retinet. Et quod ethnicus poeta dixit, Naturam expellas furca, tamen vsq; recurrit, hic maxime locum habet. Sic Israelitæ olim, Ægyptiorum idololatriæ assueti, ad vituli cultum relabuntur, licet terricam Dei concionantis, & omnem imaginum vsum prohibentis, maiestatem non multis ante diebus vidissent. Hinc etiam pertinax illa excelsorum superstitio in libris Regum tam diu seruata mihi videtur, quam nepissimi quidem reges in vniuersum tollere potuerunt. Et vtinam nō hodie etiam exempla extarent, quæ quod dicimus luculentissimè comprobarent. Est vero huius considerationis vsus, vt partim discamus, quàm referat in reformationibus radicitus euellere quæcunq; alicuius erroris vel speciem vel occasionem præ se ferunt: partim vero æquiores simus ijs, qui cum veteribus superstitionibus bellum perpetuò gerunt, quando omnium seculorum exemplis compertum est, nullam diligentiam hac in re nimiam, & nullum studium superuacaneum esse posse.
units.tr: Another benefit, moreover, comes to us from the error of the apostles. For their example teaches how difficult and laborious it is to remove from men's minds errors that are long rooted, errors in which they themselves have grown old and which are confirmed by the public example of many. For, as was said a little before, this error about a earthly kingdom of the Messiah for the Jews was old and common, and in correcting it Christ Jesus is read to have laboured more than almost anywhere else. For as often as the apostles, led astray by this error, contend about primacy, so often he admonishes them of humility, and testifies that the order of his kingdom is very different from that of this world. See Matt. 18 and 20; Luke 22. Nor did this dispute arise only once after the day of resurrection. When two men were going to Emmaus, and this mistaken opinion gave occasion for stumbling, and they complained that he had been crucified and killed, whom they had hoped would be the redeemer of Israel, Christ answers: O foolish men and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Luke 24. Moreover, Luke above reminded us that Christ spent forty days with the apostles and spoke with them about the kingdom of God, and so about all the mysteries of his kingdom. Why, then, is this question, so often refuted and most firmly overthrown, brought forward again? It comes from nothing else but the corrupt disposition of our nature, which as it readily imbibes errors, so it holds them most stubbornly. And what the heathen poet said, "You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she always comes back," applies especially here. So the Israelites of old, accustomed to the idolatry of the Egyptians, relapsed into the worship of the calf, although not many days before they had seen the terrifying majesty of God speaking and forbidding every use of images. Hence also that stubborn superstition of the high places seems to me to have been kept up so long in the books of Kings, although the most pious kings could by no means wholly remove it. And would that examples of this were not still present today, which would most clearly prove what we are saying. The use of this consideration is, first, that we learn how much it matters in reforms to root out completely whatever bears even the appearance or occasion of some error; and second, that we be more fair to those who wage constant war against old superstitions, since by the examples of all ages it has been found that no care in this matter can be excessive, and no zeal superfluous.

units.la: Porrò tempus mihi postulare videtur, ut Christi responsionem explicemus, quæ duabus partibus constat. Prima apostolorum quæstionem, ceu ineptam & responsione indignam, reijcit: altera vero regni sui rationem clarius explicat, & ita quidem, ut & apostolos formidolosos consoletur, & quo efficio ipsi in suo regno functuri sint, exponat. Ad primam partem hæc verba pertinent: Non est vestrum nosse tempora & articulos temporum, quos pater in sua ipsius potestate constituit. Et initio quidem nihil de regno suo, nec aliquid aduersus falsam ipsorum de suo regno opinionem dicit, quia & alibi multis hoc egerat, & spiritus sancti aduentus instabat, qui omnem veritatem ipsos erat docturus. Perinde autem verba hæc sonant, ac si diceret: Sæpe quidem de meo regno disserui, nec quicquam, ut video, hucusq; potui proficere. Sed esto, in fatis esset, ut regnum, quale vos somniatis, in Israelitica gente constituerem, vestra tamen curiositas reprehendi meretur, qui temporis articulum inquiritis, de quo nihil me vnquam disseruisse audiuistis, & quem vos in patientia & spe expectare decebat, non autem inutili & confidenti temeritate Dei reuelationem anteuertere. Sunt hæc Christi verba diligenter obseruanda. His enim ingenij humani audacē curiositatē cohercet, & Christianæ sapientiæ terminos describit, quos transfilire nephas est. Quia enim hoc nomine reprehenduntur discipuli, quòd quæ pater in sua ipsius potestate constituit, curiosius inquirerent: satis constat, hunc nobis sapiendi modulum & limitem præscriptū esse, vt in illorum inquisitione & consyderatione assidui versemur, quorum notitia deus sibi soli reseruare, sed in scripturis nobis quoq; reuelare dignatus est. Quæcunq; vero is abconsa & incognita esse voluit, ipsius potestati, sapientiæ & iudicio iustissimo relinquamus, vsq; in eum diem, quo non ex parte cognoscemus, sed facie ad faciem regni cælorum mysteria intuebimur. 1. Cor. 13. Idem sapiens ille monet, cuius verba vtinam curiosorum multorum animis inscripta essent. Altiora te (inquit) ne quaeras, & ne scruteris stultè quæ vires tuas superant. Quæ tibi mandata sunt à Deo, sanctè meditare, nec plurium
units.tr: Moreover, the time seems to call on me to explain Christ's answer, which consists of two parts. The first rejects the apostles' question as foolish and unworthy of an answer; the second explains more clearly the nature of his kingdom, and does so both to console the fearful apostles and to set out what they themselves are to do in his kingdom. The following words pertain to the first part: "It is not yours to know the times and seasons, which the Father has placed in his own power." And at the start he says nothing about his kingdom, nor anything against their false opinion about it, both because he had already done this often elsewhere, and because the coming of the Holy Spirit was at hand, who was to teach them all truth. Yet these words sound as if he were saying: "I have indeed often discoursed about my kingdom, and so far, as I see, have achieved nothing. But grant that it was fated that I should establish a kingdom in the Israelite nation such as you dream of; still, your curiosity deserves reproof, you who ask about a point of time of which you have never heard me say anything, and which you ought to await in patience and hope, not anticipate God's revelation by useless and presumptuous rashness." These words of Christ are to be carefully observed. For by them he restrains the bold curiosity of the human mind, and describes the limits of Christian wisdom, which it is wrong to overstep. For since the disciples are rebuked on this ground, that they inquired too curiously into what the Father has placed in his own power, it is quite clear that a measure and limit of wisdom has been prescribed for us, so that we busy ourselves with the study and contemplation of those things whose knowledge God has chosen to keep to himself, yet has deigned to reveal to us in the Scriptures. But whatever he wished to remain hidden and unknown, let us leave to his power, wisdom and most just judgment, until that day when we shall know not in part, but face to face shall behold the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. 1 Cor. 13. That wise man also warns, and would that his words were written on the minds of many curious people: "Do not seek things too high for you" (he says), "and do not foolishly search out what is beyond your strength. Meditate reverently on what God has commanded you, and do not be curious about his many works."

units.la: Sapientiæ Christianæ termini. plurium optrum eius esto curiosus. Non enim opus est, ut oculis tuis arcana praenideas. Plura negotiis tuis ne cura, nec superuacanea scruteris multiuariam. Nam plura quam pro humano captu tibi sunt patefacta. Multos enim decepit vana sua opinio, & praua coniectura sensus sui labefactauit. Ecclesiastici tertio. Quo & illud Solomonis referri debet: Qui scrutatur maiestatem, opprimetur a gloria. Prouerb. 25.
units.tr: Limits of Christian wisdom. Do not be curious about many of his works. There is no need to look into hidden things with your eyes. Do not trouble yourself with matters beyond your business, and do not search into many superfluous things. For more has been revealed to you than human capacity can grasp. Vain opinion has deceived many, and a wicked guess drawn from their own senses has undermined them. Ecclesiasticus 3. To this should also be referred that saying of Solomon: he who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. Prov. 25.

units.la: Confutantur ergo & damnantur hac Christi sententia fatidicae Mathematicorum artes, inter quas Astrologia iudiciaria fere primatum obtinet. Nam temporum articulos, id est, quid vno quoque tempore fieri debeat, vel quod nam tempus cuius rei destinatum sit, Christus inquirere prohibet. Atqui hic praecipuus Astrologiae usus est, ut rerum euentus in certa tempora praenunciet. Indicatur enim natiuitatis hora, & mox horoscopo vel caeli figura inspecta de totius vitae cursu vaticinantur: nec iis quae corporis & fortunae bona attinent, contenti, in animam quoque sibi ius sumunt, quasi hominis virtutes & vitia, & per consequens salus quo aeterna, ex astris dependeant. Simili ratione de singulorum annorum euentibus prognostica edunt, in quibus de bellis, de morbis, de rerum penuria & caritate, deniq; de vitiis & sceleribus venturi anni, tanquam ex tripode differunt. Quid vero isti homines aliud faciunt, quam quod in discipulis reprehenditur, qui tamen non per artem aliquam diuinitus prohibitam tale quidpiam cognoscere, sed ex Christi ore, qui nobis a puero sapientia factus est, discere studuerunt? Nec est, quod nobis prophetarum exempla obijciant, quorum vaticinia de futuris rebus extant, quibus futuris interdum certa tempora assignauere, quod Ieremiam in primis & Danielem fecisse constat. Hi enim quae ex spiritus sancti reuelatione acceperant, ad hominum institutionem & consolationem prodiderunt.
