Et solet frequenter Deus per prophetas suos futura praedicere, ut hominum saluti consulat: idem vero artes fatidicas, quibus futurorum cognitio humani ingenij solertia inquiratur, nusquam tradidit, sed damnauit, illarum studiosos a populi & regni sui consortio excludit, ut videre est Deut. 18. & Michaeae 5. capite.
units.tr: Therefore Christ's saying refutes and condemns the fortune-telling arts of the mathematicians, among which judicial astrology holds almost first place. For Christ forbids us to inquire into the articles of time, that is, what ought to be done at each time, or what time has been appointed for each matter. Yet this is the chief use of astrology: to foretell the outcomes of events at certain times. For the hour of a birth is noted, and then, having examined the horoscope or the figure of the heavens, they prophesy about the whole course of a life. Not content with the goods of body and fortune, they also claim authority over the soul, as if the virtues and vices of a man, and consequently his eternal salvation, depended on the stars. In the same way they publish predictions about the events of each year, in which they discourse, as from a tripod, about the wars, diseases, shortages and abundance of goods, and finally the vices and crimes of the coming year. But what else do these men do than what is rebuked in the disciples, who nonetheless did not seek to know such things through some art forbidden by God, but wished to learn them from the mouth of Christ, who was made wisdom for us from boyhood? Nor should they object to us the examples of the prophets, whose prophecies of future things survive, and for which they sometimes assigned fixed times, as is known to have been done above all by Jeremiah and Daniel. For these men published what they had received by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, for the instruction and consolation of men. God is accustomed often to foretell future things through his prophets, so that he may provide for the salvation of men. But the fortune-telling arts, by which knowledge of the future is sought through the cleverness of human intellect, he never taught anywhere; rather he condemned them, and excludes their practitioners from the fellowship of his people and kingdom, as may be seen in Deut. 18 and Micah chapter 5.

units.la: Damnantur etiam hoc ipso loco, quorum curiositas longius progressa nouissimi diei & aduentus Christi terminum inquirere audet, quem in solius patris potestate ita Christus constituit, ut nec angelis nec sibi ipsi, quatenus homo est, cognitum esse dicat. Marc. 13. Quaecunque vero nos nouisse prodest, abunde sacris literis sunt tradita. De signis enim illum diem praecessuris admonemur, non ut ex illis de temporis illius articulo disputemus, sed ut a somno vitiorum excitati, leuemus capita nostra, ut appropinquante redemptionis nostrae die, famuli fidi & industrij reperiamur. Luc. 21.
units.tr: Those too are condemned in this very place whose curiosity goes further and dares to inquire into the limit of the last day and the coming of Christ. Christ has so fixed this limit in the power of the Father alone that he says it is known neither to the angels nor to himself, insofar as he is man. Mark 13. But whatever it is useful for us to know has been abundantly handed down in the sacred letters. For we are warned about the signs that will precede that day, not so that we may dispute from them about the moment of that time, but so that, roused from the sleep of vices, we may lift up our heads, and, as the day of our redemption draws near, be found faithful and diligent servants. Luke 21.

units.la: Simili ratione hic mihi reprehendi videntur, qui aeternae praedestinationis & prouidentiae Dei arcana altius scrutantur, dum electorum numerum inquirunt, & dei iudicia, quibus ille & eligit & reprobat, ad humanae rationis calculum reuocant, quae ut humanum captum longe superant, ita sine maximo periculo inuestigari non possunt. At quae in illa causa nostra tam institutioni quam consolationi seruiunt, Deus reuelare dignatus est. Constat enim fideles ab aeterno ex mera gratia Dei, in solo Christo, nullo nostrorum operum siue meritorum respectu, electos esse. Constat electionem hanc esse firmam & stabilem, cuius Deum (ut Paulus inquit) poenitere non potest. Rom. 11. Constat electionis huius signum esse infallibile fidem, qua & Christum Iesum & in hoc iustitiam atq; salutem ipsam apprehendimus. Constat electionis finem & scopum esse, ut sancti & irreprehensibiles simus, quoad praesenti vita fruimur, hac autem exempti, in caelestibus aeternum viuamus cum Christo Iesu, Ephes. 1. Haec reuelauit dominus, & his nos contentos esse oportebat. In illis vero, quae humana ratione nec percipi nec inuestigari possunt, cum Paulo nos pia & sancta ignorantia nostrae confessione obstupescere decebat, & exclamare: O profunditatem diuitiarum & sapientiae & cognitionis Dei: quam inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, & imperuestigabiles viae eius? Quis enim cognouit mentem Domini? Aut quis illi fuit a consilijs? Aut quis prior dedit ei, & reddetur illi? Quoniam ex illo, & per illum, & in illum omnia, &c. Rom. 11. cap.
units.tr: In a similar way, those seem to me to be rebuked who search too deeply into the hidden things of eternal predestination and the providence of God, while they inquire into the number of the elect and bring God's judgments, by which he both elects and reprobates, back to the reckoning of human reason. These judgments, as they far surpass human understanding, cannot be investigated without the greatest danger. But God has deigned to reveal those things in this matter that serve both our instruction and our consolation. For it is certain that the faithful were chosen from eternity by the mere grace of God, in Christ alone, with no regard to any of our works or merits. It is certain that this election is firm and stable, and that God (as Paul says) cannot repent of it. Rom. 11. It is certain that the infallible sign of this election is faith, by which we lay hold of Jesus Christ and, in him, righteousness and salvation itself. It is certain that the end and goal of election is that we should be holy and blameless while we enjoy the present life, and that, freed from it, we should live eternally with Christ Jesus in heaven. Eph. 1. The Lord has revealed these things, and we ought to be content with them. But in those things which cannot be perceived or investigated by human reason, we should, with Paul, be astonished in a holy and pious confession of our ignorance, and exclaim: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things," etc. Rom. 11.

units.la: Porro alteram quoque responsionis Christi partem videamus, qua de regno suo repetit, quae praesenti instituto seruire videbantur. Ita vero negotium hoc tractat (quod & supra monuimus) ut & discipulos mirifice consoletur, & sui eosdem officij admoneat. Ait enim: Accipietis virtutem, cum spiritus sanctus aduenerit super vos. Et eritis mihi testes tam Hierosolymis quam in tota Iudaea, & in Samaria, & usque ad extremum terrae.
units.tr: Next let us also look at the other part of Christ's answer, in which he returns to his kingdom, which seemed to serve the present purpose. He treats this matter (as we have also noted above) in such a way that he both wonderfully comforts the disciples and reminds them of their office. For he says: "You shall receive power, when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. And you shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth."

units.la: Primò quidem promissionem spiritus sancti repetit, qua & consolatur discipulos, & regni sui conditionem describit. Nolim (inquit) vos animo deijci, quando vos regni mei propagationi inter gentes destinatos esse auditis. Nec enim humanis viribus, quas in vobis exiguas & contemptas esse non ignoro, hoc opus perficiendum est. Caelesti & divina virtute opus erit, quam vobis non defore sepius promisi, & nunc iterum promitto. Veniet enim super vos spiritus sanctus, qui & animum & vires addet, ut commissa vobis muneri sufficere possitis. Admonemur autem hoc loco, Christi regnum (ut ipse coram Pilato Iohan. 18. fatetur) non mundanum sive terrenum, sed spirituale esse, nec huius seculi potentia, honore, gloria, triumphis, opibus & voluptatibus, sed iustitia, pace & gaudio in spiritu sancto constare. Rom.14. Inde rursum colligimus nec carnalibus armis & principum huius seculi viribus regnum illud propagari & defendi, sed verbi praedicatione, cui spiritus Christi in hominum mentibus efficaciter cooperari solet. Docent hoc Pauli verba, quibus ait: In carne ambulantes, non secundum carnem militamus. Siquidem arma militiae nostrae non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Deo ad demolitionem munitionum, quibus consilia demolimur & omnem celsitudinem, quae extollitur adversus cognitionem Dei, & captivam ducimus omnem cogitationem ad obediendum Christo, &c. 2. Cor. 10. Frustra ergo laborant, quicunque humanis consiliis, foederibus, armis, principum favore & amicitiis, & quibuscunque eius generis mediis, Christi regnum promovere conantur. In animis enim hominum Christus regnum obtinet, qui nulla humana vi, sed solius spiritus potentia & operatione cogi possunt. Reges equidem & principes ecclesiae Christi nutritios & defensores esse decet, veluti Isaias monet, sed idem externis viribus atque armis Christi regnum minime propagabunt. Et exempla omnium seculorum luculenter docent, nunquam feliciter cessisse, quaecunque humanis consiliis atque viribus in illum finem instituta sunt.
units.tr: First, he repeats the promise of the Holy Spirit, by which he both comforts the disciples and describes the condition of his kingdom. "I would not have you cast down in mind," he says, "when you hear that you are destined to propagate my kingdom among the nations. For this work is not to be accomplished by human strength, which I know is small and despised in you. It will need heavenly and divine power, which I have often promised you would not be lacking, and now promise again. For the Holy Spirit will come upon you, who will add both courage and strength, so that you may be able to suffice for the task committed to you." Here we are reminded that the kingdom of Christ (as he himself confesses before Pilate, John 18) is not worldly or earthly but spiritual, and that it consists not in the power, honour, glory, triumphs, wealth and pleasures of this age, but in righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Rom. 14. From this we again gather that that kingdom is neither propagated nor defended by carnal weapons and the strength of the princes of this age, but by the preaching of the Word, with which the Spirit of Christ is accustomed to co-operate effectively in the minds of men. The words of Paul teach this, where he says: "Walking in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds, by which we pull down counsels and every height that is raised up against the knowledge of God, and bring every thought captive to the obedience of Christ," etc. 2 Cor. 10. Therefore they labour in vain who try to advance the kingdom of Christ by human counsels, alliances, arms, the favour of princes and friendships, and by whatever means of that kind. For Christ obtains his kingdom in the hearts of men, who cannot be compelled by any human force, but only by the power and operation of the Spirit alone. Kings and princes ought indeed to be nursing fathers and defenders of the Church of Christ, as Isaiah counsels, but they will by no means propagate Christ's kingdom by external forces and arms. And the examples of all ages clearly teach that whatever has been undertaken to that end by human counsels and strength has never turned out well.

units.la: Deinde officium, quod apostoli in hoc suo regno administraturi sint, diserte exprimit, & ut ita dicam, specificat. Eritis mihi testes, inquit. Hoc vestrum illud regnum erit, hoc vestrum munus, & haec vestra dignitas, ut de mea doctrina, vita, miraculis, passione, morte, sepultura, resurrectione ex mortuis, ascensione in caelos, de omnibus deniq; quae salutis humanae causa tam feci quam passus sum, ingenuè testemini. Nec historiam modo rerum abs me gestarum exponetis, sed eius finem & usum urgebitis, ut videlicet me doctorem unicum, salvatorem & redemptorem suum omnes gentes agnoscant. Voluit autem Christus hoc loco, ut etiam Iohan. 15. cap. testis vocabulo uti, ut tam apostolos quam illorum auditores officij sui admoneret. Discunt enim ex testis officio apostoli, & qui horum successores sunt, qua ratione euangelium Iesu Christi praedicari debeat. In teste veritatis studium cumprimis requiritur, & mendacem testem odit Dominus. Prouerb. 6. Deinde testis est, non nisi comperta loqui, quae tam certo ipse vidit & audiuit, ut de illorum veritate dubius esse non possit. Adhaec affectus praui remouendi sunt, ne quid vel odio vel metu vel fauore impulsus sive addat sive celet & reticeat, sed ingenuè quae ipsi comperta sunt proferat. Eiusmodi testes apostolos fuisse legimus. Quaecunq; enim Christum docentem & facientem audiuerant videranta, ingenuè praedicauerunt, nec hostium minis fracti sunt, quo minus de ijs testarentur, id quod per omnem historiam patebit. Nec verbis modo, sed vita, sed morte & sanguine suum illud de Christo testimonium confirmauere. Horum fidem & constantiam verbi ministros imitari decet, qui si in hominum gratiam, vel periculi metu, in Christi causa quicquam mutare, vel saltem dissimulare audent, horribili crimine sese polluunt, & Christi sententiae subiacent: Quemcunq; mei puduerit coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero, eius & me pudebit, ubi venero cum angelis sanctis in gloria patris mei. Marc.8.
units.tr: Next he states plainly, and, so to speak, specifies the office which the apostles are to carry out in this kingdom of his. "You shall be my witnesses," he says. This will be your kingdom, this your task, and this your dignity: to testify candidly about my teaching, life, miracles, passion, death, burial, resurrection from the dead, ascension into heaven, and finally about all the things which I have done and suffered for the sake of human salvation. You will not only set forth the history of the things done by me, but you will also urge its purpose and use, namely that all nations may acknowledge me as their only teacher, saviour and redeemer. Christ wished to use the word "witness" in this place, as also in John chapter 15, so that he might remind both the apostles and their hearers of their office. From the office of witness the apostles, and those who are their successors, learn in what manner the gospel of Jesus Christ ought to be preached. In a witness above all a zeal for truth is required, and the Lord hates a lying witness. Prov. 6. Next, a witness ought to speak only of things that have been ascertained, which he himself has seen and heard so surely that he cannot be in doubt about their truth. Besides, wicked affections must be removed, so that, impelled by hatred or fear or favour, he neither adds nor conceals or suppresses anything, but candidly sets forth what has been ascertained to him. We read that the apostles were witnesses of this kind. For they preached candidly whatever they had seen and heard of Christ teaching and acting, and they were not broken by the threats of enemies so as to stop testifying about these things, as will become clear throughout the whole history. They confirmed this testimony about Christ not only by words but by their life, by their death and by their blood. The ministers of the Word ought to imitate the faith and constancy of these men. If they dare to change anything in the cause of Christ, or at least to dissemble, in order to win the favour of men or for fear of danger, they pollute themselves with a horrible crime and fall under the sentence of Christ: "Whoever shall be ashamed of me before this faithless and adulterous world, of him will I also be ashamed, when I come with the holy angels in the glory of my Father." Mark 8.

units.la: Rursum admonentur hic apostolorum & doctrinae apostolicae auditores, quam atrox sceleus sit euangelio fidem negare, vel etiam contradicere. Nec enim simplex de Christo praeconium, vel historica narratio censeri debet, sed testimonium est, quod apostoli, ceu iurati testes, ab ipso dei filio in mundum producti, non modo coram vili plebe, verumetiam coram sacerdotibus, cocilijs, principibus & regibus, tulerunt. At qui in forensi actione iuratis testibus fidem derogat, & illorum testimonio palam contradicit, capitali periculo sese inuoluit. Quid ergo de illis dicemus, qui apostolis, Christi testibus, obloqui non verentur? Nec enim apostolos modo mendacij insimulant, sed ipsum Christum (quantum in ipsis est) imò deum patrem suspectum faciunt, quasi is falsos testes sistere, & filij sui causam subornatis testibus obtinere voluerit. Vidit hoc dilectus ille Christi discipulus, cum ait: Si testimonium hominum accipiaccipimus, testimonium dei maius est: quoniam hoc est testimonium dei, quod testificatus est de filio suo. Qui credit in filium Dei, habet testimonium in seipso. Qui non credit deo, mendacem fecit eum: quia non credit in testimonium, quod testificatus est deus de filio suo, & c. 1. Iohan. 5. Haec si expendamus o fratres, praecipuam malorum nostri seculi causam deprehendimus. Quia enim pro lusu & ioco habetur ea in quaestionem & dubium vocare, quae de Christo Iesu ab apostolis traduntur, imo illis multi improbe contradicunt, & testimonium illud Iesu Christi ferro & igne persequuntur, fieri nequit, quin deum mundus sibi iratum habeat, & proinde omni malorum genere implicetur. Baptista enim ait: Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit illi in manum. Qui credit filio, habet vitam aeternam. Qui non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Iohan. 3.
units.tr: Again, the hearers of the apostles and of apostolic teaching are reminded here how atrocious a crime it is to deny the gospel or even to speak against it. For this is not to be regarded as a mere proclamation about Christ, or a simple historical narrative, but as a testimony, which the apostles brought forth into the world as sworn witnesses, sent out by the Son of God himself, and which they gave not only before the common crowd but also before priests, councils, princes and kings. Whoever in a court of law detracts from sworn witnesses and openly contradicts their testimony puts himself in danger of capital punishment. What then shall we say of those who do not hesitate to speak against the apostles, the witnesses of Christ? For they not only charge the apostles with lying, but, so far as they can, they make Christ himself, indeed God the Father, open to suspicion, as if he had wished to produce false witnesses and to win his Son's cause by suborned witnesses. That beloved disciple of Christ saw this when he said: "If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God, which he has testified concerning his Son. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he does not believe the testimony which God has testified concerning his Son," and so on (1 John 5). If we weigh these things, brothers, we discover the chief cause of the evils of our age. For since it is counted as a jest and a game to call into question and doubt those things which are handed down by the apostles concerning Jesus Christ, and indeed many wickedly contradict them and persecute that testimony of Jesus Christ with sword and fire, it cannot but be that the world has God angry with it, and is therefore entangled in every kind of evil. For the Baptist says: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3).

units.la: Postremo regni sui terminos, quos illi Israelitica gentis finibus contineri putabant, Christus describit. Nam cum apostolos sibi testes fore dicit usq; ad extremum terrae, non obscure innuit, ipsius regnum ad omnes gentes per universum terrarum orbem extendi. Significanter vero & diserte locorum aliquot meminit, nec id temere. Quia enim Hierosolymorum urbs propter immanissimum facinus, in filium dei designatum, salutari evangelicae gratiae testimonio indigna videbatur, illam quoque nominari oportuit, ut scirent, illic praeconij salutis initium fieri debere, ubi maxime abundarat iniquitas. Rursum, quia inveterato & ingenito sine haereditario odio Samaritanos Iudaei persequebantur, Samariae quoq; mentionem expressam fieri oportuit, ne apostoli, communi Iudaeorum exemplo, ab ea gente sibi abstinendum esse putarent. Quam vero necesse fuerit, alias gentes omnes per totum orbem dispersas, finibus hisce regni Christi comprehendere, Petri exemplum abunde docet, qui tunc quoque cum Samaria Christo nomen dedisset, aliarum gentium conversatione abstinet, donec visione caelesti instituitur. Actorum 10.
units.tr: Lastly, Christ describes the limits of his kingdom, which they thought were confined within the borders of the Israelite nation. For when he says that the apostles shall be his witnesses even to the end of the earth, he plainly hints that his kingdom is to be extended to all nations throughout the whole circuit of the earth. He mentions certain places significantly and expressly, and not without reason. For since the city of Jerusalem, on account of the most monstrous crime committed against the Son of God, seemed unworthy of the saving testimony of the gospel of grace, it had to be named too, so that they might know that the beginning of the proclamation of salvation must be made there, where iniquity had most abounded. Again, since the Jews persecuted the Samaritans with an ingrained and inherited hatred, Samaria too had to be expressly mentioned, lest the apostles, following the common practice of the Jews, should think they ought to keep away from that people. How necessary it was that all other nations scattered throughout the whole world should be included within these bounds of Christ's kingdom, the example of Peter abundantly teaches, who, even when Samaria had embraced Christ, abstained from fellowship with the other nations until he was instructed by a heavenly vision (Acts 10).

units.la: Caeterum eos regni sui fines in praesenti Christus constituit, quos in prophetis iam olim spiritus sanctus designauerat. Nota sunt enim quae Psalm. 2. & 72. habentur, quorum supra meminimus. Adhaec Zacharias cap. 9. de Christo loquens ait: Imperium eius pertinget a mari usq; ad mare, & a fluvio usq; ad fines terrae. Omnium vero evidentissimum est, quod apud Isaiam cap. 49. his verbis continetur: Leve fit quod servus meus sis ad erigendas tribus Iacob, & ad reducendas vastitates Israelis, nisi te dedero, ut lux sis gentium, & sis salus mea usq; ad extremum terrae. Extant infinita alia huius generis testimonia, quae prophetas legentibus passim occurrent. Est autem hoc consolationis plenum, quod Christum Iesum communem omnium gentium salvatorem esse videmus, in quo (ut Paulus & Petrus inquiunt) non est Iudaeus vel Graecus, non Barbarus nec Scytha, non servus neq; liber, non mas neq; foemina: sed in quavis gente, qui timet ipsum & operatur iustitiam, acceptus est illi. Galat. 3. Colos. 3. Actor. 10. Admonentur etiam hic officij sui, quos Euangelij praecones Christus esse voluit, ne unius tantummodo gentis saluti studeant, sed quantum in ipsis est, Christi Iesu & salutis cognitionem tam docendo quam scribendo (quod apostolos quoq; fecisse legimus) in universo orbe disseminent. Omnium vero & singulorum est, Christi bonitatem amplecti, qui salutem suo sanguine partam omnibus tam liberaliter offert. Excipiamus ergo gratis animis regnum hoc salutis, ut aliquando in caelis cum Christo regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the limits of his kingdom which Christ now sets are those which the Holy Spirit had already long before designated in the prophets. For what is found in Psalms 2 and 72, which we have mentioned above, is well known. Besides, Zechariah in chapter 9, speaking of Christ, says: "His dominion shall extend from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth." But the most evident of all is what is contained in Isaiah chapter 49 in these words: "It is a light thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to restore the ruins of Israel; I will make you also a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth." There are countless other testimonies of this kind, which occur everywhere to those who read the prophets. Now this is full of consolation, that we see Jesus Christ to be the common Saviour of all nations, in whom (as Paul and Peter say) there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him (Gal. 3; Col. 3; Acts 10). Here also those whom Christ willed to be preachers of the gospel are reminded of their duty: that they should aim not at the salvation of one nation only, but, so far as lies in them, spread the knowledge of Christ Jesus and of salvation throughout the whole world, both by teaching and by writing, as we read the apostles also did. It is, however, the duty of all and each to embrace the goodness of Christ, who offers salvation, won by his own blood, so generously to all. Let us therefore receive this kingdom of salvation with grateful minds, that we may at last reign with Christ in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA V.
units.tr: HOMILY V.

units.la: Atq; haec locutus, videntibus illis in altum sublatus est, & nubes subduxit illum ab oculis eorum. Quum autem essent defixis in caelum oculis, eunte illo, ecce viri duo astiterunt illis, amicti vestibus albis, qui & dixerunt: Viri Galilaei, quid statis intuentes in caelum? Hic Iesus, qui assumptus est a vobis in caelum, sic veniet, quemadmodum ipsum vidistis euntem in caelum.
units.tr: And when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. As they were gazing intently into heaven while he went, behold, two men in white robes stood beside them, and said: "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."

units.la: Quoniam diuus Lucas, spiritus sancti suggestione motus, apostolorum acta commemorare instituit, non incommode ab illorum narratione orditur, quae dominus & salvator noster Iesus Christus, iam terras hasce relicturus, cum apostolis egit. Ex illis enim evidentissime conijci potest, apostolos nihil privata authoritate vel temeritate gessisse, sed eorum fuisse executores, quae Christus. ipsis iniunxerat, & proinde illorum doctrinam non pro humana censeri, sed pro ipsius Christi doctrina agnosci & recipi debere. Sequitur tandem Iesu Christi è terris discessus in coelos, quem & ipse Lucas magna diligentia describit, & nos singulari studio considerare decet: eò quòd in huius descriptione duo insignes fidei Christianae articuli comprehenduntur, in quibus potissima Christianorum spes fundata est, Ascensio nimirum Christi Iesu in coelos, & eiusdem reditus, quo in seculorum consummatione in nubibus coeli veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Praestat autem singula eo, quo à Luca describuntur ordine, considerare.
units.tr: Since the blessed Luke, moved by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, undertook to record the acts of the apostles, it is fitting that he begins with the account of what our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ did with the apostles when he was about to leave this earth. From these things it can most clearly be inferred that the apostles did nothing on their own authority or by rashness, but were the carriers out of what Christ had enjoined on them, and therefore their teaching is not to be regarded as human, but is to be acknowledged and received as the teaching of Christ himself. Last comes the departure of Jesus Christ from the earth into heaven, which Luke himself describes with great care, and which we ought to consider with special zeal, because in this description two outstanding articles of the Christian faith are contained, on which the chief hope of Christians is founded: namely the Ascension of Jesus Christ into heaven, and his return, when at the consummation of the ages he will come in the clouds of heaven to judge the living and the dead. It is worthwhile to consider each thing in the order in which Luke describes them.

units.la: Ascensionis Christi Iesu historiam paucis absoluit hoc loco. Nam haec locutus (inquit) videntibus illis in altum sublatus est, & nubes subduxit illum ab oculis illorum. Breuitatis huius causa videtur, tum quòd angelorum orationem subijcit, qui rem omnem differtius exponunt, tum quòd ipse Lucas circa finem euangelicae historiae pluribus de hac egerat. Illic enim ait: Eduxit Iesus discipulos foras vsq; in Bethaniam, & sublatis in altum manibus suis, benedixit eis. Et factum est, dum benediceret illis, recessit ab eis, ac ferebatur in coelum. Quibus coniungi debent, quae Marci 16. cap. scribuntur in hanc sententiam: Dominus postquam locutus fuisset eis, receptus est in coelum, & consedit à dextris Dei. Summa verò omnium est, Iesum Christum, qui hucusq; in terris egerat, corpus suum ex mundo hoc subduxisse in coelum, & ibi à dextris dei patris sui collocauisse, iuxta illud Dauidis: Dominus dixit domino meo, sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Psal. 110. Quamuis verò tanta sit huius historiae simplicitas, ut his ipsis verbis fere inter fidei Christianae vel symboli apostolici articulos relata sit, in quibus maiores nostri omnia simplicissima esse voluerunt, ita ut à pueris quoq; comprehendi & intelligi possent: diligentius tamen per singulas circumstantias nobis excutienda est propter eos, qui nostro seculo illam maxima ex parte eleuare audent, dum ex Ascensione disparitionem vel euanitionem fingunt, & nihil praeter inane spectrum nobis reliquum faciunt. Eò autem delabuntur isti homines, ut localem & substantialem corporis Christi in pane dominico praesentiam statuant. Sed non obseruant contentionis studio fascinati, quòd dum Christi corpus certo loco contineri negant, eidem nec in Coena locum relinqui posse. Videamus ergo primò quid per ascensionem proprie intelligi debeat? Deinde quis ascenderit? Quo item modo & in quem locum? His deinceps causas ascensionis subijciemus, quibus etiam fructus continentur, qui ex illa ad nos redeunt.
units.tr: Luke finishes the history of Christ's ascension briefly in this place. For, he says, "when he had said these things, while they were watching, he was lifted up on high, and a cloud took him out of their sight." The brevity seems to be due both to the fact that he adds the words of the angels, who explain the whole matter more clearly, and to the fact that Luke himself had dealt with it at greater length near the end of the gospel history. For there he says: "Jesus led the disciples out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he parted from them and was carried up into heaven." To these should be joined what is written in Mark chapter 16 to the same effect: "After the Lord had spoken to them, he was received into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God." The sum of all is that Jesus Christ, who had until then lived on earth, withdrew his body from this world into heaven, and there placed it at the right hand of God his Father, according to the saying of David: "The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool." Psalm 110. Although this history is so simple that almost in these very words it is recounted among the articles of the Christian faith or the Apostles' Creed, in which our forefathers wished everything to be most simple, so that it could be grasped and understood even by children, nevertheless it must be examined more carefully, circumstance by circumstance, on account of those who in our age dare to explain it away for the most part, while they make up a disappearance or vanishing out of the ascension, and leave us nothing but an empty phantom. These men go so far as to maintain a local and substantial presence of Christ's body in the Lord's bread. But they do not notice, bewitched by the zeal of controversy, that while they deny that Christ's body is contained in a certain place, no place can be left for it in the Supper either. Let us therefore first see what is properly to be understood by ascension. Then who ascended. Likewise, in what manner and into what place. After these things we shall set out the causes of the ascension, which also include the fruits that come back to us from it.

units.la: Ascendere proprie dicuntur, qui ex loco inferiori in superiorem euadunt. Quare ascensio motus est siue φορὰ, ut Graeci nominant, ex loco in locum, & quidem ex inferiori in superiorem. Atqui tale quid hic quoq; intelligendum esse, nemo nisi contentiosissimus negabit. Hoc enim huius libri initio Lucas innuit, cùm de Christi ascensione loquens, ἀνελήφθη, inquit, quod in praesenti loco, ἐπήρθη dixit. Verumq; verò assumptionem vel subuectionem ex loco inferiori in alium sublimiorem significat. Nec cauillum admittimus, quo verba haec per illud exponunt, quòd nubes ipsum ab oculis ipsorum subduxerit, unde illi suam disparitionem fingunt. Nam illic quoq; de nube dicitur, ὑπέλαβε, id est, in altum assumpsit. Vt interim taceam, Christum non potuisse non certo in loco esse, quando in nube fuit, cuius opera vti voluit. Accedit hìs, quòd apostoli oculis & visu sequuntur, euntem, non autem disparentem aut euanescentem oculis hinc inde iactatis aut circumactus requirunt. Nam [illegible, ~2 words] id est, eunte illo (obserua locutionem qua motus de loco in locum diserte exprimitur) apostoli defixis in coelum oculis constiterunt. Quid autem opus erat oculos in coelum defigere, si non in coelum ferebatur dominus? Quin potius aerem hinc inde visu lustrantes eum quaerebant, qui tam subito disparuerat? Sed & angeli postea non ideo apostolos reprehendunt, quasi falso putent in coelum illud elementale Christum penetrauisse, quin illud ipsum fatentur, & de eiusdem ex coelis reditu non obscure verba faciunt. Ascensio igitur motus de loco inferiori in superiorem est, quo Christus è terris subuectus est. Nisi enim hoc fateamur, spiritus sanctus incusandus erit, qui sine causa in simplicis historiae narratione, quam omnibus notissimam esse oportebat, inanibus verbis nobis fucum facere voluerit.
units.tr: Those are properly said to ascend who pass from a lower place to a higher. Hence ascension is a motion, or phora [φορὰ] as the Greeks call it, from place to place, and indeed from a lower to a higher. That something of this kind is to be understood here too, no one but the most contentious will deny. For Luke hints at this at the beginning of this book, when speaking of Christ's ascension he says anelēphthē [ἀνελήφθη], and in the present place he uses epērthē [ἐπήρθη]. Indeed these words signify a taking up or lifting up from a lower place to another higher one. Nor do we admit the quibble by which people explain these words through that phrase, that the cloud took him from their eyes, from which they make up their disappearance. For there too it is said of the cloud, hypelabe [ὑπέλαβε], that is, it took him up on high. To say nothing for now of the fact that Christ could not but be in a certain place when he was in the cloud, whose services he chose to use. Add to this that the apostles follow him with their eyes and sight as he goes, and do not look for him, when he has disappeared or vanished from their eyes, by casting their gaze hither and thither or turning around. For [illegible, ~2 words], that is, while he was going (note the wording by which motion from place to place is plainly expressed), the apostles stood with their eyes fixed on heaven. Why, however, would there have been any need to fix their eyes on heaven, if the Lord were not being carried into heaven? Would they not rather have been searching the air on every side with their sight, for the one who had vanished so suddenly? Moreover, the angels afterwards do not rebuke the apostles on the ground that they wrongly thought that Christ had penetrated that elemental heaven; rather they confirm this very thing, and speak not obscurely about his return from the heavens. Ascension, therefore, is a motion from a lower place to a higher, by which Christ was carried up from the earth. For unless we acknowledge this, the Holy Spirit will have to be blamed, who in the narrative of a plain history, which ought to have been most familiar to all, would without reason have wanted to deceive us with empty words.

units.la: Proximum est, ut quis ascenderit, videamus. Atqui de Christo Iesu sermo est, qui à mortuis resuscitatus, corporis sui veritatem per dies quadraginta quam pluribus argumentis asseruit. Caterum quando de Christo scripturae differunt, naturarum distinctio probè obseruanda est, quibus illum constare omnis scriptura docet. Qui enim ab aeterno verus deus est, eiusdem cum patre maiestatis & gloriae consors, imò patri consubstantialis, in constituto tempore ex muliere (vt Paulus ait) homo factus est, est, id est, humanam naturam assumpsit. Quare in una eademq; Christi persona duae naturae, divina & humana, conveniunt, ut unus & idem Christus, & verus Deus & verus homo sit. Nec tamen propter personae unitatem, naturae vel confunduntur vel mutantur, sed distincta & integra manet utriusq; naturae proprietas. Propter unitatem vero personae fit, ut quod unius tantummodo naturae proprium est, toti Christo tribuatur, & totus Christus fecisse vel passus esse dicatur, quod uni duntaxat naturae proprium est, quod veteres idiomatum communicationem dixerunt. Ad hanc pertinet, quod Christus ab aeterno fuisse dicitur, & priusquam Abraham nasceretur, qui tamen quoad humanitatem praefinito demum tempore natus est. Et filius Dei passus & mortuus dicitur, cum divinitas nec pati nec mori posset. Vere tamen hoc dicitur, quia qui vere filius dei est, secundum id quod mori potuit, mortuus est. Eadem ratione filius hominis in coelo esse dicebatur, quando in terris agebat, quia idem ille quoad divinitatem coelos quoq; penetrabat, licet secundum carnem in terris ageret, & ibi cum Nicodemo colloqueretur. Quae si hoc loco observemus, patebit, Christum Iesum humanam naturam, quam ex virgine utero assumpserat, in coelos subuexisse. De divinitate enim hoc minime intelligi potest, de qua dicitur: Coelum & terram ego impleo. Ierem. 23. Item, Coelum mihi thronus est, & terra scabellum pedum meorum. Isa. 66. Et quia divinitas de loco in locum non movetur, imo immensa & infinita est, in illam ascensio minime competit. Interim deum ascendisse recte dicimus, quia Christus, qui vere deus est, in assumpta hominis natura ascendit. Nec propterea Christum in partes distrahimus, aut unionem personalem negamus, ut olim Nestorius fecit: sed inter naturas Christi & earundem proprietates distinguimus: ut nec hominem sciudit, qui inter animae & corporis actiones quas diversissimas esse constat, distinguit. Et hic cum primis illud Augustini tenendum est, quo probibet, ne omne id quod in deo est, perinde ut deum ubiq; esse statuamus. Et Christus suae divinitatis praesentiam, non corporis sui extensione in omnes locos, sed spiritus sui operatione probari voluit.
units.tr: Next let us see who ascended. Surely it is about Jesus Christ, who, raised from the dead, proved over forty days by many arguments the reality of his body. But when the Scriptures speak of Christ, the distinction of his natures must be carefully observed, of which all Scripture teaches that he consists. For he who from eternity is true God, a partner in the same majesty and glory with the Father, indeed consubstantial with the Father, was made man at the appointed time of his birth from a woman (as Paul says), that is, he took on human nature. Hence in one and the same person of Christ two natures, divine and human, come together, so that one and the same Christ is both true God and true man. Yet on account of the unity of the person, the natures are neither confused nor changed, but the properties of each nature remain distinct and whole. But on account of the unity of the person it comes about that what belongs to one nature only is attributed to the whole Christ, and it is said that the whole Christ did or suffered what belongs to one nature alone; this the ancients called the communication of properties. To this belongs the fact that Christ is said to have existed from eternity, and before Abraham was born, although as regards his humanity he was born at a time appointed at last. And the Son of God is said to have suffered and died, although the divinity could neither suffer nor die. Yet this is truly said, because he who is truly the Son of God died according to that which could die. For the same reason the Son of man was said to be in heaven while he was living on earth, because that same one, as regards his divinity, was also penetrating the heavens, although according to the flesh he was living on earth, and talked there with Nicodemus. If we observe these things in this place, it will be plain that Christ Jesus carried up into heaven the human nature which he had taken from the Virgin's womb. For this cannot at all be understood of the divinity, of which it is said: "I fill heaven and earth." Jeremiah 23. Likewise: "Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet." Isaiah 66. And because the divinity is not moved from place to place, but is rather immense and infinite, ascension does not at all apply to it. Meanwhile we rightly say that God ascended, because Christ, who is truly God, ascended in the assumed nature of man. Nor on that account do we divide Christ into parts or deny the personal union, as Nestorius once did; rather we distinguish between the natures of Christ and their properties, just as one does not tear a man apart when one distinguishes between the actions of the soul and of the body, which are plainly very different. And here above all that saying of Augustine must be held, by which he forbids us to suppose that everything which is in God is everywhere, just as God is. Christ also wished the presence of his divinity to be proved not by the extension of his body into all places, but by the working of his Spirit.

units.la: Sed locum quoq; in quem Christus ascendit, scripturae monstrant. Et Lucas quidem illum in altum sublatum esse dicit. At angeli postea coelum nominant, ut constaret nobis, quo nam locorum ille abiisset. Et Marcus in ipso coelo locum significantius exprimens, ipsum in dextra patris consedisse scribit. Scimus quid multi de coelis philosophentur, qui per hos regnum & praesentiam dei intelligunt. Scimus etiam dextram dei pro divina maiestatis & regni consortio sumi posse, in quod Christum vere assumptum esse fatemur, iuxta id quod dicit: Data est mihi omnis potestas in coelo & in terra. Matthaei 28. Sed certum aliquem locum hic designari dicimus, & illum quidem ipsum, in quem nos olim recipiemur, aeternum cum Christo regnaturi. Et hunc sensum ex Christi verbis haurimus, qui de suo discessu loquens ait: In domo patris mei multae mansiones sunt. Quod si secus esset, dixissem vobis. Vado parpaturus vobis locum. Et si abiero ad parandum vobis locum, iterum veniam & assumam vos ad me ipsum, ut ubi sum ego & vos sitis. Iohan. 14. Num vero apertius & magis diserte locum aliquem certum designare poterat? Paulus certe in coelesti loco & beatorum sede Christum nobis monstrat, dicens: Conversatio nostra in coelis est, ex quibus & salvatorem nostrum expectamus, dominum Iesum Christum, &c. Philip. 3. Annon hic eundem locum Christo tribuit, in quem nostra corpora olim sint transferenda? Coniungi his debet, quod modum & ordinem omnem futurae resurrectionis describens, ait: Ipse dominus cum hortatu & voce archangeli ac tuba dei descendet de coelo: & mortui in Christo resurgent primum, deinde nos qui vivemus, qui reliqui erimus, simul cum illis rapiemur in nubibus in occursum domini in aera, & sic semper cum domino erimus. 1. Thess. 4. De coelo venturum, imo descensurum, dicit Christum dominum, & ut constaret quo nam de coelo istud deberet intelligi, nos nubibus ad domini occursum in aerem abripiendos esse dicit. De sublimiori igitur loco aliquo in coelestibus omnia haec intelligenda sunt, in quo & Christus suo corpore regnans sedet, & in quem electi omnes olim transferentur.
units.tr: But the Scriptures also show the place into which Christ ascended. Luke says that he was lifted up on high, and the angels afterwards name it heaven, so that we might know to what place he had gone. Mark, expressing the place more clearly still, writes that he sat down at the right hand of the Father. We know how many people philosophise about the heavens and understand by them the kingdom and presence of God. We also know that the right hand of God can be taken for the fellowship of the divine majesty and kingdom, into which we confess Christ was truly taken up, according to what he says: "All power is given to me in heaven and on earth" (Matt. 28). But we say that a certain definite place is designated here, and indeed that very place into which we ourselves shall one day be received, to reign eternally with Christ. We draw this sense from Christ's own words, when speaking of his departure he says: "In my Father's house there are many mansions. If it were otherwise, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be" (John 14). Indeed, could he have designated a definite place more openly and more plainly? Paul certainly shows Christ to us in a heavenly place and the seat of the blessed, saying: "Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ," etc. (Phil. 3). Does he not here assign to Christ the same place into which our bodies are one day to be transferred? To these words should be joined what he says, describing the whole manner and order of the future resurrection: "The Lord himself with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord" (1 Thess. 4). He says that the Lord Christ will come from heaven, or rather will descend, and so that it might be clear in what sense "from heaven" is to be understood, he says that we shall be caught up in the clouds into the air to meet the Lord. All these things, therefore, are to be understood of some higher place among the heavenly things, in which Christ sits reigning in his body, and into which all the elect will one day be transferred.

units.la: Caeterum in modo ascensionis describendo diligentissimus est Lucas. In quo primum locum obtinet quod manibus in coelum sublatis Christus apostolis benedixit, id est, valedixit, eosq; pro communi discedentium more divinae protectioni commendavit. Deinde ipsis videntibus in altum subuectus est. Quod unum unitatis & turpissimi erroris eos conuincit, qui Christum disparuisse & inuisibilem factum fuisse dicunt. Si enim hoc vere dicunt, quomodo videntibus discipulis in altum sublatus est? Vel num ideo ascendere videri voluit, ut nos illum in terris adhuc versari credamus? Accedit hic
units.tr: Moreover, Luke is most careful in describing the manner of the ascension. First in this is that Christ, with his hands lifted up to heaven, blessed the apostles, that is, bade them farewell, and commended them to the divine protection, according to the common custom of those departing. Then, while they were looking on, he was carried up on high. This one fact refutes those who say that Christ vanished and became invisible, a view of the most obvious and disgraceful error. For if they say this truly, how was he lifted up on high while the disciples were looking on? Or did he wish to be seen ascending so that we might believe that he still dwells on earth? To this is added

units.la: Quo ascenderit Christus.
units.tr: Where Christ ascended.

units.la: Ascensionis modus. nubis ministerium, quæ vt illum à terris instar vehiculi subuexit, ita illum altius, quàm hominis visus assequi posset, subductum tandem illorum oculis abstulit. Nube autem vehiculi loco vsus est, iuxta illud Psalmi 104. oraculum: Qui ponis nubem ascensum tuum. Hæc enim & cœli symbolum est, quò ille erat ascensurus, & de illius cœlesti ac diuina maiestate non obscurè testabatur. Quò & angelorum apparitio referri debet, quos non testes modò, verumetiam ministros ascensionis adhiberi voluit. Conueniebat enim vt qui in conceptione, natiuitate, tentatione, morte & resurrectione angelorum ministerio vsus erat, nunc quoq; eosdem ministros haberet, quando maximum diuinæ maiestatis opus erat designaturus. Sed & nobis proderat regis & saluatoris nostri maiestatem agnoscere, vt sciremus illum, licet corpore absentem, nos & spiritu suo protecturum esse, & angelorum ministerio facile defensurum, quorum potestas immensa & inuicta esse multis exemplis iam olim comprobata est.
units.tr: The manner of the ascension. The ministry of a cloud, which, like a vehicle, lifted him from the earth, and at last, carrying him higher than human sight could follow, withdrew him from their eyes. He used the cloud in place of a vehicle, according to the saying of Psalm 104: "who makes the clouds your chariot" (Ps. 104). For this is also a symbol of heaven, to which he was about to ascend, and it bore witness plainly to his heavenly and divine majesty. To this the appearance of the angels should also be referred, whom he wished to be present not only as witnesses but as ministers of the ascension. For it was fitting that he who in his conception, birth, temptation, death and resurrection had used the ministry of angels, should now also have the same ministers, since he was about to mark out the greatest work of the divine majesty. It also benefits us to acknowledge the majesty of our King and Saviour, so that we may know that, though absent in body, he will protect us by his Spirit and will readily defend us by the ministry of angels, whose power, immense and invincible, has already been proved by many examples from of old.

units.la: Atqui magna licet & præclara sint hæc diuinæ Christi maiestatis & potentiæ indicia, plus tamen consolationis ex causis percipere poterimus, quæ Christum vt in cœlos ascenderet, mouerunt. Quia ex his eximij, qui inde ad nos redeunt, fructus elucent. Et primò quidem exigebat hoc nostræ redemptionis atq; salutis ratio, quæ aliter perfici non poterat. Quia enim propter peccatum regni cœlorum fores nobis occlusæ erant, tantaq; est nostræ naturæ corruptio, vt Paulus carnem & sanguinem (id est, hominem carnalibus affectionibus & ingenitæ corruptioni adhuc obnoxium) regni cœlorum hæreditatem adire posse neget: necessariò cœlos per Christum reserari & rursum patefieri oportebat, si quidem pro saluatore & redemptore volebat haberi. Commodissimè verò hoc præstitit, suam carnem, quam ex nobis assumpserat, cœlis inferendo. Quis enim non intelligat, carni nostræ aditum in cœlos patere, quando Christi carnem, nostræ per omnia similLimam (vno peccato excepto) in cœlis residere audit? Vt interim de permutatione, quæ hic facta est, nihil dicamus. Nam vt suum spiritum animis nostris Christus inserit, vt is in hoc mundo agentibus salutis nostræ pignus & arrhabo sit: ita vicissim carnem nostram, quam ex Maria virgine assumpserat, cœlis intulit, vt eo quasi pignore nobis certum fiat, nos quoq; olim vnà cum corporibus nostris regni cœlorum hæreditatem adituros. Quò Paulus respiciens scribit: Deus qui dives est in misericordia, propter multam charitatem suam, qua dilexit, nos, etiam cum essemus mortui per delicta, conuiuificauit nos vnà cum Christo (per gratiam estis seruati) simul, cum eo resuscitauit, & simul cum eo sedere fecit in cœlestibus, &c. Ephes. 2. Nec temere ista Paulus pronuntiat, sed sententiæ suæ suffragatorem, imò authorem habet Iesum Christum, cuius hoc quasi testamentum est: Volo pater, vt vbi ego sum, illi etiam mecum sint, quos dedisti mihi. Iohan. 17. Quapropter omnium animis ex ascensionis consideratione fortis illa & inuicta fiducia oboriri debet, quam Tertullianus his verbis exprimit: Securi estote caro & sanguis, usurpastis & cœlum & regnum Dei in Christo.
units.tr: Yet, although these are great and notable tokens of the divine majesty and power of Christ, we may gather more consolation from the causes which moved Christ to ascend into heaven, because from these the outstanding fruits which flow from it to us are made clear. And first of all the plan of our redemption and salvation required this, since it could not be accomplished otherwise. For because of sin the gates of the kingdom of heaven were closed to us, and the corruption of our nature is so great that Paul denies that flesh and blood (that is, man still subject to carnal affections and innate corruption) can inherit the kingdom of heaven. It was necessary that the heavens be unlocked through Christ and opened again, if he was to be regarded as our Saviour and Redeemer. He accomplished this most conveniently by bringing his flesh, which he had taken from us, into the heavens. For who does not understand that a way into the heavens lies open for our flesh, when he hears that the flesh of Christ, in all things most like ours (sin alone excepted), sits in the heavens? Let us say nothing for now of the exchange that is made here. For just as Christ implants his Spirit in our minds, so that he may be a pledge and earnest of our salvation to those who live in this world, so in turn he has carried our flesh, which he took from the Virgin Mary, into the heavens, so that by this pledge, as it were, it may be made certain to us that we too shall one day, together with our bodies, enter upon the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. Looking to this, Paul writes: "God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our sins, made us alive together with Christ (by grace you have been saved), raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him in the heavenly places," etc. (Eph. 2). Paul does not pronounce these things rashly, but has Jesus Christ as the supporter, indeed the author, of his statement, whose testament this is: "Father, I will that where I am, those also whom you have given me may be with me" (John 17). Therefore from the consideration of the ascension there ought to arise in the minds of all that strong and invincible confidence which Tertullian expresses in these words: "Be secure, flesh and blood, you have seized both heaven and the kingdom of God in Christ."

units.la: Deinde ascensione Christi in cœlos, ceu publico triumpho, nos de victoria, quam is de Satana reportauit, certiores fieri oportuit. Vt enim principes huius seculi, vbi hostes debellarunt, ad suos cum triumpho redeunt, in quo & hostium duces capti ducuntur, & eorundem signa ostentantur, quæ omnia victoriam verissimè partam esse demonstrant: ita dei filius cum contra mundi principem, diabolum, bellum suscepisset, eumq; deuicisset penitus, hac quasi solenni pompa in suorum conspectu cœlos repetere voluit, vt certò nobis constaret, diaboli vires fractas, & nos ex illius tyrannide reuera liberatos esse. Et in hunc finem Paulus illud Psalmi 68. adducere videtur: Cum ascendisset in altum, captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dedit dona hominibus. Ephes. 4. Et alibi scribit: Expoliatos principatus & potestates ostentauit palàm, triumphans de illis per semetipsum. Col. 2. Quoties ergo Satanæ, peccati & mortis vires nobis formidinem & terrorem incutere incipiunt, toties ad ascensionem Christi confugiamus, qua victoriæ suæ contra has euidentissimum signum dedit Dominus, & redemptionis nostræ negotium ceu publico triumpho obsignare voluit.
units.tr: Next, by the ascension of Christ into the heavens, as by a public triumph, we needed to be made certain of the victory which he won over Satan. For just as the princes of this age, when they have defeated their enemies, return to their own people in triumph, in which the captive leaders of the enemy are led in chains and their standards are displayed, all of which show that the victory has been most truly won, so the Son of God, when he had waged war against the prince of this world, the devil, and had utterly conquered him, wished to return to the heavens in this solemn procession in the sight of his own people, so that it might be certain to us that the powers of the devil were broken and that we were truly freed from his tyranny. To this end Paul seems to cite the words of Psalm 68: "When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men" (Eph. 4). And elsewhere he writes: "Having stripped the principalities and powers, he displayed them openly, triumphing over them in himself" (Col. 2). Whenever therefore the powers of Satan, sin and death begin to strike fear and terror into us, let us always flee to the ascension of Christ, in which the Lord gave the most evident sign of his victory over these, and wished to seal the business of our redemption as with a public triumph.

units.la: Tertiò vt Christus in cœlos ascenderet, sacerdotij ratio postulabat, cui illum destinatum fuisse testatur Dauid, dicens: Iurauit Dominus, & non pœnitebit eum. Tu es sacerdos in æternum iuxta ordinem Melchisedech. Psalm. 110. Atqui sacerdos summus olim semel quotannis Sanctum sanctorum, quod intra velum erat, ingrediebatur, nec id sine sanguine. Leuit. 15. Qui cum rerum futurarum typus fuerit, Christum quoq; semel in verum illud sanctuarium, cœlos nimirum, cum vero suo corpore & sanguine, quæ ex nobis assumpserat, ingredi oportuit, vt illic in conspectu Dei pro nostris peccatis compareret. pareret & placaret iram Dei. Huc pertinet quod Paulus ait: Non in manu facta sancta ingressus est Christus, sed in ipsum cœlum, vt appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis: Item: Christus accedens Pontifex futurorum bonorum, per maius & perfectius tabernaculum, non manu factum, hoc est, non huius structura, neq; per sanguinem hircorum ac vitulorum, sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sanctta, aeterna redemptione reperta. Hebr.9. Ex quibus colligitur Christum postquam executus est quaecunq; in terris agenda erant, cœlos ingressum esse, vt quod illic agendum restabat, per ageret, id est, vt ibi seipsum pro nobis mediatorem, intercedentem & aduocatum sisteret. Quo referri debent, quaecunq; de intercessoris & aduocati officio in scripturis habentur. Et est hic non poenitendum ascensionis Christi fructus. Quoties enim peccatorum conscientia nos exagitat, & nobis propter peccata aditum in cœlos praeclusum esse sentimus, toties in ascensionis consyderationem, ac tutissimum asylum nos recipere possumus, ac certò statuere, quòd in cœlis sit, qui pro nobis interpellet, qui sui meriti respectu nostram immunditiam tegat, nosq; cum Deo reconciliet. Docet hoc Ioannes apostolus his verbis, Filioli, haec scribo vobis ne peccetis. Quòd si quis peccauerit, aduocatum habemus apud patrem, Iesum Christum iustum. 1. Ioan. 2. Et Paulus: Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat, quis illi qui condemnet? Christus est qui mortuus est, imò qui & suscitatus est, qui etiam est ad dextram Dei, qui & intercedit pro nobis. Rom.8.
units.tr: Thirdly, the nature of the priesthood required that Christ ascend into the heavens, to which David testifies that He was appointed, saying: "The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." Psalm 110. But the high priest of old entered once a year into the Holy of Holies, which was within the veil, and not without blood. Leviticus 16. Since he was a type of things to come, Christ too had to enter once into that true sanctuary, namely heaven, with His true body and blood, which He had taken from us, so that there He might appear in the sight of God on behalf of our sins, and appease and placate the wrath of God. To this pertains what Paul says: "Christ entered not into a holy place made with hands, but into heaven itself, that He might now appear in the sight of God for us." Likewise: "Christ, coming as high priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this construction, nor through the blood of goats and calves, but through His own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption." Hebrews 9. From these things it is gathered that Christ, after He had carried out all that had to be done on earth, entered heaven, so that He might do there what remained to be done, that is, so that He might present Himself there as mediator, intercessor and advocate for us. To this must be referred whatever is found in the Scriptures about the office of intercessor and advocate. And here is the fruit of Christ's ascension, which we should not despise. For whenever the awareness of sins troubles us, and we feel that the way into heaven is closed to us because of our sins, we can then take refuge in the contemplation of the ascension, as in a very safe asylum, and firmly determine that there is in heaven one who intercedes for us, who by the regard of His merit covers our uncleanness and reconciles us to God. The apostle John teaches this in these words: "My little children, I write these things to you so that you do not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." 1 John 2. And Paul: "Who shall bring a charge against the elect of God? God is the one who justifies; who is the one who condemns? Christ is the one who died, or rather who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us." Romans 8.

units.la: Porrò quia haec nondum videbant apostoli, & proinde subito Christi discessu obstupefacti, cœlos defixis oculis intuebantur, & corporalem Christi praesentiam, cui tam diu assueuerant, requirebant, plenius illos oportebat institui. Apparent ergo angeli, albis amicti vestibus, qui illos in hunc modum compellant: Viri Galilaei, quid statis intuentes in cœlum? Hic ipse Iesus, qui assumptus est à vobis in cœlum, sic veniet, quemadmodum ipsum vidistis euntem in cœlum. Inest verbis hisce primum reprehensio quaedam, deinde & consolatio haud vulgaris. Nos itaq; de utraque, quantum praesens locus exigit dicemus.
units.tr: Moreover, because the apostles did not yet see these things, and therefore, astonished by Christ's sudden departure, they gazed fixedly up into heaven and sought the bodily presence of Christ, to which they had been so long accustomed, they needed to be instructed more fully. Therefore angels appear, clothed in white garments, who address them in this way: "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This same Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw Him going into heaven." In these words there is first a certain rebuke, and then a consolation not at all ordinary. We shall therefore speak of both, as far as the present passage requires.

units.la: Reprehensionis speciem habet orationis huius initium: Viri Galilaei, quid statis intuentes in cœlum? Non autem discipulorum factum simpliciter accusant angeli, sed animi potius affectum & ignorantiam. In cœlum enim ideò oculos defixerant apostoli, quòd Christum illuc in nube subuectum esse vidissent. Nec id negatur ab angelis, qui id verissimè factum fatentur. Reprehensione verò dignum erat, quòd toties de Christi discessu admoniti, & tot promissionibus de spiritu sancto instructi, adhuc corporalem Christi praesentiam desiderant, illam mente & oculis requirunt, & quodammodo expectant, vt denuo ad illos delabatur. Hoc ergo reprehendunt angeli, quasi dicant: Quae haec vestra est ignorantia & animorum crassities? Quid adhuc Christi discessum miramini? Nonne hunc talem fore iam ante audiuistis? Nonne spiritum sanctum vobis consolatorem & tutorem promisit? Quin ergo illum expectatis, & corporalem praesentiam in illum diem vsq; reijcitis, quo in gloria patris ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos venturus est, vt illum praedixisse meministis?
units.tr: The beginning of this speech has the appearance of a rebuke: "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?" The angels do not simply accuse the disciples' action, but rather their state of mind and their ignorance. For the apostles had fixed their eyes on heaven because they had seen Christ carried up thither in a cloud. The angels do not deny this, but confess that it truly happened. But it deserved rebuke that, although so often warned of Christ's departure and so often instructed with promises about the Holy Spirit, they still desire the bodily presence of Christ, seek it with their minds and eyes, and in a way expect that He will glide down to them again. This, then, the angels rebuke, as if they were saying: "What is this ignorance of yours and this dullness of your minds? Why do you still marvel at Christ's departure? Did you not hear beforehand that this would be so? Did He not promise you the Holy Spirit as comforter and guardian? Why, then, do you not await Him, and why do you defer His bodily presence until that day on which, as you remember Him foretelling, He will come in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead?"

units.la: Quòd si verò angelorum verba cum iis, quae paulò ante in ascensionis historia dicta sunt, conferamus, luce clarius patebit, nullam posthac corporalem Christi Iesu in terris praesentiam statui debere, qualem illi fingunt, qui corpus Christi, quod ex Maria virgine natum est, quod in cruce pependit & sepultum est, in Cœna corporaliter, substantialiter & realiter fidelium manibus contrectari & manducari dicunt. Vident illi crassa huic opinioni ascensionis historiam obstare. Quare ex illa disparitionem faciunt, vt supra diximus. Deinde & scripturae locus abutuntur. Primò Pauli verba allegant: Christus ascendit supra omnes cœlos, vt impleret omnia. Ephef. 4. Vnde colligunt, illum corporis conditione mutata, per omnes tam superos quàm inferos locos diffusum esse, & corpore suo omnia implere. Deinde ad diuinitatem confugientes, huius ratione humanam quoq; naturam vbique necessariò esse contendunt, quia cum diuina coniuncta & vnita sit. Et Gordium quendam nodum sereperisse putant, cùm dicunt: Ea est naturarum in Christo coniunctio, vt nec morte dirimi potuerit: quantò minus ergo crassa haec locorum distantia illam separare potest? Habent etiam Christi promissiones, quibus opinionem suam stabiliri putant. Eius enim verba sunt: Vbicunque duo aut tres congregati sunt in nomine meo, ibi sum in medio eorum. Matth. 18. Item: Ego vobiscum sum vsque ad consummationem seculi. Matth. 28. Coniungunt his Cœnae verba, & ad nauim vsque clamante Hoc est corpus meum: quae & promissionis verba faciunt, quasi illis Christus realem & substantia-
units.tr: But if we compare the words of the angels with what was said a little earlier in the account of the ascension, it will be clearer than light that no bodily presence of Christ Jesus on earth should be posited from now on, of the kind those imagine who say that the body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin Mary, which hung on the cross and was buried, is handled and eaten corporally, substantially and really by the hands of the faithful in the Supper. They see that the account of the ascension stands in the way of this crude opinion. Therefore they make a separation out of it, as we said above. Then they also abuse a passage of Scripture. First they allege the words of Paul: "Christ ascended above all the heavens, that He might fill all things." Ephesians 4. From this they conclude that, His bodily condition having been changed, He has been diffused through all places, both higher and lower, and fills all things with His body. Then, taking refuge in the divinity, they contend that from its nature the human nature too must necessarily be everywhere, because it is joined and united with the divine. And they think they have untied a kind of Gordian knot when they say: "Such is the union of the natures in Christ that it could not be dissolved even by death; how much less, then, can this crude distance of places separate it?" They also have the promises of Christ, by which they think their opinion is confirmed. For His words are: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the midst of them." Matthew 18. Likewise: "I am with you always, even to the end of the age." Matthew 28. They join to these the words of the Supper, and the cry "This is my body" repeated even to a nausea, which also make up words of promise, as if by them Christ promised a real and substantial presence of His body

units.la: ¶ lem corporis sui praesentiam polliceatur. Sed facilis est ad omnia haec responsio.
units.tr: ¶ Yet the answer to all these things is easy.

units.la: Quoad Pauli locum, nos de Coelis philosophice disputare nolumus. Scimus Aristotelem extra coelorum orbem extremum nullum locum amplius statuere. Sed nefas est hominis ethnici authoritate niti, quando fidei causa contrauertitur. Paulus de coelis qui supra nos sunt loquitur, quia & hi inter mundi partes numerantur, & nouissimi diei igne liquescent, Christum supra hos ascendisse dicit, ut testetur illum iam extra mundum hunc corruptibilem positum esse, & in eum locum receptum, qui ab aeterno electis destinatus, & omnis corruptionis expers est. Quo magis ergo illi hoc vrgent, Christum supra omnes coelos ascendisse, eo magis liquet, illum e mundo exiuisse. Addit Paulus: Ut impleret omnia. Quod ipsi de corpore Christi exponunt, ut satis crassos & ridiculos sese praebeant. Quis enim non videat ineptam, & plus quam puerilem consequentiam: Christus corpus suum euexit supra omnes coelos, & omnes mundi huius visibilis partes: Ergo corpus Christi mundum hunc totum implet corporaliter & substantialiter? Aequi ad hunc modum illi argumentantur. At Paulus hic de veteris scriptura oraculis, siue (ut alij sentiunt) de Christi potentia & maiestate loquitur. Alij de spirituali gratia & donis locum exponunt, quae Christus post acceptam omnem potestatem in homines effundere coepit, sicuti Ioel olim praedixerat. Sed vtrum intelligas, nulla statuitur corporalis Christi in terris praesentia. Impleuerat Christus quae de ipsius incarnatione, passione, morte & resurrectione praedicta erant. Luc. 24. Restabat ascensio, de qua extabant oracula, & qua redemptionis nostrae negotium (ut supra demonstrauimus) consummari & perfici oportebat. Ascendit ergo ne quid in hoc infectum relinqueret. Quod si quis de maiestate potius & potentia Christi hoc dictum velit, quam donorum coelestium distributione declarat, cum illo non contenderim. Eodem enim sententia recidit, quia Christus perfecto demum salutis negotio (quoad humanam naturam) se potestatem accepisse dicit in coelo & in terra. Matth. 28. Et idem se tunc demum spiritum missurum ait, quando ex hoc mundo ad patrem discessit. Ioan. 14. Imo expedit vobis (inquit) ut vadam. Nam si non abiero, consolator ille non veniet ad vos.
units.tr: As for the passage of Paul, we do not wish to dispute philosophically about the heavens. We know that Aristotle posits no place beyond the outermost sphere of the heavens. But it is wrong to rely on the authority of a heathen man when the matter at issue is faith. Paul speaks of the heavens which are above us, because these too are counted among the parts of the world, and they will melt in the fire of the last day; he says that Christ ascended above these, to testify that He is now placed outside this corruptible world and received into that place which from eternity has been destined for the elect and is free from all corruption. Therefore the more they press that Christ ascended above all the heavens, the more it is clear that He has departed out of the world. Paul adds: "that He might fill all things." This they expound of the body of Christ, so that they show themselves to be quite crude and ridiculous. For who does not see the inept and more than childish inference: Christ lifted His body above all the heavens and all the parts of this visible world; therefore the body of Christ fills this whole world corporally and substantially? In this way they argue. But Paul here speaks either of the oracles of the Scriptures of old, or (as others think) of the power and majesty of Christ. Others expound the passage of spiritual grace and gifts, which Christ, after receiving all power, began to pour out on men, as Joel had foretold long before. But whichever you understand, no bodily presence of Christ on earth is established. Christ had fulfilled what had been foretold concerning His incarnation, passion, death and resurrection. Luke 24. There remained the ascension, of which there were oracles, and through which, as we have shown above, the work of our redemption had to be consummated and perfected. Christ therefore ascended so that He might leave nothing undone in this matter. But if anyone wishes this saying to refer rather to the majesty and power of Christ, which He declares by the distribution of heavenly gifts, I will not contend with him. For the sense comes to the same thing, since Christ says that, when the work of salvation was at last completed (as regards His human nature), He received all power in heaven and on earth. Matthew 28. And He says that He would send the Spirit only when He had departed from this world to the Father. John 14. Indeed, He says, "It is expedient for you that I go. For if I do not go away, that Comforter will not come to you."

units.la: Non minus friuolum est, quod a diuinitate ad humanitatem Christi argumentantur. Fatemur equidem duas hasce naturas in Christo coniunctas esse, nec personam Christi propter has scindi aut diuidi debere: nec morte disiunctas esse dicimus. Sed quod in morte factum esse nemo pius negat, id hic quoque obseruandum est. Mansit in morte salua & integra naturarum & proprietatum distinctio. Humana siquidem natura mortem subiit, quam diuina sustinere non poterat. Humana crucem & dolores pertulit, qui in diuinam non cadunt. Et qui ut verus homo in cruce moriebatur, mortuus sepeliebatur, idem ut verus Deus terram quatiebat, Soli lucem eripiebat, in animis hominum efficaciter operabatur, & verissima edebat diuinitatis suae indicia: Idem si hic obseruetur, res erit perspectu facilis. Christus enim quoad diuinam naturam, vbiq; est & vbique operatur. Idem vero quoad humanam, certo coeli loco, aeterna nimirum beatorum sede continetur. Nec propterea diuinitatem ab humanitate separamus, quando illam omnia implere & vbiq; praesentem esse dicimus: sed Augustini regulam sequimur, dicentis: Cauendum est, ne ista diuinitatem astruamus hominis, ut veritatem corporis auferamus, &c.
units.tr: It is no less frivolous when they argue from the divinity to the humanity of Christ. We certainly grant that these two natures are joined together in Christ, and that the person of Christ ought not on account of them to be split or divided; nor do we say that they were separated by death. But what no godly person denies happened in death must be observed here too. In death the distinction of the natures and their properties remained safe and whole. For the human nature underwent death, which the divine nature could not undergo. The human nature endured the cross and pains, which do not fall upon the divine. And he who, as true man, was dying on the cross and, dead, was buried, was also, as true God, shaking the earth, taking the light from the sun, working effectively in the minds of men, and displaying the most true tokens of his divinity. If this is observed here, the matter will be easy to see. For Christ, according to the divine nature, is everywhere and works everywhere. But the same Christ, according to the human nature, is contained in a certain place in heaven, namely the eternal seat of the blessed. Nor on that account do we separate the divinity from the humanity when we say that the divinity fills all things and is present everywhere; rather we follow the rule of Augustine, who says: We must take care lest, in asserting the divinity of the man, we take away the truth of the body, etc.

units.la: His autem simul, quo sensu Christi promissiones accipi debeant, edocemur, quibus se nobis affuturum dicit praesentem vsq; ad consummationem seculi. De diuinitatis enim potentia & virtute illas exponimus. Adest quippe suis Christus diuina virtute & spiritus sui operatione, qua illos regit, ducit, tuetur & defendit. Adest illis sua gratia & merito, ne in peccati & satanae laqueos relabantur, sed in Dei patris fauore & amicitia firmi maneant. De corporali autem praesentia nihil hic illum dicere, alijs eiusdem Christi verbis edocemur, quibus se e mundo abiturum, & non amplius in mundo moraturum, non semel inculcat. Ioan. 14. 16. Quod si vero priores illas promissiones de corporis praesentia exponere libet, altera illa, quibus se posthac in mundo mansurum esse negat, de diuinitatis absentia intelligi necesse erit. Nisi enim per naturarum distinctionem vel idiomatum communicationem locos hosce, alioqui diuersos, conciliemus, incerti & perplexi haerebimus. Quid ergo aliud isti obtinebunt, quam quod de corpore Christi contendentes, spiritu illius & diuina protectione sese scientes & volentes spoliant, & quod Comicus dixit, cum ratione insaniunt? Neque hic frigidum illud & ignobile suffugium admittimus, quo ad visibilem corporis Christi in mundo conuersationem elabuntur. Nec enim de qualitate aut modo rei, sed ipsa re Christus loquitur, & se in mundo posthac mansurum negat. At qua ratione hoc diceret, si in mundo inuisibiliter erat mansurus? Et Matthaei 24. illis credere vetat, qui ipsum hinc inde in penetralibus vel penuarijs & ciborijs nouissimo seculo sint monstraturi.
units.tr: At the same time, from these points we are taught in what sense the promises of Christ ought to be understood, by which he says that he will be with us, present, even to the end of the age. For we explain them of his divine power and virtue. Christ is indeed present with his own by divine power and by the working of his Spirit, by which he rules, leads, guards and defends them. He is present to them by his grace and merit, so that they do not fall back into the snares of sin and Satan, but remain firm in the favour and friendship of God the Father. But that he says nothing here about bodily presence we are taught by other words of this same Christ, in which he repeatedly impresses that he is leaving the world and will no longer remain in the world. John 14, 16. But if we wish to explain those earlier promises as concerning the presence of the body, then those other words, in which he denies that he will remain in the world henceforth, must necessarily be understood of the absence of the divinity. For unless we reconcile these places, otherwise diverse, by the distinction of the natures or the communication of properties, we shall remain uncertain and perplexed.
