What, then, will they gain by this, other than that, while contending about the body of Christ, they deprive themselves of his Spirit and divine protection, and, knowing and willing it, they act madly in the way the comic poet said? Nor do we admit here that cold and ignoble refuge by which they slip away into the visible conversation of Christ's body in the world. For Christ speaks not of the quality or manner of a thing but of the thing itself, and he denies that he will remain in the world henceforth. But for what reason would he say this if he was going to remain in the world invisibly? And in Matthew 24 he forbids us to believe those who will show him here and there, in inner chambers or storerooms and cupboards, in the last age.

units.la: Ex his vero facile colligitur, quo sensu Cœnæ verba accipi debeant. Scimus Christum panem porrexisse discipulis, & dixisse: Hoc est corpus meum, quod pro vobis traditur. Sed sacramentalem locutionem esse dicimus, qua (vt vulgo fieri solet) signo rei signatæ nomen tribuitur. Qua ratione circuncisio fœdus dicebatur, & paschale epulum transitus nomine appellabatur. Nec id temere in præsenti causa obseruamus, quia id suadet corporis Christi veritas, de qua iam aliquoties diximus. Et ipse Christus apud Ioannem discipulis crassam de carnis suæ manducatione opinionem eximere volens eos ad ascensionem relegat, vt ex ea videlicet discant, corpus suum substantialiter & realiter manducari non posse, sed spiritualem manducationem, quæ fide conficitur, intelligi debere. Vide Ioan. 6. cap. Transeo infinita alia quæ dici poterant, ne verbosior sim. Nostrum est, simplicem tenere ascensionis Christi historiam, in cælo quaerere, vt carnis ipsius & sanguinis virtute & merito æternum pascamur.
units.tr: From these things it is easily gathered in what sense the words of the Supper ought to be taken. We know that Christ handed bread to the disciples and said: This is my body, which is given for you. But we say that it is a sacramental expression, by which (as commonly happens) the name of the thing signified is given to the sign. In this way circumcision was called the covenant, and the paschal feast was called by the name of passover. Nor do we observe this rashly in the present case, because the truth of Christ's body, which we have already discussed several times, persuades us to it. And Christ himself, in John, wishing to remove from the disciples the crude opinion about eating his flesh, sends them away to the ascension, so that they may learn from it that his body cannot be eaten substantially and really, but that a spiritual eating, which is accomplished by faith, must be understood. See John 6. I pass over the infinite other things that could be said, so as not to be too wordy. It is our part to hold to the simple history of Christ's ascension, to seek him in heaven, so that we may be fed eternally by the power and merit of his flesh and blood.

units.la: Sed ad angelos reuertamur, quorum oratio consolatione quoq; habet mirificam. Nam vt crassam discipulorum opinionem reprehendunt, qua illi corporalem Christi præsentiam desiderabant: ita eos dem promissione nouissimi aduentus consolantur. Hic ipse Iesus (inquiunt) qui assumptus est à vobis in cælum, sic veniet, quemadmodum ipsum abeuntem vidistis. Visibilem Christi aduentum pollicentur angeli. Inuisibilem, præter eum qui spiritu constat, scriptura prorsus ignorat. Visibilis vero ille est, quem in fidei articulis profitemur, quo venturus est ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Multa de hoc in scripturis extant, vt videre est, Dan.7.12. Et Christus eundem diligenter describit. Matth.24. & 25. Ioan.5. Voluit autem huius in præsenti apostolos quoq; admoneri, quia & institutioni & consolationi nostræ huius meditatio plurimum feruit. Si enim iuxta Ecclesiastici dictum, mortis recordatio peccandi cupiditatem reprimit, quanto plus efficietur, si nouissimi iudicij imaginem animo volu-mus, quo omnes nos coram tribunali Christi sistemur, vt vnusquisq; in corpore suo reportet iuxta id quod fecit, siue bonum siue malum? 2. Cor. 5. Rom. 14. Quid enim tunc homini proderit, si totum mundum lucrifecerit, animæ vero suæ iacturam faciat? Matth.16. Rursum mirifica ad nos redit ex eius diei recordatione consolatio. Qui enim vindex malorum & ultor aduenient impijs, suorum redemptor apparebit, quos corpore & anima glorificatos sui regni & suæ mensæ consortes faciet. Quapropter de signis nouissimum diem præcessuris loquens ait: His fieri incipientibus attollite capita vestra, quia appropinquat redemptio vestra. Luc.21. Et Iob de Christo ad iudicium venturo loquens, Scio (inquit) quod vindex siue redemptor meus viuit, &c. Iob. 19. Huius ergo admoneri oportuit discipulos, vt imminentia pericula & labores grauissimos, qui ipsos manebant, hac spe animati vincere possent. Interim nostri quoq; muneris esse intelligamus, vt in eadem meditatione frequenter versemur, quæ & carnis prauas cupiditates reprimere, & inter labores ac pericula spem inuictam animis nostris addere poterit, qua animati vitæ præsentis cursum feliciter superabimus, æternum aliquando victuri cum Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us return to the angels, whose speech also has a wonderful consolation. For just as they rebuke the crude opinion of the disciples, by which they were longing for the bodily presence of Christ, so they console them with the promise of his last coming. This same Jesus, they say, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come, just as you saw him going away. The angels promise a visible coming of Christ. Scripture altogether knows nothing of an invisible coming, apart from that which consists in the Spirit. But that coming is visible which we profess in the articles of faith, by which he is going to come to judge the living and the dead. Many things about this are found in the Scriptures, as may be seen, Dan. 7.12. And Christ describes it diligently, Matt. 24 and 25; John 5. We ought, however, to be reminded of this at present, because the meditation on it is very useful both for our instruction and for our consolation. For if, according to the saying of Ecclesiasticus, the remembrance of death restrains the desire to sin, how much more will it be effected if we bring before our mind the image of the last judgement, when all of us shall be set before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive in his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil? 2 Cor. 5; Rom. 14. For what will it profit a man then, if he has gained the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Matt. 16. Again, a wonderful consolation returns to us from the recollection of that day. For he who will come as avenger and punisher of the wicked will appear as redeemer of his own, whom, glorified in body and soul, he will make partners of his kingdom and of his table. Therefore, speaking of the signs that will precede the last day, he says: When these things begin to happen, lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near. Luke 21. And Job, speaking of Christ who is to come to judgement, says: I know that my avenger or redeemer lives, etc. Job 19. It was therefore fitting that the disciples be reminded of this, so that, encouraged by this hope, they might be able to overcome the impending perils and the very grievous labours that awaited them. Meanwhile let us understand that it is also our duty to dwell frequently in this same meditation, which can both restrain the wicked desires of the flesh and add to our minds an unconquerable hope amid labours and dangers, by which, encouraged, we shall happily get through the course of the present life, to live for ever at last with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VI.
units.tr: HOMILY VI.

units.la: Tunc reuersi sunt Hierosolymam, à monte qui vocatur Oliueti, qui vicinus est Hierosolymæ, distans Sabbati iter. Et cum ingressi essent ascenderunt in cœnaculum, vbi manebant, nimirum Petrus & Iacobus Iohannes & Andreas, Philippus & Thomas, Bartholomæus & Matthæus, Iacobus Alphæi & Simon Zelotes, & Iudas Iacobi. Hi omnes perseverabant vnanimiter in oratione & deprecatione cum mulieribus & Maria matre Iesu, & cum fratribus illius.
units.tr: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. When they had entered, they went up into the upper room where they were staying, namely Peter and James, John and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot, and Judas the son of James. All these continued together with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, with Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.

units.la: Quamuis dominus & saluator noster Iesus Christus corpus suum per ascensionem gloriosam ex terris hisce in cœlos subuexerit, non tamen ideo nostræ salutis curam deposuisse putari debet: quia fieri non potest, vt eorum obliuiscatur bonus ille pastor, quos sanguinis sui pretio redimere dignatus est. Patet hoc tum multis alijs argumentis, tum maximè eo, quod in ipsam ascensionem, vt nuper vidimus, incidit. Cum enim apostoli subito Christi discessu stupefacti, cœlum intuerentur, rerumq; suarum omnium essent incertissimi, angelos misit, quorum ministerio non tantum de ascensione ipsius edocentur, verumetiam de eiusdem reditu amplissimam consolationem audiunt. Quam efficacem fuisse, ex sequenti rerum eventu cernere licebit. Pergit enim in instituta narratione Lucas, & quid apostoli, postquam Christus ab illis sublatus est, fecerint, commemorat. Nos de singulis ordine dicemus, vt plus inde ad nos doctrinæ vel institutionis & consolationis redire possit.
units.tr: Although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ has carried his body up from this earth into heaven by his glorious ascension, we must not therefore suppose that he laid aside the care of our salvation. That good shepherd cannot forget those whom he deigned to redeem at the price of his blood. This is shown by many other arguments, but chiefly by the fact that it fell upon the ascension itself, as we saw recently. For when the apostles, stunned by Christ's departure, were gazing at heaven and were utterly uncertain about all their affairs, he sent angels, through whose ministry they were taught about his ascension and heard a most ample consolation about his return. How effective this was can be seen from what followed. Luke goes on with his narrative and recalls what the apostles did after Christ had been taken from them. We shall speak of each point in order, so that more teaching, instruction and consolation may come back to us from it.

units.la: Primum verò hic locum ipsorum in vrbem reditus obtinet. Postquam enim adoraverunt (vt Lucæ 24. legitur) reuersi sunt Hierosolymam, & in superiori domus parte (cuius vsus ipsis concessus erat) congregati, promissum à Deo patre & Christo Iesu spiritum expectauerunt. Fuit autem ex monte Oliueti, ex quo cælos Christus petierat, in vrbem vsq; sabbati iter, quod bis mille passuum fuisse, ex Hieronymi authoritate traditur.
units.tr: First, then, comes their return to the city. For after they had worshipped (as is read in Luke 24), they went back to Jerusalem and, gathered in the upper part of the house (which had been granted them for use), they waited for the Spirit promised by God the Father and Christ Jesus. Now the distance from the Mount of Olives, from which Christ had sought heaven, to the city was a Sabbath day's journey, which, on the authority of Jerome, is said to have been two thousand paces.

units.la: Habemus in his non vulgare obedientiæ fidei exemplum, in cuius imitatione nos versari decet. Vrbem enim non priuato humanæ rationis consilio, sed ex Domini mandato apostoli repetunt, qui (vt circa initium libri huius vidimus) præceperat, ne Hierosolymis discederent, nec ab inuicem separarentur ante acceptum cælitus spiritum sanctum. Atqui multa erant, quæ diuersum suadere poterant. Inter quæ non leue videri debebat vndique imminentis periculi metus, & hostiles Iudæorum insidiæ. Et quis nam sibi tutam sperare eam vrbem, quæ & prophetarum sanguini assueuerat, & manus filij Dei sanguine adhuc madentes habebat? Deinde non exigua loci incommoditas multorum animos auertere poterat. Nam vnica in domo, imò parte duntaxat domus vnicæ, homines circiter centum viginti (vt ex sequentibus colligi potest) simul cohabitant, quod absq; singulari molestia fieri non potuisse, quius cordatus intelligit. Accedebat his grauior adhuc tentatio, fidei & religionis prætexto palliata: quod nimirum scirent spiritum sanctum, cuius causa ipsis in ea vrbe manendum erat, nulli certo loco alligatum esse, sed (vt Christus Iohan 3. ait) spirare vbicunque ipse vult. Vnde non frustraneum modo, sed stultum quoque facinus putare poterant, loco tam periculoso spiritus sancti missionem expectare, quæ alibi quoque non minus quàm illic perfici poterat. Et sanè cogitationes eiusmodi non paucas animis illorum obortas esse verisimile est, cum nemo non norit, quàm multa metu perculsis in mentem incidere soleant. At omnia hæc vna fide, quam Christi verbis adhibere dicerunt, superant, ac omni siue periculo siue rationis humanæ consilio spreto & contemptoq; Christi præceptis obedire statuunt. Nec deest felicissimus tam sanctæ obedientiæ eventus. Nam & tutò agunt in vrbe sanguinaria, & spiritum sanctum non multis elapsis diebus, quemadmodum Christus promiserat, accipiunt. Debet ex hoc exemplo generalis lex siue regula constitui, vt nimirum in Dei vocatione & præceptis Dei quacunq; obedienter ambulemus, nec vllis rationibus, quas caro dictare solet, nos ab officio nostro reuocari patiamur. Quia enim sanctus est Deus noster, & humani generis pater indulgentissimus, nihil quod non & sanctum & nobis salutare sit, præcipit. Nam iudicia eius omnia sunt iustitia & veritas, & iuxta Pauli sententiam, hic diuinæ voluntatis scopus & finis est, vt homines salui fiant. 1. Tim. 2. Et quia idem omnipotens est, in vocatione sua & præceptorum suorum obseruatione ambulantes protegit atq; tuetur, nec illis quicquam noxij euenire patitur. Tentantur quidem interdum sancti cultores Dei, quia fidem ipsorum exerceri & probari opus est. Sed quia fidelis est Deus, illos vltra vires tentari non finit, imò cum tentatione euentum largitur, vt sufferre possint. 1. Corinth. 10. Extant huius rei exempla, præter hoc quod in præsenti habemus, infinita alia. Euocatur ex patrio & natali solo Abraham, & in terram alienam & ignotam, quaq; ab impijs vsurpatoribus tenebatur, abire iubetur. At quia vocanti Deo obedit, res omnis succedit felicissimè, & in ea terra non diuitijs modò augetur, verumetiam amicitijs cum potentissimis quibusuis contrahit. Manent in eadem ipsius posteri, & quia Dei vocatione ambulant, tutò agunt inter eos quoq; quos vrbis Sichem excidium iusta vindicta cupiditate contra illos armare posse videbatur. Sed Deum protectorem habent fidelissimum, qui in Chananæorum animis & auribus vocem hanc resonare faciebat: Nolite tangere Christos meos, & prophetis meis nihil mali inferatis. Psal. 165. Transferant horum meditationem ad sese omnes homines, cuiuscunque sint loci aut ordinis, & meminerint, Dei mandatis benedictionem amplissimam & infallibilem diuini auxilij promissionem coniunctam, atq; adeò inclusam esse, quia haud dubiè fruentur, si illis obtemperare studeant. Vide de hoc Deut. 28. & Leuit. 26. cap. In primis verò cauendum, ne carnis rationes admittamus in ijs, quæ expressis Dei verbis vel præcepta vel prohibita videmus. Hæc enim præsentissima pestis est, quæ obedientiæ studium omne excutit, & totam vitam Deo inuisam reddit. Quia nullum Dei præceptum tam sanctum, tam facile & salutare est, in quo non caro nostra & difficultatem & periculum, imò & iniustitiæ & ni quitatis speciem aliquam deprehendat. Fidei obedientia requiritur, quæ (vt Paulus ait) omnem intellectum captiuum ducit, omnia humanæ rationis consilia demolitur, & totum hominem vni Deo ac verbo ipsius subijcit. 2. Corinth. 10. Huc referri debet, quod in lege Dominus his verbis præscribit: Ne peruestigetis post cor vestrum, nec post oculos vestros, post quos scortari soletis. Quin memores sitis, & facite omnia præcepta mea, eritisq; sancti Deo vestro. Numeri 15. Et rursum: Ad verbum meum, quod ego præcipio vobis, nihil adijcietis, nihil item ei detrahetis, &c. Deut. 4. & 12. Quòd si quis exempla eorum requirat, quibus infelicissimè cessit præceptorum Dei transgressio, tum alibi, tum in Saulis historia non pauca reperiet. Vide 1. Samuel. 13. & 15. cap. Sed pergamus ad reliqua.
units.tr: In this we have an uncommon example of obedient faith, and it is fitting that we should imitate it. For the apostles went back to the city not on a private decision of human reasoning but on the Lord's command, for he (as we saw near the beginning of this book) had ordered them not to leave Jerusalem nor to separate from one another before they received the Holy Spirit from heaven. Yet there were many things that could have persuaded them otherwise. Among these the fear of danger threatening on every side, and the hostile plots of the Jews, must have seemed no small matter. And who could hope that city to be safe, which was accustomed to the blood of the prophets and still had its hands stained with the blood of the Son of God? Besides, the considerable inconvenience of the place could have turned many minds away. For in one house, or rather in one part only of a single house, about one hundred and twenty people (as can be gathered from what follows) lived together at the same time, which, as any sensible person understands, could not have been done without great discomfort. A heavier temptation was added to these, cloaked under the pretext of faith and religion: they knew that the Spirit, for whose sake they had to remain in that city, is bound to no certain place, but (as Christ says in John 3) breathes where he wills. Hence they could think it not only a pointless but also a foolish thing to wait in so dangerous a place for the sending of the Spirit, which could be accomplished elsewhere no less than there. And indeed it is likely that many thoughts of this kind arose in their minds, since everyone knows how many things tend to occur to those struck with fear. Yet they overcame all these by the one faith which they gave to the words of Christ, and, despising every danger and every counsel of human reason, they resolved to obey Christ's commands. Nor is the most fortunate outcome of so holy an obedience lacking. For they lived safely in a bloodthirsty city, and within a few days, as Christ had promised, they received the Spirit. From this example a general rule should be laid down: that in God's calling and God's commands we should walk obediently wherever we are, and not allow ourselves to be called back from our duty by any reasons that the flesh is accustomed to dictate. For since our God is holy, and the most indulgent Father of the human race, he commands nothing that is not both holy and salutary for us. His judgments are all justice and truth, and, according to the saying of Paul, the goal and purpose of the divine will is that men be saved (1 Tim. 2). And since he is also almighty, he protects and guards those who walk in his calling and in the observance of his precepts, and he does not allow anything harmful to befall them. The worshippers of God are indeed sometimes tempted, because their faith must be exercised and proved. But since God is faithful, he does not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength, but with the temptation he also grants the outcome, so that they may bear it (1 Cor. 10). There are, besides what we have here, countless other examples of this. Abraham is called from his native land and birthplace, and is ordered to go into a foreign and unknown land, which was held by impious usurpers. But because he obeyed God's call, everything turned out most happily, and in that land he was not only increased in riches but also formed friendships with the most powerful men of any kind. His descendants remained in the same place, and because they walked in God's calling, they lived safely even among those whom the destruction of the city of Shechem seemed able to arm against them with a just desire for vengeance. But they had God as their most faithful protector, who caused this voice to resound in the ears and minds of the Canaanites: "Touch not my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm" (Ps. 105). Let all men, of whatever place or rank they may be, turn this meditation to themselves, and let them remember that the most ample blessing and the infallible promise of divine help are joined to, and indeed included in, God's commands, since they will undoubtedly enjoy them if they strive to obey them. See on this Deut. 28 and the chapter of Leviticus 26. Above all, however, we must take care not to admit the reasonings of the flesh in those matters which we see commanded or forbidden in the express words of God. For this is the most present plague, which shakes out all zeal for obedience and makes the whole of life hateful to God. For no command of God is so holy, so easy and so salutary that our flesh does not find in it some difficulty and danger, or even some appearance of injustice and iniquity. The obedience of faith is required, which (as Paul says) takes every thought captive, overthrows all the counsels of human reason, and subjects the whole man to the one God and his word (2 Cor. 10). To this should be referred what the Lord prescribes in the law in these words: "Do not search after your heart, nor after your eyes, after which you are accustomed to play the harlot. Rather, be mindful and do all my commandments, and you shall be holy to your God" (Num. 15). And again: "You shall add nothing to my word, which I command you, nor take anything from it," etc. (Deut. 4 and 12). If anyone seeks examples of those in whom the transgression of God's commands turned out most unhappily, he will find not a few, both elsewhere and in the history of Saul. See 1 Sam. 13 and chapter 15. But let us proceed to the rest.

units.la: Secundo loco apostolorum nomina Lucas recenset, nec id temere. Præter id enim quod notissimos esse oportebat, quos Christus Iesus totius orbis doctores fecerat, ne illud munus eiusq; muneris authoritatem seductores improbi sibi vendicarent: necesse erat, vt certò sciremus, illos post turpem defectionē à Christo priori dignitati & loco restitutos fuisse. Notum siquidem est omnibus, quàm turpes se se dederint, cùm Christus à militibus & sacerdotum seruis caperetur. Tunc enim omnes illo derelicto, fugerunt. Et Petrus, qui maxima quaq; de sua fortitudine erat pollicitus, turpiori flagitio sese polluit, dum eundem tertia vice negat. Non immeritò igitur dubitari poterat, num tales in gratiam recepisset Dominus, & num defectoribus tam ignauis fides haberi deberet. Ne quid ergo dubij animis nostris inhæreret, & ne prioris lapsus turpitudine veritatis doctrinæ officere putaremus, spiritus sanctus nominatim illos ipsos (vno Iuda excepto) recenseri voluit, qui priusquam Christus pateretur, euangelio per orbem diuulgando ordinati erant. Et si huius loci catalogum cum ijs, qui Matth. 10. Marc. 3. & Luc. 6. habentur, conferas, nihil discriminis reperies.
units.tr: Second, Luke lists the names of the apostles, and not carelessly. Besides the fact that they had to be very well known, since Christ Jesus had made them teachers of the whole world, this was so that wicked seducers could not claim that office and its authority for themselves. It was also necessary that we know for certain that they were restored to their former dignity and place after their shameful desertion of Christ. For everyone knows how disgracefully they behaved when Christ was seized by the soldiers and the servants of the priests. Then they all abandoned him and fled. Peter, who had promised great things about his courage, polluted himself with an even more shameful crime when he denied him a third time. It was therefore not unreasonable to doubt whether the Lord had taken such men back into favour, and whether men who had deserted so cowardly should be trusted. So that no doubt might cling to our minds, and so that we might not think the truth of the doctrine was impaired by the disgrace of their earlier fall, the Holy Spirit wished those very men to be named individually (Judas alone excepted) who had been ordained, before Christ suffered, to spread the gospel throughout the world. And if you compare this list with those in Matthew 10, Mark 3 and Luke 6, you will find no difference.

units.la: Est autem hoc singulare diuinæ bonitatis exemplū, quæ tam turpis defectionis crimini, non ignoscere modò, verumetiam illius reos in prioris officij atq; dignitatis gradū restituere voluit. Verè enim hic iuxta Pauli dictum abundat gratia, vbi abundarat delictū. Rom. 5. Nam Petrus, qui plus alijs peccauerat, ter sibi à Christo dici audit: Pasce oues meas. Iohan. 21. Hinc consolationem petant, qui peccatorum conscientia exagitantur, ne ob illorum vel atrocitatem vel multitudinem animum despondeant. Conuertimini ad me (inquit Dominus) & ego conuertar ad vos. Zach. 1. Viuo ego, quòd nolo mortem peccatoris, sed potius vt conuertatur, & viuat. Ezech. 16.
units.tr: This is a singular example of divine goodness, which was willing not only to forgive those guilty of so shameful a desertion, but also to restore them to the rank of their former office and dignity. For here, truly, according to Paul's saying, grace abounds where sin abounded. Rom. 5. Peter, who had sinned more than the others, hears from Christ three times: Feed my sheep. John 21. Let those who are troubled by the awareness of their sins take comfort from this, lest they lose heart because of the atrocity or the multitude of their sins. "Turn to me," says the Lord, "and I will turn to you." Zech. 1. "As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live." Ezek. 16.

units.la: Adhæc obseruatione non indignum est, quod in catalogo hoc non nisi vilißimorum & mundi itä dicio contemptißimorum hominum nomina recenseatur. Primi enim ponuntur Petrus, Iacobus, Iohannes & Andreas, quos ante ignobiles piscatores fuisse legimus. Numeratur hic & Matthæus publicanus, & vitæ prioris conditione infamis. De aliorum vel nobilitate vel opibus ac honoribus nihil vspiam extat. Atqui poterat Dei filius, cui in animos quoque hominum ius est, & sacerdotum & principum filios in suum obsequium pertrahere, vt illorum ministerio euangelium vulgaretur, qui authoritate & potentia in mundo præclari habebantur. Sed viles & contemptos eligere ipsi placuit, tum vt sciremus Deum neminem, quantumuis in mundo contemptum ac vilem, fastidire, tum vt de fidei & religionis causa non ex hominum authoritate, sed ipsius veritatis cognitione & verbo Dei iudicare discerēmus. Grauis enim & periculosissimus illorum error est, qui de fidei causa pronuntiaturi ad hominum authoritatem oculos conuertunt, quasi fides & religio ab hominum iudicio dependeat, & non potius Dei solius verbo nitatur. Ridentur apud Tertullianum, vetustissimū scriptorem, Romani, quòd deos suos senatus decreto crearent, nec pro diis agnoscerent, nisi qui senatui placuissent. Atqui idem faciunt hodie, qui pro hominum authoritate & gloria de fide & fidei doctrina pronunciant. Quod hominum genus vulgò cernitur, & eo nomine ab aduersarijs maximè nostra fides & religio damnatur, quòd paucos ex Cæsarum & Regum numero, paucos item ex Pontificum & Cardinalium atq; Episcoporum grege sectatores habeat. Sed quàm turpiter isti homines fallantur, Iudæorum exemplum docet, quos ad eundem lapidem offendisse legimus. Cum enim ministris suis Christi doctrinam nonnihil arridere cernerent, mox hominum authoritate ipsos obruere conantur, dicentes: Num & vos seducti estis? Num quis ex principibus credidit in eum, aut ex pharisaeis? Sed turba haec, quae non novit legem, execrabiles sunt. Iohan. 7. Nos ergo Dei consilium spectemus, qui (ut Paulus monuit) quae stulta, contempta & ignobilia & quasi nulla sunt in hoc mundo, eligere consueuit, ut mundi sapientiam, potentiam & authoritatem omnem confundat. 1. Corinth. 1. Nec id temere facit: quia hoc argumento constat, in solo Deo nobis gloriandum esse. Objiciant alij nobis Imperatores & Reges, Pontifices & Cardinales, Concilia & Scholas vniuersales, Doctores Seraphicos & illuminatos, Magistros nostros & quicquid vspiam in mundo sapientia & sanctitatis nomine praelucet, & vicissim miseram & contemptam in mundo condition eorum exagitent, qui euangelio nomen dederunt nos cum Christo Iesu saluatore & doctore nostro respondebimus: Gratias agimus tibi pater, Domine coeli & terrae, quod abscondevis haec a sapientibus & prudentibus, & reuelasti ea paruulis. Certè pater, sic fuit bona voluntas apud te. Matth. 11.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth observing that this catalogue records only the names of the most lowly men, those most despised by the judgment of the world. Peter, James, John and Andrew are placed first, and we read that they were humble fishermen before. Matthew the tax collector is also listed here, and infamous because of the condition of his former life. Nothing anywhere records the nobility, wealth or honours of the others. Yet the Son of God, who has rights over men's minds too, could have drawn the sons of priests and princes into his service, so that the gospel might be spread by the ministry of those who were famous in the world for authority and power. But he chose the base and the despised himself, partly so that we might know that God despises no one, however scorned and lowly in the world, and partly so that we might learn to judge matters of faith and religion not by the authority of men, but by the knowledge of the truth itself and the word of God. The error of those who, when about to pronounce on a matter of faith, turn their eyes to the authority of men is grave and most dangerous, as if faith and religion depended on the judgment of men, and did not rest on the word of God alone. In Tertullian, the most ancient writer, the Romans are mocked because they created their gods by decree of the senate, and acknowledged as gods only those who pleased the senate. Yet those who today pronounce on faith and its doctrine by the authority and glory of men do the same. This kind of men is commonly seen, and our faith and religion is condemned by our adversaries chiefly on this ground: that it has few followers among the Caesars and kings, and few likewise from the flock of popes, cardinals and bishops. But how shamefully these men are deceived is taught by the example of the Jews, whom we read stumbled over the same stone. When they saw that their servants were somewhat taken with Christ's teaching, they at once tried to crush them by the authority of men, saying: "Have you too been led astray? Has any of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed." John 7. Let us then look to the counsel of God, who (as Paul warned) is accustomed to choose what is foolish, despised, base and as it were nothing in this world, so that he may confound all the wisdom, power and authority of the world. 1 Cor. 1. Nor does he do this rashly, for this argument establishes that we must glory in God alone. Let others object to us emperors and kings, popes and cardinals, councils and universal schools, seraphic and enlightened doctors, our own masters, and whatever shines in the world under the name of wisdom and holiness, and let them in turn mock the wretched and despised condition in the world of those who have given their name to the gospel. We will answer with Christ Jesus, our Saviour and teacher: "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was good in your sight." Matt. 11.

units.la: Caeterum apostolorum congregationi mulieres etiam interfuisse Lucas scribit. Quas aliquot eas tantummodo fuisse putant, quae cum Christo Iesu postrema profectione ex Galilaea Hierosolymam ascenderant. Atqui ut negare nolim, ex illarum numero aliquas cum apostolis mansisse, ita de apostolorum uxoribus locum hunc commodissimè intelligi posse existimo. Petro equidem uxorem fuisse euangelica historia diserte docet. De Matthaeo si idem asseramus, non absurde faciemus, quando illum familiam aluisse, & domum habuisse propriam, satis constat. Et Paulus non obscurè testatur, apostolos uxores circunduxisse, quando euangelij doctrinam per omnes gentes diuulgabant. 1. Corinth. 9. Quamuis non ignorem, impuri caelibatus defensores illum locum de Christianis mulieribus, quae apostolos secutae sint, exponere. Sed non animaduertunt inepti homines, se apostolis magnam iniuriam facere, dum ista afferunt. Quam enim excusationem habebunt reliquam apostoli, si proprijs uxoribus relictis, mulieres alienas circunduxerunt? Absit ergo, ut tam absurda & inepta, nec etiam honesta, de sanctissimis Christi Iesu legatis cogitemus. Ego certè apostolorum uxores cum illis e Galilaea ascendisse, & cum apostolis, maritis suis, quibus ab vrbe non licebat discedere, in hunc vsque diem mansisse credo. Quia enim omnium & laborum & periculorum socia apostolis futura erant, ipsas quoque non vulgari spiritus sancti dono praeparari & confirmari oportebat. Qui caelibatum ecclesiae ministris necessarium esse contendunt, ineptiores sunt, quam ut in tanta euangelij luce multis confutari debeant, quando omnibus constat, coniugium in omni hominum ordine honorabile, & torum coniugalem impolutum esse. Hebr. 13.
units.tr: Luke writes that women also were present at the gathering of the apostles. Some think these were only a few who had gone up to Jerusalem with Christ Jesus on his last journey from Galilee. But although I would not deny that some of their number remained with the apostles, I think this passage can most fittingly be understood of the apostles' wives. The gospel history plainly teaches that Peter had a wife. If we make the same claim of Matthew, we will not be unreasonable, since it is quite clear that he supported a household and had a home of his own. Paul also testifies not obscurely that the apostles led about wives when they were spreading the doctrine of the gospel among all nations. 1 Cor. 9. I am not unaware that the defenders of impure celibacy explain that passage as referring to Christian women who followed the apostles. But these foolish men do not notice that they do great wrong to the apostles by bringing forward such claims. For what excuse would the apostles have left if, having left their own wives, they led about the wives of others? Far be it from us, then, to think such absurd, foolish and even dishonourable things about the most holy legates of Christ Jesus. I believe that the apostles' wives went up with them from Galilee, and remained with them, their husbands, until this day, since they were not permitted to leave the city. For since they were to be companions in all the labours and dangers of the apostles, they too had to be prepared and strengthened by no ordinary gift of the Holy Spirit. Those who contend that celibacy is necessary for the ministers of the Church are too foolish to need refuting at length in such a great light of the gospel, since everyone agrees that marriage is honourable in every rank of men, and the marriage bed is undefiled. Heb. 13.

units.la: Mulieribus verò istis diua quoq; virgo, Christi Iesu mater, affuit vna cum aliquot Christi fratribus, quos iuxta Hebraici sermonis consuetudinem, cognatos illius fuisse intelligimus. Commendarat hanc Christus moriens Iohanni dilecto discipulo, qui illam ad se receptam fidelissimè custodiuit. Atqui hoc loco postremam illius mentionem faciunt sacrae literae. Nicephorus illam regnante Claudio mortuam esse scribit: cum annum ageret quinquagesimum nonum. Eusebius in Chronicis in coelum assumptam tradidit, sed traditionem hanc incertam esse, ipse non dissimulat, cum addit: ut quidam fuisse sibi reuelatum scribit. Secuti sunt postremi temporibus monachi, quos non puduit totam Assumptionis historiam confingere: quam veteribus plane ignotam fuisse, ex Epiphanio patet, qui contra Antidicomarianitas sic scribit: Si videntur quidam errasse, quaerant vestigia scripturarum, & inuenient neque mortem Mariae, neque an mortua sit, aut non mortua: neque an sepulta sit, aut non sepulta. Et paulo post, Non dico quod immortalis mansit, sed nec affirmo quod mortua sit. Excessit enim scriptura mentem humanam, & in suspenso reliquit propter vas pretiosum & excellentissimum, ut ne quis in suspicionem veniat carnalium de ipsa rerum, &c. Quibus ego addo, non credibile videri spiritum sanctum miraculosam Mariae assumptionem voluisse tacere, si quae fuisset facta, cum Enochi & Eliae translationem tam diligenter describi curarit. Quae verò post Christi ascensionem illi acciderunt, obliuione sepulta voluit, ne quam superstitioni causam praeberet, quam circa illius cultum orituraм sciebat. Et sanè mirum videri poterat, illius facta taceri, cum apostolorum res gestas & doctrinam tam diligenti studio Deus conscribi voluerit. Sed admonemur ea re, nos non circa superstitionem hominum cultum, sed apostolorum potius doctrinam occupari debere. Interim observasse prodest, Christum Iesum dilectissimæ matri, & cognatis suis itidem charissimis, tutelam & patrocinium tam infirmum & imbecillum constituisse. Nam si iuxta mundi iudicium apostolos æstimes, nullæ illorum vires fuerunt, nullæ opes, nulla nominis authoritas, nulla denique arma, quibus sanctissimum illud vas gloriæ & gratiæ Dei contra mundi conatus possent defendere. Quin ergo potius potentissimi alicuius regis fidei matrem tuendam commisit, cuius animum & voluntatem facile, ut illius curam suscipere, inclinare poterat? Sed qui in animos hominum ius habet, externis armis & carnali præsidio ad suos tuendos non indiget. Sufficiens ergo fuit hæc tutela diuæ virgini, quam ab Iohanne suscipi voluit. Discamus itaque & nos, non in hominum præsidiis, sed in Dei protectione spem omnem collocare, nec animum despondere, si à potentioribus derelicti, amicos & fautores eos tantum habeamus, qui & viribus omnibus destituti sunt, & ipsi patronis & tutoribus opus habent, vel etiam omnium iniurijs sunt expositi. Cum Dauide enim nos imperterrito animo exclamare conuenit: Dominus lux mea & salus mea, à quo nam timerem? Dominus robur vitæ meæ, à quo expauescerem? Dominus mihi adiutor, non timebo quid faciat mihi homo, &c. Psalm. 27. & 118.
units.tr: The blessed virgin also was present with these women, the mother of Christ Jesus, together with some brothers of Christ, whom, according to the custom of the Hebrew language, we understand to have been his kinsmen. Christ, dying, had commended her to his beloved disciple John, who received her into his home and faithfully looked after her. Yet here the sacred letters make their last mention of her. Nicephorus writes that she died in the reign of Claudius, in her fifty-ninth year. Eusebius in his Chronicle handed down that she was taken up into heaven, but he himself does not conceal that this tradition is uncertain, when he adds that someone wrote that it had been revealed to him. In later times monks followed, who were not ashamed to invent the whole history of the Assumption, which was plainly unknown to the ancients, as is clear from Epiphanius, who writes against the Antidicomarians thus: "If some seem to have erred, let them seek the traces in the Scriptures, and they will find neither Mary's death, nor whether she died or did not die, nor whether she was buried or not buried." And a little later: "I do not say that she remained immortal, but nor do I affirm that she died. For Scripture has gone beyond the human mind, and left the matter in suspense on account of the precious and most excellent vessel, so that no one may fall under the suspicion of carnal thoughts about the thing itself, etc." To these I add that it does not seem credible that the Holy Spirit would have wished to pass over in silence a miraculous assumption of Mary, if it had happened, since he took such diligent care to describe the translation of Enoch and Elijah. What happened to her after Christ's ascension he wished to be buried in oblivion, lest it give some occasion for superstition, which, as he knew, would arise around her worship. Indeed it might seem strange that her deeds are passed over in silence, since God wished the deeds and teaching of the apostles to be written down with such diligent care. But we are reminded by this that we ought to be occupied not with the superstitious worship of men, but rather with the teaching of the apostles. Meanwhile it is useful to observe that Christ Jesus appointed for his most beloved mother, and likewise for his very dear kinsmen, a guardianship and protection so weak and feeble. For if you judge the apostles by the judgment of the world, they had no strength, no wealth, no authority of name, and finally no arms with which they could defend that most holy vessel of God's glory and grace against the attempts of the world. Why then did he not rather commit the mother of the faith to the protection of some most powerful king, whose mind and will he could easily have inclined to take up her care? But he who has right over men's minds does not need external arms and carnal help to protect his own. This guardianship, which he wished to be undertaken by John, was therefore sufficient for the divine virgin. Let us too learn to place all our hope not in the help of men but in God's protection, and not to lose heart if, abandoned by the more powerful, we have as friends and supporters only those who are destitute of all strength, who themselves need patrons and guardians, or who are even exposed to the injuries of all. For with David we ought to cry out with fearless mind: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; of whom shall I be afraid? The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be terrified? The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me, etc." Ps. 27 and 118.

units.la: Postremò exponit Euangelista, quid omnes isti interea temporis fecerint, dum spiritus sanctus mittendus differtur. Nam si dies supputemus, decimo demum ab ascensione Christi die illum datum esse reperiemus. Per quadraginta enim dies continuos cum discipulis Christus conuersatus est, & suæ resurrectionis veritatem argumentis pluribus affuerit. Quinquagesimo autem die à festo paschatis misum esse spiritum infrà capite secundo Lucas indicat. Interea temporis vnanimiter perseuerauerunt in orationibus & deprecationibus. Quamuis vero precationum, quas habuerunt, argumenta non explicentur, ex circumstantijs tamen, quid precati sint, facile coniici potest. Quid enim aliud orassent qui infirmitatis suæ conscij tantum onus humeris suis impositum videbant, quam ut Deus spiritus sui missionem maturare, & ipsos à lapsu omni clementer seruare dignaretur? Prioris etenim defectionis exemplo didicerant, quàm inanes & nullæ sint in diuinis rebus hominis vires, nisi præsenti diuinæ gratiæ auxilio sustentemur.
units.tr: Finally, the evangelist sets out what all these men did in the meantime, while the sending of the Holy Spirit was being put off. For if we count the days, we shall find that he was given only on the tenth day after Christ's ascension. For Christ dwelt with the disciples for forty continuous days and showed himself to them by many proofs of his resurrection. Luke indicates in the second chapter above that the Spirit was sent on the fiftieth day from the feast of Passover. Meanwhile they persevered together in one accord in prayers and supplications. Although the subjects of the prayers they made are not spelled out, what they prayed for can easily be guessed from the circumstances. For what else would they have prayed, who were conscious of their own weakness and saw so great a burden laid on their shoulders, than that God would deign to hasten the sending of his Spirit and in his kindness keep them safe from every fall? For from the example of their earlier defection they had learned how empty and worthless human powers are in divine matters, unless we are sustained by the present help of divine grace.

units.la: Obseruemus autem in his, quòd orationem & deprecationem assiduam illis Lucas tribuit, qui promissionibus amplissimis & fide instructi erant. Nam si ea legas, quæ apud Iohannem Christus, iam mortem aditurus, cum discipulis egit, spiritus sancti promissionem tantum non ad fastidium vsq; repetitam fuisse cernes. Et de eadem non semel, à mortuis resuscitatus, eos admonuerat. Ipsos verò pro missionibus Christi fidem adhibuisse, ex illorum in vrbem reditu clarissimè constat. Nisi enim credidissent Christum promissis staturum, in vrbem sanguinariam & periculi plenam minimè fuissent reuersi. Fides ergo non obstat, quò minus in precibus & bonorum operum studio assidui ac frequentes simus. Scio equidem multos, quæ de sola fide iustificante & saluante dicuntur, hoc modo cauillari, quasi & preces inutiles reddant, & bonorum operum studia vel extinguant, vel saltem magna ex parte remorentur. Sed tam longè à vero aberrant isti homines, vt non aliud efficacius ad preces & bona opera incitamentum sit, quàm quod ex fide in animis nostris oboritur. Imò nisi fide instructi simus, nec cum fructu orare, nec in bonis operibus feruere poterimus. Quomodo enim inuocabunt eum, in quem non crediderunt? inquit Paulus. Rom. 10. Et quomodo gratæ erunt Deo preces nostræ, nisi de ipsius benigna in nos voluntate certam fiduciam conceperimus? Deniq; cum natura à bonorum operum studio abhorrea mus, fieri nequit, vt illis nos totos consecremus, nisi illa Deo patri propter fidem in Christum Iesum placere certi simus. Vt iam de eo nihil dicam, quòd sine fide aliquem Deo placere impossibile est, & quòd peccatum est, quicquid sine fide fit. Hebr. 11. Rom. 14.
units.tr: Let us observe in this that Luke ascribes continual prayer and supplication to those who were furnished with the most ample promises and with faith. For if you read what Christ, about to go to his death, said with the disciples in John, you will see that the promise of the Holy Spirit was repeated almost to the point of weariness. And, raised from the dead, he had more than once admonished them about the same thing. That they put faith in Christ's promises is made quite clear by their return to the city. For unless they had believed that Christ would stand by his promises, they would by no means have returned to a city full of bloodshed and danger. Faith therefore does not stand in the way of our being constant in prayer and in the zeal for good works. I know indeed that many scoff at what is said about faith alone justifying and saving, as if it rendered prayers useless and either extinguished or at least greatly hindered the pursuit of good works. But these men are so far from the truth that nothing is a more effective incitement to prayer and good works than what arises from faith in our hearts. Indeed, unless we are furnished with faith, we shall be able neither to pray with profit nor to glow in good works. For, as Paul says, how shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Rom. 10. And how will our prayers be pleasing to God, unless we have conceived a firm trust in his kindly will towards us? Finally, since by nature we shrink from the pursuit of good works, it cannot happen that we devote ourselves wholly to them, unless we are certain that they please God the Father because of faith in Christ Jesus. To say nothing more of this, it is impossible to please God without faith, and whatever is done without faith is sin. Heb. 11. Rom. 14.

units.la: Precibus autem suis duo coniungunt Apostoli & qui cum ipsis agunt, sine quibus nulla apud Deum precum nostrarum potest esse virtus, siue authoritas, Vnanimitatem nimirum & Perseuerantiam. Vnanimitate opus est, quia eiusdem patris filij sumus, quod in oratione dominica profitemur, dicentes, Pater noster qui es in cœlis, &c. At quis obsecro pater tam vecors & ignauus est, qui filios inter se dissidentes ferre possit? Et natura ea lex est, vt qui eodem femine prognati, & eandem hereditatem aditurî sunt, mutuo amori & concordiæ studeant. At quotquot Christo per fidem sunt insiti, ex eodem femine, verbo scilicet Dei incorruptibili & immortali renati sunt in filios Dei, & eiusdem regni in cœlis hæredes erunt: imò vt maius aliquid addamus, eiusdem corporis membra facti, vnum caput agnoscunt, & vno eodemq; spiritu animantur. Num ergo fieri poterit, vt tales à charis tate & vnanimitatis studio alieni sint? Nónne dum odijs & inimicitijs indulgent, sese à corpore Christi auellunt, & hypocrisim execrabilem exercent, dum vt germani filij Dei, quasi communibus votis, in Dei conspectu apparere audent? In precibus ergo cumprimis locum habere debet, quod Christus de sacrificaturis admonet, dicens: Si obtuleris munus tuum ad aram, & illic recordatus fueris, quòd frater tuus habet aliquid aduersum te, relinque illic munus tuum coram altari, & abi, prius reconciliêris fratri tuo, & tum veniens offer munus tuum. Matth.5. Si enim cauendum est, ne quam odij contra nos causam frater habeat, quantò minus admitti debet, vt nos fratris odio ringamur? Non minor verò perseuerantiæ etiam ratio in precibus habenda est, eò quòd interdum promissam opem diu differt Deus, adeoq; nostri curam omnem deposuisse videtur. Quæ res sanctissimis quoque viris voces illas extorsit: Quousq; obliuisceris mei ô domine? Num perpetuò? Quousque faciem tuam à me abscondis? Quousque domine clamo, & non exaudis? Psalm.13. Hab.1. &c. Caeterum in eiusmodi cogitationibus animo repetendum est, Deum nostri curam & memoriam deponere non posse, quos filij sui sanguine redimere dignatus est. Nam apud prophetam ait: Num obliuioni tradit mulier infantem suum, quò minus misereatur filij vteri sui? Sed esto obliuiscantur illæ, ego tamen tui non obliuiscar. Ecce in manibus istis ambabus insculpsi te, &c. Isa.49. Et Dauid: Fugas meas tu numeratas habes, & lachrymas meas reponis in lagunculam tuam, annon in rationario tuo? Psalm.56. Quoties ergo opem petitam differt dominus, hac vna de causa fit, vt nostram patientiam atque fidem exerceat, nec tamen (quod supra monuimus) vltra vires tentari patitur. Quapropter tunc maximè fidei neruos intendere, & illius robur assiduis precibus testari conuenit. Et quanta huius perseuerantiæ adeoq; importunitatis vis sit apud Deum, Christus Iesus elegantissimis parabolis adumbrat, Luc.11. & 18. cap. Quodigitur Apostoli, dum spiritum sanctum expectarunt, fecere, id nos quoque faciamus sedulò. Spiritu sancto enim & nobis opus est ad coercenda carnis desideria & firmandam fidei constantiam. Præparemur ad hunc suscipiendum obedientiæ studio, vnanimitate & precum perseuerantia, vt illo animati & illustrati in præsenti seculo diuinæ maiestati vitam nostram approbare, & olim in cœlis viuere possimus cum Iesu Christo, saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The apostles and those who acted with them joined two things to their prayers, without which there can be no power or authority in our prayers before God: namely, unanimity and perseverance. Unanimity is needed, because we are sons of the same Father, which we profess in the Lord's Prayer when we say, Our Father who art in heaven, etc. But what father, I ask, is so senseless and sluggish that he could bear his sons quarrelling among themselves? And it is the law of nature that those born of the same seed, and destined to receive the same inheritance, should strive for mutual love and harmony. Yet all who have been engrafted into Christ through faith have been born of the same seed, that is, of the incorruptible and immortal word of God, into sons of God, and will be heirs of the same kingdom in heaven; indeed, to add something greater still, they have been made members of the same body, acknowledge one head, and are quickened by one and the same Spirit. Can it then happen that such people are estranged from charity and from the zeal for unity? Do they not, while they indulge in hatreds and enmities, tear themselves from the body of Christ and practise a loathsome hypocrisy, when they dare to appear in God's sight, as true sons of God, with what are as it were common prayers? Therefore, above all, in prayers ought to have a place what Christ warns those who offer sacrifice, saying: If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. Matt. 5. For if care must be taken that a brother has no cause for hatred against us, how much less should we allow ourselves to be entangled in our brother's hatred? Nor is there less reason to practise perseverance in prayers, because God sometimes delays the help he has promised for a long time, and seems to have laid aside all concern for us. This has wrung from even the holiest men those cries: How long, O Lord, will you forget me? Forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long, O Lord, do I cry, and you do not hear? Psalm 13. Hab. 1. etc. Yet in such thoughts the mind must recall that God cannot lay aside his care and remembrance of those whom he has deigned to redeem with the blood of his Son. For he says through the prophet: Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? But though those women forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on both of my hands, etc. Isa. 49. And David: You have counted my wanderings, and put my tears into your bottle; are they not in your record? Psalm 56. Whenever therefore the Lord delays the help we seek, he does so for this one reason: to exercise our patience and faith, yet he does not allow us to be tried beyond our strength, as we noted above. Therefore it is then especially fitting to strain the sinews of faith and to bear witness to its strength by constant prayer. And how great the power of such perseverance, and indeed of importunity, is with God, Christ Jesus shadows forth in most elegant parables, Luke 11 and 18. Therefore what the apostles did while they waited for the Holy Spirit, let us also do diligently. For we too need the Holy Spirit, to restrain the desires of the flesh and to strengthen the constancy of faith. Let us prepare ourselves to receive him with zeal for obedience, with unanimity and perseverance in prayer, so that, animated and enlightened by him, we may in the present age approve our life to the divine majesty, and hereafter live in heaven with Jesus Christ, our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VII.
units.tr: Homily VII.

units.la: In diebus illis exurgens Petrus in medio discipulorum, dixit: (erat autem turba nominum simul ferè centū viginti) Viri fratres, oportuit impleri scripturam hanc, quam prædixit spiritus sanctus per os Dauidis, de Iuda, qui fuit dux iss qui coprehenderunt Iesum, qui & coopta-tus erat in numerum nostrum, & sortitus erat partem ministerij huius. Et is quidem possedit agrū ex mercede iniquitatis, suspensus crepuit medius, & effusa sunt omnia viscera eius. Et innotuit omnibus habitantibus Hierosolymis: ita vt vocatus sit ager ille propria illorum lingua, Aceldama, hoc est, ager sanguinis.
units.tr: In those days Peter stood up in the midst of the disciples and said (now the number of names together was about one hundred and twenty): "Men, brethren, this Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was the guide of those who arrested Jesus, and who was numbered among us and had obtained a share in this ministry. Now this man bought a field with the reward of his iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the middle, and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, the field of blood."

units.la: EXposuit hucusque diuus Lucas, quid Apostoli in sua priuata causa post Christi è terris discessum fecerint, quibus obedientiam veram, animorum concordiam & preces assiduas tribuit. Sunt hæc verè salutaria exercitia, quibus & nos ad spiritum sanctum rite excipiendum præparari oportet, qui animam malignam ingredi non solet, nec à mundo percipi potest, qui eiusmodi studia contemnit & ridet. Porrò in præsenti primum apostolorum opus commemorare incipit, quo illi commisse sibi ecclesiæ ministerium publicè inchoauerunt. Est hoc diui Matthiæ in locum Iudæ proditoris & reprobi surrogatio. Quia enim duodenarium esse voluerat Christus apostolorum numerum, quos duodecim tribuum Israelis iudices constituerat, illum suppleri oportuit, ne Iudæ perfidia Christi instituto aliquid derogauisse videretur. Interim admonemur Apostolorum exemplo, hanc in ecclesia primam curam esse debere, vt ministri sint idonei. Quomodo enim credent in eum (inquit Paulus) de quo non audierunt? Quomodo autem audient absq; prædicante? Quomodo verò prædicabunt nisi missi fuerint? Rom.10. Et alibi idem Apostolus seipsum & Apollon & Cephas ministros Dei fuisse dicit,
units.tr: Up to this point Luke has set out what the apostles did in their own private affair after Christ's departure from the earth, and he ascribes to them true obedience, harmony of minds, and constant prayer. These are truly wholesome exercises, by which we too ought to be properly prepared to receive the Holy Spirit, who does not enter a malicious soul, nor can be grasped by the world, which scorns and mocks such pursuits. Now he begins to recount the first public work of the apostles, by which they openly began the ministry of the Church entrusted to them. This is the substitution of Matthias in the place of Judas, the traitor and reprobate. For since Christ had wished the number of apostles to be twelve, those whom he appointed as judges of the twelve tribes of Israel, it was necessary to fill that place, lest it seem that the treachery of Judas had detracted something from Christ's institution. Meanwhile we are reminded, by the example of the apostles, that in the Church the first care should be to have suitable ministers. For "how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard?" (says Paul) "And how will they hear without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?" Rom. 10. And elsewhere the same apostle says that he himself, Apollos and Cephas were ministers of God,

units.la: In ecclesia primā de ministris idoneis curaha beri debet. dicit per quos Corinthij crediderint. 1. Cor. 3. Nam licet solius Dei sit fidem largiri, & in illam spiritus sui virtute in animis hominum operetur (qua ratione Christi cultores Θεοδίδακτοι apud prophetam dicuntur, Isa. 54.) propter nos tamen externo verbi ministerio vt dignatur, cuius vsum & dignitatem in ecclesia asseri & retineri oportet. Quae causa est, quod & apud prophetas inter Dei beneficia idonei doctores primo loco numerantur, & Christus Apostolos Deum orare iubet, vt in messem suam operarios dignos & fideles extrudat. Matth. 9. Et Paulus alibi Christi maiestatem & fidelem pro sua ecclesia curam hoc vno argumento maxime demonstrat, quod ex alto dona sui spiritus largiatur, & alios quidem det Apostolos, alios vero Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios vero pastores ac doctores ad instaurationem sanctorum in opus administrationis, in aedificationem corporis sui. Ephes. 4. Debent horum meminisse, quicunque hodie in ecclesia Christi ius aliquod sibi vendicant, siue illi doctrinae antistites sint, siue politicum magistratum gerant, nec in hac parte omnium maxime necessaria ecclesiis desint, quin ita res omnes instituant, vt posteris quoque vera doctrinae praecepta integra & illaesa relinquant. Quo cumprimis pertinet scholarum & iuuentutis institutio, cuius praecipuam curam & prophetas olim in veteri Testamento, & postea Christianos Imperatores habuisse legimus. Quas quicunque vel negligentia vel ecclesiasticarum opum direptione dissipant, pro maximis ecclesiae hostibus censeri debent, & tam atrocis flagitij graues poenas Christo olim exoluent. Sed vt praesentis loci expositionem aggrediamur, mira diligentia historiae huius narrationem Lucas contexit: cuius hic praecipuus vsus est, vt apostolorum exemplo discamus, quid in ministris ecclesiae eligendis ac ordinandis praecipue obseruari conueniat.
units.tr: In the primitive Church, care must be taken over suitable ministers. (He says) through whom the Corinthians believed. 1 Cor. 3. For although the bestowing of faith belongs to God alone, and he works faith in men's minds by the power of his Spirit (for which reason the worshippers of Christ are called "taught by God" [Θεοδίδακτοι] by the prophet, Isa. 54), yet he is pleased to do so for our sake through the external ministry of the Word, whose use and dignity must be asserted and maintained in the Church. This is why, among the gifts of God, the prophets also list suitable teachers in the first place, and why Christ bids the apostles pray the Lord to thrust out faithful and fit labourers into his harvest. Matt. 9. And Paul, elsewhere, demonstrates the majesty of Christ and his faithful care for his Church chiefly by this one argument: that from on high he bestows the gifts of his Spirit, and some indeed he gives as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of his body. Eph. 4. Those who today claim any right in the Church of Christ, whether they are leaders of doctrine or hold the civil magistracy, ought to remember these things; nor should those things be lacking in this respect, which are most necessary of all for the churches, so that they arrange all matters in such a way that they hand down the true precepts of doctrine whole and unharmed to posterity as well. To this especially belongs the instruction of schools and youth, to whose chief care we read that the prophets of the Old Testament, and afterwards Christian emperors, devoted themselves. Whoever wastes these, either through negligence or through plundering of church resources, ought to be counted among the greatest enemies of the Church, and will one day pay grievous penalties to Christ for so atrocious a crime. But to come to the exposition of the present passage: Luke weaves the narrative of this history with remarkable care; its chief use here is that, by the example of the apostles, we may learn what ought especially to be observed in choosing and ordaining ministers of the Church.

units.la: Orditur autem ab ecclesia, quae tunc temporis erat, descriptione. In diebus illis (inquit) quando vnanimiter collecti, spiritum sanctum expectabant, Petrus in medio discipulorum exurgens oratio- nem habere coepit, quarem ad omnes ex aequo pertinentem tractandam proposuit. Erat autem credentium numerus, cum nominatim censerentur, circiter centum & viginti. Hic vero & paucitas credentium in primitiua ecclesia, & Petrus apostolus nobis obseruandi veniunt. Etenim quoad eorum numerum, qui iam tum Christo & ecclesiae suae nomina dederant, neminem esse puto, cui non mirum videatur, tam paucos in vrbe tam celebri & populosa Christi cultores esse inuentos. Quid enim in illa intentatum reliquerat Christus? Nam vt ea omittamus, quae prophetae docendo, monendo & hortando egerunt, si quae ab eo tempore in illa vrbe facta sunt, consideres, quo Christus manifestari coepit, incredibilem illius gentis duritiem & pertinaciam deprehendemus. Christum praecesserat Ioannes Baptista, qui & doctrinae perspicuitate & vitae austeritate quosuis permouere poterat. Sed quam parum profecerit, res ipsa testatur. Mox ergo Christus insecutus est, qui doctrinae (quam nullo non dicendi genere ipsis gratiorem reddere studebat) miracula coniunxit, & tanta quidem, quae vel ipsis hostibus veritatis confessionem extorquere poterant. Certe Nicodemus fatetur, neminem, nisi a Deo missum, ea facere posse, quae Christum quotidie facere videbant. Iohan. 3. Et vulgo audita fuit multorum vox, dicentium: Christus cum venerit, num signa edet plura his, quam hic edidit? Iohan. 7. Taceo prodigia & signa, quae mortem Christi partim comitata, partim secuta fuerant, quae & militum immanissimorum animos emollire potuerunt. At post omnia haec in credentium censu non plures quam centum viginti reperiuntur, Luca teste veracissimo. Apparet in his diuina Christi Iesu potentia, qui ex pauculis hisce reliquiis (sicuti olim prophetae praedixerant) ecclesiam suam instauravit, quae intra paucos annos per totum orbem terrarum propagata est. Simul vero discamus humani ingenij duritiem & tantumnon incurabilem malitiam agnoscere, nec offendamur, si hodie quoque euangelij doctrinae paucissimos credere videamus. Hoc ipsum enim Isaias olim praeuidit, & proinde de redemptione per Christum peragenda concionaturus, exclamat: Quis credidit praedicationi nostrae? & brachium domini cui reuelatum est? Isa. 53. Et Christus gregem suum alloquens, ait: Ne timeas pusille grex, quia complacitum est patri vestro, dare vobis regnum. Luc. 12. Idem de nouissimis temporibus differens, eam tunc mundi formam fore testatur, vt Christus in aduentu suo fidem omnino nullam reperturus esse videri possit, Luc. 18.
units.tr: He begins with a description of the Church as it then was. "In those days" (he says), when they were gathered together with one accord and were waiting for the Holy Spirit, Peter, standing up in the midst of the disciples, began to speak, proposing a matter to be dealt with which pertained equally to all. Now the number of believers, when they were listed by name, was about one hundred and twenty. Here we must observe both the small number of believers in the primitive Church and the apostle Peter. For as to the number of those who had already given their names to Christ and his Church, I think there is no one who does not find it remarkable that so few worshippers of Christ were found in so famous and populous a city. For what had Christ left untried in that city? For, to leave aside what the prophets accomplished by teaching, admonishing and exhorting, if you consider what happened in that city from the time Christ began to be made manifest, you will find the incredible hardness and obstinacy of that nation. John the Baptist had gone before Christ, who could move anyone by the clarity of his teaching and the austerity of his life. But how little he profited the thing itself bears witness. Soon afterwards Christ followed, who joined to his teaching (which he took pains to make more agreeable to them by every kind of eloquence) miracles, and very great ones, which could wring a confession of the truth even from his enemies. Certainly Nicodemus confesses that no one could do the things which they saw Christ doing every day, unless he were sent from God. John 3. And the voice of many, saying, "When Christ comes, will he do more signs than these which this man has done?" was commonly heard. John 7. I pass over the portents and signs which partly accompanied and partly followed the death of Christ, and which were able to soften even the hearts of the most savage soldiers. Yet after all these things, in the number of believers no more than one hundred and twenty are found, as Luke, the most truthful witness, testifies. In these things the divine power of Jesus Christ appears, who from these few remnants (as the prophets had foretold long before) restored his Church, which within a few years was spread throughout the whole world. At the same time let us learn to recognise the hardness of the human mind and its almost incurable malice, and let us not be offended if today too we see very few believing the doctrine of the gospel. For Isaiah foresaw this very thing long ago, and, about to preach concerning the redemption to be accomplished through Christ, he cries out: "Who has believed our preaching? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Isa. 53. And Christ, addressing his flock, says: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." Luke 12. Speaking of the last times, he likewise testifies that the state of the world will then be such that Christ, at his coming, may seem likely to find no faith at all. Luke 18.

units.la: Grauis ergo illorum error est, qui de fide & fidei doctrina ex sectatorum multitudine siue paucitate pronunciant, quod hodie nimium frequens est. Atqui olim quoq; ea fuit mundi conditio, vt paucissimi semper veritatis doctrinam secuti sint. Vnus Noe cum suis prisco illo seculo diuersam ab alijs fidem & religionem sectatur, toto reliquo mundo ad superstitiones & impietatem dilapso. Sed illum nec suorum paucitas salute spoliat, nec aduersariorum multitudo damnat, imò omnibus pereuntibus saluatur, & Deum fidei suæ tum probatorem tum assertorem habet. Idem de Loto Sodomis agente dicimus. Quid quòd Elias vnus tam Baalitis quàm regi Achab & aulicis vniuersis sese in fidei & religionis causa opponit? 3.Reg. 18. Et Micheas solus cum quadringentis pseudoprophetis, quos etiam regis fauor protegebat, congreditur? 3.Reg.22. Quare ipsam potius veritatis doctrinam re spicere, quæ ex Dei ore progressa sacris literis continetur, non hominum authoritatem sequi conuenit, quando omnis homo mendax est, vnus autem Deus verax. Rom. 3.
units.tr: Grievous, therefore, is the error of those who pronounce about faith and the doctrine of faith from the multitude or the paucity of its adherents, which is far too common today. And yet in former times too the condition of the world was such that very few always followed the doctrine of truth. Noah alone, with his family, in that ancient age, held a faith and religion different from others, while the rest of the world had slipped into superstition and impiety. But neither the fewness of his own people deprived him of salvation, nor the multitude of his opponents condemned him; rather, while all others perish, he is saved, and he has God as both the examiner and the defender of his faith. We say the same of Lot, when he dwelt among the Sodomites. And what of the fact that Elijah alone set himself against the Baalites, against King Ahab and all his courtiers, in the cause of faith and religion? 1 Kings 18. Or that Micaiah alone contended with four hundred false prophets, whom even the king's favour protected? 1 Kings 22. Therefore it is fitting to look rather to the doctrine of truth itself, which proceeded from the mouth of God and is contained in the sacred letters, and not to follow the authority of men, since every man is a liar, but God alone is true. Rom. 3.

units.la: Operæpretium vero est, vt Petrum quoque consideremus, qui inter discipulos assurgens, causam hanc publicè tractandam proponit. Hinc enim primatus sui, imò tyrannidis potius, patrocinium quærunt Romani pontifices, vt ex alijs etiam locis, qui Petro alicuius prærogatiuæ vel primatus speciem inter Apostolos tribuere videntur. Perinde autem mihi faciunt, vt qui in fluuijs vorticosis & profundis periclitantur. Vt enim illi quiduis obuium arripiunt: ita isti vndique captant, quo primatus sui dignitatem, iam conquassatam & vniuersalem ruinam minantem, instaurare possint. Hac ratione vni Petro claues regni cœlorum vendicant, quas tamen omnibus apostolis simul datas esse ex Iohan. 20. capite, euidentissimè constat. Ita vni Petro ouium Christi curam, ceu principi, commissam esse contendunt, nec animaduertunt, quanta iniuria reliquis Apostolis fiat, quasi illos non ouium suarum, sed porcorum aut asinorum pastores Christus fecerit. Ad eundem modum, cum Petrum audiunt primum in ecclesia sermonem fecisse, mox illum & Christi vicarium, & ecclesiæ caput, omniumq; Apostolorum principem fuisse fingunt. Ac longius progressi, omnem istum honorem sibijpsis, ceu legitimis & ordinarijs Petri successoribus, transcribunt. Sed quàm vana hæc sint & friuola, res ipsa declarat. Nec enim, vt ecclesiæ princeps & reliquorum Apostolorum dominus, quicquam ex suo arbitrio præscribit Petrus, sed in medio discipulorum, quibus se æqualem esse agnoscebat, rem maximi momenti omnibus tractandam proponit, in qua tractatione vnicuiuis liberam secundum spiritus suggestionem dicendi & agendi facultatem permittit. Et quod primus ipse loquitur, singulari spiritus sancti suggestione factum est, qui exemplum gratiæ, quod in Petro à turpi lapsu restituto Christus edidit, hac etiam ratione illustrius fecit. Quòd verò ipsum dicentem reliqui patienter audiunt, vnanimitatis signum est, quam supra illis Lucas tribuit, & non tam propter primatus dignitatem fit, quàm propter ordinis conseruationem, sine quo nihil vel in ecclesia vel repub. integrum subsistere potest. Quare & Paulus in ecclesia omnia decenter & diligenti ordinis legitimi obseruatione fieri iuber. 1.Cor.14. Quòd verò apostolorum omnium conditionem attinet, eosdem omnes æquales siue pares facit, & qui alibi se minimum apostolorum nominat, ad vita suæ prioris indignitatem respiciens, idem de ministerio loquens, seipsum Petro coniungere non veretur, dicens: Qui efficax fuit in Petro ad apostolatum circuncifionis, idem efficax fuit in me erga gentes. Galat.2. Et apud Corinthios factiosa Paulinorum, Petrinorum & Apollinianorum nomina extirpare volens, ait: Quis igitur Paulus? quis Apollo? nisi ministri, per quos credidistis, & quantum vnicuiq; dominus dedit? 1.Cor.3. Agnoscit hoc ipse Petrus, qui paulò post de Iuda loquens, ipsum partem ministerij huius ecclesiastici sustinuisse testatur. Quòd si verò partem illius sustinuit Iudas, quæ erit inscitia totum Petro vendicare? Nisi forte Petrum dicamus in gratiam improbi proditoris adulari, & quod ad se solum pertinebat, in filium perditionis transferre voluisse? Sed quid verbis opus est? quando constat, Christum Iesum ambitiosam inter apostolos primatus assectationem non semel magna cum seueritate redarguisse. Nota sunt, quæ in hanc sententiam extant, Matth.18. & 20. Luc.22. Iohan.13. Et Petrus ecclesiarum pastores graviter monet, ne sibijpsis aliquod dominium vendicent in ecclesiam, quæ Christi patrimonium & quasi sors hæreditaria ab ipso nominatur. 1.Pet.5. Quem enim tantæ authoritatis esse putabimus, vt illi imperium in gregem illum pretiosum decernamus, qui Christi sanguine redemptus est? Quòd si ipsi gregi dominico nemo principum huius seculi more dominari debet, quanto absurdius erit, si dominium quoddam inter sese constituant, quorum vna & eadem debet esse in illo grege pascendo authoritas? Quid ergo aliud tam pertinaci primatus assectatione euincunt Romani pontifices, quàm quòd se Christi præceptorum parum memores, & nihil minus quàm legitimos Petri successores esse produnt? Sed omissis illis ad Petri orationem transeamus. Constat ea duabus partibus. Prima offendiculo medetur, quod ex horribili Iudæ lapsu in sim⁠plicium & rudiorum animis oboriri poterat. Quando enim Christum Iesum ab Iuda proditum, & illum ipsum postea corpore & anima miserrimè periisse videbant, proclive erat, vel de Christi omni⁠scientia dubitare, vel omnem apostolorum ordinem vnà cum ipsorum doctrina suspectum habere. Non temere igitur tanto malo Petrus initio suæ orationis occurrit. Altera vero parte discipulos hortatur, vt alium quendam in Iudæ locum surrogent, ne Christi instituto illius perfidia aliquid de⁠cessisse videretur.
units.tr: It is worth considering Peter too, who, rising up among the disciples, puts this matter forward to be dealt with publicly. The Roman pontiffs seek from this passage the patronage of his primacy, or rather of his tyranny, and likewise from other places which seem to grant Peter some appearance of prerogative or primacy among the apostles. But they act toward me like men who are in danger in swirling and deep rivers: just as those men grab at whatever comes to hand, so these men snatch at everything from every side, so that they may prop up the dignity of their primacy, now shaken and threatening universal ruin. In this way they claim the keys of the kingdom of heaven for Peter alone, though it is quite clear from John 20 that they were given to all the apostles together. Likewise they contend that the care of Christ's sheep was entrusted to Peter alone, as to a prince, and they do not notice what an injury is done to the other apostles, as if Christ had made them shepherds not of his sheep but of swine or asses. In the same way, when they hear that Peter made the first speech in the Church, they immediately imagine that he was both Christ's vicar and the head of the Church and prince of all the apostles. Going further, they transfer all this honour to themselves, as the lawful and ordinary successors of Peter. But how empty and frivolous these claims are, the thing itself shows. For Peter does not, as prince of the Church and lord of the other apostles, prescribe anything at his own pleasure. Instead, in the midst of the disciples, whom he acknowledged as his equals, he puts a matter of the greatest moment before them all to be dealt with, and in that discussion he allows each one the freedom to speak and act according to the prompting of the Spirit. And that he himself speaks first was done by a singular prompting of the Holy Spirit, who by this means also made more illustrious the example of grace which Christ displayed in Peter, restored from his shameful fall. That the others listen patiently while he speaks is a sign of the unanimity which Luke attributes to them above, and this is done not so much on account of the dignity of primacy as for the preservation of order, without which nothing, either in the Church or in the commonwealth, can stand whole. Therefore Paul also orders that everything in the Church be done decently and with careful observance of lawful order (1 Cor. 14). As for the condition of all the apostles, he makes them all equal or peers. And he who elsewhere calls himself the least of the apostles, looking back at the unworthiness of his former life, when speaking of the ministry, does not hesitate to join himself to Peter, saying: "He who was effective in Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision was also effective in me toward the Gentiles" (Gal. 2). And among the Corinthians, wishing to root out the factious names of Paulines, Petrines and Apollonians, he says: "Who then is Paul? Who is Apollos? Only ministers, through whom you believed, and as the Lord gave to each" (1 Cor. 3). Peter himself acknowledges this, for shortly afterwards, speaking of Judas, he testifies that Judas had shared in the part of this ecclesiastical ministry. But if Judas shared in part of it, what folly would it be to claim the whole for Peter? Unless perhaps we say that Peter was flattering the wicked traitor, and wished to transfer to the son of perdition what pertained to himself alone? But why use words? It is established that Christ Jesus more than once rebuked, with great severity, the ambitious pursuit of primacy among the apostles. The passages which stand on this point are well known: Matthew 18 and 20, Luke 22, John 13. And Peter earnestly warns the ministers of the churches not to claim any lordship for themselves over the Church, which Christ names his patrimony and, as it were, his hereditary portion (1 Pet. 5). For whom shall we think so authoritative that we should grant him dominion over that precious flock which was redeemed by the blood of Christ? And if no one ought to lord it over the Lord's own flock in the manner of the princes of this world, how much more absurd would it be if they set up a certain lordship among themselves, when the authority over feeding that flock ought to be one and the same for all?
