What else, then, do the Roman pontiffs prove by such stubborn pursuit of primacy, than that they are forgetful of Christ's precepts, and that they show themselves to be no lawful successors of Peter at all? But setting those aside, let us pass to Peter's speech. It consists of two parts. The first remedies a stumbling block which could arise in the minds of the simple and less learned from the horrible fall of Judas. For when they saw that Christ Jesus had been betrayed by Judas, and that Judas himself afterwards had perished most wretchedly in body and soul, it was easy for them either to doubt Christ's omniscience, or to regard the whole order of apostles, together with their teaching, with suspicion. So it is not without reason that Peter, at the very beginning of his speech, meets such a great evil. In the second part he urges the disciples to appoint someone else in Judas's place, lest it seem that Christ's institution had been diminished by that man's treachery.

units.la: Priorem partem à scripturæ sacræ testimonio orditur, quo non obscurè æternum diuinæ prouiden⁠tiæ decretum producit: quæ validissima ratio est declinandi offendicula, si nimirum, nihil temere, sed ex Dei decreto omnia facta esse, homines intelligant. Quare ait: Viri fratres, oportuit impleri scri⁠pturam hanc, quam prædixit spiritus sanctus per os Dauidis de Iuda, qui fuit dux iis, qui compre⁠henderunt Iesum. Quorum hic mihi sensus esse videtur: Nolo fratres atroci Iudæ flagitio & eius⁠dem horribili exitu quenquam ex vobis offendi, quasi hæc vel temere facta sint, vel Dei filius, ab im⁠probo homine circumuentus, illius dolos & insidias effugere non potuerit. Nolo item hæc aliquem ita accipere, quasi nostro ordini & sanctissimæ functioni, quam ex Christi mandato sustinemus, scelerati hominis perfidia quicquam derogare debeat. Hæc enim vt ita fierent, Deo visum est, cuius hoc erat consilium & decretum, vt dilectus filius suus à discipulo, eoq; non vulgari, proderetur. Nec id nos la⁠tere voluit. Nota sunt enim, quæ Psalmo 41. leguntur, quorum ipse Christus in vltima cœna nos com⁠monefecit, dicens: Qui mecum edit panem, sustulit aduersum me calcaneum suum. Nunc dico vobis priusquam fiat, vt cum factum fuerit, credatis quòd ego sum. Ioan. 13. Quare in Dei prouidentiam oculis coniectis, ipsius bonitatem & veritatem admiremini, nec vos offendat, quæ ipsius & decreto & iusta permissione facta sunt.
units.tr: He begins the first part from the testimony of holy Scripture, by which he clearly brings forward the eternal decree of divine providence. This is a most powerful reason for avoiding stumbling blocks, if men understand that nothing has been done rashly, but that all things have been done by the decree of God. Therefore he says: "Brothers, it was necessary for this Scripture to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was the guide for those who seized Jesus." The sense of this, as I take it, is: "Brothers, I do not want any of you to be offended at the atrocious crime of Judas and his horrible end, as if these things had happened by chance, or as if the Son of God, circumvented by a wicked man, had been unable to escape his tricks and snares. Nor do I want anyone to take this as if the wickedness of a criminal could detract anything from our order and from the most holy office which we exercise by Christ's command. For it seemed good to God that these things should happen in this way, since it was his plan and decree that his beloved Son should be betrayed by a disciple, and indeed by no ordinary disciple. Nor did he wish to conceal this from us. For the words in Psalm 41 are well known, and Christ himself warned us of them at the last supper, saying: 'He who eats bread with me has lifted his heel against me. Now I tell you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am he' (John 13). Therefore, fix your eyes on the providence of God, and admire his goodness and truth, and do not be offended by what has been done both by his decree and by his just permission.

units.la: Nemo tamen hæc intelligat, quasi Petrus Iudæ immane facinus excusare, omnemque illius cul⁠pam in ipsum Deum reijcere velit. Nec enim ea diuinæ prouidentiæ, quæ omnia gubernat, ratio est, vt nostrorum scelerum culpa in Deum authorem recidat, quando quæcunque male faciunt homi⁠nes, non ideo ab illis fiunt, vt Dei decretum exequantur, sed vt propriæ malitiæ, desiderijs & cupidi⁠tatibus satisfaciant. Dei quidem hoc decretum fuisse constat, vt filius ipsius, Iesus Christus, discipu⁠li fraude & perfidia proditus, in hostium manus deueniret, inde ab illis capitis damnatus in crucem ageretur, vbi corporis sui victima mundi peccatum expiaret. At si Iudam spectes, proditionis il⁠lius ministrum, is in tanto facinore nihil minus quàm Dei decretum & humani generis redemptionem ob oculos habuit, sed auaritiæ scino excæcatus & extimulatus, primò quidem furti (vt Ioan. 12. ca⁠pite, legitur) deinde etiam proditionis crimine sese polluit. Eadem Annæ & Caiaphæ, Pilati denique & aliorum omnium ratio est, quos mortis Christi executores fuisse euangelica historia testatur. Ple⁠ni sunt huius generis exemplorum sacræ scripturæ libri, quibus vt grauiter peccent homines, admone⁠mur, dum ea faciunt, quæ fieri Deus decreuit, quia cæcis & illicitis corruptæ naturæ affectibus im⁠pulsi faciunt. Quis obsecro tam vecors est, vt Josephum sine singulari diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio in Ægyptum peruenire putet, quando de posteritatis Abrahamicæ in Ægyptum descensu, Deus ipsum Abrahamum iam olim admonuisse legitur? Quis item non agnoscat in toto illo negotio admirabi⁠lem Dei sapientiam, quæ singula & prudentissimè & vtilissimè gubernauit? Num verò idcirco Io⁠sephi fratres culpa liberamus, qui inuidia moti, fratrem melius de se meritum vendidere? Imò omne hoc negotium Josephi verbis interpretamur: Vos cogitastis aduersum me malum, at Deus cogitauit idipsum in bonum, vt faceret quemadmodum hodie apparet, vt scilicet seruaret in vita populum mul⁠tum. Genef. 50. Sed & similium casuum exempla quotidiana experientia suppeditat. Quis enim à la⁠trone viatorem sine diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio occidi dicat, quando & dies vitæ nostræ & pilos ca⁠pitis nostri apud Deum numeratos esse scimus? Psalm. 90. Matth. 10. Attamen quia improbo af⁠fectu impulsore tantum facinus latro committit, in illo peccati culpa merito hærere dicitur, & eiusdem pœnas iure exoluit. Nemo igitur in Dei prouidentia scelerum suorum excusationem quærat, nec Deum peccatorum authorem facere audeat, sed ex illius meditatione consolationes petamus, quibus contra horribiles, qui in vita hac occurrunt, easus præmuniamur. Et huc Petrum quoque respexisse certò constat, in cuius verbis alia quoq; nobis obseruanda restant.
units.tr: Yet let no one understand these things as if Peter wished to excuse Judas's monstrous crime and to throw all his guilt back upon God himself. For it is not the case of divine providence, which governs all things, that the guilt of our wicked deeds should fall back upon God as its author, since whatever wicked things men do are not done by them in order to carry out God's decree, but in order to satisfy their own malice, desires and lusts. It is certain that this was God's decree: that his Son, Jesus Christ, should be betrayed by the fraud and treachery of a disciple, should fall into the hands of enemies, and should then be condemned to death by them and led to the cross, where as a victim of his own body he would expiate the sin of the world. But if you look at Judas, the agent of that betrayal, in so great a crime he had in view nothing less than God's decree and the redemption of the human race. Rather, blinded and goaded by the itch of greed, he first defiled himself with theft (as is read in John 12) and then also with the crime of betrayal. The same is true of Annas and Caiaphas, of Pilate finally, and of all the others whom the gospel history attests to have been the executors of Christ's death. The books of holy Scripture are full of examples of this kind, by which we are warned that men sin gravely when they do the things which God decreed should be done, because they do them impelled by the blind and unlawful affections of corrupted nature. Who, I beg you, is so mad as to think that Joseph came into Egypt without the singular counsel of divine providence, since it is read that God had long ago warned Abraham himself of the descent of Abraham's posterity into Egypt? Who likewise does not acknowledge in that whole affair the wonderful wisdom of God, which governed each thing most wisely and most usefully? Do we then, for that reason, free Joseph's brothers from blame, who, moved by envy, sold their brother who had deserved better of them? Rather, we interpret this whole affair in Joseph's words: "You planned evil against me, but God planned the same thing for good, to bring about what appears today, that is, to save a great people alive" (Gen. 50). Daily experience also supplies examples of similar cases. For who would say that a traveller is killed by a robber without the counsel of divine providence, when we know that both the days of our life and the hairs of our head are numbered before God (Ps. 90; Matt. 10)? Nevertheless, because the robber commits so great a crime, impelled by a wicked desire, he is rightly said to cling to the guilt of the sin, and he justly pays its penalties. Therefore let no one seek an excuse for his sins in divine providence, nor dare to make God the author of sins. Rather, let us seek from its contemplation consolations by which we may be fortified against the horrible chances which occur in this life. And it is certain that Peter also had this in view, and other things remain for us to observe in his words.

units.la: Et primò quidem memorabili exemplo docemur, quanta sit piarum precum efficacia. Supra enim monuit Lucas, apostolos vnanimiter in precibus perseuerauisse. Quibus quid effectum sit, modò cernitur. Petrus enim, qui paulò ante veram regni Christi rationem ignorabat, & de articulo restitutionis ipsius ineptam cum alijs quæstionem mouerat, repente ex scripturis concionari incipit, quas & propriß ime allegat, & dexterrime interpretatur. Adeò verum est, quod Apostolus monet: Si cui vestrũ deest sapientia, postulet ab eo qui dat, nempe Deo, & dabitur ei. Iac.1.
units.tr: And first of all we are taught by a memorable example how effective pious prayers are. Luke had already noted above that the apostles persevered together in prayer. What came of it can now be seen. Peter, who a little before had not understood the true nature of Christ's kingdom and had raised with the others an unseemly question about the restoration of that kingdom, suddenly begins to preach from the Scriptures, which he cites most aptly and interprets most skilfully. So true is what the Apostle advises: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of him who gives, namely God, and it shall be given him." James 1.

units.la: Deinde Petri exemplo admonemur, nihil in ecclesia sine scripturarum authoritate instituì debere. Vt enim in bene constitutis rebus pub. certa leges sunt, adeoq; codex legum habetur authenticus, in quem nemini aliquid iuris permittitur, vt pro suo arbitrio quicquam in illo vel auferat vel addat, aut etiam contra illius præscriptum in repub. aliquid statuat: ita ecclesiæ suæ veteris & noui Testamenti libros Christus tradidit, quibus regni cœlorum mysteria & beatæ æternumq; viuendi leges continentur. Ex his ergo consilia omnia deduci, & ex ijsdem sermonum omnium in ecclesia argumenta sumi debent. Nec quisquam eo loco est aut ordine, vt sibi quicquam ab his diuersum statuendi ius esse putet. Olim equidem regibus liber ille tradebatur, non vt hunc suo imperio subiectum putarent, sed vt inde bene regnandi leges peterent. Deut.17. Et prophetæ hoc mandato astringebantur, vt conciones suas ex ore domini sumerent (Ezech.3. & 33.) quod nos non aliud quàm scripturas interpretari possumus, quia per has, tanquam os quoddam, suæ voluntatis mysteria nobis reuelat. Sed & ipse Christus frequenter ex scripturis concionatur, & libros sacros contrectare, & locos ex illis petitos populo exponere non dedignatur, cuius rei exemplum in schola Nazarethana præbuit. Luc.4. Præceptoris ergo exemplum Petrus imitatus, ex scripturis dicendi initium facit. Quem vtinam illi quoq; imitarentur, qui cum Petri successione glorientur, multa tamen cum scripturis ex diametro pugnantia, non alia quàm humana authoritate, ecclesijs obtrudere audent.
units.tr: Next, Peter's example warns us that nothing should be established in the Church without the authority of Scripture. In well-ordered commonwealths there are fixed laws, and an authentic code of laws is kept, into which no one is permitted to add or remove anything at his own discretion, or to enact anything in the state contrary to its prescriptions. In the same way Christ handed over to his Church the books of the Old and New Testaments, in which the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven and the laws of blessed and eternal life are contained. All counsels, therefore, ought to be derived from these, and all arguments of all sermons in the Church ought to be drawn from them. No one holds a position or rank so that he may think he has any right to decree anything different from these. Formerly, indeed, that book was handed to kings, not so that they might regard it as subject to their own power, but so that they might seek from it the laws for ruling well. Deut. 17. The prophets too were bound by this command to take their sermons from the mouth of the Lord (Ezek. 3 and 33), and we can do no other than interpret the Scriptures, since through them, as through a kind of mouth, he reveals to us the mysteries of his will. But Christ himself also frequently preaches from the Scriptures, and he does not disdain to handle the sacred books and to expound to the people passages taken from them; he gave an example of this in the synagogue at Nazareth. Luke 4. Peter, then, following the example of his Teacher, makes a beginning of his speech from the Scriptures. Would that those also would imitate him who boast of their succession from Peter, yet dare to thrust upon the churches many things utterly at odds with the Scriptures, on no other authority than human authority.

units.la: Præterea insigni elogio scripturas Petrus ornat, cum illarum authorem spiritum sanctum dicit, qui per os Dauidis ista promulgare voluerit. Idem alibi fatetur, quando Christi spiritu prophetas afflatos fuisse & illius instinctu oracula edidisse scribit. 1. Pet. 1. Et 2. Pet. 1. Nec aliud Paulus sentit, qui scripturam θεόπνευστον, id est, diuinitus inspiratam, appellare non veretur. 2. Tim. 3. Vsus vero horum est, vt scripturæ dignitate & authoritate cognita, Dei verba agnoscamus, quæ in illa traduntur, nec nobis permissum putemus illius præceptis quocunq; modo contradicere.
units.tr: Moreover, Peter adorns the Scriptures with a distinguished commendation, when he says that the Holy Spirit is their author, who willed to publish these things through the mouth of David. He says the same elsewhere, when he writes that the prophets were inspired by the Spirit of Christ and uttered oracles at his prompting. 1 Pet. 1, and 2 Pet. 1. Paul thinks no differently, who does not hesitate to call Scripture theopneustos [θεόπνευστον], that is, divinely inspired. 2 Tim. 3. The use of these things is that, once we recognise the dignity and authority of Scripture, we should acknowledge the words of God that are delivered in it, and not think it permitted to us to contradict its precepts in any way.

units.la: Pergit autem in prima orationis parte apostolus, & Iudæ dignitatem, quæ illi antequam exciderat cum reliquis apostolis communis erat, diligenter commemorat. Nam ait: Qui cooptatus erat in numerum nostrum, & sortitus erat partem ministerij huius. Cogitaret enim aliquis, Iudam inter apostolos quidem fuisse numeratum, sed non alia causa quàm vt numerum impleret, homo alioqui otiosus & nullius momenti. Sed occurrit Petrus, qui illum non tantùm ex apostolorum numero fuisse, sed eidem ministerij quoq; partem obtigisse dicit. Idem Euangelistæ testantur, dum illis Iudam connumerant, qui à Christo adhuc in terris agente ad prædicandum emissi, & miraculorum virtute instructi fuerunt, qui q; ad Christum reuersi felicem legationis suæ successum cum gaudio narrauerunt, Matth.10. Marc.3. Luc.6. & 9. Et tam abest, vt ab illorum numero vspiam secernatur Iudas, vt tunc quoq; ex illo fuisse ab Euangelistis dicatur, quando immane ipsius facinus, quo Christum prodidit, commemorant. Marc.14.
units.tr: The Apostle, moreover, continues in the first part of his speech, and carefully recalls the dignity of Judas, which he had shared with the other apostles before he fell away. For he says: "who was numbered among us and had obtained a part of this ministry." For someone might think that Judas was indeed counted among the apostles, but only so that the number would be filled, a man otherwise idle and of no importance. But Peter meets this by saying that he was not only of the number of the apostles but also had obtained a share in this same ministry. The Evangelists also bear witness to this, when they count Judas among the Twelve, who, while Christ was still living on earth, were sent out to preach and were furnished with the power of miracles, and who returned to Christ and joyfully reported the happy success of their mission. Matt. 10; Mark 3; Luke 6 and 9. And so far is Judas from being set apart anywhere from their number, that he is even said by the Evangelists to have belonged to it at the very time when they record his monstrous crime, by which he betrayed Christ. Mark 14.

units.la: Quam verò causam esse dicemus, quòd toties tamq; diligens huius rei mentio & antea facta est, & nunc quoq; à Petro repetitur? Num verò vel Iudæ improbo spiritus sanctus adulari, vel apostolorum ordinem hac labe inficere & contaminare voluit? Nequaquam. Imò aliud docet obseruatu & dignißimum & maximè necessarium: ne videlicet excellentißimorum hominum vitijs offendamur, nec propter illa omnem illorum conditionem temere damnemus. Quod in verbi ministrorum delictis multi nimium inepte faciunt. Vbi enim illos fædè prolapsos vident, in quibus paulò ante doctrinæ syncericatem cum prudentia & forti Christi veritatem afferendi constantia coniunctam admirati sunt, non contenti illorum vitijs succensuisse, in totum ministrorum ordinem ora laxant, omnes in vniuersum hypocritas & nebulones esse clamant, & vlterius progressi, doctrinam quoq; in dubium vocare non verentur. Quia ergo Christus Iesus verbi sui ministros homines fore, & pro humanæ infirmitatis ratione interdum grauissimè lapsuros præuidebat, ne quis illorum vitijs offensus, euaneuangelij doctrinam in vniuersum damnaret, apostolorum vitijs & in primis horrendo Iudæ lapsu cauere voluit. Etenim si ab omni labe apostoli alieni fuissent, non immerito de illorum doctrina hodie dubitaremus, quos non raro turpiter peccare cernimus. At quia nec ambitionis crimen, quod non semel in illis Christus reprehendit, nec turpem Petri Christum abnegantis lapsum, nec immane Iudæ proditoris scelus, quicquam euangelij doctrinæ derogasse constat, nimium profecto ineptus est, qui nostri seculi ministrorum vitijs ita offenditur, vt propter illa veritatis doctrinã mendacij accuset. Atqui nullus hominum ordo est, qui non bonos pariter & malos habeat. Et si apostolorum ordini propter Iudæ lapsum nihil decedit (instauratur enim Matthiæ successione) quanto minus per hunc apostolorum doctrinæ aliquid derogari potuit? Neq; hæc ideo dicimus, vt verbi ministris licenter peccandi fenestram aperiamus. Scimus enim eo grauiores scelerum pœnas ipsos daturos esse, quo grauius & nocentius est offendiculum, cuius ipsi auctores sunt. Sed infirmis consulimus, ne cum ministrorum vita improba, veritatis salutarem doctrinam magno suo malo abijciant. Quod ipsum Christus de Iudæorum scribis loquens, admonuit his verbis: In cathedra Mosis sedent scribæ & pharisæi, Omnia ergo quæcunq; iusserint vos seruare, seruate & facite: secundum opera vero eorum nolite facere: dicunt enim, & non faciunt. Matth. 23.
units.tr: But what cause shall we say there is that this matter has been mentioned so often and so carefully, both earlier and now again by Peter? Did the Holy Spirit wish to flatter the wicked Judas, or to stain and defile the order of the apostles with this blot? By no means. Rather, he teaches something that is both most worthy of observation and most necessary: namely, that we should not be offended by the faults of the most excellent men, nor rashly condemn their whole condition on account of those faults. Many people do this far too foolishly with the failings of the ministers of the Word. When they see those men fallen shamefully, men whom a little before they had admired for the purity of their teaching, joined with prudence and with a steadfast courage in proclaiming the truth of Christ, they are not content to be angry at their faults; they open their mouths against the whole ministry, cry out that all ministers without exception are hypocrites and scoundrels, and, going further still, do not hesitate to call even the doctrine itself into doubt. Because Christ Jesus foresaw that the ministers of his Word would be men, and that, according to the frailty of human nature, they would sometimes fall grievously, he wished to guard against anyone being offended by the faults of the apostles, and especially by the dreadful fall of Judas, and so condemning the doctrine of the gospel as a whole. For if the apostles had been free of every stain, we would perhaps rightly doubt their doctrine today, seeing that we often observe them sinning shamefully. But since it is clear that neither the crime of ambition, which Christ more than once rebuked in them, nor Peter's shameful fall in denying Christ, nor the monstrous wickedness of Judas the traitor, has detracted anything from the doctrine of the gospel, he is truly very foolish who is so offended by the faults of the ministers of our age that he accuses the doctrine of truth of falsehood on account of them. Yet there is no order of men that does not contain both good and bad alike. And if nothing was taken from the order of the apostles because of Judas's fall (for it was restored by the succession of Matthias), how much less could anything have been taken away from the apostles' doctrine through him? We do not say this so that we may open a window for ministers of the Word to sin freely. For we know that they will pay the heavier penalties for their crimes, the more gravely and harmfully the stumbling-block is one whose authors they themselves are. But we are looking after the weak, lest, on account of the wicked life of ministers, they cast away to their great harm the saving doctrine of truth. Christ himself warned of this when he spoke of the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews in these words: "The scribes and the Pharisees sit in the seat of Moses. Therefore whatever they bid you observe, observe and do; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not." Matt. 23.

units.la: Deinde alij offendiculo horum obseruatio medetur. Communis enim hæc fidelium Christi adeo, totius ecclesiæ fors est, vt domesticorum insidijs, maximè petantur. A fratre germano & uterino pius Abel cæditur, Esauum hostem acerrimum Iacob experitur, Ioseph à fratribus venditur. Et Moses Israelitas fratres, quorum causa Ægypti opes & delicias reliquerat, ipsis Ægyptijs fere inhumaniores sentit. Dauides item de illorum insidijs maximè conqueritur, qui aliquando intima familiaritas ei ipsi coniuncti fuerant. Psal. 55. 41. & c. Et quotidie experimur illud Christi: Inimici hominis domesti ci ipsius. Matth. 10. Atqui multos ista offendunt, qui suorum animos ab ipsis abalienari molestè ferunt, & finistrè multa de ea doctrina cogitare incipiunt, quam dissensionum & dissidiorum causam præcipuam esse suspicantur. Vt interim de illis nihil dicam, qui priorum mores tam duros & asperos esse putant, vt nemo ipsis diu amicus esse possit. Caeterum omnibus istis unicum hoc exemplum occurrit, quo filium Dei, summum mansuetudinis & humilitatis exemplar, à discipulo intimo & domestico proditum fuisse docemur. Quid ergo de hominis ingenio nobis ultra pollicebimur? Velnum rem indignam putabimus, vt eam experiamur fortem, quam filius Dei nostri causa subire dignatus est?
units.tr: Next, the observation of this remedies the stumbling-block for others. For this lot is common to the faithful of Christ and to the whole Church, that they are assailed especially by the plots of their own household. The godly Abel is slain by his own brother, born of the same mother; Jacob experiences Esau as a most bitter enemy; Joseph is sold by his brothers. And Moses finds the Israelites, his brothers, for whose sake he had left the wealth and delights of Egypt, almost more inhumane than the Egyptians themselves. David too laments most of all the plots of those who had once been most intimately bound to him in friendship. Ps. 55; 41, etc. And every day we experience that saying of Christ: "A man's foes will be those of his own household." Matt. 10. Yet many are offended by these things, grieving that their minds are estranged from their own people, and they begin to think unfavourably about that doctrine which they suspect is the chief cause of quarrels and divisions. To say nothing for now of those who think that the characters of their predecessors were so harsh and rough that no one could long remain their friend. But for all these there is this one example which comes to mind, by which we are taught that the Son of God, the highest model of gentleness and humility, was betrayed by an intimate and household disciple. What further promise, then, shall we make about the nature of man? Or shall we think it an unworthy thing to experience that lot which the Son of God deigned to undergo for our sake?

units.la: Sed ad Petrum redeamus, qui vt Iudæ priorem dignitatem & scelus exposuit, it eiusdem horrendum exitum graphicè depingit, & quasi spectandum oculis subijcit: non quidem, vt infelicis hominis recordatione animum odio flagrantem exatiet, sed vt atrocis exempli memoria Dei timorem & pietatis verè studium in omnium animis accendat. Nec alienum ab instituto erat huius memi-nisse, quando de noua apostolo eligendo consultabatur: vt inde in diligentem sui muneris considerationem & ardens illud obeundi studium abriperentur. Dicit ergo: Et is quidem possedit agrum ex mercede iniquitatis, suspensus, crepuit medius, & effusa sunt omnia viscera eius. Et innotuit omnibus habitantibus Hierosolymis: ita vt vocatus sit ager ille propria illorum lingua Acceldama, id est, ager sanguinis. Prodest autem singula hæc ordine, quo contigerunt, inspicere. Nam vt Euangelistæ tradunt, vbi Iudas Christum Pilato traditum vidit, scelerisi pœnitentia ductus, ad sacerdotes reuertitur, scelus suum fatetur, & pecuniam proditionis nefandæ pretium reddit. Ab illis verò delusus, & cum indignatione reiectus, pecuniam in templum abijcit, ac inde se proripiens laqueo gulam sibi frangit. Sacerdotes, quia pecuniam nec in templo sparsam relinquere bonestè poterant, nec intra templi thesauros reponere audebant, quam pretium sanguinis esse nouerant, ex ea agrum figuli emunt in peregrinorum sepulturam, nimirum hoc opere immane scelus expiaturi, cuius fuerant paulò ante authores. At hoc pacto sempiternam scelerus infamiam sibijpsis conscisculunt, dum diuina prouidentia fit, vt ager ex pecunia sanguinis denominatus, de illorum nefando flagitio testetur. Hunc vero agrum ipsum Iudam possedisse Petrus dicit, tum quia ipsius pecunia emptus erat, tum quia ad Iudam non minima infamis illius & ignominiosæ memoriæ pars redibat. Porrò in his primò æstuantis in Iuda conscientiæ dolores animo concipe, quos atrocissimos fuisse constat, adeoq; inferni cruciatibus intolerabiliores, quando & pecuniæ non contemptum modo, sed odium quoq; auarissimo homini extorquere potuerunt, & ad peccati confessionem adigere, quem Christus in Cœna frustra
units.tr: But let us return to Peter, who, having set out Judas' former dignity and crime, now vividly describes his dreadful end and places it, as it were, before our eyes. He does this not to satisfy our minds, inflamed with hatred, by recalling the unhappy man, but so that the memory of a horrible example may kindle in everyone's mind the fear of God and a true zeal for godliness. Nor was it out of place for the purpose of his speech to recall this when a new apostle was being chosen, so that men might be drawn to careful consideration of their own office and to that ardent eagerness to perform it. He therefore says: "And this man indeed possessed a field with the reward of iniquity, and falling headlong he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, the field of blood." It is useful to look at these things one by one, in the order in which they happened. For as the Evangelists relate, when Judas saw that Christ had been handed over to Pilate, driven by remorse for his crime he returned to the priests, confessed his sin, and gave back the money, the price of his accursed betrayal. But they mocked him and rejected him with scorn, so he threw the money into the temple, and then, hurrying away, broke his throat with a noose. The priests, since they could not decently leave the money lying in the temple, nor dared to put it back among the treasures of the temple, because they knew it was the price of blood, bought with it a field of the potter as a burial place for strangers, plainly intending by this work to atone for the monstrous crime of which a little before they had been the authors. Yet in this way they brought upon themselves an everlasting infamy, since by divine providence it came about that the field, named from the money of blood, bore witness to their unspeakable wickedness. Peter says that Judas himself possessed this field, both because it had been bought with his money and because no small part of that infamous and disgraceful memory fell back upon Judas. Moreover, first of all, conceive in your mind the pangs of conscience that raged in Judas, which are known to have been most atrocious, and more intolerable than the torments of hell, when they were able to wring from that most covetous man not only a disregard for the money but even a hatred of it, and to drive him to confess his sin, which Christ had in vain urged upon him at the Supper, and to produce in him a weariness of the present life.

units.la: Domesticorum insidijs petuntur fideles.
units.tr: The faithful are sought out by the treachery of their own household.

units.la: Iudæ horribilis exitus. admonuerat, & vitæ præsentis tædium in ipso parere. Adde his horrendum mortis genus. Ipse sibi laqueum nectit. Ipse collo proprio laqueum induit. Ipse sibi proprij suspendij author est, quo infelicem animam exhalat. Accedit quod mortis atrocitatem amplificet. Nam medium crepuit, & effusa sunt omnia viscera ipsius. Merebatur enim vt vitalia viscera profunderet, qui Christi vitæ veræ authorem vnicum turpi lucro vendere non erat veritus. At neq; hic quidem diuini iudicij rigor finitur, sed sempiterna accedit tam immanis flagitij memoria. Ita fit vt nec vita, nec pecunia (quam ipsa vita chariorem habuerat) diu fruatur infelix ille perditionis filius. In hoc speculum oculos mentis suæ defigant, quicunq; turpis lucri & priuati cômodi gratia Christum prodere, veritatem negare, & ecclesiæ Christi turpiter illudere consueuerunt. Obseruent eadem hac, quicunque ex sanguine viuunt, hācq; sibi præcipuam laudem ducunt, si mercenarijs bellis ditati, opes suas ædificiorum structura, prædiorum magnifico cultu, supellectilis superbo apparatu, vestium luxu, & totius vitæ immani fastu & insanis sumptibus testentur. Quid enim isti aliud faciunt, quàm quòd se sanguinarios esse produnt, & vitæ mmaniter transactæ monumenta sibiipsis relinquunt? At quia in sequentibus quædam dicenda restant, quæ ad hunc locum pertinent, hæc modò sufficiant. Moueat verò nos infelix Iudæ exitus, vt syncero Dei timore mortificati, Christum Iesum firma fide amplectamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The dreadful end of Judas. Add to these the dreadful kind of death. He himself ties the noose. He himself puts the noose about his own neck. He himself is the author of his own hanging, by which he breathes out his unhappy soul. Added to this is what increases the atrocity of his death: for he burst asunder in the middle, and all his inner organs gushed out. For he deserved to pour out his vital organs, who had not been ashamed to sell for base gain the one author of true life, Christ. Yet the rigour of divine judgment does not end here, but there is added the everlasting memory of so monstrous a crime. So it comes about that the unhappy son of perdition enjoys neither his life nor the money, which he had held dearer than life itself, for long. Let all who are accustomed to betray Christ, to deny the truth, and to mock shamefully the Church of Christ for the sake of base gain and private advantage, fix the eyes of their mind on this mirror. Let those also observe these things who live by blood and count it their chief praise if, enriched by mercenary wars, they bear witness to their wealth by the building of houses, the magnificent upkeep of estates, the proud display of furniture, the luxury of clothing, and the monstrous arrogance and mad expense of their whole life. For what else do such men do than reveal themselves as bloodthirsty, and leave to themselves the monuments of a life spent monstrously? But since some things remain to be said in what follows that pertain to this place, let these suffice for now. May the unhappy end of Judas move us, so that, mortified by sincere fear of God, we embrace Christ Jesus with firm faith, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA VIII.
units.tr: HOMILY VIII.

units.la: Scriptum est enim in libro Psalmorum: Fiat habitatio eius deserta, & non sit qui habitet in ea. Et episcopatum eius accipiat alius. Oportet igitur vt ex ijs, qui nobiscum fuerunt congregati toto tempore, quo intrauit & exiuit inter nos dominus Iesus, exorsus à baptismo Iohannis vsque in eum diem quo assumptus à nobis, vnus aliquis constituatur, qui sit vnà nobiscum testis resurrectionis eius.
units.tr: For it is written in the book of Psalms: Let his habitation be desolate, and let there be none to dwell therein. And let another take his bishopric. It is therefore necessary that of those who have been with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us, one of them be appointed to be a witness with us of his resurrection.

units.la: QVoniam dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus, apostolos suos nostræ redemptionis, quæ ipse suo merito nobis acquisiuit, testes esse voluit, minimè superuacaneum est, vt quæ de illorum vocatione & ordinatione dicuntur, aliquanto diligentius expendamus. Nisi enim hæc nobis probè comperta fuerint, non ea apud nos esse poterit testimonij ipsorum authoritas, quam esse oportet. Quæ causa est, quòd illorum vocatio, quos Christus Iesus adhuc in terris agens elegit, ab Euangelista ea diligentia describitur, vt ipsos diuinitus ordinatos esse, nemo dubitare possit. At quia Matthiæ authoritas minor videri poterat, qui post Christi ascensionem demum in Iudæ locum succedens, apostolorum collegio adnumeratus est, illius quoq; electionem ita describit Lucas, vt illum non minus quàm reliquos ab ipso Christo in huius muneris administrationem constitutum fuisse pateat. Nam nec sponte cucurrit, nec Petrus, qui causam hanc ecclesiæ consulctandam proposuit, quicquam priuato siue consilio siue authoritate egit, sed cum toto fidelium cœtu ad preces conuersus, omne hoc negotium diuinæ voluntati permisit, vt sequenti Homilia dicetur. Quo exemplo admonemur, legitimam vocationem ministris expectandam esse, nec alicui permittendum, vt vel seipsum vel alios temere & priuata authoritate ecclesiæ obtrudat. Nam apud prophetam grauissimè reprehenduntur, qui sponte currebant, non legitima domini vocatione expectata. Ierem.23. Et Paulus ait: Quo modo prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Rom.10. Atqui non ignorabat Paulus, multos non missos à domino prædicare (quos alibi ψευδαποστόλους, id est, falsos fratres vocat, qui absq; legitima ordinatione irrepant. Galat.2.) Sed tales officio suo vere defungi posse negat. Quid? quòd nec ipse Christus docendi munus aggressus est, priusquam solenni inauguratione à Deo patre orbi totius doctor esse declararetur: cuius rei etiam author epistolæ ad Hebræos cap.5.meminit. Quæ ratio nisi obseruetur, nec populus pro Dei ministris agnoscere poterit, de quorum vocatione incertus est, nec ipsi ministri qua decet fide & constantia in suo officio versabuntur. Quibus enim rationibus contra mundi minas, tyrannorum conatus & vndiq; imminentia pericula sese armabunt, qui temerariæ vsurpationis sibi conscij, de Dei auxilio spem nullam possunt concipere?
units.tr: Since our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, wished his apostles to be witnesses of our redemption, which he himself acquired for us by his own merit, it is by no means superfluous that we weigh rather carefully what is said about their calling and ordination. For unless these things have been properly established for us, their testimony will not have the authority among us that it ought to have. This is the reason why the calling of those whom Christ Jesus chose while still living on earth is described by the Evangelist with such diligence, so that no one can doubt that they were ordained by God. But because the authority of Matthias might seem less, who, succeeding into the place of Judas only after Christ's ascension, was numbered among the college of apostles, Luke also describes his election in such a way that it is plain he was appointed to this office by Christ himself no less than the others. For he did not run of his own accord, nor did Peter, who proposed that this matter be taken counsel of by the church, do anything by private counsel or authority; rather, turning to prayer with the whole company of the faithful, he left the whole business to the divine will, as will be told in the following homily. By this example we are admonished that a lawful calling is to be awaited by ministers, and that no one should be permitted to thrust either himself or others upon the church rashly and by private authority. For in the prophet those are most gravely rebuked who ran of their own accord, without awaiting the lawful calling of the Lord (Jer. 23). And Paul says: How shall they preach unless they are sent? (Rom. 10). Yet Paul was not unaware that many preach without being sent by the Lord (whom elsewhere he calls pseudapostoloi, that is, false brethren, who creep in without lawful ordination; Gal. 2). But he denies that such men can truly discharge their office. Moreover, Christ himself did not undertake the office of teaching before he was declared by God the Father, with solemn inauguration, to be the teacher of the whole world; the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews also mentions this matter in chapter 5. If this order is not observed, the people will not be able to acknowledge as ministers of God those whose calling is uncertain, nor will the ministers themselves persevere in their office with the faith and constancy that befit it. For with what resources will they arm themselves against the threats of the world, the attempts of tyrants and the dangers hanging over them on every side, when they are conscious of a rash usurpation and can conceive no hope of God's help?

units.la: Sed ad Petrum reuertamur, qui prima suæ orationis parte (vt heri monuimus) offendiculo me-detur, quod ex Iudæ lapsu oriri poterat, dum ad diuinæ prouidentiæ decretum ipsos relegat, quod ante secula aliquot spiritus sanctus per Dauidem reuelarat. Et quia scripturæ sacræ mentionem fecerat, in præsenti quædam illius testimonia profert. Omissis tamen illis, quibus Iudæ scelus (quod satis superque satis notum erat) prædicitur, ea tantummodo recenset, quæ de eiusdem horribili pœna extant. Et duo quidem coniungit, quorum prius ex Psal.69. alterum ex 109. desumptum est. Scriptum est (inquit) in libro Psalmorum: Fiat habitatio eius deserta, & non sit qui habitet in ea. Et episcopatum eius accipiat alter. Nec obstat, quod totus illis Psalmus de suis hostibus Dauid loquitur. Quia enim in persecutione, quam sub Saule tyranno sustinuit, Christi Iesu typum gessit, quæcunque de ipsius hostibus dicuntur, ad Christi hostes, & Iudam in primis, qui omnium quasi antesignanus est, referri debent.
units.tr: But let us return to Peter, who in the first part of his speech (as we noted yesterday) remedies the stumbling-block that could arise from Judas's fall, while he refers them to the decree of divine providence, which the Holy Spirit had revealed through David some centuries earlier. And since he had made mention of the holy Scripture, he now brings forward some of its testimonies. Yet, leaving aside those in which Judas's crime (which was already sufficiently and more than sufficiently well known) is foretold, he recounts only those which exist concerning his dreadful punishment. And he joins two, of which the first is taken from Psalm 69 and the other from Psalm 109. It is written (he says) in the book of Psalms: Let his habitation be desolate, and let there be none to dwell therein. And let another take his bishopric. Nor does it stand in the way that David speaks of his own enemies throughout that whole Psalm. For since in the persecution which he endured under the tyrant Saul he bore the type of Christ Jesus, whatever is said of his enemies must be referred to the enemies of Christ, and above all to Judas, who is, as it were, the standard-bearer of them all.

units.la: At priusquam de pœnis illorum dicamus, illud minime prætermitti debet, quod non de proditionis scelere tantum, quod Iudas commissurus erat, verumetiam de eiusdem horrendis pœnis spiritus sanctus prophetare voluit. Quia enim Iudas auaritiæ affectu extimulatus Christum prodidit, non autem vt iuxta Dei decretum humani generis redemptionem promoueret, illius facinus nulla ratione excusari potest, sed atroces pœnas meretur. Et eadem omnium impiorum est ratio: quam si obseruemus, facile constabit, prouidentiam Dei impijs non patrocinari, nec peccatorum culpam Deo transcribi debere, quando spontanea & libera voluntate peccant homines, qui nisi efficaci spiritus & gratia Dei virtute regenerentur, ex semetipsis nihil quam peccare possunt. Quia tamen Dei prouidentia res cunctas gubernari constat, ab huius gubernatione peccata eximi non debent, nisi Dei omnipotentiam negare & homini vires contra Dei voluntatem aliquid agendi tribuere velimus. Non autem in hominum peccatis subsistit Dei prouidentia: sed longius progressa peccatis dignas pœnas decernit, & illarum executores varios pro sua voluntate constituit. Peccatorum ergo nostrorum non authorem, sed vindicem potius Deum agnoscamus ex prouidentiæ ipsius contemplatione, & mox omnia illius iudicia iustitiam & veritatem esse deprehendemus.
units.tr: But before we speak of their punishments, this must by no means be passed over: that the Holy Spirit wished to prophesy not only of the crime of betrayal which Judas was about to commit, but also of the dreadful punishments of the same man. For since Judas, stirred by the affection of greed, betrayed Christ, and not in order to advance the redemption of the human race according to God's decree, his deed cannot be excused on any ground, but he deserves atrocious punishments. And the same is the case with all the wicked; if we observe this, it will readily be established that the providence of God does not patronise the impious, nor is the guilt of sins to be transferred to God, since men sin by a spontaneous and free will, who, unless they are regenerated by the efficacious Spirit and the power of God's grace, can of themselves do nothing but sin. Yet since it is agreed that all things are governed by the providence of God, sins ought not to be exempted from its government, unless we wish to deny the omnipotence of God and to attribute to man the power to do anything against God's will. But the providence of God does not stop at men's sins; rather, going further, it decrees punishments worthy of the sins and appoints various executors of them according to its own will. Therefore, from the contemplation of providence itself, let us acknowledge God as the avenger rather than the author of our sins, and presently we shall find that all his judgments are justice and truth.

units.la: Cæterum pœnas videamus, quibus & Iudæ perfidiam olim Deus vltus est, & omnium suorum hostium impietatem vlcisci consueuit. Sunt hæc multa & varia, quarum mentionem copiose Dauides facit in locis modò citatis. At duabus in præsenti Petrus contentus esse voluit, quæ & in Iudæ euidentissimè cernuntur, & reliquas pene omnes comprehendunt. Primùm his verbis exprimit: Fiat habitatio eius deserta, & non sit qui habitet in ea. Minatur hic illis excidium, & quod patrijs sive auitis sedibus eijciendi sint. Videtur enim hæc cum Mosaica illa maledictione conuenire: Domum extrues, & alius in ea habitabit. Deut.28. Nam quod hic dicitur: Et nemo habitet in ea, de posteris impiorum intelligendum esse videtur, qui vnà cum patribus eijci & dissipari mereantur. Atqui grauissima hæc pœna est, si rem penitius excutias. Comprehendit enim quæcunque in hominis fortunas & corpus aduersa incidere possunt. Excidium etenim præcedit bellum, & quicquid malorum belli fortuna secum trahit. Comitantur illud paupertas, fames, labor, cura, sollicitudo, ignominia & omnis generis calamitatum vicissitudo indefinens, quæ non nisi lenta tabe finitur, & plerunque infamem scelerum memoriam post se relinquit. Quæ omnia Iudæ accidisse, nemini dubium videri potest. Nam licet ipse longas huius vitæ calamitates præcipiti suspendio effugisse videatur, Dei tamen iudicium posteritas ipsius effugere non potuit. Et quid illa perpessa sit, ex vniuersali gentis Iudaicæ excidio facile colligi potest. Nec enim solus Iudas Christi proditi & crucifixi culpam sustinet, sed eadem totius gentis culpa est, cuius proceres Iudam ad tantum facinus conduxerunt, & quæ procerum consilia coram Pilato iudice vnanimi consensu approbauit, clamans: Crucifige, crucifige. Sanguis eius super nos, & super filios nostros. Nec diu cessauit Dei iustitia, quin innocentem filij sui sanguinem de illorum capitibus requireret. Et quod Christus non semel ipsis interminatus erat, non multò post tempore euenit. Christi enim minæ fuerunt: Hierusalem Hierusalem, quæ occidis prophetas, & lapidas eos qui ad te missi sunt: Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, vt gallina congregat pullos suos, & tu noluisti? Ecce relinquitur vobis domus vestra deserta. Matthæi 23. cap. Et rursum: Non relinquetur hic lapis super lapidem, qui non destruetur. Matth. 24. Alibi item non sine lachrymis infelici vrbi excidium denunciat, dicens: Venient dies in te, & circundabunt te inimici tui vallo, &
units.tr: Moreover, let us see the punishments by which God once avenged the treachery of Judas, and by which he is accustomed to punish the impiety of all his enemies. They are many and various, and David makes copious mention of them in the passages just cited. But Peter in the present place chose to be content with two, which are most plainly seen in Judas and comprehend almost all the rest. First he expresses it in these words: Let his habitation be desolate, and let there be none to dwell therein. Here he threatens them with destruction, and with being cast out from their ancestral or paternal dwellings. For this seems to agree with that Mosaic curse: You shall build a house, and another shall dwell in it (Deut. 28). For what is said here, And let no one dwell in it, seems to be understood of the posterity of the impious, who deserve to be cast out and scattered together with their fathers. And yet this is a most grievous punishment, if you examine the matter more deeply. For it comprehends whatever adversities can befall a man's fortunes and body. Indeed, destruction is preceded by war, and whatever evils the fortune of war brings in its train. Poverty, famine, toil, care, anxiety, ignominy and an unending succession of calamities of every kind accompany it, which end only by a slow wasting and generally leave behind an infamous memory of crimes. That all these things befell Judas no one can doubt. For although he himself seems to have escaped the long calamities of this life by a headlong hanging, yet his posterity could not escape the judgment of God. And what they suffered may easily be gathered from the universal destruction of the Jewish nation. For Judas alone does not bear the guilt of betraying and crucifying Christ, but it is the guilt of the whole nation, whose leaders hired Judas for so great a crime, and which, with unanimous consent, approved the counsels of the leaders before Pilate the judge, crying: Crucify, crucify. His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matt. 27). Nor did the justice of God delay long before it demanded the blood of its innocent Son from their heads. And what Christ had not once threatened them with came to pass not long afterwards. For Christ's threats were: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who killest the prophets and stonest those who are sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chickens, and you would not? Behold, your house is left to you desolate (Matt. 23). And again: There shall not be left here one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down (Matt. 24). Elsewhere too he announces, not without tears, destruction to the unhappy city, saying: The days shall come upon you, and your enemies shall cast a trench about you...

units.la: Oracula de pœnis Iudæ.
units.tr: Oracles concerning the punishments of Judah.

units.la: Dei prouidentia sceleribus non patrocinatur.
units.tr: God's providence does not defend wickedness.

units.la: Pœnæ hostium Christi.
units.tr: The punishments of Christ's enemies.

units.la: Excidium. cingent te, & coangustabunt te vndiq, & solo æquabunt te, & filios tuos qui in te sunt. Et non relin-quent in te lapidem super lapidem, eò quòd non cognoueris tempus visitationis tuæ. Luc æ 19. Cum bis fi historiam conferas, & Iudæorum conditionem, qua hodie, in totum orbem dispersi, vtuntur, verissimè impleta videbis quæcunq; dominus prædixerat. Idem Dei iudicium Romana vrbs olim experta est. Cùm enim post excisam Iudæorum gentem ipsa in Christi ecclesiam gladium stringeret, & sanctorum sanguine tota maderet, cæpit illi tandem Deus rependere. Nam intra annos centum triginta & nouem, septies capta in manus deuenit barbarorum. Primùm Visigothi duce Alarycho ceperunt vrbe & diripuerunt, anno à nato Christo saluatore CCCCXII. Mox post annos XLIIII. duce Genserycho Vandali illam irruperunt, in eius direptione omnia ea patrantes, quæ auarissimus hostis in capta vrbe patrare consuevit. Insecuti sunt hos anno salutis humanæ CCCCLXXI. Heruli, qui eandem Odacre duce occuparunt. Quorum æmulatione excitatus Theodoricus Ostrogothorum rex, illa quoq; potitus est. Et cùm annus circiter quinquaginta euolutis, vrbem recuperauisset Belisarius, intra annos duodecim proditione à Totila Ostrogotho capitur, qui direptam ferro & igne vastat, munitionibus nudat, mænia plus tertia parte solo æquat, Capitolium cum multis ædificijs publicis & priuatis incendit. Inde Roma egressus, ne vnum quidem viuentium, vel marem vel fœminam, in ea remanere passus est, vt omni humano cultu vrbs, quondam rerum domina, deserta iacaret. Quam licet mox sequenti anno restauret Bellisarius, idem tamen Byzantium reuocatus, Totila denuò occupandam relinquit. Possent infinita huius generis exempla produci, quæ certissimum excidium Christi & ecclesiæ hostibus imminere testantur.
units.tr: Destruction. They will surround you and close you in on every side, and will level you to the ground, and your sons who are in you. And they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognise the time of your visitation. Luke 19. If you compare this history with the condition of the Jews, who today are scattered throughout the whole world, you will see that everything the Lord foretold has been most truly fulfilled. The city of Rome has also at some time experienced the same judgment of God. For after the Jewish nation was destroyed, Rome itself drew the sword against the Church of Christ and was soaked with the blood of the saints, and at last God began to repay her. For within 139 years she was captured seven times and fell into the hands of barbarians. First the Visigoths under their leader Alaric took and plundered the city, in the year 412 after the birth of Christ the Saviour. Then, forty-four years later, the Vandals under Gaiseric broke in, committing in its plunder all the things that a most greedy enemy is accustomed to commit in a captured city. In the year of human salvation 471 the Heruli followed them and occupied it under their leader Odoacer. Stirred on by their rivalry, Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, also seized it. About fifty years later Belisarius recovered the city, but within twelve years it was taken by treachery by the Ostrogoth Totila, who plundered it, laid it waste with sword and fire, stripped its fortifications, levelled more than a third of its walls, and burned the Capitol together with many public and private buildings. Leaving Rome, he allowed not one living person, male or female, to remain in it, so that the city, once mistress of the world, lay deserted and stripped of all human habitation. Although Belisarius restored it the following year, he was soon recalled to Byzantium and left it to be occupied again by Totila. Countless examples of this kind could be brought forward, which testify that a most certain destruction hangs over the enemies of Christ and of the Church.

units.la: Alterum pœnæ genus est: Et episcopatum ipsius accipiat alter. Quibus verbis testatur, tales homines nullis vel dignitatibus vel donis eximijs, quibus instructi sunt, ab imminenti Dei iudicio eripi posse. Quæcunq; enim Dei beneficio excellentia & præclara habent, in alios transferuntur. Exemplum huius Iudas est luculentissimum. Erat is ad apostolatum vocatus, & cum hoc œconomiæ Christi administrationem sustinebat. Summa ergo fuit illius hominis dignitas, cui nec regia nec imperatoria conferri meretur. Accedebat huic diutina cum filio Dei conuersatio, & quòd cum reliquis apostolis multa viderat & audiuerat, quæ multis prophetis & iustis, quantumuis magno desiderio flagrantibus, non contigerat videre & audire. At non iuuant hæc infelicem hominem, qui perfidia sua omnibus istis spoliari meruerat. Nam & ipse horribili exitu è mundo hoc migrat, & in Matthiam transfertur apostolatus dignitas. Idem Dei iudicium in Saule cernitur, qui Dauidem, Christi typum, persequi ausus est. Vt primùm enim hoc in animum induxit, bono Dei spiritu priuatur, in cuius locum malignus satanæ spiritus succedit, quo eò vsq; exagitatur, donec & violentæ mortis sibi ipsi author est, & regnum Dauidi possidendum relinquit. Huc referri debet Christi sententia: Omni habenti dabitur. Ab eo autem, qui nihil habet, etiam quod habet auferetur. Matth. 25. Habere enim Christo dicuntur, qui Dei donis instructi, illa in se agnoscunt, & ijsdem ad Dei gloriam multorum salutem prouehendam studiose vtuntur. Auget in illis dona sua beneficus & liberalis Deus, vt indies in melius proficiant & illustriores fiant. At qui perinde ac si nihil donorum à Deo accepissent, illa negligunt, ac suis rebus intenti, quæcunq; ad Dei gloriam spectant, securè contemnunt, eas tandem suæ negligentiæ & improbitatis pœnas exoluunt, vt omnibus facultatibus spoliati, infelices, contempti & infames reddantur. Æternum enim stabit, nec vllis mundi conatibus infringetur Dei sententia, qua sacerdoti Heli iram suam & iustam pœnam denuncians, inter alia dicit: Honore prosequar eos, qui me honore prosequuntur: & qui me contemnunt, ignominia afficientur. 1. Sam. 2. Et alibi extremam ignominiam sacerdotibus improbis & diuinæ gloriæ contemptoribus minatur: Mittam (inquit) in vos execrationem, maledicamq; benedictionibus vestris. Ecce ego increpabo vobis semen, & spargam stercus in facies vestras, stercus, inquam, dierum vestrorum solennium. Malach. 2. In horum meditatione vtinam hodie frequentes essemus, & non miraremur omnium fere eorum authoritatem collapsam esse, quicunq; in ecclesia & repub. obseruari debebant. Queruntur de hoc malo episcopi, & quo nam ecclesiastica authoritas translata sit, ignorant. Sed conqueri & mirari desinent, si doctrinæ verè adulterationem, sacrorum nundinationem, morum corruptionem, auaritiam, fastum & alia huius generis ipsis authoribus in ecclesiam inuecta esse cogitent: quibus se Iudæ potius quàm Petri successores fuisse abunde declararunt. Queruntur & euangelici doctores de ministerij fterij & functionis suæ contemptu, & ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ authoritatem omnem extinctam esse clamant. Atqui id mirum non est, quando in illorum numero plures parum industrios in Christi gloria afferenda videre licet, alij vero sub plausibili euangelicæ doctrinæ prætextu auaritiæ, gulæ, ventri & libidini student. Iure ergo ab illis auferetur dignitas & authoritas, quam ministerij nomine me rebantur. Quare quisquis gradum suum, in quem à Deo collocatus est, tueri, & authoritatem suam retinere voluerit, diuinæ gloriæ studium sibi vnicè commendatum habeat, illud vrgeat, & vel inuito mundo omnibus viribus promouere cotendat, nec à sua vocatione latû vnguè sese dimoueri patiatur.
units.tr: The other kind of punishment is: "and let another take his bishopric." By these words it is shown that such men cannot be rescued from the impending judgment of God by any dignities or outstanding gifts with which they have been endowed. For whatever excellent and distinguished things they have by God's benefit are transferred to others. The example of Judas is most striking. He had been called to the apostleship and shared in the administration of Christ's household. Therefore the dignity of that man was very great, one that deserved to be conferred on no king or emperor. To this was added a long companionship with the Son of God, and the fact that with the other apostles he had seen and heard many things which many prophets and righteous men, though burning with great desire, had not been granted to see and hear. But these things did not help that unhappy man, who by his treachery had deserved to be stripped of all of them. For he himself departed from this world by a dreadful end, and the dignity of the apostleship was transferred to Matthias. The same judgment of God is seen in Saul, who dared to persecute David, a type of Christ. For as soon as he took this into his mind, he was deprived of the good Spirit of God, in whose place the evil spirit of Satan succeeded, by which he was so driven about that at last he became the author of his own violent death, and left the kingdom to be possessed by David. To this belongs the saying of Christ: "To everyone who has, more will be given; but from him who has nothing, even what he has will be taken away." Matthew 25. For those are said to have something from Christ who, endowed with God's gifts, recognise them in themselves and diligently use them to advance the salvation of many to the glory of God. God, who is generous and bountiful, increases his gifts in them, so that they make daily progress and become more illustrious. But those who neglect these gifts as if they had received nothing from God, and, intent on their own affairs, despise with impunity whatever pertains to the glory of God, at last pay the penalty of their negligence and wickedness, so that they are stripped of all their resources and made wretched, despised and infamous. For the sentence of God will stand for ever, and will not be broken by any efforts of the world; in it, announcing his anger and just punishment to the priest Eli, he says among other things: "I will honour those who honour me, and those who despise me will be dishonoured." 1 Samuel 2. And elsewhere he threatens the wicked priests, and the despisers of divine glory, with the extreme of dishonour: "I will send," he says, "a curse upon you, and I will curse your blessings. Behold, I will rebuke your seed and spread dung on your faces, the dung, I say, of your solemn days." Malachi 2. Would that we were many today in the meditation on these things, and did not wonder that the authority of nearly all those who ought to be observed in the Church and in the commonwealth has collapsed. The bishops complain of this evil, and do not know to whom the ecclesiastical authority has been transferred. But they would cease to complain and wonder, if they truly considered that the corruption of doctrine, the trafficking in sacred things, the corruption of morals, avarice, pride and other things of this kind have been brought into the Church by these very men, by whom they have amply shown themselves to be successors of Judas rather than of Peter. The evangelical teachers also complain about the contempt of the ministry and of their office, and cry out that all authority of church discipline has been extinguished. Yet this is not surprising, since among their number one can see many who are not very diligent in advancing the glory of Christ, while others, under the plausible pretext of the evangelical doctrine, pursue avarice, gluttony, the belly and lust. Therefore, rightly, that dignity and authority which they thought they held in the name of the ministry will be taken from them. Wherefore, whoever wishes to guard the rank in which God has placed him, and to keep his authority, let him hold the zeal for divine glory as his sole commitment, let him press it, and strive with all his strength to advance it, even if the world is opposed, and let him not allow himself to be moved a finger's breadth from his calling.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram orationis Petri partem, qua ecclesiam, vt de alio in Iudæ locum surrogando cogitet, hortatur. Comodè vero ex præmissis scripturæ oraculis argumenta desumit, qui- bus hoc illis persuadeat. Sic enim dicere videtur: Quoniam de Iuda spiritus sanctus prædixit, quòd & Christum prodituros esset, & post horribilem vitæ finem episcopatum suum & apostolicam functionem alij relicturus, ex eorum numero illi successor à nobis quærendus erit, qui hucusq; nobiscum versati, omnium quæ Christus in terris hisce gesserit, spectatores fuerunt. Est autem obseruatione digna Petri argumentatio, quæ (si paucis comprehendatur) talis est: Iudæ episcopatum iuxta spiritus sancti oraculum alius debet suscipere. Ergo nostrum est, vt illi de successore idoneo & digno prospiciamus. Atqui absurda videbitur prima fronte huius consequentiæ ratio. Esto enim, vt Iudæ episcopatus in alium transferri debeat: num vero inde sequetur, apostolorum & eorum, qui cum ipsis congregati erant, hoc munus esse, vt ipsi eum deligant, in quem episcopatus ille transferri possit? Sed omnis absurditatis species remouetur, si apostolorum functionem, quam ex Christi institutione suscinebant, consideremus. Illis enim ecclesiæ suæ curam Christus, è terra abiturus commendarat, & ex eorum numero erant, qui familiæ dominicæ (vt Matth. 24. cap. legitur) cibum depromere debebant. Quia ergo ad ecclesiæ curam & conseruationem hoc cumprimis facit, vt digni & idonei ministri habeantur: non temerè Petrus nouî apostoli ordinationem ad ipsos pertinere colligit, cùm euidens extaret de nouo aliquo in Iudæ locum substituendo spiritus sancti oraculum.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the second part of Peter's speech, in which he urges the Church to think about substituting another in Judas's place. He draws the arguments from the aforesaid oracles of Scripture with good reason, in order to persuade them of this. For he seems to say: Since the Holy Spirit foretold of Judas both that he would betray Christ, and that after a dreadful end he would leave his bishopric and apostolic function to another, a successor to him must be sought by us from among those who have associated with us up to now and have been witnesses of all that Christ did on this earth. Peter's argument, if it is summarised briefly, is worth noting, and it is this: According to the oracle of the Holy Spirit, another must take Judas's bishopric. Therefore it is our duty to provide a suitable and worthy man for it. At first sight, however, the reasoning of this consequence will seem absurd. Suppose that Judas's bishopric ought to be transferred to another: does it follow from this that it is the task of the apostles and of those who were gathered with them to choose the one into whom that office can be transferred? But every appearance of absurdity is removed if we consider the apostolic function which they undertook by Christ's institution. For Christ, about to depart from the earth, had entrusted to them the care of his Church, and they were among those who, as is read in Matthew 24, were to bring food out for the household of the Lord. Therefore, since it contributes above all to the care and preservation of the Church that worthy and suitable ministers be had, Peter rightly gathers that the ordination of a new apostle belongs to them, since there was clearly an oracle of the Holy Spirit about substituting someone new in Judas's place.

units.la: Admonemur autem Petri exemplo, vt nos in scriptura sacra lectione versari conueniat. Hîc enim ante omnia nostræ vocationis ratio semper ob oculos haberi debet, vt quicquid ad illam pertinet, nobis dici putemus. Nam ad nostram institutionem scripturas diuinitus traditas esse, Paulus testatur. Rom. 15. 2. Tim. 3. Quare grauis illorum error est, qui sacros libros non maiori attentione quàm prophanos scriptores legunt, mente inter legendum in varias cogitationes distracta, quasi lectio hæc non nisi oblectationis aut ocij fallendi causa institui debeat. Obseruemus ergo diligenter quæ nostræ vocationis siue functionis præcepta atq; exempla sint, vt illis insistere, & studium nostrum Deo approbare possimus. Hac ratione verbi minister sibi dicta putabit, quæcunq; vel prophetis vel apostolis de suo officio eiusq; administratione dicuntur. Et qui in magistratu versantur, ad se pertinere putent, quæcunq; de magistratuum officijs, præcepta in scripturis extant, vnà cum prisco rum magistratuum exemplis, siue illi boni siue mali fuerint. Idem priuati quoque homines obseruabunt cuiusq; loci sint aut ordinis. Sic fiet, vt vnà cum sancta animi voluptate ex scripturarum lectione incredibilem vtilitatem capiant.
units.tr: We are admonished by Peter's example that we should apply ourselves to the reading of holy Scripture. Above all, the purpose of our calling must always be kept before our eyes, so that we take to ourselves whatever pertains to it. For Paul testifies that the Scriptures were given by divine inspiration for our instruction. Rom. 15. 2. Tim. 3. Therefore those people are gravely mistaken who read the sacred books with no more attention than they give to profane writers, letting their minds wander into various thoughts as they read, as if this reading ought to be undertaken only for pleasure or to pass idle time. Let us therefore observe carefully what precepts and examples there are for our calling or office, so that we may keep to them and make our zeal pleasing to God. In this way the minister of the Word will think that whatever the prophets or apostles say about their office and its administration is said to him. Those who hold magistracy should consider that whatever precepts about the duties of magistrates are found in the Scriptures apply to them, together with the examples of earlier magistrates, whether they were good or bad. Private persons likewise will observe what their place or rank is. In this way, along with a holy delight of the mind, they will gain an incredible benefit from reading the Scriptures.

units.la: Excutiamus autem diui Petri verba, quibus duo, ad præsens institutum quàm maximè pertinentia, tractantur. Primò enim qualis ad apostolicam functionem deflinari debeat, docet. Deinde apostoli officium definit: & de his quidem sic disputat, vt omnium ministrorum verbi & ecclesiæ institutioni seruire possint.
units.tr: Let us examine the words of the divine Peter, in which two matters most pertinent to our present subject are treated. First, he teaches what sort of person ought to be chosen for the apostolic office. Then he defines the office of an apostle. He discusses these things in such a way that they can serve the institution of all ministers of the Word and of the Church.

units.la: Ad primum membrum pertinet, quod dicit: Oportet igitur, vt ex iis, qui nobiscum fuerunt congregati toto tempore, quo intrauit & exiuit inter nos dominus Iesus, exorsus à baptismo Iohannis vsque in eum diem, quo assumptus est à nobis, vnus aliquis constituatur, &c. Requirit hic duas res maximi momenti Petrus. Prima est certa & solida Iesu Christi, omniumq; eorum quæ inter suos conuersatus fecit, cognitio. Nam Hebræo idiomate vsus, per duo extrema, intrandi videlicet & exeundi verba, vniuersam Christi conuersationem comprehendit. Ne quis tamen curiosius quædam inquirendi occasionem hinc sumeret, cognitioni huic terminos statuit, baptismum scilicet Iohannis & gloriosam Christi in cælos ascensionem. Priusquam enim ab Iohanne Christus baptizaretur, in Nazareth Galilææ priuatam vitam agebat, parentibus obsequentem sese præbens, & cum nutricio Iofepho artem fabrilem plerunq; exercens, vt ex ijs conijci potes{ε}, quæ Luc.2. & Marci 6.cap. habentur. Ea verò, quæ ad publicam nostræ redemptionis causam, & Messiæ officium spectabant, tunc demum obire cœpit, postquam ab Iohanne baptizatus, & visibili spiritus sancti vnctione ac patris testimonio, cœlitus delato, inauguratus est. Matth.3. Quæ causa est, quòd Euangelistæ contenti ipsius incarnationem descripsisse, de illius pueritia & iuuenili ætate paucißima tradidere. Voluit enim spiritus sanctus ineptam humani ingenij curiositatem cohercere, quæ nouissimis seculis per egregios, si dijs placet, scriptores sese exeruit, qui vitam Christi & illius pueritiam, non sine publico Christiani nominis ludibrio, nobis tradiderunt. Atqui diuo Petro, eorum cognitio sufficiens esse videtur, quæ Christus post solennem illam inaugurationem fecit. Necessaria autem erat hæc, quia apostolos rerum abs se gestarum testes fidelißimos Christus esse voluerat. Secundo loco certum ac euidens perseuerantiæ specimen requirit. Non enim ex illorum numero quenquam vult deligi, qui in Christiani nominis professione nouitij adhuc erant, & ante paucos dies fidelium cœtui sese coniunxerant. Sed de illis loquitur, qui circa initium conuersationis Christi Iesu inter homines ipsum sequi cœperant, & cum eo perseuerarant, vt nec persecutionum periculis, nec crucis & infamis mortis offendiculo absterreri potuerint. Atqui eadem hæc in ministrorum verbi electionibus siue ordinationibus hodie quoq; obseruari oportebat, si ecclesiam Christi saluam & incolumem vellent, qui in hanc sibi ius vendicant. Constat enim præcipuam ministri functionem circa doctrinam versari, quod & dominus per prophetam admonuit, dicens: Labia sacerdotis custodient scientiam, legemq; ex ore eius requirent: Legatus est enim domini exercituum. Malach.2. At quomodo docebit, qui ipse indoctus & rudis est? Paulus certè in episcopo hoc cumprimis requirit, vt διδακτικὸς sit, id est, docendi facultate præditus, vtq; non modò trac abilioris ingenij hominibus simplicem veritatis doctrinam tradere, verumetiam contradicentes (quorum ingens semper multitudo erit) refellere & refutare queat. 1. Tim.3. Tit.1. Necessaria igitur in verbi ministro est Christi & mysteriorum ipsius cognitio, vnà cum omnibus ijs quæ ad fidei Christianæ articulos & fidelium officia spectant. Requiritur ab eodem diligens scripturæ studium, in quo ipsum probè versatum esse oportet. Opus eidem est linguarum cognitione, ne in scripturis legendis ab aliorum sensu pendere, adeoq; alienis oculis videre & alienis pedibus incedere cogatur. Adhæc dicendi artibus instructum esse conuenit, vt quid, quo loco & ordine, & quomodo proponi debeat, possit perspicere. Quæ omnia tanti momenti sunt, vt Paulus non temere Timotheum ad assiduum legendi studium hortetur, quem tamen à puero sacras literas didicisse fatetur. Deinde quia ministrorum functioni infinita vndiq; pericula imminent, animi fortitudo requiritur, ne periculorum metu superatus in medio cursu subsistat. Atqui hæc in sola perseuerantia perspicietur, cuius non obscura specimina ipsum dedisse oportuit. Idem Paulus obseruauit, dum monet episcopum non debere neophytum vel nouitium esse, ne dignitate subita inflatus aliquid perperam agat, & calumniandi occasionem præbeat aduersarijs. 1. Tim.3. Sed & ipse Christus apostolos, quos multis vitijs & infirmitatibus laborauisse constat, hoc elogio præcipuè commendat in vltima Cæna, quòd ipsos secum perseuerauisse dicit in omnibus tentationibus suis. Luc.22.
units.tr: As to the first point, Peter says: "It is necessary, therefore, that one of those who have been with us all the time that the Lord Jesus came in and went out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until that day on which he was taken up from us, be appointed," etc. Peter requires two things of the greatest importance here. The first is a sure and solid knowledge of Jesus Christ and of all that he did while he lived among his own. For, using a Hebrew idiom, by the two extremes, namely the words "coming in" and "going out," he comprehends the whole conversation of Christ. Lest anyone seek occasion from this to inquire into things too curiously, he sets limits to this knowledge: namely, the baptism of John and Christ's glorious ascension into heaven. For before Christ was baptized by John, he lived a private life in Nazareth of Galilee, obeying his parents and often practising the carpenter's trade with his foster-father Joseph, as you may conjecture from what is related in Luke 2 and Mark 6. But the things that pertained to the public cause of our redemption and to the office of the Messiah he began to undertake only after he had been baptized by John and inaugurated by the visible anointing of the Holy Spirit and the Father's testimony delivered from heaven. Matt. 3. This is why the Evangelists, content to describe his incarnation, handed down very little about his childhood and youth. For the Holy Spirit willed to restrain the foolish curiosity of the human mind, which in the latest ages has put itself forward through certain outstanding writers, if you please, who have handed down to us the life of Christ and his childhood, not without public ridicule of the Christian name. Yet for the divine Peter, that knowledge seems sufficient which Christ gave after that solemn inauguration. This was necessary because Christ wished the apostles to be most faithful witnesses of the things he had done in their presence. Secondly, Peter requires a certain and evident proof of perseverance. For he does not want anyone chosen from among those who were still novices in profession of the Christian name, and who had joined the assembly of the faithful only a few days before. Rather he speaks of those who had begun to follow Christ Jesus among men near the start of his life among them, and had persevered with him, so that they could not be terrified either by the dangers of persecutions or by the stumbling-block of the cross and of an infamous death. Indeed, these same qualities ought to be observed today too in the elections or ordinations of ministers of the Word, if those who claim this right for themselves wish the Church of Christ to be safe and unharmed. For it is agreed that the chief function of the minister lies in doctrine, as the Lord also warned through the prophet, saying: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts." Mal. 2. But how will he teach who is himself untaught and unskilled? Paul certainly requires this above all in a bishop, that he be διδακτικὸς [didaktikos], that is, endowed with the ability to teach, and able not only to deliver the plain doctrine of the truth to men of rather slow understanding, but also to refute and overthrow those who contradict it (and there will always be a huge number of these). 1 Tim. 3. Tit. 1. Therefore in a minister of the Word there is necessary a knowledge of Christ and of his mysteries, together with all that pertains to the articles of the Christian faith and to the duties of the faithful. He must also apply diligent study to Scripture, in which he ought to be thoroughly versed. He needs knowledge of languages, so that in reading the Scriptures he does not have to depend on the sense of others, and so be forced to see with other people's eyes and walk on other people's feet. Besides this, it is fitting that he be equipped with the arts of speaking, so that he can discern what ought to be put forward, in what place and order, and how. All these things are of such importance that Paul does not carelessly urge Timothy to a constant study of reading, although he confesses that Timothy had learned the sacred letters from boyhood. Then, since infinite dangers hang over the function of ministers on every side, courage of mind is required, so that he is not overcome by fear of dangers and stop halfway along the course. This will be seen only in perseverance, of which the candidate ought to have given clear proofs. Paul also observed this when he warns that a bishop must not be a neophyte or a novice, lest, puffed up by a sudden dignity, he do something amiss and give his adversaries occasion to slander him. 1 Tim. 3. But Christ himself, too, commends the apostles, whom it is certain labored under many faults and weaknesses, chiefly by this praise at the Last Supper: that they had continued with him in all his temptations. Luke 22.

units.la: Sed vlcima Petri verba videamus, quibus apostoli officium definit. Constituatur (inquit) vnus quispiam, qui vnà nobiscũ fit testis resurrectionis eius. Primò collegam aliquem vndecim apostolis vule coniungi, non seruum, cui ipsi pro suo arbitrio imperitent. Æqualitatem enim inter Christi ministros esse debere nouerat. Deinde testem vocat, quo nomine Christus illos, iam discessurus, appellarat. Et prodest non parum crebro huius nominis repetitio & consideratio diligens. Ex eo enim Christianæ fidei dignitas & euangelicæ doctrinæ certitudo æstimari potest, quòd Christus non præcones modò rerum abs se gestarum, sed iuratos testes habuit, qui fidem in ipsum tradiderunt. Postremò, qua de re testari debeat, ostendit: Vt fit testis resurrectionis eius. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi de sola Christi resurrectione apostoli verba facere debuerint, sed præcipuum articulum nominare voluit Petrus, quo reliqui omnes continentur, imò qui perspicuè monet, quò reliqui omnes referri debeant. Resurrectioni certè mortis prædicatio necessariò inclusa & coniuncta est. Quomodo enim Christum à mortuus resurrexisse docebit, qui illum mortuum fuisse, non ante docuit? At si mortuū Christum quis prædicare velit, de natura Christi, secundum quam mori potuit, prius loquatur, oportet. Docebit ergo, Dei filium, qui patri coæternus & consubstantialis est, definito tempore humanam naturam ex virginiũ ginis vtero induisse, in qua post multas variasq; vitae huius molestias acerbam mortem in ara crucis tandem perpessus sit. Quare qui resurrectionis Christi Iesu testis & praeco esse voluerit, minime omittet quaecunq; illam praecesserunt.
