Sed & alia causa est, propter quam resurrectionis potissimū mentionem voluit facere Petrus. Haec enim nostrae redemptionis quasi colophon est & complementum, vt Paulus in priori ad Corinthios epistola cap.15. multis demonstrat. Mortis etenim, cuius omnes homines rei erant, aculeus & potentia peccatum est. Atqui mortem deuictam esse, Christi resurrectio luculentissime testatur. Quare & peccatum, per quod nobis mors dominabatur, eiusdem Christi merito sublatum esse oportuit. Quod si vero peccati noxa sublata est, & mors exarmata, quis non videt, seu pentis caput contritum & diaboli tyrannidem funditus euersam esse? Insanit quidem adhuc, & horrendum tumultuatur: sed illius terrores Christianae mentes non expauerunt. Quibus enim viribus noceret, qui si peccati tela & mortis cuspidem illi auferas, totus inermis erit? Atqui haec Christus ab stulit, dum in ara crucis expiauit peccata mundi, & mortis vires gloriosa resurrectione enervauit. Quapropter dum resurrectionis Christi testem fieri vult eum Petrus, qui in apostolorum ordinem cooptari debebat, hoc ipsum munus illi iniungit, quod reliqui sustinebant, quibus dictum erat: Ite in orbem vniuersum, & praedicate euangelium omni creaturae. Quisquis crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Marc.16. Interim officij admonentur, qui hodie apostolorum successores dici & haberi volunt. Quamvis enim ab illis nemo exigere possit, vt resurrectionis Christi testes sint oculati, hoc tamen illorum munus sit, vt de Christo & omnibus ijs, quae ille propter nos tam fecit quam passus est, ingenuè ac intrepidè testentur, vt omnes, in vno Christo humani generis redemptionem & salutem contineri intelligant. Quicunq; enim nudo titulo inflati, pro apostolicis haberi volunt, cum nec concionari velint, nec possint, non legitimi apostolorum successores, sed stulti pastores sunt, quorum descriptionem habet Zachar. 11. cap. Et in illos Paulinum illud merito torquetur: Vae mihi, si non euangelizem. 1.Cor.9. Nostrum vero est, dei bonitatem agnoscere, qui filium suum propter peccata nostra mori, & nostrae iustificationis causa exsuscitari voluit, simul vero mortis & resurrectionis Christi salutiferae testes dedit locupletissimos. Credamus itaq; illorum testimonio, vt per semē immortalis verbi regenerati, haeredes dei efficiamur, coheredes autem Iesu Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us look at the last words of Peter, in which he defines the office of an apostle. "Let there be appointed," he says, "one who together with us may be a witness of his resurrection." First, he wants some colleague to be joined to the eleven apostles, not a slave whom they might order about at their own pleasure. For he knew that there ought to be equality among the ministers of Christ. Next, he calls him a witness, the name by which Christ had called them when he was about to depart. And the frequent repetition and careful consideration of this name are of no small profit. For from it the dignity of the Christian faith and the certainty of the gospel doctrine can be judged, in that Christ had not merely heralds of the things he had done, but sworn witnesses who handed over their faith in him. Lastly, Peter shows what they must bear witness to: "that he may be a witness of his resurrection." This should not be taken to mean that the apostles were to speak only of Christ's resurrection, as if Peter wished to name a single article, while all the others are contained in it. Rather, he clearly indicates the point to which all the rest must be referred. Certainly the preaching of death is necessarily included in and joined to the preaching of resurrection. For how will he teach that Christ rose from the dead who has not first taught that he died? But if anyone wishes to preach a dead Christ, he must first speak of the nature of Christ, according to which he could die. He will therefore teach that the Son of God, who is co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, at a set time put on human nature from the womb of the virgin, and in that nature at last endured a bitter death on the altar of the cross after many and varied troubles of this life. Therefore whoever wishes to be a witness and herald of the resurrection of Jesus Christ will by no means omit those things which went before it. But there is also another reason why Peter chose especially to mention the resurrection. For this is, as it were, the seal and completion of our redemption, as Paul shows at length in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 15. For the sting of death, to which all men were liable, is sin, and its power is sin. Yet the resurrection of Christ most brilliantly testifies that death has been overcome. Therefore sin, through which death had dominion over us, must also have been taken away by the merit of this same Christ. But if the harm of sin has indeed been removed and death disarmed, who does not see that the serpent's head has been crushed and the tyranny of the devil overthrown to its foundations? He still rages and makes a dreadful uproar, but Christian minds have not been terrified by his terrors. For with what strength could he harm, who, if you take away from him the weapons of sin and the point of death, will be altogether unarmed? Yet Christ has removed these things, when he made expiation for the sins of the world on the altar of the cross, and weakened the powers of death by his glorious resurrection. Therefore, when Peter wants the one who was to be enrolled in the order of the apostles to be a witness of Christ's resurrection, he lays upon him the same duty that the others bore, to whom it was said: "Go into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved." Mark 16. Meanwhile, those who today wish to be called and regarded as successors of the apostles are reminded of their office. For although no one can demand of them that they be eyewitnesses of Christ's resurrection, yet it is their duty to bear witness frankly and fearlessly about Christ and all the things he did and suffered for us, so that all may understand that the redemption and salvation of the human race are contained in Christ alone. For those who, puffed up by a bare title, want to be regarded as apostolic, though they neither wish nor are able to preach, are not lawful successors of the apostles but foolish shepherds, whose description is given in Zechariah chapter 11. And upon them rightly falls that saying of Paul: "Woe is me if I do not preach the gospel." 1 Cor. 9. It is our part to acknowledge the goodness of God, who willed that his Son should die for our sins and be raised up for the sake of our justification, and at the same time has given us most abundant witnesses of the death and resurrection of Christ. Let us therefore believe their testimony, so that through the seed of the immortal word we may be born again and become heirs of God and co-heirs with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honor, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA IX.
units.tr: HOMILY IX.

units.la: Tunc statuerunt duos, Iosephum, qui vocabatur Barsabas, cognomine Iustum, & Matthiam; & precantes dixerunt: Tu domine, qui nouisti corda omnium, ostende vtrum elegeris ex duobus his, qui accipiat sortem ministerij huius & apostolatus, ex quo Iudas excidit, vt abiret in locum suum. Et dederunt sortes eorum, & cecidit sors super Matthiam, & cooptatus fuit inter vndecim Apostolos.
units.tr: Then they appointed two men, Joseph, called Barsabas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias. And praying, they said: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen to take up this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas fell away, to go to his own place." And they gave their lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

units.la: VT ecclesia verbi ministris cumprimis opus habet, quorum opera in dei cognitione & vera fidei mysterijs erudiatur ac confirmetur: ita eosdem legitimè ac ritè eligi & ordinari oportet, vt ipsos diuinitus electos esse, omnibus constare possit. Quae causa est, quod in noui apostoli electione, qui in Iudae locum surrogari debebat, tam religiose egit vetus ecclesia. Et voluit spiritus sanctus historiam hanc omnem diligenter describi, vt certa ad posteritatem formula transmitteretur, ad cuius imitationem electiones ministrorum institui possent. Primum vero in hac locum obtinet, quod diuus Petrus rem omnem ad ecclesiam refert, communi & vnanimi omnium consilio discutiendam. Docemur eo exemplo, nihil in ecclesia cuiusquam priuata authoritate institui siue decerni debere. Quia enim ecclesia, vt Paulus 1.Cor.3. admonet, dei aedificatio & dei agricolatio est, imò domus & familia dei (1. Tim.3. Matth.24.) nemo sibi tantum authoritatis vendicare debet, vt sibi in illam ius esse putet, quippiam priuato consilio instituendi. Et licet eosq; progrediatur alicuius temeritas, nihil tamen inter veras Christi oues proficiet, quae vnius Christi vocem audire & sequi consueuerunt. Iohan. 10. Sed ad institutam à Luca historiae narrationem reuertamur, qui vbi diui Petri orationem recitauit, modò ipsam electionem noui apostoli commemorat, quae nobis per singulas partes diligentius erit excutienda. Primò enim duos publicè nominatos esse, & in totius ecclesiæ conspectum productos esse dicit. Deinde piis & devotis precibus electionem ipsam Dei iudicio commiserunt: de cuius voluntate religiosis sortibus scisciscati sunt.
units.tr: Just as the Church has great need of ministers of the Word, by whose work it is taught and strengthened in the knowledge of God and in the mysteries of the true faith, so these men must be chosen and ordained lawfully and properly, so that it may be evident to all that they have been chosen by God. This is why the ancient Church acted so scrupulously in the choice of the new apostle who was to be put in Judas's place. The Holy Spirit wanted this whole story described carefully, so that a certain pattern might be handed down to posterity, by whose imitation the election of ministers could be carried out. The first thing to notice here is that blessed Peter refers the whole matter to the Church, to be discussed by the common and unanimous counsel of all. From this example we are taught that nothing in the Church should be set up or decided by anyone's private authority. For the Church, as Paul reminds us (1 Cor. 3), is God's building and God's field, indeed the house and family of God (1 Tim. 3; Matt. 24). Therefore no one should claim so much authority for himself that he thinks he has the right to set up anything by his own private counsel. Even if someone's recklessness goes so far, it will achieve nothing among the true sheep of Christ, who are accustomed to hear and follow the voice of Christ alone (John 10). But let us return to Luke's narration of the history. After reciting Peter's speech, he now records the election of the new apostle itself, which we must examine more carefully part by part. First, he says that two men were publicly named and brought forward into the sight of the whole Church. Then, with pious and devout prayers, they committed the election itself to God's judgment, and they sought his will by sacred lots.

units.la: Tunc statuerunt (inquit) duos, Iosephum, qui vocabatur Barsabas, cognomine Iustū, & Matthiam. Quamuis vero modus, quo hoc factum est, non exprimatur, publico tamen & unanimi ecclesiæ totius consensu illud factum esse, verisimile videtur. Quia enim ad totam ecclesiam rem hanc omnem Petrus referre voluit, ecclesiæ iudicium non potuit praetermittere. Videntur ergo viritim rogatæ fuisse sententiæ, & singulos, quos apostolicæ functioni idoneos censebant, nominatim ecclesiæ indicauisse: Hic ergo ecclesiæ consensus tandem fuit, ut vel Iosephus vel Matthias apostolorum numero accenseretur, qui nimirum omni virtutum genere reliquis præstantiores habebantur. Et uterque haud dubie talis fuit, ut fors errare non posse videretur, utrum designaret. Nominatos autem in medium progredi iusserunt, ut ab omnibus possent conspici & agnosci.
units.tr: "Then they appointed two," he says, "Joseph, called Barsabas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias." Although the manner in which this was done is not stated, it seems likely that it was done with the public and unanimous consent of the whole Church. For since Peter wanted the whole matter referred to the entire Church, he could not have omitted the Church's judgment. It seems therefore that the opinions were asked one by one, and that each man named to the Church those whom he considered fit for the apostolic office. The outcome of this common consent was that either Joseph or Matthias should be counted among the apostles, both of whom were regarded as surpassing the others in every kind of virtue. And both were doubtless such men that it could not seem that lot might err in designating either one. They ordered the named men to step forward into the midst, so that they could be seen and recognized by all.

units.la: Est itaque cum primis memorabile hoc primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplum. Quo admonemur, ministrorum verbi & ecclesiæ electiones atque ordinationes, non in angulis & occultè intra priuatos parietes, à paucis hominibus, sed publicè ab ecclesia, & in totius ecclesiæ conspectu fieri debere. Si enim ab exterorum quoque testimonio commendari debet episcopus (quod Paulus monuit 1. Tim. 3.) quanto magis illius ipsum notum esse oportet, quibus præficitur? Cuius rei obseruatio si negligatur, vel ignoti & obscuri homines, vel etiam flagitiosi & corruptissimi moribus praediti ecclesijs obtruduntur, & ecclesiarum antistites fiunt, qui ne extremum quidem in ecclesia locum merentur. Monet idem veteris Testamenti ritus, quo ex Dei mandato Aaron & filij ipsius publicè & tota spectante ecclesia ministerio sacro destinati & initiati sunt. Leuit. 8. Num. 30. Neque nos mouet, quòd Paulus alibi uni Tito vel Timotheo ius & potestatem episcopos eligendi tribuere videtur. Non enim illos priuata authoritate quicquam agere voluit, sed pro antistitu officio iubet curare, ut ministri digni & idonei legitimè ordinentur. Nec verisimile est, illius plus concessum fuisse, quam apostolis ipsis, qui inconsulta ecclesia nihil in hac causa unquam statuerunt. Nam & paulò post diaconos coram ecclesia publicè eligunt, & Paulus cum Barnaba collectis viritim suffragijs presbyteros per ecclesias singulas ordinauisse leguntur. Actto 6. & 14. cap.
units.tr: This is therefore a notable example, especially from the early Church. It reminds us that the elections and ordinations of ministers of the Word and of the Church ought to be made not in corners and secretly within private walls, by a few men, but publicly by the Church and in the sight of the whole Church. For if even a bishop must be commended by the testimony of outsiders (as Paul warned in 1 Tim. 3), how much more ought he to be known to those over whom he is set? If this observance is neglected, either unknown and obscure men are foisted upon the churches, or men of disgraceful and thoroughly corrupt character become the overseers of the churches, although they do not deserve even the lowest place in the Church. The same is taught by the ritual of the Old Testament, in which Aaron and his sons were publicly appointed and consecrated to sacred ministry by God's command, in the sight of the whole congregation (Lev. 8; Num. 30). Nor are we troubled by the fact that Paul elsewhere seems to give to Titus or Timothy alone the right and power to choose bishops. For he did not want them to do anything on their own private authority, but ordered them, as part of their office of oversight, to take care that worthy and fit ministers were lawfully ordained. Nor is it likely that they were granted more than the apostles themselves had, who never decided anything in this matter without consulting the Church. For shortly afterward they publicly chose deacons before the Church, and we read that Paul and Barnabas, after the votes were collected one by one, ordained elders in each church (Acts 6 and 14).

units.la: Arguitur exemplo hoc corruptissimus idemque perniciosissimus ministros eligendi mos, quem iam seculis aliquot hac in causa imperium obtinuisse constat. Quo fit, ut non raro unus aliquis in pluribus ecclesijs priuata authoritate ministros & eligat & ordinet: qua re potissimùm ab Abbatibus, episcopis & præpositis peccatur. Nec melius rem administrat nonnulli inter eos qui euangelij nomine gloriantur, & ecclesiarum reformatores haberi volunt. Dum enim isti male usurpata possessione monachos & episcopos (ut par est) eijciunt, ecclesijs tamen libertatem, illorum tyrannide ereptam, non restituunt, sed pro suo arbitrio administrant, quæ olim ab episcopis & monachis administrari solebant. Et hinc præposterus ille ordo multis in locis obtinuit, ut ministros ecclesiarum eligant & ordinent, qui nec ipsos ministros nec ecclesias, quibus illi præfici debent, satis nouerunt. Et quia ignoratiæ malo plerunque affectus improbissimi coniuncti sunt, ita interdum ijs abripi solent, ut absque omni religione in tanto negotio versantes, hoc unum agere videri possint, ut suam in ecclesias potestatem non minori cum fastu, quàm episcopi olim & monachi, ostentent. Quod malum, nisi breui reprimatur, & Simoniam & exitialem omnis ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ confusionem nobis pariet. Atqui omne hoc Romanus Pontificibus debetur, qui non fine cruentissimis bellis ab Imperatoribus hoc extorserunt, ut ipsis solis episcopatus & quæcunque alia sunt beneficia ecclesiastica conferendi ius concederetur. Extant adhuc in Germania non pauci loci, qui præliorum & effusi sanguinis Christiani memoriam referunt. Certè Heinrychum quartum Imperat. constat tum hac ipsa tum alijs de causis cum pontificibus commissum, sexagies bis collatis signis pugnauisse. Tandem vero filium hostem sensit, quem episcoporum artes & consilia aduersus patrem armauerant. Qui cum tandem illorum dolos animaduerteret, sese illis opponere coepit: sed pertinaci ipsorum improbitate & audacia superatus, Califto II. omnem hanc authoritatem concessit, ex quo tempore ecclesiæ libertas ceu lethali morbo contabescens, tandem in vniuersum euanuit. Quam quicunque restitutam voleat, siue illi verbi ministri sint, siue magistratus, huc incumbendum sibi esse sciant, ut vetus ministrorum eligendorum consuetudo reducatur.
units.tr: This passage exposes the most corrupt and at the same time most pernicious custom of choosing ministers, which has held sway for several centuries. As a result, it often happens that a single man, by private authority, both chooses and ordains ministers for several churches. This abuse is especially committed by abbots, bishops and provosts. Nor do some of those who boast of the gospel and want to be regarded as reformers of the churches manage the matter any better. For while they drive out monks and bishops (as is right) from a possession wrongly seized, they do not restore to the churches the liberty that was snatched from them by those tyrants. Instead they administer, at their own discretion, the things that used to be administered by bishops and monks. From this the perverse order has taken hold in many places, that men who know neither the ministers themselves nor the churches over which they are to be set choose and ordain the ministers of the churches. And since the evil of ignorance is usually joined with the most wicked passions, these men are sometimes so carried away that, handling so great a business without any reverence, they seem to aim at nothing else than to display their power over the churches with no less pride than the bishops and monks of old. Unless this evil is checked soon, it will bring upon us both simony and the deadly confusion of all church discipline. And yet all this is owed to the Roman pontiffs, who obtained from the emperors, not without the bloodiest wars, that the right to confer bishoprics and all other ecclesiastical benefices should be granted to them alone. There are still not a few places in Germany that recall the memory of battles and of Christian blood poured out. It is certain that Emperor Henry IV, who was at odds with the pontiffs for this and other reasons, fought sixty-two pitched battles. At last, however, he found an enemy in his own son, whom the arts and counsels of the bishops had armed against his father. When at last he perceived their tricks, he began to resist them; but, overcome by their stubborn wickedness and boldness, he yielded all this authority to Calixtus II. From that time the liberty of the Church, wasting away as if from a deadly disease, finally vanished altogether. Whoever wants it restored, whether ministers of the Word or magistrates, should know that they must work toward reviving the ancient custom of choosing ministers.

units.la: Anno 1122. Vide Vrspurgen. Porrò vt ad historia præsentis expositionem redeamus, cùm duos in conspectu ecclesiæ statuissent, Iosephum & Matthiam, omni virtutum genere instructissimos viros, nemo tamen apostolorum tantum sibi authoritatis vendicare ausus est, vt alterutrum ex illis apostolum pronunciare vellet. Imò nec suffragiorum numero rem tanti momenti satis tutò committi posse putauerunt, sed ad preces devotissimas conuersi, omnem huius rei euentum infallibili Dei iudicio commisere. Dicunt enim: Tu domine, qui nouisti corda omnium, ostende vtrum elegeris ex duobus hîs, &c. Præclarum hoc est pijssimorum animorum, nihilq; audacius in dei causa sibi ipsis vendicare volentium, specimen. Quod exemplum si pari religione imitarentur, qui hodie ecclesiæ munera tractant, felicius haud dubiè pleraque succederent.
units.tr: Year 1122. See Vrspurgen. But to return to the explanation of the present history: when they had set two men before the sight of the Church, Joseph and Matthias, men most fully endowed with every kind of virtue, yet none of the apostles dared to claim so much authority for himself as to declare either of them an apostle. Indeed, they did not think that a matter of such great importance could be safely left to the number of votes, but turned to most devout prayers and committed the whole outcome of this matter to God's infallible judgment. For they say: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen," and so on. This is a remarkable example of the most pious minds, who wanted nothing in God's cause to be claimed by themselves rashly. If those who now handle the offices of the Church imitated this example with equal reverence, things would undoubtedly turn out far more happily in most cases.

units.la: Hinc verò colligimus, ministrorum electionem ab vno Deo pendere, & ad illum debere referri. Ecclesiæ partes hîc esse putamus, vt legitimè congregata, priuatis affectibus positis, aliquos inquirat, quibus ecclesiastica functio commodè & tutò credi possit. Et hic in primis ardens religionis studium exigimus, cui ieiunia quoque aliquando coniuncta fuisse constat, quò ardentiores essent preces. Act.13. & 14. At vbi aliquot reperti sunt, quos tanto munere dignos censeri æquum est, ne tunc quidem hominum iudicio nimis indulgere oportet. Sed commodissima tutissimaq; ratio videtur, si ad dei iudicium omnis nostrorum consiliorum euentus referatur. Quamuis non ignorem, aliquos scripturæ locos reperiri, in quibus ex hominum iudicio ministri creati esse videantur, nec res (vt in præsenti) fortibus transacta appareat. Quò cumprimis referri possunt, quæ in Pauli epistolis habentur. 1. Timoth. 3. & 5. Tit.1. Sed illic eorum duntaxat mentionem fieri puto, quæ in hac causa ab hominibus, tanquam rei agendæ ducibus siue ministris agi debeant, salua interim hac primitiuæ ecclesiæ forma, quam in ecclesia integram obseruari propter grauissimas rationes necesse est. Primò enim ecclesiam dei domum & familiam esse constat, vt initio monuimus, in qua œconomorum siue dispensatorum vices ministri obeunt. Matth 24. Item 1.Cor.4. Atqui nemo sapiens tantum sibi permittit, vt in aliena domo pro suo arbitrio vilissimum famulum, nedum dispensatorem constituat. Quæ ergo absurditas fuerit, hoc in Dei domo audere, & tanti momenti rem cæcæ rationis nostræ iudicio committere? Præterea in electionibus ministrorum animi potissimam rationem haberi debere, nemo negauerit: quia in animo earum virtutum sedes est, quas in ministro spiritus sanctus requirit. At quis obsecro hominum, de alterius animo iudicans, iudicij sui certus esse potest? Nonne hic homines quotidie falli fatendum erit, quando manifestis signis illorum improbitate tandem deprehendimus, quos omnibus numeris absolutos esse putabamus? Exemplo hic nobis sunt ipsi apostoli, quos Iudas, quamuis fur esset, & sacrilegus, tam diu latere potuit. Dei autem ea natura est & conditio, vt nullo fuco aut simulatione falli possit. Nec enim externa modò videt, sed corda & renes scrutatur, imò hominum cogitationes & consilia, priusquam animis nostris oboriantur, longè præuidet. Nulli ergo tutius, quàm ipsius iudicio, causa hæc omnis committitur. Id quod apostolos quoq; in præsenti maximè mouit, cum dicunt: Tu domine, qui omnium corda nouisti, ostende nobis, vtrum ex duobus hisce elegeris, &c. Quibus verbis non obscurè causam fatentur, qua impulsi, ad dei iudicium recurrant: eam nimirum, quòd aliorum corda ipsi inspicere non possint. Cum autem idem nos quoq;, quoties de ministris eligendis consultatio habetur, fateri cogamur, temerarij nimis videri possumus, quòd in ea causa nihilominus iudices nos constituimus, in qua animorum examen maximè requiritur. Accedit bis postremo loco, quòd electionis formula siue ritus, quo apostoli vti voluerunt, & ministris authoritatem non paruam in auditorum mentibus conciliat, & ijsdem contra impiorum minas & conatus, atque aliunde impendentia pericula animos addit. Sic enim fit, vt minister ne malsuolis quidem & hostibus (siquidem verum fateri velint) vel temeritatis vel doli mali suspectus esse possit. Nam quis malis artibus in ecclesiæ ministerium irrepsisse, vel hominum fauore & potentia eò euectus esse censeri poterit, qui Dei iudicio minister declaratus est? Vel quis saluo conscientiæ propriæ testimonio illum contemnere & odisse audeat, cuius electionem & ordinationem ecclesiæ totius, adeoq; suis ipsius precibus, impetratam esse nouit? Simili ratione hæc ipsis ministris animum addere solent, quo illis propter minas & conatus mundi huius cumprimis opus est. Quia enim se non hominum fauore & consilio, sed diuinitus electos & ordinatos esse certò norunt, dei auxilium & protectionem sibiipsis, si in commisso munere fideles fuerint, certò polliceri possunt. Sibi ipsis dictum esse intelligunt: Cau metuas vultus eorum, ego enim tecum sum, ut te liberem, ait dominus. Ierem. 1. Rursum se deum vindicem & ultorem habituros esse dubitare non possunt, si in officio suo ignavi, vel etiam improbi & perfidi fuerint. Sciunt enim omnibus ministris dici, quod propheta dicitur: Cum ego dixero impio, Certissimè morieris: atq; tu non monueris eum diserte, neq; locutus fueris diserte, dehortando impium à via sua impia, ut viuat: ille quidem impius morietur in iniquitate sua, sanguinem vero eius de manu tua requiram. Ezech. 3. & 33. Quorum consideratio eos animos mihi in prophetis & apostolis peperisse videtur, quos nec blanditiæ falsorum fratrum, nec impiorum hostium minæ frangere potuerunt. Etenim hac ratione Amoz propheta astutissimi Amaliæ subdolum consilium eludit. Cum enim hic fugam prophetæ suaderet, ne ab Ieroboamo rege comprehensus ob conciones suas, minarum & increpationum plenas, aduersi aliquid pateretur, illum respondisse legimus: Ego neq; propheta eram, neq; filius prophetæ, sed bubulcus, sycomora stringens. Tulit autem me dominus cum greges sequerer, dixitq; mihi: Vade, & vaticinare contra populum meum Israel, &c. Amoz 7. Quibus verbis non aliud vult propheta, quam se nihil temere aut priuato consilio egisse, sed munus obire diuinitus iniunctum, & proinde stationem eam se deserere non posse, in quam ab ipso domino collocatus sit. Idem cap. 3. ait: Leo si rugiat, quis est qui non timeat? Dominus Deus cum loquitur, quis non propheteret? Quo illa quoque referri debent, quæ apostoli in senatu Hierosolymitano pari animorum fiducia egerunt. Cum enim illis interdiceretur, ne in nomine Iesu loquerentur amplius, responderunt: Obedire oportet deo magis, quam hominibus. Item: Ipsi iudicate, an iustum sit in conspectu dei, vos potius audire quam deum? Actor. 5. & 4. cap. Qua vero ratione ista dicere licuisset apostolis, nisi se diuinitus ad hanc functionem electos & vocatos fuisse certò intellexissent? Et jane eandem παρρησίαν & dicendi agendiq; fiduciam frustra in ijs requires, qui non expectata vocatione legitima, malis artibus & hominum fauore irrepunt. Nam & propter ingressum suum subdolum male sibi conscij, & illis deinceps quorum beneficio ad hanc dignitatem subleuati sunt, pro veritate & Dei gloria afferenda nihil egregij audent, sed mirifici tergiuersatores tam Deo quam hominibus placere studeant, imò tandem excusso Dei timore omni, in populari aura captanda toti occupantur, ficq; suo sese indicio ut sorices produnt, quòd iuxta Pauli sententiam, Dei serui non sint, cum hominibus placere studeant. Gal. 1. Quare quisquis in ecclesia & veterem disciplinæ authoritatem, & prophelicam apostolicamq; in ministris agendi fiduciam, adeoq; totius ecclesiæ antiquam integritatem, restituram cupit, veterem hanc, & apostolorum exemplo monstratam, ministros eligendi rationem reuocare studeat.
units.tr: Hence we gather that the election of ministers depends on the one God alone and ought to be referred to him. We think the role of the Church here is this: when lawfully gathered, with private feelings set aside, it should seek out those to whom the ecclesiastical office can be entrusted safely and fittingly. And here above all we require a burning zeal for religion, to which fasting too was sometimes joined, as is known, so that their prayers might be more fervent (Acts 13 and 14). But when some have been found who are fitting to be judged worthy of so great an office, it is not right even then to indulge too much in human judgement. Rather the most suitable and safest course seems to be to refer the whole outcome of our counsels to the judgement of God. Although I am not unaware that there are some passages of Scripture in which ministers seem to have been appointed by human judgement, and the matter does not appear to have been settled by lot, as in the present case. To these especially may be referred what is found in Paul's epistles (1 Timothy 3 and 5; Titus 1). But I think there he mentions only those things which, in this matter, ought to be done by men as leaders of the business or ministers, while the form of the primitive Church is preserved, which, for very weighty reasons, must be kept whole in the Church. For, first, it is plain that the Church of God is a house and a household, as we noted at the beginning, in which ministers take the place of stewards or managers (Matthew 24; likewise 1 Corinthians 4). Yet no wise man allows himself so much that in another's house he would appoint, at his own discretion, even the lowliest servant, let alone a steward. What absurdity, then, would it be to dare this in God's house, and to entrust a matter of such moment to the judgement of our blind reason? Moreover, that in elections of ministers the disposition of the mind ought chiefly to be taken into account, no one will deny: for the mind is the seat of those virtues which the Holy Spirit requires in a minister. But which of men, I beg you, judging another's mind, can be certain of his judgement? Must we not confess that men are deceived every day, when by manifest signs we at last discover the wickedness of those whom we thought perfect in every respect? Here the apostles themselves are an example to us: Judas, though a thief and a sacrilegious man, could remain hidden so long. But God's nature and condition is such that he cannot be deceived by any pretence or disguise. For he sees not only outward things, but searches hearts and reins, and indeed far foresees human thoughts and plans before they arise in our minds. Therefore this whole matter is committed to no one more safely than to his judgement. This is what moved the apostles also especially in the present case, when they say: "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show us which of these two you have chosen," etc. By these words they plainly confess the reason that drove them to recur to God's judgement: namely, that they themselves could not look into the hearts of others. Yet since we too are compelled to confess the same whenever consultation is held about choosing ministers, we may seem overly rash, because in a matter where the examination of minds is especially required, we nevertheless set ourselves up as judges. Added to this, lastly, is that the form or rite of election which the apostles chose to use both brings no small authority to the ministers in the minds of the hearers, and gives them courage against the threats and attempts of the wicked and against dangers hanging over them from elsewhere. For thus it comes about that a minister cannot be suspected of rashness or of wicked deceit, even by his ill-wishers and enemies (if they are willing to tell the truth). For who could be thought to have crept into the ministry of the Church by evil arts, or to have been raised to it by the favour and power of men, when he has been declared a minister by the judgement of God? Or who would dare, with his conscience still intact, to despise and hate him whose election and ordination he knows to have been obtained for the whole Church, and so by its own prayers? In a similar way this practice is wont to give courage to the ministers themselves, which they especially need because of the threats and attempts of this world. For since they know for certain that they have been chosen and ordained not by the favour and counsel of men but by divine appointment, they can with certainty promise themselves God's help and protection, if they are faithful in the office entrusted to them. They understand that the words have been spoken to them: "Do not fear their faces, for I am with you, to deliver you," says the Lord (Jeremiah 1). Again, they cannot doubt that they will have God as avenger and punisher, if they are slothful in their duty, or even wicked and faithless. For they know that what the prophet says is said to all ministers: "When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him plainly, nor speak plainly, dissuading the wicked from his wicked way so that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at your hand" (Ezekiel 3 and 33). The consideration of these things seems to me to have produced in the prophets and apostles those minds which neither the flatteries of false brothers nor the threats of impious enemies could break. For in this way the prophet Amos thwarts the crafty plan of Amaziah. When Amaziah urged him to flee, lest he be seized by King Jeroboam and suffer some harm on account of his sermons, full of threats and rebukes, we read that he replied: "I was neither a prophet nor a son of a prophet, but a herdsman, cutting sycamore figs. But the Lord took me as I followed the flock, and said to me: Go, prophesy against my people Israel," etc. (Amos 7). By these words the prophet wishes nothing else than to show that he had not acted rashly or on private counsel, but was discharging a office divinely enjoined, and therefore could not abandon the post in which the Lord himself had placed him. Likewise in chapter 3 he says: "If a lion roars, who will not fear? When the Lord God speaks, who will not prophesy?" To this also must be referred what the apostles did with equal confidence of spirit before the council at Jerusalem. When they were forbidden to speak any more in the name of Jesus, they answered: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Again: "Judge for yourselves whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God" (Acts 5 and 4). But by what reasoning could the apostles have been permitted to say these things, unless they had understood for certain that they had been chosen and called by God to this function? And indeed you will look in vain for the same boldness of speech and confidence in acting in those who, without waiting for a lawful calling, creep in by evil arts and the favour of men. For, conscious of their deceitful entry, and toward those by whose kindness they have been raised to this dignity, they dare nothing noble in defence of the truth and the glory of God; instead, as remarkable evaders, they strive to please both God and men. Indeed, at last, with all fear of God cast aside, they occupy themselves wholly in catching popular favour, and so by their own judgement they betray themselves like mice, since, according to Paul's saying, they are not servants of God if they strive to please men (Galatians 1). Therefore whoever desires to restore in the Church both the ancient authority of discipline and the prophetic and apostolic confidence in ministers' acting, and indeed the ancient integrity of the whole Church, let him take care to recall this ancient manner of choosing ministers, shown by the example of the apostles.

units.la: Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, quibus verbis apostolicam functionem describant, videndum erit. Vocant enim sortem ministerij & apostolatus. Sortis vocabulo ad sortiendi actionem alludunt, qua paulo post dei mentem inquirere statuebant. Atqui in rerum diuisionibus fors frequenter pro parte sumitur, quæ per sortem obtingit. Quo sensu & hic sortem ministerij & apostolatus pro parte dicunt. Subinde ergo æqualem inter apostolos & euangelij ministros conditionem agnoscunt & fatentur. Si enim Matthias eius ministerij partem accepit, quod tam Petro quam alijs æque commissum erat: nemo certè illorum totum obtinuit, ut aliorum caput aut dominus habere debeat. Nec maior esse debuit Petri in euangelizando authoritas, quam vel Iohannis, vel Matthiæ, vel alterius cuiusdam apostoli, quando vnum & idem mandatum omnes illos à domino Iesu accepisse constat. Deinde ministerij & apostolatus nomina coniungunt, ut & ambitioni occurrant, & functionis huius dignitatem afferant. Quia enim ministerium est, de quo hic agitur, stultum & absurdum fuerit, sub huius prætextu dignitatem popularem quærere, vel dominium tyrannicum exercere. Quin potius Christi regulam obseruare decet: Quicunq; voluerit inter vos magnus fieri, sit vester minister, & qui voluerit inter vos primus esse, sit vester seruus. Matth. 20. Et hac ratione Paulus multis apostolis præferri mereretur, quia plus quam omnes alij in Christi ecclesia laborauit. 1. Cor. 15. 2. Cor. 11. & 12. cap. Præpositerus autem in ecclesia nostri seculi ordo est, quando primi & præstantissimi habentur, qui quàm minimum laborant in ecclesiæ ministerio, ex ecclesiæ vero bonis splendidius quam reliqui viuunt, & ex ijsdem thesauros sibi ac posteris suis congregant. Rursum ne ministerij nomen sordidius quiddam significare videretur, & ex eo impietatis ansam caperent euangelij contemptores, vel ipsi quoq; ministri de suo officio contemptius iudicarent, apostolatus simul mentionem faciunt. Qua
units.tr: Before we leave this passage, we should look at the words they use to describe the apostolic office. They call it a "lot" of ministry and apostleship. By the word "lot" they allude to the act of casting lots, by which they had decided shortly afterwards to inquire into God's mind. In divisions of things, however, "lot" is often taken to mean a share that falls to someone by lot. In this sense they also call it a share of the ministry and apostleship. Hence they acknowledge and affirm that the apostles and the ministers of the gospel have an equal standing. For if Matthias received a share of that ministry, which had been committed equally to Peter and to the others, then certainly none of them held the whole, so that the rest ought to have him as their head or lord. Nor should Peter have had greater authority in preaching the gospel than John, Matthias, or any other apostle, since it is clear that all of them received one and the same commission from the Lord Jesus. Next, they join the words "ministry" and "apostleship," so that they both guard against ambition and bring out the dignity of this office. Since the matter under discussion is a ministry, it would be foolish and absurd to seek popular esteem or to exercise tyrannical lordship under its pretext. Rather, we ought to observe Christ's rule: "Whoever wishes to become great among you, let him be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your servant" (Matt. 20). On this ground Paul deserves to be preferred to many apostles, because he laboured more than all the others in Christ's Church (1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 11 and 12). But the order in the Church of our own age is upside down, when those are held to be first and most distinguished who labour as little as possible in the ministry of the Church, yet live more splendidly than the rest from the Church's goods, and gather treasures for themselves and their posterity from them. Again, lest the word "ministry" seem to signify something rather mean, and lest the despisers of the gospel take from it an occasion for impiety, or the ministers themselves judge their office too contemptibly, they also mention apostleship.

units.la: Quia voce admonemur, Christi & ecclesiae ipsius ministros esse, qui in illo ministerio versantur. Apostolus enim legatum sonat. At legatus nō est, qui sponte currit & propria negotia tractat: sed qui ab alio excellentiori missus, publicis negotijs apud alios transfigendis destinatur. Unde apud cordatos legati non ex propria ipsorum persona aestimantur, sed ex illorum dignitate, à quibus missi sunt. Apostolos autem à Christo Iesu missos esse, supra audiuimus: qui ipsos humanae redemptionis & salutis, quam ille nobis suae incarnationis & mortis merito acquisiuit, testes in toto terrarum orbe esse voluit. Tales ergo aestimari debent, nec propter externam speciem, vilem & abiectam mundi iudicio, contemni. Christi enim vox est: Si quis recipit quemcunq; ego misero, me recipit. Qui autem me recipit, recipit eum qui misit me. Iohan. 13. Et Paulus eodem respiciens ait: Nomine Christi legatione fungimur, tanquam Deo vos obsecrante per nos, &c. 2. Corinth. 5. Ut ergo in apostolatu ministerium considerari debet, ne ambitione elati ministri dominium affectent: ita in ministerio apostolatus meminerint tam ministri quàm illorum auditores, ne vel hi ministros contemnant, vel illi de suo ministerio contemptius iudicantes, officij sui & dignitatis obliuiscantur.
units.tr: The word reminds us that those who engage in that ministry are ministers of Christ and of the Church itself. For "apostle" means one who is sent. But a legate is not one who runs of his own accord and handles his own affairs; he is one who is sent by someone more excellent and appointed to carry out public business among others. Hence, among sensible people, legates are not judged by their own persons but by the dignity of those who sent them. We have heard above that the apostles were sent by Christ Jesus, who wished them to be witnesses throughout the whole world of the human redemption and salvation which he obtained for us by the merit of his incarnation and death. Such men ought therefore to be esteemed, and not despised because of their outward appearance, which the judgment of the world considers cheap and abject. For this is Christ's word: "Whoever receives anyone whom I send, receives me; and whoever receives me, receives him who sent me" (John 13). And Paul, looking to the same thing, says: "We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting you through us," etc. (2 Cor. 5). Therefore, just as in apostleship the ministry must be considered, so that ministers, elated by ambition, do not aim at lordship, so in the apostolic ministry both the ministers and their hearers should remember: the hearers must not despise the ministers, and the ministers, judging their own ministry too contemptibly, must not forget their office and dignity.

units.la: Transeamus vero ad postremam huius loci partem, qua narratur, vt dei mentem fortibus iactis explorauerint. Dederunt fortes eorum (inquit) & cecidit fors super Matthiam, & cooptatus fuit in ter vndecim apostolos. Vbi de fortibus primo loco dicendum erit. Extant enim scripturae loci non pauci, quibus fatidicae artes & humani ingenij curiositas in futuris & arcanis inuestigandis serió damnantur. Vide Leuit. 19. Deut. 18. cap. Et Isaias propheta cap. 8. ad legem & testimonium omnes reuocat, & reliquos inquirendi diuini consilij modos magna cum authoritate prohibet. Sed & Micheas cap. 5. fatidicos, hariolos & alios eius farinae homines à regno Christi excludit. Sed obseruare conuenit, duo esse fortilegij genera, quorum alterum illicitum, alterum vero licitum habetur. Illicitum est, quando res futuras & occultas, quarum cognitio ad nos minime spectat, humana curiositate per artes diuinitus damnatas inuestigare conamur. Hoc vtuntur Meonenim, id est, qui ex nubibus vel astris & caeli influentijs de sequentium annorum cursu & successu prognostica edunt: quod hominum genus hodie inter Christianos non sine graui Christiani nominis infamia regnat. Connumerandi sunt his, qui data natiuitatis hora horoscopum inspiciunt, & ex caeli themate siue figura de totius vitae cursu, imò etiam de nati hominis natura, moribus ac ingenio vaticinantur, eò impietatis progressi, vt hominem praestantissimam Dei creaturam, omnium rerum creatarum dominum, astris subijciant. Ad eundem ordinem pertinent, qui geomantiae studio inflati, consiliorum & rerum omnium euentus se praedicere posse confidunt. Quotquot item aliqua arte, quae diuinis legibus prohibita est, res vel futuras vel occultas inquirunt. Quia enim illi homines in dei arcana audaci curiositate penetrare conantur, illorum audacia palam impia esse deprehenditur. Licitum vero fortilegij genus est, quo rei per se licitae, imò necessariae & ad nos pertinentis, euentus dei iudicio per fortes committitur. Solet hoc fere fieri, vt maior sit rerum agendarum authoritas, vel vt contentiosis occurratur, qui priuati commodi studio, & aliorum odio, lites & rixas captant. Et hunc sortiendi vsum Solomon nobis monstrat, quam do ait: Sors contentiones sedat, & praeduros componit. Prouerb. 18. Fuit autem eiusmodi fortium antiquissimus vsus, nec à religione alienus esse, etiam ab ethnicis creditus est. Hoc olim Graecos vsos Homerus scribit, quando aliquem e fortissimorum ducum numero deligebant, quem Hectori, singulare certamen petenti, obijcerent. Eodem Romani Cos. prouincias sortiebantur, ne illarum administrationem sine numine adire viderentur. Per fortes quoq; terram Chanaan Israelitae diuidere iussi sunt. Num. 33. Et fortium vsus in hereditatibus diuidundis ad nos quoque manauit, ac salua Christiana religione retineri potest, siquidem non alia quapiam superstitione corrumpatur. Nihil ergo ab apostolis à pietate alienum fit hoc loco, cum de sola Dei voluntate cognoscenda soliciti fuerint, & precationem fidei ac religionis plenam praemiserint. Nec peccaturos esse, qui fortibus in simili casu pari religione hodie vterentur, ex Solomone constat, qui eas à fortuitis casibus longissimè separans, diuinae prouidentiae gubernationi subijcit, dicens: In sinum deijciuntur fortes, at omne iudicium earum pendet à domino. Prouerb. 19.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the last part of this place, in which it is narrated that they inquired into God's mind by casting lots. "They gave their lots," it says, "and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." Here we must first speak about the lots. For there are not a few passages of Scripture in which fortune-telling arts and the curiosity of the human mind in searching out future and hidden things are seriously condemned (see Lev. 19; Deut. 18). And the prophet Isaiah, in chapter 8, calls everyone back to "the law and the testimony," and with great authority forbids the other methods of inquiring into the divine counsel. Micah also, in chapter 5, excludes soothsayers, diviners, and men of that sort from the kingdom of Christ. But we should observe that there are two kinds of divination: one is unlawful, the other lawful. It is unlawful when we try, through human curiosity and by means of arts divinely forbidden, to investigate things future and hidden, the knowledge of which does not pertain to us at all. The Meonenim, that is, those who make predictions about the course and outcome of the coming years from clouds, stars, and the influences of heaven, practise this; and this class of men now reigns among Christians, not without a serious disgrace to the Christian name. In the same category are those who, on being given the hour of a birth, examine the horoscope and from the heavenly theme or figure prophesy the whole course of a life, and even the nature, morals, and character of the person born, advancing so far in impiety as to subject man, the most excellent creature of God and lord of all created things, to the stars. Those belong to the same order who, puffed up with the study of geomancy, trust that they can foretell the outcome of counsels and of all things. Likewise, all who by some art forbidden by divine laws inquire into things either future or hidden: since these men try with bold curiosity to penetrate God's secrets, their audacity is plainly seen to be impious. The lawful kind of divination, on the other hand, is that by which the outcome of a matter that is in itself lawful, indeed necessary and pertaining to us, is committed to God's judgment by means of lots. This is usually done so that the authority of the things to be done may be greater, or so that the quarrelsome may be checked, those who, out of desire for private gain or hatred of others, seek out lawsuits and brawls. Solomon shows us this use of lots when he says: "The lot settles contentions and separates the most stubborn" (Prov. 18). This use of lots is very ancient, and it is not foreign to religion; even the heathen are believed to have practised it. Homer writes that the Greeks once did this when they chose one of the bravest leaders to oppose Hector, who sought single combat. In the same way the Roman consuls drew lots for their provinces, so that they would not seem to undertake their administration without the divine will. Israel was also commanded to divide the land of Canaan by lot (Num. 33). And the use of lots in dividing inheritances has also passed down to us, and it can be retained with the Christian religion intact, provided it is not corrupted by some other superstition. Therefore nothing alien to piety is done by the apostles in this place, since they were anxious to learn only God's will and prefaced their prayer with full faith and religious devotion. And that those who today use lots in a similar case with equal piety will not sin is clear from Solomon, who, separating lots far from chance events, subjects them to the governance of divine providence, saying: "Lots are cast into the lap, but every judgment of them depends on the Lord" (Prov. 19).

units.la: Caeterum praeterito siue reiecto Iosepho, Matthias designatur, qui in apostolorum ordinem Iudae succedat. At quantum ex praesenti loco videre datur, hominum iudicio praestantior habitus fuisse Ioseph videtur, qui praeter Barsabae cognomen (quod iurisiurandi filium, id est, fidelissimum ac ve-
units.tr: Moreover, Joseph having been passed over or rejected, Matthias is designated to succeed Judas in the order of the apostles. But, as far as can be seen from the present place, Joseph seems to have been held by men's judgment to be the more outstanding. Besides the surname Barsabbas (which means son of the oath, that is, most faithful and

units.la: Matthias deputatur apostolus. racissimum sonat) Iustus quoq; dictus est. De Matthia vero nihil praeter nudum illud nomen in sacris literis extat. Idem tamen hic dei iudicio priori illi praefertur. Seruit hoc nostrae tam institutioni quam consolationi. Docemur enim, ne hominum iudicijs, & magnifica, quam de nobis conceperunt, aestimatione efferamur. Nam vt iudicijs suis falli possunt homines, ita sententiam frequenter mutant, prout fortunas hominum immutari vident. Et exempla extant in omnibus gentibus, quibus docemur, in extremam ignominiam frequenter praecipitatos esse, quos paulo ante multiceps bestia, vulgus, fauore suo ad sydera vsq; euexerat. Dei igitur iudicio approbari studeamus, qui vt falli nequit, ita quos semel complexus est, nunquam abijcit, siquidem in officio perstiterint. Rursum vero consolari nos debet exemplum hoc, quando ab hominibus nos iniquis praeiudicijs grauari, imo in vniuersum reijci, videmus. Nec enim ideo statuendum est, nos a Deo quoq; contemni, cum is ab hominum authoritate minime pendeat, & plerunq; contemptissimos ex mortalium genere ad res maximas deligat, vt ipsi cedat omnis gloria, & non superbiat coram illo vlla caro. Vide 1.Cor.1.
units.tr: Matthias is appointed an apostle. (most truthful, is what the name means.) Nothing about Matthias exists in the sacred letters except that bare name. Yet here he is preferred by God's judgment to that other man. This serves both our instruction and our consolation. For we are taught not to be puffed up by men's judgments and by the high estimation they have formed of us. For just as men can be mistaken in their judgments, so they often change their opinion, as they see men's fortunes change. And examples exist among all nations which teach us that those whom the many-headed beast, the common crowd, had lifted to the stars by its favour, are often hurled into the utmost disgrace. Let us therefore strive to be approved by God's judgment, which, since it cannot be deceived, never casts off those whom it has once embraced, provided they persevere in their duty. Again, this example ought to console us when we see ourselves burdened by unjust prejudices of men, and indeed rejected altogether. For it must not be concluded that we are also despised by God, since he does not depend on men's authority, and often chooses for very great matters those most despised among mortals, so that all glory may belong to him and no flesh may boast before him (see 1 Cor. 1).

units.la: Adhaec non praetermittendum est in praesentis loci consideratione, quod nec Iosephus, nec qui eius partes tutati fuerant, murmurauisse leguntur, quando Matthiam a domino receptum vident. Nec propterea animum despondisse Iosephum verisimile est, quando non poterat ignorare, multas alias vocationes siue conditiones restare, in quibus suum obsequium Deo praestare poterat. Imitemur nos tantae modestiae exemplum, & nostra forte contenti, altiora ne affectemus, ne & Dei iudicium temere accusemus, & dum maiori honore nos dignos putamus, eo etiam loco indigni esse deprehendamur, in quem nos Deus collocare dignatus est. Multa vasa sunt in domo diuite, & magna etiam in vasis honestis diuersitas. Primus in his locus apostolis merito debetur, qui ipsis mera gratia Dei contigit, tenuerunt vero eundem constanti fide, suiipsius contemptu, innocentia & charitatis studio. Quorum vestigia quicunq; secuti fuerint, vna cum ipsis vitam immortalem & beatam vivent in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, in considering this passage we must not pass over the fact that neither Joseph nor those who took his side are read to have complained when they saw Matthias received by the Lord. Nor is it likely that Joseph lost heart on that account, since he could not be unaware that many other callings or conditions remained in which he could render his obedience to God. Let us imitate this great modesty, and be content perhaps with what is ours, lest we aspire to higher things, lest we rashly accuse God's judgment, and, while we think ourselves worthy of greater honour, be found unworthy of the very place in which God has deigned to set us. In a great house there are many vessels, and among honourable vessels there is great variety. The first place among these is rightly owed to the apostles, to whom it fell by the pure grace of God, and who held it with steadfast faith, by contempt of themselves, by innocence and by zeal for love. Whoever follows their footsteps will live with them an immortal and blessed life in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: HOMILIA X.
units.tr: HOMILY X.

units.la: ET dum compleretur dies Pentecostes, erant omnes vnanimiter congregati in eodem loco. Et factus est repente e coelo sonitus, quasi irruente flatu violento, & impleuit totam domum, vbi sedebant. Et visae sunt illis dissectae linguae, tanquam igneae, seditq; super vnumquenq; illorum, & impleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto.
units.tr: When the day of Pentecost had come, they were all together in one place with one accord. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them tongues as of fire, divided asunder, and it sat upon each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.

units.la: INTER promissiones, quibus saluator noster Iesus Christus apostolos suos frequenter consolari solet, omnium creberrime repetitur, quae de spiritu sancto est. Nam quando illos coram principibus causam dicturos esse praedicit, hoc argumento metum omnem illorum animis eximit, quod spiritum sanctum consultorem habituri sint, qui & argumenta & eloquendi facultatem suggerat. Et cum mortem iam adituras esset, eandem spiritus sui promissionem terq; quaterq; iterat, quem ipsis consolatorem, consultorem & rerum agendarum ducem fore pollicetur. Deniq; a mortuis resuscitatus & promissionis illius denuo illos admonet, & spiritum ipsos Hierosolymis expectare iubet. Atqui minime superuacanea censeri debet tam diliges promissionis huius iteratio. Nam & apostolorum institutioni seruire potuit, ne vel imparati ad muneris tam ardui functionem excurrerent, vel periculorum metu consternarentur: & nobis hodie vtilissima est, cum inde colligere detur, apostolorum doctrinam diuinitus inspiratam esse, nec sine manifesta impietate contemni posse. Caeterum, ne qua tanta rei obscuritas vel ambiguitas restaret, totiesq; promissum spiritum non occulto aliquo inspirationis modo apostolorum animis inseri, sed visibiliter, & non sine publico miraculo, mirti oportuit: quod & reuera factum esse, & quomodo id factum fit, in praesenti diligenter & summa cum perspicuitate diuus Lucas commemorat. Est autem cumprimis digna historia, cuius singula circumstantiae penitius inspectae excutiantur.
units.tr: Among the promises with which our Saviour Jesus Christ often comforts his apostles, the most frequently repeated is the one concerning the Holy Spirit. When he foretells that they will have to plead their cause before rulers, he removes all fear from their minds by this argument: that they will have the Holy Spirit as their counsellor, who will supply both the arguments and the power of speech. And when he was about to go to his death, he repeated this same promise of his Spirit three and four times, and promised that the Spirit would be their comforter, counsellor and guide in what they had to do. Finally, after he was raised from the dead, he reminds them again of that promise and bids them wait for the Spirit in Jerusalem. Indeed, this so frequent repetition of the promise ought not to be thought superfluous. For it could serve the instruction of the apostles, so that they would not rush unprepared into the performance of so arduous a duty, or be dismayed by fear of dangers. And it is most useful for us today, since from it we may gather that the apostles' teaching was divinely inspired, and that it cannot be despised without manifest impiety. Moreover, so that no such great matter should remain obscure or ambiguous, and so that the Spirit, promised so often, should not be infused into the minds of the apostles by some hidden mode of inspiration, but visibly and not without a public miracle, it was fitting that it should be shown forth. That this was indeed done, and how it was done, the divine Luke relates here carefully and with the greatest clarity. The story is especially worthy of attention, and its individual circumstances should be examined more closely.

units.la: Priusquam vero Euangelistæ verba aggrediamur, de spiritu sancto quædam dicenda erunt, vt quid apostoli acceperint, probè intelligamus. Primò enim minimè putabimus, spiritum sanctum vel ante hoc tempus non fuisse, vel illo in vniuersum tempore apostolos. Nam illum ab æterno esse, Deo consubstantialem, multis veteris scripturæ testimonijs liquet. Dauid certè à spiritu Domini exercitus cœlorum conditos esse fatetur. Psal.33. Et Petrus Christi spiritu prophetas olim prædictos fuisse docet: quo reuelante illi & afflictiones in Christum venturas & eiusdem gloriam prædixerint. 1. Petri.1. Sed & archangelus Gabriel spiritus sancti operatione virginem Mariam concepturam & parituram esse pollicetur. Luc.1. Quoad apostolos vero, illos spiritu Dei in vniuersum tarvisse ante hanc Pentecostes diem, nemo sanus affirmare poterit. Magna enim licet illorum fuerit infirmitas & imperfectio, Christum Iesum tamen & cognouerunt & promissum humani generis saluatorem esse ingenuè confessi sunt, quod ipso Christo teste abs q. spiritus reuelatione fieri non poterat. Matth. 16. Iohan.6. Deinde nec de substantia spiritus sancti historiam hanc exponere licebit, quasi ea (quam tertiam trinitatis personam veteres dixerunt) in apostolorum animos demissa, & in illis inclusa fuerit. Ea enim loco certo contineri non potest, sed (quæ diuinitatis proprijssima nota est) omnia penetrat & replet tam in cœlo quam in terra. Quo Dauid respiciens, air: Quo discedam à spiritu tuo? & quo à facie tua fugiam? Si ascendero in cœlum, tu ibi es: & si sternam lectum meum in infernum, ades, &c. Psal.139. Constat ergo de operatione & donis spiritus sancti historiam hanc omnem exponi debere: & spiritum sanctum apostoli accepisse dicuntur, eò quod ille (qui alioqui incomprehensibilis est) in illis efficaciter operatus est, & illos omnibus donis instruxit, quibus ad tanti muneris executionem instructos esse oportebat. Quo sensu passim in scripturis Deum & spiritum Dei præsentè, adeoq. in seipsis habere dicuntur, in quibus ille operatur, & qui sese ab illo dirigi patiuntur. Deo autem & Dei spiritu carent, qui illius operationi resistere, & improba carnis ac mundi desideria potius quam spiritus sancti regimen sequi constituerunt. Euidentiora tamen hæc erunt ex ipsius historiæ contextu, in quo primùm temporis notationem, deinde apostolorum personas, postremò autem missionis huius modum, ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: Before we take up the words of the Evangelist, some things must be said about the Holy Spirit, so that we may rightly understand what the apostles received. For first, we shall by no means think that the Holy Spirit did not exist before this time, or that the apostles had him at no time at all. For that he is from eternity, consubstantial with God, is clear from many testimonies of the Old Scripture. David certainly confesses that the hosts of heaven were made by the Spirit of the Lord (Psalm 33). And Peter teaches that the prophets of old were foretold by the Spirit of Christ, by whose revelation they foretold the sufferings to come upon Christ and his glory (1 Peter 1). Also the archangel Gabriel promises that the Virgin Mary will conceive and bear a son by the working of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1). As for the apostles, however, no sane person can affirm that the Spirit of God had not at all touched them before this day of Pentecost. For although their weakness and imperfection were great, they nevertheless both knew Christ Jesus and freely confessed that he was the promised Saviour of mankind, which, with Christ himself as witness, could not have happened without a revelation of the Spirit (Matthew 16; John 6). Next, we may not expound this history as though the substance of the Holy Spirit (whom the ancients called the third person of the Trinity) had been sent down into the minds of the apostles and enclosed within them. For that substance cannot be contained in any certain place, but (which is the most proper mark of divinity) it penetrates and fills all things, both in heaven and on earth. David, considering this, says: "Whither shall I go from your Spirit? or whither shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I make my bed in hell, you are present," etc. (Psalm 139). It is clear, therefore, that this whole history must be explained in terms of the operation and gifts of the Holy Spirit. The apostles are said to have received the Holy Spirit because he (who in himself is incomprehensible) worked effectively in them and furnished them with all the gifts by which they had to be equipped for the carrying out of so great a task. In this sense, throughout the Scriptures, God and the Spirit of God are said to be present and to dwell in those in whom he works and who allow themselves to be directed by him. Those, however, lack God and the Spirit of God who have resolved to resist his working and to follow the wicked desires of the flesh and the world rather than the rule of the Holy Spirit. These matters will be clearer from the context of the history itself, in which we shall examine in order first the notice of time, then the persons of the apostles, and last the manner of this sending.

units.la: A temporis notatione non tam historico more, vt maior rei gestæ fides sit, Lucas orditur, quam vt mysteriorum maximorum nos admoneat, quorum rationem cumprimis habuit diuina prouidentia. Fuit autem dies Pentecostes, quem alibi festum hebdomadum siue nouarum frugum scriptura nominat: eò quod illo die panes propositionis ex nouis frugibus offerrentur. Pentecostes nomen ex numero sumptsit apud Græcos, quod quinquagesima post pascha die celebraretur. Ceremonias, quæ illo die obseruabantur, qui volet requirat Leuit.23. & Deut.16.cap. Præcipuum verò in hoc erat promulgatæ legis memoria, quam illo die diuinæ maiestatis voce editam fuisse, scriptura sacra monet. Non temere autem præsenti negotio hunc diem diuinitus destinatum fuisse patebit, si & populi frequentiam, quæ tunc maxima esse solebat, consideremus, & Christum verissimum ac optimum veteris legis interpretem esse animaduertamus. Ea enim Dei consuetudo passim cernitur, quod quæ saluti nostræ seruiunt, omnibus notissima & maximè publica esse cupit. Vult enim, Paulo teste, omnes homines saluos fieri, & in veritatis cognitionem peruenire. 1. Tim.2. Comodissimum ergo erat, in celeberrimo festo & maxima hominum frequentia euangelicæ prædicationis initium fieri, & vt plures simul erudiri possent, & missi spiritus miraculum, in varias gentes breui vulgatum, apostolis quodammodo ad prædicandum viam sterneret. Et in apostolis obseruat Dominus, quod ipsum, lquando in terris agebat, obseruauisse legimus. Nam vt publicos locos delegit, in quibus prædicaret: ita festis diebus Hierosolymas proficisci solitus fuit, vt tam miracula quàm doctrina ipsius pluribus innotescerent. Imò paschalis festi tempore crucifigi voluit, vt salutaris mortis ipsius notitia & citius & latius vulgaretur. Prodest autem diuinæ bonitatis argumenta diligenter obseruasse, quæ redemptionem per Christum factam toti humano generi diuinitus offerri, & ad omnes pertinere docent. Nec enim aliunde firmior consolatio in tentationibus peti poterit. Non equidem Christum Iesum saluatorem & redemptorem esse, Satan facile negauerit. Eo autem in fide nostra oppugnanda stratagemate vtitur, quod redemptionem, quæ in Christo habetur, ad nos pertinere negat, & Christi meritum eius q. terminos ex nostra dignitate vel indignitate metiri docet. Et hic non potest non succumbere fides nostra, quando nemo est, qui non se salute indignissimum esse deprehendit. dat, vbi suam naturam penitius inspexerit. Atqui fidem iam nutantem fortissime suffulcit eorum consideratio, quae Christum vniuersalem saluatorem omnium credentium esse docent, & liberalem salutis authorem, qui quam pluribus benefacere gaudeat.
units.tr: Luke begins with the notice of time, not so much in the manner of a historian, to lend greater credibility to the event, but to remind us of the greatest mysteries, which divine providence especially took into account. Now it was the day of Pentecost, which Scripture elsewhere calls the feast of weeks or of new fruits, because on that day the loaves of the presentation were offered from the new fruits. The name Pentecost, among the Greeks, is taken from the number, because it was celebrated on the fiftieth day after Passover. Whoever wishes may look up the ceremonies observed on that day in Leviticus 23 and Deuteronomy 16. But the chief thing in it was the remembrance of the law being given, which Holy Scripture tells us was proclaimed on that day by the voice of the divine majesty. It will be plain that this day was not chosen by God rashly for the present business, if we consider both the great crowd of people, which was then usually very large, and notice that Christ is the most true and best interpreter of the old law. For it is evident everywhere in God's practice that he wishes the things that serve our salvation to be most widely known and most public to all. For he wills, as Paul witnesses, that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2). It was therefore most convenient that the beginning of the gospel preaching should be made at a most celebrated feast and in the greatest gathering of people, both so that many might be taught at once and so that the miracle of the Spirit's coming, soon made known among the various nations, might in a way prepare the way for the apostles to preach. And in the apostles the Lord observes what we read he himself observed when he was living on earth. For just as he chose public places in which to preach, so he was accustomed to go up to Jerusalem on festival days, so that both his miracles and his teaching would be made known to more people. Indeed, he willed to be crucified at the time of the Passover feast, so that the knowledge of his saving death might be spread both more quickly and more widely. It is profitable, moreover, to observe carefully the signs of divine goodness, which teach that the redemption made through Christ is offered by God to the whole human race and pertains to all. For a firmer consolation in temptations cannot be sought from elsewhere. Satan will not easily deny that Christ Jesus is Saviour and Redeemer. But in assailing our faith he uses this stratagem: he denies that the redemption which is in Christ pertains to us, and he teaches that the merit of Christ is measured by the limits of our worth or unworthiness. And here our faith cannot but give way, when there is no one who does not find himself most unworthy of salvation, once he has examined his own nature more closely. Yet the consideration of those things which teach that Christ is the universal Saviour of all believers, and a generous author of salvation, who rejoices to do good to very many, strongly supports a faith now wavering.

units.la: Sed diligentius inuestiganda est altera causa, qua propter legem olim hoc ipso die promulgatam Christi spiritum in Pentecoste datum fuisse diximus. Constat enim, omnia quae in veteri populo contigerunt, typos & figuras fuisse rerum futurarum, quibus perficiendis Christus Iesus ab aeterno praedestinatus est. Quare non superuacanea nec curiosa mihi videtur D. Augustini obseruatio, qui in praesentis historiae consideratione, illam cum veteris testamenti typo, legis promulgatione, confert, cum magna omnium circunstantiarum similitudo & mysteriorum plena analogia vtrinque deprehendatur, quam ipsius Augustini verbis exponendam esse duximus. Occiditur ouis (inquit) celebratur pascha, & interpositis quinquaginta diebus datur lex ad timorem scripta digito Dei. Occiditur Christus, qui tanquam ouis ad immolandum ductus est, sicut Isaias testatur, celebratur verum pascha, & interpositis quinquaginta diebus datur ad charitatem spiritus sanctus, qui est digitus Dei, &c. Sed & Paulus apostolus euangelij praedicationem, cuius initium die Pentecostes factum est, cum legis promulgatione diligenter confert, & illa collatione illius authoritatem afferere conatur. 2. Cor. 2. Et Christum Iesum legis finem esse, scriptura docet, cuius interpretem verum ipse se profitetur. Matth. 5. Nullum itaque missioni spiritus sancti tempus commodius designari poterat, quam quinquagesimus a pascha die, legis memoria celebris. Hinc enim admonemur, eundem esse veteris & noui Testamenti spiritum, non duos & diuersos, vt olim Manichaei somniabant. Nec enim legis interpretem se praebuisset Christus, si illa ab alio quam Dei spiritu fuisset promulgata, nec tam salutari miraculo illius memoriam commendari & celebrari voluisset. Deinde veram legis sententiam non aliunde quam ex Christi spiritu hauriri posse, admonemur. Quia enim illi vnus Christus satisfecit, cui illa nos paedagogi instar adducebat (Galat. 4.) frustra in illius consideratione versabuntur, quicunque Christi spiritu & fide in Christum, quam is in nobis gignit, destituuntur. Quae causa est, quod Iudaeos adhuc velamen habere Paulus testatur, quo impediti in Mosis faciem inspicere, id est, verum & genuinum legis sensum intelligere non possint. 2. Corinth. 3. Frustra igitur nobis legem & huius opera Iudaei & pseudochristiani, humanae iustitiae assertores, obiiciunt, quando & Christus legis finis sive scopus est, & sine hoc nulla legis cognitio vera esse potest. Interim etiam veteris Testamenti contemptores arguuntur, qui illius nullam inter Christianos rationem haberi debere exisistimant. Quasi vero non eadem hodie, quae olim, Dei voluntas sit, & quasi non nobis quoque legis manuductione ad Christum sit opus, vt de nostra iustitia desperantes, Dei iustitiam in Christo Iesu per fidem apprehendere discamus. Ceremonias equidem legis abolitas esse fatemur, quia in Christo figurae omnes impletae sunt: saluus tamen & integer manet vsus legis, quae nostram iniustitiam & ingenitam naturae corruptionem arguere, & satisfactionem omnem in Christo monstrare debet.
units.tr: But the other cause, for which we said that the Spirit of Christ was given at Pentecost on the very day on which the law was promulgated long ago, must be investigated more carefully. For it is agreed that all the things which happened to the ancient people were types and figures of things to come, for the accomplishment of which Christ Jesus was predestined from eternity. Therefore the observation of St. Augustine seems to me neither superfluous nor curious, who, in considering the present history, compares it with the type of the Old Testament, the promulgation of the law, since a great similarity of all the circumstances and a full analogy of mysteries are found on both sides; and we have thought fit to set it out in Augustine's own words. A lamb is slain, he says, the Passover is celebrated, and after fifty days the law is given, written with the finger of God, for fear. Christ is slain, who was led as a sheep to the slaughter, as Isaiah testifies; the true Passover is celebrated, and after fifty days the Holy Spirit is given for love, who is the finger of God, etc. But the apostle Paul also carefully compares the preaching of the gospel, whose beginning was made on the day of Pentecost, with the promulgation of the law, and by this comparison he tries to assert its authority (2 Corinthians 2). And Scripture teaches that Christ Jesus is the end of the law, and he himself professes to be its true interpreter (Matthew 5). Therefore no more fitting time could be marked out for the sending of the Holy Spirit than the fiftieth day from Passover, famous for the remembrance of the law. For from this we are reminded that the Spirit of the Old and New Testament is one and the same, not two and different, as the Manichaeans once dreamed. For Christ would not have presented himself as the interpreter of the law if it had been promulgated by another than the Spirit of God, nor would he have wished its memory to be commended and celebrated by so saving a miracle. Next, we are reminded that the true sense of the law can be drawn from nowhere but from the Spirit of Christ. For since the law led us to Christ like a schoolmaster (Galatians 4), and since Christ alone has fulfilled it, those who lack the Spirit of Christ and faith in Christ, which he begets in us, will labour in vain in its consideration. This is why Paul testifies that the Jews still have a veil, by which, hindered, they cannot look into the face of Moses, that is, understand the true and genuine sense of the law (2 Corinthians 3). Therefore the Jews and the false Christians, assertors of human righteousness, object the law and its works to us in vain, since Christ is the end or goal of the law, and without him there can be no true knowledge of the law. Meanwhile, too, those who despise the Old Testament are rebuked, who think that no account of it should be taken among Christians. As if God's will were not today the same as it was of old, and as if we too did not need the law as our guide to Christ, so that, despairing of our own righteousness, we may learn to grasp God's righteousness in Christ Jesus through faith. We indeed confess that the ceremonies of the law have been abolished, because all the figures have been fulfilled in Christ; yet the use of the law remains safe and whole, since it ought to convict us of our unrighteousness and of our inborn corruption of nature, and to show us all satisfaction in Christ.

units.la: Porro apostolorum personas quoque inspicere conuenit, vt quid illi hoc tempore fecerint, intelligamus. Vbi quaedam ex primo capite repetenda erunt. Primo enim Christi iam caelos ascensuri mandato ipsos paruisse audiuimus, qui Hierosolymas reuerti, & illic promissum spiritum expectare iusserat. Eo igitur reuersi, ibidem in hunc vsque diem constiterunt, quo spiritus missus est, vt paulo post vi debimus, quando Lucas haec Hierosolymis contigisse, diserte docet. Deinde vnanimitatem & concordiae studium illis tribuit. Nec enim per vrbem dispersi & palantes oberrauerunt, nec rixis & contentionibus (vt saepe alias) conflictati sunt, sed vnanimiter vno in loco congregati mansere. Coniungendum his tertium, cuius supra quoque mentio facta est, quod nimirum in precibus perseuerauerunt assidue. Nec enim putandum est, illos in precibus remissiores factos esse, quando & periculis vndiq; circumstantibus premebantur, & ad functionem sibi comissam (vt ex Matthiae electione conijci potest) sese non ofcitanter praeparabant. Seruiunt haec publicae omnium nostrum institutioni. Nam docent, vt eos praeparari oporteat, qui spiritum sanctum sibi quoq; donari, & illius dona augeri cupiunt. Opus hoc nobis est propter ingenitam naturae nostrae corruptionem. Quo nisi regeneremur, regnum Dei videre non dabitur. Iohan. 3. Opus eodem propter mundi exemplum & carnis desideria, quibus a salutis via frequenter reuocamur. Opus illo etiam propter tentationes, quibus salutis & redemptionis nostrae certitudinem in dubium vocare satan saepe conatur, & facile vincit, nisi spiritu Christi, qui (ץ) (vt Paulus monet.2.Cor.1.& 5.Eph.1.)salutis nostræ certissimus arrhabo est, confirmemur. Atqui idem ille in animam malignam non ingreditur. Præparatione igitur opus erit qua illius capaces reddamur. Primus in hac locus obedientiæ debetur, qua nos diuinæ voluntati & ipsius præceptis subijci conuenit, in ijs quoq; rebus, quæ nostræ rationi & periculosæ & noxiæ vel saltem superuacaneæ videri poterant.
