Qua enim ratione fieri posse putabimus, vt spiritu Dei donentur, qui Deo rebelles esse non erubescunt? Non fert Deus, vt lege & verbo suo glorientur, qui inobedientes esse pergunt. Psal.50. Quanto minus ergo spiritu suo tales donare dignabitur? Deinde vnanimes & charitatis studiosos esse conuenit, qui spiritum accipere desiderant. Nam quia Deus ipsa charitas est, illius studium à suis vnicè requirit, imò hanc tesseram Christus constituit, ex qua sui cognoscantur. Iohan.13. Nec fieri potest, vt Christianæ fraternitatis spiritu dignos Christus iudicet, quicunq; odio, æmulatione, simultatibus & apertis inimicitijs scinduntur, & ita se à Christi corpore, quæ ecclesia est, alienos esse probant. Porrò obedientiæ & concordiæ studio preces ardentes & assiduas coniungi oportet. Nam licet Deus spiritum suum gratis polliceatur, & eundem ex mera gratia donet, à nobis tamen orari vult, & vt illum oremus tam Dei ipsius maiestas, quàm officium quo illi obstricti sumus, requirit. Nec aliud euidentius fidei nostræ argumentum edere possumus, quàm si precibus à Deo impetrare studeamus quæ nostræ saluti seruiunt. Ideò Dauidem dicere audimus: Spiritum rectum innova in me ne abijcias me à facie tua, nec spiritum tuum sanctum à me auferas. Psal.51. Et Christo iubente ipsi quotidie clamamus: Adueniat regnum tuum. Imò idem Christus promissione animos nostros confirmat, ne quis frustra se spiritum à Deo petiturum esse existimet, cùm ait: Si vos cum sitis mali, nostis bona dona dare filijs vestris: quanto magis pater vester cœlestis dabit spiritum sanctum poscentibus se? Luc.11. Tria ergo hæc, obedientiam, vnanimitatem & preces apostolorum exemplo coniungamus hodie, & mirificos in vera pietate progressus ac saluberrima spiritus sancti incrementa in nobis sentiemus.
units.tr: Moreover, we should also consider the persons of the apostles, so that we may understand what they did at this time. Some points from the first chapter must be repeated here. First, we heard that they obeyed the command of Christ, who was about to ascend to heaven, and who had ordered them to return to Jerusalem and wait there for the promised Spirit. So they returned and remained there until the day the Spirit was sent, which, as we shall soon see, Luke plainly teaches happened in Jerusalem. Next, he credits them with unanimity and a zeal for harmony. They did not wander about the city scattered and aimless, nor were they torn by quarrels and disputes, as often happens elsewhere, but they stayed together in one place, of one mind. To these we must add a third point, which was also mentioned above: they persevered constantly in prayer. We should not suppose that they grew lax in prayer, since they were pressed on every side by dangers, and (as may be gathered from the choice of Matthias) they prepared themselves diligently for the office entrusted to them. This example serves the instruction of us all. For it teaches that those who desire the Holy Spirit to be given to them, and his gifts to be increased, must prepare themselves in this way. We need this because of the inborn corruption of our nature: unless we are born again, we shall not be permitted to see the kingdom of God (John 3). We need it also because of the example of the world and the desires of the flesh, by which we are often called back from the way of salvation. We need it too because of the temptations by which Satan often tries to call into doubt the certainty of our salvation and redemption, and easily prevails, unless we are strengthened by the Spirit of Christ, who is the most certain pledge of our salvation (as Paul warns: 2 Cor. 1 and Eph. 1). But that same Spirit does not enter a malicious soul. Therefore preparation will be needed, by which we may be made capable of receiving him. The first place in this preparation is owed to obedience, by which we ought to submit ourselves to the will of God and to his commands, even in those matters which might seem to our reason dangerous, harmful, or at least superfluous. For by what reasoning shall we think that those are to be given the Spirit of God who are not ashamed to rebel against God? God does not endure that those should boast of his law and word who persist in disobedience (Ps. 50). How much less, then, will he deign to give his Spirit to such people? Next, those who desire to receive the Spirit ought to be of one mind and eager for love. For since God is love itself, he requires that love above all from his own, and Christ has appointed this as the token by which his people are recognised (John 13). Nor can it be that Christ should judge those worthy of the spirit of Christian brotherhood who are torn apart by hatred, rivalry, quarrels, and open enmities, and so prove themselves estranged from the body of Christ, which is the Church. Moreover, fervent and constant prayers ought to be joined to the zeal for obedience and concord. For although God freely promises his Spirit, and gives him from sheer grace, he nevertheless wishes to be asked, and both the majesty of God himself and the duty by which we are bound to him require that we pray for him. Nor can we give a clearer proof of our faith than by striving to obtain from God by prayer the things that serve our salvation. Therefore we hear David say: "Renew a right spirit within me; cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (Ps. 51). And at Christ's command we cry out to him every day: "Your kingdom come." Indeed, Christ himself strengthens our minds by a promise, so that no one may think he will ask the Spirit from God in vain, when he says: "If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?" (Luke 11). Let us therefore join these three things, obedience, unanimity, and the prayers of the apostles, to their example today, and we shall feel wonderful progress in true piety and most wholesome increases of the Holy Spirit in ourselves.

units.la: Docet præterea apostolorum consideratio, spiritum Christi, qui per euangelij prædicationem operatur, concordiæ & sanctimoniæ spiritum esse, non dissidiorum & carnalis licentiæ authorem, vt qui dam hodie clamitant, qui hoc nomine euangelij doctrinam suspectam & inuisam reddere conantur, quòd per hanc dissidia seminari & quiduis audendi licentiam plantari dicunt. Sed facile est illorum calumnijs respondere. Vt enim vnanimes & concordes apostoli illum receperunt: ita illorum concordiam post acceptum spiritum minimè interturbatam, sed indies magis magusq; confirmatam fuisse constat. Et idem in omnibus credentibus eiusdem spiritus effectus est. Nec enim fieri potest, vt dissidiorum author in illis sit, quos sub vno capite, Christo Iesu, vnitos, vnius & eiusdem corporis membra, ac eiusdem regni coheredes facit. Et vt eiusdem corporis membra, quæ vno spiritu animantur, dissidere impossibile est: ita inter se dissidere non possunt, quotquot per euangelij doctrinam Christo adducti, ipsius spiritu donantur. Quod autem nostri illi de carnis licentia obijciunt, minimè agnoscimus. Hanc enim per euangelij prædicationem quàm maximè oppugnari fatebuntur, quotquot vel minimum ipsius gustum percepere. Nec externo tantùm verbo illam oppugnat Christi spiritus, sed simul animos Deo consecrat, vt qui paulò ante peccati mancipia fuerant, Dei viuentis templu efficiantur. Interim non inficiamur, complures esse, qui euangelij prætextu ad dissidia seminanda & carnis licentiam plantandam abutantur. Sed num id euangelio fraudi esse debet? Vel quis cordatus magistratum damnat, quòd huius prætextu multi tyrannidem affectando, patriæ libertatis oppressores extitérunt? Quin potius vsum magistratus respicimus, quem in eum finem institutum esse constat, vt priuatorum hominum libidini, violentiæ & tyrannidi occurratur. Ita euangelij hunc vsum, & hunc spiritus sancti effectum esse agnoscamus, quòd veram concordiam sanctamq; vitæ honestatem vnicè promouere solet. Imò si verum fateri libeat, non alia concordia Deo accepta esse potest, quàm quæ in Christo Iesu inter fideles Christi verbo & spiritu regeneratos extat: nec alia esse poterit vera sanctitas & innocentia, quàm cuius spiritus Christi author est. Quam enim sine hoc homines simulant, hypocritica est, & Dei iudicium sustinere nequit, vtpote à Christi iustitia aliena quæ si delium defectus sarcire solet.
units.tr: Moreover, consideration of the apostles teaches that the Spirit of Christ, who works through the preaching of the gospel, is the Spirit of concord and holiness, not the author of divisions and of carnal licence, as some people shout today. These people try to make the doctrine of the gospel suspect and hateful under this name, claiming that through it dissensions are sown and a licence to dare anything is planted. But it is easy to answer their calumnies. For just as the apostles received him in unity and concord, so it is plain that their concord was not at all disturbed after they had received the Spirit, but was daily made stronger and firmer. And the same effect of the Spirit is found in all believers. For it cannot be that the author of dissensions is in those whom he unites under one head, Christ Jesus, and makes members of one body and co-heirs of one kingdom. And just as the members of one body, which are quickened by one Spirit, cannot disagree, so those who have been brought to Christ through the doctrine of the gospel and are given his Spirit cannot quarrel among themselves. As for what our opponents object about licence of the flesh, we do not acknowledge it. For all who have tasted even a little of the gospel will admit that it is most strongly opposed by the preaching of the gospel. Nor does the Spirit of Christ oppose it only by the outward word, but at the same time consecrates minds to God, so that those who a little before were slaves of sin become a temple of the living God. Meanwhile we do not deny that there are many who abuse the pretext of the gospel to sow dissensions and to plant licence of the flesh. But ought this to be counted against the gospel? Or what sensible person condemns the magistrate because many, under its pretext, have aspired to tyranny and become oppressors of the liberty of their country? Rather, we look to the use of the magistrate, which is known to have been instituted for this purpose: to check the lust, violence, and tyranny of private men. In the same way we should recognise that this is the use of the gospel and this the effect of the Holy Spirit, namely that it is accustomed to promote solely true concord and the honesty of a holy life. Indeed, if we are willing to speak the truth, no concord acceptable to God can exist except that which is found in Christ Jesus among the faithful who have been regenerated by the word and Spirit of Christ; nor can there be any true holiness and innocence except that whose author is the Spirit of Christ. For whatever holiness men feign without him is hypocritical, and cannot withstand the judgement of God, since it is alien to the righteousness of Christ, which is accustomed to make up for the defects of the faithful.

units.la: Subiungit his Lucas missionis huius modum, qui visibilis fuit, tum propter apostolos, vt maiorem ex spiritus præsentia in comisso sibi munere fiduciam conciperent, tum propter nos, vt certò constaret, quòd Spiritus sanctus sit.
units.tr: Luke goes on to describe the manner of this sending, which was visible: partly for the sake of the apostles, so that they might gain greater confidence in the presence of the Spirit for the office committed to them, and partly for our sake, so that it might be clearly established that the Holy Spirit is.

units.la: III. Modus missionis Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: III. The manner of the sending of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: QVamuis promissiones domini & saluatoris nostri Iesu Christi, apostolis primùm data sunt, & ad illos solos pertinere videri possunt, constat tamen easdem generales esse, & ad omnes credentes extendi debere. Nam vt apostoli propter imperfectionem suam & omnis generis vitia spiritu sancto opus habuerunt, nec sine huius ope & auspicijs commissum sibi munus obire potuissent: ita nobis quoq; eodem spiritu opus est, cùm illo destituti nec vitam Christianè instituere, nec fidei certitudinem contra satanæ tentationes retinere possemus. Nemini ergo vel inutilis vel superuacanea censeri debet praesentis historiæ consideratio, quæ & apostolicæ doctrinæ authoritatem fortissimè asserit, & nos instituit multiuariam. Docet enim, vt ad excipiendum spiritum praeparari, & vt spiritus dijudicare debeamus. De primo in hesternis dictum est. Alterius ratio ex praesenti loco discipoterit. Pergit enim in historiæ descriptione Lucas, & effectus spiritus sancti, quos tam in apostolis, quàm in illorum auditoribus exeruit, commemorat.
units.tr: Although the promises of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ were given first to the apostles, and may seem to pertain to them alone, it is nevertheless agreed that they are general and ought to be extended to all believers. For just as the apostles, on account of their imperfection and vices of every kind, had need of the Holy Spirit, and could not have discharged the duty committed to them without his help and guidance, so we too have need of the same Spirit: without him we could neither order our Christian life nor retain the certainty of faith against the temptations of Satan. Therefore no one should regard the consideration of the present history as useless or superfluous, since it powerfully asserts the authority of the apostolic doctrine and instructs us in many ways. For it teaches us both how to prepare ourselves to receive the Spirit and how we ought to discern the Spirit. The first has been discussed yesterday. The reason for the second can be gathered from the present passage. For Luke goes on with his description of the history and recounts the effects of the Holy Spirit which he displayed both in the apostles and in their hearers.

units.la: Ab apostolis verò dicendi initium sumens, duo illis tribuit, quæ ex spiritus sancti operatione acceperant. Primum est, quòd mox accepto spiritu alienis, ijsq; diuersissimas linguas loqui coeperunt. Est hoc ingens miraculum & stupendum, quo nescio an aliquod maius inter homines vnquam contigerit. Quis enim ignorat, quanti laboris & industriæ opus sit, si quis à pueris diuersas linguas discere conetur? Homines verò adultos vix vnam aliquam discere, & perfectum illius vsum assequi posse videmus. At apostoli, adultæ & prouectæ aetatis homines, adhæc rudes & idiotæ, qui pueritiam & iuuenilem aetatem non in literarum studijs, sed manuarijs artificijs contriuerant, vno quasi momento nō vnius tantùm vel alterius, sed omnium simul linguarum cognitione & vsu insignes ac praeclari fiunt. Quis hic euidens Dei opus non agnoscat? Quis non spiritus sancti operationem admiretur? Quid enim tam breui tempore humani ingenij industria siue dexteritas efficere potuisset?
units.tr: Beginning with the apostles, he attributes to them two things which they had received from the working of the Holy Spirit. The first is that, as soon as they received the Spirit, they began to speak in foreign and very diverse tongues. This is a great and astonishing miracle, and I do not know whether any greater one has ever occurred among men. For who does not know how much labour and diligence it takes if anyone tries to learn different languages from boyhood? We see that grown men can scarcely learn one language and attain a perfect use of it. Yet the apostles, men of mature and advanced age, and moreover unskilled and untrained, who had spent their boyhood and youth not in the study of letters but in manual crafts, in a moment, as it were, became distinguished and eminent, not merely in the knowledge and use of one or another language, but of all languages at once. Who here would not recognise the evident work of God? Who would not marvel at the operation of the Holy Spirit? For what could the industry or skill of the human mind have accomplished in so short a time?

units.la: Nec verò superuacaneum est hoc miraculu, quod nudæ duntaxat & inani ostentationi (vt quæ à circulatoribus & praestigiatoribus fiunt) seruire debuerit: sed apostolis in comisso sibi munere obeundo vtilissimum & summopere necessarium. Quia enim hos totius orbis doctores Christus Iesus constituere, vt illorum ministerio euangelij doctrina in vniuersis gentibus vulgaretur, illos ab omnibus intelligi necesse erat. At quomodo ab omnibus intelligi poterant, si sua tantùm lingua vbiuis terrarum vti potuissent? Imò non aliam ipsis hucusq; maiorem in sua functione remoram obiectam fuisse puto, quàm quòd necessaria diuersarum linguarum cognitione se destitutos viderent. Et tantum fuit diuersitatis linguarum incommodum, quod audax humanæ superbiæ facinus (vt Moses docet) inuexerat, vt per hoc saluberima euangelij doctrina impediri, illiq; ad diuersas gentes aditus praeclu di videretur. Sed omnem difficultatem siue remoram vno momento Deus remouet, & primo statim spiritus aduentu se eo impedimento leuatos sentiunt apostoli, quod plurimum illis obfuturum putabatur. Potest hinc communis & generalis consolatio peti, ne quis in Dei vocatione ambulans, de illius ope & gratia diffidat. Solent equidem multa talibus ab ipso Deo obici, quæ quò minus comissam sibi prouinciam exequi possint, obstare videntur. Sed non tam illos impedire vult Deus, quàm illorum fidem & patientiam exercere. Constanti ergo fide & intrepido animo ea etiam, quæ humanas vires excedunt, aggredi oportet, & Dei fidas manus in ijs experimur, quæ nobis effectu impossibilia erunt. Sic Mosi nec exilium nec linguæ balbuties obstare potuit, quin Israelem Ægypto educeret. Imò cum Dei vocationi insistentibus mare rubrum obijceretur, & cœptum cursum inhiberet, illud è medio tolli & exiccari oportuit. Transeo infinita huius generis exempla, quæ tum in sacris tum in prophanis historijs passim occurrunt. Horum itaque memores inuictam animorum spem concipiant, quicunq; vel doctrinæ antistites sunt, vel in magistratu constituti publicam populi curam sustinent. Meminerint horum & priuati homines, & pari constantia vocationi suæ insistant. Consummabit enim opus suum dominus, quod in nobis coepit, siquidem nos laboris, qui illius nomine sustinendus est, non piguerit.
units.tr: Nor is this miracle superfluous, as if it were meant only for bare and empty display, as are the tricks of mountebanks and conjurers; rather, it was most useful and altogether necessary to the apostles in discharging the office committed to them. For since Christ Jesus appointed them teachers of the whole world, so that through their ministry the doctrine of the gospel might be spread among all nations, it was necessary that they be understood by all. But how could they be understood by all, if they could use only their own tongue wherever they went on earth? Indeed, I think that no greater obstacle had hitherto been placed in the way of their work than that they saw themselves lacking the necessary knowledge of various languages. And the inconvenience of diversity of tongues was so great that the bold crime of human pride (as Moses teaches) had brought it in, so that by this the most salutary doctrine of the gospel seemed to be hindered and access to the various nations seemed closed. But God removes every difficulty or hindrance in a moment, and at the very first coming of the Spirit the apostles feel themselves freed from that impediment which was thought likely to be most harmful to them. From this a common and general consolation may be drawn, so that no one walking in the calling of God should despair of his help and grace. Indeed, many things are commonly set in the way of such men by God himself, which seem to stand in the way of their being able to carry out the province entrusted to them. But God wills not so much to hinder them as to exercise their faith and patience. Therefore with steadfast faith and fearless spirit one ought to attempt even those things which exceed human strength, and in those things which will be impossible for us in effect we experience the faithful hands of God. Thus neither exile nor a stammering tongue could prevent Moses from leading Israel out of Egypt. Indeed, when the Red Sea stood in the way of those who persisted in God's calling and blocked the course they had begun, it had to be removed from the midst and dried up. I pass over the endless examples of this kind which occur everywhere in sacred and profane histories. Let therefore those who are either teachers of doctrine or set in magistracy and bear the public care of the people, mindful of these things, conceive an invincible hope of soul. Let private persons also remember them, and persevere in their calling with equal constancy. For the Lord will complete the work which he has begun in us, provided we do not shrink from the labour which must be undertaken in his name.

units.la: Obseruemus autem hoc loco, Christum Iesum, qui idiotas & rudes elegerat apostolos, ijsdem notis prius per orbem praedicandi copiam fecisse, quàm vbi instructissimos reddidit, omnium q; peritissimos, quæ ad docendi functionem necessaria sunt. Qui enim paulo ante solam Syrorum linguam noverant, & ne hanc quidem tam perfectè, quin ex pronuntiatione (vt in Petro patet) pro Galilæis agnosci possent, nunc omnium linguarum cognitione instructi prodeunt. Accedit scripturæ veteris peritia, quam eodem spiritu authore exactissimam consecuti sunt, vt illorum conciones testantur. Arguit hoc Anabaptistarum insolentem barbariem, qui à stiua & bobus imparati ad docendi munus prorumpunt, & tunc demum se vere apostolicos esse arbitrantur, si & bonis literis & bonis moribus destituti, omne sapientiae studium contemnant, & ecclesiae ordinem vniuersum euertant. At tam abest, vt apostolorum exemplum ipsis patrocinetur, vt potius illius authoritas ipsos ad ea studia releget, quae ministro verbi necessaria sunt. Paulus certè ecclesiae antistitem δ ἱδαχτικὸν, id est, docendi facultate instructum esse vult, nec simplicem articulorum fidei & salutis cognitionem in illo requirit, sed talem postulat, qui etiam contradicentes refellere possit. 1. Timoth. 3. Tit. 1. Ideo Timotheum, quem à pueris intra sacrae scripturae studia enutritum fuisse testatur, assiduae lectioni incumbere iubet. Fatemur equidem, non ea omnium linguarum cognitione opus esse, quae apostolis miraculose contigit: nec nostrum est, tale quid à deo petere, qui si nouis apostolis opus fuerit, eos & facilè inueniet, & donis instruet idoneis. Earum autem cognitionem merito exigimus, sine quibus scripturae sacri libri commodè & sufficienter explicari non possunt: de Hebraea & Graeca dico, quarum illa vetus Testamentum conscriptum extat, haec verò nouum ab apostolis vulgatum est. Et Paulus alibi praecipuum linguarum vsum in scripturarum interpretatione versari docet. 1. Cor. 14. Quibus quicunque carent, solidam & certam scripturae sacrae cognitionem assequi nunquam poterunt. Dum enim ab aliorum interpretationibus pendent, ijs similes videri possunt, qui alienis oculis videre, alienis auribus audire, & alienis pedibus ambulare instituunt. Linguarum cognitioni rerum notitia, & in primis dicendi facultas, accedant oportet, quibus si quis careat, na is mihi perexiguo cum fructu in ecclesiae ministerio versari dicetur.
units.tr: Let us observe here, moreover, that Christ Jesus, who had chosen the unlearned and untrained apostles, first gave them the means of preaching throughout the world in these same rough ways, before he made them most thoroughly equipped and most skilled in all the things needed for the office of teaching. For those who a little before knew only the Syrian tongue, and not even that so perfectly that from their pronunciation (as is plain in Peter's case) they could be recognised as Galileans, now go forth endowed with the knowledge of all languages. To this is added a skill in the Old Scripture, which they acquired most exactly under the same Spirit as their author, as their sermons bear witness. This shows up the insolent barbarism of the Anabaptists, who, unprepared and fit only for the plough and the oxen, rush forward to the office of teaching, and then think themselves truly apostolic if, destitute of sound learning and good morals, they despise all zeal for wisdom and overturn the whole order of the Church. But so far is the example of the apostles from defending them that rather its authority sends them back to those studies which are necessary for a minister of the Word. Paul certainly wants a bishop of the Church to be διδακτικός [didaktikos], that is, skilled in the faculty of teaching, and does not require in him a mere simple knowledge of the articles of faith and of salvation, but demands one who can also refute those who contradict. 1 Tim. 3; Tit. 1. Therefore he bids Timothy, whom he testifies to have been brought up from childhood in the studies of the sacred Scripture, to apply himself to constant reading. We grant indeed that we do not need that knowledge of all languages which was miraculously granted to the apostles, nor is it for us to ask such a thing of God, who, if new apostles should be needed, will both easily find them and furnish them with suitable gifts. But the knowledge of those languages without which the books of sacred Scripture cannot be conveniently and sufficiently explained, we rightly demand: I mean Hebrew and Greek, of which the former is the language in which the Old Testament stands written, and the latter that in which the New was published by the apostles. And Paul elsewhere teaches that the chief use of languages lies in the interpretation of Scripture. 1 Cor. 14. Whoever lacks these can never attain a solid and sure knowledge of the sacred Scripture. For while they depend on the interpretations of others, they may seem like those who undertake to see with other men's eyes, to hear with other men's ears, and to walk with other men's feet. To the knowledge of languages must be added a knowledge of things, and above all the power of speaking, and if anyone lacks these, he will, in my judgement, be said to serve in the ministry of the Church to very little profit.

units.la: At quia haec non omnibus miraculose conferri solent, & paucis aliis contigit quod hic de apostolis legimus, nostra in ijs assequendis industria, noster labor & nostrorum studiorum assiduitas requiruntur. Vbi & scholarum vsus sese exerit, & eorum ministerio opus esse patet, qui verbi ministerio destinatos à pueris instituant. Nec quenquam ignorare arbitror, in populo dei scholarum rationem praecipuam semper habitam fuisse. Huc enim referri debent quae de filijs prophetarum & illorum collegijs habentur, quibus sanctissimos prophetas, Samuelem, Elisaeum & plures alios, magna cum solicitudine & cura praefuisse constat. Et apud prophetam grauissimè reprehendi legimus eos, qui dissolutiori morum disciplina dei & ecclesiae ministerio destinatos iuuenes corrumpebant. Amos 2. Enimuero quantum in religione propagan-da & feruanda momenti habeat vera & legitima scholarum institutio, sanctissimi principes olim perspexerunt, qui vt haec salua & incolumes manerent, illis non modò consilijs & authoritate sua, verumetiam opibus suis succurrendum esse putarunt, quod ex vetustissimorum collegiorum fundationibus facilè deprehenditur, quae postquam ita degenerauerunt, vt otiosorum hominum, gulae & ventri deditorum, vel inepte superstitiosorum, lustra facta sint, horribilis inde ecclesiarum ruina & vastitas enata est. Quod non obscurè Iulianus apostata, homo versipellis & subdolus praeuidit, qui ideo à literarum studijs Christianos repelli volebat, vt ignorantia & inscitia impediti, philosophorum argutijs & ludibrijs paterent. Nisi ergo Iuliani socij & aemuli haberi velint Christianorum principes, scholarum curam sibi cumprimis commendatam esse debere intelligant.
units.tr: But since these things are not usually bestowed miraculously on all, and what we read here of the apostles has fallen to few others, our own diligence, our own labour, and the constant application of our studies are required to attain them. Here both the use of schools shows itself, and it is plain that there is need of those who educate from boyhood those destined for the ministry of the Word. Nor do I think anyone is unaware that in the people of God the arrangement of schools was always chiefly regarded. For to this must be referred what is said of the sons of the prophets and their colleges, over which it is clear that the most holy prophets, Samuel, Elisha and many others, presided with great concern and care. And we read that the prophet most gravely rebuked those who, by a looser discipline of morals, corrupted the young men destined for the ministry of God and the Church. Amos 2. Indeed, the most holy princes of old perceived how great a weight a true and lawful institution of schools has for propagating and preserving religion; and, so that these might remain safe and unharmed, they judged that they must be helped not only by their counsels and authority but also by their resources. This is easily seen from the foundations of the most ancient colleges, which, after they so degenerated that they became dens of idle men, of those given over to gluttony and the belly, or of the foolishly superstitious, a horrible ruin and desolation of the churches arose from them. Julian the apostate, a shifty and deceitful man, foresaw this not obscurely, who for that reason wanted Christians to be kept away from literary studies, so that, hindered by ignorance and lack of learning, they might be exposed to the subtleties and mockeries of the philosophers. Unless, therefore, Christian princes wish to be regarded as the allies and rivals of Julian, let them understand that the care of schools ought to be especially committed to them.

units.la: Sed ad apostolos reuertamur, quos linguarum dono per spiritum sanctum instructos fuisse diximus. Quamuis enim in solis apostolis hoc effectum fuisse videri possit, latius tamen hoc ipsum extendi debet, & perpetuus hic spiritus sancti effectus est, quod linguas credentium mutat & instruit. Quia enim homo animalis non intelligit ea quae sunt spiritus dei, de ijsdem, vt par erat, differere non potest, & quoties de diuinis rebus disputare instituit, toties suam prodit stultitiam & infantiam, quod ethnicorum philosophis accidisse, Paulus docet. Rom. 1. Adhaec vanitate delectatur homo, & turpiloquio gaudet, imo frequenter ad blasphemias linguae habenas laxat, quod in filiorum huius seculi quotidianis sermonibus facilè animaduertitur. Accedit hisce malis, quod ne tunc quidem loqui potest homo, quando religiosissimus haberi vult. Cum enim precibus dei opem implorare instituit, vel cogitationibus vanissimis mens distrahitur, vel peccatorum conscientia turbatur, quo minus certa animi fiducia orare possit. At quae sine fide manat oratio, efficax esse non potest. Caeterum omnibus hisce vitijs spiritus Christi medetur. Quia enim mentes hominum regenerat, & ijsdem veram Dei & mysteriorum salutis cognitionem instillat, idoneos reddit, ut de dei natura, voluntate & iudicijs differere possimus. Et linguas, quae blasphemijs, obtrectationibus, conuitijs, periurijs, obscaenis dicte- rijs & omnis generis impuritati assueuerant, in dei laudem & gratiarum actionem soluit, ut ea loquantur, quae dei gloriam prouehunt, & quae aliorum aedificationi seruiunt, abstineant vero ab ijs, quibus boni mores corrumpuntur. Rursum quia adoptionis spiritus est, & nos dei filios esse certo testatur, eius nobis fiducia author est, qua deum patrem invocare audemus, nec amplius illius voluntati & gratiae diffidimus. Et hunc spiritus effectum Paulus exprimit, dicens: Non accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus, Abba pater. Idem spiritus testatur una cum spiritu nostro, quod sumus filij dei, &c. Rom. 8. Et rursum: Quoniam estis filij, emisit deus spiritum filij sui in corda vestra, clamantem, Abba pater. Galat. 4. Quo etiam referri debent Christi promissiones amplissimae, quibus patrem in suo nomine orantes exauditurum pollicetur. Iohan. 14. & 16. Obstat praeterea spiritus hic carnis cogitationibus, & mentes salutis ac gloriae dei studio inter precandum accendit. Praeterea hic nouum quoddam spiritus Christi miraculum edit. Ut enim apostolorum linguas diuisit, ut diuersa omnium gentium idiomata sonare possent: ita omnium gentium fidelibus unam & eandem linguam largitur, qua ex universis mundi partibus unum & eundem patrem uno & eodem sono, & una eademque fide invocant. Sicut vnitae sunt linguae, quas insolens & audax superbia dissipauerat. Et hac mihi illa lingua Chanaan videtur, qua propheta urbes Aegypti, adeoque omnium gentium, locuturas esse vaticinatur. Isa. 19.
units.tr: But let us return to the apostles, whom we said were equipped by the Holy Spirit with the gift of tongues. Although this may seem to have been effected only in the apostles, it ought to be extended more widely: this same work of the Holy Spirit is perpetual, namely that he changes and instructs the tongues of believers. For since natural man does not understand the things of the Spirit of God, he cannot speak of them as he ought, and whenever he undertakes to dispute about divine matters, he betrays his own folly and infancy. Paul teaches that this happened to the philosophers of the heathen (Rom. 1). Moreover, man delights in vanity and takes pleasure in foul speech; indeed, he often lets loose the reins of his tongue in blasphemies, as is easily seen in the daily talk of the children of this age. To these evils is added this: man cannot even pray when he most wishes to be counted religious. When he sets about imploring God's help by prayer, his mind is either distracted by the most empty thoughts or troubled by the consciousness of sin, so that he cannot pray with a sure confidence of heart. But a prayer that flows without faith cannot be effective. Yet the Spirit of Christ heals all these vices. For since he regenerates men's minds and instils in them the true knowledge of God and of the mysteries of salvation, he makes them fit to speak of the nature, will and judgements of God. He also loosens tongues, which had been accustomed to blasphemies, detractions, reproaches, perjuries, obscene words and every kind of impurity, so that they speak to the praise of God and in thanksgiving, saying what advances the glory of God and serves the edification of others, and refrain from those things by which good morals are corrupted. Again, since he is the Spirit of adoption and certainly assures us that we are sons of God, he is the author of that confidence by which we dare to call upon God as Father, and no longer distrust his will and grace. Paul expresses this effect of the Spirit, saying: "You have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father. The same Spirit bears witness together with our spirit that we are sons of God," etc. (Rom. 8). And again: "Because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father" (Gal. 4). To this also should be referred Christ's most ample promises, by which he pledges that he will hear those who pray in his name (John 14 and 16). Moreover, this Spirit resists the thoughts of the flesh, and in praying he kindles minds with zeal for the salvation and glory of God. Furthermore, the Spirit of Christ works a certain new miracle. For as he divided the tongues of the apostles, so that they could sound forth the diverse languages of all nations, so he bestows on the faithful of all nations one and the same tongue, by which from every part of the world they call upon one and the same Father with one voice, and with one and the same faith. Thus the tongues are united which proud and insolent arrogance had scattered. And this seems to me to be that language of Canaan, of which the prophet foretells that the cities of Egypt, and so of all nations, will speak (Isa. 19).

units.la: Quod si vero spiritus sanctus hominum linguas mutat, ut quae sancta & diuina sunt ac aedificationi multorum seruiunt loquantur, ut denique certa animorum fiducia dei opem implorent: facile patet, quo spiritu agantur, qui blasphemias & execrationes plenis buccis tonant, qui conuitiorum & maledicentiae virus spirant, qui obscaenis & turpibus verbis multorum animos offendunt, nulla vel sexus vel aetatis ratione habita: qui deniq; in precibus vel omnino frigent, vel creaturas invocare, & gloriam unius dei illius ascribere non verentur, vel saltem certa illa deum invocandi fiducia destituuntur. Non enim sancti illius spiritus, sed maligni & immundi effectus hi sunt. Atqui Christus ex cordis abundantia os loqui testatur. Matth. 15. Talium ergo corda ab immundo Satanae spiritu certo possideri constat. Non temere ergo Christus Iesus, nos ex dictis nostris vel iustificari vel condemnari fatetur. Matth. 12. Et Dauid inter vitae praecepta grauiter omnino hoc primum numerat: Custodi linguam tuam a malo, & labia tua ne loquantur dolum. Psalm. 34. Adde quod & Paulus apostolus, scurrilem linguae petulantiam omnemque sermonem spurcum a Christianorum ore alienissimum esse iubet, & turpiloquium in eorum peccatorum catalogo numerat, propter quae ira dei contra inobedientes filios enascitur. Ephes. 4. & 5. Coloss. 3. Familiarissima ergo sit Christianis hominibus Dauidis oratio, dicentis: Pone domine custodiam ori meo, & conserua ostium labiorum meorum. Psalm. 141.
units.tr: But if indeed the Holy Spirit changes men's tongues so that they speak what is holy and divine and serves the edification of many, and so that at last they implore God's help with a sure confidence of soul, it is easy to see by what spirit those are moved who thunder blasphemies and curses with full mouths, who breathe out the poison of reproach and slander, who offend the minds of many with obscene and shameful words, regardless of sex or age, and who finally either grow cold in prayer altogether, or do not hesitate to invoke creatures and to ascribe to them the glory due to the one God alone, or at least are deprived of that sure confidence in calling upon God. For these are not the effects of that holy Spirit, but of an evil and unclean one. And yet Christ testifies that the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart (Matt. 15). It is therefore plain that the hearts of such people are surely possessed by the unclean spirit of Satan. Christ Jesus, then, rightly declares that we are either justified or condemned by our words (Matt. 12). And David, among the precepts of life, numbers this first and foremost of all: "Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit" (Ps. 34). Add that the apostle Paul also commands that scurrilous wantonness of the tongue, and every filthy speech, be utterly foreign to the mouths of Christians, and counts foul talk among those sins on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the disobedient children (Eph. 4 and 5; Col. 3). Let the prayer of David therefore be most familiar to Christians, saying: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth, and keep the door of my lips" (Ps. 141).

units.la: Videamus autem alterum quoque in apostolis spiritus sancti effectum, quem ex toto praesentis historiae contextu colligere datur. Est magnanimus & omnis trepidationis expers Christi Iesu confessio. Publice enim hunc pasim quibusque obuijs praedicare incipiunt, & diuersis linguis magnifica dei opera enunciant, ut auditorum verba testantur. Christi vero praedicationem vel euangelium, μεγαλεῖα τῶν θεοῦ, id est magnalia dei vocant: quia in Christo universa dei maiestas omnium euidentissime cerni solet. Et licet multa extent dei opera, quibus suam naturam & virtutes suas nobis cognoscendas praebet, in illis tamen Christi negotio primus locus facile debetur. In hoc enim diuinae iustitiae rigor conspicitur, qui nec filio proprio parci voluit, ut dignis poenis peccata expiarentur. Hoc etiam de ineffabili dei gratia & misericordia testatur, qua tam tenere dilexit nos, ut filium proprium in cruce potius morientem, quam nos aeternum damnatos videre maluerit. Ex eodem infallibilis dei veritas elucet. Qui enim tunc fallere noluit, quando de filij vita agebatur, cur in alijs fallere? Hoc ipsum insuperabilem dei omnipotentiam nobis commendat, qui vili & mortali carne tectus, Satanam deuincere, & omnem illius potestatem una cum peccato, morte & inferorum portis conterere potuit. Sapientiae vero inscrutabilis hoc specimen est, quo ea via in redimendo humanae nere inuenti potuit, quae & misericordiae dei inseruiret, & iustitiae diuinae rigori satis faceret. Deniq; quisquis, quae in Christo contigerunt, perspexerit, is dei maiestatem, quatenus nobis in hoc car-nis
units.tr: Let us now consider the other effect of the Holy Spirit in the apostles, which can be gathered from the whole context of the present history. The confession of Christ Jesus is magnanimous and free from all trembling. For they begin to preach him publicly everywhere and to anyone they meet, and they proclaim the magnificent works of God in diverse tongues, as the words of the hearers bear witness. They call the preaching of Christ, or the gospel, the mighty works of God [μεγαλεῖα τῶν θεοῦ], that is, the magnalia of God, because in Christ the whole majesty of God is most clearly seen. And although many works of God exist, by which he shows us his nature and his powers to be known, yet the first place in them is readily owed to the work of Christ. For in this the rigour of divine justice is seen, which did not wish to spare even his own Son, so that sins might be expiated by worthy punishments. It also bears witness to the ineffable grace and mercy of God, by which he loved us so tenderly that he preferred to see his own Son dying on the cross rather than to see us eternally damned. From the same thing the infallible truth of God shines forth. For he who would not deceive when the life of his Son was at stake, why should he deceive in other matters? This also commends to us the invincible omnipotence of God, who, though clothed in base and mortal flesh, was able to overcome Satan and to crush all his power together with sin, death and the gates of hell. And it is a specimen of inscrutable wisdom that, in redeeming the human race, he found such a way as both served the mercy of God and fully satisfied the rigour of divine justice. Finally, whoever has looked carefully at what happened in Christ, he has most fully perceived the majesty of God, so far as it can be perceived by us who live in this prison of the flesh.

units.la: Contra blasphemos, turpiloquos.
units.tr: Against blasphemers and foul-mouthed people.

units.la: Spiritus sanctus magnanimos reddit in Christi confessione. nis carcere agentibus patere potes̄. plenissimè perspexit. Recte ergo Dei magnifica prædicauisse dicuntur apostoli, quando Christum prædicauerunt.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit makes men magnanimous in the confession of Christ. ...can be seen by us who live in this prison of the flesh. He has perceived it most fully. Therefore the apostles are rightly said to have proclaimed the magnificent works of God when they proclaimed Christ.

units.la: Debet verò etiam alter hic spiritus sancti effectus ad omnes vere credentes extendi. Ut enim apostoli, qui non multò antequam hæc gererentur diebus periculorum metu superati Christum defecerant, & clausis præ timore foribus latitabant, statim ut spiritu sancto donati sunt, omni metu posito, Christum publicè prædicare incipiunt, & in ea quidem vrbe, quæ Christi sanguinem fuderat, & in qua acerrimi Christi hostes rerum potiebantur, nec etiam multitudinem verentur, quæ maxima conuenerat: ita quoscunque idem spiritus afflauit, eos omni metu liberatos in Christi confessione sic animat, ut in vna Christi gloria afferenda se occupari debere existiment, nec quenquam admittunt, qui vel mundi illecebris retrahere, vel minis ab instituto abstTerrere conatur. Nobis autem pro hoc spiritus dono quàm maximè laborandum est, quando à vera fide confessionem nullo modo separari posse constat. Christi enim vox est: Quisquis me confitebitur coram hominibus, illum & ego confitebor coram patre meo cœlesti, &c. Matth. 10. Et rursum: Quencunque mei ac meorum sermonum puduerit coram generatione hac adultera & peccatrice, illius pudebit & filium hominis, vbi venerit in gloria patris sui cum angelis sanctis. Marc. 8. Ex quibus suum illud apophthegma Paulus desumpsit: Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem fit confessio ad salutem. Rom. 10. Hæc obseruare conueniebat nostri seculi tergiuersatores, qui fidei confessionem inter indifferentia numerant, quasi sufficiat animum fide imbutum esse, nec aliqua fidei significatio requiratur. Gloriantur quidem fide isti homines, sed illius vim & ingenium prorsus ignorant. Fidei enim spiritus sanctus necessariò coniungitur, qui nec ipse torpet, nec eos torpere finit, quos suo afflauit numine. Et quia idem amore Christi animos accendit, quo abrepti vnum Christum quærunt, vnum illum in ore habent, vnum illum per tela, per ignes (vt poetæ verbis vtar) sequuntur, absurdum foret, eos Christi nomen & fidem negare, qui spiritum eius hauserunt. Quòd si istorum hominum sententia valere debet, & stultitiæ & dementiæ martyres omnes merito accusabimus, qui diris cruciatibus sese temere obiecerint, cum simulando illos (si dijs placet) effugere potuissent. Quanto sanctius Iuliani milites egerunt, qui vbi Imperatoris dolo se circumuentos per ignorantiam dijs thus adoleuisse senserunt, per errorem commissum dissimulatæ fidei facinus publicè testati sunt, & Christi gloriam, quam errore violauisse videbantur, mortis supplicio sibi afferendam esse putauerunt. At nostri illi scioli venia & laude dignum facinus, imò summam hanc sapientiam esse existimant, si per fida dissimulatione Christi fidem conculcent. Præstaret sanè illos omnino frigidos esse, quando calidi esse nolunt. Sed quia tepidi sunt, euomet illos dominus. Apoc. 3.
units.tr: Moreover, this other effect of the Holy Spirit ought to be extended to all who truly believe. For just as the apostles, who a little before these events had been overcome by fear of dangers and had denied Christ, and who lay hidden with the doors shut for fear, immediately after they were endowed with the Holy Spirit, cast off all fear and began to preach Christ publicly, and that in the very city which had shed Christ's blood, where his most bitter enemies held power, and they did not fear even the great crowd that had gathered: so those whom the same Spirit has breathed upon, freed from all fear, he so encourages in the confession of Christ that they think they ought to devote themselves to bringing glory to Christ alone, and they admit no one who tries either to draw them back by the allurements of the world or to turn them from their purpose by threats. But for this gift of the Spirit we ourselves must labour most earnestly, since it is plain that confession cannot in any way be separated from true faith. For the voice of Christ is: "Whoever shall confess me before men, him will I also confess before my Father in heaven," etc. (Matt. 10). And again: "Whoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words before this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of man also will be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (Mark 8). From these words Paul took that well-known saying of his: "With the heart man believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom. 10). Those evaders of our age ought to have taken note of this, who count the confession of faith among matters of indifference, as if it were enough for the soul to be imbued with faith, and no outward sign of faith were required. These people indeed boast of their faith, but they utterly ignore its power and nature. For faith is necessarily joined with the Holy Spirit, who neither grows sluggish himself nor allows those whom he has breathed upon with his divine power to grow sluggish. And since the same Spirit kindles hearts with the love of Christ, by which, being carried away, they seek Christ alone, have him alone in their mouths, and follow him alone through weapons and fires (to use the words of the poet), it would be absurd that those who have drunk in his Spirit should deny Christ's name and faith. But if the opinion of these men were to hold, we would rightly accuse of folly and madness all the martyrs who recklessly exposed themselves to dreadful tortures, when they could have escaped by pretending (if it pleases the gods). How much more holily did Julian's soldiers act, who, when they perceived that they had been tricked by the emperor's deceit into unknowingly offering incense to the gods, openly confessed the deed of dissembled faith committed through error, and judged that the glory of Christ, which they seemed to have violated through error, must be asserted by the punishment of death! But those shallow men of ours think that a deed worthy of pardon and praise, indeed the highest wisdom, is to trample underfoot the faith of Christ by a faithless pretence. Certainly it would be better for them to be altogether cold, since they will not be hot. But because they are lukewarm, the Lord will spit them out (Rev. 3).

units.la: Porrò quia de apostolis & ijs, quæ in ipsis spiritus sanctus operatus est, hucusq; diximus, ad ea tandem transfire conuenit, quæ inter apostolorum auditores contigerunt, quorum ingentem multitudinem illico conuenisse, Lucas dicit. Numerantur autem plurimæ gentes, & hæ quidem inter se diuersissimæ ac longissimis locorum spatiis distantes, quod ad miraculi amplificationem facit, quando inter tam longè diuisos nulla potuit esse linguarum affinitas. De gentium verò harum nominibus, situ, origine, moribus, differere non huius loci est, quando illa ex Geographorum libris commodissimè peti possunt. Et de omnibus quidem in genere dicitur, quòd attoniti, vel etiam territi, miraculo hoc & παρρησία apostolorum obstupuerint. Fit hoc quando euangelium prædicatur. Terretur huius prædicatione boni & pij: sed salutaris ille terror & stupor est, quia aures præbent, & salutis doctrinam auidè amplexantur. Terrentur impij quoq; sed in belluinum stuporem terror ille definit, quem postea impijs sannis & petulantibus dicteriis excutere conantur. Vtriusque stuporis exempla hoc loco proponuntur, quando vtrunq; auditorum genus hic adfuisse, Lucas scribit. De singulis ergo quædam erunt dicenda.
units.tr: Since we have so far spoken about the apostles and what the Holy Spirit accomplished in them, it is now fitting to turn to what happened among the apostles' hearers, whose great crowd Luke says gathered at once. Many nations are listed, and these are very different from one another and separated by very long distances, which adds to the amplification of the miracle, since among peoples so widely separated there could be no kinship of languages. As for the names, locations, origins and customs of these nations, it is not the place here to discuss them, since they can be conveniently sought in the books of the geographers. And of all of them in general it is said that they were astonished, or even terrified, at this miracle and at the boldness [παρρησία] of the apostles. This happens whenever the gospel is preached. Good and godly people are moved by its preaching, but that saving terror and amazement leads them to lend their ears and eagerly embrace the doctrine of salvation. The impious are also terrified, but their terror ends in brutish stupor, which they then try to shake off with godless jeers and wanton taunts. Examples of both kinds of amazement are set before us here, since Luke writes that both kinds of hearers were present. So something must be said about each.

units.la: Primò religiosi quidam & pij viri adfuisse dicuntur, ex Iudæorum gente quidem oriundi, sed qui per gentes omnes dispersi diuersas sedes tenebant. Patet enim ex historijs, varias dispersiones Iudæorum causas in Babylonica captiuitate & ab eo tempore fuisse enatas. Nam & maxima illorum pars inter Assyrios mansit, nec redeundi libertate, per Cyrum ipsis concessa, vti voluit. Dispersit eos, qui redierant, Antiochi rabies, & aliorum tyrannis, de quibus plura dicere omittimus. Interim si qui religiosiores erant, diebus festis frequenter Hierosolymam adire solebant, vt cœtibus sa-
units.tr: First, it is said that religious and godly men were present, born indeed of the Jewish people but scattered among all the nations and holding various dwelling places. For it is clear from the histories that the various dispersions of the Jews arose from the Babylonian captivity and from that time onward. For a very large part of them remained among the Assyrians, nor did they wish to use the freedom to return that Cyrus had granted them. The fury of Antiochus and the tyranny of others scattered those who had returned, though of these we omit saying more. Meanwhile, the more religious among them were accustomed to go frequently to Jerusalem on the festival days, so that they might take part in the sacred

units.la: Auditores apostolorum ex omnibus gentibus
units.tr: The hearers of the apostles from all nations

units.la: Pij et religiosi cris & sacrificijs à deo per Mosem instituris interesssent. Ex quorum numero non paucos conueniss dicitur, quibus pietatis & religionis laudem Lucas tribuit, eò quòd in dei promissionibus & præceptis pijs medicationibus vterentur, & promissum mundi saluatorem constanti spe expectarent. Magnum verò hoc est diuinæ bonitatis argumentum, quæ inter Iudæos, propter peccata hinc inde dissipatos, electorum reliquias ad salutè seruare voluit, sicut per prophetas olim prædixerat. Vide Isa.1. & 10. Rom.10. &c. Et ex ijs quidem non paucos hoc ipso die Hierosolymam perrahit, quo spiritus sanctus apostolis datus est : vt inter primos per apostolorum prædicationem Christo lucrifierent, quemadmodum circa finem huius cap. audiemus. Nunc verò illi ingens dei miraculum, quod in apostolis editum videbant, admirantur, imò obstupescunt, & illud ipsum multis verbis celebrant, nihil eorum omittentes, quæ ad huius amplificationem facere poterant. Nam & apostolos Galilæos esse fatentur, & de propria diuersorum idiomatum elocutione ingenuè testantur, simulq; gentium, quarum linguis illos vt audiebant, catalogum contexunt. Non tamen in hoc stupore subsistunt, sed vlterius progressi, rei huius finem & vsum inquirunt, quando aiunt: Quid sibi vult hoc? Docemur horum exemplo, qui nam idonei euangelicæ doctrinæ auditores sint, & in quibus hæc fructus dignos possit edere. Tales sunt, qui religione non omnino vacui, ad dei miracula humiliter obstupescunt, nec in externa duntaxat illorum contemplatione hærent, sed de fine & vsu eorundem diligenter cogitant. Horum studia frustrari non sinit dominus, cuius hæc voluntas est, vt homines in veritatis cognitionem veniant. Et Solomonem dixisse legimus: Si sapientiam vt aurum quæsiueris, inuenies illam. Prouer. 2. Ac Christus: Quærite (inquit) & inuenietis. Matth.7.
units.tr: assemblies and sacrifices instituted by God through Moses. Among their number it is said that not a few had gathered, to whom Luke gives the praise of piety and religion, because they made use of God's promises and precepts as holy remedies and with steadfast hope awaited the promised Saviour of the world. This is a great proof of divine goodness, which wished to preserve the remnant of the elect for salvation, though the Jews were scattered here and there because of their sins, as he had foretold long ago through the prophets. See Isa. 1 and 10, Rom. 10, etc. And from among these he brought not a few to Jerusalem on this very day on which the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles, so that among the first they might be gained for Christ through the apostles' preaching, as we shall hear near the end of this chapter. But now they marvel at the great miracle of God that they saw displayed in the apostles, indeed they are astonished, and they celebrate it in many words, omitting nothing that could add to its magnification. For they confess that the apostles are Galileans, and they honestly bear witness to the speaking of their own dialects, and at the same time they draw up a list of the nations in whose tongues they heard them speak. Yet they do not stop at this wonder, but going further they inquire into the end and purpose of the matter, when they say: What does this mean? By their example we are taught who are the fit hearers of the evangelical doctrine, and in whom it can bring forth worthy fruit. They are those who, not wholly devoid of religion, are humbly amazed at God's miracles, and do not cling merely to the outward contemplation of them, but carefully consider their end and use. The Lord does not allow their zeal to be frustrated, for it is his will that men come to the knowledge of the truth. We read that Solomon also said: If you seek wisdom as gold, you will find it. Prov. 2. And Christ: Seek, he says, and you will find. Matt. 7.

units.la: His verò aliud hominum genus opponitur, quos canum & porcorum nomine Christus appellat, scriptura verò alibi illusores vocat. Nam fuisse dicit Lucas, qui tam apostolos quàm illorum admiratores irriderent, dicentes: Musto pleni sunt. Proponitur autem & horum exemplum, vt videamus, quousq; tandem illorum progrediatur impietas, qui veritatem deuota mente persequi cœperunt. Incurabiles enim fiunt, nec vllis vel verbis vel operibus emendari possunt. Quo enim miraculo mouebuntur, quos præsens hoc mouere non potuit, quo nullum vnquam maius inter homines editum est? Sed adeò non mouentur, vt inde potius calumniandi & blasphemandi occasionem arripiant, & teterrimo ebrietatis vitio tribuunt, quam vel inuiti operationem spiritus sancti esse intelligebant. Extant multa eius generis exempla, quorum omnium hic finis est, ne offendamur iniquis mundi huius de veritate iudicijs. Perpetuum enim hoc est, vt euangelij doctrina alijs quidem sit odor vitæ ad vitam, alijs verò odor mortis ad mortem. 2. Cor. 2. Et Christum crucifixum Iudæis offendiculum, Græcis verò stultitiam censeri, Paulus admonet. 1. Cor. 1. Relinquamus ergo tales dei iudicio. Nos verò euangelij doctrinæ ita nos accommodemus, vt ea per spiritus sancti operationem in animis nostris viuificata, dignos fructus edat, ex quibus pro verè credentibus agnoscamur, æternùq; fruiposimus euangelij promissionibus in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Opposed to these is another kind of people, whom Christ calls by the names of dogs and swine, and whom Scripture elsewhere calls mockers. For Luke says there were those who mocked both the apostles and their admirers, saying: They are full of new wine. An example of these is also set before us, so that we may see how far at last the impiety of those progresses who have begun to pursue the truth with a devoted mind. For they become incurable and cannot be corrected by any words or works. For by what miracle will those be moved whom this present one could not move, a miracle greater than any ever displayed among men? But they are so far from being moved that they rather seize on it as an occasion for slander and blasphemy, and they attribute it to the most vile vice of drunkenness, though even unwillingly they understood it to be the working of the Holy Spirit. Many examples of this kind exist, and the purpose of all of them here is that we should not be offended by the unjust judgments of this world concerning the truth. For it is a constant feature that the doctrine of the gospel is to some indeed a fragrance of life unto life, and to others a fragrance of death unto death. 2 Cor. 2. And Paul warns that Christ crucified is considered a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks. 1 Cor. 1. Let us therefore leave such people to the judgment of God. But as for us, let us so adapt ourselves to the doctrine of the gospel that, quickened in our souls by the working of the Holy Spirit, it may bring forth worthy fruits, by which we may be recognized as truly believing, and may enjoy the promises of the gospel in Christ Jesus forever, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XII.
units.tr: Homily XII.

units.la: Stans autem Petrus cum vndecim, extulit vocem suā, & locutus est eis: Viri Iudæi, & omnes qui habitatis Hierosolymis: notum sit hoc vobis, & auribus percipite verba mea. Non enim sicut vos existimatis, isti ebrij sunt: est enim hora diei tertia. Sed hoc est, quod dictum est per prophetam Iohel: Et erit in nouissimis diebus, dicit deus, effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem. Et prophetabunt filij vestri, & filiæ vestræ: iuuenes vestri visiones videbunt, & seniores vestri somnia somniabunt. Equidem super seruos meos, & super ancillas meas in diebus illis effundam de spiritu meo, & prophetabunt.
units.tr: Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice and spoke to them: "Men of Judea, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen closely to my words. For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. Rather, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel: 'And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh. Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon my servants and my handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy.'"

units.la: Quando dei filius, Iesus Christus, recens in mundum natus, à Maria matre iuxta legis Mosaicæ mandatum deo sistebatur, sanctus & venerandus senex Simeon, ex spiritus sancti suggestione de illo prophetans, inter cætera ait: Ecce positus est hic in ruinam, & in resurrectionem multorum
units.tr: When the Son of God, Jesus Christ, newly born into the world, was presented to God by his mother Mary according to the command of the Mosaic law, the holy and venerable old man Simeon, prophesying about him under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, said among other things: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and the rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that is spoken against." (Luke 2.)

units.la: {y} illusores, canes & porci. torum in Israel, & in signum cui contradicitur. Luc. 2. Caeterum quod de Christo Iesu dicitur, hoc idem de evangelio Christi per apostolos praedicato, debet intelligi. Quamuis enim eius doctrina simplex sit & perspicua, simulq; & salutem & veram salutis consequendae rationem praedicet, semper tamen diversa erunt de hac hominum iudicia, nec paruus eorum numerus erit, qui illi palam contradicant. Vidit hoc olim Isaias propheta, qui cum prophetiam de Christo & eius doctrina instituisset, ad hunc modum exordiri voluit: Quis credidit praedicationi nostrae? & brachium domini cui revelatum est? Isa.53. Omnium vero horum causam dominus exponit, quando mundum hunc lucis impatientem esse testatur, eo quod opera ipsius prava sint. Iohan.3. Simul autem multa eius rei exempla scripturae proponunt, quorum omnium hic finis & scopus est, ne similibus, quae hodie contingunt, offendamur. Inter hac cumprimis memorabile est, quod apostoli primo statim die, quo spiritum sanctum acceperunt, & commisso sibi munere fungi coepere, experti sunt. Cum enim insigni & inaudito hucusque miraculo omnium linguarum cognitionem vsumq; tenerent, & Christum Iesum propter diversarum nationum auditores diversis linguis praedicarent, illico scinditur incertum studia in contraria vulgus. Qui enim religiosiores sunt, dei opus admirantur, & illius finem diligenter inquirunt. Impij vero illusores ebrietatis illos insimulant. Adeo verum est, quod Paulus dicit, Christum sapientibus mundi huius stultitiam videri. Sed quia de his proximo sermone dictum est, ad praesentis loci explicationem properemus, quo apostolorum fides & magnanimitas clarius & euidentius consideranda proponitur. Tam enim abest, ut iniquis impiorum hominum conuicijs sese moueri vel abster reri patiantur, ut hinc potius dicendi occasionem diuus Petrus arripiat, & concione saluberrima complures Christo lucrifaciat.
units.tr: {y} Mockers, dogs and swine. What is said of Christ Jesus must be understood in the same way of the gospel of Christ preached by the apostles. For although his teaching is simple and plain, and at the same time proclaims both salvation and the true way of obtaining it, nonetheless people's judgments about it will always differ, and the number of those who openly contradict it will not be small. The prophet Isaiah foresaw this long ago. When he had set out the prophecy about Christ and his teaching, he wanted to begin in this way: "Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" (Isa. 53.) The Lord himself explains the cause of all this, when he testifies that this world is impatient of the light because its works are evil. (John 3.) Meanwhile, the Scriptures set forth many examples of this matter, and the whole purpose and aim of these is that we should not be offended by things like those that happen today. Among these, the following is especially worth remembering: the apostles experienced it on the very first day on which they received the Holy Spirit and began to perform the office entrusted to them. For when they possessed, by an extraordinary miracle unheard of until then, the knowledge and use of all languages, and preached Christ Jesus to hearers of different nations in their different tongues, the crowd was at once divided into opposing camps. Those who were more devout admired the work of God and diligently inquired into its purpose, but the impious mockers accused them of drunkenness. So true is what Paul says, that Christ seems folly to the wisdom of this world. But since this was discussed in the previous sermon, let us hasten to the explanation of the present passage, where the faith and greatness of spirit of the apostles are set before us to be considered more clearly and evidently. For they are so far from allowing themselves to be moved or diverted by the unjust abuse of wicked men, that Peter seizes on this very occasion for speaking, and by a most salutary sermon wins many for Christ.

units.la: Priusquam vero concionem Petri exponere tentemus, inspicienda sunt, quae de illo simul & reliquis apostolis dicuntur. Stans (inquit) Petrus cum vndecim, extulit vocem suam, &c. Constituerunt ergo imperterriti, nec ideo sibi fugiendum vel officium suum deferendum putauerunt, quod tam iniquè de se iudicari audirent. At non exigua videri poterat timoris & desperationis causa. Quid enim verbis se effecturos sperarent apud eos, quorum impias mentes & proteruiam tantum miraculum, quo nullum vnquam maius accidit, mollire & mouere non potuerat? Sed intrepidi manent: nec modo manent, sed Christi Iesu causam magno animo agere incipiunt. Horum itaque exemplo quam efficax spiritus sancti operatio sit, videre licet. Qui enim paulo ante manuaria opificia exercuerant, rudes & imperiti homines, nunc tantae multitudinis conspectum & varias perstrepentium voces constanti animo sustinere possunt. Et quos antea leuissima quaeq; occasio terrebat, vt ne coram paucis quidem, ijsq; vilissimis hominuncionibus, Christi nomen profiteri auderent: nunc illius causam coram ecclesia, ex omni hominum ratione & ordine congregata, constantissime defendunt: nec tortorum manus expectant, quibus veritatem fateri cogantur, sed sponte se illi patronos praebent. Hinc disce, quibus argumentis nos testari & probare oporteat, num in nobis regnet Christi spiritus. Nisi enim zelus iste & inuictus Christi ac veritatis defendendae animus in nobis conspiciatur, spiritu hoc frustra gloriabimur. At hodie inter illos, qui hunc maxime iactant, laudi ducitur, si quis atrocissima conuicia in Christum & veritatem euangelicam ab impijssimis hominibus prolata, tanquam Syrenum cantus surdis auribus praetereat. Longè alios se hic apostoli praebent, inter quos Petrus leuissimo (vt videri poterat) dissentio lacessitus, Christi & euangelij causam libera voce agere incipit.
units.tr: Before we attempt to expound Peter's sermon, we must look at what is said about him and the other apostles together. "Peter," it says, "standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice," and so on. They stood therefore undaunted, and did not think they should flee or abandon their office because they heard themselves judged so unjustly. Yet there seemed to be no small cause for fear and despair. For what could they hope to accomplish by words among people whose impious minds and insolence a miracle so great, greater than any that had ever occurred, had not been able to soften or move? But they remain fearless; and not only do they remain, they begin to plead the cause of Christ Jesus with great courage. From the example of these men, then, we can see how powerful the operation of the Holy Spirit is. For men who a little before had practised manual trades, rough and unlearned, can now bear with steady mind the sight of so great a crowd and its various clamouring voices. And men whom the slightest occasion had frightened before, so that they did not dare to profess the name of Christ even before a few, and those the most worthless of men, now most steadfastly defend his cause before the congregation, gathered from every rank and order of men; nor do they wait for the hands of torturers to force them to confess the truth, but of their own accord offer themselves as its defenders. Learn from this by what marks we ought to test and prove whether the spirit of Christ reigns in us. For unless this zeal and unconquered desire to defend Christ and the truth is seen in us, we shall boast of this spirit in vain. But today, among those who most boast of it, it is counted praiseworthy if someone lets the most atrocious insults against Christ and the gospel truth, uttered by the most impious men, pass by with deaf ears, like the songs of the Sirens. The apostles here show themselves to be very different men: Peter, provoked by a most slight dispute (as it could seem), begins with a free voice to plead the cause of Christ and the gospel.

units.la: Deinde non obiter praetereundum est, quod cum vndecim Petrus stetisse dicitur. Est hoc euidens aequalitatis argumentum, quam inter se apostoli summo studio conseruarunt. Quia enim vnum & idem munus omnibus à Christo iniunctum erat, cuius rationem nunc accepto spiritu clarius quam antea intelligebant, euanuit prorsus inter illos vanissimum, quo antea flagrabant, primatus studium. Non igitur solus Petrus in solio residet, reliquis ministrorum & satellitum instar astantibus. Non ab illis separatur. Sed cum illis coniunctus, non obscuris signis se vnum ex illorum numero esse docet. Et licet ipse solus verba faciat, non suam tamen, sed communem omnium causam suscipit & defendit: adeo vt hic potius aliorum minister, quam princeps, Petrus videri possit. Valeant ergo, qui Petri exemplo primatum sibi in ecclesia vendicant, & Persico saltu turgent. Humilitatis exemplo apostolis Christus praeluxit, cuius imitatores esse conuenit omnes Christianos, nedum illos, quos ecclesiae suae pastores idem ille constituit. Debet huc Pauli locus referri, qui grauissimis obtes
units.tr: Next, we must not pass over in silence that Peter is said to have stood with the eleven. This is clear evidence of the equality which the apostles preserved among themselves with the greatest care. For since one and the same office had been enjoined on all of them by Christ, the nature of which they now understood more clearly than before, that most vain zeal for primacy, which they had burned with before, vanished altogether among them. Therefore Peter does not sit alone on a throne, with the rest standing about him like attendants and bodyguards. He is not set apart from them. But joined with them, he shows by no obscure signs that he is one of their number. And although he alone speaks, he takes up and defends not his own cause but the common cause of all; so much so that Peter may seem here to be rather the minister of the others than their prince. Let those then be gone who claim primacy in the Church by Peter's example and swell with a Persian pride. Christ shone before the apostles as an example of humility, and it is fitting that all Christians should imitate him, much more those whom that same Christ has appointed as ministers of his Church. Here should be cited the passage of Paul, who, using the most serious arguments, urges only this: that those who wish to be and be regarded as ministers of Christ should strive for unanimity and for humility, which is its parent. "Let nothing be done," he says, "through contention or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem the other better than himself. Let no one look on his own things, but on the things of others. For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God," and so on. See the passage in Philippians 2.

units.la: Efficax spiritus sancti operatio.
units.tr: The operation of the Holy Spirit is powerful.

units.la: Apostoli se omnes aequales et pares esse cognoscunt. flationibus vtens, hoc vnū vrget, vt qui Christi ministri esse & haberi volunt, vnanimitati & (quae huius parens est) humilitati studeant. Ne quid fiat (ait) per contentionē aut inanem gloriam: sed per humilitatem animi, alium quisq; seipso praestantiorem existimet. Ne quisquam, quae sua sunt, spe-ctet: sed quae sunt aliorum. Is enim affectus fit in vobis, qui fuit & in Christo Iesu, qui cum esset in forma Dei, &c. Vide locum ad Philip. 2. cap.
units.tr: The apostles all know that they are equal and alike. Using the most serious arguments, Paul presses this one point, that those who wish to be and be regarded as ministers of Christ should strive for unanimity and for humility, which is its parent. "Let nothing be done," he says, "through contention or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem the other better than himself. Let no one look on his own things, but on the things of others. For let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God," and so on. See the chapter of Philippians 2.

units.la: Sed Petri concione videamus, in qua spiritus sancti effectus & vis clarius elucebit. Exordium huius minimè affectatum & ambitiosum est. Simplex enim est veritatis doctrina, nec verborū leno-cinio comendari opus habet, quando seipsam commendat, dum salutis rationem luculentissimè tradit. Quare eos duntaxat compellans Petrus, quibus verba facere instituerat, ait: Viri Iudaei, & omnes qui habitatis Hierosolymis, notum sit hoc vobis, & auribus percipite verba mea. Iudaeorum nomine vti voluit, vt veteris simul gloriae & officij illos admoneat. Ipsos enim olim sibi elegerat deus, & Iebudim, id est, confessores fecerat, per quos celebrari & coli volebat. Unde alibi notus in Iuda deus dicitur. Psal. 67. Eadem ratione & Hierosolymorum meminit, quae frequenter vrbs sancta nominatur, vt offendat, vel loci religione ipsos moueri debere, vt attenti audiant, quae ad Dei gloriam & propriam ipsorum salutem pertinent. Vult enim non obiter modo tanquam ab aliud agentibus audiri, sed auribus percipi, & proinde animis recondi quae dicuntur. Sunt autē orationis partes duae. Prior conuitio respondet, quo illos ebrietatis insimulauerant impij illusores. Quod primò omnium dilui oportebat, eò quòd nulla potuisset dictorum authoritas & fides esse, si pro ebrijs & temulentis fuissent habiti. Altera pars Christum Iesum praedicat, & omnem salutis rationem comprehendit.
units.tr: But let us look at Peter's sermon, in which the effect and power of the Holy Spirit will shine out more clearly. Its opening is by no means affected or ambitious. For the doctrine of truth is simple, and does not need to be commended by the enticement of words, since it commends itself while it sets out the way of salvation most clearly. Therefore Peter, addressing only those to whom he had determined to speak, says: "Men of Judea, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen closely to my words." He wished to use the name of Jews, so as to remind them at once of their former glory and of their duty. For God had chosen them long before, and had made them Iebudim [יהודים], that is, confessors, through whom he wished to be celebrated and worshipped. Hence God is said elsewhere to be known in Judah. (Ps. 67.) For the same reason he also mentions Jerusalem, which is often called the holy city, so as to show that they ought to be moved by the sanctity of the place to listen attentively to what pertains to the glory of God and their own salvation. For he wants his words not merely to be heard in passing, as by people doing something else, but to be taken in by the ears and therefore stored in the minds of those who hear. The speech has two parts. The first answers the insult with which the impious mockers had charged them with drunkenness. This had to be wiped away first of all, since the words spoken could have no authority or credibility if the speakers were thought to be drunk and intoxicated. The second part proclaims Christ Jesus and comprehends the whole way of salvation.

units.la: Prioris exemplo docemur, licere vt conuitijs respondeamus, & contra illa afferamus nominis & famae nostrae integritatem. Nam iuxta Solomonis sententiam, bonum nomen & fama honesta mul-tis opibus praeferri debet. Prouerb. 22. In primis autem eius rationem illos habere conuenit, qui in verbi ministerio versantur, eò quòd conuitia, quibus illorum nomen & aestimatio laeditur, non tam ipsorum personas petunt, quàm ipsum Deum, in cuius contemptum maximè tendunt. Quae causa est, quòd Apostolus, episcopum exterorum quoq; testimonijs commendari vult. 1. Tim. 3. Quanto magis ergo, ne ab illis contemnatur, quibus ipsum praeesse oportet, videndum est? At quia eousq; multorum improbitas progreditur, vt falsa crimina sanctis dei ministris intentare non erubescant, quò facilius veritatis doctrinam inuisam & suspectam reddant, excusationes & purgationes & licita & necessaria sunt. Illis enim Christum quoq; frequenter vsum fuisse legimus, vt suam doctrinam à contemptu vindicaret. Et Paulus non semel contra aemulos suos de apostolatu suo, de vocatione item ad apostolatum & sua fide, qua in hoc versatus sit, copiosè disputat: quia se non posse contemni videbat, nisi fi-mul & euangelij praedicatio in multorum animis vilesceret. Recte ergo Petrus concionem suam à criminis purgatione orditur, vt apostolos omni suspicione liberet. Nec audiendi sunt in simili casu, qui patientiam requirunt. Nec enim obstat Christiana patientia, quo minus veritatem & ipsum Christum pro virili defendamus. Qui autē eo animo praediti sunt, vt quaeuis conuitia, quae cum Christi & euangelij contemptu coniuncta esse vident, surda aure praeterire sinant, ij nec patientiae nec modestiae nomen merentur, sed tepidi & ignaui suae stationis desertores potius dici debent.
units.tr: We are taught by Peter's example that it is lawful to answer insults and to defend, against them, the integrity of our name and reputation. For according to Solomon's saying, a good name and an honest reputation ought to be preferred to great riches (Prov. 22). This applies above all to those who serve in the ministry of the Word, because the insults that damage their name and standing are aimed less at their persons than at God himself, whose contempt they chiefly serve. This is why the Apostle wants a bishop to be commended even by outsiders (1 Tim. 3). How much more, then, must care be taken that he is not despised by those over whom he ought to preside?
