And since the wickedness of many goes so far that they are not ashamed to bring false charges against God's holy ministers, so that they may more easily make the doctrine of truth hateful and suspect, excuses and clearings are both permitted and necessary. We read that Christ himself often used them, to vindicate his teaching from contempt. Paul too, more than once, argues at length against his rivals about his apostleship, about his call to the apostleship, and about his faithfulness in that office, because he saw that he could not be despised without the preaching of the gospel also becoming worthless in the minds of many. Peter, therefore, rightly begins his sermon with the clearing of the charge, so as to free the apostles from every suspicion. Nor should those who call for patience be listened to in such a case. Christian patience does not prevent us from defending the truth and Christ himself to the best of our strength. Those, however, who are so disposed that they allow any insults that they see joined with contempt of Christ and the gospel to pass by with a deaf ear do not deserve the name of patient or modest, but should rather be called lukewarm and idle deserters of their post.

units.la: Caeterum in crimine diluendo non simplici negatione vtitur, nec etiam morosè in illos conuitium regerit, sed argumentis euincit, falsum esse quod illi intentabant. Primum à temporis circumstantia sumit. Non (inquit) vt vos existimatis, isti ebrij sunt: est enim hora diei tertia. At solebant veteres duodecim diei horas numerare, vt ex euangelij historia & prophanis scriptoribus colligi potest. Et quia à diluculo vel Solis ortu initium faciebant, tertia ad matutinum tempus referri debet, & nobis aestiuo tempore vel septima vel octaua antemerdiana dici posset. Petri ergo argumentum tale est: Qui inebriantur, circa vesperam & noctis principium comessari solent. Atqui cum modò matutinum tempus sit, ebrietatis nullo iure accusari possumus. Sed ô felicem illius seculi statum quando ad hunc modum argumentari licebat. Quamuis enim credibile sit, ebrietati quoq; (vt etiam alijs flagitijs) multos deditos fuisse, ea tamen fuit honestas, vt ebrietas dedecori esset, & qui inebriantur (quod & Paulus alicubi monuit) noctu ebrij essent, ne publicè infames fierent. Hodie non magna esset huius argumenti vis & authoritas, quando ij passim regnant, qui mane surgunt ad bibendum vinum, vt Isaias de sui seculi moribus conqueritur. Isa. 5. Imò inter principes inuenire est, qui qui Solomonici dicti obliti, mane ebrij sunt. Eccles. 10. Sed quid de principibus loqnor, quando ne theologi quidem a tam fœdo crimine immunes sunt? Memini me quondam in Comitijs Imperiali-bus, quibus de summa religionis & publicæ pacis per Germaniam constituendæ agebatur, magni no-minis theologum, adeoq; aduersæ partis antesignanum, vidisse, qui se sobrium de tanta causa disputaturum negabat. Dicti vero tam fuit constans, ut non semel prima diei hora non male potum vide-rim. Sed vtinam non inter nostros quoq; inuenirentur, qui communis huius & publici per Germaniam mali contagio infecti, poculis plus satis student. Et sane, si nullum aliud argumentum extaret, vnum hoc ad arguendum nostri seculi corruptionem sufficeret: Quis enim negabit dies Noæ & Loti esse, quando vna omnium vox de poculis sonat, & ebrietas apud omnis ordinis locis, homines laudi & honori ducitur? Huic malo non morum tantummodo corruptionem, verumetiam iustitiæ legum; euersionem, & religionis occasum, patriæ; libertatis oppressionem debemus.
units.tr: Moreover, in clearing the charge, Peter does not rely on a bare denial, nor does he peevishly return insult for insult, but he proves by arguments that what they alleged against them is false. First he takes the argument from the time of day. "These men," he says, "are not drunk, as you suppose, for it is the third hour of the day." Now the ancients used to count twelve hours of the day, as can be gathered from the gospel history and from secular writers. And since they began from daybreak or sunrise, the third hour must be referred to the morning, and in summer it could be called either the seventh or the eighth hour before noon. Peter's argument, then, is this: those who get drunk usually carouse toward evening and at the beginning of the night. But since it is now morning, we cannot rightly be accused of drunkenness. O the happy state of that age, when it was permitted to argue in this way! For although it is credible that many were given to drunkenness, as to other crimes, yet it was held in such honour that drunkenness was a disgrace, and those who got drunk (as Paul also warned somewhere) were drunk at night, so that they would not become publicly infamous. Today this argument would have little force or authority, since those who rise early in the morning to drink wine rule everywhere, as Isaiah complains about the morals of his own age (Isa. 5). Indeed, among princes one may find who, having forgotten Solomon's saying, are drunk in the morning (Eccles. 10). But why do I speak of princes, when not even theologians are free from so foul a crime? I remember that once, at the Imperial Diet, where the highest matters of religion and the establishment of public peace throughout Germany were being discussed, I saw a theologian of great name, and indeed a champion of the opposing party, who declared that he would not discuss so great a cause while sober. And his drinking was so constant that I have seen him drink not badly even in the first hour of the day. But would that such men were not found also among our own people, who, infected by the contagion of this common and public evil throughout Germany, are more than eager for cups. And indeed, if no other argument existed, this one alone would be enough to prove the corruption of our age. For who will deny that the days of Noah and Lot have returned, when the one voice of all is for cups, and drunkenness is esteemed as a matter of praise and honour in every rank of life? To this evil we owe not only the corruption of morals, but also the overthrow of the laws of justice, the ruin of religion, and the oppression of the fatherland and of liberty.

units.la: Sed ad Petri concionem reuertamur, qui alterum argumentum a pronuntiatis producit, quo apostolos ebrietatis suspicione liberat. Cum enim non immerito boni quoq; admirarentur, homines idiotas tam repente πολυγλωτ-τας, adeoq; omnium linguarum peritos euasisse, impij vero & illu-fores temulentiam hoc esse dicerent, opus erat rei veritatem apertius declarare. Ostendit ergo Petrus hoc spiritus sancti opus esse, cuius missionem in Messiae regno olim promissam fuisse ex Ioelis 2. capite probat. Prophetauit is ijsdem temporibus, quibus & Isaias & Micheas insignes fuerunt, & bellum, quod Sennacherib illaturus erat, prædixit. Ne vero pij animum desponderent, & Deum populi sui nullam amplius rationem habiturum putarent, illos consolatur, & Israelem non penitus excindendum esse docet: eo quod Messias ex illa gente prodire debeat, quem Deus humano generi saluatorem & redemptorem destinauerit: & vt maior sit consolationis vis, Messiæ regnum paucis describit. Quem locum diligentius paulo & copiosius Petrus citat, vt eos nimirum turpis socordiæ & ignauiæ accusat, qui manifestissimos spiritus sancti effectus ebrietati vel temulentiæ tribuebant. Ete nim fœdissimus hic error erat, tantum Dei beneficium, & id quidem olim promissum & descriptum quàm diligentissimè, non obseruare, imò conuicijs proscindere. Sunt autem loci huius partes tres. Prima de vbere & liberali spiritus sancti effusione, quæ Christi tempore futura sit, vaticinatur. Altera turbulentum mundi huius statum in Christi regno describit, adeoq; pœnas recenseт, quibus Deus mundi ingratitudinem & incredulitatem vlturus sit. Tertia salutis modum exponit, & viam ostendit, qua homines ex periculis omnibus salui & incolumes euadere queant. Caterum in præsenti primam duntaxat partem explicabimus.
units.tr: But let us return to Peter's sermon, in which he brings forward a second argument, drawn from the event itself, by which he frees the apostles from the suspicion of drunkenness. For since the good, not without reason, were amazed that uneducated men had so suddenly become many-tongued [πολυγλώσσους] and skilled in all languages, while the impious and mockers said that this was drunkenness, it was necessary to declare the truth of the matter more plainly. Peter therefore shows that this is a work of the Holy Spirit, whose mission was long ago promised in the kingdom of the Messiah, and he proves this from Joel chapter 2. Joel prophesied at the same times when Isaiah and Micah were notable, and he foretold the war that Sennacherib was about to wage. Lest the godly should lose heart and think that God would no longer take any account of his people, he consoles them and teaches that Israel is not to be utterly destroyed, because the Messiah, whom God has appointed as the Saviour and Redeemer of the human race, must come from that nation. And so that the force of the consolation might be greater, he briefly describes the kingdom of the Messiah. Peter quotes this passage somewhat more carefully and fully, in order to accuse of shameful sloth and cowardice those who attributed the most manifest effects of the Holy Spirit to drunkenness or intoxication. For this was a most foul error: not to observe, or rather to tear apart with insults, so great a benefit of God, promised and described long ago with the greatest care. Now there are three parts to this passage. The first foretells the abundant and generous outpouring of the Holy Spirit that is to come in the time of Christ. The second describes the turbulent state of this world under the reign of Christ, and so recounts the punishments with which God will avenge the world's ingratitude and unbelief. The third sets out the manner of salvation and shows the way by which men may escape from all dangers safe and unharmed. For the present, however, we will explain only the first part.

units.la: Eam his verbis dominus apud prophetam enuntiat: Et erit nouissimis diebus, dicit Deus, effundam de spiritu meo super omnem carnem: & prophetabunt filij vestri & filiæ vestræ. Iuuenes vestri visiones videbunt, & seniores vestri somnia somniabunt. Equidem super seruos meos & super ancillas meas in diebus illis effundam de spiritu meo, & prophetabunt. Sunt verba hæc per se clara & perspicua, penitius tamen inspici merentur, propter ea, quæ in his comprehensa, nostræ institutioni seruiunt.
units.tr: The Lord declares it through the prophet in these words: "And it shall come to pass in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy." These words are clear and plain in themselves, yet they deserve to be examined more closely, because of the things contained in them that serve our instruction.

units.la: Primò in his obseruandum venit, quòd de Christi regno vaticinium contexturus propheta, inter eximia & infinita beneficia, quæ per Christum Iesum nobis collata sunt, spiritus sancti donum cum-primis celebrat. Causa mihi videtur, non quòd alia diuinus vates vel ignorarit, vel contempserit: sed quòd post Christum Iesum nihil præstantius à Deo nobis dari potest, quàm spiritus ille Christi, de quo hic agitur. Conclusit equidem in Christo filio suo cœlestis pater vniuersos suæ gratiæ & nostræ salutis thesauros, sed per spiritum sanctum regenerantur homines, vt filij Dei & honorum, quæ Christus nobis acquisiuit, capaces fieri possint. Quæ regeneratio tam nobis necessaria est, vt nisi illa innouemur, regnum Dei (sicut ipse Christus testatur) videre non possimus. Iohan. 3. Idem ille spiritus mentes nostras illuminat, vt mysteria regni cœlorum intelligamus, & eorundem desiderium in nobis accendit. Sine qua illuminatione animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. 1. Cor. 2. Spiritus hic consolator est, quo animati quæcunq; in hoc mundo propter Christum nobis aduersa ac cidunt, sustinere & vincere possumus. Nec consolatoris modò officium obit, verumetiam consultor est fidissimus. Suggerit enim quid agendum sit, & perplexis nobis veritatis lumen accendit, cuius duce fidei & salutis nostræ pericula euitemus. Iohan. 14. & 16. Accedit omnibus iis, quod idem
units.tr: First, it must be observed that the prophet, about to weave a prophecy concerning the kingdom of Christ, celebrates above all the gift of the Holy Spirit among the outstanding and countless benefits conferred upon us through Christ Jesus. The reason, it seems to me, is not that the divine seer was ignorant of other things or despised them, but that after Christ Jesus nothing more excellent can be given us by God than that Spirit of Christ of whom he is speaking here. Indeed, the heavenly Father has enclosed in his Son Christ all the treasures of his grace and of our salvation, but men are regenerated through the Holy Spirit, so that they may become sons of God and capable of the good things that Christ has won for us. This regeneration is so necessary for us that, unless we are renewed by it, we cannot see the kingdom of God (as Christ himself testifies, John 3). The same Spirit illuminates our minds so that we may understand the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, and kindles in us the desire for them. Without this illumination the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). This Spirit is a comforter, by whom, being animated, we can endure and overcome whatever adversities befall us in this world for Christ's sake. And he does not perform only the office of comforter, but is also a most faithful counsellor. For he suggests what must be done, and when we are perplexed he kindles the light of truth, by whose guidance we may avoid the dangers to our faith and salvation (John 14 and 16). To all these things is added the fact that the same

units.la: f nostræ redemptionis & salutis arrhabo & pignus est infallibile. Vt enim Christus Iesus carnem, quam ex nobis assumpsit, in cœlos subuectam illic nostræ salutis pignus esse voluit: ita suum spiritum arrhabonis loco animis nostris inserit, vt salutis fiducia in nobis obsignet, & in tentationibus armet fortissimè. Quare adoptionis spiritus à Paulo dicitur, eò quòd per illum regenerati, eiusdem testimonio certiores reddimur, nos Dei filios & hæredes esse. Vide Rom 8. Galat. 4. Non temere ergo fit, quòd huius donum ex aliorum numero maximè sibi celebrandum sumpsit propheta. Admonemur hîc, quid à nobis quoque in Christi regno potissimum quæri debeat. Quo loco varios & cumprimis noxios hominum errores videre licet, qui dum carnalia tantummodo sectantur, & sub Christi prætextu mundi bonis inhiant, Christum quem ore profitentur, vita plerunq; abnegare consueuerunt, & illis adnumerandi veniunt, quibus olim dicetur: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, domine domine, ingredietur regnum meum, sed qui fecerit voluntatem patris mei, qui in cœlis est. Matth. 7. Spirituale est Christi regnum, & non de mundo hoc. Spiritus ergo dona affectemus, quibus si instructi fuerimus, reliqua sponte accedent, quibus nobis opus est. Matth. 6.
units.tr: It is also the infallible earnest and pledge of our redemption and salvation. Just as Christ Jesus wished the flesh he took from us, carried up into heaven, to be a pledge of our salvation there, so he places his own Spirit in our hearts in the place of an earnest, to seal in us confidence of salvation and to arm us most strongly in temptations. For this reason the Spirit is called the Spirit of adoption by Paul, because through him we are regenerated and, by his testimony, made more certain that we are God's sons and heirs. See Rom. 8 and Gal. 4. It is not by chance, then, that the prophet took the gift of the Spirit above all others as the one to be celebrated. Here we are reminded what should above all be sought by us in the kingdom of Christ. Here we can see various and especially harmful errors of men, who, while they pursue only carnal things and, under the pretext of Christ, gape after the goods of the world, often deny in their lives the Christ whom they profess with their mouths. They belong to those to whom it will be said one day: "Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter my kingdom, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 7. The kingdom of Christ is spiritual and not of this world. Let us therefore desire the gifts of the Spirit, and if we are furnished with these, the other things we need will come of their own accord. Matt. 6.

units.la: Deinde modum promissionis huius, & ad quos illa pertineat, videre conuenit. Modu vero vnica effundendi voce exponit, qua amplam & liberalem spiritus gratiam pollicetur. De personis, quibus illum dare veli· diligentius tractat. Effundam (inquit) de spiritu meo, super omnem carnem. Vniuersalis ergo est promissio hæc. Sed addit expositionis loco, filios & filias, iuuenes & senes, vt ostendat, nullum in Christi regno vel sexus vel ætatis discrimen esse. In Christo enim, vt Paulus ait, non est Iudæus neq; Græcus, non seruus neq; liber, non masculus neq; fœmina. Galat. 3. Interim ne quis promiscue, tam impijs, quàm pijs, spiritum sanctum dari putaret, promissionem ad seruos & ancillas suas Deus restringit, vt de solis illis vniuersaliter exponendam esse intelligamus. Quia enim adoptionis spiritus est, non nisi ab illis percipi poterit, quos pro filijs suis Deus agnoscere dignatur. At filij Dei sunt, qui illum patrem agnoscunt & inuocant, qui illi seruiunt, qui illum colunt, obseruant & adorant. Et quamuis quæ filiorum Dei sunt non ante exequi possint, quàm gratuito Dei beneficio per spiritum hunc regenerentur, & nos propterea plerunq; latent, priusquam spiritus sancti effectus in illis videamus: constat tamen spiritus huius non alios capaces fore, quàm quos pro suis dominus agnouerit. At nouit ille qui nam sui sint, & ita nouit, vt eosdem è manu ipsius nemo possit eripere. 2. Tim. 2. Iohannis 10.
units.tr: Next, it is fitting to see the manner of this promise and to whom it pertains. The manner he expresses by the single word "pour out", by which he promises an ample and generous grace of the Spirit. He treats more carefully of the persons to whom he wishes to give it. "I will pour out," he says, "my Spirit upon all flesh." This promise, then, is universal. But by way of explanation he adds "your sons and your daughters, your young men and your old men", to show that in the kingdom of Christ there is no distinction of sex or age. For in Christ, as Paul says, there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female. Gal. 3. Meanwhile, lest anyone think that the Holy Spirit is given indiscriminately to the wicked as well as the godly, God restricts the promise to his menservants and maidservants, so that we understand it is to be expounded universally of those alone. For since it is the Spirit of adoption, it can be received only by those whom God deigns to acknowledge as his sons. But those are the sons of God who acknowledge and call upon him as Father, who serve him, worship, obey and adore him. And although the things that belong to the sons of God cannot be carried out before they are regenerated by this Spirit through the free benefit of God, and for this reason they often lie hidden until we see the effects of the Holy Spirit in them, yet it is certain that only those whom the Lord has acknowledged as his own will be capable of this Spirit. And he knows who are his, and so knows them that no one can snatch them out of his hand. 2 Tim. 2; John 10.

units.la: Cæterum hoc loco nobis obiter inspiciendum venit veteris & noui Testamenti discrimen. Quamuis enim vnus & idem Christus, vna & eadem fides & salutis ratio, vnus & idem spiritus vtrobiq; pronatur, non exiguum tamen discrimen deprehendi potest, in quo facile elucet, quanto maior fit nostra quàm veterum dignitas & felicitas. Patet hoc primum in fidelium numero, deinde in tradendi modo. In veteri enim Testamento exiguum cultorum Dei numerum fuisse constat, & inter Iudaici populi fines salutis cognitio conclusa videri poterat. Nota enim sunt Dei verba, quibus Israelitas alloquitur: Vos eritis mihi peculium præ omnibus populis. Mea quidè est omnis terra: vos autem eritis mihi regnum sacerdotale, & gens sancta. Exod. 19. Item: Duntaxat vos agnoui ex omnibus cognationibus terræ. Amoz 3. cap. Qua ratione illa quoq; in Psalmis mihi dicta videntur: Notus in Iudæa Deus, præclarum nomen eius in Israele. In Salem est tabernaculum eius, & mansio eius in Zione. Nuntiat verbum suum Iacobo, & decreta sua ac iudicia sua Israeli. Non egit adhunc modum cum vllis gentibus, nec manifestauit eis iudicia sua. Psal. 76. & 147. At in nouo Testamento super omnem carnem spiritus Domini effunditur, & salutis ratio extenditur ad omnes cardines orbis terrarum. Illic dicitur, ab oriente & occidente venturos, qui accumbant in regno Dei cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo. Matth. 8. Ibi mandatum euangelij per omnem orbe prædicandi accipiunt apostoli. Marci. 16. Ibidem Petrus discit, non esse personarum respectum apud Deū, sed in quauis gente ipsi gratos & acceptos esse, qui ipsum timent & iustitiam operantur. Act. 10. Et hic impletur, quod per prophetam prædictum erat, plures fore filios sterilis & desolatæ quàm maritatæ. Isa. 54. Rursum & si præclara extent fidelium veteris Testamenti exempla, quorum similia hodie difficulter reperias: constat tamen nunc longè perspicaciori modo salutis ratione tradi, quàm olim in veteri Testamento factum fit. Ante legis promulgationem promissiones extabant, amplæ quidem & liberales, sed obscuræ satis, si hominum illius seculi conditionem æstimes, qui illas impleri nondum videbant. In lege
units.tr: Meanwhile, in this place we have to examine in passing the difference between the Old and New Testaments. For although one and the same Christ, one and the same faith and way of salvation, and one and the same Spirit are proclaimed in both, a not small difference can nevertheless be detected, in which it easily becomes clear how much greater our dignity and happiness are than those of the ancients. This appears first in the number of the faithful, and then in the manner of handing down. For it is established that in the Old Testament the number of worshippers of God was small, and the knowledge of salvation seemed confined within the borders of the Jewish people. The words of God by which he addresses the Israelites are well known: "You shall be my own possession above all peoples. Indeed all the earth is mine; but you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Exod. 19. Likewise: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth." Amos 3. For this reason those things said to me in the Psalms also seem to apply: "God is known in Judah, his name is great in Israel. In Salem is his tabernacle, and his dwelling in Zion. He declares his word to Jacob, and his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not dealt thus with any nation, nor made known to them his judgments." Ps. 76 and 147. But in the New Testament the Spirit of the Lord is poured out upon all flesh, and the way of salvation is extended to all the corners of the earth. There it is said that men will come from east and west to recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Matt. 8. There the apostles receive the command to preach the gospel throughout the whole world. Mark 16. There too Peter learns that there is no respect of persons with God, but that in every nation those who fear him and work righteousness are acceptable and pleasing to him. Acts 10. And here is fulfilled what was foretold by the prophet, that the sons of the barren and desolate woman would be more numerous than those of the married one. Isa. 54. Again, although there are notable examples of the faithful of the Old Testament, of which it is hard to find similar ones today, it is nevertheless certain that the way of salvation is now handed down in a far clearer manner than it was formerly in the Old Testament. Before the law was promulgated, promises existed, ample and generous indeed, but dark enough if you consider the condition of the men of that age, who did not yet see them fulfilled. In the law

units.la: Quomodo & quibus detur spiritus sanctus.
units.tr: How and to whom the Holy Spirit is given.

units.la: Discrimen veteris & noui Testamenti. typus & figuris salutis negotium adumbrari coepit, sed eiusmodi, ex quibus multi operum iustitiam stabiliendi occasionem sumpsere. Secuti sunt prophetae, qui alibi obscurius, clarius alibi & evidentius Christi mysteria annuntiarunt. At quae nobis in illorum scriptis luculentissima videntur, haud dubie illis seculis satis obscura visa sunt. In novo autem Testamento velum obscuritatis scissum, & illa lux illata est, quae suo in mundum adventu omnem hominem illuminat. Ioan. 1. In Evangelio clare & perspicue traduntur, quae olim obscuriora erant. Et illic piscatores & publicani vident & audiunt, quae multi prophetae & iusti olim videre & audire desiderauerunt. Matth. 13. De hac tam uberi & effusa spiritus sancti & verae illius lucis donatione Ioel quoque vaticinatur. Omnium vero hic finis & usus est, ut dignitatis nostrae & divinae erga nos liberalitatis consideratione excitati, Dei beneficentiam celebremus, & gratos nos praebeamus pro donis, quae in nos tanta benignitate confert mitis & clemens dominus.
units.tr: The difference between the Old and New Testaments. The matter of salvation began to be shadowed forth in types and figures, but of such a kind that many took from them an occasion to establish the righteousness of works. The prophets followed, who announced the mysteries of Christ, here more obscurely, there more clearly and evidently. But those things which seem most lucid to us in their writings were doubtless thought rather obscure in those ages. In the New Testament, however, the veil of obscurity has been torn, and that light has been brought in which, by its coming into the world, enlightens every man. John 1. In the Gospel those things that were formerly more obscure are handed down clearly and plainly. There fishermen and tax collectors see and hear what many prophets and righteous men long ago desired to see and hear. Matt. 13. Joel also prophesies of this so abundant and poured-out gift of the Holy Spirit and of the true light. The end and use of all this is that, stirred up by consideration of our dignity and of the divine generosity toward us, we should celebrate the kindness of God and show ourselves thankful for the gifts which the gentle and merciful Lord bestows upon us with such great goodness.

units.la: Postremo effectus spiritus sancti, qui omnibus credentibus communes futuri sint, Ioel commemorat. Quo loco prophetiae meminit, cuius donum & iuvenes & senes, filios & filias, accepturos dicit. Per prophetiam vero nos non tam vaticinandi facultatem, quam veram & certam rerum divinarum mysteriorum & salutis cognitionem, & in primis veteris scripturae intelligentiam, accipi debere putamus, iuxta illa Pauli, quae 1. Cor. 14. cap. habentur. Per expositionem vero visiones & somnia adijcit, eo quod illis fere mediis olim Deus prophetis suam voluntatem revelabat, ut videre est Numerorum cap. 12. Solent enim prophetae Christi mysteria dicendi formulis, quae illorum seculo visitata & omnibus nota erant, explicare, cuius rei exempla in illorum scriptis versantibus passim occurrent. Prophetandi itaque verbo veram & omnibus in regno Christi communem divinae voluntatis & salutis nostrae cognitionem sive intelligentiam pollicetur, quam & alibi promitti legimus. Isaias certe terram plenam fore dicit scientiae & cognitionis Dei. Isa. 11. Et Iere. 31. cap. dicit dominus: Inferam legem meam in interiora eorum, & cordibus illorum inscribam illam, eroque Deus eorum, ipsique erunt mihi populus. Et non docebit aliquis ultra proximum suum, aut fratrem suum, dicens: Cognosce dominum. Sed omnes me cognoscent a minimo eorum usque ad maximum eorum, etc. Et Christus ex propheta suos omnes θεοδιδάκτους, id est, divinitus doctos fore testatur. Ioan. 6. Isa. 54. Principalis ergo & communis omnibus credentibus spiritus sancti effectus est, divinae voluntatis certa cognitio, salutis & mysteriorum regni Dei peritia, & quatenus cuius opus est scripturae tum veteris tum novae intelligentia. Ex his ergo illos aestimare licet, qui divinae voluntatis cognitionem nihili faciunt, & cum illam per se non intelligant, a nemine tamen volunt institui: quos spiritu Christi carere, unus hic locus probare potest. Quibus coniungi debent fidei dominatores & ecclesiarum tyranni, qui plebem Christianam a scripturarum lectione arcent, & commune illud spiritus sancti beneficium, quod tantopere propheta praedicat, haeresum & errorum seminarium dicere audent. Nostrum est, fratres, divinae gratiae donum agnoscere, & spiritum Christi ampletti, ut huius operatione renati, illuminati & ad omne opus bonum idonei facti, aeterna regni caelorum haereditate fruamur, una cum filio Dei Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Joel recalls the effects of the Holy Spirit which are to be common to all believers. In this place he mentions prophecy, the gift of which he says young and old, sons and daughters will receive. By prophecy, however, we think we should understand not so much the faculty of foretelling as the true and certain knowledge of divine mysteries and of salvation, and above all the understanding of the Scripture of the Old Testament, in accordance with those words of Paul which are found in 1 Cor. 14. By the addition "explanation" he adds visions and dreams, because by these almost means God formerly revealed his will to the prophets, as may be seen in Num. 12. For the prophets were accustomed to explain the mysteries of Christ by means of forms of speech which were in use and known to all in their age; examples of this occur everywhere in their writings. Therefore by the word "prophesy" he promises a true knowledge or understanding of the divine will and of our salvation, common to all in the kingdom of Christ, which we read is also promised elsewhere. Isaiah certainly says that the earth will be full of the knowledge and understanding of God. Isa. 11. And in Jer. 31 the Lord says: "I will put my law within them, and write it on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one shall teach his neighbour or his brother, saying, Know the Lord; but they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest of them," etc. And Christ, quoting the prophet, testifies that all his people will be taught of God, that is, divinely taught. John 6; Isa. 54. The principal and common effect of the Holy Spirit for all believers is therefore a sure knowledge of the divine will, skill in salvation and in the mysteries of the kingdom of God, and, insofar as it is its work, understanding of Scripture both Old and New. From this we may judge those who make nothing of the knowledge of the divine will, and who, since they do not understand it themselves, nevertheless do not want to be instructed by anyone; that they lack the Spirit of Christ this one passage can prove. To these must be joined the lords of the faith and the tyrants of the churches, who keep the Christian people away from reading the Scriptures, and who dare to call that common benefit of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet proclaims so strongly, a seedbed of heresies and errors. It is our duty, brothers, to acknowledge the gift of divine grace and to embrace the Spirit of Christ, so that, renewed, enlightened and made fit for every good work by his operation, we may enjoy the eternal inheritance of the kingdom of heaven together with the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XIII.

units.la: Et dabo prodigia in caelo supernè, & signa super terram infernè, sanguinem & ignem, & vaporem fumi. Sol convertetur in tenebras, & Luna in sanguinem, priusquam veniat dies ille domini magnus & illustris. Et erit, omnis quicunque invocauerit nomen domini, salvus erit.
units.tr: And I will show wonders in heaven above, and signs on the earth beneath: blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before that great and notable day of the Lord come. And it shall come to pass that whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved.

units.la: Dulus Petrus primae concionis suae, quam accepto spiritu sancto Hierosolymis habuit, eum finem constituit, quem in omnibus aliis apostolos observauisse constat, nimirum, ut in Christi cognitionem adducat auditores, & eosdem Christo ad salutem lucrifaciat. Quod ut facilius obtinere possit, initio statim cauet, ne doctrina ipsius, priusquam audita & cognita fuerit, explodatur. Occurrit enim diligenter omnibus iis, quae auditoribus aliquam sinistrae suspicionis causam vel occasionem praebere poterant. Erant inter hos religiosi quidam & pii; plures tamen impii & proterui. Et religiosi quidem ignorantia obstabat, qua impediti, tanto miraculo obstupefacebant quidem, rerum autem incerti haesitabant, nec quicquam poterant splendi statuere. Deteriori autem loco alteri erant, qui cauillo & conuicio omnem miraculi sensum eludebant, apostolos nimirum temulentia, illorum verò auditores stultitiae insimulantes. Praesenti igitur remedio opus erat, quod ex Ioelis secundo cap. producit. Illo enim docet, nihil hic humano vel errore vel affectu agi, sed negotium hoc omne diuinum, & olim quidem per prophetas diuinitus esse promissum. Diligentissimus verò est in prophetae verbis citandis, eò quòd locus iste non modò calumniae diluendae seruiebat, sed vniuersum Petri in statutum vehementer iuuare poterat. Tres enim (vt priori sermone diximus) loci istius partes sunt. Prima magnificam & liberalissimam spiritus sancti promissionem comprehendit. Secunda turbulentissimum mundi statum describit, qui sub Christi regno in finem mundi vsq; futurus sit, adeoq; poenas commemorat, quibus filij sui & euangelij contemptum Deus sit vindicaturus. Quae pars Iudaeorum animis perterrefaciendis mirificè seruiebat, ne Christi & euangelij contemptum se impune laturos sperarent. Tertia, ex tantis malis euadendi viam & rationem monstrat. Primam partem heri explicuimus. Restat, vt posteriores duas modò declaremus.
units.tr: In his first sermon, which he preached at Jerusalem after receiving the Holy Spirit, Peter set himself the aim that the apostles are known to have pursued in all their other sermons: to bring his hearers into the knowledge of Christ and to win them to salvation through Christ. To achieve this more easily, he takes care at the very start that his teaching is not rejected before it has been heard and understood. He carefully meets everything that could give the hearers any cause or occasion for ill suspicion. Among them were some who were religious and devout, but most were impious and insolent. The religious were held back by ignorance: hindered by it, they were indeed astonished at so great a miracle, but being uncertain of the facts they hesitated and could not decide anything certain. On the worse side were others, who by mockery and insult made light of the whole sense of the miracle, charging the apostles with drunkenness and their hearers with folly. So a present remedy was needed, and he brings it forward from the second chapter of Joel. For in that passage he teaches that nothing here is done by human error or passion, but that this whole business is divine, and was promised by God long ago through the prophets. He is most careful in quoting the prophet's words, because this passage served not only to refute the slander but could also greatly help the whole purpose of Peter's speech. For, as we said in the earlier sermon, this passage has three parts. The first contains a magnificent and most generous promise of the Holy Spirit. The second describes the most turbulent state of the world, which is to continue under the reign of Christ until the end of the world, and so recalls the punishments with which God will avenge the contempt of his Son and of the gospel. This part was wonderfully useful for frightening the minds of the Jews, so that they would not hope to bear the contempt of Christ and the gospel with impunity. The third shows the way and method of escaping such great evils. We explained the first part yesterday. It remains that we now explain the last two.

units.la: Quia verò dubitari & disceptari video de magno illo & illustri die domini, cuius mentionem hoc loco propheta fecit, principio mea de hoc sententia proferenda videtur. Sunt qui resurrectionis dominicae diem intelligant, & signa ac prodigia, quae hic ventura praedicuntur, de iis quae in morte & resurrectione Christi contigerunt, exponant. Primus quidem illorum sensus est: sed propter Christi Iesu vaticinia, quae ille ijsdem ferè verbis de nouissimorum temporum conditione prodidit, diei huius terminus longius extendendus esse videtur. Alij vniuersum tempus, ex quo Christus in mundum natus est, huius diei significatione comprehendunt. At mihi non inepte gloriosus & illustris domini aduentus, quo orbem vniuersum iudicabit, intelligi posse videtur. Quia enim nouissimi temporis paulo ante meminerat, eam quam modò describit, illius conditionem fore dicit, donec illius terminus appropinquet, quando Christus in gloria patris comparens, & sententiam finalem de omni carne pronuntians, plenam & omnis doloris ac periculi expertem fidelium suorum beatitudinem constituet, quam & animabus & corporibus suis percipient.
units.tr: Since I see that there is doubt and dispute about that great and notable day of the Lord, which the prophet mentions in this place, I think my view on it should be stated at the outset. There are those who understand it as the day of the Lord's resurrection, and who explain the signs and wonders foretold here as the things that happened at the death and resurrection of Christ. This first view is indeed one sense, but on account of Christ Jesus's prophecies, which he gave in almost the same words about the condition of the last times, the limit of this day seems to be extended further. Others take the whole time from the birth of Christ into the world as included in the meaning of this day. But to me it seems that the glorious and notable coming of the Lord, by which he will judge the whole world, can be understood not without reason. For since the prophet had just spoken of the last time, he says that the condition he now describes will continue until its end draws near, when Christ, appearing in the glory of the Father and pronouncing the final sentence on all flesh, will establish the blessedness of his faithful, full and free of all grief and danger, which they will receive both in their souls and in their bodies.

units.la: Oportuit autem turbulentum mundi statum, qui Christo Iesu incarnato & perac-to redemptionis nostrae negotio futurus est, tam diligenter describi, ne quis propter magnificam spiritus sancti & diuinae gratiae promissionem, omnia in hoc mundo tuta & tranquilla sibi polliceretur. Quo errore Chiliastas olim dementatos fuisse legimus. Et hodie non desunt, qui vniuersalem & stabilem in hoc mundo pacem rerumq; tranquillitatem sub Christo expectant, quam quia nondum florere vident, quaecunq; de fide & religione traduntur, suspecta habent. Erroris causam ex propheticis regni Christi descriptionibus hauriunt, quales tum alibi, tum apud Isaiam cap. 11. & 65. extant. Sed simul alij scripturae loci cum illis conferendi erant, quibus abundè docemur, nihil tale in hoc mundo nobis expectandum esse. Dauid enim, Christum in medio inimicorum suorum regnaturum dicit. Psal. 110. Et Christus regnum suum de hoc mundo esse negat. Ioan. 18. Idem passim suos de cruce & acerbissimis afflictionibus admonet, quibus illos praeparari vult. In mundo (inquit) afflictionem habebitis. Ioan. 16. Ridiculi ergo reuera sunt, qui contra Christi pronuntiatum, in mundo tam sibi ipsis quàm aliis pacem, otium & tranquillitatem pollicentur. Nec interim quae de pacifico regni Christi statu apud prophetas dicuntur, negamus. Sed illa partim de animorum tranquillitate & spirituali fidelium gaudio, partim de solis fidelibus & conuersatione, quam illi soli inter se habent, intelligimus. Ita enim verè tranquilli & salutis certi sunt, & cum illis tutò cohabitant, qui cum antea persecutores essent, & lupi leonesq; videri poterant, ad Christum conuersi, oues & agni placidissimi facti sunt. Manent interim illos afflictionum palaestrae, quae (vt Christus non obscurè admonet) eò graviores erunt, quò propius vniuersalis illa piorum redemptio, quae in ipsius aduentu perficienda erit, accedet. Vide Matth. 24. Marc. 13. Luc. 21. cap. Sed vt ad prophetae verba tandem accedamus, duo in illis praecipuè consideranda videntur: quorum alterum turbulentus & infelix mundi status est, quem post Christi in carnem aduentum fore praedicit: alterum verò malorum & calamitatum causas habet, quarum consideratio nostrae tam institutioni quàm consolationi haud parum seruire potest.
units.tr: Now the turbulent state of the world, which is to follow the incarnation of Christ Jesus and the completion of the work of our redemption, had to be described so carefully so that no one, because of the magnificent promise of the Holy Spirit and divine grace, would promise himself that everything in this world is safe and calm. We read that the Chiliasts once went mad through this error. And today there are not lacking those who expect a universal and lasting peace and tranquillity of things in this world under Christ. Because they do not yet see this flourishing, they regard with suspicion whatever is handed down about faith and religion. They draw the cause of this error from the prophetic descriptions of Christ's kingdom, such as are found both elsewhere and in Isaiah chapters 11 and 65. But other passages of Scripture had to be compared with those, which teach us abundantly that nothing of that kind is to be expected for us in this world. For David says that Christ will reign in the midst of his enemies (Ps. 110). And Christ denies that his kingdom is of this world (John 18). He also repeatedly warns his followers about the cross and the most bitter afflictions, for which he wants them to be prepared. "In the world," he says, "you will have tribulation" (John 16). So those who, against Christ's pronouncement, promise themselves and others peace, leisure and tranquillity in the world are truly ridiculous. Yet meanwhile we do not deny what the prophets say about the peaceful state of Christ's kingdom. But we understand those things partly of the tranquillity of minds and the spiritual joy of the faithful, and partly of the faithful alone and of the fellowship they have among themselves. For they are truly calm and certain of salvation, and live safely with one another, those who, though they were once persecutors and might have seemed wolves and lions, have been converted to Christ and have become sheep and most gentle lambs. Meanwhile the struggles of affliction remain for them, which (as Christ clearly warns) will be the heavier the nearer that universal redemption of the godly draws, which is to be completed at his coming. See Matt. 24, Mark 13, Luke 21. But to come at last to the prophet's words, two things seem chiefly to be considered in them. One is the turbulent and unhappy state of the world which he foretells will follow Christ's coming in the flesh. The other has the causes of evils and calamities, and the consideration of these can serve no little purpose both for our instruction and for our consolation.

units.la: Nouissimi seculi statum his verbis describit: Dabo prodigia in coelo supernè, & signa super terram inferne, sanguinem & ignem, & vaporem fumi. Sol conuertetur in tenebras, & Luna in sanguinem. Prodigiorum meminit, quae quia rerum futurarum indicia sunt, in illorum consideratione calami-lamilamitates, quas illa portendunt, simul animo comprehendere oportet. Nec enim is Dei mos est, ut vanis & inanibus spectris hominum mentes deludat. Et Christus Iesus in evangelio haec ipsa repetens, afflictiones quoq; quarum haec signa & prognostica sunt, simul commemorat. Audietis (inquit) bella, & rumores bellorum. Consurget enim gens contra gentem, & regnum contra regnum, & erunt pestilentia, & fames, & terraemotus singulis locis, &c. Matth. 24. Varias autem ponit prodigiorum species, ut attentiores nos reddat propheta. Prodigia in caelo fore dicit, in quorum albo Cometes, faces, lampades, dracones volantes, xiphiae, bolides & quaecunq; alia sunt eius generis, recenseri possunt. Quae licet Meteorologici inter naturalia numerant, prodigia tamen & futurarum calamitatum praesagia esse, locus hic satis docet. Deinde in terris quoq; signa fore dicit, in quibus primum locum non immerito terraemotibus dabimus, quibus ingentes rerum mutationes plerunque denuntiatas fuisse constat. Huc quoq; insolitae aquarum inundationes pertinent, monstrosi item partus, portentosae animalium voces, sanguinolentae fontium scaturigines, monstrosi arborum & plantarum fructus, cum infinitis aliis, quorum exempla historiae & experientia quotidiana suppeditant. Sed in caelos redieus propheta, peculiariter Solis & Lunae meminit, quorum splendorem atrus tenebris & terrifica sanguinis aspersi specie obscurandum praedicit. Omnium vero sensus est: eam fore novissimo saeculo mundi totius faciem, ut quocunq; vertamus oculos, horrenda appareant irae Dei & iudiciorum ipsius indicia, in iis quoq; creaturis, quarum in Dei bonitate declaranda & hominibus consolandis praecipuus usus sit, inter quas solem & lunam cum primis intelligimus. Porro si quae hic dicuntur cum historiis conferamus, multiariam omnia haec iam aliquot saeculis impleta esse videbimus. Sed quid ad historias recurrere opus est, cum nostro saeculo horum exempla plurima viderimus, & quotidie nova videre detur? Quod unquam saeculum fuit ab ipsa rerum origine, quo tot Cometae visi sint, quot intra annos viginti tres apparuerunt? Taceo cuspides, enses, tela, equos, virorum species, imo armatas acies, leones, & infinita alia, quae in nubibus conspicua spectatorum animos terruerunt. Terraemotus & aquarum inundationes horrendas quis ignorat? Monstrosos partus tum hominum, tum pecorum, nemo facile numeraverit, quos annis iam triginta editos esse novimus. E terra sanguinis scaturigines non uno in loco emicuerunt. Vidimus in spicis rerum novarum praesagia. Barbatae vuae vel botri, e quorum acinis pili densi enati sunt, ebrietatem Germanis exprobraverunt, utpote viris fortibus ad bibendum vinum, ut propheta ait.
units.tr: He describes the state of the last age in these words: "I will show wonders in heaven above, and signs on the earth beneath: blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood." He mentions wonders, and since these are signs of things to come, we must in considering them also grasp in our minds the calamities which they portend. For it is not God's way to deceive men's minds with vain and empty apparitions. Christ Jesus, repeating these very things in the gospel, also recalls the afflictions of which these are the signs and omens. "You will hear," he says, "of wars and rumours of wars. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there will be pestilences, and famines, and earthquakes in various places," and so on (Matt. 24). The prophet, moreover, lists various kinds of wonders so as to make us more attentive. He says there will be wonders in heaven, and in the catalogue of these may be listed comets, torches, lamps, flying dragons, swords, fireballs, and whatever else is of that kind. Although the meteorologists count these among natural things, this passage sufficiently teaches that they are wonders and forerunners of future calamities. Then he says there will also be signs on the earth, and among these we rightly give first place to earthquakes, by which it is well known that great changes of affairs were commonly announced. Here also belong unusual floods of waters, monstrous births, portentous voices of animals, bloody springs of fountains, monstrous fruits of trees and plants, together with countless other things, of which history and daily experience supply examples. But returning to the heavens, the prophet makes special mention of the sun and moon, whose brightness he foretells will be obscured by darkness and by the terrifying appearance of sprinkled blood. The meaning of the whole is this: in the last age the face of the whole world will be such that wherever we turn our eyes, the dreadful anger of God and the signs of his judgments will appear, even in those creatures whose principal use is to declare God's goodness and to console men, among whom we understand the sun and moon above all. Moreover, if we compare what is said here with histories, we will see that all these things have been fulfilled in many ways for some centuries now. But why is it necessary to turn back to histories, since in our own age we have seen many examples of these, and it is given us to see new ones every day? What age has there ever been, from the very origin of things, in which so many comets have been seen as have appeared within these twenty-three years? I say nothing of spear-points, swords, weapons, horses, shapes of men, indeed armed battle-lines, lions, and countless other things, visible in the clouds, which have terrified the minds of onlookers. Who does not know of the dreadful earthquakes and floods of waters? No one could easily count the monstrous births, both of men and of cattle, which we know have been produced now for thirty years. Springs of blood have burst forth from the earth in more than one place. We have seen omens of new things in ears of grain. Bearded grapes or clusters, from whose berries thick hairs have sprung, have reproached the Germans with drunkenness, as men strong for drinking wine, as the prophet says.

units.la: Observandus autem est in his perpetuus Dei mos, qui poenas nunquam nisi per prodigia admonitis immittit, & ne inani sit prodigiorum contemplatio, iisdem plerunq; verbum suum coniungit, quo diserte de imminentibus Dei iudiciis homines admonentur. Quia enim saluos vult homines, non facit quicquam (ut propheta ait) nisi arcanum suum servis suis prophetis antea revelet. Amos 3. capite. Potest hoc omnium saeculorum, a prima mundi origine, exemplis demonstrari. Diluuium praecessit Noah, iustitiae praeco, cuius voce ad poenitentiam mundus excitari posset. Sodomitae, priusquam perirent, Lotum miserunt, cuius verbis & exemplo admonerentur. Aegyptii praeter Mosem & Aaronem, portenta viderunt horrenda, quae, si sensus aliquis in ipsis fuisset reliquus, animos illorum mollire poterant. Chananaeus non defuisse venturi excidii praesagia, Rachab meretrix non obscure testatur. Babylonicam captivitatem quam multae & quam fidae admonitiones praecesserint, nemo ignorat in prophetarum scriptis mediocriter versatus. De prodigiis & signis, quae ultimum illud Hierosolymorum & Iudaicae gentis excidium praecesserunt, horrenda & stupenda Iosephus & Egesippus tradiderunt. Taceo, quae reliquis historiis continentur, quorum fidem eventus semper comprobavit. Ex illis vero Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, & de nostri saeculi prodigiis & signis iudicare discamus, ne dum illa caeci surdique negligimus, numinis contemptores esse deprehendamur, & contemptus illius poenas luamus atroces.
units.tr: Moreover, God's consistent custom is observed in these matters: he never sends punishments except through portents, and so that the contemplation of portents may not be empty, he commonly joins his word to them, by which people are plainly warned of the judgements of God that are coming. For since he wants people to be saved, he does nothing (as the prophet says) without first revealing his secret to his servants the prophets. Amos 3. This can be shown by examples from every age, from the very beginning of the world. Noah, a herald of righteousness, went before the flood, through whose voice the world could have been roused to repentance. Before the Sodomites perished, they sent away Lot, by whose words and example they might have been warned. The Egyptians saw dreadful portents besides Moses and Aaron, which, if any sense had been left in them, could have softened their hearts. That the Canaanites did not lack signs of the coming destruction, Rahab the harlot bears clear witness. How many and how faithful the warnings were that preceded the Babylonian captivity, no one who is moderately versed in the writings of the prophets is ignorant. Josephus and Hegesippus have handed down dreadful and astonishing accounts of the portents and signs that came before the final destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation. I pass over what is contained in the other histories, whose truth the outcome has always confirmed. From these examples let us acknowledge the goodness of God, and let us learn to judge the portents and signs of our own age, so that we are not found to be despisers of the divine majesty, and to pay the dreadful penalty of that contempt, if we neglect these things like the blind and deaf.

units.la: At miretur aliquis, quae tam infelicis & turbulenti status causa esse possit, postquam filius Dei in carne manifestatus est, qui pacem inter nos & Deum constituit, & in cuius nativitate angelorum canentium voces auditae sunt: Gloria Deo in excelsis, in terris pax, in hominibus bona voluntas, &c. Atqui modo Deus magis iratus magisq; terris infensus videri potest, quam ante filii sui incarnationem fuerit. Hinc certe olim Christiani nominis hostes occasionem sumpsere contra Christi religionem inuehendi, utpote pos cuius ortum mare malorum in terras & humanum genus irrupisset: quae
units.tr: But someone may wonder what could be the cause of so unhappy and turbulent a condition, since the Son of God was manifested in the flesh, who established peace between us and God, and at whose birth the voices of angels singing were heard: "Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good will toward men," etc. And yet God now seems more angry and more hostile to the earth than he was before the incarnation of his Son. Certainly, in the past, enemies of the Christian name have seized on this as an occasion to attack the religion of Christ, as if since his coming a sea of evils had burst in upon the lands and the human race. Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, Arnobius and others of the ancients, we read, answered these calumnies vigorously.

units.la: Prodigiorum usus.
units.tr: The use of portents.

units.la: Causae malorum nouissimi seculi. rum calumnijs Tertullianum, Cyprianum, Augustinum, Arnobium & alios veterum graviter re- spondisse legimus. Sed & inter Christiana fidei sectatores, quosdam invenire licet, quos horum con- sideratio non parum labefactare solet. Non inutilis ergo & superuacanea est causae malorum o- mnium consideratio, quae bifariam habeti debet. Est enim tam in pijs quàm in impijs inueniganda, & sic facile patebit, in nobis causam calamitatum haerere, fidem vero Christianam & Christum i- psum extra omnem culpam esse. In impijs non laboriosa est causae huius inquisitio, cùm palàm mul- ta patrent quotidie, quae Dei iram & poenas merentur, In illis enim vel Epicureismus regnat & se- curus Dei omnium sacrorum contemptus, vel superstitio & idololatria. Verunq; veritatis odium gi- gnit, & persecutiones contra Christi ministros excitat, qui veritatis luce scelerum licentiam & super- stitiones arguunt atque accusant. Regnant haec nostro saeculo, imò grassantur, ut nemo tam caecus sit qui non videat, nemo tam impudens qui negare possit. Audiuntur passim illusorum voces, qui (ut Petrus praemonuit) nouissimi iudicij diem disseris vellicant, & resurrectionem mortuorum in du- bium vocant, imò aperte negant. Et qui linguas frenare possunt, vitae tamen licentia se eadem im- pietatis labe infectos esse, testantur. His opponunt sese religionis professores, sed superstitiosi homi- nes & crassissimae idololatriae dediti, qui pro frigidissimis ceremonijs, pro humanis traditionibus, pro fucata suorum operum iustitia, non minori impietate & pertinacia pugnant, quàm olim pro le- gis iustitia Iudaei pugnauerunt. Vtrunq; vero hoc hominum genus in veritate oppugnanda consen- tit, ut olim Pharisaeos cum Herodianis contra Christum collusisse traditur. Nec verbis & argu- mentis res transfigitur, sed vinculis, carceribus, laqueo, igne & gladio. Et eò vsq; multis in locis pro- cessit impietas, ut non aliud atrocius flagitium sit, quàm Christum ingenuè fateri, & euangelij ve- ritatem ac fidei Christianae fynceritatem fortiter asserere. Haec quia palàm fiunt, calamitatum & malorum huius saeculi causas laboriosius inquirere non est opus, quando ob haec ipsa scelera Israe- lem olim in Babylonem abductum, & postea sirpitus excisum esse constat. Lege 2. Paral. 36. Mat- thaei 23. Lucae 19. cap.
units.tr: The causes of the evils of the latest age. But among those who profess the Christian faith, one may find some whom the consideration of these things commonly shakes not a little. Therefore the consideration of the cause of all evils is neither useless nor superfluous, and it must be undertaken in two ways. For it is to be sought both in the godly and in the ungodly, and so it will easily be made plain that the cause of our calamities lies in ourselves, while the Christian faith and Christ himself are free of all blame. In the ungodly the inquiry into this cause is not laborious, since many things are plainly done every day which deserve God's anger and punishments. For in them either Epicureanism reigns, and a secure contempt of all that is sacred to God, or superstition and idolatry. And hatred of the truth breeds persecutions against the ministers of Christ, who by the light of the truth expose and accuse the licence of their sins and superstitions. These things reign in our age, indeed they rage, so that no one is so blind as not to see them, and no one so shameless as to be able to deny them. On every side the voices of mockers are heard, who (as Peter forewarned) tickle the ears with talk of the day of the last judgement, and call the resurrection of the dead into doubt, indeed openly deny it. And those who can restrain their tongues nonetheless bear witness, by the licence of their lives, that they are infected with the same stain of impiety. Against these stand the professors of religion, but they are superstitious men and devoted to the grossest idolatry, who fight for frigid ceremonies, for human traditions, for the painted-over righteousness of their own works, with no less impiety and obstinacy than the Jews once fought for the righteousness of the law. Yet both kinds of men agree in attacking the truth, just as the Pharisees are said once to have colluded with the Herodians against Christ. Nor is the matter settled by words and arguments, but by chains, prisons, the noose, fire and the sword. And in many places impiety has advanced so far that there is no more atrocious crime than to confess Christ openly and to assert boldly the truth of the gospel and the sincerity of the Christian faith. Since these things are done openly, there is no need to inquire with great labour into the causes of the calamities and evils of this age, since it is established that for these very crimes Israel was once led away into Babylon, and afterwards utterly destroyed. Read 2 Chron. 36; Matt. 23; Luke 19.

units.la: At scio (inquis) malorum authores esse impios, & illorum mores graviora adhuc multò mere- ri quàm quae modo sentiunt. Sed quid ista apud pios & ingenuos Christianos cultores faciunt, quos ijsdem malis inuolui, adeoq; primos esse videmus, qui ista sentiunt? Num verò impiorum audacia & pro- teruia illis fraudi esse debet? Caeterum in pijs non modò doctrinae veritatem, fidei fynceritatem & religionis integritatem, verumetiam imperfectionem & quae ex carne illis inhaerent vitia, spectare oportet, & illos non extra culpam esse, nec aliorum scelerum poenas exoluere patebit. In illis enim fre- quenter saeculi huius studium sibi exerit, & non raro cum filijs Zebedaei priuatos honores & digni- tates vel opes sub Christi praetextu quaerunt. Necesse ergo est, ut calicem Christi bibant, & afflictio- nibus exerciti discant, regnum Christi non esse de hoc mundo. Praeterea pijs non raro confidentia ma- lum obrepit, quo securiores facti in enormia scelera prolabuntur, quod Dauidi & multis alijs acci- disse constat. Afflictione ergo & cruce securitatem illam excuti oportet, ne ipsi quoq; enormiter pec- cent: vel vbi peccauerunt poenitere discant, & cum eodem Dauide dicant: Bonum mihi quòd humi- liauisti me, ut discam mandata tua. Humiliatus sum vsquequaq; domine: quare viuifica me secun- dum verbum tuum. Psal. 119. Et quia contritos corde Deus respicit, & Christus laborantes & onera- tos ad se inuitat, afflictionibus nos conteri opus est, ut cùm nos laborare & oneratos esse sentimus, alacriores ad Christum contendamus. Accedit hû, quòd seruus, qui nouit voluntatem domini sui nec facit eam, grauius vapulat. Luc. 12. Quòd si nosipsos iudicaremus, non iudicaremur à domino. 1. Cor. 11. At quia plerunq; & proprijs blandimur, & ad alienà conniuemus, Dei iudicio opus est, ne pecca- torum ratio ab humana authoritate pendere videatur. Postremò Dei gloria illud postulat, ut impij mundi flagitia puniturus, iuxta apostoli sententiam iudicii à sua domo incipiat, ne in suis probare videatur, quod in alijs seuerè vindicat. 1. Pet. 4. Haec si consideremus, non habebimus quod de Deo conqueramur. Consolatio autem magna ex eo oritur, si discrimen, quod inter piorum & impiorum afflictiones est, obseruemus. Hi enim, quia poenitere nesciunt nec volunt, afflictionum suarum finem non habent, quas aeternus inferorum cruciatus excipit. At pijs eadem paternae virga instar sunt, quibus ad vitae emendationem, fidei zelum, pietatis ardorem & verbi diuini studium excitantur, earum finis est & vsus, ne cum infelici mundo pereant. 1. Cor. 11. Ita omnibus seculis seruiunt, quae de nouissimi temporis turbulentissimo statu & aerumnis traduntur. Nam & impios minus terrent, vt quid ex Christi & euangelij contemptu sperandum sit, intelligant. Pij vero ijsdem admonentur sui officij, & de dei voluntate praemoniti, contra offendiculum, quod ex aduersis eiusmodi enascitur, animos obfirmant. Sed ad propheta locum redeamus.
units.tr: But I know (you say) that the authors of the evils are the ungodly, and that their morals deserve things far worse than what they now suffer. But what do these things have to do with the godly and sincere worshippers of Christ, whom we see to be the first to feel these same evils and to be involved in them? Surely the audacity and insolence of the ungodly ought not to be a loss to them? Moreover, in the godly one must regard not only the truth of doctrine, the sincerity of faith and the integrity of religion, but also imperfection and the vices that cling to them from the flesh, and it will be plain that they are not free of blame, nor do they escape paying the penalties of others' sins. For in them the zeal for this world often takes hold, and not seldom, under the pretext of Christ, they seek private honours and dignities or wealth, like the sons of Zebedee. It is therefore necessary that they drink the cup of Christ, and, being exercised by afflictions, learn that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world. Besides, to the godly a confidence often creeps in, by which, made too secure, they slide into enormous sins, as is known to have happened to David and many others. Therefore that security must be shaken off by affliction and the cross, lest they too sin grievously; or where they have sinned, let them learn to repent, and let them say with the same David: "It is good for me that you have humbled me, that I may learn your commandments. I am utterly humbled, O Lord; quicken me according to your word." Ps. 119. And because God regards those who are crushed in heart, and Christ invites the labouring and burdened to himself, we need to be crushed by afflictions, so that when we feel that we are labouring and burdened, we may hasten the more eagerly to Christ. To this is added that the servant who knows his master's will and does not do it is beaten more severely. Luke 12. "But if we judged ourselves, we should not be judged by the Lord." 1 Cor. 11. But since we often flatter ourselves and wink at the faults of others, the judgement of God is needed, lest the reckoning of sins seem to depend on human authority. Lastly, the glory of God requires that, since he is about to punish the wickedness of the world, judgement should begin, in the words of the apostle, at his own house, lest he seem to approve in his own people what he punishes severely in others. 1 Pet. 4. If we consider these things, we shall have nothing of which to complain against God. Great comfort, moreover, arises from this, if we observe the difference between the afflictions of the godly and of the ungodly. For the latter, since they neither know how nor want to repent, have no end to their afflictions, which eternal torment of the underworld awaits. But for the godly these same afflictions are like a father's rod, by which they are stirred to amendment of life, zeal for the faith, ardour of piety and study of the divine word; their end and purpose is that they may not perish with the unhappy world. 1 Cor. 11. Thus these things serve in every age, what is handed down about the most turbulent state and miseries of the last time. For they also terrify the ungodly less, so that they understand what is to be expected from contempt of Christ and the gospel. But the godly are reminded of their duty by these same things, and, forewarned of God's will, they strengthen their minds against the stumbling-block that arises from such adversities. But let us return to the passage of the prophet.

units.la: Tertia enim & postrema loci huius parte tantis malis remedium adhibet, & viam monstrat, qua ex illis euadere & elabi possint. Nec omittere tam partem Petrus voluit, vt viderent Iudaei, à prophetis olim hanc ipsam salutis viam monstratam fuisse, quam ipse modo praedicabat. Et est hoc ingens diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quae in mediis afflictionibus viam elabendi tam benigne monstrat. Quàm enim terrifica sunt quae de nouissimorum temporum statu praecesserunt, tam laeta & consolationis plena sunt, quae his subijciuntur. Ait enim propheta: Et erit, omnis quicunq; inuocauerit nomen domini, saluus erit. Memorabilis omnino & verè euangelica sententia, qua Paulus quoq; ad euertendum legis & operum iustitiam vti voluit. Rom. 10. Et in praesenti Petrus ex eadem de Christo plenius differendi occasionem sumit. Nos paucis, quae in hac obseruanda videntur, absoluemus.
units.tr: For Peter wanted this third and final part of the passage to supply a remedy for such great evils and to show the way by which people might escape and get clear of them. He also wished that the Jews should not leave out this part, so that they would see that this very path of salvation, which he himself was now preaching, had been shown long ago by the prophets. This is a great proof of divine goodness, which in the midst of afflictions so kindly shows the way of escape. For just as the things that precede the last times are terrifying, so the things that are added after them are joyful and full of consolation. The prophet says: "And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved." This is a truly memorable and entirely evangelical saying, which Paul too wished to use to overthrow the righteousness of the law and of works (Rom. 10.). And here Peter takes from the same words an occasion to speak more fully about Christ. We shall deal briefly with the points that seem worth noting in this.

units.la: Primum salutem & liberationem in Inuocatione monstrat, quam vni & soli deo deberi scriptu- ræ omnes magno consensu docent. In nobis ipsis ergo salutis & liberationis spes nulla esse potest. Nã si aliquae in nobis ad nos saluandum vires extarent, absurdum esset salutem alibi quaerere. Sed nec salutem quae extra nos posita in vno deo monstratur, proprijs viribus per nos apprehendi posse similiter constat. Inuocatione enim & precibus opus est, quae non nisi apud eum locum habent, cuius meræ beneficentiæ & gratuitæ liberalitati confidimus. Nam qui se meruisse aliquid perfuesum habet, non precibus, sed iure suo in ijs, quae ipsi debentur, exigendis vtitur. Constat ergo & in vno deo salutem inueniri, & eandem gratuitum diuinae liberalitatis donum esse, & proinde precibus & inuocatione assidua per nos impetrari oportere.
units.tr: First, he shows salvation and deliverance in invocation, which all the Scriptures with one accord teach is owed to the one and only God. Therefore there can be no hope of salvation and deliverance in ourselves. For if there were any strength in us to save ourselves, it would be absurd to seek salvation elsewhere. But it is equally clear that the salvation which is placed outside us and shown to be in the one God cannot be grasped by us through our own strength. For we need invocation and prayers, which have their place only before him in whose pure beneficence and free generosity we trust. For someone who thinks he has earned something does not pray, but rather claims what is owed to him by his own right. It is therefore established that salvation is found in the one God, that it is a free gift of divine generosity, and that accordingly it must be obtained by us through prayers and constant invocation.

units.la: Deinde modum inuocationis exponit, in quo multi anxiè haerent. Sunt enim qui in deo solo salutem omnem repositam esse intelligunt, sed à dei maiestate propter peccata se arceri existimant, & proinde ab inuocatione vel in vniuersum abstinent, tanquam inutili & superuacanea, vel illam minimis frigidè & sine fide exercent. Sed his non simpliciter dominum, sed nomen domini inuocandum propheta proponit. At quodnam illud nomen domini esse dicemus? Num peculiare aliquod, literis & syllabis constans, quo (vt in aliarum rerum nominibus fieri solet) dei natura, ingenium & proprietates omnes comprehendantur? Neminem equidem tam simplicem esse putauero, qui aeternam, immensam & infinitam ineffabilemq; dei essentiam ac naturam paucis literis comprehendi posse existimet. Dei ergo nomen humano more dicitur, quod nobis Deum quoad fieri potest cognoscendum proponit, & ad hoc referri debent quaecunq; de illius maiestate, veritate, iustitia, bonitate, sapientia, gratia, potentia, misericordia, natura denique eius vniuersa dicuntur. At quia haec in vno Christo omnia luculentissimè conspiciuntur, qui & expressa dei patris imago & gloriæ ipsius splendor est, illi coaeternus & consubstantialis, merito dei nomen dici debet, in quo inuocationem omnem fieri conuenit. Hic enim in carne manifestatus est, & de deo reuelauit quaecunque nos scire fas est. Iohan. 1. Eundem nobis & altare & propitiatorium deus constituit, in quo preces & omnem cultum ipsi offeramus. Illi testimonium coelitus tulit, dicens: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui. Matth. 2. & 17. Et per hunc nobis ad thronum gratiae aditum patere, apostolus docet. Ad Hebraeos quarto. Ad hunc ergo relegantur quicunque deum inuocare volunt, vt & talem esse credant deum, qualis in scriptura nobis proponitur, & se ab illo propter Christum Iesum exaudiri & saluari petat. Arguit hoc nostram iniustitiam, & nos omni merito apud deum destitutos esse docet. Si enim in precibus alieno praesidio nobis opus est, quae nisi per Christum offerantur, Deo grata esse non poterunt, qui obsecro nobis spei in reliqua vita superest, si Christum hunc auferas? At quia hic fide apprehenditur, ex fide preces promanare conuenit, & ea quidem fide, qua nos propter Christum deo patri placere certò credimus. Hinc vetus ille ecclesia mos manauit, quo preces fere omnes Iesu Christi nomine concluduntur. Nouerant enim Christi dictum sanctissimi patres: Nemo venit ad patrem nisi per me, &c. Iohan. 14. Simul verò mirifica consolatione hoc ipsum animos peccati conscientia exterritos recreat. Licet enim nos indignos videamus, quibus benefaciat deus, & quos clementer exaudiat: nouā tamen & certa ac infallibilis fiducia animis nostris oboritur, quòd Christum Iesum nostrum strum esse, & nos propter fidem in ipsum exaudiri cogitamus. Et hac vera illa inuocatio est, quam ipse dominus in spiritu & veritate consistere docet. Iohan. 4. Ex spiritu sancto enim enata in nobis fides, nostras mentes & spiritus in dei contemplationem abripit. Et quia certam in nobis gignit diuinæ gratiæ fiduciam, preces nostræ simulatæ esse non possunt, sed veracissimum sunt fidei & spei nostræ testimonium.
units.tr: Next he sets out the manner of invocation, about which many are anxiously uncertain. For there are those who understand that all salvation is laid up in God alone, but who think that they are shut out from the majesty of God on account of their sins; and so they either abstain altogether from invocation as useless and superfluous, or they perform it in the smallest measure, coldly and without faith. But to these the prophet does not propose that the Lord himself simply be called upon, but the name of the Lord. But what shall we say that this name of the Lord is? Is it some peculiar name, made up of letters and syllables, in which (as is usually the case with the names of other things) the nature, character and all the properties of God are comprehended? Certainly I would not think anyone so simple as to believe that the eternal, immense, infinite and ineffable essence and nature of God can be comprehended in a few letters. Therefore the name of God is spoken in human fashion, since it sets God before us to be known as far as possible; and to this must be referred everything that is said of his majesty, truth, justice, goodness, wisdom, grace, power, mercy, and in short of his whole nature. But because all these things are most brilliantly seen in Christ alone, who is the express image of God the Father and the splendour of his glory, coeternal and consubstantial with him, the name of God ought rightly to be said to be in him, and in him all invocation ought to be made. For he was manifested in the flesh and has revealed whatever we are permitted to know about God (John 1.). God has appointed him to us as both altar and mercy-seat, on which we offer our prayers and all worship to him. The Father bore witness to him from heaven, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 2. and 17.). And the apostle teaches that through him access to the throne of grace lies open to us (Heb. 4.). Therefore all who wish to call upon God are to be referred to him, so that they both believe God to be such as he is set before us in Scripture, and ask to be heard and saved by him for Christ Jesus' sake. This shows our unrighteousness and teaches that we are wholly destitute of any merit before God. For if in prayers we need the help of another, which cannot be pleasing to God unless they are offered through Christ, what hope, I beseech you, would remain for us in the rest of life if you took away this Christ? But because he is apprehended by faith, prayers ought to spring from faith, and indeed from that faith by which we certainly believe that we please God the Father for Christ's sake. Hence that ancient custom of the Church arose, by which almost all prayers are concluded in the name of Jesus Christ. For the most holy Fathers knew the saying of Christ: "No one comes to the Father except through me," etc. (John 14.). And at the same time this very thing refreshes with wonderful consolation souls terrified by a conscience of sin. For although we see ourselves to be unworthy of God's kindness and of his gracious hearing, yet a new and certain and infallible confidence arises in our minds, because we think that Jesus Christ is ours and that we are heard on account of our faith in him. And this is that true invocation which the Lord himself teaches must consist in spirit and truth (John 4.). For faith born in us from the Holy Spirit carries our minds and spirits up into the contemplation of God. And because it begets in us a sure confidence in divine grace, our prayers cannot be feigned, but are the most truthful witness of our faith and hope.

units.la: Quapropter fructum illis excellentissimum propheta pollicetur, quando eum, qui nomen domini inuocauerit, saluum fore dicit. Vbi duplicem consolationem obseruare conuenit. Primo enim vniuersalis est promissio, quæ omnibus nomen domini inuocantibus salutem pollicetur. Communis ergo omnibus hic patefit salutis ianua, à cuius ingressu non paupertate nec mundi infamia, non morbus nec acerbis cruciatibus, nonsexu nec ætate, non nationis nec generis discrimine arcebimur. Imò nec peccatis nec morte prohiberi poterimus, cum in Christo peccatorum omnium expiationem habeamus, & idem ille mortem & inferorum portas deuicerit. Deinde salus absolutè promittitur, vt nomen domini inuocantibus omnia sciremus obuentura, quæcunque ad salutem consequendam necessaria sunt. Vnde colligimus, eos qui nullum ex precibus salutis gustum vel consolationem capiunt, non inuocare nomen domini, id est, fide in Christum destitui, quæ preces nostras irritas esse non patitur. Atqui hæc est vnica salutis ratio, quam passim tradunt sacra litera. Et voluit huius mentionem in præsenti Petrus facere, vt intelligerent Iudæi, se ex imminentibus malis & horribili dei iudicio non alia via elabi posse, quàm si omni suorum operum & propriæ iustitiæ fiducia abiecta, ad gratiam thronum per fidem in Iesum Christum conuertantur. Eadem nobis quoque consideranda sunt hodie. Vrgent passim quæcunque nouissimi seculi mala fore, dominus & apostoli prædixerunt. Consulatur passim à summis viris de remedij & salutis ratione. Infelices verò rerum euentus docent, quanta sit consiliorum omnium vanitas, quæcunque humana ratio inuenit. Hanc ergo teneamus, quæ vt simplicissima est, & multis nos curis & laboribus liberat: ita infallibilis & certa est, eò quòd dei promissione nititur, quam nulla mundi vis euertet. Quare peccata agnoscamus, & in illis quæramus malorum causas, quæ patimur. Peccatorum agnitione ad coercendam propriæ iustitiæ fiduciam vtamur. Inde ad Deum conuersi illius nomen inuocemus: qui certò nos exaudiet & liberabit propter nomen suum in Iesu Christo filio suo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore the prophet promises a most excellent fruit to those who call upon the name of the Lord, when he says they will be saved. Here two kinds of consolation are to be observed. First, the promise is universal, offering salvation to all who call upon the name of the Lord. So the gate of salvation lies open to all in common, and from its entrance we shall be kept back by neither poverty nor the disgrace of the world, neither sickness nor bitter torments, neither sex nor age, nor any distinction of nation or race. Indeed we cannot be barred even by sins or death, since in Christ we have the expiation of all sins, and he himself has overcome death and the gates of hell. Second, salvation is promised absolutely, so that we may know that all things necessary for obtaining salvation will come to those who call upon the name of the Lord. From this we gather that those who take no taste or consolation of salvation from their prayers do not call upon the name of the Lord, that is, they lack faith in Christ, which does not allow our prayers to be in vain. And yet this is the only way of salvation which the holy Scriptures everywhere deliver.
