Peter wished to mention it here so that the Jews might understand that they could not escape the impending evils and the dreadful judgment of God by any other way than by casting off all confidence in their own works and their own righteousness, and turning to the throne of grace through faith in Jesus Christ. These same things must also be considered by us today. Whatever evils the last age will bring, the Lord and the apostles foretold, and everywhere the greatest men are consulted about the method of remedy and salvation. But the unhappy outcomes of affairs show how great is the vanity of all the plans that human reason devises. Let us therefore hold to this way, which, being most simple, frees us from many cares and labours; and it is as infallible and certain as it is simple, because it rests on the promise of God, which no power of the world will overturn. Therefore let us acknowledge our sins, and seek in them the causes of the evils we suffer. Let us use the recognition of our sins to restrain the confidence of our own righteousness. Then, turning to God, let us call upon his name, who will certainly hear and deliver us for his name's sake in Jesus Christ his Son, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XIV.

units.la: Viri Israelitæ, audite verba hæc: Iesum Nazarenum, virum à deo approbatum erga vos virtutibus & prodigijs & signis, quæ fecit per ipsum deus in medio vestri, quemadmodum & ipsi scitis: hunc, inquam definito consilio & præscientia dei traditum, accepistis per manus iniquorū, & cruci affixum interemistis. Quem deus suscitauit, solutis doloribus mortis, quatenus impossibile erat, ipsum ab illa teneri.
units.tr: Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by mighty works and wonders and signs, which God did by him in the midst of you, as you yourselves also know: him, I say, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken and, by the hands of wicked men, have crucified and slain. Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it.

units.la: Audiuimus primam concionis Petri partem, qua apostolos ebrietatis crimine liberat, & spiritu sancto donatos esse docet. Vtitur autem demonstrationis loco Iohelis propheta testimonio, quod ita recenset, vt simul pœnas horribiles, quæ euangelij contemptores manent, exponat, & vnicam effugij siue salutis viam commonstret, quæ in vna fide Iesu Christi versatur. Quæ quia sufficere poterant ijs terrefaciendis, qui non prorsus incurabiles erant, ad alteram partem transit apostolus, qua Christum prædicat, quem præcipuum apostolicæ doctrinæ scopum esse, nuper diximus. Ne verò inanis sit illa prædicatio, ita rem omnem proponit, vt peccatorum conscientia illorum mentes exagitet, vt illa territi, Christum Iesum, in quo salutem prædicari audiebant, auidius & ferentiori fide amplectantur. In primis autem breuitati & perspicuitati studet, ne quis Christi cognitionem, & salutis rationem, quæ hac continetur, philosophorum somnijs similem putaret, quæ nec infinitis voluminibus explicari, nec disputationibus vllis excuti, nec à quoquam plenè comprehendi possunt. Paucis enim verbis præcipuos nostræ fidei articulos comprehendit, quos quicunque intelligit, is & Christi Iesu cognitionem & salutis rationem omnem assecutus est. Primus etenim Christi persopersonam describit, & qualem agnoscere debeamus, docet. Secundus de passione & morte Christi disserit. Tertius eiusdem resurrectionem explicat. De his quantum ipsius spiritus dederit, in praesenti dicemus.
units.tr: We have heard the first part of Peter's sermon, in which he clears the apostles of the charge of drunkenness and teaches that they have been endowed with the Holy Spirit. He uses the testimony of the prophet Joel as proof, which he recounts in such a way as to set out at the same time the dreadful punishments that await the despisers of the gospel, and to point out the only way of escape or salvation, which lies in faith in Jesus Christ alone. Since these things were enough to terrify those who were not wholly incurable, the apostle passes to the second part, in which he preaches Christ, who, as we said recently, is the chief aim of apostolic teaching. Lest this preaching be empty, he sets out the whole matter in such a way that the consciousness of sin stirs their minds, so that, struck with fear, they might embrace more eagerly and with a firmer faith Christ Jesus, in whom they heard salvation was proclaimed. Above all he aims at brevity and clarity, so that no one should think the knowledge of Christ and the way of salvation contained in it to be like the dreams of philosophers, which can be explained by no endless volumes, shaken by no disputations, and fully grasped by no one. For in a few words he comprehends the chief articles of our faith, and whoever understands them has attained both the knowledge of Christ Jesus and the whole way of salvation. For first he describes the person of Christ and teaches what we ought to acknowledge him to be. The second treats of the passion and death of Christ. The third explains his resurrection. Of these things we shall speak now, as far as his Spirit has given us.

units.la: De Christi personam locuturus, prudenter & circumspecte agit omnia, ne qui adhuc infirmiores erant, offendiculi occasionem habeant. Nam ubi attentos reddidit breui exhortatiuncula, sensim illos in Christi cognitionem subuehere instituit, dicens: Iesum Nazarenum, virum a deo approbatum erga vos, virtutibus & prodigijs & signis, quae per ipsum Deus fecit in medio vestri, quemadmodum & ipsi scitis, &c. Quibus verbis duo de Christo praedicat. Primo hominem fuisse docet. Nam Nazarenum vocat, quod nomen illi a Ciuitate Galilaeae Nazareth, vbi educatus fuerat, obtigit, sicuti Euangelica historia docet. At quia hoc non satis firmum videri poterat, virum quoque dicit, quod nomen non nisi in verum hominem competere potest. Et vere vir Christus dicitur, quia (vt Paulus monet) non angelos aut caelestem aliquam essentiam, sed semen Abrahae assumpsit. Hebr.1. Porro ne quis vulgarem aliquem hominem fuisse putaret, a reliquis illum distinguit, addens: Approbatum a deo erga vos, virtutibus, &c. Et licet diuinitatem Christi docere instituerit, prudenter tamen diuinitatis nomen adhuc celat, quod Iudaeorum auribus nimium insolens videbatur. Vult autem, vt ipsis rebus discant, verum deum esse, quem hactenus vulgarem tantummodo hominem fuisse putauerant. Perinde enim est ac si dicat: Iesum Nazarenum praedico, quem pleriq; vestrum nudum hominem fuisse existimant. At cogitandum erat, deum palam in illo multa edidisse diuinae naturae indicia, quorum omnium finis hic fuit, vt illum vobis commendaret, & doceret expectatum illum humani generis saluatorem esse, quem olim promiserat. Et opera quidem Christi, quibus illum deus pater commendauit, tribus titulis insignit & ornat. Primo virtutes vocat, ne quid cum praestigiatoribus commune habuisse putetur. Vere enim facta sunt, quae de illo ab Euangelistis commemorantur: nec aliena, sed propria ipsius virtute facta sunt, quod Lucas diserte testatur, dum ex illo virtutem, qua infirmi sanabantur, exiuisse scribit. Luc. 6. Sed & ipse alibi virtutem ex se egressam esse dicit, quae sanguinis profluuio laborantem sanauerat. Luc.8. Deinde prodigia dicuntur Christi opera, eo quod communem naturae cursum praetergressa, in admirationem & stuporem spectatorum animos abripuerunt. At quia prodigiorum loco saepe habentur quorum causas ignoramus, cum reuera nihil portendant, postremo signa vocat quae Christus edidit: Certum enim operum Christi finis fuit, quod de illius diuinitate & officio testari debuerunt. Ex illis enim & dei filius & promissus mundi redemptor esse agnoscitur. Quae causa est, quod & Iohannis discipulos ad operum suorum considerationem relegat (Matth.11.) & Iudaeis crebro eadem opera inculcat & exprobrat, vt maior fit incredulitatis ipsorum culpa. Opera (inquit) quae dedit mihi pater vt perficiam ea, ipsa inquam opera quae ego facio, testificantur de me, quod pater me miserit. Iohan.5. Si non facio opera patris mei, nolite credere mihi. Sin vero facio, etsi mihi non credatis, operibus credite, vt cognoscatis & credatis quod pater in me est, & ego in eo. Iohan.10. Et rursum: Si opera non fecissem inter eos, quae nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. Iohan.15. Recte ergo Petrus Christi opera signa nominauit. Haec autem inter ipsos edita fuisse dicit, nec alios quam illos ipsos, quibus loquebatur, testes sistit, qui omnium spectatores fuerunt. Ita vero insignem illorum pertinaciam & ingratitudinem perstringit, quae tot tantisq; Christi beneficijs, miraculorum & prodigiorum plenis, emolliri & vinci non potuerat. Simul autem eorundem consideratione in diuinitatis Christi cognitionem illos deducere conatur, de qua paulo post apertius disserit. Licet enim hic deum haec in Christo edidisse dicat, illud tamen Christi potestati & diuinitati nihil deroagt, cum ipse fateatur, opera sibi a patre data, se vero & patrem vnum esse. Iohan.14.
units.tr: About to speak of the person of Christ, he acts prudently and circumspectly in everything, so that those who were still weaker might not have occasion for stumbling. For when he had made them attentive by a brief exhortation, he gradually sets about lifting them up to the knowledge of Christ, saying: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by virtues and wonders and signs, which God did by him in the midst of you, as you yourselves also know, etc. In these words he preaches two things about Christ. First he teaches that he was a man. For he calls him "of Nazareth," a name he received from the city of Galilee, Nazareth, where he had been brought up, as the evangelical history teaches. But because this might seem not firm enough, he also calls him a man, a name which can apply only to a true man. And Christ is rightly called a man, because (as Paul warns) he took on not angels or some heavenly essence, but the seed of Abraham. Heb. 1. Moreover, lest anyone think him some ordinary man, he distinguishes him from the rest, adding: approved by God among you, by virtues, etc. And although he has begun to teach the divinity of Christ, he prudently still conceals the name of divinity, which seemed too strange to the ears of the Jews. He wishes them to learn from the facts themselves that the one whom until now they had thought to be merely an ordinary man is the true God. For it is just as if he said: I preach Jesus of Nazareth, whom most of you think to have been a bare man. But they ought to consider that God had openly displayed in him many signs of the divine nature, the whole purpose of which was to commend him to you, and to teach that he is the expected Saviour of mankind whom he had long ago promised. And the works of Christ, by which God the Father commended him, he marks and adorns with three titles. First he calls them virtues, lest it be thought that he had anything in common with mountebanks. For the things recorded of him by the evangelists were truly done; they were done not by another's but by his own power, as Luke clearly testifies, when he writes that virtue went out from him by which the sick were healed. Luke 6. But he himself elsewhere also says that virtue went out from him, which healed the woman suffering from a flow of blood. Luke 8. Then the works of Christ are called wonders, because, passing beyond the common course of nature, they carried the minds of spectators into admiration and amazement. But because things whose causes we do not know are often held to be wonders, though in truth they portend nothing, lastly he calls them signs which Christ performed. For the certain end of Christ's works was that they should bear witness to his divinity and office. For from them both that he is the Son of God and the promised Redeemer of the world is recognised. This is why he also refers John's disciples back to the consideration of his works (Matt. 11.), and repeatedly urges and reproaches the Jews with the same works, so that the guilt of their unbelief may be greater. The works, he says, which the Father has given me to finish, these very works which I do, bear witness of me that the Father has sent me. John 5. If I do not the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do, though you believe not me, believe the works, that you may know and believe that the Father is in me, and I in him. John 10. And again: If I had not done among them works which no one else has done, they would not have sin. John 15. Rightly therefore Peter calls Christ's works signs. He says moreover that these were done among them, and he sets up as witnesses none other than those very persons to whom he was speaking, who were all spectators. Thus he sharply censures their notable obstinacy and ingratitude, which could not be softened or overcome by so many and so great benefits of Christ, full of miracles and wonders. At the same time, by the consideration of these things he endeavours to lead them to the knowledge of Christ's divinity, which he discusses more openly a little later. For although here he says that God did these things in Christ, this does not in any way detract from Christ's power and divinity, since he himself confesses that the works were given to him by the Father, and that he and the Father are one. John 14.

units.la: Docetur hic vera Christi Iesu cognitio. Est is verus deus & homo in vna inseparabili persona. Deus quidem verus ab aeterno ex patre genitus, homo autem factus ex muliere, quando praefinito tempore in mundum venire debuit, vt humani generis redemptor fieret. Et probe obseruanda est naturarum, diuinae scilicet & humanae, distinctio, quae nec personae vnitatem scindunt, nec propter hanc inter se confunduntur. Manent enim veriusq; naturae proprietates inuiolatae & illaesae, quemadmodum Euangelistae passim docent. Sed & ipse Christus, qui iuxta diuinitatem cum patre vnum est, de humana natura loquens, patrem se maiorem esse fatetur. Ioan.10. Et in humanitate Christus mo-
units.tr: Here the true knowledge of Jesus Christ is taught. He is true God and man in one inseparable person. He is indeed true God, begotten from the Father from eternity, and man, made of a woman, when at the appointed time he was to come into the world, that he might become the Redeemer of mankind. And the distinction of the natures, namely the divine and the human, must be carefully observed, which neither divides the unity of the person nor confuses the natures with one another because of that unity. For the properties of each nature remain inviolate and unharmed, as the evangelists teach throughout. But Christ himself too, who according to his divinity is one with the Father, speaking of his human nature, confesses that he is greater than the Father. John 10. And in his humanity Christ

units.la: t. Christi persona ritur, cuius diuinitas nec morti nec vlli alij corruptioni subiacet. Talem vero Christum passim scriptura sacra praedicat. Quem enim prophetae germen & filium Dauidis nominant, eundem aeternitatis patrem, dominum & deum appellare consueuerunt. Isa. 11. & 9. Ierem. 23. Et quem in Bethlehem nasciturum praedicunt, eius exitum siue progressum ab aeterno esse fatentur. Mich. 5. Quid? quòd ipse dominus de Christo loquens ait: Excitare o gladie super pastorem meum, & super virum socium meum, vel (vt alij interpretantur) coaequalem mihi, &c. Zach. 13. Quibus verbis vtraq; in Christo natura luce clarius conspicitur. Nam & virum, id est, hominem verum deus vocat, & eundem sibi coaequalem esse testatur. Possent multa alia in hanc sententiam adduci testimonia, si necesse foret, quae scripturas legentibus passim occurrent. His autem niituntur primi, quos de Christo profitemur, fidei nostrae articuli. Testamur enim, nos credere in filium Dei vnigenitum, dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: qui conceptus est ex spiritu sancto, natus ex Maria virgine, &c. Quorum explicationi inseruiunt, quaecunq; apud euangelistas de illius incarnationis mysterio habentur. Vide Luc. 1. & 2. Iohan. 1. Matth. 1. cap.
units.tr: ... the person of Christ, whose divinity is subject neither to death nor to any other corruption. Holy Scripture everywhere preaches such a Christ. For he whom the prophets call the Branch and Son of David, they have customarily also called the Father of eternity, Lord and God. Isa. 11. and 9. Jer. 23. And he whom they foretell is to be born in Bethlehem, they confess to have his going forth or origin from eternity. Mic. 5. What of the fact that the Lord himself, speaking of Christ, says: Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who is my fellow, or (as others interpret) equal to me, etc. Zech. 13. By these words both natures in Christ are seen more clearly than light. For he calls him a man, that is a true man, and God, and testifies that he is equal to himself. Many other testimonies could be brought to this effect, if it were necessary, which will meet readers of the Scriptures everywhere. But upon these rest the first articles of faith which we profess concerning Christ. For we testify that we believe in the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, etc. Whatever is found in the evangelists concerning the mystery of his incarnation serves to explain these articles. See Luke 1. and 2., John 1., Matt. 1. chapter.

units.la: Prodest autem vtriusq; in Christo naturae cognitionem probè tenere, eò quòd ex his & Christi officium & nostrae salutis certitudo dependet. Quia enim illum & deum & hominem esse constat, eundem inter Deum & homines mediatorem esse certò credimus: quoniam ea mediatoris siue sequestri conditio sit oportet, vt ab vtraq; diffidentium parte admitti & ferri queat. At hominis infirmitas diuini iudicij rigorem & maiestatem sustinere non poterat, vt nec illa hominis iustitiam, quae plane nulla est, approbat. Quare Christus Iesus inuentus fuit, qui cum dei filius, patri coaeternus & consubstantialis esset, homo factus est, & vtranq; naturam in sua persona ita coniunxit, vt per illum nobis coram deo pax redintegrata, & liber accessus ad thronum gratiae paratus sit. Eius meritum pater aspernari non potest, eò quòd & filius ille dilectus est, & omnis peccati siue sceleris expers. Eidem & nos tuto confidere possumus, quando nostras infirmitates ipse expertus ijdem condolere poterit. Quò Paulus respexit, dicens: Non habemus pontificem, qui non possit affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum, sed tentatum per omnia iuxta similitudinem, absq; peccato. Hebr. 4. Item: Posteaquam pueri commercium habent cum carne & sanguine, ipsi quoq; similiter eorundem particeps factus est, vt per mortem aboleret eum, qui mortis habebat imperium, hoc est, diabolum, & liberos redderet eos, quicunque metu mortis per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti. Non enim angelos assumit, sed semen Abrahae assumit. Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis reddi, vt misericors esset & fidelis pontifex in his quae apud deum forent agenda ad expiandum peccata populi. Nam ex hoc quod ipsi contigit tentatum esse, potest & ijs, qui tentantur, succurrere. Hebr. 2. Horum consideratio docere potest quam delirent, quotquot vnico hoc mediatore, Iesu Christo relicto, ad creaturas conuertuntur, & diuorum intercessionibus causam suam sustineri oportere existimat. Quo facto non obscurè testantur, se à Christi cognitione alienos esse, quando illius officium & causas ignorant, propter quas, qui ab aeterno Deus est, hominem verum in vnitate personae assumere voluit. Ipse certè in euangelio ait: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Iohan. 14. Et Paulus vt vnum deum agnoscit, ita vnum inter deum & homines mediatorem, Iesum Christum, esse testatur. 1. Tim. 2. At quia de his alibi copiosius dicendi occasio dabitur, paucula haec in praesenti sufficiant. Et consolationis summae loco habeamus, quòd eius diuinitatem tot argumentis demonstratam esse videmus, quo saluatore & redemptore gloriamur, & cuius nomine Christiani dicimur. Sed ad Petri concionem & illius explicationem reuertamur.
units.tr: It is useful to hold firmly to a sound knowledge of both natures in Christ, because on these depend both Christ's office and the certainty of our salvation. For since it is established that he is both God and man, we firmly believe that he is the one mediator between God and men, since a mediator or go-between must be of such a kind that he can be accepted and trusted by both the distrustful parties. But human weakness could not endure the rigour and majesty of divine judgement, nor does God approve of human righteousness, which is plainly nothing. Therefore Jesus Christ was found, who, since he was the Son of God, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, became man and joined the two natures in his one person, so that through him peace with God is restored to us and a free approach to the throne of grace is prepared. The Father cannot reject his merit, since that Son is beloved and free from all sin and wickedness. We too can confidently trust in him, since he himself, having experienced our weaknesses, can sympathise with them. Paul had this in view when he said: "We do not have a high priest who cannot be touched by the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been tested in all things, according to the likeness of ours, apart from sin" (Heb. 4). Likewise: "Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise took part in the same, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their lives. For he does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brethren in all things, so that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in the things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For since he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted" (Heb. 2). Reflection on these things can teach us how far astray they are who, leaving aside this one mediator, Jesus Christ, turn to creatures and think their cause must be upheld by the intercessions of the saints. In doing so they plainly testify that they are strangers to the knowledge of Christ, since they are ignorant of his office and of the reasons for which he who is God from eternity willed to take to himself a true man in the unity of his person. He himself certainly says in the Gospel: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14). And Paul, as he acknowledges one God, so he testifies that there is one mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2). But since there will be occasion to speak of these things more fully elsewhere, let these few points suffice for the present. And let us count it a supreme comfort that we see his divinity demonstrated by so many arguments, in whom we glory as our Saviour and Redeemer, and in whose name we are called Christians. But let us return to Peter's sermon and his explanation of it.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Secundo loco passionem & mortem Christi praedicat, & ita quidem, vt ipsorum animis terrorem conscientiae ob tantum facinus incutere studeat. Ait enim: Hunc Iesum praefinito consilio & praescientia dei traditum, accepistis per manus iniquorum, & cruci affixum interemistis. Tria dicuntur ad Christi mortem pertinentia. Primò totum populum tam nefandae caedis reum facit. Vos (inquit) cruci affixum interemistis. Atqui non ignorabat Petrus, militum manibus in crucem suspensum fuisse. Vere tamen hoc facinus vniuerso populo tribuit, qui in Christi mortem non modò consenserat, sed eundem ad crucis supplicium improbis & seditiosis clamoribus postulauerat, adeoq; sua improbitate Pilatum diu renitentem vicerat, vt euangelistae docent. Docemur hoc Petri exemplo, vnde euangelicae praedicationis initium fieri debeat: nimirum à peccatorum redargutione, quae & in publicum cum protrahi & accusari oportet. Nisi enim illa agnoscant homines, Christum magni facere nō possunt, quo se nequaquam indigere arbitrabuntur. Eadem siquidem hic, quæ & morborum corporis, est ratio. Qui morbos suos vel ipsi non sentiunt, vel dissimulare studeunt, medicinam non curant, nec sponte se offerentem medicum admittunt. Ita quicunq; nulla tanguntur peccatorum conscientia, vel peccata dissimulari aut suis ipsorum satisfactionibus expiari posse existimant, Christum nec ipsi studiose quærunt, nec illum se in evangelio manifestantem digne amplectuntur, imo priuatæ iustitiæ fiducia elati, huic se opponere non verentur. Cuius rei exempla in pharisæis multa extant. Quæ causa est, quòd Christus se ægrotantium medicum esse profitetur, nec venisse ut iustos salvet, sed ut peccato res vocet ad pœnitentiam. Matth.9. Luc.5. Et de spiritu sancto loquens, inter illius officia primo loco recensét, quòd mundum peccati arguat & accusat. Iohan. 16. Deniq; cum evangelij prædicationem apostolis commendat, pœnitentiam primò doceri vult, cui deinde peccatorum remissio subiungi debeat. Luc.24. Non temere ergo Petrus hoc ordine progreditur, ut de Christi morte dicturus, auditores huius reos & authores esse, ante omnia demonstret. Et hodie ita mortem Christi prædicari necesse est, ut singuli propter sua ipsorum peccata dei filium mortuum esse, adeoq; se mortis illius authores esse intelligant. Ita enim fiet, ut & de peccatis ex animo dolere discant homines, & salutem, quæ in Christo offertur, maiore fidei feruore amplectantur.
units.tr: Secondly, he preaches the passion and death of Christ, and does so in such a way as to strive to strike terror of conscience into their minds on account of so great a crime. For he says: "This Jesus, delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, you took and by the hands of wicked men crucified and slew." Three things are said that pertain to the death of Christ. First, he makes the whole people guilty of so dreadful a slaughter. "You" (he says) "crucified and slew him." Yet Peter was not unaware that he had been hung on the cross by the hands of soldiers. Nevertheless he rightly ascribes this deed to the whole people, who not only had consented to Christ's death but had also demanded his execution on the cross with wicked and seditious shouts, and so by their wickedness had overcome Pilate, who had long resisted, as the evangelists teach. We are taught by this example of Peter where the beginning of evangelical preaching ought to be made: namely, from the rebuke of sins, which must also be brought out into the open and accused. For unless men acknowledge these, they cannot esteem Christ highly, since they will not think they need him at all. Indeed, here the principle is the same as with bodily diseases. Those who either do not feel their sicknesses or strive to conceal them do not seek a cure, nor do they admit a physician who offers himself freely. So too, whoever is not troubled by any awareness of sins, or believes that sins can be concealed or expiated by their own satisfactions, neither eagerly seek Christ themselves nor worthily embrace him when he reveals himself in the Gospel; indeed, puffed up with confidence in their private righteousness, they do not hesitate to set themselves against him. Many examples of this are found among the Pharisees. This is why Christ professes that he is the physician of the sick, and that he came not to save the righteous but to call sinners to repentance (Matt. 9; Luke 5). And speaking of the Holy Spirit, he lists among his offices, in the first place, that he convicts and accuses the world of sin (John 16). Finally, when he commends the preaching of the Gospel to the apostles, he wills that repentance be taught first, to which the forgiveness of sins should then be added (Luke 24). Peter therefore does not proceed in this order without reason, so that, about to speak of Christ's death, he first shows that his hearers are guilty of it and its authors. And today Christ's death must be preached in such a way that each person understands that the Son of God died on account of his own sins, and that he himself is an author of that death. For in this way people will learn to grieve from the heart over their sins, and will embrace with greater fervour of faith the salvation that is offered in Christ.

units.la: Caterum ne Petrus ignobile vulgus duntaxat accusare videretur, aliud addit, quo primi tanti facinoris duces arguuntur. Nam per manus iniquorum acceptum interemistis, ait. At qui nam illi & iniusti? Primus inter hos Iudas est olim Christi discipulus & apostolus, sed postea dux factus eorum, qui Christum comprehenderunt. Proximi ab hoc sunt summi pontifices cum toto scribarum & sacerdotum collegio, quos pecunia Iudam corrupisse & ad tam immane flagitium conduxisse constat. In eodem numero & Pilatus censetur, qui Romani Imperatoris nomine pro tribunali considens in illum mortis sententiam tulit. Nec omnino extra culpam Herodes est, qui cum ad se transmissum absoluere potuisset, illusum potius ad Pilatum remittere maluit. Hos (inquam) omnes iniquorum nomine Petrus comprehendit, quorum summa erat in Hierosolymorum urbe authoritas & potestas. Quàm vero hoc dicere periculosum fuerit, facile videbit, qui hominum mores paulo diligentius inspexerit. Capitale scelus habetur iudicis sententiam, qua fontes damnantur, iniquam & iniustam dicere. Atqui hoc Petrus intrepidè facit in urbe populosissima, & in qua recens adhuc erat mortis Christi memoria, quæ tam honorificè ab illo prædicatur. Hic igitur ceu in speculo videre est, quàm fortes & intrepidos Christi assertores faciat, quos suo numine spiritus sanctus afflare dignatur. Simul etiam admonemur, quæ in verbi ministris publica flagitia accusandi libertas & παρρησία esse debeat, & quàm minimè audiendi sint, qui nescio quam modestiam in ministris requirunt. Nec enim peccata extenuari opus est, quæ ipsa alioqui (ut Dauid monet) nobis blandiri consueuerunt. Psal.36. Nec personarum ratio haberi debet, quando peccatum authoris persona non excusat, imò eo grauiori offendiculo nocet, quo maior est delinquentis authoritas. Adde, quòd publica persona minister est, cuius muneri omnes hominum ordines subiecti esse constat. Familiæ enim suæ illum Christus dispensatorem constituit, in qua diuites & egeni, nobiles & ignobiles, magistratus & subditi continentur. Matth.24. Et omnibus dicitur quod Ieremiæ dicit dominus: Ecce ego facio te hodie ciuitatem munitam, columnam ferream & murum æneum, contra omnem terram, contra reges Iuda, contra principes eius, contra sacerdotes & contra vniuersum populum terræ. Ierem.1. Nullas ergo mundi & carnis rationes admittant, quibus abster-reantur, quicunq; docendi munus in ecclesia fuscepserunt, sed Christi Iesu, prophetarum & apostolorum exempla imitentur, quos omnes simili libertate in peccatis corripiendis vtos esse constat, qua in præsenti Petrus vtitur.
units.tr: But lest Peter seem to accuse only the common crowd, he adds something else by which the leaders of so great a crime are charged. For he says, "you took by the hands of the wicked and slew." But who were these wicked men? First among them is Judas, once a disciple and apostle of Christ, but afterwards the leader of those who seized Christ. Next after him are the chief priests with the whole college of scribes and priests, whom it is known that Judas was bribed with money to join in so monstrous a crime. Among the same number Pilate is also counted, who, sitting in judgement in the name of the Roman emperor, pronounced the sentence of death against him. Nor is Herod altogether free of blame, who, although he could have released him when he was sent to him, preferred to send him back, mocked, to Pilate. All these, I say, Peter included under the name of the wicked, whose authority and power were greatest in the city of Jerusalem. How dangerous it was to say this, anyone will easily see who has examined men's ways a little more carefully. It is a capital crime to call a judge's sentence, by which the guilty are condemned, wicked and unjust. Yet Peter does this fearlessly in a most populous city, where the memory of Christ's death was still fresh, a death which he proclaims so honourably. Here, then, one may see as in a mirror how brave and fearless defenders of Christ the Holy Spirit makes those whom he deigns to inspire with his power. At the same time we are also admonished what freedom of speech and [παρρησία] there ought to be in ministers of the Word in rebuking public scandals, and how little those should be listened to who demand I know not what modesty in ministers. For sins need not be softened, since they are otherwise wont (as David warns) to flatter us (Ps. 36). Nor should the person be considered, since the sinner's person does not excuse the sin; rather, it harms all the more as an offence the greater the authority of the one who offends. Add that the minister is a public person, to whose office it is established that all orders of men are subject. For Christ appointed him as steward of his household, in which the rich and the needy, the noble and the commoners, magistrates and subjects, are contained (Matt. 24). And what the Lord said to Jeremiah is said to everyone: "Behold, I make you today a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall, against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against its priests and against all the people of the land" (Jer. 1). Therefore let those who have undertaken the duty of teaching in the Church admit no considerations of the world or of the flesh by which they may be frightened off; rather, let them imitate the examples of Jesus Christ, of the prophets and of the apostles, all of whom are known to have used the same freedom in rebuking sins that Peter uses in the present passage.

units.la: Quoniam vero quæ de Christi morte dixerat, magni offendiculi causam præbere poterant, quasi hominum astutia & viribus Christus oppressus fuisset, & proinde pro deo agnosci non deberet: offendiculo medetur Petrus, quando Christum definito sue certo dei consilio in mortem & iniquorum manus traditum fuisse dicit. Hoc enim perinde est, ac si diceret: Nemo putauerit, vel Iudæ proditori, vel sacerdotibus, vel Pilato tantum consilij aut virium fuisse, ut quicquam hic vel ignorante vel in uito deo fecerint. Huius enim & præscientia & decreto factum est, quicquid Christo accidit. Quò etiam in sua epistola respexisse videtur, quando Christum priusquam mundus hic conderetur, in hunc finem præordinatum fuisse dicit. 1.Pet. 1. Demonstrationis loco adduci possunt promissiones dei in mundi exordio datæ, & prophetarum oracula, quæ non aliam redemptionis & salutis nostræ rationem tradunt, quàm quæ filij dei sanguine parta est. Isaias certè dominum effecisse scribit, ut in Christum incurreret omnium nostrum iniquitas.Isa. 53. Eiusdem ergo domini decretum & opus fuit, ut illius sanguine nostra iniquitas expiaretur. Est autem hic insignis locus, quo de dei providentia rectè iudicare discimus.
units.tr: Since the things Peter had said about Christ's death could give great offence, as if Christ had been overcome by human cunning and strength and so ought not to be acknowledged as God, Peter remedies this offence by saying that Christ was delivered into death and into the hands of wicked men by the fixed and certain counsel of God. This is as much as to say: let no one suppose that Judas the traitor, or the priests, or Pilate had so much counsel or power that they could do anything here either without God's knowledge or against his will. For whatever happened to Christ happened by God's foreknowledge and decree. Peter seems to have had this in mind in his epistle as well, when he says that Christ was foreordained to this end before the world was made. 1 Pet. 1. As proof one may cite the promises God gave at the beginning of the world and the oracles of the prophets, which set out no other way of redemption and salvation for us than that which was won by the blood of the Son of God. Isaiah certainly writes that the Lord caused the iniquity of us all to fall upon Christ. Isa. 53. So the decree and the work of the same Lord was that our iniquity should be atoned for by his blood. This is a notable passage, from which we learn to judge rightly of God's providence.

units.la: Observemus igitur, quòd non obiter præscientiæ, sed etiam consilij siue decreti dei meminit, imò præscientiæ illud præponit, quod & certum & definitum fuisse testatur: quod perinde est, ac si humano more loquens, omne hoc negotiū præmeditatè & maturo Dei consilio transactum esse diceret. Confutatur hic illorum commentum, qui in deo nihil ferè quàm præscientiam fingunt, & deum quæ præsciuit fore, per prophetas prædixisse aiunt, interim omnem rerum agendarum administrationem illi adimentes. Qui mihi ex deo otiosum mundi spectatorem facere videntur, adeoq; ignauum etiam & inertem, qui multa contra voluntatem suam, & secus quàm constituerat, permittat fieri. At longè aliter Dauid, qui deum ita quæ in cœlis & in terra fiunt, inspicere docet, ut simul regnorum vices administraret, & omnia suo nutu dirigat.Psalm.113.Et Petrus in præsenti deum non modò Iudæ perfidiam, sacerdotum sanguinarios conatus & Pilati iniquitatem præuidisse, & hæc otiosa quadam permissione Dei accidisse fingit: sed omnem huius negotij euentum ex certo & definito Dei consilio siue decreto deducit. At quod in dei filio accidit, de vniuersa humani generis gubernatione, quam Deus sustinet, intelligi debet, nisi deum, qui sibi ipsi semper constat, à communi ordine & more suo declinauisse putemus.
units.tr: Let us therefore observe that Peter speaks not merely in passing of God's foreknowledge, but also of his counsel or decree, and indeed he puts foreknowledge first, which he affirms was certain and fixed. This is as if, speaking in human fashion, he said that the whole affair was carried out by deliberate forethought and the mature counsel of God. Here the invention of those is refuted who imagine almost nothing in God but foreknowledge, and say that God foretold through the prophets what he foreknew would happen, while taking away from him all direction of the affairs to be done. They seem to me to make God an idle spectator of the world, and indeed a sluggish and inert one, who permits many things to happen against his will and otherwise than he had decided. But David teaches quite differently, that God so watches over what happens in heaven and on earth that at the same time he governs the changes of kingdoms and directs all things by his nod. Ps. 113. And Peter here not only imagines that God foresaw Judas's treachery, the bloody attempts of the priests and Pilate's wickedness, and that these things came about by a kind of idle permission of God; he derives the whole outcome of this affair from the certain and fixed counsel or decree of God. But what happened to the Son of God should be understood of the whole government of the human race, which God sustains, unless we suppose that God, who always agrees with himself, has departed from his common order and custom.

units.la: In primis verò finem respicere conuenit, cuius gratia diuinæ prouidentiæ decretum Petrus allegat. Quem quia multi non obseruant, illico vociferantur, nos deum malì authorem facere, quando ex illius consilio & nutu omnia dependere dicimus. Atqui Petrus nec Iudam nec huius complices hic excusat, nec in Deum transfert, quæ illi impiè & iniustè designarunt. Quia enim voluntaria malitia peccauere, nec dei consilium & humani generis redemptionem sibi ipsis ob oculos posuerunt, sed improbos auaritiæ, ambitionis & odij affectus secuti sunt, in ipsis peccati culpa hæret, cuius pœnas merito exoluerunt. Prouidentiæ verò & diuini decreti ideò Petrus meminit, ut offendiculo crucis medeatur, & de vniuersa Christi ac redemptionis nostræ causa iudicare doceat. Idem ergo prouidentiæ vsus etiam nobis propositus esse debet, ut tam fidei vitæq; institutioni, quàm consolationi in aduersis seruiat. Ita ex prouidentiæ decreto docent scripturæ, salutem ex mera dei gratia dependere, qui priusquam mundus hic conderetur, Christum Iesum nobis redemptorem prædestinarit, nosq; in illo elegerit. Vide Ephes.1 Rom.9.10.11. &c. Et eodem Christus nos relegat, dicens: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego vos elegi. Item: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Iohan.15. Humanæ igitur iustitiæ crista & exitialem huius fiduciam sola prædestinationis & gratuitæ electionis consideratio reprimit. Eadem in aduersis & impiorum successibus firmissimam consolationem affert. Cur enim illis offendatur, quinos sub diuinæ prouidentiæ tutela, siue præsidio agere, nec quicquam nobis aduersi absque huius decreto accidere nouit? Ideo Christus ad flores agri & volatilia cœli, in quibus dei prouidentia euidentissimè cernitur, nos relegat, & apostolos contra persecutionum scandala argumentis ex hac petitis consolatur, dicens: Nónne duo passerculi minuto asse vœneunt? At vnus ex illis non cadet in terram sine patre vestro. Vestri verò etiam pili capitis omnes numerati sunt, &c. Matth.6. & 10. Agnosco hic hyperbolem, si ad nostræ rationis captum Christi verba examines. Sed si dei sapientiam & omnipotentiam, quæ omnem captum hominis longè superat, consideremus, nihil tam hyperbolicum dici potest, ad quod non illius vis & potentia penetret. Vide quæ habentur Psalm.139. & 147. Hæc si ob oculos nobis ponamus, plurimum doctrinæ & consolationis prouidentiæ consideratio dabit. Quòd si qui longius vagari & septa transilire cupiunt, ijs Solomonicum illud obijcimus: Qui scrutatur maiestatem, opprimetur à gloria, Prouerb.25. Et Paulinum hoc: Tu quis es, ô homo, qui ex aduerso respondes deo? &c. Vide locum Rom.9. Nec enim absque numine factum est, quòd apostolus, qui in tertium cœlu abreptus, verba audiuit quæ homini eloqui fas non est, in prouidentiæ & prædestinationis causa curiosis quæstionibus respondere dedignans, omnem illam disputationem exclamatione admirationis & stuporis plena concludit: O profunditatem diuitiarum, & sapientiæ & co& cognitionis Dei. Quàm inscrutabilia sunt iudicia eius, & imperuestigabiles viae eius? Quis enim cognouit mentem domini? Aut quis illi fuit à consilijs? Aut quis prior dedit illi, & reddetur ei? Quoniam ex illo, & per illum, & in illum omnia. Ipsi gloria in secula, Amen. Rom.11.
units.tr: Above all, we must look to the end for the sake of which Peter cites the decree of divine providence. Many do not observe this, and at once cry out that we make God the author of evil when we say that all things depend on his counsel and nod. Yet Peter neither excuses Judas nor his accomplices here, nor transfers to God what they impiously and unjustly planned. For since they sinned by voluntary malice, and did not keep before their eyes the counsel of God and the redemption of mankind, but followed the wicked affections of greed, ambition and hatred, the guilt of sin clings to them alone, and they have justly paid its penalties. Peter mentions providence and the divine decree so that he may remedy the stumbling-block of the cross and teach us to judge rightly of Christ and of the whole cause of our redemption. Therefore this same use of providence ought to be set before us as well, so that it may serve both the framing of our faith and life and our consolation in adversity. Thus the Scriptures teach from the decree of providence that salvation depends on the mere grace of God, who before the world was made foreordained Christ Jesus as our Redeemer and chose us in him. See Eph. 1; Rom. 9, 10, 11, etc. And Christ refers us to the same, saying: You did not choose me, but I chose you. Again: Without me you can do nothing. John 15. The consideration of predestination and gratuitous election alone therefore restrains the trust in human righteousness, which is both a pillar and a deadly thing. The same consideration brings the most firm consolation in adversity and in the prosperity of the wicked. For why should we take offence at them, when we know that we live under the protection and defence of divine providence, and that nothing happens to us adverse except by its decree? Therefore Christ refers us to the flowers of the field and the birds of the air, in which the providence of God is most plainly seen, and he comforts the apostles against the scandals of persecution with arguments drawn from this, saying: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? And one of them shall not fall to the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered, etc. Matt. 6 and 10. I acknowledge hyperbole here, if you examine Christ's words by the measure of our reason. But if we consider the wisdom and omnipotence of God, which far surpass every grasp of man, nothing can be said too hyperbolic that his power and might do not reach. See what is found in Ps. 139 and 147. If we set these before our eyes, the consideration of providence will give us much teaching and consolation. But if some wish to wander further and leap over the hedges, we oppose to them that saying of Solomon: He who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. Prov. 25. And this of Paul: Who are you, O man, who answers back to God? etc. See Rom. 9. For it was not without divine will that the apostle, who was caught up into the third heaven and heard words which it is not lawful for a man to utter, declined to answer curious questions about providence and predestination, and concluded that whole discussion with an exclamation full of wonder and amazement: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For of him, and through him, and in him, are all things. To him be glory for ever. Amen. Rom. 11.

units.la: Postremò Petrus Christi Iesu resurrectionem ex mortuis subijcit, his verbis: Quem Deus suscitauit, solutis doloribus mortis, quatenus impossibile erat ipsum ab illa teneri. Medentur etiam haec crucis offendiculo, potius tamen ad redemptionis & salutis nostrae rationem, quam tradere instituit, referri debent. Quia vero de resurrectione Christi plura ipse Petrus dicet in sequentibus, modò breuiores erimus. Inter alia tamen potissimum considerandum venit, quòd post personam Christi describtam, omissis multis alijs, solius mortis & resurrectionis ipsius mentionem facit. Causa haec est, quòd duobus hisce vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio continetur. Morte enim peccati culpam expiauit, quae aliter expiari non poterat. Resurrectione vero mortem, quae peccati poena erat, superauit & illius vires attriuit, iuxta illud prophetae, quod à Paulo citatur: Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Vbi tuus mors aculeus? Vbi tua inferne victoria? Hos.13.1. Cor.15. Idem in praesenti Petrus sentire videtur, quando mortis dolores per Christi resurrectionem solutos esse dicit, eò quòd impossibile esset, ipsum ab ea detineri. Nec enim de corporis doloribus, qui mortem comitantur, exponi potest, cùm illos adhuc acerbissimos esse experiamur. Vires autè mortis solutae sunt, & sublati terrores, quibus olim hominum mentes excruciabat. Peccato enim ceu aculeo vrebatur, cuius poenam Deus hanc constituerat, & pro inde non poterat non terrifica esse, cum peccati poena esset. At quia peccatum Christus sustulit, manifit quidem mors, quae è vita & mundo hoc migramus, sed Christi merito vitae ianua facta est, & proinde credentes amplius terreri nequit, Christo dicente: Qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam, & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit à morte in vitam. Ioh.5. Ideò alibi Apostolus dicit, Christum per mortem suam eum superauisse & aboleuisse, qui mortis habebat imperium. Hebr.2. Quod dici non poterat, nisi mortem resurrectio fuisset subsecuta. Semper igitur duo haec coniungi debent, quod Paulum diligentissimè obseruare videmus, quando Christu propter peccata non stra traditum esse, & propter iustificationem nostri resuscitatum dicit. Rom.4. Item: Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus: Si confessus fueris ore tuo dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quòd Deus illum excitauit à mortuis, saluus eris. Rom.10. Vbi solius quidè resurrectionis meminit, sed illa mortem simul includit, eò quòd illa sine hac considerari non potest. Discamus itaq; Iesum Christum agnoscere, qui cùm verus ab aeterno Deus sit, propter nos homo factus, peccata nostra morte sua expiauit, mortis verò dolores & vires resurrectione gloriosa vicit, & in coelos sublatus pro nobis interce dit. Rom.8. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Peter adds the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, in these words: Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. These also serve as a remedy for the stumbling-block of the cross, though they ought rather to be referred to the account of our redemption and salvation, which he sets out to deliver. Since Peter himself will say more about the resurrection of Christ in what follows, I will be briefer for now. Among other things, however, this above all must be considered: after describing the person of Christ, he mentions only his death and resurrection, leaving out many other things. The reason is that the whole account of our salvation is contained in these two. For by his death he atoned for the guilt of sin, which could not otherwise be atoned for. By his resurrection he overcame death, which was the penalty of sin, and wore down its power, according to the saying of the prophet, which Paul cites: Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your sting? O grave, where is your victory? Hos. 13.1 Cor. 15. Peter seems to think the same here when he says that the pains of death were loosed through Christ's resurrection, because it was not possible for him to be detained by death. For this cannot be explained of the bodily pains that accompany death, since we experience those to be still most bitter. Rather, the power of death was loosed and its terrors taken away, which once tormented men's minds. For it burned with sin as with a sting, and the penalty of which God had appointed to be death, and therefore it could not but be terrifying, since it was the penalty of sin. But because Christ took away sin, death indeed still removes us from this life and world, but by Christ's merit it has become the gate of life, and so it can no longer terrify believers, Christ saying: He who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. John 5. Therefore elsewhere the Apostle says that Christ by his death destroyed and abolished him who had the power of death. Heb. 2. This could not be said unless the resurrection had followed death. These two, therefore, must always be joined together, which we see Paul observing most carefully, when he says that Christ was delivered for our sins and raised again for our justification. Rom. 4. Again: This is the word of faith which we preach: If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Rom. 10. Here he mentions only the resurrection, but it includes death at the same time, because the one cannot be considered without the other. Let us therefore learn to acknowledge Jesus Christ, who, though he is true God from eternity, was made man for our sake, expiated our sins by his death, and by his glorious resurrection overcame the pains and power of death, and having been taken up into heaven intercedes for us. Rom. 8. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XV.
units.tr: HOMILIA XV.

units.la: Dauid enim dicit de ipso: Prouidebam dominum coram me semper, quoniam à dextris est mihi, ne commouear. Propter hoc laetatum est cor meum, & exultauit lingua mea, quin & caro mea requiescet in spe. Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in inferno, nec permittes vt sanctus tuus videat corruptionem. Notas mihi fecisti vias vitae; replebis me laetitia cum facie tua.
units.tr: For David says of him: "I set the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart is glad, and my tongue rejoices; my flesh also shall rest in hope. For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you suffer your Holy One to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness with your presence."

units.la: EXposuit diuus Petrus in besternis praecipuos fidei Christianae articulos, quibus Iesum Christum verum hominem & Deum esse, pro nobis autem mortem subijsse & à mortuis resurrexisse docuit. Omnium verò hic scopus & finis est, vt ipsum promissum humani generis redemptorem esse agnoscamus. Atqui resurrectionis articulus inter Iudaeos multas ob causas incredibilis videripoterat. Nam praeter id, quod humanae rationi dubius videtur, non exiguus erat Sadducaeorum numerus, qui resurrectionem aperte negabant. Et milites à sacerdotibus pecunia corrupti, rumorem falsum sparserant, quo discipulos Christi corpus è sepulchro furtim sustulisse ferebatur. Sed & ipse Christus post resurrectionem non vt prius toti populo sese videndum exhibuerat, sed cum solis discipulis fuerat conuersatus. Quamobrem necesse fuit, articulum hunc & illustrari copiosius & argumentis confirmari solidioribus, maxime cum apostolorum fides omnibus suspecta essēt. Itaq; Petrus ad Dauidis, celeberrimi inter Iudaeos regis & prophetae authoritatem confugit, cuius testimonio ex Psalmo decimo sexto producto, euincit, resurrectionem Christi nec nouam nec incredibilem videri debere, quando ex Dei consilio & decreto haec quoque euenerit, & iam olim prophetarum oraculis fuerit praedicta. Quia vero testimonij huius authoritatem ipse Petrus postea afferet & illud soli Christo conuenire demonstrabit, superuacaneum foret in illius assertione diutius commorari. Sufficere enim nobis debet tanti apostoli authoritas, quam nec Iudaei, quibus illa dicebantur, refellere potuerunt. Illud potius obseruemus, Dauidem haec ita sub Christi persona dicere, ut simul ipse sibi ex illis consolatione petat, quae similiter ad omnes Christi cultores referri debet, quando a membris prosus aliena esse non possunt, quae de capite dicuntur. Diligenti ergo consideratione in hoc loco vt nos conuenit, qui omnem verae pietatis rationem vna cum fructibus tam sancti studij saluberrimis absolutissime comprehendit, inter quos & corporum resurrectio numeratur, quam multis & diligenter diuinus vates illustrat.
units.tr: The blessed Peter, the day before yesterday, set out the chief articles of the Christian faith, teaching that Jesus Christ is true man and true God, that he submitted to death for us, and that he rose from the dead. The aim and purpose of all of this is that we should acknowledge him to be the promised Redeemer of the human race. Yet the article of the resurrection could seem incredible to the Jews for many reasons. Apart from the fact that it seems doubtful to human reason, the Sadducees were not a small number, and they openly denied the resurrection. Moreover, soldiers bribed with money by the priests had spread a false rumour that the disciples of Christ had secretly carried off his body from the tomb. And Christ himself, after the resurrection, had not presented himself to be seen by the whole people as he had before, but had associated only with the disciples. Therefore it was necessary to explain this article more fully and to confirm it with stronger arguments, especially since the faith of the apostles was suspect to everyone. So Peter takes refuge in the authority of David, the most celebrated king and prophet among the Jews. By producing his testimony from Psalm 16, he shows that the resurrection of Christ ought to seem neither new nor incredible, since it has also happened by the counsel and decree of God, and was foretold long ago by the oracles of the prophets. Since Peter himself will afterwards set forth the authority of this testimony and demonstrate that it applies to Christ alone, it would be pointless to linger longer over its proof here. The authority of so great an apostle ought to be enough for us, and the Jews, to whom these words were addressed, could not refute it. Rather let us observe this: David speaks these words in the person of Christ, and at the same time seeks for himself comfort from them, which likewise ought to be referred to all the worshippers of Christ, since what is said of the head cannot be altogether foreign to the members. So it is fitting for us to consider carefully in this place the whole rule of true piety, together with the most wholesome fruits of so holy a pursuit, among which the resurrection of the bodies is also counted, which the divine prophet illustrates in many ways and with care.

units.la: I. Summa pietatis et religionis.
units.tr: I. Summa pietatis et religionis.

units.la: Pietatis & omnem vitae religiosae rationem uno verbo explicat, cum ait: Prouidebam dominum coram me semper, quoniam a dextris mihi est, ne commoueat. Duo autem dicuntur. Primo quid faciat, dicit. Deinde sui instituti aut facti rationem reddit. Quoad primum: Prouidebam dominum coram me semper, inquit: Vel vt Hebraea habent: Posui dominum in conspectu meo, siue ob oculos meos. Hanc ergo vitae suae rationem Christus secutus est, vt dominum semper sibi ob oculos poneret, & coram illo se viuere putaret. Hoc vt rite fiat, duo requiruntur obseruatu dignissima. Alterum est obedientiae studium. Quia Deum ob oculos sibi ponere dicuntur, qui ad ipsius praecepta respiciunt, & sancto Dei timore excitati, illi placere studeunt, quem nihil latere posse nouerunt. De hoc studio ipse Deus loquitur, quando Abrahamum coram se, vel in suo conspectu ambulare iubet. Gene. 17. Alterum fides est, qua in aduersis coflituti ad vnum Deum respicimus, & ab illo vno opem & auxilium siue liberationem expectamus. De hoc alibi Dauid disserit, cum ait: Ecce vt oculi seruorum intenti sunt ad manum dominorum suorum, & vt ancillae oculi ad manum suae dominae respiciunt: sic nostri oculi conuerti sunt ad dominum Deum nostrum, donec nobis benefaciat. Psal. 123. Vtrunq; vero hoc in Iesu Christo facile conspicitur. Tanto enim reuerentia studio patrem Deum obseruauit, vt Paulo teste, obediens factus sit vsque ad mortem, & quidem crucis mortem. Phil. 2. Eorumq; quos pater illi commendauerat, curam tanta diligentia gessit, vt iam mortem aditurus comisisi sibi muneris rationem reddere posset, dicens: Quos dedisti mihi, ego custodiui, & nemo ex eis periit, nisi filius ille perditus. Item: Ego te glorificaui super terram, opus consummaui quod dedisti mihi vt facerem. Ioan. 17. Adhaec tanquam verus homo firma & constanti fide mentis oculos in vnum Deum direxit, quem & vnum inuocauit in aduersis omnibus, & vni pro acceptis beneficijs gratias egit, vt euangelica historia docet. Vere igitur per Dauidem dicere potuit, Posui dominum coram me semper. Ad hoc exemplar vitam suam & actiones omnes instituere debent, quicunq; pro veris Dei cultoribus & filijs haberi volunt. Et haec omnium virtutum vnica causa est, quibus sanctos olim floruisse legimus. Sene ca olim ad vitanda vitia clancularia suadebat, vt quando soli nobiscum versamur, seuerissimum aliquem virum, qualis fuit Scipio, Laelius, Cato, nobis & testem & inspectorem nostrarum rerum adesse censeamus. At quanto plus momenti habebit, si nos Deum cogitemus habere omnium, quae a nobis dicuntur & fiunt, inspectorem? Quia hunc sibi semper ob oculos posuit Ioseph, nec herae illecebris a recti & honesti tramite abduci, nec in carcere & aduersis animo suo frangi potuit. Gen. 39. Eadem omnium aliorum ratio habenda est. Et hic ingens illud discrimen prodit, quo a Dei cultoribus impij differunt. Hi enim quando illis bene est, non Deum ob oculos sibi statuunt, sed (vt Dauid testatur, impia stoliditate excaecati Deum esse negant. Psal. 14. & 36. Quo fit, vt tanquam effrenes equi, omni repagulo sublato, laxis habenis in omne scelus erumpant. Nam vt alibi dicitur, Deum & oculis & auribus carere persuasum habent, quibus illorum flagitia videre & audire possit. Psal. 94. Atqui Deus, quem ipsi sibi ob oculos ponere nolunt, ipsorum oculis sese iratu proponit, & vt Psal. 50. habetur, ipsis in faciem resistit, ac scelerum poenas exigit: rursum illum refugiunt, nec ab eo qui ipsos percutit (qui filiorum Dei mos est, Isa. 9.) liberationem & opem petunt: sed aliquandiu proprijs viribus Dei iudicio oblectantur, quibus vbi nihil profici vident, ad creaturas conuerti illas inuocant, vel tota mente consternati in desperationis barathrum praecipites ruunt. Extant infinita eiusmodi bo-minum exempla, quorum hic apud nos visus esse debet, ut Deum nobis ob oculos ponere discamus, cui nos et vitam nostram approbare, et in eodem omnem fiduciam sitam habere debemus.
units.tr: In one word he explains the whole of piety and the entire religious manner of life when he says: "I set the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, that I should not be moved." Two things are said here. First he says what he does; then he gives the reason for his purpose or action. As to the first: "I set the Lord always before me," he says. Or, as the Hebrew texts have it: "I have placed the Lord before my eyes, or in my sight." Christ therefore followed this rule of life, to keep the Lord always before his eyes, and to think that he lives in his presence. For this to be done properly, two things are required that are most worthy of notice. The first is zeal for obedience. For those are said to set God before their eyes who look to his commands, and, roused by a holy fear of God, strive to please him, knowing that nothing can be hidden from him. God himself speaks of this zeal when he bids Abraham walk before him, or in his sight (Gen. 17). The second is faith, by which, placed in adversity, we look to the one God and expect help and deliverance from him alone. David discourses on this elsewhere when he says: "Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he shows us mercy" (Ps. 123). Both of these are easily seen in Jesus Christ. For he observed the Father with such reverent zeal that, as Paul witnesses, he became obedient even to death, indeed to the death of the cross (Phil. 2). And he cared for those whom the Father had committed to him with such diligence that, about to face death, he could render an account of the trust committed to him, saying: "Those whom you gave me I have kept, and none of them has perished, except that son of perdition." Again: "I have glorified you on the earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do" (John 17). Moreover, as a true man, with a firm and constant faith he directed the eyes of his mind to the one God, whom he called upon alone in all adversities, and to whom alone he gave thanks for the benefits received, as the gospel history teaches. Truly, then, he could say through David: "I have set the Lord before me always." All who wish to be regarded as true worshippers and children of God ought to shape their lives and all their actions by this pattern. And this is the sole cause of all the virtues by which we read that the saints flourished of old. Seneca once advised, to avoid secret vices, that when we are alone with ourselves we should think that some most stern man, such as Scipio, Laelius or Cato, is present as a witness and overseer of our affairs. But how much more weight will it have if we think that God is the overseer of all that is said and done by us? Joseph set this before his eyes, and so he could be drawn from the path of right and honest conduct neither by the allurements of his mistress, nor was he broken in spirit by prison and adversity (Gen. 39). The same rule must be observed in all others. And here appears that great difference by which the impious differ from the worshippers of God. For when things go well for them, they do not set God before their eyes, but (as David testifies) blinded by impious stupidity they deny that God exists (Ps. 14 and 36). Hence it comes about that, like unbridled horses, with every restraint removed and the reins loose, they burst into every crime. For, as is said elsewhere, they are persuaded that God lacks eyes and ears by which he could see and hear their wickedness (Ps. 94). Yet God, whom they refuse to set before their eyes, shows himself to their eyes in anger, and, as is said in Psalm 50, resists them to their face and exacts the penalty of their crimes. Again they flee from him, and do not seek deliverance and help from him who strikes them (which is the custom of the sons of God, Isa. 9). But for a while they take pleasure in their own strength and in the judgment of God; and when they see that nothing is gained by these, they turn to creatures and call upon them, or, utterly dismayed in mind, they rush headlong into the abyss of despair. There are countless examples of men of this kind, and they ought to be set before us here, so that we may learn to set God before our eyes, to whom we ought to commend both our life and ourselves, and in whom we ought to place all our trust.

units.la: Sed causam sui instituti tam sancti et religiosi Christus indicat, addens: Quoniam a dextris mihi est, ne commovear. Ideo (inquit) Deum mihi ob oculos pono, quia mihi semper adest, sive illud ego faciam, sive non faciam. Si observem illum, astat mihi auxiliator, ne villis terroribus commoveor, Sin negligam, astat inspector aliorum omnium et olim iudex erit seuerissimus. Eadem causa cultores quoq; Christi, ut Deum ob oculos habeant, moventur, quam etiam ipsi non raro profitentur. Huc enim pertinet, quod Davidem et sui similes dixisse legimus: Dominus lux mea et salus mea, a quo nam timerem? Dominus robur vitae meae, a quo expauescerem? Psal. 27. Deus nobis suffugium et robur est, premente necessitate auxilium praestantissimum. Idcirco nihil timebimus, etiamsi loco moveatur terra, et nutent montes siti in medio mari, etc. Psal. 46. Item: Deus est petra mea, et salus mea, ipse arx mea sublimis, ideo non labascam, etc. Psal. 62. Nemo autem hanc inanem verborum iactantiam esse existimet. Dei enim promissionibus et experientia siue exemplis quotidianis haec fan&ctorum fiducia nititur. Dei siquidem verbum est: In die tribulationis tuae invoca me, et liberabo te. Psal. 50. Item: Quoniam mihi adhaeret, eruam eum, et superiorem illum faciam: nam agnouit nomen meum. Me inuocabit, ideo ei respondebo, adero ei in afflictione, eripiam cum, et glorificabo eum. Psal. 91. Confirmantur promissiones istae exemplis plurimis, qualia in sacris literis Iosephi, Davidis, Danielis et sociorum eius, Susannae, Ezechiae et multorum aliorum leguntur. At veteribus opus non est, quando ipsi quotidie promissionum Dei veritatem experimur. Licet enim multa huius saeculi tribulationes sint, ex omnibus tamen Deus suos eripit, et quasi labascentes nos suffulturus dexter nobis astat, nec tentari finit vltra quam ferre possumus. 1. Cor. 10. Et quod David fatetur, pro eius cogitatio num et tentationum nostrarum, suis consolationibus animas nostras recreat. Psal. 94. Et haec illa pio rum securitas est, longe alia quam quae impios infoelicere facit, dum propter opes et mundi gloriam se extra omnem telum iactum consistere arbitrantur. Quos falli necesse est, eo quod omnis caro faenum est, et gloria carnis flos agri, etc. Isaiae. 40.
units.tr: But Christ indicates the reason for his so holy and religious purpose, adding: "because he is at my right hand, that I should not be moved." That is, he says, I set God before my eyes because he is always present to me, whether I do this or not. If I observe him, he stands by me as a helper, so that I am not moved by any terrors; if I neglect him, he stands by as the overseer of all others and will one day be the most severe judge. The worshippers of Christ are moved by the same reason to have God before their eyes, and they often profess it too. To this belongs what we read that David and those like him have said: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom then shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" (Ps. 27). God is our refuge and strength, the most excellent help in pressing need. Therefore we will fear nothing, even if the earth should be moved from its place, and the mountains should totter in the midst of the sea, etc. (Ps. 46). Likewise: "God is my rock and my salvation, he is my lofty fortress; therefore I shall not fall," etc. (Ps. 62). Let no one think that this is empty boasting of words. This confidence of the saints rests on the promises of God and on experience, or the daily examples. For this is the word of God: "In the day of your trouble call upon me, and I will deliver you" (Ps. 50). Again: "Because he has cleaved to me, I will deliver him, and I will make him high; for he has known my name. He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I will be with him in affliction, I will rescue him and glorify him" (Ps. 91). These promises are confirmed by very many examples, such as are read in the sacred writings of Joseph, David, Daniel and his companions, Susanna, Hezekiah and many others. But there is no need for the old examples, since we ourselves daily experience the truth of God's promises. For although there are many tribulations in this age, God nevertheless delivers his people from all of them, and, as one about to uphold us when we are falling, he stands at our right hand, nor does he allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear (1 Cor. 10). And as David confesses, in the multitude of our thoughts and temptations he refreshes our souls with his consolations (Ps. 94). This is the security of the godly, far different from that which makes the wicked unhappy, when they think that they stand beyond every missile because of their wealth and the glory of the world. They must be deceived, because "all flesh is grass, and the glory of flesh is the flower of the field," etc. (Isa. 40).

units.la: Caeterum pergit Christus, spiritu suo per Davidem loquens, et studij huius eximios fructus recenset. Propter hoc (inquit) laetatum est cor meum, et exultauit lingua mea, quin et caro mea requiescet in spe. Tria dicuntur quae singula vniuersas mundi opes longe superant, quae (ut capimus) et in Christo et in membris ipsius considerare oportet. Primo gaudij meminit, et quidem de gaudio cordis loquitur, ut illud verum, solidum et stabile esse doceat. Hoc ipsum enim intelligit, quod postea discipulis pollicetur, cum ait: Nunc quidem maerore habetis, sed iterum videbo vos, et gaudebit cor vestrum, et gaudiu vestrum nemo tollit a vobis. Ioan. 16. De eode Paulus loquens, Christianos semper gaudere iubet. 1. Thess. 6. Phil. 4. In primis vero gaudij causam obseruare decet. Propter hoc (ait) laetatum est cor meum: quia videlicet dominus mihi a dextris est. In domino igitur gaudent fideles. Laetantur et gaudent impij etiam, adeoq; prae gaudio frequenter insaniunt. Id vero vel propter opes faciunt, et honores et noxias carnis voluptates, vel etiam propter scelera, ut de nonnullis Solomon admonet. Proverb. 1. At illorum gaudia nec syncera sunt nec certa, sed luctu grauissimo terminantur. Iam olim enim in illos Christi sententia lata est, quae in euangelio habetur: Vae vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia lugebitis et flebitis. Luc. 6. At piorum laetitia siue gaudium, quia domino nititur, euerti et mutari non potest. Nam in afflictionibus quoq; gloriantur et gaudent, eo quod se in omnibus superiores fore sciunt, per eum qui ipsos in Iesu Christo dilexit. Vide Rom. 5. et 8. cap.
units.tr: Moreover, Christ goes on, speaking through David by his Spirit, and lists the notable fruits of this devotion: "For this reason my heart has rejoiced, and my tongue has exulted; indeed my flesh will rest in hope." Three things are named, each of which far surpasses all the riches of the world, and which we must, as we understand it, consider both in Christ and in his members. First, he mentions joy, and speaks of joy of the heart, to teach that it is true, solid and stable. He means the same thing that he later promises the disciples: "Now indeed you have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one takes your joy from you" (John 16). Paul, speaking of the same thing, bids Christians always to rejoice (1 Thess. 5; Phil. 4). Above all, we ought to note the cause of the joy. "For this reason," he says, "my heart has rejoiced": namely, because the Lord is at my right hand. The faithful rejoice in the Lord. The impious also rejoice and exult, and often in their gladness they go mad. They do so because of riches, honours and the harmful pleasures of the flesh, or even because of their crimes, as Solomon warns concerning some (Prov. 1). But their joys are neither sincere nor certain, and they end in the most grievous sorrow. Indeed, long ago Christ's sentence was pronounced against them, as it is in the Gospel: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep" (Luke 6). But the gladness or joy of the godly, because it rests on the Lord, cannot be overturned or changed. For even in afflictions they glory and rejoice, because they know that they will be more than conquerors in all things, through him who loved them in Jesus Christ. See Rom. 5 and chapter 8.

units.la: Secundus fructus pietatis est linguae exultatio. Exprimitur per hanc gaudij magnitudo, quae ne mente quidem contineri potest, sed per linguam erumpit. Exultat enim haec in pijs, non quidem leui et scurrili affectu et procacibus dictis, sicut in impijs est videre: sed pia gratulatione, qua Dei nomen, et illius beneficia celebrat. Et sane magna haec piorum gloria est, quod nouis quotidie beneficijs Deo sese obstringi sentiunt, propter quae nomen ipsius praedicent. Gloriantur principum fauore multi, et hoc sibi potissimum laudi ducunt, si principum beneficentiam iusto aliquo titulo praedicare possint. At maior multo Christiani hominis gloria est, qui Dei bonitatem praedicandi causas quotidie nouas et grauissimas inuenit. Atqui in hoc non postrema nostrorum officiorum pars versatur.
units.tr: The second fruit of piety is the exultation of the tongue. Through it the greatness of the joy is expressed, which cannot even be contained in the mind but breaks out through the tongue. For this exultation is found in the godly, not indeed in a light and buffoonish mood or with shameless words, as may be seen in the impious, but in a pious thanksgiving, by which they celebrate the name of God and his benefits. Truly this is a great glory of the godly: that they feel themselves bound to God by new benefits every day, for which they may proclaim his name. Many glory in the favour of princes, and count it their chief praise if they can proclaim the kindness of princes on some just ground. But far greater is the glory of a Christian man, who finds new and most weighty reasons every day to proclaim the goodness of God. And indeed, no small part of our duties lies in this.

units.la: III. Pietatis fructus. Gaudium.
units.tr: III. The fruit of piety. Joy.

units.la: Lingua exultatio. Vult enim a nobis praedicari Deus, nec aliud pro beneficentia sua a nobis exigit, cum nostri minimè indigeat. Premente aduersitate(inquit)invoca me: & cùm te eripio, gloriam meam celebra. Psal. 50. Hinc illa sanctorum vota sunt, quibus carmina & hymnos Deo pollicentur. Christus certè alibi quoq; per Davidem hoc unum Deo patri suo vovet, dicens: Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in media congregatione laudabo te. Dete est laus mea in concione magna, vota mea coram timentibus ipsum persoluam. Psal. 22. Et David, cùm Dei opem petijset, in eandem sententiam dicit: Laudabo nomen Dei cum cantico, & extollam illud celebri laude. Gratius id erit domino, quàm si bovem offeram cornubus & unguis praestantem. Psal. 69. Quò & illa piorum vox apud prophetam referri debet: Aufer omnem iniquitatem & accipe bonum, & persoluemus iuuencos labiorum nostrorum. Hos. 14. Potest hic obiter cognosci nostrorum temporum infelicitas. Quia enim paucissimi sunt, quorum lingua exultet ad gratiarum actionem & nominis divini praeconium, rarum quoq; esse constat gaudium illud verum, quod ex fide & obedientia sancto studio concipitur. Quo argumento firmissimè concluditur, fidei quoq; & pietatis studium esse rarissimum.
units.tr: Exultation of the tongue. For God wishes to be proclaimed by us, and he requires nothing else from us in return for his kindness, since he has no need of us at all. "In the time of trouble," he says, "call upon me; and when I deliver you, you shall glorify me" (Ps. 50). Hence come those vows of the saints, by which they promise songs and hymns to God. Christ, certainly, elsewhere too, through David, vows this one thing to his Father: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you. From you is my praise in the great assembly; my vows I will pay before those who fear him" (Ps. 22). And David, when he had asked for God's help, says to the same effect: "I will praise the name of God with a song, and will extol it with a celebrated praise. This will be more pleasing to the Lord than if I offered an ox that has horns and hooves" (Ps. 69). To this also the voice of the godly in the prophet should be referred: "Take away all iniquity and receive what is good, and we will render the calves of our lips" (Hos. 14). Here, in passing, the unhappiness of our times may be recognised. For since there are very few whose tongue exults in thanksgiving and in the proclaiming of the divine name, it is plainly also rare that true joy, which is conceived from faith and obedience in holy zeal. From this argument it is most firmly concluded that the zeal for faith and piety is also very rare.

units.la: Tertius pietatis fructus est: Caro mea requiescet in spe. De morte autem loquitur, quam sibi laetam & omnis molestiae expertem pollicetur. Interim absolutissima felicitas hic adumbratur, quae nec morte (quae ultima linea rerum a poeta dicitur) interturbari possit. Morte, quae plerunq; inopinato obrepit, turbantur omnia, quibus infelix mundus felicitatem metitur. Ad huius mentionem divites consternantur, ambitiosi trepidant, voluptuarij tremunt, & fortissimi quiq; metuunt. At Christus hac gloriatur, ut quiete spei maximae plena. Eadem omnium membrorum Christi est ratio, quibus hoc prae caeteris hominibus datum est, ut mortem contemnere, imò morte gaudere possint: cuius conditionem omnem propheta hoc loco proprijssimè explicat. Primò enim solius carnis vel corporis mentionem facit, offendens, morti in animam, quae potior hominis pars est, nihil licere. Illa enim e corpore migrans, in vitam aeternam abit, ut alias diximus. Quae causa est, quòd Paulus cupit dissolui, & esse cum Christo. Phil. 1. Deinde de carne aut corpore loquens, illi nequaquam interitum minatur, sed ait: Caro mea requiescet in spe. Quietem ergo carni promittit, quam in morte tutissimam pij inuenerunt. Scatet malorum & periculorum examinibus totus vitae nostrae curcus. Undique labores imminent. Curae & solicitudines nunquam non novae exoriuntur. Deniq; breuis haec vita infinitis & continuis aerumnarum procellis absq; vlla intermissione exagitari solet: ut verè propheta dicat: Dies annorum nostrorum anni sunt septuaginta, aut ad summum octoginta: iam praestantissimum horum labor est & molestia. Psal. 90. Et alibi scriptura hominem ad laborem, ut auem ad volandum nasci testatur. Iob. 5. At in morte quies est, & qui hanc subijt, vniuersam & laborum & curarum palaestram, morbos item & instabiles fortunae vicissitudines euasit.
