Ne quis verò non alia nobis in morte quietem parari putaret, quàm quae etiam iumentis & reliquis animantibus paratur, quibus vita nulla post hanc reliqua est, docet nostram carnem in spe quiescere. Resurrectionis verò spem intelligit, quae & certa est, & consolationis verae causa vnica. Spem enim hanc nobis Deus facit, qui se eorum quoq; Deum nominat, qui è vita hac migrauerunt, quod de Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo Christus admonuit. Matth. 22. Et in prophetis resurrectionem fore constanter pollicetur. Vide Ezech 37. Dan. 12. Isa. 26. & 68. &c. De eadem Christus non semel disserit in euangelio. Veniet hora (inquit) in qua omnes, qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem meam, & prodibunt, &c. Iohan. 5. Plura vide Matth. 25. Iohan. 11. &c. De hac spe Iob loquens, ait: Scio quòd vindex meus viuit, & nouissimo tempore adhibebit suam vim pulueri. Vbi verò circumdederint hoc mea cute, spectabo Deum è carne mea. Quem ego mihi contemplabor, & oculi mei videbunt, & non alius: quod vnicum est meum desiderium. Iob. 19. Nec dubium est, quin hac spe animati sancti martyres, dolores omnes tanta cum animi constantia superauerint. Quare non temere Paulus ex eadem consolationis argumenta in funeribus desumere iubet. 1. Thess. 4.
units.tr: The third fruit of piety is: "my flesh will rest in hope." He speaks of death, which he promises will be joyful and free from all trouble. Meanwhile, the most complete happiness is here foreshadowed, which cannot be disturbed even by death (which the poet calls the last boundary of things). At death, which usually creeps upon us unexpectedly, everything in which the unhappy world measures happiness is thrown into confusion. At its mention the rich are dismayed, the ambitious tremble, the pleasure-seekers shake, and all the most courageous fear. But Christ glories in this, as one full of the greatest hope and rest. The same is the case for all the members of Christ, to whom it has been given above other men to despise death, indeed to rejoice in death; and the prophet in this place explains the whole condition of this most precisely. For first he mentions only the flesh or body, showing that death has no power over the soul, which is the nobler part of man. For the soul, passing out of the body, goes into eternal life, as we have said elsewhere. This is why Paul desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. 1). Then, speaking of the flesh or body, he does not threaten it with destruction at all, but says: "my flesh will rest in hope." He therefore promises rest to the flesh, which the godly find most secure in death. The whole course of our life abounds with swarms of evils and dangers. Labours press in on every side; cares and anxieties always arise anew. Finally, this brief life is wont to be tossed about without any interruption by the endless and continual storms of troubles, so that the prophet truly says: "The days of our years are seventy years, or at most eighty; and even the best of these is labour and sorrow" (Ps. 90). And elsewhere Scripture testifies that man is born for toil as the bird is born to fly (Job 5). But in death there is rest, and he who has undergone it has escaped the whole arena of labours and cares, as well as diseases and the unstable changes of fortune. Lest anyone think that no other rest is prepared for us in death than that which is prepared even for beasts and the other living creatures, to whom there is no life left after this one, he teaches that our flesh rests in hope. By hope he means the hope of the resurrection, which is both certain and the sole cause of true consolation. For God gives us this hope, he who calls himself the God of those also who have departed from this life, as Christ reminded us concerning Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt. 22). And in the prophets he constantly promises that there will be a resurrection. See Ezek. 37; Dan. 12; Isa. 26 and 68, etc. Christ speaks of the same more than once in the Gospel: "The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear my voice and will come forth," etc. (John 5). See more at Matt. 25; John 11, etc. Speaking of this hope, Job says: "I know that my redeemer lives, and at the last time he will exert his power over the dust. And when they have thus surrounded my skin, I shall behold God from my flesh; whom I shall contemplate for myself, and my eyes shall see, and not another; this is my one desire" (Job 19). And there is no doubt that the holy martyrs, animated by this hope, overcame all their pains with such constancy of mind. Therefore Paul rightly bids us draw arguments of consolation from the same at funerals (1 Thess. 4).

units.la: Porrò quia in resurrectionis mentionem propheta incidit, hanc sub Christi persona loqui pergens, plenius illustrat. Ait enim: Quoniam non derelinques animam meam in inferno, nec permittes ut sanctus tuus videat corruptionem. Notas mihi fecisti vias vitae, replebis me laetitia cum facie tua. Insunt his nonnulla, quae de solo Christo intelligi possunt, quemadmodum in sequentibus Petrus admonet. Quia tamen nostrae resurrectionis certitudo à Christi resurrectione dependet, quem idcirco Paulus eorum qui obdormierunt primitias vocat (1. Cor. 15.) omnium eorum, quae in Christi resurrectione contingerunt, fructus & effectus ad nos pertinent. Prodest ergo diligenter in illorum, quae hic dicuntur, consideratione versari. Nam ut Christi resurrectionem explicant, ita quid nobis saepe randum fit docent, & nostrae quoque resurrectionis modum & ordinem, una cum beatitudine vera, quae hanc sequetur, depingunt.
units.tr: Moreover, since the prophet has come to mention the resurrection, he goes on to speak in the person of Christ and illustrates it more fully. For he says: "For you will not leave my soul in hell, nor will you suffer your Holy One to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness with your countenance." Some of these words can be understood of Christ alone, as Peter points out in what follows. Yet because the certainty of our resurrection depends on Christ's resurrection, whom Paul therefore calls "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Cor. 15), all the fruits and effects of what happened in Christ's resurrection pertain to us. It is therefore profitable to dwell diligently on what is said here. For just as they explain Christ's resurrection, so they also teach what must often be done by us, and they portray the manner and order of our resurrection too, together with the true blessedness that will follow it.

units.la: Primo ait: Non derelinques animam meam in inferno. Inferi Hebraeis nunc pro sepulchro dicuntur, nunc pro mortuis & defunctis: Quo sensu Iosephi fratres dicunt: Deducent servi tui canitiem patris nostri cum tristitia ad inferum sive inferos. Sensus ergo verborum est, animam Christi non manssuram diutius a corpore separatam in loco ubi beatorum animae collectae sunt, sed brevi ad corpus reditypam. Intellexerunt nonnulli haec de Christi ad inferos descensu, quem inter fidei articulos profitemur. Quorum sententia mihi non omnino reijcienda videtur. Disputatum est de hoc multis apud veteres, & nostro quoque seculo prodierunt fanatici homines, qui animam Christi apud inferos damnatorum cruciatus subiisse dicerent. Sed confutat hos ipse Christus, qui latroni iam moriturus dicit: Hodie mecum eris in paradiso. Luc. 23. Adhaec animam exhalaturus, illam non ad inferos ablegat, sed in manus patris sui commendat. Praeterea constat, in ara crucis ipsum pro peccatis totius mundi perlitauisse, & plene absoluisse nostrae redemptionis negotium, ut vere dixerit: Consummatum est. Iohan. 19. Minime ergo admittendum, ut animam Christi post exitum e corpore aliquid passam esse dicamus. Contristata fuit & mortis terrores sensit ad oliveti montem, quem admodum ipse fatetur. Eadem irati patris vultum & iram, qua in peccata persequitur, sensisse videtur, quando in cruce clamavit: Deus meus, Deus meus, cur me dereliquisti? At quia haec passio peccatis nostris expiandis sufficiens fuit, absurdum est & parum Christianum, quicquam aliud illi addere. Simplicissime ergo Christi ad inferos descensus intelligi posse videtur, si vel vere mortuum dicamus, & ad mortuos collectum, vel meritum mortis ipsius ad eos quoque penetrasse, qui ante illum a prima mundi origine mortui fuerant. Quod D. Petrus alibi innuere videtur, quando Christum defunctis, qui in carcere erant, praedicavisse dicit. 1. Pet. 3. & 4. Seruiuit hoc ad ampliorem consolationem ijs, qui promissionibus de ipso datis crediderant: auxit vero impiorum poenas & cruciatus, qui ipsius promissiones improbe contempserant. Interim ad nos quoque eorum, quae hic dicuntur, fructus extenditur. Ut enim Christi anima non derelicta est: ita nostrae animae in Dei tutela & manu sunt (Sap. 3. cap.) & ad corpora nouissimo die reuertentur.
units.tr: First he says: "You will not leave my soul in hell." "Hell" (inferi) is used by the Hebrews sometimes for the grave, sometimes for the dead and departed. In this sense the brothers of Joseph say: "Your servants will bring down the grey hairs of our father with sorrow to the lower world, or to the underworld." The sense of the words, then, is that Christ's soul would not remain separated from the body for long in the place where the souls of the blessed are gathered, but would soon return to the body. Some have understood these words of Christ's descent to the dead, which we profess among the articles of faith. Their opinion does not seem to me to be altogether to be rejected. The matter was debated by many among the ancients, and in our own age there have appeared fanatical men who said that the soul of Christ underwent the torments of the damned in hell. But Christ himself refutes them, when he says to the thief, about to die: "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23). Moreover, when about to breathe out his soul, he did not send it away to hell, but commended it into the hands of his Father. Furthermore, it is agreed that on the altar of the cross he himself made atonement for the sins of the whole world and fully completed the business of our redemption, so that he truly said: "It is finished" (John 19). It is by no means to be admitted, therefore, that we should say that the soul of Christ suffered anything after its departure from the body. It was saddened and felt the terrors of death at the Mount of Olives, as he himself confesses. He seems also to have felt the face and wrath of the angry Father, which pursues sins, when on the cross he cried out: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" But because this suffering was sufficient to expiate our sins, it is absurd and little Christian to add anything else to it. Therefore the descent of Christ to the dead seems to be understood most simply if we say either that he truly died and was gathered among the dead, or that the merit of his death also reached those who had died before him from the beginning of the world. St Peter seems to hint at this elsewhere, when he says that Christ preached to the dead who were in prison (1 Pet. 3 and 4). This served for the greater consolation of those who had believed the promises given concerning him, but it increased the punishments and torments of the impious, who had wickedly scorned his promises. Meanwhile, the fruit of what is said here extends to us as well. For just as the soul of Christ was not forsaken, so our souls are in God's keeping and hand (Wisdom 3), and they will return to the bodies on the last day.

units.la: Secundo igitur subiungit: Nec dabis, ut sanctus tuus videat corruptionem. Pertinet hoc aliquo modo ad prioris expositionem. Interim ut de anima dixerat, ita quid de corpore futurum sit, indicat. Negat hoc corruptionem visurum esse. Quod de solius Christi corpore intelligendum esse, postea multis docebit. Et sane omnium nostrum corpora corruptioni subiacere constat, quia Dei sententiam impleri oportet: Pulvis es, & in pulverem reuerteris. Gen. 3. Nec iuuant hominum artes, qui aromatum condimentis magnatum corpora conseruare studient. At Christi corpus, quia illucescente tertio a morte die rususcitatum est, corruptionem ne videre quidem, nedum subire potuit, sed gloriosum & omni corruptibilitate liberatum resurrexit. Asseritur autem hic etiam nostrorum corporum resurrectio. Licet enim illa corrumpantur & in pulverem abeant, Christi tamen virtute, vbi nouissimus dies aduenerit, restituentur, ut supra docuimus. Oportet enim nostra haec mortalia corpora (ut Paulus monet) corpori Christi glorioso conformia fieri. Phil. 3. Nec impossibile erit ei, e pulueribus corpora nostra excitare, qui initio hominem e luto finxit, imo omnem huius mundi machinam e nihilo produxit. Possunt hic etiam obiter refutari, qui corpus Christi in resurrectione exinanitum fuisse & veri corporis conditiones depositsse dicunt, quales sunt, palpabile esse, certo loco contineri, de loco in locum moueri, &c. Si enim corruptionem nullam vidit, quomodo ea amittere potuit, sine quibus corporis veritas constare non potest?
units.tr: Secondly, then, he adds: "Nor will you let your holy one see corruption." This relates in some way to the explanation of the previous point. He has said what will become of the soul, and now he indicates what will become of the body. He denies that it will see corruption. He will later show with many proofs that this is to be understood of Christ's body alone. And it is certain that the bodies of all of us are subject to corruption, because God's sentence must be fulfilled: "Dust you are, and to dust you shall return." Gen. 3. The arts of men do not help, who try to preserve the bodies of great men with spices and seasonings. But Christ's body, since it rose again on the third day as the day dawned after his death, could not even see corruption, let alone undergo it; it rose glorious and freed from all corruptibility. This passage also asserts the resurrection of our bodies. For although those bodies are corrupted and turn to dust, yet by the power of Christ they will be restored when the last day has come, as we have taught above. For these our mortal bodies must (as Paul admonishes) be made conformable to the glorious body of Christ. Phil. 3. Nor will it be impossible for him to raise our bodies from the dust, he who at the beginning formed man from clay, indeed who brought the whole machinery of this world out of nothing. Here, too, those can be refuted in passing who say that the body of Christ was emptied in the resurrection and laid aside the conditions of a true body, such as being palpable, being contained in a certain place, being moved from place to place, and so on. For if he saw no corruption, how could he have lost those things without which the reality of a body cannot stand?

units.la: Tertio ait: Notas mihi fecisti vias vitae. Id est, in vitam eduxisti me. Et dextera tua aeternaque ibi loquitur, quae sola hoc nomine digna est. Resurrectionem ergo vita aeterna sequitur, quam ut Christus assecutus est, ita & nos in illo assequemur. Est autem obseruatu dignum, quod via vitae Christo manifestata fuisse dicitur. Adam peccando mortem meruit, & paradisi ostium, postquam ille eiectus fuit, igneo gladio muniuit Deus, ne eo reuersus de arbore vitae manducaret. Gen. 3. Significauit
units.tr: Thirdly he says: "You have made known to me the ways of life." That is, you have led me out into life. "And at your right hand there are pleasures forever," which alone is worthy of this name. Therefore resurrection is followed by eternal life, which Christ attained, and in him we too shall attain it. It is worth noting that the way of life is said to have been made manifest to Christ. Adam, by sinning, merited death, and after he was cast out, God guarded the gate of paradise with a fiery sword, so that he could not return and eat from the tree of life. Gen. 3. By this God signified

units.la: { } ea re Deus, homines suis viribus ad vitam penetrare non posse. In Christo autem via vitae manifestata & reclusa est, ut quemadmodum per unum hominem peccatum in mundum transiit, & per peccatum mors, ita per unum Christum iustitia & vita nobis restaurata haberetur. Vide Rom.5. Ideo Apostolus de Christo loquens, vitam nobis manifestatam fuisse dicit. 1.Iohan. 1. Et Christus passus panis vitae, lux & via vitae, adeoque ipsa resurrectio & vita dicitur. Ioan.6.14.1. & 11. &c. Est ergo hic amplissimus fructus, quem Christi resurrectio peperit, quod ad caelestem & aeternam vitam resuscitabimur, non ad terrenam & mortalem, qualem nunc viuimus, quae mors potius quam vita dici meretur. Huius autem ratio in uno Christo habetur, quem qui aspernati fuerint, vitam consequi non poterunt, ipso dicente: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Iohan.14.
units.tr: by this fact that men cannot reach life by their own strength. But in Christ the way of life has been made manifest and opened, so that just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so through the one Christ righteousness and life might be restored to us. See Rom. 5. Therefore the Apostle, speaking of Christ, says that life was made manifest to us. 1 John 1. And Christ, who suffered, is called the bread of life, the light and the way of life, and even the resurrection and life itself. John 6, 14, 11, etc. So this is the very ample fruit which Christ's resurrection has produced: that we shall be raised to heavenly and eternal life, not to the earthly and mortal life we now live, which deserves to be called death rather than life. The reason for this is found in Christ alone, and those who spurn him will not be able to obtain life, since he himself says: "No one comes to the Father except through me." John 14.

units.la: Ultimo loco addit, Replebis me laetitia cum vultu tuo. Explicatur hic vitae aeternae & caelestis condicio, quae longe alia est quam praesentis huius, quam in terris agimus. Haec enim, ut supra diximus, laborum, dolorum & curarum turbis scatet. Aeterna autem laetitiae & exultationis plena est. Ibi enim abstergèt Deus omnem lachrymam ab oculis suorum fidelium. Et mors ultra non erit, neque luctus, neque clamor, neque dolor. Apoc.21. At his sublatis, nihil nisi gaudium superesse poterit. Ideo Christus servo fideli se dicturum ait: Intra in gaudium domini tui. Matth.25. Hoc gaudium alibi Christus gloriam vocat, quam apud patrem, priusquam mundus hic conderetur, se habuisse testatur. Ioan.17. In eam gloriam & laetitiam Christi humanitas subuecta est, ut & ipsa eiusdem regni consors sit, quod iuxta diuinam naturam ab aeterno Christus possederat. Ita enim olim promissum illi fuisse legimus, domino dicente: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Psal.110. Continetur itaque his fidei articulus, quo Christum in caelos conscendisse, & ad dexteram patris sui omnipotentis considere fatemur. Interim haec ad nos quoque pertinere putabimus, qui per fidem Christo insiti & illius membra facti sumus. Nec enim fieri potest, ut a capite membra avellantur. Et Christi promissio est: Ubi ego sum, illic & minister meus erit. Iohan.12. Hanc pluribus exponens alibi, ait: In domo patris mei mansiones multae sunt. Quod si secus esset, dixissem vobis. Vado paraturus vobis locum. Et si abiero ad parandum vobis locum, iterum veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum, ut ubi sum ego & vos sitis. Ioan.14. Imo iam mortem adituros, cum de sua voluntate quasi testamento disponit, dicit: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, illi sint mecum. Ioan.17. Quae ne de solis apostolis intelligerentur, ingenue testatur se non pro illis tantum, sed pro omnibus orare, qui apostolorum sermone edocti in illum credant. Nemini ergo dubium esse potest, quin & nos gaudio & laetitia replendi simus in aeterna illa & caelesti vita, quae corporum resurrectionem sequetur.
units.tr: Lastly he adds: "You will fill me with joy with your face." Here the condition of eternal and heavenly life is explained, which is far different from the present life we lead on earth. For this life, as we said above, teems with the crowds of labours, pains and cares. But eternal life is full of gladness and exultation. For there God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his faithful, and there will be no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain. Rev. 21. With these removed, nothing but joy can remain. Therefore Christ says that he will say to the faithful servant: "Enter into the joy of your lord." Matt. 25. Elsewhere Christ calls this joy glory, which he testifies he had with the Father before this world was founded. John 17. Into that glory and joy the humanity of Christ has been raised, so that it too may share in that kingdom which Christ had possessed from eternity according to his divine nature. For we read that this was promised to him of old, when the Lord said: "Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." Ps. 110. Thus this article of faith is contained in these words, by which we confess that Christ ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of his almighty Father. Meanwhile we shall think that these things pertain to us as well, who by faith have been grafted into Christ and made his members. For it cannot happen that members are torn away from the head. And Christ's promise is: "Where I am, there my minister will be too." John 12. Expounding this more fully elsewhere, he says: "In my Father's house there are many mansions. If it were otherwise, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you. And if I go to prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you may be too." John 14. Indeed, when he was about to die and disposed of his will as if it were a testament, he said: "Father, those whom you have given me, I want them to be with me where I am." John 17. Lest these words be understood of the apostles alone, he openly testifies that he prays not only for them but for all who, taught by the apostles' word, believe in him. Therefore there can be no doubt that we too shall be filled with joy and gladness in that eternal and heavenly life which will follow the resurrection of the body.

units.la: Non praetermittendum vero est, quod gaudij huius causam efficientem indicat faciem Dei. Intelligitur hic benignus & propitius Dei vultus, quo nos propter Christum clementer aspicit, ut nulla veteris irae, quam peccatis meruéramus, vestigia appareant. Nam ut Solomone teste, serenus regis vultus vita est, & gratioso ipsius intuitu malum omne dissipatur (Prouerb.16. & 20.) ita in Dei conspectu omnis veri gaudij satietas habetur credentibus. Quo mihi Christus respicere videtur, cum dicit: Beati mundo corde, quoniam illi Deum videbunt. Matth.5. Ideo & pij orant: Ostende nobis faciem tuam, & salui erimus. Psal.80. Unde colligi potest, quanta illorum miseria futura sit, qui a Dei facie repulsi in exteriores tenebras eijcientur. Et hactenus quidem uniuersam pietatis & beatitudinis verae rationem paucis verbis propheta descripsit. Discamus nos Deum ob oculos nobis ponere, illum reuereri obedienter, & ipsi uni fidere. Oriatur ex hoc studio verum animi gaudium, & novae indies causae offerentur celebrandi Dei beneficentiam, & e vita migrantes laeta spe requiescemus. Sequetur autem beata resurrectio, qua & animae corporibus restituentur, & in vitam veram asserti coram Dei facie omni laetitia replebimur, una cum Iesu Christo fratre & coharede nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It must not be passed over that he indicates the face of God as the efficient cause of this joy. Here is meant the kindly and gracious countenance of God, with which he looks upon us mercifully for Christ's sake, so that no traces of the old wrath, which we had deserved by our sins, appear. For, as Solomon testifies, the serene face of the king is life, and by his favourable look all evil is scattered (Prov. 16 and 20); so in the sight of God is found the fullness of all true joy for believers. To this Christ seems to refer when he says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Matt. 5. So also the godly pray: Show us your face, and we shall be saved. Ps. 80. From this it can be gathered how great the misery of those will be who, cast out from the face of God, shall be thrown into outer darkness. And so far, indeed, the prophet has described in a few words the whole account of true godliness and blessedness. Let us learn to set God before our eyes, to revere him obediently, and to trust in him alone. From this zeal there arises true joy of mind, and fresh causes for celebrating God's goodness are offered daily, and departing from this life we shall rest in happy hope. Then will follow the blessed resurrection, in which both souls shall be restored to bodies, and, restored to true life, we shall be filled with all joy before the face of God, together with Jesus Christ, our brother and fellow heir: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVI.
units.tr: Homily XVI.

units.la: Viri fratres, licet liberè dicere apud vos de patriarcha Dauid, quòd & mortuus est, & sepultus, & sepulchrum eius apud nos est usque in hunc diem. Propheta igitur cùm esset, & sciret, quòd iureiurando iurasset sibi Deus, futurum ut de fructu lumbi ipsius, quoad carnem, Christus exoriretur, riretur, ac sederet super thronum eius: praescius locutus est de resurrectione Christi, quod non derelicta sit in inferno anima eius, neque caro eius viderit corruptionem. Hunc Iesum suscitavit deus, cuius omnes nos sumus testes: Dextera igitur dei exaltatus, & promissione spiritus sancti accepta a patre, effudit hoc, quod nunc vos videtis & auditis. Neque enim David ascendit in coelos, sed ipse ait: Dixit Dominus domino meo, sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Certò sciat ergo tota domus Israel, quod dominum & eundem Christum fecerit deus hunc Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis.
units.tr: Brothers, I may speak freely to you about the patriarch David: that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is among us to this day. Since he was a prophet, and knew that God had sworn an oath to him that Christ would arise from the fruit of his loins according to the flesh, and would sit upon his throne, he spoke in advance concerning the resurrection of Christ, that his soul would not be left in hell, nor would his flesh see corruption. "God raised up this Jesus, of whom we all are witnesses. Therefore, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out what you now see and hear. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ."

units.la: Quoniam vniuersa nostrae salutis ratio resurrectione corporum quasi absolvitur, in ea afferenda scripturae omnes crebrò versantur. Quae causa est, quod & Petrus de Christi resurrectione, e qua nostram dependere constat, tam diligenter disserit. Nec enim contentus est simplici illius praedicatione, sed omnem illius rationem & ordinem ex Psalmo decimo sexto describit, cuius etiam authoritate ad illam afferendam utitur. Cui tractationi & praesens hic locus seruit. Primò enim praeoccupatione aduersariorum obiectionem praeueniens, probat Psalmum hunc de Christo exponi debere. Deinde ad Christum redit, & in illo impletum esse docet quicquid à Davide praedictum sit. Tandem graui obtestatione sermoni suo fidem imponit.
units.tr: Since the whole account of our salvation is, as it were, completed by the resurrection of the body, the Scriptures everywhere dwell on establishing it. This is why Peter also discourses so carefully on the resurrection of Christ, on which, as is plain, ours depends. Nor is he content with a bare proclamation of it; he sets out the whole reasoning and order of it from Psalm 16, and he uses that Psalm's authority to establish it. The present passage serves this same discussion. First, by forestalling the objection of opponents, he proves that this Psalm must be explained of Christ. Then he returns to Christ and teaches that whatever was foretold by David was fulfilled in him. Finally, by a solemn adjuration he puts a seal of faith on his speech.

units.la: Quoad Psalmi testimonium, duo agit Petrus. Primò illud de Davide nullo pacto intelligi posse docet. Deinde Davidem de Christo vaticinari probat. Quia vero magna erat apud Iudaeos Davidis authoritas, praefatiuncula auditorum animas praemollit, ne quid contemptius de illo dicere videatur, adeoque illos ipsos eorum, quae dicere instituit, testes citat. Licet mihi (inquit) de patriarcha Davide apud vos verba facere, quos rerum Davidis non ignaros, & oraculorum ipsius studiosos esse scio. Quia autem quibusdam videri poterat, de seipso dixisse quae modo citauimus, penitius res omnis inspicienda erit, & illos sua opinione falli, euidentissimè patebit. Nam de quodam Davides loquitur, cuius anima non mansura sit inter defunctorum animas, & qui corpore suo nullam sit subiturus corruptionem. Atqui Davidem mortuum esse constat, & illius sepulchrum hodie apud nos extat, in quo corpus ipsius iuxta viam vniuersae terrae (sicuti ipse de seipso testatus est, 1. Reg. 2.) consumptum, in pulverem abijt. Quare de illo Psalmi verba nequaquam intelligi debent. Licet vero firma & indubitata sit huius argumenti veritas, non tamen sufficere poterat, nisi simul de Christo exponendum esse probaret. Quare addit: Propheta cum esset David, & sciret, quod iureiurando iuraret sibi deus, futurum ut de fructu lumbi ipsius, quod carnem Christus exoriretur, ac sederet super thronum eius, praescius locutus est, &c. Quibus verbis docere vult, nemini mirum videri debere, quod de Christo, promisso saluatore, ista Davides praedixerit. Vtitur autem duplici argumento. Primum à persona Davidis eiusque officio sumptum est. Prophetam enim fuisse, omnibus constabat. Atqui prophetarum hoc commune officium fuit, ut per Christi spiritum ipsius mysteria, maximè verò mortem & resurrectionem eius inuestigarent, quemadmodum Petrus alibi diligentius ad monet. 1. Pet. 1. Item 2. Pet. 1. Et si prophetarum libros euoluas, in singulis clara & perspicua de Christo & regno ipsius vaticinia inuenire licebit, quod ipsum Christum agnouisse legimus, quando postea resurrectionem suam ait: Necesse fuit impleri omnia, quae scripta sunt in lege Moysis, in Prophetis & Psalmis de me, &c. Luc. 24. Quid ergo mirum videtur, si David, qui propheta erat, de Christo vaticinatus est? Alterum argumentum dei promissiones complectitur. Deus iureiurando fidem suam Davidi obstrinxerat, quod ex ipsius lumbis enasciturus esset promissus ille saluator, qui regni sui thronum confirmaret & aeternum teneret. Debuit ergo David & facillime potuit promissi Messiae mysteria exponere, de quo peculiares promissiones acceperat. Et de eodem, quae modo adducta sunt, intelligi debere palam est, quando nec de Davide, nec de quoquam alio exponi possunt. Pertinent autem ad huius loci explicationem promissiones olim Davidi exhibitae. Inter quas primus locus est debetur, quam Nathan propheta, quando de templo extruendo consultabat, domino suggerente nuntiauit his verbis: Quum exacti fuerint dies tui, dormieris cum patribus tuis, excitabo semen tuum post te, quod egredietur de utero tuo, regnumque eius firmabo. Is extruet domum nomini meo, & ego confirmabo folium regni eius in sempiternum, &c. 2. Sam. 7. Quem locum de Solomone intelligi non posse, facile cernitur, cum is viuente adhuc Dauide natus & regno inauguratus fit, nec perpetuum fuerit regni illius folium. In Christo Iesu autem impleta est haec promissio, qui ex Dauids familia longo post tempore carnem assumpsit, domum dei, id est, ecclesiam, ex omnibus nationibus & populis constituit, & cuius regnum (sicut angelus testatur) finem nullum habet. Luc. 1. Accessit autem promissioni huic iuramentum, ne quid dubij superesset, cuius hic quoq; Petrus meminit, & quod in scripturis expressum habetur. Huc enim pertinet quod Psal. 89. legitur: Semel per sanctitatem meam iuraui, haudquaquam Dauidem fefellero. Semen eius in aeternum erit, solium eius coram me ut Sol perstabit. Firmum ut Luna manebit, quae est certus in aethere testis, &c. Et rursum: Iurauit dominus Dauidi veritatem, neq; discedet ab ea: De fructu ventris tui solio tuo imponam. Psal. 132. Nec inepte huc referetur, quod sacerdotium quoq; Christi iureiurando Dei confirmatum fuisse legimus. Nam de hoc Dauid vaticinans ait: Iurauit dominus, nec poenitebit eum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum iuxta ordinem Melchisedech. Psalm. 110. Tot ergo tantis q; promissionibus dei cum Dauides instructus fuerit, facile constat, de Messia vero Dauidis filio exponi debere, quaecunq; sublimiora & magis augusta sunt, quam ut in ipsum Dauidem aut reliquos ipsius filios competere possint. Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, duo obseruanda erunt.
units.tr: As to the testimony of the Psalm, Peter does two things. First he teaches that it cannot in any way be understood of David. Then he proves that David prophesied of Christ. Because the authority of David was great among the Jews, he softens his hearers' minds with a short preface, so that he may not seem to say anything disparaging about him, and so he cites those very hearers as witnesses of what he is about to say. "It is permitted to me," he says, "to speak to you about the patriarch David, whom I know you are not ignorant of David's affairs and are keen students of his oracles." But because some might think that he was speaking of himself in the words we have just quoted, the whole matter must be examined more closely, and it will be most evident that they are mistaken in their opinion. For David speaks of someone whose soul will not remain among the souls of the dead, and who will undergo no corruption in his body. Yet it is plain that David is dead, and his sepulchre is still visible among us today, in which his body, having gone the way of all the earth (as he himself testified of himself, 1 Kings 2), was consumed and turned to dust. Therefore the words of the Psalm can by no means be understood of him. But although the truth of this argument is firm and indubitable, it could not have been enough unless he also proved that it must be explained of Christ. So he adds: "Since David was a prophet, and knew that God had sworn an oath to him, that from the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, Christ would arise and sit upon his throne, he spoke by foresight," and so on. By these words he wishes to show that no one should think it strange that David foretold these things about Christ, the promised Saviour. He uses a twofold argument. The first is taken from the person of David and his office. For it was known to all that he was a prophet. But the common office of the prophets was to inquire, by the Spirit of Christ, into his mysteries, and above all into his death and resurrection, as Peter elsewhere more carefully reminds us (1 Pet. 1; likewise 2 Pet. 1). And if you go through the books of the prophets, you will find in each clear and plain prophecies about Christ and his kingdom, which we read that Christ himself recognised when afterwards he spoke of his resurrection: "All things must be fulfilled which are written in the law of Moses, in the Prophets and the Psalms, concerning me," etc. (Luke 24). Why then should it seem strange if David, who was a prophet, prophesied of Christ? The second argument concerns God's promises. God had bound his faith to David by an oath, that that promised Saviour would be born of his loins, who would confirm the throne of his kingdom and hold it for ever. David ought therefore, and could most easily, to set forth the mysteries of the promised Messiah, of whom he had received particular promises. And it is plain that what has been quoted must be understood of the same Messiah, since it cannot be explained of David or of anyone else. Now the promises once given to David bear on the explanation of this passage. Among them the first place belongs to the one which Nathan the prophet announced to him, when he was consulting about building the temple, at the Lord's suggestion, in these words: "When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever," etc. (2 Sam. 7). That this passage cannot be understood of Solomon is easily seen, since he was born and anointed king while David was still alive, and that throne was not perpetual. But this promise was fulfilled in Christ Jesus, who long afterwards took flesh from the family of David, established the house of God, that is the Church, out of all nations and peoples, and whose kingdom, as the angel testifies, has no end (Luke 1). To this promise an oath was added, so that nothing of doubt might remain; Peter also mentions this, and it is expressly stated in the Scriptures. For to this belongs what is read in Psalm 89: "Once by my holiness have I sworn; I will not deceive David. His seed shall be for ever, his throne shall stand before me like the sun. It shall remain firm like the moon, which is a faithful witness in the sky," etc. And again: "The Lord has sworn to David in truth, and he will not turn from it: I will set upon your throne the fruit of your body" (Psalm 132). Nor is it out of place to refer here what we read about the priesthood of Christ also being confirmed by the oath of God. For David, prophesying of this, says: "The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110). Therefore, since David was furnished with so many and such great promises of God, it is easily established that whatever is loftier and more majestic than can apply to David himself or his other sons must be explained of the Messiah, the son of David. Before we depart from this point, two things must be observed.

units.la: Primo docemur, veteribus Christi mysteria non omnino ignota fuisse, & quidem ea cumprimis quae eius mortem & resurrectionem attinent. Fatemur equidem plenam huius cognitionem praefinito tempori fuisse reseruatam. Interim vniuersam Christi notitiam prisci illis negare, nimis temerarium est, quando dominum de Abrahamo testari scimus, quod exultarit videre diem eius, quod viderit & gauisus sit. Iohan. 8. Et ut modo diximus, idem Mosem & prophetas de suis mysteriis prophetauisse dicit. Posset hoc & promissionum veterum authoritate & libris prophetarum abunde probari, si opus esset. Caeterum illud didicisse sufficiat, quod ad nos quoq; veteris Testamenti libri pertineant, quod multi hodie nimis audacter negare consueuerunt. Atqui constat, illis Christi cognitionem tradi. Eosdem ergo ad nos pertinere fatendum erit, nisi Christi cognitionem, quasi nihil ad nos pertinentem, reijcere libeat. Quanto rectius Paulus, qui ait: Quaecunq; scripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus. Rom. 15. Adde his, quae idem in posteriori ad Timoth. cap. 3. admonet.
units.tr: First, we are taught that the mysteries of Christ were not entirely unknown to the ancients, and especially those which concern his death and resurrection. We grant indeed that the full knowledge of these was reserved for a set time. Yet to deny the ancients all knowledge of Christ is too rash, since we know that the Lord testified of Abraham that he rejoiced to see his day, that he saw it and was glad (John 8). And, as we have just said, the same Lord says that Moses and the prophets prophesied of his mysteries. This could be sufficiently proved, if it were needed, both by the authority of the ancient promises and by the books of the prophets. But it is enough to have learned this, that the books of the Old Testament also pertain to us, something which many today are accustomed to deny all too boldly. Yet it is certain that knowledge of Christ is handed down in those books. Therefore we must confess that they pertain to us as well, unless we prefer to reject the knowledge of Christ as if it had nothing to do with us. How much more rightly does Paul say: "Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope" (Rom. 15). Add to these what the same apostle admonishes in his second letter to Timothy, chapter 3.

units.la: Deinde obseruatu dignissimum est, quod Deus nostrae redemptionis & salutis causam, quae vno Christo continetur, iurisiurandi religione interposita confirmare & stabilire dignatus est. Atqui ea est dictorum dei fides & authoritas, ut omnem iuramentorum authoritatem longe superent. Demittit tamen se ad nostrum captum supremus ille deus, ne quid in salutis causa dubij nobis relinquatur. Nec Dauidi soli se ad hunc modum obstrinxit, verumetiam Abrahamo, ut Paulus Hebr. 6. obseruauit. Illi enim dicitur: Per memetipsum iuraui, dicit dominus: quoniam rem hanc fecisti, nec pepercisti filio tuo, &c. Vide locum Genes. 22. Instauratur postea huius iurisiurandi veritas, quando Isaaco dicit dominus: Confirmabo iuramentum, quod iuraui Abrahamo patri tuo, &c. Gen. 26. Et huc cumprimis referri debent feriae illae & solennes dei patris conteststiones, quibus Iesum Christum filium suum dilectum esse caelitus testatur, cuius nomine nobis reconciliatus fit. Matth. 3. & 17. Et ipse filius toties suam fidem iureiurando nobis obstringit, quoties illud euangelicum repetit, Amen amen dico vobis &c. Seruiunt haec vehementer nostrae institutioni & consolationi. Docemur enim Christum magni facere, nec aspernari salutem, quae ipsius merito acquisita est, & ex eiusdem iussu per euangelij praedicationem nobis offertur. Olim quidem (ut Paulus admonet) qui Mosis legem transgressi fuerant, absq; misericordia sub duobus aut tribus testibus moriebantur. Quanto igitur peioribus afficietur supplicijs, qui filium dei conculcarit, & sanguinem noui Testamenti prophanum duxerit? &c. Hebr. 10. Et Ioannes apostolus de eadem re nos serio admonens, ait: Si testimonium hominum accipimus, testimonium dei maius est, quod testificatus est de filio suo. Qui credit in filium dei, habet testimonium in seipso. Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum, quia non credidit in testimonium, quod deus testificatus est de filio suo, &c. 1. Iohan. 5. Atqui quid atrocius dici poterat, quam deum mendacij insimulare, qui & veritas aeterna est, & cui tam facile est fuit contemptum vlcisci? Porro non minus consolationis haec ipsa nobis afferunt, qua in tentationum palaestra nos sustentemus. mus. Conatur saepe in dubium vocare Satan salutis nostrae certitudinem. At si cogitemus, hanc dei iuramento confirmatam & obsignatam esse, fides nostra nutare non poterit. Verax enim est deus, & verbum eius manet in aeternum.
units.tr: Next, it is most worthy of notice that God was pleased to confirm and establish the cause of our redemption and salvation, which is contained in Christ alone, by interposing the solemnity of an oath. Yet the faith and authority of God's words is such that they far surpass the authority of all oaths. Still, that supreme God condescends to our capacity, so that nothing doubtful may be left to us in the cause of salvation. Nor did he bind himself in this way to David alone, but also to Abraham, as Paul observed in Hebrews 6. For to him it is said: "By myself have I sworn, saith the Lord, because thou hast done this thing and hast not spared thy son," etc. See the passage in Genesis 22. Afterwards the truth of this oath is renewed, when the Lord says to Isaac: "I will perform the oath which I swore to Abraham thy father," etc. Genesis 26. To this should especially be referred those solemn testimonies of God the Father from heaven, by which he bears witness that Jesus Christ is his beloved Son, in whose name we are reconciled. Matthew 3 and 17. And the Son himself binds his own faith to us by an oath as often as he repeats that gospel formula, "Verily, verily, I say unto you," etc. These things serve greatly for our instruction and comfort. For we are taught to value Christ, and not to despise the salvation which was acquired by his merit and is offered to us by the preaching of the gospel at his command. Formerly (as Paul warns) those who had transgressed the law of Moses died without mercy under two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, then, will they deserve who have trampled underfoot the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant unclean? etc. Hebrews 10. And the apostle John, earnestly admonishing us on this same matter, says: "If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, which he has testified concerning his Son. He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. He who does not believe God makes him a liar, because he has not believed the testimony which God has testified concerning his Son," etc. 1 John 5. Now what more atrocious could be said than to accuse of lying God, who is eternal truth, and to whom it is so easy to avenge contempt? Moreover, these same things bring us no less comfort, by which we may sustain ourselves in the wrestling-ground of temptations. Satan often tries to call into doubt the certainty of our salvation. But if we consider that this is confirmed and sealed by God's oath, our faith will not be able to waver. For God is true, and his word endures for ever.

units.la: Sed redit ad Christi causam Petrus, & in hoc impleta esse docet, quacunq; de Messia olim a Dauide praedicta sint. Scopus omnium est, ut Iesum Nazarenum, promissum illum mundi saluatorem esse intelligant. Ex multis vero, quae adduci poterant, solius resurrectionis & ascensionis meminit, eo quod duo haec instituto sufficiebant, & praesenti causae & concertationi (quae ob spiritus sancti missionem exorta erat) cum primis seruiebant. Nos de singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: But Peter returns to the cause of Christ, and teaches that in this have been fulfilled all the things that David formerly foretold concerning the Messiah. The aim of all is that they understand Jesus of Nazareth to be that promised Saviour of the world. Of the many things that could be adduced, however, he mentions only the resurrection and the ascension, because these two were sufficient for his present purpose and especially served the present dispute (which had arisen from the sending of the Holy Spirit). We shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Resurrectionis articulum repetit, ut Christum Iesum promissum saluatorem esse probet, quo argumento Paulus quoq; Rom. 1. cap. v. sus est. Potest autem ex Petri verbis eiusmodi argumentumconstituì: De Messia olim a Dauide praedictum est, quod nec anima eius cum aliis defunctorum animabus diutius mansura esset, nec corpus corruptionem subiturum, eo quod deus illum excitaturus esset a mortuis. Illud vero in Iesu Nazareno praestitum & impletum est. Iesum ergo hunc Messiam & saluatorem esse constat. De maiori nullum reliquabat dubium. In minori itaque probanda Petrus versatur, cuius veritatem communi omnium apostolorum testimonio asserit. Huius rei (inquit) nos omnes sumus testes. Nec facile ab iis, qui saniorum mentis erant, testes hi contemni aut reici poterat, in quibus tam luculenta erant spiritus sancti & divinae operationis indicia. Ex resurrectione vero, Christum saluatorem esse frequenter probant apostoli, quia per mortem nobis dominabatur Satan, quam peccatum inuexerat. Nec Christum pro saluatore tuto agnoscere potuissemus, nisi illum mortis vires superauisse nobis certo constitisset.
units.tr: He repeats the article of the resurrection in order to prove that Jesus Christ is the promised Saviour; Paul also used this argument, Romans 1 (verse 4). The argument can be framed from Peter's words in this way: it was foretold of the Messiah by David that his soul would not remain long with the other souls of the dead, nor would his body undergo corruption, because God would raise him from the dead. But this has been performed and fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth. Therefore it is certain that this Jesus is the Messiah and Saviour. Concerning the major premise there was no remaining doubt. Peter therefore labours to prove the minor, and asserts its truth by the common testimony of all the apostles. "Of this," he says, "we are all witnesses." Nor could these witnesses easily be despised or rejected by those who were of sound mind, in whom there were such clear signs of the Holy Spirit and of divine working. Now the apostles frequently prove from the resurrection that Christ is Saviour, because Satan ruled over us through death, which sin had brought in. Nor could we have acknowledged Christ safely as Saviour unless it had been made certain to us that he had overcome the power of death.

units.la: Interim non ofcitanter nobis consideranda est Petri & reliquorum apostolorum fides atque integritas. Hos sibi testes delegerat dominus, ut primo cap. dictum est. Testium igitur officio bona fide & intrepide funguntur, non vlla alicuius periculi ratione habita. Nam in Hierosolymorum urbe & in concione frequentissima, Iesum diuina virtute a mortuis resuscitatum esse testantur. Atqui in eadem urbe longe alius rumor iam ante sparsus erat. Milites enim, ut Matthaei vltimo habetur, a sacerdotibus pecunia corrupti, discipulos noctu corpus Iesu furto subtulisse testati fuerant. His in publico contradicere quam periculosum fuerit, quiuis aestimare potest, quando & sacerdotum & Pilati Romani praesidis authoritate defendebantur. Sed vincunt periculi timorem fide in Christum apostoli, & suum exemplum omnibus imitandum relinquunt, quibuscunque testimonium Iesu Christi creditum est.
units.tr: Meanwhile, we must consider with care the faith and integrity of Peter and the other apostles. The Lord had chosen them as his witnesses, as was said in the first chapter. They therefore discharge the duty of witnesses in good faith and fearlessly, taking no account of any danger. For in the city of Jerusalem, and in a most crowded assembly, they testify that Jesus was raised from the dead by divine power. Yet in that same city a quite different rumour had already been spread. For the soldiers, as is recorded in the last chapter of Matthew, bribed with money by the priests, had testified that the disciples had stolen the body of Jesus by night. Anyone can judge how dangerous it would have been to contradict this in public, when it was defended by the authority both of the priests and of Pilate the Roman governor. But the apostles overcome the fear of danger by faith in Christ, and leave their own example to be imitated by all to whom the testimony of Jesus Christ has been entrusted.

units.la: Alterum argumentum, quo Iesum promissum Messiam esse probat, ab ascensione desumit. Et hoc propter illos maxime vti videtur, quibus ridiculum videri poterat, saluatorem praedicare eum qui nuspiam inter homines compareret. Quo vitio hodie quoque laborant, quibus non aliter saluator esse creditur, nisi se nobis corporaliter praesentem exhibeat. Sic vero loquitur Petrus: Dextera dei exaltatus, & promissione spiritus sancti, id est, promisso spiritu accepto a patre, effudit hoc, quod nunc vos videtis & auditis. Obscuriora sunt quae dicuntur, quia propter breuitatem non illico videri potest, quorsum referri debeant. Facile autem tollitur obscuritas, si Dauidis oraculum, quod ille de Christi ascensione protulit, interseras. Ex hoc enim & ijs quae Petrus dicit, argumentum integrum constitues hoc pacto: Dauid Christum non modo a mortuis resurrecturum esse praedixit, verumetiam in caelos ascensurum esse docuit. Ita enim ait Psal. 67. Ascendisti in altum, captiuam duxisti captiuitatem, & dedisti dona hominibus. Hoc ipsum vero, ut & prius illud, in Iesu impletum est. Is enim postquam resurrexit, dextera potenti dei exaltatus, nobis videntibus in caelum ascendit, & impetratum a deo patre spiritum super nos effudit, qui dona haec linguarum, sicuti videtis & auditis, in nobis operatus est. Eundem ergo hunc Messiam esse constat. Porro neminem offendere debet, quod Christus a patre spiritum accepisse dicitur, quasi ipse non pari cum hoc potestate fit praeditus. Petrus enim pro ratione humanitatis Christi loquitur, secundum quam ipse loquens, patrem se maiorem esse fatetur (Ioan. 10.) cum alibi se & patrem vnum esse pronunciet, nimirum diuinitatis respectu. Et ipse Christus nodum hunc pulchre dissecat, de spiritus sancti missione ad hunc modum differens: Ille me glorificabit, quia de meo accipiet, & annunciabit vobis. Omnia quaecunque habet pater, mea sunt. Propterea dixi quod de meo accipiet, &c. Ioan. 16. Item: Cum venerit paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis à patre, spiritus veritatis, qui à patre procedit, ille testimonium perhibebit, &c. Iohan.15. Caeterum ne quis, quae de ascensione Christi dicuntur, de Dauide exponenda esse putaret, vel in dubium vocaret, alio testimonio occurrit, dicens: Neq; enim Dauid ascendit in coelos, sed ipse ait: Dixit dominus domino meo, sede à dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Bipertitum est argumentum hoc. Primò, Dauid non ascendit in coelos. Ergo haec de Dauide non debent intelligi. Dauidem vero in coelum ascendisse negat, non quòd damnatorum numero illum ascribendum putet, sed de corpore illius loquitur, quod (vt supra diximus) in pulverem & terram abijt. Quoad animam, ratum manet illud Christi: Qui credit in me, habet vitam aeternam, & in iudicium non veniet, sed transiuit de morte in vitam. Iohan. 5. Alterum argumentum Dauidis testimonio nititur, qui ipse haec non de seipso, sed Christo, ex se nascendo, intelligi debere docet. Nam Psal.110. ait: Dixit dominus domino meo, &c. Qui locus tam clarus & irrefragabilis est, vt Christus ipse illo contra scribas vti voluerit. Matth.22. Interim Petri exemplo docemur scripturas aliorum locorum collatione exponi debere, ne vni alicui temere insistentes multis aliis contradicamus, quae multorum errorum in ecclesia causa est.
units.tr: The second argument, by which he proves that Jesus is the promised Messiah, he takes from the ascension. And this seems to be used especially for those to whom it might appear ridiculous to preach as Saviour one who appeared nowhere among men. Men still suffer from this fault today, who believe that no one is a saviour unless he presents himself to us bodily. But Peter speaks thus: "Exalted by the right hand of God, and by the promise of the Holy Spirit, that is, having received the promised Spirit from the Father, he has poured out this which you now see and hear." What is said is somewhat obscure, because on account of its brevity it cannot at once be seen to what it should be referred. The obscurity, however, is easily removed if you insert the oracle of David which he uttered concerning Christ's ascension. From this, together with what Peter says, you will construct the whole argument in this way: David foretold that Christ would not only rise again from the dead, but also taught that he would ascend into heaven. For he says in Psalm 68: "Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive, and hast given gifts to men." This very thing, as well as the former, has been fulfilled in Jesus. For he, after he rose again, exalted by the mighty right hand of God, ascended into heaven in our sight, and, having obtained the Spirit from God the Father, poured him out upon us, who has worked in us these gifts of tongues, as you see and hear. Therefore it is certain that this is the same Messiah. Moreover, no one ought to be offended that Christ is said to have received the Spirit from the Father, as if he were not himself endowed with equal power. For Peter speaks according to the human nature of Christ, according to which he, speaking, confesses that the Father is greater than he (John 10), whereas elsewhere he declares that he and the Father are one, plainly with respect to his divinity. And Christ himself neatly cuts this knot, discussing the sending of the Holy Spirit in this manner: "He will glorify me, because he will receive of mine and will declare it to you. All things whatsoever the Father has are mine. Therefore I said that he will receive of mine," etc. John 16. Likewise: "When the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness," etc. John 15. But lest anyone should think that what is said of Christ's ascension must be explained of David, or should call it into doubt, he meets this with another testimony, saying: "For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says: The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet." This argument has two parts. First, David did not ascend into heaven; therefore these things must not be understood of David. Now he denies that David ascended into heaven, not because he thinks David is to be counted among the damned, but he speaks of David's body, which (as we said above) passed into dust and earth. As to his soul, that saying of Christ remains firm: "He who believes in me has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life," John 5. The second argument rests on the testimony of David, who himself teaches that these things must be understood not of himself but of Christ, who was to be born from him. For in Psalm 110 he says: "The Lord said to my Lord," etc. This passage is so clear and irrefutable that Christ himself wished to use it against the scribes, Matthew 22. Meanwhile, by Peter's example we are taught that the Scriptures ought to be expounded by comparing other passages, lest, by rashly insisting on one single text, we contradict many others, which has been the cause of many errors in the Church.

units.la: Obseruabis autem, quòd ascensioni Christi in coelos spiritus sancti missionem coniungit. Prudenter hoc & admodum opportunè facit. Sic enim docet, Christum Iesum, licet corpus è mundo subduxerit, minimè tamen contemni debere: quia non ideo ecclesiae curam abiecit, sed eidem spiritu suo adest, per quem efficacius multò in suorum animis operatur, quàm olim cum corpore suo nobis conuersaretur. Quare discipulis dicit, expedire nobis, vt mundo relicto ad patrem abeat. Sic enim spiritui sancto locum dari, quem habere non possumus, quoad corporali praesentiae inhaeremus. Iohan.16. Et sanè postquam Christus in ara crucis corpus pro mundi vita tradidit, & eiusdem resuscitatione mortem deuicit, nihil in terris agendum corpori restabat. Restabat autem, vt gloriosa ascensione coeli portas, quas peccati culpa nobis clauserat, reseraret, & pignus fieret in coelis, quo de coelorum haereditate & possessione certiores redderemur. Ideo illud in coelum subuexit dominus, & ad patris dextram collocauit, nobis verò in terra agentibus vicariam (vt Tertulliani verbo vtar) vim spiritus sancti misit. Cuius operatione nos per semen immortale verbi dei regenerat, vt filij dei efficiamur. Iohan.3.1. Pet.1. Per eundem nos docet & consolatur. Iohan.14.&15. Idem ille salutis nostrae pignus est. 2.Cor.1.&5. Ephes.1. Illo animati, clamamus, Abba pater. Rom.8. Galat.4. Per illum fit, vt & Christus in nobis maneat, & nos in illo. Quae omnia cum in nobis spiritu suo efficacissimè operetur Christus, non est quòd de corporis absentia quicquam queramur, quod nostrae salutis causa in coelis resident. Et qui illius praesentiam expetunt, illudq; sibi in terris monstrari cupiunt, admonitionum Christi parum mihi memores videntur, quae Matth.24.cap.leguntur, &c.
units.tr: You will notice that he joins the sending of the Holy Spirit to Christ's ascension into heaven. He does this wisely and very appropriately. For he teaches that Christ Jesus, although he withdrew his body from the world, must by no means be despised; because he did not therefore abandon the care of the Church, but is present to it by his Spirit, through whom he works far more effectively in the minds of his people than when he lived with us in his body of old. Therefore he tells the disciples that it is expedient for them that he leave the world and go to the Father. For thus room is made for the Holy Spirit, whom we cannot have so long as we cling to his bodily presence. John 16. And indeed, after Christ gave up his body on the altar of the cross for the life of the world, and by his resurrection overcame death, there was nothing left for the body to do on earth. What remained was that by his glorious ascension he should open the gates of heaven, which the guilt of sin had closed against us, and become a pledge in heaven, by which we might be made more certain of the inheritance and possession of heaven. So the Lord carried that body up into heaven and set it at the right hand of the Father, and for us who are still working on earth he sent the vicarious power (to use Tertullian's word) of the Holy Spirit. By his working he regenerates us through the immortal seed of God's word, so that we become children of God. John 3; 1 Pet. 1. Through the same Spirit he teaches and comforts us. John 14 and 15. The same Spirit is the pledge of our salvation. 2 Cor. 1 and 5; Eph. 1. Animated by him we cry, Abba, Father. Rom. 8; Gal. 4. Through him it comes about that Christ abides in us and we in him. Since Christ works all these things in us most effectively by his Spirit, there is no reason for us to complain about the absence of his body, which remains in heaven for the sake of our salvation. And those who long for his presence and wish to see it displayed to them on earth seem to me to have little regard for the warnings of Christ, which are read in Matthew 24, etc.

units.la: Simul verò Christi regnum Dauidis verbis Petrus describit, in cuius consideratione nos frequenter versari, multùm prodest. Primum hic locum tenet, quòd Christum dextra dei exaltatum, & in coelum ascendisse dicit. Coeleste ergo illius regnum est, non de hoc mundo, quemadmodum ipse coram Pilato fatetur. Iohan. 18. Data quidem est illi omnis potestas in coelo & in terra: non autem more principum huius seculi regnat, in quorum regnis incertas & instabiles rerum vices oboriri necesse est, cum incerta & inani carnis potentia imperium obtinere studeant. Simul verò admonemur, in regno Christi minimè quaerenda esse mundi bona, qualia sunt opes, honores, voluptates, amicitiae mundi, & quaecunq; aliasunt huius generis. Aeterna & coelestia sunt, quae in Christo deus pater exhibuit. In illorum igitur studio nos totos occupari oportet. Deinde, Christum ad dextram dei considere docet, qua locutione & certus beatitudinis locus designatur, & aequalis cum patre regni siue imperij potestas. Pater enim diligit filium, & omnia illi in manum tradidit. Iohan.3. Idem quoque vt omnes filium honorent praecipit, quemadmodum honorant patrem. Iohan.5. Quò & sedendi verbum referri debet, quo & Christi regnantis maiestas, & regni ipsius inconcussa stabilitas, potentia exprimitur. Postremò, omnes hostes subijciendos dicit, vt scabellum pedibus Christi praebeant. Victoriosus ergo rex Christus est, & inuictus suorum inimicorum domitor. Princeps & caput horum Satan est, cui prima salutis promissio per Christum mortem iam olim minata est, deo dicente: Semen mulieris caput serpentis conteret. Gene.3. Et Christus illum iam iudicatum & eiectum esse docet. Iohan.16. & 12. Simili ratione peccatum deuictum esse constat. Deus enim (vt Paulus ait) misso filio suo peccatum condemnauit, per peccatum, id est, per hostiam filij sui, in ara crucis pro peccato oblatam, peccati reatum aboleuit, illudque ne noceret posthac, armis & viribus exuit. Roman. 8. At peccato abolito mortem quoque deuictam esse constat, quae non alio quam peccati aculeo contra nos pugnabat. 1. Corinth. 15. Vere ergo per Christum vniuersa inferorum potestas deuicta est. Idem vero & mundum vincit, & tyrannos cum tota impiorum cohorte. Quia iam olim a patre decretum legimus, vt qui salutari filij verbo gubernari nolunt, ferreo eiusdem sceptro comminuantur penitus. Psalm. 2. Nec desunt prisci & nostri seculi exempla, quibus docemur quam splendidos de hostibus ecclesiae suae triumphos Christus agere soleat. Discamus ergo regem hunc agnoscere, nec timere mundum hunc, qui cum maxime furit, excidio proximus est, nec quicquam contra eos poterit, quorum curam Christus suscepit, cui nec portae inferorum praevalent. Matth. 16. Et quamuis in mundo afflictiones nos maneant, illius dicto animemur, quo se mundum vicisse, nosque in se pacem habituros esse pollicetur. Iohan. 16.
units.tr: At the same time Peter describes the kingdom of Christ in the words of David, and it greatly profits us to dwell often on this consideration. First, he here asserts that Christ, exalted at the right hand of God, has ascended into heaven. His kingdom is therefore heavenly, not of this world, as he himself confesses before Pilate. John 18. All power is indeed given to him in heaven and on earth; yet he does not reign after the manner of the princes of this age, in whose kingdoms uncertain and unstable changes of fortune necessarily arise, since they strive to hold power by the uncertain and empty might of flesh. At the same time we are reminded that in the kingdom of Christ we must by no means seek the goods of the world, such as wealth, honours, pleasures, and the friendships of the world, and whatever else is of this kind. Eternal and heavenly are the things which God the Father has bestowed in Christ. We ought therefore to occupy ourselves wholly in the pursuit of these. Next, he teaches that Christ sits at the right hand of God, a phrase which designates both a certain place of blessedness and an equal power of kingdom or rule with the Father. For the Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. John 3. He also commands that all should honour the Son just as they honour the Father. John 5. To this too the word sitting ought to be referred, by which both the majesty of the reigning Christ and the unshaken stability and power of his kingdom are expressed. Lastly, he says that all enemies are to be made subject, so that they become a footstool for Christ's feet. Christ is therefore a victorious king and the unconquered subduer of his enemies. The prince and head of these is Satan, to whom the first promise of salvation through Christ's death was already threatened long ago, when God said: The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. Gen. 3. And Christ teaches that he has already been judged and cast out. John 16 and 12. In a similar way it is clear that sin has been overcome. For God (as Paul says) sent his Son and condemned sin in the flesh; that is, through the sacrifice of his Son, offered for sin on the altar of the cross, he abolished the guilt of sin and stripped it of its arms and strength, so that it might not harm us henceforth. Rom. 8. And with sin abolished, it is clear that death too has been overcome, for death fought against us with no other weapon than the sting of sin. 1 Cor. 15. Truly, then, through Christ the whole power of the underworld has been conquered. He likewise conquers the world, and tyrants with the whole band of the impious. For we read that the Father decreed long ago that those who refuse to be governed by the saving word of his Son should be utterly crushed by his iron sceptre. Ps. 2. Nor are there lacking examples from ancient and from our own age by which we are taught what glorious triumphs over the enemies of his Church Christ is accustomed to win. Let us therefore learn to acknowledge this king, and not to fear this world, which, raging as it does at its utmost, is close to ruin, and can do nothing against those whose care Christ has taken up, against whom the gates of hell do not prevail. Matt. 16. And although afflictions remain for us in the world, let us be encouraged by his word, in which he promises that he has overcome the world and that we shall have peace in him. John 16.

units.la: Sed concionis huius finem videamus, quem his verbis Petrus infert: Certo sciat ergo tota domus Israel, quod dominum & eundem Christum fecerit Deus hunc Iesum, quem vos crucifixistis. Breuis & grauis sententia, vereque apostolica, cuius singula verba prolixae orationis materiam suppeditare possent. Sed quia de singulis copiosius dicendi locus subinde offeretur, paucis quid his effectum vult Petrus indicabimus. Primo totam domum Israelis alloquitur. Domus vero nomine omnes cuiuscunque loci siue ordinis homines comprehendit, vt Christum omnibus nobis vniuersalem salvatorem esse doceat, penes quem personarum respectus nullus sit. Et est hoc non contemnendum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quod in corruptissimo & madente adhuc Christi sanguine Iudaeorum populo, salutem in filio suo omnibus polliceri dignatur. Deinde, certo sciat, inquit. Certa ergo est salutis nostrae ratio in Christo, cui tuto quis inniti possit: quia fallere non potest, qui ipsissima est veritas. Tertio quid omnes nouisse debeant, edicit: Quod nimirum deus Iesum Nazarenum fecerit dominum & Christum. Dominum vocat, quia redemptor noster est. Quis enim ignorat, redemptoribus in eos, quos suis pecunijs aut periculo vitae suae redemerunt, dominij ius esse? Hac ratione apud prophetam ait: Ego dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Isa. 42. Christum, id est, vnctum vocat, quia rex & sacerdos est. Antiquitus enim reges & sacerdotes vngi solitos fuisse, ex scripturis constat. Et de regis quidem officio paulo ante quaedam diximus, ad quod etiam redemptoris vel domini nomen pertinet. Certe regis instar leges fert Christus, secundum has regni sui ciues gubernat, eosdem defendit, & caelestibus thesauris ditat liberalissime. Idem etiam sacerdos est. Nam & olim docuit, & hodie docet per verbi ministerium, cuius ipse in ecclesia author est. Et sacrificio corporis sui, semel in cruce oblato, pro peccatis totius mundi satisfecit. Et vt olim in terris agens pro nobis orauit, ita hodie pro nobis in dei conspectu fidelis pontifex & aduocatus comparet. Hebr. 2.1. Iohan. 2. Vere ergo Christus sit vnctus dei est, & horribiliter peccare constat omnes, qui hoc reiecto, alios sibi dominos, reges, sacerdotes & redemptores constituunt. Caeterum vt in principio tractationis de Christo, ipsos sceleris contra hunc commissi admonuit: ita eiusdem mentione sermone suum concludit, de eo se loqui significans, quem ipsi crucifixerint. Facile vero aestimare licet sceleris atrocitatem ex ijs, quae de Christo tam honorifice praedicauit. Non alia autem ratione hoc exprobrat, quam vt peccati conscientia extimulatos, Christi & salutis amore inflammaret, quemadmodum ex rei euentu sequenti sermone patebit.
units.tr: But let us look at the end of this sermon, which Peter draws from these words: Let all the house of Israel therefore know assuredly that God has made this same Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ. It is a brief and weighty statement, truly apostolic, and each of its words could supply material for a long discourse. But since opportunity for speaking more fully about individual points will often arise, we shall briefly indicate what Peter intends to accomplish by these words. First, he addresses the whole house of Israel. By the name house he includes all men of whatever place or rank, so as to teach that Christ is the universal Saviour of all of us, with whom there is no regard of persons. And this is no small proof of divine goodness, that it deigns to promise salvation in his Son to all, even to the Jewish people, most corrupt and still dripping with the blood of Christ. Next, he says, let them know assuredly. The ground of our salvation is therefore sure in Christ, on whom anyone may safely rest, because he cannot deceive who is very truth itself. Third, he declares what all ought to know: that God has made this Jesus of Nazareth both Lord and Christ. He calls him Lord because he is our Redeemer. For who does not know that those who have redeemed others with their money or at the risk of their own life have a right of lordship over them? For this reason he says through the prophet: I am the Lord, this is my name, and I will not give my glory to another. Isa. 42. He calls Christ, that is, anointed, because he is king and priest. For it is established from the Scriptures that kings and priests were anointed in ancient times. Concerning the office of a king we have said something a little earlier, and to this the name of redeemer or lord also belongs. Certainly Christ gives laws as a king, governs his subjects of the kingdom according to them, defends them, and enriches them most generously with heavenly treasures. He is also a priest. For he both taught of old and teaches today through the ministry of the word, of which he himself is the author in the Church. And by the sacrifice of his body, once offered on the cross, he made satisfaction for the sins of the whole world. And just as while on earth he prayed for us, so today he stands before the face of God as our faithful high priest and advocate. Heb. 2; 1 John 2. Truly, then, Christ is the anointed of God, and it is certain that all who reject him and set up for themselves other lords, kings, priests and redeemers sin dreadfully. Moreover, just as at the beginning of his discourse about Christ he reminded them of their crime against him, so he concludes his speech by mentioning him, signifying that he is speaking of the one whom they crucified. Yet one may easily judge the atrocity of their crime from what he has said about Christ so honourably. He reproaches them with this for no other reason than to stir them, pricked by the awareness of their sin, to a flame of love for Christ and salvation, as will be clear from the outcome of the matter in the sermon that follows.

units.la: Exhibuit nobis Lucas apostolicae praedicationis specimen. Comprehendit his paucis Petrus omnes fidei Christianae articulos. Disseruit de deo patre, omnium creatore. Disseruit de Deo filio, qui homo factus sit ex Dauidis progenie, & proinde in persona vnitate verus deus & homo agnosci debeat. Docuit hunc pro nobis mortuum esse, sepultum, & ad inferos descendisse, resuscitatum vero ascendisse in caelos, vbi ad dextram dei patris confideat, ad iudicium venturus, in quo hostes suos omnes pedibus subijciet, imo in stagnum ardens sulphure praecipitabit. Offendit ab hoc missum venisse sanctum spiritum, qui ecclesiam & singulos fideles regat. Denique hunc Iesum nobis dominum & salvatorem factum esse probauit, in quo peccatorum remissio, resurrectio carnis, & vita aeterna credentibus parta sit. Nihil hic de nostris satisfactionibus, nihil de absolutione priuata, auriculari confesfione, indulgentijs, purgatorio & alijs huius farinæ rebus dicitur. Retineamus ergo apostolicæ doctrinæ simplicitatem, & Christum Iesum firma fide amplectamur, ut in illo saluemur: cui omnis debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke has given us a sample of apostolic preaching. In these few words Peter summed up all the articles of the Christian faith. He spoke of God the Father, the creator of all things. He spoke of God the Son, who was made man from the line of David, and so should be acknowledged as true God and true man in one person. He taught that this Jesus died for us, was buried, and descended into hell; that he rose again, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come to judgment, when he will subject all his enemies under his feet, or rather hurl them into the lake burning with sulphur. He showed that the Holy Spirit, who was sent from him, rules the Church and each of the faithful. Finally, he proved that this Jesus has been made our Lord and Saviour, in whom forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life are obtained for believers. Nothing is said here about our satisfactions, nothing about private absolution, auricular confession, indulgences, purgatory, and other things of that kind. Let us therefore keep the simplicity of the apostolic teaching, and embrace Christ Jesus with a firm faith, so that we may be saved in him, to whom all blessing, honour, glory and power are due for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XVII.

units.la: His vero auditis, compuncti sunt corde, & dixerunt Petro, & reliquis apostolis: Quid faciemus viri fratres? Dixit illis Petrus: Poenitentiam agite, & baptizetur unusquisque vestrum in nomine Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum, & accipietis donum Spiritus sancti. Vestra enim est promissio, & filiorum vestrorum, & omnium qui procul sunt, quoscunque aduocauerit dominus deus noster.
units.tr: When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, "Men, brothers, what shall we do?" Peter said to them, "Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children and to all who are far off, whomever the Lord our God shall call."

units.la: EXposuit hucusque Lucas primam euangelij concionem, quam D. Petrus postquam acceptum spiritum sanctum Hierosolymis habuit. Status illius fuit, Iesum Nazarenum, quem Iudæi crucifixerunt, esse Christum & promissum humani generis redemptorem. At quia Petri institutum fuit, illud non docere modo, sed homines (vt olim monitus erat) viuos capere, & Christo lucrifacere, immane scelus, quo in Christum peccauerant, illis luculenter ob oculos statuit. Nam circa principium tractationis de Christo ipsos eum crucifixisse docet, quem deus multis miraculis filium suum & promissum saluatorem esse defignasset. Deinde summam omnium, quæ de Christo dicta erant, colligens, rursum hunc ab illis cruci affixum esse admonet, & hoc quasi aculeo in animis illorum relicto, orationem concludit. Atqui hæc à Petro, non conuiciandi libidine, sed salutis ipsorum promouendæ studio dicta esse, rei euentus testatur, quam modo Lucas describit, memorabile simul exemplum proponens, quo vera salutis per Christum consequendæ ratio, absolutissimè traditur. Dignus ergo est locus hic, in cuius consideratione diligenter versemur, quæ vt maiorem fructum afferat, de singulis ordine dicendum erit. Primo enim de auditoribus agit Euangelista. Deinde quid Petrus cum illis porrò egerit, recenset.
units.tr: Up to this point Luke has set out the first sermon that Saint Peter preached at Jerusalem after receiving the Holy Spirit. Its theme was that Jesus of Nazareth, whom the Jews crucified, is the Christ and the promised redeemer of mankind. But Peter's aim was not merely to teach this but to take people alive (as he had once been told to do) and win them to Christ. So he placed before their eyes, clearly, the monstrous crime by which they had sinned against Christ. Near the start of his discussion of Christ he tells them that they themselves crucified him whom God had marked out by many miracles as his Son and the promised Saviour. Then, gathering up the sum of everything that had been said about Christ, he reminds them again that he was fastened to the cross by them, and having left this like a sting in their minds, he ends his address. That these words were spoken by Peter not out of a desire to insult, but out of a zeal to advance their salvation, is shown by the outcome of the event, which Luke now describes, setting forth a memorable example by which the true way of obtaining salvation through Christ is most fully taught. This passage is therefore worth our careful study. So that it may bear greater fruit, we shall have to speak about each part in order. For first the evangelist deals with the hearers, and then he recounts what Peter went on to do with them.
