units.la: De auditoribus agens, effectum concionis Petri indicat. His auditis (inquit) compuncti sunt corde, & dixerunt Petro & reliquis apostolis: Quid faciemus viri fratres? Duo illis tribuuntur. Primum corde compuncti sunt. Intelliguntur autem conscientiæ terrores, qui ex peccati agnitione & iræ dei sensu siue timore in illis orti sunt. Ab his initium fieri oportet, siquidem ex verbi prædicatione fructum aliquem referre volumus. Quoad enim securi viuentes, nullo peccatorum nostrorum & iudiciorum dei metu constringimur, de salutis ratione seriò cogitare non possumus, vt pote cuius curam inutilem & superuacaneam esse ducimus. Quia verò ex naturæ corruptione hoc nobis vitij adhæret, vt peccati blanditijs capti, nos peccatores esse nö agnoscamus, peccata per dei verbum argui & accusari necesse est, quod inter spiritus sancti opera primum à Christo recensetur. Qua ratione euangelij verbum gladius & lux dici consueuit, quia quouis gladio ancipiti penetrantior in cordis arcana & compagum medullarum, intima penetrat, adeoque cogitationes occultas eruit, & quæ nosipsos latebant, non nobis modo verumetiam aliis inspicienda proponit. Hebr. 4. Iohan. 3. Atqui hoc factu necessarium esse, non tantum expresso dei verbo, verumetiam exemplis electorum dei docemur, vt interim nullus nobis de impuris & pænitere nescijs huius sæculi filijs sermo fit. Dauid certè, quanquam vir esset iuxta cor dei, non tamen immania adulterij & homicidij scelera cum multis alijs, quæ hæc comitabantur, agnoscit, donec dei verbo illa per Prophetam arguuntur. Tunc demum exclamare incipit: Peccaui domino. Item: Transgressiones meas agnosco, & peccatum meum assiduè mihi obuersatur. Contremiscunt offa mea, & anima mea territa est vehementer. Nihil integrum est in carne mea propter indignationem tuam, non est pax ossibus meis propter peccatum meum. Et reliqua quæ Psal. 51. 6. 38. & alibi habentur. Eandem in nostris hisce rationem cernimus. Iam enim à Christi morte dies quinquaginta & amplius elapsi erant. Et quotus quisque Hierosolymis pœnitentiæ specimen ediderat, ex eorum numero, qui Christi sanguinem impia temeritate sibi & filijs suis imputari debere clamauerant? Quin potius securi vitam degunt, & haud dubiè periculi erant, nisi deus securitatem hanc animis illorum excussisset. Petri enim prædicatione excitij, iam demum
units.tr: In speaking of the hearers, Luke indicates the effect of Peter's sermon. "When they heard this," he says, "they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, 'Men, brothers, what shall we do?'" Two things are attributed to them. First, they were cut to the heart. By this are meant the terrors of conscience that arose in them from the recognition of sin and from a sense or fear of God's wrath. This must be the beginning, if we wish to gain any fruit from the preaching of the Word. For as long as we live secure, and are not bound by any fear of our sins or of God's judgement, we cannot think seriously about the way of salvation, since we regard concern for it as useless and superfluous. But because by the corruption of nature this fault clings to us, that, captivated by the flatteries of sin, we do not acknowledge ourselves to be sinners, it is necessary that sins be reproved and accused by the Word of God. This is listed first among the works of the Holy Spirit by Christ. For this reason the Word of the gospel is customarily called a sword and a light: as any two-edged sword, it penetrates more deeply into the secret places of the heart and the marrow of the joints, reaching the innermost parts, and so it drags out hidden thoughts and sets before us, and before others, things that were hidden even from ourselves. Heb. 4. John 3. Moreover, that this must happen we are taught not only by the express Word of God but also by the examples of God's elect, so that no discourse should be addressed to us about the impure sons of this world who know nothing of repentance. David, certainly, although he was a man after God's own heart, did not acknowledge the enormous crimes of adultery and murder, together with many other sins that accompanied them, until those things were reproved by the Word of God through the prophet. Only then did he begin to cry out: "I have sinned against the Lord." Likewise: "I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is constantly before me. My bones tremble, and my soul is greatly terrified. There is nothing sound in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sin." And the rest, which are found in Ps. 51, 6, 38, and elsewhere. We see the same pattern in the events before us. For more than fifty days had now passed since the death of Christ. And how few at Jerusalem had given any sign of repentance, among those who had cried out with impious rashness that the blood of Christ should be imputed to themselves and to their children? Rather, they lived in security, and were without doubt in danger, unless God had shaken that security out of their minds. For, roused by Peter's preaching, they now at last began to be pricked in their hearts, to tremble, and to think about salvation. We shall say the same about ourselves, if we are willing to admit the truth. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who refuse to have their sins reproved by the Word of God, and who loudly maintain that it is not the job of ministers to do this, that they should busy themselves with exposing the sins of others. Such people sometimes find dumb dogs that accommodate their teaching to their lusts, but then that saying of the prophet is fulfilled: the sword of the Lord comes suddenly, and the blood of the perishing is required at the hand of the flattering prophets. See Ezek. 3 and 33.

units.la: I. Effectus concionis Petri. demum animis compungi & contremiscere ac de salute cogitare incipiunt. Idem de nobis ipsis dicemus, modò verum fateri libeat. Vehementer ergo fallu ntur, qui peccata verbo Dei argui nolùt, & præter officium hoc ministros f acere clamitant, quòd aliorum sceleribus traducendis occupentur. Inueniunt tales aliquando mutos canes, qui doctrinam ipsorum libidini attemperant, sed tunc illud prophetæ impletur, quòd & gladius domini secur ùs superuenit, & pereuntium sanguis de manu blandiloquentium prophetarum exigitur. Vid Ezech.3. & 33.
units.tr: I. The effect of Peter's sermon. At last their minds are pricked, they tremble, and they begin to think about salvation. We shall say the same of ourselves, provided we are willing to confess the truth. Those therefore are greatly mistaken who will not have sins reproved by the Word of God, and who cry out that it is outside the ministers' duty to be occupied with exposing the crimes of others. Such people sometimes find dumb dogs that adapt their teaching to their lusts, but then that saying is fulfilled: the sword of the Lord comes suddenly, and the blood of the perishing is required at the hand of the flattering prophets. See Ezek. 3 and 33.

units.la: Accedit autem animorum compunctioni & conscientiæ terroribus alterum, quòd nimirum con-silium à Petro & apostolis requirunt, quod secuti, peccati noxa liberari, & cum Deo in gratiam redire queant. Est hoc non minus necessarium quàm prius illud, de quo modò diximus. Conflat enim verbo Dei & peccatorum accusatione impios quoq; compungi. Sed ut electis omnia cooperantur in bonù, ita illi vndequaq; grauius peccandi occasionem arripiunt, quod & hic fieri confuerit. Nam vbi peccatai psorum palàm accusantur, vel impatienti ferocia aduersùs Dei verbum insurgunt, nec peccasse videri volunt, cuius rei exempla in Achabo, & postea in Iudæorum sacerdotibus habentur: vel ad sua opera conuersi, in illis quærunt quo Dei iustitiæ satisfacere & iram illius declinare possint. At vbi nihil præter peccati atrocitatem & horribilem Dei iram videre possant, cum Caino clamare incipiunt: Maior est iniquitas mea, quàm vt remitti possit, & ita tandem cum Iuda infelicem exitum foreiuntur. Horum igitur exemplo longius nos progredi, nec inter acerbos conscientiæ terrores consistere decet. Consilium verò inde petendum, vnde terrorem nobis obortum esse sentimus, è Dei verbo nimirum, quod (vt Pelias hasta olim in Telepho fecit) conscientijs & vulnera infligit, & medicinam simul affert saluberrimam. Neq; hic peccatorum atrocitate nos ita terreri conuenit, vt ab omni salutis spe nos excidisse putemus. Rata enim manet Dei sententia, dicentis: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur, & viuat Ezech.18. Et Christus dominus non modò quærentibus pollicetur quòd inuenturi sint, verumetiam illorum sese medicù profitetur, qui conscientijs suis sauciį sunt, & passim eos qui laborant & onerati sunt, ad se inuitat. Isa.61. Matth.11. Nec sine numine factum putabimus, quòd primæ concionis apostolicæ auditores fuerunt, quorum manus filij Dei sanguine adhuc madere poterant. Eo enim exemplo nobis ipsum facere voluit Deus, vt Christi Iesu meritum & suæ bonitatis liberalitatem nullis peccatis superari posse credamus, modò bis per fidem vti libeat. Sed petri consilium audiamus, breue & saluberrimum.
units.tr: Now to the pricking of minds and the terrors of conscience there is added a second thing: namely, that they ask Peter and the apostles for counsel, by following which they may be freed from the harm of sin and be restored to favour with God. This is no less necessary than the first, of which we have just spoken. For it is established by the Word of God and the accusation of sin that even the wicked are pricked. But whereas all things work together for good for the elect, the wicked seize on every occasion for sinning more grievously, and this too is what usually happens here. For when their sins are openly accused, they either rise up in unbridled fury against the Word of God and do not want to seem to have sinned (examples of which are found in Ahab, and afterwards in the priests of the Jews), or they turn to their own works and seek in them a means of satisfying the justice of God and turning aside his anger. But when they can see nothing but the atrocity of sin and the dreadful wrath of God, they begin to cry out with Cain: "My iniquity is greater than can be forgiven," and so at last they meet an unhappy end with Judas. It is therefore fitting that we not advance further in the footsteps of these people, nor remain among the bitter terrors of conscience. Counsel, however, must be sought from the same place from which we feel the terror has arisen, that is, from the Word of God, which (as the spear of Pelias once did to Telephus) inflicts wounds on the conscience and at the same time brings the most wholesome remedy. Nor is it fitting that we be so terrified by the atrocity of our sins that we think we have fallen from every hope of salvation. For God's sentence stands firm, saying: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live" (Ezek. 18). And Christ the Lord not only promises to those who seek that they will find, but also professes himself the physician of those whose consciences are wounded, and everywhere invites to himself those who labour and are burdened (Isa. 61; Matt. 11). Nor shall we think it happened without God's will that the first hearers of the apostolic sermon were men whose hands could still be wet with the blood of the Son of God. For by this example God wished to show us that we should believe that the merit of Christ Jesus and the generosity of his goodness cannot be overcome by any sins, provided it pleases us to use them through faith. But let us hear Peter's counsel, brief and most wholesome.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Pœnitentiam agite, & baptizetur vnusquisq; vestrum in nomine Christi, in remissionem peccatorum. Et accipietis donum spiritus sancti. Vestra enim est promissio, &c. Tria ab illis exigit, sed in præsenti priora duo execut iemus, de tertio in sequenti Sermone dicturi.
units.tr: Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Christ, for the forgiveness of sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is yours, etc. He demands three things from them, but for now we will deal with the first two, and speak of the third in the following sermon.

units.la: Primum vno verbo absoluit: Μετάνοεῖτε, inquit, quod Latinus interpres vertit: Pœnitentiam agite. Ab eo autem orditur, quod passim scriptura exigit. Moses certè ijs, qui peccatorum & transfregeffe legis pœnas exoluunt, in vna pœnitentia salutis viam commonstrat. Leuit.26. Deut.32. In Prophetis hanc præcipuè vrgeri notius est, quàm vt multis probari opus sit. Baptista, primus nouì Testamenti minister, ab eadem prædicandi initium facit. Et Christus docere incipiens, clamat: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquauit enim regnum cælorum. Matth. 3. Huius prædicationem apostolis quoq; non semel commendauit, vt videre est Matth.10. & Luc.24.cap. Magistri ergo sui & præcepti ab illo traditi memor Petrus, pœnitentiam hiis quoq; præcipit, & eorum quæ hucusq; de ipsorum scelere dixerat, hunc scopum esse testatur, non vt desperabundi pereant, sed vt pœnitentiam agant & salvuntur. Quia verò consilium hoc propter nos literis consignari voluit spiritus sanctus, de pœnitentia quædam dicenda erunt, vt quid à nobis quoq; exigatur, intelligamus.
units.tr: He settles the first in a single word: Μετάνοεῖτε [metanoeite], he says, which the Latin translator renders "Repent" (Pœnitentiam agite). He begins with this, which Scripture demands everywhere. Moses certainly shows the one way of salvation, repentance alone, to those who pay the penalties for transgressing the law and their sins. Lev. 26; Deut. 32. That the Prophets press this most of all is too well known to need proof from many passages. John the Baptist, the first minister of the New Testament, makes this preaching the beginning of his own. And Christ, beginning to teach, cries: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Matt. 3. He also commended this preaching to the apostles more than once, as may be seen in Matt. 10 and Luke 24. Peter, then, mindful of his Master and of the precept handed down by him, also commands repentance to these men, and he declares that the aim of all that he has said so far about their wickedness is not that they should perish in despair, but that they should repent and be saved. Since the Holy Spirit wished this counsel to be recorded in writing for our sake, something must be said about repentance, so that we may understand what is required of us as well.

units.la: Pœnitere Latinis dicuntur, quos rei comissæ piget tædetq;, vnde pœnitentiæ vocabulum ductum Græci μετάνοιαν dicunt ἀπὸ τοῦ μετανοεῖν, quod animi correctionem & emendationem sonat, vnς quid sit. enim præstantiorem illam animæ partem significat, quam nostri mentem dixerunt. Vnde vocῖν Græci dicunt, quod nos intelligere dicimus aut mente percipere. Μετάνοεῖν ergo dicitur, qui errore intellecto de illius emendatione serio cogitare incipit. Hebrei Thefchubah dixerunt, quod proprie conuersionem sonat. At quia conuersio hæc, vt Græci nominis etymon docet, ad animum refertur, pœnitentiam breuiter definire licebit, esse conuersionem mentis ad Deum ab eo quod prauum & malum est. Definitionem hanc Dei verba probant, qui per Ieremiam dicit: Si reuerti voles Israel, ad me reuertere. uertere. Ierem. 4. Sed & alibi scriptura eos, qui peccauerunt, à Deo recessisse dicit. Unde necessario sequitur, pœnitentiam, qua peccatis renunciatur, reditum & conuersionem ad Deum dici debere. Atqui diligens huius definitionis consideratio grauissimis erroribus medetur. Sunt enim, qui ubi se peccauisse cognouerunt, ad creaturas vel manuum suarum opera conuerti solent, & ita duplici adhuc peccato (ut dominus monet) se polluunt, dum & fontem aquæ viuentis deserunt, & cisternas fodiunt aquis carentes. Ierem. 2. Sunt rursum, qui ex pœnitentia theatricum ludum fingunt, & sufficere putant, si Iudaicorum hypocritarum more cerea incendant, suffitus faciant, nudus pedibus incedant, ciliciis vestiantur, & alia eius generis faciant, quorum superstitio iam olim prophetarum sermonibus damnata est. Vide Isa. 1. 58. Hos. 6. Mich. 6. Zach. 7. &c. At omnibus hisce nihil profici intelligemus, si statuamus, pœnitentiam mentis conversionem esse ad Deum. Quò cumprimis facit, quod apud Iobelem cap. 2. dominus ait: Conuertimini vsq; ad me in toto corde vestro, ieiunio, fletu & lamento. Scindite cor vestrum, & non vestimenta vestra: & conuertimini ad dominum Deum vestrum, &c.
units.tr: Among the Latins, those are said to repent (pœnitere) who are grieved and wearied by a deed they have done, whence the word pœnitentia is derived. The Greeks call it μετάνοια [metanoia], from μετανοεῖν [metanoein], which signifies a correction and amendment of the mind. For νοῦς [nous] denotes that more excellent part of the soul which our writers called the mind (mens). Hence the Greeks say νοεῖν [noein], which we say means to understand or to perceive with the mind. So μετανοεῖν [metanoein] is said of one who, having recognised his error, begins to think seriously about amending it. The Hebrews called it teshuvah, which properly means conversion. But since this conversion, as the etymology of the Greek word teaches, relates to the mind, we may briefly define repentance as the conversion of the mind to God away from what is perverse and evil. The words of God confirm this definition, when through Jeremiah he says: "If you will return, Israel, return to me." Jer. 4. But elsewhere too Scripture says that those who have sinned have withdrawn from God. Hence it necessarily follows that the repentance by which sins are renounced must be called a return and conversion to God. Moreover, careful consideration of this definition cures very grave errors. For there are those who, when they have recognised that they have sinned, are accustomed to turn to creatures or to the works of their own hands, and so pollute themselves with a double sin (as the Lord warns), since they forsake the fountain of living water and dig cisterns that hold no water. Jer. 2. There are again those who make a theatrical show of repentance, and think it enough if, after the manner of Jewish hypocrites, they light candles, offer incense, walk barefoot, clothe themselves in sackcloth, and do other things of this kind, a superstition long ago condemned in the words of the Prophets. See Isa. 1 and 58; Hos. 6; Mic. 6; Zech. 7, etc. But we shall understand that nothing is gained by all these things if we maintain that repentance is the conversion of the mind to God. This agrees especially with what the Lord says in Joel 2: "Turn to me with your whole heart, with fasting, weeping and lamentation. Rend your heart, and not your garments; and turn to the Lord your God," etc.

units.la: Simul autem quæ pœnitentiæ partes sint, & in quibus illa versetur, hinc disci potest. Primas hîc peccatorum agnitioni tribuimus, quia nisi hæc adsit, de peccato nec dolere, nec ab illo ad Deum conuerti poterimus. Sumitur hæc ex legis speculo, quod non aperta modo flagitia, verumetiam latentem in nobis peccati naturam arguit, vt Paulus monet. Rom. 7. Peccati agnitionem conscientia terror, animi dolor & contritio sequitur, de quibus modò dictum est. Fieri enim nequit, quin totus terreatur, doleat & conteratur animo suo, quicunq; cum peccati atrocitate Dei irati vultum in lege contemplatus fuerit. Ea autem huius contritionis & doloris vis est, vt confessionem quoq; peccati extorqueat: non quidem auricularem illam (cuius nullum in sacris literis siue præceptum siue exemplum extat) sed qua Deo nos miseros & peccatores esse confitemur, cuius Iohannes apostolus in priori epistola, capite primo meminit. Confessioni inuocatio Dei coniuncta est, quæ ab illa nullo modo separari potest. Oritur verò ex omnibus istis ardens vitæ emendandæ studium, nec vitæ modò, verumetiam totius (si fieri possit) naturæ. Iam enim carnem mortificare homo incipit. Iam mundo mori & cum Christo crucifigi exoptat. Flagrat totus sanctimoniæ & innocentiæ studio. Recti & veri amore ardet. Operibus bonis, quorum studium à Deo commendari audit, totus occupatur, nulla interim illorum ratione habita, quæ superstitiosis hominum traditionibus præscribuntur. Denique quia inde omnis malifontem exortum esse nouit, quòd à Deo & verbo Dei secessionem fecit, Dei verbo se totum accommodare & Dei exemplum vitæ totius regulam sibi constituere studet. Nec momentaneum aut paucorum dierum hoc studium est, sed assiduum & iuge, utpote quod propter quotidianos lapsus quotidie instaurari opus est. Nam vt septies in die iustus labitur, ita septies à lapsu resurgere solet. Prouerb. 24.
units.tr: At the same time, from this it can be learned what the parts of repentance are and in what it consists. Here we assign the first place to the recognition of sins, for unless this is present we can neither grieve over sin nor turn from it to God. This recognition is drawn from the mirror of the law, which reveals not only open crimes but also the nature of sin lying hidden in us, as Paul warns. Rom. 7. Recognition of sin is followed by terror of conscience, and grief and contrition of spirit, of which we have just spoken. For whoever contemplates in the law the face of God angry at the enormity of sin cannot help being wholly terrified, grieved and crushed in his soul. The force of this contrition and grief is such that it wrings out a confession of sin as well: not indeed that auricular confession (for there is no precept or example of it anywhere in the sacred letters), but that by which we confess to God that we are wretched sinners, which the apostle John mentions in the first chapter of his first epistle. Invocation of God is joined to confession, and can in no way be separated from it. From all these things there arises an ardent zeal to amend one's life, and not only one's life but, if it were possible, the whole of one's nature. For now a man begins to mortify the flesh; now he desires to die to the world and to be crucified with Christ. He burns wholly with zeal for holiness and innocence. He glows with love of what is right and true. He is wholly occupied with good works, the zeal for which he hears is commended by God, and yet he takes no account of those rules that are prescribed by superstitious human traditions. Finally, since he knows that all evil has arisen from his having withdrawn from God and the word of God, he strives to conform himself wholly to the word of God, and to make the example of God the rule of his whole life. Nor is this zeal momentary or for a few days only, but continual and unceasing, since, because of daily lapses, it must be renewed daily. For as the righteous man falls seven times a day, so he is wont to rise seven times from his fall. Prov. 24.

units.la: Patet ex his, quid ab his fieri voluerit Petrus: nimirum vt peccata sua agnoscant, Dei iudicium timeat, de peccatis doleant, animis totis conterantur, coram Deo culpam confiteantur, & illius gratiam implorent, deniq; totius vitæ emendationi, carnis mortificationi, innocentiæ, sanctimoniæ, iustitiæ & charitati studeant. In hanc sententiam propheta clamat: Derelinquat impius viam suam, & omnis iniquus cogitationes suas, & conuertatur ad dominum, &c. Isa. 55. Ista singuli ad se transferant, cumq; his vitam suam componant, ac facile patebit, quas vias deserere, quas verò capessere & ingredi debeant.
units.tr: From these things it is clear what Peter wished them to do: namely, to recognise their sins, to fear the judgment of God, to grieve over their sins, to be crushed in their whole souls, to confess their guilt before God, to implore his grace, and finally to strive for the amendment of their whole life, the mortification of the flesh, innocence, holiness, righteousness and charity. The prophet cries out to this effect: "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him turn to the Lord," etc. Isa. 55. Let each one apply these things to himself and shape his life by them, and it will readily become plain which ways they ought to forsake, and which they ought to take up and walk in.

units.la: Secundum quod præcipit Petrus, his verbis explicat: Baptizetur vnusquisq; vestrum in nomine Iesu Christi, in remissionem peccatorum. Duplex videtur esse præceptum hoc. Primò enim quia illos in nomine Christi baptizari vult, ad Christum illos relegat, & salutem ac peccatorum remissionem in solo hoc inueniri docet. Sic autem Christus prædicare iusserat, quando peccatorum remissionem in suo nomine monstrari debere admonet. Luc. 24. Et erat id factu necessarium propter pharisaicam doctrinam, quæ proprijs operibus homines iustificari tradebat: quæ & hodie apud multos obtinuit. Et sanè, si nihil præter pœnitentiam requisiuisset Petrus, illorum doctrinæ consentire visus fuisset. At quia pœnitentes ad Christum relegat, non obscurè docet, pœnitentiam ex officio præstari debere, iustificationis verò meritum in vno Christo inueniri posse. Peccant igitur contra Petri exemplum, quicunq; in pœnitentiæ doctrina nullam Christi mentionem faciunt. Sic enim rerum imperitis authores sunt, vt propriam iustitiam stabilire conentur, in qua nihil certi aut solidi inuenire possunt.
units.tr: Next, Peter explains what he commands in these words: "Let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of sins." This precept seems to have a double aim. For first, because he wishes them to be baptized in the name of Christ, he refers them to Christ, and teaches that salvation and forgiveness of sins are to be found in him alone. Christ had indeed commanded that preaching in this way, when he admonished that the forgiveness of sins must be shown in his name. Luke 24. And this was necessary because of the Pharisaic doctrine, which taught that men were justified by their own works, and which even today has held sway among many. And indeed, if Peter had required nothing but repentance, he would have seemed to agree with their doctrine. But because he refers the penitent to Christ, he teaches, not obscurely, that repentance ought to be performed as a duty, while the merit of justification is to be found in Christ alone. Therefore those who make no mention of Christ in their teaching on repentance sin against the example of Peter. For they become authors of error to the ignorant of things, in that they strive to establish their own righteousness, in which they can find nothing certain or solid.

units.la: Deinde de baptismo externo admonet, quem ipsos in remissione peccatorum accipere iubet. Quae verba non eo sensu accipi debent, quasi baptismus a peccatis abluat. Constat enim, nos sanguine filij Dei emundari ab omnibus peccatis. 1. Ioh. 1. Baptismo autem tale quiddam tribuitur, quia beneficium emundationis, per Christi sanguinem factae, obsignat. Quod in Circuncisione cernere licet. Cum enim fide iustificatus esset Abraham, circuncisionem accepit, signaculum iustitiae fidei. Rom. 4. Ita ijs, qui Christi testamento continentur, & propterea iustificati sunt, baptismus in remissionem peccatorum datur: id est, baptismo obsignatur iustitia Dei, quam ille per Christum nobis contulit. Quare locutione hac illos salutis suae certos facit Petrus, & argumento a baptismi fine ducto consolationem adhibet. Interim quia baptismo in Christi ecclesiam assumimur, & Christo initiamur, vtpote illius auspicijs contra mundum & principem huius militaturi: simul liberam & minime fucata fidei in Christum confessionem ab illis Petrus exigit. Nec enim cultores habere vult Christus, quos sui pudeat. Marc. 8. Atqui coram Pilato Christum palam abnegauerant Iudaei, dū se nullum regem fiue Messiam habere clamant, praeter Caesarem. Quapropter necesse erat, vt eadem libertate Christum confiterentur, ne amplius ex perfidorum abnegatorum numero censeri possent. Id nulla ratione commodius, quam per baptismum fieri poterat, quem Christus in hunc finem administrari voluit, vt discipulis sibi colligendis & adducendis seruirent, vt Matth. 28. legitur.
units.tr: Then he admonishes about external baptism, which he bids them receive for the forgiveness of sins. These words should not be taken in the sense that baptism washes away sins. For it is certain that we are cleansed from all sins by the blood of the Son of God. 1 John 1. But baptism is credited with something of this kind, in that it seals the benefit of cleansing accomplished through the blood of Christ. This can be seen in circumcision. For when Abraham had been justified by faith, he received circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith. Rom. 4. Thus baptism is given for the forgiveness of sins to those who are contained in the covenant of Christ and are therefore justified: that is, the righteousness of God, which he has bestowed on us through Christ, is sealed by baptism. Wherefore by this expression Peter makes them certain of their salvation, and by an argument drawn from the purpose of baptism he offers them consolation. Meanwhile, since we are received into the Church of Christ by baptism and are initiated into Christ, as those who are to fight under his auspices against the world and the prince of this world, Peter at the same time requires from them a free and unfeigned confession of faith in Christ. For Christ does not wish to have as worshippers those of whom he is ashamed. Mark 8. Yet the Jews had openly denied Christ before Pilate, when they cried out that they had no king or Messiah except Caesar. Therefore it was necessary that they should confess Christ with the same freedom, lest they could still be counted among the number of the faithless deniers. This could be done in no more suitable way than by baptism, which Christ willed to be administered for this purpose, that his disciples might serve to gather and bring in others for him, as is read in Matt. 28.

units.la: Iam vero si quae hucusque dicta sunt, in vnum conferas, patebit quo ordine iustificationis & salutis viam Petrus docuerit. Exorsus est a peccatorum redargutione, vt supra vidimus. Deinde vbi animis compunctos & contritos vidit, poenitentiam praecepit, hoc ipso gratiae spem illis facere incipiens. Rursum vero, ne poenitentiae operibus confisi, in propria iustitia acquiescerent, ad Christi nomen & meritum illos relegat. Tandem vt Christo publice nomen dent praecipit, & in illius ecclesiam transeant. Hunc salutis tradendae ordinem passim ab apostolis obseruatum esse videmus, quem Christo praeceptore ipsos didicisse nemo negare potest. Ita enim ille iam discessurus loquitur: Praedicari oportet in nomine meo poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes. Profecti ergo in orbem vniuersum, praedicate euangelium omni creaturae, & discipulos mihi adducite ex omnibus gentibus, baptizantes eos in nomen patris & filij & spiritus sancti, &c. Luc. 24. Marc. 16. Matth. 28. Quae si cum his conferas, quae hodie poenitentiam afferunt de Confessione auriculari, de satisfactionibus, operum meritis, indulgentijs, anniuersarijs, purgatorio & sexcentis alijs traduntur, toto coelo distare videbis.
units.tr: If you now put together what has been said so far, it will be plain in what order Peter taught the way of justification and salvation. He began with the rebuke of sins, as we saw above. Then, when he saw men pricked and broken in heart, he commanded repentance, thereby beginning to give them hope of grace. Again, lest they rest in their own righteousness, trusting in the works of repentance, he refers them to the name and merit of Christ. Finally, he commands them to give their names publicly to Christ and to pass over into his Church. We see this order of conveying salvation observed everywhere by the apostles, and no one can deny that they learned it from Christ as their teacher. For he, about to depart, speaks thus: "Repentance and remission of sins must be preached in my name among all nations." "Go therefore into the whole world, preach the gospel to every creature, and bring me disciples from all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit," etc. (Luke 24; Mark 16; Matthew 28). If you set these beside what is taught today about repentance, namely auricular confession, satisfactions, the merits of works, indulgences, anniversaries, purgatory and six hundred other things, you will see they are a whole heaven apart.

units.la: Porro quia Petro cum ijs res erat, qui se atrocissimi & exemplo carentis flagitij reos esse sentiebant, duplici promissione illis animum addit, ne desperatione absorbeantur, quod proprium euangelij munus est. Primo, accipietis (inquit) donum spiritus sancti. Videtur autem de peculiari spiritus dono loqui, quod primitiuae ecclesiae tempore credentibus obtingebat, vt vel linguis diuersis loquerentur, vel alijs signis illustres fierent, sicuti infra Cap. 8. clarius patebit. Oportuit enim apostolorum ministerium singulari aliquo dono ornari, quo facilius homines Christo lucrifacerent. Et licet illa maxima ex parte cessarint hodie, manent tamen magis necessarij effectus spiritus, cuius operatione credentes regenerantur, mortificantur, innouantur, salutis certi fiunt, animantur & confirmantur, vt in periculis intrepidi stare & nomen Christi fortiter confiteri possint. Est enim adoptionis spiritus, qui omnia ea operari consueuit, quae filios Dei in hoc mundo habere necesse est. Singularem vero consolationem promissio haec trepidantibus ob peccati conscientiam afferre potuit. Qua ratione enim de peccatorum remissione dubitarent, qui se eiusdem spiritus cum apostolis confortes fore audiebant? Interim nostra institutioni eadem promissio seruit. Docet enim a credentibus & vere Christianis spiritus sancti dona in vniuersum abesse non posse. Variae quidem operationes sunt, & dona spiritus varia, vt Paulus inquit, & alios alijs praestare cernimus. At ne infimus quidem spiritu in vniuersum caret, quando qui spiritum Christi non habent, Christi membra non esse possunt. Rom. 8. Vana ergo est Christiani nominis professio, nisi nos Christi spiritu animari & regi testemur. Quae causa est, quod apostolus fidem ex operibus agnosci docet, & Christus factis nos Deum patrem imitari iubet. Iacobi 2. Matth. 5.
units.tr: Moreover, since Peter was dealing with men who felt themselves guilty of the most atrocious crime, a crime without parallel, he encourages them with a twofold promise, so that they would not be swallowed up by despair, which is the proper office of the gospel. First, he says: "You will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit." Now he seems to speak of a particular gift of the Spirit, which was granted to believers in the time of the primitive Church, so that they spoke in various tongues or were made remarkable by other signs, as will be made clearer below in chapter 8. For the ministry of the apostles needed to be adorned with some singular gift, by which they could more easily win men to Christ. And although those gifts have for the most part ceased today, the more necessary effects of the Spirit remain, by whose working believers are regenerated, mortified, renewed, made certain of salvation, quickened and strengthened, so that they can stand fearless in dangers and confess the name of Christ boldly. For it is the Spirit of adoption, who customarily works all those things that the sons of God must have in this world. Indeed, this promise could bring a singular consolation to those trembling over the awareness of sin. For by what reasoning could they doubt the forgiveness of sins, when they heard that they would share in the same Spirit as the apostles? Meanwhile this same promise serves our instruction. For it teaches that the gifts of the Spirit cannot be wholly absent from believers and true Christians. There are indeed varied operations and varied gifts of the Spirit, as Paul says, and we see some excel others. Yet not even the least lacks the Spirit altogether, since those who do not have the Spirit of Christ cannot be members of Christ (Rom. 8). Therefore the profession of the Christian name is empty unless we testify that we are animated and ruled by the Spirit of Christ. This is why the apostle teaches that faith is recognised by works, and why Christ bids us imitate God the Father by our deeds (James 2; Matthew 5).

units.la: Secundo veterem promissionem allegat: Vestra est (inquiens) promissio, & filiorum vestrorum, & omnium qui procul sunt, quoscunq; vocauerit dominus Deus noster. Intelligenda sunt haec de fadere & promissionibus in veteri Testamento datis, quarum summa Genef.17.cap.habetur. Extendit vero has ad eos, qui procul sunt, id est, ad gentes, quas à repub. populi Dei adhuc alienas & longè remotas esse constabat, quò ipsis facilius fidem faciat. Nec enim de Dei bonitate amplius dubitare poterant qui ab Abrahamo erant prognati, quando eam in gentes quoq; extendi debere audiebant. Docent hac, quis promissionū diuinarum vsus esse debeat, vt nimirum fidem nutantem in tentationibus & aduersis quibuscunq; confirment. Sed priusquam sermoni finis imponatur, duo in his obseruanda erunt.
units.tr: Second, he cites the ancient promise: "The promise is yours, and that of your children, and of all who are far off, whomever the Lord our God shall call." These words must be understood of the covenant and the promises given in the Old Testament, the sum of which is found in Genesis 17. But he extends them to those who are far off, that is, to the nations, which were known to be still foreign to the commonwealth of the people of God and far removed from it, so that he might more easily make them believe. For those who were descended from Abraham could no longer doubt the goodness of God, when they heard that it ought to be extended to the nations too. These things teach what the use of the divine promises ought to be, namely to strengthen faith that wavers in temptations and all adversities. But before the discourse is brought to an end, two things must be observed in these words.

units.la: Primum, promissionem non ad patres modò, verumetiam ad filios pertinere dicit. Monent idem ipsius fœderis verba, quibus sic ait dominus: Confirmabo fœdus meum inter me & te, interq; semen tuum post te in generationibus suis fœdere perpetuo, vt sim scilicet Deus tuus & seminis tui, &c. Gen.17. Vnde colligimus, fœdere salutis non modò adultos & patres, verumetiam credentium infantes contineri, quos à seminis vocabulo excludere non possumus. Nec enim illorum obiectio alicuius authoritatis esse debet, qui Dei verba de iis tantùm Abrahami posteris intelligi debere dicūt, qui iam adulti fidem profiteri possunt: quando Isaacum & Iacobum priusquam nascerentur, fœderi salutis inclusos fuisse constat, vt videre est Gen.17. & 25. Rom. 9. Et Paulus eos liberos, qui alterutrum modò parentem fidelem habebant, sanctos dicere non dubitauit.1. Corinth.7. Christus deniq; regnum Dei puerorum esse non obscurè fatetur. Mar.10. Confutantur hîc Papistarum & Anabaptistarum errores: quorum illi infantibus sine baptismo natis salutem & Dei conspectum negant: hi verò infantes à baptismo arcent, quos Christus sibi adducere præcipit.
units.tr: First, he says the promise pertains not only to the fathers but also to their children. The very words of that covenant confirm this, in which the Lord says: "I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you in their generations, an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed," etc. (Gen. 17). From this we gather that not only adults and fathers, but also the infants of believers, are included in the covenant of salvation, and we cannot exclude them from the word "seed." Nor ought the objection of those carry any weight who say that the words of God are to be understood only of those posterity of Abraham who are already grown and able to profess faith, since it is certain that Isaac and Jacob were included in the covenant of salvation before they were born, as may be seen in Genesis 17 and 25 and Romans 9. And Paul did not hesitate to call holy those children who had only one believing parent (1 Cor. 7). Finally, Christ plainly declares that the kingdom of God belongs to little children (Mark 10). Here the errors of the Papists and of the Anabaptists are refuted. The former deny salvation and the sight of God to infants who die without baptism; the latter keep from baptism the infants whom Christ commands to be brought to him.

units.la: Deinde promissionem salutis explicans, simul vocationis diuinæ meminit, ne quis Dei filios vel ex carne nasci, vel humani arbitrij & virium merito fieri putaret. Non enim qui filij carnis hi sunt, filij Dei, sed filij promissionis. Et non est volentis aut currentis, sed miserentis Dei. Rom.9. Proposita quidem est in Christo Iesu salus, & vt euangelica parabola monet, nuptiarum tempus appropinquauit, & parata sunt omnia. Sed vocatione opus est, qua inuitati ad epulas euocentur. Emittit ergo euangelij præcones Deus, quorum vox iam olim totum orbem personuit. At quia ijdem in animis hominum nihil possunt, tractu diuino & spiritus operatione mentes moueri necesse est, iuxta illud Christi: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit illum. Iohan.6. Atqui pro sua libera & sancta voluntate operatur Deus, & spiritus vbi vult spirat. Iohan.3. Quibus palàm fit, salutem nostram ex mera Dei gratia dependere, qui quos vult vocat, quos vult trahit, & imagini filij sui conformes reddit. Interim nostri officij est, vt vocati respondeamus, tracti non reluctemur, & euangelio per fidei obedientiam subiecti vocationem & electionem nostram (vt alibi apostolus monet) firmam faciamus.2.Pet.1. Hæc de Petri consilio, quo peccatorum conscientia perterritus salutis viam monstrat, modò dicta sufficiant. Quæ in hoc restant, proximè tractabimus. Sequamur autem consultorem spiritum, qui per os Petri locutus est. Pœnitentiam verè agamus. In Christo quæramus quæcunque saluti seruiunt. Huic nos consecremus totos & illum fateamur liberè. Fidem in baptismo datam non fallamus, & vitam Christo dignam viuamus, cum illo olim in cœlis victuri: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Then, in explaining the promise of salvation, he also mentions the divine calling, lest anyone think that the children of God are born of the flesh, or become such by the merit of human choice and strength. For "those who are the children of the flesh are not the children of God, but the children of the promise." And it is "not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy" (Rom. 9). Salvation has indeed been set forth in Christ Jesus, and, as the parable of the gospel warns, the time of the wedding has drawn near and all things are ready. But a calling is needed, by which those invited are summoned to the feast. God therefore sends forth the heralds of the gospel, whose voice has long since sounded through the whole world. But because these men can do nothing upon the minds of men, the minds must be moved by the divine drawing and the working of the Spirit, according to that saying of Christ: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him" (John 6). Yet God works according to his free and holy will, and "the Spirit breathes where he wills" (John 3). From these things it is plain that our salvation depends upon the sheer grace of God, who calls whom he wills, draws whom he wills, and makes them conformed to the image of his Son. Meanwhile it is our duty, when called, to answer, not to resist when drawn, and by obedience of faith to submit to the gospel, and so make our calling and election firm, as the apostle elsewhere admonishes (2 Pet. 1). Let these things about Peter's counsel, by which he shows the way of salvation to a man terrified by the awareness of sin, suffice for now. What remains we shall take up next. Let us follow the counselling Spirit, who spoke through the mouth of Peter. Let us truly repent. Let us seek in Christ whatever serves our salvation. Let us consecrate ourselves wholly to him and freely confess him. Let us not betray the faith given in baptism, and let us live a life worthy of Christ, since we shall one day live with him in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XVIII.

units.la: Plurimis etiam aliis sermonibus testificatus est & exhortatus, dicens: Seruemini à generatione hac praua. Qui ergo libenter amplexi sunt sermonem eius, baptizati sunt, & additæ sunt die illa animæ circiter ter mille. Erant autem perseuerantes in doctrina apostolorum, & communicatione, & fractione panis, & precibus. Obortus est autem omni animæ timor, multaq; prodigia & signa per apostolos edebantur.
units.tr: Peter also bore witness and exhorted them with very many other words, saying: "Save yourselves from this perverse generation." So those who gladly embraced his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day. They continued steadfastly in the apostles' teaching, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers. Fear came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.

units.la: Dluus Petrus primam euangelij concionem ita instituit, vt auditoribus atrox & immane factinus, quod ab illis in Dei filium fuit commissum, seriò & grauiter exprobrarit. Postquàm vero illi peccatorum conscientia superati, salutis consilium quærere cœperunt, iisdem amicè & fideliter consuluit, eam salutis viam monstrans, quam & hodie omnes ingredi oportet, quicunq; saluari cupiunt. Nam poenitentiæ studium illis præscripsit, & ad Christum relegauit, cui externo & publico baptismo consecrari debeant, ut in illius nomine peccatorum remissionem & spiritus sancti donum consequi possint. Caeterum, quia non pauci erant, quorum authoritate à salutis via revocari, vel saltem vehementer impediri poterant, de illis etiam eos admonet, quæ prima præsentis loci pars est, cui postea consilij apostolici effectum & fructum Lucas subijcit, vnà cum eleganti veteris & primitiuæ ecclesiæ typo, quæ singula diligenti consideratione cum primis digna sunt.
units.tr: At the very beginning of the gospel sermon, Peter so arranged his speech that he sharply and seriously rebuked his hearers for the monstrous and atrocious crime they had committed against the Son of God. Afterwards, when they, overcome by the consciousness of their sins, began to seek counsel for salvation, he advised them kindly and faithfully, pointing out the way of salvation which everyone who wishes to be saved must still walk today. For he prescribed to them the practice of repentance, and referred them to Christ, to whom they ought to be consecrated by outward and public baptism, so that in his name they might obtain the forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit. But since there were not a few whose authority could draw them back from the way of salvation, or at least greatly hinder them, Peter also warns them about those things, which is the first part of the present passage. Luke then adds the effect and fruit of the apostolic counsel, together with a fine picture of the old and primitive Church, all of which is especially worthy of careful consideration.

units.la: De Petro sic tradit Euangelista: Plurimis alijs sermonibus testificatus est & exhortatus, dicens: Seruemini à generatione hac prava. Sufficiens videri poterat admonitio, quam supra vidimus, & quidem illa verae salutis rationem omnem comprehendit. Sed quia durum & graue videri poterat, veteri & avita religione abiecta, nouam amplecti, & multorum exempla obstabant, alijs etiam admonitionibus opus fuit, in quibus magno serio & vehementia singulari Petrum versatum fuisse docet. Nec enim simpliciter monuit, sed obtestationibus & exhortationibus vsus est. Omnium vero summa & scopus fuit: Seruemini à generatione hac prava. Seruandi verbo admonet, de salutis ipsorum periculo agi, quam, nisi ab his separentur, retinere non possint.
units.tr: Of Peter the evangelist thus reports: "He bore witness and exhorted them with very many other words, saying: Save yourselves from this perverse generation." The admonition we saw above might seem sufficient, and indeed it embraces the whole reasoning of true salvation. But because it could seem hard and burdensome to cast off their old and ancestral religion and embrace a new one, and because the examples of many stood in the way, other admonitions were needed. Luke shows that Peter engaged in these with great earnestness and singular vehemence. For he did not admonish them simply, but used entreaties and exhortations. Yet the sum and aim of them all was this: "Save yourselves from this perverse generation." By the word "save" he warns that their own salvation is at stake, which they cannot keep unless they separate themselves from these people.

units.la: Principio autem, de quibus loquatur, videndum est. Nam quanquam de vniuersa Iudaeorum gente hoc dictum videri posset, quæ sanguinis Christi ream sese fecerat, & omnium grauissimo scelere erat polluta: maxime tamen ad scribas & sacerdotes titulus iste referri debet, quos omnium malorum in illa gente præcipuos authores fuisse constat. Superbiebant illi splendidissimis sanctissimisq; titulis. Præterquam enim quod communem filiorum Abrahami titulum sibi vendicabant, legis quoque cognitionem penes se solos haberi arbitrabantur, & publice pro caecorum ducibus, pro lucernis in tenebris ambulantium, pro insipientium eruditoribus, & imperitorum doctoribus habebantur, vt ex Pauli verbis elucet. Rom. 2. cap. At Petrus magna cum ingenuitate illos prauam, peruersam, siue distortam generationem vocat, Baptistæ nimirum & Christi exemplum secutus, qui iam ante eodem titulo illos insignierant. Ab illo enim progenies viperarum dicuntur. Matth. 3. Hic vero illos generationem prauam & adulteram, imo diaboli prolem diserte nominat. Matth. 12. & 16. Iohan. 8. Nemo autem hoc maledicentiæ tribuat, quæ à spiritus sancti ingenio alienissima est, sed gravissimae causæ Petrum, vt hoc nomine illos notaret, impulerunt. Primo enim cum fidem Abrahami aspernarentur, quæ sola Dei filios efficere potest, interim filiorum Dei titulum sibi vendicarent, pro talibus minime censeri potuerunt. Deinde quia magna erat apud omnes illorum authoritas, eo quod munere olim diuinitus institute fungerentur, & sanctissimorum hominum successione sese vendicarent, necesse fuit illos argui, vt ab omnibus degeneres esse agnoscerentur, ne cui titulorum splendore & successionis gloriatione imponerent. Prudenter ergo, pie & fortiter agit Petrus, quando illos prauam & peruersam generationem nominat. Sic enim & illos fugiendos esse monet, & inani metu simplicium mentes liberat, quibus religio erat à talibus apertam secessionem facere.
units.tr: First, we must consider who it is he is speaking of. For although this might seem to be said of the whole Jewish nation, which had made itself guilty of the blood of Christ and was polluted with the gravest of all crimes, yet this title ought to be referred chiefly to the scribes and priests, who are known to have been the principal authors of all the evils in that nation. They were proud of the most splendid and holy titles. For besides claiming the common title of the sons of Abraham, they also thought that knowledge of the law was in their hands alone, and they were publicly regarded as guides of the blind, lights for those walking in darkness, instructors of the foolish, and teachers of the unlearned, as is clear from the words of Paul (Rom. 2). But Peter, with great frankness, calls them a crooked, perverse, or twisted generation, following the example of the Baptist and of Christ, who had already marked them with the same title. For the Baptist called them a brood of vipers (Matt. 3). Here Peter plainly names them an evil and adulterous generation, indeed the offspring of the devil (Matt. 12, 16; John 8). No one should attribute this to slander, which is most alien to the spirit of the Holy Spirit; rather, the most serious causes moved Peter to mark them with this name. First, since they despised the faith of Abraham, which alone can make the sons of God, while at the same time claiming for themselves the title of the sons of God, they could in no way be counted as such. Second, since their authority was great among all, because they held an office once instituted by God and boasted of a succession from most holy men, it was necessary that they be exposed, so that they might be recognized by all as degenerate, lest they impose on anyone by the splendour of their titles and their boasting of succession. Peter therefore acts wisely, piously and bravely when he calls them a perverse and crooked generation. For thus he warns that they must be shunned, and frees simple minds from empty fear, for whom religion meant making an open break with such men.

units.la: Admonemur Petri exemplo, quid hodie etiam factu opus sit. Arbitrantur multi, simplicem nunc damnā veritatis cognitionem sufficere, qua etiam inter veritatis studiosos mirifice gloriari solent. Interim vero impij conuersantur, & cum professis Christi hostibus, imo falsæ doctrinæ authoribus commercia exercent, quos ab euangelij ministris publice argui, indignissime ferunt. At longe aliam mentem Petro apostolo fuisse constat, qui fideles ab impijs separari vult, & impostores contra communem totius populi opinionem prauæ generationis titulo notare non veretur. Exemplum huius rei ex Christo sumpsit, qui pa.ssim falsos doctores vitare iubet, & illorum commercia pijs exitialia esse docet. Vide Matth. 7. 15. 23. 24. Iohan. 10. &c. Idem reliquos apostolos fecisse constat, qui parum se officio functos esse putarunt, si fui seculi impostores digito notarent, nisi de illis etiam nos admonerent, quos nouissimo seculo venturos esse, ex spiritus suggestione noverant: cuius rei testimonia extant. 1. Tim. 4. 2. Tim. 3. & 4. 2. Theff. 2. 1. Iohan. 2, & 4. &c. Horum ergo fidem & diligentiam imitentur, quibus hodie euangelij ministerium commissum est, quando eam esse constat ovium stoliditatem, vt lupos etiam admonitæ vix fugiant, imo tenuis lucelli spe illorum fauci bus se temere ingerant. Suis itaque coloribus depingant, & veris proprijsq; nominibus notent, quoscunque seductores esse intelligunt, nullo illorum respectu habito, qui vt priuato commodo consu-
units.tr: By Peter's example we are reminded what must also be done today. Many think that a simple condemnation of error is now enough, and they are wont to boast wonderfully of it even among the zealous for truth. Meanwhile, however, the wicked live among us and carry on dealings with the open enemies of Christ, indeed with the authors of false doctrine, whom they very unworthily bear it when the ministers of the gospel publicly rebuke. But it is clear that the apostle Peter had a very different mind, who wants the faithful separated from the wicked, and does not hesitate, against the common opinion of the whole people, to mark impostors with the title of a perverse generation. He took this example from Christ, who everywhere orders false teachers to be avoided, and teaches that dealings with them are deadly to the pious (see Matt. 7, 15, 23, 24; John 10, etc.). It is clear that the other apostles did the same, who thought they had not discharged their office well if they merely pointed a finger at the impostors of their own age, unless they also warned us about those who, they knew by the Spirit's prompting, would come in the last age. Evidence of this exists (1 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 3 and 4; 2 Thess. 2; 1 John 2 and 4, etc.). Let those to whom the ministry of the gospel is entrusted today therefore imitate their faith and diligence, since it is plain that the stupidity of the sheep is such that, even when warned, they scarcely flee from wolves; indeed, for the hope of a little gain they rashly thrust their throats into them. Let them therefore paint such men in their own colours and mark with their true and proper names whoever they understand to be seducers, having no regard to any of those who, for the sake of private advantage,

units.la: {*} Generatio prava, sacerdotes & scribae. lant, talibus patrocinantur. Discant etiam reliqui fidis admonitionibus parere, & professos Christi hostes fugere, quos nisi deuitent, pro Christi membris agnosci non poterunt. Moueantur saltem periculi metu, quod tam illis quam horum sectatoribus imminere scimus. Qui enim: Babylonem scortatio mum matrem exire detrectant, plagas, quas illi destinauit dominus, ipsi quoque sentient. Vide Apocal. 18. cap.
units.tr: {*} Perverse generation: priests and scribes. take counsel and defend such men. Let the rest also learn to obey faithful warnings and to flee the open enemies of Christ, whom, unless they avoid them, they will not be recognized as members of Christ. At least let them be moved by fear of the danger which we know hangs over both these men and their followers. For those who refuse to go out from the harlot Babylon, their mother, will also feel the plagues which the Lord has prepared for her (see Rev. 18).

units.la: Habemus itaque Petri de salutis ratione consilium, cui Lucas insignem illius effectum siue fructum subijcit. Ait enim: Qui libenter amplexi sunt sermonem eius, baptizati sunt, & additae sunt die illa animae circiter ter mille. Mira breuitate rem maximam diuinus scriptor comprehendit. Nam hic impletur, quod Petro, cum ad apostolatum vocaretur, a Christo dictum fuerat: Posthac homines viuos capies. Luc. 5. Qui enim paulo ante rudis piscator fuerat, euangelij sagena proiecta, tria millia hominum Christo domino sub fidei obedientiam adduxit: qui & libenter sermonem eius amplexi sunt, & in eodem perseuerauisse dicuntur. Admonet nos locus hic de duobus cognitu valde necessarijs.
units.tr: So we have Peter's counsel concerning the way of salvation, to which Luke adds its remarkable effect or fruit. For he says: "Those who gladly embraced his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added that day." The divine writer comprehends this very great matter with wonderful brevity. For here is fulfilled what Christ said to Peter when he was called to the apostleship: "From now on you will catch men alive" (Luke 5). For he who a little before had been a rude fisherman, having cast the net of the gospel, brought three thousand men under the obedience of faith to the Lord Christ. They are said both to have gladly embraced his word and to have persevered in it. This passage reminds us of two things that are very necessary to know.

units.la: Primo docemur, Dei verbum a pijs & fidis ministris nunquam frustra praedicari, quamuis multa sint, quae illius profectum impedire posse videantur. Testatur hoc apud prophetam dominus: Vt imber aut nix de caelo descendit, & illo non redit, sed irrigat terram, & parere atq; germinare eam facit, vt det serenti semen, & panem ad edendum: ita erit verbum meum, quod exit de ore meo: non redibit ad me vacuum, sed faciet quaecunque volo, & prosperabitur in his ad quae misi illud. Isa. 55. Exemplum huius in praesenti luculentissimum proponitur, cum omnia hic inuenire liceat, quibus verbi Dei profectus impediri potest. Populus natura rebellis & contumax, qualem Moses & prophetae describunt. Hostes doctrinae sunt quotquot in populo authoritate & potestate valent. Periculum ex recepta euangelij doctrina praesens, quando iam ante excommunicationis sententia in omnes lata erat, qui Christi partes sectarentur. Iohan. 9. Apostoli rudes hucusq;, viles, ignobiles & contempti. At omnia obstacula perrumpit Dei verbum, impetuosi imbris instar ab eo vento supremi numinis impulsum, qui Christo teste spirat vbicunq; ipse voluerit. Iohan. 3. Debet hoc nos consolari nostro seculo, ne de ecclesia Christi aut verbi profectu desperemus, quando multa passim contra hoc magno cum molimine ne insurgere cernimus, &c.
units.tr: First, we are taught that the word of God is never preached in vain by pious and faithful ministers, although there may seem to be many things that could hinder its progress. The Lord testifies to this through the prophet: "As the rain or snow comes down from heaven and does not return there, but waters the earth and makes it bring forth and sprout, so that it gives seed to the sower and bread to eat: so shall my word be, which goes out of my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I please, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it" (Isa. 55). Here is a most striking example of this, since here one can find all the things by which the progress of the word of God could be impeded. The people are by nature rebellious and stubborn, such as Moses and the prophets describe. The enemies of the teaching are all who have authority and power among the people. The danger from the accepted doctrine of the gospel is immediate, since a sentence of excommunication had already been pronounced against all who took the side of Christ (John 9). The apostles were until now rude, base, ignoble and despised. Yet the word of God breaks through all obstacles, like a violent storm driven by that wind of the supreme Deity which, as Christ bears witness, blows wherever it wishes (John 3). This ought to comfort us in our own age, lest we despair of the Church of Christ or of the progress of the word, when we see that many forces are everywhere rising up against it with great effort, etc.

units.la: Deinde quae fidei natura, quod q; electorum Dei ingenium fit, docemur. Duo enim his tribuuntur. Alterum quod libenter sermonem Petri amplexi sint. Quia enim spiritu Dei trahuntur credentium animi, mox veri illius & summi pastoris vocem agnoscunt, & sequuntur agnitam. Iohan. 10. Nec alia ex re maiorem voluptatem capiunt, quam ex verbi Dei studio, quo clementissimum illum patrem, vnicumq; saluitis suae authorem secum colloqui intelligunt. Alterum est, quod illos perseuerauisse Lucas tradit, quo non minus quam priori opus est: Nam Christo teste, qui perseuerauerit in finem saluus erit. Qui autem manu aratro admota, a tergo respexerit, non est idoneus nec dignus regno Dei. Matth. 24. Luc. 9. Haec si cum nostri seculi moribus conferamus, facile patebit quanta illorum sit infelicitas. Vix enim multis & assiduis concionibus pauculos aliquos lucrifacere datur. Et in illis, qui iam Christo nomen dederunt, vel negligentem verbi Dei contemptum, vel leuitatem detestandam est videre, qua ob leuissimam quanq; occasionem ab agnita veritate turpissime deficiunt.
units.tr: Next we are taught what the nature of faith is and what kind of disposition the elect of God have. Two things are attributed to them. The first is that they gladly embraced Peter's preaching. For since the minds of believers are drawn by the Spirit of God, they straightway recognise the voice of that true and chief Shepherd, and follow the voice once recognised (John 10). Nor do they take greater delight from any other source than from the study of God's Word, through which they understand that most merciful Father, the sole author of their salvation, speaks with them. The second is that Luke records that they persevered; this is no less necessary than the first, for, as Christ testifies, whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. But whoever, having put his hand to the plough, looks back, is not fit and not worthy of the kingdom of God (Matt. 24; Luke 9). If we compare these things with the manners of our own age, it will be easy to see how great their happiness was and ours is not. Scarcely can anyone win a few by many and constant sermons. And among those who have already given their name to Christ, one may see either a careless contempt for the Word of God, or a detestable fickleness, by which, on the slightest occasion, they most shamefully fall away from the truth they have acknowledged.

units.la: Sed ad Lucam reuertamur, qui paucis verbis primitiue ecclesiae formam, mores, ritus & exercitia comprehendit, cuius loci praecipuus vsus est, vt veteris & apostolicae ecclesiae forma hodie etiam agnoscere, & vbi illa collapsa est, restituere discamus. Erant (inquit) perseuerantes in doctrina apostolorum, in communicatione, in fractione panis, & precibus. Quatuor enumerantur, de quibus singulis quaedam dicenda erunt.
units.tr: But let us return to Luke, who in a few words sets out the form, manners, rites and exercises of the primitive Church. The principal use of this passage is that we may learn to recognise today the form of the ancient and apostolic Church, and to restore it where it has fallen. "They were continuing," he says, "in the teaching of the apostles, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Four things are listed, and something must be said about each of them.

units.la: Primus locus doctrinae apostolorum tribuitur. Quae vero illa fuerit, aliunde patebit. Christi praeceptum erat, vt ea docerent omnes gentes, quae ab ipso ante didicerant. Matth. 28. Idem in suo nomine poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum praedicare iusserat. Luc. 24. Quibus articulis totius legis & diuinae voluntatis cognitionem, ac vniuersam salutis rationem contineri constat. Eius doctrinae speciem in praecedenti Petri sermone vidimus. Et hanc doctrinae formam ab illis passim obseruatam esse illorum scripta abunde testantur. In ea ergo doctrina primitiue ecclesiae fideles perstiterunt, quam hodie apostolorum libris comprehensam & traditam habemus, nec ulla hic humanarum traditionum siue fine figmentorum mentio fit. Primum vero locum doctrinae tribuit Lucas, eo quod per hanc ecclesia colligitur, per eandem (ut Paulus monuit) fides traditur, adeoq; credentes omnes ex verbo immortali & aeterno regenerantur: de quo vide Rom. 10. 1. Pet. 1. &c. Discimus hic, primam in ecclesia doctrinae curam habere debere. Quia enim per hanc (ut modo dictum est) in fidei unitatem colligi nos oportet, fieri non potest, quin turpiter & miserè dispergantur, quicunq; doctrinas varias & incertas admittunt. Incertae autem & variae sunt, quaecunq; ab hominum arbitrio dependent. Quapropter apostolicam retinere convenit, quam Christo dictante olim didicerunt apostoli, & quam spiritu sancto illuminati, ecclesijs per totum orbem tradidere. Haec & certa est & simplex, perfecta denique & authentica, ut illam nec humanis figmentis farciri, nec alicuius hominis authoritate commendari sive confirmari necesse sit. De hac ipse Iohannes loquens, ait: Quod ab initio audiuistis, in vobis permaneat, &c. 1. Iohan. 2. Et Paulus nec sibi ipsi credi vult, imo ne angelo quidem caelitus delapso, si aliud evangelium aliamque salutis rationem praedicare ausit, quam quae ab apostolis primo tradita est. Arguit ergo locus hic inconstantes nostri seculi vertumnos, quibus volupe est in religionis doctrina ludere, quam pro suo arbitrio & priuati commodi ratione in dies mutare audent, sicut olim Ieroboamum fecisse legimus: 1. Regum 12. Quasi vero non alius religionis & doctrinae visus sit, quam ut inanibus terriculamentis in officio homines continere debeat. Arguuntur etiam leues isti, qui puerorum instar, contra Pauli praeceptum, seipsos quouis doctrinae vento agitari patiuntur. Ephes. 4. Fidelium enim & verè Christianorum prima nota est, apostolicae doctrinae fidelis & constans observatio. Eam quicunq; temere deserunt, fateantur oportet, se quid Christi ecclesia sit prorsus ignorare.
units.tr: The first place is given to the teaching of the apostles. What that teaching was will be plain from elsewhere. Christ's command was that all nations should be taught the things which the apostles had learned from him beforehand (Matt. 28). He had likewise ordered that repentance and the forgiveness of sins be preached in his name (Luke 24). It is agreed that the knowledge of the whole law and of the divine will, and the entire account of salvation, is contained in these articles. We saw an outline of this teaching in Peter's preceding sermon. And the writings of the apostles abundantly attest that this form of teaching was everywhere observed by them. In this teaching, then, the faithful of the primitive Church persevered, which we today have comprehended and handed down in the books of the apostles; nor is there any mention here of human traditions or of figments. Luke assigns the first place to teaching because through it the Church is gathered, and through it (as Paul warned) faith is handed on, and so all believers are born again from the immortal and eternal Word (see Rom. 10; 1 Pet. 1, etc.). Here we learn that the Church ought to take first care for doctrine. For since through doctrine (as has just been said) we must be gathered into the unity of faith, it cannot be but that those who admit various and uncertain doctrines are shamefully and wretchedly scattered. Uncertain and various, however, are all those things which depend on the judgement of men. Therefore it is fitting to keep the apostolic teaching, which the apostles once learned from Christ's dictation, and which, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, they handed down to the churches throughout the whole world. This teaching is both certain and simple, perfect in short and authentic, so that it need not be stuffed with human figments, nor commended or confirmed by the authority of any man. John himself, speaking of it, says: "What you have heard from the beginning, let it abide in you," etc. (1 John 2). And Paul does not wish even himself to be believed, nor even an angel fallen from heaven, if he should dare to preach another gospel and another way of salvation than that which was first delivered by the apostles. This passage therefore condemns the inconstant weathercocks of our age, who delight in playing with the doctrine of religion, and dare to change it day by day at their own pleasure and for the sake of private advantage, as we read Jeroboam once did (1 Kings 12). As if religion and doctrine were meant to be nothing more than empty terrors to keep men in their duty. Those lightweights are also condemned, who, like children, contrary to Paul's command, allow themselves to be tossed about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4). For the first mark of the faithful and truly Christian is the faithful and constant observance of apostolic doctrine. Whoever rashly abandons it must confess that he is wholly ignorant of what the Church of Christ is.

units.la: Secundò in communicatione ipsos perseuerauisse dicit. Intelligitur autem mutuae beneficentiae studium, iuxta illud apostoli: Beneficentiae & communicationis ne obliuiscamini. Heb. 13. Hanc autem commodissime doctrinae subiungit, eo quod per illam (ut modo dictum est) tanquam vnius corporis membra sub Christo capite vnimur. Quare tam laeta quàm tristia inter se communia habere debent, quicunque ita uniti sunt. Quo mihi Christus respexisse videtur, quando dilectionem fidelium & discipulorum suorum tesseram constituit. Iohan. 13. Et magna quidem & praeclara beneficentiae laus est, quod ei inter ecclesiae exercitia secundus locus tribuitur. Unde facile cernitur, quid de illis sentiendum sit, quos nulla egentium fratrum cura solicitos reddit, sed stertenti animo quosuis egere patiuntur, dummodo ipsis inter opes & mundi delitias versari liceat. Sed quia de his plura dicentur insequentibus, haec modo sufficiant.
units.tr: Secondly, he says they persevered in fellowship. This is understood as the zeal for mutual beneficence, according to the saying of the apostle: "Do not forget beneficence and fellowship" (Heb. 13). He most fittingly joins this to doctrine, because through doctrine (as has just been said) we are united under Christ our head as members of one body. Therefore those who are thus united ought to hold in common both joys and sorrows. Christ seems to have had this in view when he established love among his faithful disciples as their badge (John 13). Truly great and splendid is the praise of beneficence, that it is given the second place among the exercises of the Church. Hence it is easy to see what must be thought of those who are not made anxious by any care for needy brethren, but allow anyone to be in want with a sleepy mind, provided they themselves may live amid wealth and the delights of the world. But since more will be said about these things in what follows, let these words suffice for now.

units.la: Tertio loco fractionem panis recensset. Quo nomine Caenam illam mysticam Domini & salutoris nostri Iesu Christi intelligit. Voluit autem hoc nomine uti, quod in hac panis publice & solenniter frangitur, partim quidem ut dominicae mortis memoria celebretur, partim vero ut admonea-mur nos Christo Iesu mortis authores fuisse, quando ipsum propter peccata nostra pati & mori oportuit. Solius autem Caenae meminit, non quod baptismum ab ecclesia excludat, sed quod huius iam ante mentionem fecerat, quando illos baptizatos fuisse scribit. Et de illis loquitur, qui iam ecclesiae nomen dederant, non de illorum liberis vel nouitiis Christianis, qui postea accesserunt. Unde colligimus, baptismi iterationem fieri non debere, quia semel in Christi ecclesiam adoptatum esse sufficit. Alia autem Caenae ratio est, quam mortis suae solennem memoriam Christus esse voluit, quae etiam eo nomine frequentius celebrari debet. Interim hic veteris ecclesiae simplicitatem observa, quae ritibus & sacramentis a domino traditis contenta, nec noua fingere ausa est, nec vetera nouis ceremonijs commendare voluit, ne Christo praescribere videretur. Quanquam enim ritum & ordinem Caenae mysticae, quo illi usi sunt, Lucas non exprimat, nemini tamen dubium est, eos ad Christi institutionem respexisse, cum Paulus postea ingenuè fateatur, se formulam à Christo acceptam tradidisse fidelibus, eosque qui ab illa deflexerant, ad illius observationem revocet. Erant haec ijs observanda, qui cum evangelij nomine glorientur, tantum sibi permittere audent, ut Caenae dominicae ritum & ordinem, ab ipso Christo traditum, mutare non vereantur. Nam ut de luminaribus, vestium luxu, ineptis gesticulationibus, & infinitis alijs omittam dicere, quibus illi bono fortassis zelo Caenae authoritatem commendatiorem facere studenti, illud certè nulla venia mihi dignum videtur, quòd fractionem panis è Caena sustulerunt, dum panis mystici partes priusquam ad Caenam perueniatur, rotundas fingunt, easq; integras in ora fumentium inserunt. Quid enim hac sublata, nobis reliquum faciunt, quo vel mortis dominicae memoria refricetur, vel ipsi peccatorum & poenitentiae admoneamur? Atqui fractionem panis tantae in primitiva ecclesia authoritatis fuisse ex hoc loco constat, ut illius nomine vniuersam Coenam comprehenderint. Retinenda igitur est vetus simplicitas, quae si cui sordet, ne ille Christi authoritatem nimis audacter contemnit, cuius institutione illa commendata est.
units.tr: Thirdly, he lists the breaking of bread. By this name he means that mystical supper of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. He chose to use this name because in it the bread is broken publicly and solemnly, partly so that the memory of the Lord's death may be celebrated, and partly so that we may be reminded that we were the authors of Christ Jesus' death, since it was necessary for him to suffer and die for our sins. He mentions only the Supper, not because he excludes baptism from the Church, but because he had already mentioned it earlier, when he writes that those people had been baptized. And he speaks of those who had already given their name to the Church, not of their children or of the new Christians who came afterwards. From this we gather that baptism ought not to be repeated, since it is enough to have been once adopted into the Church of Christ. The Supper has another purpose, which Christ wished to be a solemn memorial of his death, and which for that reason too ought to be celebrated more often. Meanwhile, observe here the simplicity of the ancient Church, which, content with the rites and sacraments delivered by the Lord, neither dared to invent new things nor wished to commend old things with new ceremonies, lest it should seem to prescribe to Christ. For although Luke does not set out the rite and order of the mystical Supper which they used, no one doubts that they looked to Christ's institution, since Paul later frankly confesses that he had handed on to the faithful the form he had received from Christ, and calls back those who had turned aside from it to its observance. Those who glory in the name of the gospel ought to observe these things; yet they dare to permit themselves so much that they do not hesitate to change the rite and order of the Lord's Supper, which was delivered by Christ himself. For, to omit saying anything about lights, luxury of vestments, silly gestures, and countless other things, by which they, perhaps with a good zeal, have sought to make the authority of the Supper more commendable, this certainly seems to me in no way pardonable: that they have removed the breaking of bread from the Supper, while they shape the parts of the mystical bread into round pieces before it is brought to the Supper, and insert them whole into the mouths of those who receive. For, with this breaking removed, what do they leave us by which either the memory of the Lord's death may be refreshed, or we ourselves may be reminded of sin and repentance? And yet it is plain from this passage that the breaking of bread had such authority in the primitive Church that they used its name to comprehend the whole Supper. The ancient simplicity must therefore be retained; and if anyone finds it distasteful, let him beware lest he too boldly despise the authority of Christ, by whose institution it was commended.

units.la: Postremo de precibus loquitur, quod nos de publicis intelligendum esse putamus. Nec enim quid priuatim domi sua singuli egerint, docere instituit Lucas, sed quae publica veteris ecclesiae exercitia fuerint. Non potuit autem publicarum precum obliuisci, quas propria & insigni promissione Christus nobis commendauit, cum ait: Si duo ex vobis consenserint super terram, de omni re, quamcunque petierint, fiet illis a patre meo, qui in coelis est. Matth. 18. Et apud Ioelem prophetam afflictissimis temporibus publicas preces sedulo commendari legimus. Quia enim piorum siue credentium vnanimitate deus gaudet, non potest non ratas habere preces, quibus multi simul vno ore & corde in illum quodammodo impressionem faciunt. Nec frustra illas nobis commendari patebit, si quam multa nos vndiq; pericula circumstent, paulo attentius expendamus. Quare multis nominibus eorum caecitas & oscitantia deplorari debet, qui & domi suae priuatim Deum rarissime compellant, & publicas ecclesiae preces plane fastidiunt & negligunt, imo sacros coetus scurriliter irrident, quos propter verbi praedicationem & publicas preces ecclesia instituit.
units.tr: Finally, he speaks of prayers, which we think should be understood of public prayers. For Luke did not undertake to teach what individuals did privately at home, but what were the public practices of the early Church. Nor could he forget public prayers, which Christ commended to us with his own distinct promise, when he said: "If two of you agree on earth concerning anything they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven." Matt. 18. And we read that in the prophet Joel public prayers were earnestly commended in the most afflicted times. For since God delights in the unanimity of the pious or believing, he cannot but hold valid prayers in which many together, with one mouth and heart, make a kind of impression upon him. Nor will it appear in vain that these are commended to us, if we weigh a little more carefully how many dangers surround us on every side. Therefore the blindness and indolence of those must be lamented on many counts: those who rarely call upon God privately in their own homes, who plainly despise and neglect the public prayers of the Church, and who even mock the holy assemblies in a scurrilous way, though the Church established them on account of the preaching of the Word and public prayers.

units.la: Habemus ergo veteris & primitiuae ecclesiae exercitia, quam apostolicam & Christianam fuisse nemo opinor negabit.
