Perseuerauit illa in apostolorum doctrina, per quam collecta & baptismo initiata fuerat. Beneficentiae mutuae & publicae erga quosuis gentes fluduit. Coenae mysticae formulam, a Christo traditam obseruauit. Et in precibus constans fuit & assidua. His quicunque hodie fluduerint, pro ecclesiae membris & Christianis censeri debent, vt vt multis inuisi & exosi sint. Quoscunque vero ab his alienos esse viderimus, illos Christianos & apostolicos esse impossibile est. Gloriantur hodie ecclesiae titulo Romanae sedis cultores, & nos eo nomine haereseos damnant, quod ab ipsis secessionem fecerimus. At probent prius necesse est, penes se ecclesiae titulum esse debere. Hunc si merentur, cur apostolorum doctrinam negligunt? Cur illam ferro & igne persequuntur? Cur novis traditionibus eos grauant, quos a legis iugo sanguinis sui precio Christus asseruit? Cur bona ecclesiae principum & priuatorum hominum liberalitate in pauperum subuentionem collata, impudenter dilapidant, eaque scurris plerunq; & cynaedis distribuunt? Cur Coenam domini prophanant, & in sacrificium pro viuis & mortuis conuertunt? Cur publicarum precum loco theatricum boatum & cantum linguae peregrinae inuexerunt? Possent haec latissime diduci, vt omnibus palam fieret, ipsos ecclesiae nomine indignissimos esse. Sed sufficiat cogitandi ansam praebuisse non ignauis verbi auditoribus. Interim nemo inter nos, qui euangelij titulo superbimus, omnia sarta tecta haberi exisiimet, cum etiam nobis multa corrigenda supersint. Sonat quidem in ecclesijs nostris apostolorum doctrina. Sed quam vilis sit illius apud plerosq; authoritas, res ipsa docet. Charitatis & communicationis studium refriguit. Coenae vsus apud alios a veteri simplicitate multum degenerauit, apud alios nimium leuiculè contemnitur. Quanta vero in publicis precibus negligentia regnet, ex sacris coetibus iudicare licet, ad quos pauci rariq; conueniunt. Ad veterem ergo formam & nos emendari oportet, si non frustra ecclesiae titulo gloriari volumus.
units.tr: We have, then, the practices of the old and primitive Church, which no one, I think, will deny were apostolic and Christian. That Church persevered in the teaching of the apostles, by which it had been gathered and initiated through baptism. It flourished in mutual and public beneficence toward whatever people. It observed the form of the mystical supper handed down by Christ. And it was constant and persistent in prayers. Whoever flourish today in these things ought to be counted members of the Church and Christians, even though they may be hated and detested by many. But whomever we see to be alien to these things, it is impossible that they are Christian and apostolic. The worshippers of the Roman see today boast of the title of the Church, and they condemn us on the ground of heresy because we have seceded from them. But they must first prove that the title of the Church ought to be in their possession. If they deserve it, why do they neglect the doctrine of the apostles? Why do they persecute it with sword and fire? Why do they burden with new traditions those whom Christ freed from the yoke of the law by the price of his own blood? Why do they shamelessly squander the goods of the Church, gathered for the relief of the poor by the generosity of princes and private persons, and distribute them mostly to buffoons and catamites? Why do they profane the Lord's Supper and turn it into a sacrifice for the living and the dead? Why have they introduced, in place of public prayers, theatrical bawling and singing in a foreign tongue? These things could be spread out at great length, so that it might become plain to all that they are most unworthy of the name of the Church. But let it suffice to have offered an occasion for thought to those who are not idle hearers of the Word. Meanwhile, let no one among us, who glory in the title of the gospel, think that all things are sound and in order, since many things among us still need correcting. The apostolic teaching indeed resounds in our churches, but how cheap its authority is among many, the thing itself shows. Zeal for charity and fellowship has grown cold. The use of the Supper among some has greatly degenerated from the old simplicity, and among others it is contemned too lightly. And how great the negligence in public prayers that reigns may be judged from the holy assemblies, to which few and rare people come. Therefore we ought to be amended to the old form as well, if we do not wish to glory in the title of the Church in vain.

units.la: At miretur quis, quo praesidio primitiua ecclesia inter tam infestos hostes in vrbe sanguinaria tuta esse potuerit. Id Lucas indicat, dicens: Obortus est omni animae timor, multaque prodigia & signa per apostolos edebantur. Occulto igitur timore impiorum animi detenti fuerunt. Videbant ad mirabilem apostolorum audaciam & confidentem loquendi libertatem. Videbant subito mutatos, qui paulo ante Christi hostes fuerant. Videbant prodigia & signa per apostolos edi. Mirantur ergo & obstupescunt. Accedit his spiritus Christi, qui vt in electis filialem timorem, spem, fidem & obedientiae studium operatur: ita impios peccati conscientia turbat & horribiliter terret. Timent itaq; & trepidant, ne quicquam contra herbescentem Christi segetem audeant instituere. Ita deus in medio luporum suos tueri potest. Nec enim ex hostium vel voluntate vel potentia, sed ex diuina prouidentiae consilio dependemus. Hoc olim quoq; patriarchas inter sanguinariam Chananeorum gentem detem defensos fuisse legimus, domino in illorum animis tonante: Nolite tangere Christos meos, &c. Vide Psal. 105. Eodem praesidio hodie quoq; ecclesia tuta est, cui Christus se perpetuo affuturum esse promisit. His nos excitari & animari decet. In baptismo nomen Christo dedimus. Studeamus ergo ijs, quae Christianos decent, nec mundi conatus formidemus. Fides enim, quae victoria nostra est, vincit mundum. 1. Iohan. 5. Hac Christum vere ampleCtamur, quo duce & protectore superiores e-rimus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But someone may wonder by what protection the primitive Church could be safe in the bloody city amid such hostile enemies. Luke indicates this, saying: "Fear came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles." Therefore the minds of the wicked were held by a hidden fear. They saw the wonderful boldness of the apostles and their confident freedom of speech. They saw men suddenly changed who a little before had been enemies of Christ. They saw wonders and signs done through the apostles. So they marvel and are astonished. To these things is added the Spirit of Christ, who, as he works in the elect a filial fear, hope, faith and eagerness for obedience, so he disturbs the impious with the consciousness of sin and terrifies them dreadfully. So they fear and tremble, lest they dare to undertake anything against the sprouting crop of Christ. Thus God can keep his own safe in the midst of wolves. For we depend not on the will or power of enemies, but on the counsel of divine providence. We read that the patriarchs too were once defended in this way among the bloody nation of the Canaanites, the Lord thundering in their minds: "Touch not my anointed ones," etc. See Psalm 105. By the same protection the Church is safe today too, to which Christ promised that he would be present forever. We ought to be stirred and encouraged by these things. In baptism we have given our name to Christ. Let us therefore strive for the things that become Christians, and let us not fear the attempts of the world. For faith, which is our victory, overcomes the world. 1 John 5. By this faith we truly embrace Christ, under whose leadership and protection we shall be superior. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XIX.
units.tr: Homily XIX.

units.la: Omnes autem credentes erant coniuncti, & habebant omnia communia: possessionesq; & substantias vendebant, ac diuidebant illa omnibus, prout cuique opus erat. Quotidie autem perseuerantes vnanimiter in templo, & frangentes per domos panem, sumebant cibum in exultatione & simplicitate cordis, laudantes Deum, & habentes gratiam apud totum populum. Dominus autem quotidie addebat congregationi, qui salui fierent.
units.tr: All who believed were together and had all things in common. They sold their possessions and goods and divided them among all, as each had need. Day by day, continuing with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they ate their food with gladness and simplicity of heart, praising God and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the congregation daily those who were being saved.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus omnem nostrae salutis rationem in vnico filio suo, Iesu Christo, comprehensam esse voluit: ita salutem illam ad eos solummodo pertinere constat, qui ecclesiae membra sunt. Haec enim ideo Christi corpus dici consueuit, quod per fidem vnita vni capiti Christo connectitur, qui in singula membra salutis & vitae spiritum diffundit. Vt autem fieri nequit, vt aliquod membrum a corpore ex capite vitalis spiritus communicationem sentiat: ita impossibile est, Christi spiritu eos animari, qui ab ecclesia, quae ipsius corpus est, separati sunt. Quia vero ecclesiae Dei titulum omnes sibi vendicant: necesse est exactam verae ecclesiae cognitionem tenere, ne vel alij, vel nos ipsi nobis falso ecclesiae titulo imponamus. Quae causa est, quod D. Lucas spiritus sancti suggestione excitatus, veterem illam & primitiuam ecclesiam tanta diligentia describit. Huius enim descriptionis hic finis & scopus est, vt inde veram & absolutam ecclesiae formam constituamus, secundum quam tum de alijs iudicare, tum nosipsos regere possimus. Praemisit autem in hesternis praecipua & magis generalia rerum ad ecclesiam pertinentium capita, exponens nimirum, vt primi credentes Petri praedicatione collecti, & baptismo in Christi & ecclesiae ipsius consortium adoptati fuerint. Adhaec eorundem studia & exercitia recensuit, qualia fuere perseuerantia in doctrina apostolorum, communicatio vel mutuae beneficentiae studium, pius & legitimus mysticae Coenae vsus, & preces assiduae. At quia in his nonnulla insunt, quae ampliori declaratione opus habent, eam modo subijcit, & primo quidem communicationis rationem explicat. Deinde de publicis illorum coetibus aliquid dicit. Tertio reliquam vitae ipsorum conuersationem, & quae ad oeconomiam pertinent, describit. Tandem vero, quantum hoc studio profecerint commemorat.
units.tr: Just as God willed that the whole plan of our salvation should be comprised in his one Son, Jesus Christ, so it is clear that this salvation belongs only to those who are members of the Church. For the Church is called Christ's body for this reason: that, united by faith, it is joined to its one head, Christ, who pours the spirit of life into each member. As it cannot happen that any member of a body receives the communication of vital spirit from the head unless it is joined to the head, so it is impossible for those to be quickened by the Spirit of Christ who are cut off from the Church, which is his body. But since all men claim for themselves the title of the Church of God, it is necessary to hold a precise knowledge of the true Church, lest either others or we ourselves impose on ourselves the title of the Church falsely. This is why St Luke, stirred by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, describes that ancient and primitive Church with such care. For the aim and purpose of this description is that we may thereby establish the true and complete form of the Church, by which we may both judge others and govern ourselves. In yesterday's lesson he set out the principal and more general heads concerning the things that pertain to the Church, namely how the first believers, gathered by Peter's preaching, and adopted by baptism into the fellowship of Christ and of the Church itself, were brought in. Besides this, he recounted their pursuits and exercises: such as their perseverance in the teaching of the apostles, their fellowship and the practice of mutual beneficence, the devout and lawful use of the mystical Supper, and their constant prayers. But since some of these things need fuller explanation, he now adds it. First, he explains the manner of their fellowship. Then he says something about their public assemblies. Third, he describes the rest of their way of life and what pertains to household management. Finally, he records how much they profited by this zeal.

units.la: Ad communicationem pertinet quod dicit: Omnes credentes erant coniuncti, & habebant omnia communia: possessiones & substantias vendebant, ac diuidebant illa omnibus, prout cuique opus erat. Primo animorum coniunctionem illis tribuit, quae beneficentiae verus fons est. Quamuis enim Graeca locutio, ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, ad locum quoq; referri queat, commodius tamen de animorum coniunctione exponetur, cum sequentia abunde doceant, eos non vno in loco sed in diuersis domibus habitauisse. Animorum coniunctio beneficentiam peperit & omnis generis officia, quae eo vsq; processerunt, vt multi sua diuenderent, adeoq; sua omnibus communia facerent, ne pauperioribus aliqua daretur, vel impatientiae, vel defectionis occasio.
units.tr: To the fellowship belongs what he says: All who believed were together and had all things in common; they sold their possessions and goods and divided them among all, as each had need. First he attributes to them a union of minds, which is the true source of beneficence. For although the Greek phrase ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ could also be referred to a place, it will be more fittingly explained as a union of minds, since what follows abundantly shows that they did not dwell in one place but in different houses. The union of minds produced beneficence and every kind of duty, which went so far that many sold their goods and so made their possessions common to all, lest any occasion of impatience or defection should be given to the poorer.

units.la: Est autem diligenter inquirendum, quae communicationis huius ratio fuerit. Hanc enim quia non vident Anabaptistae & alij turbarum ac nouarum rerum studiosi homines, Platonicam quandam bonorum omnium communionem inuehere student, ac nefas esse clamant, si quis Christianus aliquid proprij possideat. Quibus paucis respondere poteramus, ex singulari exemplo communem & vniuersalem regulam non constituì debere. Sed propter simplices argumentis euincendum erit, illos turpissime falli. Primo autem cum illorum opinione diserta Dei praecepta pugnant. Is enim Oeconomię leges tradidit, & diuitum officia præscripsit, quibus minimè opus erat, si nihil proprij Christia-no possidere liceret. Paulus certè diuites, non opes omnes deferre vel abijcere, sed illis piè vti & Iani-tus operibus studere iubet. 1. Tim. 6. Idem eos, qui suis non prospiciunt, ethnicis deteriores esse dicit. 1. Tim. 5. Atqui quorsum cura & prouidentia in nostris alendis opus est, si nihil proprij possidere, sed aliorum bonis, tanquam communibus, vti debemus? Similiter à Deo furtum prohiberi constat, vna cum omni impostura, fraude & dolo. Quis vero furto locus esse poterit, si communia sunt omnia? At quia aduersarij exemplo nituntur, exemplis nos quoq; contra illos pugnabimus, & facilè euincemus, nequaquam hanc fuisse apostolis mentem fiue sententiam, vt rerum proprietate sublata, confusa bo-norum omnium communio inueheretur. Diues simul & Christi discipulus fuit Ioseph Arimathæen-sis, qui sepulturæ honorè dei filio exhibuit. Matth. 27. Idem de Nicodemo dicere licet, Lazaro item & sororibus, ac Simone leproso, qui & domos suas retinuerunt, & opes, quibus ad suorum & ipsius Christi discipulorum, ipsius sustentationem vsi sunt. Eodem pertinent mulieres, quæ Christo de suis (non alienis vel communibus) facultatibus ministrauisse dicuntur. Luc. 8. Constat præterea, domi-num nostrum nullius opes vnquam inuito illo vsurpauisse. Nam & asinum, quo in vrbem vehe-retur, precario accepit, & hospitium ad vltimi paschatis celebrationem sibi cum bona gratia patrūfa-milias concedi voluit. Quæ ergo iniquitas fuerit, homines in alienis opibus sibi plus iuris & imperij vendicare, quàm Christi exemplum patiatur, cui omnis potestas in cœlo & in terris data est? Et hoc ipso libro multorum exempla recensebuntur, quorum fides magnificè prædicatur, cum nec domus vendiderint, nec communia fecerint bona, quæ possidebant. Ex quorum numero Thabita, Lydia, Maria mater Marci, Simon coriarius, Cornelius Centurio, Philippus & plures alij habentur. Quid autem de Caio, totius ecclesiæ hospite, dicemus? Rom. 16. Quid de Philemone, qui & seruum habuit ære suo emptum, quod adeò non reprehendit apostolus, vt seruum fugitiuum ipsi remittat? Sed quid exemplis aliunde petitis opus est, quando præsens hic locus rerum proprietatem euidentissimè asse-rit? Primò enim possessiones suas vendiderunt Christiani. Quòd si rerum proprietate peccatur, ipsos alijs peccati authores fuisse dicemus, quibus sua vendidere. Imò illos dolo malo vsos fuisse constabit, ea alijs accepta pecunia addicentes, quæ diuino iure vt propria possideri non poterant. At alienissi-mi ab vtroq; flagitio haud dubiè fuerunt, quorum fidem, pietatem & religionem spiritus sanctus tam splendidè prædicat. Deinde distributionis hic meminit Lucas, qua vnicuiq;, pro vt opus habebat, da-batur, nemini vero liberum erat pro suo arbitrio quod vellet rapere. Accedit hūs, quòd nemo, vt sua vel venderet vel in commune deponeret, cogebatur, sed ex vniuscuiusq; arbitrio pendebat vniuersa beneficentiæ huius & communionis ratio, vt infra Ananiæ & Sapphiræ exemplo discemus. Quam-obrem communionis nomine non aliud quàm spontanea & voluntaria contributio intelligitur, ad quam singuli fidelium pro suarum facultatum ratione, quantum ipsis libebat, contulerunt, vt inde alerentur qui egeni & inopes erant, ne paupertate & impatientia superati, vel ad malas artes con-uerterentur, vel ad Iudaismum & superstitionem denuò redirent. Impulit hos diligens communica-tionis, quæ nobis omnibus in Christo est, consideratio, & ardens dilectionis dei studium, qua quisquis ardet, vt vbi fratrem egentem viderit, viscera misericordiæ claudere non poterit. 1. Iohan. 3. Erant præterea per voluntariam istam communicationem assuefaciendi primi credentes, ne opum iacturam, quam exoriente persecutione mox facturi erant, impatientius ferrent, cum illas iam pridem alijs ero-gare, & ipsi pauco contenti viuere didicissent, &c.
units.tr: Now we must inquire carefully what the manner of this fellowship was. For the Anabaptists and other men who are eager for disturbances and novelties, not seeing this, strive to introduce a certain Platonic communion of all goods, and cry out that it is wicked if any Christian possesses anything of his own. To these we might answer briefly that a common and universal rule ought not to be drawn from a single example. But since they are simple, it must be shown by arguments that they are shamefully mistaken. First, the plain precepts of God contradict their opinion. For he has given the laws of household management and prescribed the duties of the rich, which would be quite unnecessary if it were not lawful for a Christian to possess anything of his own. Paul indeed bids the rich not to surrender or cast away all their wealth, but to use it piously and to be diligent in good works (1 Tim. 6). The same Paul says that those who do not provide for their own are worse than unbelievers (1 Tim. 5). Yet why is care and foresight needed in providing for our own, if we must use nothing of our own but everything as if it were common goods? Likewise it is clear that God forbids theft, together with all deceit, fraud and guile. But where could there be any place for theft if all things were common? And since our opponents rest on example, we will also fight against them with examples, and will easily prove that the apostles never intended this, that the ownership of goods should be abolished and a confused communion of all goods introduced. Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and also a disciple of Christ, who gave honour of burial to the Son of God, was at the same time both rich and a disciple of Christ (Matt. 27). The same may be said of Nicodemus, of Lazarus likewise and his sisters, and of Simon the leper, who both kept their houses and their wealth, by which they served both their own people and Christ's disciples and Christ himself in supporting him. To the same category belong the women who are said to have ministered to Christ from their own (not others' or common) means (Luke 8). Moreover, it is certain that our Lord never seized anyone's goods against their will. For he took the ass on which he rode into the city by request, and he willed that a lodging for the celebration of his last Passover be granted to him by the householder with good will. What injustice, then, would it be for men to claim for themselves more right and power over others' goods than Christ's example allows, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given? And in this very book the examples of many will be recounted, whose faith is proclaimed splendidly, though they neither sold their houses nor made their goods common. Among them are Tabitha, Lydia, Mary the mother of Mark, Simon the tanner, Cornelius the centurion, Philip and several others. What shall we say of Gaius, host of the whole Church (Rom. 16)? What of Philemon, who also had a slave bought with his own money, whom the apostle so little reproves that he sends back the fugitive slave to him? But why need we examples drawn from elsewhere, when this very passage most plainly asserts the ownership of goods? For first, Christians sold their possessions. If ownership of goods were a sin, we would have to say that they were the authors of sin to others, to whom they sold their goods. Indeed it would follow that they acted with evil deceit, since they handed over to others what they had received for money, and assigned what by divine right could not be possessed as one's own. But they were most remote from either crime, without doubt, whose faith, piety and religion the Holy Spirit so splendidly proclaims. Next, Luke here mentions a distribution by which something was given to each as he had need, yet no one was free to seize at his own discretion whatever he wished. Add to this that no one was forced to sell his goods or to deposit them in common, but the whole manner of this beneficence and communion depended on the will of each, as we shall learn below from the example of Ananias and Sapphira. Therefore by the name of communion nothing else is understood than a spontaneous and voluntary contribution, to which each of the faithful gave, according to his means, as much as he pleased, so that those who were needy and destitute might be supported from it, lest, overcome by poverty and impatience, they should turn to bad arts or return again to Judaism and superstition. The diligent consideration of the communion which we all have in Christ moved them, and the burning zeal of love for God, which whoever burns with, cannot close his bowels of mercy when he sees a needy brother (1 John 3). Moreover, through this voluntary communion the first believers were being trained, so that they would bear with less impatience the loss of goods which they were soon to suffer when persecution arose, since they had long been accustomed to giving them to others and had learned to live content with little, etc.

units.la: Non igitur confusionis exemplum locus hic præbere debet, quo fanatici rerumpub. turbatores sibi patrocinentur, sed beneficentia in pauperes commendatur, quam in ecclesia sua semper florere voluit Deus. Notum enim est illud quod Deuteron. 15. cap. dicitur: Omnino non sit inte mendicus. Atqui non ignorabat Deus, semper fore quos dura egestas premeret. Sed eosdem publica inopia & egestatis exempla circumuagari, à charitatis ingenio, qua populum Dei constringi decet, alienissi-mum est. Et extant aliæ Dei leges, quibus ratio indicatur, qua pauperibus commodissimè prospici possit, ne ostiatim mendicare cogantur: de quibus vide quæ habentur Deuteron. 14. 15. 16. 24. &c. Hinc est, quod etiam prophetæ pauperes passim commendant. Et Christus illorum curam & sub-uentionem tanto præconio dignatur, vt testetur, se nouissimo die eos, qui pauperibus suo nomine be-nefecere, perinde remuneraturum esse, ac si in ipsum beneficia illa contulissent. Vide Matth. 25. & 26. Quæ instituřio tantum apud apostolos momenti & authoritatis habuit, vt pauperum curam ipsos suscipere non puduerit: imò cum Paulus & Barnabas sui ministerij rationem Iohanni, Petro & Iacobo reddidissent, de hoc vno illos admonendos esse putauerunt, ne pauperes negligerent, quos à Christo tam studiose commendatos esse sciebat. Galat. 2. Quid? quòd Paulus Corinthios hortatur, vt non suos modò alant, verùmetiam (quia opulentissimi erant) egenis Syriæ fratribus, quos maior premebat inopia, subueniant. Vide 1. Corinth. 16. Item 2. Corinth. 8. & 9. Et sanè magnam huius rei curam veteribus fuisse constat, si donationes & fundationes cùm principum tum priuatorum hominum consyderes, qui opes suas ecclesijs magna liberalitate contulerunt, vt illis & doctrinæ puritas conseruari & pauperibus subueniri posset. Hodie autem eò vsq; ascendit religionis contemptus, vt pauci & rari sint, qui priuatim de suo aliquid conferant, multi verò passim exoriantur, qui ab alijs collata turpissimè diripiunt & dilapidant. Sentient illi aliquando Christum vindicem, qui pauperum suorum clamorem non contemnet, & ecclesiæ suæ direptionem seuerissimè vlciscetur. Et periculum est, ne impijs ecclesiæ & fidei hostibus diripienda relinquant, quæ in Christi fratres, & membra distribuere dedignantur.
units.tr: This passage, then, should not offer an example of disorder that fanatics, the disturbers of the commonwealth, can use to defend themselves. Rather, it commends the beneficence towards the poor that God has always wished to flourish in his Church. For that saying in Deuteronomy 15 is well known: "There shall be no beggar among you." Yet God did not fail to know that there would always be people pressed by harsh need. For the poor to wander about as public examples of want is most alien to the spirit of charity, which ought to bind the people of God. There are also other laws of God that show a method by which the poor may be most conveniently provided for, so that they are not forced to beg from door to door. On these see what is found in Deuteronomy 14, 15, 16, 24, and elsewhere. Hence the prophets too commend the poor everywhere. And Christ thinks their care and relief worthy of such high praise that he testifies that on the last day he will reward those who have done good to the poor in his name just as if they had conferred those benefits on himself. See Matthew 25 and 26. This teaching had such weight and authority among the apostles that they were not ashamed to take up the care of the poor themselves. Indeed, when Paul and Barnabas gave an account of their ministry to John, Peter and James, those men thought they should be admonished on this one point, not to neglect the poor, whom they knew Christ had so earnestly commended. Galatians 2. What of the fact that Paul exhorts the Corinthians not only to feed their own, but also (since they were very wealthy) to help the needy brothers in Syria, whom greater want pressed? See 1 Corinthians 16, likewise 2 Corinthians 8 and 9. And it is certain that the ancients had a great concern for this matter, if you consider the endowments and foundations of both princes and private persons, who with great generosity conferred their wealth on the churches, so that both the purity of doctrine could be preserved and the poor could be relieved. Today, however, contempt for religion has risen so far that few and rare are those who privately contribute anything of their own, while many arise everywhere who most shamefully seize and squander what others have contributed. Someday they will feel Christ as avenger, who will not disregard the cry of his poor and will most severely punish the plundering of his Church. And there is danger that they leave to the impious enemies of the Church and the faith what they refuse to distribute to the brothers and members of Christ.

units.la: Sed ad Lucam reuertamur, qui publicos & sacros veteris ecclesiæ cœtus describit, dum illos quotidie in templo vnanimiter perseuerauisse dicit. In templo igitur conuenerunt sæpissimè, non quidem, vt Iudæorum sacris interessent, quæ per Christi sanguinem abolita esse nouerant: sed propter populi frequentiam, vt plures docere ac Christo lucrifacere possent. Docemur autem hoc exemplo, vndiq; cauendam esse occasionem prouehendi regni Christi, & eius gratia sacros cœtus & frequenter & in publico quidem colligi debere, vt verbum dei plures audire possint. Quia enim veritatis luce fideles reguntur, eius illos pudere non potest, nec tenebras quærunt, vt ij solent, quorum opera prava sunt. Iohan. 3. Christum certè semper in publico docuisse legimus, quo nomine se, cum caperetur & postea apud Caiaphàm, excusat. Luc. 22. Iohan. 18. Et Paulus apostolus sacros & publicos cœtus in priori ad Corinthios cap. 11. & 14. diligentissimè describit: quod nunquam faceret, nisi illos in religionis causa prouehenda plurimum momenti habere intellexisset.
units.tr: But let us return to Luke, who describes the public and sacred assemblies of the ancient Church, when he says that they persevered daily with one accord in the temple. They therefore met very often in the temple, not indeed to take part in the rites of the Jews, which they knew had been abolished through the blood of Christ, but because of the large crowd of people, so that they could teach more and win more people to Christ. We are taught by this example that every occasion for advancing the kingdom of Christ must be taken, and that for its sake sacred assemblies should be gathered often and openly, so that more people may hear the Word of God. For since the faithful are ruled by the light of truth, they cannot be ashamed of it, nor do they seek darkness, as those do whose works are evil. John 3. We read that Christ certainly always taught in public, and he excuses himself on this ground when he was seized and afterwards brought before Caiaphas. Luke 22; John 18. And Paul the apostle describes most carefully the sacred and public assemblies in his earlier letter to the Corinthians, chapters 11 and 14. He would never have done so unless he understood that they were of the greatest importance for advancing religion.

units.la: Duo autem veteri ecclesiæ tribuuntur, perseuerantia nimirum & vnanimitas, quibus tum semper aliàs tum maximè in conuentibus sacris opus est. Quia enim hos (vt aliàs diximus) singulari pro missione commendauit deus, frequens studium & diligens in his retinendis perseuerantia Christianos decet. Rursum, quia cætus isti, cùm docendi causa, tum propter preces publicas & sacramentorum vsum instituti sunt, vnanimitas cumprimis requiritur. Hac coniunctos esse decet verbi ministros, ne partium & sectarum authores sint, quales olim in Corinthiaca ecclesia fuisse scimus: sed vnanimi studio veritatis doctrinam vrgeant, & Christo discipulos adducere contendant, quemadmodum iis Matthæi 28. cap. præcepit. In precibus verò vnanimitatem plurimum apud deum ponderis habere, vel hinc constat, quòd dilectionis mutuæ studiū passim præcipitur, & Christus tam enixè hoc à patre flagitat, vt omnes credentes vnum sint, sicut ipse & pater vnum sint. Iohan. 17. cap. Eadem omnino est Sacramentorum ratio. Cum enim hac & Christi beneficia nobis obsignent, & Christianæ communionis ac vnitatis symbola sint, quorum vsu in vnum ecclesiæ corpus cooptamur, fieri nequit, vt his digne vtantur, qui hostilibus animis inter se dissident. Erant hac nostro seculo diligenter consideranda, quando vtrinq; plurimum peccatur. Qui enim euangelij doctrina & diutino illius vsu gloriantur, fere remissi sunt & ab omni studio perseuerantiæ alienissimi, quasi ad metā peruenerint iam, nec aliquid ipsis agendum supersit. Idem varijs & diuersis sectis scinduntur, seq; inuicem mutuis anathematismis deuouent. Vnde illud Pauli impleri necesse est, dicentis: Quòd si alius alium vicißim mordetis & devoratis, videte ne vicißim alius ab alio consumamini. Galat. 5. Nec mirum est, parum feliciter progredi euangelij cursum, quando nec perseuerantiæ studio flagrat, nec vnanimitate coniuncti sunt, quibus huius cura commendatißima esse debebat. Legat qui volet Esebij in octauum Ecclesiasticæ historiæ librum proœmium, & nostrorum temporum descriptionem luculentissimam quidq; nobis sperandum sit, inueniet.
units.tr: Two things are attributed to the ancient Church, namely perseverance and unanimity, which are needed at all times, but most of all in sacred gatherings. For since God, as we have said elsewhere, has especially commended these gatherings, Christians ought to show constant zeal and diligent perseverance in maintaining them. Again, since these assemblies were instituted both for the sake of teaching and for public prayers and the use of the sacraments, unanimity is especially required. The ministers of the Word ought to be united in this, so that they do not become authors of parties and sects, as we know they once were in the Corinthian church; rather, with united zeal they should press the doctrine of truth and strive to bring disciples to Christ, as he commanded them in Matthew 28. In prayers, indeed, that unanimity carries great weight before God is clear from this: mutual love is everywhere enjoined, and Christ so earnestly asks this of the Father, that all believers may be one, just as he and the Father are one. John 17. The reasoning about the sacraments is entirely the same. For since they seal to us both the benefits of Christ, and are symbols of Christian communion and unity, by whose use we are joined into the one body of the Church, it cannot happen that those who are divided among themselves in hostile minds use them worthily. These things ought to be considered carefully in our own age, when on both sides there is very much sin. For those who glory in the doctrine of the gospel and in its long use are for the most part careless and utterly without any zeal for perseverance, as if they had already reached the goal and nothing remained for them to do. The same people are torn into various and differing sects and devote one another to mutual anathemas. Hence that saying of Paul must necessarily be fulfilled: "But if you bite and devour one another, take heed that you are not consumed by one another." Galatians 5. Nor is it surprising that the course of the gospel advances without much success, when those who ought to have had this as their most pressing concern are neither aflame with zeal for perseverance nor united in unanimity. Let whoever wishes read the preface of Eusebius to the eighth book of his Ecclesiastical History, and he will find a most vivid description of our own times, and of what we may hope for.

units.la: His vero Lucas priuatam vitæ rationem, qua veteres & primi Christiani inter se vsi sunt, subiungit. Frangentes (inquit) per domos panem, sumebant cibum in exultatione & simplicitate cordis laudantes Deum. Quanquam enim quod de panis fractione dicit, aliquo modo de mystica Cœna (vt in praecedenti sermone) exponi possit, quia tamen communis simul cibi meminit, commodissimè de priuata vita ipsorum ratione & conuiuijs quibus se inuicem exceperunt, locus hic totus exponi posse videtur. Docet autem Lucas, non modò in publicum depositsse aliquam bonorum suorum partem qui opulentiores erant, verumetiam ex ijs, quae sibi reseruarant, beneficentiam in pauperes & in quosuis alios exercuisse. Et diserte quidem domorum meminit, vt constet, plurimos ex credentium numero domus suas vnà cum facultatibus suis retinuisse, quo confusa illa & seditiosa rerum communio, quam Anabaptistae fingunt, validissimè oppugnatur. Caeterum ea vitae & conuersationis ratio exprimitur, quae officij, amoris & beneficentiae mutua plena fuerit. Et quia conuiuiorum immoderato luxu & fastu plurimum peccatur, de ijs potissimum Lucas dicere voluit, in quibus tria ab illis obseruata fuisse dicit. Primò in hilaritate conuiuati sunt, iuxta illud Pauli: Qui miseretur, in hilaritate. Rom.12. Nam hilarem datorem diligit deus. 2. Corinth. 9. Abfuit ergo ab illorum conuiuijs malignitas, quae facit, vt nos beneficiorum pigeat: sed hilari & alacri mente quosuis excepere, maximè tamen eos, quibus victum deesse noverant. Ita enim Christus egenos inuitare iubet, qui collata in se beneficia rependere non possunt. Luc.14. Hilaritati simplicitas cordis iungitur, per quam animi integritatem intelligit, ab omni fuco & dolo alienam, quae illorum vitio opponi solet, qui cum alijs benefacere videri volunt, nō de aliorum salute & vtilitate cogitant, sed priuato duntaxat commodo & honori consulunt. Tertio loco gratiarum actionem commemorat, qua Dei beneficentiam celebrauerunt, qui vt omnia condidit, ita omnium conseruator & nutritor est. Vide Psalm. 147. Matth. 6. Quòd si verò tria haec simul coniungas, facile patebit, illos cumprimis temperantiae studuisse, quia hac sublata, nullus hilaritati & Christianae simplicitati, multoque minus gratiarum actioni locus superest. Ex his ergo oeconomia & conuiuiorum regulam sibi constituere debent Christiani homines. Sciant in his beneficentiae & charitati primum locum deberi. Hospitalitati igitur studeant, & seopum, quas habent, dispensatores, non dominos constitutos esse intelligant. Sint autem in largiendo laeti ac hilares, cum Christo teste, beatius sit dare quàm accipere. Actor. 20. Accedat his animi simplicitas & Christianis hominibus digna integritas. In primis verò Dei memores sint, illum omnium, quae vitae seruiunt, authorem agnoscant, ab illo petant necessaria, & eidem pro acceptis gratias agant. Per fidem enim & gratiarum actionem (vt Paulus ait) sanctificantur cibi. 1. Tim. 4. Exemplum huius in Christo habemus, qui nunquam fine benedictione siue gratiarumactione panem fregisse legitur, vt videre est, Matth. 14. & 15. Lucae 24. Ioban. 6. &c. Docent haec quid de illorum conuiuijs iudices, qui vel pauperes omnino negligunt, vel maligne illis largiuntur, gratiarumactionis obliuiscuntur, scurrilitate gaudent, & intemperantiam obstrepero cantu & intempestiua Musica magis accendunt. Extant contra hos prophetarum sermones, Isa. 5. & Amos 6. cap.
units.tr: Luke then adds the private manner of life that the ancients and the first Christians practised among themselves: "Breaking bread from house to house, they took food with exultation and simplicity of heart, praising God." For although what he says about the breaking of bread can in some sense be explained of the mystical Supper (as in the preceding sermon), yet because he is speaking of a common meal, this passage seems able to be explained entirely with reference to their private way of life and the feasts with which they welcomed one another. Luke teaches us that not only did the wealthier members put a part of their goods into the common fund, but also that from what they had kept for themselves they practised beneficence towards the poor and towards anyone else. He clearly mentions houses, so that it is evident that many of the believers kept their houses together with their possessions; by this the confused and seditious communal ownership of goods that the Anabaptists invent is most strongly refuted. Moreover, the manner of life and conduct described is one full of duty, love and mutual kindness. And because much sin is committed through immoderate luxury and pride at banquets, Luke wished to speak especially about those, in which he says three things were observed by them. First, they took their meals in cheerfulness, according to that saying of Paul: "He who shows mercy, let him do it cheerfully." Romans 12. For God loves a cheerful giver. 2 Corinthians 9. So there was no ill will at their feasts, which makes us grudge our benefits; rather they received whomever it might be, with a cheerful and eager mind, and especially those whom they knew lacked food. For Christ thus bids us invite the needy, who cannot repay the benefits conferred on them. Luke 14. Joined to cheerfulness is simplicity of heart, by which he means integrity of soul, free from all pretence and deceit, which is usually opposed to the vice of those who wish to seem to do good to others, yet do not think of the salvation and advantage of others, but look only to their private gain and honour. Third, he mentions the thanksgiving by which they celebrated God's beneficence, who as he created all things, so he is the preserver and nourisher of all. See Psalm 147; Matthew 6. If you join these three things together, it will easily be clear that they especially cultivated temperance, because without it there is no room for cheerfulness and Christian simplicity, and much less for thanksgiving. From these things, then, Christians ought to set for themselves a rule for household management and for feasts. Let them know that in these matters the first place is owed to beneficence and charity. Let them therefore be eager for hospitality, and let them understand that the goods they have are set up as stewards, not as masters. Let them be joyful and cheerful in giving, since, as Christ testifies, it is more blessed to give than to receive. Acts 20. Let simplicity of mind and the integrity worthy of Christians be added to these. Above all, let them be mindful of God, acknowledge him as the author of all things that serve life, ask him for what is necessary, and give him thanks for what they have received. For (as Paul says) food is sanctified through faith and thanksgiving. 1 Timothy 4. We have an example of this in Christ, who is never read to have broken bread without blessing or thanksgiving, as may be seen in Matthew 14 and 15, Luke 24, John 6, and elsewhere. These things teach what to judge of the banquets of those who either altogether neglect the poor or give to them grudgingly, forget thanksgiving, delight in buffoonery, and inflame intemperance with noisy singing and untimely music. Against such people there are the sermons of the prophets, Isaiah 5 and Amos 6.

units.la: Porrò ne quis tam ardens pietatis studium fructu omni caruisse putaret, quid hoc effectum sit, Lucas docet, cum ait: Habebant gratiam apud omnem populum. Dominus autem quotidie addebat, &c. Duplicem fructum commemorat. Primò, gratia & authoritate valuerunt apud omnes, qui nimirum mentis saniores erant. Nam palàm impijs illos terrori fuisse, supra dictum est. Docemur hic, vnde vera authoritas hominibus cociliari possit. Nimirum ex pietatis & gloriae dei studio. Ratum enim erit, quod per prophetam dicit dominus: Honore persequar eos, qui me honore prosequuntur: & qui me contemnunt, ignominiosi erunt. 1. Samuel. 2. Obseruent hoc tum ecclesiarum ac verbi antistites, tum qui in magistratu versantur. Sciunt hi, authoritate & gratia ipsis opus esse, sed non semper ea qua decet via illam assequi student, dum alij auram popularem immodicis obsequijs venantur, alij opibus accumulandis inuigilant, alij fastu & pompa seculari sese venditant, nihil interim de dei gloria & honore soliciti. At huius ardens studiu compendiosissima gloriae consequenda via est. Remunerator siquidem illius est deus, qui hominum corda facile in quamcunq; partem voluerit, inclinat, quisque suorum memoriam (vt Psaltes ait) custodit in aeternum. Psalm. 34. Accedit & alter fructus, quòd dominus quotidie addit ecclesiae alios quoq; qui salui fiant. Incrementum ergo accepit ecclesia, & qui prius ad illam accesserant, fidem in se quoq; augeri sentiebat. Nemo igitur frustra laborauit in vinea domini, modò vocationi suae sedulò inuigilet. Interim obseruabis domino tribui omne ecclesiae incrementum. Dominus (inquit) addebat quotidie congregationi, qui salui fiebant. mi fierent. Prædicabant quidem apostoli, & verbi prædicatione trahebant. At omnis studij ipsorum effectus vni Deo transcribi debet, cui soli in animos hominum ius est. Nam Christo dicente didicimus, neminem ad illum venire, nisi quem pater trahere dignatus fuerit. Iohan. 6. Explicatur hoc à Paulo eleganti agriculturæ parabola in priore ad Corinth. 3. cap. Et apud prophetam fatetur dominus, se velle legem suam animis fidelium inscribere, vt alia in institutione non sit opus. Ierem. 31. Unde alibi credentes proprijssime Θεοδίδακτοι, id est, diuinitus edocti, vel Dei discipuli dicuntur. 54. Sed & ipse Christus spiritum suum consultorem & magistrum nobis fore dicit, qui nos in omnem veritatem inducat. Iohan. 14. Arguitur hic illorum impudentia, qui sibi ipsis discipulos colligunt, quos suo etiam nomine volunt appellari. Et cum iisdem peccant, quicunque alios magistros, præter Christum, agnoscunt, & illorum potius quàm Christi nomine gloriantur, quos ab ipso Christo & Paulo graviter impugnari constat. Matth. 23. 1. Corinth. 1. & 3. &c. Nemo tamen hinc ignaviæ occasionem sibi dari existimet. Singuli enim suam vocationem respicere & in illa ambulare debent, effectum verò omnem non suæ industriæ, sed gratiæ Dei, acceptum ferre, qui in nobis pro suo arbitrio, quæ ipsius gloriæ & nostræ aliorumq; saluti seruiunt, operatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone think that such a fervent zeal for godliness bore no fruit at all, Luke shows what came of it when he says: "They had favour with all the people. And the Lord added to them daily," and so on. He records a twofold fruit. First, they were held in favour and authority by all who were, of course, of sounder mind; for it was said above that they were a terror to the impious. Here we are taught where true authority among men may be won: namely, from zeal for godliness and for the glory of God. For what the Lord says through the prophet will surely hold: "I will honour those who honour me, and those who despise me will be brought to shame" (1 Samuel 2). Let the ministers of the churches and those who hold office in the magistracy observe this. They know that authority and favour are necessary to them, but they do not always pursue them by the proper way: some hunt after popular applause with excessive flattery, others are intent on piling up wealth, others display themselves with worldly pomp and show, all the while caring nothing for the glory and honour of God. Yet the earnest pursuit of this is the shortest way to obtain glory. For God is its rewarder, who easily inclines the hearts of men towards whatever side he wishes, and who (as the Psalmist says) "keeps the memory of his own for ever" (Psalm 34). There is also a second fruit: the Lord daily adds to the Church others also who are being saved. The Church therefore received an increase, and those who had earlier joined it perceived that faith was growing in them too. No one, then, labours in vain in the vineyard of the Lord, provided he diligently attends to his own calling. Meanwhile you will observe that all increase of the Church is to be ascribed to the Lord: "The Lord," it says, "added daily to the congregation those who were being saved." The apostles indeed preached and drew people by the preaching of the Word. But the whole effect of their labour must be credited to the one God, to whom alone the hearts of men belong. For we have learned from Christ's saying that no one comes to him unless the Father has deigned to draw him (John 6). Paul explains this by a fine parable from agriculture in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3. And the Lord, speaking through the prophet, declares that he will write his law in the hearts of believers, so that there is no need of other instruction (Jeremiah 31). Hence elsewhere believers are called most properly theodidaktoi, that is, taught by God, or disciples of God (John 6:45). But Christ himself also says that his Spirit will be our counsellor and teacher, who will lead us into all truth (John 14). Here is exposed the impudence of those who gather disciples to themselves, and want them to be called by their own name. And those sin in the same way who acknowledge other teachers besides Christ, and boast in the name of those men rather than of Christ, whom it is well established were sharply attacked by Christ himself and by Paul (Matthew 23; 1 Corinthians 1 and 3, etc.). Yet let no one think that an occasion for idleness is given him by this. For each ought to regard his own calling and walk in it, and to ascribe the whole effect not to his own industry but to the grace of God, who works in us according to his own will, whatever serves his glory and the salvation of ourselves and others.

units.la: Hæc de veteris ecclesiæ forma dixisse sufficiat. Nostrum verò esse sciamus, iisdem studijs occupari, quibus illos olim intentos fuisse videmus. Scopus verò omnium esto Dei gloria & multorum salus, quos Christo adducere curæ sit. Sic enim fiet, vt gratia & authoritate valeamus inter homines, & nostrorum studiorum fructus saluberrimos recipiamus in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let it be enough to have said this about the form of the ancient Church. We ought to know that it is our duty to be occupied with the same pursuits in which we see those men of old were engaged. Let the aim of all be the glory of God and the salvation of many, whom it is our care to bring to Christ. For in this way it will come about that we may have favour and authority among men, and receive the most wholesome fruits of our labours in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: HOMILIA XX.
units.tr: HOMILY XX.

units.la: SImul autem Petrus & Iohannes ascendebant in templum circiter horam precationis nonam. Et quidam vir, qui erat claudus ab utero matris suæ, baiulabatur: quem ponebant quotidie ad portam templi, quæ dicitur Speciosa, vt peteret eleemosynam ab introeuntibus in templum. Is cum vidisset Petrum & Iohannem ingressuros in templum, rogabat vt eleemosynã acciperet. Defixis autem in eum oculis, Petrus cum Iohanne dixit: Respice in nos. At ille ipsis attendebat, sperans se aliquid accepturum ab eis. Petrus autem dixit: Argentum & aurum non est mihi: quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do. In nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge, & ambula. Et apprehensa manu eius dextera, erexit eum. Protinus autem confirmatæ sunt illius plantæ ac tali. Et exiliens stetit, & ambulauit, & ingressus est cum illis in templum, inambulans, & saliens, ac laudans Deum.
units.tr: Now Peter and John were going up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer. And a certain man, who had been lame from his mother's womb, was carried there, whom they laid every day at the gate of the temple called Beautiful, to ask alms of those who entered the temple. When he saw Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked them for alms. But Peter, fixing his eyes on him along with John, said: "Look at us." And he gave them his attention, expecting to receive something from them. Then Peter said: "I have no silver or gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk." And taking him by his right hand, he raised him up. Immediately his feet and ankle bones were made strong. And leaping up, he stood and walked, and went with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.

units.la: Idimus in ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, quæ primitiuæ ecclesiæ forma, progressus & incrementa fuerint. Fuit in his memorabile omnino, quòd credentes apud plerosque gratia & authoritate valuerunt, impijs autem terrori fuere. Inter alia verò miraculorum mentio facta est, quæ multa & varia per apostolos edita fuisse dixit Lucas. Quapropter ex illorum numero vnum delegit, per quod nouæ concioni occasio est exhibita, qua millia aliquot hominum in Christi agnitionem Petrus pertraxit, vt suo loco videbimus. Quia autem tam insignis miraculi huius vsus fuit, æquum est, vt singulas eius circumstantias ea diligentia excutiamus, quæ illæ à Luca descriptæ sunt, qui primò occasionem miraculi commemorat. Deinde claudi personam in qua illud editum est, describit. Tandem miraculi progressum, & quid à claudo, postquam saluti restitutus est, factum sit, indicat.
units.tr: We have seen, in what went before, what the form, progress and growth of the primitive Church were. In these things one thing was altogether remarkable: that the believers were held in high regard and authority by many, while they were a terror to the wicked. Among other matters, mention was made of miracles, which Luke said were performed by the apostles in great number and variety. Therefore he chose one of them, through which an occasion for a new sermon was given, by which Peter drew some thousands of men to the knowledge of Christ, as we shall see in its place. Since the use of this so remarkable miracle was great, it is fitting that we examine its individual circumstances with the care with which Luke describes them. He first mentions the occasion of the miracle. Then he describes the person of the lame man in whom it was performed. Finally he indicates the course of the miracle, and what the lame man did after he was restored to health.

units.la: Occasio miraculi ea fuit, quòd Petrus & Iohannes circiter nonam precationis horam in templum ascenderunt, quo tempore & claudus hic ad petendum eleemosynam eodem deportatus fuit. Nona autem diei hora illis erat, quæ nobis tertia pomeridiana est, vt ex ijs quæ secundo cap. de horarum ratione diximus, colligitur. Eam precationis horam vocat, eo quod stata in populo Dei horae habebantur, quibus publicae preces fiebant, quemadmodum tum alibi, tum apud Danielem cap.6. videre est. Et in lege matutinum & vespertinum sacrificium Deus instituerat, quod sine precibus actum fuisse, nemo sana mente dixerit. Vide Exod.29. Num.28. De meridiei hora, quae & ipsa precibus destinata fuit, infra cap.10. dicetur, ubi Petrus illa hora in domo Simonis coriarij precationis gratia in superius coenaculum ascendisse legitur. Nec temere fit, quod de precationum horis mentionem tam diligentem scripturae faciunt. Primo enim docemur, cum numinis invocatione omnia a nobis inchoari, perfici & finiri debere, quando absque huius gratia & auxilio quicquam a nobis feliciter & bene tractari, impossibile est. Nam cor hominis (ut Salomon inquit) deliberat quidem de via sua, dominus autem dirigit gressum eius. Proverb.16. Unde etiam Iacobus apostolus eos severissime corripit & accusat, qui nulla divinae voluntatis ratione habita de suis rebus ita deliberant, quasi illorum eventus & successus a proprijs ipsorum viribus dependeat. Iac.4. Deinde admonemur, disciplina in ecclesijs opus esse, secundum quam legitime & decenter (ut Paulus docet) fiant, quaecunque ad fidei rationem & cultum Dei pertinent. Fatemur equidem, Christianorum esse, ut ubiuis locorum puras manus ad Deum attollant, quando ubiq; & Dei auxilio opus est, & a Deo exaudiri possumus. Interim quia publicas preces peculiari promissione nobis Christus commendavit, illas praecipue nobis cura esse convenit, nec temere negligendi sunt sacri coetus, quos tum doctrinae tum precum causa olim instituros esse constat. Nec obstare debet, quod pleraq; in superstitionem postea degenerarunt. Hanc enim tolli oportet, veterem vero & legitimum usum restitui. Hodie praeter pulsum nolarum vel campanarum nihil nobis superest, quo cum summo mane, tum meridiano & vespertino tempore ad preces excitamur. Cuius superstitiosum usum multi accusant, sed ut solennes precationis horae nobis restituantur, pauci laborant.
units.tr: The occasion of the miracle was that Peter and John went up into the temple about the ninth hour of prayer, at which time this lame man was also carried there to ask for alms. Now the ninth hour of the day was, for them, what is our third hour in the afternoon, as may be gathered from what we said in the second chapter about the reckoning of the hours. He calls it the hour of prayer because fixed hours were observed among the people of God, at which public prayers were made, as one may see both elsewhere and in Daniel, chapter 6. And in the law God had instituted the morning and evening sacrifice, which no one of sound mind would say was done without prayers. See Exodus 29 and Numbers 28. Concerning the midday hour, which was also set apart for prayer, it will be said below, chapter 10, where we read that Peter, at that hour, went up to the upper room in the house of Simon the tanner for the sake of prayer. Nor is it without reason that Scripture makes such careful mention of the hours of prayer. For, first, we are taught that all things must be begun, carried out and ended with invocation of the divine majesty, since without his grace and help nothing can be handled by us happily and well. For, as Solomon says, "The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps" (Proverbs 16). Hence also the apostle James sharply rebukes and accuses those who deliberate about their affairs without any regard to the will of God, as if their outcome and success depended on their own powers (James 4). Next, we are reminded that there must be discipline in the churches, by which, as Paul teaches, all things pertaining to the account of faith and the worship of God are done lawfully and decently. We admit, indeed, that it is the duty of Christians to lift up pure hands to God in every place, since we always need God's help and can be heard by him everywhere. Yet, because Christ has especially commended public prayers to us with a particular promise, it is fitting that we take special care of them, and the sacred assemblies, which it is established were instituted for the sake of both teaching and prayer, must not be lightly neglected. Nor should it be an obstacle that many of these things later degenerated into superstition. For that superstition ought to be removed, and the old and lawful practice restored. Today, apart from the ringing of handbells or church bells, nothing remains to us by which we are called to prayer at early morning, midday and evening. Many accuse the superstitious use of this, but few take pains that the solemn hours of prayer be restored to us.

units.la: Praecipue vero apostoli nobis observandi veniunt, qui precationis hora in templum ascendisse dicuntur. Quod non sacrificij causa, quod tum immolabatur, factum esse alias diximus. Sed impulit eos cum precandi studium, tum quod docendi occasionem se inventuros esse sperabant. Nec propter ineptam Iudaicae gentis superstitionem, quae facile corrigi poterat, suo officio deesse, & occasionem rei bene & feliciter gerendae negligere voluerunt. Quo exemplo docemur, omnem a nobis occasionem captari debere, ut evangelij doctrina ac Christi cognitio proveniat. Iubet hoc officij ratio, quo Christus nos sibi devinxit. Ut enim is nihil eorum intermisit, quae nostrae saluti serviebant: ita nec nos nostro officio in regni ipsius terminis provendis deesse debemus. Ideo Paulus omnium ecclesiarum curam suis humeris sustineri debere putabat. 2.Cor.11. Et alibi aemulorum & adversariorum suorum conatibus gaudet, quod eos evangelio propagando aliqua ratione servire videret. Phil.1. Pudeat ergo nos nostrae socordiae & ociosos cantias, quae occasiones, quas ipse dominus nobis offert quotidie, nimium ociose tanter (ne quid gravius dicam) negligimus. Atqui hic cumprimis locum habet illud propheta: Maledictus, qui facit opus domini negligenter. Ierem.48.
units.tr: Above all, the apostles deserve our attention, who are said to have gone up into the temple at the hour of prayer. We have said elsewhere that they did not go for the sake of the sacrifice, which was then being offered. Rather, both their zeal for prayer and the hope that they would find an opportunity for teaching moved them. Nor did they wish, on account of the foolish superstition of the Jewish people, which could easily be corrected, to fail in their duty and neglect an opportunity of doing the work well and happily. From this example we are taught that every opportunity must be seized by us, so that the doctrine of the gospel and the knowledge of Christ may come forth. The reason of the office by which Christ bound us to himself demands this. For just as he omitted nothing of those things that served our salvation, so we too ought not to fail in our office of advancing the bounds of his kingdom. Therefore Paul thought that the care of all the churches ought to be borne on his shoulders (2 Corinthians 11). And elsewhere he rejoices over the attempts of his rivals and adversaries, because he saw that in some way they were serving the spread of the gospel (Philippians 1). Let us therefore be ashamed of our sloth and our idle lukewarmness, which, to say nothing more severe, too idly neglect the opportunities that the Lord himself offers us every day. Indeed, that saying of the prophet applies here especially: "Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently" (Jeremiah 48).

units.la: Secundo claudi personam Lucas diligentissime describit, in quo miraculum postea editum fuit. Ex qua descriptione miraculi excellentia & Christi virtus, qui miraculi author fuit, maxime elucent. Primo claudus fuisse dicitur ab utero matris, & ea quidem membrorum luxatione debilitatus, ut omni membrorum usu destitutum ab aliis gestari oportuerit. Quibus ex iis, quae postea sequuntur, aetatem iungito (nam quadragenarius fuit) & morbum humana arte incurabilem fuisse intelliges. Tales enim fere sunt, quicunq; vel ex natiuitate hominis inhaerent, vel diutina mora & aliquot annorum spatio in habitum transierunt. Atqui omnium horum finis est felicissimus. Nam ad Dei gloriam illustrandam faciunt, quae hominis calamitosi miseriam aggravare videbantur. Parua etenim Christi gloria videri potuisset, si illius virtute morbum, humana arte curabilem, depulisset Petrus. At cum eum Christi nomine sanat, de cuius salute nemo quicquam sperare poterat, Christum divina virtute & omnipotentia praeditum, & proinde verum Deum esse, evidentissime patet. Et hic plerunq; atrocissimorum malorum usus est apud Deum, ut per ea, quibus nullo hominum consilio sive auxilio succurri poterat, sui nominis gloriam illustret. Cuius rei exemplum cum hic, tum in eo, qui caecus ex natiuitate fuerat, Iohan.9. habetur. Nam discipulis, an ipsius vel parentum vitio factum esset, ut caecus nasceretur, interrogantibus Christus respondet: Neq; hic peccavit, neque parentes eius: sed vt manifestentur opera Dei in illo. Seruit hoc nostrae tum institutioni tum consolationi. Docet enim, ne de aliorum aerumnis temere iudicemus, quasi suis peccatis & sceleribus illas meruerint, qui ista laborant. Frequenter enim fieri solet, vt non alia de causa nos affligi Deus permittat, quam vt nomen & gloria ipsius per nos illustretur. Quare iudicium nostrum minime praecipitare conuenit, ne ad illum scopulum impingamus, ad quem Iobs amicos olim impegisse legimus, qui ex aerumnis colligebant, Iobem immanibus vitiis & sceleribus Dei iram meruisse. Simul vero hinc consolationem sumant, quorum tantae sunt calamitates, vt nihil spei & auxilij ipsis apud homines reliqui sit: ne videlicet propterea se a Deo quoq; derelictos arbitrentur. Quin Deo sese patienter exercendos praebeant, & breui experientur ad Dei gloriam & propriam ipsorum salutem pertinuisse, quae ipsi irati Dei indicia esse arbitrantur. Quo Paulus quoq; respexit, dicens: Scimus, quod ijs, qui Deum diligunt, omnia cooperantur in bonum. Rom. 8.
units.tr: Second, Luke describes most carefully the person of the lame man, in whom the miracle was afterwards performed. From this description the excellence of the miracle and the power of Christ, who was the author of the miracle, shine forth most clearly. First, he is said to have been lame from his mother's womb, and so weakened by a dislocation of the limbs that, having no use of his limbs at all, he had to be carried by others. If you add to this his age, which you will learn from what follows (for he was forty years old), you will understand that the disease was incurable by human skill. For those who suffer such things, either from birth or who have passed into such a condition through long delay over some years, are almost always of this kind. Yet the outcome of all these things is most fortunate. For they serve to make the glory of God shine, though they seemed to aggravate the misery of this unhappy man. For the glory of Christ would have seemed small if Peter had driven away by Christ's power a disease that could be cured by human art. But when he heals him in the name of Christ, from whose salvation no one could hope for anything, it is most clearly evident that Christ is endowed with divine power and omnipotence, and therefore that he is true God. And here, as often, God makes use of the most atrocious evils, so that through those things which could be relieved by no counsel or help of men, he may illustrate the glory of his own name. We have an example of this both here and in the man who was blind from birth (John 9). For when the disciples asked whether it was the sin of this man or of his parents that caused him to be born blind, Christ answered: "Neither this man sinned, nor his parents, but that the works of God might be made manifest in him." This serves both our instruction and our consolation. For it teaches us not to judge rashly the troubles of others, as if those who suffer these things had deserved them by their own sins and crimes. For it often happens that God allows us to be afflicted for no other reason than that his name and glory may be illustrated through us. Therefore we ought by no means to make our judgment hasty, lest we strike against that rock against which we read that Job's friends once struck, who gathered from his troubles that Job had deserved God's anger by monstrous vices and crimes. At the same time, let those whose calamities are so great that no hope or help is left to them from men take comfort from this, lest they think on that account that they have also been forsaken by God. Rather, let them offer themselves to be patiently exercised by God, and they will soon experience that what they think are signs of God's anger has served the glory of God and their own salvation. Paul also looked to this, saying: "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God" (Romans 8).

units.la: Accidit deplorato hominis morbo, quod egenum fuisse, Lucas testatur. Et extremae inopiae argumentum est, quod quotidie ad portam templi, quae propter structuram magnificentiam Speciosa nomen acceperat, deponitur, vt a praetereuntibus eleemosynam, vnde alatur, exigat. Atqui hoc contra legem domini factum esse, ex ijs, quae proximis sermonibus dicta sunt, patet. Dei enim lex extat, quae mendicum in Israele esse prohibet. Deut. 15. Et multa habentur de pauperum subuentione a Deo tradita, quam ita institui voluit, ne fratres publica egestatis & miseriae exempla esse paterentur. Quorum illos immemores fuisse miseri huius exemplum abunde docet, quem Hierosolymitanum & opulentissimae vrbis incolam fuisse ex eo patet, quod ad templi portam quotidie defertur. Et tamen inter fratres & innumerabilem sacerdotum turbam, victum mendicare cogitur. Tales & alij describuntur, Ioan. 9. & Marc. 10. cap. Arguit hoc summam Iudaicae gentis corruptionem. Quia hinc constat, opes, quas pauperum alimoniae destinarat Deus, ab ipsis alienatas & per abusum alio translatas fuisse. Adeo verum est, nihil inter illos integri manere, qui in Dei cultu contra verbum ipsius temere dispensare audent. Atqui extremam hanc corruptionem extremum excidium paulo post secutum est. Unde aestimare licet, quid nobis hodie sperandum sit, qui eodem cum Iudaeis crimine tenemur. Nam & ipsi contra primitiuae ecclesiae exemplum mendicos esse patimur, quos fratrum loco habere & amare debebamus. Dissipatus est verus ecclesiasticorum bonorum vsus per Papistas, & otiosis hominibus cesserunt, ex quibus ecclesiae pauperes alioportuerat. Licet vero superstitiones & idololatriam ause-rant, qui euangelij titulo gloriantur, hic tamen fere omnes ecclesiae reformationes pedem fixerunt, vbi de bonorum ecclesiasticorum vero vsu & Christiana pauperum subuentione agitur. Quo argumento patet, oblerosq; sub euangelij praetextu priuato duntaxat commodo studere. At non deerit suo officio Christus, qui pauperum vindex nouissimo die venturus est. Vide Matth. 25.
units.tr: It happened that, besides his incurable illness, the man was poor, as Luke testifies. The clearest sign of his utter want is that every day he was set down at the gate of the temple, which was called Beautiful because of its magnificent construction, so that he might beg from passers-by the alms on which he lived. Yet from what was said in the preceding sermons it is plain that this was done contrary to the Lord's law, for God's law exists which forbids there to be a beggar in Israel (Deut. 15). God has also given many instructions on the relief of the poor, which he wished to be arranged so that the brothers would not allow public examples of want and misery to exist. That this man was a case in point shows well enough that they had forgotten these instructions. He was a native of Jerusalem and an inhabitant of the richest city, as is clear from the fact that he was carried daily to the temple gate, and yet among his brothers and an countless crowd of priests he was forced to beg for his food. Such men are described elsewhere too (John 9; Mark 10). This shows the great corruption of the Jewish nation, for it is evident that the wealth which God had designated for the feeding of the poor had been diverted from them and transferred to other uses by abuse. So true it is that nothing remains whole among those who rashly dare to dispense in the worship of God contrary to his word. And indeed this extreme corruption was followed soon after by the utmost destruction. From this we may judge what we ought to expect today, we who are held guilty of the same crime as the Jews. For we too, contrary to the example of the primitive Church, suffer beggars to exist, whom we ought to regard as brothers and love. The true use of ecclesiastical goods has been squandered by the Papists, and it has passed to idle men, from whom the poor of the Church ought to have been supported. Yet although those who boast of the title of the gospel have removed superstitions and idolatry, almost all the reformations of the Church have taken root here, where the true use of Church goods and Christian relief of the poor are concerned. By this argument it is clear that they are guilty, and that under the pretext of the gospel they pursue only private advantage. But Christ, who is to come on the last day as the avenger of the poor, will not fail in his duty. See Matt. 25.

units.la: Postremo in claudi personam considerandum venit, quod ab apostolis quoq; eleemosynam postulare dicitur. At cum quotidie ad templi portam deponeretur, haud verisimile est, ipsum miraculorum, quae per apostolos quotidie edebantur, prorsus ignarum fuisse. Cur igitur non corporis potius salutem postulat? Num ex nostri saeculi mendicorum ingenio ipsum aestimabimus, qui morbos ipsi sibi conficiunt, & medicinam omnem repudiunt, quo maius ex mendicitate lucrum faciant? Absit. Nec enim in tam prophanum Dei & gratiae diuinae contemptorem tantum beneficium cadere potuisset. Ea potius mihi causa videtur, quod de morbi curatione totus iam desperauerat. Extabant quidem multorum exempla, quos priscinae sanitati Christus Iesus restituerat, sed neminem ab ipso curatu esse nouerat, qui ex vtero matris claudus natus esset. Quare cum valetudinem bonam ne sperare quidem ausit, illam a quoquam petere absurdum esse existimat, nec alia de re quam victu quotidiano solicitus, quae ad hunc pertinebat, ab apostolis exigit. At plus accipit, quam vel sperare vel petere audeat. Nam & morbo liberatur, & insigne bonitatis & gloriae Dei vas efficitur, quo in multorum salutem Deus vti voluit. Est haec eximia in nos Dei bonitas, quia frequenter nostram spem & preces praevenire & superare solet, vt & plura & maiora largiatur, quam nobis sperare liceat. Sic Abrahae, de Ismaelis duntaxat vita solicito, Isaacum ex Sara filium pollicetur. Gen. 17. Sic Israelem, qui vix liberationem ex Aegypto sperare poterat, cum omni substantia, additis simul Aegyptiorum bonis, eduxit. Exod. 12. Eandem bonitatem Dauid experitur & praeclare praedicat, quando Messiae e sua stirpe nasciturí promissionem, quam nunquam postulare ausus fuisset, accipit. 2. Sam. 7. Praetereo mul-
units.tr: Finally, we must consider the person of the lame man, who is said to have begged alms even from the apostles. But since he was laid daily at the gate of the temple, it is hardly likely that he was utterly ignorant of the miracles that the apostles were working every day. Why then did he not ask for the restoration of his body rather than for alms? Shall we judge him by the character of the beggars of our own age, who bring illnesses upon themselves and refuse every remedy so that they may profit more from begging? Far from it. Such a benefit could never have fallen upon a man so profane a despiser of God and of divine grace. The reason seems rather to be that he had already given up all hope of being cured of his disease. Indeed there were many examples of men whom Christ Jesus had restored to their former health, but he knew of no one who had been healed by Christ from birth, that is, lame from his mother's womb. Therefore, since he did not even dare to hope for good health, he thought it absurd to ask it of anyone, and, anxious only about his daily food, which was what concerned him, he asked the apostles for that. Yet he received more than he dared either to hope for or to ask. For he was both freed from his disease and became a remarkable vessel of God's goodness and glory, which God wished to use for the salvation of many. This is the outstanding goodness of God towards us: it is accustomed to anticipate and exceed our hope and our prayers, so that it bestows more and greater things than we may hope for. So Abraham, who was concerned only for the life of Ishmael, was promised a son Isaac by Sarah. Gen. 17. So God led Israel out of Egypt with all their possessions, and with the goods of the Egyptians added besides, when they could hardly hope for deliverance from Egypt. Exod. 12. David experienced the same goodness and proclaims it nobly, when he receives the promise that the Messiah would be born from his line, a promise he had never dared to ask for. 2. Sam. 7. I pass over many examples of this kind, since we experience similar things every day: when we are thinking only of those things which can serve the body alone, God of his own accord offers us in his Son that blessedness of his heavenly kingdom which surpasses all human sense and the capacity of the mind. Isa. 64.

units.la: Mendicus. ta huius generis, eo quod similia ipsi experimur quotidie: quando de ijs, quae soli corpori seruire poterant, cogitantibus nobis, in filio suo eam regni sui caelestis beatitudinem sponte offert, quae omnem hominis sensum & ingenij captum superat. Ila. 64. Discamus igitur bonitati & gratiae ipsius confidere, nec de voluntate ipsius, quae liberalior est & beneficentior, quam ut nostris votis sine desideriis exhauriri possit, desperemus.
units.tr: Beggar. I pass over many examples of this kind, since we experience similar things every day: when we are thinking only of what can serve the body, he of his own accord offers us in his Son that blessedness of his heavenly kingdom which surpasses all human sense and understanding. Isa. 64. Let us therefore learn to trust in his goodness and grace, and not despair of his will, which is too generous and bountiful to be exhausted by our prayers without leaving any desires unfulfilled.

units.la: Transeamus autem ad tertiam historiae partem, quae miraculi per Petrum editi descriptionem diligentem continet, cuius circumstantiae nobis quoque non minus diligenter consyderandae sunt. Ab attentione vero orditur Petrus, clauso dicens: Respice in nos. Vult eo dicto attentum reddere, ut beneficij, quod mox accepturus erat, authorem agnosceret, ne quid vel fortuito vel humana arte, aut etiam magicis praestigijs factum putaret. Constat enim eos tantum Dei beneficia cum fructu percipere qui in Deum authorem respiciunt, & illi gloriam omnem & gratiarum actionem tribuunt. At qui in gelido Christo in solis ministris haerent, ijs fere miracula superstitionum causa sunt: ut in nostri saeculi hominibus est videre, qui diu orum cultum miraculis per illos editis praecipue defendunt. Modestia vero est, quod non de se solo Petrus loquitur, sed ait: Respice in nos. Simul ergo Ioannem collegam & Symmystā agnoscit, multum alienus a Pontificum fastu, qui cum Petri successores haberi velint, episcopi omnibus imperiose dominantur, & sibi solis omnem in ecclesia potestatem vendicant.
units.tr: We now pass to the third part of the story, which contains a careful description of the miracle wrought through Peter, and whose circumstances we must likewise consider no less carefully. Peter begins with attentiveness, saying, "Look upon us." By these words he wishes to make them attentive, so that they may recognise the author of the benefit they were about to receive, and not think that anything was done by chance, by human skill, or even by magical trickery. For it is certain that people receive God's benefits with profit only when they look to God as the author and give him all the glory and thanks. But those who cling to a dead Christ and to ministers alone, for them miracles are generally a cause of superstition, as we can see among the men of our own age, who chiefly defend the worship of the dead by miracles performed through them. Yet there is modesty in the fact that Peter does not speak of himself alone, but says, "Look upon us." At the same time he acknowledges John as his colleague and fellow-minister, very far removed from the pride of the Pontiffs, who, though they wish to be held the successors of Peter, lord it over everyone imperiously, and claim for themselves alone all power in the Church.

units.la: Deinde, cum claudi animum & spem pecuniae accipiendae nnn ignoraret, eam eximere & maiorem illi spem facere studet, dicens: Argentum & aurum non est mihi, quod autem habeo, hoc tibi do. Spiritualium enim bonorum & mysteriorum Dei (ut Paulus ait) dispensatores sunt apostoli, non pecuniarum, quales plerunque impijs maiori copia quam pijs affluere videmus. 1. Cor. 4. Duo autem profitetur Petrus, quorum observatio non parum iuvare potest. Primo paupertatem testatur, & quod argentum sive aurum non possideat. Erat enim ex illorum numero, qui omnia reliquerant, & Christum erant secuti. Mar. 10. Quare mundi opes habere non potuit. Num vero illum ideo infelicem & miserum putabimus? Absit. Nemo igitur felicitatem opibus & mundi huius bonis metiatur. Nam miser esse non potest, qui Christum possidet, licet opibus & bonis vniuersis spoliatus, cum Petro nec aurum nec argentum habeat. Quod si vero Petrus ista caruit, unde tanta horum copia Petri successoribus contigit? Quod obsecro & unde Petri patrimonium, quod hodie non modo auri & argenti amplissimos census, verumetiam terras & regna tota comprehendit? Scripturis certe nihil de hoc traditum habemus, nec fide digna historia aliquam eius rei mentionem faciunt. Vnus Iudas habetur, qui argentum & aurum malis artibus acquirere studuit, quod illi desperationis & exitij causam dedit. Et de Antichristo oraculum extat, quod thesauros terrae possessurus fit. Dan. 11. Desinant ergo Petri patrimonio gloriari Pontifices, cum illos Petrus tam libere mendacij arguat. Sed cur desinerent, qui eo impudentiae processerunt, ut verbis Petri per ludibrium abuti non verentur? quando novus Papa e sede, quam illi stercorariam vocant, subleuatus, pecuniam vilem, cui nihil vel auri vel argenti inest, in populum spargens, ait: Argentum & aurum non est mihi, &c.
