Mox vero in alium locum translatus, suis creaturis aurum & argentum distribuit, illis acclamantibus: Dispersit, dedit pauperibus, iustitia eius manet in saeculum saeculi, &c. Quid obsecro est verbum Dei ludibrio habere, si hoc non est? Egregie profecto iustorum hominum impios & degeneres animos Thomas Aquinas perstrinxit. Cum enim in Concilio Lugdunensi Neapolitanae pecuniae ad Gregorium X. deferretur, non potuit eum Thomae dicere: Non possumus nunc, ut olim Petrus, dicere: Aurum & argentum non habemus. At huic ille respondit: Sed nec dicere potes: Surge & ambula. Vidit enim vir doctissimus, Pontificum auaritia & ecclesiam dissipari & dona spiritus sancti restingui, quae veterem ecclesiam olim illustrabat. Vident hoc hodie plerique, sed ea est nostri saeculi peruersitas, ut multi scientes seducere velint. Nos vero, quorum oculos euangelij lux illustrauit, fugiamus illorum laqueos & impudentem tyranidem, neque nos illis vltra illudendos & expilandos propinemus.
units.tr: Next, since he knew that the lame man's mind and hope were set on receiving money, Peter strives to remove this and to give him a greater hope, saying: "Silver and gold I have none; but what I have, that I give you." For the apostles are, as Paul says, dispensers of spiritual goods and of the mysteries of God, not of money, which we generally see flowing in greater abundance to the wicked than to the godly (1 Cor. 4). Peter professes two things, the observance of which can help us not a little. First, he testifies to his poverty, and that he possesses neither silver nor gold. For he was of the number of those who had left everything and followed Christ (Mark 10). Therefore he could not have the riches of the world. Shall we then think him unhappy and wretched on that account? Far from it. Let no one measure happiness by wealth and the goods of this world. For he cannot be wretched who possesses Christ, even though he is stripped of all riches and goods, and, like Peter, has neither gold nor silver. But if Peter lacked these things, whence has such abundance of them fallen to the successors of Peter? I ask, and from where comes the patrimony of Peter, which today embraces not only the vast revenues of gold and silver, but also lands and whole kingdoms? Certainly we have nothing handed down in the Scriptures about this, nor do trustworthy histories make any mention of such a thing. Only Judas is recorded as having eagerly sought silver and gold by wicked arts, which brought him to despair and to his end. And there is an oracle about Antichrist, that he will possess the treasures of the earth (Dan. 11). Let the Pontiffs therefore cease to boast of Peter's patrimony, since Peter so freely convicts them of falsehood. But why should they cease, who have gone so far in shamelessness that they do not hesitate to abuse the words of Peter for mockery? When a new Pope, raised up from that seat which they call dung-heap (stercoraria), scatters base money among the people, in which there is neither gold nor silver, and says: "Silver and gold I have not," etc. Soon afterwards, moved to another place, he distributes gold and silver to his creatures, while they cry out: "He has scattered, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever," etc. What, I ask, is this but making a mockery of the Word of God? Thomas Aquinas, a truly learned man, excellently censured the impious and degenerate minds of such men. For when Neapolitan money was brought before Gregory X at the Council of Lyons, Thomas could not refrain from saying to him: "We cannot now say, as Peter once did: I have neither gold nor silver." But Gregory answered him: "Nor can you say: Rise and walk." For that most learned man saw that through the avarice of the Pontiffs the Church was being destroyed and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which once illuminated the ancient Church, were being quenched. Many see this today, but such is the perversity of our age that many, knowing it, wish to deceive. But we, whose eyes the light of the gospel has illuminated, let us flee their snares and their shameless tyranny, and let us not expose ourselves any longer to be mocked and plundered by them.

units.la: Secundo animi promptitudinem & voluntatem benefaciendi profitetur Petrus, cum ait: Quod autem habeo, hoc do tibi. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset: Si pecuniam haberem, illam quoque libenter largirer. Dabo autem quicquid habuero. Praebent hac animi benefici exemplum, quo in beneficentia excendanos quoque affectos esse oportet. Sunt enim qui ardens beneficentiae studium profesi, se ignorare dicunt, quid & quantum pauperibus largiri debeant. At quaestionibus vniuersis beneficentiae charitatis lex respondet, quae iubet vt proximum tanquam nosipsos diligamus. Hoc quicunque faciunt, non quid dare debeant, quaerunt: sed quibus nam proximus indigeat, vident, & si illa penes se esse cernunt, liberalissime largiuntur. Quare si pecuniam habent, peccunia iuuant indigos. Si victu abundant, hunc in pauperes distribuunt. Si vestes habent, vestiunt quos nudos conspicantur. Quod si nihil horum ipsis superfit, falt em animum impertiuntur egenis fratribus, cuius beneuolentiam amicis verbis, consilio item & consolatione, quibus afflictos erigunt, testantur. Ita petri exemplum secuti, dant quodcunque habuerint. Vnde colligimus, eos charitate vacuos esse, nec vllo benefaciendi studio teneri, qui quid & quantum pauperibus dari debeat, interrogant.
units.tr: Second, Peter declares his readiness of mind and will to do good when he says: "What I have, I give you." This is as if he had said: "If I had money, I would gladly give that too. But I will give whatever I have." Peter's words set before us an example of a benevolent mind, and we ought to be disposed in the same way to be generous. There are those who profess an eager zeal for beneficence and yet say they do not know what, or how much, they ought to give to the poor. But the law of charity answers all such questions, for it commands us to love our neighbour as ourselves. Those who act on this do not ask what they ought to give, but see what their neighbour lacks, and if they find they have the means, they give most generously. So if they have money, they help the needy with money. If they have food in abundance, they distribute it to the poor. If they have clothing, they clothe those they see naked. But if nothing of these things is left to them, they at least offer their goodwill to needy brothers, and they show that goodwill by friendly words, and likewise by counsel and comfort, by which they raise up the afflicted. Following Peter's example, they give whatever they have. From this we conclude that those who ask what and how much should be given to the poor are empty of charity and are not held by any zeal for doing good.

units.la: Quid vero illud est, quod Petrus habuit, & quod claudo dedit quàm liberalissime? Addit: In nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni surge & ambula. Et apprehensa manu eius dextera, erexit eum, &c. Corporis ergo valetudinem integram illi largitur, quam potestatem à Christo acceptam cum aliis apostolis habebat. Ita autem hanc largitur, vt omnibus notum fit, ipsum non propria virtute miraculum edere, sed authorem huius esse Christum, cuius imperio, virtute & operatione omne hoc factum fit: de quo ipse postea pluribus apud populum differet. Simul autem multa congeruntur, quae ad miraculi veritatem & amplificationem faciunt. Nam claudi prehensa eius manu, Petrus erigit. Subito autem & repente tali ipsius & plantae vires & robur concipiunt, vt non difficulter exurgat, vt solent, quorum membra diutinis morbis debilitata sunt, sed exilit. Nec momentaneus est ille impetus, vt eorum, quos furor aut occultior aliquis spiritus exagitat: sed insistit pedibus, & obambulat. Adhaec cum apostolis templum ingreditur, subinde exultans & subsiliens, & Dei beneficium praedicans. Vere ergo curatus fuit claudus hic, vt nullum prioris morbi vestigium remanserit. Perfecta enim sunt Dei opera, nec quicquam illis doli sive fraudis & impostura continetur. At priusquam sermoni finem imponamus, de duobus, quae fidei nostrae institutioni seruiunt, dicendum erit.
units.tr: But what was it that Peter had, and which he gave so very generously to the lame man? He adds: "In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk." And taking his right hand, he raised him up, and so on. Therefore he restores to him the soundness of his body, a power which he had received from Christ together with the other apostles. He grants it in such a way that it is known to all that he himself did not perform the miracle by his own power, but that Christ is its author, by whose command, power and working all this was done. Of this Peter himself will speak at length afterwards before the people. At the same time, many things are brought together that serve to establish the truth and the greatness of the miracle. For Peter raises the lame man by taking his hand. Suddenly and at once, the strength and vigour of his feet and soles are restored, so that he does not rise with difficulty, as those usually do whose limbs have been weakened by long illness, but he leaps up. Nor is his movement momentary, like that of those who are driven by madness or some hidden spirit; rather, he stands firm on his feet and walks about. Moreover, he enters the temple with the apostles, leaping and bounding again and again, and proclaiming God's benefit. Truly, then, this lame man was healed, so that no trace of his former illness remained. For the works of God are perfect, and there is in them nothing of trickery, fraud or imposture. But before we end this discourse, two things must be said which serve the instruction of our faith.

units.la: Primum, spiritualis nostrae restitutionis typus est, quem hoc miraculo spiritus sanctus proponere voluit. Omnium enim nostrum, quoad animam eadem est quae claudi huius conditio. Ex natiuitate in morbum traxit, qui omnium membrorum vsum ipsi abstulit. Ita nos ex matris vtero peccatores nascimur, & tanta est haereditarij mali, quod ex Adamo parente in omnem posteritatem defluxit, vt nihil in nobis virium relinquat, quibus Dei legem exequi, & ea obire possimus, quae saluti conseq uendae seruiunt. Lex enim Dei spiritualis est, nos autem carnales, venundati sub peccatum, &c. Deinde vt claudum nihil salutis sperantem sua bonitate praeuenit clemens dominus: ita primum parentem, qui peccati conscientia territus Dei conspectum fugiebat, Deus prior inuisit, quaesiuit & vocauit, ac eundem salutis promissione gratuita consolatus est. Vt vero claudus Christi Iesu nomine sanatur, quod illi Petrus praedicat, eundemque manu prehensa erigit: ita Christi merito nobis salus parta est, & illam euangelij praedicatio nobis offert, quam vbi fide percipimus, mox Christi spiritum in nobis efficaciter operantem sentimus, qui manum praebet, erigit & vires suggerit, quibus peccati tyrannidem excutere & in domini vijs ambulare possimus. Illius enim opus est, quod regenerat, caelestium amore incendit, salutis fiduciam excitat, & de adoptione certiores factos clamare docet, Abba pater. Adhaec mentes Dei & voluntatis ipsius cognitio ne illuminat, in omnem veritatem ducit, & in aduersis omnibus consolatur. Huius ergo operatione fit, vt qui antea claudi eramus & infirmi, nunc omnia possumus in Christo, qui nos corroborat. Et licet carnis ingenium maneat, quod nos & labi facit interdum, & variis tentationibus solicitat, vincit tamen semper Christi spiritus, nec vltra vires nos tentari patitur. Perfecta enim salus est, quae in Christo nobis obtigit, quae nullis mundi aut principis ipsius conatibus turbari potest.
units.tr: First, this miracle is a type of our spiritual restoration, which the Holy Spirit wished to set forth. For the condition of all of us, as regards the soul, is the same as that of this lame man. From birth he was afflicted with a disease that took from him the use of all his members. So we are born sinners from our mother's womb, and the evil of inherited sin, which has flowed from our parent Adam into all his posterity, is so great that it leaves us no strength by which we can fulfil God's law and perform those things that serve to obtain salvation. For God's law is spiritual, but we are carnal, sold under sin, and so on. Then, just as the merciful Lord, by his goodness, anticipated the lame man, who hoped for no salvation, so God first visited our first parent, who, terrified by the consciousness of sin, was fleeing from the sight of God; God sought him out and called him, and consoled him with the free promise of salvation. And just as the lame man is healed in the name of Jesus Christ, which Peter proclaims to him, and Peter raises him up by taking his hand, so salvation has been obtained for us by the merit of Christ, and the preaching of the gospel offers it to us. When we receive it by faith, we at once feel the Spirit of Christ working effectively in us. He offers his hand, raises us up, and supplies strength by which we can shake off the tyranny of sin and walk in the ways of the Lord. For it is his work that regenerates, kindles the love of heavenly things, stirs up confidence in salvation, and teaches us, made certain of our adoption, to cry out: "Abba, Father." Moreover, he enlightens our minds with the knowledge of God and of his will, leads us into all truth, and comforts us in all adversity. By his working, therefore, we who were once lame and weak can now do all things in Christ, who strengthens us. And although the nature of the flesh remains, which at times makes us stumble and tempts us with various trials, the Spirit of Christ always conquers and does not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength. For the salvation that has been granted to us in Christ is complete, and no efforts of the world or of its prince himself can disturb it.

units.la: Secundò restitutorum officia claudi exemplo docentur. Is vbi in Christi nomine salutem sibi promitti audit & Petri manu erigitur, illico exilit. Ita postquam euangelij praedicatione salus in Christo offertur, & spiritus sancti suggestione nos animari & excitari sentimus, e luto peccatorum exurgamus illico, & beneficium Christi alacri mente complectamur. Nec enim in peccatis amplius viuere possunt, quos ex illorum seruitute Christi meritum asseruit, vt multis Paulus docet, Deinde cum apostolis templū ingreditur. Atqui templum ecclesiae Christi typū gessisse constat. Huic ergo nos iungamus, idq; apostolis ducibus, qui euangelij praedicatione viam, qua Christo & ecclesiae ipsius iungamur, nobis monstrant. At in Christi ecclesiam recipi non possumus, nisi desertis prius sa-tanae castris, cuius militiae eos renuntiare convenit, quicunque Christi milites fieri cupiunt. Adhaec exultauisse & Deum laudauisse dicitur. Exultemus & nos in domino, & laudemus illius bonitatem, quam nos ingenue fateri & praedicare couenit. Frustra enim redempti & liberati sunt, quos Christi redemptoris & beneficij per ipsum accepti pudet. Ideo & fidei confessionem a nobis passim exigit, & mortis suae memoriam mystica Coena, quam in ecclesia perpetuam obseruari vult, consecrauit. His itaq; studere nos conuenit, vt Christo vere insiti, & ipsius spiritu animati, cum eodem in coelis regne-mus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Second, the duties of the restored are taught by the example of the lame man. When he hears that salvation is promised to him in the name of Christ, and is raised up by Peter's hand, he at once leaps up. So, after salvation in Christ is offered through the preaching of the gospel, and we feel ourselves stirred and roused by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, let us immediately rise up out of the mire of our sins and embrace the benefit of Christ with a willing mind. For those whom the merit of Christ has freed from the bondage of sin cannot live any longer in sins, as Paul teaches in many places. Then he enters the temple with the apostles. And it is certain that the temple bore the figure of the church of Christ. Let us therefore join ourselves to this church, and that under the leadership of the apostles, who by the preaching of the gospel show us the way by which we may be joined to Christ and to his church, to which we are joined in the way that the apostles show us, and ... But we cannot be received into the church of Christ unless we first abandon the camp of Satan, from whose service all who desire to become soldiers of Christ must renounce. Moreover, he is said to have rejoiced and praised God. Let us also rejoice in the Lord, and praise his goodness, which we ought to confess and proclaim openly. For those are vainly redeemed and freed who are ashamed of Christ their Redeemer and of the benefit received through him. Therefore he also requires from us a confession of faith everywhere, and in the mystical Supper, which he wished to be observed perpetually in the church, he consecrated a memorial of his death. Let us therefore take care to be truly grafted into Christ, animated by his Spirit, so that with him we may reign in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXI.
units.tr: Homily 21.

units.la: Et vidit eum omnis populus ambulantem ac laudantem Deum. Et agnouerunt illum, quod is esset, qui solitus erat ad eleemosynam sedere iuxta Speciosam portam templi. Et impleti sunt admiratione & stupore super eo, quod acciderat illi. Cum vero claudus, qui sanatus fuerat, teneret Petrum & Iohannem, cucurrit totus populus ad eos in porticum, quae appellatur Solomonis, obstupefactus. Quo viso Petrus allocutus est populum: Viri Israelitae, quid miramini super hoc, aut nos intuemini, quasi propria potentia aut pietate effecerimus, vt hic ambularet?
units.tr: And all the people saw him walking and praising God. And they recognized him, that it was the man who used to sit for alms beside the Beautiful Gate of the temple. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. But when the lame man who had been healed held on to Peter and John, the whole crowd, astonished, ran to them in the portico called Solomon's. When Peter saw this, he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, or look at us as though by our own power or piety we had made this man walk?"

units.la: EXposuit Lucas insigne miraculum, quo diuus Petrus eum, qui ab vtero matris claudus fuerat, curauit. Finis huius miraculi idem est, qui & aliorum omnium, vt videlicet apostolicae doctrinae confirmandae seruiat. Quare illius narratione non contentus euangelista, simul etiam, quid per hoc effectum sit commemorat. Et primo quidem, vt Christi beneficium claudus exceperit, docet: quem sese apostolis coniunxisse, & cum illis templum intrauisse, deinde laudes publice praedicauisse dicit. Adumbratur eo exemplo, quid eos facere deceat, quos Christus sui meriti virtute restituit. Debent illi apostolorum doctrinam amplecti, & per hanc ecclesiae palam coniungi, & diuinae gratiae beneficium praedicare, ne illud in indignos collatum esse videatur. Sed ad alia quoq; transit Lucas, exponens, quis miraculi tanti effectus in populo fuerit, & vt inde Petro praedicandi occasio oblata sit, vbi proprijssimus & verus totius historiae vsus sese proferet.
units.tr: Luke sets out the remarkable miracle by which the divine Peter healed the man who had been lame from his mother's womb. The purpose of this miracle is the same as that of all the others, namely to confirm the apostolic teaching. For this reason the evangelist, not content with the account of the miracle, also records what came of it. First he shows that the lame man received Christ's benefit, saying that he attached himself to the apostles and entered the temple with them, and then that he publicly praised God. In this example is shown what those ought to do whom Christ restores by the power of his merit. They should embrace the teaching of the apostles, join themselves openly to the Church through it, and proclaim the benefit of divine grace, lest it seem to have been bestowed on the unworthy. But Luke also passes on to other matters, explaining what effect so great a miracle had on the people, and how an occasion for Peter to preach was offered, where the true and proper use of the whole story will appear.

units.la: Populus claudum vidisse dicitur, qui iam ambulabat ac laudabat Deum. Nec ambulante modo vidit, sed certo agnouit eum esse, qui ad templi portam eleemosynae colligendae gratia solitus erat sedere. Quod ad veritatem miraculi afferendam facit, ne quis fucum aliquem factum esse putaret. Inde autem admiratione pleni in stuporem rapiuntur, & turmatim ad apostolos, quos claudus prae animi laetitia nondum dimiserat, confluunt. Vbi duo nobis obseruanda veniunt, quorum alterum laude dignum est, alterum reprehensionem meretur, vt ex Petri verbis plenius patebit.
units.tr: The people are said to have seen the lame man, who now walked and praised God. They saw him not only walking but knew for certain that he was the one who used to sit at the temple gate to collect alms. This serves to establish the truth of the miracle, so that no one might think it was some trick. Then, filled with wonder, they were swept into amazement, and they flocked in crowds to the apostles, whom the lame man, in his joy, had not yet left. Here two things come to our attention, one of which deserves praise, the other rebuke, as will become clearer from Peter's words.

units.la: Primo admiratione repleti excitati fuisse dicuntur, vt ad apostolos concurrerent, & de re noua & insolita inciperent cogitare: & miraculi nouitate, quod & merito & bene ab illis factum esse, ne mo negare poterit. Debemus enim Dei opera non ofcitanter obseruare, & admirari illorum excellentiam, in quem finem homines a Deo conditos esse, quidam philosophorum non omnino inepte tradiderunt. Quia obseruatio illa & admiratio non in caeco & attonito mentis stupore subsistit, sed praeparatio quaedam animi est, qua ad veram Dei cognitionem perducimur. Reuelat quidem seipsum & voluntatem suam Deus in verbo suo, quod olim literis mandatum in ecclesia perpetuo praedicare iussit. At ea est in nobis animorum corruptio, vt nisi violento aliquo motu impellantur, a terrenis nunquam abduci possint & in coelestium consyderationem subuehi. Quare verbo suo plerunque signa aut opera quaedam excellentissima Deus coniungit, vt illa animos a sopore illo stupido excitatos in verbi & voluntatis suae consideracionem abripiant. Et Christus hanc ipsam ob causam doctrinae suae miracula frequenter aut praemittit aut interserit, vt ad doctrinam percipiendam attentiores reddat. Quae quantum profecerint, ex Nicodemi & aliorum exemplis patet, qui ex illis cognitionis Christi initium sumpserunt. Iohan.3. & 7. Debet autem eadem esse omnium signorum ratio, adeoq; omnium iudiciorum & operum Dei, vt ex illis ansam arripiamus in diuinæ voluntatis cognitionem altius ascendendi. Sed deploranda hic venit nostri seculi socordia, quo pleriq; ita obsurduerunt, vt nihil vel videant vel audiant eorum, quibus nos ad salutis cognitionem Deus excitat. Prædicatur euangelij verbum, & vigilare iubet dominus. Extant paßim horrenda iudiciorum Dei exempla, quibus mûdi incurabilem impietatem cohercet atq; punit. Eduntur signa, portenta & prodigia omnis generis. Fiunt deniq; in omnium conspectu quacunq; nouissimo seculo ante gloriosum suum aduentum euentura esse Christus prædixit. Matth.24. Luc.21. Atqui omnia hæc quasi supino naso stertentes negligimus, vt si non alio signo siue argumento, certè ex mundi securitate nimia intelligi possit ea esse tempora, de quorum periculis nos apostoli non semel admonuerunt. Vide 1. Thess.5.2. Pet.3. Sed excitemur, o fratres, & præsenti exemplo Dei opera admirari discamus, vt illorum admiratio nobis ad perfectiorem Dei cognitionem adminiculo esse possit.
units.tr: First, they are said to have been stirred by wonder so that they ran to the apostles and began to think about a new and unusual thing, and to be struck by the novelty of the miracle. That they did this rightly and well no one can deny. For we ought not to observe God's works carelessly, and to admire their excellence; and some of the philosophers did not altogether foolishly teach that this is the purpose for which men were created. For that observation and admiration does not consist in a blind and dazed stupor of mind, but is a certain preparation of the soul by which we are led to the true knowledge of God. God indeed reveals himself and his will in his Word, which he once committed to writing and commanded to be preached perpetually in the Church. But such is the corruption of our souls that unless they are driven by some violent motion, they can never be drawn away from earthly things and carried up to the contemplation of heavenly things. Therefore God often joins signs or certain most excellent works to his Word, so that these may rouse souls from that dull stupor and snatch them into consideration of his Word and will. Christ, for this very reason, often either sends his miracles before his teaching or inserts them among it, so as to make his hearers more attentive in receiving the teaching. How much these have profited is clear from the examples of Nicodemus and others, who from them took the beginning of knowledge of Christ (John 3 and 7). The reason for all signs ought to be the same, and so for all the judgments and works of God, so that we may seize on them as an occasion to rise higher into knowledge of the divine will. But here comes the deplorable sloth of our age, in which many have grown so deaf that they neither see nor hear anything by which God rouses us to knowledge of salvation. The Word of the gospel is preached, and the Lord bids us watch. Everywhere there are dreadful examples of God's judgments, by which he restrains and punishes the incurable impiety of the world. Signs, portents and wonders of every kind are put forth. Finally, in the sight of all, there happen the things which Christ foretold would take place in the last age before his glorious coming (Matt. 24; Luke 21). Yet we neglect all these things, snoring with our noses turned up, so that, if not by any other sign or argument, at least from the excessive security of the world, it could be understood that these are the times of whose dangers the apostles warned us more than once (see 1 Thess. 5:2; 2 Pet. 3). But let us be roused, brothers, and let us learn from the present example to admire the works of God, so that their admiration may serve us as an aid to a more perfect knowledge of God.

units.la: Alterum in populo reprehensionem meretur, quòd etsi signo tam memorabili ipsos Deus excitarit, animis tamen & oculis in solos apostolos intenti, ipsos tanquam miraculi authores suspicerent, cum in Christi Iesu, cuius nomine & virtute miraculum editum erat, confyderationem animos suba uehere deberent. Est hoc carnis ingenium, præsentibus & proximis causis inhærere, nec altius animum attollere, vt verum & vnicum omnium, quæ fiunt, authorem agnoscat. Nec leuiculus hic error est, cum ex hoc omnis superstitio & idololatria initium sumpserit. Hinc enim factum, quòd gentes Solem & Lunam cum reliquis astris deorum loco habuerunt. Nam cum illis accepta ferrent beneficia, quæ per illa humano generi Deus confert, aliter facere non potuere. Idem error eosdem, vt homines, qui publici alicuius boni authores fuerant, in deorum numerum referrent, commouit. Nec in hominibus error iste subsitit, sed propter beneficia animalibus brutis, fluminibus, fontibus, arboribus, & plantis numen inesse putauerunt, & gloriam immortalis dei in imagines hominum, volatilium & quadrupedum transtulere. Rom.1.cap. Nec alia ratione inter Christiani nominis profesfores idololatriam exortam esse constat. Posteaquam enim miracula, quæ olim à sanctis edita fuere, ab indoctis nimium aliter conscribi, & in suggestu ineptius prædicari cæperunt, mox illa sanctorum virtute edita esse rudis populus existimauit. Opinionem falsam alius error excepit, vt diuis vota facere inciperent, qui vel morbis vel alijs periculis impliciti erant, ex quibus aut diuos ipsos, aut alios illorum ministerio liberatos esse audiuerant. Et quia sanctorum suorum memoriam aliquando miraculis, iuxta illorum sepulchra editis, Deus asseruit, locis illis numen inesse putauerunt, & inde factum est, vt cultum & inuocationem certis quoq; locis alligarent. Ne quid vero superstitioni & idololatriæ deesset, imagines diuorum signis & miraculis nobilitare cœpit Satan, per quæ eo dementiæ peruentum est, vt iam non diuis modo tribuerentur, quæ solius Christi sunt, verumetiam diuorum simulachris, quæ contra diuinæ maiestatis præceptum superstitiosi homines erexerant. Et parum prodesse videbantur vota, quæ diuis nuncupantur, nisi & locus & imago diui celebrior diserte expri meretur. Vere autem hæc dici, tum historiæ docent, tum exempla, quorum ingentem copiam nostro quoq; seculo superstitiosi nobis exhibent. Quapropter cum negligentior miraculorum consyderatio, eorumque admiratio stulta, turpissimi erroris & impietatis manifestæ causam præbuerit, admonemur, miracula quæcunq; fiunt, nunquam absq; verbi diuini doctrina consyderari debere, quæ sola de illis vere iudicare docet. Nam diuersa inter homines miracula siue signa edi, scripturis sacris edocemur, vera nimirum & falsa. Vera dicuntur, in quibus vere fit quod fieri dicitur, & quæ veritatis doctrinæ testimonium ferunt, qualia olim apostolorum opera miraculosa ex Christi institutione fuerunt. Mar.16. Matth.10. Falsa dicuntur, quæ vel mendacì specie decipiunt, vt incantatores & præstigiatores solent: vel quæ à Deo & veritatis doctrina & fide homines auocant. Qualia olim fuere, quæ Iannes & Iambres coram Pharaone edebant. Et qualia Antichristo & nouissimi seculi impostoribus tribuuntur.2. Thess.2. Matth.24. Et permittit illa interdum suorum oculis Deus obijci, vt in electis quidem fidei ipsorum constantiam exploret, quemadmodum Moses testatur. Deut.13. in reprobis autem iudicij sui seueritatem exerceat, quando efficacia erroris (vt Paulus ait) seducuntur, qui dilectionem veritatis nolunt admittere. Nunquam ergo miracula ita arripi debent, vt in illis vel illorum doctrina temere hæreamus, à quibus ea eduntur: sed ad diuini verbi regulam examinari debent, vt in ijs, quæ veritati testimonium ferunt & Christo confidere docent, Deu authorem agnoscamus: alia vero omnia pro falsis reijciamus, utpote quorum illecebris fidei & saluti nostrae Satan insidiari solet. Hoc nisi observetur, non falsis modo signis, verumetiam miraculis veris, quorum deus ipse author est, nostro vitio seducemur, dum personis intenti, finem, in quem ista fiunt, minus observuamus. Cuius rei evidens exemplum praesens hic locus exhibet, & aliud infra de Lystrensibus traditur, qui ex miraculo per Paulum edito, idololatriae occasionem arripuere, ut suo loco patebit. Actorum 14.
units.tr: The second thing deserves rebuke in the people: although God had roused them by so memorable a sign, they, intent with their eyes and minds only on the apostles, looked up to them as the authors of the miracle, when they ought to have lifted their minds to the consideration of Christ Jesus, in whose name and power the miracle had been performed. It is the nature of the flesh to cling to present and nearby causes and not to raise the mind higher, so as to acknowledge the one true author of all that happens. Nor is this a trifling error, since all superstition and idolatry have taken their beginning from it. For this is why the nations regarded the sun and moon, along with the other stars, as gods; since they received benefits through them which God bestows on the human race, they could do no other. The same error led people to count among the gods those men who had been the authors of some public good. Nor did this error stop at men; on account of their benefits they thought that a divinity dwelt in animals, rivers, springs, trees and plants, and they transferred the glory of the immortal God to images of men, birds and four-footed beasts (Rom. 1). Nor is it clear that idolatry arose among professors of the Christian name in any other way. For when the miracles once performed by the saints began to be written down too differently by the unlearned, and to be preached more foolishly from the pulpit, the ignorant people soon supposed that they had been performed by the power of the saints. Another error followed this false opinion, so that men who were caught in sicknesses or other dangers began to make vows to the saints, since they had heard that they or others had been delivered from these dangers through the saints' ministry. And because God once confirmed the memory of his saints by miracles performed beside their tombs, they thought that a divinity dwelt in those places, and from this it came about that they bound worship and invocation to certain places too. And lest anything be lacking to superstition and idolatry, Satan began to lend renown to images of the saints by signs and miracles, through which madness reached the point that things belonging to Christ alone were attributed not only to the saints but also to the likenesses of the saints, which superstitious men had set up against the command of the divine majesty. And vows made to the saints seemed to avail little unless the place and the image of the saint, made more famous, were expressly named. That these things are rightly said is taught both by history and by examples, of which superstitious people show us an enormous supply even in our own age. Therefore, since a careless consideration of miracles and a foolish admiration of them has provided the cause of the most shameful error and manifest impiety, we are warned that whatever miracles happen must never be considered apart from the teaching of the divine Word, which alone teaches how to judge them truly. For Scripture teaches us that there are different miracles or signs performed among men, true and false, of course. They are called true when what is said to be done is truly done, and when they bear witness to the teaching of truth, as once were the miraculous works of the apostles, performed by Christ's appointment (Mark 16; Matt. 10). They are called false when they deceive with the appearance of a lie, as sorcerers and conjurers usually do, or when they draw men away from God, from the doctrine of truth and from faith. Such were once those which Jannes and Jambres performed before Pharaoh, and such are attributed to Antichrist and the impostors of the last age (2 Thess. 2; Matt. 24). Sometimes God also allows such things to be put before the eyes of his people: in the elect, to test the constancy of their faith, as Moses bears witness (Deut. 13); in the reprobate, to exercise the severity of his judgment, when, as Paul says, they are led astray by the efficacy of error because they are unwilling to receive the love of the truth. Therefore miracles must never be seized upon in such a way that we rashly cling to them, or to the teaching of those by whom they are performed; rather they must be tested by the rule of the divine Word, so that in those which bear witness to the truth and teach us to trust in Christ, we may acknowledge God as the author, and reject all the others as false, since it is by their enticements that Satan usually lays snares for our faith and salvation. Unless this is observed, we shall be led astray, through our own fault, not only by false signs but also by true miracles, whose author is God himself, while we are intent on the persons and pay less heed to the end for which these things happen. The present passage shows clear proof of this, and another example is given later concerning the Lystrans, who from the miracle performed by Paul seized an occasion for idolatry, as will appear in its place (Acts 14).

units.la: Sed Petrum videamus, qui ex populi stupore praedicandi occasionem arripit. Num vero populi ignorantia sive errore abutitur? Num per hunc sibi & collegis suis authoritatem conciliare studet, quod non incommodè fieri potuisset? Nequaquam. Imo de Christo concionari incipit, & illius honorem ac gloriam asserit. Sunt autem concionis huius partes quatuor. Prima ignorantiae vulgi medetur, & ostendit, nihil hic vel potentia & virtute vel sanctitate hominum esse effectum. Secunda, Deum miraculi authorem praedicat, qui illud per filium suum ediderit, ubi simul illos immanis flagitij, in filium Dei commissi admonet. Tertia, poenitentiam ab illis exigit. Postrema, quia cum Mose & prophetis pugnare videbatur Christiana religio, docet Christum ab his tradi, & necessario illi credendum esse, nisi in Mosen & prophetas graviter peccare velint: simul vero ne peccatorum conscientia toti absorberentur, testatur Christum, qui patribus promissus fuit, ad ipsos etiam pertinere. At in praesenti primam duntaxat partem excutiemus, de reliquis suo loco & tempore dicturi.
units.tr: But let us look at Peter, who seizes on the people's amazement as an opportunity to preach. Does he take advantage of the people's ignorance or error? Does he seek through this to win authority for himself and his colleagues, which could easily have been done? By no means. Rather, he begins to preach about Christ and asserts his honour and glory. This sermon has four parts. The first remedies the ignorance of the crowd and shows that nothing here was accomplished by any power, virtue or holiness of men. The second proclaims God as the author of the miracle, who worked it through his Son, and at the same time reminds them of the monstrous crime they committed against the Son of God. The third demands repentance from them. The last, since the Christian religion seemed to be at odds with Moses and the prophets, teaches that Christ is handed down by them and that he must necessarily be believed, unless they wish to sin gravely against Moses and the prophets; at the same time, so that their consciences of sin would not be wholly overwhelmed, he testifies that Christ, who was promised to the fathers, belongs to them too. But at present we will examine only the first part, and we will speak of the rest in their place and time.

units.la: Principio ignorantiam & errorem ex auditorum animis remouet. Est hic legitimus & commodissimus veritatem docendi ordo. Ea enim hominis conditio est, quae & terra, unde ille originem trahit. Haec sentes & vepres sponte gignit, nec semen bonum cum aliquo foenore reddit, nisi ab illis sedulo repurgetur. Ita hominis mens, haereditario peccati malo corrupta, errores sponte parit, quibus nisi strenuè occurratur, veritatis doctrinam nec admittit, nec fructum ex ea aliquem percipit. Quapropter prophetam dominus diruere & extirpare iubet, priusquam aedificet atq; plantet. Ierem. 1. Nec frigidus est in hac parte Petrus, quasi civilitatis & modestiae ergò honorem detrectet, ut ambitiosuli sofolent, qui eo ipso gloriam venantur, quòd se illius contemptores esse simulant. Sed interrogatione orationem figurans, illam vehementiorem reddit, dicens: Viri Israelitae, quid miramini super hoc, aut nos intuemini, quasi propria potentia aut pietate effecerimus, ut hic ambularet? Reprehensionem spirant verba haec. Quae obsecro (inquit) causa vos impellit, ut hoc miraculo tantum stuporem concepe- ritis, cum non ita pridem infinita huius generis à Christo edita sint? Cur non illa in mentem veniunt? & facile pateret, quis nam huius quoq; author fuerit. Frustra certè nos intuemini, imò hic vester error tam gravis est, ut dissimulari non debeat. Nihil enim hic nostra vel potentia vel sanctitas effecit. Sed alterius hoc opus est, cui laudem facti omnem transcribi necesse est.
units.tr: First, he removes ignorance and error from the minds of his hearers. This is the lawful and most suitable order for teaching the truth. For such is the condition of man, which is like the earth from which he takes his origin: this earth spontaneously produces thorns and briars, and does not return a good seed with any increase unless it is diligently weeded. So the human mind, corrupted by the hereditary evil of sin, spontaneously brings forth errors, and unless these are vigorously opposed, it neither admits the doctrine of truth nor receives any fruit from it. Therefore the Lord bids the prophet to pull down and root out before he builds and plants (Jer. 1.). Nor is Peter cold in this matter, as if he were rejecting honour out of courtesy and modesty, as ambitious people do, who hunt for glory precisely by pretending to despise it. Rather, by framing his speech as a question, he makes it more forceful, saying: "Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, or look at us, as if by our own power or piety we had made this man walk?" These words breathe reproof. "For what cause," he says, "does this miracle so astonish you, since not long ago infinite works of this kind were performed by Christ? Why do these not come to mind? It would have been easy to see who was the author of this one too. You are certainly looking at us in vain; indeed, your error here is so serious that it ought not to be overlooked. For nothing here was accomplished by our power or holiness. It is the work of another, and the whole praise of the deed must be ascribed to him."

units.la: Observemus hoc loco apostolorum modestiam & fidem, qua Christo honorem & gloriam omnem ita vendicant, ut nihil sibi referunt ex eo quod illi debetur. Est hoc omnibus sanctis proprium. Agnoscunt enim Christi vocem, apud prophetam dicentis: Ego dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Isa. 42. Exempla huius studij non hic modo, verumetiam alibi multa extant. Baptista, cum de salvatore Messia interrogaretur, omnem hanc laudem uni Christo transcribit, cuius praecursorem se tantum esse profitetur. Ioan. 1. Idem coram discipulis, qui carnali zelo Christum persequebantur, illum ecclesiae sponsum esse testatur, cui omnes adduci oporteat, & huic omnem à Deo patre potestatem & gloriam concessam esse docet, & discipulos suos ad Christum ablegat. Ioan. 3. Matth. 11. Et Paulus lapidari mauult, quàm diuinos honores, cum sponte illi à Lystrensibus offerrentur, recipere. Acto. 14. Similiter & angelos affectos esse constat. Cum enim Iohannes, revelationum excellentia abreptus, angelum adorare vellet, illum dicentem audit: Vide ne feceris, conservus enim tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum prophetarum, & eorum qui servant verba prophetiae libri huius. Deum adora. Apoc. 22. Unde D. Augustinus epistola 49. de cultu soli deo exhibendo disputans, de angelis, quos spirituales creaturas vocat, sic scribit: Quanto magis pia est & subdita deo, tanto minus se tali honore dignatur, quem scit non deberi nisi deo. Et paulo post malos angelos (quos hominum erroribus delectari adeo, quasi pasci dicit) cum bonis conferens addit: Proinde sicut impia superbia, sive hominum sive daemonum, sibi hos diuinos honores exhiberi vel iubet vel cupit: ita pia humilitas vel hominum vel angelorum sanctorum, haec sibi oblata recusavit, & cui deberetur ostendit. Potestc Potestem ex his certa desumi de omnibus tam apparitionibus quàm doctrinis iudicandi regula. Quicunque enim Deo fidere, & seruire, & Deum vnum in Christo Iesu adorare docent, siue angeli siue homines fuerint, pro sanctis Dei ministris haberi debent, & illis tutò credere licebit. Quisquis verò falsitatis gloriam à Christo vel in seipsum, vel in alias creaturas transferre, ac salutem in proprijs hominum operibus quaerere docent, anathema sit, etiamsi angelus de caelo fuerit. Galat. 1. Iugulantur hoc telo omnes spirit​uum apparitiones, qui animarum de mundo digressarum personam simulant, & Missarum sacrificijs alijsque eius generis operibus sese redimi posse docent. Arguuntur item falsi doctores, qui hominum simplicitate abutuntur, vt sibi redemptionis & remissionis peccatorum gloriam vendicent. Et damnat suo exemplo Petrus Romanos Antichristos, qui sede & successione Petri gloriantur, e quorum numero quidam dixisse fertur, nihil vtilius & fecundius esse Christianas persuasione: per hanc enim fieri, vt ipsi & sui similes rerum domini habeantur. Ita vnius vox, temere elapsa, omnium illorum animos prodidit.
units.tr: Let us observe here the modesty and faithfulness of the apostles, by which they claim all honour and glory for Christ, so that they reckon nothing to themselves from what is due to him. This is proper to all the saints. For they acknowledge the voice of Christ speaking through the prophet: "I am the Lord; that is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42.). Examples of this zeal exist here and also in many other places. When the Baptist was asked about the Saviour, the Messiah, he transferred all this praise to Christ alone, whose forerunner only he professes himself to be (John 1.). Likewise, in the presence of his disciples, who pursued Christ with carnal zeal, he testifies that Christ is the bridegroom of the Church, to whom all must be brought; he teaches that all power and glory have been granted to him by God the Father, and he sends his own disciples away to Christ (John 3.; Matt. 11.). Paul also preferred to be stoned rather than receive divine honours when the Lystrians offered them to him freely (Acts 14.). It is evident that the angels are similarly disposed. For when John, carried away by the excellence of his revelations, wished to worship an angel, he heard him say: "See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant and of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of the prophecy of this book. Worship God" (Rev. 22.). Hence Augustine, in his letter 49, disputing about the worship to be rendered to God alone, writes thus of the angels, whom he calls spiritual creatures: "The more devout an angel is and subject to God, the less he deems himself worthy of such honour, which he knows is due to God alone." And a little later, comparing the evil angels (whom he says delight in the errors of men as if they fed on them) with the good ones, he adds: "Therefore, just as impious pride, whether of men or of demons, either commands or desires that these divine honours be paid to itself, so holy humility, whether of men or of holy angels, has refused what was offered to it and has shown to whom it is due." From these things a certain rule for judging all apparitions and doctrines can be drawn. For whoever teaches that we must trust and serve God, and worship the one God in Christ Jesus, whether they be angels or men, ought to be held as holy ministers of God, and it will be safe to believe them. But whoever teaches that the glory of Christ is to be transferred to themselves or to other creatures, and that salvation is to be sought in men's own works, let him be anathema, even if he were an angel from heaven (Gal. 1.). By this weapon all apparitions of spirits are slain, which feign the persons of souls departed from the world and teach that they can be redeemed by the sacrifices of the Masses and other works of this kind. The false teachers too are refuted, who abuse the simplicity of men in order to claim for themselves the glory of redemption and forgiveness of sins. And Peter condemns by his own example the Roman Antichrists, who glory in the seat and succession of Peter; of whom one is reported to have said that nothing is more useful and more fruitful than the persuasion of Christians, for through it they and men like them come to be regarded as masters of things. Thus the voice of one man, carelessly uttered, betrayed the minds of all of them.

units.la: Admonemur etiam Petri verbis, ad quem authorem signa & miracula omnia referri debeant. In quibus duo fere respiciunt homines, Potentiam vimirum & Pietatem siue sanctitatem eorum, quorum ministerio illa fiunt. Sed Petrus neutrum ex his miraculorum causam efficientem esse docet, dum Iudaeos eo nomine reprehendit, quòd apostolorum potentia & pietate tantum opus confectum fuisse putarent. Nec rationes desunt, quibus Petri sententia probari possit. Miracula enim dicuntur, quae contra aut praeter naturae ordinem fiunt. Atqui natura dominus solus deus est, qui vni Christo potestatem omnem tradidit in caelo & in terra. Matth. 28. Ioan. 3. Quare hunc quoque vnicum omnium miraculorum authorem agnoscere conuenit. Quid enim cotra naturae ordinem possent homines, qui nec in ijs aliquid possunt, quae iuxta naturae leges fiunt? Naturale est, vt aetate augeatur hominis statura, donec ad iustam mensuram peruenat, & vt idem senecta appropinquante canescat. Quis verò hominum est qui sua solicitudine & industria staturae suae vnicum cubitum addere, aut pilum capitis vel nigrum vel album facere possit? Matth. 5. & 6. At nec sanctitati hominum hic quicquam tribui debet, quasi hac miraculorum fit causa efficiens, quando multos constat sanctissimos fuisse, quos miraculorum dono destitutos fuisse legimus. Nec enim propter illos, quorum ministerio eduntur, sed aliorum salutis causa plerunque miracula fieri consueuerunt. Qua causa est, quòd impiorum opera non raro deus vti voluit, ne quid hominum meritis tribueretur. Sic Iudam proditorem in illorum numero censeri videmus, quibus euangelij praedicationem dominus commisit, & miracula edendi virtutem concessit. Et alibi dominus, multos in nouissimo die miraculis gloriaturos dicit, quos se reiecturum testatur, non quòd falsa iactitent, sed quòd iniquitatis sint operarij. Matth. 7. Quare vt miracula non semper certa sunt sanctitatis hominum testimonia, ita nec illorum sanctitati, per quos fiunt, adscribi debent. Quid enim mereatur homo contra naturae cursum facere, qui propter innatam corruptionem naturalibus quoq; & quotidianis Dei beneficijs indignus est? Solus ergo Deus miraculorum author censeri debet, eorum inquam, quae saluti & fidei nostrae confirmandae seruiunt. Operatur autem haec, non quia nos meremur, sed quia saluti nostrae consulitum cupit. Sunt enim doctrinae veritatis testimonia, & hominum mentes ad illius considerationem excitant. Eadem quoq; illorum ratio est, quae circa sanctorum tumbas olim contigisse legimus. Nam illis doctrinam ipsorum confirmare voluit dominus, & de illorum immortalitate & beatitudine testari, qui diris tormentis per impios fidei persecutores excruciati fuerant, vt consolationem accipe-rent, qui illorum morte & interitu offendi potuissent. Intra hosce ergo limites miraculorum rationem omnem contineamus, vt vni Deo omnis illorum gloria transcribatur. Hos quicunque transgressi fuerint, vel suis miraculis alios parum cautos seducent, vel ipsi ab alijs seducentur.
units.tr: We are also admonished by Peter's words as to the author to whom all signs and miracles ought to be referred. Two things mostly concern men in this matter: namely, the power and the piety or holiness of those through whose ministry they happen. But Peter teaches that neither of these is the efficient cause of the miracles, when he rebukes the Jews for thinking that so great a work had been accomplished by the power and piety of the apostles. Nor are there lacking reasons by which Peter's opinion can be proved. For miracles are said to be those things which happen against or beyond the order of nature. But nature's Lord is God alone, who has given all power in heaven and on earth to Christ alone (Matt. 28.; John 3.). Therefore it is fitting to acknowledge him also as the one author of all miracles. For what can men do against the order of nature, who can do nothing even in those things which happen according to the laws of nature? It is natural that a man's stature should grow with age until it reaches its proper measure, and that in old age the same man should grow grey. But which of men, by his own care and effort, can add a single cubit to his stature, or make one hair of his head black or white? (Matt. 5. and 6.). Nor ought anything to be attributed here to the holiness of men, as if it were the efficient cause of miracles, since it is clear that many were most holy, whom we read to have been deprived of the gift of miracles. For miracles have usually happened not on account of those through whose ministry they are performed, but for the salvation of others. For this reason God has often chosen to use the works of the wicked, so that nothing might be attributed to the merits of men. Thus we see Judas the betrayer counted among those to whom the Lord committed the preaching of the gospel and granted the power of working miracles. And elsewhere the Lord says that many will boast of miracles on the last day, whom he declares he will reject, not because they boast falsely, but because they are workers of iniquity (Matt. 7.). Therefore, just as miracles are not always certain testimonies of men's holiness, so they ought not to be ascribed to the holiness of those through whom they happen. For what does a man deserve by doing something against the course of nature, who on account of innate corruption is unworthy even of God's natural and daily benefits? God alone, therefore, ought to be counted the author of miracles, I mean those which serve for our salvation and the confirmation of our faith. He works these not because we deserve them, but because he desires to provide for our salvation. For they are testimonies of the doctrine of truth, and they stir men's minds to consider it. The reason is the same as that which we read once happened at the tombs of the saints. For the Lord willed to confirm their doctrine by these means, and to bear witness to the immortality and blessedness of those who had been tortured with dreadful torments by the impious persecutors of the faith, so that those who might have been offended by their death and destruction might receive consolation. Let us therefore keep the whole account of miracles within these limits, so that all their glory is transferred to the one God alone. Whoever shall have gone beyond these, will either lead other less cautious people astray by their miracles, or will themselves be led astray by others.

units.la: Nemo tamen nostra haec ita accipiat, quasi sanctis dei cultoribus suum honorem & gloriam ideamus. Tribuimus enim illis, quicquid illis in scripturis spiritus sanctus tribuit. Agnoscimus illos, cum in terris agerent, diuinae gloriae & gratiae vasa ac organa electissima fuisse, quorum doctrinam, fide firma apprehendere, & vitae exemplum imitari debeant, quicunq; salutem consequi cupiunt. Christum enim dixisse scimus: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Matth. 10. Ioan. 13. Et illud Pauli exosculamur: Imitatores mei estote, quemadmodum & ego Christi sum. 1. Cor. 11. Nunc autem illos ipsos in caelis agere credimus, exemptos omnibus huius seculi curis, laboribus & molestijs, quemadmodum de Abrahamo & aliis patriarchis sancti apud prophetam testantur. Isaiae 63. Interea quaecunque ad mundi huius gubernationem & nostrae redemptionis rationem spectant, uni Deo per Iesum Christum tribui debere docemus. Ut enim in mundi creatione nullius ope & auxilio sive consilio usus est: ita nec redemptionis gloriam cum aliquo communem habet. Quare nefas ducamus, quicquam illi eripere, & vel nobis vel aliis vendicare. Sed illi fidamus constanter, & uni baereamus per filium suum dilectum, Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet let no one take these things as if we were seeking the honour and glory of the holy worshippers of God. For we ascribe to them whatever the Holy Spirit ascribes to them in the Scriptures. We acknowledge that, while they lived on earth, they were the most chosen vessels and instruments of divine glory, whose teaching all who desire salvation ought to grasp with firm faith and whose example of life they ought to imitate. For we know that Christ said: "He who hears you hears me," etc. Matth. 10. Ioan. 13. And we gladly embrace that saying of Paul: "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ." 1. Cor. 11. Now, however, we believe that they themselves are at work in heaven, freed from all the cares, labours and troubles of this age, as the saints testify through the prophet concerning Abraham and the other patriarchs. Isaiae 63. Meanwhile, we teach that whatever pertains to the governance of this world and the manner of our redemption must be ascribed to God alone through Jesus Christ. For just as in the creation of the world he used no one's help, assistance or counsel, so he does not share the glory of redemption with anyone. Therefore we consider it wicked to snatch anything from him and to claim it for ourselves or for others. But let us trust him steadfastly and cling to him alone through his beloved Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXII.

units.la: Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, Deus patrum nostrorum, glorificauit filium suum Iesum, quem vos tradidistis, & quem negastis coram Pilato, cum ille iudicasset absoluendum. Vos autem sanctum & iustum negauistis, & postulauistis, ut virum homicidam donaret vobis, auctorem vero vitae interfeciistis. Quem Deus suscitauit a mortuis, cuius nos testes sumus. Et in fide nominis ipsius hunc, quem videtis & nouistis, confirmauit ipsius nomen: & fides, quae per ipsum est, dedit ei integram hanc sanitatem coram omnibus vobis.
units.tr: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied before Pilate, when he had judged that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One, and asked that a murderer be granted to you, while you killed the Author of life. Whom God raised from the dead, and of whom we are witnesses. And through faith in his name, this man whom you see and know has been made strong by his name, and the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the sight of you all.

units.la: Expositus primam concionis Petri partem, qua vulgi ignorantiae medetur, & miraculum, quod in claudo editum fuerat, nec potentiae nec sanctitati hominum tribui debere ostendit. Videamus nunc secundam, qua miraculi authorem Deum facit, & in Christum Iesum, cuius nomine illud factum sit, ipsos respicere docet. Et quia haec totius concionis praecipua pars est, illam magno studio & ordine commodissimo tractat. Primo enim summam totius negotii paucis verbis comprehensam proponit. Deinde illos immanissimi sceleris, in filium Dei commissi, admonet. Tandem vero ad propositum rediens, miraculi rationem omnem diserte exponit.
units.tr: Having explained the first part of Peter's sermon, which cures the ignorance of the crowd, he has shown that the miracle performed on the lame man ought to be attributed neither to the power nor to the holiness of men. Let us now see the second part, in which he makes God the author of the miracle and teaches them to look to Christ Jesus, in whose name it was done. And because this is the chief part of the whole sermon, he treats it with great zeal and in a most convenient order. For first he sets out the summary of the whole matter, comprehended in a few words. Then he admonishes them of the most monstrous crime committed against the Son of God. Finally, returning to his purpose, he clearly expounds the whole reason of the miracle.

units.la: Summa totius causae est: Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, Deus patrum nostrorum, glorificauit filium suum Iesum. Comprehendit hic tum miraculi authorem, Deum, tum eiusdem causam finalem, glorificationem scilicet filii Dei, Iesu Christi. Et quemadmodum prius nihil vel potentiae vel sanctitati hominum tribui debere ostendit: ita nunc ad Deum authorem unicum & filii ipsius gloriam sive illustrationem omne hoc referri debere docet. Interim duo nobis obseruanda veniunt.
units.tr: The summary of the whole case is: The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus. Here he comprehends both the author of the miracle, God, and its final cause, namely the glorification of the Son of God, Jesus Christ. And just as before he showed that nothing should be attributed either to the power or to the holiness of men, so now he teaches that all this is to be referred to God as the sole author, and to the glory or illustration of his Son. Meanwhile two things come to be observed by us.

units.la: Primum, quod de Deo loquens, Deum Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi, deniq; Deum patrum nominat. Quo titulo Deus ipse non semel in veteri Testamento vtitur, & est hoc ingens diuini amoris argumentum, quo suam bonitatem ille nobis commendat. Solent huius seculi reges a deuictis & vastatis gentibus nomina sibi sumere, & gloriam ex eo magnam quaerunt, si Parthici, Gothici, Alemannici, Africani, Numidici, dicantur. At quae alia istorum nominum ratio est, quam quod populos istos exciderunt, & illorum terras igne ac ferro vastarunt? Longe aliter Deus, qui ab hominibus ijs denominari vult, quos nihil tale meritos sibi ex gratia perpetuo foedere obstrinxit, & a quibus nec pradam opimam, nec aliquem fructum sperare potest, nisi quem ipse in illis produxerit. In praesenti tamen altius quiddam spectauit Petrus, & eos titulos Deo tribuit, quos praesenti negotio in primis conuenire videbat. Primo enim cum patres nominat, illos promissionum admonet, quas olim patribus de Christo Deus dedit. Abrahamo enim dictum erat: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui post te. In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terrae. Gen. 22. Quam promissionem in Isaaco & Iacobo postea repetitam fuisse legimus. Genes. 26. & 28. Vt iam de Dauide nihil dicamus & prophetis, qui in eadem promissione explicanda plurimum versantur. Proderat autem, imo necesse erat promissiones illas repeti, eo quod illas omnes Iudaei paulo ante coram Pilato negauerant, dum se nullum alium regem, praeter Caesarem, sperare & habere clamant, ut infra audiemus. Quapropter, ne se a Dei foedere & promissionibus in vniuersum excidisse putarent, omnemq; salutis spem abiicerent, ostendit Petrus, Deum illum adhuc viuere & regnare, qui olim cum patribus foedus inierit, nec illum adhuc Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi pigere, sed ut olim, ita nunc quoq; ab ipsis denominari velle, modo ipsi ad illum conuertantur. Deinde ad declinandum suspicionem, qua apostoli grauabantur, hic Dei titulus non parum parum faciebat. Plerisque enim suspecti erant, quasi nouum Deum, nouam fidem, nouamque religionem, patribus hucusque incognitam praedicarent. Quae causa erat, quod à multis non audiebantur, à multis vero digni putabantur, qui iuxta Mosis legem mortis iudicium sustinerent. Deut. 13. At hoc Dei titulo Petrus tam ingenuè & magnificè utens, publicè quodammodo protestatur se nullum alium Deum agnoscere, quàm qui se patribus olim manifestauerit, nec aliam fidem siue religionem praedicare, quàm qua patres olim Deo se approbarint, & per quam ipsi saluati sint. Postremò, quos patres Iudaei in religionis & fidei causa obseruare atque imitari debeant, illos non obscurè admonet. Gloriabantur illi patribus, qui recentiores erant, quique post Mosem & prophetas subingressi nouarum traditionum & multiplicis superstitionis authores fuerant. Quorum traditiones tam anxiè obseruabant, vt Dei potius leges transgredi, quàm in illis quicquam negligere aut mutare auderent, quod ipsis à Christo non semel exprobratum fuisse legimus. Matth. 15. & 23. &c. Nec alia res erat, quae ipsos tum Christo tum apostolis infensiores redderet, quàm quod isti maiorum traditiones sua do &trina impugnarent. Abrahami ergo, Isaaci & Iacobi meminit Petrus, vt offendat, non quosuis patres in religione esse imitandos. Vt enim vnus omnium pater Deus est, & vnus omnium magister, Iesus Christus, quem pater toti terrarum orbi doctorem constituit: ita illorum duntaxat vestigiis nos insistere decet, quorum fidem & religionem Deo placuisse constat, & quibus fidei & integritatis testimonium ferre Deus dignatus est. In quorum numero principatum tenet Abraham, quem credentium & multorum populorum patrem ideo scriptura vocat, quod ad illum pertinent, quotquot fidem in Iesum Christum, quae illi ad iustitiam imputata est, amplexantur. Roman. 4. Eidem Christus testimonium fert, quando illum exultauisse dicit, vt diem suum videret, & cum illo discubituros air in caelorum regno, quotquot ab Oriente & Occidente in ecclesiam Dei confluunt. Ioan. 8. Matth. 8. Discant hinc nostri saeculi homines, quàm inanis sit recentiorum patrum gloriatio, qui nouam salutis rationem extra Christum vel commenti vel secuti sunt. Nisi Abrahami filij per fidem in Christum reddamur, nullo aliorum patrocinio & authoritate defendi poterimus, etiamsi reges & Imperatores fuerint, &c.
units.tr: First, when he speaks of God, he names him the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and finally the God of our fathers. God himself uses this title more than once in the Old Testament, and it is a great proof of divine love, by which he commends his goodness to us. The kings of this age are wont to take names for themselves from conquered and devastated peoples, and they seek great glory from this, if they are called Parthian, Gothic, Alemannic, African, Numidian. But what other reason is there for these names, than that they have destroyed those peoples and laid waste their lands with fire and sword? God is far otherwise, who wishes to be named from those men whom, having deserved nothing of the kind, he has bound to himself by grace in a perpetual covenant, and from whom he can hope for neither rich booty nor any fruit, except what he himself has produced in them. Yet in the present case Peter looked to something deeper, and attributed to God those titles which he saw to be especially fitting to the present matter. For first, when he names the fathers, he reminds them of those promises which God once gave to the fathers concerning Christ. For it had been said to Abraham: I will be your God and the God of your seed after you. In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. Gen. 22. We read that this promise was afterwards repeated to Isaac and Jacob. Gen. 26. and 28. Not to mention David now, and the prophets, who are much occupied in explaining this same promise. Moreover, it was useful, indeed it was necessary, that those promises be repeated, because the Jews had a little before denied them all before Pilate, when they cried out that they had and hoped for no other king but Caesar, as we shall hear below. Wherefore, lest they should think that they had fallen altogether from God's covenant and promises, and should cast away all hope of salvation, Peter shows that God, who once made a covenant with the fathers, is still alive and reigning, and that he is not yet ashamed of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, but, as before, so now also wishes to be named from them, provided they themselves turn to him. Next, to remove the suspicion under which the apostles labored, this title of God did not a little to help. For they were suspected by many, as if they were preaching a new God, a new faith and a new religion, hitherto unknown to the fathers. This was the reason why they were not heard by many, and by many were thought worthy to undergo the sentence of death according to the law of Moses. Deut. 13. But Peter, using this title of God so frankly and nobly, publicly declares in a way that he acknowledges no other God than the one who once made himself known to the fathers, and that he preaches no other faith or religion than that by which the fathers once pleased God, and by which they themselves were saved. Lastly, he clearly admonishes them which fathers the Jews ought to observe and imitate in matters of religion and faith. They boasted of those fathers who were more recent, and who, coming after Moses and the prophets, had become the authors of new traditions and manifold superstition. These traditions they observed so anxiously that they would rather transgress God's laws than dare to neglect or change anything in them, which we read Christ rebuked them for more than once. Matth. 15. and 23. etc. Nor was there any other thing which made them more hostile to Christ and the apostles than that these men opposed the traditions of their elders with their teaching. Peter therefore mentions Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so as to show that not just any fathers are to be imitated in religion. For as God is the one Father of all, and Jesus Christ is the one Teacher of all, whom the Father has appointed as teacher for the whole world, so it becomes us to follow only the footsteps of those whose faith and religion are known to have pleased God, and to whom God has deigned to bear witness of faith and integrity. At the head of these stands Abraham, whom Scripture calls the father of believers and of many peoples, for the reason that all who embrace faith in Jesus Christ, which was imputed to him for righteousness, belong to him. Rom. 4. Christ himself bears witness to him, when he says that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and that he said that all who flow together into the Church of God from East and West shall sit down with him in the kingdom of heaven. John 8. Matth. 8. Let the men of our age learn from this how empty is the boasting of the more recent fathers, who have either devised or followed a new way of salvation apart from Christ. Unless we are made the children of Abraham through faith in Christ, we shall be able to be defended by the patronage and authority of no others, even if they were kings and emperors, etc.

units.la: Secundò obseruemus, quod ait: Deus patrum nostrorum glorificauit filium suum, Iesum. Atqui de miraculo in claudi persona edito loquitur, cuius finem his verbis indicat. Docemur hic, glorificationem siue illustrationem filij Dei, Iesu Christi, omnium miraculorum noui Testamenti finem & scopum esse, ad quem eos quoq; omnes respicere oportet, quicunq; miraculis gloriari audent. Hunc finem euangelista diserte verbis exprimit, dicens: Multa alia signa fecit Iesus, quae non sunt scripta in hoc libro: haec autem scripta sunt, vt credatis, quod Iesus est Christus ille, filius Dei, &c. Iohan. 20. Sed & ipse Christus de potestate edendi miracula & iudicandi, sibi à patre tradita, loquens, hunc eius finem esse docet, vt omnes honorent filium, sicut honorant patrem. Iohan. 5. Et de Lazari morbo apud discipulos differens, ait: Infirmitas haec non est ad mortem, sed pro gloria Dei, vt glorificetur filius Dei per eam. Iohan. 11. Hinc patet, quo loco haberi debeant miracula & signa, quibus nonnulli suam priuatam gloriam illustrare student, vt sibi discipulorum & seruorum instar subijciant, quos Christus sanguinis sui pretio redemptos sibi sanctificauit.
units.tr: Second, let us observe what he says: The God of our fathers has glorified his Son Jesus. And yet he speaks of the miracle performed on the lame man, and indicates its purpose in these words. Here we are taught that the glorification or illustration of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, is the end and aim of all the miracles of the New Testament, and that all those who dare to glory in miracles ought to look to this end. The evangelist expresses this end plainly in words, saying: Jesus did many other signs which are not written in this book, but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, etc. John 20. And Christ himself, speaking of the power given him by the Father to perform miracles and to judge, teaches that this is its purpose, that all should honor the Son just as they honor the Father. John 5. And speaking to his disciples about the sickness of Lazarus, he says: This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it. John 11. From this it is clear in what light miracles and signs are to be regarded, by which some men strive to make their own private glory shine, so as to subject to themselves, as disciples and servants, those whom Christ, redeemed by the price of his blood, has sanctified to himself.

units.la: Caeterùm, quia in Christi mentionem Petrus incidit, commodè auditores immanis flagitij admonet, quod in hunc ab illis patratum erat. Nec leuiter illud perstringit, sed omnem illius atrocitatem ipsis ob oculos statuit. Crescit enim ceu gradibus quibusdam oratio, cuius hic finis est, vt tanti sceleris agnitione consternati, paenitentiae studio & salutis per Christum assequendae desiderio inflammentur. Primò, illos filium Dei tradidisse dicit, nimirum gentibus ad illudendum & crucifigendum. Atqui immane sceleus est, innocentem in mortem tradere, & horrenda extant Dei iudicia in eos, qui sanguine se polluunt. Vide Numer. 35. Sed hic maius quiddam & atrocius subest. Quia enim Iudaeos, ex omnium gentium numero selectos, sibi consecrauerat Deus, nemo illorum gentibus prophanis ad illudendum & in mortem tradi poterat, sine prophano & sacrilego Dei & gloriae diuinitus concessae contemptu & conculcatione. Quae mihi causa esse videtur, quod Christus frequenter, quando de morte sua loquitur, huius facinoris meminit, quod ipsum gentibus traditurus sint. Matth. 20. Luc. 18. &c. Id autem non temere & incogitanter, sed publico & communi seniorum consilio & populi applausu, qui ipsos ad Pilatum vsq; comitatus est, factum esse euangelista testantur. Matt. 27.
units.tr: Moreover, since Peter has happened upon the mention of Christ, he fittingly reminds his hearers of the monstrous crime they committed against him. He does not touch on it lightly but sets its full atrocity before their eyes. His speech rises by degrees, and its aim is that they, dismayed at the recognition of so great a wickedness, may be inflamed with zeal for repentance and with desire to attain salvation through Christ. First, he says they handed over the Son of God, namely to the Gentiles, to be mocked and crucified. Now it is a monstrous wickedness to deliver an innocent man to death, and God's dreadful judgements stand against those who pollute themselves with blood. See Numbers 35. But something greater and more atrocious lies beneath this. For God had consecrated the Jews, chosen from among all nations, to himself, so none of them could be handed over to profane Gentiles to be mocked and put to death without a profane and sacrilegious contempt and trampling of God and of the glory divinely bestowed on them. This, it seems to me, is why Christ, when he speaks of his death, so often mentions this deed, that they would hand him over to the Gentiles. Matt. 20; Luke 18, etc. The evangelists testify that this was done not rashly or thoughtlessly, but by the public and common counsel of the elders, and with the applause of the people, who accompanied him right up to Pilate. Matt. 27.

units.la: Luc.23. Accedit his secundo loco, quod ait: Et negauistis illum coram Pilato. Atqui non de leui ali-qua Iesu abnegatione loquitur, sed ea, qua omnibus Dei promissionibus, de Messia & rege redem-ptore exhibitis, renuntiauerant, spemq; patrum, qua tot seculis liberatoris aduentum expectauerant, negauere. Quod ipsos fecisse, Iohan.19. legimus. Cum enim Pilatus, illis iubinde regis nomen ingemi-naret, haud dubie ad promissum & ab omnibus hucusq; expectatum Messiam respiciens, illi immani impietate exclamant: Non habemus regem, nisi Cesarem. Ergone de Cesare intelligi debebat promissio Dauidi facta, quod ex ipsius stirpe nasciturus esset, cuius regnum aeternum maneret? Et num de Tiberio, flagitioso & impuro homine, intelligendum quod dicitur, Ecce rex tuus veniet tibi, iustus & seruator & mitis? etc Zach.9. Hanc ergo impietatem, qua sese & salute & promissionibus salutis, omniq; salutis spe spoliauerant, hic illis Petrus exprobrat. Ne vero flagitium in Pilatum transferre possent, quasi illius metu eo impulsi essent, hoc ipsos fecisse dicit, cum Pilatus Christum absoluendum iudicasset, & publicum de illius iustitia & integritate testimonium tulisset. In Iudaeis ergo culpam hanc haerere dicit, qui (ne quid sceleris omitteret) tam se quam filios suos sanguinis huius reatu solenni & publica protestatione obstrinxerant. Horrenda sunt haec, sed nondum in his quieuit Iudaeorum impietas. Nam addit Petrus: Vos Sanctum & Iustum abnegauistis, & postulauistis vt vir homicida donaretur vobis, authorem vero siue principem vitae interfeci-stis. Eam odij in Christum acerbitatem exprobrat, qua ita excaecati fuere, vt no puderet ipsos, latronem sanguinarium Christo praeferre. Et vt euidentior fit sceleris atrocitas, collatione vtitur. Iesum negauistis, qui sanctus erat & iustus, in quo nec sacerdotes (licet omnem lapidem mouerint) nec Pilatus, nec Herodes quic-quam criminis deprehendere potuerunt. Adhaec interfecistis eum, quem vitae authorem, imo vitae & mortis principem ac dominum esse, tot miraculis & recenti Lazari resuscitatione agnoscere debebatis. Interim latronem, sicarium & seditiosum hominem vobis donari postulauistis. Et cum vestra esset electio, beneficiorum Christi omnium oblitis, latronem nefarium illi praeferre non puduit. Quid vero atrocius & grauius & magis horrendum dici poterat? Atqui haec Petrus in ea vrbe, imo in templo loquitur, vbi rerum potiebantur qui primi huius facinoris authores fuerant, quosq; odia in Christum adhuc spirare nouerat. Rursum ergo docemur, qua libertate publica scelera argui debeant ab ijs, quos in sua ecclesia speculatores dominus constituit, vt gladium imminentem praenuntient, ne quis illorum incuria & negligentia pereat. Nec est quod eos audiamus, qui hac vehementia minime opus esse dicunt hodie, quando nemo sit, cui tam atrox facinus obijci queat. Nec enim soli Iudaei peccauere, sed hodie no minus atrociter, quam ab illis peccatum fuit, a multis peccatur. Traditur a multis Christus in mortem, dum passim in fideles Christi ferro & igne saeuitur. Eundem multi metu, plures autem hominum fauorem secuti abnegant. Nec simplicitate & ignorantia peccatur, quo nomine paulo post Petrus Iudaeos excusabit. Sed multos reclamante multum conscientia Christum negare vidimus. Horret animus, quando atrocis flagitij recordor, quod ab illis commissum est nuper, qui non modo ipsi veritatem abnegarunt, sed suos ad eandem abnegationem coegerunt, & eam religionis formam amplexi sunt, quae nec ab eius authore & inuentore probabatur. Exemplo caret impietas, quae tunc designata est, & vtinam vere sceleris paeniteret omnes, qui eo polluti fuerunt. Interea regnare, florere & in precio haberi cernimus sanguinarios Barrabas, qui mercenariae sanguinis effusioni assueerunt, quia dei iram & horribile exitium in miseram patriam sua improbitate prouocant. Tales ergo accusari conuenit, nec vllus modestiae locus superest, vbi haec palam fiunt, & pro flagitij haberi desierunt. Sed o scelus, Non licet hodie inter Christiani nominis professores, quod Petro in sanguina ria Hierosolymorum vrbe licuit. Iudaeis igitur hoc nomine deteriores sumus, quod cum eadem cum ipsis faciamus, verbi tamen disciplinam non eadem cum ipsis patientia suscipimus.
units.tr: Luke 23. Second, he adds: "And you denied him before Pilate." He is not speaking of some slight denial of Jesus, but of a denial by which they renounced all God's promises concerning the Messiah and the redeeming king, and gave up the hope of the fathers, by which for so many ages they had awaited the coming of the liberator. We read that they did this in John 19. For when Pilate kept repeating the title of king to them, looking undoubtedly to the promised Messiah, long expected by all, they cried out with monstrous impiety: "We have no king but Caesar." Was the promise made to David, that one would be born from his line whose kingdom would endure forever, to be understood of Caesar? Or is what is said, "Behold, your king comes to you, just, a saviour and meek," etc. (Zech. 9), to be understood of Tiberius, a shameful and impure man? So this impiety, by which they had stripped themselves of salvation, of the promises of salvation and of all hope of salvation, is what Peter here reproaches them with. Lest they could shift the crime onto Pilate, as if fear of him had driven them to it, he says they did this when Pilate had judged Christ to be acquitted and had publicly borne witness to his justice and integrity.
