The guilt therefore clings to the Jews, who, lest they leave out any wickedness, bound themselves and their sons to the guilt of this blood by a solemn and public declaration. These things are dreadful, but the impiety of the Jews did not yet rest there. For Peter adds: "You denied the Holy and Just One, and asked that a murderer be granted to you, but you killed the author or prince of life." He reproaches them with the bitterness of their hatred against Christ, by which they were so blinded that they were not ashamed to prefer a bloody robber to Christ. To make the atrocity of the crime more evident, he uses a comparison. You denied Jesus, who was holy and just, in whom neither the priests (though they turned over every stone), nor Pilate, nor Herod could find any crime. Besides, you killed him whom you ought to have acknowledged, by so many miracles and by the recent raising of Lazarus, as the author of life, indeed the lord of life and death. Meanwhile you asked that a robber, an assassin and a seditious man be given to you. Although the choice was yours, forgetful of all Christ's benefits, you were not ashamed to prefer a wicked robber to him. What could be said that is more atrocious, more grave and more dreadful? Yet Peter speaks these things in that city, indeed in the temple, where those who were the first authors of this crime held power, and whom he knew still breathed hatred against Christ. Again, then, we are taught with what frankness public crimes ought to be denounced by those whom the Lord has set as watchmen in his church, so that they may announce the sword hanging over, lest anyone perish through their carelessness and negligence. Nor should we listen to those who say that such vehemence is by no means needed today, since there is no one to whom so atrocious a deed can be imputed. For not only the Jews sinned; today many sin no less atrociously than they did. Christ is handed over to death by many, while everywhere fury is unleashed with sword and fire against the faithful of Christ. Many deny him out of fear, and more out of pursuit of men's favour. Nor is this sin committed through simplicity and ignorance, which Peter will soon plead in excuse for the Jews. Yet we have seen many deny Christ while their conscience loudly protested. My mind shudders when I recall the atrocious crime lately committed by those who not only denied the truth themselves, but forced their own people into the same denial, and embraced a form of religion that was not even approved by its own author and inventor. That impiety, which was then foreshadowed, has no precedent; and would that all who were polluted by it truly repented of their crime. Meanwhile we see bloodthirsty Barabbases reigning, flourishing and held in high esteem, men accustomed to shedding blood for hire, who by their wickedness provoke God's anger and dreadful ruin upon their wretched country. Such men ought to be accused, and no room for moderation remains when these things are done openly and have ceased to be regarded as crimes. But, o wickedness, what was permitted to Peter in the bloody city of Jerusalem is not permitted today among the professors of the Christian name. We are therefore worse than the Jews in this respect: that, while we do the same things they did, we do not receive the discipline of the word with the same patience.

units.la: Redit autem ad institutum Petrus, vt deum miraculi huius authorem, omnemque illius rationem luculentius describat. Prius tamen resurrectionem Christi praedicat, tum quod in ea potissimum salutis per Christum acquisitae ratio versatur, tum quod Crucis offendiculo pulchre medetur. Vos quidem interfecistis (inquit) vitae authorem, sed deus illum resuscitauit ex mortuis, cuius rei nos sumus testes. Necesse autem erat, haec praecedentibus subijci, ne quis impiorum libidini nimium permissum fuisse putaret. Docent enim, illorum truculentiam & iniquitatem Christo nihil potuisse adimere, vt pote qui e mortuis resuscitatus, nunc in caelis viuat & regnet. Hinc vero communem conso-lationem lationem petere licebit. Vt enim Christo nihil detrahere potuit Iudaicæ gentis improbitas & tyrannis: ita nec Christi membris nocere poterunt, quicunque Iudaicam impietatem & tyrannidem imitantur. Concurrant quidem mundi principes, & Christi regnum euertere cupiunt. Sed dominus ex alto illorum consilia ridet, cuius consilium in æternum stabit. Vide Psal. 2. & 33. Nemo igitur homines timeat, qui vt maxime insaniant, in solas fortunas & corpus nostrum, alioqui mortale & perituru, aliquid poterunt. Imo nec in illa quidem quicquam possunt, nisi dominus permittat, qui capitis nostri pilos numeratos habet. Anima vero extra omnem fortunæ aleam posita, Christo redemptore fidit, nec spes sua vnquam fraustrabitur. Matth. 10.
units.tr: Peter now returns to his subject, so that he may describe more clearly God as the author of this miracle and the whole account of it. Yet first he preaches the resurrection of Christ, both because the manner of the salvation acquired through Christ turns chiefly on it, and because it fittingly heals the stumbling-block of the cross. "You indeed," he says, "killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead, and of this we are witnesses." It was necessary to add this to what has gone before, lest anyone think that the cruelty of the impious had been allowed too much licence. For it shows that the savagery and iniquity of those men could take nothing away from Christ, who, raised from the dead, now lives and reigns in heaven. From this we may draw a common consolation. For just as the wickedness and tyranny of the Jewish nation could take nothing from Christ, so neither can those who imitate Jewish impiety and tyranny harm the members of Christ. Indeed the princes of the world may gather together and desire to overthrow Christ's kingdom. But the Lord laughs at their plans from on high, whose counsel will stand forever. See Psalms 2 and 33. Let no one therefore fear men, who, however madly they rage, can do something only against our fortunes and our body, which is otherwise mortal and perishable. Indeed they can do nothing even against these unless the Lord permits it, who has even the hairs of our head numbered. The soul, however, placed beyond all the hazard of fortune, trusts in Christ the Redeemer, and its hope will never be disappointed. Matt. 10.

units.la: Sed videamus, vt miraculi rationem Petrus explicet. In fide nominis ipsius (inquit) hunc, quem videtis & nouistis, consolidauit nomen ipsius. Obscura videtur oratio, nisi verborum contextum observes. Et imponit multis, quod nomen in accusandi casu positum esse existimant, cum nominatiui casus illud esse tota verborum series non obscure testetur. Sic autem constrvi & contexi debet oratio: Nomen Iesu Christi consolidauit & sanauit hunc, quem coram conspicitis, idq; propter fidem, quam hic nomini Christi adhibuit. factum est. Et vt planior esset sensus, per expositionem adijcit: Fides, quæ per ipsum est, dedit ei integram hanc sanitatem coram omnibus vobis. Sensus vero omnium est, Christum Iesum per suum nomen, id est, sua virtute, potentia & merito, claudo sanitatem & incolumitatem contulisse, eò quòd ille in Christum Iesum crediderit. Frequentius autem Christi nomen & fidem in Christum repetit, vt euidentior fit Christi gloria, in qua afferenda nunquam fidelibus satisfaciunt apostoli, vt in illorum scriptis & sermonibus passim appareat. Sunt autem non osciter prætereunda verba hæc. Quia enim in claudo totius humani generis typum nobis propositum esse diximus, in eiusdem curatione vniuersam nostræ salutis rationem cernere licebit. Comprehenditur ergo hic salutis author verus, deinde & medium quo salus a nobis percipitur, & eiusdem finis, in quem omnia ista tendunt.
units.tr: But let us see how Peter explains the manner of the miracle. "By faith in his name," he says, "his name has made this man, whom you see and know, strong." The wording seems obscure unless you observe the connection of the words. Many are misled because they think "name" is in the accusative case, when the whole sequence of words clearly shows it is in the nominative. The sentence must be construed and arranged thus: "The name of Jesus Christ has strengthened and healed this man whom you see before you, and that because of the faith which he placed in the name of Christ." And so that the sense may be plainer, he adds by way of explanation: "The faith which is through him has given him this complete soundness in the sight of you all." The meaning of all of it is that Christ Jesus, through his name, that is, by his power, might and merit, gave soundness and wholeness to the lame man, because the man believed in Christ Jesus. Peter repeats the name of Christ and faith in Christ more often so that the glory of Christ may be more evident, and the apostles never tire of asserting it, as appears everywhere in their writings and sermons. These words, moreover, must not be passed over lightly. For, as we have said, the lame man is set before us as a type of the whole human race, and in his healing we can discern the whole manner of our salvation. Here, therefore, is comprehended the true author of salvation, then the means by which salvation is received by us, and its end, to which all these things tend.

units.la: De salutis authore Petrus differens, Christi Iesu nomen allegat, quem paulo ante authorem & principem vitæ dixerat. Nomen vero pro virtute, imperio aut merito accipi, notius est, quàm vt multis demonstrari debeat. Quia autem prius omnem potentiam & sanctitatem hominum ab hoc negotio exclusit, & nunc vnius Christi meminit, cuius nomine & potentia hoc omne transactum esse testatur facile patet, salutis nostræ originem ad vnum Christum referri debere. Huius enim merito ex peccatis liberati & mortis satanæq; tyrannide redempti sumus. Et ipse apud prophetam nullum alium redemptorem, præter se vnicum esse profitetur. Isa. 43. At plura de hoc dicendi locus cap. 4. offeretur, vbi nullum aliud nomen sub cœlo hominibus datum esse Petrus testatur, per quod saluari possint, &c.
units.tr: Peter, discussing the author of salvation, names Jesus Christ, whom he had just called the author and prince of life. That the name stands for power, authority or merit is too well known to need proof. Peter first removed all human power and holiness from this business, and now he mentions Christ alone, by whose name and power he testifies that all this was accomplished; it is therefore plain that the origin of our salvation must be referred to Christ alone. For it is by his merit that we have been freed from sins and redeemed from the tyranny of death and Satan. And he himself, through the prophet, declares that there is no other redeemer besides him, who is alone. Isa. 43. But an opportunity to say more on this will be offered in chapter 4, where Peter testifies that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which they can be saved, etc.

units.la: Atqui non satis est nouisse, in Christo omnem salutis rationem contineri, nisi qua ratione nos salutem, quæ in ipso est, consequi & apprehendere possimus, intelligamus. Sed & hanc Petrus exponit, dum in fide, id est, propter fidem nominis Iesu Christi, hunc consolidatum & sanatu fuisse dicit: Item: Fides, quæ per ipsum est, dedit ei hanc integritatem, &c. Fide ergo salus apprehenditur, nec extra fidem quicquam in nobis est, quo illa apprehendi possit: eò quòd non alia re quàm fide Christo insectimur. Qui edit carnem meam & sanguinem meum bibit, in me manet, & ego in ipso. Iohan. 6. Quia enim corpore a nobis discedit, & spiritu nos inhabitat, spiritu in nobis viuit & regnat, solius fidei illud opus est, quòd illum & in illo salutem apprehendimus. Quæ causa est, quòd frequenter fides saluare & iustificare dicitur. Sic sanguinis profluuio laboranti dicit dominus, Fides tua saluauit te. Matth. 9. Et peccatrici ijsdem verbis salutem pollicetur. Luc. 7. Saluat quidem & iustificat vnus Christus. In illo enim est vita, & hic nobis a Deo patre factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio & redemptio. 1. Cor. 1. At quia fides nos Christo inserit, & bonorum, quæ in illo sunt, confortes facit, non immeritò illi salus & iustificatio tribui consueuit. Obserua autem fidei definitionem quam verbis hisce Petrus comprehendit, cùm ait: Fides nominis ipsius, & fides quæ per ipsum est. His enim docet, se de ea fide loqui, quæ Christo nititur, & quæ talem agnoscit & credit Christum, qualis nomine suo describitur. Nomen filij Dei incarnati est, IESVS CHRISTVS. Iesus nomen, ab angelo priusquam nasceretur nominatum, in Circuncisione, solenni more gentis Iudaicæ accepit: quod Saluatorem & redemptorem sonat, angelo dicente: Vocabis nomen eius IESVM. Is enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis suis. Matth.1. CHRISTI vox Latinis vnctum significat, & salvationis siue redemptionis modum exprimit. Vngebantur enim antiquitus ex Dei institutione, Reges & sacerdotes, & propterea Mefchijm & Christi, id est, vnčti dici solebăt. Ita autem promissum saluatorem appellari decuit, eo quòd is verus ille Rex est, quem Deus super Zion, montem suum sanctum, constituit, & cuius regnum per totum orbem extenditur. Vide Psal.2. 72. Zach. 9. &c. Hic enim fidelis regis instar, suos ex tyrannide diaboli asseruit, eosdem regit & gubernat, tuetur, & coelestis regni sui thesauris liberalissimè ditat. Idem sacerdos est in aeternum iuxta ordinem Melchisedech. Psal.110. Docuit enim olim, & quotidie docet in sua ecclesia. Vnico autem corporis sui sacrificio omnia hominum peccata expiauit. Et nunc pro nobis intercedit apud patrem, fidelis Pontifex in omnibus ijs transfigendis, quae nobis apud Deum agenda restant. Hebr.2. Quicunque ergo Dei filium regem & sacerdotem ecclesiae Dei & vnicum saluatorem verè agnoscunt, & illo vno solo niituntur, in nomen filij Dei verè credunt, quod praecipuum Dei mandatum esse apostolus testatur. 1.Iohan.3.
units.tr: Yet it is not enough to know that the whole method of salvation is contained in Christ, unless we also understand how we may obtain and grasp the salvation that is in him. Peter explains this too, when he says that by faith in the name of Jesus Christ this man was made strong and healed, that is, through faith in that name. Likewise: "The faith which is through him has given him this wholeness," etc. Salvation is therefore grasped by faith, and nothing in us outside faith can grasp it, since we cling to Christ by no other means than faith. "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him." John 6. For since he is absent from us in body, yet dwells in us by his Spirit, and lives and reigns in us by the Spirit, it is the work of faith alone that we grasp him and, in him, salvation. This is why faith is often said to save and justify. So the Lord says to the woman suffering from a flow of blood, "Your faith has saved you." Matt. 9. And in the same words he promises salvation to the sinful woman. Luke 7. Christ alone saves and justifies. For in him is life, and he has been made by God the Father our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. 1 Cor. 1. But because faith joins us to Christ and makes us partakers of the good things that are in him, it is not undeservedly that salvation and justification are customarily attributed to faith. Note, moreover, the definition of faith that Peter sets out in these words, when he says: "faith in his name, and the faith which is through him." By these words he teaches that he is speaking of that faith which rests on Christ, and which acknowledges and believes Christ to be such as he is described by his name. The name of the incarnate Son of God is JESUS CHRIST. Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was born, was received at circumcision in the solemn manner of the Jewish people; it means Saviour and redeemer, the angel saying: "You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Matt. 1. The word Christ means "anointed" in Latin, and expresses the manner of salvation or redemption. For kings and priests were anointed of old by God's appointment, and therefore were commonly called Messiah and Christ, that is, anointed. It was fitting that the promised Saviour should be so called, because he is that true King whom God has set upon Zion, his holy mountain, and whose kingdom extends through the whole world. See Ps. 2, 72; Zech. 9, etc. For he, like a faithful king, has delivered his people from the tyranny of the devil, rules, governs and protects them, and most generously enriches them with the treasures of his heavenly kingdom. He is also the priest forever after the order of Melchizedek. Ps. 110. For he taught in former times, and teaches daily in his Church; and by the single sacrifice of his body he has expiated all the sins of men. And now he intercedes for us with the Father, a faithful High Priest in all those matters which remain to be transacted for us before God. Heb. 2. Therefore whoever truly acknowledges the Son of God as King and Priest of the Church of God and as the only Saviour, and rests on him alone, truly believes in the name of the Son of God, which the apostle testifies is God's chief commandment. 1 John 3.

units.la: Finis autem siue fructus fidei huius est, ὁλοκληρία, id est, integritas totius hominis, quam clau- do huic obtigisse vidimus. Contulit illi Christus propter fidem integras vires corporis, vt iam & incedere & saltare ac exultare posset. Sed & animam eius non immunem salutis fuisse ex eo patet, quod Deum praedicauit, & apostolorum socius indiuulsus factus est. Totos ergo nos per fidem Christus restituit. Nec enim à peccatis tantummodo & peccatorum poena liberat, verumetiam per verbum Dei immortale spiritus sui operationem nos regenerat. 1. Pet.1. Quo fit, vt caelestia sapere, diuinae voluntati nos accommodare, carnis cupiditatibus resistere, omnia deniq; possimus in Christo, qui nos corroborat. Philip.4. Excipit autem nos perfecta salus & vera beatitudo, quae in coelis parata est. In hanc anima, per fidem è mundo migrans, recipitur, nec in aliquod iudicium venit. Corpus verò, vbi corruptionem omnem exuerit, in nouissimo die tuba & voce archangeli excitatum resurget. Vide Iohan.5. 1. Thess.4. Amplissimus ergo hic fidei fructus est, quem etiam non alia ratione, quàm fide in Christum assequi licebit. Studeamus itaq; verbo Dei, per quod fidem largitur dominus. Iungamus studijs nostris ardentes preces, vt hac fide animati perfectam tum corporis tum animae salutem consequi & in coelis possidere possimus in Iesu Christo, saluatore, Rege & Sacerdote nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The end or fruit of this faith is wholeness (holoklēria), that is, the integrity of the whole man [ὁλοκληρία], which we saw had been granted to this lame man. Christ restored to him, on account of his faith, the full strength of his body, so that he could now both walk and leap and exult. And that his soul was not excluded from salvation is plain from the fact that he proclaimed God and became an undivided companion of the apostles. Christ therefore restores us wholly through faith. For he frees us not only from sins and the punishment of sins, but also regenerates us through the living Word of God by the working of his Spirit. 1 Pet. 1. Hence we are able to savour heavenly things, to accommodate ourselves to the divine will, to resist the desires of the flesh, and finally to do all things in Christ, who strengthens us. Phil. 4. Moreover, perfect salvation and true blessedness, which are prepared in heaven, receive us. The soul, departing from the world through faith, is received into this, and does not come into judgment. The body, when it has put off all corruption, will rise on the last day, raised by the trumpet and the voice of the archangel. See John 5; 1 Thess. 4. This is therefore the very great fruit of faith, which can be attained in no other way than by faith in Christ. Let us therefore devote ourselves to the Word of God, through which the Lord bestows faith. Let us join ardent prayers to our studies, that animated by this faith we may obtain and possess in heaven the perfect salvation of both body and soul, in Jesus Christ, our only Saviour, King and Priest, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIII.
units.tr: Homily 23.

units.la: Et nunc, fratres, scio quòd per ignorantiam fecistis, quemadmodum & principes vestri. Deus autem, quae praenuntiauerat per os omnium prophetarum suorum, Christum passurum esse, sic impleuit. Poenitentiam ergo agite, & convertimini, vt deleantur peccata vestra: vt cum venerint tempora refrigerij à conspectu domini, & miserit eum, qui ante praedicatus est vobis, Iesum Christum: quem oportet quidem coelos accipere vsque in tempora restitutionis omnium, quae locutus est Deus per os omnium suorum sanctorum prophetarum à seculo.
units.tr: And now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as your rulers also did. But God fulfilled in this way what he had foretold through the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ would suffer. Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, so that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and he may send Jesus Christ, who was preached to you before, whom indeed heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things, which God has spoken through the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.

units.la: Dicit Petrus secunda sua concionis parte, miraculi in claudo editi, authorem Deum ita indicauit, vt Iudaeos simul immanissimi sceleris, quod in Dei filium Iesum Christum commiserant admonuerit. At quia nihil hoc atrocius & horribilibus fingi poterat, dubium non est, quin multorum mentes non mediocriter perculsae & territae fuerint. Quare illis refipiscentiae & salutis viam monstrari necesse fuit. Facit hoc in praesenti, quae tertia concionis huius pars est, in qua illorum ingenio & capiti prudentissimè sese accommodat. Primò enim quia in desperationis praecipitio consistere videbantur, veniae & salutis spem adhuc superesse docet. Deinde salutis viam ostendit, & simul gravissimis rationibus hortatur & vrget, vt illam capessere velint. Quae singula si excutiantur, nostrae institutioni non parum seruient. Docent enim, ijs quoq; apud Deum veniae spem esse, qui grauissimè peccarunt: & simul salutis viam monstrant, quam eos ingredi oportet, qui cum Deo reconciliari & salutem consequi cupiunt.
units.tr: In the second part of his sermon, after the miracle wrought on the lame man, Peter named God as the author in such a way that he also reminded the Jews of the most monstrous crime they had committed against God's Son, Jesus Christ. But since nothing more atrocious or horrible could be imagined, there is no doubt that the minds of many were not a little struck and terrified. Therefore it was necessary to show them the way of repentance and salvation. He does this in the present part, which is the third part of this sermon, and in it he very wisely adapts himself to their disposition and understanding. For first, because they seemed to be standing on the precipice of despair, he teaches that there is still hope of pardon and salvation. Then he shows the way of salvation and, at the same time, urges and presses them with the weightiest reasons to take hold of it. If each of these points is examined, they will serve our instruction not a little. For they teach that there is hope of pardon with God even for those who have sinned most grievously, and at the same time they show the way of salvation which those must enter who desire to be reconciled with God and obtain salvation.

units.la: Prudenter vero & commode ab eo orditur, quod ipsos nondum omni salutis spe excidisse docet. Nisi enim hoc intelligant peccatores, frustra illos ad poenitentiam hortaberis, quam sibi nihil profuturam putabunt. Unde fit, ut vel contumaces facti scelus sceleri addant, adeoque cum Deo certamen suscipiant, cuius rei exempla in Caino, Saule & aliis extant: vel desperationis barathro absorbeantur, quod Iudae accidisse legimus. Quae causa est, quod prophetae gravissimis increpationibus, quibus & populi peccata accusant, & poenas meritas minantur, promissiones & oracula de Christo salutare interserunt, ut peccatorum conscientia perterriti, animos per fidem promissi salvatoris denuo erigant, & in illo salutem quaerere discant. Imitatur horum industriam Petrus, qui hoc sui officij esse noverat, ut homines non abster reret minacibus dictis a Christo, sed illos huic lucrifaceret: quem scopum hodie etiam Christi ministris propositum esse decet. Sed argumenta Petri videamus, quibus illos ad veniam & salutis spem erigit.
units.tr: Peter begins wisely and fittingly by teaching that they have not yet fallen from every hope of salvation. For unless sinners understand this, you will be exhorting them to repentance in vain, since they will think it will do them no good. Hence it happens that they either become obstinate and add crime to crime, and so take up a contest with God (examples of this are found in Cain, Saul and others), or they are swallowed up in the pit of despair, which we read happened to Judas. This is the reason why the prophets, in their most severe rebukes, in which they both accuse the people of their sins and threaten the punishments they deserve, interpose promises and oracles about Christ that bring salvation, so that those terrified by the consciousness of their sins may raise their spirits again through faith in the promised Saviour, and learn to seek salvation in him. Peter imitates their diligence. He knew it was his duty not to let men be driven away from Christ by threatening words, but to win them to him; and this aim ought to be set before Christ's ministers today too. But let us look at Peter's arguments, by which he raises them up to pardon and hope of salvation.

units.la: Primo ignorantiae praetextu scelus mitigat. Scio (inquit) quod per ignorantiam fecisti, quem admodum & principes vestri. Si enim illi (ait Paulus) cognouissent, nunquam dominum gloriae crucifixissent. 1. Corinth. 2. At non ita accipi debent Petri verba, quasi scelus ipsorum, quod ante horrendum in modum amplificaverat, nunc extenuare & excusare velit: quod sine levitatis crimine fieri non potuisset. Et ignorantia per se non excusat ea, quae in Dei gloriam committuntur, imo ipsa non levi peccatum est, cum homines in eum finem conditos esse sciamus, ut Deum norint, colant & glorificent. Sed Iudaeorum peccatum a peccato in spiritum sanctum distinguere vult. Est hoc, quando homines agnitam veritatem & Christum, qui animus illorum immotuit, scientes & volentes abiciunt, adeoque cum Deo & Christo eius bellum suscipere audent, quod Iudam proditorem, Iulianum apostatam & alios eius farinae fecisse constat. Horum peccatum remissionem nullam invenire, Christus testatur, Matth. 12. Et Iohannes pro eo precari vetat. 1. Ioan. 5. Rationem huius sententiae Apostolus ad Hebr. cap. 6. simili eleganti a terra petito reddit. Ut enim haec, si & studiose colatur & caelestibus influentijs irrigetur, nihilominus tamen sterilis manet & infrugifera, eo argumento satis docet, se maledictioni obnoxiam & desperatae sterilitatis esse: ita si qui Christi Iesu cognitione, quae sola hominum mentes ad salutem excolit & ad bonum fecundas reddit, non emolliuntur, sed efferatores facti, illam scientes volentes reijciunt & impugnant, nae illi satis aperte produnt, se ex reprobo rum numero esse, de quorum salute nihil sperari posse. Hoc igitur ab auditoribus suis removet Petrus, ut ostendat, de remissione peccati & salute non desperandum esse ipsis, cum ignorantia seducti, non devota impietate peccarint. Et verisimile est, ipsum ad Christi preces respexisse, qui hoc ipso nomine pro iis a quibus crucifigebatur, orat dicens: Pater remitte eis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt. Luc. 23. Est autem locus hic non oscitanter praetereundus, ut discamus, quae illa ignorantia sit, per quam peccata mitigari, adeoque excusari possint. Duplicem enim in scripturis ignorantiam invenimus. Prima impiorum est & eorum qui palam Deo rebelles facti sunt, quam voluntariam dicere possumus, quia ignorare volunt homines, quod scire & assequi poterant. Exemplum huius in Pharaone habetur, qui Iehouam se ignorare dicit, cum illum ex prodigijs quotidianis iam pridem agnouisset, & apud illum pro se orari vellet, iamque moriturus diceret, Iehoua Hebraeorum pugnat contra nos. Vide Exod. 5. & 14. Talis Iudaeorum est, qui cum a Ieremia consilium petijssent, eidem in faciem discere audent, se verbo ipsius minime obtemperaturos esse. Ierem. 44. Talis multorum est hodie qui superstitiones suas ignorantiae praetextu magnifice excusant, nec se aliter edoctos esse profiteantur: interim vero oblatam ipsis veritatem respuunt, audire nolunt, monitores fugiunt, & serpentum instar aures obturant. Est haec in excusabilis, quia emendationi viam praecludit. Imo Christus banc mundi condemnationem esse testatur, quod lucem fugiat, ac sciens volensque tenebris inuolvatur, ne arguantur ipsius prava opera. Ioan. 3. Alterum ignorantiae genus est, quod ex pietatis & gloriae Dei zelo enascitur, quo homines veritatem perseququntur, non quidem veritatis nomine, sed quod per hanc Dei gloriam & cultum imminui exfistimant. Hac multos contra Christum peccavisse credibile est, quod illum Mosis & legis, templi & universi cultus diuinitus instituti hostem esse putarent. Et Paulus eodem zelo seductus, ecclesiam Christi perseque ausus est. 1. Tim. 1. Phil. 3. Ac eodem Iudaeorum plerosque peccavisse olim, author est: Rom. 10. Excusationem vero meretur ignorantia haec, non alio nomine, quam quod institutionem admittit & emendatur: quam si respuant homines, ad primum illud & incurabile genus ignorantiæ referri debent. Obseruent discrimen hoc, qui vel sibijpsis vel alijs hominibus ignorantiæ prætextu hodie blandiùtur, cùm plerosque malitia & contumacia peccare constet.
units.tr: First he mitigates the crime by the pretext of ignorance. "I know," he says, "that you did it in ignorance, as your rulers also did." For, says Paul, if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). But Peter's words should not be taken as if he wished to lessen and excuse a crime that he had previously magnified in such a horrible way; that could not have happened without the charge of levity. Ignorance in itself does not excuse what is committed against God's glory; indeed, it is itself no small sin, since we know that men were created for this very end, that they might know, worship and glorify God. But Peter wishes to distinguish the sin of the Jews from the sin against the Holy Spirit. That sin occurs when men knowingly and willingly reject a truth they have recognized, and Christ, by whom their minds have been moved, and dare to wage war against God and his Christ. It is well known that Judas the traitor, Julian the apostate, and others of that stamp did this. Christ testifies that the sin of such men finds no forgiveness (Matt. 12), and John forbids prayer for them (1 John 5). The Apostle, in Hebrews 6, gives the reason for this view by an elegant comparison taken from the earth. For as land which, though diligently cultivated and watered by heavenly influences, remains barren and unfruitful, and by this shows sufficiently that it is liable to curse and of hopeless sterility, so those who are not softened by the knowledge of Christ Jesus, which alone cultivates men's minds for salvation and makes them fruitful for good, but become brutal, knowingly and willingly reject and assail it, plainly show that they belong to the number of the reprobate, of whose salvation nothing can be hoped. Peter therefore removes this from his hearers, to show that they need not despair of forgiveness of sin and of salvation, since they sinned through ignorance and not through settled impiety. It is likely that he had in mind Christ's prayer, in which, under this very name, he prays for those by whom he was being crucified: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23). This passage should not be passed over carelessly, so that we may learn what kind of ignorance it is by which sins can be mitigated and so excused. For we find a twofold ignorance in Scripture. The first belongs to the impious and to those who have openly become rebels against God; we may call it voluntary, because men wish to be ignorant of what they could know and attain. An example of this is Pharaoh, who says he does not know Jehovah, though he had long ago recognized him from the daily portents, and who, when he was about to die, said: "Jehovah fights against us, the God of the Hebrews" (Exod. 5 and 14). Such is the case of those Jews who, when they asked counsel of Jeremiah, dared to declare to his face that they would by no means obey his word (Jer. 44). Such, today, is the case of many who magnificently excuse their superstitions under the pretext of ignorance and profess that they have been taught nothing else; yet meanwhile they reject the truth offered them, refuse to hear, flee from those who warn them, and stop their ears like serpents. This is inexcusable, because it cuts off the way of amendment. Indeed Christ testifies that this is the condemnation of the world: that men flee the light and, knowingly and willingly, wrap themselves in darkness so that their evil works may not be exposed (John 3). The other kind of ignorance arises from zeal for piety and for the glory of God, by which men persecute the truth, not indeed in the name of truth, but because they think God's glory and worship are diminished by it. It is credible that many sinned against Christ in this way, since they thought him an enemy of Moses and the law, of the temple and of the whole worship divinely instituted. Paul too, seduced by the same zeal, dared to persecute the church of Christ (1 Tim. 1; Phil. 3). And he is the authority for saying that most of the Jews formerly sinned in the same way (Rom. 10). This ignorance deserves pardon for no other reason than that it admits instruction and is corrected. If men reject that, they must be placed under the first and incurable kind of ignorance. Let those who today flatter themselves or others with the pretext of ignorance observe this distinction, since it is clear that most people sin through malice and obstinacy.

units.la: His argumentum à Dei prouidentia desumptum subijcit, vt maiorem illis veniæ & salutis spem faciat. Deus (inquit) quæ prænuntiauerat per os omnium suorum prophetarum, Christum videlicet passurum esse, sic impleuit. Argumenti vis in eo est, quòd Deus illorum peccato bene vsus sit, & proinde ipsos de Dei gratia non debere diffidere. Perinde enim est, ac si diceret: Vos quidem immanissimum facinus designauisse nec potestis nec debetis negare. Sed ideò desperandum non est, quin potius facti vestri finem respicite, ad quem Dei immensa bonitas omne hoc negotium direxit. Vobis quidem animus fuit, Christi memoriam delere è terra viuentium, eò quòd illum Deo & religioni verae aduersum esse putaretis. Excæcauit vos ignorantiæ malum, quo factum est, vt in filium Dei insana mente grassaremini. Sed omnis huius Tragœdiæ finis fuit lætissimus. Nam quod nemo sperauisset, Deus hoc pacto æternum suum consilium de humani generis redemptione executus est, & impleuit quæcunque per prophetas olim prædicta fuere. Cur ergo spem salutis abijceretis, quam modò partam esse auditis? Cur de Dei bonitate desperaretis, quam in ipso scelere vobis tam propitia affulsisse cernitis? Nunquam certè propter hoc peccatum vos reijciet Deus, quo tam feliciter abusus est, modò vos salutis consilium, quod nunc aperiam, non reiecerítis. Admonemur bis rursum, quis nobis diuinæ prouidentiæ vsus esse debeat: non quidem vt in hac scelerum nostrorum patrocinium, sed fidei vitæq; institutionem & animorum consolationem quæramus. Non enim occisi Christi scelus à Iudæis in Deum transfert apostolus, sed Deum Iudæorum facto bene vsum fuisse docet. Ita si quid vel à nobis vel alijs delinquitur, culpam delicti in nobis agnoscamus, nec ita nos excusemus, vt Deum flagitij authorem statuamus. Quòd si verò quid boni ex nostro scelere enascitur, nec tunc quidè nos omni culpa liberatos esse putemus, sed Dei bonitatem exosculemur, quæ flagitijs quoq;, quibus damnationem merebamur, ad nostram salutem abutitur. Exemplum huius rei supra ex Iosephi historia, à fratribus venditi, adduximus, cui si præsens hoc coniungas, omnem huius causæ rationem ceu in speculo cernere licebit. Præterea nec eos audiamus, qui peccandum esse dicunt intrepidè, quando peccatis quoq; nostris Dei gloria & salus nostra prouebi potest. Nec enim (vt Paulus monet) facienda sunt mala, vt veniant bona. Rom. 3. Imò quo plura in nos extant diuinæ bonitatis argumenta, eò quoq; plus de peccatis dolere, & diuinæ voluntati obedire debemus. Obseruemus etiam hic, non temere nos de aliorum peccatis iudicare debere. Examinanda quidem sunt illa ad verbi diuini regulam, damnationis verò sententia non temere intonanda est, quando diuinæ prouidentiæ consilium non semper nobis notum est, quæ fortasse in multorum salutem vtetur illius opera, quem priuato & nimis præcipiti affectu damnare instituerimus. Vide quæ de iudicijs eiusmodi habentur Matth. 7.
units.tr: To these arguments he adds one drawn from God's providence, to give them greater hope of pardon and salvation. God (he says) fulfilled what he had foretold through the mouth of all his prophets, namely that Christ would suffer. The force of the argument lies in this: God made good use of their sin, and therefore they ought not to distrust God's grace. It is just as if he said: "You neither can nor ought to deny that you planned a most monstrous deed. But you must not despair; rather, look to the end of your deed, to which God's immense goodness directed this whole affair. You indeed intended to blot Christ's memory from the land of the living, because you thought him opposed to God and the true religion. The evil of ignorance blinded you, so that you raged with a mad mind against the Son of God. But the outcome of this whole tragedy was most joyful. For, as no one would have hoped, God by this means carried out his eternal plan for the redemption of the human race, and fulfilled whatever had been foretold of old by the prophets. Why then would you cast away the hope of salvation, which you hear has now been won? Why would you despair of God's goodness, which you see shone so favourably upon you even in the crime itself? Certainly God will never reject you on account of this sin, which he has used so happily, if now you do not reject the plan of salvation which I am about to reveal." We are admonished once more how we ought to use divine providence: not to find in it a defence for our wickedness, but to seek instruction for faith and life and consolation for our minds. For the apostle does not transfer the crime of killing Christ to God, but teaches that God made good use of the Jews' deed. So if anything is sinned by us or by others, let us acknowledge the guilt of the offence in ourselves, and not excuse ourselves in such a way as to make God the author of the wrong. But if something good arises from our wickedness, let us not on that account think ourselves freed from all blame; rather, let us embrace God's goodness, which turns even the crimes by which we deserved condemnation to our salvation. We adduced an example of this above from the history of Joseph, sold by his brothers; if you join this passage to it, you will be able to see the whole reasoning of this matter as in a mirror. Moreover, let us not listen to those who boldly say that we should sin, since God's glory and our salvation can be advanced even by our sins. For, as Paul warns, evil things are not to be done that good may come (Rom. 3). Indeed, the more evidence of divine goodness there is toward us, the more we ought to grieve over our sins and obey the divine will. Let us also observe here that we ought not to judge the sins of others rashly. Those things indeed must be examined by the rule of the divine Word, but the sentence of condemnation is not to be pronounced rashly, since the counsel of divine providence is not always known to us. It may perhaps use the work of the very man whom we had set out to condemn from a private and overly hasty feeling, for the salvation of many. See what is said about judgments of this kind in Matthew 7.

units.la: II. Salutis consilium præscribit.
units.tr: II. He prescribes the plan of salvation.

units.la: Videamus autem salutis consilium, quod Petrus paucis verbis complectitur, dicens: Pœnitentiâ agite, & conuertimini, vt deleantur peccata vestra. Habet sententia hæc præceptum & promissionem. Præceptum idem est, quo supra eos instruxit, qui peccatorum agnitione compungebantur. Rem verò vnam & eandem duobus verbis enuntiat. Primò enim pœnitentiâ agere iubet, quæ proprie peccatorum agnitionem & cordis contritionem comprehendit. Ab his passim exordiuntur, quicunq; de salute consulunt. Quia nisi peccata agnoscamus & de ijsdem doleamus, nunquam de emendatione & reconciliatione cum Deo cogitabimus. At quia interdum impij quoq; peccata agnoscunt, & de ijs dolent (quemadmodum in Iuda cernimus) alterum quoq; addit, nimirum vt Conuertantur. Conuersionem verò eò fieri oportet, vnde peccando receditur. At peccatis à Deo recedi notius est, quàm vt multis probari oporteat. Ideò enim vias domini reliquisse dicuntur in scripturis, quorum peccata accusantur. Ad Deum ergo per pœnitentiam nos conuerti oportet. Fit hoc partim vitæ emendatione, partim fide in Iesum Christum. Illa enim efficit, vt à peccatis discedamus, quibus Dei iram prouocauimus: hæc verò iustitia Christi nos induit, & facit, vt in illius conspectu consistere possimus. Quia in Christo pacem nobis reconciliatum esse euangelica doctrina testatur. Ex fide autem & inuocatio Dei, & quicunq; alij sunt pœnitentiæ fructus, enasci consueuerunt. Eandem ergo salutis rationem Petrus, quam supra vidimus, hic quoq; tradit, quam non minus ad nos, quàm ad Iudæos, pertinere putabimus. Breuiores verò hic sumus, quia quæ dici poterant, superius dicta sunt, vnde plura petat qui volet.
units.tr: Let us now consider the plan of salvation, which Peter sums up in a few words: "Repent, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out." This saying contains a command and a promise. The command is the same one by which he earlier instructed those who were pricked in conscience over their sins. He expresses one and the same thing in two words. First he bids them repent, which properly includes the recognition of sins and the contrition of heart. Everyone who seeks salvation generally begins here, because unless we recognise our sins and grieve over them, we will never think about amendment and reconciliation with God. But since the wicked too sometimes recognise their sins and grieve over them, as we see in Judas, he adds the second word, namely that they be converted. Conversion must take place from the very point where we turn away by sinning. That we turn away from God through sins is too well known to need proof. For this reason the Scriptures say that those whose sins are condemned have "forsaken the ways of the Lord." We must therefore be converted to God through repentance. This happens partly by amendment of life and partly by faith in Jesus Christ. The first makes us turn away from the sins by which we provoked God's wrath; the second clothes us with the righteousness of Christ and makes it possible for us to stand in his sight, since the gospel teaching testifies that we are reconciled to God in Christ and at peace with him. From faith arise the invocation of God and all the other fruits of repentance. So Peter here sets out the same way of salvation that we saw above, and we must think it pertains to us no less than to the Jews. We are briefer here because what could be said has been said above, and whoever wishes more may seek it there.

units.la: Præcepto autem siue consilio promissionem coniungit, vt magis moueat. Pollicetur autem peccatorum remissionem, de qua illos cumprimis solicitos fuisse credibile est. Sed obserua locutionis genus, quo non temere vti voluit. Conuertimini (inquit) vt deleantur peccata vestra. Non ipsis hanc meriti gloriam tribuit, quasi pœnitentiæ operibus peccata delere & pro illis satisfacere possint. Sed illa ab alio deleri oportere docet, à Deo nimirum, cui peccamus & peccando debitores reddimur. Metaphora enim est à creditoribus sumpta, penes quos solos debita è rationum suarum libris delendi ius est atq; potestas, vbi vel satisfactum fuerit à debitoribus, vel ipsi debitum omne ex gratia remiserint. Atqui Deo debitores fiunt quicunque peccant, iuxta illud Dauidis: Tibi domine peccaui. Et peccatum reuera est, quod contra Dei voluntatem committitur. Nisi ergo Deus peccatorum debita deleat, illis nos nemo alius liberare poterit. Consenserunt in hoc sapientissimi quiq; ex Iudæis & gentibus. Etsi enim hæc suis superstitionibus multum tribuerent, eas tamen irritas esse fatebantur, nisi peculiaris aliqua numinis gratia accederet. Inter Iudæos vero plurimum quidem suis operibus pharisæi tribuebant: at illos ipsos palam confessos fuisse legimus, quòd solus Deus peccata remittendi potestatem habeat. Matth.9. Remittit autem ea, siue delet, non quod nostrarum virium sit illa expiare & pro ipsis satisfacere (quia coram illo non iustificatur vlla caro, & omnes nostræ iustitiæ, veteris, attritæ & lacerææ vestis instar sunt, quæ nec tegere nec calefacere possunt). Psal.143. Isa. 64.) Sed quòd filius Dei, Iesus Christus, illa sua mortis merito in ara crucis expiauit, adeoq; sui sanguinis pretio omne hoc deleuit, quod nos mortis reos coram Deo faciebat. Eodem sensu dominus apud Isaiam cap.43. & 44. delendi metaphora utitur, omnemq; huius causæ rationem Christus eleganti parabola Matth. 18. explicat. Huius ergo Petrus Iudæos admonet, vt iam nunc deleta esse intelligant peccata sua, siquidem Christum Iesum, cuius merito deleta sunt, ex animo amplectantur. Quod vero illis dicitur, nobis quoq; dici putemus, quibus hoc ante omnia curæ esse debet, vt dum pœnitentiam agimus, in gratuitam peccatorum nostrorum remissionem oculos defigamus, ne impia & nimis audaci confidentia nobisipsis & nostrorum operum meritis vendicemus quod solius gratiæ Dei beneficium est, Christi merito impetratum.
units.tr: Peter joins a promise to the command, or exhortation, so as to move them more. He promises the forgiveness of sins, which they were very likely especially anxious about. But notice the kind of expression he chose to use: "Be converted, that your sins may be blotted out." He does not ascribe the glory of merit to them, as if by works of repentance they could blot out their sins and make satisfaction for them. He teaches rather that they must be blotted out by another, namely by God, against whom we sin and by whose sin we become debtors. This is a metaphor taken from creditors, who alone have the right and power to strike debts from their account books, either when the debtors have paid or when they themselves have freely forgiven the whole debt. Now everyone who sins becomes a debtor to God, according to David's words: "Against you only have I sinned." And truly it is sin that is committed against the will of God. Unless God therefore blots out the debts of sins, no one else can free us from them. The wisest people, both among the Jews and among the Gentiles, agreed on this. For although they attributed much to their superstitions, they admitted that these were in vain unless some special favour of the deity was added. Among the Jews, the Pharisees attributed very much to their own works; yet we read that they openly confessed that God alone has the power of forgiving sins (Matt. 9). He forgives them, or blots them out, not because it lies within our strength to expiate them and make satisfaction for them, since "no flesh is justified in his sight," and all our righteousnesses are like a filthy rag, which can neither cover nor warm (Ps. 143; Isa. 64). Rather, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, expiated them on the altar of the cross by the merit of his death, and so by the price of his own blood blotted out all that made us guilty of death before God. In the same sense the Lord uses the metaphor of blotting out in Isaiah 43 and 44, and Christ explains the whole reason for this cause in an elegant parable (Matt. 18). Peter therefore admonishes the Jews of this, that they should understand their sins to be already blotted out, provided they embrace with their whole heart Jesus Christ, by whose merit they have been blotted out. And what is said to them, let us think is said to us as well, for whom this ought above all to be a concern: that while we repent, we fix our eyes on the free forgiveness of our sins, lest in impious and overly bold confidence we claim for ourselves and our own works' merits what is the benefit of God's grace alone, obtained by the merit of Christ.

units.la: Porrò vt nihil vel salutarius est vel homini magis necessarium pœnitentia & conuersione ad Deum quam in præsenti Petrus suadet: ita caro vix quicquam aliud sibi difficilius persuaderi patitur. Nam & ea est natura corruptio, vt peccatis delectemur, & ita superbimus vt culpam agnoscere & emendare pudeat. Argumentis ergo cunctabundos vrget apostolus, quæ & validissima & præsenti causæ cumprimis conuenientia adhibet. Nouissimi enim diei memoriam & gloriosum Christi iudicis aduentum ipsis ob oculos statuit. Est autem ecliptica oratio, quæ facile farciri poterit hoc modo: Non fructra pœnitentiam & conuersionem ad Deum à nobis exigo. Ea enim vobis salutaris & necessaria erit, vt olim subsistere possitis, cum venerint tempora refrigerij à conspectu domini, & miserit eum, qui ante prædicatus est, Iesum Christum, quem oportet quidem cœlos accipere vsq; in tempus restitutionis omnium, &c. Ex quibus duplex argumentum elici potest. Primum à tempore sumitur, cuius sensus est: Non semper durabit hæc mundi forma, nec semper ea erit rerum & hominum ratio, quæ hodie conspicitur. Veniet enim dies refrigerij & restitutionis, quo & pij libertabuntur, & ab impijs exigetur restitutio. Quàm ergo vobis salus vestra chara est, tam studiose curate, vt & vobis dies ille refrigerium & salutem, non autem terrorem & cruciatum afferat. Alterum argumentum à iudicis persona producit. Mittet Deus hunc ipsum iudicem, de quo nunc agitur, Iesum Christum videlicet, coram huius tribunali omnes homines sisti oportebit, vt ibi recipiant in corporibus suis retributionem factorum suorum omnium, siue illa bona siue mala fuerint. Annon ergo necesse erit, vt cum illo iudice in gratiam redeatis, priusquam ille scelerum pœnas à vobis exigat? Videtur autem & tertium argumentum ex his colligi posse, cum dicit, eum iudicem venturum, qui nunc ipsis prædicetur. Sic enim ignorantia prætextum illis aufert, ne in iudicij die per ignorantiam (qua in præsenti illorum facinus mitigarat Petrus) se excusari posse existimarent. Atqui tantum habent ponderis quæ hic dicuntur, vt si quem illorum consyderatio mouere nequit, na ille frustra aliis argumentis vrgebitur.
units.tr: Moreover, just as nothing is more salutary or more necessary for a human being than the repentance and conversion to God that Peter here urges, so the flesh scarcely allows itself to be persuaded of anything more difficult. For it is our corrupt nature to take pleasure in sins, and we are so proud that we are ashamed to acknowledge and amend our fault. The apostle therefore presses the hesitant with arguments, and brings forward ones that are very strong and especially suited to the present cause. He sets before their eyes the memory of the last day and the glorious coming of Christ as judge. The sentence is elliptical, and it can easily be filled out in this way: "I do not demand repentance and conversion to God from you in vain. For it will be salutary and necessary for you, so that you may stand when the times of refreshing come from the presence of the Lord, and he sends Jesus Christ, who was preached to you before, whom indeed heaven must receive until the time of the restoration of all things," etc. Two arguments can be drawn from this. The first comes from time, and its sense is: this form of the world will not last forever, nor will the present order of things and of human beings always remain as it is today. For the day of refreshing and restoration will come, on which the righteous will be set free and restitution will be demanded from the wicked. As your salvation is dear to you, therefore, take earnest care that that day brings you refreshing and salvation, not terror and torment. The second argument is drawn from the person of the judge. God will send this very judge of whom we now speak, namely Jesus Christ; before his tribunal all human beings must appear, so that there they may receive in their bodies the recompense of all their deeds, whether good or evil. Will it not therefore be necessary for you to be reconciled with that judge before he exacts the penalties of your crimes from you? A third argument also seems to be gathered from these words, when he says that the judge who is now preached to them is the one who will come. For in this way he takes away from them the pretext of ignorance, lest they think they can excuse themselves on the day of judgement on the ground of ignorance, which Peter had lessened their guilt by in the present. Indeed, what is said here has such weight that if a person cannot be moved by consideration of it, he will be urged in vain by other arguments.

units.la: Venit autem hic nobis obseruanda nouissimi diei conditio, quam duobus epithetis exprimit. Primo diem refrigerij vocat per Synechdochen. Ad solos enim pios istud pertinet, qui tunc refrigerium sentient, & omni molestia liberabuntur. Tunc abstergat Deus omnem lachrymam ab oculis eorum Et mors vltra non erit, neq; luctus, neq; clamor, neq; dolor, &c. Apoc. 21. Tunc item iis bonis beatum tur, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec hominis ratione comprehendi possunt. Isa. 64. Tu u è carne sua (sicut Iob ait) Deum videbunt, qui cum in mundo viuerent, in carne sua omnis generis molestias patienter sustinuerunt. Iohan. 19. Quæ causa est, quòd Christus nos capita attollere iubet, quando signa nouissimum diem præcessura videmus, eò quòd tunc redemptio nostra appropinquet. Luc. 21. cap. Nec enim terribilis esse poterit piis Christi iudicis conspectus, cum hunc suum saluatorem & aduocatum esse intelligant. Et hoc ingens illud fidei bonum est, quod non aliunde homini obtingere poterit. Sola fides nos ad Christi aduentum intrepidos reddit & salutis certos. 1. Ioban. 2. Nulla tunc ex opibus, ex honoribus, ex mundi amicitia salutis spes affulgere poterit iis, qui fidem in Christum, cum hic agerent, aspernati sunt. Hac itaq; spe nos in aduersis huius mundi contra omnes tentationes armari conuenit, nec unquam à salutis via dimouebimur.
units.tr: Here we must note the condition of the last day, which he expresses by two epithets. First he calls it the day of refreshing, by synecdoche; for this belongs only to the godly, who will then feel refreshment and be freed from all trouble. "Then God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain" (Rev. 21). Then too they will be blessed with those good things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor can be grasped by human reason (Isa. 64). They will see God "in their flesh," as Job says, they who, while they lived in the world, bore all kinds of trouble patiently in their flesh (John 19). This is why Christ bids us lift up our heads when we see the signs that will precede the last day, because then our redemption draws near (Luke 21). For the sight of Christ the judge cannot be terrible to the godly, since they know him to be their saviour and advocate. This is the great good of faith, which cannot come to a person from any other source. Faith alone makes us fearless at the coming of Christ and certain of salvation (1 John 2). Then no hope of salvation from wealth, from honours, or from friendship with the world will shine on those who scorned faith in Christ while they lived here. Therefore it is fitting that in the adversities of this world we arm ourselves with this hope against all temptations, and we will never be moved from the way of salvation.

units.la: Deinde restitutionis diem vocat, quia tunc omnium restitutio fiet, & perfecta immutabilisq; reducetur rerum conditio siue forma. Qua, quoad hic vixerimus, frustra à multis expetitur & quaeritur. Plenus enim confusionis est mundus hic, & turbas quotidie nouas dare consueuit, quibus etiam Christi regnum sic interdum petitur, ut prorsus corruisse videri possit. At nouissimo die ita constitue tur regnum illud, sicut prophetæ futurum prædixerunt. Abolita enim & pedibus Christi subiecta omni aduersaria potestate, nihil erit amplius, quod fideles turbare possit; tuncq; erit læta illa, pacifica & tranquilla rerum conditio, cuius frequenter prophetæ meminerunt. Isa. 9. & 11. Iere. 23. Amos 9. cap. &c. Restituentur eodem die corpora, qualicunq; modo corrupta fuerint. Dabit enim mare mortuos, qui in ipso sunt, similiter & mors & infernus. Apoc. 20. Restituetur felix & læta mundi conditio, & quæ nunc sub corruptionis pondere ingemiscit, mundi machina liberabitur. Rom. 8. qualis prius quam ob hominis peccatum maledictione feriretur, extitit. Erunt enim cæli noui & terra noua, in quibus iustitia inhabitat. Apoc. 21. 2. Pet. 3. Retribuetur vnicuiq; in corpore suo prout egit, siue bene siue male. 2. Corinth. 5. Sed & ipse Christus, vbi omnem principatum aboleuerit, & sibi subiecerit omnia, tunc subijcietur ei, qui illi subiecit omnia, & tradet regnum patri, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus. 1. Corinth. 15. Deniq; ea tunc erit omnium restitutio, quam modo nec verbis explicare, nec ratione humana complecti possumus. Quia nunc ex parte cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: at vbi venerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur. Nunc per speculum cernimus in ænigmate, tunc autem facie ad faciem, &c. Corinth. 13. Interea autem horum consyderatio institutionis ferre debet, vt huius restitutionis spe suffulti, patienter feramus quæcunq; ferenda veniunt, & ita vitæ conuersationem per fidem in Christum instituamus, vt nobis quoq; cum reliquis pijs, consolationem & refrigerium magnus ille dies domini afferat, &c.
units.tr: Then he calls it the day of restitution, because on that day all things will be restored, and the condition or form of things will be brought back perfect and unchangeable. Until we have lived here, this is sought and asked for in vain by many. For this world is full of confusion and daily produces new disturbances, by which even the kingdom of Christ is sometimes so attacked that it might seem altogether to have collapsed. But on the last day that kingdom will be established just as the prophets foretold it would be. For once every hostile power has been abolished and placed under the feet of Christ, nothing will remain that could disturb the faithful; then will come that joyful, peaceful and tranquil condition of things, which the prophets often mention. Isa. 9 and 11; Jer. 23; Amos 9, etc. On that same day bodies will be restored, however they may have been corrupted. For the sea will give up the dead who are in it, and likewise death and hell. Apoc. 20. The happy and joyful condition of the world will be restored, and the frame of the world, which now groans under the weight of corruption, will be set free. Rom. 8. It will be such as it was before it was struck by the curse because of man's sin. For there will be new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. Apoc. 21; 2 Pet. 3. Each one will be repaid in his body according to what he has done, whether good or bad. 2 Cor. 5. But Christ himself also, when he has abolished every rule and subjected all things to himself, will then be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, and will hand the kingdom over to the Father, so that God may be all in all. 1 Cor. 15. Finally, that will then be the restitution of all things, which we cannot now explain in words or grasp by human reason. For now we know in part and prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, then what is in part will be abolished. Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face, etc. 1 Cor. 13. Meanwhile, the consideration of these things ought to furnish instruction, so that, supported by the hope of this restitution, we may patiently bear whatever must be borne, and so order our manner of life through faith in Christ that that great day of the Lord may bring consolation and refreshment to us too, along with the other godly, etc.

units.la: Atqui multis mirum videtur, quòd aduentum suum tam diu dominus differat, & de hoc fortasis Iudæi quæstionem mouere poterant. Quia enim ex nostræ carnis ingenio Deum metimur, non possumus non mirari iudiciorum Dei dilationem & moram. Sed præoccupat eiusmodi quæstiones Petrus, cum ait, Christum oportere cœlos capere, vel in cœlis regnare, donec omnia restituantur & impleantur, quæ Deus olim per prophetas prædixit. Absoluit ille quidem in terris nostræ redemptionis negotium. Sed restabant adhuc peragenda quædam, olim diuinitus decreta & prædicta. Nam euangelium in toto orbe prædicari & gentes in ecclesiæ communionem vocari oportebat, sicuti magno consensu omnes prophetæ testantur. Restabat & Antichristi mysterium, cuius tyrannide ecclesia exerceri & numerum martyrum Christi impleri opus erat. 2. Thess. 2. Apoc. 7. His ergo locum cessit Christus, in cœlos receptus, & omni tam in cœlis quam in terris potestate accepta. Nemo igitur illu vel nostri vel sui officij oblitum esse putet, quando aduentum suum & iudicij diem differt. Certa enim illi constat omnium quæ facit ratio. Consoletur interim nos, quòd eum in cœlis regnare nonimus. Ibi illu animis per fidem eleuatis quæramus, de corporali eius præsentia in terris nihil soliciti, donec magnus ille dies illuxerit, quando fulgur is instar repente apparebit. Matth. 24. Vtinam vero Petri verba diligentius excuterent, qui bodie vt corporalem Christi in terris præsentiam statuant, humanam eius naturam propter diuinæ communionem siue coniunctionem ita per omnia extendi dicunt, vt nullo vel loco vel tempore circumscribi possit. Quid igitur Petro respondeant viderint, qui & loci & tempus eidem assignat; imo sic diuinitus constitutum esse ait, vt in cœlos assumptus illic confideat vsque dum nouissinouissimus ille dies adueneric, quo iudex redibit, & olim promissam pijs restitutionem plenè conse-ret. Scio illos cœlum terræ miscere, & cœli nomine gloriam & conuersationem cœlestem intelligere, quæ etiam in terris agenti contingat. Sed commentum hoc vt scripturis probari nequit, ita erudita vetustati plane ignotum fuit, & proinde operosa confutatione non opus habet. Omissis ergo illorum argutijs, discamus ex tertia huius concionis parte, ne in peccatis de Dei gratia desperemus, sed per pœnitentiam fidemq; veram conuertamur ad Deum, ac ita nos præparemus, vt & nobis felix & lætus illucescat dies ille, quo suorum assertor & impiorum iudex veniet Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet to many it seems strange that the Lord delays his coming so long, and perhaps the Jews could raise this question about it. For since we measure God by the nature of our flesh, we cannot help but wonder at the delay and postponement of God's judgments. But Peter anticipates questions of this kind when he says that Christ must receive heaven, or reign in heaven, until all things are restored and fulfilled which God long ago foretold through the prophets. He indeed completed the business of our redemption on earth. But certain things still remained to be carried out, which had been decreed and foretold by God of old. For the gospel had to be preached throughout the whole world and the nations had to be called into the communion of the Church, as all the prophets with one accord bear witness. There also remained the mystery of Antichrist, by whose tyranny the Church had to be harassed and the number of Christ's martyrs completed. 2 Thess. 2; Apoc. 7. To these things, then, Christ, received into heaven and having received all power in heaven and on earth, gave place. Let no one therefore think that he has forgotten either our office or his own when he delays his coming and the day of judgment. For the reason of all that he does is certainly known to him. Let it console us meanwhile that we do not see him reigning in heaven. There let us seek him with our minds lifted up through faith, being in no way anxious about his bodily presence on earth, until that great day dawns, when he will suddenly appear like lightning. Matt. 24. Would that they examined Peter's words more carefully, those who today maintain a bodily presence of Christ on earth, and who say that his human nature, because of its communion or conjunction with the divine, is so extended in every respect that it can be confined to no place or time. Let those who assign both place and time to him see for themselves what they will answer Peter; indeed he says that it has been divinely ordained that he, taken up into heaven, should remain there until that last day arrives, on which the judge will return and fully bring about the restitution promised long ago to the godly. I know that these people mix heaven with earth, and understand by heaven the glory and heavenly conduct which may befall a man even while living on earth. But this invention cannot be proved from Scripture, and it was entirely unknown to learned antiquity, and therefore it does not need a laborious refutation. Setting aside, then, their subtleties, let us learn from the third part of this sermon not to despair of God's grace in our sins, but to be converted to God through repentance and true faith, and so prepare ourselves that that day will dawn happily and joyfully for us, on which Jesus Christ, the vindicator of his own and the judge of the wicked, will come, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 24.

units.la: Moses quidem ad patres dixit: Prophetam vobis suscitabit Dominus Deus vester ex fratribus vestris, mei similem. Illum audietis iuxta omnia quæcunq; locutus fuerit vobis. Erit autem, vt omnis anima, quæ non audierit prophetam illum, exterminetur è populo. Quin & omnes prophetæ à Samuele ac deinceps, quotquot locuti sunt, annuntiaue-runt dies istos.
units.tr: Moses indeed said to the fathers: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your brothers, like me. You shall hear him in all things whatever he speaks to you. And it shall be that every soul which does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from the people." Moreover, all the prophets from Samuel onward, as many as spoke, announced these days.

units.la: Postquam diuus Petrus immane Iudæorum facinus, quod in Dei filium designauerant, graviter accusauit, ijsdem tertia suæ concionis parte salutis consilium præbuit, quod proximo sermone explicuimus. Iussit autem illos pœnitere & ad Deum conuerti, quod partim per vitæ emendationem fit, partim per fidem in Iesum Christum, cuius merito Deo patri reconciliati sumus. Atqui non leuis erat remora, quæ Iudæos Christum amplecti prohibebat. Quia enim illius cognitionem nondum affectuti erant, timebant plerique, ne illum amplectendo, in Mosen & legem diuinitus per Mosen datam peccarent: & graue illis videbatur eum cultum abijcere, quem à Deo traditum & maiorum exemplo confirmatum tot iam seculis tenuerant. Huic igitur errori quarta suæ orationis parte medetur apostolus, docens, tam Mosen quam prophetas ad Christum relegare veros Dei cultores, & proinde tam ab esse, vt fide in Christum contra legem peccent, vt potius nec Mosi obedire nec prophetis vere credere possint, nisi Christum, cui illi testimonium dederunt, recipiant. Simul vero ne Christi bonitati diffide-rent, quem abs se tam immani crudelitate graviter offensum esse, iam multoties audiuerant, ostendit hunc, qui patribus promissus fuit, ad ipsos quoq; pertinere, ac illis non minus, quam patribus, salutarem fore, si ipsum vera fide complectantur. At in præsenti ea tantum modo executimus, quæ de Christi mysterio, in veteris Testamenti libris fundato, Petrus affert.
units.tr: After blessed Peter had severely accused the Jews of the monstrous crime they had committed against the Son of God, in the third part of his sermon he offered them the counsel of salvation, which we explained in the previous sermon. He ordered them to repent and turn to God, which happens partly through amendment of life and partly through faith in Jesus Christ, by whose merit we have been reconciled to God the Father. Yet there was no slight obstacle preventing the Jews from embracing Christ. For since they had not yet grasped knowledge of him, many feared that by embracing him they would sin against Moses and the law given by God through Moses; and it seemed hard to them to cast off that worship which they had held for so many ages, handed down by God and confirmed by the example of their ancestors. The apostle therefore remedies this error in the fourth part of his speech, teaching that Moses and the prophets alike refer true worshippers of God to Christ, and that therefore it is so far from being a sin against the law to believe in Christ that rather they cannot truly obey Moses nor truly believe the prophets unless they receive Christ, to whom those men bore witness. At the same time, lest they distrust the goodness of Christ, whom they had heard many times they had gravely offended by their monstrous cruelty, he shows that this one, who was promised to the fathers, pertains to them also, and will be no less saving for them than for the fathers, if they embrace him with true faith. But at present we have dealt only with those things which Peter brings forward about the mystery of Christ, founded in the books of the Old Testament.

units.la: A Mose vero orditur, eò quòd summa illius esset apud Iudæos authoritas. Cuius cum multa posset testimonia proferre, vnum è multis deligit, quo Christum populo Dei iam olim doctorem & ma-gistrum destinatum esse docet, quod præsenti causæ plurimum seruiebat, cum (vt modo diximus) multis religio esset à Mose deficere, quem sibi à Deo legislatorem & magistrum datum esse noverant. Ostendit igitur, nec ipsi Mosi eum animum fuisse, vt in ipso hærerent perpetuò, sed alium monstrauisse prophetam, qui perfectius omnia traditurus esset. Extat locus Deuteron. 18. cap. Prohibentur illic superstitiosæ & fatidicæ ethnicorum artes, quibus in futurorum & arcanorum Dei cognitionem diuinatione, mathesi impia, augurijs, necromantia & alijs eius generis vaticinandi modis penetrare conati sunt: & monet Moses, vt his abiectis, ad vnum Dei verbum conuertantur, totiq; ab vno illo pendeant. Ne vero Dei verbum inuentu difficile putarent, nunquam defuturos dicit prophetas, quos ex ipsis Deus suscitaturus sit, & quorum ministerio de Dei voluntate in omnibus, quæ agenda sunt, erudiri possint. Nec falluntur, qui eo loco vniuersalem promissionem contineri dicunt, quæ prophetiæ donum in Dei populo siue ecclesia stabilitur. At generalem promissionem ad Christum non inepte Petrus restringit, quem prophetarum principem esse constat, & cuius spiritu prophetas omnes instigatos & instructos fuisse alibi tradit. 1. Pet. 1. Et in Christum competere quæ hic à Mose dicuntur, euidentius est, quàm vt prolixiori demonstratione opus habeat. Nam & ille ex Iudæis natus est, & à Deo missum fuisse ex miraculis & doctrina constat, quam prophetarum doctrinæ omni ex parte con-formem esse videmus. Quare validissimum videtur Petri argumentum, quo Christi fidem eu Mofis oraculo illis persuadere nititur, perinde ac si diceret: Moses adeo non sibi soli omnem docendi authoritatem vendicavit, vt cuius propheta Dei verbum praedicanti, aures & fidem praebere iusserit, poenamq; capitalem decreuerit vniuersis propheticorum sermonum contemptoribus. Quanto magis ergo Christo vos credere decet, quo non alius Dei patris voluntatem perfectius & euidentius declarauit, & in quem verissime quadrant quaecunq; a Mose de propheta dicuntur? Sicq; propositi sui finem & scopum pulchre attingit Petrus, vt nimirum praepositera religione illorum animos liberet, qui Mosis & legis nimia veneratione & inepto sensu impediti, Christum amplecti renuebant. Quia tamen locum Mosis tum Petrus tum Stephanus (vt infra patebit) de Christo exponunt, nobis quoq; ea hic inuestiganda erunt, quae nos in Christi cognitione instruere possunt. Et primo quidem Christum non inelegantur nobis Moses describit. Deinde officij, quo illi obstricti sumus, admonet. Simul vero capitalem sententiam in Christi contemptores stringit.
units.tr: He begins from Moses, because Moses' authority was supreme among the Jews. Although he could bring forward many testimonies from him, he selects one of many, by which he teaches that Christ was long ago destined as teacher and master for God's people. This served the present cause very well, since (as we have just said) many were in danger of deserting Moses, whom they knew had been given by God as lawgiver and master. He shows, therefore, that Moses himself did not intend that they should cling to him forever, but pointed to another prophet who would deliver everything more perfectly. There is a passage in Deuteronomy 18. There the superstitious and fortune-telling arts of the heathen are forbidden, by which they tried to penetrate the knowledge of future and hidden things through divination, impious astrology, augury, necromancy and other kinds of prophesying. Moses warns that, these being rejected, they should turn to the one word of God and depend wholly on it. Lest they think the word of God hard to find, he says that prophets will never be lacking, whom God will raise up from among them, and through whose ministry they can be instructed in God's will in all things that must be done. Nor are they mistaken who say that a general promise is contained in that place, by which the gift of prophecy is established in God's people or church. But Peter not unfittingly restricts the general promise to Christ, who is known to be the prince of the prophets, and by whose Spirit he elsewhere says all the prophets were stirred and instructed (1 Pet. 1). And that what is said here by Moses applies to Christ is too evident to need a lengthier demonstration. For he too was born of the Jews, and it is clear from his miracles and teaching that he was sent by God; we see that this teaching agrees in every respect with the teaching of the prophets. Hence Peter's argument seems most powerful, by which he strives to persuade them of faith in Christ from the oracle of Moses, just as if he said: Moses by no means claimed for himself alone all authority to teach, since he ordered that those who hear the prophet he speaks of should give ear and faith to the one proclaiming God's word, and he decreed capital punishment for all despisers of the prophetic words. How much more, then, ought you to believe Christ, through whom no other has declared the will of God the Father more perfectly and clearly, and to whom fit most exactly all that Moses says about the prophet? Thus Peter neatly attains the end and aim of his purpose, namely to free from misguided religion the minds of those who, hindered by an excessive reverence for Moses and the law and by a foolish understanding, refused to embrace Christ. Since, however, both Peter and Stephen (as will become clear below) expound the passage of Moses about Christ, we too must examine here those things which can instruct us in the knowledge of Christ. First, Moses describes Christ for us not inelegantly. Then he reminds us of the office to which we are bound. At the same time he sets forth the capital sentence against the despisers of Christ.

units.la: In Christi descriptione primo, vnde hic exoriturus sit docet, Suscitabit illum Dominus Deus vester ex fratribus vestris. E Iudaeis ergo nasci debuit, quod infallibile incarnationis ipsius & verae humanitatis argumentum est, quo conuincuntur, qui Christum carnem coelitus attulisse, & non ex virginis substantia, sed per virginem (vt per canalem aqua defluere solet) in mundum venisse dicunt. Paulus certe, illum non angelos aut coelestem aliquam creaturam, sed semen Abrahami assumpsisse testatur. Hebr.2. Et de Iudaeorum praerogatiuis loquens, quibus illos prae aliis gentibus Deus illustrare dignatus est, inter alias huius quoq; meminit, quod ex illis Christus secundum carnem natus sit, qui est Deus in omnibus, laudandus in secula. Rom.9. Quo & veteres promissiones referri debent, in quibus frequenter modo mulieris, modo Abrahami & Dauidis semen appellatur. Gen.3.&22.Psal.132.Isa.11.&c. Obseruanda vero hic nobis venit insignis Dei bonitas, qui cum nobis filium saluatorem & doctorem destinauisset, eundem incarnari & homine fieri voluit, ne vel illius maiestate terrefieremus, vel nostras infirmitates illi minus cordi esse putaremus, quod & Paulus obseruauit. Hebr.2.&4.cap.
units.tr: In the description of Christ, he first teaches whence he is going to arise: "The Lord your God will raise him up from your brothers." He ought therefore to be born of the Jews, which is an infallible proof of his incarnation and true humanity. By this those are refuted who say that Christ brought flesh from heaven and did not take it from the substance of the virgin, but came into the world through the virgin, as water usually flows through a channel. Paul certainly testifies that he took on not angels or some heavenly creature, but the seed of Abraham (Heb. 2). And speaking of the privileges of the Jews, by which God deigned to honour them above other nations, he also mentions among the others this one: that from them Christ was born according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. 9). To this the ancient promises must also be referred, in which the seed is frequently named, now of the woman, now of Abraham and David (Gen. 3 and 22; Ps. 132; Isa. 11, etc.). Here we should observe the remarkable goodness of God, who, when he had destined for us a Son as Saviour and teacher, willed him also to be made flesh and become man, lest we be terrified either by his majesty or think our weaknesses less dear to him, as Paul also noted (Heb. 2 and 4).

units.la: Secundo officium Christi denotat, dum propheram dicit. Atqui non ignorauit Moses, Christum & regem fore & humani generis redemptorem, nec id in praesenti negat, sed eius officij meminit, quod in ea causa, quam tunc tractabat, cumprimis erat obseruandum. Prophetae vero dicuntur diuinae voluntatis interpretes, siue illi futura praedicant, siue de praesenti rerum conditione homines ex Dei verbo admoneant. Quia vero Christus sacerdotio aeterno in ecclesia sua fungi debebat, a docendi munere abstinere non poterat, quod in sacerdote non postremo loco requirebatur, vt videre est Malachi.2.cap. Quare etiam alibi in prophetae persona describitur, vt Isaiae 61.cap. quem locum ipse in schola Nazarethana de seipso exponere dignatus est, Luc.4. Nec in veteri tantum Testamento talis fore praedicitur, sed iam in terris agentem, Deus solenni & illustrissima inauguratione confirmatum, toti orbi doctorem vniuersalem & irrefragabilem proposuit: quando in monte Thabor, ostendit cum ex defunctorum tum ex viuentium numero locupletissimis testibus, Mose nimirum & Elia, Petro item, Iohanne & Iacobo, praeclaram illam sententiam pronuntiat: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui: Hunc audite. Matth.17. Sed & ipse Christus, docendi munus magno studio & sedulitate obiuit, seq; illius causa missum esse, nonobscure fatetur. Mar.1.Luc.4.Non temere ergo propheta a Mose & Petro dicitur.
