Et admonemur hoc loco, non sufficere, si Christum saluatorem & redemptorem nostrum esse fateamur, nisi eundem doctorem nobis a Deo datum agnoscamus, & officium illi praestemus, quod discipuli fido doctori debent. Obseruabis praeterea quanta penes nos esse debeat ministerij dignitas, quo enim argumento splendidius & magnificentius commendari poterat, quam filij Dei exemplo, qui illud & ipse in terris gessit, & in ecclesia sua perpetuum esse voluit? Quo Paulus respiciens, nos nomine Christi legatione fungi & reconciliationis sermonem mundo annuntiare dicit. 2.Cor.5. Cuius vtinam & auditores & ministri semper meminissent, ne vel illi contemptius de ministerio iudicarent, nec hi illud sua improbitate deridendum praberent.
units.tr: Second, he denotes Christ's office when he says "prophet." Moses did not fail to know that Christ would be both king and redeemer of the human race, nor does he deny it at present; but he mentions that office which, in the matter he was then treating, was especially to be observed. Prophets are called interpreters of the divine will, whether they foretell future things or admonish people about the present state of affairs from God's word. Since Christ was to exercise his eternal priesthood in his church, he could not abstain from the office of teaching, which in a priest was not required in the last place, as may be seen in Malachi 2. Therefore he is also described elsewhere in the person of a prophet, as in Isaiah 61, a passage which he himself deigned to expound concerning himself in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4). Nor is he foretold to be such only in the Old Testament; already acting on earth, he was confirmed by God with a solemn and most illustrious inauguration, and set forth to the whole world as universal and irrefutable teacher. This happened when on Mount Tabor, with the most weighty witnesses from the number both of the dead and of the living, namely Moses and Elijah, and likewise Peter, John and James present, he pronounced that famous saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him" (Matt. 17). But Christ himself also undertook the office of teaching with great zeal and diligence, and he plainly confesses that he was sent for that purpose (Mark 1; Luke 4). Therefore the prophet is not rashly named by Moses and Peter. And we are admonished at this point that it is not enough to confess Christ as our Saviour and Redeemer, unless we also acknowledge him as the teacher given to us by God and render to him the duty that faithful disciples owe to a faithful teacher. You will observe, moreover, how great the dignity of the ministry should be among us; for by what argument could it be commended more splendidly and magnificently than by the example of the Son of God, who himself carried it on upon earth and willed it to be perpetual in his church? Looking to this, Paul says that we act in the name of Christ as ambassadors and proclaim the word of reconciliation to the world (2 Cor. 5). Would that both its hearers and its ministers had always kept this in mind, lest the former judge the ministry more contemptuously, or the latter give occasion for it to be mocked by their wickedness.

units.la: Tertio, qualis propheta Christus futurus sit, indicatur: nimirum Mosi similis. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi nihil in Christo excellentius & praestantius Mose agnoscere debeamus, cum hic merus homo & peccator fuerit, Christum vero Deum & hominem nostraq; saluti authorem esse cōstet. Sed ad officium prophetæ & typum Christi, quem Moses gessit, similitudo hæc sive comparatio restringi debet, ubi multa occurrunt consyderatu iucunda & utilia. Primò de Mose Paulus testatur, quòd cum populo Dei laboribus & ærumnis affligi maluerit, quàm Pharaonis nepos censeri, & Ægypti thesauris atq; delitijs frui. Heb.11. Idem affectus in Christo cernitur, qui cum in forma Dei esset, seipsum humiliavit & exinaniuit, ac forma servi accepta nobiscum potius affligi, adeoq; pro nobis mori voluit, quàm nostram diutius videre miseriam. Deinde ut Mosem indignissimè reprobaverunt fratres sui: ita cum in sua venisset Christus, sui illum non receperunt, & coram Pilato abnegarunt, dicentes: Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem. Iohan.1. & 19. Sed & hodie adhuc indignissimis modis reijcitur à multis, quibus seipsum, & in sese vitam atq; salutem æternam per euangelium offert. Tertiò, ut Moses Dei populum ex immani Pharaonis tyrannide liberatum Ægypto eduxit, & Pharaonem maris rubri fluctibus obrutum suffocavit: ita Dei filius humanum genus ex diaboli potestate asseruit, disruptis peccati & mortis vinculis, simulq; spiritualem Pharaonem, Satanam, cum omni suo apparatu armisq; vniuersis sanguinis sui merito occidit. Quartò, ut Moses Israelem fidelis pastoris instar per inuia deserti loca tuto deduxit: ita Iesus Christus fidelis ille pastor est, qui oues suas præcedit, nosq; per mundi huius desertū, omni periculorum genere plenum, sui verbi lucerna & spiritus moderatione tuto traducere solet. Psalm. 24. Iohan.10. Quintò, quemadmodum Moses populo esurienti Manna exhibuit, & sitientibus ex petra fontes aquarum elicuit: sic Christus Iesus suæ carnis merito animas cibat ad vitam æternam, & in suo latere vberrimum salutis fontem aperuit, quo solo omnes sitientes animæ æstus restingui possunt. Vide Iohan. 4.6.7. 19. cap. Sextò, ut Moses diuini sermonis interpres fuit apud populum, cum hic Dei loquentis maiestatem sustinere non posset. Exod.20. Deut.5. ita cum nemo nostrum Deum viderit, nec videre possit, quoad carne hac mortali vestimur, filius Dei, qui est in sinu patris, nobis enarrauit quæcunq; de Deo nos scire oportebat, idemq; eo argumento probat, se nos amicorum loco habere, quòd nihil eorum nos celauerit, quæ à patre audiuit. Iohan.1. & 15. Septimò, ut ad Mosen referri solebant quiq; graviores casus, qui ab ordinatis iudicibus discuti non poterant, ille verò sententiam è Dei ore acceptam proferebat, quæ irrefragabilis habebatur, ut videre licet Exod.18. & 33. Leuit.24. Num.15. &c. ita quæcunq; tum in fidei & regni cœlorum mysterijs, tum in vniuersa vitæ nostræ conuersatione nostræ rationis captum superant, ad vnum Christum referri conuenit, & illius standum est sententiæ, sic ut fidei obedientiæ intellectum omnem subijciamus, quem euangelij finem & scopum esse Paulus testatur. 2. Cor.10. Rom.1. Octauo, ut Moses pro populo nunquam non apud Deum intercessit, quoties ille peccando Dei iram prouocauerat, idq; tanta fide egit, ut propter ipsos è libro Dei deleri posset. Exod.32. & 33. Num.11. & 21. &c. ita Christus, cum damnationis sententia omnium nostrum ceruicibus imminerer, se medium interposuit, & ipse execratio fieri voluit, ut nos à legis execratione liberaret. Gal.3. Idem etiam mediator inter Deum & homines factus, perpetuò pro nobis apud patrem intercedit, & illo aduocato apud Deum uti debent, quicunq; peccatis se Dei iram meruisse sentiunt. 1. Tim.2.1. Iohan.2. Possent multa alia produci, in quibus Christum Mosi similem vel potius eorum absolutum & perfectum executorem esse constat, quæ per illum præfigurabatur: sed sufficiat occasionem præbuisse ijs, qui illa altius & exactius scrutari voluerint.
units.tr: Thirdly, we are shown what kind of prophet Christ is to be: namely, one like Moses. This should not be taken to mean that we must recognise nothing in Christ more excellent and outstanding than in Moses, since Moses was a mere man and a sinner, whereas Christ is known to be God and man and the author of our salvation. The likeness or comparison is to be restricted to the office of prophet and to the type of Christ that Moses bore, and here many things present themselves that are pleasant and useful to consider. First, Paul testifies of Moses that he chose to be afflicted with the people of God in their labours and hardships rather than be counted the grandson of Pharaoh and enjoy the treasures and delights of Egypt. Heb. 11. The same disposition is seen in Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, emptied and humbled himself, and taking the form of a servant, wished rather to suffer with us, and so to die for us, than to see our misery any longer. Next, just as his own brothers most unworthily rejected Moses, so when Christ came to his own, they did not receive him, and before Pilate they denied him, saying: "We have no king but Caesar." John 1 and 19. Even today he is still rejected in the most unworthy ways by many, to whom he offers himself, and in himself life and eternal salvation, through the gospel. Thirdly, as Moses led the people of God, freed from the savage tyranny of Pharaoh, out of Egypt, and drowned Pharaoh under the waves of the Red Sea and suffocated him, so the Son of God rescued the human race from the power of the devil, breaking the bonds of sin and death, and at the same time killed the spiritual Pharaoh, Satan, with all his equipment and all his weapons, by the merit of his blood. Fourthly, as Moses safely led Israel through the pathless places of the desert like a faithful shepherd, so Jesus Christ is that faithful shepherd who goes before his sheep and is accustomed to lead us safely through the desert of this world, full of every kind of danger, by the lamp of his word and the guidance of his Spirit. Ps. 24. John 10. Fifthly, just as Moses gave manna to the hungry people and drew springs of water from the rock for the thirsty, so Christ Jesus by the merit of his flesh feeds souls to eternal life, and opened in his side the most abundant fountain of salvation, by which alone the burning of every thirsty soul can be quenched. See John 4, 6, 7 and chapter 19. Sixthly, Moses was the interpreter of the divine word to the people, since they could not bear the majesty of God speaking. Exod. 20. Deut. 5. So, since none of us has seen God or can see him while we are clothed in this mortal flesh, the Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared to us all that we needed to know about God. He proves by this argument that he holds us in the place of friends, because he has hidden from us nothing that he heard from the Father. John 1 and 15. Seventhly, the more serious cases that the ordinary judges could not settle used to be referred to Moses, and he pronounced a sentence received from the mouth of God, which was held to be irrefutable, as can be seen in Exod. 18 and 33, Lev. 24, Num. 15, and so on. So whatever surpasses the grasp of our reason, whether in the mysteries of faith and the kingdom of heaven or in the whole conduct of our life, ought to be referred to Christ alone, and we must abide by his sentence, subjecting every understanding to the obedience of faith, which Paul testifies is the end and aim of the gospel. 2 Cor. 10. Rom. 1. Eighthly, as Moses always interceded with God on behalf of the people whenever they had provoked God's wrath by sinning, and did this with such faith that he could be blotted out of God's book for their sake. Exod. 32 and 33. Num. 11 and 21, etc. So Christ, when the sentence of damnation hung over the necks of all of us, placed himself in between, and willed himself to become a curse, to free us from the curse of the law. Gal. 3. Likewise, having been made mediator between God and men, he constantly intercedes for us before the Father, and all who feel that by their sins they have deserved God's wrath ought to use him as their advocate before God. 1 Tim. 2. 1 John 2. Many other things could be brought forward in which it is clear that Christ is like Moses, or rather that he is the complete and perfect executor of those things which were foreshadowed through Moses; but it is enough to have offered an occasion to those who wish to examine these things more deeply and exactly.

units.la: Cæterum Christi descriptioni officium, quod illi debemus, subijcitur. Dicit enim Moses: Illum audietis iuxta omnia, quæcunq; locutus fuerit vobis. Idem Deus pater in monte Thabor iubet (ut paulò ante monuimus) cum ait: Hunc audite. Nemo tamen Dei præcepto satisfactum putet, si auribus Christi verba perceperit, quod & Iudam & Pharisæos cum Pilato multiq; alijs olim fecisse constat. Sed primò studium euangelij requiritur, quod inter multa alia, quibus vanissime occupantur homines, vnum est necessarium, ut Christus admonet, Luc.10. A studio verbi nō abesse potest fides, quā illi habemus. Cur enim illud assequi conaremur, cuius fides & veritas nobis suspecta esset? Fidem obedientia sequitur, qua Christum fidei, religionis & vitæ totius magistrum agnoscimus, eiq; pro virili obtemperamus. Has ipse filiorum Dei notas constituit, cū ait: Qui ex Deo est, verba Dei audit. Iohan.8. Item: Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur me. Iohan.10. Vnde certò colligimus, nec Dei filios, nec Christi oues esse, quicunq; Christi vocem in euangelio sonantem audire detrectant. Cumprimis autem obseruare decet, quòd omnia, quæcunq; Christus loquitur, audire iubemur.
units.tr: Next, the description of Christ is followed by the office that we owe him. For Moses says: "You shall hear him in all things that he shall say to you." God the Father himself commands the same on Mount Tabor (as we noted a little earlier) when he says: "Hear him." Yet let no one think that he has satisfied God's command if he has merely received Christ's words with his ears, as Judas and the Pharisees, and with Pilate and many others, are known to have done in times past. But first, zeal for the gospel is required, which, among the many other things with which men are most vainly occupied, is the one thing necessary, as Christ admonishes in Luke 10. Faith cannot exist without diligence in the Word. For why would we strive to attain that whose faith and truth were suspect to us? Obedience follows faith, by which we acknowledge Christ as teacher of faith, of religion and of the whole of life, and obey him to the best of our strength. He himself laid down these marks of the sons of God when he said: "He who is of God hears the words of God." John 8. Likewise: "My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me." John 10. Hence we certainly conclude that those who refuse to hear the voice of Christ sounding in the gospel are neither sons of God nor sheep of Christ. Above all, it is fitting to observe that we are commanded to hear all things, whatever Christ says.

units.la: Christo debetur fides & obedientia. Sunt enim qui audiunt quidem Christum, sed in ijs duntaxat, quæ carni adlubescunt: cui si quid aduersum fuerit, illud nihil ad se pertinere putant. Ex illorum numero sunt, qui euangelij promissiones, quibus gratia Dei & peccatorum remissio gratuita prædicatur, libenter audiunt & mirifice amplectuntur: sed ijdem pœnitentiæ doctrinam, quæ peccata accusat & corripit, nolunt admittere. Similes illorum sunt, qui veritatis doctrinā vtcunq; prædicari patiuntur: indignissime autem ferunt, si quis seductores & Antichristos arguat. Plerosq; etiam ita affectos esse videmus, vt magnis laudibus extollant quæcunq; de Christi regno, de illius victoria, & electorum gloria, quam in cœlis possident, dicuntur: crucem vero & persecutiones ita horrent, vt non aliquam illarum mentionem ferre possint. At toto cœlo errant isti homines. Nec enim scinditur Christus, nec separari debent doctrinæ Christi partes. Qui enim in suo nomine peccatorum remissionem prædicare iussit, idem pœnitentiam ab omnibus exigit. Luc.24. Et qui peccatrici peccata sua deflenti dixit: Remittuntur tibi peccata tua. Luc.7. idem paralytico per se restituto dicebat: Ecce sanus factus es, ne posthac pecces, ne quid deterius tibi contingat. Iohan.5. & postea per Paulum fornicatores & adulteros pœnitere nescios, regnum Dei ingressuros esse negauit. 1. Cor.6. Similiter, qui se lucem & veritatem profitetur & in se ambulare nos iubet: ide pseudochristos & antichristos arguit, & illos cauere iubet. Matth.7. & 24. Item qui regni cœlorum thesauros suis pollicetur: idem ipsos in mundo tribulationem passuros, constanter affirmat. Iohan.15. & 16. Et qui a mortuis gloriose resuscitatus, magnifico triumpho cœlis in vectus est: idem paulo ante inter latrones medius pependerat. Vt ergo Christum totum nos amplecti oportet: ita doctrinam illius omnem audire necesse est, nisi illo in vniuersum spoliari velimus. Figura huius rei in agno paschali præcessit, quem totum manducare, ossa vero & quæcunq; comedi non possunt, igne comburere iubebantur. Ita totus Christus recipiendus erit, & si quid in illo intolerabile videtur, id fidei & charitatis diuinæ flammis consumi & superari debet.
units.tr: Faith and obedience are owed to Christ. For there are some who hear Christ indeed, but only in those things that please the flesh; if anything is contrary to it, they think it has nothing to do with them. Among their number are those who gladly hear the promises of the gospel, by which the grace of God and the free remission of sins is proclaimed, and embrace them wonderfully, but the same people are unwilling to admit the doctrine of repentance, which accuses and rebukes sins. Similar to them are those who allow the doctrine of truth to be preached in whatever way, but bear it most unworthily if anyone refutes seducers and Antichrists. We see many so disposed that they extol with great praises whatever is said of Christ's kingdom, of his victory and of the glory of the elect that they possess in heaven; but they so shrink from the cross and persecutions that they cannot bear any mention of them. But these men are wholly in error. For Christ is not divided, nor should the parts of Christ's doctrine be separated. He who commanded that the remission of sins be preached in his name also demands repentance from all. Luke 24. And he who said to the sinful woman weeping over her sins, "Your sins are forgiven," Luke 7, said to the paralytic he had restored, "Behold, you are made well; sin no more, lest something worse befall you." John 5. And afterwards, through Paul, he declared that fornicators and adulterers who do not repent will not enter the kingdom of God. 1 Cor. 6. Similarly, he who professes himself to be the light and the truth and bids us walk in him is the same who refutes pseudo-christs and antichrists and bids us beware of them. Matt. 7 and 24. Likewise, he who promises the treasures of the kingdom of heaven to his own also constantly affirms that they will suffer tribulation in the world. John 15 and 16. And he who, gloriously raised from the dead, was carried up to heaven in magnificent triumph, is the same who had hung in the midst of thieves a little before. Therefore, just as we ought to embrace the whole Christ, so it is necessary to hear all his doctrine, unless we wish to be stripped of him altogether. The figure of this preceded in the paschal lamb, which they were commanded to eat whole, while the bones and whatever could not be eaten were to be burned with fire. So the whole Christ must be received, and if anything in him seems intolerable, it must be consumed and overcome in the flames of faith and divine love.

units.la: Porrò quia hic plurimum reluctatur caro nostra, quæ iugum hoc inuita suscipit, graui comminatione nos vrget Moses. Erit (inquit) vt omnis anima, quæ non audierit prophetam illum, exterminetur e populo. Comprehendit pœna hac totius hominis interitum, corporis nimirum & animæ. Quæ enim salutis spes ei superesse poterit, qui a populo Dei & ecclesia, quæ sola in bonorum Dei communione admittitur, exclusus & excisus fuerit? At cur non ab eius consortio reiciatur, qui magistrum & doctorem ecclesiæ, quem Deus illi imposuit, audire detrectat? Qui aspernatus fuerit Mosis legem, absq; misericordia, sub duobus aut tribus testibus moritur. Quanto igitur maiores pœnas meretur, qui filium Dei conculcare ausus fuerit? Hebr.10. Hinc graues illæ in euangelio comminationes sumuntur, quæ multis nimiæ & æquo atrociores videntur. Qualis illa Baptistæ sententia est: Qui non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super illum. Iohan.3. Et Christus, cum euangelio credentibus vitam æternam pollicitus esset, addit: Qui non crediderit, condemnabitur. Marc.16. Atqui horum Iudæos admonere voluit Petrus, ne lusum iocumq; putarent euangelicæ doctrinæ & Christi contemptum: sed animarum salutem hic periclitari scirent. At qui nobis idem dici putemus. Ea enim est Christi Iesu apud patrem authoritas, vt nemo huic gratus & acceptus esse possit, nisi qui illi insitus fuerit. At illi nos non nuda & inanis nominis Christiani professio inserit, sed viua fides, quæ vt doctrinæ ipsius obtemperemus, & illi firmiter inhæreamus, efficit. Vide quæ de veris falsisq; Christi auditoribus habentur Matth.7. & Luc.6. cap.
units.tr: Moreover, since our flesh struggles hard against this yoke, which it takes up unwillingly, Moses presses us with a grave threat: "It shall be that every soul which does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from the people." This penalty includes the ruin of the whole man, of body and soul alike. For what hope of salvation can remain for one who has been shut out and cut off from the people of God and from the Church, the only place into which the good things of God are admitted? And why should he not be rejected from her fellowship who refuses to hear the teacher and master of the Church whom God has set over him? He who has despised the law of Moses dies without mercy under two or three witnesses (Heb. 10). How much greater punishments, then, does he deserve who has dared to trample underfoot the Son of God? (Heb. 10.) Hence come those grave threats in the Gospel, which seem excessive to many and far more severe than is fair. Such is the sentence of the Baptist: "He who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3). And Christ, when he had promised eternal life to those who believe the Gospel, adds: "He who does not believe shall be condemned" (Mark 16). Peter wished to warn the Jews of this, so that they would not think the Gospel teaching and the contempt of Christ a game or a joke, but would know that the salvation of souls was here at stake. Let us not suppose that the same can be said of us. For such is the authority of Christ Jesus with the Father that no one can be pleasing and acceptable to him unless he has been grafted into him. And it is not the bare and empty profession of the Christian name that grafts us into him, but living faith, which makes us obey his teaching and cling firmly to him. See what is said of the true and false hearers of Christ in Matthew 7 and Luke 6.

units.la: Quamuis vero magna esset Mosis apud Iudæos authoritas, ne quid tamen omittat Petrus, prophetarum testimonia illi coniungit, quorum aliquot illum recensuisse verisimile est. Hic vero omnes simul complectens, ait: Quin & omnes prophetæ a Samuele ac deinceps, quotquot locuti sunt, annuntiauerunt dies iflos. A Samuele vero prophetarum numerum siue chorum orditur, quia ante hunc nemo prophetarum fuit postea Mosen, cuius scripta extent. Imo priusquam ille prophetaret, sermo diminuti pretiosus & rarus fuisse legitur (1. Samuel. 3.) qui postea per multos prophetas luculentissime & passim cum prædicari tum scribi cœpit. Omnes vero, quotquot ab illo tempore extiterunt, de Christo Iesu vaticinatos esse, omnibus illis liquido constat, qui illorum sermones siue libros non ofcitanter legerunt. Clarum omnino & minimè ambiguum est Dei oraculum, quod Dauidi de Christo, e sua stirpe nascendo, Nathan annuntiauit. 2. Samuel. 7. Clariora sunt hoc multa, quæ ab ipso Dauide edita sunt, vt quæ extant, Psalm.2. 22. 89. 110. &c. De Isaia quid attinet dicere, qui omnium eorum corum, quæ à Christo geri debuerunt, narrationem tam perspicuam contexit, ut (teste D. Hie-ronymo) multis locis Euangelista potius quàm propheta censeri mereatur. Eadem omnium alio-rum est ratio, quorum oracula si verbotenus recensere vellemus, dicendi initium facilius quàm fi-nem inuenire liceret. Illud admonuisse sufficiat, nihil in Christo tam minutum esse, quod non veteris Testamenti oraculis comprobari posset. Unde simul colligimus, veteris Testamenti libros ne-quaquam contemni debere, ut fanatici quidam solent, qui illos ad solos Iudæos pertinere clamant. Peccant illi in Dei bonitatem & industriam, qui salutis nostræ causam omni modo illustrare & con-firmare voluit.
units.tr: Although Moses had great authority among the Jews, nevertheless, so that Peter might leave nothing out, he joins to him the testimonies of the prophets, some of whom he very probably had in mind. Embracing them all together, he says: "Indeed all the prophets, from Samuel onwards, as many as have spoken, have foretold these days." He begins the number, or company, of the prophets from Samuel, because before him there was no prophet, after Moses, whose writings survive. Indeed, before he prophesied, we read that the word of God was rare and precious (1 Sam. 3), but afterwards it began to be proclaimed and written most brilliantly and widely through many prophets. And it is quite clear to all those who have read their sayings or books with attention that all who have arisen from that time on prophesied about Christ Jesus. The oracle of God which Nathan announced to David concerning Christ, who would be born from his stock, is altogether clear and not at all ambiguous (2 Sam. 7). Many things published by David himself are clearer still, such as those which survive: Psalms 2, 22, 89, 110, etc. What need is there to speak of Isaiah, who wove together so plain an account of all the things that were to be done by Christ that (as witness Jerome) he deserves to be counted an evangelist rather than a prophet in many places? The reasoning is the same for the others, whose oracles, if we wished to recite them word for word, we would find it easier to find a beginning of speaking than an end. It is enough to have pointed out this: there is nothing so small in Christ that it cannot be confirmed by the oracles of the Old Testament. From this we gather at the same time that the books of the Old Testament must by no means be despised, as certain fanatics are accustomed to do, who cry out that they belong to the Jews alone. Those men sin against the goodness and diligence of God, who wished to illuminate and confirm in every way the cause of our salvation.

units.la: Obseruemus igitur hic euangelicæ doctrinæ & fidei Christianæ tum certitudinem tum antiqui-tatem. Si enim prophetarum & Mosis testimonijs legales typos & veteres promissiones, olim pa-triarchis exhibitas coniungamus, facile videbis, nullum unquam doctrinæ genus siue religionem tot tantisque testimonijs confirmatam & illustratam fuisse. Prima enim promissione nititur, quam in paradiso primis parentibus de semine mulieris, quod serpentis caput conterere debeat, exhibuit. Magna igitur illorum est stultitia siue temeritas (ne quid grauius dicam) qui doctrinæ euangelij vel palàm contradicere, vel Concilia alia expetere audent, quorum authoritate de fide & religione statuatur. Quid enim isti homines aliud faciunt, quàm quòd Deum, qui per Mosen & prophetas locutus est, mendacij arguunt, vel saltem illius veritatem in dubium vocant? Ad hæc stultè admo-dum hominum authoritatem requirunt, cum ne angelo quidem diuersum docenti credi debeat. Galat.1. Quare omissis illis, Christum amplectamur, quem vnanimis scripturæ consensus proponit, in quo solo omnis iustitia, sanctificatio, veritas & salus continetur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us observe here, then, both the certainty and the antiquity of the evangelical teaching and of the Christian faith. For if we join to the testimonies of the prophets and of Moses the legal types and the ancient promises once exhibited to the patriarchs, you will easily see that no kind of teaching or religion has ever been confirmed and illustrated by so many and so great testimonies. For it rests upon the first promise, which he gave to our first parents in paradise, concerning the seed of the woman, who was to crush the head of the serpent. Great, therefore, is the folly or rashness of those (to say nothing more harshly) who dare either openly to contradict the teaching of the Gospel or to seek other councils by whose authority matters of faith and religion are to be decided. For what else do such men do than accuse of lying God, who spoke through Moses and the prophets, or at least call his truth into doubt? Besides, they foolishly seek the authority of men, when not even an angel who teaches otherwise is to be believed (Gal. 1). Therefore, setting those aside, let us embrace Christ, whom the unanimous consent of Scripture sets forth, in whom alone all righteousness, sanctification, truth and salvation are contained. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXV.
units.tr: HOMILY XXV.

units.la: Vos estis filij prophetarum & testamenti, quod testatus est Deus patribus vestris, dicens ad Abraham: En in semine tuo benedicentur omnes familiæ terræ. Vobis primùm Deus, cum suscitauisset filium suum Iesum, misit eum benedicentem vobis, dum vnumquenque conuertit ab iniquitatibus suis.
units.tr: "You are the children of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham: In your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed. To you first, God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him to bless you, by turning each one of you from his iniquities."

units.la: Dluus Petrus salutis viam & rationē Iudæis sic monstrat, ut simul omnibus ijs occurrat, quà ipsos, quo minus per hanc ingrederentur, impedire poterant: vbi duo potissimum occurrebant. Primum erat præpostera Mosis & auitæ religionis obseruantia. Timebant enim, ne Christum amplexi in legem & religionem diuinitus patribus traditam peccarent. Docet ergo nullum subesse periculum, eò quòd cum Moses cum prophetæ ad Christum relegare soleant. Quin potius eos in Mosem peccare, qui Christum amplecti dedignantur, cum talibus iam olim Moses capitalem pœnam constituerit. Restabat verò alterum obstaculum, scelcris in Christum commissi conscientia. Quia enim hùc (ut supra Petrus monuit) improbè negauerant, iustum & æquum esse videbant, ut ipsos quoq; Christus auersaretur, nec ipsorum pœnitentiam gratā & acceptam haberet. Nec ignorare poterat, Deum per prophetam illorum preces reijcere, qui manus sanguinis plenas coram ipso extendebant. Isa. 1. Quapropter huic malo in præsenti Petrus medetur, & firmis rationibus probat, Christum Iesum adipsos quoq; pertinere, nec auersaturū ipsos, si ad illum totis animis conuertantur: qui principalis huius loci status est, quo etiam concionem suam feliciter omnino absoluit.
units.tr: Saint Peter shows the Jews the way and manner of salvation in such a way that he meets, at the same time, all the objections that could keep them from entering by it. Two in particular presented themselves. The first was the supposed fidelity to Moses and to the religion of their forefathers. They feared that by embracing Christ they would sin against the law and the religion handed down by God to their fathers. Peter therefore teaches that there is no danger here, since Moses and the prophets always refer people to Christ. Indeed, those who disdain to embrace Christ are the ones who sin against Moses, since Moses long ago laid down the death penalty for such people. The second obstacle remained: the awareness of the crime committed against Christ. For, as Peter had already warned, they had wickedly denied him, and they thought it right and fair that Christ should also turn away from them and not accept their repentance as pleasing and acceptable. Nor could they fail to know that God, through the prophet, rejects the prayers of those who stretch out hands full of blood before him (Isa. 1). Therefore Peter, at this point, remedies this evil and, with firm reasons, proves that Jesus Christ pertains to them too, and that he will not turn away from them if they convert to him with their whole hearts. This is the principal point of this passage, and with it he brings his sermon to a happy conclusion.

units.la: Priusquam verò Petri verba aggrediamur, exemplum illius obseruandum venit, quo de vera euangelij prædicandi ratione admonemur. Quæ in hoc versatur, ut singuli intelligant, euangelij promissiones ad se pertinere. Nisi enim de hoc certi sint, illas nec magni facere possunt, nec illis tutò & certò inniti. Quæ causa est, quòd in gentium vocatione afferenda tam multum Paulus versatur, quia frustra illis prædicatum fuisset euangelium, nisi cognouissent, salutem per Christum partam non minus ipsis, quàm Iudæis destinatam esse. Eandem ob causam euangelij promissiones omnes vniuersales sunt, & singulis bas vera fide amplectentibus accommodari possunt. Venite ad me (inquit Christus) omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, &c. Matth.11. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum
units.tr: Before we take up Peter's words, we should observe the example of how the gospel is to be preached, by which we are reminded of the true method of proclaiming it. This method consists in helping each person understand that the promises of the gospel pertain to him. For unless people are certain of this, they can neither value the promises nor rest securely and confidently upon them. This is why Paul labours so much in proclaiming the calling of the Gentiles: the gospel would have been preached to them in vain unless they had come to know that the salvation obtained through Christ was destined for them no less than for the Jews. For the same reason, all the promises of the gospel are universal, and they can be applied to each person who embraces them with true faith. "Come to me," says Christ, "all you who labour and are heavy laden, etc." (Matt. 11). So God loved the world that he gave his son

units.la: Euangelij prædicandi ratio. vnigenitum pro illo traderet, vt omnis, qui credit in illum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam, Ioan. 3. Et alibi se pro omnibus orare dicit, qui in ipsum per apostolorum sermonem credityri sint, Ioan. 17. Quo etiam referri debet, quod Iohannes, omnes qui peccant, Christum aduocatum habere docet, cum is se dederit propitiationem pro peccatis totius mundi. 1. Iohan. 2. Et Paulus frequenter omnem personarum respectum a salutis negotio excludit, & omnibus in Christum credentibus salutem in illo diuinitus conferri testatur. Vide Rom. 10. Galat. 3. Coloss. 3. &c. Debent horum ita memi-nisse ministri, vt ab vniuersalibus Dei promissis neminem excludant, sed euangelij sermonem ita fe-cent, ne quis dubitare possit de sua salutis certitudine, & Christi meritum ad se quoque pertinere intelligat. His præmissis ad Petri sermonem accedamus, qui tribus argumentis Iudæorum fidem va-lidissimè confirmat.
units.tr: Method of preaching the gospel. the only begotten for it, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John 3). And elsewhere he says that he prays for all who will believe in him through the apostles' word (John 17). To this also belongs what John teaches: that all who sin have Christ as their advocate, since he is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world (1 John 2). And Paul frequently excludes all regard for persons from the business of salvation, and testifies that salvation is conferred by God in Christ on all who believe in him (see Rom. 10; Gal. 3; Col. 3, etc.). Ministers ought to remember these things, so that they exclude no one from God's universal promises, and so shape the word of the gospel that no one can doubt the certainty of his salvation, and each understands that the merit of Christ pertains to him as well. With these things premised, let us come to Peter's sermon, which very powerfully confirms the faith of the Jews by three arguments.

units.la: I. Iudæi filij prophetarum
units.tr: I. The Jews, sons of the prophets

units.la: Primo veteris dignitatis & maiorum suorum admonet, dicens: Vos estis filij prophetarum. Id est, ex ea gente estis oriundi, quæ prophetas genuit. Vel potius patriarcharum filij estis, quos præstan-tissimos prophetas fuisse constat, vt pote per quos salutis promissiones humano generi primò omnium innotuerunt. Quæ causa est, quod à spiritu sancto prophetæ olim dicti sint. Psal. 105. Hinc verò colligit Petrus, non dubium esse, quin ad Iudæorum gentem promissiones, per prophetas olim reuelatæ, pertineant, siquidem illas amplexi, & maiorum suorum fidem imitari velint. Nec enim carnali generationi quicquam hic tribuere vult Petrus, quam apud degeneres & palàm impios nullius mo-menti esse constat, quemadmodum grauissimæ illæ Iohannis Baptistæ & Christi expostulationes do-cent, quibus Iudæos, inani Abrahami titulo gloriantes seuerissimè increpant. Matth. 3. Iohan. 8. Sed desperabundos hoc argumento confirmat Petrus, vt intelligant, non inane fore ipsorum fludium, si patres prophetas imitati, Christum saluatorem, cuius aduentum illi prædixerunt, amplectantur.
units.tr: First, he reminds them of their ancient dignity and of their forefathers, saying: "You are the sons of the prophets." That is, you are born of that nation which bore the prophets; or rather, you are the sons of the patriarchs, who are known to have been most eminent prophets, since through them the promises of salvation first became known to the human race. This is why they were long ago called prophets by the Holy Spirit (Ps. 105). From this Peter infers that there can be no doubt that the promises revealed of old through the prophets pertain to the Jewish nation, provided that they embrace them and wish to imitate the faith of their forefathers. Peter does not want to attribute anything here to carnal descent, which is known to be of no weight among degenerate and openly impious people, as the most weighty rebukes of John the Baptist and Christ teach, by which they severely scolded the Jews who boasted in the empty title of Abraham (Matt. 3; John 8). But Peter strengthens these despairing people with this argument, so that they may understand that their zeal will not be in vain if, imitating the fathers, they embrace Christ the Saviour, whose coming those fathers foretold.

units.la: Obseruabis autem, quod salutis spem Iudæis facturus Petrus, primo loco prophetarum mention-em facit. Agnouit ergo, hoc præcipuum esse diuini erga nos fauoris argumentum, si suæ volun-tatis interpretes Deus largiatur, eò quod nisi hæc nobis bene comperta fit, salutem consequi non possu-mus. Ideo inter veteris Testamenti beneficia, quæ olim suo populo Deus contulit, hoc semper in pri-mis commemorari solet, quòd prophetas illos instruxerit, per quos de Dei voluntate edocerentur. Vide Mich. 6. Amos 2. Psalm. 107. 2. Paral. 36. Quid? quòd ipse Christus hoc argumento euincit, se apostolos amicorum suorum loco habuisse, quòd nihil eorum ipsos celarit, quæ à patre illi manife-sta erant. Vnde colligitur, quanta illorum sit ingratitudo & improbitas, qui Dei verbum con-temnere audent, & prophetas quorum ministerio illud prædicatur, explodunt. Sentient illi olim Christi sententiam, qua seruorum suorum contemptum seuerissimè vindicabit, quemadmodum mi-natur, Matth. 10. cap.
units.tr: Moreover, you will observe that Peter, about to offer the Jews hope of salvation, first makes mention of the prophets. He therefore recognised that this is the chief proof of God's favour towards us, if God grants us interpreters of his will, because unless this is well made known to us, we cannot obtain salvation. Therefore, among the benefits of the Old Testament which God long ago bestowed upon his people, this has always been commemorated first of all: that he instructed those prophets through whom they might be taught about God's will (see Mic. 6; Amos 2; Ps. 107; 2 Chron. 36). Why, Christ himself proves by this argument that he had regarded his apostles as his friends, because he had hidden nothing from them that had been made manifest to him by the Father. From this we gather how great is the ingratitude and wickedness of those who dare to despise the word of God and to reject the prophets through whose ministry it is proclaimed. They will one day feel the sentence of Christ, by which he will most severely avenge the contempt of his servants, as he threatens (Matt. 10).

units.la: II. Iudæi filij testamenti
units.tr: II. The Jews, sons of the covenant

units.la: Secundo Dei vocationem & promissionem illis in mentem reuocat, dum fœdus siue testamen-tum Dei olim cum Abrahamo factum, allegat. Vos, inquit, estis filij testamenti, quod testatus est Deus patribus vestris, dicens ad Abraham: Et in semine tuo benedicentur omnes familiæ terræ. Vi-detur autem filios testamenti Hebraica phrasi dicere, pro iis ad quos testamentum pertinebat, qui testamento Dei hæredes scripti erant. Sic enim & filios iræ aut mortis dici legimus, quos deus iratus morti destinauit. Videtur autem dupliciter argumentari Petrus. Primò à pronunciato argu-mentum ducens, ait: Deus in testamento, quod patribus testatus est, vos quoque hæredes scripsit. Ergo salus, quæ Dei testamento continetur, non minus ad vos quàm patres pertinet. Antecedens multis probari non opus erat apud eos, quibus Dei promissio notissima erat: Ero tibi Deus, & semi-nis tui post te. Genesis decimo septimo. Deinde summam & compendium testamenti illius produ-cens à comparatis probat, illos ab hoc non posse excludi. Ita enim patri Abrahamo testatus est Deus, quòd in illius semine benedici debeant omnes familiæ terræ. Quòd si ad exteras gentes testamentum Dei extenditur, quis obsecro illud ad eos pertinere dubitabit, qui ex Abrahamo progeniti sunt? Semper tamen meminerimus, Petrum hæc omnia conditionaliter loqui, & illis salutem polliceri, qui Abrahami fide prediti Christum apprehendunt: ne simpliciter carnali generationi tribuere vi-deatur, quod ex mera Dei gratia & gratuita illius electione dependet, vt multis Paulus probat, ad Rom. 9. cap.
units.tr: Secondly, he recalls to their minds God's calling and promise, when he cites the covenant or testament of God once made with Abraham. "You," he says, "are the sons of the testament, which God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham: In your seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed." He seems to use the Hebrew idiom "sons of the testament" for those to whom the testament pertained, who were written down as heirs of God's testament. So we also read of "sons of wrath" or "of death," whom an angry God has destined to death. Peter seems to argue in two ways. First, drawing his argument from the premise, he says: God, in the testament which he made with your fathers, has also written you down as heirs. Therefore the salvation contained in God's testament pertains to you no less than to the fathers. The antecedent needed no proof among those to whom God's promise was well known: "I will be a God to you and to your seed after you" (Genesis 17). Then, setting out the sum and substance of that testament, he proves from the comparison that they cannot be excluded from it. For God thus made his testament to the father Abraham, that in his seed all the families of the earth ought to be blessed. But if God's testament extends to the foreign nations, who, I ask, will doubt that it pertains to those who are descended from Abraham? Yet let us always remember that Peter speaks all this conditionally, and promises salvation only to those who, endowed with Abraham's faith, lay hold of Christ. This keeps us from seeming to ascribe to carnal generation what depends entirely on God's pure grace and free election, as Paul proves at length in Romans 9.

units.la: Potest autem ex hoc loco confutari Anabaptistarum vasania, qui paruulos ex fidelibus prognatos in Dei & ecclesiæ Christi consortium admittere nolunt. Atqui nemo nostrum negat, electionis Dei salutem esse, non carnalis generationis. Interim cùm Deus testamento suo olim paruulos ex fidelibus natos includerit, non leuis temeritas videri debet, illis testamenti & ecclesiæ Dei communionem negare. Num vero noui Testamenti conditiones nostris liberis duriores & grauiores esse putabimus, quàm veteres olim fuerint, quibus octauo die per circuncisionem in populi Dei consortium aditus patebat? Gen.17. Et an nulla erit apud nos Christi authoritas, qui & paruulis fidem tribuit, & ad eosdem regnum cœlorum pertinere affirmat? Matth.18. & 19. Marc.10. Vel quid Paulo respondebimus, qui de imparibus coniugijs loquens, liberos eos sanctos dicere non veretur, qui ex alterutro tantum parente Christiano nati erant? 1. Corinth.7. Fugiamus ergo præcipitem nostri iudicij audaciam, & diuini fœderis articulos constanter retineamus, quibus paruulis quoq; salutis communionem promissam esse constat.
units.tr: This passage can also refute the madness of the Anabaptists, who refuse to admit the children born of believers into fellowship with God and the Church of Christ. Yet none of us denies that salvation comes from God's election, not from carnal generation. Still, since God in his testament once included the children born of believers, it should seem no slight rashness to deny them communion in God's testament and Church. Shall we really think the conditions of the New Testament are harder and heavier for our children than they were for those of old, to whom on the eighth day the entrance into the fellowship of God's people lay open through circumcision? (Genesis 17.) And will Christ's authority count for nothing among us, he who grants faith even to little children and affirms that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them? (Matthew 18 and 19; Mark 10.) Or what shall we answer Paul, who, speaking of mixed marriages, does not hesitate to call holy those children who were born of only one Christian parent? (1 Corinthians 7.) Let us therefore avoid the headlong boldness of our own judgment, and hold fast constantly to the articles of the divine covenant, by which it is plain that the fellowship of salvation is promised also to little children.

units.la: Est autem diligenti obseruatione dignum, quòd nostræ redemptionis & salutis negotium fœdere vel testamento comprehensum esse voluit Deus. Quod vt in Abrahamo cœpit, ita postea non semel cū Abrahami posteris innouatum ac instauratum esse constat. Huc enim pertinent, quæ de Dauide habentur, Psal.89. & 132. & quæ Ierem.31. de nouo Dei testamento legimus. Nec testamentum modò constituit Deus, sed illud ipsum iurisiurandi religione interposita confirmauit. Iurauit enim Abraham, & per seipsum quidem, cùm per maiorem iurare non posset. Hebr.6. Seruiunt hæc salutis nostræ certitudini asserendæ. Nam si hominis testamentum, postquàm legitimè conscriptum & cõfirmatum fuerit, nemo reijcit vel infringit: nemini tantum authoritatis esse poterit, vt Dei testamentum irritum faciat. Gal.3. Dei enim dona &αμεταμελητα, & illius vocationem inuiolabilem esse Paulus testatur. Rom.11. Idem ipse Deus apud Ieremiam cap.33. affirmat, dicens: Si irritum fieri potest fœdus meum, quod inij cum die & nocte, vt non sit dies & nox suo tempore: etiam irritum fieri poterit fœdus meum, quod inij cum Dauide seruo meo, &c. Et alibi naturales parentum erga liberos affectiones, quas Græci sorgyas vocant, nö tam vehementes & certas esse testatur, quàm ipsius cura & fides est, qua sui testamenti veritatem & salutis nostræ certitudinem inuiolatam seruare studer. Ifa. 49.
units.tr: It is worth careful notice that God willed the business of our redemption and salvation to be comprehended in a covenant or testament. As this began with Abraham, so it is plain that it was afterwards renewed and restored, more than once, with Abraham's posterity. To this belong what we read about David in Psalms 89 and 132, and what we read in Jeremiah 31 about God's new testament. Nor did God only establish the testament, but he also confirmed it by interposing the solemn obligation of an oath. For Abraham swore, and that by himself, since he could not swear by a greater. (Hebrews 6.) These things serve to establish the certainty of our salvation. For if no one rejects or annuls a man's testament once it has been lawfully drawn up and confirmed, then no one will have such authority as to make void God's testament. (Galatians 3.) For Paul testifies that God's gifts and calling are without repentance and inviolable. (Romans 11.) The same God affirms through Jeremiah in chapter 33: "If my covenant with day and night can be broken, so that there is no day or night in their time, then my covenant with David my servant can also be broken," and so on. And elsewhere he testifies that the natural affections of parents toward their children, which the Greeks call storgai, are not so strong and certain as his own care and faithfulness, by which he takes pains to keep the truth of his testament and the certainty of our salvation inviolate. (Isaiah 49.)

units.la: Prodest autem diuini testamenti summam, quæ à Petro ex Genesis 22.cap. allegatur, diligentius inspicere, In semine tuo (dicit Deus Abrahamo) benedicentur omnes familiæ terræ. Quibus verbis tria comprehendit dominus. Primò enim quid ex testamento suo nobis boni obtingat, docet. Deinde mediatorem, per quem illud simus acceptur, indicat. Tertiò ad quos testamenti huius hæreditas extendatur, admonet.
units.tr: It is useful to look more carefully at the sum of the divine testament, which Peter cites from Genesis 22. "In your seed," God says to Abraham, "shall all the families of the earth be blessed." In these words the Lord comprehends three things. First, he teaches what good things come to us from his testament. Second, he points out the mediator through whom we shall receive it. Third, he reminds us to whom the inheritance of this testament extends.

units.la: Primò benedictionem promittit Deus, quæ maledictioni opponitur, vt patet Deut.27. &28.cap. Comprehendit hæc omnem hominis incolumitatem, & in primis Dei fauorem, qui omnis generis bonis suos accumulare solet. Nec enim fieri potest, vt quicquam illius vel corpori vel animæ desit, qui Deo propitio & benigno vtitur. Oportuit verò hanc nobis diserte promitti, eò quòd natura maledicti sumus, quotquot ex Adami progenie nascimur. Peccato enim maledictionem deberi passim scriptura docet, & lex maledictum pronuntiat eum, qui nõ omnia fecerit, quæ Deus mandat. Deut.27. Quia er go peccatores sumus omnes, gloria & gratia Dei destituti, illius iræ & iudicio subiacemus. Rom.3.5. &c. At quemadmodum peccato transgressionis omne malorum genus mundo inuectum est: ita benedictione omne bonum Deus pollicetur. Quare amplißima est hæc promissio, & totam hominis salutem completitur.
units.tr: First, God promises a blessing, which is set against a curse, as is plain from Deuteronomy 27 and 28. This includes every kind of human well-being, and above all God's favour, which he is accustomed to heap upon his people with every kind of good. For nothing can be lacking to body or soul in one who enjoys the favour and kindness of God. But it was necessary that this be promised to us plainly, because by nature we are under a curse, all of us who are born of Adam's line. Scripture teaches everywhere that a curse is owed to sin, and the law pronounces a curse on whoever does not do all that God commands. (Deuteronomy 27.) Therefore, since we are all sinners, destitute of God's glory and grace, we lie under his wrath and judgment. (Romans 3 and 5, etc.) But just as every kind of evil has been brought into the world through the sin of transgression, so God promises every good through blessing. Therefore this promise is most ample, and it fulfils the whole of human salvation.

units.la: Quia verò inter Deum & nos propter peccati culpam inimicitia obortæ erant, cum illo absq; mediatoris intercessione reconciliari non poteramus, nec benedictionem illius consequi. Ostendit ergo hunc Deus, cùm in semine Abrahami benedictionem pollicetur. Quem locum Paulus apostolus mira simplicitate de Christo Iesu exponit, quem Abrahami semen assumpsisse legimus. Scribit enim ad Galat. 3.cap. Abrahamo dictæ sunt promissiones & semini eius. Non dicit, & seminibus, tanquam de multis, sed tanquam de vno: Et in semine tuo, qui est Christus. Neq; hic Iudæorum cauillationes moramur, qui seminis vocabulum, quia colleƈtiuum est, de tota Iudæorum gente exponunt, & comparationem faciunt, quasi iuxta illius gentis exemplum reliqui populi benedici debeant. Quia enim constat omne genus mortalium maledictioni subiacere, nullius momenti fuisset Dei testamentum, nisi aliquem designasset, qui à maledictionis sententia liberatis benediceret. At quis nam ille sit, Iudæi nunquam offendere poterunt, si Christum abijcere velint, cùm in omnibus aliis Abrahami posteris peccata non pauca nec leuia deprehendi possint, quibus maledictionem in ipsis etiam haberi fisse constat. Vere enim apud Isaiam illis dixit Dominus: Pater tuus primus peccauit, & interpretes tui praeuaricati sunt. Isa.43. Vnus Christus habetur, in cuius ore non inuentus est dolus, & qui hostibus suis dicere potuit: Quis ex vobis arguet me de peccato? Et idem ille solus à Deo patre caelitus is esse declaratus est, in quo benedictionem consequamur: Illi enim dixit Deus, Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui, &c. Matth.3. & 17. Et ipse in vltima Cœna, noui testamenti consummationem in sanguine suo consistere palam testatus est. 1. Corinth.11. Illius enim sanguine peccata nostra expiata sunt, propter quae maledictionis sententia grauabamur. Hunc ergo amplectantur, quicunque benedictionis haereditatem volunt consequi.
units.tr: But because enmity had arisen between God and us on account of the guilt of sin, we could not be reconciled to him, nor obtain his blessing, without the intercession of a mediator. So God shows this mediator when he promises the blessing in the seed of Abraham. The apostle Paul expounds this place with remarkable plainness, of Christ Jesus, whom we read took up Abraham's seed. For he writes to the Galatians (chapter 3): "The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed." He does not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one: "and to your seed, which is Christ." Nor do we here linger over the cavils of the Jews, who, because the word "seed" is a collective noun, expound it of the whole Jewish nation, and make a comparison as if the other peoples ought to be blessed according to the example of that nation. For since it is plain that every kind of mortal lies under the curse, God's testament would be of no weight at all, unless it had designated someone who would bless those freed from the sentence of the curse. But who that is, the Jews will never be able to deny, if they are willing to reject Christ, since in all the other posterity of Abraham not a few and not slight sins can be detected, for which they are known to have been held under the curse. For the Lord truly said to them through Isaiah: "Your first father sinned, and your interpreters have transgressed." (Isaiah 43.) Christ alone is held to be one in whose mouth no guile was found, and who could say to his enemies: "Which of you convicts me of sin?" And that same one alone was declared from heaven by God the Father to be the one in whom we obtain the blessing: for God said to him, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," and so on. (Matthew 3 and 17.) And he himself, at the last Supper, openly testified that the consummation of the New Testament consists in his blood. (1 Corinthians 11.) For by his blood our sins, on account of which we were burdened with the sentence of the curse, have been expiated. Let whoever wishes to obtain the inheritance of the blessing therefore embrace him.

units.la: Caeterum ne paucorum hominum vel vnius tantum gentis haec felicitas esse videretur, diserte quousque illa extendi debeat, edocet. Includit autem benedictioni huic, quae in Christo obtingit, omnes familias terrae. Nec enim Iudaeorum duntaxat Deus est (vt Paulus inquit) qui ista fanciuit, verum etiam gentium. Rom.3. Et passim admonemur in salutis causa nullum esse coram Deo gentium discrimen, sed (vt infra Petrus testabitur) in omni gente eos ipsi probari, qui illum timent, & operantur iustitiam. Act.10. Adhaec ipse Christus salutem, cuius ipse author est, ad omnes gentes pertinere testatur, cùm in euangelio dicit: Multi venient ab Oriente & Occidente, & accumbent cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo in regno coelorum. Matth.8. Quò in primis referri debet, quod apostolis euangelium in toto terrarum orbe praedicandi mandatum dedit. Marc.16. Act.1. Vt enim primis parentibus prima salutis promissio facta est: ita omni illorum posteritati illam communem esse voluit Deus. Nec alia ratio est, propter quam Abraham multarum gentium pater dici possit, quàm quòd omnes omnium gentium fideles, in Christo Iesu coniuncti, illius filij & promissionum salutis in Christo propositae haeredes per fidem reddi solent. Est autem haec consyderatio institutionis & consolationis plena. Docet enim ne quem temere contemnamus, nec inani nostrae gentis praerogatiua, quae plerunque à nobis terrenis & insano hominum iudicio dependet, superbiamus: quando Christus Iesus, qui nostra salus & gloria est, ad omnes gentes pertinet. Rursum in fidei tentationibus nos confirmat, ne nos à Christo excludi patiamur, in quo omnes familias terrae benedici audimus: quo argumento hic quoq; Iudaeis certam salutis suae spem facere conatur.
units.tr: Lest this happiness should seem to belong to a few people or to only one nation, he plainly teaches how far it ought to extend. Moreover, this blessing that is obtained in Christ includes all the families of the earth. For God is not only the God of the Jews (as Paul says), who ordained these things, but also of the Gentiles. Rom. 3. And everywhere we are reminded that in the matter of salvation there is no distinction of Gentiles before God, but (as Peter will testify below) in every nation those who fear him and work righteousness are approved by him. Acts 10. Besides, Christ himself testifies that the salvation of which he is the author pertains to all nations, when he says in the gospel: Many will come from east and west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Matt. 8. To this should chiefly be referred the command he gave the apostles to preach the gospel throughout the whole world. Mark 16. Acts 1. For just as the first promise of salvation was made to our first parents, so God willed it to be common to all their posterity. Nor is there any other reason why Abraham can be called the father of many nations, than that all the faithful of all nations, joined together in Christ Jesus, are made by faith his sons and heirs of the promises of salvation set forth in Christ. This consideration is full of instruction and consolation. For it teaches us not to despise anyone rashly, nor to take pride in the empty privilege of our nation, which for the most part depends on earthly things and the foolish judgment of men, since Christ Jesus, who is our salvation and glory, belongs to all nations. Again, in the temptations of faith it strengthens us, so that we do not allow ourselves to be shut out from Christ, in whom we hear that all the families of the earth are blessed; by this argument he also tries to give the Jews a sure hope of their salvation.

units.la: III. Iudaeis primis missus Christus.
units.tr: III. Christ sent first to the Jews.

units.la: Tertiò recenti Dei beneficio & praesenti rerum statu ipsos consolatur. Vobis primùm Deus, cùm suscitauisset filium suum Iesum, misit illum benedicentem vobis, dum vnumquenque conuertit ab iniquitatibus suis. Suscitandi verbo non resurrectionem Christi à mortuis intelligit, sed ad Mosis oraculum, quod paulo ante citauerat, alludit. Quasi dicat: Praestitit Deus quod promisit, & prophetam illum magnum ac humani generis redemptorem ex fratribus vestris suscitauit. Suscitatum verò & incarnatum, non ad alias gentes misit, sed vobis illum destinauit, eundemq; inter vos primùm innotescere & redemptionis causam peragere voluit. Nec quisquam est, qui hoc negare possit. Inter vos enim Christus docuit. Inter vos miraculis claruit. Vobis seipsum familiarissimum exhibuit. Imò diserte fatetur, se ad perditas Israelis oues cumprimis pertinere. Matth.15. Adhaec, cùm nos primùm ad praedicandum emitteret, iussit, vt intra vestrae gentis terminos nos contineremus, nec iremus in viam gentium. Matth.10. Et vltimum ipsius, iam caelos ascensuri, mandatum fuit, vt praedicationis euangelicae initium Hierosolymis fieret, quam per Iudaeam quoq; prius vulgari, & inde demum ad reliquas gentes transferri voluit. Act.1. Quare nulla vobis iusta dubitandi causa relinquitur, nisi praesentem Dei gratiam aspernari, & de ijs dubitare libeat, quae tantum non manibus contrectanda Deus offert. At non lactat is vanis pollicitationibus homines. Non vana beneficiorum ostentatione ludit, sed illa conferre gaudet, nec aliunde maiorem, quàm ex nostra salute delectationem capit. Docemur hic, vt & ipsi ex euangelij praedicatione certam salutis nostrae spem capiamus. Quia enim salutis nuntium est, salutem vere offert Deus ijs, quos per hoc in filij sui cognitionem & consortium inuitat. Nec alia hodie via, siue ratio superest, per quam nobis filium suum Deus mittat, quàm euangelij praedicatio, quae omnem salutis benedictionem absolutè comprehendit. Paucis vero Christi officium Petrus describit, cum illum a Deo missum esse dicit, ut nobis bene dicat. Unde etiam colligimus, ipsum per semen Abrahami non alium, quam Christum intellexisse, ut supra ex Paulo demonstrauimus. Benedicit autem nobis Christus tanquam sacerdos. Sacerdotum enim erat benedicere populo, ut Moses Numerorum cap. 6. docet. Quanquam magna inter hos & Christum sit differentia. Illi enim figurae & vmbrae tantummodo ministri erant, Christus vero bona non modo imprecatur, verumetiam confert, & in hoc nobis Deus benedicit omni spirituali benedictione, ut Paulus Ephes. 1. monet. At modu quoq; benedictionis huius explicat Petrus, addens: Dum conuertit vnumquemq; ab iniquitatibus suis. Quia enim peccata maledictionem gignunt, benedictioni locus esse non potest, nisi his e medio sublatis. Aufert autem illa Christus, imo iam olim mortis suae merito expiauit, vnde a Baptista agnus Dei dicitur, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Ioan. 1. Non autem semel duntaxat peccata tollit, sed in se credentes conuertit a peccatis. Quia enim spiritu suo il los donat, per eundem regenerantur & innouantur, ut qui antea peccatorum seruituti editi fuerant, illius iugo excusso, Deo viuere, & illi per innocentiam & charitatis studium seruire incipiant. Unde colligimus, vehementer hallucinari eos, qui Christum carnalis licentiae patronum fingunt, & illius praedicatione in hominum animis peccandi securitatem plantari clamant. Ideo certe in mundum venit Christus, ut opera diaboli dissoluat. 1. Ioan. 3. At inter haec peccato primum locum debeori, nemo esse qui nesciat. Quin potius, si verum fateri libet, nulla in nobis vera esse poterit a peccatis conuersio, nisi cuius author Christus suo spiritu fuerit, iuxta illud Ieremiae: Conuerte me & conuertar. Ierem. 31. Item: Conuerte nos ad te, o domine, & conuertemur. Thren.
units.tr: Thirdly, he comforts them with the recent benefit of God and the present state of affairs. "God, having raised up his Son Jesus, sent him first to you, blessing you, while he turns each one of you from your iniquities." By "raising up" he does not mean the resurrection of Christ from the dead, but alludes to the oracle of Moses, which he had quoted a little earlier. As if he said: God has performed what he promised, and has raised up from your brothers that great prophet and redeemer of the human race. But having been raised up and made flesh, he did not send him to other nations, but destined him for you, and willed that he should first become known among you and accomplish the cause of redemption. Nor is there anyone who can deny this. For Christ taught among you. Among you he shone forth by miracles. To you he showed himself most familiarly. Indeed, he plainly confesses that he belongs chiefly to the lost sheep of Israel. Matt. 15. Besides, when he first sent us out to preach, he ordered us to keep within the bounds of your nation, and not to go into the way of the Gentiles. Matt. 10. And his last command, when he was about to ascend to heaven, was that the beginning of the evangelical preaching should be made at Jerusalem, which he wished to be published first through Judea also, and only then carried over to the rest of the nations. Acts 1. Therefore no just cause for doubt is left to you, unless you wish to spurn God's present grace and to doubt those things which God offers, almost to be handled with the hands. But he does not delight men with empty promises. He does not play with an empty show of benefits, but rejoices to bestow them, nor does he derive greater pleasure from anywhere than from our salvation. We are taught here that we too should take from the preaching of the gospel a sure hope of our salvation. For since it is a message of salvation, God truly offers salvation to those whom he invites through it into the knowledge and fellowship of his Son. Nor is there another way or means left today by which God may send us his Son, than the preaching of the gospel, which absolutely comprehends every blessing of salvation. Peter describes the office of Christ briefly, when he says that he was sent by God to bless us. Hence we also gather that by the seed of Abraham he understood no one other than Christ, as we showed above from Paul. Christ blesses us, moreover, as a priest. For it was the office of priests to bless the people, as Moses teaches in Numbers chapter 6. Yet there is a great difference between these and Christ. For those were ministers only of the figure and shadow, but Christ not only pronounces good things but also bestows them, and in him God blesses us with every spiritual blessing, as Paul admonishes in Ephesians 1. But Peter also explains the manner of this blessing, adding: while he turns each one from his iniquities. For since sins beget a curse, there cannot be room for blessing unless these are taken out of the way. Christ, however, takes them away; indeed, by the merit of his death he long ago made expiation for them, whence he is called by the Baptist the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. John 1. Nor does he take away sins only once, but he turns those who believe in him from their sins. For since he gives them his Spirit, by the same Spirit they are regenerated and renewed, so that those who before were given over to the bondage of sin, having shaken off its yoke, begin to live to God and to serve him through innocence and zeal for love. Hence we gather that those are greatly mistaken who imagine Christ as a patron of carnal license, and cry out that by his preaching a security for sinning is planted in men's minds. Surely Christ came into the world for this very purpose, that he might destroy the works of the devil. 1 John 3. But that among these things sin must first be owed its place, no one is there who does not know. Indeed, rather, if we wish to confess the truth, there can be no true conversion from sins in us, unless Christ, its author, is by his Spirit, according to that saying of Jeremiah: Convert me, and I shall be converted. Jer. 31. Likewise: Turn us to yourself, O Lord, and we shall be turned. Lam.

units.la: Porro priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, obseruandum est, quod tot praerogatiuis insignes Iudaei, quot cum his tum Rom. 9. & alibi commemorantur, nihil ex illis omnibus vtilitatis percepe- runt, sed a Deo repudiati sunt, cum pertinaci incredulitate Christum contemnere & euangelij praedicationem aspernari pergerent, qua de re multa Paulus tradit, Rom. 11. Vana ergo sunt externa omnia, nisi Christum vera fide complectamur, qui solus a peccatis conuertit, peccata expiat, & cum Deo reconciliatos, regni caelorum haeredes facit. Hunc sua concione Petrus tradidit, & in hoc apertum salutis thesaurum ijs ostendit, qui omni salutis & gratiae Dei ipse excidisse videri poterant. Nobis ergo haec ipsa dici putemus, & in hoc incumbamus, ut vera illius membra facti, illius spiritu animemur, & cum eodem in caelis olim regnemus. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, before we make an end of speaking, it must be observed that the Jews, distinguished by so many privileges, as many as are recorded both here and in Romans 9 and elsewhere, received no profit at all from all of them, but were rejected by God, since they persisted in despising Christ with stubborn unbelief and in spurning the preaching of the gospel; Paul treats this matter at length in Romans 11. Therefore all external things are vain, unless we embrace Christ with true faith, who alone turns us from sins, expiates sins, and, having reconciled us to God, makes us heirs of the kingdom of heaven. Peter delivered him in his sermon, and in him he showed to those who might seem to have fallen away from all salvation and the grace of God an open treasury of salvation. Let us therefore think that these very things are said to us, and let us labor in this, that having been made true members of him, we may be quickened by his Spirit and with him may one day reign in heaven. To him belong blessing, honor, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 26.

units.la: Loquentibus autem illis ad populum, superuenerunt illis Sacerdotes, & praefectus templi, & Sadducaei, aegre ferentes quod ipsi docerent populum & annunciarent in Iesu Christo resurrectionem ex mortuis, & iniecerunt eis manus, & posuerunt in custodiam vsque in crastinum. Erat enim iam vespera. Multi autem eorum, qui audierant sermonem, crediderunt; & factus est numerus virorum circiter quinque millia.
units.tr: While they were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed that they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus Christ the resurrection from the dead. They laid hands on them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the message believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.

units.la: Escripsit hucusque Lucas primitiuae ecclesiae initium et progressum. Vidimus illic, quaenam apostolorum doctrina fuerit, quam illi ecclesiae tradiderunt, quae item ecclesiae veteris studia fuerint & exercitia. Subijcitur his commodissime, ut doctrinam hanc mundus exceperit: vbi hoc ipsum factum fuisse videbimus, quod Christus iam olim apostolis praedixerat. Nam apud Iohannem ait: Non est seruus maior domino suo. Si me persecuti sunt, & vos persequentur. Si sermonem meum seruauerunt, & vestrum seruabunt. Iohan. 15. Item: Tradent vos in concilia, & in conciliabulis suis caedent vos flagris, &c. Matth. 10. Atqui haec iam experiri incipiunt apostoli, quos hucusque ab hostium furore tutos fecerat Deus, donec ecclesiae principium firmius & stabilius collocari posset. Iam vero repente illis acerrimi hostes irruunt, comprehensos carceribus includunt, in Concilio examinandos sistunt, tandemq; longa disceptatione vexatos non fine gravissimis miſniſ dimittunt. Nobis vero in vniuersa hac narratione illud ante omnia confyderandum erit, quod nostrae institutioni & consolationi cumprimis feruit, ne videlicet impiorum conatibus, quibus hodie Christi doctrinam & ecclesiam oppugnant, offendamur. Nec enim aliquid nouum aut insolens facit mundus hic, cuius ingenium est, veritatis lucem odisse & persequi, eo quod per hanc opera illius praeua arguuntur. Iohan. 3. Hic vero primitiuae ecclesiae constantia nos armari conuenit, ne oppugnati loco cedamus, sed forti & inuicta fide Dei opem & tentationis euentum expectemus, quem felicissimum illis largitur dominus, quos Cruce probatos & meliores factos esse viderit. 1. Cor. 10. Sed quia de his dicendi locus frequenter sese offeret, paucis haec praelibaiuffe sufficiat, ne scopum, ad quem finagula dirigi oportet, amittamus. Nunc vero quae a Luca dicuntur, per singulas partes fiue circumstantias ordine excutiemus. Describit enim, qui apostolorum hostes & persecutionis authores fuerint, qua astutia & quibus artibus vsi sint, quid suo conatui impio & iniquo praetexuerint, qua violentia manus iniecerint apostolis, & quam vanus illorum conatus fuerit, cum fidelium numerus illorum rabie auctus potius quam imminutus fit.
units.tr: Up to this point Luke has described the beginning and progress of the primitive Church. We have seen there what the doctrine of the apostles was, which they handed on to the Church, and what the zeal and practices of the early Church were. What follows fittingly is how the world received this doctrine, and there we shall see the very thing that Christ had long before foretold to the apostles. For in John he says: "The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also. If they have kept my word, they will keep yours" (John 15). Likewise: "They will deliver you up to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you," etc. (Matt. 10). Indeed, the apostles now begin to experience these things, those whom God had hitherto kept safe from the fury of their enemies, until the foundation of the Church could be laid more firmly and securely. Now suddenly their most bitter enemies rush upon them, shut them up in prison, bring them before the council to be examined, and at last, after a long dispute, dismiss them, harassed but not without severe threats. In this whole narrative we must above all consider what is especially useful for our instruction and comfort: that we should not be offended by the attempts of the impious, with which today they assail the doctrine of Christ and the Church. For this world does nothing new or strange; its nature is to hate and persecute the light of truth, because by that light its evil works are exposed (John 3). Here we ought to be armed with the constancy of the primitive Church, so that when assailed we do not give ground, but with a strong and unconquered faith await God's help and the outcome of the temptation, which the Lord grants most happily to those whom he sees to have been proved by the cross and made better (1 Cor. 10). But since the occasion for speaking of these matters will often present itself, it is enough to touch on them briefly here, lest we lose sight of the goal toward which our course must be directed. Now, however, we shall go through the particulars and circumstances of what Luke relates, one by one in order. He describes who were the enemies of the apostles and the authors of the persecution, by what cunning and what arts they acted, what pretext they put forward for their impious and unjust undertaking, with what violence they laid hands on the apostles, and how vain their attempt was, since the number of believers was increased rather than diminished by their rage.

units.la: Inter apostolorum hostes tria hominum genera recensentur. Primi sacerdotes sunt, quos totius nostri gotij authores & duces fuisse, ex circumstantijs facile colligitur. Aequi horum potius erat veritatis patrocinium suscipere, & Christum, cui Moses & prophetae testimonium ferebant, populo praedicare. Comitatur hos templi praefectus, quem Romanum aliquem militum Tribunum fuisse verisimile est. Quia enim templum in loco vrbis munitissimo situm, ipsum quoq; munitionibus probe defendebatur, illius curam a Romanis praetoribus vel praesidibus Iudaeae cumprimis commendatam fuisse credederim, ne quid ibi turbarum Iudaei sub sacrorum coetuum & religionis praetextu concitarent. Adduxit vero haud dubie templi praefectus suos satellites siue milites, qui illius seruitio & obsequio semper praesto erant. Accedit his tertium hominum genus, Sadducaei, quos omnem religionem ludibrio habuisse constat. Negabant enim corporum resurrectionem & quaecunq; de vita aeterna mysterijs traduntur, vt videre est Matth. 22. & Act. 23. cap. At qui fieri non potest, vt aliquid syncerae religionis in ijs superfit, qui ista negare audet, quibus sublatis, nullus religionis vsus superesset. Quod si vero rem probe expendamus, eosdem contra Christi apostolos conuenisse patebit, qui ad Christum capiendum admon tem oliuarum exiuerunt, sicuti Lucas in euangelica historia cap. 22. narrat.
units.tr: Among the enemies of the apostles three kinds of men are listed. The first are the priests, whom it is easily gathered from the circumstances were the authors and leaders of our whole nation's opposition. It would rather have been their duty to take up the defence of the truth and to preach to the people Christ, to whom Moses and the prophets bore witness. With these comes the captain of the temple, who was probably some Roman military tribune. For since the temple, situated in the most fortified part of the city, was itself well defended by fortifications, I should think its guard was especially entrusted to him by the Roman governors or the prefects of Judaea, lest the Jews stir up some disturbance under the pretext of sacred assemblies and religion. The captain of the temple doubtless brought with him his attendants or soldiers, who were always at hand for his service and command. To these is added a third kind of men, the Sadducees, who are known to have made a mockery of all religion. For they denied the resurrection of the body and all the teachings about the mysteries of eternal life, as can be seen in Matthew 22 and Acts 23. But how can any part of pure religion survive in those who dare to deny these things, once they are removed nothing of religion would remain? And if we weigh the matter carefully, it will be clear that these are the same men who gathered against the apostles of Christ, the very ones who went out to the Mount of Olives to seize Christ, as Luke relates in the gospel history, chapter 22.

units.la: Obseruemus hic, qui semper acerrimi ecclesiae & doctrinae Christi hostes ac persecutionum authores futuri sint. Sacerdotes nimirum, id est, ij qui doctrinae & totius ecclesiae gubernationem sibi vendicant. Vt primum enim illi, ambitione & auaritia superati, priuato honori studere & religionem in quaestum mutare incipiunt (quod Iudaicos illos fecisse euangelica historia abunde docet, Matth. 7. 23. Iohan. 5. &c.) fieri non potest, quin primi se veritati opponant, eo quod primi illius luce arguuntur. Hinc factum videmus, vt per eiusmodi homines omnibus seculis contra veritatis doctrinam tur bae concitatae fuerint. Docent hoc prophetarum tempora, quibus religionis antistites & sacerdotes prae alijs negotium fecerunt. Idem Baptista sensit, cuius doctrinam & baptismum primi ab Hierosolymis misi Leuitae carpere coeperunt. Ioan. 1. Et Christus non alios acerbiores hostes habuit quam sacerdotes, quorum consilijs tandem captus, damnatus & cruci affixus fuit. Eosdem nunc quoq; apostoli infensissimos sentiunt, & quibus per Pilatum & Romanos milites bucusq; de Christo praedicare liberum fuerat, ab ijs interturbantur, quorum patrocinio & fauore in propagando Christi regno defendi debuissent. Horum memores, non offendamur, si hodie etiam illos nobis aduersari videamus, qui hactenus doctrinae & sanctitatis titulos in ecclesia sibi vendicarunt, Pontifices dico cum vniuerso episcoporum & monachorum grege. Cum enim auaritia & ambitione totos regi constet, & humanis traditionibus veritatis doctrinam iam olim obscurarint, ac religionem sibi quaestum fecerint, fieri nequit, quin lucem veritatis odio prosequantur & extinctam cupiant.
units.tr: Let us observe here who will always be the most bitter enemies of the Church and of the doctrine of Christ, and the authors of persecutions. Namely the priests, that is, those who claim for themselves the teaching and the whole government of the Church. For as soon as they, overcome by ambition and greed, begin to pursue private honour and turn religion into a source of gain (which the gospel history abundantly shows the Jewish leaders did: Matt. 7, 23; John 5, etc.), it cannot but be that they are the first to oppose the truth, since they are the first to be exposed by its light.
