Hence we see that through men of this sort, in every age, tumults have been stirred up against the doctrine of truth. The times of the prophets teach this, when the guardians of religion and the priests were more troublesome than all others. John the Baptist also experienced it; the Levites sent from Jerusalem first began to carp at his teaching and baptism (John 1). And Christ had no more bitter enemies than the priests, by whose counsels he was at last seized, condemned and fixed to the cross. Now too the apostles find these same men most hostile, and they are harassed by those who, under Pilate and the Roman soldiers, had until then allowed them freedom to preach about Christ, and who ought to have defended them by their patronage and favour in spreading the kingdom of Christ. Mindful of these things, we should not be surprised if today we see those also opposing us who have hitherto claimed for themselves the titles of doctrine and holiness in the Church: I mean the Pontiffs, together with the whole flock of bishops and monks. For since it is plain that they are wholly governed by avarice and ambition, and have long since obscured the doctrine of truth with human traditions, and made religion a source of gain for themselves, it cannot be that they do not pursue the light of truth with hatred and wish it extinguished.

units.la: Sed astutiam horum videamus, qua in apostolis oppugnandis vsi sunt. Primo non foli templum ingrediuntur & apostolis manum iniiciunt. Sic enim omnibus videri poterant, non nisi priuati bonorus & quaestus studio duci. Et periculum erat, ne populi furorem contra se prouocarent. Quapropter templi praefectum sibi adiungunt, cuius erat publica authoritate probibere, ne quid turbarum in templo excitaretur: sicq; videri poterant pro publica pace soliciti esse, cum non alio animo hos ab ipsis fieret, quàm quòd magistratus praesidio ad suae tyrannidis defensionem abuti cuperent. Deinde Sadducaeos quoq; sibi coniungunt, homines ab omni religione alienissimos, eò quòd tales ipsorum instituto cumprimis idoneos esse viderent. Qui enim tales sunt, vel stulti vel seditiosi animi indicium esse putant, si quis in religione contra receptam consuetudinem quicquam immutare velit. Postremò docentibus superveniunt, & quidem de improviso, quod ad populum perterrefaciendum non parum serviebat. Unde etiam colligere licet, ipsos occasionem iam ante captauisse, nec quicquam hic fortuito & inconsulto esse factum. Ventur eadem astutia quicunque contra veritatem iam aliquot seculis conspiraverunt. Nam & Daniel Antichristo oculos hominis, id est, prudentiam & providendi astutiam tribuit, & Christus filios huius seculi in sua generatione prudentiores esse dicit, quàm filios lucis. Dan.7. Luc.16. Et sane si Pontificum Rom. historias consyderemus, ea calliditate iam aliquot seculis vsos fuisse constabit, ut tum maximè suas res gesserint, quando nihil minus facere videbantur, & carnali brachio suffulti in tantum tyrannidis fastigium ascenderint. Sic Bonifacius tertius Phocam, indigna Mauricij Imperatoris cade madentem, Imperij honore sibi demeretur, ut illius authoritate vicissim primatum ecclesiae obtineat. Ita Longobardorum viribus Gracos Imperatores Italia expulere, & cum Longobardi ipsis intolerabiliores viderentur, Francorum auxilio in illis debellandis vsi sunt. Nec alia causa Imperatorem Occidentis Carolum creauerunt, cum annis plus trecentis Romanum Imperium vacauisset, quàm ut Templi praefectum haberent, cuius opera occupatam in ecclesia tyrannidem tueri, & contradicentes cohercere possent. Apertissimè autem hos suos animos prodidere, quando Imperij titulo ad Germanos translato, Imperatores in verba sua iurare coegerunt, ac sibi ipsis Imperatorem confirmandi & coronandi ius referuarunt, ne quis alius quàm illorum votis respondens, ad eam dignitatem ascendere posset. Fatebuntur me vera dicere, quicunque iurisiurandi formulam, qua Imperatores obstringuntur, quamq; inter sui Iuris Canones retulerunt, adhaec Bonifacij octaui Canonem de Maioritate & obedientia legerint. Is enim de duobus gladijs, id est, ecclesiastica & politica potestate loquens, verunq; Romanus Pontificibus diserte vendicat his verbis: Vterq; est in potestate ecclesiae, spiritualis scilicet gladius & materialis. Sed vt quidem pro ecclesia, ille vero ab ecclesia exercendus. Ille sacerdotis, vt manu regum & militum, sed ad nutum et patientiam sacerdotis, &c. Agnoscamus ergo veteris typi veritatem, quando Pontifices regum armis contra veritatem pugnare videmus. Agnoscamus bestiae huius astutiam, quae alienis viribus res suas conficit. Cogitemus indefessum esse illius in opprimenda veritate studium, nec ex nostra socordia illos aestimemus. Vigilant illi nobis securè dormitantibus. Excitemur ergo & ipsi, ac iuxta Christi admonitionem caveamus nobis ab hominibus. Matth.10.
units.tr: But let us look at the cunning these men used in attacking the apostles. First, they do not enter the temple and lay hands on the apostles alone. For in this way they could appear to be moved only by a desire for private honour and gain, and there was a danger that they would provoke the people's rage against themselves. Therefore they associate with themselves the captain of the temple, whose duty by public authority was to prevent any disturbance from arising in the temple; and so they could appear to be anxious for public peace, since it could be thought that they were acting with no other intention than to use the protection of the magistrate to defend their own tyranny. Then they also join the Sadducees with themselves, men most alien to all religion, because they saw that such men were especially suited to their purpose. For those of this kind think that if anyone wishes to change anything in religion against the accepted custom, it is a sign of a foolish or seditious mind. Finally they come upon the teachers, and indeed unexpectedly, which contributed not a little to terrifying the people. From this we may also gather that they had sought the opportunity beforehand, and that nothing here was done by chance or without deliberation. The same cunning has been used by all who for some centuries have conspired against the truth. For Daniel attributes to Antichrist the eyes of a man, that is, prudence and skill in foreseeing, and Christ says that the sons of this age are more prudent in their generation than the sons of light (Dan. 7; Luke 16). And indeed, if we consider the Roman histories of the Pontiffs, it will be evident that for some centuries they have used such craft that they accomplished their aims most of all when they seemed to be doing nothing of the kind, and, propped up by the carnal arm, ascended to such a height of tyranny. Thus Boniface III, who had gained the honour of the empire for Phocas, though he was stained with the unworthy slaughter of the emperor Maurice, won for himself in return, by Phocas's authority, the primacy of the Church. So too the Greek emperors were expelled from Italy by the strength of the Lombards, and when the Lombards themselves seemed more intolerable, they used the help of the Franks to crush them. Nor for any other reason did they create Charles emperor of the West, after the Roman empire had been vacant for more than three hundred years, than that they might have a captain of the temple, by whose work they could defend the tyranny they had seized in the Church and restrain those who opposed them. Moreover they revealed their intentions most plainly when, the title of empire having been transferred to the Germans, they compelled the emperors to swear in their words, and reserved to themselves the right of confirming and crowning the emperor, so that no one could rise to that dignity except one who answered to their wishes. Those who have read the formula of the oath by which emperors are bound, which they have included among their own canons, and besides that the canon of Boniface VIII on the Majority and Obedience, will admit that I speak the truth. For he, speaking of the two swords, that is, the ecclesiastical and the political power, clearly claims both for the Roman Pontiffs in these words: "Both are in the power of the Church, the spiritual sword and the material. But the one is to be wielded for the Church, the other by the Church. The one is in the hand of the priest, the other in the hand of kings and soldiers, but at the will and sufferance of the priest," etc. Let us therefore recognise the truth of the old type, when we see the Pontiffs fighting against the truth with the arms of kings. Let us recognise the cunning of this beast, which accomplishes its ends by foreign strength. Let us consider that its zeal in suppressing the truth is never weary, and let us not judge it by our own sloth. They are watchful while we sleep securely. Let us therefore be roused ourselves, and according to Christ's warning beware of men (Matt. 10).

units.la: Atqui nimis insolens & tyrannicum videri poterat, homines nullo iuris praetextu violenter abripere. Indicat ergo Lucas quid facto suo praetexuerint: Molestè ferebant (inquit) quòd ipsi docerent populum, & annuntiarent in Iesu resurrectionem ex mortuis. His enim verbis non modò quid ipsis doluerit, verumetiam quibus criminibus apostolos grauarint, docet. Duo autem recensentur. Primò illis intolerabile videtur, quòd Petrus & Iohannes, rudes & illiterati, qui ex piscatura hucusq; vitam quaesiuerant, nec vllis sacris erant initiati, docerent populum. Videbatur hoc schisma spirare, & quòd ab ecclesiae vnitate populum abducere conarentur. Eò quippe inter Iudaos res deuenerat, vt omne ecclesiae administrandae ius penes sacerdotes esset, qui ad docendi munus neminem admitterebant, nisi qui in illorum verba iurauisset: quod a Romanis quoq; Pontificibus iam seculis aliquot vsurpatum videmus, in quorum ecclesia (sicuti Christus in sua Revelatione praedixit) nemini licet aut emere aut vendere, nisi charactere bestiae acceperit, &c. Apoc.13. Nec tamen hoc ita accipi volumus quasi cuiusdam docendi ius esse debeat. Scimus enim quid de ministrorum ordinatione apostoli tradiderint. 1. Tim.3. & 5. &c. Sed illorum damnamus tyrannidem, qui sibi solis omnem potestatem vendicant, cùm ipsi omnium in ecclesia malorum praecipui authores sint, & ne extremum quidem in illa locum habere mereantur. Secundò illud etiam animaduersione dignum ducunt, quòd Iesum à mortuis resurrexisse praedicarent. Damnabatur quidem à Sadducaeis in vniuersum resurrectionis doctrina. Sed dolet caeteris aliud quiddam grauius. Ex resurrectione enim cuius colligere licebat, Christum Dei filium & vitae authorem, à sacerdotibus & Pilato, iniusto & iniquo iudicio fuisse damnatum, quod inter concionandum non obscurè Petrus dixerat. Illud vero non intolerabile modò conuitium, verumetiam seditiosum videri poterat, quasi populum contra iudices iniquos & sanguinarios concitare cuperent. Duobus ergo grauissimis criminibus grauantur apostoli, schismatis nimirum in ecclesia & seditionis in republica, quorum utrumque omnibus bonis merito exosum & detestabile videtur. Quod si vero sacerdotum animos & mores inspicias, vanum hunc praetextum fuisse facile patebit. Si enim schisma in ecclesia ferre nolunt, cur Sadducaeos in pretio habent, quos praecipuum fidei & salutis articulum corporum scilicet resurrectionem, palam negare non pudebat? Cur Essenos & Pharisaeos, homines plane sectarios & diuersissimarum opinionum professores ferunt? Si seditionis scelus tantopere horrent, cur populo authores fuerunt, ut Barrabam, hominem seditiosum & latronem, sibi donari peteret, Christum vero ad Crucem postularet? Non ergo vel schismatis vel seditionis periculum, sed veritatis odium illos exagitat, & graue illis est, quod veritatis luce illorum malitia & improbitas argueretur.
units.tr: Yet it might have seemed too arrogant and tyrannical to seize men by violence without any pretext of right. Luke therefore states what they used as a pretext for their deed: "They were greatly troubled," he says, "that they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead." These words show not only what grieved them but also the charges with which they burdened the apostles. Two are listed. First, it seemed intolerable to them that Peter and John, uneducated and unlettered men who until then had earned their living from fishing and had not been initiated into any sacred office, should teach the people. This seemed to breathe schism, as if they were trying to draw the people away from the unity of the Church. Things had indeed come to such a point among the Jews that all right to govern the Church rested with the priests, who admitted no one to the office of teaching unless he had sworn to their words. We see this practice adopted by the Roman Pontiffs too, for many centuries now, and in their church (as Christ foretold in his Revelation) no one may buy or sell unless he has received the mark of the beast, and so on. Rev. 13. Yet we do not want this taken to mean that there should be some right of teaching restricted to a few. We know what the apostles handed down about the ordination of ministers. 1 Tim. 3 and 5, etc. But we condemn the tyranny of those who claim all power for themselves alone, when they are themselves the chief authors of all the evils in the Church and do not deserve to hold even the lowest place in it. Second, they also thought it worth noting that the apostles proclaimed that Jesus had risen from the dead. The doctrine of the resurrection was indeed rejected in general by the Sadducees, but something else grieved them more. From the resurrection it could be inferred that Christ, the Son of God and author of life, had been condemned by the priests and Pilate in an unjust and iniquitous judgment, which Peter had not obscurely said in his sermon. This could seem not only an intolerable insult but also seditious, as if the apostles wanted to stir up the people against unjust and bloodthirsty judges. So the apostles are burdened with two most serious charges, namely schism in the Church and sedition in the commonwealth, and both seem rightly hateful and detestable to all good men. But if you look closely at the minds and morals of the priests, it will easily be plain that this pretext was empty. If they cannot bear schism in the Church, why do they hold the Sadducees in such esteem, men who did not hesitate openly to deny the principal article of faith and salvation, namely the resurrection of the body? Why do they tolerate the Essenes and Pharisees, men who are plainly sectarian and profess the most diverse opinions? If they so dread the crime of sedition, why did they urge the people to ask that Barabbas, a seditious man and robber, be released to them, while demanding that Christ be crucified? Therefore it is not the danger of schism or sedition that torments them, but hatred of the truth, and it grieves them that their malice and wickedness are exposed by the light of truth.

units.la: Interim videre licet, quo praetextu contra veritatem pugnetur ab impijs. Huius enim propugnatores omnibus saeculis pro schismaticis & seditiosis habitos fuisse constat. Eliae obijcitur, quod Israelem turbet. 1. Regum 18. cap. Amos propheta seditionis apud Ieroboamum accusatur. Amos 7. Christus quoque coram Pilato populum seducere & contra Caesarem regnum affectare dicitur. Eadem crimina olim quoque Christianis intentata fuisse Imperatorum temporibus, ex Tertulliani, Cypriani, Arnobij, Lactantij & aliorum scriptis colligere licet, quibus illi gentilium calumnijs respondérunt. Hodie quoque hoc potissimum nomine euangelij doctrina male audit, quod inconsutilem Christi tunicam, ecclesiam nimirum, scindat, animos disiungat, & bellorum faces subministret. Sed facilis est ad illa responsio, nec obscurum est longe aliud illis hominibus dolere. Si enim ecclesiam scindi nolunt, cur obsecro Monachorum regulas & ordines tantopere commendant, quibus in diuersissimos ritus & factiosa nomina scinduntur, quos vnius Christi nomen profiteri decebat? Cur non Paulum apostolum, ista grauissime damnantem audiunt? 1. Corinth. 1. & 3. Si dissidia tantopere abominantur, qui fit, quod iam saeculis aliquot omnium bellorum authores Romani Pontifices fuerint? Illos debemus horrendum & Christiano orbi nunquam satis deplorandum schisma, quo Oriens ab Occidente reuulsus, & tandem Turcarum impia tyrannidi subiectus est. Quis belli sacri author indicari poterit alius, quam Romana sedes, quo totus terrarum orbis infelicissime commissus & riui sanguinis humani effusi sunt? Historias appello, quae me vera dicere, non affectui indulgere testabuntur. Nonne etiam nostro saeculo horum legati in Regum castris & inter militaria signa visuntur? An non illos regum dissidijs crescere, & suam in ecclesia tyrannidem stabilire cernimus? Haec dum euangelij lux arguit, ilico nos schismatum & seditionum accusant. Agnoscite ergo dolum o Christiani principes, & toties ista fallaces, nec contra fratres & Christi membra saeuite in illorum gratiam, quos publicae pacis & salutis maximas pestes esse constat.
units.tr: Meanwhile we can see under what pretext the impious fight against the truth. For it is well established that in every age the defenders of this truth have been regarded as schismatics and seditious men. Elijah is charged with troubling Israel (1 Kings 18). Amos the prophet is accused of sedition before Jeroboam (Amos 7). Christ too is said before Pilate to seduce the people and to aspire to a kingdom against Caesar. That the same charges were once also brought against Christians in the times of the emperors we can gather from the writings of Tertullian, Cyprian, Arnobius, Lactantius and others, who answered the slanders of the Gentiles. Even today the teaching of the gospel is ill spoken of chiefly on this ground, that it is said to tear the seamless tunic of Christ, that is the Church, to separate minds and to supply the torches of wars. But the answer to these charges is easy, and it is not hard to see that these men are grieved by something quite different. For if they do not want the Church torn apart, why, I ask, do they so highly commend the rules and orders of the monks, by which the Church is torn into very diverse rites and factious names, when they ought to profess the name of Christ alone? Why do they not listen to the apostle Paul, who condemns these things most severely? 1 Cor. 1 and 3. If they so abhor divisions, how is it that for several centuries now the Roman Pontiffs have been the authors of all wars? They are responsible for that dreadful schism, never sufficiently to be lamented by the Christian world, by which the East was torn from the West and finally subjected to the impious tyranny of the Turks. What author of a holy war could be named other than the Roman see, by whom the whole world has been most unhappily committed to war and rivers of human blood poured out? I appeal to the histories, which will bear witness that I speak the truth and do not indulge feeling. Are not their legates seen in the camps of kings and among military standards even in our own age? Do we not see them feeding on the quarrels of kings and establishing their own tyranny in the Church? While the light of the gospel exposes these things, they at once accuse us of schisms and seditions. Recognise the trick, then, O Christian princes, and do not be so often deceived by these men; do not rage against your brothers and the members of Christ for their benefit, when it is plain that they are the greatest plague to public peace and safety.

units.la: At miretur aliquis, quod ad intentata crimina non responderint apostoli. Sed quid obstiterit fatis aperte Lucas docet. Mox enim manibus in illos iniectis, in carcerem abstraxerunt, idque eo festinantius fecerunt, quo minor ipsis sese coram populo purgandi facultas daretur. Est hoc veritatis hostibus proprium, quod aperta vi in huius professores grassantur, in hoc vnum maxime intenti, ne vllus excusationis locus fidelibus concedatur. Norunt enim eam veritatis vim esse, ut suo fulgore omnes illorum machinationes facile discutiat, nec alia re magis, quam vulgi ignorantia, se tutos esse intelligunt. Vt ergo falsa crimina de pijs in vulgus spargere solent: ita ne quis illorum innocentiam cognoscere possit, summo studio obstant. Quare vbi rationibus & scripturis agi oportebat, apertam vim, laqueos, carceres, enses, faces & alia eius generis proferunt. Notius hoc est, quam vt multis probari opus sit. Meminerint tamen hanc, Christo teste, tenebrarum potestatem esse, & cum tenebrarum principe se aliquando tyrannidis & impietatis suae poenas esse daturos. Luc. 22. Animemur autem apostolorum exemplo, qui indignam pietatis & studij sui fidelis ab ingrato mundo mercedem recipiunt, nec offendamur, si quid tale nobis etiam accidere sentiamus.
units.tr: But someone may wonder why the apostles did not answer the charges brought against them. Luke clearly teaches what prevented it. For as soon as they had laid hands on them, they dragged them off to prison, and they did so all the more hastily the less opportunity was given the apostles to clear themselves before the people. It is characteristic of the enemies of truth that they rage with open force against its professors, being intent above all on this, that no opportunity of excuse be granted to the faithful. For they know that the power of the truth is such that by its brightness it easily scatters all their schemes, and they understand that they are safe only through the ignorance of the common people. So, just as they are accustomed to spread false charges about the godly among the crowd, so with the greatest zeal they block anyone from recognising their innocence. Therefore, where the matter ought to be settled by reasons and Scripture, they bring out open force, nooses, prisons, swords, torches and other things of that kind. This is too well known to need proof by many examples. Yet let them remember that, as Christ bore witness, this is the power of darkness, and that they will one day pay the penalty for their tyranny and impiety together with the prince of darkness. Luke 22. Let us be encouraged by the example of the apostles, who received an unworthy reward for their piety and zeal from an ungrateful world, and let us not be offended if we perceive that something of the sort happens to us as well.

units.la: Caeterum ne qua nobis esset iusta offendiculi occasio, quam parum tyrannide sua contra Christum & ecclesiam eius impij hostes profecerint, euangelista docet. Multi (inquit) eorum, qui audierant sermonem, crediderunt: & factus est numerus virorum circiter quinque millia. Quid hic primum explicemus & admiremur, o fratres? Ineffabilem ne Dei potentiam, aut admirandam fidelium illius temporis
units.tr: Moreover, so that we might have no just occasion for stumbling, the evangelist shows how little the impious enemies gained by their tyranny against Christ and his Church. "Many of those," he says, "who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men became about five thousand." What shall we first explain and marvel at here, brothers? The ineffable power of God, or the admirable constancy and courage of the faithful of that time?

units.la: IIII. Aperta vi pugnatur contra veritatem.
units.tr: IIII. Open force is used against the truth.

units.la: V. Persecutione augetur ecclesia. temporis constantiam & fortitudinem? Inuicta enim hic elucet Christi potentia, quae hostium con-silia non modo dissipat, sed etiam inuertit, quod illum facturum Dauid olim testatus est. Psal. 2. & 33. Conantur illi euangelij cursum impedire, & terrore iniecto homines à Christi ecclesia auellere. Sed adeo falluntur, vt admirabilis potius euangelij fructus conspiciatur, & noui ecclesiae Christi discipuli accedant. Est autem haec perpetua ecclesiae fors, quod ex persecutionibus incrementum sumit. Factum hoc olim in Babylone, quando Assyriorum & Persarum reges veri Dei & religionis praeco nes facti sunt. Dan 3. & 6. Sub Imperatoribus autem quo feruentior fuit persecutio, eo plures inuenti sunt, qui Christum sanguine confiteri pulchrum duxerunt. Hoc illud est, quod Dauid Christum in medio hostium suorum dominaturum esse vaticinatur. Psal. 110. Imitemur vero nos primitiuae ecclesiae fortitudinem, nec cruce vel persecutorum rabie terreamur. In corpus saeuiunt quantum domi-nus permiserit, sed in animam iuris nihil habent. Matth. 10. Vinciuntur ab his verbi praecones & fidi auditores, ac sermo Dei vinciri nequit. 2. Tim. 2. Spirat enim domini spiritus, non vbi mundo libuerit, sed vbi ipse vult. Iohan. 3. Adhaec maior est qui in nobis agit, quam qui in mundo furit. 1. Iohan. 4. In hoc enim diabolus agit, quem iam olim superatum esse scimus. Iohan. 12. & 16. In nobis Christus operatur, quo nos confortante, possumus omnia. Philip. 4. Est hic fortis & fidelis pastor, qui oues sibi eripi non patitur. Iohan. 10. Praeparauit is nobis in caelis locum, ad quem nos inconcussa fide per Crucem & tribulationes omniuarias contendere decet, vt cum illo viuamus & regnemus in domo patris ipsius: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: V. The Church is increased by persecution. For here the constancy and courage of that time shine forth, and the invincible power of Christ is clearly seen, which does not merely scatter the plans of its enemies but overturns them, as David long ago testified that he would do (Ps. 2 and 33). Those men try to hinder the course of the gospel and by casting terror to tear men away from the Church of Christ. But they are so deceived that an admirable fruit of the gospel is seen instead, and new disciples of the Church of Christ come forward. This is the constant lot of the Church, that it gains increase from persecutions. This happened once in Babylon, when the kings of the Assyrians and Persians became heralds of the true God and of religion (Dan. 3 and 6). Under the emperors, the fiercer the persecution, the more were found who thought it fine to confess Christ with their blood. This is what David prophesied, that Christ would rule in the midst of his enemies (Ps. 110). Let us imitate the courage of the primitive Church, and let us not be terrified by the cross or the rage of persecutors. They rage against the body as far as the Lord permits, but they have no power over the soul (Matt. 10). The preachers of the word and the faithful hearers are bound by these men, yet the word of God cannot be bound (2 Tim. 2). For the Spirit of the Lord breathes not where it pleases the world, but where he himself wills (John 3). Moreover, greater is he who works in us than he who rages in the world (1 John 4). For the devil acts in this way, whom we know was overcome long ago (John 12 and 16). Christ works in us, by whose strengthening we can do all things (Phil. 4). He is the strong and faithful minister who does not allow his sheep to be snatched from him (John 10). He has prepared for us a place in heaven, towards which we ought to strive with unshaken faith through the cross and all manner of tribulations, so that we may live and reign with him in the house of his Father, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVII.
units.tr: Homily 27.

units.la: Factum est autem postridie, vt congregarentur eorum principes & Seniores & scribae Hierosolymis, & Annas summus Sacerdos, & Caiaphas, & Iohannes, & Alexander, & quicunque erat ex genere pontificio. Et cum statuissent eos in medio, interrogauerunt: In qua virtute, aut in quo nomine fecistis hoc vos? Tunc Petrus repletus spiritu sancto dixit illis: Principes populi & Seniores Israel, si nos hodie examinamur de beneficio in hominem infirmum collato, quomodo ille sanatus sit: notum sit vobis omnibus & toti populo Israel, quod in nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni, quem vos crucifixistis, quem Deus excitauit a mortuis, hic stat coram vobis sanus. Hic est lapis ille, qui reiectus a vobis aedificantibus, factus est in caput anguli: nec est in vllo alio salus. Nec enim aliud nomen est sub caelo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri.
units.tr: It happened on the following day that their rulers, elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. And when they had set the apostles in their midst, they asked: "By what power, or in whose name, have you done this?" Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: "Rulers of the people and elders of Israel, if we are today being examined about a kindness shown to a sick man, and how he was made well, then let it be known to all of you and to the whole people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you whole. This is the stone which was rejected by you builders, and has become the head of the corner. Nor is there salvation in anyone else; for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved."

units.la: Quamuis Dominus & saluator noster Iesus Christus, iuxta promissiones suas nunquam deficit iis, qui ipsum vera fide amplexi sunt, praecipue tamen illis se praesentem exhibet, quando per persecutionibus per fidei hostes excitatis premuntur, nec aliquod vident in hominibus praesidium, quo niti possint. Et tunc quidem illos spiritu suo non modo consolatur, verumetiam, quid faciant quidue loquantur, edocet. Matth. 10. Marc. 13. Luc. 21. Exemplum eius rei praesens historia exhibet, dum eos, qui cum sapientia tum potentia instructissimi erant, per apostolos Christi, rudes & nullius pretii homines (si mundi iudicium audias) superati & turpiter confusi sunt. Vidimus enim, vt in carcerem abducti sint apostoli, eo quod docendi munus, non ordinati a sacerdotibus, susceperint, & Christum Iesum a mortuis resurrexisse praedicarent. At in praesenti, vt causam Christi coram senatu Hierosolymitano egerint, Lucas commemorat: qui locus tum ob multa alia, tum maxime hoc nomine memorabilis est, quod hostium veritatis artes & pontificij Concilij, contra veritatem congregati, typum elegantem continet.
units.tr: Although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, according to his promises, never fails those who have embraced him with true faith, he nevertheless shows himself present especially to those who are pressed by persecutions stirred up by the enemies of the faith, and who see no help in men on which they can lean. At such times he comforts them by his Spirit, and also teaches them what to do and what to say (Matt. 10; Mark 13; Luke 21). The present history gives an example of this, in which the apostles of Christ, plain men of no account (if you listen to the judgement of the world), overcame and shamefully confounded those who were most thoroughly equipped with both wisdom and power. For we saw the apostles led off to prison because they had taken up the office of teaching without being ordained by the priests, and because they preached that Jesus Christ had risen from the dead. Now Luke relates how they pleaded the cause of Christ before the Jerusalem senate. This passage is memorable for many reasons, but above all for this: it contains an elegant picture of the arts of the enemies of truth, and of a papal council gathered against the truth.

units.la: Orditur autem a Iudicum consessu, quem diligenti singulorum, qui hic conuenerunt, enumeratione depingit, non modo vt intelligamus, qui & quales conuenerint, sed vt constet, veritatis hostes humana potius authoritate & potentia quam vlla alia fiducia niti. Factum est (inquit) vt congregarentur principes, & Seniores, & scribae Hierosolymis. Tribus ordinibus quicquid inter Iudaeos
units.tr: He begins with the assembly of the judges, and by a careful listing of each of those who gathered here he paints it for us. This is not only so that we may understand who and what sort of men came together, but so that it may be clear that the enemies of truth rely on human authority and power rather than on any other confidence. "It happened," he says, "that the rulers, elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem." He has included in these three orders whatever was outstanding among the Jews.

units.la: 1 4 eximij erat, comprehendit. Principes sunt, quibus per Romanos rerum administratio comissa erat, earum cumprimis, quae ad Iudaicam politiam, quatenus illa à reliquis differebat, attinebant. Senio- rum ordo idem qui Senatorum erat, vt ex alijs scriptura locis patet. Scribae autem dicebantur, qui legis & totius scripturae notitiam sibi vendicabant, & penes quos erat tabularum seu instrumento- rum publicorum custodia. Non contentus vero ordines hos nominauisse, quorundam nomina recen- set, qui maiori inter alios authoritate praestabant. Annam nimirum, qui summus sacerdos hic dici videtur, non quòd pontificatum tunc gereret (nam illum Caiaphan adhuc tenuisse historia docent) sed quòd in illo aliquando fuisset: Caiaphan item: Iohannem & Alexandrum, quibus tandem om- nes alios subijcit, quicunq; ex pontificio genere inueniebantur. Quòd si vero hunc confessum inspicias, nihil illo tempore hoc magnificentius fingi potuisse patebit. Conuenerunt enim, quorum potentia Ro- manorum praesidum authoritate nitebatur. Adsunt, quibus publice commissa erat ecclesiae cura. Ne desunt, qui eruditionis & doctrinae titulo omnibus suspiciendi erant. Omnibus vero his accede- bat, quòd horum ordo tum diuina institutione, tum successione annorum plus mille quingentorum (si ab exitu Aegypti seu Aaronis pontificatu ad Christi & apostolorum tempora annorum nume- rum supputes) commendabatur. Et reuera sese Aaronis, Eleazari, Abiathari, Iehosua & aliorum successores dicere poterant, quibus non vulgaris laus in veteri scriptura tribuitur. Cum his apostoli committuntur, imò inter illos sistuntur captiui & rei, quibus illo tempore vix aliquis hominum ordo abiectior erat & contemptior, cum illos nec generis nobilitas, nec successionis amplitudo, nec opum & honorum huius saeculi dignitas commendaret, multos autem infame Crucis supplicium, quod il- lorum magister & institutor Christus perpessus erat, offenderet. Hos tamen illorum victores fuisse exitus tragoediae huius docebit. Nec mirum alicui videri debet, quòd tot tantiq; viri contra veritatis praecones coiuenerint, cum eius rationem nobis non semel euangelistae reddant. Quia enim priuati commodi studio & ambitione seducti doctrinam humanis traditionibus corruperant, & religionem omnem in quaestum commutarant, veritatis lucem sustinere non poterant: cuius odium illos in Christum armarat, & nunc eosdem extimulat, vt contra apostolos tanquam ad commune incendium restinguendum concurrant. Interim nostrae institutioni horum consyderatio seruire debet. Primò enim docemur, neminem hostium Christi potentia & authoritate offendi debere, vt vel illos turpiter metuat, vel praepostera reuerentia se & religionis causam illorum iudicio submittat. Vt enim Deus suos contra omnem mundi potentiam facile tuetur: ita nulla hominum dignitas est, quae Dei verbo praeiu- dicare possit. Vendicant sibi hanc potestatem hodie Rom. pontifices, & vt Conciliorum suorum de- cretis omnes obtemperent, satis pro imperio postulant. Argumenta illorum praecipua sunt, quòd Petri cathedram teneant, quòd successione apostolica commendentur, quòd regum & principum authoritate confirmata sit illorum potestas. Atqui vt haec illis demus, quae tamen falso sibi ipsis tribuunt, omnia ista hic quoq; concurrunt, vt paulò ante diximus. Non tamen ideo illis cedunt apostoli, quia degeneres iam pridem exorbitarant, cum & doctrinam corrupissent, & cultum externum sibi quaestum fecissent, & veritatem aperte persequerentur. Eadem ergo cum sit nostrorum temporum ratio, cur nobis non idem, quod apostolis, liceat? Neq; audiendi sunt, qui sibi nescio quid magni pollicentur ex istorum hominum Concilijs. Non potest arbor mala fructus bonos facere. Et quid boni statuant, qui Dei verbum persequuntur, & de stabilienda tyrannide sua dies noctesq; cogitant? qui denique, suis praeiudicijs nos iam olim damnarunt, nec aliquem habent qui ipsos in ordinem redigat? Veritatem illi oppressam cupiunt, cuius fulgorem ferre non possunt. Illis ergo credant doctrinae & religionis iudicium, quicunq; veritatem proditam volunt. Sed stupenda est nostri seculi caecitas, qua fit, vt multi scientes volentes non religionis modo causam, verumetiam fortunas suas omnes, & patriae communis libertatem, hominum ambitiosorum libidini insatiabili subijciant. Sed quaestionem videre prodest, qua Iudaeorum sacerdotes apostolos in medium producetos agrediuntur. Comprehendunt hanc paucis verbis, vt satis pro imperio loquantur, & inani authoritatis usurpatione ipsos perterrefaciant. Aiunt enim: In qua virtute, & in quo nomine fecistis hoc vos? Habent haec aliquam pietatis & zeli diuini speciem. Hoc enim ex officio interrogare videri volunt, vtpote quorum sit cauere, ne populo vel doctrina peruersa vel falsis signis imponatur. Reuera autem tentandi gratia interrogant, vt ex illorum verbis calumniandi occasionem venentur, quo dolo non II. Quaestio sacer dotalis Cœcilij. non semel contra Christum quoq; vsi fuerunt. Quid enim opus erat de hoc quaerere, cuius rationem in templo tam euidenter apostoli reddiderant? Vel num obliti erant, Christum Iesum propria vir- tute, apostolos vero illius iam pridem ipsius Christi nomine miracula edere coepisse? Non ergo veri- tatem discere cupiunt, sed dolo malo incautos circumuenire studeunt. Similes sunt illorum quaestiones, qui hodie nostros interrogant, vnde nouam doctrinam didicerint, qua authoritate noua dogmata spargant & ecclesiarum reformationem aggrediantur? Atqui iam olim de omnibus istis rationem reddidimus, quam illi ignorare non possunt. Longe alio igitur quam veritatis discenda studio tenentur, nec aliud perinde cupiunt, quam vt ex verbulo aliquo incautius elapso ansam calumniandi apprehendant. Suspecta ergo nobis sint eiusmodi hominum consilia & instituta omnia, & sicut Christus admonuit, serpentina in illis cauendus prudentia vtamur. Nec illorum astutia nos terreri conuenit, quando suum spiritum Christus promisit, cuius suggestione Petrus instructus magna cum animi constantia respondet.
units.tr: The rulers were those to whom the administration of affairs had been entrusted by the Romans, especially those matters which pertained to the Jewish polity, insofar as it differed from other states. The order of elders was the same as that of the senators, as is clear from other passages of Scripture. Scribes were those who claimed for themselves knowledge of the law and of all Scripture, and in whose keeping were the public records and documents. Not content, however, with naming these orders, he also lists certain individuals who were more influential than the rest. He names Annas, who seems here to be called high priest, not because he was then holding the high priesthood (for history shows that Caiaphas already held it), but because he had once been high priest. Likewise Caiaphas; then John and Alexander, to whom he finally adds all the others who were found to be of the high-priestly family. If you look closely at this assembly, it will be clear that nothing more imposing could have been imagined at that time. For there came together men whose power rested on the authority of the Roman governors. There were present those to whom the care of the church had been publicly committed. Nor were lacking those who, by the title of learning and teaching, were to be respected by all. To all these was added the fact that their order was commended both by divine institution and by a succession of more than fifteen hundred years (if you reckon the number of years from the exodus from Egypt, or from the priesthood of Aaron, to the times of Christ and the apostles). And indeed they could say that they were the successors of Aaron, Eleazar, Abiathar, Joshua and others, to whom no ordinary praise is given in the Old Testament. The apostles are handed over to these men; indeed they are brought before them as prisoners and accused. At that time hardly any class of men was more despised and looked down upon. Neither noble birth, nor the length of a line of succession, nor the dignity of wealth and honours of this age commended them, and many were offended by the infamous punishment of the cross, which their master and teacher Christ had suffered. Yet the outcome of this tragedy will show that these men were the victors over their opponents. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that so many great men gathered against the heralds of truth, since the evangelists give us the reason for this more than once. For these men, seduced by the pursuit of private gain and by ambition, had corrupted doctrine with human traditions and had turned all religion into a source of profit. They could not bear the light of truth, and hatred of that light had armed them against Christ; and now it spurs them on to run together against the apostles, as if to put out a common fire. Meanwhile, the consideration of these men ought to serve our instruction. For, first, we are taught that no one should be offended by the power and authority of Christ's enemies, either so as to fear them shamefully, or so as to submit himself and the cause of religion to their judgement through misplaced reverence. For just as God easily defends his own against all the power of the world, so there is no dignity of men which can override the word of God. The Roman pontiffs claim this power for themselves today, and they demand, quite sufficiently for their sovereignty, that all should obey the decrees of their councils. Their chief arguments are that they hold the chair of Peter, that they are commended by apostolic succession, and that their power has been confirmed by the authority of kings and princes. But even if we grant them these things, which they wrongly attribute to themselves, all these things meet in this assembly too, as we said a little earlier. Yet the apostles did not yield to these men because they had long since gone astray and degenerated, having both corrupted doctrine and made external worship a source of gain, and because they openly persecuted the truth. Since, then, the situation of our own times is the same, why should it not be permitted to us what was permitted to the apostles? Nor should we listen to those who promise themselves I know not what great benefit from the councils of such men. A bad tree cannot bear good fruit. And what good will they decide, those who persecute the word of God and think day and night about establishing their tyranny? Those who, finally, have long since condemned us on their own prejudices, and have no one who might bring them into order? They desire the truth to be suppressed, because they cannot bear its brightness. Therefore let those who want the truth revealed trust in them for the judgement of doctrine and religion? No indeed. Yet the blindness of our age is astonishing, by which many, knowingly and willingly, subject not only the cause of religion and all their fortunes, but also the common liberty of their country, to the insatiable lust of ambitious men. But it is worth looking at the question with which the Jewish priests confront the apostles, when they are brought forward into the midst. They express it in a few words, so as to speak with sufficient authority and to frighten the apostles by a vain assumption of authority. For they say: "By what power, and in whose name, have you done this?" These words have some appearance of piety and zeal for God. For they wish to seem to ask this out of duty, since it is their office to take care that the people are not imposed upon either by a perverse doctrine or by false signs. In truth, however, they ask in order to trap him, so that they may hunt for an occasion of slander in his words, by the same deceit which they had more than once used against Christ too. For why was there any need to ask about this, when the apostles had so clearly given the reason for it in the temple? Or had they forgotten that Jesus Christ had begun to work miracles by his own power, and that the apostles had long since begun to perform miracles in the name of Christ himself? Therefore they do not desire to learn the truth, but eagerly seek to ensnare the unwary by wicked deceit. Like these are the questions of those who today interrogate our people: where did they learn the new doctrine, by what authority do they spread new dogmas, and undertake the reformation of the churches? Yet long ago we gave an account of all these things, and those men cannot be ignorant of it. They are therefore held by a purpose far other than the desire to learn the truth, and they desire nothing so much as to seize on some word carelessly slipped out, as an occasion for slander. Therefore such counsels and all the institutions of such men should be suspect to us, and, as Christ has warned, we should use a serpent's prudence in guarding against them. Nor is it fitting for us to be frightened by their cunning, since Christ has promised his Spirit, by whose prompting Peter, instructed, answers with great steadfastness of mind.

units.la: Sunt autem responsiones Petri partes duae: quarum altera quaestioni Iudicum respondet, altera Christum praedicat. Priorem partem admirabili prudentia tractat. Priusquam enim Christum miraculi authorem esse doceat, illorum iniquitatem, & praepositerum iudicium grauiter reprehendit. Inter honore, qui ex Dei mandato magistratibus debetur, illos non defraudat, ne quid ex affectu pro aut linguae petulantia dicere videatur. Sic autem ait: Principes populi & Seniores Israelis: Si nos hodie examinamur de beneficio in hominem infirmum collato, quomodo ille sanatus sit, notum sit vobis omnibus, &c. Sic autem dicere videtur: Mirabamur equidem, qua de causa in carcerem heri abducti simus, & quae nostra culpa sit, in quam tanto studio inquiritis. Cum enim magistratus officium esse constet in maleficos inquirere, nobis autem nullius maleficij conscij essemus, veStrum hoc institutum non potuimus non admirari. At quantum nunc videtur, propter beneficium in hominem miserum collatum, iudicio sistimur. Haec mihi verborum Petri sententia esse videtur. In his vero euidens hostium veritatis typus depingitur, quorum iudicio ij soli peccant, qui Christo vni seruiunt. Quot enim illo tempore Hierosolymis fuisse putas, qui dolis, mendacijs, calumnijs, vsura, rapinis, aperta vi & homicidijs quam plurimos laeserunt? Quot item, qui falsa doctrina, superstitione, blasphemijs & infinitis aliis flagitijs Dei iram prouocabant? At nullus illorum iudicio sistitur. In nullius mores egregij illi censores inquirunt. Imo in illorum consessu non postremum locum obtinet, qui tales erant. Apostoli autem in ius vocantur, in carceres ducuntur, examinantur, qui bucusq; laeserant neminem, profuerant plurimis. Ita hodie vbi veritatis odio flagrat homines, ibi omnibus impune licet malis esse. At Christum praedicare, & illius doctrina hominum mentes a superstitione & idololatria reuocare, hoc demum maximi flagitij loco habetur. Est haec vetus mundi corruptio, quae nunquam a scelerum poenis sibi metuit, sed vos duntaxat abominatur & odit, qui ipsum Deo reconciliare studenti.
units.tr: The replies of Peter are in two parts: the first answers the question of the judges, the second preaches Christ. He handles the first part with admirable prudence. Before teaching that Christ is the author of the miracle, he sharply rebukes their injustice and their perverse judgment. He does not defraud them of the honour that God's command owes to magistrates, so that he may not seem to speak out of passion or wanton tongue. He says: "Rulers of the people and elders of Israel: if we are examined today about the kindness done to a sick man, how he was made well, let it be known to you all, etc." What he seems to say is this: "We were indeed wondering why we have been dragged off to prison yesterday, and what our fault is, which you investigate with such zeal. For since it is the office of the magistrate to inquire into wrongdoers, and we are conscious of no wrongdoing, we cannot but marvel at this proceeding of yours. But it now appears that we are brought before your judgment on account of a kindness done to a wretched man." This, it seems to me, is the sense of Peter's words. In them is portrayed a clear type of the enemies of the truth, whose judgment condemns only those who serve Christ alone. For how many, do you think, were in Jerusalem at that time who had injured very many by deceit, lies, slander, usury, robbery, open violence and murder? And how many who provoked God's wrath by false doctrine, superstition, blasphemies and countless other crimes? Yet none of these is brought before their judgment. Those splendid censors make no inquiry into anyone's morals. Indeed, those who were such men hold no small place in their assembly. But the apostles are summoned to court, led into prison, and examined, though they had harmed no one and had benefited very many. So today, where people burn with hatred of the truth, there everyone is free to do evil with impunity. But to preach Christ, and by his teaching to call men's minds back from superstition and idolatry, this is counted at last the greatest of crimes. This is the old corruption of the world, which never fears the punishments of crimes, but detests and hates only you, who strive to reconcile men to God.

units.la: Postquam vero Petrus iniquitatem horum reprehendit, quaestioni ipsorum euidentius respondet, & miraculi authorem esse testatur vnum Iesum Christum. Notum sit (inquit) vobis omnibus & toti populo Israel, quod in nomine Iesu Christi Nazareni, quem vos crucifixistis, quem Deus excitauit a mortuis, hic stat coram vobis sanus. Idem hic, quod in templo dixerat, repetit. Ita enim vni Christo miraculi gloriam vendicat, vt simul in faciem illis exprobret commissum in filium Dei facinus. Simul vero resurrectionis Christi meminit, vt ipsos fructra cum illo certamen suscepisse doceat, cum morte deuicta nunc gloriose viuat, quem illi sublatum voluerunt. Est autem probe obseruandum Petri exemplum, quo docemur, vt cum professis veritatis hostibus agere conueniat. Honore quidem, quo Deus iudices donare dignatus est, illos (vt modo diximus) non defraudat. Interim ab assentatione ignobili prorsus abstinet: quin potius libere & fortiter ea profert, quae Christi gloriae & veritati asserendae seruiebant. Nam & sceleris illos admonet, & eu viuere & regnare docet, quae illi perseguebantur. Hac via & nobis incedendum est, ne vel linguae petulantiae aliquid permittamus, vel ignauo metu siue fauoris captatione veritate dissimulemus. Vt enim nos indigni sumus, qui maledicentia seculi filios imitemur: ita veritatis hostes nequaquam digni sunt, quorum tyrannidi & sceleribus parcatur. Extant & alia huius generis exempla cum in prophetis tum in apostolis. At consultissimum erit sancti spiritus suggestionem sequi, qui Christi zelo flagrantibus nunquam deerit.
units.tr: But after Peter has rebuked their iniquity, he answers their question more plainly, and declares that the author of the miracle is one man, Jesus Christ. "Let it be known," he says, "to you all and to the whole people of Israel, that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you whole." He repeats here what he had said in the temple. Thus he claims the glory of the miracle for Christ alone, while at the same time he throws in their faces the crime committed against the Son of God. At the same time he mentions the resurrection of Christ, to show that they fought against him in vain, since he now lives gloriously, victorious over death, whom they wished removed. Peter's example is also to be carefully observed, by which we are taught how we ought to deal with professed enemies of the truth. He does not, as we have just said, defraud them of the honour which God has deigned to give to judges. Yet he abstains entirely from base flattery; rather he freely and boldly utters those things which served the glory of Christ and the assertion of the truth. For he both warns them of their crime and teaches that the one they were persecuting lives and reigns. By this way we too must proceed, so that we neither allow ourselves any wantonness of tongue, nor, through cowardly fear or the seeking of favour, dissemble the truth. For just as we are unworthy to imitate the slanderers who are sons of this age, so the enemies of the truth are in no way worthy that their tyranny and crimes should be spared. There are other examples of this kind, both among the prophets and among the apostles. But it will be most prudent to follow the prompting of the Holy Spirit, who never fails those who burn with zeal for Christ.

units.la: Caeterum, quia apostoli in hoc potissimum instituti fuerunt, vt Christum orbi praedicarent, hoc quoque sui officij Petrus minimè obliuiscitur, & ex praecedentibus occasione sumpta, paucis, in vno Christo salutis rationem omnem comprehensam esse docet. At obstabat hic vehementer, quod Christum Iesum ab illis damnatum viderent, qui ex Dei institutione in ecclesia veteri docendi & quaeuis administrandi potestatem habebant. Huic igitur offendiculo primum medetur, Dauidis verba ex Psalmo 118. producens, quibus ipsum Christum quoq; in euangelio vsum fuisse legimus. De seipso enim loquens Dauid, qui simul & Christi typus erat, ait: Lapis, quem reiecerunt aedificantes, factus est caput anguli. Quae verba Petrus de Christo & Iudaeorum sacerdotibus diserte exponens, dicit: Hic est lapis ille, qui reiectus à vobis aedificantibus factus est in caput anguli. Sensus autem verborum est: Scio tum vobis tum alijs mirum videri, quod Christo Iesu tantam laudem & gloriam tribuimus, & illum à mortis resuscitatum viuere & regnare dicimus, quem vos ignominiosa morte sublatum voluistis. At hoc neminem offendere debet. Quin hinc potius discite eum esse Iesum hunc, quem olim prophetae praedixerunt. An vero Dauidicum illud excidit, qui sic à Domino decretum esse docet, vt Messias ab illis ipsis reprobetur, qui ecclesiam Dei aedificare debebant, & illi quosuis adducere? Aedificantes illi vos ipsi estis. Vobis enim commissum est docendi munus & tota religionis administratio. Vos Iesum reiecistis, nec aliquem illi locum concedere dignati estis in templo Domini. Illum vero Deus à mortuis suscitatum, caput anguli fecit, id est, dominum & saluatorem constituit, adeoq; ecclesiae suae principem. Et salutis rationem omnem ita in hoc solo comprehensam esse voluit, vt illa extra hunc nusquam inueniri possit. Nec enim aliud nomen est sub caelo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri. Sic ergo Iesum saluatorem esse praedicat Petrus, vt simul omnem salutis spem illis deneget, quicunq; hunc ampleti dedignantur. Tria autem hic continentur, quorum consideratio non tam vtilis est quam necessaria.
units.tr: Moreover, since the apostles were appointed chiefly for this purpose, that they should preach Christ to the world, Peter does not forget this duty of his, and, taking occasion from what has gone before, briefly teaches that the whole manner of salvation is comprehended in Christ alone. But what stood strongly in the way was that they saw Jesus Christ condemned by those who, by God's appointment in the old Church, had the power of teaching and of administering all things. So he first remedies this stumbling block, by bringing forward the words of David from Psalm 118, by which we read that Christ himself also used them in the gospel. For David, speaking of himself, who was also a type of Christ, says: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Peter, expounding these words plainly of Christ and of the priests of the Jews, says: "This is that stone which was rejected by you builders and has become the head of the corner." The sense of the words is this: "I know that it seems strange to you and to others that we ascribe such great praise and glory to Jesus Christ, and say that he, raised from death, lives and reigns, whom you wished removed by a shameful death. Yet this ought to offend no one. Rather, learn from this that he is the Jesus whom the prophets foretold long ago." Has the Davidic saying then escaped you, which teaches that it has been so decreed by the Lord, that the Messiah should be rejected by those very men who ought to build the Church of God, and to bring others to it? You yourselves are the builders. For the office of teaching and the whole administration of religion has been committed to you. You rejected Jesus, and you did not deign to allow him any place in the temple of the Lord. But God, raising him from the dead, made him the head of the corner, that is, appointed him Lord and Saviour, and so the prince of his Church. And he willed that the whole manner of salvation should be comprehended in him alone, so that it can be found nowhere outside him. For there is no other name under heaven given to men, in which we must be saved. Thus Peter proclaims Jesus as Saviour in such a way that at the same time he denies all hope of salvation to those who disdain to embrace him. Three things are contained here, the consideration of which is not so much useful as necessary.

units.la: Primum, quod Christum ab ijs reijciendum fore spiritus sanctus praedixit, qui ex Dei institutione in illius populo primatum tenebant. Arguit hoc Roman. pontificum impiam superbiam, qui se errare posse negant. Nam licet illos diuinitus institutos esse constaret, hoc tamen illis nunquam concedi posset, cum toties errarint, quorum institutio diuina erat. Sed ita produnt suam impudentiam, dum se errare negant, cum impijs. illorum errores non iam lippis & tonsoribus, verumetiam pueris noti sint. Agnouit iflorum crassam ignorantiam vel potius impudentem mentiendi libidinem Clemens VII. Papa. Cum enim ad illius mensam duo Monachi pro more disputarent, An Papa errare possit? multis vltro citroq; dictis, illum quidem errare posse dixerunt, quatenus homo est: ab omni autem errore alienissimum esse, quatenus papam agat & Christi in terris vicarium. Tunc Clemens impudentissimis hisce & plus quam seruilibus adulationibus offensus non fine stomacho dixit: Imò, quoad Papae munus, me errare posse & frequenter errare fateor. Dum enim sacerdotia & ecclesiasticas dignitates in viros bonos & pios me conferre puto, illos postea nebulones & nullo honore dignos esse comperio. Audiant hoc fui Caiphae oraculum, qui hodie cornutos episcopos ita admirantur, vt scelus esse putent ab illorum decretis latum vnguem discedere. Deinde monet locus hic, ne offendamur, quando Christum à praestantissimis in mundo, imò ab ijs etiam reijci videmus, qui ecclesiae columnae, cardines & capita à plerisq; habentur. Vetus enim hoc in mundo malum est, qui tenebras luci plerunq; praefert. Quod & Isaias conqueritur, quando Christi mysteria explicaturus, paucos fore dicit, qui illi fidem adhibeant & Domini brachium vere agnoscant. Isa.53. Et Christus mysteria haec paruulis reuelata, à sapientibus vero mundi huius abscondita esse testatur. Matth.11. Quid, quod idem publicanos & meretrices ijs in regno Dei praefert, cum quibus in praesenti Petrus disputat? Matth.21. Consoletur autem nos, quod Christo honorem suum saluum & integrum fore scimus, vt vt contra illum infelix mundus saeuiat. De illo enim ab aeterno Deus praedixit: Ego constitui regem meum super Zion montem meum sanctum. Recensebo decretum, Dominus dixit mihi: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Postula à me, dabo gentes, vt sint hereditas tua, &c. Psalm.2.
units.tr: First, that Christ would be rejected by those whom the Holy Spirit foretold, who by God's appointment held the primacy among his people. This is an argument against the impious pride of the Roman pontiffs, who deny that they can err. For although it is plain that they were divinely instituted, this could never be granted to them, since they have so often erred, though their institution was divine. But they betray their own shamelessness when they deny that they err, in the face of the fact that their errors are known not only to the bleary-eyed and the barbers, but even to boys. Clement VII, the Pope, acknowledged their gross ignorance, or rather their shameless lust for lying. For when two monks were disputing at his table, as was their custom, whether the Pope could err, after much had been said on both sides, they said that he could indeed err, insofar as he is a man, but that he was most free from all error, insofar as he acts as Pope and as Christ's vicar on earth. Then Clement, offended by these most shameless and more than servile flatteries, said not without irritation: "Indeed, as far as the papal office is concerned, I confess that I can err, and often do err. For while I think I am conferring priesthoods and ecclesiastical dignities on good and pious men, I afterwards discover that they are scoundrels and worthy of no honour. Let the men who today so admire the horned bishops, as to think it a crime to depart a finger's breadth from their decrees, hear this oracle of Caiaphas." Next, this passage warns us not to be offended when we see Christ rejected even by the most distinguished men in the world, indeed by those too who are commonly regarded as the pillars, hinges and heads of the Church. For this is an old evil in the world: men often prefer darkness to light. Isaiah also complains of this, when he is about to explain the mysteries of Christ, saying that few will give faith to him and truly recognise the arm of the Lord. Isa. 53. And Christ testifies that these mysteries have been revealed to babes, but hidden from the wise of this world. Matt. 11. What of the fact that he also places tax collectors and harlots before those men in the kingdom of God, with whom Peter is now disputing? Matt. 21. But let us be comforted by knowing that the honour of Christ will remain safe and whole, however wretchedly the unhappy world may rage against him. For God foretold of him from eternity: "I have set my king upon Zion, my holy mountain. I will declare the decree: the Lord said to me, You are my son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance, etc." Ps. 2.

units.la: Secundò, Allegoria obseruanda venit, qua ecclesiae antistites aedificantibus fiue architectis conferuntur. Hae enim illos & officij admonet, & omnem illius rationem explicat. Architecti nomen non honoris sed officij est, nec quicquam ab architecto tam alienum esse potest, quam ocium. Illi enim non labores modò ut alijs operarijs, sed totius ædificij cura & solicitudo incumbit. Finis verò illi propositus est, domus ædificatio decora & stabilis. Quem finem ut assequatur, fundamentum iacit solidum, super quod ædificium totum extruit, & ut idem decore absoluatur, curat. Hæc ecclesiarum ministris obseruanda veniunt, quos ad labores & curas vocauit Dominus. Sunt autem architecti domus Dei, quæ est ecclesia, sicut Paulus admonet. 2 Cor. 6. 1. Tim. 3. Ad huius ædificationem omnia conferant, memores, se ad ædificandum, non ad destruendum potestatem accepisse. 2. Corinth. 10. Fundamentum verò non nouum iaciant, sed super illud ædificent, quod à Deo iactum, quodq; prophetarum & apostolorum fundamentum à Paulo nominatur, quod est Iesus Christus. 1. Corinth. 3. Ephes. 2. Hic enim pretiosus ille lapis est in fundamentis Zion collocatus. Isa. 28. Hæc illa petra est, cui nos viuos lapides super ædificari oportet, & cui portæ inferorum non præualebunt. 1. Pet. 2. Matt. 16. Ut autem ab hoc incipiendum ædificium, ita idem illius caput & summus angulus lapis est. In hoc enim nostra perfectio habetur, & hic duos populos, gentes nimirum & Iudæos, in vnum ecclesiæ corpus (ut duos parietes angulares lapis) connectit. Ephes. 2. Idem se huius domus ostium quoq; profitetur. Iohan. 10. Idem verus ille paterfamilias est, qui domus curam ministris commisit, ab ijsdem olim administrationis suæ rationem requisituros. Matth. 24. & 25. In hunc ergo ministri omnes respiciant, & curent ne fœnum aut stipulam ædificio isti admisceant, in quo nullus humanis traditionibus locus est. Matth. 15. Quotquot ergo hic fallunt, cum Iudæis, male fidei architectis, Christum reijciunt, in quem impingentes, sibijpsis malum consciscent. Ad quam regulam si examinentur, qui hodie architecti ecclesiæ haberi volunt, facile patebit quales censeri debeant.
units.tr: Second, the allegory of builders must be observed, by which the bishops of the Church are compared with those who build or with architects. For it reminds them of their office and sets out the whole of their task. "Architect" is a name not of honour but of duty, and nothing is further from an architect than idleness. For he is burdened not only with labour, as the other workmen are, but with the care and concern for the whole building. The end set before him is a building that is handsome and stable. To attain this end he lays a solid foundation, on which he erects the whole structure, and he takes care that it is finished in good order. These things are to be observed by the ministers of the churches, whom the Lord has called to labour and care. They are the builders of the house of God, which is the Church, as Paul reminds us (2 Cor. 6; 1 Tim. 3). They should all contribute to its building, mindful that they have received power to build up and not to destroy (2 Cor. 10). Nor should they lay a new foundation, but build upon that one which God has laid, which Paul calls the foundation of the apostles and prophets, namely Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 3; Eph. 2). For this is that precious stone laid in the foundations of Zion (Isa. 28). This is the rock on which we, as living stones, ought to be built, and against which the gates of hell shall not prevail (1 Pet. 2; Matt. 16). As the building begins with him, so he is also its head and chief corner stone. In him our perfection is found, and he joins the two peoples, namely the Gentiles and the Jews, into one body of the Church, as a corner stone joins two walls (Eph. 2). He also declares himself to be the door of this house (John 10). He is the true householder who committed the care of the house to the ministers, and of whom they will one day have to give an account of their stewardship (Matt. 24 and 25). Let all ministers, then, look to him, and take care not to mix hay or straw into this building, in which there is no place for human traditions (Matt. 15). Therefore, whoever deceives here, like the Jews, bad builders of faith, rejects Christ, and by stumbling against him brings ruin upon themselves. If those who today wish to be considered architects of the Church are examined by this rule, it will easily be seen what sort of men they ought to be counted.

units.la: Postremò imis animis recondi debet præcipuum hoc Christianæ fidei principium, quo vni & soli Christo omnem nostræ redemptionis & salutis gloriam Petrus transcribit, dicens: Non est in vllo alio salus. Id verò Dei decreto probat, cum subijcit: Nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos saluos fieri. Vt enim in rerum natura vnam quamq; rem ijs medijs confici oportet, quæ Deus illi destinata esse voluit: ita salute alijs medijs acquiri impossibile fuit, quàm Christi merito, quem Deus (qui vnicus salutis humanæ author est) ab æterno ad hoc negotium præordinauit. 1. Pet. 2. Et quia Dei decretum inuiolabile esse constat, vnum hoc ad huius dogmatis assertionem abunde sufficere putauit Petrus, cui alioqui non deerant infinita scripturæ loca, quibus hoc probari poterat. Etenim saluatorem agere nemo potest, nisi peccata tollere, mortem vincere, apud Deum pro nobis intercedere, iustitiam & vitam in se credentibus conferre possit. Hæc autem in solius Christi manu esse, omnis scriptura docet, & ipse apud prophetam clamat: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Et de hoc vno Deus pater cœlitus testari voluit: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui. Matth. 3. & 17. De hoc olim per prophetam pronuntiauit: Ecce seruus meus, quo nitar: electus meus, quo placatur anima mea, &c. Isa. 42. In hoc data nobis veritas & gratia. Iohan. 1. In eodem omnes scientiæ, sapientiæ & bonitatis diuinæ thesauri aperti sunt. Col. 1. & 2. Hic nobis à Deo factus est sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, redemptio & sanctificatio. 1. Cor. 1. Hic esuirientibus panis vitæ, & sitientibus fons aquæ viuentis est. Iohan. 4. 6. & 7. Hic laborantibus & oneratis refocillationem pollicetur & præstat. Matth. 11. Vnus hic via est, quam qui non ingreditur, ad patrem venire nequit. Iohan. 14. Hic agnus ille Dei est, mactatus ab origine mundi, cuius merito & veteres Dei cultores saluati sunt, & saluabuntur quotquot in illum credent vsq; in consummationem seculi. In hoc denique nos Paulus electos esse testatur, priusquam mundi fundamenta iacerentur. Ephes. 1. Confutantur igitur hoc loco omnes aliæ religiones, quæ noua salutis media extra Christum monstrant. Hoc ariete gentilium idololatria, Iudæorum legalis iustitia, pharisæorum gloriatio & hypocrisis, papatus cum toto indulgentiarum & meritorum foro, & totum illud Monasticorum ordinum chaos, conuellitur, disijcitur, euertitur & prosternitur. Quicquid enim extra Iesum est, saluare nunquam poterit. Non nos ergo, sed Petrum hæreseos damnant, qui ideo nos excommunicant hodie, quòd vno Iesu saluatore nitamur, contemptis ijs, quæ hominum superstitio peperit. Sed facile illorum iudicia contemnimus, qui ex Petro discimus, non mirum esse, si lapidem hunc pretiosum architecti plerique abijciant. Illum verò ampletimur constanti fide, extra quem salus nulla est, & qui omnibus in se credentibus salutem vitamq; promisit æternam. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, this chief principle of the Christian faith must be stored deep in our hearts, by which Peter ascribes all the glory of our redemption and salvation to Christ alone, saying: "There is salvation in no one else" (Acts 4). He proves this by God's decree, when he adds: "For there is no other name under heaven given to men, by which we must be saved." For just as in the order of nature each thing must be accomplished by those means which God has willed to be appointed for it, so salvation could not be obtained by other means than by the merit of Christ, whom God, the only author of human salvation, predestined from eternity for this task (1 Pet. 2). And since it is certain that God's decree is inviolable, Peter thought that this one point was enough to establish this doctrine, although there were, besides, countless passages of Scripture by which it could have been proved. For no one can act as Saviour unless he can take away sins, overcome death, intercede with God on our behalf, and bestow righteousness and life on those who believe in him. Now all Scripture teaches that these things lie in the hand of Christ alone, and he himself cries out through the prophet: "I am the Lord, that is my name, and I will not give my glory to another" (Isa. 42). And of this one alone God the Father wished to bear witness from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3 and 17). Of him God once declared through the prophet: "Behold my servant, in whom I trust; my chosen one, in whom my soul delights," etc. (Isa. 42). In him truth and grace have been given to us (John 1). In him are all the treasures of divine knowledge, wisdom and goodness opened up (Col. 1 and 2). He has been made by God our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. 1). To the hungry he is the bread of life, and to the thirsty the fountain of living water (John 4, 6 and 7). To those who labour and are burdened he promises and gives refreshment (Matt. 11). He alone is the way, and whoever does not enter by him cannot come to the Father (John 14). He is that Lamb of God, slain from the foundation of the world, by whose merit the ancient worshippers of God were saved, and will be saved, as many as believe in him to the end of the age (Rev. 13). Finally, Paul bears witness that we have been chosen in him before the foundations of the world were laid (Eph. 1). Therefore, at this point all other religions which show new means of salvation outside Christ are refuted. By this battering ram the idolatry of the Gentiles, the legal righteousness of the Jews, the boasting and hypocrisy of the Pharisees, the papacy with its whole market of indulgences and merits, and that whole chaos of monastic orders are shaken, broken, overturned and thrown down. For whatever is outside Jesus can never save. Therefore it is not we, but Peter, whom they condemn as a heretic, those who today excommunicate us because we rest on the one Saviour Jesus, having despised those things which human superstition has produced. But we easily despise the judgements of those who learn from Peter that it is no wonder if many architects cast away this precious stone. We embrace him with steadfast faith, apart from whom there is no salvation, and who has promised eternal salvation and life to all who believe in him. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXVIII.
units.tr: Homily 28.

units.la: Videntes autem Petri in dicendo libertatē & Iohannis, & reputan-tes quòd homines essent illiterati & idiotæ, mirabantur & agnoscebant eos quòd cum Iesu fuissent. Hominem verò videntes ipsis astantem, qui sanatus fuerat, nihil habebant quod contradicerent. Iussis autem illis ex concilio secedere, conferebant inter se, dicentes: Quid faciemus hominibus istis? Nam conspicuum signum editum esse per eos, omnibus incolis Hierosolymæ manifestum est: nec possumus negare. Sed ne amplius diuulgetur ad populum, minando minemur illis, ne cui hominum post hac loquantur in hoc nomine. Tunc vocatis ipsis, præceperunt, ne omnino loquerentur, neue docerent in nomine Iesu.
units.tr: When they saw the boldness of Peter and John in speaking, and understood that they were uneducated and common men, they were amazed and recognised that they had been with Jesus. Seeing the healed man standing beside them, they had nothing to say in reply. But when they had ordered them to withdraw from the council, they conferred among themselves, saying: "What shall we do with these men? For it is plain to all who live in Jerusalem that a notable sign has been done through them, and we cannot deny it. But so that it may spread no further among the people, let us threaten them, so that they speak to no one in this name from now on." Then they called them in and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

units.la: Dluus Petrus quæstioni, in Concilio Hierosolymitano sibi & Iohanni ob claudum sanatum propositæ ita respondet, vt non modò quod ipsi quærebant doceat, verumetiam vniuersam salutis rationem, breui compendio comprehensam illis exponat. Docemur eo exemplo, cum professis quod veritatis hostibus ita agendum esse, vt illos Christo & saluti lucrifacere studeamus. Quem finem ipsi Christo etiam, quotiescunque illi cum aduersarijs dimicadum fuit, propositum fuisse constat. Sed videamus modò, quis responsionis Petri effectus fuerit, qui in tanta dicendi vehementia ac præsenti spiritus sancti operatione, non potuit vulgaris esse. Vbi mira se profert animorum confusio, quæ vt euidentior esset, ita à Luca describitur, vt primò quidem quomodo animis suis affecti fuerint, deinde quid de iis consilij ceperint, exponat. Quæ & nos singula ordine consyderabimus.
units.tr: Saint Peter, in answer to the question put to him and John in the council at Jerusalem about the lame man who had been healed, does not only address what they were asking, but sets out for them, in a short summary, the whole method of salvation. From this example we are taught that when we deal with enemies of the truth we must act so as to win them for Christ and for salvation. It is clear that Christ himself had this aim whenever he had to contend with his adversaries. But let us now see what effect Peter's answer had, which, given such vehemence in speaking and the present working of the Holy Spirit, could not have been ordinary. Here a remarkable confusion of minds appears, and so that it may be more evident, Luke describes it, first setting out how they were affected in their minds and then what plans they made. We shall consider each of these in order.

units.la: Primò quidem admiratione & stupore replentur, ac consiliorum incerti fiunt, adeo vt non habeant quod contradicere possint. At ne quis illos vel ingenita mentis inopia laborauisse, vel panico quodam terrore perculsos putaret, causa indicantur, quæ tam perplexos in suis consilijs reddiderint. Prima apostolorum in dicendo libertas siue fiducia est, quam vtiq; inexpectatam audiunt. Sciebant enim homines esse illiteratos & idiotas, qui præter vernaculam linguam artes nullas didicissent. Nouerant illos à repisicatoria inter Christi discipulos fuisse adoptatos. Et nimirum nunc quoque illorum mentes vetus illa opinio dementabat, quam olim dixerant, neminem ex pharisæorum aut scribarum numero, sed execrabile vulgus & plebeios homines, legis & scripturæ ignaros, Christi partes tueri. Iohan. 7. Facilem ergo sibi de apostolis victoriam polliciti, non possunt nō obstupescere, vbi illos ad quæstionem propositam tam cordate respondere, iniustitiam illorum tam fortiter arguere, & Christi causam tanta prudentia & constantia tueri audiunt. Coguntur enim, velint nolint, diuinum quiddam in illis agnoscere, illosque longè alia quàm carnis prudentia regi vident. Atqui hæc potissima causa est, propter quam rudes & illiteratos apostolos eligere Christus voluit, vt euangelij doctrina non hominum sapientia, facundia vel authoritate, sed diuina virtute propagata esse agnosceretur, ac omnis illius laus siue gloria vni Deo cederet, quia de re multis Paulus disputat. 1. Corinth. 1. cap. Altera fluporis causa est euidens signi, per apostolos editi, veritas, quam nec in dubium vocare, nec aliqua magiæ siue incantationis suspicione aggrauare possunt. Coràm enim astare vident hominem, cui salutis beneficium contulerant, siue ille ab ipsis vocatus sit, siue sponte apostolis sese coniunxerit, cum illis omnem rei euentum communem habiturus. Harent itaq; animis, nec verbulo quidem respondere possunt. Turpissimè ergo victi & confusi sunt, qui vnius quæstionis obiectione apostolos vinci & capi posse sperauerant. Hic autem impletur, quod Christus promiserat, dicens: Dabo vobis os & sapientiam, cui non poterunt contradicere, neque resistere omnes, qui aduersabuntur vobis. Luc. 21. Simul verò patet quàm vana sint hominum contra Christum consilia. Nouit is illorum cogitationes vanas esse, & gentium consilia dissipat, ipsius verò consilium in æternū stabit, sicut Dauid admonet. Psal. 94. & 33. Vere etenim is est, qui (vt Eliphaz Themanites ait) cogitationes callidorum irritas facit, vt nihil solidi efficiant manus eorum. Et capit sapientes in ipsorum calliditate, & consilium versutorum subuertitur. Iob. 5. Exemplum eiusdem generis euangelica historia exhibet de cæco per Christum illuminato, qui & illiteratus & mendicus totum sacerdotum & scribarum Concilium mirifice exagitat, vt quò magis instant quærendo, eò magis sese ridiculos præbeant. Iohan. 9. Ne-mo mo igitur hostium siue potentia siue calliditate terreatur, cum vtranq; tam facile subuertat dominus. Nec enim nostra causa est, quam agimus, sed Dei, qui os & linguam suppeditat: nec nos sumus loquentes, sed spiritus patris nostri, qui in nobis est. Matth. 10. At priusquam hinc discedamus, de duobus obseruatu dignissimis, pauca dicenda sunt.
units.tr: First, they are filled with wonder and astonishment, and become uncertain of their plans, so that they have nothing to say in reply. But lest anyone think they were suffering from some natural weakness of mind, or were struck by a kind of panic, the causes are indicated which made them so perplexed in their deliberations.
