The first is the apostles' freedom, or confidence, in speaking, which they plainly did not expect to hear. For they knew that these men were uneducated and common, who had learned no skills apart from their native tongue. They knew that they had been taken from the fishing trade to be disciples of Christ. And certainly now also that old opinion, which they had once voiced, that none of the Pharisees or scribes, but the despised crowd and common people, ignorant of the law and Scripture, defended the cause of Christ, was confusing their minds (John 7). So, having promised themselves an easy victory over the apostles, they cannot help being astonished when they hear them answer the question put to them so wisely, argue so boldly against their injustice, and defend the cause of Christ with such prudence and constancy. For they are compelled, whether they like it or not, to recognise something divine in them, and they see that the apostles are governed by something quite other than worldly wisdom. Indeed this is the chief reason why Christ chose uneducated and unlettered apostols, so that the teaching of the gospel would be seen to have spread not by human wisdom, eloquence or authority, but by divine power, and so that all its praise and glory would belong to God alone. Paul discusses this at length (1 Corinthians 1). The second cause of their amazement is the plain truth of the sign done through the apostles, which they can neither call into doubt nor burden with any suspicion of magic or enchantment. For they see before them the man to whom they had brought the benefit of healing, whether he had been called by them or had joined the apostles of his own accord, to share in whatever came of the affair. So they are stuck in their minds, and cannot answer even a word. Therefore those who had hoped to defeat and seize the apostles by objecting to a single question were shamefully beaten and confused. Here what Christ had promised is fulfilled, when he said: "I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all who oppose you will not be able to contradict or resist" (Luke 21). At the same time it is evident how vain the plans of men against Christ are. He knows that their thoughts are empty, and he scatters the counsels of the nations, but his own counsel will stand for ever, as David reminds us (Psalms 94 and 33). Indeed he is truly the one who (as Eliphaz the Temanite says) makes void the thoughts of the crafty, so that their hands achieve nothing sound. He takes the wise in their own craftiness, and the counsel of the crafty is overturned (Job 5). The gospel history provides an example of the same kind in the blind man illumined by Christ, who, though uneducated and a beggar, wonderfully harassed the whole council of priests and scribes, so that the more they pressed their questions, the more ridiculous they made themselves (John 9). Let no one, therefore, be terrified by the power or cunning of enemies, since the Lord overturns both so easily. For the cause we are pleading is not ours but God's, who supplies the mouth and the tongue; nor are we the speakers, but the Spirit of our Father who is in us (Matthew 10). But before we leave here, two points most worthy of notice must be briefly discussed.

units.la: Primo nontemere fit, quòd dicendi fiducia & libertate, qua apostoli vtebantur, impios Christi hostes attonitos & confusos fuisse scribit Lucas. Eo enim exemplo docemur nihil ad coercendum impios tam efficax esse, quàm ingenuam dicendi libertatem, qua in faciem redarguuntur, & veritatis causa, cui illi se opponunt, forti constantia asseritur. Nam ea verborum vis est, vt animos facile penetrent. Quòd si vero ijsdem diuina veritatis & gloriae Dei zelus accedat, fieri nequit, quin auditorum conscientiae feriantur, vtcunq; illud interdum dissimulent. Quò fit, vt si non semper veram poenitentiam agant, plerunq; tamen se poenitere simulent, & à malefaciendo abstineant. Cuius rei exemplum euidens in Achabo cernitur, postquam indignam Nabothi caedem propherica libertate ipsi Elias exprobrauit. 1. Regum 21. cap. Rursum vbi linguis frenum iniici patiuntur verbi ministri, vel ipsi sibi silentium imponunt, vt mundo placeant, mox impijs animos addi videmus, qui in omnem peccandi licentiam erumpendo, mensuram iniquitatis complent, tandemq; cum caecis suis speculatoribus & canibus mutis infelicissimis pereunt. Vide Ezech. 3. & 33. cap. Quae causa est, quòd arguendi libertas passim à verbi ministris exigitur. Isaiae dicit dominus: Clama ex gutture, ne parcas, exaltain star tubae vocem tuam, & annuntia populo meo praeuaricationem suam, & domui Iacob peccata sua. Isa. 58. Et Ieremiam contra sacerdotes, populum, principes & reges intrepidum a benemuri instar stare iubet idem dominus. Ierem. 1. Idèo & Paulus eos qui peccauerunt, coram omnibus vult argui, vt & caeteri timorem habeant. 1. Timot. 5. Imò cum in vinculis agens se causam, quam ecclesiae precibus commendat, Vigilate (inquit) cum omni sedulitate & precatione pro omnibus sanctis, & pro me, vt mihi detur sermo in apertione oris mei, cum libertate, vt notum faciam mysterium euangelij, super quo legatione fungor in catena, vt in eo libere loquar, sicut oportet me loqui. Ephes. 6. cap. Nunquam ergo dicendi liberam fiduciam sibi eripi patiantur ministri, pro qua tantum apostolum tam solicitum fuisse videmus.
units.tr: First, it is not without reason that Luke writes that the impious enemies of Christ were astonished and confused by the confidence and freedom in speaking which the apostles used. For from this example we are taught that nothing is so effective in restraining the impious as free and open speech, by which they are rebuked to their faces and the cause of the truth, against which they set themselves, is asserted with brave constancy. For such words have the power to pierce minds easily. And if the zeal for divine truth and for the glory of God is added to them, it cannot be but that the consciences of the hearers are struck, however much they sometimes pretend otherwise. Hence, if they do not always repent in earnest, they often at least pretend to repent, and they refrain from doing evil. A clear example of this is seen in Ahab, after Elijah rebuked him with prophetic freedom for the unworthy murder of Naboth (1 Kings 21). Again, when ministers of the Word suffer their tongues to be bridled, or impose silence on themselves in order to please the world, we soon see impious minds emboldened, who, breaking out into every licence to sin, fill up the measure of their iniquity, and at last perish with their blind watchmen and dumb dogs, most unhappily (see Ezekiel 3 and 33). This is why freedom to rebuke is everywhere demanded from ministers of the Word. The Lord says to Isaiah: "Cry aloud, do not spare; lift up your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their transgression, and to the house of Jacob their sins" (Isaiah 58). And the same Lord bids Jeremiah stand fearless against the priests, the people, the princes and the kings, like a bronze wall (Jeremiah 1). Therefore Paul also wants those who have sinned to be rebuked before all, so that the others may also have fear (1 Timothy 5). Indeed, when he was in chains and commended his own cause to the prayers of the Church, he said: "Watch with all diligence and prayer for all the saints, and for me, that speech may be given to me when I open my mouth, with freedom, to make known the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that I may speak freely in it, as I ought to speak" (Ephesians 6). Ministers should never allow the free confidence in speaking to be taken from them, which we see the apostle so anxious to keep.

units.la: Deinde non oscitanter obseruari decet, quòd claudum sanatum apostolis, cùm causam banc ageret, afflixisse, & proinde cum ijsdem periclitatum fuisse scribit. Admonet hoc quae sanctorum in hoc mundo fors sit & conditio. Vt primum illi salutis beneficium à Christo recipiunt, periculis & minis impiorum obijci solent. Ita Lazarus per Christum resuscitatus, praesens periculum sibi imminere sentit, dum ipsum vnà cum Christo interfectum volunt Iudaeorum sacerdotes. Iohan. 12. Vt enim gloriae Christi fulgorem extinctum cupiunt impij: ita nec illos ferre possunt, per quos illum excitari & augeri vident. Est hoc non vulgari diligentia obseruandum, ne dum salutem aeternam nobis Christus offert, nos felicitatem huius saeculi & mundi amicitiam nobis promittamus, & ipse falsa inescati postea cruce ex improuiso nobis incidente offendamur: quod hodie multis non sine salutis periculo accidere videmus. Simul verò gratitudinis & fortitudinis Christianae exemplum est claudus hic, dum benefactores suos in periculo non deserit, sed illorum causam pro virili adiuuat. Atqui multae rationes erant, quibus seipsum excusare, & recepti per apostolos beneficij veniā à principibus petere poterat. At nihil tale de illo legitur. Arguuntur illius exemplo, qui salutis quidem beneficium à Christo recipere cupiunt, sed cum eodem pericula & crucem subire nolunt. Ex quorum numero sunt, qui quacunque salutis rationem in Christo comprehensam explicant, praedicari volunt, ea verò adijci non patiuntur, quae idem Christus contra Antichristos & seductores pronuntiauit, eò quòd illis plerosq; in mundo offendi vident. Quorum similes sunt, qui salutis doctrinā à ministris nuntiatā auidè arripiunt, sed errorum laqueis liberatos gaudent. At vbi mundum contra ministros furere & fremere vident, omne illis opem & patrocinium denegant, imò illorum conspectum subterfugiunt, ne ipsis fauere videantur. Plenus hodie talium hominum mundus est, & optimi haberi possunt, qui non aperte ministros Christi periclitantes calumnijs & conuitijs proscindunt, adeoq; in cruce suspensis acerum propinant. At meminerint illi, Christum diuidi non posse, & nobis aut illo in vniuersum cardendum, aut tale recipiendam esse, qualis à patre datus est. Crucifixum verò scripturae proponunt, & illum per Crucem in patris gloriam transiuisse docent. Talem & nos amplectamur, & eadem via ad cœlestem gloriam tendamus, oportet. Ad crucem ferendam suos inuitat, nec illis melior em in mundo fortem pollicetur, quàm quæ illi in mundo obtigit. Matth. 16. Ioan. 15. & 16. Idem discipulos & seruos ferre nequit, quos sui pudet coram mundo hoc prauo, adultero & degenere. Marc. 8. Christiana igitur fortitudine, iuxta claudi exemplum armemur, & cum Paulo singuli dicamus: Non me pudet euangelij Christi. Nam potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti. Rom. 1.
units.tr: Second, we should observe carefully that Luke writes that the healed lame man afflicted the apostles while they were pleading this cause, and so was in danger together with them. This reminds us what the lot and condition of the saints in this world is. As soon as they receive the benefit of salvation from Christ, they are usually exposed to the dangers and threats of the impious. So Lazarus, raised up by Christ, feels the danger hanging over him, when the priests of the Jews wanted him killed together with Christ (John 12). For just as the impious wish the brightness of Christ's glory extinguished, so they cannot bear those through whom they see it raised up and increased. This must be noted with no ordinary care: lest, while Christ offers us eternal salvation, we promise ourselves the happiness of this age and friendship with the world, and then, deceived by false bait, we are struck down when the cross falls on us unexpectedly. We see this happening to many today, not without danger to their salvation. At the same time this lame man is an example of gratitude and Christian courage, since he does not desert his benefactors in danger, but helps their cause as far as he can. Yet there were many reasons by which he could have excused himself, and sought pardon from the rulers for the benefit he had received through the apostles. But nothing of the kind is read of him. He is set as a rebuke to those who wish to receive the benefit of salvation from Christ, but are unwilling to undergo dangers and the cross with him. Among them are those who expound whatever account of salvation is contained in Christ and wish it preached, but do not allow those things to be added which Christ himself pronounced against antichrists and seducers, because they see that many in the world would be offended by them. Like them are those who eagerly seize the teaching of salvation announced by ministers, and rejoice in being freed from the snares of error; but when they see the world raging and fuming against the ministers, they deny them all help and protection, and indeed flee from their sight, lest they seem to favour them. Today the world is full of such people, and they may be thought the best, who do not openly tear apart with slanders and insults the ministers of Christ who are in danger, and thus offer vinegar to those hanging on the cross. But let them remember that Christ cannot be divided, and that we must either cling to him entirely, or receive him as the Father gave him. They set before us the crucified One in the Scriptures, and teach that through the cross he passed into the Father's glory. We too must embrace him in this way, and by the same road we must strive for heavenly glory. He invites his own to bear the cross, and promises them no better lot in the world than he himself had in the world (Matthew 16; John 15 and 16). He cannot endure as disciples and servants those who are ashamed of him before this wicked, adulterous and degenerate world (Mark 8). Let us therefore arm ourselves with Christian courage, following the example of the lame man, and let each of us say with Paul: "I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes" (Romans 1).

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua Concilij decretum contra apostolos contine-tur. Nam illis secedere iußis, inter se consultare cœperunt: vbi mira animorum perturbatio & incerta consiliorum confusio cernitur. Primò, Quid faciemus (aiunt) hominibus istis? O inepta & praeposteram quæstionem. Num vero ignorabant, innocentes dimitti debere, & eos qui beneficium dederant, remuneratione dignos esse? Sed hoc modo deuotam animi malitiam produnt, qua sibi occasionem dari vellent in innocentes & beneficos sæuiendi. Sed vlterius progressi, magis seipsos produnt, dum miraculi veritatem confitentur, dicentes: Conspicuum signum per eos editum esse, omnibus incolis Hierosolymis manifestum est, nec id possumus negare. Imp'i ergo, quòd in signi authorem, Iesum Christum, adhuc conspirant. Simul vero, quid ipsos maximè vrgeat, fatentur. Nullam enim vel Dei ipsius vel Christi mentionem faciunt: sed populo rem hanc innotuisse conqueruntur. Maiorem ergo populi quàm Dei respectum habent, vt potè qui toti ab inani imperitia & superstitiose plebis existimatione dependerent, nec vllam haberent diuinae gloriae rationem, quam incurabilis ipsorum incredulitatis præcipuam causam esse, Christus alibi dixerat. Iohan. 5. Tandem vero concludunt quid fieri debeat. Quod factum est, infectum fieri nequit. At quia ex populi defectione periculum imminere videbatur, obstandum putant, ne huius rei fama amplius vulgetur. Ita enim ἀμνησία & oblivione omnem Christi memoriam obliterari posse confidunt. Illud vero minis & tyrannide confictre studeant, cum rationibus se destitutos videant. Minaciter interminentur illis (inquiunt) ne cui bominum possit hac loquantur in hoc nomine. Et mox accersitis apostolis, magna verborum grauitate, egregium hoc sacrosancte (si diis placet) Synodi decretum denuntiant. Quid vero hic primum admirabimur, imò detestabimur o fratres? Impudentiam ne & impiam tyrannidem, aut stupendam hominum stultitiam? Miraculum se negare non posse palam fatentur, & tamen illud obliteratum volunt. Et quod in ore erat omni populo, ab apostolis prædicari prohibent. Adhæc cum Christo certamen suscipiunt, quem ne mortuum quidem & sepultum armata militum cohorte & Romani præsidii authoritate, qui sepulchri lapidem obsignauerat, in sepulchro retinere potuerunt. Nunc vero viuentis & regnantis gloriam inanibus minis reprimi & extingui posse putant flolidissimi homines.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the other part of this passage, in which the decree of the Council against the apostles is contained. For when the apostles had been ordered to withdraw, they began to consult among themselves, and there is seen a remarkable disturbance of minds and a confused uncertainty of plans. First, they say: "What shall we do with these men?" O foolish and absurd question! Did they really not know that innocent people ought to be released, and that those who had conferred a benefit deserved a reward? But in this way they reveal the devoted malice of their minds, by which they wished an occasion to be given them of raging against the innocent and the beneficent. Going further, however, they reveal themselves more, while they confess the truth of the miracle, saying: "That a notable sign has been done through them is manifest to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it." Therefore they are impious, because they still conspire against Jesus Christ, the author of the sign. At the same time, they admit what most of all presses upon them. For they make no mention of God himself or of Christ, but complain that the matter has become known to the people. They have, therefore, more regard for the people than for God, since they wholly depended on the empty ignorance and superstitious opinion of the common folk, and had no consideration of the divine glory, which Christ had elsewhere said was the chief cause of their incurable unbelief. John 5. Finally they conclude what ought to be done. What has been done cannot be undone. But because a danger from the defection of the people seemed to threaten, they think it must be opposed, lest the report of this matter be spread any further. For they trust that by forgetfulness and oblivion (ἀμνησία) all memory of Christ can be wiped out. Yet they strive to achieve this by threats and tyranny, since they see themselves left without arguments. "Let them threaten us," they say, "that they will speak to no man in this name." And soon, having summoned the apostles, with great solemnity of words they announce this remarkable decree of the most sacred Council (if it pleases the gods). But what here shall we first marvel at, or rather detest, brothers? Their impudence and impious tyranny, or the amazing stupidity of men? They openly confess that they cannot deny the miracle, and yet they want it to be obliterated. And what was on the lips of every people, they forbid to be preached by the apostles. Moreover, they take up a contest with Christ, whom, though dead and buried, they could not keep in the sepulchre with an armed cohort of soldiers and the authority of a Roman garrison, which had sealed the stone of the tomb. Now, however, the most foolish of men think that the glory of the living and reigning one can be repressed and extinguished by empty threats.

units.la: Obseruemus hic, quorsum abducat deuota mentis impietas & semel conceptum veritatis odium. Hi ne tunc quidem quiescere possunt, quo minus contra Dei consilium pugnent, vbi propria conscientiae testimonio se conuictos esse sentiunt. Verè enim impijs non est pax, vt propheta ait, & instar Eripi fremit illorum animus, affectuum æstu turbidus. Isa. 48. & 57. Exempla huius passim extant, & hodie plurima visuntur. Quis enim ignorat, eousque penetrauisse veritatis lucem nostro seculo, vt Pontifices quoq; graues in sua ecclesia abusus esse, non semel confessi sint? Norunt item de religionis causa iam non doctos modo, verumetiam artifices manuarios, nautas, aurigas, rusticos, pueros deniq; & mulierculas disputare & iudicare posse. Vident se passim ministrorum verbi concionibus argui, vulgi dicterijs derideri, canticis publicis accusari, pictura & hieroglyphicis omnis generis ad viuum exprimi. Adhuc tamen sibi omnem in ecclesia iudicandi authoritatem vendicant. Adhuc se errare posse negant, obliti nimirum, quòd abusus in Romanam ecclesiam multos irrepsisse, saepius confessi sunt. Adhuc ministros silentium mandare audent, cum non ignorent, ipsis tacentibus lapides concionaturos esse, quod iam annis aliquot in Pasquillo suo experti sunt. Adhuc bullarum suarum crepitus & inania e pelui fulgura tanti momenti esse putant, vt regnantis Christi veritas ijs opprimi possit. O caecos & stultos, qui lucem tantam non vident. O impios, qui in totius mundi theatro θεομαχεῖν non verentur. Sed experientur olim quàm infelix sit illorum exitus, qui Saulis instar Dauidem regnare nolunt, & cum Iudaeorum Pontificibus Dauidis filium, Iesum Christum, ecclesiae suae regno exturbare conantur. Vide Psal. 2.
units.tr: Let us observe here whither the devoted impiety of the mind and a hatred of the truth once conceived lead. These men cannot even then be quiet, so as not to fight against God's counsel, when they feel themselves convicted by the testimony of their own conscience. For truly, as the prophet says, "there is no peace for the wicked," and their mind rages like a fierce wave, turbid with the heat of their passions. Isa. 48. and 57. Examples of this are found everywhere, and very many are seen today. For who does not know that the light of truth has penetrated so far in our age that even the grave Pontiffs have more than once confessed that there were serious abuses in their Church? They also know that not only the learned but even manual craftsmen, sailors, charioteers, peasants, boys and little women can dispute and judge about religion. They see themselves everywhere refuted by the sermons of the ministers of the Word, mocked by the jests of the common people, accused in public songs, and portrayed to the life in pictures and hieroglyphs of every kind. Yet still they claim for themselves all authority to judge in the Church. Still they deny that they can err, plainly forgetting that they have more than once confessed that many abuses have crept into the Roman Church. Still they dare to order the ministers to be silent, although they are not unaware that, even if they themselves keep silent, stones will preach, as for some years now they have experienced in their Pasquil. Still they think that the rattling of their bulls and the empty lightnings from their chamber pot are of such importance that the truth of the reigning Christ can be crushed by them. O blind and foolish men, who do not see so great a light! O impious men, who do not fear to fight against God in the theatre of the whole world! But they will one day experience how unhappy is the end of those who, like Saul, are unwilling that David should reign, and who, with the high priests of the Jews, try to thrust David's son, Jesus Christ, out of the kingdom of his Church. See Ps. 2.

units.la: Praeterea horum exemplo admonemur, quàm noxium sit, dominium & regnum ecclesiae hominibus religione & Dei metu vacuis committere. Nulla in illis sapientia esse potest, cùm illius prin-cipum cipium (Solomone teste) sit timor domini. Prouerb.1. &c. Omni ergo rationis repagulo perrupto in caecam affectuum licentiam effunduntur, & tunc demum se magistratu probe functos exist imant, si omnibus testatum fecerint, quod nulla vel legum authoritate vel religionis maiestate potestatem suam circumscribi velint. Cumprimis ergo curandum, vt in eligendis tum rerumpub. tum ecclesiarum praesidibus prima religionis ratio habeatur, quod & Iethro Mosen admonuit, cuius consilium diuina authoritate probatum est. Exod.18. Et qui in magistratu se collocatos vident, non sibi merum quidum pro sua libidine agendi imperium traditum, sed suam potestatem diuinis iustitiae & religionis legibus limitatam esse cogitent, & Deo olim rationem reddendam esse, qui verus iudiciorum praeses in scripturis traditur. Deut.1. Psal.82. Haec nisi considerent magistratus, illorum potestas perinde erit, vt gladius in manu furiosi, & tam sibi ipsis quam reipub. exitiales erunt, qui patriae patres & conseruatores esse debebant. Vide Psal. 94. &c.
units.tr: Besides, by the example of these men we are warned how harmful it is to entrust the rule and kingdom of the Church to men empty of religion and fear of God. There can be no wisdom in them, since (as Solomon testifies) the beginning of their wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Prov. 1, etc. Therefore, once every barrier of reason has been broken through, they pour themselves out into the blind licence of their passions, and then at last they think they have discharged their magistracy well, if they have made it known to all that they wish their power to be limited by no authority of laws or majesty of religion. Above all, therefore, care must be taken that in choosing the leaders both of commonwealths and of churches, the first consideration is religion, as Jethro also admonished Moses, whose counsel was approved by divine authority. Exod. 18. And those who see themselves placed in magistracy should not think that a mere arbitrary power of acting according to their own lust has been handed to them, but that their power is limited by the laws of divine justice and religion, and that they must one day render an account to God, who is in the Scriptures set forth as the true president of judgments. Deut. 1. Ps. 82. If magistrates do not consider these things, their power will be just like a sword in the hand of a madman, and those who ought to be the fathers and preservers of their country will be deadly both to themselves and to the commonwealth. See Ps. 94, etc.

units.la: Postremo mundi ingenium hic ceu in speculo conspiciendum proponitur. Sunt in hoc tria hominum genera, omnia autem veritatis odio flagrant, & Christi nomen oppressum cupiunt. Primum eorum est, qui redemptionis & salutis humanae gloriam sibi vendicant: quo in numero Iudaeorum sacerdotes olim fuisse constat, cum templum & cultum omnem in forum & nundinationem turpissimam conuerterint, quod non semel illis Christus exprobrauit. Iohan.2. Matth.15.21.&c. Istorum locum hodie tenent, qui claues regni coelorum sibi solis vendicant, peccantes ad suorum pedum oscula inuitant, ijs peccatorum remissionem & indulgentias diuendunt, & penes se esse dicunt, vt vel canonizatos coelis inuebant, vel damnatos in tartara praecipitent. Qui cum proprium nomen stabilire velint, Christi nomen, quo omnis illorum quaestus & gloria euertitur, nullo modo ferre possunt. Secundu genus horum similimum est, & eos habet, qui non eam quidem sibi potestatem vendicant, quod alios saluare possint, sed se sibi ipsis ad salutem sufficere putant, & cum vulgo Iudaeorum propriam iustitiam (vt Paulus inquit) stabilire volentes, Dei iustitiae, quam is in filio suo nobis offert, subiici nolunt. Rom.10. Niruntur isti ieiuniis, feriis, eleemosynis, rosariis, chameunis, matutinis, cucullis, cilicijs, rasuris & infinitis aliis rebus, in quas & corporis vires exhauriunt, & sumptus ingentes faciunt. Hi quoque nominis Christi hostes sunt. Vident enim hoc admisso omnem ipsorum iustitiam intercidere, seque ridiculos fore, qui inanibus laboribus & sumptibus se fatigarint. Tertio genere palam impij & Epicuri de grege porci continentur, qui religionis nomen ideo tantum profitentur, ne pro ἀθέοις & prophanis habeantur. Horum flagitia & scelera quia Christi verbum arguit, illud ferre nequeunt, quemadmodum ipse olim monuit. Iohan.3. Nam intelligunt, aut morum mutationem faciendam esse, aut ipsos infames fore coram veris Dei cultoribus. Interim tamen omnes isti astute ingenij sui corruptionem dissimulare norunt, & ne suas res agere videantur, seditionis & turbarum nomine Christi doctrinam infamant, eamque publicarum calamitatum causam esse clamitant. Notum enim illud Achabi est, quo Eliam Israelitici regni turbatorem esse ait. primi Regum, decimo octauo. Notum illud Amasiae sacerdotis Bethel, qui Amos prophetam contra regem coniurauisse dicit, nec terram illius sermones sustinere posse. Amos 7.cap. Quo etiam referri debent, quae Iudaei in Aegypto Ieremiae in faciem exprobrant, vt libri ipsius cap.44. legitur. Nec alio praetextu hos vsos esse quinto capite patebit. Atqui vtinam ijs, quae olim mundus fecit, contentus esset, & non hodie suum illud ingenium referret. Prodest autem haec nouisse, ne mirum nobis videatur, quando salutarem Christi praedicationem prohiberi audimus. Imitemur autem apostolorum constantiam, de qua sequenti sermone dicetur, vt mundi minis & conatibus superiores salutem veram consequamur in Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, the nature of the world is set before us here as if to be seen in a mirror. There are three kinds of men in this, and all of them burn with hatred of the truth and desire that the name of Christ be crushed. The first of these is of those who claim for themselves the glory of human redemption and salvation; among this number it is well known that the priests of the Jews once were, when they turned the temple and all worship into a market and most shameful trade, which Christ more than once reproached them for. John 2. Matt. 15, 21, etc. Today those hold this place who claim for themselves alone the keys of the kingdom of heaven, invite sinners to kiss their feet, sell to them the remission of sins and indulgences, and say that it lies in their power either to carry men canonized into heaven or to hurl the damned into hell. Since they wish to establish their own name, they cannot in any way bear the name of Christ, by which all their gain and glory is overturned. The second kind is very like the first, and includes those who do not claim for themselves that power of saving others, but think that they are sufficient for their own salvation, and, wishing with the crowd of the Jews to establish their own righteousness (as Paul says), are unwilling to submit to the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son. Rom. 10. These men strive with fasts, holy days, almsgivings, rosaries, chamuns, matins, hoods, hair shirts, tonsures and countless other things, by which they exhaust their bodily strength and make huge expenses. These also are enemies of the name of Christ. For they see that, once this is admitted, all their own righteousness will perish, and that they will be ridiculous, who have wearied themselves with empty labours and expenses. The third kind, openly impious and the herd of Epicurus' pigs, profess the name of religion only so that they may not be regarded as atheists and profane persons. Because the word of Christ condemns their shameful deeds and crimes, they cannot bear it, just as he himself once warned. John 3. For they understand that either a change of morals must be made, or that they themselves will be infamous before the true worshippers of God. Meanwhile, however, all these men know cunningly how to disguise the corruption of their character, and, lest they seem to be pursuing their own affairs, they defame the doctrine of Christ under the name of sedition and disturbance, and cry out that it is the cause of public calamities. Well known is that saying of Ahab, by which he calls Elijah a troubler of the kingdom of Israel. 1 Kings 18. Well known is that of Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, who says that Amos the prophet has conspired against the king, and that the land cannot bear his words. Amos 7. To this too should be referred what the Jews in Egypt throw in Jeremiah's face, as is read in chapter 44 of his book. Nor will it be clear that they used any other pretext in the fifth chapter. Would that they were content with what the world once did, and did not today renew that same disposition! It is useful, however, to know these things, so that it does not seem strange to us when we hear that the saving preaching of Christ is forbidden. Let us imitate the constancy of the apostles, of which it will be spoken in the following sermon, so that, rising above the threats and attempts of the world, we may obtain true salvation in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXIX.
units.tr: Homily 29.

units.la: At Petrus & Iohannes respondentes, dixerunt illis: An iustum sit coram Deo, vos potius audire quam Deum, iudicate. Nos enim non possumus, quae vidimus & quae audiuimus, non loqui. At illi additis minis dimiserunt eos, nihil inuenientes cur punirent eos, propter populum: quia omnes glorificabant Deum super eo, quod acciderat. Annorum enim plus quàm quadraginta erat homo, in quem editum fuerat signum istud sanationis. Dimissi autem venerunt ad suos & annuntiarunt quæcunq; ipsis summi sacerdotes & Seniores dixerant.
units.tr: But Peter and John answered them and said: "Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God. For we cannot help speaking of what we have seen and heard." And they, after adding threats, let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, since all were glorifying God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing had been performed was more than forty years old. When they had been released, they went to their own people and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said to them.

units.la: NOn temere saluator noster Iesus Christus frequenter de persecutionibus & cruce coram Apostolis concionatur, quam omnibus paratam dicit, quicunq; ipsius discipuli esse velint. Non verò earum admonitionum hic finis est, ut metu perculsos à fide abstrerat, sed fidi Imperatoris instar hoc quærit, ut aduersus præuisa pericula fide & patientia armemur. Quare præsens etiam auxilium pollicetur, nosq; omnibus periculis & hostium conatibus superiores fore dicit. Euidens borum exemplum primus ille, qui apostolos excepit, tumultus exhibet, qui eo maiori diligentia inspici meretur, quòd & consolationem affert tam fidele Christi patrocinium, quo suos periclitantes defendit, & apostolorum exemplo nos in simili casu constitutos officij admonet. Contra apostolos siquidem omnes eos conspirauisse audiuimus, qui inter Iudæos potentia & authoritate valebant: quorum tyrannide factum est, ut primo quidem in carceres abducerentur, deinde in Concilio sisterentur, ut coram iniquissimis iudicibus fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem redderent. Vincit tamen veritas, & ita vincit, ut stupore repleantur omnium qui consiliorum incerti fiant, qui paulò ante victoriam & triumphos animo suo conceperant. Nec aliam rationem sibi restare vident, quàm quod minacibus editis apostolorum constantiam coherceri posse existimant. Quare edicunt, ne quam in posterum Iesu Christi mentionem faciant, nec doctrinam illius spargere pergant. Perpetuus hic mundo mos est, ut euangelij prædicationem tum editis publicis tum aperta vi opprimere conetur. Sed qua animorum constantia illius conatibus & minus resistere debeant Christiani homines, felix huius Tragœdia exitus docet, quem modò Lucas exponit, cuius singulæ partes diligentius excuti debent, ut plus inde consolationis & institutionis percipi possit.
units.tr: It was not without reason that our Saviour Jesus Christ so often preached to the Apostles about persecutions and the cross, which he said awaits all who wish to be his disciples. The purpose of these warnings is not to frighten them away from the faith in fear. Rather, like a faithful commander, he intends that we be armed with faith and patience against the dangers he has foreseen. For this reason he also promises present help, and says that we will be superior to all dangers and the attempts of enemies. The clear example of this is the tumult that first met the Apostles, which deserves to be examined with all the more care, because the faithful protection of Christ, by which he defended his people in peril, brings consolation, and the example of the Apostles reminds us of our duty when we find ourselves in a similar situation. We have heard that all those who were powerful and influential among the Jews conspired against the Apostles. Through their tyranny it came about that they were first led off to prison and then brought before the Council, so that they might give an account of their faith and teaching before most unjust judges. Yet truth prevails, and prevails in such a way that all who had conceived victory and triumph in their minds only shortly before are filled with astonishment and become uncertain of their plans. They see no other course left to them than to think that the Apostles' steadfastness can be restrained by threats issued. So they command that the Apostles make no further mention of Jesus Christ and not continue to spread his teaching. This is the perpetual custom of the world: it tries to suppress the preaching of the gospel both by public edicts and by open force. But how steadfast of spirit Christians ought to be, and how little they should yield to such attempts, the happy outcome of this tragedy teaches, which Luke now sets forth. Each of its parts must be examined more carefully, so that more consolation and instruction may be drawn from it.

units.la: Primum verò hic locum apostolorum responsio tenet, qua diserte testantur, se illorum mandatis obedire nec posse nec debere. Ne tamen proterui & impudentes siue temerarij videantur, rationibus agunt, quas nemo reijcere potest facile. Prima Dei authoritate nititur, quæ maior est, quàm ut homi num quantumuis excellentium edictis cedere debeat. Argumentum tale est: Deo magis obedire oportet quàm hominibus. Deus verò nos prædicare iussit, & filij Dei mandatum est: Ite in orbem universum, & prædicate euangelium omni creaturæ. Marc. 16. Item: Eritis mihi testes Hierosolymis, in Iudæa, &c. Act. 1. Quare vobis diuersum mandantibus obedire non licet. Maiorem verò per concessionem enuntiant, ipsorum iudicio causam hanc subijcientes, ut in rebus extra omnem controuersiam positis fieri solet. Et sanè plus quàm Luciferiana impietas esset, si quis sibi inter homines maiore ea, quæ Deo debetur, authoritatem & obseruantiam vendicaret: cùm palàm constet, ipsum non primatorum modò hominum, verumetiam regum & principum Dominum esse, cui omnes sacramentis publicis obstricti sumus. Altera apostolorum ratio eiusmodi est: Vidimus & audiuimus isthæc omnia quæ docemus. Ergo illa silentio prætereire aut reticere non possumus. Consequentiæ huius vis in to uersatur, quòd non otiosi rerum à Christo gestarum spectatores, sed ut testes adhibiti & delecti fuerant, quemadmodum dominus fatetur. Iohan. 15. Nihil ergo illorum, quæ viderant & audiuerant, reticere potuerunt, nisi falsi testimonij scelus incurrere vellent, quod Deo cumprimis detestabile videri Solomon docet. Prouerb. 6. Adhæc quia redemptionis & salutis humanæ ratio in ijs cōfistit, quorum prædicatio apostolis, ut pote oculatis testibus, commissa erat, nihil ab illis abs manifesta publicæ salutis & gloriæ Christi iactura fieri potuit. Ica enim & Christi gloriam, quantum in ipsis erat, silentio oppressissent, & multorum hominum saluti obstitissent, qui euangelij prædicatione lucrifieri poterant. Vere ergo argumentatur Petrus, & potuisset esse apud Iudices illorum argumentorum magna authoritas, nisi palàm cum Deo bellum suscepissent, quod postea illis Gamaliel exprobrat.
units.tr: First of all, here stands the Apostles' answer, in which they clearly testify that they can neither obey nor ought to obey these men's commands. Yet, so that they may not seem shameless, impudent or rash, they argue with reasons that no one can easily reject. The first rests on the authority of God, which is greater than that it should yield to the edicts of men, however excellent. The argument runs thus: we must obey God rather than men. But God has commanded us to preach, and the command of the Son of God is: "Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature" (Mark 16). Likewise: "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judea," etc. (Acts 1). Therefore it is not lawful to obey you when you command the opposite. They state the major premise by way of concession, submitting the case to the judgement of their hearers, as is usually done in matters placed beyond all dispute. And indeed it would be more than Luciferian impiety if anyone claimed for himself among men an authority and obedience greater than what is owed to God, since it is plain that he is the Lord not only of leading men but also of kings and princes, to whom we are all bound by public sacraments. The Apostles' second argument is of this kind: we have seen and heard all these things that we teach. Therefore we cannot pass them over in silence or keep them hidden. The force of this consequence lies in the fact that they were not idle spectators of the things Christ did, but were appointed and chosen as witnesses, as the Lord himself affirms (John 15). Therefore they could not suppress anything of what they had seen and heard, unless they wished to incur the guilt of false testimony, which Solomon teaches is especially detestable to God (Prov. 6). Moreover, since the means of redemption and human salvation consist in those things whose proclamation was entrusted to the Apostles as eyewitnesses, nothing could be done by them that would be a manifest loss to the public salvation and the glory of Christ. For they would have, as far as lay in them, suppressed the glory of Christ by silence, and would have stood in the way of the salvation of many people who could be gained by the preaching of the gospel. Peter therefore argues rightly, and their arguments could have carried great authority before the judges, had they not openly waged war against God, which Gamaliel later reproaches them for.

units.la: Est autem perquàm memorabilis hæc apostolorum responsio. Primò enim veram obedientiæ rationem tradit, circa quam variè & perniciosè errari solet. Vt enim obedientiam cùm publicæ in rep ub. & ecclesia, tum priuatim in omni vitæ genere necessariam esse, omnes intelligunt: ita fere in hominum decretis & constitutionibus omnium seuerissimè exigitur, qui maximorum errorum, & interdum scelerum quoq; fons est. Hinc enim sit, quòd principes & magistratus defectione à fide Christi, ve fli, veritatis abnegationem, superstitionem & idololatriam edictis suis mandare audent, & quod multi eo facilius ipsorum mandatis obtemperant, quod se illis obedientiam debere, & extra omnem culpam fore arbitrantur, si illis obtemperauerint. Ex eodem fonte emanat, quod liberi cum infidelibus coniugia contrahunt, ad infideles commigrant & inter illos domicilia sibi constituunt, ne parentibus rebellare videantur. Et eodem errore decepti nonnulli monasticam vitam & superstitiones mordicus retinent, quibus se per obedientiae votum obstrinxerunt. At omnibus hisce Petrus medetur, dum obedientiae rationem ad Dei iudicium reuocat. An iustum sit (inquit) coram Deo, vos potius audire quam Deum, iudicate. Non ergo quid hominibus iustum & aequum videatur, respici debet, sed quid Deus a nobis exigat. Huic omnes homines sacramentis obstrictos esse modo diximus. Illius minister est magistratus, sicuti Paulus admonet. Rom. 13. Ille in iudicum consessu arbiter & iudicij praeses, in scripturis esse traditur. Psal.82. Huic olim rationem reddent parentes, & quicunq; aliqua authoritate nobis praecellunt. Quapropter illius ratio cumprimis haberi debet, nec alicuius hominis tanta sit authoritas, ut illa nos ab obedientiae officio, quo Deo obstricti sumus, auocari patiamur. Huc illud Christi pertinet, qui ita nos quae Caesaris sunt exoluere iubet, ut simul Deo quod demus, quae Dei sunt. Matth.22. Dei sunt vera fides, religio syncera & inuiolata, innocentia & charitatis studium, inuocatio & quae alia sunt eius generis. Haec nullius imperio nobis extorqueri patiamur, quo minus Deo nos obsequentes praebeamus. Horum consyderatione moti Danielis socij Nabuchodonosoris edicto parere recusant, quo ille statuam contra Dei praeceptum adorare iubebat. Et Daniel contra regis edictum in veri Dei inuocatione constanter pergit. Vtrorumq; vero inobedientiam non vulgaribus miraculis Deus approbauit. Dan.3.&6. Infinita huius generis exempla sunt in Martyribus, quos extreme stultos fuisse quis negare posset, si principum regumq; edicta Dei praeceptis praescribere deberent? Idem in officijs quae parentibus debentur obseruari debet, quod Christi exemplo docemur, qui a matre obiurgatus, quod ipsa & Ioseph inscijs in vrbe remansisset, respondet: An nesciebatis, quod in his quae patris mei sunt, oportet me esse? Luc.2. Stultissima vero est monasticorum votorum religio, & duplicis peccati reos facit horum obseruatores. Peccant enim turpissime, dum ea vouent, quae partim praestare nequeunt, partim vero cum Dei praeceptis ex diametro diffident. Deinde vero ne parum religiosi habeantur, ea pertinaciter obseruant etiam meliora edocti, quae & impie & imprudenter vouerunt, Herodis similes, qui ne periurus videretur, temerario iuramento parricidium coniunxit. Tutissima igitur ratio est, ut officij, quod Deo debemus, memores nihil vel polliceamur vel praestemus in alicuius hominis gratiam, quod cum illo pugnat. Quod si quid imprudentia peccatum est, culpam agnoscamus, nec maiori impietate promissa praestemus, quam illa a nobis facta sunt. Quod si qui eo insolentiae efferuntur, ut suam authoritatem diuina maiorem habe ri velint, sancta & pia fortitudine illorum impietati nos opponamus, ut hic Petrum & Iohannem fecisse cernimus.
units.tr: This answer of the Apostles is indeed most worthy of remembrance. For, first, it sets forth the true reason for obedience, a matter in which people commonly err in varied and harmful ways. Everyone understands that obedience is necessary both in public life, in the commonwealth and the Church, and privately in every kind of life. Yet obedience is most strictly demanded in human decrees and constitutions, which are also the source of the greatest errors and sometimes of crimes too. From this it happens that princes and magistrates dare by their edicts to command defection from the faith of Christ, denial of the truth, superstition and idolatry; and many obey their commands all the more readily because they think they owe them obedience and will be free of all blame if they comply. From the same source it springs that children contract marriages with unbelievers, move among unbelievers and set up homes among them, so that they may not seem to rebel against their parents. And deceived by the same error, some cling stubbornly to monastic life and its superstitions, to which they have bound themselves by a vow of obedience. But Peter heals all these ills when he refers the reason for obedience to the judgement of God: "Judge for yourselves," he says, "whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God." Therefore we must look not to what seems just and fair to men, but to what God demands of us. As we have just said, all men are bound to him by sacraments. The magistrate is his minister, as Paul reminds us (Rom. 13). In Scripture he is set forth as the arbiter and president of judgement, seated in the assembly of judges (Ps. 82). To him parents and all who excel us in any authority will one day give an account. Therefore his reckoning above all must be kept in view, and no man's authority should be so great that we allow ourselves to be drawn away by it from the duty of obedience by which we are bound to God. To this belongs Christ's saying, who bids us so to pay what is Caesar's that at the same time we give to God what is God's (Matt. 22). What belongs to God is true faith, pure and inviolate religion, innocence and zeal for charity, invocation, and other things of this kind. Let us not allow these to be wrested from us by anyone's command, so that we fail to show ourselves obedient to God. Moved by consideration of these things, Daniel's companions, under Nebuchadnezzar, refused to obey the edict by which he ordered them to worship a statue contrary to God's command; and Daniel steadfastly persisted in invoking the true God against the king's edict. God approved the disobedience of both not by ordinary miracles (Dan. 3 and 6). There are endless examples of this kind among the martyrs, whom anyone could call extremely foolish if they had to shape the commands of princes and kings by the precepts of God. The same must be observed in the duties owed to parents, as Christ's example teaches us. When his mother rebuked him because he had stayed behind in the city without her and Joseph knowing it, he answered: "Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?" (Luke 2). But the religion of monastic vows is most foolish, and makes those who keep them guilty of a double sin. For they sin most shamefully when they vow things that they are partly unable to perform and partly utterly at odds with God's commands. Then, so that they may not be thought insufficiently religious, they keep them stubbornly even after being taught better, having vowed impiously and rashly, like Herod, who, so as not to seem a perjurer, joined murder to a reckless oath. The safest course, therefore, is to remember the duty we owe to God and never to promise or perform anything to please any man that conflicts with it. If we have sinned through thoughtlessness, let us acknowledge the fault, and not fulfil promises with greater impiety than that with which they were made. And if some are so puffed up with arrogance that they wish their own authority to be regarded as greater than the divine, let us oppose their impiety with holy and godly courage, as we see Peter and John did here.

units.la: Docet praeterea apostolorum responsio, quibus argumentis contra mundi conatus euangelij ministri sese armare debeant. Illum enim euangelij praedicationem prohibiturum esse semper, supra monuimus, & quotidianus rerum euentus docet. Sed principio illos cogitare decet, Dei mandatum esse, ut euangelium praedicetur, & ad ipsos huius praedicationis ministerium pertinere, cum diuinitus ad hoc munus vocati & missi sint. Impiae ergo & infelicis temeritatis esset, Deo obsequium negare, quod Amos vidit, dum sui seculi hominibus prophetica obiurgationes digne ferentibus, ait: Leo si rugiat, quis non timeat? Dominus Deus cum loquitur, quis non prophetaret? Viderat enim quam infeliciter Ionae succesisset, cum apud Niniuitas prophetandi officium vellet subterfugere. Ideo & Paulus exclamat: Vae mihi, si non euangelizem. 1.Corinth.9. Deinde, veritatis testimonium sibi commissum esse cogitent, & eius quidem veritatis, quae & praecipuam Christi gloriam & publicam humani generis salutem comprehendit. Si quid ergo in hominum gratiam reticuerint, fieri nequit, quin laese diuinae maiestatis crimen incurrant, & pro publicis humani generis hostibus habeantur. Deniq; rationem sibi olim reddendam esse cogitent coram Christo iudice, qui non modo perfidos commissi talenti adulteratores, verumetiam eos aeterno supplicio multabit, qui talentum defossum occultant, nec pro virili Christo quam plurimos lucrifacere studient. Matthai 25.capite Haec (inquam) vanis & inanibus mundi terriculamentis opponi debent, nec multum eos mora-
units.tr: The apostles' reply also teaches with what arguments the ministers of the gospel ought to arm themselves against the attempts of the world. As we noted above, the world will always try to forbid the preaching of the gospel, and the daily course of events shows this. But first they should reflect that it is God's command that the gospel be preached, and that the ministry of this preaching belongs to them, since they have been called and sent by God to this office. It would therefore be a wicked and unhappy rashness to deny obedience to God, as Amos saw when, speaking to the men of his age who rightly bore prophetic rebukes, he said: "If a lion roars, who will not fear? When the Lord God speaks, who will not prophesy?" For he had seen how unhappily Jonah fared when he tried to escape the duty of prophesying at Nineveh. So too Paul cries out: "Woe is me, if I do not preach the gospel" (1 Cor. 9). Next, let them reflect that the witness of the truth has been committed to them, and of that truth which embraces both Christ's special glory and the public salvation of the human race. If therefore they keep silent to win men's favour, it cannot but be that they incur the crime of wounding the divine majesty and are regarded as public enemies of the human race. Finally, let them reflect that they will one day have to render an account before Christ the judge, who will punish not only the faithless who adulterate the talent committed to them, but also those who hide the buried talent and do not eagerly strive to gain as many as they can for Christ (Matth. 25). These things, I say, ought to be set against the empty and vain terrors of the world, and I will not dwell long on

units.la: Quibus armis ministri mundo sese opponere debeant. bimur, qui nec salutis rationem simpliciter tradi, nec pseudochristos argui, nec palàm flagitiosos accu-sari volunt.
units.tr: With what weapons ministers ought to oppose themselves to the world: those who wish neither that the way of salvation be simply taught, nor that false christs be exposed, nor that open scandals be publicly accused.

units.la: Caeterum cumprimis admirandum est, quòd Lucas apostolos, cùm palàm obsequium detrectas-rent, dimissos esse scribit, cùm tamen obstinata maneret in iudicibus euangelium per lequendi volun-tas. Nam ne quis illos rationibus cessisse putaret, ait: Additis minis dimiserunt eos. Exprimunt haec impiorum mores & implacabile veritatis odium, quo excaecati, nullis rationibus cedere nec Dei iudicium extimescere norunt. Nec habent quod Petri rationibus obijciant. Et tamen minantur. Non ergo alio praetextu id facere possunt, quàm quòd apostolos indignos censent, quibus cùm difpu-rationem prolixiorem instituant. Interim admonet exemplum hoc, ita vincere fideles in hoc mundo, vt nulla tamen aut saltem perexigua illis detur securitas. Spirat enim minas indesinenter mundus, & semel superati veritatis hostes pugnam subinde instaurant. Ita Elias quamuis in Carmelo Baa-lis sacerdotes & doctrina & diuinitus edito miraculo vicisset, eofdemq; iugulasset, nouis tamen Ifa-bellae reginae insidijs & persecutionibus excipitur. Nunquam ergo securitati se dedant Christi mili-tes, quantumuis se hostibus superiores factos esse viderint, sed sub crucis vexillo sibi triumphandum esse meminerint, quoad carnis carcere liberati in caelis cum Christo regnabunt, vbi nulla supererit ty-rannos extimescendi occasio.
units.tr: Moreover, it is especially to be admired that Luke writes that the apostles, when they openly refused obedience, were dismissed, although the will of the judges to speak against the gospel remained obstinate. For lest anyone think they had yielded to reasons, he says: "Having added threats, they dismissed them." These things express the manners of the wicked and their implacable hatred of the truth, by which, blinded, they know how to yield to no reasons and do not fear God's judgement. Nor have they anything to set against Peter's arguments. And yet they threaten. They can therefore do it on no other pretext than that they judge the apostles unworthy of a longer disputation with them. Meanwhile this example warns that the faithful conquer in this world in such a way that yet no security, or at least very little, is granted them. For the world breathes out threats without ceasing, and enemies of the truth, once defeated, renew the fight again and again. Thus Elijah, although on Carmel he had conquered the priests of Baal both by doctrine and by a miracle divinely wrought, and had slain them, was nonetheless met with fresh plots and persecutions from Queen Jezebel. Christ's soldiers should therefore never give themselves over to security, however much they see themselves to have become superior to their enemies, but should remember that they must triumph under the banner of the cross, until, freed from the prison of the flesh, they reign in heaven with Christ, where there will be no further occasion to fear tyrants.

units.la: At miretur aliquis apostolos ab infenfiffimis hostibus liberos dimissos esse, cùm illi & potentia & authoritate praevalerent. Causam ergo rei Lucas exponens, addit: Nihil inuenerunt cur punirent eos propter populum: quia omnes glorificabant Deum super eo, quod acciderat. Annorum enim plus quàm quadraginta erat homo, in quem editum fuerat signum iflud fanationis. In his obseruanda venit admirabilis Dei potentia, cui tam facile est impijs frenum injicere. Eam enim in praece-dentibus vidimus horum authoritatem & potentiam, vt foli pro rerum dominis haberi potuerint, quibus nullorum aliorum vis fuerit timenda. Sed ecce populum timent & ignobile vulgus. Ita Deus qui mari, elemento furiofiffimo, arenam labilem & inconstantem termini loco posuit, quem nisi ille permittat, transgredi nequit: potentissimus tyrannus fere plebem, qua nihil inconstantius habetur, obijcere solet, vel etiam aliis medijs insolitis ac inexpectatis eos constringit, vt in inermes & im-belles ea exequi non possint, quae maximè vellent, & quae facillime posse videbantur. Sic in media Chananaeorum gente patriarchas olim defendit, occulto quodam Chananaeorum animis timore im-misso. Vide Gen. 35. Pfal. 105. Sic Saulem à Dauidis persecutione per Philifteos retraxit, & per eos Dauidem tutatus est, qui eiusdem hostes erant infenfiffimi. 1. Sam. 23. Et nunc illius populi me-tu sacerdotes, quò minùs apostolis manus inferans, cohercet, qui antea vafano & impio clamore Chri-ftum ad crucis immane supplicium postulauerat. Sunt infinita eius generis exempla, quibus edo-cemur, non semper licere tyrannis quicquid libet. Illorum verò hic apud nos vsus esse debet, ne ina-nibus mundi minis terreamur, sed intrepidi sectemur vocationem nostram, nec dubitemus de Dei praesidio, qui cùm pilos capitis nostri numerauerit, nihil nobis praeter suae prouidentiae decretum acci-dere patietur. Matth. 10. Tuetur ille suos in medio Babylonis & Aegypti, quàm diu ipsos gloriae suae afferenda & aliorum saluti prouehenda seruire posse viderit. Vbi verò ijdem cursum suum comple-uerint, eos ad fe euocat, & licet tunc impijs aliquid contra hos permitti videatur, hoc ipsum tamen nihil aliud est, quàm quòd pios infelici carnis ergastulo liberant, ipsi verò interea sua iniquitatis mensuram complent, vt ad eos colligantur apud inferos, qui terrorem suum posuerunt in terra vi-uentium. Ezech. 32.
units.tr: But someone may wonder that the apostles were released unharmed by their most hostile enemies, when those enemies prevailed both in power and in authority. Explaining the reason for the matter, Luke adds: "They found nothing by which to punish them, because of the people, since all were glorifying God for what had happened. For the man on whom that sign of healing had been wrought was more than forty years old." Here the admirable power of God is to be observed, to whom it is so easy to put a bridle on the wicked. For we saw in the preceding chapters that the authority and power of these men were such that they alone could be regarded as masters of affairs, and no force of others was to be feared by them. But see, they fear the people and the common crowd. Thus God, who set the shifting and unstable sand as the boundary for the sea, the most furious of elements, so that it cannot cross it unless he permits, often restrains the most powerful tyrant with the people, which is held to be the most inconstant thing, or even binds them with other unusual and unexpected means, so that they cannot carry out against the unarmed and unskilled what they most wish and what seemed most easy for them to do. So in the midst of the Canaanite nation he once defended the patriarchs, sending a secret fear into the minds of the Canaanites (see Gen. 35; Ps. 105). So he restrained Saul from persecuting David by means of the Philistines, and protected David through them, who were his most bitter enemies (1 Sam. 23). And now the priests, through fear of that people, restrain themselves from laying hands on the apostles, although formerly, with a mad and impious shout, they had demanded Christ's execution on the cross. There are countless examples of this kind, by which we are taught that tyrants are not always permitted whatever they please. The use of these examples here among us ought to be this: that we not be terrified by the empty threats of the world, but fearlessly pursue our calling, and not doubt God's protection, who, since he has numbered the hairs of our head, will suffer nothing to befall us except by the decree of his providence (Matth. 10). He keeps his own safe in the midst of Babylon and Egypt for as long as he sees them able to serve the bringing of glory to himself and the advancement of the salvation of others. But when they have completed their course, he calls them to himself, and although then something seems to be permitted to the wicked against them, this itself is nothing other than that they free the godly from the unhappy prison of the flesh, while the wicked in the meantime fill up the measure of their iniquity, so that they are gathered together among the dead in the underworld, who spread their terror in the land of the living (Ezech. 32).

units.la: Praeterea tyrannorum fortem & conditionem videre licet, quam tunc quoq; sustinent, quando cum primis potentia & authoritate praualere omnibus videntur, vt nimirum multos timeat, qui à multis timeri volunt. Idem enim illis, quod immanibus belluis, vrsis, leonibus, pantheris aliisq; similibus, ac cidit. Saeuiunt istae in quosuis obuios, & ab omnibus timentur. Sed ijsdem quàm plurimi laqueos ten-dunt & foueas effodiunt, ac in illarum necem tela parant: quò fit, vt frequenter vilissimi alicuius & formidolosissimi mortalium manu conficiatur fera, quae toti alicui regioni paulò ante terribilis erat. Eandem sibi fortem plerunq; accidere ipsi tyranni norunt, & proinde hoc praepostero metu vexan-tur, vt populum adeoq; suos domesticos timeant, qui ab omnibus timeri volunt, quod & nostris hisce in praesenti Lucas tribuit. Hinc exquisitae illae tyrannorum custodia, quibus corpora & vitam suam tueri conantur. Ideo fere ex peregrinis gentibus armatos custodes & satellites conducunt, & inter peregrinorum arma plus sibi praesidij, quam inter suos pollicentur: eo quod inter illos neminem inuenire sperant, ad quem aliquod ex ipsorum morte emolumentum redire possit. Eandem ob causam Masinissa Numidiae rex, cum & Pop. Romano amicitia & foedere iunctus, & quinquaginta quatuor filiorum pater esset, corporis salutem canum custodia vallauit, plus in his praesidij repositum esse putans, quam in hominibus, quos multoties se offendisse noverat. Quid de Dionysio dicemus, qui filias tonsorum artem edoceri voluit, ne alicuius viri manibus iugulum suum credere cogeretur: & ne filiabus quidem amplius fidere potuit, postquam illae nubiles facta sunt: nec ad coniuges suas vnquam, nisi prius excussas diligenter, accessit? Sed plenae sunt eiusmodi exemplorum historiae, quae & nobis contra tyrannos consolationi esse debent, & omnibus iis, qui in magistratu versantur, documento esse, vt iustitiae & aequitati studeant, nec in effraeni potestate salutis suae praesidium collocent. Quo enim plures terrore suo concusserint, eo plures vitae & fortunarum suarum insidiatores contra se provocabunt. Quicunque vero Dei timore ducti, illius praeceptis obsequendum esse ducunt, & secundum illa suae potentiae vires moderantur, licet interdum impiorum artibus & insidijs petantur, Deum tamen tutorem sentient, qui quosuis seditiosorum conatus facile dissipat, quemadmodum Dauidis & Ezechiae exemplis docemur.
units.tr: Furthermore, one may see the lot and condition of tyrants, which they endure even then, when they seem to prevail above all by power and authority; for surely he fears many who wishes to be feared by many. What happens to them is the same as what happens to savage beasts, bears, lions, panthers and other similar creatures. These rage against whoever they meet and are feared by all. But many lay snares for them, dig pits, and prepare weapons for their destruction; as a result, the beast, which shortly before had been terrible to a whole region, is often killed by the hand of some most worthless and most timid of mortals. Tyrants themselves know that the same lot often befalls them, and so they are harassed by this perverse fear, that they fear their own people and even their household, although they want to be feared by all; which Luke also attributes to our own times at present. Hence those exquisite guards of tyrants, by which they try to protect their bodies and lives. Therefore they often hire armed guards and bodyguards from foreign nations, and they promise themselves more protection among foreign arms than among their own, because among their own they hope to find no one to whom any gain from their death could return. For the same reason Masinissa, king of Numidia, although he was joined to the Roman people by friendship and treaty, and was the father of fifty-four sons, fenced in his bodily safety with a guard of dogs, thinking more protection was placed in them than in men, whom he knew he had offended many times. What shall we say of Dionysius, who wished his daughters to be taught the barber's art, lest he be forced to entrust his throat to any man's hands; and who could not trust even his daughters once they had become marriageable, nor ever approached his wives unless they had first been carefully searched? But the histories are full of such examples, which ought both to console us against tyrants and to serve as a lesson to all who hold office, that they should strive for justice and fairness, and not place the protection of their safety in unbridled power. For the more people they have shaken with their terror, the more plotters against their life and fortunes they will provoke against themselves. But whoever, led by the fear of God, judges that obedience is owed to his precepts, and moderates the strength of his power according to them, although at times he is assailed by the arts and snares of the wicked, will nonetheless find God as his protector, who easily scatters whatever attempts of the seditious, as we are taught by the examples of David and Hezekiah.

units.la: Adijcit autem postremo Lucas, quid apostoli dimissi fecerint, dicens: Venerunt ad suos, & illis annuntiarunt quaecunque ipsis summi sacerdotes & Seniores dixerant. Ecclesiae ergo rem omnem ex posuerunt, tum vt ad preces illam extimularent, vt sequentia testantur: tum vt singuli hostium minus & conatibus perspectis, Christiana fortitudine & patientia sese armarent, & quantum religio permittebat, sibi ab illorum insidijs cauerent. Quo exemplo docemur, licere verbi ministris, vt ecclesijs publice exponant quaecunque profesi veritatis hostes contra Christum & gregem ipsius moliuntur, Quod multis hodie non modo superuacaneum esse, verumetiam aliquam seditionis speciem referre videtur, quando vel Pontificum Bullae, vel Comitiorum aut Conciliorum decreta & horribiles Antichristorum minae coram ecclesijs recitantur. At horum iudicio cum Christus tum apostoli seditionis accusabuntur, quos hoc ipsum non semel fecisse constat. Quin potius meminerimus ministros ecclesiae pastorum & speculatorum instar datos esse. Officij ergo illorum est lupos arguere, & oues de periculis imminentibus admonere. Iohan. 10. Omnium vero hic finis fit, vt ad Dominum per preces & vitae emendationem conuersi fideles, Christiana fortitudine & fidei constantia armentur, vt omnibus hostium conatibus superiores facti, tandem in beatum Christi Iesu regnum recipiantur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke then adds, at the end, what the apostles did after they were released: "They came to their own people and reported to them all that the chief priests and elders had said." The congregation therefore laid out the whole matter before it, partly to rouse it to prayer, as what follows bears witness, and partly so that each one, having seen the plans and attempts of the enemies, might arm himself with Christian courage and patience and, so far as religion allows, guard himself against their plots. From this example we learn that it is lawful for ministers of the Word to make public to the churches whatever enemies of the truth are devising against Christ and his flock. Today many think this is not only pointless but even has the appearance of sedition, when the bulls of the Popes, the decrees of Diets or Councils, and the dreadful threats of the Antichrists are read out in the presence of the churches. Yet by their judgment both Christ and the apostles would be accused of sedition, though it is certain that they did this very thing more than once. Rather, let us remember that the ministers of the Church have been given as shepherds and watchmen. It is therefore their duty to warn against wolves and to alert the sheep to impending dangers (John 10). The final purpose of all this is that the faithful, turned to the Lord through prayer and amendment of life, may be armed with Christian courage and constancy of faith, so that, having risen above all the attempts of the enemy, they may at last be received into the blessed kingdom of Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXX.

units.la: Illi autem cum audissent, vnanimiter extulerunt vocem ad Deum, & dixerunt: Domine tu es Deus, qui fecisti coelum & terram, mare & omnia, quae in eis sunt. Qui per os Dauidis serui tui dixisti: Quare fremuerunt gentes, & populi meditati sunt inania? Adstiterunt reges terrae, & principes conuenerunt in vnum aduersus Dominum, & aduersus vnctum eius. Vere enim conuenerunt in hac vrbe aduersus sanctum filium tuum Iesum, quem vnxisti, Herodes simul & Pontius Pilatus cum gentibus & populis Israel, vt facerent quaecunque manus tua & consilium tuum prius decreuerat fieri. Et nunc domine, aspice in minas eorum, & da seruis tuis, vt cum omni fiducia loquantur sermonem tuum, manum tuam porrigendo in hoc, vt sanatio, & signa & prodigia edantur, per nomen sancti filij tui Iesu. Et cum illi precati essent, motus est locus, in quo erant congregati. Et repleti sunt omnes spiritu sancto.
units.tr: When they heard this, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord and said: "Lord, you are God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. You said by the mouth of your servant David: 'Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together against the Lord and against his anointed.' For truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy Servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your purpose had decided beforehand should happen. And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants that they may speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus." And when they had prayed, the place where they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quemadmodum Dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus, de piorum persecutionibus frequenter disserit: ita spiritus sanctus primitiuae ecclesiae persecutiones per Lucam diligenter describi voluit, non quidem ea duntaxat causa, vt oraculorum Christi veritatem assereret, sed partim ne aduersis & tribulationibus, quibus hodie ecclesia vexatur, tanquam insolitis, offendamur: partim vero vt primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplo edoceremur, quid nos in persecutionibus facere cœueniat. Et hæ quidem cum primis referri debent, quæ hucusq; de apostolis dicta sunt. Illi in Concilium producti ingenuè & intrepidè Christum confitentur. Deinde, cum euangelij prædicationem hostes prohiberent, admirabili constantia, se impio mandato obedire non posse protestantur. Tandem cum rationibus nihil apud impios profici, & ab illis minas ingeminari viderent, ad ecclesiam rem omnem referunt, vt singuli de imminentibus periculis admoniti, sibi facilius prospicere possint. Hæc ministri imitentur, quoties persecutionum procellas mundus excitat. Ingenua Christi confessione alijs exemplo sint. Impijs principum edictis nequaquam cedat. Ecclesiæ autem fidis admonitionibus adsint, ne alicuius salus illorum ignauia periclitetur. Pergit autem in cœpta narratione Lucas, & quid ecclesia per apostolos admonita fecerit, docet: cuius exemplo patebit, quid singulos Christianos quando persecutores grassari vident, tum publice, tum priuatim facere deceat.
units.tr: Just as our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, often speaks about the persecution of the godly, so the Holy Spirit wished the persecutions of the primitive Church to be carefully described by Luke. He did this not only to confirm the truth of Christ's sayings, but also in part so that we would not be shocked by adversities and tribulations, with which the Church is harassed today, as if they were unusual; and in part so that we might be taught by the example of the primitive Church what we ought to do in persecutions. Those things which have been related so far about the apostles should be considered first of all. Brought before the council, they openly and fearlessly confess Christ. Then, when the enemies forbade the preaching of the gospel, they declared with remarkable steadfastness that they could not obey the impious command. Finally, when they saw that nothing was gained with the impious by reasons, and that threats were being repeated against them, they reported the whole matter to the Church, so that individuals, warned of the dangers at hand, might more easily provide for themselves. Let ministers imitate this whenever the world stirs up the storms of persecution. Let them be an example to others by their frank confession of Christ. Let them never yield to the impious edicts of princes. Let them, moreover, stand by the Church with faithful warnings, so that no one's salvation is endangered by their cowardice. Luke goes on with his narrative and teaches what the Church did when it had been warned by the apostles; from its example it will be clear what individual Christians ought to do, both publicly and privately, when they see persecutors rampaging.

units.la: Illi, inquit, cum audissent apostolos, vnanimiter extulerunt vocem ad Deum. Atqui vnicum hoc ecclesiæ factum commemorat, quod per preces ad Dei auxilium confugerit. Non ergo securi imminentia pericula contempserunt. Nec etiam ad humanæ sapientiæ consilia aut humana præsidia sese contulerunt, sed in precibus omne quasiuerunt præsidium & auxilium. Est hoc tutissimum ecclesiæ asylum, eò quòd passim Deus suam opem postulantibus se propitium & assertorem fore pollicetur. Et quod passim pollicetur, exemplis infinitis præstitit, vt de promissionum ipsius veritate nemo Christianus dubitare possit. Huc enim pertinet, quod ad mare rubrum Ægyptiorum armis inclusos Israëlitas, per Mosis preces excitatus liberat. Exod. 14. Et postea eiusdem precibus victoriam contra Amelechitas concedit. Exod. 17. In Psalmis vero infinita exempla habentur eorum, qui Deum precibus suis benignum annuisse testantur. Sed & Ioel propheta ecclesiæ periclitanti hoc vnum consulit, vt omnes ad Deum conuersi, illius gratiam & opem implorent, simulq; formulam præscribit, quæ in precibus publicis vti debeant. Ioel. 2. Nec irritum fuisse istud consilium, rei euentus docuit. Misit enim angelum suum Deus, qui cæsis vna nocte Assyriorum copijs, vrbem Ierosolymam ex immani Sennacheribi tyrannide asseruit. Quare nihil à primitiua ecclesia melius & salutarius fieri potuit, quàm quòd Dei auxilium pijs precibus sibi impetrandum esse putauerunt. Arguuntur hoc exemplo corruptissimi nostri seculi mores. Plerofq; enim pericula ecclesiarũ, cum adhuc longius absunt, nimia securitate contemnere, admonitiones omnes scurriliter insectari, & voluptatum intempestiuis studijs se totos addicere videmus. Vbi vero persecutionis ignem iam ardere sentiunt, vel carnis consilia securi fidem dissimulant, vel principum sæderibus & humanis præsidijs sese tueri conantur. Quæ cum sa est, vt quò magis eluctantur, eò maioribus pluribusq; periculis sese implicent.
units.tr: He says: "When they heard that the apostles had been ordered, they lifted up their voices to God with one accord." Yet he records this one action of the Church, that it fled for God's help through prayer. It did not therefore despise the dangers threatening it in security. Nor did it turn to the counsels of human wisdom or to human protections, but sought every defence and help in prayer. This is the safest refuge of the Church, since God promises everywhere to be gracious to those who ask his aid and to be their defender. And what he promises everywhere he has shown by countless examples, so that no Christian can doubt the truth of his promises. To this belongs what he did at the Red Sea, when, moved by the prayers of Moses, he freed the Israelites who were shut in by the armies of the Egyptians. Exod. 14. And afterwards, at Moses' prayer, he granted them victory over the Amalekites. Exod. 17. In the Psalms there are countless examples of those who testify that God has graciously listened to their prayers. The prophet Joel, too, advises the Church in danger of this one thing: that all should turn to God and implore his grace and help; at the same time he prescribes a form of words to be used in public prayers. Joel 2. The outcome of the event showed that this counsel was not in vain. For God sent his angel, who in one night slew the forces of the Assyrians and rescued the city of Jerusalem from the monstrous tyranny of Sennacherib. Therefore nothing better or more wholesome could have been done by the primitive Church than to think that God's help was to be obtained for itself by godly prayers. By this example the most corrupt morals of our age are condemned. For we see many who, while the dangers to the Churches are still far off, despise them out of excessive security, mock all warnings in a buffoonish way, and devote themselves entirely to the untimely pursuit of pleasures. But when they feel the fire of persecution already burning, either they carelessly dissemble the faith and follow the counsels of the flesh, or they try to protect themselves by alliances with princes and human defences. And the result is that the harder they struggle, the more they entangle themselves in greater and more numerous dangers.

units.la: Simul vero pauci verbis veram precandi rationem Lucas comprehendit. Primò Deum invocarunt, quem solum invocandum esse, tum fœdus cum Abrahamo initum, tum primum Decalogi præceptum & Dominicæ orationis formula admonet. Et multis exemplis constat, illum solum nos & passim exaudire & liberare posse. Quapropter enormis illorum error est, quicunque vota sua creaturis nuncupare audent. Deinde sublata voce orant. Atqui constat, Deum gemitus quoque audire, & lachrymas oppressorum atque afflictorum ipsi indesinenter ob oculos versari. Psalm. 12. & 56. Sed ingenuitatem fidei vocis elatione exprimere voluerunt, & testari quòd ipsos precum & invocationis diuini auxilij minimè pudeat. Non postrema enim hæc confessionis fidei pars est: quod Danielem intellexisse videmus, qui cum prius occultius orauisset, vbi numinis invocationem regis edicto prohibitam sensit, apertis fenestris & quasi in publico orat, ne impio edicto subscripsisse videretur. Postremò vnanimitatem illis tribuit, quam nisi ecclesia obseruet, nec in precibus exaudiri, nec pro ecclesia Dei censeri poterit. Ea enim sub vno capite Christo vnum corpus effecta, vno eodemq; spiritu animatur, vnum & eundem patrem invocat, simulq; vnam & eandem in cœlis hæreditatem repositam habet. At qui in his vere conueniunt, animis scindi non poterunt. Imitemur ergo à primitiua ecclesia vsurpatam precandi rationem, & præsentissimum in aduersis Dei auxilium experimur.
