Præstat autem ipsam precationem, quæ vsi sunt, diligentius excutere, cuius tres partes constitui poterunt.
units.tr: At the same time, Luke sums up in a few words the true manner of praying. First, they called upon God, whom alone we ought to call upon, as both the covenant made with Abraham and the first commandment of the Decalogue and the form of the Lord's Prayer remind us. And many examples show that he alone can hear and deliver us everywhere. Therefore the error of those is monstrous who dare to address their vows to creatures. Next, they prayed with raised voices. Yet it is certain that God also hears groans and that the tears of the oppressed and afflicted are constantly before his eyes. Ps. 12 and 56. But they wished to express the sincerity of their faith by raising their voices, and to bear witness that they were not ashamed of prayer and of calling upon the divine help. For this is not the least part of the confession of faith. We see that Daniel understood this, who, when he had earlier prayed more secretly, and perceived that the invocation of the Deity had been forbidden by the king's edict, prayed with the windows open, as if in public, so that he would not seem to have subscribed to the impious edict. Finally, Luke ascribes to them unanimity, which, unless the Church keeps, it can neither be heard in prayer nor be considered the Church of God. For under the one head, Christ, it has been made one body, is animated by one and the same Spirit, calls upon one and the same Father, and has one and the same inheritance laid up in heaven. But those who truly agree in these things cannot be torn apart in their minds. Let us therefore imitate the manner of prayer used by the primitive Church, and we shall find God's help most present in adversity. It is worthwhile to examine carefully the prayer itself which they used, which may be divided into three parts.

units.la: Prima Dei descriptionem habet, qua illum totius mundi Creatorem agnoscunt. Creationis verò cum primis mentionem faciunt, vt omnipotentiam Dei & merum illius in omnes creaturas imperium sibi ipsis ob oculos statuant, vnde consolationem non vulgarem poterant percipere. Admonebantur enim, impios Christi hostes nec Dei opus impedituros esse suis machinationibus, nec ipsis quicquam citra Dei consilium & permissionem nocere posse. Eadem ratione nos quoq; Dei omnipotentiam consyderare decet, vt non creatorem modò, verumetiam gubernatorem omnium creaturarum agnoscamus, qui licet in alto throno suum collocarit, demittit tamen se, vt inspiciat quaecunque in coelo & in terra sunt. Psal.113. Quae cosyderatio vt ad vitae morum institutionem plurimùm conducit, ita in tribulationibus consolationem affert, & in precibus fidem (ex qua precum effectus maximè dependet. Iac.1. Matth.21.) quàm maximè confirmat. Et hic praecipuus articuli primi in Symbolo apostolico vsus est, quo nos in Deum patrem, coeli & terrae Creatorem, credere profitemur. Facit enim ad fidei confirmationem, & omnes causas diffidentiae adimit, quae plerunque ex eo enascitur, quòd Deum vel non posse, vel non velle nobis auxilium ferre cogitamus. At quid impossibile erit ei, qui coelum & terram verbo suo condidit, & orbem hunc totum hucusq; conseruauit? Vel num homines rerum creatarum dominos negligere volet, qui rebus inanimatis prospicere & illas suo imperio continere solet?
units.tr: The first part contains a description of God, by which they acknowledge him as the Creator of the whole world. They make mention of creation above all, so that they might set before their own eyes the omnipotence of God and his sheer dominion over all creatures, from which they could derive no ordinary comfort. For they were reminded that the impious enemies of Christ would be unable to hinder God's work by their schemes, nor could they harm anyone except by God's counsel and permission. In the same way we too ought to consider God's omnipotence, so that we acknowledge him as the creator and governor of all creatures, who, though he has set his throne on high, nevertheless humbles himself to look upon whatever is in heaven and on earth. Ps. 113. This consideration, as it greatly contributes to the instruction of our life and conduct, so in tribulations it brings consolation, and it very greatly strengthens faith in prayers (on which the effect of prayers chiefly depends. James 1; Matt. 21). This is the principal use of the first article in the Apostles' Creed, in which we profess that we believe in God the Father, Creator of heaven and earth. For it helps to confirm faith and removes all the causes of distrust, which commonly arise from our thinking that God is either unable or unwilling to bring us help. But what will be impossible for him who made heaven and earth by his word, and has preserved this whole world until now? Or will he, who is accustomed to look after inanimate things and to hold them under his command, be willing to neglect human beings, the lords of created things?

units.la: Secunda parte narrationem contexunt, qua hostium conatus & imminentia pericula Deo exponunt, non quòd illum ista ignorare putent, sed vt in Dei sinum depositis querelis suis, animos suos curis & solicitudinibus aliqua ex parte liberent: qui praecipuus narrationum vsus est, quas sanctì orationibus suis interserere consueuerunt. Commendatur autem hoc argumento Dei bonitas, qui querelis nostris aures tam facilè praebet, & de nostris miserijs aut periculis conquerentes clementer audit. Narrandi verò exordium sumunt ex Psalmo secundo, quo Dauid, Dei spiritu illuminatus, Christi regnum descripsit, vnà cum improbis mundi conatibus, quibus is contra illud pugnaturus sit. Sensus omnium est: Reipsa nunc experimur, quod tu, ô Deus, per Dauidem olim praedixisti. Verè enim in hac Hierosolymorum vrbe, quae & sancta & iustitiae sedes olim dicta est, contra filium tuum conspirauerunt Herodes & Pilatus, milites item ex gentibus collecti & populus Israel, qui tibi totus consecratus esse debuit, &c. Non temere autem vetus vaticinium repetunt. Eo enim docent, nihil hic noui aut insoliti accidisse, & proinde improbis hostium Christi conatibus neminè offendi debere. Docemur autem illorum exemplo, vt ipsi quoq; quando persecutionum procellis agitamur, scripturae oracula in mentem reuocemus, & ea cumprimis, quibus ipse Christus testatur, perpetuas inter mundum & suos cultores inimicitias fore. Si de mundo esset (inquit) mundus, quod suum est, diligeret. At nunc ego vos selegi ex mundo, & ideo mundus vos odit. Iohan.15. & 16. Et Paulus persecutionem omnibus propositam esse dicit, qui volunt pie viuere in Christo. 2. Tim.3. Quò in primis pertinet, quòd in ipsa mundi origine Deus praedixit, perpetuas inimicitias fore inter serpentem & semen mulieris, id est, inter diabolum, mundi principem, & Christum, qui simul corpus suum, ecclesiam, sub se comprehendit. Horum consyderatione fit, vt persecutionibus non offendamur, quando ita diuinitus constitutum esse cernimus, vt mundi intemperie & furoribus pij quasi per ignem probentur. Quò illud Petri referri debet: Charissimi, ne miremini dum per ignem exploramini, quae res ad experimentum vestri fit, perinde ac si nouum aliquid vobis obtingat. Imò in hoc, quòd confortes estis affli&ionum Christi, gaudete, &c. 1. Pet.4. Caeterum prodest diligentius paulò inspicere, vt de hostium Christi conatibus spiritus sanctus cùm per Dauidem tum per ecclesiam credentium loquatur.
units.tr: In the second part they set out the narrative, in which they lay before God the plots of the enemies and the dangers that are hanging over them. They do not think he is ignorant of these things, but they want to unburden their minds of some of their cares and anxieties by setting down their complaints in God's bosom. This is the chief use of such narratives, which holy people were accustomed to weave into their prayers. This argument also commends God's goodness, who lends his ears so readily to our complaints and kindly listens to those who grieve over our miseries or dangers. They take the opening of the narrative from the second Psalm, in which David, illumined by the Spirit of God, described the kingdom of Christ together with the wicked efforts of the world by which it would be attacked. The sense of them all is: "Now we actually experience what you, O God, foretold long ago through David. For truly, in this city of Jerusalem, once called holy and the seat of righteousness, Herod and Pilate conspired against your Son, and the soldiers gathered from the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, who ought to have been wholly consecrated to you, etc." They do not repeat this old prophecy without reason. By it they teach that nothing new or unusual has happened here, and that therefore no one should be offended by the wicked attempts of Christ's enemies. We are taught by their example that when we are tossed by the storms of persecution we should call to mind the oracles of Scripture, and especially those in which Christ himself testifies that there will be perpetual enmity between the world and his worshippers. "If you were of the world," he says, "the world would love what is its own. But now I have chosen you out of the world, and therefore the world hates you" (John 15 and 16). And Paul says that persecution awaits all who wish to live godly in Christ (2 Tim. 3). To this belongs above all that God, at the very origin of the world, foretold that there would be perpetual enmity between the serpent and the seed of the woman, that is, between the devil, the prince of the world, and Christ, who at the same time comprehends under himself his body, the Church. By considering these things we are kept from being offended by persecutions, when we see that it has been so ordained by God that the godly are tested, as it were by fire, by the rage and fury of the world. To this should be referred the saying of Peter: "Beloved, do not be surprised when you are tried by fire, as if something new were happening to you. But rejoice insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, etc." (1 Pet. 4). Moreover, it is useful to look a little more carefully at how the Holy Spirit speaks of the attempts of Christ's enemies, both through David and through the Church of believers.

units.la: Primò ipsos conatus describit, dum illos fremere, meditari, insurgere & concurrere vel foederibus coniungi dicit. Exprimunt haec ardens & deuotum Christi & regni ipsius odium, quod omni modo euersum cupiant. Et pulchrè quidem studia illorum moresq; depingit. Cum enim gentes & populos, & reges inter Christi hostes numeret, singulis quod ipsis proprium est, tribuit. Gentes incredulae fremunt, vt quae affectuum potius rabie quàm consilio ducuntur. Populi (quo nomine ignobile vulgus intelligitur) meditantur siue loquuntur inania, dum inter pocula fere de Christi regno opprimendo verba faciunt. At reges & principes, quos regnorum suorum cura solicitos habet, exurgunt, conueniunt & publicè consultant, quibus armis aut rationibus Christus opprimi possit. Interim omnes hosce inania moliri siue meditari dicit. Quid enim contra Dominum mortales efficerent, quorum cogitationes vanæ sunt? Psalm.94. Concipiunt molestiam, parturiunt vanitatem, & pariunt mendacium. Psal.7. Et facile dissipat gentium consilia Deus, cuius consilium æternum stabit. Psalm.33. Huc pertinet quod pij apud prophetam dicunt: Congregamini populi, & vincemini: & audite vniuersæ procul terræ, confortamini, & vincemini: accingite vos, & vincemini: inite consilium, & dissipabitur: loquimini verbum, & non fiet, quia nobiscum Deus. Ifa.8. Exempla huius historias tum sacras tum ecclesiasticas legenti passim occurrunt, vt illorum prolixa commemoratione non fit opus. Memorabile tamen Iuliani apostatæ est, qui iam morituus adhuc Christi odio flagrans, dicere coactus est: Vicisti Galilæe, vicisti. Vt non temere pius quidam Christi cultor impio Sophistæ, quid faber Galilæus ageret, interroganti, responderit: Iuliano loculum parat aut feretrum.
units.tr: First, he describes the attempts themselves, saying that they rage, plot, rise up, and gather together or join in alliances. These words express the burning and devoted hatred of Christ and of his very kingdom, which they desire to overthrow by every means. And he paints their pursuits and characters beautifully. For when he numbers the nations, peoples, and kings among Christ's enemies, he assigns to each what is proper to it. The unbelieving nations rage, since they are driven more by the frenzy of their passions than by counsel. The peoples (by which name the common, ignoble crowd is meant) plot or speak empty things, while over their cups they talk almost entirely about crushing Christ's kingdom. But kings and princes, whom the care of their realms makes anxious, rise up, assemble, and publicly deliberate by what arms or arguments Christ might be crushed. Meanwhile he says that all of these are devising or plotting empty things. For what could mortals accomplish against the Lord, whose thoughts are vain? (Ps. 94). "They conceive trouble, they bring forth vanity, and they bring forth falsehood" (Ps. 7). And God easily scatters the counsels of the nations, whose eternal counsel shall stand (Ps. 33). To this pertains what the godly say through the prophet: "Gather together, O peoples, and you shall be broken; and give ear, all you far countries; gird yourselves, and you shall be broken; take counsel, and it shall come to nothing; speak the word, and it shall not stand, for God is with us" (Isa. 8). Examples of this are met everywhere in the reading of both sacred and ecclesiastical histories, so there is no need for a lengthy recital of them. Yet the case of Julian the Apostate is worth remembering, who, already dying and still burning with hatred of Christ, was compelled to say, "You have conquered, Galilean, you have conquered." So too a certain pious worshipper of Christ, when an impious sophist asked him what the Galilean carpenter was doing, did not answer at random: "He is preparing a coffin or a bier for Julian."

units.la: Deinde aduersus quem isti conatus tendant, indicatur. Conuenerunt in vnum aduersus dominū & aduersus vnctum eius. Leue videri poterat cum Christo susceptum certamen, propter vilem & abiectam assumptæ ab illo humanitatis speciem. Sed non tam Christi incarnati, quàm ipsius Dei hostes sunt. Vt enim qui vnicum regis filium regni hæredem & regem agnoscere dedignatur, & contra illum seditionum author est, cum ipso rege bellum suscepisse merito censetur: ita qui Dei filium regem & saluatorem agnoscere noluerit, ipsius Dei hostis dicitur, qui illi soli omnem potestatem regni sui, omnemq; humanæ redemptionis gloriam tradidit, vt omnes honorent filium, sicut honorant patrem. Ioban.5. Nec aliter quàm in filio Deus agnosci & honorari potest. Quare necessario Deum nec agnoscunt nec honorant, qui filium agnoscere & colere nolunt. Quod si ijdem contra filium Dei turbas excitent & arma capessant, impiorum gigantum instar, Deum ipsum bello nefario oppugnare censentur. Vidit hoc Baptista, cum ait: Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit illi in manum. Qui credit filio, habet vitam æternam. Qui verò non credit filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Ioban.3. Quis verò Dei hostem esse dubitet eum, qui iram Dei irreconciliabilem contra se prouocauit? Seruiunt hæc nostræ tum institutioni, ne tam immani impietate nos polluamus: tum consolationi, ne hostium viribus terreamur, quando nos illis impares esse videmus. Nec enim nostra hæc pugna est, sed Dei auspicijs bellum hoc geritur, cuius facillimum erit illorum conatus & vires pe-stundare. De quo Iohannes admonet, quando eum qui in nobis est, maiorem esse ait, quàm eum qui in mundo est. 1. Ioban. 4.
units.tr: Next, it is indicated against whom these attempts are directed. "They have gathered together against the Lord and against his Anointed" (Ps. 2). The contest undertaken with Christ might seem a slight one, because of the lowly and abject appearance of the humanity he had assumed. But they are enemies not so much of Christ incarnate as of God himself. For just as one who refuses to acknowledge the king's only son as heir and king of the realm, and is the author of sedition against him, is rightly judged to have waged war against the king himself, so one who will not acknowledge and honour God's Son as King and Saviour is said to be an enemy of God himself, who has given to him alone all power over his kingdom and all the glory of human redemption, "that all may honour the Son, even as they honour the Father" (John 5). Nor can God be acknowledged and honoured in any other way than in the Son. Therefore those who are unwilling to acknowledge and worship the Son necessarily neither acknowledge nor honour God. If they stir up tumults against the Son of God and take up arms, like the giants of impiety, they are judged to assail God himself in a wicked war. The Baptist saw this when he said: "The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand. He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not believe the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3). And who could doubt that he is an enemy of God who has provoked against himself the irreconcilable wrath of God? These considerations serve our instruction, lest we pollute ourselves with such monstrous impiety; and they serve our consolation, lest we be terrified by the strength of the enemies when we see ourselves unequal to them. For this battle is not ours; it is waged under God's auspices, and his will easily crush their attempts and their power. John warns of this when he says that he who is in us is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4).

units.la: Postremò effectum & finem impiorum eiusmodi conatuum euidentius exprimunt fideles, quando aiunt: Conuenerunt, vt facerent quæcunq; manus tua & consilium tuum priùs decreuerat fieri. Atqui non ideo conueniunt & consultant impij, vt Dei decretum exequantur. Sed illos non aliud efficere posse ostendunt, quàm quod Deus fieri decreuit, & tunc maximè Dei consilia adiuuare, quando illa impedire student. Manifestum hoc fiet, si quid Iudæorum sacerdotes fecerint, consyderet. Voluerunt illi prohibere ne regnum acciperet Christus. Ideo contra illum Romanos præsides & plebem concitant, nec ante desistunt, donec in cruce defunctum & sepultum vident. At quid omnibus hisce aliud effecerunt, quàm quòd Christus iuxta æternum patris decretum, mundi saluator factus, regnum accepit? Et horum quidem consyderatione offendiculo medentur, quo illi impingunt, qui impios suis viribus Christo superiores factos esse putant. Est autè hic singularis prouidentiæ Dei vsus, vt intelligamus impiorum conatus non vlterius posse progredi, quàm à Deo constitutum est. Obseruandum verò, illos in diuina prouidentia, non præscientiam modò, verumetiam decretum stabile & manum agnoscere, qua ipse quod decreuit pro suo arbitrio administrat & exequitur, vt ipse sit omnia in omnibus. Nec ideo excusantur impij, quando illos non ad Dei voluntatem & decretum respicere constat, sed corruptissimus suis affectibus indulgere, vt iam sæpe diximus. Et licet hoc verè sentiat & ingenuè profiteatur primitiua ecclesia, orat tamen, & Dei opem precibus ardentissimis implorat. Minimè ergo preces tollit ea doctrina, quæ diuinæ prouidentiæ res omnes & illarū euentus subijcit. Vult enim orari & invocari Deus: & hoc eò ardentius faciunt pij, quòd illius nutu res omnes administrari norunt. Faciunt enim quod ille iussit, consilia verò eius arcana non scrutantur curiosius, sed euentum omnem illi permittunt, quem fidelem esse sciunt, qui nos non vltra vires tentari patiatur, ac se diligentibus omnia ad finem lætum deducat.
units.tr: Finally, the faithful express more clearly the outcome and end of attempts of this kind when they say: "They have gathered together to do whatever your hand and your counsel had decided beforehand to be done" (Acts 4:28). Yet the wicked do not gather and consult in order to carry out God's decree. Rather, the words show that they can accomplish nothing but what God has decided shall be done, and that they then most of all further God's counsels when they strive to hinder them. This will become clear if we consider what the priests of the Jews did. They wished to prevent Christ from receiving his kingdom. Therefore they stirred up the Roman governors and the common people against him, and they did not stop until they saw him dead and buried on the cross. But what else did all these things accomplish, except that Christ, made the Saviour of the world according to the eternal decree of the Father, received his kingdom? By considering these things we also remedy the stumbling-block on which those stumble who think the wicked, by their own strength, have become superior to Christ. Here is a distinctive use of God's providence: we understand that the attempts of the wicked cannot proceed any further than God has appointed. We must observe that in divine providence we recognise not only foreknowledge but also a firm decree and a hand by which he administers and carries out, according to his own pleasure, what he has decreed, so that he may be all in all. Nor are the wicked thereby excused, since it is clear that they do not look to God's will and decree, but indulge their own corrupt affections, as we have often said. And although the primitive Church truly thinks this and openly professes it, it nonetheless prays and implores God's help with most ardent prayers. Therefore the doctrine that subjects all things and their outcomes to divine providence does not in the least take away prayer. For God wishes to be entreated and called upon, and the godly do this all the more eagerly because they know that all things are administered by his nod. For they do what he has commanded, and they do not pry too curiously into his hidden counsels, but commit every outcome to him, whom they know to be faithful, who will not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, and who will lead all things to a happy end for those who love him.

units.la: Porrò tertiam precationis huius partem videamus, quæ petitiones continet earum rerū, quibus se tunc quàm maximè opus habere videbant. Prima harum est: Et nunc Domine, inspice in minas eorum. Inspiciendi verbo iudicium & animaduersionem intelligūt, & perinde est, ac si Deum causæ huius vindicem expetant. Quis enim meliori iure se vindicem præbeat, quàm ille, cum aduersus hūc bellum hoc geri, Psalmi verbis probauerint? Est autem hoc peculiare pijs, vt quando vel vocatione sua se impediri, vel viribus inferiores esse sentiunt, Dei iudicium appellent, quod Dauidem in Saul linis persecutionibus frequenter facere videmus. Psalm. 7. 17. 26. & . Nunquam tamen maiori fiducia illud fieri potest, quàm cum ipsius Dei gloria ab impijs aperte petitur. Sic Ezechias Assyrij regis blasphemam epistolam in Domini conspectu expandit, & illum vt causæ suæ assertor esse dignetur, inuocat. Isa. 37. Nec dubium est, quin de sui nominis gloria solicitos exaudiat, qui priuatas suorum querelas tam clementer suscipere solet. Sed ne ita causam hanc Deo commendare videantur, vt ipsi sese omni periculo subducere conentur, eam quoq; sibi gratiam dari expetunt, vt cum fiducia Dei sermonem eloqui possint. Quod cumprimis de apostolis & reliquis verbi ministris intelligi debet, qui nisi Dei spiritu animentur & regantur, mundi minis & machinationibus facilè terreri possunt, vt officium suum intermittant. Quod & Paulus post multiuarios sui ministerij labores agnoscit, & proinde publicis ecclesiarum precibus se adiuuari vult, vt aperto & libero ore Christi verbum proferre possit. Ephef. 6. Interim ad singulos fideles hoc etiam referri debet, & pro singulis orari conuenit, vt Christum ingenuè & intrepidè coram mundo hoc prauo & adultero confiteantur. Necesse autem est, vt hanc fiduciam nobis diuinitus conferri intelligamus. Ita enim extimulamur, vt pro fidei incremento subinde oremus, cum apostolis clamantes: Domine, adauge nobis fidem. Luc. 17. Tertiò miraculorum virtutem augeri postulant, eò quòd illa Christus doctrinæ apostolorum quasi sigilla & publica testimonia constituit. Marc. 16. Ioban. 14. Per Christi verò nomen illa fieri cupiunt, vt testentur, se de solius Christi gloria solicitos esse. Admirabilis autem hic elucet primitiuæ ecclesiæ fortitudo, & flagrantissimus Christi zelus. Senserant paulò ante apostolorum doctrina & miraculis Pontificum animos exacerbatos esse. Attamen maiorem dicendi fiduciam apostolis concedi & miraculorum dona augeri petunt, tam abest, vt hostium furori ad tempus cedendum esse existiment: quod nostri seculi homines solent, qui eam docendi rationem optimam esse ducunt, quæ professis etiam veritatis hostibus probari potest, nec aliud quàm ocium & mundi pacem quærunt, de regni Christi incremento nihil aut parum soliciti. Qui tales sunt, ministros nimium feruere putant, & sæpe eos quoq; qui plus satis tepent. Quæ mihi potissima caussa videtur, quòd parum feliciter inter nos Christi regnum propagatur.
units.tr: Next let us consider the third part of this prayer, which contains the petitions for the things they then saw they needed most. The first of these is: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats." By "look upon" they understand judgment and punishment, and it is as if they were asking God to be the avenger of this cause. For who could more rightly show himself the avenger than he, since by the words of the Psalm they have proved that this war is waged against him? It is, however, peculiar to the godly that whenever they feel hindered in their calling or weaker than their enemies, they call upon God's judgment, as we often see David doing against Saul in his persecutions. Psalm 7, 17, 26. Yet this can never be done with greater confidence than when the glory of God itself is openly sought from the ungodly. So Hezekiah spread out the blasphemous letter of the king of Assyria before the sight of the Lord, and calls upon him to deign to be the champion of his cause. Isa. 37. Nor is there doubt that he who so graciously receives the private complaints of his own people will hear those who are anxious for the glory of his name. But lest they seem to commend this cause to God in such a way that they themselves try to withdraw from every danger, they also ask for this grace to be given them, that they may be able to speak the word with confidence in God. This ought to be understood especially of the apostles and the other ministers of the Word, who, unless they are animated and governed by the Spirit of God, can easily be frightened by the threats and plots of the world, so that they abandon their duty. Paul also acknowledges this after his many labours in the ministry, and therefore wants to be helped by the public prayers of the churches, so that he may be able to utter the word of Christ with an open and free mouth. Eph. 6. Meanwhile, this ought also to be applied to each of the faithful, and it is fitting to pray for each one, that they may confess Christ frankly and fearlessly before this perverse and adulterous world. But we must understand that this confidence is conferred on us from heaven. For we are so stirred up that we pray from time to time for an increase of faith, crying out with the apostles: "Lord, increase our faith." Luke 17. Thirdly, they ask that the power of miracles be increased, because Christ established those miracles as, so to speak, seals and public testimonies to the teaching of the apostles. Mark 16. John 14. They desire that these be done through the name of Christ, so that they may bear witness that they are concerned for the glory of Christ alone. Here the remarkable courage of the primitive Church and its most ardent zeal for Christ shine forth. A little before, they had perceived that the minds of the high priests had been inflamed by the apostles' teaching and miracles. Yet they ask that greater confidence in speaking be granted to the apostles and that the gifts of miracles be increased; so far are they from thinking that they should yield for a time to the fury of their enemies. This is what the men of our age are accustomed to do, who consider the best method of teaching to be one that can win approval even from professed enemies of the truth, and who seek nothing but leisure and the peace of the world, being little or not at all concerned about the growth of Christ's kingdom. Such men think ministers burn too hotly, and often they think even those who are lukewarm enough are too zealous. This seems to me the chief reason why Christ's kingdom is spread so unsuccessfully among us.

units.la: Postremò, quis precum effectus fuerit, docet Lucas. Exaudiuit enim precantes Deus, quod tum sensibili signo, loci nimirum concussione (quæ numinis præsentiam significabat) tum effectu saluberrimè declarauit. Nam spiritu sancto repleti sunt, id est, efficacem spiritus consolationem & animos sibi addi senserunt, quos periculorum metus nonnihil terruerat. Et quibus euangelij ministerium commissum erat, summa constantia illud prædicauerunt: sic vt hostium minis accen-sos potius & inflammatos, quàm territos putares: de quo in sequenti sermone plura dicentur. Docemur hoc exemplo, piorum preces à Deo nequaquam negligi, cuius oculi ad iustos intenti sunt, & illorum votis aures ipsius patent. Psalm. 34. Imitemur ergo primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplum nostro seculo, quando passim contra veritatem luculentissimi hostes conspirant: & ad Dominum per preces conuersi, illi causam omnem committamus, petamus autem ab illo fidei & spiritus sancti incrementa, ne vllis periculis & terroribus vincamur, sed felici vitæ cursu peracto, in cœleste regnum transferamur, cum Iesu Christo victuri: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Luke shows what the effect of their prayers was. For God heard those who prayed, and declared this most salutarily both by a visible sign, namely the shaking of the place (which signified the presence of the divine power), and by the result. For they were filled with the Holy Spirit, that is, they felt the effective consolation of the Spirit and their courage was increased, though the fear of dangers had somewhat terrified them. And those to whom the ministry of the gospel had been entrusted preached it with the greatest constancy, so that you would think them kindled and inflamed by the threats of their enemies rather than frightened; more will be said about this in the following sermon. We are taught by this example that the prayers of the godly are by no means neglected by God, whose eyes are fixed on the righteous, and whose ears are open to their prayers. Psalm 34. Let us therefore imitate the example of the primitive Church in our own age, when most brilliant enemies everywhere conspire against the truth; let us turn to the Lord by prayer, commit our whole cause to him, and ask of him increases of faith and of the Spirit, so that we may not be overcome by any dangers or terrors, but, having finished the course of this life happily, may be carried into the heavenly kingdom to live with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXI.

units.la: Et loquebantur sermonem Dei cum fiducia. Multitudinis autem credentium erat cor vnum & anima vna: nec quisquâ aliquid eorum quæ possidebat, dicebat suum esse: sed erant illis omnia communia. Et magna virtute reddebant apostoli testimonium resurrectionis Domini Iesu: magnaq; gratia erat super omnes ipsos. Nec enim inter ipsos aliquis egenus erat. Quotquot enim erant possessores agrorum vel domorum ijs diuenditis, illorū pretia afferebant, & ponebant ad pedes apo‑stolorum. Distribuebatur autem singulis, prout cuiq; opus erat. Ioses au‑tem cognominatus Barnabas ab apostolis (quod est, filius consolatio‑nis) Leuita, Cyprius genere, cum haberet agrum, vendidit illum, & at‑tulit pecuniam, & posuit ad pedes Apostolorum.
units.tr: "And they spoke the word of God with boldness. The multitude of those who believed had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. And with great power the apostles gave witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. Nor was there any among them who lacked, for as many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them at the apostles' feet. And distribution was made to every man according as he had need. And Joses, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, The son of consolation), a Levite, and of the country of Cyprus, having land, sold it, and brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet."

units.la: Quemadmodum diuus Lucas primam, quae aduersus apostolos concitata est, persecutionem diligenter descripsit: ita non minori diligentia, quid in illis turbis fideles fecerint, commemorat. Finis omnium est, ut inde quid in simili casu nos facere conueniat, discamus. Primus autem locus precibus datus, quas vnanimi & ardenti studio ad Deum fuderunt. Ad Deum ergo nos quoq; in aduersis conuerti decet, non ad vana carnis praesidia. Petenda vero sunt, non quae carnis securi‑tati & ocio seruiant, sed quae ad regni Christi propagationem facere possunt. Sed videamus reliqua ecclesiae primitiuae studia, ex quibus patebit, illos nihil eorum intermisisse, quae officij ipsorum erant.
units.tr: Just as the divine Luke described carefully the first persecution stirred up against the apostles, so with no less care he records what the faithful did in those troubles. The purpose of it all is that we may learn what we ought to do in a similar case. The first place is given to prayers, which they poured out to God with one mind and burning zeal. So we too, in adversity, ought to turn to God and not to the vain protections of the flesh. We must ask not for what serves the security and ease of the flesh, but for what can advance the kingdom of Christ. But let us look at the other endeavours of the primitive Church, from which it will be clear that they neglected none of the things that belonged to their office.

units.la: Primò de apostolis agit & omnibus ijs, quibus docendi munus commissum erat. Dicitur de hu‑quod sermonem Dei cum fiducia, id est, ingenuè & liberè praedicarint. Quibus paulò post additur: Magna virtute reddebant apostoli testimonium resurrectionis Domini Iesu. Fecerunt ergo, quod facturos esse contra Concilij decretum protestati erant. Solius vero resurrectionis meminit Lucas, non quod hanc solam praedicarint, sed quia per hanc redemptionis & salutis nostrae negotium Chri‑stus absoluit, & ne apostolos Sadducaeis, qui tunc primatum tenebant, quicquam concessisse putemus. Non temere vero doctrinae ante omnia alia mentionem facit Lucas, quandoquidem prima semper illius ratio haberi debet. Quia enim per hanc nos regenerari constat, & eadem fidelium ecclesia colli‑tur, sine hac ecclesia statu salvo & incolumi seruari non potest. Nec absq; spiritus sancti suggestione olim Solomon dixit: Cum defecerit prophetia, dissipatur populus. Et hoc vere dictum esse, omnium saeculorum exempla abunde testantur. Quare vt supra ecclesiam in apostolorum sermone & doctrina perseuerauisse dixit: ita nunc apostolos quoq; sui officij memores & studiosissimos fuisse testatur. Quo exemplo ministri admonentur, ne persecutionum metu & hostium minus praedicandi libertatem sibi extorqueri patiantur, nec periculis imminentibus Christi oues verbi doctrina & consolatione deficiant. Hoc enim mercenariorum est, ut Christus admonet, non eorum, qui iuxta Christi exemplum animas suas pro ouibus suae fidei commissis deponere parati sunt. Iohan.10. At quia plurimum in hoc peccatur, prodest exemplum hoc diligentius excutere, ut ex eo ministri intelligat, quid ipsos facere conueniat. Et primò quidem ingenua docendi libertas & intrepida animi fiducia apostolis tribuitur. Quam omnibus ministris necessariam esse constat, eò quòd semper inueniri solent, qui ipsis frenum inijcere conantur. Nam veritatis lucem mundo inuisam esse Christus testatur. Iohan.3. Idem admonitionum quoq; & correptionis impatientissimus est. Quare olim exiterunt, qui prophetis dicere auderent: Ne prophetetis. Ne contemplemini nobis plana, loquimini nobis blanda, contemplamini nobis illusiones, recedite a via, declinate a semita, facite quiescere a facie nostra sanctum Israel. Amos 2. Isa.30. Et Paulus nouissimo saeculo eos regnaturos dicit, qui veritatis sermonem sustinere non possint, quiq; auribus prurientibus eiusmodi doctores coacernaturi sint, qui ipsorum affectibus conuenientem doctrinam afferant. 2. Tim.4. Quod autem ille praedixit, passim fieri cernimus. Hic ergo apostolica libertas & intrepida praedicandi fiducia requiritur, qua opportune & importune suo officio insistant ecclesiarum antistites, vt & alijs animos addant, de quibus spes bona superest, & suas animas liberent, ne ab ipsorum manibus pereuntiu sanguis exigatur. Ezech.3. & 33. Deinde resurrectionis Christi articulum prae alijs inculcauisse dicuntur apostoli. At qui hic ipsius erat, quo praecipue offendebantur Iudaeorum antistites. Partim enim per hunc iniustae caedis Christi commincebantur, partim Sadducaeis intolerabilis erat illius praedicatio, eum illi resurrectione aperte negarent. Nihilominus tamen hunc constanter & intrepide praedicant, ita vt de hoc vno soliciti esse videri possint. Docet exemplum hoc, eos articulos praecipue vrgendos esse, qui ab aduersarijs quam maxime oppugnantur. Ad aedificationem enim omnia destinari decet in verbi ministerio. 1. Cor.14. 2. Cor.10. Proxima vero cura sit, ne quod aedificatum est, denuò collabatur. Atqui neutrum ex his feliciter exequetur, qui non ea parte se constantissimè opposuerit, vbi doctrinæ veritas, aduersario-rum artibus & tyrannide oppugnata, præcipuè laborat. Qui vrbibus & castris præsidio dati sunt, illuc ferè vires omnes conferunt, vbi hostes fortissimi impressionem faciunt. Idem obseruent, quos ec-clesiæ suæ præsides & pastores dedit dominus. Nec audiendi sunt, qui ea reticenda & supprimenda esse censent, quorum prædicatione hostes exacerbari solent. Verbi enim ministros nos dominus con-stituit, non iudices siue magistros, ex quorum arbitrio doctrina pendere debeat. Impijssima ergo est illorum confidentia, qui tantum sibi tribuunt, vt spiritui sancto, qui vnicus ecclesiæ & doctrinæ gu-bernator est, præscribere audeant.
units.tr: First, he speaks of the apostles and of all those to whom the office of teaching had been entrusted. It is said of them that they preached the word of God "with boldness," that is, that they preached openly and freely. A little later it is added: "With great power the apostles gave witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus." They therefore did what they had declared they would do against the decree of the Council. Luke mentions only the resurrection, not because they preached this alone, but because by it Christ completed the business of our redemption and salvation, and so that we might not think the apostles yielded anything to the Sadducees, who then held the chief place. Luke does not mention doctrine before all other things without reason, since its due place must always be first. For it is certain that we are regenerated through it, and by it the faithful Church is gathered together, and without it the Church cannot be preserved in a sound and safe condition. Nor did Solomon say without the prompting of the Holy Spirit: "When prophecy fails, the people is scattered" [Prov. 29.18]. That this is truly said, the examples of all ages abundantly bear witness. Therefore, just as he said above that the Church persevered in the apostles' teaching and doctrine, so now he testifies that the apostles too were mindful of their office and most diligent in it. By this example ministers are admonished not to allow the freedom of preaching to be wrung from them by fear of persecutions or by enemies, nor to let Christ's sheep fail, in the face of impending dangers, of the teaching and comfort of the word. For this, as Christ warns, belongs to hired men, not to those who, following Christ's example, are ready to lay down their lives for the sheep committed to their faith [John 10]. Because this is sinned against most often, it is useful to examine this example more carefully, so that ministers may understand what they ought to do. And first, boldness of teaching and fearless confidence of spirit are attributed to the apostles. It is clear that this is necessary for all ministers, since there are always people who try to put a bridle on them. For Christ testifies that the light of truth is hateful to the world [John 3]. The same world is most impatient of admonition and correction. So long ago there arose men who dared to say to the prophets: "Do not prophesy. Do not look at us for plain things; speak to us smooth things, look for us deceits; get out of the way, turn aside from the path, cause the Holy One of Israel to cease from before us" [Amos 2; Isa. 30]. And Paul says that in the last age there will be those who cannot endure the word of truth, and who will heap up for themselves teachers of this sort, who bring doctrine suited to their own desires, having itching ears [2 Tim. 4]. What he foretold we see happening everywhere. Here, then, the apostolic freedom and fearless confidence in preaching is required, by which the leaders of the churches may keep at their office in season and out of season, both to add courage to others, in whom good hope remains, and to free their own souls, so that the blood of those who perish is not required at their hands [Ezek. 3 and 33]. Next, the apostles are said to have inculcated before others the article of Christ's resurrection. But this was the very thing by which the chief men of the Jews were chiefly offended. For partly by it they were convicted of the unjust murder of Christ, and partly the Sadducees found its preaching intolerable, since they openly denied the resurrection. Nevertheless, the apostles preach it constantly and fearlessly, so that they may seem to be concerned about this one thing alone. This example teaches that those articles especially must be pressed which are most strongly attacked by opponents. For in the ministry of the word all things ought to be directed to edification [1 Cor. 14; 2 Cor. 10]. The next care must be that what has been built is not thrown down again. But neither of these will be successfully carried out by one who has not most steadfastly opposed the point where the truth of doctrine, assailed by the arts and tyranny of adversaries, is especially in danger. Those who are set to guard cities and camps generally bring all their strength to bear where the fiercest enemies make their assault. Let those whom the Lord has given as overseers and pastors of his church observe the same. Nor are those to be heard who think that those things should be passed over and suppressed by whose preaching enemies are commonly provoked. For the Lord has appointed us ministers of the word, not judges or masters, on whose judgment doctrine ought to depend. Therefore the confidence of those is most impious, who claim so much for themselves as to dare to prescribe to the Holy Spirit, who alone is the governor of the Church and of doctrine.

units.la: Secundò vnanimitati & concordiæ totam ecclesiam studuisse docet. Multitudinis (inquit) cre-dentium erat cor vnum, & anima vna. Sensus est, vnam eandemque omnibus voluntatem siue studium fuisse, cuius finis haud dubiè non fuit alius, quàm regni Christi propagatio. Hæc voluntatum & studiorum similitudo, veram amicitiam & stabilem concordiam gignit. Qui enim ad hanc metam simul contendunt, vt Christi regnum propagent, à priuati commodi studio alienissimi sunt, quod vnum omnes amicitias interturbare solet. Insigne autem hoc spiritus sancti opus fuisse patebit, si cogitemus multitudinem credentium quinque millia virorum habuisse, in quorum omnium studijs consensus hic euidenter apparet. Est autem hæc propria verè fidelium nota, qua ipsos carere impossibile est. Qui enim vnum in cœlis patrem agnoscunt, vno baptismo initiati sunt, vnum sub Christo capite corpus sunt, & vno spiritu Christi omnes animantur, fieri nequit, vt mutuis dissidijs discerpantur. 1. Cor. 12. Ephes. 4. Ideò Christus hanc ipsam suorum tesseram constituit, dicens: In hoc cognoscent omnes, quòd discipuli mei estis, si charitatem inter vos habueritis mutuam. Iohan. 13. Et vicissim Paulus Corinthios adhuc carnales esse hoc argumento euincit, quòd æmulationibus, contentionibus & factionibus mutuis scinderentur. 1. Corinth. 3. Est verò obseruatione dignissimum, quòd hostium minis & impijs conatibus auditis, animorum coniunctioni & mutuæ concordiæ tam ardenter studerent. Est id proprium charitati, vt tum maximè suos effectus prodat, quando periculis & necessitate fratres circumuentos, ope & auxilio cumprimis indigere videt. Arguuntur autem exemplo hoc nostri seculi mores, quos ab vnanimitatis & concordiæ studio alienissimos esse constat. Audimus inter euangelicæ doctrinæ & fidei professores factiosa Zuinglianorum & Lutheranorum nomina. Et æmulationum studio ac feruore eousque progressum est, vt cum alterutri parti periculum imminet, reliqui fratres periclitantes deserant, & omni commiserationis affectu posito, tacitè in finum gaudeant, imò gaudium suum non raro acerbis scommatis testentur, adeoque Christi membris in cruce pendentibus acetum felle mixtum propinent. Vt interim de contentionibus, conuitijs, opprobrijs & obtrectationibus mutuis nihil dicam. Periculum itaque est, ne dum inuicem mordemus, mutuis morsibus consumamur. Galat. 5. Animis per charitatem prius coniungi oportet, quicunque Dei præsentem opem in periculis expetunt.
units.tr: Second, he teaches that the whole Church was zealous for unanimity and harmony. "The multitude," he says, "of those who believed had one heart and one soul." The meaning is that there was one and the same will or zeal in all, whose end was undoubtedly nothing other than the propagation of Christ's kingdom. This likeness of wills and zeal produces true friendship and lasting concord. For those who strive together toward this goal, that Christ's kingdom may be spread, are most alien to the pursuit of private advantage, which alone is wont to throw all friendships into confusion. This will be seen to be a remarkable work of the Holy Spirit if we consider that the multitude of believers numbered five thousand men, in whose zeal this agreement clearly appears. Moreover, this is the proper mark of those who are truly faithful, and it is impossible for them to lack it. For those who acknowledge one Father in heaven, have been initiated by one baptism, are one body under Christ the head, and are all quickened by the one Spirit of Christ, cannot be torn apart by mutual dissensions [1 Cor. 12; Eph. 4]. Therefore Christ made this very thing the token of his own, saying: "By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one to another" [John 13]. And conversely, Paul proves by this argument that the Corinthians were still carnal, because they were torn apart by emulations, contentions and mutual factions [1 Cor. 3]. It is most worthy of notice that, on hearing of the threats of enemies and their impious attempts, they were so eager for the joining of minds and mutual harmony. It is the nature of love to show its effects most of all when it sees brothers beset by dangers and need, and especially in want of help and assistance. The customs of our own age are also rebuked by this example, for it is clear that they are most alien to the zeal for unanimity and concord. We hear among the professors of the evangelical doctrine and faith the factious names of Zwinglians and Lutherans. And by the zeal and heat of emulation it has gone so far that when danger threatens one side, the other brothers abandon those in peril, and, laying aside all feeling of compassion, rejoice in secret, indeed often show their joy by bitter taunts, and so give vinegar mixed with gall to drink to the members of Christ hanging on the cross. I say nothing for now of contentions, reproaches, insults and mutual slanders. There is therefore a danger that while we bite one another, we are consumed by mutual bites [Gal. 5]. Whoever seeks the present help of God in dangers ought first to be joined in heart through love.

units.la: Cæterum ne quis putaret animorum coniunctionem in nudo & inani affectu subsistisse, tertio loco vt hanc ipsis rebus testati sint, docet. In primis autem beneficentiæ & subuentionis pauperum meminit, cuius studium non possunt intermittere, quorum animi in Christo concordes sunt. Et est locus ille consideratione dignissimus, tum propter Anabaptistas, qui (vt supra Cap. 2. diximus) hinc Platonicam rerum communionem elicere conantur: tum propter pseudoeuangelicos, qui Christianæ communicationis studium omne intermittunt. Vtque euidentior sit totius loci tractatio, primò summam negotij huius, deinde ordinem & modum à fidelibus hic obseruatum, tandem verò qui huius effectus siue fructus fuerint, consyderabimus.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone think that this union of minds consisted only in an inward and empty feeling, he teaches that, in the third place, the faithful should attest it by deeds. He mentions above all the beneficence and relief of the poor, a zeal which those whose minds are united in Christ cannot give up. That passage deserves close attention, both because of the Anabaptists, who (as we said in chapter 2 above) try to draw from it a Platonic communion of goods, and because of the pseudo-evangelicals, who abandon all zeal for Christian fellowship in giving. So that the treatment of the passage may be clearer, we will consider first the substance of this matter, then the order and manner observed here by the faithful, and finally what the effects or fruits of it were.

units.la: Summam huius negotij paucis verbis complectitur, cùm ait: Nemo aliquid eorum, quæ possidebat, dicebat suum esse, sed erant illis omnia communia. Non negatur hic rerum proprietas, cum possessionis mentio differtè fiat: sed animi affectum exprimit, quo fideles præditi fuerunt. Qui licet domus, prædia & alia eius generis bona possiderent, nemo tamen illa sibi ita vendicabat, vt sibi soli data putaret, sed eadem aliorum quoque vsui & necessitati patere volebat. Vnde colligimus, voluntate ipsis omnia communia fuisse, non legibus: qua ratione amicorum omnia communia esse, proverbio dicitur. Atqui hoc loco verus Christianæ beneficentiæ & communicationis fons indicatur, animus nimirum, qui diuitiarum studio minimè addictus est, sed de illis & illarum vsu verè iudicat. Nam iuxta Pauli sententiam opum huius seculi usus in solo victu & amictu (sub quo domicilium quoque comprehendimus) versatur, cùm nudi in mundum nascamur, nec quicquam inde nobis efferre liceat, 1. Timoth. 6. At quia fidelis intelligit, pauca humanæ naturæ sufficere posse, nimio accumulandarum opum studio immergi nequit, nec in illis thesaurum suum situm putat, & licet eas sibi affluere videat, non tamen illis cor apponit. Psal. 62. Matth. 6. Imò dispensationem solam sibi commissam intelligens, de iniquo Mammone sibi amicos facere satagit, qui ipsum, ubi defecerit, in æterna tabernacula recipiant. Luc. 16. Facit consyderatio hæc, ut fideles cum aliis sua communia habeant ut re, licet proprietatis ius sibi ipsis retineant.
units.tr: Luke sums up the substance of the matter in a few words when he says: "None of those things which he possessed said that any of them was his own, but they had all things in common." Private ownership is not denied here, since mention is made of possession in plain terms; rather, the passage expresses the disposition of mind with which the faithful were endowed. Although they owned houses, estates and other goods of that kind, no one so claimed these for himself as to think they were given to him alone; instead, he was willing that they should be open to the use and need of others also. From this we gather that all things were held in common by their will, not by law. This is the sense of the proverb that the goods of friends are common. Indeed, in this passage the true source of Christian beneficence and fellowship is pointed out, namely a mind that is not devoted to the pursuit of riches, but judges rightly about them and about their use. For according to Paul's teaching, the use of the riches of this world lies only in food and clothing (under which we include a dwelling), since we are born naked into the world and can carry nothing out of it (1 Tim. 6). But because the faithful man understands that few things suffice for human nature, he cannot be swallowed up in the excessive pursuit of heaping up wealth; he does not place his treasure in such things, and although he sees them flowing in upon him, he does not set his heart upon them (Ps. 62; Matt. 6). Indeed, understanding that the stewardship alone has been entrusted to him, he takes care to make friends for himself by the unrighteous mammon, who, when it fails, will receive him into the eternal tabernacles (Luke 16). This consideration brings it about that the faithful hold their goods in common with others in fact, although they retain the right of ownership for themselves.

units.la: Ad illustrationem huius sententiæ facit modus & ordo, quem in communicatione ista observarunt. De hoc enim ait Lucas: Quotquot erant possessores domorum & agrorum, iis diuendebant, illorum pretia afferebat, & ponebant ad pedes apostolorum. Distribuebatur autem singulis prout cuique opus erat. Primò domos & prædia diuendita fuisse dicit, quod nec ab omnibus, nec ita factum est, ut omnibus venditis nihil sibi retinerent. Extant enim multorum exempla, qui domus proprias posuerunt, & familias aluerunt, quod à Paulo non permissum modò esse, verumetiam graviter præcipi legimus. 1. Tim. 5. Vendiderunt ergo quantum præsens ecclesiæ necessitas requirere videbatur, & ex unius cuiusque arbitrio pendebat, sua vel retinere vel diuendere, ut ex Petri verbis ad Ananiam infra patebit. Deinde pretia sive pecuniam non in commune palàm deponebant, sed afferebant ad pedes apostolorum, quibus hanc distribuendi ius permissum esse volebant, donec publico ecclesiæ consensu diaconi ordinati sunt, qui isti negotio præessent. Act. 6. At nec apostoli quidem ad se delatas pecunias ita publicabant, ut unicuique liceret inde quod libebat auferre: sed distribuebatur singulis prout cuique opus erat. Nulla igitur hic fuit inordinata bonorum communicatio, nulla rerum confusio, nulla violenta alienarum opum usurpatio, qualem fanatici & seditiosi homines somniant. Et si circumstantias omnes expendamus, facile patebit, communicationem hanc eo duntaxat nomine fuisse institutam, ut publicas haberet opes ecclesia, quæ pauperum subuentioni seruirent, ne illi egestate coguntur à Christi fide & corpore ecclesiæ deficere: nec admittebantur in illorum bonorum usurpationem, qui vel proprias facultates habere, vel honesto aliquo labore victum sibi parare poterant. Interim hic obseruanda venit ecclesiasticorum bonorum ratio. Origo illorum est, quæ hic describitur. Ut enim in primitiua ecclesia opulentiores sanctâ liberalitate suas opes ecclesiæ contulerunt, ita sequentibus posteâ seculis factum est, ut crescente Christianorum numero, reges & principes alii, quorum lautior fortuna fuit, horum exemplum imitati, ecclesias & collegia annuis reditibus ac decimis dita rent, quemadmodum fundationes antiquæ testantur. Vsum verò bonorum eiusmodi esse voluerunt, ut ex illis doctrina conseruaretur, & pauperes alerentur: quos ecclesiæ à Christo cumprimis commendatos esse noverant. Quem usum hodie quoque in ecclesiis vel seruari, vel collapsum restitui oportet, si veteris & primitiuæ ecclesiæ formam aliquam extare volumus. Sed facilius est hunc cum gemitu requirere, quàm reducere. Eò enim audaciæ peruenit impietas, ut plerique non vereantur sibi vendicare, quæ ecclesiis olim ex maiorum liberalitate donata sunt. Et hic fere reformationes ecclesiarum, quotquot nostro seculo tentatæ sunt, substitisse vidimus, quasi satis sit monachis & sacrificulis bonorum ecclesiæ administrationem eripuisse, cùm veteris & legitimi usus restitutio potius exigatur. Imò præstaret, impuris hypocritis illa relinquere, quàm ad eundem cum ipsis lapidem offendere. Quòd si verò veteris ecclesiæ exemplo nostra, si ita necessitas ferat, ecclesiis conferre debemus: atrocem illorum culpam esse oportet, qui cùm nihil de suo largiantur, quæ ab aliis data sunt palàm diripiunt. Hinc fieri videmus, ut & pauperes negligantur, & ministri rariores sint, omnisque religio pa- sim euanescat.
units.tr: The manner and order which they observed in this fellowship help to illustrate this teaching. Luke speaks of this: "As many as were possessors of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them down at the apostles' feet. And distribution was made to every man according as he had need." First he says that houses and lands were sold, which was done neither by all, nor in such a way that they kept nothing for themselves after everything had been sold. For there are many examples of people who gave up their own houses and yet supported their households, and we read that Paul not only permitted this but strictly commanded it (1 Tim. 5). They therefore sold as much as the present need of the Church seemed to require, and it depended on the judgement of each person whether he would keep his goods or sell them, as will become clear below from Peter's words to Ananias. Next, they did not openly deposit the money or proceeds as common property, but brought it to the feet of the apostles, to whom they wished the right of distributing it to be granted, until by the common consent of the Church deacons were ordained to take charge of this business (Acts 6). Yet not even the apostles so made the money that had been brought to them common that each might take from it whatever he liked; rather, distribution was made to each according as he had need. Therefore there was here no disorderly sharing of goods, no confusion of property, no violent seizure of other people's wealth, such as fanatics and seditious men dream of. And if we weigh all the circumstances, it will readily become plain that this fellowship was established for the sole purpose that the Church might have public resources to serve the relief of the poor, so that they would not be forced by want to fall away from the faith of Christ and the body of the Church. Nor were those admitted to the use of these goods who could have their own means or could provide for themselves by some honest labour. Meanwhile, the account of church property must be observed here. Its origin is what is described in this passage. For just as in the primitive Church the wealthier contributed their resources to the Church out of holy generosity, so in the following centuries it came about that, as the number of Christians grew, kings and other princes whose fortunes were more abundant imitated this example and endowed churches and colleges with annual revenues and tithes, as the ancient foundations bear witness. But they wished the use of such goods to be that by them teaching might be maintained and the poor fed, whom they knew the Church had been especially commended to by Christ. This use ought to be either kept today in the churches or restored where it has collapsed, if we wish any form of the old and primitive Church to remain. But it is easier to lament this with groans than to bring it back. For impiety has come to such audacity that many do not hesitate to claim for themselves what was once given to the churches out of the generosity of their forebears. And we have seen that most of the reformations of the Church attempted in our century have stopped here, as if it were enough to have taken the administration of the Church's goods away from monks and little priests, when what is really demanded is the restoration of the old and lawful use. Indeed, it would be better to leave these things to impure hypocrites than to stumble over the same stone as they do. But if, following the example of the old Church, we ought to contribute to the churches out of our own means, if necessity so requires, then surely those who give nothing of their own yet openly plunder what others have given must bear the monstrous guilt. Hence we see both that the poor are neglected and that ministers are scarcer, and that all religion is fading away everywhere.

units.la: Sed eximium Christianæ communionis fructum videamus, quem huic descriptioni Lucas interserit, ut hinc colligamus, quid nobis hodie sperandum sit, qui illius studium tam facilè neglige- gimus. Duplicem hunc indicat euangelista. Primò enim effectum est, ut nemo inter illos egenus haberetur. Quare legi satisfecerunt, quæ prohibet, ne sit mendicus in Israel. Deut. 15. Videtur hoc multis impossibile hodie, dum pauperum multitudinem respiciunt. Sed confutantur primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplo. Qua ratione enim impossibile videri debet in pace & ocio agentibus, quod inter medios hostes in urbe sanguinaria pij homines effectum dederunt? Potuerunt illi suis opibus pauperes omnes alere, & nos opulentißimarum donationum & maximarum opum, quibus iam olim ecclesiæ donatæ sunt, subsidio instructi, hoc nobis impossibile factu putabimus? Seruetur modus, ut cuique detur prout opus habuerit, & benedictione domini ac piorum liberalitate nos adiuuari sentiemus, ut nulla nobis difficultas sit reliqua. Difficile autem & impossibile est quod exigimus, quia præposteró modo & ordine res agitur. Minimum enim accipiunt, qui pluribus indigebant: & plurimum in eos confertur, quorum erat propriας opes ecclesiæ largiri. Quòd si vero expendamus, quantum periculi, molestiæ & incommodi cum publice tum priuatim ex mendicorum & egentium multitudine enasci soleat, inæstimabilis erit primus hic Christianæ communicationis fructus, quem inde primitiua ecclesia percepit. Sed alius ex hoc enatus est, quòd magna erat super omnes ipsos gratia: id est, gratiosi & accepti fuerunt toti populo, & ijs etiam, qui Christi cognitione nondum illustrati erant. Ea enim beneficentia vis est, ut hostes quoq; in sui admirationem & amorem abripiat. Et quia dominus sibi collatum putat, quod in pauperes ipsius nomine confertur, hoc præmio beneficos remunerare consueuit, ut apud plerosq; hominum gratia & authoritate valeant. Hoc unum si hodie consyderemus, non mirabimur, cur omnibus inuisi & exosi sint, quicunq; euangelij nomen profitentur. Nam præter illud, quod veritatis lucem mundus odit, & huius improbitate nos Deus exerceri vult, meretur hoc animorum duritia, qua Christi egenos negligimus: ut interim de improbitate ea nihil dicam, qua ecclesiæ bona sub euangelicæ reformationis prætextu diripimus, clamante interim pauperum turba, in quorum alimoniam illa impendi oportebat. Conferamus primitiuæ ecclesiæ morem cum ijs, quæ ipsi facimus, & nisi nos nostrijpsorum pudebit, non perfrictæ modò, sed plusquam meretriciæ frontis homines merito dicemur.
units.tr: But let us look at the remarkable fruit of Christian fellowship which Luke inserts into this account, so that from it we may gather what we ought today to hope for, we who so easily neglect its zeal. The evangelist points out this twofold fruit. First, it came about that no one among them was regarded as needy. Hence they satisfied the law which forbids that there be a beggar in Israel (Deut. 15). Many think this impossible today, when they look at the multitude of the poor. But the example of the primitive Church refutes them. For why should it seem impossible to people living in peace and leisure what godly men achieved in the midst of enemies in a bloodthirsty city? They were able to feed all the poor from their own means; and shall we, furnished with the help of the most abundant gifts and the greatest wealth with which the churches were long ago endowed, consider this impossible for us to do? Let the order be kept, that each be given according as he has need, and we will feel that we are helped by the blessing of the Lord and the generosity of the godly, so that no difficulty will remain for us. But what we demand is difficult and impossible, because the matter is handled in a preposterous manner and order. For those who needed most receive least, and most is given to those whose duty it was to bestow their own resources on the churches. But if we weigh how much danger, trouble and inconvenience usually arises, both publicly and privately, from the multitude of beggars and needy people, the first fruit of Christian fellowship which the primitive Church gathered from this will be beyond price. But another came from it, namely that there was great grace upon them all: that is, they were gracious and acceptable to the whole people, and also to those who were not yet enlightened by the knowledge of Christ. For such is the power of beneficence that it draws even enemies into admiration and love of those who practise it. And because the Lord counts as done to himself what is bestowed on the poor in his name, he is accustomed to reward the benefactors with this recompense, that they gain influence and authority with many people. If we consider this one thing today, we will not be surprised why those who profess the name of the gospel are hated and detested by all. For apart from the fact that the world hates the light of truth, and God wills that we be exercised by its wickedness, this hardness of heart by which we neglect the needy of Christ deserves it. Meanwhile, I say nothing of the wickedness by which we plunder the goods of the Church under the pretext of evangelical reform, while the crowd of the poor, for whose food those goods ought to be spent, cries out. Let us compare the custom of the primitive Church with what we ourselves do, and unless we are ashamed of ourselves, we will rightly be called men not merely of brazen but of more than harlot's brow.

units.la: Cæterum subijcit tractationi huic singulare beneficentiæ & Christianæ communicationis exemplum, quod Iosès quidam Leuita Cyprius edidit, qui agrum proprium vendidit, & omne illius pretium apostolorum pedibus siue administrationi subiecit. Videtur hoc Ananiæ & Sapphiræ exemplo præmitti, ut luculentior sit illorum improbitas, quos tam celebre opus non mouere potuit. Simul vero admonet spiritus sanctus laude decorandos esse, quicunque singulare aliquod virtutis specimen edunt, ut laudis stimuli alios quoq; quorum animi generosiores sunt, ad imitationem excitent. Duo autem in Iosè commemorantur, quæ illum celebriorem reddunt. Nam cùm Leuita esset, ad Christi fidem conuersus est, cui Leuitarum ordo infensissimus erat, eò quòd Christus illorum quæstui & honori plurimum derogaret. Sed spirat domini spiritus vbicunque voluerit, nec propter vitæ genus de cuiusquam hominis salute desperandum est. Deinde cum Cyprius esset, Hierosolymitanos fideles tanto amore complexus est, ut tantum in illos ederet liberalitatis specimen. Intellexit nimirum, in Christo sublata esse nationum discrimina, ut alibi scriptura monet. At non caruit insigni fructu tanta viri liberalitas. Nam & sempiternæ memoriæ illius virtus consecrata est, & apostoli dignū censuerunt, qui cognomento Barnabas, id est, consolationis filius diceretur. Merebatur enim tam insigne nomen, qui beneficentia sua multis insigne solatium præbuerat. Interim admonemur, quos titulos mereantur, qui ecclesiasticorum bonorum direptione Christi egenos defraudant, & religionem atq; doctrinam, quantum in ipsis est, remorantur. Sunt hi revera turbationis & perditionis filij, quorum iudicium non dormitat, ut sequens Ananiæ exemplum docebit. Obseruemus autem primitiuæ ecclesiæ exercitia, & ijsdem nostro hoc turbulentißimo seculo studeamus, quando passim contra veritatis doctrinam persecutores satan excitat. Armentur ingenua docendi libertate verbi præcones, & meminerint se Dei servos esse, quos nulla hominum authoritas mouere debeat. Vnanimes in Christo sint, quotquot Christi nomen profitentur. Vnanimitatem & concordiam beneficentiæ operibus, & in primis pauperum subuentione testari studeant. Hæ Christianorum notæ sunt, & hæc ipsa eorundem fortissima præsidia & arma sunt. Ex his enim dignoscuntur Christi Iesu discipuli esse, qui contra quosuis mundi conatus ipsos facile tueri possit, & tandem omni periculo ereptos in cæleste regnum transferet. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, he adds to this discussion a singular example of beneficence and Christian fellowship, which a certain Levite from Cyprus, Joses, set forth: he sold his own field and placed the whole price at the feet of the apostles, that is, at their disposal for administration. This seems to be placed before the example of Ananias and Sapphira so that their wickedness may stand out more clearly, since such a famous deed could not move them. At the same time the Holy Spirit reminds us that whoever displays some singular specimen of virtue ought to be honoured with praise, so that the spur of praise may also stir others, whose minds are more generous, to imitate them. Two things are recorded about Joses that make him more notable. First, although he was a Levite, he was converted to faith in Christ, toward which the order of the Levites was most hostile, because Christ greatly diminished their gain and honour. But the Lord's Spirit breathes where he wills, and no one's salvation should be despaired of because of his way of life. Second, although he was a Cypriot, he embraced the faithful of Jerusalem with such love that he gave so great a proof of liberality toward them. Of course he understood that in Christ the distinctions of nations have been removed, as Scripture elsewhere teaches. Nor did such generosity of the man go without remarkable fruit. For his virtue has been consecrated to everlasting memory, and the apostles judged him worthy to be called by the surname Barnabas, that is, son of consolation. For he who had offered a notable comfort to many by his beneficence deserved so notable a name. Meanwhile we are warned what titles they deserve who, by plundering church goods, defraud Christ's poor and, as far as they are able, hinder religion and doctrine. They are truly sons of disturbance and destruction, whose judgment does not sleep, as the following example of Ananias will teach. Let us observe the practices of the primitive Church, and let us strive in this most turbulent age of ours, when Satan everywhere stirs up persecutors against the doctrine of truth. Let the heralds of the Word be armed with the free liberty of teaching, and let them remember that they are servants of God, whom no authority of men ought to move. Let all who profess the name of Christ be of one mind in Christ. Let them take pains to bear witness to their unity and concord by works of beneficence, and above all by relieving the poor. These are the marks of Christians, and these very things are their strongest defences and weapons. For by these it is recognised that they are the disciples of Jesus Christ, who is able easily to protect them against whatever attempts of the world, and at last, snatched from every danger, will transfer them into the heavenly kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Iosès Barnabæ beneficentia.
units.tr: The beneficence of Joses Barnabas.

units.la: CAPUT V. HOMILIA XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. HOMILY XXXII.

units.la: Vir autem quidam, Ananias nomine, cum Sapphira vxore sua vendidit possessionem, & subduxit de precio, conscia etiam vxore sua, & partem afferens ad pedes apostolorum posuit. Dixit autem Petrus: Anania, cur impleuit satan cor tuum, vt mentireris spiritui sancto, & subduceres ex precio agri? Annon manens tibi manebat, & venditus in tua erat potestate? Quare posuisti in corde tuo rem istam? Non es mentitus hominibus, sed Deo. Auditis vero his sermonibus Ananias, collapsus expirauit. Et ortus est timor magnus super omnes, qui haec audierunt. Surgentes autem iuuenes collegerunt ipsum, elatumque sepelierunt.
units.tr: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession and kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and bringing a part he laid it at the feet of the apostles. But Peter said: Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back part of the price of the field? While it remained unsold, did it not remain yours, and once sold, was it not in your power? Why have you conceived this thing in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God. When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and expired. And great fear came upon all who heard these things. The young men arose, wrapped him up, carried him out and buried him.

units.la: EXposuit Lucas, quibus studijs & exercitijs primitiua ecclesia periculosissimo persecutionis tempore dedita fuerit. Vidimus illic quaecunque ad perfectam omnibusque numeris absolutam ecclesiae formam siue constitutionem pertinent. Nam Dei verbum intrepide & syncere praedicarunt apostoli. Idem vero vt par erat excepit populus, sicuti vnanimis illorum concordia & ardens charitatis studium abunde testantur. At non ignorauit spiritus sanctus semper fore fanaticos & turbulentos homines, qui ex his occasionem accepturi essent quasi suis ecclesias temere damnandi, in quibus non omnia primitiuae ecclesiae perfectioni respondent. Quapropter Ananiae & Sapphirae historiam subiici voluit, qua admonemur, satanam in hoc etiam tam sancto coetu sua habuisse manicipia, quorum hypocrisis tandem erupit. Nihil ergo omni ex parte beatum est: nec audiendi sunt, qui integras ecclesias propter paucorum hypocrisim siue libidinem damnant, quando inter Christi discipulos Iudam quoque fuisse legimus, & ipse testatur per euangelij praedicationem tam bonos quam malos attrahi solere. Matth. 13. Priusquam vero historiam aggrediamur, obseruandum est, quod vt Iudas ex ecclesiae bonis sui peccati occasionem accepit: ita Ananias ad eundem lapidem impingens primas in ecclesia turbas dedit. Voluit nos iste exemplo admoneri spiritus sanctus, periculosam esse bonorum ecclesiasticorum tractationem, nec in ea fine euidenti salutis tutura peccari posse. Diligenter ergo sibi cauebant, quicunque Christi & euangelij nomine gloriantur. At si vnum hoc expenderent, nunquam vt corui famelici ad illorum administrationem tanto cum studio accurrerent. Historiae partes duae sunt. Prior quid cum Ananias, altera quid cum Sapphira illius vxore actum sit commemorat. Sed vt euidentior sit prioris partis tractatio, principio Ananiae factum, deinde Petri de hoc iudicium, postremo poenam a Deo illi immissam videamus.
units.tr: Luke sets out the pursuits and exercises to which the primitive Church devoted itself at a most dangerous time of persecution. We have seen there everything that pertains to the form or constitution of the Church, perfect and complete in every respect. For the apostles preached the word of God fearlessly and sincerely, and the people received it as was fitting, as the united harmony of their hearts and their ardent zeal for love amply bear witness. Yet the Holy Spirit did not fail to foresee that there would always be fanatical and turbulent men who would take from this an occasion to condemn rashly the churches of their own day, in which not everything corresponds to the perfection of the primitive Church. For this reason he wished the history of Ananias and Sapphira to be set before us, by which we are warned that Satan had his own henchmen even in this so holy assembly, whose hypocrisy at last broke out. Nothing, therefore, is blessed in every respect; nor should they be listened to who condemn whole churches for the hypocrisy or lust of a few, since we read that Judas too was among the disciples of Christ, and he himself testifies that through the preaching of the gospel both good and bad are wont to be drawn in. Matth. 13. Before we take up the history, it must be observed that just as Judas took an occasion of sin from the goods of the Church, so Ananias, stumbling on the same stone, stirred up the first troubles in the Church. The Holy Spirit wished us to be warned by this example that the handling of ecclesiastical goods is dangerous, and that no sin committed in it can remain without clear harm to salvation. Let those, therefore, who boast in the name of Christ and the gospel be diligently on their guard. If they weighed this one thing, they would never rush to the administration of those goods with such eagerness, like hungry ravens. The history has two parts. The first recounts what Ananias did, the second what was done with Sapphira his wife. But so that the treatment of the first part may be clearer, let us look first at the deed of Ananias, then at Peter's judgement on it, and lastly at the punishment God brought upon him.

units.la: Ananiae factum mira simplicitate narratur, ne quid affectibus datum putemus. Vir quidam, Ananias nomine, cum Sapphira vxore sua vendidit possessionem, & subduxit de precio, conscia etiam vxore sua, & partem afferens ad pedes apostolorum posuit. Inquirendum hic ante omnia, quod illud peccatum sit, quod paulo post repentina morte puniuit Dominus. Nam si carnis iudicium audiamus, nihil hic peccatum esse, sed Ananiam laude & praemio dignum putabimus. Nec enim peccatum fuit agrum vendere, cum id diuinis simul & humanis legibus facere liceat, & nulla hic fraudoli mali in contractu commissi mentio. Similiter nec id a Domino prohibitum est, ne honorum nostrorum partem nostris necessitatibus referuemus, cum Paulus ethnicis deteriores esse dicat eos, qui suis non prospiciunt. 1. Timoth. 5. Et idem eleemosynas non ita faciendas esse docet, vt nostra liberalitate alijs quidem relaxationis, nobis ipsis vero inopiae & angustiae authores simus. 2. Corinth. 8. Ad haec ingens beneficium ecclesiae Christi conferre videtur, quisquis vel dimidiam vel tertiam quartamve suarum opum partem illius vsibus consecrauit. Praeterea Christo teste praemium meretur, quisquis vel aquae frigidae poculum alicui ex discipulis eius nomine ipsius dederit. Matth. 10. Animus ergo Ananiae inspiciendus erit, quem in altera historiae parte ex Sapphirae verbis deprehendere licebit, & qua in re peccarit, videbimus: hypocrisi nimirum & fucata fidei ac charitatis simulatione, qua tam Deo ipsi quàm ecclesiæ imponere conatus est. Viderat enim homo ambitiosus, quantam sibi ipsi laudem & gloriam Iosès Leuita liberalitate sua acquisiuisset. Quare ipse etiam celebrari cupiens, simile quid faciendum esse putauit. Quia tamen idem auarus est, futuræ inopiæ consultum volens, partem precij clàm suis & uxoris necessitatibus reseruat, in eorum interim numero censeri volens, qui omnia sua ecclesiæ Christi addixerant. Concurrunt huic peccato multa alia, quæ illius atrocitatem amplificant. Nam ut de ambitione & auaritia, quæ infelicem hypocritæ istius animum contrarijs quodammodo fluctibus agitarunt, nihil dicamus, diffidentiæ malo ipsum laborauisse, & fide prorsus caruisse patet, qui omnium flagitiorum fons est. Christi enim promissionibus diffidit, quibus se ecclesiæ suæ semper affuturum esse, & suis de victu & amictu liberaliter prospecturum pollicetur. Matth.6.& 28. Quibus si fidem habuisset, nec inopiam futuram potuisset metuere, nec sibi dolo malo in posterum prospexisset. Diffidentiæ malo immanis Dei contemptus coniunctus fuit, qualis à Dæmone illis tribuitur, qui in cordibus suis vel Deum esse negant, vel illum mortalia non curare sibi per suadent. Psal.14.& 94. Et cum hominibus solis sibi negotium fore putat, quod omnibus hypocritis proprium est. Nec enim verisimile est, tale quid ausurum fuisse, si Deum tum animorum tum operum nostrorum inspectorem esse credidisset. Accedit hùc sacrilegium, quod in proprijs pecunijs comitit.
