Quia enim credi vult, vniuersum agri precium ecclesiæ abs se consecratum esse, non obscurè fatetur illud ecclesiæ deberi. Quare sacrilegij notam effugere nequit. Et quia ex ecclesiæ ærario postea alebantur, quicunque sua omnia in illud contulerant, sacrilegus dolus fuit, quo ecclesiæ imponere voluit, ijs se admiscendo, quibus ab illa victus necessarius debebatur. Adeò fœcundum est diffidentiæ malum & nouis subinde vitijs pullulat. Interim omnium pseudochristianorum typus est Ananias, qui ita Christum profiteri instituunt, ne vnquam illud ipsis damno aut fraudi esse possit. Quando enim vident Christum in gente aliqua regnum obtinuisse, de eiusdem verò perpetuitate dubitant, præsenti quidem reformationi consentiunt, sed diligenter cauent, ne aliquorum consiliorum authores sint, quæ collabentibus ecclesiæ fortunis, alicuius mali causam ipsis præbere queant. Conantur illi duobus dominis, Christo nimirum & mundo seruire, quod impossibile factu Christus ipse pronuntiat. Matth. 6. Atqui tales plerunque sapientiæ & modestiæ laudem inter homines merentur. Sed revera Ananiæ sunt, quorum cor non est rectum cum Domino, licet aliqua ipsorum in ecclesiam beneficia extare videantur. Regnat hoc hominum genus hodie, & vtinam solum regnaret. Maior enim ferè illorum numerus, qui cùm nihil ecclesiæ boni conferant, illius tamen bonis dicescere cupiunt, & ab alijs collata sibi vendicant. Quorum exemplar Iudas est, qui & ipse cùm nihil Christo contulisset, ea subripuit, quæ ab alijs dari solebant. Iohan.12. Nec eo flagitio contentus, Christum insuper prodidit: ut eo exemplo disceremus, quid à sui similibus nobis sperare liceat.
units.tr: The deed of Ananias is narrated with remarkable simplicity, so that we may not think anything was done out of passion. A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a possession and kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and bringing a part he laid it at the feet of the apostles. Here we must first inquire what the sin was that the Lord punished shortly afterwards by sudden death. For if we listen to the judgement of the flesh, we shall think that there was no sin here at all, but that Ananias deserved praise and reward. For it was no sin to sell a field, since both divine and human laws permit it, and there is no mention here of any fraud committed in the contract. Likewise the Lord has not forbidden us to set aside a part of our goods for our own needs, since Paul says that those who do not provide for their own are worse than unbelievers. 1 Tim. 5. And the same Paul teaches that alms ought not to be given in such a way that by our generosity we become the cause of relief for others but of want and distress for ourselves. 2 Cor. 8. Moreover, whoever has dedicated half, a third or even a quarter of his wealth to the needs of the Church of Christ seems to confer a great benefit upon it. Besides, whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of Christ's disciples in his name earns a reward, Christ being witness. Matth. 10. We must therefore look at the mind of Ananias, which in the second part of the history may be grasped from the words of Sapphira, and we shall see in what respect he sinned: namely in hypocrisy and the feigned pretence of faith and love, by which he tried to deceive God himself as much as the Church. For the ambitious man had seen how great praise and glory Joses the Levite had won for himself by his generosity. Wishing therefore to be celebrated too, he thought he should do something similar. Yet, being also greedy, and wishing to provide for future want, he secretly kept back part of the price for himself and his wife's needs, while wishing meanwhile to be counted among those who had devoted all their goods to the Church of Christ. Many other sins come together in this offence and magnify its atrocity. For not to speak of the ambition and avarice which tossed the unhappy soul of this hypocrite as if by contrary waves, it is clear that he was afflicted with the evil of distrust and wholly lacked faith, which is the fount of all wickedness. For he distrusted the promises of Christ, in which he promises that he will always be present with his Church and will generously provide for his own in food and clothing. Matth. 6 and 28. If Ananias had believed these, he would neither have feared future want nor have made provision for himself by crooked means. Joined to the evil of distrust is the scorn of God, such as the devil attributes to those who in their hearts either deny that God exists or persuade themselves that he does not concern himself with mortal affairs. Ps. 14 and 94. And he thinks that he will have to do only with men, as is proper to all hypocrites. For it is not likely that he would have dared such a thing if he had believed God to be the inspector of both our minds and our works. Added to this is sacrilege, which he committed with his own money. For since he wished it to be believed that the whole price of the field had been consecrated by him to the Church, he plainly confessed that it was owed to the Church. Therefore he cannot escape the mark of sacrilege. And since those who had contributed all their goods to the Church were afterwards supported from its treasury, the fraud was sacrilegious, by which he wished to deceive the Church, mingling himself with those to whom necessary sustenance was due from it. So fruitful is the evil of distrust, and it constantly sprouts forth new vices. Meanwhile Ananias is the type of all pseudo-Christians, who so arrange their profession of Christ that it can never be to their loss or harm. For when they see that Christ has obtained a kingdom among some nation, but doubt its perpetuity, they consent to the present reformation, but take care not to be authors of any counsels which, when the Church's fortunes collapse, could give them some cause of harm. They try to serve two masters, namely Christ and the world, which Christ himself declares to be impossible. Matth. 6. Yet such people commonly win the praise of wisdom and moderation among men. But in truth they are of the kind of Ananias, whose heart is not right with the Lord, although some of their benefits to the Church seem to exist. This kind of men reigns today, and would that it reigned alone. For their number is almost greater of those who, while conferring nothing good on the Church, still wish to draw from its goods, and claim for themselves what others have contributed. Judas is their model, who, though he had given nothing to Christ, stole what was usually given by others. John 12. Not content with that crime, he further betrayed Christ, so that by this example we might learn what we may hope for from those like themselves.

units.la: Porrò cùm hodie tales passim conspiciantur, & ferè ecclesiarum nutritij & reformatores haberi velint, multis rationibus sese tueri conantur, & ferè cùm ecclesiarum tum rerumpub. incolumitatem, ad hæc iura humana, feuda & collationes, aliaque eius generis innumera sua auaritiæ prætexunt. Sed spiritus sancti iudicium audiamus, quod per Petrum Apostolum pronuntiat, ut inde constet, quales censeri debeant, qui Ananiæ hodie deteriores sunt. Sensit enim ex spiritus reuelatione fraudem Petrus, & quantamcunque versutiæ laudem sibi vendicet Ananias, Petri tamen spiritum latere non potest, adeò verum est illud Christi, quo nihil tam occultum esse dicit, quod non reueletur. Matth.10. Nec dissimulat deprehensam fraudem apostolus, sed seuerissimè accusat. Quo exemplo docemur publicè à ministris argui debere non modò manifesta scelera, verumetiam quacunque occultius contra veritatem & Christi ecclesiam impij moliuntur. Nam ut boni Imperatoris est, non apertis modò hostium conatibus resistere, sed insidias quoque detegere & præuenire: ita aduersus omnes impiorum machinationes verbi ministros summa alacritate pugnare decet. Admirabilis autem inest Petri verbis vehementia, & gradibus quibusdam insurgit oratio, ut euidentior fiat sceleris atrocitas. Initio fontem omnis mali detegit, inquiens: Anania, cur impleuit satan cor tuum? Quibus verbis, ipsum à fide alienissimum esse testatur, & plane reprobum. Tentantur enim etiam pij & electi à satana, qui nunquam non vt leo rugiens obambulat, & quærit quem deuoret. Sed quia eidem fortes in fide resistunt, corda illorum implere nequit. Alia autem est impiorum ratio, qui vbi à fide semel defecerunt, toti à satana occupantur, vt nullus in ipsis spiritui sancto locus sit reliquus. Simul verò admonemur, satanæ man
units.tr: Moreover, since such men are seen everywhere today and want to be regarded almost as the nurturers and reformers of the churches, they try to defend themselves with many arguments. They pretext their greed with the safety of the churches and of the commonwealth alike, with human laws, fiefs, benefices, and countless other things of that kind. But let us hear the judgement of the Holy Spirit, which he pronounces through the apostle Peter, so that it may be clear what sort of men should be counted who are today worse than Ananias. For Peter perceived the fraud by a revelation of the Spirit, and however much credit for cunning Ananias claims for himself, the Spirit of Peter cannot be hidden. So true is that saying of Christ, that he says nothing is so hidden that it will not be revealed (Matt. 10). Nor does the apostle conceal the fraud he has detected, but accuses it most severely. From this example we are taught that ministers ought to denounce publicly not only manifest crimes but also whatever the wicked secretly contrive against the truth and the Church of Christ. For just as it is the mark of a good general to resist not only the open attempts of the enemy but also to detect and forestall their ambushes, so ministers of the Word ought to fight against all the schemes of the impious with the greatest eagerness. There is, moreover, a remarkable vehemence in Peter's words, and his speech rises by certain steps, so that the atrocity of the crime becomes more evident. At the outset he uncovers the source of all evil, saying: "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?" By these words he testifies that Ananias was utterly alien to faith and plainly reprobate. For the godly and the elect too are tempted by Satan, who never ceases to walk about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. But because they stand firm in faith and resist him, he cannot fill their hearts. The case of the wicked is otherwise: once they have fallen away from faith, they are wholly possessed by Satan, so that no place remains in them for the Holy Spirit. At the same time we are warned that all hypocrites who use deceit in religion are Satan's slaves. But to return to the narrative: was Ananias's deed seen as so atrocious by Peter alone? Nay, in God's judgement it is more atrocious, as the outcome of the event shows. For when he heard these words, he ended his life by a sudden and instant death, striking great fear into all those to whom the report of the event spread, of which we will speak later, when we treat of the similar death of his wife Sapphira. But first we must observe here the efficacy of God's Word, which God wills to be binding even when it is pronounced through a man. For its force does not depend on the authority of the man but stands by itself. This must be understood of promises as much as of threats which are found in the Scriptures. For whatever the evangelists promise to the faithful worshippers of God will be no less sure than if God himself, thundering from heaven, had promised them. And whatever threats are drawn from the Scriptures against the impious and profane despisers of God will undoubtedly come upon them. The voice of Christ bears witness to this, when he says that whatever his ministers bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven (Matt. 16; John 20). Nor let anyone object here that God does not always use such an immediate execution of his judgements as we see here. For although the wicked seize on this as an occasion to mock, and securely scorn all threats, this security will cost them dearly when they hear the voice of Christ the judge, which it will be impossible for them to endure. Rather let us acknowledge the long-suffering of God, who is accustomed to defer punishments at times so as to grant a time for repentance; yet at the same time he also sets forth some examples of his judgements, so as to confirm the faith and authority of his word.

units.la: II. Petri de Ananiæ facto iudicium. cipia esse omnes hypocritas, quicunq; in religione dolo malo ѵtuntur. Hunc enim mendacij patrem Christus esse docet, & hoc ipso argumento pharisæos diabolo progenitos esse probat. Iohan. 8. Quo etiam Iudæ exemplum referri potest, in quem satan ingressus esse dicitur, postquam pertinaci hypocrisi tam ipsi Christo quàm apostolis in vltima Cœna fucum facere conatus est. Iohan. 13. Deinde effectum satanæ exprimit Petrus, dum Ananiam eò adductum esse dicit, vt spiritui sancto mentiri voluerit: quod bifariam potest intelligi: partim enim se spiritu sancto agi falso simulauit: partim verò Christi ecclesiam fallere conatus est, quam spiritu donatam esse, tot argumentis hactenus cognouerat. Vtero, sensus impudentem & impiam hominis audaciam arguit, & ostendit quousq; progrediantur homines, si semel Satanæ in suos animos imperium permiserint. Tertiò ad ipsum Ananiæ factum propius accedens, eo nomine illum accusat, quòd ex precio agri partem subduxerit. Furti ergo & sacrilegij illum accusat, quod (vt paulò ante monuimus) in proprijs opibus à nobis committi potest. Et Ananiæ confortes sunt, qui opes, quas se egenis debere intelligunt, vel auari sibi solis vsurpant, vel luxu dissipant. Peccatur in hoc publicè & priuatim. Publicè, dum opes, quas ecclesiasticas vocant, multi in vsus prophanos conuertunt, esurientibus interim non modò egenis, verumetiam ipsis ecclesijs, quæ pastoribus fidis & idoneis destitutæ dissipantur. Priuatim quoq; peccatur, quando nos opum dispensatores à Deo constitutos esse gloriamur, interim verò illas, neglectis pauperibus, vel improbè dilapidamus, vel domino nostræ coaceruamus, vt nec nobis nec alijs sint vtiles. Conquerunturferè tales de egentium multitudine, quibus omnibus subuenire fit impossibile. At ijdem falsi conuincuntur per suum luxum, cui ipsorum opes sufficiunt, per rubiginem item nummorum, quos insatiabili cupiditate reconditos in arcis suis contemplantur: adhæc vestium multitudine, quas à tineis potius arrodi patiuntur, quàm vel illas ipsas, vel illarum venditarum precium in egenos conferant. Et ita (sicut Iacobus ait) olim per illa ipsa damnationem suam augeri sentient, quibus se totis animis addixerunt. At ne quam excusationem institueret Ananias, nulla illum necessitate ad tantum facinus ad ductum fuisse ostendit Petrus, dicens: Annon manens tibi manebat ager, & venditus in tua erat potestate? Licebat vel agrum possidere, vel totum illius precium retinere, nec quisquam te propterea Christianorum consortio indignum censuisset. Vnde liquidò colligi potest, neminem lege communi, vt sua bona publicaret, coactum fuisse, sed voluntariam & arbitrariam fuisse communionem, de qua præcedenti Sermone dictum est. NEC adhuc substitit Petrus, sed eam testatur huius flagitij atrocitatem esse, vt à Christiano homine nihil tale vel cogitari, nedum fieri debeat. Nam ait: Quare posuisti in corde tuo rem istam? Tam syncerum enim integritatis studium à suis Christus requirit, vt non mores duntaxat & externam vitæ conuersationem, verumetiam animos & cogitationes illorum ab hypocrisi alienissimas esse velit. Postremò, quod totius negotij caput est, repetit. Non es mentitus hominibus, sed Deo. Nec enim cum hominibus solis, sed cum Deo tibi res est, qui corda & renes scrutatur, quem tuæ impietatis vindicem & vltorem senties. Obseruemus autem in his, quo loco haberi debeant, quicunq; sub fidei & religionis prætextu homines fallere conantur. Inter quos cum Anania primum locum tenent, qui in duas partes claudicando, Christianismum ita profitentur, vt sibi interim corruente etiam in terris Christi regno prospectum velint. Proximi ab his sunt, qui Iudæ insitar Christum & ecclesiam ipsius vel dolo malo vel etiam aperta vi spoliant, & tandem osculo pro dunt. Quibus etiam adnumerari debent Ieroboamici principes, qui religione ad tyrannidem suam flectendam ѵtuntur, dum eos fidei articulos præscribunt eosq; externæ religionis ritus obtrudunt, quos nullo Dei mandato traditos esse, sed ex meris hominum traditionibus dependere non ignorant, nec aliud quærunt, quàm vt in officio contineantur quibus ipsi imperitare cupiunt, quod olim Ieroboamum, primum Israeliticæ tyrannidis authorem fecisse legimus. 1. Reg. 12. & 13. Nec ab his alieni sunt, quicunq; sub euangelij & Christianæ fidei prætextu peccandi licentiam quærunt, quorum infinitus bodie est numerus. Atqui omnibus istis facile est hominibus vel fucum facere, vel silentium imponere, ne quis illorum hypocrisim detegat. Sed quia non hominibus solis, verum ipsi Deo mentiuntur, id inultum nunquam ferent. Nam vt illum nihil latere potest, ita mendaces quàm maximè abominari & odisse solet. Psal. 5. Prouerb. 12. Et eosdem regno suo excludendos esse Christus testatur. Apoc. 12. Quis enim virum bonum dicat, qui alijs sui nominis prætextu imponi pateretur? Quæ ergo stultitia sive dementia, Deum talem fingere, qui ipsissima est Veritas? Sed vt ad historiam reuertamur, num soli Petro tam atrox visum est Ananiæ facinus? Imò atrocius est Deo iudice, quemadmodum rei euentus declarat. Nam auditis his sermonibus repenti-na & subita morte vitam finiuit, magnum omnibus illis timorem suo tam infelici exitu incutiens, ad quos rei gestæ fama dimanauit: de quo postea dicemus, vbi Sapphiræ vxoris similem interitum tractabimus. Primò autem hic nobis verbi Dei efficacia obseruanda venit, quod ratum esse vult Deus, etiamsi per hominem enuntietur. Nec enim ab hominis authoritate illius vis dependet, sed per sese subsistit. Intelligendum hoc tam de promissionibus quam de minis, quæ in scripturis extant. Quæ cunque enim fidis Dei cultoribus euangelistæ pollicentur, non minus rata erunt, quam si illa cœlitus intonans Deus polliceretur. Et quæcunque item impijs & prophanis Dei contemptoribus ex scripturis interminantur, indubie illis euenient. Testatur hoc Christi vox, qui in cœlis solutum sine ligatum fore ait, quodcunque ipsius ministri in terris ligauerint siue soluerint. Matth. 16. Ioan. 20. Nec hic mihi quisquam obijciat, non semper tam præsenti suorum iudiciorum executione Deum vti, qualem hic cernimus. Nam licet inde illudendi occasionem impij arripiant, & securi minas omnes contemnant, magno tamen hæc illis securitas constabit, quando Christi iudicis vocem audient, quam sustinere ipsis impossibile erit. Agnoscamus potius Dei longanimitatem, qui pœnas ideo interdum differre solet, vt pœnitentiæ tempus concedat: idem vero simul aliqua edit suorum iudiciorum exempla, vt verbi sui fidem & authoritatem afferat.
units.tr: Peter's judgement on the deed of Ananias (II.). All who use deceit in religion as hypocrites are Satan's slaves. For Christ teaches that he is the father of lies, and by this very argument he proves that the Pharisees were begotten of the devil (John 8). To this may also be referred the example of Judas, into whom Satan is said to have entered, after he tried with obstinate hypocrisy to deceive both Christ himself and the apostles at the last Supper (John 13). Next, Peter expresses the effect of Satan, when he says that Ananias was brought to the point of wishing to lie to the Holy Spirit. This can be understood in two ways: partly, because he falsely pretended to be moved by the Holy Spirit; partly, because he tried to deceive the Church of Christ, which he had hitherto known by so many proofs to be endowed with the Spirit. Either way, the sense condemns the shameless and impious audacity of the man, and shows how far men advance once they have allowed Satan dominion over their minds. Thirdly, drawing nearer to the deed of Ananias itself, he accuses him on this count, that he had withheld part of the price of the field. He accuses him therefore of theft and sacrilege, which (as we noted a little earlier) can be committed by us even with our own resources. And they are companions of Ananias who, though they understand that they owe their resources to the needy, either greedily appropriate them to themselves alone or squander them in luxury. Sin is committed in this both publicly and privately. Publicly, when many turn to profane uses the resources which they call ecclesiastical, while meanwhile not only the needy go hungry but the churches themselves, deprived of faithful and fit ministers, are being wasted. Privately too sin is committed, when we boast that we have been appointed by God as stewards of wealth, yet meanwhile, neglecting the poor, we either wastefully squander it or heap it up in our own houses, so that it is useful neither to us nor to others. Such men often complain of the multitude of the needy, to all of whom it is impossible to bring help. But these same men are shown to be liars by their own luxury, which their resources suffice for; likewise by the rust on the coins which they gaze upon in their strongboxes, hidden away by insatiable greed; and besides by the multitude of garments which they allow to be gnawed by moths rather than give them, or the price of them when sold, to the needy. And so (as James says) they will one day feel their damnation increased by those very things to which they gave themselves wholeheartedly. But lest Ananias should devise any excuse, Peter shows that he was driven to so great a crime by no necessity, saying: "Did not the field remain yours while it remained unsold, and after it was sold was it not in your power?" You were free either to keep the field or to retain the whole of its price, and no one would therefore have judged you unworthy of fellowship with Christians. Whence it can clearly be gathered that no one was compelled by common law to make his goods public; the fellowship was voluntary and optional, as was said in the previous sermon. Nor did Peter stop there, but he testifies that the atrocity of this shameful act is such that nothing like it should be thought of by a Christian, much less done. For he says: "Why have you conceived this thing in your heart?" For Christ requires such a sincere zeal for integrity from his people that he wishes not only their morals and outward conduct, but also their minds and thoughts, to be wholly free from hypocrisy. Lastly, which is the heart of the whole matter, he repeats: "You have not lied to men, but to God." For your business is not with men alone, but with God, who searches the hearts and reins, and whom you will feel as the avenger and punisher of your impiety. Let us observe, moreover, in what rank those should be held who, under the pretext of faith and religion, try to deceive people. Among these, those hold the first place with Ananias who, limping between two sides, profess Christianity in such a way that they wish to provide for themselves meanwhile, even should Christ's kingdom fall on earth. Next to these are those who, like Judas, plunder Christ and his Church either by deceit or even by open force, and finally betray them with a kiss. To these also should be added the princes who imitate Jeroboam, who use religion to bend it to their tyranny. While they prescribe articles of faith to people and force upon them the rites of external religion, which they know were handed down by no command of God but depend purely on human traditions, they seek nothing else than that those over whom they wish to rule should be kept in obedience, as we read that Jeroboam, the first author of Israelite tyranny, once did (1 Kings 12 and 13). Nor are they unlike those who, under the pretext of the gospel and the Christian faith, seek licence to sin, and whose number today is endless. Yet it is easy for all these people to deceive men, or to impose silence so that no one uncovers their hypocrisy. But because they lie not only to men but to God himself, they will never bear this unavenged. For just as nothing can be hidden from him, so he is wont to abominate and hate liars above all (Ps. 5; Prov. 12). And Christ testifies that they are to be shut out from his kingdom (Apoc. 12). For who would call a good man one who would allow others to be deceived under the pretence of his name? What folly or madness, then, is it to imagine God as such a one, who is Truth itself?

units.la: Præterea non negligendum est, quòd Ananiam verbo & diuini iudicij denuntiatione Petrus occidit. Cui non absimile est, quod Paulus Elymam Magum cæcitate ferit, vt cap. 13. videbimus. Videri hæc poterant ab illorum functione alienissima esse, quibus vitæ & salutis ministerium commissum est. Sed nullam reprehensionem apostoli merentur, quibus inter alia spiritus sancti dona efficaciam potentiarum, id est, efficacem ea quæ dicebant exequendi vim diuinitus concessam esse, Paulus admonet. 1. Corinth. 12. Asseritur hic etiam ius gladij, quo magistratus improbos coherceat. Si enim Petrum & Paulum excusat, quòd diuinitus concessō dono aduersus Ananiam & Elymam Magum vsi sunt, qua ratione magistratum accusabimus, cui ius gladij non minus à Deo collatum esse constat? Rom. 13. Nec prolixa disputatione contra eos mihi opus esse videtur, qui in religionis causa gladij ius omnino cessare volunt. Nam vt hoc illis demus, neminem violenter ad fidem cogi posse, cum ea Dei donum sit, magistratus tamen est cum blasphemos tum seductores & pseudoprophetas gladio coherceat, ne contra Dei gloriam & publicam salutem impune grassentur. Vide legem Leuit. 24. Deut. 13. Nec aliam quàm religionis causam cùm Petrus præsenti hoc loco, tum Paulus postea asseruisse videntur. In primis autem præcipuum huius historiæ caput memoriæ reconda-mus, & infelici Ananiæ exemplo territi, hypocrisim fugiamus, colamus autem Deum in spiritu & veritate, animisque sancta fide flagrantibus Christo Iesu adhæreamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, we must not neglect the fact that Peter killed Ananias by the word and by the announcement of divine judgment. Not unlike this is what Paul does when he strikes Elymas the magician with blindness, as we shall see in chapter 13. These things might seem to be utterly foreign to the office of those to whom the ministry of life and salvation has been entrusted. But the apostles deserve no rebuke: Paul reminds us that among the other gifts of the Spirit is the power of working, that is, the divinely granted ability to carry out effectively what they said (1 Corinthians 12). Here also the right of the sword, by which magistrates restrain the wicked, is affirmed. For if Peter and Paul are excused because they used a gift given by God against Ananias and Elymas the magician, by what reasoning shall we accuse the magistrate, to whom the right of the sword is plainly granted no less by God? (Romans 13). Nor does it seem to me that I need a lengthy argument against those who want the sword to have no place at all in matters of religion. For even if we grant them that no one can be forced to faith violently, since faith is a gift of God, it is nonetheless the magistrate's duty to restrain with the sword both blasphemers and seducers and false prophets, lest they run riot with impunity against the glory of God and the public good. See the law in Leviticus 24 and Deuteronomy 13. And the apostles, both Peter in the present passage and Paul later, seem to have asserted no other cause than religion. Above all, let us keep in memory the chief point of this history, and, terrified by the unhappy example of Ananias, let us flee hypocrisy, and worship God in spirit and in truth, and, with hearts burning with holy faith, cleave to Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIII.

units.la: Intercesit autem circiter trium horarum spatiū, vxor quoq; ipsius, nesciens quid factum esset, ingressa est. Dixit autem illi Petrus: Dic mihi, num tanti agrum vendidistis? At illa dixit: Certè, tanti. Petrus autem illi dixit: Quid hoc est, quòd consensistis inter vos ad tentandum spiritum Domini? Ecce pedes eorum, qui sepelierunt virum tuum, ad ianuam adsunt, & efferent te. Repente autem concidit ad pedes eius, & expirauit. Ingressi verò iuuenes, inuenerunt eam mortuam, & elatam sepelierunt iuxta virum suum.
units.tr: About three hours later his wife also came in, not knowing what had happened. Peter said to her, "Tell me, did you sell the field for so much?" She said, "Yes, for so much." Then Peter said to her, "Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Look, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." At once she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in, they found her dead, carried her out, and buried her beside her husband.

units.la: Quoniam non ignorauit Iesus Christus, semper in ecclesia falsos fratres & hypocritas fore, qui maximorum offendiculorum authores futuri sint, in eosdem circa principium nascentis ecclesiæ horrendum exemplum edi voluit, quo edoceremur, quid tales sperare debeant. Vidimus illius priorem partem in Ananias, qui hypocritarum mores egregiè exprimit. Deflectuuntur hi fide vera, qui omnium malorum fons atque origo est. Inde enim fit, vt tam Deum quàm ecclesiam ipsius ludibrio habeant & improbè contemnant. Accedit his vitiorum colophon, incurabilis pertinacia, qua fit vt manifestos peccatores facilius conuertere liceat, quàm tales, qui Christum & ecclesiam sua hypo-crisi fallere semel in animum induxerunt. Clariora autem erunt ista, si alteram quoq; huius historiæ partem videamus, quæ Sapphiræ non minus tristem exitum continet, quam horis circiter tribus elapsis Ananiæ mariti mortis ignaram, ad Petrum & fideles qui cum ipso erant ingressam esse Lucas ait. Fere enim ita fieri consueuit, vt postremi ea resciscamus, quæ nos cumprimis scire oportebat, cum plerique potius clam nobis vitia nostra traducere, quàm nos in faciem redarguere soleant. Deinde pios charitatis quoq; affectus mouet, vt ægrè eorum vuntij fiant, quæ proximo dolendi causam præbere possunt. Quæ mihi causa videtur, quòd Sapphira mariti mortem hucusq; ignorauisse dicitur. Caterum vt ex historiæ huius consyderatione plus ad nos vtilitatis redeat, primo loco Petri quæstionem, qua illam aggressus est, deinde verò confidentem Sapphiræ audaciam, & postremò pœnam, qua hanc Deus vindicauit, consyderabimus.
units.tr: Since Jesus Christ knew that in the Church there would always be false brothers and hypocrites, who would be the authors of the greatest stumbling-blocks, he wished a dreadful example of them to be set near the beginning of the infant Church, so that we might learn what such people ought to expect. We have seen the first part of it in Ananias, who vividly expresses the character of hypocrites. These men turn aside from true faith, which is the fount and origin of all evils. From this it follows that they both mock God and his Church and shamelessly despise them. To these vices is added, as the finishing touch, incurable obstinacy, so that manifest sinners can more easily be converted than those who have once resolved to deceive Christ and the Church by their hypocrisy. These matters will be clearer if we also look at the other part of this history, which contains no less sad an end for Sapphira. Luke says that about three hours after her husband's death, she came in to Peter and the faithful who were with him, unaware of her husband's death. For it usually happens that we learn last the things we most needed to know, since most people prefer to speak ill of our faults behind our backs rather than rebuke us to our face. Then, godly feelings of charity also move us to be reluctant to tell what may give our neighbour cause for grief. This seems to me the reason why Sapphira is said to have been ignorant of her husband's death until now. But so that more usefulness may come to us from considering this history, we will consider first Peter's question, with which he addressed her, then Sapphira's bold confidence, and lastly the punishment with which God avenged her.

units.la: Petri quæstio nec leuis nec superuacanea est. Hac enim Sapphiræ impietas manifesta fit, quæ alioquin videri poterat vel fraudis per maritum commissæ ignara, vel mariti authoritate ad simu-lationem & hypocrisin pertractata fuisse. Ab ipsa ergo facti huius rationem exigit Petrus, inquiens: Dic mihi, num tanti vendidisti agrum? Porrò cum rei euentus doceat, Petrum nihil priuato affec-tu, sed diuino spiritus sancti instinctu, hic omnia egisse, Dei morem hic obseruare conuenit, quo in pu-niendis sceleratis vtitur. Non poterat hunc latere incurabilis Sapphiræ improbitas, nec aliquis pro-hibebat, quò minus illam repente vindicaret. Sed pœnitentiæ tempus ipsi concedi, & illius animum quæstione insolita tentari & excitari voluit, ne nimia alicui videretur iudicij ipsius seueritas. Simi-lia diuinæ longanimitatis exempla passim extant. Cauet enim Deus, ne tyrannorum instar in fontes seuiat, sed vt ijdem intelligant, quibus delictis Dei iram & pœnas contra se prouocarint. Ita cum primis parentibus illum egisse legimus. Genes.3. Et primo mundo centum viginti annorum spacium concessit, quibus pœnitentiam agere posset, & eidem Noah iustitiæ præconem dare dignatus est. Gen.6. 2.Pet.2. Chananæos autem & Amorrhaos non ante delere instituit, quàm ipsos iniquitatis mensuram impleuisse, & plane incurabiles factos esse videret. Genes.15. Sed quid exemplis opus est, cum ea non in sacris modò, verumetiam prophanis historijs passim occurrant? vt interim ea omit-tamus, quæ cùm in alijs tum in nobis ipsis quotidie experimur. Transferamus hæc potius ad nostram institutionem, & primò quidem Dei longanimitate non abutamur. Ad pœnitentiam enim nos inuitat. Ne ergo reproborum instar, nobis iram Dei conflemus, dum pœnitere nescij peccando pergi-mus, & quotidie deteriores reddimur. Rom.2. Nam lento quidem gradu ad vindictam Deus procedit, sed tarditatem hanc (vt ethnici quoq; olim monuerunt) supplicij gravitate compensat. Deinde Dei bonitatem ipsi quoq; imitemur, nec præcipitemus iudicium nostrum, etiamsi pœnam aliquos meruisse constet. Quia enim salutem potius hominum quàm interitum Deus passim requirit, quæ obsecro audacia est, si nostro rigore & seueritate Dei iustitiam superare contendamus? Quod ijs maximè ob-seruandum fuerit, qui in alios animaduertendi potestatem & ius diuinitus acceperunt, ne nimia se-ueritate & iudicij præcipitantia animabus quoque, quarum saluti maximè studeri debet, periculum struant.
units.tr: Peter's question is neither trivial nor superfluous. By it Sapphira's impiety is made manifest, which otherwise might seem to be either ignorance of the fraud committed by her husband, or a matter of being drawn into pretence and hypocrisy by her husband's authority. So Peter demands from her an account of the deed itself, saying: "Tell me, did you sell the field for so much?" Moreover, since the outcome shows that Peter acted here not from private feeling but by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, it is fitting to observe the manner of God which he uses in punishing the wicked. Sapphira's incurable wickedness could not be hidden from him, nor was anything preventing him from punishing her at once. But he wished to grant her time for repentance, and to test and stir her mind by an unusual question, lest his judgment seem too severe to anyone. Similar examples of divine long-suffering are found everywhere. God takes care not to rage against the springs like a tyrant, but so that those same people may understand by what offences they have provoked God's wrath and punishments against themselves. Thus we read that he dealt in this way with our first parents. Gen. 3. To the first world he granted a span of one hundred and twenty years in which it could repent, and he deigned to give Noah as a herald of righteousness. Gen. 6. 2 Pet. 2. He did not decide to destroy the Canaanites and Amorites until he saw that they had filled up the measure of their iniquity and had plainly become incurable. Gen. 15. But why do we need examples, since they occur everywhere not only in sacred but also in profane histories? Let us pass over those which we daily experience both in others and in ourselves. Let us rather apply these things to our own instruction, and first of all not abuse God's long-suffering. For it invites us to repentance. Lest, therefore, like the reprobate, we heap up God's wrath against ourselves, while we go on sinning without repenting and are made worse every day. Rom. 2. For God indeed proceeds to vengeance at a slow pace, but he compensates for this tardiness (as the heathen also once warned) by the severity of the punishment. Next, let us also imitate God's goodness, and not rush to judgment, even if it is clear that some have deserved punishment. Since God everywhere seeks the salvation of men rather than their destruction, what audacity is it, I ask, if we strive by our rigour and severity to outdo God's justice? This ought especially to be observed by those who have received from God the power and right to punish others, lest by excessive severity and hasty judgment they put in danger also the souls for whose salvation the greatest care ought to be taken.

units.la: Sed Sapphiram audiamus, quæ confidenter mentitur, omni tum timore Dei tum pudore posito. Nec simpliciter, sed adhibita contestationis nota, quasi iuramento affirmat, quod falsum esse nouerat. Atqui si non Dei timor, saltem quæstionis nouitas illam terrere debebat. Quia enim cuius liberum erat pro suo arbitrio conferre quantum volebat, verisimile est, à nemine antehac postulatum fuisse, vt accepti datiq; rationem coram ecclesia redderet. Cogitareergo debebat Sapphira, non sine mysterio fieri, quod talis iam mouebatur quæstio, maximè cum flagitij sibi conscia esset. At cum sec-cura animi & confidens mentiri audeat, infallibili argumento se prorsus incurabilem esse probat. Quid enim boni sperare possis, vbi pudor semel explosus est, quo generosi animi tanquâ fræno in ossi-cio retinentur? Interim confidentem audaciam, quod hypocritarum proprium est, Sapphira exprimit. Quem enim verentur possunt, qui Deum fallere instituerunt, nec illius conspectum expauescunt? Quare nihil hypocrisi confidentius & audacius esse, scriptura multis exemplis probat. Et cum pa-lam flagitiosi ad primam fere Dei vocem concidant, et in eius conspectum prodire metuat, hypocrita cnut tunc quoque suam integritatem ostentare audent, quando conscientias suas saucias & Dei iudicio patefactas esse sentiunt. Exemplum eius rei Cainus exhibet, qui de Abelo fratre interrogatus, Deo responsare audet, & dicere: Quis me constituit custodem fratris mei? Gene.4. Et apud prophetam hypocritae cum Deo, tanquam nimis querulo, expostulant, cum aiunt: Quare ieiunauimus, & tu non aspicis? Affligimus animas nostras, & tu ignoras? Isa.58. Item: Frustra feruitur Deo. Quae enim utilitas quod instituta eius obseruamus, & quod pullati coram Domino exercituum incedimus? Malach.3. Quid de Iuda proditore dicemus? Qui cum Christum facinus ipsius minime ignorare, seque argui & grauissime reprehendi sentiret, cum alijs tamen apostolis interrogare Christum audet, num se de tanto scelere suspectum habeat? Matth.26. Nec minor est Sapphirae confidentia, cum tot extarent exempla, quibus edocebatur, apostolos spiritu sancto donatos esse. Prodest autem haec obseruare, ne confidentia & temeritate sua nobis hypocritae imponant, aut suis dictis improbis nos protelent.
units.tr: But let us hear Sapphira, who lies confidently, with all fear of God and all shame laid aside. And she affirms it not simply, but with the mark of an oath, as if swearing to what she knew to be false. Yet if the fear of God did not terrify her, at least the novelty of the question should have done so. For since it was up to each person's free choice how much to contribute, it is likely that no one before had been asked to render an account of what was received and given before the Church. Sapphira ought therefore to have considered that it was not without a mystery that such a question was now raised, especially since she was conscious of her crime. But since she dares to lie with a calm and confident mind, she proves by an infallible argument that she is utterly incurable. For what good can you hope for where shame has once been burst through, by which the feelings of noble minds are kept in check as if by a bridle in the mouth? Meanwhile Sapphira expresses the bold confidence which is characteristic of hypocrites. For whom can those fear who have set out to deceive God and do not dread his sight? Wherefore Scripture proves by many examples that nothing is more confident and bold than hypocrisy. And although the openly wicked collapse at almost the first voice of God and fear to come into his sight, the hypocrite dares even then to display his integrity, when he feels his conscience wounded and laid open by God's judgment. Cain offers an example of this: asked about his brother Abel, he dares to answer God and say, "Am I my brother's keeper?" Gen. 4. And in the prophet, hypocrites complain against God, as if he were too querulous, when they say, "Why have we fasted, and you do not look? We afflict our souls, and you take no notice?" Isa. 58. Likewise: "It is vain to serve God. For what profit is it that we keep his ordinances, and that we walk in mourning before the Lord of hosts?" Mal. 3. What shall we say of Judas the traitor? Although he knew that Christ was not ignorant of his deed, and felt himself being refuted and gravely rebuked, he nevertheless dares, along with the other apostles, to ask Christ whether he is suspected of so great a crime. Matt. 26. Nor is Sapphira's confidence any less, when so many examples existed by which she was taught that the apostles had been endowed with the Holy Spirit. It is useful to observe these things, so that hypocrites do not impose on us by their confidence and boldness, or put us off with their wicked words.

units.la: Caeterum ad Petrum reuertamur, qui ex spiritus suggestione dolum & fraudem intelligens, muliebri & hypocritica confidentia se moueri non patitur, sed Dei sententiam, quam idem spiritus suggerebat, in illam stringit, cuius duae partes sunt. Prima peccatum accusat & arguit. Nec enim quenquam punit Deus, nisi peccati conuictum, ut quae poenae causa sit, intelligat. Quid hoc est (inquit) quod consensistis inter vos ad tentandum spiritum Domini? Admiratione & interrogatione facti audaciam & atrocitatem amplificat: & ipsos in hoc conspirauisse clamat, ut spiritum Domini tentarent. At si quis Ananiam & Sapphiram de hoc suo facto interrogasset, hunc illis animum esse, constanter negaturos fuisse crediderim. At non refert quod nam nostrum sit de peccatis nostris iudicium: quia ad diuinae legis regulam illa examinantur. Et quia coniuges ipsi ecclesiam fallere instituerunt, in qua spiritus Dei praesidet & regnat, negari non potest, ipsos impia temeritate Dei spiritum tentauisse. Quare hypocritico suo dolo in eam legem peccauerunt, quae Deum tentare prohibet. Deuter.6. Eiusdem vero criminis reatu tenentur, quicunque ecclesiae Christi hodie etiam falsa fidei & pietatis simulatione imponere conantur, qui & ipsi sentient, Deum a nemine impune tentari posse.
units.tr: But let us return to Peter, who, understanding by the prompting of the Spirit the deceit and fraud, does not allow himself to be moved by the woman's confidence and hypocrisy, but aims at her the sentence of God, which the same Spirit suggested. This sentence has two parts. The first accuses and convicts the sin. For God punishes no one unless he is convicted of sin, so that the one being punished may understand the cause of the punishment. "What is this," he says, "that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?" By exclamation and question he amplifies the boldness and atrocity of the deed, and cries out that they had conspired together to test the Spirit of the Lord. If someone had asked Ananias and Sapphira about this deed, I believe they would have constantly denied that they had such an intention. Yet it does not matter what our own judgment of our sins is, since they are examined by the rule of divine law. And since the couple themselves set out to deceive the Church, in which the Spirit of God presides and reigns, it cannot be denied that by impious rashness they tempted the Spirit of God. Wherefore by their hypocritical trickery they sinned against that law which forbids tempting God. Deut. 6. Moreover, those are bound by the guilt of the same crime who today also try to impose on the Church of Christ by a false show of faith and piety; they too will feel that God can never be tempted with impunity by anyone.

units.la: At ne mariti authoritate & imperio excusari posse videretur Sapphira, consensum, qui inter ipsos fuit, cumprimis accusat Petrus, & eo argumento omnem excusationem illi adimit. Quo loco docemur, neminem malis consentire debere, qui Dei iudicium effugere cupiat: & ne ijs quidem, qui aliquod in nos ius habent diuinitus concessum. Marito etenim a Domino in vxorem potestas facta est, quando Euae dicitur: Ad virum erit respectus tuus, & ipse tibi dominabitur. Genes. 3. capite. Et apostoli mulieres virorum imperio subditas esse iubent. Ephes.5. Coloss.3 capite &c. Atqui hoc vnum Sapphirae vitio vertitur, quod marito consenserit, cum ille partem pecuniae, quam ecclesiae consecratam esse volebat, dolo malo seposuisset. Peccatum ergo quod contra Dei leges committitur, nullius hominis authoritas siue imperium excusat: eo quod Deo potius obediendum est quam hominibus, quemadmodum supra Petrus monuit, & hoc ipso Capite denuo repetetur. Quod si vero illorum peccatis consentire nefas est, qui aliquam in nos potestatem ex Dei ordinatione gerunt: quid de illis fiet, qui eorum scelera non consensu animi modo, verumetiam illicitis commercijs, & publicis laudibus approbant & defendunt, quorum commercio in vniuersum abstinere poterant, imo iuxta Dei leges abstinere debebant? Vt interim de illis nihil dicam, qui laborum & periculorum socios sese praebent, & sceleratos in flagitijs designandis adiuuant.
units.tr: But lest Sapphira seem to be excused by her husband's authority and command, Peter especially charges her with the consent that existed between them, and by this argument takes away every excuse from her. Here we are taught that no one who wishes to escape God's judgment should consent to evil, not even to those who hold some right over us granted by God. For power over a wife was given to the husband by the Lord, when it is said to Eve: "Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you." Gen. 3. And the apostles bid wives be subject to the authority of their husbands. Eph. 5. Col. 3, etc. Yet the only fault laid against Sapphira is that she consented to her husband, when he had secretly set aside by fraud part of the money which he wanted consecrated to the church. Therefore the authority or command of no human being excuses a sin committed against God's laws, since we must obey God rather than men, as Peter warned above and as will be repeated again in this chapter. But if it is wrong to consent to the sins of those who hold some power over us by God's ordinance, what will become of those who approve and defend the wicked deeds of others not only by consent of mind but also by unlawful dealings and public praise, when they could altogether abstain from their company, and indeed were bound by God's laws to abstain? I say nothing for now of those who make themselves partners in labours and dangers, and help the wicked in planning their crimes.

units.la: Altera sententia diuinae, per Petrum enunciata, pars poenam continet, quae Sapphirae cum marito communis futura sit. Ecce (inquit) pedes eorum, qui sepelierunt virum tuum, ad ianuam adsunt, & efferent te. Nec mora, quin ad pedes Petri extemplo collapsa expiret, & elata iuxta virum suum sepeliatur. Hic enim diuinae iustitiae tenor est, ut qui idem flagitium designant, eodem etiam supplicio multentur, sicut ipse apud prophetam testatur, dicens: An super his non visitarem, & gentem huic simile non vlcisceretur anima mea? Ierem.5. Debet hinc generalis doctrina sumi, quae ad omnia peccata & scelera extendatur. Qui enim olim pauperum oppressionem, iniustam vim, tyrannidem, vsuras, caedes, adulteria, stupra & quaecunque alia sunt huius generis, grauissime vindicauit, eadem in nobis etiam hodie vindicabit, nisi poenitentiam agamus Christiani hominibus dignam. Praecipuum tamen huius loci caput est, ut quid eos maneat discamus, qui sub Christi praetextu sua quaerunt, & ecclesiae Christi fucum facere audent. Videntur illi interdum laetis vti rerum suarum successibus, sed instabilis est illorum felicitas, nec diu per fraudem partis bonis fruuntur. Nam cito finitur impiorum iubilatio, & momentanea est hypocritae laetitia. Iob.20. Exemplum huius rei in Iuda quoq; proditore habemus, qui cum rebus suis optime consulcum esse putaret, & iam sacerdotum favore magnus videri posset, eam experitur divina iustitia seueritatem, quae ipsum ad restim adigit, ut nec vita nec pecunijs, quas vita chariores habuerat, diu frui possit. Et utinam non hodie eadem poenas multi experirentur, qui sub euangelij praetextu, nihil aliud quam ecclesiasticorum bonorum vsurpationem & direptionem quaesiuerunt. Hos certe a Monachis & episcopis denuo eiectos vidimus, nec aliquid ex illis opibus praesidij senssse, quas in eum vsum seposuerant, ut contra apertos religionis hostes ecclesias armata manu tueri possent. Nec melior fortuna omnibus ijs speranda est, qui similii exemplo peccant. Si enim subitam mortem Ananias & Sapphira meruerunt, quos non quicquam ecclesiae surripuisse, sed de suis opibus aliquid hypocritica fraude seposuisse Lucas scribit, quas mortes & quae infortunia non merentur, qui ecclesias aperta vi & publica authoritate diripere audent? Agnoscamus ergo in his Christi Iesu potentiam, qui ut ecclesiae suae propitius semper adest, ita illi fucum fieri non patitur, sed cum apertos eius hostes & persecutores, tum hypocritas impostores dignis supplicijs coercet, ut veri cultus syncritas retineri possit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The other part of the divine sentence, pronounced through Peter, contains the punishment that was to fall upon Sapphira together with her husband. "Behold," he says, "the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." And without delay she fell at Peter's feet at once, expired, and was carried out and buried beside her husband. For this is the tenor of divine justice: those who commit the same crime are punished with the same penalty, as he himself testifies through the prophet, saying: "Shall I not visit these things? Shall not my soul avenge itself on such a nation?" Jer. 5. From this a general doctrine should be drawn, extending to all sins and crimes. For he who once most severely avenged the oppression of the poor, unjust violence, tyranny, usury, murder, adultery, fornication and whatever else is of this kind, will avenge them in us today as well, unless we do repentance worthy of Christians. The principal point of this passage, however, is that we learn what awaits those who seek their own gain under the pretext of Christ and dare to make a mask of Christ's church. Such people sometimes seem to enjoy happy outcomes in their affairs, but their happiness is unstable, and they do not long enjoy goods gained by fraud. For the rejoicing of the wicked is quickly ended, and the joy of the hypocrite is momentary. Job 20. We have an example of this in Judas the traitor too, who thought his affairs were going very well and already seemed great through the favour of the priests, yet experienced the severity of divine justice, which drove him to the halter, so that he could not long enjoy either his life or the money which he had prized more than life. And would that many did not today suffer the same punishments, who under the pretext of the gospel have sought nothing but the seizure and plundering of church goods. Certainly we have seen these men cast out again by monks and bishops, and they felt no help from those resources which they had set aside for that purpose, so that they might defend the churches by armed hand against open enemies of religion. Nor should a better fortune be hoped for by all who sin by a similar example. For if Ananias and Sapphira deserved sudden death, though Luke writes that they had stolen nothing from the church but had only set aside part of their own resources by hypocritical fraud, what deaths and misfortunes do they not deserve who dare to plunder churches by open force and public authority? Let us therefore acknowledge in these things the power of Christ Jesus, who, as he is always present and propitious to his church, does not allow it to be made a mask, but restrains with fitting punishments both his open enemies and persecutors and his hypocritical impostors, so that the sincerity of true worship may be preserved. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIV.

units.la: Et factus est timor magnus super totam ecclesiam, & super omnes qui haec audierunt. Per manus autem apostolorum signa fiebant & prodigia multa in populo, (Et erant vnanimiter omnes in porticu Solomonis. Aliorum autem nemo audebat se illis coniungere, sed magnificabat illos populus. Magis autem accrescebat multitudo credentium Domino, virorum simul & mulierum:)ita ut in plateas exportarent infirmos, & ponerent in lectulis & grabbatis, ut veniente Petri vel vmbra obumbraret aliquem eorum. Conueniebat autem & multitudo vicinarum ciuitatum Hierosolymam, afferens aegros ac vexatos a spiritibus immundis, qui sanabantur omnes.
units.tr: And great fear came upon the whole Church, and upon all who heard these things. Through the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people. (And they were all with one accord in Solomon's porch. Of the rest none dared join himself to them, but the people magnified them. Yet believers were increasingly added to the Lord, both men and women.) So that they carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on beds and couches, so that when Peter came by, at least his shadow might fall on some of them. A crowd also came together from the neighbouring towns to Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, and they were all healed.

units.la: Vidimus horribile iudicij diuini exemplum, quo Ananias & eius vxor Sapphira morte repentina multati sunt, quod & fidem in Christum falso simulassent, & ecclesiae conati essent fucum facere, quoad bona publica, quae in pauperum subuentionem contribuebantur. Docet hoc, quanta sit Dei in puniendis hypocritis seueritas: qui ut falli nequit, ita non potest non graviter irasci ijs, qui ipsum fallere conantur. Vidimus praeterea, quam ardens fuerit in primitiua ecclesia disciplina conseruandae studium, ne vel hypocrita vel palam scelerati obrepentes, fidem Christi infamem aut bonis suspectam redderent. Vt vero ad huius imitationem accenderetur tota posteritas, sequitur praesens locus, qui huius exempli fructus plures & eximios commemorat: quibus primitiuae ecclesiae studia & exercitia interseruntur: ut ex ijs discamus, quid hodie fieri oporteat, si regnum Dei propagare, & Christo propitio vti velimus.
units.tr: We have seen a horrible example of divine judgement, by which Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck down by sudden death, because they had falsely pretended to faith in Christ and had tried to deceive the Church about the public goods that were contributed for the relief of the poor. This teaches how great God's severity is in punishing hypocrites. He cannot be deceived, and so he cannot but be gravely angry with those who try to deceive him. We have also seen how eager the primitive Church was to keep up discipline, so that neither hypocrites nor openly wicked people might creep in and make the faith of Christ infamous or suspect to good men. And so that all posterity might be inflamed to imitate this, the present passage follows, which recounts several outstanding fruits of this example. Among them are interwoven the practices and exercises of the primitive Church, so that from them we may learn what ought to be done today, if we wish to spread the kingdom of God and enjoy the favour of Christ.

units.la: Primo ait Lucas: Factus est timor magnus super totam ecclesiam, & super omnes qui haec audierunt. Timuerunt ergo tam Christiani quam exteri, ad quos huius rei fama dimanauit. Nec inutilis fuit hic timor. Per hunc enim factum est, ut pij quidem cautiores essent, & ferio magis agerent Dei negotium: hostes vero minus auderent contra ecclesiam, cui spiritum tam efficaciter adesse videbant. Est hic praecipuus disciplinae ecclesiasticae fructus, quod & pios in officio continet, & impijs timorem incutit. Hodie quia quidem licet omnibus, ecclesiae inseptina licentia dissipata hostibus praeda fiunt. Obseruandus est hic simul iudiciorum Dei vsus, qui in hoc consistit, ut ex illis Dei iusticiam agnoscamus & eius pia consyderatione territi emendemur. Tradidit hunc ipse Deus, quando Abrahamo Sodomarum horribile excidium denuntians, dicebat: Scio, quod mandaturus sit filijs suis
units.tr: First, Luke says: "And great fear came upon the whole Church, and upon all who heard these things." Therefore both the Christians and the outsiders, to whom the report of this matter had spread, were afraid. Nor was this fear useless. For through it the godly became more cautious and carried on God's business more fervently, while enemies dared less against the Church, which they saw the Spirit so effectively present with. This is the chief fruit of ecclesiastical discipline: it keeps the godly in their duty and strikes fear into the ungodly. Today, because everyone is free to do as he likes, and the Church's discipline has been dissolved by unbridled licence, she is made a prey to her enemies. We must also observe here the practice of God's judgements, which consists in this: that from such judgements we recognise the justice of God and, struck with pious reflection on it, we are corrected. God himself handed this down, when announcing to Abraham the horrible destruction of Sodom, he said: "I know that he will command his sons and his household after him that they keep the way of the Lord, and do justice and judgement," etc.

units.la: Disciplina piost & impios in officio continet.
units.tr: Discipline keeps the godly and the ungodly in their duty.

units.la: Vsus iudiciorum Dei. suis & domui suae posse, ut custodiant viam Domini, & faciant iustitiam & iudicium, &c. Nec aliam ob causam veteta iudiciorum suorum exempla literis consignari, & in ecclesia cum publice tum priuatim praedicari voluit, sicut Asaph Psalm. 78. testatur, vbi sic scribit: Constituit contestationem in Iacob, & legem tulit in Israele Deus, quam praecepit patribus nostris, ut haec nota faceret filijs suis: Ut cognoscat aetas posterà, filij scilicet qui nati sunt, cum adoleuerint, narrent ea filijs suis: Indeque in Deo fiduciam suam ponant, nec obliuiscantur operum Dei, mandataque eius obseruent. Nec euadant similes patribus suis, &c. Debet ergo hic iudicij diuini, quo Ananiae & Sapphirae hypocrisis punita est, vsus hodie etiam retineri, ut vero Dei timore concepto, ab hypocrisi nobis caueamus, Deum autem colamus in spiritu & veritate, sicut Christus nobis praecepit. Imo hoc exemplo singuli excitati, ad se transferant quaecunque huius generis passim in historijs habentur, ut ex aliorum exemplis discant sibi quid facto opus sit, si Dei iram effugere cupiant.
units.tr: The practice of God's judgements. (…) his sons and his house after him, that they keep the way of the Lord, and do justice and judgement, etc. Nor did he wish the ancient examples of his judgements to be recorded in writing, and proclaimed in the Church both publicly and privately, for any other reason, as Asaph testifies in Psalm 78, where he writes thus: "He established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children: that the generation to come might know them, the children who were yet to be born; who should arise and declare them to their children; that they might put their confidence in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments, and not be like their fathers," etc. Therefore the use of this divine judgement, by which the hypocrisy of Ananias and Sapphira was punished, ought to be retained today too. And so that, with the fear of God conceived, we may guard ourselves against hypocrisy, and worship God in spirit and truth, as Christ has taught us. Indeed, let each one be stirred by this example to apply to himself whatever things of this kind are found everywhere in histories, so that from the examples of others they may learn what must be done for themselves, if they wish to escape the wrath of God.

units.la: Secundo de apostolis dicitur, quod illorum ministerio multa signa & prodigia in populo publice edita sint. Vnde constat hac etiam parte exauditas fuisse fidelium preces, qua petierunt, ut miraculis instruerentur apostoli, quorum authoritate in Christi regno propagando adiuuari possent. Nec vulgaria tantummodo edunt, sed eousque virtus illa extenditur, ut in plateas expositi aegroti vmbram Petri transeuntis expetant, & hanc sibi salutarem experiantur. Iam ergo impleri coepit illud Christi: Qui credit in me, signa quae ego facio, faciet etiam ipse, & maiora his faciet. Est autem hic secundus disciplinae ecclesiasticae fructus, quod ecclesiae preces exaudit Deus, & dona spiritus sui auget: cum eorum preces abominari soleat, qui aures suas ad legem eius obturant. Proverb. 28. Patet hoc ex historijs, quae luculenter docent, insigniora illa spiritus dona, simul cum miraculis tunc extinguì coepisse, cum disciplina dissolui coepit, & morum licentia introducta est. Nemo tamen superstitiosis patrocinari putet, quod hic de Petri vmbra scribitur: ut nec illud, quod infra de Pauli sudarijs audiemus. Solent quidem hinc nonnulli argumentari: Si Petri vmbra multis salutaris fuit, quanto magis vestes & offa? &c. Et hinc totum illud superstitionum chaos exortum est, quod circa peregrinationes & Diuorum, vel potius reliquiarum (quarum maxima pars falsa & ementita est) cultum versatur. At nos signa ista non in eum finem facta dicimus, ut de Petri aut Pauli virtute testarentur, sed ut euangelij praedicationem, cuius illi ministri erant, confirmarent. Ad huius ergo commendationem referri debent, & ad Christum eos remittere, quos hactenus vana superstitio circa res inutiles occupatos detinuit. Praeterea ex ipsius Petri verbis, quae cap. 3. audiuimus, nos firmius multo argumentabimur: Maior est apud Deum virtutis & pietatis quam vestium, aut totius corporis humani, ratio. At neque sanctorum virtus neque pietas ad miracula quicquam contulit. Ergo multo minus illorum vestibus aut ossibus illa ascribi debent. Addemus huic argumento, quod alibi virtus ex ipso Christo, non ex eius tunica exiuisse dicitur. Luc. 6. & 8. Sed facile cadet superstitio, si miraculorum omnium finem siue scopum consyderemus, qui duplex est. Primo iste apostolorum doctrinam obsignari oportuit, quemadmodum ipse Christus admonet, Matth. 10. Marc. 16. Vnde colligitur, huic credendum esse, nec nouis hodie miraculis nos indigere. Si enim apostolicam doctrinam ministri praedicant, illa iam olim innumeris signis probata atque confirmata est. Quod si vero diuersam ab hac tradunt, nequaquam recipi merentur, etiamsi miracula edant plurima: quando falsis quoque & Antichristianis doctoribus illud permitti constat, ut electorum fides perspicacior & euidentior fiat. Vide Deut. 13. Matth. 24. 2. Thess. 2. Alter miraculorum finis & vsus est, ut Christi Iesu cognitionem tradant, in cuius nomine ab apostolis virisque apostolicis edita sunt. Curantur ab apostolis in Christi nomine variis morbis & infirmitatibus obnoxij, & cum his etiam daemoniaci, quos malignus Satanae spiritus exagitabat. Christum Iesum ergo eum esse agnoscamus, qui (ut propheta ait) nostros languores & infirmitates pertulit, quique non corporum modo, verumetiam animarum & corruptae nostrae naturae vitiis medetur. Illius enim spiritu & verbo regenerati nouas vires concipimus, ut illo nos confortante possimus omnia. Phil. 4. Idem a Satanae tyrannide solus liberat. Idcirco enim in mundum venit (teste Iohanne apostolo) ut opera diaboli dissoluat. 1. Iohan. 3. Et prima salutis promissio illius potentia & merito serpentis caput conterendum esse docet. Genes. 3. Quod effectum esse partim ipse in euangelio testatur, partim per apostolos illius nomine edita miracula abundè probant. Et omnes quidem sanatos fuisse Lucas admonet, qui ad apostolos adducti fuerunt, ut Christi nomine sanarentur. Unde colligimus, vniuersalem esse salvatorem Christum, qui ut omnes laborantes & oneratos ad fide inuitat: ita ad se venientes minime excludit. Matth. 11. Iohan. 6.
units.tr: Second, it is said of the apostles that through their ministry many signs and wonders were publicly performed among the people. From this it is clear that in this respect too the prayers of the faithful were heard, by which they asked that the apostles be equipped with miracles, so that by their authority they might be helped in spreading the kingdom of Christ. Nor do they perform only ordinary works, but that power extends so far that the sick, laid out in the streets, long for the shadow of Peter as he passes and experience it as healing for themselves. Now that saying of Christ begins to be fulfilled: "He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also, and greater works than these will he do." This second fruit of ecclesiastical discipline is that God hears the prayers of the Church and increases the gifts of his Spirit, whereas he is wont to abominate the prayers of those who stop their ears against his law (Prov. 28). This is evident from the histories, which clearly teach that those more outstanding gifts of the Spirit, together with the miracles, then began to be extinguished, when discipline began to be dissolved and licence in morals was introduced. Yet let no one think that superstitious people are being supported by what is written here about Peter's shadow, nor by what we shall hear later about Paul's handkerchiefs. Some indeed are accustomed to argue from this: "If Peter's shadow was healing to many, how much more his garments and bones?" etc. And from this arose that whole chaos of superstitions which revolves around pilgrimages and the cult of the saints, or rather of relics, most of which are false and fabricated. But we say that these signs were not done for the purpose of bearing witness to the power of Peter or Paul, but to confirm the preaching of the gospel, whose ministers they were. Therefore they must be referred to the commendation of this, and those whom vain superstition has hitherto kept occupied with useless things must be sent back to Christ. Moreover, from Peter's own words, which we heard in chapter 3, we shall argue much more firmly: "The reckoning with God is greater in virtue and piety than in garments or in the whole human body." But neither the virtue nor the piety of the saints contributed anything to miracles. Therefore much less should those miracles be ascribed to their garments or bones. We may add to this argument that elsewhere it is said that virtue went out from Christ himself, not from his tunic (Luke 6 and 8). But superstition will easily fall, if we consider the end or purpose of all the miracles, which is twofold. First, that doctrine of the apostles had to be sealed, as Christ himself warns (Matt. 10; Mark 16). Hence it is gathered that this doctrine must be believed, and that we have no need of new miracles today. For if ministers preach the apostolic doctrine, that doctrine has long since been proved and confirmed by countless signs. But if they teach something different from this, they do not deserve to be received at all, even if they perform very many miracles, since it is plainly permitted that false and Antichristian teachers too should do so, so that the faith of the elect may become more keen and clearer (see Deut. 13; Matt. 24; 2 Thess. 2). The other end and use of the miracles is that they might convey the knowledge of Jesus Christ, in whose name they were performed by the apostles and men of apostolic character. By the apostles, in the name of Christ, those liable to various diseases and infirmities were cured, and with them also the demoniacs, whom the wicked spirit of Satan tormented. Let us therefore acknowledge Christ Jesus as he who (as the prophet says) bore our languors and infirmities, and who heals not only the bodies but also the souls and the vices of our corrupted nature. For we, regenerated by his Spirit and word, conceive new strength, so that with him strengthening us we can do all things (Phil. 4). He alone also frees us from the tyranny of Satan. For he came into the world (as the apostle John testifies) to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3). And the first promise of salvation teaches that by his power and merit the head of the serpent is to be crushed (Gen. 3). This was partly fulfilled, as he himself attests in the gospel, and partly the miracles performed in his name through the apostles abundantly prove it. And Luke reminds us that all those brought to the apostles to be healed in Christ's name were in fact healed. From this we gather that Christ is the universal Saviour, who invites all who labour and are burdened to faith, and in the same way does not in the least exclude those who come to him (Matt. 11; John 6).

units.la: Apostolorum miraculis publicum totius ecclesiae exercitium subijcit, quando eos qui credidernt, vnanimiter in porticu Solomonis fuisse ait. Quod de sacris illorum coetibus intelligendum esse, ex secundi capitis fine discimus, vbi domorum mentio fit, in quibus panem fregerint. Non aliud igitur hoc loco euangelista docere vult, quam praecipuam fidelibus hanc curam fuisse, vt sacros coetus frequentarent, & in ijs non tam corporibus quam animis suis per fidem & charitatem vnirentur. Vbi Christianae fortitudinis & constantiae exemplum nobis exhibent, qui cum Concilij minas & edicta non ignorarent, propter illa tamen ne a coetibus quidem publicis abstinere voluerunt. Atqui humanae prudentiae sufficere potuisset, si in animis suis fidem retinere, & intra priuatos parietes de Christo cum fidis fratribus verba facere licuisset. Et hodie multi istis rationibus suam ignauiam excusant, qua Christi confessionem inter indifferentia numerant, & illam principum edictis sibi extor queri patiuntur. Imo prudentiae esse putatur, inter pericula fidem dissimulare, coetus & sacra omnia intermittere, controuersos articulos vel omnino non attingere, vel ambigue tractare, vel etiam fidem omnino abnegare. Sed quam infelices sint huius prudentiae effectus, ecclesia non sine dolore & multorum interitu experitur. Rectius multo isti, qui ex Christi verbis didicerunt, confessionem a fide separari non posse. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Rom. 10. Et Christi vox est: Quecunque puduerit mei & sermonum meorum in generatione hac adultera & peccatrice, pudebit illius & filium hominis, vbi venerit in gloria patris sui cum angelis sanctis. Marc. 8. cap. Obseruemus autem, non temere toties sacrorum coetuum mentionem fieri. Hinc enim colligitur, ecclesiam illis nullo modo carere posse, cum propter preces publicas quas peculiari promissione nobis Christus commendauit, tum ne falsis doctoribus clam subrependi occasio detur, quibus hoc proprium esse Paulus scribit, quod in familias subeant, & captiuas ducant mulierculas, & quotquot harum similes, ipsorum dolis patent. 2. Tim. 3. Et ne quis tam necessarium ordinem turbandi occasionem aliquam haberet, Christus quoque coetus publicos nunquam deuitauit, sed in illis publice docuit, & eo argumento, sene nec seductorem nec schismaticum censeri debere probat. Ioan. 18. Nec alia causa videtur, quod primi credentes ne Iudaicum quidem tem plum horruerunt, cum nullus alius commodior locus ipsis in vrbe daretur. Confutantur hoc exemplo Anabaptistae, fanaticum & seditiosum hominum genus, qui nefas esse ducunt nostra templa noftrosq; coetus ingredi, & anxie cauent, ne ijs polluantur: cum interim illis non graue videatur, in Christi ecclesia schisma facere, quo non aliud crimen magis horrendum & detestabilius censeri debebat.
units.tr: He sets before us, in the miracles of the apostles, the public exercise of the whole Church, when he says that those who believed were all together in Solomon's porch. From the end of the second chapter, where mention is made of houses in which they broke bread, we learn that this must be understood of their sacred assemblies. The evangelist therefore wishes to teach nothing else here than that the chief care of the faithful was to attend the holy assemblies, and in them to be united not so much in body as in soul, through faith and love. Here they set before us an example of Christian courage and steadfastness: though they were not ignorant of the threats and edicts of the Council, they nevertheless were unwilling to abstain even from the public assemblies because of them. And yet it would have sufficed for human prudence to keep the faith in their hearts, and, if it had been allowed, to speak of Christ within private walls with trusted brothers. And today many excuse their cowardice on these grounds: they count the confession of Christ among things indifferent, and suffer it to be wrung from them by the edicts of princes. Indeed, it is thought to be prudence to hide one's faith amid dangers, to give up assemblies and all sacred duties, to avoid disputed articles altogether or handle them ambiguously, or even to deny the faith outright. But how unhappy the effects of this so-called prudence are, the Church experiences not without grief and the death of many. Far better are those who have learned from the words of Christ that confession cannot be separated from faith: "With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom. 10). And the voice of Christ is: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him also will the Son of man be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (Mark 8). Let us note, moreover, that the mention of sacred assemblies is not made so often without reason. For from this it is gathered that the Church can by no means do without them, both because of the public prayers which Christ commended to us with a special promise, and so that no occasion be given for false teachers to slip in secretly, of whom it is Paul's writing that this is their characteristic: that they creep into households and lead captive silly women, and whoever are like these are open to their deceits (2 Tim. 3). And lest anyone have any occasion for disturbing so necessary an order, Christ too never avoided public assemblies, but taught publicly in them, and by this argument he proves that one who does so ought not be judged a seducer or a schismatic (John 18). Nor does there seem to be any other reason why the first believers did not shrink even from the Jewish temple, since no other more convenient place was given them in the city. By this example the Anabaptists are refuted, a fanatical and seditious kind of men, who count it an abomination to enter our churches and our assemblies, and anxiously take care lest they be polluted by them; while meanwhile it does not seem grave to them to make a schism in the Church of Christ, a crime than which none ought to be judged more horrible and detestable.

units.la: Sed ad fructus disciplinae & exercitiorum veteris ecclesiae reuertamur, inter quos tertio loco refertur Maiestas, quae illam hostibus formidabilem, & toti populo venerabilem fecit. Ait enim Lucas: Nemo aliorum sese ipsis coniungere audebat. Sed magnificabat eos populus. Quod de ijs intelligi debet, qui non prorsus impij & a religione alieni erant, mundi tamen & carnis studijs adhuc detinebantur. Nam cum horrendum & infelicem Ananiae & Sapphirae exitum vidissent, timebant torum coetui se coniungere, in quo hypocrisis tam seuere punita fuerat, sua nimirum imperfectionis sibi probe conscij. Purior ergo ab eo tempore fuit externus ecclesiae coetus, in quem fortasse prius multi dolo irrepserant, qualem vidimus Ananiam fuisse. Interim magnifice de illis isti sentiebant, & illorum mores publicis quoq; laudibus celebrabant: eo quod coelestis & angelicae vitae speciem in illis viderent relucere. Plura eius generis exempla in historijs leguntur. Et sub Traiano Imperatore tam inculpata & integra fuit Christianorum conuersatio, vt cum is contra illos persecutionem decreuisset, Plinij Secundi (qui ex Iudicum numero erat) intercessione liberati sint. De duobus autem obseruatu dignissimis, nos hic locus admonet. Primo, ecclesiam solis fidelibus & veris Christi cultoribus patere, nec vllo modo in illa mendaces & hypocritas admitti. Quia enim veritatis rex Christus est (quemadmodum coram Pilato testatur) mendaces & hypocritas ferre nequit. Et in euangelio a nuptijs suis eijciendos dicit, quicunque fine veste nuptiali ingressi fuerint. Matth. 22. Eosdem alibi quoq; vna cum timidis & incredulis, cum homicidis, fornicatoribus, veneficis & idololatris, aeternae damnationi adiudicat. Apocal. 21. Deinde vnde Christianus authoritas & gratia inter homines conciliari possint, discimus. Inde nimirum, si suae professioni respondeant, vitamq; viuat Christo dignam, per quam Deus cœlestis pater glorificari possit. Matth.5. Firmū enim ratumq; manet, quod per prophetam sacerdoti Heli Deus denuntiat: Honore prosequar eos, qui me honoraverint: at qui me probro affecerint, ignominiosi fient. 1.Sam.2. Quae si paulò attentius consyderaremus, facile pateret, quî fiat, quòd euangelij nomen passim hodie inuisum, eiusq; professores fere exosi & infames habentur. Meretur hoc effrænis nostra licentia, qua in omne scelus sub euangelij prætextu erumpimus, quique aliis sanctiores volumus haberi, fere omnes alios peccandi libidine superamus. Corrigamus hæc, & veteri maiestate ecclesiam venerabilem fore breui experiemur.
units.tr: But let us return to the fruits of discipline and of the exercises of the ancient Church, among which in the third place is mentioned the majesty which made it formidable to its enemies and venerable to the whole people. For Luke says: "None of the others dared join himself to them; but the people magnified them" (Acts 5:13). This must be understood of those who were not wholly impious and alien to religion, yet were still held by the pursuits of the world and the flesh. For when they had seen the dreadful and unhappy end of Ananias and Sapphira, they feared to join themselves to that assembly in which hypocrisy had been punished so severely, being of course well aware of their own imperfection. The external assembly of the Church was therefore purer from that time on, whereas before, many had perhaps crept in by guile, as we saw Ananias had. Meanwhile they thought highly of them, and celebrated their conduct with public praises, because they saw in them the appearance of a heavenly and angelic life shining forth. Many examples of this kind are read in histories. And under the Emperor Trajan the conduct of the Christians was so blameless and upright that, when he had decreed persecution against them, they were freed through the intercession of Pliny the Younger, who was of the number of the judges.
