Now, this passage reminds us of two things most worthy of observation. First, that the Church is open only to the faithful and true worshippers of Christ, and that liars and hypocrites are in no way admitted into it. For since Christ is the king of truth (as he testifies before Pilate), he cannot bear liars and hypocrites. And in the Gospel he says that those who enter without the wedding garment are to be cast out from his wedding (Matt. 22). Elsewhere too he condemns these same people, together with the fearful and unbelieving, with murderers, fornicators, sorcerers and idolaters, to eternal damnation (Rev. 21). Second, we learn how Christians can win authority and grace among men: certainly, if they live up to their profession and lead a life worthy of Christ, through which the heavenly Father God may be glorified (Matt. 5). For what God declares through the prophet to the priest Eli stands firm and fixed: "I will honour those who honour me, but those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed" (1 Sam. 2). If we considered these things a little more carefully, it would easily be clear why the name of the gospel is everywhere hated today, and its professors are for the most part held in odium and infamy. Our unbridled licence deserves this, by which we break out into every crime under the pretext of the gospel, and while we want to be considered holier than others, we surpass almost all others in the lust of sinning. Let us correct these things, and we shall soon find the Church venerable again with its ancient majesty.

units.la: Quarto loco nouos quotidie Christi cultores, tam viros quàm mulieres, ecclesiæ numero accessisse dicit, qui nimirum vera fide imbuti & diuino spiritu moti pertrahebantur. Docet hoc quàm inanes & vani sint hostium Christi conatus, quando qui in vrbe Hierosolymorum primatum tenebant, nascentis ecclesiæ incrementa impedire nequiuerunt. Nam sicuti Christus ait, spirat spiritus vbicunq; voluerit, nec vllis hominum legibus subijcitur. Ioban.3. Et exempla docent, ecclesiam inter persecutionum procellas semper auctam potius quàm imminutam esse. Hoc enim Christi proprium est, vt in medio inimicorum suorum dominetur. Psal.110. Nemo igitur impiorum hostium minus terreatur, quasi in illorum potestate consistat ecclesiæ euersio. Christo enim illa nititur, cui inferorum portæ prævalere nequeunt. Matth.16.
units.tr: In the fourth place he says that daily new worshippers of Christ, both men and women, were added to the number of the Church, being of course imbued with true faith and drawn along, moved by the divine Spirit. This teaches how empty and vain are the attempts of the enemies of Christ, since those who held the leading position in the city of Jerusalem could not hinder the growth of the newborn Church. For, as Christ says, the Spirit breathes where he wills, and is subject to no laws of men (John 3). And examples teach that the Church, amid the storms of persecutions, has always been increased rather than diminished. For it is peculiar to Christ to rule in the midst of his enemies (Ps. 110). Let no one therefore be terrified by the impious enemies, as if the overthrow of the Church rested in their power. For it rests on Christ, against whom the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. 16).

units.la: Accedit hùs, quòd Christi regnum ad finitimas quoq; ciuitates propagari incipit. Vulgata enim hinc inde miraculorum fama, excitantur quàm plurimi, vt & ipsi suos ægrotos & dæmoniacos Hierosolymam deportari curent, eaq; occasione in Christi cognitionem perueniant. Præcipuus verò hodie huius loci vsus est, vt quibus medijs Christi regnum propagari possit, intelligamus. Qua in re varie & diuersimodè ab ijs consultatur, qui sub fidei prætextu carnali sapientiæ indulgent, nec illam adhuc fidei obedientiæ subiecerunt. Sunt enim qui consultissimum esse putent, vt fideles tempori inseruiant, multa concedant & dissimulent, donec noua aliqua mundi facies sese exerat, & mitiores sint illorum animi, qui nunc veritatis odium profitentur. Alij rursum ad carnus præsidia conuersi, fœderibus & armis rem transfigendam esse arbitrantur. Vtrosq; verò perniciosissimè falli, rerum euentus testatur. Dei enim hoc opus est, nec alijs armis aut viribus confici poterit. Non per exercitum, neq; per fortitudinem (ait per prophetam Dominus) sed per spiritum meum. Zach.4. Et rursum: Seruabo eos in Domino Deo eorum, non autem seruabo eos per arcum, neq; per gladium, neq; per bellum, nec per equos, nec per equites, &c. Scimus equidem illum nonnunquam hominum & principum ministerio adeoq; armis vti (sicuti Machabæorū, Constantini & Theodosij exempla testantur) sed ita tunc res moderari solet, vt inter hæc ipsa spiritus sui virtus elucescat, & sola emineat. In hunc itaq; solum respiciant, quicunque de ecclesia afferenda & Christi regno propagando consilia ineunt. Quia nullus Deo operandi locus superest, vbi humanis cōsilijs aut præsidijs res peragi incipitur. Primitiuæ igitur ecclesiæ studijs insistamus, quæ hucusq; Lucas recensuit. Veritatis doctrinam constanter prædicent doctores, nec ab ea se diuelli patiantur, quæ tot miraculis olim obsignata est. Eandem studiose audiant, quicunque Christiani haberi volunt, & verbi studio assiduas preces coniungant, quando sine Dei interna suggestione nihil efficitur. Vigeat ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ authoritas, ne vel hypocritis vel palàm flagitiosis in ecclesia locus concedatur. Regnet charitatis studium & liberalis in pauperes beneficentia, ne fidei domestici propter nostram auaritiam publica egestatis exempla conspician-tur. Hæc quia hodie non modò negliguntur, verumetiam inuertuntur, mirum non est, quòd exiguos videmus euangelicæ doctrinæ professus. Adista igitur accingamur totis animis, nec deerit conatibus pijs Dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the kingdom of Christ begins to spread also to the neighbouring cities. For when the fame of the miracles has spread abroad on every side, very many are roused, so that they also take care to have their sick and demoniacs brought to Jerusalem, and on that occasion come to the knowledge of Christ. But the principal use of this passage today is that we may understand by what means the kingdom of Christ can be propagated. In this matter men consult in various and diverse ways, those who, under the pretext of faith, indulge in carnal wisdom and have not yet subjected it to the obedience of faith. For there are those who think it most prudent that the faithful should serve the times, concede many things and dissemble, until some new face of the world shows itself, and the minds of those who now profess hatred of the truth become milder. Others again, turning to fleshly defences, think the matter must be carried through by alliances and arms. But the outcome of events shows that both are most perniciously mistaken. For this is God's work, and it cannot be accomplished by other arms or strength. "Not by an army, nor by strength," says the Lord through the prophet, "but by my Spirit" (Zech. 4). And again: "I will save them in the Lord their God, but I will not save them by the bow, nor by the sword, nor by war, nor by horses, nor by horsemen," etc. We indeed know that he sometimes uses the ministry of men and princes, and so also arms, as the examples of the Maccabees, Constantine and Theodosius testify; but then the matter is usually so ordered that the power of his Spirit shines forth amid these very things, and alone stands out. Therefore let all those who devise plans for the establishment of the Church and the propagation of the kingdom of Christ look only to him. For there is no room left for God to work where the thing is begun by human counsels or defences. Let us therefore devote ourselves to the pursuits of the primitive Church, which Luke has so far recounted. Let the teachers preach the doctrine of truth steadfastly, and not allow themselves to be torn from it, which was once sealed by so many miracles. Let all who wish to be considered Christians hear it diligently, and join constant prayers to their zeal for the Word, since nothing is accomplished without God's inward prompting. Let the authority of ecclesiastical discipline flourish, so that no place be granted in the Church either to hypocrites or to those openly shameful. Let zeal for charity and generous beneficence toward the poor reign, lest the household of faith, on account of our avarice, be seen as public examples of want. Since these things are today not only neglected but even overturned, it is no wonder that we see few professors of the evangelical doctrine. Let us therefore gird ourselves for these things with all our hearts, and our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, will not fail our pious efforts: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Christum propagari ad finitimos.
units.tr: Christ is propagated to the neighbouring places.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXV.
units.tr: Homily 35.

units.la: Exurgens autem summus Pontifex, & omnes qui cum eo erant (quæ erat secta Sadducæorum) repleti sunt zelo, & iniecerunt manus in apostolos, posuerunt́ eos in custodiam publicam. Angelus autè Domini nocte aperuit ianuā carceris, & educens eos, dixit: Ite, & stantes loquimini in templo populo omnia verba vitæ huius. Illi verò cùm hoc audiuissent, sub auroram ingressi sunt templum, & docebant.
units.tr: Then the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (which was the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with jealousy. They laid hands on the apostles and put them in the public prison. But the angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, brought them out, and said: "Go, stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this life." When they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach.

units.la: PErquàm memorabile est Dauidis regis & prophetæ oraculum, quo Christum Iesum in medio inimicorum suorum regnaturum esse vaticinatur. Psal.110. Inde colligitur, regnaturum quidem Christum etiam in hoc seculo, ita tamen, vt nunquam defuturi sint, qui regnum ipsius euertere conentur. Exempla huius rei passim in scripturis & ecclesiasticis historijs obuia sunt. Omnium vero clarissimè in præsenti libro hoc cernitur, cùm in apostolicarum rerum commemoratione & primitiuæ ecclesiæ descriptione, duo hæc, felices nimirum regni Christi progressus, & insanos contra hoc impiorum conatus semper Lucas coniungit. Vsus horum est, vt nec cruce & aduersis offendamur, de quibus toties Christus admonuit, nec perpetuam in hoc mundo speremus ecclesiæ tranquillitatem, sed tunc quoque ad crucem ferendam præparemur, quando ecclesia in portu tutissimo consistere videtur. Quò cum primùs præsens historia referri debet. Præmisit enim nuper Lucas florentissimum primitiuæ ecclesiæ statum, illam & authoritate præclaram & nouis indies incrementis auctam fuisse docens, adeò vt iam Hierosolymorum vrbs angustior esset, quàm quæ Christi regnum posset completi, quod iam ad exteros quoq; propagari incipiebat. Cæterum tantis tamen prosperis successibus grauis persecutio & ingens periculum subijcitur, quando tantum hostibus suis permittit Christus, vt apostolis manus inijciant, & in carcerem abductos extremo supplicio multare instituant. Interim plus consolationis quàm terroris ista afferunt, dum apostolis pro sui nominis gloria periclitantibus tam præsentiope af-fulget dominus. Sed vt plus hinc vtilitatis ad nos redeat, primò Christi & apostolorum hostes consyderandi erunt. Deinde vt illorum conatus dominus eluserit, inspiciemus. Postremò de eo dicetur, quod apostoli periculo ereпti fecerunt.
units.tr: How memorable is the oracle of King David and prophet, in which he foretells that Christ Jesus will reign in the midst of his enemies (Ps. 110). From this it is gathered that Christ indeed reigns even in this age, yet in such a way that there will never be lacking those who try to overthrow his kingdom. Examples of this are found everywhere in the Scriptures and in the church histories. Yet most clearly of all this appears in the present book, where in the account of the apostolic affairs and the description of the primitive church, Luke always joins these two things: on the one hand the happy progress of Christ's kingdom, and on the other the mad efforts of the impious against it. The use of this is that we should not be offended by the cross and adversity, of which Christ warned us so often, nor hope for lasting tranquillity in this world, but that we should prepare ourselves to bear the cross even when the church seems to rest in the safest harbour. With this the present history must now be taken up. For Luke had recently set forth the most flourishing state of the primitive church, teaching that it had been made famous by its authority and enlarged daily by new increases, so that the city of Jerusalem was now too narrow to contain the kingdom of Christ, which was already beginning to spread also to foreigners. Yet amid such prosperous successes a grievous persecution and great danger is laid upon them, when Christ allows his enemies so far that they lay hands on the apostles and resolve to lead them off to prison and punish them with the utmost penalty. Meanwhile these things bring more comfort than terror, since the Lord shines forth with such presence to the apostles who are in peril for the glory of his name. But so that more profit may come back to us from this, we must first consider the enemies of Christ and the apostles. Then we shall look at how the Lord thwarted their efforts. Lastly, we shall speak of what the apostles did when they were rescued from danger.

units.la: De hostibus siue persecutoribus ecclesiæ & eorunde conatu diligenter Lucas disserit. Nam summum Pontificè contra apostolos insurrexisse ait, nec solū hunc, sed cum illo collegas siue Symmystas ipsius, vnà cum omnibus ijs, quos sibi familiariores fecerat. Et hos quidè Sadducæorū sectatores suis-se dicit, vt intelligamus, quanta tunc fuerit in Iudaica gente corruptio, quando illi primas in religione tenebant, quibus mortuorū resurrectio (quod præcipuum fidei & religionis caput est, 1. Cor. 15.) Iusus erat, vt iam sæpe diximus. Et sanè nisi ab omni religione alieni fuissent, ipsos quoq; vel apostolicæ doctrinæ syncericas, vel veneranda ecclesiæ maiestas, vel miraculorū admiranda dignitas, tantusq; omnis generis hominū ad Christi regnum concursus, mouere potuisset, ne tam indomitū furerent. Simul verò quid illos extimularit, indicatur. Zelo enim, id est, inuidia & æmulatione repletos fuisse Lucas dicit. Nec enim ferre poterant, eos in precio & honore esse, quorū doctrina ipsorum honori & quæstui derogabat. At dubiū non est, ipsos zelum Dei & publicam totius populi vtilitatem priuatorū affectuum prætextum fecisse, quod Caiapham cum suis antea fecisse legimus. Quorsum verò zelus iste erupit? Eòusq;, vt manus inferrent apostolis, & captos publico carceri mandarent, quasi publicæ pacis turbatores & palàm flagitiosos. Sunt autem hæc ad nostra quoq; tempora transferenda, cùm constet propter nos scripta esse omnia, vt inde institutionem & consolationem habeamus. Rom. 15.
units.tr: Luke discusses carefully the enemies or persecutors of the church and their efforts. For he says that the high priest rose up against the apostles, and not only he but his colleagues or fellow office-holders with him, together with all those whom he had made more familiar to himself. And he says that these were followers of the Sadducees, so that we may understand how great the corruption of the Jewish people then was, when such men held the first places in religion, men to whom the resurrection of the dead (which is the chief article of faith and religion, 1 Cor. 15) was a laughing-stock, as we have often said already. And indeed, unless they had been utterly estranged from all religion, neither the soundness of the apostolic doctrine, nor the venerable majesty of the church, nor the wonderful dignity of the miracles, nor such a great gathering of men of every kind to the kingdom of Christ could have moved them to prevent them from raging so untamed. At the same time, what stirred them up is indicated. For Luke says they were filled with zeal, that is, with envy and rivalry. For they could not bear that those whose teaching detracted from their honour and profit should be held in esteem and honour. Yet there is no doubt that they made the zeal of God and the public good of the whole people a pretext for their private passions, as we read that Caiaphas and his men had done before. But where did this zeal break out? So far that they laid hands on the apostles and handed them over to the public prison, as if they were disturbers of the public peace and openly wicked men. These things, however, are to be applied also to our own times, since it is established that all things were written for our sake, so that we may have instruction and consolation from them (Rom. 15).

units.la: Primo enim docemur exemplo hoc, qui semper acerrimi veritatis Christianæ persecutores futuri sint. Illi nimirum, qui cum sacerdotij titulo glorientur, primiq; ecclesiæ antistites haberi velint, illam publicè tueri & prædicare debebant. Vt primùm enim illi sub religionis prætextu sua quærere incipiunt, mox nec ipsi credere possunt, nec veritatis lucem ferunt, cuius fulgore ipsorum nequitia & imposturæ arguuntur. Et tales quidem plerunq; Sadducæi, imò Epicuri de grege porci sunt. Nisi enim Apinis & Siculis gerris vaniora putarent, quæ de cœlis & inferis, de animarum immortalitate & corporum resurrectione in scripturis traduntur, nunquam vel scripturas tam improbè suis traditionibus corrumperent, vel religionem tam impudenter in quæstum conuerterent. Ideò in ipsa ecclesia Antichristi sedem Christus & apostoli nobis monstrant, vt intelligamus vnde maximum periculum timeri debeat. 2. Thess. 2. 1. Iohan. 1. Etsi nostra hæc tempora inspiciamus, soli illi euangelicæ doctrinæ & regni Christi hostes videri possunt, qui ecclesiæ primi antistites esse antehac crediti sunt. Quæ enim à principibus & regibus tentantur, in horum gratiam & his ipsis impulsoribus & authoribus fieri, clarius est, quàm vt multis demonstrari debeat. Offendit hoc multos hodie, qui vix sibi persuaderi patiuntur, veram esse ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam, quæ ipsos Pontifices & Episcopos inimicos habeat. At stultum est eo offendi, quo iam inde ab orbe condito nihil fuit vulgarius atque frequentius, vt alibi dictum est. Sed non minus diligenter obseruandum est, quibus artibus & armis isti pugnent. Vbi primum occurrit, quòd zelum Dei egregie simulare norunt, cuius gloriam calcari & ecclesiam perniciose dissipari queritantur. At corruptus ille zelus est, qualem in Caiapha videre licet, cui veritatis confessio quam Christus protulerat, blasphema videtur & intolerabilis. Ita enim nostris illis nihil vel impium vel intolerabile videtur, quàm quod euangelij veritatem redolet, & ipsorum quaestui & superbae tyrannidi aduersatur. Nec aliter de nostrorum hostium zelo iudicari debere ex eo patet, quòd vt Iudaeorum antistites Sadducaeorum furiosos errores ferre potuerunt, modò in Christo oppugnando suam illius operam locarent: ita nostri illi impiam & Pontificum canonibus damnatam sacrorum nundinationem, doctrinae Dei adulterationem, deteriorationes horrendas, stupra & effrenem morum licentiam ferre possunt, modò illis intacta relinquas, quae ad ipsorum quaestum & inanem gloriam faciunt. Sed vt demus, illos reuera diuinae gloriae zelo agi, excusari tamen non merentur, sed Iudaeorum similes sunt, qui & ipsi (Paulo teste, Rom.10.) zelo Dei flagrarunt, sed à quo omnis veri recti, scientia ab esset. Nec enim nostri zeli, sed verbi sui nos sectatores esse vult Deus, quod ideò omnibus seculis reuelare dignatus est, ne quis humanae sapientiae & carnis dictata consuleret. Sed qualis eiusmodi hominum zelus censeri debeat, rei euentus declarat. Qui enim verbi Dei dispensatores erant, & diuinis rationibus errantes in viam reducere, & contradicentes conuincere debebant, ceu officij sui obliti ad vim conuertuntur, & nullius adhuc criminis conuictos, publicis carceribus includunt. Atqui hoc ipsum est, quod Christus illis exprobrat, quando gladijs & fustibus armati ad ipsum capiendum egressi erant, quem tamen quotidie in templo docentem audiebant, vbi conuincendus erat, si quid à diuina veritate alienum docuisset. Luc.22. Imò ne in Concilio quidem vim apertam prohibent, cùm Christi à Pontificis seruo impunè vapulare permittunt. Iohan.18. Ijsdem armis iam seculis aliquot pugnatum esse aduersus veritatis doctrinam, historiae docent. Nec exempla coaceruare opus est, quando vnicum illud Constantiensis Concilij facinus sufficere potest, quod in sanctissimum Christi martyrem, Iohannem Hussium desiguarunt Romanae ecclesiae antistites: quem nec publica fides, nec Imperatoria Maiestas, nec ius gentium, nec piorum preces & Bohemorum minae, è cruentis illorum manibus liberare potuerunt. Nec bodie aliis argumentis frequentius aduersus veritatis doctores, Magistri nostri & Pontifices pugnant, quàm quòd principes contra veritatem & illius doctores, armant, qui tunc se ecclesiae propugnatores esse arbitrantur, si veram Christi ecclesiam ferro & igne vastare pergant. Vt interim de illis nihil dicam, qui eiusmodi causarum cognitionem nihil ad principes pertinere clamant, & indicta causa Christi martyres ad supplicia rapiunt, prius tamen linguis exectis, ne spectanti populo fidei & mortis suae rationem reddere possint. Sed quanto isti Iudaeorum sacer dotum tyrannidem superant, tanto grauiores impietatis poenas Christo exoluent, cuius regnum humanis viribus opprimi non potest.
units.tr: For first we are taught by this example who will always be the most fierce persecutors of Christian truth. Surely those who glory in the title of priesthood and wish to be regarded as the first leaders of the church ought publicly to defend and proclaim it. For as soon as those men begin to seek their own ends under the pretext of religion, soon they can neither believe themselves nor bear the light of truth, by whose brightness their wickedness and deceits are exposed. And such men are for the most part Sadducees, or rather swine from the herd of Epicurus. For unless they thought the things that are handed down in the Scriptures about heaven and hell, about the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies, more trifling than the fables of Apinus and the Sicilian trifles, they would never have corrupted the Scriptures so shamelessly by their traditions, nor turned religion so impudently into a source of gain. Therefore Christ and the apostles show us that the seat of Antichrist is in the church itself, so that we may understand whence the greatest danger ought to be feared (2 Thess. 2; 1 John 2). If we look at our own times, only those can seem enemies of the evangelical doctrine and of the kingdom of Christ who were formerly believed to be the first leaders of the church. For it is clearer than that it needs to be shown to many that what is attempted by princes and kings is done for their benefit, and with these very men as instigators and authors. This offends many today, who scarcely allow themselves to be persuaded that the doctrine of our churches is true, since it has as its enemies the Pontiffs and Bishops themselves. But it is foolish to be offended by what, from the creation of the world, has been nothing more common and frequent, as has been said elsewhere. Yet we must observe no less carefully by what arts and arms these men fight. The first thing that meets us is that they know very well how to feign zeal for God, whose glory they complain is trampled on and whose church is perniciously scattered. But that zeal is corrupt, such as one may see in Caiaphas, to whom the confession of truth that Christ had made seems blasphemous and intolerable. For in the same way, nothing seems to our opponents either impious or intolerable except what smells of the truth of the gospel and stands against their profit and their proud tyranny. Nor does it become clear otherwise that the zeal of our enemies ought to be judged thus: just as the Jewish high priests could bear the mad errors of the Sadducees, provided they devoted their effort to attacking Christ, so those men of ours can bear the impious sale of sacred things, condemned by the canons of the Pontiffs, the adulteration of God's teaching, horrible corruptions, debaucheries, and unbridled licence of morals, provided you leave untouched those things which serve their profit and empty glory. But even if we grant that they are really moved by zeal for the divine glory, they do not deserve to be excused, but are like the Jews, who also (as Paul testifies, Rom. 10) burned with zeal for God, but without knowledge of what is right. For God wills us to be followers not of our zeal but of his word, which he has deigned to reveal in every age, so that no one should consult human wisdom and the dictates of the flesh. But what kind of zeal such men ought to be judged to have, the outcome of the matter declares. For those who were dispensers of the word of God, and who ought to have brought back those who erred by divine reasons and convicted those who contradicted, as if forgetful of their office, turn to force and shut up in public prisons men not yet convicted of any crime. And yet this very thing is what Christ rebukes them for, when they went out armed with swords and clubs to seize him, whom they nevertheless heard teaching daily in the temple, where he ought to have been refuted if he had taught anything alien to the divine truth (Luke 22). Indeed, not even in the council do they forbid open violence, when they allow Christ to be beaten with impunity by the servant of the high priest (John 18). History teaches that the same weapons have been used against the doctrine of truth for several centuries. Nor is it necessary to heap up examples, since that single deed of the Council of Constance can suffice, in which the leaders of the Roman church condemned to death the most holy martyr of Christ, John Hus; him neither public faith, nor imperial majesty, nor the law of nations, nor the prayers of the pious and the threats of the Bohemians could rescue from their bloody hands. Nor today do our teachers and Pontiffs fight against the teachers of truth by any other arguments more often than by arming princes against the truth and its teachers, thinking themselves then to be defenders of the church, if they go on laying waste the true church of Christ with sword and fire. To say nothing for now of those who cry that the cognizance of such causes has nothing to do with princes, and who drag the martyrs of Christ to punishment without a hearing, yet first with their tongues cut out, lest they be able to give an account of their faith and death to the watching people. But the more these men surpass the tyranny of the Jewish priests, the heavier the penalties of impiety they will pay to Christ, whose kingdom cannot be crushed by human strength.

units.la: Docet hoc altera historiae pars, qua quid dominus interea egerit, explicatur: qui ecclesiae suae curam depositae & nimium hostibus suis permisisse videri poterat. Sed non dormitat, nec pro suo nomine periclitantes deserit. Venit enim angelus domini, qui nec Sacerdotum authoritate terretur, nec ius violati carceris formidat, sed illius ianuas referat, apostolos educit, & in templum reuerti ac ibidem illos verba vitae (id est, euangelium de Christo Iesu, in quo solo vita habetur) praedicare iubet. Docent haec, Deo suos curae esse, nec vinciri posse verbum Dei, etiamsi illius ministri carceribus inclusi detineantur. Spirat enim spiritus domini vbi vult, nec mundi iudicio regitur. Et Paulus se quidem vinctum detineri dicit, idem verò Dei verbum vinctum esse negat. 2. Tim.2. Nemo igitur ministrorum verbi vinculis offendatur, imò ne morte quidem, cùm non ex nobis, sed ex Dei arbitrio & potestate, verbi ipsius propagatio dependeat. Praestat autem liberationis huius modum & finem diligentius inspicere.
units.tr: This is taught by the other part of the history, which explains what the Lord was meanwhile doing. He might seem to have neglected the care of his Church and allowed too much to his enemies. But he does not sleep, and he does not abandon those who are in danger for his name. An angel of the Lord comes, who is not terrified by the authority of the priests nor afraid of the law of the violated prison. He opens its doors, leads the apostles out, and orders them to return to the temple and there preach the words of life (that is, the gospel of Christ Jesus, in whom alone life is found). These things teach that God cares for his own, and that the word of God cannot be bound, even if its ministers are kept shut up in prisons. For the Spirit of the Lord breathes where he wills, and is not governed by the judgment of the world. Paul says that he himself is held bound, but he denies that the word of God is bound. 2 Tim. 2. Therefore no minister of the Word should be offended by chains, or even by death, since the spread of the word itself depends not on us but on God's will and power. It is worth examining more carefully the manner and the end of this deliverance.

units.la: In liberationis modo obseruatu dignissimum est, quòd angeli ministerio carceris portas aperiri Deus voluit, quod infinitis aliis medijs effici poterat. Sed ita testari & docere vult, quae & quanta sit electorum suorum dignitas, cùm illorum seruitio non terrenae modò & inferiores creaturae, verùm etiam cœlestes spiritus & angeli destinati sint. Generale enim dogma hinc constitui debere, multis scripturae locis edocemur. Paulus certè, angelos ministratorios spiritus esse dicit, qui emittantur in ministerium propter eos, qui salutis haeredes erunt. Heb.1. Et notum est illud Dauidis: Angelus do-
units.tr: Regarding the manner of the liberation, the most noteworthy thing is that God chose to have the prison doors opened by the ministry of an angel, though he could have done it by countless other means. He wishes thereby to witness and teach how great is the dignity of his elect, since not only earthly and lower creatures but even heavenly spirits and angels are appointed to serve them. Many passages of Scripture teach us that a general doctrine should be drawn from this. Paul certainly says that the angels are ministering spirits, sent out for service on account of those who will be heirs of salvation. Heb. 1. And that saying of David is well known: The angel of the Lord

units.la: Hostium veritatis artes.
units.tr: The arts of the enemies of the truth.

units.la: Deus hostium suorum conatus cludit, & suos asserit.
units.tr: God shuts off the attempts of his enemies and vindicates his own.

units.la: Angeli electorum ministri & custodes. mini castrametatur circa eos, qui ipsum timent, & eripit eos. Psal.34. Et quod de vno Christo malignus ille tentator exponit, ad singula illius membra referri debet, quos angelorum curæ & custodiæ commendauit deus, ne pedibus suis ad lapidem offendant. Psal.91. Nec desunt exempla eorum, qui visibili angelorum ministerio vsi sunt. Per angelos Sodomarum incendio eripitur Lot. Gen.19. Angelorum castra Iacob cernit, & illorum præsidio se tutum fore intelligit. Gen.32. Elizeum angelicæ copiæ à Syrorum manibus liberant. 2. Reg. 6. Daniel angelum domini Leonum ora constrinxisse fatetur, ne quid mali ipsi inferrent. Dan.6. Tobiæ filio multis diebus fidele obsequium angelus, visibili specie assumpta præstitit. Quid? quod angelus Aegyptiorum primogenita cædit, & Israeli itineris ducem se exhibet. Et Assyriorum obsidione Ezechiam angeli ope liberatum esse constat. Isa.37. Commemorantur hæc & alia eius generis exempla, non vt visibili forma angelorum ministeria ipsi quoque requiramus, sed vt de horum præsidio & custodia non dubitemus, licet nobis non conspicui sint. Experimur hoc frequenter, quado occultis periculis eripimur, & nullo vel consilio vel auxilio hominum adiuti pericula ignota declinamus. Agnoscamus ergo nostræ naturæ & conditionis dignitatem, in quam diuinæ gratiæ beneficio collocati sumus. Seruiat autem eadem nostræ tum consolationi, ne in aduersis desperemus: tum institutioni, ne vitæ impuritate & improbitate angelos offendendo, tam sanctum tamq; necessarium præsidium à nobis propulsemus.
units.tr: Angels are the ministers and guardians of the elect. encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. Ps. 34. And what that malignant tempter applies to Christ alone must be referred to each of his members, whom God has committed to the care and guard of the angels, so that they do not strike their feet against a stone. Ps. 91. Nor are there lacking examples of those who made use of the visible ministry of angels. Through angels Lot is snatched from the burning of Sodom. Gen. 19. Jacob sees the camps of angels and understands that he will be safe under their protection. Gen. 32. A host of angels frees Elisha from the hands of the Syrians. 2 Kings 6. Daniel confesses that an angel of the Lord shut the mouths of the lions, so that they could do him no harm. Dan. 6. An angel, taking on a visible form, rendered faithful service for many days to Tobias' son. Tob. What more? An angel strikes down the firstborn of the Egyptians and shows himself as leader of Israel on the journey. And it is established that Hezekiah was delivered from the Assyrian siege by the help of an angel. Isa. 37. These and other examples of this kind are recalled, not so that we should seek the ministry of angels in visible form, but so that we should not doubt their protection and guardianship, even though they are not seen by us. We often experience this when we are rescued from hidden dangers and avoid unknown perils with no counsel or help of men. Let us therefore acknowledge the dignity of our nature and condition, into which we have been placed by the benefit of divine grace. Let this serve both for our consolation, that we do not despair in adversity, and for our instruction, that by impurity and wickedness of life we do not offend the angels and so drive away from ourselves so holy and so necessary a protection.

units.la: Porrò liberationis finem angelus indicat, cum apostolis carcere ereptis ait: Ite, & stantes loquimini in templo populo omnia verba vitæ huius. Ad muneris ergo siue officij executionem, cui ipsos dominus destinarat, illos redire iubet, & regnum Christi, cuius tam præsens auxilium senserint, pro virili propagare. Conuenit hoc cum eo, quod alibi Deus ipse iubet, vt ex malis liberati ipsum glorificemus. Psal.50. Nec enim apostolis solis hoc dictum est, sed ad omnes ex æquo pertinet. Vult enim Deus, vt singuli suæ vocationi insistant, & periculis erepti eò ardentiori studio ad illam redeant, quò diutius illam intermittere coacti sunt. Grauis ergo illorum culpa est, qui morbis aut egestate alijsue calamitatibus erepti, vitijs & sceleribus sese consecrant, & dei nomen vitæ impuritate polluunt. Qui mihi eorum militum similes esse videntur, qui ad Christum capiendum emissi, cum illius occulta virtute prostrati essent, subitò tamen in pedes erecti, manus & vincula illi intecerunt. Nec multò leuior illorum culpa est, qui vbi semel & iterum pro Christi nomine periclitati sunt, quasi suo iam officio defuncti, omnia in posterum pericula & omnes pro Christo labores detrectant. Quibus grauius adhuc peccant, qui vt sese à periculis tutos faciant, veritatem abnegare non verentur. Atqui iuxta Pauli exemplum consummare nos decet cursum nostrum. Nec enim in nostro arbitrio situm est, vt ipsi nobis laborum & periculorum finem statuamus: sed domini voluntatem expectemus, qui licet opera suam ad tempus dilulerit, non deerit tamen firma & constanti fide in ipsum sperantibus. Habak.2. Nec ideo nenus est ad regnum Christi, qui vbi manum aratro admouit, à tergo respicit: sed qui in finem perseuerat, saluus erit. Luc.9. Matth.24.
units.tr: Further, the angel indicates the end of the liberation, when, the apostles having been led out of prison, he says: Go, and stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life. So he orders them to return to the duty or office for which the Lord had destined them, and to advance the kingdom of Christ, whose present help they have felt, as far as they are able. This agrees with what God himself commands elsewhere, that we, freed from evils, should glorify him. Ps. 50. For this was said not to the apostles alone but pertains equally to all. God wills that each person should keep to his calling, and that those delivered from dangers should return to it with all the more eager zeal, the longer they were forced to be away from it. Grievous, therefore, is the fault of those who, rescued from sickness or poverty or other calamities, dedicate themselves to vices and crimes, and pollute the name of God by an impure life. They seem to me like those soldiers who, sent out to seize Christ, when they had been struck down by his hidden power, yet immediately got to their feet and bound him. Not much lighter is the fault of those who, once or twice having been in danger for the name of Christ, as if they had already finished their duty, shrink from all future dangers and all labours for Christ. They sin even more gravely who, to keep themselves safe from danger, do not hesitate to deny the truth. Yet, following Paul's example, it becomes us to finish our course. For it is not in our power to set for ourselves the end of labours and dangers; we should await the Lord's will, who, although he defers his work for a time, will not fail those who hope in him with firm and constant faith. Hab. 2. Nor is anyone fit for the kingdom of Christ who, having put his hand to the plough, looks back; but he who perseveres to the end will be saved. Luke 9. Matt. 24.

units.la: Cumprimis vero memorabile est, quòd euangelium de Christo Iesu verbum vitæ angelus nominat. Decoratur alijs quoq; titulis in scriptura. Nam verbum gratiæ dicitur, eò quòd gratia Dei in Christo nobis collatam nuntiat. Paulus idem reconciliationis verbum vocat, propter Christum, qui nobis deum patrem reconciliauit. 2. Corinth.5. Idem hoc potentiam Dei salutificam esse testatur. Rom.1. Alibi veritatis & salutis verbum dicitur. At præstantissimus hic titulus est, quo verbum vitæ esse prædicatur, qui etiam illi proprius & germanus est. Nam & ipsum verbum immortale viuit & manet in æternū (1. Pet.1. Isa.40.) & vitam omnibus confert, qui illud vera fide amplectti dignantur. Christum Iesum enim nobis prædicat, qui solus verba vitæ æternæ habet. Iohan.6. In eodem omnia monstrat & exhibet, quæ nobis ad vitam consequendam necessaria sunt. In hoc enim habemus peccatorum expiationem, satisfactionem, iustitiam, sanctificationem, redemptionis pretium, & quæcunq; alia sunt eius generis. Et per fidem in hunc non modò in filios Dei nos regenerat verbum hoc, verumetiam regeneratis adoptionis spiritum largitur, in quo clamamus Abba pater, quia infallibilis nostræ salutis arrahabo est. Rom.8. Ephes.1. &c. Atqui hoc nomine omnem mundi sapientiam euangelica doctrina excellit, quòd æternæ vitæ dux est, cum aliarum scientiarum professores ne præsentis quidem vitæ tranquillitatem & felicitatem nobis tuò polliceri possint. Vere ergo margaritæ preciosissimæ & thesauro incomparabili confertur, cuius gratia omnium facultatum tum iacturam hilari & spontanea mente facere debeat, quisquis salutem veram expetit. Rursum, quia propter Christum, qui vita & salus est, hoc tam illustri titulo euangelium decoratur, mortiferae & exitiosae omnes doctrinae censeri debent, quaecunq; Christi meritum obscurant, & à fide Christi hominum mentes auocant. Quas qui profitentur, fures & latrones sunt, tum quia Christum sua gloria spoliant, tum quia incautis sectatoribus pro verbo vitae letiferum humanarum traditionum venenum propinant. Ioan.10.
units.tr: Especially worth remembering is that the angel calls the gospel of Christ Jesus the word of life. Scripture adorns it with other titles too. It is called the word of grace, because it announces the grace of God conferred on us in Christ. Paul calls it the word of reconciliation, on account of Christ, who reconciled us to God the Father. 2 Cor. 5. The same Paul testifies that it is the saving power of God. Rom. 1. Elsewhere it is called the word of truth and of salvation. But this is the most excellent title, by which it is proclaimed the word of life, which is also its own and proper title. For the word itself lives and remains forever (1 Pet. 1; Isa. 40), and confers life on all who deign to embrace it with true faith. For it preaches to us Christ Jesus, who alone has the words of eternal life. John 6. In the same gospel he shows and sets forth everything that is necessary for us to obtain life. For in him we have expiation of sins, satisfaction, righteousness, sanctification, the price of redemption, and whatever else is of this kind. Through faith in him this word not only regenerates us as children of God, but also bestows on the regenerate the spirit of adoption, in which we cry "Abba, Father", since it is the infallible pledge of our salvation. Rom. 8; Eph. 1, etc. Indeed, by this name the evangelical doctrine surpasses all the wisdom of the world, because it is the leader to eternal life, whereas the professors of other sciences cannot promise us even the tranquillity and happiness of the present life. Rightly, then, it is compared to the most precious pearl and to an incomparable treasure, for the sake of which whoever seeks true salvation ought to give up the loss of all his possessions with a cheerful and willing mind. Again, since the gospel is adorned with this so illustrious title on account of Christ, who is life and salvation, all doctrines that are deadly and destructive, whatever obscures the merit of Christ and turns men's minds away from faith in Christ, must be judged so. Those who profess them are thieves and robbers, both because they strip Christ of his glory and because they give to unwary followers, in place of the word of life, the deadly poison of human traditions. John 10.

units.la: Sed ad Apostolos redeamus, quos Lucas angeli mandato obedientes fuisse, ac mox sub auroram templum ingressos, ibidem docuisse scribit. Atqui multa diversum suadere poterant, cum & periculi metus recens esset, & nota omnibus aduersariorum potentia, qua nulla alia re magis quam euangelij praedicatione prouocari posse noverant: adhaec, ex hoc ipsorum facto ad totam ecclesiam periculum commune rediturum videbatur, si hostium rabiem nouis furoribus magis accenderent. At tantum abest, ut his ab officio se revocari patiantur, ut potius nulla ampliori deliberatione habita, dei manda to sese obsequentes praebeant. Nobis autem in exemplum illorum obedientia proponitur. Generale siquidem Dei praeceptum est, ut non quod nobis bonum videtur faciamus, sed illius iussa exequamur. Num.15. Nec alia nocentior pestis est, quam si carnis rationem in consilium admittamus, vbi suam voluntatem disertis mandatis expressit dominus, quod tum Saulis tum aliorum exempla abunde declarant. Et Paulus frequenter fidei obedientiam euangelicae praedicationis scopum & finem esse testatur.2. Cor.10. Rom.1.&16. Quicunq; igitur hac abiecta, carnis consilia audiunt, nam illi euangelio & fide Christi fraustra gloriantur. Quare & nos transferamus apostolorum exemplum, & spretra mundi tyrannide, quod Deus iniunxit sedulò exequamur, nec deerit suo praesidio & ope pijs coeptis Christus Iesus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us return to the apostles, who, Luke writes, obeyed the angel's command and, as soon as dawn broke, entered the temple and taught there. Yet many considerations could have persuaded them otherwise: the fear of danger was fresh, and the power of their adversaries was well known to all, a power which they knew could be provoked by nothing more than the preaching of the gospel. Moreover, it seemed that from this deed of theirs a common danger would come back upon the whole Church, if they inflamed the enemy's rage with fresh fury. But so far are they from allowing themselves to be called back from their duty by these things that, without any further deliberation, they readily submit themselves to God's command. Their obedience is set before us as an example. For it is a general command of God that we do not do what seems good to us, but carry out his orders (Num. 15). Nor is there a more harmful plague than when we admit the reasoning of the flesh into our counsel, where the Lord has expressed his own will in plain commands; the examples of Saul and of others declare this abundantly. And Paul often testifies that obedience of faith is the aim and end of evangelical preaching (2 Cor. 10; Rom. 1 and 16). Therefore, whoever, rejecting this, listens to the counsels of the flesh, boasts in vain of the gospel and the faith of Christ. Wherefore let us also imitate the example of the apostles, and, scorning the tyranny of the world, diligently carry out what God has enjoined; nor will Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever, fail to aid our godly undertakings with his protection. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILIA XXXVI.

units.la: Aduenientes autem summus Pontifex, & qui cum eo erant, conuocarunt Concilium & totum Seniorum ordinem filiorum Israel, & miserunt ad carcerem, ut adducerentur. Cum autem venissent ministri, non inuenerunt eos. Itaq; reuersi nuntiarunt, dicentes: Carcerem quidem inueni mus clausum cum omni diligentia, & custodes foris stantes ad ianuam. Vbi vero aperuimus, neminem intus inuenimus. At postquam audierunt hos sermones tum summus Pontifex, tum praefectus templi & sacerdotes, anxij erant super his, quidnam hoc esset. Aduenientes autem quidam nuntiauit eis: Ecce viri quos posueratis in carcerem, stant in templo, & docent populum. Tunc abiens praefectus cum ministris adduxit eos sine vi. Timebant enim populum, ne lapidarentur.
units.tr: Then the high priest and those who were with him came and called together the council and all the senate of the sons of Israel, and sent to the prison to have the apostles brought. But when the officers came, they did not find them there. So they returned and reported: "We found the prison shut with all care, and the guards standing outside at the door; but when we opened it, we found no one inside." When the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were anxious about them, wondering what this could mean. Then someone came and told them: "Behold, the men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people." Then the captain went with the officers and brought them, without violence, for they feared the people, lest they should be stoned.

units.la: CUm Christi saluatoris & redemptoris nostri regnum Regius ille & diuinus Psaltes, Dauid, describere instituisset, ab insanis contra hoc impiorum hostium conatibus exordiu sumens, air: Quare fremuerunt gentes, & populi meditantur inania? Concurrunt reges terrae, & principes vna consultant aduersus dominum & aduersus Christum eius. Rumpamus (inquiunt) vincula eorum, & lora eorum à nobis abiciamus. Mox vero terrificis illorum conatibus Dei consilium opponens, subiicit: Qui sedet in coelis, ridet: dominus subsannat eos. Tunc loquetur ad eos in ira sua, & in furore suo terrebit eos, &c. Psal.2. Quibus docemur, non irritos modo, verumetiam ridiculos esse hostium Christi conatus, nec alijs quam authoribus suis perniciosiores. Possent huius rei multa exempla produci, inter quae non postremus locus illi debetur, quod modo diuinus scriptor, Lucas proponit. Capti sunt enim sacerdotum suasu & impulsu apostoli, & in publico carcere non seris modo & portis, verumetiam custodibus adhibitis asseruantur. Mox sequentis diei diluculo concurrunt sacerdotes, concilium & Senatum congregant, de supplicio nimirum & modo euangelicum ignem extinguendi consilium inituri. At Dominus ex alio illos deridens & totimundo deridendos propinare volens, vnius angeli ope apostolos vinculis eripuit, & mirifice illorum consilia frucтratur, qui sibi plus fatis afluti videbantur. Quia vero spiritui sancto visum est, singulas huius historiae partes describere, nos quoq; in illis excutiendis nullius diligentiae aut studij pigere debet, cum praeclaros studij huius fructus referre liceat.
units.tr: When the royal and divine psalmist David set out to describe the kingdom of Christ our Saviour and Redeemer, he began with the mad attempts of the impious enemies against it, and said: "Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth stand up, and the rulers take counsel together against the Lord and against his Anointed. Let us break their bonds," they say, "and cast away their cords from us." But straightway he sets the counsel of God against their terrifying attempts and adds: "He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his wrath he will terrify them," and so on (Psal. 2). From these words we are taught that the enemies of Christ's attempts are not only vain but ridiculous, and more harmful to none than to their own authors. Many examples of this could be brought forward, and no small place among them belongs to the one which the divine writer Luke now sets before us. The apostles were seized at the instigation and urging of the priests, and they were kept not only with bars and gates in the public prison but with guards set over them. Then at dawn the next day the priests gather, call together the council and the senate, and plan, of course, how to deal with them by punishment and how to extinguish the gospel fire. But the Lord, mocking them from another quarter and wishing to offer them up to be mocked by the whole world, rescued the apostles from their chains by the help of one angel, and wonderfully defeated the plans of men who seemed to themselves too wise by far. Yet because it has pleased the Holy Spirit to describe each part of this history, we too ought not to grudge any diligence or effort in examining these parts, since it is permitted to report the excellent fruits of such study.

units.la: Principio igitur Concilium videamus, ad quod illos magno studio concurrauisse diximus: cuius partes si excutias, omnia videbis, quae legitimi Concilij speciem & formam referre possunt. Primas in hoc tenet summus Pontifex, penes quem in eiusmodi causis ius summum Deus esse voluerat, & cui ex dei institutione obedientia summa debebatur. Capitalis enim iam olim in illos sententia lata erat, qui Sacerdotis sententiam contumaciter spernere audebant. Deut.17. Coniunguntur huic sacerdotes reliqui, ne quis Pontificem priuato affectu quicquam egisse arbitretur. Et ne quis vniuersum sacerdotum ordinem suspectum habeat, Seniores quoque vocantur, quorum ordo olim diuinitus institutus erat, & totius ecclesiae formam repraesentabat. Num.11. Adhaec templi quoq; praefectum vna cum publicis ministris sibi adiunxunt, ne quid contra rempub. moliri videantur. Haec cum ita sint, quid obstat, quo minus legitime collectum putari debeat Concilium? Sane quod externam formam attinet, non facile quicquam aliud requirere possis. At si finem consyderes, quem isti homines sibi proposuerunt, non in sancto spiritu, sed satanae auspicijs illos conuenisse patebit, & proinde neminem bonum piumue illis se subijcere, vel obedire debuisse. Nam veritatis opprimendae causa conuenerunt, & contra Christum conspiratione facta illius regnum euertere conantur.
units.tr: Let us look first at the council, to which we said they had hurried with great zeal. If you examine its parts, you will see everything that can represent the form and figure of a lawful council. The first place in it is held by the high priest, in whose hands God had wished the supreme right to lie in such cases, and to whom, by God's own institution, the highest obedience was owed. For long ago a capital sentence had been passed against those who dared obstinately to scorn the priest's judgment (Deut. 17). The other priests are joined to him, so that no one may think the high priest acted from private feeling. And lest anyone regard the whole order of priests with suspicion, the elders are also called, an order which had been instituted by God of old and represented the whole form of the Church (Num. 11). Besides, they joined to themselves the captain of the temple together with the public officers, so that they might not seem to be plotting anything against the commonwealth. Since these things are so, what prevents us from thinking that the council was lawfully convened? Certainly, as far as the outward form goes, you could hardly require anything else. But if you consider the end which those men set before themselves, it will be plain that they gathered under the auspices not of the Holy Spirit but of Satan, and therefore that no good or pious man ought to have submitted to them or obeyed them. For they came together for the sake of suppressing the truth, and by conspiring against Christ they try to overthrow his kingdom.

units.la: Docet nos locus hic de Concilijs iudicare, quae hodie in omnium ore versantur, quando controuersam religionis causam non aliter quam Concilij generalis authoritate componi posse, multi sibi persuaserunt. De quorum sententia vt nunc non disputo, ita mihi quoq; vtilissimum videtur, si quae Synodus impetrari posset libera, in qua ex solo Dei verbo controuersiae omnes componerentur: qualis Apostolica illa fuit, de qua Cap.15. dicetur, & quales veteres illas fuisse scimus, Nicenam nimirum, Constantinopolitanam, Ephesinam, Chalcedonensem, & similes, quas pij Imperatores sua authoritate gubernarunt, ne episcoporum ambitio rixas maiores accenderet. Num vero talis hodie sperari possit, ego affirmare non ausim, quando neminem ex aduersae partis hominibus video, qui male vsurpata in ecclesia possessione cedere, & se aliorum iudicio subijcere velit. Rursum si videamus, qualia iam saeculis aliquot fuerint Concilia, ex quo Romani Pontifices summum in ecclesiam ius obtinuerunt, nemo sanae mentis ex illis boni aliquid sperare poterit, cum in illis ne externa quidem Concilij legitimi forma siue species habeatur. Nam vt a capite exordiamur, a Romanis Pontificibus illa indici & conuocari solent, quorum primatus nec a Deo institutus est, & Christi gloriae quam maxime aduersatur. Idem Conciliorum praesides & supremi iudices haberi volunt, qui causam potius dicere & suae dispensationis rationem, iam saeculis aliquot requisitam, reddere debebant. Assessores horum sunt Episcopi: non quales a Paulo describuntur, sed quales terrestris ille Deus creare consueuit, a quibus si ineptum ac histrionicum ornatum & inanes titulos auferas, nihil relinquetur, quod aliquam episcopalis officij siue dignitatis speciem referat. Et illis solis sententiam dicendi ius datur, quinepostremo quidem in ecclesia Christi loco digni, sed iam olim Dei sententia excommunicati sunt. Chananeis enim, id est, sacrorum nundinatoribus, nullum in aede domini locum fore propheta affirmat. Zach.12. Et tales olim Christus templo Iudaico eiecit. Ioan.2. Matth.21. Idem in Reuelatione sua incredulis, homicidis, scortatoribus, veneficis, idololatris & omnibus mendacibus in stagno, igne & sulphure ardenti locum paratum esse dicit. Apoc.21. At quis obsecro tam impudens est, vt scelerib. hisce pollutos esse neget plerosque illorum, quibus solis de religionis causa decernendi potestas datur? Nec obstat, quod imperatores quoq; vna cum regibus & principibus ad Concilium vocare solent, cum omnes hoscè in Pontificum verba iurauisse constet, nec pro catholicis agnoscantur, nisi qui Romanae sedi se totos consecrarint. Quare ne externa quidem species legitimum Concilium referat, sed inani larua incautos decipit. Quod si vero finem spectes, in quem isti omnia referunt, veritatis & euangelij oppressionem ab ipsis vnice quaeri, notius est, quam vt multis demonstrari debeat. Testatur enim hoc fusius ab his martyrum Christi sanguis, quem auidissime fuiunt. Probant idem bella, quorum ipsi contra verae fidei cultores primi authores fuerunt. Fatentur hoc ipsi in Bullis suis, quibus Concilia indicunt & conuocant. Tam acerbo enim veritatis odio flagrant, vt cum toti hypocrisin induerint, & ad quiduis simulandum vel dissimulandum instructissimi sint, hic tamen nihil aut certe certè parum simulare possint, quò minus odium immane, quod iam olim aduersus euangelium conce-perunt, palàm profiteantur. Horum igitur iudicio fidei & religionis causam subijciunt, qui ecclesiam & regnum Christi euersum cupiunt, quiq; scientes & videntes perire volunt. Quibuscunq; verò cùm propria ipsorum salus, tum Christi gloria & ecclesiæ incolumitas cordi est, Dauidicum illud cum-primis huc pertinere intelligant: Beatus vir ille, qui non ambulauit in consilio impiorum, nec in via peccatorum stetit, nec in consessu irrisorum sedit. Psal.1.
units.tr: This passage teaches us to judge those councils which today are on everyone's lips, since many have persuaded themselves that a controversy of religion can be settled only by the authority of a general council. I shall not now dispute their opinion; yet it seems to me most useful, if a free synod could be obtained, in which all controversies would be settled from the Word of God alone, such as the apostolic council was, of which we shall speak in chapter 15, and such as we know the ancient councils were: the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, the Ephesine, the Chalcedonian, and similar ones, which pious emperors governed by their own authority, so that the ambition of bishops might not kindle greater quarrels. Whether such a council can be hoped for today I would not venture to affirm, since I see no one from the opposing party who is willing to yield a possession wrongly seized in the Church and to submit himself to the judgment of others. Again, if we look at what councils have been for some centuries, since the Roman pontiffs obtained the supreme right over the Church, no sane man can hope for anything good from them, since in them not even the outward form or appearance of a lawful council is kept. For, to begin at the head, these councils are usually announced and convened by the Roman pontiffs, whose primacy was not instituted by God and is most opposed to the glory of Christ. The same men want to be the presidents and supreme judges of the councils, although they ought rather to plead their cause and give an account of their stewardship, which has been demanded for some centuries. Their assessors are bishops, not such as Paul describes, but such as that earthly god is accustomed to create; and if you strip them of their silly and theatrical trappings and empty titles, nothing will remain that shows any semblance of episcopal office or dignity. Only these men are given the right to give a vote, men who are indeed in the Church of Christ in the last place, but who long ago were excommunicated by God's sentence. For the prophet declares that the Canaanites, that is, the sellers of sacred things, will have no place in the house of the Lord (Zech. 12). And Christ once cast such men out of the Jewish temple (John 2; Matt. 21). In his Revelation he likewise says that for unbelievers, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars there is a place prepared in the lake burning with fire and brimstone (Rev. 21). But who, I beg you, is so shameless as to deny that most of those to whom alone the power of deciding matters of religion is given are polluted by these very crimes? Nor does it count against this that the emperors too, together with kings and princes, are customarily summoned to the council, since it is certain that all of these have sworn to obey the words of the Pontiffs, and they are not acknowledged as Catholics unless they have wholly consecrated themselves to the Roman see. Therefore not even the outward appearance represents a lawful council; it is an empty mask that deceives the unwary. And if you look at the end to which all these men refer everything, it is too well known to need demonstration by many arguments that their sole aim is the oppression of truth and of the gospel. The blood of Christ's martyrs, which they have thirstily shed, bears witness to this more fully. The wars also prove it, of which they themselves were the first authors against the worshippers of the true faith. They confess this themselves in their Bulls, by which they announce and convene the councils. For they burn with such bitter hatred of the truth that, although they have put on hypocrisy entirely and are most skilled at pretending or dissembling anything, here they can pretend little or nothing, so that they do not openly profess the monstrous hatred which they long ago conceived against the gospel. Therefore those who wish the Church and the kingdom of Christ to be overthrown, and who want to perish knowingly and deliberately, are the ones who submit the cause of faith and religion to their judgment. But for those whose own salvation, together with the glory of Christ and the safety of the Church, is dear to their heart, let them understand that the words of David apply above all: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of scoffers" (Psal. 1).

units.la: Cæterum omissis his ad Sacerdotes & Seniores reuertamur, qui consilio de apostolis inito mi-niftros ad carcerem mittunt, qui illos in Concilio sistant. Ibi verò mirificè illos rider & ludit Christus dominus, cum quo ipsi certamen susceperant. Ministri siquidem apostolos è carcere liberatos esse inueniunt. Reuersi ad suos heros rem ita narrant, ut non obscurè de diuino auxilio & miraculosa apostolorum liberatione testentur. Dicunt enim carcerem probè clausum fuisse, & custodes excu-bias egisse sedulò, neminem tamen in carcere repertum. Quid verò hinc aliud colligi potuit, quàm dei hoc opus esse? Quis enim custodes ita fallere potuisset, & apostolos ipsis insciis educere? Non frustra ergo animis suis anguntur, & rerum incerti hærent. Sentiunt enim conscientiæ stimulos, qui etiam impijssimis frequenter obrepere solent. Sed aliud accedit nuntiū, quo magis irritantur. Nam venit, qui apostolos in templo intrepidè & palàm docere refert. Quod non potuit non maximi doloris causam præbere ambitiosissimis hominibus, quando nec authoritatem suam obseruari, nec potentiam timeri intellexerunt. Docet autem exemplum hoc, quàm facile sit deo improbos suorum hostium conatus eludere. Quis enim sperasset, apostolos insciis custodibus è carcere educi potuisse? At quod hominibus impossibile videtur, deo tam facile est quàm vento puluis diffi-citur. Nam potest hic vel somno, vel sensuum obstipatione, vel vertiginis spiritu, vel infinitis alijs modis eos fallere, qui nulla astutia & dolo capi posse videbantur. Adhæc, eos miraculi testes & præcones habent, quorum ministerio ad veritatis oppressionem abuti solebant. Idem ergo hic illis accidit, quod prius, quando ad Christum capiendum emissi ipsorum serui, non modò sine hoc reuertuntur, sed etiam de illius doctrina testimonium insigne & præclarum perhibent. Ioban.7. Cui non absimile fuit, quod milites de Christi resurrectione testati sunt, quos ipsi, ut illam impedirent sepulchro adhibuerant. Matth.28. Similia exempla passim in scripturis leguntur. Israelis oppressionem & interitum meditatur Pharao: Idem tamen domi suæ eum alit, & gremio suo fouet, quem populi sui assertorem & vindicem dominus esse voluit. Postea verò cum Mosi Magos opponeret, illos ipsos palàm testari audit, Dei digitum per Mosem operari. Exod.8. Nec absimile est quòd Balaam à Moabita rege ad maledicendum Israeli conductus, eidem etiam inuitus benedicit. Numer.23. & 24. Quid de Achabo dicemus, qui cum prophetas domini truculentissimè persequeretur, fidelissimum prophetarum patronum, adeóq; unicum illius seculi Mecœnatem inter aulæ suæ principes fouet & veneratur? Taceo infinita eius generis, quæ tum ex recentioribus tum prisci̇s historijs adduci poterant, & quæ experientia quotidiana offert. His tantummodo fideles Christi cultores excitare volui, ut similia diligenter obseruent. Magnus quippe & salutaris eiusmodi exemplorum usus est. Primò enim consolationem in aduersis afferūt, quando humanas vires diuina potentia longè inferiores esse, nec Dei consilia hominum conatibus impediri posse videmus. Deinde ad vitæ institutionem conducunt, ne temere Dei consilijs & decretis nos opponamus. Quid enim impossibile Deo erit, qui olim linguarum mirifica diuisione primorum bo-minum conatus dissipauit, & non semel vnius duntaxat angeli ministerio reges & principes omniū ludibrio exposuit? Quare sub illius potenti manu humiliari tutissimum simul & saluti nostræ consul-tissimum est.
units.tr: But let us set these matters aside and return to the chief priests and elders, who, having taken counsel about the apostles, send ministers to the prison to bring them before the Council. There Christ the Lord mocks and derides them wonderfully, though they had taken up the contest with him. For the ministers find that the apostles have been freed from prison. They return to their masters and report the matter in such a way that they bear witness, not obscurely, to divine help and a miraculous deliverance of the apostles. For they say that the prison was securely locked and the guards had kept watch diligently, yet no one was found inside. Yet what else could be gathered from this than that this was the work of God? For who could have deceived the guards like that and led the apostles out without their knowledge? So they are not troubled in their minds for nothing, and they remain uncertain of the facts. For they feel the stings of conscience, which often creep even upon the most wicked. But another messenger comes, and this makes them even more enraged. For he reports that the apostles are teaching openly and fearlessly in the temple. This could not fail to cause the greatest grief to these ambitious men, since they realised that their authority was not respected and their power was not feared. Yet this example also teaches how easily God can frustrate the attempts of the wicked against his people. For who would have expected that the apostles could be led out of prison without the knowledge of the guards? But what seems impossible to men is as easy for God as it is for the wind to scatter dust. For he can deceive those who seemed unable to be caught by any cunning or trickery, whether by sleep, by a stupor of the senses, by a spirit of giddiness, or by countless other means. Moreover, God has as witnesses and heralds of the miracle those through whose service they had been accustomed to abuse the suppression of the truth. So the same thing happens to them here as happened before, when their servants were sent out to seize Christ: they not only return without him, but also bear a remarkable and noble testimony to his teaching (John 7). Not unlike this was the testimony the soldiers gave about Christ's resurrection, whom they themselves had posted at the sepulchre to prevent it (Matt. 28). Similar examples are read everywhere in the Scriptures. Pharaoh plots the oppression and destruction of Israel; yet he nourishes and cherishes in his own house the one whom the Lord wished to be the champion and avenger of his people. Afterwards, when he set the magicians against Moses, he is heard himself openly testifying that the finger of God was working through Moses (Exod. 8). Nor is it unlike that Balaam, hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel, nevertheless blesses them against his will (Num. 23 and 24). What shall we say of Ahab, who, while he savagely persecuted the prophets of the Lord, nevertheless cherished and honoured the most faithful patron of the prophets, and so the only patron of that age, among the princes of his court? I pass over the countless instances of this kind which could be adduced both from more recent and from ancient histories, and which daily experience offers. I have wished only to rouse the faithful worshippers of Christ to observe similar things carefully. For the use of examples of this kind is great and salutary. First, they bring consolation in adversity, since we see that human powers are far inferior to divine power, and that the counsels of God cannot be hindered by the efforts of men. Second, they serve to instruct our lives, so that we do not rashly set ourselves against the counsels and decrees of God. For what will be impossible for God, who once scattered the plans of the first men by the wonderful division of tongues, and who more than once, by the ministry of a single angel alone, exposed kings and princes to the mockery of all? Therefore, to be humbled under his mighty hand is at once the safest course and the one most advantageous to our salvation.

units.la: Porrò Sacerdotes & reliquos Concilij huius assessores videamus, qui ne nunc quidem Deo cede re norunt, nec contenti stultitiam suam iam omnibus patefactam esse, incurabilem quoq; animorum impietatem produnt. Abillis enim missus templi præfectus, apostolos sine vi in Concilium adducit. Et a violentia quidem sibi temperant, non quòd diuini operis siue miraculi consyderatio mitiores reddiderit, sed quòd populum timent, ne forte ab illo lapidentur. Hic verò non modò sacerdotes cum suis complicibus, verumetiam ipse Deus, & cum hoc apostoli quoq; consyderandi veniunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us consider the chief priests and the rest of the assessors of this Council, who, even now, do not know how to yield to God, and, not content that their folly has already been made plain to all, also reveal the incurable impiety of their minds. For the prefect of the temple, sent by them, leads the apostles into the Council without violence. And they refrain from violence, not because the consideration of the divine work or miracle has made them milder, but because they fear the people, lest perhaps they be stoned by them. Here, then, we must consider not only the priests with their accomplices, but God himself, and with him the apostles too.

units.la: In sacerdotibus & templi præfecto incurabilis impiorum malitia & pertinax animorum excaecatio cernitur. Nam anxios rerum, incertosque fuisse, antea dictum est. Vnde facilè colligitur, illos aliquo saltem rei gesta sensu fuisse perculsos. At non eòusq; progrediuntur, vt miraculum ex animo agnoscant & Deo cedere velint. Imò ad institutum redeunt, & (vt sequentia docebunt) occidere etiā conantur, quos tam præsenti Dei ope paulò ante seruatos viderant. Hoc impijs omnibus ingenium esse, infinita exempla probant. Pharao certè non semel miraculorum maiestate & plagarum dolore victus, Deum Israëlis confitetur, Mosis intercessionem flagitat, Deiq; mandato se obtemperaturum esse promittit. Mox verò ad ingenium redit, quasi nouum cum Deo bellum suscepturus. Et quod hic isti faciunt, iam ante in Christi resurrectione fecerunt. Cum enim illam ex militibus resciuissent, nec veritati cedere, nec Christi inuictam potentiam formidare norunt: sed auro corruptis militibus falsos in vulgus rumores spargunt, quasi mendacijs Christi gloria obscurari posset, quem nec Imperatoria maiestatis authoritas (cuius nomine sepulchri lapis obsignatus erat) in sepulchro retinere potuerat. Atqui vtinam vetera tantummodo huius pertinacia exempla haberemus, & non hodie quoque passim inuenirentur, qui nec Dei iudicijs, nec propriæ conscientiæ testimonio se superari patiuntur, vt Christo & veritati cedant. Est autem hoc infallibile reprobationis argumentum, & dignum contempti verbi Dei supplicium, quod per prophetam olim, & postea in euangelio hostibus suis intermi-natus est Christus, quando ait: Auribus audietis, & non intelligetis: & videntes videbitis, & non cernetis. Incrassatum est enim cor populi huius, & auribus grauiter audierunt, & oculos suos obcluserunt, ne quando viderent oculis & auribus audirent, & corde intelligerent, & conuerterentur & sanarem illos. Isa. 6. Matth. 13. Debent autem ista nos terrere, ne indulgeamus veritatis odio, cuius tam infelix est exitus.
units.tr: In the priests and the prefect of the temple the incurable malice of the wicked and the stubborn blindness of their minds are seen. For it was said before that they were anxious and uncertain about the facts. From this it is easily gathered that they were at least struck by some sense of the deed. But they do not go so far as to acknowledge the miracle from their hearts and to be willing to yield to God. Rather, they return to their purpose and (as what follows will show) even try to kill those whom they had seen preserved a little before by such a present help of God. Countless examples prove that this is the disposition of all the impious. Pharaoh, certainly, more than once overcome by the majesty of the miracles and the pain of the plagues, confesses the God of Israel, begs for Moses' intercession, and promises that he will obey God's command. Soon, however, he returns to his nature, as if about to wage a new war with God. And what these men do here, they had already done before in Christ's resurrection. For when they learned of it from the soldiers, they knew neither how to yield to the truth nor to fear the unconquered power of Christ. Instead, they bribe the soldiers with gold and spread false rumours among the people, as if the glory of Christ could be obscured by lies, when he could not be kept in the sepulchre even by the authority of the imperial majesty, in whose name the stone had been sealed. Would indeed that we had only old examples of this obstinacy, and that they were not found today too, everywhere, among those who suffer themselves to be overcome neither by the judgements of God nor by the testimony of their own conscience, so as to yield to Christ and the truth! This, moreover, is an infallible sign of reprobation, and a punishment worthy of contempt for the Word of God, with which Christ once threatened his enemies through the prophet and afterwards in the Gospel, when he said: "Hearing you shall hear, and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see, and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them" (Isa. 6; Matt. 13). These things ought indeed to terrify us, so that we do not indulge in hatred of the truth, whose outcome is so unhappy.

units.la: Præterea docemur, non semper licere impijs quod libet, sed occulta Dei potentia frequenter illos coherceri. Hac enim fit vt manus abstineat præfectus cum suis, metuens nimirum, ne à populo lapidetur. Ignobile ergo vulgus metuit, qui Deum se impunè contemptURUM putabat. Est hoc proprium impijs, vt diuersa omnino sint illorum & piorum sententiæ. Pij enim & fidelis hominis vox est: Dominus lux mea & salus mea, à quo nam timerem? Dominus robur vitæ meæ, à quo nam expauescerem? Dominus mihi adiutor, non timebo quid faciat mihi homo. Psalm. 27. & 118. Impiorum autem voces sunt: Dominus non videt, neq; Deus Iacob intelligit. Psalm. 94. At ijdem illi, qui Dei metum abiecerunt, mortales homines, & plerunq; seruos, imò proprios liberos timere coguntur: & qui generoso Dei timore duci nolunt, ignauo & ignobili miserrimorum hominum metu vexantur. Ita sui contemptum Deus vlciscitur. Et est præposterus hic metus, dignum tyrannidis contra iustitiam & veritatem institutæ supplicium. Quod obseruare debent magistratus, quicunq; cum laude in suo officio versari voluerint.
units.tr: Besides, we are taught that it is not always permitted to the wicked to do whatever they please, but that they are frequently restrained by the hidden power of God. For it comes about that the prefect with his men keeps his hands off, fearing, no doubt, lest he be stoned by the people. The common crowd, therefore, is what he fears, though he had thought he could despise God with impunity. It is characteristic of the impious that their opinions and those of the pious are altogether different. For the voice of the godly and faithful man is: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; of whom shall I be afraid? The Lord is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be terrified? The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me" (Ps. 27 and 118). But the voices of the impious are: "The Lord does not see, neither does the God of Jacob understand" (Ps. 94). Yet those very men who have cast off the fear of God are compelled to fear mortal men, and often their own servants, indeed their own children; and those who will not be led by the noble fear of God are harassed by the cowardly and base fear of the most wretched men. Thus God avenges their contempt of himself. And this fear is perverse, a punishment worthy of tyranny established against justice and truth. Magistrates, whoever wish to conduct themselves with praise in their office, ought to observe this.

units.la: At miretur aliquis, quòd Deus apostolos denuo duci & comprehendi passus est, quos paulò ante per angeli ministerium liberauerat. Num verò illos amplius defendere non potuit? Vel num eorum curam abiecit, qui ipsius mandato tam studiosè obtemperauerant? Nequaquam. Inuicta enim illorum constantia docet, ipsos Deo cumprimis curæ fuisse. Sed docere voluit dominus, sub crucis vexillo pijs triumphandum esse. Quia enim Christus in cruce suspensus mundum cum principe suo, simulq; peccatum, mortem & inferos deuicit, iniquum foret, si nos victoriæ modum faciliorem affectaremus, sed illius vestigijs nos insistere decet, vt Petrus admoneat. 1. Pet. 2. Debet hoc carnis socordiæ & secupитaнi mederi, vt nunquam non cruci ferendæ nos accingamus.
units.tr: Someone may wonder why God allowed the apostles to be led away and arrested again, when he had just freed them through an angel's ministry. Could he not defend them any longer? Or had he abandoned the care of those who had so eagerly obeyed his command? By no means. The unbroken constancy of the apostles shows that they were especially dear to God. But the Lord wished to teach that the godly must triumph under the banner of the cross. For Christ, hanging on the cross, conquered the world with its prince, and at the same time sin, death and hell. It would be unjust if we sought an easier way to victory, but it becomes us to follow in his footsteps, as Peter admonishes (1 Pet. 2). This should cure the sluggishness and softness of the flesh, so that we never fail to prepare ourselves to bear the cross.

units.la: Præclarum verò Christianæ modestiæ exemplum apostoli præbent, qui in diuina vocatione capti & abducti, nec contra Deum murmurant impatienter, nec populum contra magistratum ad seditionem excitant. Nouerant enim Deum sapienter, iustè & vtiliter omnia administrare. Nouerant Christi regnum nec mundanum esse, nec mundi armis propagari. Nouerant Deum sibi affuturum, si ita ipsius gloria & illorum salus exigat. Huius igitur curæ sese committunt, & illius opem patienter expectant. Arguuntur horum exemplo, quicunq; Deo obmurmurare & illius iudicia nimium audacter carpere audent. Quotquot item seditionibus iniquis sibi consulere studeant, quasi illæ aliquid ad Christi regnum propagandum momenti habeant. Scimus sanè, puniri interdum tyrannos seditionibus, & iusto Dei iudicio fieri, vt seditiosis præda fiant, qui in pios moderato & iusto imperio uti nolunt. At pios seditionum authores nunquam fuisse legimus. A quibus Dauidem ita abhorruisse constat, vt Saulem apertum hostem occidere noluerit, ne in vnctum domini aliquid proteruiùs designadesignaret.1. Samuel. 24. & 26. De priuatis loquor, alia enim magistratuum ratio est, qui si Christiani fuerint, gladio diuinitus sibi commissō, cumprimis ad piorum & gloriæ Christi defensionem uti debent. Quid autem in eiusmodi casu episcopi & ecclesiarum ministri faciant, D.
