Ambrosij exemplo admonemur: qui cum Arrianis templa tradere iuberet Imperator, & inde non modò ecclesiæ turbatio, sed urbis totius tumultus esset exortus, ipse nec ecclesiam in periculo constitutam deserere, nec arma contra Imperatorem excitare voluit. Eius si quidem verba ad populum, inter multa alia, hæc quoq; fuerūt: Metuistis ne ecclesiam desererem, & dum saluti meæ timeo, vos relinquerem. Sed quid & ipse mandauerim (de responso tribunis Imperatorijs dato loquitur) potuistis aduertere: deserenda ecclesiæ voluntatem mihi subesse non posse: quia plus Dominum mundi, quàm seculi huius Imperatorem timerem. Sane si me vis aliqua abduceret ab ecclesia, carnem meam exturbari posse, non mentem: Paratum me esse, ut si ille faceret quod solet esse regiæ potestatis, ego subirem quod sacerdotis esse consueuit. Quid ergo turbamini? Volens nunquam ius deseram, coactus repugnare non noui. Dolere potere, potero flere, potero gemere: aduersus arma, milites, Gotthos quoque, lachrymæ meæ arma sunt. Talia enim munimenta sunt sacerdotis. Aliter nec debeo, nec possum resistere. Fugere autem & relinquere ecclesiam non soleo, &c. Et cum eidem à tribunis Gotthis diceretur, ut populum compesceret, respondit: In meo iure est, ut non excitem, in Dei manu, ut mitiget. Libuit hæc isto loco annotare, ut ex his ministri constantiam discant cum vera & Christiana prudentia coniunctam. Interim singulorum est, vocationi suæ constanter insistere, pericula patienter ferre, Dei opem firma spe expectare, nec fallet Christus, qui se suis tutorem pollicitus est. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The apostles set a remarkable example of Christian moderation. Though seized and led away in the course of their divine calling, they neither murmured impatiently against God nor stirred up the people to sedition against the magistrate. For they knew that God governs all things wisely, justly and profitably. They knew that Christ's kingdom is neither worldly nor advanced by worldly arms. They knew that God would be at their side, if his glory and their salvation required it. So they committed themselves to his care and patiently awaited his help. All who dare to grumble against God and to criticise his judgments too boldly are rebuked by this example, and so are all who strive to look after themselves by unjust seditions, as if such things had any weight in extending Christ's kingdom. We certainly know that tyrants are sometimes punished by seditions, and that by God's just judgment those who refuse to use a moderate and just rule over the godly become the prey of the seditious. Yet we read that the godly were never the authors of sedition. It is well established that David so abhorred this that he would not kill Saul, his open enemy, lest he should dare to mark the Lord's anointed with anything more insolent (1 Sam. 24 and 26). I am speaking of private persons; the situation of magistrates is different. If they are Christians, they ought, above all, to use the sword committed to them by God for the defence of the godly and of the glory of Christ. What bishops and ministers of the Church should do in such a case we learn from the example of Ambrose. When the emperor ordered him to hand over the churches to the Arians, and this led not only to disturbance in the Church but to a tumult throughout the whole city, he neither wished to abandon a church placed in danger nor to stir up arms against the emperor. Among many other things, his words to the people were these: "You feared that I would desert the church, and that while I cared for my own safety I would leave you behind. But you could have noticed what I myself had ordered (he is speaking of the reply given to the imperial tribunes): that it cannot be my will to desert the church, because I fear the Lord of the world more than the emperor of this age. Indeed, if some force were to drag me away from the church, it could drive out my flesh, not my mind. I am ready, if he does what is customary for royal power, to undergo what is customary for a priest. Why then are you troubled? I will never willingly give up my right; I know not how to resist under compulsion. I can grieve, I can weep, I can groan; against arms, soldiers and even Goths, my tears are my weapons. For such are the defences of a priest. I can neither resist otherwise, nor ought I to. But I am not accustomed to flee and abandon the church, etc." And when the Gothic tribunes told him to restrain the people, he replied: "It is within my right not to stir them up; it is in God's hand to calm them." I have been pleased to note this passage here, so that ministers may learn from it a constancy joined with true and Christian prudence. Meanwhile it is for each one to hold constantly to his calling, to bear dangers patiently, and to await God's help with firm hope; and Christ, who promised to be the guardian of his own, will not deceive. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVII.

units.la: Cum vero adduxissent illos, statuerunt coram concilio. Et interrogauit eos summus Pontifex, dicens: Annon præcipiendo præcepimus vobis, ne doceretis in nomine isto? Et ecce repleuistis Hierosolymam doctrina vestra; & vultis adducere super nos sanguinem hominis istius. Respondens autem Petrus & apostoli, dixerunt: Obedire oportet Deo magis quàm hominibus. Deus patrum nostrorum excitauit Iesum, quem vos in ligno suspensum interemistis. Hunc Deus principem & seruatorem exaltauit dextera sua, ad dandam pœnitentiam Israeli, & remissionem peccatorum. Et nos sumus eius testes de verbis istis, & insuper spiritus sanctus, quem dedit Deus obedientibus ipsi.
units.tr: When they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, saying: Did we not strictly command you not to teach in this name? And behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us. But Peter and the apostles answered and said: We ought to obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted this man at his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are his witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.

units.la: Quamuis Deus apostolos per angeli ministerium è carcere liberauerit, permitterit tamen, ut iidem denuò comprehensi coram Concilio immanissimorum hostium sistantur. Ita enim docere voluit, se non modò ex periculis imminentibus suos liberare, verumetiam in periculis constitutos tueri & conseruare posse. Cuius doctrinæ vsus est, ne de salute nostra & Dei auxilio desperemus, si quando cum periculis & aduersitatibus nos diutius conflictari patitur Deus, nec à nobis calicem transfert, quem semel ebibendum propinauit. Tutus enim & securus agit, qui in abdito excelsi & sub umbra omnipotentis commoratur, etiamsi cadunt à latere ipsius mille, & à dextris ipsius decem millia, &c. Psalm. 91. Exemplum huius euidens in præsenti historia Lucas proponit, qua quid cum apostolis in Concilio gestum sit, commemoratur: in quo virgis quidem cæsos esse, hostium verò manus euasisse audiemus. Priusquam tamen illud exponat euangelista, primò sacerdotum criminationem, deinde apostolorum responsionem siue apologiam describit: de quibus in præsenti (quantum Dominus dederit) dicemus.
units.tr: Although God freed the apostles from prison through the ministry of an angel, he nevertheless permitted them to be seized again and brought before the council of their most savage enemies. For he wished to teach that he can not only deliver his people from impending dangers, but also protect and preserve those who are placed in danger. We should make use of this teaching, so that we do not despair of our salvation and of God's help whenever God allows us to be struggling for a long time with dangers and adversities, and does not take from us the cup which he has once handed us to drink. For he who dwells in the secret place of the Most High and abides under the shadow of the Almighty acts safely and securely, even if a thousand fall at his side and ten thousand at his right hand, and so on. Psalm 91. Luke sets before us a clear example of this in the present history, where he recounts what was done with the apostles in the council. In it we hear that they were indeed beaten with rods, but escaped the hands of their enemies. Before the evangelist explains this, however, he first describes the accusation of the priests and then the apostles' answer or defence. With the Lord's help, I will speak of these things, as far as he gives me to do so, in the present lecture.

units.la: Accusantur apostoli à summo Pontifice, qui idem supremus huius causæ iudex erat. Nec ita accusantur, quasi dubium adhuc sit ipsos peccauisse, sed magno verborum fastu tanquam scelerum conuictos perterrefacere & tantum non obruere studet. Ait enim: Annon præcipiendo præcepimus vobis, ne doceretis in nomine isto? Et ecce repleuistis Hierosolymam doctrina vestra, & vultis adducere super nos sanguine hominis istius. Qua verba, si penitius inspiciantur, non vnius modò, sed plu sua ad dandam poenitentiam Israeli, & remissionem peccatorum. Et nos sumus eius testes, &c. Describitur bis tum ipse Christus, tum modus & ratio, qua ille in conferenda nobis salute utitur. Et Christum quidem non saluatorem modo, sed principem salutis, Dei dextra & virtute exaltatum esse dicunt. Frequenter autem Christi regis & principis mentio fit in scripturis, praecipue in Psalmis & Prophetarum sermonibus. Huc enim pertinent, quae leguntur Psalm.2.45.89.110.&c. Mich.5. Et angelus Gabriel ad illa allusisse videtur, quando ipsum in solio Dauid regnaturum, nec vllum regni ipsius finem fore dicit. Luc.1. Ita vero docere vult spiritus sanctus, Christum salutis nostrae non ministrum modo, sed authorem esse, qui virtute propria nos ex diaboli tyrannide asseruerit: adhaec potentem esse saluatorem, cui nemo resistere possit. Nec enim ipse sibi honorem illum raptu vendicauit, sed cum extremè humiliatus esset, datum est ei nomen illud, quod est supra omne nomen, in quo omne genu flectitur, &c. Philip.2. Seruit vero hoc consolationi nostrae in tentationibus. Quia enim potens ille rex Christus est, quem Dei dextera exaltauit, & cui omnis potestas data est in coelo & in terris, facile illi erit nos tueri, nec quisquam oues de manu ipsius rapiet. Matth.28. Ioban.10. Vtq; impia sacerdotum rabies obstare nequiuit, quo minus illum Dei dextera exaltaret: ita nec hodie impij principum & mundi huius conatus, illius regno & gloriae quicquam derogare poterunt.
units.tr: The apostles are accused by the high priest, who was also the supreme judge of this case. Nor are they accused as though it were still doubtful whether they had done wrong; rather, he strives to terrify them, as if they were already convicted of crimes, and almost to overwhelm them with a great show of words. For he says: Did we not strictly command you not to teach in this name? And behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring the blood of this man upon us. If these words are examined more closely, they show not one thing only but many: ... to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are his witnesses, and so on. Here Christ himself is described, and also the manner and method by which he uses to bestow salvation upon us. They say that Christ is not only Saviour but also Prince of salvation, exalted by the right hand and power of God. Now, mention of Christ as King and Prince is frequent in the Scriptures, especially in the Psalms and the sayings of the prophets. To this belong the passages read in Psalms 2, 45, 89, 110, and so on; Micah 5. And the angel Gabriel seems to have alluded to these when he said that Christ would reign on the throne of David and that his kingdom would have no end. Luke 1. The Holy Spirit wishes to teach in this way that Christ is not merely a minister of our salvation but its author, who by his own power has rescued us from the tyranny of the devil; moreover, he is a mighty Saviour, whom no one can resist. For he did not claim that honour for himself by seizure; rather, when he had been utterly humbled, that name was given to him which is above every name, at which every knee bows, and so on. Philippians 2. This also serves our comfort in temptations. For since Christ, whom God's right hand has exalted and to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, is a mighty King, it will be easy for him to protect us, and no one will snatch his sheep from his hand. Matthew 28; John 10. And just as the impious rage of the priests could not prevent God's right hand from exalting him, so today the attempts of the ungodly rulers and of this world will be unable to take anything away from his kingdom and glory.

units.la: Sed modum quoq; & rationem indicant, qua Christus salutem confert, & quae omnibus necessario ampleCtenda est, qui per ipsum saluari cupiunt. Duabus vero partibus ea comprehenditur, poenitentia nimirum & remissione peccatorum, & vtriusq; author vnicus Christus esse traditur. Poenitentiam totius hominis conuersionem ad Deum esse, non semel dictum est. Necessaria autem est omnibus nobis haec ad Deum conuersio, eò quòd omnes peccando exorbitauimus, & quotidie à salutis via deflectimus. Atqui eam non humanarum virium opus esse, non scripturis modo, verumetiam experientia quotidiana edocemur, nec quisquam, nisi à Deo conuertatur, conuerti poterit. Vide Ierem.31. Thren.5. Hanc vero conuersionem solus Christus vere in nobis operatur, dum per verbi sui semen & regenerationis spiritum nouos homines facit, quos & Dei cognitione illuminat, voluntate noua ac sancta imbuit, & viribus instruit, quibus ea exequantur, quae humanis viribus alioqui perfici non possunt. Confutantur hi, qui vbi poenitentiam exigi audiunt, mox inde iustitiae propriae meritum stabiliri arbitrantur, & liberi arbitrij vires extollunt. At quid nostro arbitrio gloriamur, si conuersionis istius author nobis est Christus? Et quid obsecro merebimur poenitentia nostra, qui nisi Christi spiritu excitemur & ducamur, illam agere non poterimus? At licet ad Deum conuersus sit homo, nondum tamen absoluta est nostrae salutis ratio. Quia enim peccatores sumus, peccatorum quoq; remissione & satisfactione opus est, ne quid diuinae iustitiae decedat. Caeterum cum modo dictum sit, nos nisi per Christum regeneremur, ad Deum conuerti non posse, multo minus pro peccatis nostris satisfacere poterimus. Et Christus peccata tale debitum esse docet, cui soluendo nos non possimus sufficere. Matth.18. Luc.7. Quare vt in priori parte nostrae infirmitati Christus succurrit, ita hic quoq; nobis medetur. Nam & mortis suae merito peccati debitum ac culpam expiat, & in Dei conspectu iustos facit, dum suam iustitiam nobis in se credentibus communicat. Ideo enim peccatum pro nobis factus est, vt nos efficeremur Dei iustitia per illum. 2.Cor.7. Quia vero vtraq; haec, sine quibus saluari nemo potest, vnius Christi beneficio contingunt, firmissime hinc colligimus, extra Christum salutem nullam inueniri posse. Quae causa est, quod euangelij summam ipse paucis comprehensurus, in suo nomine cum poenitentiam tum peccatorum remissionem praedicare docet. Luc.24. Interim & hoc discimus, quàm errent, qui sub Christi praetextu vel peccandi licentiam quaerunt, vel illa hoc plantari putant, quando vnus hic verus vere & salutifera poenitentiae author est.
units.tr: But the Spirit also indicates the manner and method by which Christ bestows salvation, and which all who desire to be saved through him must necessarily embrace. This method is comprised in two parts, namely repentance and forgiveness of sins, and Christ alone is delivered as the sole author of both. We have already said that repentance is the conversion of the whole man to God. This conversion to God is necessary for all of us, because by sinning we have all gone astray and daily turn aside from the way of salvation. Yet we are taught not only by the Scriptures but also by daily experience that this is not the work of human strength, and that no one can be converted unless he is converted by God. See Jeremiah 31; Lamentations 5. Christ alone truly works this conversion in us, while through the seed of his word and the Spirit of regeneration he makes us new men, whom he illuminates with the knowledge of God, endows with a new and holy will, and equips with strength to carry out those things which otherwise cannot be accomplished by human powers. Those are refuted who, as soon as they hear that repentance is required, at once think that the merit of their own righteousness is thereby established and extol the powers of free will. But why do we boast of our own will, if Christ is the author of this conversion? And what, I ask, will our repentance merit, when we cannot perform it unless we are roused and led by the Spirit of Christ? But although a man has been turned to God, the reckoning of our salvation is still not complete. For since we are sinners, we also need the remission of sins and satisfaction, lest anything be lacking to divine justice. Moreover, since it has just been said that we cannot be converted to God unless we are regenerated through Christ, much less will we be able to make satisfaction for our sins. And Christ teaches that sin is a debt which we are not able to pay in full. Matthew 18; Luke 7. Therefore, just as Christ comes to help our weakness in the former part, so he also heals us here. For by the merit of his death he both expiates the debt and guilt of sin, and makes us righteous in the sight of God, since he imparts his righteousness to us who believe in him. For he was made sin for us, so that through him we might become the righteousness of God. 2 Corinthians 7 [5:21]. And because both of these things, without which no one can be saved, come to us solely by the benefit of Christ, we firmly conclude from this that salvation cannot be found outside Christ. This is why, when he is about to sum up the gospel briefly, he teaches that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be preached in his name. Luke 24. Meanwhile, we also learn here how wrong those are who seek under the pretext of Christ either a licence to sin, or who think that repentance is planted by that licence, when this one is the true and only author of saving repentance.

units.la: Porrò praedicationem de Christo testimonijs confirmant, cum addunt: Et nos sumus eius testes de verbis istis, insuper & spiritus sanctus, quae dedit Deus obedientibus ipsi. Nec cuiquam temerarium aut insolens videri debet, quòd suum testimonium allegant apostoli coram ijs, à quibus rei agebantur. Quia enim Christus hos rerum abs se gestarum testes esse voluerat, hoc officij detrectare non potuerunt. Vide Ioban.15. Act.1. Et magna hinc accedit doctrinae ipsorum authoritas, quam nemo negare poterit, nisi Christum falsi accusare velit. At cum non ignorarent apostoli non multu ponderis coram sacerdotibus hoc ipsorum testimonium habere, alterum quoq; adijciùt spiritus sancti nimirum, quem Deus
units.tr: Furthermore, the apostles confirm their preaching about Christ with testimonies when they add: And we are his witnesses of these words, and also the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him. Nor ought it to seem rash or insolent to anyone that the apostles appeal to their own testimony before those by whom they were being tried. For since Christ had wished them to be witnesses of the things he had done, they could not refuse this duty. See John 15; Acts 1. From this there also arises a great authority for their teaching, which no one can deny unless he is willing to accuse Christ of falsehood. But since the apostles were not unaware that this testimony of theirs carried little weight before the priests, they added another, namely that of the Holy Spirit, whom God

units.la: Modus salutis.
units.tr: The way of salvation.

units.la: Euangelij testes apostoli & spiritus sanctus. Deus ijs largitur, qui Christo obediunt. Quamuis vero eius testimonium singuli fideles intra animos suos sentiant, & per hoc salutis suæ certi reddantur, præcipuè tamen de donis & operationibus spiritus sancti ista intelligi debent, quibus is euangelij doctrinæ in primitiua ecclesia testimonium fere-bat. Illius enim virtute fiebat, quòd linguis nouis loquebatur fideles, quòd toti subitò innouabantur, quòd miracula edebant. Quibus vt hodie non opus est, cum apostolorum doctrina iam satis comprobata sit: ita nobis spiritus testimonium sufficere debet, quo animos nostros confirmari sentimus, & quo animati clamamus, Abba pater. Attamen non ofcitanter præteriri debet, quòd spiritus ijs dari dicitur, qui Christo obediunt. Quos equidem iam ante spiritu prædictos esse oportet, cùm sine hoc nec credere nec obedire Christo possint. Sed augentur in illis spiritus dona, iuxta illud Christi: Omni habenti dabitur. Matth.25. Vnde rursum colligimus, spiritum sanctum penes illos locum habere non posse, qui Christo reluctantur. Talem enim ipse esse fatetur, quem mundus capere non potest. Ioban.14. Patet hinc, cur tam raræ sint nostro seculo spiritus sancti operationes & dona: idcirco nimirum, quòd paucos est videre, qui Christo obedire studeant. Nos verò istis ad sanctam fidei obedientiā excitari decet, vt spiritu sancto donati proficiamus in omni bono, & salutem consequamur in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The apostles and the Holy Spirit are witnesses of the gospel. God bestows the Spirit on those who obey Christ. Although each faithful person indeed feels the Spirit's testimony within his own heart, and is by this made certain of his salvation, still those things ought chiefly to be understood of the gifts and operations of the Holy Spirit, by which in the primitive Church he bore witness to the doctrine of the gospel. For by his power the faithful spoke in new tongues, were all suddenly renewed, and worked miracles. As these are not needed today, since the doctrine of the apostles has now been sufficiently proved, so the testimony of the Spirit ought to suffice for us, by which we feel our hearts strengthened, and by which, being stirred up, we cry out, Abba, Father. Yet it must not be passed over carelessly that the Spirit is said to be given to those who obey Christ. These men indeed must already have been endowed with the Spirit beforehand, since without him they can neither believe nor obey Christ. But the gifts of the Spirit are increased in them, according to that saying of Christ: To everyone who has, more will be given. Matt. 25. Hence again we gather that the Spirit cannot have a place among those who resist Christ. For he himself declares that he is such a one whom the world cannot receive. John 14. It is plain from this why the operations and gifts of the Holy Spirit are so rare in our age: no doubt because few are to be seen who are eager to obey Christ. But we ought to be stirred up by these things to a holy obedience of faith, so that, endowed with the Holy Spirit, we may make progress in every good thing and obtain salvation in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXVIII.

units.la: His auditis dissecabantur, & consultabant vt interficerent illos. Surgens autem quidam in Concilio pharisæus, nomine Gamaliel, legis doctor, pretiosus toti populo, iussit paulisper apostolos educi foras: dixitq; illis: Viri Israelitæ, attendite vobisipsis quoad homines istos, quid sitis facturi. Nā ante hos dies surrexit Theudas, dicens se esse aliquem, cui adhæsit numerus virorum circiter quadringentorū: qui occisus est, & dissipati sunt omnes, qui illi obedierant, & redacti in nihilum. Post hunc surrexit Iudas Galilæus in diebus census, & abduxit populum multum post se. Ille quoq; periit, & omnes qui illi paruerāt, dispersi sunt. Et nunc dico vobis, abstinete ab hominibus istis, & finite eos. Nam si ex hominibus est consilium vel opus hoc, dissoluetur. Sin verò ex Deo, non poteritis dissoluere: ne quando etiam cum Deo pugnare reperiamini.
units.tr: When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and took counsel to kill them. Then a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law and held in honour by all the people, stood up in the council and ordered the apostles to be put outside for a little while. He said to them: "Men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what you intend to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be someone, and about four hundred men joined him. He was slain, and all who had obeyed him were scattered and came to nothing. After him Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the census and drew many people after him. He too perished, and all who had obeyed him were dispersed. And now I say to you: keep away from these men and let them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will come to nothing; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, lest you be found even fighting against God."

units.la: NArrauit in hesternis diuus Lucas, quæ crimina à summo Sacerdote apostolis obiecta sint, & vt hi ad illa responderint. Cuius narrationis præcipuus vsus est, vt intelligamus quibus criminibus impij veritatem simul & huius ministros infamare soleant, quàm itē constantia & fortitudine nos in veritate asserenda vti conueniat. Vbi prima eius officij, quo deo obstricti sumus, cuna esse debet, ne quid in hominum gratiam aduersus illud peccemus. Deinde cauendum, ne nostra pusillanimitate insolentiores reddantur veritatis hostes, quod illis proprium esse constat. Adhæc constanter retinenda est Christi confessio, ne illius nos coram hominibus pudeat, quem nostri causa hominem fieri & mortem subire non puduit. Sequitur autem, quis responsionis seu apologiæ huius effectus apud improbos Christi hostes fuerit, qui locus cumprimis memorabilis est, tum quòd incurabilem impiorum pertinaciam arguit, tum quòd docet, quàm facilè sanguinarios illorum conatus Deus dissiper.
units.tr: Yesterday St Luke related what charges the high priest brought against the apostles and how they answered them. The chief use of this narrative is that we may understand with what accusations the wicked are accustomed to defame both the truth and its ministers, and likewise with what steadfastness and courage we ought to maintain the truth. Here the first duty of our office, by which we are bound to God, ought to be the rule: we must not sin against it to win the favour of men. Next, we must take care that our timidity does not make the enemies of the truth more insolent, which is known to be their nature. Moreover, the confession of Christ must be steadfastly held, lest we be ashamed of him before men, he who was not ashamed to become man for our sake and to undergo death. Next follows what effect this answer or defence had upon the wicked enemies of Christ. This passage is especially worth remembering, both because it shows the incurable obstinacy of the impious and because it teaches how easily God scatters their bloody attempts.

units.la: Primò enim de ijs sermonem instituens, qui irreconciliabile veritatis odiū conceperant, ait: His auditis dissecabantur, animis nimirum, adeoq; ira rumpebantur. Dolebat enim superbis & ambitiosis hominibus, quòd suam authoritatem vilipendi viderent, & intolerabilis ipsis videbatur tam libera & intrepida Christi & veritatis assertio. Quare præsentibus adhuc apostolis de mortis supplicio aduersus illos cōsultare incipiunt. Et verisimile est, ipsos furiosis potius clamoribus, quàm maturis deliberationibus vsos esse. Admonemur autem hoc exemplo, impios & improbos, qui in Christi odio induruerunt, nullis rationibus emolliri ac mitigari posse. Nam spiritum sanctum, qui solus corda mutare potest, tales capere non possunt, vt proximo Sermone diximus. Verbum Dei verò æternum, licet ipsorum animos penetret & conscientias perstringat, ferociores tamen reddit & ma-
units.tr: For first, in speaking of those who had conceived an irreconcilable hatred of the truth, he says: "When they heard this, they were cut to the heart," that is, in their minds, and so they were torn with anger. For it grieved these proud and ambitious men to see their authority held cheap, and the free and fearless assertion of Christ and the truth seemed intolerable to them. Therefore, while the apostles were still present, they begin to deliberate about putting them to death. And it is likely that they used furious shouts rather than mature deliberation. We are admonished by this example that the impious and wicked, who have grown hard in hatred of Christ, cannot be softened or mollified by any reasoning. For such men cannot receive the Holy Spirit, who alone can change hearts, as we said in the last sermon. The eternal Word of God, though it penetrates their minds and pierces their consciences, nevertheless makes them fiercer and

units.la: I. Apostolis mors intentatur. gis indurat. Et quemadmodum in superiori aeris regione ingens calor frigidiorem materiam eo loci euectam, non dissoluit, sed in glaciem congelascere facit: ita impiorum animi, quo vehementius Dei verbo vrgentur, eo magis indurescunt & ferociunt. Vel vt Solis calor ceram quidem liquefacit, lutum vero indurat: sic Dei verbum, quo piorum mentes doceri & formari solent, impios praefractiores reddit. Non quod haec divini verbi culpa sit, sed quod ea sit naturae corruptio in impiis, qua verbi germanum effectum impedit. Exempla huius in Caino extant & Pharaone, Saule item & Achabo, Iuda proditore & infinitis aliis, quibus hos quoq; annumerari debere, res ipsa docet. Hinc discimus, quid de nostri seculi hominibus iudicari debeat, qui verbi odium inueteratum non obscuris indiciis produnt: simulq; admonemur, quam immane scelus sit veritatis persecutio, maxime si ea non ex ignorantia & stulto Dei zelo, sed corruptissimis affectibus suasoribus instituatur. Meretur haec, vt ad divini verbi medicinam inepti reddamur, quae sola salutי & vita nos restituere potest.
units.tr: I. The apostles are threatened with death. harder. And as in the upper region of the air an intense heat does not dissolve a colder matter carried up there, but makes it freeze into ice, so the minds of the impious, the more vehemently they are pressed by the word of God, the more they harden and grow fierce. Or as the heat of the sun melts wax but hardens clay, so the word of God, by which the minds of the godly are usually taught and shaped, makes the impious more stubborn. This is not the fault of the divine word, but of the corruption of nature in the impious, which hinders the true effect of the word. Examples of this are found in Cain and Pharaoh, likewise in Saul and Ahab, in Judas the traitor and in countless others, and the thing itself teaches that these too ought to be counted among them. From this we learn what ought to be judged of the men of our own age, who betray their long-standing hatred of the word by no obscure signs; and at the same time we are warned how monstrous a crime is the persecution of the truth, especially when it is undertaken not from ignorance and foolish zeal for God, but at the urging of the most corrupt passions. This deserves that we should be made unfit for the medicine of the divine word, which alone can restore us to salvation and life.

units.la: Praeterea docet exemplum hoc, quem finem & scopum consiliorum suorum impij veritatis hostes habeant: eum videlicet, vt e medio tollantur veritatis ministri, quos solos suis cupiditatibus obstare existimant. Est enim hoc omnibus illis proprium, vt nihil sibi magis aduersum sentiant, quam Dei verbum, quo scelera ipsorum arguuntur. Quo fit, vt illos non pudeat vires suas omnes contra pauperculos homunciones proferre, & summo conatu aduersus illos pugnare, quos viri fortes & magnanimi vix dignos putarent, propter quos aliquid laboris aut molestiae suscipi debeat. Aliter autem isti sentiunt, quia iam sibi persuaserunt, tum demum res suas in portu fore, si molestissimis diuini verbi sermonibus non amplius obturbentur. Sic Achab vnum Eliam Israelis turbatorem & hostem suum esse arbitratur. Et de Syris victoriam certam sibi promittit, modo Micheam non admittat in consilium, quem infaustis nuntijs gaudere sibi plane persuaserat. Ita isti tunc se a reatu sanguinis Christi immunes, adhaec per omnia tutos & tranquillos fore credunt, si apostoli e medio sublati, auribus ipsorum oggannire desinant. Et si hodie aliquos interroges, quid ipsis in vita molestissimum sit, de solis verbi diuini ministris conquerentur. Atque hinc fit, quod tam immani rabie contra veritatis praeones mundus hic tumultuatur, quod hos publica pacis & tranquillitatis turbatores esse credit. Quod cum omnibus seculis factitatum sit, non miremur nostri seculi mores, nec impiorum conatibus offendamur, de quibus toties nos Christus admonuit. Armemus nos potius constantia, fortitudinis & patientia spiritu, adhaec cauti & circumspecti in vocatione, cui nos dominus destinauit, versemur, quemadmodum Christus iam olim docuit. Matth. 10. &c.
units.tr: Moreover, this example teaches what end and aim the enemies of the truth have in their plans: namely, that the ministers of the truth should be removed from the midst, since they alone, they think, stand in the way of their desires. For it is characteristic of all such men that they feel nothing more opposed to them than the word of God, by which their wickedness is rebuked. Hence it happens that they are not ashamed to bring all their strength against poor little men, and to fight with the utmost effort against those whom brave and great-hearted men would hardly think worth any trouble or annoyance. But they think otherwise, because they have already persuaded themselves that their affairs will be safe in harbour only when they are no longer disturbed by the most troublesome sermons of the divine word. So Ahab thought that Elijah alone, the troubler of Israel, was his enemy. And he promised himself certain victory over the Syrians, provided he did not admit Micaiah into his counsel, whom he had quite persuaded himself would rejoice in unlucky messages. Thus these men believe that they will then be free from the guilt of Christ's blood and safe and calm in all things, if the apostles are taken out of the way and stop buzzing in their ears. And if today you ask some people what is most troublesome to them in life, they will complain of the ministers of the divine word alone. And from this it comes that this world rages with such monstrous fury against the heralds of the truth, because it believes they are the disturbers of public peace and tranquillity. Since this has been done in every age, let us not wonder at the manners of our own age, nor be offended by the attempts of the wicked, of whom Christ has so often warned us. Let us rather arm ourselves with a spirit of constancy, courage and patience, and let us, cautious and circumspect, live in the calling to which the Lord has appointed us, as Christ taught long ago. Matt. 10, etc.

units.la: 11. Gamaliel apostolos mortis eripit.
units.tr: 11. Gamaliel rescues the apostles from death.

units.la: At miretur aliquis, cuius ope aut intercessione apostoli immanissimorum hostium manibus & praesenti mortis periculo erepti sint. Quem enim alium isti vererentur, penes quos summa rerum potestas erat? Sed ex ipsorum consessu sive numero apostolis patronum & assertorem exurrexisse, Lucas docet, Gamalielem nimirum, cuius personam diligenter describit. Nam Pharisaeum fuisse dicit, quae secta vt iustitiae externa splendorem sibi vendicabat, ita Christianae doctrinae & fidei erat infensissima. Deinde doctor legis fuit, cui illum attentius, quam alios eius ordinis, studuisse res ipsa declarat, nec studij fructu caruit. Accessit his summa auctoritas, quae ipsum toti populo venerabilem & charum fecerat. Et hoc quidem in praesenti causa quam plurimum momenti habebat. Quia enim alteri illi populum timebant, illius authoritatem reijcere non poterant, a cuius nutu totum vulgus sciebant dependere. Is ergo importunis collegarum consilijs prouocatus, & illorum furori se obijcere volens, apostolos paulisper secedere iubet, quo liberius causam hanc agere posset: hoc ipso facto declarans quantum reliquos prudentia & sapientia anteiret, qui praesentibus apostolis animorum impotentiam & rabiem prodiderant. Mox vero sententiam suam exponit, qua miriores reddit eos, qui apostolos morte multandos esse iudicarant. Priusquam vero Gamalielis verba explicemus, obseruandum venit, quam facile sit Deo suos periculis eripere, cum ex hostium quoque numero ipsis tutores dare, & vnius consilio sive authoritate multorum conatus dissipare possit. Nam vt modo dictum est, nullus hominum ordo Christo & doctrinae ipsius infensior fuit, quam pharisaeorum, qui iam olim excommunicationis sententiam in omnes Christi fectatores strinxerant. Iohan. 12. Verumtamen ordo hic Nicodemu habuit, cuius patrocinio ante etiam Christi causa defensa fuit. Iohan. 7. Ex eodem nunc Gamaliel prodit, cuius opera ad liberandos apostolos suos dominus vti dignatur. Et quidem vnus hic absque armis, prudenti tantum consilio adhibito totius Concilij conatus disturbat. bat. Extant & alia huius generis exempla, quae nos generalem doctrinam & consolationem hinc petere docent. Huc enim pertinet, quòd unus Ruben, qui tamen & ipse hostili in Iosephum animo praeditus fuerat, eundem postea praesenti mortis periculo eripit. Gen. 37. Eodem referri meretur, quòd Davidem Philistaei liberant, cum Saulinis copijs undiq; inclusus teneretur. 1. Samuel. 23. Quid de Mose dicemus, Israelitici populi vindice, quem Pharaonis immanissimi hostis filia inter Nili fluctus periclitantem saluat? Exod. 2. Sed longum foret, si quis omnibus exemplis, quae adduci poterant, recitandis immorari vellet. Vsum potius illorum nos obseruare conuenit, qui est, ne hominum conatibus terreamur, quos leui momento dissipare potest dominus, cuius seruitio addicti sumus. Quod unum si tam publicè quàm priuatim meditarentur homines, non vllis rationibus sese abduci patenter, quò minus suae vocationi insisterent, &c.
units.tr: Someone may wonder by whose help or intercession the apostles were rescued from the hands of the most savage enemies and from the immediate danger of death. For whom else would these men have feared, in whose hands lay the supreme power of affairs? Yet Luke shows that a patron and defender of the apostles arose from their own council, or from among their number: namely Gamaliel, whose character he describes carefully. For he says that Gamaliel was a Pharisee, a sect which, while it claimed for itself the splendour of outward righteousness, was most hostile to Christian doctrine and faith. Next, he was a teacher of the law, and the thing itself shows that he studied it more diligently than others of that order, nor did he lack the fruit of his study. Added to this was great authority, which had made him venerable and dear to the whole people. And in the present case this counted for a great deal. For since they feared the people, they could not reject the authority of the man on whose nod, they knew, the whole crowd depended. So he, provoked by the importunate advice of his colleagues, and wishing to expose himself to their fury, orders the apostles to withdraw for a little while, so that he might handle the case more freely. By this very act he declared how far he surpassed the rest in prudence and wisdom, since they had revealed their lack of self-control and their rage while the apostles were present. Soon he sets out his opinion, which makes those who had judged the apostles worthy of death look more foolish. Before we explain Gamaliel's words, we should observe how easily God can rescue his people from dangers, since he can provide them with defenders even from the number of their enemies, and by the counsel or authority of one man scatter the efforts of many. For, as has just been said, no order of men was more hostile to Christ and his teaching than the Pharisees, who had long before launched the sentence of excommunication against all Christ's followers (John 12). Yet this same order had Nicodemus, by whose patronage the cause of Christ was defended even earlier (John 7). Now from the same order comes Gamaliel, through whose work the Lord deigns to free his apostles. And indeed this one man, without arms, merely by applying prudent counsel, disturbs the efforts of the whole council. There are other examples of this kind, which teach us to draw from this a general doctrine and consolation. To this belongs the fact that Reuben, though he too had been filled with hostile feeling towards Joseph, later rescued him from the immediate danger of death (Gen. 37). To the same place may be referred the fact that the Philistines set David free, when he was held enclosed on every side by Saul's forces (1 Sam. 23). What shall we say of Moses, the champion of the Israelite people, whom the daughter of the most savage enemy of Pharaoh saved while he was in peril among the waves of the Nile (Exod. 2)? But it would be a long business if someone wanted to linger over reciting all the examples that could be adduced. Rather we should observe their use, which is that we should not be terrified by the efforts of men, whom the Lord, to whose service we are devoted, can scatter in a moment. If men meditated on this one thing, both publicly and privately, they would not allow themselves to be drawn away by any reasons from persisting in their calling, etc.

units.la: Videamus autem Gamalielis consilium, prudentiae quidem plenum, sed in quo nonnulla desyderes, quae illum in veritatis causa nondum perfectè institutum esse docent. Voluit tamen illius opera vel dominus, & ipes est illum postea maiores in pietate progressus fecisse. Sunt autem orationis ipsius partes tres. Primò exordiolo vtitur, quo furentes mitigat, & hortatur ne quid temere aut inconsultò agant. Attendite vobisipsis (inquit) quoad homines istos, quid sitis facturi. Quasi dicat, Audio quidem à vobis decerni, vt mortis supplicium luant. Sed metuo, ne praeceps nimium sit, & proinde periculosa vestri consilij ratio. Maturam ergo & diligentem deliberationem adhiberi velim, ne quid ab iratis designetur, cuius nos postea paenitear. Est autem haec vtilissima & omnibus seculis necessaria admonitio, ne irati quid statuamus vel agamus. Pessimum enim consultorem iram esse veteres dixerunt, vtpote quae breuis insania est. Quid autem ab insano aut mente capto boni aut aequi speres? Quam ob rem verissimè Iacobus dicit: Ira viri iustitiam Dei non operatur. Iacob. 1. Atqui vtinam tanta hodie inter Christianos esset harum sententiarum authoritas, quantam olim inter ethnicos fuisse legimus. De Augusto fertur, quòd Athenodori philosophi conuersationem sibi necessariam esse duxerit, eò quòd illum iam abiturus monuisset, vt iratus nihil decerneret, nisi prius viginti quatuor literarum siue elementorum nomina recitauisset. Intelligebat enim vir prudentissimus iram morā mitescere. Nec minus memorabile est, quòd alius quidam è philosophorum numero, seruo, qui peccarat, dixit: Vapulares, nisi iratus esset. At hodie inter Christianos plerique ita sentiunt, vt iratis quiduis licere existiment, & irae praetextu atrocissima & iniquissima quaeque facinora excusare conentur. Quòd si leones aut vrsos nos creauisset dominus, aliquem fortasse locum illorum excusatio habere t. At quia homines sumus, quos tum rationis fraeno, tum Dei verbo regi decet, inexcusabiles erunt, quicunque affectuum libidini sese regendos permittunt. In primis tamen horum iudices & principes meminisse decet, ne ira abrepti ab aequitate & iustitia exorbitent.
units.tr: Let us look, however, at Gamaliel's counsel, full of prudence, but in which you may miss some things which show that he was not yet fully instructed in the cause of truth. Nevertheless the Lord wished to use his work, and it is indeed certain that he afterwards made greater progress in piety. The speech has three parts. First he uses a little preamble, by which he calms the raging and urges them not to act rashly or without deliberation. "Take heed to yourselves," he says, "as to these men, what you are about to do." As if he said: I hear indeed that you have decided that they should pay the penalty of death. But I fear that this is too hasty, and that the plan of your decision is therefore dangerous. I would therefore wish a mature and careful deliberation to be applied, lest anything be decided by angry men which we may afterwards regret. This admonition is most useful and necessary in every age: that we should not decide or do anything while angry. For the ancients said that anger is the worst counsellor, being as it is a brief madness. What good or fairness can you hope for from a madman or someone out of his mind? Wherefore James rightly says: "The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God" (James 1). And yet would that today among Christians the authority of these sayings were as great as we read it was once among the heathen. It is related of Augustus that he judged the company of the philosopher Athenodorus necessary to him, because when about to depart he advised him that, when angry, he should decide nothing until he had first recited the names of the twenty-four letters of the alphabet. For that most prudent man understood that anger is softened by delay. No less memorable is what another of the philosophers said to a slave who had done wrong: "You would be beaten, if I were not angry." But today among Christians most people think so as to suppose that the angry may do anything at all, and they try to excuse the most atrocious and unjust deeds under the pretext of anger. But if the Lord had created us as lions or bears, perhaps such an excuse would have some place. But since we are men, who ought to be ruled both by the bridle of reason and by the Word of God, those will be inexcusable who allow themselves to be governed by the lust of their passions. Above all, however, judges and rulers of this kind should remember not to be carried away by anger and to stray from equity and justice.

units.la: Est praeterea diligenti consideratione digna Gamalielis locutio: Attendite vobisipsis, &c. Atqui de apostolis agebatur, quorum vita in periculo consistuta erat. Caeterum videbat vir prudentissimus, & diligentissimus legis diuinae obseruator, ex iniquis iudicijs plus periculi iudicibus, quàm reis ipsis imminere. Quid enim his potest morte durius accidere, qua vitam mortalem cum immortali permutant? Illi verò Dei iram contra se prouocant, qui illorum consessibus (vt Psal. 82. scribitur) medius interest, nec inultam finit eorum audaciam, qui sub iudiciorum diuinorum praetextu iniustitiam exercent. Sibi ergo hoc dici putent quicunque in magistratu sunt constituti, & sibijpsis attendant, ne affectibus excaecati à iustitiae tramite exorbitent.
units.tr: Moreover, Gamaliel's expression is worthy of careful consideration: "Take heed to yourselves," etc. Yet it was about the apostles that he was speaking, whose life was placed in danger. But this most prudent man, and most diligent observer of the divine law, saw that more danger threatens the judges from unjust judgements than the accused themselves. For what can happen to these men more harshly than death, by which they exchange mortal life for immortal? Yet the judges provoke the wrath of God against themselves, who, as is written in Psalm 82, stands in the midst of their assemblies, and does not allow the audacity of those to go unpunished who practise injustice under the pretext of divine judgements. Let therefore all who are set in the magistracy think that this is said to them, and let them take heed to themselves, lest, blinded by their passions, they stray from the path of justice.

units.la: Secunda orationis parte narrationem exemplis constantem texit, ex quibus suae sententiae argumenta paulò post desumit. Prudenter verò exempla praemittit, & ita narrat, vt in quam partem inclinare velit, primò videri non possit, ne sententia ipsius vel non audiatur, vel non expensa explodatur. E multis autem duo potissimum deligit, quae vt omnibus notissima erant: ita illorum mentes acrius commouere poterant: quorum alterum Theudae, alterum Iudae Galilaei est. Meminit horum Iosephus quoque, sed quoad ordinem à Luca plurimùm differt, cùm Iudam multis annis Theuda priorem fuisse scribat, quem Gamaliel postea hunc demum exurrexisse palàm testatur. Sed maior apud nos esse debet sacri scriptoris authoritas, quàm Iosephi, quem in multis alijs quoque falsum esse constat, & cuius scripta facilè corrupti & inuerti potuerunt. In historijs difficultas nulla est, nec aliud hic docere vult Gamaliel, quàm nemini hactenus impune fuisse, Messiae nomen & of-
units.tr: In the second part of his speech he weaves a narrative consisting of examples, from which he afterwards draws the arguments for his opinion. He prudently puts the examples first, and so tells them that one cannot at first see which way he wishes to lean, lest his opinion either not be heard or be rejected without being weighed. Of the many he chooses two principal ones, which, as they were most familiar to everyone, could the more keenly move their minds: one concerns Theudas, the other Judas the Galilean. Josephus also mentions these, but as to their order Luke differs considerably, since Josephus writes that Judas came many years before Theudas, whereas Gamaliel plainly testifies that the latter arose later. But the authority of the sacred writer ought to be greater for us than that of Josephus, who is known to be false in many other things too, and whose writings could easily be corrupted and altered. There is no difficulty in the histories, nor does Gamaliel wish to teach anything else here than that no one up to now has gone unpunished for claiming for himself the name and office of the Messiah,

units.la: III. Gamalielis consilium.
units.tr: III. Gamaliel's counsel.

units.la: Lib. antiq. 18. cap. 1. & lib. 20. cap. 4. cium sibi vendicare, imò cum omni sua secta perijsse eos omnes, qui hoc prætextu res suas agere vo luerint. Vnde postea colligit, idem etiam Christianorum sectæ euenturum, si quid dolo malo Christus egerit: & proinde Dei iudicium expectari debere, &c. Nobis verò in exemplorum narratione ob seruandum est obicer, quid fere eos maneat, qui verum Messiam, Iesum Christum, ampleƈti nolunt. Tales enim plerunq; seditiosis & improbis hominibus præda fiunt, qui ipsis publicorum malorum authores sunt. Quis enim hic non videat illud Christi impletum esse: Ego veni nomine patris mei, nec recipitis me: Si alius venerit in nomine suo, illum recipietis? Ioan. 5. Quod ipsum hodie quoq; fieri cernimus. Incurabile enim manet mundi ingenium, qui impostoribus gaudet & seductoribus, veritatis verò ministros odio irreconciliabili prosequitur. Iusto igitur Dei iudicio fit, vt efficacem illusionem sentiant, & scientes simul ac volentes in exitium ruant. Vide 2. Thess. 2. cap.
units.tr: (Antiquities 18, ch. 1, and book 20, ch. 4), and that all those who wished to pursue their own affairs under this pretext have perished, together with their whole sect. From this he afterwards infers that the same would befall the sect of the Christians, if Christ had acted with evil intent; and therefore that God's judgement should be awaited, etc. But for us, in the narration of these examples, we must observe what usually awaits those who refuse to embrace the true Messiah, Jesus Christ. For such people are usually the prey of seditious and wicked men, who are themselves the authors of public evils. For who here does not see that the saying of Christ has been fulfilled: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him" (John 5)? This we see happening even today. For the nature of the world remains incurable: it rejoices in impostors and deceivers, but pursues the ministers of truth with irreconcilable hatred. It is therefore by the just judgement of God that they feel a powerful delusion and, knowingly and willingly, rush to their destruction. See 2 Thess. 2.

units.la: Sed ad Gamalielem reuertamur, vt videamus quomodo exemplis hisce vsus fit. Ex his enim sententia sua fundamentum colligit, cuius propositio siue conclusio est: Abstinete ab hominibus istis, & finite eos. Quod vt persuadeat, argumentationem per dilemma figurat hoc modo. Aut humanum aut diuinum sit oportet hoc negotium, cuius ministri siue dispensatores sunt apostoli, quos necandos censetis. At qualecunque sit, ego à sanguinis effusione abstinendum censeo. Si enim humanum est, nec aliis quàm humanis consilijs regitur, sponte dissoluetur, id quod Theudæ & Iudæ exempla superioribus annis abunde docuerunt. Quæ ergo dementia foret vulgi furorem concitare, vt id tollatur, quod iamiam (etsi nemo impellat) collapsurum est? Quòd si verò diuinum hoc opus est, Deoq; auctore & moderatore regitur, nullis hominum vel viribus vel consilijs dissolui poterit. Quid enim contra Deum homo efficiat, qui puluis & cinis est? Adhæc, cum Deo bellum suscepisse deprehendemini, cuius non poterit non esse infelicissimus exitus. Diligenter autem consilij huius scopus obseruandus est, quem dum multi negligunt, perniciosissimi dogmatis occasionem hinc venantur, quo nullius conatus quantumuis improbos, nullius etiam errores quantumuis impios & blasphemos vi coercendos esse clamant. Vnde aliud sequi non potest, quàm vniuersæ disciplinæ cùm politicæ tum ecclesiasticæ conuulsio. Frustra enim geret magistratus gladium. Et frustra Paulus eiusmodi ministros ecclesijs vult præficī, qui non modo veritatem docere, verumetiam contradicentes refutare & conuincere possint. Quis autem prudentissimo viro hunc animum fuisse putet, vt omnes ecclesiæ & politiæ neruos dissolutos voluerit? Hoc illum potius spectauisse constat, vt apostolos iudicium furori & imminenti mortis periculo eriperet, quod commodissimè fieri posse videbat, si offenderet contra illos sine euidenti discrimine nihil acerbius aut durius statui posse. Aut enim ex Deo periculum fore, si illi bene sentiant & Dei ministri sint: aut ex vulgo, cuius furorem ipsi declinare potius quàm prouocare debeant, maximè in tali causa, quæ si nudis hominum consilijs administretur, diu stare non posset. Adhæc siue veritatem intellexerit siue ignorarit, dubius tamen & ambiguus in sermone apparet. Longè igitur alia illorum ratio est, qui veritatis cognitione vera illuminati, illam ex officio tueri, & errores ac impietates extirpare debent.
units.tr: But let us return to Gamaliel, so that we may see how he used these examples. From them he draws the foundation of his opinion, whose proposition or conclusion is: Keep away from these men and leave them alone. To persuade them of this, he sets out an argument by dilemma, in this way: this business, whose ministers or stewards are the apostles, whom you think should be put to death, must be either human or divine. But whatever it is, I judge that bloodshed should be avoided. For if it is human, and is governed by nothing but human plans, it will dissolve of its own accord, as the examples of Theudas and Judas taught well enough in former years. What madness, then, would it be to stir up the mob's fury in order to remove something that is already about to collapse, even if no one pushes it? But if this work is divine, and is governed by God as its author and director, it cannot be dissolved by any human strength or plans. For what can a man do against God, who is dust and ashes? Besides, you will be found to have taken up war against God, and it cannot fail to end most unhappily for you. Moreover, the aim of this counsel must be carefully observed. Many neglect it, and while they do so they hunt for an occasion for a most destructive doctrine, by which they cry out that no attempts, however wicked, and no errors, however impious and blasphemous, should be restrained by force. From this nothing else can follow but the overthrow of all discipline, both civil and ecclesiastical. For the magistrate would bear the sword in vain, and Paul would wish such ministers set over the churches in vain, men who can not only teach the truth but also refute and convince those who contradict it. Who, then, would think that such a mind belonged to a most prudent man, that he wished to loosen all the sinews of the Church and the state? It is clear rather that he aimed at this: to snatch the apostles from the judgement of a furious mob and from the imminent danger of death. He saw that this could be done most easily if he showed that nothing harsher or more severe could be decided against them without an obvious risk. For either the danger would come from God, if they were of good mind and were God's ministers; or it would come from the mob, whose fury they ought rather to avoid than provoke, especially in such a cause, which, if it were managed by mere human plans, could not stand for long. Besides, whether he had understood the truth or had been ignorant of it, he nonetheless appears doubtful and ambiguous in his speech. Far different, therefore, is the case of those who, enlightened by the true knowledge of the truth, must by their office defend it and root out errors and impieties.

units.la: Interim oraculi instar nobis esse debet, quòd Dei consilia nullis hominum viribus impediri possunt, humana verò sua sponte collabi discimus. Nam vt Deus æternus est & immutabilis, ita æternum est verbum domini, nec vllis rationibus conuelli potest. Isa. 4.0. Et Deum gentium consilia absque negotio dissipare, suum verò consilium perpetuò stabilire, Dauid testatur. Psalm. 33. Exempla, quæ id probent, passim sunt obuia. Dei consilio, quo Dauidem Israelis regem facere decreuerat, multum diuque reluctatur Saul. Sed quò magis pugnat, eò minus se proficere sentit, & infelicem sortitur certaminis cum Deo suscepti exitum. In primis tamen ad fidei & religionis causam hoc transferri debet. Dei consilium est, vt filius quem ab æterno genuit, regnum obtineat in monte suo sancto, qui est ecclesia, Psalmo secundo. Huic dictum est: Sede à dextris mihi, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum. Item: Dominare in medio inimicorum tuorum. Psal. 110. Isti consilio abipsa mundi origine sese cum suis membris satan opposuit, & in Abele (quem idcirco primum Christi martyrem dicere fas est) cœpit persecutio, quæ sequentibus seculis continuata, bodie adhuc durat. Sed vicisim durat Christi regnum & ecclesia, cùm ei petræ innitatur, contra quam portæ inferorum non præualent. prima Corinthiorum tertio. Matth. decimo sexto. Quòd si è contra gentilismum & immane illud idololatriæ chaos inspicias, quod à potentissimis regibus obseruatum, multorum seculorum spacio confirmatum, nationum & gentium fere omnium consensu approbatum, nullius vero vnquam armis oppugnatum fuit: sponte tamen collapsum & spi- ritu ac verbo Christi dissipatum esse videbis. Eadem est scriptura sacra ratio, quam à Deo inspi- ratam vocat Apostolus. Nam si prophanos scriptores inspicias, illorum libri in pretio fuerunt, nec hostes habuerunt vllos, qui illos extinctos vellent. Perijt tamen maxima illorum pars, & vix nomi- na extant librorum, quos olim opulentissimi reges summo studio & immani pretio conquisierunt, sicut de Ptolemaeo Philadelpho & alijs similibus traditur. At sacri libri toties exusti, proscripti, & in super principibus potentissimis exosi, adhuc extant, & in omnes prope linguas translati, per totum orbem magistrorum officio funguntur. Seruiant ergo haec institutioni & consolationi nostrae, ne quid temere aduersus Deum instituamus, neue mundi & tyrannorum minacibus contra Christi regnum instituti terreamur. Ita vero Deum causae suae assertorem & vindicem agnoscamus, vt ipsi quoque pro nostrae vocationis ratione, in aedificanda ecclesia fidelem operam nauemus, tanquam cooperarij Ie su Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile, we ought to have this as an oracle: that the counsels of God cannot be hindered by any human strength, while human plans, we learn, fall of their own accord. For as God is eternal and unchangeable, so the word of the Lord is eternal, and it cannot be overthrown by any arguments (Isa. 40). And David testifies that God scatters the counsels of the nations without any trouble, while he establishes his own counsel forever (Ps. 33). Examples that prove this are everywhere at hand. Saul struggles long and hard against the counsel of God, by which he had decreed to make David king of Israel. But the harder he fights, the less he feels himself prospering, and he meets an unhappy end to a contest undertaken against God. Yet above all this must be applied to the cause of faith and religion. It is God's counsel that the Son, whom he begat from eternity, should obtain the kingdom on his holy mountain, which is the Church (Ps. 2). To him it was said: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet. And again: Rule in the midst of your enemies (Ps. 110). Against this counsel Satan has set himself with his members from the very beginning of the world, and in Abel (who may rightly be called the first martyr of Christ) persecution began, which, continued through the following ages, lasts even today. But in turn the kingdom of Christ and the Church endure, since they rest upon the rock against which the gates of hell shall not prevail (1 Cor. 3; Matt. 16). But if, on the other hand, you look at paganism and that monstrous chaos of idolatry, which was observed by the most powerful kings, confirmed through the space of many ages, and approved by the consent of nearly all nations and peoples, yet was never attacked by the arms of anyone, you will see that it collapsed of its own accord and was dissipated by the Spirit and the word of Christ. The reasoning of Holy Scripture is the same, which the Apostle calls inspired by God. For if you look at profane writers, their books were held in high esteem, and they had no enemies who wished them destroyed. Yet the greatest part of them has perished, and hardly the titles of the books remain, which once the most wealthy kings sought out with the greatest zeal and at enormous price, as is recorded of Ptolemy Philadelphus and others like him. But the sacred books, so often burned, banned, and moreover hated by the most powerful princes, still survive, have been translated into almost all languages, and throughout the whole world discharge the office of teachers. Let these things therefore serve for our instruction and comfort, so that we may not rashly undertake anything against God, nor be frightened by the threats of the world and of tyrants against the kingdom of Christ. Rather, let us acknowledge God as the defender and vindicator of his own cause, so that we too, according to the measure of our calling, may apply faithful labour to building up the Church, as fellow workers with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XXXIX.

units.la: Paruerunt autem illi, & cùm aduocassent apostolos, caesis praecepe- runt, ne loquerentur in nomine Iesu, & dimiserunt eos. Et illi quidem i- bant gaudentes à conspectu Concilij, quòd digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine eius contumelia afficerentur. Et quotidie in templo & per singu- las domus non cessabant docere & annuntiare Iesum Christum.
units.tr: They yielded to him. When they had called in the apostles, they had them beaten and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and then they let them go. The apostles went out from the presence of the council rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for his name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease to teach and to proclaim Jesus Christ.

units.la: QVoniam ita comparatum est, vt omnes homines naturali quodam instinctu incolumitatis & felicitatis appetentes sint, fieri non potest, quin aduersis & tribulationibus vehementer offendantur, maximè verò ijs, quae propter religionem excitari & oboriri consueuerunt. Fit enim vt de religione & doctrina ex euentu iudicent, & mox falsi insimulent eam religionem, cuius profes- fores persecutionibus & aduersis exerceri vident. Quare non tam vtile quàm necessarium est, vt con- tra omnes offendiculorum occasiones probè instituamur. Quae causa est, quòd primitiuae ecclesiae afflì- ctiones tam diligenter per Lucam spiritus sanctus describi voluit: in quibus praecipuè obseruandum est, quae semper in hoc mundo ecclesiae Christi fors fuerit, & vt praesenti fidoq; domini praesidio iam olim inter maximas tribulationes conseruata sit: ne vel nostri seculi aerumnis, tanquam insolitis, offendamur, vel de Dei auxilio & ecclesiae conseruatione desperemus. Vtriusq; exemplum praesens histo- ria nobis exhibet, cuius exitum modò describit euangelista, & primò quidem quid coniurati Christi hostes, deinde verò quid apostoli fecerint, commemorat.
units.tr: Since it is the case that all people, by a natural instinct, seek safety and happiness, it cannot but happen that they are deeply disturbed by adversities and tribulations, and especially by those that usually arise and break out on account of religion. For people judge a religion and its teaching by the outcome, and they soon declare false the religion whose professors they see harassed by persecutions and misfortunes. Therefore it is not only useful but necessary that we be thoroughly instructed against all occasions of stumbling. This is the reason why the Holy Spirit wanted Luke to describe so carefully the afflictions of the primitive Church. In them we must above all observe what the lot of the Church of Christ has always been in this world, and how, under the present and faithful protection of the Lord, it was preserved long ago amid the greatest tribulations. The aim is that we should not be thrown off balance by the miseries of our own age, as though they were unusual, nor despair of God's help and of the Church's preservation. The present history sets before us an example of both. The evangelist now describes its outcome, and first recounts what the conspiring enemies of Christ did, and then what the apostles did.

units.la: De Christi hostibus in Concilio congregatis sic scribit Lucas: Paruerunt Gamalieli, & cùm ad vocassent apostolos, caesis praeceperunt, ne loquerentur in nomine Iesu, & dimiserunt eos. Paruisse di- cuntur Gamalielis sententiae, cùm duo addiderint, quae ille nequaquam facienda censuerat. Nam virgis caedunt apostolos, & prius edictum renouant, quo euangelij praedicationem prohibere conaban- tur. Ita igitur paruerunt Gamalieli, ne occiderent Christi seruos, quemadmodū facere instituerant. Interim sibi temperare non possunt, quin flagris & virgis caedant homines innoxios. Magnam ergo & effrenem fuisse oportuit illorum rabiem, quae ne tunc quidem omnino sopiri potuit, cùm iam plane restincta esse videretur. Est autem hoc proprium impijs Christi persecutoribus, vt cùm placati esse putantur, animorum tamen rabiem & veritatis odium occulte foueant, & raro fine aliqua ignominia aut publicae poenae nota Christi ministros dimittant, ne iniusto & impio ausu contra illos insurrexisse videantur, & vt vel aliquam erroris speciem ipsorum sectatoribus obijciant. Ita Pilatus, licet Christum innocentem pronuntiet, non tamen nisi virgis caesum dimittere instituit. Luc.23. Consolationis tamen plenum est, quòd tantam rabiem vnica Gamalielis oratione eorum frenauit dominus, vt mortis supplicium in sontibus inferre non ausi fuerint. Vnde colligimus, non semper impijs licere, quicquid libet, sed quamuis inuitos diuina prouidentia habenis gubernari. Insunt autem huic exemplo praeter hoc alia quaedam, quorum obseruatio nobis hodie vtilissima est.
units.tr: Luke writes thus about the enemies of Christ gathered in the council: "They yielded to Gamaliel, and when they had called in the apostles, they had them beaten and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and they let them go." They are said to have yielded to Gamaliel's opinion, although they added two things which he had by no means advised doing. For they beat the apostles with rods, and they renewed the earlier edict by which they had tried to forbid the preaching of the gospel. So they yielded to Gamaliel only in this respect: they did not kill Christ's servants, as they had planned to do. Yet they could not restrain themselves from striking innocent men with whips and rods. Their rage must therefore have been great and unbridled, and it could not be entirely calmed even then, when it seemed already quite extinguished. It is, however, characteristic of the impious persecutors of Christ that, when they are thought to be appeased, they nonetheless secretly nourish the rage of their minds and their hatred of the truth. Rarely do they dismiss Christ's ministers without some disgrace or mark of public punishment, lest they seem to have risen against them in an unjust and impious undertaking, and in order to throw at their followers some appearance of error. So Pilate, although he pronounced Christ innocent, nonetheless resolved to release him only after having him scourged (Luke 23). Yet it is full of consolation that the Lord, through the single speech of Gamaliel, restrained such great rage that they did not dare to inflict the penalty of death on the guilty. From this we gather that it is not always permitted to the impious to do whatever they please, but that, however unwilling, they are governed by the reins of divine providence. Besides this, the example contains several other lessons, whose observation is most useful for us today.

units.la: Et primò quidem admonemur, nihil noui aut insoliti accidere, etiamsi hodie quoq; pij & sancti cultores Christi, impiorum libidini permittantur, & afflictionem sentiant. De hoc enim Christus ipse iam olim praemonuit, & ostendit tempus fore, quo cultum deo praestare videatur, quicunq; aliquem è suis occiderit. Ioban. 16. Idem ad crucem suos inuitat, & suo exemplo praeire voluit, ne nostram fortem illa praestantiorem fore speraremus, quam ipse sustinuit. Matth. 16. Ioban. 15. Sentiunt id nunc apostoli, nec offenduntur, quin potius nos frequenter admonent, ne tanquam re insolita offendamur, si quando per ignem exploramur. Vide. 1. Pet. 4. Prodest autem in horum consyderatione diligenter versari. Ita enim fiet, ut nec secundis rebus insolenter abutamur, nec aduersis frangamur, cum illa iam ante à nobis praeuisa sint.
units.tr: First, we are reminded that nothing new or unusual happens, even if today too the godly and holy worshippers of Christ are given over to the lust of the impious and suffer affliction. Christ himself long ago foretold this, and showed that there would be a time when whoever killed one of his followers would seem to render worship to God (John 16). He also invites his own to the cross, and wished to go before them by his example, so that we would not hope that our lot would be better than that which he himself endured (Matthew 16; John 15). The apostles now feel this, and they are not offended; rather, they frequently admonish us not to be offended, as though by something unusual, if at any time we are tested by fire (see 1 Peter 4). It is profitable to dwell diligently on these considerations. For thus it will come about that we neither abuse prosperity arrogantly nor are broken by adversity, since these things have already been foreseen by us.

units.la: Secundò non indignum consyderatu est, quòd apostoli, electa Christi organa, in causa optima & sanctissima, cuius patrocinium ex Christi mandato susceperant, ignominiose vapulat. Vnde non obscure colligimus, quàm turpis & pudendus illorum error sit, qui afflictiones malas & iniustas causa argumentum siue indicium esse existimant: è quorum numero sunt, qui nobis hodie clades & omnis generis infortunia obiiciunt, quibus patere dicunt, nos in fidei & religionis causa exorbitare. At ipsos mentis & rationis non satis compotes esse, vel hinc constat, quòd ea videre nequeunt, de quibus ethnicorum poetae aequius multò iudicauerunt. Notum est enim illud Nasonis: Careat successibus opto, Quisquis ab euentu facta notanda putet. Nam si horum iudicia valere debent, paucos adeoq; nullos ex sanctissimorum Dei cultorum numero dabimus, qui non ipsi quoq; damnari mereantur: cum vel caecus videat, plerosq; ipsorum, non modò variis laborum & persecutionum vicibus vexatos, verumetiam immanissimorum hostium iniquis manibus necatos fuisse. Nec meliora nobis hodie sperande esse, Christi oracula, quibus ille nos de nouissimorum temporum statu admonuit, abunde docent. Quare quicunq; religionis causam ex euentu & successibus huius seculi dijudicant, Iudaeorum & militum similes censeri debent, quos Christo in cruce pendenti acetum propinauisse, & dixisse legimus: Sirex Israel est, descendat nunc de cruce, & credemus ei. Confidit in Deo, liberet eum nunc, si vult eum. Dixit enim, se esse Dei filium, &c. Matth. 27. Et sanè quod nam acetum asperius & acerbius esse potest, quàm eiusmodi exprobrationes, quibus & Dei gloria oppugnatur, & salutis nostrae certitudo atq; diuini verbi veritas in dubium vocari solet?
units.tr: Second, it is not unworthy of consideration that the apostles, the chosen instruments of Christ, were shamefully beaten in a most excellent and most holy cause, the defence of which they had undertaken at Christ's command. From this we may clearly gather how base and shameful is the error of those who think that evil and unjust afflictions are a proof or sign of a bad cause. Among these are those who today throw at us defeats and every kind of misfortune, and say that they show that we have gone astray in the matter of faith and religion. That such people lack sufficient sense and reason is evident from the fact that they cannot see what the poets of the heathen judged far more fairly. For that saying of Naso is well known: "I wish that he who thinks deeds must be judged by their outcome may lack success." For if the judgements of such people were to hold, we would find few or no ones among the most holy worshippers of God who would not themselves deserve to be condemned. Even a blind man can see that most of them were not only harassed by various rounds of labours and persecutions, but were also killed by the unjust hands of the most savage enemies. Nor are we to hope for better things today; the oracles of Christ, in which he warned us about the state of the last times, teach this abundantly. Therefore, whoever judge the cause of religion by the outcome and the successes of this age ought to be counted like the Jews and soldiers who, we read, offered vinegar to Christ hanging on the cross and said: "If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he wills him, for he said that he is the Son of God," etc. (Matthew 27). And indeed, what vinegar can be more bitter and sharp than such reproaches, by which the glory of God is assailed, and the certainty of our salvation as well as the truth of the divine Word are usually called into doubt?

units.la: Nec tamen idcirco temere ferri putabimus res mortalium, quando pios & religiosos Dei seruos affligi videmus. Sunt enim infinitae aliae causae, propter quas Deus ista euenire patitur, ut interim de occultis iudiciorum ipsius arcanis nihil dicamus. Ita enim carnis latentem improbitatem & ferociam interdum coherceat dominus, quae nisi coherceretur, magno suorum malo erumperet. Nec est quòd interdum coherceri dicamus eos, qui plus satis abiecti & humiles, nullum vnquam ferociae signum dedere. Nouit enim humani ingenij improbitatem Deus, & quibus rebus nobis opus sit, melius & certius, quàm nos ipsi perspectum habet. In tempore ergo castigat, & interdum nostram malitiam praeuenit, ne illa viribus augeatur, & incurabiles reddat, qui cum mundo condemnari mereamur. Praeterea fidem nostram ea ratione explorat, non quòd illum quicquam lateat, sed vt tum alijs exemplo simus, tum ipsi experiamur quanta adhuc in nobis infirmitas haeret, quamq; nobis Dei opem & gratiam adhuc sit opus. Accedit hìs, quòd mundo testatum facere vult, quàm illi displiceat peccatum, quando electorum suorum leuia delicta, imò latentem adhuc corruptionem tam seuere castigat. Et hucquidem Petrus respexit, cùm ait: Tempus est, vt incipiat iudicium à domo Dei. Quòd si primùm incipit à nobis, quis erit finis eorum, qui non credunt Dei euangelio? Et si iustus vix saluatur, impius & peccator vbi comparebit? 1. Pet. 4. Haec vt inam obseruarent, qui hodie ex nostris afflictionibus, quarum consyderatio vitae ipsorum emendationi seruire debebat, maioris impietatis & blasphemandi occasionem arripiunt.
units.tr: Yet we should not therefore think that the affairs of mortals are carried on rashly when we see the pious and religious servants of God afflicted. For there are countless other causes on account of which God allows these things to happen, not to mention the hidden secrets of his judgements. Thus the Lord sometimes restrains the hidden wickedness and fierceness of the flesh, which, unless it were restrained, would break out to the great harm of his people. Nor should we say that they are sometimes restrained who were most humble and abject and never gave any sign of fierceness. For God knows the wickedness of the human mind, and he understands better and more surely than we ourselves what we need. He therefore chastises in due time, and sometimes forestalls our malice, lest it be strengthened by its own power and make incurable those who, along with the world, deserve to be condemned. Besides, he tests our faith in this way, not because anything is hidden from him, but so that we may both be an example to others and experience ourselves how much weakness still clings to us, and how much we still need God's help and grace. In addition, he wishes to show the world how displeasing sin is to him, since he chastises so severely the slight offences, indeed the still hidden corruption, of his elect. Peter had this in mind when he said: "It is time for judgement to begin at the house of God. And if it begins first with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the gospel of God? And if the righteous is scarcely saved, where will the impious and the sinner appear?" (1 Peter 4). Would that those who today seize upon our afflictions as an occasion of greater impiety and blasphemy would observe these things, since the consideration of them ought to serve the amendment of their lives.

units.la: Tertiò minimè negligendum est, quòd ex mortis quidem periculo apostolos Christus eripit, permittit autem, vt ijdem ignominiose virgis caedantur. Quo exemplo securitatem animis nostris excutere vult, ne periculo aliquo exempti, nobis omnia tuta & tranquilla polliceamur: sed potius cogitemus, alia nos manere certamina, ad quae nos praeparari oporteat. Quae causa est, quòd pasim ad vigilantiam & preces assiduas nos dominus exhortatur. Nec exempla desunt, quibus docemur, quàm infelix sit carnalis securitatis & socordiae exitus.
units.tr: Thirdly, we must not neglect the fact that Christ rescued the apostles from the danger of death but allowed them to be shamefully beaten with rods. By this example he wants to shake our minds out of their complacency, so that, once freed from some danger, we do not promise ourselves that everything is safe and calm. Rather, let us think that other struggles await us, for which we ought to prepare ourselves. This is why the Lord everywhere urges us to watchfulness and constant prayer. Nor are examples lacking that teach us how unhappy the outcome of carnal security and sloth is.

units.la: Sed alterum quoq; videamus, quod præter Gamalielis consilium fecerunt Concilij impij assessores siue antistites.
