Renouarunt illi impiū edictum, cuius mentio precedenti cap. facta est, & præceperunt apostolis, ne posthac in nomine Iesu loquerentur, id est ne euangelium prædicarent. Est hoc ingens pertinacię argumentum, quæ impijs propria est. Cum enim in omnibus alijs studijs, per incertos & varios affectus abrepti, nimium leues & inconstantes sint, veritatis tamen odium constanter retinent, & pertinaciter vrgent quæcunq; ad huius oppugnationem facere arbitrantur. At non ofcitanter prætereunda est edicti siue decreti formula, qua ne in nomine Iesu loquantur, prohibetur. Iesu Christi ergo nomen impijs cumprimis exosum est. Potest alioqui cum pœnitentia tum remissionis peccatorum doctrinam mundus vtcunq; ferre. Nam & olim de pœnitentia & peccatorum expiationibus multa à gentium sapientibus tradita sunt, & hodie inter Papistas multa ac frequens est vtriusq; articuli tractatio. At quia quæ ab his dicuntur, ex humanæ rationis scrinio promanant, non difficulter illa admittunt, qui & ipsi ratione carnis duci consueuerunt. Sed quàm primum iuxta Christi præceptum in ipsius nomine tum pœnitentia tum peccatorum remissio prædicatur, intolerabilis videtur mundo doctrina hæc, eò quod ijs inimica sit, quæ humana prudentia in reli gione & salutis nostræ negotio excogitauit, ac quibus vt plurimum homines gloriari solet. Si enim pœnitentiam veram nobis Christus largiatur (vt superius Petrus docuit) nec nos illius in nobis fumus authores, iam collapsa iacet nostri arbitrij libertas, hominis vires extinctæ sunt, nec aliqua superest nostrorum meritorum gloria. Imo verum esse deprehenditur, quod Christus dicit: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Ioan. 15. Item illa Pauli: Deus est, qui in nobis operatur & velle & facere. Phil. 2. Item: Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Quòd si accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? 1. Cor. 4. Rursum, si in Christi nomine obtingit nobis peccatorum remissio, corruit iam nostrarum satisfactionum gloria, inutilis & vana est nostrorum operum fiducia, ridicula, imo impia & blasphema depre benditur sacrorum nundinatio, quam auari homines, qui religionem quæstum ducunt, inuexerunt. Adhæc, quando ea est peccatorum atrocitas, vt solius Christi sanguine expiari potuerint, facile pa tet, quàm serio & ardenti studio nobis incumbendum sit, ne à sanctitate & libertate, in quam Christi beneficio asserti sumus, denuo excidamus. Et hic aperiuntur Christianæ disciplinæ fontes, sine qua Christiani nominis professio damnationi potius quàm saluti seruit. Atqui ab omnibus istis pro inanito carnis ingenio homines abhorrent. Quapropter fieri nequit, vt Iesu Christi doctrinam patientibus animis & auribus ferant. Prodest autem hæc obseruauisse, ne ignaris horum suspecta sit euangelij doctrina, quam mundo tam inuisam & exosam esse cernimus.
units.tr: But let us also consider the other thing that the impious assessors, or leaders, of the council did, contrary to Gamaliel's advice. They renewed the impious edict mentioned in the preceding chapter, and they ordered the apostles not to speak any more in the name of Jesus, that is, not to preach the gospel. This is a great proof of obstinacy, which is proper to the impious. For while in all other pursuits they are carried away by uncertain and shifting passions and are too fickle and inconstant, they nonetheless hold fast to their hatred of the truth and stubbornly press whatever they think will serve its opposition. But the wording of the edict or decree, by which they are forbidden to speak in the name of Jesus, must not be passed over carelessly. Therefore the name of Jesus Christ is especially hateful to the impious. Otherwise the world can somehow bear the teaching of both repentance and the forgiveness of sins. For of old much was handed down about repentance and the expiation of sins by the wise men of the nations, and today among the Papists the treatment of both articles is abundant and frequent. But because what these men say comes from the chest of human reason, those who are themselves accustomed to be led by carnal reason do not find it hard to accept. But as soon as repentance and the forgiveness of sins are preached in Christ's name, according to his command, this teaching seems intolerable to the world. It is hostile to those things that human prudence has devised in religion and in the business of our salvation, and in which men usually take pride. For if Christ grants us true repentance (as Peter taught above), and we are not its authors in ourselves, then the liberty of our will lies fallen, the strength of man is extinguished, and no glory of our merits remains. Indeed, what Christ says proves true: "Without me you can do nothing" (John 15). Likewise that of Paul: "It is God who works in us both to will and to do" (Phil. 2). Likewise: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" (1 Cor. 4). Again, if forgiveness of sins comes to us in the name of Christ, the glory of our satisfactions collapses, our trust in our works is useless and vain, and the sale of sacred things, which greedy men who make a profit of religion have introduced, is found to be ridiculous, indeed impious and blasphemous. Besides, since the atrocity of sins is such that they could be expiated by the blood of Christ alone, it is easy to see with how serious and ardent a zeal we must labour not to fall back from the holiness and liberty into which Christ's benefit has restored us. Here the springs of Christian discipline are opened, without which the profession of the Christian name serves damnation rather than salvation. But men shrink from all these things because of the empty nature of the flesh. Therefore it cannot happen that they bear the teaching of Jesus Christ with patient minds and ears. It is useful, however, to have observed these things, so that the teaching of the gospel, which we see so hated and detested by the world, may not be suspect to the ignorant.

units.la: Transeamus vero ab impijs Christi hostibus ad electa ipsius organa, apostolos, & quales sese hi gesserint, videamus. Et de his quidem duo præcipuè Lucas narrat. Primum, quòd à Concilij conspectu abierint gaudentes, quòd digni habiti essent, qui pro nomine Christi contumelia afficerentur. Alterum, quòd nò cessarint quotidie cum in templo tum per domus singulas docere & prædicare Iesum Christum. De vtroq; autem nobis diligentius dicendum est, cum hæc multum ad nostram consolationem & institutionem faciant.
units.tr: Let us now pass from the impious enemies of Christ to his chosen instruments, the apostles, and see how they conducted themselves. Luke relates two things about them in particular. First, that they departed from the sight of the council rejoicing, because they had been judged worthy to be disgraced for the name of Christ. Second, that they did not cease daily, both in the temple and from house to house, to teach and preach Jesus Christ. We must speak about both more carefully, since these things contribute much to our consolation and instruction.

units.la: Gaudent, quòd virgis contumeliosè cæsi sint, apostoli. Nemo autem Stoicam in illis ἀπάθειαν fuisse suspicetur, aut ita mente captos, vt nullum inter honores & contumelias discrimen habere potuerint. Nam & homines fuisse constat, & humanis affectionibus obnoxios, quiq; sui nominis famam non semel ab improborum calumnijs asseruerunt. Gaudent verò, quòd propter Christi nomen ipsos ignominiam pati licuerat. Vbi duæ concurrunt non leues & vulgares gaudij causæ. Primò enim constat, peccatores esse omnes homines, & in sanctis quoq; carnis reliquias superesse, quibus abrepti non raro grauissimè delinquunt, vt diuinitus puniri mereantur. At ea est Dei bonitas & clementia, vt sub Christi fui & veritatis nomine ea immittat, quæ scelerum pœnæ esse debebant. Quod perinde est, ac si princeps furem, qui suspendium meruerat, infami morti subducat, & inter primos suæ aulæ nobiles in prima acie pro regni sui libertate & incolumitate pugnare velit. Et in horum quidem consideratione versatos esse apostolos verisimile est, quibus nondum excidisse potuerant, quæ partim ignobili fuga, partim abnegatione turpi ab ipsis fuerant designata, cum Christus caperetur. Et cum hucusq; nutare potuerint illorum animi, nunc infallibile habent Christi reconciliati argumentum, quando se crucis & afflictionum ipsius consortes factos esse vident. Accedit his altera causa ex Chrifti promissionibus, quibus cælestis regni gaudia ijs pollicetur, qui propter iustitiam ac nomen ipsius persecutionem sustinent. Ait enim: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam illorum est regnum cælorum. Beati estis, cum probra in vos iecerint homines, & insectati fuerint, & dixerint omne malum verbum aduersus vos, mentientes propter me. Gaudete & exultate, quoniam merces vestra multa est in cælis. Matth.5. Item: Vos estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis. Et ego dispono vobis, sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, vt edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo, &c. Luc.22. Quas promissiones, quia in Christo confirmatas & impletas se videbant, qui per crucem de omni potestate inferorum triumphauit, & per mortem patris sui ingressus est, non potuerunt non singulari gaudio perfundi, cum istis principijs ad promissam sibi cœlestis regni sortem se contendere viderent. Cæterum vt hæc apostolis gaudij causam præbuerunt: ita nobis quoq; in afflictionibus gaudium & lætitiam afferre debent. Omnibus enim Christianis hoc proprium esse Paulus testatur, quòd afflictionibus glorientur & gaudeant. Rom.5. Et sanè non vulgares causæ sunt, quæ hodie nos ad horum consyderationem excitare debebant, quando iam annis aliquot grassantes videmus in Germania Christi hostes, qui eo nomine nos crudelissimè persequuntur, quòd Christo potius quàm Antichristo obedire instituimus. Quorum victorijs & successibus multi sic offenduntur, vt veritatis doctrinam quasi suspectam habeant, & multos (prob dolor) circa fidem naufragium fecisse vidimus. At si nostra peccata ob oculos reuocemus, & in eius ingratitudinis consyderatione diligenter versemur, qua Germania iam annis aliquot ineffabile verbi Dei & Christiana libertatis beneficium partim neglexit, partim vero prodidit, & effræni vitæ licentia prophanauit, admirabilem in nos Dei bonitatem videbimus, qui propter verbi sui veritatem nos periclitari & filij sui martyres fieri vult, qui peccatis & sceleribus excidium meruimus. Et vt constet nos non propter scelera, sed solius religionis & veritatis causa periclitari & pati, eos nobis hostes immisit, quorum mores abunde cestantur, ipsos non peccatis nostris, sed sola veritatis confessione aduersus nos esse prouocatos. Quod ergo euidentius diuinæ bonitatis & gratiæ argumentum nobis exhiberi poterat, quàm quòd nobis datur, vt non modò credamus in Christum, verumetiam pro illius nomine patiamur? Hinc enim cum Paulo concludere licet: Si commorimur Christo, eidem conuiuemus. Si cum illo patimur, cum illo etiam regnabimus, &c. 2. Tim.2. Hanc Crucis nostræ gloriam quia multi non vident, vel à fidei professione turpiter deficiunt, vel impijs conuitijs fidem nobis exprobrant, & sub Christi cruce gementes contumeliosè proscindunt. Quotquot vero ista digne expendunt, non possunt non gloriari & exultare in Christo, cum illius stigmata in suis corporibus comparere cernunt. Vehementer ergo illorum stultitia deploranda est, quos Christi crux & afflictiones offendunt, ex quibus consolationis & gaudij argumenta sumere debebant.
units.tr: The apostles rejoice that they were beaten with rods in dishonour. Yet no one should suspect in them a Stoic apatheia [ἀπάθειαν], or think that they were so out of their minds that they could make no distinction between honours and insults. For it is agreed that they were men, subject to human feelings, and that they more than once defended the reputation of their name against the slanders of the wicked. But they rejoice because it had been granted them to suffer disgrace for Christ's name. Here two not slight or common causes of joy meet. For first, it is agreed that all men are sinners, and that remnants of the flesh remain even in the saints, and carried away by these they not infrequently sin grievously, so that they deserve to be punished by God. But such is God's goodness and clemency that, under the name of Christ and of the truth, he sends what ought to have been the penalties for their crimes. This is just as if a prince were to rescue from an infamous death a thief who had deserved the gallows, and wished him to fight in the front line for the liberty and safety of his kingdom, among the first nobles of his court. And it is likely that the apostles were occupied with the consideration of these things, since they could not yet have forgotten what had been marked out by them, partly by an ignominious flight and partly by a shameful denial, when Christ was seized. And although their minds could have wavered up to this point, they now have an infallible pledge of Christ's reconciliation, since they see themselves made partners in his cross and afflictions. To this is added another cause, drawn from Christ's promises, by which he promises the joys of the heavenly kingdom to those who endure persecution for righteousness and for his name. For he says: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven" (Matt. 5). Likewise: "You are those who have continued with me in my trials. And I appoint for you a kingdom, as my Father appointed for me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom," etc. (Luke 22). Since they saw these promises confirmed and fulfilled in Christ, who through the cross triumphed over all the power of the underworld and entered through his Father's death, they could not but be filled with singular joy, when they saw themselves, by these beginnings, striving toward the heavenly kingdom promised to them. Yet just as these things gave the apostles cause for joy, so they ought to bring us joy and gladness in our afflictions. For Paul testifies that it is proper to all Christians to glory and rejoice in afflictions (Rom. 5). And indeed the causes that ought to rouse us today to consider these things are not slight. For we see the enemies of Christ raging for some years now in Germany, who persecute us most cruelly on this account, that we have chosen to obey Christ rather than Antichrist. By their victories and successes many are so offended that they regard the doctrine of truth as suspect, and we have seen many (alas!) shipwrecked in the faith. But if we call our sins before our eyes and dwell diligently on the ingratitude by which Germany, for some years now, has partly neglected and partly betrayed the unspeakable benefit of God's word and Christian liberty, and has profaned it by an unbridled licence of life, we shall see the wonderful goodness of God towards us. He wishes us, for the sake of the truth of his word, to be endangered and to become martyrs of his Son, although we have deserved destruction by our sins and crimes. And so that it may be clear that we are endangered and suffer not because of our crimes but solely for the cause of religion and truth, he has set against us enemies whose morals are abundantly known, who have been provoked against us not by our sins but solely by our confession of the truth. What more evident proof of divine goodness and grace could be shown us than that it is given to us not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for his name? For from this we may with Paul conclude: "If we die with Christ, we shall also live with him. If we endure with him, we shall also reign with him," etc. (2 Tim. 2). Since many do not see this glory of our cross, they either shamefully fall away from the profession of faith, or they cast the faith in our teeth with impious reproaches, and, groaning under the cross of Christ, they mock it with insults. But all who weigh these things rightly cannot but glory and exult in Christ when they see his marks on their own bodies. Therefore the folly of those is to be deeply deplored, who are offended by Christ's cross and afflictions, from which they ought to draw arguments of consolation and joy.

units.la: Postremò de apostolis Lucas tradit, quòd nulla imperij decreti ratione habita, non cessarint docere & euangelizare in nomine Iesu Christi. Et id quidem publice in templo fecere, quam diu hoc ipsis permissum fuit. Vbi vero hostium tyrannus illos templo eiecit, in fidelium ædibus concliones saceras instituerunt. Nec enim certis locis alligata est Dei veritas, sed vbiuis doceri potest, modò ordinis & decori ratio habeatur, sicuti Paulus admonet. 1.Corinth.14. Reipsa ergo præstant, quod in Concilio protestati erant, Deo nimirum plus obediendum esse, quàm hominibus: & suo exemplo eos confutant, qui hodie in fidei & religionis causa magistratibus simpliciter obtemperandum esse contendunt. Quasi vero seipsum & cultum suum hominum libidini & arbitrio Deus subiecerit. At quia de hoc iam semel & iterum diximus, plura in præsenti dicere non attinet. Interim memorabilis est apostolorum constantia, qua diuinitus sibi commissam functionem, etiam plagis affecti, intrepidè obeunt. Confutatur hoc exemplo nostri seculi hominum ignauia, qui vbi aliquid passi sunt, omni officio sese iam defunctos esse putant, nec amplius vel labores vel pericula sustinere volunt. Posset equidem illorum rationibus aliquid tribui, si nobis liberum esset laborum nostrorum finem & limites constituere. Sed quia serui sumus, Dei voluntatem nos obseruare, & illum cum silentio expectare decet. Nec eos regno suo idoneos Christus dicit, qui à tergo respiciunt, sed qui in finem vsque perseuerant. Vide Luc.9. Matthæi 24. Adhæc Domini præceptum est, vt angustijs & periculis illius beneficio erepti, ipsum glorificemus. Psal.50. Quod ab ijs nequaquam fieri potest, qui suam stationem deserunt, & periculorum metu superati, otio & quieti suæ consulunt. Quapropter apostolorum
units.tr: Lastly, Luke records that the apostles, without regard to the decree of the authorities, did not cease to teach and preach the gospel in the name of Jesus Christ. They did this openly in the temple for as long as it was permitted them. But when the tyrant of their enemies drove them out of the temple, they set up holy assemblies in the houses of the faithful. For the truth of God is not bound to fixed places but can be taught anywhere, provided that order and decency are observed, as Paul admonishes, 1 Cor. 14. So in practice they do what they had declared before the Council, namely that God must be obeyed rather than men. By their example they refute those who today contend that in matters of faith and religion the magistrate must be obeyed without qualification, as if God had subjected himself and his worship to the whim and judgment of men. But since we have already said this once and again, there is no need to say more at present. Meanwhile the apostles' steadfastness is remarkable: once entrusted by God with their office, they undertake it fearlessly, even when they have been beaten. This example refutes the cowardice of the men of our age, who, once they have suffered something, think they have now discharged every duty and no longer wish to endure either labours or dangers. Their excuses might carry some weight if it were ours to set the limits and the end of our labours. But since we are servants, it becomes us to observe God's will and to wait for him in silence. Nor does Christ count fit for his kingdom those who look back, but those who persevere to the end. See Luke 9 and Matthew 24. Moreover, it is the Lord's command that, delivered from distress and dangers by his benefit, we glorify him, Ps. 50. This cannot be done by those who desert their post and, overcome by fear of danger, look only to their own leisure and quiet. Wherefore the apostles'

units.la: Apostolorum in docendo perseverantia. lorum constantiam singuli in sua vocatione imitentur, maxime vero, quibus ecclesiæ & verbi sui dispensationem Dominus commendauit: nec de illius ope diffidant, quem gregis sui curam iam olim tanta fide gessisse vident. Huic quicunq; fui ministerij rationem iustam reddere possunt, regni ipsius consortes fient. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Perseverance of the apostles in teaching. constancy should be imitated by each one in his own calling, and especially by those to whom the Lord has committed the stewardship of his Church and his Word. Let them not distrust his help, since they see that he himself once bore the care of his flock with such faith. Whoever can give a just account of his ministry to him will become a partner in his kingdom. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HOMILIA XL.
units.tr: HOMILY XL.

units.la: IN diebus autem illis crescente numero discipulorum, ortum est murmur Græcorum aduersus Hebræos, quòd despicerentur in ministerio quotidiano illorum viduæ. Duodecim itaq; conuocata multitudine discipulorum, dixerunt: Non conuenit, vt nos derelicto sermone Dei, ministremus mensis. Dispicite ergo, fratres, viros ex vobis testatæ probitatis septem, plenos spiritu sancto & sapientia, quos præficiemus huic negotio. Nos autem precationi & ministerio verbi incumbemus.
units.tr: In those days, as the number of the disciples grew, a murmuring arose among the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily ministration. So the Twelve called together the multitude of the disciples and said: "It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God in order to serve tables. Therefore, brethren, select from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint to this business. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word."

units.la: Xposuit hucusq; Diuus Lucas primitiuæ ecclesiæ originem, progressum, incrementa & formam: in quibus omnia secundum Dei verbum optimè instituta, & felicißimo successu inter horribiles persecutiones & diros hostium conatus administrata fuisse vidimus. Quia tamen generaliora sunt, quæ illic tractantur, nunc tandem ad specialiora diuinus scriptor descendit, ostendens vt quidam peculiari studio insignem operam nauarint in Christi regno proue-hendo. Inter quos cum primum locum Stephanus obtineat, qui ex Diaconorum numero fuit, quorum nulla antehac mentio facta est, commodißimè illius historiam ab illorum institutione orditur, & in præsenti quidem loco docet primùm, qua occasione Diaconorum ordo institutus fit: deinde quo ritu & modo primi illi ab Apostolis electi & ordinati sint, commemorat. Insunt verò narrationi huic non pauca, quorum hodie in ecclesia præcipuus vsus est, quare de singulis non indiligenter distendum erit.
units.tr: Up to this point St. Luke has set out the origin, progress, growth and form of the primitive Church, in which we have seen that everything was rightly ordered according to the word of God and carried on with the happiest success amid terrible persecutions and the savage attempts of enemies. Because what has been treated so far is rather general, the divine writer now comes down to more particular matters, showing how certain men, by a special zeal, have laboured remarkably to advance the kingdom of Christ. Among these, Stephen holds the first place. He was one of the deacons, a group not mentioned before this point. Quite fittingly, Luke begins his account of him from the institution of the deacons, and in this passage he first teaches on what occasion the order of deacons was instituted, and then relates the manner and rite by which the first men were chosen and ordained by the apostles. This narrative contains not a few things which are of especially common use in the Church today, so each of them will need to be examined with some care.

units.la: Occasionem siue causam noui in ecclesia ordinis creandi credentium multitudo, & quod in ea exortum fuit murmur, præbuit. Creuit enim & mirificè auctæ est illo tempore Christi ecclesia, & irriti plane fuerunt impiorum antistitum conatus, quibus illam opprimere studuerunt. Cæterum quia ex diuersis hominum generibus multitudo ista confluxerat, non diu consentire potuit. Ortum enim est murmur siue querela Græcorum aduersus Hebræos. Græcos verò dicit vel proselytos, qui ex genealissimo ad Iudaismum transierant, vel qui ex parentibus quidem Iudæis, sed in gentes dispersis, nati fuerant. Constat enim hoc tempore gentes in ecclesiæ communionem nondum admissas fuisse, cum longo post tempore Petro illud vitio detur, quòd euangelium Cornelio & familiæ ipsius, hominibus nimirum incircumcisis, prædicauisset, vt infra cap.11. patebit. Causam verò murmuri præbuit, quòd Græcorum viduæ negligerentur in ministerio quotidiano, id est, in distributione victus quæ inter credentes quotidie fiebat. Supra enim indicatum fuit, multos pecunias suas in publicum contulisse & Apostolorum administrationi subiecisse, qui ex illis vnicuiq;, prout opus erat, distribuebant. Ibi acci-dit, vt vel negotiorum multitudine obruti apostoli aliquos neglexerint, vel illi se neglectos esse putarint: id quod peregrini (suspicax hominum genus) præ aliis amarulenter conquesti sunt. Et ea res causa fuit, propter quam vsitata hucusq; administranda ecclesiæ forma & ratio nonnihil immutanda esse videretur. Sed priusquam de eo dicamus, quædam hic nobis obseruanda erunt.
units.tr: The occasion, or cause, for creating a new order in the Church was the great number of believers, and the murmuring that arose among them. For the Church of Christ grew and was marvellously increased at that time, and the attempts of the wicked chief priests, by which they tried to crush it, came to nothing. But since this multitude had gathered from many different kinds of people, it could not agree for long. A murmuring, or complaint, arose among the Grecians against the Hebrews. By "Grecians" he means either proselytes, who had passed over from the Gentiles to Judaism, or those who were born of Jewish parents but scattered among the nations. For it is clear that at this time the Gentiles had not yet been admitted to fellowship in the Church; long afterwards Peter was blamed for having preached the gospel to Cornelius and his household, that is, to uncircumcised men, as will become clear below in chapter 11. The cause of the murmuring was that the widows of the Grecians were being overlooked in the daily ministration, that is, in the daily distribution of food that took place among the believers. For it was said above that many had brought their money into common funds and placed it under the administration of the apostles, who distributed it to each person as need required. It happened that the apostles, either overwhelmed by the multitude of their business, neglected some people, or those people thought they had been neglected. The foreigners, a suspicious kind of people, complained of this more bitterly than the others. This matter was the reason why the form and manner of administering the Church, used until then, seemed to need some change. But before we speak of that, some things must be noted here.

units.la: Et primò quidem memorabile est, quòd primitiuam ecclesiam suis quoq;, vitijs laborauisse cernimus, quæ hactenus omni ex parte beata videri poterat. Nec leuia delicta sunt, sed horrenda, quæ hic commemorantur. Nam & nationum discrimina obseruant, quæ in Christo nulla sunt (In hoc enim non est vel Iudæus vel Græcus, vel Scytha vel Barbarus. Galat.3. Col.3.) & factionibus scissi, non iam occultas simultates exercent, sed animorum amarulentiam murmure iniquißimo produnt. Eò ipso igitur peccato primitiuam ecclesiam infectam esse videmus, propter quod sub Mose multa mil-
units.tr: And first, it is worth remembering that we see the primitive Church also suffering from its own faults, although until now it could seem to be blessed in every respect. The offences recorded here are not slight but dreadful. For they observe distinctions of nations, which do not exist in Christ (for "there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither Scythian nor barbarian," Gal. 3; Col. 3). Split into factions, they no longer carry on hidden enmities but reveal the bitterness of their minds by a most unjust murmuring. By this very sin, then, we see that the primitive Church was infected, on account of which, under Moses, many people are read to have been struck down in the wilderness by the terrible judgment of God (1 Cor. 10).

units.la: Causa propter quam electi diaconi.
units.tr: The reason why the deacons were chosen.

units.la: Primitiua ecclesia non caret vitijs. lia olim in deserto horribili Dei iudicio prostrata fuisse legantur. 1. Cor. 10. Accedit hùc ingratitudo detestabilis erga apostolos, quos infinitis alij negotijs occupatos esse non ignorabant, imò quos iam semel & iterum in carcerem abductos esse, & solos fere communis ecclesiae periculum sustinere viderant. Et cum scelus sit graue de benefactoribus & bene meritis aliquid finistre suspicari, illi murmurando ipsorum fidem in dubium vocant, & seditiose rebus nouis studeant: & quidem perfectionis tempore hoc faciunt, quando de mutua animorum coniunctione & charitatis studio omnes solicitos esse oportebat. Quo exemplo docemur, nunquam tam perfecte constitui posse ecclesiae formam, quin semper aliquid correctione dignum incidat: non quidem quòd ea diuini verbi vel obscuritas vel incertitudo sit, vt nihil ex eo perfecti instituì queat: sed quòd nostri ingenij corruptio nusquam non occasionem inuenit, qua sanctissimas Dei constitutiones conuellat. Stulta igitur & nimis insolens est illorum hominum confidentia, qui se supremam perfectionem assecutos esse putant, nec aliquem monitorem ferre norunt. Praeterea illorum quoq; arguitur temeritas, qui ab ecclesijs, in quibus nauos aliquos deprehendunt, secessionem faciunt, & schismatum authores sunt: quo vitio Anabaptistae vt plurimum laborant. At si horum ratio valere debet, nec primitiua ecclesia satis tuta foret, nec digna censeri potuisset, cui quis se coniungeret. Porrò cum Christus vnitatis studium maximè commendarit, facile cernitur, quo spiritu regantur, quibus leuiculum videtur ecclesiae vnitatem scindere. Vide de Ioan. 17. Item 1. Ioan. 2.
units.tr: The primitive Church is not free from faults. To this must be added the detestable ingratitude shown to the apostles, whom they knew to be occupied with countless other tasks, and whom they had seen more than once led away to prison and almost alone bearing the danger of the common Church. Since it is a grave crime to entertain any sinister suspicion of benefactors and those who have deserved well, these people, by murmuring, call the apostles' faithfulness into doubt and seditiously aim at new arrangements. And they do this at a time when everyone ought to have been concerned for mutual fellowship of minds and the pursuit of love. From this example we are taught that the form of the Church can never be set up so perfectly that something worthy of correction does not still arise. This is not because the word of God is so obscure or uncertain that nothing perfect can be established from it, but because the corruption of our nature finds an occasion everywhere to overturn the most holy ordinances of God. Foolish and far too arrogant, therefore, is the confidence of those men who think they have attained supreme perfection and know how to bear no one as a monitor. Besides, the rashness of those is also condemned who withdraw from churches in which they detect some faults, and become the authors of schisms; the Anabaptists in particular are very often troubled by this vice. But if their reasoning ought to hold, neither the primitive Church would have been safe enough, nor could it have been deemed worthy of anyone joining himself to it. Moreover, since Christ especially commended the pursuit of unity, it is easy to see by what spirit those are ruled who think it a trifle to split the unity of the Church (see John 17; also 1 John 2).

units.la: Deinde obseruandum venit, quòd crescente Christianorum numero murmur illud obortum fuisse dicitur: quando nimirum Dei gratiam agnoscere, & vnitati quàm maximè studere debebant. Sed vulgare hoc est, vt vbi multitudo est, ibi quoq; murmur fit & confusio, eò quòd impossibile est omnium votis satisfacere in tanta animorum & desideriorum varietate. Et natura sic comparatum est, vt vndiquaq; quiritandi occasionem arripiant, qui sibi aliquid deesse sentiunt. Expertus hoc est fidelis ille Dei seruus, Moses, quem non semel lapidare conati sunt Israelitae, si quando ollarum Ægypti memoria animis illorum denuò occurrebat. Tale quid nunc apostoli sentiunt, qui tamen in rebus administrandis haud dubiè summa fide & studio indefesso vsi sunt. Nemo igitur mirum & insolens esse putet, si hodie quoq; in tanta, quae passim cernitur, pauperum & egentium multitudine, murmura & querelae acerbae exaudiantur: quod vt vbiq; aliàs, ita maximè in ptochotrophijs & xenodochijs, locisq; similibus fieri consueuit. Nam vt nullae aliae causae accedant, paupertas per se querula est. Quod vitium vel hoc nomine veniam meretur, quòd multae indies causae incidunt, quae mentes alioqui constantissimas permouere possunt. Hoc potius sibi cauendum ducant, quibus pauperum cura commissa est, ne illis iustas quiritandi & murmurandi causas praebeant, dum vel maligne distribuunt necessaria, vel quae pauperibus alendis impendi debebant, impiè suffurantur. Nec enim leue aut simplex est peccatum, quod hic committitur. Nam & immani sacrilegio sese polluunt, & spiritui sancto mentiuntur, simulq; pauperibus non parui peccati authores sunt, dum impatientiae causas illis praebent, qui potius consolationem merebantur. Moneat hos, quòd primitiua ecclesia non aliis turbis vexata est, quàm quae ex publicorum bonorum administratione vel iniqua vel negligenti exortae sunt. Hic enim Iudam proditorem impegisse scriptura docet. Ioan. 12. Ad eundem scopu Ananiam & Sapphiram salutis naufragium fecisse, supra vidimus. Et nunc murmuris seditio occasionem non aliunde Graeci arripiunt, quàm quòd suas viduas in publica bonorum ecclesiae distributione negligi putarent. Quae exempla ideo tam diligenter conscribi voluit spiritus sanctus, vt notum facerent quos scopulos cumprimis vitare debeant, qui Christiani nominis professione non inutiliter gloriari, sed ipsis factis respondere instituerunt. Minimè enim decet, vt ecclesiae bona maligne dispensent, qui sua pro Christi nomine vel iam reliquerunt, vel relinquere debent, si ita ferat necessitas. Et absurdum est, nulloq; supplicio satis expiandum facinus, ea suffurari, quae alij in pauperum subuentionem contulerunt, quorum alimoniae nostra omnia impendere iubemur. Sed vtinam tam facile esset hoc loco corrigere nostri seculi mores, quàm merito illos deploramus.
units.tr: Next, it should be observed that this murmuring is said to have arisen when the number of Christians was growing, that is, at a time when they ought to have been acknowledging the grace of God and pursuing unity as much as possible. But it is a common thing that where there is a multitude, there also arise murmuring and confusion, because it is impossible to satisfy everyone's wishes amid such variety of minds and desires. And by nature it is so arranged that those who feel that something is lacking seize on every occasion for complaining. The faithful servant of God, Moses, experienced this, whom the Israelites more than once tried to stone whenever the memory of the pots of Egypt came back to their minds. Something of the same kind the apostles now experience, although in administering these matters they undoubtedly used the greatest faithfulness and tireless diligence. Let no one, therefore, think it strange or unusual if even today, in such a great multitude of poor and needy people as is seen everywhere, murmurings and bitter complaints are heard. This is customary everywhere, but especially in almshouses, hospices and similar places. For even if no other causes were added, poverty of itself is querulous. This fault deserves pardon for this reason alone, that daily there arise many causes which can move even the most steadfast minds. Rather, those to whom the care of the poor has been entrusted should take this as a warning to themselves, lest they give the poor just grounds for complaining and murmuring, whether by distributing necessities meanly, or by impiously stealing what ought to have been spent on feeding the poor. For the sin committed here is neither slight nor simple. Such men both defile themselves with monstrous sacrilege and lie to the Holy Spirit, and at the same time they become authors of no small sin against the poor, while they give them causes of impatience who ought rather to have deserved comfort. Let them be warned that the primitive Church was troubled by no other storms than those which arose from the unjust or negligent administration of public goods. For Scripture teaches that Judas the traitor fell into this (John 12). Ananias and Sapphira suffered shipwreck of their salvation on the same rock, as we saw above. And now the sedition of murmuring gives the Grecians their occasion for nothing else than that they thought their widows were being overlooked in the public distribution of the goods of the Church. The Holy Spirit wanted these examples to be recorded so carefully so that they might make known which rocks especially ought to be avoided by those who have not been content to glory uselessly in the profession of the Christian name, but have resolved to answer with their deeds. For it is by no means fitting that those who have already left, or ought to leave if necessity so requires, their own possessions for the name of Christ should wickedly dispense the goods of the Church. And it is absurd that anyone should steal, a crime that no punishment is enough to atone for, those things which others have contributed for the relief of the poor, and on whose support we are commanded to spend everything we have. But would that it were as easy to correct the morals of our own age in this place as we rightly lament them.

units.la: Quid autem oborto murmure faciunt apostoli? Num maledictis eos incesserunt, quos de iniqua dispensatione contra se murmurare audiunt? Num ingratos murmuratores deserunt, & omnem administrandae ecclesiae curam indignabundi abijciunt? Num priuata authoritate nouam ecclesiae formam obtrudunt? Vel quod charitatis speciem repraesentasset, num dissimulant, & mo-tas vas nectant, quaß dißimulando & cunctando malum hoc sopiri possit? At nihil horum Lucas commemorat. Nec enim maledictis animos plus satis exacerbatos magis irritandos esse vident: nec ecclesiæ curam à Christo ipsis creditam, propter paucos querulos deserere possunt: nec clero siue hæreditati domini quicquam priuata authoritate prascribunt, quasi tyrannidem affectent: nec dissimulandum putant, aut ignauiter negligendum non obscure glíscens incendium. Sed in tempore remedium adhibent, & vniuersa multitudine conuocata, publice & amice de constituenda meliori ecclesia forma consultant. Est autem exemplum hoc omnibus seculis non obseruandum modo, verumetiam imitandum summo studio, siquidem ecclesiam saluam & incolumem volumus. Nam nec paucorum hominum ea debet tolerari licentia, vt pro suo arbitrio quiduis agant, & ecclesiæ domini superbè dominentur (1. Pet. 5. cap.) nec dissimulari debent aperta vitia, ea cumprimis, quæ murmurus & querelarum siue dissidiorum seminaria sunt. Nam & vires colligunt diutina mora, serpuntq; longius & animos inflammant, vt incurabile malum fiat, quod circa initium facilè tolli potuisset. Fit etiam, vt temerarijs & seditiosis occasio detur, qua ipsi ecclesiæ dominium inuadere & pro sua libidine nouas reformationes instituere conantur. Debebant hoc obseruare, qui hodie falsa apostolorum successione gloriantur, & primi ecclesiæ antistites haberi volunt, quibus intolerabile videtur si sanctì magistratus ecclesiarum suarum reformationem instituant: cum ipsos totius orbis querela iam multis seculis non potuerint excitare, vt manifestos & horribiles abusus tollerent, quorum ipsi tum authores tum patroni iam nimis diu fuerunt. Sed & nobis hoc obseruandum erat, qui euangelij nomine gloriamur, & ecclesias reformauisse videri volumus. Quis enim tam vecors est, qui non audiat hodie simili de causa murmurantes & quiritantes pauperes? Et vtinam non iustior multò esset illorum querela, quàm illorum fuit, de quibus hic agitur. Nam plerisque in locis à magistratibus diripiuntur ecclesiæ bona, luxu & fastu dilapidantur ab ijs, qui nec ecclesijs ministrant, nec euangelicæ veritatis studio tenentur: egentibus interim & extrema inopia fameque laborantibus tum pauperibus, quos ecclesiæ commendatissimos esse voluit Christus (Matthæi vigesimo sexto capite) tum ecclesiarum ministrũ. Vt nihil interim de studiorum neglectu & scholarum dissipatione & neglecta morum disciplina diçam, & infinitis alijs malis, quæ omnia impiæ illi ecclesiarum & collegiorum direptioni accepta ferri debent. Vident hæc cordati multi, & ingemiscunt. Arguunt hæc non pauci ecclesiarum fidi pastores, & emendationem flagitant. Multi palàm conquerantur, nec desunt qui seditioso murmure animorum indignationem testantur. Quid vero omnibus istis proficitur? Sunt qui minis & atrocibus edictis, vel etiam pœnis murmuratores eiusmodi cohercendos putent. Et qui optimi videntur, supina & ocistanti ignauia omne hoc negligunt. Interim nemo de reformatione seriò cogitat, quia nemo ex bonorum ecclesiasticorum possessione vult deijci. Sed inueniet viam aliquam dominus, & horribili iudicio ignauos illos expergefaciet, quos nulla vel verbi diuini admonitiones, vel pauperum querela excitare possunt.
units.tr: But what do the apostles do when the murmuring arises? Do they attack with insults those whom they hear complaining against them about an unfair distribution? Do they abandon the ungrateful grumblers and indignantly throw off all care of governing the Church? Do they impose a new form on the Church by private authority? Or, since it would have looked like charity, do they pretend not to notice and weave vain schemes, as if this evil could be lulled by pretending and delaying? Luke records none of this. They see that minds already too inflamed with insults are not to be provoked further, nor can they desert the care of the Church, which Christ entrusted to them, on account of a few complainers. Nor do they think they should prescribe anything by private authority over the clergy or the Lord's inheritance, as if they were aiming at tyranny. Nor do they think they should overlook or carelessly neglect a fire that is openly smouldering. Instead they apply a remedy in time: they call the whole multitude together and consult publicly and amicably about setting up a better form for the Church. This example ought not only to be observed in every age, but also imitated with the utmost zeal, if we want the Church to be safe and sound. For the licence of a few men should not be tolerated, so that they do whatever they like by their own judgement and lord it over the Church's ministry (1 Pet. 5), nor should open vices be overlooked, especially those which are seedbeds of grumbling, complaints and dissensions. For they gather strength through long delay, creep further and inflame minds, so that what could easily have been removed at the beginning becomes an incurable evil. It also happens that rash and seditious men are given an opportunity to seize control of the Church and attempt to institute new reforms at their own pleasure. Those who today boast of a false succession from the apostles, and wish to be regarded as the first leaders of the Church, ought to have observed this. To them it seems intolerable if holy magistrates institute a reform of their churches, although for many centuries the complaints of the whole world have not been able to move them to remove manifest and horrible abuses, of which they themselves have for far too long been both the authors and the patrons. But we too ought to observe this, we who glory in the name of the gospel and want to seem to have reformed the churches. For who is so mad as not to hear the poor murmuring and complaining today for a similar reason? And would that their complaint were not far more just than that of those of whom we are speaking here! For in most places the goods of the Church are plundered by the magistrates, and squandered in luxury and pride by men who neither minister to the churches nor are devoted to the study of evangelical truth, while meanwhile the poor, whom Christ wished to be most commended to the Church (Matthew 26), and the ministers of the Church, labour in utter want and famine. I say nothing for now of the neglect of studies, the breaking up of schools, the neglected discipline of morals, and the endless other evils, all of which must be credited to that impious plundering of churches and colleges. Many thoughtful people see these things and groan. Not a few faithful ministers of the churches point them out and demand a remedy. Many complain openly, and there are those who bear witness to their indignation with seditious murmuring. But what comes of all this? Some think that murmurers of this kind should be restrained with threats, harsh edicts, or even punishments. And those who seem best neglect all this with idle and lazy inactivity. Meanwhile no one seriously thinks about reform, because no one wants to be thrown out of the possession of ecclesiastical goods. But the Lord will find some way, and with a dreadful judgement he will rouse those idle men whom neither the admonitions of the divine Word nor the complaints of the poor can stir.

units.la: Caeterum quia magni momenti res est, de qua hic agitur, apostolorum orationem quoq; Lucas recitat, qua illi causam hanc toti ecclesiæ excutiendam proposuerunt. Est ea deliberatiui generis, eiusq; status est, creandos esse diaconos, quibus tum pecuniæ publicæ dispensatio, tum pauperum cura & subuentio committatur. Sunt autem orationis partes tres. Prima breuem excusationem habet, qua & præsentis instituti rationem reddunt, & crimen, quod à murmuratoribus intendebatur, modestè diluunt, ita vt in seipsos omnem culpam recipiant, ne qua restet suspicionum exprobrationumue occasio. Aiunt enim: Non conuenit, vt nos derelicto sermone Dei, ministremus mensis. Ratio est ab impossibili. Ostendunt enim, fieri non posse, vt vtriq; muneri, quod haḃtenus administrarant, sufficiant, quapropter necessarium sit, vt alterutrum in alios transferatur. Simul verò admonent, neminem hoc iniquius ferre debere, si quid peccatum sit ab ijs, qui tanta negotiorum mole bucusq; occupati fuerant. Perinde enim est, ac si dicerent: Quia ad nos delata fuerunt pecuniæ, quas ecclesiæ conseratas esse voluerunt pij & benefici quidam, illarum dispensationem non inuiti suscepimus, ne aliqua in re ecclesiæ commodo deesse videremur. At experientia discimus non potuisse nos simul tum docendi officio tum œconomiæ huic satisfacere, & fatemur inter tot tantasq; occupationes aliquid à nobis neglectum esse. Quare aut huic aut illi officio nosmetipsos addicere oportet. At docendi munus intermittere non possumus, cum illud nobis Christus ipse commendarit, nosq; rerum abs se gestarum testes esse voluerit. Alterum ergo illud in alios transferri oportet, qui mensis ministrent, id est, qui eorum curam suscipiant, quæ pauperum fubuentioni & alimoniæ seruiunt.
units.tr: Moreover, since the matter under discussion is of great importance, Luke also recites the speech of the apostles, by which they proposed that this cause be examined by the whole Church. It is of the deliberative kind, and its issue is that deacons are to be appointed, to whom the administration of public money and the care and relief of the poor are to be entrusted. The speech has three parts. The first contains a brief excuse, by which they both give the reason for the present plan and modestly dispel the accusation brought by the murmurers, so that they take all the blame upon themselves and no occasion for suspicion or reproach remains. For they say: "It is not right that we, leaving the word of God, should serve tables." The reasoning is from impossibility. For they show that it is impossible for them to be equal to both duties they have hitherto carried out, and so it is necessary that one of them be transferred to others. At the same time they advise that no one should take it too unfairly if something has been neglected by men who have hitherto been so occupied with such a heavy load of business. It is as if they said: "Because money was brought to us, which certain pious and generous people wished to be contributed to the Church, we took up its distribution not unwillingly, lest we should seem to be lacking in any respect for the Church's advantage. But from experience we learn that we could not at once satisfy both the duty of teaching and this economy, and we admit that amid so many and such great occupations something has been neglected by us. Therefore we must devote ourselves either to this duty or to that one. But we cannot give up the office of teaching, since Christ himself has entrusted it to us and wished us to be witnesses of the things he has done. So the other task must be transferred to others, who will serve at tables, that is, who will take up the care of those things which serve the relief and sustenance of the poor."

units.la: Docemur prima huius relationis parte, quanta fit euangelij & verbi diuini dignitas, cum huius prædicationem apostoli œconomiæ ecclesiastica & pauperum fubuentioni, rei nimirum sanctissimæ & cumprimis necessariæ, præferant. Nec ignorauerunt ab euangelij ministris pauperes nullo modo negligi debere, cum illorum curam Paulo & Barnabæ postea tam ferio commendarint. Galat. 2. At vbi eò deuentum est, vt vel mensarum vel verbi miniflerium intermitti oporteat, indignifsimû factu putant, vt verbi prædicatio ab ipsis hoc prætextu negligatur. Quia maior animarum, quæ verbo Dei aluntur, quàm corporum & corporalis victus cura haberi debet, quemadmodum Christus ipse admonet: Quærite ante omnia regnum Dei, &c. Matth. 6. Quid quòd ipse Christus verbi fui studium omnibus aliis officijs, quæ ipsi olim impendi potuerunt, præferri? Mulieri enim exclamanti, Beatus venter, qui te portauit, & beata vbera quæ suxisti, respondet: Quin imò beati, qui audiunt ser monem Dei, & custodiunt illum. Luc. 11. Quò & referri debet, quæ apud eundem euangelistam habetur Marthæ & Mariæ, fororum Lazari, biftoria. Luc. 10. Et Paulus maiorem euangelij quàm Sacramentorum curam sibi habendam esse putauit, quando testatur, fe non ad baptizandum, sed euangelizandum missum esse. 1. Cor. 1. Adhæc non obscure in præsenti docent apostoli, tantam esse huius muneris excellentiam & grauitatem, vt peculiarem hominem, omnibus aliis curis & laboribus liberatum, requirat. Quæ causa est, quòd Christus apostolos mundi huius imperijs & regnorum administratione occupari noluit. Matth. 20. Luc. 22. Peccatur ergo hic vehementer à personatis nostri seculi episcopis, qui quiduis potius quàm prædicandi munus subire volunt, & in aulis regum, imò castris etiam frequentius quàm in suggestu conspiciuntur, cum præcipuam in episcopo virtutem hanc Paulus esse velit, vt docendi facultate fit præditus. 1. Tim. 3. Sed vtinam ab illis solis peccaretur, & non inter nos haberentur, qui vel opum studio immodico, vel vanissimis rebus, computationibus nimirum, aut venationi & aucupio, ac interdum parum honestis exercitijs, maximam temporis partem, quæ lectioni & doctrinæ debebatur, impendunt. Experientur illi aliquando horribile Dei iudicium, quando ab ipsorum manibus requiretur illorum sanguis, qui ipsorum negligentia perierût. Ezech. 3. & 33. Matth. 24.
units.tr: From the first part of this statement we are taught how great is the dignity of the gospel and of the divine Word, since the apostles place the preaching of it above ecclesiastical economy and the relief of the poor, a matter most holy and especially necessary. Nor did they overlook that the poor must in no way be neglected by the ministers of the gospel, since they later commended their care so earnestly to Paul and Barnabas (Galatians 2). But when it comes to the point that either the ministry of tables or the ministry of the Word must be dropped, they think it most unworthy that the preaching of the Word should be neglected by them on this pretext. Because the care of souls, which are nourished by the Word of God, ought to be held more important than the care of bodies and bodily sustenance, as Christ himself warns: "Seek first the kingdom of God," etc. (Matthew 6). What of the fact that Christ himself preferred zeal for his Word to all the other duties which could once have been rendered to him? For when a woman cried out, "Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you," he replied: "Yes, rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it" (Luke 11). To this also should be referred the story in the same evangelist of Martha and Mary, the sisters of Lazarus (Luke 10). And Paul thought that he should have a greater care for the gospel than for the sacraments, when he testifies that he was sent not to baptize but to preach the gospel (1 Cor. 1). Besides, in the present passage the apostles clearly teach that the excellence and weight of this office is so great that it requires a particular man, freed from all other cares and labours. This is why Christ did not want the apostles to be occupied with the administration of the empires and kingdoms of this world (Matthew 20; Luke 22). Therefore those bishops of our age who wear only the mask of office sin grievously here: they want to undertake anything rather than the duty of preaching, and they are seen more often in the courts of kings, indeed even in camps, than in the pulpit, although Paul wants this to be the chief virtue in a bishop, that he be endowed with the ability to teach (1 Tim. 3). But would that only those men sinned, and that others were not counted among us who spend the greatest part of their time, which was owed to reading and teaching, on an immoderate pursuit of wealth, or on the most vain things, such as reckoning, hunting and fowling, and sometimes on rather dishonourable pastimes! Those men will one day experience the dreadful judgement of God, when their blood will be required at their hands, the blood of those who perished through their negligence (Ezek. 3 and 33; Matthew 24).

units.la: Secunda parte orationis, quid factu opus fit docent, vt afflictis ecclesiæ rebus consulatur, cum aiunt: Dispicite ergo ex vobis viros testatæ probitatis septem, plenos spiritu sancto, & sapientia, quos præficiemus huic negotio. Diaconos siue dispensatores constituendos esse censent, ad quos hæc cura peculiariter pertinere debeat. Et septem quidem eligi volunt, eò quòd illum numerum pro illorum temporum ratione sufficere putarent, non quòd omnes ecclesias eidem numero alligatas esse oporteat. Quamuis vile hoc esse videatur, ne paucioribus publicarum opum cura credatur: quia fere fit, vt tales vel ferocius insolescant, vel priuatis commodis prospiciant, nisi aliorum imperio & authoritate coherceantur. Et si nihil horum fiat, attamen pauciores citius in suspicionem veniunt, quàm si plures hoc munus inter se distribuant. At ne electione aberretur, diligenter quales ordinari debeant, exponunt. Primò ex fidelium cœtu eligi volunt. Nemo igitur admittendus, qui fidei aduersarius, aut fidem à fide alienus fuerit. Deinde testatæ probitatis viros requirunt, vt nimirū publicæ opes illis tuto committi possint. Tertiò spiritu sancto plenos postulant, nō eos, qui affectibus turpissimis toti regantur. Postremò sapientiæ, id est, rerum gerendarum peritiæ & dexteritatis rationem haberi volunt, cum fine hac non possit legitima exerceri opum eiusmodi dispensatio. His coniunge, quæ de Diaconis Paulus tradit, & quid hodie obseruandum fit, facile constabit. 1. Tim. 3. Sed vt alibi, ita hic etiam turpissimè aberratur. Apud Papistas enim inane diaconorum nomen remansit. At qui euangelici dicuntur, cum ecclesiarum opes vel ærario publico vendicent, vel in alios vsus maximam illarum partem conuertant, fere eos dispensatores constituunt, qui à fide alieni, verbum Dei eiusq; ministros summo odio persequuntur, quiq; vbi sua bona dilapidarunt, ecclesiæ opibus ditescere studeant, & quos vino potius quàm spiritu sancto plenos esse, & non tam sapientiæ spiritu quàm impotentissimis esse- ctibus regi videas. Peccant hi quidem grauissime, sed non minus peccant, quorum suffragijs talis creantur. Nam hos alienis peccatis communicare, Paulus testatur. 1. Tim. 5. Tertia & postrema parte, quid ipsi facturi sint, repetunt, ne quis illos otium affectare suspicaretur. Nos autem (dicunt) precationi & ministerio verbi incumbemus. Incumbendi verbo ardens & serium studium exprimunt, quo verbi ministris opus est, siquidem in suo munere cum fructu aliquo versari velint. Duobus vero officijs praecipuas ecclesiastici ministerij partes comprehendunt. Primas in hoc doctrina tenet. Quae quia ex ore Dei desumi debet, diligenti scripturae sacrae, in qua nobis Deus loquitur, studio opus est. Ideo Paulus Timotheum lectioni iubet intendere. 1. Tim. 4. Rursum quia eadem ad aedificationem tendere debet, probe curandum est, ut rite secetur verbum Dei, ut singulorum tum institutioni cum consolationi seruiat. Caeterum quia inane est ministri studium, nisi dominus incrementum dederit (1. Cor. 3.) assiduis precibus ille fatigandus est, ut auditorum mentes suo spiritu imbuere & trahere dignetur. Coniunxit vtrunq; Christus dominus, cuius exemplum apostoli hoc loco sibi imitandum proponunt. Imitentur idem quotquot ecclesijs seruiunt, nec inaniter sese laboraturos sentient. Aderit enim illorum studijs sui numinis gratia verus & summus ille ecclesiae Rex, Iesus Christus, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The second part of the prayer teaches what must be done to relieve the afflicted affairs of the Church, when they say: "Look out therefore among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business" (Acts 6:3). They judge that deacons, or stewards, should be appointed, to whom this care should belong in particular. They wish seven to be chosen, not because every church must be bound to that number, but because they thought it sufficient for the circumstances of those times. It may seem unwise to entrust the care of public resources to fewer people, because such men are apt either to grow more arrogant or to look after their own advantage, unless they are restrained by the command and authority of others. Yet even if none of this happens, fewer officers quickly fall under suspicion, whereas if several share the office among themselves, that suspicion is less likely. So that they may not go wrong in the choosing, they explain carefully what kind of men ought to be ordained. First, they want them chosen from the assembly of believers. Therefore no one should be admitted who is an enemy of the faith or estranged from the faith. Next, they require men of proven honesty, so that the public resources may be safely committed to them. Third, they demand men full of the Holy Spirit, not those who are wholly governed by the most shameful passions. Last, they want them to have wisdom, that is, skill and dexterity in managing affairs, since without this the lawful administration of such funds cannot be carried out. Add to these what Paul teaches about deacons (1 Tim. 3), and what must be observed today will easily be made plain. But, as elsewhere, so here too the error is most shameful. Among the Papists the empty name of deacons has remained. Yet those who are called evangelical, although they claim the resources of the churches either for the public treasury or convert the greater part of them to other uses, generally appoint as stewards men who are estranged from the faith, who persecute with the greatest hatred the Word of God and its ministers, who, once they have squandered their own goods, eagerly seek to grow rich from the resources of the Church, and whom you may see to be full of wine rather than of the Holy Spirit, and ruled not so much by the spirit of wisdom as by the most unbridled passions. These men certainly sin most gravely, but no less sin those by whose votes such men are created. For Paul testifies that these share in the sins of others (1 Tim. 5). In the third and last part, they repeat what they themselves will do, lest anyone suspect them of seeking leisure. "But we," they say, "will give ourselves continually to prayer and to the ministry of the Word." They express an ardent and earnest zeal for the Word, which the ministers of the Word need, if they wish to be occupied with any fruit in their office. Indeed, they comprehend the chief parts of the ecclesiastical ministry under two duties. Doctrine holds the first place in this. Since it must be drawn from the mouth of God, it needs diligent study of holy Scripture, in which God speaks to us. Therefore Paul bids Timothy to give attention to reading (1 Tim. 4). Again, since teaching must aim at edification, care must be taken that the Word of God be rightly divided, so that it serves both the instruction and the comfort of each person. Moreover, since the minister's study is empty unless the Lord gives the increase (1 Cor. 3), he must be wearied with constant prayers, that the Lord may deign to imbue and draw the minds of his hearers with his Spirit. Christ the Lord joined these two together, and the apostles set his example before themselves here to be imitated. Let all who serve the churches imitate it likewise, and they will not feel that their labours are in vain. For the grace of his divine power, the true and supreme King of the Church, Jesus Christ, will be present with their studies, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLI.

units.la: Et placuit hic sermo coram tota multitudine: & elegerunt Stephanum, virum plenum fide & spiritu sancto, & Philippum, & Prochorum, & Nicanorem, & Timonem, & Parmenam, & Nicolaum proselytum Antiochenum. Hos statuerunt coram apostolis, & cum orassent, imposuerunt eis manus. Et sermo Dei crescebat, & multiplicabatur valde numerus discipulorum Hierosolymis, multaque turba sacerdotum obediebat fidei.
units.tr: And this speech pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles, and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. And the word of God increased, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great crowd of priests obeyed the faith.

units.la: Quemadmodum optimam perfectissimamq; primitiuae ecclesiae formam Lucas descripsit: ita vitium quoque, quod in illa obortum fuit, magna diligentia commemorat. Origo eius circa ecclesiae opes extitit, & multipliciter peccatum fuisse nuper vidimus. Errarunt ignorantia & negotiorum multitudine circumuenti apostoli, cum duobus simul officijs sufficere non possent. Sed leniculum errorem atrox flagitium sequitur. Simultatum enim femina quaedam concipiunt, & murmuratores fiunt: ut longe alia nunc ecclesiae facies fit, quam quae hactenus fuerat, quando vnam & eandem omnium animam atq; voluntatem fuisse dixit. Voluit autem de his nos admoneri spiritus sanctus, ne qui tanquam re insolita offendantur, si quos naevos aut vitia in ecclesijs oriri videant. Quid enim tam humanum est, quam falli & errare? De correctione ergo potius cogitandum, ne longius serpant vitia, aut dilatione incurabilia fiant. Obseruarunt hoc apostoli, qui multitudine convocata modestissime sese excusant, simulq; quid factu opus sit, ingenue consulunt. Is vero consilij ipso rum finis & scopus est, ut diaconi sive dispensatores eligantur, quibus cum publicorum bonorum tum pauperum ecclesiae cura committatur: & ne in electione aberretur, qui & quales eligi debeant, diligenter admonent. Sequitur ergo, quid factum sit, vbi apostolorum consilium ecclesiae totius auctoritas comprobauit. Est haec altera historia praesentis pars, qua diaconorum ecclesiae electio describitur, in cuius consyderatione nos non officiter versari conuenit, ut quid hodie nos facere deceat, intelligamus.
units.tr: As Luke has described the best and most perfect form of the primitive Church, so he also records with great care the fault that arose within it. Its origin lay in the Church's wealth, and we have just seen that the sin spread in many ways. The apostles, beset by ignorance and the multitude of their business, went astray, since they could not manage two offices at once. But a small error was followed by a shameful crime: certain women began to nurse grudges and became murmurers. So the face of the Church is now quite different from what it was before, when Luke said that all had one and the same soul and will. The Holy Spirit wished us to be warned of these things, so that people would not be offended, as if at something unusual, when they see spots or faults arise in the churches. For what is so human as to be deceived and to err? We should therefore think rather about correction, lest the faults creep further or, by delay, become incurable. The apostles observed this: having called the multitude together, they excuse themselves very modestly, and at the same time frankly ask what needs to be done. The aim and purpose of their counsel is that deacons, or stewards, should be chosen, to whom the care both of the Church's public goods and of the poor should be committed; and, lest they go wrong in the choice, they carefully instruct who and of what kind should be chosen. It follows, then, what was done once the authority of the whole Church had approved the counsel of the apostles. This is the second part of the present history, in which the choosing of the Church's deacons is described; in considering it we ought not to be idle, so that we may understand what it becomes us to do today.

units.la: Principio autem, a quibus diaconorum electio facta fit, docet. Placuit (inquit) hic sermo toti multitudini, & elegerunt Stephanum, &c. Totius ergo ecclesiae consensu & authoritate diaconi electi sunt. Ad ecclesiam ergo totam pertinet diaconorum electio, quibus ecclesiae bonorum administratio committatur. Quia enim haec illi consecrata sunt, minime permittendum est ut pauci aliquot illa pro suo arbitrio dispensent, aut illorum dispensatores eligant. Ita enim fit, ut dissipationi ecclesiarum occasionem praebeant opes illae, quas in illarum conseruationem pij & fideles sancto studio & Christiano zelo contulerunt. Magnam vero laudem meretur, quod illis apostolorum consilium placuisse dicit. Videbant enim aequum & iustum esse, ne temporarijs rebus granarentur, quos euangelij praedicationi Christus consecratos esse voluerat. Videbant item Christi exemplo institutum hoc conuenire, qui & ipse loculos & victus quotidiani pauperum curam Iudae comiserat, quo minus vel ipse vel re liqui apostoli in verbi ministerio impedirentur. Quapropter absque omni controuersia in apostolorum sententiam pedibus eunt. Est autem haec germana & propria ecclesiae nota, quòd pastoris sui vocem audit, nec Christi consilijs siue exemplis reluctatur. Iohan.10. Et inexcusabilis illorum contumacia est, qui ne errauisse videantur, quicquam mutari & corrigi nolunt, etiamsi horrendis abusibus ecclesiae formam & ordinem omnino conturbatū esse videant. Peccatur in hoc à Romanis, qui axioma hoc mordicus sibi defendendum esse existimant, Romanam ecclesiam non posse errare, &c. Nec reformationem aliquam admittere volunt, etiamsi errores & abusus ingentes nec dissimulare nec excusare possint. Ad eundē lapidem non paucos ex euangelicorum numero offendere videmus, qui dum à prima ecclesiarum suarum reformatione ne latum vnguē discedere volunt, non veteres modò errores in quibusdam articulis retinent, sed nouos quotidie succrescere patiuntur. Veteris ergo & primitiue ecclesiae facilitate imitemur, ne dum omni erroris suspicione liberari volumus, erroribus toti deformemur.
units.tr: First, he teaches by whom the election of the deacons was made. "The speech," he says, "pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen," etc. Therefore the deacons were chosen by the consent and authority of the whole Church. The election of deacons, to whom the administration of the Church's goods is committed, therefore belongs to the whole Church. For since these goods have been consecrated to that purpose, it must by no means be allowed that a few men should dispense them at their own discretion, or choose their stewards. For thus it happens that those riches, which pious and faithful people have contributed with holy zeal and Christian earnestness to the maintenance of the churches, provide an occasion for their dissipation. Great praise is due to them, because Luke says that the counsel of the apostles pleased them. For they saw that it was fair and just that those whom Christ had wished to be consecrated to the preaching of the gospel should not be burdened with temporal matters. They saw too that this arrangement agreed with the example of Christ, who had himself committed the purse and the daily support of the poor to Judas, so that neither he nor the other apostles would be hindered in the ministry of the Word. Therefore they go without any dispute, on foot, to the apostles' judgment. This is the genuine and proper mark of the Church, that it hears the voice of its own minister and does not resist the counsels or examples of Christ (John 10). Inexcusable is the stubbornness of those who, lest they seem to have erred, refuse to have anything changed or corrected, even when they see the form and order of the Church utterly thrown into confusion by horrible abuses. The Papists sin in this, who think that this axiom must be defended tooth and nail: that the Roman Church cannot err, etc. Nor are they willing to admit any reformation, even though they can neither dissemble nor excuse their great errors and abuses. We see not a few of the evangelicals stumbling over the same stone: while they do not wish to depart a hair's breadth from the first reformation of their churches, they not only retain old errors in certain articles, but allow new ones to grow up every day. Let us therefore imitate the simplicity of the old and primitive Church, so that, while we wish to be freed from every suspicion of error, we do not become wholly disfigured by errors.

units.la: Secundò, qui nam ab ecclesia electi fuerint, indicatur. Texitur enim septem virorum catalogus, in quo vt primum locum Stephanus obtinet, ita singulari elogio commendatur, dum fide & spiritu sancto plenus fuisse dicitur. Cuius commendationis partim causa est sequens Stephani historia, partim vt intelligamus, quid in electione ista praecipuè ecclesia obseruarit. Nihil enim priuatim affectibus datum, nec admissae sunt ambitiosorum hominum artes, quos priuatae vel gloriae vel utilitatis cupiditas exagitauit. Sed tales sibi eligendos esse censuerunt, qui Canoni ab apostolis praescripto responderent. Attamen inter hos Nicolaus censetur, quem veteres vxorem publicauisse, & execrabilis Nicolaitarum sectae (cuius opera Christus se odisse testatur. Apoc.2.) authorem fuisse tradunt. Nec tantū, vel apostolorum exhortatione, vel sancto totius ecclesiae studio effici potuit, quò minus sanctissimo diaconorum ordini impurus & flagitiosus homo obreperet. Quod sane admirabile simul & absurdum videri poterat, nisi diuina prouidentia cum totius humani generis tum ecclesiae Christi negotia omnia regi constaret. Et permisit hunc iusto suo iudicio dominus in ecclesia locum aliquem insignem obtinere, quòd haec ad nostram institutionem plurimum facere poterant. Primò etenim admonemur, bonorum & piorum coetibus frequenter improbos obrepere. Nec enim cessat Satan bono semini, dum dormiunt homines, zizania superseminare. Matth.13. Sic Iuda inter apostolos recenseri videmus, quem Christus diabolum & proditorem esse nouerat. Iohan.6. Quapropter nemo offendi debet, si quid simile hodie accidat. Vult enim suos exerceri dominus. Et oportet haereses esse, vt electi probentur. 1.Cor.11. Praeterea attentos nos reddit, tum in nobis ipsis, tum in aliis examinandis, ne vel ipsi nobis imponamus, vel ab aliis tum nobis tum ecclesiae imponi patiamur. Quod in electionibus ante omnia obseruari conuenit. Si enim primitiua ecclesia suo iudicio falsa est, cum sancto Christi zelo ferueret, quid forè sperabimus, si corruptissimi carnis affectus in consilium admittantur, vel inconsulto praecipitentur iudicia? Docet insuper Nicolai exemplum, quanta cura & studio illis etiam opus sit, qui stare videntur, ne quando & ipsi cadant. 1.Cor.10. Nam vt natura ad omne vitiorum genus proclines sumus: ita non otiatur communis noster hostis diabolus, sed nunquam non rugientis leonis instar obambulat, quaerens quem deuoret. 1.Pet.5. Nec sibi securitate polliceri debent, qui tot sanctissimorum hominum lapsus ob oculos habent, & qui iustum in die septies cadere non ignorant. Prouerb. 24. Postremò arguuntur exemplo hoc, qui nudo antecessorum suorum & successionis titulo gloriantur, cùm in Dei leges palàm peccent. Nicolaitas enim, qui Gnostici, turpissimo hominum generi, quo nihil vnquam flagitiosius orbis terrarum habuit, initium dedisse videntur, authorem habuisse cernimus Nicolaum, quem primitiua ecclesia, non modò fidelium numero dignum esse iudicauit, sed quasi reliquos excelleret, in diaconorum numerum accersuit. Quid quòd Antichristum in ipsa ecclesia sedem habiturum esse Paulus docet, & abominationem in loco sancto fore ex prophetis Christus testatur? 2. Thess.3. Matth.24. Stultum ergo est, successionem & ordinis sanctitatem iactare, & non potius in hoc incumbere, vt vocationi nostrae respondeamus.
units.tr: Second, it is indicated who were chosen by the Church. For a list of seven men is set out, in which Stephen holds the first place, and he is commended with a special eulogy, since he is said to have been full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. The reason for this commendation is partly the following history of Stephen, and partly that we may understand what the Church especially observed in that election. For nothing was granted to private affections, nor were the tricks of ambitious men admitted, men driven by a private desire either for glory or for gain. Rather, they judged that such men should be chosen as would answer to the rule prescribed by the apostles. Yet among these Nicolaus is counted, whom the ancients report to have made his wife common, and to have been the author of the execrable sect of the Nicolaitans, whose works Christ testifies that he hates (Rev. 2). Nor could it be brought about, either by the exhortation of the apostles or by the holy zeal of the whole Church, that an impure and shameless man should slip into the most holy order of deacons. This indeed could seem both remarkable and absurd, unless it were established that all the affairs of both the whole human race and of Christ's Church are governed by divine providence. And the Lord, by his just judgment, allowed this man to hold some prominent place in the Church, because these things could contribute greatly to our instruction. First, we are reminded that the wicked often creep into the assemblies of the good and pious. For Satan does not cease, while men sleep, to sow tares over the good seed (Matt. 13). So we see Judas counted among the apostles, though Christ knew him to be a devil and a traitor (John 6). Therefore no one ought to be offended if something similar happens today. For the Lord wishes his people to be tested, and there must be heresies, so that those who are chosen may be approved (1 Cor. 11). Moreover, it makes us attentive, both in ourselves and in examining others, so that we neither deceive ourselves nor allow ourselves, or the Church, to be deceived by others. This ought above all to be observed in elections. For if the primitive Church was deceived by its own judgment, though it burned with the holy zeal of Christ, what shall we hope for if the most corrupt affections of the flesh are admitted into counsel, or judgments are hastily made without consultation? Furthermore, the example of Nicolaus teaches how great the care and zeal needed even by those who seem to stand, lest at some time they too fall (1 Cor. 10). For just as we are naturally prone to every kind of vice, so our common enemy the devil is not idle, but always prowls like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5). Nor should those promise themselves security who keep before their eyes the falls of so many most holy men, and who know that the just man falls seven times a day (Prov. 24). Lastly, by this example are rebuked those who boast of the bare title of their predecessors and of their succession, while they openly sin against God's laws. For we see that the Nicolaitans, who are called Gnostics, and who seem to have given a beginning to the most shameful kind of men, to whom the world has never had anything more disgraceful, had Nicolaus as their author; the primitive Church judged him worthy not only of the number of the faithful, but, as though he excelled the rest, summoned him to the number of the deacons. What of the fact that Paul teaches that Antichrist will have his seat in the Church itself, and that Christ testifies from the prophets that there will be an abomination in the holy place (2 Thess. 2; Matt. 24)? It is foolish, therefore, to boast of succession and of the holiness of an order, and not rather to labour at answering our calling.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Sed reuertamur ad diaconos, quos modò electos fuisse diximus, & quid praeterea factum sit, videamus. Nec enim illicò munus suum inuadunt, sed publica prius inauguratione confirmantur. Et primò quidem coram apostolis sistuntur, tanquam ijs, ad quos tum totius ecclesiae tum pauperum cura imprimis pertinebat. Qua de re admonebantur noui illi diaconi, ita ipsis in dispensatione sua munere versandum esse, vt apostolis, qui verbi Dei ministri erant, ratione possent reddere, quorum circa
units.tr: But let us return to the deacons, who, as we said, have just been chosen, and see what happened next. They do not take up their office at once, but are first confirmed by a public inauguration. They are first presented before the apostles, as those to whom the care of the whole church and especially of the poor belonged. The newly chosen deacons were reminded that in their administration they must so conduct themselves that they could give an account to the apostles, who were ministers of the Word of God, of those things which

units.la: Catalogus diaconorum ecclesiae.
units.tr: The catalogue of the deacons of the church.

units.la: Diaconi inaugurantur publicè. circa hoc negotium seueritas in Ananiæ & Sapphiræ exemplis non ita pridem eluxerat. Quo exemplo arguuntur nostri seculi homines, qui verbi & ecclesiarum ministros ab inspectione & cura publicorum bonorum omnino arcendos esse censent, & indignum putant, si illi de ecclesiasticarum opum dispensatione ac earundem dispensatoribus verba faciant. Atqui constat, pauperum curam non posse ab ijs negligi, quibus totius ecclesiæ curam Christus commendauit. Qua ratione enim partem negligent, qui totum curare debent? Vel ergo pauperes ad ecclesiam pertinere negabunt illi homines, vel ministris illorum curam permittere cogentur. At quomodo negabunt pauperes ecclesiæ partem esse, cum hos Christus ita complectatur, ut in se collatum putet, quicquid illis fit?
