Caterum non clam est, quid nostri illi venentur: hoc nimirum, ut omni freno abiecto, & vniuerso disciplinæ atq; correptionis metu soluti, pro suo arbitrio in ecclesiæ bonis libidinentur, quæ pauperum subuentioni destinari oportebat. Nec horum tyrannidi cedere debent, quicunq; in ecclesiæ ministerio fideliter & cum laude versari voluerint. Secundò precum mentionem Lucas facit. Fudit has vnanimi consensu pro diaconis recens electis ecclesia, ut spiritus sancti dona impetrarent, quibus illos quàm maximè opus habere noverat. Nobis vero suo exemplo religionis studium commendant, quod ut in omni alia re, ita in ijs maximè adhiberi debet, quæ ad communem ecclesiæ administrationem pertinent. Nec immeritò impij censentur, qui preces tum priuatas tum publicas prophano contemptu negligunt.
units.tr: The deacons are inaugurated publicly. In this matter the severity shown in the examples of Ananias and Sapphira had recently shone forth. By this example are rebuked the men of our own age, who judge that ministers of the Word and of the churches should be wholly kept away from the oversight and care of public goods, and who think it unworthy if these men speak about the distribution of church resources and of those who distribute them. Yet it is clear that the care of the poor cannot be neglected by those to whom Christ has entrusted the care of the whole church. For how will those who ought to care for the whole neglect a part? Either those men will deny that the poor belong to the church, or they will be compelled to entrust their care to ministers. But how will they deny that the poor are part of the church, since Christ embraces them so closely that he counts whatever is done to them as done to himself? Moreover, it is no secret what those men are hunting for: namely, that, with every bridle cast off and freed from all fear of discipline and correction, they may indulge their own will in the goods of the church, which ought to have been set aside for the relief of the poor. Nor should those who wish to serve faithfully and with commendation in the ministry of the church yield to their tyranny. Secondly, Luke mentions prayers. The church, with one accord, poured out these prayers for the newly chosen deacons, that they might obtain the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the church knew they very greatly needed. By its example it commends to us zeal for religion, which ought to be applied in every matter, and especially in those that pertain to the common administration of the church. Nor are those rightly judged ungodly who neglect prayers, both private and public, with profane contempt.

units.la: Præterea docemur pro omnibus illis sedulò orandum esse, qui in publico aliquo munere versantur. Vt enim isti non sibi solis laborant, sed publicæ saluti inuigilant: tita si quid ab ipsis peccatum fuerit, id ferè publici alii cuius mali causam præbere solet. Ideò ecclesiam paulò ante pro apostolis publicas & communes preces habuisse vidimus. Et Paulus sese ecclesiarum publicis precibus commendat, ut aperto ore & liberè salutis verbum prædicare possit. Ephes. 6. Idem pro magistratibus & omnibus in eminentia constitutis Christianos orare iubet, ut qui non alia re, saltem precibus publicam salutem adiuuent. Quod in veteri ecclesia ita obseruatum fuisse ecclesiastici scriptores testantur, ut pro Romanis Imperatoribus à fide adhuc alienis, quotidianis precibus Christiani apud Deum intercederent. Et sane tum ingrati tum stupidi animi argumentum est, nulla eorum cura tangi, quibus publica rerum administratio commissa est. Tertium in horum inauguratione locum obtinet manuum impositio, quæ partim quidem consecrationis, partim verò commissionis symbolum erat. Nam vt victimis manus imponebant sacerdotes, & sic eas Deo consecratas esse testabantur: ita ecclesiæ ministris manus imponi solebant, ut se Deo consecratos esse scirent, & suæ vocationis certiores essent. Nec parum referebat illos eius rei, publica ceremonia admoneri. Nisi enim quis certò intelligat, se diuinitus vocatum & ordinatum esse, munere quidem suo, dum felici successu omnia procedunt, fungetur, ut primùm vexerò fortuna aduersa tonare cœperit, nulla diuini auxilij spe suffultus, stationem suam turpissimè deseret. Interim probè obseruemus, quòd manuum impositioni preces coniungunt. Ita enim docent, non externo symbolo spiritus gratiam alligatam esse, sed diuinitus obtingere, & pijs precibus esse impetrandam. Atqui hæc est simplicissima ministros ecclesiæ & diaconos inaugurandi ratio, qua primitiuam ecclesiam aliquot seculis vsam fuisse constat. Cum qua si conferas, quæ hodie à Papistis fiunt, veterem simplicitatem omnino obsoleuisse, & frigidissimis ceremoniis omnia ea obliterata esse videbis, quæ ad verum Dei cultum spectant, & homines officij sui admonere poterant.
units.tr: Furthermore, we are taught that we must pray diligently for all those who hold some public office. For as these men do not labour for themselves alone, but watch over the public welfare, so if anything is sinned by them, it usually provides a cause of some public evil. For this reason we saw that the church had previously offered public and common prayers for the apostles. And Paul commends himself to the public prayers of the churches, that he may be able to preach the word of salvation with an open mouth and freely (Eph. 6). He likewise bids Christians pray for magistrates and for all who are set in high places, so that those who cannot help the public welfare in any other way may at least help it by their prayers. Ecclesiastical writers testify that this was observed in the ancient church, so that Christians interceded with God by daily prayers even for the Roman emperors, who were still strangers to the faith. Indeed, it is a sign of an ungrateful and stupid mind not to be moved by the concerns of those to whom the public administration of affairs has been committed. The third element in their inauguration is the laying on of hands, which was partly a sign of consecration and partly a sign of commission. For just as priests laid their hands on victims and so testified that they were consecrated to God, so hands were customarily laid on the ministers of the church, so that they might know that they were consecrated to God and be more certain of their calling. And it mattered not a little that they were reminded of this by a public ceremony. For unless someone clearly understands that he has been called and ordained by God, he will perform his office while all goes well with success; but as soon as adverse fortune begins to thunder, supported by no hope of divine help, he will shamefully desert his post. Meanwhile let us carefully observe that prayers are joined to the laying on of hands. For this teaches that the grace of the Spirit is not bound to an external sign, but comes from God and is to be obtained by devout prayers. Yet this is the most simple manner of inaugurating ministers of the church and deacons, which we know the primitive church used for several centuries. If you compare with it what is done today by the Papists, you will see that the ancient simplicity has entirely fallen into disuse, and that all those things which pertain to the true worship of God, and which could remind men of their duty, have been obliterated by the coldest ceremonies.

units.la: Caterum ne quis diaconorum institutionem & erroris huius tam diligentem correctionem sua peruacaneam siue inutilem fuisse putaret, insignem & multiplicem fructum ex ea enatum esse Lucas docet. Creuit enim verbum Dei, tum quòd ad alios quoq; propagatum est, tum quòd maiores in illorum animis fructus fecit, à quibus antea auditum & receptum fuerat. Deinde fidelium numerus, quem primates & antistites non modò imminutum, sed omnino sublatum cupiebant, mirificè auctus est, idq; Hierosolymis, vbi maxima erat hostium potentia atq; authoritas. Præterea non modò vulgares & plebeij, sed iam sacerdotes quoq; obedientia fidei sese submittere, & Christo nomina dare inciperunt. Habent hæc multiplicem consolationem, si penitius paulò inspiciantur. Docent enim, quibus armis & studijs ecclesia Christi felicissimè propagetur & conseruetur. Non quidem humanæ siue carnalis prudentiæ consilijs & mundi machinationibus: sed doctrinæ puritate & disciplina sancta. Cuius hic finis esse debet, ut doctrinæ Christi externa omnia respondeant, & errores, si qui incidunt, studiose emendentur: scopus verò omnium sit Dei gloria & multorum salus. Hæc cùm sedulò obseruantur, cordatiores quiq; (quos prius nouitas terrebat) aures & animos præbere incipiunt. Nec dubium est, hodie etiam feliciores fore in ecclesia rerum successus, nisi in hac parte prorsus obsurduissemus. Quasi enim inanis Christiani nominis professio ad salutem sufficiat, in illa otiosi subsistimus, nec publica morum corruptione & manifestis erroribus, nec iustissimis piorum querelis excitamur, vt serio emendemus, quæ emendari oportebat. Nostra igitur negligentia & fecunditate fit, vt minus feliciter hodie procedat euangelij negotium. Rursum euidenti exemplo docemur, quam irrici & vani sint impiorum aduersus Christi regnum conatus. Quo magis enim ili furunt, eo magis illud propagatur, & iam in sacerdotum ordine Christiana fides locum inuenit, quam illi in vulgo minime tolerandam esse putabant. Simile quid Christo adhuc in terris agente contigit: quando Nicodemus & Iosephus Arimathæus in illum crediderunt, quem reliqui omnes extinctum volebant. Quid, quod Nerone crudelibus edistis contra ecclesiam fulminante, in illius tamen aula reperti sunt, qui Christo nomen dederant, sicuti Paulus ad Philippenses testatur? Simul vero singulare hoc est diuinæ bonitatis & mansuetudinis specimen, quod ex eorum numero non paucos veritatis cognitione illustrare dignatur, qui Christi sanguinem fuderant, primiq; mortis ipsius authores habebantur. Quis ergo posthac in peccatis suis desperet, quando hos venia consecutos esse videmus? Christum potius audiamus, qui peccatoribus remissione & pacem sponte pollicetur, & pro ijs, à quibus cruci affigebatur, orare dignatus est. Nec tamen consolationi tantum, verumetiam institutioni exemplum hoc seruire debet, vt nimirum ipsi quoque pari facilitate ijs condonemus, qui iniuriji nos afficiunt. Ita enim fiet, vt vero filiorum dei spiritu donati, & omni liberati nostrorum peccatorum debito, cœlestis & æterni regni hæreditatem adeamus, cum filio Dei vnigenito, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But lest anyone think that the institution of the deacons and this very careful correction of error were superfluous or useless, Luke teaches that a notable and manifold fruit arose from them. The word of God grew, both because it was spread also to others and because it produced greater fruit in the minds of those who had previously heard and received it. Then the number of believers, which the chief men and bishops had wished not only to diminish but to abolish altogether, increased wonderfully, and this at Jerusalem, where the power and authority of the enemies were greatest. Moreover, not only common and plebeian people, but now also priests, began to submit themselves to the obedience of faith and to give their names to Christ. These things offer a manifold consolation, if they are examined a little more closely. For they teach by what arms and efforts the church of Christ is most happily propagated and preserved: not indeed by the counsels of human or carnal prudence and the machinations of the world, but by the purity of doctrine and holy discipline. The aim of this ought to be that all the external things of Christ's doctrine correspond to it, and that errors, if any creep in, be diligently amended; and the goal of all should be the glory of God and the salvation of many. When these things are diligently observed, the more discerning people (whom the novelty had previously frightened) begin to lend their ears and minds. Nor is there doubt that today too the affairs of the church would be happier, unless we had grown utterly deaf in this respect. For as if the empty profession of the Christian name were sufficient for salvation, we remain idle in it, and we are roused neither by the public corruption of morals and manifest errors, nor by the most just complaints of the pious, to amend seriously what ought to be amended. Therefore it is through our negligence and sluggishness that the business of the gospel is less prosperous today. Again, we are taught by a clear example how vain and empty are the attempts of the ungodly against the kingdom of Christ. For the more they rage, the more it spreads, and now the Christian faith has found a place even in the order of priests, which they thought could scarcely be tolerated among the common people. Something similar happened while Christ was still acting on earth, when Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea believed in him whom all the others wanted extinguished. What of the fact that, while Nero was hurling cruel edicts against the church, there were still found in his court men who had given their name to Christ, as Paul testifies to the Philippians? At the same time this is a singular specimen of divine goodness and gentleness, that it deigns to enlighten with the knowledge of the truth not a few of those who had shed Christ's blood and were regarded as the first authors of his death. Who then should despair of his sins hereafter, since we see these men obtained pardon? Let us rather listen to Christ, who freely promises remission and peace to sinners, and who deigned to pray for those by whom he was fastened to the cross. Nor should this example serve only for consolation, but also for instruction, so that we too may likewise with equal readiness forgive those who wrong us. For in this way it will come about that, endowed with the Spirit of the sons of God and freed from all the debt of our sins, we shall come to the inheritance of the heavenly and eternal kingdom, with the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLII.

units.la: Porrò Stephanus, plenus fide & potentia, edebat prodigia & signa magna in populo. Surrexerunt autem quidam ex Synagoga, quæ vocatur Libertinorum, & Cyrenensium, & Alexandrinorum, & eorum qui ex Cilicia erant & Asia, disputantes cum Stephano, & non poterant resistere sapientiæ & spiritui, quo loquebatur. Tunc subornarunt viros, qui dicerent: Audiuimus hunc loquentem verba blasphema in Mosen & deum. Commouerunt quoque populum, & Seniores & scribas: & inuadentes corripuerunt eum, & adduxerunt in Concilium, statuerunt quoque falsos testes, qui dicerent: Homo iste non cessat loqui verba blasphema aduersus locum hunc sanctum & legem. Audiuimus enim eum dicentem, quod Iesus hic Nazarænus destruet locum hunc, & mutabit instituta, quæ nobis tradidit Moses. Et cum omnes, qui sedebant in Concilio, intuiti essent in eum, viderunt faciem eius, tanquam faciem angeli.
units.tr: Moreover, Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and signs among the people. But some men arose from the synagogue called that of the Freedmen, and of the Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and those from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen. They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. Then they suborned men who said, "We have heard this man speak blasphemous words against Moses and God." They also stirred up the people, the elders and the scribes; and, rushing in, they seized him and brought him before the council. They also set up false witnesses who said, "This man does not cease to speak blasphemous words against this holy place and the law. For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs which Moses handed down to us." And when all who sat in the council fixed their eyes on him, they saw his face as the face of an angel.

units.la: Cum dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus, per acerbam crucis mortem in dei patrii sui regnum & gloriam ingressus fit: eadem sors omnibus sustinenda erit, quicunq; in illo pie viuere & cœlestis regni consortes cum illo fieri cupiunt. At quia non alia re magis quam cruce offenditur, non præceptis modo, verumetiam primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplo nos instrui & confirmari voluit deus, ne persecutionibus & aduersis, tanquam re noua & insolita offenderemur: quando olim lætis successibus horribiles persecutiones intermixtas fuisse videmus, crescere nihilominus ecclesia. Cuius rei exemplum præsens, quam modo tractabimus, historia exhibebit, si cum ijs, quæ proximè præcesserunt, conferatur. Narrauit enim Lucas felicissimos euangelij progressus, & quod illi iam non modo vulgares homines, verumetiam multi ex sacerdotum numero credere cœperint. Quare ecclesia rei iam in portu tuto & pacato constituta videri poterant, quando tantis patronis tamq; præclaris defendebantur. Ecce vero nouum certamen oboritur, quo nullum hucusque atrocius & periculosius extitit, & in quo Stephanus, per cuius latus tota Christi ecclesia petebatur, Christi causam non verbis modo & constanti fidei confessione, sed etiam sanguine tueri coactus fuit. Vt hic historiae praecipuum est, ne offendamur, si subito graves motus surgant, quando omnia in tuto videtur, & ij iuuare vel no possunt, vel etiam non volunt, quos nobis fidissimos patronos fore sperauerant. Patitur enim hoc fieri Deus, vt nos a carnalium praesidiorum fiducia abstrahat, & reipsa discamus, Christi regnum neque per exercitum, neque per vim (sicut Zacharias) sed per spiritum Domini propagari. Quia vero hic multa alia concurrunt, quae ad nostram institutionem & consolationem faciunt, historia tota cum suis partibus singulari studio a Luca describitur. Primo enim a persona descriptione exorsus, quis & qualis Stephanus fuerit, docet. Deinde illius hostes & eorundem aduersus ipsum conatus describit. Tertio qualem se in huius causae certamine Stephanus gesserit, & eiusdem gloriosum martyrium commemorat. Nunc vero de iis dicemus, quae ad praesentis loci tractationem pertinere videbuntur.
units.tr: When our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ entered into the glory and kingdom of his heavenly Father through the bitter death of the cross, the same lot must be endured by all who wish to live godly in him and to become partners with him in the heavenly kingdom. Since nothing offends us more than the cross, God wished us to be instructed and strengthened not only by precepts but also by the example of the primitive Church, so that we would not be offended by persecutions and adversities as if they were something new and unusual. For we see that in former times, amid prosperous successes, dreadful persecutions were mixed in, and yet the Church nevertheless grew. The present history, which we shall now treat, will furnish an example of this, if it is compared with what has just gone before. For Luke has related the most happy progress of the gospel, and how not only ordinary people but also many from the number of the priests had begun to believe. Therefore the Church might seem to have been already set in a safe and peaceful harbour, since it was defended by such great patrons and such distinguished ones. But behold, a new conflict arises, more savage and more perilous than any hitherto, and in it Stephen, through whose side the whole Church of Christ was attacked, was compelled to defend the cause of Christ not only with words and a steadfast confession of faith, but also with his blood. The chief lesson of this history is this: we should not be dismayed if sudden grave disturbances arise when all seems secure, and when those whom we had hoped would be our most faithful patrons either cannot help us or do not wish to. God permits this to happen so that he may draw us away from trust in carnal protections, and so that we may learn in fact that the kingdom of Christ is propagated neither by an army nor by force (as Zechariah says), but by the Spirit of the Lord. Since many other things also concur here which serve our instruction and consolation, Luke describes the whole history with its parts with singular care. First, beginning with a description of the person, he teaches who and what sort of man Stephen was. Then he describes his enemies and their attempts against him. Third, he recounts how Stephen conducted himself in the conflict of this cause, and he recalls his glorious martyrdom. Now we shall speak of those matters which seem pertinent to the treatment of the present passage. ## Description of Stephen.

units.la: Stephanum in diaconorum numero primum locum tenuisse supra ostendit Lucas. Nunc vero ea adijcit, quae ad praesentem historiam faciunt. Et primo quidem fide plenum fuisse docet, vt intelligamus ipsum non inani fidei gloriatione superbiuisse, sed vera fide animatum, zelo Christi & gloriae ipsius flagrauisse. Fidei potentiam addit, cuius nomine miraculorum donum intelligimus, iuxta illud Pauli, quod de donorum diuisione in priori ad Corinth. cap. 12. habetur. Vt autem fidem zeli ardore declarauit, ita alterum illud spiritus sancti donum miraculis & prodigiis praeclaris testatus est. Et quamuis de publicis concionibus nihil dicatur, constat tamen ex historiae contextu, ipsum has & frequentes & efficaces maxime, ferias habuisse. Quapropter obiter & quasi in transcursu hic videre licet, primitiuae ecclesiae diaconos, a verbi ministerio non omnino alienos fuisse: sed licet circa bonorum ecclesiae dispensationem praecipue occupaarentur, suam tamen operam in reliquis quoque ministeriis ecclesiae, quoad fieri licuit, impenderunt, vt iuxta Pauli sententiam hoc pacto bonum gradum sibi ipsis acquirerent. 1 Timoth. 3. In primis vero obseruanda hic est promissionum Christi veritas, quibus ille fideles & industrios seruos instruit. Ait enim, super multa & magna constituendos esse, qui in paruis fideles fuerint. Idem eos qui habent, plura adhuc accepturos esse pollicetur. Matth. 25. Experitur hoc Stephanus, vt hic locus docet. Quia enim donis spiritus, quae initio habuit, bene vsus est, & temporariorum honorum dispensationem summa fide administrauit, pluribus donis augetur, & in altiorem gradum euectus, adeoque ipsis apostolis par factus, aeternos & coelestes euangelii thesauros magna cum laude & fructu dispensare pergit: imo primus est, quem Christus martyrij corona ornari voluit. Excitemur igitur huius exempli consideratione, nec conditionis nostrae vilitate nos ab industria reuocari patiamur, quando fide & diligentia spiritus sancti incrementa assequi, & nobis ad praeclarior ministeria gradum siue aditum praeparare possumus.
units.tr: Luke has already shown that Stephen held the first place among the number of the deacons. Now he adds those things which bear on the present history. And first he teaches that Stephen was full of faith, so that we may understand that he was not puffed up with empty boasting about faith, but was animated by true faith and burned with zeal for Christ and his glory. He adds that he was full of power, by which we understand the gift of miracles, according to the saying of Paul in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 12, concerning the distribution of gifts. And just as he showed his faith by the ardour of zeal, so he attested that other gift of the Holy Spirit by remarkable miracles and wonders. And although nothing is said about public sermons, it is nevertheless clear from the context of the history that he held these, and frequent and very effective ones. Hence here one may see, in passing and as it were incidentally, that the deacons of the primitive Church were not entirely strangers to the ministry of the Word; but although they were chiefly occupied with the distribution of the goods of the Church, they nevertheless devoted their labour to the other ministries of the Church as far as this was possible, so that, according to Paul's judgment, they might thereby acquire for themselves a good standing. 1 Timothy 3. Above all, the truth of Christ's promises is to be observed here, by which he instructs faithful and diligent servants. For he says that those who have been faithful in small things will be set over many great things. Likewise he promises that those who have will receive more still. Matthew 25. Stephen experienced this, as this passage teaches. For because he made good use of the gifts of the Spirit which he had at the start, and administered the distribution of temporal goods with the utmost faithfulness, he was enriched with more gifts. Raised to a higher rank, and made in effect the equal of the apostles themselves, he went on to dispense with great praise and fruit the eternal and heavenly treasures of the gospel. Indeed, he was the first whom Christ wished to adorn with the crown of martyrdom. Let us therefore be roused by the consideration of this example, and let us not allow ourselves to be called back from diligence by the lowliness of our condition, since by faith and diligence we can attain increases of the Holy Spirit, and prepare for ourselves a way or access to more distinguished ministries. ## Stephen's antagonists.

units.la: Caeterum mox inuenit fortis & strenuus Christi miles, qui ipsius studijs & sanctis conatibus se opponerent. Insurgunt enim diuersarum nationum viri ex schola siue collegio Libertinorum, qui ipsi negotium faciant: Nam cum Hierosolymorum ciuitas tum cultui externo tum scholae & legis studio destinata esset, diuersa in ea habeantur Iudaeorum, qui ex diuersis gentibus vel religionis vel studiorum ergo illuc commeabant, collegia: e quorum numero haec quoque Libertinorum Synagoga fuit, qui coniurationis contra Stephanum institutae duces vel antesignani fuerunt. Vnde vero ipsi Synagogae nomen hoc obtigerit, variae sunt interpretum sententiae. Mihi prae aliis eorum arridet, qui a libertis Romanis collegium quoddam extructum fuisse putant, in quo extranei instituebantur. Scimus enim magnam fuisse Libertorum eiusmodi potentiam: & eiusmodi officijs multos populi fauorem captauisse, Centurionis exemplo docemur, quem eo nomine sacerdotes Christo comendant, quod ipsorum Synagogam aedificasset. At non temere factum est, quod a diuersarum nationum hominibus, ijsque doctis rerum peritis, Stephanus oppugnatur. Vt enim a sapientibus huius seculi abscondita fere sunt regni Christi mysteria: ita maior eo est sanctorum gloria, quam ex congressibus eiusmodi reportant. Tum etiam consolationi feruit, ne ignauo metu succumbamus, si quando a multis simul & instructissimis hostibus nos peti videamus. Est autem operae precium videre, quo ordine & quibus artibus pugnam contra Stephanum coniurati illi instituant.
units.tr: But soon the brave and vigorous soldier of Christ found men who opposed his efforts and holy endeavours. For men from various nations arise from the school or college of the Freedmen, who make trouble for him. For since the city of Jerusalem was set aside both for external worship and for the study of the school and of the law, various colleges of Jews are found there, who came thither from different nations for the sake of religion or study; and of their number this synagogue of the Freedmen was one, whose leaders or front men were the instigators of the plot against Stephen. As to where this synagogue got its name, there are various opinions among the interpreters. Of these, the one that pleases me more than the others is the view of those who think that a certain college was built by Roman freedmen, in which foreigners were taught. For we know that freedmen of this kind had great power, and by such services won the favour of many people; we are taught this by the example of the centurion, whom the priests commend to Christ on the ground that he had built their synagogue. But it was not by chance that Stephen was attacked by men of various nations, and by learned men skilled in affairs. For just as the mysteries of Christ's kingdom have been largely hidden from the wise of this age, so the glory of the saints is greater in the contests of this kind which they win. Moreover, it is a consolation not to yield to cowardly fear if we ever see ourselves attacked at once by many and very well-equipped enemies. It is, however, worth the effort to see in what order and by what arts these conspirators set about their fight against Stephen.

units.la: A disputatione initium factum esse Lucas dicit, cuius finem & scopum non alium fuisse verisimile est, quam quod ipsum suis sermonibus capere & irretire studuerunt, quod non semel in Christo quoque scribae tentauerunt. Ingenio enim & eruditione freti, facilem sibi ea in re victoriam pollicebantur.
units.tr: Luke says that the contest began with a dispute. It is likely that its aim and purpose was nothing other than to catch him and ensnare him in his own words, which the scribes also attempted against Christ more than once. For, relying on their talent and learning, they promised themselves an easy victory in this matter. ## Stephen is attacked in disputation.

units.la: Stephani descriptio.
units.tr: Description of Stephen.

units.la: Stephani antagonista.
units.tr: Stephen's opponent.

units.la: Disputatione oppugnatur Stephanus. bantur aduersus rudem & illiteratum hominem, vel saltem nullo adhuc eruditionis titulo insignem. At longè aliter cadit negotium, quàm ipsi instituerant. Quem enim illi rudem & imparatum putabant, cœlesti sapientia & spiritu suggestore sine consultore instructus, non modò ad propositas quæstiones respondet, sed tanta argumentorum copia & vi pugnat, ut ipsi nullo pacto resistere possint. Quo loco rursum cernimus, nunquam promissum suis deesse Christum, qui ipsissima est veritas. Promisit is spiritum consolatorem & consultorem, qui in omnem veritatem suos ducturus sit, Iohan. 14. Promisit os & sapientiam, cui homines resistere non possint. Luc. 21. Promissa autem fideliter prestaﬁt hucusque, ut in apostolorum exemplis vidimus. Nec adhuc exhaustus est cœlestis sapientiæ thesaurus, sed ex eo Stephanus quoque haurit, quæ ipsi in hoc certamine necessaria erant. Neminem ergo mundi vel sapientia vel authoritas terreat, quando non nostra est causa quam agimus, sed Christi, qui nobis à patre sapientia factus est, & in quo omnes scientiæ & sapientiæ thesauri reconditi sunt. 1. Corinth. 1. Coloss. 2. Cogitemus item, maiorem esse illum, qui in nobis est, quàm qui in mundo tumultuatur. 1. Iohan. 4.
units.tr: Stephen is attacked in debate. They thought they were arguing against a rough and unlettered man, or at least one not yet marked by any title of learning. But the affair turned out very differently from what they had planned. Stephen, taught by heavenly wisdom and prompted by the Spirit, without any adviser, not only answers the questions put to him but fights with such abundance and force of argument that they cannot in any way resist him. Here again we see that Christ, who is truth itself, never fails his own. He promised the Spirit, the Comforter and Counsellor, who would lead them into all truth (John 14). He promised a mouth and a wisdom which men could not withstand (Luke 21). And he has faithfully kept these promises up to this point, as we have seen in the examples of the apostles. Nor is the treasure of heavenly wisdom yet exhausted; from it Stephen too draws what was necessary for him in this contest. Let no one's fear, then, of the wisdom or authority of the world terrify us, since the cause we are pursuing is not ours but Christ's, who has been made our wisdom from the Father, and in whom all the treasures of knowledge and wisdom are hidden (1 Cor. 1; Col. 2). Let us also consider that he who is in us is greater than he who rages in the world (1 John 4).

units.la: Num verò disputatione victi cedunt Libertini Sophistæ? Nequaquam. Imò ad malas artes conversi, falsis testibus & mendacijs eum opprimere conantur, quem veritate suffultum, & proinde invictum esse cernebant. Subornant enim venales linguæ viros, qui calumnijs toti populo invisum & infamem reddant fidelissimum Christi præconem. Et de his quidem paulò post dicetur. Nunc verò observemus, quousque progrediantur, qui veritatis odium, quod semel animis conceperunt, pertinaciter alunt, & ne victi quidem cedere volunt. Traduntur tales in reprobum sensum, & eò caecitatis deveniunt, ut sub zeli divini prætextu, quo improbe gloriantur, quidvis sibi licere putent, & ne manifesta quidem & atrocissima flagitia exhorreant. Nec enim ignorare poterant Libertini isti, talionis legem falsis testibus divinitus impositam esse. Deut. 19. Et si nulla vsquam extarent leges, communi tamen sensu dictat, immani flagitio omnes eos polluì, quicunque vel ipsi falsum testimonium dicunt, vel falsos testes fiiunt. At omnia hæc fusè deferunt, qui veritatis odio flagrant. Et iusto Dei iudicio fieri solet, ut communi quoque sensu destituantur, & proinde immanibus flagitijs se polluant, qui veritatem, ubi illa animis ipsorum illuxit, improbè exhibilant. Extant multa eius generis exempla, tum vetera tum recentia, inter quæ cumprimis memorabile est, quod Constantiensis Concilij antistites contra commune gentium ius in Iohannem Hussium designarunt, quem non veriti sunt violata fide publica & Imperatoria, immanibus flammis tradere, nec alio prætextu tanti facinoris indignitatem excusarunt, quàm quòd hæreticis fidem servandam esse negaverunt. Nemini ergo mirum videri debet, si se quoque indignis & iniquis modis tractari sentiat. Interea dicamus glisçentiæ contra veritatem odij ignem in primis initijs restinguere, ne in similem cæcitatem & incurabilem pertinaciam ipsi quoque abripiamur.
units.tr: Do the Libertine sophists, then, yield once they are defeated in debate? By no means. Instead they turn to wicked arts and try to crush with false witnesses and lies the man whom they see supported by the truth and therefore unconquerable. They suborn men with venal tongues who, by slanders, make the most faithful herald of Christ hateful and infamous to the whole people. I will speak of these men a little later. For now let us observe how far those people advance who stubbornly nourish the hatred of truth that they have once conceived in their minds, and who will not yield even when they are beaten. Such people are given over to a reprobate mind, and they fall into such blindness that, under the pretext of a divine zeal in which they wrongly boast, they think everything is permitted to them, and they do not shrink from even plain and most atrocious crimes. Nor could those Libertines have been ignorant that the law of retaliation was imposed by God upon false witnesses (Deut. 19). And even if no laws existed anywhere, common sense itself dictates that all who either give false testimony themselves or suborn false witnesses are defiled by a monstrous crime. But those who burn with hatred of the truth carry out all these things without restraint. And by the just judgment of God it usually happens that those who shamelessly hiss at the truth, once it has shone into their minds, are deprived even of common sense, and so defile themselves with monstrous crimes. There are many examples of this kind, both old and recent, among which the most memorable is this: the prelates of the Council of Constance, against the common law of nations, condemned John Hus, and did not hesitate, with public and imperial faith violated, to hand him over to the cruel flames. They excused the enormity of so great a crime by no other pretext than that they held that faith need not be kept with heretics. Therefore no one should think it strange if he finds himself also treated in unworthy and unjust ways. Meanwhile let us quench, at its very first beginnings, the growing fire of hatred against the truth, lest we ourselves be swept into a similar blindness and an incurable obstinacy.

units.la: Quia verò paucorum improbitas contra veritatis doctrinam parum aut nihil proficere poterat, in hoc incubuerunt callidissimi sophistæ, ut populum totum unà cum Senioribus & scribis aduersus Stephanum concitarent. Et quantum ex circunstantijs conijci potest, publico in urbe tumultu excitato, illum comprehendi, & in Concilium abripi curauerunt. Quod vetus satanæ stratagema est, ut seditionibus absorbeantur, quos veritatis & legum patrocinio tutos esse videt. Fit autem fere, ut per seditiones miserè pereant, qui veritatem seditiosis artibus oppugnant, quod Iudæorum etiam genti accidisse constat. Infigne verò hic proponitur leuitatis & inconstantiæ vulgi exemplum. Supra enim indicatum est, apostolos & totam ecclesiam apud populum in summo pretio extitisse, tum propter miraculorum splendorem, tum propter diuinam & cœlestis maiestatis speciem, qua fulgebant. At nunc Sophistarum artibus pleriq; decepti, aduersus veritatis doctrinam insurgunt. Eandem vulgi leuitatem Christus quoque expertus est, quem modò regem facere conantur, modò insanis clamoribus ad immane crucis supplicium deposcunt. Ita Paulum Lystrenses primò quidem Deum esse clamant, mox verò lapidibus obruunt. Act. 14. Et multa huius generis passim in omnium gentium historijs leguntur, quorum omnium hic vsus est, ne popularem auram venemur, nec mundo placere studeamus, sed Deo potius, cuius voluntas certa, stabilis & inconcussa manet.
units.tr: But since the wickedness of a few could accomplish little or nothing against the doctrine of truth, the most cunning sophists set themselves to this task: to stir up the whole people, together with the elders and scribes, against Stephen. And, as far as can be conjectured from the circumstances, they arranged for a public tumult to be raised in the city, and for him to be seized and dragged before the council. This is an old stratagem of Satan: to swallow up in sedition those whom he sees to be safe under the protection of truth and of the laws. It usually happens that those who attack the truth by seditious arts perish wretchedly through sedition, as is known to have happened also to the Jewish nation. Here is set before us a notable example of the fickleness and inconstancy of the crowd. For it was shown above that the apostles and the whole church stood in the highest esteem with the people, both on account of the splendour of their miracles and because of the divine and heavenly majesty that shone in them. But now many, deceived by the arts of the sophists, rise up against the doctrine of truth. Christ too experienced this same fickleness of the crowd: they now try to make him king, now with mad shouts demand for him the dreadful punishment of the cross. So too the Lystrians first cried out that Paul was God, but soon afterwards stoned him (Acts 14). Many things of this kind are read everywhere in the histories of all nations. The use of all of them here is that we should not hunt after popular applause, nor strive to please the world, but rather to please God, whose will remains certain, stable and unshaken.

units.la: Videamus nunc quidnam criminis Stephano intentarint per falsos testes, quos in Concilium producios fuisse Lucas testatur. Summa accusationis est: Homo iste non cessat loqui verba blasphe mia aduersus ma aduersus locum hunc sanctum & legem. Impietatis ergo accusatur, nec eius tantummodo, verum etiam incurabilis pertinacia, qua nullis hucusq; rationibus emolliri potuerit. Nominatim vero vr-bis sanctæ & templi meminerunt, eo quòd intolerabilis impietas Iudæis videbatur, quicquam ad-uersus ipsa vel dicere vel instituere, cum tot diuinis promissionibus passim commendarentur. Ideo Ieremiæ etiam hoc cumprimis vitio datur, quod aduersus ciuitatem sanctam & templum prophe-taret. Ierem. 26. Cæterum quia crimen testibus euinci oportebat, & apertius exponi qua nam ipsa essent blasphemia, addunt: Audiuimus enim eum dicentem, quòd Iesus iste Nazarenus destruet lo-cum hunc, & mutabit instituta, qua tradidit nobis Moses. Quia ergo æternitatem sibi tum de tem-plo & externo cultu, tum de ciuitate pollicebantur, impiũ putabant, quicunq; de horum destructione aliquid diceret. Porrò vnde huius accusationis ansam arripuerint, facile ex apostolorum doctrina conijcere licet. Docebant enim illi, mera dei gratia propter meritum Iesu Christi iustificari & sal-uari homines, nec quicquam in salutis negotio vel hominum operibus vel externis ceremonijs tribuŭ debere. Illa enim imperfecta & polluta esse, has vero futurae in Christo redemptionis vmbras & fi-guras fuisse, quas fui corporis sacrificio Christus sustulerit, sicuti ex veli scissione, in Christi morte facta colligere liceat. Simul vero hortabantur omnes homines, vt abiecta inani iustitiæ legalis fidu-cia, dei iustitiam, quæ in Christo nobis offertur, firma fide amplecti dignarentur. Quod vt facilius persuaderent, imminentis excidij periculum, de quo non semel Christus admonuerat, ob oculos reuo-cabant. Ex his ergo accusandi occasionem arripiunt astutissimi impudentissimiq; calumniatores: de externi cultus abolitione & vrbis excidio quidem Stephanum verba fecisse clamant, astutè vero & improbè causas reticent, quæ illum ista dicere coegerant. Quin ita causam hanc proponunt, vt ipse Stephanus templo flammas minatus fuisse videri potuerit & de Christo contemptim admodum lo-quendo, hunc cum templi splendore & magnificentia quasi conferunt, vt magis inuisam reddant do-ctrinam eius omnem. Est autem singulari diligentia obseruandus locus hic. Nam vt docet menda-cijs ferè veritatem oppugnari: ita non obscurè admonet, illius doctrinam nunquam tam cordatè & modestè prædicari posse, quin calumniandi occasionem mundus infelix arripere possit. Experimur hoc nostro tam exulcerato seculo, quo iniquissimè carpitur, quicquid fidi veritatis doctores prose-runt. Nam cum docemus, mera dei gratia iustificari homines, & nullam in salutis causa laudem no-stris viribus siue operibus deberi: mox bonorum operum hostes, & carnalis licentiæ fautores esse di-cimur. Rursum si in vno Christo contineri dicamus quæcunq; saluti nostræ seruiunt, eò quòd ille no-bis vnicus inter deum & nos mediator, vnicus aduocatus & intercessor constitutus sit: mox in Di-uam virginem & sanctos impij & blasphemi iudicamur. Item, si Christi ecclesiam humanarum tra-ditionum intolerabili iugo liberare, abusus corrigere & veterem primitiuæ ecclesiæ simplicitatem reducere conemur: illico prosiliunt, qui nos religionis, & cultus diuini aduersarios, sacramentorum prophanatores, adeoq; sacrilegos esse vociferentur. Quòd si mundo impuris scelerum vorticibus im-merso, imminentem dei iram & dignas iamq; olim commeritas pœnas denuntiamus: pro publica pa-cis hostibus & seditiosis rerumpub. turbatoribus damnamur et proscindimur. Deniq; nihil tam verè, tam pie, tamq; modestè à veritatis præconibus dici potest, quod Zoilorum iniquam censuram subter fugere possit. At nemo istis ita moueri debet, vt à domino sibi commissam prouinciam deferat. Cogite mus veterem hunc mundi morem esse, cui nos constanter simul & prudenter obluctari decet. Ani-memur item scripturæ testimonijs, quæ piorum memoriam à deo conseruari, & ijsdem in cœlis am-plissimam mercedem repositam esse pollicetur. Psal. 34. Matth. 5. Interim non inultam feret mun-dus impudentem calumniandi licentiam: sed vt Iudæi horrendum sua vrbis & gentis excidiũ, quod ab apostolis denuntiari nolebant, summa cum miseria subire coacti sunt: ita perpetuum hoc est, vt plagas sentiant, qui verbis emendari nolunt, & minas audire dedignantur.
units.tr: Let us now see what charge they brought against Stephen through the false witnesses whom Luke says were produced before the council. The sum of the accusation is: "This man does not cease to speak blasphemous words against this holy place and the law." He is accused of impiety, and not only of impiety but also of an incurable obstinacy, by which, as yet, he has not been moved by any reasoning. They mention specifically the holy city and the temple, because it seemed to the Jews an intolerable impiety to say or undertake anything against them, since they were everywhere commended by so many divine promises. So too Jeremiah was especially charged with this fault, that he prophesied against the holy city and the temple (Jer. 26). Moreover, since the crime had to be proved by witnesses, and it had to be stated more plainly what the blasphemies actually were, they add: "For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs which Moses delivered to us." Since they claimed eternity for themselves, both for the temple and external worship and for the city, they thought it impious for anyone to say anything about their destruction. Furthermore, it is easy to conjecture from the teaching of the apostles where they seized the occasion for this accusation. For those apostles taught that men are justified and saved by the pure grace of God, on account of the merit of Jesus Christ, and that in the business of salvation nothing should be attributed either to human works or to external ceremonies. For these were imperfect and defiled, while the latter were shadows and figures of the redemption to come in Christ, which Christ abolished by the sacrifice of his body, as may be gathered from the tearing of the veil at Christ's death. At the same time they urged all men, setting aside the empty confidence in legal righteousness, to deign to embrace with firm faith the righteousness of God that is offered to us in Christ. To persuade them more easily, they kept before their eyes the impending danger of destruction, of which Christ had warned more than once. From these things the most crafty and shameless slanderers seize the occasion for accusation: they cry out that Stephen spoke about the abolition of external worship and the destruction of the city, but cunningly and wickedly they conceal the causes that forced him to say these things. Indeed, they present the case so that Stephen might seem to have threatened the temple with fire, and speaking quite contemptuously about Christ they set him beside the splendour and magnificence of the temple, so as to make his whole doctrine more hateful. This passage, however, must be observed with particular care. For just as lies usually assail the truth, so it clearly warns us that its doctrine can never be preached so wisely and modestly that the unhappy world cannot seize the occasion to slander it. We experience this in our own age, so exasperated, in which whatever the preachers of faithful truth bring forward is most unjustly torn to pieces. For when we teach that men are justified by the pure grace of God, and that no praise for the cause of salvation is due to our own strength or works, we are at once called enemies of good works and supporters of carnal licence. Again, if we say that everything that serves our salvation is contained in Christ alone, because he is the only mediator between God and us, the only advocate and intercessor appointed, we are at once judged impious and blasphemous towards the blessed Virgin and the saints. Likewise, if we try to free the church of Christ from the intolerable yoke of human traditions, to correct abuses, and to restore the old simplicity of the primitive church, at once there leap forth those who cry out that we are adversaries of religion and of divine worship, profaners of the sacraments, and therefore sacrilegious. And if, when the world is plunged in the impure whirlpools of its crimes, we announce the wrath of God that hangs over it and the punishments already long deserved, we are condemned and torn apart as enemies of public peace and seditious disturbers of the commonwealth. Finally, nothing can be said so truly, so piously and so modestly by the heralds of truth that it can escape the unjust censure of the Zoili. Yet no one should be so moved by these things that he abandons the province committed to him by the Lord. Let us consider that this old custom of the world is one against which we ought to struggle both steadfastly and wisely. Let us also keep in mind the testimonies of Scripture, which promise that the memory of the godly is preserved by God, and that a most ample reward is laid up for them in heaven (Ps. 34; Matt. 5). Meanwhile the world will not bear unavenged the shameless licence of slandering; but just as the Jews, who did not want to hear the dreadful destruction of their city and nation announced by the apostles, were forced to undergo it with the greatest misery, so it is a constant rule that those who will not be corrected by words feel blows, and those who disdain to hear threats are struck.

units.la: Quid vero ad ista Stephanus, qui vt ouis in medio luporum ab omnibus iniquissimè petitur? Num metu consternatur? Num animi terrores pallore aut tremore prodit? Num supplex veniam sibi dari petit, & culpam deprecatur? Imò potius insigni & intrepida libertate suæ fidei & doctrinæ rationem reddit, & illorum improbitatem, & incurabile deo reluctandi studium acerrimè corripit, vt sequenti capite videbimus. Ne quis vero maledicentiæ id tribueret, animi intrepidi & læta in Christo conscientiæ indicium in illius vultu refulsisse dicitur. Cum enim Iudices (vt fieri solet) ipsum intentis oculis inspicerent, viderunt illius faciem vt faciem angeli. Id de insolito & plus quàm humano splendore mihi exponendum esse videtur, quo hostiū oculos perstringere deus voluit, vt se quàm minimè timeri intelligerent. Nec dubium est, incredibilem spiritus consolationem in animo Stephani interim obortam fuisse. Adhæc futuræ glorificationis gustum siue typum exhibet dominus, cuius spe aduersa omnia vincant, quoscunq; pro ipsius nomine periclitari contingit. Exempla huius rei in Martyrum historijs multa occurrunt: inter quæ æterna memoria dignum est, quod non procul à nobis ante annos triginta contigit. Adiguis supplicium propter euangelij professionem ducebatur rusticus quidam: qui cum multa prius in carcere dedisset Christianæ fortitudinis specimina, eò tamen illa in eo efficacior elucebat, quo propius ad mortem accedebat. Nam machinæ alligatus, cum in ignem iam mittendus esset, præfectum supplicíorum postremò alloqui se velle clamauit, & post multas tergiuersationes accedenti tandem sic dixit: Tu me hodie sub hæreseos crimine igni adiudicauisti. At ego etsi me peccatorem esse fatear, hæreseos tamen crimen in me nullum agnosco. Eam enim fidem profiteor, & toto corde amplector, quæ Symbolo apostolico continetur. Et mox recitatis illius articulis, adiecit: Hoc nunc abs te postremum peto officium, mi domine, vt manum meo primum pectori, hinc tuo admoueas: deinde astanti populo bona fide testeris, tuum ne an meum cor praemetu & angustia magis palpitet. Ego quidem læto corde nunc ad Christum contendo, cui credidi. Quis vero tibi sit animus, ipse videris. Non habuit præfectus quod responderet, sed supplicium maturari iussit: læta tamen, vt maior in illius quàm in Martyris vultu tristitia conspiceretur. Est autem hæc ingens fidei nostræ gloria, quòd tum maximè consolatur & exhilarat mentes hominum, quam do omnia terroris & consternationis plena esse videntur. Hanc ergo retinere studeamus omni diligentia, vt huius vitæ curriculum & persecutionum pelagus latis animis & hilari conscientiæ applausu emensi, promissæ nobis glorificationis gaudium in cœlis assequamur tandem in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But what does Stephen do in the face of all this, he who is most unjustly assailed by everyone like a sheep in the midst of wolves? Is he dismayed by fear? Does his soul betray its terrors by pallor or trembling? Does he humbly beg that pardon be granted him and plead for his fault? Rather, with remarkable and fearless frankness he gives an account of his faith and teaching, and sharply rebukes their wickedness and their incurable zeal for resisting God, as we shall see in the following chapter. Lest anyone should ascribe this to malice, it is said that a sign of a fearless spirit and a joyful conscience in Christ shone forth in his face. For when the judges, as is customary, fixed their eyes upon him, they saw his face as the face of an angel. This seems to me to be explained as a splendour unusual and more than human, by which God willed to dazzle the eyes of his enemies, so that they might understand how little he was to be feared. Nor is there any doubt that an incredible consolation of the Spirit arose in Stephen's soul in the meantime. Moreover, the Lord here gives a foretaste or type of the future glorification, by hope of which all adversities are overcome by those who happen to be in danger for his name. Many examples of this occur in the histories of the Martyrs, among which is one worthy of eternal remembrance, which happened not far from us some thirty years ago. A certain country man was being led to execution for the profession of the gospel at Aidigui [Adiguis]; although he had previously in prison given many proofs of Christian fortitude, these shone forth all the more effectively in him the nearer he drew to death. For, bound to the engine, when he was about to be thrown into the fire, he cried out that he wished at last to speak to the prefect of the executions, and after many evasions, when he came near, he said to him: "Today you have condemned me to the fire under the charge of heresy. But although I confess that I am a sinner, I acknowledge no charge of heresy against me. For I profess and embrace with my whole heart that faith which is contained in the Apostles' Creed." And presently, having recited its articles, he added: "This last service I now ask of you, my lord: that you place your hand first on my breast, then on yours, and testify in good faith to the bystanding people whether your heart or mine throbs more with fear and anguish. For my part, with a joyful heart I now hasten to Christ, in whom I have believed. As for what your own mind is like, you yourself must see." The prefect had nothing to answer, but ordered the execution to be hastened; yet a greater sadness was seen in his face than in the Martyr's. This, however, is the great glory of our faith, that it most of all consoles and cheers the minds of men when things seem wholly full of terror and consternation. Let us therefore strive with all diligence to hold fast to this, so that, having run the course of this life and the sea of persecutions with glad hearts and the cheerful applause of a good conscience, we may at last attain in Christ Jesus the joy of the glorification promised us in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: Chapter 7

units.la: HOMILIA XLIII.
units.tr: Homily 43

units.la: DIxit autem summus Sacerdos: Num hæc ita habent? At ille aits Viri fratres & patres, audite: Deus gloriæ apparuit patri nostro Abrahæ, cum esset in Mesopotamia, priusquam habitaret in Charran. Et dixit ad illum: Exi è terra tua & è cognatione tua, & veni in terram, quamcunq; tibi monstrauero. Tunc egressus è terra Chaldæorum, habitauit in Charran. Et illinc, postquam mortuus est pater eius, transtulit eum in terram hanc, in qua nunc vos habitatis.
units.tr: And the high priest said, "Are these things so?" And he said, "Men, brethren and fathers, hear me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran, and said to him, 'Get you out of your country and from your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you.' Then he came out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charran. And from there, after his father was dead, God removed him into this land, in which you now dwell."

units.la: DIuum Stephanum ab hostibus suis per falsos testes accusatum fuisse audiuimus, quod tam in Deum quàm in legem per Mosen latam blasphemet, vrbi simul & templo excidium minitetur. Proponuntur hæc in eum finem, vt intelligamus, primum statim ecclesiæ apostolicæ martyrem, vt postea reliquos omnes, falsis criminibus obrutum fuisse: & hinc quoque discamus, quæ in hoc mundo ministrorum veritatis sors sit, adeoq; omnium eorum, qui Dei gloriæ & publicæ hominum saluti consultum cupiunt. Tales enim impij diuinæ gloriæ ac communis pacis hostes censentur, sicuti Christus non semel monuit, & multorum exemplis iam olim demonstratum est. Neminem ergo iniqua nostri seculi hominum de veritatis ministerio & ministris iudicia offendere debent, quo minus Deum vocantem audiat. At quia de his tum proximo sermone, tum sæpe aliàs di ctum est, modo omissis illis, præsentem locum tractabimus, in quo vt causa hæc in Concilio acta sit, Lucas commemorat.
units.tr: We have heard that the divine Stephen was accused by his enemies through false witnesses, on the charge that he blasphemed both God and the law given through Moses, and threatened the city and the temple with destruction. These things are set out for this purpose: that we may understand that he was the first martyr of the apostolic Church, and that, like all the others afterwards, he was overwhelmed with false charges. From this we may also learn what the lot of the ministers of truth is in this world, and so the lot of all who desire to promote the glory of God and the public salvation of men. For such men are regarded as enemies of divine glory and of the common peace, as Christ warned more than once, and as the examples of many already demonstrated long ago. Therefore the unjust judgments of the men of our age about the ministry of truth and its ministers ought not to deter anyone from hearing God calling. But since these matters have been discussed both in the previous sermon and often elsewhere, we will set them aside now and treat the present passage, in which Luke records how this case was conducted before the council.

units.la: Et primo quidem à summo sacerdote exorsus, hunc interrogauisse dicit, num hæc ita sese habeant, quemadmodum ab accusatoribus Stephani proposita erant? Vbi eximium nobis proponitur callidi tatis & astutiæ exemplum, quia falsi antistites aduersus veritatis ministros & sectatores pugnare solent. Ideo enim Stephanum interrogat & ad respondendum inuitat, vt simulato iustitiae fuco incautioribus imponat, quasi liberum fecerit Stephano causam suam dicere & eandem ingenuè tueri: cum nihil minus illum voluisse constet. Nam ratum adhuc erat apud illos homines impij decreti praeiudicium, quo edixerant, ne quis in nomine Iesu praedicaret. Et modò non de iure facti, sed de solo facto simpliciter interrogat, quasi sufficiens crimen omnibus videri debeat, si quid eorum Stephanus dixisse deprehendatur, quae ab impijs accusatoribus illi obiecta erant. Obseruatur hoc ipsum nostro etiam seculo a persecutoribus nostris, nec aliter dicendi copiam faciunt fidis Christi cultoribus, quàm quod ex illorum ore cognoscere cupiunt, num quid ab ipsis contra receptam superstitionem & abusus siue errores papisticae tyrannidis dictum sit. Quod vt primùm constiterit, mox capitalis sententia stringitur, nec vllae rationes audiuntur, quibus illi causam suam defendere poterant. Itaque quis fateatur, se Diuorum intercessionem negauisse, & eorundem superstitiosos cultus impugnauisse, illicò haereseos damnatur, nec permittitur, vt suae doctrinae rationem reddat. Simili ratione haereticus censetur, quicunque Missae sacrificium, purgatorium ignem, Romanae sedis primatum, indulgentiarum nundinationem, & infinita alia eius generis oppugnare audet, nec facti vel doctrinae ipsius rationes aliae audiuntur. Notemus haec diligenter, ne incautius fucum faciant, quando in Concilijs liberam nobis potestatem se facturos esse dicunt causam nostram dicendi. Nam latet anguis in herba: nec aliud ex nobis, quam veritatis confessionem elicere cupiunt, quae ipsis plus quàm capitalis esse videtur.
units.tr: And first of all he says that the high priest began by asking him whether these things were so, as they had been put forward by Stephen's accusers. Here we are given a notable example of cunning and craftiness, for false bishops are accustomed to fight against the ministers and followers of the truth in this way. He questions Stephen and invites him to answer so that he may deceive the less cautious with a pretence of justice, as if he had freely allowed Stephen to state his case and to defend it honestly, when it is plain that he wanted nothing less. For that wicked decree, by which they had ordered that no one should preach in the name of Jesus, still stood firm in their minds, and so the judgment had already been made. He asks not about the legal merits but simply about the fact, as if the charge should seem sufficient to everyone if it were found that Stephen had said any of the things that the impious accusers had brought against him. This same practice is observed in our own age by our persecutors, who grant no freedom of speech to the faithful worshippers of Christ except this: they want to learn from their mouths whether anything has been said against the received superstition and the abuses or errors of papal tyranny. As soon as this is established, a sentence of death is pronounced at once, and no reasons are heard by which they could defend their cause. So whoever admits that he has denied the intercession of the saints and attacked their superstitious worship is immediately condemned as a heretic, and he is not permitted to give an account of his teaching. By the same reasoning, whoever dares to oppose the sacrifice of the Mass, purgatory fire, the primacy of the Roman see, the trade in indulgences, and countless other things of this kind is judged a heretic, and no other grounds of fact or doctrine are heard. Let us note this carefully, so that they do not deceive us more carelessly when in councils they say they will give us free power to state our cause. For there is a snake in the grass. They wish to draw from us nothing but a confession of the truth, which seems to them worse than a capital crime.

units.la: Sed Stephani responsionem audiamus, quae continua narratione (cuius initium a prima gentis Iudaicae origine ducitur) conflat, & praecipua dei in patres olim collata beneficia comprehendit, vnà cum ijs, quae ab illis vel bene vel male facta sunt. Quis vero narrationis totius finis & scopus fit, ex accusationis capitibus facilè colligi poterit. Praecipua illic sunt, quod in deum & legem blasphemia locutus fit. Impietatis ergo crimine seipsum purgare instituit, & ne vanis & inanibus argumentis alii cui fucum facere videretur, reipsa testari vult, se a dei & institutorum ipsius impio siue prophano contemptu alienissimum esse. Primum quidem argumentum in eo consistit, quod illum ipsum deum agnoscit & praedicat, qui olim cum patribus multa gesserit, & quem illi vnicè coluerunt. Deinde nec propter legis & ceremoniarum abrogationem impium censeri debere probat, quando patres olim sine lege & ceremonijs per solam fidei obedientiam deo placuisse constet: multos vero post legem latam & instituta sacra externa illi idem improbarit. Inde vero non obscurè colligit, longè alium legis & ceremoniarum vsum aut finem esse, quàm vt illis iustificari siue saluari possimus: imò ijs eam salutis rationem adumbrari, quae in Christo demum completa sit: & proinde omissis illis, hunc vera fide recipiendum esse. Tandem vero, vt inanem patrum fiduciam ipsis excuteret, illorum pertinacem & incurabilem impietatem ipsis ob oculos reuocat, hoc simul grauissimis verbis accusans, quòd horum potius imitatores sese praebeant, quàm veterum illorum & vere sanctorum patrum, qui per fidem deo placuerunt. Et haec quidem totius orationis Stephani summa est, qua docemur, quomodo & quàm fortiter veritatis causa aduersus illius hostes asseri debeat. Elucet praeterea hic admirabilis spiritus sancti virtus, qui illum tam perfecta rerum diuinarum cognitione & tam imperterrita animi fortitudine instruere potuit, vt in medio luporum constitutus, doctrinae & fidei suae rationem tam prudenter reddere, & hostium minas tam constanter contemnere potuerit. Quod exemplum nos quoque consolari debet, ne impiorum audacia & proteruitate spiritus sancti virtutem superari possepuremus. Videamus autem orationis initium, quod praesenti loco continetur.
units.tr: But let us hear Stephen's reply. It is made up of a continuous narrative, which begins from the first origin of the Jewish nation, and it contains the chief benefits of God conferred on the fathers long ago, together with the good and bad deeds of those same people. The purpose and aim of the whole narrative can easily be gathered from the heads of the accusation. The main charges there are that he spoke blasphemy against God and the law. Therefore he sets out to clear himself of the crime of impiety, and, so that he should not seem to deceive anyone with empty and idle arguments, he wants to show in fact that he is most remote from any impious or profane contempt of God and of God's ordinances. The first argument consists in this: he acknowledges and proclaims the very God who long ago dealt with the fathers and whom they alone worshipped. Next, he proves that he should not be judged impious because the law and the ceremonies have been abolished, since it is established that the fathers pleased God long before the law and the ceremonies, through obedience of faith alone, while many after the law was given and the external sacred institutions were set up, displeased him by the same unbelief. From this he clearly concludes that the use and purpose of the law and the ceremonies is quite different from making us righteous or saved through them. Rather, they foreshadowed that way of salvation which was at last completed in Christ, and therefore, setting those aside, Christ must be received with true faith. Finally, so that he might shake from them their empty confidence in the fathers, he calls before their eyes their stubborn and incurable impiety, and at the same time accuses them in the gravest words that they rather imitate their own unbelief than those ancient and truly holy fathers who pleased God through faith. This is the sum of the whole of Stephen's speech, and from it we are taught how and how boldly the cause of the truth ought to be maintained against its enemies. Here too shines the admirable power of the Holy Spirit, who could so fully instruct him in divine things and give him such fearless courage of mind, that, placed among wolves, he could give an account of his teaching and faith so wisely and despise the threats of his enemies so steadfastly. This example ought also to console us, so that the audacity and insolence of the wicked may not overcome the power of the Holy Spirit. Let us now look at the beginning of the speech, which is contained in this passage.

units.la: Exordium breue est. Ait enim: Viri fratres & patres, audite. Et fratres quidem vocat propter cognationem, quo titulo frequenter se inuicem Israelitae compellant: patres vero dicit, propter loci & officij dignitatem, quam ex Dei institutione tenebant, cuius authoritatem non inuitus agnoscit, quantumuis corruptos & impios esse sciret. Interim non ita ad illorum dignitatem obstupescit, vt nefas esse ducat, ab illis dissentire: quin potius ingenuè & liberè suam sententiam profert, & ipsos erroris accusat. Docemur hoc exemplo, Christianam fidem minimè abolere humanitatis & civilitatis officia, quae cum honore & veneratione illis debemus, qui nos aliquo dignitatis gradu praecedunt. Licet enim quoad salutis nostrae causam, in Christo Iesu nulla sint personarum discrimina (sicuti Paulus admonet, Galat. 3. Col. 3. &c.) manent tamen dignitatis gradus, neque dei patris legem abo-
units.tr: The exordium is short. For he says, "Men, brethren and fathers, hear me." He calls them brethren because of kinship, the title by which the Israelites often address one another; he calls them fathers because of the dignity of their place and office, which they held by God's appointment. Stephen acknowledges their authority, though unwillingly, even though he knew they were corrupt and impious. Yet he is not so awed by their dignity that he thinks it wrong to dissent from them; rather, he states his opinion openly and freely, and accuses them of error. From this example we learn that the Christian faith does not abolish the duties of courtesy and civility which we owe with honour and reverence to those who stand above us in some degree of dignity. For although, as far as the cause of our salvation is concerned, there is no distinction of persons in Christ Jesus (as Paul reminds us, Gal. 3; Col. 3, etc.), nevertheless degrees of dignity remain, and the law of God the Father is not abo-

units.la: Oratonis Stephani argumentum.
units.tr: The argument of Stephen's oration.

units.la: Attentionis et benevolentiae captatio. leuit Christus, qua parentes honorare, & coram cano capite assurgere iubet: & eodem apostolo teste, Christianæ modestiæ est, ut nos inuicem honore præueniamus. Rom.12. Præcipua tamen habeatur diuinæ voluntatis & officij, quo deo obstricti sumus, ratio, ne in hominum gratiam veritatem dissimulemus, cuius confessionem à nobis passim Christus exigit. Nec vnquam nobis apostolicum illud & vere Christianum axioma excidere debet, quo admonemur, deo plus quàm hominibus obediendum esse. Vt ergo Stephani exemplo barbara fanaticorum quorundam inciuilitas arguitur, qui vt se fatus Christianos præbeant, principes quoq; & quosuis in eminentia constitutos, non alio quàm fratrum nomine compellant: ita illorum quoq; tyrannis confuratur, qui iniquum putant, vt quisquam Romanæ sedis præsulibus contradicat, eo quod illorum authoritas tot seculorum præscriptione & plurimorum principum authoritate confirmetur. Atqui vana & ridicula est humanæ authoritatis gloriatio, quando apostolis licuit ab illis dissentire, quorum potestas diuinitus instituta erat, & quos propter diuinam institutionem pro patribus agnoscebant. Probatur ethnici philosophi ingenuitas, qui dixisse fertur: Amicus Socrates, sed magis amica veritas. Quæ ergo iniquitas est à Christianis hominibus exigere, vt maiorem Antichristi Romani, quàm Christi & æternæ veritatis rationem habeant?
units.tr: Gaining attention and goodwill. Christ taught this, when he bade us honour parents and rise up in the presence of grey hair; and, as the same apostle testifies, it is a mark of Christian modesty that we go before one another in honour (Rom. 12). Yet the chief consideration should be the will of God and the duty by which we are bound to God, so that we do not dissemble the truth to win men's favour, a confession which Christ demands of us everywhere. Nor should that apostolic and truly Christian maxim ever fall from our minds, by which we are reminded that we must obey God rather than men. So, just as by Stephen's example the barbarous rudeness of certain fanatics is refuted, who, in order to appear as Christians, address princes and all who are set in high positions by no other name than brothers, so too the tyranny of those is overthrown who think it unjust that anyone should contradict the bishops of the Roman see, on the ground that their authority is confirmed by the prescription of so many centuries and by the authority of many princes. Yet the boast of human authority is empty and ridiculous, since the apostles were allowed to dissent from those whose power had been instituted by God, and whom, because of God's institution, they acknowledged as fathers. The frankness of the heathen philosopher is praised too, who is said to have said: "Socrates is a friend, but truth is a greater friend." What injustice, then, is it to demand of Christian men that they should have more regard for the Antichrist of Rome than for Christ and eternal truth?

units.la: Sed ad Stephanum reuertamur, qui narrationem ab Abrahamo Iudaicæ gentis patre orditur, eo quod illo potissimum gloriarentur. Et illius quidem exemplo probat, legales cultus ad salutem non esse necessarios, nec impios siue blasphemos censeri debere, qui illorum abrogationem prædicant, quando constet, Abrahamum sine his olim deo placuisse. Ad amplificationem vero argumenti faciunt circumstantia loci & temporis. Ne enim promisse terræ aliquam apud deum rationem fuisse putarent, in Chaldæa siue Mesopotamia adhuc agentem Abrahamum, diuinitus euocatum fuisse, & mortuo demum patre Thare (cuius senio vel morbo ipsum in Charris detentum fuisse verisimile est) in terram Chanaan deuenisse ostendit, vbi Circuncisionis sigillum acceperit. Cæterum, quia ad nostram institutionem scripta sunt omnia, Abrahami exemplum, non præsenti modò causæ, verumetiam nobis applicari debet: nec parum inde ad nos fructus redibit, si dei vocationem & Abrahæ fidem siue obedientiam probè consyderemus.
units.tr: But let us return to Stephen, who begins his narrative with Abraham, the father of the Jewish nation, because the Jews above all boasted in him. By Abraham's example he proves that the legal ceremonies are not necessary for salvation, and that those who preach their abrogation should not be judged impious or blasphemous, since it is clear that Abraham once pleased God without them. The circumstances of place and time also add weight to the argument. Lest they think that God had some regard for the promised land, Stephen shows that Abraham, while still living in Chaldea or Mesopotamia, was called by God, and that he came into the land of Canaan only after the death of his father Terah (who, it is likely, had been detained at Haran by his old age or sickness), and there received the seal of circumcision. Moreover, since all things are written for our instruction, the example of Abraham applies not only to the present case but to us as well, and no small benefit will come to us if we carefully consider God's calling and Abraham's faith or obedience.

units.la: In dei vocatione, qua Abraham ex Vr Chaldæorum in terram Chanaan translatus est, duo cum primis memorabilia habentur. Primum est, quòd nullo precedente merito vocatus est. Nam inter idololatras illum habitasse, & dijs alienis seruiuisse, Iosue author est, Cap.24. Imò Epiphanius ex veterum traditione docet, patrem Abrahami Tharan primum ex luto statuas fecisse, & ideo diuinitus fuisse punitum, vt filij Haran mortem videret, quem primum ex veteribus patrem suum morte naturali præuenisse scribit. Nec circuncisione aut templo commendari potuit, cum illud aliquot post seculis demum extructum, hæc vero fœderis cum illo initi signum fuerit, quo fidei iustitia quam iam assecutus erat, obsignabatur. Rom.4. Alterum est, quòd à nudo dei verbo tota hæc vocatio dependet. Nam iubetur quidem patrium solum & cognatos deserere, nihil verò oculis ipsius subijcitur, quod ipsum meliora & præstantiora sperare iubeat. Nec enim fideliores amicos aut terram fertiliorem deus pollicetur, sed indefinite loquens: Veni (inquit) in terram, quancunq; tibi monstrauero. Sunt hæc diligenti obseruatione digna. Primò enim docent, nos ad salutem & cœlestem patriam (cuius typum olim gessit terra Chanaan) ex mera dei gratia vocari, nec aliquem esse nostrorum operum siue meritorum in salutis causa respectum. Quid enim meruimus, quando priusquam mundus hic conderetur, in Christo electi sumus? Ephes.1. Vel quid iactare possunt, qui nihil habent, quod non acceperint? 1.Corinth.4. Et sane si nostræ naturæ ingenium consyderes, patebit nos de cœlesti patria, priusquam diuinitus vocemur & trahamur, non magis solicitos esse, quàm Abraham de terra Chanaan fuerit, cuius nomen quoq; ignorabat. Imò cum nos vocat dominus, improbum carnis diuinæ vocationi reluctantis ingenium experimur, quod nunquam, nisi efficaci spiritus tractu adiuti superare possumus. Deinde admonemur vocationem nostram, quæ salutem nobis offert, à solo dei verbo dependere, & proinde non carnis sensu aut humana ratione, sed sola fide (quæ & ipsa dei donum est, Ephes.2.) percipi posse. Animalis enim homo non percipit, quæ sunt spiritus Dei.1.Cor.2. Et ea diligentibus se præparauit deus, quæ nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in cor hominis ascenderunt. Isa.64. Atqui hic demum fidei virtus præclara se se exerit, quòd sola dei promissionem arripit, & quæ sub sensum non cadunt, omnému humanæ rationis captum superant, firmissimè complectitur: quapropter à Paulo eorum quæ sperantur substantia, & infallibilis eorum, quæ non videntur, apprehensio dicitur. Hebr. 11. Debebant hæc obseruare, quibus doctrina de iustificatione fidei leuicula videtur, quasi salutis rationem nimis facilem indicet, & ita carnis securitatem atq; licentiam foveat. Quomodo enim leuiculum & facile nimium censeri potest, quod omnes hominis facultates excedit? Vel num maioris apud deum momenti erit, quod homines proprijs viribus faciunt quàm quod non nisi spiritus sancti virtute perfici potest? Conferamus fidem cum omnibus omnium monachorum operibus, & hæc quidem in gentium philosophis plura & perfectiora reperiemus: illam vero in nullo monstrare poterunt, nisi qui ex Dei verbo per spiritum renatus fuerit. Merito ergo rei omnium maximæ, & quà nihil præstantius homo in terris viuens habere potest, salutis & iustificationis nostræ ratio tribuitur.
units.tr: In God's calling, by which Abraham was brought out of Ur of the Chaldeans into the land of Canaan, two things are especially worth noting. The first is that he was called without any preceding merit. For Joshua testifies (chap. 24) that Abraham lived among idolaters and served strange gods. Indeed Epiphanius, from ancient tradition, teaches that Abraham's father Terah first made images out of clay, and was therefore punished by God, so that he saw his son Haran die; Epiphanius writes that Haran was the first of the ancients to precede his father in natural death. Nor could he have been commended by circumcision or by the temple, since the temple was built many centuries later, while circumcision was the sign of the covenant made with him, by which the righteousness of faith that he had already attained was sealed (Rom. 4). The second is that this whole calling depends on the bare word of God. For he is indeed ordered to leave his native soil and his kinsfolk, but nothing is set before his eyes that would lead him to hope for better and more excellent things. God does not promise him more faithful friends or a more fertile land, but speaks indefinitely: "Come," he says, "into the land that I shall show you." These things deserve careful attention. For first they teach us that we are called to salvation and to the heavenly fatherland (of which the land of Canaan once was a type) by God's pure grace, and that no regard for our works or merits enters into the cause of salvation. For what did we merit, when before the world was founded we were chosen in Christ? (Eph. 1). Or what can those boast of who have nothing that they have not received? (1 Cor. 4). And indeed, if you consider the disposition of our nature, it will be plain that we are no more concerned about the heavenly fatherland before we are called and drawn by God than Abraham was concerned about the land of Canaan, whose name he did not even know. Indeed, when the Lord calls us, we experience the wicked disposition of the flesh resisting the divine calling, which we can never overcome unless we are helped by the effectual pull of the Spirit. Next we are reminded that our calling, which offers us salvation, depends on the word of God alone, and therefore can be grasped not by the sense of the flesh or by human reason, but by faith alone (which is itself a gift of God, Eph. 2). For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). And "God has prepared for those who love him things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man" (Isa. 64). Here, indeed, the excellent power of faith shows itself, in that it lays hold of God's promise alone and firmly embraces what does not fall under the senses and surpasses the whole grasp of human reason; therefore Paul calls it the substance of things hoped for and the sure apprehension of things not seen (Heb. 11). Those who think the doctrine of justification by faith is a trifling thing, as if it pointed to too easy a way of salvation and so fostered the security and licence of the flesh, ought to observe these things. For how can that be thought trifling and too easy which exceeds all the faculties of man?
