Or will what men do by their own powers have greater weight with God than what cannot be accomplished except by the virtue of the Holy Spirit? Let us compare faith with all the works of all the monks, and we will find more and more perfect such works among the philosophers of the Gentiles; but none of them will be able to exhibit faith, except one who has been born again through the Word of God by the Spirit. Rightly, therefore, the reckoning of our salvation and justification is attributed to the greatest of all matters, and than which a man living on earth can have nothing more excellent.

units.la: Admirabilis autem est Abrahami fides & obedientia, qua dei vocationem secutus est. Infinita enim erant, quæ ipsum impedire & remorari poterant. Nam vt alia omittamus, magna est natalis soli vis, quod (vt poeta inquit) mira dulcedine captos Attrahit, immemores nec finit esse sui. Nec parua est cognatorum & affinium authoritas, quorum amore tunc vehementiori corripimur, si quando deferendi sunt. Obstare etiam poterat patris senectus & imbecillitas, quæ mortem illi attulit, priusquam terræ promissæ fines attingeret. Et verisimile est, honoribus quoq; claruisse inter suos Abrahamum, quos inter exteras nationis homines non facile sperare poterat. At nihil horum diuinum illud pectus remorari potuit, quin omni mora abiecta, deum vocantem sequitur, nec etiam cu-riosius de terræ promissæ conditione quicquam quærit. Hæc illa fidei obedientia est, quam toties Paulus commendat, & quam euangelij finem esse docet. 2. Corinth. 10. Rom. 1. & 16. Hanc Christus à nobis exigit, quando parentes, sorores & fratres, vxores & liberos nos relinquere, ad ipsos abnegare iubet, si ipsius discipuli effici velimus. Matth. 10. & 16. Atq; huius quidem rei tàm difficilis tamen, ardua est executio, vt nobis præstitu plane impossibilis fit, nisi cœlesti spiritu regeneremur, quemadmodum Christus cum Nicodemo disputans admonet. Ioan. 3. Ad hanc ergo regulam seipsos examinent, qui Christianum nomen affectant, ne dum illo temere superbiunt, stultorum architectorum instar sint, qui priusquam sumptuum rationem subduxerint, ædificium ingens & arduum moliuntur. Luc. 14. Excitet nos hæc consyderatio, vt indefesso pietatis studio ardentes preces iungamus, quibus fidei augmenta impetremus, vt omnium huius mundi bonorum iactura facta, cœlestis patriæ hæreditatem adire possimus cum Iesu Christo saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Abraham's faith and obedience, by which he followed God's calling, are admirable. For there were countless things that could have hindered and delayed him. To pass over other things, the power of the native soil is great, which (as the poet says) "by a wondrous sweetness captures and does not let those it has captivated be mindful of themselves." Nor is the authority of kinsfolk and relatives small, by whose love we are then seized more strongly, when we must leave them. The old age and weakness of his father, which brought him death before he reached the borders of the promised land, could also have stood in the way. And it is likely that Abraham was held in honour among his own people, whom he could hardly hope to find among foreign nations. Yet none of these things could hold back that divine heart; casting aside every delay, it follows God calling, nor does it inquire any more curiously into the condition of the promised land. This is the obedience of faith which Paul so often commends, and which he teaches to be the goal of the gospel (2 Cor. 10; Rom. 1 and 16). Christ requires this of us when he bids us leave parents, sisters and brothers, wives and children, and deny them, if we wish to be his disciples (Matt. 10 and 16). Yet the carrying out of this matter is so difficult and arduous that it is utterly impossible for us to achieve it unless we are regenerated by the heavenly Spirit, as Christ, disputing with Nicodemus, reminds us (John 3). Let those who aspire to the name of Christian therefore examine themselves by this rule, lest, while rashly boasting of that name, they become like foolish builders who undertake a huge and costly building before they have reckoned the expense (Luke 14). Let this consideration stir us to join ardent prayers with an unflagging zeal for piety, by which we may obtain increases of faith, so that, having suffered the loss of all the goods of this world, we may be able to enter the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland with Jesus Christ our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIIII.
units.tr: Homily 44

units.la: Et non dedit illi hæreditatem in ea, ne vestigium quidem pedis: & promisit illi eam se daturum in possessione, & semini eius post ipsum, cum illi non esset filius. Locutus est autem deus sic: Semen tuum inquilinum erit in terra aliena, & subijcient illud seruituti, & male tractabunt annis quadringentis. Et gentē, cui seruierint, ego iudicabo, dixit deus. Et post hæc exibunt, & seruient mihi in loco hoc.
units.tr: "And he gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on; yet he promised that he would give it to him in possession, and to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child. And God spoke on this wise: that his seed should sojourn in a strange land, and that they should bring them into bondage and entreat them evil four hundred years. And the nation to which they shall be in bondage will I judge, said God: and after that shall they come forth, and serve me in this place."

units.la: Quoniam Diuus Stephanus propter doctrinam de legis & ceremoniarum abrogatione, publicus diuinæ gloriæ & totius religionis hostis accusatus est, eum suæ responsionis flatum & vsus præsensive scopum constituit, vt euincat, se licet legalium ceremoniarum abrogationem doceat, non tamen idcirco impium & diuini cultus hostem censeri debere. Id vero non inani verborum strepitu, sed rerum ipsa demonstrare instituit. Diligentem enim rerum olim à deo cum patribus gestarum narrationem contexit: partim quidem, vt probet se, verum deum, quem patres olim coluerint, agnoscere: partim vero, vt doceat iustificationem & salutem minimè legalibus ceremonijs esse alligatam, quando sine his patres deo seruiuisse, & eidem placuisse constet. Vnde colligit, se quoq; veræ religionis aduersarium non esse, cum ea solummodo oppugnet, quibus olim patres feliciter caruerint, & quæ in eum duntaxat finem sint institutæ, vt veram salutis rationē, quæ in vno Christo continetur, figurarent.
units.tr: Because St Stephen was accused of teaching the abrogation of the law and the ceremonies, and was charged as a public enemy of the divine glory and of the whole religion, he set his speech and his whole aim on proving that, although he taught the abrogation of the legal ceremonies, he ought not on that account to be judged impious or an enemy of divine worship. He undertook to demonstrate this not by empty noise of words but by the facts themselves. For he wove together a careful narrative of the things God had earlier done with the fathers: partly to show that he acknowledges the true God whom the fathers worshipped long ago, and partly to teach that justification and salvation are by no means bound to the legal ceremonies, since it is clear that the fathers served God and pleased him without them. From this he infers that he is not an opponent of true religion either, since he attacks only those things which the fathers happily lacked, and which were instituted only for this purpose, to prefigure the true way of salvation contained in Christ alone.

units.la: Narrandi vero initium ab Abrahamo sumit, cuius nomine illi maxime gloriabantur. Et primo quidem, illum cum adhuc trans fluuium inter alienorum deorum cultores versaretur, ex mera gratia ad terrae Chananaicae (quae caelestis patriae typus est) euocatum esse ait, cum nec templum adhuc staret, nec instituta essent legales ceremoniae. Et in Abrahamo nihil praeter fidei obedientiam in scripturis praedicari docet, qua deum vocantem secutus, & oblatam sibi gratiam amplexus sit. Quo exemplo Iudaeorum proceres extimulare conatur, vt omissa iuperstitiosa ceremoniarum obseruatione, Christum Iesum, vnicum verae salutis authorem firma fide recipiant. Caeterum quia carnis iudicio fides non tanti momenti res esse videtur, quae salutem nobis conciliare possit, in Abrahami fide illustranda diligenter versatur Stephanus, vt offendat, eam fidei virtutem esse, quae omnes hominum vires & humanae rationis captum longe superet. Per hanc enim Abraham patriae dulcis desyderium, cognatorum conuersationem, opum & honorum splendorem, itinerum labores & moléstias, solicitudines, curas, denique omne id, quod carni nostrae vel iucundum vel aduersum est, ita superauit, vt absque omni mora & tergiuersatione deo vocanti obediret. Ad eandem vero demonstrationem praesens quoque locus facit, quo insignis illa Abrahami fides plenius illustratur, si quo modo illius studium & amorem in illis possit accendere: quo cum nobis quoque opus sit, diligenter singula considerare proderit.
units.tr: He begins his narrative with Abraham, in whose name the Jews especially boasted. First he says that Abraham, while he was still living across the river among worshippers of strange gods, was called out of sheer grace into the land of Canaan (which is a type of the heavenly fatherland), at a time when there was not yet a temple and the legal ceremonies had not been instituted. And he teaches that in the Scriptures nothing is proclaimed of Abraham except his obedience of faith, by which he followed God calling him and embraced the grace offered to him. By this example he tries to stir up the leaders of the Jews, so that, setting aside the superstitious observance of ceremonies, they may receive Jesus Christ, the only author of true salvation, with a firm faith. But because by human judgement faith seems to be a thing of little weight to win us salvation, Stephen works diligently at making Abraham's faith plain, so as to show that this faith is a power which far surpasses all human strength and the grasp of human reason. For through this faith Abraham overcame the sweet longing for his homeland, the company of his kinsfolk, the splendour of wealth and honours, the labours and troubles of journeys, anxieties, cares, and in short everything that is either pleasant or hostile to our flesh, so that without any delay or evasion he obeyed God calling him. This present passage also serves the same demonstration, in which that remarkable faith of Abraham is set out more fully, if in some way it can kindle in them a zeal and love for it. Since we too have need of this, it will be profitable to consider each detail carefully.

units.la: Valet autem exponere Stephanus, quid cum Abrahamo, postquam in terram promissam venit, gestum sit, & sic ait: Et non dedit illi deus haereditatem in ea, ne vestigium quidem pedis. Sed promisit illi eam se daturum in possessionem, & feminini eius post ipsum, cum illi non esset filius. Quibus verbis tria continentur, quae ad fidei Abrahami amplificationem faciunt. Primo, vbi per multos labores & multa pericula in terram diuinitus promissam & monstratam ventum est, non vacuam inuenit, sed a Chananaeis, ferocissima gente, occupatam. Et tam abfuit, vt illam possideret, vt ne pedis quidem vestigium posset suum dicere. Imo nouis subinde infortunijs excipitur. Nam vix tenetoris fixis, fame compulsus in Aegyptum abit. Inde reuersus, propter pastorum iurgia a nepote suo Lot separatur, qui vnicum inter infestas gentes solatium videri poterat. Nec multo post periculoso bello contra Orientis reges implicatur. Et vt multa alia omittamus, Sara vxore mortua, sepultura locum ab Ephrone Hethaeo emit. Annon ergo spe sua falsus videri poterat? Deinde, quid inter tot & tantas aerumnas Abrahamum sustentarit, docet: nimirum promissio, qua illi deus terram illam sponderat. At quam graue sit nudae promissioni inniti, si nihil aliud sit quo confirmeris, experientia quotidiana discimus, maxime si rerum euentus cum promissionibus pugnare videantur: quod hic euenisse, modo diximus. Sed tertium accedit longe grauissimum, quod nimirum dei promissio humanae sapientiae ridicula videri poterat. Promittebat enim terram hanc feminini siue posteritati Abrahamicae deus, cum ille filium non haberet aliquem, nec generationi propter aetatem posthac idoneus esset, vtpote prope centenarius, & coniugem Saram hucusque sterilem esse sensisset. Quis ergo non videat quam multis quamque validis arietibus Abrahami fides oppugnata & concussa sit, & quam graues de dei promissis dubitandi causas habuerit? At nihil horum diuinum illud pectus expugnare potuit. Nam praeter spem sub spe credidit, nec consyderauit suum ipsius corpus iam emortuum, nec emortuam vuluam Sarae, verum ad promissionem dei non haesitabat per incredulitatem, sed robustus factus est fide, tribuens gloriam deo, certa persuasione concepta, quod is qui promiserat, idem posset etiam praestare. Rom. 4. Atqui haec illa fides est, quam Moses illi ad iustitiam imputatam fuisse dicit. Gene. 12.
units.tr: Stephen then sets out what happened to Abraham after he came into the promised land, and says: "And God gave him no inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on; yet he promised that he would give it to him in possession, and to his seed after him, when as yet he had no child." Three things are contained in these words which add to the amplification of Abraham's faith. First, when after many labours and many dangers he came into the land divinely promised and shown to him, he found it not empty but occupied by the Canaanites, a most fierce nation. And so far was he from possessing it that he could not even call a footprint his own. Indeed he was met again and again by fresh misfortunes. For scarcely had he fixed his tents when, driven by famine, he went down into Egypt. Returning from there, because of the quarrels of the herdsmen he was separated from his nephew Lot, who alone seemed to be a comfort among hostile nations. Soon after he was caught up in a dangerous war against the kings of the East. And to pass over many other things: when his wife Sarah died, he bought a burial place from Ephron the Hittite. Could he not therefore seem to have been deceived in his hope? Second, Stephen shows what sustained Abraham amid so many and great troubles: namely the promise by which God had pledged that land to him. But we learn from daily experience how hard it is to rest on a bare promise, if nothing else confirms it, especially when the outcome of events seems to conflict with the promises, which we have just said happened here. But there is a third thing, far the heaviest, namely that God's promise could seem ridiculous to human wisdom. For God promised this land to his seed, or to Abraham's posterity, when Abraham had no child, and was no longer fit for begetting on account of his age, being nearly a hundred, and he had perceived that his wife Sarah had been barren until then. Who then does not see how many and how strong battering rams assailed and shook Abraham's faith, and how serious were the grounds for doubting God's promises that he had? Yet none of this could overcome that divine heart. For he believed in hope against hope, nor did he consider his own body, already dead, nor the dead womb of Sarah; but he did not waver at God's promise through unbelief, and was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, with the firm persuasion that he who had promised could also perform it. (Rom. 4.) Yet this is that faith which Moses says was imputed to him for righteousness. (Gen. 12.)

units.la: Porrò vt Stephanus Abrahami exemplo Iudaeos ad fidem excitare studet: ita nostrae etiam institutioni eiusdem exempli consyderatio seruire debet. Nam vt Paulus ait, non propter illum tantum, sed etiam propter nos haec scripta sunt, quibus simili ratione fides ad iustitiam imputabitur, si Abrahami exemplum sedulo imitemur. Rom. 4. Plurimum vero ad fidei confirmationem facit, si obseruemus, vt deus suos exercere soleat, dum ita res huius mundi moderatur, vt omnis harum euentus cum ipsius promissionibus pugnare videatur, quod in Abrahami exemplo clarius est, quam vt multis repeti debeat. Nec melior fuit filij Isaaci, & postea Iacobi fors. Hic certe, cum primogeniturae ius in ipsum deus transtulisset, & promissionibus amplissimis exornasset, Esau fratris metu ad redire cogitur, vnde auus Abraham venerat, & ibi apud iniquum aununculum durissimam seruitutem uitutem seruit, Esauo interim opibus affluente & regnum constituente, qui à Deo reiectus erat. Idem Dauidi accidisse legimus, qui cum regni Israelitici promissionem à Deo accepisset, priusquam ad regni solium peruenirat, in exilium eiectus, publicus regni & communis patriae hostis declaratur. Nec alia omnium nostrum fors est, si salutis nostrae negotium & regni Christi, cui per fidem inserti sumus, conditionem expendamus. Promittitur in Christum credentibus pax, incolumitas, gaudium, salus, victoria item contra mundum & satanam mundi principem. At si rerum huius seculi cursum consyderes, perpetuis turbis, aduersis & calamitatibus fideles exerceri, & tyrannorum libidini subiacere videbis. Num vero dum ista fiunt, Dei veritatem in dubium vocabimus, & falsis promissis nos lactatos esse conqueremur? Nequaquam. Imo discamus potius, non de hoc mundo esse Christi regnum, nec iuxta externam rerum faciem de illo iudicari debere. Discamus item longius extendere fidei oculos, & in Dei promissiones respicere, quae nunquam fallent, vtue infelix hic mundus caelum terris miscere conetur. Dei enim vox est: Non prophanabo foedus meum, quod egressum est de labiis meis non mutabo. Psal.89. Videt ille gentium & regum consilia, nec videt modo, sed etiam dissipat, ipsius vero consilium aeternum stabit. Psal.2. & 33. Atqui hoc maxime de salutis nostrae promissionibus intelligi debet, quarum veritas inuiolabilis est, eo quod Christo Iesu nituntur, contra quem nec inferorum portae praevalere possunt. Matth.17. Huic quicunque iuxta Abrahami exemplum constanter adhaerent, experientur tandem, se & mundo & diabolo superiores fore, & pedibus suis eos substerni videbunt, qui nunc immani insolentia illorum capitibus insultant. Vincunt enim in omnibus per eum qui dilexit nos, & filium suum pro nobis tradidit: adeo ut cum Paulo exclamare possint: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? Rom.8.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Stephen labours to stir the Jews to faith by Abraham's example, so the consideration of the same example ought to serve our instruction too. For as Paul says, these things were written not for his sake alone but for ours too, to whom faith will likewise be imputed for righteousness, if we diligently imitate Abraham's example. (Rom. 4.) It contributes very much to the strengthening of faith if we observe how God is accustomed to exercise his own people, while he so governs the affairs of this world that the outcome of all of them seems to conflict with his promises; which is clearer in Abraham's example than it needs to be repeated at length. Nor was the lot of Isaac's son, and afterwards of Jacob, any better. Jacob, when God had transferred the right of the firstborn to him and adorned him with the most ample promises, was forced by fear of his brother Esau to return to where his grandfather Abraham had come from, and there he served as a slave, most harshly, under a dishonest uncle, while Esau, who had been rejected by God, grew rich and established a kingdom. We read that the same happened to David, who, although he had received from God the promise of the kingdom of Israel, before he reached the throne of the kingdom was cast into exile and declared a public enemy of the kingdom and of the common fatherland. Nor is the lot of all of us any different, if we weigh the business of our salvation and the condition of the kingdom of Christ, into which we are grafted through faith. Peace, safety, joy, salvation, and likewise victory over the world and over Satan, the prince of this world, are promised to those who believe in Christ. But if you consider the course of the affairs of this age, you will see the faithful exercised by constant tumults, adversities and calamities, and subject to the lust of tyrants. Shall we then, while these things happen, call God's truth into doubt and complain that we have been elated by false promises? By no means. Rather let us learn that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, nor should it be judged by the outward appearance of things. Let us also learn to stretch the eyes of faith further and to look to God's promises, which never fail, however much this unhappy world may try to mix heaven with earth. For this is the voice of God: "My covenant I will not profane, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips." (Ps. 89.) He sees the counsels of the nations and of kings, and not only sees them but also scatters them; but his own counsel stands for ever. (Ps. 2 and 33.) And this must be understood above all of the promises of our salvation, whose truth is inviolable, because they rest on Jesus Christ, against whom the gates of hell cannot prevail. (Matt. 17.) Whoever constantly cleaves to him after Abraham's example will at last experience that they will be superior both to the world and to the devil, and they will see those who now insult their heads with monstrous insolence placed under their feet. For they conquer in all things through him who loved us and gave his Son for us; so that with Paul they can cry out: "If God be for us, who can be against us? Who shall separate us from the love of God?" (Rom. 8.)

units.la: Pergit vero in coepta narratione Stephanus, & oraculum Dei de Israelitica gentis seruitute in Aegypto recenset, quod Genes.15.cap.habetur. Et quamuis de hac infra quoque dicturus sit, huius tamen loci mentionem facere voluit, ne fortuito & nullo praefinito Dei consilio ista accidisse putaretur. Ad eundem vero finem, quo & priora omnia, locus hic referri debet. Nam & Abrahami fides elucet ex eo, quod nec tristi vaticinio succubuit, & simul docet olim in Aegypto ecclesiam fuisse, quam Deus pro suo peculio agnouerit, & quam singulari beneficio in libertatem asseruerit, cum nec templi haberent, nec Leuiticis ceremoniis vterentur. Unde quivis colliget, gratiam Dei & salutem non externis sacris alligatam esse, sed à mera Dei gratia pendere, quae non alio modo, quam fide vera percipi potuit. Constabat enim hoc, Aegyptiacam liberationem futuræ salutis typum fuisse. Quod si ergo corporum seruitus non nisi potenti manu Dei depelli potuit, quis non videat, sine Dei ope & gratia in animarum seruitute excutienda, humanis viribus aut meritis nihil profici posse? SVNT autem haec quoque, ad nostram institutionem transferenda, eo quod ecclesiae Dei conditionem omnem ceu in speculo contemplandam nobis proponunt.
units.tr: Stephen then continues his narrative and recounts God's oracle about the servitude of the Israelite people in Egypt, which is found in Genesis 15. Although he will speak of this again later, he wanted to mention it here so that these events would not seem to have happened by chance and without any predetermined counsel of God. This passage should also be referred to the same purpose as everything before it. For Abraham's faith shines out in this, that he did not give way to the sad prophecy, and at the same time it teaches that the Church existed even then in Egypt, a people whom God acknowledged as his own possession and whom he rescued into liberty by a singular benefit, though they had neither a temple nor used the Levitical ceremonies. From this anyone may gather that God's grace and salvation are not tied to external rites but depend on God's mere grace, which could be received in no other way than by true faith. For this was clear: the Egyptian deliverance was a type of future salvation. If, then, the servitude of the body could be thrown off only by the mighty hand of God, who does not see that in casting off the servitude of souls nothing can be achieved by human strength or merits, without God's help and grace? These things are also to be applied to our instruction, since they set before us, as in a mirror, the whole condition of the Church of God to be contemplated.

units.la: Primo enim obseruandum venit, quod de semine Abrahami loquens, cui Chananaicae terrae haereditas promissa erat, dicit: Inquilinum erit in terra aliena, & subijcient illud seruituti, & male tractabunt annis quadringentis. Docent haec, quae nam fidelium in terris sit conditio. Hos enim verum illud Abrahami semen fuie filios esse, tum Christus, tum Paulus testantur. Iohan. 7. Rom.9. Est his promissa caelestis patriae hereditas, Christo teste, qui ait: Noli timere pusillegrex, quia complacitum est patri vestro vobis dare regnum. Luc.12. Item: Volo pater, vt vbi ego sum, etiam hi sint mecum. Iohan.17. Et rursum: In domo patris mei mansiones multae sunt: Vado vobis praeturus locum. Et iterum veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum, vt vbi sum ego, & vos sitis. Iohan.14. Quo Paulus respexisse videtur, cum πολίτευμα nostrum in caelis esse dicit, vnde saluatorem Christum expectamus. Phil.3. Quamuis vero caelestis patriae haeredes simus, nondum tamen apparet mundo, nos tales aliquando fore, sed interea temporis in terra aliena, id est, mundo hoc peregrinamur, nec quicquam habemus proprij. Et peregrinationis instar esse vitam hanc, non scripturae modo oraculis, sed experientia quotidiana docemur, cum nudi mundum hunc ingrediamur, & nudi exeamus. 1. Tim.6. Nec peregrini modo sumus, verumetiam à seculi huius filijs, qui sibi ipsis mundi dominium vendicant, oppressi infinitis modis affligimur, vt non temere propheta ecclesiam saxo conferat, quo subleuando omnes populi vires suas exercere & ostentare soleant. Zach.12. Et historiae docent, ab mundi origine persecutionibus obnoxios fuisse, quotquot Deo se per veram fidem consecrauerunt.
units.tr: First, we must notice that, speaking of Abraham's seed, to whom the inheritance of the land of Canaan was promised, he says: "Your seed shall be a stranger in a land not theirs, and they shall enslave it and afflict it for four hundred years." These words teach what the condition of the faithful on earth is. For both Christ and Paul testify that those who are the true seed of Abraham are the children of Abraham: John 8; Romans 9. To these is promised the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland, as Christ testifies, who says: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" (Luke 12). Likewise: "Father, I will that where I am, there these also may be with me" (John 17). And again: "In my Father's house are many mansions. I go to prepare a place for you. And I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, there you may be also" (John 14). To this Paul seems to have looked when he says that "our citizenship [πολίτευμα] is in heaven, from which we await the Saviour Christ" (Philippians 3). Although we are heirs of the heavenly fatherland, it does not yet appear to the world that we will ever be such; meanwhile we are strangers in a foreign land, that is, we are pilgrims in this world, and we possess nothing of our own. That this life is like a pilgrimage we are taught not only by the oracles of Scripture but by daily experience, since we enter this world naked and leave it naked (1 Timothy 6). And we are not only pilgrims, but we are also oppressed and afflicted in countless ways by the sons of this age, who claim dominion of the world for themselves. So the prophet does not without reason compare the Church to a stone, by lifting which all peoples are accustomed to test and display their strength (Zechariah 12). And histories teach that, from the beginning of the world, all who have consecrated themselves to God through true faith have been exposed to persecutions.

units.la: Narrandi vero initium ab Abrahamo sumit, cuius nomine illi maximè gloriabantur. Et primò quidem, illum cum adhuc trans fluuium inter alienorum deorum cultores versaretur, ex mera gratia ad terra Chananaica (quæ cœlestis patriæ typus est) euocatum esse ait, cum nec templum adhuc staret, nec instituta essent legales ceremoniæ. Et in Abrahamo nihil præter fidei obedientiam in scripturis prædicari docet, qua deum vocantem secutus, & oblatam sibi gratiam amplexus sit. Quo exemplo Iudæorum proceres extimulare conatur, ut omissa superstitiosa cæremoniarum obseruatione, Christum Iesum, vnicum verè salutis authorem firma fide recipiant. Cæterum quia carnis iudicio fides non tanti momenti res esse videtur, quæ salutem nobis conciliare possit, in Abrahami fide illustranda diligenter versatur Stephanus, vt ostendat, eam fidei virtutem esse, quæ omnes hominis vires & humanæ rationis captum longè superet. Per hanc enim Abraham patriæ dulcis desyderium, cognatorum conuersationem, opum & honorum splendorem, itinerum labores & molestias, solicitudines, curas, denique omne id, quod carni nostræ vel iucundum vel aduersum est, ita superauit, vt absque omni mora & tergiuersatione deo vocanti obediret. Ad eandem verò demonstrationem præsens quoque locus facit, quo insignis illa Abrahami fides plenius illustratur, si quo modo illius studium & amorem in illis possit accendere: quo cum nobis quoque opus sit, diligenter singula consyderare proderit.
units.tr: Moses begins his narrative with Abraham, in whose name the Jews especially gloried. And first he says that Abraham, while he was still living across the river among worshippers of foreign gods, was called out of sheer grace into the land of Canaan (which is a type of the heavenly fatherland), at a time when the temple did not yet stand and the legal ceremonies had not been instituted. And he teaches that in Abraham nothing is proclaimed in the Scriptures except obedience of faith, by which he followed God calling him and embraced the grace offered to him. By this example Stephen tries to rouse the leaders of the Jews, so that, setting aside the superstitious observance of ceremonies, they may receive Jesus Christ, the only true author of salvation, with firm faith. But because by carnal judgment faith seems a matter of little weight to win salvation for us, Stephen labours diligently in illustrating Abraham's faith, so that he may show that it is that virtue of faith which far surpasses all human strength and the grasp of human reason. For through this faith Abraham overcame the sweet desire of his homeland, the company of his kinsfolk, the splendour of wealth and honours, the labours and troubles of journeys, anxieties, cares, and finally everything that is either pleasant or hostile to our flesh, so that without any delay or evasion he obeyed God calling him. And the present passage also serves this same demonstration, by which that remarkable faith of Abraham is more fully illustrated, if somehow it can kindle in us a zeal and love for it. Since we also need this, it will be useful to consider each point carefully.

units.la: Valet autem exponere Stephanus, quid cum Abrahamo, postquam in terram promissam venit, gestum sit, & sic ait: Et non dedit illi deus hereditatem in ea, ne vestigium quidem pedis. Sed promisit illi eam se daturum in possessionem, & semini eius post ipsum, cum illi non esset filius. Quibus verbis tria continentur, quæ ad fidei Abrahami amplificationem faciunt. Primò, vbi per multos labores & multa pericula in terram diuinitus promissam & monstratam ventum est, non vacuam inuenit, sed à Chananæis, ferocissima gente, occupatam. Et tam abfuit, vt illam possideret, vt ne pedis quidem vestigium posset suum dicere. Imò nouis subinde infortunijs excipitur. Nam vix tenetorijs fixis, fame compulsus in Ægypeum abit. Inde reuersus, propter pastorum iurgia à nepote suo Lot separatur, qui vnicum inter infestas gentes solatium videri poterat. Nec multò post periculoso bello contra Orientis reges implicatur. Et vt multa alia omittamus, Sara vxore mortua, sepultura locum ab Ephrone Hethæo emit. Annon ergo spe sua falsus videri poterat? Deinde, quid inter tot & tantas ærumnas Abrahamum sustentarit, docet: nimirum promissio, quam illi deus terram illam spoponderat. At quàm graue sit nudæ promissioni inniti, si nihil aliud sit quo confirmeris, experientia quotidiana discimus, maximè si rerum euentus cum promissionibus pugnare videantur: quod hic euenisse, modò diximus. Sed tertium accedit longè grauissimum, quòd nimirum dei promissio humanæ sapientiæ ridicula videri poterat. Promittebat enim terram hanc feminis siue posteritati Abrahamicæ deus, cum ille filium non haberet aliquem, nec generationi propter ætatem posthac idoneus esset, vt pote prope centenarius, & coniugem Saram hucusque sterilem esse sensisset. Quis ergo non videat quàm multis quamq; validis arietibus Abrahami fides oppugnata & concussa sit, & quàm graues de dei promissis dubitandi causas habuerit? At nihil horum diuinum illud pectus expugnare potuit. Nam præter spem sub spe credidit, nec consyderauit suum ipsius corpus iam emortuum, nec emortuam vuluam Sarae, verum ad promissionem dei non hæsitabat per incredulitatem, sed robustus factus est fide, tribuens gloriam deo, certa persuasione concepta, quòd is qui promiserat, idem posset etiam præstare. Rom. 4. Atqui hæc illa fides est, quam Moses illi ad iustitiam imputatam fuisse dicit. Gene. 12.
units.tr: Stephen goes on to explain what happened to Abraham after he came into the promised land, and says: "And God gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth. But he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his seed after him, though he had no child." In these words three things are contained, which serve to magnify Abraham's faith. First, when after many labours and many dangers he came into the land divinely promised and pointed out to him, he found it not empty but occupied by the Canaanites, a most fierce people. And so far was he from possessing it that he could not even call a footprint his own. Indeed, new misfortunes followed him at every turn. Hardly had he pitched his tents when, driven by famine, he went down into Egypt. Returning from there, because of quarrels among the herdsmen he was separated from his nephew Lot, who alone seemed to be a consolation among hostile nations. Not long after, he became entangled in a dangerous war against the kings of the East. And to pass over many other things: when his wife Sarah had died, he bought a burial place from Ephron the Hittite. Could he not then seem to have been deceived in his hope? Next, he teaches what sustained Abraham amid so many and so great distresses: namely, the promise which God had given him of that land. But how hard it is to rely on a bare promise, if nothing else is there by which you may be confirmed, we learn from daily experience, especially when the outcome of events seems to contradict the promises; and this, as we have just said, happened here. But a third thing is added, far the most serious: namely, that God's promise could seem ridiculous to human wisdom. For God was promising this land to Abraham's seed or posterity, when Abraham had no son, and was no longer fit for begetting children, being nearly a hundred years old, and he had perceived that his wife Sarah was barren up to that time. Who, then, does not see how many and how strong battering rams assailed and shook Abraham's faith, and how serious were the causes he had for doubting God's promises? But none of these things could overcome that divine heart. For beyond hope he believed in hope, nor did he consider his own body already dead, nor the dead womb of Sarah; but he did not waver in unbelief at God's promise, but was made strong in faith, giving glory to God, with the firm persuasion that he who had promised could also perform. (Romans 4.) Indeed, this is that faith which Moses says was reckoned to him for righteousness (Genesis 15).

units.la: Porrò vt Stephanus Abrahami exemplo Iudæos ad fidem excitare studet: ita nostræ etiam institutioni eiusdem exempli consyderatio seruire debet. Nam vt Paulus ait, non propter illum tantum, sed etiam propter nos hæc scripta sunt, quibus simili ratione fides ad iustitiam imputabitur, si Abrahami exemplum sedulo imitemur. Rom. 4. Plurimum verò ad fidei confirmationem facit, si obseruemus, vt deus suos exercere soleat, dum ita res huius mundi moderatur, vt omnis harum euentus cum ipsius promissionibus pugnare videatur, quod in Abrahami exemplo clarius est, quàm vt multis repeti debeat. Nec melior fuit filij Isaaci, & postea Iacobi fors. Hic certè, cum primogeniturae ius in ipsum deus transtulisset, & promissionibus amplissimis exornasset, Esaui fratris metu ò redire cogitur, vnde auus Abraham venerat, & ibi apud iniquum auunculum durissimam seruitutem
units.tr: Moreover, just as Stephen seeks by the example of Abraham to rouse the Jews to faith, so too the consideration of the same example ought to serve our instruction. For as Paul says, these things were written not for him alone, but for us also, to whom in a similar way faith will be reckoned for righteousness if we diligently imitate Abraham's example (Romans 4). And it contributes very much to the confirmation of faith if we observe how God is accustomed to exercise his own people, while he so governs the affairs of this world that the outcome of all of them seems to conflict with his promises; this is clearer in Abraham's example than that it needs to be repeated at length. Nor was the lot of Isaac's son, and afterwards of Jacob, any better. He, certainly, when God had transferred the right of the firstborn to him and adorned him with the most ample promises, was compelled by fear of his brother Esau to flee back to where his grandfather Abraham had come from, and there, among an unjust uncle, endured the harshest servitude

units.la: Deus suorum fidem & patientiam exercet.
units.tr: God exercises the faith and patience of his people.

units.la: Abrahami fides illustratur. uitutem seruit, Esauo interim epibus affluente & regnum cõstituente, qui à Deo reiectus erat. Idem Dauidi accidisse legimus, qui cum regni Israelitici promissionem à Deo accepisset, priusquàm ad regni solium peruenisset, in exilium eiectus, publicus regni & communis patriæ hostis declaratur. Nec alia omnium nostrûm fors est, si salutis nostræ negotium & regni Christi, cui per fidem inserti sumus, conditionem expendamus. Promittitur in Christum credentibus pax, incolumitas, gaudium, salus, victoria item contra mundum & satanam mundi principem. At si rerum huius seculi cursum considereS, perpetuis turbis, aduersis & calamitatibus fideles exerceri, & tyrannorum libidini subiacere videbis. Num verò dum ista fiunt, Dei veritatem in dubium vocabimus, & falsis promissis nos laetatos esse conqueremur? Nequaquam. Imò discamus potius, non de hoc mundo esse Christi regnum, nec iuxta externam rerum faciem de illo iudicari debere. Discamus item longius extendere fidei oculos, & in Dei promissiones respicere, quæ nunquam fallent, ut infelix hic mundus cælum terræ miscere conetur. Dei enim vox est: Non prophanabo fœdus meum, quod egressum est de labiis meis non mutabo. Psal.89. Videt ille gentium & regum consilia, nec videt modò, sed etiam dissipat, ipsius verò consilium æternum stabit. Psal.2. & 33. Atqui hoc maximè de salutis nostræ promissionibus intelligi debet, quarum veritas inuiolabilis est, eò quòd Christo Iesu nituntur, contra quem nec inferorum portæ prævalere possunt. Matth.17. Huic quicunque iuxta Abrahami exemplum constanter adhærent, experientur tandem, se & mundo & diabolo superiores fore, & pedibus suis eos substerni videbunt, qui nunc immani insolentia illorum capitibus insultant. Vincunt enim in omnibus per eum qui dilexit nos, & filium suum pro nobis tradidit: adeò ut cum Paulo exclamare possint: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? Rom.8.
units.tr: Abraham's faith is illustrated. ...serving in slavery, while Esau meanwhile, abounding in wealth, was establishing a kingdom, he who had been rejected by God. We read that the same thing happened to David, who, although he had received from God the promise of the kingdom of Israel, was driven into exile before he came to the throne and was declared a public enemy of the kingdom and of his common homeland. Our own lot is no different if we weigh the matter of our salvation and the kingdom of Christ, into which we have been grafted through faith. To those who believe in Christ are promised peace, safety, joy, salvation, and likewise victory against the world and Satan, the prince of this world. But if you consider the course of affairs in this age, you will see the faithful harassed by constant disturbances, adversities and calamities, and subject to the lust of tyrants. Shall we then, while these things are happening, call God's truth into doubt, and complain that we have been made happy by false promises? By no means. Rather let us learn that the kingdom of Christ is not of this world, and that it must not be judged by the outward appearance of things. Let us also learn to extend the eyes of faith further, and to look to God's promises, which never fail, however much this unhappy world may try to mix heaven with earth. For this is the voice of God: "I will not profane my covenant, nor alter the thing that has gone out of my lips" (Ps. 89). He sees the counsels of the nations and of kings, and not only sees them but also scatters them; but his own counsel will stand forever (Ps. 2 and 33). And this must be understood especially of the promises of our salvation, whose truth is inviolable, because they rest upon Christ Jesus, against whom the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. 16). Whoever clings constantly to him, after Abraham's example, will at last experience that they are superior to both the world and the devil, and they will see those trampled under their feet who now insult their heads with monstrous arrogance. For they conquer in all things through him who loved us and gave his Son for us; so that, with Paul, they can cry out: "If God is for us, who can be against us? Who shall separate us from the love of God?" (Rom. 8).

units.la: Pergit verò in cœpta narratione Stephanus, & oraculum Dei de Israelitica gentis seruitute in Ægypto recenset, quod Genes.15.cap.habetur. Et quamuis de hac infra quoque dicturus sit, huius tamen loci mentionem facere voluit, ne fortuitò & nullo præfinito Dei consilio ista accidisse putaretur. Ad eundem verò finem, quò & priora omnia, locus hic referri debet. Nam & Abrahami fides elucet ex eo, quòd nec tristi vaticinio succubuit, & simul docet olim in Ægypto ecclesiam fuisse, quam Deus pro suo peculio agnouerit, & quam singulari beneficio in libertatem asseruerit, cùm nec templū haberent, nec Leuiticis cæremoniis uterentur. Unde quivis colliget, gratiam Dei & salutem non externis sacris alligatam esse, sed à mera Dei gratia pendere, quæ non alio modo, quàm fide vera percipi possit. Constabat enim hoc, Ægyptiacam liberationem futuræ salutis typum fuisse. Quòd si ergo corporum seruitus non nisi potenti manu Dei depelli potuit, quis non videat, sine Dei ope & gratia in animarum seruitute excutienda, humanis viribus aut meritis nihil profici posse? SVNT autem hæc quoq; ad nostram institutionem transferenda, eò quòd ecclesiæ Dei conditionem omnem ceu in speculo contemplandam nobis proponunt.
units.tr: Stephen, however, continues his narrative and recounts God's oracle about the servitude of the Israelite people in Egypt, which is found in Genesis 15. And although he will speak of this again below, he wished to mention it here, lest these things be thought to have happened by chance and without any predetermined counsel of God. For the same purpose, to which all the earlier material is also directed, this passage ought to be referred. For Abraham's faith shines forth from the fact that he did not give way to the sad prophecy, and at the same time it teaches that there was once a Church in Egypt which God acknowledged as his own possession, and which he claimed for liberty by a singular kindness, although they had neither a temple nor used the Levitical ceremonies. Hence anyone may conclude that God's grace and salvation are not bound to external rites, but depend on the mere grace of God, which can be received in no other way than by true faith. For it was established that the Egyptian deliverance was a type of future salvation. If then the bondage of bodies could be cast off only by the mighty hand of God, who does not see that, without God's help and grace, nothing can be achieved by human strength or merits in shaking off the bondage of souls? These things, moreover, are also to be applied to our instruction, since they set before us the whole condition of the Church, to be contemplated as in a mirror.

Docent hæc, quæ nam fidelium in terris sit conditio. Hos enim verum illud Abrahami semen siue filios esse, tum Christus, tum Paulus testantur. Iohan. 7. Rom.9. Est his promissa cœlestis patriæ hereditas, Christo teste, qui ait: Noli timere pusillegrex, quia complacitum est patri vestro vobis dare regnum. Luc.12. Item: Volo pater, ut ubi ego sum, etiam hi sint mecum. Iohan.17. Et rursum: In domo patris mei mansiones multæ sunt: Vado vobis paraturus locum. Et iterum veniam, & assumam vos ad meipsum, ut ubi sum ego, & vos sitis. Iohan.14. Quò Paulus respexisse videtur, cùm πολίτευμα nostrum in cœlis esse dicit, unde saluatorem Christum expectamus. Phil.3. Quamuis verò cœlestis patriæ hæredes simus, nondum tamen apparet mundo, nos tales aliquando fore, sed interea temporis in terra aliena, id est, mundo hoc peregrinamur, nec quicquam habemus proprij. Et peregrinationis instar esse vitam hanc, non scripturæ modò oraculis, sed experientia quotidiana docemur, cùm nudi mundum hunc ingrediamur, & nudi exeamus. 1. Tim.6. Nec peregrini modò fumus, uerumetiam à seculi huius filijs, qui fibijpsis mundi dominium vendicant, oppressi infinitis modis affligimur, ut non temere propheta ecclesiam saxo conferat, quæ subleuando omnes populi vires suas exercere & ostentare soleant. Zach.12. Et historiæ docent, ab ipsa mundi origine persecutionibus obnoxios fuisse, quotquot Deo se per veram fidem consecrauerunt. runt. Quorum nos meminisse oportet, ne ijs, quae nostro seculo contingunt, tanquam nova & insoli-tis offendamur. 1. Pet. 4. Illud autem pro confesso habeamus, nihil nobis fortuito accidere, sed certo & praefinito divinae providentiae consilio, quae res omnes iustissimè moderatur. Nec quicquam contra nos posset mundus hic aut huius princeps satan, nisi dominus permitteret. Permittit vero is, non quod nostris calamitatibus & eiulatibus gaudeat, tyrannorum instar, sed quòd ingenitam & adhaeren-tem nobis carnis corruptionem hoc modo cohercendam esse novit, qua fit, ut modò ad opum contem-plationem, modò ad honorum splendorem, modò ad voluptatum carnalium desyderia attoniti subsi-stamus, vel etiam à via salutis declinemus. Tum ergo noxium illum stuporem excuti, & carnis desy-deria per crucem restingui oportet, ut mundum hunc odisse discamus, & flagranti coelestis patriae amo-re accendamur. Nec fortem nobis in mundo meliorem promittamus, quando & mundus suum inge-nium, veritatis impatiens, perpetuò retinebit, & nostrae carnis corruptio utcunque corrigatur, leuiss-ima quaque occasione recurrit.
units.tr: First, we must observe what Stephen says about the seed of Abraham, to whom the inheritance of the land of Canaan was promised: "Your seed shall be a sojourner in a land not their own, and they shall be enslaved and ill-treated for four hundred years." These words teach what the condition of the faithful is in the world. For both Christ and Paul testify that these are the true seed or children of Abraham (John 7; Rom. 9). To them is promised the inheritance of the heavenly fatherland, as Christ testifies, who says: "Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" (Luke 12). Again: "Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me" (John 17). And again: "In my Father's house there are many dwelling places. I go to prepare a place for you. And I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you may be also" (John 14). To this Paul seems to have looked when he says that our citizenship [πολίτευμα] is in heaven, from which we await the Saviour Christ (Phil. 3). Although we are heirs of the heavenly fatherland, it does not yet appear to the world that we will ever be such; meanwhile we are pilgrims in a land not our own, that is, in this world, and we possess nothing of our own. That this life is like a pilgrimage we are taught not only by the oracles of Scripture but also by daily experience, since we enter this world naked and leave it naked (1 Tim. 6). And we are not only pilgrims, but also, oppressed by the sons of this age, who claim dominion of the world for themselves, we are afflicted in infinite ways; so the prophet is not without reason compared the Church to a stone, which all the peoples who try to lift it are accustomed to test and display their strength upon (Zech. 12). And histories teach that, from the very beginning of the world, all who consecrated themselves to God through true faith have been liable to persecutions. We ought to remember them, lest we be offended by what happens in our age as if it were something new and unusual (1 Pet. 4). Let us, moreover, hold this as settled: nothing happens to us by chance, but by the certain and predetermined counsel of divine providence, which governs all things most justly. Nor could this world, or Satan its prince, do anything against us unless the Lord permitted it. He permits it, not because he rejoices in our calamities and laments, like a tyrant, but because he knows that the inborn corruption of the flesh, which clings to us, must be restrained in this way; the result is that we stand dazzled, now gazing at riches, now at the splendour of honours, now at the desires of carnal pleasures, or even stray from the way of salvation. Therefore that harmful torpor must be shaken off, and the desires of the flesh must be quenched through the cross, so that we may learn to hate this world and be kindled with a burning love of the heavenly fatherland. Nor should we promise ourselves a better lot in the world, since the world, impatient of truth, will always keep its own nature, and the corruption of our flesh, however it may be corrected, runs back at the slightest occasion.

units.la: Interim summae consolationis loco nobis esse debet, quod hic Deus subijcit, dicens: Gentem, cui servierint, ego iudicabo. Est enim Deus iudex universae terrae, nec suo officio deest, licet interdum, nec im-piorum feroces & impios conatus, nec piorum afflictiones cernere & audire videatur. Quomodo enim non videret, qui oculum finxit? & quomodo non audiret, qui aurem fecit? Psal. 94. Non autem, ut otiosi spectatores, mundi huius theatrum intuetur, sed ut iustus iudex res omnes mortalium spe-ctat. Et quia nihil illi carius est quam ecclesia, quam filij sui sanguine redemptam voluit, neminem aduersus illam impune grassari patitur: imò pupillam oculi ipsius tangere putantur, quicunque fidos Dei cultores audacius tangunt. Zach. 2. Extant passim horrenda in tales iudiciorum Dei exem-pla, inter quae primo loco numerari meretur, quod in Aegyptios, sicuti hic minatus est, exercuit. Ex-perti sunt idem Assyrij, qui gravissimas suae in populum Dei tyrannidis poenas dederunt. Nec diu con-tra hunc impune saevijt Antiochus. Quid Herodi evenerit, notius est, quàm ut multis narrari debe-at. Quod si vero ea, quae Christi incarnationem secuta sunt, consyderes, neminem horrendas Dei iudi-cij manus evasisse videbis, qui ecclesiam persequi ausus fuit. Primus in horum numero est Nero, qui cum Romanos cives urbis incendium, cuius ipse author fuerat, iniquius ferre sentiret, Christianos tanti flagitij insimulavit, & omni suppliciorum genere in illos grassatus est, sicuti Cornelius Ta-citus de illo prodidit. Et eò usque truculentissimi tyranni rabiem progredi passus est Deus, ut apostolo-rum quoque Petri & Pauli sanguinem fudisse legatur. Sed mox horribili iudicio suorum sangui-nem vindicavit dominus. Secuta enim pestis est, quae plus quàm triginta millia hominum absumpsit. Accessit pesti Romani exercitus clades in Britannia accepta, & defecerunt in Armenia provincia, nec sine publica infamia Romanae legiones sub iugum missae sunt. Et tandem ipsum tyrannum di-uina vindicta corripuit, qui à senatu hostis iudicatus, primò in turpi & ignobili fuga salutem quae-siuit, deinde vero ipse sua falsus, sibijpsi violentas manus intulit. Neronem imitatus Domitianus, ipse quoque Deum iudicem sensit, dum à domesticis suis confossus obijt. Traianus vero, licet crudelis aduersus Christianos edicta revocasset, Deum tamen iratum sensit. Nam aurea domus Romae con-flagravit, fames & pestis immaniter saevierunt, ac terraemotu non pauca Asiae, Galatiae & Graeciae oppida euersa sunt. Quartus tamen à Nerone ex Imperatorum ordine contra ecclesiam M. Anto-ninus Verus insurrexit: nec multò post Germanorum tumultus & immanis pestis inualuit, cuius cõtagio aliquot Italiae oppida & villae habitatoribus suis in universum exhaustae & euacuatae sunt.
units.tr: Meanwhile, as a source of the greatest consolation, we should bear in mind what God adds here: "The nation which they serve, I will judge." For God is the judge of all the earth, and he does not fail in his office, although at times he may seem neither to see nor to hear the fierce and impious attempts of the ungodly, nor the afflictions of the godly. For how should he not see, who formed the eye? And how should he not hear, who made the ear? (Ps. 94). He does not, however, look upon the theatre of this world like an idle spectator, but as a just judge he watches all the affairs of mortals. And since nothing is dearer to him than the Church, which he willed to redeem with the blood of his Son, he allows no one to rage against it with impunity; indeed, whoever boldly touches the faithful worshippers of God is thought to touch the apple of his eye (Zech. 2). Everywhere there are dreadful examples of God's judgments against such men, among which the first place deserves to be given to what he carried out against the Egyptians, just as he threatened here. The Assyrians too experienced this, who paid the most grievous penalties for their tyranny against the people of God. Nor did Antiochus rage long against him with impunity. What happened to Herod is too well known to need to be recounted at length. But if you consider those events which followed the incarnation of Christ, you will see that no one who dared to persecute the Church escaped the dreadful hand of God's judgment. Foremost in this number is Nero, who, when he perceived that the Roman citizens were more unhappy about the fire of the city, of which he himself was the author, charged the Christians with so great a crime and raged against them with every kind of punishment, as Cornelius Tacitus has reported of him. And God allowed the rage of this most savage tyrant to proceed so far that it is read that he also shed the blood of the apostles Peter and Paul. But the Lord soon avenged their blood by a dreadful judgment. For a plague followed, which carried off more than thirty thousand people. To the plague was added the defeat of the Roman army received in Britain, and the province of Armenia revolted, and Roman legions were sent under the yoke not without public disgrace. And at last divine vengeance seized the tyrant himself: declared an enemy by the senate, he first sought safety in a shameful and ignoble flight, and then, being himself deceived, he laid violent hands upon himself. Domitian, imitating Nero, also felt God as judge, when he died, stabbed by his own household. Trajan, although he had revoked his cruel edicts against the Christians, nevertheless felt God's anger. For the Golden House at Rome burned down, famine and plague raged dreadfully, and by an earthquake not a few towns of Asia, Galatia and Greece were overthrown. Fourth in the order of emperors after Nero, Marcus Antoninus Verus rose up against the Church; and not long after, a tumult of the Germans and a dreadful plague grew strong, by whose contagion several towns and villages of Italy were utterly drained and emptied of their inhabitants.

units.la: Quintam persecutionem L. Septimius Seuerus mouit, qui & bellis ciuilibus vexatus est, & in An-glia probè Eboracum praematura morte extinctus. Quorum exemplis cum parum moveretur Iu-lius Maximinus, sed impia audacia in ecclesiam fureret, iusto Dei iudicio euenit, ut unà cum filio à militibus discerperetur, acclamantibus universis, ne catulum quidem habendum esse à pessimo gene-re. Nec dissimilis multum exitus Decium mansit, qui & ipse post effusum Christi martyrum san-guinem, unà cum filio in solo barbarico perijt, adeò ut nec mortui cadauer ad sepulturam inueniri po-tuerit. Quid de Licinio Valeriano dicemus, octauo Christianorum persecutore? qui à Sapore Per-sarum rege captus, equum conscensuro tergum scabelli loco substernere coactus est. Val. Aurelianus vero, qui nonus in hoc ordine esse voluit, primum quidem fulmine ante pedes delapso territus, mox autem cum nulla institutae tyrannidis poenitentia duceretur, suorum insidijs occisus est. Cum vero post omnes hosce maiori conatu contra Christi ecclesiam sese armaret Diocletianus cum Maximia no & Galerio Maximino collegis, non obscure Dei ecclesiam suam vindicantis manum senserunt. Terramotu enim multa millia hominum absumpta fuisse leguntur. Diocletianus autem & Maximianus vno die imperium volentes deposuerunt: vel dolore, quòd non perfici posse viderent quod moliti fuerant, vel metu Constantini: Et ille quidem postea sibijpsi mortem consciuit, cùm Maxentium à Constantino victum & occisum esse audiuisset: hic verò cùm ad imperium redire cuperet, à Maxentio expulsus ad generum Constantinum confugit, cui cùm strueret insidias, filia maritum patri prætulit, & insidias detexit: Itaq; Massiliæ occisus est. Et hic exitus fuit duorum sæuissimorum tyrannorum, qui decennio toto ecclesiam crudeliter afflixerant. Galerius verò atrocissimo morbi incurabilis doloribus superatus, sanguinaria edicta, quibus Christianorum sanguis petebatur, reuocauit. Atqui omnia hæc intra trecentos annos vsq; ad Constantini magni Imperium eueniesse constat. Nec ab illo tempore quieuit dominus. Sed cùm Iulianus apostata tum aperta vi, tum dolo & fraude ecclesiâ infestaret, in acie victus, & conto vulneratus, exclamauit: Vicisti Galilæe, vicisti. Ita enim Christum per contemptum nominare consucuerat. Possent his infiniti alij adnumerari, si opus esset. Nec recentiora desunt exempla, quibus nostro seculo iudiciorum suorum seueritate Deus in ecclesiæ suæ persecutores exercuit. Perpetuò igitur ratum erit, Deum suo iudicio de illis vindictam sumptu-rum, qui suum populum impia tyrannide vexare ausi fuerint. Debent hæc nostræ tum consolationi tum institutioni seruire. Cõsoletur enim nos, quòd Deo vindice ecclesiam defendi audimus, ne nos ab illo inter afflictiones negligi putemus. Simul verò admonemur, vt insanum priuatæ vindictæ studium deponamus, ac omne de hostibus nostris iudicium Deo commendemus, dicenti: Mea est vindicta, ego retribuam. Deut 32. Interim latius quoq; eadem doctrina extendi potest, vt à violenta quorumuis hominum oppressione abstineamus, nec dubitemus, Deum iniurias, quæ infirmioribus infe-runtur, vlcisci. Christi enim vox est: Qua mensura metimini, eadem vobis metientur alij. Matth. 7. Et propheta clamat: Væ qui prædaris, quoniam prædafies, &c. Isa. 33. Item: Væ ei, qui ædificat ci-uitatem in sanguine. Væ ei, qui adauget non sua. Habak. 2. Quò referri debent, quæ viduarum, or-phanorum & peregrinorum oppressoribus in lege sua Deus minitatur. Vide Exod. 22. In quorum consyderatione vtinam frequentius versarentur, qui hodie in mercenaria militia potissimâ viri lau-dem & rerumpub. salutem collocant.
units.tr: The fifth persecution was stirred up by Lucius Septimius Severus, who was harassed by civil wars and died prematurely at York in England. Although Julius Maximinus was little moved by these examples, he raged against the Church with impious boldness, and by the just judgment of God it happened that he was torn apart by the soldiers along with his son, while everyone shouted that not even a puppy should be kept from so wicked a breed. The end of Decius was not much different: after he had shed the blood of Christ's martyrs, he perished with his son in a barbarian land, so that not even his corpse could be found for burial. What shall we say of Licinius Valerian, the eighth persecutor of the Christians? He was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and was forced to lie down as a footstool for him when he was about to mount his horse. Valerian Aurelian, who wished to be ninth in this line, was first terrified when a thunderbolt fell at his feet, and afterwards, though he showed no repentance for his tyranny, he was killed in an ambush by his own men. When, after all these, Diocletian armed himself with greater effort against the Church of Christ, along with his colleagues Maximian and Galerius Maximinus, they clearly felt the hand of God defending his Church. For we read that many thousands of people were swept away by an earthquake. Diocletian and Maximian laid down the empire on the same day, either from grief that they could not see what they had planned carried through, or from fear of Constantine. Diocletian later took his own life when he heard that Maxentius had been defeated and killed by Constantine. Maximian, however, wanting to return to power, was driven out by Maxentius and fled to his son-in-law Constantine; when he plotted against Constantine, his daughter preferred her husband to her father and revealed the plot, and so he was killed at Massilia. This was the end of the two most savage tyrants, who for a whole decade had cruelly afflicted the Church. Galerius, overcome by the most dreadful pains of an incurable disease, revoked the bloody edicts by which the blood of Christians had been sought. Yet it is agreed that all these things happened within three hundred years, up to the rule of Constantine the Great. Nor did the Lord rest from that time on. For when Julian the apostate attacked the Church, sometimes by open force and sometimes by trickery and fraud, he was defeated in battle, and wounded by a spear, he cried out: "You have conquered, Galilean, you have conquered." For he had been accustomed to name Christ with contempt in this way. Countless others could be added to these, if there were need. Nor are more recent examples lacking, in which God in our own age has shown, by the severity of his judgments, his power against the persecutors of his Church. It will therefore always be certain that God, by his judgment, will take vengeance on those who have dared to harass his people with impious tyranny. These things ought to serve both our consolation and our instruction. For they console us, in that we hear the Church is defended by God as its avenger, so that we should not think we are neglected by him amid our afflictions. At the same time we are admonished to lay aside the mad zeal for private revenge, and to commit all judgment concerning our enemies to God, who says: "Vengeance is mine, I will repay" (Deut. 32). Moreover, this same teaching can be extended more widely, so that we abstain from the violent oppression of any men whatever, and do not doubt that God avenges the wrongs inflicted on the weaker. For it is Christ's word: "With what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you by others" (Matth. 7). And the prophet cries: "Woe to you who plunder, for you shall be plundered," etc. (Isa. 33). Likewise: "Woe to him who builds a city with blood; woe to him who increases what is not his" (Hab. 2). To this should be referred what God threatens in his law against the oppressors of widows, orphans and strangers. See Exod. 22. Would that those who today place the greatest praise of a man and the safety of the commonwealth in mercenary soldiering would dwell on these considerations more often.

units.la: Cæterum non ofcitanter dissimulari debet, quod de liberationis fine dominus addit, dicens: Et posthæc exibunt, & seruient mihi in hoc loco. Est hoc vniuersale præceptum, vt qui Deum libera-torem senserunt, illi seruiant, de quo etiam Psalmo 50. admonemur. Debet hoc ante omnia in salutis negotio consyderari. Liberati sumus è satanica tyrannide & horribili peccatorum seruitute, singu-lari Dei beneficio, qui filium suum pro nobis dare dignatus est. Exeamus ergo Ægyptum, & abie-ctis infelicis mundi studijs, Deo seruiamus in sanctimonia, puritate, innocentia, fide & dilectione non ficta: qua de re vide quæ passim in Apostolorum scriptis habentur. Rom. 6. Tit. 2. & 3. 1. Thess. 4. &c. Eadem eorum, qui ex alijs ærumnis liberati sunt, ratio sit. Qui ex morbis conualuerunt, sen-tiant sibi di-ctum esse, quod paralytico Christus dicit: Vide ne posthac peccaueris, ne quid tibi dete-rius accidat. Iohan. 5. Idem cogitent: qui ex egestate, fame, peste, bellorum tumultibus & quibuscun-que alijs calamitatibus erepti sunt. Admonebant de hoc olim sacrificia σωτήρια, quæ Deus pro ac-ceptis beneficijs sibi offerri volebat: & quæ gentibus quoq; in vsu fuerunt, quamuis à vero cultu alie-næ essent. Et in eum vsum à Christo tradita est Cœna mystica, quam veteres Eucharistiam, id est, gratiarumactionem vocarunt, quòd illam in commemorationem mortis Christi scirent esse in-stitutam. Nec potest non damnari illorum impietas, qui cum redemptionis beneficio glorientur, & quotidie Dei vindicis sui manum sentiant, illi tamen non seruiunt, sed se totos diaboli & peccati seruitio mancipant. Præcipuè verò animis nostris fixum inhæreat, quod vnicum Stephanus vrget, nos solius diuinæ gratiæ beneficio ex peccatorum & satanæ tyrannide liberatos esse, nec quicquam hic vel operibus nostris, vel frigidissimis ceremonijs tribui debere. Fide ergo ampleƈtamur benefi-cium hoc, & Deo liberatori seruiamus in spiritu & veritate, vt cum eodem cœlestis regni gaudio ö-lim fruamur per Iesum Christum, dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & pote-stas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet it must not be passed over carelessly what the Lord adds about the purpose of the deliverance, saying: "And after this they shall come out and serve me in this place." This is a general precept: that those who have felt God as their deliverer should serve him, which we are also reminded of in Psalm 50. This must be considered above all in the matter of salvation. We have been freed from satanic tyranny and the dreadful servitude of sins by the singular kindness of God, who deigned to give his Son for us. Let us therefore leave Egypt, and, casting aside the pursuits of this unhappy world, serve God in holiness, purity, innocence, faith and sincere love. On this matter see what is found throughout the writings of the apostles: Rom. 6; Tit. 2 and 3; 1 Thess. 4, etc. The same principle should hold for those who have been freed from other troubles. Those who have recovered from sickness should feel that what Christ said to the paralytic is said to them: "See that you sin no more, lest something worse befall you" (John 5). Let those think the same who have been rescued from poverty, famine, plague, the tumults of war and any other calamities. The sacrifices of salvation [σωτήρια], which God wished to be offered to him for benefits received, once reminded people of this, and they were also in use among the Gentiles, although they were alien to the true worship. And the mystical supper, which the ancients called the Eucharist, that is, thanksgiving, because they knew it had been instituted in remembrance of Christ's death, was handed down by Christ for this same purpose. The impiety of those cannot but be condemned who boast of the benefit of redemption, and who feel daily the hand of God their avenger, and yet do not serve him, but surrender themselves wholly to the service of the devil and sin. Above all, let this be firmly fixed in our minds, which Stephen alone urges: that we have been freed from the tyranny of sin and Satan by the benefit of divine grace alone, and that nothing should be attributed here either to our works or to the coldest ceremonies. Let us therefore embrace this benefit by faith, and serve God our deliverer in spirit and in truth, so that we may one day enjoy with him the joy of the heavenly kingdom, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom blessing, honour, glory and power are due for ever. Amen.

units.la: Liberati Deo seruiant.
units.tr: Those who have been set free should serve God.

units.la: CAPVT VII. HOMILIA XLV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 7. SERMON XLV.

units.la: Et dedit illi testamentum Circuncisionis: atque hic genuit Isaacum, & circuncidit eum octavo die. Et Isaac genuit Iacobum, & Iacob duodecim patriarchas. Et patriarchae invidia extimulati, Iosephum vendiderunt in Aegyptum. Et erat Deus cum illo, & eripuit eum ex omnibus afflictionibus eius: ac dedit illi gratiam & sapientiam coram Pharaone rege Aegypti: & constituit eum principem super Aegyptum & totam domum ipsius
units.tr: And he gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so he begat Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day. And Isaac begat Jacob, and Jacob begat the twelve patriarchs. And the patriarchs, moved by envy, sold Joseph into Egypt. But God was with him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions, and gave him favour and wisdom in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt; and he made him governor over Egypt and over all his house.

units.la: Diuus Stephanus accusatus fuit impietatis in Deum, legem & locum sanctum rotumq; cultum Leviticum. Accusationis causam inde sumpserunt aduersarij: quod doceret externa haec per Christum esse abrogata, nec illis homines iustificari posse, sed ex sola fide in Christum Iesum hominibus iustitiam & salutem obtingere, nec alium ceremoniarum legis fuisse vsum, quam vt salutis rationem, quae in vno Christo continetur, adumbrarent, ac illi adducerent homines. Quapropter gratui & feria defensionis ipsi opus erat, maxime apud eos, qui toti ceremonijs nitebantur. Hanc ergo sic instituit, vt ipsis rebus testetur, se ab impietate esse alienissimum. Nam quacunq; olim Deus cum patribus egit, diligenter recensetur: partim quidem vt offendat se veterem patrum fidem agnoscere & retinere: partim vero vt intelligant Iudaei, patres olim sine ceremonijs per solam fidem fuisse salvatos. Vnde quiuis facile colliget, nihil obstare, quo minus hodie etiam sine ceremonijs Leviticj cultus per fidem in Christum homines salvari possint, & proinde non esse impietatis accusandos, qui de huius abrogatione differunt. Ab Abrahamo autem exorsus, illius fidem, qua gratuitam Dei vocationem (nullo praecedente operum merito) secutus est, diligentissime illustrauit, vt Iudaeos ad illius imitationem extimularet. Caeterum quia non ignorabat sanctus Christi martyr, Circuncisionis & patrum gloriatione contra gratiam Dei in Christo collatam, Iudaeos cumprimis superbire, in coepta narratio ne sic pergit, vt vtranq; gloriationem ipsis excutiat.
units.tr: Saint Stephen was accused of impiety against God, the law, the holy place and the whole Levitical worship. His opponents took the ground of the accusation from this: that he taught these external things had been abrogated through Christ, that men could not be justified by them, but that righteousness and salvation come to men through faith alone in Christ Jesus, and that the ceremonies of the law had no other use than to foreshadow the way of salvation contained in Christ alone and to lead men to it. Therefore he needed a free and well-ordered defence, especially before those who relied entirely on the ceremonies. He therefore arranged his defence so that by the very facts he would show that he was far removed from impiety. For all the things God once did with the fathers are carefully recounted: partly so that he might show that he acknowledged and held to the ancient faith of the fathers, and partly so that the Jews might understand that the fathers were once saved without ceremonies, through faith alone. From this anyone can easily gather that nothing prevents men today from being saved through faith in Christ even without the ceremonies of the Levitical worship; and therefore those who argue about its abrogation are not to be accused of impiety. Beginning with Abraham, he set out very carefully his faith, by which he followed God's free call (with no prior merit of works), so as to stir the Jews to imitate him. Moreover, since the holy martyr of Christ knew that the Jews especially boasted, against the grace of God offered in Christ, of circumcision and of the fathers, he does not continue the narrative as begun in such a way as to strike down both of their boasts.

units.la: De Circuncisione paucis agit, dicens: Et dedit illi testamentum Circuncisionis, atque hic genuit Isaacum & circuncidit eum octavo die. Fatetur Circuncisionem a Deo institutam esse, sed dum ista praecedentibus connectit, illius fiduciam eo argumento demolitur, quod hanc post omnia ea, quae hucusque expositae sunt, Abrahamo datam esse docet. Postquam enim e Chaldaea euocatus, fidem suam multis & praeclaris indicijs publice declarauit, & per illam iustificatus est, Deus illi testamentum Circuncisionis dedit, id est, foedus siue testamentum cum illo constituit, quod circuncisione, tanquam signillo, confirmatum & obsignatum est. Vnde sequitur, circuncisione non iustificatum fuisse Abrahamum, sed hanc iustitiae, quam fide iam erat assecutus, fuisse signaculum. Quo argumento Paulus etiam ad Roma. cap. 4. vsus est. Et quemadmodum Abraham circuncisionis institutionem simplicem a domino accepit: ita eandem simplici obseruatione posteris commendauit. Nam Isaacum octavo natiuitatis die, iuxta domini institutum, nullo alio superstitiose ritu adhibito, circuncidit. Quod & Isaacum in Iacobo filio, & hunc rursum in duodecim filijs suis, qui Israelitice gentis patriarchae sunt, obseruauisse nemo pius dubitauerit. Voluit autem spiritus sanctus paucula, & fere nulla de hac re annotari, vt inde constaret, sanctissimos patres noluisse in externis haerere, sed diuinis foederis siue testamenti, quo salutis promissiones continebantur, maiorem, quam externae ceremoniae rationem habuisse. Faciunt ad horum explicationem, quae Genes. 17. cap. leguntur. Interim non obscure praeposteram Iudaeorum religionem reprehendit diuus Stephanus, qui circuncisionis gloriatione elati, foederis illius salutiferi, quod Christi merito obsignatum & ratificatum est, nulla cum tangebantur.
units.tr: He deals briefly with circumcision, saying: "And he gave him the covenant of circumcision; and so he begat Isaac, and circumcised him the eighth day." He confesses that circumcision was instituted by God, but in linking this to what precedes, he overthrows their confidence in it by the argument that it was given to Abraham after all the things that have been set out so far. For after he was called out of Chaldea and had publicly declared his faith by many and notable signs, and was justified through it, God gave him the covenant of circumcision: that is, God established with him a covenant or testament, which was confirmed and sealed by circumcision as by a seal. From this it follows that Abraham was not justified by circumcision, but that circumcision was a seal of the righteousness which he had already obtained by faith. Paul also used this argument in Romans chapter 4. And just as Abraham received the institution of circumcision from the Lord in its simplicity, so he commended the same to his posterity with simple observance. For he circumcised Isaac on the eighth day after his birth, according to the Lord's command, with no other superstitious rite added. No pious person will doubt that Isaac observed it in his son Jacob, and Jacob in turn in his twelve sons, who are the patriarchs of the Israelite nation. The Holy Spirit, however, wished only a few things, and almost nothing, to be recorded about this matter, so that it would be evident that the most holy fathers did not cling to external things, but gave greater regard to the divine covenant or testament, in which the promises of salvation were contained, than to the external ceremonies. Genesis chapter 17, which is read there, serves to explain these matters. Meanwhile, Saint Stephen clearly rebukes the perverse religion of the Jews, who, elated by their boasting in circumcision, made no mention of that saving covenant which was sealed and ratified by the merit of Christ.

units.la: At simul docet nos locus iste iudicare de sacramentis & locutionibus sacramentalibus, ex quibus hodie superstitiosi & contentiosi quidam indesinenter rixandi ansam accipiunt: quando in illis τὸν ψιλὸν literam vrgent, nec illarum mysteria aliori sensu inuestigant. Stephanus dicit, Abrahamo datum esse testamentum siue foedus Circuncisionis: neq; illud ex se dicit, sed in Dei verba respicit, qui olim Abrahamo dixerat: Hoc est foedus meum, quod obseruabitis inter me & vos, deinq; inter semen suum tuum posse te: Circuncidatur vobis omnis mas, &c. Quae si iuxta literam accipias, Circuncisio ipsum faedus fuisse dicetur: nec dubium est, quin hoc ipsum multis olim imposuerit, qui se omni pietatis officio defunctos putabant, quod circuncisi essent. At aliter ista accipi debere, res ipsa probat. Primo enim circuncisionem cordis Deus in lege & prophetis requirit. Deut.10. Ier.4. Deinde apud Ieremiam eos in foedere suo perstitisse negat, quos tamen circuncisos fuisse scimus. Iere.31. Accedit bis, quod Abraham priusquam circumcideretur, iam ante habuit, quae Deus in foedere suo pollicetur. Iam ante enim Deum vocantem secutus fuerat: iam ante promissiones eius fide apprehenderat: iam ante fidem illam Deus ipsi ad iustitiam imputarat, & proinde Christo erat insitus, sine quo nec iustitia nec salus hominibus obtingit. Foedus ergo dicitur Circuncisio, propter analogiam, quae in sacramentis est inter signa & res significatas, & quod hoc signaculo Deus testaretur, se pro confoederatis & haeredibus suis eos agnoscere qui foederi sui capita fideliter custodirent. Et ut per illam in populi Dei societatem recipiebantur, sic eadem in tentationibus fidem confirmabat, cui Deus propter carnis ingenium externa quoque fulcra adhibet. Eadem plane fuit ratio sacrificiorum, quae in lege & peccata & expiatio peccatorum dici solent. At si quis illic τὸ χαρτὸν seu literam vrgere velit, apostolum contra clamantem audiet: Non potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Et Deum per prophetas pro immundis & sceleratis eos reijcere scimus, qui in sacrificando assidui, nullis vel impensis vel laboribus parcebant. Num ergo Deum alibi vanis promissis suos lusisse dicemus, quando tam magnificis titulis sacrificia ornauit? Nequaquam. Sed eorum ratio certa & vera fuit, quod Christum adumbrarent, verum illam agnum Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi: quem qui tunc fide non fucata apprehendebant, propter illum a peccatis suis omnibus liberabantur. Si qui vero fide vacui sacrificarent, non magis gratas habebat Deus illorum victimas, quam si canem aut porcum immolauissent, sicut apud Isaiam ipse testatur. Quod si ad novi Testamenti sacramenta transfeamus, eandem horum quoque rationem esse reperies. Baptismum enim innouationis & regenerationis lauacrum vocat Apostolus. At quam multos, prob dolor, reperias, qui cum baptizati sint, nulla tamen praesferunt bominis innouati aut regenerati indicia? Nec tamen falsis elogijs baptismum spiritus sanctus commendat, sed ad illius vsum respicit: quod nimirum ex Dei instituto, regenerationem & innouationem, cuius nobis author est Christus, in electis vere & efficaciter obsignat. Sic in Coena mystica panis Christi corpus, vinum illius sanguis dicitur.
