Unde nonnulli colligunt, in illis verum Christi corpus & sanguinem realiter & substantialiter manducari atque bibi cum a pijs tum ab impijs. At nos ipsum Christum huius disceptationis arbitrum constituentes, ex re ipsa argumentamur ad hunc modum: Quisquis carnem Christi edit, & sanguinem eius bibit, in Christo manet, & Christus in illo. At multi, qui ex pane Coenae edunt, & eius poculo bibunt, neque in Christo manent ipsi, neque hunc in se manentem habent. Ergo in pane & vino hoc mystico Christi corpus & sanguis non realiter & substantialiter percipiuntur, neque externis hisce symbolis sunt alligata. Maiorem ipsius Christi esse negabit. Minorem probat ipsa rerum experientia, & vtinam non illorum exemplis probaretur, qui quam alieni sint a Christo, hoc ipso abunde docent, quod suis contentionibus horribilem ecclesiarum dissipationem inuehunt, & veros Christi Iesu cultores hostiliter persequuntur. Quis ergo non videat Coenae verba sacramentaliter accipi debere? Imo ut olim sacrificia non nisi illis prodepant, qui vera fide praediti, Christum ad illa ipsi adferebant: Ita nec ex Coena aliquis ad nos fructus redibit, nisi ipsi illum fide vera apprehensum adferamus, & animis supra caelos euectis per fidem illo vescamur: Qua quicunque destituuntur, a Christo alieni sunt, & Coenam sua hypocrisi prophanant, & proinde sibi ipsis iudicium edunt & bibunt. Sunt haec nobis in eum finem observanda, ut discamus errorem esse perniciosum, si externis actionibus addicti, in illis quaeramus, quod solius Christi est, & per solam fidem in illo inueniri potest. Ita ergo sacramentis vti conuenit, ut primo Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui externis quoque symbolis & actionibus fidem nostram fulcire dignatur, deinde vero illorum vsu excitati animos subuehamus ad ea, quae his adumbrantur: in primis autem ea praestemus, quae Deus in illis praescribit. Facit huc D. Augustini regula, quae in libris eius de Doct. Christiana hisce verbis traditur: Pauca quaedam promultis, eademque facilia, & intellectu augustissima, & obseruatione castissima, ipse Dominus & apostolica tradidit disciplina: sicuti est
units.tr: At the same time this passage teaches us how to judge concerning sacraments and sacramental expressions, from which some superstitious and contentious people today constantly take occasion to quarrel: when in these they insist on the bare letter [τὸν ψιλὸν] and do not search out their mysteries in any other sense. Stephen says that the covenant or testament of circumcision was given to Abraham; he does not say this on his own, but refers to the words of God, who once said to Abraham: "This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you, and between your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised," etc. If you take these words according to the letter, circumcision would be said to be the covenant itself; and there is no doubt that this very error once deceived many who thought they had discharged every duty of piety simply because they were circumcised. But the thing itself shows that these words must be understood otherwise. For, first, God requires in the law and the prophets circumcision of the heart (Deut. 10; Jer. 4). Next, through Jeremiah he denies that those remained in his covenant who, however, we know were circumcised (Jer. 31). Moreover, in addition to this, Abraham, before he was circumcised, already had what God promises in his covenant. For he had already followed God calling him; he had already laid hold of his promises by faith; God had already imputed that faith to him for righteousness; and therefore he was already grafted into Christ, without whom neither righteousness nor salvation comes to men. Circumcision is therefore called a covenant on account of the analogy that exists in sacraments between signs and the things signified, and because by this seal God attested that he acknowledged as his confederates and heirs those who faithfully kept the terms of his covenant. And just as by it they were received into the fellowship of God's people, so in temptations it confirmed their faith, for which God, on account of the weakness of the flesh, also provides external supports. The reasoning concerning sacrifices, which in the law are commonly called sins and the expiation of sins, is exactly the same. But if anyone wishes to insist there on the letter [τὸ χαρτὸν], he will hear the Apostle crying out against him: "It is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" (Heb. 10). And we know that God through the prophets rejected as unclean and wicked those who were diligent in sacrificing and spared no expense or labour. Shall we then say that God mocked his people elsewhere with empty promises, when he adorned sacrifices with such magnificent titles? By no means. Rather, their purpose was certain and true: that they foreshadowed Christ, the true Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; and those who then laid hold of him in unfeigned faith were freed from all their sins through him. But if any offered sacrifices without faith, God regarded their victims no more favourably than if they had sacrificed a dog or a pig, as he himself testifies through Isaiah. And if we turn to the sacraments of the New Testament, you will find that their reasoning is the same. For the Apostle calls baptism the washing of regeneration and renewal. Yet, alas, how many will you find who, though baptized, show no signs of a renewed or regenerated man? Nor does the Holy Spirit commend baptism with false praises, but looks to its use: namely, that by God's appointment it truly and effectively seals, in the elect, the regeneration and renewal of which Christ is our author. So in the mystical Supper the bread is called Christ's body and the wine his blood. From this some conclude that in these the true body and blood of Christ are really and substantially eaten and drunk, both by the godly and by the ungodly. But we, setting Christ himself as the judge of this dispute, argue from the matter itself in this way: whoever eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood abides in Christ, and Christ in him. But many who eat of the bread of the Supper and drink from its cup neither abide in Christ themselves nor have him abiding in them. Therefore in this mystical bread and wine the body and blood of Christ are not really and substantially received, nor are they bound to these external symbols. The major premise Christ himself will not deny. The minor premise is proved by experience itself, and would that it were not proved by the examples of those who by this very fact abundantly show how far removed they are from Christ, in that by their quarrels they bring about the dreadful dissipation of churches and hostilely persecute the true worshippers of Jesus Christ. Who then does not see that the words of the Supper must be understood sacramentally? Indeed, just as the sacrifices of old profited only those who, endowed with true faith, brought Christ to them, so no fruit from the Supper will return to us unless we ourselves bring him, apprehended by true faith, and feed on him by faith, our minds lifted above the heavens. Those who lack this are alien to Christ, profane the Supper by their hypocrisy, and therefore eat and drink judgment to themselves. These things are to be observed by us for this purpose: that we may learn it is a pernicious error, if, devoted to external actions, we seek in them what belongs to Christ alone and can be found in him through faith alone. Thus it is fitting to use the sacraments in such a way that, first, we acknowledge the goodness of God, who deigns to support our faith also with external signs and actions; and then, stirred by their use, we raise our minds to those things which are foreshadowed by them; and above all, that we perform those things which God prescribes in them. The rule of Saint Augustine, which is handed down in his book On Christian Doctrine in these words, bears on this: "The Lord himself and apostolic discipline have handed down a few things, many in number yet easy, most august in understanding and most chaste in observance, just as is the sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord."

units.la: Lib.3.cap.9. Baptismi sacramentum & celebratio corporis & sanguinis domini: Quae unusquisque percipit, quae referantur imbutus agnoscit: ut ea non carnali seruitute, sed spirituali potius libertate veneretur. Vt autem literam sequi, & SIGNA PRO REBUS, quae his significantur, accipere, seruilis infirmitatis est: ita inutiliter signa interpretari, male vagantis erroris est, &c. Et sane miserabilis est animarum seruitus externis inhaerere, nec animos in caelum attollere posse, ut Christo Iesu ad dexteram patris in supernis regnante frui possint.
units.tr: Book 3, chapter 9: "The sacrament of baptism and the celebration of the body and blood of the Lord: each one who receives them, being instructed, recognises what they refer to, so that he venerates them not with carnal servitude but with spiritual liberty. To follow the letter and take the SIGNS FOR THE THINGS signified by them is the mark of servile weakness; to interpret the signs so uselessly is the error of one who wanders badly, etc." Indeed it is a miserable servitude of souls to cling to outward things and be unable to lift their minds to heaven, so that they might enjoy Christ Jesus reigning at the Father's right hand on high.

units.la: Quod si vero diuinitus institutae ceremoniae nos nec iustificare nec saluare possunt, imo noxius quoque illarum vsus est, si absque fide administrentur: quanto detestabilior illorum error est, qui humanis constitutionibus & frigidissimis ceremonijs, hominum audaci curiositate inuentis, iustificationis & salutis gloriam tribuunt? Nam vt olim hominum traditiones in vniuersum omnes damnauit Dominus (Isaiae 29. Matthaei 15.) ita luce clarius est, eiusmodi ceremonias cum fide administrari non posse, eo quod haec non alio fundamento, quam Dei verbo niti possint, sicuti Paulus ad Romanos cap. 10. admonet. Vnico igitur hoc ariete totus Papatus sternitur, quem vna cum omnibus suis ritibus, ineptissimis superstitiosorum hominum decretis stabiliri notius est, quam vt longiori demonstratione opus habeat.
units.tr: But if divinely instituted ceremonies can neither justify nor save us, and their use is even harmful when they are administered without faith, how much more detestable is the error of those who ascribe the glory of justification and salvation to human constitutions and very cold ceremonies, invented by men's bold curiosity? For just as the Lord once condemned all human traditions in general (Isaiah 29; Matthew 15), so it is clearer than light that ceremonies of this kind cannot be administered with faith, because they can rest on no foundation other than the word of God, as Paul admonishes at Romans 10. By this one battering-ram, therefore, the whole Papacy is overthrown, which, together with all its rites, established by the most foolish decrees of superstitious men, is too well known to need any longer demonstration.

units.la: Pergit autem in instituta narratione Stephanus, & inanem patrum fiduciam oppugnat, quibus illi, vt supra diximus, mirum in modum superbiebant. Et vt probet, patres nec circumcisione iustificatos, vel aliqua ex parte meliores factos fuisse, nec vllis operibus salutem meruisse, sed mera & ineffabili Dei bonitate aut gratia esse saluatos, immane & exemplo carens illorum facinus quod in Iosephum fratrem designarunt, commemorat: quod paucis quidem verbis, sed talibus comprehendit, vt facile pateat, quanta illius flagitij atrocitas fuerit. Dicit enim: Patriarchae inuidia exti-mulati, Iosephum vendiderunt in Aegyptum. Extat historia apud Mosen Genes. 37. cap. Primo autem huius sceleris fontem indicat, inuidiam scilicet, qua aduersus innocentem fratrem Æstuarunt, non aliam ob causam, quam quod illi diuinitus amplissimos honores & dignitatem destinatos esse viderent. Eodem igitur vitio, quo Cainus olim laborarunt. Nam & hic Abelem fratrem inuidia & odij affectu exacerbatus occidit. Genes. 4. Nam licet hi sanguine abstinuerint, homicidij tamen reatu tenentur, tum propter destinatam animi voluntatem, cuius executioni Deus per Ruben obstitit, tum quod vendiderunt fratrem alienigenis, quod scelus postea ex Dei instituto capitali poena vindicari debuit. Vide Exod. 21. Coniunge his infinita alia, quae in huius facinoris designatione concurrerunt, & constabit, illos vno hoc facto meruisse, vt in aeternum abijcerentur: & proinde non ipsorum iustitiae, sed diuinae bonitati tribuendum esse, quod gentem, quae ex ipsis descendit, suum peculium Deus facere dignatus est. Nam audaci impietate cum Deo certamen suscepe-runt, cuius consilia hoc pacto impedire conati sunt. Impij quoque in patrem fuerunt, cui Iosephum in delicijs esse nouerant, & cuius senium consolari potius, quam contristare debebant. De impietate in fratrem quid attinet dicere, quem, quantum in ipsis fuit, non corporis modo, verumetiam animae iacturam facere voluerunt, dum illum Ismaelitis in Aegyptum vendunt, vt inter illos infelicem seruitute seruiat, quos a veri Dei cognitione & cultu alienissimos esse non ignorabant. Quae ergo supplicia, qui inferi huic flagitio vindicando potuissent sufficere, si iustitiae suae rigorem potius quam bonitatem suam & misericordiam Deus exercere voluisset?
units.tr: Stephen goes on with his narrative and attacks the empty confidence of the fathers, in which they, as we said above, took a wonderful pride. To prove that the fathers were neither justified by circumcision nor made better in any respect, nor earned salvation by any works, but were saved by the mere and ineffable goodness or grace of God, he recalls the monstrous and unparalleled crime they committed against their brother Joseph. He sums it up in few words, but in such a way that it is easy to see how atrocious that crime was. For he says: "The patriarchs, moved by envy, sold Joseph into Egypt." The story is found in Moses, Genesis 37. But he first points out the source of this crime, namely the envy they nursed against their innocent brother, for no other reason than that they saw God had destined the greatest honours and dignity for him. So they suffered from the same vice that Cain once had, for he too, provoked by envy and hatred, killed his brother Abel (Genesis 4). For although these men abstained from blood, they are nevertheless guilty of homicide: both because of the intention of their minds, whose execution God hindered through Reuben, and because they sold their brother to foreigners, a crime which afterwards, by God's institution, ought to have been avenged by capital punishment (see Exodus 21). Join to these the countless other things that came together in the planning of this deed, and it will be clear that by this one act they deserved to be cast off for ever. It must therefore be ascribed not to their own righteousness but to divine goodness that God deigned to make the nation descended from them his own possession. For with bold impiety they entered into a contest with God and tried to thwart his counsels. They were also impious toward their father, who they knew was fond of Joseph, and whose old age they ought to have comforted rather than grieved. Why speak of their impiety toward the brother whom, so far as lay in them, they wished to harm not only in body but also in soul, when they sold him to the Ishmaelites to serve as an unhappy slave among people they knew to be utterly alien from the knowledge and worship of the true God? What punishments, then, could have sufficed to avenge this crime, if God had wished to exercise the rigour of his justice rather than his goodness and mercy?

units.la: Simul vero nostrae institutioni seruit locus hic, & vanam esse docet gloriationem, quaecunque ex patrum siue maiorum virtute quaeritur. Non quod singulare Dei beneficium esse negemus, si cuius maiores praeclari & egregij contigerunt, sed non idcirco nos habere dicimus, quo coram Deo possimus gloriari. Nam etsi optimi fuerint maiores nostri, hoc ipsum tamen ex Dei gratia fuerunt, ad nos vero nihil ex illorum virtute praesidij redit, nisi illam imitari studeamus, quod pluribus apud Ezechielem cap. 18. exponitur. Et constat nunquam graujoribus minis cum Iudaeis concertauisse Deum, quam quoties illi Abrahami virtute gloriari coeperunt. Tunc enim & viperarum soboles ab Iohanne, & a Christo diaboli filij dicuntur. Matthaei 3. Iohan. 8. Et quod in Iudaeis Stephanus animaduertit, id in omnium nationum gentibus tum publice tum priuatim euidentissime cernitur. Nam sint licet inter maiores ipsorum aliquot, qui virtutibus & egregijs factis aliquam inter homines laudem meruerunt, non deerunt tamen infiniti alij, quorum scelera non gentis modo excidium, sed aeternam damnationem & totius posteritatis repudium mereri poterant, nisi peculiari & gratuito beneficio illos Deus seruatos voluisset. Humiliemur ergo omnes in conspectu Domini, & qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, qui misericors est & beneficus, patiens item & magnae benignitatis, qui non tractat nos pro peccatis nostris, neq; reprendit nobis, quod iniquitates nostrae merentur, &c. Vide Psalm. 103.
units.tr: At the same time this passage serves our instruction and shows that any boasting sought from the virtue of fathers or ancestors is vain. Not that we deny it is a singular benefit of God if one's ancestors happen to be distinguished and outstanding, but we do not say that we possess such things so that we may glory before God. For although our ancestors were excellent, even this was from the grace of God, and nothing of their virtue returns to us as protection unless we strive to imitate it, which is set out at greater length in Ezekiel 18. And it is clear that God never contended with the Jews with heavier threats than whenever they began to glory in the virtue of Abraham. For then the brood of vipers is addressed by John, and the children of the devil by Christ (Matthew 3; John 8). And what Stephen noticed in the Jews is most plainly seen, both publicly and privately, among the peoples of all nations. For although some among their ancestors have earned praise among men by their virtues and outstanding deeds, there will nevertheless be no lack of countless others whose crimes could have deserved not only the destruction of the nation but eternal damnation and the rejection of all their posterity, unless God had wished to save them by a peculiar and gratuitous benefit. Let us therefore all be humbled in the sight of the Lord, and let him who glories glory in the Lord, who is merciful and beneficent, patient also and of great kindness, who does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities, etc. See Psalm 103.

units.la: Quia vero in Iosephi historiam incidit Stephanus, cuius casitas, prudentia, iustitia & pietas meruisse videbantur, ut & ipse magnus fieret, & propter ipsum tota Iudaeorum cognatio honoribus & beneficijs accumulaterur, huic etiam errori occurrens, docet Iosepho quoq; ex Dei gratia, non ullo suo merito obtigisse quicquid habuit. Deus erat cum illo (inquit) & eripuit eum ex omnibus afflictionibus. Quod igitur Iosephus aduersa constanter pertulit, quod meretricis impudicae herae blanditijs non fuit superatus, quod fidem hero seruauit impollutam, quod carceris & captiuitatis squalore non offensus fuit, illud omne Dei beneficium fuit, qui ipsum sua gratia noluit deflituere. Eiusdem quoq; gratia factum est, quod Iosephi prophetico spiritu instructus, sana consilia regi proponere, & illius gratiam demereri potuit. Quapropter nec Iosephi ingenio, nec Pharaonis clementia, sed divinae bonitati tribuendum est, quod ad totius Aegypti dominium ille conscendit. Adde his, quod in prophana terra, cum nullum adhuc in populo Dei templum extructum, nec legis ceremoniae institutae essent, omnia ista Deus fieri voluit. Unde rursum colligitur, ceremonias, quae longo post tempore demum secutae sunt, non iustificationis ergo fuisse traditas, sed ut veram iustificationis & salutis rationem, quae a prima mundi origine primis promissionibus tradita erat, & praefinito correctionis tempore per Christum impleri debebat, nobis adumbrarent. Quid ergo propter illa tumultua-ri libet, sine quibus olim veteres Deo placuisse & saluatos esse constat? Restant autem in Iosephi exemplo, quae singulorum hominum institutioni & consolationi seruire possunt, de quibus nonnihil dicendum est.
units.tr: But since Stephen has come to the history of Joseph, whose chastity, prudence, justice and piety seemed to have earned that he himself should become great, and that because of him the whole kindred of the Jews should be heaped with honours and benefits, he meets this error too, and teaches that whatever Joseph had came to him from the grace of God, not from any merit of his own. "God," he says, "was with him, and rescued him from all his afflictions." Therefore that Joseph bore adversity steadfastly, that he was not overcome by the flatteries of his mistress's shameless wife, that he kept his faith to his master unstained, that he was not broken by the squalor of prison and captivity: all that was a benefit of God, who did not wish to abandon him by his grace. It was also by the same grace that Joseph, instructed by the prophetic Spirit, was able to set sound counsels before the king and win his favour. Wherefore it must be ascribed neither to Joseph's ingenuity nor to Pharaoh's clemency, but to divine goodness, that he rose to rule over the whole of Egypt. Add to this that in a profane land, when no temple had yet been built among the people of God and the ceremonies of the law had not been instituted, God willed all these things to happen. From this again it is gathered that the ceremonies, which followed only after a long time, were not handed down for the sake of justification, but to set before us the true way of justification and salvation, which had been handed down from the first promises at the very beginning of the world and which had to be fulfilled through Christ at the appointed time of correction. Why then should we be inclined to make a tumult over those things without which the men of old are known to have pleased God and been saved? What remains in the example of Joseph are things that can serve the instruction and consolation of individual men, and something must be said about them.

units.la: Primum inter haec est, quod Deum Iosepho affuisse dicit. Non ergo vel fratrum perfidia, vel herae impudens calumnia, vel inconsulta Putipharis iniquitas diuino praesidio Iosephum, fidum Dei cultorem, priuare potuit. Et quod in illo accidit, id omnibus pijs commune est. Nam oculi domini intenti sunt super iustos, & aures eius illorum precibus patent. Psalm. 34. Et singulis nobis cum Davide dicere licet: Vbi pater meus & mater mea deflituunt me, dominus colligit me. Psal. 27. Vt enim Christus se solum fore negat, etiamsi omnes discipuli illum deserant (Ioban. 16.) ita soli non possunt esse, quicunq; Christo per fidem insiti sunt: cum ad ipsos pertineant Christi promissiones, quales sunt: Non derelinquam vos orphanos, Ego vobiscum sum vsq; ad mundi consummationem. Ioban. 14. Matth. 28. Interim obseruemus, Iosephum variis calamitatibus exercitatum fuisse, licet Dei praesenti praesidio sustentaretur. Nam a fratribus venditur, herae blanditijs tentatur, ab eadem improbe accusatus capitis periculum incurrit, & diuturnis carceris terroribus concutitur. Nemo igitur tunc modo Deum sibi adesse putet, quando tutus & ab omni tribulatione liber agit. Nemo etiam sub Dei praesidio carnis securitatem & tuta omnia sibi polliceatur. Sed intelligamus, ita nos a Domino liberari & defendi, ut interim crux ferenda sit, nihilominus vero nunquam nos Deo magis curae esse, quam cum omni afflictionum genere tentamur. Tunc enim fugas nostras numerat, & in ipsius conspectu, ceu in vrceolo quopiam, lachrymae nostrae colliguntur. Psal. 55.
units.tr: First among these is that he says God was present with Joseph. Therefore neither the treachery of his brothers, nor the shameless slander of his mistress, nor the ill-advised injustice of Potiphar could deprive Joseph, a faithful worshipper of God, of divine protection. And what happened in him is common to all the godly. For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers (Psalm 34). And each of us may say with David: "When my father and my mother forsake me, the Lord gathers me up" (Psalm 27). For just as Christ says that he will not be alone even if all the disciples desert him (John 16), so those who are implanted in Christ through faith cannot be alone, since the promises of Christ pertain to them, such as: "I will not leave you orphans"; "I am with you even to the end of the world" (John 14; Matthew 28). Meanwhile let us observe that Joseph was exercised by various calamities, although he was sustained by the present protection of God. For he is sold by his brothers, tempted by his mistress's flatteries, wickedly accused by the same woman and put in danger of his life, and he is shaken by the long terrors of prison. Let no one therefore think that God is with him only when he lives safe and free from all tribulation. Let no one either promise himself, under God's protection, security of the flesh and all things safe. But let us understand that we are so freed and defended by the Lord that the cross must meanwhile be borne; yet we are never more the care of God than when we are tried by every kind of affliction. For then he counts our flights, and our tears are gathered in his sight, as into some little urn (Psalm 55).

units.la: Deinde notemus, Iosephum a Deo sapientiam & gratiam habuisse. Dei ergo donum est quicquid boni & eximij habemus. Et eiusdem beneficium est, si dona, quae in nobis sunt, cum fructu aliquo vti, & reliquis grati vel accepti esse possumus. Nam si hominis naturam cognoscimus, corrupta in illo sunt omnia. Non percipit intellectus noster ea, quae sunt spiritus Dei. 1. Cor. 2. Voluntas nisi terrena sectatur, & carnis desyderijs regitur, cuius figmenta ab ineunte aetate prava sunt. Gene. 8. Vires ad bene agendum nullae sunt. Nisi ergo Dominus nos regeneret, & suo spiritu instruat, nihil in nobis sanum erit & integrum. Rursum nisi ille nos & nostra omnia alijs placere faciat, nihil proficiemus. Quid enim in alijs efficias, qui teipsum docere & gubernare nescis? Vt ergo Dei beneficium fuit, quod Iosephi consilia Pharaoni grata fuerunt: ita nisi Deus hominum mentes inclinet, inutilia & inania erunt, quae nos instituimus, omnia. Quod in verbi ministerio Paulus obseruauit, quando ait: Nihil est qui
units.tr: Next, let us note that Joseph had wisdom and grace from God. Therefore whatever good and excellent thing we have is God's gift. And it is by his kindness that we can use the gifts that are in us to some profit, and be pleasing and acceptable to others. For if we consider human nature, everything in it is corrupt. Our understanding does not grasp the things of the Spirit of God. 1 Cor. 2. The will seeks only earthly things and is ruled by the desires of the flesh, whose figments are evil from early youth. Gen. 8. We have no strength to act well. Unless the Lord regenerates us and instructs us by his Spirit, nothing in us will be sound and whole. Again, unless he makes us and all our efforts pleasing to others, we will achieve nothing. For what can you accomplish in others when you do not know how to teach and govern yourself? So just as it was God's favour that Joseph's counsels pleased Pharaoh, so unless God inclines the minds of men, everything we undertake will be useless and vain. Paul observed this in the ministry of the Word when he said: "Neither is he that plants anything, nor he that waters, but God who gives the increase."

units.la: Dei donum est quicquid exi-mij habemus. rigat, nihil qui plantat, sed Deus qui dat incrementum. Admonet autem huius rei consyderatio, ne Dei donis superbiamus, & ut ijsdem recte utamur. Quid enim habes, quod non acceperis? Quod si acceperis, quid gloriaris ac si non acceperis? 1.Cor.4. Quod si accepisti, utiq; accepti & dati ratio olim reddenda erit, sicut in talentorum parabola Christus docuit. Matth.25.
units.tr: God's gift is whatever excellent thing we have. Consideration of this matter should also warn us not to be proud of God's gifts, and to use them rightly. For what do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? 1 Cor. 4. And if you have received it, an account of what was received and given will surely one day have to be rendered, as Christ taught in the parable of the talents. Matt. 25.

units.la: Postremo non abs re fuerit, si Christi typum, quem Iosephus gessit, consyderemus, cum hic totius orationis a Stephano institutae scopus sit, ut Christo Iudaeos adducat. Ut enim Iosephum fratres dominum & regem suum agnoscere noluerunt: ita cum Christus in sua veniret, sui illum recipere dedignati sunt. Iohan.1. Ut Iosepha fratribus: ita Christus a Iuda venditus, & postea a Iudaeis, qui ipsius iuxta carnem fratres erant, gentibus traditus est. Ut Iosephus cum pistore & pincerna aduersa multa pertulit, quorum ille quidem periit, hic vero seruatus est: ita Christum in medio duorum latronum passum esse legimus, quorum alter Dei gratia seruatus est, alter a salute excidit. Ut Iosephus per multa pericula & horribiles casus ad summos regiae dignitatis honores ascendit: ita Christus per acerbam & diram mortem crucis patris gloriam ingressus, nomen accepit, quod est super omne nomen, & in quo omne genu flecti conuenit. Philip.2. Omitto multa alia, quae suo loco & tempore commodius tractari poterunt. Nostrum est, Christum Iesum, cuius typum Iosephus gessit, vera fide amplecti, & per varios huius vitae casus ad caelestis regni hereditatem eniti, quae credentibus ab aeterno praeparata, & pretioso Christi sanguine acquisita est: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, it will not be out of place to consider the type of Christ which Joseph bore, since the whole aim of the speech delivered by Stephen is to lead the Jews to Christ. For just as the brothers refused to acknowledge Joseph as their lord and king, so when Christ came to his own, his own people disdained to receive him. John 1. As Joseph was sold by his brothers, so Christ was sold by Judas and afterwards handed over to the Gentiles by the Jews, who were his brethren according to the flesh. As Joseph endured many hardships with the baker and the cupbearer, of whom the one indeed perished and the other was saved, so we read that Christ suffered between two robbers, of whom one was saved by the grace of God and the other fell away from salvation. As Joseph, through many dangers and dreadful misfortunes, rose to the highest honours of royal dignity, so Christ, entering into his Father's glory through a bitter and dreadful death on the cross, received the name which is above every name, and at which every knee should bow. Phil. 2. I pass over many other matters, which can be treated more fittingly in their proper place and time. It is our task to embrace in true faith Christ Jesus, whose type Joseph bore, and through the various chances of this life to strive for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, which has been prepared from eternity for believers and purchased by the precious blood of Christ: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVI.

units.la: Venit autem fames super universam terram Aegypti & Chanaan, & afflictio magna, nec inveniebant frumenta patres nostri. Cum vero audiuisset Iacob, esse frumenta in Aegypto, misit illuc patres nostros primum. Secundo autem aduentu agnitus fuit Ioseph a fratribus suis. Et innotuit Pharaoni genus Iosephi. Misit ergo Ioseph, & euocauit patrem suum Iacob, & universam cognationem suam in animabus septuaginta quinque. Descendit autem Iacob in Aegyptum, & mortuus est ipse & patres nostri, & translati sunt in Sichem, & positi sunt in sepulchro, quod emerat Abraham pretio argenti a filiis Hemor, filii Sichem.
units.tr: Now a famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great affliction, and our fathers could find no food. But when Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there the first time. At their second coming Joseph was recognised by his brothers, and Joseph's family became known to Pharaoh. Joseph therefore sent and called his father Jacob and all his kindred, seventy-five souls. Jacob went down into Egypt, and he died, he and our fathers, and they were carried over to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor, the son of Shechem.

units.la: Pergit in coepta narratione rerum cum patribus olim gestarum Stephanus: cuius hic praecipuus finis est, ut euincat, se veterem patrum religionem firmiter tenere, quos sine templo & sine ceremoniis Deo placuisse, & salvatos esse constet. Unde colligit templum ne nunc quidem ad salutem necessarium esse, sed in eum potius debere respici, qui hoc praefiguratus fuit. Inter alia vero singulari diligentia Iosephi historiam tractat, eo quod is (ut praecedenti Sermone diximus) Christi Iesu typum gessit. Et in iis quidem, quae praecesserunt, ut Ioseph in Aegyptum venditus & ibidem ex gratia Dei non modo seruatus, verum etiam Aegypti dominus factus fit, expositus. Subiungitur his in praesenti totius Israeliticae gentis descensus in Aegyptum, cuius author idem ille Ioseph fuit. Ad eundem vero scopum haec narrationis pars referri debet, ad quem praecedentia referre docuimus. Vult enim docere Stephanus, religionem veram & salutis humanae rationem adeo non alligatam esse ei cultui, qui per Mosem institutus, & in terra Chanaan aliquot seculis obseruatus fuit, ut olim patres famis necessitate e terra illa excedere coacti, in Aegyptum venerint, vbi annis circiter ducentis & decem (totidem enim a descensu Aegypti vsq; ad exitum filiorum Israelis numerantur) Dei populus fuerint, licet nec templo nec legalibus ceremoniis vterentur. Nihil ergo obstare, quo minus hodie quoque sine templo seruentur, imo hoc cum toto Leuitico cultu necessario abrogari debere, quando illum exhibitum esse constet, cuius typum ista olim gesserunt. Extat historia Genes.42.43. & deinceps, vbi prolixe narrantur, quae pauca Stephanus perstringit. Ne vero inutilis nobis fit illius narratio, summa rerum capita distinguere, & ea ad nostram institutionem transferre conuenit. Videamus ergo causam, quae Israelem in Aegyptum descendere compulit: deinde ipsum descensum: postremo autem quae de patriarcharum morte simul & sepultura dicuntur. Causam in Ægyptum descendendi Iacobo fames præbuit, qua in terra Chanaan vexatus esset, & quam non alia commodiori ratione effugere potuit, cum in sola Ægypto frumenta, ex Iosephi consilio reposita, inuenirentur. Hic verò diligenti obseruatione dignum est, quòd Iacobum, fidelissimum suum cultorem & sanctissimum virum, Deus cum fame conflictari patitur. Poterat hoc filiorum improbitati acceptum ferri, nisi idem Abrahamo & Isaaco euenisse legeremus. Gen.12. & 26. Nec exempla desunt, quibus docemur aliis quoq; ærumnis & aduersis fidos sanctosq; Dei cultores obnoxios fuisse. Vnde colligimus, aduersa & afflictiones non semper irati numinis argumenta esse, nec propter has nobis esse desperandum, quasi à Dei gratia in vniuersum exciderimus. Nam vel paterna cura lapsus nostros Deus præuenit, & ne quando turpiter peccemus, carnis feroces spiritus coercet: vel delicta nostra paternè castigat, & castigando in viam reducit: vel occulta & nobis ignota adhuc iudicia hoc modo exequitur: quod in præsenti historia factum fuisse constat. Fame enim in Ægyptum abire Iacob cogitur cum omni sua familia, vt oraculo locus fit, quo Abrahamo prædixerat Deus, semel ipsius peregrinum fore in aliena terra, vnde post multas afflictiones diuina ope sint educendi. Gen.15. Et quotidiani afflictionum nostrarum euentus abunde docent, multa per has iusto & salutari iudicio facere Deum, quæ prius ignorabamus. Cæterum haud vulgarem consolationem affert, quòd vt Iacobum fame vexari voluit: ita Iosephum in Ægyptum præmisit & totius regni dominium constituit, vt illius consilio & ope cum vniuersa familia sua aleretur. Prædicatur hæc Dei bonitas & fides in Psal.105. vbi sic scribitur: Vocauit Deus famem super terram, & omnem bacu-lum panis contriuit. Misit ante illos virum, Iosephum venditus est in seruitutem, &c. Hinc igitur præcipua salus Iacobo contigit, vnde is præcipuam doloris causam se habere putabat. Iosephum enim, vt vita defunctum summa animi acerbitate luxerat, cuius beneficentia & liberalitate modò alitur. Agnoscit hoc Dei consilium Ioseph, quando fratres sceleris conscientia perterritos, hoc argumento consolatur, quòd non sine Dei prouidentia, publicæ & communis salutis ergo, in Ægyptum præmissus fit. Gen.45. Et frequenter fieri solet, vt quæ ab hostibus nostris summa cum inhumanitate & iniquitate contra nos instituuntur, nostro commodo & saluti inseruiant. Nec ideo illorum improbitas excusatur, quando illi non vt Dei consilia exequantur, ista faciunt, sed vt effreni affectuum suorum libidini indulgeant: qua de re iam sæpe dictum est.
units.tr: Stephen continues his account of what was done long ago with the fathers, and his chief purpose here is to show that he firmly holds to the ancient religion of the fathers, who, as is plain, pleased God and were saved without a temple and without ceremonies. From this he infers that even now the temple is not necessary for salvation, and that men ought rather to look to him who was foreshadowed by these things. Among the other matters, he treats with special care the history of Joseph, because he (as we said in the previous sermon) bore the type of Christ Jesus. In what has gone before, he sets out how Joseph was sold into Egypt, and there, by the grace of God, was not only preserved but made lord of Egypt. Following on from this, the present passage describes the descent of the whole Israelite people into Egypt, of which the author was that same Joseph. This part of the narrative must be referred to the same goal to which we showed that the preceding parts are referred. Stephen wishes to teach that true religion and the way of human salvation are by no means bound to that worship which was instituted through Moses and observed for some centuries in the land of Chanaan. For the fathers, compelled by the need of famine to leave that land, came into Egypt, where for about two hundred and ten years (for so many are counted from the descent into Egypt to the exodus of the sons of Israel) they remained the people of God, although they had neither a temple nor the legal ceremonies. Nothing therefore stands in the way of its being observed today also without a temple; indeed, it is plain that this, together with the whole Levitical worship, ought of necessity to be abrogated, since he has been revealed whose type those men once bore. The history is found in Genesis 42-43 and following, where it is related at length, and Stephen touches on only a few points. So that the account may not be useless to us, it is fitting to mark the main heads of the matter and apply them to our instruction. Let us consider, then, the cause that compelled Israel to go down into Egypt; next the descent itself; and lastly what is said of the death and burial of the patriarchs. Famine gave Jacob the cause for going down into Egypt, since he was distressed in the land of Chanaan, and he could not escape it by any more convenient means, since grain, laid up on Joseph's advice, was to be found in Egypt alone. Here it is worth careful notice that God allowed Jacob, his most faithful worshipper and most holy man, to be struck by famine. This could have been ascribed to the wickedness of his sons, were we not also to read that the same befell Abraham and Isaac (Gen. 12 and 26). Nor are examples lacking by which we are taught that faithful and holy worshippers of God were subject to other troubles and adversities as well. Hence we gather that adversities and afflictions are not always signs of an angry deity, nor should we despair on account of them, as though we had altogether fallen from the grace of God. For either God anticipates our lapses with a fatherly care and restrains the fierce impulses of the flesh, lest we ever sin shamefully; or he chastises our offences as a father and, by chastising, brings us back to the way; or he carries out his hidden judgments, which are still unknown to us, in this manner, as is plainly what happened in the present history. For Jacob is compelled to go away into Egypt with all his household by famine, so that there might be fulfilment of the oracle by which God had foretold to Abraham that his seed would be strangers in a foreign land, whence, after many afflictions, they would be led out by divine help (Gen. 15). And the daily outcomes of our afflictions teach abundantly that God, by a just and salutary judgment, does through these many things that we did not previously understand. Moreover, it brings no common consolation that, just as he willed Jacob to be vexed by famine, so he sent Joseph before into Egypt and set him over the whole kingdom, so that by his counsel and help the whole family might be fed. This goodness and faithfulness of God is proclaimed in Psalm 105, where it is written thus: "God called a famine upon the land, and broke every staff of bread. He sent a man before them, Joseph was sold into servitude," etc. Thus the chief salvation came to Jacob from the very thing which he had thought to be the chief cause of his grief. For he had mourned Joseph, as one dead, with the utmost bitterness of spirit, and now he is fed by his beneficence and liberality. Joseph acknowledges this counsel of God when he consoles his brothers, terrified by the consciousness of their crime, with this argument: that he was sent before into Egypt not without the providence of God, for the sake of the public and common salvation (Gen. 45). And it often happens that the things which our enemies undertake against us with the utmost inhumanity and injustice turn out to serve our advantage and our welfare. Nor is their wickedness on that account excused, since they do these things not in order to carry out God's counsels, but to indulge the unbridled lust of their own passions; about this matter it has already been said often enough.

units.la: Simul verò Pharaonem & Iosephum hic obseruare conuenit. Ille enim non exiguam prudentiæ & gratitudinis laudem meretur, quòd Iosephum, quem præ cæteris sapientia & consilijs instructum videbat, regni gubernaculis præficit, etiamsi peregrinum & seruilis conditionis hominem esse nouisset: & quòd illius consilijs feliciter vsus, non Iosepho modò, verumetiam toti ipsius cognationi gratias liberalissimè referre studet. Quo exemplo non tantum gratitudinem discunt qui in magistratu versantur, verumetiam admonentur, quàm referat, pios & sanctos Dei cultores publicis officijs adhibere: eò quòd tales Dei benedictio sequitur, & quod illis fit, sibi factu esse Deus reputat. Sentit hoc antea Putiphar, quamuis parum gratus, quem in omnibus negotijs fortunauit Deus, quando Iosephum domus suæ gubernatorem habebat. Idem nunc Pharao experitur, quando Iosephi studio seipsum opibus immensis augeri, totamque simul Ægyptum & finitimas nationes conseruari videt. Sic infra propter Paulum è naufragio seruantur, quotquot cum illo nauigabant. Vt verò ex pijs ad multos alios magna vtilitas redire solet: ita frequenter paucos impios, si honoribus & potentia subl- limes fiant, vel saltem impune grassentur, publicorum malorum authores fieri constat. Vnus Achan certè sacrilegio suo, quamuis occulto, publicæ cladis causam præbuit. Ios.7. Et Ionas, à Dei conspectu fugiens, non seipsum modò, verumetiam nautas & quotquot in ea naui cum ipso vehebantur, in capitis periculum adduxit. Adeò periculosa & noxia est impiorum consuetudo siue societas. Quid ergo sperandum erit, si publicis officijs & rerum gubernaculis tales præficiantur? Non aliud certè, quàm quòd publici alicuius mali, adeoque vniuersalis excidij authores futuri sint. Cuius rei exemplum in Manasse habetur, cuius sanguinaria tyrannide & impietate factum est, vt implacabili aduersus Iudæorum gentem Deus ira excandescens, in Babylonem abducendos traderet, templo & vrbe prius ferro & igne vastatis. Prima ergo in rerumpublicarum & ecclesiarum præsidibus deligendis pietatis cura esse debet, nisi vastatores potius quàm conseruatores regnare velimus. Et sane huius loci consyderatio vel sola docere potest, quæ potissima malorum nostri seculi causa fit, quando passim rebus publicis ij praficiuntur, quorum animi à religione & pietatis studio alienissimi sunt.
units.tr: At the same time it is fitting to observe Pharaoh and Joseph here. Pharaoh deserves no small praise for prudence and gratitude, in that he set Joseph, whom he saw to be endowed with wisdom and counsel above others, over the reins of the kingdom, even though he knew him to be a foreigner and of servile condition; and in that, having profited happily from his counsels, he takes pains to repay thanks most generously not only to Joseph but to his whole family. By this example, those who hold office learn not only gratitude but are also reminded how much it profits to employ pious and holy worshippers of God in public duties, since God's blessing follows such men, and God counts as done to himself what is done to them. Potiphar felt this earlier, although he was ungrateful enough, whom God prospered in all his affairs when he had Joseph as steward of his house. Pharaoh now experiences the same, when through Joseph's zeal he sees himself increased in immense riches and sees all Egypt and the neighbouring nations preserved together. So, later on, for Paul's sake, all who sailed with him are saved from shipwreck. But just as great benefit is wont to flow from the pious to many others, so it is plain that when a few impious men are raised to honours and power, or at least are allowed to rage with impunity, they become the authors of public evils. Achan alone, by his sacrilege, though it was secret, was the cause of the public disaster (Josh. 7). And Jonah, fleeing from the sight of God, brought into danger of life not only himself but the sailors and all who were carried in that ship with him. So dangerous and harmful is the company and fellowship of the wicked. What then is to be expected if such men are set over public offices and the reins of affairs? Certainly nothing other than that they will become the authors of some public evil, indeed of universal ruin. An example of this is found in Manasseh, by whose bloody tyranny and impiety it came about that God, kindled with implacable anger against the nation of the Jews, handed them over to be led away to Babylon, the temple and city having first been laid waste by sword and fire. The first concern, therefore, in choosing rulers of commonwealths and churches should be piety, unless we want rulers who are destroyers rather than preservers. And indeed the consideration of this passage alone can teach what is the chief cause of the evils of our age, when everywhere those are placed over commonwealths whose minds are most alien to religion and the pursuit of piety.

units.la: In Iosepho autem fraternæ charitatis ingenium, æquitatis & iustitiæ regula temperatum, consyderandum venit. Nam fratres, à quibus indignissimè inhumanissimeq; tractatus fuerat, agnoscit, & ijsdem alimenta præbet liberalissimè: interim tamen illorum animos simulata quadam austeritate & verborum duritia explorat, nec prius sese illis cognoscendum præbet, quàm emendatos videret. Exprimit ea in re Dei patris & filij ipsius, Iesu Christi, ingenium: qui cum nullum non à nobis iniuriarum genus olim perpessus sit, & quotidie patiatur, nihilominus tamen charitatis suæ & beneficentiæ obliuisci non potest, verum etiam pro fratribus nos agnoscit, & illis benefacit, qui mille cruces & mortes meruerunt. Imitemur hoc Dei patris ingenium, siquidem illius filij dici & haberi volumus. Matth. 5. Interim nihil obstat, quo minus illorum peccata argui & accusari debeant, quos præter officium multa indignè facere & fecisse videmus. Nec ita condonandum ijs, qui in nos iniuria fuerunt, ut nimia indulgentia corrumpantur, sed hoc præcipuum charitatis officium esse intelligamus, si à peccatis & interitu revocentur, qui à pœnitentiæ studio adhuc alieni sunt.
units.tr: In Joseph, however, the spirit of brotherly love, tempered by the rule of fairness and justice, deserves consideration. For he recognises his brothers, by whom he had been treated most shamefully and inhumanely, and provides them with food most generously. Meanwhile, however, he tests their hearts by a feigned sternness and harshness of words, and he does not make himself known to them until he sees them reformed. In this matter he expresses the spirit of God the Father and of his Son, Jesus Christ, who, though he has long suffered every kind of injury from us and daily endures it, nevertheless does not forget his love and kindness, but even acknowledges us as brothers and does good to those who have deserved a thousand crosses and deaths. Let us imitate this spirit of God the Father, since we wish to be called and to be regarded as his children. Matt. 5. Meanwhile nothing stands in the way of the sins of those being rebuked and accused, whom we see doing many unworthy things beyond their duty and having done them. Nor should those who have wronged us be forgiven in such a way that they are corrupted by excessive indulgence; rather, let us understand that this is the chief duty of love, if those who as yet have no zeal for repentance are called back from their sins and from ruin.

units.la: Sed alteram huius loci partem videamus, qua Iacobus cum vniuersa familia & cognatione sua in Ægyptum descendisse dicitur. Unde constat neminem in terra Chanaan remansisse ex illorum numero, qui populus Dei esse censebantur: sed simul omnes in Ægypto exulauerunt, & illic absque vllis ceremonijs & absque omni cultu legali, mera Dei gratia conseruati sunt. Non temere autem factum putabimus, quod numerum animarum tam diligenter Stephanus recenset. Eius enim consyderatio ineffabilem & inuictam Dei potentiam nobis ob oculos ponit, qui tantillam gentem intra ducentos & decem annos innumerabilem efficere potuit. Nam, ut Moses testatur, cum Ægyptum exirent, in censu Israelis sexcenta & triginta millia, quingenti & quinquaginta ad militiam instructorum reperti sunt. Cum quo si tyrannicos Pharaonis conatus conferas, qui populum hunc omni modo delere & extirpare instituit, facile patebit, Dei promissionem Abrahamo olim factam (Gen.15. & 17.) humanis consilijs & viribus nequaquam impediri potuisse. Debet hoc omnium nostrum institutioni & consolationi seruire, ne mundi minus & conatibus perterreamur, quando huius vires aduersus Deum irritas omnino & nullius momenti esse constat. Transferamus hoc ad Christum & ecclesiam eius. Promisit illi regnum Deus, quod inuitis hostibus ille obtinet & in æternum tenebit. Promisit porro ecclesiam fore numerosissimam: quod ipsum quoq; impleri videmus, ut non vnus Pharao illa extinctam cupiat. Singuli item hoc obseruent in tentationibus, ne fidem suam euerti patiantur, cum Paulo teste, nihil sit, quod nos separare possit à dilectione Dei, &c. Rom.8.cap.
units.tr: But let us look at the other part of this passage, in which Jacob is said to have gone down into Egypt with his whole household and kindred. From this it is clear that none of those who were considered the people of God remained in the land of Canaan; rather, all of them together went into exile in Egypt, and there, without any ceremonies and without any legal worship, they were preserved by the pure grace of God. We shall not think it done without reason that Stephen so carefully recounts the number of souls. For that reckoning sets before our eyes the ineffable and unconquered power of God, who was able to make so small a nation innumerable within two hundred and ten years. For, as Moses testifies, when they left Egypt, there were found in the census of Israel six hundred and thirty thousand, and five hundred and fifty men equipped for war. If you compare with this the tyrannical attempts of Pharaoh, who set out to destroy and root out this people by every means, it will easily be evident that the promise of God once made to Abraham (Gen. 15 and 17) could in no way be hindered by human counsels and strength. This ought to serve the instruction and consolation of all of us, so that we are not terrified by the attempts of the world, since it is clear that its strength against God is utterly vain and of no moment. Let us apply this to Christ and his Church. God promised him a kingdom, which he holds and will hold forever though his enemies are unwilling. Furthermore, he promised that the Church would be most numerous; we see this also being fulfilled, so that no single Pharaoh can desire to extinguish her. Let each individual likewise observe this in temptations, that they not allow their faith to be overthrown, since, as Paul testifies, nothing can separate us from the love of God, etc. Rom. 8.

units.la: Postremo huius loci membro, patres in Ægypto mortuos, & postea in Sichem translatos esse, Stephanus docet. Atqui de Iacobo diserte Moses scribit, illius funus in Chanaan fuisse delatum. Gen.50. Et Iosephi offa ex Ægypto ab Israelitis, quemadmodum ipse mandauerat, translata fuisse, similiter scriptura admonet. Exod.13. Ios.24. De reliquis patriarchis, licet nihil tradat Moses, verisimile tamen est, illorum quoq; offa à suis posteris simul asportata fuisse, cum id tam libere Stephanus afferat coram ijs, quos verborum suorum intentissimos iudices esse nouerat. Porro in Abrahami nomine liberariorum incuria erratum esse, notius est, quàm ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Videlicet quæ de hoc agro, quem Iacob à filijs Emor emit, habentur Gen.33. & Ios.24. In Ægypto autem mortuos esse patriarchas ideo asserit, ut constet illos in ea religione diem obijsse, quæ nullis externis ceremonijs nitebatur, sed in sola fide, qua Dei promissiones amplectebantur, consistebat. Unde colligitur, illos per fidem, ex mera Dei gratia, non Leuitico cultu iustificatos & saluatos esse. Interim admonemur, fideles vbiuis terrarum feliciter mori, nec miseros censendos esse, qui extra patriae fines in exilio vita hac defunguntur. Quia enim vita hac, vbicunque agatur, peregrinatio est, & patriam siue ciuitatem permanentem in cœlis habemus, in exilio mori non potest, qui peregrinationis cursum per fidem consummato in cœlestis patriæ portum recipitur. Beati enim dicuntur ab angelo mortui, qui in domino moriuntur. Apoc.14. Et Christus eos, qui in se credunt, ex morte in vitam transfire tentatur. Iohan.5. Præterea vbiq; locorum Deus suis moriturus adest: & in nouissimo die omnis terra, imò & mare, adeoq; omnes mundi partes reddere cogentur, quoscunq; absumpserunt. Vide Apoc.20. Ridicula ergo & stulta est illorum hominum superstitio, qui locorum religione beatitudinem metiuntur, riuntur, nec parum referre putant, quo loco quis sepeliatur: cum omnem terram Domini esse constet, cuius potentia & gratia certo loco nec concludi nec alligari potest. Nec mihi patriarchas obijcient illi homines, qui ossa sua in terram Chanaan ex Ægypto transferri voluerunt. Nec enim hoc ideo fecere, quod salutis spem in sepultura loco haberent repositam: sed fidei hoc opus fuit, quam nec mortis terror illis excutere potuit. Et ut omnibus testatum facerent, se Dei promissionibus firmiter credere, quibus ipsorum posteris huius terrae hereditatem erat pollicitus, & nepotes suos in huius terrae amorem raperet, in ea sepeliri voluerunt: adeo ut in ipsa morte fidem & spem retinuisse dici possint. Nec id temere factum esse ex posterorum moribus patet, qui cum non sine maximis miraculis essent liberati, subinde tamen in Ægyptum respexerunt, & terram illam aspernati sunt, in qua patres sepeliri voluerant. Quid vero non facturi erant illi, si patres sibi in Ægypto sepulturae locum delegissent? Nihil ergo horum exempla illorum superstitioni patrocinantur, qui in sepulchris non posteram salutis spem & hominis gloriam consistere arbitrantur. Nos potius loci huius & totius orationis a Stephano institutae caput teneamus, & omissis ceremoniarum observationibus, fidem & spem seruemus inconcussam, ut cum sanctissimis patriarchis in regno caelorum discumbere nobis liceat, sicut promisit Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Stephen teaches that in this part of the passage the fathers died in Egypt and were afterwards carried over to Shechem. Yet Moses writes plainly of Jacob that his funeral was taken to Canaan. Gen. 50. And Scripture likewise reminds us that the bones of Joseph were carried out of Egypt by the Israelites, just as he himself had commanded. Exod. 13. Josh. 24. Concerning the other patriarchs, although Moses records nothing, it is nevertheless likely that their bones too were carried away together by their posterity, since Stephen states this so freely before those whom he knew to be the most attentive judges of his words. Moreover, that an error was made by the copyists in the name of Abraham is better known than that it needs to be demonstrated to many. Clearly, this concerns the field which Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor, which is described in Gen. 33 and Josh. 24. But he asserts that the patriarchs died in Egypt so that it may be established that they ended their days in that religion which relied on no external ceremonies, but consisted solely in faith, by which they embraced God's promises. From this it is gathered that they were justified and saved through faith, by the pure grace of God, and not by the Levitical worship. Meanwhile we are reminded that the faithful die happily wherever they are on earth, and that those who depart this life in exile beyond the borders of their homeland are not to be counted wretched. For since this life, wherever it is lived, is a pilgrimage, and we have a lasting homeland or city in heaven, he cannot die in exile who through faith has brought the course of his pilgrimage to completion and is received into the harbour of the heavenly homeland. For the dead who die in the Lord are called blessed by the angel. Rev. 14. And Christ teaches that those who believe in him pass from death into life. John 5. Moreover, God is present everywhere to his own who are about to die, and on the last day the whole earth, and indeed the sea, and thus all parts of the world, will be compelled to give back all whom they have consumed. See Rev. 20. Ridiculous and foolish, therefore, is the superstition of those men who measure blessedness by religious attachment to places, and who think it matters much in what place someone is buried, since it is clear that the whole earth belongs to the Lord, whose power and grace cannot be confined or bound to any one place. Nor will those men who wished their bones to be carried from Egypt into the land of Canaan raise the patriarchs as an objection against me. For they did not do this because they had the hope of salvation placed in a burial place; it was rather a work of faith, which the terror of death itself could not shake out of them. And so that they might show to all that they firmly believed God's promises, by which he had pledged the inheritance of this land to their descendants, and so that they might draw their grandchildren to love of this land, they wished to be buried in it, so that they may be said to have kept faith and hope even in death itself. That this was not done rashly is clear from the conduct of their descendants, who, though they had been freed not without very great miracles, nevertheless from time to time looked back to Egypt and despised that land in which the fathers had wished to be buried. But what would those men not have done, had the fathers chosen a place of burial for themselves in Egypt? Therefore these examples lend no support to the superstition of those who think that the hope of salvation and the glory of man lie in tombs. Rather, let us hold to the heart of this place and of the whole discourse instituted by Stephen, and, setting aside the observance of ceremonies, keep faith and hope unshaken, so that it may be granted to us to recline with the most holy patriarchs in the kingdom of heaven, as Jesus Christ has promised, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVII
units.tr: Homily 47

units.la: Vt autem appropinquauit tempus promissionis, quam iurauerat Deus Abrahamo, creuit populus & multiplicatus est in Ægypto, donec surrexit rex alius, qui non nouerat Iosephum. Hic dolose circumueniens genus nostrum, afflixit patres nostros, ut exponerent infantes suos, ne sobole augerentur. Quo tempore Moses natus est, qui Deo gratus fuit: & nutritus est per tres menses in domo patris. Expositum vero illum sustulit filia Pharaonis, & educauit eum sibi in filium. Et institutus est Moses in omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, erat-que potens in factis & in dictis.
units.tr: But as the time of the promise drew near, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until another king arose who did not know Joseph. He, deceitfully dealing with our race, afflicted our fathers, so that they exposed their infants, lest they be increased by offspring. At that time Moses was born, who was pleasing to God; and he was nurtured for three months in his father's house. When he was exposed, Pharaoh's daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in deeds and in words.

units.la: ETsi Deus fidem & salutis rationem, quae solius Iesu Christi merito nititur, primos parentes docuerit, & eius doctrina ideo sola & vetustissima & veracissima sit, passim tamen nouitatis & falsi accusatur. Causa est, quod homines non in Dei verbum, sed externa respiciunt, & quidem in ea plerunque, quae ipsi ex suo cerebro finxerunt. Fit ergo, ut illis solis intenti, pro nouorum dogmatum auctoribus eos habeant, qui diuersum quid docent, & a Deo traditam salutis nostrae cultumque diuini rationem reducere student. Accidit hoc Stephano: qui cum Ierosolymae euangelium Iesu Christi praedicaret, & populum a legalibus ceremoniis ad Christum remitteret, mox ac cusatur, quasi templum & Dei cultum hostiliter oderit. Excusat se ille non verbis nudis sed reipsa. Nam patrum historiam contexens, illos quoque non aliam fidei & salutis rationem secutos fuisse docet, quam quae in Christo habetur. Deduxit vero narrationem hanc ab ipsa gentis origine usque ad descensum Israelis in Ægyptum & patriarcharum mortem. Nunc ergo eiusdem populi incrementa & liberationem narrare incipit: vbi singulari diligentia vtitur, eo quod Ægyptiaca liberatio redemptionis per Christum facta typus fuit, quo simul admonemur, quae omnibus seculis ecclesiae in hoc mundo fors fuerit, atque semper futura sit. Idem vero huius partis, qui & superiorum omnium scopus est, nimirum Iudaeis liberationem hanc non aliquo operum ipsorum aut legalis iustitiae merito, sed singulari gratia Dei beneficio iuxta promissiones veteres contigisse. Vnde colligit, veram religionis & salutis rationem non in externis ceremoniis, sed potius in fide, qua Dei gratiam & promissiones apprehendimus, consistere. At quia de singulis suo loco dicetur, in praesenti de populi multiplicatione & eius assertore Mose, agemus, quae vtraque in ijs, quae modo praelecta sunt, Stephanus tractat.
units.tr: Although God taught the first parents the faith and the way of salvation, which rests solely on the merit of Jesus Christ, and although his teaching is therefore the only, the most ancient and the most true, it is nonetheless everywhere accused of novelty and falsehood. The reason is that people look not to God's Word but to external things, and for the most part to those things which they have fashioned out of their own brains. So it comes about that, intent only on these, they regard as authors of new doctrines those who teach something different and strive to lead back the way of our salvation and worship of God, handed down by God. This happened to Stephen: when at Jerusalem he preached the gospel of Jesus Christ and referred the people from the legal ceremonies to Christ, he was at once accused of hating the temple and the worship of God as an enemy. He defends himself not with empty words but by deeds. For in weaving together the history of the fathers, he shows that they too followed no other way of faith and salvation than that which is found in Christ. He drew out this narrative from the very origin of the nation down to Israel's descent into Egypt and the death of the patriarchs. Now he begins to narrate the increase and the deliverance of the same people, and here he uses singular diligence, because the deliverance from Egypt was a type of the redemption made through Christ; by this we are also reminded what fortune the Church has had in this world in every age, and what it will always be. Moreover, the aim of this part, which is also the aim of all that precedes, is clearly that this deliverance came to the Jews not by any merit of their own works or of legal righteousness, but by the singular grace of God's benefit, according to the ancient promises. Hence he gathers that the true religion and way of salvation consists not in external ceremonies, but rather in faith, by which we lay hold of God's grace and promises. But since these matters will be discussed each in its place, in the present we shall deal with the multiplication of the people and with Moses, its champion, which two things Stephen treats in what has just been read.

units.la: Populi multiplicationem in Ægypto, non vllis hominum consilijs, sed Dei gratiae transcribere duobus argumentis probat. Primum a causa efficienti, alterum a temporum illorum conditione deducit. Vt enim (inquit) tempus promissionis appropinquauit, quam Deus iurauerat Abrahamo, multiplicatus est populus in Ægypto. At promissionem gratuitam fuisse nemo negauerit, cum nondum natus Iudaeis facta fit, & ipsum Abrahamum mera gratia electum & ex Chaldaea evocatum fuisse constat. Unde colligitur populum hunc Dei gratia conservatum fuisse, & in tantam multitudinem excreuisse, quanta a Mose alibi recensetur. Num. 1. cap.
units.tr: Stephen proves by two arguments that the multiplication of the people in Egypt is to be ascribed not to any human counsels but to the grace of God. The first he draws from the efficient cause, the second from the condition of those times. For (he says) as the time of the promise drew near, which God had sworn to Abraham, the people multiplied in Egypt. But no one will deny that the promise was free, since it was made to the Jews before they were born, and it is established that Abraham himself was chosen by sheer grace and called out of Chaldea. From this it is gathered that this people was preserved by the grace of God and grew into so great a multitude as Moses records elsewhere. Num. 1.

units.la: Est autem obseruatione dignissimum, quod diuinae promissioni certum tempus tribuit diuinus martyr, cuius mentionem in ipsius Dei verbis fieri non ignorabat, ut videre est, Genes. 15. cap. ubi quarta generatione e seruitutis iugo afferendi dicuntur Abrahami posteri. Promissioni autem historia pulchre conuenit, quae docet Mosem, populi vindicem, a Iacobo quartum fuisse. Hic enim genuit Leui, Leui genuit Cahad, ex Cahad natus est Amram, qui Mosis & Aaronis pater fuisse perhibetur. Docemur hoc loco, Dei prouidentia non modo summam rerum, quae inter mortales fiunt, verum etiam rerum causas vna cum reliquis circumstantijs comprehendi. Quid enim negligere posset aeterna illa mens, quae & capitis pilos numerat, & florum agri atq; volatilium coeli rationem habet exactissimam? Matth. 6. & 10. Eandem vero temporum articulos completi, ipse Christus fatetur, quando apostolos hoc nomine reprehendit, quod de ijs inquirerent, qui in solius patris potestate sunt repositi. Act. 1. Debet horum consyderatio nostrae consolationi seruire, quando in grauissimis angustijs constituti, diuinam opem eousq; differri sentimus, ut nostri simul & promissionum suarum Deus oblitus esse videri possit. Tunc enim meminerimus, Dei promissionibus certum tempus constitutum esse, quod nunquam elabi patietur Deus, quin in se sperantes adiuuet. Nostrum vero est interea expectare Dei opem, nec illi rerum agendarum formam aut tempus praescribere. Expecta Dominum (inquit Dauid,) forte fit & roboretur cor tuum, & expecta dominum. Psal. 27. Quid? quod alibi Deum tentauisse dicuntur, qui terminos certos diuinae vel potentiae, vel voluntati praescripserunt, quales fuere, qui carnes in deserto postulare ausi sunt & Bethuliani proceres, qui quinq; duntaxat dierum spacio Dei opem expectare statuerant. Num. 11. Psal. 78. Iudith. 8. Vtamur igitur hoc contra carnis impatientiam antidoto, ut Deum certis locis & temporibus res omnes agere cogitemus, nec interim in se sperantes deserere. Vide Habac. 2.
units.tr: It is most worthy of note that the divine martyr assigned a definite time to the divine promise, and he was not unaware that mention of it is made in God's own words, as may be seen in Genesis 15, where Abraham's descendants are said to be brought out of the yoke of slavery in the fourth generation. The history agrees well with the promise, which teaches that Moses, the deliverer of the people, was the fourth from Jacob. For he begot Levi, Levi begot Kohath, from Kohath was born Amram, who is said to have been the father of Moses and Aaron. We are taught in this place that the providence of God comprehends not only the sum of the things that happen among mortals, but also the causes of things together with the other circumstances. For what could that eternal mind neglect, which counts the hairs of the head and takes the most exact account of the flowers of the field and the birds of the heaven? Matt. 6 and 10. Christ himself also acknowledges that the same God fixes the appointed times, when he rebukes the apostles for this very thing, that they inquired about those things which are kept in the power of the Father alone. Acts 1. The consideration of these things ought to serve our consolation, when we are placed in the heaviest distress and feel that divine help is so long delayed that God may seem to have forgotten both us and his promises. For then let us remember that a fixed time has been appointed for God's promises, which God will never let slip away without helping those who hope in him. Meanwhile it is our part to await God's help, and not to prescribe to him the form or the time of his doings. "Wait for the Lord," says David, "and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord." Ps. 27. What then? It is said elsewhere that those tested God who prescribed fixed limits to his power or his will, as did those who dared to demand flesh in the wilderness, and the leaders of Bethulia, who had resolved to wait for God's help for only five days. Num. 11; Ps. 78; Judith 8. Let us therefore use this as an antidote against the impatience of the flesh, that we may think of God as doing all things in fixed places and times, and meanwhile not forsake those who hope in him. See Hab. 2.

units.la: Alterum argumentum a temporum illorum, quo populus multiplicatus est, conditione sumitur. Nec enim magnum videri poterat, si inter eos creuisset populus, qui Iosephi & beneficiorum ipsius memores, illum tuebantur & omni officiorum genere prosequebantur, quod primos Aegypti reges fecisse constat. At inuitis & multum reluctantibus ijs, quorum arbitrio omnia regebantur, multiplicata est Iudaeorum gens. Nam surrexit rex alius, qui non nouerat Iosephum, nec aliqua veterum beneficiorum cura tangebatur. Is non modo neglexit Israelem, & aliorum libidini vexandum permisit, sed ipse dolo malo populum illum aggressus, toti Aegypto suspectum & inuisum reddidit, & eousq; tyrannidis sua saeuitiam extendit, ut non contentus libertatem abstulisse & turpi seruitute oppressisse, foetus quoque illorum tum in ipso partu occidi, tum recens natos a parentibus exponi, aut per crudelitatis sua ministros inuestigari, & immanissime extingui curauit. Vide Exod. 1. Nihilominus tamen creuit in immensum populus, & palmae instar vrgentis tyrannidis ponderi reluctatus est. Quis ergo hoc non agnoscat singulare quoddam diuinae bonitatis opus fuisse, nec vllis ceremonijs, quae tunc nulla erant, acceptum ferri debere?
units.tr: The second argument is taken from the condition of those times in which the people multiplied. For it could not seem remarkable if the people had grown among those who, mindful of Joseph and his benefits, protected him and showed every kind of service to his people, as it is established that the first kings of Egypt did. But the nation of the Jews multiplied while those by whose will all things were governed were unwilling and strongly resisted. For another king arose who did not know Joseph, and was moved by no care for the earlier benefits. He not only neglected Israel and allowed it to be harassed at the lust of others, but himself with malicious deceit attacked that people and made it suspect and hateful to all Egypt; and he extended the cruelty of his tyranny so far that, not content with having taken away their liberty and oppressed them with shameful slavery, he saw to it that their offspring were killed, both in the very birth, and that the newborn were exposed by their parents or sought out by the agents of his cruelty and most savagely destroyed. See Exod. 1. Nevertheless the people grew immensely, and like a palm tree resisted the weight of the pressing tyranny. Who then would not acknowledge this as a singular work of divine goodness, and one that ought to be credited to no ceremonies, since there were none at that time?

units.la: Primo autem hic obseruemus, quod cum tempus promissionis instaret, eiusmodi regem excitauit Deus, qui iniusta tyrannide populum opprimeret, & eousque grassaretur, ut vix aliqua liberationis spes reliqua esset. Est hic vetus Dei mos, ut laetis tristia permisceat, & impios tunc maxime ferociri sinat, quando illorum interitus prae foribus adest. Ita enim suorum fidem exercet, & cauet ne securi nimis insolescant, & libertate abutantur. Sunt huius generis exempla passim obuia in Dauide, Ezechia & infinitis alijs. Pertinet huc etiam quod post reditum e Babylone circa vrbis restaurationem contigit, quando nec Cyri regis authoritas improbos hostium conatus reprimere potuit, & hunc secutus Cambyses filius ecclesiae hostes suo fauore armauit: adeo ut qui in vrbis aedificatione laborabant, altera manu opus facere, altera pugnare cogeretur. Nehem. 4. Prodest vero nobis, ut dili genter in horum meditatione versemur, ne prosperis successibus nimium confisi, securitatis laqueo circumueniamur, sed potius cogitemus, nobis sub cruce triumphandum esse, & proinde ad hanc, cum maxime tuta videntur omnia, praeparari debere.
units.tr: But first let us observe here that, when the time of the promise was at hand, God raised up a king of this kind, who oppressed the people with unjust tyranny and raged so far that there was scarcely any hope of deliverance left. This is God's ancient custom, to mingle sad things with joyful ones, and to allow the wicked to grow most fierce just when their destruction is at the door. For so he exercises the faith of his own people, and guards against their becoming too secure and abusing their liberty. Examples of this kind are found everywhere, in David, Hezekiah and countless others. To this belongs also what happened after the return from Babylon, about the restoration of the city, when the authority of King Cyrus could not restrain the wicked attempts of the enemies, and his son Cambyses, following him, armed the enemies of the Church with his favour, so that those who were labouring at the building of the city were compelled to do the work with one hand and to fight with the other. Neh. 4. It profits us, however, to dwell diligently on these things, lest, trusting too much in prosperous successes, we be caught in the snare of security, but rather that we may consider that we must triumph under the cross, and therefore must prepare ourselves for it, especially when all things seem most safe.

units.la: Deinde obferuandu venit, quod rex exortus esse dicitur, qui Iosephum non nouerit. At si historiam excutiamus, vix quinquaginta annorum spatium inter Iosephi mortem & tyrannidis huius initium intercessisse patebit. Iosephus enim trigesimo aetatis anno Aegypti dominus factus est: Secuti sunt septem anni fertiles, & secundo sterilitatis anno patrem Iacobum ad se euocauit. Quare si quid temporis praeparationi ad iter & ipsi itineri tribuamus, non vltra quadragesimum Iosephi annum Israelis in Aegyptum descensus extrahetur. Vixit ab eo tempore Iosephus annis adhuc septuaginta, nam centesimo decimo demum anno illum obdormiisse Moses testatur. Fuerunt autem in Aegypto Israelitae annis ducentis & decem, a quibus si septuaginta Iosephi annos & octuaginta, quibus Moses vixit, priusquam populum educeret, subtrahas, soli sexaginta anni reliquunt, qui inter Iosephi mortem & Mosis natiuitatem intercurrunt. A quibus tamen auferendi erunt anni, ad minus decem, quibus Amram in matrimonio (quod feruente iam persecutione demum ab illo contractum fuit) priusquam illi Moses nasceretur, vixit. Tribus enim annis ante Mosen Aaronem natum esse constat, & cum Moses in fluuio reperiretur, eius soror Maria ea aetate fuit, vt cum regis filia colloqui, & non omnino inepta de seruando puero consilia suggerere posset. Docet horum consyderatio, quam fluxa sit apud potentes & principes huius seculi beneficiorum memoria, quando Iosephum Aegypti reges, tam breui tempore secuti, ignorant, cuius consilijs & Aegyptus seruata, & regum potestas in immensum aucta fuerat. Ebrij enim fortuna facile insolescunt, & nefas esse ducunt, vt se alicui mortalium debitores esse agnoscant. Recte ergo & prudenter Dauid clamat: Nolite confidere principibus, nec filijs hominum, in quibus non est salus. Psal. 146. Item: Spem habere in domino melius est, quam fidere principibus. Psal. 118. Simul vero admonemur quam noxia sit regnis & rebuspublicis veterum actorum, legum & priuilegiorum ignorantia siue obliuio. Hanc enim crudelissimae tyrannidis tandem horribilis interitus causam fuisse, hic locus diserte testatur. Memorabilis ergo est Persarum & Medorum mos, quorum reges in annalium lectione frequenter versatos fuisse, historici docent. Quantum enim inde commodi enatum sit, vnius Mardochai historia abunde monet. Vide Esth. 6. cap.
units.tr: Next we should observe that the text says a king arose who did not know Joseph. But if we examine the history, it will be clear that scarcely fifty years passed between Joseph's death and the beginning of this tyranny. Joseph became lord of Egypt in his thirtieth year. Seven fruitful years followed, and in the second year of famine he summoned his father Jacob to himself. So if we allow some time for preparing the journey and for the journey itself, the descent of Israel into Egypt is not put later than Joseph's fortieth year. From that time Joseph lived another seventy years, for Moses testifies that he fell asleep in his hundred and tenth year. The Israelites were in Egypt for two hundred and ten years. If you subtract from this Joseph's seventy years and the eighty years Moses lived before he led the people out, only sixty years remain between Joseph's death and Moses' birth. From these, however, at least ten years must be deducted, the years Amram lived in marriage before Moses was born to him. (That marriage was contracted only when the persecution was already raging.)
