For it is certain that Aaron was born three years before Moses, and when Moses was found in the river, his sister Miriam was old enough to speak with the king's daughter and to suggest, not altogether foolishly, plans for saving the boy. This consideration shows how fleeting is the memory of benefits among the powerful and princes of this age. The kings of Egypt who followed so soon after Joseph did not know him, though through his counsel Egypt had been saved and the king's power had been enormously increased. Men raised by fortune easily become insolent, and they think it wrong to acknowledge that they owe anything to any mortal. Rightly and wisely, then, David cries out: "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation" (Psal. 146). Again: "It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in princes" (Psal. 118). At the same time we are warned how harmful to kingdoms and commonwealths is ignorance or forgetfulness of past acts, laws and privileges. That this was the cause of the dreadful downfall of the most cruel tyranny is clearly attested by this passage. Memorable, therefore, is the custom of the Persians and Medes, whose kings, the historians tell us, were often occupied with reading the annals. How much advantage came from this is amply shown by the history of Mordecai alone. See Esther chapter 6.

units.la: Tertio tyrannorum artes, quibus in alijs opprimendis vtuntur, consydera. Nec enim absoluta potentia vti videtur Pharao, sed callide & miro dolo Israeliticum populum circumuenit, & in hoc est, vt cum publicae paci quam maxime consulere, tum aequitatis summam rationem habere videatur, quando gentem auita libertate exutam tanta immanitate persequitur. Nam haud dubie conquestus est, rem iniquam & absurdam esse, homines peregrinos immanitate gaudere, & ipsis Aegyptijs esse liberiores. Praeterea periculum imminere ostendit, ne si bellum ab exteris inferatur, hostibus coniunctis, Aegypti tyrannidem affectent. At si exitum rei consyderes, omnium consiliorum & argumentorum finis fuit auaritia, quae Aegyptios aliorum oppressione & gratuitis seruitijs ditescere docuit. Hinc exemplo carens tyrannis secuta est, cuius saeuitiem ne infantibus quidem recens natis effugere licuit. Adeo sibi quiduis licere putant, qui iuris & aequi leges semel violare ausi sunt, & aliquem inde priuati commodi gustum perceperunt. Agnoscamus eiusmodi artes, quo facilius agnitas cauere possimus. Interim non despondeamus animos, quando plerunque fit, vt tyrannorum conatus Dei gloriam & virtutem illustrent, quibus facillimum est gentium consilia euertere, sicut diuinus Psalmes admonet, & hoc loco euenisse patet.
units.tr: Third, consider the arts by which tyrants use to oppress others. Pharaoh does not seem to use absolute power, but cunningly and with a remarkable trick he circumvents the Israelite people. He aims to appear to consult the public peace as far as possible, and to have the highest regard for fairness, when he persecutes with such savagery a nation stripped of its ancestral liberty. For he doubtless complained that it was an unjust and absurd thing for foreigners to enjoy liberty while the Egyptians themselves had less. Besides, he points to a danger hanging over them: if war were waged against them by external enemies allied with them, they might seize the tyranny of Egypt. But if you consider the outcome of the affair, the aim of all his counsels and arguments was greed, which taught the Egyptians to grow rich by oppressing others and by unpaid services. From this came a tyranny without precedent, whose savagery not even newborn infants could escape. So much do those who have dared once to violate the laws of justice and right think they may do anything, once they have tasted some private gain. Let us recognise such arts, so that we may guard against them more easily once recognised. Meanwhile, let us not despair, since it very often happens that the attempts of tyrants bring out the glory and power of God, to whom it is very easy to overturn the plans of nations, as the divine Psalmist reminds us, and as is clear to have happened in this place.

units.la: Caeterum pergens in coepta narratione Stephanus, Mosen producit, quo assertore vel vindice & legislatore Iudaei maxime gloriabantur. Docet autem, hunc quoque singulari Dei beneficio seruatum & ad tam altum functionis gradum euectum esse, nec habere, quo glorietur. Vnde cuiuis facile est concludere, multo magis eos diuina gratia omnia debere, quos illius ministerio Deus liberari & legem accipere voluit. Sunt vero tria potissimum, quibus probat, quod modo diximus. Primo a tempore conditione argumentari pergens, illo ipso tempore natum fuisse dicit, quando maxime feruebat tyrannus, & quando non alia ratione quam occulta Dei potentia & gratia seruari poterat. Addit & aliud, quod in recens nato infante non obscura diuina gratiae indicia apparuerint, quae certe ad nullum Mosis meritum referri possunt. Interim probe tenendum, quod eo tempore vindex & assertor populi nascitur, quo vix aliqua liberationis spes superesset, & quando ipsum primi periclitari oportebat, quam illum futurae magnanimitatis aut liberationis specimen edere posset. Solet ita
units.tr: Stephen, continuing the account he has begun, brings forward Moses, in whom the Jews especially gloried as their champion, defender and lawgiver. He shows that Moses too was preserved by a singular benefit of God and raised to so high a rank of office, and that Moses had nothing in which to glory. From this it is easy for anyone to conclude that those whom God wished to free through Moses's ministry and to give the law much more owe everything to divine grace. There are three main arguments by which he proves what we have just said. First, arguing from the time and circumstances, he says that Moses was born at the very time when the tyrant raged most fiercely, and when he could be preserved by no means other than the hidden power and grace of God. He adds another point: in the newborn infant there appeared clear signs of divine grace, which can certainly not be ascribed to any merit of Moses. Meanwhile we must hold firmly that the champion and defender of the people was born at a time when there was scarcely any hope of deliverance left, and when he himself had to be in danger before he could show any sign of future greatness or of deliverance.

units.la: Deus præter omnem spem suis adesse, & (vt Isaias inquit) opus suum alienum facere, eiusque, quodammodo obliuisci, quò maiori cum gloria illud posteà exequatur, Isa.28. Proprium enim Dei opus est, saluare homines: quod tum facit, quando cum salute spes quoque omnis intercidisse videtur. Simile quid in Christi natiuitate contigit. Quando enim Iudæi libertate amissa, extero principi, eique ethnico, censum siue tributum exoluere coguntur, & viritim omnes censentur à Cyrenio, promissus ille & tanto tempore expectatus orbis saluator nascitur. Imò ex Dauidis familia nascitur, cum illa ex omni dignitate decidisset, & iam truncus aliquis putris & inutilis videri posset, sicuti olim Isaias prædixerat. Isa.11. Nemo igitur propter imminentes afflictiones de Dei ope desperet, &c.
units.tr: God is present to his people beyond all hope and (as Isaiah says) does his work as a stranger, and in a sense forgets it, so that he may afterwards carry it out with greater glory (Isa. 28). For it is God's proper work to save men, and he does this when all hope of salvation seems to have perished. Something similar happened at the birth of Christ. When the Jews, having lost their liberty, were forced to pay the census or tribute to a foreign prince, and a pagan at that, and all were enrolled man by man by Cyrenius, then the promised Saviour of the world, who had been awaited for so long, was born. Indeed he was born from the family of David, when that family had fallen from all dignity and might already seem like some rotten and useless stump, just as Isaiah had foretold long before (Isa. 11). Therefore let no one despair of God's help because of the afflictions that threaten, etc.

units.la: Secundum argumentum, quo Moses ex gratia seruatus esse docetur, à parentibus deducit, qui illum contra regis edictum tribus mensibus occultatum domi suæ aluerunt. Id enim (Paulo teste & interprete, Hebr.11.) fidei opus fuit, qua in Dei gratiam & promissiones respicientes, ita confortati sunt, vt regis mandato se opponere auderent. At fidem animi, constantiam, Dei dona esse, non tantum est, quàm vt multis demonstrari debeat. Ita tamen parentum Mosis fides considerari debet, vt eius imitatione accensi, impia tyrannorum edicta, quibus nemo salua pietate obedire potest, contemnere discamus. In talibus enim Petri regula audiri debet, qui nos Deo potius, quàm hominibus, obedire oportere, diserte testatur.
units.tr: The second argument by which Moses is shown to have been preserved by grace he draws from his parents, who, against the king's edict, hid him in their house and nourished him for three months. For this (as Paul, the witness and interpreter, says in Heb. 11) was a work of faith, by which, looking to the grace and promises of God, they were so strengthened that they dared to oppose the king's command. But that faith and constancy of mind are gifts of God is not something that must be shown to many people. Yet the faith of Moses's parents should be considered in such a way that, kindled by their example, we learn to despise the impious edicts of tyrants, which no one can obey and keep his piety. For in such cases Peter's rule ought to be heard, which expressly declares that we ought to obey God rather than men.

units.la: Tertiò liberationis modum & ordinem, quo Moses seruatus est, recensset, vt Dei gratia & vires magis illustretur. Nam expositum suffulit filia Pharaonis, & educauit eum sibi in filium. Adhæc in aula tyranni omni Ægyptiorum sapientia institutus, omnibus animi facultatibus, quæ rebus agendis necessariæ sunt, instructissimus euasit. Vide Exod.2. Quis verò hic humanis consiliis sine meritis quicquam tribuat? Quis non Dei gratiam singularem agnoscat? Est autem memorabilis hoc loco Dei potentia, qua tyrannorum conatus ridere & ludere consueuit. In aula, adeoque sinuo eius populi vindicem alit fuerat Pharao, quem maximè oppressum cupiebat. Sic Achabo prophetas & ecclesiam persequente, in aula honore & authoritate excellit Abdias, fidelissimus prophetarum & purioris doctrinæ patronus. Sic sub Romanis Imperatoribus olim militarunt Christianorum & veræ fidei propugnatores: cùm illi hanc extinctam vellent. Et multa alia exempla extant, quæ acerrimos Christi hostes ecclesiæ salutem adiuuisse docent. Quis ergo illorum conatibus exhorrescat, quos diuinæ potentiæ & prouidentiæ fræno gubernari nouit? Simul verò obseruemus, quod Mosen omni Ægyptiorum sapientia institutum fuisse tradit. Licet ergo pijs gentilium quoque libros & philosophiam attingere, quod Paulum etiam fecisse, illius scripta & sermones testantur, quibus ethnicorum sententias aliquando non ineptè nec sine gratia inseruit. Interim modus seruetur, ne gentilitia philosophia curgidus verbi Dei mysteria sordere incipiant, nèue in philosophorum scriptis ea admiremur, quæ cælestis sapientiæ oraculis palàm repugnant. Solet hoc astrologis & nimium anxijs naturalium causarum indagatoribus contingere, quos interim non pudet suam impietatem Mosis exemplo tueri. At huius potius modestiam imitari debebant, qui cùm in opificio mundi descriptione amplissimam haberet Ægyptiacam sapientiam ostentandi occasionem, mira breuitate & simplicitate omnia ea complexus est, quæ iam seculis aliquot mathematicorum & philosophorum curiosa ingenia inutiliter fatigauerunt. Quia enim rerum causas ad vnum Deum refert (quod passim scriptura faciunt) facile vidit, impiam esse tam ingenij ostentationem, quæ Deum aliqua suæ gloriæ parte spoliat, & mundi gubernationem creaturarum statis legibus subijcit. Detestabilis ergo est illorum studitia & vesania, qui astrologiæ & iudiciariæ impietatem ad Abrahamum & Mosen ex gratia elegit, nobisque filium suum saluatorem & regem per bos pollicitus est. Cui cum omnis potestas data sit in cælo & in terra, debetur eidem benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Third, he recounts the manner and order of the deliverance by which Moses was preserved, so that God's grace and power may be shown all the more clearly. For Pharaoh's daughter took him up when he was exposed and brought him up as her son. Moreover, instructed in the court of the tyrant in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he became most thoroughly equipped with all those mental abilities which are necessary for carrying out affairs. See Exod. 2. But who here would ascribe anything to human counsels without merit? Who would not acknowledge God's singular grace? Memorable in this place is the power of God, by which he is accustomed to mock and make sport of the attempts of tyrants. Pharaoh had nourished in his own court and bosom the champion of the people whom he most wished to oppress. So when Ahab was persecuting the prophets and the Church, Obadiah, the most faithful of the prophets and a patron of purer doctrine, excelled in honour and authority at court. So too under the Roman emperors, defenders of the Christians and of the true faith once served as soldiers, while the emperors wished to extinguish that faith. And many other examples exist which show that the bitterest enemies of Christ have helped the salvation of the Church. Who, then, should tremble at the attempts of those whom he knows to be governed by the bridle of divine power and providence? At the same time let us observe that he says Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. It is therefore lawful for the godly to touch also the books and philosophy of the Gentiles, as Paul's own writings and speeches show that he did, in which he sometimes wove in the opinions of the pagans not inaptly and not without grace. Meanwhile moderation must be kept, lest, puffed up with Gentile philosophy, they begin to despise the mysteries of God's Word, or we admire in the writings of philosophers those things which openly contradict the oracles of heavenly wisdom. This tends to happen to astrologers and to overly anxious investigators of natural causes, who nonetheless are not ashamed to defend their impiety by the example of Moses. But they ought rather to imitate the modesty of Moses, who, when in describing the creation of the world he had the greatest opportunity to display Egyptian wisdom, embraced with wonderful brevity and simplicity all those things which for several centuries the curious minds of mathematicians and philosophers have wearied themselves over to no purpose. For because he refers the causes of things to the one God (which the Scriptures do everywhere), he easily saw that it is impious to make such a display of ingenuity as strips God of some part of his glory and subjects the governance of the world to fixed laws of creatures. Detestable, therefore, is the zeal and madness of those who transfer the impiety of astrology and judicial astrology to Abraham and Moses, whom God chose by grace, and through whom he promised his Son as Saviour and King to us. To him, to whom all power has been given in heaven and on earth, belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XLVIII.

units.la: Vt verò illi impletum fuit quadraginta annorum tempus, subiit in cor eius, vt inuiseret fratres suos, filios Israel. Et cùm vidisset quendam iniuria affectum, defendit, & vindicauit eum qui affligebatur, cæso Ægyptio. Existimabat autem intelligere fratres suos, quòd Deus per manum ipsius daret illis salutem. At illi non intellexerunt. Et sequenti die conspectus est illis litigantibus, & reduxit eos in concordiam, dicens: Viri, vos estis fratres, cur vos inuicem læditis? Cæterum is, qui iniuriam faciebat proximo, repulit eum dicens: Quis te constituit principem & iudicem super nos? Nunquid me interficere tu vis, quemadmodum heri interfecisti Ægyptium? Fugit autem Moses ad dictum hoc, & factus est aduena in terra Madian, vbi generauit filios duos.
units.tr: When the forty years were fulfilled for him, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. And when he saw one of them suffering wrong, he defended him and avenged the one who was oppressed, striking down the Egyptian. He supposed that his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation through his hand. But they did not understand. And on the following day he appeared to them as they were quarrelling, and he reconciled them, saying: "Men, you are brothers; why do you wrong one another?" But the one who was doing wrong to his neighbour pushed him away, saying: "Who made you a prince and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" At that word Moses fled, and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.

units.la: Cum Diuus Stephanus, veterum patrum historiæ filum & ordinem secutus, in Mosis mentionem incidisset, quo liberatore & legislatore Iudæi quàm maximè gloriari solebant, illius historiam singulari diligentia tractat: partim quidem, quia Moses hic, quoad Ægyptiacam liberationem, Christi Iesu typum gessit, & eidem testimonium tulit: partim vero, vt seipsum contempti Mosis crimine liberet, cuius illum accusabant, eò quòd contra templum & Leuitici cultus ceremonias esset concionatus. Vt verò inanem & vanam rerum externarum fiduciam illis penitus auferat, ostendit has ad hominis iustificationem & salutem adeò nihil conferre, vt nec ipse Moses aliquid habeat, quo coram domino glorietur, cum nulla humana ope, sed solius Dei gratia seruatus, & in tantum honoris fastigium euectus sit. Vnde sequitur, diuinæ gratiæ ascribi debere, quicquid ab illo postea præclarè & bene gestum est. Id verò præsenti loco plenius illustratur, quo recenset, vt Moses officium, cui illum Deus destinauerat, obire cœperit, & vt oblatum liberationis beneficium patres indignißimè fastidierint, Mosenq; vindicem reiecerint plusquam inhumaniter.
units.tr: When St Stephen, following the thread and order of the histories of the ancient fathers, had come to mention Moses, in whom the Jews were wont above all to glory as their deliverer and lawgiver, he treats his history with singular care. He does so partly because this Moses, in the matter of the deliverance from Egypt, bore the figure of Jesus Christ and bore witness to him; and partly so that he may clear himself of the charge against Moses, of which they accused him, namely that he had preached against the temple and the ceremonies of the Levitical worship. But so that he may wholly strip them of their empty and vain confidence in external things, he shows that these things contribute so little to a man's justification and salvation that not even Moses himself has anything in which he may glory before the Lord, since he was saved by no human help but by the grace of God alone, and was raised to such a height of honour. Hence it follows that whatever was afterwards done by him nobly and well must be ascribed to divine grace. This is set forth more fully in the present passage, where he recounts how Moses began to undertake the office to which God had destined him, and how the fathers most shamefully spurned the offered benefit of deliverance, and rejected Moses the avenger more than inhumanly.

units.la: Orditur autem à Mosis ætate & causa, quæ illum vt populi afflictissimi curam susciperet, impulit. Quadragenarium enim factum fuisse dicit, priusquam aliquod liberationis specimen exhibueret. Interea verò temporis in aula regis inter regni proceres vitam ducens, non magnam populi sui rationem habuisse videtur. Quod non obscurè monet Stephanus, quando post quadraginta demum annos, eas cogitationes animum ipsius subijsse dicit, quæ illum vt fratres suos inuiseret, solicitauerunt. Quis verò eas suggessit? Vel num sponte enasci potuere in eo homine, qui à pueris inter aulæ delitias educatus, & Ægyptiaca sapientia imbutus fuerat? Nequaquam. Diuinus ergo & arcanus spiritus sanctus hic motus fuit, qui Mosis quasi stertentis aures vellicauit, & veterum promissionum meditatione animum illius expergefecit, vt ei populo sese adiungere cuperet, è cuius stirpe promissum humani generis saluatorem enasciturum esse intelligebat. Consentit hîc Paulus, qui Mosis factum fidei tribuit, quam diuinæ gratiæ donum esse vniuersa scriptura docet. Ait enim: Per fidem Moses iam grandis, renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis, potius eligens simul malis afflici cum populo Dei, quàm temporarijs peccati commodis frui, maiores arbitratus diuitias probrum Christi, quàm Ægyptiorum thesauros. Heb. xi. cap. Simul verò ex his luce clarius pater, liberationis laudem omnem vni Deo deberi, qui Mosen non viribus modò instruxit, sed animum quoq; & voluntatem inseruit.
units.tr: He begins from Moses' age and the cause which moved him to take up the care of the most afflicted people. For he says that Moses was forty years old before he showed any sign of deliverance. Meanwhile, living at the king's court among the nobles of the realm, he seems not to have had much regard for his people. Stephen clearly indicates this when he says that only after forty years did those thoughts come into his mind which stirred him to visit his brothers. But who suggested them? Could they have sprung up of their own accord in a man who had been brought up from boyhood amid the delights of the court and steeped in Egyptian learning? By no means. This was therefore a divine and hidden movement of the Holy Spirit, which plucked at the ears of Moses, as though he were sleeping, and by meditating on the ancient promises roused his mind, so that he desired to join that people from whose stock he understood the promised Saviour of mankind would be born. Paul agrees here, who ascribes Moses' deed to faith, which the whole of Scripture teaches to be a gift of divine grace. For he says: "By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God than to enjoy the temporary pleasures of sin, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt" (Heb. 11). At the same time it is clearer than light that all the praise of deliverance is owed to the one God alone, who furnished Moses not only with strength but also inspired in him both mind and will.

units.la: Interim ad nostram quoq; institutionem transferri debet, quòd Moses non prius, quàm à domino excitetur, fratrum suorum curam suscipit. Generalis hinc doctrina colligitur, eos qui mundo & carnis studijs adhuc immersi hærent, & mundi sapientia reguntur, in ijs quæ ad Dei gloriam & salutem faciunt, nihil boni aut præclari facere, nisi diuini spiritus motu trahantur: quando ex nobis ipsis (sicuti Paulus monet) non sumus idonei ad cogitandum. 2. Corinth. 3. Et Christus neminem, nisi qui à patre trahitur, ad se venire docet. Ioan. 6. Quare sponsa apud Solomonem nô immeritò clamat: Trahe me post te. Cant. 1. Vnde rursum sequitur, nullam meriti laudem nostris operibus deberi, sed vnius gratiæ esse quicquid bene agimus.
units.tr: Meanwhile this too ought to be applied to our instruction, that Moses did not take up the care of his brothers until he was roused by the Lord. From this a general teaching is drawn: those who still lie immersed in the pursuits of the world and the flesh, and are governed by worldly wisdom, do nothing good or excellent in those things which serve God's glory and salvation, unless they are drawn by the motion of the divine Spirit; since of ourselves (as Paul warns) we are not sufficient to think anything (2 Cor. 3). And Christ teaches that no one comes to him unless he is drawn by the Father (John 6). Therefore the bride in Solomon rightly cries out: "Draw me after you" (Song 1). Hence again it follows that no praise of merit is owed to our works, but whatever we do well is due to grace alone.

units.la: Simul verò officij nos admonet Mosis exemplum, vt Deo nos excitanti & trahenti accommodè mus, & illi nos obsequentes præbeamus. Ea enim diuinæ vocationis apud fideles vis est, vt effectu carere non possit: quando hoc ouibus suis proprium esse dicit Christus, quòd vocem suam agnoscant, & auditam sequantur. Ioan. 10. Quod tanto ardore & zelo ab ipsis fieri consueuit, vt omnia simul fastidiant & ceu noxia quædam excrementa abijciant, quæcunque ipsos in vocatione sua remorate.
units.tr: At the same time the example of Moses also reminds us of our duty, that we should accommodate ourselves to God when he rouses and draws us, and yield ourselves obedient to him. For such is the power of divine calling among the faithful that it cannot fail to have its effect, since Christ says that it is peculiar to his sheep that they know his voice and follow it when heard (John 10). And they are wont to do this with such ardour and zeal that they despise everything together and cast away, like harmful excrement, whatever holds them back in their calling.

units.la: Nisi diuinitus trahamur, nil boni facimus.
units.tr: Unless we are drawn by God, we do nothing good.

units.la: Vocanti & trahenti Deo obedire decet. ri possunt: nec vicissim illis quicquam intolerabile videtur, quod cum Dei vocatione coniunctum esse vident. Utrunque in Mosis exemplo cernitur. Nam mox, ut domini vocem in animo suo loquentem audit, omni mora abrupta, aulae lautitias, regni splendorem, officiorum publicorum dignitates, precerum amicitias, opes, otium, & quicquid eius generis in aulis habebatur, procul reijcit. In eorum vero locum eligit aerumnas, inopiam, infamiam, labores & infinita pericula, quibus populum Dei sub immanissimis hostibus quotidie vexari videbat. Et quod Mosen fecisse dicimus, idem in apostolis cernitur, qui etsi non tantas opes reliquerint, non minori tamen zelo & studio sua illa, quantulacunque deseruerunt. Quibus Zachaeus & infiniti alij adnumerari debent. Ad quorum exempla si nostrum torporem & socordiam conferamus, quibus intolerabile & iniquum videtur, quicquid propter Christum vel amittere vel pati, non obscure patebit, quam procul adhuc a Christiana perfectione absimus. Haec enim abnegatio illa est, quam a suis discipulis Christus exigit. Haec fidei obedientia est, quam Paulus ubique urget, & sine qua inutilis est Christiani nominis professio.
units.tr: It is fitting to obey God who calls and draws us. Nor, conversely, does anything seem intolerable to them which they see is joined with God's calling. Both are seen in the example of Moses. For as soon as he heard the voice of the Lord speaking in his mind, he broke off every delay and cast far away the luxuries of the court, the splendour of the kingdom, the dignities of public office, the friendship of the nobles, wealth, leisure, and whatever of that kind was held in high esteem at court. In their place he chose hardships, poverty, infamy, labours and endless dangers, by which he saw the people of God being daily harassed under most savage enemies. And what we say Moses did is seen also in the apostles, who, although they did not leave such great riches, nevertheless gave up their own possessions, however small, with no less zeal and eagerness. Zacchaeus and countless others must be counted among them. If we compare our sluggishness and laziness with their examples, to whom nothing seems intolerable or unjust that they must either lose or suffer for Christ's sake, it will become plain enough how far we are still from Christian perfection. For this is the self-denial which Christ demands of his disciples. This is the obedience of faith which Paul urges everywhere, and without which the profession of the Christian name is useless.

units.la: Caeterum obijciat aliquis: Fatemur equidem, quae de Mose dicta sunt, omnia. At credibile est, patres suorum operum meritis hoc assecutos esse, ut hic illis assertor & vindex a domino daretur. Huic ergo obiectioni prudenter occurrit Stephanus, & ostendit, patres Iudaeorum in liberatione ex Aegypto adeo nullam laudem & gloriam meruisse, ut potius digni fuerint, qui perpetuo servirent, eo quod Mosen & divinitus oblatum redemptionis beneficium iniquis & indignis modis reiecerint. Et demonstrationis loco historiam, quae Exod. 2. cap. habetur, recenset: unde plura petat, si cui breviora videntur, quae Lucas scribit. Finis vero omnium est, patres & Dei beneficiis & Mosen vindicem spreuisse, quare vniuersum Aegyptiacae liberationis negotium ad solius Dei gratiam referri debeat. Simul vero non obscure Stephanus Mosis contemptum, cuius accusabatur, in ipsorum patres retorquet, & illis ipsis auitam improbitatem & ingratitudinem exprobrat: non quidem connitian dilibidine, sed ut ostendat, ipsos patrum vestigia probe sectari, quando Christum simili contumacia reijciant, quem Moses olim observare & audire iusserit.
units.tr: But someone may object: "We admit that everything said about Moses is true. Yet it is credible that the fathers obtained this, that he should be given to them by the Lord as their champion and avenger, by the merits of their works." Stephen prudently meets this objection and shows that the fathers of the Jews deserved so little praise and glory in the deliverance from Egypt that they were rather worthy to be kept in perpetual slavery, because they rejected both Moses and the redemption offered them by God, in wicked and unworthy ways. And as proof he recounts the history which is found in Exodus 2; from which, if the things Luke writes seem too brief to someone, he may seek more. The aim of it all is that the fathers spurned both the benefits of God and Moses the avenger, and therefore the whole business of the deliverance from Egypt must be referred to the grace of God alone. At the same time Stephen clearly turns the contempt of Moses, of which he was accused, back upon their fathers, and reproaches them with the ancestral wickedness and ingratitude; not indeed to speak ill of them, but to show that they are carefully following in their fathers' footsteps, since they reject Christ with similar obstinacy, whom Moses long ago commanded them to observe and hear.

units.la: Sed ut ea, quae nostrae institutioni servire possunt, non omittamus, primo omnium Moses, & in hoc boni principis siue magistratus officium, consyderari debet. Non pudet illum populi, cuius pastor & vindex a Deo constitutus erat. Ita populi diuinitus commissi neminem pudere debet, quantacunque coram mundo gloria excellat. Nam ut contemptissima sic plebecula mundi iudicio, in Dei tamen oculis pretiosissima habetur, qui illam sanguine filij sui redimere dignatus est. Deinde contra apertam vim & tyrannidem illos armata quoque manu, nec sine vitae periculo tuetur. Decet hoc omnes eos, qui cum laude in magistratu versari voluerint. Ita enim principis officium Solomon describit: Liberabit pauperem clamantem, & afflictum, cui deest adiutor: Beneficus erit in attritos & inopes, & animas pauperum seruabit. Redimet animas eorum a faenore & violentia, & pretiosus erit sanguis illorum in oculis suis. Psalmo 72. Et Paulus magistratui in eum finem gladium diuinitus datum esse docet, ut improborum petulantiam coheerceat, probos vero & bonos tueatur. Rom. 13. Quare vehementer errant, qui inani titulo & vano splendore turgidi, nulla populi cura tanguntur, sed illum aliorum tyrannidi vexandum permittunt. At haec potissimum in religione locum habent, quam in populo suo conseruare debent principes, ne superstitiosis hominum traditionibus a Deo abstrahantur, qui huic consecrati esse debent. Ideo reges ecclesiae nutritios vocat Isaias, cuius tituli gloriam vtinam hodie agnoscerent, qui suae fidei commissum populum immani Pontificum tyrannidi & impijs Conciliorum decretis subijci patiuntur. Accedit hus, quod fratribus concordiae author est: cuius studium inter suos ante omnia conseruare decet eos, qui respublicas suas saluas esse voluerint. Multorum enim regnorum & populorum exemplis illud Romani historici dictum comprobatum est: Concordia parvae res crescunt, discordia magnae dilabuntur. Nec dubium est, infelicem semper fore illorum exitum, qui dissidijs mutuis scinduntur. Quod si vero Mosis aut mores cum ijs conferamus, qui hodie inter Christianos rerum potiuntur, infelice nostri status minus mirabimur: quando ij passim regnant, quos & sui populi pudet, & illum vel supina quadam officiantia negligunt, vel exactionibus immodicis totum exhauriunt, adhaec lites in illo fouent, deniq; in temere suscepti bellis, & minime necessaria sanguinis effusione, potissimam laudem sibi esse ducunt.
units.tr: But so that we do not omit the things that can serve our instruction, first of all Moses should be considered, and in this the office of a good prince or magistrate. He was not ashamed of the people whose shepherd and defender God had appointed him to be. So no one should be ashamed of the people committed to him by God, however much he may stand out in glory before the world. For just as the people of the world regard the lowliest commoners as the most contemptible, in the eyes of God they are most precious, since he has deigned to redeem them with the blood of his Son. Next, Moses defends them against open violence and tyranny, even with an armed hand, and not without danger to his own life. All who wish to hold office with praise ought to do the same. Solomon describes the prince's duty in this way: "He will deliver the poor who cries out, and the afflicted who has no helper. He will be merciful to the broken and the needy, and will save the souls of the poor. He will redeem their souls from usury and violence, and their blood will be precious in his sight" (Ps. 72). And Paul teaches that the magistrate has been given the sword by God for this end: to restrain the wantonness of the wicked and to protect the upright and good (Rom. 13). Therefore they greatly err who, puffed up with an empty title and vain splendour, are moved by no care for the people, but allow them to be harassed by the tyranny of others. Yet this matters above all in religion, which princes ought to maintain among their people, so that they are not drawn away from God by superstitious human traditions, since they ought to be consecrated to him. For this reason Isaiah calls kings the nursing fathers of the Church. Would that those who allow the people entrusted to their faith to be subjected to the monstrous tyranny of the Pontiffs and the impious decrees of Councils would acknowledge the glory of that title today! In addition, Moses was the author of concord among his brothers, and those who wish their commonwealths to be safe ought above all to preserve this zeal for harmony among their own people. For the examples of many kingdoms and peoples confirm that saying of the Roman historian: "By concord small things grow, by discord great things fall apart." Nor is there any doubt that the outcome is always unhappy for those who are torn apart by mutual quarrels. But if we compare the conduct of Moses with that of those who today hold power among Christians, we will be less surprised at the unhappy state of our own times. For these rule everywhere, men whom their own people are ashamed of, who either neglect their office with a kind of idle indifference or drain everything away with immoderate exactions, who moreover foster quarrels, and who, finally, count it their chief glory to wage rashly undertaken wars with bloodshed that is by no means necessary.

units.la: Simul vero, quam gratiam tam pio officio apud Iudaeos Moses inierit, videamus. Pessimam hanc fuisse, Stephanus ait. Nam improbus ille, qui fratri iniuriam facere non dubitarat, scelerus con scientia efferatus, petulantis linguae habenas in conuitia & probra laxat, dicens: Quis te constituit principem & iudicem super nos? Nunquid me interficere tu vis, quemadmodum heri interfecisti Aegyptium? Quibus verbis affectati regni accusat eum, qui regni honores & opes ipsorum causa reliquerat. Homicidij item, imo latrocinij reum agit eum, qui cum sui capitis periculo populi salutem tueri studebat. Et quamuis vnius duntaxat improbitas notetur, multorum tamen similes fuisse animos hinc patet, quod & huius petulantia nemo coercuit, & Pharaoni tyranno Moysis facinus pati ho post innotuit, cuius nemo Aegyptius spectator fuerat. Israelitam ergo delatorem fuisse oportet. Nec meliores sunt, cum ex Aegypto liberati, infinitis signis & prodigijs didicissent, illu ipsis a Deo vindice & ducem datum esse. Quoties enim non pro voto omnia ipsis succedunt, toties Mosem proditionis & perfidiae accusant. Est autem hoc mundi ingenium, qui hoc pacto summos benefactores suos remunerare consueuit. Et quod Mosi accidit, hoc ipsum Dauidi, Ezechiae, Iosiae, prophetis omnibus, & inter ethnicos Miltiadi, Phocioni, Camillo, Scipionibus & infinitis alijs euenisse legimus. Quorum consyderatio eum vsum habere debet, ne mundi ingratitudine offendamur, nec eius causa vocationem nostram & officium deseramus. Meminerimus potius nos Dei seruos esse. Ab illo igitur mercedem expectemus, qui remunerator est liberalissimus. Cogitemus iam nunc nobis in coelo amplissimam mercedem repositam esse, & super multa olim constituendos fore, qui hic in paucis & exiguis fideles fuerint. Vide Matth. 5. 25. cap.
units.tr: But let us see what thanks Moses won from the Jews for such a dutiful office. Stephen says it was the worst. For that wicked man, who had not hesitated to do wrong to his brother, was driven to frenzy by a guilty conscience and loosed the reins of his insolent tongue into insults and abuse, saying: "Who made you a prince and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" With these words he accuses of seeking power the man who had left behind the honours and riches of a kingdom for their sake. Likewise he charges with murder, indeed with robbery, the man who, at risk to his own life, was eager to protect the people's safety. And although only one man's wickedness is noted, it is plain from this that many shared his feelings: no one restrained this man's insolence, and afterwards the tyrant Pharaoh was told of Moses' deed, though no Egyptian had witnessed it. So the Israelite must have been the informer. Nor were they any better when, freed from Egypt, they had learned from countless signs and wonders that Moses had been given to them as leader by God, their avenger. For whenever things did not turn out as they wished, they accused Moses of treason and faithlessness. Such is the disposition of the world, which is accustomed to repay its greatest benefactors in this way. And we read that what happened to Moses also happened to David, Hezekiah, Josiah, all the prophets, and among the heathen to Miltiades, Phocion, Camillus, the Scipios and countless others. Consideration of these things ought to serve to keep us from being offended by the ingratitude of the world, and not to abandon our calling and duty for its sake. Let us rather remember that we are servants of God. Let us therefore look for our reward from him, who is the most generous rewarder. Let us consider now that a most ample reward is laid up for us in heaven, and that those who have been faithful in a few and small things here will be set over many things (see Matt. 5). Cap. 25.

units.la: Praeterea redemptionis nostrae mysteria Mosis exemplum comprehendit, & nostram ingratitudinem, qua in Christum peccamus, nobis exprobrat. Nam vt Moses relicta Pharaonis aula & Aegypti opibus fratres inuisit & illorum causam suscepit: ita Iesus Christus, cum esset in gloria patris, propter nos humiliari & exinaniri, adeoque per incarnationem frater noster fieri voluit, vt nostram causam suscipere & tueri posset. Phil. 2. Rursum, vt Moses caeso Aegyptio Israelitam vindicauit & defendit: ita Iesus Christus caeso & deiecto Satana, nos in libertatem asseruit. Est enim promissum illud mulieris semen, cuius merito serpentis caput debebat conteri. Et vt Moses charitatis & concordiae author suaforq; inter fratres fuit: ita Iesus Christus ijs, quos mortis suae merito liberatos, sui corporis membra & Dei filios fecit, non alia quam charitatis praecepta praescribit, adeoque hanc tesseram esse vult, ex qua pro discipulis ipsius agnosci possint. Iohan. 13. & 15. Caeterum vt Mosi obmurmurare non veriti sunt Israelitae: ita plerique hominum Christi legibus indignissime & iniquissime obmurmurare non verentur, & paucos videre est, qui ipsum principem & vindicem suum agnoscant, cum maxima hominum pars gloriam, quam solus meruit, vel in creaturas transferant, vel sacrilego ausu sibi ipsis & suorum operum meritis vindicent. Impudenter ergo nimis Iudaeis ingratitudinis crimen exprobramus, qui maiori multo ingratitudine in Dei filium delinquimus.
units.tr: Moreover, the example of Moses contains the mysteries of our redemption, and it rebukes us for our ingratitude, by which we sin against Christ. For just as Moses, leaving behind the court of Pharaoh and the riches of Egypt, visited his brothers and took up their cause, so Jesus Christ, though he was in the glory of the Father, chose to be humbled and emptied for our sake, and so by the incarnation to become our brother, that he might take up and defend our cause (Phil. 2). Again, just as Moses avenged and defended the Israelite by striking down the Egyptian, so Jesus Christ, by striking down and overthrowing Satan, has asserted us into liberty. For that promise of the woman's seed is fulfilled, by whose merit the serpent's head was to be crushed. And just as Moses was the author and advocate of love and concord among his brothers, so Jesus Christ, to those whom he has freed by the merit of his death and made members of his body and sons of God, prescribes no other rule than the precepts of love, and he wills that this be the token by which they may be recognised as his disciples (John 13 and 15). But just as the Israelites did not shrink from murmuring against Moses, so most men do not shrink from murmuring most unworthily and unjustly against the laws of Christ; and few are to be seen who acknowledge him as their prince and defender, while the greater part of mankind either transfers to creatures the glory that he alone has earned, or with sacrilegious boldness claims it for themselves and the merits of their own works. Therefore we rightly charge the Jews with ingratitude too boldly, since we sin with far greater ingratitude against the Son of God.

units.la: Prodest vero poenam, qua in ingratissimos homines animaduertit Deus, inspicere. Fugatur Moses, & in Madian ab Iethrone receptus, illius filiam vxorem ducit, ex qua liberos duos, exilij solatium, suscipit. Interim vindice & liberatore suo destituuntur Israelitae, & quadraginta adhuc annis tyrannidem sustinent, qua iam primo liberari poterant, nisi Moses abs se repulisset. Ita frequenter fieri solet, vt nostra improbitas obstet, quo minus Deus pro sui ingenij bonitate nos iuuare possit. Simile huic est, quod ad terminos terrae Chanaan perducti, suo murmure merentur, vt in desertum denuo reducantur, & quadraginta annis omni malorum genere afflicti corruant. Numeri decimo quarto. Immerito igitur Dei voluntatem accusant, qui ipsi sibi malorum authores esse consueuerunt. Obseruent hoc qui de morbis conqueruntur, quos ipsi sibi sua intemperantia accersunt. Item qui egestatem impatienter ferunt, quam luxus immodicus ipsis peperit. Idem hoc in salutis causa locum habet. Quia enim iustitiam Dei, quam is in suo filio nobis offert, multi ampletti dedignantur, & propriam iustitiam statuere audent, merito fit, vt nec suam illam in Dei conspectu constituere, nec per Christum iustificari & saluari possint. Rom. 10.
units.tr: It is useful, however, to look at the punishment with which God punished these most ungrateful men. Moses is put to flight, and received in Midian by Jethro, he marries his daughter, and by her has two sons, the consolation of his exile. Meanwhile the Israelites are left without their avenger and liberator, and for forty more years they endure the tyranny from which they could have been freed at once, had Moses not been rejected by them. Thus it often happens that our wickedness stands in the way, so that God cannot help us as the goodness of his nature would wish. Similar to this is what happens when they are led to the borders of the land of Canaan and by their murmuring deserve to be led back again into the wilderness, and to fall there, afflicted for forty years with every kind of evil (Num. 14). Therefore they unjustly accuse the will of God, who have made themselves the authors of their own evils. Let those who complain of diseases which they bring upon themselves by their own intemperance take note of this. Likewise those who bear poverty impatiently, which their immoderate luxury has brought upon them. The same holds in the matter of salvation. For since many disdain to embrace the righteousness of God, which he offers us in his Son, and dare to establish their own righteousness, it follows deservedly that they can neither establish that righteousness of their own in the sight of God, nor be justified and saved through Christ (Rom. 10).

units.la: Postremo fuga Moses consyderanda venit, cuius exemplo admonemur, licere aliquando, vt suga nobis consulamus, nosq; melioribus temporibus referuemus. Hoc enim Christum quoq; non semel fecisse, & apostolis praecepisse legimus. Matth.10. Hic vero diligenti cura & circumspectione opus est, ne sub Christi praecepto nostra pusillanimitati & ignauo timori praetextum quaeramus, & turpi fuga stationem a domino nobis commendatam deseramus. Fugit Moses, nec alicuius peccati accusatur, quia ex indignissima illa, quam passus est, repulsa, facile intelligebat nondum instare liberationis tempus: nec fieri poterat, ut eos educeret, a quibus tanta improbitate reiciebatur. At vbi illi vindicem a Deo datum agnoscere, & Dei vocationi se accommodare coeperunt, nullis tyranni minis se consternari patitur, ut denuo fugiat: nec perfidia notam effugisset, si tunc sibi potius consulere, quam Dei mandatis obedire voluisset. Ita Christus tunc fugisse dicitur, quando horam suam nondum instare nouerat. At vbi illa venit, mortem patienter & intrepide adit. Hanc ergo regulam sibi proponant quicunq; in publico aliquo officio versantur, nec sibi licere putent eos deserere, quorum animos ita affectos vident, ut diuinae vocationi insistere cupiant. Quod si vero eousq; euadat populi improbitas, ut ipse prior officium detrectet, & antistites suos (siue illi magistratus siue verbi praecones fuerint) officio suo fideliter fungentes improbe reiciat, nihil obstabit, quo minus illi iuxta Christi praeceptum fuga sibi consulant, seq; melioribus temporibus & locis referuent. Multum hic proderit fidei obedientia, Dei & proximi charitate temperata. Ea enim faciet ne priuatis affectibus exaecati seducamur. Faxit Deus, ut ipsius gratia & voluntatis memores, vocationem nostram singuli sedulo tueamur, ut bono cursu ad felicitatis metam delati, in coelis viuamus cum Iesu Christo domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, the flight of Moses must be considered, by whose example we are reminded that it is sometimes lawful to take flight and to keep ourselves for better times. For we read that Christ too did this more than once, and instructed the apostles to do the same (Matt. 10). Here, however, diligent care and caution are needed, lest under the pretext of Christ's precept we seek an excuse for our own timidity and cowardly fear, and by shameful flight abandon the post entrusted to us by the Lord. Moses fled, and he was accused of no sin, because from the most unworthy rejection he had suffered he readily understood that the time of liberation was not yet at hand, nor could he lead out those by whom he was rejected with such wickedness. But when they began to acknowledge the one whom God had given them as avenger, and to accommodate themselves to God's calling, he did not allow himself to be dismayed by any threats of the tyrant so as to flee again; nor would he have escaped the mark of faithlessness if he had then chosen to consult his own safety rather than obey the commands of God. So Christ is said to have fled when he knew that his hour was not yet at hand; but when it came, he met death patiently and fearlessly. Let therefore all who hold some public office set this rule before themselves, and let them not think it permitted to desert those whom they see so disposed that they desire to persevere in the divine calling. But if the wickedness of the people should go so far that they themselves first refuse the office, and wickedly reject their leaders (whether they are magistrates or heralds of the Word) who faithfully discharge their duty, nothing will stand in the way of their taking flight for their own safety, according to Christ's precept, and keeping themselves for better times and places. Obedience of faith, tempered by love of God and neighbour, will be of great help here. For this will keep us from being blinded and led astray by private passions. May God grant that, mindful of his grace and will, each of us diligently guard his calling, so that, having run a good race to the goal of blessedness, we may live in heaven with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XLIX.

units.la: Et expletis annis quadraginta, visus est illi in deserto montis Sina angelus domini in flammeo incendio rubi. Moses autem vt vidit, admiratus est visionem. Porro cum accederet ad consyderandum, facta est ad eum vox domini: Ego sum Deus patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi. Tremefactus autem Moses, non audebat attendere. Dixit autem illi dominus: Solue calceamentum pedum tuorum. Locus enim, in quo stas, terra sancta est. Videns vidi afflictionem populi mei in Aegypto, & gemitum eorum audiui, & descendi ad eos liberandos. Et nunc veni, & mittam te in Aegyptum.
units.tr: And when forty years were completed, there appeared to him in the desert of Mount Sinai an angel of the Lord in the flame of a burning bush. When Moses saw it, he marvelled at the vision. As he drew near to look more closely, the voice of the Lord came to him: "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses, trembling, did not dare to look. The Lord said to him: "Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground. I have surely seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come, and I will send you into Egypt."

units.la: QVoniam Diuus Stephanus ab aduersarijs suis accusatus erat, quod impia & blasphema aduersus Mosen totumq; cultum Dei per Mosen traditum esset locutus: vniuersam Moysis historiam paucis quidem, sed sufficienti expositione comprehendit: partim quidem, vt offendat se de Mose honorifice sentire: partim vero vt euincat salutem hominum non vllis ceremonijs tribui debere, quando Mosi quoque nullo suo merito, sed mera Dei gratia obtigerit, quicquid in illo praeclarum fuit & eximium. Omnium ergo principalis scopus & finis est, vt Iudaeos ab inani cultu Leuitici ducia auocet, & in sola Dei gratia per Christum confidere doceat. Et in hunc finem Moysis natales, educationem & primam cum Israelitis conuersationem exposuit, ostendens simul quam indignos tanto liberatore se praebuerint illorum patres, quando summa iniquitate & ingratitudine ipsum repulerunt, adeo vt inter Madianitas exulare coactus sit. Sequitur solennis vocatio Moysis, qua officio suo restitutus est: in qua vt euidentiora sint diuina gratia argumenta, singulas illius partes ordine consyderabimus.
units.tr: Since the blessed Stephen had been accused by his adversaries of speaking impious and blasphemous words against Moses and against the whole worship of God delivered through Moses, he sums up the whole history of Moses in a brief but sufficient account. He does this partly to show that he thinks highly of Moses, and partly to prove that the salvation of men is not to be ascribed to any ceremonies, since whatever was outstanding and remarkable in Moses also came to him not by any merit of his own but by the sheer grace of God. The chief aim and purpose of the whole is therefore to call the Jews away from the empty worship of the Levitical law, and to teach them to trust in the grace of God alone through Christ. To this end he sets out Moses' birth, his upbringing, and his early dealings with the Israelites, showing at the same time how unworthy their fathers proved themselves of so great a deliverer, since with the greatest wickedness and ingratitude they rejected him, so that he was forced to live in exile among the Midianites. Next follows the solemn calling of Moses, by which he was restored to his office. In it, so that the proofs of divine grace may be clearer, we will consider its parts one by one in order.

units.la: Primo tempus, quo Moses vocatus est, notatur. Fuit autem quadragesimus exilij Madianitici annus, qui in octuagesimum aetatis annum incidit. Simul vero locus & vitae conditio concurrunt. Nam in deserto fuisse dicitur, vbi Iethronis soceri sui oues pauit, sicuti videre est Exod.3. At sitis tum hunc quadraginta annorum cursum consyderes, sine templo & legalibus ceremonijs Moses Deo placuisse patebit, quando constat, has postea demum institutas fuisse: & quia a conuersatione simul himul & repub. Israelis interea exclusus fuit, nihil praeter solam & meram dei gratiam restat, ad quam vocatio haec referri debet. Interim non oscitanter nobis Moses hic considerandus est, qui ve primum ecclesiae dei coniungi voluit, diutini exilij labores senserit, & ex principe ovium pastor factus est. Hinc enim generalis doctrina colligi potest, qua admonemur, quid omnes eos maneat, qui mundo relicto ecclesiae dei coniunguntur. Excipit hos varia afflictio, eo quod mundus hic nec defectionem illam, nec veritatis lucem ferre poterit. Et sicuti Moses Iethronem quidem hospitem & socerum invenit, apud illum vero non maioris fit, quam quod pastoritio muneri destinatur: Ita fere fieri solet, ut pij apud eos quoq; inglorij & contempti vivant, qui illis hospitium praebent, & ipsorum causae egregie fauere videntur. Est haec omnium gravissima tentatio, quae interdum animos magis vulnerat, quam quae hostes aperti contra nos crudeliter designant. Ideo Christus monet, ne temere nominis sui professionem suscipiamus, sed vires prius exploremus, num ipsius nomine (sita necessitas ferat) exilij aerumnas, egestatem, infamiam, persecutiones, & si quae alia sunt eius generis, ferre possimus. Luc.14. Ubi vero ista incidunt, Mosis modestiam & constantem fidem imitemur, quam variè tentatam fuisse nemo dubitauerit. Vincit tamen fide, quae illum ut Christi probrum Aegypti diuitiis praeferret, antea impulerat. Eadem ergo & nos vincamus tentationum assultus, nec pudeat nos crucis Christi, quam ipse prior propter nos ferre dignatus est. Ita enim fiet, ut nec illum nostri pudeat, quando in gloria patris veniet ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos. Marc.8.
units.tr: First, the time at which Moses was called is noted. It was the fortieth year of his exile among the Midianites, which fell in his eightieth year of life. At the same time the place and the condition of his life coincide. For he is said to have been in the desert, where he pastured the flocks of his father-in-law Jethro, as may be seen in Exodus 3. Now if you consider this course of forty years, when Moses lived without the temple and the legal ceremonies, it will be plain that he pleased God, since it is certain that these were instituted only later; and because he was meanwhile shut out from the common life and from the commonwealth of Israel, nothing remains but the sole and pure grace of God, to which this calling must be referred. Meanwhile we must not carelessly pass over Moses here, who, when he first wished to join the church of God, endured the hardships of a long exile, and from being the prince of the flocks became a shepherd. For from this a general doctrine can be drawn, by which we are warned what awaits all those who, having left the world, join the church of God. Various afflictions await them, because this world can neither bear that departure nor the light of the truth. And just as Moses found Jethro indeed a host and father-in-law, yet with him he was held of no more account than to be assigned to the shepherd's task, so it generally happens that the godly live without honour and despised even among those who give them lodging and seem to favour their cause warmly. This is the most serious of all temptations, and it often wounds the minds more than enemies openly raging against us do. Therefore Christ warns us not to take up the profession of his name rashly, but first to test our strength, whether for his name (should necessity so require) we can bear the hardships of exile, poverty, disgrace, persecutions, and whatever else is of that kind (Luke 14). But when such things befall us, let us imitate the modesty and steadfast faith of Moses, which no one will doubt was tried in many ways. Yet he conquered by faith, which had earlier moved him to prefer the reproach of Christ to the riches of Egypt. Let us, therefore, likewise conquer the assaults of temptations, and let us not be ashamed of the cross of Christ, which he himself deigned first to bear for us. For so it will come about that he will not be ashamed of us when he comes in the glory of the Father to judge the living and the dead (Mark 8).

units.la: Secundò, quis Mosem vocarit, indicat Stephanus: nimirum angelus domini, quem ipsi in deserto apparuisse dicit. Atqui idem ille paulò post dicit: Ego sum Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci & Iacobi. Et rursum is ipse fuisse dicetur, cuius operatione & virtute Moses in Aegypto prodigia & signa edidit, quia populo per desertum via dux fuit: quem Paulus apostolus Iesum Christum, promissum humani generis saluatorem fuisse testatur. 1. Cor.10. Hunc ergo Stephanus angelum domini vocat, non quod nihil in illo diuinius aut excellentius agnoverit, sed Isaiam imitatus esse videtur, qui illum olim angelum magni consilij nominauit: non quod angelicam naturam assumpserit (id quod Paulus ad Heb.cap.2. diserte negat) sed quod à Deo patre in mundum missus, magnum illud et aeternum Dei consilium de humani generis redemptione executus est. In illo enim nos electos fuisse Paulus docet, priusquam mundi fundamenta iacerentur. Ephes.1. Et Petrus illum ab aeterno praedestinatum fuisse dicit, ut illius merito redimeremur. 1. Pet.1. Non autem temere factum putabimus, quod is Mosi apparuisse dicitur. Hinc enim constat, Christum non tunc demum, quando ex Maria homo natus est coepisse, sed ab aeterno fuisse, imò cum patribus olim egisse, quaecunq; ad illorum salutem pertinebant. Etsi enim nondum incarnatus esset, non potuit tamen diuina sua bonitate & potentia illis deesse ex quibus praefinito tempore hominem erat assumpturus. Ideo se Abrahamo priorem esse, & Abrahamo visum fuisse dicit. Iohan.8. Et Daniel in nubibus caeli iudicem, similem filio hominis vidit, qui usque ad proueetum aetate pertingebat. Dan.7. cap. Adhaec Christi spiritus prophetas olim animatos fuisse & futura praedixisse, Petrus ingenuè fatetur. 1. Pet.1. Magnaigitur est illorum temeritas, qui veteres in vniuersum omnes abijciunt, & illorum libros nihil ad nos pertinere clamant, cum & Christi spiritu donati fuerint, & de eodem multifariam testati sint. Vide Iohan.5. Luc.24. Dei bonitatem potius agnoscamus, qui olim veteribus se ipse reuelare, & nobis fidei nostrae vetustatem & certitudinem hoc pacto cognoscendam proponere dignatus est.
units.tr: Second, who called Moses is indicated by Stephen: namely the angel of the Lord, whom he says appeared to him in the desert. Yet that same one, a little later, says: "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and of Jacob." And again he is said to be the one by whose working and power Moses performed wonders and signs in Egypt, and who was a guide for the people along the way through the desert; of him the apostle Paul testifies that he was Jesus Christ, the promised Saviour of the human race (1 Cor. 10). Stephen therefore calls him the angel of the Lord, not because he recognised nothing more divine or excellent in him, but he seems to have imitated Isaiah, who once named him the Angel of great counsel. Not that he took on an angelic nature (which Paul expressly denies in Hebrews 2), but because, sent into the world by God the Father, he carried out that great and eternal counsel of God concerning the redemption of the human race. For Paul teaches that we were chosen in him before the foundations of the world were laid (Eph. 1). And Peter says that he was predestined from eternity so that we might be redeemed by his merit (1 Pet. 1). Nor shall we think it was without reason that he is said to have appeared to Moses. For from this it is clear that Christ did not begin only when he was born a man of Mary, but existed from eternity, and indeed once dealt with the fathers in all things that pertained to their salvation. For although he was not yet incarnate, nevertheless by his divine goodness and power he could not be absent from those from whom at the appointed time he was to assume a human nature. Therefore he says that he was before Abraham, and that he was seen by Abraham (John 8). And Daniel saw in the clouds of heaven one like the Son of Man, a judge, who reached to the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7). Besides, Peter frankly admits that the Spirit of Christ once animated the prophets and foretold future things (1 Pet. 1). Great, then, is the recklessness of those who reject the ancient writers altogether, and cry out that their books have nothing to do with us, when they were both endowed with the Spirit of Christ and bore witness to him in many ways (see John 5; Luke 24). Let us rather acknowledge the goodness of God, who deigned in former times to reveal himself to the ancients, and in this way to set before us the antiquity and certainty of our faith to be known.

units.la: Porrò qua forma aut specie Christus Mosi apparuerit, Stephanus diligenter docet. Nam angelum domini, qui Christus erat, in rubo ardente. Mosi apparuisse dicit. Est enim hic vetus dei mos, ut visibili aliqua specie cum hominibus olim egerit, qui essentiae diuinae maiestatem sustinere non poterant. Exempla sunt passim obuia in patriarcharum & prophetarum historiis. Facit hoc ad attentionem, & ut in Dei admirationem rapiantur homines, qui alioqui supino contemptu diuina omnia negligunt. Interim eas species & formas fere assumpsit Deus, quae praesentibus negotijs, temporibus & personis maximè conueniebant. Quod & hoc loco factum fuisse videmus. Voluit enim per rubum ardentem populi sui, qui in Aegypto affligebatur, conditionem Mosi ob oculos statuere. Ardebat ille immani Pharaonis tyrannide succensus, non autè consumebatur, eò quod in eius medio dei filius erat, qui ex illorum posteritate constituto tempore homo nasci debebat. Eadem verò est omnibus seculis ecclesiae Christi conditio, in cuius consyderatione nos frequenter versari, vehementer prodest. Est haec
units.tr: Moreover, Stephen carefully teaches in what form or appearance Christ appeared to Moses. For he says that the angel of the Lord, who was Christ, appeared to Moses in a burning bush. For this is God's ancient custom, that he once dealt with men in some visible shape, since they could not bear the majesty of his essence. Examples lie everywhere in the histories of the patriarchs and prophets. This serves to draw attention, and to carry men into the admiration of God, who otherwise neglect all divine things in careless contempt. Meanwhile God has taken on those forms and shapes which were most suited to the present affairs, times and persons. This we also see was done in this place. For through the burning bush he wished to set before Moses the condition of his people, who were being afflicted in Egypt. That bush blazed, set on fire by the monstrous tyranny of Pharaoh, but was not consumed, because in its midst was the Son of God, who was to be born a man of their posterity at the appointed time. Indeed this is the condition of the church of Christ in every age, and it greatly profits us to dwell on it frequently. This is

units.la: II. Angelus domini vocat Mosem.
units.tr: II. The angel of the Lord calls Moses.

units.la: Rubus ardens. rubi instar, imbellis nimirum & infirmus grex: sed quem non facile dissipes, eo quod per fidem in Christo capite arctissime coniungitur. Ut ergo rubus & spinetus inter se indiuulsè cohærentibus igne subijciunt agricolæ, ut illa simul exurant: Ita ecclesiæ persecutionum faces mundus hic subijcit, & uno incendio totam simul vastare conatur. Et ignem hunc suscitari Christus permittit: quia suorum fidem hoc pacto probari & carnis ingenium coherceri necesse est. Idem tamen ecclesiam suam in universum consumi non patitur, in cuius medio versari solet. Ipsius enim vox est: Non relinquam vos orphanos. Ego vobiscum sum usque in consummationem seculi. Ioban. 14. Matth. 28. Pertinent huc quæcunque ab ipsa mundi origine pro ecclesiæ suæ defensione deus egit. Primus illi faces subiecit Cain, qui licet Abelum fratrem sustulerit, fidem tamen illius tollere non potuit, & multo minus obstare, quo minus in Setho nouum suæ ecclesiæ seminarium deus excitaret. Nec id postea potuerunt Nephilim, qui diluuium proximè præcesserunt, quin illis male pereuntibus, ecclesiæ suæ reliquias Deus arcæ beneficio mirificè seruauit. Arsit item sæpenumero iudicum tempore rubus hic, sed præsenti dei auxilio semper conseruatus est. Arsit in Babylone, unde tamen reduxit & liberauit dominus. Arsit post reditum è Babylone non semel, & tandem Antiocho regnante, iam exitio proxima videri potuerat ecclesia, quando Deus Machabæos excitauit, qui & cultum suum repurgarunt, & populum in libertatem asseruerunt. Arsit post Christum natum totis ferè trecentis annis usque ad Magni Constantini tempora. Nunquam tamen illi deus defuit, qui ut olim Danielis socios, in medijs ardoribus tueri potest. Ardet hodie, & passim sunt, qui funestas faces subijciant, & potentissimos monarchas ecclesiæ odio inflamment. Nunquam tamen proficient illi quantum volunt, sed dei vindicis iram sentient, in cuius oculis suorum mors preciosa est, quia suorum sanguinem inultum non feret. Psal. 116. Imò dum ecclesiæ ignem subiciunt tyranni persecutores, ipsi lignorum instar ab igne diuini iudicij consumuntur, manente interim in medijs persecutionum ardoribus ecclesia catini instar, in quo metallici aurum & argentum conflare atque purgare solent. Vide quæ de his similibus habentur Zachariæ 12. & 13. cap.
units.tr: The burning bush. Like the bush, indeed, the flock is unwarlike and weak, yet it cannot easily be scattered, because through faith it is most closely joined to Christ its head. Just as farmers set fire to a bramble and thornbush whose stems hold fast together, so that they burn up together, so this world sets torches to the churches of persecution and tries to lay waste the whole of them at once in one blaze. And Christ permits this fire to be kindled, since the faith of his people must be tested in this way and the nature of the flesh restrained. Yet he does not allow his church to be consumed entirely, and he is present in its midst. For this is his own word: "I will not leave you orphans; I am with you always, even to the end of the age." John 14; Matt. 28. To this belong all the things God has done from the very beginning of the world in defence of his church. Cain first set the torch to it: although he killed his brother Abel, he could not take away Abel's faith, and much less prevent God from raising up in Seth a new seedbed for his church. Nor could the Nephilim, who immediately preceded the flood, do this, but when they perished miserably, God by the help of the ark marvellously preserved the remnants of his church. This bush has also often burned in the time of the judges, yet it was always kept safe by God's present help. It burned in Babylon, yet the Lord led it back and set it free. It burned more than once after the return from Babylon, and at last, under King Antiochus, the church might have seemed close to destruction, when God raised up the Maccabees, who both purified his worship and vindicated the people's liberty. It burned for almost the whole of three hundred years after the birth of Christ, down to the times of Constantine the Great. Yet God was never lacking to it, and he who once guarded Daniel's companions in the midst of the flames can still protect it. Today it burns again, and there are everywhere those who set deadly torches to it and inflame the most powerful monarchs with hatred of the church. Yet they will never achieve as much as they wish; they will feel the anger of God the avenger, in whose eyes the death of his people is precious, for he will not let the blood of his servants go unavenged. Ps. 116. Indeed, while the tyrant persecutors set fire to the church, they themselves are consumed like wood by the fire of divine judgement, while the church remains in the midst of the heat of persecutions like a crucible, in which metalworkers are accustomed to melt and refine gold and silver. See what is said of such things in Zechariah chapters 12 and 13.

units.la: III. Ipsa Moysis vocatio.
units.tr: III. The calling of Moses itself.

units.la: Sed ipsam vocationem videamus, qua officio, quod ante annos quadraginta exequi cœperat, Moses restituitur. Constat hæc suis partibus, quarum consyderatio veilissima est. Primò enim seipsum declarat dominus, ne de vocationis suæ certitudine Moses quicquam dubitet. Nam rubi ardentis spectaculo obstupefacto dicit: Ego sum Deus patrum tuorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci et Deus Iacobi. Voluit vero ex multis titulis hunc potissimum vsurpare dominus, ut Mosi fœdus cum Abrahamo initum, & promissiones patribus olim factas in memoriam reuocaret: ostendens simul se nec patrum nec promissionum aut fœderis sui oblitum esse, licet populum hucusque affligi passus sit. Quo exemplo admonemur, in aduersis ad Dei promissiones ante omnia respici debere, quarum Deus nec obliuisci potest, nec fidei suæ deesse. Imò tam infallibilem esse cernimus diuinarum promissionum veritatem, ut Deus ne mortuos quidem deserat, quos semel in tutelâ suam suscepit. Est enim mortis simul & vitæ dominus. Quare nec vita nec mors nos à dilectione Dei separare poterit. Rom. 8. cap. Nam sive viuamus sive moriamur, domini sumus. Et huc facit, quod hic Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi deum esse profitetur, qui tamen iam olim vita defuncti erant, cum hæc deus loqueretur. Et Christus eadem ratione Lazarum & mortuum & sepultum, amicum suum vocare dignatur. Iohan. 11. Quo cumprimis pertinet, quod idem ex hoc loco generalem doctrinam desumit, qua mortuorum resurrectionem & vitæ cœlestis certitudinem contra Sadducæorum cauillationes asserit. Matth. 22. Versemur igitur in huius tituli meditatione, quoties mortis metus nobis obuersatur, & omni solicitudine nos statim liberari sentiemus.
units.tr: But let us look at the calling itself, by which Moses is restored to the office he had begun to carry out forty years before. It consists of several parts, and their consideration is most useful. First, the Lord makes himself known, so that Moses should have no doubt about the certainty of his calling. For, amazed at the sight of the burning bush, he is told: "I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." Now the Lord chose especially to use this title out of many, so as to call to Moses' mind the covenant made with Abraham and the promises once given to the fathers, showing at the same time that he had not forgotten the fathers, the promises or his covenant, although he had allowed the people to be afflicted until now. From this example we are reminded that in adversity we ought above all to look to God's promises, which God can neither forget nor fail to keep. Indeed, we see that the truth of divine promises is so infallible that God does not abandon even the dead whom he has once taken into his protection. For he is the Lord of death and of life alike. Therefore neither life nor death will be able to separate us from the love of God. Rom. 8. For whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. And this is to the point: he declares himself to be the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who had long since departed this life when God spoke these words. And Christ, for the same reason, deigns to call Lazarus, who was dead and buried, his friend. John 11. To this especially belongs the fact that from this passage he also draws a general doctrine, by which he asserts the resurrection of the dead and the certainty of heavenly life against the cavils of the Sadducees. Matt. 22. Let us therefore dwell on the meditation of this title whenever the fear of death presents itself to us, and we shall feel ourselves freed from all anxiety.

units.la: Caeterum cum Moses tam rubi ardentis spectaculo quàm subita dei voce territus, propius accedere non auderet, mox quid facere debeat, audit. Subjicit enim dominus: Solue calceamentum pedum tuorum. Locus enim in quo stas, terra sancta est. Ita vero dicitur propter Dei præsentiam, & quòd illam legis promulgationi destinasset. Non temere autem huius præcepti mentionem fecit Stephanus. Sic enim Iudæos admonere voluit, quid tum olim ab ipso Mose deus requisierit, et quid idem à nobis hodie requirat: nempe non templum, non legalem cultum, non frigidas ceremonias sive hircorum taurorumve sanguinem: sed ut animos nostros pecuniis affectibus (qui per calceos figurantur) liberemus, & ipsi syncera fide & animorum integritate toti vniamur. Hic enim verus ille Dei cultus est. ws est, quem alibi in spiritu & veritate consistere Christus testatur. Iohan. 4. Et huc eiusdem praeceptum de pedibus abluendis pertinet, cuius multo maior, quàm omnium externorum, ratio à nobis haberi debet. Iohan. 13. Passim quoq; observari conuenit, cum Deum nobis vbiq; locorum praesentem esse, scripturae omnes testentur, & exempla quotidiana abundè probent.
units.tr: Moreover, since Moses, terrified both by the sight of the burning bush and by the sudden voice of God, did not dare to come nearer, he now hears what he ought to do. For the Lord adds: "Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground." It is called holy because of God's presence, and because he had set it apart for the proclamation of the law. Nor did Stephen mention this command without reason. For he wished to remind the Jews what God once required of Moses himself, and what he requires of us today: not a temple, not legal worship, not cold ceremonies, nor the blood of goats and bulls, but that we free our minds from earthly affections (which are signified by the sandals) and that we ourselves be united to him in sincere faith and integrity of heart. For this is the true worship of God, which Christ elsewhere testifies consists in spirit and truth. John 4. To this also belongs the command about washing the feet, the reason for which ought to be held by us in far greater regard than that of all external things. John 13. It is also fitting to observe everywhere that all the Scriptures testify that God is present with us in every place, and daily examples abundantly prove it.

units.la: Postremò mentem & voluntatem suam reuelat Mosi dominus: Videns vidi (inquit) afflictionem populi mei in Ægypto, & gemitum eorum audiui, & descendi ad eos liberandos, &c. Quae verba instituto Stephani proprijssimè seruiunt. Docent enim in Israelitis nullum fuisse meritum, propter quod liberari debuerint, nec quicquam in illis respexisse dominum praeter afflictiones, quibus miserrimè vexabantur. Vnde sequitur totum liberationis beneficium ad Dei meram gratiam pertinere. Simul verò docemur, deum suos nequaquam negligere, licet interdum dissimulet. Videt illorum lachrymas, quas coram ipso in lagenulam colligi Dauid testatur. Psalm. 56. Audit non modò clamores illorum, verumetiam gemitus, eò quòd renes & corda scrutatur. Et passim occurrunt historias legentibus exempla, quibus id probari potest. Seruiat ergo hoc nobis ad consolationem, quando ab hominibus perfidis & inmitibus deserimur. Seruiat item institutioni, ne eos temere affligamus, quos deo tam curae esse constat. Pertinet huc quod Exo. 22. de viduis, pupillis & peregrinis, ad ipsum clamantibus habetur. Et quod Zach. 2. cap. dicitur: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Praecipua verò nobis cura sit, vt huic Deo nos totos consecremus, qui communi humani generis afflictione perspecta, nobis assertorem & vindicem dedit filium suum, Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, the Lord reveals his mind and will to Moses: "I have seen," he says, "the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them," etc. These words serve Stephen's purpose most exactly. For they teach that there was no merit in the Israelites on account of which they ought to be delivered, nor did the Lord regard anything in them except the afflictions by which they were most miserably harassed. Hence it follows that the whole benefit of deliverance belongs to God's mere grace. At the same time we are taught that God by no means neglects his people, although at times he seems to overlook them. He sees their tears, which David testifies are gathered by him into a bottle. Ps. 56. He hears not only their cries but also their groans, because he searches the reins and hearts. And many histories present examples to those who read them by which this can be proved. Let this therefore serve us for consolation when we are forsaken by faithless and merciless men. Let it also serve as instruction, that we should not rashly afflict those whom it is clear are so dear to God. To this belongs what is said in Exodus 22 about widows, orphans and strangers crying out to him. And what is said in Zechariah chapter 2: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Our chief care, however, should be to consecrate ourselves wholly to this God, who, having seen the common affliction of mankind, gave us as our advocate and avenger his Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA L.
units.tr: HOMILY 50.

units.la: Hunc Mosem, quem negauerant, dicentes: Quis te constituit principem & iudicem? Hunc, inquam, deus principem & redemptorem misit in manu angeli, qui illi apparuerat in rubo. Hic eduxit eos, edens prodigia & signa in Ægypto, & in mari rubro, & in deserto annis quadraginta. Hic est Moses, qui dixit filijs Israel: Prophetam vobis suscitabit dominus Deus vester, ex fratribus vestris, sicut me; Ipsum audite.
units.tr: This Moses, whom they had denied, saying, "Who made you a prince and judge?" This one, I say, God sent as prince and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who had appeared to him in the bush. He led them out, doing wonders and signs in Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the desert for forty years. This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; hear him."

units.la: Et si Diuus Stephanus non aliam fidei & salutis rationem tradiderit, quam quae promissi salvatoris, Iesu Christi merito nituntur, cui Moses & prophetae testimonium tulere: accusatur tamen, quòd fidem doceat nouam atq; erroneam, imò quod in Mosem & patres contumeliosus, fidem ab illis traditam & obseruatam abolere conetur. Eadem ergo fuit illius seculi ratio, quae hodie est, quando qui ab apostolis traditam, & martyrum sanguine obsignatam fidem sectantur, passim audiunt, quòd veteres cultus euertant, diuos violent et prisios patres ignominiosè damnent. Quid verò hic nobis agendum sit, Stephani exemplo docemur.
