Is de patrum fide diligenter & prolixè disserit, in primis verò Mosis historiam ex ordine recenseт, vt ea commemoratione partim ostendat, se de illo magnificè sentire, partim verò euincat, se veteris patrum religionis hostem minimè esse, quàmuis eos ritus iam abrogandos esse doceat, sine quibus ipsi olim deo seruierint, imò sine quibus Moses quoq; deo placuerit, & in tam sublime honoris fastigium sit euectus. Ita hodie quoq; edocendi sunt imperitiores, quae olim Martyrum fides & doctrina fuerit, & illi sine istis seruati sint, de quibus hodie tanta cum animorum exacerbatione contenditur. Caeterum postquam Stephanus narrationem suam vsq; ad folennem Mosis vocationem deduxit, nunc tandem liberiori cursu & plenis velis, quod aiunt, in illius laudes digreditur: & primò testatur, se in Mose omnia ea agnoscere, quae in illum deus contulerit: Deinde suam de Christo doctrinam ipsius Mosis testimonio probat, cuius nō eam sententiam fuisse docet, vt in lege & ceremonijs per se traditis Israelitae acquiescant, sed vt in prophetam illum eximium respiciant, quem olim Deus missurus sit, & cuius typum ipse modò sustineat. Est autem insignis hic locus, quo docemur, ita nobis de sanctorum virtutibus & ministerio magnificè sentiendum atq; loquendum esse, vt interim Christo Iesu suus honor salvus maneat, qui solus in omnibus ijs eminere debet, quae ad Dei cultum & salutis nostrae rationem faciunt.
units.tr: And although holy Stephen delivered no other account of faith and salvation than that which rests on the merit of the promised Saviour, Jesus Christ, to whom Moses and the prophets bore witness, he is nevertheless accused of teaching a new and erroneous faith, and indeed of speaking insultingly against Moses and the fathers and trying to abolish the faith handed down and observed by them. The situation of that age was therefore the same as today, when those who follow the faith handed down by the apostles and sealed with the blood of the martyrs hear on every side that they overturn the old worship, violate the divine things and shamefully condemn the ancient fathers. What we ourselves ought to do here we are taught by the example of Stephen. He discusses the faith of the fathers carefully and at length, and above all he recounts the history of Moses in order; by this recital he shows partly that he thinks highly of Moses, and partly that he proves himself by no means an enemy of the old religion of the fathers, although he teaches that those rites, without which they had once served God, and without which Moses too had pleased God and been raised to so lofty a height of honour, must now be abrogated. So today the less learned too must be taught what the faith and teaching of the martyrs once was, and that those men were saved without those things over which such great bitterness of spirits is now contended. Moreover, after Stephen had brought his narrative down to the solemn calling of Moses, he now at last, with a freer course and full sails, as they say, turns to praise him; and first he testifies that he recognises in Moses all those things which God bestowed upon him. Then he proves his own doctrine concerning Christ by the testimony of Moses himself, whose purpose he shows was not that the Israelites should rest in the law and ceremonies handed down in themselves, but that they should look to that outstanding prophet whom God would one day send, and whose type Moses himself bore. This is a notable passage, by which we are taught that we ought to think and speak so highly of the virtues and ministry of the saints that Christ Jesus meanwhile keeps his own honour intact, he who alone ought to stand out in all those things which pertain to the worship of God and the manner of our salvation.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Primò autem à Mosis officio exorditur, quo nihil excellentius dici vel cogitari poterat. Nam illum à Deo Israelitica genti principem simul & redemptorem datum fuisse dicit. Illud verò sic proponit, vt simul patrum ingratitudinem, qua illi Mosem indignissimè reiecerunt, illus denuò exprobret, & contempti Mosis crimen in illorum maiores, quibus ipsi cumprimis gloriabantur, retorqueat. Ait enim: Hunc Mosem, quem negauerant, dicentes: Quis te constituit principem & iudicem? Hunc, inquam, deus principem & redemptorem misit, in manu angeli, &c. Quia verò principem & redemptorem populi Dei Mosem agnoscit, vnum hoc sufficientis excusationis loco esse poterat contra aduersarios, qui illum in Mosem impia quaedam dixisse quiritabantur.
units.tr: First he begins with the office of Moses, than which nothing more excellent could be said or thought. For he says that God gave Moses to the Israelite nation as prince and at the same time redeemer. He sets this out in such a way that he also reproaches the fathers again for their ingratitude, by which they had shamefully rejected Moses, and turns the crime of despising Moses back upon their forefathers, in whom they especially gloried. For he says: "This Moses, whom they had denied, saying: Who made you prince and judge? This one, I say, God sent as prince and redeemer, in the hand of the angel, etc." Since he acknowledges Moses as prince and redeemer of God's people, this alone could serve as a sufficient excuse against adversaries, who complained that Moses had said certain impious things.

units.la: Nobis autem hic ante omnia obseruandum venit, quod eum sui populi principem & vindicem constituit deus, qui iam Aegyptijs exosus, & ab Israelitis fratribus suis reiectus, longo tempore exulauerat. Quo exemplo admonemur tam de nostris quàm aliorum fortunis nequaquam secundum mundi sententiam iudicandum esse: cum frequenter fieri soleat, vt deo acceptissimi sint, quos mundus nimis contemptim fastidit & abominatur. Nam proprius hic dei mos est, vt humilia eligat, & per illa mundi fastum confundat. Et in Psalmo 113. legimus: Deus erigit tenuem ex puluere & pauperem è stercore euehit. Vt collocet eum cum principibus, cum principibus inquam sui populi. Cui non absimile est, quod Diua virgo canit: Detraxit potentes de sedibus, & exaltauit humiles. Luc.1. Exempla huius rei non modò in Mose, verumetiam multis alijs habentur. Ita Saulem ex agasone regem fecit, & Danidem ex caula extractum regali solio imposuit. Quo etiam quod in apostolis factum est, referri poterat: qui cum piscatores maxima ex parte, & nullius in mundo authoritatis essent, eousque electi sunt, vt totius orbis victores dici possint, quem verbi praedicatione intra paucos annos Christo subiugauerunt. Debent hinc consolationem petere qui abiecti et inglorij habentur. Simul verò huius memores qui in sublimi aliquo gradu constituti sunt, humilitatem sectari studeant, ne exaltatio (vt Solomon inquit) ruinam praecedere videatur. Prouerb.16.
units.tr: Here we must above all observe that God appointed as prince and deliverer of his people the man who, already hated by the Egyptians and rejected by his Israelite brothers, had spent a long time in exile. From this example we are taught that both our own fortunes and those of others must by no means be judged by the opinion of the world, since it often happens that those whom the world despises and loathes are most acceptable to God. For it is God's characteristic way to choose the lowly and through them to confound the world's pride. And in Psalm 113 we read: "God raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dunghill, that he may set him with princes, with princes, I say, of his people." Not unlike this is what the virgin Mary sings: "He has put down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble." Luke 1. Examples of this are found not only in Moses but in many others. Thus he made Saul a king from a herdsman, and placed David, taken from the sheepfold, on the royal throne. This could also be applied to what happened with the apostles, who, being for the most part fishermen and of no authority in the world, were chosen to such an extent that they can be called conquerors of the whole world, which they subdued to Christ within a few years by preaching the Word. Those who are regarded as abject and inglorious should draw consolation from this. At the same time, those who have been placed in some high rank should remember this and earnestly strive for humility, lest exaltation, as Solomon says, seem to go before ruin. Prov. 16.

units.la: Praeterea qua ratione Moses populi dei redemptor dicatur, videndum est. Nec enim hoc ita intelligi debet, quasi priuata & propria authoritate siue potentia quicquam effecerit: cum non obscure Stephanus testetur, illum in manu angeli, qui ipsi in rubo apparuerat, redemptorem missum esse: id est, Iesu Christi (quem angelum illum fuisse proximo Sermone demonstrauimus) auspicijs & imperio omnia ea obiuisse, quae ad populi redemptionem pertinebant. Mosem ergo ministrum fuisse, & omnem redemptionis gloriam vni & soli Christo deberi constat. Quo sensu omnes scripturae loci exponi & accipi debent, in quibus quod dei proprium est, hominibus tribuitur. Id enim non alia quàm, ministerij ratione fit, quod ex dei mandato obeunt. Ita ministri ecclesias plantare & aedificare, homines item deo lucrifacere, peccata remittere & retinere dicuntur: non quòd illa ab ipsorum arbitrio et potestate dependeant: sed quòd illorum ministerio in istis rebus conficiendis deus vti dignatur, qui etiam sine his pro suo arbitrio res omnes versare & gubernare potest.
units.tr: Next, we must consider in what sense Moses is called the redeemer of God's people. This must not be understood as if he accomplished anything by his own private authority or power, since Stephen clearly testifies that he was sent as redeemer in the hand of the angel who had appeared to him in the bush; that is, under the auspices and command of Jesus Christ (whom we showed in the previous sermon to have been that angel), he performed all those things that pertained to the redemption of the people. Moses, then, was a minister, and all the glory of redemption is owed to one and only Christ. In this sense all passages of Scripture must be explained and understood in which what belongs to God alone is attributed to men. This happens only by way of ministry, which they perform by God's command. Thus ministers are said to plant and build churches, and likewise to win men for God, to forgive and retain sins: not because these depend on their own will and power, but because God deigns to use their ministry in accomplishing these things, although he can also govern and direct all things without them, as he pleases.

units.la: Caeterum, quia Mosem populi dei principem & redemptorem factum fuisse dixerit, vt hoc suo officio functus sit, docet: Hic eduxit eos, edens prodigia & signa in Aegypto, & in mari rubro, & in deserto annis quadraginta. Non ergo nudum redemptoris titulum in Mose agnoscit Stephanus, sed illum suo officio fideliter functum esse, ingenuè fatetur. Et ne quid reticere videatur, quod ad illius gloriam facere poterat, prodigiorum quoq; & signorum meminit, quae diuina virtute per illum edita fuerunt. Distinguuntur haec tribus ordinibus, & in scriptis Mosis diligentius recensentur. Primus ordo ea habet, quae in Aegypto contigerunt. Inter quae primus locus ijs dari potest, quibus sua vocationi fidem facere debuit, quale fuit virga in serpentem conuersio, qui Magorum virgas, incantationum praestigijs transformatas, deuorauit. Secuta sunt mox plagae prodigiosae & horribiles, quibus Pharaonem & Aegyptios deus mirificè exercuit. Nam omnes Aegypti aquae in sanguinem conuersae, non modò usui inutiles fiunt, verumetiam cruentam tyrannidem & infanticidia Aegyptijs exprobrant. Immittuntur mox ranae, quae non agris modò, verumetiam domibus oberrantes, molestia coaxatione sceleris conscientiam exagitant. Has pediculi excipiunt, eò his molestiores, quòd ipsis coporibus foedo cruciatu inhaerent. Accedunt mox varia infectorum genera, quae magnus examinibus improbè tum hominies tum pecora molestant. Et quia haec leuiora videri poterant, grauioribus petuntur. Horribilis enim & contagiosa lues armenta & greges depopulatur. Enascuntur in hominum
units.tr: Moreover, since he said that Moses was made prince and redeemer of God's people, he shows that Moses discharged this office: "He led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, and in the Red Sea, and in the desert, for forty years." Stephen therefore does not acknowledge in Moses a bare title of redeemer, but frankly confesses that he faithfully discharged his office. And lest he seem to omit anything that could add to Moses' glory, he also mentions the wonders and signs which were performed through him by divine power. These are divided into three orders, and are recorded more carefully in the writings of Moses. The first order contains those things which happened in Egypt. Among these, the first place can be given to those by which he had to confirm his calling, such as the turning of the staff into a serpent, which swallowed the staffs of the magicians, transformed by the tricks of incantations. Soon followed prodigious and horrible plagues, by which God wonderfully afflicted Pharaoh and the Egyptians. For all the waters of Egypt were turned into blood, which not only became useless but also reproached the Egyptians with bloody tyranny and the murder of infants. Then frogs were sent, which wandered not only over the fields but into houses, and by their annoying croaking goaded the conscience of their crime. Lice followed, all the more troublesome because they clung to the bodies themselves with foul torment. Soon came various kinds of gnats, which in great swarms wickedly harassed both men and cattle. And because these might seem rather light, heavier ones were sent. For a horrible and contagious pestilence laid waste the herds and flocks. Foul ulcers broke out on the bodies of men, and scab, consuming the limbs with horrible decay. By a prodigious hailstorm the whole hope of the year was overwhelmed. And what the hail had left untouched, or what had sprung up from the earth, was devoured by locusts that laid waste the fields far and wide. And because they persisted knowingly and willingly in their blind ignorance of God, God sent terrifying darkness that could be felt. At last, through the destroying angel, all Egypt was thrown into turmoil by the slaughter of the firstborn, so that no house was free of deadly mourning. The consideration of all these shows how easily God can restrain and overcome the most powerful tyrants. For he is truly the Lord of hosts, who is accustomed to use against his enemies both good angels and demons, and indeed all creatures in general. No animal is so weak and unwarlike that it is not sufficient to torment and kill men, if God wishes to arm it. By his judgment Pharaoh is afflicted with frogs and tormented by swarms of lice and gnats, he who had shortly before proudly rejected the God of the Hebrews. Thus through mice he punished the impious contempt of his name among the Philistines, when they had brought the ark, which was a sacrament of his presence, into their power. And we read that Antiochus, Sulla, Herod and countless others were devoured by lice and worms born from their own flesh. Let us therefore humble ourselves in the sight of the Lord, and not allow ourselves to be driven mad by the insane confidence placed in temporal things.

units.la: {y} num corporibus fœda vlcera, & horribili tabe membra depascens scabies. Grandine prodigiosa anni spes tota obruitur. Et quod à grandine intactum mansit, vel possé hanc è terra enatum fuit, à locu-ftis agros longè latéq; vastantibus devoratur. Et quia scientes & volentes in caeca Dei ignorantia perseverant, terrificas & palpabiles tenebras immittit Deus. Tandem verò per angelum vastato-rem omnium primogenitorum caedibus tota Ægyptus turbatur, ut nulla domus funesti luctus ex-pers fuerit. Quorum omnium confyderatio docet, quàm facile Deo sit potentissimos tyrannos coher-cere & vincere. Est enim revera dominus exercituum, qui tam angelis bonis quàm daemonibus, adeoq; omnibus in vniuersum creaturis contra hostes suos vti consueuit. Nec vllum animal tam ve-le & imbelle habetur, quod non hominibus excruciandis & enecandis sufficiat, si illud armare velit Deus. Huius iudicio fit, quòd ranis infestatur Pharao, & pediculorum infectorumq; examinibus ex-cruciatur, qui paulò ante Deum Hebraeorum superbè reiecerat. Ita per mures impium sui nominis contemptum inter Palestinos vltus est, cum illi arcam, quae sua praesentia sacramentum erat, in suam potestatem redegissent. Et Antiochum, Syllam, Herodem & infinitos alios à pediculis & ver-mibus ex propria ipsorum carne enatis, depastos fuisse legimus. Humiliemur ergo in conspectu domini, nec insani rerum temporariarum fiducia nos dementari patiamur. Secundus miraculorum, quae per Mosem edita sunt, ordo, quae in mari rubro acciderunt, continet. Cum enim Israelitae Ægy-ptiorum curribus & equitatu inclusi, sibi vel hostili ense, vel maris vorticibus pereundum esse puta-rent, subito mare ex Dei mandato Mosis virga percussum, late diductum instar murorum duorum utrinq; conflitit, et ventus vehementiori flatu spirans caenosi vadi voragines exiccauit, ut siccus Israelitis per medium mare transitus daretur: quos cum hostili animo Ægyptij insectarentur, repente cor-ruentibus utrinq; aquarum cumulis oppressi & absorpti sunt. Quo miraculo non obscure docuit Deus, quòd suos per ea quoq; iuuare & saluare possit, quae ipsis cumprimis noxia & aduersa videntur, & per quaedam obstacula effugij viam aperire ijs, qui in sua vocatione ambulant. Rursum verò idem ho-stes suos ijs rebus punire & vlcisci solet, in quibus illi non postremam salutis suae spem collocantrimo eosdem excaecare & spiritu vertiginis impellere potest, ut sponte ruant in exitium, & ne oculis qui-dem exposita pericula declinent. Nam Ægyptios rubrum mare firmissimi propugnaculi loco ha-buisse constat, & in hoc Israelitae omnes simul cum vxoribus & liberis periturì videbantur. Ita verò rem omnem diuina prouidentia administrat, ut hi quidem corporibus simul & rebus suis salvis tran-seant, illi verò submergantur: & quidem sponte in profundum maris vadum inter vtrinq; erectos aquarum cumulos descendant, cum Dei vltricem manum iam toties essent experti. Vnde discimus, nec vllis aduersis nos à fide deijci, nec in externis fiduciam aut spem aliquam collocare debere, quan-do rerum vices tam facilè immutat dominus. Tertio ordine ea comprehendit Stephanus, quae in deserto facta sunt, ubi Manna datum, quod annis quadraginta populū aluit: ubi coturnices castris illatae sunt, ubi è duris petris viuorum fontium venas Moses aperuit: ubi piis precibus ab Ameleki eis victoriam gloriosam retulit: ubi Balaami praestigia mirificè elusit dominus: ubi prodigiosis pla-gis impij murmuratores prostrati perierunt: vbi illorum vestes per annos quadraginta nec vsu attri-tae sunt, nec vetustate computruerunt. Taceo infinita alia, quae ab ipso Mose diligentius commemo-rantur. At cum omnia illa Stephanus tam ingenuè agnoscat, tamq; magnificè praedicet, abundè sa-tis demonstrauit, sibi haud vulgarem iniuriam fieri, dum contempti Mosis accusatur. Quia tamen Israelitas à Mose ad Christum remittit, non obscure docet, signa haec omnia ad confirmandam Mo-fis doctrinam seruiuisse, nec eo debere detorqueri, ut illi inhaerendum esse putent. Et confutantur hoc loco, qui signis per Diuos olim editis abutuntur, dum superstitiosam illorum inuocationem & cul-tum per illa probant, quae doctrinae potius ipsorum testimonium tulerunt, qua ad vnum Christum relegamur.
units.tr: The second order of the miracles performed through Moses comprises those which happened at the Red Sea. For when the Israelites, shut in by the chariots and horsemen of the Egyptians, thought they must perish either by the hostile sword or by the whirlpools of the sea, suddenly, at God's command, the sea was struck with Moses' staff, and, drawn back widely, it stood on both sides like two walls; and a wind blowing with a very strong blast dried up the whirlpools of the muddy shallows, so that a dry passage through the middle of the sea was given to the Israelites. When the Egyptians pursued them with hostile intent, suddenly the heaps of water collapsed on both sides, and they were overwhelmed and swallowed up. By this miracle God clearly showed that he can help and save his people even through those things which seem most harmful and adverse to them, and can open a way of escape through certain obstacles for those who walk in their calling. Again, he is accustomed to punish and avenge his enemies by those very things in which they placed no small hope of their safety; for he can first blind them and drive them on with a spirit of giddiness, so that they rush headlong to destruction and do not avoid the dangers placed before their very eyes. For it is established that the Egyptians regarded the Red Sea as a most secure stronghold, and in it the Israelites, with their wives and children, seemed destined to perish. Yet divine providence so orders the whole matter that the former pass through safe in body and possessions, while the latter are submerged; and indeed they go down of their own accord into the depths of the sea between the heaps of water raised on either side, although they had already so often experienced the avenging hand of God. Hence we learn that we should not be cast down from faith by any adversities, nor place any confidence or hope in external things, since the Lord so easily changes the course of affairs. In the third order Stephen includes those things which were done in the desert: where manna was given, which fed the people for forty years; where quails were brought into the camp; where Moses opened streams of living water from hard rocks; where by pious prayers he won a glorious victory for them over Amalek; where the Lord wonderfully defeated the sorceries of Balaam; where the impious murmurers were struck down by prodigious plagues and perished; where their garments were worn neither by use nor decayed by age for forty years. I pass over countless other things which are recounted more fully by Moses himself. But since Stephen acknowledges all these things so frankly and proclaims them so magnificently, he has amply shown that no ordinary injury is done to him when he is accused of despising Moses. Yet since he sends the Israelites from Moses to Christ, he clearly teaches that all these signs served to confirm Moses' teaching, and ought not to be twisted so that men think they must cling to Moses himself. And here are refuted those who abuse the signs once performed through the saints, while they prove by them the superstitious invocation of the saints and their worship, when these signs rather bore witness to the doctrine by which we are directed to Christ alone.

units.la: Quoniam verò non ignorabat, aduersarios hoc potissimum argumento niti, quòd à sacris lega-libus ad Christum & fidem in hunc sua doctrina auditores relegaret, illum abs se non in Mosis con-temptum, sed iuxta illius exemplum & mandatum fieri probat. Nam hic ipse Moses est (inquit) qui dixit filijs Israelis: Prophetam vobis suscitabit dominus Deus vester ex fratribus vestris sicut me: ipsum audite. Vnde colligit, nec ipsi Mosi eum animum fuisse, vt in ceremonijs per ipsum tradi-tis haererent Iudaei, sed alium prophetam promisisse, cuius dictis omnes attendere debeant, nisi corporibus simul & animabus interire velint. Est Christus, quem prophetarum omnium principem esse, & cuius spiritu reliquos omnes animatos fuisse, scriptura docet. 1. Pet. 1. &c. Simul vero contempti Mosis crimen in ipsos retorquet, dum Christum Iesum ab illis reiici ostendit, quem tanta authoritate tamen, serio Moses commendavit. Extat locus Deuteron. 18. cap. in cuius explicatione plura diximus Sermone 24. vbi Petri concionem eundem locum adducentis exposuimus. Nos discamus, Dei patris voluntatem esse, vt Christum audiamus, eiq; subijciamur vera fidei obedientia, & in illo salutem consequamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But since he was not unaware that his opponents rest chiefly on this argument, namely that he referred his hearers from the sacred laws to Christ and to faith in him, he proves that he did this not out of contempt for Moses but in accordance with Moses' own example and command. For Moses himself (he says) is the one who said to the sons of Israel: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; hear him." From this he gathers that Moses himself had no intention that the Jews should cling to the ceremonies handed down through him, but had promised another prophet, to whose words everyone ought to attend, unless they wish to perish in both body and soul. This is Christ, whom Scripture teaches to be the prince of all the prophets, and by whose Spirit all the rest were inspired (1 Pet. 1, etc.). At the same time he turns the charge of contempt for Moses back upon them, since he shows that they reject Jesus Christ, whom Moses nevertheless commended so earnestly and with such authority. The passage is found in Deuteronomy chapter 18, in whose explanation we said more in Sermon 24, where we expounded Peter's sermon which cites the same passage. Let us learn that it is the will of God the Father that we should hear Christ, submit ourselves to him in true obedience of faith, and obtain salvation in him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LI.
units.tr: HOMILY LI.

units.la: Hic est, qui fuit in ecclesia in deserto cum angelo, qui loquebatur ei in monte Sina, & cum patribus nostris, qui suscepit sermonem viuum, vt daret nobis. Cui noluerunt obedire patres nostri, sed repulerunt, & auersi sunt corde suo in Aegyptum, dicentes Aaroni: Fac nobis deos, qui nos praecedant. Nam huic Mosi, qui eduxit nos de terra Aegypti, nescimus quid acciderit. Et vitulum fecerunt in diebus illis, & obtulerunt hostiam idolo, & laetati sunt super operibus manuum suarum.
units.tr: "This is he who was in the congregation in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received the living oracles to give to us. To him our fathers would not be obedient, but thrust him from them, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt, saying to Aaron: Make us gods who shall go before us. For as for this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him. And they made a calf in those days, and offered a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands."

units.la: QVoniam Iudaei omnem salutis suae fiduciam in externis ceremonijs repositam habebant, sed prisco rum patrum fidem tenere gloriabantur: omnes eos, qui salutem in vno Christo quaerere docebant, summae impietatis cum in deum ipsum, tum in Mosem & patres accusare consueuerant. Idipsum ergo Stephanus quoq;, vt supra vidimus, expertus est: qui vt se facilius purget, inter multa alia in Mosis laudes digreditur, quem magnifice praedicat, exponens simul quam indigne ab illorum patribus habitus sit. Finis vero omnium est, vt crimen, quod ipsi intentabatur, cum in illorum patres, quibus mirifice gloriari solebant, tum in illos ipsos retorqueat, qui similí peruicacia Christum reiciebant, cui Mosem testimonium dedisse ostendit. Simul vero inde colligitur, patribus nullo suo merito, sed ex mera dei gratia salutem contigisse, nec aliunde hanc ipsos sperare debere. Idem praesentis quoq; loci finis & scopus est, quo primum quidem legis promulgationem, cuius minister fuit Moses, commemorat: inde vero immane maiorum facinus, quo in Mosem & legem Dei peccaverunt, exponit.
units.tr: Since the Jews placed all their hope of salvation in external ceremonies, but boasted that they held the faith of the ancient fathers, they were accustomed to accuse of the greatest impiety all who taught that salvation is sought in Christ alone, both against God himself and against Moses and the fathers. Stephen therefore experienced the same thing, as we saw above. In order to clear himself more easily, he digresses, among many other things, into praise of Moses, whom he extols magnificently, and at the same time explains how unworthily he was treated by their fathers. The purpose of the whole is that the charge brought against him should be turned back both upon the fathers in whom they took such pride and upon those very men who, with the same obstinacy, rejected Christ, to whom he shows that Moses bore witness. At the same time it is gathered from this that the fathers obtained salvation not by any merit of their own but by the pure grace of God, and that they ought not to hope for it from any other source. This is also the purpose and aim of the present passage: first, Stephen recalls the promulgation of the law, of which Moses was the minister; then he sets out the monstrous crime of their forefathers, by which they sinned against Moses and the law of God.

units.la: Atqui de legis promulgatione loquens, duo alia praemittit, quae Mosi haud vulgarem authoritatem conciliare poterant. Primo illum in deserto cum patribus in ecclesia Dei versatum fuisse dicit. Comprehendit hoc quadraginta annorum spacium, quo Israeliticam gentem tanta fide & patientia sustinuit, vt nemo ex omnium seculorum historiis inueniatur, qui cum illo conferri possit. Est hoc singularis fidei argumentum, qua nec periculorum terroribus, nec continuis laborum vicibus, nec populi ingratitudine superari potuit, quin a domino mandatam prouinciam strenuè tueretur. Alterum est, quòd cum angelo illum collocutum fuisse ait, qui & antea ipsi apparuerat, & postea ipsi familiariter conuersatus est, quando illum dei interpretem apud populum constituit. Exod. 20. & 24. Angelum vero hunc Christum fuisse supra ex Paulo docuimus. Quare hic ea Mosis dignitas indicatur, qua is omnes omnium seculorum prophetas longe superauit. Ita enim deum dixisse ldimus: Si fuerit propheta domini inter vos, per visionem ei apparebo, & per somnium loquar ei. At non sic seruo meo Mosi, qui in tota domo mea fidelis est. Ore ad os loquar ei, &c. Num. 12. Haec itaq; in memoriam revocat Stephanus, vt intelligant, quanta olim apud patres merito esse debuerit, & nunc apud ipsos esse debeat, Mosis simul & oraculorum, quae per hunc deus tradidit, authoritas. Et in eum finem subijcit: Hic suscepit sermonem viuum, vt daret nobis. Nec temere legem viuum sermonem vocat. Ita enim se à contempta legis crimine liberat, & huius effectum vno verbo comprehendit. Verè enim lex sermo viuus, vel etiam viuificus dicitur, licet alicubi Paulus illam potentiam peccati & mortis ministerium vocet. 1. Cor. 15. 2. Cor. 3. Nam sanctè viuendi regulam praescribit, & vitam omnibus, qui hanc obseruant, pollicetur. Leuit. 18. Deinde ad Christum ducit, in quo vniuersa salutis ratio, adeoq; ipsa vita continetur. Quo nomine Paulus illam pædagogo conferre
units.tr: Yet in speaking of the promulgation of the law, he first sets down two other points which could win Moses no ordinary authority. First, he says that Moses dwelt in the congregation of God with the fathers in the wilderness. This covers the space of forty years, during which he sustained the Israelite people with such faith and patience that no one can be found in the histories of all the ages who could be compared with him. This is a singular proof of faith, by which he could be overcome neither by the terrors of dangers, nor by the constant turns of labour, nor by the ingratitude of the people, but he bravely defended the charge committed to him by the Lord. The other point is that he says Moses spoke with the angel, who had both appeared to him before and afterwards dealt with him familiarly, when he appointed him interpreter of God to the people (Exod. 20 and 24). We have shown above from Paul that this angel was Christ. Hence the dignity of Moses is here indicated, by which he far surpassed all the prophets of all ages. For God said thus, as we have read: "If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will appear to him in a vision and speak to him in a dream. But it is not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. I will speak to him mouth to mouth," etc. (Num. 12). Stephen therefore recalls these things so that they may understand how great the authority of Moses, and of the oracles which God delivered through him, ought to have been among the fathers of old, and ought now to be among themselves. And to this end he adds: "He received the living oracles to give to us." Nor does he call the law "living oracles" rashly. For in this way he frees himself from the charge of despising the law, and sums up its effect in one word. For the law is truly called living speech, or even life-giving, although elsewhere Paul calls it the power of sin and the ministry of death (1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 3). For it prescribes the rule of holy living and promises life to all who keep it (Lev. 18). Then it leads to Christ, in whom the whole plan of salvation, and so life itself, is contained. For this reason Paul likens it to a tutor.

units.la: {} fert. Gal.3. Et Moses ideo se Iudaeis vitam proposuisse dicit, quod in lege veram vitae consequendae rationem monstrauisset. Et haec quidem in lege agnoscere nos decet, fi illius ingenium recte aftimemus. At fi cum hac nostrae naturae corruptionem conferas, non inepte potentia peccati & mortis ministerium dicetur. Nam peccatum, quod alioqui latet & ignoratur, arguit, & nos mortem meruisse testatur. Adhaec infirmiores nos esse docet, quam qui legis iustitiam implere, & proprijs viribus fiue meritis Dei iram declinare possimus. Sed plura de his Paulus habet Rom.7. & 8. cap.
units.tr: Paul compares it to a tutor (Gal. 3). And Moses says that he set life before the Jews because in the law he had shown the true way of attaining life. We ought to recognise these things in the law, if we rightly estimate its nature. But if you compare with it the corruption of our nature, it will not be inappropriately called the power of sin and the ministry of death. For it convicts sin, which otherwise lies hidden and unknown, and it testifies that we have deserved death. Moreover, it teaches that we are too weak to fulfil the righteousness of the law, or by our own strength or merits to avert the wrath of God. But Paul treats these matters at greater length in Romans 7 and 8.

units.la: Obseruemus autem, quod Mosen non fui ingenij figmenta aut placita, sed sermonem viuum, a Deo acceptum, Israelitis tradidisse dicit. Quod tanta diligentia illum praestitisse constat, vt sine certo & expresso Dei mandato in dubijs rebus nihil vnquam statuere aut decernere ausus sit: vt videre est in causa blasphemi, & eius qui sabbati religionem violarat, illorum ite, qui mortticini tactu polluti, paschale epulum cum ecclesia non potuerant accedere. Vide Leuit.24. Num.9. & 15. Quod autem Moses obseruauit, hoc ipsum prophetis & apostolis diuinitus mandatum fuit olim, ne quid ex proprio cerebro sub diuini nominis praetextu docerent, sed Dei per scripturas loquentis verbum sedulo proponerent. Ita Ieremiae verba sua in os ponit dominus, & Ezechielem ex suo ore verbum, quod annunciet populo, sumere iubet. Ierem.1. Ezech.3. Et apostoli ea docere iubentur omnes gentes, quae Christo docente prius didicerint. Matth.28. Hoc si simili studio obseruauissent, qui apostolorum successione postea gloriati sunt, plus in ecclesia pietatis & verae fidei, minus autem erroris & superstitionis haberemus. Et si Mosen cum prophetis & apostolis inspicias, detestabilem esse deprehendes Romanorum Pontificum audaciam, qua sibi potestatem vendicant nouas leges nouos fidei articulos condendi: quorum licentia & libidine factum est, vt Christianorum iugum Iudaico grauius & molestius fuerit.
units.tr: Let us observe, however, that he says Moses delivered to the Israelites not his own inventions or opinions, but the living word received from God. It is well established that Moses showed such great diligence in this that, in doubtful matters, he never dared to decide or determine anything without a clear and express command of God. This may be seen in the case of the blasphemer, and of the man who had broken the sabbath, and of those who, polluted by touching a corpse, could not come with the congregation to the Passover feast (see Lev. 24; Num. 9 and 15). Now what Moses observed was itself commanded by God of old to the prophets and apostles, that they should not teach anything out of their own head under the pretext of the divine name, but should faithfully set forth the word of God speaking through the Scriptures. So the Lord puts his words into the mouth of Jeremiah, and bids Ezekiel take from his mouth the word to announce to the people (Jer. 1; Ezek. 3). And the apostles are commanded to teach all nations what they have first learned from Christ teaching them (Matt. 28). If those who afterwards boasted of succession from the apostles had observed this with a similar zeal, we would have more piety and true faith in the Church, and less error and superstition. And if you look at Moses together with the prophets and apostles, you will find detestable the audacity of the Roman Pontiffs, by which they claim for themselves the power of framing new laws and new articles of faith. By their licence and lust it has come about that the yoke of Christians has been heavier and more burdensome than the Jewish one.

units.la: Deinde obseruandum venit, quod legem non patribus modo, qui Mosis seculo vixerunt, sed etiam posteris latam fuisse, Stephanus testatur, adeoque, seipsum cum reliquis omnibus, qui iam Christo nomen dederant, illorum numero includit, quibus illa data sit. Quo loco aperte confutatur illorum error, qui ad patres solummodo pertinere putant, quaecunque olim per Mosen & prophetas ex Dei instituto gesta sunt. Atqui Deum aeternum esse constat & immutabilem. Aeterna ergo sit oportet illius voluntas. Nec obstat, quod multa abrogata sunt, quae olim veteribus tradita fuerunt. Ea enim in tempus correctionis duntaxat durare debuerunt, & illorum vmbram referre, quorum veritas in Christo debebat impleri. Nec in illis consistebat Dei cultus, quem spiritualem esse oportet, cum ipse Deus spiritus sit. Iohan.4. Interim vero salua & rata manent vera fidei & religionis capita, quae in mundi exordio primum exposita, deinde vero per Mosen & prophetas plenius illustrata sunt. Quo respiciens propheta, verbum Dei in aeternum manere dicit. Isa.40. Et Christus mundum quidem interiturum fatetur, nullum vero apicem legis irritum fore testatur. Matth.5. Nemo igitur falsa speciem ipsi imponat, quasi non nobis quoque dicta sint, quae patribus olim Deus tradidit, quando ad veteris legis regulam nostram quoque fidem & totius vitae nostrae actiones examinari oportet, &c.
units.tr: Next we must observe that Stephen testifies that the law was given not only to the fathers who lived in the age of Moses, but also to posterity, and so he includes himself with all the rest who had already given their name to Christ among those to whom it was given. In this passage the error of those is openly refuted who think that whatever was done of old through Moses and the prophets by God's appointment pertains only to the fathers. But it is certain that God is eternal and unchangeable. Therefore his will must be eternal. Nor does it stand in the way that many things were abrogated which were of old handed down to the ancients. For those were to last only for the time of correction, and to represent the shadow of those things whose truth was to be fulfilled in Christ. Nor did the worship of God consist in those things, which must be spiritual, since God himself is Spirit (John 4). Meanwhile the true heads of faith and religion remain safe and valid, which were first set forth at the beginning of the world, and then more fully illustrated through Moses and the prophets. Looking to these, the prophet says that the word of God endures for ever (Isa. 40). And Christ indeed confesses that the world will perish, but testifies that not one jot of the law will be void (Matt. 5). Let no one therefore put a false appearance upon it, as if the things God once delivered to the fathers were not also spoken to us, since our faith and all the actions of our whole life must be examined by the rule of the old law as well, etc.

units.la: Sed ad Stephanum reuertamur, qui diuinae legis promulgationi patrum ingratitudinem & improbitatem opponit, qua illi & Mosen & legem iniquissime reiecerunt. Et quamuis innumera prodire posset flagitia, vnicum tamen idololatriae facinus adducit, quo satis patet, quam exigua apud illos fuerit diuinae legis authoritas, quando contra illius edictum Dei imaginem fingere, & nouos cultus instituere ausi sunt, cum paucis diebus ante terribilem diuinae maiestatis voce auribus suis hausissent. Extat historia Exod.32.cap. Finis vero & scopus is Stephano propositus est, vt euincat, patres semper Mosis contemptores fuisse, & ipsos illorum peruicaciam egregie imitari: quare vt mera gratia patres olim saluati sint, ita ipsis quoque non aliam salutis spem restare, quam quae in Dei gratia sit fundata. Prodest autem paucula haec, quibus atrox inobedientiae facinus comprehenditur, diligenter inspicere, eo quod idololatriae fontem & progressum nobis diligenter depingunt.
units.tr: But let us return to Stephen, who sets against the promulgation of the divine law the ingratitude and wickedness of the fathers, by which they most unjustly rejected both Moses and the law. And although he could list countless crimes, he cites only one act of idolatry, from which it is plain enough how slight the authority of the divine law was among them, since they dared to make an image of God and to institute new forms of worship against his command, after they had heard the terrifying voice of the divine majesty with their own ears only a few days before. The history is in Exodus chapter 32. Stephen's aim and purpose is to prove that the fathers were always despisers of Moses and remarkably imitated the obstinacy of their own forebears. Therefore, just as the fathers were once saved by sheer grace, so no other hope of salvation remains for us than that which is founded on the grace of God. It is useful to examine carefully these few words, which describe the dreadful act of disobedience, because they set out for us in detail the source and progress of idolatry.

units.la: Primo omnis mali origine indicans, patres viuo sermoni diuinae legis noluisse obedire dicit, sed corde suo in Aegyptum auersos fuisse. Et Aegypti nomine abominabilem superstitionem, quae in illa gente regnauit, complectitur, cui illos animum denuo adiecisse affirmat. Hic vero execrabilem animorum leuitatem notat, qua factum est, vt tum grauissimae seruitutis, tum miraculosae liberationis tam cito obliuiscerentur, & eos sibi imitandos putarent, ad quorum mentionem totis animis horas rere debuissent. Est autem hic omnis impietatis fons, si Dei verbo contempto & reiecto, ad hominum commenta & exempla animos nostros conuersi, illis potius quam Deo placere studeamus. Hinc enim detestabilis illa leuitas initium sumit, quae nos non modo diuinae legis oblivisci facit, sed infelicis tyrannidis & seruitutis, quam aliquando sustinuimus, memoriam omnne animo excutere solet. Exempla huius rei hodie passim extant in illis, qui ut mundo probentur, illius superstitionem sibi imitandam proponunt, & horrenda Antichristianismi grauamina, quibus olim oppressi fuerunt, mirifice extenuant, ne quid nimis impie designare videantur.
units.tr: First, pointing to the origin of all evil, he says that the fathers were unwilling to obey the living word of the divine law, but that in their hearts they had turned back to Egypt. By the name of Egypt he takes in the abominable superstition that reigned in that nation, and he affirms that they had again given their minds to it. Here he notes the wretched fickleness of mind, by which it came about that they so quickly forgot both the most grievous slavery and the miraculous deliverance, and thought that they should imitate those people whose memory ought to have turned all their minds away from them. Now this is the source of all impiety: when the word of God has been despised and rejected, and we turn our minds to human inventions and examples, and strive to please them rather than God. For that detestable fickleness takes its beginning from here, which not only makes us forget the divine law, but is wont to banish from the mind all memory of the unhappy tyranny and slavery we once endured. Examples of this are still to be found everywhere today in those who, in order to win the approval of the world, propose for themselves that superstition as something to imitate, and wonderfully downplay the horrible burdens of Antichristianity by which they were once oppressed, lest they seem to speak of them in too impious a way.

units.la: At diuinae legis contemptu Mosis contemptus sequitur, quem non obscuris verbis exprimunt, cum aiunt: Huic Mosi, qui nos eduxit de terra Aegypti, nescimus quid acciderit. Fatentur ergo beneficium, quod ipsis per Mosen contigerat, interim quid illi acciderit, incertum esse dicunt. Atqui illum domino vocante in montem ascendisse viderant. Ab eodem mandatu acceperant, quo illius adventum iusti erant expectare. Habebant praeterea a Mose constitutos vicarios, Hur & Aaronem. Adhuc tamen quasi omnium rerum dubij & incerti reliqui sint, conqueri audent. Vnde facile constat, perquam exilem fuisse apud illos homines Mosis authoritatem, qui legem Dei tanta improbitate ab iicere instituerant. Ita vero semper verbi contemptus, vbi is semel animo conceptus fuerit, ministrorum Dei contemptum & fastidium parere consueuit. Quia enim hos nobis ceu εγγελιώντας & speculatores a Deo constitutos esse satan nouit, quorum admonitionibus, vel in officio retineamur, vel in viam reuocemur, si quando exorbitauimus, hoc vnum effectum cupit, vt illorum intercidatin animis nostris authoritas. Et docet locus hic, quid de illis iudicemus, qui verbi ministros scurriliter contemnere & maledictis incessere audent. Eo certe argumento probant, se ipsius Dei & verbi ipsum contemptores esse, licet id constanter pernegent. Nam vt legatum contemnere non solet, qui principem a quo ille missus est, magnificat: ita nisi illi Deum parui facere didicissent, illius ministros & legatos contemnere non possent.
units.tr: But contempt for the divine law is followed by contempt for Moses, which they express in no obscure words when they say: "As for this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him." So they admit the benefit that had come to them through Moses, yet they say that what has become of him is uncertain. And yet they had seen him go up the mountain when the Lord called him. They had received from the same command that they were to await his coming. Besides, he had appointed deputies, Hur and Aaron. Yet they dare to complain, as if everything were still doubtful and uncertain. From this it is easily established that the authority of Moses was very slight among those men, who had resolved to cast away the law of God with such wickedness. Indeed, contempt for the Word, once it has taken hold of the mind, is wont to produce contempt and disdain for the ministers of God. For Satan knows that these men have been set up by God as messengers [ἀγγέλους] and watchmen, by whose admonitions we are either kept in our duty or called back to the way if ever we have strayed. He desires only this one result, that their authority should perish in our minds. And this passage teaches us what we should think of those who dare to despise the ministers of the Word with scurrilous talk and to assail them with abuse. Certainly by this argument they prove that they are despisers of God himself and of his Word, although they stubbornly deny it. For just as a man does not usually despise the envoy of a prince whom he honours, so unless they had learned to hold God in small esteem, they could not have despised his ministers and envoys.

units.la: Ex istis fontibus idololatriae peccatu promanare coepit. Dum enim se nescire dicunt, quid Mosi acciderit, mox addunt: Fac nobis deos, qui nos praecedant. Num vero eo dementiae ipsos progressos fuisse putabimus, vt putarent hominum manibus Deos fieri posse? Minime gentium. Sed visibile dei & praesentiae Dei signum sibi dari volunt, quo de praesenti Dei auxilio certiores fieri, & ad quod externi cultus ceremonias dirigere possint. Et quia semel a Dei verbo ad humanae rationis figmenta exorbitare coeperant, vitulum aureum conflant, Aegyptios imitati, quos Apim suum sub viculi figura coluisse constat. Vbi multiplex error sese exerit. Primo enim de Dei praesentia dubitat, cuius tam multa & insignia argumenta hucusque viderant. Et iam nec prodigiorum, quae in Aegypto & mari rubro viderant, meminere: nec ad columnam nubis & ignis, quae castra praecedebat, respiciunt: nec tremendae maiestatis, quae in monte Sinai apparuerat, recordantur. Deinde contra Dei praeceptum imaginem fusilem faciunt, qua Dei formam exprimere conantur, & (vt propheta inquit) permutant maiestatem Dei sui effigie bouis comedentis faenum. Psal. 106. Deum ergo extrema ignominia afficiunt, & nouos deos fingunt, dum longe alium imaginantur, quam reuera sit. Est autem hic proximus ad idololatriam gradus, quando non ijs mediis contenti sunt homines, quibus sese Deus reuelare dignatur, sed nouos ex semetipsis fingere audent. Reuelat autem sese per verbum & sacramenta deus, item per mundi huius machinam & creaturas, in quibus singulis non obscura diuinae sapientiae, bonitatis, iustitiae & omnipotentiae indicia apparent. Et vt ijs visis in Dei & cultus veri consydratio nem excitemur, nihil vere totus hic orbis cotinet, e quo non parabolas desumpserit spiritus sanctus, quibus Dei & salutis nostrae mysteria adumbrat. Vndique ergo in oculos nostros incurrunt per dei verbum consecratae imagines, quae nos officij admonere possunt. Ista quicunque negligunt, & carnis rationi indulgent, non possunt no idololatriae vitio pollui. Nam quod Iudaeis hoc loco accidisse videmus, idem gentibus quoq; euenisse legimus. Rom. 1. Nec aliam inter Christianos idololatriae originem fuisse, notius est, quam vt multis demonstrari debeat. Praeterea admonemur, quam referat, a pueris recte circa religionem institui, quando post tot visa prodigia & post auditam Dei vocem ad illud idololatriae genus relabuntur Israelitae, cui in Aegypto assueuerant.
units.tr: From these sources the sin of idolatry began to spring forth. For when they say that they do not know what has happened to Moses, they immediately add: "Make us gods who will go before us." Shall we suppose that they had gone so far in madness as to think that gods could be made by human hands? By no means. But they wanted a visible sign of God and of his presence, by which they might be made more certain of God's present help, and to which they might direct the outward ceremonies of worship. And because they had once begun to wander from the word of God into the inventions of human reason, they cast a golden calf, imitating the Egyptians, who are known to have worshipped their Apis under the figure of a little ox. Here many errors break out. First, they doubt the presence of God, whose many great and remarkable proofs they had seen up to that time. And now they no longer remember the prodigies they had seen in Egypt and at the Red Sea, nor do they look to the pillar of cloud and fire that went before the camp, nor do they recall the dreadful majesty that had appeared on Mount Sinai. Then, against God's command, they make a cast image, by which they try to express the form of God, and (as the prophet says) they exchange the glory of their God for the likeness of an ox that eats grass (Ps. 106). So they treat God with the utmost dishonour, and they invent new gods, since they imagine him to be quite different from what he really is. Now this is the step nearest to idolatry, when people are not content with the means by which God deigns to reveal himself, but dare to invent new ones out of themselves. God reveals himself through his Word and sacraments, and likewise through the frame of this world and its creatures, in each of which appear clear signs of divine wisdom, goodness, justice and omnipotence. And so that we may be stirred by these to contemplate God and the true worship, the whole of this world truly contains nothing from which the Holy Spirit has not taken parables, by which he sketches the mysteries of God and of our salvation. Therefore consecrated images, which can remind us of our duty, meet our eyes from every side through the Word of God. Whoever neglects these things and gives way to the reasoning of the flesh cannot be free from the vice of idolatry. For what we see happened here to the Jews, we read also happened to the Gentiles (Rom. 1). Nor is it better known that there was any other origin of idolatry among Christians than that it should have to be shown to many. Furthermore, we are reminded how much it matters that people be rightly instructed in religion from childhood, when after so many prodigies seen and after hearing the voice of God, the Israelites fall back into that kind of idolatry to which they had been accustomed in Egypt.

units.la: Noui deum cultus sequitur. Quare illos vitulo immolauisse dicit. Atqui Deo vero, qui ipsos de terra Aegypti eduxerat, immolare videri volebant. Veri enim Dei mentionem faciunt, & Aaron festum festum diem domino indixisse legitur. Quia tamen vitulus hic nec verus Deus erat, nec Dei imago (quis enim deum vitulo similem dixerit?) verissimè vitulo immolauisse dicuntur. Habes ergo quod ijs respondeas, qui imaginum cultum boni zeli prætextu excusari putant, & Deo acceptum esse dicunt, quicquid in illius honorem fit, etiamsi à verbi ipsius regula interdum deuiemus. At longè alia est spiritus sancti mens, qui per Stephanum loquitur. In imaginibus enim omnis iste cultus hæret, nec ad Deum vsq; extenditur, cuius similitudinem minimè referunt. Quomodo enim Deum, qui ipsa veritas est, idola repræsentarent, quæ mendacès magistri à propheta dicuntur? Hab.2. Quod si cul rum hunc longius extendi dixeris, diabolo illum impendi fatebor, qui & mendacij patr est, & mendacijs vnicè delectatur. Vidit hoc Paulus, quando in priori ad Corinth. cap.10. scribebat: Quæ immolant gentes, dæmonijs immolant, & non Deo.
units.tr: The worship of a new god follows. Therefore it is said that they sacrificed to the calf. And yet they wanted to seem to sacrifice to the true God, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. For they make mention of the true God, and it is read that Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD. Yet because this calf was neither the true God nor an image of God (for who would call God like a calf?), they are rightly said to have sacrificed to a calf. You therefore have here an answer to those who think that the worship of images can be excused under the pretext of good zeal, and who say that whatever is done to honour God is acceptable to him, even if we sometimes stray from the rule of the Word itself. But the mind of the Holy Spirit, who speaks through Stephen, is quite different. For all this worship clings to images and does not reach as far as God, whose likeness they by no means represent. For how could they represent God, who is truth itself, by idols, which the prophet calls lying teachers? (Hab. 2). And if you should say that this worship is extended further, I will admit that it is offered to the devil, who is both the father of lies and takes delight in lies alone. Paul saw this when in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 10, he wrote: "What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God."

units.la: Accedit omnibus hïs, quòd lætati sunt super operibus manuum suarum. Exprimitur hïs partim animi fiducia & quod inde enascitur gaudium, quæ vtraq; in vno Deo quæri & collocari debebant; partim externum gaudium, in quod omnes modestiæ terminos transgressi, idololatræ effundi solent. Vtrunq; hïc accidisse, historia sacra docet. Nam vitulo primum conflato & exsculpto ingenti cum applausu acclamant: Isti sunt dij tui ô Israel, qui te eduxerunt ex Ægypto. Deinde idolothytorum carnibus saturi, surgunt ad ludendum. Est autem hoc idololatræ proprium. Auferunt enim idola cor hominis, vt propheta inquit. Hos.4. Vnde fit, vt illis gaudeant, qui in vno Deo exultare debebant: & immodicis intempestiuisq; ludis infantant, quos Dei spiritu regi decebat. Quòd si verò quæcunque hactenus dicta sunt, cum ijs, quæ in Papatu contigerunt, conferas, plane eadem esse videbis. Quem enim alium idololatriæ fontem dabis, quàm quòd homines Dei verbo abiecto ad gentium Iudæorum abominationes, vnde diuino beneficio liberati fuerant, cordibus suis denuo conuersi sunt? Patet hoc inde, quod pleraq; cum gentilium sacris & Iudaicis ritibus conueniunt. Verbi dei contemptum mox ministerij contemptus subsecutus est, quem vehementer promouit sacrificulorum stolidi tas, qui rudes homines ad mutas statuas relegarūt, vt inde discerent quæ saluti seruiunt. Ex hïs foetibus noui dij prodierunt, quorum alij virili, alij muliebri forma expressi sunt, alij rursum senili, alij iuuenili specie sese commendarunt. Quid quòd humanis formis, quadrupedum, volatilium, reptilium & aquatilium imagines intermixta sunt? Taceo deformes militum habitus, & meretricium mundum, quo exornatæ sunt imagines, quæ diuorum & Dei ipsius formam repræsentare debebant. At noui dij nouos cultus exigebant. In illorum ergo honorem extructa sunt templa, consecratæ aræ, suspensa anathemata, instituta passagia, accensæ lampades, indictæ feriæ, oblatæ victimæ, nihil denique omissum est, quod olim in gentium sacris vsurpatum fuit. Et quasi peccatorum sarcina in vniuersum liberati essent homines, bisce manuum suarum operibus mirificè gloriati sunt. Nec defuit carnalis gaudij licentia, quæ nunquam magis quàm in deorum istorum festis & dedicationibus reg-nauit. Tam grauis & atrox fuit cæcitas, è qua per euangelij lucem nos liberauit dominus. Viue-mus ergo in posterum nostri ingenij adinuentiones & nostrarum manuum opera. Seruiamus autem in spiritu & veritate Deo patri Iesu Christi, domini nostri: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Add to all this that they rejoiced in the works of their own hands. This describes partly the confidence of their minds and the joy that springs from it, both of which ought to have been sought and placed in the one God alone; and partly an outward joy, in which idolaters, overstepping all bounds of moderation, are wont to pour themselves out. Sacred history teaches that both happened here. For first, after the calf was cast and carved, they shouted with great applause: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of Egypt." Then, glutted with the flesh of things sacrificed to idols, they rose up to make merry. Indeed this is characteristic of idolatry: idols take away the heart of man, as the prophet says (Hos. 4). Hence it comes about that they rejoice in the things which ought to have made them exult in the one God, and they dissolve into immoderate and untimely games, when they ought to have been ruled by the Spirit of God. But if you compare all that has been said so far with what happened under the Papacy, you will see that they are plainly the same. For what other source of idolatry will you give than that men, having cast off the Word of God, were turned again in their hearts to the abominations of the Gentiles and Jews, from which they had been freed by the divine benefit? This is evident from the fact that many of the practices agree with the rites of the Gentiles and the Jews. Contempt for the Word of God was soon followed by contempt for the ministry, which the foolishness of the sacrificing priests greatly promoted, when they sent simple people off to dumb statues to learn from them what serves salvation. From these offspring new gods were born, some represented in male form, some in female, some again displayed themselves in old age, others in youthful appearance. Why speak of the mingling of human forms with images of four-footed beasts, birds, reptiles and fish? I say nothing of the ugly soldiers' garb and the harlot's finery with which those images were adorned, which were supposed to represent the saints and God himself. But these new gods demanded new forms of worship. So temples were built in their honour, altars consecrated, votive offerings hung up, feasts of Passover instituted, lamps lit, holy days proclaimed, victims offered; in short, nothing was left out that had once been used in the rites of the Gentiles. And as if men had been freed in general from the burden of their sins, they took wondrous pride in these works of their hands. Nor was there any lack of licence for carnal joy, which has never reigned more than at the festivals and dedications of those gods. So grievous and savage was the blindness from which the Lord has freed us through the light of the gospel. Let us therefore live henceforth by the inventions of our own minds and the works of our own hands? No: let us serve God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ in spirit and in truth, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LII.
units.tr: HOMILY 52.

units.la: Conuertit autē se deus, & tradidit eos, vt colerent militiā cœli, quemadmodum scriptum est in libro prophetarum: Numquid victimas & hostias obtulistis mihi per annos quadraginta in deserto, domus Israel? Et suscepistis tabernaculum Moloch, & sydus dei vestri Remphan, figuras quas fecistis ad colendum eas. Ideo transferam vos vltra Babylonem.
units.tr: But God turned himself away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, the figures which you made to worship them. Therefore I will carry you beyond Babylon.

units.la: Inter multa alia, quæ Christus Iesus fidis euangelij sui præconibus euenturā prædixit, non postre-mum est, quòd mundus illos tanquam publicos veræ religionis hostes persecuturus fit. Illud cir-ca initium nascentis ecclesiæ apostolos expertos fuisse vidimus, & inter hos Stephanum in primis, qui dum Christo homines lucrifacere studet, hoc nomine accusatur, quòd aduersus Deum, Mosen, legem, torumq; legalem cultum impia & blasphema locutus sit. Prudenter verò & fortiter tam impudentibus calumniis respondet, dum veterem patrum religionem, qua illi servati sunt, repetit, & quae per Mosen gesta sunt diligentissimè exponit, & ingenuè fatetur hunc viuum sermonem a Deo acceptum patribus tradidisse. Simul vero ostendit, patres nunquam divinis praeceptis fuisse morigeros, sed externis duntaxat caeremoniis addictos, multa ex semetipsis finxisse verae religioni contraria. Et hoc modo inanem patrum & avitae religionis fiduciam animis illorum excutere conatur, qua non alia perniciosior est remora in salutis negotio versantibus. In eum ergo finem aurei vituli historiam produxit, qua summae impietatis patres illorum convincit, eosque mera Dei gratia servatos esse demonstravit, quando vnico illo facinore excidium meruissent. Commodè vero has praesentem locum connectit, quo non simpliciter scelere ab illis modo peccatum fuisse, sed posteros quoque patrum impiorum vestigiis insistitisse docet.
units.tr: Among the many other things which Christ Jesus foretold would befall the faithful heralds of his gospel, it is not the least that the world would persecute them as public enemies of the true religion. We saw this happen near the beginning of the infant Church, when the apostles were tried, and above all Stephen, who, while he strove to win men to Christ, was accused of speaking impious and blasphemous words against God, Moses, the law and the legal worship. Stephen answers such shameless slanders wisely and bravely. He recalls the ancient religion of the fathers, by which they were saved, explains with great care what was done through Moses, and frankly admits that Moses handed on to the fathers the living word received from God. At the same time he shows that the fathers were never obedient to the divine precepts, but were devoted only to outward ceremonies, and had invented for themselves many things contrary to true religion. In this way he tries to shake from their minds their empty confidence in the fathers and in the religion of their ancestors, which is no more harmful obstacle for those who are concerned with the business of salvation. To this end he brought forward the story of the golden calf, by which he convicts the fathers of the greatest impiety and shows that they were saved by pure grace of God, since by that single crime they had deserved destruction. He connects this passage well with the present place, where he teaches that the sin was committed by them not merely once, but that their descendants also trod in the footsteps of their impious fathers.

units.la: Videtur autem praeoccupationis speciem habere, quòd posterorum quoque idololatriam recenset. Ita enim cauere vult, ne quis erecti vituli scelus vel extenuaret, vel posterorum pietate tam olim expiatum esse diceret: Nec enim aliquis excusationi locus superesset, quando primus ille lapsus adeò non meliores reddidit, ut potius sequentis impietatis foecundissimum seminarium fuerit. Quia enim Dei verbum semel abiecerant & devotis ad impietatem animis in exitium ruebant, Deus, qui antea illis benignè fauebat, tergum obvertens, ipsos in reprobum sensum tradidit, ut vniuersam caeli militiam sibi colendam putarent, omnemque gentium superstitionem sedulò imitarentur. Atqui paucis hisce verbis comprehendit Stephanus, quicquid posteà in religione ab ipsis contra Dei leges designatum fuit. Primus enim omnium mali author Salomon in uxorum alienigenarum gratiam diversis Sidoniorum, Moabitarum, & Ammonitarum & aliarum gentium diis templa condidit. 1.Reg.11. Vitulorum superstitione Ieroboam postliminio revocavit. 1.Reg.12. & 13. Baalis cultus per Achabum inductus est. 1.Reg.16. Amasias Idumaeorum deos, abs se deiectos, insano consilio adorandos proposuit. 2.Paral.25. Syrorum diis & religione captus est Achaz. 2.Paral.28. Tandem Manasses secutus, qui omnem maiorum impietatem longè supergressus, quicquid vspiam inter gentes superstitionis & idololatriae fuit, in Iudaeam intulit, & impios cultus iniusta vi contra fidos Dei cultores defendit, adeò vt Hierosolymam sanctorum sanguine repleuisse legatur. 2.Reg.21. Cuius impietas tam profundè radices egit, vt ne Iosiae quidem temporibus tota excindi & deleri potuerit, quemadmodum Ieremiae & Sophoniae Sermones abundè testantur. Ne vero alicui mirum videretur, haec poëna à Deo legem facta esse, non temere à Deo derelictos & in reprobum sensum traditos, adeoque excaecatos fuisse dixit. Id autem iusto Dei iudicio factum esse ex ijs, quae proximè praecesserunt, facile colligitur. Hoc enim merebatur illorum impietas & ingratitudo, quos nec Dei verbum, nec infinita alia, quibus Deus illis se revelare dignatus erat, in officio retinere potuerant. Digni ergo erant, qui videntibus oculis caecutirent, & auribus audientibus obsurdescerent, animúque totis indurarentur, vt apud Isaiam cap.6. minatur dominus. A T similia iudiciorum Dei exempla in alijs quoque gentibus inuenire licet. Idem certè de ethnicorum superstitione Paulus affirmat. Rom.1. Et vtinam non similia inter eos cerneremus, qui Christi nomine gloriantur. Postquam enim apud illos verbi Dei authoritas euanuit, & ex imaginibus mutis potius quàm viuo Dei sermone discere voluerunt, tous superstitionis licentia progressa est, vt Iudaeis simul & Turcis sese deridendos praebuerint. Atque hic mihi succurrit memorabile Turcici legati dictum, qui in magni inter Christianos regis aula terrogatus, cur Christianam religionem tam infestis animis Turcae persequantur, nec vt illi nomen dent adduci possint? Respondit, nemini sanae mentis eam religionem probari posse, quae deos colat, qui suis ipsorum cultoribus inferiores & impotentiores sint. Id vero paulò post de Christo impanato & idolis, quae in templis adorantur, expositum, quae cum illorum opera fiunt, à quibus coluntur, satis constat praepositorum hunc cultum esse, & communi sensui contrarium. Norunt haec Christiani principes, norunt antistites, norunt plebeii: nemini tamen dolet tam atrox, quae inde infertur Christiano nomini iniuria: vt non temere cordati quiuis metuant multos nostro quoque seculo in reprobum sensum traditos, vertiginis spiritu agitari.
units.tr: Yet he seems to anticipate an objection, in that he also recounts the idolatry of their descendants. For he wishes to guard against anyone either lessening the guilt of the erected calf, or saying that it had long since been atoned for by the piety of their descendants. For there would be no room left for excuse, since that first fall did not make them better, but rather became the most fruitful seedbed of the impiety that followed. For since they had once cast aside the word of God and rushed to destruction with minds given over to impiety, God, who had formerly favoured them kindly, turned his back and gave them over to a reprobate mind, so that they thought the whole host of heaven was to be worshipped and eagerly imitated all the superstition of the nations. Stephen in these few words sums up whatever was afterwards devised in religion by them against the laws of God. For first of all the author of evil, Solomon, for the sake of his foreign wives, built temples to the various gods of the Sidonians, Moabites, Ammonites and other nations (1 Kings 11). Jeroboam recalled the superstition of the calves (1 Kings 12 and 13). The worship of Baal was introduced by Ahab (1 Kings 16). Amaziah, in his mad counsel, proposed that the gods of the Edomites, which he himself had cast down, should be worshipped (2 Chron. 25). Ahaz, taken captive, adopted the gods and religion of the Syrians (2 Chron. 28). Finally Manasseh followed, who far surpassed the impiety of his forefathers, and brought into Judea whatever superstition and idolatry existed anywhere among the nations, and by unjust violence defended impious worship against the faithful worshippers of God, so that it is recorded that he filled Jerusalem with the blood of the saints (2 Kings 21). His impiety struck such deep roots that it could not be wholly uprooted and destroyed even in the time of Josiah, as the sermons of Jeremiah and Zephaniah abundantly testify. Lest anyone should think it strange that this punishment was laid upon them by God, he said that they had been abandoned by God, and given over to a reprobate mind, and so blinded. It is easily gathered from what has immediately preceded that this came about by the just judgment of God. For the impiety and ingratitude of these people deserved it: neither the word of God nor the countless other means by which God had deigned to reveal himself to them had been able to keep them in their duty. They were therefore worthy to grow blind with their eyes open, to grow deaf with their ears hearing, and to be hardened in heart, as the Lord threatens in Isaiah 6. Similar examples of God's judgments may be found among other nations also. Paul certainly affirms the same of the superstition of the heathen (Rom. 1). And would that we did not see similar things among those who glory in the name of Christ! For after the authority of the word of God had vanished among them, and they chose to learn from dumb images rather than from the living word of God, the license of superstition advanced so far that they exposed themselves to be mocked by the Jews and the Turks alike. Here there comes to my mind the memorable saying of a Turkish envoy, who, when he was asked at the court of a great Christian king why the Turks persecuted the Christian religion with such hostile minds and could not be brought to take its name, replied that no man of sound mind could approve a religion which worships gods who are inferior and less powerful than their own worshippers. Shortly afterwards, when Christ incorporated in the bread and the idols which are adored in the temples were explained, it is well established that this worship is set up by those who make these things and by those who worship them, and that it is contrary to common sense. Christian princes know this, bishops know it, common people know it; yet no one is troubled by how great an injury is thereby done to the Christian name. Thus it is no wonder that thoughtful men fear that many in our own age too, given over to a reprobate mind, are driven by a spirit of giddiness.

units.la: Admonet praeterea nos locus hic, neminem in religionis causa rectam viam tenere posse, nisi qui Dei manu & spiritu regatur. Animalis enim homo non capit ea, quae sunt spiritus dei. 1.Cor.2. Nec quisquam venit ad Christum, nisi quem pater traxerit. Ioban.6. Quia vero is per verbum suum ducit & cit & trahit, illius studio opus est. Quicunq; enim illud parui faciunt & abijciunt, Dei gratia sese in dignos reddunt. Quare iuste tergum vertit Deus, & omni veritatis luce spoliatos tenebris inuoluit. Solicita ergo verbi cura nos teneri conuenit, & ab illo ita pendere, ut recta via ingressi, nec ad dextram nec ad sinistram declinemus. Deut. 4. & 12.
units.tr: Moreover, this place admonishes us that no one can keep to the right path in matters of religion unless he is ruled by the hand and Spirit of God. For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). And no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6). But since he leads, calls and draws men by his word, it is necessary to be eager for that word. For whoever make little of it and cast it aside make themselves unworthy of the grace of God. Therefore God justly turns his back and wraps in darkness those who are stripped of all the light of truth. It is fitting, then, that we be held by a careful attention to the word, and depend upon it so that, having entered the right way, we do not turn aside to the right or to the left (Deut. 4 and 12).

units.la: Caeterum ne quis tam perfrictae frontis esset, ut ista a patribus facta esse negaret, propheticum testimonium Stephanus producit, quod Amos 5. cap. habetur. Accusat ibi Israeliticam gentem dominus, cum propter alia vitia, tum propter hoc, quod parum syncere in ipsius cultu versarentur. Et ut maior appareat peccati atrocitas, & omnibus constet, Deum non immerito hanc tum ipsis expostulationem suscepisse, ostendit vetus hoc malum esse, quod olim in deserto inceptum, temporis progressu maiores vires sumpserit, adeo ut incurabile factum, non aliter quam excidio totius gentis tolli possit. Non parum autem ad nostram institutionem faciet, si singula quae dicuntur, penitius inspiciamus.
units.tr: But lest anyone be so brazen as to deny that these things were done by the fathers, Stephen brings forward the testimony of the prophet, which is found in Amos chapter 5. There the Lord accuses the people of Israel, both for their other vices and for this, that they dealt too insincerely in his worship. And so that the greater enormity of the sin may appear, and it may be clear to all that God had not undeservedly brought this complaint against them, he shows that this is an ancient evil which, begun in the wilderness, had gathered greater strength as time went on, so that it had become incurable and could be removed only by the destruction of the whole nation. Nor will it contribute little to our instruction if we examine closely each thing that is said.

units.la: Primo de patrum, qui in deserto fuerunt, inobedientia & impietate disserit his verbis: Numquid victimas & hostias obtulistis mihi per annos quadraginta in deserto, domus Israel? Interrogatione sermonem intendit, & patres totis quadraginta annis Deo sacrificasse negat. At constat illos ex Dei mandato tabernaculum construxisse & altaria, in quibus omnis generis sacrificia Deo obtulerunt, qui ipsos de terra Aegypti eduxerat. At Deus in suum honorem impensum fuisse negat, quod alio fine, quam ipse praescripserat, fuit factum. Eum enim omnis externi cultus finem esse voluit Deus, ut promissi saluatoris typos praeferret, & ipsos sui officij tam in fide & religione, quam totius vitae conversatione admoneret. Illi autem horum immemores, nudis ceremonijs occupabantur, & his Deo satisfieri atque peccata expiari putabant. Qua ratione fiebat, ut toto Levitico cultu in licentiae & scelerum praetextum abuterentur. Merito igitur cultum hunc omnem Deus reijcit, & ad se pertinere negat. Et alia quoq; extant scripturae loca, quibus idem constanter vrget, & inutile esse docet eorum administrationem, quae tanta diligentia in lege praescripserat. Vide Psal. 50. Isa. 1. & 43. Mich. 6. Hos. 6. Imo Circumcisionem quoque inutilem esse clamat, cum illos hac insolentius gloriari videret, nulla interim spiritualis circuncisionis ratione habita. Iere. 4. Docemur igitur hoc loco, vanum esse omnem eum cultum, qui non ad illum finem destinatur, qui a Deo praescriptus est. Fieri enim nequit, ut absq; fidei obedientia aliquis cultus Deo placeat. Hebr. 11. At ubi Dei verbum neglitur, ibi nec fidei nec obedientiae locus est reliquus: quare pro impuris & prophanis habentur, quaecunq; fiunt, etiamsi quoad externam speciem cum verbo Dei conuenire videantur. Quid ergo de ijs ceremonijs dicemus, quae sola hominum authoritate & humanis traditionibus nituntur? Iugulauit has olim vna sententia dominus, dicens: Frustra me colunt docentes doctrinas hominum. Omnis plantatio, quam non plantauit pater meus, eradicabitur. Isa. 29. Matth. 15.
units.tr: First, he speaks of the disobedience and impiety of the fathers who were in the wilderness, in these words: Did you offer victims and sacrifices to me for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? By this question he makes his point, and denies that the fathers sacrificed to God through all forty years. Yet it is established that by God's command they built the tabernacle and altars, on which they offered sacrifices of every kind to God, who had led them out of the land of Egypt. But God denies that what was done with another end than the one he had prescribed was done for his honour. For God willed that the whole outward worship should have this end: that it should prefigure the promised Saviour, and remind them of their duty both in faith and religion and in the whole conduct of life. But they, forgetting these things, busied themselves with bare ceremonies, and thought that God was satisfied and sins atoned for by these. The result was that they abused the whole Levitical worship as a pretext for licence and for crimes. Rightly, then, God rejects all this worship and denies that it pertains to him. There are other passages of Scripture too in which he insists on the same thing, and teaches that the administration of those things which he had prescribed in the law with such great care is useless (see Ps. 50; Isa. 1 and 43; Mic. 6; Hos. 6). Indeed he cries out that circumcision too is useless, when he saw them boasting of it more arrogantly, while taking no account of spiritual circumcision (Jer. 4). We are taught therefore in this place that all worship which is not directed to the end prescribed by God is vain. For no worship can be pleasing to God without the obedience of faith (Heb. 11). But where the word of God is neglected, there is no room left either for faith or for obedience; therefore whatever is done is regarded as impure and profane, even if it seems in outward appearance to agree with the word of God. What then shall we say of those ceremonies which rest only on human authority and human traditions? The Lord once overthrew these with a single sentence, saying: In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men. Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Isa. 29; Matt. 15).
