units.la: Pergens autem in recensendis Israelitarum peccatis deus, quid posteri occupata iam terra Chanaan fecerint commemorat. Suscepistis (inquit) tabernaculum Moloch, & sydus Dei vestri Remphan, figuras quas fecistis ad colendum eas. Tribus autem speciebus omnem idololatriam comprehendit. Primum cultum Moloch habuit, quem Ammonitarum Deum fuisse ex rebus Solomonis constat, qui illi primus templum constituisse legitur. Videtur aute Deus genitalis fuisse, cuius honori infantes igne lustrati consecrabantur, quod a Manasse factum est, qui filium suum per ignem traduxit. Statuerat huic impietati capitalem poenam Deus, quae Leuit. 20. cap. his verbis continetur: Quicunq; e filijs Israel aut ex incolis, qui commorantur in Israele, de semine suo dederit ipsi Moloch, morte multabitur, populus terrae lapidibus eum obruet. Et ego statuam faciem meam contra virum eiusmodi, eumq; de medio populi sui excindam, eo quod dederit de semine suo ipsi Moloch, ut contaminaret sanctuarium meum, & prophanaret nomen meum sanctum. Et si omnino populus regionis oculos suos absconderit a viro isto, qui de semine suo dederit ipsi Moloch, & eum non interfecerit, statuam ego faciem meam contra virum eiusmodi, & contra cognationem eius, & excindam eum, & omnes qui scortantur post eum, ut scortentur post Moloch, e medio populi sui. At non potuit tanta esse tam seueri edicti auctoritas, quin vulgare esset nefandum hoc turpissimae lustrationis flagitium, ut ex Ieremiae oraculo, quod cap. 32. extat, facile liquet. Altera idololatriae species syderis cultu habuit, quod Deo Remphan (de quo nihil certi traditur) sacrum fuisse perhibet. Sunt qui Saturni sydus interpretentur, alij Remphan.
units.tr: Continuing in his recital of the sins of the Israelites, God now recalls what their descendants did once the land of Canaan was occupied. "You have taken up" (he says) "the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the figures which you made in order to worship them." He comprehends all idolatry under three kinds. The first was the worship of Moloch, who is known from the history of Solomon to have been the god of the Ammonites, and to whom he is said to have first built a temple. Moloch seems to have been a god of generation, in whose honour infants were consecrated by being passed through the fire, which Manasseh did when he made his son pass through the fire. God had decreed capital punishment for this impiety, which is contained in Leviticus 20 in these words: "Whoever of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel, shall give of his seed to Moloch, shall be put to death; the people of the land shall stone him with stones. And I will set my face against that man and will cut him off from the midst of his people, because he has given of his seed to Moloch, to defile my sanctuary and to profane my holy name. And if the people of the land shall at all hide their eyes from that man, who gives of his seed to Moloch, and do not kill him, I will set my face against that man and against his kindred, and will cut him off, and all who go whoring after him, to go whoring after Moloch, from the midst of his people." Yet the authority of so severe an edict could not prevent this unspeakable shame of most filthy purification from being widely known, as is easily made clear from the oracle of Jeremiah which stands in chapter 32. The second kind of idolatry had the worship of a star, which is said to have been sacred to the god Remphan (about whom nothing certain is handed down). Some interpret it as the star of Saturn, others as Mars.

units.la: Locus Amos 5. cap.
units.tr: The passage in Amos, chapter 5.

units.la: Cultus Moloch.
units.tr: The worship of Moloch.

units.la: Deus Remphan. uerem, quidam vero Martem fuisse existimant. Fuit autem apud omnes gentes admodum frequens syderum cultus, eò quòd mirabilis illorum motus, sp'endor item & forma illis diuini quiddam inesse simplicioribus facile persuaderet. Et huc referri debent scripturæ loci, in quibus militiam cœli adorauisse Iudæi dicuntur. Nobis vero obseruandum est, syderum cultum non adoratione modò & sacrificijs constare, quæ olim apud gentes in vsu fuêre: verumetiam ab ijs illa coli, qui rerum euentus, bella, pacem, famem, anni prouentum, morbos, tempestates, & si quæ alia sunt eius generis, ab illis pendere putant. Constat enim omnia hæc diuinæ prouidentiæ legibus gubernari, cuius iudicia non astris alligata sunt, sed verbi Dei & æternæ illius voluntatis regula diriguntur. Quicunque ergo ista astris tribuunt, deo honorem suum negant, & hominem quæ præstantissima dei creatura est, stellarum motibus subijciunt. Quare deploranda est nostri seculi cæcitas, quæ eòusque progressa est, vt maximarum rerum auspicia è stellis petantur, & inde vel felices rerum euentus pleriq; sperent, vel infelices & tristes metuant. Quin potius prophetam dicentem audimus: Viam gentium ne discatis, & à signis cœli ne formidetis. Nam gentes ab illis sibi metuunt. Ierem.10. Tertio loco figuras reprehendit, quas ipsi cultus gratia fecerint. Et mitiori vocabulo vtitur deus, vt non modo ea sibi improbari doceat, quæ notoria impietate in alienorum deorum cultu siunt, verùm ea quoq;, quibus ipsum honorare volunt homines. Quales sunt, qui dei operum, illius memoriâ imaginibus conseruare student, vel qui eas rudium & illiteratorum institutioni seruire clamant. Peccant hi, quia suopte ingenio & consilio in sidei & religionis causa instituunt, quod à deo nusquam traditum legitur. Beneficiorum suorum memoriam sacramentis paucis, ijsq; obseruatu facillimis, consecrauit. Institutioni nostræ verbum destinauit, & cùm ipse concionaretur, solam vocem audiri, imaginè verò nullam apparere voluit. Deut.4. Hîs ergo contenti, immoderatæ carnis sapientiæ frænum injiciamus, ne dum plus æquò sapere volumus, stulti reddamur, quemadmodum de gentium philosophis Paulus admonet. Rom.1.
units.tr: The god Remphan. Indeed, the worship of the stars was very common among all nations, because the wonderful motion of the stars, and likewise their brightness and form, easily persuaded simple people that something divine resided in them. And to this belong the passages of Scripture in which the Jews are said to have worshipped the host of heaven. For our part we must observe that the worship of the stars consists not only in adoration and sacrifices, which were once in use among the nations, but also in that they are worshipped by those who think that the outcomes of events, wars, peace, famine, the yield of the year, diseases, storms, and whatever else is of that kind, depend upon them. For it is certain that all these things are governed by the laws of divine providence, whose judgments are not bound to the stars but are directed by the rule of the Word of God and of that eternal will. Whoever therefore ascribes these things to the stars denies to God his honour, and subjects man, who is the most excellent creature of God, to the motions of the stars. Therefore the blindness of our age is to be deplored, which has advanced so far that the auspices of the greatest affairs are sought from the stars, and from them many hope for happy outcomes of affairs, or fear unhappy and sad ones. Rather, let us hear the prophet saying: "Do not learn the way of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of heaven; for the nations are afraid of them." Jeremiah 10. In the third place he reproves the figures which men made for the sake of worship. And God uses a milder word, so that he teaches that not only those things are disapproved by him which are done with notorious impiety in the worship of strange gods, but also those by which men wish to honour him itself. Such are those who strive to preserve the memory of God's works by images, or who cry out that they serve for the instruction of the unlearned and the illiterate. These err, because they institute on their own wit and counsel, in matters of faith and religion, what is nowhere read to have been handed down by God. He consecrated the memory of his benefits with a few sacraments, and those very easy to observe. He appointed the Word for our instruction, and when he himself preached, he wished only the voice to be heard, and no image to appear. Deuteronomy 4. Content with these, let us curb the unrestrained wisdom of the flesh, lest while we wish to be wiser than is right, we become foolish, as Paul warns concerning the philosophers of the nations. Romans 1.

units.la: Postremò incurabili & subinde in deterius ruenti impietati pœnâ minatur, dicens: Transferam vos vltra Babylonē. Amoz Damascum habet, vt decem tribubus inanem Syriaci fœderis fiduciam auferat. At Stephanus sensum potius respiciens, vltra Babylonè transferendos fuisse dicit. Id enim reuera factū esse constat. Nam Salmanazar Assyriorum tyrannus capta Samaria decem tribuum regnum euertit, & captiuos in Assyriam transtulit. Nec multò post Iudæâ grauissimè afflixit Sanherib. At quia Ezechia authore ad dominum conuersi idola deiecerant, è tyranni manu per angeli auxilium liberati sunt. Vbi verò sub Manasse ad vomitum reuersi, superstitiones nefandas, & idololatriam reduxerunt, nec reformationem, quam Josias cœperat, admiserunt, quin clancularium in ædibus superstitionem exercerent, vt ex Sophoniæ sermonibus colligitur, Nabuchodonozorem induxit Deus, qui vrbe excidit, templum exussit, & infelicis populi reliquias vltra Babylonè abductas per omnia Babylonicæ monarchiæ regna dispersit. Ita Deus incurabile idololatriâ & prophanū sui nominis contemptum vltus est. Idem postea euenijse legimus. Cùm enim è Babylone reuersi, templum & religionem omnem quæstum fecissent & speluncam latronū, nec Christum reformatorem admittere, nec apostolos audire vellent, Vespasianum & Titum reformatores adduxit Deus, qui vrbe & templo excisis, Iudæos superstites per omnes orbis terrarum prouincias dissiparunt. In horum consideratione nos hodie versari decebat. Inualuit inter Christianos infelix idololatriæ malum. Nec deest Moloch, qui inter Monachorum ordines delitescens, Christo per baptismum initiatos sibi vendicat & impiè vrit. Superstitiosa syderū obseruatione multi seducuntur. Prostant passim ad cultū & ad doctrinam factæ imagines. Reformationem iam annis aliquot per euangelij sui præconium Deus nequicquam flagitauit. Quare periculū est, ne excidium sentiant qui reformari nolunt, ne haētenus errauisse videantur. Nec vanus certè illorum metus est, qui Turcarum manibus hæc tolli oportere suspicantur. Constat enim propter imagines Orientis imperium ab Occidente diuisum esse, & ea diui sione Sarracenorū & Turcarū vires in immensum creuisse, vt nō obscurè deus innuisse videri possit, quos nam & quales idololatriæ extirpatores iam olim constituerit. Et experientia docet, quàm dira quotidie per Turcas in pertinaces imaginum cultores exempla Deus edat. Nec sine numine factum putemus, quòd Solimannus Turcarum Imperator non multùs ab hinc annis Buda Hungarorum superatum gum sede potitus, præcipuū illius vrbis templum, quod Virgini matri sacrū erat, confessim altarium & imaginū sordibus purgari voluit, priusquàm in eo pro victoria sibi concessa Deo optimo maximo gratias.
units.tr: Finally, he threatens punishment upon an incurable impiety which keeps rushing into worse, saying: "I will carry you away beyond Babylon." Amos has Damascus, so that he may take from the ten tribes their vain confidence in the Syrian covenant. But Stephen, looking rather to the sense, says that they were to be carried away beyond Babylon. For it is certain that this really happened. For Shalmaneser, tyrant of the Assyrians, after Samaria was taken, overthrew the kingdom of the ten tribes and carried the captives into Assyria. Not long after, Sennacherib afflicted Judah most grievously. But because, under the leadership of Hezekiah, they had turned to the Lord and cast down the idols, they were freed from the hand of the tyrant by the help of an angel. But when, under Manasseh, they returned to their vomit and brought back the accursed superstitions and idolatry, and did not admit the reformation which Josiah had begun, but even practised secret superstition in their houses, as is gathered from the sermons of Zephaniah, God brought in Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed the city, burned the temple, and scattered the remnants of the unhappy people, carried away beyond Babylon, through all the kingdoms of the Babylonian monarchy. Thus God avenged incurable idolatry and the profane contempt of his name. We read that the same thing happened later. For when they returned from Babylon and had made the temple and all religion a source of gain, and a den of robbers, and would admit neither Christ the reformer nor listen to the apostles, God brought Vespasian and Titus as reformers, who, with the city and the temple cut off, scattered the surviving Jews through all the provinces of the world. It behoved us today to dwell upon the consideration of these things. The unhappy evil of idolatry has prevailed among Christians. Nor is Moloch lacking, who, hiding among the orders of monks, claims for himself those initiated into Christ through baptism and burns them impiously. Many are led astray by superstitious observation of the stars. Images made for worship and doctrine stand everywhere. For some years now God has in vain demanded reformation through the proclamation of his gospel. Therefore there is danger lest those who refuse to be reformed feel destruction, lest they seem to have erred until now. Nor is the fear of those vain who suspect that these things must be removed by the hands of the Turks. For it is established that on account of images the empire of the East was divided from the West, and by that division the strength of the Saracens and Turks grew to an immense degree, so that God may seem not obscurely to have indicated whom and what kind of destroyers of idolatry he has already long ago appointed. And experience teaches how dire the examples are which God daily gives through the Turks against the obstinate worshippers of images. Nor let us think it done without the divine will, that Suleiman, emperor of the Turks, not many years ago, after taking possession of Buda, the seat of the Hungarians, wished the chief temple of that city, which was sacred to the Virgin Mother, at once to be cleansed of altars and the filth of images, before he gave thanks to God most good and great in it for the victory granted to him.

units.la: Vide Paulum Iouium bist. sui temporis libro 40. gratias ageret. Eo enim facto deus aperte testari voluit, idololatriam, quae sub Christi & sanctorum ipsius praetextu exercetur, potissimam Turcicarum cladium causam esse. Quare expergisci nos tandem tempus iubet, & abiectis vanissimis hominum adinuentionibus deum patrem secundum ipsius praescriptum in veritate & spiritu adorare per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: See Paulus Jovius, in the fortieth book of his history of his own times. For by this deed God wished to testify plainly that the idolatry which is practised under the pretext of Christ and his saints is the chief cause of the Turkish defeats. Therefore he bids us at last to awake, and, having cast aside the most vain inventions of men, to worship God the Father according to his prescription, in truth and in spirit, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LIII.

units.la: Tabernaculum testimonij fuit patribus nostris in deserto, quemadmodum ordinauerat is, qui cum Mose loquebatur, vt faceret illud secundum formam quam viderat. Quod etiam qui successerunt patres nostri, induxerunt cum Iesu in possessionem gentium, quas expulit deus a facie patrum nostrorum, vsque ad dies Dauid: qui inuenit gratiam coram deo, & petijt, vt inueniret habitaculum deo Iacobi. Solomon autem aedificauit illi domum. Sed altissimus ille non in manufactis templis habitat, quemadmodum propheta dicit: Coelum mihi sedes est, terra vero scabellum pedum meorum. Qualem domum aedificabitis mihi? dicit dominus: aut quis locus requietionis meae? An non manus mea fecit haec omnia?
units.tr: Our fathers had the tabernacle of testimony in the wilderness, just as he ordained who spoke with Moses, that Moses should make it according to the pattern he had seen. Our fathers who came after them also brought it in with Joshua into the possession of the nations whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, until the days of David. David found grace before God and asked that he might find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But Solomon built him a house. Yet the Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says: Heaven is my throne and earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me? says the Lord. Or what is the place of my rest? Did not my hand make all these things?

units.la: ACcusationis contra Stephanum instituta duo praecipua capita fuerunt: alterum, quod legem abrogare conetur: alterum vero, quod in templum adeoque omnem cultum externum blasphemus fuerit. Ad primum hucusque respondit, diligenter simul & magnifice de lege & huius ministro, Mose differens. Ostendit enim diuinitus per Mosem datam esse, & verbum vivificum esse fatetur, eo quod feliciter viuendi regulam comprehendit, & paedagogi instar Christo adducit. Simul vero, quia illi patrum titulo potissimum gloriabantur, illos semper inobedientes fuisse docuit, vt ipsos non legalis iustitiae merito, sed diuinae gratiae beneficio seruatos esse constaret. His vero absolutis, ad alterum accusationis caput transitum faciens, de loco sancto siue templo disputat, in quo praecipuam salutis spem repositam habebant. Omnium vero, quae a Stephano dicuntur, finis est, vt euincat, deum & cultum dei nequaquam templo alligatum esse. Unde sequitur, non statim blasphemos & in deum contumeliosos censeri debere, qui de huius abrogatione differunt. Primo autem de tabernaculo, deinde de templo post annos circiter quadringentos & octuaginta ab exitu Aegypti extructo agit.
units.tr: Two main heads were brought in the accusation against Stephen. The first was that he tried to abolish the law. The second was that he blasphemed the temple and therefore all external worship. To the first he has so far replied, speaking carefully and with honour both of the law and of its minister, Moses. He shows that the law was given by God through Moses, and he acknowledges that it is a living word, because it contains the rule of living well and leads to Christ like a schoolmaster. At the same time, since the Jews especially boasted in the title of "fathers," he taught that those fathers were always disobedient, so that it is plain they were saved not by the merit of legal righteousness but by the benefit of divine grace. Having finished this, he turns to the second head of the accusation and discusses the holy place, or temple, in which they had placed their chief hope of salvation. The aim of everything Stephen says is to prove that God and the worship of God are in no way tied to the temple. It follows that those who discuss its abolition should not at once be judged blasphemers and insulters of God. He speaks first of the tabernacle, and then of the temple built about four hundred and eighty years after the exodus from Egypt.

units.la: Fuit tabernaculum locus sacris destinatus, tabulis cedrinis & cortinis maxima ex parte constans, quarum illae circulis aureis & per hos traiectis vectibus, hae vero fibulis & ansulis connectebantur. In hoc erant arca foederis, mensa aurea, candelabrum, ara thymiamatis, altare holocaustorum, labrum aeneum, vna cum reliquis instrumentis ad sacra pertinentibus: de quibus vide Exod. 25.26.27.30. &c. Haec omnia patres in deserto ex Moysis qui dei interpres erat, traditione habuisse, ingenue fatetur. Et testimonij tabernaculum vocat, eo quod per hoc deus suam praesentiam testaretur, & ibi in rebus dubijs responsa daret. Tria vero addit, quibus probat, cultum dei deumque ipsum minime loco isti alligatum fuisse. Primo secundum formam siue exemplar, quod Moysi in monte exhibitum erat, illud extructum fuisse dicit. Unde constat typicum fuisse, & caelestium rerum mysteria adumbrasse: quod Paulus quoque ad Hebraeos cap. 8. & 9. annotauit. Figurabat enim scena haec Ecclesiam, quam vnam esse vult deus, licet ex variis ijsque diuersis hominum ordinibus constet. Habet enim doctores, qui columnarum instar sunt, quales Paulus Iacobum, Petrum & Iohannem vocat. Gal. 2. Habet tabulas cedrinas & deauratas, quibus singuli fideles significantur, quos fides incorruptos simul & caelesti fulgore illustres reddit. Coniunguntur omnes isti tum doctrinae, tum fidei & charitatis vinculo, & Christo innituntur, qui totius ecclesiae vnica basis & fundamentum est. Idem in hac arca est, veros caelestium mysteriorum thesaurus continens. Idem mensam nobis instruit, e qua aeternae vitae panem petamus. Idem ille candelabri locum tenet, & ecclesiam sui verbi lumine illustrat. In hoc etiam oblatae preces grati thymiamatis instar sunt apud deum patrem. Et hic altare verum est, in quo nos ipsos et totam vitae conversationem Deo immolari oportet. Poterant
units.tr: The tabernacle was a place set apart for sacred use, made for the most part of cedar boards and curtains. The boards were joined by golden rings through which bars were passed, and the curtains by clasps and loops. In it were the ark of the covenant, the golden table, the lampstand, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offerings, and the bronze laver, together with the other instruments belonging to the sacred service. On these see Exod. 25, 26, 27, 30, and so on. Stephen openly confesses that the fathers in the wilderness had all these things by tradition from Moses, who was God's interpreter. He calls it the tabernacle of testimony because through it God bore witness to his presence and gave answers in doubtful matters there. He adds three things by which he proves that worship and God himself were by no means bound to that place. First, he says it was built according to the form or pattern that had been shown to Moses on the mountain. From this it is plain that it was typical and shadowed the mysteries of heavenly things, which Paul also noted in Hebrews 8 and 9. For this scene (the tabernacle) was a figure of the Church, which God wills to be one, although it consists of various and different orders of men. It has teachers, who are like pillars, such as Paul calls James, Peter and John (Gal. 2). It has boards of cedar and gold, by which individual believers are signified, whom faith makes incorruptible and at the same time bright with heavenly splendour. All of these are joined together by the bond of teaching, of faith and of love, and they rest upon Christ, who is the sole base and foundation of the whole Church. In this ark too is the true treasure of heavenly mysteries. The same tabernacle furnishes us with a table, from which we may seek the bread of eternal life. The same figure holds the place of the lampstand and lights the Church with the light of his Word. In it the prayers offered are, before God the Father, like a pleasing incense. And here is the true altar, on which we ourselves and the whole course of our life ought to be offered up to God. They could

units.la: 1. Tabernaculo non fuit alligatus cultus Dei.
units.tr: 1. The worship of God was not bound to the tabernacle.

units.la: Tabernaculum typus fuit caelestium rerum.
units.tr: The tabernacle was a type of heavenly things.

units.la: Templorum aliquando culpa fuit. hæc copiosius tractari, sed summa rerum capita adumbramus, vt cuius pateat, cur Stephanus tabernaculum ad cœleste exemplar extructum fuisse dicat: vt nimirum hinc intelligamus, neminem olim tabernaculo inhærere, sed per fidem in Christi & ecclesiæ ipsius consyderatione versari debuisse, cuius mysteria per hoc adumbrabantur. Nam veteres quoq; tunc demum Deo placuisse, quando animis in cœlum sublatis, illum in spiritu & veritate adorabant. Iohan.4. Et multi extant scripturæ loci, in quibus grauissimè increpantur, qui externis ceremonijs occupati, spiritualem cultum negligebant. Vide Psalm.50. Isa.143. Mich.6. Ierem.7. &c. Interim admonemur, nihil in cultu Dei & religione ex hominum placito statui debere. Si enim olim, quando plurimus externorum vsus erat, formam diuinitus præscriptam Moses observare debuit, & horrenda in illos exempla extant, qui aliquid secus agere ausi sunt: maiori utiq; diligentia nobis hodie opus est in ijs observandis, quae filius Dei in ecclesia perpetua esse vult, donec nouissimi aduentus ipsius tempore in cœlestia tabernaculacum illo transferamur.
units.tr: Sometimes the fault lay with the temples. These things are treated more fully elsewhere, but we sketch the main heads, so that it may be clear why Stephen says the tabernacle was built according to a heavenly pattern. Namely, we may understand from this that no one in former times ought to have clung to the tabernacle, but should have dwelt by faith in the contemplation of Christ and of his Church, whose mysteries were shadowed by it. For the ancients too pleased God only when, with their minds lifted up to heaven, they worshipped him in spirit and in truth (John 4). And there are many passages of Scripture in which those are most severely rebuked who, occupied with external ceremonies, neglected spiritual worship. See Ps. 50, Isa. 143, Mic. 6, Jer. 7, and so on. At the same time we are warned that nothing in the worship and religion of God ought to be established by human decision. For if formerly, when the use of external things was very great, Moses had to observe the form prescribed by God, and there are dreadful examples of those who dared to act otherwise, then surely we today need much greater diligence in observing those things which the Son of God wills to be perpetual in the Church, until at the time of his last coming we are transferred to the heavenly tabernacle with him.

units.la: Secundò tabernaculum à patribus duce Iosua in possessionem gentium, id est, in terram prophanam translatum fuisse, dicit. Vnde rursum patet, cultum Dei & salutis rationem illi non potuisse alligari. Hic verò obiter docemur, dei instituta sancta, non pollui ex loco, modò vsus verus & legitimus obseruetur. Vbiq; enim præsens est Deus, & sua præsentia tum ipsos cultores suos, tum absque traditos ritus sanctificat. Ideo in prophana terra, cuius incolæ paulò ante idolorum cultores fuerant, tabernaculum collocari et totus ille cultus exerceri potuit. Quod de externis ritibus dicitur, idipsum de precibus intelligi debet: quæ si ex fide promanent, deo gratæ & acceptæ erunt, quocunq; tandem in loco fundantur. Iohan.4. Ita Ionam in ventre ceti orantem exaudiuit Deus, & Danielis socij ex fornace clamantes Deum liberatorem senserunt, nec leonum rugitus obstare potuit, quo minus Danielis preces in domini conspectum ascenderent.
units.tr: Second, he says that the tabernacle was carried by the fathers under the leadership of Joshua into the possession of the nations, that is, into a profane land. Here again it is plain that the worship of God and the way of salvation could not be tied to it. Here we are also taught in passing that God's holy institutions are not polluted by the place, provided the use is true and lawful. For God is present everywhere, and by his presence he sanctifies both his worshippers and the rites handed down to them. So the tabernacle could be set up in a profane land, whose inhabitants had shortly before been worshippers of idols, and the whole worship could be carried on there. What is said of external rites must also be understood of prayers. If they come forth from faith, they will be pleasing and acceptable to God, wherever they are poured out. John 4. Thus God heard Jonah praying in the belly of the whale, and the companions of Daniel, crying out from the furnace, felt God as their deliverer. Nor could the roaring of lions prevent Daniel's prayers from ascending into the sight of the Lord.

units.la: Addit ur his alterum argumentum à loco desumptum, quo dei cultum tabernaculo minime alligatum fuisse probat. Nam incertis sedibus illud per annos quadringentos hinc inde translatum fuisse dicit, vsq; ad Dauidis tempora, qui primus hoc singularis beneficij loco à deo accepit, vt ipsi per angelum locus certus, in quo templum extrui deberet, revelaretur: quod illum ardentissimis precibus impetrauisse legimus, cum ait: Male sit mihi, si tabernaculum domus meæ subiero, si conscendero sponsam lecti mei, si concessero oculis meis somnum, & palpebris meis dormitionem: Donec inueniam locum domino, & habitacula potenti deo Iacob, &c. Psal.132. Historiam vide 2. Samuel. 24. Item. 1. Paral.21. Ante illa vero tempora variam fuisse tabernaculi sedem scriptura non obscure docet. Primò enim in Silo collocatum fuit, vbi vsq; ad Heli tempora hæsisse videtur. Iof.18.1. Sam.1. &c. Regnante Saule, in Gilgal, deinde etiam in Nobe, sacerdotali vrbe sedem habuit. 1. Sam.11. & 20. Sub Dauide autem in Gabaon constitit: 1. Paral. 21. Tandem omnia quæ ad hoc pertinebant, à Solomone, vt thesaurus aliquis, in templum recondita fuere. Quis verò sanæ mentis tabernaculo dei cultum & salutis rationem alligatam fuisse dicet, cum ipsum certam sedem nunquam habuerit? Est autem obseruatione dignum, quòd singulari diuinæ gratiæ beneficio hoc Dauidi obrigisse dicitur, vt certum locum cognosceret, in quo deus cultum suum vsq; ad tempus correctionis peragi volebat. Faciebat hoc ad regni confirmationem & stabilitatem, quod non obscure Ieroboam obseruauit, qui regnum suum sine certa religionis sede infirmum & instabile fore videbat. 1. Reg.12. Interim admonemur, præcipuum hoc in terris dei donum esse, si externa religio firmiter constituta sit, & hanc tutò homines exercere possint. Est hoc firmissimum ecclesiasticæ vnitatis conseruandæ vinculum, & inæstimabile diuini fauoris argumentum. Agnoscunt hoc & anxiè desyderant, qui sub tyrannis ecclesiæ persecutoribus agunt. Agnoscamus & nos, qui ocio & pace abundamus, ne enormi ingratitudine dei iram prouocemus, & in arumnis constituti intelligamus, quantum illud bonum sit, quod nunc pleriq; nihili facere confuerunt.
units.tr: He adds a second argument taken from place, by which he proves that the worship of God was by no means tied to the tabernacle. For he says that for four hundred years it was carried hither and thither to uncertain seats, right up to the time of David, who first received from God this singular benefit, that a certain place, where a temple ought to be built, should be revealed to him through an angel. We read that he obtained this with most ardent prayers when he said: "I will not go into the tent of my house, nor climb into my bed, nor give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the Mighty God of Jacob," etc. (Ps. 132). See the history in 2 Sam. 24 and 1 Chron. 21. Before those times, Scripture plainly teaches that the seat of the tabernacle varied. First it was placed at Shiloh, where it seems to have stayed until the time of Eli (Josh. 18; 1 Sam. 1, etc.). In the reign of Saul it was at Gilgal, and then also at Nob, a priestly city, where it had its seat (1 Sam. 11 and 20). Under David it stood at Gibeon (1 Chron. 21). Finally, all the things that belonged to it were placed by Solomon in the temple, as a treasure is stored away. But who of sound mind would say that the worship of God and the way of salvation were bound to a tabernacle that never had a fixed seat? It is worth noting that this was granted to David as a singular benefit of divine grace, that he should know the certain place where God willed his worship to be carried on until the time of correction. This served the confirmation and stability of the kingdom, which Jeroboam clearly observed, since he saw that his kingdom would be weak and unstable without a fixed seat of religion (1 Kings 12). At the same time we are warned that it is a chief gift of God on earth when external religion is firmly established and men can safely practise it. This is the most firm bond for keeping ecclesiastical unity, and an inestimable proof of divine favour. Those who live under tyrants and persecutors of the Church recognise this and long for it anxiously. Let us also recognise it, we who abound in leisure and peace, lest by enormous ingratitude we provoke the anger of God; and let us, placed in troubles, understand how great a good that is which many now are accustomed to regard as worth nothing.

units.la: Expositis autem ijs, quæ ad tabernaculum spectabant, de templo quoq; disserit, quod in huius locum successerat, & cuius idem omninò erat vsus. Illud, cum nondum certo constituto religionis loco nullum fuisset, à Solomone extructum fuisse, scriptura tradit. 1. Reg.6. At quia huius locum diuina reuelatione Dauid cognouerat, non inepte facere videbantur Iudæi, quòd illi cultum alligatum esse putarent. Quare illorum stoliditatem grauiter arguit Stephanus. Nam vt templum ex dei mandato datorextruƈtum fuisse concediti: ita mox subijcit: Sed altissimus ille non in manufactis templis habi-tat. Et ne temeritatis accusaretur, dei verba, apud Isaiam cap.66. in hunc modum loquentis produ-cit: Cœlum mihi sedes est, terra vero scabellum pedum meorum. Qualem domum ædificabitis mihi? dicit dominus. Aut quis locus requietionis meæ? Annon manus mea fecit hæc omnia? Argumen-tu ex natura sua sumptis probat se nec loco certo concludi, nec externis hisce, quæ ab hominibus fiunt, indigere: Quia enim immensus & infinitus est, quemá cæli cælorum non capiunt (sicuti ipse So-lomon fatetur. 1. Reg. 8.) Ieum domo aliqua contineri impossibile est. Rursum, qui omnium creator est & dominus, nostris officijs indigere non potest, quem admodum pluribus docet Psal. 50. Ista vero consolationi simul & institutioni seruiunt. Quia enim vbiq; præsens est deus, vbiq; etiam à nobis coli poterit, vt nec sumptibus immodicis, nec superuacaneis laboribus nos vexari opus sit. Et quia no-stris non indiget, externis hisce vera cultus ratio & illius gratia non potest esse alligata. Turpis ergo & fœdus hypocritarum error est, qui dum illa peregerunt, se omni erga deum officio defunctos esse putant. Quapropter quis verus & legitimus externorum omnium vsus sit, nos potius obseruare conuenit. Possunt hæc tempore, loco, & ceremonijs comprehendi. Tempus & locus ordini seruiunt. Nam vt dies certos religionis officijs consecrari oportet, ita hæc ipsa absq; loco certo peragi non pos-sunt. Sed vt dierum obseruationi non alligatur salus, ita nec locorum spacijs. Habent tamen hæc suum in religione vsum. Nam cœtibus sacris seruiunt, quos propter verbi sui prædicationem, publi-cas preces & sacramentorum administrationem crebro conuenire prodest. Et quia istis studijs tem-pla consecrata sunt, illa ab omni prophano vsu separata esse conuenit, ne de diuinis parum honorificè sentire videamur. Quæ causa est, quòd templi extructionem tantopere Haggeus propheta vrget. Interim abest luxuriosa superstitio, quæ immodicam loci obseruationem in hominum animis exci-tare solet. Ceremoniarum vero diuinitus traditarum (nam de humanis constitutionibus nullus hic nobis sermo est) quæ recepto vocabulo Sacramenta dicuntur, vsus est, quòd dei beneficia obsignant, & proinde animos per fidei contemplationem in cœlos subuehunt, nosq; nostri cum erga Deum, tum erga fratres officij admonent. Hæc nos obseruare & isdem contentos esse conuenit: ne dum externis occupati, vetesto Iudæorum errore inuoluimur, cœlestiŭ bonorum iacturam faciamus. Colamus ergo in spiritu & veritate deum patrem, qui quæ olim patribus templi & ceremoniarum typis figurauit, nobis vere & plenè exhibuit in filio suo & vnico Sacerdote nostro Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedi-ctio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Having set out the things that pertained to the tabernacle, he also discusses the temple, which succeeded to its place and had entirely the same use. Scripture relates that it was built by Solomon, at a time when no fixed place for religion had yet been established. 1. Reg.6. But since David had learned the place of it by divine revelation, the Jews did not seem unreasonable in thinking that worship was bound to it. Therefore Stephen strongly charges them with their stupidity. For although it is granted that the temple was built by God's command, he immediately adds: "But the Most High does not dwell in temples made by hands." And lest he be accused of rashness, he brings forward the words of God, speaking in this manner in Isaiah chap. 66: "Heaven is my seat, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What kind of house will you build for me? says the Lord. Or what place is there for my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?" By an argument drawn from God's own nature, he proves that he is neither confined to a certain place nor in need of these external things that are made by men. For since he is immeasurable and infinite, whom the heavens of heavens cannot contain (as Solomon himself confesses, 1. Reg. 8.), it is impossible for him to be contained by any house. Again, he who is the creator and lord of all cannot need our services, as he teaches at greater length in Psal. 50. These things serve at once for consolation and for instruction. For since God is present everywhere, he can be worshipped by us everywhere too, so that we need not be troubled either by immoderate expense or by superfluous labours. And since he does not need our things, the true manner of worship and his grace cannot be bound to these external things. Therefore the error of hypocrites is base and foul, who, when they have performed those things, think they have discharged every duty towards God. Wherefore it is rather fitting for us to observe what the true and lawful use of all external things is. These can be comprehended under time, place and ceremonies. Time and place serve order. For just as certain days ought to be consecrated to the duties of religion, so these things cannot be carried out without a fixed place. But just as salvation is not bound to the observance of days, so neither is it bound to the extent of places. Nevertheless these have their use in religion. For they serve the sacred assemblies, which it is profitable to gather together often for the preaching of God's Word, public prayers and the administration of the sacraments. And because temples have been consecrated for these pursuits, it is fitting that they be separated from every profane use, lest we seem to think meanly of divine things. This is the reason why the prophet Haggai urges so strongly the building of the temple. Meanwhile, the luxurious superstition, which is wont to stir up immoderate reverence for a place in men's minds, is absent. As for the use of the ceremonies handed down by God (for we are not speaking here of human constitutions), which are called by the received name sacraments, they seal God's benefits, and therefore lift up our minds to heaven through the contemplation of faith, and remind us of our duty both towards God and towards our brothers. We ought to observe these and be content with them, lest, while we are occupied with external things, we become entangled in the old error of the Jews and suffer the loss of heavenly goods. Let us therefore worship God the Father in spirit and truth, who has truly and fully shown to us in his Son, our only Priest, Jesus Christ, what he once figured to the fathers by the types of the temple and the ceremonies: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 54.

units.la: Duri ceruice & incircuncifi corde & auribus: Vos semper spiritui sancto resistitis. Sicut patres vestri, ita & vos. Quem prophetarum non persecuti sunt patres vestri? & occiderunt eos, qui prænuntiarunt de aduentu Iusti illius: cuius vos nunc proditores & occisores facti estis. Qui accepistis legem per dispositiones angelorum, nec seruastis. Porrò hæc audientes, dissecabantur cordibus suis, & stridebant dentibus suis in ipsum.
units.tr: "Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of that Just One, whom you have now become the betrayers and murderers. You who received the law through the dispositions of angels, and did not keep it." And hearing these things, they were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at him.

units.la: REspondit hucusq; ad obiecta sibi crimina Diuus Stephanus, & prolixa narratione demonstra-uit, se nec in Deum, nec in legem Dei, nec item in templū vnquam consumeliosum fuisse. Nam ab ipso Abrahamo exorsus, se veri illius & vnici dei cultore esse testatur, qui patribus sese olim re-uelare ijsq; gratiam suam offerre dignatus fit. Deinde de Mose & lege splendidè disseruit, & in hac Christum non obscurè patribus promissum fuisse docuit. Tandem de templo & externo cultu agens, bis nec dei gratiam, nec verum cultum, nec item salutis humanæ rationem alligari, fortissimis argu-mentis euicit. AT quia nec ipse Stephanus ignorare poterat, quales causæ suæ Iudices haberet: nec illi animorum suorum rabiem diutius dissimulabant, sicuti quiuis ex circunstantijs facilè colliget, graui & vehementi increpatione in illos inuehens, orationi finem imponit. Vbi hunc finem Stephano propositum fuisse patet, quòd ecclesiæ titulo superbè turgentibus et potestate sua turpiter abutentibus laruam hanc detrahere conatur, ne diutius hoc fuco rudes & imperitos terreant. Est hoc factū perquàm necessarium, quando cum ijs nobis rem esse videmus, apud quos verbi doctrina nihil prosi-citur. Et sanè nostro seculo non aliud veritati magis officit quàm quòd eos hostes habet, qui ecclesiæ titulum & gubernacula sibi iam annis aliquot vendicarunt. Quare necesse erit, ut hodie quoq; Stephani exemplum sibi imitandum proponant, quibus ecclesiarum cura commissa est. Sed ut ad præsentis loci tractationem accedamus, tria præcipuè erant, quæ illos insolentiores faciebant: Circun-cisio nimirum, Patrum gloria & dignitas, Lex item, quæ illis peculiari quodam dei beneficio obti-gerat. De omnibus verò hisce sic loquitur divinus Christi martyr, ut perspicuè doceat, vanam esse omnem ipsorum fiduciam, quam in his collocatam habebant.
units.tr: Up to this point Saint Stephen has answered the charges brought against him, and by a lengthy narrative he has shown that he never spoke insultingly against God, nor against the law of God, nor likewise against the temple. For beginning with Abraham himself, he testifies that he is a worshipper of that true and only God, who deigned to reveal himself to the fathers of old and to offer them his grace. Then he spoke splendidly about Moses and the law, and in it he taught that Christ had been promised to the fathers, not obscurely. Finally, dealing with the temple and external worship, he proved by the strongest arguments that neither the grace of God, nor true worship, nor the way of human salvation is bound to these things. But since Stephen himself could not fail to know what sort of judges his case had, and since they no longer concealed the rage of their minds, as anyone may easily gather from the circumstances, he brought his speech to an end with a severe and vehement rebuke aimed at them. It is clear that Stephen intended this ending, because he tries to tear off this mask from those who swell proudly with the title of the Church and shamefully abuse their power, so that they may no longer frighten the crude and unlearned with this paint. This is very necessary when we see ourselves dealing with those among whom the teaching of the Word makes no progress. And indeed in our own age nothing hinders the truth more than that it has as enemies those who for some years now have claimed for themselves the title and the helm of the Church. Therefore it will be necessary that today also those to whom the care of the churches has been entrusted should set before themselves the example of Stephen to imitate. But to come to the matter at hand, there were three things especially that made those men more insolent: namely circumcision, the glory and dignity of the fathers, and also the law, which had been granted to them by a peculiar benefit of God. Now the divine martyr of Christ speaks of all these things in such a way as to teach clearly that all their confidence, which they had placed in these things, is empty.

units.la: A Circuncisione autem exorsus, ipsos hac frustra gloriari monet, quando illos duræ ceruicis homines & tam corde quàm auribus incircuncisos vocat. Videtur autem ad Mosis & Dei verba, quæ Deut. 10. & Ierem. 4. extant respicere, quasi dicat: Scio vos in circuncisione non exiguam salutis fi-duciam repositam habere: sed hæc vanissima est, quando spiritualis circuncisio à vobis negligitur. Voluit quidem Deus vos externo symbolo fœdus suum profiteri: sed idem vos corda gladio spiritus circuncidere, & ceruices nimium antehac intractabiles obedientiæ iugo submittere iussit. At nihil horum à vobis factum esse res ipsa loquitur. Indesinenter enim spiritui sancto, per scripturas & prophetas vobis loquenti resistitis. Ita verò Stephanus non vulgaris tantùm inobedientiæ, verumetiam atrocis perfidiæ ipsos accusat, ut qui circuncisione, quæ fœderis diuini symbolum erat, deo turpiter ludere conentur. Admonet autem locus hic, nihil externis symbolis iuuari homines, nisi ijs studeant, quæ per hæc adumbrantur. Quia enim spiritus est Deus, non inanibus ceremonijs, sed spiritu & veritate coli vult. Has verò propter nos instituit, ut animos in fidei contemplationem abreptos, officij admoneant. Quòd si à nobis negligatur, perfidiam nostram symbola arguunt, non excusant. Quæ cau-sa est, quòd immodicos externorum ritùum obseruatores tanta fœueritate prophetæ accusant, & spi-ritualis cultus curam ijsdem anxiè commendant. Idem nostræ quoq; institutioni feruit, ne Baptismo & Cænæ intenti, fidem in Christum, innocentiæ & charitatis studium negligamus, sine quibus Chri-stiana religio consistere nequit. At si frigida ritùum diuinitus traditorum obseruatio saluare nequit, quid de humanarum traditionum obseruatoribus dicemus, quas diuinæ sententiæ gladio (ut alibi quoque monuimus) iam olim iugulatas esse constat? Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Docemur præterea, quales Dei iudicio censeantur, qui verbo Dei per homines prædicato improbè resistunt, quod Iudæos fecisse constat. Hos enim Stephanus, non prophetis, sed spiritui sancto resistisse dicit. Nec temere hoc dictum illi excidisse putabimus. Quia enim spiritu sancto authore ministri loquuntur, & idem hominum animis sese insinuans, obedientiam suadet, & frequentes de vita emendanda cogitationes sug-gerit, reuera spiritui resistunt, quicunq; verbo parere recusant. Et hoc quidem infallibile incircuncisorum cordium & indurataë ceruicis hominum argumentum est. Habes ergo, unde nostri seculi homines æstimes, qui eo sibi mirificè placent, quòd ministrorum verbi sermones audacter contemnere, & scurriliter insectari audeant.
units.tr: Beginning with circumcision, he warns them that they boast of it in vain, when he calls them men stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart as well as in ears. Now he seems to be looking to the words of Moses and of God, which are found in Deut. 10 and Jer. 4, as if he were saying: I know that you have placed no small hope of salvation in circumcision; but this hope is most vain when spiritual circumcision is neglected by you. God indeed willed that you should profess his covenant by an outward sign; but he also commanded you to circumcise your hearts with the sword of the Spirit, and to submit your necks, too stubborn until now, to the yoke of obedience. But the thing itself shows that none of this has been done by you. For you continually resist the Holy Spirit, who speaks to you through the Scriptures and the prophets. Stephen accuses them not merely of ordinary disobedience but of atrocious faithlessness, in that they try shamefully to mock God with circumcision, which was the sign of the divine covenant. This passage also teaches that men gain nothing from outward signs unless they strive for those things which these signs foreshadow. For since God is Spirit, he wishes to be worshipped not with empty ceremonies but in spirit and truth. He instituted these signs for our sake, so that they might remind us of our duty, when our minds have been carried away into the contemplation of faith. But if they are neglected by us, the signs accuse our faithlessness; they do not excuse it. This is why the prophets so severely accuse those who keep outward rites immoderately, and earnestly commend to them spiritual worship. The same applies to our own instruction, so that, being intent on Baptism and the Lord's Supper, we do not neglect faith in Christ and the pursuit of innocence and charity, without which the Christian religion cannot stand. But if the cold observance of rites handed down by God cannot save, what shall we say of the observers of human traditions, which, as we have also noted elsewhere, were long ago slain by the sword of the divine sentence? Isa. 29; Matth. 15. We are further taught what sort of people are judged by God: those who stubbornly resist the Word of God preached through men, which the Jews are known to have done. For Stephen says that these men resisted not the prophets but the Holy Spirit. Nor shall we think this was said by him carelessly. For since the ministers speak with the Holy Spirit as their author, and the same Spirit, insinuating himself into human minds, urges obedience and suggests frequent thoughts of amending life, those who refuse to obey the Word truly resist the Spirit. And this is indeed an infallible sign of uncircumcised hearts and of men with hardened necks. You have, therefore, a means of judging the men of our age, who take such delight in themselves because they dare to scorn boldly and to attack with buffoonery the sermons of the ministers of the Word.

units.la: Sed ad Stephanum redeamus, qui eam, quæ ex maiorum dignitate ab ipsis quærebatur, gloriam similì ratione euertit. Iudæos enim his quàm maximè confisos fuisse, vel ex eo constat, quòd Baptista & ipsi Christo, de vitæ emendatione cum ipsis agentibus, Abrahamum patrem & generis sui præro-gatiuam obijcere audent. Matth. 3. Iohan. 8. At inter illorum maiores discrimen facit Stephanus. Erant in his boni aliquot & eximij dei cultores, Abraham nimirum, Isaac, Iacob & horum similes: quibus ipsi gloriari non poterant, cum horū essent dissimillimi, utpote degeneres & spurij filij. Rur-sum verò alij erant, impietate & sanguinaria aduersus prophetas tyrannide infames. Iis ipsos si-miles esse dicit, eò quòd illorum ingenium & mores egregie referrent, imò etiam superarent. Sicut patres vestri: ita & vos. Quem prophetarum non sunt persecuti patres vestri? & occiderunt eos, qui prænuntiarunt de aduentu Iusti illius. Ita verò Christū Iesum vocat, qui & ipse absolutè iustus est, in cuius ore dolus inueniri non potuit (Isa. 53.) & nobis iustitia à deo patre factus est. 1. Corinth. 1. Quare apud Ieremiam ipsi nomen inditur, Dominus iustitia nostra. Ierem. 23. Porrò ut huius prænuntios, prophetas, patres vestri occiderunt, quemadmodum monumenta in illorum bonorem vbiq; extantia restantur: ita vos ipsum Christum prodidistis Romano præsidi, & eundem immanibus au-sis diro crucis supplicio sustulistis. Patrum ergo mensuram non impleuistis modò, sed longè supera-nistis. misti. V T vero non sine arcano spiritus sanctimotu hæc à Stephano dicta sunt, ita non sine numine factum putabimus, quòd eadem scriptis mandata & ad posteritatem transmissa sunt. Docent enim, vt cum illis agi debeat, qui maiorum virtutibus & legitimæ successionis titulo gloriantur, & temere sibi vendicata potestate rudibus imponunt. Quo in numero Romanos Pontifices hodie videmus, qui cum apostolorum doctrinam ferro & igne persequantur, corruptissimæ vitæ exemplo vniuersum terrarum orbem inficiant, sacra omnia sibi quæstum faciant, adhuc tamen se Christi vicarios, Petri & Pauli successores esse venditant, & Romanam ecclesiam errare posse constantissimè negant. Et horum quidem artibus aliquot seculis orbem circumuentum esse constat. Detrahenda ergo est illis larua hæc, nec permittere debent fideles ecclesiæ ministri, vt Cumanus ille asinus asciti tio leoninæ prætextu simplices hominum conscientias terrere pergat. Nec hic audiendi sunt, qui hæc vel taceri volunt, vel modestiæ & mansuetudinis leges præscribunt. Vbi enim Christi gloria oppugnatur, & animarum salus periclitatur, nullas ignauiæ aut mansuetudini locus superest. Vidit hoc Christus, quo cum nemo opinor mansuetudinis aut modestiæ certamen facilè susceperit. Idem vero summa seueritate potius quàm ignaua aut præpostera lenitate, falsos antistites oppugnandos esse putauit. Cuius exemplum tum Stephanus, tum reliqui Apostoli rectissimè imitati sunt. Priusquam ve rò hinc discedamus, obiter notabis, prophetas Christi prænuntios fuisse. Fatetur hoc ipse Christus, Luc. 24. cap. Et Petrus hoc ipsum illis tribuit. 1. Pet. 1. cap. Facit hoc ad fidei nostræ dignitatem & certitudinem, ne illam vel nuper inuentam, vel incertam pauculorum hominum persuasionem esse putemus.
units.tr: But let us return to Stephen, who overthrew in a similar way the glory that they sought from the dignity of their ancestors. For it is clear that the Jews relied greatly on this, since when John the Baptist and Christ himself dealt with them about amending their lives, they dared to set against them Abraham their father and the privilege of their race. Matth. 3; John 8. But Stephen makes a distinction among their ancestors. Among them there were some good and outstanding worshippers of God, namely Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and men like them; in these they could not boast, since they were most unlike them, being degenerate and spurious sons. On the other hand there were others, infamous for impiety and for bloody tyranny against the prophets. He says that they are like these, because they strikingly resembled them in disposition and manners, and even surpassed them. As your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of that Just One. Now he calls Christ Jesus "the Just One", who is himself absolutely just, in whose mouth no deceit could be found (Isa. 53), and who was made for us righteousness by God the Father, 1 Cor. 1. Therefore in Jeremiah he is given the name: The Lord our righteousness, Jer. 23. Moreover, just as your fathers killed the prophets, the heralds of this one, as the monuments everywhere standing in honour of those men attest, so you betrayed Christ himself to the Roman governor, and with monstrous audacity removed him by the dreadful punishment of the cross. Therefore you have not only filled up the measure of your fathers, but have far surpassed it. Now, that these things were said by Stephen not without the secret movement of the Holy Spirit, so we shall think it was not without divine will that they were committed to writing and transmitted to posterity. For they teach how one ought to deal with those who boast of the virtues of their ancestors and of the title of lawful succession, and who, having rashly claimed power for themselves, impose on the simple. Among this number we see today the Roman pontiffs, who, while they persecute the doctrine of the apostles with fire and sword, infect the whole orb of the earth with the example of a most corrupt life, make a profit from all sacred things, and yet still boast that they are Christ's vicars, the successors of Peter and Paul, and most stubbornly deny that the Roman Church can err. And it is well known that by the arts of these men the world has been taken in for several centuries. This mask must therefore be torn off them, and the faithful ministers of the Church must not permit that Cuman ass to go on terrifying the simple consciences of men under the pretext of a lion's skin. Nor should we listen to those who want these things either to be passed over in silence, or who prescribe the laws of moderation and gentleness. For where the glory of Christ is attacked and the salvation of souls is in danger, there is no room left for cowardice or gentleness. Christ saw this, and I think no one has ever more easily undertaken a contest of gentleness or moderation than he. Indeed he thought that false prelates must be opposed with the greatest severity rather than with cowardly or misplaced leniency. Stephen and the other apostles imitated this example most rightly. Before we depart from here, you will note in passing that the prophets were heralds of Christ. Christ himself admits this, Luke 24, and Peter ascribes the same to them, 1 Pet. 1. This contributes to the dignity and certainty of our faith, so that we may not think it a persuasion recently invented or uncertain, held by a few men.

units.la: Pergit autem in suo instituto Stephanus, & legis inanem fiduciam illis eximit, quæ inter dei beneficia primum quodammodo locum tenere videbatur, Dauide teste, qui deum in nulla alia gente simili argumento suæ bonitatis vsum fuisse, dicit. Psal. 147. Fatetur autem, hanc illis diuinitus datam esse per angelorum ministerium, quorum præsentia maiestatis suæ gloriam deus illis testari voluit. At inanem esse gloriationem, quam illi inde petebant, docet, eò quòd legi nunquam obedientes fuerint. Nam peccatorum desyderijs abrepti illam negligebant, & insuper Christum, cui illa adducit, improbè persequebantur. Vnde colligimus vanam esse eam quoq;, quæ ex verbo dei & euangelij doctrina sumitur gloriationem, nisi factis exequamur, quæ per hanc præscribuntur. Beati enim (inquit Christus) qui audiunt verbum meum, & faciunt illud. Luc. 11. Et alibi procul abs se relegat iniquitatis operarios, qui patris sui voluntatem facere negligunt. Matth. 7. In quorum consyderatione nos hodie diligentius versari oportebat. Si enim legis, per Mosem latæ, transgressores grauissimè puniti sunt, quid eos manebit, qui euangelij verbum, Christo authore nobis traditum, improbè contempserint? Christus certè hos graniori iudicio, quàm Sodomeos & Gomorrheos puniendos dicit. Matth. 10. Vide item Heb. 10.
units.tr: Stephen goes on with his argument and strips them of their empty confidence in the Law, which seemed to hold first place, as it were, among God's benefits, as David attests, who says that God had shown his goodness in this way to no other nation. Psalm 147. He admits that this Law was given to them by God through the ministry of angels, by whose presence God wished to bear witness to the glory of his majesty. But he teaches that the boasting they drew from it was empty, because they never obeyed the Law. For, carried away by the desires of sin, they neglected it, and moreover they persecuted with wicked hatred Christ, to whom the Law leads. From this we gather that the boasting which is drawn from the Word of God and the doctrine of the gospel is also vain, unless we carry out in deeds what they prescribe. For Christ says, "Blessed are those who hear my word and do it." Luke 11. And elsewhere he banishes far from himself the workers of iniquity, who neglect to do their Father's will. Matthew 7. We ought to have considered these more carefully today. For if the transgressors of the Law given through Moses were punished most severely, what will await those who have wickedly despised the word of the gospel, handed down to us with Christ as its author? Christ certainly says that these will be punished with a heavier judgment than the Sodomites and Gomorrhites. Matthew 10. See also Hebrews 10.

units.la: Et hæc quidem grauissima simul & iustissima est Stephani protomartyris apologia, quæ vt apud pios maximum pondus habuisset, ita apud professos Christi hostes non modò profectu caruit, verùm etiam illorum animos maiori & acutiori impietatis stimulo exacerbauit. Scribit enim Lucas: Hiis auditis dissecabantur cordibus suis, & stridebant dentibus suis in eum. Cordium dissectio furentis animi & æstuantis dolorem notat, quo acerrimè compuncti sunt. Tantus enim is fuit, vt illu in loco iustitiæ & religioni sacro dissimulare nequiuerint. Nam dentium stridore, rabidorum canum instar, illum testati sunt. Exprimitur hîs impiorum ingenium, qui quo magis vrgentur verbo dei, eò intolerabilius furunt, & in eos armantur, quos Deus verbi sui præcones apud ipsos constituit. Ita Cainum diuinis admonitionibus magis exasperatum fuisse legimus. Et extant infinita istorum hominum exempla, quibus recensendis immorari non est opus, quando similia quotidie experimur. Discamus autem hanc infallibilem esse extremæ impietatis notam. Quid enim de eo speres, qui verbo dei non melior, sed deterior efficitur? Reprimamus ergo affectum hunc, vt primùm illius sensu tangimur. Interim discamus, non ideo tacendum esse verbi ministros, quia illorum increpationibus impij efferantur. Hos enim Paulus opportunè simul & importunè instare iubet. 2. Tim. 4. Nec quenquam offendat, quòd verbo nihil apud tales proficitur. Nam si nullus alius sequatur verbi effectus, suam saltem animam fidelis verbi minister liberabit. Ezech. 3. Nec interea deerunt electi Christi serui, quorum institutioni seruiet, quod impijs in iustæ damnationis testimonium præsdicatur. Faxit deus pater misericordia, vt oracula verbi sui rite audiamus, & in illa transformati ipsius maiestati nulla ex parte displiceamus, per Christum Iesum dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: This is indeed both the most grave and the most just defence of Stephen, the first martyr; and although it ought to have carried the greatest weight among the godly, among the open enemies of Christ it not only failed to achieve any result, but even inflamed their minds with a greater and sharper goad of impiety. For Luke writes: "When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed on him with their teeth." The cutting of the heart denotes the pain of a raging and seething spirit, by which they were most sharply pierced. For this was so great that they could not conceal it in a place sacred to justice and religion. And by the grinding of their teeth, like rabid dogs, they bore witness against him. Here the nature of the impious is expressed, who, the more they are pressed by the Word of God, the more intolerably they rage, and arm themselves against those whom God has appointed among them as heralds of his Word. Thus we read that Cain was made more bitter by divine admonitions. And there are countless examples of these men, which need not detain us to recount, since we experience similar ones every day. Let us learn, however, that this is an infallible mark of extreme impiety. For what can you hope of one who is made not better but worse by the Word of God? Let us therefore restrain this passion as soon as we feel it stirring. Meanwhile let us learn that the ministers of the Word are not to be silent because the wicked are roused by their rebukes. For Paul bids them to press on, in season and out of season. 2 Timothy 4. Nor should it trouble anyone that nothing is achieved by the Word among such people. For even if no other effect of the Word follows, a faithful minister will at least deliver his own soul. Ezekiel 3. Nor will the elect servants of Christ be lacking, for whose instruction it serves that the wicked are preached to, as a testimony of their just condemnation. May God the Father of mercies grant that we hear the oracles of his Word rightly, and, transformed into them, that we in no way displease his majesty, through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LV.
units.tr: Homily 55.

units.la: Cum autem esset plenus spiritu sancto, intentis in coelum oculis, vidit gloriam dei, & Iesum stantem à dextris dei, & dixit: Ecce, video coelos apertos, & filium hominis stantem à dextris Dei. Clamantes autem voce magna, continuerunt aures suas, & impetu fecerunt vnanimiter in eum, & eiectum extra vrbem lapidarunt. Et testes deposuerunt vestimenta ad pedes adolescentis, qui vocabatur Saulus. Et lapidarunt Stephanum invocantem & dicentem: Domine Iesu, suscipe spiritum meum. Positis autem genibus clamauit voce magna: Domine, ne statuas illis hoc peccatum. Et cum hoc dixisset, obdormiuit. Saulus autem consentiebat in necem eius.
units.tr: Then Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadily into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and said: "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." But they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed upon him with one accord, and cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul. And they stoned Stephen as he called upon God and said: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And kneeling down he cried with a loud voice: "Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge." And when he had said this, he fell asleep. And Saul was consenting to his death.

units.la: Quamuis Dei verbum frugiferum & salutare sit, apud eos tamen solos fructificat, qui animis rectè dispositis illud audiunt. Impijs verò adeò non prodest, vt hoc exacerbentur potius & peiores fiant. Quia enim horum animi vt mare aestuant, quo magis vrgentur, eò magis furere consueuerunt. Extant eius rei exempla passim: inter quae cumprimis memorabile est, quod in Concilij aduersus Stephanum congregati assessoribus proponitur. Cum enim Stephanus & innocentia suam grauissimis argumentis asseruisset, & illorum inueteratam malitiam dignis verbis corripuisset, tam abest, vt poenitentiae stimulis ad vitae emendationem excitentur, vt potius totis animis implacabilem furorem concipiant, & eundem (quod in iudice turpissimum est) non modò vultus mutatione, verumetiam canino dentium stridore testentur. Atqui tolerari hoc aliquo modo poterat, si vel manus cohibuissent. Sed quasi parum adhuc insanierint, sanctissimi viri necem & indignu supplicium adijciunt: in cuius descriptione diligens omnino est Lucas, eò quòd de martyrum supplicijs non instruit, & multa alia, quae nostrae tum consolationi tum institutioni seruiunt, complectitur.
units.tr: Although the word of God is fruitful and saving, it bears fruit only among those who hear it with minds rightly disposed. For the impious it is so far from profitable that it rather exasperates them and makes them worse. For their minds boil like the sea, and the more they are pressed, the more they are accustomed to rage. There are examples of this everywhere, and among them the most memorable is what is set before the members of the council gathered against Stephen. For when Stephen had asserted his innocence with very weighty arguments, and had rebuked their long-ingrained malice in fitting words, they were so far from being stirred to repentance and amendment of life that they conceived a wholly implacable fury, and displayed it (which is most shameful in a judge) not only by changing their countenance but even by gnashing their teeth like dogs. And yet this might have been borne in some fashion, if they had at least restrained their hands. But as if they had not yet raged enough, they add the murder and unworthy punishment of this most holy man. Luke is entirely careful in describing it, in that he does not give an account of the sufferings of the martyrs, and yet he includes many other things that serve both our comfort and our instruction.

units.la: Ab ijs verò narrandi initiu sumit, quia deus cum suo martyre, tantis periculis implicito, gessit. Cum enim is se in medio luporum versari videret, nec vlla appareret alicuius auxilij spes, oculus in coelum eleuatis diuinam opem requirere coepit. Nec hanc illi diu negauit deus, sed illico visione oculis ipsius obijcit, qua & ipse confirmetur, & hostes terrefiant. Quo loco admonemur, deum suos, dum periclitantur, nequaquam deserere. Videt enim hos & audit, quod passim scriptura testatur. Et quia pater est, illorum arumnis tangitur, periclitantium miseretur, & se vindicem praebet fidelissimum. Et quamuis non semper praesentibus malis eripiat, animos tamen consolatur, vt malis sustinendis possint sufficere. Discamus ergo, non ad hominum auxilia, quae vanissima sunt, respicere, sed animi oculos in coelum attollere, nec spe nostra frustrabimur. Omnium enim piorum vox est, qua Dauid vtitur, dicens: Leuo meos oculos ad montes, vnde nam veniat auxilium meum. Auxilium meum venit à domino, conditore coeli & terrae. Psalm. 121. Et propheta felicem pronuntiat eum, cuius spes & fiducia est in domino. Execrabilem verò eum vocat, qui confidit in homine, & carnem ponit brachium suum, & c. Ierem. 17.
units.tr: He begins the narrative with these events because God acted with his martyr, who was caught in such great dangers. For when he saw that he was living in the midst of wolves, and no hope of any help appeared, he began to lift his eyes to heaven and to seek divine aid. Nor did God long deny it to him, but at once set before his eyes a vision, by which he himself might be strengthened and his enemies terrified. In this place we are reminded that God by no means forsakes his people when they are in peril. For he sees them and hears them, as Scripture testifies everywhere. And because he is a Father, he is moved by their troubles, has mercy on those in danger, and shows himself a most faithful avenger. And although he does not always snatch them from present evils, he still comforts their minds, so that they may be equal to bearing the evils. Let us learn, therefore, not to look to the help of men, which is most vain, but to lift the eyes of our minds to heaven, and we shall not be disappointed in our hope. For this is the voice of all the godly, which David uses, saying: "I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where shall my help come? My help comes from the Lord, the maker of heaven and earth." (Ps. 121.) And the prophet pronounces blessed the one whose hope and trust is in the Lord, but calls cursed the one who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, etc. (Jer. 17.)

units.la: Prodest autem modum & rationem diuinae consolationis, qua Stephanus subleuatus est, inspicere. In hac primum locum tenet spiritus sanctus, quo Stephanum repletum fuisse, Lucas dicit. Praestitit hic dominus, quod promittur, vbi nos non orphanos fore, sed spiritum consolatorem habituros dicit. Iohan. 14. Eo autem nobis propter carnis infirmitatem omnino opus est, & hunc à Deo iubente Christo petimus, dicentes: Adueniat regnum tuum. Hoc animati fideles, mundi conatus facile contemnunt. De hoc enim illud Iohannis intelligi debet: Maior est, qui in vobis est, quàm qui in mundo. 1. Iohan. 4. At quia vndiq; instabant, quae terrorem incutere possent etiam fortissimo martyri, externam quoq; consolationem illi Deus adhibere voluit. Visionem ergo exhibet, vniuersam salutis rationem continentem. Videt etenim apertos esse coelos, quod ipsum in Christi baptismo contigisse-gimus. gimus. Apparet item Christus in gloria, ad patris dextram stans. Quae cum visionis nomine commemorentur, & antea oculos in cælum ab illo sublatos esse dictum fit, ego hæc illi revera visibiliter apparuisse, nec mentis duntaxat contemplationi obiecta fuisse intelligo. Nec opus puto, ut de naturali visu multa disputemus, quando hæc soli Stephano apparere debuerunt, cuius oculos insolita acie denare, Deo facillimum fuit. Atqui opus erat ista a primo martyre conspici, ut quid reliqui omnes sperare debeant, intelligamus. Significant enim, patere nobis iam Christi merito cælos, & in his iuxta ipsius promissionem nobis locum paratum esse: adhæc Christum in cælis regnare, nec inertem & otiosum causam suorum negligere, sed in procinctu stare, ut ipsos liberet & conservet, ut pote fidelis ille pastor, qui oves suas manibus suis eripi non patitur Iohan. 10. Et huc mihi videntur referendæ sanctorum preces, quibus petunt, ut dominus exurgat ad salvandum ipsos. Psal. 3. 35. 44. &c. Quanquam autem soli Stephano hæc videre licuerit, illum tamen ut eadem iniquis iudicibus nuntiaret, suo spiritu impulit dominus. Quod magna libertate factum est. Inde vero intelligere debebant, irritos fore omnes ipsorum aduersus Christum conatus: quando iam in cælis gloriose regnet, quem ipsi paulo ante infami crucis supplicio extinctum putabant. Generalis autem hinc doctrina desumi debet, qua admoneamur, Christi vires invictas esse, & perpetuo hunc regnaturum, ut tum contra illum infelix hic mundus tumultuetur. Illius enim proprium hoc fore olim Davides prædixit, ut dominetur in medio hostium suorum. Psal. 110.
units.tr: It is also profitable to look at the manner and reason of the divine consolation by which Stephen was upheld. In this the Holy Spirit holds the first place; Luke says Stephen was filled with him. The Lord has fulfilled here what he promised, when he said that we would not be orphans but would have the Spirit as Comforter (John 14). Yet we absolutely need him because of the weakness of the flesh, and we ask for him from God, as Christ bids us, saying: "Thy kingdom come." Encouraged by this, the faithful easily despise the efforts of the world. For this is what that saying of John must be understood to mean: "He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world" (1 John 4). But because on every side there were things that could strike terror even into the bravest martyr, God chose to supply him also with an outward consolation. He therefore grants him a vision containing the whole manner of salvation. For he sees the heavens opened, which we have seen happen at Christ's baptism. Christ also appears in glory, standing at the Father's right hand. Since these things are recorded under the name of a vision, and since it was said earlier that he had lifted his eyes to heaven, I understand that these things truly appeared to him visibly, and were not merely set before the contemplation of his mind. Nor do I think it necessary to dispute at length about natural sight, since these things were to appear to Stephen alone, and it was very easy for God to make his eyes see with an unusual keenness. Yet it was necessary that these things be seen by the first martyr, so that we may understand what all the rest ought to hope for. For they signify that heaven is now open to us by the merit of Christ, and that a place has been prepared for us there according to his promise; moreover, that Christ reigns in heaven and does not idly and lazily neglect the cause of his own, but stands ready for battle, to deliver and preserve them, as that faithful shepherd who does not allow his sheep to be snatched from his hands (John 10). And it seems to me that the prayers of the saints, by which they ask that the Lord would arise to save them, should be referred to this (Ps. 3, 35, 44, etc.). Although it was allowed to Stephen alone to see these things, nevertheless the Lord moved him by his Spirit to announce the same to the unjust judges. This was done with great boldness. And from this they ought to have understood that all their efforts against Christ would come to nothing, since he now reigns gloriously in heaven, whom they had supposed to be put out by the infamous punishment of the cross just before. A general doctrine should also be drawn from this, by which we are reminded that the power of Christ is invincible, and that he will reign forever, however wretched this world may rage against him. For David long ago foretold that this would be his proper role: to rule in the midst of his enemies (Ps. 110).

units.la: Quid vero inter hæc Stephani hostes egere? Num vel horum denuntiatione moti impios furores remiserunt? Minime gentium. Primo enim vesanis clamoribus viro sanctissimo obstrepunt, & aures obturant, ne Dei verbum vel inviti audire cogantur. Est hoc impiis omnibus proprium, quod nihil perinde ut Dei verbum audiant, nec illud audire vel ferre possunt, cum nihil ipsorum desyderii aut conatibus magis contrarium fit. Quare David illos aspidibus confert, quæ aures, ne incantatorum carmina audiant, obturare solent. Psal. 58. At meretur ista impietas, ut & ipsi aliquando clament, nec audiantur a domino, sicut propheta admonet. Mich. 3. Tandem vero ultimam & atrocem Christi iudicis sententiam audire cogentur, qua illos cum satana, principe ipsorum, ad æterni ignis cruciatus relegabit. At non contenti clamoribus obstrepuisse Stephano de Christi gloria concionanti, ad iniustam vim convertuntur. Nam vnanimi consensu in illum ruunt, & urbe eiectum lapidant. Vbi apparet, quibus argumentis contra veritatem ab impiis disputetur: Clamoribus nimirum seditiosis, iniusta vi, lapidibus, gladiis, facibus, & quæcunque alia potestatis tenebrarum instrumenta sunt. His olim prophetas oppugnatos fuisse legimus. Isdem contra Christum disputatum est. Et apostolos similia esse expertos sequens historia docebit. At quia de his non semel nos Christus admonuit, minime nos offendi decet. Præparemur potius, ne hæc inopinantibus accidant.
units.tr: But what did Stephen's enemies do amid these things? Did they, moved by his warning, abandon their impious fury? Not at all. For first they drown out the most holy man with frenzied shouts and stop their ears, so that they may not be compelled to hear the word of God even against their will. This is peculiar to all the impious: they cannot hear or endure the word of God at all, since nothing is more contrary to their desires and efforts. Therefore David compares them to adders, which are accustomed to stop their ears so that they will not hear the songs of enchanters (Ps. 58). Yet such impiety deserves that they themselves too should someday cry out and not be heard by the Lord, as the prophet warns (Mic. 3). Finally they will be compelled to hear the last and dreadful sentence of Christ the judge, by which he will consign them with Satan, their prince, to the torments of eternal fire. But not content with having drowned out Stephen with shouts while he preached of Christ's glory, they turn to unjust violence. For with one accord they rush upon him and, having cast him out of the city, stone him. Here it becomes clear by what arguments the impious dispute against the truth: namely, seditious shouts, unjust violence, stones, swords, torches, and whatever other instruments of the power of darkness there are. We read that the prophets were attacked by these means of old; the same was done against Christ; and the following history will teach that the apostles experienced similar things. But since Christ has warned us of these things more than once, we ought by no means to be offended. Rather let us prepare ourselves, lest these things befall us unawares.

units.la: Singulari autem observatione dignum est, quod dum maxime iniusta vi furunt, iuris tamen speciem observare possunt. Nam quia blasphemiæ in Deum & falsa doctrinæ accusarunt, eam pœnam de illo sumunt, quæ blasphemis & seductoribus a Deo constituta erat. Leuit. 24. Deut. 12. & 17. Et testes, sicuti in lege describebatur, primos lapides iaciunt, quod ut expeditius faciant, vestes deponunt, quas Saulo (qui postea ad Christum conuersus Pauli nomen accepit) custodiendas tradunt. Nihil ergo quoad iuris formulam, desyderare possis. Et Stephanus iure & legibus pœnas dediisse videri potest. Sed non semper iure fit, quod iuris speciem refert, & penitius causæ suppliciorum excutiendæ sunt, nisi graviter offendere volumus. Interim observa quantum impiis interdum permittat Deus, quorum furoribus suos exerceri, illos autem impietatis mensuram implere vult. Et testium exemplo docemur, quousque tandem procedat impietas, nisi initiis obstare studeamus. Peccarunt illi falso testimonio, cum nec Dei legem, nec pœnam, quæ falsis testibus constituta est, ignorare possent. Nec illos terret, quod Solomon falsum testem Deo exosum & abominabilem esse pronunciat. Proverb. 6.
