Quia tamen seipsum abnegare & carni renunciare non studuit, quod verù Chriftianismi initium est, fides haec προσκαιρος fuit (sicuti Christus illam vocat, Mar.5.) & proinde in tentationis æstu non potuit subsistere. Admiranda autem hic elucet Christi Iesu potentia, qui tam grauem remoram, quæ euangelico cursui per Simonem obiecta videbatur, tam facile tollit: & improbum præstigiatorem, satanicis artibus instructissimum, ita subiugat, ut Philippo, peregrino & ignobili homini, addictus haereat, qui paulo ante se magnā Dei potentiam esse dixerat. Eodem pertinet, quòd alibi absq; negotio ipsum satanam expellit, ut plane constet ipsum satanæ victorem & fortissimum humani generis vindicem esse. Adhæc euangelij haec maxima laus est, cuius simplici praedicatione, versuta & subdola cum mundi tum diaboli sapientia nimium ridiculè confunditur. Videt. Cor.1. Deinde baptizatur quoq; Simon, & assiduè Philippo adhaeret. Cuius studij non postrema causa fuisse videtur, quòd se quoq; simili edendorum miraculorum facultate instrui cupiuit, ut sequentia docebunt. Hic vero admonemur, semper in ecclesia falsos fratres fore, qui aut fidem falso simulent, aut momentanea tantum præditi denuo deficiant. Verriculo enim confertur euangelium, quo tam mali quam boni pisces trahuntur. Neminem igitur offendat, si quando sibi à similibus imponi sentiat: quando Christum in suo comitatu Iudam habuisse legimus, & Paulus non raro de falsis fratribus conqueritur. Nimium enim inepti & impatientes sunt, qui ab vno & altero decepti, omnes promissæ fastidiunt, nec aliquem veri Christiani aut fratris nomine dignantur. Praeterea docemur Simonis exemplo, Dei gratiam Sacramentis minimè alligatam esse, quando signum gratiae sine fructu Simon accipit. Et Paulus, licet veteres ijsdem nobiscum Sacramentis vsos fuisse fateatur, eos tamen Deo minimè placuisse dicit, quia fide caruerint. Nec Iudæ profuit, quod mensæ dominicæ accumbens, de manu Domini panem sumpsit. Sola ergo fides est, quæ & Christo nos inserit, & donorum Dei consortes facit, quæ per Sacramenta repræsentari & adumbrari solent.
units.tr: Luke now returns to Simon, so that we may understand what he did when he saw the people deserting him and rushing to give their names to Christ. He says first that Simon believed. I do not think this should be explained as mere pretence. That his mind was touched and struck by some sense of faith is clear from the fact that, having attached himself to Philip, he was astonished at the miracles and the outstanding works of the Holy Spirit. Yet since he did not take care to deny himself and renounce the flesh, which is the true beginning of Christianity, this faith was temporary (as Christ calls it, Mark 5), and so it could not hold up in the heat of temptation. Here, however, the wonderful power of Jesus Christ shines out, who so easily removes so serious a hindrance, which Simon seemed to put in the way of the gospel's course, and who subdues the wicked sorcerer, most skilled in satanic arts, so that he clings bound to Philip, a foreigner and a man of humble birth, although a little before he had called himself the great power of God. To the same point belongs the fact that elsewhere he drives out Satan himself without any difficulty, so that it is plain that Christ is the conqueror of Satan and the most mighty defender of the human race. Moreover, this is the greatest praise of the gospel: by its simple preaching, the crafty and deceitful wisdom of both the world and the devil is ridiculously confounded (see 1 Cor. 1). Then Simon too is baptized and constantly adheres to Philip. The reason for his zeal seems to have been not the least that he also wished to be equipped with a similar power of working miracles, as what follows will show. Here we are warned that there will always be false brothers in the church, who either feign faith falsely, or, endowed only for a moment, fall away again. For the gospel is compared to a dragnet, in which bad fish are caught as well as good. Let no one therefore be offended if he ever finds that he has been deceived by such men, since we read that Christ had Judas in his company, and Paul not infrequently complains of false brothers. Those are too foolish and impatient who, deceived by one or another, despise all who have been promised, and do not deign to call anyone a true Christian or brother. Moreover, we are taught by the example of Simon that God's grace is not bound to the sacraments, since Simon receives the sign of grace without fruit. And Paul, although he admits that the ancients used the same sacraments as we do, nevertheless says that they did not please God, because they lacked faith. Nor did it profit Judas that, reclining at the Lord's table, he took bread from the Lord's hand. Faith alone, therefore, both engrafts us into Christ and makes us partakers of God's gifts, which the sacraments are wont to represent and foreshadow.

units.la: Quia autem in Hierosolymitana ecclesia admirabiles spiritus sancti effectus floruisse, supra vidimus, Lucas apud Samaritanos quoq; eandem spiritus efficaciam fuisse docet, ne quis gentium ecclesias Iudaicis inferiores putaret. Dona autem haec per apostolos administrata fuisse scribit: quod ideo factum est, ut fortius coalesceret inter populos totis animis antehac disiunctos, ecclesiæ vnitas. Quanta enim animorum dissensio inter Iudæos & Samaritanos fuerit, ex Iohan.4.cap.& aliunde patet. Et Iudæi nimium arroganti praeiudicio reliquas gentes fastidire solebant. Non temere igitur apostolorum ministerio hic quoq; Deus vti voluit: ut clarissimè constaret, vnam & eandem esse apud omnes ecclesias Christi fidem, & vno eodemq; spiritu fideles omnes animari, adeoq; nullum in Christo gentis discrimen esse. Rom.10. Galat.3. Colos.3.
units.tr: Since we saw above that the remarkable effects of the Holy Spirit flourished in the Jerusalem church, Luke teaches that the same efficacy of the Spirit was present among the Samaritans as well, lest anyone think the churches of the Gentiles inferior to the Jewish ones. He writes that these gifts were administered through the apostles, and this was done so that the unity of the church might be more firmly joined among peoples who had hitherto been divided in heart. How great the dissension between Jews and Samaritans was is clear from John 4 and from elsewhere. And the Jews, with an excessively arrogant prejudice, used to despise the other nations. Not without reason, therefore, did God wish to use the ministry of the apostles here too, so that it might be most clearly established that there is one and the same faith in all the churches of Christ, that all believers are animated by one and the same Spirit, and that there is no distinction of nation in Christ (Rom. 10; Gal. 3; Col. 3).

units.la: Dicit autem Lucas, ab Hierosolymis Petrum & Iohannem missos fuisse, qui Samariam profecti, pro iis qui Christo nomen dederant, orauerint, ut etiam ipsis spiritus sanctus conferretur. Causa vero huius instituti assignatur, eò quòd super neminem adhuc spiritus sanctus incidisset, sed in Christi tantummodo nomine essent baptizati. Qui locus non ita accipi debet, quasi spiritu sancto in vniuersum caruerint Samaritani fideles. Quia enim fidem habuerunt, quæ spiritus donum atq; effectus est, & baptismo non indignè Christo initiati fuerunt, ijs omnino carere non potuerunt, quæ per hunc nobis obsignantur Christi beneficia. Sunt haec peccatorum ablutio, regeneratio, mortificatio veteris hominis, adoptio item in filiorum Dei numerum. At haec non aliunde quàm ex spiritus operatione nobis contingere, omnis scriptura testatur. Et sunt haec vulgaria spiritus sancti dona, sine quibus nemo Christianus vere dici poterit. Quare hos Samaritanos caruisse, verisimile non est. Spiritus autem nomine hoc loco excellentiora illa dona significantur, quibus vetus ecclesia floruit, quæq; visibili modo credentibus conferebantur, ut apostolos in Pentecoste spiritu sancto repente donatos fuisse, supra vidimus. Potest id exemplis probari, ijs maximè, quæ alibi de Cornelij familiarib. & Ephesijs quibusdam leguntur, supra quos visibili specie spiritus incidit, cum ab apostolis baptizarentur. Actor.10.& 19. Haec tam luculenta spiritus dona primitiua ecclesia, tam Samariæ quàm alibi conferri necesse fuit, ut maiori felicitate Christi regnum propagaretur. Hodie verò, licet haec maxima ex parte cessarint, is tamen inde ad nos fructus redit, quod spiritum sanctum ecclesiæ Christi praesidem & gubernatorem esse discimus, sicuti ille pollicitus est. Iohan.14.
units.tr: Luke says that Peter and John were sent from Jerusalem, and that when they had gone to Samaria, they prayed for those who had given their names to Christ, that the Holy Spirit might be conferred on them too. The reason for this arrangement is given: the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon anyone, but they had only been baptized in the name of Christ. This passage should not be understood as if the Samaritan believers were altogether without the Holy Spirit. For since they had faith, which is the gift and effect of the Spirit, and had been rightly initiated into Christ by baptism, they could not lack those benefits of Christ which are sealed to us through it. These are the washing away of sins, regeneration, the mortification of the old man, and likewise adoption into the number of the sons of God. That these come to us from nothing other than the working of the Spirit, all Scripture testifies. These are the common gifts of the Holy Spirit, and without them no one can truly be called a Christian. It is therefore unlikely that these Samaritans lacked them. By the name of Spirit in this place, however, are meant those more excellent gifts by which the early church flourished, and which were conferred on believers in a visible manner, as we saw above that the apostles were suddenly endowed with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. This can be proved by examples, especially those read elsewhere concerning Cornelius's household and certain Ephesians, upon whom the Spirit came in visible form when they were baptized by the apostles (Acts 10 and 19). These so splendid gifts of the Spirit had to be conferred on the primitive church, both in Samaria and elsewhere, so that the kingdom of Christ might be spread with greater success. Today, although these have for the most part ceased, the fruit still comes down to us, in that we learn that the Holy Spirit is the president and governor of the church of Christ, as he promised (John 14).

units.la: Nobis autem apostolorum industria hoc loco consyderanda venit. Vt primum enim Samariæ Philippum in opere Domini laborare audiunt, è suis mittunt etiam non rogati, qui laboranti opem ferant. Nec aliqua apparet stolidæ ambitionis species. Nam Petrum & Ioannem mittunt, quorum opera hucusq; præ aliis conspicua fuerat. Et illi se ab aliis mitti patiuntur, nec superbè sibi solos legatos à latere mittendi potestatem vsurpant. Philippus verò ad se venientes non ambitiosè reijcit, vt qui in alienam messem falces mittere, & ipsum aliqua gloriæ & honoris parte spoliare velint. Sed humaniter illis quoq; in eæ ecclesia locum concedit, cuius fundamentum ipse primus iecerat. Vnde docemur, animorum coniunctionem & operas mutuas in Christi regno propagando cumprimis requiri. At quia his inter ambitiosos locus nullus est, humilitatis non temere Christus suos toties admonet. Quibus studijs si hodie intenti essent, qui ecclesijs præsunt, maiori certè professu commissas sibi provincias administrarent.
units.tr: Now let us consider the diligence of the apostles here. As soon as they hear that Philip is labouring in the Lord's work in Samaria, they send men from among themselves, even though they are not asked, who might bring help to the one labouring. Nor does any sign of foolish ambition appear. For they send Peter and John, whose work had hitherto been more conspicuous than that of others. And they allow themselves to be sent by others, nor do they proudly claim for themselves alone the power of sending legates at their side. Philip, for his part, does not ambitiously reject those who come to him, as if they wished to put their sickles into another's harvest and strip him of some part of glory and honour. Rather, he humanely grants them a place also in that church, whose foundation he himself had first laid. Hence we are taught that a joining of hearts and mutual labours are especially required in propagating the kingdom of Christ. But since there is no room for these among the ambitious, Christ not without reason so often admonishes his people about humility. If those who preside over churches today were intent on these pursuits, they would certainly administer the provinces committed to them with far greater profit.

units.la: Cæterum quoad ritum & ordinem, non alia ceremonia, quàm manuum impositione, quæ à Christo tradita fuerat, vtuntur, ne quis sibi aliquid mutandi potestatem temere arroget. Preces autem præmittunt, ne quis spiritum sanctum externæ ceremoniæ alligatum putaret, sed hunc diuinitus conferri, & precibus à Deo impetrari omnes intelligerent. Nec defuit felix rei euentus. Scimus ex hoc loco Confirmationis sacramentum Papistas inuexisse: sed tam ridiculum est horum commentum, eamq; manifesta temeritas, vt multis refutari non mereatur. Nostrum erit Samaritanorum exemplo fidei vnitati studere, vt ipsi quoq; feliciter coalescamus in Christo Iesu, capite & saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, as to rite and order, they use no other ceremony than the laying on of hands, which had been handed down by Christ, lest anyone rashly arrogate to himself the power of changing anything. They also send prayers ahead, so that no one would think the Holy Spirit bound to an external ceremony, but everyone would understand that he is conferred by God and obtained from God through prayer. Nor was the outcome of the matter unhappy. We know that the Papists have introduced the sacrament of Confirmation from this passage; but this invention is so ridiculous, and so manifest a rashness, that it does not deserve to be refuted at length. It will be ours, following the example of the Samaritans, to strive for unity of faith, so that we too may happily be joined together in Christ Jesus, our head and saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 59.

units.la: Cum vidisset autem Simon, quòd per impositionem manuum apostolorum daretur spiritus sanctus, obtulit illis pecunias, dicens: Date & mihi potestatem hanc, vt cuicunq; imposuero manus, accipiat spiritum sanctum. Petrus autem illi dixit: Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem: quia donum Dei existimauisti pecuniis parari. Non est tibi pars neque sors in ratione hac. Cor enim tuum non est rectu coram Deo. Resipisce igitur ab hac tua malitia, & ora Deum, si forte remittatur tibi cogitatio cordis tui. Nam in felle amaritudinis & colligatione iniquitatis video te esse. Respondens autem Simon dixit: Orate vos pro me apud Dominum, ne quid eorum, quæ dixistis, mihi eueniat.
units.tr: When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying: "Give me this power too, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit." But Peter said to him: "May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be bought with money. You have no part or lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity." Simon answered and said: "Pray to the Lord for me yourselves, that none of the things you have said may come upon me."

units.la: Diuus Lucas communi scripturarum more, non modò felices primitiæ ecclesiæ progressus, & illustria verè fidelium exempla describit: verumetiam pseudochristianorum & hypocritarum mores vnà cum vitijs, quæ illi in ecclesiam inuexerunt, commemorat. Ita superius Ananiæ historiam, & obortum in ecclesia murmur exposuit. Et eadem ratione nunc horribile Simonis exemplum narrat, qui sacrilega ambitione & auaritia fidei professionem contaminauit. Vsus omnium horum est, vt intelligamus, semper in ecclesia hypocritas fore, qui grauissimorum offendiculorum authores sint: quibus tamen fideles non ita offendi debent, vt vel omnes promiscuè damnandos esse censeant, vel ab ecclesia secessionem faciant, quod ab Anabaptistis nostro seculo factum fuisse vidimus. Diligenter verò præsens locus inspici meretur, qui primò quidem Simonis peccatum, deinde acerrimam increpationem, qua contra illum Petrus innectus est, commemorat: tandem verò, vt hac affectus sit Simon, docet.
units.tr: Luke, in the usual manner of Scripture, does not only describe the happy progress of the early Church and the illustrious examples of true believers, but also records the conduct of false Christians and hypocrites, together with the vices they brought into the Church. So earlier he related the story of Ananias and the murmuring that arose in the Church. For the same reason he now tells the dreadful example of Simon, who defiled the profession of faith with sacrilegious ambition and greed. The purpose of all this is that we may understand that there will always be hypocrites in the Church, who are the authors of very grave stumbling-blocks. Yet the faithful ought not to be so offended by them that they either judge all men indiscriminately to be damned, or withdraw from the Church, as we saw the Anabaptists do in our own age. This passage deserves careful examination: it first recounts Simon's sin, then the very sharp rebuke with which Peter confronted him, and finally shows how Simon was affected by it.

units.la: Simonis peccatum paucis comprehendit Lucas. Cum vidisset (inquit) quòd per impositionem manuum apostolorum daretur spiritus sanctus, obtulit illis pecunias, dicens: Date & mihi potestatem hanc, vt cuicunq; imposuero manus, accipiat spiritum sanctum. Ante quidem credidisse Simonem dictum est, & miraculorum nouitate attonitum baptismum cum reliquis accepisse. Sed ex eorum numero fuit, qui licet carnis suæ studijs valedicere nolint, aliquo tamen Dei timore perculsi, cum illo palam contendere nolunt: & hi vtcunq; animi corruptionem ad tempus dissimulent, non tamen semper latere possunt. Et horum exemplo Simon etiam sese prodit, & bifariam peccat. Primò enim ambitionis malo inflatus, apostolis ministerij dignitate similis esse cupit, adeoq; diuinos honores sibi arrogat, dum sibi eam potestatem dari cupit, vt pro suo arbitrio spiritum sanctum hominibus con-
units.tr: Luke sums up Simon's sin in a few words. "When Simon saw" (he says) "that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying: Give me this power too, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit." It is said that Simon had earlier believed, and, astonished by the novelty of the miracles, had received baptism along with the others. But he belonged to the number of those who, although they are unwilling to renounce the pursuits of the flesh, yet, struck by some fear of God, are unwilling to contend openly with the truth. Such men, however much they may for a time conceal the corruption of their minds, cannot always stay hidden. And in the manner of such men Simon also betrayed himself, and sinned in two ways. For first, inflated by the disease of ambition, he desires to be like the apostles in the dignity of the ministry, and so arrogates to himself divine honours, while he wishes to be given the power to confer the Holy Spirit on men at his own pleasure. Ambition, moreover, is accompanied by avarice, by which, blinded, he makes religion a source of gain, and thinks that a trade in the gifts of the Holy Spirit can be set up. For he wanted to buy this power with money so that he might at some point make a greater profit from it. This thought about God and his gifts was far too profane, and utterly alien to the mind of Christ, who, when he equipped the apostles with these very gifts, said: "You have received freely, give freely." Matt. 10.

units.la: Simonis peccatum. ferre possit. Ambitioni autem auaritia comes est, qua excæcatus, religionem quæstum ducit, & spi-ritus sancti doni negotiationem instituí posse arbitratur. Ideo enim potestatem hanc pecunijs redi-mere voluit, vt ex ea maius lucrum aliquado faceret. Quæ nimis prophana fuit de Deo & donis il-lius cogitatio, & à Christi mente alienissima, qui cum apostolos donis bisce instrueret, dixit: Gratis accepistis, gratis date. Matth.10. Docet autem Simonis exemplum, superbiam omnis mali causam, adeoq; (vt sapiens ille monuit) peccati initium esse. Eccli.10. Hæc angelis ruinæ causam præbuit. Et illius tumore inflammatus Adam, diuini præcepti transgressor factus est, dum Deo similis fieri cupit. Deniq; quotidiana exempla docent, à superbis & ambitiosis nihil rectè fieri, & tales plerunq; perniciosissimos rerumpub. turbatores esse. Sed cum vbiq; locorum pestilens sit ambitionis malum, ecclesijs pestilentissimum est. Vbi enim has inuasit, dissidiorum semina inter eos spargit, quorum concordibus studijs ecclesiæ pax & incolumitas conseruari debebat. Cuius rei exempla nobis in Co-re, Mosis æmulo, & crebris apostolorum contentionibus proponuntur, quas toties tamq; graviter Christus repressit. Num.16. Matth.18. & 20. Luc.22. At leue videri poterat dissensionis malum, vt-cunque ecclesijs fere exitiale sit, nisi maior pestis accederet, impia nimirum & sacrilega sacrorum nundinatio, qua religionem omnem euertit, & hominum mentes ab hac in vniuersum alienare con-suevit. Euidentius hoc est in Simonis exemplo, quàm vt multis demonstrari opus sit. Vt primùm e-nim is in religionis causa ambitionem & auaritiam, consultores pessimos, admisit, ad sacrilegum il-lud spiritualis nundinationis consilium descendit. Sed vtinam solus Simon hac infamia teneretur, & non hodie pasim eos videremus, qui maiori impietate peccant. Postquam enim religionis studium ecclesias diuitijs maximis instruxit, & in honore ac precio esse cœperunt harum antistites, illico ma-lis artibus ad illarum gubernacula contenderunt parum synceri Simones, quos ambitionis & ava-ritiæ spiritus exagitavit. Hi postea primatu potiti, vias excogitarunt, quibus ea recuperarent, qua in coemendis suffragijs erogarant, & mox infamis nundinatio sacrorum instituta est. Hinc ini-tijs debemus sacramenta venalia, indulgentiarum contractus, conducticias preces, supererogationis merita, dispensationes quæstuosas, venales sepulturæ honores, & quæcunq; alia eius generis excogi-tata vidimus. Vt mirum sit eò impudentiæ progressos esse præcipuos ecclesiarum antistites, vt Simo-nis Petri successione gloriari voluerint, qui tam luculentis indicijs prodebant, se Simonis Magi po-tius successores esse. Regnauerunt isti homines iam seculis aliquot in ecclesia, donec verbi sui flagel-lo illos eijcere cœpit Dominus. Sed ne sic quidem resipiscunt, quin potius in scelere deprehensi, se ve-ros & legitimos ecclesiarum antistites esse vociferantur. Nec tamen solos illos accusamus, verum dolemus inter euangelij professores eiusmodi pestes non raro inueniri. Plerosq; enim non alijs animis ad euangelium contendere videmus, quàm quod hoc tam plausibili prætextu muniti, ecclesiarum bo-na auidissimè inuadunt, ijsq; turpissimè abutuntur. Et inueniunt illi nonnunquam sui similes minis-tros, qui cum & ipsi malis artibus ecclesiarum gubernacula inuadant, raptores bosce nec arguere nec cohercere possunt. Longè ergo lateq; imperij sui ditiones Simonis spiritus hodie extendit, qua mihi maxima ecclesiarum pestis esse videtur, qua fit, vt parum proficiant euangelij prædicatione, qui to-dem cum Antichristianis crimine tenentur.
units.tr: The sin of Simon. Simon's example also teaches that pride is the cause of every evil, and therefore (as that wise man warned) "the beginning of sin." Sirach 10. This pride was the cause of the fall of the angels. And Adam, inflamed by its swelling, became a transgressor of the divine command, while he desired to become like God. Finally, daily examples teach that nothing is done rightly by the proud and ambitious, and that such men are generally the most pernicious disturbers of commonwealths. But although the evil of ambition is harmful everywhere, it is most harmful to churches. For wherever it has gained entrance, it sows the seeds of dissension among those whose harmonious efforts ought to preserve the peace and well-being of the Church. Examples of this are set before us in Korah, the rival of Moses, and in the frequent contentions among the apostles, which Christ so often and so severely suppressed. Num. 16; Matt. 18 and 20; Luke 22. Yet the evil of dissension might seem slight, however nearly fatal it is to churches, unless a greater plague were added, namely the impious and sacrilegious bartering of holy things, which overturns all religion and is accustomed to estrange men's minds from it altogether. This is more evident in Simon's example than it needs to be demonstrated by many arguments. For as soon as he had admitted ambition and avarice, the worst counsellors, into the cause of religion, he descended to that sacrilegious plan of spiritual trafficking. But would that Simon alone were held by this infamy, and that we did not today see on every side those who sin with still greater impiety. For after the zeal for religion had endowed the churches with very great riches, and their leaders began to be held in honour and high esteem, at once men of little sincerity, Simons driven by the spirit of ambition and avarice, strove by wicked arts for the helm of those churches. Afterwards, having gained primacy, they devised ways to recover what they had spent in buying votes, and soon an infamous trade in sacred things was established. From these beginnings we have seen venal sacraments, contracts for indulgences, hired prayers, merits of supererogation, profitable dispensations, the sale of burial honours, and whatever else of this kind has been invented. So it is astonishing that the chief leaders of the churches advanced so far in impudence that they wished to boast of the succession of Peter, when by such clear signs they showed that they were rather the successors of Simon Magus. These men have held sway in the Church for several centuries, until the Lord began to drive them out with the scourge of his Word. But even so they do not repent; rather, caught in their crime, they cry out that they are the true and lawful leaders of the churches. Nor do we accuse them alone; we grieve that such plagues are not rare even among professors of the gospel. For we see many who approach the gospel with no other intention than that, protected by this very plausible pretext, they may most greedily seize the goods of the churches and most shamefully abuse them. And sometimes they find ministers like themselves, who, since they too seize the helm of the churches by wicked arts, cannot rebuke or restrain these plunderers. Therefore the spirit of Simon today extends its realms far and wide, and it seems to me the greatest plague of the churches, through which it comes about that those who are still held by Antichristian crime make little progress by the preaching of the gospel.

units.la: Sed Petri orationem videamus, qua cum Simone expostulat. Est hæc grauissima simul & acer-rima, & duabus partibus constat. Prima peccatum illius accusat, & pœnam meritam denunciat. Figuratur autem imprecatione, à qua dicendi initium facit. Pecunia tua(inquit)tecum sit in per-ditionem: id est, Male pereas cum tua pecunia maledicta & execrabili. Ita verò orditur apostolus, non impotenti irae affectu abreptus, sed spiritu sancto motus, qui & sceleris & pœnae atrocitatem hac loquendi formula illustrare voluit. Quare ad vaticiniorum species eiusmodi imprecationes referri debent, quales non pauca in Psalmis & prophetarum scriptis extant. Magis autem alia adiecta sententia pœnae atrocitas amplificatur, cum addit: Non est tibi pars neq; hæreditas in ratione hac. Quibus verbis illum ab omni spiritualium donorum communione omnino exclusum, adeoq; ab eccle-sia Domini excommunicatum esse testatur. Et ne temere debacchari videretur, causam tam dirè comminationibus interseris: Quia donum Dei existimauisti pecunijs parari. Quæ vna res abunde do-cet, animum tuum non esse rectum siue syncerum coram Deo, quando hunc auaris mercatoribus & nundinatoribus vsurarijs simile esse suspicaris. Generalis autem hinc sententia colligitur, qua docemur.
units.tr: But let us look at Peter's speech, with which he rebukes Simon. It is most severe and at the same time most sharp, and consists of two parts. The first accuses his sin and announces the punishment he deserves. It is framed as a curse, with which he begins to speak. "May your money perish with you" (he says), that is, "May you perish cursed and damned along with your money." The apostle begins in this way not carried away by an impotent passion of anger, but moved by the Holy Spirit, who wished by this form of speech to set forth the atrocity both of the crime and of the punishment. Hence such curses should be referred to the kind of prophecy that is found in no small number in the Psalms and in the writings of the prophets. The atrocity of the punishment is further magnified by another added sentence, when he adds: "You have no part or inheritance in this matter." By these words he testifies that Simon has been wholly excluded from every communion of spiritual gifts, and so excommunicated from the Church of the Lord. And lest he seem to rage rashly, he joins a reason to such terrible threats: "Because you thought that the gift of God could be bought with money." This one thing sufficiently shows that your mind is not right or sincere before God, since you suspect it is like greedy merchants and usurious traders. From this a general statement is drawn, by which we are taught

units.la: II. Expostulatio Petri cum Simone. mur, omnium illorum animos Deo probari non posse, quicunq; religionem quaestu ducunt, & sub huius praetextu priuatis commodis consulunt. Simul vero Petri exemplo admonemur, quo zelo & ardore spiritus ministri eos arguere debeant, qui turpis quaestus studio Dei gloriae derogant. Ita enim cum illis agendum est, vt se horribiliter peccauisse, & atrocem damnationis aeterna poenam meruisse intelligant. Nec enim aliquis modestiae & mansuetudinis locus superest, vbi Dei gloria apertis armis petitur, & diuinae gratiae dona auarissimorum hominum quaestuosae libidini subiacent. Simili ergo zelo Elisaeum quoq; aduersus nequam seruum Giezi vsum esse legimus, quem subita lepra plaga percussit, quod ab Naamano Syro sanitatis diuinitus concessa premium postulauisset. 2. Reg. cap. 5. Et Christus Iesus, perfectissimum mansuetudinis exemplar, impia sacrorum nundinatione irritatus fuisse legitur, vt manus quoque tanti facinoris authoribus iniicere, & eosdem flagello, tanquam canes impudentes, templo eijcere voluerit. Vide Iohan. 2. Matth. 12. Marc. 11. Merito igitur de illorum iniquitate hodie conquerimur, qui nos contra Christianae modestiae & charitatis leges peccare dicunt, quando Romanum Antichristum & huius creaturas, Cardinales, episcopos, monachos & sacrificulos accusamus, qui impia & profana nundinatione iam seculis aliquot religionem Christianam Iudaeis & Turcis deridendam exposuerunt, nec dum hodie, quamuis passim reprehendantur, de reformatione & emendatione serio cogitant. Atqui perpetuum & aeternum Dei decretum est, quo per prophetam statuit, ne in sua domo Chananaeis siue nundinatoribus locus aliquis relinquatur. Zach. 14.
units.tr: ...we are taught that the minds of all those cannot be approved by God who make religion a source of profit and use it as a pretext for their private advantage. At the same time, Peter's example teaches us with what zeal and fervour of spirit ministers ought to rebuke those who, out of a desire for shameful gain, detract from the glory of God. For they must be dealt with in such a way that they understand they have sinned dreadfully and deserve the terrible punishment of eternal damnation. There is no room left for gentleness and mildness where the glory of God is openly attacked and the gifts of divine grace are subjected to the greedy lust of the most avaricious men. In the same way we read that Elisha, with similar zeal, dealt with the wicked servant Gehazi, whom a sudden leprosy struck down because he had demanded a reward from Naaman the Syrian for the health that God had granted. 2 Kings 5. And Christ Jesus, the most perfect model of gentleness, is read to have been roused by the impious trade in sacred things, so that he wished to lay hands on the authors of so great a crime and drive them out of the temple with a whip, like shameless dogs. See John 2, Matthew 12, Mark 11. Rightly, therefore, we complain today about those who say that we sin against the laws of Christian gentleness and charity when we accuse the Roman Antichrist and his creatures, the cardinals, bishops, monks and little priests, who for several centuries have exposed the Christian religion to be mocked by Jews and Turks through their impious and profane trade, and who, although they are rebuked on every side, still do not think seriously about reform and amendment. Yet it is the perpetual and eternal decree of God, by which he declared through the prophet that no place be left in his house for Canaanites, that is, traders. Zech. 14.

units.la: Adhaec obseruatione dignum est, quod non Simonem modo, verum etiam Simonis pecuniam hac tam graui sententia Petrus multat. Execrabile ergo vna cum impijs est, quicquid illis ad gloriae Dei derogationem seruit. Ita merces iniquitatis dicitur ea pecunia, qua Balaamum rex Balak aduersus Dei populum ad impediendum Dei decretum conduxerat. 2. Pet. 2. Et Iudae pecuniam, qua is Christum prodidit, maledictioni obnoxiam fuisse, vel ex eo constat, quod nec Iudas illa diu frui potuit, nec in alium vsum sacerdotibus seruiuit, quam quod ex ea perpetuam sanguinariae suae impietatis memoriam sibi comparauit. Quid vero de monasteriorum bonis & redditibus dicere attinet, quos ex parte Simoniacis artibus collectos fuisse constat, ab iis hominibus, qui sacra omnia venalia habuerunt? Nam luce clarius constat, tam infelicem horum fortem esse, vt euangelij luce illustratis fere offendiculi lapis sint, dum horum potius direptioni, quam Christi gloriae propagandae studeant. Adeo infelix est Simoniae malum. Ac quod de his opibus dicitur, hoc ipsum de omnibus iniuste partis diuitijs debet intelligi, quibus hoc proprium est, quod maledictionem & execrationem horribilem suis possessoribus afferunt. Nota enim est domini sententia: Vae ti, qui adaugct non sua. Habakuk 2. cap.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth noting that Peter condemns with such severe judgement not only Simon but also Simon's money. Whatever serves to detract from the glory of God is therefore cursed together with the wicked. Thus the money with which King Balak hired Balaam to hinder God's people is called the wages of iniquity. 2 Pet. 2. And that the money with which Judas betrayed Christ was liable to a curse is clear from this: Judas could not enjoy it for long, nor was it applied to any other use by the priests, except that through it he gained for himself an everlasting memorial of his bloody impiety. But what need is there to speak of the goods and revenues of monasteries, which are known to have been gathered partly by simoniacal arts from men who treated all sacred things as saleable? For it is clearer than light that their lot is so unhappy that, although they are illuminated by the light of the gospel, they are almost a stone of stumbling, since they are more eager to plunder these goods than to spread the glory of Christ. So unhappy is the evil of simony. And what is said of these riches must be understood of all wealth unjustly acquired, which has this peculiar feature, that it brings a curse and terrible execration upon its possessors. For the Lord's sentence is well known: Woe to him who increases what is not his own. Habakkuk 2.

units.la: Altera orationis parte, illum ad poenitentiam hortatur, qua non obscure illi veniae spem facit. Cur enim poeniteret & resipiscceret, qui studiu hoc inutile & superuacaneum esse crederet? Patet autem hic, quis in ecclesia increpationum omnium finis & scopus esse debeat: vt homines a peccatis conuersi, Deo reconciliantur. Qui scopus nisi obseruetur, corripiendi libertas a scurrili maledicentia nihil differet. Quare ne Petri verba eo nomine Simon suspecta habere posset, subijcitur: Resipisce ab hac tua malitia, & ora Deum, si forte remittatur tibi cogitatio cordis tui. Cogitationis mememinit, vt maior eluceat facti atrocitas, cuius cogitatio a Christiani hominis mente alienissima esse debebat. Et obiter admonemur, non operibus modo, verum etiam cogitationibus & desyderijs peccari. Quia enim homines animo simul & corpore Deo addicti esse debent, peccati nome meretur, si vel minimam sui partem a Dei obedientia subtraxerint. Pertinent huc quae Christus in legis expositione dicit apud Matthaeum 5. cap. Porro vt fortius feriret Simonis animum, quem non leuiter a satana tentatum videbat, peccati fontes & radices perstringit, ita ostendens, ipsi serio plane poenitentiae studio opus esse: in quem fine id quoq; referri debet, quod quasi dubitabundus dixit, Si forte remittatur tibi, &c. At nunc addit: Na in felle amaritudinis, & in colligatione siue vinculo iniquitatis video te esse. Prima membro ad Mosaicum illud alludit, quo Israelitae sibijpsis cauere iubentur, ne in ipsis locum habeat radix germinans fel & absynthium. Deut. 29. Notatur autem interna animi malitia siue corruptio, qua fit, vt corda Deo amara & ingrata sint, quaecunq; homines faciunt. Nam vt e bono cordis thesauro bonum profert pius dei cultor: ita nihil nisi malum ex malo cordis thesauro impij proferunt.
units.tr: In the second part of his speech, Peter urges Simon to repentance, which does not obscurely give him hope of pardon. For why would a man repent and come to his senses if he believed that his effort was useless and vain? Here it is plain what the aim and purpose of all rebukes in the Church ought to be: that people turned from their sins may be reconciled to God. If this aim is not kept in view, the freedom to rebuke will differ in nothing from scurrilous slander. Therefore, lest Simon might regard Peter's words with suspicion on that account, it is added: Repent of this your wickedness, and pray to God, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. He mentions the thought so that the greater atrocity of the deed may shine forth, since such a thought ought to have been most alien to the mind of a Christian man. And we are admonished in passing that sin is committed not only by deeds but also by thoughts and desires. For since men ought to be devoted to God both in soul and in body, they deserve the name of sinner if they withdraw even the smallest part of themselves from obedience to God. To this belong the words Christ speaks in his exposition of the law in Matthew 5. Moreover, in order to strike more forcefully the mind of Simon, whom he saw to be sorely tempted by Satan, Peter touches the sources and roots of sin, thus showing that Simon needed to apply himself to repentance with complete seriousness. To this same end should also be referred what he said as if in doubt: If perhaps it may be forgiven you, etc. But now he adds: For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity. The first phrase alludes to that passage of Moses in which the Israelites are ordered to take care lest a root bearing gall and wormwood spring up among them. Deut. 29. The phrase denotes the inner malice or corruption of the mind, by which it happens that whatever men do is bitter and unpleasing to God. For just as the pious worshipper of God brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart, so the wicked bring forth nothing but evil from the evil treasure of the heart.

units.la: x ea nimirum quibus homine reuera pollui Christus testatur. Matth.12.&15. Ac per colligationem iniquitatis, eorum conditio exprimitur, qui peccatorum laqueis prorsus impediti, se ex illis non nisi summo studio & flagranti poenitentia zelo extricare possunt. Eam Simonis conditionem esse docet, ne frigidam & superuacaneam poenitentiae simulationem sufficere putaret, &c.
units.tr: Indeed, these are the things by which, as Christ testifies, a man is truly defiled. Matt. 12 and 15. And by the bond of iniquity is expressed the condition of those who, entirely entangled in the snares of sins, can free themselves from them only by the greatest effort and burning zeal of repentance. Peter teaches that this was Simon's condition, so that he might not think a cold and useless pretence of repentance was enough, etc.

units.la: Admonet nos locus hic, quo nam peccatores relegari debeant. Ad Deum nimirum, quo cum nisi in gratiam redeant, nulla de salute ipsorum spes esse potest. Ideo apud prophetas hoc unum ingeminari videmus, ut ad Deum convertantur, qui peccando ab hoc secessione recesserunt. At ut id commode fiat, duo observare conuenit, quae utraque Petrus Simoni praescribit. Primum, resipiscentia opus est, quae ut alibi monuimus, peccati agnitionem, cordis contritionem & totius vitae emendationem complectitur. Alterum in piis precibus versatur, quibus peccatorum remissio peti debet, eo quod illa gratuita est, nec vllis nostrorum operum meritis obtingit. At verum, unus Christus operatur, qui & spiritu suo credentes regenerat, & sua mortis merito peccata diluit, patremque nobis reconciliat. In fide ergo, qua is a nobis apprehenditur, vniuersa salutis ratio versatur. Fidem itaque ante omnia vrgeri conuenit, non mortuam illam, qua hypocritae gloriantur, sed viuam & efficacem spiritus virtutem, qua fit, ut & ipsi in Christo viuamus, & ille in nobis suo spiritu operetur. Haec enim sola de Dei gratia hominis fluctuantem conscientiam certiorem reddit, & vberrimos in nobis verae pietatis fructus gignere consueuit.
units.tr: This passage admonishes us where sinners ought to be sent back to. Namely to God, since unless they return into favour with him there can be no hope of their salvation. Therefore we see that the prophets repeat this one thing again and again: that they should be converted to God, from whom they have withdrawn by sinning and turning away. But so that this may be done properly, two things should be observed, both of which Peter prescribes to Simon. The first is that there must be repentance, which, as we have said elsewhere, includes the acknowledgement of sin, contrition of heart and amendment of the whole life. The second consists in pious prayers, by which forgiveness of sins ought to be sought, because it is a free gift and comes to us by no merit of our works. For truly, Christ alone works, who both regenerates believers by his Spirit and washes away sins by the merit of his death, and reconciles the Father to us. The whole order of salvation therefore rests on faith, by which he is apprehended by us. Faith must therefore be urged above all, not that dead faith in which hypocrites boast, but the living and effective power of the Spirit, by which it comes about that we also live in Christ and he works in us by his Spirit. For this alone makes the wavering conscience more certain of God's grace, and it is accustomed to bring forth the most abundant fruits of true godliness in us.

units.la: Vt vero Simon hac tam gratu & salutari expostulatione affectus est? Perculsum animo fuisse, verba illius declarant. Nam ait: Orate vos pro me apud dominum, ne quid eorum, quae dixistis mihi euenient. Videtur se ecclesiae precibus commendare, sed non obscurum diffidentiae argumentum est, quod nihil de seipso dicit, sed aliorum duntaxat precibus se iuuari posse putat. Atqui irrita & inanes pro nobis sunt aliorum preces, nisi ipsi ad dominum reuertamur. Docent hoc prophetarum loci, in quibus ipsi prophetae pro impiis & poenitere nescijs orare prohibentur. Vide Ierem.7. 14.15. Ezech.14. Ridiculus ergo & noxius illorum error est, qui conductitijs & redemptis monachorum sacrificulorum preculis se iuuari sperant, cum & ipsi in impietate sua pergant, & precatiunculae alienà lingua demurmuratae, plerunque ne ab ipsis quidem monachis demurmuratoribus intelligantur. Scimus quidem non inefficaces esse fidelium preces, quibus confratrum suorum labores Deo commendant, cum ijs Paulus quoque sublevari voluerit. Rom.15. Ephes.6. Sed hae in illis locum habent, qui ipsi quoque sui officij meminerunt, & constanti fide pro sua salute inuigilant. Horum itaque memores, vigilemus & oremus sedulo, ne ambitionis & auaritiae affectibus excaecati, salutis iactuam faciamus, sed syncero corde Deo seruientes salutem consequamur in Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But how was Simon affected by this so serious and salutary rebuke? His words show that he was struck in mind. For he says: Pray for me to the Lord yourselves, that none of the things you have said may come upon me. He seems to commend himself to the prayers of the Church, but it is no obscure sign of distrust that he says nothing about himself and thinks he can be helped only by the prayers of others. Yet the prayers of others for us are vain and empty unless we ourselves return to the Lord. The passages of the prophets teach this, in which the prophets themselves are forbidden to pray for the impious and for those who do not know how to repent. See Jer. 7:14-15, Ezek. 14. Therefore the error of those is ridiculous and harmful who hope to be helped by the hired and purchased prayers of monks and little priests, when they themselves persist in their impiety, and little prayers muttered in a foreign tongue are for the most part not understood even by the monks who mutter them. We know indeed that the prayers of the faithful, by which they commend the labours of their brothers to God, are not without effect, since Paul also wished to be supported by them. Rom. 15, Eph. 6. But these prayers have a place among those who also remember their own duty and watch over their salvation with steadfast faith. Mindful of these things, then, let us watch and pray diligently, lest, blinded by the passions of ambition and avarice, we make shipwreck of our salvation, but serving God with a sincere heart, let us obtain salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LX.
units.tr: HOMILY LX.

units.la: Porrò illi testificati, & locuti sermonem domini, redierunt Hierosolymam, & multis pagis euangelizauerunt. Angelus autem domini locutus est Philippo, dicens: Surge, & vade meridiem versus, ad viam, quae descendit ab Hierusalem ad Gazam: haec est deserta. Et surgens profectus est. Et ecce vir Aethiops, eunuchus, praefectus Candaces reginae Aethiopum, qui praerat toti eius gazae: qui venerat adoraturus Hierosolymam, reuertens & sedens in curru suo, legebat prophetam Esaiam. Dixit autem spiritus Philippo: Accede & adiungere ad hunc currum. Accurrens autem Philippus, audiuit eum legentem prophetam Esaiam, & dixit: Intelligis ne quae legis? At ille ait: Quomodo possem, nisi aliquis mihi dux viae fuerit? Et rogauit Philippum, vt ascenderet ac sederet secum.
units.tr: Then those men, having borne witness and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem and preached the gospel in many villages. But the angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, "Rise and go towards the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza; this is the desert road." And he rose and went. And behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure, had come to worship at Jerusalem. On his way back, sitting in his chariot, he was reading the prophet Isaiah. Then the Spirit said to Philip, "Go up and join this chariot." So Philip ran up and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, "Do you understand what you are reading?" He answered, "How could I, unless someone guides me?" And he asked Philip to come up and sit with him.

units.la: Quoniam Deus filium suum, Iesum Christum, vniuersalem totius orbis saluatorem constituit, euangelium quoque, quo salutis per illum partae ratio continetur, in omnibus gentibus praedicari oportuit. Id quomodo fieri ceperit, hoc Capite Lucas commemorat. Orditur autem a Samariae conuersione, quam ipse Christus disertè apostolis commendauerat, sicuti in Ascensionis ipsius historia vidimus. Et illuc quidem Philippus venit, primusq; euangelicæ doctrinæ & fidei semina sparsit. Mox verò eodem missi apostoli, ijs qui iam ante per baptismum Christo nomen dederant, spiritus sanctI dona contulerunt: quæ res actioni cum Simone Mago institutæ, occasionem præbuit. Ad conuersæ autem Samariæ historiam præsentis quoq; loci initium pertinet, cui deinde noua narratio subtexitur, quæ vt Christi cognitio ad Æthiopes vsque penetrauerit, docet.
units.tr: Since God appointed his Son, Jesus Christ, to be the universal Saviour of the whole world, the gospel, which contains the account of the salvation obtained through him, had to be preached among all nations. Luke relates in this chapter how this began. He starts with the conversion of Samaria, which Christ himself had expressly committed to the apostles, as we saw in the account of his Ascension. Philip came there first and scattered the first seeds of evangelical teaching and faith. Soon afterwards the apostles, who had been sent there, conferred the gifts of the Holy Spirit on those who had already given their names to Christ through baptism. This matter, arising from the dealings with Simon Magus, gave the occasion for it. The story of the converted Samaria also gives the starting point for the present passage, to which a new narrative is then joined, showing how the knowledge of Christ reached as far as the Ethiopians.

units.la: Et initiò quidem superiorem narrationē conclusurus Lucas, quid apostoli præterea Samariæ secerint, paucis comprehendit, dicens: Illi testificati, & locuti sermonem dei, redierunt Hierosolymam, & multis pagis euangelizarunt. Quibus verbis tria apostolis tribuuntur. Primò testificati sunt de Christo, què Philippus prædicarat. Suo igitur officio functi sunt, cui illos Christus destinauit, quando testes suos esse iubet. Ioh. 15. Act. 1. Deinde annunciarunt verbum Dei, non suæ rationis commenta. Et hic quoq; ad Christi præceptum respiciunt, qui illos ea prædicare iussit, quæ ipse tradiderat. Matth. 28. Tertiò, in reditu ne obscuriores quidem locos negligunt, verumetiam passim in pagis euangelium Iesu Christi prædicant. Est hoc magni & feruentis zeli argumentum, quo inflammati, nullam occasionem sibi prætermittendā esse putarunt, quæ propagando Christi regno inseruire posset. His verò ministrorum verbi & ecclesiæ officium plenissimè continetur. Meminerint illi, se nō modò præcones verumetiam testes Christi esse. At testium est veritati studere, & intrepidè ingenuē proferre, quæ ipsis comperta fuerint. Nec fidus testis dicetur, quisquis in hominum gratiam, quocunque tandē affectu superatus, veritatem obscurare audet. Præterea, dei verbū sibi comissum esse intelligant, cuius præcones, non aut nouorum dogmatū authores, illos dominus constituit. Quare sibi dictū putent, quod Ezechieli dicitur, qui ex ore domini verbum sumere iubetur. Ezech. 3. Nec sibi concessum putent, dei verbo sua commenta admiscere. Quid enim paleæ cum tritico? Ierem. 23. Cæterū in omnibus hisce zelus requiritur, quo nisi inflammati fuerint, haud magnum fructū facient. Christum ergo imitentur, quem vndiquaq; docendi & prædicandi occasionem arripuisse videmus. Et Paulus se omnia omnibus factum fuisse testatur, vt quàm plurimos Christo lucrifaceret. 1. Corinth. 9.
units.tr: Luke, about to conclude the earlier narrative, briefly sums up what the apostles did further in Samaria, saying: "They, having borne witness and spoken the word of God, returned to Jerusalem and preached the gospel in many villages." Three things are attributed to the apostles in these words. First, they bore witness to Christ, as Philip had preached him. In this they performed their office, to which Christ appointed them when he bade them be his witnesses (John 15; Acts 1). Second, they proclaimed the word of God and did not offer the inventions of their own reason. Here too they look to the command of Christ, who ordered them to preach what he himself had taught (Matt. 28). Third, on their return they did not neglect even the more obscure places, but preached the gospel of Jesus Christ everywhere in the villages. This is a sign of great and fervent zeal, by which, inflamed, they judged that no opportunity should be let slip which could serve the spread of Christ's kingdom. In these words the office of the ministers of the Word and of the Church is fully set out. Let them remember that they are not only heralds but also witnesses of Christ. It is the task of a witness to pursue the truth and to report boldly and honestly what has been made known to him. Nor will a man be called a faithful witness who, to win men's favour, and overcome by whatever feeling, dares to obscure the truth. Furthermore, let them understand that the word of God has been entrusted to them, and that the Lord has appointed them as its heralds, not as authors of new doctrines. Let them therefore take to themselves what is said to Ezekiel, who is bidden to take the word from the mouth of the Lord (Ezek. 3). Nor let them think it allowed them to mix their own inventions with God's word. For what has chaff to do with wheat? (Jer. 23). Moreover, in all these things zeal is required, and unless they are inflamed by it they will bring forth no great fruit. Let them therefore imitate Christ, whom we see seizing every opportunity to teach and preach. Paul also testifies that he became all things to all men, so that he might win as many as possible to Christ (1 Cor. 9).

units.la: Cæterùm hīs nouam (vt initiò monuimus) historiam subijcit Lucas, qua euangelij doctrinam ad Æthiopes vsq; peruenisse docet, vnius quidem ministerio, sed quem non frustra laborauisse putamus, cùm summa illius esset apud eam gentem authoritas. Atqui hīc luculentissimè implctur, quod de Æthiopibus Christi regno subijciendis olim prædictum fuit. Vide Psal. 68. 72. & 87. Quia autem verè conuersionis exemplum historia hæc comprehendit, non piguit diuinum scriptorem omnes illius circunstantias exponere. Et in præsenti quidem, primùm de Philippo agit, cuius ministerio hac in re deus vti voluit. Mox verò diligenti prosopopœia Æthiopem, qui ad Christi fidem conuersus est, depingit. Tandem modum actionis, quæ inter hunc & Philippum intercessit, narrare incipit.
units.tr: Next, as we noted at the beginning, Luke adds a new narrative, which shows that the teaching of the gospel reached as far as the Ethiopians. This was done through the ministry of one man, but we think his labour was not in vain, since he had great authority among that people. Indeed, what was foretold long ago about the subjection of the Ethiopians to Christ's kingdom is fulfilled most clearly here (see Ps. 68, 72 and 87). And because this history contains a true example of conversion, the divine writer did not hesitate to set out all its circumstances. In the present passage he first speaks of Philip, through whose ministry God chose to act in this matter. Then, with a careful prosopopoeia, he portrays the Ethiopian who was converted to faith in Christ. Finally he begins to relate the manner of the dealings that took place between this man and Philip.

units.la: In Philippo, cuius opera Æthiops Eunuchus conuersus est, duo nobis obseruanda proponuntur. Vocatio nimirum specialis, qua illum præsenti negotio deus destinauit, & eiusdem obedientia, qua deum vocantem secutus est. Fuit autem valde illustris vocatio, cùm non parui momenti res esset, quæ ex dei ordinatione peragi debebat. Apparet enim Philippo angelus domini, & quid illi agendū sit, magna diligentia monet. Surge (inquit) & vade meridiem versus, ad viam, quæ descendit ab Hierusalem ad Gazam, &c. Et licet nondum disertè exprimát angelus, quid illic loci fieri debeat, facile tamen fuit Philippo coniicere, se ad magnum aliquod & diuinum opus vocari. Obiter autem de euangelij dignitate nos locus hic admonet, quando Philippum ad huius prædicationem per angelum vocari audimus. Cùm enim angelos ceu maiestatis suæ apparitores constituerit deus, quos in electorum suorum salutem (teste Paulo ad Hebr. 1. cap.) emittit, magnum & excellens esse oportet, quodcunq; illorum ministerio peragitur. Simul etiam salutis nostræ originem ad meram dei gratiam referri debere discimus. Vt enim is præsenti Eunucho nihil tale cogitanti, salutis præconem destinat: ita nobis quoq; salutis doctrinam plerunq; inopinantibus offerre consueuit. Quam dei gratiam ita nos agnoscere conuenit, ne quid nobis ipsis in salutis negotio insolentius tribuamus, quod diuinæ gratiæ maiestatem obscuret.
units.tr: In Philip, through whose work the Ethiopian eunuch was converted, two things are set before us to observe: namely, his special calling, by which God appointed him to this business, and his obedience, by which he followed God calling him. The calling was very remarkable, since the matter that was to be carried out by God's ordinance was of no small importance. For an angel of the Lord appears to Philip and carefully instructs him what he must do: "Rise," he says, "and go towards the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza," and so on. And although the angel does not yet clearly state what ought to be done there, Philip could easily guess that he was being called to some great and divine work. Incidentally, this passage reminds us of the dignity of the gospel, since we hear that Philip was called by an angel to preach it. For since God has appointed angels as the attendants of his majesty, whom he sends for the salvation of his elect (as Paul says in Heb. 1), whatever is accomplished by their ministry must be great and excellent. At the same time we learn that the origin of our salvation must be referred to God's pure grace. For just as he appoints a herald of salvation for this eunuch, who was thinking of no such thing, so he is accustomed to offer us the doctrine of salvation, often when we least expect it. We ought to acknowledge this grace of God in such a way that we do not presume on ourselves in the business of salvation, lest we obscure the majesty of divine grace.

units.la: Singularem verò laudem meretur Philippi obedientia, qui nec responsat angelo, nec diuini præcepti rationes curiosius inuestigat: sed omni mora abrupta eò pergit, quò iussus erat, deo iubenti omnem rei euentum permittens. Eandem à nobis etiam requiri credamus, ne dum Dei præcepta adnostræ rationis calculum reuocamus, primò quidem inepti cunctatores, mox verò etiâ temerarij transgressores efficiamur. Et quoties aliquid simpliciter mandat dominus, nec aliquam sui mandati rationem reddit, toties illum nostram obedientiam probare cogitemus, & ad illius studium generalibus promissionibus accendamur, quibus felices rerum successus in suis præceptis ambulantibus pollicetur. Huius studij exemplum in Abrahamo cernitur, qui patrio solo exire iussus, diuinæ vocationi obediendum esse putauit, quàmuis rerum suarū per omnia incertus esset. Gen.12. Quod vt felicißimè illi cessit: ita horrendis calamitatibus Saulem implicitum fuisse legimus, qui suæ potius rationis placita, quàm Dei præcepta obseruanda esse putabat. Vide 1.Sam.13.& 15.
units.tr: Philip's obedience deserves special praise: he neither answers the angel nor investigates the reasons for the divine command too curiously. Instead, with all delay set aside, he goes where he was bidden, leaving the outcome of the matter entirely to God, who commanded it. Let us believe that the same obedience is required of us as well, lest, while we weigh God's commands on the scales of our own reason, we become first foolish hesitators and then even rash transgressors. And whenever the Lord commands something plainly and gives no reason for his command, let us consider that he is testing our obedience, and let us be stirred to this eagerness by the general promises with which he assures happy outcomes to those who walk in his precepts. An example of this eagerness is seen in Abraham, who, bidden to leave his native land, thought he must obey the divine call, although he was completely uncertain about his affairs. (Gen. 12). As this turned out most happily for him, so we read that Saul was entangled in dreadful calamities, since he thought that the decisions of his own reason ought to be observed rather than the commands of God (see 1 Sam. 13 and 15).

units.la: Sed Æthiopem videamus, cuius diligens descriptio proponitur. Primò autem illius conditionem exprimit, quando Eunuchum fuisse ait, quo nomine Orientalium regum & reginarum aulici & ij cumprimis, qui illis à cubiculo fuerunt, vocatos fuisse constat, etiamsi non omnes castrati essent. Quare ad huius nominis expositionem facere videtur, quòd illam Δωάσλω, id est, principe, & totius regiæ gazæ præfectum fuisse dicit, quem nos supremum regni Quæstorem siue thesaurarium appellare possemus. Quibus satis patet, non vulgarem aliquem aulicum, sed è principum numero illum fuisse.
units.tr: But let us look at the Ethiopian, whose careful description is set before us. First, Luke describes his condition, when he says that he was a eunuch. It is well known that this name was given to the courtiers of Eastern kings and queens, and especially to those who were attendants of their bedchamber, even though not all of them were castrated. Therefore, to explain this title, it seems relevant that he is said to have been a dynast [δυνάστην], that is, a prince, and the chief officer over the whole royal treasury, whom we might call the chief treasurer or steward of the kingdom. From these details it is quite clear that he was not some ordinary courtier, but one of the number of the princes.

units.la: Docet autem locus hic, principes viros propter magistratum, quem gerunt, nequaquam à Christi regno excludi, sicuti Anabaptistæ seditiosi vociferantur. Tales enim Paulus Dei ministros esse, dissertè fatetur. Rom.13. Et multorum exempla extant, qui cùm in magistratu essent, Christi cognitione illuminati, nec tamen magistratu sese abdicare iussi sunt. Ex horum numero Josephus Hierosolymitanus Senator fuit, quem & Christi discipulum fuisse, & Christo sepulturæ honore pio officio impendisse, euangelistæ tradunt. Ita Cornelio Centurioni officio minimè interdicit Petrus Act.10. Et Sergio Paulo ad fidem conuerso Cypri proconsulatu fungi licuit. Act.13. Vanissimi ergo sunt Anabaptistarum clamores, quibus illi magistratum à Christianis hominibus geri posse, pertinaciter negant.
units.tr: This passage teaches that princes, because of the magistracy they hold, are by no means excluded from Christ's kingdom, as the seditious Anabaptists shout. For Paul openly confesses that such men are God's ministers. Rom. 13. And there are many examples of men who, while holding office, were enlightened by the knowledge of Christ, and yet were not ordered to give up their magistracy. Of this number Joseph of Arimathea, a senator of Jerusalem, was one, whom the evangelists tell us was both a disciple of Christ and rendered Christ the pious service of burial. So Peter does not forbid the centurion Cornelius his office, Acts 10. And Sergius Paulus, once converted to the faith, was allowed to hold the proconsulship of Cyprus. Acts 13. Therefore the clamours of the Anabaptists, by which they stubbornly deny that the magistracy can be exercised by Christian men, are most empty.

units.la: Deinde Eunuchi huius mores & studia duobus argumentis exponit. Nam illum Hierosolymâ ad adorandum ascendisse, & in itinere scripturæ sacræ lectioni intentum fuisse dicit. Licet ergo alienigena esset, aliquam tamen veri illius Dei cognitionem habuit, qui in Iudæa potissimùm priscis temporibus voluit innotescere, vt Psal.76. testatur. Nec illum inepta superstitione deceptum, religione locis certis inclusisse dicemus. Quia enim scripturarum studiosus fuit, externum cultum ad verbi diuini regulam reuocauit, quæ vnica est verę religionis ratio: & haud dubiè Dei promissionem respexit, qui tum Iudæorum tum alienigenarum preces se in templo hoc exauditurum esse, olim pollicitus fuerat. 1.Reg.8.cap. Cuius promissionis ratio in Christo Iesu fundata erat, cuius typum gerebant tam templum ipsum, quàm sacra, quæ in hoc peragebantur. Admonet nos autem Eunuchi exemplum, quæ principum studia esse debeant. Religionem sibi ante omnia curandam esse meminerunt. Eam verò non ex suo cerebro (vt olim Ieroboamum stabiliendæ tyrannidis studio fecisse legimus. 1.Reg.12.) sed ex Dei verbo instituant, cuius auditores simul & lectores diligentissimos esse illos conuenit. Dei enim ministros hos esse, supra dictum est. Idem illos suæ ecclesiæ nutritios constituit, vt propheta monet. Ifa.49. Is ipse illorum iudicijs & consessibus medijs interest. Psal.82. Et huic olim suæ administrationis rationem reddent: quæ ipsis nunquam solida & salua constare poterit, nisi religionis studio incensi, Dei verbum sibi ante omnia obseruandum esse statuant. Ideo legis epitomen olim rex penes se habere, & in eius lectione frequenter versari, iussus est. Deut.17. Et horum quidem studiosissimos fuisse constat omnes eos principes, qui laudem aliquâ coram Deo meruerunt, quales fuere Dauid, Solomon, Asa, Ezechias, Iofias, & post apostolorum tempora Constantinus, Theodosius, Carolus, & plures alij, quorum pietatem ecclesiarum & collegiorum fundationes passim bodie testantur. Iisdem studijs si hodie etiam occuparentur reges, & quotquot in magistratu sunt, selicius res Christianæ cederent. At quia in horum locum caeca libido, insanum aleæ studium, Sybaritica mensæ, venationes immodicæ, verbi Dei & sacrorum omnìù cõtemptus, & insatiabilis bellandi rabies successit, nihil ab eiusmodi principibus sperare licebit, quod vel publicæ saluti vel ecclesiarum reformationi & gloriæ Dei seruire possit.
units.tr: Next, Luke describes the character and pursuits of this eunuch in two respects. For he says that he had come up to Jerusalem to worship, and that on the journey he was occupied with the reading of Holy Scripture. Although he was a foreigner, he nevertheless had some knowledge of that true God who chose above all to make himself known in Judea in former times, as Psalm 76 testifies. Nor shall we say that he was deceived by foolish superstition and shut up religion in certain places. For because he was a diligent student of the Scriptures, he referred outward worship back to the rule of the divine Word, which is the only way of true religion; and without doubt he had regard to God's promise, who had long before pledged that he would hear the prayers of both Jews and foreigners in this temple. 1 Kings 8. The ground of this promise was laid in Christ Jesus, of whom both the temple itself and the sacred rites performed in it were a type. But the example of the eunuch warns us what the studies of princes ought to be. Let them remember that religion is to be looked after above all else. Let them establish it not from their own brain (as we read that Jeroboam did in his zeal to establish his tyranny, 1 Kings 12), but from the Word of God, of which they ought to be the most diligent hearers and readers at once. For it has been said above that these men are God's ministers. He also appoints them to be nursing fathers of his Church, as the prophet warns. Isa. 49. He himself is present at their judgments and meetings. Psalm 82. And to him they will one day render an account of their administration; it can never stand firm and safe for them unless, fired with zeal for religion, they resolve that the Word of God must be observed above all else. Therefore the king was ordered to keep a copy of the law by him and to be frequently occupied in reading it. Deut. 17. And it is plain that all those princes who have won some praise before God were most devoted to these studies: such as David, Solomon, Asa, Hezekiah, Josiah, and, after the time of the apostles, Constantine, Theodosius, Charlemagne, and many others, whose piety the foundations of churches and colleges bear witness to everywhere even today. If kings and all who hold office were occupied with these same studies today, the affairs of Christendom would turn out more happily. But since blind lust, a mad passion for dice, Sybarite tables, immoderate hunting, utter contempt for the Word of God and the sacred rites, and an insatiable rage for war have taken their place, nothing can be hoped from princes of this kind that could serve public welfare, the reform of the churches, or the glory of God.

units.la: His ipsam actionem, quæ Philippo cum Æthiope intercessit, Lucas subiungit. Iubetur enim Philippus ad currum propius accedere, iamq; spiritus domini bene agendi occasionem offert, quàmuis nuluis nullam hucusq; Philippus viderit. Nam vt propius accesserit, eunuchum Isaiae prophetae illustrem de Christo locum alta voce legentem audiuit, moxq; spiritu extimulatus, num locum hunc intelligat quaerit. Vbi parum ciuilis quibusdam videri poterat Philippus, qui & principis currui non vocatus appropinquat, & ignotum quaestione eiusmodi compellat, qua non obscure ignorantiam exprobrabat. Sed quia deo se totum addixerat, contemptis stolidae carnis rationibus, quicquid deus iubet, sedulò exequitur. Nec infeliciter cedit, quod ex Dei mandato facit. Nam insignia summae modestiae & humanitatis argumenta in peregrino principe deprehendit. Qui cum maximam occasionem haberet Philippum pro communi diuitum & principum more contumeliosis dictis propulsandi, modestissimè tamen & ignorantiam propriam fatetur, & quia arcano spiritus motu de Philippo praeclarius sentire incipit, illum ad se inuitat, & scripturae interpretem adiungit. Enimuero insignem laudem hic princeps meretur, dum nec proprij ingenij fiducia inflatus, interpretem alienum respuit, nec scripturas fastidit, quarum maximam partem abstrusiorem sentiebat, quàm vt abs se intelligi posset. Atqui tales verbi sui auditores Deus probat, qui humili mente praediti, ad verbum suum reuerenter contremiscunt. Isa.66. Interim docemur, scripturas interpretationibus illustrari oportere. Eas autem per homines Deus profert, qui spiritu illuminati, mutua illarum collatione & obseruata fidei analogia, sensus veros eruunt. Quod donum inter praecipua Paulus numerat. 1.Corinth.12.& 14. Ephes. 4. Vehementer ergo ineptiunt, qui revelationes coelitus expectant, & ecclesiae ministerium stolidè & impiè aspernantur. Imitemur nos eunuchi huius pietatem, modestiam, humilitatem & ardens salutis studium. Ita enim fiet, vt & ipsi salutis cognitionem veram assequamur in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke goes on to add to these the encounter that took place between Philip and the Ethiopian. For Philip is bidden to draw nearer to the chariot, and now the Spirit of the Lord offers him an opportunity to do good, although Philip had not seen the man before. For as he came closer he heard the eunuch reading aloud the notable passage about Christ from the prophet Isaiah, and at once, stirred by the Spirit, he asks whether he understands what he reads. Here Philip might seem to some rather lacking in courtesy: he approaches the prince's chariot without being invited, and he addresses a stranger with a question of this kind, which plainly reproaches him for his ignorance. But because he had given himself wholly to God, he disregarded the foolish reasoning of the flesh and diligently carried out whatever God commanded. Nor does it turn out unhappily that he did what was commanded by God. For he found in this foreign prince clear signs of the greatest modesty and courtesy. Although he had the greatest opportunity to repel Philip with insulting words, as is the common habit of the rich and powerful, he nevertheless most modestly confesses his own ignorance, and because by a hidden movement of the Spirit he begins to think more highly of Philip, he invites him to himself and takes him on as an interpreter of Scripture. Indeed this prince deserves remarkable praise, since, not puffed up with confidence in his own wit, he does not spurn an outside interpreter, nor does he scorn the Scriptures, most of which he felt were too obscure for him to understand by himself. Yet God approves such hearers of his word, who, endowed with a humble mind, tremble reverently at his word. Isa. 66. Meanwhile we are taught that the Scriptures ought to be made clear by interpretations. God brings these forth through men who, enlightened by the Spirit, bring out the true senses by comparing passages with one another and by observing the analogy of faith. Paul counts this gift among the chief ones. 1 Cor. 12 and 14; Eph. 4. Therefore those are very foolish who look for revelations from heaven and foolishly and impiously despise the ministry of the Church. Let us imitate this eunuch's piety, modesty, humility and ardent zeal for salvation. For in this way we too shall attain the true knowledge of salvation in Christ Jesus, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXI.
units.tr: Homily 61.

units.la: Porrò argumentū scripturae, quam legebat, erat hoc: Tanquam ouis ad mactationem ductus est, & tanquam agnus coram tondente se mutus: sic non aperuit os suum. In humilitate eius iudicium eius sublatum est. Generationem verò eius quis enarrabit? Quoniam tollitur de terra vita eius. Respondens autem Eunuchus Philippo, dixit: Quaeso te, de quo hoc dicit propheta? de seipso an de alio quopiam? Aperiens autem Philippus os suum, & exorsus à scriptura hac, praedicauit illi Iesum.
units.tr: The argument of the Scripture he was reading was this: "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation? For his life is taken from the earth." The eunuch answered Philip and said: "I ask you, of whom does the prophet say this? Of himself, or of some other man?" Then Philip opened his mouth, began from this Scripture, and preached Jesus to him.

units.la: Diuus Lucas Aethiopis ad Christum conuersi historiam diligentissimè describit, tum ob multas alias causas, tum quòd verae conuersionis exemplum continet, quo docemur, vt nobiscum Deus agat, quando in salutis consortium nos assumere instituit. Primò enim conuersionis huius causa efficiens Deus fuisse indicatur, qui ex mera gratia Philippum, cuius ministerio Aethiops Eunuchus conuerteretur, submisit. Idem ille, vt omnes credentes, nullo nostrorum operum respectu habito elegit, priusquàm mundi fundamenta iacerentur: ita per gratiam suam omnia ea subministrat, & saepe nihil tale cogitantibus submittit, quae saluti nostrae inserviunt. Deinde instrumentum conuersionis Philippus est, cuius opera hic pro suo more Deus vtitur. Quia enim maiestatem Dei nostra infirmitas ferre non potest, hominum ministerio nos doceri & duci vult; quod praecipuum est diuinae erga nos bonitatis argumentum, & proinde passim inter Dei beneficia primo loco numeratur. Organum verò, quo Philippus vetitur, Verbum Dei est, non quidem imaginarium quoddam & ineffabile (quale Seraphici quidam & fanatici Theologastri fingunt) sed illud ipsum, quod scripturis continetur. Ex ijs enim conciones sacrae & vniuersa salutis doctrina peti debent, nec nouum aliquod & inauditum hactenus doctrinae genus expectandum est. Inter omnia verò haec Eunuchi animus, ad veritatem & salutis doctrinam digne percipiendam rectè dispositus, elucet. Religionis enim studiosum fuisse, longinqua peregrinatio, laboris & periculi plena, abunde docet. Discendi cupiditatem diligens scriptura lectio arguit, & quod hominem ignotum sibi comitem iungit, ex quo veritatis vberiore cognitionem sperabat. Quae omnia illi ex diuina gratia obtigisse constat, cum in nemine mortalium haec apparearent, nisi singulari spiritus illuminatione aliquis illustretur. Sed ipsam actionem videamus; quam in praesenti Lucas describit, verbatim locum Isaiae recensens, qui Philippo occasionem praebuit cum Æthiope de salutis & Christi negotio disputandi.
units.tr: Saint Luke describes very carefully the history of the Ethiopian's conversion to Christ, both for many other reasons and because it contains an example of true conversion, by which we are taught how God deals with us when he determines to take us into fellowship of salvation. First, the efficient cause of this conversion is shown to be God, who, from pure grace, sent Philip, through whose ministry the Ethiopian eunuch was converted. The same God, as he chose all believers without regard to any of our works, before the foundations of the world were laid, so through his grace he supplies all those things that serve our salvation, and often sends them to us when we are thinking of nothing of the kind. Next, the instrument of the conversion is Philip, whom God, as is his custom, uses here. For since our weakness cannot bear the majesty of God, he wills that we be taught and led through the ministry of men. This is a chief proof of the divine goodness toward us, and therefore it is everywhere counted first among God's benefits. The organ through which Philip was moved is the Word of God, not some imaginary and unspeakable thing (such as certain seraphic and fanatical little theologians invent), but that very Word which is contained in the Scriptures. For sacred sermons and the whole doctrine of salvation ought to be sought from them, and no new and hitherto unheard-of kind of doctrine is to be looked for. Among all these things, the mind of the eunuch stands out, rightly disposed to receive the truth and the doctrine of salvation worthily. For that he was zealous for religion, his long journey, full of toil and danger, sufficiently shows. His careful reading of Scripture proves his eagerness to learn, and that he takes on as companion a man unknown to him, from whom he hoped for a fuller knowledge of the truth. It is clear that all these things came to him from divine grace, since they would not appear in any mortal unless he were enlightened by a singular illumination of the Spirit. But let us look at the action itself, which Luke describes here, quoting word for word the passage of Isaiah that gave Philip the occasion to dispute with the Ethiopian about salvation and the matter of Christ.

units.la: Extat is cap.53. nec vllus est alius, qui Christi Iesu mysteria euidentius comprehendat, ut non temere D. Hieronymus Isaiam Euangelistā potius quàm propheta adnumerandum esse iudicarit. Interim obseruanda est Dei prouidentia, quae res mortalium administrat, nec quicquam temere fieri finit: cuius argumentum euidens est, quod eo ipso temporis articulo, quo Philippus cum Æthiope colloqui incipit, in huius loci lectione hic incidisse dicitur. Hoc ethnicus aliquis fortunae casum aut contingentiam fuisse diceret. Sed nos Dei prouidentiam agnoscimus, quae non modo rerum euentus, sed reliqua quoq; omnia moderatur, quae ad hos spectant. Cur enim hominum res, quantumuis minutas, negligeret, qui capitis nostri pilos numeratos habet; quiq; caeli volucres pascit; & flores agri tam mirificè vestit? Porrò quoad Isaiae locum, vniuersam nostrae redemptionis rationem comprehendit. Explicat enim mortis Christi mysterium & victoriam, qua in patris gloriam ingressus, regnum immortale & aeternum acquisiuit. Praestat autem singula eo, quo dicuntur, ordine inspicere.
