units.tr: This is found in chapter 53, and there is no other passage that sets forth the mysteries of Christ Jesus more clearly; so Saint Jerome did not rashly judge that Isaiah should be counted rather an evangelist than a prophet. Meanwhile, we must observe the providence of God, which governs human affairs and allows nothing to happen by chance. The proof of this is plain: at the very moment when Philip began to talk with the Ethiopian, he is said to have fallen upon this passage in reading. A heathen might call this a chance or accident of fortune. But we acknowledge the providence of God, which governs not only the outcome of events but also all the other circumstances that pertain to them. For why would he neglect the affairs of men, however small, he who has numbered the hairs of our head, who feeds the birds of heaven, and clothes the flowers of the field so wonderfully? Moreover, as to the passage of Isaiah, it comprehends the whole plan of our redemption. For it explains the mystery and victory of the death of Christ, by which he entered into the glory of the Father and obtained an immortal and eternal kingdom. We should, however, examine each part in the order in which it is spoken.

units.la: Primò mortem Christi exponit, his verbis: Tanquam ouis ad mactationem ductus est, & tanquam agnus coram tondente se mutus. His autem non modò patientiam Christi exprimit, quae vt saepe alias, ita in passione & morte eluxit perfectissima: verumetiā illum sua sponte mortem subiturum esse docet, adeò vt nihil hic hostium consiliis aut viribus tribuendum sit. Consultarunt quidē ad versus illum sacerdotes & scribae. Prodendi illum occasionem feliciter captauit Iudas. Mortis reum pronunciauerunt Pontifices in Concilio. Pilatus damnatum virgis caedi, & in crucem affigi curauit. Quid verò omnes isti efficere potuissent, si diuinae suae potentiae & maiestatis vires proferre & exercere voluissent? Quis item illum è patris sinu in terras detraxerat? Quorum consiliis factum est, vt in virginis vtero incarnaretur? Quis illis resurgendi vires dedit, qui ad ipsum capiendum emissi, ad vnicam illius vocem supini conciderant? Docent ergo haec, ideo mortuum esse, quia mori voluit: quando non aliam ob causam in mundum venerat, quam vt animam suam daret pro mundi vita. Matthaei 20.cap. Quare cum hostium conatibus fortissimè resistere posset, instar ouis & agni duci voluit, vt ne verbo quidem aliquod impatientis animi & mortem detrectantis argumentum praebere videretur. Pertinet huc quod in euangelio dicit: Propterea me pater diligit, quia ego pono animam meam, vt iterum sumam eam. Nemo tollit eam à me, sed ego pono eam à meipso. Potestatem habeo ponendi eam, & potestatem habeo rursus iumendi eam, &c. Iohan.10. Et Paulus haec exponens, patri obedientem factum fuisse dicit vsque in mortem crucis, & serui formam assumpsisse, cùm esset in forma Dei. Phil.2. Porrò ista partim redemptioni & saluti nostrae, partim nostrae institutioni seruierunt. Ita enim nostrae inobedientiae culpam expiari oportuit, quae nos aeternae damnationi subiicerat. Praeterea suo exemplo patientiam & obedientiam in ferenda cruce nos docuit Christus, quemadmodum ipse frequenter in Euangelio admonet. Et Petrus in eandem sententiam scribit: Christus afflictus est pro nobis, relinquens nobis exemplum, vt insequamur vestigia ipsius, qui peccatum non fecerat, nec inuentus est dolus in ore illius: qui cum maledictis incesseretur, non regesserit maledicta: cùm malis afficeretur, non minabatur. 1.Pet.2.
units.tr: First, he sets forth the death of Christ in these words: "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent." By these words he expresses not only the patience of Christ, which shone forth most perfectly, as it often did elsewhere, in his passion and death, but he also teaches that he would undergo death of his own accord, so that nothing here is to be attributed to the counsels or strength of his enemies. True, the priests and scribes plotted against him. Judas seized eagerly the occasion to betray him. The chief priests in council pronounced him guilty of death. Pilate saw to it that he was condemned, scourged, and fastened to the cross. But what could all of them have accomplished if he had wished to bring forth and exercise the powers of his divine might and majesty? Or who had drawn him down from the Father's bosom to the earth? By whose counsels was it brought about that he was incarnate in the womb of the virgin? Who gave strength to those who were sent to seize him, so that they fell prostrate at his single word? These things therefore teach that he died because he willed to die, since he had come into the world for no other reason than to give his life as a ransom for the life of the world (Matt. 20). Therefore, since he could have resisted the attempts of his enemies most strongly, he willed to be led like a sheep and a lamb, so that he might not seem to give, even by a single word, any sign of an impatient spirit or of one who shrank from death. To this pertains what he says in the Gospel: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again," etc. (John 10). And Paul, explaining this, says that he became obedient to the Father, even to the death of the cross, and took the form of a servant, though he was in the form of God (Phil. 2). Moreover, these things served partly for our redemption and salvation, and partly for our instruction. For thus it was necessary that the guilt of our disobedience, which had made us liable to eternal damnation, be expiated. Besides, Christ taught us by his example to bear patience and obedience in bearing the cross, as he often reminds us in the Gospel. And Peter writes to the same effect: "Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in his steps; he who did no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth; who, when he was reviled, did not revile again; when he suffered, he did not threaten" (1 Pet. 2).

units.la: Caeterum morti Christi victoriam eiusdem, quam moriendo obtinuit, subijcit propheta, dicens: In humilitate eius iudicium sublatum est. Humilitatis nomine crucis & mortis conditio intelligitur, quae extremè humiliatum fuisse constat. Sensus ergo verborum est: Cùm omnino oppressus, adeoq; desperatus videretur, deus iusto suo iudicio illius casum attulit, et mortis satanaeq; victorē huc declarauit, qui iam victus esse putabatur. Conuenit hoc cū prima promissione, qua serpens Christi calcaneo insidiaturus esse dicitur, ita tamen, vt hic illius caput conterat. Gen.3. Idē Dauid fore praedixit, quando ait: De torrente in via bibet, ac propterea caput attollet. Psal.110. Quia enim mortis suae merito peccatum expiauit & sustulit, ipsam quoq; mortem exarmauit, quae propter peccatum in nos grassabatur, adeoq; omne diaboli tyrannidem euertit. Mox verò a mortuus resuscitatus, palàm ostendit, nihil in eis fuisse diabolo et morti, quapropter de omni aduersaria potestate gloriosissimè triumphauit. Quare vide 1.Cor.15.Col.2. Atqui haec illa gloria est, quā toties sibi à patre tribui postulat. Ioā.12.13.17. &c. Est autem cumprimis necessaria haec consyderatio. Nā fidei confirmandae feruit, ne vel Christi vel nostra cruce offendamur. Vt enim Christus per crucem in gloriam patris ingressus est, & propter nos mortuus & à mortuis resuscitatus est, vt se tam mortuorum quàm viuentium saluatorem & dominum esse testaretur: ita nos quoq; per mortem vincimus, & siue viuamus,siue moriamur,domini sumus. Rom.14. Et vt Christi causam deus asseruit, licet omnino oppressus videretur: sic idem ille suorum memoriam afferere & tueri consueuit, vt posteris illorum pietas testata sit, qui modò vt scelerati & malefici infamibus supplicijs excruciantur. Psal.34. Quo cùm prophetarum tum apostolorum exem-pla referri debent.
units.tr: Furthermore, the prophet adds to the death of Christ the victory which he obtained by dying, saying: "In his humiliation his judgment was taken away." By the name of humiliation is understood the condition of the cross and death, by which he was known to have been most deeply humbled. The sense of the words therefore is this: when he seemed altogether crushed, and so desperate, God, by his just judgment, brought about his fall, and declared him to be the conqueror of death and of Satan, who was thought already to have been conquered. This agrees with the first promise, in which the serpent is said to lie in wait for the heel of Christ, yet in such a way that he crushes its head (Gen. 3). David also foretold the same, when he said: "He shall drink of the brook in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head" (Ps. 110). For since by the merit of his death he expiated and took away sin, he also disarmed death itself, which raged against us because of sin, and so overthrew all the tyranny of the devil. Soon after, having been raised from the dead, he openly showed that there was nothing in them that belonged to the devil and to death; therefore he triumphed most gloriously over every hostile power. See therefore 1 Cor. 15 and Col. 2. Indeed, this is that glory which he so often asks the Father to give him (John 12, 13, 17, etc.). This consideration is especially necessary. For it serves to confirm faith, so that we are not offended either by the cross of Christ or by our own. For just as Christ entered into the glory of the Father through the cross, and died for us and was raised from the dead, so that he might testify that he is the Saviour and Lord both of the dead and of the living, so we too conquer through death, and whether we live or die, we are the Lord's (Rom. 14). And just as God vindicated the cause of Christ, though he seemed altogether crushed, so he is accustomed to defend and preserve the memory of his own people, so that their piety might be attested to posterity, even though these people are now tormented with infamous punishments as if they were wicked and criminals (Ps. 34). To this the examples of both the prophets and the apostles ought to be referred.

units.la: Porrò victoriam regnum sequitur,cui & æternitatem & ineffabilem potentiam tribuit,dicens: Generationem verò eius quis enarrabit? Generationis enim vocabulum, Hebræorum more,tum pro seculo alicuius hominis,tum pro posteritate sumi potest. Vtrunq; verò durabilem regni perpetui tatem notat. Nam Christi & regni ipsius seculum æternum esse angelus testatur,cùm Mariæ ait: Regni ipsius non erit finis. Luc.1. Similiter æterna quoq; est Christi posteritas. Qui enim per ipsum fili dei facti sunt,nunquam deficient. Et vt in terris semper erunt,quos ille pro Dei filijs & coheredibus agnoscit: ita ijdem hoc seculo exempti cum illo æternum viuent & regnabunt. Hæc enim extremæ ipsius voluntatis summa est, quam moriturus iam coram patre ratam esse voluit: Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo vt vbi sum ego,& illi sint mecum: vt videant gloriam meam,quam dedisti mihi,&c. Iohan. 14. & 17. De vtroq; verò nos spiritus sanctus per prophetam admonet,dicens: Semen Dauidis in æternum erit, solium eius coram me vt Sol perstabit. Firmum vt Luna manebit, quæ est perpetuus in æthere testis. Psalm. 89. Atqui hoc illud est, quo Christi regnum ab omnibus mundi regnis differt. Hæc enim omnia intereunt,nec ullum ex priscis illis ac opulentis.saluum restat,& quæ hodie florent, non obscuris argumentis excidia sua & ruinas præsagiunt. Possunt autem hinc duo colligi,quorum cognitio vtilissima est. Primò,ecclesiæ Christi perpetuitas,quæ ab ipsa mundi origine oppugnata,in hunc vsq; diem durat,& durabit vsque in consummationem seculorum, sicuti ille pollicitus est. Matth.28. Quo argumento nos aduersus omnes tyrannorum conatus consolari possumus. Deinde vitæ æternæ certitudo hinc patet,sine qua vanissimum est, quicquid de fide & religione traditur, sicuti Paulus de mortuorum resurrectione differens admonuit.1.Cor.15. Si enim Christi posteritas ineffabilis,& proinde æterna est,huius vitæ cursum alia vita, cœlesti nimirum & æterna,excipi oportet. Atq; sic ratum firmumq; manet,quòd Paulus nec vita nec morte nos à dei dilectione separari posse,dicit. Rom.8.
units.tr: Victory is followed by the kingdom, to which he also ascribes eternity and an unspeakable power, saying: "But who shall declare his generation?" The word "generation," in the Hebrew manner, can be taken either for the lifetime of a single person or for posterity. Both meanings signify the lasting character of a perpetual kingdom. For the angel bears witness that the age of Christ and of his kingdom is eternal, when he says to Mary: "Of his kingdom there shall be no end." Luke 1. Likewise the posterity of Christ is eternal. For those who have been made sons of God through him will never fail. And just as they will always be on earth, those whom he acknowledges as sons of God and fellow heirs, so these same people, freed from this age, will live and reign with him for ever. For this is the sum of his final will, which he wished to be ratified before the Father as he was about to die: "Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory, which you have given me," etc. John 14 and 17. The Holy Spirit warns us of both through the prophet, saying: "The seed of David shall endure for ever, and his throne shall stand before me like the sun. It shall be established for ever like the moon, which is a faithful witness in the sky." Psalm 89. This is indeed the point at which the kingdom of Christ differs from all the kingdoms of the world. For all these perish, and not one of those ancient and wealthy kingdoms remains intact; and those which flourish today, by no obscure signs, foretell their own downfall and ruin. Two things may be gathered from this, and knowledge of them is most useful. First, the perpetuity of the Church of Christ, which, though attacked from the very origin of the world, has endured to this day, and will endure until the consummation of the ages, as he promised. Matt. 28. By this argument we can console ourselves against all the attempts of tyrants. Second, the certainty of eternal life is made plain from this, without which whatever is taught about faith and religion is utterly vain, as Paul admonished when discussing the resurrection of the dead. 1 Cor. 15. For if the posterity of Christ is unspeakable, and therefore eternal, then the course of this life must be followed by another life, namely a heavenly and eternal one. And so it remains firm and sure that Paul says that neither life nor death can separate us from the love of God. Rom. 8.

units.la: At quia maximi momenti sunt,quæ de Christi victoria & regno dixit, causam illorum denuò repetit,quæ est: Quia tollitur de terra vita eius. Quid verò,si carnis iudicium audias,absurdius dici poterat? Christum victorem fore & perpetuò regnaturum dixit. Causam verò victoriæ & regni ac quisiti hanc subijcit,quòd illius vita de terra tolli & excindi debeat. Sed hoc cum prima promissione conuenire,supra diximus. Et Paulus loci huius fidelißimus interpres est,quando ait: Christus Iesus,cum esset in forma dei,non rapinam arbitratus est, vt esset æqualis deo, sed semetipsum exinaniuit,forma serui sumpta,in similitudine hominum constitutus, & figura repertus vt homo, humiliauit semetipsum,factus obediens vsq; ad mortem,mortem (inquam)crucis.Quapropter & deus illum in summam extulit sublimitatem, ac donauit illi nomen,quod est supra omne nomen, vt in nomine Iesu fleCtatur omne genu cœlestium ac terrestrium & infernorum, omnisq; lingua confiteatur, quòd dominus sit Iesus Christus,ad gloriam dei patris.Phil.2.Seruiunt verò hæc nostræ consolationi, ne morte offendamur. Vt enim Christum de terra excindi oportuit, vt victoriam & regnum in cœlis obtineret:ita in cœlis nos viuere & regnare impossibile est,nisi ipsi quoq; præsentem hanc vitam cum æterna permutemus. Oportet enim (vt Paulus ait) corruptibile hoc induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc immortalitatem sumere necesse est.1.Cor.15. Ea denique est nostræ cum Christo societatis ratio & ius,vt non alia via quàm per mortem,qua ipse ingressus est,vitam consequamur. Vnde apostolus dicit: Si commorimur,etiâ conuiuemus. Si susferimus,etiam conregnabimus.2. Tim.2. Nam filij sui conformes nos esse vult deus, vt qui cum illo patiuntur, vnâ cum illo glorificentur. Roman. octauo. Et hæc quidem in prophetici loci, quem Æthiops in manibus habuit, expositionem dicta sint.
units.tr: But because the things he said about the victory and kingdom of Christ are of the greatest importance, he repeats their cause, which is: "Because his life is taken from the earth." Yet what could be said more absurdly, if you listen to the judgement of the flesh? He said that Christ would be victor and would reign for ever. But he adds the cause of the victory and the kingdom and of what was sought, namely that his life must be taken from the earth and cut off. But we have said above that this agrees with the first promise. And Paul is the most faithful interpreter of this passage, when he says: "Christ Jesus, though he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Therefore God also exalted him to the highest place and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father." Phil. 2. These things serve our consolation, that we should not be offended by death. For just as it was necessary for Christ to be cut off from the earth in order to obtain victory and kingdom in heaven, so it is impossible for us to live and reign in heaven unless we also exchange this present life for the eternal. For (as Paul says) "this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." 1 Cor. 15. Finally, this is the principle and right of our fellowship with Christ, that we attain life by no other way than by death, through which he himself entered. Hence the apostle says: "If we die with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him." 2 Tim. 2. For God wishes us to be conformed to his Son, so that those who suffer with him may be glorified together with him. Rom. 8. These things have been said by way of explanation of the prophetic passage which the Ethiopian held in his hands.

units.la: Videamus nunc,vt inde occasione sumpta, Æthiops Christi cognitionem sit assecutus. Cùm enim ignorantiam suam paulò ante confessus esset,nunc de vero loci huius sensu serió interrogat. Quaso te
units.tr: Let us now see how, taking occasion from this, the Ethiopian came to the knowledge of Christ. For when he had a little before confessed his ignorance, now he earnestly asks about the true sense of this passage. I beseech you

units.la: Christi regnum eternum & inuictum.
units.tr: The eternal and unconquerable kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Mors ingressus ad Christi regnum.
units.tr: Death as the entrance to the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Eunuchi zelus, multa tamē adhuc ignorantis. (inquit) de quo haec dicit propheta? Est hoc magni zeli argumentum, quòd qui principis dignitate suspiciendus erat, vili & ignoto ante hac homunculo quodammodo supplex fit, vt scripturae sensum verum discat. Interim nō oscitanter praeteriri debet, quòd tanto religionis studio flagrans eunuchus, bucusq; ea ignorauit, quae salutis nostrae rationem omnem comprehendunt. Permittit hoc frequenter Deus, non quòd vel promissionum suarum immemor fit, vel nobis sui verbi notitiam inuideat: sed quòd dilatione eiusmodi maius discendi desyderium in nobis accendit, fidem nostram exercet, & suae sapientiae mysteria sublimiora esse docet, quàm vt humani ingenij captu atq; folertia apprehendi possint. Neminem ergo mora hac offendat: quin potius pergamus flagranti veritatis studio, & inuestigemus salutaria diuinae sapientiae mysteria, nec deerit promissus Iuis Christus, qui à quaerentibus inueniri cupit. Matth.7.
units.tr: The zeal of the eunuch, yet still much ignorant. "Of whom," he says, "does the prophet speak this?" It is a sign of great zeal that he, who ought to have been regarded for his princely dignity, becomes in a manner a suppliant before a poor and previously unknown little man, so that he may learn the true sense of Scripture. Meanwhile it must not be passed over carelessly that the eunuch, burning with such great zeal for religion, had until then been ignorant of those things which comprehend the whole reason of our salvation. God allows this often, not because he forgets his promises or begrudges us knowledge of his word, but because such delay kindles in us a greater desire to learn, exercises our faith, and teaches that the mysteries of his wisdom are too lofty to be grasped by the capacity and cleverness of the human mind. Let no one, therefore, be offended by this delay. Rather let us press on with an ardent zeal for the truth, and let us search out the saving mysteries of divine wisdom; nor will Christ be wanting, who has promised and who desires to be found by those who seek him. Matt. 7.

units.la: Simul verò Philippi facilitas obseruari debet, qui mox os aperit, id est, diligenter orditur de propheta loco orationem, qua ex hoc loco exorsus, quaerenti Aethiopi Christum Iesum praedicauit. Et verisimile est, ipsum omnia quoq; alia, quae eodem capite de Christo habentur, copiosè expositisse, & demonstrauisse, ea de solo Iesu Christo, dei & Mariae filio, intelligi debere. Hic autem duo obseruanda veniunt. Primum, quid praedicari debeat: Iesus Christus, & is quidem solus. Non quod huius nomen solum inepta iteratione subinde repeti & inculcari debeat: sed in vno hoc monstrari debent, quaecunq; ad nostram salutem faciunt. Quia hunc solum dedit pater, in quo nobis vera poenitentia & peccatorum remissio obtingit, quemadmodum supra Petrus docuit. Act.5. Et in illo solo vita salusq; inuenitur. Act.4. Quare inepti simul & falsi doctores sunt, quicunq; haec sine Christo docent, vel extra illum monstrant. Alterum est, quo admonemur, doctrinam & praedicationem Christi ex prophetarum libris desumi & discì posse. Imò inter externa omnia nihil aliud extat, quo illa probari possit. Fatetur hoc Christus, dum in Mose & prophetis ea contineri dicit, quae ipse nostrae salutis causa fecit & passus est. Luc.24. Idem in schola Nazarethana verae salutis & suijpsius cognitionem traditurus, Isaiae locum, qui cap.61. habetur, interpretandum sumit. Luc. 4. Impia ergo & execrabilis illorum ingratitudo est, qui veteris testamenti libros improbè contemnunt. Agnoscamus potius Dei gratiam, qui filij sui cognitionem tot tamq; luculentis testimonijs fulcire voluit, eandem verò inquiramus ardenti zelo, vt iuxta eunuchi exemplum, illa imbuti cum Christo regnemus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time the readiness of Philip must be noted, who at once opened his mouth, that is, began diligently with the prophetic passage, and from this text, taking his start, preached Christ Jesus to the Ethiopian who asked. And it is likely that he also fully expounded and demonstrated all the other things which are found about Christ in the same chapter, and that they must be understood of Jesus Christ alone, the Son of God and of Mary. Two things here deserve attention. First, what ought to be preached: Jesus Christ, and he alone. Not that his name alone should be repeatedly brought up and pressed in with foolish repetition; but in him alone should be shown everything that pertains to our salvation. For the Father has given him alone, in whom true repentance and forgiveness of sins are obtained for us, as Peter taught above. Acts 5. And in him alone life and salvation are found. Acts 4. Therefore those teachers are both foolish and false who teach these things without Christ, or point to them apart from him. The second thing is that we are admonished that the teaching and preaching of Christ can be drawn from the books of the prophets and learned there. Indeed, among all external things there is nothing else by which it can be proved. Christ himself acknowledges this, when he says that those things which he did and suffered for our salvation are contained in Moses and the prophets. Luke 24. Likewise in the school at Nazareth, about to deliver the knowledge of true salvation and of himself, he takes up for interpretation the passage of Isaiah which is found in chapter 61. Luke 4. Impious and detestable, therefore, is the ingratitude of those who shamelessly despise the books of the Old Testament. Let us rather acknowledge the grace of God, who wished to support the knowledge of his Son with so many and so clear testimonies, and let us seek the same with ardent zeal, so that, imbued with these things after the example of the eunuch, we may reign with Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXII.
units.tr: Homily 62.

units.la: Cum autem pergerent in via, venerunt ad quandam aquam. Et dixit Eunuchus: Ecce aqua, quid obstat, quo minus baptizer? Dixit autem Philippus: Si credis ex toto corde, licet. Et respondens ille, dixit: Credo filium Dei esse Iesum Christum. Et iussit sisti currum, ac descenderunt ambo in aquā, Philippus simul & Eunuchus, & baptizauit eum. Cum autem ascendissent ex aqua, spiritus domini rapuit Philippum, nec vidit eum amplius Eunuchus. Pergebat enim per viam suam gaudens. Philippus autem repertus est Azoti, & pertransiens euangelizabat omnibus ciuitatibus, donec veniret Caesaream.
units.tr: And as they went on their way, they came to a certain water. And the eunuch said: "See, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?" Philip said: "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught up Philip, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azotus, and passing through he preached the gospel in all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

units.la: Audiuit heri charitas vestra Diui Philippi concionem, qua Aethiopem Eunuchum converti. Desumpsit hanc ex Isaiae scriptis. Argumentum fuit Iesus Christus: cuius mysteria haud dubie diligenter expositum docens, hunc esse promissum humani generis saluatorem, in quo nobis Deus pater (vt Petrus supra admonuit) poenitentiam simul & remissionem peccatorum conferat. Sequitur nunc concionis huius effectus, qui in eo apparet, quòd Eunuchus, Christi cognitione imbutus, publicè illi in baptismo nomen dare, & externae ecclesiae visibili signo inseri & accenseri cupit. Quod nunquam fecisset, nisi mirificè in illius animo vim suam exeruisset dei spiritus, quem electis suis ille promisit. Videamus ergo Eunuchi huius baptismum, cuius descriptionem diligentissimam Lucas proponit, eò quòd singulae circunstantiae cum institutioni tum consolationi nostrae seruiunt.
units.tr: Yesterday your charity heard the sermon of Saint Philip, in which he converted the Ethiopian eunuch. He took it from the writings of Isaiah. Its subject was Jesus Christ, whose mysteries he expounded with great care, teaching that this is the promised Saviour of mankind, in whom God the Father (as Peter earlier reminded us) bestows both repentance and the forgiveness of sins. Now follows the effect of this sermon, which appears in the fact that the eunuch, imbued with the knowledge of Christ, desires to be publicly given his name in baptism and to be incorporated and enrolled in the visible external Church by its sign. He would never have done so unless the Spirit of God, whom he promised to his elect, had mightily exerted his power in his mind. Let us therefore look at the baptism of this eunuch, whose very careful description Luke sets before us, because each of its particular circumstances serves both our instruction and our comfort.

units.la: (Primus vero hic ipse Eunuchus prodit, qui cum Philippum de Christi mysterijs prolixè differentem audiuisset, & spiritus virtute animum suum illuminari trahiq, sentirèt, mox aqua confpetta, baptismum sibi conferri cupit. Est enim hæc ardentis defyderij vox: Ecce aqua, quid obstat, quò minus baptizer? Unde colligi potest, Philippum inter alia de baptismo quoque ex Christi institutione disseruisse, quo ille in fe credentes sibi consecrari, & in vnū ecclesiæ corpus cooptari vult: quo item beneficia sua nobis obsignat, vt olim in Circuncifione fieri consueuerat, sicuti Paulus tradidit. Roman. 4. cap. Quare cum Christum toto animo hausisset Eunuchus, sibi temperare non potest, quin ipse quoque fidem suam publicè profiteri, & Christi ecclesiæ folenni ceremonia adscribi velit. At qui hic nobis fidei ingenium obseruandum venit, in quo duo notabis. Primum, quòd illa nequaquam latere cupit: sed potius, postquam Christum animo concepit, & hominem totum Christi cognitione vera imbuit, palàm quoque sese exerere, & externa nominis professione ab alijs seiungi, Christo autem inferi & consecrari defyderat. Scit enim deum zelotem esse, qui in suis alterius religionis commercium non ferat. Scit Christum Iesum fibijpfi peculiarem populum è mundo selegisse, quem etiam sibi foli consecratum esse velit. Huius igitur ingenio sese accommodat, nec aliud perinde cupit, quàm vt omnibus conspicua fit, cum in solo Christo sibi gloriandum esse putet. Arguunt hæc ignauos nostri seculi hominum animos, quos Christi pudet, & qui fidem dissimulandam esse dicunt, sicubi ex illius confessione periculum aliquod oriri possit. Atqui multa erant, quæ Æthiopem, quò minus baptismo initiaretur, absterrere poterant, cum & reginam Candacem, & omnes suæ gentis homines à Christi cognitione alienifimos esse sciret, quæ res euidens illi cùm famæ tum fortunarum omnium periculum minabatur. Sed omnes remoras vincit & perrumpit viua Christi fide flagrans animus: cui iam baud dubiè per spiritus suggestionem inscripta erat Christi sententia: Quencunq, mei & sermonum meorum puduerit in generatione hac adultera & peccatrice, illius pudebit etiam filium hominis, vbi venerit in gloria patris fui cum angelis sanctis. Marc. 8. Deinde ad fidei ingenium illud quoq, pertinet, quod licet fe in Christo omnes diuinæ gratiæ thesauros & infallibilem salutis certitudinem habere intelligat Eunuchus, non tamen idcirco baptismi vsum inutilem aut superuacaneum esse putat. Nouit enim fides, nihil à Christo temere & inutiliter institui, cum hunc æternam Dei patris sapientiam esse agnoscat, in quo omnes scientiæ thesauri reconditi sunt. Colof. 1. & 2. cap. Nouit præterea nostræ carnis corruptionem multis indigere, & vix multis stimulis ad capessendam salutis viam fatis impelli posse. Vnde constat tam à Christi quàm fuijpfius cognitione alienifimos adhuc esse, quicunque sacramenta aspernari & fastidire solent. Nam licet in Christo per fidem consequamur, quæcunque nobis ad salutem necessaria sunt, prodest tamen propter carnis ingenium, vt dei beneficia externis quoq, signaculis obsignentur, & vt ijsdem nostri officij admoneamur, cuius alioqui frequenter obliuiscimur.
units.tr: First, the eunuch himself comes forward. When he had heard Philip speaking at length about the mysteries of Christ, and felt his mind being enlightened and drawn by the power of the Spirit, he at once, on seeing water, desires to be baptized. For this is the voice of an ardent desire: "See, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?" From this it can be gathered that Philip, among other things, also discoursed about baptism, according to Christ's institution, by which he wills that those who believe in him be consecrated to him and enrolled into the one body of the Church. Likewise by it he seals his benefits to us, as used to be done in circumcision, as Paul teaches (Rom. 4). Therefore, since the eunuch had drunk in Christ with his whole soul, he cannot restrain himself from wishing to profess his faith publicly too, and to be admitted to the solemn ceremony of Christ's Church. Here we must observe the character of his faith, in which two things are to be noted. First, that he by no means wishes to keep it hidden; rather, having conceived Christ in his heart and imbued his whole person with the true knowledge of Christ, he also wishes to show himself openly, to be set apart from others by an outward profession of the name, and to be given to Christ and consecrated to him. For he knows that God is a jealous God, who will not tolerate fellowship with another religion among his own. He knows that Jesus Christ has chosen for himself a peculiar people out of the world, which he wishes to be consecrated to himself alone. He therefore accommodates himself to this character of faith, and desires nothing so much as to be visible to all, since he thinks he must glory in Christ alone. These things reproach the cowardly spirits of the men of our age, who are ashamed of Christ, and who say that faith must be concealed wherever some danger might arise from its confession. Yet there were many things that could have deterred the Ethiopian from being initiated into baptism, since he knew that both Queen Candace and all the people of his nation were most alien to the knowledge of Christ, a fact which clearly threatened him with danger to both his reputation and all his fortunes. But a soul burning with the living faith in Christ overcomes and breaks through all these hindrances. For to it, without doubt, through the prompting of the Spirit, the saying of Christ had been written: "Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed, when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels" (Mark 8). Second, this also belongs to the character of his faith: although the eunuch understands that in Christ he has all the treasures of divine grace and an infallible certainty of salvation, he nevertheless does not therefore think the use of baptism useless or superfluous. For faith knows that Christ institutes nothing rashly or to no purpose, since it acknowledges him to be the eternal wisdom of God the Father, in whom all the treasures of knowledge are laid up (Col. 1 and 2). Faith knows, moreover, that our flesh's corruption needs many things, and can scarcely be driven by many goads to take up the way of salvation. Hence it is plain that those who are wont to scorn and despise the sacraments are still wholly alien both to the knowledge of Christ and to their own. For although in Christ we obtain by faith whatever is necessary for our salvation, it is nonetheless profitable, on account of the nature of the flesh, that God's benefits should be sealed also by outward signs, and that we should be reminded of the duty which otherwise we often forget.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque huius actus personam Lucas producit, Philippi nimirum, qui Eunucho non statim morem gerit, ne quid vel splendori vel humanitati ipsius tribuisse videatur: sed fidei veræ Confessionem ab illo requirit, dicens: Si credis ex toto corde, licet tibi baptismum recipere. Fidei ergo rationem habet, eamq, omnis fuci & subdolæ simulationis expertem esse vult. Quo exemplo admonemur, sacramenta non temere prophanari debere, sic nimirum, vt infidelibus communicentur. Quia enim fidei tessera & ecclesiæ Christi Symbola sunt, minimè decet, vt illis temere committantur, qui à fide & ecclesia sunt alieni: eò quòd tales ferè canes & porci sint, quibus margaritas proijcere Christus vetat. Matth. 7. Et fi Christi mandatum inspiciamus, patebit apostolos prius docere debuisse, & tunc demum baptizandos fuisse eos, qui doctrinæ fidem adhibebant. Ait enim: Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine patris, &c. Matth. 28. Nemo tamen nos Anabaptistarum furoribus patrocinari putet. Errant enim illi & perniciosè tumultuantur, dum quod in alienis & adultis obseruari debet, ad Christianorum infantes restringunt, eosq, à baptismo temere arcent. Etenim eos, qui antehac ab ecclesia Christi alieni fuerunt (quales olim Iudæi & gentes erant, hodie vero Iudæi & Turcæ alijq, eius farinæ homines sunt) minimè baptizandos esse dicimus, nisi baptismum nimis crassa impietate prophanare libeat, donec fidei suæ professionem edant. At lon-gè alia infantium, qui ex Christianis nascuntur, ratio est. Hi enim fœderis lege inter ecclesiæ filios fiue domesticos censentur. Iidem sancti sunt, & illos Christus sibi adduci vult. Eosdem quoq, deo platere constat, quandoquidem illorum angeli semper vident faciem patris. Et quamuis illorum condi-tionem nostrer captus assequi nequeat, Christus tamen illos fidem habere testatur, & eosdem spiritus sancti capaces esse, cum Iohannes Baptista, tum aliorum etiam exempla docent. Quare talibus bap-tismum negare, non vulgaris impietatis & audaciae plusquam Cyclopicae facinus est. Quia tamen de his alibi plura diximus, in praesenti paucula haec sufficiant.
units.tr: But Luke also brings forward the other person in this act, namely Philip, who does not immediately comply with the eunuch, lest he seem to have yielded to his rank or his humanity. Instead he requires from him a true confession of faith, saying: "If you believe with all your heart, you may receive baptism." He therefore has regard to faith, and wishes it to be free of all pretence and deceitful simulation. From this example we are warned that the sacraments must not be profaned rashly, so as to be communicated to unbelievers. For since they are the tokens of faith and the creeds of Christ's Church, it is by no means fitting that they be rashly entrusted to those who are alien from faith and Church, since such people are for the most part dogs and swine, to whom Christ forbids us to cast pearls (Matt. 7). And if we look at Christ's command, it will be clear that the apostles ought first to have taught, and only then to have baptized those who gave assent to the doctrine. For he says: "Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, etc." (Matt. 28). Yet let no one think we are defending the frenzies of the Anabaptists. For they err and riotously stir up trouble, while they restrict to the infants of Christians what ought to be observed in strangers and adults, and rashly bar those infants from baptism. For we say that those who were formerly alien from the Church of Christ (as the Jews and Gentiles once were, and today the Jews and Turks and other men of that stamp are) are by no means to be baptized, unless one wishes to profane baptism with gross impiety, until they make a profession of their faith. But the case of the infants who are born of Christians is entirely different. For by the law of the covenant they are counted among the sons, or household members, of the Church. They are holy, and Christ wishes them to be brought to him. It is also certain that they are pleasing to God, since their angels always see the face of the Father. And although our capacity cannot grasp their condition, Christ nevertheless testifies that they have faith, and that they are capable of the Holy Spirit, as the examples both of John the Baptist and of others also teach. Therefore to deny baptism to such children is no common impiety, and a deed of more than Cyclopean audacity. Yet since we have said more about these matters elsewhere, these few words will suffice here.

units.la: Porro audiamus Eunuchi confessionem, quae mira brevitate res maximas comprehendit. Credo (inquit) filium Dei esse Iesum Christum. Similis est haec confessio ei, quam Petrus omnium apostolorum nomine fecisse legitur. Matth. 16. Iohan. 6. Tribuit autem Christo, quaecunque de hoc sacris literis traduntur. Imo, si penitius rem inspicias, omnes fidei nostrae sive Symboli apostolici articulos comprehendit. Nam deum agnoscit, eum haud dubie, quem caeli & terrae creatorem scripturae esse docent. Non autem eiusmodi fatetur, qualem Iudaei & Turcae somniant, sed talem agnoscit, qui filium habeat ex se genitum, sibi coaeternum & consubstantiale. Filii huius incarnationem credit, ut ex iis, quae apud Isaiam legerat, colligere licet. Adhaec filium dei, Christum, id est, unctum esse fatetur. Quo nomine & sacerdotium & regnum illius comprehendit. Ad sacerdotium vero tota Christi passio pertinet, qua corporis & sanguinis sui hostiam pro totius mundi peccatis immolavit. Regni autem titulo gloriosa eiusdem resurrectio continetur, qua mortem devicit: ascensio item, qua coelos ingressus est: & sessio ad dextram patris, quae illum regem potentissimum declarat, cui omnis potestas data sit in coelo & in terris, quique olim ad iudicium vniuersae carnis sit venturus. At qui regem agnoscit Christum, idem hunc ecclesiam habere fateatur oportet, in qua regnet. Est haec omnium sanctorum communio, cui inaestimabiles thesauros suos Christus concredidit, remissionem scelicet peccatorum, carnis resurrectionem & aeternae vitae consortium. Haec (inquam) mysteria breviis haec Eunuchi confessio comprehendit. Qua docemur, qualem nos quoque Christum agnoscere & fateri debeamus. In primis vero observandum, quod fidei cordis confessionem oris coniungi videmus. Duo enim haec necessario coniungi oportere, supra quoque monuimus, & Paulus diserte monet, cum inquit: Hoc est verbum fidei, quod praedicamus: Nempe si confessus fueris ore tuo dominum Iesum, & credideris in corde tuo, quod Deus illum excitavit a mortuis, salvus eris. Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Rom. 10.
units.tr: Next let us hear the eunuch's confession, which comprehends the greatest matters in wonderful brevity. "I believe," he says, "that Jesus Christ is the Son of God." This confession is similar to the one which Peter is read to have made in the name of all the apostles (Matt. 16; John 6). It ascribes to Christ whatever the sacred writings deliver concerning him. Indeed, if you look into the matter more deeply, it embraces all the articles of our faith, or of the Apostles' Creed. For it acknowledges God, undoubtedly the one whom the Scriptures teach to be the Creator of heaven and earth. Yet it confesses him not in the way that the Jews and Turks dream, but as one who has a Son begotten of himself, coeternal and consubstantial with himself. It believes in the incarnation of this Son, as can be gathered from what he had read in Isaiah. Moreover, it confesses the Son of God to be Christ, that is, anointed. By this title his priesthood and his kingship are comprehended. To the priesthood belongs the whole passion of Christ, by which he offered up the sacrifice of his body and blood for the sins of the whole world. The title of king contains his glorious resurrection, by which he conquered death; likewise his ascension, by which he entered the heavens; and his sitting at the right hand of the Father, which declares him the most mighty king, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, and who will one day come to judge all flesh. But whoever acknowledges Christ as king must also confess that he has a Church in which he reigns. This is the communion of all the saints, to which Christ has entrusted his inestimable treasures, namely the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and fellowship in eternal life. These mysteries, I say, this brief confession of the eunuch comprehends. By it we are taught what kind of Christ we too ought to acknowledge and confess. Above all, we must observe that we see the confession of the heart joined with the confession of the mouth. For we have also reminded you above that these two must necessarily be joined, and Paul plainly warns of this when he says: "This is the word of faith which we preach: namely, if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom. 10).

units.la: Ubi vero Philippus, quod unicum cupiebat, ab Eunucho elicuit, mox omni mora abrupta, cum illo in aquam descendit, & ibi illum baptizat. Quo loco observare conuenit, quod aqua communi baptismus confertur, sive ille fluvius, sive fons (ut Hieronymo placuit) fuerit. Nec aliqua fit vel nova consecrationis, vel asperssi salis & chrismatis, vel exorcismi mentio, qualia multa posterioribus seculis Pontificum superstitio inuexit. Noverat enim Philippus Iohannis exemplum, qui in Iordanis flumine baptizarat. Sciebat item Christi institutione omnem aquam ad baptismi usum consecratam esse, nec novis expiationibus sive exorcismis indigere. Procul ergo facessant impiae simul & ineptae audacissimorum hominum adinuentiones, qui religione honoris privati & quaestus aucupium esse voluerunt. Interim nemo ex huiusmodi exemplis occasionem sumat, passim in fontibus aut fluminibus baptizandi. Nam ut hoc pie fieri scimus, si ita suadeat rei necessitas: ita ubi ecclesiae constitutae sunt, omnia decenter & legitimo ordine administrari debent, ne in effrenem licentiam erumpens libertas, ecclesiarum cum disciplinam tum unitatem dissipet. 1. Corinth. 14.
units.tr: But when Philip had drawn from the Eunuch the one thing he desired, he at once broke off all delay, went down with him into the water, and baptized him there. At this point it is fitting to observe that baptism is conferred with ordinary water, whether it was a river or a spring (as Jerome thought). There is no mention of any new consecration, of sprinkling with salt and chrism, or of exorcism, which the superstition of the Popes introduced in great number in later centuries. For Philip knew the example of John, who had baptized in the river Jordan. He also knew that by Christ's institution all water is consecrated for the use of baptism, and that it does not need new expiations or exorcisms. Let the impious and foolish inventions of the most audacious men, who wished it to be a matter of private honour in religion and a means of seeking gain, depart far from us. Meanwhile, let no one take occasion from such examples to baptize at random in springs or rivers. For as we know this may be done devoutly, if the necessity of the situation so requires, so where churches have been established, everything ought to be administered becomingly and in good order, lest liberty, bursting into unbridled licence, scatter both the discipline and the unity of the churches. 1 Corinthians 14.

units.la: Restat totius historiae Catastrophe, quae Philippi ab Eunucho discessum comprehendit, quem miraculosum fuisse, Lucas docet. Nam cum ex aqua ascenderent, spiritus domini rapuit Philippum, nec vidit illum amplius Eunuchus. Voluit autem illius fidem hoc miraculo confirmare dominus. Ita enim intelligere poterat, nihil in tota actione hac fortuito contigisse, sed divina providentia esse omnia administrata. Interim quid vterq; postquam disiuncti fuerunt, fecerit, videamus.
units.tr: There remains the conclusion of the whole history, which covers Philip's departure from the Eunuch, and Luke teaches that it was miraculous. For when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the Eunuch saw him no more. The Lord wished to confirm the Eunuch's faith by this miracle. For in this way he could understand that nothing in the whole transaction had happened by chance, but that all had been ordered by divine providence. Meanwhile, let us see what each of them did after they were separated.

units.la: Eunuchus (inquit Lucas) pergebat per viam suam gaudens. Non ergo de Philippi repenti no discessu improbe conquestus est, nec eundem anxie quaesuit, & multo minus illum ut praesentem aliquem detestatus est. Id vero nec ingrati nec levis animi argumentum putari debet. Sed quia fide donatus, spiritu sancto doctore iam utebatur, qui illi iuxta Christi promissionem suggerebat omnia, suoque testimonio fidei doctrinam a Philippo traditam confirmabat, animo suo facile conquiescere poterat. Quo exemplo docemur, non ita ministris inhaerendum esse, ut illis sublatis de fidei causa desperemus. Agnoscamus hos Dei cooperarios esse, per quos ille fidem nobis largitur, & mysteriorum Dei dispensatores. 1. Corinth. 3. & 4. Rursum intelligamus, spiritum Christi doctoris officio verissime fungi, nec nobis defuturum Christum, etiamsi eos interdum auferat, quibus nos quam plurimum debere scimus. Nec enim personis aut locis alligari potest Dei spiritus, qui ubicunque voluerit, spirat. Iohan. 3.
units.tr: The Eunuch (Luke says) went on his way rejoicing. He therefore did not complain bitterly of Philip's sudden departure, nor anxiously seek him, and much less did he rage against him as if he were still present. This ought not to be taken as a sign of an ungrateful or fickle mind. Rather, since he had been given faith and now had the Holy Spirit as his teacher, who, according to Christ's promise, suggested all things to him and confirmed by his own witness the doctrine delivered by Philip, he could easily find rest in his own mind. From this example we are taught not to cling so closely to the ministers that we despair of the cause of faith when they are taken away. Let us acknowledge that these men are God's fellow-workers, through whom he bestows faith upon us, and the stewards of God's mysteries. 1 Corinthians 3 and 4. Again, let us understand that the Spirit of Christ performs the office of teacher most truly, and that Christ will not be lacking to us, even if he sometimes takes away those to whom we know we owe so very much. For God's Spirit cannot be bound to persons or places; he breathes where he wills. John 3.

units.la: Simul vero fidei fructus, quem Eunuchus retulit, indicatur, quando illum laetum & gaudio perfusum in cepto itinere perrexisse, dicit Lucas. Ita supra Samariae ingens gaudium obortum fuisse scripsit, quando in ea urbe euangelium Philippus praedicauit. Intelligi vero debet fidelis mentis gaudium, quod ex conscientiarum pace enasci consueuit. Postquam enim Christus per fidem receptus est, Deum patrem sibi reconciliatum esse homo intelligit, cuius iram & horribile iudicium antea pertimescebat. Ut vero pax illa Dei (Paulo teste, Phil. 4.) vincit omnem intellectum: ita omnes quoque tristitiae nebulas pellit, animum totum serenat, & in mediis afflictionibus intrepidum reddit. Omnium enim fidelium vox est: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat, quis ille qui condemnet? Rom. 8. Norunt enim nec inferorum portas Christo, petrae viventi, cui illi innituntur, praevalere posse. Hanc ergo tranquillae mentis fiduciam quia Eunuchus affectus est, maiori laetitia perfusus domum properat, quam si maximos regum thesauros acquisiuisset, aut superatis Aethiopici regni hostibus, triumphans ad Candacem fuisset reuersus. Quae enim divitiae cum caelestis regni thesauris conferri merentur? Aut quae tam praeclara victoria est, quam ea, quae fidelibus cum Christo Iesu aduersus satanam & inferos commune est? Hanc si tanto desyderio affectarent principes, quanto ardore pro mundi regnis & inani gloria hodie belligerantur, & ipsi maiori gaudio exultarent, et melius haberent vniuersae res mortalium.
units.tr: At the same time, the fruit of faith which the Eunuch showed is indicated, when Luke says that he went on his begun journey glad and filled with joy. So too he wrote that great joy arose in Samaria when Philip preached the gospel in that city. But we should understand this as the joy of a faithful mind, which is wont to be born from peace of conscience. For once Christ has been received through faith, a man understands that God the Father has been reconciled to him, whose anger and dreadful judgment he had feared before. Now that peace of God (as Paul witnesses, Philippians 4) surpasses all understanding; so it also drives away all clouds of sadness, makes the whole mind serene, and renders it fearless in the midst of afflictions. For the voice of all the faithful is: "If God is for us, who is against us? Who will bring charges against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns?" Romans 8. For they know that the gates of hell cannot prevail against Christ, the living rock, on whom they rest. Therefore, because the Eunuch was moved by this confidence of a tranquil mind, he hastens home filled with greater gladness than if he had gained the greatest treasures of kings, or, having overcome the enemies of the Ethiopian kingdom, had returned triumphant to Candace. For what riches deserve to be compared with the treasures of the heavenly kingdom? Or what victory is so splendid as that which the faithful share with Christ Jesus against Satan and the powers of hell? If princes aspired to this with as great a desire as they now wage war for the kingdoms of the world and empty glory, they would themselves exult with greater joy, and the affairs of mortals would be in a better state.

units.la: Sed ad Philippum redeamus, qui repertus est Azoti, & inde maritimam oram obambulans vniuersis in eo tractu ciuitatibus euangelium praedicauit, Caesaream usque, vbi domicilium collocauisse videtur, cum apud eum Paulus illic diuertit, sicuti Cap. 21. videbimus. Obseruabis vero diligenter ardens & indefessum primitiuae ecclesiae hominum in propagando Christi regno studium. Quamuis enim Philippus in conuertenda Samaria multum laborauisset, & iam de conuerso Aethiope principe gloriari posset, nondum tamen suo se officio defunctum putat, sed nouos labores ipse sibi imponit, nec noua detrectat pro Christo subire pericula. Idem studium in Paulo cernitur, qui cum plus omnibus apostolis laborasset, indefinenti tamen ardore pergit. Vide 1. Cor. 15. 2. Cor. 11. Rom. 15.
units.tr: But let us return to Philip, who was found at Azotus, and from there, walking along the coast, preached the gospel in all the cities of that region, as far as Caesarea, where he seems to have settled his home, when Paul stayed with him there, as we shall see in chapter 21. Now you will observe carefully the ardent and tireless zeal of the men of the primitive Church in spreading the kingdom of Christ. For although Philip had laboured much in converting Samaria, and could already boast of the Ethiopian prince he had converted, he does not yet think he has discharged his duty, but imposes new labours upon himself, and does not shrink from undertaking new dangers for Christ. The same zeal is seen in Paul, who, though he had laboured more than all the apostles, nevertheless pressed on with unfailing ardour. See 1 Corinthians 15, 2 Corinthians 11, Romans 15.

units.la: Arguunt haec nostri seculi ignauiam, quando omnes hominum ordines, vt primum paucula quaedam perpessi sunt, ipsi sibi ferias indicunt: quasi vero nostri arbitrij & iuris sit, a Dei vocatione & commisso nobis officio discedere. Praeterea docent haec quam irriti impiorum aduersus Christi doctrinam conatus sint. Quo magis enim illi furunt, eo magis glisicit & vincit veritas. Imo in persecutionibus eorum opera fere omnibus conspicua fit, qui antea ignaui & ignobiles habebantur. Exemplum huius in Philippo habetur, cuius nulla fere mentio facta fuit, cum Hierosolymis tuto ageret ecclesia: nisi quod inter diaconos adnumeratum fuisse audiuimus: At idem nunc extorris & exul factus, Samariam Christo lucrifacit, Aethiopiae apostolum emittit Eunuchum, quem ipse conuerterat, & totam Palestinam euangelij praedicatione percurrit. Ita hostium suorum conatus eludere solet deus. Quare neminem tyrannorum minae offendere debent, quibus illi hodie euangelio & ecclesijs nostris excidium denunciant. Quin potius in Deo speremus, qui electos suos tum in hoc seculo seruare, tum in altero Christi sui cohaeredes efficere potest: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: These things expose the sloth of our age, when all orders of men, as soon as they have suffered a few small trials, declare holidays for themselves, as if it were in our power and right to depart from God's calling and the office committed to us. Besides, these things teach how futile the attempts of the impious against the doctrine of Christ are. For the more they rage, the more the truth shines forth and prevails. Indeed, in their persecutions the work of those who were previously regarded as idle and ignoble becomes conspicuous almost to everyone. An example of this is found in Philip, of whom almost no mention was made while the Church was safely at work in Jerusalem, except that we hear he was counted among the deacons. But now, made an exile and a fugitive, he wins Samaria for Christ, sends forth the Eunuch, whom he himself had converted, as apostle to Ethiopia, and runs through all Palestine with the preaching of the gospel. Thus God is wont to frustrate the attempts of his enemies. Therefore the threats of tyrants, with which they today threaten the gospel and our churches with destruction, ought to offend no one. Rather let us hope in God, who can both preserve his elect in this age and make them co-heirs of his Christ in the next, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIII.

units.la: SAulus autem adhuc spirans minas & caedem aduersus discipulos domini, veniens ad summum Sacerdotem, petijt ab eo epistolas Damascum ad synagogas, vt si quos inueniret huius sectae, seu viros seu mulieres, vinctos duceret Hierosolymam. Cum autem iter faceret, accidit ut appropinquaret Damasco: & repente circumfulgurauit illum lux è coelo, & collapsus in terram, audiuit vocem, dicentem sibi: Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris? Dixit autem: Quis es Domine? Dominus autem dixit: Ego sum Iesus, quem tu persequeris. Durum est tibi contra stimulum calcitrare.
units.tr: Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any followers of this sect, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he journeyed, it happened that he drew near to Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" He said, "Who are you, Lord?" The Lord said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad." (Acts 9:3–5; cf. 26:14)

units.la: Emorabilis illa Iesu Christi vox est: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Iohan.6. Nec illi absimilis est, qua alibi discipulis dicit: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Iohan.15. Docet enim utraque salutem & quaecunque ad hanc faciunt, ex mera Dei gratia hominibus contingere, nec quicquam nostris operibus sive meritis esse tribuendum. Suns autem eius rei multa exempla, inter quae cumprimis insigne, quod nuper in Aethiope vidimus, cui Philippus, verae salutis praeco, ut cogitanti quidem nedum quaerenti, mero Dei beneficio submittitur. Quia tamen praeclaris aliquot virtutibus illum floruisse dictum est, ne quis illarum merito illi salutem obtigisse putaret, commodè illius conversioni, Sauli ad Christum conversi historia subiicitur, quem invitum & reluctantem, imo acerrimum fidei hostem, Christus Iesus ad salutem non modo invitat & trahit, sed (ut in parabola de quibusdam dicitur, Luc.14.) intrare compellit. Et sane historiam hanc omnem ita narrat Lucas, ut nihil hic hominis merito, sed solius gratiae Dei beneficio Sauli salutem tribuendam esse, quius videat. Sed & ipse Paulus diserte monet, ad hunc finem exemplum hoc potissimum referri debere, cum se ideo in medijs institutae contra ecclesiam tyrannidis conatibus interceptum & vocatum esse scribit, ut in ipso primo ostenderet Iesus Christus omnem clementiam, ad exprimendum exemplar ijs, qui credituri sunt. 1. Tim.1. Et alias se apostoli nomine indignum esse fatetur, si ipsius meritum spectes, Dei autem gratia esse quicquid est. 1. Cor.15. Caeterum cum multa huic historiae insint scitu & consyderatu dignissima, singulas eius partes inspicere prodest. Et in praesenti, primo quidem Sauli descriptionem proponit Lucas, deinde conversionis ipsius historiam orditur.
units.tr: That memorable saying of Jesus Christ is: "No one can come to me unless my Father draws him." (John 6:44) It is not unlike the other saying, which he addresses to the disciples elsewhere: "You did not choose me, but I chose you." (John 15:16) For both teach that salvation, and everything that pertains to it, comes to men from the pure grace of God, and that nothing is to be ascribed to our works or merits. There are many examples of this, among which is especially notable the one we saw recently in the Ethiopian, to whom Philip, the herald of true salvation, was sent by the mere benefit of God, though he was not thinking of it, let alone seeking it. But because it has been said that this man flourished in several outstanding virtues, lest anyone should think that salvation came to him on account of those merits, the story of Saul's conversion to Christ is fittingly added. Christ Jesus invites and draws him to salvation, though he was unwilling and resisting, indeed the fiercest enemy of the faith; and he compels him to come in, as is said in the parable about certain people (Luke 14:23). And Luke narrates this whole story in such a way that anyone can see that Saul's salvation is to be attributed to nothing in man's merit, but solely to the benefit of God's grace. Paul himself also plainly warns that this example ought to be referred to this end above all: he writes that he was stopped and called in the middle of his attempts at tyranny against the Church, so that Jesus Christ might first show in him all his mercy, as a pattern for those who would believe (1 Tim. 1:16). Elsewhere too he confesses that he is unworthy of the name of apostle, if you look at his own merit, but that whatever he is, he is by the grace of God (1 Cor. 15:9–10). Yet since this story contains many things most worthy of knowledge and consideration, it is useful to examine its individual parts. At present, Luke first sets out a description of Saul, and then begins the account of his conversion itself.

units.la: Diligens autem est in Saulo describendo Lucas, eò quòd ex illius descriptione Dei tum potentiae tum bonitas euidentius cognoscitur. Primùm enim ingenium eius & naturam exprimit, cum illum minas & caedem spirauisse dicit. Animo igitur in ecclesiam infenso & inflammato fuit, cuius speciem iam ante in Stephani lapidatione dederat, & cum Hierosolymis ecclesiam omnem vastaret, ut supra dictum est. Nunc tamen, vbi se nihil proficere, ecclesiam verò quotidie latius propagari videt, immanem toto animo furorem concipit, ut iam nihil aliud quàm atroces minas, sanguinarias caedes & excidia spirare & somniare possit. Ea enim (ut supra quoq; monuimus) tyrannorum & hostium ecclesiae natura est, ut postquam semel gustarunt piorum sanguinem, magis furant, adeoq; belluarum instar omnem humanitatis sensum exuant, nec ponere possint semel conceptam animorum rabiem, nisi potenti dei manu cicurentur. Exempla huius saeuitiae passim in historijs occurrunt. Eò autem nobis seruire debet illorum consyderatio, ut quid de nostri seculi tyrannis sperari debeat, intelligamus, quos sanctorum sanguinis iam adhuc videmus, ut hunc maiori truculentia quàm ullae tygrides sitiant. Quos certè, nisi dominus cicurauerit, nullae humanae aut vires aut rationes mansuefacere poterunt.
units.tr: Luke is careful in describing Saul, because from that description the power and goodness of God are more clearly known. First he expresses Saul's character and nature, when he says that Saul was breathing threats and slaughter. He was therefore hostile to the Church and inflamed in mind; he had already shown this in the stoning of Stephen, and when he was ravaging the whole Church at Jerusalem, as was said above. Now, however, when he sees that he is making no headway, and that the Church is spreading more widely every day, he conceives a monstrous fury with his whole soul, so that he can now breathe and dream of nothing but savage threats, bloody murders, and destruction. For this is (as we also noted above) the nature of tyrants and enemies of the Church: once they have tasted the blood of the godly, they rage all the more, and, like wild beasts, they cast off every feeling of humanity. Nor can they put down the rage once conceived in their minds, unless they are tamed by the mighty hand of God. Examples of this savagery occur everywhere in histories. Yet the consideration of these examples ought to serve us, so that we may understand what should be expected from the tyrants of our own age, whom we already see thirsting for the blood of the saints with greater ferocity than any tigresses. Certainly, unless the Lord tames them, no human powers or plans will be able to make them gentle.

units.la: At quia animi furorem armis instructum esse oportebat, de his quoq; sibi Saulus profexit. Summum enim sacerdotem accessisse dicitur, à quo literas accepit ad Damasci synagogas, quibus illi plena potestas dabatur, quosvis vinciendi, quos Christiani nominis cultores esse inueniisset. Vnde colligimus, religionis causam à Romanis praesidibus illo tempore summis sacerdotibus commissam fuisse. Quia enim illi gentilicia superstitione excaecati erant, credibile est, illos quotidianis de religione controuersijs statim fatigatos fuisse, et vias omnes quaesiuisse, quibus & molestijs eiusmodi sese liberarent, & inuidiam odiumq; plebis in alios deriuarent. Fuit autem occasio haec sacerdotibus exoptatissima, quorum quaestus & honor euangelij praedicatione in periculum vocabatur. Horum ergo authoritate munitus Saulus, adhibitis etiam satellitibus, sceleris ministris, Damascum pergit, eam mimirum ob causam, quòd illic Christi regnum mirifice surgere & florere sciret. Admonet autem locus hic acerrimos semper veræ religionis & doctrinæ Christianæ hostes fore antistites, quorum studio & diligentia hanc prouehi oportebat. Vt primum enim isti religionem quæstum faciunt, veritatis lucem, quæ ipsorum arguitur nequitia, ferre non possunt. Tales vero istos fuisse, ex evangelica historia notius est, quam ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Quid ergo de nostri seculi præsulibus spe-remus, facile videbit, qui illorum avaritiam & ambitionem observauerit. Interim principum & magistratuum prophana ignauia obseruanda venit, qui cum religionem non magni faciant, eius nomine inuidiam vel odium sibi conflare nolunt. Ne vero pro impijs & alienis a religione videantur, illius causam episcopus & Cardinalibus committunt, eo prætextu & summam pietatis exist-imatione captantes, & excusationem quærentes, si quis illos veritatis persecutores esse dicat. Nec enim ad se pertinere dicunt eiusmodi controversias, nec magis pie se facere posse sibi persuadent, quam si negotium hoc omne ecclesiarum præsidibus committant. In qua sententia a personatis episcopis mirifice confirmantur. Ita enim illi omnem de religione iudicandi potestatem sibi vendicant, quorum ambitio & avaritia pejus iret, nisi veritatis doctrina extingueretur. Sed dabunt illi cum Iudæorum Pontificibus graues pœnas Deo, qui dolum hunc inultum abire non patietur. Nec excusabit prætextus hic principes, cum ad ipsos ecclesiæ cura & religionis cognitio quam maxime pertineat. Ideo enim legis liber Regi tradebatur. Deut. 17. Et Reges ecclesiæ nutritios esse debere, propheta docet. Isa. 49. Nec exempla desunt clarissima regum, qui veritatis & ecclesiarum propagatione summam sibi ipsis laudem acquisiuere.
units.tr: But because the fury of his mind had to be equipped with weapons, Saul also provided himself with these. It is said that he went to the high priest, from whom he received letters to the synagogues of Damascus, by which full power was given to him to bind whomever he found to be worshippers of the Christian name. From this we gather that at that time the cause of religion had been entrusted by the Roman governors to the high priests. For since they were blinded by pagan superstition, it is credible that they were wearied at once by daily controversies about religion, and sought every way by which they might free themselves from such troubles, and divert the hatred and odium of the common people onto others. Now this opportunity was most eagerly desired by the priests, whose gain and honour were put in danger by the preaching of the gospel. Therefore Saul, armed with their authority and accompanied by attendants, servants of his crime, sets out for Damascus, for the reason, of course, that he knew Christ's kingdom was rising and flourishing wonderfully there. This passage also warns us that the bitterest enemies of true religion and Christian doctrine will always be the bishops, through whose zeal and diligence this doctrine had to be advanced. For as soon as such men make religion a source of profit, they cannot bear the light of truth, which exposes their wickedness. And that such men were of this kind is better known from the evangelical history than it needs to be shown by many arguments. What we should hope for from the prelates of our own age will easily be seen by anyone who has observed their greed and ambition. Meanwhile, the profane indolence of princes and magistrates must be noted, who, since they do not hold religion in high regard, are unwilling to bring odium or hatred upon themselves on its account. Yet lest they seem impious and alien to religion, they commit its cause to bishops and cardinals, seeking by this pretext a high reputation for piety, and looking for an excuse should anyone call them persecutors of the truth. For they say that such controversies do not concern them, and they persuade themselves that they cannot act more piously than by committing this whole business to the overseers of the churches. In this opinion they are wonderfully confirmed by the masquerading bishops. For they claim for themselves all power of judging about religion, and their ambition and greed would be even worse, were not the teaching of the truth extinguished. But these men will pay heavy penalties to God, together with the high priests of the Jews, for God will not allow this deceit to go unpunished. Nor will this pretext excuse the princes, since the care of the Church and the knowledge of religion pertain to them above all. For this reason the book of the law was handed to the king (Deut. 17:18), and the prophet teaches that kings ought to be nursing fathers of the Church (Isa. 49:23). Nor are there lacking most famous examples of kings who won for themselves the highest praise by spreading the truth and the Churches.

units.la: Sed finem quoque & scopum, quem sibi Saulus propositum habuit videamus. Fuit is, vt quoscunq; Christianæ sectæ inueniret, siue viros siue mulieres, vinctos duceret Hierosolymam. Nullum ergo apud illum sexus discrimen erat, & qui eousq; immanitatis processerat, haud dubie nec ætati quo que parcendum esse putabat. Iam enim illi propositum erat, omnibus Christianis deletis, ipsius Christi nomen in vniuersum extinguere. Tam immanis vero institutii causa ab ipso alibi indicatur, auita ni mirum religionis zelus, quam omni modo defendendam & seruandam esse putabat. Pharisæum enim fuisse constat, & legis studio se Christi nomen & ecclesiam persecutum esse, ipse non semel fatetur. Act. 26. Phil. 3. Galat. 1. cap. &c. Obseruemus autem hoc loco primum, quantum impijs permittat Deus. Nam contra discipulos, & quidem Christianas fœminas hac tentata fuisse, Lucas docet. Sed ita fore dominus prædixerat, nimirum vt cultus Dei putaretur, aliquem in se credentium iugulare. Ioban. 16. Et frequenter de his nos apostoli admonent, ne quis persecutionum procellis & cruce offendatur. Cur enim meliorem nobis hodie fortem optaremus, quam ipsius Christi, apostolorum & primitiuæ ecclesiæ olim fuit? Deinde docet Sauli exemplum, quam parum ad salutis causam faciat præposterus in religione zelus, quem abs q; diuini verbi præscripto, humanis traditionibus abrepti interdum homines concipiunt. Nam quo frequentius hoc ardet Saulus, eo longius a Christo, qui vnica salutis via est, recedit. Quo fortius pro legis iustitia pugnat, eo alienior est a iustitia Christi, quæ sola coram Dei iudicio defendit. Et quod Saulo accidit, hoc ipsum ille Iudæus euenisse testatur. Hos enim zelo Dei flagrare dicit, sed non secundum scientiam. Quare illis hoc mali contigit, quòd dum suam iustitiam statuere conantur, à Dei iustitia exciderunt. Rom. 10. Poterat idem de Monachis dici, nisi maxima illorum pars ventris & ocij studio magis quam religione flagraret. Illud tamen verissime dici tur, eo ardentius euangelium persequi tyrannos, quo constantius maiorum religionem & cultum retinere student. Confutatur vero hic noxius illorum error, qui zelo pietatis ea excusari posse existimat, quæ contra pietatem veram & religionem instituuntur. Quasi vero verbi sui canones frustra Deus dederit, & non bi potius observari debeant, quemadmodum alibi diximus. Præterea Dei cum bonitas tum potentia hic observanda venit, qui tam immanem lupum repente, non modo cicurare, verum etiam fidelissimum gregis sui pastorem efficere potuit. Nemo igitur vel de ecclesia vel de alicuius homi-nis salute temere desperet, quando Deus & hominum animos subito mutare & ecclesiæ suæ tutores facere potest, qui illam iamiam dissipaturi esse videbantur.
units.tr: But let us also look at the end and aim that Saul had set before himself. It was this: that he should bring bound to Jerusalem whichever followers of the Christian sect he found, whether men or women. So there was no distinction of sex for him, and one who had advanced so far into savagery undoubtedly thought that age should not be spared either. For it was already his purpose, once all Christians had been destroyed, to wipe out the very name of Christ entirely. Such a monstrous undertaking is elsewhere attributed to him by himself, namely, the zeal for his ancestral religion, which he thought must be defended and preserved by every means. For it is established that he was a Pharisee, and he himself more than once confesses that he persecuted the name of Christ and the Church out of zeal for the law (Acts 26:5; Phil. 3:5–6; Gal. 1:13–14, etc.). Let us observe here first how much God permits the wicked. For Luke shows that the disciples, and indeed Christian women, were attacked in this way. But the Lord had foretold that this would happen: that men would think they were serving God by killing any of those who believed in him (John 16:2). And the apostles often warn us about this, that no one should be offended by the storms of persecution and the cross. For why should we hope today for a better lot than that which Christ himself, the apostles, and the primitive Church once had? Next, the example of Saul teaches how little a preposterous zeal in religion contributes to the cause of salvation, the kind of zeal that men sometimes conceive, carried away by human traditions without the prescription of the divine Word. For the more eagerly Saul burns in this way, the farther he withdraws from Christ, who is the only way of salvation. The more strongly he fights for the righteousness of the law, the more alien he is to the righteousness of Christ, which alone defends us before the judgement of God. And what happened to Saul, that same Jew testifies happened to his own people. For he says that they burn with zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. So the evil that came upon them was this: while they tried to establish their own righteousness, they fell away from the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:2–3). The same could be said of the monks, were it not that the greater part of them burns more with the pursuit of belly and leisure than with religion. Yet this is said most truly: the more constantly tyrants strive to keep up the religion and worship of their ancestors, the more fiercely they persecute the gospel. But here the harmful error of those is refuted who think that things which are set up against true piety and religion can be excused by zeal for piety. As if God had given the rules of his Word in vain, and they ought not rather to be observed, as we have said elsewhere. Moreover, the goodness and the power of God are to be noted here, for he could suddenly tame so savage a wolf, and make him not only gentle but also the most faithful shepherd of his flock. Therefore let no one rashly despair either of the Church or of the salvation of any man, since God can suddenly change the minds of men and make tutors of his Church those who seemed about to scatter it altogether.

units.la: Transeamus autem ad Conuersionis Sauli historiam, quam vius quodammodo coloribus Lucas depingit. Et a tempore quidem & loco exorsus. Cum (inquit) iter faceret, accidit vt appropinquaret Damasco. Tunc ergo Sauli conatibus occurrit Christus, cum de illorum successu & euentu quam maxime sperare poterat. Iam enim Damascum coram intuetur, & fortasse, vt lupus cospectu præda, de rapiendis Christi ouibus terribiles cogitationes animo suo voluit. Obseruabat vero Dei con-filium & morem, qui hostes suos non raro eò vsq; progredi sinit, vt vix latum vnguem à consiliorum suorum meta abesse videantur. Quæ causa est, vt horribiles interdum terrores sentiat Christi cultores, in quorum excidium illi conspirauerunt: quos Damasci quoq; obortos fuisse verisimile est, cùm Saulū hostem aduentare & ipsorum ceruicibus imminere audirent. Sed ita solet Deus, vt & potentiā suam aduersus impios gloriosius exerat, & pios doceat non terreri nec timere, si quando ab hostibus se vn-diq; circumuentos vident. Ita Pharaonem eò vsq; progredi passus est, vt non iam de effugij via, sed sepulchris cogitare inciperent Israelitæ. Sed eundem subitò deleuit, cum hiantis lupi instar Israelem deglutire conaretur. Possent multa eius generis recenseri, nisi temporis angustia obstaret. Verum hic cium vsus esse debet, ne deo præscribere velimus, quæ nulla rerū gerendarū occasio latere aut subterfu-gere potest. Sed illud prophetæ obseruemus, Expecta dñm, forte sit & roboretur cor tuū, &c. Psal.27.
units.tr: Let us now turn to the history of Saul's conversion, which Luke paints, as it were, with vivid colours. He begins with the time and place: "As he was journeying, it came about that he drew near to Damascus." Christ met Saul's endeavours at the very moment when he could hope most eagerly for their success and outcome. For now he sees Damascus before his eyes, and perhaps, like a wolf at the sight of its prey, he was turning over in his mind terrible thoughts of seizing Christ's sheep. God's counsel and custom, however, is to observe this: he often lets his enemies advance to the point where they seem scarcely a hair's breadth from the goal of their plans. This is why Christ's worshippers, against whose destruction they have conspired, sometimes feel dreadful terrors; and it is likely that such terrors arose at Damascus too, when they heard that Saul the enemy was approaching and was about to fall upon their necks. Yet God is accustomed both to display his power more gloriously against the wicked, and to teach the godly not to be terrified or afraid when they see themselves surrounded on every side by enemies. So he allowed Pharaoh to advance so far that the Israelites began to think not of a way of escape but of their graves; yet he suddenly destroyed him, when he was trying to swallow Israel like a gaping wolf. Many examples of this kind could be listed, were it not for the shortness of time. Yet here we ought to use restraint, lest we prescribe to God what no opportunity of doing his work can lie hidden from or escape him.
