Rather let us observe the words of the prophet: "Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage," etc. Ps. 27.

units.la: Deinde modum conuersionis Euangelista exponit, dicens: Repente circumfulgurauit eum lux è cælo, & collapsus in terram audiuit vocem dicentem sibi: Saul, Saul, &c. Terribilis hæc est huma-nis sensibus rerum facies, sed quæ abunde doceat abfq; negotio hac à domino perfecta fuisse. Lucem e-nim fulguris instar cœlitus immittit, quod illi tam facile fuit, quàm Solem educere & reducere. Re-pente verò lucem hanc emicare voluit, vt magis terreretur immanis ille lupus, qui ecclesiam Christi inexplebili auiditate iam quodammodo deuorarat. Fulguri vox accedit, quæ fulminis loco est, & ni-hil tale timentem subitò prosternit. Docent hæc, quàm facile sit Deo hostium suorum conatus infrin-gere. Quia enim exercituū dominus est, quauis contra illos armare potest, nec aliqua tam vilis crea-tura est, quæ non ijs puniendis sufficiat, quos Deus punire instituit. Ita aquis olim repente immissis mundum totum delere potuit. In Sodomas sulphur & ignem cœlitus depluit. Ægyptiorum feroces spi-ritus modo tenebris fregit, modo muscarum examinibus, modo ranarum fœdis obsultationibus, mo-do pediculorum infestis morsibus emolliuit. Antiochum & Herodem vermibus ex ipsorum carne e-natis necauit. Saulem tyrannum proprio ipsius gladio iugulauit. Taceo infinita eius generis, quia hic Sauli lapsus multorum exemplorum instar esse potest. Prodest enim hunc diligenter inspicere. Quid nunc impetrata à Pontifice summo litera repente collapso prosunt? Quid iuuat illius authoritas concessa in Christianos sæuiendi potestas? Num satellitum, quos scelerum ministros adduxerat, mi-nisterio vel sustineri vel subleuari potest? Minimè. Quibus verò armis tantus modo gigas & secun-dus Enceladus deiectus iacet? Nullus adhuc auditus tonitruum sonitus, nullus collidentium nu-bium fragor, nullus ruentis fulminis stridor. Sola cœlestis lux oculis percepta, & intonans auribus Christi vox, corpus & animum ita perculit, vt supinus victori Christo manus dedat, qui illius nomen paulò ante extinguere conabatur. Hæc verò vt nostræ consolationi aduersus impios Christi hostes ser-uiunt, ita ad nostram quoq; institutionem transferri debent. Docent enim quàm infelix illorum sit insolentia, qui cùm quotidie diuinæ potentiæ & maiestatis exempla cernant, adhuc tamen aduersus Deum & verbum eius insolescere & ferocire audent: quod ego non postremum nostræ corruptionis ar-gumentum esse arbitror: quando vel formæ, vel generis, vel honorum aut opum fiducia elati, Dei ob-liuiscimur, cui tam facile est feroces animos deijcere. Agnoscamus potius Dei potentiam, & humi-liemur sponte sub victrici illius manu, ne magno nostro malo, quantum ille possit, experiamur.
units.tr: Next the Evangelist sets out the manner of the conversion, saying: "Suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him, and falling to the ground he heard a voice saying to him: Saul, Saul, etc." This aspect of events is frightening to human senses, yet it sufficiently teaches that the thing was accomplished by the Lord without any difficulty. For he sends down light from heaven like lightning, which was as easy for him as to bring the sun out and back again. He willed that this light should flash forth suddenly, so that that vast wolf, who had already in a sense devoured the Church of Christ with insatiable greed, might be more terrified. To the lightning is added a voice, which takes the place of thunder, and suddenly prostrates him, who feared nothing of the kind. These things teach how easily God can break down the endeavours of his enemies. For since he is the Lord of hosts, he can arm any creature against them, and there is no creature so worthless that it is not sufficient for punishing those whom God has determined to punish. Thus once, by suddenly loosing the waters, he could destroy the whole world; he rained brimstone and fire from heaven upon Sodom. He broke the fierce spirits of the Egyptians now with darkness, now with swarms of flies, now with the foul leaping of frogs, now he softened them with the harassing bites of lice. He killed Antiochus and Herod with worms bred from their own flesh. He slew the tyrant Saul with his own sword. I pass over the countless examples of this kind, since this fall of Saul can serve as an instance of many. For it is useful to examine it carefully. What now avail the letters obtained from the chief Pontiff, once he has suddenly collapsed? What good is the authority granted to him, the power to rage against Christians? Can he be upheld or supported by the service of the attendants whom he had brought along as ministers of his crimes? Not at all. By what weapons is such a giant and second Enceladus lying cast down? No sound of thunder is yet heard, no crash of colliding clouds, no hiss of falling lightning. Only the heavenly light perceived by the eyes, and the voice of Christ thundering in the ears, struck body and soul so that he, on his back, gives his hands to Christ the victor, whose name a little before he had been trying to extinguish. These things serve for our consolation against the impious enemies of Christ, and they ought also to be carried over to our instruction. For they teach how unhappy is the insolence of those who, although they daily see examples of divine power and majesty, still dare to grow proud and fierce against God and his Word. I consider this no small proof of our corruption, when, lifted up by confidence in beauty, birth, honours or wealth, we forget God, who can so easily cast down proud spirits. Let us rather acknowledge God's power, and humble ourselves willingly under his victorious hand, lest to our great harm we experience how much he is able to do.

units.la: Porrò Saulum iacentem inuisamus, qui audita cœlitus voce, quærit: Quis es domine? O socor-diam. Ab eo se prostratum audiuerat, quem persequebatur, & adhuc quis nam ille sit interrogat. Est tamen vox hæc humiliati & manuefacti animi indicium. Quod vtinam in ijs hodie videre liceret, qui à Deo vel morbis prostrati, vel paupertate humiliati, vel alijs plagis afflicti, nondum tamen se à Deo prostratos, nec illum dominum suum esse agnoscunt.
units.tr: Let us further look upon Saul lying prostrate, who, having heard the voice from heaven, asks: "Who are you, Lord?" O dullness! He had been told that he was being cast down by the one whom he was persecuting, and still he asks who he is. Yet this utterance is a sign of a humbled and tamed spirit. Would that today we could see it in those who, though they are prostrated by God with sicknesses, or humbled by poverty, or afflicted with other plagues, do not yet acknowledge that they have been cast down by God, nor that he is their Lord.

units.la: At quia mitiorem iam se præbet Saulus, illum responso dignatur dominus, dicens: Ego sum Ie-sus, quem tu persequeris. Durum est tibi contra stimulum calcitrare. Qua responsio bipartita est. Pri-ma enim parte quis sit docet, simulq; sceleris concepti atrocitatem arguit, quasi dicat: Tu quidem in homines te persecutionem instituisse arbitraris, & in eos quidem, qui vt apud omnes odio laborant, ita vindicem & assertorē inter homines habent neminē. At nec illi vindice carent, nec illos solos perse-queris. Ego enim ille Iesus sum, quē illi profitetur. Ego in cœlis regnans illorū fortē sedulum obseruo. Ego me illis patronum & tutorem fore olim promisi. Imò ea mihi cum illis intercedit coniunctio, vt mihi fieri putem, quodcunq; minimo illorum fecerit, &c. Hinc vero generalis doctrina colligi debet, Christo fieri, quodcunq; illius cultoribus fit. Eius enim vox apud prophetam legitur: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Zach.2. Et Isaias Cap.63. de Dei erga suum populum benevolentia loquens, inter alia ait: In omni afflictione illorum, ipse afflictus est. Seruiat hoc tyrannorum institutioni, ut meminerint se Christum hostem habituros, quando ecclesiam persequuntur, qui illos aliquando regit & comminuet sceptro ferreo, ut vasa figuli. Psal.2. Rursum hinc consolationem petant fideles, quod in cruce Christi socium habent, quo cum si patiantur, cum eode olim regnaturi sunt.2, Tim.2.
units.tr: But because Saul now shows himself milder, the Lord deigns to answer him, saying: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. It is hard for you to kick against the goad." This reply is in two parts. In the first part he declares who he is and at the same time exposes the atrocity of the crime conceived, as if to say: "You indeed think you have begun a persecution against men, and against those who, since they are hated by all, have no avenger or defender among men. But they are not without an avenger, nor do you persecute them alone. For I am that Jesus whom they profess. I, reigning in heaven, watch carefully over their lot. I promised long ago that I would be their patron and protector. Indeed such a union is between me and them that I count whatever is done to the least of them as done to me," etc. From this a general doctrine should be drawn: whatever is done to the worshippers of Christ is done to Christ. For his voice is read in the prophet: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye." Zech. 2. And Isaiah, chapter 63, speaking of God's goodwill towards his people, says among other things: "In all their affliction he was afflicted." Let this serve as a warning to tyrants, that they will have Christ as their enemy when they persecute the Church; he who one day will rule them and break them with an iron sceptre, like the vessels of a potter. Ps. 2. Again, let the faithful draw consolation from this, that they have a companion in the cross of Christ; if they suffer with him, they will one day reign with him. 2 Tim. 2.

units.la: Altera responsionis parte poenam illi ob oculos statuit, dicens: Durum est tibi contra stimulu calcitrare. Metaphora autem a bubus siue equis desumpta vtitur, qui si stimulo recalcitrent, non modo nihil proficiunt, sed aculeu ipsi sibi altius infigunt, & maioris mali sibi ipsis authores sunt. Ide Saulo & omnibus alijs, qui ipsius exemplo ecclesiam persequuntur, eeuenturum dominus minatur, nimirum ut illorum conatus non irriti modo, sed ipsis authoribus exitiales futuri sint. Est enim Christi ecclesia lapis oneris, in quo subleuando nemo suarum virium periculum impune faciet, sicut apud prophetam Deus pollicetur. Zach.12. Necexempla desunt, quibus id probari poterat. Huc enim Pharao pertinet, qui contra stimulum calcitrans maris rubri vndas suo suorumq; interitu nobilitauit. Sentit idem iudicium Sanherib, qui cum Israeli & illius Deo bellum indixisset, vnius angeli manu & exercitum amisit, & castris exutus est. De Antiocho & Herode paulo ante diximus. Quibus adnumerari poterant Romanorum Imperatores, quotquot post Christi tempora ecclesiam persecuti sunt, & statim atroces tantae impietatis poenas exoluerunt. His si ea coniungas, quae nostro seculo iudiciorum Dei exempla in ecclesia hostes edita sunt, infallibilem huius sententiae, quam hic Christus pronunciat, veritatem esse fateberis. Nobis vero hic omnium vsus esse debet, ne in persecutionibus mundi & tyrannorum potentia territi, animum despondeamus. Viuit enim adhuc Christus ille, nec ecclesia suam deseret, cui se affuturum promisit vsq; in consummationem seculi: Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the second part of the reply he sets the punishment before his eyes, saying: "It is hard for you to kick against the goad." He uses a metaphor taken from oxen or horses, which, if they kick back against the goad, not only gain nothing but drive the sting deeper into themselves and become the authors of greater harm to themselves. The Lord threatens that the same will happen to Saul and to all others who follow his example in persecuting the Church: namely, that their attempts will not only be futile but will prove deadly to themselves as their authors. For the Church of Christ is a stone of burden, and no one who tries his strength against it in lifting it will do so with impunity, as God promises through the prophet. Zech. 12. Nor are examples lacking by which this could be proved. To this belongs Pharaoh, who, kicking against the goad, made the waves of the Red Sea famous by his own and his people's destruction. Sennacherib shared the same judgment: when he declared war on Israel and its God, he lost his army to the hand of one angel and was stripped of his camp. Of Antiochus and Herod we spoke a little before. To these could be added the Roman emperors, all who after the time of Christ persecuted the Church, and who immediately paid the dreadful penalties of such impiety. If you join to these the examples of God's judgments on the enemies of the Church which have been published in our own age, you will confess the infallible truth of this sentence which Christ here pronounces. For us, however, the whole of this ought to serve so that we are not terrified by the persecutions of the world and the power of tyrants, and do not lose heart. For that Christ lives still, and the Church will not be deserted by him, to whom he promised to be present even to the end of the age. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIIII.
units.tr: Homily 64.

units.la: Tum[Saulus] tremens & stupens dixit: Domine, quid me vis facere? Et dominus ad illum: Surge, & ingredere in urbem, & dicetur tibi, quid te oporteat facere. Viri autem, qui cum illo proficiscebantur, stabant attoniti, audientes quidem vocem, neminem vero videntes. Surrexit autem Saulus a terra, & cum aperti essent ipsius oculi, neminem videbat, sed manu agentes eum, adduxerunt Damascum. Et fuit tres dies non videns, & non edit neq; bibit.
units.tr: Then Saul, trembling and astonished, said: "Lord, what do you want me to do?" And the Lord said to him: "Arise and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do." The men who were travelling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul got up from the ground, and when his eyes were opened he could see no one. So they led him by the hand and brought him to Damascus. For three days he was without sight, and he neither ate nor drank.

units.la: Quemadmodum Saulus, priusquam ad Christum Iesum conuerteretur, singulari immanitate nomen & ecclesiam Christi persecutus est: ita illum elegit Deus, vt in ipso peculiare boni tatis & gratiae suae exemplum proponeret, quo admoneremur, nihil nos habere, quo coram Deo nobis gloriari liceat, sed cum ipsam salutem, tum quaecunq; nobis ad hanc consequendam adiumento esse solent, ad meram Dei gratiam & bonitatem referri debere. Quamuis enim non omnes simili immanitate cum Paulo in Christi ecclesiam grassentur, nec omnes aperta vi ad subeundam salutis viam dominus cogat: omnium tamen ea conditio est, vt potenti Dei manu ipsos conuerti & trahi oportear. Nam si hominem, quatenus naturali anima regitur, consyderes, illum minime intelligere videbis quae sunt spiritus Dei.1.Corinth.2. Quare intellectu corrupto voluntatem quoq; prauam & corruptae esse necesse est, quae impura & iniqua carnis desyderia generat: vt vere Deus olim, humani cordis figmenta ab ineunte aetate praua esse dixerit. Gen.8. At quia peccati malo vires omnes ita debilitatae sunt, vt ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, satis constat, neminem mortalium de salute sua serio cogitare vel posse vel velle, nisi diuinitus illuminetur, trahatur & emolliatur: licet nonnullorum corruptio apertior sit & magis conspicua. Quia tamen in Sauli couersione multa alia concurrunt, quae nostrae institutioni seruiunt, diligentissime in eius descriptione Lucas versatur. Et in praesenti quidem, postquam primum illius actum exposuit, effectum tam duri congressus, & alia quaedam huic cohaerentia commemorat.
units.tr: Just as Saul, before he turned to Christ Jesus, persecuted the name and the Church of Christ with extraordinary savagery, so God chose him to set before us in his person a singular example of his goodness and grace, so that we might be reminded that we have nothing in which we may glory before God, but that both salvation itself and whatever usually helps us to attain it must be ascribed to God's mere grace and goodness. For although not everyone rages against the Church of Christ with the same savagery as Paul, and the Lord does not compel everyone by open force to enter the way of salvation, the condition of all is nonetheless that they must be turned and drawn by the powerful hand of God. For if you consider a man as far as he is governed by his natural soul, you will see that he does not understand the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). Hence, once the understanding is corrupted, the will too must be perverse and corrupt, and it produces impure and unrighteous desires of the flesh; so God truly said of old that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth (Gen. 8). But since the power of all our faculties has been so weakened by the evil of sin that we are not even fit to think from ourselves, it is clear enough that no mortal can seriously think about his salvation, or wish to, unless he is enlightened, drawn and softened by God, although the corruption of some is more open and more conspicuous. Yet because many other things came together in Saul's conversion which serve our instruction, Luke dwells with great care on his account. And at present, having first set out the beginning of that event, he relates the effect of so harsh an encounter and certain other things connected with it.

units.la: Paucis vero insignem diuinae castigationis effectum in Paulo comprehendit. Is enim (inquit) tremens & stupens dixit: Domine, quid me vis facere? Et dominus ad illum: Surge, & ingredere in urbem, &c. Nobis autem cum Pauli tum Dei persona hoc loco diligentius considerandae sunt. Et in Paulo quidem haud vulgare animi humiliati, & ad obsequium omne propensi specimen est videre. Iam enim domini titulo dignatur, quem paulo ante cane & angue peius oderat. Et sponte de illius voluntate interrogat, eos famulos imitatus, qui nondum prolatis herorum iussis, illa fideli & sedulo obsequio praeuertere studenr. Hinc autem duo, ad nostram institutionem pertinentia, elici poterunt.
units.tr: Briefly, he records the remarkable effect of divine chastisement in Paul. For he says: "He, trembling and astonished, said: Lord, what do you want me to do? And the Lord said to him: Arise and go into the city, etc." But in this passage we must consider more carefully both the person of Paul and the person of God. In Paul we can see a not ordinary example of a humbled spirit, inclined to every obedience. For now he honours him with the title of Lord, whom shortly before he hated worse than dog or snake. And he asks of his own accord what his will is, imitating those servants who, before their masters have even issued their orders, strive to anticipate them with faithful and diligent obedience. From this two points may be drawn which pertain to our instruction.

units.la: Primo, officij sui admonentur, quicunque Dei castigantis manum sentiunt. Agnoscant illi se a Deo puniri, qui parentis instar ideo percutit, ut sanet: & suos corrigit, ne cum mundo poenitere nescio condemnentur. 1. Corinth. 11. Quae causa est, quod propheta beatum illum pronunciat, quem dominus castigauerit. Psal. 94. Rursus hunc dominum suum agnoscant, & de eius voluntate serio inquirant, ut norint, quibus studijs ille placari possit. Est hoc electis Dei proprium, quibus nihil durius & intolerabilius videtur, quam si Deum sibi iratum esse senserint. At longe alia impiorum & reproborum mens est, qui licet interdum Deo cedere & obsequium praestare coguntur, fremunt tamen, & se illud inuitos facere multis argumentis testantur. Quare mox quoque ad ingenium & vix intermissa impietatis studia redeunt. Exempla huius rei in Pharaone & Saule rege scriptura proponit. Quibus connumerari debent sacerdotum ferui, ad Christum capiendum emissi, qui licet & ipsi illius verbo profrati essent, mox tamen exurgunt, & ei impias manus iniiciunt, quem dominum suum agnoscere debebant. Iohan. 18. Paulum ergo imitemur, quoties vel morbis sternimur, vel paupertate opprimimur, vel hostibus praedae fumus, vel quibuscunque alijs aerumnis vexamur, & ex animo dicamus: Domine, quid nos vis facere? Ita enim ad salutem cedent, quae cumprimis noxia videbantur.
units.tr: First, all who feel the hand of God chastising them are reminded of their duty. Let them recognise that they are punished by God, who strikes as a parent does, so that he may heal; and who corrects his own, lest they be condemned along with the world (1 Cor. 11). This is why the prophet pronounces blessed the man whom the Lord has chastened (Ps. 94). Again, let them acknowledge this one as their Lord, and inquire seriously into his will, so that they may learn by what pursuits he can be appeased. This is peculiar to the elect of God, for whom nothing seems harsher or more intolerable than to perceive that God is angry with them. But the mind of the ungodly and the reprobate is far different. Although they are sometimes compelled to yield to God and render obedience, they nonetheless rage, and they attest by many arguments that they do it unwillingly. Hence they soon return to their natural bent and to pursuits of impiety scarcely interrupted. Scripture sets before us examples of this in Pharaoh and King Saul. To these must be added the servants of the priests, sent to seize Christ, who, although they had been overthrown by his word, nevertheless soon rose up and laid impious hands on him whom they ought to have acknowledged as their Lord (John 18). Let us therefore imitate Paul whenever we are laid low by sickness, or oppressed by poverty, or made prey to enemies, or harassed by whatever other troubles, and let us say from the heart: "Lord, what do you want us to do?" For in this way those things which seemed especially harmful will turn to our salvation.

units.la: Secundo docet exemplum hoc, quam necessaria interdum fit, etiam in salutis & fidei causa, seuerior paulo castigatio. Multos enim eo ingenio praeditos esse videmus, ut nisi vi cogantur, Dei verbo colla non submittant. Quapropter Christus quosdam ad coelestes nuptias cogi & compelli vult. Luc. 14. Ex quorum numero Paulum fuisse notius est, quam ut multis demonstrari oporteat. Non leuis ergo illorum error est, qui in fidei & religionis causa nemini vim adhibendam esse clamant, cum solus Deus in hominum animos ius & imperium habeat. Nam ut fatemur, solius Dei esse animos illuminare, trahere & fidem largiri: ita a Deo praeceptum esse nouimus, ut falsi doctores tum argumentis & scripturis conuincantur, tum magistratus gladio coerceantur, si incurabiles esse pergant. Vide Deut. 13. vbi eadem ratione superstitiones, falsos cultus & blasphemias excindere iubentur. Absurdum quippe foret, eos cohercere, qui fortunis aut corporibus insidiantur, illis vero impune quidum permittere, qui & Dei gloriam improbe oppugnant, & animabus damationis laqueos struunt. Et exempla passim extant eorum, qui seueriori castigatione cohibiti, postquam blasphemare desierunt, in veritatis cognitionem perducti sunt. Sed ut in omnibus alijs causis, ita hic maxime prudentia & moderatione opus esse admonemus.
units.tr: Second, this example teaches how necessary, even for the sake of salvation and faith, a somewhat severer chastisement sometimes is. For we see many who are so constituted that, unless they are compelled by force, they will not submit their necks to the word of God. Therefore Christ wills that some be forced and compelled to the heavenly marriage feast (Luke 14). It is better known that Paul was one of this number than that it needs to be demonstrated to many. It is therefore no slight error of those who cry out that force must be applied to no one in matters of faith and religion, since God alone has right and dominion over the minds of men. For while we admit that it belongs to God alone to enlighten, draw and bestow faith on minds, we also know that God has commanded that false teachers be refuted both by arguments and by the Scriptures, and be restrained by the sword of the magistrate if they persist in being incurable (see Deut. 13), where in the same way they are commanded to root out superstitions, false worship and blasphemies. For it would indeed be absurd to restrain those who plot against goods or bodies, while allowing those to go unpunished who wickedly assail the glory of God and set snares of damnation for souls. And there are examples everywhere of those who, restrained by a severer correction, after they ceased to blaspheme were led to the knowledge of the truth. But, as in all other matters, so here above all we remind you that prudence and moderation are needed.

units.la: Sed Christum audiamus, qui mox amicum se & benignum ei exhibet, quem iussa subire paratum vidit. Vt enim pater apud prophetas clamat: Reuertimini ad me, & ego reuertar ad vos: ita illum in euangelio omnes laborantes ad se inuitare, & palam testari legimus, quod neminem ad se venientem reijcere velit. Matth. 11. Iohan. 6. cap. Iubet autem illum in vrbem pergere, vt illic ex Anania discat, quid faciendum sit. Duplex vero huius praecepti causa adduci potest. Nam & Pauli modestiam hoc modo tentat dominus, dum ad eos illum relegat, quos paulo ante violentius inuadere statuerat: & simul suam verbi ministerio authoritatem dignitatemque asserit. Quia enim hoc frequenter ab hominibus contemni nouit, non raro docet, eius vsum ad salutem consequendam necessarium esse. Vidimus id in Aethiopis historia, quem cum occulta spiritus virtute illuminare potuisset, Philippi ministerio instituì voluit. Et nunc licet Saulo colloqui dignetur, eundem tamen ad Ananiam relegat, ex quo fidei & salutis mysteria discat, eiusdem minis terio baptizatus in ecclesiae consortium adoptetur. Cui simile est, quod de Cornelio Centurione infra referetur, quem angelo missio, ut Petrum accersat & ab illo edoceatur, admonet. Docent haec, ne verbi ministerium inutile & superuacaneum putemus, nec coelestes aut angelicas reuelationes expectemus, quae nos coelestium cognitione instruant. Quia enim scripturis & verbi praedicatione nos doceri vult dominus. minus, quisquis illa contemperit, seipsum regno ipsius plane indignum esse testatur, nec ad fidei cognitionem vnquam peruenient. Cur enim ordinis diuini contemptorem noua methodo dignaretur Deus? Firmum ergo illud Paulinum manet: Quomodo credent, si non audierint? Quomodo autem audient absque prædicante? Rom. 10. Item illud Christi: Mosen habent & prophetas, quos qui non audierint nec illos audient, qui à mortuis reuersi, salutis rationem exposuerint. Luc. 16. Admonemur præterea neminem, vel vilissimum Christi & verbi ministrum contemni debere, modò legitimè ordinatus sit, quando præclarum illud Dei organum Paulus, ad Ananiam, cuius nulla hucusque mentio facta est, relegatur. Nec enim ex hominum dignitate diuini verbi authoritas dependet, sed ea nobis inuiolata & integra consistere debet, quisquis tandem ille sit, quem nobis doctorem & suæ voluntatis præconem dominus destinauit.
units.tr: But let us hear Christ, who soon shows himself friendly and kind to him whom he saw ready to submit to his commands. For as the Father cries through the prophets: "Return to me, and I will return to you" (Zech. 1), so we read that in the gospel he invites all who labour to come to him, and openly testifies that he wishes to reject no one who comes to him (Matt. 11; John 6). Now he bids him go into the city, so that there he may learn from Ananias what must be done. A double reason for this command may be adduced. For the Lord tests Paul's humility in this way, while he sends him back to those whom he had just resolved to attack more violently; and at the same time he asserts the authority and dignity of the ministry of his Word. For since he knows that this is often despised by men, he frequently teaches that its use is necessary for obtaining salvation. We saw this in the history of the Ethiopian, whom he could have enlightened by the hidden power of the Spirit, but whom he willed to instruct through the ministry of Philip (Acts 8). And now, although he deigns to speak with Saul, he nevertheless sends him back to Ananias, so that from him he may learn the mysteries of faith and salvation, and, baptised by the same ministry, be admitted into fellowship with the Church. Similar to this is what is reported below about Cornelius the centurion, whom an angel admonishes to summon Peter and be taught by him. These things teach us not to think the ministry of the Word useless and superfluous, nor to look for heavenly or angelic revelations to instruct us in the knowledge of heavenly things. For since the Lord wills us to be taught by the Scriptures and the preaching of the Word, whoever despises these shows himself plainly unworthy of his kingdom, and will never come to the knowledge of the faith. For why should God honour a contemner of his divine order with a new method? Therefore that firm word of Paul remains: "How will they believe, if they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?" (Rom. 10). Likewise that saying of Christ: "They have Moses and the prophets; if they do not hear them, neither will they hear those who return from the dead and explain the way of salvation" (Luke 16). We are further reminded that no one, however lowly, should be despised as a minister of Christ and of the Word, provided he has been lawfully ordained, since the noble instrument of God, Paul, is sent back to Ananias, of whom no mention has been made until now. For the authority of the divine Word does not depend on the dignity of men; rather it must remain inviolate and whole for us, whoever he may be whom the Lord has appointed to us as teacher and herald of his will.

units.la: Porrò interserit hîs, de Pauli comitibus narratiunculam Lucas, quos attonitos fuetisse, & vocem quidem audiuisse, neminem verò vidisse dicit. At si Paulum hæc eadem coram Agrippa narrantem audiamus, ipsos etiam inirio collapsos fuisse constabit, & licet priores surrexerint, adhuc tamen mente captis similes, terrore & metu omnino absorpti fuere. Videtur autem nonnihil à Pauli narratione Lucas variare, cum ille eos nec vocem audiuisse, nec quenquam vidisse dicat. Sed nulla in his contradicentia est. Nam vocem audiuisse hic dicuntur, quia sonum audiuere. Eandem verò audiuisse negantur, quia quid diceretur, non intellexerunt, nec illos ea intelligere voluit dominus, quæ non ad ipsos pertinebant. Vel quod de voce dicitur hoc loco, ad solius Pauli vocem referri debet, quam quidem audierant eius comites, cum Christi cum ipso colloquentis vocem non audirent, vt quæ nihil ad eos pertineret. Et hoc innuere videntur Pauli verba, quæ infra Cap. 22. sic habentur: Qui mecum erant, lucem quidem viderunt, & expauefacti sunt: vocem autem non audierunt eius, qui mecum loquebatur. Est autem hoc loco cumprimis obseruandum, quid omnes eos maneat, qui apertis Christi hostibus coniunguntur, & illorum consilijs sese immiscent. Cum ijdem enim pœnas dant, siue illi serui, siue subditi, siue filij fuerint. Cedit enim humana iura omnia ei obedientia, qua nos sibi obstrictos vult esse Deus: & firma rataq; perpetuò manet illius dicti authoritas: Oportet Deo plus obedire quàm hominibus. Quotquot ergo in hominum gratiam eius officij obliuiscuntur, quo Deo de uincti sunt, mererentur, vt cum ijs pereant, quos Deo chariores habuerunt. Docent hæc fugienda esse malorum consortia: & fiid non datur, saltem cauendum est, ne illorum conatus improbos vel nostro consensu approbemus, vel authoritate tueamur. Notus est in ethnicorum scriptis de Ciconia, inter grues capta, apologus, quam nequicquam de sua innocentia differentem iugulauit agricola, eò quòd cum gruibus, quæ ipsius segetem depasta fuerant, capta esset. Sed & Paulus alibi, non modò eos qui mala faciunt, verumetiam hos, qui illis consentiunt, pœna dignos esse pronunciat. Rom. 1. Quæ si hodie consyderemus, nostri seculi multiplices calamitates minus mirabimur, quando contempti & oppressi euangelij reatu omnes fere homines tenentur, dum alij quidem illud immani crudelitate persequuntur, alij persecutorum amicitias & fœdera solicitè curant, alij vero otiosi spectatores eos perire & opprimi sinunt, quos suo patrocinio tueri debebant.
units.tr: Luke then adds a short account of Paul's companions. He says they were astonished, that they heard the voice but saw no one. But if we listen to Paul telling the same story before Agrippa, it becomes clear that they too fell to the ground, and although the first ones rose, they were still like men out of their minds, completely overwhelmed by terror and fear. Luke does seem to differ a little from Paul's account, since Paul says they neither heard the voice nor saw anyone. But there is no contradiction here. They are said to have heard a voice because they heard a sound. They are said not to have heard it because they did not understand what was being said, and the Lord did not mean them to understand what did not concern them. Or what is said here about the voice should be referred to the voice of Paul alone, which his companions did hear, while they did not hear the voice of Christ speaking with him, since that did not concern them. Paul's words in chapter 22 seem to point to this: "Those who were with me saw the light indeed, and were afraid; but they did not hear the voice of him who spoke with me." Here we must especially observe what awaits all those who join themselves to the open enemies of Christ and mix themselves into their counsels. Such people pay the penalty, whether they are servants, subjects or sons. For all human rights give way to the obedience by which God wills us to be bound to himself, and the authority of that saying remains firm and unchanging: "We ought to obey God rather than men." So all who, to win the favour of men, forget the duty by which they are bound to God, deserve to perish with those whom they held dearer than God. These things teach that the company of evil men must be avoided; and where this cannot be done, at least we must take care not to approve their wicked attempts by our consent, or defend them by our authority. In the writings of the heathen there is a well-known fable about the stork, caught among cranes, which a farmer slaughtered although she protested her innocence in vain, because she had been caught with the cranes that had eaten up his crop. Paul also says elsewhere that not only those who do evil but also those who consent to them are worthy of punishment (Rom. 1). If we consider these things today, we will be less surprised at the many calamities of our own age, when almost all men are held guilty of despising and oppressing the gospel: some persecute it with savage cruelty, others carefully seek the friendship and alliances of the persecutors, and others, idle spectators, allow those to perish and be crushed whom they ought to have defended with their protection.

units.la: Cæterum ad Paulum redeamus, cuius fortem modò describit Lucas. Et primò quidem illum surrexisse dicit, cùm nimirum surgendi copiam illi fecisset Christus dominus. Addit autem, quòd cùm aperuisset oculos, nihil tamen viderit, cœlestis nimirum lucis fulgore excæcatus. Quare comitum siue famulorum ductu Damascum peruenit, vbi toto triduo neq; comedisse neq; bibisse dicitur. Sunt autem hæc omnia haud vulgaris consternationis indicia, quæ illius tum corpus tum mentem perculerat. Quæ ab alijs hoc loco de Pauli raptu in Paradisum referuntur, vt incerta relinquimus, ne quid audacius afferere videamur. Interim obseruasse sufficiat, vt suorum hostium conatus eludere soleat Deus, & in illorum capita retorqueat, quæ illi aduersus fideles suos machinantur. Visus est hucusque multis alijs oculatior Paulus, vtpote qui supra multos æquales suos profecit, quemadmodum ipse alibi testatur. Gal. 1. At nunc tam corpore quàm mente cæcus est, donec diuinitus illuminatur. Idem comitum & seruorum caterua flipatus aduenit, quos in eum finem elegerat, vt Christianos vinctos Hierosolymam abducerent. Sed ab illis ipse plus quàm vinctus & captiuus ducitur. Similiter multis illum fatis & inopiæ authorem fuisse credibile est. At nunc ipse toto triduo famem sustinet, adeoq; rerum omnium incertus est. Sunt eius generis exempla passim in scripturis. Ita Balaamum & Balakum de-
units.tr: Let us return, however, to Paul, whose fortune Luke now describes. First he tells us that Paul rose from the ground, since Christ the Lord had indeed given him the power to rise. He adds that, although he had opened his eyes, he nevertheless saw nothing, being blinded, of course, by the brilliance of the heavenly light. Therefore, led by his companions or servants, he came to Damascus, where for three whole days he is said to have neither eaten nor drunk. All these things are signs of no ordinary consternation, which had struck both his body and his mind. As for what others here refer to Paul's rapture into Paradise, we leave it uncertain, lest we seem to assert something too bold. Meanwhile it is enough to have observed that God is accustomed to frustrate the attempts of his enemies and turn back upon their heads what they plot against his faithful. Up to this point Paul seemed to many others more clear-sighted, as one who had advanced beyond many of his contemporaries, as he himself testifies elsewhere (Gal. 1.). But now he is blind both in body and in mind, until he is enlightened by God. He arrives with the same band of companions and servants whom he had chosen for this purpose, to lead Christians away bound to Jerusalem. But by them he himself is led away, more than bound and a captive. Similarly, it is credible that he had been the author of many people's ruin and want. But now he himself endures hunger for three whole days, and is utterly uncertain of everything. Examples of this kind are found everywhere in Scripture.

units.la: J. s lusos videmus, dum benedictionibus Israelem accumulat, quem maledictionibus obruere instituerunt. Ita Ægyptij proprijs opibus onustos extrudunt, quos perpetuo seruitutis iugo opprimere volebant. Sic Saul Dauidi gloriæ maioris materiam indies subminiſtrat, dum illum oppreſſum cupit. Eodè Haman & Mardochæi hiſtoria debet referri cum infinitis alijs, quæ Dauidis dictum confirmant, quo il le Deum hostium suorum consilia ex alto deridere testatur. Pfal.2. Discamus ergo saluatoris nostri, Iesu Christi, potentiam agnoscere, nec vllis hostium ipsius minis & conatibus terreamur. Illi verò sub ijciamur fideli obedientia, vt in cælis olim promissæ gloriæ cum illo hæredes fimus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Thus we see Balaam and Balak deceived, while he heaps blessings upon Israel, whom they had set out to overwhelm with curses. Thus the Egyptians thrust out, loaded with their own wealth, those whom they had wanted to crush under the perpetual yoke of slavery. So Saul supplies David with ever greater matter for glory day by day, while he desires to see him oppressed. To the same class belongs the history of Haman and Mordecai, along with countless others, which confirm the saying of David, in which he testifies that God laughs at the counsels of his enemies from on high (Ps. 2.). Let us learn, then, to acknowledge the power of our Saviour, Jesus Christ, and let us not be terrified by any threats or attempts of his enemies. Rather, let us submit ourselves to his faithful obedience, so that we may one day be heirs with him of the glory promised in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXV.
units.tr: Homily 65.

units.la: Erat autem quidam discipulus Damasci, nomine Ananias, & dixit ad illum in visione dominus: Ananía. Ille autem ait: Ecce ego, domine. Dominus autem ad eum: Surge & vade in viam, quæ vocatur Recta, & quære in domo Iudæ Saulum, nomine Tarsensem. Ecce enim orat. Et vidit in visione virum, Ananiam nomine, introeuntem & imponentem sibi manum, vt visum reciperet. Respondit autem Ananias: Domine, audiui ex multis de viro hoc, quanta mala fecerit sanctis tuis Hierosolymis: & hic habet potestatem à summis sacerdotibus vinciendi omnes, qui inuocant nomen tuum. Dixit autem illi dominus: Vade, quia organum electum mihi est iste, vt portet nomen meum coram gentibus, & regibus, & filijs Israel. Ego enim ostendam ei, quanta oporteat ipsum pro nomine meo pati.
units.tr: There was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." He answered, "Behold, I am here, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Arise, and go into the street called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judas for a man of Tarsus named Saul. For behold, he is praying. And he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hand on him, so that he might receive his sight." But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem; and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name." But the Lord said to him, "Go, for this man is a chosen instrument to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, kings and the sons of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name."

units.la: Quamuis omnium apostolorum conuersiones & vocationes diligenter à nobis considerari debeant, singularem tamen diligentiam Pauli conuersio meretur: partim quidem quod illustre & praeclarum diuinæ bonitatis erga peccatores exemplum habet: partim verò, quòd Paulus hic plus omnibus alijs apostolis laborauit, nec alius est, cuius scripta cum à veteribus tum recentioribus ecclesiæ doctoribus, in fidei & salutis causa explicanda frequentius adducantur. Necesse ergo est, vt sciamus, quis ille fuerit, quomodo eunde vocarit & converterit Deus, vt maior apud nos esse possit authoritas. Qua causa est, quòd illius historiam tam diligenter Lucas describit. Et buc quidem exposuit, vt illius ferociam & horribiles conatus in medio cursu dominus interruperit, tanta violentia, vt se iam docilem & morigerum offerret domino, qui paulò ante hostis acerrimus fuerat. Hic commodè ipsius ordinationem ad apostolicum munus subjicit, quæ præclaram actionem continet inter dominum Iesum Christum & Ananiam, cuius ministerio Paulus ordinari debuit. Huius singulas partes, quantum dominus dederit, explicabimus.
units.tr: Although the conversions and callings of all the apostles ought to be carefully considered by us, the conversion of Paul deserves particular attention: partly because it offers a remarkable and outstanding example of divine goodness towards sinners, and partly because Paul labored more than all the other apostles, and no other writings are more often cited, both by the ancient and by the more recent teachers of the Church, in explaining the cause of faith and salvation. It is necessary, therefore, that we know who he was and how God called and converted him, so that his authority may carry greater weight with us. This is why Luke describes his history so carefully. He has set out here how the Lord interrupted Paul's fierceness and terrible efforts in the midst of his course, with such force that he who had shortly before been a most bitter enemy now offered himself to the Lord as teachable and compliant. Here Luke rightly adds Paul's ordination to the apostolic office, which contains a notable action between the Lord Jesus Christ and Ananias, through whose ministry Paul was to be ordained. We shall explain each of its parts as far as the Lord grants.

units.la: Primum, à domino vocatur Ananias, vt illius ministerio Paulus ordinetur. Et de hoc quidem in præsenti pauca Lucas dicit, pluribus autem de illo ipse Paulus differet, quando illum pietatis nomine commendat, & apud omnes Iudæos probitatis & innocentiæ testimonium meruisse dicit. Act. 22. Hunc per visionem suæ voluntatis certum facit dominus, & simul Paulum assiduis precibus vacantem alia visione ad excipiendum digne Ananiam præparat. Hic verò obseruandus est nobis Christus dominus, qui vtrunque visione luculenta instruere voluit. Ex eo eo enim ardens Christi pro humani generis salute studium agnoscitur, quo cum omnes prosequi soleat, in primis tamen illud in quarendis & saluandis perditis ouibus adhibere consueuit, quemadmodum ipse alibi fatetur. Luc. 15. Quod vt consolationem nobis adfert, ita nostræ etiam institutioni feruit, vt nimirum saluandis potius quàm perdendis peccatoribus studeamus, nec illos imitemur, qui dum feruenti diuinæ gloriæ zelo gloriantur, omnes eos temerè abijciunt & damnant, quos semel à via veritatis exorbitauisse videnti. Deinde admonemur simul, quàm referat, vt in externo verbi ministerio omnia rite & legitimè administrentur. Nisi enim illic & ministri digne vocentur, suaeq; vocationis certi sint, & rite præparentur ad hos excipiendum auditores, fructus dignus sequi non poterit. Quomodo enim prædicabunt, nisi missi fuerint? Rom. 10. Vel quibus rationibus aduersus impiorum minas & improbos conatus
units.tr: First, Ananias is called by the Lord so that Paul may be ordained through his ministry. Luke says only a little about this here, but Paul himself will speak at greater length about him, when he commends him for his piety and says that he had won a testimony of uprightness and innocence from all the Jews. Acts 22. The Lord makes known his will to Ananias by a vision, and at the same time prepares Paul, who was occupied in constant prayer, by another vision to receive Ananias worthily. Here we must observe Christ the Lord, who wished to instruct both of them by a clear vision. For from this we recognize Christ's burning zeal for the salvation of the human race: although he is accustomed to care for all, he has especially applied himself to seeking and saving the lost sheep, as he himself testifies elsewhere. Luke 15. This both comforts us and serves our instruction, so that we may strive to save sinners rather than destroy them, and not imitate those who, while they boast of a fervent zeal for the divine glory, rashly cast off and condemn all whom they see to have wandered from the way of truth. Next, we are reminded at the same time how much it matters that everything in the outward ministry of the Word be administered duly and lawfully. For unless the ministers themselves are worthily called and certain of their calling, and unless the hearers are duly prepared to receive them, no worthy fruit can follow. For how shall they preach unless they are sent? Rom. 10. Or with what arguments shall we rise against the threats of the impious and the wicked efforts of those who have seized the office of teaching by evil arts?

units.la: Ananias vocatur, vt Paulum ordinet. conatus erigentur, qui malis artibus docendi officium vsurparunt? Rursus, nisi praeparati & ritè instructi ad verbum Domini auditores accesserint, salutare illud semen, vel in viam, vel in loca petricosa, vel in spinas excipient, & multa obstabunt, quò minus fructus dignos facere possint. Quare bonestos animos Christus requirit, qui semel exceptum semen tenaciter servent, & aduersus omnes Satanae simul & mundi propriaeq; carnis suggestiones armati, fructus dignos ferant in patientia. Luc. 8. Ad illud vero diligenti praeparatione opus esse, quiuis intelliget, qui humanae naturae corruptionem rectè perspectam habuerit. Haec si hodie expendamus, facile patebit, cur passim fere abfq; fructu praedicetur. Nam & maxima minis trorum pars, non expectata legitima vocatione Domini, malis artibus ecclesiae ministerium ventris gratia & studio inuadunt, & qui verbi auditores non omnino impij videri volunt, ita ad illud accedunt, vt illos hoc potius ex consuetudine vulgari, quàm serio emendationis studio facere videas, ijs omnino similes, qui apud prophetam dicebant: Venite quaeso, & audite quod nam verbum egressum sit à Domino &c. Vide locum Ezech. 33. cap.
units.tr: Ananias is called so that he may ordain Paul. Shall efforts be raised up against those who have usurped the office of teaching by evil arts? Again, unless hearers come to the word of the Lord prepared and rightly instructed, that saving seed will be received either by the wayside, or on rocky places, or among thorns, and many things will hinder them from bearing worthy fruit. Therefore Christ requires honest hearts, who hold fast the seed once received, and who, armed against all the suggestions of Satan, of the world and of their own flesh, bear worthy fruit in patience. Luke 8. That such careful preparation is necessary anyone will understand who has rightly grasped the corruption of human nature. If we weigh these things today, it will be easy to see why preaching is almost everywhere without fruit. For a great part of the ministers, without waiting for the lawful calling of the Lord, seize the ministry of the Church by evil arts, for the sake of their belly and for their own ambition; and those who do not wish to seem altogether impious among the hearers of the Word come to it in such a way that you may see them doing so more from common custom than from a serious desire for amendment, altogether like those who said to the prophet: "Come, we pray, and hear what word has gone out from the Lord," etc. See the passage, Ezek. 33.

units.la: Praeterea Paulus quoque consyderandus venit, quem Dominus Ananiae loquens, orauisse testatur. Id verò de assiduis precibus, quibus toto illo triduo vacauit, intelligendum esse, ex circumstantijs facile liquet, cum multa fuerint, quae Paulum ad precandum excitare potuerunt. Senserat enim horribilem Dei manum, qua profratus fuerat. Audiuerat se caelitus accusari tanquam publicum filij Dei hostem. Obuersabantur ergo illius animo improbi conatus & immanis saeuitia & impietas, quibus in Christi nomen & ecclesiam peccauerat: piorum item exilia, vincula, carceres, tormenta, vnà cum mulierum & parvulorum eiulatu & clamoribus, quorum omnium ipse author fuerat. Exagitabat consternatum adhuc mens sibi male conscia. Deinde etiam promissa revelationis & institutionis expectatio, haud vulgare sedulò precandi zelum in ipso excitare potuit. Attamen tam sedulò tamque ardenter orantem toto triduo fructratur (vt ita dicam) Dominus. Commendant haec nobis indefinens orandi studium, cum non pauciores nec leuiores causae sint, quae nos quoque ad illud excitare possunt. Nam si in nosmetipsos descendamus, peccata haud vulgaria deprehendemus, quibus Dei iram meruimus. Sentimus frequenter Dei irati manum. Exagitat frequenter scelerum conscientia. Diuina institutione omnes indigemus. Instant & vrgent passim omnis generis aduersa. Quorum meditatio, nisi precandi ardorem in nobis excitare poterit, ferrei & glaciei frigidiores merito dicemur. Paulus certè has ob causas nos indesinenter orare iubet. 1. Thessal. 5. cap. Ita verò precibus instandum esse meminerimus, ne diffidentiae aut impatientia malo superati, Deo temere praescri bamus. Differt enim ille interdum promissam nobis opem, non quòd in se sperantes fructrari velit, sed vt fidem nostram exerceat: cuius rei exempla tum in Paulo hoc loco, tum in Abrahamo, Cananea muliere, & multis aliis passim proponuntur. Hic ergo fidei neruos intendamus, & viduae illius exemplum imitemur, cuius importunitate iniustum quoq; iudicem superatum esse, Christus testatur. Luc. 18. Sed ô miseros & infelices nos, qui vt ad preces vix extrema necessitate accedimus, ita in iisdem languemus & deficimus illico, vt primum non nostris votis per omnia dominus annuerit, nostrae nimirum conditionis parum memores, qui cum ferui simus, Dominum expectare, non autem illi imperiose praescribere, debebamus.
units.tr: Next, we must consider Paul, whom the Lord, speaking to Ananias, testifies to have been praying. From the circumstances it is easy to see that this must be understood of the constant prayers with which he occupied himself throughout those three days, since there were many things that could stir Paul to pray. He had felt the terrible hand of God by which he had been struck down. He had heard that he was accused from heaven as a public enemy of the Son of God. The wicked efforts, the monstrous cruelty and the impiety by which he had sinned against the name of Christ and the Church were before his mind; likewise the exiles, chains, prisons and tortures of the godly, together with the wailing and cries of women and little children, all of which he himself had caused. His mind, still dismayed and conscious of wrong, tormented him. Then also the expectation of the promised revelation and instruction could stir in him no common zeal for earnest prayer. Yet the Lord, so to speak, disappointed him for three days though he prayed so diligently and so fervently. These things commend to us an unceasing zeal for prayer, since there are no fewer or lighter reasons which can also stir us to it. For if we descend into ourselves, we find sins that are not ordinary, by which we have deserved God's wrath. We often feel the hand of the angry God. The consciousness of our crimes often torments us. We all lack divine instruction. Adversities of every kind press upon us and urge us on everywhere. If the meditation on these things cannot kindle in us the ardor of prayer, we shall rightly be called colder than iron and ice. Paul certainly bids us to pray without ceasing for these reasons. 1 Thess. 5. And we must remember that we should press on with prayers in such a way that we do not, overcome by distrust or impatience, rashly prescribe to God. For he sometimes delays the help he has promised us, not because he wishes to disappoint those who hope in him, but in order to exercise our faith. Examples of this are set forth, in this passage in Paul, and in Abraham, the Canaanite woman, and many others. Here, then, let us stretch the sinews of faith, and imitate the example of that widow, by whose persistence Christ testifies that even an unjust judge was overcome. Luke 18. But woe to us, wretched and unhappy, who scarcely come to prayer except in extreme necessity, and then at once grow weary and faint in it, if the Lord does not in every respect grant our wishes straightaway, forgetting, of course, our own condition, since we are servants and ought to wait for the Lord rather than prescribe to him imperiously.

units.la: Sed Ananiam videamus, qui periculi metu superatus, aduersus euidens & disertum Domini mandatum tergiuersatur. Ait enim: Domine, audiui ex multis de viro hoc, quanta mala fecerit sanctis tuis Hierosolymis, & hic habet potestatem à summis sacerdotibus vinciendi omnes, qui inuocant nomen tuum. Aliorum testimonia producit, ne fructra sibi metuere videatur. At ridiculum est, hominum potius testimoniis, quàm Dei verbo niti. Ridiculum item ex aliorum ore Saulis gestas coram Domino recensere, quasi hae illum hucusq; latuissent. Sed eò nos deducit pessimus & stultissimus consultor, metus, si illu semel in Dei mandatis discutiendis adhibuerimus. Constat tamen exemplo hoc, illum, non raro in sanctos etiam & fidos Dei cultores cadere. Eodem Abrahamu superatum legimus, vt Saram sibi coniugem esse negaret. Gen. 12. & 20. Eodem perculsus Moses, agerrime adduci potest, vt liberandi populi Israelitici munus aggrediatur. Exod. 3. & 4. Sensit hunc Elias propheta, quàdo posse deuictos & iugulatos Baalis sacerdotes, muliebribus regina Iezabelis minis animo fractus incertam fugam capessit. 1. Reg. 19. Metu quoque deceptus Ionas, inter marinos fluctus & barbaros nautas maiorem sibi securitatem spondet, quàm in Domini vocatione & praesidio. Possent hic aliorum quoq; prophetarum & apostolorum exempla adduci. Sed est haec humana infirmi‐tas, propter quam nemo temere damnari debet, quando non obscura illius indicia in Christo quoq;, cum mortis hora instaret, eluxisse videmus. Curandum vero, ne hac ita nos absorberi patiamur, ut iniunctam nobis a Domino prouinciam omnino deseramus. Quin potius in Dei prouidentiam respi‐ciendo, nos totos ipsius voluntati committamus, sicuti apostolos Christus admonet. Matth. 10. Quo etiam generales diuini auxilij promissiones referri debent, quae certum & fidum praesidium in Dei vocatione ambulantibus pollicentur. Et his quidem Ananiam quoq; confirmatum esse crediderim, qui licet initio subtimidus videatur, cedit tamen instanti Domino, & denuo mandanti fidele obse‐quium praestat.
units.tr: But let us look at Ananias, who, overcome by fear of danger, shrinks from the clear and express command of the Lord. For he says: "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem, and here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name." He produces the testimonies of others, as if he feared in vain. But it is ridiculous to rely on the testimonies of men rather than on the word of God. It is equally ridiculous to recount to the Lord, from the mouths of others, the deeds of Saul, as if they had been hidden from him until now. But the worst and most foolish counselor, fear, leads us to this, if we once allow it to be used in examining the commands of God. Yet this example shows that it often befalls even the saints and faithful worshipers of God. We read that Abraham was overcome by the same fear, so that he denied that Sarah was his wife. Gen. 12 and 20. Moses, struck by the same fear, could most readily be brought to undertake the task of freeing the people of Israel. Exod. 3 and 4. The prophet Elijah felt the same, when, broken in spirit by the threats of Queen Jezebel, he took to flight in uncertainty, although he could have destroyed and slain the priests of Baal. 1 Kings 19. Jonah, too, deceived by fear, promised himself greater safety among the sea waves and the barbarian sailors than in the calling and protection of the Lord. Examples of other prophets and apostles could be brought forward here as well. But this is human weakness, on account of which no one ought to be rashly condemned, since we see clear signs of it shining forth even in Christ, when the hour of death was at hand. We must take care, however, that we do not allow ourselves to be so absorbed by it that we altogether abandon the task laid upon us by the Lord. Rather, looking to the providence of God, let us commit ourselves wholly to his will, as Christ admonishes the apostles. Matth. 10. To this also the general promises of divine help should be referred, which promise a sure and faithful protection to those who walk in God's calling. And I think Ananias too was confirmed by these, who, although he at first seems rather timid, yields nonetheless to the Lord who presses him, and renders faithful obedience when he is commanded again.

units.la: Est autem cumprimis praeclara consolatio, qua nutantem & meticulosum Ananiae animum Dominus erigit & confirmat. Vade (inquit) quia organum electum mihi est iste, ut portet nomen meum coram gentibus, & regibus, & filijs Israel. Ego enim ostendam ei, quanta oporteat ipsum pro nomine meo pati. Videntur autem duae rationes adduci, propter quas non timere debeat Ananias, & vtraq; a Pauli persona desumitur. Primo enim, illum non ut antehac tyrannum & perse‐cutorem esse ait, sed ex electorum numero, adeoq; fortissimum fidelissimumq; Christiani nominis pro‐pugnatorem in posterum fore. Deinde tam abesse docet, ut a Paulo aliqua persecutio timeri debeat, ut potius ipse nihil non propter Christi nomen sit passurus. Comprehendunt autem haec verba praeclarum & illustre Pauli praeconium, in cuius consyderatione non indiligenter nos versari oportet, cum ut plenius a nobis cognoscatur diuinae bonitatis excellentia, tum ut intelligamus, quanta apud nos esse debeat Paulinae doctrinae authoritas.
units.tr: It is indeed a most excellent consolation by which the Lord raises up and strengthens Ananias's hesitant and fearful mind. "Go," he says, "for this man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the sons of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name." Two reasons seem to be given why Ananias should not fear, and both are drawn from Paul's own person. First, Christ says that Paul is not, as before, a tyrant and persecutor, but one of the number of the elect, and that in future he will be the bravest and most faithful champion of the Christian name. Second, he teaches that Paul is so far from being someone from whom any persecution should be feared, that rather he himself is going to suffer everything on account of the name of Christ. These words contain a remarkable and illustrious eulogy of Paul, and we ought not to dwell on its consideration carelessly, both so that the excellence of divine goodness may be more fully known by us, and so that we may understand how great the authority of Pauline doctrine should be among us.

units.la: Primo vas electionis Hebraica phrasi dicitur, id est, organum electissimum. Solent enim Hebrai vasis nomine omne genus armorum siue instrumentorum complecti. Et ijdem genitiuo substantiui pro adiectiuo vtuntur. Dicuntur autem homines vasa siue organa Dei, eo quod per illos sua iudicia hic exequitur. Ita Paulus alibi vasa gloriae & misericordiae, pro electis, & rursum vasa irae pro reprobis vsurpat. Rom. 9. Et Sanherib eadem ratione virga furoris Domini dicitur. Isa. 10. Electum vero organum Christus Paulum vocat, eo quod per hunc maxima & saluberrima opera in euangelij & fidei salutifice promulgatione executus est. Interim admonet vasis siue organi vocabulum, ut homines suae conditionis memores, si quid in seipsis eximium & praeclarum vident, illud non sibi ipsis proprium esse putent, sed omnem laudem & gloriam Deo deberi intelligant, qui ipsorum operati dignatus est. Non intelligunt hoc reprobi & Dei cognitione vacui: quare sua viribus & con‐silijs arroganter tribuunt, quicquid in ipsis eximium habetur. Quam vero illud Domino displiceat, Sanherib Assyrij & Nabuchodonosoris Babylonij exempla abunde docent. Vide Isa. 10. Dan. 4. cap. Multo rectius haec Paulus obseruauit, qui quicquid est, se ex Dei gratia esse ingenue fatetur. 1. Cor. 15. Idem ministros omnes admonet, ne quid vel sibi ipsis vel aliis tribuant, sed omnem ministerij effectum Dei esse meminerint, qui solus dat incrementum. 1. Cor. 3. Plurimum vero ad animos homi‐num humiliandos haec consyderatio seruit. Solicitos enim reddit, ne insolentia aut securitate excidentes irae vasa & organa efficiantur.
units.tr: First, he is called a chosen vessel in a Hebrew manner of speaking, that is, a most choice instrument. For the Hebrews are accustomed to embrace under the name of vessel every kind of weapon or implement, and they also use the genitive of a substantive in place of an adjective. Men are called vessels or instruments of God because through them he carries out his judgments here. Thus Paul elsewhere uses "vessels of glory and mercy" for the elect, and again "vessels of wrath" for the reprobate. Rom. 9. And Sennacherib for the same reason is called the rod of the Lord's wrath. Isa. 10. Christ calls Paul a chosen instrument because through him he carried out the greatest and most salutary works in the saving proclamation of the gospel and of faith. Meanwhile the word vessel or instrument admonishes people, that mindful of their condition, if they see anything outstanding and remarkable in themselves, they should not think it belongs to themselves, but understand that all praise and glory is owed to God, who has deigned to work through them. The reprobate, who lack knowledge of God, do not understand this; therefore they arrogantly ascribe to their own strength and counsels whatever is considered outstanding in them. How much this displeases the Lord, the examples of Sennacherib the Assyrian and Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian abundantly teach. See Isa. 10 and Dan. 4. Paul observed these things far more rightly, who frankly confesses that whatever he is, he is by the grace of God. 1 Cor. 15. He likewise admonishes all ministers not to ascribe anything either to themselves or to others, but to remember that all the effect of the ministry is of God, who alone gives the increase. 1 Cor. 3. This consideration serves very much to humble people's minds. For it makes them anxious lest, falling through arrogance or complacency, they become vessels and instruments of wrath.

units.la: Secundo finem & vsum huius organi Christus exprimit, & eo destinatum esse docet Paulum, ut nomen ipsius portet, id est, euehat & extollat, coram gentibus & regibus & filijs Israel. Intelligitur autem euangelij praedicatio, qua Christi nomen extolli & celebrari solet, quando in illo paenitentia & remissio peccatorum praedicatur. Hic autem officij admonentur ministri omnes. Horum enim est nomen Iesu Christi portare, id est, illum praedicare saluatorem, regem & sacerdotem, & in illo vno monstrare, quaecunq; saluti nostrae inseruiunt. Ita Paulus se nihil aliud nouisse fatetur, praeter Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum. 1. Cor. 2. Idem in solius Christi cruce sibi gloriandum esse clamat. Galat. 6. Idem nomen Petrus portauit, quando nullum aliud sub Sole hominibus datum esse dixit, in quo saluari ipsos oporteat. Act. 4. Unde colligimus, non Christi ministros esse, sed Antichristi spiritu omnes eos agitari, quicunq; aliud nomen proferunt, in quo paenitentiam aut remissionem peccatorum praedicant. Vide de his 1. Iohan. 4. Simul vero meminerint ministri, non in angulis hoc nomen portandum esse, sed coram gentibus, regibus & Iudaeis. Licet enim non omnes apostoli fuimus, omnium tamen est, ne nos Christi pudeat, & ut de testimonijs ipsius (sicuti Dauid ait) coram regibus loquamur, parati ad reddendam fidei nostræ rationem omni petenti. 1. Pet. 2. Quanta vero fide & studio commissum sibi à Christo munus Paulus obierit, historiæ contextus docebit. Et ipse fatetur, se ab Hierosolymis & circumiacentibus regionibus ad Illyricum usq; euangelium impleuisse. Rom. decimo quinto.
units.tr: Second, Christ sets out the purpose and use of this instrument, and teaches that Paul was destined for this, that he should carry his name, that is, lift it up and exalt it, before the Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel. Now what is meant is the preaching of the gospel, by which the name of Christ is usually exalted and celebrated, when repentance and the forgiveness of sins are proclaimed in him. Here all ministers are admonished of their office. For it is theirs to carry the name of Jesus Christ, that is, to preach him as Saviour, King and Priest, and to show in him alone whatever serves our salvation. So Paul confesses that he knew nothing else except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. 1 Cor. 2. He cries out that he himself should glory in the cross of Christ alone. Gal. 6. Peter carried the same name when he said that no other name under heaven has been given to men, in which they must be saved. Acts 4. Hence we gather that all those who proclaim another name in which they preach repentance or forgiveness of sins are not ministers of Christ, but are all driven by the spirit of Antichrist. On these things see 1 John 4. At the same time, ministers should remember that this name is not to be carried in corners, but before the Gentiles, kings and Jews. For although not all of us are apostles, it is nevertheless the duty of all not to be ashamed of Christ, and, as David says, to speak of his testimonies before kings, ready to give an account of our faith to everyone who asks. 1 Pet. 2. How greatly, with what faith and zeal, Paul performed the task entrusted to him by Christ, the context of the history will show. And he himself confesses that from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions he had fully preached the gospel as far as Illyricum. Rom. 15.

units.la: Tertiò, ne quis tantum Christi ministrum priuilegio quodam immunitatis donatum putaret, de illius quoq; afflictionibus mentionem facit. Ego (inquit) ostendam ei, quanta ipsum oportet pati pro nomine meo. Quæ verba non comminationem, sed potius promissionem habent. Primò enim scimus, Christum suæ gloriæ consortes facere eos, quos crucis suæ socios habere dignatur. Unde Paulus postea Philippenses hoc nomine commendat, quòd ipsis datum fit, ut non modò in Christum credant, verumetiam pro illo patiantur. Deinde inuitatum quoq; fore prædicit, adeoq; suum auxilium in ferenda cruce illi pollicetur. Optimus verò huius dicti interpres ipse Paulus erit, qui Corinthijs scribens, ait: A Iudæis quinquies quadragenas plagas, vna minus, accepi. Ter virgis cæsus fui: semel fui lapidatus: ter naufragium feci, noctem & diem in profundo egi, in itineribus sæpe, in periculis fluminum, periculis latronum, periculis ex genere, periculis ex gentibus, periculis in ciuitate, periculis in deserto, periculis in mari, periculis inter falsos fratres, &c. Vide locum 2. Cor. 11. & 12. cap. Porrò docent hæc euangelium sine cruce prædicari non posse. Nec enim eius lucem mundus hic ferre potest, cum illius opera prava sint. Ioban. 3. Quare ut Paulum hic, ita passim suos de cruce ferenda Christus admonet. Stultissimi ergo mortalium sunt, qui in euangelij ministerio rem sine periculo concifci posse existimant, & mundo huic placere student. Imò functioni huic parum idoneus erit, nisi qui ad crucem & quæuis aduersa ferenda semetipsum præparauerit. De qua re vide apud Lucam cap. 14. Meminerimus autem, vires & facultates ab uno Domino dari, cuius dilectionem, qua ille nos complexus est, si probè perspectam habuerimus, in omnem euentum (ut Paulus postea monuit) parati & inuicti erimus. Rom. 8. Hunc ergo assiduis precibus fatigemus, ut & nobis detur pro Christi nomine pati, & cum eodem cœlestis regni hereditatem adire: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Third, lest anyone think that a minister of Christ is granted some privilege of immunity, he also makes mention of his afflictions. "I," he says, "will show him how much he must suffer for my name." These words contain not a threat but rather a promise. For first, we know that Christ makes those whom he deigns to have as companions of his cross sharers in his glory. Hence Paul afterwards commends the Philippians on this account, because it has been granted to them not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for him. Second, he foretells that Paul will be invited to it too, and so he promises his help in bearing the cross. The best interpreter of this saying will be Paul himself, who, writing to the Corinthians, says: "From the Jews I received five times forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I spent in the deep, often on journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers, etc." See the passage in 2 Cor. 11 and the 12th chapter. Moreover, these things teach that the gospel cannot be preached without the cross. For the world here cannot bear its light, since its works are evil. John 3. Therefore, as he admonishes Paul here, so Christ admonishes his people everywhere to bear the cross. Most foolish, then, are those mortals who think that in the ministry of the gospel something can be done without danger, and who strive to please this world. Indeed, one will be little fit for this function unless he has prepared himself to bear the cross and every adversity. On this matter see Luke 14. Let us remember, however, that strength and abilities are given by the one Lord, whose love, with which he has embraced us, if we have rightly perceived it, we shall be ready and unconquered in every outcome (as Paul afterwards admonished). Rom. 8. Let us therefore weary him with constant prayers, that it may be granted to us too to suffer for the name of Christ, and with him to enter into the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVI.
units.tr: Homily 66.

units.la: Abijt autem Ananias, & ingressus est in domum, & cum imposuisset ei manus, dixit: Saul frater, Dominus misit me, Iesus scilicet, qui tibi apparuit in via, qua veniebas, ut visum recipias, & implearis spiritu sancto. Et continuò deciderunt ab oculis eius tanquam squamæ, & visum recepit: & surgens baptizatus est, & sumpto cibo conualuit. Fuit autem Saulus cum discipulis, qui Damasci agebant, per dies aliquot. Et continuò in Synagogis prædicauit Christum, quòd hic esset filius dei. Obstupescebant autem omnes qui audiebant, & dicebant: Nonne hic est, qui vastauit Hierosolymis eos, qui inuocabant nomen hoc: & eo consilio venit huc, ut eos vinctos duceret ad summos Sacerdotes. Saulus autem corroborabatur, & confundebat Iudæos, qui habitabant Damasci, confirmans quòd hic esset Christus.
units.tr: Ananias went away and entered the house, and laying his hands on him said: "Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me, Jesus himself, who appeared to you on the road by which you were coming, so that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight. He rose and was baptized, and after taking food he regained his strength. Saul stayed for some days with the disciples who were at Damascus. And at once he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God. All who heard were astonished and said: "Is this not the man who in Jerusalem destroyed those who called upon this name, and who came here for the purpose of leading them bound to the chief priests?" But Saul grew stronger and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this man is the Christ.

units.la: Dui Pauli conuersionem summa diligentia Lucas describit, partim quidem ut ex hac Dei gratiam & bonitatem, qua ut peccatores complectitur, agnoscamus: partim verò, ut maior apud nos sit doctrinæ Pauli authoritas, quam ille tam graui protestatione commendauit, ut ne angelo quidem diuersum docenti credendum esse dixerit. Ad utrunq; præclarum illud & illustre testimonium pertinet, quo ipse Christus (sicuti heri audiuimus) Paulum exornauit. Nam electum organum vocat eum, qui paulò ante vas iræ videri poterat. Adhæc illi in rebus agendis fidem, dexteritatem, animi constantiam & patientiam tribuit. Unde colligimus, magnam esse Dei erga peccatores bonitatem, nec contemni a nobis posse Pauli doctrinam, nisi in ipsum Christum contumeliosè peccare, & illius testimonium mendacij arguere velimus. Sed præsentem locum videamus, qui Pauli restitutionem, & primum illius actum in apostolatu siue euangelij ministerio comprehendit.
units.tr: Luke describes Paul's conversion with the greatest care, partly so that we may recognise in it God's grace and goodness, by which he embraces sinners, and partly so that the authority of Paul's teaching may be greater among us, which he commended with such a solemn protestation that he said not even an angel was to be believed if he taught something different. To both purposes belongs that famous and illustrious testimony with which Christ himself (as we heard yesterday) honoured Paul. For he calls him a chosen instrument, though a little before he might have seemed a vessel of wrath. Besides, Christ ascribes to him faithfulness, skill, steadfastness of spirit and patience in carrying out his tasks. From this we gather that God's goodness towards sinners is great, and that Paul's teaching cannot be despised unless we wish to insult Christ himself and charge his testimony with lying. But let us look at the present passage, which contains Paul's restoration and his first act in the apostleship or ministry of the gospel.

units.la: Quoad Pauli restitutionem, qui toto triduo oculis captus, tandem visum recepit, & baptismo in Christi ecclesiam adoptatus est, personae tum Ananiae tum Pauli consyderandae veniunt, vnà cum mirabili effectu, quem mox secutum esse Euangelista tradit. Primò autem de Anania dicemus, cuius ministerio hic Dominus vti voluit. Dicitur is abijsse, & ingressus esse domum Iudae, in qua Paulum diuersari audiuerat. Excussit ergo illi ignauum metum, quo ante correptus fuit, tam seria diuini mandati repetitio, nec amplius vel vulgi rumores, vel carnalis prudentiae rationes Domini praeceptis opponit. Quem animum in omnibus Dei cultoribus videre licet, qui hoc vnum anxie cauent, ne ignobili metu ab obedientiae officio, quo Deo obstricti sunt, reuocentur. Imitemur hos etiam nos, & omni venia siue excusatione indignos esse intelligamus, quos ita absorbet carnis infirmitas & periculorum metus, vt tum Dei tum sui officij immemores, omne Deo obsequium negare pergant.
units.tr: As for Paul's restoration, who for three whole days was deprived of sight and at last recovered it, and was received by baptism into the Church of Christ, we must consider the persons both of Ananias and of Paul, together with the wonderful effect which the evangelist tells us followed soon after. First, however, we shall speak of Ananias, through whose ministry the Lord wished to act. He is said to have gone away and entered the house of Judas, in which he had heard that Paul was staying. The earnest repetition of the divine command therefore drove out the cowardly fear by which he had been seized before, and he no longer set against the Lord's precepts either the rumours of the common people or the reasoning of worldly prudence. We may see this spirit in all the worshippers of God, who take anxious care above all that they not be turned back by base fear from the duty of obedience by which they are bound to God. Let us also imitate them, and understand that those are unworthy of any pardon or excuse who are so overwhelmed by the weakness of the flesh and the dread of dangers that, forgetful both of God and of their own duty, they persist in refusing all obedience to God.

units.la: Deinde manus Saulo impositas dicitur Ananias. Quae ceremonia e veteri Testamento non inepte ad ministrorum ordinationem siue inaugurationem translata est. Olim enim sacrificijs manus imponebant sacerdotes, quae res testabantur, communem hic populi causam agi, & simul altari astantes pecudes Deo consecrabant. Simili ratione per manuum impositionem ministris publica totius ecclesiae cura commendatur, & ipsi admonentur, vt sese Deo consecratos esse meminerint, & proinde in illius gloriam omnia sua studia, curas, labores & vigilias conferant. At quia nullus inanis ceremonia visus esse poterat, verbum simul adhibet Ananias, quo illi nunciat, quaecunque à Christo dicere iussus erat. Vbi intrepidus Ananiae animus obseruandus est, qui & Iesu Christi nomen ingenuè profitetur, & illius seruum sese agnoscit coram illo, quem hucusque acerrimum Christi hostem fuisse nouerat. Rursum vero, quia Christi de Paulo testimonium audierat, illum fratrem appellare non dedignatur. Coniungi ergo debet in ministris fortis & intrepida animi magnitudo cum leni & affabili facilitate, ne videlicet, vel Christi confessionem & debitae obedientiae studium sibi excuti patiantur, vel nimiae & importunae seueritatis supercilio eos improbe repellant, quos fratrum loco completi & Christo per omnia lucrifacere debebant.
units.tr: Next, Ananias is said to have laid his hands on Saul. This ceremony was not unsuitably carried over from the Old Testament to the ordination or installation of ministers. For formerly the priests laid their hands on the sacrifices, which signified that the common cause of the people was being transacted, and at the same time, standing by the altar, they consecrated the beasts to God. In a similar way, by the laying on of hands the public care of the whole Church is committed to ministers, and they are reminded that they should remember they have been consecrated to God, and therefore should devote all their zeal, cares, labours and watchings to his glory. But because no empty ceremony could seem sufficient, Ananias at the same time adds a word, by which he announces to Saul whatever he had been ordered to say by Christ.
