Here we must notice Ananias's fearless spirit, who both openly professes the name of Jesus Christ and acknowledges himself to be the servant of him whom he knew to have been until then the fiercest enemy of Christ. Again, because he had heard Christ's testimony about Paul, he does not disdain to call him brother. Therefore in ministers a strong and fearless greatness of spirit ought to be joined with a gentle and affable kindness; so that they neither allow their confession of Christ and their zeal for due obedience to be shaken from them, nor, with the haughty frown of excessive and unseasonable severity, wrongly repel those whom they ought to have gained as brothers and won for Christ in every way.

units.la: His vero mirabilem effectum Lucas subijcit. Nam à Pauli oculis squamarum instar aliquid decidisse, & hunc illico visum recepisse, scribit. Squamarum vero mentionem facit, vt intelligamus non leuiter tantum oculos, vt fulgure fieri consueuit, perstrictos, sed crassam & miraculosam caecitatem illis indutam fuisse. Nec enim miraculo caret, quod intra paucos dies squamae in illis enasci potuerunt, quae omnem visus facultatem adimerent. Nec minus miraculosa est tam subita amissi visus restitutio. Interim patet, Dominum non obscurè Saulum pristinae conditionis, quam in Iudaismo, seu potius Pharisaismo agens sustinuerat, admonere voluisse. Tunc enim ad Gamalielis pedes institutus, cum inter aequales omnes mirificè proficeret, sibi ipsi prae caeteris oculatus esse & sapere videbatur. Atqui mera caecitas erat, quae illi tantopere placebat, sapientia. Adhuc enim illi ob oculos expansum erat velum, quo Iudaei prohibentur, quò minus germanam Mosis faciem intueri possint: eò quod Christi cognitione careant, in quo solo caelestem lucè Deus pater exhibuit, quae omnes ignorantia & carnalis zeli tenebras discutere potest. Haec quia Paulo illucescere coepit, ab oculis illius squamae decidunt, & caeco ignorantiae zelo se hucusque miserè & turpiter seductum fuisse videt. Christum ergo lucem sequantur, & in illo ambulent, quicunque absque offendiculo in salutis & fidei causa versari voluerint. Vide Iohan. 1. 8. & 12. cap.
units.tr: To these things Luke adds the wonderful effect. For he writes that something like scales fell from Paul's eyes, and that he immediately recovered his sight. He mentions scales so that we may understand that his eyes were not merely dazzled slightly, as is usual with lightning, but that a thick and miraculous blindness had come upon them. For it is no small miracle that within a few days scales could grow in them which took away all power of sight. Nor is the restoration of the sight so suddenly lost less miraculous. Meanwhile it is plain that the Lord wished to remind Saul, not obscurely, of his former condition, which he had endured while living in Judaism, or rather Pharisaism. For then, when he had been trained at the feet of Gamaliel and was making remarkable progress among all his peers, he seemed to himself to be keener-sighted and wiser than the rest. Yet the wisdom which pleased him so much was sheer blindness. For the veil was still spread over his eyes, by which the Jews are prevented from beholding the true face of Moses, because they lack the knowledge of Christ, in whom alone God the Father has shown the heavenly light, which can disperse all the darkness of ignorance and carnal zeal. Since this light began to shine upon Paul, the scales fall from his eyes, and he sees that until then he had been miserably and shamefully led astray by a blind zeal of ignorance. Let all who wish to live without stumbling in the cause of salvation and faith therefore follow Christ the light, and walk in him. See John 1, 8, and chapter 12.

units.la: Quid vero Paulus recepto visu fecit? Surgens baptizatus est, & sumpto cibo conualuit. Primò baptizatum fuisse dicit, eò quod de hoc etiam ab Ananias admonitus fuerat, quemadmodum ipse Act. 22. testabitur. Atqui superuacaneus videri poterat baptismus in eo, quem ipse Christus organum electum esse agnosceat, qui mirificam Christi virtutem senserat, qui iam spiritu sancto erat donatus, & cuius oculos tum mentis tum corporis singulari beneficio Dominus illuminauerat. Sed nihil superuacaneum & inutile iudicant sancti, quod à Domino institutum esse norunt. Et quia eorum obseruationem, quae in veteri Testamento ad tempus correctionis vsq; tradita fuere, tanta seueritate praecepta fuisse legunt, vt ea transgredi capitale esset: nunquam sibi tantum permittunt, vt in ijs aliquid neglgant, quae Christus abs se tradita vsq; ad mundi consummationem obseruari vult. Execrabilis ergo est illorum impudentia & temeritas, qui Baptismi & Cœnae dominicae vsum hodie impudenter negligunt, & ea demum re fidei suae perfectionem obtentant, quòd Domini instituta improbè aspernari audeat. Deinde cibo sumpto amissas & collapsas corporis vires Paulus recreat & revocat. Vtuntur ergo ijs sanctis, quae naturae nostrae conseruandae seruiunt, quaeq; in eum vsum nobis à Deo sunt tradita: qualia sunt cibus, potus, vestitus, & si qua alia sunt eius generis. Ita ipse Paulus Timotheum monet, vt propter stomachi imbecillis cruditatem vino modico vtatur. 1. Tim. 5. Confutatur ijs exemplis inepta illorum superstitio, qui eo nomine singularis sanctitatis titulum venantur, quod necessariis abstineant. Licet enim non damnemus ieiunia, quibus lasciuientis carnis ferocia domatur, vt sponso Christo libentius obtemperet: ita probare non possumus eos, qui meritum in eo constituunt, siue quaerunt, quod diuinis literis nusquam mandatum est. In illos enim illud Domini competit: Quando comeditis & bibitis, annò vobis comedistis, & vobis bibistis? Zach. 7. Qua ratione etiam ijsdem dici potest: Quando ieiunastis, vobis ieiunastis. Quid? quod Paulus ab illis cauendum esse docet, qui superstitiose quibusdam abstinere docent, & eos daemoniorum doctrinam afferre dicit, qui cibis à Domino in vsum humanum creatis abstinere iubent. Coloss. 2. 1. Tim. 4.
units.tr: But what did Paul do when he had recovered his sight? "He rose and was baptized, and after taking food he regained his strength." First, Luke says that he was baptized, because Ananias had also admonished him about this, as Paul himself will testify in Acts 22. Yet baptism might seem superfluous in one whom Christ himself acknowledged as a chosen instrument, who had felt Christ's wonderful power, who had already been given the Holy Spirit, and whose eyes, both of mind and of body, the Lord had illuminated by a singular benefit. But the saints judge nothing superfluous or useless which they know to have been instituted by the Lord. And since they read that the observances which were handed down in the Old Testament for a time of correction were prescribed with such strictness that to transgress them was a capital offence, they never permit themselves so much as to neglect anything in those things which Christ has handed down and wishes to be observed until the end of the world. Therefore the impudence and rashness of those is detestable who today shamelessly neglect the use of Baptism and the Lord's Supper, and who claim as the perfection of their faith the fact that they dare to scorn the Lord's institutions wickedly. Then, after taking food, Paul restored and recalled his bodily strength, which had been lost and had collapsed. Therefore they use those holy gifts which serve the preservation of our nature, and which God has given us for that purpose: such as food, drink, clothing, and any other things of that kind. So Paul himself advises Timothy to use a little wine because of the weakness and indigestion of his stomach. 1 Tim. 5. By these examples the foolish superstition of those is refuted, who hunt for the title of singular holiness on the ground that they abstain from necessary things. For although we do not condemn fasts, by which the wild lust of the flesh is tamed so that it may more willingly obey its spouse Christ, we cannot approve of those who place merit in such things, or seek it there, when nothing of the kind has ever been commanded in the sacred writings. For against them the Lord's words apply: "When you eat and drink, do you not eat for yourselves, and drink for yourselves?" Zech. 7. In the same way it may be said to them: "When you fast, you fast for yourselves." What of the fact that Paul teaches that they must be guarded against, who superstitiously teach abstinence from certain things, and says that they bring in the doctrine of demons, who order abstinence from foods which the Lord created for human use? Col. 2. 1 Tim. 4.

units.la: Sed pergamus in suscepta loci tractatione, & primum Pauli in euangelij ministerio actum consyderemus, de quo duo dicuntur. Primò cum discipulis, id est Christianis, qui Damasci fuerunt, conversatus fuisse scribitur. Non ergo Iudaeis aut gentibus, publicis Christi inimicis, sed fidelibus, qui & ipsi nomen Christi profitebantur, sese coniunxit. Admonemur exemplo hoc, piorum comercijs eos vti debere, qui Christiani haberi volunt, ab illis autem abstinere, quos Christiani nominis hostes ex professo esse nouerunt. Licet enim pio cum alienis à fide conuersari permissum sit, quatenus illud publica necessitas requirit, ea tamen commercia sibi noxia esse intelligant fideles, quae nulla necessitate iubente, solius amicitiae mundanae & voluptatis gratia cum impijs contrahuntur. Legimus equidem Iesum Christum nonnunquam pharisaeorum & publicanorum conuiuijs interfuisse. Illud vero ipsum non animi gratia, sed vt illos saluti lucrifaceret, fecisse constat. Nunquam enim sui officij ita oblitus est, vt ad illorum errores conniueret, sed conuiuales quoq; sermones salutaribus praeceptis & regni coelorum mysterijs condiuit. Quod si qui ad eum modum incredulorum consortia quaerunt, merito illorum studium probamus. At ijs, qui ad impiorum blasphemias, nefandam idololatriam, ineptam superstitionem, corruptissimos mores & studia turpissima ignauo & oscitanti animo conniuent, vt illis belli homines videri, illorumq; stabili amicitia & fauore frui possint, Dauidicum illud occinimus, qui eum inter coelestis regni ciues ascribit, qui nullius reputat impium, eos autem qui Dominum timent, honorat. Psal. 15. Idem se sanctis, qui in terra sunt, delectari dicit. Psal. 16. Cur enim in satanae & Antichristi castris Christi miles otiosus & iners conspiciatur? Cur illorum dictafactaq; ferat, quos Christi honori & gloriae derogare nouit?
units.tr: But let us go on with the subject of this passage and first consider the first of Paul's actions in the ministry of the gospel, about which two things are said. First, he is recorded as having associated with the disciples, that is, the Christians, who were at Damascus. So he joined himself not to the Jews or the Gentiles, the public enemies of Christ, but to the faithful, who also professed the name of Christ. This example teaches us that those who wish to be considered Christians ought to have dealings with pious people, and should keep away from those whom they know to be the open enemies of the Christian name. For although it is permitted for a godly person to deal with outsiders to the faith, so far as public necessity requires, the faithful should understand that those dealings are harmful to them which are entered into with the ungodly, without any necessity demanding them, merely for the sake of worldly friendship and pleasure. We indeed read that Jesus Christ sometimes attended the banquets of the Pharisees and tax collectors. But it is clear that he did this not for the sake of enjoyment, but so that he might win them to salvation. For he never forgot his office so far as to connive at their errors, but he seasoned even their table talk with wholesome precepts and with the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. If anyone seeks the company of unbelievers in this way, we rightly approve his purpose. But as for those who, with idle and drowsy minds, wink at the blasphemies of the ungodly, their unspeakable idolatry, their foolish superstition, their most corrupt morals and their most shameful pursuits, so that they may seem to be fine fellows to them and may enjoy their steady friendship and favour, we sing that verse of David's, who counts among the citizens of the heavenly kingdom the one who does not regard the ungodly as worthy, but honours those who fear the Lord (Ps. 15). He also says that he takes delight in the saints who are on the earth (Ps. 16). For why should a soldier of Christ be seen idle and slothful in the camp of Satan and of Antichrist? Why should he bear the sayings and deeds of those whom he knows to detract from the honour and glory of Christ?

units.la: Secundo loco de Pauli doctrina agitur, quae in hoc actu merito primas tenet. Dicitur autem publice in synagogis praedicauisse. Et quid nam praedicauit nouus ille apostolus? Iesum, & hunc quidem esse filium Dei & Christum. Haec vero non perfunctorie modo & frigide docuit, sed argumentis & scripturis validissimè confirmauit, vt Iudaeos omnes, qui infensissimi Iesu Christi hostes erant, plane confunderet, & suarum in religione rerum incertos faceret.
units.tr: In the second place, the teaching of Paul is treated, which in this action rightly holds the first place. It is said that he preached publicly in the synagogues. And what, pray, did that new apostle preach? Jesus, and that this same Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ. He did not teach this merely in a superficial and cold manner, but confirmed it most powerfully with arguments and with the Scriptures, so that he utterly confounded all the Jews, who were the most hostile enemies of Jesus Christ, and made them uncertain of their own beliefs in religion.

units.la: Habemus in his summam doctrinae Pauli, cuius praecipua nobis esse debet authoritas. Fatetur hic alibi, se nihil praeter Iesum Christum nouisse. 1. Corinth. 2. cap. Quem ergo solum nouit, solum quoque praedicare voluit. Paucis autem, adeoq; duobus capitibus comprehendit, quaecunq; de illo prophetiis simul & apostolicis scriptis fusissime tractata sunt. Primò enim Iesum, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, Dei quoq; filium esse docuit. Ita vero complexus est quaecunq; ad Christi personam cognoscendam faciunt, in qua nisi humanam simul & diuinam naturam agnoscamus, salua & integra subsistere nequit salutis nostrae ratio, quam yni Christo inniti omnis scriptura passim testatur. Vtrunq; vero Paulus agnoscit. Quomodo enim non humanam in Iesu naturam fateretur, qui de illo loquebatur, quem à Iudaeis captum, crucifixum, & mortuum fuisse nouerat, & quem alibi ex Iudaeis hominem verum secundum carnem natum esse testatur? Rom. 9. cap. At cum eundem filium Dei esse dicit, diuinitate eius negare non potest. Quid enim ex Deo, nisi Deus, nascereretur? Verum ergo Deum & hominem esse docuit Iesum: Deum quidem ab aeterno, hominem vero factum con-stituto siue praefinito tempore, quemadmodum alibi monet. Gal. 4. Deinde efficium quoq; illius exposuit, & ostendit CHRISTVM, id est, nullum Dei esse. Vngebantur olim ex veteri instituto reges & sacerdotes. Et quia tum regis tum sacerdotis munere promissus humano genere saluator fungi debebat, illum Christi siue Messiae, id est, vncti nomine Deus insignire voluit. Alterum ergo Saulinae doctrinae caput fuit, Iesum hunc, qui verus Deus & homo est, simul etiam promissum esse mundi saluatorem, quem legales ceremoniae adumbrarint, & prophetarum oracula venturum esse praedixerint. Atqui haec illa doctrina est, quae sola apostolica dici meretur. Cum ea enim confessione conuenit, quam quaerente Christo, omnium apostolorum nomine Petrus edidit, dicens: Tu es Christus ille filius Dei viuentis. Et tu verba vitae aeternae habes. Matth. 16. Ioan. 6. Et haec illa fides est, quae Christo petrae superstructa, vacillare nequit, nec illi portae inferorum praevalent. Hanc ergo doctrinam constanter feruet, quicunq; Christi cultores dici & apostolica fide gloriari voluerint. De hac enim Paulum pronunciauisse constat: Etiamsi nos, aut angelus e caelo praedicauerit vobis euangelium, praeter id quod praedicauimus vobis, anathema sit. Galat. 1.
units.tr: We have here the sum of Paul's teaching, whose chief authority ought to be ours. He declares elsewhere that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 2). Therefore he wished to preach only the one whom he alone knew. But in a few words, and indeed in two chapters, he sums up everything that the prophecies and the apostolic writings have treated at length concerning him. For first he taught that Jesus, who was born a man of the Virgin Mary, is also the Son of God. He so comprehended everything that contributes to knowing the person of Christ, in which, unless we acknowledge both his human and his divine nature, the ground of our salvation cannot stand safe and whole, and all Scripture everywhere testifies that this ground rests on Christ alone. Paul acknowledges both. For how would he not confess a human nature in Jesus, when he was speaking of one whom he knew to have been seized, crucified and killed by the Jews, and whom elsewhere he testifies to have been born as a true man according to the flesh from the Jews (Rom. 9)? But when he calls him the Son of God, he cannot deny his divinity. For what could be born of God except God? Therefore he taught that Jesus is true God and true man: God indeed from eternity, but made man at a fixed or predetermined time, as he warns elsewhere (Gal. 4). Next he set out his office and showed that he is the CHRIST, that is, the anointed one of God. Kings and priests were anointed of old by ancient custom. And since the Saviour promised to the human race was to exercise the office of both king and priest, he wished God to mark him with the name of Christ or Messiah, that is, the Anointed. The second head of Paul's doctrine, therefore, was that this Jesus, who is true God and man, is also the promised Saviour of the world, whom the legal ceremonies foreshadowed and the oracles of the prophets foretold would come. And indeed this is that teaching which alone deserves to be called apostolic. For it agrees with that confession which Peter, when Christ asked, made in the name of all the apostles, saying: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and "You have the words of eternal life" (Matt. 16; John 6). And this is the faith which, built upon Christ the rock, cannot waver, nor do the gates of hell prevail against it. Therefore whoever wishes to be called a worshipper of Christ and to glory in the apostolic faith should hold firmly to this teaching. For it is clear that Paul pronounced concerning this: "Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1).

units.la: Num vero obiter duntaxat & perfunctorie doctrinam hanc Paulus proposuit? Nequaquam. Imo, quia Damasci Iudaeorum scholae erant, quorum delirijs vera Iesu Christi cognitio obscurabatur, illa sibi confutanda & veram de Christo doctrinam scripturarum authoritate confirmandam esse putauit. Constat enim Iudaeos agnouisse quidem veteres de Messia promissiones. Sed quia hunc terrenum tantummodo principe fore imaginabantur, qui vetus illud Israeliticae gentis regnum instaurare, illius maiestatem reducere, & populum Romanae tyrannidis iugo liberare deberet: nunquam adduci potuerunt, vt Iesum, cuius aduentus humillimus, conuersatio vilissima, & mors ignominiosa fuerat, Messiam illum agnoscerent. Horum ergo errores fortiter oppugnauit Paulus, & Iesum hunc Dei filium & Messiam esse, tanta scripturarum authoritate & argumentorum vi asseruit, vt doctissimos quosq;, qui illud hucusq; negare ausi fuerant, pudore suffusos miserè turbaret, rerumq; suarum incertos faceret. Quod omnibus euenire solet, quibus turpe videtur, Christo & veritati manus dare.
units.tr: Did Paul, then, set forth this teaching only in passing and superficially? By no means. Indeed, because there were synagogues of the Jews at Damascus, whose delusions obscured the true knowledge of Jesus Christ, he thought that this teaching had to be refuted and the true doctrine about Christ confirmed by the authority of the Scriptures. For it is certain that the Jews did indeed acknowledge the ancient promises about the Messiah. But because they imagined that he would be only an earthly prince, who ought to restore that old kingdom of the Israelite nation, bring back its majesty, and free the people from the yoke of Roman tyranny, they could never be brought to acknowledge as that Messiah Jesus, whose coming was most humble, whose life was most lowly, and whose death was ignominious. Paul therefore vigorously attacked their errors, and asserted with such weight of Scripture and such force of argument that Jesus is the Son of God and the Messiah, that he sorely troubled the most learned men, who had until then dared to deny it, filling them with shame and making them uncertain of their own position. This is what usually happens to all those for whom it seems shameful to give their hand to Christ and to the truth.

units.la: Admonet locus hic, vt euangelij doctrina praedicari debeat. Qua in re multorum ea est sententia, vt sufficere putent simplicem planamq; mysteriorum salutis explicationem: eos vero inanem operam sumere & intolerabiles dissidiorum authores esse, qui Antichristi tyrannidem arguunt, superstitionem oppugnant, & cum professis veritatis hostibus certamen publicè suscipiunt. Atqui suf-ficere poterat simplex illa salutis doctrina, nisi essent, qui illam erroribus ac tenebris inuoluere, & incautos à veritatis semita abducere studerent. Tales vero cum & olim fuerint, & hodie passim reperiantur, moneri oportet fideles, ne illis aures praebeant. Id vero nunquam efficies, nisi illos toto caelo errare demonstraueris. Rursum cum eo vsq; multorum impudentia progrediatur, vt palam veritati contradicere audeant, hi quoq; publicè confutandi sunt, ne sua temeritate veritatis causam suspicionem reddant. Vtrunq; non apostolos modo, verumetiam Christum fecisse legimus, cuius exemplum merito imitari debent, quicunq; ecclesiae ipsius ministri dici & haberi volunt. Quae causa est, quòd eiusmodi doctores Paulus esse vult, qui non modo sana doctrina rudiores instituere, verumetiam contradicentes conuincere possint. Tit. 1. Et idem scripturas quoq;, in eum finem datas esse testatur, vt aduersarijs redarguendis seruiant. 2. Tim. 3. Quae res tanti momenti esse spiritui sancto visa est, vt per apostolos non modo illius saeculi impostores argui, verumetiam de illis nos admoneri voluerit, qui nouissimis temporibus ecclesiam turbaturi erant. Quo igitur iure illis hodie in ecclesia grassantibus, silentium ministris imponent, qui nullius impietatem traduci volunt?
units.tr: This passage admonishes that the doctrine of the gospel ought to be preached. On this matter many hold the opinion that a simple and plain explanation of the mysteries of salvation is enough, and they regard as men who waste their effort and as intolerable authors of dissension those who expose the tyranny of Antichrist, attack superstition, and publicly take up the contest with the professed enemies of the truth. Yet that simple doctrine of salvation would have been sufficient, were it not that there are people who strive to wrap it in errors and darkness and to lead the unwary away from the path of truth. Since such people have existed in the past and are found everywhere today, the faithful must be warned not to lend them their ears. But you will never accomplish this unless you show that they are wrong by the whole breadth of the heavens. Again, since the impudence of many goes so far that they dare openly to contradict the truth, these too must be refuted publicly, lest by their rashness they bring suspicion upon the cause of the truth. We read that not only the apostles but Christ himself did both, and those who wish to be called and considered ministers of the Church itself rightly ought to imitate his example. This is why Paul wants teachers of this kind, who are able not only to instruct the more ignorant in sound doctrine, but also to convince those who contradict (Titus 1). He likewise testifies that the Scriptures too were given for this very purpose, that they might serve to refute adversaries (2 Tim. 3). The Holy Spirit has regarded this matter as of such great importance that, through the apostles, he wished not only the impostors of that age to be exposed, but also us to be warned about those who were going to trouble the Church in the latter times. By what right, then, will men today who are running riot in the Church impose silence on the ministers, when they wish no one's impiety to be exposed?

units.la: Porrò primi huius speciminis siue congressus effectum videamus. Obstupescebant omnes (inquit Lucas) & dicebant: Nonne hic est, qui vastauit Hierosolymis eos? &c. Hic vero de pijs loquitur, de impiorum conatibus improbis posteà dicturus. Conferunt autem illi cum anteactis praesens Pauli studium, & sic maiorem admirationis causam inueniunt. Addit alibi Paulus, quod in ipso Deum glorificauerint. Galat. 1. Quo exemplo obiter docemur, ita nos in sanctorum admiratione versari debere, vt ad Deum omnem laudem & gloriam referamus, qui hac illos gratia dignatus est. Admonet praeterea Pauli exemplum, ne quem pudeat agnitos errores abnegare & oppugnare. Quamuis enim hoc multis inconstantis & impudentis animi indicium videatur, Deo tamen hoc debemus & proximo. Iubet ille, vt veritati volentes cedamus, & proximum ab errore reuocemus. Impudentiae ergo & impietatis summae facinus est, si quis agnitos errores mordicus retinere, & quod apud proprophetam dominus accusat, videntibus oculis caecutire velit. Nostrum est, Iesum, quem Paulus praedicauit, filium Dei & Christum agnoscere, illi fidere & seruire, ut cum eodem in caelis viuamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now look at the outcome of this first encounter. Luke says: "All who heard him were amazed and said, 'Is not this the man who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who call on this name?' etc." Here Luke speaks of the godly, intending to speak later of the wicked attempts of the impious. The hearers set Paul's present zeal against his past conduct, and so they find a greater cause for wonder. Paul adds elsewhere that they glorified God in him (Galat. 1.). From this example we are taught in passing that when we admire the saints we should refer all praise and glory to God, who graced them in this way. Paul's example also warns us not to be ashamed to renounce and oppose errors that we have recognised. Although this may seem to many a sign of an inconstant and shameless mind, we owe it to God and to our neighbour to do so. He bids us yield willingly to the truth and call our neighbour back from error. It is therefore a deed of great shamelessness and impiety if anyone stubbornly clings to errors he has recognised, and wishes, with his eyes open, to grow blind, which the Lord rebukes through the prophet. It is our duty to acknowledge Jesus, whom Paul preached, as the Son of God and the Christ, to trust in him and serve him, so that we may live with him in heaven, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXVII.

units.la: Cum autem dies complures transfacti essent, consilio inter se inierunt Iudaei, ut illum interficerent. Sed cognitae sunt Saulo illorum insidiae. Et custodiebant portas die noctuque, ut eum interficerent. Cum autem illum accepissent discipuli noctu, per murum depositerunt, demittentes in sportam. Porro cum veniisset Saulus Hierosolymam, tentabat se adiungere discipulis, & omnes timebant eum, non credentes, quod esset discipulus. Barnabas autem assumptum illum duxit ad apostolos, & narrauit illis, quomodo in via vidisset dominum, & quod locutus esset ei, & quomodo Damasci confidenter egisset in nomine Iesu. Et versatus est cum ipsis Hierosolymis, & confidenter locutus est in nomine domini Iesu. Loquebatur & disputabat cum Graecis. Illi autem conati sunt eum interficere. Quod cum cognouissent fratres, deduxerunt eum Caesaream, & emiserunt eum in Tarsum.
units.tr: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted together to kill him. But Saul learned of their plots. They also watched the gates day and night so that they could kill him. But his disciples took him by night and lowered him through the wall, letting him down in a basket. When Saul came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. Barnabas, however, took him and brought him to the apostles, and related to them how on the road he had seen the Lord and that the Lord had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. And he stayed with them in Jerusalem and spoke boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He spoke and disputed with the Grecians, but they tried to kill him. When the brothers learned of this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

units.la: VT in Pauli conuersione describenda diligens admodum fuit Lucas, ita non minori studio eiusdem doctrinam nuper expositi. Summa eius fuit, Iesum, qui ex Maria virgine homo natus est, simul etiam esse Dei filium & Christum, id est, Regem & Sacerdote nostrum, adeoque olim promissum humani generis redemptorem. Conuenit cum apostolorum confessione, quam omnium illorum nomine Petrus edidisse legitur: & simul omnem nostrae salutis rationem comprehendit, quemadmodum proximo Sermone dictum est. Quare sicut alias Paulus admonet, ea animi constantia in retinenda doctrina hac nos uti conuenit, ut nullius authoritate, ne angeli quidem, nos ab ea auocari patiamur. Quia vero Paulum electum organum fore Christus dixerat, breuem eorum, quae Paulus circa sui apostolatus initia gessit, expositionem praesenti hoc loco euangelista subiicit: ut ea ostendat, qua fide & industria ille usus sit, ut tanto de se Christi praeconio responderet. Est autem narratio haec diligentius consideranda, quod perspicue docet, quam varij quamque graues in hac vita fidelium Christi ministrorum casus sint, & quam fideliter ijsdem pro sui nominis gloria periclitantibus, promisso auxilio ille adesse soleat.
units.tr: Just as Luke was very careful in describing Paul's conversion, so with no less zeal he sets out the teaching that Paul had recently been preaching. Its sum was that Jesus, who was born a man of the virgin Mary, is also at the same time the Son of God and the Christ, that is, our King and Priest, and so the Redeemer of the human race promised long ago. This agrees with the confession of the apostles, which Peter is read to have made on behalf of them all; and at the same time it comprehends the whole manner of our salvation, as was said in the previous sermon. Therefore, as Paul elsewhere admonishes, we ought to hold to this teaching with such steadfastness of mind that we never allow ourselves to be drawn away from it by anyone's authority, not even an angel's. But because Christ had said that Paul would be a chosen vessel, the evangelist here adds a brief account of what Paul did at the beginning of his apostleship, so as to show with what faith and diligence he acted, so as to answer to such a great proclamation of Christ concerning himself. This narrative, moreover, is to be considered more carefully, because it clearly teaches how varied and how grave are the trials of Christ's faithful ministers in this life, and how faithfully he is wont to stand by them with the promised help when they are endangered for the glory of his name.

units.la: Ab ijs vero narrandi initium sumit Lucas, quae Damasci Paulo acciderunt. Sed priusquam eius verba attingamus, historiae ordo contexendus erit, quem non adeo anxie a Luca obseruatum fuisse constat, utpote cui non propositum fuit singulatim omnes res gestas commemorare, sed ea exponere, quae ecclesiae institutioni sufficere poterant. Et multa se scientem volentemque praeteriisse, non obscure monet, quando post multos dies a Pauli conuersione, quae hic recenset, accidisse fatetur. Quare complanandus & farciendus nobis erit historiae ordo ex ijs, quae ipse Paulus de rebus abs se gestis commemorat. Is autem ad Galatas scribens, primum se Damasco in Arabiam concessisse dicit, priusquam Hierosolymam proficisceretur. Ex Arabia vero, quam abillo Christi praedicatione illustratam esse credibile est, reuertus Damascum, in insidias, de quibus hic agitur, incidit. Authores barum Iudaei fuisse, hic dicuntur. At in posteriori ad Corinth. cap. 11. ab Aretae regis praefecto excubias haec ad se comprehendendum dispositas fuisse, scribit. Vnde colligimus, hunc a Iudaeis solicitatum hoc consilij cepisse: quod illi vel hoc nomine facilius persuaderi potuit, quod Arabiam, quae Aretae parebat, euangelij praedicatione Paulus tentauisset. Pauli ergo profectionem in Arabiam Lucas omisit, quam priusquam his insidijs peteretur, peractam fuisse oportuit, cum paulo post, insidijs elapsus Hierosolymam venisse dicatur.
units.tr: Luke takes his beginning of the narrative from what happened to Paul at Damascus. But before we touch on his words, the order of the history must be laid out, which it is agreed Luke did not observe so very strictly, since it was not his purpose to recount every single deed, but to set out those things which could suffice for the instruction of the Church. And he openly warns that he has knowingly and willingly passed over many things, when he admits that this happened many days after Paul's conversion, which he recounts here. Therefore the order of the history must be filled out and supplemented for us from those things which Paul himself recounts of his own deeds. Now writing to the Galatians he says that he first withdrew to Arabia from Damascus before he went to Jerusalem. From Arabia, which it is credible was illumined by Christ's preaching, he returned to Damascus and fell into the plots of which we are speaking here. The Jews are here said to have been the authors of them. But in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 11, he writes that guards were posted by the prefect of King Aretas to seize him. From this we gather that he was stirred up by the Jews to this plan; and they could more easily be persuaded of it for this reason, that Paul had attempted to preach the gospel in Arabia, which was subject to Aretas. Luke therefore omitted Paul's journey into Arabia, which must have been completed before he was attacked by these plots, since he is said shortly afterwards, having escaped the plots, to have come to Jerusalem.

units.la: Porro quoad praesentem historiam, praecipuum illius caput est, ut videas, quid a mundo expectes, ut primum te Christo coniunxeris. Quia enim suos e mundo selectos sibi uni Christus consecrat, eos mundus postea ferre non potest, quemadmodum ipse admonet, Iohan. 15. Et tot passim exempla ex-
units.tr: Moreover, as far as the present history is concerned, its chief lesson is this: that you should see what you may expect from the world as soon as you have joined yourself to Christ. For since Christ consecrates to himself alone those whom he has chosen out of the world, the world afterwards cannot bear them, as he himself warns in John 15. And there are so many examples everywhere that prove this,

units.la: Historiae ordo sive contextus complanatur.
units.tr: The order or sequence of the history is made plain.

units.la: Persecutio mo net Christi ministros. tant, quibus hoc probari poterat, vt mirum sit hodie tam multos ijs aduersis offendi, de quibus totius nos scriptura admonet, & quibus omnes Christi cultores à prima mundi origine exercitatos fuisse con-stat. Interim obseruemus, quòd pofἓ multos dies hæc accidisse Lucas ait. Datum igitur Paulo tem-pus prædicandi, & interea temporis hostium rabiem Deus cohibuit, qui haud dubiè primis initijs ob-stitissent, nisi freno per illum iniecto fuissent retracti. Vnde discimus non semper licere impijs quic-quid libet, & quod cumprimis posse videbantur. Eadem enim illorum, quæ & capitis ipsorum ratio est. Nam vt satan diuinæ prouidentiæ habenis subiacet, nec quicquam aduersus homines, nisi Deo permittente, moliri potest: ita vel inuitos & multum reluctantes tyrannos dominus frænat, & id quidem sæpe occultis modis, vt ipsi mirentur sua consilia tam parum succedere, quibus neminem qui-dem mortalium obstare posse vident, Deum autem non vident, qui illa dissipare solet. Psal. 33. Semper ergo Dei prouidentiam ob oculos nobis ponamus, quoties hostium verbi conatus audimus, & pilos capitis nostri numeratos esse meminerimus. Matth. 10.
units.tr: Persecution warns the ministers of Christ. that it is a wonder today that so many are offended by those adversities of which all Scripture warns us, and by which it is established that all the worshippers of Christ have been exercised from the very beginning of the world. Meanwhile let us observe that Luke says these things happened after many days. Paul was therefore given time to preach, and in the meantime God restrained the rage of the enemies, who would undoubtedly have opposed him at the very beginning had they not been held back by a bridle placed on them through him. From this we learn that the wicked are not always permitted to do whatever they like, even when they seem able to do the most. For the same rule applies to them as to their head. For just as Satan is subject to the reins of divine providence and can attempt nothing against men except with God's permission, so the Lord also restrains even unwilling and strongly resisting tyrants, and often does so in hidden ways, so that they themselves marvel that their plans turn out so poorly, plans which they see no mortal able to obstruct, while they do not see God, who is wont to scatter them. Psalm 33. Therefore let us always keep God's providence before our eyes whenever we hear of the attempts of the enemies of the Word, and remember that the hairs of our head are all numbered. Matthew 10.

units.la: Quid verò Damasceni fideles, cùm Paulo insidias impij hostes struerent, fecere? Num pericli-tantem sua destituerunt ope & auxilio? Vel num illud domini vsurparunt: Ne resistatis malo? Vel secuti rerum, domini auxilium ita expectarunt, vt ipsi nihil interea pro Pauli salute sibi audendum aut faciendum esse putarent? Nihil sane horum de illis dicitur. Imò capitis sui periculo Paulum liberare sategerunt, violata etiam lege publica, quæ mœnia sacrosancta esse iubet. Constat enim veteres mœnia & portas inter res sanctas numerasse, & mœnia diis consecrauisse: nimirum quòd sci-rent, res mortalium (vt iuris consultus ait) nulla humana ratione satis à quoquam regi & dispensari posse in tanta hominum perfidia, obrepente quandoque & ciuibus negligentu, aut finitimorum co-riente grassante, latius inuidia, &c. Mœnia ergo transfilire, aut portas effringere, capitale erat, etsi nullum aliud crimen accederet. Pia tamen & sancta dispensatione absque legum ciuilium contem-ptu fratres isti vsi sunt, & proinde excusationem merentur. Videbant enim maiorem diuinæ legi ratione habendam esse, quæ periclitanti succurrere, & humanas constitutiones ita obseruare iubet, ne vel Dei leges abrogent, vel pijs & bonis fraudi sint. Sporta ergo per mœnia demissum periculo im-minenti eripiunt, nec pium officium, quod ipsi offerebant, Paulus detrectat. Quo exemplo primùm admonemur, permitti interdum Christianis hominibus, imò verbi quoq; ministris, vt fuga sibi con-sulant, nec temere capitis periculum sibi accersant. Nam & Christum non semel fugisse legimus, quando vel Iudæorum, vel Herodis furori & insidijs sese subduxit: & idem suos monet, vt sibi cau-ant ab hominibus, & persecutione oborta, ex vna ciuitate in aliam fugiant. Matth. 10. Ea autem adhibenda est cautio, vt tunc nobis fugam concessam putemus, quando hæc nec Dei gloriæ derogat, nec ab officio cui nos dominus destinauit, reuocat. Nisi enim in hac duo intenti simus, dum nobis con-sulimus, Dei gloriam turpiter prodemus, & nostri officij immemores, illorum salutem negligemus, qui nobis commendatissimi esse debebant. Vtriusque verò rationem Paulus habuit, quando ipso per fugam elapso, erant nihilominus qui Damasci communem Christi causam sustinerent: & ipse non ignobili ocio sese dedidit, sed tum Hierosolymis tum alibi salutis doctrinam magno cum fructu vul-gauit, sicuti sequens historia docet.
units.tr: But what did the faithful at Damascus do when the wicked enemies were laying plots against Paul? Did they abandon him in his peril, without help or aid? Or did they seize on the Lord's saying, "Do not resist evil"? Or did they follow the course of events and wait for the Lord's help in such a way that they thought they had nothing to dare or do in the meantime for Paul's safety? Certainly none of these things is said of them. On the contrary, they strove to free Paul at the risk of their own heads, even violating the public law which orders the walls to be held sacred. For it is well known that the ancients counted walls and gates among holy things, and consecrated walls to the gods: plainly because they knew that the affairs of mortals (as a jurist says) cannot be sufficiently governed and arranged by any human reasoning, in such great faithlessness of men, when sometimes, through the negligence of citizens, or through the spreading envy of neighbours, and so on. Therefore to leap over the walls or break open the gates was a capital offence, even if no other crime were added. Yet these brothers acted with a pious and holy discretion, without contempt for the civil laws, and so they deserve to be excused. For they saw that the divine law must be given greater regard, which bids us help one in danger, and observe human constitutions in such a way that they neither abrogate God's laws nor become a snare to the pious and good. So they rescued Paul, who was in imminent danger, by letting him down through the wall in a basket, and Paul did not refuse the pious service they offered him. From this example we are first admonished that Christians, and even ministers of the Word, are sometimes permitted to look to their own safety by flight, and not to bring the danger to their own heads rashly. For we read that Christ too fled more than once, when he withdrew himself from the fury and plots of the Jews or of Herod; and he likewise warns his own to beware of men, and when persecution arises, to flee from one city into another. Matthew 10. But this caution must be exercised, so that we think flight is allowed us only when it does not detract from God's glory and does not recall us from the office to which the Lord has appointed us. For unless we are intent on these two things while we look after ourselves, we shamefully betray God's glory, and, forgetting our office, we neglect the salvation of those who ought to have been most commended to us. Paul did have regard for both, when, though he himself had escaped by flight, there were still those at Damascus who upheld the common cause of Christ; and he did not give himself over to idle leisure, but then at Jerusalem and elsewhere he spread the teaching of salvation with great fruit, as the following history shows.

units.la: Præterea officij sui fideles admonentur, quo illos doctoribus suis dominus obstrinxit. Requirit hoc, vt ministrorum saluti proprij capitis periculo consulant. Constat enim illos parentum loco cense-ri debere, quando illorum ministerio (quemadmodum Paulus monet) ad vitam æternam regenera-mur. 1. Cor. 4. Gal. 4. Turpis ergo & pudenda illorum ingratitudo & perfidia est, qui vt primùm persecutionis periculum imminet, in verbi ministros linguæ petulantis habenas laxant, & illorum capitibus pacem redemptam vellent. At si priuati hominis est, sui capitis periculo ministros tueri, quanto magis hoc officij à ciuilibus magistratibus requiri debet, quos Christus olim suæ ecclesiæ nu-tritios & tutores fore prædixit? Isa. 49. Quare inepta plane illorum sententia est, qui mœnibus & armis religionis causam à magistratibus minimè defendi debere clamant, cùm propter vnius Pauli salutem, mœniorum religionem Damasceni fratres magna cum laude violauerint.
units.tr: Moreover, the faithful are reminded of the duty the Lord has laid on them toward their teachers. This requires them to look after the safety of the ministers of the Word even at risk to their own heads. For it is certain that ministers ought to be regarded in the place of parents, since through their ministry (as Paul admonishes) we are born again to eternal life. 1 Cor. 4. Gal. 4. Shameful and disgraceful, therefore, is the ingratitude and treachery of those who, as soon as the danger of persecution threatens, loosen the reins of their unruly tongues against the ministers of the Word and would buy peace for themselves at the price of the ministers' heads. But if it is the duty of a private person to protect ministers at risk to his own head, how much more should this duty be required of the civil magistrates, whom Christ foretold would one day be the nurses and guardians of his Church? Isa. 49. Therefore the opinion of those is plainly foolish who cry out that the cause of religion must by no means be defended by the magistrates with walls and arms, since the Damascene brothers, for the sake of the safety of Paul alone, breached the walls of religion's city, and were greatly praised for it.

units.la: Porrò quid Paulus è Damasco feliciter elapsus fecerit, Lucas narrat: & Hierosolymam venisse scribit, quod anno conuersionis ipsius quarto demum factum fuisse, ipse docet ad Galat. 1. cap. Vbi cum se discipulis, & Petro in primis, coniungere vellet, illum propter priscinam in fideles Christi tyrannidem... sti tyrannidem suspectum habuerunt. Barnabas autem, de quo in fine Cap. 4. quaedam dicta sunt, cum illius res propius nouisset, illius ministerium illustri & amplissimo testimonio apostolis, Petro nimirum et Iacobo (quos solos se vidisse ad Galatas scribit) commendauit. Cum his ergo quindecim dierum spacio conuersatus, Christi causam constanter asseruit, donec nouis insidijs petitus denuo fugere coactus est.
units.tr: Next, Luke relates what Paul did after he had happily escaped from Damascus, and he writes that Paul came to Jerusalem; Paul himself shows in Galatians 1 that this happened only in the fourth year after his conversion. When he wished to join the disciples, and Peter in particular, they held him in suspicion because of his former tyranny against the faithful of Christ. Barnabas, however, of whom some things were said at the end of chapter 4, knew his case more closely and commended his ministry with an illustrious and very weighty testimony to the apostles, namely Peter and James (the only ones, he writes to the Galatians, whom he saw). So Paul, living with them for fifteen days, steadfastly maintained the cause of Christ, until, attacked by new plots, he was again forced to flee.

units.la: Hic vero nobis discipuli Hierosolymitani consyderandi veniunt, quos sibi a Paulo timuisse Lucas scribit. Fuit hic non ignauus metus, sed prudens, qualem Christus commendat, dum serpentinam prudentiam a suis requirit. Matth. 10. Quia enim vix credibile videbatur, tam immane tyrannum subito mutatum esse, merito sibi cauendum putauere, ne incautis imponeret. Nouerant enim illud Christi, qui filios huius seculi in sua generatione prudentiores filijs lucis esse testatur. Luc. 16. Postea aute rei veritatem edocti, illum humaniter, vt fratrem & fidelem symmystam, excipiunt. Habemus in his Christianae tum prudentiae tum charitatis exemplu, quo vtrang; virtute coniungere docemur. Quia enim omnis homo mendax est, non temere quibusuis credendum, qui pietatis studium egregie simulare nouerunt. Quam enim falsi fratres noceant, Paulus ipse se non sine periculo expertum esse fatetur. 2. Cor. 11. Et idem eam ob causam a nouitijs cauendum esse iubet, & eum, qui ad episcopi functionem aspirat, exterorum quoq; testimonio comendari vult. 1. Tim. 3. Rursum vero nimius ille rigor cauendus erit, quo multi ita obduruerunt, vt omnes peregrinos & ignotos semel explodendos esse putet. Vt enim Christianae charitatis est, de omnibus bene sperare: ita honesta & fide digna de igno tu fratribus testimonia facile recipit, & ijsdem ante conceptas suspiciones dilui patitur. Vtamur ergo moderatione hac hodie, quando passim exules Christi oberrant, nec illorum sententijs acquiescamus, qui in vtranq; parte nimij, vel facilitate nimia se omnibus deridendos & decipiendos praebent; vel immodica austeritate & rigore exasperati, omnes simul nullo adhibito discrimine, reiiciunt.
units.tr: Here the disciples of Jerusalem come before us for consideration, whom Luke writes were afraid of Paul. This was not a lazy fear but a prudent one, of the kind Christ commends when he requires serpent-like wisdom from his own. Matt. 10. For since it seemed scarcely credible that so savage a tyrant had suddenly changed, they rightly thought they should be on their guard, lest he deceive them unawares. For they knew that saying of Christ, who testifies that the sons of this age are wiser in their generation than the sons of light. Luke 16. Afterwards, however, having been informed of the truth of the matter, they received him kindly, as a brother and a faithful fellow-partaker. In these men we have an example both of Christian prudence and of Christian charity, and we are taught to join the two virtues together. For since every man is a liar, one must not lightly believe just anyone who knows how to counterfeit zeal for godliness with distinction. For Paul himself confesses that he experienced how much harm false brothers can do, and not without danger. 2 Cor. 11. For this reason he also bids us beware of novices, and wishes that one who aspires to the office of bishop be commended even by the testimony of outsiders. 1 Tim. 3. On the other hand, we must also beware of that excessive rigour by which many have grown so hardened that they think all strangers and unknown persons should be rejected at once. For it belongs to Christian charity to hope well of everyone; so it readily accepts honest and trustworthy testimonies about unknown brothers, and allows the suspicions conceived beforehand to be dispelled by them. Let us therefore use this moderation today, when Christ's exiles wander everywhere, and let us not assent to the opinions of those who, excessive on either side, expose themselves to be mocked and deceived by everyone through too great credulity, or, exasperated by immoderate severity and rigour, reject everyone together without any distinction.

units.la: Deinde Barnabas nobis obseruandus erit, qui vt supra liberalitate sua communis ecclesiae inopia subleuauit, & filius consolationis dici meruit: ita nunc periclitantem Pauli famam suo testimonio egregie sustinet, nec eius illum pudet, quem omnibus suspectum esse videbat. Est hoc charitatis opus cumprimis eximium & necessarium, cum vix quicquam inter homines vberius quam sinistrarum & pessimarum suspicionum seges proueniat. Vt enim philautia excaecati nobis ipsis blandimur, ita alio rum mores sedulo & magligno oculo obseruamus, & occasione omnem captamus, qua illorum famae detrahere liceat. Graue ergo illorum peccatum est, qui immerito suspectos magis aggrauant, quorum famae potius consulere oportebat.
units.tr: Next, Barnabas is to be observed by us, who, as above, relieved the poverty of the common Church by his liberality and deserved to be called a son of consolation; so now, by his testimony, he splendidly sustains the endangered reputation of Paul, and is not ashamed of the man whom he saw to be suspected by all. This is an especially outstanding and necessary work of charity, since scarcely anything grows more abundantly among men than the crop of sinister and wicked suspicions. For as we are blinded by self-love and flatter ourselves, so we diligently and with an evil eye watch the conduct of others, and seize every occasion by which it may be permitted to detract from their reputation. Therefore it is a grave sin of those who harm more severely those who are suspected undeservedly, when they ought rather to have looked after their good name.

units.la: Tertio Paulum videamus, quem eximijs virtutibus fidem sua Hierosolymis declarauisse Lucas docet. Et primo quidem illum ecclesiae & discipulorum Christi commercium quaesiuisse, scribit. Est hoc laude dignissimum, si cogites Paulum non multo ante in ea vrbe inter primates non postremum locum habuisse. At vt iam sic concul canda putans, quaecunq; in mundo eximia habentur, vnum Christum assequi, & illius ecclesiae coniungi cupit. Vide Philip. 3. Nobis ergo exemplum hoc ob oculos ponamus, quando mundi amicitia & gloria nos ad defectionem solicitat. Nam pusillus licet sit Christi grex, & vilis ac infelix videatur ecclesiae conditio, quae in mundo hoc instar vetustae casae ruinam in singulas horas minetur: in ea tamen sola salus est, & tutissimum est eius contubernium. Communis ergo hac omnium piorum vox est: Potior est dies in atrijs domini, quam alias mille dies. Malo ad limen defidere domus Dei, quam habitare in tentoriis impiorum. Deinde magnum Christianae modestiae argumentum Paulus praebet, dum suspectus pijs, & ab ijsdem reiectus, non tamen improbe obmurmurat, non ipse suarum laudum immodicus praeco est, nec ab ecclesia indignabundus resilit, sed patienter hoc omne sustinet. Anteacta enim vitae memor, non miratur haec fieri. Imo Dei iudicium agnoscit, qui ita ipsum humiliari voluit & exerceri, vt supplex quodammodo illorum commercium expeteret, quos antea immani fastu contempserat, & crudelissime fuerat persecutus. Imitemur exemplum hoc, quotiens dolor aliquis ex iniuria ab alijs illata animo nostro oboritur. Et licet nos iniuste ab ijs lesos sciamus, cogitemus tamen nos, iniuria hac non indignos esse, & grauiora meruisse, si nobiscum Deus iure vellet concendere. Postremo, vbi se fratribus reconciliatu videt, reipsa se verum Christi discipulum esse probat. Nam confidenter & liberè loquitur in nomine Iesu Christi. Est autem haec euangelij descriptio, quod nobis in solius Iesu Christi nomine poenitentiam simul & remissionem pec-
units.tr: Third, let us consider Paul, whom Luke teaches declared his faith at Jerusalem by outstanding virtues. And first, he writes that Paul sought fellowship with the Church and with the disciples of Christ. This is most worthy of praise, if you consider that Paul had not long before held no mean place among the leaders in that city. But although he thinks that he must now be cast down, and that whatever is held outstanding in the world is to be counted as nothing, he desires to attain Christ alone and to be joined to his Church. See Phil. 3. Let us then set this example before our eyes, when the friendship and glory of the world entice us to defection. For although the flock of Christ is small, and the condition of the Church may seem mean and wretched, and in the world, like an old and crumbling house, threatens ruin every hour, yet salvation is in her alone, and her fellowship is the safest. So this is the common voice of all the godly: "A day in the courts of the Lord is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather stand at the threshold of the house of God than dwell in the tents of the wicked." Psalm 84. Next, Paul provides a great proof of Christian modesty, since, though suspected by the godly and rejected by them, he does not complain shamelessly, is not himself an immoderate herald of his own praises, and does not leap away from the Church in indignation, but endures all this patiently. For mindful of his past life, he does not wonder that these things happen. Indeed he acknowledges the judgment of God, who willed that he should be so humbled and exercised that he should in a manner humbly seek the fellowship of those whom he had formerly despised with monstrous pride and had most cruelly persecuted. Let us imitate this example whenever some grief arising from an injury inflicted by others arises in our mind. And although we know that we have been unjustly harmed by them, let us nevertheless consider that we are not undeserving of this injury, and that we have deserved more grievous things if God wished to contend with us by right. Lastly, when he sees himself reconciled to the brothers, he proves in fact that he is a true disciple of Christ. For he speaks confidently and freely in the name of Jesus Christ. Now this is the description of the gospel, that in the name of Jesus Christ alone we preach repentance and at the same time the remission of sins,

units.la: Discipuli a Paulo sibi metuunt. catorum prædicat, vt iam sæpe monuimus. Simul vero cum Helliftinis disputat, quos supra quoq; ecclesiæ turbatores, & indignissimi murmuris authores fuisse vidimus. Actò.6. Solebant hi euangelio legem miscere, & operum iustificatione fidem in Christum euertere. Quibus confutandis Paulus peculiari Dei consilio destinatus fuit, vt illius epistolæ testantur. Admonet autem locus hic, ita in vno Christo prædicandam esse salutis rationem, vt simul omnibus ijs sedulò occurratur, quæ hanc euertere videntur. De quæ re cum præcedenti Sermone dictum sit, hæc obiter annotauisse sufficiat.
units.tr: [The disciples fear Paul for themselves.] as we have often admonished already. Yet at the same time he disputes with the Hellenists, whom we saw above to have been troublers of the Church and authors of most unworthy murmuring. Acts 6. These men used to mix the law with the gospel and to overthrow faith in Christ by the justification of works. To refute them Paul was appointed by a special counsel of God, as his epistles testify. This passage, however, warns us that the way of salvation must be preached in Christ alone, and at the same time that all those things which seem to overthrow it must be diligently opposed. Since this matter was discussed in the preceding sermon, it is enough to have noted these things in passing.

units.la: Cæterum postremo loco, Paulum non meliori successu Hierosolymis, quàm ante Damasci visum fuisse dicitur. Rursus enim contra illum conspirant Iudæi, & occisum volunt. Et hæc hypocritarum argumenta sunt, qui cum pro operum iustitia acerrimè digladiantur, pro leuissimo ducunt, insontes iugulare & sanguinem innoxium fundere. Sed rursus discipulorum fides & charitas elucet, qui Cæsaream vsque deductum, in Tarsum Ciliciæ emittunt, quæ Paulo patria fuit. Est autem summa admiratione digna Pauli constantia, qui cum nouis vndiq; periculis petatur, nō tamen à fide & Christo deficit. Nouerat enim ex prophetarum lectione, multas esse tribulationes iustorum. Sciebat ad crucem ferendam inuitari omnes, qui Christo nomen dant. Nouerat item se grauiora meritum, qui aliquando Christianis similium malorum author fuisset. Quare gaudere potius debuit, quando pro Christi nomine ea ipsum pati contigit, quæ vt scelerum pœnas dominus immittere potuisset. Quæ vna consideratio si animis nostris obuersetur, facilè efficiet, ne vllis aduersis offendamur. Interim insignem laudem Paulus eo quoq; nomine meretur, quòd iubente domino (vt infra cap.22. patebit) elapsus Tarso, patriæ suæ euangelij lucem inferre fluduit, Christi exemplū imitatus, qui & ipse patriæ suæ, quantumuis ingratæ, rationem habuit. Imitemur nos Pauli fidem, pietatem & constantiam. Itafiet, vt Deo protectore & vindice omnibus præsentis vitæ molestijs erepti, in cælis olim viuamus cum Iesu Christo, filio Dei, saluatore nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, at the last point, it is said that Paul fared no better at Jerusalem than he had before at Damascus. For again the Jews conspire against him and want him killed. These are the arguments of hypocrites, who, while they fight most fiercely for the righteousness of works, count it a trifle to cut the throats of the innocent and shed innocent blood. But again the faith and charity of the disciples shine forth, who, having led him as far as Caesarea, send him away to Tarsus in Cilicia, which was Paul's homeland. Now Paul's constancy is worthy of the greatest admiration, since, though attacked on every side by new dangers, he nevertheless does not fall away from the faith and from Christ. For he knew from the reading of the prophets that the tribulations of the righteous are many. He knew that all who give their name to Christ are invited to bear the cross. He knew too that he himself had deserved heavier things, having once been the author of similar evils against Christians. Therefore he ought rather to have rejoiced when it was his lot to suffer for the name of Christ those very things which the Lord could have sent as punishments for sins. If this one consideration is kept before our minds, it will easily bring it about that we are not offended by any adversities. Meanwhile Paul deserves remarkable praise also on this account, that, at the Lord's command (as will appear below in chapter 22), having escaped from Tarsus he undertook to bring the light of the gospel to his own homeland, imitating Christ, who himself also took account of his own country, however ungrateful it was. Let us imitate the faith, godliness and constancy of Paul. So it will come about that, with God as our protector and avenger, delivered from all the troubles of this present life, we shall one day live in heaven with Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our only Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 68.

units.la: Porrò ecclesiæ per totam Iudæam, & Galilæam, & Samariam, habebant pacem, & ædificabantur, & ambulabant in timore domini, & consolatione sancti spiritus replebantur. Accidit autem, dum Petrus per omnes peragraret, vt veniret etiam ad sanctos, qui habitabant Lyddæ. Inuenit autem illic hominem quendam, Æneam nomine, ab annis octo decumbentem in grabato, qui erat paralyticus. Et ait illi Petrus: Ænea, sanet te Iesus Christus. Surge & sterne tibi ipsi. Et continuò surrexit: & viderunt eum omnes, qui habitabant Lyddæ & in Assarone, qui conuersi sunt ad dominum.
units.tr: Meanwhile the congregations throughout all Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace, were being built up, walked in the fear of the Lord, and were filled with the comfort of the Holy Spirit. As Peter was travelling through all the regions, it came about that he also came down to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been lying on a pallet for eight years, for he was paralysed. Peter said to him: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Rise and make your bed for yourself." And immediately he rose. All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

units.la: Vidimus hucusque Diui Pauli tyrocinia, quibus apostolatum suum auspicatus est. Fuerunt hæc laboris simul & periculi plena. Bis enim vitæ periculum subiit, & bis fideli quidem discipulorum ope & industria, non tamen sine eorundem periculo, elapsus est. Docent illa, quid in hoc mundo fidos Christi cultores maneat, quos tamen Pauli constantiam & fidem imitari decet, ne vllis periculis & aduersis sese à Christo abduci patiantur. Beatus enim, qui in finem vsque perseuerauerit. At qui manu aratro admota, à tergo respexerit, ea re satis declarat, se regno Christi idoneum & dignum non esse. Luc.9.cap. Cæterum, quia quæ hucusque commemorata sunt, talia videri possunt, quæ vniuersalem ecclesiæ ruinam & excidium minitentur, non sine spiritus sancti suggestione diuinæ scriptor, abrupta Pauli historia, ad Petrum apostolum transfitum facit, & lætiores, qui mox secuti sunt ecclesiæ progressus describit: in quorum consyderatione, eò diligentius nos versari decet, quòd magis illa nobis consolationem afferre possunt, qua nobis inter mundi huius procellas quàm maximè opus est.
units.tr: So far we have seen the apprenticeship of the blessed Paul, with which he began his apostleship. It was full of labour and of danger alike. For twice he underwent peril of his life, and twice he escaped, by the help and diligence of faithful disciples, yet not without danger to them as well. Those events teach us what awaits the faithful worshippers of Christ in this world, whom nevertheless it becomes to imitate Paul's steadfastness and faith, so that they do not allow themselves to be drawn away from Christ by any dangers or adversities. For "blessed is he who has endured to the end." But whoever, having put his hand to the plough, looks back, by that very act shows sufficiently that he is not fit and worthy for the kingdom of Christ. Luke 9. Moreover, since the things recounted so far may seem such as to threaten the utter ruin and overthrow of the Church, the writer, not without the prompting of the Holy Spirit, breaks off the history of Paul and turns to the apostle Peter, and describes the more cheerful progress of the Church that followed soon after. In considering these things we ought to labour all the more diligently, because they can bring us the consolation which we need most of all amid the storms of this world.

units.la: Orditur autem à generali omnium ecclesiarum, quæ per Iudæam, Galilæam, & Samariam hucusque collectæ & fundatæ erant, conditione, & horribilium turbarum & motuum, quorum veritatis boates antehac authores fuerant, lætissimum & felicem cumprimis exitum fuisse, scribit. Ecclesiæ (inquit) habebant pacem. Mira hæc & præter omnem expectationem exorta rerum vicissitudo fuit, si priorem ecclesiæ statum, hostium feroces animos, consilia & vires cum hac conferas. At hic deimos est, quòd nostræ infirmitatis rationem habens, læta tristibus interserit, nec nos vltra id quod ferre possumus tentari finit. 1. Corinth. 10. Et vbi afflictiones abundant, ibidem consolationem vberiorem adhibet. 2. Cor. 1. Psal. 94. Nec id difficile est, qui quotidie eius generis exempla in ijs edit, quæ certis naturæ legibus feruntur. Ita hyemem frigore & gelu molestam amœnum ver, læta æstas & frugifer autumnus excipere consueuerunt. Ita continuos imbres & horribiles grandinis procellas, lætior rediens post nubila Phœbus discutit. Et nauta post aduersa tempestatis terrores, optatam serenitatem & fecundos ventorum flatus experiuntur. Et eadem vicissitudine ecclesiæ statum gubernari, omnium seculorum exempla testantur. Sed vnus ludicum liber ijs confirmandis abunde sufficere poterit. Neminem ergo præsentium malorum facies ita perterreat, vt sibi prorsus pereundum existimet. Nam vel in hac vita agentibus melior & felicior rerum conditio affulgebit: vel vita hac & omnibus mundi procellis exemptos ad cœlestis regni hæreditatem benignus Deus transferet. Interim admonet locus hic, crucem non perpetuam ecclesiæ notam esse, quia illa nunquam carere possit, cum & hic primitiuam ecclesiam vniuersali pace donatam fuisse audiamus, & hæc ipsa sequentibus quoque seculis non semel contigerit. Vanissima igitur eorum est sententia, qui quasi ecclesias, quibus tranquillior rerum conditio ex Dei beneficio obtingit, temerè damnant, & Christianis nullum à cruce respirandi tempus concedi volunt. Rursum admonemur, ad pacem consequendam nec ignaua dissimulatione, nec perfida abnegatione fidei opus esse, sed potius constantia & magnanimitate in verbi & fidei doctrina retinenda. Tunc enim pacem secuta esse Lucas tradit, quando Paulus veritatis hostes tum Damasci cum Hierosolymis, constanti prædicatione & infinitis aduersus illos disputationibus quàm maximè irritauerat. Frustra ergo dissimulationem veri à nobis quidam hodie exigunt, qui liberiori errorum & superstitionis insectatione hostium animos magis exacerbari dicunt. Quasi vero Deus non eos quoq; cohercere possit, qui in omne rabiem effusi nil nisi cædes & flammas spirant. Imò exemplis edocemur, raro fideli hominum amicitia eos vsos esse, quicunq; in horum gratiam fidem & veritatem abnegare in animum induxerunt.
units.tr: He begins with the general condition of all the churches that had hitherto been gathered and founded throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria, and he writes that, after the dreadful disturbances and commotions of which Saul had been the author, the outcome was most joyful and happy. "The churches," he says, "had peace." This change of fortune was wonderful and arose beyond all expectation, if you compare the earlier state of the Church with the fierce spirits, plans and strength of its enemies. But here the Lord shows his care, for, taking account of our weakness, he mingles joys with sorrows, and does not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear. 1 Corinthians 10. And where afflictions abound, there he supplies a richer consolation. 2 Corinthians 1. Psalm 94. Nor is this hard to believe, since he displays daily examples of this kind in those things which move by fixed laws of nature. Thus a winter made troublesome by cold and frost is wont to be followed by a pleasant spring, a joyful summer and a fruitful autumn. Thus the cheerful sun, returning after the clouds, scatters the continual rains and dreadful hailstorms. And the sailor, after the terrors of the storm, enjoys the longed-for calm and the fruitful winds. And that the state of the Church is governed by the same alternation, the examples of all ages bear witness. But the single book of Judges will suffice to confirm these things abundantly. Let no one, therefore, be so terrified by the face of present evils that he thinks he must utterly perish. For either a better and happier state of affairs will shine upon those who are still living in this life, or else the kindly God will carry those who are freed from this life and from all the storms of the world to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Meanwhile this passage reminds us that the cross is not a permanent mark of the Church, since the Church could never be without it, for we hear that the primitive Church was granted universal peace here, and that the same thing has happened more than once in the following ages too. Therefore the opinion of those is most empty who rashly condemn churches in which, by God's benefit, a calmer state of affairs is granted, and who wish that Christians be allowed no time to breathe from the cross. Again we are admonished that to obtain peace there is need neither of idle dissimulation nor of faithless denial of the faith, but rather of steadfastness and magnanimity in holding fast to the word and the doctrine of the faith. For Luke relates that peace followed only when Paul, by constant preaching and countless disputations against them both at Damascus and at Jerusalem, had greatly provoked the enemies of the truth. It is in vain, then, that some today demand from us the concealing of the truth, who say that the enemies' minds are rather exasperated by a freer assault upon errors and superstition. As if God could not restrain even those who, poured out in every kind of rage, breathe nothing but slaughter and flames! Indeed, the examples teach us that those who have resolved to deny the faith and the truth for the sake of such men have seldom been benefited by the friendship of men.

units.la: Deinde pacis concessæ fructum Lucas subijcit, quando ecclesias ædificatas fuisse scribit. Potest boc bifariam intelligi. Nam ædificari dicuntur ecclesiæ, quando vel noui credentes accedunt: vel qui iam ante crediderunt, donis spiritus sancti vberioribus donati, in fide proficiunt. Nec temere ædificandi metaphora spiritus sanctus vtitur, quando ecclesia domus Dei dicitur, quæ ex viuis lapidibus, ijs nimirum qui in Christum credunt construitur, (1. Tim. 3. & 1. Pet. 2. cap.) & singuli fideles spiritus exempla esse alibi dicuntur. Quæ etiā causa est, quòd doctores architecti vocantur, & ecclesiæ constructio dei ædificatio appellatur. 1. Cor. 3. Porrò præter id, quòd hostium Christi in extirpanda ecclesia conatus vanos & irritos esse hoc exemplo cōstat, admonemur etiam, quòs omnibus in ecclesia vt sanctibus finis & scopus propositus esse debeat: vt nimirum vt ecclesia feliciter ædificetur. Inculcat hunc diligentissimè Paulus, quando de publicis ecclesiæ exercitijs in priori ad Corinth. cap. 14. loquitur. In hunc ergo ministri totis viribus tum doctrina tum redargutione incumbant, semperq; Pauli illius meminerint, quo sibi & reliquis ministris potestatem diuinitus concessam esse ait, ad ædificationem, non autem ad destructionem. 2. Corinth. 10. Nihil ergo in ecclesia esse patiantur, quod ad illius destructionem facere possit. Eundem scopum reges quoq; & magistratus sibi proponant, quos suæ ecclesiæ nutritios dominus constituit, vt iam sæpe monuimus. Ad hunc respiciant Seniores, quibus ecclesiæ disciplina & morum censura commissa est. In hunc omnia sua referunt parentes & quicunq; puerorum institutioni præpositi sunt. Priuatos deniq; homines hæc cura indesinenter extimulare debet. Quisquis enim ad hanc spiritualem ecclesiæ Christi ædificationem aliquid contulerit, & vel vni cum hominem, viui lapidis instar Christo fundamento superstruxerit, nā is maiorem multò laudem meretur, quàm qui insanis sumptibus marmorea templa excitant.
units.tr: Next, Luke adds the fruit of the peace granted, when he writes that the churches were built up. This can be understood in two ways. For churches are said to be built up either when new believers are added, or when those who had already believed, endowed with richer gifts of the Holy Spirit, grow in faith. Nor does the Holy Spirit use the metaphor of building rashly, when the Church is called the house of God, which is constructed of living stones, namely those who believe in Christ (1 Timothy 3 and 1 Peter 2), and when individual faithful are elsewhere said to be the Spirit's building. This is also why teachers are called architects, and the construction of the Church is called the building of God. 1 Corinthians 3. Moreover, besides the fact that this example makes it clear that the attempts of Christ's enemies to root out the Church are vain and fruitless, we are also admonished what end and aim ought to be proposed to all in the Church, as to holy people: namely, that the Church may be happily built up. Paul urges this most diligently when, in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14, he speaks of the public exercises of the Church. Let ministers, then, devote all their strength to this, both in teaching and in rebuke, and let them always remember that saying of Paul, by which he declares that the power given to him and to the other ministers by God is for building up and not for destruction. 2 Corinthians 10. Let them therefore allow nothing in the Church that could serve its destruction. Let kings and magistrates also set this same aim before themselves, whom the Lord has appointed as nurses of his Church, as we have often admonished. Let the elders, to whom the discipline of the Church and the censure of morals are committed, look to this. All parents, and whoever are set over the instruction of children, refer all their efforts to this. Finally, this care ought to stir up private persons without ceasing. For whoever contributes anything to this spiritual building of Christ's Church, and who builds even one man upon Christ the foundation as a living stone, deserves far greater praise than those who raise marble temples at mad expense.

units.la: Postremò, vt pace & rerum tranquillitate vsi sint fideles, indicatur: Ambulabant (inquit) in timore domini, & consolatione sancti spiritus replebantur. Timorem domini illis tribuit, quo omnia ea comprehendit, quæ ad religionem veram faciunt: Dei nimirum cognitionem, fidem synceram, amorem Dei, piam diuini verbi obseruationem, & fidele quod eidem debetur obsequium. Quomodo enim Deum timebit, qui illum non agnoscit? Quomodo autem fide carebit Dei cognitio, & quomodo
units.tr: Lastly, the passage indicates how the faithful used peace and the tranquillity of affairs: "They walked," it says, "in the fear of the Lord, and were filled with the comfort of the Holy Spirit." He attributes to them the fear of the Lord, by which he comprehends everything that pertains to true religion: namely, the knowledge of God, sincere faith, love of God, pious observance of the divine word, and the faithful obedience that is owed to him. For how will one fear God who does not know him? And how can knowledge of God lack faith, and how can it be deprived of the same love of God?

units.la: ℨ 3 eadem Dei amore destituetur? At vbi hæc fuerint, ibidem & verbi studium & obedientiam vigere oportet. Addit autem, consolatione spiritus sancti repletos fuisse. Possumus per hanc cùm euangelij prædicationem, tum internam spiritus suggestionem intelligere, quam Christus suis pollicetur, Iohan.14. & 16.cap. Vtraq; certè hominum mentes & afflictas conscientias mirificè consolatur, quando Deum nobis Christi merito placatum & propitium factum esse docet, & in medio afflictionum æstu, diuini auxilij promissiones, tanquam saluberrimos fontis viui latices, aspergit. Et in his animorum recreationem, gaudia & delitias suas primitiuam ecclesiam quasiuisse, Lucas docet. Vnde colligimus, quæ nam illorum exercitia esse debeant, quibus pace & rerum tranquillitate frui datur. Immane ergo illorum scelus est & ingratitudo execrabilis, qui pace & ocio ad carnis licentiam & turpissima scelerum studia abutuntur: nec interim eos vel auxilio vel consilio, aut saltem consolatio ne subleuant, quos propter testimonium Iesu Christi varijs malis affligi vident. Est hoc peccatum vt atrox, ita animis vulgare hodie. Quò fit, vt quemadmodum pace abutimur, ita leuissimis quoq; afflictionibus facile offendamur & absorbeamur penitus.
units.tr: But where these things are, there the zeal for the word and obedience ought also to flourish. He adds, moreover, that they were filled with the comfort of the Holy Spirit. We may understand this both as the preaching of the gospel and as the inward prompting of the Spirit, which Christ promises to his own, John 14 and 16. Both certainly comfort the minds of men and afflicted consciences wonderfully, when they teach that God has been made placated and propitious to us by the merit of Christ, and, in the midst of the heat of afflictions, sprinkle the promises of divine help like the most wholesome streams of living water. And Luke teaches that the primitive Church sought in these its recreation of spirit, its joys and its delights. From this we gather what exercises ought to be those of men to whom it is granted to enjoy peace and the tranquillity of affairs. Therefore the crime of those who abuse peace and leisure for the licence of the flesh and the most shameful pursuit of wickedness is monstrous and detestable ingratitude, and who meanwhile do not relieve by help, counsel, or at least consolation, those whom they see afflicted with various evils on account of the testimony of Jesus Christ. This sin is as atrocious as it is, today, common among minds. Hence it comes about that, just as we abuse peace, so we are easily offended by even the slightest afflictions and utterly swallowed up.

units.la: His autem præmissis ad res siue acta Petri apostoli transitum facit, è quorum numero miracula duo continua serie exponuntur, quorum alterum Lyddæ, alterum Ioppæ contigit. Occasio horum ea fuisse indicatur, quod Petrus, apostoli officio fungens, ecclesias omnes peragrauit: non quidem indolenti dominandi studio, sed vt laborantibus, sicubi opus erat, succurreret: nutantes confirmaret: errores, si qui oborti fuissent, euelleret: beneficia deniq; in quàm plurimos conferret. Hæc enim apostolorum officia fuisse, ex multis alijs locis patet, & ipsum apostoli nomen docet, quod illos certam sixamue sedem habere vetuit. Eandem rationem Paulus postea obseruauisse, & ecclesias passim confirmasse legitur. Idem sibi omnium ecclesiarum curam incumbere dicit. 2. Corinth. 11. Stultè ergo & ridiculè ex hoc loco primatum suum Romani Pontifices tueri solent. Primò enim vni Petro tribuunt, quod reliquis etiam apostolis mandatum fuisse constat. Deinde impudenter Petri munus in se transferunt, Petro per omnia dissimiles. Adhæc dum omnium ecclesiarum curam ad se rapiunt, ne vni quidem ea officia præstant, quæ fidelem apostolum siue pastorem decent.
