Præterea autem admonemur, ecclesijs tunc quoque fideli cura & inspectoribus opus esse, quando omnia in tu o collocata esse videntur. Nam vt ex ocio proclivius ad carnis licentiam lapsus est, ita pace & ocio securi, satanæ insidijs quàm maximè patent, sicuti Christus monuit. Matth. 12.
units.tr: Having made these preliminary remarks, he now turns to the deeds, or acts, of the apostle Peter. In a continuous sequence he sets out two miracles, one of which took place at Lydda and the other at Joppa. The occasion for these is stated to have been that Peter, discharging the office of an apostle, travelled through all the churches: not indeed out of a restless desire to lord it over them, but so that he might help the labouring wherever there was need, strengthen the wavering, root out errors if any had arisen, and finally bestow benefits on as many as possible. That these were the duties of the apostles is clear from many other places, and the very name "apostle" shows it, since it forbade them to have a fixed and settled seat. Paul is read to have followed the same plan afterwards, and to have strengthened the churches everywhere. He also says that the care of all the churches rests upon him (2 Cor. 11). It is therefore foolish and ridiculous for the Roman Pontiffs to defend their primacy from this passage. For, first, they attribute to Peter alone what is known to have been commanded to all the other apostles as well. Next, they shamelessly transfer Peter's office to themselves, although they are in every respect unlike Peter. Moreover, while they seize to themselves the care of all the churches, they do not even perform for any one of them those duties which become a faithful apostle or minister. Furthermore, we are reminded that churches need faithful care and overseers even at the time when all things seem to be settled in your favour. For just as a slide into the indulgence of the flesh comes more easily from idleness, so when men are secure in peace and leisure they lie most open to the snares of Satan, as Christ warned (Matt. 12).

units.la: Caeterum hac occasione factum est, vt Petrus ad sanctos (id est, fideles Christi merito sanctificatos) qui Lyddæ habitabant, perueniret: vbi Æneam quendam, paralysi debilitatum, & continuo octo annorum spacio decumbentem, Christi Iesu nomine restituit. Sunt autem in eo miraculo diligenter excutiendæ personarum circumstantiæ. Atqui in Ænea quædam commemorantur, quæ ad miraculi amplificationem faciunt. Paralysi enim laborauit, quæ vt difficulter curatur si quis initijs obstet, ita temporis diuturnitate planè incurabilis redditur. Eadem verò humanæ corruptionis typus est. Nam & nos omnes peccati culpa debilitauit, vt viribus melioris naturæ destituti, ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus. 2.Cor.3. Nec vllo hominum consilio aut ratione morbus iste curari potest, qui à primo parente in nos deriuatus, nobiscum & concipitur, & nascitur, & adolescit, veluti de semetipso Dauid testatur. Psal.51. Quare nisi è supernis regeneretur homo, nulla illi aliunde salutis spes offerri potest. Iohan.3. Et id quidem diserte Petrus in præsenti docet, quando spiritus sancti suggestione excitatus, illum accedit, & magna confidentia ait: Æneas, sanet te Iesus Christus, Surge & sterne tibi ipsi. Ita enim hæc profert, vt diserte fateatur, omnem miraculi huius effectum & laudem vni Christo deberi, ad se verò illius ministerium duntaxat pertinere. Et hoc ab apostolis passim obseruatum fuisse, supra in claudi restitutione, quæ cap.3. describitur, demonstratum est. Idem Lyddæ etiam fideles agnoscunt, qui cùm ad Iesu Christi nomen Æneam conualescere viderent, ad dominum Iesum illicò conuersi sunt. Estq; hic omnium miraculorum vsus, vt apostolicæ doctrinæ testimonium ferant, & Christo Iesu, cuius virtute fiunt, adducant. Stulti ergo & inepti nimis sunt, qui miracula, sanctorum ministerio edita, ita commemorant, vt ad illos confugere, & illos adorare doceant. Atque falsa esse constat miracula, quæ cunq; in eum finem fiunt, vt creaturæ alicuius cultum stabiliant, & à Deo rerum omnium creatore auocent. Possent hîc multa dici. Sed quia alibi eadem causa tractata est, & sapius tractanda recurret, consultò breuitati stu demum. demus. Illud admonuisse sufficiat, Iesum Christum unicum cum corporis tum animæ medicum, & eundem ecclesiæ suæ fidelissimum vindicem & tutorem esse, qui & illam inter persecutionem fluctus servare, & afflictæ pacem subito concedere solus potest. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Meanwhile, on this occasion it came about that Peter came to the saints (that is, the faithful of Christ, rightly sanctified) who lived at Lydda, where in the name of Jesus Christ he restored a certain Aeneas, crippled with palsy and lying bedridden for a continuous span of eight years. In this miracle the circumstances of the persons must be carefully examined. Now certain things are recorded of Aeneas which add to the magnitude of the miracle. He suffered from palsy, which, as it is cured with difficulty if someone resists it at the start, so by the length of time it runs on it becomes utterly incurable. Indeed this is a type of human corruption. For we all have been weakened by the guilt of sin, so that, stripped of the powers of a better nature, we are not even fit to think (2 Cor. 3). Nor can this disease be cured by any human counsel or reasoning, since it was derived to us from our first parent, and is conceived with us, born with us, and grows up with us, as David himself testifies of himself (Ps. 51). Therefore unless a man is regenerated from above, no hope of salvation can be offered to him from any other source (John 3). Peter teaches this plainly in the present passage, when, roused by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, he approaches the man and says with great confidence: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed for yourself." For he so puts it that he openly confesses that the whole effect and praise of this miracle is owed to Christ alone, while his own part is only that of minister. That the apostles observed this everywhere has been shown above, in the restoration of the lame man described in chapter 3. The believers at Lydda also acknowledge the same, for when they saw Aeneas recover at the name of Jesus Christ, they immediately turned to the Lord Jesus. And this is the purpose of all miracles: to bear witness to apostolic doctrine and to lead people to Christ Jesus, by whose power they are wrought. Therefore those are foolish and altogether silly who recount miracles performed through the ministry of saints in such a way as to teach people to flee to them and to adore them. Indeed it is certain that miracles are false whatever their purpose, if they are done to establish the worship of some creature and to draw people away from God, the Creator of all things. Much could be said here. But since the same cause has been treated elsewhere and will often return to be treated, I have deliberately chosen to spare the brevity. It is enough to have pointed out this: that Jesus Christ is the only physician both of body and soul, and the most faithful defender and guardian of his Church too, who alone can both preserve it amid the waves of persecution and suddenly grant peace to the afflicted. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXIX.

units.la: Ioppæ autem quædam erat discipula, nomine Thabita, quæ si interpreteris, dicitur Dorcas. Hæc erat plena bonis operibus & eleemosynis, quas faciebat. Accidit autem in diebus illis, ut ægrotaret & moreretur. Cum autem lauissent, posuerunt in cœnaculo: & cum vicina esset Lydda Ioppæ, discipuli qui audierant Petrum illic esse, miserunt ad eum, rogantes, ne grauaretur ad eos usque venire. Surgens autem Petrus, venit cum illis: quem cum adesset, subduxerunt in cœnaculum, & astiterunt illi omnes viduæ flentes, & ostendentes tunicas & vestes, quas cum ipsis manens Dorcas, faciebat. Eiectis autem omnibus foras, Petrus positis genibus orauit, & conuersus ad corpus dixit: Thabita surge. Illa autem aperuit oculos suos, visoque Petro resedit. Data vero ei manu erexit illam, & cum vocasset sanctos ac viduas, exhibuit eam viuam. Innotuit autem hoc per totam Ioppen, & multi crediderunt in dominum. Accidit vero, ut ipse dies multos maneret Ioppæ, apud quendam Simonem coriarium.
units.tr: There was at Joppa a certain female disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas. She was full of good works and of the almsdeeds she performed. It came to pass in those days that she fell sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. And since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent to him, begging him not to hesitate to come to them. So Peter rose and went with them. When he arrived, they brought him into the upper room, and all the widows stood around him weeping and showing the tunics and garments that Dorcas had made while she was still with them. Peter put everyone out, knelt down and prayed, and turning to the body said, "Tabitha, arise." She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. He gave her his hand and raised her up, and calling the saints and the widows, he presented her to them alive. This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And it came to pass that he stayed for many days in Joppa with a certain Simon, a tanner.

units.la: VT Dei filius, & saluator noster Iesus Christus, discipulos suos ad euangelizandum misit: ita eosdem miraculis instruxit, quibus & doctrinæ suæ fidem facerent, & vim sine fructum meriti Iesu Christi declararent. Debent ad hunc finem cumprimis duo hæc referri, quæ Petri ministerio edita fuisse Lucas in huius cap. fine commemorat. Primum est Æneæ restituti, qui octo annorum spacio paralyticus decubuerat, sed invocato Christi nomine conualuit. Quo docemur per Christum medicum collapsas naturæ vires restitui, & in hoc nos posse omnia, qui alioqui ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus. Subiungitur huic alterum, quod ut reipsa maius est & admirabilius, ita maiorem quoque nobis consolationem affert. Mortuam enim Thabitam siue Dorcadem resuscitat Petrus, eo facto demonstrans, Iesum Christum mortis quoque victorem esse, & proinde nullo huius metu teneri debere, quicunque illi per fidem insiti fuerint. Commodissima autem huius consyderatio erit, si personas de quibus hic Lucas agit, ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: Since the Son of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ sent his disciples to preach the gospel, he also equipped them with miracles, by which they might confirm the faith of his teaching and show the power and fruit of the merit of Jesus Christ. To this end, two events above all should be noted, which Luke records at the end of this chapter as having been performed through Peter's ministry. The first is the restoration of Aeneas, who had lain paralysed for eight years but recovered when the name of Christ was invoked. From this we are taught that through Christ the physician the failing powers of nature are restored, and that we can do all things in him, though of ourselves we are not even fit to think. The second follows, which, as it is in fact the greater and more wonderful, so also brings us greater comfort. For Peter raised Tabitha, or Dorcas, from the dead, thereby showing that Jesus Christ is also the victor over death, and that therefore no one who has been grafted into him by faith ought to be held by fear of it. The most convenient way to consider this will be to look at the persons of whom Luke speaks here, in order.

units.la: Ab ea autem miraculi descriptionem orditur, in qua illud editum fuit. Et quamuis non magni momenti res esse videatur, quo quis nomine appelletur, eius tamen meminisse voluit, ut certior esset tanta rei fides. Syrus itaque Thabitam, Græcus Dorcadem (quæ vox Latinis Capream sonat) dictam fuisse ait. Sed in eorum consyderatione potius nos versari conuenit, quæ de hac dicuntur. Primum in huius locum fidei & religionis professio habet, quando discipulam, id est, Christianam fuisse scribit. Solebant enim in primitiua ecclesia discipuli dici credentes, donec Antiochiæ Christiani denominati sunt, ut infra cap. 11. audiemus. Nec mysterio carebat iste titulus. Admonebat enim præceptoris Christi, & Christianismum non inani nominis professione, sed potius doctrina siue præceptis & diligenti illorum obseruatione constare tetabatur. Quo Paulus respexisse videtur, quando fidei obedientiam euangelicæ prædicationis & totius apostolicæ functionis finem constituit. 2. Cor. 10. Rom. 1. & 16. Vt igitur huius nominis consyderatione docemur, vanam & inutilem esse Christiani nominis professionem, nisi Christo Iesu, cui nomen dedimus, fidelem obedientiam præstemus: ita simul admonemur, primum hunc nostræ salutis gradum esse, ut Christi discipuli simus. Est enim hic fundamentum tam propheticæ quam apostolicæ doctrinæ, cui omnes eos superædificari oportet, quicunque voluerint salui fieri. Ephes. 2. 1. Cor. 3. Quæ causa est, quod in Dorcadis commendatione huic etiam primus locus tribuitur. Arguit hoc omnium illorum superstitionem, qui cum pietatis & religionis titulum sibi vendicent, abiecto tamen Christi nomine, quod in baptismo suscepere, hominum potius discipuli dici volunt. Quorum vanitas ab apostolo olim grauissime reprehensa & confutata est. Vide 1. Cor. 1. & 3. Deinde plenam fuisse dicit bonis operibus. Et vt pateret, quae nam illa opera fuerint, per expositionem Eleemosynas subijcit. Comprehendit ea vox omnia misericordiae et charitatis officia, quibus proximus iuuatur, dum vel esurienti cibus, vel sitienti potus praebetur, vel nudus vestitur, vel captiuus redimitur, vel aegrotus inuisitur, vel in afflictione constitutus consilio aut consolatione subleuatur. Eleemosyna enim Graecis a misericordia nomen habet. At ne quis inanem in illa affectum duntaxat fuisse putaret, eleemosynas siue misericordiam fecisse dicitur. Admonet exemplum hoc, fidem, quae nos Christi discipulos facit, minime otiosam esse, nec in ignaua et inerti rerum caelestium contemplatione subsistere. Quia enim animum, qui potior hominis pars est, occupat, et ex animo vere credit, fieri non potest, quin totum hominem in Dei obedientiam rapiat, et multiplicem fructum ferat. Ideo Christus Iesus ait: Qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic fert fructum multum. Iohannis decimo quinto. Et Iacobus apostolus a vanis fidei ostentatoribus hoc potissimum exigit, vt fidem, quam ore iactant, ipsis quoque rebus ostentent. Iacob. 2. Merito igitur nobis atrocem iniuriam fieri conquerimur, quando bonorum operum hostes nos esse dicunt qui propriae iustitiae merito gloriantur, cum ipsi fateamur, fidem non esse, nisi quae ipsis factis se exerit, nec opera bona a quoquam posse fieri, nisi qui per fidem Christo coniunctus fuerit. Eius enim vox est: Sicut palmes non potest ferre fructus a semetipso, nisi manserit in vite: sic nec vos, nisi in me manseritis. Quia sine me nihil potestis facere, &c. Iohan. 15. Rursum, quae nam vere bona opera sint, idem exemplum admonet. Nam discipulam Christi fuisse audiuimus, et iam charitatis officia illi tribuuntur. Bona opera igitur sunt, quae a Christi cultoribus ex fide fiunt iuxta charitatis regulam. Nam cum ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus, quicquid ex nobis ipsis sine fide facimus, peccatum esse oportet, sicut Paulus testatur. Rom. 14. Praeterea bonum dici non potest, quodcunque nullius commodo feruit, cum vel ipse deus hoc potissimum nomine bonus dicatur, quod in creaturas suas suae gratiae thesauros liberalissime effundat. Ideo Christus charitate legem a nobis impleri docuit, et apud prophetas charitatis officia passim ab illis exigit, qui legalium ceremoniarum fiducia inflati, harum obseruatione homines saluari putabant. Vide Isa. 58. Hos. 6. Imo charitatem suorum tesseram fore docet, ex qua agnosci queant, et in nouissimi iudicij die huius potissimam rationem sese habiturum monet. Iohan. 13. Matth. 25. Confutantur ergo hic quaecunque homines ex semetipsis confingunt, dum frigidissimis caeremonijs, a fide et charitate alienis, salutem tribuunt, quarum obseruationem inutilem omnino esse, omnis scriptura constanter docet. Vide Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Col. 2. &c.
units.tr: He begins with a description of the woman in whom the miracle was performed. And although it may seem a matter of little moment what name someone bears, he nevertheless wished to record it, so that the faith in so great a thing might be more certain. The Syrian name, then, was Tabitha, and the Greek name Dorcas (a word which in Latin means "roe" or "gazelle"). But it is better for us to dwell on what is said about her. First, her profession of faith and religion is shown in that he calls her a disciple, that is, a Christian. For in the early Church believers were commonly called disciples, until they were named Christians at Antioch, as we shall hear in chapter 11. Nor was this title without mystery. For it reminded them of their teacher, Christ, and showed that Christianity consists not in an empty profession of a name but rather in doctrine, that is, in precepts and in their diligent observance. Paul seems to have had this in view when he set the obedience of faith as the goal of evangelical preaching and of the whole apostolic office (2 Cor. 10; Rom. 1 and 16). So by considering this name we are taught that the profession of the Christian name is vain and useless unless we render faithful obedience to Christ Jesus, whose name we have taken; and at the same time we are admonished that the first step of our salvation is to be disciples of Christ. For this is the foundation of the prophetic as well as the apostolic doctrine, upon which all must be built who wish to be saved (Eph. 2; 1 Cor. 3). This is why, in commending Dorcas, this title is also given first place. It exposes the superstition of all those who, while claiming for themselves the title of piety and religion, nevertheless put aside the name of Christ, which they received at baptism, and wish rather to be called disciples of men. The vanity of such people was long ago most severely rebuked and refuted by the apostle (see 1 Cor. 1 and 3). Next, he says she was full of good works. And so that it might be clear what those works were, he adds by way of explanation, "almsdeeds." That word embraces all the offices of mercy and charity by which a neighbour is helped: when food is given to the hungry or drink to the thirsty, when the naked are clothed, when the captive is ransomed, when the sick are visited, or when someone in affliction is relieved by counsel or comfort. For the Greek word for almsgiving derives from the word for mercy. And lest anyone should think that in her there was only an empty feeling, he says she performed almsdeeds, that is, mercy. This example admonishes us that the faith which makes us disciples of Christ is by no means idle, nor does it rest in a sluggish and inert contemplation of heavenly things. For since faith occupies the mind, which is the more important part of a man, and since one who truly believes from the heart cannot fail to draw the whole man into obedience to God and to bear manifold fruit, therefore Christ Jesus says, "He who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit" (John 15). And the apostle James especially demands of those empty boasters of faith that they show by their deeds the faith they vaunt with their mouths (James 2). Therefore we rightly complain of a grievous wrong when those who boast of their own righteousness call us enemies of good works, although they themselves admit that there is no faith except that which shows itself in actual deeds, and that no good work can be done by anyone who is not joined to Christ through faith. For this is his word: "As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, unless it abides in the vine, so neither can you, unless you abide in me. For without me you can do nothing," etc. (John 15). Again, this example shows what good works truly are. For we have heard that she was a disciple of Christ, and now offices of charity are attributed to her. Good works, therefore, are those which are done by the worshippers of Christ from faith, according to the rule of charity. For since we of ourselves are not even fit to think, whatever we do of ourselves without faith must be sin, as Paul testifies (Rom. 14). Moreover, that cannot be called good which benefits no one, since God himself is called good chiefly for this reason, that he most generously pours out the treasures of his grace upon his creatures. Therefore Christ taught that the law is fulfilled by us through charity, and among the prophets he everywhere demands offices of charity from those who, puffed up with confidence in legal ceremonies, thought that men were saved by observing them (see Isa. 58; Hos. 6). Indeed he teaches that charity will be the token of his own, by which they may be recognised, and he warns that he will take this above all into account on the last day of judgment (John 13; Matt. 25). Therefore whatever men fashion for themselves out of their own heads is refuted here, when they ascribe salvation to frigid ceremonies alien to faith and charity; and all Scripture constantly teaches that the observance of these is wholly useless (see Isa. 29; Matt. 15; Col. 2, etc.).

units.la: Sequitur vero in Dorcadis descriptione, illam eo tempore, quo Lyddae agebat Petrus apostolus, morbo lethali correptam esse, ex quo postea obierit. Atqui facile obstare poterat dominus, quo minus vel in morbum incideret, vel ex eo moreretur, cum olim quoq; Ezechiae dies prolongauerit, et Christum multorum morbos lethales curauisse constet. Sed permittit, vt morbi doloribus superata mortem subeat. Vnde colligimus, electos non immunes esse communium calamitatum, quibus humanum genus affligi consueuit. Nam et morbis conflictantur, et inopia laborant, et fame premuntur, et exilij molestias sentiunt, et quaecunque alia eius generis sunt aduersa experiuntur. At Paulo teste omnia illis cooperantur in bonum. Rom. 8. Ita enim per illos dei gloria illustratur, et illorum fides exercetur, et nunquam non in illis euidentia diuinae bonitatis argumenta elucent. Docet hoc caeci exemplum, quem caecum natum fuisse Christus monet, vt in illo manifestarentur opera dei. Iohan. 9. Et Lazarum aegrotare audiens ait: Infirmitas haec non est ad mortem, sed pro gloria dei, vt glorificetur filius dei per eam. Iohan. 11. Et huc Dorcadis quoq; exemplum referri debere, laetus et felix rei exitus declarat. Nam et ipsa vita restituitur, et per illam multi Christo lucrifiunt. Docent hae ne vel ipsi ijs offendamur, quae nobis aduersa eueniunt, vel de alijs temere iudicemus, quos infelicius et miserius tractari contingit. Saepe enim misericordiae et gratiae dei praeclara vasa sunt, qui propter assiduas aerumnas mundi iudicio irae vasa esse videbantur.
units.tr: Next, in the description of Dorcas, it is said that at the time when Peter the apostle was at Lydda she was seized by a deadly sickness, from which she afterwards died. Yet the Lord could easily have prevented her from falling ill or from dying of it, since he had of old prolonged the days of Hezekiah, and it is well established that Christ healed many deadly diseases. But he permits her to undergo death, overcome by the pains of sickness. From this we gather that the elect are not exempt from the common calamities with which the human race is wont to be afflicted. For they too are beset by diseases, they suffer want, they are oppressed by hunger, they feel the troubles of exile, and they experience whatever other adversities are of that kind. Yet, as Paul testifies, all these things work together for good for them (Rom. 8). For in this way the glory of God is made illustrious through them, their faith is exercised, and in them the evident tokens of divine goodness always shine forth. The example of the blind man teaches this, whom Christ said was born blind so that the works of God might be made manifest in him (John 9). And when he heard that Lazarus was sick, he said, "This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified through it" (John 11). And that the example of Dorcas too should be referred to this is shown by the joyful and happy outcome of the affair. For her life was restored, and through her many were won to Christ. These examples teach us neither to be offended by the adversities that befall us, nor to judge rashly of others who happen to be treated more unhappily and wretchedly. For often those who seemed, in the world's judgment, to be vessels of wrath because of their constant troubles are in fact noble vessels of God's mercy and grace.

units.la: Porrò ijs, quae de Dorcade dicta sunt, quid illius domestici et Ioppenses aliquot viduae, illa iam defuncta fecerint, subijcit. Et primò quidem mortuae cadauer ab illis ablutum, et in cœnaculo depositum esse dicit. Solebant enim antiquitus lauari funera, cum propter resurrectionis spem, tum quod purificatione eos opus habere nouerant, qui e vita migrantes dei tribunal subeunt. Ea autem figurabatur purificatio, quae in Christi sanguine fidelibus offertur. Eadem quoque aromatum et unguentorum guentorum ratio fuit, quibus funera condiebantur, priusquam sepulchris mandarentur. Et poterant in primitiua ecclesia tolerari aliquandiu eiusmodi ceremonia, quoad in fide firmiores facti omnibus istis simul renunciarent. Interim docemur, honestè à Christianis hominibus funera curari debere. Licet enim nec gentilitius luctus ab ijs adhiberi debeat, qui resurrectionem olim fore sciunt, (1. Thess. 4.) nec Iudaeorum ceremonijs opus sit, quando in Christo abunde impleta sunt, quae nostrae saluti seruiunt: debet tamen cum honestatis tum pietatis diligens ratio haberi, quam & charitatis lex requirit, & Christiana religio obseruare iubet, qua fit, vt corpora nostra spiritus sancti templa fiant. Cur ergo inhumaniter abijcerentur, quae spiritus Christi paulo ante inhabitare dignatus est? Moabitis certè hoc praecipuè propheta exprobrat, quòd humanitatis omnis obliti, Regis Idumaei ossa combusserint. Amos. 2. Graue ergo illorum hodie scelus est, qui belluarum instar in mortuos quoq; saeuiunt, aut funera inhumaniter abijciunt.
units.tr: Next, as to what is said of Dorcas: he goes on to tell what her household and some of the widows of Joppa did for her after she had died. And first, he says, the dead woman's body was washed by them and laid in an upper room. For in antiquity bodies were washed before burial, both because of the hope of resurrection and because they knew that those who depart this life and go before the judgment seat of God need purification. This purification was prefigured by the one offered to believers in the blood of Christ. Likewise, spices and ointments were used to prepare the dead before they were committed to the tomb. In the primitive Church such ceremonies could be tolerated for a while, until those who were firmer in faith renounced all of them together. Meanwhile we are taught that Christians ought to attend to funerals in a decent manner. For although the mourning of the Gentiles should not be practised by those who know that the dead will one day rise (1 Thess. 4), and although there is no need for the ceremonies of the Jews, since in Christ what serves our salvation has been fully accomplished, yet a careful regard for both decency and piety must still be kept, which the law of love requires and the Christian religion commands, since our bodies are made temples of the Holy Spirit. Why then should those bodies be cast out inhumanly, which the Spirit of Christ a little while before deigned to dwell in? It is especially for this that the prophet rebukes the Moabites, who, forgetting all humanity, burned the bones of the king of Edom (Amos 2). Grave, therefore, is the guilt of those today who rage like beasts even against the dead, or cast out funerals in an inhuman way.

units.la: Sed alterum quoque officium praestant. Nam missis nuncijs Petrum accersunt, quem Lydda vocatur Peruersari & miraculis clarere audiuerant. Quod non vulgare fidei simul & charitatis opus est. Nam & defunctam per Christi ministrum vitae restitui posse sperant, & id cupiunt fieri, eò quòd Christi ecclesiam tali membro adhuc indigere scirent. Et est hoc fidei ingenium, quòd nec in morte sperare definit, cum hanc à Christo deuictam esse nouerit: & quos semel syncero charitatis affectu complexa fuerit, eorum curam ne post mortem quidem abijcit. Simul vero praeclarum pietatis & Christianae beneficentiae praemium elucet. Quia enim huic studuit Dorcas, cum in viuis ageret, non desunt iam qui mortuae fidelem curam gerunt. Ita suorum memoriam deus afferere & tueri solet. Et frequenter fit, vt qui propter pietatem omnibus inuisi videbantur, postquam vita defunguntur, subito nominis sui assertores quam plurimos inueniant. Cuius rei exemplar in capite nostro, Iesu Christo, praecessit. Hunc enim ignominiosa crucis morte sublatum honorificè sepeliunt Iosephus & Nicodemus, qui prius occulti duntaxat eius discipuli fuerant. Nemo igitur infamem mortem pro Christi nomine perpeti detrectet, quando suorum memoriam tam fideliter Deus vindicat. Psalm. 34. capite.
units.tr: But they also performed a second duty. For they sent messengers and summoned Peter, whom they had heard was staying at Lydda and was famous for his miracles. This was no common work of faith and love together. For they hoped that the dead woman could be restored to life through the minister of Christ, and they desired this, because they knew that the Church of Christ still needed such a member. Such is the nature of faith that it does not cease to hope even in death, since it knows that death has been conquered by Christ; and those whom it has once embraced with sincere affection, it does not abandon even after death. At the same time the splendid reward of piety and Christian beneficence shines forth. For because Dorcas had cared for these people while she lived, there are now those who look after her, though dead, with faithful care. So God is wont to defend and protect the memory of his own. And it often happens that those who seemed hated by all because of their piety, after their life ends, suddenly find very many who vouch for their name. An example of this went before in our Head, Jesus Christ. For Joseph and Nicodemus, who had been only secret disciples of his before, honourably buried him after he was taken away by the shameful death of the cross. Let no one, therefore, shrink from enduring an infamous death for the name of Christ, since God so faithfully vindicates the memory of his own (Ps. 34).

units.la: Accedit omnibus hīs, quòd praesente iam Petro, dolorem quem ex Dorcadis morte conceperant, fletu pio testantur, & apostolo vestes monstrant, quas illa cum viueret, in pauperum vsum fieri curauerat. Vbi praeter pietatis officium, de quo iam diximus, videre est, quae vera sint sanctorum & fidelium Christi reliquiae, quas pij & palam ostendere, & exosculari ac venerari debent: charitatis nimirum opera, & vestigia horum. De his dicitur, quòd mortuos sequi, & his sublatis superesse solent. Apoc. 14. cap. Haec in Maria Christus commendat, & propter extremum vnctionis officium, quod ipsi impenderat, eius memoriam in ecclesia perpetuam fore pollicetur. Marc. 14. cap. Exhibent nobis reliquias eiusmodi passim sacrae & ecclesiasticae historiae. Eas nos pio officio laudare & diligenti imitatione colere decet. Ossa vero eorundem superstitiose venerari, nullo vel testimonio vel exemplo scripturae iubemur. Porrò vt magna piorum laus est, charitatis vestigia & exempla apud posteros relinquere: ita turpe est & miserum, si quis auaritiae, libidinis, iniustitiae, luxus & intemperantiae signa posteris relinquat. Eiusmodi vero sunt immodicae opes, & quaecunque ex his nequitiae instrumenta parantur, quae apostolus testimonium iustae damnationis olim fore dicit. Iacob. 5. capite. O infelicem ergo illorum fortem, quorum memoriam viduae & orphani propter ereptas sibi fortunas fletu prosequuntur. Infeliciores autem multò, qui quasi parum in vita peccarint, ad sepulchra sua clypeos & gladios suspendi, & ibidem cataphractti conspici volunt, vt diuturnior sit vitae in rapinis & caedibus transfactae memoria. O durum pectus, quod nec mortis amarae mentio emollire potest.
units.tr: To all this is added that, with Peter now present, they bear witness with pious tears to the grief they had felt at Dorcas' death, and they show the apostle the garments which she, while she lived, had made for the use of the poor. Here, besides the duty of piety of which we have already spoken, one may see what the true relics of the saints and faithful of Christ are. The godly ought both to display these openly, and to kiss and venerate them: namely, the works of charity and the traces of such people. Of these it is said that their works follow them when they die, and that they remain after these are taken away (Rev. 14). Christ commends this same thing in Mary, and, because of the final anointing that she gave him, he promises that her memory will be perpetual in the Church (Mark 14). Sacred and ecclesiastical histories everywhere offer us relics of this kind. It is fitting for us to praise them with a pious duty and to honour them by diligent imitation. But we are commanded by no testimony or example of Scripture to venerate superstitiously the bones of the same people. Moreover, just as it is a great praise of the godly to leave traces and examples of charity to posterity, so it is shameful and wretched if someone leaves to posterity the marks of greed, lust, injustice, luxury and intemperance. Such are immoderate riches, and whatever instruments of wickedness are acquired from them, which the apostle says will one day be a witness of just condemnation (James 5). O unhappy, then, is the lot of those whose memory widows and orphans follow with weeping, because their fortunes were snatched from them. Far more unhappy are those who, as if they had sinned too little in life, want shields and swords hung at their tombs and want them to be seen there in full armour, so that the memory of a life spent in plunder and slaughter may last longer. O hard heart, which not even the mention of bitter death can soften!

units.la: Caeterum videamus tandem quid Petrus ab illis vocatus egerit. Dicitur is illico eos comitatus esse, qui ad ipsum missi fuerant. Quod magnum facilitatis & zeli in prouehendo Christi regno argumentum est. Vnde facile colligas, quo spiritu ducantur, quicunq; in ijs sese difficiles praebent, quae gloriae Christi illustrandae & aliorum saluti seruiunt. Porrò vbi loppen aduenit, & in coenaculum, in quo funus iacebat, deductus est, viduarum fletus non multum curans, eò quòd agente in illo spiritu sancto, maius quoddam opus meditabatur, omnibus e coenaculo eiectis, ipse in genua prouolutus, & ad preces ardentes conuersus est. Recte autem Dicus apostolus vetera exempla imitatur, quando tundem modum in resuscitandis mortuis, Elifeum prophetam & Christum Iesum obseruauisse, con-
units.tr: But let us at last see what Peter did after he was summoned by them. He is said to have immediately gone with those who had been sent to him. This is a great proof of readiness and zeal in advancing the kingdom of Christ. From this you may easily gather by what spirit those are led who show themselves reluctant in matters that serve the glory of Christ and the salvation of others. Moreover, when he arrived at Joppa and was led into the upper room in which the body lay, he did not greatly heed the weeping of the widows, because, the Holy Spirit working in him, he was contemplating a greater work. Having put everyone out of the room, he himself fell on his knees and turned to fervent prayer. Peter the apostle rightly imitates ancient examples when he observed the same manner in raising the dead as Elisha the prophet and Christ Jesus observed, con-

units.la: flat.2.Reg.4. Matth.9. Nam ut secessum & solitudinem preces requirunt, ita modestia videtur, quod rem tanti momenti non inter multos cum ambitiosa ostentatione, sed solus peragere voluit. Et dum preces tam ardentes adhibet, non obscure testatur, ad Christum Deum omnem miraculi euentum & laudem referri debere, de quo iam saepe nobis dictum est. Peraltis vero precibus, mortuam alloquitur, illam, surgere iubet. Quod ridiculum videri poterat, nisi idem Christus fecisset, quando Iairi filiam & Lazarum resuscitauit. Sunt autem eiusmodi voces tremendae illius et altisonae vocis praeludia, qua olim in nouissimo die mortui omnes excitabuntur, sicut ipse Christus docuit. Ioan.5. Imo infallibile hoc futurae resurrectionis argumentum est, quod ad hominis vocem, Christi spiritu & nomine pronunciatam, mortui resurrexisse leguntur. Nec enim irritam fuisse Petri vocem, rei euentus docet. Nam mox apertis oculis Petrum intuetur Dorcas: deinde considet: tandem Petri manu erigitur, & intro vocatis omnibus viua exhibetur. Quo miraculo euidenter probatum fuit, viuificam esse doctrinam cuius minister fuit Petrus, & illius authorem, Iesum Christum, vitae si mul & mortis dominum esse. Agnouerunt hoc electi omnes, qui mox viso miraculo in dominum crediderunt dicuntur.
units.tr: flat (2 Kings 4; Matt. 9). For just as prayer requires seclusion and solitude, so it is a mark of modesty that he wished to carry out a matter of such weight alone, not among many with ambitious display. And while he offers such fervent prayers, he clearly testifies that every outcome and praise of the miracle ought to be referred to Christ God, a point about which we have often been told already. And after his earnest prayers, he addresses the dead woman and bids her arise. This might have seemed ridiculous, had not Christ himself done the same when he raised the daughter of Jairus and Lazarus. Such words are, moreover, the prelude to that dreadful and loud voice by which all the dead will be raised on the last day, as Christ himself taught (John 5). Indeed this is an infallible proof of the future resurrection, that at a man's voice, pronounced in the Spirit and name of Christ, the dead are read to have risen. For the outcome of the event shows that Peter's voice was not in vain. For Dorcas immediately opened her eyes and looked at Peter; then she sat up; finally she was raised by Peter's hand, and when all had been called in, she was presented alive. By this miracle it was clearly proved that the doctrine whose minister Peter was is life-giving, and that Jesus Christ, its author, is Lord both of life and of death. All the elect, who soon after seeing the miracle are said to have believed in the Lord, acknowledged this.

units.la: Subijcit autem narrationi huic paucula quaedam Lucas, quae sequentium praeparationi seruiunt. Petrum enim aliquot diebus Ioppae mansisse ait apud Simonem quendam coriarium: in cuius domo caelesti visione de gentibus in ecclesiam vocandis admonitus, & a Cornelio Centurione vocatus fuit, vt sequenti Capite dicetur. Hic vero obseruemus, e quali hominum genere primitiua ecclesia collecta fuerit, quando non alius hospes Petro obtingit, quam qui manuario artificio, eoq; non omnino nobili, victum quaerebat. Admonet de hoc Paulus, vt in solo domino gloriandum esse doceat. 1.Corinth.1. Adhaec Petri modestia exprimitur, qui tale hospitium non dedignatus est, cum hodie personatum illius successorem vix regum palatia capiant. Imitemur nos modestiam apostolicam, & in hac Christo Iesu credamus atque seruiamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke adds a few things to this narrative, which serve to prepare what follows. For he says that Peter stayed for some days at Joppa with a certain Simon, a tanner; in whose house, warned by a heavenly vision about calling the Gentiles into the Church, and summoned by Cornelius the centurion, he was to go on, as will be told in the next chapter. Here we should observe what kind of people the primitive Church was gathered from, since the only host Peter found was one who earned his living by a manual trade, and one that was not at all noble. Paul warns about this, to teach that we must glory only in the Lord (1 Cor. 1). In addition, Peter's modesty is shown, since he did not disdain such lodging, whereas today his self-styled successor can scarcely find room in the palaces of kings. Let us imitate the apostolic modesty, and in this believe in and serve Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: HOMILIA LXX.
units.tr: HOMILY LXX.

units.la: VIr autem quidam erat Caesareae, nomine Cornelius, Centurio ex cohorte, quae dicitur Italica, pius ac timens Deum cum tota domo sua, faciensq; eleemosynas multas populo, & orans Deum assidue. Is vidit in visione manifeste circiter horam nonam diei, Angelum Dei ingredientem ad se, & dicentem sibi: Corneli. At ille intuitus eum, & territus, dixit: Quid est domine? Dixit autem illi: Precationes tuae & eleemosynae tuae ascenderunt in memoriam coram Deo. Et nunc mitte loppen viros, & accerse Simonem, qui cognominatur Petrus. Hic diuertatur apud Simonem quendam coriarium, cui domus est ad mare. Hic dicet tibi, quid te oporteat facere.
units.tr: There was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian, a devout man who feared God with all his household, who gave many alms to the people and prayed to God continually. About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God coming in to him and saying to him: "Cornelius." And he, looking at him and afraid, said: "What is it, lord?" The angel said to him: "Your prayers and your alms have come up for a memorial before God. Now send men to Joppa and call for Simon, who is surnamed Peter. He is staying with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea. He will tell you what you ought to do."

units.la: Expositae est hucusque prima huius historiae pars, qua vt Apostoli iuxta Christi mandatum salutare euangelij verbum Iudaeis passim praedicarint, narratur. Simul vero indicatum est, vt verbi huius praedicationem Iudaei exceperint. Crediderunt quidem non pauci, & mirificos ecclesiae fideiq; Christianae progressus Lucas commemorauit. Maior tamen illorum pars, & ij praecipue, qui authoritate valebant, Christi doctrinam oppugnauisse dicti sunt. Nam & Apostolis manus iniiciunt, & Stephanum lapidibus obruunt, & Hierosolymis ecclesiam vniuersam horribili persecutione populantur, & Saulum cum publicis mandatis Damascum vsque emittunt, vt ibi nascentem Christi ecclesiam in herba, quod aiunt, opprimat. Et quod de Saulo scribitur, a multis aliis factitatum fuisse verisimile est. Merebatur ergo incurabilis et pertinax salutaris doctrina strinæ contemptus, vt tandem regnum dei à Iudæis ad gentes transferretur, sicuti venturũ Christus prædixerat, Matth.21. Id vt fieri cœperit, hoc Cap. Lucas commemorat, & Cornelij historiam ex-ponit, quem nos vocationis gentium primitias dicere possumus, cum is à deo delectus fit, qui tantæ rei initium præberet. Debet autem ante omnia principalis historiæ huius vsus obseruari, qui in eo consistit, quòd deus ingratos & impios euangelij hostes iusto iudicio reijcere soleat, nec vlli genti ita alli gatus fit, vt illam, quantumuis indignam, ferre cogatur. Accedit huic & alterum, salutem nimirum, quæ in Christo continetur, non ad solos Iudæos, verumetiam ad gentes pertinere. Quod vt nobis consolationem affert haud vulgarem, qui ex gentibus oriundi sumus: ita Iudaicæ gentis repudio nunquam non nos terreri conuenit, ne simili ingratitudine & inobedientia ipsi quoque à deo reijci merea mur. Rata enim & firma erit in omne æuum Pauli apostoli ratio, dicentis: Si deus naturalibus ramis non pepercit, vide ne qua fiat, vt nec tibi parcat, &c. Rom.11. Sed & Christi sententia iam olim lata est, qua omnem palmitem, qui fructum non fert vllum, abscindi & in ignem abijci debere minatur. Iohan.15. Cæterum quia Iudæis absurda simul & iniqua videbatur gentium incircuncisarum vocatio & adoptio in regnum Dei, (eò quòd soli illi iam multis seculis hoc titulo digni habiti fuissent, & ipsi reliquas gentes, perinde vt nos hodie Iudæos & Turcas solemus, abominabantur) primò quidem per prophetas vocationem gentium prædici voluit deus, cuius rei præclara extant apud illos testimonia, vt Psal.2.et 27.Isa.2.et 19.Item 42.& 49.Zach.9.&c. Deinde verò illius initium cumprimis illustre fecit in Cornelio, quem ita vocauit, vt nemo non diuinæ prouidentiæ consilium agnoscat. Nam et angelum suum cœlitus Cornelio transmittere dignatur, & Petrum cœlesti visione instruit, qua gentes in ecclesiam vocandas esse testatur, vt suo loco videbimus. In præsenti verò Cornelius nobis consyderandus venit, & quid cum illo dominus agere dignatus sit.
units.tr: So far we have set out the first part of this history, which tells how the Apostles, in obedience to Christ's command, preached the saving word of the gospel everywhere among the Jews. At the same time it is shown that the Jews received this preaching of the word. Indeed, not a few believed, and Luke recorded the remarkable progress of the Church and of the Christian faith. Yet the greater part of them, and especially those who held authority, are said to have opposed the teaching of Christ. For they laid hands on the Apostles, stoned Stephen, and ravaged the whole Church at Jerusalem with dreadful persecution; and they sent Saul to Damascus with official warrants, so that he might crush the young Church of Christ in the blade, as they say. And what is written of Saul was very likely done by many others as well. Therefore that incurable and obstinate people deserved to see the saving doctrine despised, so that at last the kingdom of God would be transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles, as Christ had foretold, Matt. 21. That this began to happen, this chapter records, and Luke sets out the history of Cornelius, whom we may call the firstfruits of the calling of the Gentiles, since he was chosen by God to be the beginning of so great a thing. But before all else the principal use of this history must be observed, which consists in this: that God is accustomed, by a just judgment, to cast off ungrateful and impious enemies of the gospel, and he is not bound to any nation so as to be forced to endure it, however unworthy. To this is added another point, namely that the salvation contained in Christ pertains not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles. This brings us no slight comfort, since we are born of the Gentiles; yet we ought always to be made afraid by the rejection of the Jewish nation, lest we too, by similar ingratitude and disobedience, deserve to be rejected by God. For the argument of the Apostle Paul will be valid and firm for all time, when he says: "If God did not spare the natural branches, take heed lest he also not spare you, etc." Rom. 11. And Christ's sentence was pronounced long ago, in which he threatens that every branch that bears no fruit must be cut off and cast into the fire. John 15. Moreover, because the calling of the uncircumcised Gentiles and their adoption into the kingdom of God seemed to the Jews both absurd and unjust (since they alone had for many centuries been held worthy of this title, and they themselves abhorred the other nations, just as we today are accustomed to abhor Jews and Turks), God wished first to proclaim through the prophets the calling of the Gentiles, of which there are clear testimonies among them, such as Ps. 2 and 27, Isa. 2 and 19, likewise 42 and 49, Zech. 9, etc. Then indeed he made its beginning especially illustrious in Cornelius, whom he called in such a way that no one fails to recognise the counsel of divine providence. For he deigns to send his angel from heaven to Cornelius, and he instructs Peter by a heavenly vision, by which he testifies that the Gentiles are to be called into the Church, as we shall see in its place. But at present Cornelius comes before us to be considered, and what the Lord has deigned to do with him.

units.la: Sumit enim narrandi exordium à Cornelij descriptione Lucas, quam mira tum breuitate tum per spicuitate contexit. Primò vitæ genus siue conditione exprimens, Centurionem fuisse dicit ex cohorte Italica. Solebant enim Romani cohortes suas ex diuersis nationibus & gentibus conscribere, ex qui bus postea nomina imponebantur. Et quia inter omnes nationes nulla illis Italica potior erat & excellentior, Italicæ etiam cohortes reliquis præferebantur. Nec dubium est Cornelium quoq; Italum fuisse, cum in eius gentis cohorte non postremum dignitatis locum tenuerit. At quia Cæsareæ habita uisse dicitur, quæ veteribus Turris Stratonis dicta est, illius seculi militiũ conditio obseruanda erit, vt eò clarius Cornelij conditione videre liceat. Tradunt itaq; Romani scriptores, post Pom. Magni victorias, qui primus Syriam & Iudæam Romano Imperio subiecit, nullos molestiores Romano populo hostes fuisse Parthis, quos & Crassi interitus et Romanarũ legionum clades captaq;, aquilæ nobilitarunt. Quorum excursionibus cum assidue obstandum esset, cohortes aliquot in Romani Imperij finibus per vrbes dispositæ fuerunt, ex quibus breui temporis spacio (si ita necessitas ferret) iustius exercitus, ad reprimendam hostilem vim, colligi possent. Simul verò Iudææ vrbibus præsidio erant cohortes illæ, vt ad seditiones & nouarum rerum studia proclives Iudæorũ animos in officio retinerent. Hinc illa tam frequens in euangelistarum scriptis militum & Centurionum mentio, quorum pleriq, inter Iudæos fixas sedes habebant, & familias alebant, non venalium Carum instar incertis hinc inde sedibus vagabantur. Ex eo autem hominũ genere, gentium in ecclesia Christi primitias deo colligere placuit, vt clarior eluceret ipsius gratia & bonitas, quando constat militari vitæ plerunq, summam licentiam, effrænem morũ corruptelam & nihil non audendi libidinę coniunctam esse. Interim ex ijs, quæ de illius seculi militibus diximus, colligi potest, quæ nam sit populi aliquando liberi conditio, postquam libertatis donum ingratitudine & inobedientia amisit. Tales enim Iudæos fuisse constat, quos deus Ægypto eductos in libertatem asseruerat, vt nulla exterorum regum tyrannide pressi, legitimis magistratibus parerent. At tanto bono abusi, libertatem simul & fortunas maxima ex parte amiserunt. Iam ergo non præsidum modò Romanorũ libidini et auaritiæ subiacent, verumetiam per singulas fere vrbes disposita habent exterorum militum præsidia, inter quos licet aliqui pietatis & aequitatis nomine commendentur, plerosq, tamen illorum nimis militares, id est feroces & temerarios fuisse, multa exempla docent. Atqui olim eam infelicitatem inobedientibus deus minatus fuerat. Discant ergo Iudæorum exemplo legitimis magistratibus & sanctis legibus parere, quicunque libertatis bono frui untur, ne similem & ipsi aliquando tyrannidem sentiant.
units.tr: For Luke begins his narrative with a description of Cornelius, which he weaves together with such remarkable brevity and clarity. First, expressing his way of life or condition, he says that he was a centurion of the Italian cohort. For the Romans used to enlist their cohorts from different peoples and nations, and names were afterwards given to them from these. And since among all nations none was more esteemed or more excellent than the Italian, the Italian cohorts were also preferred to the others. Nor is there doubt that Cornelius was also an Italian, since he held no lowly rank of dignity in a cohort of that people. But since he is said to have lived at Caesarea, which was formerly called the Tower of Strato, the condition of the soldiery of that age must be observed, so that Cornelius's position may be seen more clearly. Roman writers therefore relate that after the victories of Pompey the Great, who first brought Syria and Judea under the Roman Empire, the Parthians were the most troublesome enemies of the Roman people; the destruction of Crassus and the defeat and capture of the Roman legions made them famous, along with the eagle. Since it was necessary to resist their raids constantly, several cohorts were stationed in towns throughout the boundaries of the Roman Empire, so that from them, within a short time (if necessity so required), a more regular army could be gathered to check the hostile force. At the same time those cohorts were a garrison in the towns of Judea, so that they would keep the minds of the Jews, who were prone to sedition and the desire for revolution, in obedience. Hence that frequent mention of soldiers and centurions in the writings of the evangelists; many of them had settled homes among the Jews and supported families, and they were not wandering about from place to place with uncertain dwellings like mercenaries. From this class of men God was pleased to gather the firstfruits of the Gentiles into the Church of Christ, so that the grace and goodness of God might shine more brightly, since it is agreed that the military life is generally joined with the greatest licence, unbridled corruption of morals, and a lust for daring anything. Meanwhile, from what we have said about the soldiers of that age, one may gather what the condition of a free people becomes once it has lost the gift of liberty through ingratitude and disobedience. For it is certain that the Jews were such, whom God, having led them out of Egypt, had established in liberty, so that they, pressed by no tyranny of foreign kings, might obey their lawful magistrates. But having abused so great a good, they lost both their liberty and their fortunes to a very great extent. Now therefore they are subject not only to the lust and greed of Roman governors, but they also have garrisons of foreign soldiers stationed in almost every town; and although some of these are commended for their piety and fairness, many examples show that most of them were excessively military, that is, fierce and reckless. Yet God had long ago threatened this misery to the disobedient. Let therefore all who enjoy the good of liberty learn from the example of the Jews to obey lawful magistrates and holy laws, lest they too one day experience a similar tyranny.

units.la: Sed ad Cornelium redeamus, cuius studia & mores magnifice commendantur. Nam pietatem & dei timorem illi tribuit Lucas. Unde constat, eum a gentilium idololatria, qui multos deos inepte & impie colebant, alienissimum fuisse. Atqui magnum & praeclarum facinus illud fuisse patebit, si illorum temporum conditionem expendamus, quando Romanorum tyrannidi omnes prope nationes parebant, quorum legibus caveba-tur, ne quis alienam religionem profiteretur. Nam ut Tertullianus author est, nemini divinus cultus impendi poterat, nisi quem Senatus in deorum numerum retulisset: adeo ut Christum deum hanc potissimum ob causam reiecerint, quod Tyberius cum fuisset fragii sui praerogativa de illius cultu ad Senatum retulisset. Magnam ergo hanc animi constantiam fuisse oportet, qua Cornelius, abiectis gentilium Dijs, verum Deum colere ausus est, cum in publico officio versaretur, & vel eo nomine se minus latere posse sciret. Confutantur autem hoc exemplo nostri seculi homines, qui in religionis causa infimis magistratibus, priusquam summi magistratus consensus accedat, nihil tentandum, sed supremis Regibus simpliciter obediendum esse clamitant. At ut non negamus reddenda esse Caesaribus & Regibus, quaecunque illorum iuris sunt: ita religionem ad unum deum referimus, nec hanc, ut illis placeamus, violari debere contendimus. Nobiscum vero olim Danielis socios & ipsum Danielem fenisse scimus, qui in fornacem ardentem & Leonum speluncas potius abijci, quam religionem veram prophanare voluerunt. Et Cornelij haec potissima laus est, quod non expectato Romanorum Imperatoris decreto, verum deum publice coluit. Sed & Christus Centurionis fidem, qui se alterius imperio subesse ingenue fatetur, praeclaro testimonio simul & miraculo commendavit. Luc.7.
units.tr: But let us return to Cornelius, whose zeal and character are praised in noble terms. For Luke attributes to him piety and the fear of God. From this it is evident that he was utterly alien from the idolatry of the Gentiles, who foolishly and impiously worshipped many gods. Moreover, that deed will appear great and remarkable if we weigh the condition of those times, when almost all nations obeyed the tyranny of the Romans, by whose laws it was provided that no one should profess a foreign religion. For, as Tertullian is the authority, no divine worship could be offered to anyone unless the Senate had enrolled him among the gods; so much so that they rejected Christ as God chiefly for this reason, that Tiberius, when he had brought the matter of his worship before the Senate by the prerogative of his office, was refused. Great constancy of mind must therefore have been required for Cornelius, who, having cast aside the gods of the Gentiles, dared to worship the true God, while he was engaged in public service and knew that on this account he could hardly remain hidden. By this example, however, those men of our own age are refuted, who cry out that in matters of religion nothing must be attempted with the lower magistrates before the consent of the highest magistrate is obtained, and that supreme kings must simply be obeyed. But just as we do not deny that what belongs to Caesars and kings must be rendered to them, so we refer religion to the one God, and we contend that it must not be violated in order to please them. Indeed we know that Daniel's companions and Daniel himself lived with us, who preferred to be cast into a burning furnace and the dens of lions rather than profane the true religion. And this is Cornelius's chief praise, that without waiting for the decree of the Roman Emperor, he publicly worshipped the true God. But Christ also commended the centurion's faith, who frankly confessed that he was under another's command, with a remarkable testimony and a miracle. Luke 7.

units.la: At quia pietatis & timoris dei laudem Cornelio tribuit euangelista, externa quoque illius studia, quibus animi religionem declaravit & exercuit, recensset. Inter quae primum locum habet, quod non ipse modo deum timuit, sed familiam quoque in vera pietate & dei timore probe institutam habuit. Est enim hoc proprium pijs, quod ut seipsos, ita suos quoque omnes deo consecratos esse volunt. Cur enim a deo alienos esse paterentur, quos a deo sibi concreditos esse norunt? Abraham certe hoc nomine commendatur, quod & ipse veri dei cultor fuerit, & eiusdem cultum verum domui suae commendarit. Gen.18. Et quia in eam sententiam dei praecepta extant (sicuti videre est Deut.6. & Psal.78.) non immerito ipsis patribus domesticorum impietas imputatur, si illi negligentia sua huius authores fuerint. Exemplum eius rei cumprimis memorabile in Hel: scriptura proponit. 1. Samuel. 2. & 3. &c. Sed & Saba regina Solomonem propter bene institutos vulgos laudat, & eidem postea uxorum impietas, vitio datur. 1. Regum 10. & 11. cap. Quotquot ergo religionis laudem sibi vendicare volunt, non in hoc se officio suo functos putent, si ipsi dei cultores fuerint, sed quoscunque ipsorum curae deus commiserit, illi adducere & consecrare studeant.
units.tr: But because the evangelist ascribes to Cornelius the praise of piety and the fear of God, he also recounts his outward practices, by which he displayed and exercised the religion of his soul. Among these, the first place belongs to the fact that he not only feared God himself but also had his household thoroughly trained in true piety and the fear of God. For this is the mark of the godly: they want not only themselves but all their household to be consecrated to God. For why would they allow those to be estranged from God whom they know have been entrusted to them by God? Abraham is certainly commended on this account, that he was himself a worshipper of the true God and also commended that true worship to his household (Gen. 18). And because God's precepts to this effect exist (as may be seen in Deut. 6 and Ps. 78), the impiety of household members is not unjustly imputed to their fathers if, through their negligence, they were the authors of it. Holy Scripture sets before us a very memorable example of this in Eli (1 Sam. 2 and 3, etc.). But also the queen of Sheba praises Solomon for his well-ordered people, and afterward the impiety of his wives is laid to his charge (1 Kings 10 and 11). Therefore, whoever wish to claim the praise of religion should not think they have discharged their duty if they themselves are worshippers of God, but should earnestly strive to bring to God and consecrate all those whom God has committed to their care.

units.la: Deinde eleemosynas, id est misericordiae opera, exercuisse dicitur Cornelius. Unde constat tantas in animo illius vires acquisivisse religionis studium, ut eo inflammatus, hominibus quoque omne officiorum genus praestaret. Et verisimile est, non ignarum fuisse eius regulae, quam Baptista interrogantibus ipsum militibus praescripserat, dicens: Ne quem concutiatis, ne quem calumniemini, & contenti estote stipendijs vestris. Luc.3. At quasi parum fecisset haec praestando, aliorum simul necessitatibus subveniendum esse putat. Et sane, qui hunc animum in se nondum deprehendit, nam in religionis titulo gloriari desinat: quando Paulus ea, quae maximi momenti esse videntur, pro inutilibus habet, si charitate vacui simus. 1. Corinth.3.
units.tr: Next, Cornelius is said to have practised almsgiving, that is, works of mercy. From this it is clear that the zeal for religion had gained such strength in his soul that, inflamed by it, he also showed every kind of duty toward men. And it is likely that he was not ignorant of the rule which the Baptist prescribed to the soldiers who asked him: "Do not intimidate anyone, do not accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your wages" (Luke 3). But as if it were too little to do these things, he thinks he must also come to the aid of others in their needs. Indeed, whoever does not find this disposition in himself should cease to boast of the name of religion, since Paul counts as worthless those things which seem of the greatest importance if we are empty of love (1 Cor. 13).

units.la: Accedit his tertio loco assiduum & indefinens orandi studium. Quod veritatis cognoscendae desyderio in illo excitatum fuisse crediderim. Nam in eorum numero censendus esse videtur Cornelius, qui olim Dei cognitionem veram assecuti, salvatorem a deo promissum esse noverant, sed quis nam ille esset, ignorabant. Hunc ergo sibi revelari orauit, ne forte suis rationibus in salutis causa fallere-tur. Quem sensum ex angeli verbis postea colligere licet, qui Petrum ipsi annunciaturum esse dicit, quid facere debeat.
units.tr: In the third place, there is added a constant and unceasing zeal for prayer. I am inclined to believe that this was stirred up in him by a desire to know the truth. For Cornelius seems to be counted among those who, having already attained the true knowledge of God, knew that the Saviour had been promised by God, but did not know who he was. He therefore prayed that this be revealed to him, lest perhaps he be deceived in his reasoning about the cause of salvation. This sense may afterward be gathered from the words of the angel, who says that Peter will tell him what he ought to do.

units.la: Conferamus autem cum Centurione hoc nostri seculi milites, qui tam huius quam aliorum eius generis exemplis sibi ipsis patrocinari solent, & facile patebit, quam parum haec illis seruiant. Cornelius pietatis nomine commendatur: at illi pietatis studium ad monachos, non ad milites pertinere putant. Cornelius cum tota sua domo deum timuisse dicitur: at nostri illi eos demum vere militares animos esse ducunt, qui omni metu tam dei quam hominum vacui fuerint. Cornelium eleemosynis mosynis egenos subleuasse Lucas scribit: at illi rapto viuunt, nec sacris nec prophanis abstinentes. Cornelius in precibus assiduus promissi saluatoris notitiam sibi reuelari petijt: at illorum linguae ad deie rationes, execrationes & blasphemias proclives, Christi saluatoris crucem, passionem, vulnera, & quid non? impio ausu polluunt. Taceo nunc quod Cornelius legitimo magistratus sui imperio militiam secutus est, vt hostilem vim arceret, seditionibus resisteret, pacem publicam tueretur: nostri vero illi Carum instar mercede conducti, bellis nihil ad se pertinentibus se immiscent, & publicae pacis nomen cane peius & angue oderunt. Quid vero de militibus dicere attinet, quando nec illi Cornelio conferri merentur, qui hodie in Christianismo se omnium perfectissimos esse gloriantur? Adeo in omnium animis Dei timor extinctus: adeo priuati quaestus studium apud omnes ordines inualuit: & tam frigisunt in precibus ad Deum fundendis omnium fere hominum animi, vt nec vndiq; premen-tibus aduersis securitatem hanc sibi excutei patiantur.
units.tr: But let us compare with this Centurion the soldiers of our own age, who are accustomed to defend themselves by examples of this kind and of others like it, and it will easily be seen how little these examples serve them. Cornelius is commended for his piety; but they think the zeal for piety belongs to monks, not to soldiers. Cornelius, it is said, feared God with his whole household; but those men of ours judge that only those are truly soldierly in spirit who are free from all fear of God and of men. Luke writes that Cornelius relieved the needy with alms; but they live by plunder, abstaining from neither sacred nor profane things. Cornelius, persistent in prayer, asked to have the knowledge of the promised Saviour revealed to him; but their tongues, prone to oaths, curses and blasphemies, with impious daring defile the cross, the passion and the wounds of Christ the Saviour, and whatever else. I say nothing now of the fact that Cornelius followed the military life under the lawful command of his magistrate, to repel hostile force, to resist sedition, and to maintain public peace; but those men of ours, hired like Carian mercenaries, involve themselves in wars that have nothing to do with them, and hate the name of public peace worse than a dog or a snake. But why should I speak of soldiers, when not even those are worthy to be compared with Cornelius who today boast that they are the most perfect of all in Christianity? So completely has the fear of God been extinguished in the minds of all, so strongly has the pursuit of private gain prevailed among every rank, and so cold are the minds of almost all men in pouring out prayers to God, that they do not even allow this security to be shaken off when adversities press on them from every side.

units.la: Porro personae descriptionem Cornelij vocatio sequitur: cuius initium ab apparitione angelica factum est. Vbi magnum diuinae bonitatis argumentum elucet. Poterat enim Deus nos vel abiectissimae creaturae ministerio indignos putare. At non contentus omnia alia nostro vsui destinauisse, angelos quoq; (quod & Paulus monuit) in suorum ministerium emittit. Hebr.1. Ea autem huius apparitionis ratio est, vt ab omni doli fraudisque suspicione sit alienissima. Nam clara luce, circa horam diei nonam, angelus visibili specie (nimirum aliquid plus quam humanum referens) ingreditur & proprio nomine Cornelium appellat, vt sic ad percipienda Dei mandata attentiorem reddat. Solet enim ingenue & ea fide nobiscum agere Deus, vt nullus nobis dolus timendus sit, qui diabolicis apparitionibus, obscuris semper & ambiguis, admiscerí confuerit. At magnum licet & ardens fuerit in Cornelio religionis studium, consternatur tamen viso angelo. Quod vt humanae infirmitati tribui poterat, ita pijs proprium est, vt diuinae maiestatis praesentia terreantur. Hoc enim olim Danieli, & postea tribus Christi discipulis in monte Thabor accidisse legimus. At eadem nos quoq; erga verbum Dei reuerentia affici decebat, cum non alia re se nobis magis praesentem Deus exhibere soleat. Quare cum Cornelio dominum agnoscamus in verbo suo nobis loquentem, & ad iussa illius capessenda nos paratos & spontaneos offeramus. Praecipuum vero in hoc actu locum Angeli oratio obtinet, quam bipartitam esse constat. De singulis igitur partibus ordine agemus.
units.tr: Next to the description of the person comes Cornelius's calling, whose beginning was made by an angelic appearance. Here a great proof of divine goodness shines forth. For God could have regarded us as unworthy of the ministry of even the most lowly creature. But not content to have destined all other things for our use, he also sends out angels into the service of his own people (as Paul also reminded us, Heb. 1). The reason for this appearance is that it is entirely free from any suspicion of deceit. For in clear daylight, about the ninth hour of the day, the angel enters in visible form (surely representing something more than human) and calls Cornelius by name, so as to make him more attentive to receiving God's commands. For God is accustomed to deal with us openly and in good faith, so that we have no deception to fear, which is usually mixed into diabolical apparitions, always obscure and ambiguous. But although the zeal for religion in Cornelius was great and burning, he was nonetheless dismayed at the sight of the angel. This could be attributed to human weakness, but it is proper to the godly to be terrified at the presence of the divine majesty. For we read that this happened long ago to Daniel, and afterward to three of Christ's disciples on Mount Tabor. Yet we too ought to be moved by the same reverence toward the Word of God, since God usually presents himself to us in no other thing more fully. Therefore, together with Cornelius, let us acknowledge the Lord speaking to us in his word, and let us offer ourselves ready and willing to take up his commands. But the angel's speech holds the chief place in this action, and it is clearly twofold. We shall therefore treat each of its parts in order.

units.la: Prima pars consolationem habet, qua diu iam anxium Cornelij animum subleuat. Ait enim: Precationes tuae & eleemosynae tuae ascenderunt in memoriam coram Deo. Quae verba non ofcitanter transiliri debent, cum bifariam illis abutantur Papistae, dum pro humanae iustitiae gloria aduersus Christi meritum dimicant. Primo enim hinc colligunt, homines suis viribus & operibus praeparari, vt postea digni habeantur ad percipiendum maiorem gratiam & salutem in Christo. Deinde absolute & simpliciter operibus meriti laudem tribuunt, quasi illis iustificemur & saluemur. At in vtroq; illos hallucinari, res ipsa clamat. Nam quoad primum, vanissimum est, quod de suis praeparationibus ex hoc loco somniat, cum satis constet, Cornelium nihil horum, quae ante de illo dicta sunt ex seipso habuisse aut fecisse. Quomodo enim homo gentilis, in superstitione natus & a pueris institutus, Deum verum popria industria agnoscere & timeret, cum homo ille animalis non percipiat ea quae sunt spiritus Dei? 1.Corinth.2. Quomodo item orationes Deo gratas sine fide funderet, cum sine fide Deo nemo placere possit? Hebr.11. Quod si fidem habuit (vt sane negari non potest) ex Dei dono hanc habuerit, oportet. Ephes.2. At eadem sine regeneratione spiritus non est, qui & pium Dei veri timorem, & beneficentiae studium, & quaecunq; alia in ipso praeclara fuerunt, progenuit. Eadem autem est omnium nostrum ratio, quae Cornelij, nec quisquam sese ad percipiendum gratiam Dei propriis viribus praeparare poterit, cum ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus. 2.Cor.3. Deinde ridiculum est meriti titulum operibus tribuere, & illis coram Dei iudicio gloriari. Quis enim haec abs se facta esse, dicere poterit? Et num illius Paulini fumus obliti: Quid habes quod non acceperis? Quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis? 1.Corinth.4. Praeterea, velimus nolimus, agnoscere nos oportet, imperfecta esse quaecunq; ex nobis emanant opera, etiamsi ad diuini verbi praescriptum, agente in nobis gratia Dei, instituantur. Concurrunt enim illis nostrae carnis affectus, & cupiditates improbae, quibus illa inficiuntur. Vnde sancti apud prophetam clamant, iustitias nostras esse instar lacerae vestis aut panni menstruae mulieris Isa.64. Postremo cum in nobis corrupta sint omnia, propter solam fidem in Iesum Christum Deo placet, quicquid placet. In illo enim huic complacuit. Matth. 3. 17. Interim non negamus, mercedis nomine frequenter scripturam uti. Sed hoc ipsum diuinae gratiae donum est, quae sua dona (ut D. Augustinus ait) in nobis coronat, qui alias serui inutiles dici merebamur. Luc. 17. Longe ergo alia verborum angeli mens est. Docere enim vult, Deum hucusque Cornelij rationem habuisse, nec neglexisse ipsius orationes et quaecunque alia ex pietatis studio fecerat. Adeoque Christi promissionem illi in mentem reuocat: Omni habenti dabitur. Habere enim dicuntur, qui concessis sibi diuina liberalitate donis, ut par est, uti consueuerunt. Hinc vero vniuersalis consolatio decerpi potest, non inane aut inutile esse pietatis et precandi studium, et haud dubie ingens donorum Dei incrementum sensuros nos, si domino fenerari velimus. Refer huc talentorum parabolam, quae Matth. 25. cap. habetur.
units.tr: The first part contains a consolation, by which he raises up the long-anxious soul of Cornelius. For he says: "Your prayers and your alms have come up for a memorial before God." These words ought not to be passed over carelessly, since the Papists misuse them in two ways, while they fight against the merit of Christ for the glory of human righteousness. First, from this they gather that men are prepared by their own strength and works so that afterward they may be deemed worthy to receive greater grace and salvation in Christ. Then they attribute the praise of merit absolutely and simply to works, as if we were justified and saved by them. But that they go astray in both respects the matter itself cries out. For as to the first, it is most vain that they dream about their own preparations from this passage, since it is quite certain that Cornelius had none of the things said of him before, either from himself or by himself. For how could a Gentile man, born in superstition and trained from boyhood in it, come by his own effort to recognise and fear the true God, when "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2)? Likewise, how could he pour out prayers pleasing to God without faith, since "without faith no one can please God" (Heb. 11)? But if he had faith (as indeed it cannot be denied that he did), he must have had it by the gift of God (Eph. 2). But that gift is not without the regeneration of the Spirit, who has begotten both the godly fear of the true God, and the zeal for beneficence, and whatever other excellent things were in him. Moreover, the case of all of us is the same as that of Cornelius; nor can anyone prepare himself by his own powers to receive the grace of God, since of ourselves we are not even fit to think anything (2 Cor. 3). Then it is ridiculous to attribute the title of merit to works and to glory in them before the judgment of God. For who will be able to say that these things were done by himself? And have they forgotten that saying of Paul: "What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" (1 Cor. 4). Besides, whether we like it or not, we must acknowledge that whatever works come forth from us are imperfect, even if they are performed according to the prescription of the divine word, with grace of God working in us. For our fleshly affections and wicked desires mingle with them and stain them. Hence the saints cry out through the prophet that our righteousnesses are like a filthy rag (Isa. 64). Finally, since all things in us are corrupted, whatever pleases God pleases him only through faith alone in Jesus Christ. For in him he was well pleased (Matt. 3:17). Meanwhile we do not deny that Scripture frequently uses the word reward. But even this is a gift of divine grace, which, as Augustine says, crowns its own gifts in us, though we deserved to be called unprofitable servants (Luke 17). Therefore the angel's meaning is quite different. For he wants to teach that God has hitherto taken account of Cornelius, and has not neglected his prayers and whatever else he had done from zeal for piety. And so he recalls to his mind the promise of Christ: "To everyone who has, more will be given" (Matt. 13 / Luke 19). For those are said to have, who, having been given gifts by divine liberality, are accustomed to use them as is fitting. From this, indeed, a universal consolation may be drawn: that the zeal for piety and for prayer is not empty or useless, and that without doubt we shall experience a great increase of God's gifts, if we are willing to lend to the Lord. Refer here the parable of the talents, which is found in Matthew 25.

units.la: Altera parte, quid facere debeat, admonet. Summa vero mandati est, ut Simonem Petrum accersat, qui illi rerum agendarum minister et doctor futurus sit. Est hoc euidens diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quod itineris molestiam in Petrum potius quam Cornelium transfert. Ita enim gratiam et salutem nobis, vel non quaerentibus, offerre consueuit, non ut carnis ignauiam foueat, sed ut suo studio nos ad simile salutis nostrae et suae gloriae studium accendat. Exemplum huius in primis parentibus extat, qui cum non ipsi priores Deum vel quaerent vel vocarent, ab illo quaesiti et vocati sunt. Praeterea ad externi verbi et ecclesiastici ministerij commendationem facit locus hic. Vt enim Paulum antea ad Ananiam relegauit, ita Petrum Cornelio doctorem destinat, quem per angelum instituere poterat. Constat quidem, neminem ad Christum venire, nisi quem pater traxerit, et fidem Dei donum esse: sed interim ratus et stabilis manet ordo Dei, quod fides ex auditu est, auditus vero per verbum Dei. Rom. 10. Quotquot igitur verbum ex hominis ore audire dedignantur, hoc ipso sese regno Dei indignos esse declarant, quod illius constitutionem improbe contemnunt, et ab ipso institutum salutis ordinem euersum cupiunt. Vtamur ergo et nos apostolorum doctrina, ut per hanc instituti faciamus quae Deo accepta sunt, et salutem consequamur in Iesu Christo, saluatore nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the second part, he advises what Cornelius ought to do. The sum of the command is that he should send for Simon Peter, who is to be his minister and teacher in the matter at hand. This is a clear sign of divine goodness that the trouble of the journey is laid upon Peter rather than Cornelius. For God is accustomed to offer grace and salvation to us even when we do not seek them, not so as to indulge our sloth, but so that by his own zeal he may kindle in us a like zeal for our salvation and for his glory. The first parents provide an example of this, for when they neither sought nor called upon God first, they were sought and called by him. Moreover, this passage serves to commend the outward Word and the ecclesiastical ministry. For just as he had earlier sent Paul to Ananias, so he appoints Peter as teacher for Cornelius, although he could have instructed him through an angel. It is certainly true that no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him, and that faith is the gift of God; yet meanwhile the order of God remains fixed and stable, that faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the Word of God (Rom. 10). Therefore, all who disdain to hear the Word from the mouth of a man declare by this very fact that they are unworthy of the kingdom of God, since they wickedly despise its appointment and wish to overturn the order of salvation instituted by him.
