Let us therefore also make use of the apostles' teaching, so that, instructed by it, we may do what is acceptable to God and obtain salvation in Jesus Christ, our one Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXI.

units.la: Postquam vero abijt angelus, qui locutus erat Cornelio, vocauit duos ex famulis suis, et militem pium ex his qui sibi adhaerebant: et cum narrauisset illis omnia, misit ipsos Ioppen. Postridie vero cum illi iter facerent, et appropinquarent urbi, ascendit Petrus super tectum domus, ut oraret, circiter horam sextam. Erat autem ieiunus, et voluit gustare. Parantibus vero illis, incidit super eum mentis excessus: et vidit coelum apertum, et descendens ad se vas quoddam, instar lintei magni, quatuor initijs alligatum, et demissum in terram: in quo erant omnia quadrupedia terrae, et feræ, et reptilia, et volatilia coeli. Et facta est vox ad eum: Surge Petre, macta, et vescere. Petrus autem dixit: Nequaquam domine, quia nunquam comedi quicquam commune vel immundum. Et vox rursus ad eum secundo: Quae Deus mundauit, tu communia ne dixeris. Hoc autem accidit ter, et rursus receptum est vas in coelum.
units.tr: After the angel who had spoken to Cornelius had gone away, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him. When he had told them everything, he sent them to Joppa. The next day, as they were on their journey and drawing near the city, Peter went up onto the roof of the house to pray, about the sixth hour. He was hungry and wanted something to eat, and while the meal was being prepared he fell into a trance. He saw heaven opened and a certain vessel descending to him, like a great sheet, bound at the four corners and lowered to the earth. In it were all the four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles and birds of the air. And a voice came to him: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." But Peter said, "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean." And the voice came to him again a second time: "What God has cleansed, do not call common." This happened three times, and then the vessel was taken back up into heaven.

units.la: Quemadmodum Deus in Iudaici populi electione singularem gratiam et bonitatem exercuit, quam passim Moses et prophetae praedicant: ita cum eundem repudiauit, adoptatis in illius locum gentibus, peculiare iustitiae suae et irae exemplum edidit: in cuius consideratione eo diligentius nos versari decet, quod generalem inde doctrinam Paulus deducit, ostendens, neminem Dei gratiam et bonitatem, quae in Christo offertur, impune contemptum iri, quando in naturalibus ramis detruncandis tanta iudicij seueritate Deus vsus fit. Rom. 11. Quia autem ea res Iudaeis dictu et creditu digna videri poterat, sic ut apostoli quoq; circa hanc aliquandiu dubij haesisse legantur, et ipsis gentibus non parua erat, ob antecedentem vitae conditionem, dubitandi occasio: illustre cumprimis illius initium esse oportuit. Deligitur ergo ex militari ordine Centurio Cornelius, ut diuinae bonitatis indulgentia gentia clarior eluceret. Idem ille per angelu coelitus missum de Petro ad se vocando admonetur: quo vnico argumento abunde patebat, diuina administratione omne istud negotium transfigi. Plenius tamen & euidentius hoc ipsum in sequentibus patebit, & ad eius rei demonstrationem non parum facit praesens hic locus, qui Cornelij per angelum admoniti fidelem obedientiam exponit, simulq; docet, vt Petrus quoq; coelesti visione admonitus fit, ne petenti Cornelio euangelizandi officium denegaret.
units.tr: Just as God, in choosing the Jewish people, showed singular grace and goodness, which Moses and the prophets proclaim everywhere, so when he rejected that people and adopted the Gentiles in their place, he displayed a remarkable example of his justice and his wrath. It is fitting that we dwell on this with greater care, because Paul draws a general teaching from it, showing that no one who spurns the grace and goodness of God offered in Christ will go unpunished, since God has used such severity of judgment in cutting off the natural branches (Rom. 11). Moreover, since this matter could seem worthy of being spoken of and believed by the Jews, and since the apostles too are read to have hesitated over it for some time, and since the Gentiles themselves had no small occasion for doubt because of their previous way of life, that beginning had to be notable above all. Therefore a centurion, Cornelius, is chosen from the military ranks, so that the kindness of God toward the Gentiles might shine more clearly. This same man is instructed by an angel sent from heaven to summon Peter to himself, and by this single argument it was abundantly clear that this whole affair was carried out by divine direction. Yet this will become clearer and more evident in what follows, and the present passage contributes not a little to demonstrating this matter. It sets out the faithful obedience of Cornelius, who was warned by an angel, and at the same time teaches that Peter too was admonished by a heavenly vision not to deny the office of preaching the gospel to Cornelius, who asked for it.

units.la: Est autem perquam diligens in Cornelij obedientia describenda Lucas, eo quod haec luculentum praebet de fide ipsius testimonium: quod euidentius erit & locupletius, si expendamus, quam multa ob-stare potuerint, quo minus angeli dictis fidem & obedientiam praestaret. Periculosum erat nouitatis in religione studium, maxime in eo homine, cuius erat cauere, ne qui in Syria nouarum rerum studio tumultuarentur. Nec aliquod in humanis praesidium apparebat, quo contra Rom. Imperatoris potentiam se defendi posse speraret. Adhaec suspectum esse poterat, quod apud coriarium monstrabatur, qui salutis & vitae doctor esse debebat. Quis enim e tali schola tantum magistrum expectaret? Quis item non suspectum haberet eum, qui tam ignobili loco quasi latitabat? At omnia haec vna fides superat, cuius obedientia iam pridem sese submiserat Cornelius. Et non immerito ijs exemplis praesens hoc adnumerari meretur, quae Paulus ad Hebr. cap. xi. recenset. Nostra vero institutioni seruit, ne vllis periculis nos a veritatis doctrina abstrahi patiamur, nec fidei causam propter vilem speciem vlla ex parte suspectam habeamus. Et Cornelium imitati, abfq; omni mora Dei mandata exequamur. Hic enim mox vocatis ad se duobus famulis, & milite religioso, illos Ioppen ablegat, vt Petrum accersant. Quo loco haud vulgaris fructus apparet, quem ex religiosa familia sua institutione Cornelius retulit. Habet enim nunc fidos famulos, quibus tanti momenti negotium tuto committere possit. Cuius rei exemplu in Abrahamo & famulo ipsius Moses proponit, Gen. 24. Atqui longe alia illorum fors est, qui familiam suam ita negligunt, vt domesticorum suorum institutionem nihil ad se pertinere putent. Quia enim illi Deo suum ius vendicare nolunt, infida fere illorum opera vtuntur, quos sua negligentia a religione alienos fecerunt. Sensit hoc Nero tyrannus, quem in ipso mortis articulo de suorum fide conquestum esse historici tradunt. Cur autem fidos experiretur, quos aduersus Deum & Christum eius impie armauerat? Debent ergo hinc vniuersalem doctrinam petere magistratus omnes, vt Dei cultibus & religioni suos assuefaciant. Nec enim fieri potest, vt magistratibus fides sint, quicunq; Deo fidem negare audent. Vidit hoc olim Constantius Magni Constantini pater, qui aula sua eijciendos putauit eos, qui ad ipsius mandatum dijs adoleuerant, nec quicquam fidelis operae se ab ijs sperare posse dixit, qui in Deum ingrati & cultus diuini proditores fuerant.
units.tr: Luke is very careful in describing the obedience of Cornelius, because it provides a clear testimony of his faith. That testimony will be more evident and fuller if we weigh how many things could have stood in the way of his giving faith and obedience to the angel's words. Eagerness for novelty in religion was dangerous, especially in a man whose duty it was to guard against anyone stirring up riots in Syria by a desire for change. Nor did any human protection appear by which he could hope to defend himself against the power of the Roman emperor. Moreover, he could be suspected because Peter was lodging with a tanner, when he ought to have been a teacher of salvation and life. For who would expect such a master from such a school? Who would not also regard with suspicion a man who lay hidden in so lowly a place? Yet faith alone overcomes all these things, and to this faith Cornelius had long since submitted his obedience. And not without reason this passage deserves to be counted among those examples which Paul recounts in Hebrews chapter 11. Our own instruction serves this end: that we should not allow ourselves to be drawn away from the teaching of truth by any dangers, nor regard the cause of faith with suspicion in any way because of a base appearance. Let us imitate Cornelius and carry out God's commands without any delay. For he at once calls two of his servants and a devout soldier to himself and sends them to Joppa to fetch Peter. Here appears no ordinary fruit which Cornelius gained from the religious upbringing of his household. For he now has trusted servants, to whom he can safely entrust a matter of such importance. Moses sets before us an example of this in Abraham and his servant (Gen. 24). But far different is the fate of those who so neglect their households that they think the instruction of their domestics is no concern of theirs. Because they are unwilling to claim their right for God, they generally use the services of those whom their own negligence has estranged from religion. Nero the tyrant felt this, of whom the historians report that, at the very point of death, he complained about the faithfulness of his own people. But why should he have tested those whom he had impiously armed against God and his Christ? Therefore all magistrates ought to learn from this a general lesson: to accustom their subjects to the worship of God and to religion. For those who dare to deny faith to God cannot be faithful to magistrates. Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, saw this long ago. He thought that those who had grown up in the worship of the gods, at his own command, should be expelled from his court, and he said that no faithful service could be expected from those who had been ungrateful to God and traitors to divine worship.

units.la: Praeterea non negligendum est, quod rursum militi, qui Cornelio adhaerere solebat, religionis laudem tribuit. Nam praeter id, quod hinc patet, quantum ad pietatem & salutem momenti afferat pio-rum conuersatio, docemur quoq; nullum vitae genus a religione alienum esse debere, quando ea in militia quoq; locum habet, quae multorum iudicio tunc demum nomine suo digna videtur, si religionis curam omnem abiecerit. Atqui Deum huius ducem felicissimum esse, scriptura docet. Huius auspicijs cum Syrorum ingenti manu Ioab congressus, praeclaram victoriam retulit. 2. Sam. 10. Illius o-pem Dauid cum Golia manum conferturus, inuocat. 1. Sam. 17. Eidem quoque omnes victorias & vniuersum militiae decus acceptum fert, cum per hunc manus suas ad praelium instrui fatetur. Psal. 18. & 144. Quid, quod Constantinus, oraculo admonitus, salutifera Crucis signum exercitibus suis praetulit? Sub hoc nimirum felicem belli euentum expertus, quam sub Romanis aquilis sperare potuisset. Et Theodosium in difficili bello contra Eugenium & Arbogastum, cum noctem totam in precibus transegisset, & oblata specie angelorum ad pugnam ipsum exhortantium confirmatus esset, postero die ventus adiutum victoriam retulisse legimus. Indignissimae ergo illorum voces sunt, qui vt Romanus ille leges inter armorum strepitus exaudiri posse negauit, ita abfq; religione bella gerere censent. Quam si suffuleris, illa a belluina rabie nihil different, nec aliquo honesto titulo defendi poterunt, imo contra omne ius & fas immani crudelitate grassabuntur. Docent haec simul, minime ferendam esse Anabaptistarum intemperiem, qui Christianum hominem arma gestare, nefas esse du-cunt: quando & nostri illi, & plures alij milites in euangelio religionis & fidei nemine commendan-tur. Et sane tam absurda est illorum sententia, vt potius dicendum sit, neminem arma digne gestare posse, nisi qui Christianus fuerit.
units.tr: Besides, we must not overlook the fact that once more Luke gives praise for religion to the soldier who used to attend Cornelius. For apart from what this shows, namely how much the godly way of life of believers contributes to piety and salvation, we are also taught that no way of life ought to be estranged from religion, since religion has its place even in military service, which in the judgment of many is then at last worthy of its name when it has cast off all care for religion. Yet Scripture teaches that God is the most fortunate leader of such men. Under his auspices Joab, meeting the great army of the Syrians, won a splendid victory (2 Sam. 10). David, about to engage Goliath in battle, calls upon his help (1 Sam. 17). To him also he ascribes all his victories and the whole glory of his warfare, when he confesses that by him his hands are trained for battle (Ps. 18 and 144). What of the fact that Constantine, warned by an oracle, carried the saving sign of the Cross before his armies? Surely under this sign he experienced a more fortunate outcome of war than he could have hoped for under the Roman eagles. And we read that Theodosius, in a difficult war against Eugenius and Arbogastes, spent the whole night in prayer, and when he had been strengthened by the appearance of angels urging him on to battle, he won the victory the next day, the wind being in his favour. Therefore the most unworthy are the words of those who, like that Roman who denied that laws could be heard amid the clash of arms, think that wars should be waged without religion. If you remove religion, such wars differ in nothing from the rage of beasts, and they cannot be defended by any honourable title; rather, they will rage with monstrous cruelty against all right and justice. These same points teach that the wantonness of the Anabaptists is in no way to be tolerated, they who hold that it is wrong for a Christian man to bear arms, since in the gospel neither that centurion nor many other soldiers are commended for any lack of religion or faith. Indeed their opinion is so absurd that it should rather be said that no one can bear arms worthily unless he is a Christian.

units.la: Transeamus vero ad Petrum apostolum, quem peculiari visione Deus instruit, ne communi Iudaeorum errore deceptus, Cornelij legatos reijceret. Nec dissimile ab eo est, quod hic fit, quod supra inter Saulum & Ananiam accidisse audiuimus. Nam vt illic, ita hic quoque primò quidem de Petro accersendo Cornelius admonetur: deinde autem Petrus quoq; suae vocationis certus fit, ne pietatis officium tam Christo quàm Cornelio deneget. Est hoc illustre & praeclarum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quae homines saluos fieri & in veritatis cognitionem peruenire cupit. Praestat vero singulas visionis huius circumstantias excutere, vt plenior eluceat eorum cognitio, quae ad communem nostrae salutis causam faciunt.
units.tr: But let us pass on to the apostle Peter, whom God instructed by a special vision, so that, deceived by the common error of the Jews, he would not reject the messengers of Cornelius. What happens here is not unlike what we heard happened above between Saul and Ananias. For here, as there, Cornelius is first warned about summoning Peter, and then Peter too is made certain of his calling, so that he will not deny Christ or Cornelius the duty of godliness. This is an illustrious and remarkable proof of divine goodness, which desires that men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. It is worth examining each circumstance of this vision, so that the understanding of those things which pertain to the common cause of our salvation may shine more fully.

units.la: Primus hic locus Petro debetur, quem circiter sextam diei horam, ieiunum adhuc, in superiorem domus partem ad orandum ascendisse dicitur, dum interea prandium illi esurienti pararetur. Certas enim precationis horas antiquitus constitutas fuisse, supra Cap. 3. dictum est. Nam licet precum effectus nec loco nec tempori alligetur, in iis tamen opportunitatem obseruare oportet, & certa precibus tempora constitui necesse est, ne aliorum negotiorum occupationibus distracti, rem omnium maximè necessariam negligamus. Admonet simul Petri exemplum, preces vt secessum, ita sobrietatem exigere, ne ventris studio & crapula illarum deuotio extinguatur. Quae causa est, quod scriptura cum veteris tum noui Testamenti, frequenter preces cum ieiunijs coniungunt. Arguit hoc hypocritarum ineptias, qui vt preces ad ostentationem instituunt, ita ieiunijs absolute meriti laudem transcribunt, cum non alius illorum vsus sit, quàm vt carni subigendae seruiant, ne illa insolentior & ferocior facta, tam preces quàm reliqua verae pietatis exercitia extinguat & interturbet. Vide Mat. 9. Isa. 58. cap.
units.tr: This first place is due to Peter, who is said to have gone up to the upper part of the house to pray, about the sixth hour of the day, while he was still fasting and while dinner was being prepared for him in his hunger. That certain hours of prayer were appointed in ancient times has been said above, in Cap. 3. For although the effect of prayer is bound neither to place nor to time, it is right to observe opportunity in prayer, and it is necessary to set fixed times for it, lest, distracted by the cares of other business, we neglect what is most necessary of all. Peter's example also shows that prayer requires both retirement and sobriety, lest devotion be extinguished by attention to the belly and by drunkenness. This is why the Scriptures of both the Old and New Testament frequently join prayers with fasts. It also exposes the folly of hypocrites, who undertake prayers for show and claim the praise of merit for their fasting, when its only use is to subdue the flesh, lest the flesh, grown more insolent and fierce, extinguish and disturb prayer and the other exercises of true piety. See Matt. 9. and Isa. 58.

units.la: Deinde ecstasis super illu irruisse scribitur, vt intelligamus, nihil hic naturali visui esse tribuendum, nec organicorum sensuum defectu Petrum fuisse ludificatum. Nam extra se raptus mentis oculis ista subijci sensit, quod fieri necesse erat. Quia enim animalis homo (sicuti Paulus admonet) non percipit ea quae sunt spiritus Dei, diuino spiritus raptu mentem supra mundum euehi oportet, vt caelestis regni mysteria percipiat. Hoc ipsum Paulus suo exemplo docet, quando de raptu suo in tertium caelum scribens, ingenuè fatetur, se ignorare num in corpore vel extra corpus existenti illud contigerit. 2. Corinth. 12. Et firmior certiorq; rei huius fides est, quod non corporeis sensibus, qui vt plurimum falli consueuerunt, ista obiecta fuere.
units.tr: Next it is written that an ecstasy fell upon him, so that we may understand that nothing here is to be attributed to natural sight, and that Peter was not deceived by a failure of the bodily senses. For, carried out of himself, he felt that these things were placed before the eyes of his mind, as had to happen. For since the natural man (as Paul warns) does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, the mind must be lifted above the world by a divine rapture of the Spirit, so that it may perceive the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom. Paul teaches this very thing by his own example, when, writing of his rapture into the third heaven, he frankly confesses that he does not know whether it happened to him while in the body or outside the body. 2 Cor. 12. And the faith in this matter is firmer and more certain because these objects were presented not to the bodily senses, which are wont for the most part to deceive.

units.la: Subijcitur his diligens admodum visionis descriptio. Videt aperiri caelos, demitti vas ingens instar magni lintei siue veli: quod à quatuor angulis alligatum in terram descendit. Apparuerunt in eodem omnis generis animalia, tam quadrupedia, quàm reptilia & volatilia, & ea in primis, quae in lege immunda & illicita dicebantur, de quibus videre est, Leuit. 11. Deut. 14. Accedit vox, quae Petrum surgere, animalia omnis generis macta re, & vesci iubet. Ante omnia vero visionis scopum observare conuenit, quem non alium fuisse ex sequentibus patet, quàm quòd docere voluit Deus, sublatum esse omne illud discrimen, quod hucusque per legis ceremonias inter Iudaeos & gentes positum videbatur, nec quicquam obstare, quo minus gentes quoq; in euangelij & salutis per Christum partem communionem admittantur.
units.tr: A very careful description of the vision follows. He sees the heavens opened, and a great vessel like a large linen sheet or sail let down, bound at its four corners and descending to the earth. In it appeared animals of every kind, quadrupeds, reptiles and birds alike, and especially those which in the law were called unclean and unlawful, as may be seen in Lev. 11. and Deut. 14. A voice is added, bidding Peter rise, kill animals of every kind, and eat. Above all, however, it is fitting to observe the aim of the vision, which, as is clear from what follows, was none other than to teach that all the distinction which had hitherto seemed to be set between Jews and Gentiles by the ceremonies of the law had been removed, and that nothing stood in the way of Gentiles also being admitted to a share in the gospel and in salvation through Christ.

units.la: Mirificè autem praesenti negotio visionem hanc seruire patebit, si singula quae huic insunt mysteria penitius inspiciantur. Nam & Petri animum fluctuantem confirmat, & ecclesiae totius conditionem pulchrè adumbrat. Esuriuisse Petrum eo tempore dictum est. Atqui non tam corpore quàm animo illum esuriuisse constat, qui totus desyderio prouehendi regni Christi & propagandae ecclesiae flagrabat. Incidebant autem quae animum miserè excruciare poterant. Iudaei enim, quibus salus cumprimis deberi videbatur, illa indignis modis abijciebant, imò persequebantur. Gentes vero salutis communione indignas putabat: cum Christum olim praecepisse sciret, ne in viam gentium abirent, sed potius perditis Israelis ouibus euangelium praedicarent: meminisset item, ab ipso Christo gentes canum loco habitas fuisse, quando Cananaea dixit: Non decet panem filiorum proijcere canibus. Matth. 15. Licet enim postea Christus euangelium omni creaturae praedicare iussisset, de ijs tamen gentibus solummodo hoc intelligi debere videbatur, quae reliquis gentilitijs cultibus ad Iudaismum transfirent, & circuncisae legis iustificationibus vterentur. Quid ergo hic aliud faceret Petrus, quàm dubijs animi aestuantis cogitationibus torqueretur? Nec enim videbat, ex quibus ecclesia illa Christo colligi posset, in qua illum regnaturum toties audiuerat. Hic vero commodùm succurrit Deus, & colligenda ecclesia rationem omnem explicat, imò ecclesiam typum euidentissimum proponit. E cœlis enim, quos insolito modo diduci & aperiri videbat, ingens linteum, quatuor angulis alligatum, demittitur, quod ecclesiæ typum gerebat. Ita vero docebatur Petrus, non ex legis iustificationibus, sed è cœlis expectandam esse ecclesiam, quæ noua Hierusalem dici consueuit. Apoc. 21. Nisi enim quis renatus fuerit è supernùs, non videbit regnum Dei. Iohan. 3. At quatuor angulis alligatum linteum, significabat ex toto terrarum orbe ecclesiam hanc colligendam fore. Insunt animalia, quæ lex immunda esse pronunciabat, ea autem Petrus mactare, & illorum esu famem sedare iubetur. Admonebat hoc gentes etiam, quæ hucusque pro immundis & à republica populi Dei alienis habitæ erant, spirituali gladio, id est, euangelij prædicatione (nullo habito legis & ceremoniarum Iudaicarum respectu) iugulandas & mortificandas, ficq; in Christi & ecclesiæ communionem recipiendas esse. Iam enim aduenisse correctionis tempus, quo velum templi scissum, & per Christum maceria diruta est, qui vtrunque populum in vnam fidem & eiusdem regni hereditatem coniunxerit. Ephes. 2. Atque hunc visionis sensum fuisse, rei exitus Paulo postea docebit.
units.tr: It will become clear how greatly this vision serves the present business if the individual mysteries contained in it are examined more closely. For it both strengthens Peter's wavering mind and beautifully shadows forth the condition of the whole Church. It was said that Peter was hungry at that time. Yet it is evident that he was hungry not so much in body as in mind, he who burned entirely with desire to advance the kingdom of Christ and to spread the Church. And there came into his thoughts things that could miserably torment his spirit. For the Jews, to whom salvation seemed chiefly owed, were rejecting it in unworthy ways, indeed persecuting it. The Gentiles, however, he thought unworthy of a share in salvation, since he knew that Christ had once commanded that they should not go the way of the Gentiles but rather preach the gospel to the lost sheep of Israel. He also remembered that Christ himself had counted the Gentiles as dogs, when he said to the Canaanite woman: It is not fitting to throw the children's bread to dogs. Matt. 15. For although Christ afterwards ordered the gospel to be preached to every creature, it seemed that this ought to be understood only of those Gentiles who, abandoning their other heathen cults, passed over to Judaism and used the justifications of the circumcised law. What else, then, was Peter doing here but being tormented by the doubtful thoughts of a restless mind? For he did not see from what people that Church could be gathered to Christ, in which he had so often heard that Christ would reign. But here God comes to the rescue at the right moment, explains the whole reasoning for gathering the Church, and indeed sets forth the Church as a most evident type. For from heaven, which he saw opened and parted in an unusual way, a great sheet bound at four corners is let down, which bore the image of the Church. Peter was thus taught that the Church, which is commonly called the new Jerusalem, is to be looked for not from the justifications of the law but from heaven. Rev. 21. For unless a man is born from above, he will not see the kingdom of God. John 3. And the sheet bound at four corners signified that this Church was to be gathered from the whole orb of the earth. Among the animals contained in it are those which the law pronounced unclean, and Peter is ordered to kill them and to satisfy his hunger by eating them. This admonished that the Gentiles too, who hitherto had been regarded as unclean and alien to the commonwealth of God's people, were to be slain and mortified with the spiritual sword, that is, by the preaching of the gospel, with no regard for the law and Jewish ceremonies, and so were to be received into communion with Christ and the Church. For the time of correction had now arrived, in which the veil of the temple was torn and the wall was broken down through Christ, who joined both peoples into one faith and into the inheritance of the same kingdom. Eph. 2. And that this was the meaning of the vision, the outcome of the event will show later, when Paul teaches it.

units.la: Caeterum nondum intelligit domini mentem Petrus, sed nimia legis obseruantia adhuc detentus, Dei præceptum tanquam impium abominatus, respondet: Nequaquam domine, quia nunquam commedi quicquam commune vel immundum. Mox vero graui sententia illius iudicium confutat dominus, dicens: Quae dominus mundauit, tu communia ne dixeris. Quae sententia præsenti quidem negotio fecit, & nec cibos, qui lege interdicti fuerant, nec gentiles homines, qui per hos figurabantur, posthac pro immundis habendos esse docet: simul vero generalem doctrinam continet, qua nihil ex nostro arbitrio aduersus Dei iudicium & decretum nos statuere debere admonemur. Et in hanc sententiam peccant, quicunque illicitum & profanum ducunt, quod Deus nobis licitum & sanctum esse voluit. Confutantur ergo hic, qui post abrogatam legem nouam inducunt ciborum discrimina, cum omnes cibos Dei verbo sanctificatos esse, nec per ea quæ os ingrediuntur, hominem pollui posse constet. 1. Timoth. 4. Matth. 15. Nec illorum cauillum audimus, qui carnis nostræ cohercendæ gratia hæc constituta esse dicunt, non quòd cibos per se immundos censeant. Si enim hæc illis mens est, cur conscientijs eo præcepto laqueum ponunt? Cur certis diebus abstinentiam illam astringunt? Cur pauperes maximè grauant, quos alioqui plus satis coherceri constat assiduis laboribus & inopia? Cur opulentioribus permittunt, vt illi interea piscibus, longè petitis edulijs & aromaticis cibis, ad excitandam carnis ferociam maximè idoneis, saginentur? Cur vini vsum concedunt, in quo luxus est, vt Apostolus ait, & quo nihil est ad excitandam carnis libidinem efficacius? Confutantur item, qui matrimonio abstinere docent, quasi hoc ad regnum Dei tendentibus impedimento sit, cum illud diuinitus institutum, & proinde licitum sanctumq;, imò ad vitam sanctè transigendam, necessarium esse constet. Nec temere duos hosce articulos dæmoniorum doctrinis Paulus adnumeravit. 1. Timoth. 4. Nam plus quàm diabolica audacia est, illud pleno ore damnare, quod Deus sanctum esse voluit. Rursum vero eadem illorum ratio est, qui quod diuinis legibus prohibitum est, licitum esse docent, vel in commissis contra Dei legem sceleribus, pecunia accepta, dispensare audent. Vtrunque vero in Papatu tam vulgare est, vt ex vna hac nota Antichristum agnoscere possis, cui Daniel illud tribuit, quòd leges & tempora mutaturus sit. Discamus ergo à Dei ore pendere, nec vllas hominum constitutiones diuinis contrarias admittere.
units.tr: Meanwhile Peter does not yet understand the mind of the Lord, but, still held back by excessive observance of the law, he abhors God's command as impious and replies: "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean." Soon, however, the Lord refutes his judgment with a weighty saying: "What the Lord has cleansed, do not call common." This saying did what the present matter required, and it teaches that neither the foods which the law had forbidden nor the Gentile men who were figured by them are to be regarded as unclean from now on. At the same time it contains a general doctrine, by which we are warned that we ought to decide nothing by our own judgment against God's judgment and decree. And those sin in this way who count unlawful and profane what God has willed to be lawful and holy for us. Therefore those are refuted here who, after the law has been abrogated, introduce distinctions among foods, since it is established that all foods are sanctified by the word of God, and that a man cannot be defiled by what enters his mouth. 1 Tim. 4. Matt. 15. Nor do we listen to the quibbles of those who say that these rules were established to restrain the flesh, not because they think foods are unclean in themselves. For if this is their mind, why do they set a snare for consciences with that precept? Why do they impose that abstinence on fixed days? Why do they especially burden the poor, who by constant labour and want are already restrained more than enough? Why do they allow the richer to be stuffed meanwhile with fish, delicacies brought from afar, and aromatic foods most suited to rousing the fierceness of the flesh? Why do they permit the use of wine, in which there is luxury, as the Apostle says, and than which nothing is more effective for stirring up lust? They are likewise refuted who teach abstinence from marriage, as if it were an impediment to those tending toward the kingdom of God, when it is established that marriage was divinely instituted, and therefore lawful and holy, and indeed necessary for living a holy life. Nor did Paul rashly number these two articles among the doctrines of demons. 1 Tim. 4. For it is more than diabolical audacity to condemn with full mouth what God has willed to be holy. Again, the reasoning is the same for those who teach that what is forbidden by divine laws is lawful, or who dare to dispense, for money received, with crimes committed against God's law. Both practices are so common in the Papacy that from this one mark alone you can recognise the Antichrist, to whom Daniel ascribed the intention to change laws and times. Let us therefore learn to hang upon God's mouth, and to admit no human constitutions contrary to divine ones.

units.la: Porrò adijcit Lucas, hæc tertiò facta, & tandem linteum illud in cælum receptum esse, vnde de scenderat. Ter vero ista repeti voluit Deus, vt maiorem & certiorem Petro fidem faceret. Et in cælum recipitur linteum hoc vnà cum animalibus, tum vt sciret Petrus, diuina prouidentia negotium hoc omne administrari: tum vt constaret, ijs quoq; in cælis locum paratum esse, qui antehac propter legis discrimen exclusi videbantur. Est q; hæc generalis consolatio. Cælos enim, quos Adami lapsus nobis clauserat, Christi meritum denuo patefecit, & in illis locum nobis paruit, vt sæpe alias dictum est. Illum ergo vera fide amplexi, mortificemus spiritus gladio veterem hominem, vt è supernis renati, eodem transferamur in consortium saluatoris & domini nostri Iesu Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke then adds that these things happened three times, and that at last the sheet was taken back up into heaven from where it had been let down. God wished this to be repeated three times so that he might make Peter's faith firmer and more certain. The sheet with the animals is taken up into heaven, first so that Peter would know that the whole matter was being managed by divine providence, and second so that it would be plain that a place in the heavens was prepared also for those who had seemed shut out until then because of the distinction of the law. This is also a general consolation. For Christ's merit has opened again the heavens that Adam's fall had closed to us, and has made a place for us in them, as has often been said elsewhere. Let us therefore embrace him with true faith, and with the sword of the Spirit put to death the old man, so that, reborn from above, we may be carried over into the fellowship of our Saviour and Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Á 2 hanc quoq; Paulus recensendam esse putauerit. 1. Tim. 3. Arguitur igitur Petri exemplo illorum morositas, qui vt authoritatem suam satis tueantur, omnibus sese difficiles praebet, nec vllum amicae familiaritatis officium vel peregrinis vel domesticis praebent. Quos si non Petri exemplum, certe Christi authoritas mouere debebat, quem tunc quoq; amicè quosuis excepisse Marcus scribit, quando prae populi irruentis importunitate, ne cibum quidem capere poterat. Marc. cap. 6.
units.tr: Paul also thought this hospitality worth recounting. 1 Tim. 3. Peter's example therefore rebukes those who are so surly that, in order to guard their authority well enough, they make themselves hard to approach for everyone, and offer no office of friendly familiarity either to strangers or to members of their household. If Peter's example did not move them, certainly the authority of Christ ought to, for Mark writes that he too once received anyone kindly, even when, because of the crowd's pressing importunity, he could not even take food. Mark ch. 6.

units.la: Porrò his primum Cornelij & Petri congressum Lucas describit. Et de Cornelio quidem duo dicit. Primum est, quòd conuocatis cognatis, affinibus & omnibus aliis, qui ipsi aliquo necessitudinis gradu coniuncti erant, Petri aduentum expectarit. Exprimunt haec vera fidei ingenium. Quia enim haec vni Dei verbo nititur, illud etiam anxiè quaerit & expectat. Rursum vero, quia & diuinae gloriae studio & proximi charitate ardet, salutem multis quoq; aliis communicare cupit. Vtrunque Cornelius praestat, & quidem non sine periculo. Periculosam enim fuisse apud Romanos religionis mutationem, iam saepe diximus. Non potuit ergo non periculosissimum esse, multos illius testes adhibere. At omnem periculi metum fide superari, tum infinita alia exempla, tum scripturae passim indicant. Imitemur vero studium hoc, ne dum nobis tantum consulimus, Dei gloriam prodamus, & illorum salutem negligamus, qui iuxta naturae leges nobis commendatissimi esse debent. Sed alterum quoq; Cornelius addit. Nam viso Petro apostolo, mox in illius occursum effunditur, ad ingredientis pedes procidit, illum venerabundus adorat. Sunt haec religiosi animi & magnificè de Dei verbo eiusq; ministro sentientis indicia. Interim nimius est hac in re Cornelius, & immodica veneratione non leuiter peccat, dum (vt ex Petri verbis colligi potest) aliquid plus quàm humanum Christi ministro tribuit. Solet id plerunque fieri, quando inconsultum nostrae rationis zelum in ministrorum Dei veneratione adhibemus. Nec aliunde superstitiosus ille diuorum cultus, peregrinationes religionis ergò suscepta, reliquiarum deosculationes & infinita alia eius generis exorta sunt, quàm quòd homines immodico & inconsulto religionis zelo seducti, diuinitatis aliquid ijs inesse putauerunt, quibus Deus aliquando ad suae gloriae & aliorum salutis propagationem vsus est. Prodest ergo in ipsum Deum mentis oculos attollere, ne dum nimium religiosi haberi volumus, Deum debito cultu fraudemus.
units.tr: Next, Luke describes first the meeting of Cornelius and Peter. And he says two things about Cornelius. The first is that, having called together his relatives, kinsmen and all the others who were joined to him by some degree of kinship, he waited for Peter's arrival. These things express the nature of true faith. For since faith rests on the word of God alone, it also seeks and awaits that word anxiously. Again, since it burns both with zeal for God's glory and with love for its neighbour, it also wishes to share salvation with many others. Cornelius shows both, and indeed not without danger. For we have often said already that a change of religion was dangerous among the Romans. It could not therefore but be most dangerous to call many as its witnesses. Yet that every fear of danger is overcome by faith is shown both by countless other examples and by Scripture everywhere. Let us imitate this zeal, so that while we look only to ourselves we do not betray God's glory, and neglect the salvation of those who, by the laws of nature, ought to be most commended to us. But Cornelius adds a second thing. For as soon as he sees the apostle Peter, he rushes out to meet him, falls at the feet of the one who enters, and worships him with reverence. These are signs of a devout mind that thinks highly of God's word and of its minister. Yet in this matter Cornelius goes too far, and by excessive reverence he does not sin lightly, since (as can be gathered from Peter's words) he attributes to Christ's minister something more than human. This usually happens when we show an ill-considered zeal in venerating God's ministers. Indeed, that superstitious worship of saints, pilgrimages undertaken for the sake of religion, kissing of relics and countless other things of that kind arose from nothing else than this: people, led astray by immoderate and ill-considered zeal for religion, thought that some divinity dwelt in those whom God at some time used to propagate his glory and the salvation of others. It is therefore useful to lift the eyes of the mind to God himself, so that, while we want to be thought overly devout, we do not defraud God of the worship that is due to him.

units.la: Facit huc Petri apostoli responsum, qui Cornelij errorem non dissimulat, sed amicè reprehendit, dicens: Surge, nam & ego ipse homo sum. Quasi dicat: Video te augustius, quàm par sit, deme sentire. Et quia diuinum quiddam mihi inesse putas, tanto honore dignum iudicauisti. Sed longè falleris. Nam licet Christi Iesu apostolum me diuina gratia fecerit, quoad tamen meam essentiam & naturam, nihil quàm homo sum, mortalis nimirum, fragilis, caducus, peccator, qui & ipse gratia Dei & Christi merito opus habeo. Define ergo diuinos honores mihi impendere, sed eos in illum transfer, cuius tam ego quàm tu ministri sumus. Haec verborum Petri sententia est, quam etiam Paulus, cum Lystrensies similí errore deceptos videret, expressit, clamans: Viri, cur ista facitis? Nos quoq; ijsdem quibus vos obnoxij malis sumus homines, &c. Actor. 14. Ita vero nimios honores à sese repulerunt apostoli, quos vel eo praetextu excusare poterant, quòd ad euangelij authoritatem facerent. Sed indignum putarunt, si quis hominum zelo abuteretur, & dolo malo doctrinae authoritatem conciliare studeret. Docent autem haec, immodicum & illicitum esse omnem eum cultum, qui sub aliqua diuinitatis opinione creaturis impenditur. Praescribit quidem & Paulus ciuilitatis officia, iubetq; vt honore nos inuicem praeueniamus. Rom. 12. Impia autem est diuini cultus prophanatio, si quod vni Deo debetur, in creaturas transferamus. Simul vero Romani Pontificis immanis fastus arguitur, qui Petri praetextu ecclesiae primatum sibi vendicans, non modò quosuis ad se venientes coram se prosterni patitur, verumetiam Reges & Imperatores ad pedum suorum oscula cogit, nec illorum colla impuris pedibus calcare veretur: qua re non fidelem Christi ministrum, sed Caligulam & Diocletianum portenta humani generis, imitatur. Quod scelus eo grauius est & intolerabilius, quòd eo praetextu admittitur, quasi diuini aliquid homini flagitiosissimo infit. Caeterum omisso Christi & salutis nostrae aduersatio, Dei gratiam agnoscamus, qua gentes adoptare dignatus est, & officij memores illi seruiamus, qui nos regni sui haeredes fecit, coheredes autem Iesu Christi filij sui & saluatoris nostri: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen. Et colloquens cum illo, introiuit: & inuenit multos qui conuenerat, dixitq; illis: Vos scitis, quòd nefas sit viro Iudaeo adhaerere alienigenae, vel ad eum accedere. At mihi Deus ostendit, nullum hominem communem vel immundum dicendum esse. Quare absq; contradictione veni accersitus. Rogo igitur, quam ob causam accersiuistis me? Et Cornelius ait: Quarto ab hinc die vsque ad hanc horam sedebam ieiunus, & hora nona precabar domi meae: & ecce vir stetit coram me in veste splendida, qui dixit: Cornely, exaudita est precatio tua, & eleemosynę tuae ascendè rūt in memoriam coram Deo. Itaq; mitte Ioppen, & accerse Simonem, qui cognominatur Petrus. Hic hospitiū habet in domo Simonis coriarij. Is simul atq; venerit loquetur tibi. Confestim ergo misi ad te, & tu bene fecisti qui aduenisti. Nunc ergo nos omnes adsumus coram Deo, ad audienda omnia, quae tibi à Deo commissa sunt.
units.tr: To this belongs the reply of the apostle Peter, who does not conceal Cornelius's error but rebukes him kindly, saying: "Stand up, for I too am a man myself." As if he were saying: "I see that you think of me more highly than is fitting; and because you think there is something divine in me, you have judged me worthy of such honour. But you are greatly mistaken. For although divine grace has made me an apostle of Jesus Christ, yet as far as my essence and nature are concerned I am nothing but a man, mortal, frail, perishable, a sinner, who myself also need the grace of God and the merit of Christ. Cease therefore to pay divine honours to me, but transfer them to him whose ministers both I and you are." This is the sense of Peter's words, which Paul also expressed when he saw the Lystrans deceived by a similar error, crying out: "Men, why are you doing these things? We too are men subject to the same evils as you, etc." Acts 14. Thus the apostles repelled from themselves such excessive honours, which they could have excused on the pretext that they served the authority of the gospel. But they thought it unworthy if anyone should abuse human zeal and, with bad intent, seek to win authority for a doctrine by such means. These passages teach that every worship which is paid to creatures under some notion of divinity is excessive and unlawful. Paul certainly prescribes the duties of civility too, and bids us to go before one another in honour. Rom. 12. But it is an impious profanation of divine worship if we transfer to creatures what is owed to the one God alone. At the same time, the monstrous pride of the Roman Pontiff is exposed, who, claiming for himself the primacy of the Church under the pretext of Peter, not only allows whoever comes to him to prostrate himself before him, but even compels kings and emperors to kiss his feet, nor does he scruple to tread upon their necks with his unclean feet. In this he imitates not a faithful minister of Christ, but Caligula and Diocletian, monsters of the human race. This wickedness is all the more grave and intolerable because it is permitted under the pretext that something divine is inherent in a most scandalous man. But, setting aside the opposition to Christ and to our salvation, let us acknowledge the grace of God, by which he has deigned to adopt the Gentiles, and, mindful of our duty, let us serve him who has made us heirs of his kingdom, and co-heirs with Jesus Christ his Son and our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. And talking with him, he went in and found many who had come together, and said to them: "You know that it is unlawful for a Jewish man to associate with, or go to, a foreigner. But God has shown me that no man should be called common or unclean. Therefore I came without objection when sent for. I ask, then, why you have sent for me?" And Cornelius said: "Four days ago, until this hour, I was sitting fasting, and at the ninth hour I was praying in my house; and behold, a man stood before me in shining clothing, and said: 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your alms have come up in remembrance before God. So send to Joppa and call Simon, who is surnamed Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon the tanner; when he comes he will speak to you.' So I sent to you at once, and you did well to come. Now therefore we are all present before God, to hear all the things that have been committed to you by God."

units.la: Quoniam gentium vocatio Iudaeis, quos legalium ceremoniarum fiducia inflabat, nō absurdâ modo, verumetiam iniqua videbatur: spiritus sanctus in Cornelij couerfione (qui primus absque Circuncisione & reliquis ceremonijs in ecclesiae communionem receptus est) singulari diligentia versatur: vt omnibus pateat, nihil hic humano, sed diuino consilio omnia transacta esse. Praecipuus vero huius historiae vsus est, vt & Iudaeorum insolens gloriatio reprimatur, & omnium nostrum animi (qui ex gentibus oriundi sumus) in fide confirmentur, quando salutis praedicationem non minus ad nos, quam ad Iudaeos pertinere cernimus. Cuius rei euidens cumprimis & infallibile argumentum est, quòd diuino iussu & ductu Petrum Caesareā venisse audiuimus, vt Cornelio salutem in Christo praedicaret. Idem vero in praesenti plenius patebit, si primum Petri colloquium cum Cornelio excutiamus: in quo ille quidem suum ad gentes ingressum excusat, ille vero sui instituti, quo Petrum ad sese euocauerat, rationem reddit.
units.tr: Since the calling of the Gentiles seemed not only absurd but also unjust to the Jews, who were puffed up by their confidence in the legal ceremonies, the Holy Spirit dwells with singular care on the conversion of Cornelius, who was the first to be received into the communion of the Church without circumcision and the other ceremonies, so that it might be plain to all that nothing here was done by human counsel but everything by divine. The chief use of this history is that the insolent boasting of the Jews may be restrained, and that the minds of all of us who are descended from the Gentiles may be confirmed in faith, when we see that the preaching of salvation pertains to us no less than to the Jews. Of this the clearest and above all infallible proof is that we hear Peter came to Caesarea by divine command and guidance, to preach salvation in Christ to Cornelius. This will appear more fully now if we examine first Peter's conversation with Cornelius, in which the one indeed excuses his entrance among the Gentiles, and the other gives the reason for his purpose, in calling Peter to himself.

units.la: Voluit autem ab excusatione dicendi initiū facere Petrus, partim quidem propter Iudaeos fratres, quos illi ex Ioppe proficiscenti itineris comites fuisse audiuimus, ne videlicet illi nouo & inso-lito facto offenderentur: partim vero propter Cornelij domesticos & cognatos, qui gentiles erant, ne illi ipsum leuitatis nomine suspectum haberent, si veterem sui populi consuetudinem temere & absq; ratione transgrederetur. Fatetur ergo Iudaeorum consuetudinem, ne huius temere oblitus esse videatur: eidem vero Dei voluntatem siue oraculum opponit, cuius authoritas vel sola ad facti huius excusationem sufficere poterat. Nobis vero de vtroq; singulatim dicendum est.
units.tr: Peter chose to begin his speech with an excuse, partly on account of the Jewish brothers who, we have heard, accompanied him on his journey from Joppa, lest they be offended by this new and unusual deed; and partly on account of Cornelius' household and relatives, who were Gentiles, lest they regard him as fickle if he rashly departed from the old custom of his people without good reason. He therefore admits the custom of the Jews, so that he may not seem to have rashly forgotten it; yet he sets against it the will or oracle of God, whose authority alone was enough to excuse this deed. We must now speak of each of these separately.

units.la: De Iudaeorū consuetudine loquens, ipsos auditores testes facit. Vos scitis (inquit) quòd nefas sit viro Iudaeo adhaerere alienigenae, aut ad eum accedere. Quamuis autem nulla Dei lex extet, quae illud diserte prohibeat, ex eo tamen consuetudo haec originem duxisse videtur, quòd gentilium, & Chanaanaeorum in primis, coniugia & foedera Deus prohibuit, ne illorum commercijs seducti, à Deo & vero illius cultu deficerent. Deut. 7. Iof. 23. Et credibile est, multos sub eorum commerciorum praetextu, quae communis necessitatis ergo inter homines exercentur, ethnicis familiariter conuersatos, & sic à Dei cultu alienos factos fuisse. Quae causa fuit, vt arctiores huius legis terminos constituerent pij sancti, patres, qui omnem à Deo deficiendi occasionem sublatam volebant. Hinc vero generale & perpetuum praeceptum sumi debet, vt qui Dei cultores dici & haberi volunt, eorum commercia detestent, quos vel falsa religione vel manifesta morum impietate corruptos & à Deo alienos esse noverunt. Quia enim natura ad malum proclives sumus, facilè alienae impietatis consuetudine inficimur: & quotidiana exempla docent, quantum ea in re malorum conuersatio & prava colloquia possint, quibus bonos quoq; mores corrumpi. Paulus author est. 1. Corinth. 15. capite. Accedit hūs, quòd poenarum quoque consortes fiunt, quicunque impiorum conuersatione delectantur: cuius rei exemplum in Loto scriptura proponit, qui Sodomarum incola factus, cum ijsdem primò quidem funesto bello implicatur, deinde verò omnium fortunarum simul & coniugis iacturam facit, & tandem in filiabus experitur, quantum illis impiae gentis commercium nocuerit, cum incestum patris concubitum tam subdolis artibus venentur. Non temere ergo Paulus, absurdum esse docet, ut cum infidelibus iugum trahant, qui Christo consecrati sunt. 2. Corinth. 6. Et Christus Dominus de Antichristi & impia Babylonis supplicio loquens, suos serio admonet, ut inde exeant, ne ijsdem poenis ipsi quoque involuantur. Apoc. 18. Quod si vero insidiosa pijs est vulgaris impiorum conuersatio, maiori utique diligentia falsi doctores cauendi erunt, qui animis hominum sese mirifice insinuare, & incautis lethiferum falsae doctrinae venenum inspirare solent. Vide de his Matth. 7. & 15. capite. 2. Iohan. 1. &c.
units.tr: Speaking of the custom of the Jews, he makes his hearers themselves witnesses: "You know," he says, "that it is unlawful for a Jewish man to associate with, or go near, a foreigner." Although no law of God exists that expressly forbids this, the custom seems nonetheless to have arisen from this: God forbade marriages and alliances with the Gentiles, and the Canaanites above all, lest, led astray by their dealings, they should fall away from God and his true worship (Deut. 7; Josh. 23). And it is credible that many, under the pretext of those dealings which are carried on among men for the sake of common necessity, became familiar with the heathen and so were estranged from the worship of God. This was the reason why the godly holy fathers set narrower limits to this law, since they wished every occasion of falling away from God removed. From this, however, a general and perpetual precept ought to be drawn: that those who wish to be called and regarded as worshippers of God should shun the company of those whom they know to be corrupted either by false religion or by manifest wickedness of life and estranged from God. For since we are by nature prone to evil, we are easily infected by the habit of another's impiety; and daily examples teach how much the company of the wicked and corrupt conversation can do, by which even good morals are corrupted. Paul is the authority (1 Cor. 15). Moreover, those who delight in the company of the impious also become sharers in their punishments. Scripture sets before us an example of this in Lot, who, becoming a dweller among the Sodomites, is first entangled with them in a disastrous war, then suffers the loss of all his goods together with his wife, and at last learns in his daughters how greatly the intercourse with that impious people harmed him, when they ensnared their father with incest by such deceitful arts. Not without reason, then, does Paul teach that it is absurd for those consecrated to Christ to draw the yoke with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6). And the Lord Christ, speaking of the punishment of Antichrist and of impious Babylon, earnestly admonishes his people to come out from there, lest they too be involved in the same plagues (Rev. 18). But if the common company of the impious is a snare to the godly, then certainly false teachers must be guarded against with even greater diligence, since they are wont to insinuate themselves wonderfully into men's minds and to breathe the deadly poison of false doctrine into the unwary. See on these matters Matt. 7 and 15; 2 John 1, etc.

units.la: Caeterum receptae Iudaeorum consuetudini recens Dei oraculum apostolus opponit, dicens: At mihi ostendit Deus, nullum hominem communem aut immundum dicendum esse. Immundos autem hoc loco intelligit, euangelij & salutis doctrina indignos. Alioqui enim satis constat immundos esse & dici debere omnes homines, quando in peccatis omnes nos concipi & nasci, figmenta item humani cordis ab ipsa pueritia praua, & iustitias nostras instar sordidorum centonum esse scripturae tantur. Psalm. 51. Gen. 8. Isa. 64. At quia Christi sanguis nos a peccatis emundat (1. Iohan. 1. cap.) & fide in hunc corda nostra purgantur, nemo purificatione ea, quam Christus summa liberalitate omnibus offert, & quibusuis in se credentibus benignissime impertit, indignus temere censeri debet: nisi quem palam deprehendamus ex canum & porcorum genere esse, quibus regni coelorum margaritas & sancta eius mysteria proijcere Christus prohibet. Matth. 7. Vehementer ergo terrant, qui salutis mysteria inuide celant, & Christi quoque nomen profesos ab illorum communione arcere consueuerunt.
units.tr: Moreover, the Apostle sets against the accepted custom of the Jews the recent oracle of God, saying: "But God has shown me that no man should be called common or unclean." By "unclean" he here understands those unworthy of the doctrine of the gospel and of salvation. For otherwise it is well established that all men are and ought to be called unclean, since we are all conceived and born in sins, and the imaginations of the human heart are evil from childhood, and our righteousnesses are, as Scripture says, like filthy rags (Ps. 51; Gen. 8; Isa. 64). But because the blood of Christ cleanses us from sins (1 John 1) and our hearts are purified by faith in him, no one should rashly be judged unworthy of that purification which Christ offers to all with the greatest liberality and most kindly bestows on whomever believes in him; unless we plainly detect someone to be of the race of dogs and swine, to whom Christ forbids the pearls of the kingdom of heaven and his holy mysteries to be thrown (Matt. 7). Therefore they terrify greatly who enviously hide the mysteries of salvation, and who are accustomed to keep from their fellowship those who have professed the name of Christ.

units.la: Est autem cumprimis obseruandum, quod veteri & receptae consuetudini expressum Dei oraculum apostolus opponit. Docemur exemplo hoc, eam esse diuini verbi authoritatem, ut huic ea quoq; cedere debeant, quae bono zelo & sancto consilio ab hominibus instituta sunt, ut primum illa Dei voluntati aliqua ex parte obstare videtur. Perniciosa igitur & absurda valde illorum pertinacia est, qui eos ritus in ecclesia retinere conantur, quos ab ineptissimis hominibus ad superstitionis confirmationem institutos esse, & Christi merito quam plurimum derogare constat. Periculosum illis videtur nouitatis studium. At multo periculosius est, veterum errorum obseruatione cum salutis iactura inhaerere. Et meminisse oportebat, fidei obedientiam veri Christianismi finem esse, quae ut nosipsos abnegemus, & resignato in vniuersum nostro arbitrio & iudicio in Dei voluntatem & potestatem nos totos tradamus, requirit. 2. Cor. 10. Matth. 16. Luc. 8.
units.tr: Now it must be observed above all that the Apostle sets against the old and accepted custom the express oracle of God. We are taught by this example that the authority of the divine word is such that even those things which have been instituted by men with good zeal and holy counsel ought to yield to it, whenever they seem in some measure to stand in the way of God's will. Therefore the obstinacy of those is pernicious and very absurd who try to retain in the Church those rites which it is plain were instituted by most foolish men to confirm superstition, and which greatly detract from the merit of Christ. The zeal for novelty seems dangerous to them. But it is much more dangerous to cling to the observance of old errors to the loss of salvation. And they ought to have remembered that obedience of faith is the end of true Christianity, which requires that we deny ourselves and, having altogether given up our own judgment and will, surrender ourselves wholly to the will and power of God (2 Cor. 10; Matt. 16; Luke 8).

units.la: II. Cornelij ad Petri orationem responsio. 1. Causam sui instituti explicat.
units.tr: II. Cornelius' reply to Peter's address. 1. He explains the reason for his undertaking.

units.la: Porro institutae apologiae quaestionem subijcit Petrus, causam requirens, ob quam ipsum accersere voluerint. Nec superuacanea videri debet quaestio haec, licet & visione coelesti & legatorum sermone Petrus antea instituerit. Ita enim in auditorum animis diligentiam & attentionem ardensq; audiendi studium excitare voluit: quae nisi adfuerint, cum fructu verbum praedicari non poterit. Nec parum docentis animum zelumq; extimulat, si attentos & cupidos discendi esse videat, quos ipsi instituendos Deus tradidit.
units.tr: Next, Peter puts to the apology undertaken the question of its cause, asking why they wished to summon him. This question should not seem superfluous, although Peter had already set it out by the heavenly vision and by the words of the envoys. For in this way he wished to stir up diligence and attentiveness in the minds of his hearers and an eager desire to listen; unless these are present, the word cannot be preached with profit. Nor does it sharpen the teacher's spirit and zeal a little if he sees that those whom God has handed over to him to be taught are attentive and eager to learn.

units.la: Sequitur ergo Cornelij responsio, quae ut simplex est minimeq; fucata, ita non pauca habet, quae communi omnium institutioni seruiunt. Nam & causam fui consilij exponit, & gratias agit Petro, quod ad ipsum venire dignatus sit, simulq; attentionem pollicetur, ubi etiam non obscure officij Petrum admonet: quae singula ordine videbimus. Ordituur autem a causa, ob quam Petrum ad se euocarit, ne aliquibus vel negligentior in propria salutis causa, vel etiam insolentior videatur, quod non ipse potius Ioppen descenderit. Repetit igitur quae iam ante de angeli apparitione dicta sunt: nec Lucam eadem toties repetere piget, ut historiae veritas & certitudo clarius elucescat. Summa omnium est, Dei mandato & oraculo euidenti se admonitu esse, ut Petrum ad se vocaret. Obseruemus autem hic, quod se ad nonam vsq; diei horam (quae nobis tertia pomeridiana est) ieiunum manssisse, & orauisse dicit. Exprimunt haec ardens veritatis studium, quo illum ob religionum diuersitatem non mediocriter vexatum fuisse credibile est: cum Iudaeos quidem a gentibus differre, & simul nouam Christianorum religionem exoriri videret. Valde ergo anxius, ne a vero deuiaret, precibus assiduis Deum fatigauit, & ijsdem, ut feruentiores essent, ieiunia sancta coniunxit: ut plane videas illum non precum & ieiuniorum merito confisum fuisse, sed ijs non aliud quam veritatis cognitionem quaesiuisse. Confer autem militem hunc cum nostri seculi Monachis, ut quantum illos tum pietate tum carnis disciplina
units.tr: Cornelius' reply follows. It is simple and by no means artificial, and yet it contains not a few things that serve the instruction of all. For he both sets out the reason for his plan, and thanks Peter for deigning to come to him, and at the same time promises attention, where he also not obscurely reminds Peter of his duty. We shall look at each of these in order. He begins with the reason why he had summoned Peter, lest he should seem to anyone either too careless about his own salvation or even too presumptuous, in that he himself had not rather gone down to Joppa. So he repeats what has already been said about the appearance of the angel; nor does Luke grudge repeating the same things so often, so that the truth and certainty of the history may shine out more clearly. The sum of it all is that by God's command and a clear oracle he had been admonished to call Peter to him. We should observe here that he says he remained fasting until the ninth hour of the day (which for us is three in the afternoon), and prayed. These things express the burning zeal for truth, by which it is credible that he was not a little troubled by the difference of religions, since he saw the Jews indeed differing from the Gentiles, and at the same time the new religion of the Christians arising. Being therefore very anxious lest he should stray from the truth, he wearied God with constant prayers, and joined holy fasts to them, so that they might be more fervent. You can plainly see that he did not trust in the merit of his prayers and fasts, but sought by them nothing other than the knowledge of the truth. Now compare this soldier with the monks of our age, that you may understand how far he surpassed them then both in piety and in discipline of the flesh.

units.la: { } Vide de his Matth. 7. & 15. capite. disciplina superarit intelligas. Et in publico quidem officio versans hisce studijs sese dedidit, ut evidens omnino illorum error sit, qui perfectum religionis studium absq; solitaria vita consistere posse negant. Elucet praterea hoc loco, quae causa sit, quod in religionis verae studio tam parum hodie proficitur. Precibus fatigari vult Deus, quae ex sobria carnis disciplina non parum feruoris accipiunt. At hodie rarissima precum cura est, & sobrietatis studium in crapulam & ebrietatem transijt, quae homines ad diuina simul & humana ineptos reddere solet. Regnat haec multis in locis inter ipsos verbi ministros, ut in illis eos mores cernas, quos infidis doctoribus Isaias Cap. 56. tribuit. Principes, & qui in magistratu versantur, fere mane comessantur, & crapulae indulgent, Solomonici illius profusi immemores: Va tibi terra, cuius rex puer est, & cuius principes mane comessantur. Eccles. 10. In vulgo autem Noae & Loti tempora videre licet, sicuti olim Christus praemonuit. Matth. 24. Luc. 17. Quid ergo miramur, raraм esse veritatis cognitionem, quando ea studia regnant, quibus illa suffocari, & in vniuersum obrui solet?
units.tr: { } See on these things Matthew, chapters 7 and 15. He gave himself to these pursuits while engaged in a public office, so that the error of those is wholly plain who deny that perfect zeal for religion can exist apart from the solitary life. This passage also makes clear the reason why so little progress is made today in zeal for the true religion. God wishes to be wearied with prayers, which receive no small fervour from a sober discipline of the flesh. But today there is very rare care for prayer, and the pursuit of sobriety has passed into gluttony and drunkenness, which are wont to make men unfit both for divine and for human things. This prevails in many places, even among the ministers of the Word themselves, so that you may see in them those manners which Isaiah in chapter 56 attributes to unfaithful teachers. Princes and those who hold office often feast in the morning and indulge in gluttony, forgetful of that lavish Solomonic saying: Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes feast in the morning (Eccles. 10). Among the common people one may see the times of Noah and Lot, as Christ once forewarned (Matt. 24; Luke 17). Why then do we wonder that knowledge of the truth is rare, when those pursuits reign which are wont to suffocate it and utterly overwhelm it?

units.la: Secundo loco gratias agit Petro Cornelius, quod ad ipsum venire dignatus sit. Hunc enim sensum habet locutio, qua vtitur: Bene fecisti, qui aduenerus. Nam quia hoc ab ipso bene factum esse agnoscit, non obscure simul se gratiam illi debere fatetur. Quo exemplo admonemur gratitudinem nos ministris verbi debere. Per hos enim pax & salus affertur, iuxta illud prophetae: Misit verbum suum, & sanauit eos. Psal. 107. Idem nobis patrum loco sunt, cum illorum ministerio regeneremur, & Dei filij atq; haeredes efficiamur: quod non semel a Paulo inculcatum esse legimus, ut 1. Cor. 4. Gal. 4. cap. Atqui philosophos ex naturae legibus docuisse constat, nunquam a filijs dignam parentibus gratiam referri posse. Quis ergo satis gratus erga eum fuerit, cuius opera & studio Dei filius & caelestis regni haeres factus est? Quae causa est, quod prophetae inter potissima Dei beneficia fidos doctores commemorare solent, ut videre est Psal. 147. Isa. 30. Amos 2. Mich. 6. &c. Et Paulus inter spiritus dona, quibus ille ex alto ecclesiam suam ornat, pastorum, doctorum, prophetarum, apostolorum & euangelistarum maxime meminit. Ephes. 4. At hodie eò ingratitudinis plerique deuenerunt, ut verbi ministros a malo daemone submitti, & publicos omnium malorum authores esse, dicere audeant. At habebunt illi aliquando se dignos doctores, quando salutis praedicationem tanta cum ingratitudine respuunt. Vide 2. Thess. 2.
units.tr: Second, Cornelius thanks Peter for deigning to come to him. For this is the sense of the expression he uses: You have done well, who have come. For since he acknowledges that this was well done by him, he at the same time not obscurely confesses that he owes him thanks. By this example we are reminded that we owe gratitude to the ministers of the Word. For through them peace and salvation are brought, according to that saying of the prophet: He sent his word and healed them (Ps. 107). They are likewise in the place of fathers to us, since we are regenerated by their ministry and made sons and heirs of God; which we read Paul has inculcated more than once, as in 1 Cor. 4 and Gal. 4. Yet it is agreed that the philosophers taught from the laws of nature that a worthy return of gratitude can never be made by sons to their parents. Who then could be grateful enough towards him by whose work and zeal someone has been made a son of God and heir of the heavenly kingdom? This is why the prophets are wont to number among the chief gifts of God faithful teachers, as may be seen in Ps. 147, Isa. 30, Amos 2, Mic. 6, etc. And Paul, among the gifts of the Spirit with which he from on high adorns his Church, especially mentions pastors, teachers, prophets, apostles and evangelists (Eph. 4). But today very many have sunk into such ingratitude that they dare to say that the ministers of the Word are sent by an evil demon and are public authors of all evils. Yet those men will one day have teachers worthy of themselves, since they reject the preaching of salvation with such ingratitude. See 2 Thess. 2.

units.la: Tertio attentionem & obedientiam Petro Cornelius pollicetur, cum ait: Nunc ergo nos omnes adsumus coram Deo, ad audiendum omnia, quae tibi a Deo commissa sunt. Sunt haec verba singulari consyderatione digna. Docent enim quales nam verbi auditores esse conueniat. Primo, ipsos coram Deo adesse dicit. Ante omnia ergo se in Dei conspectu versari meminerint, quicunq; in ecclesia Dei verbum audiunt. Christi enim vox est: Qui vos audit, me audit. Luc. 10. Et idem se inter illos medium fore promittit, qui in suo nomine congregati fuerint. Matth. 28. Deinde, se cum suis ad audiendum adesse fatetur. Est hoc alterum, cuius auditores meminisse oportet, se nimirum doctrina & institutione opus habere, & proinde non conueniens esse, ut animos suos in vanis cogitationibus peregrina ri patiantur. Qui enim id faciunt, semen verbi (ut Christus ait) in viam excipiunt, vbi ab auibus deuoratum fructum ferre nequit. Postremo, omnia audire vult Cornelius, quaecunq; Petrus a Deo commissa habet. Idem a nobis requiri cogitemus, nec tantum nobis permittamus, ut quaedam audire & ampletti, alia vero reijcere velimus, quae carnis affectibus minus adlubescunt. Haec si cum nostri seculi moribus conferas, quam horribilem, prob dolor, corruptionem videbis? Conueniunt quidem plerique, sed non tanquam in Dei conspectu: quin ijs similes sunt, de quibus apud Ezech. cap. 33. legitur. Deinde passim impios illos ardeliones andire est, qui cum verbum audiant, se tamen nec doctrina nec admonitione opus habere gloriantur. Quantus vero illorum numerus est, qui in Dei verbi censuram exercere audent, & ea quidem praedicari volunt, ex quibus lucrum sperant: rursum vero ministris silentium imponunt, si quid affectibus ipsorum aduersum aut mundo exosum dixerint? Atqui praestaret talibus verbum non praedicari, & sentient olim ipsis in testimonium cessurum esse, quod tanta improbitate contemnere ausi sunt.
units.tr: Third, Cornelius promises attention and obedience to Peter, when he says: Now therefore we are all present before God, to hear all things that have been committed to you by God. These words are worthy of particular consideration. For they teach what kind of hearers of the Word it becomes us to be. First, he says that they are present before God. Above all, therefore, let those who hear the Word in the Church of God remember that they are living in the sight of God; for it is the voice of Christ: He who hears you hears me (Luke 10). And he likewise promises that he will be in the midst of those who have gathered in his name (Matt. 28). Next, he confesses that he with his people is present to hear. This is another point which the hearers must remember: namely, that they need doctrine and instruction, and that it is therefore not fitting to allow their minds to wander abroad in vain thoughts. For those who do so receive the seed of the Word (as Christ says) on the road, where, devoured by the birds, it cannot bear fruit. Last, Cornelius wishes to hear all things that Peter has been given by God. Let us think that the same is required of us, and let us not allow ourselves to wish to hear and embrace some things while rejecting others which are less pleasing to the affections of the flesh. If you compare these things with the morals of our age, what a horrible corruption, alas, will you see? Many indeed assemble, but not as in the sight of God; rather they are like those of whom it is read in Ezekiel chapter 33. Then everywhere one hears those impious busybodies, who, though they hear the Word, yet boast that they need neither doctrine nor admonition. And how great is the number of those who dare to exercise censure over the Word of God, and want only those things preached from which they hope for gain; and on the other hand impose silence on the ministers, if they have said anything contrary to their affections or hateful to the world? Yet it would be better for such people that the Word were not preached; and they will feel that one day it will stand as a testimony against them, since they have dared to despise it with such wickedness.

units.la: Simul vero Petrum ista officij admonuerunt, ut nimirum quae ipsi a Deo commissa erant, libere praedicaret, & quidem sola illa, non suae rationis figmenta obtruderet. In quibus praecipue ministrorum officium versatur, ut saepe iam dictum est. Nos autem Cornelium nobis imitandum proponamus, vt eodem verbi studio accensi, salutis doctrinam digne percipiamus, illaq; regenerati vitam Deo dignam viuamus in Christo Iesu, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: At the same time, these words reminded Peter of his duty: namely, that he should freely preach what had been committed to him by God, and should thrust forward those things alone, not the inventions of his own reason. In this especially the office of ministers consists, as has often been said already. As for us, let us set Cornelius before ourselves as one to be imitated, so that, kindled with the same zeal for the Word, we may worthily receive the doctrine of salvation, and, being regenerated by it, live a life worthy of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXIIII.

units.la: Petrus autem aperiens os dixit: In veritate comperio, quod non fit personarum acceptor Deus: sed in omni gente qui timet ipsum, & operatur iustitiam, is acceptus est illi. Sermonem, quem misit Deus filijs Israel, annuncians pacem per Iesum Christum. (Hic est omnium Dominus) vos nouistis.
units.tr: Then Peter opened his mouth and said: "I now truly perceive that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation the man who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him. The word which he sent to the children of Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), you know."

units.la: Quamuis ardens veritatis cognoscendæ studium ante quidem pijs precibus & sanctis ieiunijs Cornelius abunde testatus sit, euidentioribus tamen signis hoc ipsum declarat, quando Petrum apostolum aduenisse videt, eumq; ad docendum paratum esse audit. Nam & gratum sibi esse fatetur apostoli aduentum, & se fidelem atq; obedientem auditorem fore promittit omnium eorum, quæ ex Dei mandato Petrus dicturus sit. Quo loco docemur, quid omnes eos facere conueniat, qui dei verbum non absq; fructu audire voluerint. Porro vt pij auditoris & studiosi exemplum præbet Cornelius: ita in eodem simul patet, pium & ardens verbi studium fructu carere non posse, sed iuxta Christi promissionem inuenturos Dei voluntatem, quicunque illam non fucato animo quæsuerint. Nam qui paulo ante cœlestis visionis oraculo Petrum excitauit, vt ad Cornelium sibi proficiscendum esse intelligeret: idem nunc quoque occulta spiritus suggestione animum eius extimulat, vt magna cum gravitate & diligentia sese ad docendum præparet. Id enim per oris apertionem significari tam ante dictum est. Concionis vero argumentum est, per solum Iesum Christum homines purificari & salutem consequi. Ordine autem commodissimo vtitur. Nam exordium habet ad captandam beneuolentiam cumprimis idoneum, cum ad gentes quoque salutis doctrinam pertinere, ingenue fatetur. Deinde summam totius euangelici negotij paucis comprehensam proponit. Quam mox bifarica narratione latius exponit, & tum apostolicis tum propheticis testimonijs confirmat. Tandem vero finem & scopum omnium subiungit, docens, vt nos tam Christi ipsius quam salutis, quæ in ipso offertur, per solam fidem conforites fieri oporteat. At in præsenti duas priores partes explicabimus, de reliquis suo loco & tempore dicturi.
units.tr: Although Cornelius had already shown abundantly, by devout prayers and holy fasts, his ardent desire to know the truth, he now declares the same thing by clearer signs, when he sees that the apostle Peter has come and hears that he is ready to teach. For he confesses that the apostle's arrival is welcome to him, and he promises to be a faithful and obedient hearer of everything that Peter is about to say by God's command. Here we are taught what all those ought to do who wish to hear the word of God not without profit. Cornelius sets an example of a devout and attentive hearer; and at the same time it is plain that a devout and ardent zeal for the word cannot be without fruit, but, according to Christ's promise, all who seek God's will with an unfeigned heart will find it. For he who a little earlier stirred up Peter, through the vision from heaven, to understand that he must go to Cornelius, now also by a hidden prompting of the Spirit stirs up his mind, so that he prepares himself to teach with great seriousness and diligence. This is what was signified before by the opening of his mouth. The subject of the sermon is that men are cleansed and obtain salvation through Jesus Christ alone. He uses a most fitting order. For he has an introduction well suited to win goodwill, since he openly admits that the teaching of salvation pertains also to the Gentiles. Then he sets forth in a few words the sum of the whole gospel business. Soon he explains this more fully in a twofold narrative, and confirms it by both apostolic and prophetic testimonies. Finally he adds the end and aim of all, teaching that we must be made conformable to Christ himself, and to the salvation offered in him, through faith alone. But at present we will explain the first two parts, and speak of the rest in their place and time.

units.la: Exordium exclamatione figurat, dicens: In veritate comperio, quod non fit personarum acceptor Deus, &c. Sensus est: Euangelium & salutis doctrinam non minus ad gentes, quam Iudæos, pertinere. Antea quidem interstitium ingens & præalta quædam maceria gentes à Iudæis dirimebat. Nam & Paulus eos qui ex gentibus sunt, à republica Israelis abalienatos, à testamentis extraneos, spei exortes, deniq; sine Christo & sine Deo fuisse scribit. Addit vero, quod ad huius loci explicationem facit: Nunc autem per Christum Iesum vos, qui quondam eratis longinqui, propinquis facti estis, per sanguinem Christi. Ipse est enim pax nostra, qui fecit ex vtrisq; vnum, & interstitium maceria diruit, &c. Ephes. 2. Hoc ipsum magna gravitate Petrus asserit, partim quidem, vt beneuolos sibi reddat auditores, quorum salutì non inuidebat, aliorum Iudæorum more: partim vero, vt ijdem attentiores sint in ijs audiendis, quæ ad ipsorum salutem spectabant. Præstat autem singula verba excutere, vt plus inde consolationis & institutionis ad nos redeat.
units.tr: He begins with an exclamation, saying: "I now truly perceive that God is no respecter of persons," and so on. The meaning is: the gospel and the doctrine of salvation pertain no less to the Gentiles than to the Jews. Before this, a great gap and a high wall of separation divided the Gentiles from the Jews. For Paul also writes that those who are of the Gentiles were alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope, and finally without Christ and without God.
