He adds, which bears on the explanation of this passage: "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who has made the two one and has broken down the dividing wall," and so on (Eph. 2). Peter asserts this with great seriousness, partly indeed to make his hearers well disposed to him, since he did not begrudge them their salvation, unlike other Jews; and partly so that they might be more attentive in hearing those things which concerned their own salvation. It is worth examining each word, so that more comfort and instruction may come to us from it.

units.la: Primum per exclamationem (vt modo monuimus) ait: In veritate, aut reipsa comperio. Quæ vox ipsum hoc mysterium ignorauisse, testatur. Antea enim communi Iudæorum errore deceptus, & cæco carnis præiudicio fascinatus, gentes tanquam prophanas & Deo abominabiles horrere consueuerat. Nunc vero cœlesti visione, angeli apparitione & verbis Cornelij aliter sentire docetur: quādo in hisce non obscura Christiani & verè regenerati animi argumenta deprehendit. Docet autem Petri exemplum, sanctos quoq; interdum aliqua latere, & proinde non credendum esse nostræ rationis præiudicio, sed illud potius ad diuini verbi regulam magna diligentia examinari debere.
units.tr: First, by the exclamation (as we have just noted) he says: "I truly perceive," or "I find in fact." This word shows that he had been ignorant of this mystery. For before, deceived by the common error of the Jews and blinded by the carnal prejudice, he had been accustomed to shrink from the Gentiles as profane and abominable to God. But now he is taught to think otherwise by the heavenly vision, the appearance of the angel, and the words of Cornelius, when in these he detects no obscure signs of a Christian and truly regenerate mind. Peter's example also teaches that even saints sometimes remain in some ignorance, and therefore we should not trust the prejudice of our own reason, but rather examine such things with great diligence by the rule of the divine word.

units.la: Secundo quidnam comperierit, docet: nimirum, quod non fit personarum acceptor Deus. Cate-rum personæ vocabulum externam hominis speciem significat, qua vel commendari vel contemptui fieri solet: cuius generis sunt, nobilitas, stemmatum splendor, opes, honores, natio siue natale solum, maiorum obscuritas, paupertas, seruitus, & infinita alia. Quorum respectum a iudicibus alienissimum esse iubet Deus, eo quod salua esse nequit iudiciorum aequitas, vt primum ille admissus fuerit. Deut. 1. Exod. 23. Psal. 82. Nequit ergo fieri, vt in Dei naturam cadat, quod is in hominibus abomi nari consueuit. Et sane passim hoc illi scripturae tribuunt, quod nec genere, nec diuitijs, nec pauperta te, nec externa conditione, nec etiam natalis soli respectu moueatur: sed aeque omnibus sese iustum atque misericordem exhibeat. Habet vero hoc haud vulgarem vsum in salutis negotio. Nam & institutioni seruit, ne quem propter externa illa contemnamus, quando Deum, cuius filij sumus, his ne quaqua moueri constat: & consolationem affert afflictis & infimae sortis hominibus, quando audiunt in Christo nec seruum nec liberum, non Iudaeum nec Graecum, non Scytham nec barbarum, non marem nec faeminam, non diuitem nec pauperem haberi. Vide Gal. 3. Colos. 3. &c.
units.tr: Second, he tells what he has perceived: namely, that God is no respecter of persons. Now the word "person" signifies a man's outward appearance, by which people are usually either commended or despised. Of this kind are nobility, the splendour of ancestry, wealth, honours, nation or native soil, obscurity of forebears, poverty, servitude, and countless others. God commands that regard for these be wholly alien to judges, because the fairness of judgments cannot remain safe if such regard is admitted even slightly (Deut. 1; Exod. 23; Ps. 82). It is therefore impossible that what God is accustomed to abhor in men should fall within his nature. And indeed Scripture everywhere attributes this to him: that he is moved neither by lineage, nor by riches, nor by poverty, nor by external condition, nor even by regard for native soil, but shows himself equally just and merciful to all. This has no small use in the business of salvation. For it serves instruction, so that we do not despise anyone on account of those outward things, since it is established that God, whose children we are, is in no way moved by them; and it brings comfort to the afflicted and to men of the lowest rank, when they hear that in Christ there is neither slave nor free, neither Jew nor Greek, neither Scythian nor barbarian, neither male nor female, neither rich nor poor (see Gal. 3; Col. 3, etc.).

units.la: Facit vero ad huius explicationem, quod mox subijcit, quales nam in omni hominum genere deus sibi acceptos habeat, ne quis illum temere res humanas administrare putet. Addit enim: Sed in omni gente, qui timet ipsum & operatur iustitiam, is acceptus est illi. Comprehendit autem duobus capitibus totius vitae integritatem, qualem a suis cultoribus Deus requirit. Nam Dei timore omnem religionem complectitur, quando constat, hunc absque Dei notitia, fide & obedientia consistere non posse. Iustitiae autem vocabulo supremam illam virtutem intelligit, qua vnicuique quod suum est tribuitur, quaeque sola totius vitae optima moderatrix est, & ex Christianae charitatis fontibus deriuatur. At si cum his corruptam hominis naturam conferas, facile patebit, haec non nisi in renatis inueniri, & sine Dei gratia, fide, in Christo minime constare. Quomodo enim propter externa opera Deo placerent, qui a Christo alieni sunt, quando solus hic mediator ille est, in quo patri complacuit? Vehementer errgo errant, qui ex hisce Petri verbis humanae iustitiae meritum stabiliri posse existimant: cum sola Dei gratia eorum causa efficiens sit, quae hic tam praeclaris laudibus vehuntur. Simul autem illorum quo que error confutandus est, qui hoc loco abutentes, vnumquemque in sua gentis religione saluari posse affirmant, siue ille Iudaeus, siue Turca fuerit, modo aliqua numinis reuerentia illuminatus communi inter homines iustitiae studeat. At longe alia hic Petri mens est: qui potius probare instituit, euan gelij doctrinam, qua salus in Christo praedicatur, ad omnes gentes ex aequo pertinere. At quor sum obsecro illam ad omnes diuulgare opus esset, si fine Christo salus obtingeret? Est autem cumprimis perniciosum istud hominum genus, qui sub Christianae modestiae praetextu, ne quem audacius damnare videantur, Christi meritum plane euacuant, imo Dei iustitiam, bonitatem, sapientiam, veritate & quicquid praeterea virtutum in Deo est, in dubium vocant. Si enim absque Christo salus cuiquam obtingit, illam ex nostro arbitrio & zelo pendere constat. Frustra ergo in mundum Christus venit. Frustra incarnatus, passus & mortuus est. Frustra a mortuis resuscitatus, caelos conscendit. Et mendacij arguetur, quod dixerit: Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Iohan. 14. Mendacij quoq; conuincetur Petrus, qui Christi spiritu suggerente nullum aliud sub caelo nomen hominibus datum esse dixit, in quo saluari possint. Adhaec quis obsecro Deum patrem vel iustum, vel sapientem, vel veracem, vel misericordem dicere poterit, qui nulla graui causa motus, tam acerbis afflictionibus filium subiecerit? Procul ergo a facessant illi homines, qui dum modesti videri volunt, religionis mysteria euacuant.
units.tr: What he adds next also serves to explain this, namely what sort of people God holds as acceptable among every kind of men, so that no one may rashly think that he manages human affairs carelessly. For he adds: "But in every nation the man who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him." He comprehends under two heads the whole integrity of life that God requires from his worshippers. For by the fear of God he embraces all religion, since it is clear that this cannot exist without the knowledge, faith and obedience of God. By the word "righteousness" he understands that supreme virtue by which each person is given what is his own, and which alone is the best governor of the whole of life, and which flows from the springs of Christian love. But if you compare with these the corrupt nature of man, it will easily be seen that these things are found only in the regenerate, and cannot exist at all without the grace of God and faith in Christ. For how could those who are alien from Christ please God by their outward works, when this mediator alone is the one in whom the Father is well pleased? Therefore those greatly err who think from these words of Peter that the merit of human righteousness can be established, since the grace of God alone is the efficient cause of those things which are here praised with such fine commendations. At the same time, the error of those must also be refuted who, abusing this passage, affirm that each man can be saved in his own nation's religion, whether he be a Jew or a Turk, provided that, enlightened by some reverence for a divinity, he strives for the righteousness common among men. But Peter's mind here is quite different: he rather sets out to prove that the doctrine of the gospel, in which salvation is preached in Christ, pertains equally to all nations. For why, I ask you, would it be necessary to publish it to all, if salvation could come without Christ? Yet that kind of men is especially pernicious who, under the pretext of Christian moderation, so as not to seem to condemn anyone too boldly, utterly empty Christ's merit, and indeed call into doubt the justice, goodness, wisdom, truth and whatever other virtues there are in God. For if salvation comes to anyone without Christ, it is clear that it depends on our own judgment and zeal. In vain, then, did Christ come into the world; in vain was he incarnate, suffered and died; in vain, raised from the dead, did he ascend into the heavens. And he will be convicted of falsehood, who said: "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14). Peter too will be convicted of falsehood, who, with Christ's Spirit suggesting it, said that there is no other name under heaven given to men by which they can be saved. Besides, who, I ask, could call God the Father just, or wise, or truthful, or merciful, if, moved by no grave cause, he subjected his Son to such bitter afflictions? Let those men, then, keep far away, who, while wishing to seem moderate, empty the mysteries of religion.

units.la: Nos vero verborum Petri scopum obseruantes, Dei iudicio eos relinquamus, ad quos euangelij & Christi lux nondum peruenit: quos, si saluantur, Christi merito saluari oportet, nisi in Christum simul & Deum contumeliosi esse velimus.
units.tr: Now, observing the aim of Peter's words, let us leave those to God's judgment to whom the light of the gospel and of Christ has not yet come. If they are saved, they must be saved by the merit of Christ, unless we wish to be insulting both to Christ and to God.

units.la: Accedamus autem ad secundam concionis huius partem, quae totius causae propositionem habet his verbis comprehensam: Sermonem, quem misit Deus filijs Israel, annuncians pacem per Iesum Christum (hic est omnium dominus) vos nouistis. Quorum hic mihi sensus esse videtur: Nolo vos nouum & inauditum aliquid expectare, o fratres. De eo enim negotio verba facturus sum, quod iam passim per omnium ora versatur, & cuius fama haud dubie ad vos quoq; peruenit: vt nimirum Deus filium suum Iesum Christum, qui ipsi coaeternus & omnium dominus est, filijs Israelis miserit, hominem factum ex Maria virgine, ijsq; per hunc pacem annunciauerit. Comprehendit his Petrus vniuersa Christi Iesu & euangelici negotij mysteria, quae mox subiecta narratione fusius explicabit. Quare in ijs ea tantum modo, quae praesenti loco seruiunt, quoad fieri potest, breuissime perstringemus.
units.tr: Let us turn to the second part of this sermon, which contains the statement of the whole matter, expressed in these words: "The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), ye know." The sense seems to me to be this: "Brethren, I do not want you to expect anything new or unheard of. For I am going to speak about a matter that is now on everyone's lips and whose report has undoubtedly reached you too: namely, that God sent his Son Jesus Christ, who is co-eternal with him and Lord of all, to the children of Israel, made man from the Virgin Mary, and through him announced peace to them." In these words Peter comprehends all the mysteries of Christ Jesus and of the gospel business, which he will later explain more fully in the narrative that follows. Therefore, as far as possible, we shall touch on only those points that serve the present passage, and do so very briefly.

units.la: Propositio.
units.tr: The proposition.

units.la: Primò quis nam Christus ille sit, non obscurè docet, quando omnium dominum vocat. Est hoc enim dininitatis ipsius testimonium. Constat enim ad solum Deum omnium rerum dominium pertinere, eò quòd idem ille solus omnium creator sit. At per æternum illud Dei verbum omnia creata esse, & eidem omne iudicium & omnem potestatem à patre datam esse constat, Ioban.1. 3. & 5. Deus ergo verus sit oportet. Neq; hic nobis dandi verbum quisquam obijciat, quasi minor sit, cui ab altero aliquid datur. Hoc enim ad assumptam hominis naturam refertur, cui præfinito tempore à patre datum est, quod iuxta diuinitatem ab æterno Christus habuit. Ita enim ipse iam mortem aditurus loquitur: Glorifica me pater apud temetipsum gloria, quâ habui priusquam hic mundus esset apud te. Ioban.17. Cofutantur his Arriani & qui horum vestigijs hodie insistunt Seruetani, simulq; Christiane fidei dignitas contra Iudæos & Turcas asseritur, qui nos nudo homine gloriari & confidere dicunt.
units.tr: First, who this Christ is he makes clear enough when he calls him Lord of all. For this is a testimony to his very divinity. It is agreed that dominion over all things belongs to God alone, because he alone is the creator of all things. But it is agreed that all things were created through that eternal Word of God, and that all judgment and all power has been given to him by the Father (John 1:3; 5). Therefore he must be true God. Nor let anyone here object to us the word "gave", as if he were lesser, since something is given to him by another. For this refers to the assumed nature of man, to which at a set time the Father gave what Christ had from eternity according to his divinity. So he himself speaks, now about to undergo death: "Glorify me, Father, with that glory which I had with you before the world was" (John 17). Arians, and the Servetians who today follow in their footsteps, are refuted by these words; and at the same time the dignity of the Christian faith is asserted against Jews and Turks, who say that we glory and trust in a mere man.

units.la: Deinde salutis modum obiter attingit Petrus, quando æternum illud Dei verbum, Iesum Christum à Deo patre missum esse dicit. Nam missionis vocabulo totum incarnationis mysterium comprehendit, quemadmodum & Paulus, quando ait: Vbi venit plenitudo temporis, emisit Deus filium suum, factum ex muliere, &c. Gal. 4. Incarnationi autem includuntur, quæcunq; in carne Christus nostræ salutis ergò fecit simul & passus est, de quibus postea dicetur. Porrò filijs Israelis missum dicit, non quòd ad solos hos pertinuerit, sed quòd ex illis carnem assumpsit, & illis primis innotescere debuit, donec propter illorum incredulitatem ad gentes transferretur. Obseruabis autem in his, universum illud Christi negotium, quod euangelio prædicatur, non humanum, sed diuinum esse. A Deo enim verbum illud missum est. Et æternum hoc Dei decretum esse constat, ut Iesus Christus Rex & sacerdos sit sui populi in æternum. Psal. 2. & 110. Vnde colligimus, frustra contra euangelium ipsius humanis viribus pugnari: quod supra Gamalielem vidisse audiuimus, & omnium seculorum exemplis abunde demonstratum est.
units.tr: Next, Peter briefly touches on the manner of salvation when he says that the eternal Word of God, Jesus Christ, was sent by God the Father. For by the word "sent" he comprehends the whole mystery of the incarnation, just as Paul does when he says: "When the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman," etc. (Gal. 4). Included in the incarnation are all the things Christ did and suffered in the flesh for our salvation, of which more will be said later. Moreover, he says that he was sent to the children of Israel, not because he pertained to them alone, but because he took flesh from them, and he had to be made known first to them, until, on account of their unbelief, he was transferred to the Gentiles. You will observe in these words that the whole business of Christ, which is preached in the gospel, is not human but divine. For that Word was sent from God. And it is agreed that this is the eternal decree of God, that Jesus Christ should be King and priest of his people forever (Ps. 2 and 110). From this we gather that it is in vain to fight against the gospel with human strength; as we heard Gamaliel had seen, and as has been abundantly demonstrated by the examples of all ages.

units.la: Postremò finem & scopum totius negotij huius attingit, qui est, ut pax annuntiaretur per Iesum Christum. Ita Isaias cap. 52. de euangelij præconibus loquens, ait: O quàm speciosi sunt super montes pedes euangelizantis, prædicantis pacem, &c. Prædicationis verò meminit Petrus, non quòd huius tantummodo minister sit Christus, sed quòd pax illa, cuius ipse author est, nobis per verbi euangelici prædicationem offertur, & fidei auditu percipitur. Præcipuè autem de ea pace loquitur, quæ nobis cum Deo per Iesum Christum intercedit. Antea enim propter peccata à Deo disiuncti, hostium loco reputabamur. Et Paulus iram Dei cœlitus patefieri scribit aduersus omnem impietatem & iniustitiam hominum. Rom. 1. Pacificatore ergo & reconciliatore opus fuit, quem in Iesu Christo nobis à patre datum esse, scripturæ docent. Is enim peccata, quæ dissidij inter nos & Deum causa erant, in se transtulit, illa mortis suæ merito expiauit, & diuinæ iustitiæ rigori satisfecit. Idemq; per fidem nostrer factus, sua iustitia nos vestit, munit & tuetur ut Dei tribunal sustinere possimus, qui pro nostris delictis æternum damnari merebamur. Ita fit, ut iuxta Pauli doctrinam, iustificati ex fide pacem habeamus erga Deum, per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. Rom. 5. Fatetur hoc ipse pater, quando cœlitus latam hanc & plenam consolationis vocem intonat: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacitum est. Matth. 3. & 17. Atqui hæc illa pax est, quæ omnem intellectum superat, quæque nullis afflictionibus interturbari potest, eò quòd has leues & iucundas efficiat ijs, qui Deum patrem sibi in Christo propitium factum, & se Dei filios factos esse intelligunt. Parit etiam pax hæc ciuilem imò fraternam inter homines concordiam, eò quòd per Christum omnis ille personarum respectus inter fideles tollitur, quo concordia mutua maximè turbari consueuit. Et quia charitatis igne hominum mentes incendit, pacis studium illorum animis ita inserit, ut cane & angue peius oderint & abominentur, quæcunq; huic aduersa esse nouerunt. Magna ergo & execrabilis est illorum hominum ingratitudo & iniquitas, qui euangelij prædicatione politias & publicam pacem turbari clamant. Ita enim Christum Iesum, veræ & æternæ pacis principem, eorum scelerum authorem faciunt, quæ mundo infelici accepta ferri debebant, quem ideò contra Christum & verbum eius tumultuari & publicas turbas excitare constat, quòd eius lucem, qua praua ipsius opera arguuntur, ferre non potest. Ioban. 3. Agnoscamus nos Dei bonitatem, qui salutis doctrinam omnibus offerre dignatur, & Christum Iesum, salutis & pacis authorem vnicum vera fide ampleCtamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, he touches on the end and aim of the whole matter, which is that peace should be announced through Jesus Christ. So Isaiah, speaking of the heralds of the gospel in chapter 52, says: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who proclaims peace," etc. Peter mentions preaching, not because Christ is merely the minister of it, but because that peace, of which he himself is the author, is offered to us through the preaching of the gospel word and is received by the hearing of faith. He speaks especially of that peace which exists between us and God through Jesus Christ. For before, separated from God on account of our sins, we were regarded as enemies. And Paul writes that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men (Rom. 1). There was need, therefore, of a peacemaker and reconciler, whom the Scriptures teach was given to us by the Father in Jesus Christ. For he transferred to himself the sins which were the cause of the quarrel between us and God, expiated them by the merit of his death, and satisfied the rigor of divine justice. And he, made our substitute through faith, clothes, fortifies and protects us with his righteousness, so that we can stand before the tribunal of God, though we deserved to be damned eternally for our offences. Thus it comes about, according to the teaching of Paul, that we, justified by faith, have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5). The Father himself confirms this when he thunders from heaven this joyful and consoling voice: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3 and 17). And this is that peace which surpasses all understanding, and which no afflictions can disturb, because it makes them light and pleasant for those who understand that God the Father has been made propitious to them in Christ, and that they have been made sons of God. This peace also brings forth civil, indeed brotherly, concord among men, because through Christ all that respect of persons which most often disturbs mutual harmony among the faithful is removed. And since it kindles men's minds with the fire of charity, it so implants a zeal for peace in their souls that they hate and abominate worse than dog and snake whatever they know to be opposed to it. Great and detestable, therefore, is the ingratitude and wickedness of those men who cry out that the preaching of the gospel disturbs public order and peace. For they make Christ Jesus, the prince of true and eternal peace, the author of those crimes which ought rather to be charged to the unhappy world; and it is clear that they stir up tumults and public disorders against Christ and his word for this reason, that they cannot bear his light, by which their wicked works are exposed (John 3). Let us acknowledge the goodness of God, who deigns to offer the doctrine of salvation to all, and let us embrace with true faith Christ Jesus, the one author of salvation and peace, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXV.

units.la: Vos[inquam] nouistis, Verbum quod diuulgatum fuit per totam Iudaeam, initio facto a Galilaea, post baptismum, quem praedicauit Iohannes: nempe Iesum a Nazareth, vt illum vnxerit Deus spiritu sancto & virtute: qui obambulauit benefaciens, & sanans omnes, qui oppressi erant diaboli tyrannide. Quoniam Deus erat cum illo.
units.tr: "You know, I say, the word that was spread throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism that John preached: namely, Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the tyranny of the devil, because God was with him."

units.la: QVamuis concionem hanc Caesareae in Cornelij Centurionis domo diuus Petrus habuerit, eadem tamen ad omnes homines spectat, & hodie etiam a nobis diligentissime consyderari meretur. Nam praeter id, quod multa praecesserunt, quae Dei spiritum huius authorem fuisse docent, hac ipsa Petrus omnem nostrae iustificationis & salutis rationem plenissime comprehendit. Et huius quidem in ipsa propositione (vt nuper vidimus) auditores admonuit, dum se de aeterno Dei verbo, Iesu Christo nimirum, dicturum esse pollicetur, qui cum omnium dominus adeo, verus Deus sit, in mundum tamen venire dignatus est, vt humanum genus Deo patri reconciliaret, & salutiferae illius pacis praeco simul & author esset. Quia vero iis verbis non obscure testatus est, salutis nostrae rationem in vno Iesu Christo comprehendi, hoc ipsum modo historica narratione latius fusius explicare incipit, & sic quidem, vt facile pateat, ea omnia a Christo peracta esse, quae ad humani generis redemptionem pertinebant.
units.tr: Although blessed Peter delivered this sermon at Caesarea in the house of Cornelius the centurion, it nevertheless applies to all men, and it deserves to be considered most diligently by us today as well. For apart from the fact that many things preceded it which show that the Spirit of God was its author, Peter here comprehends most fully the whole account of our justification and salvation. In the very opening of his speech he has already admonished his hearers, as we saw recently, when he promised to speak of the eternal word of God, namely Jesus Christ, who, though he is Lord of all and true God, deigned nevertheless to come into the world, so that he might reconcile the human race to God the Father, and be at once the herald and the author of that saving peace. But since in those words he has plainly testified that the account of our salvation is contained in Jesus Christ alone, he now begins to explain this more fully and at greater length by a historical narrative. He does so in such a way that it is easily evident that all those things were accomplished by Christ which pertained to the redemption of the human race.

units.la: Facit autem narrandi initium a loco & tempore, docens, vbi & quando Christus innotescere coeperit. Simul vero ipsos rerum, quas iam pridem fama longe lateque vulgauerat, testes sistit, ne cui narratio haec incerta & dubia fidei esse videretur. Vos (inquit) nouistis verbum, quod diuulgatum fuit per totam Iudaeam, initio facto a Galilaea, post baptismum, quem praedicauit Iohannes. Loci vero non temere meminit, cum in Galilaea Christum praedicandi initium facturum esse, olim Isaias praedixerit, quemadmodum Matthaeus quoque cap. 4. annotauit. Isa. 9. Nec alia ratio videtur, quod tempus quoque allegat, Verbum hoc post baptismum Iohannis coepisse dicens, quando hunc quoque primum noui Testamenti ministrum & promissi saluatoris praecursorem fore, prophetae vaticinati sunt. Nam in hunc competere, quae Isa. 40. de voce in deserto clamante, & apud Malachiam de Elia dicuntur, ex Euangelistarum scriptis, & ipsius Christi testimonio, quod Matth. 11. habetur, notius est, quam vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Confutantur igitur hoc loco, qui Iohannem inter euangelij ministros censeri debere negant. Atqui constat, hunc de Christo testimonium tulisse, & ad hunc discipulos suos summa fide relegauisse. Ioh. 1. & 3. Idem ille vniuersum populum tam doctrina quam baptismo ad Christum excipiendum praeparauit, quod eius officium in recens nato pater Zacharias ex spiritus suggestione agnoscit. Nobis potius studiose hoc obseruandum est, quod Christi Iesu & euangelij ipsius negotium a Iohanne coepit, qui paenitentiae doctrina & baptismo illorum animos, qui Christi discipuli futuri erant, praeparare debuit. Ita enim cauere voluit Christus, ne quis sub illius praetextu carnis & peccandi licentia quaereret, quod & olim multos fecisse constat, & hodie plerosque facere videmus, qui euangelij nomine gloriantur. Quae causa est, quod & ipse Christus a paenitentia docendi initium fecit, & inde apostolos incipere iussit. Matth. 4. & 10. Luc. 24. Nec audiendi sunt, qui paenitentiae doctrinam ab euangelio separant, cum sine hac salutis in Christo consortes fieri non possimus. Nec ideo humanae iustitiae aut illius merito salus tribuitur, cum paenitentia quoque in Christi nomine praedicare iubeamur, & Petrus supra Christum huius authorem & largitorem nobis a Deo patre constitutum esse docuerit. Act. 5. Interim illi quoque arguuntur, qui euangelij praedicatione carni ad peccandum habenas laxari calumniantur, cum ijdem illud non alio nomine magis oderint & persequantur, quam quod & aperta scelera & latentem multorum hypocrisim graviter accusat & insectatur.
units.tr: He begins the narrative with place and time, teaching where and when Christ began to be made known. At the same time he presents as witnesses the very men who had long since spread the report of these events far and wide, so that this account might not seem to anyone to be uncertain and doubtful as to its credibility. "You know," he says, "the word that was spread throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee, after the baptism that John preached." He does not mention the place carelessly, since Isaiah long ago foretold that Christ would begin to preach in Galilee, as Matthew also noted in chapter 4. Isa. 9. Nor does there seem to be any other reason why he also gives the time, saying that this word began after John's baptism, since the prophets foretold that John would be the first minister of the New Testament and the forerunner of the promised Saviour. For that what is said of the voice crying in the wilderness in Isaiah 40, and of Elijah in Malachi, applies to him, is more evident from the writings of the Evangelists and from Christ's own testimony, which is found in Matthew 11, than it needs to be shown by many arguments. Therefore those are refuted here who deny that John ought to be counted among the ministers of the gospel. Yet it is certain that he bore witness to Christ and most faithfully directed his disciples to him. John 1 and 3. That same man prepared the whole people, by both teaching and baptism, to receive Christ, a duty which his father Zacharias, moved by the Spirit, recognised in the newborn child. Rather, we ought to observe carefully that the business of Christ Jesus and of the gospel itself began with John, who was to prepare the minds of those who were going to be Christ's disciples by the teaching of repentance and by baptism. For Christ wished to guard against anyone seeking, under the pretext of this, licence for the flesh and for sinning, which is known to have been done by many in former times, and which we see very many doing today, who boast of the name of the gospel. This is why Christ himself also began his teaching with repentance, and ordered the apostles to begin there too. Matt. 4 and 10. Luke 24. Nor are they to be heard who separate the teaching of repentance from the gospel, since without it we cannot become partakers of salvation in Christ. Nor on that account is salvation attributed to human righteousness or to its merit, since we are commanded to preach repentance also in the name of Christ, and Peter has taught that God the Father appointed Christ himself as its author and giver to us. Acts 5. Meanwhile, those also are rebuked who slander the preaching of the gospel as loosening the reins for the flesh to sin, when these same men hate and persecute it for no other reason more than that it sharply accuses and attacks both open crimes and the hidden hypocrisy of many.

units.la: Deinde obseruare conuenit, vt de Iohannis ministerio apostolus loquatur. Hunc enim baptismum praedicauisse ait. Praedicationem autem baptismo coniungit, vt illum & doctrinae & sacramenti ministrum fuisse ostendat. Vt enim baptismo homines purificationis admonuit: ita illius mysteria verbis exponens, purificationem in vno Christo haberi, a purificatis vero dignos paenitentiae fructus requiri docuit. Unde patet doctrinam Sacramentis necessario coniungi debere, quando sine hac illorum mysteria intelligi non possunt. Ita olim Deus pueris paschalis epuli arcana exponere iussit. Et prophetarum sermones in explicandis sacrificiorum & legalis cultus mysterijs maximè versari videmus, dum eos grauissimè reprehendunt, qui illa quidè anxiè obseruabant, cùm interim vitæ officia, quæ his adumbrantur, negligerent. Et Christus à suis discessurus, illos non modò baptizare iubet, sed euangelij prædicationem maximè commendat. Quod ita Paulus obseruauit, ut se paßim quidem prædicauiße, paucißimos autem baptizauiße fateatur. 1. Cor. 1. Seruiunt hæc illis confutandis, qui externis signis gratiam alligantes, illorum vsum simpliciter ad salutem sufficere putant, nec doctrinam, qua illorum vsus illustretur, adhibent: imò peregrina lingua in illorum administratione vtuntur. Quàm verò id absurdum censeri debeat, Paulus in priori ad Corinth. 14. multis demonstrat.
units.tr: Next, we should observe that the apostle speaks here of John's ministry. For he says that John preached the baptism. He joins preaching to baptism, to show that John was a minister both of the teaching and of the sacrament. For just as he admonished men of purification by baptism, so, explaining its mysteries in words, he taught that purification is had in Christ alone, and that worthy fruits of repentance are required of those who have been purified. From this it is plain that doctrine must necessarily be joined to the sacraments, since without it their mysteries cannot be understood. Thus God once commanded that the secrets of the Passover feast be explained to the children. And we see that the sermons of the prophets were chiefly concerned with explaining the mysteries of the sacrifices and of the legal worship, while they most severely rebuked those who observed these outward things anxiously, but in the meantime neglected the duties of life that were foreshadowed by them. And Christ, about to leave his own, not only commanded them to baptise but most strongly commended the preaching of the gospel. Paul observed this so that he confesses that he preached everywhere, but baptised very few. 1 Cor. 1. These things serve to refute those who tie grace to external signs and think that the simple use of them is sufficient for salvation, and who do not bring in the teaching by which their use is made clear, but indeed use a foreign tongue in their administration. How absurd this ought to be judged, Paul shows at length in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 14.

units.la: II. Iesus vnctus à Deo.
units.tr: II. Jesus anointed by God.

units.la: Expositio autem euangelici negotio initij, eius authorem Iesum Christum describit, ut quis nam & qualis ille sit ac credi debeat, offendat. Differtè verò Iesum à Nazareth nominat, ut illum ipsum agnoscamus, quæ tum ob patriæ ignobilitatem, tum ob vilem totius conuersationis speciem pleriq; contempserunt. Hunc autem à Deo vnctum esse testatur, his verbis illum humani generis saluatorem, quem iam olim Deus destinauerat, esse docens. Nam vnctionis propter veterem typum meminit. Vngebantur enim antiquitus Sacerdotes & reges Israelis, quos promissi Saluatoris typum gessisse, satis constat. Et receptum erat, ut promissus Saluator Messias vel Christi, id est, vncti nomine designaretur, eò quòd ista denominatio illius sacerdotij & regnum, adeoq; omnē nostræ redemptionis modum significationem exprimebat. Quapropter in euangelio quoq; interrogati discipuli, quænam ipsi Iesum esse dicerent, hunc Christum, id est, vnctum illum Dei esse fatentur. Matth. 16. Luc. 9. Porrò, ne quis illum reliquis sacerdotibus & regibus nihilo excellentiorem esse putaret, qui propter externam vnctionem eodem nomine ornati fuerunt, Petrus hunc spiritu sancto & virtute vnctum fuisse docet: nimirum ad illud Dauidis alludens, qui de promissi Saluatoris regno vaticinans, ait: Vnxit te Deus oleo lætitiæ præ consortibus tuis. Psal. 45. Ita verò spiritu sanctum vocat, cuius auspicijs filius Dei incarnatus regnū suum & sacerdotium ita administrauit, ut nihil in illo triste & acerbum, sed omnia læta & iucunda habeantur. Sic enim ipse hoc apud prophetā interpretatur, dicens: Spiritus Domini Dei super me est, eò quòd vnxit me Dominus, & misit me, ut læta nunciem mansuetis, ut obligem vulnera corde totri torum, ut proclamem captiuis libertatem, vinctis apertionem, & cæcis visum, ut proclamem annum beneplaciti Domini, & c. Isa. 61. Præ consortibus verò vnctus fuisse dicitur, quia illi nō ad mensuram spiritum dedit Deus, sed ita, ut de eius plenitudine omnes nos accipiamus. Ioa. 1. & 3. Nam visibili columbæ specie super illū descendit, cùm à Iohanne baptizaretur, ut inde Iohannes agnosceret, hunc à Deo hominibus saluatorē esse declaratū. Vide Ioan. 1. Sunt & alia argumenta, quæ illum omnibus veteris Testamenti vnctis, siue illi reges siue sacerdotes fuerint, præstantiorem esse declarant. Licet enim illi Christi siue vnctī domini dicti sint, nemini tamen hoc datū, ut etiā subditos suos vngeret, & à se Christianos, id est, vnctos denominaret. Id verò Dei filius præstitit, qui vnxit nos & fecit nos reges & sacerdotes Deo patri suo. Apoc. 1. Nemo ite ex veteris Testamenti vnctis diuino honore & cultu dignus habitus est. Nemo totius orbis reformatione inuexit. Nemo à suis in tanto precio est habitus, vt ipso defuncto, propter ipsius nomen morte oppetere quisquā voluerit. Nullius præterea sacerdotiū aut regnum in hunc vsq; diem durat: & quia mortales illi erant, vicarijs & successoribus opus fuit, per quos officium, cui ipsi præfuerant, administraretur. At Dei filius æterni regni administrator fa-ctus omnem potestatem accepit in cælo & interra. Et quia ecclesiæ suæ præsens adest, nec vicario nec successore opus habet. Matth. 28. Idem sacerdos est in æternum iuxta ordinem Melchisedech. Psal. 110. Benedicit enim nobis omni spirituali benedictione. Ephes. 1. Docet per verbum externum & spiritus sui suggestionē, & ipse ecclesiæ suæ alios quidem dat apostolos, alios autem prophetas, alios euangelistas, alios verò pastores ac doctores, &c. Ephes. 4. Idem vnica pro nobis hostia oblata corporis & sanguinis sui precio totius mundi peccata expiauit, & vnica oblatione perfectos fecit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur. Hebr. 9. & 10. Adhæc in cælos subuectus pro nobis intercedit, & fidelem agit Pontificem in omnibus ijs, quæ nobis coram Deo agenda sunt. Heb. 2. & 4. Verè ergo Petrus dicit, hunc à Deo vnctum, id est, populi sui regem & sacerdotem constitutum esse. Vnde colligimus in æternum Dei decretum ab omnibus ijs peccari, quicunq, alios salutis suæ patronos, alios animarum saluatores, alios item saluatores & intercessores sibi faciunt. Ita enim filium Dei suo honore spoliant, quem is se nemini concessurum esse apud prophetam constanter affirmat. Isa. 42. Rursum, quia à Deo illum vnctum esse constat, insuperabilem fore credendum est regni ipsius potentiam, nec mundi aut inferorum vires illis metuendas esse, qui hunc regem agnoscunt. Quia tamen alibi quoq; hoc ipsum argumentum à nobis tractatum est, haec modò dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: The exposition of the beginning of the gospel describes its author, Jesus Christ, so that it becomes clear who and what he is and how he ought to be believed. Peter carefully names him Jesus of Nazareth, so that we may recognise this very man, whom many despised both because of the lowliness of his homeland and because of the humble appearance of his whole manner of life. He testifies that this man was anointed by God, teaching by these words that he is the Saviour of the human race whom God had long ago destined. For Peter recalls the anointing because of the old type. Priests and kings of Israel were anointed in ancient times, and it is well established that they bore the type of the promised Saviour. It was also the custom that the promised Saviour be designated Messiah or Christ, that is, by the name of the Anointed One, because that title expressed his priesthood and kingship, and so the whole manner of our redemption. Therefore in the gospel too, when the disciples were asked what they themselves said Jesus was, they confess that he is the Christ, that is, the Anointed One of God. Matt. 16; Luke 9. Furthermore, lest anyone think that he was in no way more excellent than the other priests and kings, who were adorned with the same name because of an external anointing, Peter teaches that he was anointed with the Holy Spirit and power. He clearly alludes to that saying of David, who, prophesying of the kingdom of the promised Saviour, says: God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. Ps. 45. He calls it the Holy Spirit in this way because under whose auspices the Son of God, incarnate, administered his kingdom and priesthood so that nothing in him is sad and bitter, but all things are joyful and pleasant. He himself interprets this in the prophet, saying: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me and sent me to bring good news to the meek, to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to captives, release to prisoners, and sight to the blind, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favour, and so on. Isa. 61. He is said to have been anointed above his companions because God did not give him the Spirit by measure, but so that we all receive from his fullness. John 1 and 3. For the Spirit descended upon him in the visible form of a dove when he was baptised by John, so that John might recognise that he had been declared by God to be the Saviour of men. See John 1. There are also other arguments which show that he is superior to all the anointed ones of the Old Testament, whether they were kings or priests. For although they were called the anointed lords, it was granted to none of them to anoint even their subjects and to call them Christians, that is, anointed ones, after himself. But the Son of God has done this, who anointed us and made us kings and priests to God his Father. Rev. 1. None of the anointed ones of the Old Testament was ever held worthy of divine honour and worship. None brought about a reformation of the whole world. None was held in such high esteem by his people that, after his death, anyone would wish to die for his name. Moreover, the priesthood or kingdom of none of them lasts to this day; and since they were mortal, they needed vicars and successors through whom the office they had held might be administered. But the Son of God, made administrator of an eternal kingdom, has received all power in heaven and on earth. And since he is present with his Church, he has no need of a vicar or successor. Matt. 28. He is a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek. Ps. 110. For he blesses us with every spiritual blessing. Eph. 1. He teaches through the outward Word and the prompting of his Spirit, and he himself gives to his Church some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers, and so on. Eph. 4. The same, by offering his body and blood as the one sacrifice for us, expiated the sins of the whole world, and by the one offering has made perfect for ever those who are sanctified. Heb. 9 and 10. Moreover, taken up into heaven, he intercedes for us and acts as a faithful High Priest in all those matters which must be dealt with on our behalf before God. Heb. 2 and 4. Rightly, then, Peter says that he was anointed by God, that is, appointed king and priest of his people. From this we gather that those sin against the eternal decree of God who make for themselves other patrons of salvation, other saviours of souls, and likewise other saviours and intercessors. For they strip the Son of God of his honour, which he constantly affirms through the prophet that he will give to no one. Isa. 42. Again, since it is established that he was anointed by God, we must believe that the power of his kingdom is unconquerable, and that the powers of the world or of hell are not to be feared by those who acknowledge this King. But since this same argument has been treated by us elsewhere, let what has been said here suffice.

units.la: Porrò ne quis Iesum dei filium, more vulgari hominum, nudo & inani titulo gloriari putaret, illum tam Regis quàm Sacerdotis officio fidelissimè functam esse & fungi Petrus docet. In praesenti autem generaliora praemittit, illius in nos beneficia exponens: postea de modo etiam redemptionis nostrae dicturus, vt sequens Sermo docebit. Et primò quide illum hinc inde obambulauisse & hominibus benefecisse dicit. Est hoc fidei regis simul & sacerdotis officium, non modò opem quaerentibus consilio & auxilio adesse, verumetiam hinc inde dispicere, qui nam tutore & benefactore opus habeant. Idcirco Dei filium, Iesum Christum fidelissime praestitisse, Euangelista docent. Nam vt nostrae salutis causa in mundum venit, ita salutis doctrinam & miracula, quibus hanc obsignabat, per omnes Iudaeae & Galilaeae locos circumtulit, nec alicubi diutius sedem fixam habuit, imò ingenuè confessus est, se passim omnibus euangelizare debere. Mar. 1. Luc. 4. Nec tantum ad se venientes humaniter excepit, sed etiam oneratos & laborantes amicè ad se inuitauit, omnibus ad se venientibus requiem & refocillationem pollicitus. Matth. 11. Et quod olim illud fecisse constat, id ipsum hodie etiam facit, dum euangelij sui praedicatione longè lateq; diffundit, vt illa imbris instar, modo hanc modo illam gentem coelestis verbi semine fecundam reddat: vt non immeritò hodie quoq; dici possit obambulare, & beneficia sua in quosuis obuios conferre. Nam erroribus deceptos fideliter erudit, seductos in viam reducit, vitijs corruptos amicè corrigit, afflictas conscientias humanissimè consolatur, & diuini iudicij metu consternatos, sua iustitia & satisfactione protegit. Magna ergo & enormis illorum ingratitudo est, qui tantum benefactore quasi rigidum & immitem horrere, & alibi cōsilium & opem quaerere consueuerunt. Longè tamen atrociorem illorum est iniquitas, qui verbum ipsius improbè reijciunt, nec illud audire dignantur, adeoq; salutem à se repellunt, quam obuijs vlnis amplecti, & indefesso studio inuestigare debebant. Est vtrunq; scelus nimis vulgare nostro seculo, quorum indignitatem si non oscitanter expendamus, tot tamq; pertinacium malorum, quae nos passim vrgent, causas minus mirabimur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone think that Jesus, the Son of God, is glorified in the common manner of men by an empty and bare title, Peter teaches that he has discharged the office of both King and Priest most faithfully, and continues to do so. For now he sets out more general matters, explaining his benefits towards us, and will speak later of the manner of our redemption, as the following sermon will teach. And first he says that Jesus went about here and there and did good to men. This is the office of a faithful king and priest at once: not only to be present with counsel and help for those who seek aid, but also to search out on every side those who need a guardian and benefactor. Accordingly, the evangelists teach that Jesus Christ most faithfully performed this. For just as he came into the world for the sake of our salvation, so he carried the doctrine of salvation and the miracles by which he confirmed it through all the regions of Judea and Galilee. He never settled for long in any one place, and indeed he openly confessed that he must preach the gospel everywhere. Mark 1; Luke 4. Nor did he only receive kindly those who came to him, but he also kindly invited to himself those who were burdened and labouring, promising rest and refreshment to all who came to him. Matt. 11. And what he is known to have done in the past, he does still today, while he spreads his gospel far and wide by preaching, so that, like rain, he makes now this nation, now that one, fruitful with the seed of the heavenly Word. Thus it can rightly be said today too that he goes about and bestows his benefits upon whomever he meets. For he faithfully instructs those deceived by errors, leads the strayed back onto the way, kindly corrects those corrupted by vices, most humanely comforts troubled consciences, and protects with his righteousness and satisfaction those dismayed by fear of divine judgement. Great and monstrous, then, is the ingratitude of those who are accustomed to dread him as if he were a harsh and cruel benefactor, and to seek counsel and help elsewhere. Far more atrocious, however, is the wickedness of those who wickedly reject his Word and do not deign to hear it, and so repel from themselves a salvation which they ought to embrace with open arms and seek out with tireless zeal. Both sins are far too common in our age; if we do not weigh their unworthiness carefully, we shall be less surprised at the causes of the many stubborn evils that press upon us on every side.

units.la: Alterum Iesu Christi beneficium est, quod per hunc sanatos esse dicit omnes eos, quos sua tyrannide diabolus oppresserat. Pertinet hoc proprie ad Regis officiu̅, de quo etiam Psal. 72. dicitur: Vindicabit afflictos in populo, seruabit pauperes, & violentum calumniatorem contundet, &c. At quia spiritualis redemptionis author fuit Christus, spiritualis quoq; tyranni mentionem Petrus facit: diaboli nimirum, qui postquam primos parentes transgressionis reos fecit, per eosdem omne calamitatum genus & ipsam mortem in mundum inuexit, adeoq; ex Dei permissione omne humanum genus immani tyrannide pressit, vnde etiam mundi huius princeps dictus est. Fecit enim vt per delicta morerentur, quos ad vitam Deus creauerat: vt contra naturae leges peccarent, quos ratione prae omnibus alijs animantibus Deus instruxerat: vt mendacibus daemoniorum oraculis sese dementari paterentur, qui à Dei verbo toti pendere debebant: vt ligna & lapides adorarent, & nefandis sacris daemones placarent, quos vnius Dei cultores esse decebat. Quia tamen pauci immanem agnoscebant diaboli tyrannidem, hoc quoq; permisit Deus, vt ab illo non pauci corporaliter etiam obsessi tam in seipsos quàm in alios homines indomitum furerent, sicut ex euangelij historia discere licet. At omnibus istis malis medicus datus est Iesus Christus, qui iuxta primam promissionem serpentis caput conterere, & (vt apostolus inquit) opera diaboli destruere debuit. 1. Iohan. 3. Illud verò se & velle & posse abunde testatus est, dum horrendis morborum flagellis excruciatos verbo curauit, daemonia & spiritus immundos expulit, & nec hiscere quidem illis permisit, qui paulò ante rerum domini videbatur. Referenda huc sunt quaecunq; eius generis miracula ab Euangelistis describuntur: quibus docetur fortiorem illum venisse, qui diaboli domum (mundum videlicet) ingressus, ipsum constrinxerit, & vasa illius diripuerit, sicuti ipse Christus in euangelio admonet. Luc. 11. Dei autem virtute haec omnia facta esse Petrus testatur, vt scribis respondeat, qui ipsum praesidio Beelzebul daemonia eijcere dicebant. Extant verò in historijs exempla, quae Christi virtute diaboli regnum destructum esse testantur. Nam & oracula omnia in Christi morte obmutuisse constat, & Constantinus Diocletiano regnante diabolum ex Apollinis antro conquestum fuisse scribit, quòd Christiani, quos ille iustos nominabat, obstarent, quò minus ve-ni, vt antehac oracula ederet. Veruntamen clariora Christi aduersus diabolum victoriae argumenta
units.tr: The second benefit of Jesus Christ is that, through him, all those whom the devil had oppressed with his tyranny have been healed. This properly pertains to the office of a king, of which it is also said in Psalm 72: He will defend the afflicted among the people, he will save the poor, and he will crush the violent oppressor, and so on. But since Christ was the author of a spiritual redemption, Peter also makes mention of a spiritual tyrant: namely the devil, who, after he made our first parents guilty of transgression, brought every kind of calamity and death itself into the world through them, and by God's permission pressed the whole human race with a savage tyranny; hence he is also called the prince of this world. For he made those whom God had created for life die through their sins; he made those whom God had equipped with reason above all other living beings sin against the laws of nature; he made those who ought to depend wholly on the Word of God allow themselves to be driven mad by the lying oracles of demons; he made them worship wood and stones and appease demons with unspeakable rites, when they ought to have been worshippers of the one God. Yet since few acknowledged the monstrous tyranny of the devil, God also permitted this: that not a few were possessed in body by him, and raged without restraint both against themselves and against other men, as may be learned from the gospel history. But Jesus Christ was given as a physician for all these evils, who, according to the first promise, was to crush the serpent's head and (as the apostle says) destroy the works of the devil. 1 John 3. He abundantly showed that he both wished and was able to do this, when he cured by a word those tortured by the dreadful scourges of diseases, expelled demons and unclean spirits, and did not even allow those who a little before seemed to be masters of affairs to open their mouths. To this category belong all the miracles of this kind that the evangelists describe, by which it is taught that a stronger one has come, who entered the house of the devil (that is, the world), bound him, and plundered his goods, as Christ himself admonishes in the gospel. Luke 11. Peter testifies that all these things were done by the power of God, in order to answer the scribes, who said that he cast out demons by the help of Beelzebul. There are also examples in the histories which testify that the kingdom of the devil was destroyed by the power of Christ. For it is well established that all oracles fell silent at the death of Christ, and Constantine writes that, in the reign of Diocletian, the devil complained from the cave of Apollo that the Christians, whom he called the just, were hindering him from giving oracles as he had done before. But the clearer proofs of Christ's victory over the devil

units.la: {III} Vt Christus sacerdotis & regis officio fungatur. Christus obambulauit benefaciens.
units.tr: {III} That Christ fulfils the office of priest and king. Christ went about doing good.

units.la: Christus sanauit à diabolo oppressos.
units.tr: Christ healed those oppressed by the devil.

units.la: Vide Eusebium de vita Constantini lib. 2. paulò post videbimus, vbi de illius morte & resurrectione Petrus disserit. Interim nostri nos officij meminisse decet, quod est, vt ex potestate tenebrarum in regnum filij Dei translati, libertatem nostram tueamur, & contra communem hostem Satanam assiduè pugnemus, ne quando ingrati deprehendamur liberatori Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: See Eusebius, On the Life of Constantine, book 2; we shall see shortly, where Peter discourses on his death and resurrection. Meanwhile it becomes us to remember our duty, namely that, having been transferred from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of God, we should guard our liberty and fight constantly against the common enemy Satan, lest we be found ungrateful to our deliverer Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 76.

units.la: Et nos sumus testes omnium, quæ fecit in regione Iudæorum & Hierosolymis: quæ occiderunt suspensum in ligno. Hunc Deus suscitauit tertio die, & consp icuum exhibuit, non toti populo, sed testibus prius ad hoc delectis à Deo: nobis nimirum, qui cum illo comedimus & bibimus, post quã à mortuis resurrexit. Et mandauit nobis, vt prædicaremus populo, ac testificaremur, quòd ipse sit definitus ille à Deo iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Huic omnes prophetæ testimonium ferunt, quòd remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen eius, quisquis in eum crediderit.
units.tr: "And we are witnesses of all that he did in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem, whom they killed by hanging him on a tree. God raised him up on the third day and caused him to be seen openly, not by all the people, but by witnesses chosen beforehand by God, that is, by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. And he commanded us to preach to the people and testify that he is the judge of the living and the dead, appointed by God. To him all the prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."

units.la: Duus Petrus Cornelium Centurionem, cui à Deo doctor destinatus erat, ita instituit, vt simul omnibus hominibus generalem & absolutissimam salutis doctrinam proponat. Nam vnicum humani generis saluatorem, Iesum Christum, illi prædicat, in quo omnem salutis nostræ rationem comprehendi omnis scriptura testatur. Et de hoc quidem, in ijs quæ proximè præceperunt, duo dixit. Primum, quòd ipsum Deus vnxerit, id est, populi sui regem & sacerdotem constituerit. Vnde colligimus, in aeternum Dei decretum ab omnibus ijs peccari, qui in salutis causa alios sibi assertores & mediatores constituunt. Deinde qua fide & diligentia officio suo Christus Iesus functus sit, docet. Nam illum passim obambulauisse, & salutis beneficium etiam non quærentibus singulari liberalitate obtulisse dicit. Omnium vero studiorum hic illi finis & scopus fuit, vt diaboli tyrannide oppressos in Dei regnum & libertatem filiorum Dei transferret. Cui liberationi per miracula præludum est, quibus tam morbis incurabilibus quàm daemoniorum intemperie vexatos salutari ope & verbi sui potentia fidelissimè subleuauit. His vero ea in præsenti subijcit Petrus, quæ salutis doctrinam absolunt. Nam primo quidem modum & rationem, quam Christus in redimenda mortalium genere adhibuit, recenset: deinde vero, vt horum vtilitas & fructus ad nos quoq; redire possit, docet. Est ergo locus hic dignus, in cuius consyderatione non vulgari diligentia versemur.
units.tr: While Peter instructs Cornelius the centurion, to whom God had sent him as teacher, he sets forth at the same time to all men a general and most complete doctrine of salvation. For he preaches to him the one Saviour of the human race, Jesus Christ, in whom all Scripture testifies that the whole plan of our salvation is contained. On this matter, in the words that immediately precede, he says two things. First, that God anointed him, that is, appointed him king and priest of his people. From this we gather that the decree of God is violated for ever by all those who set up other advocates and mediators for themselves in the cause of salvation. Second, he teaches with what faith and diligence Jesus Christ discharged his office. For he says that Jesus went about everywhere and, with singular generosity, offered the benefit of salvation even to those who did not seek it. The whole aim and goal of his labours was to transfer those oppressed by the tyranny of the devil into the kingdom of God and the freedom of the sons of God. This liberation was foreshadowed by miracles, by which he most faithfully relieved, by saving help and the power of his word, those afflicted with incurable diseases as well as those tormented by demons. Peter now adds those things which complete the doctrine of salvation. For first he recounts the manner and method which Christ used in redeeming the human race; then he teaches how the benefit and fruit of these things may also come back to us. This passage, therefore, is worthy of our consideration, and we should give it no ordinary attention.

units.la: Priusquam vero humanæ redemptionis modum & ordinem attingat, doctrinæ suæ confirmationem, à testibus desumptam, interserit, dicens: Et nos sumus testes omnium, quæ fecit in regione Iudæorum & Hierosolymis. Nec illud cuicquam vel absurdum vel insolens videri debet, quòd seipsum vnà cum alijs collegis dictorum testem tam audacter Petrus producit. Nam hoc illis officij à Christo impositum fuisse iam sæpe audiuimus: & paulò post dicetur, ipsos à Deo electos fuisse, vt de Iesu Christo, & ijs, quæ hic salutis nostræ causa fecit, testarentur. Docent hæc quàm graue illorum scelus sit, qui euangelio credere dedignantur. Quia enim non simplex aut vulgaris est rerum à Christo gestarum narratio, sed testimonium habet, cuius author est ipse Deus, facile patet in ipsum Deum contumeliam istam recidere: vt alibi copiosius dictum est.
units.tr: Before he reaches the manner and order of human redemption, Peter inserts a confirmation of his teaching, drawn from witnesses, saying: "And we are witnesses of all that he did in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem." Nor should this seem to anyone either absurd or strange, that Peter so boldly puts himself forward, together with his fellow apostles, as a witness of these things. For we have often heard that this duty was laid upon them by Christ; and shortly it will be said that they were chosen by God to bear witness concerning Jesus Christ and the things which he did here for our salvation. These words teach how grievous is the sin of those who disdain to believe the gospel. For since the account of the things done by Christ is not simple or ordinary, but has a testimony whose author is God himself, it is easy to see that this insult recoils upon God himself; as has been said more fully elsewhere.

units.la: Cæterum quoad nostræ redemptionis modum, quem hoc loco præcipuè tractari diximus, triadè Christo dicuntur, quibus omnia ea comprehendi constat, quæ in hac causa fieri oportebat. Inter quæ primus locus morti Christi tribuitur, quam paucis attingit, quia alioqui satis nota erat. Dicit autem in ligno suspensum à Iudæis occisum esse. Et ligni quidem meminit, non tam vt mortis genus crudele & atrox exprimat, quàm vt sacrificij mysterium, quod Christus moriens pro peccatis nostris obtulit, in mentem auditoribus reuocet. Constat enim in lignorum flrue sacrificia adoleri & offerri consueuisse. Et sic quidem ipse Petrus locum hunc interpretari videtur, quando in prioris epistolæ cap. 2. Christum peccata nostra in corpore suo super lignum tulisse, id est, corporis sui sacrificio in ara crucis expiauisse scribit. Idem Christus docet, quando ait, quòd carne suam pro mundi vita daturus sit: quod illu nos alibi quã in cruce fecisse constat. Iob. 6. Copiosius vero horum interpres est Isaias propheta, qui cap. 53. ait: Propter transgressiones nostras vulneratus est & attritus propter iniquitates nostras. Multa enim correctionis nostrae ei imposita est, & in liuore eius nobis medicatum est. Nos omnes tanquam ouis errauimus, quisq; viam suam sectatus: Dominus autem effecit vt in ipsum incurreret omnium no- strum iniquitas, &c. Id vero ad Christi sacerdotium pertinebat, quem hoc pasto (vt Paulus monet) nò per sanguinem hircorum aut vitulorum, sed per proprium sanguinem & suiipsius immolationem in cœlos ingredi oportuit, ad profligationem peccati, vt multorum peccata tolleret. Hebr.10. Atqui hinc redemptionis nostræ initium fieri oportebat, quando propter peccata nobis Deus iratus erat, vt in illius conspectu nobis comparere non liceret. Atque hæc demum salutaris est mortis Christi consy deratio, si in illa corporis sui sacrificium, quod pro peccatis nostris obtulit, meditemur. Interim non temere factum putabimus, quod cum mortis Christi simpliciter meminisse posset, illum à Iudæis oc- cisum fuisse dicit. Ita enim immemorem gentis suæ ingratitudinem accusat, maximè cum paulò ante tam diligentem beneficiorum Christi mentionem fecisset. Et obseruanda est mundi ingratitudo, quæ illi perpetua fere est, ne hodie piorum afflictiones, & persecutiones, quibus euangelij doctrina petitur, cum offendiculo admiremur.
units.tr: Furthermore, as to the manner of our redemption, which we said is to be treated chiefly in this place, the apostle refers to three things in Christ, which are known to comprise all that had to be done in this cause. Of these, the first place is given to the death of Christ, which he touches on briefly, because it was otherwise well known. He says that Christ was killed by the Jews by being hanged on a tree. He mentions the tree, not so much to express the cruel and savage kind of death, as to recall to the hearers' minds the mystery of the sacrifice which Christ offered dying for our sins. For it is established that sacrifices were customarily burned and offered upon wood. And Peter himself seems to interpret this passage in this way, when in chapter 2 of his first epistle he writes that Christ bore our sins in his body upon the tree, that is, expiated them by the sacrifice of his body on the altar of the cross. Christ himself teaches the same, when he says that he would give his flesh for the life of the world; which it is evident he did elsewhere than on the cross (John 6). But the more ample interpreter of these things is the prophet Isaiah, who says in chapter 53: "He was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed. We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; but the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all," etc. Now this pertained to the priesthood of Christ, who (as Paul warns) had to enter into heaven not by the blood of goats or calves, but by his own blood and by the offering of himself, to put away sin, so that he might take away the sins of many (Heb. 10). Yet from this the beginning of our redemption had to be made, since God was angry with us on account of our sins, so that we could not appear in his sight. And this, finally, is the saving consideration of the death of Christ, if we meditate on the sacrifice of his body which he offered for our sins. Meanwhile we shall not think it was done without purpose that, although he could have spoken simply of the death of Christ, he says that he was killed by the Jews. For in this way he accuses the ingratitude of his own nation, which was forgetful, especially since he had just made such a careful mention of the benefits of Christ. And we must observe the ingratitude of the world, which is almost perpetual in it, so that we do not now marvel with offence at the afflictions and persecutions of the pious, by which the doctrine of the gospel is assailed.

units.la: Secundus locus in redemptionis nostræ modo & ordine, resurrectioni Christi gloriosa tribuitur, de qua maiori diligentia Petrus disserit, eò quòd hæc præcipuum nostræ salutis fundamentum est. Nota enim sunt illa Pauli: Quòd si Christus non resurrexit, inanis est prædicatio nostra, inanis est & fides vestra: adhuc estis in peccatis vestris: & qui obdormierunt in Christo, perierunt, &c. 1.Cor.15. Nam vt certa nobis salus constare posset, mortem, quæ hucusq; per peccatum dominata fuerat, de- uinci & exarmari oportebat. Quæ si Christum quoq;, vt reliquos mortales detinuisset, nemo vtiq; de salute parta quicquam sperare poterat. Quare vt Lazari & quorundam aliorum resuscitatione se vitæ simul & mortis dominum antea Christus declarauerat: ita cum ipse mortem adiuisset, & sepul- tus iaceret, tertia die tanquam indomitus vitior mortis vincula disrupit, & effractis inferorum por- tis in vitam redijt. Fuitq; ea res infallibile & euidens deuictæ mortis simul & peccati argumentum. Quia vero resurrectionem Christi improbè negabant & calumniabantur Iudæi, à quibus milites quo- que in eum finem pecunijs corruptos fuisse Matthæus docet, magna constantia illam in præsenti Pe- trus asserit. Deus (inquit) suscitauit Iesum tertio die, & conspicuum exhibuit, non toti populo (neç enim digni erant, quibus tam familiariter Christus innotesceret, quem incurabili odio persequeban- tur) sed testibus prius ad hoc electis à Deo: nobis nimirum, qui cum illo comedimus & bibimus, post- quam à mortuis resurrexit. Et cum multa alia vera resuscitationis argumenta adducere posset, eo contentus est, quo & ipse Christus illius veritatem maximè asseruit, cum videlicet semel & iterum in conspectu discipulorum cibum ab ipsis oblatum sumpsit. Vide Luc.24. & Iohan.21.cap. Est autem admiranda hæc Christi facilitas, qui vt resurrectioni suæ fidem faceret apud nos, quorū tarditatem probè nouerat, eò vsq; sese demittere dignatus est, vt cibum quoq;, quo clarificatum corpus minimè opus habebat, sumpserit, ne quis illum posthac vero & organico corpore, quo ante in terris versatus erat, resurrexisse dubicaret. Quò maior est illorum improbitas & nequitia, qui ne sic quidem mortuo- rum resurrectionem negare & scurriliter insectari desinunt. Qui cum Iudæorū similes sint, ipsi quoq; indigni censebuntur, quibus gloriosa Christi resurrectio saluti cedat.
units.tr: The second place in the manner and order of our redemption is given to the glorious resurrection of Christ, on which Peter speaks with greater care, because this is the chief foundation of our salvation. Those words of Paul are well known: "If Christ has not risen, our preaching is in vain, and your faith is also in vain; you are still in your sins; and those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (1 Cor. 15). For that our salvation might be certain, death, which until then had reigned through sin, had to be conquered and disarmed. If Christ too had been held by it, like other mortals, no one could in any way hope for the salvation obtained. Therefore, just as Christ had previously shown himself to be lord of life and of death by raising Lazarus and certain others, so when he himself had undergone death and lay buried, on the third day, like an unconquered victor, he broke the bonds of death, and, the gates of the underworld being broken open, he returned to life. And this event was an infallible and evident proof that death and sin were overcome. But because the Jews wrongly denied and slandered the resurrection of Christ, and Matthew teaches that soldiers were bribed with money to this end, Peter now asserts it with great constancy. "God," he says, "raised Jesus up on the third day and caused him to be seen openly, not by all the people" (for they were not worthy that Christ, whom they persecuted with incurable hatred, should make himself so familiarly known to them), "but by witnesses chosen beforehand by God: that is, by us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead." And although he could adduce many other true proofs of the resurrection, he is content with that by which Christ himself most strongly confirmed its truth, namely when he took food offered by his disciples, once and again, in their sight (see Luke 24 and John 21). This humility of Christ is admirable: he deigned to stoop so far, so as to give us proof of his resurrection, knowing well our slowness, that he also took food, which his glorified body did not at all need, lest anyone should afterwards doubt that he had risen in the true and organic body with which he had previously lived on earth. The greater, therefore, is the wickedness and malice of those who, even so, do not cease to deny the resurrection of the dead and to mock it scurrilously. Since they are like the Jews, they too will be judged unworthy that the glorious resurrection of Christ should be for their salvation.

units.la: Porrò, licet Dei filius, Iesus Christus, morte & resurrectione sua (cui eiusdem in cœlos Ascensio commodè includi potest) omnem nostræ redemptionis & salutis rationem absoluerit, cum his & pec- cati noxam expiarit, & mortem omnemq; inferorum potestatem deuicerit: tertium tamen his Petrus subijcit, vltimum videlicet ipsius aduentum, quo ad iudicandum viuos & mortuos rediturus est. Eo enim articulo tam diuinitatis Christi, quàm regni ipsius certissimū & cumprimis euidens argumen- tum exhibet. Nam vt iudicare regis officiū est, ita diuinitatem suam ipse Christus hoc argumento asserit, quod sibi à patre omne iudicium traditum esse testatur. Iohan.5. Est autem vtilis & cum primis necessaria huius articuli consyderatio. Si quis enim rerū huius seculi cursum inspiciat, multa occurrent, quæ vt Christum Iesum humanarū rerum curam prorsus abiecisse credamus, suadere pos- sunt. Nam pios Christi cultores varijs afflictionibus vexari, egere, laborare, & impiorum libidinē subiectos esse videmus. Rursum vero lætis rerum successibus impij fruuntur, & impunè in quosuis grassantur. Quæ res quantum ad fidem labefactandam possit, prophetarum exempla docent, quos in- terdum ita cōmotos fuisse legimus, vt iustam se de Deo querendi causam habere putaret. Et sanè quiā Christum regem agnoscat, si incertas & nonnunquam indignas rerum humanarum vices consyderet? Caeterum hic succurrat, non dormitare regem nostrum & vindicem Iesum Christum, & fore aliquando iudicij vniuersalis diem, quo tam viuos quam mortuos ad Christi tribunal sisti oporteat, vt in corporibus suis recipiant iuxta id quod fecerunt, siue bonum siue malum. 2.Cor.5. Nam vt Paulus admonet, ad archangeli tubam mortui resurgent, & qui in eum vsq; diem superstites fuerint, momento temporis immutabuntur. 1.Cor.15. & 1.Thess.4.cap. Fatetur autem Petrus serio huius articuli praedicationem apostolis mandatam esse. Mandauit nobis (inquit) vt praedicaremus populo, & testificaremur, quod ipse sit definitus ille a Deo iudex viuorum & mortuorum. Nam vt ea, quae modo de Christi diuinitate & regno dicta sunt, omittamus plurimum cum vitae institutioni, tum consolationi piorum huius articuli consyderatio feruit. Cum enim plerosq; in peccandi libidinem hac potissimum causa abripi videamus, quod vel mortem vltimam lineam rerum esse & nullum post hanc vitam iudicium fore, sibi persuaserunt: vel de illo negligentius cogitant: non potest non vehementissimus ad omnis virtutis studium stimulus esse, si homo se olim Christi iudicio sistendum esse cogitet, vt ibi tam dictorum quam factorum omnium rationem reddat. Ea certe cogitatio & carnis laisciuientis af sectus, & mundi illecebras efficacissime restinguit. Rursum non alia fortior & efficacior in aduersis consolatio pijs oboriri potest, quam si iudicij diem fore intelligant, quo ipsorum innocentiam Christus manifestaturus & promissa vitae praemia largiturus sit. Ideo Christus de signis, quae nouissimis diem praecedent, differens, His (ait) fieri incipientibus, leuate capita vestra, quia redemptio vestra appropinquat. Luc.21. Et Paulus nos e coelis saluatorem expectare docet, qui corpora nostra mortalia & misera corpori suo glorioso conformia reddat. Philip.3. Idem, vt fideles nouissimi aduentus Christi mutua meditatione sese consolentur, monet. 1.Thess.4. Et est haec ingens nostrae fidei gloria, quod eum diem nobis laetum & iucundum reddat, cuius impij huius saeculi filij nunquam sine dolore & horrifico animorum terrore meminisse possunt.
units.tr: Moreover, although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, by his death and resurrection (to which his Ascension into heaven may fitly be joined), has completed the whole plan of our redemption and salvation, has by these atoned for the guilt of sin, and has conquered death and all the power of the underworld, Peter nevertheless adds a third point to these, namely his final coming, when he will return to judge the living and the dead. For in that article he presents a most certain and especially clear proof both of Christ's divinity and of his kingdom. For just as it is the office of a king to judge, so Christ himself asserts his divinity by this argument, since he testifies that all judgment has been handed to him by the Father. John 5. The consideration of this article is also useful and especially necessary. For if anyone looks at the course of affairs in this age, many things present themselves which may persuade us that Christ Jesus has utterly abandoned the care of human affairs. For we see that the pious worshippers of Christ are vexed with various afflictions, are in want, labour, and are subjected to the lust of the ungodly. Again, the impious enjoy happy outcomes of affairs and rage with impunity against whomever they please. How much this can shake faith the examples of the prophets teach, whom we read were at times so moved that they thought they had a just reason to complain about God. And indeed, how could one acknowledge Christ as king if one considers the uncertain and sometimes unworthy changes of human affairs? But let this come to mind: our king and avenger Jesus Christ is not asleep, and there will at some time be a day of universal judgment, on which both the living and the dead must be brought before the tribunal of Christ, so that they may receive in their bodies according to what they have done, whether good or evil. 2 Cor. 5. For, as Paul warns, the dead will rise at the trumpet of the archangel, and those who are alive until that day will be changed in a moment of time. 1 Cor. 15, and 1 Thess. 4. Peter also solemnly affirms that the preaching of this article was entrusted to the apostles. "He has commanded us," he says, "to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead." For, to pass over what has just been said about Christ's divinity and kingdom, the consideration of this article is very much conducive both to the instruction of life and to the consolation of the pious. For since we see that many are hurried into the lust of sinning chiefly for this reason, that they have persuaded themselves that death is the final boundary of things and that there will be no judgment after this life, or else they think about it too carelessly, the consideration of it cannot but be a most vehement spur to the pursuit of every virtue, if a man thinks that he must one day stand before the judgment of Christ, there to render an account of all his words and deeds. This thought most effectively quenches both the lustful desires of the flesh and the allurements of the world. Again, no stronger or more effective consolation can arise for the pious in adversity than if they understand that there will be a day of judgment, on which Christ will make their innocence manifest and bestow the promised rewards of life. Therefore Christ, speaking of the signs that will precede the last day, said: "When these things begin to happen, lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near." Luke 21. And Paul teaches us to expect a Saviour from heaven, who will make our mortal and wretched bodies conformed to his glorious body. Phil. 3. The same Paul urges the faithful to console one another by mutual meditation on the last coming of Christ. 1 Thess. 4. And this is the great glory of our faith, that it makes that day joyful and pleasant for us, a day which the impious sons of this age can never remember without pain and a horrifying terror of mind.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, qua docemur, vt nos salutis, quae in Christo habetur, confortes vel capaces fieri possimus. Hanc vero magna verborum gravitate Petrus enunciat, dicens: Huic omnes prophetae testimonium ferunt, quod remissionem peccatorum accipiat per nomen eius, quisquis in eum crediderit. Sunt hic singula distinguenda, vt maiorem euidentiam doctrina hac cumprimis necessaria sortiatur. Primo enim fructum eorum, quae hucusq; expositi sunt, indicans, in Christi nomine nobis peccatorum remissionem obtingere docet. At dum huius meminit, non obscure nos peccatores esse testatur, quibus illa opus sit. Dum vero eandem in Christo conferri docet, gratuitam facit, quae absq; nostro merito ex mera Dei gratia obtingat: vt hic plane illud Paulinum audias: Omnes peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei, iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu, &c. Rom.3. Et huc referri debent, quae supra de peccatorum expiatione in ara crucis facta, diximus. Ibi enim Dei filius pro nobis peccatum factus est, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum. 2.Cor.5. Tolluntur hac sententia omnes aliarum sectarum religiones. Quia enim in vnius Christi nomine peccatorum remissionem monstrat Petrus, omnem operam eos perdere docet, qui hanc extra illum quaerunt: adeoq; nouo argumento grauem illam sententiam confirmat, qua coram Hierosolymitano Senatui testatus est, nullum aliud sub coelo nomen hominibus datum esse, in quo saluari possint. Idem ipse Christus affirmat, quando ait: Ego sum via, veritas & vita. Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Iohan.14.
