For he gave an account of what he had done, most courteously and most carefully, to those from whom he could rightly have demanded an account himself. Leaving aside many other arguments, he presses this one alone: that he had done all these things not by private counsel but by God's direction and command. From this example we learn what arguments we too ought to use against those who, with similar peevishness, are accustomed to accuse us today of breaking human traditions and customs. The authority of the divine Word should be enough for us; those who dare to spurn it are unworthy that the Church of Christ should take any account of them.

units.la: Restat autem in huius historiæ tractatione, vt Petri apologiam exceperint, qui paulò ante tam rigidi censores fuerunt. Dicuntur autem quieuisse & Deum glorificauisse, dicentes: Ergo & gentibus Deus pœnitentiam dedit ad vitam. Porrò quieuerunt, nec aduersus Dei præceptum & voluntatem humanis rationibus contendere perrexerunt. Quo argumento abunde declaratur, illos non malligno ligno vel odij vel inuidiæ affectu, sed potius inconsulto & cæco pietatis zelo litem hanc instituisse: quem Paulus quoque Iudæis alicubi tribuit. Et quia hunc in illis Petrus facile deprehendebat, mitius cum ipsis agendum esse duxit. Nec enim tanquàm incurabiles negligi, aut etiam amarulentius abijci debent, quicunq; zelo gloriæ Dei agitantur, eo quòd tales rationibus cedere & acquiescere solent. Est vero hoc vere fidelium, vt rationibus è dei verbo productis libenter cedant, quamuis non plena illis omnium eorum, quæ dicuntur, ratio satis constet. Nam hoc demum verum & proprium est fidei exercitium, quando nostram rationem dei verbo & præceptis subijcimus, quod Paulus pas-sim sub fidei obedientia docet, quam euangelicæ prædicationis finem & scopum esse testatur. 2. Corinth.10. Rom.1.& 16. Unde facile patet, minimè pro fidelibus eos agnosci debere, quicunque adversus diserta Dei oracula pertinacius disputare non erubescunt.
units.tr: It remains, in treating this history, to notice that those who a little before had been such stern critics accepted Peter's defence. They are said to have become quiet and to have glorified God, saying: "So God has granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles also." They were quiet, and they did not go on contending against God's precept and will with human reasons. From this it is abundantly clear that they raised this dispute not from a malicious motive of hatred or envy, but rather from an ill-considered and blind zeal for piety; Paul also attributes this to the Jews somewhere. And because Peter readily perceived this in them, he judged that he should deal more gently with them. For those who are moved by zeal for the glory of God should not be neglected as incurable, nor cast off more bitterly, since such people are accustomed to yield to reasons and to acquiesce. It is truly the mark of the faithful to give way willingly to reasons drawn from God's Word, even when the full account of all that is said is not clear to them. For this is the true and proper exercise of faith, when we subject our own reason to God's Word and precepts, which Paul teaches everywhere under the obedience of faith, and which he testifies to be the end and aim of the evangelical preaching (2 Cor. 10; Rom. 1 and 16). Hence it is easy to see that those should by no means be counted as faithful who are not ashamed to dispute more stubbornly against the plain oracles of God.

units.la: Præterea Deum quoque glorificauisse dicuntur: quod euidentius signum est, ipsos vere & ex animo Petri excusationem recepisse. Sunt enim, qui rationibus conuicti, tacent quidem cum quod respondeant non habent, interim iuxta illud poetæ, taciti premunt alto corde dolorem. At qui Deum glorificat, infallibili argumento testatur, sibi per omnia satisfactum esse. Docemur autem, congratulandum esse ijs, quos Deus veritatis luce dignatur. Iubet hoc cum diuinæ gloriæ studium, quo Christianos homines flagrare decet, tum charitas, quæ nos totos proximi commodis prouehendis obstringit. Et sane non aliter est, quæ fidelem animam ß uberiori gaudio perfundat, quàm si veritatis lucem cum diuinæ gloriæ illustri incremento & multorum salute propagari videat. Rursum ex animo dolere nos decet, si quando aliquos vel negligi, vel à salutis via deficere videmus. Ita Samuelem propter Saulis casum infelicem iugi dolore seipsum excruciauisse legimus. Et Paulus pro Iudæis assiduè in deprecationibus versatur, & pro illis anathema à Christo fieri cupit, vt ipsi salui fiant. Rom. 9.& 10. Ac hodie vetrinque frigentium: quæ non postrema causa est, quòd minus feliciter procedit euangelicæ doctrinæ cursus.
units.tr: Moreover, they are said to have glorified God as well, which is a clearer sign that they truly and from the heart accepted Peter's excuse. For there are some who, when convicted by arguments, keep silent, since they have nothing to answer, yet, in the words of the poet, they press down their grief deep in their hearts. But one who glorifies God bears infallible witness that he is fully satisfied. We are taught, moreover, that we ought to rejoice with those whom God deigns to enlighten with the light of truth. Both the zeal for God's glory, with which Christian people ought to burn, and the love which binds us to advance the welfare of our neighbour, require this. And indeed nothing fills a faithful soul with greater joy than to see the light of truth spread abroad with the illustrious increase of God's glory and the salvation of many. Again, we ought to grieve from the heart whenever we see some either neglected or falling away from the way of salvation. So we read that Samuel tormented himself with constant sorrow over Saul's unhappy fall. And Paul is constantly engaged in prayers for the Jews, and desires to be made an anathema from Christ for their sake, that they might be saved (Rom. 9 and 10). And today there is a like coldness on both sides, which is no small reason why the course of the evangelical doctrine advances less happily.

units.la: Sed verba videamus, quibus isti animorum suorum affectum testantur. Ergo & gentibus (aiunt) dedit deus pœnitentiam ad vitam. Dicitur autem bifariam deus dare pœnitentiam: quando nimirum vel locum & tempus ad pœnitentiam concedit: vel animos hominum spiritu & verbo suo emollit & conuertit, vt per pœnitentiam ad meliorem vitæ rationem disponantur. Vtrunq; hoc loco fatu esse constat, quàmuis posterior sensus præsenti argumento magis conueniat. Est autem obseruatio dignissimum, quòd gentibus per euangelij prædicationem pœnitentiam ad vitam datam esse, dicunt. Ea enim locutione testantur, se de ea pœnitentia loqui, quæ propter fidem in Christum salutifica est, & quam totius negotij euangelici scopum dicere possumus: qui est, vt per Christum deo reconciliati, ad illum totis animis conuertamur, inq; ipso viuamus. Ita enim Paulus scribit: Deus reconciliauit sibi per Iesum Christum, dedito nobis ministerium reconciliationis. Itaq; nomine Christi legatione fungimur tanquà Deo vos obsecrante per nos, Christi nomine rogamus: Reconciliemini deo, &c. 2. Corinth.5. Pœnitentiam verò diserte nominant, nimirum ad illud Christi respicientes, qui in nomine suo cùm pœnitentiam, tum peccatorum remissionem prædicare iubet. Nec vnquam duo hæc separari debent, ne qua illis occasio detur, qui sub euangelij prætextu carnis licentiam venantur. Rur-sum consolationem insignem habet, quòd pœnitentia ad vitam dari dicitur. Nunquam ergo illa in fidelibus vana est, aut infrugifera, sed illos per Christum salutis confortes reddit. Extant Dei promissiones, quibus passim gratiam suam & vitam ijs pollicetur, qui ex animo ad illum conuertuntur. Vide Ezech.18. vbi ait: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur, & viuat. Nec putandum est, quemquam à deo vanis pollicitationibus deludi siue lactari. Pertinet huc totus ferè Iudicū liber, qui multis exemplis euincit, nunquam sine fructu Israelitas ad deum per veram pœnitentiam conuersos fuisse. Et Nineuitas iam latam aduersus se dei sententiam fideli pœnitentia reuocauisse, constat. Quid verò de illis dico, quando Achabi quoq; temporariâ pœnitentiam Dei voce commendatam fuisse legimus? 1. Reg.21. Debent hæc ijs animos addere, qui in desperationis præcipitio consistunt, dum se deo propter anteacta scelera ita displicere putant, vt nec pœnitentiam suam illam gratam esse di-cant. Quibus illa prophetæ succurrere debent: Si peccata vestra fuerint vt coccus, niue albiora red-dentur: si instar purpuræ rubeant, instar natiuæ lanæ fient. Item: Misericors est & beneficus domi-nus, patiens etiam & magnæ benignitatis. Qui non perpetuò solet litigare, &c. Vide Psal.103.
units.tr: But let us look at the words by which these men bear witness to the disposition of their minds. "So God has granted," they say, "repentance unto life to the Gentiles also." Now God is said to grant repentance in two ways: either when he allows a place and time for repentance, or when he softens and turns the minds of men by his Spirit and Word, so that they are disposed through repentance to a better manner of life. Both senses are plainly admissible here, although the latter fits the present argument better. It is also most worthy of notice that they say repentance unto life was granted to the Gentiles through the preaching of the gospel. By this expression they show that they are speaking of that repentance which is saving on account of faith in Christ, and which we may call the whole aim of the evangelical business: that, being reconciled to God through Christ, we turn to him with all our hearts and live in him. For so Paul writes: "God has reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation... Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us; we beg you in Christ's name: be reconciled to God," etc. (2 Cor. 5). They explicitly name repentance, doubtless looking to that command of Christ, who bids repentance and the remission of sins to be preached in his name. These two must never be separated, lest an occasion be given to those who, under the pretext of the gospel, hunt for licence for the flesh. Again, they have a remarkable consolation in the fact that repentance is said to be given unto life. It is therefore never empty or fruitless in believers, but through Christ makes them partakers of salvation. God's promises stand, by which he everywhere offers his grace and life to those who sincerely turn to him. See Ezekiel 18, where he says: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live." Nor should we think that anyone is deluded or flattered by God with empty promises. Almost the whole book of Judges bears on this, which proves by many examples that Israelites who turned to God through true repentance were never without fruit. And it is well known that the Ninevites by faithful repentance turned away the sentence of God already pronounced against them. But what need I say about them, when we read that even Ahab was commended for a temporary repentance by the voice of God? (1 Kings 21). These things ought to encourage those who stand on the brink of despair, thinking that because of their past sins they so displease God that they cannot say their repentance is acceptable to him. The words of the prophet ought to come to their aid: "If your sins are like scarlet, they will be made whiter than snow; if they are red like purple, they will become like natural wool." Likewise: "The Lord is merciful and bountiful, patient also and of great kindness, who does not always keep up his strife," etc. See Psalm 103.

units.la: Porrò absoluta Cornelij Centurionis historia, quae gentium vocationis principia adeoq; primitias continet, ad intermissam rerum ad communem ecclesiam pertinentium narrationem D. Lucas redit, & vt regnum Christi inter gentes longè lateq; extendi caperit, commemorat. In primis verò de Antiochia ad Christum conuersa agit, vbi Christianorum nomen primò obtinuit. Et ante omnia quidem tantæ rei occasionem attingit, quam ex persecutione propter Stephanum excitata, oblatam & à viris piis arreptam fuisse docet. Atqui cumprimis memorabile illud est, quòd tanti boni initium ex re funestissima obortu fuit. Quàm misera enim persecutionis illius tempore fuerit ecclesiae facies, supra cap. 8. vidimus. Quando eousq; deuenerat persequentium furor, vt ne clanculò quidem liceret Christianos esse, cùm ex aedibus quoq; priuatis cùm viri tum mulieres ad lanienam pertraherentur. Quae cau-sa fuit, vt ecclesia hinc inde dissipata, lacerum quoddam & nulla arte curabile corpus esse videretur. At Dei bonitate & gratia fit, vt ex singulis pene dissipatae ecclesiae membris nouum corpus enascatur. Nam quos tam diræ persecutionis tempestas hinc inde disiecit, sui officij memores, passim Christiano men prædicare incipiunt, & nonnulli ex illis in Phoeniciam & Cyprum vsq; delati, eas quoq; regiones euangelij fulgore illustrarunt. Quo exemplo primitiuam ecclesiam, adeoq; omnium seculorum fideles confirmari oportuit, ne immanibus hostium veritatis conatibus offendantur, quando his Christi regnum non euerti nec in angustum redigi, sed potius adificari & latius extendi constat. Nam quod hoc loco factum fuisse Lucas commemorat, idipsum in omnibus persecutionibus accidisse, Ecclesiastica historiae scriptores narrant. Et vt horrendas tempestates læta & stabilis cæli serenitas fere excipit: ita ecclesia faciem post persecutionū procellas semper latiorem & splendidiorem apparuisse constat. Dissipat enim gentium consilia Deus, ipsius verò consilium æternum stabit, quo filium suum totius orbis terrarum regem constituit. Vide Psal. 2. 33. & 110.
units.tr: Furthermore, when the history of the centurion Cornelius, which contains the beginnings and indeed the first fruits of the calling of the Gentiles, is finished, St Luke returns to the interrupted narrative of events concerning the common Church, and records how the kingdom of Christ began to spread far and wide among the Gentiles. In particular he treats of Antioch, where converts to Christ first obtained the name of Christians. And above all he touches on the occasion of so great a matter, which he shows was offered by the persecution stirred up over Stephen and seized upon by pious men. Indeed, it is especially memorable that so great a good had its beginning from a most deadly event. For we saw above, in chapter 8, how miserable the face of the Church was at the time of that persecution: when the fury of the persecutors had gone so far that it was not even safe to be a Christian in secret, and men and women alike were dragged from their private houses to slaughter. The result was that the Church, scattered here and there, seemed to be a torn body that no skill could heal. But by the goodness and grace of God it came about that a new body sprang up from almost every scattered member of the Church. For those whom the storm of so dreadful a persecution had driven hither and thither, mindful of their duty, began to preach the Christian name everywhere, and some of them, carried as far as Phoenicia and even Cyprus, lit up those regions too with the brilliance of the gospel. By this example the primitive Church, and indeed the faithful of all ages, ought to be strengthened, so that they are not discouraged by the savage attempts of the enemies of the truth, since it is clear that by these the kingdom of Christ is not overthrown or reduced to a narrow compass, but rather built up and extended more widely. For what Luke here records as having happened, the writers of ecclesiastical history tell us happened in all the persecutions. And just as a calm and settled serenity of the sky usually follows dreadful storms, so it is well established that after the tempests of persecution the Church always appeared broader and more splendid. For God scatters the counsels of the nations, but his own counsel will stand, by which he has set his Son as king of the whole earth (Ps. 2, 33 and 110).

units.la: Sed de illis singulari diligentia agit Lucas, quorum ministerio rem tanti momenti confecit dominus. Qui omnes quidem propter Christi fidem & doctrinam dispersi fuerunt, interim verò in euangelij ministerio eius ratione non per omnia consenserunt. Nam alij quidem solis Iudaeis prædicant, quos eorum quae inter Petrum & Cornelium contigerunt, adhuc ignaros fuisse, verisimile est. Alij verò, quos Cyprios & Cyrenaeos fuisse scribit, Antiochiam ingressi, Græcis, id est, gentibus quoq; prædicarunt. Ita non raro fieri consuevit, vt in quibusdam dissentiant, qui fidelissimi Iesu Christi serui habentur, Deo ita dispensante dona sua, vt verbo suo authoritas maior accedat, ne ex hominum conspiratione huius propagatio pendere videatur. Quò etiam referri debet, quod infra de contentione inter Paulum & Barnabam oborta dicitur, quæ in tantum efferbuit, vt disiungerentur ab inuicem præstantissima & selecta Christi organa. Neminem ergo offendat, si quid eius generis hodie quoq; in ecclesia contingat. Nam sectas esse oportere, Paulus scribit, vt electi probentur. 1. Corint. 11. Interim in omnibus hisce magna laudem meretur ardens propagandi regni Christi studium, quo inflammati, periculorum quae paulò ante sustinuerant, prorsus obliuiscuntur, & Christi verbum passim divulgant. Hac constantia fideles Christi ministros præditos esse oportet, ne se officio suo per omnia deponere putent, si semel pro Christi nomine periclitati sint. Nec aliter sibi fugam concessam esse intelligant, quàm vt periculis erepti, ad officium redeant, & quicquid illis vitae reliquum est, illud totum ad propagandam gloriam Christi insumant.
units.tr: But Luke gives particular attention to those men through whose ministry the Lord brought about a matter of such great importance. All of them were indeed scattered on account of Christ's faith and teaching, yet in their preaching of the gospel they did not all agree in every respect. For some preached only to the Jews, who were probably still unaware of what had happened between Peter and Cornelius. Others, whom Luke says were Cypriots and Cyrenians, went into Antioch and preached also to the Greeks, that is, to the Gentiles. It often happens that some disagree in certain matters, even though they are regarded as most faithful servants of Jesus Christ, because God so distributes his gifts that greater authority is added to his word, so that its spread might not seem to depend on a conspiracy of men. To this also should be referred what Luke says later about the dispute that arose between Paul and Barnabas, which flared up so greatly that the most outstanding and chosen instruments of Christ were separated from one another. Let no one, therefore, be offended if anything of this kind happens in the Church even today. For Paul writes that there must be factions, so that those who are approved may be made known. 1 Cor. 11. Meanwhile, in all these things the ardent zeal for spreading the kingdom of Christ deserves great praise; inflamed by it, they quite forgot the dangers they had endured a little earlier, and they proclaimed the word of Christ everywhere. Faithful ministers of Christ ought to be endowed with this steadfastness, so that they do not think they have wholly laid down their office if they have once been in danger for the name of Christ. Nor should they understand that their flight was granted to them otherwise than that, rescued from dangers, they might return to their duty and spend whatever life remains to them entirely on advancing the glory of Christ.

units.la: Cæterum locorum quoque, in quibus isti prædicarunt, non indiligentem mentionem facit Lucas. Et primò quidem Phoenicia nominatur, quam Iudaea vicinam esse constat, celeberrimam vrbibus & gentis vetustate, apud exteros quoque scriptores insignem. Post hanc Cyprus ponitur, poetarum carminibus decantata insula, quam illi cùm propter loci amoenitatem, tum propter incolarum mores dissolutissimos Veneri sacram dixere. Et elucet hic partim magna dei bonitas, qui tales homines filij sui cognitione illustrare dignatus est: partim admirabilis & inuicta euangelij vis, cuius prædicatione termini regni Christi adeo breui tempore eo vsq; dilatati sunt, vt ex continente maria transfire & insulas inuadere inciperet, quod fore olim à prophetis prædictum fuit. Vide Psal. 27. Isa. 60, 66. & c. Præcipuè verò Antiochiae meminit, quæ vix alia inter Syriae vrbes præstantior extitit. Nam vt Seleuco conditore superba, gloria & diuitijs illustris fuit: ita (vt postea audiemus) in illa prima ex gentibus ecclesia coaluit & tanta frequentia floruit, vt qui hactenus discipuli modò dicti fuerant, angustiori vocabulo Christiani appellari inciperent. Habuit eadem vrbs episcopos & eruditione pietate insignes: martyribus quoq; ita abundauit, vt vix alia illi conferri possit. Memorabile igitur & cumprimis obseruandum est, quòd tantam vrbem eorum ministerio Deus conuerti voluit, quo- rum ne nomina quidem extant. Nam hoc vnum de illis traditur, quod Cyprij & Cyrenæi fuerint. Atqui poterat eadem ratione insignium apostolorum opera vti dominus. Sed per contempta & vilia huius mundi, pro suo more, rem maximam confici voluit, vt in illo, non in hominibus, gloriandum no bis esse sciremus. 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke does not fail to mention the places in which these men preached. And first Phoenicia is named, which is known to be near Judea, very famous for its cities and for the antiquity of its people, and notable also among foreign writers. After it Cyprus is set down, an island celebrated in the songs of the poets, which they dedicated to Venus, both on account of the pleasantness of the place and because of the most dissolute morals of its inhabitants. Here shine forth partly the great goodness of God, who deigned to enlighten such men with the knowledge of his Son, and partly the admirable and unconquered power of the gospel, by whose preaching the bounds of Christ's kingdom were extended in so short a time that it began to cross the seas from the mainland and invade the islands, which was foretold long ago by the prophets. See Ps. 27; Isa. 60, 66, and so on. But especially he mentions Antioch, which hardly any other of the cities of Syria surpassed in distinction. For just as it was proud with Seleucus as its founder and famous for its glory and wealth, so (as we shall hear later) in that city the first church from among the Gentiles grew strong and flourished with such a crowd that those who until then had been called only disciples began to be called by the narrower name of Christians. The same city had bishops distinguished for learning and piety, and it also abounded in martyrs so much that scarcely any other could be compared with it. It is therefore a memorable thing, and above all to be noted, that God wished so great a city to be converted through the ministry of men whose very names are not extant. For only this is handed down about them, that they were Cypriots and Cyrenians. And yet the Lord could have used in the same way the work of famous apostles. But, according to his custom, he wished the greatest thing to be accomplished through the despised and base things of this world, so that we might learn to glory not in men but in him. 1 Cor. 1.

units.la: Videamus autem, quid prædicarint qui Antiochenæ ecclesiæ fundamenta iecerunt. Prædica- runt (inquit Lucas) dominū Iesum. Hic ergo illis doctrinæ argumentum fuit, quem & Paulus fo- lum se nouisse fatetur. Solius vero Iesu mentionem facit, quia in hoc continentur, quæcunque ad no- stræ salutis rationem faciunt. Hic enim nobis à Deo datus est, vt humano generi pœnitentiæ & re- missionis peccatorum author esset, sicut cap. 5. dictum est. Nam vt in illo solo peccatorum remissio inuenitur, ita nec pœnitentia ea, quæ extra fidem in Christum agitur, Deo placere potest. Habemus ergo quod illis respondeamus, qui hoc nobis vitio vertunt & per ludibrium exprobrant, quòd vnum & solum Christum in nostris concionibus inculcemus. Idem enim apostolorum exemplum secuti faci- mus, nec aliter facere possumus, quando extra Christum salus nulla inuenitur.
units.tr: Let us see, then, what those men preached who laid the foundations of the church at Antioch. They preached (says Luke) the Lord Jesus. So the subject of their teaching was he whom Paul also confesses that he alone knew. Luke mentions Jesus alone because everything that pertains to the manner of our salvation is contained in him. For he was given to us by God so that he might be the author of repentance and forgiveness of sins for the human race, as was said in chapter 5. For just as forgiveness of sins is found in him alone, so also that repentance which is undertaken apart from faith in Christ cannot please God. We therefore have an answer for those who find fault with us for this and mock us, because in our sermons we press upon one thing only, Christ alone. For we follow the same example of the apostles, and we cannot do otherwise, since no salvation is found outside Christ.

units.la: Postremò insignem professum euangelij Lucas describit, dicens: Multus numerus, cum credi- disset, conuersus est ad dominum. Præmittit vero efficientem causam, ne quis hominibus ministris il- lud acceptum ferret. Nam ait: Manus domini erat cum illis. Vnde colligimus, omnem fidei & sa- lutis profectum à solo deo pendere, nec quicquam præter externum ministerium hominibus esse tri- buendum. Exponit hoc multis Paulus in priori ad Corinth. epistola cap. 3. Et prodest eius frequen- ter meminisse, cum ne insolentiores fiant ministri, tum vt deo grati esse discant, quos ille vera fide il- luminat. Simul vero fidei Christianæ proprium finem euangelista exprimit, qui est, vt ad dominum conuertantur, qui vel ignorantia, vel superstitione & peccatis ab hoc auersi fuerunt. Non ergo in inani speculatione fides versatur, sed viua est Iesu Christi cognitio, quæ totum hominem in dei obse- quium rapit. Nec pro Christianis habendi sunt, qui vel superstitioni vel flagitijs immersi, ad domi- num conuerti nolunt. Hunc ergo nostris studijs scopum præfigamus, vt vera fide ad Deum conuersi, salutem consequamur in Iesu Christo, saluatore vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potes- tas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, Luke describes the remarkable progress of the gospel, saying: A great number, having believed, were converted to the Lord. He sets down first the efficient cause, so that no one might ascribe this to the ministers as men. For he says: The hand of the Lord was with them. From this we gather that all progress of faith and salvation depends on God alone, and that nothing beyond the outward ministry is to be attributed to men. Paul explains this at length in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3. And it is useful to remember this often, both so that ministers may not become too arrogant, and so that they may learn to be pleasing to God, whom he enlightens with true faith. At the same time the evangelist expresses the proper end of Christian faith, which is that those who were turned away from this, either by ignorance or by superstition and sins, should be converted to the Lord. Faith, therefore, is not occupied with empty speculation, but the living knowledge of Jesus Christ, which carries the whole man into obedience to God. Nor are those to be regarded as Christians who, plunged into either superstition or wickedness, are unwilling to be converted to the Lord. Let us therefore set this goal before our studies: that, converted to God by true faith, we may obtain salvation in Jesus Christ, the only Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY 80.

units.la: Peruenit autem rumor de ipsis ad aures ecclesiæ, quæ erat Hierosolymis, & miserunt Barnabam, vt transiret Antiochiam vsque. Qui cum venisset, & vidisset gratiam dei, gauisus est, adhortatus est omnes, vt propositio cordis adhærerent domino. Nam erat vir bonus, & plenus spiritu sancto & fide. Et addita est multa turba domino. Profectus est autem Barnabas Tarsum ad quærendum Saulum: quem cum inuenif- set, adduxit illum Antiochiam. Accidit autem vt totum annum conuer- farentur cum ecclesia, & docerent turbam multam, & Antiochiæ pri- mum discipuli nominarentur Christiani.
units.tr: News of them reached the ears of the church at Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to go as far as Antioch. When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and exhorted them all that with steadfast purpose of heart they should cling to the Lord. For he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great crowd was added to the Lord. Barnabas then set out for Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. And it came about that for a whole year they met with the church and taught a great crowd, and at Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.

units.la: Quoniam Deus filium suum, Iesum Christum, vniuersalem totius mundi saluatorem confi- tuit, ad eundem omnes quoque gentes per euangelij prædicationem adduci oportuit: quemad- modum ex prophetarum oraculis & ipsius Christi mandato patet, quo apostolos in omnem orbem terrarum exire & ex omnium nationum hominibus sibi discipulos adducere iussit. Porro vt hoc fieri cœperit, hoc cap. Lucas commemorat. Licet enim in præcedenti Cornelij ad fidem Christianam conuersi historia descripta sit, quia tamen singulari quodam priuilegio ille vocatus esse videri pote- rat celeberrimæ vrbis Antiochiæ conuersio subijcitur, in qua multis nominibus insignis ecclesia ex gentibus primum collecta est. Cuius rei authores fuerunt (vt beri dictum est) Cyprij, & Cyrenæi quidam, obscuri nominis viri, sed quorum nomina haud dubiè in libro vitæ apud deum scripta seruan- tur. Hi vrbem ingressi, solum Iesum Christum gentibus prædicarunt, hunc à deo patre missum esse, docentes, vt in se credentibus poenitentiam simul & peccatorum remissionem conferat. Nec defuit pio conatui felicissimus effectus. Diuina enim virtute per eorum ministerium efficaciter operante, incredibilis hominum multitudo fidem didicit, & ad dominum conuersa est. Ipsis vero ea subjicit Lucas, quae ad Antiochenae ecclesiae statum confirmandum reflabant. Et primo quidem Hierosolymitanorum in nouam Christi ecclesiam officium recenset, qui Barnabam illis quasi subsidio miserunt. Deinde Barnabae praeclarum in commisso sibi munere studium, tandemque felicem eius profectum describit.
units.tr: Since God appointed his Son, Jesus Christ, to be the universal Saviour of the whole world, it was fitting that all nations should also be brought to him through the preaching of the gospel. This is clear from the oracles of the prophets and from the command of Christ himself, by which he ordered the apostles to go out into the whole world and to bring disciples to him from the people of all nations. Luke records in this chapter how this began to happen. For although the earlier history describes the conversion of Cornelius to the Christian faith, that man could seem to have been called by a unique privilege, so the conversion of the famous city of Antioch follows, where a church, notable for many things, was first gathered from the Gentiles. The authors of this were, as has been said, some men of Cyprus and Cyrene, men of obscure name, but whose names are without doubt written in the book of life with God and kept safe. Entering the city, they preached Jesus Christ alone to the Gentiles, teaching that he had been sent by God the Father, so that he might grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to those who believe in him. Nor did their pious effort lack a most happy result. For with the divine power working effectively through their ministry, an incredible multitude of people learned the faith and turned to the Lord. Luke then adds those things which served to strengthen the state of the church at Antioch. First he sets out the duty of the Jerusalem church toward the new church of Christ, which sent Barnabas to them as a kind of support. Then he describes Barnabas's remarkable zeal in the task entrusted to him, and finally his happy progress.

units.la: Et de Hierosolymitanis quidem, inter quos apostolos quoq; fuisse verisimile est, paucis agit, quia ex Barnabae actis consilij ipsorum ratio evidentissime deprehendi potest. Hoc vnum ergo dicit, quod rumore de Antiochia ad Christum conuersa Hierosolymam vsq; vulgato, qui illic tanquam in specula vel sublimi arce ex officio pro omnium ecclesiarum salute excubabant, Barnabam eo transmiserint: nimirum, vt recentem discipulorum fidem confirmaret, & mutuā alleret inter ecclesias beneuolentiam. Quod ipsum supra quoque factum esse vidimus, quando Samariam Petrus & Iohannes miss sunt, cum illa per Philippi praedicationem deuicta, Christo portas aperuisset. Est autem cumprimis memorabile exemplū hoc, quo docemur, etiam longe distitas ecclesias, si quando vsus postulat, tum consilium fideli ministrorum opera iuuandas esse, & insignem laudem eos mereri, quicunq; hac in re diligentem operam nauare consueuerunt. Si enim pietatis officium, quod vni salcem ex Christi discipulorum numero praestatur, tantopere commendat Christus, vt illud sibi praestitum esse nouissimo die palam testaturus sit, & ei mercedem certam pollicetur, qui vel poculum frigidae aquae apostolo obtulerit: quanto maiori gloria eorum studium remuneraturus est, qui integras ecclesias suis consiliis & auxiliis vel seruant vel confirmant? Meminerint huius tum antistites tum magistratus Christiani, ne illorum calumniis se ab officio reuocari patiantur, qui & temerarios & seditiosos nouarum rerum authores eos esse dicunt, qui alienis in fidei causa vel praescribere vel consulere consueuerunt.
units.tr: He deals briefly with the men of Jerusalem, among whom it is likely the apostles were also included, because the reason for their counsel can be very clearly understood from the account of Barnabas. So he says only this: when the report that Antioch had been converted to Christ spread as far as Jerusalem, those who kept watch there, as on a lookout or a high citadel, for the salvation of all the churches, sent Barnabas thither, namely to strengthen the fresh faith of the disciples and to stir up a mutual goodwill between the churches. We saw this also done above, when Peter and John were sent to Samaria, after that city, conquered by the preaching of Philip, had opened its gates to Christ. This example is especially memorable, because it teaches us that even churches far apart, when need requires, ought to be helped by the faithful labour of ministers, and that those who are accustomed to undertake diligent work in this matter deserve remarkable praise. For if Christ so highly commends the duty of kindness shown to one of the least of his disciples that he will openly bear witness on the last day that it was done to him, and promises a sure reward to the one who offers a cup of cold water to an apostle, how much greater glory will he bestow upon those who preserve or strengthen whole churches by their counsel and help? Let the bishops and the Christian magistrates remember this, and not allow themselves to be called away from their duty by the slanders of those who say that they are rash and seditious authors of new things, when they have been accustomed to prescribe or give counsel to others in a matter of faith.

units.la: Sed Barnabam videamus, de quo diligenter Lucas agit. Nam qualis fuerit & quid in Antiochenorum causa fecerit, narrat. Et quamuis personae descriptionem rebus per illum Antiochiae gestis mediam interserat, nobis tamen ea primo loco consyderanda est, vt de causa tam insignium virtutum, quae in illo eluxerunt, melius iudicare possimus: maximè cum in eum finem illius conditionem & ingenium Lucas describat. Dicit autem, fuisse virum bonum, plenum spiritu & fide. Est hoc praeclarum viri sancti encomium, quo nullum maius vel ab ipso Demosthene & Cicerone effingi potuerat. Quae enim maior laus esse potest quam a spiritu sancto bonum dici, cum Christo teste, nemo bonus sit, praeterquam vnus Deus? Sed ne quis Lucam eius dicti parum memorem putaret, mox docet, cur hunc bonum virum dicere ausus fuerit: nimirum quod plenus esset spiritu & fide. Licet enim solus deus reuera & ex seipso bonus sit, quia tamen hic suum spiritum, & per hunc suas virtutes bominibus communicare dignatur, nihil prohibet bonos dicere, in quibus diuinae bonitatis argumenta, propter inhabitantem in illis dei spiritum, elucent. At quia diuini spiritus simul & bonorum omnium capaces nos reddit sola fides, hanc etiam Barnabae Lucas tribuit, & plenum fide fuisse ait. Per hanc enim iustificantur homines, quia hac Christum apprehendunt, cuius merito ab omni iniquitate emundantur, & ad omne opus bonum idonei redduntur, vt tam Deo quam hominibus fideliter praestent, quaecunq; illis debent officia. Prodest autem hanc boni viri definitionem memori animo recondere, vt insano mundi iudicio opponatur, qui vel egregie hypocritas, vel ad carnis voluptates & studia procliues, bonos viros appellare consueuit. Praeterea vero admonemur hoc loco, quales publicis officijs, & in primis in religionis causa, adhiberi debeant. Viri boni nimirum, quos spiritu sancto guberanari & fide praeditos esse, constat. Talibus enim quiduis tuto committi potest. Quicunq; autem improbis & a spiritu dei alienis res vel publicas vel priuatas commendant, ijs fere euenire solet, quod Noe coruum ex arca emittenti euenisse legimus. Et sapienter, vt & reliqua omnia dixit Solomon: Truncat pedes, & bibit violentiam, qui per fluitum aliquid demandat. Prov. 26. Nam & ipse sua frustrantur, & plerunq; graues suae leuitatis & imprudentiae poenas dant.
units.tr: But let us look at Barnabas, of whom Luke speaks with care. For he relates what kind of man he was and what he did in the affair of the Antiochenes. And although Luke inserts the description of the man in the middle of the events done at Antioch, we ought nevertheless to consider it first, so that we may judge better concerning the cause of such remarkable virtues as shone forth in him, especially since Luke describes his character and disposition for this very purpose. He says, moreover, that he was a good man, full of the Spirit and of faith. This is an excellent encomium of a holy man, and no greater one could have been fashioned even by Demosthenes or Cicero. For what greater praise can there be than to be called good by the Holy Spirit, when, as Christ testifies, no one is good except God alone? But lest anyone think that Luke was too careless in this saying, he immediately teaches why he dared to call this man good: namely, because he was full of the Spirit and of faith. For although God alone is truly and of himself good, yet because he deigns to communicate his Spirit to men, and through him his virtues, nothing prevents us from calling those good in whom the marks of divine goodness shine forth, on account of God's Spirit dwelling in them. But since faith alone makes us capable of the divine Spirit and of all good things, Luke ascribes this also to Barnabas, and says that he was full of faith. For through faith men are justified, because by it they lay hold of Christ, by whose merit they are cleansed from all iniquity and made fit for every good work, so that they may faithfully render to God and to men whatever duties they owe. It is useful, moreover, to keep this definition of a good man in a mindful heart, so that it may be set against the foolish judgement of the world, which is accustomed to call good men those who are notably hypocrites, or who are prone to the pleasures and pursuits of the flesh. Furthermore, we are reminded here of what sort of men should be employed in public offices, and especially in the cause of religion. Namely, good men, of whom it is plain that they are guided by the Holy Spirit and endowed with faith. For anything can safely be entrusted to such men. But those who commit public or private affairs to wicked men, who are alien to the Spirit of God, usually meet with what we read befell Noah when he sent the raven out of the ark. And Solomon wisely said, as he did of all other things: "He cuts off his feet and drinks violence who sends a message by a fool" (Prov. 26). For such men also frustrate their own affairs, and very often pay grievous penalties for their own levity and imprudence.

units.la: Porro videndum est, quid Barnabas in Antiochena ecclesia egerit: quod omne quatuor articulis Lucas comprehendit. Primo ait. Cum venisset, & vidisset gratiam Dei, gauisus est. Intelligit autem per gratiam dei, fidei profectum & quae huic comitantur spiritus sancti dona. Et gratia vocabulo cabulo vsus est, vt doceret, ex dei beneficio hæc omnia hominibus contingere. Est autem insigne boni viri & fidelis Christi ministri argumentũ, quòd aliorum profectu gaudet Barnabas. Qui enim spi-ritus sancti illuminatione & fide carent, fere alijs inuident, dum suæ duntaxat gloriæ consulunt. Nec omnes Mosis modestiam imitantur, qui omnes filios Israel Dei spiritu repleri & prophetandi dono instrui cupiebat. Imò passim, prob dolor, multa extant ambitiosorum hominum exempla, qui dum alijs debitum honorem præripere conati sunt, funestas ecclesijs contentiones excitarunt. At quos Christi spiritus regit, & qui fide vera illuminati sunt, priuatæ gloriæ iacturam facilè spernunt, dummodo Dei gloriæ consultum esse videant.
units.tr: Next we must consider what Barnabas did in the church at Antioch, which Luke sums up under four heads. First he says: "When he had come and seen the grace of God, he rejoiced." By the grace of God he understands the progress of faith and the gifts of the Holy Spirit that accompany it. And he used the word grace to teach that all these things come to men by God's benefit. It is a remarkable mark of a good man and a faithful minister of Christ that Barnabas rejoices in the progress of others. For those who lack the illumination of the Holy Spirit and faith are generally envious of others, while they look only to their own glory. Nor do all imitate the modesty of Moses, who wished that all the sons of Israel might be filled with the Spirit of God and instructed in the gift of prophecy. Indeed, alas, there are everywhere many examples of ambitious men who, while they tried to snatch away from others the honour due to them, stirred up deadly quarrels in the churches. But those whom the Spirit of Christ rules, and who have been enlightened by true faith, readily disregard the loss of private glory, provided they see that the glory of God is being served.

units.la: Deinde adhortatus est Antiochenos Barnabas, vt cordis proposito adhærerent domino. Nam vt in quouis alio studio, ita maximè in religione perseuerantia opus est. Nec enim coronatur qui cer-tat, nisi legitimè certauerit. Et Christo non probantur, qui vbi manum aratro admouerunt, à tergo respiciunt. Luc. 9. Recte ergo perseuerantiam ab Antiochenis exigit Barnabas. Sed ne externam duntaxat simulationem aut inanem verborum iactantiam exigere videretur, cordis propositum re-quirit. Ea enim demum vera perseuerantia verâq; cum domino Iesu coniunctio est, cum corda nostra illius obsequio consecrauimus. Et qui id fecère, eos nulla periculorum atrocitas à domino absterrere potest. Omnia enim pro damno ducunt, dummodo Christum lucrifaciant. At quia nō ignorabat Bar-nabas, multa esse, quæ homines à Christo reuocare solent, adhortatione opus esse putauit etiam ijs, in quibus præclara diuinæ gratiæ argumenta elucebant. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd Paulus Timotheũ indesinenter suæ fidei commissos monere & hortari, adeoq; omni modo & ratione illis instare iubet. Vide 2. Timoth. 4. Absurdissimus ergo illorum error est, qui omnem doctrinam inutilem & super-uacaneam esse putant apud eos, qui semel veritatis cognitionem assecuti sunt.
units.tr: Then Barnabas urged the Antiochenes to cleave to the Lord with a resolute heart. For perseverance is needed in religion, as in any other pursuit. Nor is the one who competes crowned unless he has competed lawfully. And those who have put their hand to the plough and look back are not approved by Christ (Luke 9). So Barnabas rightly required perseverance of the Antiochenes. But lest it seem that he demanded only outward show or empty boasting of words, he required the purpose of the heart. For that is true perseverance and true union with the Lord Jesus, when we have consecrated our hearts to his obedience. Those who have done this cannot be turned away from the Lord by any savagery of dangers, for they count all things loss, provided they gain Christ. But because Barnabas knew that many things commonly draw men away from Christ, he thought exhortation was needed even for those in whom the remarkable signs of divine grace shone forth. This is also why Paul bids Timothy to admonish and exhort those committed to his faith without ceasing, and to press them in every way and manner (see 2 Timothy 4). Therefore the error of those is most absurd who think that all teaching is useless and superfluous among those who have once attained the knowledge of the truth.

units.la: Tertiò Tarsum profectus Barnabas, inde Paulum Antiochiam deducit, vt huius etiam mi-nisterio ecclesia magis confirmetur. Est hoc alterum verè fidelis animi & Christi amore flagrantis argumentum. Nec enim ignorare potuit Barnabas, quanta essent in Pauli peǝore spiritus dona, & quantum suæ authoritati decessurum esset, si Antiochiam Paulus peruenirét, quo non aliud erat Christi organum præstantius. Sed iam ante monuimus, eos ab hominibus gloriam non quærere, qui fide inflammati, dei gloriam prouehere cupiunt. Imò fide carere certum est omnes eos, quos priuatæ gloriæ & auræ popularis studium exagitat: quo argumento aduersus Iudæorum scribas Christus etiam vtitur. Iohan. 5. Interea admonet Barnabæ exemplum, in bene constitutis ecclesijs præcipuam de idoneis ministris curam esse debere, & hos vndiquaque conquirendos & adducendos esse. Docet idem Christus, quando orare iubet dominum messis, vt is operarios extrudat. Matth. 9. Hinc sa-ctum videmus, vt & præstantissimi prophetarum, & illustrissimi reges tam diligentem scholarum rationem habuerint, cum videlicet sine his nec ecclesias consistere, nec fidei saniorem doctrinam retineri posse viderent. Quare nimis crassa illorum ingratitudo est, qui ministros, quos dominus benignè offert, non modò ceu inutiles contemnunt, verumetiam tanquam nocentissimos homines cane & an-gue peius oderunt.
units.tr: Third, Barnabas set out for Tarsus and from there brought Paul to Antioch, so that the church might be strengthened also by his ministry. This is another sure sign of a faithful mind burning with love for Christ. For Barnabas could not have been ignorant of how great the gifts of the Spirit were in Paul's breast, and how much of his own authority would have diminished if Paul had come to Antioch, where there was no more excellent instrument of Christ. But we have already noted before that those who are inflamed with faith do not seek glory from men, but desire to advance the glory of God. Indeed, it is certain that all those whom the zeal for private glory and popular applause drives on lack faith; Christ also uses this argument against the scribes of the Jews (John 5). Meanwhile the example of Barnabas admonishes that in well-ordered churches the chief care must be given to suitable ministers, and that these must be sought out and brought in from every quarter. Christ himself teaches the same when he bids us pray the Lord of the harvest to thrust out labourers (Matthew 9). Hence we see that the most outstanding of the prophets and the most illustrious kings took such diligent care of schools, since they plainly saw that without them churches could not stand, nor a sounder doctrine of faith be retained. Therefore the ingratitude of those is far too gross who not only scorn as useless the ministers whom the Lord kindly offers, but even hate them as the most harmful men, worse than dog and snake.

units.la: Adijcitur his vltimo loco, quòd toto anno vnà cum Paulo Antiochiæ permanserit Barnabas: ideo nimirum quòd operam suæ ecclesiæ vtilem & necessariam esse videret. Nec enim otiosos & in-ertes illic desedisse eos Lucas scribit: sed magnam hominum turbam ab illis in vera fide & Christi religione institutam fuisse tradit. Imitentur exemplum hoc ecclesiarum ministri, & dum alijs per-seuerantiam suadent, ipsi in suo officio constantes perseuerent: nec inani pastorum titulo glorientur, sed quod veros pastores decet, faciant: ne stulti illius pastoris æmuli & successores videantur, qui apud Zachariam cap. 11. describitur.
units.tr: Lastly, it is added that Barnabas remained at Antioch with Paul for a whole year. This was surely because he saw that his labour was useful and necessary to the church. For Luke writes that they did not sit there idle and inactive, but he relates that a great crowd of men was instructed by them in the true faith and the religion of Christ. Let the ministers of the churches imitate this example, and while they urge perseverance on others, let them themselves persevere constantly in their office. Let them not boast in the empty title of pastors, but do what true pastors ought to do, lest they seem to be the foolish rivals and successors of that shepherd who is described in Zechariah 11.

units.la: Restat sanĉti huius & ardentis studij profectus, quem insignem fuisse Lucas docet. Primò enim multam turbam domino additam fuisse, ait. Vnde constat non inutiles esse piorum ministrorum la-bores. Nam vt dei verbum per se, fœcundi seminis instar, fructificandi vim habet: ita semper in ali-quos incidit, qui ad illud excipiendum rite dispositi, fructus dignos faciunt. Et licet alij vel saxea, vel spinosa, vel omnis generis illecebris patentia corda afferant: habet tamen vbiq; dominus suos, qui honestis cordibus exceptum semen retinent, donec multiplicem fructum proferat. Vide Luc. 8. Et propheta testatur non sine fructu aut irritum redire verbum domini, sed pluuiæ instar esse, quæ terram irrigat & fœcundam reddit. Ifa.55. Præterea minijtrorum suorum studijs benedicit dcmi-nus,ne in cassum laborent. Debet hoc animos addere in ecclesia Christi laborantibus,ne se frustra la-boraturos esse putent. Nam si vel pauculas animas ab interitu liberauerint, inæstimabilem thefau-rum se :æquisuisse putent,cum Christo teste, ne vnius quidem animæ salus totius mundi substantia redimi possit. Matth.16. Interim obseruabis,domino turbam hanc addita fuisse. Non ergo sibijpsis, sed Christo discipulos collegerunt Paulus & Barnabas. Sciebant enim vno Christo doctore & ma-gistro gloriandum esse. Matth.23. Et Christi præceptum nouerant, qui sibi discipulos adducere iusse-rat. Matt.28. Enormis ergo illorum insolentia est,qui inter Christianos sectarum authores sunt, & hominum seruos faciunt eos,quos sanguinis sui precio redemptos Christus sibi vendicauit. Vide quæ aduersus hos Paulus disputet in priori ad Corinth.cap.1.3.7.&c.
units.tr: There remains the progress of this holy and ardent zeal, which Luke records as remarkable. For first he says that a great crowd was added to the Lord. From this it is clear that the labours of godly ministers are not useless. For just as the word of God, like fertile seed, has in itself the power of bearing fruit, so it always falls upon some who, rightly disposed to receive it, bring forth worthy fruit. And although others bring hearts that are stony, thorny, or open to every kind of allurement, the Lord nonetheless always has his own, who keep the seed received in honest hearts until it bears fruit a hundredfold (see Luke 8). And the prophet testifies that the word of the Lord does not return without fruit or in vain, but is like the rain which waters the earth and makes it fertile (Isaiah 55). Moreover, the Lord blesses the labours of his ministers, so that they do not toil in vain. This ought to encourage those who labour in the church of Christ, lest they think they are labouring to no purpose. For if they have rescued even a few souls from perdition, they may think they have gained an inestimable treasure, since, as Christ witnesses, the salvation of even one soul cannot be redeemed by the substance of the whole world (Matthew 16). Meanwhile you will observe that this crowd was added to the Lord. Paul and Barnabas, therefore, did not gather disciples for themselves, but for Christ. For they knew that they must glory in the one Christ as teacher and master (Matthew 23). And they knew the precept of Christ, who had bidden them make disciples for himself (Matthew 28). Therefore the monstrous arrogance of those is enormous who become authors of sects among Christians, and make slaves of men whom Christ has claimed for himself, redeemed by the price of his blood. See what Paul argues against such people in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapters 1, 3, 7, and following.

units.la: Accedit autem alius fructus,qui immortalem et æternam Antiochenæ vrbi gloriam peperit.Quia enim illic prima ex gentibus ecclesia coaluit,factu est, vt qui bucusq; discipuli disti fuerunt nunc pri-mum Christianorum nomine insigniantur. Et hoc illud nouum nomen esse videtur,quod electu suis apud Isaiam deus olim pollicitus est.Ifa.62. At quæ nam Antiochenis maior gloria contingere pote-rat? Conferantur cum his superbæ & insolentis Romæ antistites,& vel inuiti cedere cogentur. Nec tamen vnquam Antiochiæ insolente illum titulum concessum fuisse legimus, vt ecclesiarum omnium Caput diceretur. Sed omissis istis, potius nominis huius rationè expendamus,cum illud non sine nu-mine nobis obtigerit. Illo autè nos à dei filio denominari constat,qui iuxta veteris Testamenti typū, quo reges & sacerdotes vngebantur, καὶ ἐξοχὴν Græcis Christus, Hebræis Meschias, nobis verò vnctus dicitur:eò quòd illum deus vniuersale & æternum populi sui rege et sacerdotem constituerit, vt videre ess Psal.2.& 110. At quia idem suis se totum suaq; omnia communicat, illos etiam abse Christianos dici voluit:nec nudo & inaniduntaxat nominis titulo nos dignatus est,sed vt apostolus ait,vnxit nos,& fecit nos reges & sacerdotes deo patri suo.Apoc.1.cap. Multiplex ergo huius no-minis vsus est. Primò enim dignitatis,quam in Christo habemus,nos admonet, quâ exemplo carere satebuntur,quicunq; rem penitius introspexerint. Neminem enim vnquam regum fuisse constat,qui sui regni subditos omnes reges facere potuerit,imò ne aulicos quidem aut qui illi à consilijs fuere. At Christi Iesu ea potentia & virtus est,vt æterno regiæ dignitatis honore omnes eos donet,qui illū-gem suum agnoscunt. Deinde fidei confirmandæ & salutis certitudini hic titulus feruit. In Iesu Chri-sto enim deo patri complacitum esse constat. Idem ergo nobis insci nosq; auersari non potest,quos sui dilecti nomine insignire dignatus est. Hinc ergo consolationis argumenta in aduersis omnibus, maximè autem in conscientia tentationibus petere licebit. Postremò officij nos titulus iste admonet: quod est,vt nos reges & sacerdotes à Christo factos esse meminerimus, & dignitatem nominis nostri fortiter tueamur. Regis proprium est liberum esse,nec ab alio regi. Maneamus ergo in libertate, in quam dei filius nos asseruit, nec peccati seruitute , qua nulla aut fœdior est aut miserior,nos posshac opprimi patiamur. Regis est vincere & debellare hostes. Debellemus ergo hostes salutis nostræ cru-delissimos,satanam,mundum,carnem̨ cum suis concupiscentijs. Regis est imperare & regere. Re-gamus itaq;nosipsos, & potenter imperemus omnibus ijs,quæ nos à salutis via transuersos abripiunt.
units.tr: Moreover another fruit followed, which won for the city of Antioch an immortal and eternal glory. For since the first church from among the Gentiles was formed there, it came about that those who until then had been called disciples were now for the first time distinguished by the name of Christians. This seems to be that new name which God long ago promised through Isaiah to his elect (Isaiah 62). But what greater glory could befall the Antiochenes? Let them be compared with the proud and insolent bishops of Rome, and they will be forced to yield, even against their will. Nor do we read that the Antiochenes ever claimed that arrogant title of being called the head of all churches. But setting that aside, let us rather weigh the reason for this name, since it has fallen to us not without divine will. It is plain that we are named from the Son of God, who, according to the type of the Old Testament, by which kings and priests were anointed, is called Christ by the Greeks pre-eminently (kai exochēn), Messiah by the Hebrews, and by us "the Anointed." This is because God has appointed him, the eternal and universal, to be king and priest of his people, as may be seen in Psalms 2 and 110. But since he communicates himself and all his possessions to his own, he wished that they also be called Christians from him. Nor has he thought us worthy of the bare and empty title of the name only; rather, as the apostle says, he has anointed us and made us kings and priests to God his Father (Revelation 1). The use of this name is therefore manifold. First, it reminds us of the dignity we have in Christ, a dignity which those who look more deeply into the matter will confess no example can match. For it is certain that no king has ever existed who could make all his subjects kings, not even his courtiers or those who were his counsellors. But the power and virtue of Christ Jesus is such that he bestows the eternal honour of royal dignity on all who acknowledge him as their Lord. Second, this title serves to confirm faith and the certainty of salvation. For it is certain that Jesus Christ is well pleasing to God the Father. Therefore he cannot be hostile or adverse to us, whom he has deigned to mark with the name of his beloved. Hence we may seek arguments of consolation in all adversities, and especially in temptations of conscience. Last, this title admonishes us of our duty: that we remember we have been made kings and priests by Christ, and bravely defend the dignity of our name. It is the mark of a king to be free and subject to no other king. Let us therefore remain in the liberty to which the Son of God has asserted us, and let us not allow ourselves to be oppressed again by the slavery of sin, than which none is more foul or more wretched. It is the office of a king to conquer and subdue enemies. Let us therefore subdue the most cruel enemies of our salvation: Satan, the world, and the flesh with its lusts. It is the office of a king to command and rule. Let us therefore rule ourselves, and powerfully command all those things that drag us aside from the way of salvation.

units.la: Ita sacerdotis quoq; officium meditemur,cuius est Docere, Orare,Consecrare vel Offerre. Quare no-stri officij erit, docere nostros tum verbo tum vitæ exemplo , quatenus illud nostræ vocationis ratio exigit. Nostrum erit,orare tum priuatim tum publicè, & non pro nostris tantum,verumetiam alio-rum necessitatibus apud Deum intercedere. Nostrarum quoq; partiū erit,vt nos ipsos deo consecre-mus viuentem hostiam,& immolemus quotidie iuuencos labiorū nostrorum,id est, gratiarumactio-nem,qua nullum aliud est deo magis acceptum gratumq; sacrificium. Possent hæc latissimè per om-nes vitæ partes deduci:sed rudibus occasionem meditandi præbuisse sufficiat.Hæc verò quicunq; pre-stant,Christiani dici merentur. Et tales olim patriarchas fuisse constat,quos Psal.105. vnctos suos, id est,Christianos deus vocauit. Tales primos illos huius nominis vsurpatores Antiochiæ fuisse cre-dibile est.Quòd si qui nomine tanto gloriari volent temerè,seipsos quidem fallent, deum verò fallere non poterunt. Meditemur itaque hæc diligenter,vt nostræ cùm dignitatis tum officij memores, tam augu-sto & præclaro nomini respondeamus,& hac vita exempti,in cœlis regnemus cum Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum.~Amen.
units.tr: Let us therefore also consider the office of the priest, whose duty is to teach, to pray, to consecrate, and to offer. It will therefore be our task to teach our people, both by the word and by the example of our life, as far as the nature of our calling requires. It will be ours to pray, both privately and publicly, and to intercede before God not only for our own needs but also for the needs of others. It will also be our part to consecrate ourselves to God as a living sacrifice, and to offer daily the calves of our lips, that is, the thanksgiving, which is no more acceptable or pleasing a sacrifice to God than any other. These things could be drawn out at great length through all the parts of life, but it will be enough to have given the untrained an occasion for meditation. Moreover, all who perform these things deserve to be called Christians. And it is established that the patriarchs of old were such men, whom God in Psalm 105 called his anointed ones, that is, Christians. It is credible that the first users of this name at Antioch were such men as well. But if some boast of so great a name rashly, they will deceive themselves, though they will not be able to deceive God. Let us therefore meditate on these things diligently, so that, mindful both of our dignity and of our office, we may answer to so august and glorious a name, and, released from this life, reign in heaven with Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA
units.tr: HOMILY

units.la: Caeterum in illis diebus venerunt ab Hierosolymis prophetae Antiochiam. Surgens autem unus ex illis nomine Agabus, significauit per spiritum, famem magnam futuram in toto terrarum orbe, quae accidit sub Claudio Caesare. Discipuli autem, prout cuique suppetebat facultas, decreuerunt singuli in ministerium mittere fratribus, qui in Iudaea habitabant. Quod & fecerunt, mittentes ad Seniores per manum Barnabae & Sauli.
units.tr: Now in those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them, named Agabus, stood up and signified by the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole world, which came to pass under Claudius Caesar. Then the disciples, each according to his means, determined to send relief to the brothers who dwelt in Judaea. And they did so, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

units.la: Etsi dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus, ecclesiae suae nunquam non praesens adsit, eandem tamen, sicuti praedixit, varie exerceri patitur, dum continuis quodammodo vicibus aduersa secundis succedunt. Cuius rei praecipua causa est, quod partim quidem carnis nostrae ferociam cohercere, & securitatem nimiam excutere: partim vero docere vult, se non minus in aduersis quam secundis suos tueri & liberare posse. Vidimus horum memorabilia aliquot exempla hucusque. Nam initio quidem felici auspicio euangelij doctrina Hierosolymis praedicata, ingentem Christo discipulorum numerum attraxit: mox vero persecutionis tempestas oborta enascentis ecclesiae initia interturbat. Rursum tamen Saulo ad Christum converso, insperata pax ecclesijs redditur, & ad gentes usque extensa Christi doctrina incredibiles fructus polliceri coepit, postquam Antiochiae, celeberrimae totius Syriae urbis, ecclesia ex gentibus collecta, & nobile illud Christianorum nomen credentibus primum impositum fuit. Sed ecce novum & ingens malum incidit, fames nimirum, quae ut totum terrarum orbem, ita fideles cumprimis, quorum facultates partim alendis ecclesiae pauperibus exhaustae, partim inter persecutionis furores direptae erant, miserrime vexauit. Est autem utilissima nobis horum consyderatio, qua fit, ut minus offendamur, si quando eadem rerum vicissitudo hodie quoque nos exerceat. Et prae aliis praesens hic locus diligenter consyderari meretur propter multiplicem cum consolationem tum institutionem, quam hic nobis spiritus sanctus proponit. Nam & famem, quae ecclesia vexata est, commemorat, & dei paternam curam, qua ecclesiae suae prospexit, exponit: addens simul, quo consilio, imminente publica calamitate, fideles usi sint. Et de his quidem singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Although our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ is never absent from his Church, yet, as he foretold, he allows it to be exercised in various ways, while adversity follows prosperity in a kind of continual alternation. The chief cause of this is that he wishes partly to restrain the wildness of our flesh and shake off excessive complacency, and partly to teach that he can protect and deliver his people no less in adversity than in prosperity. We have seen several memorable examples of this so far. For at first, under a happy beginning, the doctrine of the gospel was preached at Jerusalem and drew a great number of disciples to Christ; but soon a storm of persecution arose and disturbed the beginnings of the infant Church. Again, however, when Saul was converted to Christ, peace was unexpectedly restored to the churches, and the doctrine of Christ, extended even to the Gentiles, began to promise incredible fruits, after the church gathered from the Gentiles at Antioch, the most famous city of all Syria, and that noble name of Christians, was first given to believers. But behold, a new and great evil has fallen upon them: famine, namely, which afflicted the faithful most miserably, just as it did the whole world, since their resources had been partly exhausted in feeding the poor of the Church and partly plundered amid the raging of persecution. Now the consideration of these things is most useful to us, so that we may be less troubled if the same changes of fortune trouble us today also. And above other passages, this place deserves to be carefully considered because of the manifold consolation and instruction which the Holy Spirit sets before us here. For he both records the famine by which the Church was afflicted, and sets out God's fatherly care, by which he watched over his Church, adding at the same time by what counsel the faithful acted when public calamity threatened. Of these matters we shall speak one by one in order.

units.la: Primo autem de fame nobis dicendum est, cuius exteri quoque scriptores, & inter hos Iosephus maxime ac Suetonius meminerunt. Hanc divino iudicio immissam fuisse, nemo negabit, nisi qui deum orbis terrarum gubernatorem esse negare velit. Nam propheta teste, non est aliquod malum in ci-uitate, cuius non author sit deus. Amos 3. cap. Et in lege inter poenas, quibus deus sui verbi contemptum vindicat, agrorum sterilitas, vitibus inopia & fames, non postremo loco numerantur. Vide Leuit. 26. Deut. 28. Nec aliquid hominibus temere euenire putandum est, quando ad passerculos vsque & flores agri divinae providentiae curam extendi constat. Matth. 6. & 10. Prodest autem iudiciorum dei causas, si quid tale accidit, scrutari, quae non alibi melius, quam in hominum moribus, deprehendi possunt. Et sane huius famis causas quasi digito Lucas monstrare videtur, quando illam sub Claudio Caesare fuisse scribit. Nam principem orbis terrarum, penes quem illo tempore summa rerum potestas erat, nominare voluit, ut ex eo de publico totius orbis statu deq; illius seculi moribus iudicare possemus: quando constat principum vitia primo quidem in proceres, inde vero in ipsum vulgus corrupti exempli contagio derivari. Atqui Claudium per omnia corruptissimum fuisse, ethnici scriptores tradiderunt. A pueritia siquidem cum variis & tenacibus morbis conflictatus est, adeo vt animo simul & corpore hebetato, ne progressa quidem aetate, vlli publico priuatoue muneri habilis existimaretur. Quare illum Antonia mater portentum hominis, nec absolutum a natura, sed tantum inchoatum, dictitabat: & si quem socordiae argueret, stultiorem aiebat filio suo Claudio. Et soror Liuilla, cum audisset illum aliquando imperaturum, tam iniquam & indignam fortem Populi Rom. palam & clare detestata est. Naturae enim corruptionem multis argumentis prodidit. Primus sane militum fauorem pecuniis redemit, quo in Imperium subuectus est: quod ita gessit, vt maiore multo ventris & eorum, quae sub ventre sunt, quam huius curam habuerit: vtpote qui a conuiuio nunquam fere nisi distentus & madens surgeret, & libidinis in foeminas esset insatiabilis. Nec verisimile est, talem principem alijs, quàm sui similibus, proceribus & consiliarijs delectari potuisse. Quanta vero publicorum morum apud omnes ordines corruptio fuerit, ex illius seculi scriptoribus, & ex assiduis Iohannis & ipsius Christi apostolorum eius de poenitentia concionibus facile conijci potest, quibus minime opus erat, nisi omnia corruptissima fuissent. Accessit tamen vitiorum colophon, divini verbi contemptus & odium. Cum enim deus, misso in mundum filio suo, homines sibi reconciliare statuisset, & salutiferum gratiae verbum passim vulgaretur, plerique illud non modo contemnere & odisse, verum etiam crudeliter persequi ausi sunt: adeo ut nec in Iudaeorum gente, quae dei nomine prae ceteris gloriabatur, dei verbum audiretur. Num ergo mirum videri debet, quod ebrio & corrupto mundo verbi coelestis salutarem cibum fastidienti telluris fruges deus negavit, & insolenter contra Christum suum ferocientes fame coercuit? Testantur certe historici, propter continuas siccitates tantâ vitus & annonae inopiam cum vbiq; terrarum tum Romae inualuisse, ut Claudio Caesari aliquando vitae periculum subeundum fuerit, cum parum abesset, quin à populo inediae impatientissimo, lapidaretur. Docent autem huius generis exempla, quae nam publicorum malorum causa sit: publica nimirum flagitia, & verbi divini contemptus. Aequi hanc causam ipse deus tum in lege tum in prophetarum scriptis monstrat. Et arguuntur hoc loco, qui ex euangelij doctrina ista enasci clamant. Licet enim malis istiusmodi fideles quoq; implicentur, longè tamen alia illorum quàm mundi infelicis ratio est. Nam dei patris castigationem & disciplinam agnoscunt, fide & patientia res aduersas superant, & quia illis ad vitae institutionem ac emendationem rite vtuntur, fere fit ut clementi dei manu malis omnibus felicissimè liberentur. Fidelis enim est deus, nec suos vltra, quàm ferre possint, tentari patitur. 1.Cor.10. Et sequentia docebunt, quàm fideliter ecclesiae suae illo seculo dominus consuluerit. Nec dissimile huic est quod post sequentibus seculis contigisse legimus. Nam Eusebius tradit Maximino regnante & Christianos immaniter persequente, tantam annonae inopiam diuinitus immissam fuisse, ut diuites quoq; & opulenti in plateis publicè morerentur, & canum praedapalam fierent, qui paulò ante Christianos feris obiecerant, ut illorum miserabili interitu crudeles oculos satiarent. Illis vero miserè pereuntibus, Christianis non modò ad victum necessaria affuerunt, sed ijdem fame intermorituros pijs officijs subleuarunt. Erant hac nobis hodie consyderanda, quando non vnus Claudius regnat, sed passim ebrietas immanis dominatur, tamen abest, ut diuinis admonitionibus emendentur homines, ut potius corruptissimis vitae moribus impium & immanem diuini verbi contemptum odiumq; implacabile coniungant. Et sanè non desunt hodie quoq; diuinorum iudiciorum exempla: nobis vero aures simul & oculi desunt, quibus ea percipiamus, quae communi saluti seruire poterant. Vide Isa.5. Eccles.10. Amos 6. Matth.24. &c.
units.tr: First, then, we must speak of the famine, which foreign writers also mention, and among them Josephus above all and Suetonius. That it was sent by divine judgement no one will deny, unless he wishes to deny that God is the governor of the world. For, as the prophet bears witness, there is no evil in a city of which God is not the author (Amos 3). And in the law, among the punishments by which God avenges contempt of his word, barrenness of the fields, scarcity of vines and famine are not counted last (see Lev. 26; Deut. 28). Nor should we think that anything happens to men by chance, since it is established that the care of divine providence extends even to the sparrows and the flowers of the field (Matt. 6 and 10). It is useful, however, when such a thing happens, to search out the causes of God's judgements, which can be discovered nowhere better than in the morals of men. And indeed Luke seems to point with his finger to the cause of this famine when he writes that it happened under Claudius Caesar. For he wished to name the prince of the world, in whose hands at that time the supreme power lay, so that from him we might judge the public state of the whole world and the morals of that age, since it is agreed that the vices of princes flow down by the contagion of corrupt example first into the nobles, and thence into the common people. Now the ethnic writers have handed down that Claudius was corrupt in every respect. From boyhood he was afflicted with various stubborn illnesses, so that, with his mind and body both dulled, he was judged fit for no public or private office even when he had grown to mature age. Hence his mother Antonia used to call him a monster of a man, not finished by nature but only begun; and if she wished to reproach anyone for laziness, she would say he was more foolish than her son Claudius. And his sister Livilla, when she heard that he would one day rule, openly and clearly detested so unjust and unworthy a lot for the Roman people. For he revealed the corruption of his nature by many proofs. Indeed, he was the first to buy the favour of the soldiers with money, by which he was raised to empire; and he so conducted himself that he took far greater care of his belly and of the things beneath his belly than of anything else: for he rose from the table almost never except stuffed and drunk, and he was insatiable in his lust for women. Nor is it likely that such a prince could have delighted in any but men like himself, nobles and counsellors. And how great the corruption of public morals was among all orders can easily be inferred from the writers of that age, and from the constant sermons of John and of the apostles of Christ himself concerning repentance, which would not have been necessary at all unless everything had been most corrupt. Yet there was added to these vices the crowning evil, contempt and hatred of the divine Word. For when God, having sent his Son into the world, had decided to reconcile men to himself, and the saving word of grace was everywhere spread abroad, many not only despised and hated it but even dared to persecute it cruelly; so that the word of God was not heard even among the nation of the Jews, who gloried above others in the name of God. Is it therefore any wonder that God denied the fruits of the earth to a drunken and corrupt world which loathed the heavenly word's wholesome food, and restrained with famine those who raged insolently against his Christ? Certainly the historians testify that, on account of continual droughts, such a want of food and grain prevailed both throughout the world and at Rome that Claudius Caesar once faced danger to his life, since he came close to being stoned by a people most impatient of hunger. Examples of this kind teach what the cause of public evils is: namely public crimes and contempt of the divine Word. God himself shows this same cause both in the law and in the writings of the prophets. And those are rebuked here who cry out that such evils arise from the doctrine of the gospel. For although the faithful also are involved in evils of this kind, their situation is far different from that of the unhappy world. For they acknowledge the chastisement and discipline of God the Father, they overcome adverse things by faith and patience, and since they use these things rightly for the instruction and amendment of their lives, it generally comes about that they are most happily delivered from all evils by the merciful hand of God. For God is faithful, and does not allow his people to be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Cor. 10). And what follows will show how faithfully the Lord provided for his Church in that age. Nor is what we read happened in later ages unlike this. For Eusebius relates that under Maximinus, who cruelly persecuted the Christians, such a scarcity of food was sent by God that even the rich and wealthy died publicly in the streets, and the dogs which had shortly before been set on Christians to be thrown to the wild beasts became openly the prey, so that the cruel eyes might be sated by their wretched death. But while these perished miserably, the Christians not only supplied what was necessary for food, but also, by pious duties, relieved those who were about to die of hunger. These things ought to be considered by us today, when not one Claudius reigns but a monstrous drunkenness rules everywhere; yet it is far from the case that men are corrected by divine admonitions, but rather they join to their most corrupt manner of life an impious and monstrous contempt and implacable hatred of the divine Word. And indeed there are today too no lack of examples of divine judgements; but we lack ears and eyes to perceive those things which could serve the common good. See Isa. 5; Eccles. 10; Amos 6; Matt. 24, etc.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Sed videamus, ut publica imminente calamitate, suae ecclesiae consuluerit dominus? Prophetas excitauit, & ex illorum numero aliquos ex Hierosolymorum urbe Antiochiam transmisit, ut recentem illic ex gentibus ecclesiam prophetiae etiam dono illustraret. Inter hos Agabus quidam, spiritus suggestione excitatus, de ventura fame Christianos admonuit, authoritate, ut tam sibi ipsis quàm aliis prospicerent. Quo loco obseruanda nobis venit paterna dei bonitas, qui cum nostris peccatis prouocatus poenas immittere statuit, de ijsdem tamen prius admonere consueuit, cum ut omnibus constet nihil in mundo temere fieri, tum ut admoniti conuertamur & saluemur. Quem morem à prima mundi origine tam constanter obseruauit, ut Amos propheta dicere ausit: Non facit Deus quicquam, nisi reuelet arcanum suum seruis suis prophetis. Patet hoc in primae aetatis hominibus, quibus Noah praeconem iustitiae dedit, & centum viginti annorum tempus ad poenitentiam concessit, priusquam illos diluuio immisso deleret. Sodomitis quoque Lotum submisit, cuius doctrina simul & vitae exemplo ad vitae emendationem reuocari poterant. Aegyptios per Iosephum de futura fame admonens, multorum saluti consuluit. Eosdem postea per Mosem non verbis modò verumetiam horrendis prodigijs excitauit, ut officium facerent. Quid verò de Babylonica captiuitate dicere attinet, quam aliquot seculis priusquam illa eueniret, prophetas praedixisse constat? Et ultimum gentis Iudaicae excidium non modò Christus praedixit, sed de eodem infinitis propemodum prodigijs Iudaeos admonitos fuisse, Iosephus author est. Et si nullis vnquam admonitionibus peccantes in viam reuocaret, generales tamen praedictiones extant, innumeris diuinorum iudiciorum exemplis confirmata, quae docere poterant, quid sperandum sit omnibus ijs, qui diuinas leges temere transgredi, & absque poenitentia
units.tr: But let us see whether the Lord, with public calamity impending, took care of his Church. He raised up prophets and sent some of their number from the city of Jerusalem to Antioch, so that the young church there, made up of Gentiles, might be adorned with the gift of prophecy. Among these was a certain Agabus, who, stirred by the prompting of the Spirit, warned the Christians of the coming famine with authority, so that they might provide for themselves and for others. Here we must observe the fatherly goodness of God. Although he is provoked by our sins and resolves to send punishments, he is accustomed to give warning of them beforehand, both so that everyone may understand that nothing in the world happens by chance, and so that, being warned, we may be turned back and saved. He has observed this practice so constantly from the very beginning of the world that the prophet Amos dared to say: "The Lord God does nothing unless he reveals his secret to his servants the prophets."
