This is evident in the people of the first age, to whom Noah preached righteousness, and to whom God granted a period of a hundred and twenty years for repentance before he destroyed them by sending the flood. He also sent Lot to the Sodomites, by whose teaching and example of life they could have been called back to amendment of life. By warning the Egyptians through Joseph of the coming famine, he cared for the safety of many. Afterwards, through Moses, he roused the same people not only with words but also with terrible portents, so that they would do their duty. And what need is there to speak of the Babylonian captivity, which, as is established, the prophets foretold some centuries before it came about? And Christ not only foretold the final destruction of the Jewish nation, but Josephus testifies that the Jews were warned of it by almost countless portents. And even if he never called sinners back to the right way by any warnings, there remain nonetheless general predictions, confirmed by countless examples of divine judgments, which could teach what is to be expected by all those who dare to transgress the divine laws rashly and to indulge in corrupt morals without repentance.

units.la: Lib.9. Eccles. hist. cap.8.
units.tr: Lib.9. Eccles. hist. cap.8.

units.la: De bello Iud. lib.7. cap.12. pœnitentia corruptis moribus indulgere audent. Vide Levit.26. Deut.28. Ierem.5. &c. Agnoscamus obsecro bonitate hanc domini nostro seculo, ne dum fidas illius admonitiones spernimus, gravioribus pœnis coherceamur.
units.tr: De bello Iud. lib.7. cap.12. Let us acknowledge, I beg you, the goodness of the Lord toward our age; so that, while we despise his faithful warnings, we are not restrained by heavier punishments. See Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28, Jeremiah 5, and so on.

units.la: Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, illud quoq; observandum est, quòd Agabus per spiritum futuram famem significauisse dicitur. Exprimitur enim modus & ratio, qua illius seculi prophetæ in vicinando vsi sunt, ne quis illos vel ex astris præsagiuisse, aut alijs illicitis artibus deditos fuisse putet. Spiritus sanctus enim illis prophetiæ author fuit, sicuti dominus olim per Ioelem promiserat. Et Paulus prophetiam inter spiritus sancti dona recenset. Minimè ergo Agabi exemplum nostri seculi impostoribus patrocinatur, qui contra diuinæ legis præscriptionem ad curiosas artes couerfi, in futuros annos de bellorum motibus, terræ proventu, morbis item & alijs eius generis rebus vaticinari audent. Quorum audaciam cum impietate coniunctam, & diuinis legibus prohibitam esse, supra demonstrauimus. Vide Homil.4. Vide præterea Michæam nostrum Homil.20.
units.tr: Before we leave this point, it must also be noted that Agabus is said to have signified the coming famine through the Spirit. For the manner and method by which the prophets of that age used to foretell the future is here set out, so that no one may think they foretold it from the stars or were given over to other unlawful arts. For the Holy Spirit was the author of their prophecy, just as the Lord had promised long before through Joel. And Paul counts prophecy among the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the example of Agabus in no way lends support to the impostors of our own age, who, turning to curious arts contrary to the prescription of divine law, dare to prophesy about the coming years: about the movements of wars, the yield of the land, diseases too, and things of that sort. We have already shown above that their audacity, joined with impiety, is forbidden by divine laws. See Homily 4. See also our Micah, Homily 20.

units.la: Restat, vt quid Antiocheni Christiani, per prophetā admoniti fecerint, consyderemus. Vbi ante omnia illorum fides elucet, quæ omnium ab ipsis rectè factorum causa fuit. Nam illos prophetanti Agabo credidisse, ex actis facile colligitur. Nec enim suspectum habere poterant, quem ea ministrari audiebant, quæ communis omnium ordinum corruptio merebatur. Est hoc salutis initium, si dei verbo credere animum inducant homines. Hoc Nineuitis olim denunciatum à Deo excidium deplorat. Rursum verò plures alios sibi ipsis extremi excidij authores fuisse constat, quòd diuini verbi veritatem suo malo potius experiri, quàm fide amplecti voluerunt. Et Christus dominus hanc vnam Hierosolymitani excidij causam fuisse docet, quòd visitationis suæ diem agnoscere noluerint. Luc.19. Ita verò tempus illud gratiæ vocat, quo Iudæos cœlestis pater, primò quidem per Iohannem Baptistam, mox verò per filium suum & apostolos de ventura ira admonere, & ad vitæ morum emendationem exhortari dignatus fuerat. Quòd si hæc ad nostra secula transferre libeat, hanc præcipuam malorum causam fateri cogemur, quòd paucissimi sint, qui diuinis oraculis fidem habere, & imminentis pœnæ præsagia metuere soleant.
units.tr: It remains for us to consider what the Christians of Antioch did when they were warned by the prophet. Here, above all, their faith shines forth, which was the cause of everything they rightly did. For from the account it is easily gathered that they believed Agabus when he prophesied. Indeed, they could not regard with suspicion the one who was announcing things that the general corruption of all ranks deserved. This is the beginning of salvation, if people are willing to believe the word of God. Nineveh, on the other hand, lamented the destruction once announced to it by God. Again, it is established that many others have been the authors of their own utter ruin, because they preferred to test the truth of the divine word at their own cost rather than embrace it in faith. And Christ the Lord teaches that this was the one cause of the destruction of Jerusalem: that they would not recognise the day of their visitation (Luke 19). Thus he calls that the time of grace in which the heavenly Father deigned to warn the Jews of the coming wrath, first indeed through John the Baptist, and soon afterwards through his own Son and the apostles, and to exhort them to amend their lives. But if we are willing to apply this to our own times, we will be forced to acknowledge this as the chief cause of evils: that there are very few who are accustomed to have faith in the divine oracles and to fear the signs of the punishment that is at hand.

units.la: Porrò postquam propheranti Agabo crediderunt Antiocheni, egentium fratrum conditionem sibi ob oculos ponentes & qualis illa tempore famis futura fit diligenter expendentes, sese ad Christianæ pietatis siue charitatis officia præparauerunt. Quod illos præter filiorum huius seculi morem fecisse constat. Hi enim si quando annonæ caritatem oboriturum vident, ad quæstuosas artes conuerti, fruges coaceruant, & intimis penetralibus recondunt, vt ex publica calamitate priuatum lucrum captare possint. Imò horum artibus feré fit, vt magis aggrauentur rerum omnium inopia qui auxilio indigebant, & diuturnior sit fames, illis subinde maioris lucri spem auidè obseruantibus. At longè alios videmus Antiochiæ fideles, quos primos omnium sui nominis titulo Christus insigniri voluit. His enim prima hæc cura animo sedet, vt egentium & famæ laborantium fratrum inopiæ consulant. Et hic quidem Iudæorum fratrum maximam curam habendam esse intelligunt: partim quidem, quòd horum facultates direptas esse scirent (quemadmodum Paulus ad Hebræos capite decimo testatur) partim verò, quòd hoc officium sese illis debere agnoscerent, à quibus salutarem euangelij doctrinam & Christi saluatoris cognitionem acceperant. Facilè enim animaduertebant cordati simul & pij viri, non sine numine factum esse, vt ipsi quorum fortuna adhuc integra erant, de futurâ fame admonerentur: ita enim deum in publica inopia egentium fratrum nomine charitatis officium ab ipsis exigere putabant. Esse autem hoc memorabile cumprimis Christianæ gratitudinis exemplum, quo docemur, quid doctoribus suis auditores debeat, quando Antiocheni se totius Iudaicæ gentis debitores esse agnoscunt, eò quòd ex Iudæis quibusdam veritatē didicissent. Communis enim sensus iudicio Paulinum illud æquissimum esse intelligunt, non magnum quiddam præstari, si qui spiritualia metuerunt, carnalia seminent. 1. Corinth.9. At hodie ingratissimi sumus, dum ipsis quoq; doctoribus, nedum illorum gentilibus, victum necessarium inuident, qui ingentes ex euangelij doctrina fructus perceperunt. Ita verò testantur, se de euangelio non magnificè sentire, quando quæ euangelij ministris numerantur stipendia tanti faciunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, after the Antiochenes believed Agabus as he prophesied, setting before their eyes the condition of their needy brothers and carefully weighing what sort of famine it would be, they prepared themselves for the duties of Christian piety and charity. It is established that they did this contrary to the custom of the children of this world. For these, whenever they see a dearth of grain about to arise, turn to profit-seeking arts: they heap up grain and hide it in their innermost storerooms, so that they may snatch private gain from public calamity. Indeed, through their devices it usually comes about that those who needed help are the more burdened by the lack of all things, while the famine lasts longer, since those men keep eagerly watching for the hope of greater gain. But we see the faithful of Antioch to be very different: they were the first of all to be honoured by Christ with the title of their name. For this is their first concern, that they provide for the want of their brothers who are in need and suffering from famine. And they understand that here, in particular, the greatest care must be taken of the Jewish brothers: partly indeed because they knew that the goods of these men had been plundered (as Paul testifies to the Hebrews in chapter ten), and partly because they recognised that they owed this duty to those from whom they had received the saving doctrine of the gospel and the knowledge of Christ the Saviour. For thoughtful and godly men readily perceived that it was not without the divine will that they themselves, whose fortunes were still intact, were warned of the coming famine: they thought that God in this way demanded from them a work of charity in the public want of their needy brothers. This is a memorable example of Christian gratitude above all, by which we are taught what hearers owe to their teachers, since the Antiochenes acknowledge that they are debtors to the whole Jewish nation, because they had learned the truth from certain Jews. For by the common judgment of sense they understand that the saying of Paul is most just: that it is no great thing if men reap carnal things when they have sown spiritual things (1 Corinthians 9). But today we are most ungrateful, when we begrudge even our teachers, let alone their kindred, the necessary sustenance, though they have received immense fruits from the doctrine of the gospel. Indeed, by this we testify that we do not think highly of the gospel, when we make so little of the stipends that are counted out to the ministers of the gospel.

units.la: Cæterum rationem, quam hac in re Antiocheni obseruarunt, Lucas diligenter exponit. Primò, discipuli singuli (inquit) decreuerunt mittere in ministerium fratribus in Iudæa habitantibus. Cum vero singulorum hoc decretum fuisse docet, voluntarium hoc officium fuisse innuit, non coactum. Tales enim esse decet, qui Deo beneficentiam suam probari volunt. Nam hilarem datorem requirit dominus, ut Paulus monet. 2. Corinth. 9. Plurimum vero ad excitandum in nobis beneficentiae studium facit, si ministerium & officium hoc esse cogitemus, quod diuino iure ditiores egenis debent. Quae causa est, quod Paulus quoq; quoties hac de causa disserit, διακονίας voce vtitur, quae ministerij & dispensationis officium significat. Quo referri debet illud Christi, qui monet, ut ex iniquo Mammona nobis amicos paremus, qui nos cum defecerimus, in aeterna tabernacula recipiant. Luc. 16. Deinde tantum illos decreuisse mittere ait, prout vnicuiq; facultas suppetebat. Eam enim beneficentiae Christianae moderationem ipse Deus exhibuit, ut neminem plus quam fortunae ipsius ferre possint, grauari velit. Nota enim sunt illa Pauli: Si prius adsit animi promptitudo, ea accepta est iuxta illud quod possidet aliquis, non iuxta id quod non possidet. Non enim ut alijs relaxatio sit, vobis autem angustia: sed ut ex aequabilitate in praesenti tempore vestra copia illorum succurrat inopiae, &c. 2. Corinth. 8. Et viduam a Christo laudatam fuisse legimus, quae duo aera minuta in gazophylacium miserat, cum maiora donaria conferre nequiret. Marc. 12. Hic vero vehementer grauatur illorum malignitas, adeoq; inexcusabilis redditur, qui beneficentiae opera eo praetextu negligunt, quod iniquum esse putent, ut suo labore & industria partas opes alijs erogent: cum nihil ab illis exigat Deus, quam quod facultatum ipsorum ratio ferre potest. Postremo singulari industria cauent, ne qua fraus tam sanctum tamq; necessarium institutum interturbet & vitiet. Collectam enim pecuniam non quibusuis temere, sed Paulo & Barnabae deferendam committunt, quorum fides tam multis argumentis abunde perspecta erat. Et sane ut omnia illa omittamus, ex Pauli scriptis constat, quanta fide in hac re vsus sit, & quam anxie commendatam sibi habuerit egentium Iudaeorum causam. Vide 1. Corinth. 16. Et posteriores cap. 8. & 9. Item Rom. 15. Praeterea ad Seniores mittunt, ut horum prudentia rite distribuatur. Habemus igitur hoc loco, quid Christianos in publicis necessitatibus facere deceat. At si haec cum ijs, quae hodie fiunt, conferantur, perexigua veteris ecclesiae vestigia inuenire licebit. Plures enim publicas ecclesiae opes maligne auertunt, & turpiter dissipant: paucissimi vero & rarissimi, adeoq; nulli sunt, qui ex suis bonis Christianae beneficentiae officia exerceant. Magnus porro illorum numerus est, qui publica calamitate ad priuatum quaestum abuntur. Et qui optimi habentur, non ante pauperum inopiae succurrendum esse putant, quam illos ad mendicitatem redactos, & ostiatim stipem petere videant. Faxit Deus Opt. Max. ut vera fide & charitate inflammati, ex operibus pro Christianis agnoscI possimus in illo die, quo in gloria patris ad iudicium veniet dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke carefully sets out the principle which the Antiochenes observed in this matter. First, he says, the disciples each determined to send relief to the brothers living in Judaea; and since he teaches that this decision was each one's own, he implies that the duty was voluntary, not compelled. For such ought to be those who wish their beneficence to be pleasing to God. For the Lord requires a cheerful giver, as Paul advises (2 Corinthians 9). Indeed, it greatly helps to arouse in us zeal for beneficence if we consider this to be a ministry and a duty which the richer owe to the needy by divine right. This is why Paul too, whenever he discusses this matter, uses the word diakonia [διακονία], which signifies the office of ministry and stewardship. To this must be referred what Christ says, urging us to make friends for ourselves by means of unrighteous mammon, who will receive us into eternal dwellings when we fail (Luke 16). Next, he says that they decided to send only as much as each one's means allowed. For God himself has prescribed this moderation in Christian beneficence, so that he does not want anyone to be burdened beyond what his fortune can bear. Those words of Paul are well known: "If there is first a willing mind, it is accepted according to what a man has, not according to what he does not have. For it is not that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that by an equal measure your abundance at the present time may supply their want," and so on (2 Corinthians 8). We read too that the widow who cast two small coins into the treasury was praised by Christ, since she could not contribute larger gifts (Mark 12). Here their malice is severely condemned, and those are rendered inexcusable who neglect works of beneficence on the pretext that it seems unjust to give away to others riches gained by their own labour and industry, when God demands nothing from them except what the state of their means can bear. Finally, they take the greatest care that no fraud should disturb or corrupt so holy and so necessary an arrangement. For they did not carelessly commit the collected money to just anyone, but resolved that it should be carried to Paul and Barnabas, whose faithfulness had been thoroughly proved by many evidences. And indeed, to pass over all those things, it is clear from Paul's writings with what great faithfulness he handled this matter, and how anxiously he kept the cause of the needy Jews in his care (1 Corinthians 16; and the later chapters 8 and 9; likewise Romans 15). Besides, they send to the elders, so that the money may be properly distributed by their prudence. We have, then, in this passage what Christians ought to do in public necessities. But if these things are compared with what is done today, we will be able to find only very slight traces of the ancient Church. For many maliciously divert the public resources of the Church and squander them shamefully; very few, and very rarely, indeed none, are those who from their own goods carry out the duties of Christian beneficence. Moreover, the number of those who are misused for private gain by public calamity is great. And those who are regarded as the best men do not think that the poverty of the poor should be relieved until they see them reduced to beggary and asking alms from door to door. May God, Best and Greatest, grant that, inflamed with true faith and charity, we may be recognised as Christians by our works on that day when our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ comes to judgment in the glory of the Father, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXII.

units.la: EOdem autem tempore iniecit Herodes rex manus, vt affligeret quosdam ex ecclesia. Occidit autem Iacobum, fratrem Iohannis gladio. Et videns quod hoc placeret Iudaeis, perrexit comprehendere & Petrum. Erant autem dies azymorum. Quem cum etiam coepisset, posuit in carcerem, tradens quatuor quaternionibus militum custodiendum volens post pascha eum producere populo. Petrus itaque custodiebatur in carcere. Fiebat autem assidua precatio ab ecclesia ad deum pro ipso.
units.tr: About that time King Herod laid hands on some of the church to afflict them. He killed James the brother of John with the sword. When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to seize Peter also. (It was the days of unleavened bread.) When he had arrested him, he put him in prison and handed him over to four squads of soldiers, four soldiers to each watch, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover. So Peter was kept in prison. But the church made constant prayer to God for him.

units.la: DEscribit antehac Dius Lucas persecutiones, a sacerdotibus contra ecclesiam excitatas: quae licet graues & horrenda videri potuerint, multo tamen grauior est, quae hoc capite commemoratur. Author enim illius est Rex potentissimus, penes quem apud Iudaeos summa erat rerum potestas. Et cum hucusq; apostolorum ordo salvus & incolumis manisset, nunc in illum quoq; tantum impio tyranno permittitur, ut non postremum inter apostolos indigna morte tollat. Est lat. Est vero totius historiæ finis, vt hinc ecclesiæ fortem agnoscamus, & Christi admonitionum memores, ad similia præparemur. Caterum cum in his magna semper eluceat carnis nostræ tarditas, diligentius paulo singulæ præsentis loci circumstantiæ nobis consyderandæ erunt.
units.tr: Earlier, St Luke described the persecutions stirred up against the church by the priests. Although these seemed grievous and dreadful, the one recorded in this chapter is much more serious. Its author is a most powerful king, in whose hands lay the supreme authority among the Jews. Until now the company of the apostles had remained safe and unharmed, but now the impious tyrant is permitted to strike even against them, and by an unworthy death to take away one who was not the least among the apostles. Indeed, the purpose of the whole history is that we may recognise the strength of the church and, mindful of Christ's warnings, prepare ourselves for similar things. But since our flesh's great slowness always shows itself in these matters, each circumstance of the present passage will need to be considered a little more carefully.

units.la: Et primo quidem cum præcedentis Cap. sine præsentem historiam Lucas connectens, à tempore narrationem orditur. Nam cum de fame ab Agabo prædicta disseruisset, eodem tempore persecutionem ab Herode contra ecclesiam institutam fuisse scribit. Et si locum hunc cum fine Capitis conse-ras, hæc vltimo anno Herodis gesta esse patebit, cum paulo post Cæsarea horribili Dei iudicio extinctus extremum diem clauserit. At si temporum rationem ex historijs colligamus, vltimum Herodis huius annum in quartum Claudij Imperatoris incidisse deprehendemus, quo famem inualuisse historici prodiderunt. Simul ergo concurrunt duo grauissima mala, fames nimirum & persecutio, quæ singula ecclesiæ intolerabilia videri poterant. Est autem nobis diligenter consideranda hæc ecclesiæ fors, quam tot malis tamque grauibus Deus exerceri patitur. Et qui paulo ante Antiochenorum aliorumque quorundam animos excitarat, vt Iudæorum fratrum inopiæ sua liberalitate subuenirent, nunc aduersus eosdem tanti regis furiosos conatus insurgere finit. Atqui nouum non est, quod hic fit, & exstant infinita huius generis exempla. De Abrahamo legimus, illum cum Dei vocationem secutus, relicto patrio solo in terram Chanaan concessisset, inde per famem obortam eiectum, & in Ægyptum vsq; compulsum fuisse. Gen.12. Eiusdem filius Isaac, eandem fortem expertus, inter infestas Chanaanæorum gentes cum fame conflictatur. Gen.26. Ita Iosephum, amissa libertate, carceres quoq; & vitæ periculum subijsse legimus. Gen.37. & 39. Quid de Iacobo illius patre dicam? qui continuis malis ita vexatus est, vt in extrema senectute, apud Pharaonem vitæ suæ dies plerosq; acerbos fuisse testetur. Gen.47. Quòd si Israelis conditionem tum in Ægypto tum in deserto consyderes, perpetuos & suis quodammodo vitijs recurrentes malorum æstus videbis. Et quod modò primitiua ecclesia experitur, idipsum sequentibus post seculis euenisse constat. Nec est quod nobis meliora polliceamur hodie, quàm Christi oracula de nouissimi seculi malis extant, quibus ecclesiam fame, peste, bellis & persecutionibus exercendam esse admonemur. Matth.24. Luc.21. Quapropter nos ad patientiam præparari decet, vt cum ista inciderint, cogitemus iudicium incipere à domo Dei, nosq; à domino iudicari, ne cum mundo pœnitere nescio condemnemur. 1.Pet.4. 1.Cor.11. Simul vero illorum error arguitur, qui ex euentibus huius seculi de fide & religione iudicant: quasi vero piorum ciuitas in terris sit, cum illam in cœlis nobis præparatam esse, passim scriptura testetur.
units.tr: And first, Luke, connecting the present history with the end of the preceding chapter, begins his narrative with the time. For after speaking of the famine foretold by Agabus, he writes that at the same time Herod began a persecution against the church. If you compare this place with the end of the chapter, it will be clear that these things happened in the last year of Herod, when shortly afterwards he died at Caesarea by a dreadful judgement of God. If we gather the chronology from the histories, we find that this last year of Herod fell in the fourth year of the Emperor Claudius, when the historians report the famine was severe. So two very grievous evils came together, namely famine and persecution, each of which might have seemed intolerable to the church. We must carefully consider this lot of the church, which God allows to be tried by so many and such grave evils. He who a little before had stirred up the minds of the Antiochenes and certain others to relieve the poverty of their Jewish brothers by their generosity, now allows the raging attempts of so great a king to rise against those same brothers. Yet this is not new, and there are countless examples of this kind. We read that Abraham, when he followed God's call and had left his native land and come into the land of Canaan, was driven from there by a famine that arose, and was compelled as far as Egypt. Gen. 12. His son Isaac, experiencing the same lot, struggled with famine among the hostile nations of the Canaanites. Gen. 26. Likewise, we read that Joseph, having lost his liberty, underwent prisons and danger of life. Gen. 37 and 39. What shall I say of Jacob, his father, who was so troubled by continual evils that in extreme old age he testifies that most of his days had been bitter before Pharaoh? Gen. 47. If you consider the condition of Israel, both in Egypt and in the wilderness, you will see perpetual waves of evils returning, in a way arising from their own vices. And what the primitive church now experiences has clearly happened in the ages that followed. Nor have we any reason to promise ourselves better things today than the oracles of Christ about the evils of the last age, in which we are warned that the church is to be exercised by famine, pestilence, wars and persecutions. Matt. 24; Luke 21. Therefore it is fitting for us to be prepared for patience, so that when these things fall upon us we may think that judgement begins at the house of God, and that we are judged by the Lord, lest we be condemned with the world that does not know how to repent. 1 Pet. 4; 1 Cor. 11. At the same time, the error of those is refuted who judge faith and religion by the outcomes of this age, as if the city of the pious were on earth, when Scripture everywhere testifies that it has been prepared for us in heaven.

units.la: Secundò persecutionis authorem nominat Lucas, & Herodem fuisse scribit. Constat autem vel ex hoc loco, Galilææ & Iudææ reges communi nomine Herodes appellari solitos fuisse, nimirum à Magno illo Herode, qui primus ex alienigenis in Iudæa regnum obtinuit. Hunc enim, de quo in præsenti Lucas agit, Agrippam fuisse certum est, Herodis Magni ex Aristobulo filio nepotem: cuius mortem Lucæ per omnia consentiens Iosephus lib. Antiq.19.cap.7. describit. Fuit hic potentissimus simul & callidissimus princeps. Nam à Caio Cæsare vinculis liberatus (in quæ à Tiberio propter nimiam Caij familiaritatem coniectus fuerat) & tetrarchiarum Philippi & Lysaniæ Rex declaratus, paulò post Herodem Antipam patruum & sororium suum regno Galilææ spoliauit, illo in exilium relegato à Caio, apud quem per literas ipsum accusauerat. Vbi autem Caio Cæsare defuncto, Claudius imperium arripuit, ab illo Iudææ simul & Samariæ prouincijs donatus est, sicque vniuersum fere aui sui, Herodis Magni, regnum Agrippa obtinuit. Præstat autem huius regis potentiam diligenter inspicere, vt maior eluceat Christi potentia, qui tantum hostem tam facile obtriuit. Talem enim cum Christo filio suo & eius ecclesia Deus committi voluit, vt singulare exemplum ederet, vanam adeoq; nullam esse mundi huius potentiam, si Christo domino conferatur. Nam Agrippa hic, qui intra breue temporis spacium felicissimo rerum suarum successu in summam regij fastigij potentiam ascenderat, qui Tiberij crudeles manus effugerat, qui Herodis Antipæ insidias mirificè eluserat, vt primum Christo congredi audet, miserrimè occidit, vt in fine Capitis audiemus. Tale quid in Iuliano cernitur, qui cum felicissimus bellator fuisset, repente imperium simul & vitam amisit, quando Christum oppugnare cœpit, quem per ludibrium solebat Galilæum dicere. Extant & nostro seculo huius generis exempla: in quorum consyderatione nos assiduos esse conuenit, ne hostium Christi potentia & viribus offendamur. Fortior enim & maior est, qui à nobis stat; & ferreum Christi sceptrum sentient quouis seculo, quicunque salutari illius disciplina coherceri non sint. Vide Psal.2. &c.
units.tr: Second, Luke names the author of the persecution and writes that it was Herod. Even from this place it is evident that the kings of Galilee and Judaea were customarily called by the common name Herod, namely after that great Herod who was the first foreigner to obtain the kingdom of Judaea. The one with whom Luke is now concerned was certainly Agrippa, grandson of Herod the Great through his son Aristobulus. Josephus, agreeing with Luke in every respect, describes his death in Antiquities, book 19, chapter 7. He was a most powerful and at the same time most crafty prince. Freed from chains by Gaius Caesar (into which Tiberius had thrown him because of his excessive intimacy with Gaius), and declared king of the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias, he shortly afterwards stripped his uncle and brother-in-law, Herod Antipas, of the kingdom of Galilee, Herod being banished into exile by Gaius, to whom Agrippa had accused him in a letter. When Gaius Caesar died and Claudius seized the empire, Agrippa was granted the provinces of Judaea and Samaria as well, and so he obtained almost the whole kingdom of his grandfather, Herod the Great. It is worth examining the power of this king carefully, so that the greater power of Christ may shine out, who so easily crushed so great an enemy. For God willed that such a man be set against Christ his Son and his church, so that he might give a singular example that the power of this world is vain and utterly nothing when it is set against Christ the Lord. For this Agrippa, who within a short time had risen by the most fortunate success of his affairs to the highest height of royal power, who had escaped the cruel hands of Tiberius, who had marvellously eluded the snares of Herod Antipas, as soon as he dared to engage Christ, perished most miserably, as we shall hear at the end of the chapter. Something similar is seen in Julian, who, though he had been a most fortunate warrior, suddenly lost both empire and life when he began to attack Christ, whom he used to mockingly call the Galilean. Examples of this kind also exist in our own age, and we should constantly keep them in mind, lest we be offended by the power and strength of Christ's enemies. For he who stands on our side is stronger and greater. All who are not restrained by his saving discipline will feel the iron sceptre of Christ in every age. See Ps. 2, etc.

units.la: Tertiò instituta persecutionis causas inuestigare decet, quarum altera subobscurius à Luca innuitur, altera verò diserte exprimitur. Primò enim Herodem manus iniecisse siue admonisse dicit, vt affligeret quosdam de ecclesia. Et quia ecclesiæ mentio fit, quæ in causa fidei & religionis âre-liquis Iudæis secessionem fecerat, illi tanquam schismatis authori, Agrippa infensus fuisse videtur. Nequeunt enim vel minimam schismatis speciem inter suos ferre tyranni, non quòd illis pax tanto pere cordi sit, sed quòd suæ potentiæ metuunt, quam schismate & dissidijs, quàm maximè imminui in telligunt. Quæ causa est, quòd cum ab omni religione alienissimi sint, religionis tamen vniformem consensum in suis regnis esse velint. Norunt enim astutissimi homines, nihil ad disiungendos hominum animos religionis diuersitate vel dissimilitudine efficacius esse. Vtriusq; rei exempla in scriptu-ris extant. Ieroboam, ne cum Dauidis domo reconciliarentur decem tribus, in quas ipse regnum arripuerat, cultus nouos instituit 1. Reg.12. Et Antiochus, vt imperium suum stabilire-t, eandem religionis formam in omnibus provincijs suis obseruari voluit. 1. Machab. Interim non ofcitanter consy-derandum est, quòd foliferè veritatis cultores pro schismaticis habentur, cum non alij vnitatis ve-ritate studio maiori teneantur, nec aliunde fecundior sectarum soboles, quàm ex superstitione enascatur. Apud Iudæos certè Pharisæorum, Sadducæorum, Essenorum & aliorum huius farinæ hominum se-ctæ habebantur. Nec tamen in aliquos horum manus Agrippa iniecit. Sola Christi ecclesia, tanquam schismatis mater, persecutionem sustinet. Simile quid nostro seculo factum vidimus. Quis enim in-numeras & diuersissimas Monachorum sectas ignorat, quibus iam seculis aliquot Christianus orbis scissus est? At quis vnquam siue Pontificum siue imperatorum & regum eos schismaticos dixit, li-cet & nomè aliud profiterentur, & vestitu simul atq; ceremonijs à reliquis differrent? Imò tales Pon-tificum authoritate defensi, & in intima regum consilia admissi sunt. Vt primùm verò orthodoxa fides, syncriori euangelij doctrina illustrata, caput exeruit, mox horrenda haereticorum, sectariorum schismaticorum nomina passim audiri coeperunt. Quia enim sola Veritas satanæ regnum validissi-mè euertit, minimè vt ferre potest, vt hanc amplectantur, qui in tenebris hucusq; agentes, illi seruien-dos præbuerunt. Interim illo instigante, pacem turbari clamitant, qui quiduis potius quàm Chri-stianam pacem in suis regnis ferre possunt.
units.tr: Third, it is fitting to inquire into the causes of this persecution. Luke hints at one of them rather obscurely, but expresses the other plainly. For first he says that Herod laid hands on, or set about, afflicting certain members of the church. Since mention is made of the church, which had separated from the rest of the Jews in matters of faith and religion, Agrippa seems to have been hostile to them as the author of a schism. Tyrants cannot bear even the slightest appearance of schism among their people, not because peace is so dear to them, but because they fear for their power, which they understand is greatly weakened by schism and dissension. This is why, although they are most alien to every religion, they nevertheless want there to be uniform agreement in religion throughout their kingdoms. The most cunning men know that nothing is more effective for dividing men's minds than diversity or disagreement in religion. Examples of both things are found in the Scriptures. Jeroboam, so that the ten tribes, over which he had seized the kingdom, would not be reconciled with the house of David, instituted new forms of worship. 1 Kings 12. And Antiochus, in order to establish his empire, wanted the same form of religion observed in all his provinces. 1 Macc. Meanwhile we must not overlook that the cultivators of the truth are almost always held to be schismatics, although no others hold more zealously to the unity of truth, and no more fruitful offspring of sects springs from anywhere than from superstition. Among the Jews there were certainly sects of Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others of that kind. Yet Agrippa laid hands on none of these. The church of Christ alone, as the mother of schism, bears persecution. We have seen something similar happen in our own age. For who does not know the countless and very diverse sects of monks, by which the Christian world has been split for some centuries? Yet who has ever called them schismatics, whether pontiffs, emperors or kings, although they profess a different name and differ from the rest in dress and ceremonies? Indeed, such men, defended by the authority of the pontiffs, were admitted even into the innermost counsels of kings. But as soon as orthodox faith, illuminated by the purer doctrine of the gospel, lifted up its head, the dreadful names of heretics, sectaries and schismatics began to be heard everywhere. For since only truth most powerfully overturns the kingdom of Satan, it cannot bear that those should embrace it who, until now walking in darkness, have given themselves over to serve him. Meanwhile, at his instigation, they cry out that peace is being disturbed, who in their kingdoms can tolerate anything rather than Christian peace.

units.la: Alteram causam, quæ Herodem sua sponte furentem, magis instigauit, diserte exprimit Lu-cas, dicens: Videns quòd hoc placeret Iudæis, perrexit comprehendere & Petrum. Voluit ergo no-uus Rex apud Iudæos, quos pro auito ingenio iugi impatientes esse, interea autem implacabili Chri-stianæ religionis odio laborare noucrat, gratiam inire. Pulchrè autem in hoc exemplo tyrannorum mores exprimuntur, quibus hoc proprium est, vt innocentium hominum sanguine suam tyrannidem stabiliant. Nec enim precio-sus est in illorum oculis pauperum sanguis, quemadmodum de bono re-ge propheta dixit. Psal.72. Sed piorum capitibus ceu telsēris ludunt, si ex illorum morte aliquid emolumenti accessurum perent. Ita olim Augustum Ciceronis capite Antonij fauorem demeruisse legimus. Et Pilatus, vt Herodi Antipæ gratificaretur, illi Christum transmisit, & eundem cuius innocentiam multis argumentis deprehenderat, in Iudaici populi gratiam cruci adiudicauit: eo ni-mirum facto illorum animos sibi reconciliaturus, quos multis indignis modis offenderat. Nec de-sunt nostro seculo huius generis exempla. Agrippam enim imitantur, quicunque Christi doctrinam & discipulos ideò hostiliter persequuntur, vt Pontificum & episcoporum amicitia frui possint. Et quod olim L. Flaminium fecisse traditur, qui in gratiam mulierculæ adamatæ quendam secuti per-cussit: id hodie inter principes nimis vulgare est, vt in Babyloniæ meretricis gratiam non secures modò & flammas, verumetiam ipsum belli terrorem aduersus Christianæ doctrinæ professores cir-cumferant. Hic verò nos consoletur, quòd Deum habemus nostræ causæ vindicem, qui vt Iudæorum gentem, implacabili odio Christi imssmatam, excidit: ita horrendis modis eorum iniustitiam vl-tus est, qui sanctorum suorum sanguine impiæ gentis fauorem redimere studuerunt. Experientur idem iudicium, quicunque etiam hodie Christum persequi audent, vt mundo infelici placeant. Com-modior tamen de his dicendi locus in fine Capitis sese offeret, vbi horribilem Herodis exitum Lu-cas commemorat. Quarto, quid tantus Rex aduersus Christi ecclesiam tentarit, quidq; effecerit narratur. Et duo quidem commemorantur illius facinora, quibus sempiternam sibi conciliauit nominis infamiam. Primum est, quod Iacobum, Iohannis apostoli & euangelistae fratrem, gladio occidit. Fuit is non postremus in apostolorum ordine. Nam eundem hunc Christus dominus vna cum Iohanne fratre & Petro sibi prae aliis familiarem fecit, quando resuscitatae Iairi filiae miraculo oculatum testem adhi-buit, & suae clarificationis spectatorem esse voluit. Idem a Christo propter ardentem pietatis zelum & dicendi vehementiam tonitrui filius dictus est. Marc.3.cap. Permittit tamen Deus arcano suo iudicio, vt primus ex apostolorum numero cadat, & tantus Christi cultor crudelissimo tyranno prae-da fiat. Quo exemplo euidenter demonstratur, crucem & infames vitae exitus, nequaquam irati Dei argumenta esse, quemadmodum impij dicere consueuerunt, quibus summa sapientia videtur, de fide & religione ex euentibus iudicare. At si illos audire libeat, cum Abelo, primo Dei cultore, prophetas simul & apostolos omnes, adeoque ipsum Dei filium, Iesum Christum, damnabimus: cum omnes bos impiorum dolis circumuentos & occisos fuisse constet. Quin potius Christum audiamus dicentem: Beati, qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam: quoniam illorum est regnum coelorum. Beati estis, cum probra iecerint in vos homines, & insectati fuerint, & dixerint omne malum verbum aduersus vos, mentientes propter me. Gaudete & exultate, quoniam merces vestra multa est in coelis. Sic enim persecuti fuerunt prophetas, qui fuerunt ante vos, &c. Matth.5. cap. Quae causa est, quod Paulus in afflictionibus nos gloriari docet. Rom.5.cap. Ita enim nos filio Dei conformes fieri conuenit, vt postquam cum illo patimur, cum eodem glorificemur & regnemus. Rom. 8.cap. & 2. Tim.2.cap.
units.tr: Another cause, which more strongly incited Herod, who was raging of his own accord, Luke states plainly: "Seeing that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also." The new king wished to win the favour of the Jews, who, by their ancestral temperament, were always impatient, and whom he knew to be burning with an implacable hatred of the Christian religion. In this example the manners of tyrants are vividly portrayed, for it is characteristic of them to establish their tyranny with the blood of innocent men. The blood of the poor is not precious in their eyes, as the prophet said of the good king (Ps. 72). But they toy with the heads of the godly as with missiles, if they think some advantage will come from their death. Thus we read that Augustus once won the favour of Antony by the head of Cicero. And Pilate, to gratify Herod Antipas, sent Christ to him, and then condemned to the cross, to please the Jewish people, the very man whose innocence he had established by many proofs; doubtless by this deed he meant to win back the minds of those he had offended in many unworthy ways. Examples of this kind are not lacking in our own age. For all those imitate Agrippa who so hostilely persecute the doctrine of Christ and his disciples in order to enjoy the friendship of the Pontiffs and bishops. And what L. Flaminius is said to have done long ago, when he struck down a man at the urging of a woman he loved, to please her, is today too common among princes. To win the favour of the Babylonian harlot, they level against the professors of Christian doctrine not only axes and fires but the very terror of war. Yet this should console us: we have God as the avenger of our cause, who destroyed the Jewish nation, stung by implacable hatred of Christ, and punished in dreadful ways the injustice of those who tried to buy the favour of that impious nation with the blood of his saints. The same judgment awaits all who today dare to persecute Christ in order to please the unhappy world. A more suitable place to speak of these matters will present itself at the end of the chapter, where Luke recounts Herod's dreadful end. Fourth, it is related what so great a king attempted against the Church of Christ and what he achieved. Two of his crimes are recorded, by which he earned for himself an everlasting infamy. The first is that he killed James, brother of John the apostle and evangelist, with the sword. He was not the least in the order of the apostles. For Christ the Lord made this same man, together with John his brother and Peter, especially familiar to himself above the others, when he made them eyewitnesses of the miracle of the raising of Jairus's daughter and wished them to be spectators of his glory. The same man was called a son of thunder by Christ on account of his burning zeal for piety and the vehemence of his speech (Mark 3). Yet God, by his secret judgment, permits the first of the apostles to fall, and so great a worshipper of Christ to become the prey of a most cruel tyrant. By this example it is clearly shown that the cross and infamous ends of life are by no means signs of God's anger, as the impious are accustomed to say, who think it the height of wisdom to judge faith and religion by outcomes. But if we were to listen to them, we would condemn along with Abel, the first worshipper of God, all the prophets and apostles, and indeed the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, since it is certain that all of them were trapped and killed by the snares of the impious. Rather let us listen to Christ saying: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when men revile you and persecute you and say every evil word against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you," etc. (Matt. 5). This is why Paul teaches us to glory in afflictions (Rom. 5). For it is fitting that we be made conformed to the Son of God, so that, after we suffer with him, we may be glorified and reign with him (Rom. 8; 2 Tim. 2).

units.la: Alterum Herodis facinus est, quod primum conatum Iudaeis placuisse videns, & proinde sibi pergendum esse existimans, Petrum quoq; comprehendit. Nam quo terribiliorem se praeberet, non in vilem plebeculam, sed in ipsos antistites grassari voluit. Nec per ipsum stetit, quo minus Petrum quoq; confestim ad supplicium raperet: sed quia dies azymorum agebantur, festi religione prohibitus est, ne huius prophanatione Iudaeorum animos, quos sibi deuincire studebat, abs se alienaret. Ita ve-rò egregie hypocritam quoq; agit crudelissimus nebulo, & religionis studium simulat, qui omnem dei sensum iam pridem animo eiecerat, vt in illius exitu patebit. Interim hoc diuinae prouidentiae opus est, quod fucata illius sanctimonia Deus ad apostoli sui liberationem vtitur. Ita enim tyrannorum conatus ipsis medijs eludere & frustrare nouit, quibus illi se res suas maxime confecturos sperant. Obserua autem, quanta diligentia in obseruando Petro tyrannus vtatur. Quatuor enim quaternionibus militum custodiendum committit, catenis vinciri & adeius latus duos ex militibus excubare iubet, vt postea in liberationis historia videbimus. At quot obsecro fures, latrones, sicarios, periuros, blasphemos & facinorosos interea per totum Herodis regnum impune grassatos fuisse putas, dum innocens Christi apostolus instar latronis nocentissimi asseruatur? Atqui hoc illud est, quod Christus etiam ad se capiendum emissus exprobrat, Luc.22.cap. dicens: Quasi ad latronem existis cum gladijs & fustibus, &c. Simul vero & hoc obseruabis, quod tempore festi in vinculis agit tantus apostolus, & in singulas horas atrocem mortis sententiam expectat, dum alij laetos dies ducunt. Huius itaq; exemplum imitati patienter feramus, si quando dies festi nobis vel propter morbos, vel carceres, vel alia eius generis aduersa in moerorem conuertantur. Nec enim festum agunt, qui vel diuinis ceremonijs vel solennibus epulis intersunt, sed qui Christi spiritu confortati, in illo gaudent, etiamsi undiq; vrgentibus malis premantur.
units.tr: The second crime of Herod is that, seeing that his first attempt had pleased the Jews, and thinking that he must therefore proceed, he seized Peter also. For in order to show himself more terrible, he wished to rage not against the common rabble but against the leaders themselves. Nor did it stand in his way that he did not at once hurry Peter off to execution; but because the days of unleavened bread were being observed, he was restrained by regard for the feast, lest by profaning it he should alienate the minds of the Jews, whom he was eager to bind to himself. Indeed the most cruel scoundrel also plays the hypocrite here, and feigns zeal for religion, though he had long since banished all sense of God from his mind, as will be clear at his end. Meanwhile it is a work of divine providence that God, using the pretended sanctity of the man, brings about the liberation of his apostle. For thus he knows how to mock and frustrate the attempts of tyrants by the very means through which they hope to accomplish their aims most of all. Observe, however, with how much care the tyrant takes to guard Peter. He commits him to four squads of soldiers to be guarded, orders him to be bound with chains and two of the soldiers to keep watch at his side, as we shall see later in the story of his deliverance. But how many thieves, robbers, assassins, perjurers, blasphemers and criminals do you suppose went about with impunity throughout Herod's kingdom meanwhile, while an innocent apostle of Christ is kept like the most guilty robber? Yet this is what Christ also rebukes, when he was sent out to seize him, saying: "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs?" etc. (Luke 22). At the same time you will also observe that during the feast the great apostle is in chains, and awaits the dreadful sentence of death every hour, while others spend joyful days. Let us, then, imitate his example and bear patiently whenever the feast days are turned to mourning for us through sickness, prisons, or other adversities of that kind. For those do not keep a feast who attend the divine ceremonies or the solemn banquets, but those who, strengthened by the Spirit of Christ, rejoice in him, even when they are pressed on every side by evils.

units.la: Caeterum postremo, quid ecclesia interea egerit, indicatur. Illa vero nec turpi ocio, nec voluptatibus interea indulsit, sed suam esse intelligens Petri causam, pro illo indesinenter preces fundit ad dominum. Est hoc gratitudinis simul & fidei argumentum. Nam agnoscunt quid Petro debeant, a quo bucusque veram salutis viam edocti fuerant. Et sperant Dei ope periclitantem liberari posse. Docet locus hic, quid fratribus pro fidei & Christi causa periclitantibus Christiani debeant. Omne nimirum officij genus pro ratione vocationis suae, in quam diuinitus constituti sunt. Et si qui omnem bos iuuandi facultatem sibi ereptam esse videnf, saltem precibus communem causam adiuuent. Monet hoc tu Christi gloria, cui promouendae omnes studere debet, tum charitatis lex & Christianae communionis ratio, quae iubet, vt nobis communes esse ducamus tribulationes, quae fratribus accidunt. Et huc quidem illud apostoli pertinet: Memores estote vinctorum, tanquam vnà cum illis vincti: eorum item qui affliguntur, velut ipsi quoq; versantes in corpore. Heb.13. Item: Gaudete cum gaudentibus, flete cum flentibus, eodem animo alij in alios affecti. Rom.12. At si haec cum nostri seculi moribus conferas, facile patebit quàm frigidi simus in re maximè neceßaria. Gemunt paßim nonin vinculis modò & carceribus verumetiam inter carnificum manus & in mediis flamis pij Iesu Christi martyres. Quotus vero quisq; est, qui illorum cruciatibus tangatur? Imò dum integrae vrbes & gentes pro fide & Christo ad sanguinem vsq; decertant, pleriq; interea voluptatibus dediti, fratrum nan fragia quasi per lusum ex portu spectant. Vt interim de illis dicere omittam, qui pfafforum hanc causam esse clamant, & proinde bene actum esse arbitrantur, si quando illi pro pietatis studio indignam mercedem referant. Testantur isti homines, se in Christi corpore non esse, cum nulla tangantur cum Christi membris sympathia. Vide 1.Corinth.12. Interim docet hic locus, quibus armis maximè pugnet ecclesia. Precibus nimirum, quibus ipsum Deum vinci quodammodo & expugnari nouit. Has igitur indesinenter ad Deum fundit, & in illis praesens subsidium aduersus tyrannorum minas, & laqueos, enses & omnis generis tormenta inuenit. Sed de his sequenti Sermone agetur, vt piorum precibus militum excubias deuitas & carceris fores reseratos fuisse patebit. Sufficiat nunc ecclesiae fortem agnouisse, quae assiduis persecutionibus exercetur. Ad hanc ergo praeparemur, vt in patientia nostra possideamus animas nostras, per Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, it is shown what the Church meanwhile did. It neither gave itself up to shameful idleness nor to pleasures in the meantime, but, understanding that Peter's cause was its own, it poured out unceasing prayers to the Lord on his behalf. This is a proof both of gratitude and of faith. For they acknowledge what they owe to Peter, by whom they had hitherto been taught the true way of salvation. And they hope that he, who is in peril, can be freed by the help of God. This passage teaches what Christians owe to brothers who are in peril for the cause of the faith and of Christ: every kind of service, according to the measure of their calling, into which they have been placed by God. And if anyone sees that every power of helping has been taken from him, let him at least help the common cause by prayers. The glory of Christ, which all ought to strive to advance, admonishes us of this, and also the law of love and the principle of Christian fellowship, which bid us count the afflictions that befall our brothers as common to us. To this indeed the words of the apostle refer: "Remember those in bonds, as if bound with them, and those who are afflicted, as being yourselves in the body" (Heb. 13). Again: "Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, being of one mind toward one another" (Rom. 12). But if you compare these things with the manners of our age, it will easily be seen how cold we are in a matter most necessary. Everywhere the pious martyrs of Jesus Christ groan, not only in chains and prisons but also in the hands of executioners and in the midst of the flames. Yet how few are there who are moved by their sufferings? Indeed, while whole cities and nations contend even to blood for the faith and Christ, many meanwhile, given over to pleasures, look on the shipwrecks of their brothers from the harbour as if it were a game. Not to mention those who cry out that this cause is that of the priests, and therefore think it well done if the priests receive an unworthy reward for their devotion to piety. Such men testify that they are not in the body of Christ, since they are touched by no sympathy with the members of Christ (see 1 Cor. 12). Meanwhile this passage teaches with what weapons the Church chiefly fights: namely with prayers, by which it knows how God himself may in some measure be conquered and overcome. Therefore it pours these out to God without ceasing, and in them it finds present help against the threats of tyrants, their snares, swords and every kind of torment. But these things will be treated in the following sermon, where it will be shown that by the prayers of the godly the guards of the soldiers were avoided and the doors of the prison were opened. Let it suffice now to have recognised the strength of the Church, which is exercised by constant persecutions. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for this, that in our patience we may possess our souls, through Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 83.

units.la: Cum autem eum productu rus esset Herodes, nocte illa dormiebat Petrus inter duos milites, vinctus duabus catenis, & custodes ante ostium seruabant carcerem. Et ecce Angelus domini astitit, & lumen refulsit in habitaculo. Percussò autem latere Petri, excitauit eum, dicens: Surge ocyus. Et exciderunt catenae de manibus eius. Dixitq; illi Angelus: Praecingere, & subliga soleas tuas. Fecit autem sic. Et dicit illi: Circunda tibi vestimentum tuum, & sequere me. Et egressus sequebatur eum, & nesciebat verum esse quod fiebat per Angelum, sed putabat se visionem videre. Cum autem pertransissent primam custodiam & secundam, venerunt ad portam ferream, quae ducit in vrbem, quae sponte aperta est illis. Et egressi processerant vicum vnum, & mox discedit Angelus ab eo. Et Petrus ad semetipsum reuersus, dixit: Nunc vere scio, quod dominus Angelum suum misit, & eripuit me ex manu Herodis, & omni expectatione populi Iudaeorum.
units.tr: When Herod had brought him forth, that same night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and the guards before the door were keeping the prison. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by him, and a light shone in the room. He struck Peter on the side and woke him, saying, "Get up quickly." And the chains fell from his hands. The angel said to him, "Gird yourself and put on your sandals." He did so. And the angel said to him, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me." So he went out and followed him, and did not know that what was done through the angel was real, but thought he was seeing a vision. When they had passed the first guard and the second, they came to the iron gate that leads into the city, which opened of its own accord for them. They went out and walked down one street, and suddenly the angel left him. Then Peter came to himself and said, "Now I truly know that the Lord has sent his angel and has rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people."

units.la: Divus Lucas in praesentis historia descriptione tria cum primis memorabilia comprehendit. Primò communem ecclesiae Christi fortem, ceu in speculo contemplandam proponit, quam Deus variis malis & tribulationibus exerceri patitur. Deinde quod nam singulorum Christianorum officium sit docet, si quando persecutionum tempestas oboriatur: nimirum vt Christianae communionis memores, suam hic causam agi credant, & sub cruce periclitantes fratres, si non alio officio iuuare possunt, saltem assiduis precibus Deo commendent. Hoc enim ecclesia, cum Petrus ab Herode in vincula coniectus esset, sedulò fecisse scribit. Tertio diuinae bonitatis exemplum proponit, quo docemur, Deum tunc suorum quàm maximè curam gerere, quando omnitum humano tum diuino auxilio destituti videntur. Atqui hoc loco piarum precum effectus cernitur, quem illius saeculi fideles diuinis pro missionibus per omnia conformè experti sunt. Miraculosè enim liberatur sanctus Christi apostolus, & ecclesiae precibus vniuersa Herodis potentia simul & prudentia cedit: quando nec militum excubiae, nec ferrea catenarum vincula, nec obseratae fores, nec portae ferreae claustra eum retinere possunt, quem Deus suorum precibus donauerat. Praestat autem diligentius paulò hunc locum excutere, cum Lucas quoq; in singulis circunstantijs describendis tanto studio vsus sit, vt ne minutissima quidem praetermittat, eò quod singula haec nostrae institutioni simul & consolationi plurimù seruire possunt.
units.tr: Luke, in describing this present history, sets out three things especially worth remembering. First, he presents the common condition of the Church of Christ, to be contemplated as in a mirror, which God allows to be harassed by various evils and tribulations. Next, he teaches what the duty of each Christian is when a storm of persecution arises: namely, that mindful of Christian fellowship, they should believe that their own cause is being fought here, and that, if they cannot help brethren in peril under the cross by any other service, they should at least commend them to God by constant prayers. For this is what the Church did, Luke writes, when Peter had been thrown into chains by Herod, and it did so diligently. Third, he sets before us an example of divine goodness, by which we are taught that God then takes the greatest care of his people, when they seem to be deprived of all human and divine help. And indeed in this place we see the effect of pious prayers, which the faithful of that age experienced in every way as answered by God. For the holy apostle of Christ is delivered by a miracle, and by the prayers of the Church the whole power and prudence of Herod give way, when neither the watch of the soldiers, nor the iron fetters, nor the barred doors, nor the iron gate can hold him whom God had granted in answer to his people's prayers. It is worth examining this place a little more carefully, since Luke also uses such great diligence in describing each circumstance that he omits not even the smallest details, because each of these can serve very much both for our instruction and for our consolation.

units.la: A tempora
units.tr: From the time

units.la: A tempore autem narrationem orditur, non tam communi historicorum more, quàm quòd hoc ad diuini beneficij illustrationem multum momenti affert. Nam ea ipsa nocte Petrum liberatum esse scribit, postquam ipsum capitis supplicio multare Herodes decreuerat. Vnde constat diebus aliquot liberationem hanc suspensam fuisse, quibus interea Petrus quidem carceris molestias pertulit, ecclesia verò in precum ardore perseuerauit, & Christi odio inflammati Iudæi indignam tanti viri necem, ceu hiantes corui, expectarunt. Sed in ipso temporis momento, cum breue tantummodo noctis spacium illorum expectationem remorari videretur, egregiè illos delusit dominus, suumque seruum tam imminenti gladio eripuit. Quo exemplo admonemur, differri quidem interdum opem à domino, non tamen ideo hunc nostri memoriam & curam deponere: sed hoc potius agere, ut & nos interea pro dignitate exerceat atq; exploret, & illustrius reddat liberationis beneficium, quando praeter omnem spem, quae in humanis superesse poterat, illud contingere videmus. Hac ipsa ratione factum est, quòd Israelem olim tunc demum in libertatem asseruit, quando infantes quoq; exponere, & quoad humana, de libertate recuperanda in universum desperare coacti sunt. Et eosdem imminentibus demum Ægyptijs & iam iam cum ipsis congressuris, per apertum maris rubri alueum traduxit. Quò & Ezechias referri debet, qui diuina ope tum demum subleuatus est, cum Sanherib iam iam urbem capturus esse videretur. Ifa.37. Omnium verò horum vsus est, ut Dei opem patienter expectare difficilis, nec illi rerum agendarum tempus aut modum praescribamus. Licet enim Christus interdum in puppi nauis suæ dormire videatur, opportuno tamen tempore afflictis rebus opem ferre, & tempestates omnes sopire consueuit. Vide Marc.4.
units.tr: He begins the narrative with the time, not so much in the common manner of historians, but because this contributes much to the illustration of the divine benefit. For he writes that Peter was freed on that very night after Herod had decided to punish him with execution. Hence it is clear that this deliverance was delayed for some days, during which Peter indeed endured the troubles of prison, but the Church persevered in the fervour of prayer, and the Jews, inflamed with hatred of Christ, waited for the unworthy death of so great a man like gaping ravens. But at the very moment of time, when only a short span of the night seemed to delay their expectation, the Lord mocked them splendidly and snatched his servant from a sword so close at hand. By this example we are admonished that help from the Lord is sometimes deferred, yet we must not therefore lay aside remembrance and care of him; rather we should do this, that he may in the meantime exercise and test us as is fitting, and make the benefit of deliverance more illustrious, when we see it come about beyond all hope that could remain in human affairs. For this very reason it came about that he once rescued Israel into liberty only when they were compelled, as far as human means went, to expose even their infants and to despair entirely of recovering their freedom. And he led the same people, when the Egyptians were at hand and about to engage them, through the open channel of the Red Sea. To this also Hezekiah should be referred, who was relieved by divine help only when Sennacherib seemed about to capture the city. Isa. 37. The use of all these examples is that we should patiently wait for God's help, and not prescribe to him the time or manner of doing his work. For although Christ sometimes seems to sleep in the stern of his ship, yet he is accustomed to bring help to afflicted people at the opportune time and to quiet all storms. See Mark 4.

units.la: Subijcitur hîc ipsius Petri descriptio, ut quomodo ut tam præsenti periculo affectus fuerit, videamus. Et sanè, si quæ vulgò fiunt, consyderes, metu tantum non exanimatus esse debuit, cum & propter recentem Iacobi mortem, & propter exquisitam custodiam nulla melioris spei occasio offerre- tur. Quid ergo aliud quàm eiularet & fortem suam deflerèt? At longè alius nobis gloriosus hic miles Christi describitur. Illum enim duabus catenis vinctum inter duos milites dormiuisse, Lucas scribit. Id verò non socordiæ aut ignauiæ, sed veræ fidei & inuictæ spei argumentum fuisse, ex eo colligitur, quòd supra apostolos, cum virgis caesi essent, lætos & gratulantes sibi ipsis exiuisse audiuimus, quòd digni habiti fuissent, qui pro Christi nomine aliquid paterentur. Conferamus autem hoc loco inter se Herodem & Petrum, & facile patebit, quantum sit inter impios & pios dei cultores discriminis. Herodem enim per omnia anxium & solicitum fuisse, ut institutam aduersus Christum persecutionem feliciter finiret, inde patet, quòd Petrum, cui ad nocendum nec voluntas nec vires adersent, instar immanissimæ belluæ catenis vinciri, & militibus ad ipsius latus & ante carceris ostium excubatibus custodiri, ferreis deniq; portis concludi curauit. Quos ergo & quantos animi tuta quæq; timentis æstus illum sustinuisse putas, qui in vno Petro asseruando tam est solicitus? At quanto meliori conditione Petrus fruitur, qui insomnes noctes tyranno agente, securus dormit? Porrò quod in hoc exemplo proponitur, ad omnes horum similes transferri debet. Ea siquidem impiorum omnium conditio est, ut sibi ipsis laborum & curarum authores sint, dum suis consilijs & viribus res omnes confici oportere credunt. Et quia illis cum Christo negotium est, cuius inuictas vires tum in externis rebus experiuntur, tum in conscientijs suis, vel inuiti, sentiunt, nunquam nō concurrant & consultant, vt illius iugum excutere, & frænum confringere possint. Vide horum imaginem à Dauide Psalm.2. depictam. Sed & dominus ideo impijs nullam pacem esse, & illorum animos Euripi instar æstuare dicit. Ifa.48. & 57. Pij verò, quia causæ bonitate freti, in dei prouidentiam recumbunt, à qua se & res suas omnes pendere sciunt, facilè curas & metum omnem animis expuunt, & ea pace fruuntur, quam Paulus omnem intellectum superare, ait. Phil.4. Nam quò propius illos mala vrgent, eò prae sentiorem sentiunt spiritus sancti illuminationem, quem suis Christus consolatorem pollicitus est. Ioban.14. Hæc itaque frequenter nobis meditanda sunt, ut spiritus consolatione confirmati, quæuis pericula pro Christi nomine subire, & fortiter vincere possimus.
units.tr: Here follows the description of Peter himself, so that we may see how he was affected by so present a danger. And indeed, if you consider what usually happens, he ought to have been almost dead with fear, since there was no occasion of better hope, both because of the recent death of James and because of the strict guard. What else, then, would he do but wail and lament his lot? But this glorious soldier of Christ is described to us quite differently. For Luke writes that he slept bound with two chains between two soldiers. That this was a proof not of sloth or cowardice, but of true faith and unconquered hope, is gathered from the fact that we heard the apostles, when they had been beaten with rods, went out joyful and rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer something for the name of Christ. Let us now compare Herod and Peter in this place, and it will easily be clear how great is the difference between impious men and pious worshippers of God. For that Herod was anxious and troubled in every way, so that he might successfully end the persecution begun against Christ, is evident from the fact that he took care to have Peter, against whom he had neither will nor strength to harm, bound with chains like a most savage beast, guarded by soldiers stationed at his side and before the door of the prison, and finally shut in by iron gates. What storms of fear, then, do you think he endured, who is so anxious in keeping safe a single Peter? But in how much better a condition is Peter, who sleeps securely in the nights when the tyrant is at work and cannot sleep! Moreover, what is set forth in this example ought to be applied to all such cases. For this is the condition of all the impious, that they are authors of their own labours and cares, while they believe that all matters must be accomplished by their own counsels and strength. And since they have to do with Christ, whose unconquered power they experience both in external affairs and in their consciences, willingly or unwillingly they feel that they always rush together and consult how they may shake off his yoke and break his bridle. See the image of these men depicted by David, Ps. 2. But the Lord also says that there is no peace for the impious, and that their minds seethe like the tides of the Euripus. Isa. 48. and 57. The pious, however, because they rely on the goodness of their cause, rest upon the providence of God, on whom they know that they and all their affairs depend, easily cast out cares and every fear from their minds, and enjoy that peace which Paul says surpasses all understanding. Phil. 4. For the nearer evils press upon them, the more they feel the illumination of the Holy Spirit present, whom Christ promised to his own as Comforter. John 14. These things therefore must often be meditated upon by us, so that, strengthened by the consolation of the Spirit, we may be able to undergo any dangers for the name of Christ and to conquer them bravely.

units.la: Sed modum liberationis videamus, quæ potissima huius loci pars est, quapropter Lucas etiam in illius descriptione admirabili diligentia vtitur, dum singula, quæ in hunc inciderunt, commemorat. Et primò quidem, deum angeli ministerio vsum fuisse, diserte docet, ut hic quoq; impletum fuisse constet, quod scriptura pollicetur, quando Angelos ad electorum seruitia diuinitus deslinatos & paratos esse tradit. Sed quae ad huius loci explicationem pertinent, ex ijs, quae in similem historiam Sermone XXXIIII. dicta sunt petantur. Illud unum adiecisse sufficiat, maximam suae dignitatis rationem hominibus habendam esse, ut angelorum praesentia memores, morum innocentiae & puritati studeant, ne sua culpa tam sancto praesidio esse spolient. Quo Paulum quoque respexisse videmus, quando mulieres monet, ut si non alia ratione ad verecundiam & habitus honestatem excitari queant, saltem Angelos vereantur, qui sanctorum coetibus intersunt. 1 Cor. 11.
units.tr: But let us see the manner of deliverance, which is the chief part of this place; for this reason Luke also uses admirable diligence in describing it, while he recounts each single thing that befell him. And first of all he plainly teaches that God used the ministry of an angel, so that it may be established that what Scripture promises is fulfilled here too, when it tells us that angels are appointed and prepared by God for the service of the elect. But what pertains to the explanation of this place may be sought from what was said in the sermon XXXIIII. on a similar history. It is enough to add this one thing: that men must have the greatest regard for their own dignity, so that, mindful of the presence of the angels, they may strive for innocence and purity of conduct, lest through their own fault they be deprived of so holy a protection. We see that Paul also had this in view when he admonishes women that, if they cannot be stirred to modesty and decency of dress by any other reason, they should at least reverence the angels, who attend the assemblies of the saints. 1 Cor. 11.

units.la: Deinde lux quaedam in carcere, tetro alioqui & obscuro, refulsisse dicitur. Cuius visus mihi videtur fuisse, ut partim quidem hunc Angelum lucis esse conflaret, partim vero Petrus videret quae sibi agenda erant. Et frequens in scripturis est, quod coelesti fulgore splendentes, Angeli boni apparuerunt, quemadmodum ex resurrectionis & ascensionis dominicae historia colligere datur. Admonet autem locus hic, Christum in medijs tenebris suos illuminare & efficaci consolatione subleuare posse, sic ut laeta & iucunda reddat, quae nobis plena terroris videntur. Ipse enim lux mundi est, quam qui sequitur, tenebris inuolui non potest. Ioban. 8. & 12.
units.tr: Then a certain light is said to have shone in the prison, which was otherwise dark and gloomy. It seems to me this happened partly so that the light might signal that this was an angel of light, and partly so that Peter could see what he had to do. And in Scripture it is frequent that good angels appeared shining with heavenly brightness, as may be gathered from the accounts of the Lord's resurrection and ascension. This passage also reminds us that Christ can illuminate his people in the midst of darkness and lift them up with effective consolation, so that he makes joyful and pleasant what seems full of terror to us. For he himself is the light of the world, and whoever follows him cannot be wrapped in darkness. John 8 and 12.

units.la: Tertio Angelus Petrum dormientem, percusso illius latere, excitat & festinanter surgere iubet, cum is de liberatione ne cogitaret quidem. Est hoc luculentum diuinae bonitatis argumentum, quae nunquam non pro nobis vigilat, ne maligno hosti praeda fiamus. Et quod hic Petro accidit, quotidie singuli experimur, sed ea est nostra caecitas, ut praesentem dei bonitatem non agnoscamus. Constat enim satanam indesinenter nostrae saluti insidias struere, & instar rugientis Leonis obambulare, & quaerere quem devoret. Qui ergo fit, quod nos in somnis non perdat, quando nec precibus illum arcere, nec quicquam pro salute nostra vel cogitare possumus? Num hic vlla ratio assignari poterit, quam quod sub dei protectione & in abdyto altissimi (ut propheta ait) tuti degimus? Psal. 91. Unde simul discitur, quanta diligentia nos ipsos quouis tempore dei custodiae & protectioni commendare debeamus. Simul vero aduersus mortis terrores haec nos consolari possunt. Quum enim in somno (quae mortis imago est) nos deo curae esse constet: minime putabimus, nos per mortem ab illius prouidentia excludi. Cuius rei exemplum in Lazaro Christus proponit, quem & mortuum & in sepulchro iacentem, amicum suum dicere dignatur. Ioban. 11. Quae causa est, quod sanctii iam animas atturi, perinde ac si ad somnum se componere velint, Deo patri se commendare consueuerunt.
units.tr: Third, the angel strikes Peter's side as he sleeps, wakes him, and orders him to rise quickly, although he was not even thinking about deliverance. This is a clear proof of divine goodness, which never ceases to watch over us, lest we become the prey of the malicious enemy. What happened here to Peter we experience daily, one by one, but such is our blindness that we do not recognise the present goodness of God. For it is certain that Satan unceasingly lays snares for our salvation, and walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Why, then, does he not destroy us in our sleep, when we can neither keep him off by prayers nor think of anything for our salvation? Can any reason be given here except that we live safe under God's protection and in the secret place of the Most High, as the prophet says? Psalm 91. From this we also learn with how great diligence we ought at all times to commend ourselves to the custody and protection of God. At the same time, this can console us against the terrors of death. For since it is certain that we are a care to God in sleep (which is an image of death), we shall by no means think that through death we are excluded from his providence. Christ sets before us an example of this in Lazarus, whom he deigns to call his friend even when he was dead and lying in the tomb. John 11. This is why holy men, when about to breathe their last, are accustomed to commend themselves to God the Father just as if they were lying down to sleep.

units.la: Quarto, ad Angeli vocem illico catenae Petri manibus excidunt, & absque omni difficultate fiunt quaecunque ad liberationem restabant. Milites enim (siue illi diuina virtute sopiti, siue fulgore angelico examines facti fuerint, ut in resurrectione domini accidisse legimus) nec veritum se Petrum, nec exeuntem remorantur: & nemine prohibente primam & secundam custodiam, angelo duce, a nemine interpellatus apostolus transit. Adhaec ferrea porta, quae sola quousque aditu & exitu arcere poterat, sua sponte aperitur. Nec ante Petrum Angelus deserit, quam illum extra omne periculum in tuto collocauit. Voluit autem successive illum educi deus, ut illustrius esset tanti miraculi beneficium: alioqui eum nouo miraculo repente in ipsas Mariae aedes transferre poterat. Hic vero inuicta dei potentia nobis considerandu venit, quam & illi facile fit suos in libertatem afferere, cui absque negotio cedunt, quae insuperabilia videntur. Nec enim in solius Petri liberatione, sed saepius hoc accidisse constat, ut rerum natura diuina voluntati cesseris, ut electis dei salutis via pateret. Huc enim maris rubri transitus, & aperti Iordanis miraculum referri debent. Ita ignem praeter naturam suam Danielis socijs, imo eorundem vestibus & capillis pepercisse legimus. Danielis tertio. Et leones ingenitam rabiem deponere potius quam dei cultorem aduersus dei voluntatem laedere maluerunt. Danielis sexto. Quod non semel in martyribus contigisse Ecclesiastica historia docet. Huc pertinet quod Ierichuntidis muri ob tubarum clangorem corruunt, quod Assyriae copiae vna nocte trucidantur, & infinita alia, quae tam sacras quam prophanas historias legenti passim occurrunt. His ergo fidem nostram aduersus tyrannorum minas confirmemus. Certo enim certius est, deum si velit ex quouis periculo suos liberare posse. Quod si id aliquando facere detrectat, ideo fit, quod aliud nostrae salutis rationem postulare nouit. Interim fidelis est, nec tentari finit vltra quam ferre possumus. 1. Cor. 10.
units.tr: Fourth, at the angel's word the chains fall from Peter's hands at once, and everything that remained for his deliverance is done without any difficulty. For the soldiers (whether they were lulled to sleep by divine power, or were made senseless by angelic brightness, as we read happened at the Lord's resurrection) neither feared Peter nor hindered him as he went out. And with no one forbidding it, the apostle, led by the angel, passes through the first and second guard, and is challenged by no one. Moreover, the iron gate, which alone could keep the way in and out closed, opens of its own accord. Nor does the angel leave Peter before he has placed him in safety, beyond all danger. God, however, willed that he be led out step by step, so that the benefit of so great a miracle might be more conspicuous; otherwise he could have suddenly transferred him by a new miracle into the house of Mary itself. Here we must consider the invincible power of God, to whom it is easy to set his people free, since those things that seem insuperable yield to him without trouble. For it is clear that this has happened not only in Peter's deliverance but often, so that the order of nature yielded to the divine will, to open a way of salvation for the elect of God. To this must be referred the passage through the Red Sea and the miracle of the Jordan being opened. So too we read that the fire, contrary to its nature, spared Daniel's companions, indeed their very clothes and hair. Daniel 3. And the lions preferred to lay aside their innate rage rather than harm a worshipper of God against God's will. Daniel 6. The Ecclesiastical history teaches that this has happened more than once to martyrs. To this belongs the fact that the walls of Jericho fell at the sound of the trumpets, that the army of the Assyrians was slaughtered in one night, and countless other things which meet the reader of both sacred and profane histories everywhere. Let us therefore strengthen our faith with these against the threats of tyrants. For it is more certain than certain that God, if he wills, can free his people from any danger. But if he at some time refuses to do so, it is because he knows that another reason for our salvation is required. Meanwhile he is faithful, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: Postremo quid Petrus inter omnia haec fecerit, narrat euangelista. Et primo quidem illum neseiuisse dicit, quod haec vere agerentur. Visionem enim esse putabat, qualis supra in Cornelij causa ipsi oblata fuerat. Estq; hoc humanae infirmitatis exemplum, qua impediti, manifesta quoq; dei opera interdum non agnoscimus, maxime si caelesti aliqua maiestate velentur. Sic cum Christum in monte clarificatum vnà cum Mose et Helia videret Petrus, inepta quaedam verba effundit, ignarus quid diceret. Luc.9. Periculosius tamen hallucinantur, qui aperta dei iudicia, quibus ad poenitentiam illos inuitat, non obseruant: quod bodie nimis vulgare est. Interim non paruam laudem meretur Petri obedientia, qui licet ignarus adhuc rerum, monenti angelo obtemperat: suo exemplo docens, ut nos ad fidei obedientiam assuefaciamus, de quo iam saepe dictum est. Deinde vbi ad seipsum reuersus, se liberatum videt, deum tanti beneficij authorem magnificè praedicat. Nunc (inquit) vere scio, quod dominus angelum suum misit, & eripuit me ex manu Herodis, &c. Quo exemplo docemur, cuiusquis liberationis gloriam vni & soli deo debere acceptam ferri.
