Licet enim is vel angelis vel hominibus ministris vtatur, illi tamen solida laus transcribi debet, qui solus creaturis suis pro sua voluntate vti solet. Docet hoc ipse, per prophetam dicens: Premente aduersitate, inuoca me: & liberabo te, & glorificabis me. Psal.50. Quò etiam illud Dauidis pertinet: In libertatem vindicati a domino, dicant quod ipse eos vindicauerit a manu hostili. Psal.107. Vere ergo Petrus vnum & solum deum vindice suum agnoscit: quod etiam Paulus facit, quando deo vindice se ex ore leonis ereptum esse fatetur. 2. Tim.4. Quare intolerabilis illorum error est, qui vel carceribus, vel morbis, vel aliis periculis liberati, Dei gloriam liberationis transferibunt. Quanto magis autem humani generis redemptio ex infernali tyrannide ad vnum deum authorem referri debebit? Agnoscamus igitur haec o fratres, & gratis animis deum patrem praedicemus, qui eripuit nos è potestate tenebrarum, & in sui regni consortium transtulit, per filium suum Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, the evangelist tells what Peter did amid all this. And first he says that Peter did not know that these things were truly happening. For he thought it was a vision, such as had been shown to him earlier in the matter of Cornelius. This is an example of human weakness, by which, hindered, we sometimes fail to recognise even the manifest works of God, especially when they are veiled in some heavenly majesty. So when Peter saw Christ transfigured on the mountain together with Moses and Elijah, he poured out some foolish words, not knowing what he said. Luke 9. Yet those who do not observe the open judgments of God, by which he invites them to repentance, go astray more dangerously; this is only too common today. Meanwhile Peter's obedience deserves no small praise, for although as yet ignorant of the facts, he obeys the angel who warns him, teaching by his example that we should accustom ourselves to obedience of faith, a point on which much has already been said. Then, when he returns to himself and sees that he is free, he proclaims magnificently God, the author of so great a benefit. "Now," he says, "I truly know that the Lord has sent his angel and has snatched me from the hand of Herod," etc. By this example we are taught that the glory of anyone's deliverance must be ascribed as received to the one God alone. For although he uses angels or human ministers, the solid praise must nevertheless be transferred to him who alone is accustomed to use his creatures at his own pleasure. He himself teaches this through the prophet, saying: "When adversity presses, call upon me, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me." Psalm 50. To this also belongs that saying of David: "Let those who have been freed by the Lord say that he has rescued them from the hand of the enemy." Psalm 107. Truly, then, Peter acknowledges the one and only God as his deliverer; Paul does the same when he confesses that he was snatched from the mouth of the lion, God being his deliverer. 2 Tim. 4. Therefore intolerable is the error of those who, freed from prisons, from diseases, or from other dangers, transfer the glory of their deliverance to others. How much more, then, must the redemption of the human race from infernal tyranny be referred to the one God as author! Let us therefore acknowledge these things, brothers, and with grateful hearts let us praise God the Father, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the fellowship of his kingdom, through his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 84.

units.la: Et re perpensa Petrus venit ad domum Mariae, matris Iohannis, qui cognominabatur Marcus, ubi erant multi congregati & orabant. Cum autem pulsasset Petrus ad ostium atrii, prodijt puella ad subaudiendum, nomine Rhode. Et cum agnouisset vocem Petri, prae gaudio non aperuit atrium, sed introcurrens nunciauit, Petrum stare ante atrium. At illi dixerunt ei: Insanis. Sed illa affirmabat, sic rem habere. Illi autem dicebant: Angelus eius est. Petrus autem perseuerabat pulsando. Vt vero aperuerunt, viderunt eum, & obstupuerunt. Cum autem innuisset eis manu, vt tacerent, narrauit illis, quomodo ipsum dominus eduxit e carcere. Dixit autem: Nunciate Iacobo & fratribus haec. Et egressus abijt in alium locum. Porro vbi dies venit, turbatio fuit non parua inter milites, quo nam deuenisset Petrus. Herodes autem, cum requisiuisset eum, nec inuenisset, examinatis custodibus, iussit eos duci. Et discedens a Iudaea Caesaream, illic commoratus est.
units.tr: And when Peter had considered this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John, who was surnamed Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying. And when Peter knocked at the door of the gate, a girl came out to listen, named Rhoda. And when she recognized Peter's voice, for joy she did not open the gate, but ran in and announced that Peter was standing before the gate. But they said to her, "You are mad." Yet she kept insisting that it was so. Then they said, "It is his angel." But Peter kept on knocking. When they opened and saw him, they were astonished. But he motioned to them with his hand to be silent, and related to them how the Lord had brought him out of the prison. And he said, "Tell these things to James and the brethren." And going out, he went to another place. Now when day came, there was no little disturbance among the soldiers as to what had become of Peter. And Herod, when he had sought him and not found him, after examining the guards, ordered them to be led away. And he departed from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

units.la: Quemadmodum Diuus Lucas ex spiritus sancti suggestione grauissimam ecclesiae Christi persecutionem hoc capite describit, cuius exemplo docemur, quae nam ecclesiae conditio sit inter vrbes vicissim memorabile diuinae bonitatis & prouidentiae exemplum proponit, quae fideles in periculis tuetur & olim promissam opem fidelissime praestat. Nam vt nuper vidimus, tunc maxime Petro apostolo praesens affuit dominus, quando tam diuino quam humano auxilio destitutus esse videbatur. Nec modò propensae voluntatis aliquod specimen edidit, sed inuita sua potentia ad ipsum liberandum vsus est. Angelo enim misso ferrea catenarum vincula dissoluit, portas mirabiliter pacit, militum excubias eludit, & Petrum, in quem iam lata erat mortis sententia, extra omne periculum eductum, in tuto collocat. Quamuis vero non omnes simili miraculo liberentur, quotquot Christi nomine vincula & carceres perferunt, extant tamen generales promissiones, sub dei prouidentia tutos degere, quotquot illius seruitio se addixerunt. Nam oculos domini super iustos intentos esse, & eiusdem aures illorum precibus patere, Dauid affirmat. Psal.34. Et Dei filius, capillos quoq; nostros numeratos esse testatur. Matth. 10. Sedomissùs istùs, de quibus iam antea dictum est, præsentem locum inspiciamus, quo docetur, quid Petrus iam vinculis et carcere liberatus, egerit: qua ecclesiæ interea temporis studia fuerint, & vt hoc Dei iudicio Herodes tyrannus affectus sit.
units.tr: As Saint Luke, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, describes in this chapter a most grievous persecution of the Church of Christ, from which we are taught what the condition of the Church is, so he also sets before us a memorable example of divine goodness and providence, which protects the faithful in dangers and most faithfully grants the help promised long ago. For, as we saw recently, the Lord was present to the apostle Peter most of all when he seemed to be deprived of both divine and human aid. Nor did he merely show some sign of his favourable will, but he used his power, though men were unwilling, to deliver him. For by sending an angel he loosed the iron chains, miraculously opened the gates, eluded the watch of the soldiers, and set Peter, against whom the sentence of death had already been passed, outside all danger and placed him in safety. Yet although not all who suffer chains and prisons for Christ's name are delivered by a similar miracle, there remain general promises that all who have devoted themselves to his service dwell safely under God's providence. For David affirms that the eyes of the Lord are fixed upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers (Ps. 34). And the Son of God testifies that even the hairs of our head are numbered (Matt. 10). But leaving aside those matters already mentioned, let us look at the present passage, in which we are taught what Peter did once he was freed from chains and prison, what the studies of the Church were in the meantime, and how Herod the tyrant was dealt with by the judgment of God.

units.la: Petrus, postquam angelo digresso se liberatum sensit, consilio apud se inito, & singulis, quæ ipsi in mentem incidere poterant, diligenter expensis, domum Mariæ petit, quam non procul abfuisse verisimile est, & vbi fideles aliquot pro more congregatos esse credebat. Dicitur autem Maria hæc mater Iohannis Marci fuisse, qui à nonnullis tam veterum quàm recentiorum, Martus euangelista putatur. Quod vt non per omnia certum est, ita Mariam hanc, rarę fidei & pietatis matronam fuisse, vel hoc vno argumento patet, quòd tam immaniter contra Christi discipulos furente Agrippa, domum tamen suam ipsidem instar communis templi, patere voluit, vbi collesti in dei verbo & precibus exercerētur: quod sine manifesto periculo fieri nō poterat. Et voluit infirmioris sexus exemplo docere dominus, quàm intrepidè inter præsentia pericula causam suam tueri & afferere, Christianos deceat. Cæterum, vbi eò peruenit Petrus, non vt ante apud ferream portam, miraculose patefiunt fores, eò quòd nouo miraculo iam non opus erat: sed pulsando aliquem ad aperiendum euocare incipit. Est autem nobis obseruandum Petri exemplum, qui vbi mortis periculum euasit, ante omnia ecclesiæ Christi denuò coniungi cupit, in cuius viscera tamen tyrannum adhuc sæuire nouerat. Docemur enim quanta nobis ecclesiastica vnitatis siue communionis cura esse debeat, & quòd spiritus Christi fideles non dissipet, sed tam interne quàm externè coniungat. Nec facile coniunctionem hanc negligere possunt, qui vt in vno Christo salutem omnem contineri sciunt: ita hanc à Christo capite in eos duntaxat deriuari intelligunt, qui corporis Christi, id est, ecclesiæ membra fuerint. Absurdus ergo & perniciosus illorum error est, qui imminentibus persecutionum procellis ecclesias deserunt, vel vbi semel periclitati sunt, quasi officio suo per omnia defuncti, illis amplius coniungino lunt, ne noua pericula subeant. Ita enim à Christo sese alienant, pro cuius nomine primo assultus sustinuerunt, & dum corpora periculis eripiunt, animabus certam perditionem et interitum accersunt.
units.tr: When Peter, after the angel had departed, perceived that he was set free, he took counsel with himself, weighed carefully each thing that could come into his mind, and made for the house of Mary, which was probably not far off, and where he believed several of the faithful were gathered together as usual. Now this Mary is said to have been the mother of John Mark, who by some both of the ancients and of more recent writers is thought to be the evangelist Mark. That this is not certain in every respect is clear, but that this Mary was a matron of rare faith and piety is shown by this one argument alone: although Agrippa raged so savagely against Christ's disciples, she nonetheless wished her house, like a common temple, to be open, where the faithful might be engaged in the Word of God and in prayers, which could not be done without manifest danger. And the Lord wished to teach by the example of the weaker sex how fearlessly Christians ought to defend and assert their cause amid present dangers. Moreover, when Peter came there, the doors were not opened miraculously, as before at the iron gate, because there was no longer any need for a new miracle; instead he began by knocking to summon someone to open. We must observe in Peter's example that when he had escaped the danger of death, he above all desired to be joined again to the Church of Christ, though he knew that the tyrant was still raging in her very heart. For we are taught how great a care for ecclesiastical unity or communion we ought to have, and that the Spirit of Christ does not scatter the faithful, but joins them both inwardly and outwardly. Nor can those easily neglect this union who know that all salvation is contained in Christ alone, and who understand that it flows from Christ the head only to those who are members of his body, that is, of the Church. Absurd and pernicious, therefore, is the error of those who desert the churches when storms of persecution are threatening, or who, once they have been in danger, as if they had fully discharged their duty, no longer join themselves to them, lest they undergo new dangers. For in this way they estrange themselves from Christ, for whose name they first endured assaults, and while they snatch their bodies from dangers, they bring upon their souls certain ruin and destruction.

units.la: Porrò quales in domo Mariæ Petrus Christianos inuenerit, videamus. Lucas tertè rem maximam paucis verbis comprehendens, multos illic collestos fuisse, & orauisse scribit. Nec tamen putandum est, omnes totius vrbis fideles in vnam domum conuenisse: sed alibi quoq; similes conuentus fuisse credibile est: & noctuarnos quidem, quòd illis tutum non esset interdiu conuenire. Atque hinc originem duxisse videntur noctuarni illi Christianorum cętus & antelucani, quorum mentio abexternis quoq; scriptoribus facta est: non quòd tempori religionem & precum efficaciam alligarent, sed quod inter persecutiones & hostiles insidias aliter conuenire vix possent. Damnantur hodie à multis eiusmodi cætus, qui illi in vniuersum putant abstinendum esse, ne vel seditionis vel impurioris licen tiæ suspicionem de se pij præbeant. Sed cur non egregij illi censores ad primitiuæ ecclesiæ exemplum respiciunt, & sub cruce constitutis fratribus idem permittunt quod olim factitatum est, quando cau sæ sunt eædem? Interim non negamus multa & diligenti cautione hic opus esse. Nam vt ea res olim impijs Christiani nominis soribus occasionem præbuit Christianam religionem atrocibus calumniis infestandi: ita sequentibus seculis superstitionis causa fuit, dum inepti quidam matutinas suas & antelucanos cantus hinc stabiliri posse putauerunt. Interim docet locus hic, quæ et qualia esse debeant Christianorum exercitia, tum quouis alio tempore, tum maximè si quando persecutiones aut alia publicæ calamitates incidant. Et hic quidem diligens sacrorum cætuum ratio habenda est. Nam vt suos vnū esse cupit Christus, ita vnitatis & communionis studium illos publicè testari conuenit. Quæ causa est, quòd in veteri Testamento de festis tam diligenter Moses disserit, in quibus omnibus sere primus locus conuocationi sanctæ tribuitur. Vide Leuit. 23. Et Iohel propheta Assyriaci belli tem pore populum officij admonens, non semel illos cætum sacrū indicere iubet. Nec temere factum est, quòd Paulus ad Corinthios scribens, per capita aliquot de sacrorū cætuum ratione rectè instituenda disserit. Nouerat enim hos peculiari promissione à Christo exornatos esse, qui se medium illis interesse testatur, qui in suo nomine congregati sunt. Matth. 18. Minimè tamen probabuntur cætus homi num, quantumuis frequentes, nisi ea fiant in illis, quæ Deus fieri præcepit. Vult ꝯ verbum suum publicè doceri. Ad illud ergo audiendum nos conuenire decet. Idem à nobis orari vult. In cœtibus ergo nos preces coiungere conuenit, vt quasi manu factâ (Tertulliani verbis vtor) deum orantes ambiamus. Hæc etenim vt illi grata est, sicuti viduæ exemplo Christus docuit, Luc.18. Verum, ab his observatum esse, satis constat. Licet enim solarum precum Lucas hoc loco mentionem facit, quia tamen hæ per Dei verbum diriguntur, & ex illius promissionibus vim concipiunt, illos in huius studio segnes fuisse, minime cogitandum est. Tales quoq; post apostolorum tempora Christianorum cætus fuisse, vetustissimi scriptores abundè testantur. Quòd si vero hæc cum nostri sæculi moribus conferas, facilè patebit, quantum à veteris ecclesiæ integritate degenerauerimus. Hæc enim nocturno tempore, cum vndiq; pericula circumstarent, convenire voluit: nos vero ne interdiu quidem, cum id tutò facere possemus, convenimus. Et si qui forte templa adeunt, eorum mores imitantur, quorum improbitatem & vanitatem Ezech.cap.33.accusat. Rursum, si qui noctu conueniunt, bi vel poculis certare, vel alea infami ludere, vel lasciuis per vicos discursibus indulgere consueuerunt. Vt interim de illis nihil dicamus, qui si quando persecutiones insurgant, ad execrationes & conuicia conuersi, in insontes verbi ministros debacchantur, quasi non communis totius ecclesiæ, sed illorum duntaxat causa agatur. Atqui hinc fieri consueuit, quod nostri sæculi calamitates tam pertinaces sentimus. Cur enim percutere desineret deus illos, qui ne inter verbera quidem manum illius agnoscunt, nec ad Deum paternè ipsos castigantem conuertuntur? Vide Isa.9. Amos 4. cap.
units.tr: Next, let us see what kind of Christians Peter found in Mary's house. Luke, summing up a very important matter in a few words, writes that many were gathered there and were praying. Yet we should not think that all the faithful of the whole city came together in one house; it is credible that similar assemblies were held elsewhere too, and by night, since it was not safe for them to meet by day. From this, it seems, arose those nocturnal assemblies of Christians and those gatherings before dawn, which are also mentioned by writers outside the faith. This was not because they bound religion and the efficacy of prayer to a time, but because amid persecutions and hostile plots they could scarcely meet in any other way. Today many condemn such gatherings, and think that they should be avoided altogether, lest the godly give cause for suspicion either of sedition or of unchecked licentiousness. But why do those distinguished critics not look to the example of the primitive Church, and permit to brethren placed under the cross the same thing that was once done, when the causes are the same? Meanwhile we do not deny that much careful caution is needed here. For just as that practice once gave wicked men an occasion to attack the Christian religion with savage slanders, so in later centuries it became a cause of superstition, when certain foolish persons thought that their early morning and before-dawn chants could be established on this basis. Meanwhile this passage teaches what and of what sort the exercises of Christians ought to be, both at any other time and especially if persecutions or other public calamities should befall. And here, indeed, a careful order of sacred assemblies must be observed. For just as Christ wishes his people to be one, so it is fitting that they publicly bear witness to their unity and communion. This is why Moses discourses so carefully about the feasts in the Old Testament, in nearly all of which the first place is given to the holy assembly. See Lev. 23. And the prophet Joel, admonishing the people about their duty in the time of the Assyrian war, bids them more than once to proclaim a sacred assembly. Nor was it by chance that Paul, writing to the Corinthians, discourses over several chapters on the proper ordering of sacred assemblies. For he knew that these were adorned with a special promise from Christ, who testifies that he is present in the midst of those who are gathered in his name (Matt. 18). Yet assemblies of men, however numerous, will by no means be approved unless those things are done in them which God has commanded to be done. He wishes his Word to be taught publicly; it is therefore fitting for us to come together to hear it. He wishes also to be prayed to by us. In assemblies, then, it is fitting that we join our prayers, so that, as it were with hands formed (to use Tertullian's words), we may seek to win God by prayer. For this is pleasing to him, as Christ taught by the example of the widow (Luke 18). And it is quite clear that these things were observed by them. For although Luke mentions only prayers in this place, since these are directed by the Word of God and draw their power from its promises, we must not think that they were slack in this study. That such assemblies of Christians existed after the time of the apostles, the most ancient writers abundantly testify. But if you compare these things with the customs of our own age, it will easily be seen how far we have fallen from the integrity of the ancient Church. For they wished to gather at night, when dangers threatened on every side; we do not gather even by day, when we could do so safely. And if some do go to churches, they imitate the conduct of those whose wickedness and vanity Ezekiel (ch. 33) condemns. Again, if some do meet by night, they are accustomed either to compete in drinking, or to play at dice shamefully, or to indulge in wanton rambling through the streets. To say nothing for now of those who, whenever persecutions rise, turn to curses and insults and rage against the innocent ministers of the Word, as if the cause at stake were not that of the whole Church in common, but only their own. Yet from this it commonly comes about that we feel the calamities of our age so stubborn. For why would God cease to strike those who do not recognize his hand even under the blows, nor turn to him as a Father who chastises them? See Isa. 9 and Amos ch. 4.

units.la: III. Vt Petri aduentu fideles affecti fuerint
units.tr: III. How the faithful were affected by Peter's arrival

units.la: Pergens verò in cæpta narratione Lucas, vt fideles isti inopino & inspérato Petri aduentu affecti fuerint, narrat. Et initio quidem ad pulsum ostij nonnihil turbatos fuisse patet, quòd Rhode accillula non ad aperiendum procurrit, sed vt tacite auscultando obseruaret, quis nam ad ostium astaret. Quia enim Herodis iram aduersus ecclesiam tanta vehementia exarsisse videbant, nihil tam tum erat, quod non illis suspectum esse posset. At Rhode Petrum adesse ex voce agnoscens, gaudio immodico perfusa & tam lætæ rei nuntia fieri gestiens, prius id intus renuntiat, quàm ostium pulsanti aperiat. Illi verò, qui tale quid vix cogitare, nedum sperare, ausi fuerant, primò illam insanire dicunt: mox, vbi constantius hoc affirmantem audiunt, non Petrum, sed Petri angelum ad ianuam comparuisse, eiusq; vocem imitatum fuisse suspicantur. Ita verò insignes Christi cultores, quos omni virtutum genere exornatos fuisse, dubium non est, affectibus diuersis exagitatos, & inter spem, metum, gaudium ac omnis generis suspiciones, suspensos fuisse vides. Procul ergo valeat Stoicorum dementia, qui dum affectuum motus à viro bono & perfecto alienos esse debere docent, ex hominibus fungos & truncos fingere conantur. Atqui Christum Iesum eiusmodi infirmitates sustinuisse, & multiariam instar veri hominis tentatum fuisse Paulus fatetur, vt nobis condolere posset. Heb.2. Sunt tamen hic duo nobis diligentius excutienda, priusquam vlterius progrediamur. Primum consolationi seruit, quo docemur, piorum vota adeò non irrita esse apud dominum, vt is illa plerunq; sua benignitate superet, dum plura largitur, quàm illi petere aussint. Licet enim isti pro Petro assiduè orauerint, illius tamen liberationem illos sperare non potuisse, ex hoc loco patet. Nouerant quidem nihil apud Deum impossibile esse. Sed non videbant, cur Petrum saluum vellet dominus, qui Iacobum indigna morte cadere permiserat. Hoc igitur illos precibus suis petijsse puto, vt in veritatis confessione per Dei gratiam confirmaretur, & pro Christo fortiter mortis terrores vinceret. Atqui præter omnem spem Petrum diuina ope restitutum sibi vident, quod infallibile erat diuinæ bonitatis argumentum, quo edocebantur, nolle ecclesiam suam tyrannis dilaniandam permittere dominum, cum illius ministros tam fideliter afferat. Extant infinita eius generis exempla, quæ scripturas, imò quasi historias legenti passim occurrunt. Et si in nostris rebus paulo attentius obseruemus Dei iudicia, frequenter nobis ipsis idem accidere experiemur. Discamus ergo constanter in domino sperare, & illius prouidentiæ nos nostrasq; res committamus. Alterum hic obseruandum venit, quod angelum Petri apparuisse putant. Agnouerunt enim sanctissimi homines, quæ de angelorum præsidio in scripturis dicuntur: nec quisquam putare debet, ipsos aliquid à religione alienum superstitiosius imaginatos fuisse. Extant enim scripturæ miracula, quibus docetur, angelos hominum ministros & tutores diuinitus constitutos esse: vt Psal.34. & 91. Nec exempla desunt, quibus illos non semel visibili forma apparuisse constat. Non inepte ergo nec impie in tam inspérato Petri aduentu, in eiusmodi verba eruperunt. Interim non ignoramus, hinc apud superstitiosos homines vulgarem errorem de binis angelis vnicuius homini destinatis, obortum esse: quem merito reijcimus, cum de angelorum numero nihil certi scriptura tradat, modò vnus, modò duo aut tres, imò turmæ angelorum in vnius bo-
units.tr: Luke now continues his account and tells how these believers were affected by Peter's unexpected and sudden arrival. At first, it is clear, they were somewhat alarmed by the knock at the door, since the servant girl Rhoda did not run to open it but listened quietly, to see who was standing at the door. Because they saw that Herod's anger against the Church had flared up with such violence, nothing at that time could fail to seem suspicious to them. But Rhoda recognised Peter's voice, and, overcome with immoderate joy and eager to announce such happy news, she told them inside before she opened the door to the one knocking. Those men, however, who had hardly dared to think such a thing, let alone hope for it, first said she was out of her mind. Then, when they heard her insisting more firmly, they suspected that it was not Peter but Peter's angel who had come to the door and had imitated his voice. So you see that these outstanding worshippers of Christ, who were beyond doubt adorned with every kind of virtue, were tossed about by different emotions, and were held in suspense between hope, fear, joy and every sort of suspicion. Let the madness of the Stoics, then, be gone, who, while they teach that movements of the emotions must be foreign to a good and perfect man, try to make men out of mushrooms and blocks of wood. Yet Paul acknowledges that Christ Jesus endured such weaknesses, and was tempted in many ways like a true man, so that he could sympathise with us (Heb. 2). There are, however, two things here that we must examine more carefully before we go further. The first serves for consolation, teaching us that the prayers of the godly are not so fruitless before the Lord that he, by his kindness, often exceeds what they dare to ask, while he grants more than they request. For although these men prayed constantly for Peter, it is clear from this passage that they could not have hoped for his deliverance. They knew indeed that nothing is impossible with God. But they did not see why the Lord would want Peter saved, when he had allowed James to fall by an unworthy death. So I think they asked by their prayers only that he might be strengthened by God's grace in confessing the truth, and might conquer the terrors of death for Christ's sake. Yet they see Peter restored to them by divine help, beyond all hope, which was an infallible proof of divine goodness, by which they were taught that the Lord was unwilling to let his Church be torn apart by tyrants, since he so faithfully preserves its ministers. There are countless examples of this kind, which occur everywhere in the Scriptures, and indeed in what one reads like histories. And if we observe the judgments of God in our own affairs a little more attentively, we shall often find the same thing happening to ourselves. Let us therefore learn to hope steadfastly in the Lord, and commit ourselves and our affairs to his providence. The second point to be noted here is that they thought it was Peter's angel who had appeared. For these holy men understood what the Scriptures say about the protection of angels, and no one should think that they imagined something superstitious and foreign to true religion. For there are scriptural miracles which teach that angels have been appointed by God as servants and guardians of men (Ps. 34 and 91), and there is no lack of examples showing that they have more than once appeared in visible form. So it was not foolish or impious that they burst out with such words at Peter's unexpected arrival. Meanwhile we are not unaware that from this passage a common error has arisen among superstitious people, about two angels assigned to each single man. We rightly reject this, since Scripture delivers nothing certain about the number of angels: sometimes one, sometimes two or three, and even whole troops of angels are said to be present for the defence of one good man.

units.la: Vide Tertul. de pologet. c. 39.
units.tr: See Tertull., De apologetico, ch. 39.

units.la: Angelorum apparitiones.
units.tr: The appearances of angels.

units.la: Piorum preces non sunt irritæ. minus defensione comparuerint, quemadmodum de Iacobo & Heliseo legimus. Gene. 28, & 32. item 2. Reg. 6. Multo minus illos audimus, qui defunctorum spiritus oberrare & apparere dicunt. Illud enim Christi doctrinae & fidei veritati repugnat, qua docemur, piorum animas ex morte in vitam transire, impiorum vero ad inferos deferri, nec aliquem illinde ad superos regressum patere. Vide de hac re Christum differentem. Iohan. 5. & Luc. 16. Sufficiat ergo nobis, angelos dei ministros esse, qui illis pro suo arbitrio ad electorum suorum salutem uti consueuit: & hominis dignitatem inde agnoscamus, quae non vulgare ad pietatem incitamentum nobis esse debet.
units.tr: The prayers of the godly are not in vain. Less as a defence, as we read of Jacob and Elisha (Gen. 28 and 32; likewise 2 Kings 6). Much less do we listen to those who say that the spirits of the dead wander about and appear. For that is contrary to the teaching of Christ and the truth of the faith, by which we are taught that the souls of the godly pass from death into life, while the souls of the wicked are carried down to hell, and that there is no way back from there to the living above. On this matter see Christ's discourse in John 5 and Luke 16. It is enough for us, then, to know that angels are God's ministers, whom he is accustomed to use at his discretion for the salvation of his elect; and from this let us recognise the dignity of man, which ought to be no small incentive to godliness for us.

units.la: Porro ut ad Petrum reuertamur, tempus admonet. Is fratribus partim in gaudium effusis, partim attonitis adhuc manu silentium indicit, & rem omnem, ut gesta erat, ordine recenseт, unum deum tanti beneficij authorem praedicans. Simul vero, ut haec reliquis fratribus, & imprimis Iacobo Alphaei filio (quem Hierosolymorum episcopum veteres fuisse scribunt) renuntient, praecipit. Cuius praecepti duplex ratio fuisse videtur. Nam & Dei gloriam grato officio latius propagare voluit, & fratres quos sua causa anxios esse nouerat, solicita cura liberatos cupit. Suo igitur exemplo nos quoque officij Petrus admonet, ne collata in nos dei beneficia vel ingratis vel inuidis animis celemus. Pius enim & eximius eius praedicationis usus est, dum alij quoque per nos excitati, in deo sperare & illum vindicem & assertorem suum in periculis inuocare discunt. Meminit huius rei Dauid, Philistaeorum manibus ereptus, initio Psal. 34. &c.
units.tr: But to return to Peter, the time reminds us to do so. He imposes silence on the brothers, some of whom were poured out in joy and some still stunned, and he recounts the whole matter in order, as it had happened, proclaiming the one God as the author of so great a blessing. At the same time he instructs them to report these things to the rest of the brothers, and especially to James the son of Alphaeus (whom the ancient writers say was bishop of Jerusalem). There seems to have been a twofold reason for this instruction. For he wanted to spread God's glory more widely by a pleasing duty, and he wished the brothers, whom he knew to be anxious on his account, to be freed by careful concern. So by his own example Peter also reminds us of our duty: we should not conceal the benefits God has given us, either with ungrateful or with envious hearts. For his preaching was a fine and remarkable use of this, since others too, stirred up by us, learn to hope in God and to call on him as their defender and champion in dangers. David recalls this matter at the beginning of Psalm 34, when he had been rescued from the hands of the Philistines, and so on.

units.la: Deinde in alium locum secessisse Petrus scribitur. Facile enim videbat, se abs quo fructu in Herodis regno versaturu. Et praesens miraculosa liberationis beneficium abunde illu docere poterat, nolle deum, ut sub Herodis manu mortem subiret, sed apostolatus munere alibi quoque fungeretur. Vtitur itaque Christi consilio, dicentis: Si vos persequantur in una ciuitate, fugite in aliam. Matth. 10. Habes ergo quod illis respondeas, qui verbi ministros temere in luporum manus deferri vellet, & eos demum vere apostolicos esse clamant, qui abs que vlla professus spe, non seipsos modo, verumetiam doctrinam suam et Christi veritatem impiorum iudicijs permittunt. At facile patet, quid istos moueat. Euangelij enim ministros ad unum omnes sublatos vellent, ut Antichristiana superstitio reduci posset. Quare contra illos, iuxta Christi praeceptum serpentina prudentia uti couenit, ne nostra temeritate Christi causae incomodemus.
units.tr: Then it is written that Peter withdrew to another place. For he easily saw what fruit he would have while he remained in Herod's kingdom. And the present miraculous benefit of his deliverance could amply teach him that God did not want him to undergo death at Herod's hand, but to carry out the office of apostle elsewhere as well. So he follows the counsel of Christ, who said: "If they persecute you in one city, flee to another" (Matt. 10). You therefore have an answer for those who rashly want ministers of the Word to be handed over into the hands of wolves, and who cry that those alone are truly apostolic who, without any hope of safety, expose not only themselves but also their teaching and the truth of Christ to the judgments of the impious. But it is easy to see what moves such people. They would have all the ministers of the gospel removed, so that Antichristian superstition could be restored. Therefore, against them, it is fitting to use serpent-like prudence according to Christ's precept, so that we do not harm the cause of Christ by our own rashness.

units.la: IIII. Vt Herodes miraculo dei affectus fuerit.
units.tr: IIII. How Herod was struck by the miracle of God.

units.la: Restat vltima huius loci pars, qua docetur, ut dei opere & miraculo Herodes affectus fuerit. Et primo quidem, vbi Petrum carceres & vincula euasisse compertum fuit, non leuis turba & animorum consternatio inter milites obortaest. Quia enim Herodis ferox ingenium perspectum habebant, nil ab illo boni sperare poterant. Nec illos fefellit opinio. Herodes enim Petrum ad supplicium poscens, vbi de illius liberatione resciuit, furenti similis, custodes per tormenta examinari iubet, ut quamuis illos extra culpam esse audiat, tamen vel ad carceres, vel (quod verisimilius est) ad mortem abduci praecipit. Est hoc memorabile cumprimis exemplum, quo docemur, impios dei iudicijs non emendari, sed deteriores fieri. Quia enim illi aduersus deum pugnare audent, iusto dei iudicio excaecantur & indurantur, ut nec in aperta luce videre, nec potenti dei manui cedere possint. Nec est quod meliora de nostri seculi tyrannis speremus, qui semel suscep tum cum deo bellum tam pertinaci veritatis odio hucusque gesserunt. Simul vero diuinae prouidentiae exemplum elucet, qua Herodes aflutia eluditur, dum ab illis ipsis dei opus praedicari audit, quorum opera aduersus deum uti consueuerat. Nec dissimile huic est, quod milites a sacerdotibus Christi sepulchro adhibiti, primi illius resurrectionem in urbe diuulgant. Matth. 28. Admonet praeterea infelix horum militum casus, quid expectent, qui tyrannis aduersus veritatem inseruiunt. Incidunt vere in foueam, quam pijs parauerunt. Psalm. 7. Et illos sibi hostes sentiunt, quorum gratiam in pios grassando demereri voluerunt. Quo fit, ut licet iniuriam illis faciant homines, iusto tamen dei iudicio puniantur, qui hominibus potius quam deo placere studuerunt. Meminerint huius, qui in hominum gratiam aliquid contra Christi fideles vel ipsi faciunt, vel alios facere permittunt. Christi vox est: Nolite tangere unctos meos. Psal. 105. Et qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Zach. 2. Denunciant haec praesentem interitum ecclesiae suae persecutoribus. Horum ergo commercijs & consilijs abstineant, quicunque veras fidei cultores haberi volunt, ne cum ijsdem pereant. Interim Christi regis & saluatoris nostri potentiam agnoscamus, qui hostium conatus tanta felicitate eludit, suosque tam fortiter asserit. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of this passage, in which we are taught that Herod was struck by the work and miracle of God. And first, when it was discovered that Peter had escaped from the prison and the chains, no small uproar and consternation of minds arose among the soldiers. For since they knew Herod's savage temper, they could hope for nothing good from him. Nor did their fear deceive them. Herod, demanding Peter for execution, when he learned of his deliverance, behaved like a madman and ordered the guards to be examined under torture; although he heard that they were free of blame, he nevertheless commanded that they be led away either to prison or (what is more likely) to death. This is a notable example above all, by which we are taught that the impious are not corrected by the judgments of God but become worse. For since they dare to fight against God, by the just judgment of God they are blinded and hardened, so that they can neither see in the clear light nor yield to the mighty hand of God. Nor is there reason for us to hope for better things from the tyrants of our own age, who have so far waged war with God, with such stubborn hatred of the truth, once they had undertaken it. At the same time, an example of divine providence shines forth, by which Herod is mocked by his own cunning, while he hears the work of God proclaimed by those very men through whose agency he was accustomed to act against God. Not unlike this is the fact that the soldiers placed at the sepulchre by the priests of Christ spread abroad in the city the news of his first resurrection. Matt. 28. Moreover, the unhappy fate of these soldiers warns what those expect who serve tyrants against the truth. They truly fall into the pit that they prepared for the godly. Ps. 7. And they find as enemies those whom they wished to win over by raging against the godly. Hence it comes about that, although men do them injury, they are nevertheless punished by the just judgment of God, who strove to please men rather than God. Let those who, to win the favour of men, either do something themselves against the faithful of Christ or permit others to do so, remember this. The voice of Christ is: "Touch not my anointed ones." Ps. 105. And he who touches you touches the apple of my eye. Zech. 2. These things announce the imminent destruction of his Church's persecutors. Therefore let all who wish to be considered true worshippers of the faith abstain from their dealings and counsels, lest they perish with them. Meanwhile let us acknowledge the power of Christ, our King and Saviour, who thwarts the attempts of his enemies with such good fortune and so bravely defends his own. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA LXXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY LXXXV.

units.la: Porrò Herodes infensus erat Tyrijs & Sidonijs. At illi vnanimiter ve-nerunt ad eum, & persuaso Blasto, qui præerat cubiculo Regis, petebant pacem: eò quòd aleretur regio ipsorum à ditione regia. Statuto autem die, Herodes indutus veste regia, consedit pro tribunali, & concionaba-tur ad eos. Populus autem acclamabat: Vox Dei, & non hominis. Conse-stim autem percussit eum Angelus domini, eò quòd nō dedisset gloriam Deo, & erosus à vermibus, expirauit. Cæterum sermo Dei crescebat & multiplicabatur. Barnabas autem & Paulus Hierosolyma reuersi sunt Antiochiam, impleto ministerio, assumpto etiam Iohanne, qui cognomi-nabatur Marcus.
units.tr: Now Herod was angry with the Tyrians and the Sidonians. But they came to him with one accord, and having won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, they asked for peace, because their country was fed from the king's territory. On an appointed day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon the throne and made an oration unto them. And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost. But the word of God grew and multiplied. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem to Antioch, when they had fulfilled their ministry, and took with them John, whose surname was Mark. [Acts 12:20-25]

units.la: ETsi Deus ecclesiam suam asiduis persecutionibus probari & exerceri patiatur, idem tamen omnibus ijs graues & horrendas pœnas constituit, qui hanc persequi & oppugnare audent. Nam apud Zacchariam lapidi oneris siue exercitij confertur, in quo pleriq; quidem virium suarum periculum facere soleant, nemo tamen illud impunè factypus sit. Et huius quidem rei memorabile exemplum in Herode Agrippa proponitur. Qui vt in initio huius capitis dictum est, aduersus ec-clesiam Christi persecutionem grauem instituit, tum quòd suæ ditionis homines diuersis religionibus noluit scindi, tum quòd Iudæis placere studuit. Et initio quidem haud infeliciter hic conatus illi succedere videtur. Nam duos primarios apostolici ordinis viros aggressus, Iacobum quidem occi-dit, Petrum verò comprehensum catenis ferreis constringit, & militibus sedecim custodiendum tra-dit. Quo tempore omnium mentes vehementer consternatas fuisse, assiduæ illorum preces testantur. Sed in puncto temporis, cùm iam deplorata viderentur omnia, Christus sese ecclesiæ suæ vindicem esse declarat. Et primò quidem Petrum miraculose liberat. Deinde in milites transfert pœnam, quæ Petro parata fuerat. Ne quis verò Herodem perpetuo felici rerum successu vsurum putaret, hunc quoque graues & horrenda Dei vindicta assequitur: quam in præsenti loco diligentissimè Lu-cas describit.
units.tr: Although God allows his Church to be tested and exercised by constant persecutions, he nevertheless appoints grave and dreadful punishments for all those who dare to persecute and assail it. For in Zechariah it is compared to a heavy stone or a test of strength, with which many are wont to try their powers, yet no one has done so with impunity. A memorable example of this is set before us in Herod Agrippa. As was said at the beginning of this chapter, he launched a grievous persecution against the Church of Christ, partly because he would not have the men of his realm divided by different religions, and partly because he was eager to please the Jews. And at first this attempt seems to have succeeded for him, not unhappily. For he attacked the two chief men of the apostolic order: he killed James, and seized Peter, bound him with iron chains, and handed him over to be guarded by sixteen soldiers. At that time the minds of all were greatly dismayed, as the constant prayers of the brethren attest. But at the critical moment, when everything seemed already lost, Christ showed himself to be the avenger of his Church. First he miraculously freed Peter. Then he transferred to the soldiers the punishment that had been prepared for Peter. Lest anyone should think that Herod would enjoy an unbroken run of good fortune, the grave and dreadful vengeance of God overtook him too, and Luke describes it most carefully in the present passage.

units.la: Orditur autem à noua historiæ commemoratione, quæ Herodis ingenium euidentius adhuc ar-guit, vt inde tam grauis supplicij causas melius cognoscamus. Summa omnium est, quòd hostili in Tyrios & Sidonios animo fuerit, quos cum publica necessitate, fame nimirum, circumuentos, sup-pliciter pacem petere coegisset, insolentior factus, Dei vindictam accelerarit. Et quamuis inimicitia-rum causas non exponat Lucas, non tamen difficile est videre, quales fuerint. Constat enim raro Monarchis cum liberis ciuitatibus conuenire, eò quod hæ ipsorum libidini & ambitioni aduersentur, & suo exemplo regum subditos ad libertatis studium extimulent. Præterea verisimile est, Tyrios & Sidonios Agrippæ fastum iniquius tulisse, vtpote noui hominis, qui vixdum carcere ereptus à Ca-ligula & Claudio in tantam potentiam euectus fuerat. Et animos illis addere poterant immodicæ opes & longè lateq; patens maris dominium, quod iam seculis aliquot mercibus suis totum ferè ob-tinebant. Inde enim ipsos quoque insolentiores factos fuisse, ex prophetarum scriptis patet. Vide Ifa. 23. Ezech. 26. 27. & 28. Et dissimulauit fortasse astutus tyrannus latens animo suo odium, donec annonæ caritas oborta, illi aliquid aduersus ipsos moliendi occasionem præbuit. Rursum ipsi quoq; cùm suas vrbes non aliunde quàm ex Herodis vicina ditione alij posse, & proinde illius amicitiam sibi necessariam esse viderent, supplices illi siunt, & vt pacem impetrent, Blastum, qui regi à cubiculo erat, in suas partes pertrahunt, quod absq; ingentibus donis & largitionibus fieri non potuit. In his vero tyrannorum mores tanquam in speculo nobis contemplandos spiritus sanctus proponit. Vt enim Herodes hic amplissimus sui regni finibus non contentus, finitimos quoq; suo imperio subiectos cupit: itanifi Dei timore insatiabilis carnis cupiditas in regum animis coberceatur, nullum tam longè la-teq; patens regnum est, quod ipsorum spiritus capere & ambitionem explere possit. Nam vt auari pecuniarum aceruos congerunt & domus domibus agrosque agris insatiabili studio coniungunt: ita tyranni regna regnis coniungere, & indefinenti desiderio imperium suum in finitimos extendere sa-tagunt, minimè interim in hoc intenti, vt ijs prudenter & rectè præsint, quos ipsis gubernandos Deus
units.tr: Luke begins with a fresh account of the story, which shows Herod's character more clearly still, so that we may better understand the causes of so severe a punishment. The sum of the matter is that he had a hostile spirit towards the Tyrians and Sidonians; when he had forced them, surrounded by public distress, that is, by famine, to beg humbly for peace, he became more arrogant and hastened God's vengeance. And although Luke does not set out the causes of the enmity, it is not hard to see what they were. For it is well known that monarchs rarely agree with free cities, because the free cities oppose their lust and ambition, and by their example stir up the subjects of kings to a zeal for liberty. Moreover, it is likely that the Tyrians and Sidonians resented Agrippa's pride the more, as he was a man of new standing, who had scarcely been rescued from prison by Caligula and Claudius and raised to such power. Their own excessive wealth and the dominion of the sea, which stretched far and wide and which for several ages they had almost entirely held through their merchandise, may also have added to their spirits. For that they had become more arrogant too is clear from the writings of the prophets. See Isaiah 23, Ezekiel 26, 27 and 28. And perhaps the crafty tyrant concealed his hatred in his mind until a rise in the price of grain gave him an occasion for some plot against them. Again, when the Tyrians and Sidonians saw that their cities could be supplied from nowhere but the neighbouring territory of Herod, and that his friendship was therefore necessary to them, they came to him as suppliants, and in order to obtain peace they won over Blastus, who was over the king's bedchamber, to their side; and this could not be done without great gifts and bribes. In these events the Holy Spirit sets before us the manners of tyrants as if in a mirror to be contemplated. For just as Herod, not content with the very wide bounds of his kingdom, desires also the neighbouring peoples to be subject to his rule, so, unless the insatiable lust of the flesh is restrained in the minds of kings by the fear of God, there is no kingdom so vast and so widely extended that their spirit cannot grasp it and satisfy their ambition. For just as misers heap up piles of money, and with insatiable zeal join house to house and field to field, so tyrants strive to join kingdom to kingdom and to extend their rule over their neighbours with unending desire, meanwhile being in no way concerned that they should govern wisely and righteously those whom God has entrusted to them to be ruled.

units.la: E concredidit. Atqui hæc assiduorum bellorum causa est, quibus infelici subditi miserè exhauriun-tur, & ab illis sese perdi sentiunt, qui ipsis pastorum & parentum loco esse debebant. Rursum, cum Reges inexplebili ambitione turgidi omnibus imperare velint, ipsi feré à vilissimis mancipijs regun-tur, qui adulatorijs artibus in illorum animos sese insinuare, & mox illorum stoliditate & ignauia ad suum quaestum abuti nouerunt. Ex quo hominum genere Blastus hic fuisse videtur, à quo totius regni administrationem dependisse, vel vnus hic locus facile indicat. Ita apud quosdam Imperato-res primum locum liberti habuisse leguntur: vt interim de illis non dicatur, qui histrionibus, morio-nibus, scortis, cynædis sese regendos præbuerunt. Hinc fieri consueuit, vt perditissimis hominibus supplices fieri cogantur, quibus cum principibus res est: nisi enim illos sibi propitios habuerint, nun-quam ipsis ad regum aures aditus patebit. At quia illi pecunijs inhiant, quibus affectata dignitatis locum tueantur, feré fit, vt in principium aulis venalia sint omnia, & iuxta poetæ dictum, ibi fas, vbi maxima merces. Dicuntur hæc in eum finem, vt & principes intelligant, à quibus vitijs sibi cauere debeant, & simul omnes homines Dei bonitatem agnoscant, qui reges populo suo tam diligenter dissuasit, vt in primo libro Samuelis cap. 8. legitur. Et quibus diuinitus datum est, vt libertate fruantur, tantum bonum tueri, & illo digne vti discant, ne illo amisso & impotentissimorum hominum libidini subiecti, amissam libertatem anxijs suspirijs & gemitibus frustra requirant. Præterea ob-serdandum hic venit, quod tam felici successu Herodes fruitur, postquam ecclesiam Dei persecutus, innoxio sanctorum sanguine sese polluit. Atqui dignus erat, quem vel fulmen cælitus delapsum per-deret, vel regno amisso inglorius & infamis oberraret. Sed ecce opulentissimæ vrbes sponte ad illius pedes deuolutæ, ab illo pacis conditiones accipiunt. Hoc illud est, quod infirmos in fide offendit, quòd nimirum impios lætis rerum successibus vti, & malorum quibus reliqui mortales premuntur (vt pro-pheta ait) immunes esse vident. Psal. 73. Et Ieremias ideò exclamat: Qui fit vt via impiorum prospe-retur, & feliciter agant omnes, qui impudentissimè prauaricantur? Ierem. 12. Adhæc impij inde oc-casione arrepta, vniuersum religionis veræ studium inutile & superuacaneum esse colligunt, vt vide-re est Malach. cap. 2. & 3. Caterum hic nos meminisse oportet, impios tunc quoq; diuinæ prouidentiæ nutu gubernari, quando illis contra Dei oracula res succedere videntur. Iusto autem iudicio Dei fit, vt fortuna ebrij altius euehantur, vt postea grauiori casu ruant. Quo Solomon respiciens superbiam siue exaltationem ruinæ præludium esse dixit. Prouerb. decimo sexto. Et Dauid impiorum gloriam & felicitatem momentaneam esse docens, ait, Vidi impium violentum & sese diffundentem instar lauri frondosæ. Et transiui, & ecce non erat: quæsiui eum, & non est inuentus. Psal. 37. Stultum ergo est, impiorum successibus offendi, cum illi ipsi potissima sint causa interitus illorum, eò quòd il-lis insolenter aduersus Deum abutantur: quemadmodum ex præsentis negotij euentu colligere licet, quem Lucas modò commemorat.
units.tr: But this is the cause of the constant wars by which subjects are wretchedly exhausted and unhappily feel themselves destroyed by those who ought to have been in place of shepherds and parents to them. Again, since kings, swollen with boundless ambition, wish to rule over everything, they are themselves for the most part governed by the vilest slaves, who know how to insinuate themselves into their minds by flattering arts, and soon to exploit their dullness and idleness for their own gain. From this class of men Blastus here seems to have been, on whom, the single fact that the whole administration of the kingdom depended on him easily shows. Thus among some emperors, freedmen are read to have held the first place; not to mention those who gave themselves over to be governed by actors, buffoons, prostitutes and catamites. From this it commonly comes about that men must humbly sue to the most worthless of men, with whom they have business at the princes' courts; for unless they have these men favourable to them, access will never lie open to the ears of kings. But because those men gape after money by which to maintain the position of dignity they pretend to, it generally happens that everything is for sale in the courts of princes, and, as the poet says, right is where the greatest reward is. These things are said to this end: that princes may understand from which vices they ought to guard themselves, and at the same time that all men may acknowledge the goodness of God, who so earnestly dissuaded his people from kings, as we read in the eighth chapter of the first book of Samuel. And that those to whom it has been divinely granted to enjoy liberty may learn to guard so great a good and to use it worthily, lest, having lost it and been subjected to the lust of the most powerful men, they seek in vain with anxious sighs and groans for the liberty they have lost. Besides, it is to be observed here that Herod enjoys such a happy outcome after he has persecuted the Church of God and polluted himself with the innocent blood of the saints. Yet he deserved to be destroyed either by a thunderbolt sent down from heaven, or to wander about inglorious and infamous with his kingdom lost. But behold, the most wealthy cities of their own accord fall prostrate at his feet and receive from him the terms of peace. This is what offends the weak in faith, namely that they see the impious enjoy happy successes and remain free from the evils by which the rest of mortals are oppressed, as the prophet says. Psalm 73. And for this reason Jeremiah cries out: Why does the way of the wicked prosper, and why do all who most shamelessly transgress live at ease? Jeremiah 12. Moreover, the impious, seizing on this occasion, conclude that the whole zeal for true religion is useless and vain, as may be seen in Malachi chapters 2 and 3. But here we ought to remember that the impious are then also governed by the nod of divine providence, when things seem to go well for them against the oracles of God. Yet by the just judgment of God it comes about that men drunk with fortune are lifted higher, so that afterwards they fall with a heavier downfall. Solomon, looking at this, said that pride, or exaltation, is the prelude to ruin. Proverbs 16. And David, teaching that the glory and the happiness of the impious are momentary, says: I have seen the wicked man violent and spreading himself like a green bay tree. And I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and he could not be found. Psalm 37. It is therefore foolish to be offended at the successes of the impious, since those very successes are the chief cause of their destruction, because they abuse them insolently against God; as may be gathered from the outcome of the present affair, which Luke has just recorded.

units.la: Herodes enim, vbi omnia pro voto sibi succedere videt, fortunæ fauore ebrius, diuinos quoq; ho-nores affectare cœpit: quod euidentius patebit, si quæ Iosephus Antiq. libro 10. 9. cap. 7. scribit, cum Luca conferas. Ludos enim ab illo in Cæsaris honorem institutos fuisse tradit, & quodam die indu-tum veste regia, quæ argeto intertexta erat, consedisse, vt publicè coram populo verba faceret. Cùm verò ad solis Orientis radios vestis fulgore suo faciem quoq; regis illustraret, inde aulici adulatores ipsum diuinis laudibus celebrandi occasionem arripuerunt, quorum exemplum populus quoque imi-tari cœpit. Primò itaq; acclamant: Vox Dei, & non hominis. Mox verò ad preces conuersi, aiunt: Propitius nobis esto, quia licet hactenus te velut hominem timuerimus, attamen nunc superioris na-turæ te esse conspicimus, &c. Videntur autem hæc ideò potissimum instituta narrationi interseri, vt populi totius vanitatem videamus, qua corruptus, à tyranno fœdissimo diuexarimeruit. Cur enim meliorem principem illis daret Deus, qui impurum & scelestum hominem diuinis laudibus vehere non erubescebant? Atqui eadem vanitas hodie passim dominatur, quando crudelissimos tyrannos qui se totos ventri & inguini manciparunt, nimium ambitiosis titulis, imò diuinis, tantum non obrui cernimus: nec iam sufficit illos beneficos dixisse aut victores, nisi Inuictissimi dicantur, & diuinâ illa Gratiæ & Maiestatis nomina ad fastidium vsq; inculcentur, quæ soli Deo conuenire ex scriptu-ris constat. Et quia hæc primi quidem faciunt aulici, illos verò non modò ignobile vulgus verum-etiam seruilia doctorum ingenia imitantur, digni sumus, qui aperta principum tyrannide & ma-nifestæ
units.tr: For Herod, when he sees everything succeeding to his liking, drunk with the favour of fortune, began to aspire to divine honours as well. This will appear more clearly if you compare what Josephus writes in Antiquities, book 19, chapter 8 (the reference printed as 10.9 cap. 7), with Luke. For he relates that games were instituted by him in honour of Caesar, and that on a certain day, clad in a royal robe woven with silver, he sat down so that he might make a public address before the people. When the sun's rays from the east struck the robe and its brightness lit up the king's face, his courtly flatterers seized the occasion to praise him with divine honours, and the people began to imitate their example. First they shouted: "The voice of God, and not of a man." Then, turning to prayer, they said: "Be gracious to us, for although hitherto we have feared you as a man, yet now we see that you are of a higher nature, etc." These things seem to have been inserted into the narrative chiefly so that we may see the vanity of the whole people, corrupted by which they deserved to be harassed by a most foul tyrant. For why should God give them a better prince, when they were not ashamed to exalt with divine praises an impure and wicked man? Yet this same vanity rules everywhere today, when we see the most cruel tyrants, who have given themselves wholly to belly and groin, almost buried under overly ambitious titles, indeed divine ones; nor is it now enough to call them beneficent or victorious, unless they are called Most Invincible, and those divine names of Grace and Majesty, which are known from the Scriptures to belong to God alone, are dinned into us to the point of disgust. And since the courtiers do this first, and not only the common crowd but also the servile wits of the learned imitate them, we deserve to be convicted of falsehood by the open tyranny of princes and the plainer proof of their own crimes.

units.la: Impiorum successus ruinæ præludium.
units.tr: The success of the wicked is a prelude to their ruin.

units.la: Herodes diuinos honores affectat. nifestiùs eorundem flagitijs magno nostro malo mendacij argùamur. Meminerint simul horum am-bitiosissimi homines, qui seruilium hominum stoliditate in hunc finem abuntur, vt ementitis & vanis titulis magni fiant. Ita enim sese cùm Herodis huius, tum Caligulæ & Domitiani aliorum qeius generis hominum socios esse declarant, & proinde cum illis Dei vindictam incurrent, quam He-rodes atrocissimam expertus est.
units.tr: Herod aspires to divine honours. Let those most ambitious men remember too, who are misused by the stupidity of servile men to this end, that they may become great by means of false and empty titles. For by doing so they declare themselves companions of this Herod, and of Caligula and Domitian and others of that kind, and therefore they will incur God's vengeance, which Herod experienced in its most terrible form.

units.la: Nam confestim percussit eum Angelus domini, quem illi visibili specie apparuisse, ex Josepho Eusebius tradit. Ex qua plaga repentinùs alui doloribus excruciari cœpit, qui quantumuis ambi-tioso pectori aliquam veritatis confessionem extorserunt. Ad suos enim conuersus, dixit: En ego ve-ster Deus nunc vitam cum morte commutare cogor. Et qui à vobis immortalis dictus sum, nunc ad mortem abducor. Lucas verò morbi genus exprimens, à vermibus erofum expirauisse dicit. Vide-tur ergo phthiriasi periisse, enascentibus ex carne sua vermiculis, qui viuentem graui simul & fœdo dolore depasti, tandem mori coegerunt. Porrò tanti mali hanc vnam causam Lucas assignat, quòd Deo non dederit gloriam. Primò enim regni decus non à Deo, sed à Cæsare sibi obtigisse credit, quem propterea ludis in ipsius honorem editis veneratur. Deinde verum Dei cultum crudeliter persequi & extinguere conatus est. Postremò blasphemiis adulatorum vocibus gauisus est, quas illum abomi-nari & detestari oportebat. Discant igitur hoc exemplo, quid expectent à Deo, qui simili impietate aduersus ipsum efferuntur. In primis verò obseruare conuenit, quàm potenter superbiam Deus vlci-scatur, quando non graues modò, verumetiam ignominiosas pœnas superbis infligit, vt illorum inso-lentes spiritus magis coherceat. Ita Pharaonem non in acie fortiter occumbere, sed aquis maris ru-bri, ignobili vtiq; mortis genere, submergi voluit. Ita Sanherib in templo dei sui à proprijs filijs mise-ré occiditur. Et eodem, qui hic describitur, morbo antea quidè Antiochus, Herodes Magnus, Sylla, & tandem Maximianus persecutor fædè consumpti sunt. Verìssimè ergo Petrus dixit, Deum su-perbis resistere, 1. Pet. 5. Discant hinc omnis ordinis homines intra suæ vocationis fines sese contine-re, & si quid in sese eximij vident, illud omne diuinæ bonitatis donum esse intelligant. Ita fiet, vt sub potenti Dei manu humiliati, donis suis rectè vtantur. Adhæc docet locus hic, quantum mali adu-latores principibus parere soleant. Natura enim philauti sumus, & placent nobis nostra omnia. Quòd si ergo adulatores accedant, prorsus excæcati, manifesta vitia non videmus, & simul veritatis atq; admonitionum impatientes reddimur. Quæ causa est, quòd amplißima regna adulatorum linguis euersa esse, historiæ tradunt. Et sane felicißimus fuisset Herodes, si apostolos potius vitia sua verbo Dei corrigentes, quàm adulatorum voces audiuisset, quæ nefario & superbo Dei contemptu in slatum horrendo interitu multauerunt.
units.tr: For at once the Angel of the Lord struck him, who, as Eusebius relates from Josephus, appeared to him in visible form. From this blow he began suddenly to be racked with pains in the bowels, which wrung from his ambitious heart some confession of the truth. For turning to his people he said: "Behold, I, your God, am now forced to exchange life for death. And I who was called immortal by you am now led away to death." Luke, describing the kind of disease, says he breathed his last, eaten away by worms. So it seems he perished of phthiriasis, with little worms breeding out of his flesh, which, feeding on the living man with grievous and at once foul pain, at last forced him to die. Furthermore, Luke assigns this one cause of so great an evil: that he did not give glory to God. For first, he believed the honour of his kingdom had come to him not from God but from Caesar, whom for that reason he venerated with games held in his honour. Next, he cruelly tried to persecute and extinguish the true worship of God. Lastly, he rejoiced in the blasphemous voices of the flatterers, which he ought to have abhorred and detested. Let those who are puffed up against God with like impiety learn from this example what they may expect from Him. Above all we should observe how powerfully God avenges pride, when He inflicts on the proud not only severe but also ignominious punishments, so as to restrain their insolent spirits the more. So Pharaoh was not allowed to fall bravely in battle, but to be drowned in the waters of the Red Sea, by an ignoble kind of death indeed. So Sennacherib was wretchedly slain in the temple of his god by his own sons. And by the same disease which is described here, Antiochus, Herod the Great, Sulla, and at last the persecutor Maximian were foully consumed. Most truly therefore Peter said that God resists the proud, 1 Pet. 5. Let men of every rank learn from this to keep themselves within the limits of their calling, and if they see anything outstanding in themselves, let them understand that all of it is a gift of divine goodness. Thus it will come about that, humbled under the mighty hand of God, they will use their gifts rightly. Moreover, this place teaches how much harm flatterers are wont to bring upon princes. For we are by nature self-loving, and all our things please us. If therefore flatterers approach, we become utterly blinded, we do not see manifest vices, and at the same time we become impatient of truth and of admonitions. This is the reason why histories relate that the most powerful kingdoms have been overthrown by the tongues of flatterers. And indeed Herod would have been most fortunate, if he had listened to the apostles correcting his faults by the word of God rather than to the voices of flatterers, which by impious and proud contempt of God condemned him to a dreadful death.

units.la: Porrò posts descriptum tyranni exitum, ad institutã ecclesiæ & propagati euangelij historiam Lucas reuertitur, vt offendat huic per Herodem nihil detractum fuisse. Nam sermo Dei (inquit) crescebat & multiplicabatur, indies nimirum ad plures diffusus. Id verò in sequentibus copiose ex-ponet, ad quæ transitum sibi facit, Pauli & Barnaba reditum ex Hierosolymis perstringens. Illuc enim missos fuisse, vt fame laborantibus in Iudæa fratribus subsidium pecuniarum ab ecclesijs hinc inde collectum afferrent, circa finem Cap. 11. audiuimus. Quo officio fideliter defuncti, Antiochiam redeunt, vnde paulò post digressi vnà cum Marco, quem secum adduxère, euangelium longè latè diuulgarunt. Est verò consolationis plenum, quòd ecclesiam omnibus tyrannis & hostibus suis su-perstitem esse cernimus. Generatur enim & conseruatur Dei verbo, quod in æternum manet, 1. Pet. 1. Docent hoc omninm gentium & temporum historiæ. Misere enim & turpiter perierunt Pharao, Chananæi, Sanherib, Babylonij, Antiochus, Herodes tres, Nero, Domitianus, Traianus, Anto-ninus, Seuerus, Maximini, Decius, Valerianus, Aurelianus, Diocletianus, Maximiani duo, Li-cinius, Maxentinus, Iulianus, & quotquot vnquam post bosce omnes Christi ecclesiam op-pugnare ausi sunt. Floret autem illa, & viuit, viuetq; perpetuò sub fidel i & in-uisto vindice & assertore suo Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, after describing the tyrant's end, Luke returns to the history of the founding of the Church and the spread of the gospel, to show that nothing was taken from it through Herod. For the word of God (he says) grew and was multiplied, that is, spread daily to more people. This he will set out at length in what follows, to which he passes over, touching briefly on the return of Paul and Barnabas from Jerusalem. We heard, near the end of chapter 11, that they had been sent there to bring to the brothers suffering famine in Judea the aid of money collected from the churches here and there. Having faithfully discharged this duty, they return to Antioch, whence, shortly afterwards, setting out together with Mark, whom they had brought with them, they widely spread the gospel. It is full of consolation that we see the Church surviving all its tyrants and enemies. For it is begotten and preserved by the word of God, which remains for ever, 1 Pet. 1. The histories of all nations and times teach this. For Pharaoh, the Canaanites, Sennacherib, the Babylonians, Antiochus, three Herods, Nero, Domitian, Trajan, Antoninus, Severus, the Maximini, Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, Diocletian, the two Maximians, Licinius, Maxentius, Julian, and as many as have ever dared to assail Christ's Church after all these, miserably and shamefully perished. But that Church flourishes and lives, and will live for ever under its faithful and invincible defender and champion, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIII. HOMILIA LXXXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. HOMILY LXXXVI.

units.la: ERant autem quidam in ecclesia, quae Antiochiae erat, prophetae & doctores, Barnabas & Simon, qui vocabatur Niger, & Lucius Cyrenaeus, & Manaen, qui cum Herode tetrarcha enutritus fuerat, & Saulus. Cùm autem illi ministrarent domino & ieiunarent, dixit Spiritus sanctus: Segregate mihi Barnabam & Saulum in opus, ad quod vocavi eos. Tunc postquam ieiunassent & precati essent, impositisque illis manus, dimiserunt eos. Illi itaque emissi à Spiritu sancto, descenderunt Seleuciam, & inde navigaverunt in Cyprum. Et cùm essent Salaminae, annunciaverunt Sermonem dei in synagogis Iudaeorum. Habebant autem & Iohannem ministrum.
units.tr: Now there were in the church at Antioch certain prophets and teachers: Barnabas, and Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. And as they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." Then, after they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they let them go. So they, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia, and from there sailed to Cyprus. And when they were at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They also had John as their assistant.

units.la: DEscribit duobus iam sequentibus Capitibus divus Lucas, ut evangelij doctrina, Paulo & Barnaba ministris, pleno cursu gentibus promiscuè praedicari coeperit. Quia enim (ut saepe iam dictum est) soli Iudaei hucusque populi Dei & ecclesiae titulum sibi vendicaverant, ad hos quoque solos redemptionis per Christum partae beneficium pertinere videbatur, & quae de Cornelio Centurione & Antiochenis dicta fuerunt, privilegio quodam evenisse videri poterant. Ne quis ergo scrupulus resţaret, salutis doctrina modo ad diversas gentes promiscuè transfertur, & implentur pa-lam, quae de gentium vocatione olim à prophetis praedicta sunt. Caeterum, ne quis Paulum & Barnabam aliquid in hac causa priuato consilio & temere fecisse putaret, ab illorum vocatione & missione historiam hanc Lucas orditur: cuius hic praecipue scopus est, regnum Dei & universum salutis negotium, non humano consilio, sed divino iussu & decreto ad gentes esse translatum, & has non minus, quàm eos qui ex Iudaeis crediderunt, ad ecclesiae Dei communionem pertinere. Et quidem diligenti demonstratione in hac causa opus fuisse, ex ea concertatione patebit, quam infra Cap. XV. describit. Imò ex Pauli epistolis videre est, gentium salutem ab Iudaeis subinde oppugnatam & in dubium vocatam fuisse: & idem non aliam ob causam Iudaeos sibi tam infensos habuit, quàm quòd incircuncisas gentes ipsis in Christo aequaret, quod illi sine notoria iniuria & prophano contemptu tum Mosaicae legis, tum Iudaici populi fieri non posse arbitrabantur. Quae etiam causa fuit, quòd in asserenda vocatione sua tam serio ubiq; versatur, qui alioqui nominis sui contemptum facile ferre poterat, nisi simul & Dei gloriam & gentium salutem periclitari vidisset. SED ut ad praesentis loci tractationem accedamus, primò quidem Antiochenam ecclesiam describit Lucas, è qua Paulus & Barnabas emissi, euangelium gentibus praedicarunt. Deinde illorum vocationem & missionem unà cum illius circumstantijs explicat. Postremò ut idem commissso sibi munere fungi coeperint, docet.
units.tr: In the two chapters that follow, St Luke describes how the teaching of the gospel, with Paul and Barnabas as ministers, began to be preached freely to the Gentiles. For, as has often been said already, the Jews alone had until now claimed for themselves the title of God's people and the Church, and it seemed that the benefit of redemption won through Christ belonged to them alone. What was said about the centurion Cornelius and the men of Antioch could therefore seem to have happened by some special privilege. So that no scruple should remain, the teaching of salvation is now carried openly to diverse nations without distinction, and what the prophets long ago foretold about the calling of the Gentiles is plainly fulfilled. Moreover, lest anyone think that Paul and Barnabas acted in this matter on their own private judgement and rashly, Luke begins this history with their calling and sending. His chief aim here is to show that the kingdom of God and the whole business of salvation were transferred to the Gentiles not by human counsel but by divine command and decree, and that the Gentiles belong to the communion of God's Church no less than those of the Jews who believed. That this matter needed careful demonstration will be clear from the dispute which he describes below in chapter 15. Indeed, from Paul's epistles it can be seen that the salvation of the Gentiles was repeatedly attacked by the Jews and called into doubt; and the Jews were hostile to him for no other reason than that he made the uncircumcised Gentiles equal to them in Christ, which they thought could not be done without open injury and profane contempt of the law of Moses and of the Jewish people. This was also why he insists so earnestly on asserting his calling everywhere, although he could easily have borne contempt of his own name, unless he saw at the same time the glory of God and the salvation of the Gentiles put in danger. But to come to the subject of this passage: first, Luke describes the church at Antioch, from which Paul and Barnabas were sent out to preach the gospel to the Gentiles. Then he explains their calling and sending together with its circumstances. Lastly, he teaches how they began to discharge the office committed to them.

units.la: Antiochenae ecclesiae descriptionem non absq; causa praemittit. Ex ea enim colligi potest, nihil tamen ab illis potuisse institui, qui tam praesenti Spiritu Dei vtebantur. Nec enim accusari possunt Paulus & Barnabas, quasi ecclesiam hanc suo ministerio destituerint, cùm illi etiam ipsis digressum optimè prospectum fuerit. Fuerunt enim in ea quidam prophetae & doctores. Prophetae autem dicuntur, tum qui ex spiritus suggestione futura praedicunt, qualem supra Agabum fuisse vidimus: tum quibus scripturas propheticas dextrè interpretari datum est: quo sensu propheticae vocabulum Paulus in priori ad Corinth. cap. 14. vsurpat. Vterq; verò sensus praesenti loco non male convenit. Nam vaticinandi donum in ecclesia primitiua multis annis durauisse ex historijs certum est: & dici non potest, scripturarum interpretatione ecclesiam tam celebrem caruisse. Doctores autem dicuntur, qui ecclesiam publicè instituunt, & scripturas sacras omnium institutioni rite accommodant, quos hodie vel pastores vel verbi ministros dicimus. Antiochiae ergo non ecclesia modò fuit, quales vulgò esse consueuerunt, verumetiam schola, è qua eruditi ministri ad alias vrbes emittebantur. Et docet locum hic, praecipuum ecclesiae decus & ornamentum esse, adeoq; omnem incolumitatem in hoc consistere, ut idoneis ministris & doctoribus instructa sit. Horum enim ministerio per verbum Dei ecclesias gubernari simul & aedificari, denique & conseruari. Paulus diserte monet. Nam quomodo credent (inquit) audiunt?
units.tr: He sets down the description of the church at Antioch not without reason. For from it one can gather that nothing could have been set up by those who had such a present gift of God's Spirit. Nor can Paul and Barnabas be accused, as if they had abandoned this church in their ministry, since provision had been made for it very well even at their departure. For there were in it certain prophets and teachers. Now those are called prophets who foretell future things by the prompting of the Spirit, as we saw Agabus was above; and also those to whom it has been given to interpret the prophetic Scriptures rightly, which is the sense in which Paul uses the word "prophets" in his first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 14. Both senses fit this place well. For it is certain from histories that the gift of prophecy lasted in the primitive Church for many years, and it cannot be said that the Church, so celebrated, lacked the interpretation of Scripture. Teachers, however, are those who publicly establish the Church and rightly adapt the holy Scriptures to the instruction of all; today we call them either ministers or ministers of the Word. At Antioch, therefore, there was not only a church, such as there usually are, but also a school, from which learned ministers were sent out to other cities. And this passage teaches that the chief glory and ornament of the Church is that it is furnished with fit ministers and teachers, and that all its safety consists in this. For by their ministry churches are governed, and at the same time built up, and finally preserved through the Word of God. Paul plainly warns of this. For "how," he says, "will they believe those of whom they have not heard?"

units.la: Antiochenae ecclesiae commendatio. Prophetae. Doctores. ut, de quo non audierunt? Quomodo autem audient absq; prædicante? Rom.10. Item: Per euangelium in Christo Iesu ego vos genui.1.Cor.4. Quò etiam in primis pertinet, quòd apostolos, prophetas, euangelistas, pastores & doctores, à Christo ad instaurationem sanctorum & in ædificationem corporis Christi, dari scribit, Ephes.4. Quia verò constat, docendi facultatem non omnibus miraculose dari, vt olim apostolis, scholis opus esse, in quibus instituantur, qui aliquando ecclesiarum ministri futuri sunt. Tales in veteri populo in Leuitarum ciuitatibus erant, & præstantissimos Dei prophetas earum præcipuam curam habuisse, ex Samuelis & Helisei historia patet. Quin & Amos propheta illos acerrimè accusat, qui Nazaraeos & sacris studijs destinatos iuuenes vino corrumpebant. Vide runt hoc in veteri ecclesia potentissimi Reges & Imperatores, qui suis sumptibus collegia instituerunt, ne quando doctorum inopia Christianæ religioni damnum daret. At hodie illa vel ab ignauis fucis occupantur, vel insolentium hominum libidini subiacent, qui ambitiosi titulos potius venari, quàm ecclesiarum consolationi consulere consueuerunt.
units.tr: The commendation of the church at Antioch. Prophets. Teachers. "And how will they hear without a preacher?" (Rom. 10.) Likewise: "In Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor. 4.). To this also belongs chiefly what he writes in Ephesians 4, that Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, ministers and teachers for the restoring of the saints and for the building up of the body of Christ. But since it is plain that the power to teach is not given miraculously to everyone, as it was once to the apostles, there must be schools in which those are trained who will sometimes become ministers of churches.
