But today matters have come to such a pass that among Christians those can be counted the best men who violate the Sabbaths of God by manual labour and by work for their living, while most profane them with abominable crimes; and never is more sinned by pride and arrogance, by drunkenness, by luxury and lust, than on that day which ought to have been wholly consecrated to God and to the meditation on his works and eternal rest. And when these things are done openly, do we still inquire into the causes of the evils of our age?

units.la: Cæterum quia in sacris cætibus, quos Moses conuocationes sanctas vocat, religio sabbatorum quoad externam obseruationem maxima ex parte consistit, quid in hoc cœtu factum sit, diligenter narrat Lucas. Et primò quidem consederunt apostoli, haud dubiè cum reliquis, qui illic congregati erant. Est hoc modestiæ & honestatis, cuius ratio tum semper alias, tum maximè in templis haberi debet, ne quid inordinatè & inhonestè fiat. Deinde mentio fit lectionis ex lege & prophetis, quam communi & solenni consuetudine inter Iudæos seruatam fuisse, paulò post ex Pauli Sermone, & cap. 15. ex Iacobi verbis intelligemus. Ita enim Moses ex Dei mandato instituerat: quem morem ab Esdra post reditum è Babylone restitutum fuisse constat ex Nehem. 8. cap. Nec alio Christus vti voluit, quando in schola Nazarethana ex Isaiæ loco salutis mysteria docuit. Luc. 4. Docent hæc in sacris cœtibus dei verbum, quod scripturis comprehensum est, tractari debere. Ideò enim Paulus ecclesiarum ministris scripturæ sacræ studium commendat, quia non alia vox, quàm quæ in hac sonat, in Dei domo audiri meretur. Enormis ergo & absurdus illorum error est, qui in ecclesiâ rudi populo ineptissimas nugas ex legendis Sanctorum prædicant, vel humanas traditiones virgent, quibus omnem cultum vitiari Christus ipse ex propheta admonet. Matth. 15. Isa. 29. cap. Quod ut hodie nimis frequens est, itasi aliquando aliquis verbo Dei locus relinquitur, illud ferè peregrina lingua vel recitari vel etiam cantari solet, ut ne ex illo quidem aliquis ad populum fructus redire possit. Sed vide de hoc Pauli sententiam 1. Corinth. 14. Tertiò, illud quoque laudem meretur, quòd nemo nisi legitimè rogatus sibi dicendi copiam vsurpat. Nam licet ex veteri consuetudine doctoribus interpretes & prophetæ assiderent, nemo tamen temere & impudenter sese ingerebat, ut nec rogatus nec vlla necessitate vrgente, coram populo verba faceret. Quare Paulus quoq; & Barnabas, licet à spiritu sancto missi essent, receptum tamen & utilem ecclesiæ ordinem minimè turbandum esse putauerunt. Minimè ergo ferenda est Anabaptistarum intemperies, qui loco Pauli 1. Corinth. 14. abutentes, cuius in ecclesiâ dicendi copiam fieri debere clamitant. De illis enim Paulus eò loci loquitur, qui interpretationis & prophetiæ dono instructi, doctoribus (ut modò diximus) assidebant. Eos verò, qui interpretes non sunt, tacere iubet. Idemq; omnia decenter & legitimè fieri præcipit. Neq; hic mihi quisquam obijciat, quid apostolos factures fuisse existimem, si illis nemo dicendi copiam fecisset? Quis enim dubitaret, illos libertate à spiritu cœcessa tunc vsuros fuisse? At quia eadem, etiam seruata ecclesiæ consuetudine, ut poterant, non potuissent non reprehendi, si hanc temere interturbare voluissent. Præterea illud quoq; ab Antiochenis rectè fit, quòd hominibus peregrinis & ignotis dicendi copiam faciunt. Nolunt enim spiritum extinguere, nec prophetias aspernantur, quâ de re Paulus alibi nos admonet. 1. Thess. 5. Hic verò præcipuè obseruandum, quòd sermonem exhortationis requirunt. Ita enim finem exprimunt, ad quem omnis doctrina & sermo in ecclesia referri debet: nimirum ut non modò quid fieri debeat, obiter edoceatur ecclesia, verumetiam pijs exhortationibus ad officium faciendum excitetur, & sic ædificetur super fundamentum apostolorum & prophetarum, ac sub capite Christo verè coalescat. Et huc illa scripturæ sacræ commendatio pertinet, quam Paulus vtilem esse dicit ad doctrinam, institutionem, correctionem, redarguationem, ad hoc deniq;, ut homo Dei integer fit, & ad omne opus bonum præparatus. 2. Timoth. 3. Erant hæc illis obseruanda, qui ad ostentationem in ecclesia sermones suos instituunt, & de sua potius quam Christi gloria soliciti sunt. Discant potius singuli ita ecclesiæ exercitia omnia instituere, ut exhortationibus sanctis ædificentur in vera fide, ad gloriam Iesu Christi cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But since the sabbath religion, as far as its outward observance is concerned, consists for the most part in the sacred assemblies, which Moses calls holy convocations, Luke carefully relates what was done in this gathering. First of all the apostles sat down, doubtless together with the others who were assembled there. This belongs to modesty and decorum, which ought always to be observed, and especially in the temples, lest anything be done in a disorderly and indecent way. Next, mention is made of the reading from the law and the prophets, which, as we shall understand shortly from Paul's sermon and from the words of James in chapter 15, was observed among the Jews as a common and solemn custom. For so Moses had instituted it by God's command, and it is well known that this custom was restored by Ezra after the return from Babylon, as is shown in Nehemiah chapter 8. Nor did Christ wish to use any other method when, in the school at Nazareth, he taught the mysteries of salvation from a passage of Isaiah. Luke 4. These things teach that in the sacred assemblies the word of God, as it is contained in the Scriptures, ought to be handled. For this reason Paul also commends the study of Holy Scripture to the ministers of the churches, because no voice other than the one that sounds in this word deserves to be heard in the house of God. Therefore the error of those is monstrous and absurd, who in the church preach most inept trifles to the unlearned people from the legends of the saints, or who cling to human traditions, by which Christ himself, quoting the prophet, warns that all worship is corrupted. Matt. 15. Isa. 29. chapter. And since this is very common today, so that if any passage of the word of God is ever read, it is usually recited or even sung in a foreign tongue, so that no profit can come to the people even from that. But see Paul's judgment on this in 1 Corinthians 14. Thirdly, this also deserves praise, that no one takes for himself the opportunity to speak unless he has been lawfully asked. For although by ancient custom the interpreters and prophets sat beside the teachers, nevertheless no one rashly and impudently thrust himself forward, so as to speak before the people unless he was asked or unless some necessity urged it. Therefore Paul and Barnabas also, although they had been sent by the Holy Spirit, thought that the received and useful order of the Church ought not to be disturbed. The intemperance of the Anabaptists is therefore by no means to be tolerated, who abuse the passage of 1 Corinthians 14, crying out that the opportunity to speak should be granted to everyone in the church. For Paul there speaks of those who, endowed with the gift of interpretation and prophecy, sat beside the teachers, as we have just said. But those who are not interpreters he bids to be silent, and he likewise commands that everything be done decently and in order. Nor let anyone here object to me: what do I think the apostles would have done if no one had given them the opportunity to speak? For who would doubt that they would then have used the freedom granted by the Spirit? But because, even had the custom of the Church been kept, they could not have avoided rebuke if they had rashly wished to disturb it. Moreover, the Antiochenes also do rightly in granting the opportunity to speak to strangers and unknown men. For they are unwilling to quench the Spirit, nor do they despise prophecies, about which Paul admonishes us elsewhere. 1 Thess. 5. Here what must above all be noted is that they ask for a word of exhortation. For in this way they express the end to which all teaching and speech in the Church ought to be directed: namely, that the Church should not only be informed in passing about what ought to be done, but should also be stirred by holy exhortations to perform its duty, and so be built up upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, and truly grow together under Christ the head. To this also pertains that commendation of Holy Scripture which Paul says is useful for teaching, instruction, correction, and rebuke, and finally so that the man of God may be complete and prepared for every good work. 2 Tim. 3. These things ought to have been observed by those who arrange their sermons in the church for display, and who are concerned for their own glory rather than the glory of Christ. Rather, let each learn to arrange all the exercises of the Church so that they may be built up in true faith by holy exhortations, to the glory of Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XIII. HOMILIA LXXXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. HOMILY LXXXIX.

units.la: Exurgens autem Paulus, cum manu silentium indixisset, ait: Viri Israelitæ, & qui ex vobis timent Deum, audite: Deus populi huius elegit patres nostros, & populum in altum euexit, cum inquilinus esset in terra Ægypti, & cum brachio excelso eos inde eduxit, & circiter quadraginta annos eorum mores pertulit in deserto. Ac deletis septem gentibus in terra Chanaan, terram ipsorum illis hæreditaria sorte distribuit. Et posthæc per annos circiter quadringentos & quinquaginta dedit Iudices usque ad Samuelem prophetam. Et exinde postularunt regem, dedit eis Deus filium Cis, virum ex tribu Beniamin, annis quadraginta.
units.tr: Then Paul stood up, and with his hand he called for silence, and said: "Men of Israel, and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people chose our fathers, and exalted the people while they were sojourners in the land of Egypt, and with an outstretched arm he led them out from there, and for about forty years he bore with their conduct in the wilderness. And when he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them as an inheritance by lot. After these things, for about four hundred and fifty years, he gave them judges, down to Samuel the prophet. And afterwards they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul, the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years."

units.la: Describit deinceps D. Lucas electi illius organi, Pauli apostoli concionem, quam in schola Antiochena habuit, estque hæc prima, quam ex Paulinis concionibus spiritus sanctus literis mandari voluit: non quod reliquas indignas cognitu putarit, sed quod ex hac de omnibus aliis iudicare licet, quas huic minime dissimiles fuisse oportet, eo quod spiritus Christi semper & vbiq; sibi conueniat. Interim non temere factum est, quod hanc potissimum ex omnibus aliis selegit Lucas, in cuius relatione diligentior esset. Vt enim hac vniuersa Iesu Christi & salutis nostræ mysteria plenissime comprehendit: ita cum illa Antiocheni contemnerent, fecerunt apostoli, quod illos rarissime fecisse legimus. Nam excusso super Iudæos pedum pulvere, salutis doctrinam ad alios transtulerunt. Porro concionis argumentum idem est, quod ipse Christus apostolos obseruare iusserat. In hoc enim totum incumbit, ut Iudæos ab inani legis & legalium ceremoniarum fiducia ad Christi fidem adducat. Quod ut facilius impetret, commodissimo ordine procedit. Primo enim, quia illos prærogatiuis aliquot insolentius gloriari nouerat, sic ut superuacaneum illis videretur, aliam salutis viam inuestigare vel ingredi, docet illos nihil ex semetipsis habere, quo gloriari possint, sed ex mera Dei gratia accepisse quicquid eximium habeant, qui propter Messiam promissum illos & seruare & prærogatiuis illis ornare dignatus fit. Inde vero colligit, necessarium omnino esse, ut Messiam hunc amplectantur, nisi a gratia Dei excidere, & bonis omnibus spoliari velint. Deinde Iesum Dei & Mariæ virginis filium, Messiam hunc & promissum saluatorem esse docet: & ibi quidem de illius officio ita disserit, ut vniuersum nostræ redemptionis negotium breuiter comprehendat, & luculentis scripturæ veteris oraculis confirmet. Tandem vero prophetarum comminationes profert, ut horribile Dei iudicium sibi imminere sentiant, quicunq; Dei filium, & oblatam in hoc salutis aspernari ausi fuerint. Et hæc quidem totius concionis summa est, quam paucis comprehendisse sufficit, cum de singulis suo loco sius dicturi simus: nunc vero ad præsentis loci tractationem accedamus.
units.tr: Luke next describes the sermon of Paul the apostle, that chosen instrument, which he delivered in the synagogue at Antioch. This is the first of Paul's sermons that the Holy Spirit wished to have committed to writing. This is not because Luke thought the others unworthy of being known, but because from this one we may judge the rest, which must have been very like it, since the Spirit of Christ always and everywhere agrees with itself. Nor was it by chance that Luke chose this one above all others, since in its report he was more careful. For just as this sermon fully comprehends the mysteries of Jesus Christ and our salvation, so the apostles did, when the Antiochenes rejected those things, what we read they very rarely did. For, shaking the dust from their feet against the Jews, they transferred the message of salvation to others. Moreover, the subject of the sermon is the same that Christ himself had ordered the apostles to observe. For it is all directed to this end: to lead the Jews from a vain trust in the law and in legal ceremonies to faith in Christ. To achieve this more easily, Paul proceeds in a most suitable order. First, because he knew that they were rather arrogant in boasting of certain privileges, so that it would seem pointless to them to seek or enter upon another way of salvation, he teaches them that they have nothing of their own in which they may glory, but have received from the pure grace of God whatever excellence they have, since God deigned, on account of the promised Messiah, both to preserve them and to adorn them with those privileges. From this he infers that it is absolutely necessary that they embrace this Messiah, unless they wish to fall from the grace of God and be stripped of all good things. Then he teaches that Jesus, the son of God and of the virgin Mary, is this Messiah and the promised Saviour. There he speaks of his office in such a way as to comprehend briefly the whole business of our redemption, and to confirm it by the clear oracles of the Old Scripture. Finally, he brings forward the threats of the prophets, so that those who have dared to spurn the Son of God and the salvation offered in him may feel the dreadful judgment of God hanging over them. This is indeed the sum of the whole sermon, which it is enough to have summarised briefly, since we shall speak of each part in its place; now let us turn to the treatment of the present passage.

units.la: I. Exordium pro more apostolico breue est, nec exquisiti artificij lenocinijs suspectum. Pramittit vero extensæ vel eleuatæ manus gestum, quo veteres publice verba facturi, silentium indicebant, sicut non uno in loco infra videbimus. Deinde attentionem captans, eiusmodi titulis illos appellat, quibus & beneuolos sibi reddere, & simul officij admonere auditores studet. Nam primo Israelitas vocat, quo nomine illi maxime gaudebant, non modo propter Iacobum patriarcham, qui primum hoc nomine ornatus fuit, sed quod illo manifesta diuini auxilij & protectionis promissio continetur, de qua videre est Genes. 32. cap. Addit vero: Et qui ex vobis timent Deum, audite: ita illos officij sui non obscure admonens, ut intelligant, si tunc demum veros Israelitas fore, si Dei timentes fuerint, & Dei verbo se morigeros præbeant. Nos vero apostolica exordij breuitas de duobus, scilicet & considerato dignissimis admonet. Primum est, quis in præfationibus titulorum, quibus auditores honorificentius compellari solent, vsus esse debeat. Vbi honori quidem non nihil tribuendum est vel Paulo authore, qui iubet ut nos inuicem honoris & reuerentiæ significatione prævenianus. Rom. 12. Diligenter tamen cauendum, ne quid adulatoria mente et lingua ambitioni insolentiu hominum indulgeatur, qui titulorum falsu inebriari consueuerunt. Et hoc potius videndum, ut titulis idoneis officij admoneantur, quibus cum nobis res est. Merito ergo laudatur veterum simplicitas, qui officiorum nominibus contenti, adulatorios illos titulorum fucos ignorauerunt. Quid enim regis titulo addes, quod illo angustius sit & præclarius, cum solus hic plus contineat, quam aliquis hominum præstare stare possit? Et inter Christianos verba factURUS, num quid fratris nomine amabilius aut Christianorum titulo honorificentius excogitabis, quo & sacerdotalis dignitas & regia maiestas, in quam nos Christus euexit, exprimitur? At hodie eò stultitiæ peruentum est, ut rustici putentur, qui non ementitis titulis, ijsq; ineptissimis & ridiculis, orationes & scripta sua farciunt, quibus homines plus satis mente alienatos prorsus ad insaniam redigant. Quanto rectius Augustus Cæsar, qui domini quoque titulum augustiorem putauit, quàm vt sibi homini mortali conueniret? Secundò admonemur, quales esse oporteat, qui verbu Dei digne & non sine fructu audire voluerint. Primum Israelitæ sint oportet, qui in tentationum luctâ Dei verbum constanter apprehendant, nec illud sibi vllis aduersis extorqueri patiantur. Fides ergo exigitur, quasola nos vincere apostolus testatur. 1. Iohan. 5. Deim de Dei timentes sint, & ad verbum eius magna reuerentia contremiscant, quemadmodum per prophetam dominus admonet. Isa. 66. Nec enim fieri potest, ut dei verbo sese morigerum præbeat, nisi qui de illo magnificè sentire didicit. Quæ causa est, quòd ad Dei colloquium accessurus Moses, calceos, id est, pecuinos & carnales affectus exuere iubetur, quibus verbi maiestas exinaniri consueuit. Tales verò auditores cum hodie rari sint, frustra fere Dei verbum prædicari videmus.
units.tr: I. The introduction, in the apostolic manner, is brief and free of the enticements of exquisite art. But he first makes the gesture of an extended or raised hand, by which the ancients, when about to speak publicly, called for silence, as we shall see more than once below. Then, seeking their attention, he addresses them with titles by which he strives both to win their goodwill and at the same time to remind his hearers of their duty. For first he calls them Israelites, a name in which they especially rejoiced, not only because of the patriarch Jacob, who was the first to bear this name, but because in it is contained a clear promise of divine help and protection, which may be seen in Genesis chapter 32. He adds: "and you who fear God, listen." Thus he reminds them of their duty not obscurely, so that they understand that they will then at last be true Israelites if they are God-fearing and submit themselves obediently to the word of God. Now the brevity of the apostolic introduction reminds us of two things which are worth considering. The first is what use should be made of titles in preface, by which hearers are customarily addressed more respectfully. Here, indeed, some honour is to be given, even on the authority of Paul, who bids us to go before one another in showing honour and reverence (Rom. 12). Yet we must take great care that no flattering mind or tongue is indulged in to the ambition of arrogant men, who are wont to be intoxicated by false titles. Rather, we should see to it that they are reminded of their office by suitable titles, with which we have to deal. Rightly, then, the simplicity of the ancients is praised: content with the names of offices, they did not know those flattering paints of titles. For what could you add to the title of king that would be narrower and more distinguished, since this one title alone contains more than any man can manage? And when speaking among Christians, what more lovely name than brother, or what more honourable title than Christian, could you devise, by which both the priestly dignity and the royal majesty to which Christ has raised us are expressed? But today folly has reached such a point that men are thought rustic who do not stuff their orations and writings with lying titles, and those most inept and ridiculous, by which men already sufficiently out of their minds are driven altogether into madness. How much more rightly did Augustus Caesar act, who thought the title of lord too grand to suit a mortal man! The second thing we are reminded of is what sort of people ought to be those who wish to hear the word of God worthily and not without fruit. First, they must be Israelites, who in the struggle of temptations hold fast to the word of God and do not allow it to be wrested from them by any adversity. Faith, therefore, is required, which alone the apostle testifies overcomes (1 John 5). They must also be God-fearing, and tremble with great reverence at his word, as the Lord admonishes through the prophet (Isa. 66). For no one can submit himself obediently to the word of God unless he has learned to think highly of it. This is why Moses, about to approach the colloquy with God, is commanded to take off his shoes, that is, the fleshly and carnal affections, by which the majesty of the word is wont to be emptied. But since such hearers are rare today, we see that the word of God is almost preached in vain.

units.la: Caeterum, vt ad Paulum reuertamur, exordio historicam narrationem subijcit, qua prima oratiònis pars absoluitur. Et narrandi quidem initium à patribus sumit, vt simul ostendat, abs se nec nouum Deum, nec nouam fidem prædicari, sed eam, qua patres quoque olim saluati sint. Nam illos quidem præclaros & eximijs bonis illustres fuisse, nihil tamen habuisse, quàm quod ex gratia Deus contulit, qui ex illorum posteris promissum orbis saluatorem nasci volebat. At quia diuinam gratiam difficulter agnoscunt, quos proprię dignitatis fiducia inflauit, Paulus diligenti beneficiorum Dei enumeratione vtitur, quæ & gratiam Dei contra suorum meritorum iactatores asserit, & lucu-lentos communis omnium nostrum redemptionis typos comprehendit. Quare non alienum à Pauli instituto fuerit, si singula percurrentes, ea quoq; expendamus, quæ nostræ institutioni seruiunt.
units.tr: But, to return to Paul, after the introduction he adds a historical narrative, with which the first part of his speech is completed. He takes the beginning of his narrative from the fathers, so as to show at the same time that he is preaching neither a new God nor a new faith, but that faith by which the fathers too were once saved. For those fathers were indeed renowned and illustrious for their outstanding goods, yet they had nothing except what God conferred from grace, he who willed that the promised Saviour of the world should be born of their posterity. But because those whom confidence in their own dignity has puffed up find it hard to acknowledge divine grace, Paul uses a careful enumeration of the benefits of God, which both asserts the grace of God against the boasters of their own merits and comprehends clear types of the redemption common to us all. Therefore it will not be out of keeping with Paul's method if, running through the individual points, we also weigh those things which serve our instruction.

units.la: Primò fontem omnium bonorum attingit, gratuitam electionem. Deus populi huius (inquit) elegit patres nostros. Vocat autem Deum populi Iudaici, non gentilium more, qui singulis populis deos suos proprios tribuebant, sed quòd Deus is, qui omnium gentium vnicus dominus & rector est, Iudaicam gentem sibi præ omnibus alijs delegit, per quam toti mundo inclaresceret, vt Dauid monuit, Psal. 76. & 147. Electionem verò hanc gratuitam fuisse passim scriptura docet. Iosue certè Abrahamum, priusquam vocaretur, diis alienis seruiuisse testatur cap. 24. Et Moses electionem hanc frequenter inculcat, vt intelligant, ad quem authorem bona illa omnia, quibus donati erant, referri debeant. Et huc quoque pertinent, quæ Ezechiel. 16. & apud Amos 3. cap. leguntur, omnesq; Iudæis gloriandi occasionem adimunt. Simul verò hinc patet, nostram quoq; salutem, & quæcunq; in nobis eximia sunt vnius Dei gratiæ acceptà ferri debere, quia nos quoq; in filio suo Iesu Christo, priusquam mundi fundamenta iacerentur, eligere dignatus est. Ephef. 1. Rectè igitur Dauid clamat: Beatus, quem tu elegeris, &c. Psal. 65. Quod si verò nihil ex nobisipsis boni habemus, sed diuinitus nos eligi oportet, quæ obsecro vocatio est, nostris operibus aut meritis salutem tribuere, quæ nisi gratuita electio prædedat, Deo placere non possunt?
units.tr: First he touches on the source of all good things, gratuitous election. "The God of this people," he says, "chose our fathers." He calls God the God of the Jewish people, not in the manner of the Gentiles, who assigned to each people its own gods, but because that God, who is the sole Lord and ruler of all nations, chose the Jewish nation for himself above all others, so that through it he might be made famous to the whole world, as David reminded us (Ps. 76 and 147). Moreover, that this election was gratuitous the Scripture teaches everywhere. Joshua certainly testifies that Abraham served strange gods before he was called (ch. 24). And Moses frequently inculcates this election, so that they may understand to whom all those good things, with which they were endowed, ought to be referred. To this also belong the passages read in Ezekiel 16 and in Amos chapter 3, which take away from the Jews every occasion of glorying. At the same time it is plain from this that our salvation too, and whatever excellence there is in us, ought to be received as coming from the grace of the one God alone, since he also deigned to choose us in his Son Jesus Christ, before the foundations of the world were laid (Eph. 1). Rightly, then, David cries out: "Blessed is the one whom you have chosen" (Ps. 65). But if we have no good from ourselves, and it is necessary that we be chosen by God, what calling, I beg you, is it to attribute salvation to our works or merits, which cannot please God unless gratuitous election goes before?

units.la: Secundò populi huius gloriam & illustrem ex Ægypto liberationem allegat. Cùm peregrinus esset & aduena in Ægypto, illum mirificè exaltauit Deus, primò quidem per Iosephum, qui Ægypti dominus factus, ipsis quoque apud illius gentis reges gratiam impetrauit: deinde verò, quòd tyrannide oppressos, excelso brachio, id est, miraculis & prodigijs conspicua virtute in libertatem asseruit, & è domo seruitutis eduxit. Sed & hoc gratuitum beneficium fuisse, ex eo patet, quòd peregrini & abiectissimæ conditionis homines fuerunt. Quid enim tales mererentur? Vt interim de eo dicere omittamus, quòd Ægyptiaca superstitione inquinati, in seruitute retineri potius quàm liberari merebantur. Habent verò hæc communis nostræ redemptionis typum, præsenti argumento mirificè seruientem. Constat enim omnes nos in terra peregrinos esse, nec vllam hic habere permanentem ciuitatem. Tales verò nos, qui nec terræ possessionem merebamur, Deus in sublimem cælestis dignitatis gradum euehere, imò filiorum loco habere dignatus est. Idem quoque nos mortifera diaboli tyrannide oppressos, excelso brachio, id est, per filium suum, quem Isaias propheta cap. 53. brachium domini nominat, liberauit.
units.tr: Second, he cites the glorious and famous deliverance of this people from Egypt. Though they were strangers and sojourners in Egypt, God greatly exalted them, first through Joseph, who became lord of Egypt and won them favour with the kings of that nation; then, because he rescued them from tyranny with a mighty arm, that is, by miracles and prodigies displayed in manifest power, and led them out of the house of bondage. That this was a free gift is clear from the fact that they were foreigners and men of the most abject condition. For what did such people deserve? Let us pass over for now the point that, defiled by Egyptian superstition, they deserved to be kept in slavery rather than set free. These events, moreover, provide a type of our common redemption, serving the present argument remarkably well. For it is certain that we are all strangers and pilgrims on earth, with no lasting city here. Yet God, who did not deserve even a possession of the land, has been pleased to raise us to the high rank of heavenly dignity, indeed to place us in the position of sons. He has likewise freed us, who were oppressed by the deadly tyranny of the devil, with a mighty arm, that is, through his Son, whom the prophet Isaiah in chapter 53 calls the arm of the Lord.

units.la: Tertiò, deū populi huius mores totùs annùs quadraginta in deserto pertulisse dicit. Notatur hic admiranda & plus quàm paterna Dei lenitas siue indulgentia, quali nemo mortalium vel erga filium vnigenitum, vel erga seruum sibi omnino necessariū vsuretur. Patet hoc si Moisis historia legamus. Quoties enim aduersus Moisen murmurauisse? quoties seditiose aduersus eundem insurrexisse? quoties morte illi intentauisse leguntur? Sed omissis ijs, quae in Moisen patrauerūt, quid non designarūt in ipsum deum? Huius certè praeceptorū obliti, vitulum fecere, & transmutarūt gloriā immortalis dei in formā bouis comedentis fœnum. Quoties verò Aegyptiacam seruitutem gloriosissimae liberationis beneficio praetulerunt? quoties dei voluntatē & potentiā tentauerunt? Tulit tamen incurabilem illorū malitiā deus, licet quotidie nouis supplicijs excindi mererentur. Stupenda haec videretur dei lenitas, nisi eandē ipsi quoq; indies experiremur. Quae enim dies, quae hora praeterit, qua non dei in nos iudiciū vel factis vel dictis vel cogitationibus & nefandis desyderijs prouocemus? Attamen parcit nobis dominus, licet illi nunquā non ad manū sint fulmina & infinita alia arma quibus nos puniat. Nouit enim (vt prophetae verbis vtar) conditionē nostrā, recordās quòd simus puluis. Psal.103. Ne quis tamen impunitatē peccandi hinc stabiliri putet, obseruemus, hanc dei lenitatē hoc tantū cauisse, ne totā gentē pro meritis excinderet. Interim tamen incurabiles & poenitere nescios grauiter multa uit. Nemo enim illorū in terrā promissam ingressus est, sed variis plagis in deserto ceciderunt: adeò vt nec Aaroni nec Moisi pepercerit deus, cùm illi quoq; offendiculi in populo authores fuissent. Nu.20.
units.tr: Third, he says that God bore with this people's conduct for forty years in the desert. Here we note the wonderful and more than paternal gentleness or indulgence of God, such as no mortal would show even to an only son or to a servant who was wholly necessary to him. This becomes plain if we read the history of Moses. How often are they read to have murmured against Moses? How often to have rebelled against him in sedition? How often to have threatened him with death? But setting aside what they did against Moses, what did they not do against God himself? Forgetting his commandments, they made a calf and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the image of an ox eating grass. How often did they prefer Egyptian slavery to the benefit of a most glorious deliverance? How often did they test the will and power of God? Yet God bore their incurable wickedness, though every day they deserved to be cut off by fresh punishments. This forbearance would seem astonishing, did we not experience the same from him day by day. For what day or hour passes in which we do not provoke the judgment of God, by our deeds, words, thoughts and wicked desires? Yet the Lord spares us, although the thunderbolts and countless other weapons with which he could punish us are always at hand. For he knows (to use the prophet's words) our frame, remembering that we are dust (Ps. 103). Lest anyone think, however, that impunity for sin is thereby established, let us observe that this gentleness of God has taken care only to prevent him from destroying the whole nation according to their deserts. Yet in the meantime he afflicted severely those who were incurable and did not know how to repent. For none of them entered the promised land; they fell in the desert by various plagues. So much so that God did not spare even Aaron and Moses, although they too had been the authors of stumbling among the people (Num. 20).

units.la: Quartò terrae promissae haereditatē cōmemorat, quam Iudaico populo, septem prius deletis potentissimis gentibus, deus forte distribuit. Exponitur hoc multis in libro Iosue. Et Moises beneficiū illud dei diligenter cōmendat, quando ait: Quū introduxerit te dominus tuus in terram, quā iurauit patrib. tuis, & dederit tibi ciuitates magnas & bonas, quas tu nō aedificasti: domos quoq; plenas omnibus bonis quas tu nō impleuisti: & puteos excisos, quos tu non effodisti: vineas & oleas, quas tu non plantasti, &c. Deut.6. Quae verba vt dei liberalitatē mirificè amplificant, ita iniustitiae & crudelitatis notam eidē inurere poterant, nisi causae consyderentur, propter quas gentes illae eiectae fuerunt. Enumerat has alibi Moises, dum libidines vagas, incestus, nefaria sacra, fortilegia & alias eius generis artes curiosas prohibet, & addit: Ne incedatis iuxta ritus gentis huius, quam ego eijcio ante vos. Quoniam omnia ista fecerunt, ideo eos cum fastidio repuli, &c. Vide Leuit.18.20. & Deut.18. Propter peccata igitur gentes istae excisae sunt, quibus cum etiam Israelitae polluerentur, ipsos quoq; eiectos fuisse legimus, vt nemo hic deum vel iniustitiae vel nimiae seueritatis accusare possit.
units.tr: Fourth, he recalls the inheritance of the promised land, which God apportioned to the Jewish people after first destroying seven very powerful nations. This is set out at length in many places in the book of Joshua. Moses also commends that benefit of God carefully when he says: "When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which he swore to your fathers, and has given you great and good cities which you did not build, houses also full of all good things which you did not fill, and cisterns hewn out which you did not dig, vineyards and olive trees which you did not plant," and so on (Deut. 6). These words greatly magnify God's liberality, but they could also brand him with the mark of injustice and cruelty, unless the reasons are considered for which those nations were cast out. Moses lists these elsewhere, when he forbids wanton lusts, incest, unlawful rites, sorcery and other arts of that kind, and adds: "Do not walk in the customs of this nation, which I am driving out before you. Because they did all these things, I therefore rejected them with loathing," and so on (see Lev. 18, 20, and Deut. 18). Those nations were therefore cut off on account of their sins; and since we read that the Israelites too were cast out when they were polluted by the same things, no one can accuse God here of injustice or of excessive severity.

units.la: Quinto loco reipub. diuinis legibus optimè constitutae beneficium proponit. Nec enim terram modo illis distribuit Deus, verumetiam iudices dedit, a quibus regerentur & afferentur ab hostium tyrannide. Obseruandus verò hoc loco manifestus error, qui librariorum incuria annorū numeros depravauit. Nam post Moisen & terrā distributa Iudices vsq; ad Samuelis tempora annis circiter quadringentis & quinquaginta praefuisse scribitur, cùm trecenti tantum anni ex infallibili cōputatione colligantur, cuius Paulus minimè ignarus fuit. Constat enim ab exitu Israelis vsq; ad templi Salomonici extructionem, cuius initium in quartum Salomonis incidit, numerari annos quadringentos octoginta. 1.Reg.6. Ab hīs subtrahendi sunt 40. anni Moisis, quibus in deserto populum duxit, 40. item Samuelis & Saulis, & totidem Dauidis vnà cum quatuor primis regni Salomonici: & remanebunt anni trecenti quinquaginta sex, quibus Iudices rempub. Israelis administrauerunt. Comprehenditur autem hīs duplex diuina bonitatis argumentum. Nam toto illo Iudicū tempore non semel excindi meruerunt, & tamen seruati sunt. Deinde cùm contempta reipub. forma, quam a Deo optimam acceperant, regem postularent, non exterum aliquem tyrannum capitibus ipsorum Deus imposuit, sed regem dedit Saulem ex fratribus ipsorum, & quidem contemptissimae tribus hominē, nemia & intolerabilis in ipso initio esset noui regis potentia. Quid quòd inconsulta illorū temeritate bene vsus est dominus? Ita enim regnum ad Iudam deuoluit, e cuius regali stirpe Messiam oriturum esse, Iacob praedixerat. Gen.49.cap. Sed de hoc postea agetur. In praesenti verò obseruemus, reipub. constitutione inter praecipua dei beneficia numerari. Quia enim natura disciplinam homines refugiunt sine qua vitam ducere quietam & tutam, impossibile foret: diuinae virtutis opus est rerumpub. & magistratuum constitutio. Cuius meminisse conuenit, quibus pace simul & bonis legibus fruendum est: nisi dum ingratos se deo praebent, reges in furore sibi dari sentiant, quod Iudaeis accidisse prophetae propheta testatur. Hos.13. In primis verò suam felicitatem Christiani agnoscant, quibus æterni & cœlestis regni consortium à Deo præparatum est in Iesu Christo, regeinuictissimo & immortali: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Fifth, he sets before them the benefit of a commonwealth excellently constituted by divine laws. For God not only distributed the land to them but also gave them judges, by whom they were governed and rescued from the tyranny of their enemies. A manifest error must be noted here, which the carelessness of copyists has corrupted in the numbers of years. For after Moses and the distribution of the land, the judges are written as having governed until the time of Samuel for about four hundred and fifty years, whereas from an infallible reckoning only three hundred years are gathered, and Paul was by no means unaware of this. For it is established that from the exodus of Israel to the building of Solomon's temple, whose beginning fell in the fourth year of Solomon, four hundred and eighty years are counted (1 Kings 6). From these must be subtracted the forty years of Moses, by which he led the people in the desert; likewise forty years of Samuel and Saul, and as many of David, together with the first four years of Solomon's reign. There remain three hundred and fifty-six years, during which the judges administered the commonwealth of Israel. Now in these years a twofold argument of the divine goodness is included. For throughout that whole period of the judges they deserved to be cut off not once, yet they were preserved. Then, when they despised the form of the commonwealth which they had received from God as the best, and demanded a king, God did not impose on their heads some foreign tyrant, but gave them Saul as king from among their own brothers, and indeed a man from the most despised tribe, so that the power of the new king might not be excessive and intolerable from the very beginning. What of the fact that the Lord made good use of their rash folly? For thus he turned the kingdom over to Judah, from whose royal stock Jacob had foretold that the Messiah would arise (Gen. 49). But this will be discussed later. For now let us observe that the constitution of a commonwealth is counted among the chief benefits of God. For since by nature men shrink from discipline, without which it would be impossible to live a quiet and safe life, the establishment of commonwealths and magistrates is a work of divine power. It is fitting to remember this, since we must enjoy both peace and good laws; unless, while they show themselves ungrateful to God, they perceive kings given to them in wrath, as the prophet testifies happened to the Jews: the prophet Hosea (Hos. 13). Above all, Christians should acknowledge their own happiness, for whom a share in the eternal and heavenly kingdom has been prepared by God in Jesus Christ, the most invincible and immortal King, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XC.
units.tr: HOMILY XC.

units.la: Et sublato Saule suscitauit illis Dauidem in Regem, cui testimonium reddens, dixit: Inueni Dauidem filium Iesse, virum secundū cor meum, qui faciet omnes voluntates meas. Huius ex femine deus iuxta promissionem adduxit Israeli saluatorem Iesum: prædicante priùs Iohanne ante faciem ingressus eius baptismum pœnitentiæ toti populo Israel. Cùm autè impleret Iohannes cursum dixit: Quem me arbitramini esse? Non sum ego. Sed ecce venit post me, cuius subligacula pedum soluere non dignus sum.
units.tr: And when he had removed Saul, he raised up David to be king over them, to whom he gave this testimony: "I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my will." From his seed, according to the promise, God brought to Israel a Saviour, Jesus. John had first preached, before his coming, a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And when John was finishing his course, he said: "Whom do you suppose me to be? I am not he. But behold, there comes one after me, whose sandal straps I am not worthy to loosen."

units.la: Dvvus Paulus hac concione sua totus in hoc incumbit, vt Iudæos ab inani & superstitiosa legis fiducia ad salutiferam IesuChristi fidem adducat. Quia verò illi prærogatiuis aliquot, quibus ipsorum gentem Deus exornauerat, ita gloriabantur, vt sibi nullo alio saluatore opus esse putarent, prima concionis parte hanc fiduciam oppugnans, docet, patres non suo merito, sed ex mera Dei gratia habuisse, quicquid in illis eximium & præclarum fuit, & id quidem propter Messiam, qui ex illorum stirpe enasci debuit. Inde verò cuius cordato colligendū relinquit, Messiam hunc constanti fide arripi simul & retineri oportere, nisi à gratia Dei & pristina dignitate omnino excidere velint. Porrò primam hanc concionis suæ partem diligenti veterum beneficiorum Dei enumeratione absoluit, in quibus singulis diuinæ gratiæ bonitas elucet, quæ vt patres initiò elegit, ita secus quàm illi merebantur seruauit, cùm non semel perdere & reijcere potuisset. Deduxit autè historiam vsq; ad Saulis tempora, cuius mentionem ideò cumprimis fecisse videtur, vt commodior esset ad Dauidem transitus, quem promissi saluatoris patrem scripturæ nominant. Et in præsenti quidem, vt ad hunc regni translatio facta sit docet: deinde ea occasione alteram concionis partem aggreditur, qua probat Iesum esse Christum, cuius officium simul & vniuersum redemptionis nostræ negotium fusius exponit.
units.tr: Paul in this sermon bends every effort toward this end: to lead the Jews from a vain and superstitious trust in the Law to the saving faith of Jesus Christ. Since they boasted of several privileges with which God had adorned their nation, so that they thought they had no need of any other saviour, he attacks this confidence in the first part of the sermon and teaches that the fathers had whatever was outstanding and remarkable in them not by their own merit but from the sheer grace of God, and this indeed on account of the Messiah, who was to be born from their stock. From this, however, he leaves it to the thoughtful to gather that this Messiah must be seized and held fast with a steadfast faith, unless they wish to fall utterly from grace and their former dignity. Moreover, he completes this first part of his sermon with a careful enumeration of God's past benefits, in each of which the goodness of divine grace shines forth. God chose the fathers at the beginning, and then preserved them, though not as they deserved, since he could have cast them off and rejected them more than once. He carried the history down to the times of Saul, and he seems to have made mention of him especially so that the transition to David would be more convenient, whom the Scriptures call the father of the promised Saviour. And for the present, he teaches that the transfer of the kingdom was made to him; then, on that occasion, he takes up the second part of his sermon, in which he proves that Jesus is the Christ, and sets out more fully his office and the whole business of our redemption.

units.la: Facit autem non parum ad Pauli institutum regni translatio. In ea enim insigne bonitatis Dei argumentum eluxit, quando reipub. formam mutare ausis, non tyrannum imposuit, sed eo sublato, optimum regem dedit, promissi Messiæ patrem, adeoq; illorum insania & temeritate, præter illorum meritum, bene vti dignatus est. Et vt luculentius esset Dei beneficum, Dauidis encomium, ab ipso deo prolatum, recitat. Nobis verò tum de Saule è regni solio deturbato, tum de Dauide in eius locū surrogato, quædam dicenda sunt, quæ & ipsum Paulum fusius tractauisse verisimile est, cùm nostræ institutioni non mediocriter seruiant. Et primò quidem, ne quis Deum in regnorum translationibus tyrannico more ludere arbitretur, sacra historia consuli debet, quæ causas repudiati Saulis diligentissimè recenset. Præcipua in his fuit insolens diuini verbi contemptus, qui priuatæ gloriæ studiosiorem quàm diuinæ fecit. Exempla huius extant in 1.Sam.cap.13. & 15. Inde secuta sunt horrenda quæq; facinora. Nam non Dauidem modò, quem diuinitus probari videbat, persequi ausus est, ve-rumetiam Ionathæ filio necem molitur, & Dei sacerdotes crudeliter occidit. Adhæc veneficam consulit, & reprobæ mentis specimen in ipso vitæ fine exhibet, sibi ipsi crudelem manū inferens. Est verò exemplum hoc cumprimis memorabile, in cuius consyderatione omnes homines maximè verò qui in magistratu sunt, crebrò versentur: vt intelligant cùm suam ipsorum tum rerumpub. suarum salutem ab vno Deo pendere, & proinde verbum Dei audiant, gloriā illius prouehant, eiq; (vt Dauides monet) in timore seruiant, & filium Dei, Iesum Christum, quem ille regem regum constituit, venerabundi & supplices exosculentur. Psal.2. At quia hodie regum & principum lusus est, contempto Dei verbo pro sua libidine omnia versari, nemini mirum videri debet, si vnà cum suis regnis miserè perear. De Christo enim dictum est: Gens & regnum, quod non seruierit tibi, peribit, & c. Isa.60.
units.tr: The transfer of the kingdom contributes not a little to Paul's purpose. For in it a remarkable proof of God's goodness shone forth: when men had dared to change the form of the commonwealth, God did not set a tyrant over them but, removing him, gave them an excellent king, the father of the promised Messiah, and so deigned, by their folly and rashness and beyond their deserving, to use them for good. And so that the kindness of God might stand out more brightly, he recites the praise of David, uttered by God himself. Now, certain things must be said to us about Saul, cast down from the throne of his kingdom, and about David, put in his place; Paul likely treated these more fully, since they serve our instruction no little. And first, lest anyone think that God plays with the transfers of kingdoms in a tyrannical manner, the sacred history must be consulted, which recounts most carefully the causes of Saul's rejection. The chief of these was his insolent contempt of the divine word, which made him more eager for his own glory than for God's. Examples of this are found in 1 Samuel chapters 13 and 15. From this followed all manner of horrible crimes. For he not only dared to pursue David, whom he saw approved by God, but also plotted the death of Jonathan's son and cruelly slew the priests of God. Besides this, he consulted a sorceress, and at the very end of his life he displayed a sign of a reprobate mind, laying a cruel hand upon himself. This example is especially memorable, and it is to be constantly pondered by all men, and most of all by those who hold office, so that they may understand that both their own safety and that of their commonwealths depends on the one God alone; and therefore they should hear the word of God, advance his glory, serve him in fear (as David admonishes), and kiss the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom he has appointed King of kings, with reverence and humility. Psalm 2. But since today it is the sport of kings and princes to set aside the word of God and to act entirely at their own pleasure, no one should think it strange if they perish wretchedly along with their kingdoms. For it is said of Christ: "The nation and the kingdom that will not serve you shall perish," etc. Isaiah 60.

units.la: Sed Dauidē videamus, quem insigni elogio ipse deus ornare dignatus est, quod partim ex Psal.89. partim verò ex cap.13. primi Samuelis concinnat Paulus, nec quicquam diuinis oraculis interserit, quàm quod filium Iesse vocat, quem Bethlehemitam & obscuræ conditionis hominem fuisse, &
units.tr: But let us look at David, whom God himself deigned to adorn with a remarkable eulogy, which Paul compiles partly from Psalm 89 and partly from chapter 13 of the first book of Samuel. And he inserts nothing from the divine oracles except that he calls him the son of Jesse, who was a Bethlehemite and a man of obscure condition, and

units.la: Regni Iudaici translatio ad Dauidem.
units.tr: The transfer of the Jewish kingdom to David.

units.la: Dauidis encomium. è re pecuaria cumprimis vitium quæfuiffe, historia sacra docet. Facit hoc ad amplificandam boni- tatem Dei, qui obscurum hominem, eumq; inter fratres suos natu minimum in tantam dignitatem euehere voluit: simulq; probibet, ne vel de ipso Dauide insolentius glorientur, quando hunc quoq; mera Dei gratia sic exaltatum fuisse constet. Et sane si Dauidem ipsum audiamus, hoc ingenuè fatetur. Auditis enim Dei promissionibus de Messia è sua stirpe nascendo, exclamauisse legitur: Quis sum ego domine Deus? & quæ domus mea, quod me tantopere euehus? &c. 2. Sam. 7. Porrò vt Saulem regno excidisse diximus propter immanem verbi contemptum & inobedientiam: ita hoc nomine potissimum Dauid condemnatur, quod omnes dei voluntates fecerit. Vnde generalis doctrina peti debet, eos demum probari Deo, qui ipsius voluntati se accommodant. Nec enim sacrificijs vllis Deus placatur, sed obedientia delectari solet. 1. Sam. 15.
units.tr: David's eulogy. Sacred history teaches that he was especially a herdsman by occupation. This serves to magnify the goodness of God, who wished to raise an obscure man, and the youngest among his brothers, to so great a dignity; and at the same time it prevents them from boasting too insolently even of David himself, since it is clear that he too was so exalted by the mere grace of God. And indeed, if we listen to David himself, he confesses this frankly. For when he heard God's promises about the Messiah to be born from his line, he is read to have exclaimed: "Who am I, Lord God? And what is my house, that you have raised me up so greatly?" etc. 2 Samuel 7. Moreover, just as we said that Saul fell from his kingdom on account of his monstrous contempt of the word and his disobedience, so David is chiefly commended on this account, that he did all of God's will. Hence a general doctrine should be drawn: that those alone are approved by God who accommodate themselves to his will. For God is not appeased by any sacrifices, but is wont to delight in obedience. 1 Samuel 15.

units.la: Caterum quæritur hoc loco, quomodo Dei voluntates omnes fecisse dicatur Dauid, qui tamen adulterio & homicidio se polluit, quiq; superbia seductus populi censum aduersus Dei voluntatem instituit? Sed facilis est ad illa responsio. Primò enim cum se promissi saluatoris patrem fore audiret, hunc constanti fide apprehendit, & propterea Deo displicere non potuit, cum eum haberet, in quo illi complacuit. Deinde ex fide hac omnes illæ virtutes germinauerunt, quibus Deum de'ectari constat. Hæc enim humilem reddidit, & magnificum beneficiorum Dei æstimatorem, vt modò dixi- mus. Eadem si quando per infirmitatem laberetur, illum denuò erexit, & ad pœnitentiam agendam extimulauit. Hæc ipsa verbi Dei amante & studiosum effecit, vt illud fauis melle stillantibus præferret. Psal. 19. Fidei quoq; opus fuit, quod verbi disciplinam patientissimè tulit, imò obsequentem se ad omnia ferenda præbuit, quæ sibi propter peccata diuinitus irrogari audiebat. Cùm enim Nathan propheta bella intestina & gladium sibi minitari audiret, non illum reiecit improbè, nec seditionis accusauit, sed hoc vnum respondisse contentus fuit: Peccaui domino. Nec socordia aut fastidientis animi ea vox fuit, sed verè dolentis & culpam deprecantis, quod ex Psalmo 51. quem eodem tempore composuit, videre licet. Nec illum quicquam simulauisse, res ipsa declarauit. Cùm enim vrbe & regno per filium pelleretur, Zadoko sacerdoti, qui arcam ad ipsum detulerat, inquit: Reduc arcam Dei in vrbem. Si natus fuero fauorem coram domino, me restituet, ostendetq; mihi & se & habitaculum suum. Quòd si dixerit, Nihil te delector: præsto sum, faciat mecum quod illi bonum visum fuerit. 2. Samuel. 15. Eiusdem animi specimen fuit, quòd maledicentem sibi Semeium non modò patienter tulit, sed eundem sua authoritate, ne quid mali pateretur, defendit. 2. Sam. 16. Quòd item optionem offerenti domino, vt ex tribus plagis quam vellet, eligeret, respondit: Supra modum angor, incidamus quæso in manum domini, &c. 2. Sam. 24. Quid quòd angelo in populo funesta lue grassanti dixit: Ego peccaui, ego iniquè egi, oues autem istæ quid fecerunt? Sit quæso manus tua contra me & contra domum patris mei. Quid hoc animo modestius, sanctius, tractabilius & manfuetius? Vt intelerim de ijs dicere omittamus, quæ in Saulem multis modis sibi iniurium, omnis officij & pietatis plena designauit. Cùm his si Saulis animum, ambitione, fastu, inuidia, odio, ira, Dei contemptu & immani contumacia æstuantem conferas, facile vidobis, quantum inter vtrunq; discriminis fuerit. Seruiunt autem hæc communi omnium hominum institutioni. Docent enim quales eos esse conueniat, qui Deo probari cupiunt. Si enim Christum Iesum vera fide complexi, obseruationi mandatorum Dei studuerint, fiet vt quod infirmitate carnis peccatum fuerit, Christi merito sarciatur, & in vitium aliquod prolapsi, huius spiritu duce per pœnitentiam à lapsu resurgent.
units.tr: Yet the question here is how David can be said to have done all of God's will, when he polluted himself with adultery and murder, and, led astray by pride, ordered a census of the people contrary to God's will. But the answer to these is easy. For first, when he heard that he would be the father of the promised Saviour, he laid hold of him with steadfast faith, and therefore could not be displeasing to God, since he had him in whom God was well pleased. Then from this faith all those virtues sprang forth, by which it is agreed God is delighted. For this faith made him humble and a great esteemer of God's benefits, as we have just said. If at any time through weakness he slipped, it raised him up again and stirred him to repent. This same faith made him a lover and diligent student of the word of God, so that he preferred it to honey dripping from the honeycomb. Psalm 19. Faith was also at work in his most patient endurance of the discipline of the word, and in his readiness to bear whatever he heard had been sent upon him by God on account of his sins. For when the prophet Nathan threatened him with civil wars and the sword, he did not wickedly reject him, nor accuse him of sedition, but was content to answer only this: "I have sinned against the Lord." That word was not spoken from carelessness or a disdainful spirit, but from one who truly grieved and sought pardon for his fault, as may be seen from Psalm 51, which he composed at the same time. And the event itself showed that he had not pretended anything. For when he was driven from the city and kingdom by his son, he said to the priest Zadok, who had brought the ark to him: "Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favour in the sight of the Lord, he will restore me and show me both himself and his dwelling. But if he says, 'I have no delight in you,' behold, I am here; let him do with me what seems good to him." 2 Samuel 15. A proof of the same spirit was that he not only bore patiently Shimei cursing him, but also, by his own authority, defended him so that he would suffer no harm. 2 Samuel 16. Likewise, when the Lord offered him a choice of three plagues, that he might choose whichever he wished, he answered: "I am in great distress; let us fall, I beg you, into the hand of the Lord," etc. 2 Samuel 24. And what of when, seeing the angel smiting the people with a deadly plague, he said: "I have sinned, I have done wrong; but these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand, I pray, be against me and against my father's house." What could be more modest, holy, tractable and gentle than this spirit? Not to mention what he showed toward Saul, who in many ways did him wrong, a man full of all duty and piety. If you compare with these the spirit of Saul, seething with ambition, arrogance, envy, hatred, anger, contempt of God and monstrous obstinacy, you will easily see how great the difference between the two was. Now these things serve the common instruction of all men. For they teach what sort of people it is fitting for those to be who wish to please God. For if they embrace Christ Jesus with true faith and strive to keep the commandments of God, it will come about that whatever sin is committed through the weakness of the flesh is made good by the merit of Christ, and those who have fallen into some vice, led by his Spirit, will rise again from their fall through repentance.

units.la: Porrò ex Dauidis historia occasione arripiens Paulus, ad secundam sua concionis partem transit, qua Iesum, quem apostoli prædicarunt, promissum illum Saluatorem esse docet, propter quem patribus olim benefecerit Deus. Et quia sibi cum Iudæis, infensissimis Christi hostibus rem esse noverat, multis simul & firmis argumentis illud asserit, è quorum numero tria præsenti hoc loco continentur, quæ ordine excutiemus.
units.tr: Taking occasion from the history of David, Paul passes to the second part of his sermon, in which he teaches that Jesus, whom the apostles preached, is the promised Saviour, on whose account God had long ago done good to the fathers. Because he knew he had to deal with the Jews, the most bitter enemies of Christ, he asserts this by many strong arguments at once. Three of these are contained in the present passage, and we will examine them in order.

units.la: Primum est, quod inde natum esse dicit, vnde nascendum prophetæ prædixerant, nimirum ex Dauidis semine. Atqui longum foret singulas promissiones producere, imò superuacaneum quoq;, cùm itaque fuerint, vt vulgò Messias Dauidis filius diceretur. Si quis tamen plura cupit, legat quæ habentur 2. Samuel. 7. Psal. 132. Isa. 11. Ierem. 23. &c. Christum verò è Dauidis semine hominem natum esse, diligenti genealogia Matthæus & Lucas euincunt. At hic simul obseruemus, quòd secundum promissionem Saluator hic excitatus fuisse dicitur. Docet hæc particula, hunc quoq; ex mera dei gratia nobis datum esse, nec alicuius hominis merito tribui debere, quòd deus filium suum saluatorem nobis misit. Promissionem enim ex gratia factam fuisse, ipse Dauides fatetur, ut paulò ante vidimus. Quòd si quis modestiæ tribuere velit, ea promissione conuincetur, quam primus parentibus, fugitiuus & mortem commeritus, factam fuisse legimus. Gene.3. Et ipse Christus ingenuè ad Dei gratiam omne hoc refert, quando Iohan.3.ait: Ita deus dilexit mundum, ut filium suum vnigenitum daret, &c. Quæ verba apostolus exponens scribit: In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dilexerimus deum, sed quòd ipse dilexerit nos, &c. 1. Iohan.4. Simul quoq; infallibilis hic elucet Dei Veritas, quæ ad omnes promissiones extendi debet, ut inde firmam in omnis generis tentationibus consolationem petamus. Qui enim fallere noluit, cum de filij ipsius morte ageretur, cur in aliis falleret?
units.tr: The first is that he says Jesus was born from the place the prophets had foretold he must be born, namely from the seed of David. It would be long, and indeed superfluous, to cite each promise, since they were such that the Messiah was commonly called the son of David. If anyone wants more, let him read what is found in 2 Samuel 7, Psalm 132, Isaiah 11, Jeremiah 23, etc. That Christ was born a man from David's seed, Matthew and Luke prove by a careful genealogy. But here let us also observe that this Saviour is said to have been raised up according to promise. This phrase teaches that he too was given to us by the sheer grace of God, and that no man's merit should be credited with God sending his Son to be our Saviour. For David himself confesses that the promise was made from grace, as we saw a little earlier. If anyone would ascribe it to modesty, he will be refuted by that promise which, as we read, was first made to our parents, fugitives who deserved death. Genesis 3. And Christ himself openly refers all this to the grace of God, when he says in John 3: "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son," etc. The apostle, expounding these words, writes: "In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us," etc. 1 John 4. At the same time the infallible truth of God shines forth here, which ought to be extended to all his promises, so that we may draw from it firm consolation in every kind of temptation. For he who was unwilling to deceive when the death of his own Son was at issue, why would he deceive in other matters?

units.la: Secundum argumentum est, quòd eo modo Iesum venire dicit, quo promissum Saluatorem venturum esse prophetæ prædixerunt. Habuit enim præcursorem, qualis describitur Isa.40. Mala.3. & 4.. Iohannes qui pœnitentiæ baptismum prædicauit, quo hominum animos ad Christum rite excipiendum præparauit. Eodem argumento Marcus euangelista vtitur, quando negotiū Iesu Christi ita cœpisse scribit, sicut à prophetis prædictum fuit. Interim obseruatu dignum est, quòd præcursore opus fuit, qui pœnitentia (quam verbis simul & sacramento commendauit) homines Christo præpararet. Arguit hoc naturæ nostræ corruptionē, quæ fit ut salutis minimè capaces simus, nisi toti mutemur & regeneremur. Adhæc eos quoq; confutat, qui Christi doctrina peccandi licentiam plantari existimant, cum nemo ad illū admittatur nisi qui vera pœnitentia digne præparatus fuerit. Quia tamen de hoc sæpe iam dictum est, et noua pastim sese occasio plura dicendi offert, hæc obiter annotauisse sufficiat.
units.tr: The second argument is that he says Jesus came in the same way as the prophets foretold the promised Saviour would come. For he had a forerunner, such as is described in Isaiah 40, Malachi 3 and 4: John, who preached the baptism of repentance, by which he prepared men's minds to receive Christ properly. The evangelist Mark uses the same argument when he writes that the work of Jesus Christ began just as the prophets had foretold. Meanwhile it is worth noting that there was need of a forerunner to prepare men for Christ by repentance, which he commended both in word and by sacrament. This proves the corruption of our nature, which makes us wholly incapable of salvation unless we are completely changed and regenerated. Besides, it refutes those who think that the doctrine of Christ plants a license to sin, since no one is admitted to him unless he has been duly prepared by true repentance. But since this has often been said already, and the opportunity to say more new things presents itself, it will suffice to have noted these points in passing.

units.la: Tertium argumentum à pronunciatis ducitur. Nam Iohannis testimonium allegat, non quòd Christi causa hominum testimonijs nitatur, sed quòd tanta esset Iohannis inter Iudæos authoritas, vt vulgò pro propheta haberetur, vt videre est Matth.11. & apud Iosephū, qui Iohannis indignam necem, cladis, quam Herodes ab Areta acceperat, causam fuisse scribit. Quo sensu ipse Christus eiusdem testimonio alicubi vsus est. Iohan.5. Hic (inquit Paulus) cum à quibusdā Messias putaretur, omni suspicione populum liberaturus ait: Quem me arbitramini esse? Non sum ego Christus. Sed ecce venit post me, &c. Explicantur hæc fusius Iohan.1. Luc.3. & Matth.3.cap. Hic autem quod nam vulgi ingenium sit in astimandis dei seruis proponitur.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from the things proclaimed. For he cites John's testimony, not because the cause of Christ rests on human testimonies, but because John's authority among the Jews was so great that he was commonly held to be a prophet, as may be seen in Matthew 11 and in Josephus, who writes that John's unworthy death was the cause of the disaster Herod suffered from Aretas. In this sense Christ himself also once used John's testimony, John 5. Here (says Paul), since by some he was thought to be the Messiah, wishing to free the people from every suspicion, he says: "Whom do you suppose me to be? I am not Christ. But behold, he comes after me," etc. These things are explained more fully in John 1, Luke 3 and Matthew 3. Here, however, the attitude of the crowd in judging God's servants is set forth.

units.la: HOMILIA XCI.
units.tr: HOMILY XCI.

units.la: Viri fratres, filij generis Abrahami, & qui in vobis timent deum, vobis sermo salutis huius missus est. Nam qui habitabant Hierosolymis, & principes eorum, cum eum ignorarent, & voces prophetarum, quæ per omne sabbatum leguntur, eo damnato impleuerunt. Cumq; nullam causam mortis inuenissent, postularunt à Pilato, ut eum occideret. Et postquam consummarunt omnia, quæ de ipso scripta sunt, sublatum è ligno posuerunt in monumentum. Deus autem suscitauit eum ex mortuis, qui visus est per dies complures his, qui simul ascenderant cum eo à Galilæa Hierosolymas, qui sunt testes eius ad populum.
units.tr: Brethren, sons of the stock of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, the word of this salvation has been sent to you. For those who dwelt in Jerusalem, and their rulers, not knowing him, and fulfilling the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath, condemned him. And though they found no cause for death, they asked Pilate that he should be put to death. And when they had accomplished all the things that were written concerning him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead, and he was seen for many days by those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people.

units.la: QVod omnis scriptura, tum veteris tum noui Testamenti, vnanimi consensu tradit, idipsum hac concione sua Paulus ingenuè simul & constanter docet: nimirum, quòd Iesus Christus vnicus humani generis redemptor & saluator sit, in quo vno nobis à deo patre benedictio, iustitia, salus & vita obtingat. Quia verò cum Iudæis ipsi res erat, quos insuperabili fere contumacia Christo aduersari nouerat, magna grauitate causam hanc agit. Et initio quidem tria argumenta præmisit, quibus id euinceret. Subiungit hıs alia, quæ ita proponit, vt simul ijs occurrat, quæ auditores in fide Christi suscipienda remorari poterant. Primò enim Christum Iesum ad ipsos pertinere testatur, ne quis illum de re prorsus aliena loqui putaret. Deinde crucis offendiculo medetur. Tandem Christi resurrectionem, quæ præcipuum diuinitatis illius argumentum est, allegat & constanter asserit. Nos verò de singulis, quod Dominus dederit, ordine dicemus.
units.tr: This is what the whole of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, teaches with one voice, and Paul in this sermon teaches it both frankly and steadfastly: namely, that Jesus Christ is the only redeemer and saviour of the human race, and that in him alone blessing, righteousness, salvation and life from God the Father are obtained for us. Since he was dealing with Jews, whom he knew to be almost unshakably opposed to Christ, he argues this case with great seriousness. At the outset he set out three arguments by which he would establish it. He then adds others, which he presents in such a way that they also meet the objections that could hold back his hearers from embracing faith in Christ. First, he testifies that Jesus Christ belongs to them, so that no one would think he was speaking of something entirely foreign to them. Then he remedies the stumbling block of the cross. Finally, he cites the resurrection of Christ, which is the chief proof of his divinity, and firmly affirms it. We shall speak of each of these in order, as the Lord grants.

units.la: Viri fratres (inquit) filij generis Abrahami, & qui in vobis timent Deum, vobis sermo salutis huius missus est. Grauis hæc est interfaciuncula, quæ illos excitari voluit, ne Christi doctrinam nihil ad se pertinere putarent. Verisimile enim est fuisse eo tempore plures, qui à sua professione alienum putarent, sese controuersijs de fide & religione obortis immiscere: quales hodie etiam passim inueniuntur, qui hac opinione primam prudentiæ laudem & gloriam sibi vendicant. At negat hoc Paulus, & vt facilius illis, quod res erat, persuaderet, magnificis titulis eos compellat. Præterid enim quòd communi & recepto more viros fratres vocat, addit: Filij generis Abrahami: quo titulo ipsos propter fœdus dei & promissiones cumprimis gloriari nouerat. Ne tamen generis prærogatiuam sufficere putarent, simul officij illos admonet, cum subijcit: Qui in vobis timent Deum. Ita enim docet, tunc demum illos genuinos & veros Abrahami filios fore, si externæ professioni Dei timorem & syncerum religionis studium coniunxerint, de qua re Christus etiā Iohannis octauo disputat. Deinde verò infert: Vobis sermo salutis huius missus est. Quasi dicat: Si filij Abrahami & veri Dei cultores censeri vultis, salutis doctrinam quæ singulari Dei beneficio vobis primis offertur, nullo modo aspernari poteritis. Nec enim eo sensu hæc à Paulo dicuntur, quòd à salutis consortio gentes adhuc exclusas putaret, quarum vocationi ipsum spiritus sanctus destinauerat. Sed dicendo filium respicit, qui vt Christi promissiones Iudæorum patribus proposuerat, eosq; populum sibi peculiarem à reliquis segregarat: ita ipsis quoq; primis salutem in Christo exhibitam prædicari voluit, quemadmodum in euangelio non obscurè Christus testatur, quando apostolos, cum primùm emitterentur, in viam gentium abire vetat. Matth. 10. At sublato in Christi morte velo, quo à Iudæis gentes distinguebantur, illis quoq; ianua patefacta est, vt per fidem Abrahami filij facti, eandē cum Iudæis vitæ hereditate adire possint. Prærogatiuæ ergo Iudæos Paulus admonet, quod deus illos exornauerat, ne Christi cognitionem, quasi nihil ad se pertinentem, inconsulta temeritate reijcerent. Est autem omnibus verbi ministris imitandum Pauli exemplum, vt meminerint ita prædicandum esse dei verbu, vt quæ dicuntur, auditores ad se pertinere intelligant. Nisi enim id fiat, cantilenæ instar inani sono illorum aures verbum dei feriet, quemadmodum Ezech. 33. legimus. Ita ergo salutis promissiones proponant, vt singuli certi fiant eas ad se pertinere, & inde consolationem accipiant. Ita dei præcepta ingerant, vt singuli abs se quoq; horum obseruationem requiri sentiant. Ita dei iudicia prædicent, vt qui similia meruerunt, sibi hæc ipsa expectanda esse norint. Ita enim demum recte secatur verbum domini, si singuli ex eo haurire possint, quæ ipsorum vel institutioni, vel consolationi, vel emendationi seruiunt. Præterea insignis euangelij lausest, quòd salutis sermo vocatur, quo sensu angelum quoq; Cornelio dixisse, supra vidimus: Simon Petrus loquetur tibi verba, per quæ seruieris tu & domus tua, &c. Illud hic monuisse sufficiat, enormem illorum ingratitudinem esse, qui verbum illud maledictis incessunt, & eosdem propriæ salutis acerrimos hostes esse.
units.tr: "Brethren" (he says), "children of the stock of Abraham, and whoever among you fears God, the word of this salvation has been sent to you." This is a weighty little interjection, meant to rouse them so that they would not think the doctrine of Christ had nothing to do with them. It is likely that at that time there were many who thought themselves exempt from their profession and kept out of controversies about faith and religion that had arisen; such people are still found everywhere today, who claim for themselves the highest praise of prudence on this very ground. But Paul denies this, and to persuade them more easily of what was the case, he addresses them with splendid titles. Besides calling them brethren in the usual and accepted way, he adds, "children of the stock of Abraham," a title by which he knew they especially boasted, on account of God's covenant and promises. Yet lest they think that their descent from the patriarchs was enough, he reminds them of their duty by adding, "whoever among you fears God." For he teaches that they will be true and genuine sons of Abraham only if they join the fear of God and a sincere zeal for religion to an outward profession; Christ also discusses this matter in John chapter 8. Then he adds: "the word of this salvation has been sent to you." As if to say: if you wish to be counted children of Abraham and true worshippers of God, you can by no means scorn the doctrine of salvation, which is offered to you first of all by a singular kindness of God. For Paul does not say this in the sense that he thought the Gentiles, whose calling the Holy Spirit had already determined, were still excluded from fellowship in salvation. Rather, by saying "son," he looks back to the promises of Christ that had been made to the fathers of the Jews, and that had set them apart as a people peculiar to God from the rest. So he wanted the salvation exhibited in Christ to be preached to them first of all, just as Christ plainly testifies in the gospel, when he forbids the apostles, at their first sending out, to go on the way of the Gentiles (Matt. 10). But once the veil that separated Jews from Gentiles was taken away at Christ's death, the door was opened to them as well, so that by faith they might become sons of Abraham and enter into the same inheritance of life with the Jews. Paul therefore reminds the Jews of the privileges with which God had adorned them, so that they would not, through thoughtless rashness, reject the knowledge of Christ as though it had nothing to do with them. Moreover, all ministers of the Word should imitate Paul's example, remembering that the word of God must be preached in such a way that the hearers understand what is said to pertain to themselves. For unless this is done, the word of God will strike their ears with empty sound, like a song, as we read in Ezekiel 33. So they should set out the promises of salvation in such a way that each one becomes certain that they pertain to him, and receives consolation from them. They should press the commands of God in such a way that each one feels that their observance is required of him too. They should proclaim the judgments of God in such a way that those who have deserved similar things know that these very things await them. For the word of the Lord is rightly handled only if each person can draw from it what serves his instruction, his consolation or his correction. Besides, the gospel's distinctive praise is that it is called "the word of salvation"; we saw above that the angel also spoke in this sense to Cornelius: "Simon Peter will speak words to you by which you and your household will be saved," and so on. It is enough to note here that those who revile this word and who are the fiercest enemies of their own salvation show an enormous ingratitude.

units.la: Hinc verò Paulus ad crucis offendiculum transit, cui diligentissimè medetur, eo quòd non sine graui causa morte Christi offendebantur, qui eius mysteria ignorabant. Et cumprimis atrox videbatur, quod Hierosolymitani antistites eius authores essent. Erat enim Hierosolyma religionis, sacerdotij & doctrinæ sedes, & inde iuxta veteres prophetias verbum salutis expectabatur. Isa. 2. Quare non poterat non absurdum videri, eum pro saluatore agnoscere, quem Hierosolymitani proceres pro schismatico & seductore in crucem egissent, & eam doctrinam ampletti, quæ Hierosolymis explosa erat. Tanta quippe erat ciuitatis sanctæ (ita enim à prophetis appellatur Hierusalem) authoritas, vt plerique impossibile putarent, eam in fidei & religionis caussa errare posse. Caeterum Paulus offendiculo isti sic medetur, vt illius ciuitatis exemplum cauendum potius, quàm imitan-dum esse doceat, ne simili ingratitudine & impietate Deum offendant. Sunt autem quatuor quae in eum finem adducit.
units.tr: From here Paul passes to the stumbling block of the cross, which he remedies most carefully, since those who did not know the mysteries of Christ were offended by his death for no slight reason. And it seemed especially monstrous that the high priests of Jerusalem were its authors. For Jerusalem was the seat of religion, of the priesthood and of teaching, and from there, according to the ancient prophecies, the word of salvation was expected (Isa. 2). Therefore it could not but seem absurd to acknowledge as Saviour the one whom the leaders of Jerusalem had handed over to the cross as a schismatic and seducer, and to embrace the doctrine that had been driven out of Jerusalem. Indeed, so great was the authority of the holy city (for the prophets call Jerusalem by this name) that most people thought it impossible for her to err in matters of faith and religion. But Paul remedies this stumbling block in such a way as to teach that the example of that city is to be avoided rather than imitated, lest they offend God with a similar ingratitude and impiety. There are four things which he brings forward to this end.

units.la: Primò, qui habitabant Hierosolymis (inquit) & principes eorum, cum eum ignorarent, dam-nauerunt. Ignorantiam ergo tanti facinoris causam fuisse dicit, vt etiam 1.Cor.2. Quis vero imita-tione dignum esse putet, quod per ignorantiam peccatum esse audit? Nec tamen eiusmodi ignoran-tia hac censeri debet, quae factum excusat. Nam simul scripturas ignorauisse dicuntur, & quidem vulgares illas, quae omnibus sabbatis legi consueuerant. At turpe simul & nulla venia dignum sa-cerdotem scripturas nescire, cum ab eo legis scientiam requirere Deus iubeat. Malach. 2. Adhaec magnam excusationis partem illis adimit, quòd ab ipso Christo, vt scripturas scrutarentur, admoniti fuerunt. Ioan.5. Atqui omnis ignorantiae causam banc vnam fuisse, alibi Paulus docet, quòd sine Christo in Mosis & prophetarum lectione versabantur. Hoc enim illud velum erat, quod obstabat, quò minus Mosis faciem, id est verum legis sensum intueri possent.2.Cor.3. Cum ergo caeci duces fuerint (quales à Christo quoq; dicuntur, Matth.15.) minimè imitandi erunt. Admonemur itaq; hoc loco, non semper clarorum virorum iudicijs & exemplis insisti debere, quin potius ad scrip-turae regulam facta omnia examinari debent, priusquam in exemplum trahantur. Si enim turpiter hallucinati sunt, qui in populo dei ex diuina institutione primum dignitatis gradum obtinuerunt, quid de reliquis omnibus sperandum erit? Simul vero confutantur, qui nobis cum dei verbum pro-ferimus, principum virorum & magnorum antistitum exempla obijciunt. Nec enim quid homines fa-ciant quaeritur, sed quid iuxta dei verbum recte aut secus fiat. Deinde docemur, non prodesse nobis quamuis frequentem scripturae sacrae lectionem, nisi sensus scripturae nobis probè perspectus sit. Legebantur veteri & recepto apud Iudaeos more in omnibus synagogis Mosesi & prophetae. Sed quia pro-priae iustitiae fiducia decepti, finem legis, Iesum Christum, ignorauerunt, nescij scripturas impleue-runt, eum immani audacia occidendo, quem Moses & prophetae saluatorem fore praedixerant. Idem iam seculis aliquot in Papatu accidisse vidimus. Leguntur enim & canuntur ab indoctis monachis & sacrificulis scripturae sacrae. Interim tamen Christus, quem illa tradunt, à plerisq; contemniturs solitur autè & adoratur Antichristus, quem vnicè cauendum esse monent. Nec alia tam foedi erro-ris causa est, quàm quòd Iudaica suorum operum fiducia inflati homines, Christi iustitiā videre non possunt, dum propriam iustitiam stabilire conantur. Vide Rom.10.
