units.tr: First, he says, "those who lived in Jerusalem, and their rulers, condemned him because they did not know him." He therefore says that ignorance was the cause of so great a crime, as also in 1 Cor. 2. But who would think that something is worth imitating when he hears that it was done through ignorance? Nor ought this kind of ignorance to be counted as one that excuses the deed. For they are said at the same time to have been ignorant of the Scriptures, and indeed of those common passages that were customarily read on every sabbath. But it is shameful, and deserving of no pardon, for a priest not to know the Scriptures, when God commands him to seek knowledge of the law from his lips (Mal. 2). Moreover, he takes away from them a large part of any excuse, since they had been urged by Christ himself to search the Scriptures (John 5). Yet Paul teaches elsewhere that the one cause of all their ignorance was this: that they were engaged in reading Moses and the prophets without Christ. For this was the veil that stood in the way, so that they could not look upon the face of Moses, that is, the true sense of the law (2 Cor. 3). Therefore, since they were blind guides (as Christ also calls such men, Matt. 15), they are by no means to be imitated. We are admonished, then, at this point, that we should not always follow the judgments and examples of famous men, but rather that all things should be examined by the rule of Scripture before they are taken as examples. For if those who held the first rank of dignity among the people of God by divine appointment went so disgracefully astray, what can we hope for from all the rest? At the same time, those are refuted who, when we bring forward the word of God, object to us the examples of leading men and great high priests. For the question is not what men do, but what is done rightly or wrongly according to the word of God. Next, we are taught that however frequent our reading of Holy Scripture, it does us no good unless the sense of Scripture has been thoroughly understood by us. Moses and the prophets were read in all the synagogues, by the old and accepted custom among the Jews. But because they were deceived by confidence in their own righteousness, they did not know the end of the law, Jesus Christ; ignorant of the Scriptures, they fulfilled them by killing with monstrous audacity him whom Moses and the prophets had foretold would be the Saviour. We have seen the same thing happen under the Papacy for several centuries now. For the Holy Scriptures are read and sung by unlearned monks and little priests. Meanwhile, Christ, whom those Scriptures set forth, is despised by most people, while Antichrist, whom we are warned above all to beware of, is honoured and worshipped. Nor is there any other cause of so foul an error than that men, puffed up with a Jewish confidence in their own works, cannot see the righteousness of Christ while they try to establish their own righteousness. See Rom. 10.

units.la: Secundo loco diuinae prouidentiae authoritatem allegat, docens ideo neminem Christi morte offendi debere, quòd nihil ille passus sit, quàm quod prophetae, quibus dei consilia & decreta spiritus re-uelauit, passurum praedixerunt. Quare sacerdotes cum scripturas ignorarent, eas tamen impleue-runt, quando Christum damnare & occidere ausi sunt. Nec dubium est, Paulum hoc loco prophetarum oracula adduxisse, quae de Christi passionibus vbiq; extant. Nobis vero obseruandum venit, quòd prophetias ab impijs Christi hostibus impletas fuisse dicit. Hoc enim docet, impios quoq; dei organa esse, quibus vt sua consilia & decreta frequenter expedire consueuit. Nec tamen ideo excusan-tur illi, quòd ea faciant, quae deus fieri vult. Quia enim audaci impietate aduersus deum furunt, & illius consilia impedire, non promouere studient, in illis quidem impietatis culpa haeret, deo autè laus & gloria debetur, qui illorum audacia optimè vti nouit. Simul autem insuperabilis dei potentia & eiusdem infallibilis veritas in eiusmodi exemplis elucet. Si enim illius consilia per hostes quoq; esse-ctum sortiuntur, illa perpetua & aeterna esse oportet. Quare hinc consolationem petant, quorum in-firmitas immanibus principum huius mundi consilijs terreri solet.
units.tr: Secondly, he appeals to the authority of divine providence, teaching that no one should be offended by Christ's death because he suffered nothing other than what the prophets, to whom the Spirit revealed God's counsels and decrees, had foretold he would suffer. Therefore, although the priests did not know the Scriptures, they nevertheless fulfilled them when they dared to condemn and kill Christ. And there is no doubt that Paul here had in mind the prophetic oracles about Christ's sufferings, which are found everywhere. But we must observe that he says the prophecies were fulfilled by impious enemies of Christ. For this teaches that the impious too are instruments through which God is accustomed to carry out his counsels and decrees. Yet they are not excused on the ground that they do what God wills to be done. For since they rage with reckless impiety against God and strive to hinder his counsels rather than advance them, the guilt of impiety clings to them, while praise and glory are due to God, who knows how to make the best use of their recklessness. At the same time, the unconquerable power of God and his infallible truth shine forth in such examples. For if his counsels are carried into effect even through enemies, they must be eternal and unchanging. Hence let those whose weakness is usually terrified by the fierce counsels of the rulers of this world draw consolation from this.

units.la: Caeterum, quia nihilominus obijci poterat, vix credi fas esse, eum à deo saluatorem datum fuisse, qui infami simul & secundum legem execrabili mortis genere sublatus sit: tertio loco, innocentem fuisse probat, nec tam mortis genus quàm causam respici debere, docet. Cum (inquit) nullam causam mortis inuenissent, postularunt à Pilato, vt eum occideret. Potuerunt haec fusius exponi, quod Pau-lum fecisse verisimile est, cum apud eos verba faceret, quibus tota Christi causa suspecta erat. Nobis vero scopum Pauli tenere sufficiat, non debere quenquam infami Christi morte offendi, quam in-iuris sustinuit, cum non raro sanctissimi quiq; indignis & iniustis modis occidi soleant. Interim verum etiam innocentiæ Christi vsus obseruari debet, qui in peccatorum nostrorum expiatione versatur. Quia nisi omnis labis expers fuisset Christus, pro nostris peccatis nunquam satisfacere potuisset. Quomodo enim alios mundaret, qui ipse immundus esset? Aut quomodo obæratus aliquis aliorum debita exolueret? Innocentem ergo Christum esse oportuit, vt mortem, quam ipse non meruerat, pro nobis illum subijsse sciremus. Meminit huius Isaias, quando cap. 53. nostræ redemptionis mysterium explicat. Et eodem illud Pauli pertinet: Deus illum, qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei per illum. 2. Cor. 5. Atqui hæc potissima causa est, quòd in Christi innocentia asserenda tam sæpe euangelistæ versantur. Porrò si Christi morte nemo offendi debet, eò quòd illam innocens perpessus est, eadem ratione indignæ & iniustæ sanctorum cædes neminem debent offendere, quibus sic, vt crucis Christi consortes facti, cum eodem glorificentur. Ro. 8. 2. Tim. 2.
units.tr: Moreover, since it could nonetheless be objected that it can hardly be right to believe that he was given by God as Saviour who was also removed by a death both infamous and, according to the law, accursed, he proves in the third place that he was innocent, and teaches that one must look not so much at the kind of death as at the cause. "When" (he says) "they had found no cause of death, they asked Pilate that he should be put to death." These matters could have been explained at greater length, as Paul probably did when he spoke among them, in words by which the whole cause of Christ was made suspect. For us, however, it is enough to keep to Paul's purpose: no one should be offended by the infamous death of Christ, which he endured unjustly, since the most holy men are often put to death in unworthy and unjust ways. Meanwhile, the true use of Christ's innocence must also be observed, for it bears on the expiation of our sins. For unless Christ had been free from every stain, he could never have made satisfaction for our sins. For how could he cleanse others if he himself were unclean? Or how could someone who is himself in debt pay the debts of others? Christ therefore had to be innocent, so that we might know that he underwent for us a death which he himself had not deserved. Isaiah makes mention of this when, in chapter 53, he explains the mystery of our redemption. And to this belongs also that saying of Paul: "God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him." 2 Cor. 5. Indeed, this is the chief reason why the evangelists so often dwell on the assertion of Christ's innocence. Furthermore, if no one ought to be offended by Christ's death because he suffered it while innocent, by the same reasoning the unworthy and unjust slaughter of the saints ought not to offend anyone, since by it they are glorified together with him, having become partners of Christ's cross. Rom. 8; 2 Tim. 2.

units.la: Quartò, ne quis Christum aduersariorum vi superatum esse putaret, & ideo illum vindicem & saluatorem esse negaret, nihil illum ex infandis sacerdotum conatibus detrimenti accepisse, docet. Consummauerunt quidem illi omnia, quæ de ipso prædicta erant, dum in cruce illum occiderunt, & mortui latus lancea transfixerunt, tandemq; ipsi è cruce sublatum depositerunt in monumentum. At nihil propterea illius gloriæ & potentiæ derogatū fuit. Deus enim (sicuti prædixerat) illum ex mortuis suscitauit, vt iam æternum viuat clarificato suo corpore, cui illi miseram hanc & corruptibilem vitam inuiderunt. Cæterum hic neminem offendat, quòd sepulturam Christi impijs hostibus tribuere videtur, cuius rei honorem fidi Christi discipuli, Iosepho & Nicodemo euangelistæ ascribunt. De eo enim Paulus loquitur, quòd sacerdotes vulgari sepultura non contenti, lapidem monumenti à Pilato obsignari, & milites adhiberi curauerunt, vt violenter in sepulchro detinerent, quem humanis viribus in cruce occisum esse putabant, ignari nimirum, quòd animam suam volens deposuisset. Iohan. 10. Facit autem ad resurrectionis certitudinem & veritatē tam diligens sepulturæ descriptio. Ita enim constat, nullam in hac fraudem committi potuisse, & mendacem fuisse rumorem, quem sacerdotes, multo auro corruptis militibus, de Christi corpore furtim à discipulis sublato, in vulgus sparserunt. Interim generalis consolatio hinc sumi poterit, frustra nimirum aduersus Christum ab impijs hostibus pugnari. Id verò ad illius membra quoq; transferri debet. Petuntur quidem hæc à multis simul & diris hostibus. Vt vt tamen illi furant, nec in corpora quidem, adeoq; nec in pilos fidelium ius habent, nisi id dominus permittat. Quòd si verò vitam eripere possunt, gloriosam tamen corporis resurrectionem & cœlestis vitæ commercium, quod suis Christus præparauit, eripere nunquam potuerunt. Frequenter ergo his meditationibus nosipsos persecutionum tempore consolemur.
units.tr: Fourthly, lest anyone think that Christ was overcome by the force of his adversaries, and therefore deny that he is the avenger and Saviour, he teaches that he suffered no loss from the unspeakable endeavours of the priests. Indeed, they fulfilled all the things that had been foretold about him, when they killed him on the cross and pierced his side, now dead, with a lance, and at last took him down from the cross and laid him in the tomb. Yet nothing was thereby taken away from his glory and power. For God (as he had foretold) raised him from the dead, so that he now lives eternally, with his body glorified, the life which they had grudged him, this wretched and corruptible life. Moreover, let no one be offended that here he seems to ascribe to Christ's impious enemies the burial, a service which the faithful disciples of Christ, Joseph and Nicodemus, the evangelists attribute to themselves. For Paul speaks of the priests who, not content with an ordinary burial, took care that the stone of the tomb should be sealed by Pilate and soldiers posted, so that they might forcibly hold in the sepulchre him whom they believed had been killed on the cross by human strength, plainly unaware that he had laid down his life of his own accord. John 10. Moreover, so careful a description of the burial contributes to the certainty and truth of the resurrection. For it is thus established that no fraud could have been committed in this matter, and that the rumour which the priests spread among the people, after bribing the soldiers with much gold, that the body of Christ had been stolen by the disciples, was a lie. Meanwhile, a general consolation can be drawn from this: plainly, fighting against Christ by impious enemies is in vain. And this must be transferred also to his members. These things are indeed sought by many and fierce enemies at once. However they may rage, they have no right over the bodies, nor even over the hairs of the faithful, unless the Lord permits it. But if they can take away life, they have never been able to take away the glorious resurrection of the body and the fellowship of heavenly life, which Christ has prepared for his own. Therefore let us often console ourselves in times of persecution with these meditations.

units.la: Porrò quia in Christi Iesu resurrectionem Paulus incidit, diligentem illius assertionem insti-tuit, eò quòd per hanc diuina Christi maiestas omnium euidentissime manifestata est, & in eadem (sicut idem apostolus in priori ad Corinth. cap. 15. admonet) præcipua nostræ redemptionis & salutis spes consistit. Et quia hanc à multis negari nouerat, multos quoq; eius rei testes producit. Visus est (inquit) per dies complures his, qui simul ascenderant cum eo à Galilæa Hierosolymas, qui sunt testes eius ad populum. De iis verò loquitur, quos in vltima profectione Christo comites fuisse euangelistæ tradunt, quorum non exiguum numerum fuisse vel ex eo constat, quòd ex illis septuaginta ordinauit Christus, quorum concionibus illi pa-ssim via pararetur. Luc. 10. Quid si eosdem cum quingentis illis fuisse putemus, quibus Christum post resurrectionem apparuisse, idem Paulus author est? 1. Cor. 15. Certè quicunq; fuerint, fides eorum laudari meretur, qua animati, Christo aduersus tot hostes suos testimonium tulerunt. Voluit verò hos apostolos priores sistere, non quòd illud ipsorum dignitas merereretur, sed quòd minus suspecta esset apud infideles illorum fides, & ne solos apostolos resurrectionis Christi testes esse putarent. Mox verò apostolorum quoq; testimonium magna cum authoritate allegat, quibus etiam prophetarum oracula coniungit, de quibus sequenti Sermone dicetur. Interea agnoscere nos conuenit dei bonitatem & fidem, qui tam certa & comperta esse voluit ea, in quibus nostræ salutis spes maximè versatur. Amplectamur ergo constanti fide seruatorem nostrum, qui ex mortuis resuscitatus, mortis tyrannidem fregit, nos in libertatem filiorum dei asseruit, qui est vnigenitus Dei filius, Iesus Christus, Deus verus & æternus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, since Paul came to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, he set out a careful assertion of it, because through it the divine majesty of Christ was most evidently made manifest, and in it (as the same apostle reminds us in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 15) lies the chief hope of our redemption and salvation. And because he knew that many denied this, he also produces many witnesses of the fact. "He was seen" (he says) "for many days by those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are his witnesses to the people." He speaks of those whom the evangelists tell us accompanied Christ on his last journey, a not small number, as is clear even from this, that Christ appointed seventy of them, by whose preaching the way was everywhere prepared for him. Luke 10. Or if we think they were the same as the five hundred to whom, the same Paul is the authority, Christ appeared after the resurrection? 1 Cor. 15. Certainly, whoever they were, their faith deserves praise, since, animated by it, they bore witness to Christ against so many enemies. But he chose to set these men forth first, not because their dignity deserved it, but because their faith would be less suspected among unbelievers, and lest they should think the apostles alone were witnesses of Christ's resurrection. Soon, however, he also cites the testimony of the apostles with great authority, to which he joins the oracles of the prophets, of which we shall speak in the following sermon. Meanwhile it becomes us to acknowledge the goodness and faithfulness of God, who wished those things in which our hope of salvation chiefly rests to be so certain and well attested. Let us therefore embrace with steadfast faith our Saviour, who, raised from the dead, broke the tyranny of death and asserted us into the liberty of the sons of God, who is the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, true and eternal God: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCII.

units.la: Et nos vobis euangelizamus promissionem patribus factam, quòd illam deus impleuerit filijs eorum, nimirum nobis, excitato Iesu, sicut & in Psalmo primo scriptum est: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Quòd autem suscitauerit eum ex mortuis, non amplius reuersurum in corruptionē, sic dixit: Dabo vobis sancta Dauid fidelia. Ideo etiam alibi dicit: Non permittes, vt sanctus tuus videat corruptionē. Nam Dauid quidem, cum suae aetati inseruisset, consilio dei obdormiuit, & appositus est ad patres suos, viditq; corruptionem. Quem autem deus excitauit, non vidit corruptionem.
units.tr: And we preach to you the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to their children, namely to us, by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you." But that he raised him from the dead, never to return to corruption, he said thus: "I will give you the holy and sure mercies of David." Therefore he also says elsewhere: "You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption." For David, indeed, after he had served his own generation by the counsel of God, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers, and saw corruption. But he whom God raised up did not see corruption.

units.la: Dlius Paulus secunda concionis suae, quam in Antiochena synagoga habuit, parte docet Iesum, qui ab apostolis praedicatus esset, esse verum dei filium, & promissum humani generis salvatorem, propter quem deus olim patribus benefecerit. Propter Iudaeos autem causam hanc magna gravitate agit, & quod docere instituit, argumentis firmis & solidis probat. Ostendit enim tum genus Iesu Christi, tum aduentus ipsius modum veterum prophetarum oraculis conuenire. Deinde Iohannis Baptistae testimonium adducit, cuius tanta erat apud Iudaeos authoritas, vt illi contradicere turum non esset. Quia autem illos cruce Christi potissimum offendi noverat, hanc quoq; olim a prophetis praedictam fuisse, nec quicquam Christo derogauisse docet, eo quòd vel invitis hostibus a mortuis resurrexerit. Porro vbi in resurrectionis mentione incidit, hanc multis & diligentissimè asserit, tum quia haec euidentissimum verae diuinitatis in Christo Iesu argumentum est, tum quia ex eadem praecipua nostrae resurrectionis spes dependet. Et primò quidem, ne soli apostoli hanc nouisse & testari viderentur, Galilaeos testes produxit, quibus Christum a mortuis resuscitatum videre contigit. In praesenti verò illorum testimonio apostolorum & prophetarum oracula subijcit.
units.tr: Paul, in the second part of his sermon delivered in the synagogue at Antioch, teaches that Jesus, who had been preached by the apostles, is the true Son of God and the promised Saviour of the human race, on whose account God in former times dealt well with the fathers. For the sake of the Jews he handles this matter with great seriousness, and he proves what he has undertaken to teach by firm and solid arguments. For he shows that both the lineage of Jesus Christ and the manner of his coming agree with the oracles of the ancient prophets. Then he brings forward the testimony of John the Baptist, whose authority among the Jews was so great that they would not contradict him. But since he knew that the Jews were chiefly offended by the cross of Christ, he teaches that this too was foretold long ago by the prophets, and that it detracts nothing from Christ, since he rose from the dead even though his enemies were opposed. Moreover, when he came to the mention of the resurrection, he asserts it with many arguments and with the greatest diligence, both because it is the most evident proof of the true divinity in Jesus Christ, and because the chief hope of our own resurrection depends upon it. And first, lest the apostles alone should seem to have known and testified this, he brought forward Galilean witnesses, to whom it happened to see Christ raised from the dead. Now, in support of their testimony, he adds the oracles of the apostles and the prophets.

units.la: Apostolicum testimonium magna cum authoritate, quasi communi omnium apostolorum nomine loquens allegat. Nos (inquit) vobis euangelizamus promissionem patribus factam, quòd illam deus impleuerit filijs eorum, nimirum nobis, excitato Iesu, &c. Nemini tamen insolens videri debet tanta apostolici dicti gravitas, cum illa vtatur Paulus, tum quòd Christus apostolos testes suos esse voluerat, tum quod ipse & Barnabas praesentem legationem ex peculiari spiritus sancti mandato susceperant, vt initio Capitis dictum est. Legationis ergo commissae mandata diserte simul & digna cum gravitate proponit, quorum haec summa est: Deum in filio suo Iesu Christo omnia ea exhibuisse posteris, quae patribus olim promiserit. Quo sensu ad Corinthios scribens Cap.1. posterioris epistola, ait: Quotquot sunt promissiones dei, per Iesum Christum sunt etiam, & per ipsum sunt Amen, id est, per ipsum impletae sunt. Adeò vt vehementer falli eos constet, qui dei promissionibus quidem & gratia gloriantur, cum Christum Iesum reijciant, in quo vno illae nobis ratae sunt. Eò quòd in illo nobis exhibita sunt, quaecunque humani generis saluti inserviunt. In illo enim iustitia est, quae coram dei tribunali nos defendit. Hic ipse sapientia, sanctificatio, redemptio & sanctificatio nobis factus est a patre. 1.Cor.1. In illo vita est. Iohan.1. Idem via, veritas & lux est. Iohan.14. & 8. In eodem adoptionis spiritus datus est, per quem clamamus, Abba pater. Rom. 8. Per hunc caelestis regni haeredes & consortes facti sumus, nimirum ipso dicente: Ego dispono vobis, sicut mihi disposuit pater, &c. Luc. 22. Item: Volo pater, vt vbi sum ego, ibi quoq; sint quos dedisti mihi. Iohan.17. Quamvis verò haec maxima ex parte in ara crucis impleta sint, Christo iam iam morituro dicente, Consummatum est: maxime tamen in resurrectione horum omnium effectus elucet. Ea enim testatur, mortis aculeum hebetatum, adeoque confractum, & proinde peccatum quoq; exarmatum esse, sicuti multis Paulus docet, 1.Corinth.15.cap. Ideo horum nunc demum mentionem facit apostolus, postquam de resurrectione agere coeperat. Sed priusquam hinc discedamus, quaedam paulo diligentius consyderanda erunt.
units.tr: He cites the apostolic testimony with great authority, speaking as if in the common name of all the apostles: "We," he says, "preach to you the promise made to the fathers, that God has fulfilled it to their children, namely to us, by raising up Jesus," and so on. Yet this solemn statement of the apostle ought to seem in no way arrogant to anyone, since Paul uses it, both because Christ had wanted the apostles to be his witnesses, and because he himself and Barnabas had received the present mission by a special command of the Holy Spirit, as was said at the beginning of this chapter. So he sets out, clearly and with fitting seriousness, the instructions of the mission entrusted to them, the sum of which is this: that God, in his Son Jesus Christ, has exhibited to posterity all those things which he had formerly promised to the fathers. In this sense he writes to the Corinthians in the first chapter of the second epistle: "However many are the promises of God, in him they are also Yes, and in him Amen," that is, in him they have been fulfilled. So much so that it is plain that those greatly err who boast of the promises and grace of God, yet reject Jesus Christ, in whom alone those promises are ratified for us. For in him there has been exhibited to us whatever serves the salvation of the human race. For in him there is righteousness, which defends us before the tribunal of God. He himself was made to us by the Father wisdom, sanctification, redemption and sanctification (1 Cor. 1). In him is life (John 1). He is the same way, truth and light (John 14 and 8). In him the spirit of adoption has been given, by whom we cry, "Abba, Father" (Rom. 8). Through him we have been made heirs and partners of the heavenly kingdom, Christ himself saying: "I appoint to you, as my Father has appointed to me," and so on (Luke 22). Also: "Father, I will that where I am, there also may be those whom you have given me" (John 17). Although these things have been for the most part accomplished on the altar of the cross, Christ being about to die and saying, "It is finished," nevertheless the effect of all these things shines forth most of all in the resurrection. For it attests that the sting of death has been blunted and so broken, and consequently that sin too has been disarmed, as Paul teaches at length in the fifteenth chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians. Therefore the apostle now at last makes mention of these things, after he had begun to speak of the resurrection. But before we depart from here, some things must be considered a little more carefully.

units.la: Primò, nos (inquit) euangelizamus promissionem patribus factam. Non ergo nouae alicuius & antehac inauditae doctrinae authores sunt apostoli, sed eam ipsam salutis rationem tradunt, quae patribus olim diuinitus promissa fuit. Ideo Christus Mosis & prophetarum testimonia allegat. Iohan. 5. Luc.24. Et Petrus supra, omnes prophetas de Christo testari dixit. Asseritur bis nostrae fidei di-
units.tr: First, he says, "we preach the promise made to the fathers." The apostles, therefore, are not the authors of some new doctrine unheard of before, but they hand down that very way of salvation which was once divinely promised to the fathers. Therefore Christ cites the testimonies of Moses and the prophets (John 5; Luke 24), and Peter above said that all the prophets bear witness concerning Christ. Thus the dignity of our faith is affirmed twice over

units.la: I. Apostolorū testimonium de Christo et eius resurrectione.
units.tr: I. The testimony of the apostles concerning Christ and his resurrection.

units.la: Apostolorū doctrina non noua est. gnitas, & salutis per Iesum Christum nobis acquisitæ certitudo monstratur. Præterea discrimen, quod inter nos & veteris Testamenti patres est, hic elucet. Promissa bis fuit salus, quā nos in Christo exhibitam habemus. Illi item futurū expectarunt, quod nos impletum esse credimus. Adhæc venturæ redemptionis typi illis dati fuerunt, quibus fidem suam alerent & exercerent: nobis vero redemptionis peractæ et exhibitæ salutis sigilla dominus instituit. Deniq; nostri oculi vident, et nostræ aures audiunt, quod olim prophetæ & sancti patres videre & audire desyderauerunt. Matth.13. Hæc vero vt fidem nostram confirmant, ita animos nostros ad gratitudinis officia excitare debent, ne exhibitam salutem ingratis animis aspernari videamur, cuius spes & expectatio patres olim inter omnis generis aduersa in officio continuit.
units.tr: The teaching of the apostles is not new, and the certainty of the salvation obtained for us through Jesus Christ is shown. Moreover, the difference which exists between us and the fathers of the Old Testament is brought out here. Salvation was promised to them as well as to us, and we have it exhibited in Christ. They likewise looked for a future thing, which we believe to have been fulfilled. In addition, types of the coming redemption were given to them, by which they might nourish and exercise their faith; but to us the Lord has instituted the seals of the redemption accomplished and the salvation exhibited. Finally, our eyes see and our ears hear what the prophets and holy fathers desired to see and hear (Matt. 13). And these things, as they confirm our faith, so ought they to stir up our minds to the duties of gratitude, lest we seem to scorn with ungrateful minds the salvation exhibited, the hope and expectation of which kept the fathers in duty of old amid every kind of adversity.

units.la: Deinde diuinarum promissionum veritas & fides dei infallibilis hoc loco cernitur. Promissionem enim patribus factam ita posteris impleuit, vt filium potius in mundo inopem & inglorium viuere, tandemq; infami supplicio mori, quàm fidem datam fallere voluerit. Vbi simul alia etiam circumstantia nobis considerandæ veniunt, quas omnes dei promissis & prophetarum oraculis conuenire constat. Nam promisso tempore in carne venit dei filius, quando iam quarta Monarchia florebat, & sceptrum à Iuda ablatū fuerat. Dan.2. Gene.49. Natus item est ex solo muliebri sexu, & matre quidem virgine. Gene.3. Isa.7. Locus natalis fuit, Bethlehem, prophetico oraculo olim prædictus. Mich.5. Miracula per illum edita sunt, qualia sub illius regno euentura Isaias cap.53. dixerat. De passione vero & morte, resurrectione item & ascensione in cœlos, quid attinet dicere, quando in hiis ad literam impleta sunt, quæ Psal.22.41.68. Isa.53.63. &c. habentur? De effectu horum, quem olim quoq; per prophetas deus promiserat, supra diximus. Verissimè ergo Paulus ait, deū impleuisse, quæcunq; olim patribus promissa fuerunt. HINC vero consolationis argumenta in tentationibus petere debent, ne de dei fide in promissa gratia & ope præstanda dubitemus, quem tam fideliter ea præstitisse audimus, quæ non nisi filio suo in mundum & mortis tenebras emisso præstari poterant.
units.tr: Next, the truth of the divine promises and the infallible faithfulness of God are seen here. For he so fulfilled to posterity the promise made to the fathers that he would rather allow his Son to live in the world poor and without glory, and at last to die by an infamous punishment, than wish to break the faith he had given. Here other circumstances also come before us for consideration, which it is agreed all agree with the promises of God and the oracles of the prophets. For at the promised time the Son of God came in the flesh, when the fourth monarchy was already flourishing and the sceptre had been taken from Judah (Dan. 2; Gen. 49). He was also born from the female sex alone, and indeed of a virgin mother (Gen. 3; Isa. 7). The place of his birth was Bethlehem, foretold long before by a prophetic oracle (Mic. 5). Miracles were performed through him, such as Isaiah in chapter 53 had said would happen under his reign. As for the passion and death, and likewise the resurrection and ascension into heaven, what need is there to speak, since in these things those words are fulfilled literally which are found in Psalms 22, 41, 68, Isaiah 53, 63, and so on? Of the effect of these things, which God also long before had promised through the prophets, we have spoken above. Paul therefore rightly says that God has fulfilled whatever was formerly promised to the fathers. FROM THIS, indeed, they ought to seek arguments of consolation in temptations, so that we may not doubt the faithfulness of God in the grace and help he has promised to supply, since we hear that he has so faithfully supplied those things which could be supplied only by his Son sent into the world and into the darkness of death.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reuertamur, qui quod tanta cum authoritate de Christo dixerat, prophetarum oraculis confirmat. Inter quæ primum locum Dauidi tribuit, quem Psalmo primo (qui hodie secundus numeratur) de Christo vaticinatum esse, ait. Atqui vnum duntaxat Psalmi versum adducit, ita tamen, vt totum Psalmum ipsis in mentem revocet, quem licet quidam de Dauide exponere conentur, verè tamen manifestam de Christi regno prophetiam continet, cum pleraq; eiusmodi sint, vt nullo modo in Dauidem referri possint. Prædicit enim ex spiritus suggestione propheta, Christum multos simul et truculentos hostes sensurum, qui regnum ipsius euertere, omnemq; eius authoritatem conuellere cupiant. Irritos tamen illorum conatus fore, eò quòd omnibus illis superior futurus sit Christus. Causa vero omnium allegatur dei decretum, dicentis: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te. Postula à me, daboq; gentes vt sint hæreditas tua, &c. Locum vero hunc de Christi resurrectione exponit Paulus, eò quòd per hanc deus illum publice filium suū declarauerit, cum maximè aduersus eum impia hostium conspiratio fureret. Nam paulò ante blasphemas illas voces audiuerat: Si filius dei es, descende de cruce. Si rex Israel est, descendat nunc de cruce, & credemus ei, &c. Imò diris mortis terroribus circumuentus clamauerat: Deus meus, deus meus, cur me deseruisti? Nec multò post ita sepulchro inclusus est, vt Romanus præses, Pilatus, Imperatoriæ authoritatis nomine illius operculum obsignaret, & custodes adhiberet milites, qui ipsius resurrectionem impedirent. Quis vero tunc filium dei putauisset, in quem tantum impijs hostibus licuerat? Sed illo ipso die eum genuit deus, id est, filium suum esse declarauit, quem alioqui ab æterno genuerat, iam vero deseruisse & abdicauisse videbatur. Cum enim impij hostes dixissent: Si filius dei es, descende de cruce: non quidem de cruce illum descendere voluit, sed quod longè maius erat, fecit, ex mortuis nimirum excitando illum, vt ex proprijs verbis impios illos iudicaret, & Iesum hunc reuera filium suum esse ostenderet. Nobis vero præter hæc obseruandum venit, quòd Iesu Christi regnum simul & diuinam maiestatem ex resurrectione cumprimis euincit ac asserit spiritus sanctus. Nam alibi quoq; Paulus, de Christo loquens, ait: Qui declaratus fuit filius dei cum potentia, secundum spiritum sanctificationis, ex eo quòd resurrexit è mortuis. Rom.1. Nam morte deuicta palam omnibus innotuit, diabolum quoq;, qui mortis habebat imperium, deuictum esse, quæ victoria non humanarum virium, sed diuinæ maiestatis opus erat. Debet vero hoc ad membra Christi extendi. Quia enim & qui sanctificat & qui sanctificantur ex uno sunt, nostra quoq; gloria, quæ filijs Dei debetur, in resurrectione demum elucebit. Clamamus quidem nunc quoq; Abba pater, & arrhabonem salutis in cordibus nostris gestamus, spiritum sanctum, & nunc filij Dei sumus, sed nondum apparuit quod futuri sumus. Scimus autem, quòd cùm apparuerit Christus nouissimo die, similes ei erimus. 1. Ioan. 3. Quæ causa est quod Christus illum diem Matth. 19. regenerationem vocat: non quòd tunc demum filij Dei efficiamur, sed quòd eo die filij Dei esse declarabuntur, qui in præsenti seculo à Deo derelicti, imò Deo inuisi putantur. Vide Sap. 5. Petamus hinc consolationem in aduersis contra mundi iniqua de nobis iudicia, & simul abiecta terrestris gloriæ cupiditate cœlestem & futuram gloriam affectemus.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who confirms by the oracles of the prophets what he had said about Christ with such authority. Among these he first assigns the place to David, whom he says prophesied of Christ in the first Psalm (which today is numbered second). But he adduces only a single verse of the Psalm, yet in such a way that he calls the whole Psalm to mind. Although some try to explain it of David, it nevertheless contains a clear prophecy of the kingdom of Christ, since most of its statements are such that they can in no way be referred to David. For the prophet, by the prompting of the Spirit, foretells that Christ will face many and fierce enemies, who desire to overthrow his kingdom and to tear down all his authority. Yet their attempts will come to nothing, because Christ will be superior to them all. The cause of all this is stated to be the decree of God, who says: "You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give the nations as your inheritance," and so on. Paul explains this place of Christ's resurrection, because by it God openly declared him his Son, when the impious conspiracy of his enemies raged most against him. For shortly before they had heard those blasphemous words: "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him," and so on. Indeed, beset by the dreadful terrors of death, he had cried out: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And not long afterwards he was so shut up in the sepulchre that Pilate, the Roman governor, in the name of imperial authority sealed the stone and set soldiers as guards to prevent his resurrection. Who then would have thought him the Son of God, when the impious enemies had been permitted so much against him? But on that very day God begot him, that is, declared him to be his Son, whom he had otherwise begotten from eternity, and who now seemed to have been forsaken and disowned by him. For when the impious enemies had said, "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross," God did not indeed want him to come down from the cross, but he did what was far greater: namely, by raising him from the dead, so that from their own words he might judge those impious men and show that this Jesus was truly his Son. Besides these things, it must be observed for us that the Holy Spirit above all proves and asserts from the resurrection both the kingdom of Jesus Christ and his divine majesty. For elsewhere also Paul, speaking of Christ, says: "who was declared the Son of God with power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by his resurrection from the dead" (Rom. 1). For by death being overcome, it became openly known to all that the devil too, who held the power of death, had been overcome; and this victory was the work not of human strength but of divine majesty. But this ought to be extended to the members of Christ. For since both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of one, our glory too, which is owed to the sons of God, will at length shine forth in the resurrection. We indeed now also cry, "Abba, Father," and we carry the pledge of salvation in our hearts, the Holy Spirit, and now we are sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know, however, that when Christ appears on the last day, we shall be like him (1 John 3). This is why Christ calls that day the regeneration (Matt. 19): not because we then first become sons of God, but because on that day those are declared to be sons of God who in the present age are thought to be forsaken by God, and even hated by God. See Wisdom 5. Let us seek from this consolation in adversities against the unjust judgements of the world concerning us, and at the same time, having cast off the desire for earthly glory, let us aspire to the heavenly and future glory.

units.la: Secundo loco Isaiam producit, apud quem Deus Cap. 55. de beneficijs, quæ per Christum collatu- rum erat, differens inter alia ait: Feriam vobiscum fœdus sempiternum, misericordias Dauidis fideles. Porrò misericordiæ vocem Paulus, vulgarem Græcorum interpretationem secutus, per Sancti vocabulum reddidit, nec inepte, cùm Christum intelligat, quo vno omnes promissiones, Dauidi & patribus olim factæ, nituntur. Sensus ergo est: Dabo vobis sanctum illum, Saluatorem nimirum, quem Dauidi olim pollicitus suam, & in quo ille omnem spem & fiduciam collocatam habuit. Locum verò totum ad Christi resurrectionem refert, ex fœderis perpetuitate argumentum ducens, quasi dicat: Deus cum Dauide æternum fœdus sanxiit, idemq; sempiternum fore posteris quoq; promisit. Atqui fœdus illud Christo innixi certum est, quem patriam Dauidis filium scriptura vocant. Ergo Christum quoque æternum & immortalem esse oportet. Nec enim æternum esse posset fœdus illud, nisi æternus & incorruptibilis esset is, in quo illud sanctum est, & qui vnicus est illius mediator. Sequitur ergo, necessarium fuisse, vt ex mortuis resurgeret Christus, semel q; resuscitatus, nullam posthac corruptionem subiret. EST autem obiter obseruandum, quòd semel duntaxat mori debuit Christus. Inde enim sequitur, semel duntaxat illum pro peccatis immolari potuisse, quando absq; sanguinis effusione peccatorum remissio nulla est. Vide quæ de hac re copiosè disputantur ad Hebr. 9. & 10. cap. quibus Missæ sacrificium ita euertitur, vt mirum sit, aliquem inter Christianos tam perfrictæ frontis esse, vt illud tueri & stabilire audeat.
units.tr: Secondly, he brings forward Isaiah, in whom God, in chapter 55, speaking among other things about the benefits that were to be conferred through Christ, says: "I will make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David." Paul, following the common Greek translation, rendered the word "mercies" by the word "holy", and not inappropriately, since he understands Christ, on whom alone all the promises made to David and the fathers rest. The sense, therefore, is: I will give you that holy one, namely the Saviour, whom he once promised to David and in whom David placed all his hope and confidence. Paul refers the whole passage to Christ's resurrection, drawing an argument from the perpetuity of the covenant, as if he said: God sanctioned an eternal covenant with David and promised that it would be everlasting for his posterity too. But that covenant certainly rests on Christ, whom the Scriptures call the son of David. Therefore Christ too must be eternal and immortal. For that covenant could not be eternal unless he in whom it is holy, and who is its only mediator, were eternal and incorruptible. It follows that it was necessary for Christ to rise from the dead, and, once raised, to undergo no corruption afterwards. It is to be observed in passing that Christ had to die only once. For it follows from this that he could be offered for sins only once, since without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins. See what is disputed at length on this matter in Hebrews chapters 9 and 10, by which the sacrifice of the Mass is so overturned that it is astonishing anyone among Christians should have such a brazen face as to dare to defend and uphold it.

units.la: Tertium testimonium ex Psalmo 16. allegat, quo Petrum quoq; in prima concione Hierosolymis vsum esse vidimus, & eodem plane modo. Simul enim euincit, locum illum non de Dauide, sed solo Christo intelligi posse. Ita enim argumentatur: Dauidis vox est, Non permittes, vt sanctus tuus videat corruptionem. Dauidem verò aliorum hominum more vitæ suæ cursum absoluisse, & postquam suæ ætati inseruiit obdormiuisse, & in puluerem abijsse constat. Non ergo de seipso Dauid loquitur, sed de Christo, quem ex se nascituram esse nouerat. Is enim priusquam corruptionem subiret, tertio die excitatus, gloriosò corpore resurrexit. Ita verò Paulus omnia Christi mysteria paucis verbis comprehendit, eumq; esse docuit, de quo prophetarum oracula passim extent. Porrò priusquam dicendi finem faciamus, obseruemus primò locutionem, qua Dauidem suæ ætati vel suo seculo inseruijsse dicit. Ea nos nostri officij simul & fortis admonet, docens, exigi à nobis mutuæ charitatis officia, quoad in hoc mundo viuimus, postquam verò vita hac exempti sumus, nos omni officio erga quosvis homines defunctos esse, nec quicquam à nobis vlterius requiri. Nihil ergo defunctis commercij est cum viuentibus, vt rectè apud prophetam sancti dicant: Abraham nos non cognoscit, nec Israel nouit nos, &c. Isa. 63. Confugiatur bis intercessio & invocatio Diuorum, quorum beatitudo integra esse non posset, si nostris ærumnis illi occuparentur. Arguuntur item apparitiones spirituum siue animarum ex quibus ingentem quæstum bucufq; fecerunt, qui purgatorium ignem commenti sunt. Deinde Dauidis mortem ita describit Paulus, vt simul quæ omnium nostrum in morte fit conditio, exponat. Nam primò illum consilio Dei obdormiuisse ait. Non ergo ab incertis fortunæ euentibus aut hominum voluntate mortis nostræ, hora dependet, sed in Dei consilio continetur, qui vt capillos nostros, ita etiam vitæ nostræ dies numeratos habet. Matth. 10. Atqui vnum hoc aduersus pericula & mortis terrores consolari poterat. Deinde illum obdormiuisse dicit. Somnum enim Christus quoque mortem appellat, eo quòd in hac omnibus vitæ molestijs defuncti, sub futuræ resurrectionis spe requiescimus à laboribus nostris. Apoc. 14. Tertiò, ad patres suos collectus esse dicitur, quæ locutio in scripturis frequens est, & certas defunctorum animabus sedes destinatas esse docet, de quibus in diuitis epulonis & Lazari parabola Christus quoq; mentionem facit, Luc. 16. Colliguntur enim inter beatos piorum animæ, quarum sedem Abrahami sinum aliquando scriptura vocat. Rursum vero apud inferos conueniunt impij & quotquot terrorem suum posuerunt in terra viuentium. Ezechielis trigesimo secundo Isa.14.30. Postremo corruptionem vidit Dauides. Ea enim Dei irreuocabilis sententia est, vt qui ex puluere originem ducimus, in puluerem conuertamur: idque nostrae salutis ratio exigit. Oportet enim vt corruptibile hoc induat incorruptibilitatem, & mortale hoc immortalitate donetur, eo quod affectibus obnoxia caro regni Dei hereditatem consequi non potest.1.Cor.15. Magna ergo nobis in ipsa corruptione spes repostia est, quam futurae regenerationis & gloriosae resurrectionis initium esse scimus. Atqui hanc vnam sanctorum spem fuisse, vnius Iobis verba, quae cap.19.extant, abunde docent. Eademigitur nos quoq; consolemur, nec mortem horreamus, post quam filio Dei, Iesu Christo, conformes reddamur: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Third, he cites a testimony from Psalm 16, which we saw Peter also using in his first sermon at Jerusalem, and in exactly the same way. For he shows at the same time that this passage can be understood not of David but of Christ alone. He argues thus: the words are David's: "You will not permit your holy one to see corruption." But it is established that David finished the course of his life like other men, and after serving his own generation fell asleep and passed into dust. Therefore David is not speaking of himself, but of Christ, whom he knew would be born from his own line. For Christ, before undergoing corruption, was raised on the third day and rose in a glorious body. Thus Paul comprehends all the mysteries of Christ in few words, and teaches that he is the one of whom the oracles of the prophets are found everywhere. Before we make an end of speaking, let us observe first the expression by which he says David served his own age, or his generation. This reminds us both of our duty and of our limits, teaching that the duties of mutual love are required of us as long as we live in this world; but once we are released from this life, we have fulfilled every duty towards any men who have died, and nothing further is required of us. Therefore the dead have no dealings with the living, so that the saints rightly say in the prophet: "Abraham does not know us, nor does Israel acknowledge us," etc., Isa. 63. Here intercession and the invocation of the saints are refuted, since their blessedness could not be complete if they were occupied with our troubles. Likewise the apparitions of spirits or souls are refuted, by which those who invented the fire of purgatory have made enormous profit up to now. Then Paul describes David's death in such a way as at the same time to set out the condition of all of us in death. For first he says David fell asleep by the counsel of God. Therefore the hour of our death depends not on the uncertain chances of fortune or the will of men, but is contained in God's counsel, who has our days numbered just as he has our hairs. Matt. 10. Yet this alone could console us against dangers and the terrors of death. Next he says David fell asleep. For Christ too calls death sleep, because in death we are released from all the troubles of this life, and under the hope of future resurrection we rest from our labours. Rev. 14. Thirdly, David is said to have been gathered to his fathers, an expression frequent in Scripture, which teaches that fixed seats have been appointed for the souls of the dead. Christ too makes mention of these in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Luke 16. For the souls of the pious are gathered among the blessed, whose seat Scripture once calls Abraham's bosom. Again, the wicked, and all who have placed their terror in the land of the living, gather together in the underworld. Ezek. 32. Isa. 14.30. Lastly, David saw corruption. For this is God's irrevocable sentence, that we who derive our origin from dust should be turned back into dust, and the reason of our salvation requires it. For it is necessary that this corruptible put on incorruptibility, and that this mortal be clothed with immortality, since flesh subject to passions cannot obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of God. 1 Cor. 15. Great hope, therefore, is laid up for us in corruption itself, which we know to be the beginning of the future regeneration and glorious resurrection. That this was the one hope of the saints, the words of Job alone, which are found in chapter 19, abundantly teach. Let us therefore console ourselves likewise, and not dread death, after which we are made conformable to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIII.

units.la: Notum ergo sit vobis, viri fratres, quòd per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur, & ab omnibus, a quibus non potuistis in lege Moysis iustificari, in hoc omnis qui credit, iustificatur. Videte igitur, ne super veniat vobis, quod dictum est in prophetis: Videte contemptores & admiramini, & euanescite: quia opus ego facio in diebus vestris, cui non credetis, si quis enarret vobis.
units.tr: Let it therefore be known to you, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and that everyone who believes in him is justified from all those things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. See to it, then, that what was said in the prophets does not come upon you: "Look, you scorners, and be astonished, and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work which you will not believe even if someone declares it to you."

units.la: Postquam Diuus Paulus perspicue & diligenter demonstrauit, Iesum Christum verum esse Dei filium & olim promissum humani generis saluatorem, simulq; omnia illa amouit, quae Iudeos quò minus Christum amplecterentur, impedire poterant, tandem praesenti loco concionem suam concludit, qui duabus partibus absoluitur. Primò enim beneficia, quae nobis in Christo conferuntur, edisserit, si forte horum consyderatio auditorum animos verae fidei studio inflammare posset. Deinde horrendum Dei iudicium illis ob oculos statuit, quo vt filij & verbi sui contemptum vindicaturus sit, si increduli & incurabiles esse pergant.
units.tr: After the blessed Paul had clearly and carefully shown that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God and the Saviour of the human race promised long ago, and at the same time had removed all those obstacles that could keep the Jews from embracing Christ, he finally brings his sermon to a close here. The close has two parts. First he sets out the benefits conferred on us in Christ, in the hope that considering them might inflame the minds of his hearers with zeal for true faith. Then he sets before their eyes the dreadful judgment of God, by which he will avenge the contempt shown to his Son and his Word if they persist in unbelief and remain incurable.

units.la: Primum graui verborum pondere absoluit, dicens: Notum ergo sit vobis, viri fratres, quod per Iesum hunc, quem hucusq; praedicaui, vobis remissio peccatorum nuntiatur, &c. Nec temere particula haec: Notum sit vobis praemittitur. Ea enim illos attentos reddere, & ad diligentem eorum, quae sequuntur, consyderationem excitare voluit. Ita enim docet, conueniens & necessarium esse, vt Christum nouerint, quicunq; saluari cupiunt. In cognitione enim hac potissimam salutis nostrae partem vt sari, ipse Christus author est, cum ait: Haec est vita aeterna (pater) vt te cognoscant solum verum Deum, & quem tu misisti, Iesum Christum. Iohan. 17. Deinde cum peculiari Dei consilio factum sit, vt per euangelij praedicationem Christi cognitio per totum terrarum orbem vulgaretur, non possunt non improbi & ingrati diuinae bonitatis contemptores censeri, quicunq; diuinitus oblatam salutis nostrae gratiam aspernantur. Confutantur igitur hoc loco, qui fidei causam nihil ad se pertinere dicunt, & voluntaria ignorantia in salutis negotio hallucinantur. Solent illi ferè Christi verbis abuti, quibus eum seruum grauius vapulaturum dicit, qui notam sibi voluntatem heri sui facere neglexerit. Luc. 17. Ita enim se coram Dei tribunali excusari posse existimant, si omnium fidei & salutis nostrae mysteriorum plane rudes & imperiti sint. At simul cogitandum erat, minime aequum & conueniens esse, vt qui Dei serui haberi & dici volunt, heri sui voluntatem ignorent, & eandem discere detrectent. Vult dominus, vt patresfamilias inter domesticos suos de ipsius praeceptis & operibus differant: & nos eo praetextu nos excusari putabimus, si volentes ignoremus, quae scriptis simul & viua voce nobis Deus reuelat. Quin Christum audimus, qui Dei verbum eos audire testatur, qui ex Deo nati sunt. Iohan. 8. Et Iacobus eos, quibus sapientia deest, ad preces relegat, vt illam a patre luminum impetrent. Iac. 1. Nec exempla desunt cum Dauidis tum aliorum sanctorum, quos in toto hoc studio caelestis sapientiae consequendae flagrantissimos fuisse constat. Vide. Psal.25.119.&c.
units.tr: He begins the first part with a weighty statement: "Let it therefore be known to you, brothers, that through this Jesus, whom I have preached to you until now, the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you," and so on. The phrase "let it be known to you" is not placed here carelessly. Paul wanted it to make his hearers attentive and to stir them to careful consideration of what follows. For it teaches that it is fitting and necessary that all who desire to be saved should come to know Christ. Christ himself is the author of this, since in the knowledge of him lies the chief part of our salvation, as he says: "This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17). Moreover, since by God's special counsel the knowledge of Christ is spread throughout the whole world by the preaching of the gospel, those who reject the grace of salvation offered to us by God can hardly be counted anything but wicked and ungrateful despisers of divine goodness. So this passage refutes those who say that the cause of faith is nothing to them, and who go astray in the matter of salvation through wilful ignorance. Such people commonly misuse the words of Christ, in which he says that the servant who neglects to do his master's will, though he knows it, will be beaten severely (Luke 12). They think they can excuse themselves before God's judgment seat if they are completely raw and unskilled in all the mysteries of faith and our salvation. But at the same time it should be considered that it is by no means fair or fitting that those who wish to be called and treated as God's servants should not know their master's will and should refuse to learn it. The Lord wishes the heads of households to speak among their household about his precepts and works; and shall we think ourselves excused on this pretext, if we willingly remain ignorant of what God reveals to us both in writing and by the living voice? Indeed we hear Christ, who testifies that those who are born of God hear God's word (John 8). And James sends those who lack wisdom to prayer, that they may obtain it from the Father of lights (James 1). Nor are examples lacking, both of David and of other saints, who are known to have burned most ardently in this whole pursuit of heavenly wisdom. See Psalms 25 and 119, etc.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui paucis verbis omnium beneficiorum Dei, quae in Christo nobis conferuntur, summam comprehendit, dicens: Per hunc vobis remissio peccatorum annuntiatur. Nam peccatorum remissione omnia ea completur, quae nostrae saluti seruiunt. Constat enim propter peccata Deum nobis iratsci, & propter illa nos a gratia, spiritu & regno Dei excludi. Vnde rursum colligitur.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who in a few words sums up all the benefits of God conferred on us in Christ, saying: "Through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you." For in the forgiveness of sins all those things are fulfilled that serve our salvation. For it is plain that God is angry with us on account of our sins, and that on account of them we are shut out from God's grace, Spirit and kingdom. From this it follows again:

units.la: Christi cognitio ad salutem consequendam necessaria est.
units.tr: The knowledge of Christ is necessary for obtaining salvation.

units.la: Remissio peccatorum in Christo confertur. gitur, non posse non Deum illis propitium esse, quorum peccata remissa & sublata sunt: ijsdem ergo spiritum suum largitur, quo regenerati & filij ipsius facti, cœlestem regni sui hæreditatem adeunt. Obseruemus autem, Paulum breui hac sententia plenissime veram salutis cognitionem tradere, quæ si in certa capita distinguatur, perspicua & facillima perceptu apparebit. Primum inter hæc est, vt nos peccatores esse intelligamus, & grauibus debitis coram Deo obstrictos: quod ex eo patet, quod remissionis peccatorum passim scripturæ meminerunt. Eadem etiam nos vbiq; peccati arguunt, & natura corruptos esse docent. Moses ex Dei ore, humani cordis figmenta ab ineunte ætate praua esse testatur. Gen.8. Idem legem speculi instar proponit, vt in illo corruptionem suam agnoscat caro, quæ alioqui sibi ipsi blandiri consueuit. In libro Iobs neminem, qui ex muliere natus est, mundum esse, scribitur. Dauid se in peccatis conceptum & genitum esse fatetur. Psal. 51. Solomon iustum quoq; septies in die cadere scribit. Et apud Isaiam fatentur fideles, iustitias quoq; nostras propter inhærentem illis ex carnis contagio labem & concurrentes affectus, coram Deo abominabiles & instar sordidi panni siue centonis esse. Isa.64. Atqui omnium horum nos ipse Christus admonet, dum orare docet: Remitte nobis debita nostra. Superuacanea enim esset illa oratio, nisi debitis maximis grauaremur. Necesse autem est hoc fundamentum in salutis cognitione iaci, eo quod de hac homo felicitus esse non potest, nisi se corruptum & perditum esse intelligat. Sed alterum accedat oportet, nempe vt nobis gratuita remissione opus esse intelligamus. Quia enim peccato æternam mortem meruimus, nec quicquam ex nobis ipsis boni habemus, adhæc corrupta sunt & imperfecta quæcunq; à nobis in speciem bene fiunt: ex gratia nobis remissio contingat, necesse est. Admonet nos huius parabola, quæ Matth. 18. habetur. Et hanc remissionem inter fidei articulos profitemur, quando nos remissionem peccatorum credere dicimus, nec aliquam allegamus, quæ ex nostris operibus dependeat, satisfactionem. Ter tio eum, in quo gratia hæc confertur, nouisse conuenit. Est is vnus & solus Christus, in quo patri com placuit, quia ille nostras iniquitates in se transtulit, easq; sanguinis sui merito in ara crucis expiauit, vnde alibi Paulus illum nobis à Deo patre iustitiam, satisfactionem & sanctificationem, adeoq; peccatum factum esse dicit, vt nos per illum iustificaremur. 1. Cor. 1. 2. Cor. 5. Hoc ipsum Iohannes Baptista docuit, quando illum agnum Dei esse dixit, qui mundi peccata tollat. Iohan. 1. Quarto modum, quo Christus hic nosterfit, tenere oportet: quem non obscure Paulus docet, quando peccatorum remissionem nobis per Christum annunciari ait. Inde enim colligitur, fide illum recipi, quando non aliud medium est, quo annuntiatum siue prædicatum verbum apprehendi queat. Apertius tamen hoc in sequentibus exprimit, dicens: In hoc omnis, qui credit, iustificatur. Quo referri debent, quæcunque de fide passim in scripturis habentur, maxime quod in vltimo suo discessu discipulis Christus mandat. Nam apud Lucam 24. cap. in suo nomine pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum prædicare iubet. Alibi vero mox subiicit: Quicunque crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Mar.16. Atqui omnia hæc breui sententia Paulus complexus est, quæ in epistolis ad Romanos, Galatas, Ephesios & alios complures fusissime exponit. Quorum si quis breuiorem summam & compendium habere vellit, illud Pauli audiat: Omnes peccauerunt, & destituuntur gloria Dei. Iustificantur autem gratis per illius gratiam, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, per fidem, interueniente ipsius sanguine, &c. Rom.3.
units.tr: Therefore God cannot but be favourable to those whose sins have been forgiven and taken away; to them he gives his Spirit, by which they are born again, become his sons, and enter upon the heavenly inheritance of his kingdom. We should observe, moreover, that Paul in this brief sentence delivers most fully the true knowledge of salvation, which, if it is divided into its particular heads, will appear clear and very easy to grasp. The first of these is that we understand ourselves to be sinners, bound by grave debts before God. This is evident from the fact that Scripture everywhere makes mention of the forgiveness of sins. The same Scripture also convicts us of sin in every place and teaches that we are corrupted by nature. Moses, speaking from God's mouth, testifies that the figments of the human heart are evil from earliest youth (Genesis 8). He also sets forth the law as a mirror, so that in it the flesh may recognise its corruption, which otherwise is accustomed to flatter itself. In the book of Job it is written that no one born of a woman is clean. David confesses that he was conceived and born in sins (Psalm 51). Solomon also writes that the righteous man falls seven times a day. And in Isaiah the faithful confess that even our righteousnesses, because of the stain of the flesh's contagion that clings to them and the concurrent passions, are abominable before God and like a filthy rag or patchwork (Isaiah 64). Christ himself reminds us of all these things when he teaches us to pray: "Forgive us our debts." For that prayer would be superfluous if we were not burdened with great debts. Now this foundation must necessarily be laid in the knowledge of salvation, because a man cannot be happy about it unless he understands that he is corrupt and lost. But a second point must be added, namely that we understand we need forgiveness given freely. For since by sin we have deserved eternal death, and since we have nothing good of our own, and since whatever we do that seems good is corrupt and imperfect, forgiveness must come to us from grace. The parable found in Matthew 18 reminds us of this. And we profess this forgiveness among the articles of faith when we say that we believe in the forgiveness of sins, and we allege no satisfaction that depends on our works. Thirdly, it is fitting to know the one in whom this grace is conferred. He is the one and only Christ, in whom the Father is well pleased, because he took our iniquities upon himself and expiated them by the merit of his blood on the altar of the cross. Hence elsewhere Paul says that God the Father made him for us righteousness, satisfaction and sanctification, and indeed sin, so that we might be justified through him (1 Cor. 1; 2 Cor. 5). John the Baptist taught this very thing when he said that he is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1). Fourthly, we must hold to the manner in which Christ becomes ours, which Paul teaches not obscurely when he says that the forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to us through Christ. For it follows from this that he is received by faith, since there is no other means by which the word proclaimed or preached can be apprehended. Paul expresses this more openly in what follows, saying: "Everyone who believes in him is justified." To this must be referred all that is said about faith throughout the Scriptures, especially what Christ commands his disciples at his final departure. For in Luke 24 he bids them preach repentance and the forgiveness of sins in his name. And elsewhere he immediately adds: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16). Now Paul has embraced all these things in this brief sentence, which he expounds at great length in the letters to the Romans, Galatians, Ephesians and several others. If anyone wishes to have a shorter summary and compendium of them, let him hear that saying of Paul: "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. They are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, through faith, by his blood interposed," and so on (Rom. 3).

units.la: Quia vero nouerat Paulus, Iudæos, quibus cum illi res erat, iustificationem legi & operibus, quæ secundum legem fiunt, tribuere, & hanc maximam illis esse fidei & salutis remoram, illorum obiectiones præoccupans ait: Et ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis in lege Mosis iustificari, in hoc omnis qui credit iustificatur. Quibus verbis Legem cum Christo conferens, ita huic iustificationis nostræ laudem & gloriam vendicat, vt hanc legi nullo modo tribui debere testetur. Lex enim (inquit) non potuit iustificare ab omnibus, peccatis nimirum, quibus tamen liberantur, quicunq; Christum vera fide apprehenderint. Nec ideo temeritatis Paulus accusari debet, quasi nimis impudenter Legis authoritatem conuellat. Vere enim hoc illum dixisse patebit, si ipsam Legem propius inspiciamus. Potest hæc duabus partibus comprehendi, quarum altera de virtutibus aut bonis operibus est, altera Ceremonias complectitur. Priori moralia simul & politica præcepta includimus, quorum omnium breue compendium Decalogus exhibet. Quod si hunc inspiciamus, patebit quidem quid à nobis Deus exigat, quid illi, quid proximo, quid deniq; nobismetipsis debeamus. Simul vero nostra patebit infirmitas & tor
units.tr: Since Paul knew that the Jews, with whom he was dealing, attributed justification to the law and to works done according to the law, and that this was the greatest obstacle to their faith and salvation, he anticipated their objections and said: "And from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses, in this everyone who believes is justified." By setting the Law against Christ in these words, he claims for Christ the praise and glory of our justification and declares that it must in no way be ascribed to the Law. For the Law (he says) could not justify from all sins, from which, nevertheless, all who have laid hold of Christ by true faith are set free. Nor should Paul be accused of rashness, as if he overthrew the authority of the Law too boldly. He will be shown to have spoken truly if we look more closely at the Law itself. It can be divided into two parts: one concerns virtues or good works, the other contains the ceremonies. The first part includes both the moral and the civil precepts, of which the Decalogue offers a brief summary. If we look at it, it will indeed be clear what God requires of us, what we owe to him, to our neighbour and finally to ourselves. But at the same time our weakness and corruption will be clear, by which we are depraved and not only fail to obey the divine law but cannot even obey it. For who among the whole race of mortals is able to subject his mind and all the affections of the flesh to obedient faith, as God demands? What else, then, is the Law than a mirror, in which the corruption of our nature is exposed and our sins, both public and secret, are brought to light?

units.la: Lex non potest iustificare. ruptio, qua depravati, divinæ legi non modò non obedimus, sed ne possumus quidē obedire. Quis enim est ex toto mortalium genere, qui animum simul & omnes carnis affectus, sicuti Deus exigit, obedientiæ fidei subijcere queat? Quid ergo aliud Lex, quàm speculum est, quo nostræ naturæ corruptio arguitur, & peccata cùm publica tùm occulta in lucem protrahuntur? Quòd si verò ad Ceremonias transeamus, quibus iustitiam suam Iudæi olim metiebantur, has quoq; inanes esse, & illis nos accusaripo-tius, quàm iustificari, apparebit. Quid enim Circuncisio, in genitali membro facta, aliud docet, quàm generationis nostræ principia corrupta esse, nosq; regeneratione opus habere? Quid sacrificia quotidiana & annua? quid sanguinis aspersiones? quid ablutiones crebræ? quid certi expiationum & purificationum ritus, aliud quàm nos expiatione & purgatione indigere docebant? Num verò in ijsdem purificatio vera consistebat? Minimè gentium. Nam apud prophetam illorum manus sanguinibus totas pollutas esse, dominus clamat, qui tamen in his exercendis assidui erant, Isa.1. Et alibi: Num comesturus sum (inquit) sanguinem taurorum, & sanguinem hircorum bibiturus? Psal.50. Et David atrocissimi facinoris conscientia exagitatus ait: Hostijs non delectaris, alioqui eas obtulissem, holocaustum non vis, &c. Imò in promissi salvatoris sanguinem & meritum respiciens, orat: Lava me plurimùm ab iniquitate mea, & à peccato meo munda me. Expia me hyssopo, & mundus ero: lava me, & niue ero candidior. Libera me de sanguinibus Deus, Deus salutis meæ, &c. 51. Unde suum illud dictum apostolus haussisse videtur: Non potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata. Heb.10. Verissimè ergo Paulus in præsenti, nos per Legem iustificari posse negat. Nec idcirco vel Legem improbè contemnit, vel Deum rei inutilis & superuacaneæ authorem facit. Manet enim illius honor, dum in hac pia fuerunt fidei exercitia, & eadem (ut alibi Paulus monet) nobis pædagogi instar fuit, quo ad Christum deducebantur, qui illius finem non ofcitanter inspiciebant. Galat.3.
units.tr: The law cannot justify. But if we turn to the ceremonies, by which the Jews once measured their righteousness, it will also appear that these are empty, and that they rather accuse us than justify us. For what does circumcision, performed on the genital member, teach except that the sources of our generation are corrupt and that we need regeneration? What do the daily and yearly sacrifices teach? What do the sprinklings of blood, the frequent washings, and the fixed rites of expiation and purification teach, except that we need expiation and purgation? But did true purification actually consist in these things? By no means. For the Lord cries out through the prophet that their hands were wholly polluted with blood, though they were busy in performing these rites (Isa. 1). And elsewhere: "Will I eat the flesh of bulls," he says, "or drink the blood of goats?" (Ps. 50). And David, goaded by the consciousness of a most atrocious crime, says: "You do not delight in sacrifices; otherwise I would have offered them; you do not want burnt offering," and so on. Indeed, looking to the blood and merit of the promised Saviour, he prays: "Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Deliver me from blood, O God, God of my salvation," and so on (Ps. 51). From this the apostle seems to have drawn his saying: "It is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats should take away sins" (Heb. 10). Paul therefore most truly denies in the present passage that we can be justified by the Law. Nor does he, for that reason, wickedly despise the Law or make God the author of a useless and superfluous thing. For its honour remains, while these were the pious exercises of faith, and the same Law (as Paul warns elsewhere) was for us like a schoolmaster, by which we were led to Christ, whose purpose they did not regard carelessly (Gal. 3).

units.la: Est autem diligenti observatione dignum, quòd nos ab omnibus peccatis per fidem in Christum iustificari Paulus ait, quod per legem fieri impossibile erat. Hac enim sententia non modò Iudaica operum legis & ceremoniarum fiducia evertitur, verumetiam totus Papatus corruit, quo vix aliud iustitiæ Dei & salutis, quæ in Christo offertur, magis contrarium inveniri potest. Gloriantur illi quidem Christo salvatore, sed eundem egregiè evacuant, dum illius merito Originale tantummodo peccatum & quæ ante baptismum receptum committa sunt, expiari fingunt, reliqua verò nostris satisfactionibus purgari docent. Has verò maxima ex parte in humanarum traditionum figmentis constituere tradunt, utpote ieiuniorum statis observationibus, feriis, chameunijs, cucullis, passagijs, bullarum redemptionibus, & id genus nugis. Ita verò Paulus mendacij arguitur, qui nos per Christum ab omnibus peccatis liberari clamat. Mendacij arguitur Christus, qui ex propheta docet, Deum patrem frustra coli hominum traditionibus, nos quoq; seruos inutiles vocat, etiamsi omnia ea faciamus, quæ nobis in lege præcepta sunt. Matth.15. Luc.17. cap. Firmiter ergo hanc Pauli sententiam tenemus, quæ ut uni Christo tribuit omnem salutis nostræ rationem, ita omnibus aliis sectis confutandis sola sufficere potest, nec Christianus vere est, nisi qui hac secutus, uni Christo induulsè hæret, illi salvatorem & redemptorem agnoscit, illi fidit, & eundem in spiritu & veritate colit. Impossibile enim est, eos Deo placere posse, qui filium Dei aspernari, & sua opera illius merito præferre audent. Paulus certè, ut hoc loco solum Christum prædicat, ita alibi se nihil præter hunc unum novisse fatetur, & abominabile flagitium esse censet, si quis alia in re confidere aut gloriari velit. 1. Cor.2. Gal.6.
units.tr: It is also worth careful attention that Paul says we are justified from all sins through faith in Christ, which was impossible through the law. For by this statement not only is the Jewish confidence in the works of the law and in the ceremonies overthrown, but the whole Papacy also collapses, to which hardly anything can be found more opposed than the righteousness of God and the salvation that is offered in Christ. They indeed glory in Christ as Saviour, but they utterly empty him of his merit, while they pretend that only original sin and the sins committed before baptism are expiated, and teach that the remaining sins are purged by our satisfactions. These they for the most part establish in the fictions of human traditions, such as the strict observances of fasts, holy days, pallets on the ground (chamaeunias [χαμευνίας]), cowls, pilgrimages, the purchase of papal bulls, and that kind of trifles. In this way Paul would be convicted of falsehood, when he proclaims that we are freed from all sins through Christ. Christ would be convicted of falsehood, who, quoting the prophet, teaches that God the Father is worshipped in vain by the traditions of men, and who calls us unprofitable servants even if we do all those things that are commanded us in the law (Matt. 15; Luke 17). Let us therefore hold firmly to this saying of Paul, which, as it ascribes to Christ alone the whole reason of our salvation, so alone is sufficient to refute all other sects. Nor is anyone truly a Christian unless he follows this and clings to Christ alone, acknowledges him as Saviour and Redeemer, trusts in him, and worships him in spirit and truth. For it is impossible that those can please God who dare to despise the Son of God and prefer their own works to his merit. Paul, indeed, as in this passage he preaches Christ alone, so elsewhere he confesses that he knows nothing except this one, and he judges it an abominable crime if anyone wishes to trust or glory in anything else (1 Cor. 2; Gal. 6).

units.la: Porrò ut cum apostolo concionandi finem faciamus, epilogus nobis considerandus restat, qui gravem & horribilem comminationem habet: cuius causa fuisse videtur, quòd in authoribus perspicua incredulitatis & contumaciæ indicia cerneret. Nec enim temere tantùm efferbuisse apostoli spiritu credibile est. Ait enim: Videte, ne superveniat vobis, quod dictum est in prophetis, &c. Ita igitur pænam minatur, ut simul veniæ spem adhuc relinquat, dum ipsos ne quid patiantur cauere iubet. Producit autem propheticum oraculum ex Habak.1. cap. quod per Collationem præsenti instituto accommodat. Constat enim Manasse regnante prædicauisse prophetam hunc, quando idololatria simul & omnis generis scelera sub impio & sanguinario rege regnabant. Dicitur enim is in errorem abduxisse Iudam & cives Hierosolymitanos, ut malitia superarent gentes, quas ante deleuerat dominus. Accessit hic immanis verbi Dei contemptus & implacabile veritatis odium, quo irritatus rex sanctam urbem innocenti sanguine compleuit. Interim tamen diuini fœderis, maiorum, templi & ceremoniarum rum fiducia inflati, se haec omnia impune facturos putabant, & meliora monentes aut Dei iudicium minitantes improbe subsannabant. Tunc ergo Chaldaeorum adventum praedixit Habakuk, qui urbem cum templo eversuri & populum omnem abducturi sint, quod illis factu impossibile videbatur. Eo igitur Paulus respiciens, sic dicere videtur: Scitis quid olim maioribus vestris acciderit, cum prophetarum sermones contemnerent. Viderunt illi urbis simul & templi excidium, nec illos superbus ille populi Dei titulus & ceremoniarum fiducia imminentibus poenis eripere potuerunt. Idem ne vobis euenia t, cavete. Licet enim incredibile vobis videatur, si quis gentem vestram Dei iudicio excindendam dicat, maiora tamen & atrociora vos supplicia manent. Transferetur enim a vobis regnum Dei, & repudiatis vobis ad gentes transferetur falsus, quae patribus vestris promissa fuit, &c. Docet autem Paulì exemplum, ita praedicandum esse verbum salutis, ut simul Dei iudicium contemptoribus & in credulis ob oculos statuatur. Minime ergo audiendi sunt, qui illud ab euangelica mansuetudine & charitate alienum esse existimant. Ita enim apostolos instituit Christus, quando Sodomis & Gomorrhaeis in die iudicii tolerabiliora eventura esse ait, quam ijs, qui ipsos audire contempserint. Quid quod, ipse ingratis urbibus, Bethsaida, Corozain & Capernaum horrendum illud Vae intonat? Matth. 11. Nonne idem Hierosolymis obsidionem, gladium, famem & excidium minatur? Luc. 19. Matth. 23. & 24. Exigit hoc humani ingenij contumacia, quam interdum minus frangi oportet; partim pastoris officium, quem decet, ut speculatoris instar imminentem populi cervicibus gladium annuntiet, ut quamvis illi incurabiles esse pergant, ipse tamen suam animam eripiat, ne de ipsius manu pereuntium sanguis requiratur. Vide Ezech. 3. & 33. Admonet praeterea locus hic, nullum esse peccatum verbi Dei contemptu atrocius, quando nullum gravioribus poenis Deus cohercere solet. Possunt enim quaecunque alia committuntur, aliquo modo humanae infirmitati condonari, qua sanctissimi quoque Dei cultores interdum superati delinquunt. At si quis peccandi licentiae verbi Dei contemptum coniungat, hoc demum diabolica simul & incurabilis malitiae argumentum est. Quae causa est, quod hunc seuerissime semper vindicavit dominus. Nota sunt, quae primo mundo, Noam iustitiae praeconem contemnenti, acciderunt. Senserunt idem Pharao, Saul, Achab, Manasses, totus denique Israel, in Assyriam abduc tus. Attamen lusus iocus, ista fuerunt prae ijs, quae postea Iudaeis propter Christum ab ipsis reiectum acciderunt, de quibus prolixius differere, temporis angustia non patitur. Interim illud monuisse necesse est, in Iudaeis commune omnibus gentibus simul & seculis exemplum nobis diuinitus propositum esse, quo docemur, neminem impune fore, si quis Christi doctrinam contemnere ausus fuerit.
