Nam qui naturalibus ramis non pepercit, alienis & insititiis, si & ipsi steriles fuerint, multo minus parcere poterit. Rom. 11. Quod iam olim expertas esse videmus Asiae & Graeciae ecclesias, quae ab ipsis apostolis quondam fundatae, nunc a Christo abscisse, horribile Mahumeticae impietatis iugum sustinent. Et utinam non hodie futuri mali praeludia videremus in quam plurimis, quos euangelicae salutis nimis fastidiose taedere coepit. Ad nos ergo transferamus quod hoc loco Paulus dicit, & euangelij doctrinam fide constanti & gratis animis complexi, totos nos consecremus salvatori & redemptori nostro, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, that we may bring our sermon to an end with the apostle, there remains for us to consider the epilogue, which contains a grave and dreadful warning. The reason for it seems to have been that he saw in these men clear signs of unbelief and obstinacy. For it is credible that the apostle did not burn with such zeal without cause. For he says: "Take heed lest there come upon you what was spoken in the prophets," and so on. Thus he threatens punishment, yet at the same time leaves a hope of pardon still open, while he bids them take care lest they suffer anything. He brings forward a prophetic oracle from Habakkuk 1, which he applies to his present purpose by way of comparison. For it is agreed that this prophet preached in the reign of Manasseh, when idolatry and every kind of wickedness reigned under that impious and bloodthirsty king. For he is said to have led Judah and the citizens of Jerusalem into error, so that they surpassed in wickedness the nations which the Lord had destroyed before them. Added to this was a monstrous contempt of the word of God and an implacable hatred of the truth, by which the king, provoked, filled the holy city with innocent blood. Meanwhile, puffed up with confidence in the divine covenant, in their ancestors, in the temple and in the ceremonies, they thought they would do all these things with impunity, and they wickedly mocked those who gave better advice or threatened the judgment of God. Then Habakkuk foretold the coming of the Chaldeans, who were about to overthrow the city together with the temple and to lead away the whole people, which seemed impossible to them. Looking to this, Paul seems to say: "You know what happened once to your ancestors when they despised the words of the prophets. They saw the destruction of the city and of the temple, and that proud title of the people of God and their confidence in the ceremonies could not snatch them from the punishments that hung over them. Take care lest the same happen to you. For although it may seem incredible to you if anyone says that your nation is to be destroyed by the judgment of God, yet greater and more atrocious punishments await you. For the kingdom of God will be taken from you, and, you being rejected, the covenant that was promised to your fathers will be transferred to the nations," and so on. The example of Paul also teaches that the word of salvation is to be preached in such a way that at the same time the judgment of God is set before the eyes of contemners and unbelievers. Those therefore are not to be listened to who think that this is alien to evangelical gentleness and charity. For Christ himself so instructed the apostles, when he said that it would be more tolerable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for those who had despised them when they heard them. What of the fact that he himself thundered the dreadful "Woe" against the ungrateful cities of Bethsaida, Chorazin and Capernaum? (Matt. 11). Does he not likewise threaten Jerusalem with siege, sword, famine and destruction? (Luke 19; Matt. 23 and 24). The obstinacy of the human mind demands this, which must sometimes be broken more sharply; and partly it is the duty of a minister, who ought, like a watchman, to announce the sword hanging over the necks of the people, so that, although they persist in being incurable, he himself may save his own soul, lest the blood of those who perish be required at his hand (see Ezek. 3 and 33). This passage also warns that there is no sin more atrocious than contempt of the word of God, since God is accustomed to restrain no sin with more severe punishments. For whatever other sins are committed can in some measure be pardoned to human weakness, by which even the most holy worshippers of God sometimes fall and transgress. But if anyone joins contempt of the word of God to the license of sinning, this is at last the proof of a diabolical and incurable malice. This is why the Lord has always punished it most severely. The things that happened in the ancient world to those who despised Noah, the herald of righteousness, are well known. Pharaoh, Saul, Ahab, Manasseh, and finally the whole of Israel, carried away into Assyria, have felt the same. Yet these were trifling jests compared with what afterwards befell the Jews, who rejected Christ, and of which the shortness of time does not permit me to speak at greater length. Meanwhile it must be noted that the Jews were divinely set before us as a common example for all nations and all ages, by which we are taught that no one will go unpunished if he dares to despise the doctrine of Christ. For he who did not spare the natural branches will be able much less to spare the grafted and alien ones, if they too prove barren (Rom. 11). We see that the churches of Asia and Greece, once founded by the apostles themselves, have already experienced this, and now, cut off from Christ, bear the dreadful yoke of Mahometan impiety. And would that we did not see in very many people today the preludes of future evils, who have begun to be wearied too fastidiously of the salvation of the gospel. Let us therefore apply to ourselves what Paul says in this passage: let us embrace the doctrine of the gospel with constant faith and a grateful mind, and let us consecrate ourselves wholly to our Saviour and Redeemer, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 94.

units.la: Exeuntibus autem e Synagoga Iudaeis, rogabant gentes, ut intermedio sabbato loquerentur ipsis verba. Soluto autem coetu, secuti sunt multi ex Iudaeis & religiosis proselytis Paulum & Barnabam, qui alloquentes ipsos suadebant, ut perseuerarent in gratia Dei. Sequenti autem sabbato, fere tota ciuitas congregata fuit ad audiendum verbum Dei. Videntes autem Iudaei turbas, repleti sunt zelo, & contradicebant his, quae a Paulo dicebantur, contradicentes & blasphemantes. Sumpta autem fiducia Paulus & Barnabas dixerunt: Vobis primum necesse erat annuntiari verbum Dei. Quoniam vero repellitis illud, & non dignos vos ipsos iudicatis vita aeterna, ecce conuertimur ad gentes. Sic enim mandauit nobis dominus: Posui te in lucem gentium, ut tu sis in salutem usque ad extremum terrae.
units.tr: As the Jews were leaving the synagogue, the Gentiles begged that these words be spoken to them on the next sabbath. When the assembly broke up, many of the Jews and devout proselytes followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and urged them to persevere in the grace of God. On the following sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of God. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with envy, and they contradicted what Paul said, opposing and blaspheming. Then Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: "It was necessary that the word of God be preached to you first. Since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us: 'I have set you to be a light to the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"

units.la: CAPUT XIII.
units.tr: Chapter 13

units.la: Praeclara simul & plena consolationis est Dei de verbo suo sententia, quam per Isaiam cap.55. ad hunc modum pronuntiat: Vt imber aut nix de caelo descendit, & illuc non redit, sed irrigat terram, & germinare eam facit: ita verbum meum, quod exit de ore meo, non redibit ad me vacuum, sed faciet quaecunq; volo, & prosperabitur in his, ad quae misi illud. Licet enim multi sint, qui illud im probè repellant, habet tamen vbiq; suos dominus, in quibus fructum ferre consueuit. Cuius rei exem plum cumprimis euidens in praesenti proponitur. Postquam enim Pauli concionem Lucas recenseuit, illi diuersa subijcit auditorum genera, quorum alij nobis imitandi sunt, aliorum autem improbitas & audacia diligenter fugienda est. Et in his quidem diuersus verbi Dei effectus cernitur, quod aliis quidem odor vitae ad vitam, aliis vero odor mortis ad mortem esse solet, sicuti in posteriori ad Corinthios cap.2. ipse Paulus testatur.
units.tr: God's statement about his word, which Isaiah sets out in chapter 55, is both remarkable and full of comfort: "As the rain or snow comes down from heaven and does not return there, but waters the earth and makes it bring forth and bud, so my word, which goes out of my mouth, shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I will and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it." Although many people wickedly reject it, the Lord always has those in whom it customarily bears fruit. A most clear example of this is set before us in the present passage. After Luke has recorded Paul's sermon, he adds the different kinds of hearers. Some of them we ought to imitate, but the wickedness and boldness of others we must carefully avoid. In these we see the varied effect of God's word: to some it is, as it were, a fragrance from life to life, and to others a fragrance from death to death, as Paul himself testifies in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 2.

units.la: Orditur autem ab ijs, quibus abs q; fructu euangelium praedicatum fuit, Iudaeis nimirum, quos e Synagoga eximiisse dicit priusquam coetus soluerentur. Id vero non alia causa factum esse, quam quod Christi doctrinam non possent ferre, ex sequentibus patebit, vbi illos nouum certamen & ingentes turbas contra apostolos excitauisse scribitur. His vero ingenium reproborum pulchrè exprimitur, qui Dei verbum nec volunt nec possunt audire. Vt enim qui ex Deo nati sunt, Christi verbu audiunt & pastoris sui vocem illico agnoscunt (Iohan.8. & 10) ita reprobi & huius saeculi filij, vocem illam caa ne & angue peius oderunt, nec adduci possunt, vt illam sponte quaerat: & si quando eam praeter spem & animi voluntatem audire contigerit, illico aures auertunt, & ex ijs locis sese proripiunt, in quibus vox illa sonat. Est hoc euidens incurabilis malitiae argumentum, quod Danidem quoq; obseruauisse legimus, quando illos aspidi surdae confert, quae aures suas mirificè obturat, ne incantatoris vocem audire cogatur. Psal.58. Et licet hoc aliquando modestiae esse videatur, semper tamen maiorū impietatis initium est. Nam qui primò verbum Dei leuiter duntaxat fastidiunt & audire detrectant, mox vbi illo fortius vrgentur, impietatis habenas laxant & indomitum furunt. Exempla huius in Pharaone, Saule, Achabo & innumeris alijs scriptura proponit, quibus commemorandis immorari superuacaneum foret, cum de his ipsis paulò post audituirimus, quanta impietate & audacia sese salutis doctrinae opposuerint.
units.tr: Luke begins with those to whom the gospel was preached without any fruit, namely the Jews, whom he says were driven out of the synagogue before the assembly broke up. That this happened for no other reason than that they could not bear the teaching of Christ will become clear from what follows, where we are told that they stirred up a new conflict and great tumults against the apostles. Here the nature of the reprobate is vividly portrayed: they neither want nor are able to hear God's word. For as those who are born of God hear the word of Christ and at once recognise the voice of their shepherd (John 8 and 10), so the reprobate, children of this age, hate that voice worse than a dog or a snake, cannot be brought to seek it of their own accord, and if by chance they happen to hear it beyond their expectation and against their will, they at once turn away their ears and flee from the places where that voice sounds. This is clear evidence of an incurable malice, and we read that David also observed it when he compared them to the deaf adder, which stops its ears tightly so that it need not hear the voice of the charmer (Psalm 58). Although this may sometimes seem to be modesty, it is always the beginning of greater impiety. For those who at first only lightly despise God's word and refuse to hear it, soon, when they are pressed harder by it, loosen the reins of impiety and rage without restraint. Scripture sets before us examples of this in Pharaoh, Saul, Ahab and countless others, and it would be superfluous to dwell on recounting them, since we shall soon hear about these very men, how great their impiety and audacity were in opposing the doctrine of salvation.

units.la: His vero alij opponuntur, qui apostolicam doctrinam digne exceperunt, quos partim ex gentibus partim ex proselytis fuisse ait Lucas. Et hos quidem ad recipiendum Christum magis idoneos fuisse constat, quod in illis minus locū haberet insolens illa propria dignitatis fiducia, quae Iudaeos (vt alibi Paulus monet) in fide Christi maximè remorabatur. Quamuis his aliquot etiam Iudai accedant, cum gentem illam ita reijceret Deus, vt interim reliquiae salua fierent. Isa.1. & 10. Rom.10. Porrò vt in prioribus illis reproborum mores proponuntur, ita in alteris istis electorum & filiorum Dei ingenium egregie describitur, quod eò diligentius consyderandum est, vt in his, quantum nobis adhuc defit, quid nos facere conueniat, intelligamus. Primò rogant apostolos, vt intermedio sabbato, eandem salutis doctrinam ipsis denuò annuntiare velint. Amant ergo Dei verbum, nec eos illius satietas capere potest, cum in hoc patris sui vocem sonare ex occulta spiritus sancti suggestione intelligant. Deinde soluto iam coetu, sequuntur apostolos, eosq; iam publice quoq; salutis & veritatis doctores agnoscunt, quos à plerisq; odio haberi non ignorabant. Minimè ergo illos verbi Dei pudet coram hominibus, & Christi gratiam totius mundi amicitiae praeferunt. Sunt haec verae pietatis rudimenta, in quibus qui se probè exercent, haud poenitendos tandem fidei & aeternae salutis fructus pariunt. Ex his vero de nostri seculi moribus iudicare licet. Hodie enim plerique verbum fastidiunt, nec quicquam illis à vera prudentia tam alienum putatur, quàm si quis ex hoc suorum consiliorum & rerum agendarū rationes petere studeat. Etsi illud non alia re, certè hoc vno indicio abunde testamur, quod ministrorum verbi nos non pudet modò, sed illos tanquam publicos salutis hostes & malorum omnium authores, odio prosequimur, abominamur, fugimus. conuitiamur & omni diuexamus iniuriarum genere. Interim magnificè, si dijs placet, euangelij studium & Christi fidem iactitamus. Sed nō fallitur inani verborū ostentatione Deus, qui nullo cultu delectatur, nisi qui cum veritate coniunctus fuerit.
units.tr: Set over against these are others who received the apostolic teaching worthily, whom Luke says were partly Gentiles and partly proselytes. It is agreed that these were better fitted to receive Christ, because in them there was less room for that insolent confidence in their own dignity which (as Paul elsewhere warns) especially hindered the Jews from faith in Christ. Yet some Jews also join these, since God so rejected that nation that meanwhile a remnant was saved (Isaiah 1 and 10; Romans 10). Moreover, as the former passage sets out the manners of the reprobate, so this latter one describes admirably the disposition of the elect and the children of God, which we must consider all the more carefully so that we may understand, in these things, what we ought to do, since we still fall short in them. First, they ask the apostles to preach the same doctrine of salvation to them again on the following sabbath. They therefore love God's word, and satiety cannot seize them, since they understand that the voice of the Father sounds in it through the secret prompting of the Holy Spirit. Then, when the assembly had broken up, they follow the apostles and acknowledge them openly as teachers of salvation and truth, though they were not unaware that these were hated by most people. Therefore they are in no way ashamed of God's word before men, and they prefer the grace of Christ to the friendship of the whole world. These are the rudiments of true piety, and those who train themselves well in them in the end bear the fruit of faith and eternal salvation, which they will not regret. From these things we may judge the manners of our own age. For today most people despise the word, and nothing is thought to be so far removed from true prudence as to seek from it the principles of one's plans and conduct. Yet, though we give witness to this by many other things, we certainly show it abundantly by this one sign: we are not only ashamed of the ministers of the Word, but we pursue them with hatred as public enemies of salvation and authors of every evil, we abominate them, flee them, revile them and harass them with every kind of injury. Meanwhile, if it please the gods, we boast magnificently of our zeal for the gospel and our faith in Christ. But God, who delights in no worship except that joined with truth, is not deceived by the empty display of words.

units.la: Quid vero ad ista apostoli? Suaserunt illis, vt perseuerarent in gratia Dei. Nouerunt enim illud Christi: Nemo qui manum aratro admota respexerit à tergo, dignus est regno Dei. Item: Qui perseuerauerit vsq; in finem, salvus erit. Et quia ijdem humani ingenij infirmitatem perspectam habebant, adhoradhortationibus quoq; opus esse nouerant apud illos, qui iam prima fidei & salutis fundamenta iecerant. Frequenter enim fit, vt qui bene coeperunt, vel periculis territi, vel affectibus abrepti, denuo concidant aut exorbitent. Obseruari ergo conuenit apostolorum exemplum, ne superuacaneas esse putemus fidas verbi adhortationes, siue quibus fidei & salutis cognitio rarissime retinentur. Interim notatu dignum est, quod in Dei gratia perseuerare dicuntur, qui in euangelio perseuerant. Per hoc enim illam nobis offerri constat. Et Christus in ea domo pacem, quae euangelio praedicatur, mansuram dicit, in qua filij pacis fuerint, qui nimirum vera fide pacem & gratiam Dei amplexi fuerint. Matth.10. Luc.10. Unde rursum colligimus, a gratia Dei omnes eos excidere, quicunq; euangelium reijcere audent, vnicum gratiae illius nuncium. Hinc vero omne genus malorum sequitur, sic vt in mundo quoq; infelicissimi habeantur, qui vt mundo placeant, Christum aspernantur. Patet hoc in Iudaeorum exemplo, quos euangelij contemptus in miserrimam conditionem detrusit, in qua iam annis plus mille quingentis laborant. Nobis ergo dictum putemus, quod illis in praesenti dixerit apostoli, & euangelium amplexi, in eodem perseueremus, vt simul nobis stabili gratia Dei & eiusdem fido auxilio in omni casu frui liceat.
units.tr: But what did the apostles say to these things? They urged the hearers to persevere in the grace of God. For they knew Christ's saying: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." Likewise: "He who perseveres to the end will be saved." And since they had seen clearly the weakness of human nature, they knew that exhortations were also needed among those who had already laid the first foundations of faith and salvation. For it often happens that those who began well, either frightened by dangers or carried away by passions, fall back again or go astray. We ought therefore to observe the example of the apostles, lest we think that the faithful exhortations of the word are superfluous, especially where the knowledge of faith and salvation is very rarely retained. Meanwhile it is worth noting that those are said to persevere in the grace of God who persevere in the gospel. For it is through the gospel, as we know, that grace is offered to us. And Christ says that peace will remain in that house to which the gospel is preached, in which there are sons of peace, that is, those who have truly embraced by faith the peace and grace of God (Matthew 10; Luke 10). From this we conclude in turn that all who dare to reject the gospel, the sole message of that grace, fall away from the grace of God. From this indeed every kind of evil follows, so that even in the world those are considered most unhappy who despise Christ in order to please the world. This is evident from the example of the Jews, whom contempt for the gospel has thrust into a most wretched condition, in which they have now been labouring for more than fifteen hundred years. Let us therefore take to ourselves what the apostles said to those people at that time: having embraced the gospel, let us persevere in it, so that we may be permitted to enjoy at all times the steadfast grace of God and his faithful help.

units.la: Caeterum graue certamen, quod felicem euangelij successum mox secutum est, Lucas subijcit, quo docemur, nunquam tam felicitur inchoari in hoc mundo Christi regnum, quin persecutionum procellae eos maneant, qui illud propagare student. Nec enim fallit Christi vox: Si meum sermonem audiuerunt, & vestrum audient. Iohan.15. Et quia mundus hic veritatis lucem alioqui odit, eo magis furere & insanire solet, quo magis illam splendere videt. Quare nemini mirum aut nouum videri debet, si quid simile etiam nostro saeculo contingat, & turbas inter illos excitari videamus, quibus euangelij doctrina primum praedicatur: Ipsum enim hic quoque fideles Christi apostoli, Paulus & Barnabas experiuntur. Nam sequenti sabbato, cum tota fere ciuitas congregata esset ad audiendum verbum Dei, Iudaei tantas turbas ad Christi regnum excipiendum paratas conspicati, zelo repleti sunt, & Paulo primum quidem contradicere coeperunt, tandem vero ad blasphemias & contumelias conuersi sunt. Quia autem eousq; certamen hoc exarsit, vt apostoli pedum puluerem contra illos excussserint (quod rarissime factum esse legimus) diligentius nos totius historiae circumstantias expendere conuenit.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke adds the severe conflict which soon followed the happy success of the gospel, from which we are taught that the kingdom of Christ never begins so fortunately in this world that the storms of persecution do not remain for those who strive to spread it. For the word of Christ is not false: "If they have heard my word, they will hear yours" (John 15). And since this world hates the light of truth in any case, it is wont to rage and rave all the more the more it sees that light shining. Therefore no one should think it strange or new if something similar happens in our own age, and we see tumults stirred up among those to whom the doctrine of the gospel is first preached. For here too the faithful apostles of Christ, Paul and Barnabas, experience this very thing. On the following sabbath, when almost the whole city had gathered to hear the word of God, the Jews, seeing such great crowds prepared to receive the kingdom of Christ, were filled with zeal, and at first began to contradict Paul, but at last turned to blasphemies and insults. Since this conflict blazed up to such a degree that the apostles shook the dust from their feet against them (which we read was very rarely done), it is fitting that we weigh more carefully all the circumstances of the whole story.

units.la: Et primo quidem quae tanti tumultus occasio fuerit, docetur: nimirum quod omnem fere totius ciuitatis multitudinem ad audiendum verbum Dei confluxisse, Iudaei viderent. Atqui satis constat, non omnes sancto animi proposito conuenisse, alioqui enim apostolos a Iudaeis (inuiso omnibus hominum genere) tam indignis modis tractari nunquam passi fuissent. Quare licet veritatis studium eos attraxerit, de quibus supra diximus, maior tamen eorum pars fuit, quos inanis curiositas pellexit. Quod quamuis apostoli facile suspicari possent, occasioni tamen tam opportunae deesse noluerunt, & ad docendum parati adsunt. Quo exemplo docemur, ardenti studio & zelo opus esse ijs, qui in Christi regno propagando cum fructu versari volunt, nec vllam occasionem, siue illa opportuna siue importuna fuerit, negligi debere, sicut Paulus alibi monet. Phil.1.2. Tim.4. Docet idem suo exemplo Christus, qui ex quauis re docendi ansam arripit, & ita neminem ad se venientem auersatus est, vt nec Nicodemum nocturno tempore, nec Samaritidem turpi quaestui addictam reiecerit: imo hanc suum cibum esse ait, vt ea exequatur, ad quae illum Deus pater miserat. Iohan.4. Arguitur hic illorum ignauia, qui sapius requisiti docere nolunt, & suo potius ocio quam hominum saluti consulunt.
units.tr: First, the author explains what occasioned such a great tumult: the Jews saw that almost the entire multitude of the city had flocked together to hear the word of God. Yet it is quite clear that not all of them came with a holy purpose in mind; otherwise the Jews, who hated every kind of person, would never have allowed the apostles to be treated in such shameful ways. So although the desire for truth drew in those of whom we spoke above, the larger part were drawn by empty curiosity. The apostles could easily suspect this, yet they were unwilling to let so opportune an occasion pass and stood ready to teach. From this example we learn that those who wish to work with profit in extending Christ's kingdom need ardent zeal, and that no opportunity, whether convenient or inconvenient, ought to be neglected, as Paul elsewhere advises (Phil. 1.2; 2 Tim. 4). Christ teaches the same by his own example: he seized the chance to teach from any matter whatever, and he so refused no one who came to him that he rejected neither Nicodemus at night nor the Samaritan woman given over to shameful gain. Indeed he said that it was his food to carry out the things for which the Father God had sent him (John 4). Here the laziness of those is condemned who, though often asked, refuse to teach and look after their own leisure rather than the salvation of others.

units.la: Deinde causa tumultus indicatur, Iudaeorum zelus, qui tot turbis vitis repleti sunt. Videntur autem partim ambitione & inuidia extimulati fuisse, dum priuato honori & gloriae suae metuunt (quod ipsum Christus quoq; illis obijcit, Iohan. 5.) partim vero propositione legis zelo id fecisse, quo abrepti, indigne tulerunt, gentes incircuncisas ipsis in salutis negotio aequari: quae res non semel Paulo ingentes turbas dedit, vt suis locis videbimus. Interim admonet locus hic, non quemuis zelum Deo probari, nec veniam statim eos mereri, qui zelo & bono quidem animi proposito veritatem oppugnant. Nam zelum Dei alibi quoq; Iudaeis Paulus tribuit, eosdem vero damnat, quod non secundum scientiam pro Dei gloria aemulentur. Rom.10. Cauendum ergo, ne quis prauus affectus concurrat, & ne diuinae voluntatis ignorantia peccemus, quae omnium nostrorum consiliorum vnica regula esse debet. Vide Num.15.
units.tr: Next the cause of the tumult is pointed out: the zeal of the Jews, who were filled with such great disorder. They seem to have been moved partly by ambition and envy, since they feared for their private honour and glory (which Christ himself also throws in their faces, John 5), and partly by zeal for the law, by which they were carried away and took it badly that the uncircumcised Gentiles should be made equal to themselves in the matter of salvation. This matter gave Paul no small trouble more than once, as we shall see in their places. Meanwhile this passage warns us that not every zeal is approved by God, and that those who oppose the truth out of zeal and with a good intention of mind do not at once deserve pardon. For elsewhere Paul also credits the Jews with zeal for God, but condemns them because they are zealous not according to knowledge (Rom. 10). Therefore we must take care that no depraved affection creeps in, and that we do not sin through ignorance of the divine will, which ought to be the only rule of all our plans. See Num. 15.

units.la: Occasio certaminis.
units.tr: The occasion of the dispute.

units.la: Causa certaminis.
units.tr: The cause of the dispute.

units.la: Tertiò, quid apostolorum antagonistæ Iudæi fecerint exponitur, qui antea cœtu nondum dimisso exiuerant, ne verbum audire cogerentur. Illi nunc dum suæ gloriæ timent, contradicunt etiam, & argumentis contra veritatem pugnare instituunt. Mox verò vbi se nihil proficere vident, ad conuicia conuertuntur, quibus haud dubiè tum doctrinam tum personas apostolorum prosciderunt, vt illos rudi vulgo inuisos & suspectos facerent. Sunt hæc impiorum artes, quibus hodie etiam pugnatur: & qui argumentis vel scripturis certaturi putantur, postquam dicendo inualuerunt, conuicia iaculantur, & frequenter in ipsum Dei nomen & verbum impiæ linguæ habenas laxant. Simul verò hic locus admonet, quò tandem infelices homines perducat veritatis odium, si quando illi indulgere caperint. Blasphemos enim & apertos hostes impudentes, & calumniatores reddit, qui initiò tolerabiles, adeoq; viri boni videbantur. Principijs ergo obstent, & aures suas veritati assuefaciant, qui vlterius progredi nolunt.
units.tr: Third, the passage sets out what the apostles' opponents, the Jews, did. Earlier, before the gathering was dismissed, they had gone out so that they would not be compelled to hear the word. Now, fearing for their glory, they also contradict, and they set about fighting against the truth with arguments. But soon, when they see that they are gaining nothing, they turn to insults, by which they undoubtedly tore apart both the teaching and the persons of the apostles, so as to make them hateful and suspect to the crude common people. These are the arts of the ungodly, by which battle is still waged today: those who are thought to be going to contend with arguments or Scripture, once they have grown strong in speaking, hurl insults, and often let loose their impious tongues against the very name and word of God. At the same time this passage warns us where the hatred of truth finally leads wretched men, if they ever begin to indulge it. For it makes blasphemers, open and shameless enemies, and slanderers of those who at first seemed tolerable and even good men. Therefore let those who refuse to go further resist the beginnings and accustom their ears to the truth.

units.la: Num verò Iudæorum audaciæ cesserunt apostoli? Minimè gentium. Imò maiori fiducia sumpta, se illis fortiter & admirabili dicendi libertate opponunt. Ita enim verbi ministros instructos esse oportet, vt non solum veritatem docere, verumetiam contradicentes confutare possint. Tit.1. Nec decet, vt mundi conatibus cedant, qui se Christi ministros esse noluerunt. Pertinent huc prophetarum exempla, quos tò constantiores fuisse legimus, quò audaciores videbant verbi Dei hostes. Vide quæ de Michea in priori Regum cap.22. & de Ieremia & reliquis passim extant. Nec aliam ob causam Christus apostolos de futuris periculis admonuisse videtur, quàm vt contradicentium audaciam sese terreri non paterentur, nec vllum ex hostibus offendiculum arriperent. Horum nos hodie meminisse decet, quando intolerabilis ferè facta est Antichristiana cohortis in oppugnanda veritate audacia. Cogitemus igitur nunc maximè nostram constantiam & fortitudinem requiri, qua periclitantem ecclesiæ causam fideliter sustineamus.
units.tr: But did the apostles yield to the audacity of the Jews? By no means. Rather, taking up greater confidence, they oppose them bravely and with a remarkable freedom of speech. For ministers of the Word ought to be so equipped that they can not only teach the truth but also refute those who contradict it (Titus 1). Nor is it fitting that they should give way to the efforts of the world, if they did not wish to be ministers of Christ. The examples of the prophets belong here, whom we read to have been the more constant the more bold they saw the enemies of God's word to be. See what is said of Micaiah in the first book of Kings, chapter 22, and of Jeremiah and the rest, which appear everywhere. Nor does Christ seem to have warned the apostles about future dangers for any other reason than that they should not allow themselves to be terrified by the boldness of those who contradict them, nor seize any stumbling block from their enemies. We ought to remember these things today, when the boldness of the Antichristian band in attacking the truth has become almost unbearable. Let us therefore consider now above all that our steadfastness and courage are required, so that we may faithfully uphold the cause of the Church, which is in danger.

units.la: Est autem cumprimis obseruanda apostolorum oratio, qua graui & diuino plane verborum pondere horribilem excommunicationis sententiam in incurabiles stringunt. Quid enim de illis sperarent amplius, quos per omnes impietatis gradus ascendisse, & primùm quidem ad verbum Dei aures obturauisse, mox verò eidem contradixisse, & tandem blasphemos factos esse videbant? Ante omnia verò pœnæ causam, ingratitudinem nimirum & incredulitatem illis exprobrant, dicentes: Vobis primum necesse erat annunciari verbum Dei, quos fœdere suo, promissionibus, & filij sui cognitione Deus exornare dignatus est. At ipsi vos tanta gratia indignos reddit, dum oblatam vobis salutem incurabili improbitate aspernamini. Quid ergo aliud restat, quàm vt ad gentes conuersi, ex ijs Deo ecclesiam colligamus, qui hactenus à testamentis & fœdere alieni fuerunt? Ita enim impleri oportet, quod Christus dixit: Transferetur à vobis regnum Dei, & dabitur genti facienti fructus eius. Matth.21. In his verò perquàm memorabile est, quòd proprio iudicio increduli pereunt, quibus in testimonium Christus prædicatur. Matth.10. Præterea, quòd propter hominum incredulitatem & ingratitudinem regno Christi nihil decedit. Potest enim Deus ex lapidibus Abrahami filios facere, qui Christum vera fide amplectantur, quemadmodum in gentium vocatione factum esse vidimus. Qui enim corda ipsis lapidibus duriora gestabant, Dei verbo & spiritu emolliti, in Christi regnum magna alacritate concesserunt.
units.tr: The apostles' speech must especially be noted, in which, with a weighty and plainly divine force of words, they pronounce the dreadful sentence of excommunication upon those beyond cure. For what more could they hope from those whom they saw to have climbed through every degree of impiety: first stopping their ears against the word of God, then contradicting it, and at last becoming blasphemers? Above all they throw in their faces the cause of the punishment, namely their ingratitude and unbelief, saying: "It was necessary that the word of God be announced to you first, whom God has deigned to adorn with his covenant, his promises and the knowledge of his Son. But they make you unworthy of so great grace, since you spurn the salvation offered to you with incurable wickedness." What then remains but that, turning to the Gentiles, we gather from them a church for God, from those who until now have been strangers to the testaments and the covenant? For what Christ said must be fulfilled: "The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits" (Matt. 21). In this it is most memorable that those who are unbelievers, to whom Christ is preached as a witness, perish by their own judgement (Matt. 10). Moreover, the kingdom of Christ loses nothing because of the unbelief and ingratitude of men. For God can make sons of Abraham from stones, who embrace Christ with true faith, as we have seen done in the calling of the Gentiles. For those who had hearts harder than stones, softened by God's word and Spirit, came into the kingdom of Christ with great eagerness.

units.la: Caterum ne quid priuato consilio & temere facere viderentur apostoli, Dei oraculum ex Isaia 49.cap. allegant, quo iam olim à Deo decretum fuisse docent, vt gentibus quoq; salus per Christum innotesceat: nec id amplius differri posse, cum Iudæi, quibus illa primùm prædicari debuerat, eam aspernentur. Asseritur igitur hic gentium vocatio, de qua iam ante non semel dictum est. Docet autem præterea Isaiæ locus, quid nobis in Christo exhibitum sit. Primum quidem lux, quæ veram Dei & se lucis cognitionem in nobis operatur, quam humanæ rationis industria per se assequi non potest. Deum enim nemo vidit vnquam, filius autem qui est in sinu patris, ipse enarrauit nobis. Iohan.1. Lucem ipsa salus sequitur. Hæc est enim vita æterna, vt cognoscamus Deum patrem, & quem illemisit, Iesum Christum. Iohan.17. Est autem hæc admiranda Dei bonitas, qui breui compendio quacunque saluti nostræ seruiunt, nobis proponere voluit. Ambulemus ergo in luce hac, ne nos tenebræ obruant, vt salutem nobis propositam in hac ipsa assequamur, nempe Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But lest the apostles seem to do anything on their own private counsel and rashly, they cite the oracle of God from Isaiah, chapter 49, by which they teach that it was decreed by God long ago that salvation through Christ should also be made known to the Gentiles, and that this could no longer be deferred, since the Jews, to whom it ought first to have been preached, reject it. The calling of the Gentiles, which has been spoken of already more than once, is therefore asserted here. Moreover, the passage of Isaiah also teaches what has been shown to us in Christ. First, the light, which works in us the true knowledge of God and of the light itself, which human reason cannot attain by its own industry. For no one has ever seen God, but the Son who is in the bosom of the Father has made him known to us (John 1). Salvation follows the light: "This is eternal life, that they know you the only true God and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (John 17). This is the admirable goodness of God, who has willed to set before us in a brief summary whatever serves our salvation. Let us therefore walk in this light, lest the darkness overwhelm us, so that we may attain in this very light the salvation set before us, namely in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCV
units.tr: Homily 95

units.la: Audientes autem gentes gauisæ sunt, & glorificabant sermonem Domini, & crediderunt quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam. Diuulgabatur autem sermo Domini per totam regionem. Iudæi autem exstimulauerunt religiosas mulieres & honestas, & primores ciuitatis, & excitauerunt persecutionem aduersus Paulum & Barnabam, & eiecerunt eos e finibus suis. At illi excussò puluere pedum in eos, venerunt Iconium. Discipuli vero repleti sunt gaudio & spiritu sancto.
units.tr: When the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. The word of the Lord was published throughout all the region. But the Jews stirred up the devout and honourable women and the chief men of the city, and raised a persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their borders. But they shook off the dust of their feet against them and came to Iconium. The disciples, however, were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quamvis Deus filio suo, Iesu Christo, regnum & omnem potestatem tradiderit, eundem tamen plures in mundo hostes habiturum, passim scripturæ docent: & ipse Christus frequenter de hoc suos discipulos admonuit, ne temporariam regni sui felicitatem sperantes, cruce & aduersis offenderentur. Exemplum vero eorum, quæ Christus euenturæ prædixit, cumprimis euidens & præclarum præsens historia exhibet. Venit enim post Cyprum & Pamphyliam conuersam Paulus Antiochiam Pisidiæ, ibiq; pro more in Iudæorum synagoga Christum prædicat. Mox ex gentibus simul & Iudæis auditores habet, qui fidei doctrinam ampleEuntur: imò tota fere ciuitas euangelio aures præbere incipit, adeò vt iam confectum videri possit negotium hoc. Sed ecce subitò Iudæi insurgunt, & publicè docentibus apostolis contradicunt, nec à conuitijs sibi temperant. In qua pugna cumprimis apostolorum constantia & fortitudo obseruari debet, qua improbis hostibus non modò restiterunt, sed ijsdem horrendum Dei iudicium denunciauerunt, quòd nimirum repudiatis Iudæis Deus regnum suum ad gentes transferre decreuerit. Nondum tamen certamen hoc sopiri potuit, quin graniora sequerentur, de quibus in præsenti agitur. Docet enim Lucas, vt inter medios hostes euangelij doctrina felicissimè propagata fit. Mox vero persecutionem nouam subijcit, qua apostoli Pisidia expulsi in Lycaoniam transierunt. Catastrophe vero tragœdiæ huius pijs quidem felix & læta, impijs vero cum primis horribilis & funesta, tandem describitur.
units.tr: Although God has given his Son, Jesus Christ, the kingdom and all power, the Scriptures teach everywhere that he would nonetheless have many enemies in the world. Christ himself often warned his disciples of this, so that they would not hope for a temporary happiness in his kingdom and be offended by the cross and by adversity. The present history sets before us, most clearly and remarkably, an example of what Christ foretold would happen. For after Cyprus and Pamphylia had been converted, Paul came to Antioch in Pisidia, and there, as was his custom, he preached Christ in the synagogue of the Jews. Soon he had hearers from both the Gentiles and the Jews, who spread the teaching of the faith. Indeed almost the whole city began to lend its ears to the gospel, so that the matter might seem already settled. But suddenly the Jews rose up, opposed the apostles while they were teaching publicly, and did not refrain from abuse. In this conflict the constancy and courage of the apostles must be noted: they not only resisted these wicked enemies but also announced to them the dreadful judgment of God, namely that, since the Jews had been rejected, God had decided to transfer his kingdom to the Gentiles. Yet this contest could not be quelled at once, and graver things followed, which are the subject of the present passage. For Luke teaches that the doctrine of the gospel was most happily propagated even amid the enemies. Soon, however, he adds a new persecution, by which the apostles were expelled from Pisidia and passed into Lycaonia. Finally he describes the outcome of this tragedy, which was happy and joyful for the godly, but for the wicked above all dreadful and deadly.

units.la: Ad primam huius loci partem pertinet, quod ait: Audientes autem gentes gauisæ sunt, & glorificabant sermonem Domini, & crediderunt quotquot ordinati erant ad vitam æternam. Diuulgabatur autem sermo Domini per totam regionem. Gauisi dicuntur qui ex gentibus erant, auditis Pauli verbis, non quidem propter Iudaicæ gentis repudium (hoc enim à fide simul & charitate Christiana alienissimum foret) sed quòd salutem ad se quoq; pertinere, & Christum, iuxta prophetarum oracula, non Iudæorum modò, verumetiam gentium saluatorem esse, audirent. Gratis ergo animis Dei verbum amplexantur & dignis laudibus vehunt: nec intra vrbis mœnia salus hæc continetur, sed per verbi prædicationem in totam Pisidiæ regionem longè lateq; diuulgatur. Sunt in his quædam diligentiori consyderatione digna, de quibus singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: To the first part of this passage belongs what he says: "When the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. The word of the Lord was published throughout all the region." Those who were from the Gentiles are said to have rejoiced when they heard Paul's words, not indeed because the Jewish nation was rejected (for that would be utterly foreign to Christian faith and love), but because they heard that salvation pertained to them also, and that Christ, according to the oracles of the prophets, was the Saviour not only of the Jews but also of the Gentiles. Therefore they embraced the word of God with glad minds and praised it with fitting praises. Nor was this salvation confined within the walls of the city; through the preaching of the word it was spread far and wide throughout the whole region of Pisidia. There are in these words some matters worthy of closer consideration, which we shall take up one by one in order.

units.la: Et primò quidem videndum, qui nam isti fuerint, de quibus hæc dicuntur: nimirum qui ordinati erant ad vitam æternam. Ita verò ista à Luca describuntur, vt manifestum fiat, quæ causa sit, quòd euangelio credunt homines, etiam tunc quando illud à multis & acerrimis hostibus impugnari vident: electio nimirum Dei libera & gratuita, qui quos vult ad vitam ordinat, quos vult exitio & æterna damnationi, quam abunde meruerunt, relinquit. Nam si hominem qualis natura est, spes, minimè in illius vel voluntate vel potestate situm esse videbis, vt euangelio credat, & Christum apprehendat. Animalis siquidem homo, non percipit ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei. 1. Corinth. 2. Et ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandū quidem idonei sumus. 2. Cor. 3. Deus ergo operatur in nobis & vt velimus & vt possimus, prout illi visum fuerit. Phil. 2. Docet hoc ipsum Christus Dominus, quando nos è superis neceßario renasci oportere ait, nec aliquem ad se venire testatur, nisi quem pater traxerit. Ioan. 3. & 6. Idem Petro, fidei confessionem edenti, dixit: Beatus es Simon Bar Iona, quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi, sed pater meus, qui in cœlis est. Matth. 16. Ex quibus luce clarius colligitur, fidem eorum duntaxat esse, quos Deus elegit & vitæ æternæ prædestinauit. Atqui electionem illam ante mundi constitutionem ab æterno factam fuisse constat, idq; in Christo, qui & ipse nobis antequam mundus hic conderetur à Deo saluator & redemptor præordinatus fuit. Ephes. 1. 1. Pet. 1. cap. Liberam ergo & gratuitam esse oportet. Porrò quos in Christo elegit, eosdem suo tempore per
units.tr: And first we must see who these were of whom this is said, namely those who were ordained to eternal life. Luke describes these things in such a way that it becomes clear what the cause is that men believe the gospel even when they see it attacked by many and most bitter enemies: namely, the free and gratuitous election of God, who ordains whom he wills to eternal life, and leaves whom he wills to destruction and eternal damnation, which they have more than fully deserved. For if you consider man as he is by nature, you will see that hope lies neither in his will nor in his power, that he should believe the gospel and lay hold of Christ. "For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Cor. 2). And we are not even sufficient of ourselves to think anything (2 Cor. 3). "God works in us both to will and to do, as seems good to him" (Phil. 2). Christ the Lord teaches this very thing when he says that we must be born again from above, and testifies that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him (John 3 and 6). He said the same to Peter, when he made his confession of faith: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven" (Matt. 16). From these things it is clearer than light that faith belongs only to those whom God has chosen and predestined to eternal life. And it is agreed that this election was made from eternity, before the foundation of the world, and that it was in Christ, who himself was foreordained by God to be our Saviour and Redeemer before this world was made (Eph. 1; 1 Pet. 1). Therefore it must be free and gratuitous. Moreover, those whom he has chosen in Christ, he calls at his appointed time by the preaching of the gospel, and draws them effectively by his Spirit, so that, being grafted into Christ through faith, they are justified by his merit and become partakers with him of heavenly glory, according to that saying of Paul: "Whom he foreknew, these he also predestined; and whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, these he also glorified" (Rom. 8).

units.la: I. Euangelij doctrina in mentibus turbis propagatur. euangelij prædicationem vocat,& spiritu suo efficaciter trahit, vt per fidem Christo insiti, illius merito iustificentur, & cœlestis gloriæ cum illo consortes fiant, iuxta illud Pauli: Quos præscieuerat, eosdem & prædestinauit: & quos prædestinauerat, eosdem & vocauit: & quos vocauit, eos & iustificauit: quos autem iustificauit, hos & glorificauit. Rom. 8. Et quicunq; ex illorum numero sunt, hi Christi vocem facile agnoscunt, seq; vocari à Deo intelligunt, eò quòd semen Dei in sese habeant, quod occultum antea, per Dei verbum viuificatur & ad maturam frugem perducitur. Hinc est quòd Christus eos, qui ex Deo nati, & sui gregis oues sunt, vocem suam agnoscere & eadem delectari ait, imò eos quoq; pro ouibus suis agnoscit, à quibus adhuc ignorabatur, & qui postea demum vocandi & trahendi erant, cum dicit: Alias quoque oues habeo, quæ non sunt ex hoc ouili, illas quoq; oportet me adducere, & vocem meam audient, & fiet vnum ouile, & vnus pastor. Iohan. 10. Ex quo ordine Antiochenos hosce Lucas fuisse docet. Nec alicui superuacanea videri debet ista tractatio, cum non aliud in salutis nostræ negotio consyderatu vtilius simul & iucundius sit. Hic enim salutis nostræ fontes patefiunt, bancq; ex mera Dei gratia pendere docemur, & proinde euersa & sepulta iacet insolens & pharisaica humanæ iustitiæ & meriti gloriatio. Hæc ipsa quoq; salutis nostræ certitudinem afferunt, & fidem nutantem in tentationibus mirificè stabiliunt. Nec enim electionis & vocationis suæ Deum pœnitere potest. Rom. 11. Et quia in Christo electi sumus, qui insuperabilis illa petra est, cui ne porta quidem inferorum prævalent, quiq; oues suas è manibus suis eripi non patitur, impossibile est, vt ijà salute excidant, qui se Christo insitos esse sentiunt. Quò etiam referri debet, quòd in præsenti omnes credidisse dicuntur, qui ad vitam æternam ordinati erant. Quantumuis enim Iudæi furerent, tamen ne vnius quidem electi fidem & salutem impedire potuerunt. Quotquot verò ad hunc modum Dei prædestinationem & electionem consyderant, fidem suam egregiè augeri sentient. Quòd si qui Dei mysteria altius scrutari volunt, eiusq; æterna consilia ad humanæ rationis calculum vocare audent, eò tandem delabuntur, vt vel Dei iudicia scurriliter reprehendant, vel homini tribuant, quod nos in sola Dei gratia quærere decebat, & Christum, qui nostræ salutis fundamentum est, maxima exparte euacuent, &c. Vide Rom. 9. & 11. cap.
units.tr: I. The doctrine of the gospel is spread among the crowds. And all who are of their number readily recognise the voice of Christ and understand that they are called by God, because they have within them the seed of God, which, hidden before, is quickened by the word of God and brought to ripe fruit. Hence it is that Christ says that those who are born of God and are sheep of his flock recognise his voice and delight in it; indeed he also acknowledges as his sheep those who were still unknown to him, and who were afterwards to be called and drawn, when he says: "I have other sheep also, which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd" (John 10). By this order Luke shows that these Antiochenes were of that number. Nor should this discussion seem superfluous to anyone, since nothing more useful and at the same time more pleasant can be considered in the business of our salvation. For here the sources of our salvation are opened, and we are taught that it depends entirely on the pure grace of God, and therefore the arrogant and Pharisaical boasting in human righteousness and merit lies overthrown and buried. These same things also bring certainty of our salvation and marvellously strengthen a faith that wavers in temptations. For God cannot repent of his election and calling (Rom. 11). And since we are elect in Christ, who is that unconquerable rock against which even the gates of hell do not prevail, and who does not allow his sheep to be snatched from his hands, it is impossible that those who feel themselves grafted into Christ should fall from salvation. To this too must be referred the fact that here all are said to have believed who were ordained to eternal life. For however much the Jews raged, they could not hinder the faith and salvation of even one of the elect. Indeed, all who consider God's predestination and election in this way will feel their faith greatly increased. But if any wish to search the mysteries of God more deeply, and dare to bring his eternal counsels to the reckoning of human reason, they will at last slip into this: either they will scoffingly find fault with God's judgments, or they will attribute to man what we ought to seek in the grace of God alone, and will largely empty Christ, who is the foundation of our salvation, etc. See Rom. 9 and 11.

units.la: Sed ad nostros illos reuersi, verbi Dei effectus videamus, qui in illis sese exeruerunt, ex quibus quæ sint electorum Dei officia, facile colligitur. Primò gauisi sunt, quantumuis crudeles contra sebastium Christi conatus viderent. Est hic mirabilis verbi Dei effectus, quòd in medijs periculorum terroribus credentium animos gaudio recreat, dum Deum patrem sibi placatam esse intelligunt. Quò Christus respexit, quando nos in persecutionibus exultare iubet, Matthæi 5. cap. Deinde Dei verbum glorificauisse dicuntur, quod gratitudinis argumentum est, quam non possunt nō præstare Deo, quicunq; gratiæ diuinæ aliquem gustum perceperunt. Glorificant autem Dei verbum, qui illud cum fide amplexi, eidem sese submittunt, omnemq; suam rationem & intellectum illi subijciunt, quinon postremus euangelicæ prædicationis finis est, sicut alibi monuimus. Docent hæc quid eos facere conueniat, qui ex electorum numero censeri volunt: simulq; confutantur, qui Christianæ pietatis exercitia per gratuitæ electionis & prædestinationis doctrinam euerti clamitant. Quia enim (vt supra monuimus) electionem vocatio, & ex hac iustificatio per fidem sequitur, fieri non potest, vt Christiani hominis studia abijciat, qui se electum esse intelligit. Simul enim nouit, in eum finem nos in Christo electos esse, vt hanc vitam puram & irreprehensibilem emensi, æternum cum Christo in cœlis regnemus. Ephes. 1. Quapropter iuxta apostoli præceptum, indefinenti pietatis & innocentiæ studio vocationem & electionem suam firmam ratamq; efficere studet. 2. Pet. 1.
units.tr: But let us return to those people of ours and see the effects of the Word of God that showed themselves in them, from which it is easily gathered what the duties of God's elect are. First, they rejoiced, however cruel the attempts against the servants of Christ they saw. This is a wonderful effect of the Word of God: in the midst of the terrors of dangers it refreshes the hearts of believers with joy, while they understand that God the Father is reconciled to them. Christ looked to this when he bids us exult in persecutions, Matthew 5. Next, they are said to have glorified the Word of God, which is a proof of gratitude that those who have tasted the grace of God cannot fail to render to God. They glorify the Word of God who embrace it with faith, submit themselves to it, and subject all their reason and understanding to it, which is not the least end of the evangelical preaching, as we have noted elsewhere. These things teach what those ought to do who wish to be counted among the number of the elect; at the same time they refute those who cry out that the exercises of Christian piety are overthrown by the doctrine of free election and predestination. For since (as we noted above) election is followed by calling, and from this by justification through faith, it cannot be that a Christian who understands himself to be elect should abandon the pursuit of godliness. For at the same time he knows that we are elected in Christ for this end: that, having passed through this life pure and blameless, we may reign eternally with Christ in heaven. Ephesians 1. Wherefore, according to the apostle's precept, he strives with unceasing zeal for piety and innocence to make his calling and election firm and sure. 2 Peter 1.

units.la: Tertio loco obseruandum venit, quod verbum Dei per totam regionem diuulgatum fuisse, Lucas scribit. Ex eo enim patet, quàm nihil contra Christum, suis conatibus impij proficiant. Spiritus enim Dei spiritus vbicunq; voluerit, nec hominum authoritate siue potentia mouetur. Idem ergo hic fit quod supra in persecutione propter Stephanum Hierosolymis exorta accidisse vidimus. Est hoc verbi Dei ingenium, quòd eò validius vim suam exerat, quò magis oppugnatur, quasi cum aduersariorum potentia colluctari gaudeat. Nec est, quòd quærat aliquis, cur non hodie tam felices regni Christi successus experiamur. Nostra enim ignauia & socordia huius limites in angustum contrahuntur, & in omni hominum ordine illud Christi dictum cernitur, quo fidem in terris nouissimis temporibus raram fore testatus est. Luc. 18.
units.tr: In the third place it must be observed that Luke writes that the Word of God was spread through the whole region. For from this it is evident how little the wicked accomplish against Christ by their attempts. For the Spirit of God blows where he wills, and is moved neither by the authority nor the power of men. So here the same thing happens that we saw happen above in the persecution that arose at Jerusalem on account of Stephen. It is the nature of the Word of God that the more it is attacked, the more forcefully it exerts its power, as if it rejoices to wrestle with the might of its adversaries. Nor should anyone ask why we do not experience such happy successes of the kingdom of Christ today. For through our sloth and carelessness its limits are narrowed, and in every order of men that saying of Christ is seen, by which he testified that faith would be rare in the last times on earth. Luke 18.

units.la: Porrò lætiùs bisce apostolorum successibus & partæ iam contra impios hostes victoriæ novus tumultus subijcitur, aperta nimirum persecutio, quam ijsdem Iudæis authoribus excitatam fuisse indicatur: eam nimirum ob causam, quòd priori certamine nihil effectum esset, & quòd firmiorem virtutem Christi doctrinam, quam quæ Sophistarum artibus, vel calumniis & conuicijs euerti posset. Frequenter autem in hoc libro Iudæi persecutionem authores introducuntur, & Paulus de ijsdem in priori ad Thessal. cap. 2. scribens, ait: Quemadmodum Dominum occiderunt Iesum, & proprios prophetas: ita & nos persequuntur, & Deo non placent, & omnibus hominibus aduersantur, qui obstant nobis, ne loquamur gentibus, quò salvæ fiant, vt expleant sua peccata semper, & c. Quæ ideo observanda sunt, vt iustum agnoscamus in illis Dei iudicium, quod merito illis horrenda illæ & exemplo carentes calamitates acciderint, quas Christus Dominus minatus fuerat, & historijs prodita sunt. Voluit enim illorum exemplo docere Deus, quid omnes filij sui contemptores & hostes maneat. In primis autem consyderatione dignum est, quibus artibus persecutionem iflam excitarint, quisq; illius effectus fuerit.
units.tr: Moreover, with these successes of the apostles and the victory already won against the impious enemies, a new tumult is stirred up: an open persecution, which is indicated to have been roused by the Jews as its authors, namely for this reason, that nothing had been accomplished by the earlier struggle, and that the doctrine of Christ was too firm to be overthrown by the arts of the Sophists, or by calumnies and reproaches. Now in this book the Jews are frequently introduced as the authors of persecution, and Paul, writing of them in his first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 2, says: As they killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, so they also persecute us, and they do not please God, and they are opposed to all men, who hinder us from speaking to the Gentiles that they may be saved, so as always to fill up their sins, etc. These things are to be observed so that we may recognise in them the just judgment of God, since those dreadful calamities, without parallel, which Christ the Lord had threatened and which histories have recorded, justly befell them. For God willed to teach by their example what awaits all his sons' despisers and enemies. In particular, however, it is worth considering by what arts they stirred up this persecution, and who was its instigator.

units.la: Primum in ijs patet, quos in suas partes pertractos contra apostolos extimulauerunt. Ponuntur inter hos primo loco mulieres, quibus religionis & honestatis laus tribuitur. Nec temere harum operam sibi ad hanc rem idoneam esse putauerunt. Est enim sexus hic vt natura superstitiosior, ita ad decipiendum mirè idoneus, maximè si illud sub religionis & recepti apud illas cultus prætextu fiat. Deinde per illas ad maritos gradus est, apud quos blanditijs suis plurimum possunt, maximè si pietatis & honestatis nomine commendentur. Exempli loco prima omnium mater Heua esse potest, qua ad decipiendum infelix hominum genus olim satan abuti voluit. Et quia illi tam feliciter primus conatus successit, eodem organo postea quoq; sibi vendum putauit. Per mulieres ergo Salomonem decepit, qui prima apud Israelitas idololatriæ femina iecit, quæ nullis postea vel regum vel prophetarum laboribus prorsus extirpari potuerunt. Et Iesabelis authoritate Baalis cultum inuexit. Taceo infinita alia, quæ adduci poterant. Paulus certè hoc ita obseruauit, vt impostoribus hoc proprium esse scribat, quòd mulierculis insidientur, ijs præcipuè, quarum conscientias grauatas esse animaduertunt. 2. Tim. 3. Id verò nostro seculo tam vulgare est, vt talpa cæcior fit, qui hoc non videt. Nemo tamen ista in huius sexus ignominiam dici putet. Quin potius institutioni seruiat, & discant hinc sibi cauere mulieres, ne falso religionis prætextu sibi imponi sinant.
units.tr: First, this appears in those whom they drew to their side and stirred up against the apostles. Among these, women are placed first, to whom a reputation for religion and honour is ascribed. Nor did they rashly think that their efforts were suited to this business. For this sex is, by nature, more superstitious, and so wonderfully apt for deceiving, especially when this is done under the pretext of religion and of the worship received among them. Next, through women there is a way to husbands, over whom they have great power by their flatteries, especially if they are commended under the name of piety and honour. The first of all, the mother Eve, may serve as an example, through whom Satan once wished to make use of the deception of the unhappy human race. And since his first attempt succeeded so happily, he thought he should use the same instrument afterwards too. Through women, therefore, he deceived Solomon, who first introduced idolatry, a female thing among the Israelites, which afterwards could not be utterly rooted out by the labours of any kings or prophets. And by the authority of Jezebel he introduced the worship of Baal. I pass over countless other things that could be adduced. Paul certainly observed this so carefully that he writes that it is characteristic of impostors to lie in wait for silly women, especially those whose consciences they notice are burdened. 2 Timothy 3. Yet in our age this is so common that he must be blinder than a mole who does not see it. Still, let no one think these things are said to the disgrace of this sex. Rather, let them serve as instruction, and let women learn from this to be on their guard, lest they allow themselves to be imposed upon under a false pretext of religion.

units.la: At quia contemni poterat muliebris sexus, ciuitatis proceres & magistratus quoq; extimulant, in quibus exacerbandis mulierum opera haud dubiè vsi sunt. Magistratus verò apostolis tanquam publicæ pacis turbatoribus infensos faciunt, quod vnicum omnibus seculis argumentum fuit, quo veritatis doctrinam impij maximè oppugnarunt, quemadmodum prophetarum historiæ docent, quos fere omnes vnà cum Christo Iesu seditionis accusatos fuisse constat. Nec quicquam bodie est vulgarium. Obseruemus autem quòd quicquid Antiochiæ vel sanctitatis vel publicæ authoritatis nomine pollet, contra apostolos armatur, à quorum partibus rude duntaxat stat & ignobile vulgus. Arguuntur exemplo hoc, qui religiones hominum authoritate metiuntur: quæ si valere debet, apostolorum causa nimium misere periclitabitur. At longè aliter nos Christus docet, qui regni cælorum mysteria sapientibus abscondita esse, paruulis autem reuelari testatur. Matth. 11. Refer huc etiam quæ 1. Cor. 1. circa finem capitis in eandem sententiam habentur.
units.tr: But since the female sex could be despised, the leaders and magistrates of the city also stir up the people, and in exasperating them they doubtless used the work of the women. The magistrates, moreover, make the apostles hostile to them as disturbers of the public peace, which was the one argument in all ages by which the impious most of all attacked the doctrine of truth, as the histories of the prophets teach, nearly all of whom are known to have been accused of sedition along with Jesus Christ. Nor is anything more common today. Let us observe, moreover, that whatever at Antioch is powerful in the name of holiness or public authority takes up arms against the apostles, on whose side stands only the rough and ignoble crowd. By this example are refuted those who measure religions by the authority of men; if that were to hold, the cause of the apostles would be in very wretched danger. But Christ teaches us quite otherwise, who testifies that the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones. Matthew 11. Refer here also what is said to the same effect in 1 Corinthians 1, near the end of the chapter.

units.la: Caterum effectus persecutionis fuit, quòd apostoli publica authoritate finibus Pisidiæ eiecti sunt. Non tamen idcirco euangelium omnino profligatum est, cum postea discipulorum mentio fiat, qui spiritus donis omniuarijs donati sunt. Frequens autem omnibus seculis fuit, vt tanquam publicæ pestes exilio multati sint veri Dei cultores, impunè interim per medias vrbes grassantibus impijs, propter quos ira Dei accendi solet. Exilium fere comitatur bonorum direptio & triste egestas. Permittit ista electis suis euenire Deus multas ob causas. Ita enim suam potentiam declarat, quæ tunc maximè elucet, quando in medijs persecutionum fluctibus ecclesiam suam conseruat. Deinde fidem suorum, vt aurum igne explorat, & infelices carnis reliquias mortificat, ne per hanc seductionem exorbitemus. Præterea filio suo conformes reddere studet, vt qui cum illo patiuntur, cum eodem regnent. 2. Timoth. 2. Adhæc mundi huius fastidium suorum animis hoc modo inferre solet, quem alioqui caro nostra nimis impotenter admiratur & colit. Neminem ergo ista offendere
units.tr: Moreover, an effect of the persecution was that the apostles were expelled from the region of Pisidia by public authority. Yet the gospel was not therefore utterly overthrown, since afterwards mention is made of disciples who were endowed with various gifts of the Spirit. It has been frequent in all ages that true worshippers of God have been punished with exile as if they were public pests, while meanwhile the impious roam unpunished through the midst of the cities, on account of whom the wrath of God is wont to be kindled. Exile is generally accompanied by the plundering of goods and sad want. God permits these things to befall his elect for many reasons. For thus he declares his power, which shines most brightly when in the midst of the waves of persecution he preserves his church. Next, as gold is tested by fire, he tests the faith of his people, and mortifies the unhappy remnants of the flesh, lest we go astray through this seduction. Moreover, he seeks to make them conformed to his Son, so that those who suffer with him may reign with him. 2 Timothy 2. Besides, he is wont in this way to bring contempt of this world into the minds of his people, which otherwise our flesh admires and worships too immoderately. Let no one, therefore, be offended by these things.

units.la: Effectus persecutionis exilium. debent: quin potius in promissionum Christi meditatione versemur, quales sunt: Nullus est, qui reliquit domum, aut fratres & sorores, aut parentes, aut uxorem, aut liberos, aut agros, mea causa & euangelij, quin recipiat centupla nunc in hoc tempore cum persecutionibus, & in seculo venturo vitam aeternam. Marc.10. Item: Vos estis, qui permansistis mecum in tentationibus meis: & ego dispono vobis, sicut disposuit mihi pater meus regnum, ut edatis & bibatis super mensam meam in regno meo, &c. Luc.22. Et rursum: Ubi ego sum, ibi & minister meus erit, &c. Iohan.12.14. & 17. Haec qui attente considerant, iis nihil molestum & intolerabile videri potest, cuius tam letum exitum fore sciunt. Interim Christi exulibus, qui suis sedibus eiecti, ad nos commigrant, charitatis officia sedulo praestemus, nec sinistris suspicionibus eos per nos gravari patiamur, qui eandem cum apostolis Christi sortem sustinent. Consyderemus diligenter illud Christi: Hospes fui, & collegistis me, &c. Matth.25.
units.tr: The effect of persecution is exile. They ought not to be offended: rather let us dwell on the meditation of the promises of Christ, such as these: There is no one who has left house, or brothers and sisters, or parents, or wife, or children, or fields, for my sake and the gospel's, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the coming age eternal life. Mark 10. Likewise: You are those who have remained with me in my trials; and I appoint to you, as my Father has appointed to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, etc. Luke 22. And again: Where I am, there also my minister will be, etc. John 12, 14 and 17. To those who attentively consider these things nothing can seem troublesome or intolerable, since they know its outcome will be so joyful. Meanwhile, to Christ's exiles, who, driven from their seats, migrate to us, let us diligently render the offices of charity, and let us not allow them to be burdened by us with sinister suspicions, since they bear the same lot as the apostles of Christ. Let us carefully consider that saying of Christ: I was a stranger, and you gathered me in, etc. Matthew 25.

units.la: II. Catastrophe persecutionis.
units.tr: II. The catastrophe of the persecution.

units.la: Videamus autem Tragediae huius exitum, quem contumacibus Iudaeis horribilem & funestem, piis vero & credentibus laetissimum fuisse, scribit Lucas. Apostoli enim, ubi Iudaeorum malitiam insuperabilem esse vident, excussio in eos pedum suorum pulvere, in Lycaoniae civitatem Iconium transeunt. Quod illos iuxta Christi praeceptum fecisse constat, quem discipulis ita dixisse legimus: Si qui non receperint vos, egressi de civitate illa, pulverem quoque e pedibus vestris excutite in testimonium adversus illos. Luc.9. Et rursum apud eundem euangelistam Cap.10. ait: In quamcunque civitatem intraveritis, & non susceperint vos, exeuntes in plateas eius, dicite: Etiam pulverem, qui adhaesit nobis de civitate vestra, excergimus in vos. Tamen hoc scitote, quod appropinquavit in vos regnum Dei. Fuit ergo pulveris excussio solenne & publicum execrationis symbolum, quo significabatur, impios euangelij contemptores instar pulveris dissipandos esse, tamque horribilem illis imminere a Deo maledictionem, ut ne pulveri quidem illorum communicare debeant, qui se salvos esse volunt. Et ista quidem adversus tales in testimonium fieri voluit Dominus, ut omnem excusationem illis adimeret. Solent enim fere ignorantiam praetexere impij, quando Dei iudicijs vrgentur. Id ne facere possent, sed propria conscientia testimonio iugulantur, apostoli non sine publica protestatione & poenae imminentis denunciatione discedere debuerunt: quasi dicerent: Innoxij nos sumus a vestro sanguine. Nostro enim officio functi, regnum Dei vobis annunciavimus. Quod quia incurabili impietate reijcitis, vos iusto Dei iudicio relinquimus, cuius tanta erit atrocitas, ut ne pulverem quidem vobiscum communem habere tutum sit. Nam Christo teste, in nouissimo die Sodomae multo tolerabilius iudicium, quam vos, sustinebunt. Quod si vero puluis, qui ministrorum Christi pedibus adhaesit, conuincendis & redarguendis euangelij contemptoribus sufficere potest, quid obsecro de eorundem concionibus, vigilijs, lucubrationibus, sanguine deniq; propter testimonium Iesu Christi effuso, iudicabimus? Transferamus haec ad nostra tempora, ut intelligamus quam inexcusabili impietate sese polluant, qui hodie regni Dei praedicationem tanta improbitate respuunt. Fugiamus ergo tam immane flagitium, simulq; illorum abominemur commercia, quos illo pollutos esse novimus. Licet enim illis ridiculae fere putentur comminationes eiusmodi, sentient tamen suo tempore illis fidem non defuisse.
units.tr: Let us now look at the outcome of this tragedy, which Luke writes was dreadful and deadly for the stubborn Jews but most joyful for the pious and believing. For when the apostles see that the malice of the Jews is beyond cure, they shake the dust from their feet and pass on to Iconium, a city of Lycaonia. That they did this in accordance with Christ's command is plain, since we read that he said to his disciples: "If any do not receive you, when you go out of that city, shake off even the dust from your feet as a testimony against them" (Luke 9). And again, in the same evangelist, chapter 10, he says: "Into whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, going out into its streets, say: Even the dust of your city which clings to us we wipe off against you. Yet know this, that the kingdom of God has drawn near to you." The shaking off of dust was therefore a solemn and public symbol of curse, by which it was signified that the impious despisers of the gospel were to be scattered like dust, and that such a horrible curse from God hung over them that people ought not even to share in their dust who wish to be saved. The Lord wished this to be done as a testimony against such people, so that he might take away from them every excuse. For the impious usually pretend ignorance when they are pressed by the judgments of God. So that they could not do this, but would be overwhelmed by the testimony of their own conscience, the apostles had to depart not without public protest and a declaration of the punishment about to fall: as if they said, "We are innocent of your blood. For we have discharged our duty and announced to you the kingdom of God. Since you reject it with incurable impiety, we leave you to the just judgment of God, whose severity will be so great that it is not even safe to have dust in common with you. For, Christ being witness, in the last day the land of Sodom will bear a more tolerable judgment than you." But if the dust that clung to the feet of Christ's ministers is enough to convict and refute the despisers of the gospel, what, I beg you, shall we judge of their sermons, watchings, labours, and finally of the blood shed for the testimony of Jesus Christ? Let us apply these things to our own times, so that we may understand with what inexcusable impiety those pollute themselves who today reject the preaching of the kingdom of God with such wickedness. Let us therefore flee such a monstrous crime, and at the same time abhor the company of those whom we know to be defiled by it. For although such threats may seem almost ridiculous to them, they will nevertheless feel in their time that the faithfulness of God was not wanting.

units.la: Perfectionum finis laetus fidelibus.
units.tr: The joyful end of the trials for the faithful.

units.la: At non tam funestus fuit impijs huius historiae finis, quam laetus piis Christi cultoribus. De illis enim subijcit Lucas: Discipuli autem repleti sunt gaudio & spiritu sancto. Antea illos gaudisse fuisse audiuimus. Gaudium vero illud persecutione hac nec turbari, nec omnino auferri potuit, sed solidum illis manet & integrum. Vere ergo illud Christi impletur: Gaudebit cor vestrum, & gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis. Ioan.16. Gaudij vero author indicatur spiritus sanctus, qui ipsos animauit & consolatus est, ne sub crucis pondere deficerent, simulq; donis varijs illustrauit, quibus veterem ecclesiam floruisse, iam saepe diximus. Elucet vero in his inuicta spiritus sancti virtus, qua Christi fideles aduersus omnem mundi potentiam & auctoritatem sustentare & tueri potest. Consoletur nos illa hodie inter pericula, nec mundi terriculamentis nos frangi patiamur, qui antequam mundus hic conderetur, ex gratia electi sumus, nunc vero per euangelij praedicationem vocamur, ut fide iustificemur & glorificemur in Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But the end of this history was not as deadly for the impious as it was joyful for the pious worshippers of Christ. For Luke adds concerning them: "The disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit." We have heard before that they had rejoiced. Yet that joy could be neither disturbed nor wholly taken away by this persecution, but remains solid and whole for them. Truly, then, that saying of Christ is fulfilled: "Your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you" (John 16). The author of this joy is shown to be the Holy Spirit, who animated and comforted them, so that they would not sink under the weight of the cross, and at the same time adorned them with various gifts, by which, as we have often said, the ancient Church flourished. In these things the invincible power of the Holy Spirit shines forth, by which he can sustain and protect Christ's faithful against all the power and authority of the world. Let this comfort us today amid dangers, and let us not allow ourselves to be broken by the terrors of the world, we who, before the world was founded, were chosen out of grace, and now are called through the preaching of the gospel, that we may be justified by faith and glorified in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVI.
units.tr: Homily 96.

units.la: FActum est autem Iconij, vt simul ingrederentur Synagogā Iudæorum, & loquerentur sic, vt crederet magna multitudo Iudæorum simul & Græcorum. Qui vero incredduli erant Iudæi concitauerūt & exacerbauerunt animos gentiū contra fratres. Porrò multo tempore manserunt confidenter se gerentes in domino, qui testimonio reddebat sermoni gratiæ suæ, dabatq; vt signa & prodigia fierent per manus eorū. Diuisa est autē multitudo ciuitatis, & alij quidem stabant à Iudæis, alij vero ab Apostolis. Cum autem factus esset impetus gentium pariter & Iudæorum vnā cum illorum principibus, vt eos iniuria afficerent & lapidarent, re intellecta fugerunt in ciuitates Lycaoniæ, Lystram & Derben, & finitimam vndiq; regionem, & ibi prædicabant euangelium.
units.tr: At Iconium it happened that they went together into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up and embittered the minds of the Gentiles against the brothers. They stayed for a long time, speaking boldly in the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace and granted that signs and wonders be done through their hands. The multitude of the city was divided: some sided with the Jews, others with the apostles. When the Gentiles and the Jews, together with their leaders, made an attack to mistreat them and stone them, they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region, and there they preached the gospel.
