units.la: VIdiuimus in præcedenti Capite, vt ex spiritus sancti mandato Paulus & Barnabas emisi, euangelium inter gentes prædicare coeperunt: quibus ita successit negotium, vt breui temporis spacio Cyprum insulam, Pamphyliā & Pisidiam Christi doctrina & fide illustrarint. At felicem euangelij cursum nonnihil impedire visa fuit Iudæorum, qui Antiochiæ fuerunt, improbitas: quæ factum est, vt apostoli Pisidiæ finibus ignominiose eiecti, pedum puluere aduersus ipsos excutere coacti fuerint, quod vix paucis in locis factum fuisse legimus. Caeterum ne quis vel apostolos ignobili metu succubuisse, vel Christi regnum aliqua ex parte labefactatum esse putaret, pergit in cæpta narratione Lucas, & quid Pisidia eiecti fecerint, commemorat. Eorum quidem expositionem præsens locus habet, quæ Iconij gesta sunt, quæ tunc perstringemus, vbi de Iconio diximus, quæ ad huius historiæ cognitionem faciunt.
units.tr: We saw in the previous chapter that Paul and Barnabas, sent out by the command of the Holy Spirit, began to preach the gospel among the Gentiles. Their work went so well that in a short time they illuminated the island of Cyprus, Pamphylia and Pisidia with Christ's teaching and faith. But the wickedness of the Jews who were at Antioch seemed to hinder somewhat the happy course of the gospel. As a result, the apostles were shamefully expelled from the borders of Pisidia and were forced to shake the dust off their feet against them, something we read has happened in only a few places. Yet lest anyone think that the apostles had yielded to a base fear, or that the kingdom of Christ had been weakened in any part, Luke goes on with his narrative and recounts what the apostles did after they were driven out of Pisidia. The present passage gives their account of what was done at Iconium. We will explain these matters when we have spoken about Iconium, as they bear on the understanding of this history.

units.la: Iconium Lycaoniæ, in quam ex Pisidia Orientem versus tendenti, transitus est, ciuitas celeberrima fuit, sic Græco nomine dicta ab imagine, quam post Deucalionis diluuiū Iouis iussu à Promotheo & Minerua factam & inspirante vento animatam fuisse, poetarum fabulæ tradiderunt. Quare vt propter opes luxu perditi, ita propter simulachri veterem superstitionem, idololatriæ & impijs cultibus eius loci ciues addictissimi fuerunt, quales fere nostro seculo videre est eos, qui imaginibus à Luca depictis, aut aliqua alia non minus mendaci opinione clariss gloriari solent. Hic vero admirabilis Dei bonitas elucet, qui eiusmodi vrbem verbi sui splendore inuisere, & ijs qui infami idolorū cultu excidium meruerant, salutem in filio suo tam clementer offerre dignatus est. Nec aliam ob causam alibi quoq; Paulus, qualis ante Christum cognitum fuerit gentium conditio, diligentissimè describit, quàm vt inde pateat, omnem salutis nostræ ratione in mera dei gratia consistere, nec quicquam humanis meritis tribui debere. Fatebuntur hoc ipsum quicunq; in semetipsos descenderint, & quales olim fuerint, priusquam ipsis Christus illucesceret, probè expenderint. S E D præmissis istis, præsentis loci historiam videamus, qua narrat Lucas quid Iconij egerint apostoli, quis studij ipsorum effectus fuerit, vt q; fideliter domino suo seruientes noua persecutionum tempestas exceperit.
units.tr: Iconium, a very famous city of Lycaonia, lies on the route from Pisidia toward the east. It was called by a Greek name from an image which, the poets' fables tell, was made by Prometheus and Minerva at Jupiter's command after the flood of Deucalion, and was brought to life by a breath of wind. So the citizens of that place, given to luxury because of their wealth, were also utterly devoted to idolatry and impious worship because of the old superstition about that statue. One sees much the same in our own age among those who are accustomed to boast of images painted by Luke, or of other things no less false. Here, however, the wonderful goodness of God shines forth, who deigned so graciously to visit such a city with the splendour of his word and to offer salvation in his Son to those who had deserved destruction through their infamous worship of idols. Paul, too, elsewhere describes most carefully what the condition of the Gentiles was before Christ was known, for no other reason than to show that the whole basis of our salvation rests in pure grace of God, and that nothing should be ascribed to human merits. All who descend into themselves and carefully weigh what they once were, before Christ dawned upon them, will confess this very thing. But, these things premised, let us look at the history of the present passage, in which Luke tells what the apostles did at Iconium, what the result of their labour was, and how a new storm of persecution received them as they faithfully served their Lord.

units.la: Primò Synagogam Iudæorum ingressi esse, & ibi docuisse dicuntur. Quid autem docuerint, non exprimit Lucas, eò quòd iam ante integras conciones aliquot suæ historiæ inseruit, è quibus quid vbi vus locorum docuerint, facile colligi potest. Nec enim diuersa & inter se pugnantia docere potuerunt, qui expressum & euidens à Christo mandatum acceperant, & qui spiritu Christi duce & authore omnia agebant, quum veritatis spiritum esse, & proinde sibi ipsi per omnia consentire constat. Quid ergo eadem subinde repetere opus erat? Caeterum illud obseruatione simul & admiratione dignissimum est, quòd Iudæorum Synagogam denuò ingrediuntur, & inter eos docent, quos acerrimos euangelij hostes esse experti erant, & quorum conuersatio ipsis ante non multos dies Antiochiæ satis infeliciter cesserat. Est hoc præclarum constantia & fidei argumentum, qua in commissio sibi munere vsi sunt. Nam (vt in fine cap. præcedentis vidimus) Iudæis authoribus ita aduersus ipsos Antiochiæ magistratus insurrexerat, vt de vita periclitandum esset, & Pisidiæ finibus non sine publica
units.tr: First, they are said to have entered the synagogue of the Jews and to have taught there. Luke does not state what they taught, because he has already inserted several complete sermons into his history, from which one can easily gather what they taught in each place. Indeed they could not teach things diverse and contradictory to one another, since they had received an explicit and plain command from Christ, and since they did everything under the guidance and authority of Christ's Spirit, and it is agreed that the Spirit is the Spirit of truth and therefore always agrees with himself. Why then was it necessary to repeat the same things again and again? Yet this is most worthy of notice and wonder: that they re-enter the synagogue of the Jews and teach among those whom they had found to be the bitterest enemies of the gospel, and whose company had turned out quite unhappily for them only a few days before at Antioch. This is a notable proof of their constancy and faith, with which they carried out the office committed to them. For (as we saw at the end of the previous chapter) the magistrates of Antioch had risen up against them at the instigation of the Jews, so that they were in danger of their lives and were driven from the borders of Pisidia not without a public mark of infamy.

units.la: H infamiæ nota afficerentur. Deinde multa erant, quæ ipsos de Iudæorum salute desperare iubebant. Nam & prophetias nouerant vnà cum Christi minis, quæ vnanimi consensu regnum Dei ab ipsis ad gentes transferendum esse docebant: & repudij tempus iamiam instare, multis argumentis deprehendere poterant. Et quid obsecro sperarent de ijs, quos filij Dei sanguine madere, & implacabili vi ritatis odio laborare videbant? Pergunt tamen constanti fide à spiritu mandatum sibi munus exqui, ne ipsorum ignauia quisquam pereat. Nec dubium est, quin quod Ezechieli dicitur, illorum auribus insonueris: Cùm dixero ego impio, Certissimè morieris: atq; tu non monueris eum diserte, debortando impium à via sua mala, vt viuat: ille quidem morietur in iniquitate sua, sanguinem verò eius de manu tua requiram, &c. Ezech.3. At quod propheta dictum est, quodq; apostolos serio obseruauisse videmus, idipsum omnes alij sibi dictum putent, quorum curæ aliquos commendauit dominus. Quo in loco magistratus, parentes, & si qui alij sunt horum similes versantur. Qui omnes minimè ad mittere debent, vt hominum malitia superentur. Licet enim incurabiles sint, quibus cum ipsis res est, magnus tamen ex fideli & constanti studio ad ipsos fructus redibit, si vel suas duntaxat animas liberauerint. Deinde memorabile hoc Christiana charitatis exemplum est, quòd tantis laboribus suis, mul & periculis inimicissimæ gentis, & iam iam ob incurabilem malitiam perituræ, salutem quaerunt apostoli. Quia enim nunquam non bene sperat charitas, ipsi quoq; saltem reliquias aliquot, tanquam ex naufragio, saluari posse sperant. Hinc est, quòd Paulus pro illis indesinenter orat, & anathema fieri cupit, modò ipsi saluentur. Rom. 9. & 10. Eundem affectum in Christo cernimus, quem totus visceribus commotum esse, Matt.cap.9.testatur, cùm tanquam oues pastore destitutas, miseré dispersos cerneret. Idem illachrymauisse dicitur ad sanguinariæ Hierosolymæ conspectum, quòd illam incurabili pertinacia in exitium ruere, nec diem visitationis suæ agnoscere videret. Luc.19. Arguuntur hîs exemplis barbari illi & nimis crassi homines, quos vel alienâ mala ita nō tanguntur, vel priuatæ vindictæ cupiditas adeò impotenter abripit, vt propter pauculos aliquos, à quibus ipsis iniuria facta est, totam aliquam gentem odisse soleant: vt interim de illis taceam, qui cùm nullam odij sui causam allegare possint, occulto corruptæ naturæ vitio in odium præcipites feruntur, & aliorum malis gaudent. At quomodo Dei filij esse potuunt, qui à Dei ingenio tam procul absunt? Is enim homines saluos fieri, & in veritatis cognitionem venire cupit. 1. Tim.2. Idem propter paucos bonos totius vrbibus parcere solet, quas illi propter paucos malos euersas cuperent. At præcipua huius mali causa est, quòd ner Dei bonitatem, qua in nos mille mortes meritos vti consueuit, nec eiusdem fidem, qua suo officio sedulò fungentes remuneratur, vt par erat, consyderamus.
units.tr: Moreover, there were many things which might have bidden them despair of the salvation of the Jews. For they knew the prophecies together with the threats of Christ, which with one voice teach that the kingdom of God was to be transferred from them to the Gentiles; and they could tell from many signs that the time of rejection was now at hand. And what, I ask, could they hope for from those whom they saw stained with the blood of the Son of God and labouring under an implacable hatred of the truth? Nevertheless, with steadfast faith they went on to carry out the task given them by the Spirit, lest anyone perish through their sloth. Nor is there doubt that what was said to Ezekiel applies to them as well: "When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not speak to warn the wicked from his evil way, that he may live, the wicked shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand," etc. Ezek. 3. What the prophet was told, and what we see the apostles earnestly observed, let all others also consider as said to themselves, those to whose care the Lord has committed some. Here magistrates, parents, and any others like them are concerned. They ought by no means to give up, lest they be overcome by the wickedness of men. For although those with whom they have to do may be incurable, yet a great fruit will return to them from a faithful and constant zeal, if they at least free their own souls. Next, this is a memorable example of Christian charity, that the apostles, amid such labours, dangers and perils from a most hostile people who were now about to perish through incurable wickedness, seek their salvation. For since charity never ceases to hope well, they too hope that at least some remnants, as from a shipwreck, may be saved. Hence Paul prays for them unceasingly, and wishes himself to be anathema, provided they be saved. Rom. 9 and 10. We see the same affection in Christ, which Matthew 9 testifies moved him to the depths of his heart, when he saw them wretchedly scattered like sheep without a shepherd. It is also said that he wept at the sight of bloody Jerusalem, because he saw that she was rushing to destruction with incurable obstinacy and did not recognize the day of her visitation. Luke 19. By these examples those barbarous and excessively coarse men are reproved, who either are not moved by the misfortunes of others, or whose desire for private revenge carries them away so intemperately that, on account of a few by whom they have been wronged, they are accustomed to hate a whole nation. To say nothing of those who, though they can give no cause for their hatred, are hurled into hatred by the hidden vice of corrupt nature and rejoice in the misfortunes of others. But how can they be sons of God who are so far from the character of God? For he desires that men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. 1 Tim. 2. He is accustomed to spare entire cities for the sake of a few good people, which those men would wish overthrown on account of a few wicked ones. But the chief cause of this evil is that we do not consider the goodness of God, by which he is accustomed to treat us, who deserved a thousand deaths, nor his faithfulness, by which he rewards, as is fitting, those who faithfully perform their duty.

units.la: II. Effectus doctrinæ apostolorum.
units.tr: II. The effect of the apostles' teaching.

units.la: Videamus autem, quid suo tam flagranti studio apostoli effecerint, vt ex eo etiam arguantur, qui ex prosectus desperatione deficiunt priusquam rem aggressi sunt. Ita locuti sunt (inquit) vt cederet magna multitudo Iudæorum simul & Græcorum. Nunquam ergo sine fructu prædicatur verbum domini, & passim inueniuntur, qui illud rite excipiunt, vt fructificare possit, de quare aliâs diximus. Nec deest sua ope Deus ijs, qui in ipsius nomine laborant fideliter. Nam vt Petrus cum domini iussu retia proijceret, ingentem piscium multitudinem traxit, cùm antea nihil cæpisset, suæ rationis consilia secutus: ita quicunq; in Dei nomine ad illius præscriptum res suas instituunt, haud vulgarem laboris sui fructum, etiam vbi minimè sperauerant, reportabunt. Nostræ ergo ignauiæ simul & perfidiæ tribui debet, quòd hodie nihil aut parum proficitur. Cur enim præsenti ope illis adesse dominus, qui de illius gloria nihil soliciti, sua duntaxat, nec vnquam aliquid pro Dei nomine & publica salute audent? Simul verò etiam hoc loco patet, quod iam sæpe monuimus, irritos nimirum esse hostium Christi conatus, & illius regnum persecutionibus prouehi potius quàm minui. Docet hoc continuus apostolicæ historiæ cursus, si illum probè inspiciamus. Agnoscamus nos in his Dei sapientiam, nec facile de Christi regno desperemus, quando hostium suorum conatus tam feliciter eludere noluit, &c.
units.tr: Let us now see what the apostles accomplished with such burning zeal, so that those who give up in despair before they have even begun a task may be shown to be in the wrong. They spoke, it says, so that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed. The word of the Lord, then, is never preached without fruit, and everywhere there are some who receive it properly so that it can bear fruit, as we have said on other occasions. Nor does God fail to help with his power those who labour faithfully in his name. For when Peter cast out his nets at the Lord's command, he drew in a huge multitude of fish, although he had caught nothing before, when he had followed the plans of his own reasoning. So too, whoever sets about his work in the name of God and according to his instructions will gain a no small reward for his labour, even where he had least hoped for it. The fact that today little or nothing is achieved must therefore be attributed to our sloth and unbelief together. For why should the Lord be present with help for those who, caring nothing for his glory, look only to their own interests, and never dare anything for the name of God and the public good? At the same time, this passage also makes plain what we have often said before: the attempts of Christ's enemies are in vain, and his kingdom is advanced by persecutions rather than diminished. The continuous course of the apostolic history teaches this, if we examine it carefully. Let us acknowledge in these things the wisdom of God, and not easily despair of the kingdom of Christ, since he has been unwilling to frustrate so successfully the attempts of his enemies, etc.

units.la: III. Persecutio contra apostolos.
units.tr: III. Persecution against the apostles.

units.la: Porrò felicem regni Christi successum nouarursum persecutionis tempestas excipit, vt verissimum esse videas, quod de improbis mundi conatibus & ministrorum suorum laboribus atq; periculis dominus prædixit. Proderit autem omnium nostrum institutioni, si singulas nouæ huius Tragædiæ circumstantias penitius inspiciamus. Primò persecutionis authores nominantur, Iudæinimirum, quos sua incredulitate non contentos fuisse, sed simul gentium animos aduersus fratres, qui iam Christo nomen dederant, exasperauisse Lucas scribit: quod absque calumnijs fieri non potuit. Nec dubium est, quin turbarum et seditionum auctores esse dixerint, cum his criminibus fidos Christi cultores omnibus seculis petitos fuisse constet. Est autem horrendum plane, Iudaeos implacabile istud veritatis odium concepisse, et infelicia irae vasa factos esse, quos olim filios suos et sacerdotale regnum Deus nominare solebat. Nemo igitur maiorum dignitate aut vllis praerogatiuis confidat, sed humilitati studeant et Deum vereantur, qui non ipsi quoq; praecipitari volunt. Obseruemus autem hoc loco, quinam seditionu et turbarum authores sint. Non quidem qui euangelio credunt, sed qui huic credere dedignantur. Illi enim pacisi studeant cum omnibus hominibus quantum in ipsis est. Hi vero, quia lucem ferre non possunt, veritatis ministros falsis criminibus vulgo suspectos facere, et veritatem seditionibus opprimere solent. Interim turbarum causas miris artibus in pios transferunt, cuius rei exempla in Achabo rege et in Iudaeis, Christum coram Pilato accusantibus, extant. Ista vero in eum finem obseruare conuenit, ne facile ijs fidem habeamus, qui euangelij doctrina hodie etiam respub. turbari pacemq; publicam scindi calumniantur. Secundo, quales se in tumultu hoc gefeferint apostoli, docetur. Pergunt illi, nec primo impiorum conatui cedunt, sed longo tempore Iconij manentes, magna cum fiducia et libertate domini negotium agunt. Nec illis suo fauore ille deest, sed per miracula et signa testimonium reddit sermoni gratia id est, euangelio, quo nobis gratia Dei in Christo praedicatur. Docet nos apostolorum exemplum, ne impiorum conatibus facile cedant, qui Christi ministri esse volunt, etiamsi ingentes turbae insurrecturas esse videant. Nec enim aduersus Dei gloriam aliquid admitti debet, vt nobis cum mundo conuenire possit, quem prauum et adulterum vel degenerem Christus vocat, et proinde indignum esse docet, cuius tantam rationem dei cultores habeant. Mar.8. Interim quis miraculorum vsus fit, locus hic docet. Fiunt haec deo authore per ministrorum manus, non vt illis plus aliquid quam humanu tribuatur, sed vt apud incredulos, qui dei verbo nondum assueuerunt, doctrinae sigilla sint. Fatetur hoc de suis miraculis Christus dominus, Iohan.5. et 10. Nec alium illorum vsum fore docet, quae apostoli edituri sint. Vide Marc.16. Arguitur ergo hic duplex error, qui hodie passim regnat. Primus eorum est, qui a nobis miracula exigunt, quorum vsus magnus esse non potest inter Christiani nominis professores, quorum fides dei verbo inniti debet, quiq; apostolorum doctrinam iam olim miraculis abunde probatam esse fatentur. Alter Papistarum est, qui ineptissima quadam miracula pro diuorum inuocatione, transsubstantiatione, purgatorio et alijs id genus nugis contra apertam veritatem allegant. Atqui Dei verbo dogmata prius probanda erant, quod cum facere non possint, falsa et mendacia signa centseri debent, quaecunq; in horum assertionem afferuntur, qualia ab Antichristianis nouissimo seculo prodituta Christus olim praedixit, Matth.24. 1.Thess.2. Tertio, quousq; persecutionis tempestas progressa fit docetur. Diuisa est (inquit) multitudo ciuitatis, et alij quidem stabant a Iudaeis, alij autem ab apostolis. Non leuis ergo haec fuit paucorum duntaxat hominum commotio, sed totius ciuitatis populus interstina seditione scissus, in partium studia transfuit, quibus nihil in repub. pestilentius accidere potest. Atqui hoc illud est, quod Christus fore praedixit: Non veni vt mittere pacem, sed gladium. Nam veni, vt disidere faciam hominem aduersus patrem suum, et filiam aduersus matrem suam, et sponsum aduersus socrum suam, et inimici hominis erunt domestici ipsius. Matth.10. Hic tamen eorum, quae supra de incredulis, persecutionis huius authoribus dicta sunt, meminisse oportet. Nec enim proprie Christus disidiorum author est, cum pacem passim commendet, et inimici quoq; diligere iubeat. At tanta est impiorum malitia, vt quo magis vrgentur salutifera Christi doctrina, eo magis illi furant, tandemq; apertas inimicitias exerceant, quae res absque seditionibus transfigi non potest. Vt enim impij suam impietatem mordicus retinere voluntsita nec pijs suam statio nem, in quam a Deo vocati sunt, deserere licet, ne mundi amicitiam Christi gloria et animarum saluti praeferre videantur. Quae etiam causa est, quod non neutrales se in hoc schismate praebent apostoli, quamuis peregrini essent, quos in alienae repub. curiosos esse, Cicero quoq; prohibet. Quia enim quidam ab ipsis fletiffe dicuntur, facile patet, ipsos quoq; se partibus adiunxisse. Parum ergo apostolici sunt, qui vt primum diss dia in religione oboriuntur, summa prudentia esse putant, si neutrales fuerint. At Solon bonum ciuem esse negabat, qui seditione exorta, neutralis esse vellet. Et nos Christianos dicemus eos, qui quando de Christi gloria pugnatur, extra omnem teli iactum otiosi spectatores
units.tr: Moreover, after this happy progress of Christ's kingdom, a storm of persecution breaks out again, so that you may see how very true it is what the Lord foretold about the wicked endeavours of the world and about the labours and dangers of his ministers. It will profit all of us in our instruction if we examine more closely the individual circumstances of this new tragedy. First, the authors of the persecution are named: the Jews, namely, who, not content with their own unbelief, also, as Luke writes, stirred up the minds of the Gentiles against the brethren who had already professed the name of Christ. This could not be done without slander. Nor is there any doubt that they called them the authors of disturbances and seditions, since it is well established that faithful worshippers of Christ have been assailed with these accusations in every age. It is indeed horrible that the Jews conceived this implacable hatred of the truth and became vessels of wrath, though God once called them his sons and a kingdom of priests. Therefore let no one trust in the dignity of his ancestors or in any privileges, but let them strive for humility and fear God, lest they too be thrown down headlong. Let us observe, moreover, in this place, who the authors of sedition and disturbance are: not those who believe the gospel, but those who disdain to believe it. For the former strive to be at peace with all men, as far as lies in them; the latter, because they cannot bear the light, are accustomed to make the ministers of the truth commonly suspected by false charges, and to suppress the truth by means of sedition. Meanwhile they shift the causes of the disturbances, by wonderful arts, onto the godly, of which examples are found in King Ahab and in the Jews who accused Christ before Pilate. We ought to note these things so that we do not readily give credence to those who today also slander the gospel doctrine as troubling the commonwealth and breaking the public peace. Second, we are taught how the apostles conducted themselves in this tumult. They go on, and do not yield to the first attempt of the impious, but remaining a long time at Iconium they carry on the Lord's work with great confidence and freedom. Nor does he fail them with his favour, but bears witness to the word of his grace, that is, the gospel, by which the grace of God in Christ is preached to us, through miracles and signs. The example of the apostles teaches us not to yield readily to the attempts of the impious, if we wish to be ministers of Christ, even if we see great tumults about to rise. For nothing ought to be admitted that is against the glory of God, so that we might come to terms with the world, which Christ calls wicked and adulterous or degenerate, and therefore teaches is unworthy that worshippers of God should have such regard for it. Mark 8. Meanwhile, what use is made of miracles is taught by this place. These things are done by God as author, through the hands of ministers, not so that anything more than human is attributed to them, but so that they may be seals of the doctrine among unbelievers who are not yet accustomed to the word of God. Christ the Lord himself confesses this about his own miracles, John 5 and 10. Nor does he teach that they will have any other use, the things which the apostles are to perform. See Mark 16. Therefore a double error is refuted here, which now reigns everywhere. The first belongs to those who demand miracles from us, whose use cannot be great among professors of the Christian name, whose faith ought to rest on the word of God, and who confess that the teaching of the apostles was long ago abundantly proved by miracles. The other belongs to the Papists, who by most absurd miracles allege, against plain truth, the invocation of saints, transubstantiation, purgatory, and other trifles of that kind. But doctrines ought to be proved first by the word of God; since they cannot do this, whatever signs are brought forward in support of these assertions ought to be counted false and lying, such as Christ foretold would be produced in the last age by the Antichristians, Matt. 24; 2 Thess. 2. Third, we are taught how far the storm of persecution advanced. The multitude of the city, it says, was divided, and some indeed stood with the Jews, others with the apostles. This was therefore no slight commotion of only a few men, but the whole people of the city, split by internal sedition, passed over into the factions, than which nothing more pestilential can happen in a commonwealth. Yet this is what Christ foretold would happen: I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man at variance against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's foes will be those of his own household. Matt. 10. Here, however, we must remember what has been said above about the unbelievers, the authors of this persecution. For Christ is not properly the author of divisions, since he commends peace everywhere and bids us love even our enemies. But such is the malice of the impious that the more the saving doctrine of Christ presses on them, the more they rage, and at last they carry on open hostilities, a thing which cannot be carried through without sedition. For just as the impious are unwilling to give up their impiety, so the godly may not desert the station to which God has called them, lest they seem to prefer the friendship of the world to the glory of Christ and the salvation of souls. This is also the reason why the apostles do not show themselves neutral in this schism, although they were strangers, whom Cicero also forbids to be meddlesome in the affairs of another commonwealth. For since some are said to have fled from them, it is easy to see that they too joined the parties. Therefore those are little apostolic who, as soon as divisions arise in religion, think it the height of prudence to be neutral. But Solon denied that a man was a good citizen who, when sedition had broken out, wished to be neutral. And we shall call Christians those who, when the glory of Christ is being fought for, remain idle spectators beyond every range of a missile.

units.la: 4. Apostoli su sedere solent? Sunt bi certè tepidi illi, quos euomiturum se Christus minatur. Apoc.3.cap. Quarto idem præsentū huius, qui supra Antiochena persecutionis, exitus fuisse ostenditur. Tanto enim su- rore vnà cum primatibus suis insurrexerunt Christi hostes, vt periculum esset, ne lapidibus obrue- rentur apostoli. Quare Christi consilium simul et exemplum secuti, fugam ceperunt, melioribus ni- mirū temporibus sese seruantes. Nec tamen illis hoc vitio vertitur, quòd propter ipsos seditione or- ta fugerunt. Quid enim facerent, qui aperta vi rem geri videbant? Cumprimis autem obseruemus, quid fuga elapsi fecerint. Nec enim turpi ocio sese dediderunt, sed in Lystram et Derben profecti, e- uangelij doctrinam per omnem Lycaoniam longè lateq; sparserunt. Vt ergo fugere licet, quando nes Christi gloria, nec ecclesiarū salus in fuga nostra periclitatur, ne nos temere periculis obijciendo deū tentare videamur: ita cauendum est, ne ignobile timoris consilium secuti, officium deseramus, cui nos deus destinauit. Semper ergo dei gloriam, vnicum consiliorum nostrorum scopum, ob oculos habeamus. Ita enim fiet, vt omnibus periculis superiores, fidem simul et animas seruemus in Iesu Christo salua- tore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: 4. Do the apostles usually sit idle? Surely those lukewarm ones whom Christ threatens to spew out are such people. Rev. 3. Fourth, the outcome of this present persecution is shown to have been the same as that of the Antiochene persecution above. For the enemies of Christ rose up together with their leaders in such fury that the apostles were in danger of being stoned. Wherefore, following both the counsel and the example of Christ, they took flight, keeping themselves, of course, for better times. Nor is this charged against them as a fault, that they fled because sedition had been stirred up on their account. For what else could they do, who saw the matter being carried on by open violence? Above all, let us observe what they did after their escape. They did not give themselves up to shameful idleness, but, having gone to Lystra and Derbe, they spread the doctrine of the gospel far and wide throughout all Lycaonia. Therefore, just as it is lawful to flee when neither the glory of Christ nor the safety of the churches is endangered by our flight, so that we do not seem to tempt God by rashly exposing ourselves to dangers, so we must take care that, following a base counsel of fear, we do not abandon the duty to which God has appointed us. Let us therefore always keep before our eyes the glory of God, the single goal of all our counsels. For so it will come about that, rising above all dangers, we keep both faith and souls in Jesus Christ our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVII.
units.tr: HOMILY XCVII.

units.la: Et quidam vir Lystris sedebat, debilis pedibus, claudus ab utero matris suæ, qui nunquam ambulauerat. Hic audiuit Paulum loquentem. Qui intuitus eum, & videns quòd fidem haberet se saluum fore, dixit magna voce: Tibi dico: In nomine domini Iesu Christi surge super pedes tuos rectus. Ille autem exiliit, & ambulabat. Turbæ verò cùm vidis- sent quod Paulus fecerat, sustulerunt vocem suam Lycaonicè, dicentes: Dij hominibus similes facti descenderunt ad nos. Et vocabant Barnabã, Iouem, Paulum verò Mercurium, eò quòd is dux esset sermonis. Sacerdos autem Iouis, qui erat ante vrbem illorum, tauros & coronas ad portas afferens, volebat cum turbis sacrificare.
units.tr: And a certain man sat at Lystra, lame in his feet, a cripple from his mother's womb, who had never walked. This man heard Paul speaking. Paul, looking at him and seeing that he had faith to be made whole, said with a loud voice: "I say to you, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, stand upright on your feet." And he leapt up and walked. But when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian language, saying: "The gods, made like men, have come down to us." They called Barnabas Jupiter, and Paul Mercury, because he was the chief speaker. The priest of Jupiter, whose temple stood before their city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wished to sacrifice with the crowds.

units.la: Quando dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus, apostolos suos primò ad prædicandū euangelium emisit, nō alia de re illos diligentius admonuit, quàm de persecutionibus, quæ hoc mu- nere occupatis obuenturæ essent. Has enim assiduas simul & graues fore prædixit, non quidem vt inde timore cōcepto animis deficerent, sed vt fide aduersus prauisa mala armati, illa superare dis- cerent. Intellexerūt hoc electa Christi organa, Paulus & Barnabas, quos singulari spiritus mandato, ad prædicandum inter gentes emissos fuisse, supra vidimus. Ea enim constantia & fide in commissⁱ munere versantur, vt ex persecutionibus quasi nouis viribus aucti feruentiores ad officiū redeant. Nam Antiochia electi Iconium Christi doctrina illustrant. Rursum Iconio per seditionē pulsi, Der- bam & Lystram petunt, ibiq; docere incipiunt: & quidem euangelium prædicauisse dicuntur, ne quis illos in hostium gratiam doctrinæ genus mutauisse putaret. Omnibus verò imitanda proponitur bo- rum constantia, ne quid impijs verbi hostibus dent, qui Christi cultores videri volunt. Nec enim Christo dignus erit, qui degeneris huius & adulteri mundi amicitiam pluris quàm illius gloriam fe- cerit. Caterum quia miraculorum mentio facta erat, quibus apostolorum doctrinæ testimonium red- didit Deus, modò vnum ex multis Lucas commemorat, quod propter rei euentum, qui inde secutus est, cumprimis dignum narratu videbatur. Nos verò, vt uberior ex eius consyderatione ad nos fru- ctus redeat, primò ipsum miraculum cum suis circumstantijs, deinde illius effectum excutiemus.
units.tr: When our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ first sent out his apostles to preach the gospel, he warned them more carefully of nothing else than of the persecutions that would befall those engaged in this task. He foretold that these would be both constant and grievous, not so that their hearts should fail through fear, but so that, armed with faith against the evils foreseen, they might learn to overcome them. The chosen instruments of Christ, Paul and Barnabas, understood this; we have seen above that they were sent out to preach among the Gentiles by a singular command of the Spirit. They carry out their charge with such constancy and faith that, as if strengthened by persecutions with new vigour, they return to their office all the more fervently. Thus at Antioch they were chosen, and at Iconium they illustrated Christ's teaching. Then, driven out of Iconium by a riot, they made for Derbe and Lystra, and there they began to teach. And it is said that they preached the gospel, lest anyone should think they had changed the kind of their teaching to win the favour of their enemies. The steadfastness of these men is set before all to be imitated, so that they give nothing to the impious enemies of the Word who wish to seem worshippers of Christ. For he will not be worthy of Christ who has valued the friendship of this degenerate and adulterous world more highly than his glory. But since mention has been made of the miracles by which God bore witness to the teaching of the apostles, Luke now recounts one of many, which seemed especially worth telling because of what followed from it. In order that a richer fruit may come to us from considering it, we shall first examine the miracle itself with its circumstances, and then its effect.

units.la: Orditur ab eius descriptione, in quo miraculū editum fuit. Fuit is Lystrensis ciuis, non vno dun- taxat modo miser. Nam pedibus captus fuisse dicitur, idq; ab vtero matris, vt inde pateat, malum fuisse incurabile, qualia ferè sunt, quæ ex natiuitate inhærent. Additur, illum nunquā ambulauisse, Facit autem ad miraculi certitudinem tam diligens claudi descriptio, vtq; clarior eluceat Christi po- tentia, cuius nomine hic paulò post sanatus est. HIC verò obseruandum venit, quòd fere Christus per eos nominis sui gloriam illustrat, qui vel ex natiuitate incurabilibus morbis laborat, vel alioqui calamitosissimi videntur. Talem enim cæcum fuisse legimus, quem Iohan.9.cap.visu donauit. Talis paralyticus, qui post triginta octauū annum demum sanitati restituitur. Iohan.5. Talis etiam mulier quæ octodecim annis contracta fuerat. Luc.13. Tales damoniaci, qui indomitum furentes, ilo- ling
units.tr: He begins with a description of the place where the miracle was performed. The man was a citizen of Lystra, and wretched in more than one respect. For he is said to have been crippled in his feet, and that from his mother's womb, so that it is clear the ailment was incurable, as those are that cling to a person from birth. It is added that he had never walked. This careful description of the lame man serves to make the miracle certain and to shed clearer light on the power of Christ, in whose name he was healed shortly afterwards. HERE it must be noted that Christ very often displays the glory of his name through those who suffer from incurable diseases from birth, or who otherwise seem most wretched. For we read of a blind man whom he gave sight to, in John 9. A paralytic was restored to health only after thirty-eight years, John 5. There was also a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, Luke 13. There were demoniacs, raging and untameable, who were freed by his benefit, Matthew 8. These things serve first for our consolation, that we may not bear impatiently the adversities sent to us by God, since Christ knows how to draw from them the matter for glorifying his name. For far from being hateful to God on account of these things, we are made instruments of God's glory by bearing them with faith and patience rather. Next, these things serve for our instruction, that we should not rashly insult those whom God has afflicted with natural defects. For just as, according to the saying of Solomon, he who mocks the poor despises his Maker, so he who by untimely and biting mockery adds greater affliction to those who have been struck or afflicted by the hand of God involves himself in the grave guilt of impiety. For this reason the law pronounces cursed the man who dares to put a stumbling block before the blind or to curse the deaf. Deut. 27. Lev. 19.

units.la: {y} Miraculū clau- di sanati.
units.tr: Miracle of the lame man healed.

units.la: Claudi cõditio miserrima. lius beneficio liberati sunt. Matth.8. Seruiunt haec primum consolationi nostrae, ne impatienter serramus quae à Deo immittuntur aduersa, quando ex ijs glorificandi nominis sui materia Christus petere nouit. Tam enim abest, ut propter illa Deo inuisi simus, ut potius illa cum fide & patienter ferendo organa gloriae Dei efficiamur. Deinde ad nostram institutionem haec faciunt, ne ijs temere insultemus, qui à Deo naturae vitijs multati sunt. Vt enim iuxta Solomonis sententiam, qui pauperem ridet, Deum illius factorem contemnit: ita atroci impietatis reatu sese implicat, qui Dei manu caesi gatis aut afflictis intempestiua & mordaci illusione maiore afflictionem affert. Qua causa est, quod maledictos pronunciat lex, qui caeco offendiculum ponere aut surdo maledicere audet. Deu.27. Leu.19.
units.tr: The wretched condition of the lame man. were set free by his kindness. Matt. 8. These things serve first to console us, so that we do not bear impatiently the adversities that God sends, since Christ knows how to draw from them the material for glorifying his name. For far from our being hated by God on account of such things, we are rather made instruments of God's glory when we bear them with faith and patience. Next, these things serve for our instruction, that we should not rashly insult those whom God has maimed with defects of nature. For as, according to Solomon's saying, whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker, so whoever by untimely and biting mockery adds to the affliction of those struck or afflicted by the hand of God entangles himself in the grave guilt of impiety. For this reason the law pronounces cursed whoever dares to put a stumbling block before the blind or to curse the deaf. Deut. 27. Lev. 19.

units.la: Videamus autem, quid claudus hic fecerit, priusquam sanaretur. Audiuit Paulum concionantem, & se saluum fore credidit. Vnde patet de Christi saluifica virtute Paulum concionatum fuisse. Quam cum claudus miraculis multis confirmatam esse audiret, suae quoque restitutionis spem animo concepit, cui peculiarem aliquam spiritus sancti suggestionem accessisse, verisimile est, cum nulla extet vniuersalis promissio, quae omnibus in Christi nomen credentibus corporis properam valetudinem pollicetur. Voluit autem Lucas causam salutis ostendere, quando illum credidisse dicit. Fide enim nos tum ipsius Christi tum omnium bonorum ipsius participes fieri, omnis scriptura docet, & ipse Christus frequenter monet, quando aliquem saluaturus ait: Fiat tibi secundum fidem tuam: vel, Fides tua te saluum fecit. EST autem consyderatu dignissimum, quod hunc audiuisse prius dicit, & postea demum fidei ex auditu verbi conceptae meminit. Docet id unde & quo ordine homini fides obtingat. Hanc equidem dei donu esse constat, nec ab alicuius siue arbitrio siue facundia aut prudentia pendere. Nemo enim nouit patrem nisi filius, & cui filius voluerit revelare. Nemo quoq; nouit filium, nisi pater, & cui is revelare dignatus fuerit. Matth.11. Vtitur autem hominibus ministris & verbi sui organo Deus, quado homines fide donare instituit, iuxta illud Pauli: Ministri Dei sumus, per quos credidistis, quantum vnicuique dominus dedit. 1. Cor.3. Quicunq; ergo fide consequi voluerint, verbu dei audiant oportet. Quomodo enim credent, nisi audierint? Quomodo autem audient absq; praedicante? Fides etenim ex auditu est, auditus vero per verbu Dei. Rom.10. Quapropter ipse Christus duo haec coniungens, ait: Qui sermone meu audit, & credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam aeternam. Ioan.5. Seruiunt ista ad externi verbi commendationem, ne contempto illo aliud quoddam dei verbum imaginemur & incognitas sanctis fidei acquirendae vias scrutemur. Quod qui faciunt, fere diaboli insidijs patent, & mirificis illusionibus irretiuntur, ijsq; similes sunt, qui cum segetes à deo incrementum accipere audiunt, agriculturae studium omittunt, quam alendo humano generi Deus destinauit.
units.tr: Let us see, however, what this lame man did before he was healed. He heard Paul preaching and believed that he would be saved. From this it is clear that Paul preached concerning the saving power of Christ. When the lame man heard that this power had been confirmed by many miracles, he also conceived in his mind the hope of his own restoration. It is likely that some special prompting of the Holy Spirit came to him in this, since there is no universal promise that offers speedy bodily health to all who believe in the name of Christ. Luke, moreover, wished to show the cause of his salvation when he says that the man believed. For all Scripture teaches that we become partakers, both of Christ himself and of all his good things, by faith, and Christ himself often admonishes this when he says to someone whom he is about to save: "Let it be done to you according to your faith," or "Your faith has made you whole." It is most worthy of consideration that Luke says he heard first, and only afterwards mentions the faith conceived from hearing the word. This teaches us whence and in what order faith comes to a man. Indeed it is plain that this faith is a gift of God and does not depend on anyone's will, eloquence or prudence. For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son is pleased to reveal him. Likewise no one knows the Son except the Father, and anyone to whom he has deigned to reveal him. Matt. 11. God, however, when he determines to bestow faith on men, uses human ministers and the instrument of his word, according to that saying of Paul: "We are God's ministers, through whom you believed, as the Lord gave to each one." 1 Cor. 3. Therefore whoever wishes to attain faith must hear the word of God. For how will they believe unless they have heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. Rom. 10. Hence Christ himself, joining these two together, says: "Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life." John 5. These things serve to commend the outward word, lest, despising it, we imagine some other word of God and search out unknown ways of acquiring faith, as the saints did not. Those who do so are commonly exposed to the snares of the devil and caught in his wonderful delusions. They are like those who, when they hear that the crops receive their growth from God, neglect the labour of farming, which God has appointed to feed the human race.

units.la: Subiungit his ipsum miraculum Lucas. Paulus enim claudum hunc intuitus, fidei argumenta in illo deprehendit: quod absq; occultiori spiritus suggestione fieri non potuit. Quis enim ex hominis vultu, quo nihil & mutabilius est & fallacius, de fide alicuius certo iudicare posset? Spiritus ergo suggestionem fuisse oportuit, qua Paulus de claudi huius fide certior factus est. Mox vero ad illum conuersus, integram corporis valetudinem ipsi largitur: & ut vetustiora aliquot fideq; dignissima exemplaria habent, ait: Tibi dico, In nomine domini Iesu Christi surge super pedes tuos rectus. Nec enim credibile est, priorem particulam, qua Christi nomen allegatur, à Paulo omissam fuisse (ut in vulgaribus exemplaribus legitur) cum hic unus apostolis cum doctrina tum miraculorum scopus fuerit, ut Christo saluatori homines adducerent. Non caruit autem felici successu opus hoc, quod ex fide vtrinq; emanabat. Illico enim exiluit qui bucusq; claudus fuerat, & ambulauit. Ita vero apostolica doctrinae testimonium miraculo hoc Deus reddidit, sicuti heri audiuimus. Quia autem eiusmodi fere sunt Christi & apostolorum miracula, ut non obscure salutis & redemptionis nostrae rationem adumbrent, eadem in hoc etiam nobis breuiter perstringenda erit.
units.tr: Luke adds the miracle itself to these words. For Paul, looking at this lame man, perceived the signs of faith in him, which could not have happened without some more hidden prompting of the Spirit. For who could judge with certainty from a man's face, which is nothing more changeable and deceptive, whether someone has faith? It was therefore necessary that there be a prompting of the Spirit by which Paul was made more certain of this lame man's faith. Then, turning to him, he gives him complete health of body, and, as some older copies, most worthy of trust, have it, he says: "I say to you, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, rise up upright upon your feet." For it is not credible that the first clause, in which the name of Christ is invoked, was omitted by Paul (as is read in the common copies), since this was the chief aim of the apostles, both in their teaching and in their miracles: to bring men to Christ the Saviour. Nor did this work lack a happy outcome, which came from faith on both sides. For at once he who had been lame until then leapt up and walked. Thus God gave this miracle as a witness to the apostolic doctrine, as we heard yesterday. Since the miracles of Christ and the apostles are of such a kind that they obscurely set forth the manner of our salvation and redemption, these same things must also be briefly touched upon here for us.

units.la: Claudus hic omnium nostrum adeoq; totius humani generis conditionem adumbrat. Nam ut hic corpore debilis est, idq; ex matris vtero: ita omnes nos ad ea, quae saluti seruiunt, infirmi & debiles sumus, hocq; vitij nobis ex matris utero agnatum habemus, ut qui in peccatis concipimur simul & nascimur. Et si anteactam vitam consyderemus, nunquam nos ambulauisse videbimus, nimirum in Dei vijs, quae ad vitae aeternae haereditatem ducunt. Omnes quippe, ut oues errauimus, singuli[q?] suas vias secuti sumus. Isa.53. Et humani cordis figmenta ab ineunte aetate praua esse, ipse Deus testatur. Gen.8. Qualis ergo claudi huius conditio fuit quoad corpus, talis omnium nostrum est quoad animam. quanto illa corpore praestantior est, tanto etiam miseriorem nostram conditionem esse constat. Nulla ergo in nobis ipsis salus est, sed hanc extra nos quaramus: oportet illic loci nimirum, ubi illam clausus hic noster invenit. Audiuit is euangelium de Iesu Christo, et huius virtute se salvum fore credidit, votis quoque, sui per fidem compos factus est. Eadem igitur ratione nobis quoque ad salutem tendendum erit. Euangelium audiamus, et Christum Iesum, qui in hoc praedicatur, fide complectamur, et statim salvabimur. Is enim omni reatu in se credentes liberat, cum pro nobis peccatum factus sit, ut nos iustitia Dei efficeremur per illum. 2. Corinth. 5. Idem ille nos regenerat et immortali aeternoque caelestis generationis semine corrupta nostrae naturae vitiis atque infirmitati medetur. Hic ipse novis viribus nos instruit, ut qui ex nobis ipsis non idonei eramus vel ad cogitandum, in ipso possimus omnia, dum in ipso manemus, fructum multum feramus. Iohan. 15. Phil. 4. Et quia solus haec operari potest, solus quoque salvator censeri debet, nec alius miseris nobis iam periturus medicus quarendus est. Simul vero quod nam eorum, qui Christi beneficio curati sunt, officium sit, claudi exemplo admonemur. Is enim Pauli voce vocatus, illico exilit et ambulat. Ita nos Christo vocante, absque mora exiliamus e luto, cui nimis diu inhaesimus, et abnegatis infelicis ac caecae carnis operibus, ambulemus in viis domini. Possent haec latissime diduci, et exemplis pluribus illustrari, sed paucis his medicandi occasionem ijs praebuisse sufficiat, quos ardentius syncerioris pietatis studium inflammauit.
units.tr: This lame man represents the condition of all of us, and so of the whole human race. Just as he is weak in body from his mother's womb, so all of us are weak and feeble for the things that serve our salvation, and we have this fault inherited from our mother's womb, since we are conceived and born in sins. If we consider our past life, we will see that we have never walked, namely in the ways of God, which lead to the inheritance of eternal life. For all of us, like sheep, have gone astray, and each of us has followed his own way. Isa. 53. And God himself testifies that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth. Gen. 8. Therefore, just as this lame man's condition was in body, so ours is in soul. As much as the soul is more excellent than the body, so much more wretched, it is plain, is our condition. There is therefore no salvation in ourselves, but we must seek it outside ourselves, namely in that place where this lame man of ours found it. He heard the gospel concerning Jesus Christ, believed that by his power he would be made whole, and, having faith, he obtained what he desired. By the same method, then, we too must strive for salvation. Let us hear the gospel, embrace by faith Christ Jesus who is preached in it, and we shall immediately be saved. For he frees from all guilt those who believe in him, since he was made sin for us, so that through him we might become the righteousness of God. 2 Cor. 5. The same Christ regenerates us, and with the immortal and eternal seed of heavenly generation he heals the corruptions and infirmities of our corrupted nature. He himself equips us with new strength, so that we who of ourselves were not fit even to think, may in him be able to do all things, and, as long as we remain in him, bear much fruit. John 15. Phil. 4. And since he alone can accomplish these things, he alone ought to be counted Saviour, and we who are miserable and otherwise destined to perish need seek no other physician. At the same time, the example of the lame man reminds us what the duty of those is who have been healed by Christ's kindness. For called by Paul's voice, he immediately leaps up and walks. So, when Christ calls us, let us without delay leap up out of the mire to which we have clung far too long, and, renouncing the works of the unhappy and blind flesh, let us walk in the ways of the Lord. These things could be spread out very widely and illustrated with many examples, but let it suffice to have offered these few points as an occasion for meditation to those whom a more ardent zeal for a purer piety has inflamed.

units.la: Accedamus nunc ad alteram huius loci partem, quae miraculi effectum describit, qui apud Lystrenses longe alius fuit, quam Paulo propositus esset. Hic enim vt doctrina, ita miraculo quoque audi-tores suos Christo adducere voluit. Illi vero a Christo resiliendi occasionem inde arripiunt. Nam vetustis poetarum fabulis decepti, deos hos esse putant, qui humana specie assumpta in terras descenderint. Et fortassis succurrit de Iouis et Mercurij ad Lycaonem progenitore ipsorum defensa fabula. Nam hos ipsos caelitus descendisse clamant, illorumque nomina in apostolos ineptissime partiuntur. Barnabā enim Iouem esse dicunt, quod vel natu maior esset vel vultus maiestate grauior: Paulum vero Mercurium putant deorum interpretem, quod is coram populo verba faceret. Superuenit in tempore Iouis sacerdos, qui insanientes magis instigat. Nam adductis simul tauris et coronis, pro more gentilium sacrificium parat. E S T vero hoc memorabile cumprimis exemplum, quo docemur, quam proclive sit a vera pietate ad superstitionem et idololatriam hominum ingenium, quamque diffi-cile sit errores exuere, qui nobiscum vna cum aetate succreuerunt. Paulo ante enim Lycaones ipsi apostolum de Christo concionantem audiuerunt. Viderunt item in Christi nomine editum esse miraculum. Manet tamen in illorum animis vetus de deorum in terras peregrinatione persuasio, et turpissimi erroris occasionem inde arripinnt, vnde pietatis semina petere debebant. Atqui ineptè simul et impie illos fecisse omnes fatemur. At quanto ineptiores iis sunt Papistae, qui tamen Christi nomine gloriari consueuerunt? Fatentur illi apostolos homines quidem, sed Christi seruos fuisse, quorum opera ille in propagando regno suo vti voluerit. Interim eosdem illos in deorum numerum referre solent, et ea illis tribuunt, quae solius Dei sunt, quaeque abs que prophano veri dei contemptu nulli creaturae tribui possunt. Illos enim in periculis inuocandos esse docent, et officia inter illos non minori ineptiia, quam olim inter suos deos ethnici partiuntur, dum alium quidem vinctis, alium naufragis, alium iter facientibus, alium in igne periclitantibus saluatorē constituunt. Et ne quis ineptiendi modus sit, cum sanctos pro Christi nomine morte oppetijsse agnoscant, in eosdem tamen praecipuam gloriae Christi partem transtulerunt, dum illos suos apud Deum intercessores et aduocatos esse fingunt, ijsque vota sua nuncupant. Pudeat ergo nos in gentium stultitia confutanda laborem suscipere, cum maiore multo inter Christiani nominis professores inueniatur. Deinde idololatriae originem et progressum hoc exemplo spiritus sanctus proponit. Erroris quidem omnis fons fuit veri Dei ignorantia, et quod alia-rum gentium more Dei naturam et essentiam ad humana rationis calculum reuocarunt. Qui titulos deorum multitudinem et crassas simul atque absurdas de ijsdem opiniones inuexit. Secutus hunc est alius, quod nimirum cum multos esse deos putarent, temere proximam quamque personam sue rem, quae ipsis alicuius boni causa erat, in deorum numerum retulerunt. Hinc factum vt caeli sydera, elementa, animalia, homines item, quorum natales et sepulchra in terris monstrabantur, pro diis baberent. Falsos vero et fictitios deos sacris etiam coli oportuit. Instituti ergo dies festi, erectae aras, extructa templa, caesae victimae, positae imagines et statuae, et infinita alia priscae superstitionis figmen-ta. ta introducta sunt. Quibus omnibus sese duces & antesignanos præbuerunt Sacerdotes, qui inde honoris simul & quæstus materiam venabantur. Quòd si ista cum ijs conferas, quæ inter Christianos iam seculis aliquot facta sunt, nullum inter veterem & novam superstitionem discrimen invenies, quàm quòd deorum nominibus mutatis, ijdem ritus & eadem sacra exercentur, eoque detestabilior error est, quòd sub eorum prætextu & nomine dei patris & Christi gloriæ derogatur, qui sanguinem suum fundendum esse putauerunt, ut sua Christo gloria integra & salua maneret. Et plebs infici-am sacrificulorum turba adauget, qui inde sibi quæstum vberrimum propositum esse vident. Quàm vero ista sanctis dei cultoribus displiceant, sequens Pauli oratio abunde docebit. Discamus nos è scripturis veri dei cognitionem petere, illum colere in spiritu & veritate, illum solum in aduersis inuocare, & illi soli vbi periculis erepti sumus, gratias agere per nomen filij sui Iesu Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now come to the second part of this passage, which describes the effect of the miracle, which at Lystra was quite different from what Paul had intended. For here, just as he wished to bring his hearers to Christ by teaching, so also by the miracle. But they seize on it as an occasion to turn away from Christ. For, deceived by the ancient fables of the poets, they think that these are gods who have come down to earth in human form. And perhaps the fable recalled concerning Jupiter and Mercury and their ancestor Lycaon comes to mind. For they cry out that these very men have come down from heaven, and they absurdly divide their names between the apostles. For they say that Barnabas is Jupiter, because he was either older or more dignified in appearance; but they think Paul is Mercury, the interpreter of the gods, because he was the one who spoke before the people. Then a priest of Jupiter arrives at the right moment and stirs up the madmen even more. For, bringing oxen and garlands together, he prepares a sacrifice in the manner of the heathens. Now this is especially a memorable example, by which we are taught how prone the human mind is to turn from true piety to superstition and idolatry, and how difficult it is to cast off errors which have grown up with us along with our age. For shortly before, the Lycaonians themselves had heard the apostle preaching about Christ. They had also seen a miracle performed in Christ's name. Yet the old persuasion about the gods' wandering on earth remains in their minds, and they seize on an occasion of the most shameful error from the very place where they ought to have sought the seeds of piety. Yet we all confess that they acted both foolishly and impiously. But how much more foolish are the Papists, who nevertheless are accustomed to boast in the name of Christ! They admit that the apostles were men, but servants of Christ, whose labours he wished to use in spreading his kingdom. Meanwhile, they are accustomed to place those same men among the number of the gods, and they attribute to them what belongs to God alone, and what cannot be ascribed to any creature without profane contempt for the true God. For they teach that the apostles are to be invoked in dangers, and they divide the offices among them with no less folly than the heathens once divided them among their gods: one they set up as saviour of prisoners, another of shipwrecked men, another of travellers, another of those in peril from fire. And lest there be any limit to their folly, although they acknowledge that the saints died for the name of Christ, they have nonetheless transferred to them the chief part of Christ's glory, while they feign that these saints are their intercessors and advocates with God, and they make their vows to them. Let us therefore be ashamed to undertake the labour of refuting the folly of the Gentiles, when a much greater measure of it is found among those who profess the Christian name. Next, the Holy Spirit sets before us in this example the origin and progress of idolatry. Indeed, the source of all error was ignorance of the true God, and the fact that, after the manner of other nations, they reduced the nature and essence of God to the reckoning of human reason. This introduced the titles of the gods, a multitude of them, and gross and at the same time absurd opinions about them. Following this came another step: since they thought there were many gods, they rashly counted among the gods whatever person or thing nearest to them had been a cause of some good to them. Hence it came about that they regarded the stars of heaven, the elements, animals, and also men whose birthplaces and tombs were pointed out on earth, as gods. Moreover, these false and fictitious gods had to be worshipped with rites. Therefore festival days were instituted, altars were raised, temples built, victims slaughtered, images and statues set up, and countless other inventions of ancient superstition were introduced. Priests went before all of these as leaders and standard-bearers, seeking from them the material of both honour and profit. But if you compare these things with what has been done among Christians for several centuries now, you will find no difference between the old superstition and the new, except that, with the names of the gods changed, the same rites and the same sacred practices are carried on. And the error is all the more detestable because, under the pretext and name of these saints, the glory of God the Father and of Christ is taken away, although Christ thought his own blood had to be shed so that his glory would remain whole and safe. And the common people increase the number of this crowd of sacrificers, who see before them a most abundant profit to be gained from it. How much these things displease the holy worshippers of God, the following speech of Paul will sufficiently show. Let us learn from the Scriptures to seek the knowledge of the true God, to worship him in spirit and in truth, to call upon him alone in adversity, and to him alone, when we have been rescued from perils, to give thanks through the name of his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 98.

units.la: Porrò cum audissent apostoli, Barnabas & Paulus, disruptis vestibus suis insilierunt in turbam, clamantes ac dicentes: Viri, cur hæc facitis? Nos quoque ejusdem quibus vos malis obnoxij sumus homines: annunciantes vobis, vt à vanitatibus istis conuertamini ad deum viuum, qui fecit cœlum, & terram, & mare, & omnia quæ in eis sunt. Qui præteritis ætatibus permisit omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis ingredi. Quanquam non sine testimonio seipsum reliquerit, benefaciens, dans nobis de cœlo pluvias, & tempora fructifera, implens cibo & lætitia corda nostra. Et hæc dicentes, vix compescuerunt turbas, ne ipsis immolarent.
units.tr: When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their garments, leapt into the crowd, and cried out, saying: "Men, why are you doing these things? We are also mortal men, of the same nature as you, and we bring you the good news that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them. In past ages he allowed all nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without witness, doing good, giving us rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness." And saying these things, they scarcely restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them.

units.la: HOmo peccati lapsu non modò à pristina dignitate, ad quam conditus erat, excidit, verumetiam extincta est in eo rationis lux, qua deum simul & dei mente perspicere solebat, adeò vt ea quæ sunt spiritus dei naturali suo intellectu percipere non possit. Quæ causa est, quòd non suis modò figmentis seipsum seducit, verumetiam ijs perniciosè abutitur, quibus illum deus in veritatis cognitionem perducere studet. Exempla huius rei passim in omnium seculorum historijs extant: at inter illa cumprimis memorabile est, quod in Lystrensibus proponitur. His etenim euangelium de Iesu Christi prædicarunt Paulus & Barnabas, nec dubium est eam illos in prædicando adhibuisse diligentiam, qua alibi vsos legimus. Accessit doctrinæ miraculum, quo claudus quidam Christi nomine & virtute restitutus est, sicque ipso opere declaratum fuit, talem omnino esse Christum, qualis ab apostolis prædicabatur, humanæ videlicet naturæ restauratorem & redemptorem potentissimum. Quid verò istis apud Lystrenses effectum est, quos diuini spiritus luce adhuc destitutos cæca carnis ratio gubernabat? Non inde Christi cognitionem hauriunt, nec hunc glorificandi occasionem ex tanto miraculo arripiunt. Sed quæ humani ingenij natura est, proxima quæque, temere arripientes, in apostolis hærent, illos solos admirantur, illos miraculi authores vnicos esse putant, & nulla Christi Iesu ratione habita, illis sacrificia & diuinos honores parant. Atqui tolerabile videri poterat, si soli Lystrenses, quos gentilitia superstitionis consuetudo dementabat, peccassent. Sed eòusque progressum est huius exempli contagium, vt inter Christiani nominis professores, pietatis & religionis summa ratio in simili Diuorum cultu consistere putetur, quibus propter vetera miracula ab ægrotis, captiuis, naufragis & quouis alio casu periclitantibus vota nuncupari, aræ constitui, imagines fabricari, templa extrui & omnis generis sacrificia offerri consueuerunt: cum interim vix minima meriti Christi ratio habeatur, in quo vno illi nobis omnem salutis spem monstrauerunt. Poterat iSTorum hominum vesania multis confutari. Sed præsens locus illis confutandis sufficit, quo narratur, vt Lystrensium facto apostoli affecti fuerint.
units.tr: Through the fall into sin, man not only fell from the former dignity for which he had been created, but the light of reason was also extinguished in him, by which he once used to perceive God and the things of God's mind. So much so that he cannot grasp by his natural understanding the things of the Spirit of God. This is why he not only deceives himself with his own fictions, but also misuses those very things by which God seeks to lead him to the knowledge of the truth. Examples of this are found everywhere in the histories of all ages, but among them the one set out in the case of the Lystrans is especially memorable. Paul and Barnabas had preached the gospel of Jesus Christ to them, and there is no doubt that they used in their preaching the same care that we read they used elsewhere. A miracle also accompanied the teaching: a certain lame man was healed in the name and by the power of Christ. In this way it was shown by the very deed that Christ was truly such as the apostles preached him to be, namely the restorer and most powerful redeemer of human nature. But what came of this among the Lystrans, who were still destitute of the light of the divine Spirit and were governed by the blind reason of the flesh? They did not draw from it a knowledge of Christ, nor did they seize from so great a miracle any occasion to glorify him. Rather, as is the nature of the human mind, grasping rashly at whatever is closest at hand, they clung to the apostles, admired them alone, thought them the sole authors of the miracle, and, with no regard for Christ Jesus, prepared sacrifices and divine honours for them. Yet it might seem tolerable if only the Lystrans, whom the custom of pagan superstition drove out of their minds, had sinned. But the contagion of this example has spread so far that among those who profess the Christian name, the highest rule of piety and religion is thought to consist in a similar worship of the saints. To them, on account of old miracles, vows are made by the sick, the captive, the shipwrecked, and all who are in danger from any other misfortune; altars are set up, images are made, temples are built, and every kind of sacrifice is offered. Meanwhile the least consideration is given to the merit of Christ, in whom alone they have shown us every hope of salvation. The madness of these people could be refuted in many ways. But the present passage, which tells how the apostles were affected by the deed of the Lystrans, is enough to refute them.

units.la: Primò enim ipsorum gestus graphicè describuntur, quibus cultum hunc sibi quàm maximè displicere, abunde testati sunt. Nam vestes scindunt pro more gentis, qui summè dolentium & ob intolerabilem blasphemiam indignantium gestus fuit, vt in Ezechiæ & Caiaphæ exemplis patet, quorum ille quidam audiens blasphemum Rapsacis Chaldæi vocibus, animi dolorem & indignationem hoc gestu testatus est: hic vero, cum in Christi causa iudex sederet, eodem blasphemiæ impatientem animum egregiè simulavit. At nihil simularunt hoc loco apostoli, qui Christi gloriam omnibus privatis affectibus anteponere soliti fuerunt. Nec etiam vestium scissione contenti, in medias turbas, ceu incendium publicum extinguturi, insiliunt, quod ab hominibus peregrinis sine manifesto capitis periculo fieri non poterat. Præterea non verbis nudis, sed clamore et vociferatione rem agunt, ut omnis modestiæ simul et mansuetudinis oblita videri possint, quos in propria causa modestissimos et patientissimos fuisse constat. Ex hoc igitur exemplo, quod nam sanctorum ingenium sit, et quàm ferventi zelo pro dei gloria asserenda pugnent, colligere licebit. Intolerabilis hæc illis blasphemia esse putatur, si quis dei cultum, vel illis ipsis, vel aliis creaturis tribuat. Ad fœdus enim dei et eius delegem anxiè respiciunt, cuius hoc præcipuum caput est, ut ipsum solum deum nostrum esse agnoscamus, et ipsum solum veneremur. Et quia zelotem esse noverunt deum hunc, acerrimumq; sui honoris vindicem, ipsos quoq; zelo haud vulgari accendi oportet, si quando deo honorē suum palam eripi, et alio transferri vident. Exempla similia supra quoq; in Iohanne et Petro apostolis vidimus, cap. 3. et 10. Et eodem ingenio angelos etiam præditos esse constat, utpote fideles dei internuncios. Vide exemplum Apoc. 19. et 22. cap. Discimus ex hoc loco, quales censeri debeant, qui sibi ipsis divinos honores vendicare audent, quales olim Herodem Agrippam, Caligulam, Domitianum, Diocletianum, et alios eius generis homines impuros et naturæ monstra, fuisse legimus: et hodie Romanos pontifices videmus, qui et sanctitatis titulum, et peccatorum remissionem, et absolutam quiduis impunè agendi potestatem sibi vendicant, adeò ut à nemine sese reprehendi velint, etiamsi animas hominum caeruatim ad inferos deduxerint. Non possunt omnes isti evidentiori argumento testari, se à Christi spiritu alienissimos esse, cum apostolos Christi tantopere ab ea gloria abhorruisse videamus, cuius illa dio ita illi rapiuntur, ut eius gratia totum orbe non modò falsa doctrina seducere, verumetiam bellis horrendis commiscere non verentur. Præterea constat exemplo hoc, minimè ab illis Diuos coli, qui invocationem et externum cultum, quem sibi soli deus vendicat, in ipsos transferre consueuerunt. Quid enim isti homines aliud agunt, quàm quòd (quantum ipsis est) ignominiæ et iræ dei vasa ex iis faciunt, qui cum in terris viverent, se totos in hoc impenderunt, ut sua deo gloria salva et immota maneret? Nec putandum est, vel illos in cœlis ingenium suum, vel ipsum deum suam voluntatem mutauisse, qui olim per prophetam dixit: Ego dominus, hoc est nomen meum, et gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Isa. 42. Evidentior tamen omnium horum demonstratio in apostolorum oratione, quam mox subiunxerunt, patebit: cuius singulas partes ordine excutiemus.
units.tr: First, their gestures are vividly described, by which they amply testified that such worship greatly displeased them. For they tore their garments according to the custom of the people, which was the gesture of those who are deeply grieved and indignant at intolerable blasphemy, as is clear from the examples of Hezekiah and Caiaphas. Hezekiah, when he heard the blasphemous words of the Chaldean Rabshakeh, showed his inner grief and indignation by this gesture. Caiaphas, when he sat as judge in Christ's cause, feigned most skilfully an outrage at blasphemy. But the apostles here feigned nothing, for they were accustomed to place the glory of Christ above all private feelings. Nor, being content with tearing their garments, did they leap into the midst of the crowd, as if to put out a public fire; yet for strangers this could not be done without obvious danger to their lives. Moreover, they did not act with bare words but with shouting and outcry, so that they might seem to have forgotten all moderation and gentleness, though it is well known that in their own cause they were most moderate and patient. From this example, therefore, we may gather what the spirit of the saints is, and with how fervent a zeal they fight to defend the glory of God. This blasphemy is regarded by them as intolerable if anyone ascribes the worship of God either to themselves or to other creatures. For they look anxiously to the covenant of God and to his law, the chief point of which is that we acknowledge him alone as our God and worship him alone. And because they know that this God is a jealous God and the most fierce avenger of his own honour, they ought also to be kindled with no ordinary zeal when they see God's honour openly snatched from him and transferred to another. We saw similar examples above in the apostles John and Peter, in chapters 3 and 10. And it is well established that the angels also have the same spirit, as faithful messengers of God. See the examples in Revelation chapters 19 and 22. From this passage we learn what kind of people deserve to be judged to be those who dare to claim divine honours for themselves. We read that Herod Agrippa, Caligula, Domitian, Diocletian, and other men of this kind were impure and monsters of nature. And today we see the Roman pontiffs, who claim for themselves the title of holiness, the forgiveness of sins, and an absolute power of doing whatever they like with impunity, so that they wish to be reproved by no one, even though they have led the souls of men in droves down to hell. All these men cannot prove by more evident argument that they are most alien from the spirit of Christ, since we see the apostles of Christ so greatly abhor that glory for which these men are so carried away that they do not hesitate to seduce not only the whole world with false doctrine, but also to involve it in dreadful wars for the sake of that glory. Moreover, this example makes it plain that those are by no means worshipped as gods who are accustomed to have invocation and the outward worship, which God claims for himself alone, transferred to themselves. For what else do such men do, so far as it lies in them, than make vessels of wrath and dishonour out of those who, while they lived on earth, devoted themselves wholly to keeping God's glory safe and unchanged? Nor should we suppose that either they in heaven have changed their disposition, or God himself has changed his will, who once said through the prophet: "I am the Lord; that is my name; I will not give my glory to another." Isa. 42. Yet the clearer demonstration of all these things will appear in the apostles' speech which they went on to add, and we shall examine its individual parts in order.

units.la: Propositio et summa orationis est, non apostolos aut quamuis aliam creaturam, sed solum verum atq; viventem deum cœli et invocari debere. Quod cum simpliciter et absq; omni sermonis involucro dicere potuissent, interrogatione mentem suam exprimere voluerunt. Aiunt enim: Viri, ut ista facitis? Conveniunt hæc pulchrè gestibus, quos modò vidimus. Paucissimis enim verbis aperiete stantur, impium, illicitum et abominabilem esse cultum hunc, in quo hodie à plerisq; Christianorum profession ibus præcipua vera pietatis et religionis laus quæritur. Nec mihi quisquam objiciat, gentilitium cultum et fictitiorum deorum nomina apostolis displicuisse, qui fortassis æquanimiter laturi fuissent, si quis eo honore illos coluisset, quo hodie in papatu coluntur. Simpliciter enim cultum omnem abominantur, eiusq; honorem uni et soli Deo vendicant.
units.tr: The proposition and the sum of the speech is that not the apostles nor any other creature, but only the true and living God of heaven, ought to be invoked. Since they could have said this simply and without any wrapping of words, they chose to express their mind by a question. For they say: "Men, why are you doing these things?" These words fit well with the gestures we have just seen. In very few words it is made clear that this worship, in which today the chief praise of true piety and religion is sought by most professors of Christianity, is impious, unlawful, and abominable. Let no one object to me that the apostles disliked pagan worship and the names of fictitious gods, as if they would perhaps have borne calmly it if someone had honoured them with the worship now paid to saints in the papacy. For they simply abhor all worship and claim its honour for the one and only God.

units.la: Id verò in secunda orationis parte evidentissimè patet, quæ propositionis confirmationem habet duobus validissimis argumentis munitam. Primum à sua ipsorum persona sive natura desumunt, dicentes: Nos quoq; ijsdem, quibus et vos, malis obnoxij sumus homines. Quasi dicant: Stultum et absurdum est eos pro Dijs adorare et colere, qui eiusdem nobiscum naturæ consortes, et ijsdem malis nobiscum obnoxij sunt. Atqui tales nos sumus, homines nimirum, à quibus nihil humani alienum est. Nam et peccatores sumus, et propter peccata communibus, quas hæc vita fert, molestiis subiacemus. Hoc ipso argumento Petrus quoq; apud Cornelium, ante pedes ipsius prostratum, vsum fuisse audiuimus. Ait enim illi: Surge, nam et ego homo sum. At si hoc argumentum probè expendatur, hoc vno omnem creaturarum cultum euerti patebit. Si enim homines ideo diuinis honoribus indignitas dicantur, quia homines sunt, quid de aliis creaturis dicemus, quas omnes homine inferiores esse constat, utpote quæ in illius gratiam et seruitium creatæ sunt? A quo ordine ne angeli quidem excluduntur. duntur, cum & ipsi ministratorij spiritus sint, qui propter eos, qui salutis haeredes erunt, in ministerium emittuntur. Heb.1. Neq; hic illorum cavillum admittimus, qui hoc argumento Diuorum cultum minimè euerti dicunt, eò quòd illi iam malis omnibus exempti, & coelestis gloriae consortes facti sint. Nam vt fateamur, ex praesenti argumento nihil de illis colligi posse, infinici tamen scripturae loci sunt, qui illos non magis nunc, quàm olim cum in terris agerent, invocari debere docent. De illis enim apud prophetam sancti testantur, quòd nostrae fortis modo ignari sint. Isa.63. Et hoc beatitudinis ratio requirit, quae nulla omnino futura esset, si nostrarum miseriarum vel spectatores vel vindices esse cogerentur. Deinde immobile & irrefragabile stat verae pietatis & religionis principium, quo unum solumq; deum adorandum & colendum esse docemur. Deut.6. Matth. 4. Quòd si vero homines nec viui nec defuncti diuinos honores merentur, quis obsecro illorum stultitiam satis ridebit, imò potius deplorabit, qui hos in manuum suarum opera, mutas nimirum imagines transferre consuerunt? Alterum argumentum ab officio suo ducunt apostoli, dum se in eum finem aduenisse & euangelium apud ipsos praedicauisse testantur, vt à vanitatibus istis conuersi, deum viuum colere incipiant, coeli, terrae, maris & omnium, quae his continentur, creatorem. Ita vero non obscure fatentur, se oblatos ipsis diuinitatis honores absq; manifesto summae in deum perfidiae & impietatis crimine recipere non posse.
