Quis enim non perfidum dicat legatum & quouis supplicio dignum, qui sub Regis sui nomine & praetextu priuatam causam ageret, suamq; apud illos tyrannidem stabiliret, quos ad Regis sui obedientiam reducere debebat? Quis non sceleratu esse clamaret, qui alterius sponsam sub amicitiae veterumq; officiorum praetextu domum suam deduceret? At apostolos simul & reliquos verbi minist-ros, Christi legatos & paranymphos esse constat, eumq; officij illorum finem esse, vt ad fidei obedientiam homines reducant, & Christo despondeant, quos ille sanguinis sui precio redemptos sibi sponsam immaculatam esse voluit. Ita de suo officio Iohannes Baptista apud suos discipulos, ita alibi Paulus disserit. Ioban.3.2. Corinth.11. Et ideo in praesenti oblatos sibi honores tanta cum detestatione reijcit, quia se proditionis simul & lenocinij crimen subiturũ videbat, si quid tale admitteret. Haec vtinam obseruarent, quibus hodie cumprimis pium & religiosum videtur, si rude & imperitum vulgus ad creaturas relegent, aut etiam in hominum meritis salutem quaerere doceant.
units.tr: This is made most clear in the second part of the speech, which confirms the proposition with two very strong arguments. The first they draw from their own person or nature, saying: "We too are men, subject to the same evils as you." As if they said: it is foolish and absurd to adore and worship as gods those who share our nature and are subject with us to the same evils. But we are such: men indeed, to whom nothing human is foreign. For we are sinners, and because of our sins we are subject to the common troubles that this life brings. We have heard that Peter used this same argument with Cornelius, when the man fell prostrate at his feet: "Rise up, for I too am a man." If this argument is weighed carefully, it will be seen that by this one point all worship of creatures is overturned. For if men are judged unworthy of divine honours because they are men, what shall we say of other creatures, which are all known to be inferior to man, since they were created for his good and service? Nor are the angels excluded from this order, since they too are ministering spirits, sent out to serve those who will be heirs of salvation (Heb. 1). Nor do we accept the quibble of those who say that this argument does not overthrow the worship of the saints, because they are now freed from all evils and have become partakers of heavenly glory. For even granting that nothing can be inferred about them from the present argument, there are nonetheless countless passages of Scripture which teach that they ought not to be invoked any more now than when they lived on earth. For the holy men testify, in the prophet, that they are ignorant of our affairs (Isa. 63). And the nature of blessedness requires this, for it would be no blessedness at all if they were compelled to be either spectators or avengers of our miseries. Furthermore, the principle of true piety and religion stands fixed and unshakeable, by which we are taught that the one and only God is to be adored and worshipped (Deut. 6; Matt. 4). But if men, whether living or dead, do not deserve divine honours, who, I beg you, would not laugh at the folly, or rather deplore it, of those who are accustomed to transfer these honours to the works of their own hands, that is, to dumb images? The second argument the apostles draw from their office, when they testify that they came for this purpose and preached the gospel among them, so that, converted from these vanities, they might begin to worship the living God, the creator of heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them. And thus they plainly confess that they could not accept divine honours offered to them without the clear crime of the greatest treachery and impiety against God. For who would not call a envoy treacherous and deserving of any punishment, if he pursued a private cause under the name and pretext of his king, and established his own tyranny over those whom he ought to have brought back to obedience to his king? Who would not cry out that a man was criminal if he led home another man's bride under the pretext of friendship and old obligations? But it is plain that the apostles, and the other ministers of the Word, are the envoys and the friend-of-the-bridegroom of Christ, and that the end of their office is to bring men back to obedience to the faith and to betroth them to Christ, whom he willed to have as his spotless bride, redeemed by the price of his own blood. So John the Baptist speaks of his office among his disciples, and so Paul elsewhere (John 3; 2 Cor. 11). And therefore here he rejects the honours offered to him with such great abhorrence, because he saw that he would incur the guilt of betrayal and of procuring at once, if he admitted anything of the kind. Would that those who today think it especially pious and religious to send the rude and unlearned crowd back to creatures, or to teach them to seek salvation even in the merits of men, would observe this!

units.la: Porrò obseruatione dignum est quòd vanitate vocant cultum hunc apostoli, quem ipsis Lystren fes impendere conabantur. Inde enim colligimus, vanam & inanem esse omnem religionem, quae ex humanae rationis figmento citra dei verbum instituitur, maximè si non in vnum deum, sed in creaturas dirigatur, quibus cum gloriam suam Deus communem habere non vult. Consentiunt his, quae Christus ex propheta allegat: Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas hominum. Matth.15. Isa.29. Respondeant hic Papistae, quorum religio vt circa creaturarum cultum maximè versatur, ita non alio fundamento, quàm humanis traditionibus nititur.
units.tr: Moreover, it is worth noting that the apostles call this worship, which the people of Lystra were trying to offer them, "vanity." From this we gather that every religion which is devised by the invention of human reason, apart from the word of God, is vain and empty, especially if it is directed not to the one God but to creatures, whom God does not wish to share his glory with. This agrees with what Christ quotes from the prophet: "In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines of men" (Matt. 15; Isa. 29). Let the Papists answer this, whose religion is chiefly concerned with the worship of creatures, and rests on no other foundation than human traditions.

units.la: Deinde ministrorum verbi officium his verbis apostoli complectuntur, dum se in hunc finem praedicare dicunt, vt à vano creaturarum cultu ad vnum viuentem Deum homines conuertantur. Duo igitur haec coniungere debent fideles Christi ministri, vt & falsam religionem euertant, & veram plantent. Quò illud apud prophetam referri debet: Ecce ego constitui te vt euellas & extirpes, vt aedifices et plantes. Ierem.1. Vt enim in agricultura irritus erit labor omnis, qui vel arando vel rigando insumitur, nisi radicitus extirpentur quae segeti officiunt, & semen bonum rite spargatur: ita in animorum cultura infelicissime laborarint, qui non vtrunque hoc summo studio & cura coniunxerint. Peccatur autem bifariam à nostri seculi hominibus. Sunt enim, qui Antichristum & illius impia sacra sic abominantur: vt solis illis euertendis occupati, de syncerioris religionis restauratione nunquam cogitent. Rursum alij inveniuntur, qui verbi praedicatione homines veram pietatem edoceri volunt, abusus autem & superstitiones taxari non volunt, ne mundum hunc sibi inimicum faciant. Et sperant quidem posteriores isti sponte cessuras superstitiones, vbi veri dei cognitione homines per eeperint: non vident ante, eam nisi illis sublatis in animis hominum locum habere non posse. Vtrunq; ergo coniungant, quicunq; in religionis negotio cum laude & fructu versari voluerint.
units.tr: Next, the apostles embrace the office of the ministers of the Word in these words, when they say that they preach for this purpose: that men may be converted from the empty worship of creatures to the one living God. Therefore faithful ministers of Christ ought to combine these two things, so that they both overthrow false religion and plant the true. To this must be referred what is said in the prophet: "Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to pull down, to build and to plant" (Jer. 1). For just as in farming all labour spent either in ploughing or in watering is futile unless the things that hinder the crop are rooted out and the good seed is properly sown, so those who do not combine both of these with the greatest zeal and care labour most unhappily in the cultivation of souls. Yet men of our age sin in two ways. For there are some who so abhor the Antichrist and his impious rites that, occupied only in overthrowing them, they never think of the restoration of purer religion. On the other hand, there are others who want men to be taught true piety by the preaching of the Word, but do not want abuses and superstitions to be censured, lest they make this world their enemy. And indeed these latter hope that superstitions will give way of their own accord once men have grasped the knowledge of the true God; they do not see beforehand that the knowledge of God cannot have a place in men's minds unless superstitions are first removed. Therefore let whoever wishes to labour in the business of religion with praise and profit join both of these together.

units.la: Tertiò qualis à nobis Deus agnosci debeat, docent apostoli: Creator nimirum coeli, terrae, maris & omnium quae in his continentur. Talem nobis deum scriptura passim proponit, & talem ex apostolorum traditione in fidei nostrae articulis publicè profitemur. At qui creatorem agnoscunt, gubernatorem. bernatorem quoq; fateantur necesse esse. Nec enim fas esset, eiusmodi opificem deum fingere, qui operis sui curam omnem abiecisset. Et David illum in alto quidem habitare, sed simul omnia inspicere dicit, quaecunq; vel in caelis vel in terris geruntur. Psal. 113. Illius enim providentia fit, quod ad regni solia plebeij homines ascendunt, quod regna transferuntur, quod steriles foecundae fiunt, quod terra foetus omnis generis producit, quod maria crescunt & decrescunt, quod vicibus variis totus mundus mutatur. Deniq; adeo nihil a dei providentia excluditur, ut haec vagos quoq; avium volatus, flores agri & capitum nostrorum pilos in numerato habeat. Confutatur hic illorum delirium, qui mundum hunc aeternum esse docent, qui primus ad impietatem gradus est. Inde enim sequitur, incerti vicibus omnia ferri, & deum aut omnino nullum esse, aut otiosum circa caeli cardines vagari, nec tamen rare ea, quae in terris geruntur. Descripsit eorum hominum, qui ista fingunt, sedulam diligentissime David Psalm. 14. & 53. Sed ita hodie regnat, ut paucos esse videas, qui deum omnium creatorem & gubernatorem esse, sibi vere persuasum habeant. Sed eorundem finem Petrus in posteriori epistola capite tertio pulchre exponit.
units.tr: Thirdly, the apostles teach what kind of God ought to be acknowledged by us: the Creator, namely, of heaven, earth, sea and all that is in them. Scripture everywhere sets forth such a God to us, and we publicly profess such a God, drawn from the apostles' teaching, in the articles of our faith. But those who acknowledge the Creator must necessarily acknowledge him as governor too. For it would not be right to imagine a God who, as a maker, had cast off all care of his work. David says that he dwells on high, yet at the same time looks upon all that is done in heaven and on earth (Ps. 113). For it is by his providence that common men rise to the thrones of kingdoms, that kingdoms are transferred, that barren women become fruitful, that the earth brings forth fruit of every kind, that the seas grow and shrink, and that the whole world is changed by its various turns. Indeed, nothing is so excluded from God's providence that he does not count even the wandering flights of birds, the flowers of the field and the hairs of our heads. Here the madness of those is refuted who teach that this world is eternal, which is the first step to impiety. For from this it follows that all things are carried along by uncertain changes, and that God either does not exist at all, or wanders idly about the poles of heaven and does not care for what is done on earth. David carefully and diligently described these men who invent such things (Ps. 14 and 53). But today it so prevails that you will see few who are truly persuaded that God is the creator and governor of all. Peter sets out well the end of these men in his second epistle, chapter three.

units.la: Caeterum ad apostolos reuertamur, qui tertia orationis sua parte ea confutant, quae ipsis obijci poterant: nimirum longi temporis praescriptionem & vnanimem totius fere orbis terrarum consensum. Quibus argumentis hodie etiam contra veritatem pugnari solet. Indignum enim & absurdum videtur, tot seculis nationes omnes errauisse, & nunc demum veritatis lucem paucis quibusdam & obscuri nominis hominibus innotuisse. At paucis verbis ad ista respondent apostoli. Deus (inquiunt) permisit praeteritis aetatibus omnes gentes suis ipsarum viis ingredi. Inest bis duplex argumentum. Alterum est, gentes non in dei praeceptis, sed in suis viis et adinuentionibus ambulauisse, quare quod illae fecerunt, minime in exemplum trahi debere. Alterum est, dei permissione hoc factum esse, non quod ipsi illarum superstitio placeret, sed quod ita meruisset curiosorum hominum audacia, qui (ut alibi Paulus docet) humani ingenij acumine dei mysteria altius scrutati sunt, quam par erat, nec iis medijs, quibus ut fui cognitione reuelauerat, contenti fuerunt. Rom. 1. Docet vero locum hic, hominum vias in salutis negotio caecas, & proinde fallaces esse, cum animalis homo (ut initio huius Sermonis monuimus) non percipiat ea quae sunt spiritus dei. 1. Corinth. 2. Nisi ergo dei verbo subijciatur humani ingenij solertia, in veram salutis cognitionem minime peruenient, imo quo altius euolabit, proprijs freta viribus, eo graviori lapsu in mare errorum decidet. Enormis ergo illorum error est, qui religionis causam, & in hac obortas controuersias, humanis rationibus componi posse exististimant. Qui perinde faciunt, ac si quis forensium causarum iudices constituerent, qui auribus simul & oculis capti, nihil vel audire vel videre possent. Admonemur praeterea hoc loco, miserè omnes eos falli, qui in religione multitudinem allegant, & ecclesiam errare posse negant. Constat enim omnibus seculis maiorem fuisse eorum numerum, qui & falsis de deo opinionibus decepti fuerunt, & eidem non rite seruierunt. Vnus Noe cum sua familia, quae non plures octo personis continebat, diuersam a toto mundo de deo & religione sententiam sequitur, eiusq; testem & vindicem habet ipsum deum. Et patriarchae pauciss mi numero, ceu stellae quaedam obscuro & nubilo caelo micantes, per incredulas gentes sparsi fuerunt. Quid vero de Israele, dei peculio, dicemus? Nonne illos vna cum suo antistite sut pitersimul & impie errauisse legimus, quando contra dei praeceptum vitulum conflare, & maiestatem dei imagine bouis (ut propheta ait) comedentis fenum, mutare ausi sunt? Psal. 106. Et ut de nouo dei populo dicamus, nonne hunc Christus pusillum gregem vocat, & paucos esse dicit, qui per angustam portam ad salutem ingrediantur? Luc. 12. Matth. 7. Quid, quod Paulus ex ecclesia graues lupos exorituros esse dicit, qui non parcant, idemq; Antichristi sedem in ipso dei templo sub limen fore docet? Act. 20. 2. Thessal. 2. Desinant ergo nobis multitudinis suffragia & ecclesiae authoritatem obijcere, qui manifestae veritati aduersantur. Dei verbum & Christi vocem requirimus, quae vnica in dijudicandis doctrinae controuersijs regula esse debet.
units.tr: But let us return to the apostles, who in the third part of their speech refute the objections that could be raised against them, namely the argument from long prescription and the almost unanimous agreement of nearly the whole world. Today too the truth is often opposed with these arguments. It seems unworthy and absurd that all nations should have erred for so many centuries, and that the light of truth should only now have become known through a few men of obscure name. The apostles answer these points in a few words: God, they say, allowed all nations in past ages to walk in their own ways. There is a double argument here. The first is that the nations walked not by God's commandments but by their own ways and inventions, so that what they did should in no way be taken as an example. The second is that this happened by God's permission, not because he approved of their superstition, but because the boldness of curious men deserved it. As Paul teaches elsewhere, these men searched the mysteries of God more deeply with the keenness of human intellect than was fitting, and were not content with the means by which he had revealed himself for knowledge. Rom. 1. This passage teaches that the ways of men are blind in the matter of salvation, and therefore deceptive, since the natural man (as we noted at the beginning of this sermon) does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God. 1 Cor. 2. Unless human ingenuity is subjected to the Word of God, it will by no means reach true knowledge of salvation; indeed, the higher it flies, trusting in its own strength, the more gravely it will fall into the sea of error. Therefore the error of those is enormous who think that the cause of religion, and the controversies that arise in it, can be settled by human reasons. They act just as if someone were to appoint judges for legal cases who, deprived of both hearing and sight, could neither hear nor see anything. We are also warned in this place that all those are miserably deceived who appeal to the multitude in religion and deny that the Church can err. For it is plain that in every age those who were deceived by false opinions about God, and did not worship him rightly, have been the greater number. Noah alone, with his family, which numbered no more than eight persons, followed an opinion about God and religion different from the whole world, and had God himself as witness and defender. And the patriarchs, in a very small number, were scattered among unbelieving nations like certain stars shining in a dark and cloudy sky. But what shall we say of Israel, God's own people? Do we not read that they, together with their high priest, also erred both foolishly and impiously, when they dared against God's command to cast a calf and to exchange the majesty of God for the image of an ox eating grass (as the prophet says)? Ps. 106. And to speak of the new people of God: does not Christ call this a little flock, and say that few are those who enter through the narrow gate to salvation? Luke 12. Matt. 7. And what of Paul, who says that grievous wolves will arise from the Church, which will spare no one, and who also teaches that the seat of Antichrist will be placed right in the temple of God? Acts 20. 2 Thess. 2. Let those who oppose manifest truth therefore cease to throw in our faces the votes of the multitude and the authority of the Church. We seek the Word of God and the voice of Christ, which alone ought to be the rule for judging controversies of doctrine.

units.la: Porrò ne quis idololatriae & superstitionis gentilitiae culpam in deum reijceret, cum ille permiserit, vt suis ipsarum viis gentes ingrederentur, praeoccupatione utuntur apostoli, qua deum extra omnem culpam constituunt. Is enim (inquiunt) nunquam non de se suaq; natura & voluntate testatus est, & per visibilia opera sua invisibilem suam essentiam & naturam mundo declarauit. Omissis autem maioribus illis & stupendis dei operibus, quae humani ingenij captum superant, ea in medium adduadducunt, quae & quotidiana sunt, & hominum bono fiunt, ut vel eo nomine quemuis in supremi illius numinis diligentem considerationem rapere possint. Quis enim adeo caecus aut hebes est, ut tempestatum vices & qui inde enascuntur frugum proventus, non videat? Quis illa fortuito fieri dicat, quae certis legibus ita astringuntur, ut portentu putetur, si quid praeter solitum naturae cursum fiat? Et quanta obsecro ingratitudo est, deum non agnoscere, qui non necessaria modo, verum etiam quae voluptati & laetitiae serviunt, nobis liberalissime largitur? Aut quam excusationem ignorantiae sua afferre possunt, qui quoties cibum capiunt, de Dei in nos beneficentia admonentur? EST autem in hoc loco utilis doctrina, & ad quorundam superstitiosam curiositatem cohercendam cumprimis necessaria: in quem authorem caelestes influentiae & terrae proventus referri debeant. De Deo creatore dicunt apostoli, quod is nobis de caelo pluvias mittat & tempora fructifera, quod nos cibo simul & laetitia impleat. Consentiunt hi, quae passim scripturae tradunt. David certe inter dei opera hoc ipsum diligenter connumerat, cum ait: Ipse operit caelum nubibus, & parat pluviam terrae, & producit foenum in montibus. Ipse dat pecori pastum suum, & pullis corvorum invocantibus se. Ipse dat nivem tanquam lanam, & pruinam spargit ut cinerem. Proiicit glaciem suam ut laminas, missoque verbo suo liquefacit ea, & vento suo afflat, ut aquae fluant. Psal. 147. Item: Rigat montes e suis caenaculis, & de fructu operum eius satura fit terra. Producit foenum pecori, & herbam ad usum hominis, ut proferat panem de terra, &c. Psal. 104. Omitto infinita alia, quae adduci poterant. Temperat autem haec pro sua iusta voluntate deus, dum in lege sua ambulantibus felicem & uberem rerum proventum, immorigeris autem sterilitatem immittit: cuius rei luculenta testimonia exstant, Levit. 26. & Deut. 28. cap. Confutantur hic astrologi, qui dum syderum positionibus ista tribuunt, prophana deorum nomina, adeoque totum pene gentilismum revocant. Arguuntur etiam superstitiosi, qui horum authores Dijvos faciunt, a quibus etiam pluvias & tempestates, instituit in eum finem publicis sacris, petere solent. Videant utrique quid dominus apud Hoseam Cap. 2. loquatur. Nos vero apostolorum doctrinam secuti, unum solumque deum horum omnium authorem & gubernatorem agnoscamus, qui nec syderum legibus astringitur, nec naturae subiacet, sed pro sua bona voluntate iusto iudicio omnia moderatur.
units.tr: Moreover, lest anyone should lay the blame for idolatry and gentile superstition on God, on the ground that he allowed the nations to walk in their own ways, the apostles anticipate this objection and place God beyond all blame. He, they say, has never ceased to bear witness of himself and of his nature and will, and through his visible works has made known his invisible essence and nature to the world. Setting aside those greater and astonishing works of God that surpass the grasp of human understanding, they bring forward those that are both everyday and done for the good of men, so that they may draw anyone at all to a diligent consideration of that supreme Deity, even on this account alone. For who is so blind or dull that he does not see the changes of the weather and the crops of fruit that come from them? Who would say that those things happen by chance which are bound by such fixed laws that, if anything happens beyond the usual course of nature, it is considered a portent? And, I beg you, how great is the ingratitude of not acknowledging God, who so generously gives us not only necessities but also things that serve pleasure and delight? Or what excuse of ignorance can they offer who, whenever they take food, are reminded of God's kindness towards us? Now this passage contains useful teaching, and is especially necessary for restraining the superstitious curiosity of some people: to whom the heavenly influences and the produce of the earth ought to be attributed. The apostles say that God, the Creator, sends us rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, and fills us with food and gladness. What the Scriptures teach everywhere agrees with this. David certainly, among God's works, diligently counts this very thing when he says: He covers the heaven with clouds, and prepares rain for the earth, and makes grass grow on the mountains. He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens that call upon him. He gives snow like wool, and scatters hoarfrost like ashes. He casts forth his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? He sends forth his word and melts them; he causes his wind to blow and the waters flow. Ps. 147. Likewise: He waters the mountains from his upper chambers, and the earth is satisfied with the fruit of his works. He causes grass to grow for the cattle, and herbs for the use of man, that he may bring forth bread from the earth, etc. Ps. 104. I pass over countless other passages that could be cited. God, moreover, tempers these things according to his just will: he gives a happy and abundant produce of things to those who walk in his law, but sends barrenness upon the disobedient. Clear testimonies of this matter exist in Lev. 26. and in Deut. 28. Here the astrologers are refuted, who, while they attribute these things to the positions of the stars, revive profane names of gods, and thus almost the whole of paganism. Superstitious people are also rebuked, who make the authors of these things into gods, and from whom they are accustomed to seek rains and storms by public sacred rites for that purpose. Let both groups consider what the Lord says through Hosea in chapter 2. But we, following the doctrine of the apostles, acknowledge one God alone as the author and governor of all these things, who is bound neither by the laws of the stars nor subject to nature, but by his good will and just judgment governs all things.

units.la: Sed effectum apostolicae concionis Lucas exponit, tamque graui verborum simul & sententiarum pondere vix prohiberi potuisse Lystrenses testatur, quo minus ipsis sacrificarent. Adeo concum ax est in retinendis superstitionibus humanum genus. Maior tamen nostri seculi contumacia est. Potuerunt isti una concione cohercer i, cum bodie passim inveniantur, quos multorum annorum labores & quotidianae conciones, ut ad mentem redeant, movere non possunt. Oremus itaque deum patrem, ut suo spiritu tam illos quam nos illuminatos, in veram & salutiferam suijpsius & filij sui, Iesu Christi, cognitionem perducat: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But Luke sets out the effect of the apostolic sermon, and testifies that the Lystrians could scarcely be restrained, by such weighty words and arguments, from sacrificing to them. So eager is the human race in holding on to superstitions. Yet the obstinacy of our own age is greater. Those men could be restrained by a single sermon, whereas today there are found everywhere people whom the labours of many years and daily sermons cannot move to come to their senses. Let us therefore pray to God the Father that, by his Spirit, he may lead both them and us, enlightened, into the true and saving knowledge of himself and of his Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA XCIX.
units.tr: HOMILY XCIX.

units.la: Superuenerunt autem ab Antiochia & Iconio Iudaei, qui cum persuasissent turbis, & Paulum lapidassent, extraxerunt eum extra vrbem, existimantes ipsum esse mortuum. Circundantibus autem eum discipulis surrexit & ingressus est ciuitatem, & postridie cum Barnaba exiuit Derben: cumque euangelizauissent illi ciuitati, multosque fore mauissent discipulos, reuersi sunt Lystram, & Iconium, & Antiochiam, denuo confirmantes animas discipulorum, & exhortantes ut perseuerarent in fide, & quod per multas afflictiones oporteat nos ingredi in regnum Dei.
units.tr: Then Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, who won over the crowds, stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered around him, he rose and entered the city. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. After they had preached the gospel to that city and made many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and saying that we must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions.

units.la: QVemadmodum dominus noster Iesus Christus humani generis salutem indefinenti studio promouere & tueri contendit: ita vicissim totus in hoc est Satan, ut euerso Christi regno, a salutis via homines retrahat. Exemplum eius rei cumprimis euidens in praesenti historia proponitur. Nam apostolis apud Lystrenses praedicantibus, primum superstitiosos quosdam Satan commouet, quibus diuinos honores impendere instituerunt, nec dubium est boc etiam quaesiisse malignum humana salutis hostem, ut ambitione tentati apostoli succumberent, cum hoc ipso ariete Christum antea oppugnare ausus fuerit. Sed non successit conatus hic. Olfaciunt enim diaboli artes Paulus & Barnabas, & maiori quàm antea zelo inflammati, veri dei gloriam constantissimè asserunt: sic ut iam Lystrenses illius cognitionem gustare & ab auctis erroribus discedere inciperent. Quare mox alia via Satan rem aggreditur, & veritatis hostes apertos armat, quorum opera alibi quoque apostolos loco cedere coegerat. Nam Iudaeos Antiochia & Iconio euocat, qui calumnijs suis Lystrensium animos ita aduersus apostolos commouent, ut furiose in illos insurgentes, Paulum lapidarent, & seminecem extra urbis suae portas extraherent. Et praecipuus quidem totius historiae usus est, ut sata nae artes, quibus ille veritatem oppugnat, obseruare, & aduersus eosdem apostolorum constantiam imitari discamus. Quia vero alia simul insunt, quae nostrae tum institutioni tum consolationi seruire possunt, singulas huius certaminis partes inspicere, non parum proderit.
units.tr: Just as our Lord Jesus Christ strives with unfailing zeal to advance and guard the salvation of mankind, so in turn Satan is wholly intent on overturning Christ's kingdom and drawing men away from the way of salvation. A clear example of this is set before us in the present story. When the apostles were preaching at Lystra, Satan first stirred up certain superstitious people, who began to pay divine honours to them. There is no doubt that the malicious enemy of human salvation also aimed at this, so that the apostles, tempted by ambition, might give way, since he had earlier dared to attack Christ with this very battering-ram. But this attempt did not succeed. For Paul and Barnabas detected the devil's arts, and, inflamed with greater zeal than before, they firmly asserted the glory of the true God, so that the Lystrans now began to taste the knowledge of him and to turn away from their increased errors. Therefore Satan soon approached the matter by another route, and armed the open enemies of the truth, by whose efforts he had also forced the apostles to yield ground elsewhere. For he summoned Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who by their slanders so stirred up the minds of the Lystrans against the apostles that, rising furiously against them, they stoned Paul and dragged him half dead outside the gates of their city. The chief use of the whole story is that we learn to observe the crafty arts by which he assails the truth, and to imitate the constancy of the apostles against them. But since other matters are also contained in it which can serve both our instruction and our consolation, it will be of no small benefit to examine the separate parts of this conflict.

units.la: Primò igitur turbarum authores producuntur, qui etiam antea apostolis negotium fecerunt, Iudaei nimirum, de quorum horribili caecitate & deplorata aduersus Christum pugnandi contumacia iam saepe dictum est. Hic vero haud vulgare Satanae stratagema obseruandum venit, quod illos Antiochia & Iconio, ceu veteranos milites, adducit. Curat enim ut ubiq; organa sua habeat, quibus Christi regnum euertere, suum vero stabilire possit. Quare si alicubi homines suis conatibus parum commodos esse viderit, alios aliunde adducit, quorum industria & tura ratis suas conficiat. Possent huius rei multa exempla recenseri, si veteribus exemplis opus esset, ubi quotidiana abunde suppeterunt. Nam eiusdem artis est, quòd hodie episcopos & male feriatos monachos submittit, qui passim obrepentes impiorum consilia adiuuant, rude & ignobile vulgus calumnijs aduersus Christi doctrinam exasperant, nobiliores promissis & interdum donis solicitant, toti denique in hoc incumbunt, ut renascentis euangelij fructum in berba suffocent. At qui hoc obseruauisse vehementer proderit, ut non minori studio & zelo, pio tamen & ab omni fraude alieno, ipsi quoq; pro veritatis defensione & propagatione inuigilemus.
units.tr: First, then, the instigators of the uproar are brought forward: the Jews, who had also caused trouble for the apostles before, of whose dreadful blindness and hardened obstinacy in fighting against Christ we have often spoken already. Here we must notice a stratagem of Satan that is not commonplace: he brings in the Jews from Antioch and Iconium as if they were veteran soldiers. For he takes care to have his instruments everywhere, by which he can overturn Christ's kingdom and establish his own. Therefore, if he sees that men are not well suited to his purposes in one place, he brings others from elsewhere, by whose diligence he may carry out his schemes. Many examples of this could be listed, if older examples were needed, but daily ones are plentiful. For it is the same art that today he sends in bishops and ill-disciplined monks, who creep about everywhere and assist the counsels of the impious, who inflame the rude and common crowd with slanders against Christ's teaching, who entice the nobler sort with promises and sometimes with gifts, and who, in short, devote themselves wholly to choking the fruit of the renewed gospel while it is still in the blade. It will greatly profit us to have observed this, so that we too may watch over the defence and spread of the truth with no less zeal and effort, yet a zeal that is pious and free from all deceit.

units.la: Secundò vulgi inconstantia nobis consideranda venit. Nam qui paulò ante apostolos decorum habebant, & illis sacra parabant, repentè ab hominibus externis & quidem diuersa religionis statoribus, persuasi, ijsdem crudelem necem moliuntur. Quid ergo illos facturos fuisse putas, si vel a suae gentis proceribus, vel Romanis praesidibus solicitati fuissent? At non tam turpis quàm vulgaris & passim obuia est ista vulgi leuitas, quae & beneficiorum acceptorum obliuionem parit, & benefactores atrocibus iniurijs adobruit. Huius exemplum in Aegyptijs ternitur, qui cum Iosephi consilijs non modò famis tempore seruati, verumetiam in summum potentiae & gloriae fastigium tuli essent, eiusdem tamen vix fato functi memoriam plane abiecerunt, & in illius posteros iniquissima tyrannide & enormi crudelitate grassati sunt. Idem Moses expertus est, qui cum Israelitica gentis saluator fuisset, ab ijsdem tamen omni conuiciorum genere obrutus, vix euasit quò minus lapidatur. Quid autem de Dauide & infinitis alijs, quorum exempla in gentilium historijs leguntur, dicere attinet, quando hanc ipsam fortem Christo quoq; contigisse constat? Nam qui huic regis titulum deferrent, & Hierosolymas ingrediunti magno cum applausu acclamare solebant, paulò post sacerdotibus & scribis coniuncti, illum ad crucis supplicium postulauerunt. Est vero non vulgaris horum exemplorum usus. Docent enim ne aurae popularis fidamus, qua nihil mobilius & inconstantius in rerum natura habetur. Nam si vel te solum inspicias, facile videbis quàm multis quamq; diuersis & contrarijs affectibus simul distrahari. Et fieri posse speras, ut vulgus, multorum capicum bellua, sibi semper constet, qua quot capita habet, tot sensibus ducitur, nouaq; quotidie eorum consilia admittit, qui illius mobilitate ad suum quaestum abuti consueuerunt? Quin potius soli deo studia nostra approbare studeamus, apud quem certa virtutum merces nobis repositae est, quam nec vulgi inconstantia, nec tyrannorum violentae manus nobis eripere possunt. Matth.6.
units.tr: Second, we must consider the inconstancy of the crowd. For those who a little before had held the apostles in honour and were preparing sacrifices for them, suddenly, persuaded by outsiders, and indeed by men who were founders of a different religion, plot a cruel death for them. What, then, do you think they would have done if they had been stirred up by the nobles of their own nation or by the Roman governors? Yet this levity of the crowd is not so shameful as it is common and met with everywhere: it both causes forgetfulness of benefits received and overwhelms benefactors with savage injuries. An example of this is found in the Egyptians, who, though they had been saved from famine by the counsels of Joseph and had been raised to the highest peak of power and glory, nevertheless, scarcely after he had died, utterly forgot his memory and raged against his descendants with the most unjust tyranny and monstrous cruelty. Moses experienced the same thing: although he had been the saviour of the Israelite nation, he was overwhelmed by the same people with every kind of abuse, and barely escaped being stoned. But why speak of David and of the countless others whose examples are read in the histories of the Gentiles, when it is established that this same lot also fell to Christ? For those who had offered him the title of king and were accustomed to shout with great applause as he entered Jerusalem, a little later, joined with the priests and scribes, demanded that he be sent to the punishment of the cross. The use of these examples is not commonplace. They teach us not to trust the breeze of popular favour, for nothing in the nature of things is more changeable and inconstant. For if you look at yourself alone, you will easily see how many and how diverse and contrary emotions tear you apart at once. And do you hope that the crowd, that beast with many heads, will always remain consistent with itself, when, as many heads as it has, so many minds lead it, and it daily admits new counsels from those who are accustomed to abuse its fickleness for their own gain? Rather, let us strive to commend our efforts to God alone, with whom a sure reward of virtues is laid up for us, which neither the inconstancy of the crowd nor the violent hands of tyrants can snatch from us. Matt. 6.

units.la: Tertiò ipse deus nobis inspiciendus est, cuius nutu & prouidentia res omnes administrari contingat. Permittit vs, ut fidelissimus Christi apostolus & electum gratiae suae organum lapidetur, & quidem ijs authoribus, quorum saluti ille cumprimis studebat, & pro quibus indesinenter precabatur. Non nouum ergo aut insolens nobis videri debet, si quid simile hodie contingat, nec ex euentu de cuiusquam fide aut doctrina iudicare debemus, quando olim prophetis hoc ipsum euenisse, Christus testatestatur. Matth.5. Quin potius ex prouidentia Dei consolationem petamus, quae hoc loco non obscuris argumentis eluxit. Quis enim non singulare Dei opus & consilium in eo agnoscat, quòd Paulus quidem lapidatur, illaesus autem manet Barnabas, Pauli collega, & quem antea Paulo praetulisse videntur, cum Iouem illum esse dixerint? Quis hunc alia quàm diuina ope seruatu fuisse dicat, cum nemo affuisse legatur, qui furentis vulgi conatibus sese opponeret? Quòd si quis interroget, cur hunc potius quàm Paulu defendere voluerit dominus, certa quidem ratio adduci non poterit, quàm quòd sic Deo visum est, cuius iudicia sunt iustitia & veritas. Si quis tamen piis coniecturis locus est, ideo Barnabae pepercisse videri potest Deus, quòd tam graui pugnae adhuc imparem & infirmiorem sciret, quàm qui tantum pondus posset sustinere. Fidelis enim est Deus, nec nos vltra quàm ferre possumus, tentari sinit. 1. Corinth. 10. cap. Nec minor in ipso Paulo Dei bonitas & cura elucet. Nam & hunc inter furiosi populi clamores & vndiq; volantia saxa ita feruat, vt lethale vulnus nullum accipiat, vel si quod accepit, saltem illius quoq; periculum euadat. Imò ita illum restituit, vt qui mortuus putabatur, & extra vrbis portas cadaueris instar extractus erat, postridie itineri faciundo idoneus esse posset. Nemo igitur in medijs periculis desperet, quando diuinae prouidentiae limites vltra omnes periculorum fines extendi constat. Nam siue viuamus, siue moriamur, domini sumus, nec quicquà nos abeius dilectione separare poterit. Rom. 8. & 14. Atq; ex hoc exemplo generalem doctrinam peti de bere ipse Paulus in posteriori ad Timotheum cap. 3. his verbis admonet: Tu verò assecutus es doctrinam meam, institutionem, propositum, fidem, lenitatem, charitatem, patientiam, persecutiones, afflictiones, quae mihi acciderunt Antiochiae, Iconij, Lystris, quas persecutiones sustinuerim, & ex omnibus eripuit me dominus. Sed & omnes, qui volunt piè viuere in Christo Iesu, persecutionem patientur. Quare primum hoc animis nostris fundamentum insideat, nihil citra Dei consilium & voluntatem nobis accidere, qui etiam capitis nostri pilos numerauit. Matth. 10. cap. Deinde iusto simul & sancto iudicio illum omnia administrare cogitemus. Tertiò firmiter persuasum sit, illum nostri curam & paterni animi affectum nunquam exuere, & tunc maximè nos tueri, quando hostium libidini plane permisi esse videmur. Liberabit ergo ex periculis, si ita è re nostra fore nouerit. Quòd si illi sectis videatur, qui omnia nostra melius quàm nos ipsi perspecta habet, nos qui sumus obsecro, vt illi obloquamur? Sed de his circa finem Sermonis plura dicendi locus erit commodior.
units.tr: Third, we must look to God himself, by whose will and providence all things are governed. He allows his most faithful apostle of Christ, the chosen instrument of his grace, to be stoned, and that by men whose salvation he especially cared for and for whom he prayed without ceasing. Therefore nothing new or strange should seem to us if something similar happens today, nor ought we to judge anyone's faith or teaching from the outcome, since Christ testifies that this same thing happened to the prophets of old. Matt. 5. Rather, let us seek consolation from the providence of God, which shines forth in this passage with no obscure proofs. For who does not recognise a singular work and counsel of God in this, that Paul is indeed stoned, while Barnabas, Paul's colleague, whom they seem to have preferred to Paul when they called him Jupiter, remains unharmed? Who would say that he was preserved by any other than divine help, since no one is recorded as having stood by to oppose the attempts of the raging crowd? But if anyone asks why the Lord chose to defend this man rather than Paul, no certain reason can be given except that it so seemed good to God, whose judgements are justice and truth. Yet if there is room for pious conjecture, God may seem to have spared Barnabas because he knew that Barnabas was not yet equal to so grievous a conflict and was too weak to bear so great a burden. For God is faithful, and does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear. 1 Cor. 10. Nor is God's goodness and care less evident in Paul himself. For amid the shouts of the furious people and the stones flying from every side, he preserves him so that he receives no mortal wound, or, if he has received one, at least escapes its danger. Indeed, he so restores him that the man who was thought dead, and had been dragged outside the city gates like a corpse, was able the next day to set out on his journey. Let no one, then, despair in the midst of dangers, since it is certain that the limits of divine providence extend beyond all the boundaries of danger. For whether we live or die, we are the Lord's, and nothing can separate us from his love. Rom. 8 and 14. From this example Paul himself, in his second letter to Timothy, chapter 3, admonishes us to draw a general doctrine, in these words: "But you have followed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance, my persecutions and afflictions, which came upon me at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; what persecutions I endured, and out of them all the Lord rescued me. Indeed, all who wish to live godly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution." Therefore let this first foundation remain fixed in our minds: nothing happens to us apart from God's counsel and will, who even numbered the hairs of our head. Matt. 10. Next, let us reflect that he governs all things by a just and holy judgement at the same time. Thirdly, let it be firmly believed that he never lays aside his care for us and his fatherly affection, and that he protects us most of all when we seem fully given over to the lust of our enemies. He will therefore deliver us from dangers if he knows that it is for our good. But if it seems good to him, who has a fuller view of all our affairs than we ourselves, we who are such, I ask, should we speak against him? But there will be a more fitting place to say more about these matters near the end of the sermon.

units.la: Quid verò in istis turbis discipuli fecere, quorum animis syncerior cognitionis Christi lux iam affulserat? Num abnegata fide, in gentilium partes denuò transierunt? vel num Pauli lapidati & ignominiose per vrbem tracti illos puduit? Nequaquam. Imò hunc circumstetisse dicuntur, quod illos officij causa fecisse. verisimile est. Cùm enim illum aduersus furiosa plebis apertam vim tueri non possent, quod possunt, faciunt. Et quem mortuum putabant, circumstant, cum plancu nimirum, & extremum sepulturae officium fortissimo Christi ministro praestare cupiunt, quodipsum Hierosolymitanos fideles in Stephani martyrio fecisse, supra audiuimus. Atqui periculo res haec non poterat carere, si quis & implacabile in Iudaeos Christi odium, & vulgi animos ex recenti facinore adhuc ferocientes, probè consyderet. Sed non deesse tam pio officio Christus dominus. Nam quem illi vt mortuum plangunt, eum ille miraculose restituit, vt subitò exuscitatus in vrbem redeat. Admonemur exemplo hoc, quid fidis Christi membris, pro communi causa periclitantibus, debeamus. Primum officium est, vt qui possunt, fideli ope laborantes sublevent: vbi varia officiorum genera occurrunt, in quibus nullum tam vile & contemptum est, quod non suam coram Deo remunerationem habeat, quando ne is quidem mercedem suam amissurus est, qui Christi discipulo poculum aquae frigidae dederit. Matth. 10. cap. Quòd si qui opem, quàm ferre poterant, negauerint, sibi dictum esse intelligant, quod Hester reginae Mardochaeus olim dixit: Si omnino tacueris hoc tempore, aliunde oberietur populo Dei respiratio & liberatio, tu verò & domus patris tui peribitis, &c. Secundus officij gradus est, vt qui iuuare non possunt, saltem impiorum Christi hostium consilijs non consentiant, & quocunq; modo possunt, se illis non vnquam consensisse testentur. Exemplum huius in Iosepho Arimathaeo euangelica historia proponit. Marc. 15. cap. Tertius & vltimus gradus est, vt aliorum improbitate & tyrannide afflictos, quibus possumus officijs consolemur, & si omnes vires desint, saltem illorum fortem pijs lachrymis doleamus: nec nos eorum pudeat, in quorum corpore Christi vinciri, eijci affligi & contristari scimus. Hoc ipsum Iosephus quoq; fidelissimè praestitit, dū honorificè sepeliendū curae
units.tr: But what did the disciples do amid these tumults, they whose minds had already been lit by a purer knowledge of Christ? Did they deny the faith and go back over to the Gentiles? Or were they ashamed of Paul, who had been stoned and dragged ignominiously through the city? By no means. Indeed, they are said to have stood around him, and this was probably done out of duty. For since they could not defend him against the furious crowd's open violence, they did what they could. They stood around the man they thought dead, certainly to mourn him, and they wished to render the last duty of burial to the most brave minister of Christ. We heard above that the faithful of Jerusalem did the same at the martyrdom of Stephen. Yet this business could not be free of danger, as anyone who carefully considers the implacable hatred of the Jews towards Christ, and the crowd's spirits still inflamed by the recent crime, will see. But Christ the Lord was not lacking to such a dutiful act. For the one whom they mourned as dead, he miraculously restored, so that he suddenly rose and returned to the city. This example teaches us what we owe to the faithful members of Christ who are in danger for the common cause. The first duty is that those who can should help those labouring in distress with faithful aid. There are various kinds of duties, and none is so humble and despised that it does not have its reward before God, since not even he who gives a cup of cold water to a disciple of Christ will lose his wage (Matt. 10). But if anyone has refused the help he could give, let him understand that what Mordecai once said to Queen Esther applies to him: "If you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will arise for the people of God from another place, but you and your father's house will perish," etc. The second step of duty is that those who cannot help may at least not consent to the counsels of the impious enemies of Christ, and by whatever means they can, bear witness that they never consented to them. The gospel story sets an example of this in Joseph of Arimathea (Mark 15). The third and last step is that we comfort, by whatever services we can, those afflicted by the wickedness and tyranny of others, and if all strength is lacking, at least grieve for their misfortune with devout tears. Nor should we be ashamed of those in whose body we know that Christ is bound, cast out, afflicted and saddened. Joseph himself also performed this most faithfully, when he took care to bury honourably

units.la: Christianorum ergà periclitantes fratres officia. Christum, quem aduersarij ignominiosè in crucem suspenderant. His officijs si Christi membra hodie prosequamur, diuinam opem, unde minimè speres, nobis obtingere videbimus. Nec enim Deus vt suorum labores irritos esse, vel impiorum conatibus Christi filij sui regnum superari & euerti patitur. Sed ad apostolos reuersi, quid tam graui certamine superato fecerint, videamus, de quibus in præsenti hæc commemorantur.
units.tr: the Christ whom his adversaries had shamefully hung on the cross. If today we attend to the members of Christ with these duties, we shall see divine help come to us from where we least expect it. For God does not allow the labours of his people to be in vain, nor the kingdom of his Son to be overcome and overthrown by the attempts of the wicked. But let us return to the apostles and see what they did after overcoming so grave a struggle, which is what is recorded here.

units.la: Postridie Paulus, Barnaba ipsum comitante, Lystris digressus, Derbam profecisci-tur, vbi euangelium Iesu Christi annunciat, & non paucos Christo discipulos adducit. Est memorabile & præclarum Christianæ constantiæ & fidelis industriæ exemplum, quod ex periculo animosiores facti, maiori & feruentiori zelo ad officium redeunt. Arguuntur hoc ignaui desertores, qui vt primum pe-riclitati sunt, quasi suo iam officio functi sint, nunquam adduci possunt, vt aliquid amplius pro Christo audendum esse putent. Atqui cogitandum erat, ex recenti liberationis & auxilij diuini beneficio argumenta peti debere, quibus ad maiorem fortitudinem excitemur. Num enim ideò nos periculis eripit Deus, vt securi posthac certaminum, quibus alij exercentur, spectatores simus? Quin potius promissiones suas sancire solet, vt maioribus animis pro illius nomine pugnemus. Horum memor Paulus, vix vnius diuculæ quietem sibi ipsi concedit, qui tamen humano iudicio dignus videri poterat, qui iam rude donaretur. Illud verò simul obseruandum venit, quòd quotiescunque de apostolorum doctrina Lucas disserit, non alterius quàm euangelij mentionem facit, cuius ministerium & prædicationem illis Christus commiserat. Marc. 16. Est hoc magnum fidei argumentum, qua in commissi-bi munere vsi sunt, simulque quid in ecclesia prædicari debeat, admonet. Si enim apostoli sibi minimè tantum permittere ausi sunt, vt à Christi mandato digressi, nouas traditiones ecclesijs obtruderent, nec inexcusabilis est illorum temeritas, qui illud hodie sub illorum nomine & prætextu tam impudenter facere audent.
units.tr: On the next day Paul, accompanied by Barnabas, left Lystra and set out for Derbe, where he proclaimed the gospel of Jesus Christ and brought many to be disciples of Christ. It is a notable and excellent example of Christian steadfastness and faithful diligence that, made bolder by danger, they return to their duty with greater and more fervent zeal. Cowardly deserters are shown up by this: as soon as they are endangered, they behave as if they had already done their duty, and can never be brought to think that anything more must be dared for Christ. Yet they should have considered that arguments must be drawn from the recent benefit of divine deliverance and help, by which we are stirred to greater courage. For does God rescue us from dangers so that we may afterwards be safe spectators of the struggles in which others are engaged? Rather, he is accustomed to confirm his promises so that we may fight for his name with greater spirit. Mindful of this, Paul grants himself scarcely a day's rest, though by human judgment he could have seemed worthy to be given a discharge. But it must be noted at the same time that whenever Luke speaks of the apostles' teaching, he mentions nothing but the gospel, whose ministry and preaching Christ had committed to them (Mark 16). This is a great proof of their faithfulness in the office entrusted to them, and at the same time it reminds us what ought to be preached in the Church. For if the apostles did not dare to permit themselves so much as to depart from Christ's command and thrust new traditions upon the churches, then the rashness of those who today shamelessly dare to do this under their name and pretext is inexcusable.

units.la: Deinde in tres vrbes vnde eiecti antea fuerant, reuertuntur apostoli, Antiochiam nimirum, Iconium & Lystram, vt quos illic Christo lucrifecerant, in fide confirmarent & in officio retinerent. Vt enim in re domestica non minor laus est, parta seruare, quàm acquirere: ita in ecclesia non modò per verbum Dei homines lucrifieri debent, sed studiosè vigilandum est, ne quis nostra negligentia a fide & officio excidat. Et vt semen non modò spargi, verumetiam custodiri & foueri necesse est, ne vel spinis succrescentibus suffocetur, aut alio vitio pessum eat: ita verbi semen, vbi semel inter homines sparsum fuerit, indefinenti studio rigari & conseruari oportet. Nota enim est Christi parabola de inimico nostro, qui dormientibus nobis zizania aspergere consueuit. Non parum ergo peccant, qui vbi verbum prædicarunt, suo se officio defunctos esse putant, cùm tunc maximè illorum fides ac industria exigatur, ne satanæ insidijs seducantur, qui Christi vocem iam audire & sequi cœperunt. Simul verò insigne Christianæ charitatis & apostolici zeli exemplum est, quòd ad eos reuertuntur Paulus & Barnabas, à quibus ignominiosè & summa cum iniuria eiecti fuerant. Nemo igitur hominum ingratitudine offendatur, nec ideò sibi licere putet, vt officium suum deserat, quòd parum æquos laborum fructum censores esse sentit, quorum saluti inuigilat. Cur enim eum imitareris, quem reprehensione dignum esse vides? Damnantur tuo iudicio, qui officium non faciunt. Cur ergo illorum inimicitate te superari patiaris, vt ipse quoq; officium negligas? Memineris potius Dei seruum te esse, & proinde ab illo mercedem expectes, non à mundo hoc stolido simul & ingrato, cuius proprium est, pef-simam suis benefactoribus gratiam referre. Testantur hoc abunde quæ Mosi, Dauidi, prophetis, Christo & apostolis acciderunt. Imò gentium historiæ huius generis exemplis referta sunt. Huc enim Aristides, Themistocles, Miltiades, Cimon, Camillus, Scipiones, Catones, Cicero & infiniti alij referri debent, qui cum patriæ liberatores fuissent, ab ingratis ciuibus vel ignominiosè patriæ finibus eiecti, vel etiam indignè occisi sunt. Sed paulò diligentius inspici debet, quid in vrbibus istis, ad quas reuersi sunt, Paulus & Barnabas egerint.
units.tr: Next, the apostles return to the three cities from which they had previously been driven out, namely Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, to strengthen in the faith those whom they had won for Christ there, and to keep them in their duty. For just as in domestic affairs it is no less praiseworthy to preserve what has been gained than to acquire it, so in the Church men must not only be won through the Word of God, but care must also be taken with watchful effort that no one falls from faith and duty through our negligence. And just as seed must not only be sown but also guarded and nourished, lest it be choked by springing thorns or perish by some other fault, so the seed of the Word, once sown among men, must be watered and preserved with unceasing care. For the parable of Christ about our enemy is well known, who is accustomed to sow tares while we are asleep. Therefore those who, once they have preached the Word, think they have done their duty are not a little mistaken, since it is then above all that the faith and diligence of those who have begun to hear and follow Christ's voice must be required, so that they are not seduced by the snares of Satan. At the same time it is a remarkable example of Christian charity and apostolic zeal that Paul and Barnabas return to those by whom they had been shamefully and grossly wronged, from whom they had been driven out. Let no one therefore be offended by human ingratitude, nor think it lawful for him to abandon his duty because he finds that those whose salvation he watches over are rather unfair judges of his labours. For why would you imitate one whom you see to be worthy of blame? Those who do not do their duty are condemned by your judgment. Why then would you allow yourself to be overcome by their hostility, so that you too neglect your duty? Rather remember that you are a servant of God, and therefore expect your reward from him, not from this foolish and ungrateful world, whose characteristic it is to repay its benefactors with the worst thanks. The things that happened to Moses, David, the prophets, Christ and the apostles bear abundant witness to this. Indeed, the histories of the nations are full of examples of this kind. For to this class belong Aristides, Themistocles, Miltiades, Cimon, Camillus, the Scipios, the Catos, Cicero and countless others, who, though they were liberators of their country, were either shamefully driven from its borders by ungrateful citizens or even unworthily killed. But we must examine more carefully what Paul and Barnabas did in those cities to which they returned.

units.la: Primò discipulorum animas confirmauisse dicuntur. Atqui solius Dei opus est animos hominum regere, confirmare & inclinare pro suo arbitrio. Confirmant tamen apostoli, quorum ministerio ad eam rem Deus vti voluit, qui cum solus omnia operetur in omnibus, medijs tamen & certo ordine vti consueuit. Quare vt per verbi prædicationem animos fide illuminat, ita per eandem hominum animos in fide confirmat. Et ita in horum consyderatione nos versari conuenit, ne vel hominum minum minisserio tribuamus, quod solius Dei opus est, vel ministerium à Deo institutum improbè con-temnamus. Grauis enim & detestabilis illorum error est, qui cum Deo suam gloriam vendicare videri volunt, à Deo traditum ordinem improbè contemnunt, verbi doctrinam aspernantur, cætus fugiunt, preces negligunt, & ita sub divini nominis prætextu impietati secure student.
units.tr: First, they are said to have strengthened the souls of the disciples. But it is the work of God alone to rule, strengthen and incline the minds of men according to his will. Yet the apostles do the strengthening, since God willed to use their ministry for this purpose; although he alone works all things in all, he is nevertheless accustomed to use means and a fixed order. So just as through the preaching of the Word he enlightens minds with faith, so through the same Word he confirms men's minds in faith. And in considering this we ought to be careful neither to attribute to the ministry of men what is the work of God alone, nor wickedly to despise the ministry instituted by God. For the error of those is grave and detestable who, wishing to appear to claim glory for themselves against God, wickedly despise the order handed down by God, scorn the doctrine of the Word, flee the assemblies, neglect prayers, and so under the pretext of the divine name diligently pursue impiety in security.

units.la: Cæterum ab ipso Luca exprimitur, ut discipulorum animas apostoli confirmauerint, cum addit: Exhortantes ut perseuerarent in fide. Exhortationibus ergo è Dei verbo adductis hominum mentes confirmari solent. Obseruemus autem, non sufficere ut semel Christo crediderint homines, sed necessariam esse in fide vera perseuerantiam. Hæc enim nisi accedat, fiunt postrema peiora primis, nec regno Dei digni putantur, qui ubi manum aratro admouerunt, à tergo respiciunt. Matth.12. Luc.9. Hinc est quod Ephesinâ ecclesiam, multis alioqui nominibus celebrem, hanc unam ob causam Christus in gloria sua agens reprehendit, quod priorem charitatem & feruentis fidei zelum amisisset: Thyatirensem verò hoc potissimum nomine commendat, quod maiores quotidie in pietate & fide vera progressus faceret. Apoc.2.cap. Diligenter ergo in horum meditatione omnes ecclesias versari conuenit, ne præclara fidei principia turpi & ignaua defectione & negligentia corrumpant. Simul verò hinc omnis ordinis & loci homines doctrinam petant, qua sui officij admoneantur, quando omnium ea conditio est, ut frustra bene cœperis, nisi in finem usque perseueres. Interim fidei doctrinam certam & inuiolabilem esse, locus hic admonet. Nec enim laudabilis esset fidei perseuerantia, si quid in eius doctrina vel corrigi vel mutari oporteret. Id quod ijs obijciendum est, qui cum apostolorum dogmata aperte damnare non audeant, multa tamen posterioribus seculis accessisse aiunt, non minus necessaria obseruatu, quam quæ illi tradiderint. At si ea cum Apostolorum doctrina conferas, huius veritatem minime saluam esse posse deprehendes, si ista admittantur. Discamus ergo ita in apostolica fide & doctrina perseuerandum nobis esse, ut nihil huic contrarium admittamus, adeoque ne angelo quidem credamus, qui nouum siue aliud euangelium prædicauerit. Galat.1. Præterea crucis offendiculo medentur, quod fieri cumprimis oportebat, quando ex temporarijs euentibus fere de fidei causa ratio humana iudicat. Et credibile est multorum animos non mediocriter tentatos fuisse, cum apostolorum doctrinam pasim explodi, & illos ipsos quotidianis periculis exerceri viderent. At breui sententia efficacissimam consolationem infirmis in fide apostoli adhibent, cum dicunt, quod per multas afflictiones oporteat nos ingredi in regnum Dei. Habet sententia hæc duas rationes ad consolandum cumprimis idoneas. Prima est, quod ita fieri oportere dicunt, nec aliter fieri posse. Atqui communis sensus dictat, patienter & moderate ferendum esse, quod mutari non potest. Ita verò conditionem fidelium, quæ in hoc mundo ipsis sustinenda est, exprimunt: quam omnis generis afflictionum refertam esse, Christus quoq; testatur, quando nos quotidie nostram crucem tollere, & ita se sequi iubet. Luc.9. Et sanè si vitæ huius cursum inspicias, nihil à malis immune videbis. Scatet enim vita hæc communibus molestijs, quarum origo ex peccato est, quales sunt morbi, labor, cura, vigilia, egestas, incertæ rerum vices, & infinita alia huius generis, propter quæ vita molestissima periculosissimaq; peregrinationi & perpetuæ luctæ confertur. Sed accedunt his aliæ afflictiones, quæ pijs Christi cultoribus ex mundo enascuntur, qui lucem veritatis ferre non possunt. Hinc est, quod odio mundi subiacent, quod contumelias & ignominiam sustinent, quod omnium iniurijs expositi sunt, quod aperta vi petuntur, quod carceres, vincula, compedes, exilium, bonorum direptionem, mortes deniq; infames & horribiles ferre coguntur. Ita verò impletur quod Dauid ait, multas esse tribulationes iustorum, & quod Christus nobis euenturum prædixit. Psalm. 34. Ioban.15.16 Porrò in omnibus his cogitandum est, hæc ita fieri oportere, nō quidem eam tantummodo ob causam ut sua constet verbo Dei veritas, sed quia sic carnem nostram coherceri, & præsentis vitæ fastidium ad cœlestis desyderium in nobis excitari necesse est. Experimur enim in nobis ipsis, quantus carni nostræ mundi amor inhæreat, & quàm difficulter ad cœlestium bonorum studia excitari possit. Quid verò futurum putas, si nihil illi in hoc mundo aduersum, sed læta & secunda omnia acciderent? Nunquam certè adduci posset, ut mundo renuntiaret, cuius fortunam tot aduersis vexari solitam, tanto desyderio admirari solet. Altera ratio est, quòd finem tribulationum lætissimum indicant, dum per has nobis in regnum Dei aditum patere docent. Quæ verba non ita accipi debent, quasi afflictionibus ferendis regnum Dei mereamur, quod vnius Christi sanguine nobis acquisitum esse conflat. Sed viam hanc Christi exemplo nobis consecratam esse docent, ut quemadmodum ille per crucem in gloriam patris ingressus est: ita nobis quoq; afflictionum finem propositum esse, caelestis vitae hereditatem, iuxta Christi promissum: Volo ut ubi ego sum, ibi etiam sit minister meus. Iohan. 12.14. & 17. Quis ergo posthac crucem horreat? Quis afflictionibus offendatur, quando eas impijs quoq; accidere, pijs autem propter Christum ad salutem seruire audit? Meditemur ista bodie, o fratres. Cogitemus à Deo ita constitutum esse, ut varijs aerumnis exerceamur, nec aliter fieri posse, quando ita exigit nostrae carnis improbitas. Respiciamus in Christi exemplum, qui ut se nobis ducem praeberet, prior haec omnia sustinuit. Praeterea in promissam caelestis vitae gloriam animi oculos defigamus, & eorum quae à tergo sunt caduca & friuola obliuiscamur. Coniungamus his ardentes preces, ut bonum opus in nobis consummare dignetur. Ita fiet, ut illius spiritu & gratia animati, vitae huius cursum feliciter absoluamus, & caelestis gloriae brauium assecuti viuamus & regnemus cum Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke also tells us that the apostles strengthened the souls of the disciples when he adds: "exhorting them to continue in the faith." Minds are usually strengthened by exhortations drawn from the Word of God. Let us observe, however, that it is not enough for people to have believed in Christ once; perseverance in true faith is also necessary. Unless this is added, "the last things become worse than the first," and those who have put their hand to the plough and look back are not considered worthy of the kingdom of God (Matt. 12; Luke 9). Hence Christ, reigning in his glory, rebukes the church of Ephesus, otherwise famous in many respects, for this one reason alone: that it had lost its first love and its zeal of burning faith. The church of Thyatira, on the other hand, he commends especially for this, that it was making greater progress every day in piety and true faith (Rev. 2). Therefore all churches ought to be diligent in meditating on these things, so that they do not corrupt the excellent beginnings of faith by shameful and lazy defection and neglect. At the same time, people of every rank and place should draw from this teaching what they are reminded of concerning their duty, since the condition of all is such that you have started well in vain unless you persevere to the end. Meanwhile this place reminds us that the doctrine of faith is certain and inviolable. For the perseverance of faith would not be praiseworthy if anything in its doctrine needed to be corrected or changed. This must be set against those who, though they do not dare openly to condemn the doctrines of the apostles, nevertheless say that many things have been added in later centuries which are no less necessary to observe than those the apostles handed down. But if you compare those things with the teaching of the apostles, you will find that the truth of the apostles cannot possibly remain safe if those additions are admitted. Let us learn, then, that we must persevere in the apostolic faith and doctrine in such a way that we admit nothing contrary to it, and so that we do not believe even an angel who should preach a new or different gospel (Gal. 1). Moreover, the passage heals the stumbling block of the cross, which was especially necessary, since human reason mostly judges the cause of faith by temporary events. And it is credible that the minds of many were not a little shaken, when they saw the teaching of the apostles everywhere being hooted down and the apostles themselves daily exposed to dangers. But the apostles, in a brief saying, apply a most effective consolation to those weak in faith, when they say that "through many afflictions we must enter into the kingdom of God." This saying contains two reasons especially suited to console. The first is that they say it must be so and cannot be otherwise. Now common sense dictates that what cannot be changed must be borne patiently and calmly. In this way they describe the condition of believers, which they must endure in this world: that it is full of afflictions of every kind, as Christ also testifies, when he bids us take up our cross daily and so follow him (Luke 9). And indeed, if you look at the course of this life, you will see that nothing is free from evils. For this life teems with common troubles, whose origin is in sin: diseases, toil, care, sleeplessness, poverty, the uncertain turns of fortune, and countless others of this kind, on account of which life is said to be most troublesome and dangerous, a pilgrimage and a constant struggle. But besides these there come other afflictions, which arise from the world for the pious worshippers of Christ, who cannot bear the light of truth. Hence they lie under the hatred of the world; they endure insults and disgrace; they are exposed to the injuries of all; they are attacked by open force; and they are forced to bear prisons, chains, fetters, exile, the plundering of their goods, and finally infamous and horrible deaths. Thus what David says is fulfilled, that there are many afflictions of the righteous, and what Christ foretold would happen to us (Ps. 34; John 15, 16). Moreover, in all these things we must consider that they must happen in this way, not only for this reason, that the truth of God's Word may stand, but because it is necessary that our flesh be restrained in this way, and that a weariness of the present life be aroused in us, leading to a desire for heavenly things. For we experience in ourselves how deeply love of the world clings to our flesh, and how difficult it is to be stirred up to the pursuit of heavenly goods. What do you think would happen if nothing adverse came to us in this world, but all things were joyful and prosperous? Certainly it could never be brought about that a man would renounce the world, whose fortune, which is usually tossed about by so many adversities, he so greatly admires. The second reason is that they point out a most joyful end to tribulations, while they teach that through these an entrance into the kingdom of God is opened to us. These words should not be understood as if we deserve the kingdom of God by enduring afflictions, which is acquired for us by the blood of Christ alone is believed. But they teach that this way has been consecrated to us by the example of Christ, so that just as he entered into the glory of the Father through the cross, so the end of afflictions is also set before us, the inheritance of the heavenly life, according to Christ's promise: "I want those who are mine to be where I am, and my minister also to be there" (John 12, 14, and 17). Who, then, after this, would shrink from the cross? Who would be offended by afflictions, when he hears that they happen to the impious also, but to the pious they serve for salvation on account of Christ? Let us meditate on these things today, brothers. Let us consider that it has been so appointed by God that we should be exercised by various hardships, and that it cannot be otherwise, since the wickedness of our flesh requires it. Let us look to the example of Christ, who, that he might present himself to us as our leader, endured all these things first. Moreover, let us fix the eyes of our mind on the promised glory of the heavenly life, and forget the frail and trifling things that lie behind us. Let us join to these fervent prayers, that he may deign to bring the good work to completion in us. Thus it will come about that, animated by his Spirit and grace, we will happily finish the course of this life, and, having won the prize of heavenly glory, we will live and reign with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA C.
units.tr: HOMILY C.

units.la: Quum autem suffragijs creauissent illis per singulas Ecclesias presbyteros, precati cum ieiunijs, commendarunt eos domino, in quem crediderant, & per Pisidiam transeuntes, venerunt in Pamphyliam. Et cum locuti essent Pergae sermonem, descenderunt in Attaliam, atq; inde nauigarunt Antiochiam, unde fuerant commissi gratiae dei in opus, quod compleuerant. Cum autem aduenissent, congregata ecclesia, narrarunt quanta per illos fecisset deus, & quod gentibus aperuisset ostium fidei. Commorati sunt autem illic non exiguum tempus cum discipulis.
units.tr: When they had appointed elders for them in every church by vote, with prayer and fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Passing through Pisidia, they came into Pamphylia. When they had preached the word at Perga, they went down to Attalia, and from there they sailed to Antioch, from where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work that they had now completed. When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported how much God had done through them and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they stayed there a considerable time with the disciples.

units.la: Quemadmodum apostoli ex omnibus gentibus domino nostro Iesu Christo discipulos adduxere, & euangelij praedicatione ecclesiam colligere debuerunt: ita officij illorum fuit, ecclesias diligenti cura & sedulo studio conseruare. Id vero summa fide Paulus & Barnabas praestant. Postquam enim Antiochiae, Iconij & Lystris ecclesias non sine periculo constituerunt, eosdem aduersus satanae insidias omni studio tueri conati sunt. Et quia illas à Iudaeis mirifice vexari nouerant, adeo reuertuntur, licet inde non sine publica ignominia eiecti essent. Nec sine fructu ad illas redeunt, sed animas discipulorum fidei admonitionibus & consolationibus confirmant, ad perseuerantiam exhortantur, & crucis offendiculo mederi studeant, de quibus singulis praecedenti Sermone dictum est. Illis vero coniungi debet, quod initio huius loci de presbyteris, per eosdem apostolos instituti, dicitur. Id vbi per Dei gratiam exposuerimus, de eorundem reditu ad Antiochenam ecclesiam, cui legationis suae & aliorum omnium rationem reddiderunt, dicemus.
units.tr: Just as the apostles brought disciples to our Lord Jesus Christ from all nations, and had to gather the church by preaching the gospel, so it was their duty to preserve the churches with careful attention and diligent zeal. Paul and Barnabas performed this duty with the greatest faithfulness. After they had established churches at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, not without danger, they strove with every effort to protect them against the snares of Satan. And because they knew that the churches were being wonderfully troubled by the Jews, they returned to them, even though they had been expelled from there with public disgrace. They did not return to them without fruit, but strengthened the souls of the disciples with admonitions and consolations, exhorted them to perseverance, and took pains to heal the stumbling block of the cross, as was said of each of these in the preceding sermon. What follows this should be joined to it, namely what is said at the beginning of this passage about the elders appointed by the same apostles. When, by God's grace, we have explained this, we shall speak about their return to the church at Antioch, to which they gave an account of their mission and of everything else.

units.la: Cum (inquit Lucas) suffragijs creauissent illis per singulas Ecclesias presbyteros, precati cum ieiunijs, commendarunt eos domino, in quem crediderant. Dicuntur autem presbyteri siue Seniores, partim quidem verbi ministri & pastores, partim vero qui pastoribus in ecclesia administranda adsunt, & publica authoritate morum disciplinam tuentur. Et quia per singulas ecclesias hos instituos fuisse dicit, facile patet, ad ecclesiarum conseruationem cumprimis requiri eos, quorum ministerio verbi doctrina in continuo vsu conseruetur. Postulat hoc carnis infirmitas & humani ingenij coruptio, quod assiduis admonitionibus in officio retineri oportet, ne diaboli insidijs & artibus in perditionem & interitum abripiatur. Quae causa est, quod Christus non apostolos modo emisit, quorum ministerio euangelium inter gentes, toto terrarum orbe dispersas praedicaretur: sed idem ecclesiae suae pastores quoq; ac doctores dedit, quorum studio fides & Dei cognitio, ab apostolis tradita, in hominum mentibus confirmaretur & conseruaretur. Vide Ephes. 4. & prioris ad Corinth. 12. cap. Et Paulus Titum hanc vnam ob causam se in Creta reliquisse scribit, ut per singulas eius insulae vrbes presbyteros constitueret. Et huc respexisse constat piissimos reges & principes, quorum liberalitate ecclesiae olim ditatae sunt, ne illarum inopia verbi ministerio officeret. Absurda ergo & turpis est illorum ignorantia & proteruia, qui verbi doctrinam, ut superuacaneam & plane inutilem, contemnunt. Nam si isti vel seipsos probe nouissent, hanc vnam ad salutem consequendam cumprimis necessariam
units.tr: "When they had appointed elders for them in every church by vote," says Luke, "with prayer and fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed." Now the elders, or seniors, are partly ministers of the Word and pastors, and partly those who assist the pastors in administering the church and who, by public authority, watch over the discipline of morals. And since he says that these were appointed in every church, it is easy to see that for the preservation of the churches, above all, those are required through whose ministry the teaching of the Word is kept in continual use. The weakness of the flesh and the corruption of human nature demand that people be kept in their duty by constant admonitions, lest they be snatched away by the snares and tricks of the devil into ruin and destruction. This is why Christ not only sent out apostles, through whose ministry the gospel would be preached among the nations scattered across the whole world, but also gave to his church pastors and teachers, through whose zeal the faith and knowledge of God, handed down by the apostles, might be confirmed and preserved in human minds. See Ephesians 4 and 1 Corinthians 12. Paul also writes that he left Titus in Crete for this one reason, that he might appoint elders in each city of that island. And it is evident that the most pious kings and princes, by whose generosity the churches were once enriched, had this in view, so that their poverty would not hinder the ministry of the Word. Absurd and shameful, then, is the ignorance and insolence of those who despise the teaching of the Word as superfluous and altogether useless. For if they had properly known themselves, they would have understood that this one thing is above all necessary for obtaining salvation, as Christ once admonished Martha, who was occupied with countless other things. Therefore, all who want the churches preserved should devote themselves especially to this, so that they are not left without suitable and worthy ministers.
