units.la: Apostoli singulis ecclesijs creant presbyteros. riam esse intelligerent, quod olim Martham, circa infinita alia occupatam, Christus admonuit. Quot quot ergo ecclesias conseruatas volunt, in hoc praecipue incumbant, ne ministris idoneis & dignis destituantur.
units.tr: Apostles appoint elders in each church. would understand it to be necessary, as Christ once admonished Martha, who was occupied with countless other things. Therefore, all who want the churches preserved should devote themselves especially to this, so that they are not left without suitable and worthy ministers.

units.la: Porrò ritum quoq; quo in eligendis presbyteris vsi sunt, Euangelista exprimit. In quo primum locus precibus & ieiunijs tribuitur, quorum mentionem supra etiam in similli causa factam fuisse vidimus. Act. 1. & 13. Quando autem duo ista scripturae coniungunt, solennem ecclesiae coetum instituum fuisse significatur. Solebant enim veteres, si quae magna vrgeret necessitas, coetus sacros indicere, in quibus ad vesperum vsq; ieiunijs simul & precibus vacabant, cuius rei non obscura testimonia apud Ioelem in 2. cap. & Regum historijs inueniuntur. Non leuibus autem causis mota est vetus ecclesia, quod haec ipsa in ministrorum electione obseruari debere putauit. Quia enim homines falli possent intellexit, nihil in re summopere necessaria humano iudicio permittere voluit, & proinde diuini spiritus illuminationem pijs precibus quaesiuit. Rursum, quia homines maximis donis instructos ad hoc munus requiri nouerat, illa quoq; à Deo supplicibus votis postulauit. Quae vt magis ferarent, ieiunia coniunxit, vt alibi quoq; monuimus. Deinde χειροτονίας mentionem facit Lucas, per quam non modo suffragiorum collectio, verumetiam manuum impositio, quae consecrationis symbolum erat, intelligi potest. Et posterius quidem magis conuenire videtur. Nec enim verisimile est, apostolos à primo ritu, quem in Matthiae electione obseruatum fuisse vidimus, recedere, & quicquam humano iudicio (vt in suffragijs fieri consueuit) permittere voluisse, cum ad preces & ieiunia ecclesiam vniuersam excitarint. EST autem diligenti obseruatione digna religiosa haec & sancta veteris ecclesiae simplicitas, cum qua si quae hodie fiunt conferas, facile patebit, quàm foeda tyrannide ecclesiarum status oppressus sit. Auaritia enim & ambitione antistitum factum est, vt omni libertate ecclesiarum concultata, ministrorum electio ab ijs pendeat, quibus vel sacra omnia venalia sunt, vel hoc vnum studium est, vt se dignos ministros habeant, qui ad ipsorum scelera conniuere & quiduis vel simulare vel dissimulare norint.
units.tr: Moreover, the Evangelist sets out the rite they used in choosing the elders. In this, first place is given to prayers and fasting, which we saw mentioned above also in a similar matter (Acts 1 and 13). When Scripture joins these two things together, it signifies that a solemn assembly of the church was held. For the ancients, if some great necessity pressed, used to call sacred assemblies, in which they gave themselves to fasting and prayer together until evening; clear testimonies of this are found in Joel chapter 2 and in the histories of the Kings. The ancient church was moved by no trivial causes to think that these very practices should be observed in the choice of ministers. For, understanding that men can be mistaken, it wished to leave nothing of the greatest necessity to human judgment, and therefore it sought the illumination of the divine Spirit by pious prayers. Again, since it knew that men endowed with the greatest gifts were required for this office, it also asked these from God with suppliant vows. And so that these might be borne more readily, it joined fasts, as we have also noted elsewhere. Next, Luke mentions χειροτονία [cheirotonia, election by show of hands], by which can be understood not only the collecting of votes but also the laying on of hands, which was the sign of consecration. And the latter seems to fit better. For it is not likely that the apostles departed from the first rite, which we saw observed in the election of Matthias, or wished to leave anything to human judgment (as is customary in votes), since they had roused the whole church to prayer and fasting. This religious and holy simplicity of the ancient church is worthy of careful observation, and if you compare with it what is done today, it will easily be seen how foully the condition of the churches has been oppressed by tyranny. For through the avarice and ambition of bishops it has come about that, with all the freedom of the churches trampled down, the choice of ministers depends on those for whom all sacred things are for sale, or whose only concern is to have ministers who know how to connive at their wickedness and either pretend or ignore whatever they wish.

units.la: Adijcit ministrorum electioni Lucas, quòd apostoli ecclesias domino commendarint, cui crediderunt. Est hoc humanitatis officium, Dei tutelae & defensioni eos commendare, quibus sua omnia salua esse cupias: simul verò fidelem apostolorum curam arguit, qui ecclesiarum salutem sibi nunquam non commendatissimam habuerunt. Quò illud Pauli referri debet: Incumbit mihi quotidiana cura omnium ecclesiarum. Quis infirmatur, & ego non infirmor? Quis offenditur, & ego non vror? 2. Corinth. 11. Interim admonemur, infirmitatem nostram Dei tutela & gubernatione opus habere. Nam vt ipsi ad lapsum proclives sumus, ita nō quiescit satan, si quo modo in insidias abducere possit: vt non temere Christus è mundo discessurus, discipulos patris protectioni commendet. Ioan. 17. Debet hoc in nobis ardens excitare religionis studium, ne salutem nostram propria ignauia prodamus. Rursum hinc nos consolationem petere decet, quòd salutem nostram à Dei protectione & prouidentia depende re constat. Quis enim non desperet, si ea à nobis pendeat & carnis arbitrio, quà nihil magis lubricum & fallacius? At desperandi causa nulla est, si hanc in Dei tutela consistere cogitemus, cui non possit non commendatissima esse, cùm ab illo flores agri & volucres caeli curentur, idemq; capitis pilos numerates habeat. Promisit us per filium suum, quod nos nolit orphanos relinquere Ioban. 14. Et Christus, cui credimus, se fidum simul & fortem pastorem esse profitetur, è cuius manu oues nemo rapere possit. Ioban. 10. cap. Quid quod alibi Paulus docet, Deum nouisse suos, nec aliquid esse quod nos à Dei dilectione separare queat? 2. Tim. 2. Rom. 8. cap. Quoties ergo fidem nostram tentat satan, ad diuinae gratiae asylum confugiamus, cui nos ipse Christus commendauit. Admonet praeterea apostolorum exemplum, quid nos, postquam officio nostro functi sumus, facere conueniat. Deo euentum omnem commendemus, cuius prouidentia res omnes administrari scimus. Est haec vnica ratio, quae consilia nostra moderari & pacare potest. Quam qui ignorant, mirifice torquentur, & saepe ab officio suo discedunt, dum suo consilio & prudentia res confici oportere arbitrantur. Nam sepe simul & metu dubij consilium suorum certum portum inuenire non possunt. At qui abs se in exequendo suo munere fidem & diligentiam requiri à Deo autem rei euentum pendere norunt, vbi se suo officio functos esse vident, quaecunq; incidunt pericula, facile contemnere possunt, nec etiam periculorum metu sese reuocari patiuntur, quò minus officium faciant.
units.tr: Luke adds to the choice of ministers that the apostles commended the churches to the Lord in whom they believed. It is an act of kindness to commend to the protection and defence of God those whom you wish to be safe in every respect; at the same time it shows the faithful care of the apostles, who always held the salvation of the churches as their dearest concern. To this should be referred what Paul says: "There presses on me daily the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" (2 Corinthians 11). Meanwhile we are reminded that our weakness needs the protection and governance of God. For just as we ourselves are prone to fall, so Satan does not rest, if in any way he can lead us into snares; so Christ, about to depart from the world, did not rashly commend his disciples to the protection of the Father (John 17). This should kindle in us a burning zeal for religion, so that we do not betray our salvation through our own laziness. Again, we ought to seek consolation from this, that it is established that our salvation depends on the protection and providence of God. For who would not despair if it depended on us and on the will of the flesh, than which nothing is more slippery and deceptive? But there is no cause for despair if we consider that it rests in the protection of God, to whom it cannot fail to be most dear, since by him the flowers of the field and the birds of the air are cared for, and he has even numbered the hairs of our head. He has promised through his Son that he will not leave us orphans (John 14). And Christ, in whom we believe, professes himself both a faithful and a strong shepherd, from whose hand no one can snatch the sheep (John 10). What of the fact that Paul teaches elsewhere that God knows his own, and that there is nothing that can separate us from the love of God (2 Timothy 2; Romans 8)? Therefore, whenever Satan tests our faith, let us flee to the refuge of divine grace, to which Christ himself has commended us. Moreover, the example of the apostles admonishes us what we ought to do after we have discharged our duty: we should commit every outcome to God, whose providence we know governs all things. This is the one reason that can regulate and calm our plans. Those who do not know it are wonderfully tormented, and often depart from their duty while they think that matters must be accomplished by their own counsel and prudence. For often, uncertain both through fear and through doubt about their own plans, they cannot find a safe harbour. But those who know that faithfulness and diligence are required of them in carrying out their office, while the outcome of the matter depends on God, when they see that they have done their duty, can easily despise whatever dangers befall them, and they do not allow themselves to be called back by fear of dangers from doing their duty.

units.la: Ritus veteris ecclesiae in eligendis presbyteris.
units.tr: The custom of the early Church in choosing elders.

units.la: Apostoli ecclesias commendant domino.
units.tr: The apostles commend the churches to the Lord.

units.la: Caeterum peractis hîs Antiochiam Syriae, unde dimissi erant, redire instituunt Paulus & Barnabas: quod ne absq; fructu fieret, in transitu Pergam quoq; Pamphyliae civitatem evangelij praedicatione illustrant. Fuit haec Dianae cultu infamis, quam inde Pergaeam dictam esse, gentilium scriptores prodiderunt. Singulare ergo bonitatis divinae opus fuit, quod superstitione & idololatria infames, salutis verbo inuisere dignatus est. Denuo autem observanda venit apostolorum sedulitas & indefessa industria, qua in euertendo Satanae regno vsi sunt. Imitentur zelum hunc, quicunq; apostolici videri volunt, & vel inuito mundo & illius principe superstitiones extirpent, & Christi regnum promouere studeant. Nec enim illi audiendi sunt, qui vel ob mundi ingratitudinem, vel vndiq; imminentia pericula, officium facere negligunt, &c. SED tempus admonet, vt quid apostoli Antiochiam reuersi fecerint, videamus.
units.tr: Now when these things were done, Paul and Barnabas resolved to return to Antioch in Syria, whence they had been sent out. And so that this would not be without fruit, on the way they also illuminated the city of Perga in Pamphylia by preaching the gospel. This place was notorious for the worship of Diana, and the pagan writers have handed down that it was from there that it got the name Pergaea. It was therefore a singular work of divine goodness that he deigned to visit with the word of salvation a place infamous for superstition and idolatry. Again, the zeal and tireless diligence of the apostles, by which they laboured to overthrow the kingdom of Satan, must be observed. Let all who wish to be thought apostolic imitate this zeal: let them root out superstitions even though the world and its prince are against it, and let them strive to advance the kingdom of Christ. For those are not to be listened to who neglect their duty either because of the ingratitude of the world or because dangers threaten on every side, etc. But the time admonishes us that we should see what the apostles did when they returned to Antioch.

units.la: Primò ecclesia congregata totum suae peregrinationis cursum exponunt, & fidelium legatorum instar rerum abs se gestarum rationem toti ecclesiae reddunt. Non ergo dominatores fidei fuerunt apostoli, qui absoluta potestate quidvis pro suo arbitrio egerint. Quin potius sese Christi seruos esse agnouerunt, nec illius sponsam, quae est ecclesia, impudenter contempserunt, vt hodie solent, qui illorum nomine & successione turgidi, nefas esse putant alterius imperio subijci, aut factorum suorum rationem cuiquam reddere. Legant illi obsecro quae habentur 1.Pet.5.cap.
units.tr: First, having gathered the church, they set out the whole course of their journey, and, like faithful envoys, they gave the whole congregation an account of what they had done. The apostles, then, were not lords over the faith, who with absolute power did whatever they liked at their own discretion. Rather, they acknowledged that they were servants of Christ, and they did not shamelessly despise his bride, which is the Church, as those do today who, puffed up with their name and succession, think it wrong to be subject to another's authority or to render an account of their deeds to anyone. I beg them to read what is found in 1 Peter 5.

units.la: Deinde nihil de seipsis arrogantius praedicant, sed ad Deum authore referunt omnia. Nec temere fieri putemus, quod hîs verbis Dei gratia & opus Lucas inculcat. Principio enim illos gratiae dei in opus hoc commissos fuisse dicit, nimirum vt tota ecclesia tuste, si absq; Dei gratia nihil effecturos essent. Deinde ipsi narrant, quanta per ipsos fecisset Deus. Quae sola locutio omnem legationis huius & ministerij ipsorum effectum vni Deo transcribit. Praeterea Deum gentibus ostium fidei aperuisse testantur. Dicitur autem fidei ostium aperiri, quando externa praedicationi efficax spiritus sancti operatio accedit, qua mentes hominum illuminantur & trahuntur, vt in fidei obsequium se totos tradant. Id vero solius Dei opus est, Christo teste, qui ait: Nemo venit ad me, nisi pater meus traxerit eum. Iohan.6. Docemur itaq; apostolorum exemplo, ne quid nostrae vel industriae vel prudentiae tribuamus. Exigitur quidè à nobis in rebus agendis fides & industria. Caeterum vt studiorum nostrorum eventus Deo committi debet, ita ad eundem omnis referri debet rerum bene & feliciter gestarum laus & gloria. Cuius doctrina non modò verbi ministros, verumetiam magistratus, patresfamilias, coniuges, servos, denique omnis loci & ordinis homines in rebus agendis meminisse conuenit, vt saepe alias monemur.
units.tr: Next, they say nothing more arrogant about themselves, but refer all things to God as the author. Nor should we think it happened by chance that Luke so insists on these words, the grace of God and the work. For first he says that they had been committed to this work by the grace of God, evidently so that the whole Church would know that they could accomplish nothing without the grace of God. Then they themselves tell how much God had done through them. This single expression ascribes the whole effect of their embassy and ministry to God alone. Moreover, they testify that God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. The door of faith is said to be opened when the effective working of the Holy Spirit is added to the external preaching, by which the minds of men are enlightened and drawn so that they give themselves wholly over to the obedience of faith. This is indeed the work of God alone, as Christ witnesses, who says: "No one comes to me unless my Father draws him" (John 6). We are therefore taught by the example of the apostles not to attribute anything to our own industry or prudence. Indeed, diligence and industry are required of us in carrying out our tasks; yet just as the outcome of our endeavours must be committed to God, so the praise and glory of things well and successfully done must be referred to the same God. His teaching makes it fitting that we remember this in our undertakings not only as ministers of the Word, but also as magistrates, heads of households, spouses, servants, and in short men of every place and rank, as we are often reminded elsewhere.

units.la: Postremò non exiguum tempus in Antiochena ecclesia manssisse dicitur, nimirum vt bono sancto ocio recrearentur, qui tot tantisq; laboribus & periculis per terras perq; maria exercitati fuerant. Aequum enim iustum est, vt laborum suorum fructum percipiant, quorum fides & industria non obscuris argumentis perspecta est. Ita Christus apostolos ab euangelij praedicatione ad se reuersos, in semotiorem locum secedere & paulisper quiescere iubet. Marc.6. Nemo tamen haec ita intelligat, quasi inertes & ignavi aliorum spectatores Antiochiae apostoli sederint. Docuerunt enim bauddie sedulò, & aliorum laboribus suo auxilio adfuerunt fideliter. Ad tempus vero peregrinationibus laborum & periculorum plenissimis, abstinuerunt. Faxit Deus, pater misericordiae, vt quotquot hodie euangelij nomine gloriantur, vitae suae cursum eadem, qua apostoli, industria & felicitate absoluant, & in caelesti patria quiete nunquam finienda fruantur cum Iesu Christo saluatore nostro, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, they are said to have stayed a considerable time in the church at Antioch, no doubt so that they might be refreshed with a good and holy rest, since they had been exercised by so many and such great labours and dangers by land and sea. For it is fair and just that they should receive the fruit of their labours, since their faith and industry have been clearly shown by unmistakable evidence. So Christ, when the apostles returned to him from preaching the gospel, bade them withdraw into a more remote place and rest awhile (Mark 6). Yet no one should understand this as if the apostles sat idle at Antioch, spectators of others' labours. For they taught diligently every day and faithfully helped others with their assistance. It was for a time only that they abstained from journeys full of labours and dangers. May God, the Father of mercies, grant that all who today glory in the name of the gospel may complete the course of their life with the same industry and success as the apostles, and enjoy in the heavenly fatherland a rest that will never end, with Jesus Christ our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XV. HOMILIA CI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV. HOMILY CI.

units.la: ET quidam qui descenderant à Iudaea, docebat fratres: Nisi circumcidamini secundum ritum Mosis, non potestis salui fieri. Quum itaq; orta esset seditio & disceptatio non exigua Paulo & Barnabae contra illos, statuerunt vt Paulus & Barnabas, & quidam alij ex ipsis, ascenderent ad apostolos ac presbyteros Hierosolymam super quaestione hac. Illi ergo deducti ab ecclesia transierunt Phoeniciam & Samariam, narrantes rantes conuersionem gentium, & attulerunt gaudium magnum omni-bus fratribus. Cum autem venissent Hierosolymam, excepti sunt ab ec-clefia, & ab apostolis ac presbyteris, annunciaruntq; quæcunq; fecisset Deus cum ipsis.
units.tr: And certain men who had come down from Judea taught the brethren: "Unless you are circumcised after the manner of Moses, you cannot be saved." When therefore dissension and no small dispute arose between Paul and Barnabas and those men, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and some others of them, should go up to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem about this question. So they were sent on their way by the church, and passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, describing the conversion of the Gentiles, and they brought great joy to all the brethren. And when they came to Jerusalem, they were received by the church, and by the apostles and elders, and they reported all that God had done with them.

units.la: PRAECEDENTI operis fui parte exposuit Lucas, vt primitiua ecclesia apostolorum prædicatione ex Iudæis simul & gentibus collecta, & admirabili Dei præsidio inter con-tinuas persecutionum procellas & fluctus conseruata fit. Istis vero noua historia hoc Cap. subiicitur, qua docet, vt eandem ecclesiam aduersus falsos fratres & impostores Dominus conferua-rit, ne vel doctrinæ simplicitatem vel fidei puritatem amitteret. Hactenus enim totis annis qua-tuordecim Paulus euangelium prædicarat, & iuxta communem apostolicæ doctrinæ consensum, in vno Christo Iesu vniuersam salutis rationem contineri docuerat. Quæ doctrina cum passim reciperetur, quidam qui ex Iudaismo, maxime autem ex Pharifæorum secta ad Christi fidem transierant, illi fe opponere cœperunt. Qui licet Christum faterentur, cum hoc tamen Circuncifionem & reliquas legis ceremonias necessario coniungi oportere contendebant. Quorum sententia cum acriter sese Paulus opponeret, ingens contentio oborta est, quæ totam ecclesiam horribiliter concussura videbatur. Sed non deserit pro fui meriti gloria pugnantes Christus Dominus, cuius prouidentia fit, vt communi & publico omnium apostolorum & totius ecclesiæ testimonio simplex Christi doctrina afferatur & confirmetur. Plurimum vero communi ecclesiarum institutioni simul & consolationi feruit huius historiæ confyderatio. Nam vt apostolorum exemplo docemur, qua ratione aduersus falsas doctrinas pugnandum fit: ita veritatis doctrinam aduersus quasuis incursiones firmam & inuictam consistere discimus. Quare singulas præfentis loci partes ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: In the earlier part of my work Luke set out how the primitive church, gathered from both Jews and Gentiles by the preaching of the apostles, was preserved amid the continual storms and waves of persecution by the wonderful protection of God. This new history is added to this chapter, in which he teaches that the Lord has likewise preserved the same church against false brethren and impostors, so that it would lose neither the simplicity of its teaching nor the purity of its faith. For Paul had preached the gospel for fourteen whole years, and, in agreement with the common consensus of apostolic teaching, had taught that the whole manner of salvation is contained in the one Christ Jesus. While this doctrine was being received everywhere, certain men who had passed over to the faith of Christ from Judaism, and especially from the sect of the Pharisees, began to oppose it. Although they confessed Christ, they nevertheless contended that circumcision and the remaining ceremonies of the law must necessarily be joined with him. When Paul opposed their opinion sharply, a great contention arose, which seemed likely to shake the whole church terribly. But Christ the Lord, whose providence it is, does not abandon those who fight for his glory, and so by the common and public testimony of all the apostles and of the whole church the simple doctrine of Christ is brought forward and confirmed. The consideration of this history is also of great use both for the common instruction and for the consolation of the churches. For, as we are taught by the example of the apostles, in what way one must fight against false doctrines, so we learn that the doctrine of truth stands firm and unconquered against whatever attacks. Therefore we shall examine the individual parts of this passage in order.

units.la: Primo qui dissensionis & turbarum authores fuerint, indicatur. Nimirum quidam qui ex Iu-dæa, adeoq; ex ipsa Hierosolyma descenderant. Non potuit ergo non maxima esse illorum auctori-tas, cum Hierofolymitana ecclesia, quasi communis quædam omnium mater effet, & non immerito ab omnibus aliis obseruaretur, eò quod ex hac euangelium salutis primum prodiisset: quo nomine il-lam Paulus quoq; commendat, cum æquum esse ait, vt gentes corporalia subsidia Hierofolymitanis subministrent, à quibus ipsæ spiritualia & æterna salutis donareceperint. Rom. 15. cap. Nec du-bium est, quin apostolorum nomen & authoritatem impostores illi magnifice iactitarint, & Pauli nomen pro virili eleuarint, quasi is in apostolorum numero minimè censeri mereretur, eò quod nō cum Christo Iesu, in carne agente, conuersatus effet. Id enim ex Pauli epistolis colligere licet, quibus con-tra illos apostolatus fui authoritatem acerrimè vindicare & afferere coactus fuit. Porrò hæc vide-re est, ex ipsa ecclesia plerunq; seductores exoriri, eos nimirum, qui vera ecclesiæ membra nunquam fuerunt. Qui enim reuera ex ecclesia sunt, cum illa manere consueuerunt. 1. Ioban. 2. Ideo Christus ouium pellibus vestitos esse ait. Matth. 7. cap. Et Paulus alibi dicit: Ex vobis ipsis exorientur lupi graues, &c. Act. 20. Et est hæc admirabilis satanæ calliditas, qua cum fe hominibus inuisum & exe-crabilem esse nō. ut, lucis angelum mentiri, & sub sanctorum persona imperitis & incautis illudere consueuit. 2. Corinth. 11. Seruit autem illis redarguendis locus hic, qui Romanam ecclesiam falli & errare posse, constanter negant, & oraculi instar recipiendum esse contendunt, quicquid ex illa prose-ctum fuerit. Æquè ex Hierosolymis pestes eiusmodi prodierunt, cum illic Apostoli suo officio sum-ma fide fungerentur. Quid ergo de ijs speres, apud quos iam fæculis aliquot nulla extiterunt apostoli-cæ doctrinæ vel vitæ vestigia?
units.tr: First, it is shown who were the authors of the dissension and the disturbances: namely, certain men who had come down from Judea, and so from Jerusalem itself. Their authority could not but be very great, since the church of Jerusalem was, as it were, the common mother of all, and was rightly honoured by all others, because the gospel of salvation had first gone forth from it. Paul too commends it under this name, when he says that it is fair that the Gentiles should supply material aid to the men of Jerusalem, from whom they had received the spiritual and eternal gifts of salvation (Rom. 15). Nor is there any doubt that those impostors boasted loudly of the name and authority of the apostles, and magnified the name of Paul as far as they could, as if he deserved to be counted in the number of the apostles least of all, because he had not lived with Christ Jesus while he was in the flesh. This can be gathered from Paul's epistles, in which he was forced to defend and assert very fiercely the authority of his apostleship against them. Moreover, it may be seen here that seducers often arise from the church itself, namely those who were never true members of the church. For those who are really of the church are accustomed to remain with it (1 John 2). Therefore Christ says that they come clothed in sheepskins (Matt. 7). And Paul says elsewhere: "From among yourselves shall grievous wolves arise," etc. (Acts 20). This is the admirable cunning of Satan, by which he is accustomed to deceive the inexperienced and the incautious under the appearance of the saints, since he cannot make himself pleasing to men, so that he may pretend to be an angel of light (2 Cor. 11). This passage also serves to refute those who firmly deny that the Roman church can be deceived and err, and who insist that whatever proceeds from it must be received like an oracle. In the same way such plagues came out of Jerusalem, when the apostles there were discharging their office with the greatest faith. What, then, can you hope for from those among whom for several centuries no traces of apostolic doctrine or life have remained?

units.la: Deinde concertationis status, quem impostores isti maxime asseruerunt, exprimitur. Gentium enim fideles ad Circuncifionem & legales ceremonias reuocarunt, dicentes: Nisi circuncidamini, non potestis salui fieri. Quam sententiam ipsos multis argumentis confirmauisse, verisimile est. Ha-bebant enim legem Dei, qui circuncifionem perpetuum in Israelitis fœderis fui signum esse voluit. Genef. 17. cap. Habebant item Hierofolymitanæ ecclesiæ exemplum, in qua Iudaeorum infirmitati hoc dabant apostoli, vt infantes circuncifionis sacramento initiarent. Præterea, quia circuncifio-ni ad legis obseruationem obstringebantur (iuxta illud Pauli, Contestor omnem hominem qui cir-cumciditur, quod debitor est totius legis feruanda, Galat. 5.) illa sublata legem totam abrogari, & effrænem peccandi licentiam inuebi clamabant. Interim Christum fatebantur, & euangelij secta-tores videri volebant: egregij nimirum compositores, cum legem euangelio & operum iustitiam cum fide commisceri posse putarent. Totius ergo controuersiæ status hic fuit, An sola fide in Christum per Dei gratiam iustificentur homines, vel num legalis iustitia ad salutem necessaria sit. Quòd si ve-rò rem propius expendas, eandem controuersiam hanc fuisse patebit, quæ nobis hodie cum Papistis intercedit, qui & ipsi Christum quidem profitentur, interim vero nostrorum operum meritis nos iu-stificari & saluari contendunt: nisi quod minus firma est Papistarum causa, quòd illi non Mosis le-ge, quæ diuinitus olim tradita fuit, sed hominum traditionibus nituntur, quas iam olim Dei sententia damnatas esse constat. Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Frustra me colunt, docentes doctrinas hominum. Ad nos igitur cumprimis pertinet huius controuersiæ cognitio. Si enim legis diuinæ operibus nullus in iusti-ficationis nostræ gloria locus debetur, miseri reuera & cæci sunt, qui laudem hanc frigidissimis bu-manarum traditionum obseruatiunculis vendicare audent. Interim prodit se hoc loco hominum per uerfitas, qui cum salutem nobis Deus gratis offert, contempta illa, sumptuosam potius & laboriosam eius consequenda rationem inquirunt. Extant huius peruerfitatis exempla omnibus seculis, & de hac Dominus apud Isaiam cap. 55. conqueritur, dicens: Cur expenditis pecuniam pro eo quod cibum non est, & laborem vestrum pro eo quod non satiat? Item Iere. 2. cap. Duo mala fecit populus meus, me deseruerunt fontem aquarum perennium, ut effoderent sibi puteos, puteos inquam pertusos, qui aquas continere non valent. Atqui vtinam non maior similiter conquerendi occasio hodie pa-sim Deo præberetur, &c.
units.tr: Next, the state of the contention, which those impostors especially maintained, is set forth. For they called back the Gentile believers to circumcision and the ceremonies of the law, saying: "Unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved." It is likely that they confirmed this opinion by many arguments. For they had the law of God, which willed that circumcision should be the perpetual sign of his covenant with the Israelites (Gen. 17). They also had the example of the church of Jerusalem, in which the apostles granted this to the weakness of the Jews, that they should admit infants by the sacrament of circumcision. Besides, since men were bound by circumcision to observe the law (according to Paul's words: "I testify to every man who is circumcised that he is a debtor to keep the whole law," Gal. 5), they cried out that once circumcision was removed the whole law would be abolished and an unbridled licence to sin would be introduced. Meanwhile they professed Christ and wished to seem followers of the gospel: clever compounders indeed, who thought that the law could be mixed with the gospel, and the righteousness of works with faith. The whole state of this controversy was therefore this: whether men are justified by faith alone in Christ through the grace of God, or whether legal righteousness is necessary for salvation. But if you weigh the matter more closely, it will be clear that this is the same controversy which today lies between us and the Papists, who also profess Christ indeed, yet meanwhile contend that we are justified and saved by the merits of our works. The only difference is that the Papists' cause is less firm, because they rest not on the law of Moses, which was once delivered by God, but on the traditions of men, which it is plain were long ago condemned by the judgment of God (Isa. 29; Matt. 15: "In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines that are the precepts of men"). Therefore the knowledge of this controversy especially concerns us. For if no place is due to the works of the divine law in the glory of our justification, then those who dare to claim this praise for the very cold little observances of human traditions are truly wretched and blind. Meanwhile this passage reveals the perversity of men who, when God offers us salvation freely, despise it and seek instead a costly and laborious way of obtaining it. Examples of this perversity exist in every age, and the Lord complains of it in Isaiah 55: "Why do you spend money on what is not bread, and your labour on what does not satisfy?" Likewise in Jeremiah 2: "My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, to dig for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns, which cannot hold water." Would that today there were not, everywhere, a greater occasion for similar complaint to be made to God, etc.

units.la: III. Effectus.
units.tr: III. The effects.

units.la: Sequitur tertio loco falsi dogmatis, quod Iudaizantes Christiani inuehebant, effectus. Fuit in se-ditio & apertum schisma, quo Antiochenam ecclesiam, quæ hucusque pacatissima & instar commu-nis asyli omnibus pijs fuerat, turbatam fuisse Lucas scribit. Ecclesiarum ergo turbatores sunt, quicun-que a simplici veritatis doctrina recedentes, nova & falsa dogmata ecclesijs obtrudunt. Hoc nomine no-stros illos Paulus exornat, cum ait: Miror quòd a Christo tam citò transferamini in aliud euange-lium, quod non est aliud, nisi quòd sunt quidam qui turbant vos. Galat. 1. Et alibi illos canes, malos operarios, concisores adeò crucis Christi inimicos appellat. Philip. 3. Scimus equidem nobis hodie a Papistis obiici, quòd ecclesiam turbaverimus & turbemus. At crimen hoc a nobis alienissimum esse constabit, si apostolicæ doctrinæ veritas inspiciatur, cuius puritas ut reduci queat, illorum otium fe-dulo turbamus, quibus sub falso Christi & ecclesiæ prætextu de miserarum ouium pellibus & carni-bus ludere volupe fuit. Porrò præcipuus huius loci vsus est, ne propter dissensiones, quæ nostro secu-lo in religionis causa oboriuntur, ita offendamur, ut omnem fidei & religionis doctrinam incertam & dubiam esse putemus. Veritatis enim doctrinam omnibus seculis varie oppugnatam, & proinde dissensiones frequenter excitatas fuisse constat. Id autem iusto iudicio & nostræ salutis cömodo fieri permittit Deus. Primò enim iuxta Pauli sententiam, sectas esse oportet, ut qui probati sunt, manifesti fiant. 1. Cor. 11. Deinde hac occasione fit, ut maiori diligentia & studio præcipui fidei & salutis nostræ articuli examinentur: qui nisi in controuersiam adducerentur, maxima ex parte inexpensi & -pulti iacerent. Ita enim quæ mala sunt moderari nouit Deus, ut suorum saluti seruiant, & ijs qui Deum diligunt, omnia cooperantur in bonum. Id verò in præsenti disceptatione luce clarius cernimus. Per hanc etenim factum est, ut vera iustificationis ratio maiori diligentia ab apostolis tractata sit, & inter Iudæos quoq; vilescere cæperint legales ceremoniæ, quibus plerique adhuc nitebantur. Itano-stro seculo non alio fortiori ariete Missæ sacrificium euersum est, quàm concertatione illa, quæ circa Cœnæ negotium oborta fuit. Absurdi ergo & nimis inepti illorum clamores sunt, qui propter fre-quentes dissensiones, fidei & salutis negotium dubium omnino & incertum esse conqueruntur. Ita enim prophanos animos, quos gerunt, mendaci prætextu occultare studeut.
units.tr: Third, we come to the effects of the false doctrine that the Judaizing Christians were spreading. There was sedition and an open schism, by which, as Luke writes, the church at Antioch was thrown into turmoil. That church had until then been most peaceful, and had been like a common refuge for all the godly. Those, then, are the disturbers of the churches who, departing from the simple doctrine of the truth, force new and false doctrines upon the churches. Paul brands our opponents with this name when he says: "I marvel that you are so quickly turning from Christ to another gospel, which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you" (Gal. 1). Elsewhere he calls them dogs, evil workers, and mutilators, enemies of the cross of Christ (Phil. 3). We know that the Papists today object to us that we have disturbed, and still disturb, the church. But this charge will prove to be most foreign to us if the truth of apostolic doctrine is examined. In order to restore its purity, we diligently disturb the ease of those men who, under the false pretext of Christ and the church, have taken pleasure in playing with the skins and flesh of wretched sheep. Moreover, the chief use of this passage is that we should not be so offended by the dissensions that arise in our age over religion that we think the whole doctrine of faith and religion is uncertain and doubtful. For it is established that the doctrine of the truth has been variously attacked in all ages, and therefore dissensions have often been stirred up. God permits this to happen by his just judgment and for the benefit of our salvation. First, according to Paul's saying, there must be factions, so that those who are approved may be made manifest (1 Cor. 11). Second, by this occasion it comes about that the chief articles of our faith and salvation are examined with greater care and zeal; unless they were brought into controversy, they would for the most part lie neglected and unexamined. For God knows how to govern even evils so that they serve the salvation of his people, and "all things work together for good for those who love God" (Rom. 8). We see this more clearly than daylight in the present dispute. For through it the true manner of justification was treated with greater diligence by the apostles, and among the Jews the legal ceremonies, on which many still relied, began to be held in contempt. In our own age the sacrifice of the Mass was overthrown by no stronger battering ram than that contention which arose over the business of the Lord's Supper. Absurd and very foolish, then, are the clamours of those who complain that, because of frequent dissensions, the matter of faith and salvation is altogether doubtful and uncertain. For they seek by this lying pretext to hide the profane minds which they bear.

units.la: IIII. Paulus & Barnabas acriter resistunt.
units.tr: IIII. Paul and Barnabas resist vigorously.

units.la: Porrò videamus, quid in disceptatione hac Paulus & Barnabas, quid item Antiochena eccle-sia fideles fecerint. Et Paulo quidem ac Barnabæ non paruas cum turbatoribus istis disceptatio-nes, adeoque disputationes quotidianas intercessisse dicitur. Non ergo canes muti fuerunt, qui quam libet doctrinam in ecclesiam subrepere permitterent, quin potius acerrime obstiterunt, ne impostorum commentis fidei veritas euerteretur. At alibi Paulus omnia fit omnibus, & ijs qui in fide firmi sunt ferió præcipit, ut infirmiores modestè & aquanimiter ferant. Cur ergo hic tam difficilem & intrac-tabilem Stabilem sese prœbet? Quia maioris momenti res erat, quàm quæ aliquam dissimulationem admit - teret. Euertebatur enim hoc dogmate fidei iustitia, quæ in solo Christo nobis obtingit. Nam qui cir - cumcisione legi sese subijciunt, ijs Christus inutilis redditur, & qui per legem iustificari volunt, à gra - tia excidunt. Gal.5. Deinde periclitabatur hic Christiana libertas, quæ non alio pretio, quàm Christi sanguine acquiri potuit: & legis imperio iugoq; intolerabili (vt Petrus postea docebit) subijcieban - tur, qui fide in Christum iustificati, & libertate filiorum Dei donati erant. Adhæc verus legis vsus peruertebatur, qui esset, vt nobis pædagogi instar fit, qui nos Christo adducat. Gal.3. Isti verò eos, qui iam Christo insiti erant, ad legis elementa relegabant. Præterea fieri nō poterat, quin legalibus vm - bris euangelij lux obscuraretur. Nihil ergo impostoribus istis dare potuit Paulus, nisi parum fidus Christi minister esse vellet. Quo exemplo docemur, pacis & concordiæ studio nihil admittendum esse, quod Christi gloriam & fidei simplicem confessionem aliqua ex parte obscurat. Verè enim exitialis est concordia, quæ nominis Christi prophanatione & fidei abnegatione redimitur. Firma enim & rata manet Christi sententia: Qui amauerit patrem & matrem supra me, non est me dignus. Matt. 10. Item: Quemcunq; mei puduerit coram mundo hoc adultero & prauo, eius etiam pudebit me, cum venerit in gloria patris mei, &c. Marc.8. Adhæc perspicuum nobis sit, Christianos homines nullam extra Christum pacem habere posse. Si enim Christiani esse velint, in mundo afflictionem, in solo autem Christo pacem habebunt. Iohan.16.
units.tr: Next, let us see what Paul and Barnabas, and likewise the faithful of the church at Antioch, did in this dispute. It is said that between Paul and Barnabas and those troublers there were no small disputes, and indeed daily debates. Therefore they were not dumb dogs, who allowed any doctrine whatever to creep into the church; rather, they resisted most fiercely, lest the truth of faith be overturned by the inventions of impostors. Yet elsewhere Paul "becomes all things to all men," and he strictly commands that those who are firm in the faith bear with the weaker ones modestly and patiently. Why, then, does he show himself here so stubborn and intractable? Because the matter was of greater weight than could admit any dissimulation. For by this doctrine the righteousness of faith, which we obtain in Christ alone, was being overturned. For those who submit themselves to the law by circumcision, Christ is rendered useless to them, and those who want to be justified by the law fall away from grace (Gal. 5). Next, Christian liberty was in danger, which could not be acquired at any price other than the blood of Christ; and those who had been justified by faith in Christ and endowed with the liberty of the sons of God were being subjected to the rule of the law and to an intolerable yoke (as Peter will later teach). Besides, the true use of the law was being perverted, which is to be for us as a tutor who leads us to Christ (Gal. 3). But these men were sending back to the elements of the law those who were already grafted into Christ. Moreover, it could not be avoided that the light of the gospel would be obscured by legal shadows. Paul could therefore give nothing to those impostors, unless he wished to be an unfaithful minister of Christ. From this example we are taught that, for the sake of peace and concord, nothing is to be admitted which in any way obscures the glory of Christ and the simple confession of faith. For that concord is truly destructive which is purchased by the profanation of the name of Christ and the denial of faith. For the saying of Christ stands firm and sure: "He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Matt. 10). Likewise: "Whoever is ashamed of me before this adulterous and wicked world, of him also will I be ashamed when he comes in the glory of my Father," etc. (Mark 8). Furthermore, let it be plain to us that Christians can have no peace apart from Christ. For if they wish to be Christians, they will have affliction in the world, but peace in Christ alone (John 16).

units.la: Cæterum Antiochenæ ecclesiæ fideles, vbi concertationem hanc indies magis magisq; exardescere viderent, tandem communi decreto statuunt, vt Paulus & Barnabas cum alijs quibusdam Hierosolymam profecti, quæstionem hanc apostolis & presbyteris, qui illic erant, discutiendam proponerent. Et huic decreto facilè acquiescit Paulus: non quidem ea mente, quòd veritatis causam hominum iudicio subijciendam esse putaret, sed quòd probè sciret, impostores illos apostolorum nomine abuti. Quare vt imperitis & rudibus mederetur, quorum oculos illi apostolicæ authoritatis fulgore perstringebant, consilium hoc, quo nullum commodius & expeditius excogitari poterat, facilè recipit. Atqui hanc præcipuam omnium Synodorum fiue Conciliorum causam fuisse constat, quæ à sanctis episcopis & regibus olim collecta sunt. Nunquam enim ea fuit sanctissimorum virorum sententia, quòd hominum iudicijs fidei & salutis causa subijci deberet. Sed quia hereticos impudenti audacia & improbitate apud rude vulgus apostolicæ doctrinæ & vniuersalis ecclesiæ consensum iactare noverant, Synodis & communi ecclesiæ testimonio illos commodissimè coherceri posse putabant, ne fidem apud aliquos posthac inuenirent. Nobis verò diligenter obseruanda est Pauli modestia, quæ hic vtitur. Ea enim constantia illum præditum fuisse certum est, vt ne apostolis quidem diuersum quid à veritatis doctrina pronunciantibus, cedere voluisset. Nam Petrum Antiochiæ palàm reprehendere ausus fuit, & idem ne angelo quidem credendum esse docet, qui aliud euangelium prædicet. Galat. 2. & 1. cap. Idem tamen pacis consilium, à pijs fratribus prodictum minimè aspernatur, cum illo Christi gloriam nullo pacto obscurari, paci autem & infirmorum offendiculis eodem consuli posse videret. Hanc modestiam constantia coniungi oportet, ne dum constantes videri volumus, præfracti & pertinaces efficiamur. Tractabilis enim est Christi spiritus, & Christi gloriæ verè studiosos efficit, qui illo consultore vtuntur. Interim minimè probanda est illorum leuitas, qui dum faciles & tractabiles videri volunt, ijs quoq; consilijs obsequuntur, quibus & Christi gloriam, & fidei veritatem palàm euerti & dissipari vident. Docet præterea locus hic, quæ optima fit componendorum dissidiorum ratio, quæ in religionis & fidei causa oboriri solent. Sunt qui humana prudentia commodissimè res transfigi posse existiment, si vtrinq; aliquid concedatur: quasi verò in diuinis perinde vt humanis rebus ludere liceat. Quin potius ad apostolos ascendere conuenit, vt quid illi docuerint & statuerint, audiamus, quorum doctrinam ipsius Christi testimonio confirmata esse constat. Illi enim dictum est: Qui vos audit, me audit, &c. Luc.10. Et proillis Christum orauisse scimus, qui in ipsum iuxta illorum sermonem crediderint. Iohan.17. Adhæc spiritu sancto palàm donati fuerunt, qui non obscura suæ præsentiæ & operationis argumenta in illis edidit. Quare anxiè cauendum est, ne vel latum vnguem ab illorum doctrina discedamus. Monet id Iohannes apostolus, cum in priori sua epistola cap.2. ait: Quod ab initio audiuistis, in vobis maneat. Si in vobis manserit, quod audiuistis ab initio, vos quoq; in filio & in patre manebitis, &c. Paulus quoq; cum de ijs monuisset, qui veritatis doctrinam peruertere audent, addit: Tu perfistito in his quae didicisti, & quae tibi concredita sunt, cū sciat à quo didiceris, & quòd à puero sacras literas noueris, quae te possunt erudire ad salutem per fidem, quae est in Christo Iesu. 2. Tim. 3. Turpissimè ergo falluntur, qui hoc exemplo Concilia nobis obtrudere volunt, quasi horum iudicijs religionis causa subijci debeat, cum constet, iam seculis aliquot eiusmodi Concilia fuisse, in quibus nullum plane apostolici spiritus vestigium apparuerit. Quòd si illi apostolos & prophetas audire voluerint, libenter iuxta Pauli & Barnabae exemplum cum ipsis ad illos ascendemus, vt audiamus, quid in illis Dei spiritus olim locutus sit. At si homines audiri volunt, procul facessant, cum nobis alium magistrum, praeter Iesum Christum, audire nefas sit.
units.tr: Moreover, when the faithful of the church at Antioch saw this contention growing hotter day by day, they at last decided by common vote that Paul and Barnabas, with some others, should go up to Jerusalem and propose this question for discussion before the apostles and the elders who were there. Paul readily agreed to this decision, not indeed because he thought the cause of the truth should be subjected to the judgment of men, but because he knew well that those impostors were abusing the name of the apostles. Therefore, in order to heal the untrained and rude people, whose eyes those men dazzled with the brilliance of apostolic authority, he readily accepted this plan, than which none could be devised more convenient and expedient. Yet it is established that this was the chief cause of all the synods or councils which were once gathered by holy bishops and kings. For it was never the opinion of the most holy men that the matter of faith and salvation ought to be subjected to the judgments of men. But because the heretics knew how to boast, with shameless audacity and wickedness, before the untaught crowd of the consent of apostolic doctrine and of the universal church, they thought that by synods and the common testimony of the church those men could be most conveniently restrained, so that they might find no further faith among anyone. But we must diligently observe the modesty which Paul shows here. For it is certain that he was endowed with such steadfastness that he would not yield even to the apostles, if they declared anything different from the doctrine of the truth. For he dared to rebuke Peter openly at Antioch, and he teaches that not even an angel is to be believed if he preaches another gospel (Gal. 2 and Gal. 1). Yet he by no means scorned the peaceful counsel put forward by the godly brethren, since he saw that by it the glory of Christ could in no way be obscured, while provision could be made for peace and for the stumbling of the weak. This modesty ought to be joined with constancy, lest, while we wish to seem steadfast, we become headstrong and obstinate. For the spirit of Christ is gentle, and makes those truly zealous for the glory of Christ who use him as their counsellor. Meanwhile, the levity of those men is by no means to be approved, who, while they wish to seem easy and pliable, also obey those counsels by which they plainly see the glory of Christ and the truth of the faith being overturned and destroyed. Furthermore, this passage teaches what is the best way of settling those disagreements which are wont to arise over the cause of religion and faith. There are some who think that matters can be most conveniently settled by human prudence, if something is conceded on both sides, as if indeed in divine matters one might play just as in human ones. Rather, we ought to go up to the apostles, that we may hear what they taught and decided, since it is established that their doctrine was confirmed by the testimony of Christ himself. For it was said to them: "He who hears you hears me," etc. (Luke 10). And we know that Christ prayed for those who would believe in him through their word (John 17). Besides, they were openly endowed with the Holy Spirit, who gave clear evidence of his presence and working in them. Therefore we must be anxiously careful not to depart even a hair's breadth from their doctrine. The apostle John warns us of this when, in his first epistle, chapter 2, he says: "What you have heard from the beginning, let it abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Son and in the Father," etc. Paul too, when he had warned about those who dare to pervert the doctrine of the truth, adds: "But you continue in the things you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, since you know from whom you learned them, and that from childhood you have known the holy writings, which can make you wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim. 3). Most foolishly, then, are those deceived who wish to thrust councils upon us by this example, as if matters of religion ought to be subjected to their judgments, when it is established that for some centuries such councils have been held in which there appeared no trace at all of the apostolic spirit. But if those men wish to hear the apostles and the prophets, we will gladly go up with them to those men, after the example of Paul and Barnabas, so that we may hear what the Spirit of God once spoke through them. But if men wish to be heard, let them depart far away, since for us it is unlawful to hear any other teacher besides Jesus Christ.

units.la: Caeterum ipsam quoque profectionem Pauli Lucas describit, cum in hac etiam quadam conti-neantur obseruatu dignissima. Inter quae primum est, quod ab ecclesia deducuntur Paulus & Barnabas, quae nimirum dignos & fidos itineris comites illis adiunxerat. Vnde patet ecclesiam abillorum partibus fletisse, nec ipsorum fidem suspectam habuisse. Imitentur hoc omnes ecclesiae, ne fideles Christi ministros suo patrocinio destituant. Quid enim illi aliud quàm commune bellum pro ecclesijs sustinent? Et sane execrabilis illorum ingratitudo est, qui si quid turbarum in religionis causa oritur, extra teli iactum certaminis spectatores esse volunt, quasi nihil ad ipsos ea res pertineat, sed priuata duntaxat ministrorum causa agatur. Deinde, ne infrugifera illis esset profectio, & sine fructu omne illud profectionis tempus transiret, paßim gentium conuersionem praedicant. Atqui haec potissima erat litis causa, quòd indigne nonnulli ferrent, gentes nondum circuncisas in Christi & ecclesia communionem receptas esse. Sed intelligunt sanctissimi viri, Dei opera, quae gloriae Christi illustrande seruiunt, propter iniqua quorundam iudicia minimè dissimulari debere. Quin potius cum mundi improbitate nobis luctandum est, ne per hanc gloriae Dei aliquid decedat. Nam quod sacerdotibus puerorum acclamationes indigne ferentibus, olim Christus respondit: Si isti tacuerint, lapides clamabunt: hoc ipsum nobis dictum putemus. Licet enim ipsi ignauiae nostrae consulentes, pro Dei gloria nihil audendum esse putemus, facile tamen illius assertores fidos Dominus inueniet, & nos ire & ignominiae vasa efficiemur, qui gratiae & gloriae vasa esse noluimus. Tertiò, gaudent gentium conuersione fratres, & nec illis salutis communionem, nec Paulo & Barnabae tam praeclaram sui ministerij laudem inuident. Est hoc proprium piorum, vt ex gloriae Christi propagatione & aliorum salute praecipuam gaudendi causam arripiant: rursum vero non aliud illis perinde dolet, quàm si Christi regnum minus feliciter promouere videant. Quarto, vbi Hierosolymam peruentum est, ab apostolis simul & tota ecclesia tanquam praeclara Christi organa excipiuntur. Decet enim vt Dei dona in illis veneremur, quorum ministerio Deus cum fructu & laude vti dignatur. Illi rursum, quae cum ipsis Deus egerit, praedicant, eò quòd hac praesenti causa plurimum seruiebant, cum gentium vocationem inepto suo dogmate aduersarij omnino euertere conarentur. Faxit Deus, vt hodie quoque sopitis contentionibus, apostolorum doctrinam omnes audiant, & omnium mentes per fidei vnitatem veraque charitatis vinculum firmissimè coniungantur in Iesu Christo, saluatore nostro vnico: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke also describes the departure of Paul itself, in which there are several things most worthy of notice. Among these, first, Paul and Barnabas are escorted by the congregation, which had of course assigned them worthy and faithful companions for the journey. From this it is plain that the church grieved at their departure and did not regard their faith with suspicion. All the churches should imitate this, so as not to leave the faithful ministers of Christ without their protection. For what else are these men doing than waging a common war on behalf of the churches? Truly, the ingratitude of those is detestable who, when some disturbance arises over the cause of religion, want to be spectators standing beyond the range of the missiles, as if the matter did not concern them at all, and as if only the private cause of the ministers were being pursued. Next, so that the journey would not be unfruitful for them, and so that all that time of travel would not pass without fruit, they preach everywhere the conversion of the Gentiles. And yet this was the chief cause of the dispute, since some took it badly that the Gentiles, not yet circumcised, were received into fellowship with Christ and the church. But these most holy men understood that the works of God, which serve to make the glory of Christ shine forth, must by no means be concealed because of the unjust judgments of certain people. Rather, we must struggle against the wickedness of the world, lest anything of the glory of God be lost through it. For what Christ once answered to the priests who took offence at the shouts of the children, "If these were silent, the stones would cry out," let us regard as said to us as well. For although we, consulting our own laziness, may think that nothing should be dared for the glory of God, the Lord will nevertheless easily find faithful defenders of it; and we will become vessels of shame, we who were unwilling to be vessels of grace and glory. Third, the brethren rejoice in the conversion of the Gentiles, and they do not begrudge them the fellowship of salvation, nor do they begrudge Paul and Barnabas such an outstanding commendation of their ministry. It is characteristic of the godly to seize upon the spread of Christ's glory and the salvation of others as the chief cause for rejoicing; on the other hand, nothing else grieves them as much as seeing the kingdom of Christ advance less successfully. Fourth, when they arrive at Jerusalem, they are received by the apostles and by the whole church as distinguished instruments of Christ. For it is fitting that we should honour the gifts of God in those through whose ministry God deigns to use them with fruit and praise. In turn, they declare what God has done with them, because in this present cause they were of great service, since the adversaries were attempting entirely to overturn the calling of the Gentiles with their unsound doctrine. May God grant that today too, with contentions laid to rest, all hear the doctrine of the apostles, and that the minds of all are most firmly joined together through the unity of faith and the true bond of charity in Jesus Christ, our one Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CII.
units.tr: HOMILY CII.

units.la: Surrexerunt autem quidam ex secta Pharisaeorum, qui crediderant, dicentes, quòd oportere eos circuncidere, & praecipere vt seruarent legem Mosis. Conuenerunt autem apostoli & presbyteri, vt dispicerent de hoc negotio. Sed cum magna disceptatio fuisset exorta, surgens Petrus dixit ad eos: Viri fratres, vos scitis quòd ab antiquis diebus deus in nobis elegit, vt per os meum audirent gentes verbum euangelij, & crederent. Et cognitor cordium deus, testimonium praebuit illis, dans eis spiritum sanctum, sicut & nobis: nihilq; discreuit inter nos & illos, cum fide purificasset corda illorum. Nunc ergo quid tentatis deum, vt imponatur iugum super ceruices discipulorum, quod neq; patres nostri, neq; nos portare potuimus? Sed per gratiam domini nostri Iesu Christi, credimus dimus nos saluari, quemadmodum & illi. Tacuit autè tota multitudo, & audiebant Barnabā ac Paulum, narrantes, quæ Deus edidisset signa & prodigia inter gentes.
units.tr: Then some of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up, saying that it was necessary to circumcise them and to command them to keep the law of Moses. The apostles and elders came together to consider this matter. When a great debate had arisen, Peter rose and said to them: Men and brothers, you know that in the early days God chose among us that the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel through my mouth and believe. And God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us. He made no distinction between us and them, since by faith he had purified their hearts. Why, then, do you now test God by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are. Then the whole multitude fell silent and listened to Barnabas and Paul, who told how many signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles.

units.la: POstquàm euangelij doctrina Pauli & Barnabæ ministerio inter gentes propagata, & hæ etiam in Christi & ecclesiæ consortium receptæ fuerunt, grauis inter ipsos fideles controuersia incidit, eò quòd nonnulli gentes circuncidendas & ad legis Mosaicæ obseruationem cogendas esse dicerent, id quod alij constantissimè negabant. Diligenter verò controuersiam hanc ex [spiritus sancti suggestione Lucas describit, quòd non parum omnium nostrum institutioni seruiat. Docet enim non nouum & insolens censeri debere, si etiam hodie inter eiusdem fidei & doctrinæ professores controuersia aliquot exoriantur: cum illas Deus non sine publico aliquo bono incidere patiatur. Rursum quid in his agendum sit, admonet. Nam Pauli & Barnabæ exemplo fortiter contra quosuis veritatem asserere, nec vllorum hominum iudicia audire, sed apostolos Iesu Christi consulere debemus, quos ille orbi doctores dedit.
units.tr: After the teaching of the gospel had spread among the Gentiles through the ministry of Paul and Barnabas, and these Gentiles had also been received into fellowship with Christ and the Church, a serious controversy arose among the believers themselves. Some said that the Gentiles must be circumcised and compelled to observe the law of Moses, while others most firmly denied it. Luke describes this controversy carefully, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, and this is of no small use for the instruction of us all. For it teaches that we should not think it strange or new if controversies arise even today among those who profess the same faith and doctrine, since God allows such disputes to arise for some public good. Again, it shows us what must be done in such cases. For following the example of Paul and Barnabas, we must assert the truth boldly against anyone whatsoever, and not listen to the judgements of any men, but consult the apostles of Jesus Christ, whom he gave to the world as teachers.

units.la: Pergens autem in cœpta historia Lucas, maiorem de hac causa disceptationem exortam esse ait, postquàm Hierosolymis in apostolorum & presbyterorum conuentu propositá est. Authores huius fuerunt, qui ex Pharisæis Christo nomen dederant, ex veteri tamen fermento illud retinentes, quòd legalis iustitiæ obseruationem pertinacius vrgerent. Constat enim vel ex euangelica historia, pharisæos iustificationem omnem in externis legalium operum exercitijs collocauisse. Quare fieri non potuit, quin in his retinendis pertinaciores essent. Cuius rei exemplum in Monachis hodie extat, quos difficile est ita à veteri secta retrahere, ut nulla illius vestigia superstint. EST autem diligenti obseruatione dignum, quòd præcipuus Christianæ religionis articulus in sanctissimorum hominum consessu & apostolorum conspectu tanta concertatione agitatur, ut vtra pars rectius sentiat, non statim possit intelligi. Inde enim docemur, non mirum videri debere, etiamsi magna ingenia interdum hallucinentur, vel etiam conceptos errores pertinacius retineant. Ita enim Deus nostræ naturæ corruptionem, quam interdum non obseruamus, nobis cognoscendam offert, vt eius cognitione humiliati, non altum sapiamus. Cæterum in disceptatione hac tacuit hucusq; Petrus apostolus, nimirum ne cui arrogantius præscribere videretur, & quòd singulorum mentes reuelari, non inutile esset. Vbi verò animos contendentium plus satis incaluisse videt, modestè simul & grauiter assurgens suam authoritatem interponit, qua Pauli & Barnabæ sententiam ingenuè tuetur, qui iustificationis & salutis humanæ rationem in sola fide Iesu Christi consistere, nec vlla legalium ceremoniarum obseruatione opus esse, imò in vniuersum nullam huius rei laudem & gloriam ad legem transferri debere, docebant. Constat tota oratio duabus omnino partibus, quarum altera à Deo non aliam iustificandi rationem obseruari docet, quàm quæ in euangelio traditur, fides nimirum in Christum Iesum: altera autem ingens scelus esse offendit, si quis legis obseruationem ad salutem necessariam esse, affirmare audeat. Sed de singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Luke goes on with his history and says that a greater dispute arose about this matter after it had been laid before the assembly of the apostles and elders at Jerusalem. The authors of it were those who, from the Pharisees, had given their names to Christ, yet still kept the old leaven, insisting more stubbornly on the observance of legal righteousness. For it is clear, even from the gospel story, that the Pharisees placed all justification in the outward exercises of legal works. So it could not be that they were not more stubborn in holding on to these things. An example of this exists today among the monks, who are hard to draw so far from the old sect that no trace of it remains. But it is worth careful notice that the chief article of the Christian religion was debated with such contention in the assembly of the most holy men and before the apostles, so that it could not at once be understood which side judged more rightly. From this we are taught that it should not seem surprising if great minds sometimes go astray, or even hold their errors more stubbornly. For in this way God sets before us the corruption of our nature, which we sometimes fail to notice, so that, humbled by knowing it, we may not think highly of ourselves. Moreover, the apostle Peter had kept silent in this dispute until now, doubtless lest he seem to dictate too arrogantly to anyone, and because it was not unhelpful for the minds of each to be revealed. But when he saw that the minds of the disputants had grown more than enough heated, he rose up modestly and gravely and brought in his authority, by which he sincerely upheld the view of Paul and Barnabas, who taught that the way of justification and human salvation rests solely on faith in Jesus Christ, and that no observance of legal ceremonies is needed; indeed, that in general no praise or glory in this matter should be transferred to the law. The whole speech consists of two parts. In one, he teaches that God observes no other way of justifying than the one handed down in the gospel, namely faith in Jesus Christ. In the other, he shows that it is a great crime if anyone dares to affirm that the observance of the law is necessary for salvation. But we shall speak of each part in order.

units.la: Prima pars Dei exemplum habet, qui primitias credentium ex gentibus non alia ratione quàm fide in Christum iustificauit. Debet autem de Cornelij Centurionis historia locus intelligi, quam Petrus commodissimè allegat, eò quòd iam ante eadem inter fideles disputationibus exagitata esset, vt Cap. 11. vidimus. Summa argumenti est: Deus, cum Cornelium & illius domesticos ex gentilismo ad Christum vocare, & in ecclesiæ suæ communionem adoptare vellet, simul in illorum exemplo veram & perfectam salutis consequendæ rationem propositum. Ab illis verò non aliud requisiuit, quàm vt ex me euangelium audirent, & crederent. Ergo ad iustificationem & salutis rationem duo ista suffi ciunt, nimirum vt euangelium audiant homines, & Christum qui per hoc prædicatur, vera fide amplectantur. Firmissimè autem ex singularibus vniuersale dogma colligit Petrus, quia certa & inuiolabilis est Deo saluandi ratio erga omnes homines, nec verisimile videri potest, Deum in propha no milite saluando eam rationem negligere voluisse, quæ filij sui sanguine sancita erat. Vt verò plus ponderis haberet argumentum, ipsos rei gestæ testes producit. Vos ipsi scitis (inquit) quòd antiquis diebus, id est, primo nascentis ecclesiæ tempore, Deus inter nos elegit vel instituit, vt per os meum gentes euangelij audirent, & crederent. Quibus inferre poterat: Cur ergo vos præter ea, quæ Deo suffitere vsa sunt, circuncisionem & legis obseruatione requiritis? Vel vnde ea vobis authoritas, quòd Dei ordinem mutare, & aliquid huic adijcere vel adimere audeatis? Sed hoc ipsis colligendum relinquit. Interim duo adijcit, quibus exemplum hoc illustrat. Primò, Deus (ait) qui cordium cognitor est, qui corda hominum respicit, nec externa specie fallitur, hanc rationem, de qua modò diximus, sufficere, abunde suo ipsius testimonio comprobauit. Vt primùm enim euangelio praedicato crediderunt, spiritum sanctum illis, perinde vt nobis, misit. Quem cum mundus hic & prophani homines, vel ipso Christo teste, capere non possint, luce clarius constat, Deum hos pro ecclesia suae membris & Christi cohaeredibus agnoscere, licet nec circuncisionem recipiant, nec vlla legali ceremonia lustrentur. Deinde modum iustificationis quasi digito monstrans ait: Nihil§ discreuit inter nos & illos Deus, cum fide purificauisset corda illorum. Ante quidem lege Iudaei à gentibus distinguebantur, Christus autem legis maceriam diruit, & ex duobus populis vnam constituit ecclesiam, & vt Iudaeos, ita gentes quoq; fide Deus purificauit. Pertinet huc Pauli locus Ephes.2. Et quae idem ad Romanos cap.3. in haec verba scribit: Arbitramur igitur fide iustificari hominem absq; operibus legis. An Iudaeorum Deus tantum? annon & gentium? Certe & gentium. Quoniam vnus Deus, qui iustificabit circuncisionem ex fide, & praeputium per fidem.
units.tr: The first part has God's example, who justified the first-fruits of believers from the Gentiles in no other way than by faith in Christ. The passage must be understood from the story of the centurion Cornelius, which Peter cites most aptly, since the same matter had already been debated among the faithful, as we saw in chapter 11. The summary of the argument is this: God, when he wished to call Cornelius and his household from heathenism to Christ and to adopt them into the fellowship of his Church, at the same time set forth in their example the true and perfect way of obtaining salvation. From them, however, he required nothing more than that they hear the gospel from me and believe. So for justification and the way of salvation these two things suffice: that people hear the gospel, and embrace with true faith Christ who is preached through it. Peter draws a universal doctrine very firmly from particular cases, because God's way of saving all people is certain and inviolable, and it cannot seem likely that God, in saving the Gentiles, wished to neglect that way which was sanctioned by the blood of his Son. But so that the argument might carry more weight, he calls forward the very witnesses of what was done. You yourselves know, he says, that in the early days, that is, at the first time of the nascent Church, God chose or appointed among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the gospel and believe. He could have added to this: Why, then, besides what has served to bring about God's purpose, do you require circumcision and observance of the law? Or where do you get the authority to change God's order and to add anything to it or take anything from it? But he leaves this for them to draw themselves. Meanwhile he adds two points by which he illustrates this example. First, God (he says), who knows the hearts, who looks upon the hearts of men and is not deceived by outward appearance, has amply confirmed by his own testimony that this way, of which we have just spoken, is sufficient. For as soon as they believed the preached gospel, he sent the Holy Spirit to them just as he did to us. Since the world and profane men, even by the testimony of Christ himself, cannot receive the Spirit, it is clearer than light that God acknowledges these men as members of his Church and co-heirs with Christ, even though they receive neither circumcision nor are cleansed by any legal ceremony. Then, as if pointing with his finger to the manner of justification, he says: God made no distinction between us and them, since he had purified their hearts by faith. Before this, the Jews were distinguished from the Gentiles by the law, but Christ broke down the dividing wall of the law and made one Church out of two peoples, and God has purified the Gentiles by faith just as he has the Jews. To this belongs the passage of Paul in Ephesians 2, and what he writes in Romans 3 in these words: We therefore conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law. Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Certainly also of the Gentiles. Since there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.

units.la: Porrò breui sententia Petrus comprehendit, quaecunq; de iustificatione nostra dici possunt. Primò enim corda purificatione opus habere fatetur. Totus igitur homo pollutus fit, oportet, quādo cor omnium actionum nostrarum fons est. Testatur hoc ipse Deus, quando figmenta cordis humanae iuuentae aetate praua esse dicit. Gen.8. Atqui vnum hoc ad euertendam nostrorum operum iustitiam abunde sufficit, vt alibi monuimus. Deinde purificationem fide fieri docet, eò quòd illa Christum apprehendit, quem nobis iustificatorem Deus constituit. Is à peccatis nos fui sanguinis merito emundat. 1.Iohan.1. Idem suam iustitiam nobis communicat, vt propter fidem, qua illi inferimur, iusti coram Deo conspectu reputemur: quare Paulus illum nobis à Deo iustitiam factum esse docet. 1.Cor.1. Item 1. Cor.5. Adhaec vnus hic carnis nostrae reliquias mortificat, dum verbo & spiritu suo regeneratos inuat, & vires suggerit, vt dignos professione nostra fructus feramus. Quo ipsius verba referri debent: Iam vos mundi estis propter sermonem meum, quem locutus sum vobis. Qui manet in me, & ego in eo, hic fert fructum multum, &c. Iohan.15. At quia nulla nobis absq; fide cum Christo communio esse potest, recte per fidem nos purificari & iustificari, scriptura tradit. Quae locutio non ita accipi debet, quasi fides virtus fit, cuius merito peccata expientur, sed quòd illa Christum, in quo omnis iustitia nostra sita est, apprehendimus. Tertiò Deum purificationis huius authorem facit. Hic idem ergo vnicus fidei nostrae author est, quam Paulus quoq; Dei donum esse testatur. Ephes.2. Et Christus neminem ad se venire dicit, nisi quem pater traxerit. Iohan.6. Quia enim animalis homo spiritus mysteria non percipit, & ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei sumus, diuinitus nos illuminari & duci oportet, vt fides in nobis locum habere possit. Ita vero ad vnum Deum redit tota nostrae iustificationis gloria, nec quicquam humanus siue viribus siue meritis relinquitur. Vidit hoc olim David, quando Deum pro peccatorum remissione inuocans, ait: Laua me tu ab iniquitate mea, & à peccato meo munda me. Expia me hyssopo, & mundus ero: laua me, & nive ero candidior. Libera me de sanguinibus ô Deus, Deus salutis meae, &c. Psal.51. Atqui haud vulgaris inde consolatio petitur, qua in tentationibus fidem nutantem erigamus. Quia enim à Deo pendet iustificatio & salus nostra, certissimam & infallibilem hanc esse oportet. Hinc illa Pauli: Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat, quis ille qui condemnet? Rom.8. Tanta autem huius doctrinae in populo Dei certitudo fuit omnibus seculis, vt Pharisaei quoq; id non obscure confessi sunt, quòd solus Deus peccata remittendi potestatem habeat. Matth.9. Non temere ergo illorum stultitiam simul & arrogantiam hodie deploramus, qui gloriam hanc vel suis ipsorum operibus, velarrogantissimis hominibus & audacissimis hypocritis tribuunt, &c. Quàm verò isti homines peccent, altera orationis suae parte Petrus docet, quam modò inspiciemus.
units.tr: Moreover, Peter has summed up in a brief sentence everything that can be said about our justification. First, he admits that the heart needs purification. Therefore the whole man must be defiled, since the heart is the source of all our actions. God himself bears witness to this when he says that the imaginations of the human heart are evil from youth (Gen. 8). Yet this one point alone is enough to overthrow the righteousness of our works, as we have elsewhere pointed out. Next, he teaches that purification is effected by faith, because faith apprehends Christ, whom God has appointed as our justifier. He cleanses us from sins by the merit of his blood (1 John 1). The same Christ communicates his righteousness to us, so that through faith, by which we are engrafted into him, we are reckoned righteous in the sight of God; for this reason Paul teaches that he was made righteousness to us by God (1 Cor. 1). Likewise (1 Cor. 5). Moreover, this one Christ mortifies the remnants of our flesh, while he helps those who have been regenerated by his word and Spirit, and supplies strength so that we may bear fruits worthy of our profession. To this his words should be referred: Now you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, etc. (John 15). But because there can be no communion with Christ for us without faith, Scripture rightly teaches that we are purified and justified through faith. This expression should not be understood as if faith were a virtue by whose merit sins are expiated, but because by it we lay hold of Christ, in whom all our righteousness lies. Thirdly, he makes God the author of this purification. This same one, therefore, is the sole author of our faith, which Paul also testifies is the gift of God (Eph. 2). And Christ says that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him (John 6). For since the natural man does not perceive the mysteries of the Spirit, and we are not fit even to think from ourselves, we must be enlightened and led by God, so that faith may have a place in us. Thus the whole glory of our justification returns to the one God, and nothing is left to man, either to his strength or to his merits. David saw this long ago, when, calling upon God for the forgiveness of sins, he said: Wash me from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, God of my salvation, etc. (Ps. 51). Yet a not common consolation is drawn from this, by which we may lift up our faltering faith in temptations. For since justification and our salvation depend on God, this must be most certain and infallible. Hence that saying of Paul: Who will bring any charge against the elect of God? It is God who justifies; who is he who condemns? (Rom. 8). Moreover, there has been such certainty of this doctrine among the people of God in all ages that even the Pharisees openly confessed that God alone has the power of forgiving sins (Matt. 9). Therefore we do not rashly deplore today the folly and at the same time the arrogance of those who attribute this glory either to their own works, or to the most arrogant men and the most audacious hypocrites, etc. How greatly these men sin, Peter teaches in the other part of his speech, which we shall now examine.

units.la: Nunc ergo (inquit) quid tentatis Deum, vt imponatur iugum super ceruices discipulorum, quod neq; patres nostri, neq; nos portare potuimus? Docet grauissimis hisce verbis, omnem salutis rationem prorsus euerti, nec sine atroci flagitio intolerabile iugum credentibus imponi, si ad legis obseruationem adigantur, vt in hac iustificationem quarant. Et Deum quidem hoc dogmate tentari dicit. Hunc enim tentant, quicunque absque Dei praecepto, vel ipsi facere conantur, vel ab aliis exigunt. gunt, quæ humanas vires superant. Quotquot item de Dei voluntate alijs rationibus edoceri volui, quàm quas ipse nobis proposuit. Ita Deum Israelitæ tentauisse dicuntur, quando posse infinita illius beneficia, bonitatem & omnipotentiam eius tum demum se agnituros esse dixerunt, si in deserto carnes largiri possit. Psal.78. Num.11. Et Deum Christus tentauisset, si diaboli consilium secutus, se- se de templi pinna præcipitans, illius erga se voluntatem & promissionum ipsius veritatem voluisset experiri. Verum, vero ab ijs fieri constat, qui legis operibus iustificari volunt. Nam quæ humanas vires longissime superant, nullo Dei verbo vocati, cum ipsi aggrediuntur, tum ab alijs exigunt.
