Lege enim ab vilo hominum impleri, tam impossibile est, quàm cælum digito contingere. Spiritualis enim est, nec externa modo opera, sed totum animi omnesq; hominis facultates in Dei obedientiam vendicat. Nos vero carnales sumus, & sub peccatum venundati. Rom.8. Et in sanctis etiam carnis reliquiæ apparent, & lex peccati, quæ vel inuitos multumq; reluctante Dei spiritu, peccatis subijcit, sicuti de semetipso Paulus fatetur. Rom.7. Adhæc maledictionis & mortis sententiam omnibus illis lex intonat, quicunq; no omnia illius præcepta impleuerint. Deut.27. Quid ergo aliud quam Deum tentant, qui per hanc iustificari volunt? Et quia idem salutis rationem, quam in Christo deus exhibuit, negligunt, nouamq; comminiscuntur, qua in Dei gratiam peruenianť, bifariam illum tentant. Quòd si alios quoq; ad eandem salutis rationem cogere velint, iugum imponunt, quod ne sanctissimi quidem patres olim ferre potuerunt. Horum enim voces sunt: Si iniquitates nostras obseruaueris domine, quis sustinebit? Nec intres cum seruo tuo in iudicium. Psal.130. & 143. Omnes iustitiæ nostræ tanquam vestis centonum, vel vt pannus menstruæ mulieris. Isa.64. Videergo quàm non temere cum illis contendamus, qui hodie etiam ad operum iustificationem homines adigunt, & pharisæorum exemplo, contempta Dei iustitia, quam ille nobis in Christo offert, propria stabilire conantur. Neq; hic aliquis obijciat: Ergo frustra lex data est? Ergo impune quod lubet faciemus? Manet enim verus legis vsus, dum nos pædagogi instar ad Christum perducit, & vitæ pie instituen dæ regulam exhibet. Nec bonis operibus ideo renuntiandum est, quòd illis iustificationis gloria non tribuitur. Licet enim hæc ad solum Deum pertineat, constat tamen perpetuo eorum, quos Deus iustificauit, officium esse, vt innocentiam & vitæ puritatem, quæ ipsis in Christo contigit, indefesso studio tueantur, de qua re multa Paulus habet ad Rom.6.cap. Quid vero gravius dici poterat, quàm quod in eos Petrus dicit, qui pro gloria Dei, pro bonis operibus, pro vitæ Christianæ officijs pugnare videri volebat? Deum illos tentare dicit, quod nulla venia dignum facinus esse, scriptura docet. Idem iugum imponunt alijs, & Christi sanguine redemptos nouæ seruituti subijciunt. Plagij ergo crimine aduersus ipsum Christum peccant. Hæc si hodie expenderent aduersarij nostri, facile viderent, se nullam in nos de bacchandi causam habere: quin potius culpam suam agnoscerent, nec tam improbe Dei gratiam & Christi meritum fœda sua hypocrisi conculcarent.
units.tr: "Now therefore," he says, "why do you tempt God by putting a yoke on the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" With these very weighty words he teaches that the whole way of salvation is utterly overthrown, and that no believers can have this intolerable yoke laid on them, if they are compelled to observe the law in order to seek justification by it, without a grievous wickedness. He says that God is tempted by this doctrine. For whoever tries, without a command of God, either to do things himself or to demand them of others, which exceed human strength, tempts him. The same is true of whoever wants to teach about God's will by other reasons than those he himself has set before us. So the Israelites are said to have tempted God when they said that they would only then acknowledge his infinite benefits, his goodness and his omnipotence, if he could furnish flesh in the desert (Ps. 78; Num. 11). And Christ would have tempted God, had he followed the devil's counsel and, throwing himself down from the pinnacle of the temple, wished to test God's will toward himself and the truth of his promises. But it is clear that those who want to be justified by the works of the law do this in fact. For when they, not called by any Word of God, undertake things that far exceed human powers, and demand them of others, they tempt him. For to fulfil the law by any man is as impossible as touching heaven with a finger. The law is spiritual; it claims not only outward works but the whole mind and all the faculties of man in obedience to God. We, however, are carnal and sold under sin (Rom. 8). Even in the saints remnants of the flesh appear, and the law of sin, which brings them under sin even against their will, while the Spirit of God struggles against it, as Paul confesses about himself (Rom. 7). Moreover, the law thunders the sentence of curse and death on all those who have not fulfilled all its precepts (Deut. 27). What else, then, do those who want to be justified by the law do but tempt God? And because they neglect the one way of salvation which God has displayed in Christ, and devise a new one by which they might reach God's grace, they tempt him in two ways. But if they want to compel others also to the same way of salvation, they lay a yoke on them, which not even the most holy fathers of old could bear. For these are their words: "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, who could stand? Do not enter into judgment with your servant" (Ps. 130 and 143). "All our righteousnesses are like a filthy garment, or like a rag of a menstruous woman" (Isa. 64). See, then, how rightly we contend with those who today also drive men to justification by works, and, following the example of the Pharisees, disregard the righteousness of God which he offers us in Christ, and try to establish their own. Nor let anyone object here: "Then was the law given in vain? Then shall we do whatever we please with impunity?" For the true use of the law remains, while it leads us, like a schoolmaster, to Christ and sets forth the rule for instructing life in godliness. Nor must good works be renounced because the glory of justification is not ascribed to them. For although this belongs to God alone, it is nevertheless certain that it is always the duty of those whom God has justified to guard with unwearied zeal the innocence and purity of life which they have received in Christ. Paul has much to say about this in Rom. 6. But what could be said more severely than what Peter says against those who wished to appear to be fighting for the glory of God, for good works, and for the duties of the Christian life? He says that they tempt God, and Scripture teaches that this is a crime deserving no pardon. They impose the same yoke on others and subject those redeemed by the blood of Christ to a new servitude. They therefore sin against Christ himself with the crime of kidnapping. If our adversaries today considered these things, they would easily see that they have no cause to rail against us. Rather they would acknowledge their own fault, and would not so shamelessly trample underfoot God's grace and the merit of Christ with their foul hypocrisy.

units.la: Porrò ne patres audacius damnare videretur Petrus, dum illos quoq; legem non potuisse ferre dicit, rationem qua illi saluati sunt, conclusione infert, dicens: Per gratiam domini nostri Iesu Christi credimus nos saluari, quemadmodum & illi. Ita vero infirmioribus medetur, quibus durum videbatur, ab ea religione discedere, in qua patres suos olim Deo placuisse & saluatos fuisse credebant: quasi dicat: Longe fallimini, si maiores nostros legis operib. iustificatos & saluatos esse putatis, cum ipsi legem se nunquam impleuisse, ingenuè confessi sint. Quòd si scire velitis, quæ salutis ipsorum ratio fuerit, non alia monstrari poterit, quàm quæ nobis hodie in Christo prædicatur. Quem enim nos exhibitum esse scimus, illi venturum expectarunt, nec alium, quàm hunc, saluatorem sperauerunt. Vna ergo & eadem est veteris & noui Testamenti fides, vna quoq; & eadē vtrobiq; salutis ratio. Testatur hoc de Abrahamo loquens Christus, quando hunc diem suum vidisse; & in hoc exultauisse dicit. Ioban.8. Et Paulus patres eundem spiritualem cibum nobiscum comedisse, & de petra Christo salutem hausisse fatetur. 1.Cor.10. Eam deniq; inter nos & patres communionem facit, vt nunc quidem illorum sacramenta ad nos transferat, nunc vero nostra illis applicet. Turpis ergo illorum error est, qui veteris Testamenti libros nihil ad nos pertinere clamant, nosq; Iudaeos esse negant, quibus hæc olim scripta sint. Quin potius cogitandum erat, Dei populū Iudaeos fuisse, quos non alia ratione Deus saluos fecit olim quàm qua nos hodie saluari solemus. Rursum vero salutis rationem Petrus breuiter perstringit. Et eius quidem fundamentum in gratia Dei collocat, qua vna voce operum iustitiā & meritum excluditur, cum hac inter se opponantur. Nam si per gratiam (vt Paulus ait) salus ob-tingit, non iam ex operibus, quandoquidem gratia non esset gratia, si nimirum operum merita ad-mitterentur. Sin vero ex operibus saluamur, non iam ex gratia. Siquidem opus meriti nomen amittit, vt primum gratia admittitur. Vide Rom. 11. cap. Qui locus abunde docet, gratia Dei & operum nostrorum merita simul consistere non posse. Deinde vero gratiae illius mediatorem siue προέϛωρ Christum Iesum esse, Petrus ostendit, in quo patrem nobis reconciliatum esse, caelesti oraculo edocemur, Matth. 3. & 17. Postremo fide gratiam hanc apprehendi testatur. Nam credimus (inquit) nos per gratiam domini nostri Iesu Christi saluari. Paucis ergo & minime ambiguis verbis vniuersa salutis ratio comprehendi poterit, si nos gratia Dei in Iesu Christo per fidem saluari dicamus, quae omnis tum propheticae tum apostolicae doctrinae summa est.
units.tr: Moreover, lest Peter seem to condemn the fathers too boldly, while he says that they too could not bear the law, he draws the conclusion about the way they were saved, saying: "We believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are." In this way he comforts the weaker ones, to whom it seemed hard to depart from that religion in which they believed their fathers of old had pleased God and been saved. As if he said: "You are greatly mistaken if you think that our forebears were justified and saved by works of the law, since they openly confessed that they had never fulfilled the law. But if you want to know what their way of salvation was, none can be shown other than that which is preached to us today in Christ. For the one whom we know has been revealed, they looked for as the one who would come, and they hoped for no other Saviour than this one. There is therefore one and the same faith of the Old and New Testaments, and one and the same way of salvation in both." Christ bears witness to this when, speaking of Abraham, he says that Abraham saw his day and rejoiced in it (John 8). And Paul confesses that the fathers ate the same spiritual food as we do, and drew salvation from the rock, which is Christ (1 Cor. 10). Finally he makes such a communion between us and the fathers that he sometimes transfers their sacraments to us, and sometimes applies ours to them. Shameful, then, is the error of those who cry out that the books of the Old Testament have nothing to do with us, and deny that we are the Jews to whom these things were once written. Rather they ought to have considered that the people of God were Jews, whom God saved of old by no other way than that by which we are wont to be saved today. Again, Peter briefly sets out the way of salvation. He lays its foundation in the grace of God, by which the merit and works of righteousness are excluded in a single word, since these are set against one another. For if salvation comes through grace (as Paul says), it is no longer from works, since grace would not be grace if the merits of works were admitted. But if we are saved by works, it is no longer by grace, since a work loses the name of merit as soon as grace is admitted. See Rom. 11. That passage teaches abundantly that the grace of God and the merits of our works cannot stand together. Then Peter shows that the Mediator of that grace is Christ Jesus, the Reconciler (προέστωρ), through whom we are taught by the heavenly oracle that the Father has been reconciled to us (Matt. 3 and 17). Last, he testifies that this grace is apprehended by faith. For he says: "We believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ." So the whole way of salvation can be comprehended in few and wholly unambiguous words, if we say that we are saved by the grace of God in Jesus Christ through faith, which is the sum of all prophetic and apostolic doctrine.

units.la: Postquam vero dicendi finem Petrus fecit, vniuersa multitudo conticuit, & silentio consensum testata est. Hinc autem omnium euidentissimo argumento colligitur, eos in spiritu sancto congregatos fuisse. Vt enim is veritatis spiritus est, ita veritati non possunt non cedere, quoscunque ille afflauerit. Nec vnquam credendum est, huius auspicijs ea Concilia gubernari, in quibus veritati aditus praclusae sunt, & aduersus hanc linguae effraeni & tumultuosa licentia laxantur, qualia fuisse constat, quae iam seculis aliquot a Romanensibus indicta & celebrata sunt. Nam vt in illis dogmata palam falsa & impia constituerunt, ita illorum decretis nemo sine manifesto vitae periculo contradicere potuit. Caeterum Paulus & Barnabas ex Petri verbis occasione sumpta, miracula & prodigia exponunt, quibus ipsorum ministerium inter gentes deus confirmauerat, vt plenius pateret hunc nullum inter has & Iudaeos discrimen posuisse, quando eadem inter gentes miracula fieri voluerit, quae inter Iudaeos fieri solebant. Ita vero miraculorum omnium hunc vsum esse videmus, vt euangelicam doctrinam confirment, de quo iam saepe dictum est. Nostrum est, salutis rationem, quam Petrus exposuit, attentis animis & firma fide amplecti. Ita enim fiet, vt ipsi quoq; ex gratia purificati cum Christo caelestis regni haereditatem accedamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: When Peter had made an end of speaking, the whole multitude fell silent and testified their agreement by their silence. From this it is gathered, by the most evident proof of all, that they were gathered together in the Holy Spirit. For he is the Spirit of truth, and so those whom he breathes upon cannot but yield to the truth. Nor should it ever be believed that those councils are governed under his auspices, in which access is closed to the truth, and unbridled and tumultuous licence of tongues is given free rein against it. Such councils, it is known, were called and held some centuries ago by the Romanists. For just as they set forth doctrines plainly false and impious in those councils, so no one could contradict their decrees without manifest danger to life. But Paul and Barnabas, taking the occasion from Peter's words, set out the miracles and wonders by which God had confirmed their ministry among the Gentiles, so that it might more fully appear that he had made no distinction between these and the Jews, since he willed the same miracles to occur among the Gentiles as used to occur among the Jews. Thus we see that the use of all miracles is this: to confirm the gospel doctrine, as has often been said already. It is our part to embrace with attentive minds and firm faith the way of salvation which Peter set forth. For so it will come about that we too, purified by grace, may come with Christ to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CIII.

units.la: Postquam vero illi conticuerunt, respondit Iacobus, dicens, Viri fratres, audite me. Simeon narrauit, quemadmodum primum Deus visitauerit, vt sumeret ex gentibus populum in nomine suo. Et huic consonant verba prophetarum, sicut scriptum est: Posthaec reuertar, & rursus aedificabo tabernaculum Dauidis, quod collapsum est, & diruta eius instaurabo, & erigam illud: vt requirant qui reliqui sunt homines dominum, & omnes gentes, super quas inuocatum est nomen meum, dicit dominus qui facit haec omnia. Nota a seculo sunt deo omnia opera sua. Quapropter ego censeo, non esse obturbandum his, qui ex gentibus conuertuntur ad deum: sed scribendum ad eos, vt abstineant ab inquinamentis simulachrorum, & scortatione, & suffocato, & sanguine. Moses enim ab aetatibus antiquis habet in singulis ciuitatibus, qui ipsum praedicent, cum in Synagogis per omne sabbatum legitur.
units.tr: When they had fallen silent, James answered, saying: "Men, brothers, listen to me. Simeon has told how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: 'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen; I will restore its ruins and set it up again, so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles over whom my name is invoked, says the Lord who does all these things. To God all his works are known from the beginning.' Therefore I judge that those among the Gentiles who turn to God should not be troubled, but should be written to, that they abstain from the pollutions of idols, from fornication, from what is strangled, and from blood. For Moses has had in every city, from ancient times, those who preach him, since he is read in the synagogues every sabbath."

units.la: Controuersiam, quae in primitiua ecclesia circa iustificationis causam exorta fuit, Lucas euangelista studiosissime describit. Vidimus in ea descriptione Diui Petri sententiam, qui solam fidem iustificandis gentibus sufficere, nec illas legis iugo onerandas esse docuit. Et quia plerorumque patrum exempla mouebant, quos per legem iustificatos esse arbitrabantur, offendiculo huic pulchre medetur, offendens illos quoq; non alia ratione saluari posse, quam gratia Dei, cuius author & mediator nobis sit Christus dominus. At quia de his priori Sermone diximus, videamus nunc Iacobi apostoli, qui Alphaei filius fuit, & cuius mentionem Paulus ad Galat. cap. 2. facit, orationem, quae ipsa duabus maximis partibus constat. Primo enim Petro subscribit: deinde consilium afferst, quo inter Iudaeos & gentes pax constituit & vera concordia foueri siue conseruari possit.
units.tr: The controversy that arose in the early Church concerning the cause of justification, Luke the evangelist describes with the greatest care. In that account we have seen the judgment of St Peter, who taught that faith alone was sufficient to justify the Gentiles, and that they should not be burdened with the yoke of the law. And because the examples of many of the Fathers, whom they thought had been justified by the law, moved the others, he cures this stumbling block well, showing that those too can be saved in no other way than by the grace of God, whose author and mediator for us is Christ the Lord. But since we spoke of these matters in the previous sermon, let us now consider the speech of the apostle James, the son of Alphaeus, whose mention Paul makes in Galatians chapter 2. This speech consists of two main parts. First he agrees with Peter; then he offers a counsel by which peace can be established between the Jews and the Gentiles, and true concord preserved or kept.

units.la: Priusquam
units.tr: Before

units.la: Priusquàm verò Iacobi verba attingamus, obseruandum erit, illum non antea dicendi initium fecisse quàm conticuisse videret alios. Ex eo enim Concilij huius verè apostolici ordinem æstimare licet, & quòd modestè omnia egerint, nec aliquis fuerit, qui reliquis insolenter præscriberet. Huius specimen supra quoq; vidimus. Nam cùm multi acriter contenderent, Petrus tacuit. Vbi verò tempus postulare videbatur, modestè simul & grauiter assurgens, sententiam dicere coepit, & ab aliis ea patientia auditus est, qua ipse paulò antea disceptantes audiuerat. Post hunc audiuntur, nemine eos interturbante, Paulus & Barnabas, qui miraculis Petri sententiam confirmant. Hi verò vbi dicendi finem fecerunt, Iacobus prodit, & tantumnon vltimus sermonem habet, quamuis inter eccle sia columnas numeraretur. Fuit modestia hæc non obscurum spiritus sancti argumentum, qui illorum mentes gubernauit, ne nimio contendendi feruore abrepti, immodestius tumultuarentur, & veritati aures præcluderent. Obseruari debet ordo hic in publicis actionibus, vt singuli non tam ad dicendum quàm ad audiendum aliorum sententias proclives sint. Nam vt ineptum, ita inutile etiam & perniciosum est illud hominum genus, qui vt soli sapere videantur, sibi solis dicendi ius faciunt, & atrocem sibi iniuriam fieri putant, si quis ab illorum sententia latum unguem discedat.
units.tr: But before we come to the words of James, it should be noted that he did not begin to speak until he saw that the others had fallen silent. From this one may judge the order of this truly apostolic council, and that they all acted modestly, and that there was no one who insolently prescribed to the rest. We have seen an example of this above also. For when many were contending vehemently, Peter kept silent. But when the time seemed to demand it, he rose modestly and gravely and began to give his opinion, and he was heard by the others with the same patience with which he himself had listened to those disputing a little before. After him Paul and Barnabas are heard, with no one disturbing them, and they confirm Peter's judgment by miracles. But when they had made an end of speaking, James comes forward and speaks almost last, although he was counted among the pillars of the Church. This modesty was no obscure sign of the Holy Spirit, who governed their minds, so that carried away by too much heat of contention they would not riot more immodestly and shut their ears to the truth. This order ought to be observed in public business, so that each is inclined not so much to speak as to listen to the opinions of others. For that kind of men is as foolish as it is useless and harmful: those who, that they may seem to be the only wise ones, claim for themselves alone the right to speak, and think it a monstrous injury done to them if anyone departs from their opinion by the breadth of a nail.

units.la: Sed omissis istis, Iacobum audiamus, qui prima sua orationis parte in Petri sententiam descendit, dicens: Simeon narrauit, vt Deus primum visitauerit vel decreuerit, vt sumeret ex gentibus populum in nomine suo. Agnoscit Dei consilium Iacobus, qui in Cornelij vocatione abunde declarauerat, gentibus non alia præparatione, quàm fide in Christum ad iustificationem & salutem opus esse, & proinde Petro ingenuè subscribit. Porrò ne apostoli soli hoc sentire putarentur, sententiam hanc vnanimi prophetarum consensu probat, licet vnum duntaxat ex his testimonium adducat. Nec enim plura adduci necesse erat, cùm omnes prophetas vno eodemq; spiritu animatos fuisse, & in tradenda salutis ratione consentire constet. Est autem diligenti obseruatione dignum, quòd nihil pro sua authoritate ecclesijs obtrudunt apostoli, sed scripturis probant quæ docent. Christi enim & ecclesiæ scriptures esse agnouerunt, & proinde nihil tradendum esse putarunt, quod cum Christi voluntate & scripturis sacris pugnaret. Quam modestiam si seruassent, qui illorum successores dici & videri voluat, minus in ecclesia superstitionum, plus verò pietatis & syncerè religionis hodie haberemus.
units.tr: But setting those aside, let us hear James, who in the first part of his speech agrees with Peter's judgment, saying: "Simeon has told how God first visited, or decreed, to take from the Gentiles a people for his name." James acknowledges God's counsel, who in the calling of Cornelius had fully declared that the Gentiles needed no other preparation for justification and salvation than faith in Christ; and therefore he frankly agrees with Peter. Moreover, lest the apostles alone be thought to hold this view, he proves this judgment by the unanimous consent of the prophets, although he brings forward only one testimony from them. Indeed there was no need to bring more, since it is agreed that all the prophets were animated by one and the same Spirit and agree in setting forth the way of salvation. It is worth careful observation that the apostles do not thrust anything upon the churches on their own authority, but prove by the Scriptures what they teach. For they recognised that the Scriptures belonged to Christ and to the Church, and therefore they thought nothing should be handed down that conflicted with the will of Christ and the holy Scriptures. If those who wish to be called and seen as their successors had kept this modesty, we would today have fewer superstitions in the Church, and much more piety and sincere religion.

units.la: Quoad autem prophetæ oraculum, extat illud apud Amos nono cap. Prædixerat paulò ante excidium Iudæis, quod effræni peccandi licentia meruerant. Sed quia Iudaicæ gentis excidio promissiones de æterno Messiæ regno intercidere & collabi videbantur, consolationem instituit dominus, qua se tabernaculum siue regnum Dauidis reflaturum pollicetur. Reuertar (inquit) & rursus ædificabo tabernaculum Dauid, quod collapsum est, & diruta eius instaurabo, & erigam illud. Et tabernaculi quidem non temere mentionem facit. Ita enim externum quoq; cultum comprehendit, quem abrogari & aboleri oporteat sub Messiæ regno. Et inde argumentari videtur Iacobus, non contendendum esse cum gentibus de ceremonijs & legis obseruatione, cùm iam olim prædictum sit, omnem illam Mosis disciplinam Messia tempore abrogandam esse. Simul verò ecclesiæ populus, qualis sub Christo futurus sit, describitur. Et in hoc primus locus reliquijs Iudæorum tribuitur, ijs nimirum, qui ex communi totius gentis interitu peculiari diuinæ gratiæ beneficio saluati fuerint, iuxta illud Isa.10. Si fuerit numerus filiorum Israel, vt arena maris, reliquiæ saluæ erunt. Sed his accedunt omnes aliæ gentes, quæ & ipsæ Dei nomine censebuntur, & cum Iudæis dominum requirent. His verò duplex argumentum continetur. Nam primò vna eademq; Iudæorum & gentium dignitas sub Messiæ regno fore dicitur. Deinde, vnum & idem vtriusq; populi officium in illo regno fore docet. Dignitas ea erit, quòd super omnes illos inuocabitur nomine domini: id est, vtriq; dei nomine & dei populus esse censebuntur. Nota enim locutio est Hebræis vsitata, quæ & Gen.48. & Isa.4.cap. inuenitur. Officium verò vtriusq; populi erit, dominum quærere. Id verò non externis ritibus, nec legalium operum obseruatione, sed fide vera fieri consueuit. Ex istis ergo prophetæ verbis firmissimè concludit Iacobus, stultum & iniquum esse, si quis propter legis ceremonias ea gloria gentes spoliare velit, qua illos donare iam olim deus dignatus sit. Porrò vt magnum consolationem affert, quòd hominum perfidia & interitu promissionibus dei nihil derogatur: (Quid enim, si quidam fuerunt increduli? Num incredulitas illorum fidem dei faciet irritam? Imò sit Deus verax, omnis autem homo mendax. Rom.3.) ita officij hoc loco admonentur, quicunq; Dei populus censeri volunt. Est hoc, ut dominum quærant, qui cum spiritus sit infinitus & omnia penetrans simul & gubernans, non loco certo alligatur, sed sola fide quæri & inveniri potest, quæ illum apprehendit, dum verbo suo se nobis manifestat. Ne vero alicui absurdum & insolens videretur, gentes subito Iudæis æquari, Amoz deum huius rei authorem facit, & illud ipsum Iacobus exponens, ait: Nota à seculo sunt deo omnia opera sua. Quasi dicat: Non est quod vel ista miremur, vel deum iniustitiæ accusemus. Licet enim hæc nobis absurda videantur, certatamen Deo constat omnium suorum operum ratio. Necillum falli posse putemus, quando iam olim, priusquam mundus hic crearetur, æterno suo consilio res omnes optimè dispositas. Hinc vero generalis doctrina peti debet, ne æterna salutis nostræ consilia ad humani ingenij calculum revocemus, sed Dei iustitiam simul & sapientiam una cum eiusdem bonitate venerabundi exosculemur. Vide de hoc Paulum ad Rom. 9. & 11. cap.
units.tr: As for the prophet's oracle, it is found in Amos chapter 9. He had foretold a little before the destruction of the Jews, which they had deserved by their unbridled license to sin. But since the promises of the eternal kingdom of the Messiah seemed to perish and fall with the destruction of the Jewish nation, the Lord set up a consolation, by which he promises to restore the tabernacle or kingdom of David. "I will return," he says, "and rebuild the tabernacle of David, which has fallen; I will restore its ruins, and set it up again." And he does not mention the tabernacle without reason. For it also comprehends the external worship, which had to be abrogated and abolished under the kingdom of the Messiah. And from this James seems to argue that one should not contend with the Gentiles about ceremonies and the observance of the law, since it was foretold long ago that all that discipline of Moses would be abrogated in the time of the Messiah. At the same time the people of the Church, as it will be under Christ, is described. And in this the first place is given to the remnant of the Jews, namely those who were saved from the common destruction of the whole nation by a special benefit of divine grace, in line with that saying of Isaiah 10: "If the number of the sons of Israel is like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved." But all the other nations are added to these, who will also be counted in the name of God, and will seek the Lord along with the Jews. This passage contains a twofold argument. First, it is said that under the kingdom of the Messiah there will be one and the same dignity for Jews and Gentiles. Second, it teaches that under that kingdom there will be one and the same duty for both peoples. The dignity will be this: that the name of the Lord will be invoked over all of them, that is, both will be counted as God's people, bearing God's name. For this is a form of speech common among the Hebrews, and it is found in Genesis 48 and Isaiah chapter 4. The duty of both peoples will be to seek the Lord. And this is accomplished not by external rites or the observance of legal works, but by true faith. From these words of the prophet, therefore, James firmly concludes that it is foolish and unjust for anyone to want to strip the Gentiles, on account of the ceremonies of the law, of that glory which God has long since deigned to bestow upon them. Moreover, just as it brings great consolation that the faithlessness and ruin of men do not take anything from God's promises (for what if some were unbelieving? Will their unbelief make the faithfulness of God void? Certainly God is true, but every man a liar, Romans 3), so in this place those who wish to be counted as God's people are reminded of their duty. It is this: to seek the Lord, who, since he is infinite spirit penetrating and governing all things at once, is not bound to a fixed place, but can be sought and found only by faith, which apprehends him while he makes himself known to us by his word. Lest it should seem absurd and strange to anyone that the Gentiles should suddenly be made equal to the Jews, Amos makes God the author of this matter, and James, explaining that very thing, says: "To God all his works are known from the beginning." As if he said: there is no reason for us either to wonder at these things or to accuse God of injustice. For although these things may seem absurd to us, yet it is certain that God has the reason for all his works. Nor should we think that he can be mistaken, since from of old, before this world was created, he disposed all things most well by his eternal counsel. From this a general teaching should be drawn: that we should not bring the eternal counsels of our salvation back to the reckoning of the human mind, but with reverence embrace the justice and wisdom of God together with his goodness. See on this Paul, Romans chapters 9 and 11.

units.la: Altera sua oratione parte consilium profert Iacobus utile simul & necessarium. Videbat enim graves exerceri inter gentes & Iudæos inimicitias, ex quibus tandem perniciosum & exitiale ineclesia schisma enasci poterat. Quare necessitas postulabat, ut de concordia coci-lianda & fovenda mare consulteretur, & quid sibi factu optimum videatur docet. Summa consilij est, salvam & integram servari debere Christianorum libertatem, ita vero hanc temperandam esse, ne in licentiam erumpens, offendiculis causam & materiam præbeat. Ad primum pertinet quod dicit: Quapropter censeo, non esse obturbandum his, qui ex gentibus converterentur ad Deum. Sensus est, non imponendum esse legis iugum, nec huius observatione tanquam ad iustificationem necessaria, grauandas esse illorum conscientias, qui relictis gentilismi superstitionibus, Christo nomen dederunt. Ne vero gentes legem ita abrogatam putarent, quasi impunitas quædam & quidus faciendi licentia constituta esset, de quibusdam illas admonendas censet, quibus cum in Christianam puritatem & sanctimoniam tum in fraternam charitatem à gentibus peccabatur. Quatuor autem prohibet, quorum duo quidem per se illicita sunt, duo vero altera media sunt & indifferentia.
units.tr: In the second part of his speech, James offers advice that is both useful and necessary. He saw that bitter hostilities between the Gentiles and the Jews were stirring, from which a harmful and destructive schism in the Church could finally arise. The need therefore called for counsel on how to secure and foster harmony, and he teaches what seems best to be done. The sum of his advice is that the Christians' liberty must be preserved whole and intact, but that it must be tempered so that it does not break out into licence and give occasion and material for stumbling. He addresses the first point when he says: "Therefore I judge that those from among the Gentiles who turn to God should not be troubled." The meaning is that no yoke of the law should be imposed, and their consciences should not be burdened by observing it as if it were necessary for justification, for those who had left the superstitions of paganism and given their names to Christ. Lest the Gentiles, however, should think that the law had been abrogated in such a way that a kind of impunity and licence to do whatever they pleased had been established, he judges that they must be warned about certain things in which they were sinning against Christian purity and holiness, and also against brotherly love. He forbids four things, of which two are unlawful in themselves, while the other two are indifferent and intermediate.

units.la: Ad primum ordine pertinent, Inquinamentum idolorum & scortatio. Admonendæ vero de hu erant gentes, quia in utroq; turpissime peccabant. Erant enim, qui cum Christo nomen dedissent, idolorum tamen templa ingrediebantur, ab amicis inuitati sacris gentilium intererant, idolothytn vescebantur, adeoq; sacris alienis communicabant, ut ex Pauli ad Corin. Epist. priori facile patet. Nec vero se hac re peccare putabant, eo quod scirent idolum nihil esse, & de fide bene essent instituti. At illorum rationibus uno verbo Iacobus occurrit, dum illos ab inquinamentis idolorum abstinere iubet. Ita enim docet, idololatriam per se illicitam & abominabilem esse, ut nemo illi abs, manifesta pollutione communicare possit. Id vero ex lege sumpsisse videtur, in qua per Mosen dominus ait: Sculptilia deorum igne comburescit, argentum & aurum quod in illis est ne concupiscas, ut tibi tollas, ne forte impingas in eo: quoniam abominanda res est domino Deo tuo. Ne ergo inferas abominationem in domum tuam, ne fias anathema quemadmodum illud est. Omnino execrerus illud, planeq; abhorreas: anathema enim est. Deut. 7. Quoad vero scortationem, quanta illius impunitas & licentia fuerit inter gentes, notius est, quam ut multus explicari mereatur. Extant fædæ libidinis exempla passim in historiis & poetarum scriptis, qui ex Venereorum descriptione maximam ingenij laudem quæsiuerunt. De utroq; ergo gentes diligenter admoneri, necesse fuit. HINC vero perpetuum & generale præceptum colligi debet, Christianorum esse, ut sese Deo per omnia puros & immaculatos sist uent. Nec enim alienis sacris communicare debent, cum Deus totum hominis cor & animum requirat. Deut. 6. Et notum est illud Pauli: Non potestis mensa domini participes esse, & mensa dæmoniorum. 1. Cor. 10. Rursum quoad vitæ conversationem, hanc quoq; Deo consecratam esse conuenit. Constat enim corpora nostra Christi sanguine in templa spiritus sancti dedicata esse. Deus ergo in corpore nostro glorificari debet. 1. Cor. 6. Quare turpis & nefandus illorum error est, qui scortationem Christianis hominibus licitam & liberam esse contendunt, cum Paulus hanc inter Christianos nemo minari quidem velit, & non adulteris modo, verumetiam scortatoribus horrendum Dei iudicium minitetur. Ephes. 5. Hebr. 13.
units.tr: The first two belong to the first category: the pollution of idols and fornication. The Gentiles had to be warned about these, because they sinned most shamefully in both. For there were some who, though they had given their names to Christ, still entered the temples of idols, attended the rites of the Gentiles when invited by friends, ate things sacrificed to idols, and so shared in alien worship, as is easily clear from Paul's first Epistle to the Corinthians. Nor did they think they were sinning in this, because they knew that an idol is nothing, and they had been well instructed in the faith. But James meets their arguments with a single word when he orders them to abstain from the pollutions of idols. For he teaches that idolatry is unlawful and abominable in itself, so that no one can take part in it without manifest pollution. He seems to have taken this from the law, in which the Lord says through Moses: "You shall burn the carved images of their gods with fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold that is on them, to take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it, since it is an abomination to the Lord your God. Therefore do not bring an abomination into your house, lest you become accursed like it. You shall utterly detest it and abhor it, for it is accursed." (Deut. 7.) As for fornication, how great its impunity and licence were among the Gentiles is too well known to deserve lengthy explanation. Examples of foul lust are found everywhere in histories and in the writings of the poets, who sought the greatest praise of their wit from describing sexual love. Therefore it was necessary to warn the Gentiles carefully about both matters. From this a perpetual and general precept ought to be drawn: that it is the duty of Christians to present themselves to God pure and unblemished in all things. For they must not share in alien worship, since God requires the whole heart and soul of man (Deut. 6.). And Paul's words are well known: "You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of demons" (1 Cor. 10.). Again, as regards the conduct of life, it is fitting that this too should be consecrated to God. For it is established that our bodies have been dedicated as temples of the Holy Spirit by the blood of Christ. God therefore ought to be glorified in our body (1 Cor. 6.). Hence it is a shameful and abominable error of those who contend that fornication is lawful and free for Christian men, since Paul does not wish even this to be named among Christians, and threatens with the dreadful judgment of God not only adulterers but also fornicators (Eph. 5.; Heb. 13.).

units.la: Secundo ordine suffocatum & sanguis comprehenduntur, à quibus gentes abstinere debeant. Licet enim præceptu hoc inter Ceremonias numeretur, quas in Christo abrogatas esse constat, quia tamen de his antiquissima lex extat, quam à diluuio toti mundo Deus imposuit, eademq; in quotidiano conuictu connectu frequenter occurrebant, non poterant non vehementer offendi quotquot inter Iudaeos infirmiores erant, si gentes his promisque vesci viderent. Aequum ergo esse censet Iacobus, ut gentes hac parte libertate suam restringant, & charitatis ergo ab ijs abstineant, quae per se licita & divinitus concessa erant, ne quem incautius libertate sua abutentes offendant. Atqui haec apostolorum mentem fuisse, ex Pauli verbis patet, quae ad Rom. 14. cap. habentur: Noui siquidem & persuasum habeo per dominum Iesum, nihil esse commune per se, nisi ei qui existimat aliquid commune esse, illi commune est. Verum si propter cibum frater tuus contristatur, non iam secundum charitatem ambulas. Ne cibo tuo illum perdas, pro quo Christus mortuus est. Ne igitur vestrum bonum hominum maledicentia fit obnoxium. Non enim est regnum Dei cibus & potus, sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in spiritu sancto; & c. Idem se a carnibus potius perpetuo abstinere velle dicit, quam alicui offendiculum praebere. 1. Corinth. 8. Minime ergo illis patrocinatur locus hic, qui sibi permissum putant, ut eadem authoritate iciunia & ferias & alia eius generis praescribant, qua apostoli a suffocato & sanguine abstinere iusserunt. Nec enim eadem ipsis est ratio, cum humanas duntaxat traditiones urgeant, quarum nulla esse debet in religione authoritas, & conscientijs laqueos inijciant, quod apostoli omni modo cauendum esse censuerunt. Sed facit huc quoque ratio, quam ipse Iacobus affert. Moses enim (inquit) ab aetatibus antiquis habet in singulis ciuitatibus, qui ipsum praedicent, cum in Synagogis per omne sabbatum legitur. Quibus non aliud docet, quam eam adhuc esse inter Iudaeos Mosis authoritatem, ut illos ab huius decretis subito reuellere impossibile sit. Tempori ergo & charitati hoc dandum esse, ut interim salua & incolumi animorum libertate, cum honore veteres ceremonias sepeliantur. Interim obseruemus, veterem hunc in Dei populo morem fuisse omnibus seculis, ut legis & scripturae sacrae studio fetus diebus exercerentur. Eundem ergo nos quoque retinere decet, & in hoc unum incumbere, ut libertatem nostram constanter tueamur, charitatis vero & puritatis memores, ab offendiculis nobis cautamus. Ita fiet ut cum ipsi saluemur, tum alios adducamus Iesu Christo, cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the second category are things strangled and blood, from which the Gentiles ought to abstain. For although this precept is counted among the ceremonies, which are known to have been abrogated in Christ, nevertheless there is a most ancient law concerning them, which God imposed on the whole world from the time of the flood, and since these things frequently came up in daily intercourse, they could not but be deeply offended, all those among the Jews who were weaker, if they saw the Gentiles eating such things freely and openly. James therefore judges it fair that the Gentiles should restrict their liberty in this respect, and for the sake of charity abstain from things that in themselves are lawful and divinely permitted, so that they do not offend anyone by using their liberty too carelessly. That this was the mind of the apostles is clear from Paul's words, which are found in Romans 14: "For I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common in itself, except to one who thinks something is common; to him it is common. But if your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let not your good be exposed to evil speaking. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit," etc. He says the same thing about meat, that he would rather abstain from it forever than give a stumbling block to anyone (1 Cor. 8.). This passage, therefore, gives no support to those who think that they have been permitted, on the same authority, to prescribe fasts, holy days and other things of that kind, by which the apostles ordered abstinence from things strangled and from blood. For their reason is not the same, since they press merely human traditions, which ought to have no authority in religion, and they cast snares on consciences, which the apostles judged must be guarded against in every way. But this reasoning that James himself brings also applies here: "For Moses (he says) from ancient generations has in every city those who preach him, since he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath." He teaches nothing else by this than that Moses still has such authority among the Jews that it is impossible to tear them suddenly away from his decrees. This must therefore be yielded to time and charity, so that the ancient ceremonies may be buried with honour while the freedom of souls remains safe and intact. Meanwhile let us observe that this ancient custom among God's people has existed in all ages, that they should be occupied on all days with the study of the law and of Holy Scripture. We too ought therefore to retain the same, and to devote ourselves to this alone: that we steadfastly defend our liberty, and, mindful of charity and purity, guard ourselves against stumbling blocks. In this way it will come about that, while we ourselves are saved, we also bring others to Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 104.

units.la: Tunc visum est Apostolis & Presbyteris cum tota Ecclesia, delectos viros ex ipsis mittere Antiochiam cum Paulo & Barnaba, Iudam cognomine Barsabam & Silam, viros primarios inter fratres, missis per manus eorum literis in hanc sententiam: Apostoli & Presbyteri & fratres, his qui sunt Antiochiae, & in Syria & Cilicia fratribus, qui sunt ex gentibus, Salutem. Quoniam audiuimus, quod quidam ex nobis egressi, turbarunt vos verbis, labefactantes animas vestras, iubentes vos circuncidi & seruare Legem, quibus no mandauieramus: visum est nobis unanimiter congregatis, delectos viros mittere ad vos, cum dilectis nostris Barnaba & Paulo, hominibus qui exposuerunt animas suas pro nomine domini nostri Iesu Christi. Misimus ergo Iudam & Silam, qui & ipsi vobis sermo ne referent eadem. Visum est enim spiritui sancto & nobis, ne quid amplius imponeremus vobis oneris, quam haec necessaria, ut abstineatis ab his, quae immolata sunt simulachris, & sanguine, & suffocato, & scortatione: a quibus si conseruaueritis vos ipsos, bene facietis. Valete.
units.tr: Then it seemed good to the apostles and elders, together with the whole Church, to send chosen men from among themselves to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas, surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, men of standing among the brothers. They sent letters by their hand, to this effect: "The apostles, the elders and the brothers, to the brothers from among the Gentiles who are at Antioch, and in Syria and Cilicia: greetings. Since we have heard that some who went out from us have troubled you with words and unsettled your souls, telling you to be circumcised and to keep the Law, which we did not command, it seemed good to us, being gathered together with one accord, to send chosen men to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves report the same things to you by word of mouth. For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell."

units.la: Quoniam Christo Iesu a Deo patre omnis potestas data est, regnum suum non modo tueri & seruare potest, sed ita res omnes moderatur & regit, ut quae contra hoc satan molitur, ad illius propagationem faciant. Exemplum huius praesens historia exhibet. Postquam enim persecutionibus & aperta vi euangelij cursum Satan impedire non potuit, intestinis dissensionibus ecclesiae aggressus, grauem de iustificatione (qui praecipuus & summus Christianae religionis articulus est) concertationem excitauit, eo nimirum consilio, ut omnem euangelij doctrinam suspectam & inuidam redderet. Sed adeo nihil profecit, ut potius hac occasione veritas magis illustrata, & fidei iustificatio contra Pharisaeos validissime asserta & defensa sit: quemadmodum in Petri, Pauli & Barnabae. bæ, & postremò Iacobi etiam sermonibus hucusq; vidimus. Quo cumprimis pertinet felix & victoriosus concertationis totius exitus, quem in præsenti Lucas describit: primo quidem totius ecclesiæ consensum, deinde verò Synodicæ epistolæ exemplum commemorans, de quibus singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Since all power has been given by God the Father to Christ Jesus, he can not only protect and preserve his kingdom, but also so order and govern all things that whatever Satan plots against it turns out to advance its spread. The present history offers an example of this. For after Satan could not hinder the course of the gospel by persecutions and open force, he attacked the Church with internal dissensions and stirred up a grievous dispute about justification (which is the chief and highest article of the Christian religion), obviously with the purpose of making all the teaching of the gospel suspect and hateful. But he gained so little that, on the contrary, on this occasion the truth was more clearly illuminated, and justification by faith was most powerfully asserted and defended against the Pharisees, as we have seen up to now in the speeches of Peter, Paul and Barnabas, and last of all of James. To this especially belongs the happy and victorious outcome of the whole controversy, which Luke describes in the present passage: first recounting the agreement of the whole Church, and then the example of the synodal letter. We shall discuss each of these in order.

units.la: Primò vnanimem omnium consensum exprimit, dum apostolos vnà cum Senioribus & totā ecclesia decreuisse scribit, vt legati cum publicis literis Antiochiam mitterentur, vbi incendium hoc primò exortum fuerat. Prudenter verò ista decernunt, quibus non modò præsentem litem sopiri, verumetiam in posterum rixandi occasiones declinari poterant. Et primò quidem quia Pauli & Barnabæ fides apud eos, quorum animi contentionibus exacerbati erant, dubia & suspecta fuisset, legatos non postremæ dignitatis ipsis adiungunt. Rursum verò, ne Silas & Iudas dolo circuuenti & malis artibus in Pauli partes pertracti esse viderentur, publicis literis illorum authoritatem muniunt atque tuentur. Quo exemplo admonemur, prudentiam in publicis ecclesiarum causis cumprimis adhibendam esse, ne inconsulta temeritas causæ per se bonæ & sanctæ obsit. Interim hoc loco veteris & primitiuæ ecclesiæ ordo consyderandus venit, quo in publicis causis illa vti solita fuit. Præfuerunt quidem rebus gerendis apostoli vnà cum Senioribus, quibus publica ecclesiæ cura mandata erat. Idem tamen non ita dominiū & imperium sibi vendicauerunt, vt populum ab eorum cognitione excluderent siue arcerent, quæ ex æquo ad totam ecclesiam pertinebant. Rursus in populo summa modestia ratio fuit, qua factum est, vt veritati omnes libenter cederent, nec quisquā vel ambitione vel alio prauo affectu extimulatus, temere tumultuaretur. Hunc ordinem quia antistitum ambitio tur bauit, qui contra Petri apostoli præceptum in Christi hæreditatem, siue ecclesiam sibi dominium vendicauerunt, nouis indies concertationibus vexantur ecclesiæ, nec aliquis vel errorum vel acerbissimarum contentionum finis apparet. S E D epistolam Synodicam videamus, qua res maximi momenti breuissimè & simplicissimè tractatur. Vt enim Veritas facilis & ab omni fuco alienaest, ita verborum ambages & affectatum ornatum minimè requirit. Sunt autem epistolæ huius partes quatuor, quas perspicuitatis causa singulas seorsim tractabimus.
units.tr: First, he expresses the unanimous agreement of all, when he writes that the apostles, together with the elders and the whole Church, decided to send envoys with public letters to Antioch, where this fire had first broken out. Their decisions were wise, since they could not only settle the present quarrel but also avoid occasions for wrangling in the future. In the first place, because Paul's and Barnabas's credibility was doubtful and suspect to those whose minds were inflamed by the dispute, they joined to them envoys of no lesser standing. Again, so that Silas and Judas should not seem to have been won over by deceit and led into Paul's party by underhand tricks, the letters public authority supports and protects their standing. From this example we are reminded that prudence must especially be employed in the public affairs of the churches, lest rash thoughtlessness harm a cause that is good and holy in itself. Meanwhile, at this point we must consider the order of the old and primitive Church, which it was accustomed to use in public affairs. The apostles indeed presided over the business, together with the elders, to whom the public care of the Church had been entrusted. Yet they did not claim such lordship and command for themselves as to shut out or keep away the people from the knowledge of matters that pertained equally to the whole Church. Again, among the people there was the greatest moderation, so that all willingly yielded to the truth, and no one, stirred up by ambition or some other wicked feeling, rushed about recklessly. Since the ambition of bishops has disturbed this order, those who, contrary to the command of the apostle Peter, claimed lordship over Christ's inheritance, that is, the Church, the churches are daily troubled by new disputes, and no end of errors or of most bitter quarrels is in sight. But let us look at the synodal letter, in which a matter of the greatest importance is treated most briefly and most simply. For just as truth is easy and free from all paint, so it least of all requires circumlocutions and affected ornament. This letter has four parts, which for the sake of clarity we shall treat separately, one by one.

units.la: 1. Inscriptio epistolæ Synodicæ.
units.tr: 1. The inscription of the synodal letter.

units.la: Prima inscriptionem habet, quæ authores epistolæ nominat vnà cum iis ad quos hæc scribitur. Ita verò omnes illi nominantur, vt nihil hic vel arrogantius vel ambitiosius dictum deprehendas. Seruatur tamen ordo, cuius in omni re potissima ratio haberi debet. Primus ergo locus apostolis tribuitur, eò quòd hos orbis totius doctores & testes suos Christus constituit, & ea dignitate ornauit, vt sal terræ & lux mundi dicti sint. Deinde Seniores ponuntur, de quorum officio iam ante diximus. Postremò omnes credentes fratrum nomine comprehenduntur. Totius ergo Synodi & ecclesiæ nomine literæ hæ scriptæ sunt. Scribuntur autē ad fratres, qui Antiochiæ, in Syria item & Cilicia habitabant, inter quos schismata & turbæ impostorum malitia & dolo excitatæ fuerant. Obseruanda autem est fraterni nominis appellatio, qua se inuicem compellant, & quam inter Christianos vetustissimam & ab apostolorum tempore vsitatam fuisse constat. Est verò duplex nominis huius ratio. Fratres enim dicimur, cùm quòd vnus & idem omnium nostrum pater in cælis est, qui vnà & eandem nobis regni sui hæreditatem præparauit: tum quòd Dei filius Iesus Christus, nos fratrum loco habet, nosq; sibi cohæredes facere dignatur. Vt ergo concordiæ inter Christianos fouendæ titulus hic plurimum feruit, ita consolationem singularem in omni tentationum genere affert. Quia impossibile est, vt Christus Iesus eos negligat, quos pro fratribus semel agnouit, & regni sui consortes habere vult. Huius tituli rationem vtinam expenderent, qui hodie odiosa nationum discrimina obseruant, quasi nullum Christianæ charitatis officium illis debeatur, quos natalis soli diuersitas à nobis distinxit. Atqui apostoli Syros & Cilices, longissimè à se diuisos, & quidem ex gentibus oriundos, fratres suos esse agnoscunt. Quæ ergo improbitas est, Christianos homines, quos Christus fratrum loco habere dignatur, ob patriam à nobis alienos ducere? An verò maior esse debet terrestris quàm cœlestis patriæ authoritas? Vide Ephes. 4. &c.
units.tr: The first part is the inscription, which names the authors of the letter together with those to whom it is written. All of them are named in such a way that you will find nothing said here either arrogant or ambitious. Yet the order is kept, which in every matter ought to be carefully observed. The first place, then, is given to the apostles, because Christ appointed them as the teachers and witnesses for the whole world, and adorned them with such dignity that they are called the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Next the elders are named, of whose office we have already spoken. Last, all the believers are included under the name of brothers. The letters were therefore written in the name of the whole synod and Church. They are addressed to the brothers who lived at Antioch, and likewise in Syria and Cilicia, among whom schisms and disturbances had been stirred up by the malice and deceit of impostors. The form of address "brothers," by which they speak to one another, is to be observed; it is well established that among Christians it is the most ancient and was in use from the time of the apostles. There is a twofold reason for this name. We are called brothers, first, because one and the same Father of us all is in heaven, who has prepared for us one and the same inheritance of his kingdom; and second, because God's Son Jesus Christ regards us as brothers and deigns to make us his co-heirs. So as this title is very useful for fostering concord among Christians, so it brings singular comfort in every kind of temptation. For it is impossible that Christ Jesus should neglect those whom he has once acknowledged as brothers and wishes to have as partners in his kingdom. I wish that those who today observe hateful distinctions between nations would weigh the reason of this title, as if no duty of Christian love were owed to those whom the difference of birthplace separates from us. Yet the apostles acknowledge that the Syrians and Cilicians, who were very far from them and indeed of Gentile origin, were their brothers. What wickedness, then, is it to regard as foreigners to us Christian men whom Christ deigns to regard as brothers, on account of their country? Or ought the authority of an earthly fatherland to be greater than that of the heavenly one? See Eph. 4. etc.

units.la: 2. Pseudoapostoli perstringuntur.
units.tr: 2. The false apostles are censured.

units.la: Secunda parte impostores & pseudoapostolos perstringunt grauissimè, prout causæ gravitas ab illis exortum salutis periculum merebantur. Et primò quidem hos ab ipsis egressos esse fatentur, ita verò vt nihil sibi cum illis commune esse doceant. Id autem vanissimæ illorum gloriationi opponunt. Nam se Hierosolymis aduenire, & suam doctrinam ab apostolis hausisse dicebant, qui eandem dem in Hierosolymitana ecclesia docerent. Non negant ergo ex sua ecclesia illos exiuisse apostoli, sed non propterea quiduis recipiendum esse monent, quod illi tradant. Ita enim fere comparatum est, ut ex ipsa ecclesia seductores exeant, quemadmodum alibi monuimus. Minime ergo sufficit inanis titulorum & successionis gloriatio, qua hodie Romani praesules suam dignitatem tuentur, dum veteris Romanae ecclesiae authoritatem & apostolos antecessores allegant. Atqui non ignoramus tam olim fuisse illius ecclesiae fidem, ut illam merito laudarit Paulus. Scimus praeterea multos in ea fediss pietate, fide & eruditione insignes episcopos, quorum non pauci martyrio coronati sunt. Sed quid haec ad nostros illos, quorum fides, doctrina ac conuersatio ab illis toto coelo dissidet? Veteris ecclesiae vestigijs insistendum erat ijs, qui huius authoritate se tueri volunt. Deinde quid impostores illi fecerint exprimunt. Turbauerunt vos verbis & labefactauerunt animas vestras. Turbatores ergo sunt ecclesiarum, non aedificatores, quod ipsum Paulus obseruauit, cum Galatis scribit: Miror quod tam cito transferamini in aliud euangelium, quod non est aliud, nisi quod quidam sunt qui turbant vos. Item: Vtinam & abscindantur qui vos labefactant. Gal.5. HIS vero falsae doctrinae esse ctus indicatur, quem in omnibus illis deprehendere licebit, qui non vni Christo omnem nostrae salutis rationem & laudem tribuunt. Primo turbant & salutis incertos reddunt auditores suos, dum fidem omnem euertunt. Nec enim fieri potest, ut quicquam stabile & certum habeant, quicunque legis operibus nituntur, quando haec perfectam & omnibus numeris absolutam obedientiam exigit, quam humanae vires praestare non possunt. Quare iuxta Pauli dictum fides euacuatur & irrita fit promissio, ut primum in operibus salutis ratio monstratur. Rom.4. Nec hac tantum ratione homines turbare dicuntur pseudoapostoli, verumetiam quod scbismatum authores sunt, quae sequi necesse est, ut primum non vni Christo salus tribuitur. Exemplo nobis est Corinthiorum ecclesia, quam falsorum doctorum impostura in multas & diuersas factiones diuisam fuisse Paulus conqueritur. Vtrunq; autem experti sunt, quotquot ante euangelicae lucis cognitionem Monacborum doctrinis circunducti fuerunt. Sed addunt memorabilem sententiam impostorum descriptioni apostoli, qua diserte testantur, se pseudoapostolis illis nihil omnino in mandatis dedisse. Mendacij itaq; illos accusant, simul& mendaces fore omnibus seculis docent, quotquot sub apostolici nominis praetextu operum iustificationem praedicant. Clament illi ad rauim vsq;, se legatos a latere esse, praetexant patres & Concilia, scripturas torqueant, principum et regum authoritate glorientur, nos vero omnibus istis Synodicam & vere apostolicam authoritatem obijciemus, quae publice testatur, apostolis nihil cum omnibus illis commune esse, quicunq; fidei iustificationem euertere, & nostrae salutis gloriam operibus aliquo modo tribuere audent. Imo huc Pauli dictum referemus, qui angelum quoq; aliud euangelium praedicare audentem, anathemate ferire non dubitauit. Gal.1.&c.
units.tr: In the second part they censure the impostors and false apostles very severely, as the gravity of the matter, and the danger to salvation that these men caused, deserved. First, they admit that these men had gone out from among themselves, yet they teach that the false apostles had nothing in common with them. They set this against the empty boasting of those men. For they used to say that they had come to Jerusalem and had drawn their teaching from the apostles, who taught the same faith in the Jerusalem church. The apostles therefore do not deny that these men had come out from their church, but they warn that nothing should be accepted merely because they hand it down. For it is generally the case that seducers come out from the very church, as we have noted elsewhere. So the empty boasting about titles and succession is of no real use. Today the Roman prelates defend their dignity by it, when they appeal to the authority of the old Roman church and to the apostles who went before them. Yet we are not unaware that the faith of that church was once so sound that Paul rightly praised it. We know too that many bishops of it were distinguished for piety, faith and learning, and that not a few of them were crowned with martyrdom. But what has this to do with those men of ours, whose faith, teaching and way of life are as far from the old church as heaven is from earth? Those who want to be protected by its authority ought to follow the footsteps of the old church. Next they state what those impostors had done: "They have troubled you with words and unsettled your souls." Those who trouble churches are therefore not builders but disturbers, as Paul also observed when he wrote to the Galatians: "I marvel that you are so quickly turning to another gospel, which is not another; only there are some who trouble you." And again: "I wish that those who unsettle you would even cut themselves off." Gal. 5. The mark of false doctrine is found in all those who do not ascribe to Christ alone the whole ground and praise of our salvation. First, they trouble their hearers and make them uncertain of their salvation, while they overturn all faith. For those who rely on the works of the law cannot have anything stable or certain, since the law demands a perfect and wholly complete obedience, which human powers cannot render. Therefore, according to Paul's saying, faith is emptied and the promise is made void, as soon as the basis of salvation is placed in works. Rom. 4. The false apostles are said to trouble people not only in this way, but also because they are the authors of schisms, which must follow when salvation is not ascribed to Christ alone. The church of the Corinthians is an example for us: Paul complains that it was divided into many and various factions by the imposture of false teachers. All who, before the knowledge of the light of the gospel, were led about by the doctrines of the monks have experienced both of these things. But they add a memorable sentence to the apostle's description of the impostors, in which he clearly testifies that he gave those false apostles no commission at all. So they accuse them of lying, and teach that those who, under the pretext of the apostolic name, preach justification by works will be liars in every age. Let those men shout themselves hoarse, let them claim to be legates from the side, let them put forward the Fathers and Councils, twist the Scriptures, and boast of the authority of princes and kings. We will oppose to all of this the synodal and truly apostolic authority, which publicly testifies that the apostles had nothing in common with all those who dare to overturn the justification of faith and in any way to ascribe the glory of our salvation to works. Indeed we will cite the saying of Paul, who did not hesitate to smite with anathema even an angel who dared to preach another gospel. Gal. 1, etc.

units.la: Tertia parte Paulum & Barnabam magnifice laudant, eo quod horum authoritatem ab impostoribus summa cum improbitate oppugnari scirent: quae etiam causa fuit, quod Paulus non semel apostolatum suum non absque ambitionis suspicione asseruit, ut illius epistolae ad Galatas & Corinthios testantur. Vocant ergo dilectos suos, qua appellatione mendacij arguunt omnes eos, qui Paulum ab apostolis dissentire clamabant. Addunt autem praeconium, quo nullum magnificentius excogitari poterat, cum hos animas suas pro nomine Iesu Christi expo-suisse, dicunt. Docet autem primitiuae ecclesiae exemplum, asseri debere eorum famam & nomen, qui de publica hominum salute bene meriti sunt. Nec id adulationi tribuendum est, quando modeste fit, & in eum finem, ut sua illis authoritas integra maneat. Ita Christus Petrum & Zebedei filios magnificis titulis ornare voluit, cum hoc illorum virtutes mereri videret. Et Paulus quandoq; in Titi, Lucae, Timothei, Epaphroditi & similium laudes digreditur, cum ut ipsis stimulos adderet, tum ut fructuosius esset illorum ministerium. Nec in ecclesia modo, verumetiam in repub. hoc obseruari conuenit, quando generosi animi non alijs incitamentis efficacius, quam laude & honoribus, ad virtutis studia & res magnas obeundas extimulari possunt. Et exempla passim extant, quibus docetur, nullas respub. diu floruisse, in quibus nulla laudis & bonorum brauia bene meritis proposita fuerunt. Porro quae vera ministri laus fit hoc loco exprimitur, nimirum si vbi necessitas ita exigit, animam suam ponat pro nomine Iesu Christi. Nam vt bonus miles dici non meretur, qui non mori paratus est, si ita ducis sui imperium & publica salus requirat: ita fidelis Christi minister non erit, qui non omnia sua & cum his vitam quoque pro Christi gloria deponere paratus fuerit. Et id quidem optimo iure à no bis Christus exigit, cum is prior animam suam pro communi hominum salute deponere dignatus sit. Nec tamen ita haec intelligi debent, vt nemo pro fideli Christi ministro agnoscatur, nisi qui vitae periculum adierit. Non enim temerarios & vitae prodigos nos esse vult Christus, quin potius serpentinam prudentiam nos in cauendis periculis adhibere iubet. Et frequenter fit, vt nullum sese periculum offerat propter quod vita nostra timere necesse fit. Interim tamen animi promptitudo & voluntas prona requiritur, ne pedem referamus, si quando cum praesenti vitae periculo Christi gloria afferenda fit. Exprimit hanc animi promptitudinem Paulus, quando de vinculis admonitus, se non ad vincula modo, verumetiam ad mortem sustinendam pro Christi nomine paratum esse fatetur. Vide Actho.20. & 21.cap. At quod de verbi ministris dicitur, ad singulos Christianos pertinet. Vniuersalis enim regula est, quae Christum coram mundo confiteri iubet, & regno dei parum idoneum esse docet eum, qui vbi manum aratro admouit, a tergo respicit. Luc.9.
units.tr: In the third part they praise Paul and Barnabas magnificently, because they knew that the impostors attacked the authority of these men with the greatest wickedness. This was also the reason why Paul more than once asserted his apostleship, not without suspicion of ambition, as his letters to the Galatians and Corinthians bear witness. So they call them "our beloved," a term by which they prove liars all those who cried out that Paul dissented from the apostles. They add an encomium, and none more magnificent could be devised, when they say that these men exposed their lives for the name of Jesus Christ. The example of the primitive church teaches that the reputation and name of those who have deserved well of the public welfare of mankind ought to be upheld. Nor should this be attributed to flattery, when it is done modestly, and to the end that their authority may remain intact. So Christ wished to adorn Peter and the sons of Zebedee with splendid titles, since he saw that they merited this because of their virtues. And Paul sometimes digresses into praise of Titus, Luke, Timothy, Epaphroditus and others like them, both to add spurs to them and so that their ministry might be more fruitful. This should be observed not only in the church but also in the commonwealth, since generous spirits can be stirred to the pursuit of virtue and to great undertakings by no incentive more effective than praise and honours. And there are everywhere examples showing that no commonwealth has long flourished in which no prizes of praise and rewards were offered to those who deserved well. Moreover, this passage sets out what the true praise of a minister is, namely, if, where necessity so requires, he lays down his life for the name of Jesus Christ. For just as a good soldier does not deserve to be called such if he is not prepared to die, when the command of his leader and the public safety require it, so a faithful minister of Christ will not be one who is not prepared to lay down all his goods, and with them his life also, for the glory of Christ. Christ rightly demands this of us, since he first deigned to lay down his life for the common salvation of mankind. Yet these words should not be understood to mean that no one is to be recognised as a faithful minister of Christ unless he has faced danger to his life. For Christ does not want us to be rash and careless of our lives; rather he bids us use serpent-like prudence in avoiding dangers. And it often happens that no danger presents itself for which our life must be feared. Meanwhile, however, a ready spirit and a willing disposition are required, so that we do not draw back if at any time the glory of Christ must be upheld at the present peril of life. Paul expresses this readiness of spirit when, warned about his chains, he confesses that he is prepared not only to be bound but even to die for the name of Christ. See Acts 20 and 21. But what is said of ministers of the Word applies to every Christian. For the universal rule is that which bids us confess Christ before the world, and teaches that he who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is unfit for the kingdom of God. Luke 9.

units.la: Quarta pars Synodi decretum exponit, in quo Petri & Iacobi sententiae repetuntur & concitantur: quo in loco tria nobis ordine consyderanda veniunt. Primo authorem decreti allegant, spiritum sanctum. Visum est (inquiunt) spiritui sancto & nobis. Seipsos autem spiritui sancto adiungunt, non quod suam authoritatem illi aequare, vel sibi priuatim absque spiritus suffragio credi velint, sed quod a Christo ministri spiritus facti erant, per quos ille oracula sua proderet. Quo sensu etiam dicitur: Qui vos audit, me audit: et qui vos spernit, me spernit: qui autem me spernit, spernit eum qui misit me, Luc.10.cap. Quia ergo nihil quam quod spiritus dixauit, pronuntiarunt apostoli, non inf olenter, sed modesta & iusta gravitate sese spiritui coniungunt, ne ab hoc dissentire videantur. Spiritus vero oraculum esse quod illi scribunt, ex eo patet, quod nihil scripturis sacris repugnans tradiderunt. Idem si de suis decretis dicere possunt papistarum Conciliorum praesides, illos quoque in spiritu sancto congregari, & quae ab ipsis sanciuntur, spiritus placita & decreta esse fatebimur. Quotiés autem dogmata a scripturis diuersa & cum his pugnantia proferent, toties illos spiritu sancto duci negabimus, eo quod vt secum ipse dissidere non potest, cum veritatis spiritus sit. Secundo, quid spiritui sancto visum sit exponunt, nimirum, Ne quid amplius oneris vobis imponeremus. Onus ergo est quicquid praeter fidem in Iesum Christum traditur. Grauantur enim conscientiae inutili traditionum obseruatione, quae salutis causam iuuare non possunt. Repetunt autem, quae de idolothytis & scortatione, de suffocato item & sanguine Iacobus admonuerat, eaque necessaria obseruatu esse dicunt. Hic vero notandum est quod praecedenti Sermone diuersam horum praeceptorum rationem esse diximus. Duo enim priora absolute & simpliciter necessaria sunt, eo quod Christianos hominem omnem idololatriae communionem horrere, & vas siue corpus suum sanctum & impollutum seruare decet, nec scorti membrum ex eo facere, quod vt spiritus sancti templum fit, Christus suo sanguine consecrauit. At quae de suffocato & sanguine dicuntur, necessaria obseruatu sunt per accidens, minimum propter offendiculum, quod horum esu infirmis ponebatur. Quia enim nefas est cibo eum destruere, quem Christus mortis sua merito redimere dignatus est, necessario illis propter infirmiores abstinere debemus, quae alioqui licita & concessa sunt, ne libertas nostra aliis perditionis causam praebeat. Alioqui firma & rata manet Christi sententia, Nihil quod per os ingreditur, hominem inquinare posse, Matth.15.cap. Et Paulus, si nullum scandali periculum subit, idolothytis vesci permittit, nec his conscientiam simpliciter pollui testatur. 1. Corinth.10.cap. Et alibi daemoniorum doctrina vocat, quae tiborum discrimina, quasi in his salutis ratio consistat, introducit. 1. Tim.4. Ineptissime ergo hoc loco abutuntur, qui Conciliorum decreta obseruatu necessaria esse clamant, cum pleraque ex his eiusmodi sint, quae graue conscientijs onus imponunt, & cum diserte scripturae oraculis ex diametro pugnant. Fatemur quidem infirmis multum tribui debere, ne quem offendamus: interea tamen Christiana libertas minime euertenda est propter eos, qui pertinaces potius quam infirmi, semel conceptos errores abijcere nolunt, sed eosdem mordicus tuentur. Contra quos Christi potius sententia vibrari debet: Sinite eos, nam caeci sunt caecorum duces. Matth.15. Postremo fructum & vtilitatem subijciunt, dicentes: Ab his si conseruaueritis vos ipsos, bene facietis. Nam & vos ipsos puros & immaculatos conseruabitis, & neminieritis offendiculo. Debet vero hic omnibus nobis scopus vnicus esse, ad quem studia nostra omnia dirigamus. In vno Christo per fidem quaerenda iustifica tio &
units.tr: The fourth part sets out the decree of the synod, in which the opinions of Peter and James are repeated and confirmed. Here three things are to be considered in order. First, they name the author of the decree, the Holy Spirit: "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." They join themselves to the Holy Spirit, not because they wish to make their authority equal to his, or to be believed on their own without the support of the Spirit, but because they had been made ministers of the Spirit by Christ, through whom he would publish his oracles. In this sense it is also said: "He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you rejects me; but he who rejects me rejects him who sent me." Luke 10. Therefore, since the apostles announced nothing but what the Spirit had dictated, they joined themselves to the Spirit, not arrogantly but with modest and just gravity, lest they should seem to differ from him. That what they write is an oracle of the Spirit is clear from the fact that they handed down nothing contrary to the holy Scriptures. If the presidents of the Papist councils could say the same of their decrees, we would also acknowledge that those councils are gathered in the Holy Spirit, and that what they enact are the pleasure and decrees of the Spirit. But whenever they put forward doctrines that differ from the Scriptures and conflict with them, we will deny that they are led by the Holy Spirit, since the Spirit of truth cannot be at odds with himself. Second, they set out what seemed good to the Holy Spirit, namely: "that we should lay no further burden upon you." Therefore whatever is handed down beyond faith in Jesus Christ is a burden. For consciences are weighed down by the useless observance of traditions, which cannot help the cause of salvation. They repeat what James had warned about meats offered to idols, fornication, and also what is strangled and blood, and they say that these things must be observed. Here, however, it must be noted that in the previous sermon we said that these precepts have different grounds. For the first two are necessary absolutely and simply, since it becomes Christians to abhor all communion with idolatry, and to keep their vessel or body holy and undefiled, and not to make a member of a harlot out of what Christ has consecrated with his blood to be a temple of the Holy Spirit. But what is said about the strangled and about blood is necessary to observe only by accident, chiefly because of the stumbling block that eating them placed before the weak. For since it is wrong to destroy by food one whom Christ deigned to redeem by the merit of his death, we ought, for the sake of the weaker brethren, to abstain from things that are otherwise lawful and permitted, so that our liberty does not give others a cause of ruin. Otherwise Christ's saying remains firm and valid: "Nothing that enters the mouth can defile a man," Matt. 15. And Paul permits eating meat offered to idols when no danger of scandal arises, and he testifies that the conscience is not simply defiled by these things. 1 Cor. 10. And elsewhere he calls doctrines that introduce distinctions of foods, as if salvation consisted in them, "teachings of demons." 1 Tim. 4. Those therefore act most foolishly here who cry out that the decrees of councils must be observed as necessary, since most of them are of such a kind that they lay a heavy burden on consciences, and openly and directly conflict with the oracles of Scripture. We admit indeed that much must be yielded to the weak, lest we offend anyone; yet Christian liberty must by no means be overturned for the sake of those who, being stubborn rather than weak, refuse to cast off errors once conceived, but cling to them tooth and nail. Against such men rather the saying of Christ should be hurled: "Let them alone; for they are blind guides of the blind." Matt. 15. Last, they add the fruit and usefulness: "If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. For you will also keep yourselves pure and unblemished, and you will give offence to no one." Yet here the single goal, to which all our endeavours should be directed, ought to be the same for all of us. In the one Christ, justification and salvation are to be sought through faith.

units.la: 110 tio & salus. Interim ab omni contaminatione tum idololatriæ tum reliquæ impuritatis nos ipsos conseruemus, & aliorum hominū saluti pro virili studeamus, ne ijs offendiculo simus, pro quibus Christus mori dignatus est. Hæc qui sedulò obseruant, falli & errare non poterunt, & ijdem huius vitæ cursum feliciter emensi, æternæ vitæ consortium obtinebunt cum Iesu Christo, domino & saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
