units.tr: 110 Meanwhile let us keep ourselves free from every contamination, both of idolatry and of other impurity, and in so far as we are able, let us work for the salvation of other people, so that we are no stumbling block to those for whom Christ deigned to die. Those who observe these things carefully will be unable to be deceived or to go astray, and having run the course of this life happily, they will obtain fellowship of eternal life with Jesus Christ, our Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CV.
units.tr: HOMILY CV.

units.la: Illi ergo dimissi venerunt Antiochiam, & congregata multitudine reddiderunt epistolam. Quam cum legissent, gauisi sunt super consolatione. Iudas autem & Silas, cum essent & ipsi prophetæ, multo sermone adhortati sunt fratres, confirmauerunt. Commorati autem illic ad tempus, dimissi sunt cum pace à fratribus ad Apostolos. Visum est autem Silæ manere ibidem. Paulus vero & Barnabas demorabantur Antiochiæ docentes & euangelizantes cum alijs etiam compluribus sermonem domini. Post aliquot autem dies dixit ad Barnabam Paulus: Reuertentes iam visitemus fratres nostros per omnes ciuitates, in quibus annunciauimus sermone domini, quomodo se habeant. Barnabas autem consulebat, ut simul assumerent Iohannem, cognomento Marcum: Paulus autem dedignabatur, ne is qui defecisset ab ipsis ex Pamphylia, nec iuisset cum eis in opus, simul assumeretur. Tam acris autem fuit inter eos disceptatio, ut alter ab altero seiungeretur: et Barnabas qui dem assumpto Marco, nauigaret in Cyprum: Paulus autem allecto Sila profectus est, traditus gratiæ dei à fratribus. Perambulabat autem Syriam ac Ciliciam, confirmans Ecclesias.
units.tr: So they were sent away and came down to Antioch, and when they had gathered the multitude together, they delivered the letter. When they had read it, they rejoiced at the comfort it gave. Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, exhorted the brothers with many words and strengthened them. After they had stayed there for a time, they were sent back in peace by the brothers to the apostles. But Silas decided to remain there. Paul and Barnabas stayed on at Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, together with many others. After some days Paul said to Barnabas: "Let us now return and visit our brothers in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing." Barnabas wanted to take John, called Mark, with them as well. But Paul thought it wrong to take with them the one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. The disagreement between them became so sharp that they parted from one another. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and set out, commended by the brothers to the grace of God. He travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

units.la: Postquam Diuus Lucas Hierosolymitani Concilij acta diligenter descripsit, et ostendit qua dexteritate ea contentio sopita sit, quæ circa iustificationis causam inter Christianos exorta fuerat, vltima huius capitis parte, quam modò recitauimus, quatuor res, cum primis memorabiles, commemorat, de quibus ordine dicemus, quantum vestris precibus exorata dei gratia dederit.
units.tr: After St. Luke had carefully described the acts of the Council of Jerusalem, and had shown with what skill that dispute was calmed, which had arisen among Christians about the cause of justification, in the last part of this chapter, which I have just read, he records four matters, especially worth remembering. With your prayers, I shall speak of them in order, as far as the grace of God, sought by your prayers, grants.

units.la: Principio, legationis quam ad Antiochenos Hierosolymitani miserunt, executio describitur, in qua quid legati simul & Paulus cum Barnaba egerint, deinde vt hos ecclesia Antiochena excepit, consyderandum venit. Et de illis quidem tria dicuntur. Primò vbi Antiochiam perueners, mox tota illius ecclesiæ multitudine congregata, epistolam à Synodo ipsis creditam reddiderunt. Quia enim de publica causa & ad omnes ex æquo pertinente agebatur, minimè admittendum censuerunt, vt aliquid populum celaretur. Vbi rursum veteris ecclesiæ morem videre licet, in qua publicè tractata sunt, quorum cognitio communi omnium saluti seruiebat. Sustulit morem hunc magna cum publicæ salutis iactura laruatorum episcoporum ambitio, qui populi ignorantiam & cæcitatem præcipuum tyrannidis suæ præsidium duxerunt. Deinde Iudas & Silas multis adhortationibus & consolationibus fratres in agnita & recepta veritate confirmauisse dicuntur. In quem finem illos missos fuisse, epistola abunde docet. Redditur tamen facti illorum ratio, eò quòd prophetæ essent, id est, publici & legitimè ordinati sacræ scripturæ interpretes. Eo enim sensu prophetæ nomen vsurpari ex priori ad Corinth. epistola cap. 14. clarissime patet. Admonet interim locus hic, neminem sibi in ecclesia aliquid publicè agendi ius vendicare debere, nisi qui legitimè vocatus & donis dignus atque necessarijs instructus fuerit. Perniciosa enim & detestabilis est Anabaptistarum impudentia, qui nec vocati nec donis instructi, ad docendi munus temerè irrumpunt. Tertiò, non ante Antiochia discedunt, priusquam cum pace & solenni benedictione dimittuntur, et turbas omnes ritè compositas esse vident. Quæ omnia si in vnum conferas, illos in legatione hac summo studio simul & fide vsos fuisse patebit: nec dubium est, quin generali exemplo docere velit spiritus sanctus, qua fide & industria publica ecclesiarum & rerumpub. negotia tractari debeant. Porrò quoad ecclesiam, illa hos cum gaudio excepisse, & non vulgariter recreata fuisse dicitur. Antea quidem dissidijs turg batos fuisse, epistola Synodica ostendit. Dolebat enim piissimus virus, Christianæ fidei articulos non sine graui offendiculo in disceptationem trahi. Altera rursum dolendi causa erat, quòd apostolos suos, Paulum & Barnabam, indignis modis proscindi, adeoq; ecclesias suas obliquè perstringi viderent. Quare non possunt non vehementer gaudere, quando pacem restitutam, doctores suos calumniis liberatos, & ecclesias suas apostolorum testimonio confirmatas esse audiunt. Hoc ingenio fideles & Christianos omnes præditos esse decet, à quo alienissimi sunt, qui dissidijs, ministrorum ignominia & contemptu, deniq; ecclesiarum dissipationibus delectantur.
units.tr: First, the carrying out of the embassy which the Jerusalem council sent to the Antiochenes is described, and we must consider what the envoys did, together with Paul and Barnabas, and then how the Church of Antioch received them. Concerning the envoys, three things are said. First, when they arrived at Antioch, they gathered the whole multitude of that church and delivered the letter entrusted to them by the synod. For since the matter concerned the public and affected everyone equally, they judged that nothing should be hidden from the people. Here again we can see the custom of the ancient Church, in which matters were treated openly, and the knowledge of them served the common salvation of all. The ambition of the masked bishops, who regarded the ignorance and blindness of the people as the chief stronghold of their tyranny, abolished this custom, to the great loss of public well-being. Next, Judas and Silas are said to have strengthened the brothers, who had acknowledged and received the truth, with many exhortations and consolations. The letter abundantly shows the purpose for which they were sent. Yet the reason for their action is given, namely that they were prophets, that is, public and lawfully ordained interpreters of Holy Scripture. That the name prophet is used in this sense is quite clear from the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 14. Meanwhile this passage warns that no one should claim for himself the right to act publicly in the Church, unless he has been lawfully called and is worthy of the gifts and equipped with what is necessary. For the impudence of the Anabaptists is pernicious and detestable, who, neither called nor equipped with gifts, rashly force their way into the office of teaching. Third, they did not leave Antioch until they had been dismissed in peace with a solemn blessing, and had seen that all the congregations were properly settled. If you put all these things together, it will be clear that in this embassy they made use of the greatest diligence and faith. And there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit wishes to teach by this general example with what faith and industry the public affairs of the churches and of the commonwealth ought to be handled. Moreover, as for the church, it is said that it received them with joy and was greatly refreshed. The synodal letter shows that before this it had been troubled by disputes. For that most pious people grieved that the articles of the Christian faith were being dragged into controversy, not without serious offence. Their second cause for grief was that they saw their apostles, Paul and Barnabas, torn to pieces in unworthy ways, and their own churches indirectly attacked. Therefore they could not but rejoice greatly when they heard that peace was restored, that their teachers were freed from calumnies, and that their churches were confirmed by the testimony of the apostles. All the faithful and Christians ought to be endowed with this disposition, from which those are far removed who delight in dissensions, in the disgrace and contempt of ministers, and finally in the scattering of churches.

units.la: II. Industria Silæ, Pauli & Barnabæ in propagando Christi regno.
units.tr: II. The diligence of Silas, Paul and Barnabas in propagating the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Secundò fidelem omnium horum in propagando & conseruando Christi regno curam atque industriam Lucas describit, quæ multis ijsq; non obscuris argumentis deprehendi potest. Et de Sila quidem dicitur, illum cum ad sua redeundi ipsi copia facta esset, Antiochiæ tamen manere voluisse, nimirum quòd operam suam, cuius fructum iam ante expertus erat, illi ecclesiæ adhuc vtilem esse videret. Maiorem ergo ecclesiæ Christi, quàm suarum rerum, rationem Silas habuit, quando Antiochiam Hierosolymorum vrbi & antiquis laribus præferit. Quod exemplum omnes Christi ministri imitari decet, vt seipsos & terrena omnia abnegent, quò in Christi & ecclesiæ ministerio expeditios res versari possint. Execrabilis ergo est illorum fordities, qui in ecclesiæ ministerio constituti prius tas suas rationes hominum saluti præferunt, & lucri gratia ecclesias relinquunt, quibus maximo cum profectu inseruire poterant. Sed de Paulo quoq; & Barnaba quædam dicuntur, nimirum quòd aliquandiu Antiochiæ commorati, euangelium vnà cum multis aliis symmystis prædicarint. Non ergo turpi ocio sese dediderunt, licet post tot labores atq; pericula iustissimam ocij quærendi causam habere viderentur. Ex eo autem quòd multi in Antiochena ecclesia euangelium prædicauisse dicuntur, facilè colligitur, qui animorum in illis candor fuerit, & quòd ab omni æmulatione alieni, non aliud magis, quàm Christi gloriam & multorum salutem quæsuerint. Est autem dignißimum obseruatione apostolorum exercitium, quos euangelicæ prædicationi cumprimis vacauisse videmus. Nouerant enim hoc salutis nuncium esse. Nouerant his armis Christo gentes subijci & mundum sub fidei obedientiam redigi. Nouerant deniq; Christum dominum vni huic rei cumprimis intentum fuisse, nec aliud fecisse frequentius. Nec veterem typum ignorabant, quo sacerdotis vestem tintinna bulis sonorum esse iusserat dominus, vt eo argumento doceret, à ministris vocis sonum, id est, euangelij doctrinam maximè requiri. Exod.28. At hodie eò deuentum est, vt episcopi à nullare magis, quàm à verbi ministerio abhorreant, & id potius sibi laudi ducant, si ex ecclesiarum redditibus canes equosúe & ignauam seruilemq; aulicorum turbam pascant, quàm si Christi oues cœlestis doctrinæ pabulo saturent. Ita suo exemplo apud reliquos quoq; hominum ordines dei verbum vile & contemptum reddunt, quæ potissima calamitatum nostri seculi causa est. Additur autem aliud quoque Paulinæ industriæ argumentum, quòd nimirum pro alijs etiam ecclesijs solicitus, cum Barnaba de illis inuisendis consultarit. Intelligebat enim uon sufficere, ecclesias semel constituisse, sed ijs conserendis maximè studendum esse, cum præter ingenitam humano generi leuitatem infinita alia quotidie occurrant, quæ à fide nos abstrahere, & optimè constitutas ecclesias turbare atq; euertere possunt. Quare strenui militis instar in excubijs frequens consistit, nec vllis laboribus parcit, vt salua maneat ecclesijs sua incolumitas, in quam semel constitutæ fuerant. Quod exemplum si cum ijs conferas, qui toti in hoc sunt, vt aliorum fide & industria constitutas ecclesias turbent & dissipent, facilè patebit, quo spiritu ducantur, & cuius principis ministri sint.
units.tr: Second, Luke describes the faithful care and diligence of all these men in spreading and preserving the kingdom of Christ, which can be discerned by many arguments, and those not obscure. Concerning Silas, it is said that when he was given the chance to return home, he nevertheless wished to remain at Antioch, clearly because he saw that his work, the fruit of which he had already experienced, was still useful to that church. Silas therefore had greater regard for the church of Christ than for his own affairs, when he preferred Antioch to the city of Jerusalem and his old home. All ministers of Christ ought to imitate this example, so that they may deny themselves and all earthly things, and so that they may be more free to occupy themselves in the ministry of Christ and of the Church. Therefore the baseness of those is detestable who, placed in the ministry of the Church, put their own affairs and gains before the salvation of men, and abandon the churches for the sake of profit, churches they could have served with the greatest benefit. But certain things are also said about Paul and Barnabas, namely that after staying for some time at Antioch, they preached the gospel together with many other fellow workers. Therefore they did not give themselves over to shameful idleness, although after so many labours and dangers they seemed to have the most just reason for seeking rest. From the fact that many are said to have preached the gospel in the church of Antioch, it is easily gathered what sincerity of mind existed among them, and that, free from all rivalry, they sought nothing more than the glory of Christ and the salvation of many. Moreover, the exercise of the apostles, whom we see especially devoted to the preaching of the gospel, is most worthy of notice. For they knew that this was the message of salvation. They knew that by these weapons the nations are subjected to Christ and the world is brought under the obedience of faith. Finally, they knew that the Lord Christ was especially intent on this one task, and did nothing more often. Nor were they ignorant of the old type, in which the Lord had commanded that the priest's robe be hung with bells sounding, so that by this sign he might teach that from the ministers above all is required the sound of the voice, that is, the teaching of the gospel. Exodus 28. But today things have come to such a point that bishops shun nothing more than the ministry of the word, and they count it more to their credit if they feed dogs, horses, and a lazy, servile crowd of courtiers from the revenues of the churches, than if they fill Christ's sheep with the food of heavenly doctrine. Thus by their example they make the word of God cheap and contemptible among the other orders of men as well, which is the chief cause of the calamities of our age. Another proof of Paul's diligence is added, namely that, anxious for the other churches too, he took counsel with Barnabas about visiting them. For he understood that it was not enough to have founded the churches once, but that the greatest care must be given to preserving them, since, besides the innate fickleness of the human race, countless other things meet us every day which can draw us away from the faith and disturb and overthrow even well-established churches. Therefore, like a vigilant soldier, he stands often on watch, and spares no labour, so that the churches may keep the safety in which they were once established. If you compare this example with those who are wholly intent on disturbing and scattering churches established by the faith and industry of others, it will be easily seen by what spirit they are led, and whose ministers they are.

units.la: III. Dissidium Pauli & Barnabæ.
units.tr: III. The Dissension of Paul and Barnabas.

units.la: Tertiò graue & infelix inter Paulum & Barnabam dissidium commemoratur, quod multis nominibus memorabile est. Hos enim spiritu sancto authore collegas & symmystas factos fuisse supra cap. 13. audiuimus. Idem multa simul pericula terra mariq; sustinuerunt, quo non aliud est firmius ad animorum coniunctionem vinculum. Adhæc mirificos suorum laborum succęssus ex dei benedictione experti fuerant. Nunc verò atroci inter ipsos contentione oborta, dissociantur, nec post hac laborum socij fuisse leguntur. Contentionis verò & dissidij materia Iohannes Marcus fuit, de cuius defectione cap.13. dictum est. Hunc denuò in gratiam & ministerij societatem recipiendum esse, Barnabas censebat, & haud dubiè consilij sui rationes graues allegabat. Apud deum enim pe-catoribus, si culpam agnoscant ac fateantur, venia locus est. Et Petrum post Christi abnegationem in pristinum dignitatis suæ gradum restitutum esse constat. Nec parum Marco patrocinari videbatur, batur Mariae matrum pietas, quae cum maxime fureret persecutionis tempestas, domum suam fidelibus portum quendam & asylum esse voluit. At rationibus hisce omnibus nunquam adduci potest Paulus, ut eum collegam habere dignetur, quem tam turpiter in medio cursu, & fortasse non fine graui multorum offendiculo, defecisse meminerat. Occurrebat enim Christi dictum, Nemo qui manu aratro admota respexerit a tergo, dignus est regno dei. Luc. 9. Et si circumstantias consyderemus, ecclesiae calculo Paulum adiutum fuisse, verisimile videbitur. Is enim alletto Sila, a fratribus gratiae dei commendatur, id est, solenni cum benedictione ad opus dimittitur. De Barnaba vero hoc unum Lucas refert, quod assumpto Marco in Cyprum navigarit (quam illi patriam fuisse supra Cap.4. dictum est) indignabundus nimirum & aestuans. Quamvis vero non per omnia excusari posse videatur Pauli seueritas, voluit tamen hoc in apostatas siue defectores exemplum extare spiritus sanctus, quo discamus ad dei gratiam aditum quidem patere peccatoribus, non temere tamen ad ecclesiae ministerium admittendos esse, qui graviores alicuius offendiculi authores fuerunt, quorumque fides ob ante commissa facinora non immerito suspecta est. Episcopum oportet enim irreprehensibilem esse, & nouitium hoc potissimum nomine Paulus arcere iubet, quod tales calumniis facile pateant. Hodie quia nimium faciles sumus in quibusvis admittendis, non mirum si indies magis vilescat ministerij authoritas. Porro mirum alicui videri poterat, quod deus electissima gratiae suae vasa tam atroci dissidio implicari passus est, & quod illorum errores spiritus sanctus scriptis mandatos ad posteros transmittere voluit. At penitius rem consideranti iustae & graues huius rei causae patebunt. Primo enim docent haec, sanctos quoque homines esse affectibus obnoxios, & proinde dei gratia indigere. Agnoscit hoc Paulus, quando sibi stimulum carnis & nuncium Satanae immissum fuisse scribit, cui non aliis armis, quam dei gratia resistere potuerit. 2.Corinth.12. Idem de lege peccati scribens, quae in singulis hominibus aduersus spiritum dei pugnat, tandem exclamat: Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex hoc corpore mortis? Illico vero subdit: Gratias ago deo per Iesum Christum, &c. Rom. 7. Vsus horum est, ut quae a sanctis egregie facta sunt, ad deum authorem referamus, & illum praedicemus vnice. Deinde ad ardens & irremissum pietatis studium icti sanctorum lapsus nos excitant, ut iuxta Pauli dictum cum timore & tremore salutem nostram operemur. Philip.2. Quis enim non expauescat? quis non ad vigilandum & ad preces excitetur, quando praeclaros dei cultores tam graviter lapsos esse videt? Quis non a lapsu sibi timeat, etiam tum quando sibi stare videtur? 1.Corinth.10.cap. Et praeterea alius quoq; huius dissidij vsus, ne hodie ministrorum verbi dissidijs offendamur, nec propter haec diuini verbi doctrinam suspectam habeamus. Nec enim ex hominibus dependet huius authoritas, sed ut Isaias clamat, in aeternum manet, etiamsi omnis caro cum gloria sua instar floris exaresc at & collabatur. Isa.40.capite.
units.tr: Thirdly, a grievous and unhappy dissension between Paul and Barnabas is recorded, which is memorable for many reasons. For we heard in chapter 13 that they had been made companions and fellow-labourers by the authority of the Holy Spirit. They had together endured many dangers on land and sea, and nothing is a firmer bond for uniting minds than this. Moreover, they had experienced wonderful success in their labours through God's blessing. Now, however, a bitter contention has arisen between them, they part ways, and we read that they were no longer companions in labour. The matter of the contention and dissension was John Mark, whose desertion was mentioned in chapter 13. Barnabas thought that he should be received again into favour and fellowship in the ministry, and he certainly argued his case with weighty reasons. For with God there is room for pardon for sinners, if they acknowledge and confess their fault; and it is agreed that Peter, after denying Christ, was restored to his former rank of dignity. Nor did the piety of Mark's mother, Mary, seem to plead little for Mark, for when the storm of persecution was raging most fiercely, she wished her house to be a kind of harbour and refuge for the faithful. But Paul could never be moved by all these arguments to count as his colleague a man who, as he remembered, had deserted so shamefully in the middle of the race, and perhaps not without serious stumbling for many. For the saying of Christ came to mind: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9). And if we consider the circumstances, it will seem likely that Paul was supported by the judgement of the congregation: for after choosing Silas, he is commended by the brothers to the grace of God, that is, he is sent out to the work with a solemn blessing. Of Barnabas, however, Luke reports only this, that he took Mark and sailed to Cyprus (which, as was said above in chapter 4, was his homeland), no doubt indignant and seething. Although Paul's severity may not seem entirely excusable in every respect, the Holy Spirit nevertheless wished this example to stand against apostates or deserters, so that we may learn that access to the grace of God is indeed open to sinners, yet that those who have been the chief authors of some serious stumbling-block, and whose faith is not unreasonably suspected on account of past misdeeds, are not to be lightly admitted to the ministry of the Church. For "a bishop must be blameless" (1 Tim. 3), and Paul bids us keep away a novice especially on this account, that such men easily lay themselves open to slander. Today, since we are far too easy in admitting whomever we please, it is no wonder that the authority of the ministry grows more contemptible by the day. Moreover, it might seem strange to some that God allowed his most chosen vessels of grace to be entangled in so bitter a dissension, and that the Holy Spirit wished their errors to be committed to writing and handed down to posterity. But to one who considers the matter more deeply, the just and weighty causes of this will become clear. For first, these things teach that holy men too are subject to passions, and therefore need the grace of God. Paul acknowledges this when he writes that a goad of the flesh and a messenger of Satan was sent to him, which he could resist with no other weapons than the grace of God (2 Cor. 12). Writing also about the law of sin, which in each man fights against the Spirit of God, he at last cries out: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" and immediately adds: "I thank God through Jesus Christ," etc. (Rom. 7). The use of these things is that we should refer to God as the author whatever has been done nobly by the saints, and proclaim him alone. Secondly, the falls of the saints, stirring us up, should rouse us to an ardent and unremitting zeal for godliness, so that, according to Paul's saying, we work out our salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2). For who would not be struck with dread? Who would not be roused to watchfulness and prayer, when he sees the outstanding worshippers of God fall so grievously? Who would not fear a fall for himself, even when he seems to himself to stand? (1 Cor. 10). And besides, there is another use of this dissension: that we should not be offended today by the quarrels of the ministers of the Word, nor on account of these things hold the doctrine of the divine Word in suspicion. For its authority does not depend on men, but, as Isaiah cries, "it remains for ever, even if all flesh with its glory withers like a flower and collapses" (Isa. 40).

units.la: Quartum & postremum huius loci caput est, Pauli & Barnabae peregrinatio, qua suum de visitandis ecclesijs & ijsdem verbo dei confirmandis consilium executi sunt. Licet enim inter se toti dissideant, neuter tamen propterea fui officij immemor est, & Barnabas quidem in Cyprum, Paulus vero in Syriam & Ciliciam, & inde in Lycaoniam transit. Estq; haec laude digna constantia, quam omnes imitari decet, ne contendendi libidine & hominum importunitate nos superari patiamur, ut nostri officij immemores, deo parum fidi simus. Interim dei bonitatem & sapientiam nos admirari conuenit, qui electorum suorum delictis optime vti nouit. Ex tristi enim apostolorum dissidio hoc boni oritur, ut plures uno eodemq; tempore inuisantur & confirmentur ecclesiae. Imo impiorum peccatis frequenter ad suae gloriae illustrationem & hominum salutem deus abutitur: cuius rei exempla in Iosephi venditione & multa alijs historijs extant. Nemo tamen idcirco nos culpa vacare putet. Peccant enim homines, & peccatis, ut irae vasa fiant, merentur. Quod si quis ex illorum delictis fructus bonus oritur, id universum diuinae bonitati & sapientiae tribui debet. Faxit haec, ut per nos quoq; diuini nominis gloria illustretur, & omnibus nostris in eum finem vtatur clementissimus pater, qui multorum saluti seruiat, nosq; in coelis viuamus cum Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: The fourth and last point of this passage is the journey of Paul and Barnabas, by which they carried out their plan of visiting the churches and strengthening them by the Word of God. For although they were completely at odds with each other, neither of them forgot his duty, and Barnabas indeed went to Cyprus, while Paul went to Syria and Cilicia, and from there passed into Lycaonia. This constancy is worthy of praise, and all ought to imitate it, lest we allow ourselves to be overcome by the lust for contention and by the importunity of men, so that, forgetful of our duty, we become less faithful to God. Meanwhile we ought to marvel at the goodness and wisdom of God, who knows how to make the best use of the sins of his elect. For from this sad dissension of the apostles this good comes, that the churches are visited and strengthened at one and the same time by more men. Indeed, God often turns the sins of the impious to the illustration of his glory and the salvation of men; examples of this exist in the selling of Joseph and in many other histories. Yet let no one therefore think that we are free from blame. Men sin, and by their sins they deserve to become vessels of wrath. But if some good fruit comes from their offences, the whole of it must be attributed to the goodness and wisdom of God. May he grant that through us also the glory of his divine name be illustrated, and that the most merciful Father use all our efforts to this end, he who serves the salvation of many, and that we may live in heaven with Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: HOMILIA CVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CVI.

units.la: PEruenit autem Derben & Lystram: & ecce discipulus quidam erat ibi nomine Timotheus, filius cuiusdam mulieris Iudaeae fidelis, patre autem Graeco. Huic testimonium bonum reddebatur a fratribus, qui Lystris erant & Iconij. Hunc voluit Paulus secum proficisci, & assumptum circuncidit propter Iudaeos, qui erant in illis locis. Sciebant enim omnes, quod pater eius esset Graecus. Cum autem pertransirent civitates, seruanda illis tradebant placita, quae decreta erant ab apostolis & senioribus, qui erant Hierosolymis. Itaque ecclesiae confirmabantur fide, & abundabant numero quotidie.
units.tr: Then he came to Derbe and Lystra: and behold, a certain disciple was there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but his father was a Greek. He was well reported of by the brethren who were at Lystra and Iconium. Paul wanted him to go forth with him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. As they went through the cities, they delivered to them the decrees to keep, which had been decided by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith and increased in number daily.

units.la: DIuus Paulus ecclesias, quas euangelij praedicatione collegerat, innisere & in fide semel recepta confirmare instituit, ne vel securitate immersi, vel satanae dolis circumuenti, vel persecutionibus superati deficiant. Id vero sic facit, ut simul ubicunque sese offeret occasio, nouas ecclesias lucrifacere studeat. Eam historiam in praesenti Lucas describit, qui in hac peregrinatione Paulo individuus comes fuit, & proinde tanquam oculatus testis, res omnes compertissimas habuit. Et principio quidem Syriam & Ciliciam ab illis lustratam fuisse audiuimus. Sequitur quid in Lycaonia factum fuerit, cuius ecclesiae propter Iudaeos, acerrimos Christi hostes, prae aliis confirmatione opus habuisse videntur: nec potuit non illis timere Paulus, cum Iudaeorum hostiles conatus & implacabiles animos ipse non semel expertus esset.
units.tr: Divine Paul resolved to strengthen and confirm in the faith, once received, the churches he had gathered by preaching the gospel, so that they would not fail, either sunk in complacency, or deceived by the wiles of Satan, or overcome by persecutions. He did this in such a way that, wherever an opportunity presented itself, he also strove to win new churches. Luke describes that history in the present passage. He was Paul's inseparable companion on this journey, and therefore, as an eyewitness, he had full knowledge of all the facts. At the start, we heard that Syria and Cilicia had been traversed by them. Next comes what happened in Lycaonia, whose churches seem to have needed strengthening more than others, because of the Jews, the bitterest enemies of Christ. Paul could not but fear for them, since he himself had more than once experienced the hostile attempts and implacable minds of the Jews.

units.la: Porro narrandi initium a Timothei vocatione facit euangelista, quem Paulus profectionis suae comitem & laborum omnium socium assumpsit. Noverat enim absque idoneis verbi ministris, Christi regnum & fidem in hunc propagari non posse. Quare ut huius saeculi principes, qui regnorum suorum fines longe late extendere student, in rerum peritis & longo usu exercitatis belli ducibus ac amicis militibus undique conquirendis toti occupantur: ita Pauli haec praecipua cura fuit, ut quam plurimos ecclesiae Christi fideles & idoneos ministros acquireret, quorum opera Christi regnum ad plures propagaretur. Imitari debent exemplum hoc, quicunque ecclesias saluas esse volunt, siue illi doctrinae antistites siue magistratus fuerint. Nam ut absque verbi praedicatione ecclesiae nouae plantari non possunt, ita sine hac nec in officio retinebuntur, quae iam plantatae & collectae sunt. Hinc illa prophetarum veteris Testamenti circa scholas cura & industria, quam maiores nostri, prudentissimi & pijssimi viri, imitati sunt, quemadmodum passim vetustissimorum Collegiorum fundationes testantur. Sunt autem in Timothei vocatione duo consyderanda, de quibus ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Moreover, the evangelist begins his narrative with the calling of Timothy, whom Paul took as the companion of his journey and the partner of all his labours. For he knew that without suitable ministers of the Word, the kingdom of Christ and the faith could not be spread among them. Therefore, just as the princes of this age, who strive to extend the borders of their kingdoms far and wide, are wholly occupied in seeking out from everywhere leaders of war skilled in affairs and experienced through long practice, and friendly soldiers, so this was Paul's chief concern: to acquire as many faithful and suitable ministers for the church of Christ as he could, through whose labour the kingdom of Christ might be spread to more people. Whoever wishes the churches to be safe should imitate this example, whether they be teachers of doctrine or magistrates. For just as new churches cannot be planted without the preaching of the Word, so churches already planted and gathered cannot be kept in their duty without it. Hence came the care and diligence of the prophets of the Old Testament concerning schools, which our forefathers, most prudent and pious men, imitated, as the foundations of the most ancient colleges testify everywhere. Now there are two things to consider in Timothy's calling, which we shall discuss in order.

units.la: Primo quis & qualis ille fuerit, describitur. Iudaea matre, eaque fideli, natus, patrem Graecum, id est, gentilem habuit. Et matris quidem Eunicae simul & Loidis aviae pietatem multis in posteriori ad Timotheum epistola Paulus praedicat, cuius hoc cumprimis euidens argumentum est, quod filium in Christiana fide & religione probe instituit curauit. Et hic illum discipulum, id est, Christianum iam antea fuisse dicit Lucas, priusquam a Paulo ad ministerij ecclesiastici munus vocaretur. Adhaec eundem communibus omnium fratrum suffragijs commendatum fuisse testatur, & quidem non Lystrenfium modo, inter quos domicilium habebat, verum etiam Iconiensium, adeo ut exteris quoque illius virtus cognita & perspecta esset. Docet haec Timothei descriptio, quales ad verbi dei & ecclesiae ministerium eligi debeant. Vbi prima religionis cura haberi conuenit, ne vel omnino alienae a fide, vel saltem neophyti aut nouitij eligantur. Nam ut hi plerunque rerum omnium incerti, tum etiam leues & inconstantes sunt: ita illi religionem quaestum ducunt, quam & ipsi in sinu improbe ridVent, & alijs quoque deridenda exponunt. Deinde vero eruditionis quoque ratio habenda est, ut ij ecclesiae gubernaculis praeficiantur, qui in sacris literis probe versati sint, in quibus Timotheum a pueris institutum fuisse Paulus testatur. 2. Tim. 3. Impossibile enim reuera est, ut alios doceat, qui non ipse prior didicit, & tales non alij quam caeci caecorum duces esse possunt, quales illos Christus nominat. Matth 15. At quia ex scripturis sacris ecclesiae doctrina peti debet, in illis exercitatissimos esse oportet ectet ecclesiarum ministros: nec illis quicquam tribuendum, etiamsi in omni philosophia peritissimi, sacrarum autem literarum imperiti & rudes fuerint. Qua causa est, quod ne apostolos quidem, nisi prius plenissime instructos, ad praedicandum erumpere Christus voluit. Tertio probata vitae testimonium accedat oportet, ne propter ipsos doctrina vel contemnatur, vel saltem suspecta fiat. Irrepre hensibilem ergo episcopum esse vult Paulus 1. Tim. 3. Tit. 1. Et quantum religioni simul & doctrinae per impuram antistitum vitam derogatur, filiorum Eli exemplum abunde docet, quorum libidine & sacrilega audacia factum fuit, ut omnis fere populus a Dei cultu abhorreret, eaque occasione ita apud omnes ordines impietas invaluit, ut non nisi publica clade & multo sanguine fuso expiari posset. Imitanda ergo hodie quoque Pauli prudentia & solertia, qui non nisi omnibus numeris absolutissimum & talem sibi in ministerio collegam adoptavit, qui spem de se conceptam ita confirmaverat, ut eam fallere nunquam posse videretur.
units.tr: First, who he was and what kind of man is described. Born of a Jewish mother, and a believing one, he had a Greek father, that is, a Gentile. Paul praises in many places in his later letter to Timothy the piety of his mother Eunice and his grandmother Lois, and this is especially clear proof of it: that she took care to bring up her son well in the Christian faith and religion. Luke also says that this man was already a disciple, that is, a Christian, before he was called by Paul to the office of ecclesiastical ministry. Besides, he testifies that he was commended by the common votes of all the brethren, and not only of the Lystrans, among whom he had his home, but also of the Iconians, so that his virtue was known and well observed even by outsiders. This description of Timothy teaches what sort of men ought to be chosen for the ministry of the Word of God and of the Church. Here the first concern of religion should be that men are not chosen who are wholly alien to the faith, or at least new converts or novices. For these, being generally uncertain about everything, are also fickle and inconstant. They regard religion as a means of profit, which they themselves secretly mock, and expose it to be mocked by others too. Next, account must also be taken of learning, so that those set over the government of the church are men well versed in the sacred letters, in which Paul testifies that Timothy was instructed from boyhood (2 Tim. 3). For it is truly impossible that a man should teach others who has not first learned himself, and such men can be none other than blind guides of the blind, as Christ calls them (Matt. 15). But because the doctrine of the Church ought to be drawn from the holy Scriptures, the ministers of the churches must be most practised in them, and nothing should be granted to men who, although most skilled in all philosophy, are inexperienced and untrained in the sacred letters. For this reason Christ did not wish even the apostles to break out into preaching unless they were first thoroughly instructed. Third, the testimony of a proven life must be added, lest the doctrine itself be despised, or at least become suspect, because of the men. Paul therefore wants a bishop to be blameless (1 Tim. 3; Tit. 1). And how much both religion and doctrine are damaged by the impure life of its teachers is amply shown by the example of the sons of Eli, by whose lust and sacrilegious audacity it came about that almost the whole people abhorred the worship of God, and on that occasion impiety so prevailed among all orders that it could be atoned for only by public slaughter and much blood shed. Therefore, the prudence and diligence of Paul should be imitated today too, who adopted as his colleague in the ministry no one but a man most perfect in every respect, and one who had so confirmed the hope conceived of him that he seemed never able to disappoint it.

units.la: Secundo, quid cum Timotheo nouo symmysta sive collega primo omnium egerit, videamus. Huc (inquit) cum vellet secum proficisci Paulus, assumptum circumcidit. Quid (inquis) audio? Quae illa levitas & inconstantia? Non multo ante acerrime se illis Paulus oppositus, qui circumcisionem a gentibus exigebant, & tanta propter hanc turba concitata fuit, ut coram apostolis & tota Hierosolymitana ecclesia causa haec difficulter componi & sopiri potuerit. Nunc vero postquam gentes circumcisione nequaquam grauandas esse apostoli decreuerunt, Paulus Timotheum, qui iam aliquanto tempore Christianus fuerat, circumcidit. At nihil hic vel leuitati vel pertinaciae tribuendum est, cum facti sui rationem grauissimam habuerit, nec ipse secum dissideat, si rem ipsam penitius inspiciamus. Pharisaeis enim sive Nazaraeis, circumcisionem ut necessariam vrgentibus, merito sese opposuit Paulus, cum ea opinio Christi meritum euacuaret, fidem inanem redderet, & libertatem Christianam everteret. Et propter hos Titum circumcidere noluit, eo quod illos libertati fidelium astute insidiari videret, Gal. 2. Hic vero Timotheum propter Iudaeos circumcidit, qui in illis locis frequentes erant, ut ea occasione Timotheo euangelium inter Iudaeos praedicandi aditus pateret. Notum enim est, quam vehementer gentes incircumcisas abominati fuerint Iudaei, quando Petrum hoc nomine palam accusauerunt, quod ad gentes esset ingressus, & Paulum postea seditiose comprehendunt, quod gentes in templum ad duxisset. Nisi ergo circumcidisset Timotheum, nunquam illi inter Iudaeos docendi facultas fuisset data, & ipsi Paulo in posterum, tanquam legis prophanatori & auitae religionis hosti, Iudaeorum aures clausae fuissent. Prudenter itaque hoc illorum infirmitati tribuit, & Timotheum circumcidit, ut illius ministerio ad Iudaeos viam sternat, & patulatim eos edoceat, ut circumcisionem cum reliquis caeremoniis in Christo abrogatam esse intelligant. Nec alia ratione Timotheum circumcidi voluit, quia suffocati & sanguinis esum apostoli in Synodo prohibuerunt. Ita ipse fatetur se Iudaeis Iudaeum factum esse, ut Iudaeos Christo lucrifaceret, non ut illos in superstitiosa legis obseruatione confirmaret 1. Cor. 9. Ex his vero vniuersalis regula constitui potest, qua docemur, quando & quomodo in externis dispensare liceat. Nimirum quando id charitas iubet, & ecclesiae aedificatio postulat. Vt primum vero cultum illis alligari, aut meriti humani fiduciam erigi, aut Christianae libertati insidias struì videmus, ne minima quidem ferri aut admitti debent. Nam quae pro medijs & indifferentibus habe riposterant, indifferentia esse desinunt, quamprimum sub his fidei nostrae professio & meriti Christi gloria periclitatur. Inepte ergo & nimis impudenter Pauli exemplum pro suis traditionibus Pontificij allegant, dum ea ratione Missas, imagines, exequiarum pompam, preces pro defunctis, ieiunia, vestium & ciborum discrimina, caelibatum, monastica vota, confessionem auricularem, absolutionem, satisfactiones & sexcenta alia eius generis a nobis retineri & obseruari debere contendunt, qua Timotheum Paulus circumciderit. Nam ut illud omittamus, quod inepta & superstitiosa humanarum traditionum figmenta cum circumcisione, cuius origo ex Deo fuit, conferunt, lippis & tonsoribus notum est, illos in his omnibus praecipuam cultus diuini partem constituere, in ijsdem maximam iustitiae & salutis suae fiduciam repositam habere, deniq; his saluis Christianam libertatem subsistere non posse, imo hac ipsa insignem illum bestiae characterem continere, quem absq; Christi abnegatione nemo vel fusci pere vel retinere potest. Quamobrem Christianos homines ista oppugnare potius, quam Christiani no minus professionem minima ex parte violare decet.
units.tr: Second, let us see what he did first of all with Timothy, his new fellow-worker and colleague. "He wanted," it says, "to go forth with him, and he took him and circumcised him." What (you say) do I hear? What levity and inconstancy is this? Not long before, Paul had most fiercely opposed those who demanded circumcision from the Gentiles, and so great a tumult was stirred up over this that the matter could hardly be settled and quieted before the apostles and the whole church of Jerusalem. But now, after the apostles had decided that the Gentiles were in no way to be burdened with circumcision, Paul circumcised Timothy, who had already been a Christian for some time. Yet nothing here should be attributed either to levity or to obstinacy, since he had a most weighty reason for his act, and if we look into the matter more deeply, he does not contradict himself. For Paul had rightly opposed the Pharisees, or Nazarenes, who urged circumcision as necessary, since that opinion made void the merit of Christ, rendered faith empty, and overturned Christian liberty. And for the sake of these men he refused to circumcise Titus, because he saw that they were craftily plotting against the liberty of the faithful (Gal. 2). But here he circumcised Timothy because of the Jews, who were numerous in those places, so that on that occasion an opening might be made for Timothy to preach the gospel among the Jews. For it is well known how vehemently the Jews abhorred uncircumcised Gentiles, when they openly accused Peter on this account, because he had gone in to the Gentiles, and afterwards seditiously seized Paul, because he had brought Gentiles into the temple. Unless he had circumcised Timothy, the opportunity of teaching among the Jews would never have been given to him, and afterwards the ears of the Jews would have been closed even to Paul himself, as a profaner of the law and an enemy of the religion of their fathers. Therefore he wisely yielded this to their weakness and circumcised Timothy, so that by his ministry he might prepare a way to the Jews and gradually teach them to understand that circumcision, together with the other ceremonies, has been abrogated in Christ. Nor did he wish Timothy to be circumcised for any other reason, since the apostles in the Synod forbade the eating of what is strangled and of blood. Thus he himself confesses that he became a Jew to the Jews, that he might win the Jews to Christ, not that he might confirm them in a superstitious observance of the law (1 Cor. 9). From these things a universal rule can be laid down, by which we are taught when and how it is lawful to dispense in external matters. Namely, when charity demands it and the building up of the church requires it. But as soon as we see that worship is bound to such things, or confidence in human merit is raised up, or snares are laid for Christian liberty, not even the smallest things ought to be tolerated or admitted. For things which had been regarded as means and indifferent cease to be indifferent as soon as the profession of our faith and the glory of Christ's merit are endangered by them. Therefore the Papists foolishly and too shamelessly allege the example of Paul in defence of their own traditions, when on this ground they contend that we must retain and observe Masses, images, the pomp of funerals, prayers for the dead, fasts, distinctions of clothes and foods, celibacy, monastic vows, auricular confession, absolution, satisfactions, and six hundred other things of this kind, just as Paul circumcised Timothy. For to pass over the fact that the foolish and superstitious inventions of human traditions are compared with circumcision, whose origin was from God, as bleary-eyed men and barbers know, these men set up in all these things the chief part of divine worship, place in them the greatest confidence of their righteousness and salvation, and finally hold that Christian liberty cannot survive if these remain; indeed, that by this very fact they bear that notorious mark of the beast, which no one can either receive or retain without denying Christ. Therefore it becomes Christians to attack these things rather than to violate, even in the smallest part, the profession of Christians.

units.la: Priusquam vero hinc discedamus, parentum Timothei impar coniugium inspiciendum erit, cum L huius mentionem diserte Lucas faciat. Matrem enim Eunicam Iudaeam, patrem vero Graecum fuisse gentilem fuisse dicit. At Iudaeis coniugia cum gentilibus interdicta fuisse legimus. Ea tamen fuit illo tempore Iudaici populi conditio, ut Romana tyrannide oppressus & hinc inde dispersis multa praeter animi sententiam ferenda fuerint. Interim piissimae foeminae Eunicae ex connubio hoc illud periculum enatum esse videmus, quod in lege Deus praedixit. Nam Timotheum filium, qui haud dubie ante Christum passum & ante legem abrogatam natus erat, circumcisione in populi Dei consortium adscribere, Deoq; consecrare non potuit, obstante nimirum marito, quem a vera religione alienissimum fuisse verisimile est, cum nullibi ipsius pietas praedicetur a Paulo, qui Eunicae & Loidis fidem dignam putavit, quae scriptis suis commendaretur. Debent haec abstterre Christianae fidei profesores, ne cum incredulis iugum ducant, sicuti alibi apostolus monet. 2. Corinth. 6. Simul tamen memorabile est Eunicae exemplum, quae filium, vel inuito marito, ab ineunte aetate sacris literis imbui curauit, ne gentilium superstitione & idolomania corrumperetur. Observent hoc matronae, quibus impari coniugio diuexari contingit. Meminerint liberos suos propter foederis promissionem sanctos esse, quod diserte Paulus docet. 1. Corinth. 7. Eosdem ergo verae pietatis doctrina imbuant & Deo adducant, cuius honor si ipsis cordi fuerit, veracem illum in suis promissis experientur, quibus se suis tutorem & vindicem fore pollicetur.
units.tr: Before we leave this point, the mixed marriage of Timothy's parents must be looked at, since Luke expressly mentions him. He says that his mother Eunice was a Jewess and his father a Greek, a Gentile. We read, however, that marriages between Jews and Gentiles were forbidden. Yet such was the condition of the Jewish people at that time, oppressed by Roman tyranny and scattered here and there, that they had to bear many things against their own judgment. Meanwhile we see that from this marriage of the most pious woman Eunice there arose the danger that God foretold in the law. For Timothy, who was undoubtedly born before Christ suffered and before the law was abrogated, could not be admitted by circumcision into the fellowship of God's people and consecrated to God, since his father stood in the way, a man who was very probably most alien to the true religion, since nowhere does Paul praise his piety, although he judged the faith of Eunice and Lois worthy to be commended in his writings. These things ought to deter professors of the Christian faith from yoking themselves with unbelievers, as the apostle warns elsewhere (2 Cor. 6). At the same time, the example of Eunice is worth remembering: she took care that her son was imbued with the Holy Scriptures from his earliest age, even against her husband's will, so that he would not be corrupted by the superstition and idolatry of the Gentiles. Let Christian matrons who happen to suffer the trouble of an unequal marriage take note of this. Let them remember that their children are holy because of the promise of the covenant, as Paul expressly teaches (1 Cor. 7). Let them therefore imbue their children with the doctrine of true piety and bring them to God; if the honour of God is dear to them, they will experience him to be true to his promises, in which he pledges himself to be the guardian and defender of their children.

units.la: Sed redeamus ad praesentis loci tractationem, quo post Timothei vocationem, quid in ecclesijs docuerint, qui cum Paulo fuerunt, indicatur. Cum transirent (inquit) civitates, seruanda illis tradebant placita, quae decreta erant ab apostolis & Senioribus, qui erant Hierosolymis. Qua verba ad nescio quas traditiones Papistae detorquent, quas ab apostolis illorum q; successoribus quasi per manus ecclesijs traditas, nunquam vero scriptis mandatas fuisse fingunt. Quod asylum vbi semel sibi constituerunt, apostolicam traditionem esse dicunt, quicquid nulla scripturae authoritate confirmari posse vident. At nihil tale Lucas dicit, sed de ijs decretis loquitur, quorum mentio superiori capite facta est. Illa vero fuerunt: Sola Dei gratia per fidem Iesu Christi, non ex legis operibus, hominem iustificari & salutem consequi. Abstinendum esse ab ijs, quae vel fidei nostrae professionem, vel sanctitatem nostram polluunt, qualia sunt Idololatriae consortium & Scortatio. Studendum esse charitati, & in externis aliquid dandum esse infirmioribus, vel etiam adhuc a fide alienis, quos lucrifieri posse speret est. Interim cauendum ne quis laqueus inijciatur conscientijs, aut onus imponatur intolerabile. Haec Paulum cum suis passim inculcauisse Lucas tradit, ut & Iudaeos reprimeret, qui gentes ad legis observationem adigebant importunius, & gentium licentiam frenaret, qui Christiana libertate non sine graui offendiculo abutebatur. Pacem enim in ecclesijs florere voluit, quae illas cum primis propagari nouerat. Simul vero, vbi nullum erat scandali periculum, libertatem Christianam constanter asseruit, ne huic praeiudicaret, quod infirmis duntaxat dandum esse apostoli censuerunt. Docet id prior ad Corinthios epistola, in qua idolothytorum esum liberum facit quoad conscientiam, si nemo adsit quem ille offendat. 1. Cor. 10. Interim admonet nos Pauli exemplum, non sufficere, si bonae leges condantur, nisi illarum executionem constanter vrgeant, quibus ea cura commissa est. Executionem enim legum animam & neruum esse, communis experientia docet. Hanc si auferas, mortuae iacebunt leges, & instar Anachariis dictum aranearum telae erunt, quas cuiusuis audacia facile perrumpet. Imitentur ergo Paulum cum ecclesiarum ministri, tum qui in magistratu versantur, siquidem officio suo fungi voluerint, & non potius inani simulatione Deo simul & hominibus illudere.
units.tr: But let us return to the treatment of the present passage, in which, after Timothy's calling, it is shown what those who were with Paul taught in the churches. "As they went through the cities," it says, "they delivered to them the decrees to keep, which had been decided by the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem." The Papists twist these words to some traditions or other, which they pretend were handed down to the churches from the apostles and their successors, as it were by hand, and never committed to writing. Once they have set up this refuge for themselves, they say that whatever they see cannot be confirmed by any authority of Scripture is an apostolic tradition. But Luke says nothing of the kind; he speaks of those decrees whose mention was made in the previous chapter. These were: that a man is justified and obtains salvation by the grace of God alone, through faith in Jesus Christ, and not by the works of the law; that one must abstain from those things which pollute either our profession of faith or our holiness, such as communion with idolatry and fornication; that one must strive for charity, and yield somewhat in external matters to the weaker, or even to those still alien to the faith, whom one may hope to gain; and that meanwhile care must be taken that no snare is cast upon consciences, nor any intolerable burden imposed. Luke records that Paul everywhere impressed these things upon his companions, both to restrain the Jews, who pressed the Gentiles more insistently to observe the law, and to check the licence of the Gentiles, who abused Christian liberty not without grave offence. For he wished peace to flourish in the churches, knowing that it above all things would spread them. At the same time, wherever there was no danger of scandal, he constantly asserted Christian liberty, lest it be prejudiced by what the apostles judged should be given only to the weak. The earlier epistle to the Corinthians teaches this, in which he makes the eating of meat offered to idols free as far as conscience goes, if no one is present whom he might offend (1 Cor. 10). Meanwhile, the example of Paul admonishes us that it is not enough for good laws to be enacted, unless those to whom that care has been committed constantly press their execution. For common experience teaches that the execution of laws is their soul and sinew. If you take this away, laws will lie dead, and like the saying of Anacharsis about spiders' webs, they will be easily torn through by anyone's boldness. Let therefore the ministers of the churches, and those who hold the magistracy, imitate Paul, if they wish to discharge their office, and not rather mock God and men alike with empty pretence.

units.la: Postremo sanctissimi studij & laboris insignem fructum Lucas subijcit, dum ecclesias in fide confirmatas fuisse, & indies numero creuisse ac magis abundauisse scribit. Quia vero fidei meminit, banc maxime, non inanes ceremonias aut frigidas traditiones, Paulum inculcauisse constat. Sunt autem bi perpetui effectus verbi Dei, quod imbris instar, nunquam sine fructu redit ad eum, qui misit illud. Haec quoq; arma sunt, quibus regnum Christi in mundo hoc felicissime propagatur, diligentia nimirum verbi praedicatio, & ardens illius conseruandi studium. Haec vbicunque cessauerint, mox quoq; fides intercidit & omnis intermoritur verae religionis amor. Exempla huius passim sunt obuia, quibus illi conuincuntur, qui sufficere putant, si nullius tyrannide cogantur, vt impijs sacris communicent, interim vero ijs locis degunt, vbi Dei verbum exulat, nec vlla exercentur Christiana religionis officia. Studeamus ergo omnes diuini verbi propagationi, vt & ipsi in fide confirmemur,
units.tr: Finally, Luke adds the remarkable fruit of this most holy zeal and labour, when he writes that the churches were confirmed in the faith and daily increased in number and grew more abundant. Now, since he mentions faith, it is clear that Paul pressed this above all, not empty ceremonies or cold traditions. These are the perpetual effects of the Word of God, which, like the rain, never returns empty to him who sent it. These too are the weapons by which the kingdom of Christ is most happily propagated in this world, namely the diligent preaching of the Word and an ardent zeal for preserving it. Wherever these have ceased, soon faith also perishes, and all love of true religion dies out. Examples of this are everywhere to hand, and they convict those who think it enough, if they are not compelled by any tyrant to take part in impious rites, while meanwhile they live in places where the Word of God is banished and no Christian duties of religion are practised. Let us all therefore strive for the propagation of the divine Word, so that we ourselves may be confirmed in the faith,

units.la: quotidie credentium numero crescat ecclesia, in qua solus regnet Iesus Christus, humani generis salvator & ecclesiae sponsus unicus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: and that the Church of believers may grow daily in number, the Church in which Jesus Christ alone reigns, the saviour of the human race and the sole bridegroom of the Church, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CVII.
units.tr: SERMON 107.

units.la: Quum autem peragrassent Phrygiam & Galaticam regionem, vetiti a spiritu sancto loqui sermonem in Asia, profecti in Mysiam, tentabant ire in Bithyniam, & non permisit eos spiritus. Quum autem pertransissent Mysiam, descenderunt Troadem. Et visio per noctem Paulo apparuit: Vir Macedo quidam erat stans & deprecans eum, & dicens: Profectus in Macedoniam succurre nobis. Ut autem visionem vidit, statim quaesivimus proficisci in Macedoniam, certo persuasi, quod vocasset nos dominus ad evangelizandum eis. Cum ergo soluissemus a Troade, recto cursu venimus in Samothracen, & postero die Neapolim, & inde Philippos, quae prima est partis Macedoniae civitas, colonia.
units.tr: When they had passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach the word in Asia, they went on into Mysia and tried to enter Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them. And passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas. And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a certain man of Macedonia stood and begged him, saying, "Come over into Macedonia and help us." When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go into Macedonia, assuredly concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the gospel to them. Therefore, setting sail from Troas, we came with a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, the chief city of that part of Macedonia, a colony.

units.la: Spiritus domini nostri Iesu Christi apostolorum peregrinationes, & inter has Pauli cumprimis, diligentissime describi voluit, eo quod hae ad nostram institutionem haud mediocriter faciunt. Elucet enim in his eximia Dei bonitas, qui tam brevi temporis curriculo totum orbem euangelij & salutis doctrina illustrare, & prophanas gentes, tunc cum modis omnibus corruptissimae essent, in filij sui cognitionem & consortium adducere dignatus est. Patet item ex historia hac, quibus armis & mediis Christi regnum in terris tum propagari tum conservari soleat: nimirum euangelij praedicatione, per quam etiam minuito mundo spirat Dei spiritus, sicuti Christus alibi testatur. Et quia ad hac hominum ministerio Deus vti dignatur, ab ijsdem sedulam industriam & vigilantem zelum requirit. Qua in re Paulus maxime nobis imitandus erit, de cuius flagranti studio multa Lucas commemorat: cuius hoc haud vulgare argumentum est, quod non contentus multas ecclesias Christo lucrifecisse, easdem denuo inuisit, & fidei verbi admonitionibus confirmat: docens nimirum, vigilandum nobis esse in salutis negotio, quando nemini non notae sunt satanae artes, quibus incautos a salutis via avertere satagit. Ita tamen Paulus ecclesias inuisit, ut simul novas quoque colligere & Christo adducere studeat, de quo in praesenti potissimum agitur.
units.tr: The Spirit of our Lord Jesus Christ wished the journeys of the apostles, and among them especially those of Paul, to be described with the greatest care, because these contribute no little to our instruction. For in them shines forth the outstanding goodness of God, who deigned, in so short a span of time, to illuminate the whole world with the teaching of the gospel and of salvation, and to bring the profane nations, when they were utterly corrupt in every way, into the knowledge and fellowship of his Son. This history also makes clear with what weapons and means the kingdom of Christ is usually both spread and preserved on earth: namely, by the preaching of the gospel, through which also, when the world is laid waste, the Spirit of God breathes, as Christ testifies elsewhere. And because God is pleased to use the ministry of men for this, he requires from them diligent effort and watchful zeal. In this matter Paul is especially to be imitated by us, of whose burning zeal Luke records many things. This is no ordinary proof of it: that, not content with having won many churches for Christ, he visits them again and strengthens them with admonitions of the word of faith, teaching us, of course, that we must be watchful in the business of salvation, since the wiles of Satan, by which he labours to turn the unwary from the way of salvation, are known to no one. Yet Paul visits the churches in such a way that at the same time he also eagerly gathers new ones and brings them to Christ, which is chiefly what is under discussion at present.

units.la: Principio Phrygiam & Galaticam regionem peragrauisse dicitur, & illic quidem ecclesias nonnullas fundatas esse, Pauli ad Galatas epistola abunde testatur, quae omnem euangelicae doctrinae summam breui & absoluto compendio comprehendit. In ea autem professione hoc cumprimis memorabile accidit, quod a spiritu sancto prohibiti sunt, ne in Asia euangelium praedicarent. Intelligitur autem sub Asiae nomine ea pars, quae ad occasum mari proxima, in mediterraneis Aeoliam & Lydiam supra Ephesum & Smyrnam, deniq; ipsam quoque Ioniam complectitur. Quae regiones vt omnium fertilissimae & opulentissimae, ita hoc nomine plus satis infelices fuerunt, quod illas tunc temporis salutis doctrinam audire Christus noluit. Eadem Bithyniae quoq; fors fuit, in quam idem Christi spiritus Paulum transfire non permisit. Quo argumento facile patet, apostolos non temere per orbem circumuagatos esse, sed Dei spiritu authore & auspice fecisse omnia. Hunc enim illis a Christo promissum simul & exhibitum fuisse scimus. Accesserunt item singulares revelationes, si quando opus fuit, cuius rei exempla in Petro & Philippo supra habuimus, quando horum ministerio Eunuchus, Aethiops & Cornelius Centurio conuerti debuerunt. Facit hoc ad apostolicae doctrinae commendationem, ne vt humanam aspernemur, quam tam euidenti spiritus sancti ductu inter homines vulgatam fuisse constat. At quaestionem mouent hoc loco aliqui grauem, cur alicubi Paulus docere permissus, alicubi vero prohibitus fuerit? Quam nonnulli commodissime solui putant, si ad Dei praescientiam omne hoc negotium referatur. Hunc enim praeuidere aiunt, qui verbo & salute digni, qui rursum indigni sunt. Sed isti homines, dum de Dei iustitia asserenda solliciti sunt, ne hunc alicuius peccati authorem faciant, eiusdem gratiam euacuant, dum salutem ex hominum dignitate metiuntur: quod facere non possunt, nisi simul meritum hominis & insolentem humanae iustitiae fiduciam stabiliant. Quam vero friuolum sit commentum hoc, vel ex eo patet, quod omnes homines ex sese salute indigni sunt. Nam Paulo teste, omnes peccauerunt & destituuntur gloria Dei, & non est iustus, ne vnus quidem. Nec quisquam ad percipiendum salutis verbum dignus fuerit, nisi quem Deus dignum & idoneum fecerit. Nam non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis vel ad cogitandum, sed omnis nostra dignitas & facultas percipiendi quod bonum est, à Deo contingit. 2. Cor. 3. Celebris deniq; & omnibus nota est Christi sententia, Nemo venit ad me, nisi quem pater traxerit. Iohan. 6. Cuius exemplum cap. 14. habuimus, vbi credidisse dicuntur, qui praedestinati fuerant ad vitam aeternam. Et sequenti Sermone Lydiae exemplum habebimus, quae ideo docenti Paulo credidit, quod dominus illius cor aperuisset. Restat ergo non aliam huius consilij rationem allegari posse, quam liberam & gratuitam Dei electionem, qui quos vult misericordia sua complectitur, quos vero vult indurat. Nec tamen quisquam Deum vel iniustitiae vel crudelitatis accusare debet: quando ille nemini quicquam debet, & iudicia sua sic regit, vt haud vulgaris ex illis doctrina ad nos redeat. In electis enim gratuitae bonitatis exemplum edit: in reprobis autem iustitiae suae severitatem exerit, vt hanc timere, illam vero amplecti & exosculari discamus. Est praeterea varius & necessarius omnino eiusdem doctrinae vsus. Nam consolationi in tentationibus mirifice seruit, quod salutem nostram non in nostris viribus, aut nostrae iustitiae merito, sed in Dei gratia ac Christi merito fundatam esse scimus. Quis enim illam euerteret? Quis à Dei dilectione separaret, quos ille semel complexus est? Rom. 8. Vel quis e Christi manibus eripere, cum illi omnis potestas data sit in caelo & in terra? Iohan. 10. Consolationis huius vim plane euenerunt, quicunq; ex nostra dignitate salutis rationem aestimare docent. Adhaec officij nos admonet doctrina haec, & Dei immensam bonitatem agnoscere docet, quando nos prae aliis à Deo quaerit & salutis verbo visitari sentimus. Vt enim non meritis nostris illud tribuit Deus, sed mera gratia nos saluare studet: ita si qui illius bonitate agnoscere dedignantur, & ingratos se illi praebent, horribilem in eos iustitiae suae severitatem exerit. Exemplo sunt Corozaim, Bethsaida, Capernaum, tota deniq; Iudaeorum gens, quam non alio nomine à Deo reiectam esse legimus, quam quod diem visitationis suae noluerunt agnoscere. Luc. 10. & 19. Eiusdem seueritatis exempla haec ipsae vrbes sunt, quas Pauli ministerio prae aliis Deus illustrari voluit. Eas enim hodie immani Turcarum tyrannide oppressas cernimus, eò quod erga Dei bonitatem se non satis gratas praebuerunt. Meditemur quaeso hoc nos, quibus iam annis aliquot libera euangelij praedicatione frui, adeoq; ocio & pace euangelica abundare licuit, multis interim miserè egentibus & famelicis vndiquaq; bolum aliquem euangelicae consolationis captantibus.
units.tr: First, it is said that he travelled through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and that several churches were indeed founded there; Paul's epistle to the Galatians bears ample witness to this, and it sums up the whole substance of evangelical doctrine in a brief and complete compendium. In that account, this above all is worthy of note: that they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach the gospel in Asia. By the name of Asia is understood that part which lies near the sea towards the west, and which includes, inland, Aeolia and Lydia above Ephesus and Smyrna, and finally Ionia itself. These regions, as the most fertile and wealthy of all, were for this very reason all the more unhappy, because at that time Christ did not wish them to hear the teaching of salvation. The same, perhaps, was true of Bithynia, into which the same Spirit of Christ did not permit Paul to pass. From this argument it is easily clear that the apostles did not wander about the world at random, but did all things with the Spirit of God as author and guide. For we know that this Spirit was both promised to them by Christ and bestowed on them. Special revelations also came in, whenever there was need; we have examples of this above in Peter and Philip, when through their ministry the eunuch, the Ethiopian, and Cornelius the centurion had to be converted. This serves to commend apostolic doctrine, so that we do not despise it as human, since it is plain that it was spread among men under such clear guidance of the Holy Spirit. But some raise here a grave question: why was Paul permitted to teach in one place, but forbidden in another? Some think this can be most conveniently resolved if the whole matter is referred to God's foreknowledge. They say he foresaw who would be worthy of the word and salvation, and who, on the other hand, would be unworthy. But these men, while anxious to vindicate God's justice, lest they make him the author of any sin, empty his grace, while they measure salvation by the worth of men; and they cannot do this unless they establish at the same time man's merit and an unseemly confidence in human righteousness. How frivolous this invention is, is clear enough from the fact that all men are by themselves unworthy of salvation. For, as Paul witnesses, all have sinned and lack the glory of God, and there is none righteous, no, not one. Nor is anyone worthy to receive the word of salvation unless God has made him worthy and fit. For we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think anything, but all our worth and our ability to perceive what is good comes from God. 2 Cor. 3. Finally, the saying of Christ is famous and known to all: No one comes to me unless the Father draws him. John 6. We had an example of this in chapter 14, where those are said to have believed who had been predestined to eternal life. And in the following sermon we shall have the example of Lydia, who believed Paul teaching because the Lord had opened her heart. It remains, therefore, that no other reason for this counsel can be alleged than the free and gratuitous election of God, who embraces with his mercy whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills. Yet no one ought to accuse God of injustice or cruelty, since he owes nothing to anyone, and governs his judgments in such a way that no ordinary teaching comes back to us from them. For in the elect he shows an example of gratuitous goodness; in the reprobate he exercises the severity of his justice, so that we may learn to fear the one and to embrace and kiss the other. Moreover, the use of this same teaching is varied and altogether necessary. For it serves wonderfully for consolation in temptations, because we know that our salvation is founded not on our own strength or the merit of our righteousness, but on the grace of God and the merit of Christ. For who could overturn it? Who could separate from God's love those whom he has once embraced? Rom. 8. Or who could snatch them from the hands of Christ, since all power has been given to him in heaven and on earth? John 10. Those who teach that the reckoning of our salvation is to be made from our own worth have plainly robbed this consolation of its force. Besides, this teaching admonishes us of our duty, and teaches us to acknowledge God's immense goodness, since we perceive that God seeks us out, and visits us with the word of salvation, before others. For as God ascribes this not to our merits but seeks to save us by sheer grace, so if any refuse to acknowledge his goodness and show themselves ungrateful to him, he exercises the dreadful severity of his justice against them. Examples are Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum, and finally the whole nation of the Jews, whom we read to have been rejected by God for no other reason than that they would not recognise the day of their visitation. Luke 10 and 19. The very cities which God wished to be enlightened above others through Paul's ministry are examples of this same severity. For today we see them oppressed by the monstrous tyranny of the Turks, because they showed themselves not thankful enough for God's goodness. Let us, I pray, meditate on this, we to whom it has been granted for some years now to enjoy the free preaching of the gospel and to abound in leisure and evangelical peace, while meanwhile many, wretchedly needy and famished, on every side catch at some morsel of evangelical consolation.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum eiusq; comites redeamus, qui licet alicubi praedicare prohibeantur, non tamen officium facere desinunt, sed Mysiam transeuntes tandem in Aeolidem & eius oppidum Troadem peruenient, vbiq; nimirum docendi occasionem auidè captantes. Illic vero oraculo admonitus Paulus sibi in Macedoniam transeundum esse intelligit. Apparet enim illi vir Macedo, quem angelum fuisse nemini dubium esse potest, & patriae opem ferri postulat. Et hic quidem non pauca cumprimis vtilia nobis obseruanda veniunt. Primum in his Pauli exemplu est, quo docemur, non turpiter cessandum esse ab officio, etiamsi in bona quoq; causa primus & alter conatus non pro voto succedeat. Illud enim non raro prophetis simul & apostolis euenisse legimus, qui tamen vocationem suam eo maiori constantia secuti sunt, quo plura ipsis resistere videbantur. Pergant horum exemplo singuli, nec deerit illorum conatibus Deus, qui suo loco & tempore occasionem simul agendi & successum felicem dare consueuit. Deinde praeclarum diuinae bonitatis exemplum locus iste proponit, qua fit, vt nescientibus quoq; nobis, adeoq; ne cogitantibus quidem, salutem nostram operetur dominus. Quem enim apud Macedones de Paulo & salutis via cogitauisse putas, quando aduenientem vix pauce aliquot mulieres audire & sequi dignatae fuerunt? Ita vero propheticum illud impletur: Inuentus fui his qui me non quaerebat, & conspicuus factus sum his qui de me non interrogabant. Isa. 65. Quod autem in Macedonibus accidisse Lucas scribit, hoc ipsum in omnibus aliis, quotquot salutem consecuti sunt, & hodie consequuntur, videre licet. Nam priusquam mundus hic fundaretur, nos in Christo electos esse, Paulus ait. Ephes. 1. Et primus parens Adam, cum in peccatum prolapsus Deum non modò non quaereret, sed etiam fugeret, ipse tamen à Deo quaesitus & vocatus, salutis promissionem gratuitam accepit. Gen. 3. Huc quoq; facit, quod in scripturis homines ouibus coferuntur, quae vbi semel à grege deuiarunt, nunquam redeunt, nisi pastoris cura reducantur. At pastor noster Christus est, qui amissam amissam ouem per valles & montes quærere, & inuentam humeris imponere & gestare solet. Vide Isa.53. Luc.15. Nec in ijs solis, quæ animarum saluti seruiunt, hæc Dei cura cernitur, verumetiam in illis sese exerit, quæ corpori seruiendo sunt necessaria. Vt enim illud benigne pascit Deus, dum ex terra victum largitur: ita angelos nobis custodes dedit, qui circa cultores ipsius castrametentur, & eosdem sedulo defendant. At quia de hoc iam ante dictum est, hæc modo sufficiant. Obseruemus tamen huius doctrinæ vsum, qui in eo potissimum versatur, vt Deo grati simus, & inuicta spe atq; fiducia divini auxilij per omnia aduersa ad tuendam nostram vocationem eluctemur. Præterea euangelij & ministerij euangelici dignitatem exemplum hoc nobis commendat. Primo enim præclarum hoc est, quod per angelum & diuino oraculo ad docendum Paulus vocatur. Ita Petrus cælesti visione, vt Cornelio & gentibus prædicaret, admonitus fuit: & Philippum spiritus duxit, vt Æthiopi salutis doctor fieret. Frustra ergo humanum ministerium, vt exile & ignobile quiddam contemnunt, & angelos doctores requirunt, quando angeli nos ad homines audiendos relegat. Quid? quod Paulus ne angelo quidem credendum esse docet, si quid diuersum ab apostolica doctrina prædicauerit? Galat.1. Deinde minísterij dignitate angeli verba quoq; commendant. Ait enim: Profectus in Macedoniam, succurre nobis. Atqui solius Dei est tam corporibus quam animabus succurrere. Quia vero euangelij verbum potentia Dei est ad salutem omni credenti, non temere eius ministri hominibus opem ferre, imo eosdem salvare dicuntur. Et hanc ob causam Abdias de Christi regno vaticinans, apostolos Saluatores vocauit. Arguitur ergo hic illorum temeritas & impietas, qui ex euangelio turbas & rerumpub. interitus exoriri clamant, cum certo constet, non posse non ad interitum ruere homines, nisi Christi prædicatione ad salutis viam revocentur, propheta dicente: Gens & regnum, quod non seruierit tibi, peribit. Isa.60.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul and his companions. Although they are forbidden to preach in some places, they do not stop doing their duty. Passing through Mysia, they at last reach Aeolis and its town of Troas, everywhere eagerly seizing any opportunity to teach. There Paul, warned by a vision, understands that he must cross over into Macedonia. For a man of Macedonia appears to him, who, there can be no doubt, was an angel, and he asks for help for his homeland. Here not a few things are especially useful for us to observe. First, this is the example of Paul, by which we are taught not to give up shamefully on our duty, even if in a good cause the first and second attempts do not succeed as we wished. For we read that this has often happened to prophets and apostles as well, and yet they pursued their calling with all the greater constancy, the more things seemed to stand against them. Let each person follow their example, and God will not fail their efforts, for he is accustomed to give, in his own place and time, both the opportunity to act and a happy outcome. Next, this passage sets before us a remarkable example of the divine goodness, by which the Lord works our salvation even when we do not know it, indeed when we are not even thinking of it. For what do you suppose anyone in Macedonia was thinking about Paul and the way of salvation, when scarcely a few women deigned to hear him and follow him as he arrived? Thus that prophetic word is fulfilled: "I was found by those who did not seek me, and I was made visible to those who did not ask about me." Isa. 65. And what Luke writes happened among the Macedonians, one can see happening in all others who have obtained salvation, and who obtain it today. For Paul says that before the world was founded we were chosen in Christ. Eph. 1. And our first parent Adam, when he had fallen into sin and not only did not seek God but even fled from him, was nevertheless sought and called by God, and received the free promise of salvation. Gen. 3. This also agrees with the way in which Scripture compares men to sheep, which, once they have strayed from the flock, never return unless they are brought back by the care of the shepherd. But our shepherd is Christ, who is accustomed to seek the lost sheep through valleys and mountains, and, when he has found it, to lay it on his shoulders and carry it. See Isa. 53, Luke 15. Nor is this care of God seen only in those things that serve the salvation of souls; it also shows itself in those things that are necessary for serving the body.
