Caveant ergo pestem hanc, quicunque iudicijs præsunt, sibiq; duas aures ideo datas esse meminerint, ut altera quidem actori, altera autem reo pateat. Cogitent deniq; deum iudiciorum præsidem esse, cui ipsi quoque aliquando rationem reddituri sint. Interim admonemur, quæ piorum in hoc mundo sors sit. Licet in hoc tuto viuere hominibus palam flagitiosis & sceleratissimis. Soli pij, omnibus fere exosi, persecutionem sustinent, & cum malefaciant nemini, benefaciant vero omnibus, pessimam in mundo gratiam ineunt. Beneficium summum erat, dæmonis imperio liberauisse puellam. At pro beneficio tanquam publici civitatis hostes virgis & carcere multantur. Exempla huius generis hodie passim extant. At quia hæc nobis eventura esse olim Christus prædixit, nostrum est non offendi, sed constanti fide & invicta patientia ad propositam nobis metam contendere, ut promissum nobis brauium assequamur in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains for us to consider the judgment of the Philippian magistrates in the present case. But why do I speak of judgment, when they raged against the apostles with monstrous fury and without any judgment at all? For straightway they tear the apostles' garments off them, as if they were the ministers of crimes. Then, though the men are innocent and no charge has been laid, they order them to be beaten with rods. And after they have been wretchedly punished with many blows, at last they cast them into prison, and at the same time order that they be guarded with special care, as if they were worthy of greater punishment than other criminals. The result was that when they were put into the inner prison their feet were fastened in the stocks. Yet what could be more unworthy or more unjust than this from men who hold the magistracy? He sins who denies the accused the opportunity to excuse himself. But these men further beat with rods strangers, and at last hand them over to custody, so that they may afterwards examine their case. The cause of this fury was that they had allowed themselves to be stirred to anger by slanders. Let those who preside over judgments beware of this plague, and let them remember that we have been given two ears, so that one may be open to the accuser and the other to the accused. Let them finally consider that God is the president of judgments, to whom they too will one day have to render an account. Meanwhile we are reminded what the lot of the godly is in this world. Men who are openly shameless and most wicked may live safely in it. The pious alone, hated almost by all, endure persecution, and although they harm no one but do good to all, they meet with the worst return in the world. The greatest benefit had been conferred in freeing the girl from the power of the demon; yet in return for this benefit they are punished with rods and prison as enemies of the public good of the city. Examples of this kind are found everywhere today. But since Christ foretold long ago that these things would befall us, it is our duty not to be offended, but with steadfast faith and unconquered patience to press on toward the goal set before us, that we may win the prize promised to us in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXI.
units.tr: Homily CXI.

units.la: Media autem nocte Paulus & Silas orantes laudabant deum. Exaudiebant autem eos qui vincti erant. Subitò verò terræmotus factus est magnus, ita ut concuterentur fundamenta carceris. Et statim aperta sunt omnia ostia, & omnium vincula soluta sunt. Experrectus autem custos carceris, cùm videret ianuas carceris apertas, evaginato gladio ipsum erat interfecturus, existimans aufugisse vinctos. Clamavit autem Paulus voce magna, dicens: Ne quid feceris tibi ipsi mali: vniuersi enim hic sumus. Postulato à lumine irrupit, ac tremefactus procidit Paulo & Silæ ad pedes, & productis illis foras, ait: Domini, quid me oportet facere ut salvus fiam? Illi verò dixerunt: Crede in Dominum Iesum, & salvus eris, tu & domus tua. Et locuti sunt ei sermonem domini, & omnibus qui erant in domo eius.
units.tr: But at midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing praises to God, and the prisoners were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. At once all the doors were opened, and everyone's chains were loosed. The jailer woke up, and when he saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped. But Paul called out with a loud voice, saying, "Do yourself no harm, for we are all here." Then the jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling at the feet of Paul and Silas. Bringing them out, he said, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" They said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household." And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house.

units.la: Quemadmodum scriptura sacra passim pios Dei cultores de persecutionibus, in hoc seculo frendis, admonet: ita vicissim ijsdem Dei opem abunde pollicetur, nec desunt exempla, quibus promissionum suarum veritatem Deus ab ipsa mundi origine declarauit: cuius generis sunt, quæ in libro habentur. Supra enim apostolos simul omnes, per angelum ex carcere eductos, in templo M docuisse audiuimus. Et Petrus vinculis liberatus, Herodis crudele consilium elusit, totiusq; populi, in necem suam intenti, expectationem fefellit. Cumprimis verò memorabile est, quod modò recitari audiuit Charitas vestra. Hic enim non modò ex carcere liberantur fideles Christi apostoli, Paulus & Silas, verumetiam & carceris custos, homo barbarus & crudelis, impietatis vinculis liberatus, & vera salutis cognitione illuminatus, ad Christum conuertitur. Quia autē historia hæc nostræ tum institutioni tum consolationi multiuariam seruire potest, singulas illius circumstantias diligentius excussisse non parum proderit. Videamus igitur quid in hac causa ab apostolis, quid rursum ab ipso Deo factum sit: quibus inspectis ipsam quoq; Carcerarij conuersionem consyderabimus.
units.tr: Just as Holy Scripture everywhere warns God's faithful worshippers of persecutions in this world, so in turn it abundantly promises them God's help. Nor are there lacking examples by which God, from the very beginning of the world, has shown the truth of his promises; of this kind are those recorded in this book. For we have heard above that the apostles, all together, were led out of prison by an angel and taught in the temple. Peter, freed from his chains, also frustrated Herod's cruel plan and disappointed the expectation of the whole people, who were bent on his death. Most memorable of all is what your Charity has just heard read. For here not only are the faithful apostles of Christ, Paul and Silas, freed from prison, but also the jailer, a cruel and barbarous man, is released from the chains of impiety, enlightened by the true knowledge of salvation, and converted to Christ. Since this story can serve our instruction and our comfort in many ways, it will be of no small profit to examine carefully its individual circumstances. Let us see, then, what was done in this matter by the apostles, and again by God himself; and having considered these, we will also consider the conversion of the jailer.

units.la: Apostolos quidem Paulum & Silam, indignissimè tractatos & virgis laniatos tandem in cippum coniectos fuisse audiuimus. Quare non immeritò aliquis muliebriter illos suum infortunium planxisse & assiduis querelis Dei iustitiam folicitauisse putauerit. Sed longè aliud de illis Lucas commemorat. Illos enim media noctē preces fudisse, Deumq; laudauisse scribit, nec id tacitis animi votis siue suspirijs, sed tam alta voce, vt à vinctis, qui in exteriori carceris parte asseruabantur facile exaudirentur. Est hoc constantis fidei simul & læta conscientiæ argumentum, quæ non apud vlos alios homines, quàm solos Christi fideles in aduersis inuenitur. Illis enim hoc quasi proprium Paulus tribuit, quòd in afflictionibus quoque glorientur & gaudeant. Rom.quinto. Causam gaudij huius capite quinto expressit Lucas, quando apostolos, cum virgis in Concilio cæsi essent, latos & cum gratiarum actione exiuisse scribit, eò quòd digni habiti essent, qui pro Christi nomine affligerentur. Respiciunt enim in promissionem Christi, qui cœlestis regni consortium illis pollicetur, qui cum ipso in tentationibus suis permanserint. Luc.22. Vnde cum Paulo colligunt, eos gloriæ Christi consortes fore & cum Christo æternum victuros esse, qui in hoc seculo crucem ferendo illius imagini conformes facti fuerint. 2. Timoth.2. Rom.8. Est autem obseruatione dignissimum, quòd apostolos tam solicitè & assiduè orauisse audimus, qui spiritu sanctò & vera fide illuminati, omnia diuinæ prouidentiæ consilio geri nouerant. Confutantur exemplo hoc nimium arguti & plus satis curiosi homines, qui precibus minimè opus esse contendunt, eò quòd Deus omnia nostra per se norit, & diuina prouidentia res omnes administrentur, cuius consilia nullis precibus reuocari aut interrumpi possint. Nec enim Deo tanquam ignoranti causam nostram exponimus, sed fida & anxia illius commemoratione fidem nostram testamur. Norunt præterea sancti, hoc quoque perpetuum diuinæ prouidentiæ decretum esse, vt exaudiantur à Deo, quicunq; in afflictionibus ad illum conuersi, illius opem inuocant. Dei enim præceptum est: In die tribulationis tuæ, inuoca me, & liberabo te, & c. Psal.50. Item, Conuertimini ad me, & ego conuertar ad vos, & c. Orant ergo in afflictionibus apostoli, & iuxta eorum exemplum non alibi, quàm apud solum Deum, pij omnes in aduersis opem & liberationem quæ rere debent. Admonemur præterea, non modò liberationem ex aduersis petendam esse, verumetiam nos Deo gratias agere, & illum laudibus vehere debere, si quando affligimur. Est enim hoc veræ pa terni animi argumentum, quando carnis nostræ petulantiam crucis disciplina cohercet. Nec alibi efficacior elucet diuinæ consolationis vis, quàm cum afflictionibus variis tentamur, iuxta illud prophetæ: Pro æstu multarum cogitationum intra me, recrearunt animam meam consolationes tuæ. Psal.94. Et Paulus ait: Sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat & consolatio nostra. 2. Corinth.1. Quò Petrus quoque respexisse videtur, quando dispersis per varias gentes fratribus scribens, à λογισμῷ & diuinæ gratiæ commendatione exordium facit. Horum nos meminisse decet, si quando carnis impatientia tentamur, ne hac superati aduersus Deum murmuramus, quo peccato ira Dei quàm maximè prouocatur, vt Israelitarum in deserto murmurantium exempla abunde docent. Vide 1. Corinth.10.
units.tr: We have heard that Paul and Silas were treated most shamefully, beaten with rods, and finally thrust into the stocks. Hence someone might not unreasonably suppose that they bewailed their misfortune like women and troubled God's justice with constant complaints. But Luke relates something quite different about them. He writes that they poured out prayers at midnight and praised God, and not with silent wishes of the mind or with sighs, but with a voice so loud that the prisoners, who were kept in the inner part of the prison, could easily hear them. This is a sign of steadfast faith and at the same time of a joyful conscience, which is found among no other men in adversity than among Christ's faithful alone. For Paul attributes this as, so to speak, a peculiar thing to them: that they glory and rejoice even in afflictions (Rom. 5). Luke expressed the cause of this joy in chapter five, when he writes that the apostles, after being beaten with rods in the Council, went out rejoicing and giving thanks, because they had been counted worthy to suffer for the name of Christ. For they look to the promise of Christ, who promises a share in the heavenly kingdom to those who have remained with him in their trials (Luke 22). Hence they conclude with Paul that they will be fellow heirs of Christ's glory and will live with Christ forever, if in this world they bear the cross and have been made conformable to his image (2 Tim. 2; Rom. 8). It is also most worthy of notice that we hear the apostles prayed so earnestly and constantly. They were enlightened by the Holy Spirit and true faith, and knew that all things are done by the counsel of divine providence. This example refutes those men who are overly clever and more than curious, who contend that prayer is not needed, because God knows all our affairs by himself, and all things are governed by divine providence, whose counsels cannot be recalled or interrupted by any prayers. For we do not set out our cause to God as if he were ignorant, but by a faithful and anxious remembrance of it we bear witness to our faith. Moreover, the saints know that it is also a settled decree of divine providence that all who turn to God in affliction and call upon his help are heard by him. For God's command is: "In the day of your trouble, call upon me, and I will deliver you, etc." (Ps. 50). Likewise: "Turn to me, and I will turn to you, etc." (Zech. 1). Therefore the apostles pray in their afflictions, and following their example, all the godly ought to seek help and deliverance in adversity from no one but God alone. We are further reminded that we should not only seek deliverance from adversity but also give thanks to God and praise him whenever we are afflicted. For this is a sign of a truly fatherly spirit, when the discipline of the cross restrains the wantonness of our flesh. Nowhere does the power of divine consolation shine more effectively than when we are tried by various afflictions, according to the prophet: "In the multitude of my thoughts within me, your comforts have refreshed my soul" (Ps. 94). And Paul says: "As the afflictions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds" (2 Cor. 1). Peter also seems to have had this in view, when, writing to the brethren scattered among the various nations, he begins with a sober mind [λογισμῷ] and the commendation of divine grace. It becomes us to remember these things, so that if at any time we are tried by impatience of the flesh, we are not overcome by it and do not murmur against God. By this sin the anger of God is most provoked, as the examples of the Israelites murmuring in the desert abundantly teach (see 1 Cor. 10).

units.la: Transeamus nunc ad secundum huius loci caput, quo quid Deus fecerit docetur. Subitò (inquit Lucas) terræmotus factus est magnus, ita vt concuterentur fundamenta carceris: & statim aperta sunt omnia ostia, & omnium vincula soluta sunt. Id verò non alterius cuiuspiam, sed solius Dei opus fuisse, nemini dubiū esse potest, quando non alius in scripturis proponitur, qui hæc facere possit.Exprimitur autem hoc loco, quanta sit fidelis orationis vis atque efficacia. Nam (vt sapiens monuit) nubes penetrat, & in Dei conspectum ascendit, qui illam minimè negligit. Ecclesiastici 35. Hinc fit quòd oratione impetrantur, quæ humanas vires longè superant, quodq; rerum natura illis ce- deræ. dere cogitur. Ita Mosen maris rubri aquas precibus scidisse legimus. Idem Amalekitis orando clam dem horribilem intulit. Eliam precibus caelum clausisse, ne pluuias daret, & idem rursus aperuisse, Iacobus apostolus testatur. Hic vero ad Pauli & Silae preces carceris fundamenta concutiuntur, vincula soluuntur & fores omnes referantur. Cui simile est, quod supra Petrum ecclesiae precibus e carcere liberatum fuisse audiuimus. Hinc ergo consolationem petamus in aduersis, ne mundi minus toti consternemur, quando preces, quas omnibus aliis armis validiores esse constat, nemo nobis eripere potest, eoque maior illorum vis est, quo grauius ipsi premimur. Rursum innocentium oppressione omnes abstinere discant, quorum preces & gemitus tanta apud deum authoritatis esse videmus.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the second point of this passage, in which what God did is taught. "Suddenly," says Luke, "there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and at once all the doors were opened, and everyone's chains were loosed." No one can doubt that this was the work of no other than God alone, since no other being is set forth in the Scriptures who could do such things. But in this place is shown how great is the power and efficacy of faithful prayer. For (as the wise man warned) it pierces the clouds and ascends to the sight of God, who does not neglect it (Ecclus. 35). Hence it happens that by prayer things are obtained which far exceed human strength, and nature itself is compelled to yield to them. Thus we read that Moses split the waters of the Red Sea by prayer; the same Moses by praying inflicted a dreadful defeat on the Amalekites. James the apostle testifies that Elijah by prayer shut up the heavens so that they gave no rain, and opened them again. Here, at the prayers of Paul and Silas, the foundations of the prison are shaken, the chains are loosed, and all the doors are thrown open. Similar to this is what we heard above, that Peter was freed from prison by the prayers of the Church. Let us therefore seek comfort in adversity from this, that we should not be utterly dismayed by the world, since no one can take from us prayer, which is known to be stronger than all other weapons; and its power is greater the more heavily we are oppressed. Again, let all learn to abstain from oppressing the innocent, since we see that their prayers and groans have such authority with God.

units.la: Porro principalem miraculi huius effectum videamus, nimirum custodis carceris conuersionem, in qua vniuersale exemplum, quod omnes homines imitentur, spiritus sanctus proponere voluit. Hab bet autem conuersio haec certos gradus, quos ordine inspexisse, non parum proderit. Primum terraemotu expergefactus, fores omnes apertas videt, & quia captiuos omnes aufugisse putat, mox euagi-nato gladio seipsum occidere inflituit, nimirum legum seueritatem pertimescens, quae carcerum custodibus, si illorum negligentia captiui elapsi essent, mortis supplicium decernebant. Cuius nimiae seueritatis exemplum supra Herodes in illos edidit, quos Petro custodes adhibuerat. Vult ergo publicae infamiae notam subterfugere custos hic, communi gentilium errore deceptus, qui summa fortitudinis laudem ex eo venabantur, si ignominiae declinandae causa sibi ipsis manum violentam inferrent. Adeo illorum mentes satan fascinauerat, vt in interitu salutem, & in infamia laude sibi quaerent. Reuera enim nihil vel exitialius vel turpius est, quam violenta morte a Deo impositum crucis onus subterfugere velle, planeque degeneres & ignauos animos ipse timor arguit, qui nihil ferre velint aut possint. Rursus hoc ipsum euidens desperati animi indicium est, quando vitam (quae nihil homini dulcius & exoptatius videtur) nemo sibi ipsi eripiet, nisi qui de Dei ope & gratia iam ante desperauerit, id quod Iudae proditoris & huius similium exempla satis probant. Recte ergo Pauli voce custos hic reuocatur, ne quid sibi ipsi mali inferat. Et minime admittenda sunt a Christianis hominum satanae suggestiones, quae vt nobis ipsis morte consciscamus, suadent. Quocunque enim illae fuco & praetextu velentur, reuera tamen diabolicae & exitiales sunt, quando constat ea esse Dei voluntatem, vt peccator non moriatur, sed conuertatur & viuat. Vide Ezech. 18. Interim docemur exemplo hoc, quae fere illorum fors fit, qui impijs vel seruiunt vel consentiunt, quod nostrum hunc, de quo iam agitur, fecisse constat. Diligens enim & nimis indulgentius impij mandati, ab impijs magistratibus accepti, executor, apostolos in interiore carceris locum conclusos cippo constrinxit. At dum re omni quasi probe curata secure dormit, in casus incidit, qui vt anima simul & corpore periclitetur, causa est. Imo iam iam totus perierat, nisi illum singulari gratia suae beneficio per Paulum salutis praeconem ab interitu reuocauisset dominus. Memorabilem ergo & vere auream putemus sententiam illam, quae primo Psalmo extat: Beatus vir ille, qui non ambulauit in consilio impiorum, nec in via peccatorum stetit, nec in consessu irrisorum sedit, &c. Praeterea Christianae charitatis exemplum in Paulo habemus, qui eius saluti tam studiose consulit, a quo paulo ante indignissime & iniquissime tractatus fuerat. Imitemur nos factum hoc, & diligamus eos, qui nos odiunt, eorumque salutem quaeramus, qui nos perditos volunt. Ita enim genuini Dei patris filij censebimur, qui Solem suum super iustos & iniustos exoriri patitur, &c. Vide Matth. 5.
units.tr: Next let us look at the principal effect of this miracle, namely the conversion of the jailer, in which the Holy Spirit wished to set forth a universal example for all men to imitate. This conversion has certain stages, and it will be of no small profit to examine them in order. First, roused from sleep by the earthquake, he sees all the doors open, and because he thinks all the prisoners have fled, he at once resolves to kill himself with his drawn sword. He was evidently dreading the severity of the laws, which decreed the punishment of death for jailers if prisoners escaped through their negligence. Herod had earlier shown an example of this excessive severity against those guards whom he had assigned to Peter. So this jailer wishes to escape the mark of public disgrace, deceived by the common error of the Gentiles, who sought the highest praise of courage from this, if they laid violent hands on themselves to avoid shame. So completely had Satan bewitched their minds that they sought salvation in destruction and glory in infamy. Indeed nothing is more deadly or more shameful than to wish to escape by a violent death the cross laid on us by God; and fear itself shows that such minds are plainly degenerate and cowardly, since they will not or cannot bear anything. Again, this very thing is a clear sign of a despairing spirit, since no one will take away his own life (which seems to man sweeter and more desirable than anything) unless he has already despaired of God's help and grace; as the examples of Judas the traitor and others like him sufficiently prove. Rightly, then, this jailer is called back by Paul's voice, lest he do himself any harm. And Christians must by no means admit the suggestions of Satan, which urge men to take their own lives. For however these are veiled with pretence and disguise, they are in truth diabolical and deadly, since it is plain that it is God's will that the sinner should not die but be converted and live (see Ezek. 18). Meanwhile this example teaches us what usually becomes of those who either serve the impious or consent to them, as this executor of which we now speak plainly did. For being a diligent and overly zealous carrier-out of the impious command he had received from the impious magistrates, he bound the apostles in the inner part of the prison, fastening them in the stocks. But while he sleeps securely, having seen to everything as if properly arranged, he falls into peril that threatens both soul and body. Indeed he had already almost perished utterly, had the Lord not called him back from destruction by his singular grace, through Paul, the herald of salvation. Let us therefore consider that famous and truly golden saying in the first Psalm: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of the scornful, etc." Moreover, we have in Paul an example of Christian charity, who so earnestly seeks the salvation of the one by whom he had been most shamefully and unjustly treated only a little before. Let us imitate this deed, and love those who hate us, and seek the salvation of those who wish us ruin. For thus we shall be counted true children of God the Father, who allows his sun to rise on the just and the unjust, etc. (see Matt. 5).

units.la: Sed ad carceris custodem reuertamur, quem subito transformatu, imo plane alium factu fuisse, Lucas scribit. Postquam enim captiuos non fugisse, sed Dei manu retentos esse audit, cum praesenti miraculo apostolorum fortitudinem & ingenuitatem, hactenus in nullis hominibus obseruatam, con-ferens, propiori numinis afflatu tactus, toto animo consternatur. Sentit enim quam graui peccato sese polluerit, eos iniquius & inhumanius tractando, quos Deo tantopere commendatos esse videbat. Quare illico postulato lumine ad eos irrumpit, pedibus illorum aduoluitur, & tandem foras eductus (id quod contra magistratus mandatum facit) ait: Domini quid me oportet facere, vt saluus fiam? Quis vero hic non potente Dei manum agnoscat, quae omne hoc operata est? Huic certe tribui meritur, quod virgis caesos & publica infamia notatos veneratur, quod magistratus impium & iniu-stum mandatum transgreditur, quod de vera salutis ratione interrogat. Docet tamen exemplo suo, non leuiter ea praeterire aut officiant er negligi debere, quae in seruis suis miraculose operatur domi-nus. nus. Vix enim quicquam aliud perniciosius stupore illo, qui ut in manifestis Dei operibus cacutia- mus, facit. Hunc olim Pharaoni exitium attulisse constat, & hodie multis hoc vnum nocet, quod sui tuitu casibus res omnes ferri arbitrantur, nec Dei iudicia in illis inquirunt, quae praeter naturae cur- sum fieri vident. Praesenti igitur animo in veram salutis rationem inquirendam semper intentisi- mus, de qua custodem hunc magno cum fructu interrogauisse modò videbimus.
units.tr: But let us return to the jailer, whom Luke writes was suddenly transformed, or rather made into a completely different man. For after he hears that the prisoners had not fled but had been held back by the hand of God, comparing the apostles' courage and frankness, never before seen in any men, with the present miracle, he is moved by a nearer breath of divinity and is struck with terror in his whole soul. For he perceives how grievously he has polluted himself by treating so unjustly and inhumanely those whom he saw so greatly commended to God. Therefore, having asked for a light, he at once rushes in to them, throws himself down at their feet, and at last, led outside (which is contrary to the magistrate's order), says: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Who here would not recognise the hand of God, mighty in all this that was done? To Him certainly must be credited that he reveres men beaten with rods and marked with public disgrace, that he disobeys the magistrate's impious and unjust command, and that he asks about the true way of salvation. Yet by his example he teaches us that the things the Lord works miraculously in his servants should not be lightly passed over or neglected. For there is scarcely anything more destructive than that stupor by which we become blind to the manifest works of God. It is known that this once brought destruction upon Pharaoh, and today it harms many people in this one respect: they think that all things happen by chance and do not inquire into God's judgments in them, which they see take place beyond the course of nature. Let us therefore always be intent, with a ready mind, to inquire into the true way of salvation, about which we shall now see that the jailer asked with great profit.

units.la: Mox enim amicè respondent apostoli, & quaerenti paucis verbis veram & absolutam salutis ba- mana rationem monstrant, dicentes: Crede in dominum Iesum, & saluus eris tu & domus tua. Vnā fidem praedicant, & eam quidem, quae non alio salutis authore, quàm Iesu Christo nititur. In hoc- nim omnis satisfactio, iustitia, redemptio & sanctificatio continetur, quae omnia nobis non alia ratione, quàm per fidem obtinguntur: quae causa est, quod fide nos iustificari & saluari scriptura docet. De quo cùm non semel dictum sit, in praesenti paucula haec sufficiant. Illud tantùm obseruemus, nō aliud in scripturis fidei obiectum, quàm Christum tradi. Inde enim colligitur, fides carere & incertis opinioni- bus miserè vagari omnes eos, qui extra Christum salutem quaerere solent. Quia tamen breuiter erat doctrina haec, quàm quae ab homine gentili & barbaro statim intelligi posset, pleniorem institutionem apostoli subiiciunt. Nam domini verbum, id est euangelium, tam ipsi quàm domesticis ipsius omni- bus annuntiant, cuius ea summa est, quòd Christi merito per fidem iustificemur & saluemur. Iui- rim admonemur, fidem non temere conceptam opinionem aut imaginariam persuasionem, sed certam & plenam Christi Iesu cognitionem esse, quae ex Dei verbo aeterno dependeat. Ex eo igitur fidei disci- debet, nec quicquam admittendum est, quod non euangelio diserte comprehendatur. Quicquid au- tem illo traditur, id omne fide constanti complectamur, ut sic ipsi quoq; saluemur per dominum Ie- sum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Straightway the apostles answer him kindly, and in a few words show him the true and complete way of human salvation, saying: "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you shall be saved, you and your household." They preach one faith, and that one which rests on no author of salvation other than Jesus Christ. For in him is contained all satisfaction, righteousness, redemption and sanctification, all of which we obtain in no other way than through faith; this is why Scripture teaches that we are justified and saved by faith. Since this has been said more than once, these few words will suffice here. Let us observe only this: that in the Scriptures no object of faith is handed down other than Christ. From this it follows that all those who seek salvation outside Christ lack faith and wander wretchedly in uncertain opinions. Yet because this teaching was brief, such that a gentile and barbarian man could not immediately understand it, the apostles add a fuller instruction. For they proclaim the word of the Lord, that is the gospel, to him and to all his household, the sum of which is that we are justified and saved through faith by the merit of Christ. We are reminded here that faith is not a rashly conceived opinion or an imaginary persuasion, but a certain and full knowledge of Christ Jesus, which depends on the eternal Word of God. From this, therefore, faith must be learned, and nothing is to be admitted that is not expressly contained in the gospel. Whatever is handed down in it, let us embrace with constant faith, so that we too may be saved through the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXII.

units.la: Et assumptis illis in illa hora nocti s, abluit plagas: & baptizatus est ipse & omnes domestici illius continuò. Cumq; perduxisset eos in do- mum suam, apposuit eis mensam, & exultauit quòd cum vniuersa do- mo sua credidisset deo. Cùm verò dies ortus esset, miserunt magistratus apparitores, dicentes: Dimitte homines illos. Nuntiauit autē custos car- ceris sermones hos Paulo: Miserunt magistratus vt dimittamini. Nunc igitur exeuntes, ite in pace. Paulus autē dixit eis: Casos nos publicè in dicta causa, cùm simus Romani, coniecerunt in carcere: & nunc occul- tè nos eiiciunt? Non profectò: sed veniant ipsi, ac nos educant. Nuntia- uerunt autem magistratibus apparitores verba haec. Qui timuerunt, au- dito quòd Romani essent. Et venientes deprecati sunt eos, & eductos rogabant, vt egrederentur ex vrbe. Egressi autem è carcere introierunt ad Lydiam, & visis fratribus consolati sunt eos, & profecti sunt.
units.tr: And taking them in that same hour of the night, he washed their wounds; and he himself was baptized, and all his household straightway. And when he had brought them into his house, he set food before them, and rejoiced that he had believed God with all his household. But when day was come, the magistrates sent the sergeants, saying: Let those men go. And the keeper of the prison reported these words to Paul: The magistrates have sent to let you go. Now therefore depart, and go in peace. But Paul said to them: They have beaten us openly, uncondemned, though we are Romans, and cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privately? Not so; let them come themselves and bring us out. And the sergeants reported these words to the magistrates. And they feared when they heard that they were Romans. And they came and pleaded with them, and brought them out, and asked them to depart from the city. And they went out of the prison and entered the house of Lydia; and when they had seen the brethren and comforted them, they departed.

units.la: Sicuti Diuus Lucas Philippensis magistratus tyrannidem & iniustitiam, qua in fideles Christi seruos, Paulum & Silam saeuierunt, diligentissimè descripsit: ita non minori studio commemo- rat, vt custos carceris, qui non minima patrati scelaris pars fuerat, ad fidem Iesu Christi conuersu- sit. Finis autem totius narrationis est, vt partim Dei gratiam agnoscamus, qui hostes quoq; veritatis cognitione illuminare dignatur: partim vt discamus exemplo hoc, quae vera conuersionis ad Dei ratio sit, quidq; eos qui conuertuntur praestare aut facere conueniat. Et ad posterius quidem mem- brum prima praesentis loci pars pertinet, qua quid custos hic, postquàm Christum amplexus est, fecit, narratur. Eam igitur ante omnia exponemus, postea quoq; de apostolorum liberatione aut dimis- sione, quantum dominus dederit, dicturi.
units.tr: Just as the divine Luke described most carefully the tyranny and injustice of the Philippian magistrates, with which they raged against Paul and Silas, the servants of Christ, so with no less care he records how the jailer, who had been no small part of the crime, was converted to the faith of Jesus Christ. The purpose of the whole narrative is, on the one hand, that we should acknowledge the grace of God, who deigns to enlighten even enemies with the knowledge of the truth; and, on the other, that we should learn from this example what the true way of conversion to God is, and what those who are converted ought to render and do. The first part of the present passage, in which it is told what the jailer does after he has embraced Christ, belongs to this latter point. We shall therefore expound that part first, and afterwards speak of the release or dismissal of the apostles, as far as the Lord shall grant.

units.la: De carceris custode, iam ad Christum conuerso, quatuor fere dicuntur. Primò apostolos eaisse noctis hora è carcere educit, eorumque plagas abluit. Id verò contra magistratus mandatum facit, qui illos diligentissimè asseruare iusserat. Imò qui eam nouerat iudicum seueritatem esse, vt sibiipsi mortem inferre voluerit, cùm vinctos aufugisse putaret, nunc illos sponte educit & liberat, ita nimi- rum
units.tr: About the jailer, now converted to Christ, about four things are said. First, he leads the apostles out of the prison in the hour of the night and washes their wounds. This he does against the magistrates' command, who had ordered that they be kept very closely. Indeed, he who knew how severe the judges were, so that he had meant to take his own life when he thought the prisoners had escaped, now of his own accord leads them out and sets them free, plainly exposing himself to the danger of his life.

units.la: Fidei Fructus & opera. Obedientia. rum manifesto vitæ periculo sese obijciens. Docet locus hic, hunc primum & principalem fidei effectum esse, quòd Deo obedientes reddit homines, ac animosos facit in ijs exequendis, quæ diuinitus manda ta esse Deo, probari nouerunt, etiamsi longè aliud mundus ille censeat. Ea enim omnium credentium, quæ & Petri apostoli sententia est, Deo nimirum potius quàm hominibus obediendum esse. Arguun- tur itaq; hoc loco, qui hodie principum authoritatem, publica iura, leges, mundi amicitiam, & infini- ta alia huius generis allegant aduersus Dei præcepta, & ignauo metu torpidi nihil vnquam pro Christo & gloria illius audendum esse existimant. Imitemur potius hunc carceris custodem, quæ nec magistratus sui authoritas, nec publicæ leges, nec violati carceris ius, nec præsens periculum abstterrere potest quin carcere educat, quos illuc iniustè conclusos & plus satis indignè tractatos esse nouerat.
units.tr: Fruits of faith and works. Obedience. This place teaches that this is the first and principal effect of faith: that it makes men obedient to God and bold in carrying out those things which they know, from the divine command, to be commanded by God, even though the world thinks quite otherwise. For this is the judgment of all believers, and also of the apostle Peter: that God must be obeyed rather than men. Therefore those are rebuked here who today allege the authority of princes, public laws, statutes, the friendship of the world, and countless other things of this kind against the precepts of God, and, numbed by a cowardly fear, think that nothing should ever be dared for Christ and his glory. Let us rather imitate this jailer, whom neither the authority of his magistrate, nor public laws, nor the right of a violated prison, nor the present danger could terrify from leading out those whom he knew had been unjustly shut up there and treated more than shamefully.

units.la: Deinde baptizatur illico, simulq; domesticos suos omnes baptizari curat. Ex euangelio enim per apostolos prædicato didicerat, eam Christi institutionem esse, vt per baptismum colligerentur in vnum ecclesiæ corpus, qui in illum vellent credere. Quare à Christo institutum baptismi sacramentum minimè negligendum esse putat, nec ex præmissa fidei doctrina paralogizat: Si sola fides in do- minum Iesum ad salutem sufficit, quemadmodum paulò ante docuistis, cur nunc baptismum exigi- tis, qui non potest non superuacaneus esse & inutilis? Nec enim Christi instityтa contemnere possunt, quotquot illi vere crediderunt, quando illa cum fide non pugnare, sed potius eius appendices, & diuinarum promissionum, quas fide percipimus, externa sigilla esse norunt. Interim zelus fidei in cute hoc obseruandus venit, quo accensus, suos quoq; per baptismum Deo consecrari vult, cuius exemplum supra in Lydia quoq; habuimus. Quod vt Anabaptistis confutandis seruit, qui Christianorum liberos à baptismo priuata temeritate arcent: ita illorum ignauiam & minimè ferendam socor- diam arguit, qui suorum domesticorum adeò nullam curam gerunt, vt ne externis quidem symbolis illos Christo & ecclesiæ suæ consecrari curent, eo argumento abundè testantes, se nec de Dei gloria multum solicitos esse.
units.tr: Next, he is baptized at once, and at the same time he takes care that all his household are baptized. For he had learned from the gospel preached by the apostles that it was Christ's institution that those who wished to believe in him should be gathered into one body of the Church through baptism. Therefore he thinks that the sacrament of baptism, instituted by Christ, is by no means to be neglected, and he does not reason inconsistently from the doctrine of faith set out before: "If faith in the Lord Jesus alone suffices for salvation, as you taught a little while ago, why do you now require baptism, which cannot but be superfluous and useless?" For all who truly believed in him cannot despise Christ's institutions, since they know that these do not clash with faith, but are rather its appendages and the outward seals of the divine promises which we receive by faith. Meanwhile, the zeal of faith is to be noted in this man, by which, being inflamed, he wills that his own people also be consecrated to God through baptism; we had an example of this above in Lydia as well. This serves to refute the Anabaptists, who by their own rash judgment keep the children of Christians from baptism; and it also rebukes the shameful and entirely intolerable indifference of those who take so little care of their own household that they do not even see to it that they are consecrated to Christ and his Church by the outward symbols, thereby amply attesting that they are not much concerned for the glory of God either.

units.la: Tertiò mensam illis domi suæ apponit, nimirum quòd illos in carcere nimis tenuiter, aut fortasse omnino non cœnatos esse sciret. Est hoc charitatis & beneficentiæ Christianæ opus, qua qui Christo crediderunt, carere non possunt. Fidem enim à Dei dilectione separari impossibile est. At qui Deum vere diligit, proximum negligere non potest, quem ad Dei imaginem conditum & Deo ita curæ esse nouit, vt illum filij sui sanguine redemptum voluerit. Quæ causa est, quòd Paulus fidem per charitatem operari ait. Gal.5. Nam licet multa sint fidei opera, ea tamen omnia ferè ad vnam charitatem referri possunt, eò quòd per hanc lex tota impletur. Matth.22. Rom.13. Et Iohannes apostolus cum, qui proximum negligit, nec Dei amantem esse, nec fidem habere docet. Rectè ergo nostrer hic charitatis operibus fidem suam probat, quibus & nos studere vnicè conuenit, siquidem non inanes fidei profesfores dici & haberi volumus.
units.tr: Third, he sets a table for them in his house, doubtless because he knew that they had been fed very meagrely in prison, or perhaps not fed at all. This is a work of Christian love and beneficence, without which those who have believed in Christ cannot be. For faith cannot be separated from the love of God. But whoever truly loves God cannot neglect his neighbour, whom he knows to have been created in God's image and so dear to God that he willed him to be redeemed by the blood of his Son. This is why Paul says that faith works through love (Gal. 5). For although there are many works of faith, nearly all of them can be referred to love alone, because through it the whole law is fulfilled (Matt. 22; Rom. 13). And the apostle John teaches that he who neglects his neighbour is neither a lover of God nor has faith. Rightly, then, this man proves his faith by works of love, to which we too ought above all to devote ourselves, since we wish to be called and regarded not as empty professors of faith.

units.la: Quartò cum tota domo sua exultat, eò quòd credidisset Deo, seq; iam ad Christi ecclesiam pertinere sciret, in qua sola salutis thesauri repositi sunt. Atqui (vt modò monuimus) graue illi periculum imminebat. Nisi enim subito mutati fuissent Iudicum animi (quos tamen ille mutatos esse nouerat) capite pœnas luissent, quòd contra magistratus sententiam vinctos liberassent. Sed vt fides Deo obedientes reddit, ita omnes labores & omnia pericula vincit, nec gaudij cœlestis sensum, quem Christi spiritus suggerit, vllis tentationibus superari aut excuti patitur. Ideò Paulus ad hos ipsos Philippenses fideles scribens, illos perpetuò & indesinenter gaudere iubet. Porrò, si quæ de Caeris custodie hactenus dicta sunt, in vnum conferas, fidem minimè ociosam esse, nec à bonorum operum studio separari posse patebit. Quid enim bonorum operum hic desyderaueris? Emendat fideliter ante illatas apostolis iniurias, Deo cum præsenti vitæ periculo debitam obedientiam præstat, vno facto declarans quàm promptus ad omnia alia in posterum esse velit. Sacramentis rite vtitur. Quia enim baptismum confessim recipit, haud verisimile est illum à Cœna abstinuisse, quando inter fideles agebatur. Adhæc de suorum quoq; salute solicitus, illos Christo & ecclesiæ suæ consecrari cu- rat. Praterea charitatem & beneficentiam liberaliter exercet, totusq; inter media pericula spiri- tuali gaudio exultat. Atqui de salutis ratione interroganti vnam fidem in Iesum Christum apostolis præscripserant. Fides verò hæc fructus tam eximios tam citò protulit, quibus tamen salutis glo- ria minimè tribui debet, eò quòd nihil horum ille facere potuisset, nisi fide Christo insitus & illius spiritu animatus fuisset. Confutantur hic primùm, qui fidei doctrinam bonis operibus inimicā esse clamant, cùm non aliunde vberior bonorum operum seges enascatur. Deinde illi quoq;, qui falso Euangelij titulo inflati, sub fidei prætextu effrænem carnis licentiam & peccandi impunitatem quærunt. Vide de his Rom.6. Iacob.2. &c.
units.tr: Fourth, he rejoices with his whole house, because he had believed God and knew that he now belonged to the Church of Christ, in which alone the treasures of salvation are laid up. Yet (as we have just noted) a grave danger hung over him. For unless the judges' minds had suddenly changed (which he knew had indeed changed), he would have paid with his head for freeing the prisoners against the magistrates' sentence. But just as faith makes men obedient to God, so it conquers all labours and all dangers, and does not allow the sense of heavenly joy, which the Spirit of Christ suggests, to be overcome or shaken by any temptations. Therefore Paul, writing to these very Philippian believers, bids them rejoice constantly and without ceasing. Moreover, if you gather together what has been said so far about the jailer, it will be plain that faith is by no means idle and cannot be separated from zeal for good works. For what good works could you miss here? He makes amends faithfully for the injuries previously done to the apostles; he renders due obedience to God at the present risk of his life, declaring by one deed how ready he is to do all other things in future. He partakes of the sacraments rightly: since he receives baptism at once, it is hardly likely that he abstained from the Supper, when it was being celebrated among the faithful. Besides, being anxious for the salvation of his own, he takes care that they are consecrated to Christ and his Church. Furthermore, he exercises love and beneficence generously, and amid the dangers all around he exults with spiritual joy. Yet when he asked about the way of salvation, the apostles had prescribed for him only faith in Jesus Christ. And this faith has so quickly produced such outstanding fruits; yet the glory of salvation must by no means be ascribed to them, because he could have done none of these things unless he had been grafted into Christ by faith and animated by his Spirit. Here, first, are refuted those who cry out that the doctrine of faith is hostile to good works, when a richer harvest of good works springs from no other source. Then also are refuted those who, puffed up with the false title of the gospel, seek under the pretext of faith an unbridled license of the flesh and impunity for sin. On these matters see Rom. 6; James 2, etc.

units.la: Caeterum absoluta custodis carceris historia ad Philippenses magistratus Lucas transiens, vt horum quoq; authoritate & sententia apostoli liberati sint, docet. Perfecta enim sunt Dei opera, nec vana & imaginaria salutis siue auxilij spe hominum mentes ludunt. Interim mirificè illos dominus exagitat, vt illum etiam inuitis impijs ad suam voluntatem exequendā vti videas. Sed singulariordine excutiamus, vt plus inde ad nos consolationis & institutionis redeat. Primùm statim exorto die à magistratibus missi apparitores adsunt, qui apostolos dimittere iubent: & occultam quidem dimissionem, quasi simul vrbe extruderentur, intelligi debere, ex Pauli verbis postea patebit. Qualiscunq; verò illa dimissio fuerit, constat Iudices hoc tum apostolorum innocentiam tum suam, quam illos saevierant, iniustitiam agnouisse. Siue verò interposita noctis mora huius cognitionis causa fuerit, siue terraemotus illorum mentes concusserit, vt in coepta tyrannide pergere timuerint, incertum est. Certè tam subita & improuisa animi mutatione suam tum iniustitiam tum leuitatem abundè testantur. Mira tamen astutia comissum flagitium, cuius iam illos pudet, tegere instituunt. Ideo enim clam dimitti volunt apostolos, vt in ipsos omnem culpam deriuent, quasi illi male sibi cōscij effractiū carceribus aufugerint. Ita verò impij, dum illos suae nequitiae pudet quidem, non autē poenitentiam ferìo meditantur, illam dolo malo tegere & fraudulenter iustitiae speciem captare solent: quae causa est, vt maiori suo dedecore pristinis peccatis noua accumulent. Docet igitur locus hic primo, qualis re sit impiorum poenitentia. Fucata nimirum, & quam hominū reuerentia sola illis extorquet, cùm interim minimè ex animo poeniteant, nec de emendatione quicquam cogitent. Ita Saulem poenituisse legimus, quando Samuelem, ne abs se recedat, sedulò precatur, ne coram senioribus & populo suae authoritas in vniuersum corruat. 1. Sam. 15. Inanem verò & inutilem esse poenitentiam hanc velexto constat, quòd interea Dei verbum cane & angue peius oderunt, eò quòd huius luce illorum nequitia arguitur. Discant igitur singuli peccata sua sic agnoscere, vt simul horum dolore tangantur, nec illa cum aliorum dedecore celata cupiant, imò ipsi potius illa publicent ad aliorum emendationem & diuinae gratiae illustrationem, cuius rei exempla in Dauide & Paulo scriptura proponit. Deinde admonet locus hic, quàm facile sibi ipsis atrocissima flagitia impij magistratus condonare soleant. Quid enim isti iniquius & sua conditione indignius facere poterant, quàm quòd innocentes indicta causa inter furentis vulgi clamores virgis caedunt, & cruentos adhuc, nondum ablutis plagis in terrimum carcerem detrudunt? At nunc sufficere putant, si non maiori ignominia affectos è viuis tollant, sed clam vrbe eijciant. Interim de satisfactione verbum nullum. Est hoc nimis frequens hodie, maximè si illorum causae agantur, qui mundo ob syncerioris religionis & veritatis studium exosi sunt: imò magnae modestiae & aequitatis laudem se mereri putant, qui honoribus simul & fortunis spoliatos Christi cultores patrijs sedibus eijciunt. Sed cogitent magistratus, se diuinitus in illum honoris & potentiae gradum collocatos esse. Rom. 13. Meminerint item iudicium Dei esse. 2. Par. 13. Deut. 1. Adhaec crebrò recordentur, se quoque olim Christi iudicio esse sistendos, vbi omnium iudiciorum suorum rationem reddituri sint. Et proinde iuxta prophetae admonitionem, pretiosum ducant sanguinem subditorum suorum in oculis suis. Psal. 72. Praeterea elucet hic inuicta dei potentia, qua impiorum manibus suos eripere & extorquere potest, licet illi impij esse pergant. Non enim istos sui facinoris pænitet, nec de emendatione cogitant, vt modò diximus, imò haud dubie male perditos voluissent Christi apostolos. Attamen occulta Dei manu coguntur illos liberos dimittere. Sic Aegyptij, licet animos non verè mutauerint, Israelem etiam auro & argento oneratum dimittere coacti fuerunt. Exod. 12. Eodem referri debet, quòd Saul Dauidem proprio ore iustum pronuntiat, & quem diu ad mortem quaesierat, inuentum non sine publico innocentiae testimonio dimittit. 1. Sam. 24. & 26. Ita apostolos quoq; in Hierosolymitano Senatu absolutos fuisse legimus, cùm tamen nemo Senatorum pristinam impietatem exuisset. Consoletur hoc nos aduersus incurabilem mundi huius malitiam. Pergant vt lubet impij, attamen Dei vasa sunt, qui illis etiam pro suo arbitrio vtitur, perq; illos etiam inuitos suam gloriam interdum illustrare consueuit.
units.tr: Now that Luke has finished the story of the jailer, he moves on to the magistrates of Philippi, to show how the apostles were released by their authority and decision. The works of God are complete, and the hope of salvation or help does not deceive human minds with empty and imagined expectations. Meanwhile the Lord wonderfully drives these men on, so that you see him using even unwilling wicked men to carry out his will. But let us examine the passage in its proper order, so that more comfort and instruction may come back to us from it. First, at dawn, the magistrates send officers who order the apostles to be dismissed. That this dismissal was secret, as though they were to be thrown out of the city at once, will become clear later from Paul's words. Whatever kind of dismissal it was, it is certain that the judges then acknowledged both the apostles' innocence and their own injustice, in beating them. Whether the delay of the night was the reason for this change of mind, or whether the earthquake shook their minds so that they feared to go on with the tyranny they had begun, is uncertain. Certainly such a sudden and unexpected change of mind bears full witness to both their injustice and their fickleness. Yet with a cunning craft they set about hiding the crime they are now ashamed of. For they want the apostles let go in secret, so that they can shift all the blame onto them, as though the apostles, conscious of wrongdoing, had broken out of the prison. Thus wicked men, when they are ashamed of their wickedness but do not repent, are accustomed to cover it by deceit and to seize the appearance of righteousness by fraud. This is the cause why they add new sins to their old ones, to their own greater disgrace. This passage therefore first teaches what the repentance of the wicked is really like. It is plainly feigned, and it is wrung from them only by respect for men, while in fact they do not repent from the heart and think nothing of amendment. So we read that Saul repented, when he earnestly begged Samuel not to leave him, lest his authority collapse entirely before the elders and the people (1 Sam. 15). That this kind of repentance is empty and useless is clear from the fact that they hate the word of God worse than dog or snake, because their wickedness is exposed by its light. Let each one learn to recognise his sins in such a way that he is at the same time moved by sorrow for them, and does not wish them hidden for fear of shame, but rather would make them public, for the amendment of others and the illustration of divine grace. Scripture sets examples of this in David and Paul. Next, this passage warns us how easily wicked magistrates are accustomed to pardon their own most atrocious crimes. For what could they have done that was more unjust and more unworthy of their office than to beat innocent men with rods, without any charge, amid the shouts of a raging crowd, and to thrust them, still bleeding and not yet washed of their wounds, into the most terrible prison? Yet now they think it enough if they do not put them to death with greater disgrace, but drive them secretly out of the city. Meanwhile there is not a word about making satisfaction. This is far too common today, especially when the causes are pleaded of those who are hated by the world for their zeal for purer religion and the truth. Indeed, they think they deserve praise for great moderation and fairness, when they cast out of their homes the worshippers of Christ, stripped of their offices and property. But let magistrates consider that they have been placed by God in that degree of honour and power (Rom. 13). Let them also remember that judgement is God's (2 Chron. 19; Deut. 1). Moreover, let them often call to mind that they too will one day have to stand before the judgement of Christ, where they will have to give an account of all their judgements. And therefore, in keeping with the prophet's admonition, let them count the blood of their subjects precious in their eyes (Ps. 72). Besides, the unconquerable power of God shines forth here, by which he can snatch his own out of the hands of the wicked and wring them from them, even though those wicked men persist in their wickedness. For these men do not regret their deed, nor do they think of amendment, as we have just said; indeed, no doubt they would have preferred the apostles of Christ to be utterly destroyed. Yet by a hidden hand of God they are compelled to dismiss them free. So the Egyptians, although they did not truly change their minds, were compelled to send Israel away, loaded with gold and silver (Exod. 12). To the same point belongs the fact that Saul, with his own mouth, pronounces David righteous, and, having long sought him for death, when he is found, dismisses him with a public testimony to his innocence (1 Sam. 24 and 26). So we read also that the apostles were acquitted in the Jerusalem council, although none of the councillors had put off their former impiety. This consoles us against the incurable malice of this world. Let the wicked go on as they please; nevertheless they are God's instruments, and he uses them according to his own judgement, and by them, even against their will, he is accustomed at times to display his glory.

units.la: Renuntiat autem Paulo Senatusconsultum custos carceris, lætus nimirum, quòd fraudem sub-esse non videret. Ea enim fere est filiorum lucis simplicitas, ut impiorum consilia non semper videre possint. Et hodie multi huius similes, rem optime gestam putant, si qui viui dimittantur, quorum vi ta periclitabatur, nec vident interea iniquissimis præiudicijs totam euangelij causam grauari, & illi estium præcludi. Rectius ergo Paulus oblatam ab impio magistratu gratiam fortissimè repsuit, di-cens: Cæsos nos publicè indicta causa, cum simus Romani, coniecerunt in carcerem, & nunc occulte nos eijciunt? Non profecto, sed veniant ipsi, ac nos educant. Quibus verbis de illata sibi & collegæ suo Silæ iniuria conqueritur, & ut grauior fit accusatio, Romanas leges allegat, quibus caucbatur, ne quis in Romani ciuis corpus indicta causa sæuiret. Adhæc non occulte ex vrbe eijci, sed honorificè dimitti vult. Nemo tamen propterea Paulum vel fastus & insolentiæ, vel impatientiæ accusef, cum sui facti causas grauissimas habeat. Primò enim curat, ne euangelij doctrina aliqua suspicione sinistra grauetur, quæ vel teneros adhuc in fide offendat, vel apertis hostibus calumniandi occasionè præbeat. Quis enim non putasset male sibi conscios fuisse apostolos, si de occulta ipsorum fuga rumor fuisset sparsus? Deinde ferocibus illis timorem incutere voluit, adeoq; illos sibi obnoxios reddere, ne posthac tam inconsultò & audacter in Christi membra sæuirent. VNDE colligimus, non eam esse Christianæ patientiæ rationem, ut quiduis impunè impijs permittatur. Quin potius arguenda si-mul & coercenda est illorum impietas, si qua ratione commoda id fieri possit. Asserenda item tum Dei gloria, tum nostra innocentia, eò quòd frequenter cum hac aliorum quoq; salus periclitetur. Ita Christus potestatis tenebrarum ministros & executores vocat eos, qui ad illum capiendum cum gladijs & fustibus exiuerant. Et sacerdotis seruum, à quo indignè percussus erat, aperte reprehendit. Sic ergo patienter ferendum est quicquid nobis aduersi accidit, ne interea Christi & veritatis causam pro damus, aut saltem turpiter deseramus. Rursum admonemur, licere pijs, ut politicis quoq; legibus & priuilegijs, quatenus illa veritati & religioni non repugnant, ad sui defensionem utantur. Nec enim Romanæ ciuitatis ius, si illud per se impium fuisset, allegasset Paulus, qui ad quiduis pro Christo paratissimus erat. Sic illum postea ad Cæsarem quoque prouocauisse, & legitimo armorum præsidio aduersus impiæ coniurationis socios vsum fuisse audiemus. Magna ergo illorum iniquitas est, qui omnem humani iuris vsum Christianis prohibitum, omnemq; defensionem legitimam ijsdem illicitam esse contendunt, & illos inconsultò in quæuis aperta pericula ruere volunt. Quid vero magistratus Philippensium, Pauli verbis auditis, egerunt? Timuerunt, non qui-dem quòd illos de iniuria sibi facta conqueri audirent, sed quòd Romanos esse intelligerent, quibus hæc facta erat. Nouerant enim, quæ esset Romanorum in vindicandis suis legibus & defendendo suo iure seueritas, adeò ut (teste Cicerone aduersus Verrem) sæpe illa vox, Ciuis Romanus sum, multis in vltimis terris inter Barbaros opem & salutem tulerit. Et sanè non alius potest religionis veræ fidium, firmior Rerumpub. neruus & validius vinculum est, quàm constans & firma publicarum legum & iuris custodia. Non ergo de nihilo illi timent, quin mox adsunt, culpam deprecantur, & honorificè deductos ex carcere rogant, ut maioris tumultus vitandi causa vrbe decedere dignentur. Vbirursum impiorum mores elucent, qui nullo numinis metu astricti, solos homines se potentiores & legum seueritatem metuunt. Quòd si apud homines peccandi impunitas detur, quiduis audent. Cuius rei non alia causa est, quàm quòd Deum esse non credunt, qui res mortalium curet. Longè aliter pij, qui in Deum intenti, scelerum atrocitatem ita horrent, ut si quando per humanam infirmitatem labi contigerit, ob admissum peccatum magis quàm ob pœnam imminentem, timeant. Interim docemur exemplo hoc, quorsum exeant temeraria & inconsulta impiorum magistratuum iudicia. Eò nimirum, ut ignominiam simul & periculum suis authoribus concilient. Hinc est, quòd nostri illi timore impediti, honorificè deducunt, quos pridie publica infamia notauerant, & sic suam temeritatem & iniustitiam accusant. Extant multa eius generis exempla, quorum vsus est, ut magistratus & quicunque in publicis officijs versantur, affectus frenare, & iuxta ethnici criptoris dictum, diu deliberare disceant de eo, quod statuendum est semel. Adhæc tantam innotentiæ vim esse, exemplum hoc docet, ut ferocissimos quoque hostes suos egregiè confundat. Huic ergo studeamus, nec dubitemus nos quoque per hanc de hostibus nostris, vtut modo ferociant, triumphaturos esse.
units.tr: Now the jailer reports the decision of the magistrates to Paul, rejoicing no doubt because he did not see any trickery underneath it. For such is nearly always the simplicity of the sons of light, that they cannot always see the plans of the wicked. And today many like him think that a matter has been very well managed if those whose lives were in danger are let go alive, and they do not see that the cause of the gospel is meanwhile burdened by the most unjust prejudices, and its entrance is shut. Paul therefore rightly and most boldly rejected the favour offered by the wicked magistrate, saying: "They have publicly beaten us without a hearing, although we are Romans, and thrown us into prison; and now do they secretly cast us out? Certainly not! Let them come themselves and lead us out." By these words he complains of the wrong done to himself and his fellow Silas, and to make the accusation more serious, he cites the Roman laws, by which it was provided that no one should be violently assaulted, without a hearing, in the body of a Roman citizen. Besides, he wants not to be cast out of the city secretly, but to be dismissed with honour. Yet no one should accuse Paul on that account of arrogance or haughtiness or impatience, since he had most serious reasons for his action. For first, he takes care that the doctrine of the gospel is not burdened with any sinister suspicion, which might either offend those still tender in the faith, or give open enemies an occasion to slander it. For who would not have thought that the apostles had a guilty conscience, if a rumour of their secret flight had been spread abroad? Next, he wished to strike fear into those fierce men, and so make them answerable to himself, lest in future they should rage so rashly and boldly against the members of Christ. From this we gather that it is not the rule of Christian patience that anything is permitted to the wicked with impunity. Rather, their impiety must at the same time be challenged and restrained, if this can be done by any suitable means. Equally, both the glory of God and our innocence must be asserted, because often the salvation of others is also endangered along with ours. So Christ calls those who had gone out with swords and clubs to seize him the ministers and executors of the power of darkness, and openly rebuked the servant of the high priest by whom he had been unworthily struck. So whatever adversity befalls us must be borne patiently, but not in such a way that we betray or at least shamefully desert the cause of Christ and of the truth. Again we are reminded that it is lawful for the godly to use the civil laws and privileges for their own defence, so far as these do not conflict with the truth and religion. For Paul, who was most ready for anything for Christ, would not have appealed to the right of the Roman citizenship if that right had been wicked in itself. So we shall hear that he afterwards also appealed to Caesar, and used the lawful protection of the authorities against the accomplices of the impious conspiracy. Great, then, is the wickedness of those who contend that the use of all human law is forbidden to Christians, and that every lawful defence is unlawful for them, and who want them to rush rashly into any open danger. But what did the magistrates of Philippi do when they had heard Paul's words? They were afraid, not indeed because they heard that he was complaining of the wrong done to him, but because they understood that they were Romans, to whom this had been done. For they knew how strictly the Romans were accustomed to avenge their laws and defend their rights; so much so that (as Cicero testifies against Verres) the phrase "I am a Roman citizen" often brought help and safety among many barbarians in the furthest lands. And indeed no other firmer sinew of the commonwealth, and no stronger bond of the faithful of true religion, can exist than the steady and firm guardianship of public laws and rights. So it was not for nothing that they feared; they came at once, begged pardon for their fault, and asked them to leave the prison with honour, so that they might deign to depart from the city to avoid a greater uproar. Here again the character of the wicked shines forth, who, bound by no fear of the divine power, fear only men who are more powerful than they and the severity of the laws. But if impunity for sin is granted among men, they dare anything. The only cause of this is that they do not believe that God exists, who cares for the affairs of mortals. Far otherwise are the godly, who, intent upon God, so shudder at the atrocity of crimes that, if at any time they happen to slip through human weakness, they are afraid of it more because of the sin committed than because of the punishment hanging over them. Meanwhile we are taught by this example where the rash and ill-considered judgements of wicked magistrates lead. Namely, they bring disgrace and danger at once upon their own authors. Hence it is that those men of ours, held back by fear, honourably escort those whom they had marked with public infamy the day before, and so accuse their own rashness and injustice. There are many examples of this kind, and their use is that magistrates and all who hold public office should learn to restrain their passions and, in the words of a pagan writer, to deliberate for a long time about what must be decided once for all. Besides, this example teaches that innocence has such great power that it utterly confounds even the fiercest enemies. Let us therefore strive for this, and let us not doubt that we too, through it, will triumph over our enemies, however fiercely they may now rage.

units.la: Restat vltima huius loci pars de apostolorum discessu, qui omnino suscipiendus fuit, cum viderent sibi posthac in ea vrbe nullum locum reliquum esse. Non tamen ita discedunt, vt simul ecclesiam in vniuersum negligant, sed prius apud Lydiam collectos fratres inuisunt, eosq; ad fidei constantiam exhortantur, & efficaci consolatione confirmant. Deinde ad illos epistolam scribit Paulus, quadocemur quàm felices posthac huius ecclesiæ progressus fuerint, cuius initium plane funestum videri potuit. Vnde patet, nullis impiorum conatibus euangelij cursum impediri posse. Vinciuntur aliquando huius ministri, sed dei sermo vinciri non potest. 2. Tim. 2. Pelluntur rursus in exilium qui illud prædicant, sed Christi spiritus in exilium relegari non potest, sed spirat vbicunq; ipsi libuerit. Imò tacentibus hominibus lapides Christum prædicant. Luc. 19. Hæc nos in fide constantes reddant, vt tandem mundo & mundi principe superiores, in cælis viuamus & regnemus cum domino nostro Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains to consider the last part of this passage, concerning the departure of the apostles, which had to be made, since they saw that from then on there was no place left for them in that city. Yet they did not depart in such a way as to neglect the Church altogether; first they visited the brethren gathered at Lydia's house, exhorted them to constancy in the faith, and strengthened them with effective consolation. Then Paul writes a letter to them, from which we learn how happy the later progress of this congregation was, though its beginning could seem altogether deadly. Hence it is clear that the course of the gospel cannot be hindered by any attempts of the wicked. The ministers of the Word are sometimes bound, but the word of God cannot be bound (2 Tim. 2). Those who preach it are again driven into exile, but the Spirit of Christ cannot be banished; it breathes wherever it pleases. Indeed, when men are silent, the stones preach Christ (Luke 19). May these things make us constant in the faith, so that at last, raised above the world and the prince of the world, we may live and reign in heaven with our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XVII. HOMILIA CXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. SERMON CXIII.

units.la: OVum autem iter fecissent per Amphipolim & Apolloniam, venerunt Thessalonicam, vbi erat Synagoga Iudeorum. Secundum consuetudinem autem suam Paulus introiuit ad eos, & per sabbata tria differebat eis è scripturis, adaperiens & allegans, quòd Christum oportuerit pati & resurgere à mortuis, & quòd hic fit Christus Iesus, quem ego (inquit) annuncio vobis. Et quidam ex eis crediderunt, & adiuncti sunt Paulo & Silæ, & religiosorum Græcorum multitudo magna, mulieresq; primariæ non paucæ.
units.tr: When they had travelled through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul, as was his custom, went in to them and for three sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures, opening them up and showing that Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and that this Jesus Christ, whom I (he said) proclaim to you, is the Christ. Some of them believed and joined Paul and Silas, and so did a great multitude of devout Greeks and not a few leading women.

units.la: DOminus noster Iesus Christus in euangelio secundum Lucam ait: Nemo qui manu aratro admota respexerit à tergo, aptus est regno dei. Quæ verba diserte monet, ab omnibus quidem Christianis, maximè verò à verbi ministris insuperabilem animi constantiam requirit, qua aduersus omnes tum labores tum pericula intrepidi pergant, nec vllis tentationibus sese auocari patiantur, vt commissum fidei suæ munus deserant. Eius constantiæ præclarum cumprimis exemplum in Paulo apostolo proponitur: qui ab eo die, quo Christo & euangelio seruire cœpit, continuis laboribus & periculis vexatus, perrexit tamen, & inuicto animo nouam quotidie propagandi regni Christi occasionem quæsiuit. Et quod alibi ante hac fecit, hoc ipsum apud Macedones incredibili studio illum fecisse, præsens historia docet. Nam Philippis, quo per visionem vocatus erat, indignissimè tractatus, non tamen Deo obmurmurat, nec vocationem suam in dubium vocat, nec officium turpi & ignobili metu deserit: sed rectà per Amphipolim & Apolloniam iter faciens, Thessalonicam totius Macedoniæ metropolim contendit, quam vbi euangelij prædicatione illustrauit, Berrhœam aggreditur, & inde Athenas delatus, illic quoq; inter doctissimos gentium philosophos, quasi in publico totius orbis theatro Christum prædicat. Sed omissis aliis, in præsenti quæ Thessalonicæ gesta sunt, ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel according to Luke: "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God." These words plainly warn that all Christians, and above all the ministers of the Word, need an unconquerable steadfastness of mind, so that they press on fearlessly through every labour and danger, and do not allow themselves to be called away by any temptations from abandoning the task entrusted to their faith. A most outstanding example of this steadfastness is set before us in the apostle Paul. From the day he began to serve Christ and the gospel, he was harassed by constant labours and dangers, yet he pressed on, and with an unconquered spirit he sought fresh opportunities each day to spread the kingdom of Christ. This present history shows that what he had done elsewhere before, he did again among the Macedonians with incredible zeal. For at Philippi, to which he had been called by a vision, he was treated most shamefully, yet he did not grumble against God, nor call his calling into doubt, nor desert his office out of base and ignoble fear. Instead, he travelled straight through Amphipolis and Apollonia and made for Thessalonica, the metropolis of all Macedonia. Once he had made it famous by preaching the gospel, he set out for Berea, and from there, having been conveyed to Athens, he preached Christ there too, among the most learned philosophers of the nations, as if on the public stage of the whole world. But setting other things aside, we shall examine in order what was done at Thessalonica in the present passage.

units.la: Et primò quidem Amphipolim & Apolloniam transiuisse dicitur, nec aliqua in illis vrbibus prædicati à Paulo Euangelij mentio fit, vt verisimile sit, nullam illi à spiritu sancto prædicandi occasionem oblatam fuisse. Thessalonicam verò ingressus, Iudæorum Synagogam, quæ illic frequens erat & celebris, intrat & in ea per tria sabbata euangelium Iesu Christi docet. Atqui mirum videri poterat, Paulum Iudæis denuò salutis doctrinam offerre, quorum incurabilē maliciam toties expertus erat, quosq; à Deo reiectos esse multis non obscurus argumentis intelligebat. Sed monit illum partim ardens prouehendi regni Christi studium, partim constans suæ gentis amor, pro qua anathema fieri aliquando optauit. Nec tamen cæcum illum affectum fuisse putabimus, quando in gentis Iudaicæ repudio reliquias saluas fore dominus iam olim prædixerat. Isa. 10. Et fortassis Eliæ exemplo moneri potuit, qui cum in vniuersum omnes à deo Israelitico defecisse putaret, audit adhuc septem millia sulia superesse eorum, qui ne genua quidem Baali flexerint. Admonemur hoc Pauli exemplo, propter multorum ingratitudinem non temere ab officio cessandum, quin potius (ut alibi apostolus docet) malos cum mansuetudine tolerandos, eos qui obsistunt erudiendos esse, si quando det illis deus paenitentiam ad agnoscendam veritatem, ut e diaboli laqueo resipiscant. 2. Tim. 2. Quia enim dei serui sumus, huius ingenium nos imitari conuenit, nec mundi ingratitudine offendi, quando nobis a domino premium repositum esse scimus, cuius spes nunquam fallet. Turpis ergo et inexcusabilis illorum morositas est, qui ut primum se nihil proficere vident, ab officio suo discedunt, nec dei et Christi exemplo ducuntur, qui erga incurabilem Iudaeorum malitiam tam fideli mansuetudine et longanimitate ab ipso statim gentis illius initio vsus est. Simul autem obseruatione dignum est, quod et sabbatorum religionem Paulus obseruat, et Synagogas ingreditur, ut illic praedicet: nimirum Christi exemplum imitatus, qui et ipse nihil in occulto, sed palam et publice docuit. Interim hanc vetustissimam in populo Dei consuetudinem fuisse videmus, quod ad sacros coetus pii conuenerunt: propter quos et dies festos et locos sacros olim diuinitus institutos fuisse legimus. Necessaria autem est horum obseruatio, tum propter doctrinam, quae non alio commodiori modo tradi potest: tum propter externam religionem, quam publice exerceri oporter, ne fidei verae professio intercidat. Quae causa est, quod suo quoq; exemplo coetus sacros Christus nobilitauit, et promissione amplissima commendauit, quod in illis rite instituendis Paulus in priori ad Corinth. epistola tam diligenter versatur. Quare non potest non detecтanda esse illorum proterua, qui publicos Christianorum coetus scurriliter subsannant, nec vllo vel saniori doctrinae vel syncerae religionis studio sese teneri testantur.
units.tr: And first, he is said to have passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, and no mention is made of Paul preaching the gospel in those cities. It is therefore likely that the Holy Spirit gave him no opportunity to preach there. But when he entered Thessalonica, he went into the synagogue of the Jews, which was well attended and famous there, and for three sabbaths he taught the gospel of Jesus Christ in it. Yet it might seem strange that Paul should again offer the teaching of salvation to the Jews, whose incurable malice he had so often experienced, and whom he understood, by many clear arguments, to have been rejected by God. But he was moved partly by an ardent zeal to advance the kingdom of Christ, and partly by a steadfast love for his own nation, for whose sake he once wished himself accursed. Nor should we think that this affection was blind, since the Lord had long before foretold that a remnant would be saved out of the rejection of the Jewish nation (Isa. 10). And perhaps he could have been reminded by the example of Elijah, who, when he thought that all had utterly fallen away from the God of Israel, heard that seven thousand remained of those who had not bowed their knees to Baal. We are taught by Paul's example that, because of the ingratitude of many, we must not rashly give up our duty. Rather, as the apostle teaches elsewhere, we must bear evil men with gentleness, and instruct those who resist, in case God at some time grants them repentance to acknowledge the truth, so that they may recover from the snare of the devil (2 Tim. 2). For since we are servants of God, it is fitting that we imitate his disposition, and not be offended by the world's ingratitude, since we know that a reward is laid up for us by the Lord, whose hope never fails. Shameful and inexcusable, therefore, is the peevishness of those who, as soon as they see they are achieving nothing, abandon their office, and are not guided by the example of God and Christ, who from the very beginning of that nation used such faithful gentleness and patience towards the incurable malice of the Jews. At the same time, it is worth noting that Paul observed the religion of the sabbaths and entered the synagogues in order to preach there, plainly imitating the example of Christ, who also taught not in secret but openly and publicly. Meanwhile, we see that this very ancient custom existed among the people of God, that the pious came together in holy assemblies, and we read that feast days and holy places were once instituted by divine command for this purpose. The observance of these is necessary, both for the sake of teaching, which cannot be handed on in any more convenient way, and for the sake of outward religion, which must be practised publicly, lest the profession of the true faith perish. This is why Christ also ennobled holy assemblies by his own example and commended them by the most ample promise. And this is the reason Paul is so diligent in his first epistle to the Corinthians in ordering them properly. Therefore the shamelessness of those must be exposed, who mock the public assemblies of Christians with buffoonery, and who claim to have no concern for sound teaching or for pure religion.

units.la: Quid vero in Iudaeorum Synagoga Paulus fecit? Hoc ipsum quod iam multis in locis illum fecisse audiuimus. Nam ex scripturis disseruit, docens Christum oportuisse pati et a mortuis resurgere, et hunc ipsum Christum esse, quem ipse praedicabat. Sunt hic nobis singula diligenter excutienda, eo quod totius apostolicae doctrinae rationem plenissime comprehendunt. Primo enim indicant, unde doctrinam suam Paulus hauserit. Ex scripturis nimirum Mosis et prophetarum, quas alibi diuinitus inspiratas esse ait, et in quibus vitae aeternae mysteria contineri, Christus testatur. 2. Tim. 3. Ioban. 5. Ex ijsdem ergo hodie etiam ecclesiarum doctrina peti debet, nec illorum impudentia ferenda est, qui nostri seculi concertationes per scripturam dirimi nolunt, sed traditiones et Canones, quos illi apostolicos dicunt, adhaec Patres et Concilia nobis ogganniunt: quasi vero illi perfectius quiddam et certius, quam apostoli, tradiderint. Deinde quomodo scripturas tractauerit Paulus, docetur.
