Aperuit, id est, interpretatione diligenti verum illarum sensum enucleauit, et quae in illis continentur, praesenti negotio applicauit, id quod non alia commodiori ratione quam per collationem fieri potest. Arguitur ergo Pauli exemplo illorum error, qui nudam scripturae sacrae lectionem in ecclesia sufficere clamant, nec illam interpretationibus illustrari volunt. Peccasset igitur horum sententia Paulus apostolus, imo ipse Christus, quem hanc ipsam docendi rationem in schola Nazarethana tenuisse legimus, Luc. 4. At peccare non potest, quisquis Christi exemplum sequitur. Et multo rectius Paulus ecclesiae doctorem eiusmodi requirit, qui dei verbum recte secare et singulorum cum institutione tum consolatione accommodare possit. 2. Tim. 2. Tertio doctrina Pauli argumentum exponitur, cuius duo praecipue capita sunt, quae totidem erroribus Iudaeorum oppositae esse videtur. Primo enim illi cruce Christi offendebantur, eo quod prophetarum oracula secundum literam intelligentes, temporale Christi regnum imaginabantur, et Messiam sine cruce expectabant: qui error hodie etiam vulgo cernitur inter illos, qui euangelium sine cruce praedicari vellent, et cum Christi merito saluari cupiant, cum eodem tamen affligi nolunt. Alter Iudaeorum error erat, quod Iesum Mariae filium Messiam siue Christum esse negarent. Vtriq; ergo Paulus mederi studet, dum scripturarum testimonijs euincit, eam iam olim ab aeterno salutis humanae rationem apud deum constitutam esse, ut filij sui incarnati morte et resurrectione saluaremur. Rursum Iesu Mariae filio ea applicans, quae de Messia olim prophetae praedixerunt, luculenter docuit, hunc pro Messia agnosci, nec quenquam alium expectari debere. Vt vero haec Paulus copiose et vndique in vnum collectis scripturis demonstrauit: ita a nobis etiam prolixe exponi poterant. Sed quia ex praecedentibus tum Pauli tum apostolorum sermonibus facile patet, quibus locis illi praecipue vsi fuerint, et scripturas legentibus passim obuia sunt, quae Christi cognitionem tradunt, breuitati consulto studemus. Interim duo hic nobis obferuanda veniunt. Primum, quid in ecclesia praedicari debeat? Nimirū unus Iesus Christus, quem solum se nouisse, alibi Paulus fatetur. Quia enim unus hic ad omnia nobis sufficit, eo quod nobis a deo patre sponsus, pastor, rex & sacerdos, caput, denique iustitia, sapientia, satisfactio, sanctificatio & redemptio, datus sit, idemque homines sibi soli adduci velit, nefas est aliquid ab hoc diuersum tradere. Alterum est, quomodo Christus praedicari debeat? Qualem scilicet scripturae proponunt, qui pro nobis in ara crucis mortuus peccata nostra expiarit, & resurrectione gloriosa mortem deuicerit: qui non regum huius seculi instar in mundo regnet, sed in caelos subuectus spiritus suo nobis adsit, & per nostras afflictiones & carnis infirmitatem de omni aduersaria potestate triumphet. Qui talem sibi Christum animo concepere, nullis mundi conatibus offendi possunt, sed securi & laeti omnia rident, quae ille aduersus ecclesiam improbe molitur. Hinc ergo de nostri seculi doctrinis iudicare discentes illos audiendos esse putato, qui in salutis negotio plura quam Christum tradunt, quando hunc solum Paulus nouit, licet in tertium caelum abreptus fuerit &c.
units.tr: But what did Paul do in the synagogue of the Jews? Exactly what we have heard he had already done in many places: he reasoned from the Scriptures, teaching that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that this very Christ is the one he was preaching. Here each point must be examined carefully, since they fully set out the whole plan of apostolic teaching. First, they show where Paul drew his teaching from: namely, from the Scriptures of Moses and the prophets, which he elsewhere says were divinely inspired, and in which Christ testifies that the mysteries of eternal life are contained (2 Tim. 3; John 5). Therefore the teaching of the churches must still be drawn from these same Scriptures today. We must not tolerate the impudence of those who in our age do not want controversies settled by Scripture, but instead bark at us with traditions and canons, which they call apostolic, and besides these with the Fathers and councils, as if they had handed down something more perfect and certain than the apostles. Next, the passage teaches how Paul handled the Scriptures. He "opened" them, that is, by careful interpretation he brought out their true sense, and applied what is contained in them to the matter at hand. This cannot be done in any more suitable way than by comparing passages. Thus Paul's example refutes the error of those who cry out that the bare reading of Holy Scripture is enough in the church, and who will not have it explained by interpretation. Then Paul the apostle would have erred in holding this opinion, and indeed Christ himself would have, since we read that he used this very method of teaching in the school at Nazareth (Luke 4). But whoever follows Christ's example cannot err. And Paul rightly requires of a teacher of the church that he be able to handle the word of God correctly, and to apply it to each person both for instruction and for comfort (2 Tim. 2). Thirdly, the content of Paul's teaching is set out, and it has two chief heads, which seem to be opposed to two errors of the Jews. For first, they were offended by the cross of Christ, because they understood the oracles of the prophets according to the letter, imagined a temporal kingdom of Christ, and expected a Messiah without a cross. This error is still seen today among those who want the gospel preached without the cross, and who wish to be saved by the merit of Christ, yet do not want to suffer with him. The second error of the Jews was that they denied that Jesus, the son of Mary, was the Messiah or Christ. Paul therefore labours to heal both, by proving from the testimonies of Scripture that God had from eternity appointed this way of human salvation: that we should be saved by the death and resurrection of his incarnate Son. Again, by applying to the son of Mary what the prophets long ago foretold about the Messiah, he clearly taught that this man is to be acknowledged as the Messiah, and that no one else ought to be looked for. Yet just as Paul demonstrated these things at length, by gathering the Scriptures together from every side, so they could also be expounded at length by us. But since it is easily clear from the preceding sermons of Paul and the apostles which passages they especially used, and since the passages which hand down the knowledge of Christ are everywhere in the hands of those who read the Scriptures, we deliberately aim at brevity. Meanwhile, two things here demand our attention. The first is: what ought to be preached in the church? Surely the one Jesus Christ, whom Paul confesses elsewhere that he knew alone. For since this one man is enough for us in all things, because he has been given to us by God the Father as bridegroom, shepherd, king and priest, head, and finally righteousness, wisdom, satisfaction, sanctification and redemption, and since he wishes men to be brought to himself alone, it is wrong to teach anything different from him. The second is: how ought Christ to be preached? Clearly as the Scriptures set him forth: he who died for us on the altar of the cross and atoned for our sins, and who by his glorious resurrection overcame death. He does not reign in the world like the kings of this age, but having been raised into heaven, he is present with us by his Spirit, and through our afflictions and the weakness of the flesh he triumphs over every hostile power. Those who have conceived such a Christ in their minds cannot be offended by any efforts of the world, but secure and joyful, they laugh at all the wicked schemes that are devised against the church. Therefore, in judging the teachings of our own age, learn to regard as worth hearing only those who, in the matter of salvation, teach more than Christ, since Paul knew only him, even though he was caught up into the third heaven, etc.

units.la: Porro non inanem fuisse Pauli praedicationem, euentus docet. Quidam enim ex Iudaeis crediderunt, pauciores tamen, quia iam incipiebat gentis illius excaecatio. Interim tamen veritatem suam deus custodit, dum ex innumerabili turba reliquias saluas facit. Vere autem illos credidisse existimandum est, quod palam sese Paulo & Silae coniungunt, tum discendi studio, tum quod ita fidem suam publice profitentur. Maior tamen multitudo Graecorum credit, quos religiosos vocat, eo quod iam aliquem syncerioris religionis gustum haberent, quem illos ex Iudaeorum conuersatione percepisse, verisimile est. Licet enim deplorata esset illius gentis incredulitas, illis tamen uti voluit deus, ut orbe dispersi, gentes ab idolomania ad vnius veri dei cultum reuocarent, & puriorus religionis principia de vno deo colendo & inuocando, passim traderent. Adnumerantur credentium numero etiam mulieres, & quidem primariae siue nobiles, ut videas deum in omni hominum ordine electorum suorum rationem habere. Docet vero locus hic, euangelium nunquam fructra praedicari, de quo iam saepius dictum est. Adumbrantur item vere credentium officia, quae sunt, ardens verae religionis & doctrinae studium, gratitudo erga salutis doctores & aperta ingenuaque verae fidei professio. Necenim ambidextros cultores vult dominus, qui quidem simulent & dissimulent. Faxit Deus, ut ipsi quoque vera fidei luce illuminati & accensi, idem tum ore tum factis testemur, & per hanc caelestis regnum reditatem adeamus cum filio Dei vnigenito, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the outcome shows that Paul's preaching was not in vain. For some of the Jews believed, though fewer, because the blindness of that nation was already beginning. Yet God keeps his truth safe, while from the countless crowd he preserves a remnant. That they truly believed may be judged from the fact that they openly joined themselves to Paul and Silas, both in their eagerness to learn and because they so publicly professed their faith. A greater multitude, however, of the Greeks believed, whom he calls "devout," because they already had some taste of purer religion, which it is likely they had received from their association with the Jews. For although the unbelief of that nation was despaired of, God nevertheless wished to use them, so that, scattered throughout the world, they might call the nations back from idolatry to the worship of the one true God, and spread far and wide the principles of a purer religion concerning worshipping and calling upon the one God. Women also are counted among the believers, and indeed women of standing, or noble ones, so that you may see that God takes account of his chosen ones in every order of men. This place teaches, moreover, that the gospel is never preached in vain, which has been said often enough already. The duties of true believers are also outlined here: an ardent zeal for true religion and doctrine, gratitude towards the teachers of salvation, and an open and sincere profession of true faith. For the Lord does not want double-dealing worshippers, who pretend and dissemble. May God grant that we too, illuminated and kindled by the light of the true faith, may bear witness to the same both with our lips and with our deeds, and through this may come to the heavenly kingdom, our inheritance, with the only-begotten Son of God, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 114.

units.la: Zelo autem commoti Iudaei increduli, & assumptis quibusdam circumforaneis, viris malis, & coacta turba concitauerunt urbem: & vrgentes domum Iasonis, quaerebant eos producere ad populum. Illis autem non inuentis, trahebant Iasonem & quosdam fratres ad principes ciuitatis, clamantes: Hi qui terrarum orbem turbarunt, huc etiam venerunt, quos clanculum excepit Iasor. Et hi omnes contra Caesaris decreta faciunt, regem alium dicentes esse Iesum. Concitauerunt autem turbam & magistratus ciuitatis audientes haec. Et acceptis satisfactione ab Iasone & a ceteris, dimiserunt eos. Fratres vero confestim per noctem emiserunt Paulum simul & Silam in Berrhoeam. Qui cum aduenissent, abierunt in Synagogam Iudaeorum.
units.tr: Stirred by jealousy, the unbelieving Jews took some idle loafers from the marketplace, wicked men, gathered a mob, and threw the city into an uproar. They attacked the house of Jason and sought to bring Paul and Silas out to the people. When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the rulers of the city, shouting: "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too, and Jason has secretly taken them in. All of them act against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus." The crowd and the magistrates were thrown into agitation when they heard this. After they had taken security from Jason and the others, they released them. That same night the brothers at once sent Paul and Silas away to Berea. When they arrived, they went into the synagogue of the Jews.

units.la: Quemadmodum deus filium suum ab aeterno praedestinauit, vt humani generis saluatorem esset: ita perpetuam inter hunc & diabolum pugnam fore, in ipsa mundi huius origine praedixit, quando serpenti ait: Ponam inimicitias inter te & mulierem, inter semen tuum & semen illius. Ipsum conculcabit tibi caput, & tu insidiaberis calcaneo eius. Gene. 3. Cuius vaticinij exempla continua nobis hic Actuum Apostolicorum liber exhibet. Vbicunque enim terrarum Christi regnum apostoli per euangelij praedicationem erigere & stabilire conati sunt, ibi per organa sua sese illis satan opposuit. Factum id primo quidem Hierosolymis per scribas & sacerdotes, deinde vero Samariae per Simonem nem Magum, mox Damasci per Aretam regem Arabiae, in Cypro per Elymam Magum, Antiochiae Pisidiae per Iudaeos, qui mox pertinaci studio & odio irreconciliabili Paulum per maria & terras secuti esse videntur, ut passim euangelij cursum impedirent. Hos ipsos enim Lystris hostes habet. Iidem Derbae docenti obstrepunt. Et nunc in Macedoniam diuinitus vocato negotium faciunt. Nam his authoribus, ut praesens locus docet, Thessalonica eijcitur, in qua urbe euangelium feliciter radices agere coeperat. Est vero praecipuus omnium horum vsus, ne similibus hodie offendamur. Sed cogitemus hanc perpetuam ecclesiae in mundo hoc forte esse, quando is suo potius principi, quam Christo, seruire studet. Sed praesentem locum videamus, qui nobis aduersus improbos diaboli & mundi conatus institutioni simul & consolationi mirifice seruire potest. Primo enim quibus organis aduersus Paulum Thessalonicae diabolus pugnarit docet. Mox vero illorum studia, & tandem felicem Tragaediae totius exitum describit.
units.tr: Just as God predestined his Son from eternity to be the Saviour of mankind, so he foretold at the very origin of this world that there would be a perpetual war between this Son and the devil, when he said to the serpent: "I will put enmity between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed. He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." (Gen. 3.) This book of the Acts of the Apostles sets before us continual examples of this prophecy. Wherever the apostles tried to raise up and establish the kingdom of Christ on earth by preaching the gospel, there Satan opposed them through his instruments. This happened first at Jerusalem through the scribes and priests, then at Samaria through Simon the Magician, soon at Damascus through Aretas the king of Arabia, in Cyprus through Elymas the Magician, at Antioch in Pisidia through the Jews. These Jews, with a stubborn zeal and irreconcilable hatred, seem to have followed Paul over seas and lands so that they might everywhere hinder the course of the gospel. For at Lystra these same men were his enemies; at Derbe they heckled his teaching; and now, when he was divinely called into Macedonia, they make trouble for him. For at their instigation, as this passage shows, he was driven out of Thessalonica, a city in which the gospel had begun happily to take root. The principal use of all these examples is that we should not be offended by similar things today. Let us reflect that this is perhaps the perpetual lot of the Church in this world, when it strives to serve its own prince rather than Christ. But let us look at the present passage, which can serve wonderfully both for instruction and for comfort against the wicked attempts of the devil and the world. First it shows with what instruments the devil fought against Paul at Thessalonica; then it describes their efforts, and finally the happy outcome of the whole tragedy.

units.la: Inter diaboli organa, quibus hic vti voluit, duo hominum genera recensentur. Primum Iudaeorum est, qui zelo commoti fuisse dicuntur. Sed hypocritae fuerunt, qui contumacia & incredulitati suae legis diuinae & auitae religionis zelum praetexere solebant, cum reuera non aliud quam priuatum quaestum & gloriam quaererent, ut ex conspiratione ipsorum facile patet. Nam adiunxerunt sibi circumforaneos quosdam, pessimae notae & peruersi ingenij homines, quorum commercia ceu pestem nocentissimam fugere debebant, siquidem illis religio & veritas cordi erant. Ita enim dicunt otiosi & ignaui sponsi Penelopes, qui vbi sua improbe dilapidarunt, ceu publicae merces in foro venales prostant, & ad quoduis facinus parati sunt, modo emptorem inueniant. Mirifica ergo haec societas est, quam inter tam dissimilium studiorum professores nemo sperare posset, nisi tanta esset odij aduersus veritatem semel concepti vis: ut dissimillimos quoq;conspergere & sociare posset. Ita contra Christum sacerdotes, scribas, pharisaeos, sadducaeos, Iudam pseudoapostolum, milites, Herodem & Pilatum conspirauisse vides, qui omnes alioqui tum patria, tum religione & professione inter sese dissidebant. Admonet autem locus hic, qui acerrimi & praecipui veritatis hostes sint. Hypocritae nimirum, qui sub falso religionis praetextu suis rebus student, & qui otio assueti atque pertatus impatientes operam suam ad quaestum patrandum venalem habent. Nam ut priores illi (Christo teste, Ioan. 5.) credere non possunt, eo quod priuatae gloriae studio flagrant: ita alteris illis ibi fas esse putatur, vbi maxima merces. Astute ergo duo haec hominum genera satan sociare confuerunt, ut hypocritarum pecuniis redempti audaces illi & mercenarij Cares aperta vi conficiant, quod illi dolis & malis artibus conficere non possunt. Haec causa est, quod hodie in regum aulis ecclesiarum antistites visuntur, quod principum comitijs intersunt episcopi, & quod inter armatas acies & classica monachi volitant, qui se mundo mortuos esse gloriantur. Nec enim alios magis fidos patronos sibi reperire possunt, quam qui venali mente & conscientia praediti religionem & veritatem quaestu metiri solent. Docent haec a quo hominum genere sibi maxime cauere debeant, quicunq; ecclesias suas saluas volunt. Blandiuscule se hodie multis in locis Abbates & Episcopi insinuant, & zelum quendam praetexunt. Sed vbi admissi fuerint, mox suis consilijs aptos homines inuenient, qui auro corrupti quiduis etiam aperta vi aduersus Christi doctrinam audebunt: & ab omni religione simul & iustitia alienissimi esse deprehendentur, qui Dei zelo toti flagrare videbantur.
units.tr: Among the instruments of the devil that he chose to use here, two kinds of men are listed. The first are the Jews, who are said to have been moved by zeal. But they were hypocrites, who were accustomed to cover their obstinacy and unbelief with a zeal for the divine law and their ancestral religion, when in truth they were seeking nothing but private gain and glory, as their conspiracy makes plain. For they joined to themselves certain loafers from the marketplace, men of the worst reputation and perverse character, whose company they ought to have avoided like a most harmful plague, since religion and truth meant nothing to them. Such are the idle and lazy suitors of Penelope, who, once they have wastefully squandered their own goods, offer themselves for sale in the forum like public merchandise, and are ready for any crime provided they find a buyer. This is a wonderful alliance, which no one could have hoped for among professors of such dissimilar pursuits, unless there were so great a force of hatred against the truth once conceived that it could bring together and unite even the most unlike. Thus you see that priests, scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, Judas the false apostle, soldiers, Herod and Pilate conspired against Christ, though otherwise they were at odds with one another in nation, religion and profession. This passage warns us who the most bitter and chief enemies of the truth are: namely hypocrites, who under the false pretext of religion seek their own advantage, and those who, accustomed to idleness and impatient of work, hold their labour for sale to gain profit. For as the former (as Christ testifies, John 5) cannot believe, because they burn with a desire for private glory, so the latter think it lawful wherever the reward is greatest. Satan therefore has cunningly been accustomed to join these two kinds of men, so that those bold and mercenary men, bought with the money of the hypocrites, might carry out by open force what the others cannot accomplish by tricks and wicked arts. This is the reason why today we see bishops of churches in the courts of kings, why bishops attend the assemblies of princes, and why monks flit among armed battle lines and trumpets, boasting that they are dead to the world. For they cannot find more faithful patrons than men who, endowed with a venal mind and conscience, are accustomed to measure religion and truth by profit. These things teach those who want their churches to be safe from what sort of men they must most carefully guard themselves. Abbots and bishops today insinuate themselves rather smoothly in many places and put on a certain zeal. But once they have been admitted, they soon find men suited to their plans, who, corrupted by gold, will dare anything against the doctrine of Christ, even by open force; and they are found to be utterly alien to all religion and justice, though they seemed to burn entirely with zeal for God.

units.la: Docet hoc altera huius loci pars, quae studia horum explicat, qui diuini nominis zelum hucusque suo instituto praetexuerunt. Primum inter haec est, quod coniuratione facta totam ciuitatem seditione turbant, quod illis facile fuit per falsos rumores, quos tum aperte tum clanculum aduersus apostolos, ceu publicae salutis hostes, spargebant. Deinde aedes alienas inuadunt violenter, illinc nimirum protracturi apostolos, si inuenissent. Quis vero ille zelus est, qui fores effringere, & insontes ad mortem deposcere iubet? Accedit tamen grauius quiddam. Nam non inuentis illis, quos quaerebant, Iasonem apostolorum hospitem, virum ob hospitalitatem non vulgari laude dignum, et cum hoc aliquos ex fratribus, qui iam Christo nomen dederant, ad iudices trahunt, & tanquam vrbis proditores accusant. Accusatione vero ita instituunt, ut impudentissimis medacijs et calumnijs omnia misceant. Hi (inquiunt) qui terrarum orbem turbarunt, huc quoque venerunt, quos clanculum excepit Iason. Turbatores orbis vocant apostolos, qui pacem nunciabant & charitatem docebant mutuam: cum ipsi modo totam ciuitatem seditione commouerint. At quia religione, cuius praetextu ipsi tumultuabantur, apud Thessalonicenses non magni fieri sciebant, crimen amplificant, & contra Cæsaris edi-cta hæc fieri clamant, adeoque læsæ maiestatis reos faciunt apostolos, dum illos alium regem orbi terrarum imponere dicunt, tantumnon illud inferentes, quod Pilato ante Hierosolymitani obiecerant: Si hos impunè dimiseritis, non estis amici Cæsaris. EST vero horum præcipuus vsus, vt discamus quibus armis & artibus fere ab impijs oppugnetur Veritas & huius ministri. Ante omnia aperta vi res agitur. Quia enim homicida est Satan, in hac summum præsidium sibi repositum esse putat. Ita aduersus Christum cum gladijs & fustibus emisit qui illum caperent, quos ille diserte potestatem tenebrarum exercere ait. Luc. 22. Ita Abelum violenter trucidauit Cain. Et Israelitas aperta tyrannide afflixit Pharao. Imò si omnium seculorum historias consyderes, potissima aduersariorum veritatis argumenta in carnali brachio fundata fuisse videbis. Et hodie fere carceribus, vinculis, bombardis, hastis, ferro deniq; & igne aduersus pios disputari solet. Quia tamen cordatiores quiq; à manifesta vi & tyrannide abhorrent, astute mendacijs huius atrocitatem satan mitigare nouit, dum calumniis & falsis criminationibus exosos & infames reddit Christi cultores & fideles veritatis ministros. Exempla huius rei alibi de Achab rege, de Iudæis item Christum coram Pilato accusantibus, produximus, vt diutius loco isti inhærere non fit opus. Discamus saltem non temere sidem adhibere iis, qui pios grauissimè accusant, quasi in Deũ blasphemi, in Diuos iniurij, & publicæ pacis turbatores sint. Ipsam potius rei veritatem inuestigemus, & fere innocentissimos esse patebit, qui paulò ante quouis supplicio digni videbantur. Docet præterea locus hic quanta totius rebuspub. pernicies ex ociosis & luxu perditis hominibus exoriri soleat. Ibi enim vbi sua dilapidarunt, aliena affectant, & nummo sese ad quæuis facinora conduci patiuntur. Quò fit, vt qui illorum mores disciplinai ustaco-hercere noluerunt, ab iisdem tandem malum accipiant, & respub. suas misere exagitari sentiant. Ita apud Thessalonicenses nimis diu toleratisti homines, eò audacia progressi sunt, vt à Iudæis pelleCti & redempti, publicæ seditionis authores fiant, & illorum petulantia bonis omnibus formido-sa esse incipiat. Quæ mihi causa videtur, quòd ad Thessalonicenses postea scribens Paulus, tamdi-ligenter monet, vt in ordinem redigantur, qui ociosi ex aliorum laboribus sibi victum quærunt. Nam vt præsens hoc exemplum omittamus, non pauca aliarum gentium exempla passim extant, quibus docentur, non aliud hominum genus maiorem rebuspub. perniciem afferre solere. Sed multorum instar esse potest quod de Catilinaria coniurationis socijs in Romana historia habetur. Prudentissimè ergò Athenienses olim cauerunt, vt inertia & otium in forum protraherentur, & publicam ignominiam subirent, qui nulla honesta arte victum quærebant. Apud eosdem Areopagitæ cius, si quos suspectos habebant, ad se vocatos interrogabant, vnde vitam suam sustentarent. Quæ seueritas & industria si hodie obseruaretur, tum respub. tum ecclesias magis pacatas & tranquillas haberemus. Sed turpe est hac parte Christianos homines ab gentilibus vinci, quos sola carnis ratio & experientia rectius sapere docuit.
units.tr: The second part of this passage teaches the same thing; it explains the pursuits of those who have hitherto used the pretext of zeal for God's name to serve their own ends. First among these is that, by forming a conspiracy, they throw the whole city into sedition; this was easy for them to do through the false rumours which they spread against the apostles, both openly and secretly, as enemies of public safety. Then they violently break into other people's houses, clearly intending to drag the apostles out if they found them. But what kind of zeal is it that breaks down doors and demands the death of innocent men? Yet something more serious follows. For when they did not find those they were looking for, they drag before the magistrates Jason, the apostles' host, a man deserving no ordinary praise for his hospitality, together with some of the brothers who had already given their names to Christ, and accuse them as traitors to the city. In making this accusation they so contrive matters that they mix everything with the most shameless lies and calumnies. "These men," they say, "who have turned the world upside down, have come here too, and Jason has secretly received them." They call the apostles disturbers of the world, though these men were proclaiming peace and teaching mutual love, while the accusers themselves had just stirred up the whole city to sedition. But because they knew that the religion in whose name they themselves were creating the tumult was not held in high regard among the Thessalonians, they magnify the charge and cry out that these things are being done against the edicts of Caesar. Thus they make the apostles guilty of treason, saying that they set up another king over the world, not far from the very thing the Jerusalemites had objected to Pilate: "If you let these men go free, you are not friends of Caesar." Indeed, the principal use of this is that we learn with what weapons and arts the impious usually attack the truth and its ministers. Above all, the matter is pursued by open force. For since Satan is a murderer, he thinks that in this his greatest help is laid up for himself. So against Christ he sent men with swords and clubs to seize him, men whom he himself openly calls the power of darkness (Luke 22). So Cain violently slew Abel, and Pharaoh afflicted the Israelites with open tyranny. Indeed, if you consider the histories of all ages, you will see that the chief arguments of the adversaries of the truth have been founded on the carnal arm. And today too, against the godly, one usually disputes with prisons, chains, bombards, spears, and finally with iron and fire. But because more prudent people shrink from manifest force and tyranny, Satan has learned to soften the atrocity of this by lies, while through calumnies and false accusations he makes the worshippers of Christ and the faithful ministers of the truth hateful and infamous. Examples of this I have produced elsewhere, concerning King Ahab and the Jews who accused Christ before Pilate, so there is no need to remain longer on this point. Let us at least learn not to lend rash credence to those who gravely accuse the godly, as if they were blasphemers against God, disrespectful toward the gods, and disturbers of the public peace. Rather let us investigate the truth of the matter itself, and it will be plain that those who a little earlier seemed deserving of any punishment were almost entirely innocent. Furthermore, this passage shows what great ruin to the whole commonwealth usually arises from idle men and men ruined by luxury. For where they have squandered their own, they covet what belongs to others, and let themselves be hired for any crime for a coin. The result is that those who would not submit to their morals and discipline at last receive harm from them, and feel that their commonwealths are miserably harassed. So at Thessalonica, men who had been tolerated far too long went so far in their boldness that, enticed and bought by the Jews, they became the authors of public sedition, and their insolence began to be a terror to all good men. This, it seems to me, is the reason why Paul, writing afterwards to the Thessalonians, so diligently urges that those be brought into order who, idle, seek their food from the labours of others. For, to pass over this present example, there are many examples of other peoples everywhere, from which it is taught that no other kind of men usually brings greater ruin to the commonwealth. But the case of Catiline's fellow conspirators, as recorded in Roman history, may serve as an example of many. Accordingly, the Athenians of old took most prudent care that idleness and sloth should be dragged into the forum and suffer public disgrace if they sought a living by no honourable art. Among the same people the Areopagites, if they held anyone under suspicion, summoned him and asked him how he sustained his life. If this strictness and diligence were observed today, we would have commonwealths and churches more peaceful and tranquil. But it is shameful that Christians should be surpassed in this respect by the Gentiles, whom mere reason and experience of the flesh taught to be wiser.

units.la: Porrò Tragœdiæ huius exitum videamus, cuius initium tale fuit, vt nemo illam absq; sanguine finiri posse putauerit. Principio enim populus simul & Iudices commouentur, quod fere in seditionibus fieri consueuit, vt primo impetu cordati quoq; & modesti tantumnon abripiantur. Sed vt minacem cæli faciem & vndiq; imminentem nubium caliginem leui aura dissipare nouit deus, ita hoc loco absque labore pacatos & tranquillos reddit, qui toti furere videbantur. Iudicum enim animos occulta spiritus sui virtute moderatur & mitigat, vt Iasonem quoq; audiant, & illum tandem cum reliquis fratribus, accepta satisfactione, liberum dimittant. Interea temporis fratres Paulum & Silam noctu Berrhœam dimiserunt, vbi Iudæorum synagogam denuò ingressi magno cum fructu docent. Cæterū vt in Thessalonicensi Senatu ciuilis iustitiæ & æquitatis exemplum, omnibus qui in magistratu versantur imitandum proponitur: ita in alijs quoq; personis quæda obseruanda veniunt. ET primò quidem consolationis plenum est, quod de Iasone narratur. Is ob pietatis officium apostolis exhibitum graui periculo implicitus hæsit. Sed ita illum liberat dominus, vt æterna simul laudem in ecclesia sanctorum obtineat. Atqui ita impletur promissio, qua Christus illi quoq; mercedem certam pollicetur, qui poculum aquæ frigidæ vni ex discipulis suis dederit. Matth. 10. Accendat hoc in nobis quoq; pietatis studium, ne nobis graue videatur pro Christi fidelibus labores & periculapericuli. Deinde gratitudinis officium Paulo & Silæ Thessalonicen. fratres præstant, dum illos noctu deduxerunt. deducentes nouo sese pro illis periculo exponunt: ut non temere illorum fidem Paulus scripta ad illos epistola praedicarit. Commendantur ab eodem hoc nomine etiam Galatae, quod oculos quoque suos dare fuissent, si illis Paulus opus habuisset. At hodie pessimam gratiam fideles ministri referunt, quando primi manifestis periculis obiciuntur, et interdum impiorum hostium manibus ab illis ipsis traduntur, qui Christianissimi et euangelicissimi haberi volunt. Postremo Paulus obseruandus venit, qui fratrum consilium de fuga suscipienda recipit, hanc nimirum a Christo permissam esse intelligens, quando nec Dei gloria, nec fratrum et ecclesiae salus periclitatur. Nec enim nos absque graui causa et nullo cum fructu perire vult dominus. Interim in ipsa fuga officij sui non obliuiscitur, sed mox ut Berrhoeam deuenit, denuo docet. Quo exemplo admonemur ita nos saluti nostrae consulere debere, ne interim stationem nostram deseramus. Sed si Dei zelo animus flagrauerit, res ipsa, tempus item et locus facile consilium dabunt. Simul vero consoletur nos Dei virtus et bonitas, qua Paulum toties defensum ac liberatum fuisse videmus, et hac freti fortiter vocationem nostram tueamur, ut ad metam usque constanti cursu delati, caelestis vitae brauium assequamur in Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria et potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now look at the outcome of this tragedy, whose beginning was such that no one would have thought it could end without bloodshed. For at the start the people and the magistrates are stirred up together, as usually happens in seditions, so that at the first onset even the sensible and moderate are all but swept away. But just as God knows how to disperse a threatening sky and the darkness of clouds hanging over us on every side with a gentle breeze, so in this place he makes peaceful and calm, without effort, those who seemed wholly raging. For he moderates and softens the minds of the judges by the hidden power of his Spirit, so that they hear Jason too and at last, once satisfaction has been given, release him free along with the other brothers. Meanwhile the brothers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where, entering the synagogue of the Jews again, they teach with great fruit. But just as in the Thessalonian senate an example of civil justice and fairness is set forth to be imitated by all who hold office, so certain things are to be observed in the other persons too. And first indeed what is narrated of Jason is full of comfort. He, on account of the duty of piety shown to the apostles, was caught in grave danger and clung fast to it. But the Lord so delivers him that at the same time he obtains eternal praise in the Church of the saints. Surely in this way the promise is fulfilled, by which Christ also promises a sure reward to the one who gives a cup of cold water to one of his disciples (Matt. 10). Let this kindle in us also the zeal for piety, so that it does not seem a burden to us to labour and face dangers for the faithful of Christ. Next, the brothers of Thessalonica perform the duty of gratitude to Paul and Silas, while they lead them away by night; in leading them they expose themselves to a new danger on their behalf, so that Paul did not rashly praise their faith in the letter he wrote to them. The Galatians too are commended by him on this same account, because they would have given their own eyes, had Paul needed them. But today faithful ministers receive the worst return for their favour, when they are first exposed to manifest dangers, and sometimes are handed over by those very men, who want to be thought most Christian and most evangelical, into the hands of impious enemies. Last, Paul is to be observed, who accepts the advice of the brothers to take flight, understanding that this was allowed by Christ, since neither the glory of God nor the salvation of the brothers and the Church is endangered. For the Lord does not wish us to perish without serious cause and to no fruit. Meanwhile, in the very flight he does not forget his office, but as soon as he reaches Berea, he teaches again. By this example we are admonished that we ought to look after our own safety in such a way that we do not desert our post in the meantime. But if the mind has burned with zeal for God, the matter itself, and likewise the time and place, will easily give counsel. At the same time let the power and goodness of God comfort us, by which we see Paul so often defended and delivered, and relying on this let us bravely guard our calling, so that, carried on by a steady course to the very goal, we may win the prize of the heavenly life in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXV.
units.tr: HOMILY CXV.

units.la: Hi autem generosiores erant quam Thessalonicenses, qui receperunt sermonem cum omni animi promptitudine, quotidie scrutantes scripturas, an haec ita se haberent. Et multi quidem ex illis crediderunt, et Graecae mulieres honestae et viri non pauci. Cum autem cognouissent Thessalonicenses Iudaei, quod et Berrhoeae annuntiatus esset a Paulo sermo dei, venerunt etiam illic commouentes turbas. Statim vero tunc fratres emiserunt Paulum, ut iret velut ad mare. Silas autem et Timotheus remanserunt ibi. Porro qui deducebant Paulum, deduxerunt eum Athenas usque. Et accepto mandato ad Silam et Timotheum, ut quam celerrime ad ipsum venirent, profecti sunt.
units.tr: Now these were more noble than the Thessalonians, for they received the word with all readiness of mind, searching the Scriptures daily, whether these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, and of Greek women of honour and of men not a few. But when the Jews of Thessalonica learned that the word of God had also been preached by Paul at Berea, they came there too, stirring up crowds. Then at once the brethren sent Paul away, as though to the sea, but Silas and Timothy stayed behind there. Those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and having received a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they set off.

units.la: Et si regnum domini nostri Iesu Christi continuis et assiduis mundi huius et ipsius principis conatibus oppugnetur, adeo tamen euerti nequit, ut inter medias persecutiones felicissime promoueat. Docet hoc continua libri huius historia, maxime autem rerum a Paulo gestarum narratio. Ut enim is plus quam omnes alij apostoli laborauit, ita plures quoque et graviores persecutiones sustinuit, passimque fidei hostes reperit, quorum insidijs pulsus est {a}. Sed quoties illum horum rabies loco aliquo decedere compulit, toties relicto prius in auditorum animis verbi Dei semine, euangelium alio transtulit, sicque plures Christo domino lucrifecit. Hoc ipsum in Macedonia accidisse Lucas docet. Philippis enim illum indigne simul et iniuque tractatum fuisse audiimus. Non tamen ipsum sine fructu illic laborauisse, scripta ad Philippenses epistola docet. Persecutio autem illi ad Thessalonicenses cum migrandi occasionem praebet, apud quos per tria sabbata docuit. Tandem illinc quoque per Iudaeos, veteres hostes, pellitur. Non autem pellitur fides Christi, quae iam in multorum animis radices egerat. Ipse vero Berrhoeam delatus magno cum fructu euangelium praedicat. Seruiunt haec consolationi nostrae aduersus mundi et diaboli conatus. Nam ut Solomon inquit: Non est consilium aduersus dominum. At huius consilium est, quod Christus omnem potestatem in caelis et in terra obtinere, et fui regni terminos per totum terrarum orbem extendere debeat. Quare id fiat necesse est, quando caelum et terram citius transfire oportet, quam Dei decreta intercidere possint. SED praesentem locum videamus, qui Pauli res Berrhoeae gestas exponit.
units.tr: Even if the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ is assailed by the constant and unceasing efforts of this world and of its prince, yet it cannot be overthrown, but advances most happily amid the persecutions. The continuous history of this book teaches this, and especially the narrative of what Paul did. For as he laboured more than all the other apostles, so he also endured more and heavier persecutions, and everywhere he met enemies of the faith, by whose plots he was driven out. But whenever the rage of these men forced him to leave some place, he always first sowed the seed of God's word in the minds of his hearers, and then carried the gospel elsewhere, and so won more people to the Lord Christ. Luke teaches that the same thing happened in Macedonia. For we hear that Paul was treated there both shamefully and unjustly at Philippi. Yet his letter to the Philippians shows that he did not labour there without fruit. The persecution at Thessalonica gave him an opportunity to move on, where he taught for three sabbaths. At last he is driven out of there too, by the Jews, his old enemies. But the faith of Christ is not driven out, for it had already taken root in the minds of many. Paul himself, having been brought to Berea, preaches the gospel with great fruit. These things serve as a comfort to us against the attempts of the world and the devil. For, as Solomon says: "There is no counsel against the Lord." But his counsel is that Christ should possess all power in heaven and on earth, and should extend the bounds of his kingdom through the whole circuit of the earth. Therefore it must happen, since heaven and earth must sooner pass away than God's decrees can fail. But let us now look at the present passage, which sets out what Paul did at Berea.

units.la: Orditur a Berrhoensium Iudaeorum commendatione, ostendens, quo ordine quamque feliciter apud ipsos euangelium profecerit. Commendatur autem per comparationem, qua illos Thessalonicensibus confert. Illi enim Dei verbum contumeliose reiecerant. At isti magis ingenui vel generosiores illud cum omni animorum promptitudine receperunt, et simul domi scripturas scrutantes, ceu Lydio lapide probauerunt ea, quae a Paulo dicebantur. Inde factum est, ut et illorum magna multitudo crederet, et ipsorum exemplo ex Graecis quoque siue ethnicis non pauci, tum viri tum mulieres, ad fidem
units.tr: It begins with a commendation of the Jews of Berea, showing in what order and how successfully the gospel advanced among them. They are commended by comparison, by which Luke sets them against the Thessalonians. For those had rejected God's word with contempt, but these, being more noble or generous, received it with all readiness of mind, and at the same time, searching the Scriptures at home, tested what Paul said as by the Lydian touchstone. The result was that a great multitude of them believed, and by their example not a few of the Greeks, that is, Gentiles, both men and women, were led to the faith of Christ.

units.la: {a} Berrhoea euangelio illustratur. Christi perducerentur. DOCET exemplum hoc, quales esse conueniat, qui euangelium non absque fructu audire volunt. Ante omnia omni promptitudine, qua verbum recipiatur, opus est. Nisi enim verbo in animis hominum locus detur, fructum ferre non poterit. Quam ob rem in ipso limine impi-gunt, qui illud ne audire quidem dignantur, quae propria filiorum diaboli nota est, sicuti Christus apud Iohan. Cap. 8. admonet. Erat exemplum hoc iis maxime obseruandum, qui generis nobilitate superbiunt, et hanc signis inanibus ostentant. Atqui quoad generationem ex carne, eadem illa est omnibus corrupta nimirum et quae peccati seruos nos nasci facit. Regenerationis vero semen est Dei verbum, ex quo per spiritum intra animos nostros viuificato Dei filij nascimur, qui prius peccati mancipia eramus. Nobiles ergo et generosi non erunt, nisi qui huic locum dederint, et ex illo renati, Dei filij facti fuerint. Quapropter recte Lucas Berrhoenses istos propter verbi studium generosos dixit. Interea tamen nimia facilitas caueri debet, ne quiduis temere recipiendo quod sub verbi Dei praetexta praedicatur, falsis dogmatibus imbuamur, et incertis doctrinis ceu ventorum turbine circumferamur. Ruminari ergo et ad scripturae sacrae Canonem examinari oportet quae dicuntur, iuxta illud Pauli: Omnia probate, quod bonum est tenete. 1. Thess. 5. Et Ioannes apostolus ait: Charissimi, ne cuiuis spiritui credatis, sed probate spiritus num ex Deo sint, etc. 1. Ioan. 4. Arguuntur hoc loco duo insignes errores, qui iam annis aliquot ecclesias grauissime turbauerunt. Alter illorum est, qui scripturas sacras a laicis et vulgo legi, nefas esse clamant. Atqui has omnibus hominum ordinibus communes esse semper Deus voluit. Legem enim coram tota Israelis multitudine, in eum finem conuocata, promulgauit. Et sacros libros non alia quam vulgari lingua conscribi spiritus sanctus curauit. Et sane absurdum foret a vitae aeternae doctrina aliquem excludi, cum et illam et veritatis cognitionem ad omnes hominum ordines Deus peruenire velit. 1 Timoth. 2. Alterilorum error est, qui doctrinam suam a nemine dijudicari volunt, sed Cyclopea arrogantia sibi quidquid docendi in ecclesia ius vendicant: imo indignissimum et plane haereticum facinus esse vociferantur, si quis ab ipsis rationes dictorum exigat. Num ergo Paulo praestantiores sunt, qui suas concio-nes ad scripturae canonem probari passus est? Vel num hodie haereticus erit, qui hoc ipsum fecerit, ob quod Berrhoenses isti, pro germanis vere, ingenuis Dei filijs commendantur? Quid quod Paulus ipse se piorum censura subijcit? Eius enim verba sunt: Si ego ipse Paulus siue angelus de caelo praedicauerit aliud euangelium, praeter id quod praedicatum est, anathema censeri meretur. Galat. 1. Et Christus hoc ouibus suis proprium esse ait, quod inter suam et alienam vocem discernant et suam solummodo sequantur. Ioan. 10. Caeterum breuis quoque credentium catalogus, quem Lucas contexit, inspiciendus est, quem ex omni hominum genere collectum esse videmus. Credunt primo ludai multi, licet gentis illius repudium iam instaret. Non potest tamen sui foederis in vniuersum oblivisci Deus, quin iuxta promissionem reliquias saluas faciat. Isa. 10. Accedunt his ex gentibus mulieres honestae siue nobiles et illustres. Demum viri quoque non pauci numerantur. Vnde patet gratiam Dei, quae in Christo nobis collata est, ad omnes hominum ordines pertinere, nec quenquam aut ob patriam et nationem, vel propter sexum aut vitae conditionem excludi. Nam in Christo Iesu non est Iudaeus neque Graecus, non est seruus neque liber, non est masculus neque foemina, etc. Galat. 3. Quod vt consolationi feruit, ita singulos docet, vt communionis Christianae memores, neminem praeperfe insolentius contemnant.
units.tr: Berea is held up by the gospel. This example teaches what sort of people ought to be, those who wish to hear the gospel not without fruit. Above all, there must be the readiness with which the word is received. For unless a place is given to the word in people's minds, it cannot bear fruit. Therefore those stumble at the very threshold who do not even deign to hear it, which is the mark proper to the children of the devil, as Christ admonishes in John chapter 8. This example ought to be especially observed by those who take pride in noble birth and display it with empty signs. Yet as to birth according to the flesh, that is the same for all, corrupted indeed, and it is what makes us born slaves of sin. But the seed of regeneration is God's word, by which, quickened within our minds through the Spirit, we are born as children of God, who before were the slaves of sin. Therefore only those will be noble and generous who have given place to this word, and who, having been born again from it, have become children of God. Hence Luke rightly called those Bereans generous for their zeal for the word. Meanwhile, however, great care must be taken lest, by receiving rashly whatever is put forward under the pretext of God's word, we become steeped in false doctrines and carried about like leaves in a whirlwind of uncertain teachings. Therefore what is said must be weighed and tested by the canon of Holy Scripture, according to Paul's words: "Test all things; hold fast what is good" (1 Thess. 5). And the apostle John says: "Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God," etc. (1 John 4). In this passage two notable errors are refuted, which for some years have sorely troubled the churches. One of them is the view of those who cry out that it is wrong for the Scriptures to be read by laymen and the common people. But God has always willed that these be common to all orders of men. For he promulgated the law before the whole multitude of Israel, gathered for that purpose. And the Holy Spirit took care that the sacred books were written in nothing other than the common language. Indeed it would be absurd for anyone to be shut out from the doctrine of eternal life, since God wishes both that teaching and the knowledge of the truth to come to all orders of men (1 Tim. 2). The other error is that of those who want their teaching judged by no one, but with Cyclopean arrogance claim for themselves whatever right there is to teach in the church; indeed they shout that it is a most unworthy and plainly heretical crime if anyone asks them for the grounds of what they say. Are they then better than Paul, who allowed his sermons to be tested by the canon of Scripture? Or will he be a heretic today who does the very thing for which those Bereans are commended, as truly generous children of God? What of the fact that Paul himself submits to the judgement of the godly? For his words are: "If I, Paul, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any gospel other than what has been preached, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1). And Christ says it is the mark of his sheep that they distinguish his voice from a stranger's and follow his voice alone (John 10). Furthermore, the short list of believers which Luke has woven together must be looked at, which we see gathered from every kind of people. First, many Jews believe, although the rejection of that nation was already at hand. Yet God cannot altogether forget his covenant, but will save a remnant according to the promise (Isa. 10). To these are added honourable, that is, noble and distinguished, women from the Gentiles. Finally, men not a few are counted. From this it is plain that the grace of God, which has been offered to us in Christ, pertains to all orders of men, and that no one is excluded because of country or nation, or because of sex or condition of life. For in Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female, etc. (Gal. 3). This, as it serves for consolation, so also teaches each one, that, mindful of Christian fellowship, no one should despise another too insolently.

units.la: Sed videamus, quid Berrhoea aduersus Christi regnum tentarit satanas. Idem nimirum quod etiam alibi. Neque enim huius progressum ferre poterat, quo suum regnum labefactari et euerti nouit. Quia vero neminem in ea vrbe suo instituto idoneum reperire potuit, Thessalonicenses Iudaeos euocat, qui Christi fidem propagari indigne ferentes aduolant, et Berrhoeae etiam turbarum auctores sunt. Eodem ergo hic stratagemate satan vtitur, quo illum apud Lystrenses quoque vsum esse, supra vidimus: id quod hodie etiam illi peculiare est, vt aliunde adducat regni Christi turbatores, si illos alicubi deesse viderit. Et mirum est quam induistrij sint in hoc officio praestando Monachi, quos afflute non per vrbes modo, verumetiam per Regum aulas dispergere, imo in intima illorum consilia insinuare nouit, vt illorum suggestionibus fascinati principes, veritatis doctrinae aures praecludant. Interim vide hoc loco incurabilem Iudaicae gentis malitiam, qua exacerbati non modo ipsi fidem Christi explodunt, sed ne alios quidem illius luce illustrari ferre possunt: vt non temere illos tam grauiter Paulus
units.tr: But let us see what Satan attempted at Berea against the kingdom of Christ. Certainly the same as elsewhere. For he could not bear its progress, since he knew that his own kingdom would be shaken and overthrown by it. But because he could find no one in that city suited to his purpose, he calls out the Jews of Thessalonica, who, indignant that the faith of Christ was spreading, rush there and are also the instigators of the uproar at Berea. So Satan uses the same stratagem here as he had used at Lystra too, as we saw above. This is even today a particular habit of his: if he sees that there are none to be found somewhere, he brings in disturbers of Christ's kingdom from elsewhere. And it is remarkable how busy the monks are in performing this office, whom he knows how to scatter not only through cities but also through royal courts, and even to insinuate themselves into the innermost counsels of princes, so that princes, fascinated by their suggestions, shut their ears to the teaching of the truth. Meanwhile, observe here the incurable malice of the Jewish nation, by which, provoked, they not only reject the faith of Christ themselves, but cannot even bear that others should be illuminated by its light; so it is no wonder that Paul rebuked them so severely.

units.la: II. Berrhoensis ecclesia turbatio. Paulus notet in priori ad Theff. epistola secundo capite. Sed similes horum sunt, quotquot hodie sese diabolo organa prabent ad Christi fidem oppugnandam, & inde summam laudem captant. Memi- nerint tamen se idem iudicium subituros, cuius exemplum magno cum totius mundi stupore in Iudaeos editum est. Iam olim enim praedixit spiritus sanctus, ferreo Christi sceptro confringendos esse omnes eos, qui verbo illius corrigi & emendari noluNt. Psal. 2. Nec desunt potentissimorum regum exempla qui seueram hanc Christi vindicis sententiam magno suo malo experti sunt: de quibus cum alibi co- piose dictum sit, in praesenti paucis iste contenti sumus.
units.tr: II. The disturbance at the church of Berea. Paul notes this in the second chapter of his first epistle to the Thessalonians. But like these are all who today lend themselves as instruments of the devil to attack the faith of Christ, and who seek great praise from doing so. Yet let them remember that they will undergo the same judgment, whose example was displayed, to the great astonishment of the whole world, in the Jews. For the Holy Spirit foretold long ago that all those who are unwilling to be corrected and amended by Christ's word will be broken with his iron sceptre. Psalm 2. Nor are there lacking examples of the most powerful kings who, to their great cost, have experienced this severe sentence of Christ the avenger. Since this has been discussed at length elsewhere, in the present place we are content with a few words.

units.la: Quid vero furentibus iam turbis fratres faciunt? Num Paulum periculis obijciunt, aut saltem omni consilio auxilioq; destitutum deserunt? Nequaquam. Quin potius reliclis Berrhaeae Sila & Timotheo, quibus non ita periculosum erat illic manere, Paulum subducunt, & ea in re singularem prudentiam adhibent. Nam iter mare versus instituunt, mox autem flexo cursu Athenas contendunt, unde postea priorem ad Thessalonicenses epistolam Paulus scripsit. Obliquo autem itinere profecti ef se videntur, quo facilius Iudaeorum insidias vitarent, quos odio Pauli tantum non furere videbant. Porro obseruandum hic venit pietatis officium, quod suo doctori Berrhaensis praestant. Quis enim dubitet rem non modo magni sumptus & laboris, verum etiam periculi plenam fuisse, quam tentant? At nihil illos in pio officio remorari potest, eo quod de accepto euangelij beneficio recte iudicant, nec magnum esse arbitrantur, si pro aeternae salutis dono externum officium praestent. Hodie vero quia pauci diuinam gratiam, quae euangelio offertur, recte agnoscunt, omne periculum & labores omnes subterfugiunt. Sed fere fit, ut qui pro Christi causa periclitari noluerunt, postea maioribus turbis ob causas minus sanctas implicentur. Admonet praeterea locus hic, prudentiam cum fide nequaquam pugnare. Iubet enim Christus, ut ab hominum insidiis caueamus, & serpentina aduersus illas utamur prudentia. Matth. 10. Opus enim illa est propter filios huius seculi, quos in sua generatione prudentiores esse quam filios lucis, ipse Christus testatur. Luc. 16. Meminerimus tamen metas certas carnis rationi ponendas esse, ne quid ex huius consilio & suasu praeter officium faciamus. Qua in re non aliud tutius remedium erit, quam si intellectum omnem fidei obedientiae subijciamus, ut alibi Paulus monet. Ita fiet, ut nec temere perilcitando Deum tentemus, nec veritatis causam turpiter deseramus, sed media via ingressi officium faciamus, cum Christo Iesu, cui seruimus, olim in caelis regnaturi. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But what do the brothers do while the mobs are now raging? Do they expose Paul to dangers, or at least abandon him destitute of all counsel and help? By no means. Rather, leaving Silas and Timothy behind in Berea, where it was not so dangerous for them to remain, they withdraw Paul, and in this matter they show singular prudence. For they set out on the way towards the sea, but soon, changing course, they make for Athens, whence Paul afterwards wrote his first epistle to the Thessalonians. They seem to have set out by an indirect route, so that they might more easily avoid the snares of the Jews, whom they saw were almost raging with hatred of Paul. Furthermore, the duty of piety that the brothers of Berea render to their teacher deserves notice here. For who would doubt that the undertaking they attempt was full not only of great expense and labour but also of danger? Yet nothing can hold them back from this pious duty, because they judge rightly concerning the benefit of the gospel they have received, and do not think it a great thing if they render an outward service in return for the gift of eternal salvation. Today, however, since few rightly acknowledge the divine grace that is offered in the gospel, people shun every danger and all labours. But it usually happens that those who were unwilling to face danger for the cause of Christ are afterwards entangled in greater disturbances for less holy causes. This passage also warns that prudence is by no means at odds with faith. For Christ commands us to beware of men's snares and to use serpent-like prudence against them. Matt. 10. Such prudence is needed on account of the sons of this age, whom Christ himself testifies to be wiser in their own generation than the sons of light. Luke 16. Yet let us remember that fixed limits must be set to human reason, lest we do anything beyond our duty on its counsel and persuasion. In this matter there will be no safer remedy than if we subject all understanding to the obedience of faith, as Paul advises elsewhere. Thus it will come about that we neither rashly tempt God by exposing ourselves to danger, nor shamefully desert the cause of truth, but walking the middle way we perform our duty, since we shall one day reign in heaven with Christ Jesus, whom we serve. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 116.

units.la: Paulus autem cum Athenis eos expectaret, incadescebat spiritus eius in ipso, cum videret idololatriae deditam ciuitatem. Disputabat igitur in Synagoga cum Iudaeis & religiosis, & in foro quotidie cum his, qui in ipsum incidebant. Quidam autem Epicurei & Stoici philosophi disce- ptabant cum eo. Et quidam dicebant: Quid sibi vult hic spermologus dicere? Alii vero: Nouorum daemoniorum videtur annuntiator esse, quod Iesum & resurrectionem annuntiaret eis. Et apprehensum eum in Areopa- gum duxerunt, dicentes: Possumus ne scire, quae sit ista noua, quae a te praedicatur doctrina? Noua enim quaedam ingeris auribus nostris. Vo- lumus ergo scire, quid nam velint haec esse. Athenienses autem omnes & qui illic versabantur hospites, ad nihil aliud vacabant, nisi ad dicendum vel audiendum aliquid noui.
units.tr: While Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred within him when he saw the city given over to idolatry. So he disputed in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to meet him. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also argued with him. Some said, "What does this babbler want to say?" Others said, "He seems to be a proclaimer of strange demons, since he preached Jesus and the resurrection to them." So they took hold of him and led him to the Areopagus, saying, "Can we know what this new doctrine is that you preach? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know, then, what these things mean." Now all the Athenians and the foreigners living there devoted themselves to nothing else but telling or hearing something new.

units.la: Descripsit hucusque Lucas varias Pauli apostoli peregrinationes, quibus tot gentes & urbes euangelij praedicatione illustrauit, ut non temere alicubi se plus omnibus aliis apostolis laborasse dixerit. Porro ne quis illum obscuros tantummodo rerum, imperitos homines elaborato dicendi artificio traxisse putaret, non sine certo diuinae prouidentiae consilio tandem Athenas venit, quae nescio si quae unquam urbs fuit celebrior. Vetustate enim plures alias vicit, ut quae primum regem Cecropem circa Mosis tempora habuerit. Postmodum victoriis aduersus Persas clara, summam liberata e Barbarorum manibus Graciae laudem sibi vendicauit. Ingeniorum felici acumine omnes alias excelluit. Huic enim Socratem, Platonem, Xenophontem, Cratem & infinitos alios, sapientiæ titulo celebres, debemus. Quæ causa fuit, vt ibi vniuersalis quædam mundi totius schola constitueretur, ad quam ex toto orbe, ceu vnicam sapientiæ sedem & arcem nobilissimi quique confluebant. Tantaque fuit penes illam sapientiæ existimatio, vt Romani, cum Asiæ domini facti essent, suos filios nusquam terrarum sapientiæ præceptis simul & exemplis melius quam Athenis instrui posse putaret, sicuti Ciceronis ad filium in libros Offic. præfatio testatur. Et vt multis aliis rebus, ita etiam religio ne & gentilitio deorum cultu reliquis præstare videbantur, eo quod apud illos Minervæ simulachrum viseretur, quod cælo delapsum esse credebatur, & inter deos multi numerarentur, quos Athenis natos esse gloriabantur. In eam vrbem Paulum apostolum dominus ablegat, vt ipsius ministerio ad veræ fidei obedientiam reducatur. Nec id absque fructu tentatum esse, rei exitus probabit. Ethoc memorabile tum bonitatis Dei tum potentiæ euangelij exemplum. Quis enim non diuinæ bonitatis ineffabilem gratiam agnoscat, quando idololatriæ simul & humanæ sapientiæ tenebris plane immersam ciuitatem tam amicè à Deo respectam fuisse audit? Rursum quis non euangelij inuictam virtutem admiretur, quando sapientissimos in vrbe viros per hoc conuictos esse videt, idque Pauli ministerio, qui nihil quàm plagarum vestigia secum afferebat, & tot vrbibus eiectus nulla in mundo authoritate pollebat? Dignissima ergo consyderatu est conuersionis Athenarum historia, cuius primum actum in præsenti Lucas commemorat, doceus primò quid ibi Paulus egerit, deinde vt eius doctrina, cùm primum prædicaretur, à plerisque illius loci hominibus fuerit excepta. Nos de singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Up to this point Luke has described the various journeys of the apostle Paul, by which he illuminated so many nations and cities with the preaching of the gospel that he could not rashly be said to have laboured more than all the other apostles anywhere. Furthermore, lest anyone think he had drawn in obscure matters and unlearned men by an elaborate art of speaking, he came at last to Athens, and not without a definite plan of divine providence. I do not know whether any city was ever more famous. By antiquity it surpassed many others, since it had Cecrops as its first king around the time of Moses. Afterwards, renowned for its victories over the Persians, it claimed for itself the highest praise of Greece, having been freed from the hands of the barbarians. In the happy keenness of its minds it excelled all others. To it we owe Socrates, Plato, Xenophon, Crates and countless others, famous for the title of wisdom. This was the reason why a kind of universal school of the whole world was established there, to which the noblest men from all over the world flocked, as to the one seat and citadel of wisdom. The esteem for wisdom there was so great that the Romans, when they had become masters of Asia, thought their sons could be taught the precepts and examples of wisdom nowhere on earth better than at Athens, as Cicero's preface to his son in the books On Duties attests. And in religion, as in many other things, they seemed to surpass the rest, because among them was seen the image of Minerva, which was believed to have fallen from heaven, and many gods were counted whom they boasted had been born at Athens. The Lord sends the apostle Paul into that city, so that through his ministry it might be brought back to obedience to the true faith. That this was not attempted without fruit the outcome of the matter will prove. This is a memorable example both of the goodness of God and of the power of the gospel. For who does not acknowledge the ineffable grace of divine goodness, when he hears that a city plunged into the darkness of idolatry and of human wisdom alike was so kindly regarded by God? Again, who would not admire the unconquered power of the gospel, when he sees the wisest men of the city convicted through it, and this by the ministry of Paul, who carried nothing with him but the marks of blows, and who, cast out of so many cities, had no authority in the world? The history of the conversion of Athens is therefore most worthy of consideration. Luke now recounts its first act, teaching first what Paul did there, and then how his teaching, when it was first preached, was received by most of the men of that place. We shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Paulus Silas & Timotheus aduentum expectans Athenis, interea vrbem vndiquaque circuit, mores & ritus consyderat, adeò vt ne templa quidem prætermittat, sed illa quoque ingressus contemplatur, quemadmodum ex ipsius oratione infra patebit. Videns autem tantam ciuitatem præ aliis, quas hucusque viderat, idololatriæ deditam & immersam esse, totus excandescit spiritu, indigne nimirum ferens Dei cultum tam iniquis modis prophanari. Nam vt non alio peccato magis quàm idololatria Deus offenditur, ita hoc ipso sanctorum animi quàm maximè irritari solent, eo quòd illi nihil antiquius & charius ducant, quàm supremi numinis gloriam. Hinc est, quòd Moses confracto vitulo aureo, sui tantùmnon oblitus, legis tabulas confringit, & in puluerem redactum vitulum in aquas spargit, vt Deum illum suum haurire & in ventrem demittere idololatræ cogerentur. Eodem zelo Elias accensus, Baalis sacerdotes propria manu iugulat, quem non male imitatus Iehu diuino testimonio commendatur. Hoc ipso Ioiam flagrauisse scriptura docet, quando idololatrarum sacerdotum offa in ipsorum altaribus combustit, vt abunde perspecta omnibus fieret tanti flagitij indignitas. Quid de prophetis dicemus, qui vix alia in re ingenij & eloquentiæ sua vires magis intendunt, quàm cum illis de simulachris sermo est? Tunc enim nec seriis nec ludicris abstinent, vt rem Deo exosissimam satis exagitent. Admiranda ergo & stupenda est illorum contumacia, qui hodie cùm Christiani & euangelici haberi velint, simulachra tamen tuentur, & pro illis contra fratres, Christianæ fidei professores, certamen suscipiunt, & inuidiosis nominibus Iconomachos & Iconoclastas eos dicunt, quorum zelus tot scripturæ testimonijs & sanctorum exemplis commendatur. Interim admonet nos Pauli exemplum, zelo opus esse omnibus ijs, qui in Christi causa & regno Dei cum laude & fructu versari voluerint. Quia enim pertinacissimum est impietatis malū, nunquam fine zelo feruentissimo euelli poterit. Excitet hunc in nobis Christi exemplum, qui cùm patris sui domum in emporium conuersam esse videret, quasi oblitus solitæ mansuetudinis, flagello è proximè collectis funibus facto impios mercatores templo eijcit, Dauidicum illud discipulis in animum reuocas: Zelus domus tuæ exedit me. Ioan. 2. Psal. 68. Admonet nos hic officij nostri dominicæ orationis consyderatio, cuius præcipuæ petitiones sunt, vt Dei nomen sanctificetur, & regnum eius adueniat. At quomodo hæc non fucato animo precabuntur, quos nulla mordet diuini nominis prophanatio & regni Dei euersio? Minimè ergo audiendi sunt ambidextri illi, qui cùm religionis causam tractant, neque frigidi sunt nec tepidi, & contra Eliæ dictum in vtranque partem claudicant, summam sibi laudem ex eo venantes, si in nullius verba iurent, & omnibus ex æquo amici sint. Tales olim Laodicenses erat, quos se euomiturum esse, Christus minatur. Apoc. 3.
units.tr: Paul, waiting at Athens for Silas and Timothy, meanwhile goes all round the city and considers its customs and rites. He does not even pass over the temples, but goes into them too and examines them, as will become clear below from his speech. Seeing such a great city, more than any other he had yet seen, given over to idolatry and sunk in it, he is wholly inflamed in spirit, indignant that the worship of God should be profaned in such wicked ways. For just as God is offended by no sin more than by idolatry, so the minds of the saints are most stirred by it, because they count nothing more precious and dear than the glory of the supreme deity. Hence Moses, when he had broken the golden calf, not unmindful of himself, breaks the tables of the law, and reduces the calf to powder and scatters it on the water, so that the idolaters were forced to drink down their god and send him into their bellies. Elijah, kindled by the same zeal, slays the priests of Baal with his own hand, and Jehu, who imitated him not badly, is commended by divine testimony. Scripture teaches that Joash burned with this very same zeal when he burned the bones of the idolatrous priests on their own altars, so that the unworthiness of so great a crime might be thoroughly seen by all. What shall we say of the prophets, who scarcely exert the powers of their wit and eloquence more in any other matter than when the talk is of images? For then they abstain neither from serious nor from mocking language, so as to vent sufficiently their hatred of a thing most hateful to God. Admirable and astounding, then, is the obstinacy of those who today, though they wish to be considered Christians and evangelicals, nevertheless defend images, take up strife on their behalf against brothers who profess the Christian faith, and call them by odious names, Iconomachs and Iconoclasts, when their zeal is commended by so many testimonies of Scripture and examples of the saints. Meanwhile the example of Paul admonishes us that zeal is needed by all who wish to live with praise and profit in the cause of Christ and the kingdom of God. For since the evil of impiety is most stubborn, it can never be uprooted without the most fervent zeal. Let the example of Christ kindle this in us. When he saw his Father's house turned into a marketplace, as if forgetful of his usual gentleness, he made a whip from cords gathered nearby and drove the impious merchants out of the temple, recalling for his disciples that saying of David: "The zeal of your house has eaten me up" (John 2; Ps. 68). Our consideration of the Lord's Prayer also admonishes us, whose chief petitions are that God's name be hallowed and his kingdom come. But how will they pray these things with a sincere mind, whom the profanation of the divine name and the overthrow of God's kingdom do not sting? Therefore those ambidextrous men are by no means to be listened to. When they handle the cause of religion, they are neither cold nor lukewarm, but limp to both sides against Elijah's saying, hunting for themselves the highest praise from this, that they swear to no one's words and are equally friends to all. The Laodiceans were once like this, and Christ threatens that he will vomit them out (Rev. 3).

units.la: Sed vt ad Paulum redeamus, num ille intra se tantum æstuat & ob idololatriam vi∫am indi- gnatur? Imo vrbis tanta reformatione meditatur, homo peregrinus & nullius apud illos nominis. Mox ergo publicè de religione vera disputat & Christum Iesum predicare incipit. At quot obsecro res erant, quæ illum revocare poterant, si carnis rationes audire voluisset? Cogitaret enim: Tune in vrbe celeberrima eam religionem labefactare audebis, quæ tot seculorum vetustissima consuetudine commendatur, totq; prosperis rerum successibus & victoriis gloriosissimis hucusq; confirmata est? Tune cum acutissimis hominibus & disputando exercitatissimis congredieris, qui philosophiæ ipsorum rudimenta vix dum salutauisti? An ignoras quàm inuisæ quamq; periculosæ sint mutationes omnes, maximè autem illæ, quarum authores peregrini sunt, quos in aliena republica curiosos esse decet communis sensus prohibet? Hæc & infinita alia Paulo in mentem venisse verisimile est, quando & homo erat, & longo rerum vsu didicerat, quid facto opus esset. At procul valere iußis rationibus illis, rem ipsam fortiter aggreditur: suo exemplo docens, eos qui in Dei vocatione versantur, nullas carnis rationes admittere debere, quibus ab officio revocari possint. Nam si has audire voluissent prophetæ & apostoli, nemo vnquam illorum officium fecisset, quin potius Ionam imitati, fuga transmarina sibi ipsis consulere conati essent. Nam Mosen Dei mandato reluctari & imperium detrectare vidimus, quàm diu ratione secutus suam infantiam & ruditatem cum illius iußis confert. Vide Exod. 4. Cogitemus ergo, non ex nostro sed Dei arbitrio res omnes pendere, qui in sua vocatione ambulantibus viam facile sternere poterit. Cogitemus item Dei verbi omnibus obstaculis, quæ mundus obijcit, potentius esse. Est enim gladius vtrinq; acutus & ad medullas vsq; penetrans: est ignis devorans & petras comminuens. Hebr. 4. Ierem. 23. Hoc igitur animati strenuè tentemus quodcunq; Deus iniunxerit, illi permittentes rei eventum, qui ipsius auspicia secuti non potest non lætissimus obtingere.
units.tr: But to return to Paul: does he merely seethe inwardly and feel indignation at the idolatry he sees? No, he plans so great a reformation of the city, though he is a foreigner of no name among them. Soon, therefore, he publicly disputes about the true religion and begins to preach Christ Jesus. But what, I ask, were the considerations that could have called him back, had he wished to hear the reasons of the flesh? He would think: "Will you dare in this most famous city to undermine that religion which is commended by the most ancient custom of so many centuries, and has been confirmed until now by so many prosperous successes and most glorious victories? Will you engage with the sharpest men, most practised in disputation, when you have scarcely greeted the rudiments of their philosophy? Do you not know how hateful and how dangerous all changes are, above all those whose authors are foreigners, whom common sense forbids to be meddling in another's commonwealth?" It is likely that these and countless other thoughts came into Paul's mind, since he was a man and had learned from long experience what needed to be done. But bidding those reasons farewell, he bravely tackles the matter itself, teaching by his own example that those who are engaged in God's calling must admit no reasons of the flesh by which they might be called back from their duty. For if the prophets and apostles had wished to hear such reasons, none of them would ever have done his duty; rather, imitating Jonah, they would have tried to save themselves by fleeing across the sea. We saw Moses, too, resisting God's command and refusing the charge, as long as he weighed his own infancy and roughness against the commands of God (see Exod. 4). Let us therefore consider that all things depend not on our judgment but on God's, who can easily smooth the way for those who walk in their calling. Let us consider also that the word of God is more powerful than all the obstacles the world throws in its path. For it is a sword sharp on both edges, penetrating even to the marrow; it is a fire that devours and crushes rocks (Heb. 4; Jer. 23). Inspired by this, let us vigorously attempt whatever God has enjoined, leaving the outcome to him, since whoever follows his auspices cannot fail to reach the most joyful result.

units.la: Porrò ordinem quoq; quem Paulus in propagando apud Athenienses Christi regno secutus est, Lucas exponit. Primò cum Iudæis ea de re sermonem contulit, eò quòd illos facillimè omnium aures præbituros sciret, Mosen & prophetas in medium adducenti. Inde eos quoq; sibi instituendos sumit, qui ex Iudæorum conuersatione aliquem syncerioris fidei & religionis gustum perceperant, nondum tamen perfectè erant instituti. His verò fundamentis iactis quosuis in foro obuios aggreditur, & eò vsq; progressus est, vt iam philosophi etiam, quibus ciuitas illa abundabat, disputationes contra Paulum instituerent. Ex multis verò illorum sectis Epicurei & Stoici potissimum in arenam descendunt, qui cum inter se toto cœlo disiderent, nunc tamen in oppugnando veritatis ministro conuenire possunt. Epicurei enim omnis verae sapientiae & politioris literaturæ hostes, summum bonum in voluptate collocabant, honesta quidem illa (vt aiebant) vtpote quæ animi tranquillitatem & corporis incolumitatem comprehenderet, interim tamen non altius ascendendo, absurdissimorum dogmatum, quæ inde consequebantur authores erant. Quia enim numinis metus & vitæ futuræ meditatio conscientijs terrores incutit, & acerba reddit externa omnia, Dei prouidentiam simul & vitam futuram negabant. Deum quippe ad cœli cardines obambulare & nulla mortalium rerum cura tangi fabulabatur, animasq; vnà cum corporibus intermori. Vnde Sardanapalicum illud concludebant, Ede, bibe, lude, post mortem nulla voluptas. Stoici autem his plane contrarij, summum hominis bonum in virtute positum esse docebant. Quod licet in speciem plausibile & sanctum videatur, non minus tamen quàm Epicurei à Deo abstrahebant, eò quòd illos in proprijs operum suorum meritis felicitate quærere docerent. Rursum quia virtutis studiû affectibus interturbari videbant, ab his alienissimos esse volebant summi boni setta-tores, adeò vt nec secundis rebus lætitia, nec in aduersis tristitia aliquâ significatione præ se ferrent.
