Ex hominibus ergo truncos & lapides faciebant, ἀ πάθεις nimirum ἡ ἀσόργυσς, qui ne naturalibus quidem affectibus, quibus parentes & liberi inter se tanguntur, obnoxij essent. Adhæc ex causarum connexione fatum fingebant, cui ipse quoq; Deus subijceretur. Docent hæc quibus cum Paulo contentio fuerit, simulq; admonent, qui nam bodie etiâ, adeoq; omnibus seculis, verae doctrinæ & euangelij hostes sint. Licet enim olim apud solas gentes Epicureorum & Stoicorum nomina in vsu fuerint, fuerunt tamen etiam in externo Dei populo qui idem cum illis sentirent, nec illi etiam bodie desunt. Certe inter Iudæos olim Nabal fuit, qui diceret, Non est Deus, & hunc suæ sententiæ innumeros socios habuisse, Dauid testatur. Psal. 14. & 53. Tales item erant, qui dicebant: Dominus non videt, neque Deus Iacob intelligit. Psal. 94. De nouissimis verò temporibus, in quæ nos incidimus, Christi & apo lorum oracula extant, quæ Epicureismum plane regnaturum docent. Ait enim Christus: Sicut acci‑dit in diebus Noe, ita erit & in diebus filij hominis. Edebant, bibebant, vxores ducebant, & daban‑tur nuptū, ad eum vsq; diem quo intrauit Noe in Arcam, &c. Luc.17. Et Petrus nouissimis diebus illusores venturos esse prædicit, qui iuxta proprias concupiscentias ambulent & dicant: Vbi est pol‑licitatio aduentus eius? Siquidem ex quo die patres dormierunt, sic omnia permanent ab initio condi‑tionis, &c.2.Pet.3. Atqui tales hodie passim cernuntur, qui licet Epicureismū non diserte profitean‑tur, ita tamen viuunt, vt illos nec deos nec vitam futurā credere cuiuis facile pateat. At ijdem euan‑gelij lucem ferre non possunt, eò quòd hac (vt Christus Iohan.3.ait) opera ipsorum mala arguantur. Simili ratione Stoicorū dogma omnibus seculis reperire licet. Hoc enim inter Iudæos olim pharifæi tenuerunt, qui vt suorum operum iustitiæ considebant, ita Christi hostes omnium acerrimi fuerunt. Horum ordo (vt vt supra Cap.15. Vidimus) primitiuæ ecclesiæ turbatores dedit, qui euangelij cum lege & operum merita cum fide miscebant. Patrum temporibus Pelagiani exorti sunt, eiusdem do‑strinæ assertores. Quòd si eosdem nostro seculo quæras, Monachos reperies, quos iuratos Zenonis di‑scipulos iure dixerū. Nam præter id quòd felicitatem suis virtutibus ascribunt, simul etiā Stoicam indolentiam docent & seuere exiguNT: imò σοφὸς, quas natura hominū mentibus inseuit, eradicare student. Quid enim aliud faciunt, cùm parentes proprios liberos abnegare, & monasterijs includere iubent? Quando item liberos instituunt, vt omni parentū amore & cura abiečta solis monasticis legi‑bus vacent? Notum est lippis & tonsoribus quàm dura & indigna distu & creditu tenellis animis instillent. Qui vero tales sunt, non possunt nō euangelij hostes esse, quod vasanos istos & furiosos erro‑res liberè accusat, & dānat. At non ideo cedendū talibus, imò contra illos sedulò, iuxta Pauli exem‑plū, pugnare conuenit. Qua vero ratione nobis pugna hæc ineunda fit, eode docemur. Nec enim dubiū est, quin argutis fallacijs & verbosis concertationibus Philosophi causam suam tueri volerint. Sed inanes verborū contentiones Paulus deuitans, vnū Christum Iesum & mortuorū resurrectionē illis proponit, doces duo hæc omnium philosophorū & hæreticorū delirijs cōfutandis sufficere. Si enim Chri‑stum Iesum expiandis hominū peccatis & saluando humano generi in mundū misit Deus, nec Epicu‑reorum nec Stoicorū siue iustitiarioru dogma subsistere potest, qui vel Deum humana curare negant, vel nostrorum operum meritis salutem tribuunt. Rursum, si mortui resurgunt, vitam aliam superesse necesse est, & proinde stultissimum fuerit hominū felicitatem in præsentu seculi voluptate collocare. Posset hoc ipsum ad omnes sectas & hæreses extendi, sed monuisse sufficiat vnius Christi Iesu cogni‑tione & resurrectionis articulo ita omnem fidei & salutis causam contineri, vt quicunq; in hū probè instructus fuerit, facile omnes hæreses confutare queat. Simplex igitur est salutis ratio, nec verbosis demonstrationibus & inanibus sophistarū argutijs indiget. Hanc qui constanter olim vrgere solebāt, omnibus hæreticis, licet argutissimis, facile superiores extiterunt. Libet hoc loco cōmemorare quod in Nicæna Synodo philosopho cuidam dialesticis argutij exercitatissimo contigisse Sozomenus refert. Cùm enim ille noua quotidie certamina episcopis moueret, qui & ipsi ingenij dexteritate & arte fre‑ti cum illo disputabant, nec à quoquam constringi posset, quidam simplicissimæ naturæ vir, qui nihil nisi Iesum Christum, & hunc crucifixum nouerat, illum aggressus ait: In nomine Iesu Christi philo‑sophe audi quæ vera sunt. Deus vnus est, qui fecit cœlum & terram, quiq; homini de terra limo for‑mato spiritum dedit, vniuersa quæ videntur & quæ non videntur virtute verbi sui creauit, & spi‑ritus sui sanctificatione firmauit. Hoc verbum & sapientia, quem nos filium dicimus, humanos mi‑seratus errores, ex virgine nascitur, & per passionem mortis à perpetua nos morte liberauit, & resur‑rectione sua æternam nobis contulit vitam. Quem & expectamus iudicem omnium, quæ gerimus, ef‑se venturum. Credis hoc ita esse philosophe? Tum ille ac si nullam vnquam contradicendi artem di‑dicisset, obstupefactus, Credo ait. Et ad discipulos totamq; auditorum coronam conuersus, dicit: Doo‑nec verbis mecū gesta res est, verba verbis opposui, & quæ dicebantur dicendi arte subuerti: vbi ve‑ro pro verbis virtus processit ex ore dicentis, non potuerunt verba virtuti resistere, nec homo Deo ad‑uersari potuit, &c. Adeò potens est simplex Christi assertio, quā quicunq; philosophorum argutijs per‑miscent, languidam reddunt & miserè eneruat, quod in schola sticis doctoribus non obscure cernitur. SED docet præterea diuersissimarum sectarum aduersus veritate conspiratio, quàm impossibile sit euangelij doctrinam absq; disceptatione mundo prædicare, quando huic contraria est, in quamcunq; partem. partem inclinet mundi sapientia, siue nimirum virtutis studium explodat, siue vrgeat & amplectatur. Reuera ergo ridiculi sunt, qui hoc à nobis hodie exigunt, quod nec Christum nec apostolos praestare potuisse constat.
units.tr: Luke also sets out the order that Paul followed in spreading the kingdom of Christ among the Athenians. First he held a discussion on this matter with the Jews, because he knew they would lend their ears more readily than anyone, and he brought forward Moses and the prophets. Then he took in hand those who, from their dealings with the Jews, had tasted some purer faith and religion but were not yet fully instructed. Once these foundations were laid, he approached whomever he met in the marketplace, and he advanced so far that the philosophers, of whom that city had plenty, began to dispute against Paul. Of their many schools, the Epicureans and Stoics especially entered the arena. Although they differed from each other entirely, they could now agree in attacking the minister of the truth. The Epicureans, enemies of all true wisdom and of more refined learning, placed the highest good in pleasure. They called it an honourable pleasure, since, as they said, it secured tranquillity of mind and soundness of body. Yet by not rising any higher, they were the authors of the most absurd doctrines that followed from it. Because the fear of God and the thought of a future life strike terror into consciences and make all external things bitter, they denied both God's providence and the life to come. They fabled that God strolls about the corners of heaven and is touched by no care for mortal affairs, and that souls die together with bodies. Hence they concluded with that saying of Sardanapalus: Eat, drink, play; after death there is no pleasure. The Stoics, on the other hand, quite opposed to these, taught that the highest good of man lies in virtue. Although this seems plausible and holy, it drew people away from God no less than the Epicureans did, since it taught them to seek happiness in the merits of their own works. Again, because they saw that the pursuit of virtue is disturbed by the emotions, the followers of the highest good wanted to be wholly free of them, so that they showed no sign of joy in prosperity or of sorrow in adversity. Thus they made men into blocks and stones, that is, apathy [ἀπάθεις] and freedom from anger [ἀοργησία], people not even subject to the natural affections by which parents and children are bound to one another. Besides this, from the connection of causes they invented fate, to which God himself would be subject. These things teach those with whom Paul had contention, and at the same time they warn us who are the enemies of the gospel and of true doctrine today, and in every age. For although the names of Epicureans and Stoics were in use only among the Gentiles in the past, there were also within God's external people those who thought the same as they did, and such people are not lacking even today. Certainly among the Jews there was once Nabal, who said, There is no God, and David testifies that this opinion had countless companions. Psal. 14. & 53. Likewise there were those who said: The Lord does not see, nor does the God of Jacob understand. Psal. 94. Concerning the last times, into which we have fallen, the oracles of Christ and the apostles stand, which teach that Epicureanism will reign completely. For Christ says: As it was in the days of Noah, so it will be in the days of the Son of man. They were eating, drinking, taking wives, and being given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered the ark, etc. Luc. 17. And Peter foretold that in the last days mockers would come, who walk according to their own lusts and say: Where is the promise of his coming? For since the day the fathers fell asleep, all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation, etc. 2. Pet. 3. Yet such people are seen everywhere today, who, although they do not openly profess Epicureanism, so live that it is plain to anyone that they believe neither in gods nor in a future life. But these same people cannot bear the light of the gospel, because (as Christ says, Iohan. 3.) their evil works are exposed by it. In a similar way the Stoic dogma can be found in every age. For among the Jews the Pharisees once held this view; they trusted in the righteousness of their own works, and they were the most bitter of all enemies of Christ. Their kind (as we saw above in chapter 15) produced the troublers of the primitive Church, who mixed the gospel with the law and the merits of works with faith. In the time of the Fathers the Pelagians arose, asserters of the same doctrine. And if you look for them in our own century, you will find monks, whom one may rightly call the sworn disciples of Zeno. For besides ascribing happiness to their own virtues, they also teach Stoic indifference and enforce it strictly; indeed they strive to root out the natural affections that nature has planted in human minds. For what else do they do when they order parents to renounce their own children and shut them up in monasteries? Or when they educate children so that, with all parental love and care cast aside, they may devote themselves only to monastic laws? It is well known to barbers and tonsurers how harsh and unworthy to say or believe are the things they instil into tender minds. Those who are like this cannot but be enemies of the gospel, since the gospel freely accuses and condemns these mad and frenzied errors. Yet we should not yield to such people. Rather, following Paul's example, we ought to fight against them diligently. The method by which this fight is to be entered upon is taught in the same place. For there is no doubt that the philosophers wanted to defend their cause with subtle fallacies and wordy disputes. But Paul, avoiding empty contests of words, sets before them only Jesus Christ and the resurrection of the dead, showing that these two are enough to refute the delusions of all philosophers and heretics. For if God sent Christ Jesus into the world to expiate human sins and save the human race, then neither the doctrine of the Epicureans nor that of the Stoics or of the self-righteous can stand, since they either deny that God takes care of human affairs or ascribe salvation to the merits of our works. Again, if the dead rise, another life must remain, and so it would be most foolish to place human happiness in the pleasure of the present age. This could be extended to all sects and heresies, but it is enough to have warned that the whole cause of faith and salvation is contained in the knowledge of the one Christ Jesus and the article of the resurrection, so that whoever is well instructed in these can easily refute all heresies. The way of salvation is therefore simple, and it needs no wordy demonstrations or empty subtleties of the sophists. Those who used to press this constantly always proved superior to all heretics, however clever. It is worth recalling here what Sozomen reports happened at the Nicene Synod to a certain philosopher highly practised in dialectical subtleties. When he kept stirring up new contests with the bishops, who also relied on their own skill and art and disputed with him, and no one could bind him, a certain man of the simplest nature, who knew nothing but Jesus Christ and him crucified, attacked him and said: In the name of Jesus Christ, philosopher, listen to what is true. God is one, who made heaven and earth, who gave spirit to man formed from the clay of the earth, who created all things visible and invisible by the power of his word, and established them by the sanctification of his Spirit. This Word and Wisdom, whom we call the Son, out of pity for our human errors, was born of a virgin, and by the passion of his death freed us from eternal death, and by his resurrection gave us eternal life. We expect him to come as judge of all that we do. Do you believe this is so, philosopher? Then he, as if he had never learned any art of contradiction, astonished, said: I believe. And turning to his disciples and the whole crowd of listeners, he said: As long as the matter was conducted with words, I opposed words to words and overturned what was said by the art of speaking; but when power came forth from the mouth of the speaker instead of words, words could not resist power, nor could a man oppose God, etc. So powerful is the simple assertion of Christ that whoever mixes it with the subtleties of philosophers makes it feeble and miserably weakens it, as is not obscurely seen in the scholastic doctors. BUT it further shows how the conspiracy of very diverse sects against the truth makes it impossible to preach the doctrine of the gospel to the world without dispute, since it is opposed to the wisdom of the world, whichever way that wisdom leans, whether it rejects the pursuit of virtue or urges and embraces it. Truly, then, those are ridiculous who demand of us today what Christ and the apostles are known not to have been able to deliver.

units.la: Restat vt videamus, quomodo ab Athenien s ibus Pauli doctrina excepta fit: vbi duo se produnt hominum genera. Alterum eorum est, qui oblatam salutis praedicationem cum conuitio excipiunt, dicentes: Quid sibi vult spermologus siue nugator ille dicere? Atqui inter sapientiae professores isti inueniuntur. Adeo inepta est ad percipiendum regnum Dei humana sapientia, vt illi stultitia videatur quicquid de Christo & vita aeterna praedicatur. Vbi habes quod illis respondeas, qui nobis hodie sapientissimorum & maximorum hominum authoritatem totumq; illud mundi supercilium obiiciunt. Nam si ista valerent, haud dubie causa fuit Paulus apud Athenienses cecidisset. Alterum vero genus curiosorum est, qui cum nouos deos aut semideos praedicari putarent, Paulum abreptum in Areopago sistunt, vt ibi publice suae doctrinae rationem reddat. Confluit ergo ad illum infinita otiosorum hominum turba, tam ciuium quam hospitum, quibus hoc vnum curae fuisse Lucas scribit, vt noua quotidie audiendi siue dicendi copia sibi fieret. Ea vero occasione Deus facit, vt in celeberrimo totius orbis loco Christum praedicet. Interim docet locus hic, quae euangelij in hoc mundo fors sit. Aut enim turpissime à manifestis hostibus explodentur, aut eo non minori turpitudine leuissimi homines abuntur, vt ipsorum affectibus inseruiat, qui si illud votis suis minus respondere videant, iam ipsi quoq; manifesti hostes fiunt. Hac vero quia omnibus seculis facilitata sunt, neminem offendere debent, quin potius Pauli constantiam in iniuria fide nitamur saluatore nostro Iesu Christo, qui electus licet sit ab ijs, qui ecclesiae Dei aedificatores haberi volunt, est tamen factus caput anguli. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains for us to see how Paul's teaching was received by the Athenians, where two kinds of people reveal themselves. One group receives the offered proclamation of salvation with mockery, saying: What does this babbler [σπερμολόγος] want to say? And yet such men are found among the professors of wisdom. Human wisdom is so unfit to grasp the kingdom of God that whatever is preached about Christ and eternal life seems foolishness to them. Here you have an answer for those who today object to us the authority of the wisest and greatest men and all that haughtiness of the world. For if those things carried weight, Paul's cause would undoubtedly have fallen among the Athenians. The other kind are the curious, who, thinking that new gods or demigods were being proclaimed, bring Paul, taken away, before the Areopagus, to give a public account of his teaching. So an endless crowd of idle people, citizens and strangers alike, flocks to him, for whom, Luke writes, this one concern was that they might have a constant supply of new things to hear or say. On that occasion God makes it so that Christ is preached in the most famous place in the whole world. Meanwhile this place teaches what the fortune of the gospel in this world is. For either it is shamefully rejected by open enemies, or else light-minded men, with no less shame, are beguiled into serving their own passions; and if they see it does not match their wishes, they too become open enemies. Since these things have been made easy in every age, they ought to offend no one. Rather let us rest on Paul's steadfastness in the face of injury, in faith in our Saviour Jesus Christ, who, though he is rejected by those who want to be regarded as the builders of God's church, has nonetheless become the chief cornerstone. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 117.

units.la: Stans autem Paulus in medio Areopagi, ait: Viri Athenienses, per omnia fere superstitiosiores vos video. Praeteriens enim & contemplans religiones vestras, inueni & aram, in qua scriptum erat, Ignoto Deo. Quem igitur ignorantes colitis, hunc ego annuncio vobis. Deus qui fecit mundum & omnia quae in eo sunt, hic coeli & terrae cum sit dominus, non in manufactis templis habitat, nec manibus hominum colitur, indigens aliquo: cum ipse det omnibus vitam & halitum per omnia.
units.tr: And Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: "Men of Athens, I see that you are in every way rather superstitious. For as I passed by and looked carefully at your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was written, 'To the Unknown God.' What therefore you worship without knowing it, I proclaim to you. God, who made the world and all things in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made by hands, nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all life and breath and all things."

units.la: Paulus apostolus in priori ad Corinthios ait: Nos praedicamus Christum crucifixum, Iudaeis quidem offendiculum, Graecis vero stultitiam. Quia enim carnis ratio in ea duntaxat, quae ob oculos versantur, respicit, nec percipit spiritus Dei mysteria, non potest illi non stultissimum videri, si quis in Christo crucifixo & publica infamia notato salutem quaerat. Id cum alibi, tum Athenis Paulus ipse expertus est. Cum enim in ea vrbe inter sapientissimos, qui illo seculo babebantur, Christum praedicaret, adeo non auditur ab illis, vt vix vsquam alibi minus profecisse videri possit. Alij enim illius doctrinam cum conuitio excipiunt & explodunt, alij vero curiositate moti suis affectibus illam accommodant. Interim in tanta hominum corruptione admirabilis Dei sapientia elucet, quae perditissimo curiosorum hominum affectu bene vtitur. Ea enim occasione fit, vt Paulus in Areopagum, ceu in frequentissimum totius orbis theatrum productus, euangelium Iesu Christi praedicet. Argumentum vero concionis est, quod Athenienses a superstitione & idololatria ad vnius & veri Dei cultum per Iesum Christum reuocare conatur. Primo igitur amice illos arguit & nimiae superstitionis accusat. Inde de Deo & vero illius cultu disserit, eorum simul stultitiam taxans, qui Deum simulachris aut vllis alijs hominum inuentionibus coli posse existimant. Tandem ad Christi causam propius descendit. In praesenti tamen exordium cum paucis alijs, quae huic cohaerent, excutiemus.
units.tr: The apostle Paul says in his first letter to the Corinthians: "We preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks." For since human reason looks only at those things which lie before the eyes, and does not perceive the mysteries of the Spirit of God, it cannot but seem utterly foolish that anyone should seek salvation in Christ crucified and marked with public infamy. Paul himself experienced this, both elsewhere and at Athens. For when he preached Christ in that city, among the wisest men who were then regarded as such, he was so little heard by them that he could scarcely seem to have made less progress anywhere else. Some received his teaching with mockery and scorned it, while others, moved by curiosity, adapted it to their own passions. Yet in so great a corruption of men, the wonderful wisdom of God shines forth, which makes good use of the most depraved curiosity of men. For by this occasion Paul was brought before the Areopagus, as onto the most crowded theatre of the whole world, and there he preaches the gospel of Jesus Christ. The argument of the sermon is that he seeks to call the Athenians back from superstition and idolatry to the worship of the one and true God through Jesus Christ. First, then, he gently accuses them and charges them with excessive superstition. Then he discourses about God and his true worship, at the same time rebuking the folly of those who think God can be worshipped by images or any other human inventions. Finally he comes closer to the cause of Christ. For now, however, we shall examine the introduction, together with a few other points that belong to it.

units.la: Exordio breui vtitur, quo se artificiose insinuans simul propositionem & summam concionis com prehendit. Viros Athenienses vocat, eo quod iste titulus apud illos honorificentissimus haberetur,
units.tr: He uses a brief introduction, by which, insinuating himself skilfully, he at the same time grasps the proposition and the substance of the sermon. He calls them "Men of Athens," because that title was regarded as most honourable among them.

units.la: I. Exordium cum insinuatione. quemadmodum Demosthenis & aliorum orationes docent. Ignorauit enim veteres ambitio forum titulorum insolentiam, quibus hodie dementari & inebriari gaudent superbissimi vanissimi homines, qui omnem gloriam in illorum splendore sitam esse arbitrantur. Porro amice admodum sese illorum animis insinuat, ne orationis principio offensi, aures praebere negarent. Ait enim: Per omnia fere superstitiosiores vos esse video. Laudatur vestra vbique sapientia & prudentia, sed in religione non nimis modo, verumetiam rerum omnino incerti esse videmini, adeo ut minimum sapiatis, vbi cumprimis sapere oportebat. Ne quis vero illum mendacij arguerēt, publica altaris cuiusdam inscriptione probat quod dicit. Quae qualis fuerit, alij curiosius inuestigauerunt. Graeca scholia Philippidae cuiusdam historiam adducunt, & inscriptione eiusmodi fuisse tradunt: ⊙ωϊς ἀσίας καὶ Ἀφρικῆς καὶ Λυβίης, Θεῷ ἀγνώσῳ κ ἀξ...
units.tr: I. The introduction with its insinuation. As the orations of Demosthenes and others show. For the ancients did not know the arrogance of empty titles, in which the proud and vain men of today delight to be intoxicated and driven mad, thinking that all glory lies in their splendour. Moreover, he insinuates himself very politely into their minds, so that they might not be offended at the beginning of the speech and refuse to give him a hearing. For he says: "I see that you are in almost every respect more superstitious. Your wisdom and prudence are praised everywhere, but in religion you appear not merely imprudent but also quite uncertain of things, so that you are least wise where above all you ought to be wise." Lest anyone should accuse him of lying, he proves what he says by a public inscription on a certain altar. What it was like, others have investigated more carefully. The Greek scholia cite a history of a certain Philippides, and report that the inscription was of this kind: ΤΩΙ ΑΣΙΑΣ ΚΑΙ ΑΦΡΙΚΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΛΥΒΙΗΣ, ΘΕΩΙ ἈΓΝΩΣΤΩΙ ΚΑΙ ἈΞ... [Ἀσίας καὶ Ἀφρικῆς καὶ Λιβύης, Θεῷ ἀγνώστῳ καὶ ἀξ...]

units.la: Athenienses reliquis superstitiosiores. Ego talem omnino fuisse crediderim, qualis a Paulo recensetur. Nec enim calumniatoris nomen effugere potuisset, si altaris inscriptionem, quae illis haud dubie sacrosancta erat, mutatis verbis citauisset. Sed institutum Pauli cumprimis observare conuenit, quod est, ut Atheniensis nihil in religione certi & solidi habere, sed incerta superstitionibus vagari euincat, quando non contemi Dijs patrijs & gentilitijs, ignotum quoq; colant.
units.tr: The Athenians were more superstitious than the rest. I should believe that it was altogether such as Paul describes. For he could not have escaped the name of a slanderer if he had quoted the altar's inscription, which was no doubt holy to them, with the words changed. But it is especially fitting to observe Paul's purpose, which is to prove that the Athenian had nothing certain and solid in religion, but wandered among uncertain superstitions, since, without despising their ancestral and national gods, they also worshipped an unknown one.

units.la: Religio absque Deicognitione nulla est. mortuis quidem securis esse licet, cum ab ipsis adhuc tributum exigat insatiabilis sacrificulorum aua ritia, quae mortuorum animas in purgatorio excruciari & excoqui fingit? Annon ibi Deus ignotus colitur, Deus Maozim nimirum, quem (ut Daniel ait) patres omnes ignorauerunt, qui vel ex pane fit, vel in panem conuertitur? Atqui vtinam haec expenderent hodie homines, & discerent quam miserum sit veritatis luce destitui. Qui enim illa carent, cum apud seipsos rerum omnium in religione incerti sunt, tum coram Deo operam omnem ludunt, qui humanis traditionibus coli nec vult nec potest. Isa.29. Matth.15. Paulum ergo & apostolos audiamus, quos in eum finem Deus instituit, ut sui cognitionem veram verumque cultum caeco mundo traderent.
units.tr: Religion without knowledge of God is nothing. Are they indeed safe from the dead, since the insatiable greed of the little priests still exacts tribute from them, pretending that the souls of the dead are tormented and purged in purgatory? Is not the unknown god worshipped there, namely the god Maozim, whom (as Daniel says) all their fathers did not know, who is either made from bread or turned into bread? Would that men today would consider these things and learn how wretched it is to be deprived of the light of truth. For those who lack it, since they are uncertain about all things in religion among themselves, also in the sight of God waste all their labour, since he neither wills nor is able to be worshipped by human traditions. Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Let us therefore hear Paul and the apostles, whom God established for this end, that they might hand down to the blind world the true knowledge of himself and a true worship.

units.la: Porro omnia haec in secunda sua concionis parte Paulus sic tradit, ut simul gentilitios errores refellat, ex quibus exorti sunt, qui hodie adhuc mundum dementant. Interim licet illi cum acutissimis philosophis & hominibus curiosissimum res sit, non tamen argute de Dei essentia (quam inscrutabilem esse, ipse Deus testatur. Exod.33.) disputat, sed ab operibus Deum describens, quid de illo credi fas sit, & quomodo coli debeat, admonet. DEVS (inquit) qui fecit mundum & omnia quae in eo sunt, hic caeli & terrae cum sit Dominus, &c. Videtur haec Epicureis opponere, quasi mundum vel ab aeterno esse, vel sponte & temere ex atomis emersisse, Deo certe nequaquam curae esse, docebant. At Paulus mundi creatorem simul & dominum esse ait Deum, & hoc quasi irrefragabile ponit suae doctrinae principium, quod nemo negauerit, nisi qui communi etiam sensu careat. Ex eo autem colligit, vanam esse templorum religionem, quae apud Graecos tanto in precio & authoritate erat, ut Persas non alio nomine magis odissent, quam quod illi templa Graeciae passim exstruxerant, eo quod illa superstitioni potius quam pietati seruire viderent. Ita vero argumentatur Paulus: Qui omnium Dominus est, vbi, praesens adesse oportet. Deus vero ut omnium creator, ita etiam omnium Dominus est. Ergo vbi praesens est, & per consequens non inhabitat templa, quae hominum manibus extructa sunt. At quod aduersus gentes dicitur, qui religionem ex templorum splendore metiebantur, & illis Dei maiestatem, potentiam & gratiam alligabant, hoc ipsum contra omnes eos facit, qui cum veri Dei cultu glorientur, hoc ipso tamen errore ebrij delirant. Solomon certe cum immensis sumptibus templum extruxisset, tandem Deo ait: En caeli caelorum te non capiunt, quanto minus aedes ista quam extruxi? 1. Reg.8. Et ipse Deus apud Isaiam cap.66. dicit: Caelum mihi solium est, terra vero scabellum pedum meorum: vbi igitur erit domus ista, quam aedificabitis mihi? Ieremias quoque duriter admodum Iudaeos, templi religione confidentes, reprehendit. Vide Ier.7. Quid, quod Christus veros adoratores non certis locis alligatos esse, sed passim in spiritu & veritate adorare docet? Idemque minime credendum esse iis monet, qui Dei gratiam vel sui meriti effectum certis in locis monstrent. Ioban.4. Matth.24. Tollitur ergo his vniuersa peregrinationum religio, in quibus fluctissimi homines, gentilitio prorsus errore, summam salutis collocatam esse putant. Nec tamen ideo templorum vsum in vniuersum damnamus. Externa enim religioni seruiunt, quae propter fidei professionem & fouendum vnanime pietatis studium necessaria est: dum in illis ad audiendum Dei verbum, ad preces publicas & sacramentorum administrationem conuenitur. Quibus rebus templa sic consecrata esse debent, ut nefas putemus illa prophanis vsibus polluere.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul sets out all these things in the second part of his sermon in such a way that he also refutes the errors of the Gentiles, from which have arisen those who even now drive the world mad. Yet although it is a matter of the greatest curiosity for him to deal with the most acute philosophers and men, he does not argue subtly about the essence of God, which God himself testifies to be unsearchable (Exod. 33.), but, describing God from his works, he admonishes what it is right to believe about him and how he ought to be worshipped. "God," he says, "who made the world and all things in it, since he is Lord of heaven and earth, etc." This seems to be set against the Epicureans, who taught that the world either was from eternity or had emerged by chance from atoms, and that God certainly had no concern for it. But Paul says that God is at once the creator and the lord of the world, and he lays this down as an unshakeable principle of his teaching, which no one would deny except one who lacks even common sense. From this he concludes that the religion of temples is vain, a religion which among the Greeks was held in such high esteem and authority that the Persians hated them for no other reason more than that they had built temples throughout Greece, since they seemed to serve superstition rather than piety. Paul argues thus: He who is Lord of all must be present wherever he is. But God, as creator of all, is also Lord of all. Therefore he is present wherever he is, and consequently does not dwell in temples which have been built by human hands. But what is said against the nations, who measured religion by the splendour of temples and bound the majesty, power and grace of God to them, applies equally against all those who boast of the true worship of God and yet rave in this very error. Solomon, certainly, when he had built the temple at immense cost, said at last to God: "Behold, the heaven of heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house which I have built?" 1 Kings 8. And God himself says through Isaiah, chapter 66: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; where then will be the house which you will build for me?" Jeremiah also reproves the Jews very harshly, who trusted in the religion of the temple. See Jer. 7. What of the fact that Christ teaches that true worshippers are not bound to fixed places, but worship everywhere in spirit and truth? And he warns that those ought by no means to be believed who point out God's grace, or the effect of their own merit, in certain places. John 4. Matth. 24. Therefore the whole religion of pilgrimages is abolished by this, in which men, wholly in the grip of a Gentile error, think that the sum of salvation is placed. Yet we do not on that account condemn the use of temples in general. For they serve external religion, which is necessary for the profession of faith and for fostering the unanimous zeal of piety, since people assemble in them to hear the word of God, for public prayers and for the administration of the sacraments. For these purposes temples ought to be so consecrated that we think it wrong to defile them with profane uses.

units.la: Sed pergens in Dei descriptione Paulus, illum nullius indigum esse dicit. Unde colligit, eundem non coli manibus, neque religionem in nullis externis hominum officiis consistere. Antecedens autem per id probat, quod illum omnibus vitam & habitum largiri docet. Eo argumento inanem sacrificiorum fiduciam impugnat, in quibus praecipuam religionis partem veteres repositam habebant. Videtur vero Paulus argumentum ex Dei verbis sumpsisse, quibus ille Israelitas accusat, quod se sacrificiis coli & placari putarent. Nam Psal.50. ait: Non est ut accipiam de domo tua iuvencum, nec de caulis tuis hircos. Meae enim sunt omnes ferae sylvarum, & pecudes in mille montibus. Noui cunctas in montibus volucres, penes me sunt animantes agrestes. Si esuriero, non est ut tibi indicem, &c. At eodem argumento totam Papisticam religionem damnari constat. Quid enim in illa aliud fit, quam quod infelici superstitione decepti homines, egentibus a Christo commendatus, officia sua subtrahunt, eaque offerunt Diuis non egentibus, imo qui nec norunt nos? Isa.63. Quid quod maxima donariorum pars simulachris cedit, sensu quoque carentibus? vel sacrificiis luxu & libidine diffluentibus? Interim tam altas radices egit superstitio, ut hominem spoliatum iugulare
units.tr: But Paul, continuing his description of God, says that he needs nothing. From this he concludes that God is not worshipped with human hands, and that religion does not consist in any external services of men. He proves the premise by showing that God gives life and all things to everyone. By this argument he attacks the empty confidence in sacrifices, in which the ancients held the chief part of religion to lie. Paul seems to have taken the argument from the words of God, in which God accuses the Israelites of thinking that he was honoured and appeased by sacrifices. For Psalm 50 says: "I will not take a bullock out of your house, nor goats out of your folds. For all the beasts of the forests are mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the mountains; the wild creatures are in my keeping. If I were hungry, I would not tell you," etc. Yet it is clear that the whole Papist religion is condemned by the same argument. For what else happens in it, than that men deceived by an unhappy superstition withdraw their duties from Christ, who commended the needy, and offer them to saints who are not needy, indeed who do not even know us? Isaiah 63. What of the fact that the greatest part of the offerings goes to images, which also lack sense, or to sacrifices dissolved in luxury and lust? Meanwhile superstition has struck such deep roots that it thinks it less wrong to clothe a naked poor man than to strip some covering from an altar or image. O death, O times!

units.la: Deus non colitur sacrificiis. minus nefas putetur, quàm ex altari aut imagine detrahto velo aliquo vestire pauperem. O morte, ô tempora.
units.tr: God is not worshipped with sacrifices. It is thought less wrong than to take some covering from an altar or image to clothe a poor man. O death, O times!

units.la: At obijciat aliquis: Si sacrificijs non colitur Deus, cur illa in populo suo per Mosem instituit & requisiuit? Sed obseruemus duo potissimum fuisse sacrificiorum genera. Primum expiatoria pro peccatis habebat, quae ita dicebantur, non quòd taurorum aut hircorum sanguine peccata expiari possent (id enim diserte Paulus negat ad Hebraeos 10. cap.) sed quòd Christum figurarent, quem pro mundi peccatis praefinito tempore moriturum sancti & pij omnes credebant. Docebant praeterea pecuinos affectus mactare, & spiritum contritum in Dei conspectum afferre, quod sacrificium Deo acceptissimum esse, Dauid testatur. Psal. 51. Alterum genus gratulatoria pro acceptis beneficijs comprehendebat. Sanguine vero constabat fere omnia, quia nondum fusus erat Christi sanguis quo solo patrem placari oportebat. Hoc igitur effuso, & peractio redemptionis nostrae mysterio, expiatorium pro peccatis, sacrificium nullum superesse. Sufficit enim Christi meritum, nec alio sacrificio opus est, quemadmodum multis epistola ad Hebraeos docet. Interim non carent sacrificijs Christiani, incrementis vero, quia postquam effusum Christi sanguinem, nullius sanguinis pecuini aut etiam humani vsus est in ijs, quae ad ordinarium Dei cultum pertinent. Seipsos enim Deo viuentes hostias statuunt. Rom. 12. Preces & gratiarum actiones per Christum offerunt. Opes vero & pecunias, adde & cibos ac vestes, & quaecunque sunt eius generis officia, in pauperes conferunt, quos sibi Christus substituit. Matth. 25.26. & Heb.13. Qui istis rite defunguntur, religioni Christiana satis faciunt. Teneamus ergo Pauli sententiam, qui Deum nullius indigere ait, colamus autem illum spiritu & veritate, & externa in viuas Dei imagines, pauperes conferamus, vt gratus Deo esse possit cultus noster per Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But someone may object: if God is not worshipped with sacrifices, why did he institute and require them among his people through Moses? But let us observe that there were chiefly two kinds of sacrifices. The first kind were expiatory for sins, and were so called not because the sins could be cleansed by the blood of bulls or goats (for Paul expressly denies this in Hebrews chapter 10), but because they foreshadowed Christ, whom all the holy and pious believed would die for the sins of the world at a set time. They also taught that the affections of the flesh were to be put to death, and that a contrite spirit was to be brought into God's sight, which David testifies is a sacrifice most acceptable to God (Psalm 51). The second kind comprised thank offerings for benefits received. Almost all of them, however, consisted of blood, because Christ's blood, by which alone the Father had to be appeased, had not yet been shed. Therefore, once this blood was shed and the mystery of our redemption accomplished, no expiatory sacrifice for sins remains. For Christ's merit is sufficient, and no other sacrifice is needed, as the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches in many places. Yet Christians are not without sacrifices, but they are of a different kind: since Christ's blood was shed, no blood of cattle, or even of humans, is used in those things that pertain to the ordinary worship of God. For they present themselves as living sacrifices to God (Romans 12). They offer prayers and thanksgivings through Christ. And their wealth and money, add food and clothing, and whatever duties are of that sort, they bestow on the poor, whom Christ has put in his place (Matthew 25, 26, and Hebrews 13). Those who properly discharge these duties sufficiently satisfy the Christian religion. Let us therefore hold to the saying of Paul, who says that God needs nothing; but let us worship him in spirit and truth, and let us bestow the external things on the living images of God, the poor, so that our worship may be pleasing to God through Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 118.

units.la: Fecit[Deus] ex vno sanguine omne genus hominum, vt inhabitaret super vniuersam faciem terrae, definiuitque praestituta tempora & terminos habitationis eorum, vt quaerent Deum, si forte palpent eum & inueniant. Quamuis nō longè absit ab vnoquoque nostrum. In ipso enim viuimus, mouemur & sumus: sicut & quidam veterum poetarum dixerunt. Nam huius progenies etiam sumus. Genus ergo cū simus Dei, non debemus aestimare auro vel argento vel lapidi, hominis arte & studio exsculpto, numen esse simile.
units.tr: God made from one blood every nation of men, that they should dwell upon the whole face of the earth, and he determined their appointed times and the bounds of their habitation, so that they should seek God, if perhaps they might grope after him and find him. Yet he is not far from any one of us. For in him we live, move and have our being, as some of the ancient poets also have said: for we too are his offspring. Since then we are God's offspring, we ought not to suppose that the Deity is like gold, silver or stone, carved by human skill and craft.

units.la: Vod in omnibus tum dictis tum factis suis quaesiuit Paulus, idipsum in concione sua Atheniis habita, maximè effectum voluit: nimirum vt auditores a superstitione & idololatriae vocatos ad veri Dei cognitionem & cultum adduceret. Id vero fieri impossibile erat, nisi confutatis erroribus, quibus battenus excaecati fuerant. Ne tamen prolixior fieret oratio, praecipuos tantum sibi confutandos sumit, ex quibus reliqui dependebant. Et in bellernis quidem contra inanem templorum & sacrificiorum fiduciam disseruit, docens nec templis Deum includi, cum infinitus sit, nec sacrificijs coli, cum nullius egeat. In quorum tractatione hic versatur, vt eadem omnibus illis confutandis seruiant, qui hodie religionem templorum & donariorum splendore aut magnificentia gloriantur. In praesenti vero ipsum impietatis caput aggreditur, fictitios nimirum gentium deos, & simulachra impiosque illorum cultus, de quibus magno sermonio disputat, offendens nimis turpem & pudendum errorem esse, quòd Dei maiestatem & gloriam in miserps mortales & muta simulachra hominess transferant. Et quia sibi cum illis rem esse nouerat, quibus in ea superstitione enutriti, hoc persuadere difficile erat, multa simul congerit, quae tanti erroris atrocitatem amplificare poterant. Nec dubium est pluribus verbis a Paulo tractata esse, quorum capita Lucas consignauit. Nos de singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: What Paul aimed at in all his words and deeds, he especially wished to accomplish in his sermon delivered to the Athenians: namely, to bring his hearers, who were called to superstition and idolatry, to the knowledge and worship of the true God. This could not happen unless the errors by which they had hitherto been blinded were refuted. Yet, so that his speech would not become too long, he takes up only the chief errors to be refuted, on which the rest depended. In the first part of his speech he argued against the empty confidence placed in temples and sacrifices, teaching that God cannot be confined to temples, since he is infinite, nor be honoured with sacrifices, since he needs nothing. The treatment of these points serves to refute all those who today boast of a religion of splendid or magnificent temples and offerings. In the present passage, however, he attacks the very head of impiety, namely the fictitious gods of the nations and their images and impious cults, about which he speaks at length, showing that it is a most shameful and disgraceful error to transfer God's majesty and glory to wretched mortals and dumb images of men. And since he knew that he was dealing with people brought up in that superstition, and that it would be hard to persuade them of this, he piles up many points at once which could magnify the enormity of so great an error. There is no doubt that Paul treated these matters at greater length, and Luke has recorded only the heads of his argument. We shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Primò humani generis originem in medium adducit. Deus (inquit) ex vno sanguine fecit omne genus hominum. Ex Adamo enim omnes omnium nationum & conditionum homines prognatos esse conflat. Quorsum vero ista allegat Paulus? Duo ex his colliguntur, quae praesenti causae non pertinent. rum seruiunt. Alterum est, non debuisse diuersis religionibus scindi eos, quorum vnus creator, vna & eadem origo est: sed potius in colendo suo creatore animos & studia sua omnia conferre. Gentium ergo leuitatem perstringit, qui non vnum tantummodo Deum falsum colebant, sed plures & diuersos deos fingendo inter sese multiuariam dissidebant, in hoc vno concordes, quod omnes simul a veritatis via declinarent. Inde vero generalis doctrina peti debet, aduersus naturae ordinem ab ijs peccari, qui in religione sectas & dissidia inuehunt. Authores enim sunt, vt suae originis obliti homines creatorem quoque suum negligant. Multo grauius ergo illud peccatum est, quam vulgo aestimari soleat. Vtinam vero inter Christianos hoc argumentum valeret, qui cum vnum creatorem & vnam eandemq; originem profiteantur, adhaec vno omnibusq; communi saluatore, Iesu Christo glorientur, infinitis tamen & nouis quotidie festis sese scindi patiuntur, quae a Deo creatore & Christo saluatore longissime abducunt. Et sane deplorandum est, hodie inter Christianos homines minorem esse huius argumenti authoritatem, quam olim inter gentes fuerit. Alterum quod ex humani generis origine Paulus colligit, est, ex hominibus no debere nec posse deos fieri: qui error longe lateq; inter gentes dominabatur. Constabat enim omnibus, homines aliquando fuisse, quos illi pro dijs colebant. In Creta siquidem Iouis cunae & sepulchrum seruabantur. Delos infula Apollinis & Diana, Thebae Bacchi & Herculis natiuitate insignes erant. Et a natali suo Venus Cypria, Mars Thracius, Vulcanus Lemnius, Priapus Lampfacenus dicebantur. At Paulus absurdum esse docet, vt dij esse credantur, qui aliquando homines fuerunt, cum ex vno eodemq; sanguine vniuersum genus humanum prodijsse constet. Caterum eodem argumento Diuorum cultus euerti poterit, quos pro dijs in Papatu coli manifestius est, quam vt multis demonstrari oporteat. Illis enim vota fiunt, illi in aduersis invocantur, illis factificatur, illis templa & aras consecrantur, illis dies festi nuncupantur, illis deniq; acceptae sanctae gloria transcribitur. Atqui illos homines fuisse scimus, & quidem nobis ὁμοιοπαθεῖς, vt supra apud Lyftrenses Paulus confessus est. Adhaec peccatores fuisse, tota scriptura testatur. Et apostoli non minus quam nos, Christo iubente orarunt: Remitte nobis debita nostra, &c. Fieri ergo nequit, vt iidem nunc dij facti, orbis dominium obtineant. Nec ideo illos contemnimus, aut debito honore spoliamus. Agnoscimus illos praeclara fuisse gratia Dei organa. Sed ex mera Dei gratia hoc illis obtigisse dicimus, id quod illi de sese passim confitentur. Quare absurdum fuerit, in illis tanquam dijs haerere, & non potius iuxta ipsorum doctrinam & exemplum, vni Deo per Christum Iesum confidere, quem nobis quoq; eiusdem gratiae mediatorem scriptura proponit. Imo non aliam maiorem Diuinam iniuriam fieri posse putamus, quam fi in illos transferatur Dei gloria, cuius acerrimi vindices illi fuerunt, adeo vt illam proprio etiam sanguine afferendam esse putauerint.
units.tr: First he brings forward the origin of the human race. "God," he says, "made every nation of men from one blood." It is agreed that all men of every nation and condition are descended from Adam. Why, however, does Paul adduce this? Two conclusions are drawn from it, which do not pertain to the present cause but serve it. The first is that those whose creator and origin are one and the same ought not to be divided into different religions, but should rather direct their minds and all their zeal to worshipping their creator. He therefore censures the levity of the nations, who worshipped not only one false God but, by inventing many diverse gods, quarrelled among themselves in many ways, agreeing only in this, that they all alike turned aside from the way of truth. From this a general teaching must be drawn: that those who introduce sects and dissensions into religion sin against the order of nature. For they are the authors of men forgetting their origin and so neglecting their creator too. This sin is therefore much graver than is commonly thought. Would that this argument carried weight among Christians, who profess one creator and one origin, and glory in one common Saviour, Jesus Christ, and yet allow themselves to be split by endless new feasts every day, which lead far away from God the creator and Christ the Saviour! And indeed it is to be lamented that today the authority of this argument among Christians is less than it once was among the nations. The second conclusion Paul draws from the origin of the human race is that men ought not, and cannot, become gods; this error held sway far and wide among the nations. For it was common knowledge that men had once lived whom they worshipped as gods. In Crete, indeed, the cradle and tomb of Jupiter were kept; the island of Delos was famous for the birth of Apollo and Diana, Thebes for the birth of Bacchus and Hercules; and Venus was called Cyprian, Mars Thracian, Vulcan Lemnian, and Priapus of Lampsacus, from their birthplaces. But Paul teaches that it is absurd for those who once were men to be believed gods, since it is agreed that the whole human race sprang from one and the same blood. Moreover, by this same argument the cult of the saints could be overthrown, which is more manifestly practised as divine in the Papacy than it needs to be demonstrated by many arguments. For vows are made to them, they are invoked in adversity, sacrifices are offered to them, temples and altars are consecrated to them, festival days are named after them, and finally the glory due to holy ones is transferred to them. Yet we know that they were men, and indeed men "of like passions" with us [ὁμοιοπαθεῖς], as Paul confessed above among the Lystrans. Furthermore, Scripture testifies throughout that they were sinners; and the apostles, no less than we, prayed at Christ's command: "Forgive us our debts," etc. It is therefore impossible that the same men, now made gods, should hold dominion over the world. Nor on this account do we despise them or deprive them of due honour. We acknowledge that they were distinguished instruments of God's grace. But we say that this came to them from sheer grace of God, as they themselves everywhere confess. Hence it would be absurd to cling to them as gods, rather than, according to their own teaching and example, to trust in the one God through Jesus Christ, whom Scripture sets before us too as the mediator of that same grace. Indeed, we believe that no greater injury to the divine majesty can be done than if God's glory were transferred to them, when they themselves were the most zealous defenders of it, so much so that they thought it ought to be maintained even with their own blood.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui homines non modo a Deo conditos, verumetiam in terram collocatos fniffe, illamq; inhabitandam a Deo accepisse dicit. Ne quis vero inde Epicureum dogma hauriret, Deumq; terras hominum arbitrio permisisse putaret, diuina prouidentia aeterno decreto hoc omne factum esse docet. Deus (inquit) praefinuit praestituta tempora & terminos habitationis eorum: id est, Deus singulis gentibus & populis suas regiones attribuit, easq; certis finibus conclusit, idemq; tempora quoq; constituit, quibus iuxta aeterna suae prouidentiae decreta vel oriri vel occidere debeant. Nihil ergo in terris fortuito & citra Dei prouidentiam geritur. Hac vero in eam finem Paulus allegat, vt euincat, omnes populos in vno vero Deo colendo occupari debere, a quo suas regiones inhabitandas acceperint, & cuius prouidentia regantur simul & conseruentur. Ita vero communem gentium errorem refutat, qui singulis nationibus & vrbibus suos deos tutelares tribuebant. Athenienses enim Palladis numine se tutos esse credebant. Ephesus Diana protectrice gloriabatur. Cyprij Venerem sibi tutricem delegerant. Carthago sub Iunonis tutela degebat. Romani Marte progenitore & praesidi nitebantur. Imo eo vsq; superstitio progressa erat, vt nulla domus esset, quae non suos lares aut penates proprios coleret. Qui error inter Christianos quoq; inualuit, cum nulla reperiatur ciuitas, quae non Diuum aliquem sibi vendicarit, cuius praesidio se tutam esse existimet. At Paulus Deum regionum omnium distributorem, omniumq; populorum vnicum praesidem esse docet: qui cum vbiq; praesit, nullo vicario indiget, qui illius vices suppleat. Interim obseruandum Deo non praescientiam modo, sed prouidentiam tribui, quae omnes cum regiones tum populos regit, & cuius decreto fiant quaecunq; fiunt. Ab huius nutu regnorum vices pendere, tota scriptura doc cet, in primis vero Danielis de quatuor mundi monarchijs vaticinia. Ab eadem priuatorum hominum fortunæ pendent. Deus enim ex puluere (vt Dauides ait) egenum extrahit, eumq; inter populi sui principes collocat. Psalm. 113. Exempla in Saule extant, Dauide, Ieroboamo, Cyro, Ottomanno & infinitis alijs, vt quotidiana omittam. Quid quòd ad minutissima quæq; sese demittit Dei prouidentia, dum volucres cæli curat, flores agri vestit, & capitum nostrorum pilos numeratos habet? Matth. 6. 10. Longè ergo facessant, qui in Deo præscientiam solam agnoscunt, eumq; otiosum rerum quæ in mundo geruntur, spectatorem esse fingunt. Nos potius illius prouidentia res omnes gubernari credamus. Id enim vt ad vitam piè instituendam plurimum momenti habet: ita in aduersis haud vulgarem nobis consolationem afferre solet.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who says that God not only created men and placed them on the earth, but also appointed the land for them to inhabit. Lest anyone should draw from this an Epicurean dogma and suppose that God had left the lands to the will of men, he teaches that all this was done by divine providence according to an eternal decree. "God," he says, "determined the appointed times and the bounds of their habitation." That is, God assigned to each nation and people its own regions, enclosed them within fixed boundaries, and likewise fixed the times at which, according to the eternal decrees of his providence, they must rise and fall. Nothing therefore happens on earth by chance and apart from God's providence. Paul adduces this for the purpose of proving that all peoples ought to be busy worshipping the one true God, from whom they have received the regions they inhabit, and by whose providence they are at once governed and preserved. In this way he refutes the common error of the nations, who assigned to each nation and city its own guardian gods. The Athenians, for instance, believed they were safe under the protection of the goddess Pallas; Ephesus boasted of Diana as its protectress; the Cypriots had chosen Venus as their guardian; Carthage lived under the protection of Juno; the Romans relied on Mars as their progenitor and defender. Indeed superstition had advanced so far that there was no household which did not worship its own household gods or penates. This error has also prevailed among Christians, since there is no city that has not claimed some saint for itself, in whose protection it thinks itself safe. But Paul teaches that God is the distributor of all regions and the sole guardian of all peoples; since he presides everywhere, he needs no vicar to fill his place. Meanwhile it should be observed that to God is ascribed not only foreknowledge but providence, which governs all regions and peoples alike, and by whose decree whatever happens comes to pass. That the changes of kingdoms depend on his nod, the whole of Scripture teaches, especially the prophecies of Daniel about the four monarchies of the world. On the same providence depend the fortunes of private men as well: for God, as David says, raises the needy out of the dust and places him among the princes of his people (Psalm 113). Examples are found in Saul, David, Jeroboam, Cyrus, the Ottoman and countless others, not to mention the daily instances. And what of the fact that divine providence descends to the smallest things, since it cares for the birds of the heavens, clothes the flowers of the field, and has the hairs of our heads numbered? (Matth. 6.) Far away, then, with those who acknowledge in God only foreknowledge and pretend that he is an idle spectator of what happens in the world! Rather let us believe that all things are governed by his providence. For this has the greatest weight in leading a godly life, and in adversity it is wont to bring us no small consolation.

units.la: Porrò istis præmissis finem infert, propter quem homines creati & terræ incolatu donati sunt: qui est, vt dominum quærant. Dicuntur autem Deum quærere, qui in eius cognitione sedulò versantur, voluntatem illius inquirunt, illum vnicè colunt, eiq; ex animo seruiunt. Atqui hunc hominis finem esse, omnis scriptura docet. Et sanè æquum est, vt qui supremum in omnes alias creaturas dominium à Deo acceperût, illi vicissim toti addicti & dediti sint. Meminit verò huius Paulus, vt ostendat finem suum eos ignorare & terræ incolatu indignos esse, quicunq; relicto Deo vero fictitios colut, & muta simulachra venerantur. Elucet autem hoc loco stupenda humani generis corruptio. Nam si finem, ad quem conditi sumus, consyderes, patebit nihil minus facere homines, quàm quod illos facere decebat. Illorum erat Deum quærere, in quo omnis nobis felicitas repositæ iacet. At plerique incertas potius opes, vagos honores & impuras mundi voluptates sectari consueuerunt. Quòd si qui alij religiosiores inueniuntur, illi quoq; creaturis potius, quàm Deo, addicti, post illas nimis impudenter securi tantur. Quæ peruersitas eò detestabilior est, quòd cum omnes aliæ creaturæ suo officio diligentissimè fungantur, solus homo sui officij planè est immemor. Vide de his Isa. cap. 1. Ierem. item 8. &c.
units.tr: Having laid down these premises, he now states the end for which human beings were created and given a dwelling on the earth: namely, that they should seek the Lord. Those are said to seek God who busy themselves diligently with knowledge of him, inquire into his will, worship him alone, and serve him wholeheartedly. And that this is the end of man, all Scripture teaches. Indeed it is only right that those who have received from God dominion over all other creatures should in turn be wholly devoted and given over to him. Paul mentions this so as to show that those who abandon the true God and worship fictitious gods and venerate dumb images do not know their end and are unworthy of a dwelling on the earth. And in this passage the amazing corruption of the human race stands out. For if you consider the end for which we were made, it will be plain that men do almost nothing that they ought to do. It was their task to seek God, in whom all our happiness lies buried. But most people are accustomed rather to pursue uncertain riches, fleeting honours and the impure pleasures of the world. And if some others are found who are more religious, they too are devoted to creatures rather than to God, and after them they are far too brazenly secure. This perversity is the more detestable because, while all other creatures diligently carry out their function, man alone is wholly forgetful of his own. See on this Isaiah chapter 1, and likewise Jeremiah chapter 8, etc.

units.la: Quia verò nimium difficile, adeoq; impossibile videri poterat, quod Deus exigit, præoccupatione Paulus omnem tergiuersandi occasionem eripit. Et primò quidem Deum ita à nobis quæri vellet, vt illum palpando quoq; assequi & inuenire liceat. Cuius dicti ratio est, quòd passim sese sensibus nostris ingerit, dum per visibilia opera inuisibilem suam potentiam, sapientiam & bonitatem reuelat, vt pluribus ad Rom. 1. cap. docetur. Et sanè nulla mundi pars est tam abiecta, nullaque vilis creatura, quæ non ineffabilem Dei potentiam nobis ob oculos statuat. Elucet hac in rudibus terræ glebis, quibus mirificam fructificandi vim inesse videmus. Eadem in temporum vicibus, in perpetuis cæli motibus, tempestatibus omnibusq; alijs cœlorum influentijs cernitur. Imò floseulum aliquod contemplare, & creatoris potentiam infinitam summæ sapientiæ coniunctam admirari cogeris. At quia infiniti operis erat singulas mundi partes percurrere, & multorum ea est stupiditas, vt nihil extra se obseruare & indagare possint: propius adhuc se nobis Deus insinuat, nec procul ab vnoquoq; nostrum abest. In ipso enim viuimus, mouemur & sumus, adeoq; ipsius sumus progenies. Quis enim nonfatea tur, nos ab illo viuendi facultatem accipere, quando nulla humana ratione inuestigari potest, quomodo in matris vtero infans viuere & augeri possit? Quis non in admirabili corporis humani fabrica, membrorum sympathia, sensu, motu & vsu, creatoris virtutem agnoscat? Quis nos in illo esse & subsistere neget, quando tot vndiq; nobis insidiantur pericula, ex quibus indies euadimus? Quis non diuini seminis vestigia deprehendat, quando perpetuos animæ motus & operationes, eiusdem immortalitatem, totius deniq; hominis dignitatem, quà reliquis creaturis præstat, consyderaurit? Inexcusabilis ergo est hominum stupiditas, Deum non agnoscens, quando in nobis ipsis eius cognitio elucet. Absurda item est dementia, Dei imagines mutas fingere, cum in nobis viuam Dei imaginem circunferamus. Id vt melius Athenienses intelligant, & simul pundore suffundantur, Arati poetæ testimonium adducit, vt ostendat, se non noua & inaudita hactenus dicere, sed eadem sapientes clim natura duce didicisse, ipsos verò nimis crassos & barbaros esse, qui naturales quoq; Dei notitias in se extingui passi sint.
units.tr: But since what God requires seemed very difficult, and even impossible, Paul takes away every opportunity for evasion by anticipating it. And first of all he wishes God to be sought by us in such a way that he can be reached and found even by groping. The reason for this statement is that God everywhere presents himself to our senses, while through visible works he reveals his invisible power, wisdom and goodness, as is taught at length in Romans chapter 1. And indeed there is no part of the world so lowly, and no creature so worthless, that does not set before our eyes the ineffable power of God. It shines forth in the rough clods of earth, in which we see a wonderful power of bearing fruit. The same is seen in the changing of the seasons, in the perpetual motions of the heavens, in storms and in all the other influences of the heavens. Indeed, contemplate any little flower, and you will be compelled to marvel at the infinite power of the Creator joined to supreme wisdom. But since it would be an endless task to run through each part of the world, and many people are so dull that they can observe and investigate nothing outside themselves, God draws even nearer to us and does not stand far from any one of us. For in him we live, move and have our being, and so we are indeed his offspring. For who would not admit that we receive from him the faculty of living, since no human reasoning can investigate how an infant can live and grow in the mother's womb? Who does not recognise the power of the Creator in the admirable structure of the human body, in the sympathy, sense, motion and use of its members? Who would deny that we exist and subsist in him, when so many dangers lie in wait for us on every side, from which we escape day by day? Who does not perceive traces of divine seed, when he considers the perpetual motions and operations of the soul, its immortality, and finally the dignity of the whole man, by which he excels other creatures? Inexcusable, therefore, is the stupidity of men who do not acknowledge God, when his knowledge shines forth in ourselves. Likewise absurd is the madness of fashioning dumb images of God, when we carry about within ourselves a living image of God. So that the Athenians may understand this better, and at the same time blush with shame, Paul adduces the testimony of the poet Aratus, to show that he is not saying new and hitherto unheard-of things, but that wise men, guided by nature, have learned the same, while they themselves are too gross and barbarous, since they have allowed even the natural knowledges of God to be extinguished within them.

units.la: Tandem verò locum concludens infert: Genus ergo cum simus Dei, non debemus æstimare auro vel argento, vel lapidi, hominis arte & studio excultpto, numen esse simile. Dei verò genus nos vocat maximè propter imaginem ad quam conditi sumus. Nec enim nunc de adoptione electorum dicendi locus fuisset apud eos, qui prima cognitionis Dei rudimenta ignorabant. Sensus ergo est: Cum Deus suam imaginem in homine, omnium creaturarum principe, elucere voluerit, nimium crassus error est, illius imaginem mutam ex re aliqua inanimata effingere velle. Nam ne hominem quidem, quatenus Dei imago est, effingere licet, cum imago hæc in anima hæreat, cuius forma & natura nullo artificio exprimi aut adumbrari potest. Quanto minus ergo Deum aliqua imagine homo exprimere poterit? Primo autem preciosissimas materias, aurum & argentum nominat, offendens ne hæc quidem ad Dei imaginem repræsentandam sufficere. Nam quantocunque in preciosis inter homines, caduca tamen & corruptibilia sunt, deus vero incorruptibilis & æternus. Deinde non de formis, quas deo hominum temeritas affingit, sed de ipsa hominum arte & industria loquitur, quasi dicat: Etsi in unum omnes suas meditationes conferant ingeniosissimi artifices, dei tamen imaginem veram ne animo quidem concipere, nedum materia aut simulachro aliquo exprimere poterunt. Refer huc quae Isa. 40. & 44. cap. habentur. Hinc autem colligimus, simulachra quae Deo fiunt, nihil quam mera esse mendacia, eo quod minime præstare possint quod pollicentur. At quae obsecro maior iniuria deo fieri poterat, quam mendacio illi similem dicere, qui æterna est veritas? Quid hoc aliud, quam ex Deo diabolum fingere, quem mendacii patrem esse Christus ait? Nemo vir bonus se latronis aut scurræ specie repræsentari, æquo animo ferret, & honesta matrona meretricis habitum sibi affingi non pateretur. Nos tamen, quasi fumus audacia, deum mendacijs referre tentabimus? Non temere profecto Lactantio, disertissimo scriptori, ea sententia excidit, qua vllam religionem esse negat, ubicunque simulachra fuerint. Utinam vero in horum consideratione versarentur, qui hodie simulachris patrocinantur, quorum temeritas non postrema causa esse mihi videtur, ob quam Turcas reformatores orbis immittit Deus, quando euangelij doctrina Christianum orbem a superstitione & idololatria repurgari principes non ferunt. Nostrum est, ut nostræ originis & dignitatis memores, unum Deum colamus in Christo Iesu redemptore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, concluding the passage, he adds: "Since we are therefore the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like gold or silver or stone, shaped by human art and skill." And God calls us his offspring chiefly on account of the image to which we were created. For there would have been no place to speak of the adoption of the elect among those who did not know the first rudiments of the knowledge of God. The sense, then, is this: since God willed his image to shine forth in man, the prince of all creatures, it is a very gross error to wish to fashion his dumb image from some lifeless thing. For it is not even permitted to fashion man himself, insofar as he is the image of God, since this image dwells in the soul, whose form and nature can be expressed or shadowed forth by no craft. How much less, then, can man express God by any image? He first names the most precious materials, gold and silver, implying that not even these are sufficient to represent the image of God. For however precious they may be among men, they are nonetheless perishable and corruptible, whereas God is incorruptible and eternal. Next, he speaks not of the shapes which human rashness attributes to God, but of human art and industry itself, as if to say: even if the most ingenious craftsmen were to bring all their designs together into one, they could not conceive a true image of God even in the mind, much less express it in some material or likeness. Compare what is found in Isaiah chapters 40 and 44. From this we gather that the images made for God are nothing but pure lies, because they cannot do what they promise. And what greater injury, I beg you, could be done to God than to call him like a lie, he who is eternal truth? What else is this than to fashion the devil out of God, whom Christ calls the father of lies? No good man would bear it calmly to be represented in the guise of a thief or a buffoon, and no honest matron would suffer herself to be dressed in the garb of a prostitute. Shall we, then, as if we were mad with audacity, attempt to ascribe lies to God? Certainly it was not without reason that Lactantius, the most eloquent writer, let fall that saying, by which he denies that there is any religion wherever images are. Would that those who today defend images would dwell on these considerations, whose rashness seems to me no small cause for which God sends the Turks as the reformers of the world, since princes do not tolerate that the Christian world be cleansed of superstition and idolatry by the teaching of the gospel. It is our duty, mindful of our origin and dignity, to worship the one God in Christ Jesus our Redeemer, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXIX.

units.la: Et tempora quidem huius ignorantiæ cum hactenus dissimularit deus, nunc annunciat omnibus hominibus, ut ubique resipiscant: eo quod statuit diem, in quo iudicaturus est orbem terrarum in iustitia, per eum virum quem definiuit, fide omnibus præstita, cum eum excitauit a mortuis. Cum autem audissent resurrectionem mortuorum, alii quidem ridebant, alii vero dixerunt: Audiemus te de hoc iterum. Sic Paulus exiit de medio eorum. Quidam tamen viri adhærentes ei crediderunt: in quibus & Dionysius Areopagita, & mulier nomine Damaris, & alij cum eis.
units.tr: God has indeed overlooked the times of this ignorance until now, but now he declares to all men everywhere that they should repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, through the man whom he has appointed, having given assurance to all by raising him from the dead. When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, "We will hear you about this again." So Paul went out from among them. Yet some men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

units.la: Audiuimus priores Paulinæ concionis partes, quibus gentium errores diligentissime apostolus confutauit. Deum enim nec templis concludi, nec sacrificijs coli docuit. Singulari autem fictitios gentium deos & simulachra impugnauit, diserte monens, naturæ ordinem ab ijs violari, qui istis colendis occupentur, & eosdem nec finis sui nec dignitatis, ad quam conditi sunt, satis memores esse. Audiamus nunc postremam istius concionis partem, qua ad pœnitentiam per Christum illos hortatur, nimirum ut ab impietate & falso deorum cultu ad verum deum convertantur. Quo loco propter Epicureos, qui omnem religionem ludibrio habebat, extremi iudicij mentionem quam maxime vrget. Singula tamen eo ordine, quo illa Paulus exposuit, confyderabimus.
units.tr: We have heard the first parts of Paul's sermon, in which the Apostle very carefully refuted the errors of the Gentiles. He taught that God is not confined to temples, nor worshipped with sacrifices. He attacked the fictitious gods of the Gentiles and their images in particular, clearly warning that the order of nature is violated by those who busy themselves with worshipping them, and that they themselves are not mindful enough of their own end and of the dignity for which they were made. Let us now hear the last part of this sermon, in which he urges them to repentance through Christ, namely that they should turn from impiety and the false worship of gods to the true God. Here, because of the Epicureans, who made a mockery of all religion, he strongly stresses the mention of the final judgment. Nevertheless, we will consider the individual points in the order in which Paul set them out.

units.la: Primo quaestioni respondet, quae omnibus seculis, quando veritas prædicatur, moueri consueuit, & hodie passim occinitur: Cur videlicet deus mundum hunc universum tot seculis seduci passus sit? Et num verisimile sit, nunc demum pauculis quibusdam & obscuris hominibus veritate innotuisse? At paucis ad ista Paulus respondet, deum ignorantiæ tempora hactenus dissimulauisse, non quod hæc illi placeret, sed quod ita ipsi visum fuerit, qui iusto iudicio omnia administrat: nec potuisse non errare mundum, quoad veritatis lucem Deus occultauit, cum ex semetipsis homines nihil diuinum sapiant. At cum occultatam prioribus seculis veritatem nunc reuelari dicit, nullam posthac ignorantiæ excusationem fore admonet. EST autem obseruatione dignissimum, quod simpliciter Dei factum Paulus allegans, de causis propter quas mundum tot seculis errare passus sit, nullam omnino
units.tr: First he answers the question that is usually raised in every age whenever the truth is preached, and that is commonly sung today everywhere: why, namely, did God allow the whole world to be led astray for so many ages? And is it likely that the truth has only now become known to a few obscure men? To these things Paul answers briefly: God has overlooked the times of ignorance until now, not because he was pleased by them, but because it seemed good to him, who administers all things by a just judgment. Nor could the world have failed to err while God hid the light of truth, since men of themselves understand nothing divine. But when he says that the truth, hidden in earlier ages, is now revealed, he warns that there will be no excuse of ignorance from now on. It is worth noticing most carefully that Paul, while citing only God's act, makes no mention at all of any dispute about the causes for which he allowed the world to err for so many centuries.

units.la: Respondetur ijs, qui maiorum ignorantia suis erroribus præ texunt. disputationem monet. Imitanda enim nobis quoq; esse modestia hæc, ne iudiciorum Dei causas alius scrutemur, aut in illum nostræ impietatis causam audacius reiiciamus. Constat enim nemini ab illo iniuriam fieri posse, cum æternam damnationem iam olim omnes meruerimus, adeoq; filij iræ nascamur. Constat utem iusto iudicio illum omnia administrare. Et alibi Paulus, de euangelij reuelatione loquens, mysterium esse dicit abscónditum à seculo. Rom.16. Idem Christus monet, quando mysteria regni cælorum non omnibus reuelari dicit, Matth.13. Stultum ergo, imò audax nimis & impius esse, ad humanæ rationis calculum reuocare quæ à Deo fiunt, cum ille fidei obedientiam a nobis requirat, nec aliud perinde filios Dei deceat, quàm ut illius voluntati, quæ in verbo & operibus ipsius elucet, sese accommodent. Præterea euangelica prædicationis finem hoc loco Paulus exprimit, quando illam nunc annuntiari dicit omnibus hominibus, ut ubique respiscant. Non ergo euangelium audiuisse vel didicisse sufficit, sed ut ab erroribus & reliquis vitiis respiscamus, opus est. Docet hoc totius euangelicæ historiæ ordo. A pœnitentiæ doctrina Iohannes Baptista orditur. Deinde Christus clamat: Resipiscite, appropinquauit enim regnum cælorum. Ita illius iussu prædicant apostoli. Et Lucas vltimo eum docendi ordinem prescribit, ut in ipsius nomine pœnitentia primum, deinde vero peccatorum remissio prædicetur. Quem ordinem ab illis sedulo obseruatum fuisse, totus liber hic & illorum epistolæ satis testantur. Falso igitur & nimis impudenter euangelicos sese dicunt, qui pristinos errores mordicus retinent, & vitijs suis effræni licentia indulgent, nec patiuntur, ut illorum mores ministri verbi arguant: quod perinde est, ac si quis à medico exigat, ut corporis valetudinem tueatur quidem, morbus tamen non obstet, nec illis remedia digna adhibeat. Admonemur præterea, neminem vel patrum vel prioris seculi ignorantia excusari coram Deo. Quod enim multis seculis errarunt maiores nostri, Dei iusto iudicio factum est, qui errores ipsos dissimulauit. At quando idem ille voluntatem suam reuelat, certum est illum ignorantiam amplius dissimulare nolle, & resipiscentiam ab omnibus exigere. Quam qui non præstant, oblata gratia contemptores sunt, & proinde pœnas grauissimas merentur. Obseruare hoc debebant, qui hodie sub plausibili maiorum & auctoritatis superstitionis titulo euangelium ferro & igne perseq uuntur. Sed Dei iudicium nunquam effugiunt, de quo in præsenti Paulus disserit.
units.tr: It is answered to those who cover their own errors with the ignorance of their forebears. For we too must imitate this modesty, so that we do not each search out the causes of God's judgments, or too boldly lay the cause of our impiety upon him. For it is clear that no one can be wronged by him, since we have all long since deserved eternal damnation and are born children of wrath. It is also clear that he administers all things by a just judgment. And elsewhere Paul, speaking of the revelation of the gospel, says that it is a mystery hidden from the age (Rom. 16.). Christ himself also warns, when he says that the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven are not revealed to all (Matth. 13.). It is therefore foolish, indeed too bold and impious, to bring what God does back to the reckoning of human reason, since he requires obedience of faith from us, and it is fitting for the sons of God to accommodate themselves to his will, which shines forth in his word and works. Moreover, in this passage Paul sets out the aim of the preaching of the gospel, when he says that it is now announced to all men, that they should repent everywhere. It is therefore not enough to have heard or learned the gospel; we must repent of our errors and of the other vices. The order of the whole gospel history teaches this. John the Baptist begins with the doctrine of repentance. Then Christ cries out, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." The apostles preach in the same way at his command. And Luke, at the end, prescribes this order of teaching, that repentance should be preached first in his name, and then the forgiveness of sins. That this order was diligently observed by them, this whole book and their epistles bear sufficient witness.
