Therefore they falsely and too shamelessly call themselves evangelical who stubbornly keep their former errors and indulge their vices with unbridled licence, and do not allow their ministers of the Word to rebuke their morals. This is just as if someone demanded that a physician look after the health of the body, yet did not let the disease stand in the way, nor apply to him proper remedies. We are further reminded that no one, whether of the Fathers or of an earlier age, is excused before God by ignorance. For that our forebears erred for many centuries happened by the just judgment of God, who overlooked their errors. But when he now reveals his will, it is certain that he is unwilling to overlook ignorance any longer, and requires repentance from all. Those who do not render it, despise the grace offered, and therefore deserve the most severe punishments. Those who today persecute the gospel with sword and fire under the plausible title of the authority and superstition of their ancestors ought to have observed this. But they never escape the judgment of God, of which Paul is speaking in this passage.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Causam enim allegat, propter quam verbu suum nunc gentibus reuelet Deus, dicens: Quia diem quam facere, nisi prius illud reuelet seruis suis prophetis. Amos 3. Exempla non in sacris modo sed puris, verumetiam gentium historijs passim sunt obuia, ut illis hoc loco recensendis immorari non sit opus. Præstat autem nouissimi iudicij rationem inspicere, quam breuiter simul & luculenter Paulus comprehendit. Primo enim propter Epicureos & horum sectatores, diem iudicij iam confiduit esse à Deo testatur, ne quis illius denuntiationem scurriliter eludat, quod illusores quosdam facturos esse Petrus monet. 2. Pet. 3. Et quod Paulus dicit, idipsum vnanimis totius scripturæ consensus probat. Huc enim pertinent quæ Daniel vltimo habentur. Quæ item Christus toties inculcat. Ioban. 5. Matth. 16. 24. 25. Et quod alibi dicitur, nos omnes coram Christi tribunali sisti oportere. 2. Cor. 5. Rom. 14. Id vero iustitiæ diuinæ ratio plane exigit, quæ subsistere nullo modo posset, nisi iudicium illud foret, quo dignam suis operibus retributionem singuli accipient, quando in hoc seculo plerunque pios absq; omni remuneratione affligi, & impios impune ferocire & libidinari videmus. Deinde quoque iudicium illud subire oportet exprimit, totum terrarum orbem nominans, quod nos in fidei articulis per vinos & mortuos exprimimus. Nemo igitur diem illum subterfugiet, sed ut antea monuimus, omnes nos coram Dei tribunali sistemur. Nec enim personarum respectus apud Deum est, nec illius oculos quisquam eludere poterit. Id quod magnates & mundi fastu turgidos modestia & humilitatis admonere debebat. Tertio modum & formam iudicij indicat, dum illum in iustitia indicaturum dicit. Non ergo vlli prætexui locus erit, sed qui sub lege peccauerunt, legis sententiam ferent, & qui absq; lege peccauerunt, absque lege damnabuntur. Rom. 2. Et vnusquisq; reportabit quod fecerit in corpore suo. 2. Cor. 5. Huius nos meminisse oportebat, quando peccatorum & carnis blanditiis obrepunt, quibus ab officio reuocamur: quando item mundi & opum splendor nos ad peccandum solicitat. Quid enim dabit homo pro redemptione animæ suæ in illa die, qua seuerissimus iudex secundum iustitiam
units.tr: For Paul gives the reason why God now reveals his word to the Gentiles, saying: "Because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world" (Acts 17:31 in the sense of the passage), "which he would not have revealed unless he first revealed it to his servants the prophets" (Amos 3). Examples of this are found everywhere, not only in the sacred writings but also in profane histories, so there is no need to linger over recounting them here. It is better, however, to consider the account of the last judgment, which Paul sets out both briefly and clearly. First, because of the Epicureans and their followers, he testifies that God has already appointed the day of judgment, so that no one may mock its announcement with buffoonery, as Peter warns that some scoffers will do (2 Pet. 3). What Paul says is also proved by the unanimous agreement of all Scripture. To this belong the things written at the end of Daniel, and the things Christ so often impresses (John 5; Matt. 16:24-25). And elsewhere it is said that we must all be brought before the tribunal of Christ (2 Cor. 5; Rom. 14). Indeed, the reasoning of divine justice plainly demands this, for it could not stand in any way unless there were a judgment in which each person receives a repayment worthy of his works, since in this age we often see the godly afflicted without any reward, and the wicked raging and indulging their lusts with impunity. Next, he indicates that the judgment must be undergone by the whole orb of the earth, naming it, which we in the articles of faith express as "the living and the dead." No one, therefore, will escape that day, but, as we said before, we shall all be brought before the tribunal of God. For there is no respect of persons with God, nor can anyone deceive his eyes. This ought to admonish the great men and those puffed up with worldly pride to modesty and humility. Third, he indicates the manner and form of the judgment, when he says that he will judge in righteousness. So no pretext will be left to anyone; those who have sinned under the law will receive the sentence of the law, and those who have sinned without the law will be condemned without the law (Rom. 2). "And each one will receive what he has done in his body" (2 Cor. 5). We ought to remember this when the enticements of sins and of the flesh creep upon us, by which we are called back from our duty, and likewise when the splendour of the world and of wealth urges us to sin. For what will a man give in exchange for his soul on that day, when the most severe judge will pronounce the sentence of justice? (Matt. 16).

units.la: Nouissimi iudicij terrore pœnitentiam vrget. iustitiae tenorem sententia proferet? Matth. 16. Postremo iudicem etiam definit, per quem deus orbem iudicaturus sit. Per virum scilicet quem praefiniuit. Ita vero Christum nominat propter humanam naturam: mitiori nimirum vocabulo uti volens apud incredulos, ut sensim ad explicanda Christi mysteria descendat. Non temere autem Christum iudicem fore passim scripturae docent. Id enim piorum consolationi mirifice feruit, quando eum iudicem venturum audiunt, quem ipsi saluatorem & Pontificem suum esse norunt. Inde enim colligunt illum ipsis non iudicem, sed vindicem potius fore, sicuti illi Iob Cap. 19. nominat: nec damnationis sententia ab illo metuere possunt, quae pro peccatis suis in Cruce immolatum esse credunt. Rursum hoc impiis magno terrori est, quando iudicem venturum cogitant, quem improbe contempserunt. Videbunt enim in quem pupugerunt, & magno suo malo eius tribunal subire cogentur, quem redemptorem suum noluerunt agnoscere. Vide Zach. 12. Ioban. 19. Psal. 2. &c.
units.tr: By the terror of the last judgment he urges repentance. Finally, he also defines the judge through whom God will judge the world: namely, "through the man whom he has appointed." He names Christ thus on account of his human nature, wishing to use a milder word before unbelievers, so that he may gradually descend to explain the mysteries of Christ. Scripture everywhere teaches that Christ will not without reason be the judge. For this brings wonderful comfort to the godly, when they hear that he will come as judge, whom they know to be their own Saviour and High Priest. From this they gather that he will be for them not a judge but rather an avenger, as Job calls him (Job 19). Nor can they fear a sentence of condemnation from him, whom they believe to have been sacrificed on the cross for their sins. Conversely, this is a great terror to the wicked when they think of the judge who is coming, whom they have wickedly despised. For they will see him whom they pierced, and to their great harm they will be compelled to undergo the tribunal of him whom they refused to acknowledge as their redeemer (Zech. 12; John 19; Ps. 2, etc.).

units.la: Quia vero in Christi mentione Paulus incidit, huius quoque mysteria tractare incipit, in qua tractatione illum prolixiorem & diligentiorem fuisse, nemo dubitare debet. Lucas vero summa duntaxat capita perstringit, quae qualis Pauli oratio & doctrina fuerit, abunde docent. Sunt ea tria numero. Primo illum a Deo praefinitum siue praedestinatum esse dicit, nimirum ab aeterno, ut alibi habetur. 1. Pet. 1. Patet id ex promissionibus, quae illum a prima origine humano generi saluatorem destinatum fuisse testantur. Inde vero (ut alibi Paulus monet) salutem nobis ex gratia, nullo nostro merito obtingere colligitur. Ephes. 1. Quis enim hominum est, qui se iam olim ab aeterno meruisse gloriari possit, ut ipsi Dei filius saluator destinaretur? Secundo Deum in Christo omnibus fide praestitisse ait, significans in illo promissiones, typos & prophetias impletas esse, quibus olim salutis ratio comprehensa fuit. Quo ipse Christus respiciens iam moriturus dixit: Consummatum est. Et a resurrectione, haec ita oportuisse fieri docet, ut implerentur, quae de ipso in Mose prophetis & Psalmis scripta extant. Luc. 24. Unde colligimus nimis turpiter omnes eos falli, qui extra Christum nouam salutis rationem & viam monstrant: quid enim illi aliud faciunt, quam quod Deum & Christum mendacii arguunt? Vide de hoc 1. Ioban. 5. Qui non credit Deo, mendacem fecit eum, &c. Tertio resurrectionis Christi meminit, per hanc nimirum probaturus, ipsum Deum et Iudicem esse omnium. Quo argumento etiam ad Rom. 1. cap. utitur. Simul vero sub hac vniuersum nostrae redemptionis negotium complexus est. Si enim resurrexit, vtiq; mortuus est: mortuus quidem (ut alibi dicitur) propter peccata nostra, & excitatus propter iustificationem nostram. Rom. 4. Sed quia de his saepe iam dictum est, & passim plura dicendi locus occurrit, paucula haec in praesenti sufficiant.
units.tr: But since Paul has come to the mention of Christ, he also begins to treat of his mysteries; no one should doubt that in this treatment he was fuller and more diligent. Luke, however, touches only the main heads, and how Paul's speech and teaching were is amply shown by them. There are three of these. First, he says that Christ was foreordained or predestined by God, namely from eternity, as is said elsewhere (1 Pet. 1). This is evident from the promises, which testify that he was appointed from the very beginning as the Saviour of the human race. From this, moreover (as Paul warns elsewhere), it is gathered that salvation comes to us from grace, by no merit of our own (Eph. 1). For who among men can boast that he had merited from eternity that the Son of God himself should be appointed Saviour? Second, he says that God has given assurance to all in Christ by faith, signifying that the promises, types and prophecies, by which the manner of salvation was once comprehended, have been fulfilled in him. Looking to this, Christ himself, about to die, said: "It is finished." And from the resurrection he teaches that these things had to happen in this way, so that those things which are written about him in Moses, the prophets and the Psalms might be fulfilled (Luke 24). From this we gather how shamefully all those are deceived who point out a new way and method of salvation outside Christ; for what else do they do but accuse God and Christ of lying? See on this 1 John 5: "He who does not believe God has made him a liar," etc. Third, he mentions the resurrection of Christ, intending by this to prove that he is God and the judge of all. He uses this argument also in Romans 1. At the same time, under this head he has embraced the whole business of our redemption. For if he has risen, then certainly he died: he died indeed (as is said elsewhere) for our sins, and was raised for our justification (Rom. 4). But since these things have often been said already, and there will be opportunity to say more at many points, let these few remarks suffice for the present.

units.la: Restat doctrinae huius effectus, varius nimirum & diuersus pro auditorum diuersitate. Quidam enim ad primam resurrectionis mentionem scurriliter ridThis, Epicurei maxime: quorum hodie non parum numerus habetur. Alij vero bis meliores, denuo de eadem re differentem audire cupiunt, itaque testantes, se aliquem veritatis gustum sensisse. Sunt rursum, quorum animos Dei spiritus illuminauit, ut credant & Paulo palam coniungantur. Ita passim impletur, quod Paulus dicit, euangelium aliis quidem esse odorem mortis ad mortem, aliis vero odorem vitae ad vitam. Inter credentes vero Dionysius numeratur, primariae dignitatis vir, utpote ex Areopagitarum iudicum numero. Accedit etiam Damaris, quam non obscura nota matronam fuisse verisimile est, cum eius mentio nominatim fiat. Nunquam ergo sine fructu euangelium praedicatur, & licet pauci initio credant, ex paruis tamen initijs maximae & celeberrimae ecclesiae exoriuntur: quod ipsum Athenis accidisse historia tradunt. Nostrum est non offendi credentium paucitate, sed euangelium salutis gratis animis amplecti, ut dignos in nobis fructus proferat, nosq; iuxta illius promissiones salutem consequamur per Christum Iesum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the effect of this teaching, which is indeed varied and different according to the difference of the hearers. For some, at the first mention of the resurrection, mocked it with buffoonery, especially the Epicureans, whose number is not small even today. Others, who are better, desire to hear again about the same matter, thereby testifying that they have tasted something of the truth. There are again those whose minds the Spirit of God has illumined, so that they believe and openly join themselves to Paul. Thus what Paul says is everywhere fulfilled: that the gospel is to some indeed a fragrance of death unto death, and to others a fragrance of life unto life. Among the believers Dionysius is numbered, a man of the first rank, as one of the number of the Areopagite judges. Damaris is added too, who was probably a matron of no obscure reputation, since her name is expressly mentioned. The gospel, therefore, is never preached without fruit, and although at first only a few believe, from small beginnings the greatest and most celebrated churches nevertheless arise; history tells us that this very thing happened at Athens. It is our part not to be offended by the paucity of believers, but to embrace the gospel of salvation with willing minds, so that it may bring forth worthy fruits in us, and that we may obtain salvation according to its promises through Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XVIII. HOMILIA CXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 18. HOMILY 120.

units.la: Posthaec Paulus digressus Athenis venit Corinthum. Et nactus quendam Iudaeum, nomine Aquilam, Ponticum genere, qui nuper venerat ab Italia, & Priscillam vxorem eius (eo quod praecepisset
units.tr: After these things Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth. And finding a certain Jew named Aquila, a Pontic by birth, who had lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla (because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome), he came to them, and because he was of the same trade, he stayed with them and worked.

units.la: Claudius omnes Iudaeos Roma decedere) accesit ad eos, & quia eiusdem erat artificij, mansit apud eos & operatus est. Erant autem tabernaculorum opifices. Disputabat autem in Synagoga per omne sabbatum, suadebatq; Iudaeis pariter & Graecis. Cum autem venissent e Macedonia Silas & Timotheus, coarctabatur spiritu Paulus, testificans Iudaeis Christum esse Iesum.
units.tr: Now they were tentmakers by trade. And he reasoned in the synagogue every sabbath, and persuaded both Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy had come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in spirit, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.

units.la: Exhibuit Dius Lucas praecedenti capite conversionem Athenarum, urbis tum sapientiae studio, tum multiplicis religionis fama celeberrimae. Huic modo commodissime subiicit Corinthi, urbis opulentissimae corruptissimaeq; ad Christum conversae historiam: in qua spiritus Christi virtus & euangelij efficacia tam luculenter & miraculose emicuit, ut Corinthiacam ecclesiam non temere Paulus sui apostolatus sigillum esse dicat. 1. Cor. 9. Ut enim Corinthus propter situm bimarem mercatura celebris & opulenta fuit, ita illam diuitiarum illecebrae & vndiq; confluentium mercatorum frequentia corruptissimis moribus infecerunt: adeo ut Proverbijs quoq; luxus ipsius notaretur. Corinthiari enim dicebatur, qui immodico luxui studebant. Et passim illud tritum ferebatur: Non omnibus licet adire Corinthum. Inter reliqua vero vitia scortatio maxime regnabat, cui sic addicti fuerunt, ut in Veneris templo circiter mille puellae prostarent: & postea inter eos quoq; qui Christo nomen dederant inueniretur, qui nouercam incesto coitu polluaret, quod illi impune licuerat, donec Paulo iubente excommunicaretur. In eam ciuitatem Paulus, relictis Athenis digreditur, nec sine numine, ut exitus docebit. Multi enim in ea populum dominus habuit, qui electos suos ex sententia flagitiorum per euangelij praedicationem saluauit. Porro insigne cum bonitatis Dei, quae illo peccatores prosequitur, tum euangelicae virtutis siue potentiae exemplum urbis huius conuersio exhibet. Nam si cum indurata peccandi consuetudine, opum splendore, delitiarum abundantia, obuijs vndiq; voluptatis illecebris, saltu deniq; mercatorio, Pauli peregrini & ignoti hominis conditionem plane abiectam & ignobilem conferas, ridiculus omnino videbitur conatus ipsius, quo reformationem cum vitae & morum tum religionis moliri coepit. At quod carnis iudicio ridiculum videri potest, non caruit euentu felicissimo, quem dominus dedit. Intra sequiquannum enim per euangelij praedicationem, cooperante spiritu Christi, nouam huic urbi faciem Paulus induxit, & reformationem inuexit publicam, quam nullus legislator, quantacunq; authoritate praeditus, illis persuadere potuisset: ut non sine causa de huius urbis conversione Paulus tantopere glorietur, cum vix vspiam alibi efficaciorem euangelij operationem senserit. Quae etiam mihi causa potissima esse videtur, quod in hac floria huius comemoratione tanta diligentia Lucas versatur, ut minutissimas quoq; circumstantias prolixe exponat, quas alibi vel omnino praeterit, vel leuiter tantummodo, & quasi aliud agens perstringit. Id quod nos quoq; ad diligentem omnium quae dicuntur consyderationem excitare debet.
units.tr: Luke set out in the previous chapter the conversion of Athens, a city famous both for its devotion to learning and for the reputation of its many religions. Right after this he fittingly adds the history of Corinth, a very wealthy and deeply corrupt city, which was converted to Christ. In it the power of Christ's Spirit and the efficacy of the gospel shone out so clearly and miraculously that Paul does not rashly call the church of Corinth the seal of his apostleship (1 Cor. 9). For Corinth, because of its position on two seas, was famous and rich in trade, and so the allurements of wealth and the crowds of merchants flocking in from every side infected it with the most corrupt morals, so much so that its luxury was noted even in proverbs. For those who devoted themselves to excessive luxury were called "Corinthianizers." And the common saying was everywhere repeated: "It is not for everyone to go to Corinth." Among its other vices, fornication reigned above all, and the people were so given over to it that about a thousand girls worked as prostitutes in the temple of Venus. Later, even among those who had given their names to Christ, a man was found who polluted his stepmother by incestuous intercourse, something that had been allowed to him with impunity until Paul ordered him to be excommunicated. Paul left Athens and went to that city, and not without the divine will, as the outcome will show. For the Lord had many people in it, whom through the preaching of the gospel he saved, his elect, out of the midst of its shameful sins. Moreover, the conversion of this city offers a striking example both of the goodness of God, which pursues sinners, and of the power or strength of the gospel. For if you compare the condition of Paul, a stranger and an unknown man, plainly lowly and obscure, with a city hardened in the habit of sinning, dazzling with riches, abounding in pleasures, surrounded on every side by the allurements of pleasure and, finally, by its commercial bustle, his attempt to bring about a reformation, first of life and morals and then of religion, will seem utterly ridiculous. But what may seem ridiculous to the judgment of the flesh did not lack a most happy outcome, which the Lord gave. For within the space of a year and a half, through the preaching of the gospel, with the Spirit of Christ working together, Paul gave this city a new face and brought in a public reformation, which no lawgiver, however great his authority, could have persuaded them to accept. So it is not without reason that Paul glories so greatly in the conversion of this city, since he had hardly felt the gospel work more effectively anywhere else. This also seems to me the chief reason why Luke spends such care on the account of this history, that he sets out in full even the smallest circumstances, which elsewhere he either passes over entirely or touches on only lightly, as if he were doing something else. This too ought to stir us to a diligent consideration of everything that is said.

units.la: Ante omnia vero hospitij, quo Paulus vsus est, mentionem facit, in quo quaerendo illum non officium tantum fuisse crediderim, cum peculiare de hoc praeceptum Christus dederit, ut se dignos hospites apostoli quarant. Paulo igitur hospes contigit Aquilas, homo Iudaeus, ex Ponto oriundus, qui non ita pridem cum reliquis Iudaeis ex Claudij Caesaris mandato Roma decedere coactus, vna cum vxore Prifcilla Corinthum venerat. Fuit enim illo tempore plus quam misera Iudaeorum conditio, eo quod filij Dei sanguine pollutos diuina vltio vbiq; locorum persequeretur. Accedebat aliud quoq;, quod qui Christum saluatorem abnegarant, nouos indies saluatores quaerendo passim turbas dabant & tumultuabantur, vnde merito omnibus inuisi erant. Communi igitur gentis infortunio abreptus Aquilas, ipse quoq; exilio multatur, non tamen citra Dei prouidentiam, qui per hunc Paulo apud Corinthios hospitium parare, & ipsius opera in celeberrimae ecclesiae fundatione vti voluit. Ita enim frequenter euenit, ut ingentis boni causa fiat, quod nobis initio nimis grave & asperum videbatur. Ad hunc itaque graues ob causas Paulus diuertit. Nam praeterquam quod in fide institutus erat, communis exilij fortuna illum omnibus peregrinis aequiorem reddebat, quos fere contemnunt, quicunq; intra patrios lares consenuerunt. Deinde cum idem cum Paulo artificium exerceret, tentoriorum nimirum textor siue sutor (quae illo seculo ex pellibus fiebant) commode cum illo apostolus versari, & eodem labore victum sibi acquirere poterat. Praestat tamen cum Aquila tum Pauli per... sonam diligentius consyderare. Et ille quidem memorabile fidei & charitatis exemplum nobis exhibet. Homo enim mechanicus & exul, in peregrina vrbe Christi ministrum hospitio excipit, suo facto non paruam ignominiæ notam opulentioribus inurens, qui in aliis sedibus peregrinos facile contemnebant. Imò tantam huius hospitalitatem fuisse, ex aliis locis constat, vt domesticam ecclesiam habuerit. Vide de hoc 1. Cor. 16. & Rom. 16. Pudeat ergo inhumanitatis suæ & sordidissimæ tenacitatis, qui cum opibus & pace abundent, nulla tamen exulum Christi cura tanguntur. Discent illi ali quando suo malo quæ sint exilij molestiæ, & quanta laborum examina trahat persecutio. At qui Christi amore feruidi, seruos suos colligunt, grauissimum remuneratorem sentiunt dominum, illi etiam merce dignam pollicetur, qui poculum aquæ frigidæ alicui discipulorum suorum dederit. Matth. 10. Idem nouissimo die sibi impensum æstimabit, quod egenus membris suis impensum fuerit. Similiter in Paulo quoq; præclaræ virtutes elucent. Fidei constantis argumentum est, quod ignobili hospitio non offenditur, vt propterea de relinquenda Corintho cogitet. Nouerat enim Deum quæ humilia sunt in hoc mundo deligere, vt illis in regni sui propagatione ad eorum confusionem vtatur, qui sibi ipsis præclari & magnifici videntur. Rursum charitatem æquitati coniunctam exercet, dum non otiosus in Aquilæ domo desidet, sed manibus operatur, & honestè sibi ipsi victum quærit. Quod exemplum vt summa laude dignum est, ita male ab illis torquetur, qui per illud omnes verbi ministros ad manuaria opificia, vel etiam ad stiluam relegant, quasi indignum sit, ex verbi ministerio viuere. Non enim ideò Paulus laborauit, quòd illicitum & nefas sibi videretur, ecclesiæ stipendio quenquam alii; sed quòd nondum constituta Corinthi ecclesia, publico stipendio ali non poterat. Interim pauculis istis ecclesiæ primitijs in Aquilæ domo, cuius fortunæ non admodum splendidæ esse potErant, oneri esse noluit. Mouerunt eum deinceps, vt iam constituta ecclesia, suo iure vti nollet, pseudoapostolorum quorundam calumniæ, qui illum & sui similes aliorum bonis insidiari dicebant, ipsi gratis docebant, quò facilius sese populo commendarent. His ergo inferior videri noluit Paulus, potius esse ducens suo iure aliquandiu cedere, quàm illud vrgendo euangelium suspectum reddere. Interea se alias ecclesias depredatum fuisse scribit, vt Corinthijs gratis prædicare posset. Et à Philippensibus missa pecunia se subleuatum esse, idem ipse fatetur. 2. Corinth. 11. Phil. 4. Arguuntur tamen Pauli exemplo laruati episcopi, qui cum ex ecclesiarum bonis persico luxu diffluant, ecclesijs tamen minime seruiunt. Nec ij solum, verumetiam Ventres quidam, qui euangelij quidem titulo gloriantur, interim toti auaritiæ dediti, ecclesias quibus magno cum fructu seruire poterant, ob leue aliquod lucellum & pinguioris stipendij spem turpissimè deserunt. Sentiet vtrunq; genus aliquando Christum iudicem, qui ecclesiæ suæ tam turpiter illudi, inultum non feret.
units.tr: Above all he mentions the lodging that Paul used. In seeking it, I would think, this was not merely a matter of duty, since Christ gave a special command about this, that the apostles should seek out worthy hosts. So Paul's host was Aquila, a Jew born in Pontus, who, not long before, had been forced to leave Rome with the other Jews by the command of Emperor Claudius, and had come to Corinth together with his wife Priscilla. For at that time the condition of the Jews was more than wretched, because divine vengeance pursued them everywhere, polluted with the blood of the Son of God. In addition, those who had denied Christ as Savior, by constantly seeking new saviors, stirred up disturbances and riots everywhere, so that they were rightly hated by all. So Aquila, carried away by the common misfortune of his nation, was himself punished with exile, yet not without the providence of God, who wished through him to prepare lodging for Paul among the Corinthians and to use his work in founding a most famous church. For it often happens that something which at first seemed to us very grievous and harsh becomes the cause of a great good. So Paul turned aside to him for weighty reasons. For apart from the fact that he had been instructed in the faith, the common fortune of exile made him more gracious toward all strangers, whom those who have grown old within their native hearths usually despise. Next, since he practised the same trade as Paul, namely the weaving or sewing of tents (which in that age were made of hides), the apostle could live conveniently with him and gain his livelihood by the same labor. It is nevertheless better to consider carefully both Aquila and Paul's person more carefully. Aquila shows us a memorable example of faith and love. For a craftsman and an exile, in a foreign city, received a minister of Christ into his house, by his deed branding a mark of no small shame upon the wealthier people who in other places readily despised strangers. Indeed, it is clear from other passages that his hospitality was so great that he had a church in his house. See on this 1 Cor. 16 and Rom. 16. Let those who abound in wealth and peace, yet are moved by no care for the exiles of Christ, be ashamed of their inhumanity and most sordid stinginess. They will learn someday, to their own harm, what the discomforts of exile are, and how many trials persecution brings. But those who, burning with love for Christ, gather in his servants, feel the Lord to be a most generous rewarder; he promises a reward worthy of himself even to one who gives a cup of cold water to one of his disciples (Matt. 10). On the last day he will count as done to himself whatever was done to his needy members. Likewise, splendid virtues shine forth in Paul too. It is a proof of a steadfast faith that he is not offended by a humble lodging, so as to think of leaving Corinth on that account. For he knew that God chooses what is lowly in this world, so that in propagating his kingdom he may use it to confound those who seem to themselves illustrious and great. Again, he exercises love joined with fairness, since he does not sit idle in Aquila's house, but works with his hands and honestly seeks his own food. This example, as it deserves the highest praise, is so wrongly twisted by those who use it to send all ministers of the Word back to manual trades or even to the pen, as if it were unworthy for anyone to live from the ministry of the Word. For Paul did not labor because he thought it unlawful and wicked for anyone to be supported by the church's stipend, but because the church of Corinth, not yet established, could not be supported by public stipend. Meanwhile he did not want to be a burden to those first beginnings of the church in Aquila's house, whose fortunes were not very splendid. Later, when the church was established, the slanders of certain false apostles moved him not to use his right. They said that he and men like him were plotting against the goods of others, and that they taught for nothing so that they might commend themselves more easily to the people. Paul therefore did not wish to appear inferior to these men, thinking it better for a while to yield his own right than by insisting on it to make the gospel suspect. Meanwhile he writes that he had despoiled other churches so that he might preach gratis to the Corinthians, and he himself confesses that he was relieved by money sent from the Philippians (2 Cor. 11; Phil. 4). Yet the example of Paul condemns those masked bishops who, while they dissolve in Persian luxury from the goods of the churches, nonetheless serve the churches not at all. And it is not only they, but certain bellies too, who boast of the title of the gospel, yet, wholly given over to greed, shamefully desert churches which they could have served with great profit, for the sake of some slight gain and the hope of a fatter stipend. Both kinds will one day feel Christ to be their judge, who will not allow his church to be so shamefully mocked without punishment.

units.la: Caterum quia non eo nomine Corinthum Paulus venerat, vt tentoria texeret, sed vt Christi regnum propagaret, qua ratione illud fecerit indicatur. Pro more autem sabbata & cætus sacros, qui illis diebus cogebantur, obseruauit. Et primò quidem doctrinam suam prudenter temperauit, auditorum captui sese accommodans, quod ipse alibi fatetur, dum se illos lacte aluisse scribit, eò quòd solidiorem cibum nondum ferre possent. 1. Corint. 3. cap. Id in præsenti Lucas persuadendi verbo exprimit, vt offendat, illum sese auditorum animis commodè insinuauisse, ne quos in ipso limine (quod aiunt) offenderet. Et sanè credibile est, ipsum eo ordine progressum fuisse, quo alias vti consueuit. Nouerat Iudæos præposfero Legis studio teneri, & in huius operibus iustificationem atque salutem quærere. Docuit ergo omnes nos peccatores esse, nec Legi humanis viribus satisfieri posse. Inde verò promptum erat colligere, alium quærendum esse, cuius merito homines iustificari & saluari possint. Quæ commodissima erat ad tradendum Christi mysteria occasio. Imitentur Pauli exemplum omnes ecclesiæ & verbi Dei ministri, ne dum nullam auditorum rationem habent, confuse omnia ingerendo a Christi regno alienissimos reddant, qui prudenti modestia facile lucrifieri poterat. Ipse certè talem ministrum esse vult, qui veritatis sermonem rite secare norit. 2. Tim. 2. Et Christus ab eodem non fidem modo in rebus agendis, verumetiam prudentiam requirit. Porrò ne quis Paulum perpetuò lacte vsum putaret, illum tandem occasione oblata maiori feruore Christi causam egisse Lucas scribit. Cùm enim ex Macedonia aduenissent Silas & Timotheus, totus spiritu coarctari cœpit: vel quòd ex illis felicè apud Macedones euangelij cursum audiret: vel quòd tanta vrbis cæcitas & infelix conditio animum eius commoueret. Quem enim non mouisset celeberrima ciuitatis ad interitum tum ruentis calamitas, toti in ea hominum miserè seipsos decipientiu ignorantia? Certè qualiscun-que illa Pauli coarctatio fuerit, illum acriori spiritus suggestione extimulatum fuisse certum est, ut publicè & aperte Iudæis testari inciperet, Iesum Mariæ filium esse Christum, id est, promissum humani generis salvatorem, cuius solius merito à legis maledictione, peccato & morte liberemur. Ita ergo prudenti modestia sibi viam sternant ministri, ut tandem in Christo tradendo & illius glo-ria afferenda verè ardeant, ne pusillanimitatem suâ modestiâ titulo palliare videantur. RVRSVM vero elucet praecipuû doctrina apostolicæ caput esse Christum, cuius testes apostoli delecti fuerunt. In hoc uno salutem omnem conclusam esse, supra Petrus docuit. Paulus postea ad Corinthios scri-bens, se nihil aliud quàm Iesum Christum, & hunc quidem crucifixum nouisse fatetur. Iohannes omnia in eum finem ab euangelistis scripta fuisse tradit, ut credamus Iesum esse Christum, & credentes vitam æternam consequamur. Eodem ergo nos quoq; contentos esse decet. Nefas enim est, quam in salutis negotio maiorem sibi cognitionem vendicare, quàm apostoli fecerunt, qui Christo praeceptore domestico & spiritu eiusdem fidelissimo consultore usi sunt. Quare Christum unum omnes sapiamus, regem & sacerdotem unicum, qui pro peccatis nostris mortuus & propter iustificationem nostram excitatus à mortuis, redemit nos, & patri suo reges & sacerdotes fecit. Ipsi debetur benedi-ctio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But since Paul had not come to Corinth for the sake of making tents, but to spread the kingdom of Christ, Luke indicates how he went about it. Following his custom, he observed the Sabbaths and the sacred assemblies that were gathered on those days. And first of all he tempered his teaching prudently, accommodating himself to the capacity of his hearers, as he himself admits elsewhere when he writes that he had fed them with milk, because they were not yet able to bear solid food (1 Cor. 3). Luke expresses this in the present passage by the word "persuading," so as to show that Paul had skilfully insinuated himself into the minds of his hearers, so as not to offend them at the very threshold (as they say). And it is certainly credible that he proceeded in the order he usually followed. He knew that the Jews were held fast by a perverse zeal for the Law, and sought justification and salvation in its works. So he taught that all of us are sinners, and that the Law cannot be satisfied by human strength. From this it was easy to conclude that another must be sought, by whose merit men can be justified and saved. This was the most suitable occasion for delivering the mysteries of Christ. Let all the churches and ministers of the Word imitate Paul's example, lest, by taking no account of their hearers and pouring everything out in confusion, they make them utterly alien to the kingdom of Christ, when they could easily have been won over by prudent moderation. Certainly he himself wills that a minister be one who knows how to handle the word of truth rightly (2 Tim. 2). And Christ requires of the same minister not only faithfulness in carrying out his work, but also prudence. Moreover, lest anyone think that Paul always used milk, Luke writes that when an opportunity arose he pleaded the cause of Christ with greater fervour. For when Silas and Timothy had arrived from Macedonia, he began to be wholly seized by the Spirit, either because he heard from them that the course of the gospel was going well among the Macedonians, or because the blindness of so great a city and its unhappy condition moved his spirit. For who would not have been moved by the calamity of that most famous city, now rushing to ruin, and by the wretched ignorance of men in it who deceive themselves? Certainly, whatever that restraint of Paul's was, it is certain that he was stirred by a more vehement impulse of the Spirit, so that he began to testify publicly and openly to the Jews that Jesus, the son of Mary, is the Christ, that is, the promised Saviour of the human race, by whose merit alone we are freed from the curse of the Law, from sin and from death. Thus ministers prepare their way by prudent moderation, so that at last they may truly burn in handing on Christ and in bringing forth his glory, lest they seem to cover their timidity with the name of moderation. AGAIN, indeed, it is plain that the chief point of apostolic teaching is Christ, whose witnesses the apostles were chosen to be. Peter taught above that all salvation is enclosed in him alone. Paul, writing later to the Corinthians, confesses that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. John records that the evangelists wrote all things with this end in view, that we may believe that Jesus is the Christ and, believing, obtain eternal life. Therefore we too ought to be content with the same. For it is wrong to claim for oneself, in the matter of salvation, a greater knowledge than the apostles had, who had Christ as their domestic teacher and his most faithful Spirit as their counsellor. Wherefore let us all be wise in Christ alone, the one King and the one Priest, who died for our sins and was raised from the dead for our justification, redeemed us, and made us kings and priests to his Father. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY 121.

units.la: Contradicentibus autem illis & blasphemantibus, excutiens vestimen-ta dixit ad eos: Sanguis vester super caput vestrum. Mundus ego pos-thac ad gentes vadam. Et migrans inde intrauit in domum cuiusdam no-mine Iusti, colentis Deum, cuius domus contigua erat Synagogæ. Cri-spus autem archisynagogus credidit domino cum tota domo sua: multiq; Corinthiorum audientes credebant & baptizabantur. Dixit autem do-minus nocte per visionem Paulo: Noli timere, sed loquere & ne taceas, propterea quod ego sum tecum, & nemo insurget contra te ut noceat: quoniam populus est mihi multus in hac urbe. Sedit autem ibi annum & sex mensescdocens eos sermonem domini.
units.tr: But when they opposed him and blasphemed, Paul shook out his garments and said to them: "Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles." And he left there and entered the house of a certain man named Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next to the synagogue. Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with his whole household, and many of the Corinthians, hearing, believed and were baptized. Then the Lord said to Paul by night in a vision: "Do not be afraid, but speak and do not keep silent, because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city." And he stayed there a year and six months, teaching them the word of God.

units.la: DOminus noster Iesus Christus non semel testatus est, se eo potissimum nomine in mundum ve-nisse, ut peccatores salvos faceret. Huius ergo memores ipsius apostoli, salutis doctrinam in-signibus peccatoribus praedicare, & hos in Christi & ecclesiae communionem adducere consueuerunt. Ita enim initio fieri oportebat, ne quis Christi meritum peccatorum nostrorum atrocitate superari pu-taret, & de salutis ratione, quae in hoc sita est, desperare inciperet. Id verò in Corinthi conuersione cumprimis obseruandum venit. Eam enim urbem omnibus modis corruptissimam fuisse nuper au-diimus. Mittitur tamen ad illam Paulus, ut in interitus praecipitio constitutos per euangelij prae-dicationem liberet. Et quidem pro more suo Iudæis primùm salutem offert, qui prae aliis digni erant, ut à Deo negligerentur. Quis ergo de Dei bonitate desperet, quae infestissimæ gentis salutem tam pro-penso studio quaesiuit? Videamus autem in praesenti, ut incurabilis horum impietas cum Dei longa-nimitate hic quoq; luctata sit, vincente tamen & triumphante in medijs turbis Christo domino.
units.tr: Our Lord Jesus Christ declared more than once that he came into the world chiefly for this purpose, to save sinners. Mindful of this, the apostles were accustomed to preach the message of salvation to notorious sinners and to bring them into the communion of Christ and the Church. For this was how it had to be done from the beginning, lest anyone think that the merit of Christ was overcome by the enormity of our sins, and begin to despair of the way of salvation, which lies in him. Now this must be especially observed in the conversion of Corinth. For we have recently heard that this city was utterly corrupt in every way. Yet Paul is sent to it, to free those who were headed for the precipice of destruction through the preaching of the gospel. And indeed, according to his custom, he first offers salvation to the Jews, who, above others, deserved to be abandoned by God. Who then should despair of God's goodness, which sought the salvation of a most hostile nation with such eager zeal? Let us see, then, how the incurable impiety of these men wrestled here also with God's long-suffering, though Christ the Lord conquered and triumphed in the midst of the crowds.

units.la: Iudaeos enim Paulo, de Christo diserte testificanti, contradixisse & tandem ad blasphemias de-uenisse scribitur. Id verò illis perpetuum fuisse, iam multis exemplis didicimus. Horribilis autem est hac illorum improbitas, si quales olim fuerint cogitemus, & eam quae hodie adhuc graßantur in Chri-stum maledicendi rabiem expendamus. Quis enim non diuinae iustitiae seueritatem exhorreat, quam do iam saeculis aliquot non alia irae vasa tam infelicia esse videt, quàm eos qui olim primogeniti Dei genus electum & sacerdotale illud Dei regnum dici solebant? EST autem obseruatione dignissi-mum, quòd nunc demum Paulo contradicunt, quando ille de Christo apertius testari coepit: cum il-lum iam sabbatis aliquot de Lege & reliquis articulis disputantem non admodum iniquis animis sustinuerint. Quod enim Corinthi factum est, hoc ipsum hodie quoq; passim fieri videmus. Ferantur vtcunq; qui manifestos abusus & mores palam corruptos oblique reprehendunt, quod ipsum regnan-te adhuc te adhuc Papatu multos fecisse constat. Vt primum vero Christus vrgetur, & illi diserte sua asse‐ritur & vindicatur gloria, mox furore concitantur, qui modestissimi videri poterant. Causa huius mali est, quod abs‐q; Christi praedicatione omnes aliae reprehensiones frigent, nec plus ponderis habent quam philosophorum sermones, quos olim magnifice & ornate de virtutum studio & vitiorum misera‐bili conditione disseruisse legimus. Christus vero ipsas hominum mentes penetrans, ad vivum vsq; omnem cum cultus divini tum vitae morumq; corruptionem resecat, & proinde intolerabiles mundo videntur, quae ex huius doctrina necessario colligi solent consequentia. Per hanc enim funditus vsq; corruit vniuersa sacrorum nundinatio. Per eandem humanae iustitiae splendor extinguitur, & euer‐titur tota nostri meriti fiducia. Eadem Christi luce morum licentiam arguit, nec theatrale modo & fucatam, sed synceraм omnibusq; numeris absolutam poenitentiam requirit, quam nec carnis nostrae corruptio admittere, nec humanae vires praestare possunt. Tolerabile quidem mundo videtur, si adul‐terum, militem, vsurarium, ebriosum arguas, modo ijsdem friuola aliqua satisfactione expiatis lo‐cum relinquas in ecclesia, licet eundem vitae cursum sedulo sequantur. At si euangelij voce damna‐tionis sententiam intones, & poenitere nescium a regno dei excludas, id demum nullo modo seren‐dum esse putatur. Est hoc evidens corruptionis nostrae argumentum, & quod revera Dei hostes sint, quicunq; devotis animis in peccata ruunt, nec sese verbo dei corrigi patiuntur. Quis enim non dei ho‐stem dicat eum, cui filius Dei sordet prae abominabili peccandi licentia? Rursum vero locutionis or‐dinem, quo Lucas vtitur, observemus. Contradixerunt (inquit) & blasphemauerunt. Primus ergo impietatis gradus est, si verbo Dei contradicamus. Quia vero id ex ignorantia multi faciunt, excusabilis primo error est. At quicunq; prauo affectu sese impelli sinunt, vt revelata veritati contradicat, primo hoc gradu non contenti, fere ad conuicia conuertuntur. Qualia autem conuicia fuerint, quae in Paulum iaculati sunt Iudaei, ex iis collige, quae supra Cap. 6. 16. & 17. audiuimus. Admonemur vero horum exemplo, principiis obstandum esse, ne dum verbo dei, prava cupiditate abrepti, contradicere non veremur, tandem contentione irritati ad blasphemandum quoq; animum applicemus. Ita enim paulatim horribili peccato in spiritum sanctum nosipsos implicamus, tandemq; gigantea audacia inflammati, Deo apertum bellum mouemus, cuius finis alius esse nequit, quam miserabilis & sempi‐terna animarum perditio. Exempla huius passim sunt obuia, &c.
units.tr: For we read that the Jews contradicted Paul when he openly testified about Christ, and at last came to blasphemies. We have already learned from many examples that this was a constant feature of theirs. But their wickedness is dreadful if we consider what they once were, and weigh the raging malice of cursing that still rages today against Christ. For who would not shudder at the severity of divine justice, when for some centuries now no vessels of wrath appear so unhappy as those who were once called the firstborn of God, the chosen race, and that priestly kingdom of God? It is also most worthy of notice that they now at last contradict Paul, when he began to bear witness to Christ more openly, whereas for some sabbaths they had endured him disputing about the Law and the other articles without too much ill will. What happened at Corinth we see happening everywhere today. Let them be borne with, however, who obliquely reprove manifest abuses and openly corrupt morals; it is well known that many did this even while the Papacy still reigned. But as soon as Christ is pressed, and his glory is plainly claimed and asserted, straightway those who might seem most gentle are roused to fury. The cause of this evil is that, apart from the preaching of Christ, all other rebukes grow cold and carry no more weight than the speeches of the philosophers, which we read were once delivered in fine and elaborate style on the pursuit of virtue and the wretched condition of vice. But Christ, penetrating the very minds of men, cuts away to the quick every corruption both of divine worship and of life and morals; and therefore those consequences which usually follow necessarily from his doctrine seem intolerable to the world. For through this doctrine the whole trade in sacred things collapses to its foundations. Through the same doctrine the splendour of human righteousness is extinguished, and the whole confidence in our own merit is overthrown. By the same light of Christ, he condemns licence of conduct, and he requires a repentance that is not theatrical or feigned, but sincere and complete in every respect, which neither the corruption of our flesh can admit nor human strength can supply. It seems tolerable to the world if you charge an adulterer, a soldier, a usurer, or a drunkard, provided you leave them a place in the Church once they have been cleansed by some trifling satisfaction, even though they continue diligently in the same course of life. But if you thunder the sentence of condemnation with the voice of the gospel, and exclude from the kingdom of God those who know not how to repent, this is thought by all means to be unbearable. This is clear evidence of our corruption, and that those are truly enemies of God who rush into sins with devoted minds and will not allow themselves to be corrected by the word of God. For who would not call an enemy of God the one for whom the Son of God is worthless in comparison with a detestable licence to sin? Again, let us observe the order of the words Luke uses: "They contradicted and blasphemed." The first step of impiety, then, is to contradict the word of God. But since many do this out of ignorance, the first error is excusable. However, those who allow themselves to be driven by a wicked disposition to contradict revealed truth, not content with this first step, almost turn to reproaches. As for what sort of reproaches the Jews hurled at Paul, gather this from what we heard above in chapters 6, 16 and 17. We are warned by their example, however, that we must resist beginnings, lest, while we are carried away by a perverse desire and do not fear to contradict the word of God, we at last, provoked by strife, apply our minds to blaspheming as well. For thus we gradually entangle ourselves in the horrible sin against the Holy Spirit, and at last, inflamed with gigantic audacity, we wage open war against God, whose end can be nothing other than the wretched and eternal destruction of souls. Examples of this are everywhere to be met with, etc.

units.la: Quid vero Paulus? Num propter incurabiles Iudaeos Corintho discedit, sic vt quorundam im‐probitas omnibus in vniuersum fraudi sit? Nequaquam. Quin potius improbis illis & pertinaci‐bus valere iussis, ad gentes conuertitur. Ne quid vero impotentis animi affectu fecisse videatur, or‐dinem a Christo praescriptum, diligenter obseruat. Primo vestes excutit, quod ipsum Antiochiae fecit, vt Cap. 13. dictum est: vnde peti possunt quae ad huius caeremonia aut chriae explicationem fa‐ciunt. Deinde poenam denunciat, illos propria ipsorum culpa perire docens. Sanguis vester (inquit) super caput vestrum. Mundus ego posthac ad gentes vadam. Alludit autem ad Dei verba, quae apud Ezechielem Cap. 3. & 33. in hunc modum extant: Fili hominis, speculatorem constituite do‐mui Israelis. Audies igitur verbum ex oremeo, & diserte monebis eos ex me. Cum ego dixero im‐pio, Certissime morieris: & tu non monueris eum diserte, dehortando illum a via sua impia vt vi‐uat: ille quidem morietur in iniquitate sua, sanguinem vero eius de manu tua requiram. Quod si tu diserte monueris impium, nec ille conuersus fuerit ab iniquitate sua, peribit is, tuq; animam tuam liberauisti. Ad haec (inquam) verba Paulus alludit, dicens: Ego quidem meo officio functus sum, & Christum salutis authorem vnicum proposui. Hunc vero quia vos reiicitis, in vobis haeret vestra perditionis culpa, ego autem immunis & liber me ad gentes conferam. Ita vero idem illis minatur quod Christus, quando scribis ait: Transferetur a vobis regnum Dei, & dabitur genti facienti fru‐ctus eius. Matth. 21. At quod Iudaeis dicitur, hoc ipsum omnes euangelij contemptores sibi dictum esse intelligant. Quia enim euangelio remedium perditionis nostrae diuinitus nobis offertur, non pos‐sunt non perire iusto dei iudicio, quicunq; illud improbe aspernati fuerint. Interim admonet nos Paulus factum, tunc demum extra culpam esse verbi ministros, quando erga peccatores officio suo fideli‐ter defuncti sunt, eos nimirum docendo, monendo, increpando & hortando. Quod si canes muti fue‐rint (quales Isaiae 56. describuntur) ab ipsis exigetur sanguis pereuntium, id est, reos aget illos Deus omnis sanguinis, qui ipsorum incuria effunditur. At atrocissimum esse sanguinis reatum,
units.tr: But what did Paul do? Did he leave Corinth because of the incurable Jews, so that the wickedness of some should be a loss to all in general? By no means. Rather, having bidden farewell to those wicked and obstinate men, he turns to the Gentiles. And lest he seem to have acted from a passion of an impatient spirit, he carefully observes the order prescribed by Christ. First he shakes out his garments, which he had also done at Antioch, as was said in chapter 13; from this one may seek what pertains to the explanation of this ceremony or sign. Then he announces punishment, teaching that they perish by their own fault. "Your blood," he says, "be upon your own heads. From now on I will go to the Gentiles." Now he alludes to the words of God which stand in Ezekiel, chapters 3 and 33, in this manner: "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear a word from my mouth, and you shall warn them plainly from me. When I say to the wicked, 'You shall surely die,' and you do not warn him plainly, dissuading him from his wicked way so that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand. But if you warn the wicked plainly, and he is not turned from his iniquity, he shall perish, and you have delivered your soul." It is to these words, I say, that Paul alludes when he says: "I have indeed discharged my duty, and I have set forth Christ, the sole author of salvation. But since you reject him, your guilt of perdition clings to you; I, however, am innocent and free, and I will go to the Gentiles." Thus he threatens them with the same thing that Christ did, when he said in the scriptures: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation bearing its fruits." Matt. 21. But what is said to the Jews, let all despisers of the gospel understand is said to themselves. For since the remedy for our perdition is offered to us from God through the gospel, all who wickedly spurn it cannot but perish by the just judgment of God. Meanwhile Paul teaches us that ministers of the word are free from blame only when they have faithfully discharged their duty toward sinners, namely by teaching, warning, rebuking and exhorting them. But if they are dumb dogs (such as are described in Isaiah 56), the blood of those who perish will be required of them, that is, God, the avenger of all blood, will hold those men guilty whose blood is shed through their negligence. But that the guilt of blood is most atrocious,

units.la: dus. passim scriptura docent. Vide Gene.9. Num.35.cap.Psal.5.&c. Non temere ergo prophetas simul & apostolos tanto zelo in docendi functione versari videmus. Huc certè Paulus respiciens ait: Vae mihi, si non euangelizem. Et Amos tertio capite dicit: Leo si rugiat, quis non timebit? Dominus Deus locutus est, & quis non prophetaret? Postremò ad Iustum quendam Paulus diuertit, non quòd Aquilam odisset, sed vt protestationi suae pondus accederet. Videtur enim Iustus hic gentilis fuisse, nisi ridiculum velimus aestimare Pauli factum, qui ex Iudaei fidelis domo in alterius Iudaei aedes migrare voluerit. Sed & verba ipsius sonant, Ego posthac ad gentes vadam. Elucet tamen in Paulo ardens suae gentis studium. Nam licet gentilem sibi hospitem deligat, Synagoga tamen vicinus habitare cupit, ne illi Iudaeos lucrifaciendi occasio defit. Imitentur exemplum hoc omnes mi niftri. Quia enim pastores & patres dicuntur, eo erga pereuntes quoq; affectu illos praeditos esse conuenit, quem in fidis pastoribus erga palantes oues, & in patribus erga liberos male pereuntes vide-mus. Eundem enim Christus declarat, quando ad vrbis Hierosolymitanae conspectum lachrymas fundit, & iusto Dei iudicio pereuntis exitium deplorat. Luc.19.
units.tr: ...as Scripture teaches throughout. See Gen. 9; Num. 35; Ps. 5, etc. It is no accident, then, that we see the prophets and apostles so zealously engaged in the work of teaching. Paul certainly had this in view when he said: "Woe is me, if I do not preach the gospel." And Amos says in chapter 3: "If a lion roars, who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken; who will not prophesy?" Lastly, Paul turned aside to a certain Justus, not because he hated Aquila, but so that his protest might carry more weight. For this Justus seems to have been a Gentile, unless we want to think Paul's action ridiculous, since he would have moved from the house of a faithful Jew into that of another Jew. His own words also sound like "From now on I will go to the Gentiles." Yet Paul's burning zeal for his own people still shines through. For although he chose a Gentile as his host, he wanted to live next door to the synagogue, so that he would not lack an opportunity of winning Jews. Let all ministers imitate this example. Since they are called shepherds and fathers, it is fitting that they should be endowed with that affection toward those who are perishing which we see in faithful shepherds toward wandering sheep, and in fathers toward children who are going badly astray. Christ shows the same feeling when, at the sight of the city of Jerusalem, he sheds tears and laments the ruin of those perishing by God's just judgment. Luke 19.

units.la: Atqui non infrugiferum fuit Pauli studium. Ex Iudaeis enim Crispus credit, princeps Synagogae, quem abs se baptizatum esse in priori ad Corinth.1.cap.scribit. Simul etiam multi ex Corinthijs credunt, qui paulo ante peccatis & perditioni toti immersi videri poterant. Nec sucatam fuisse illorum fidem, ex baptismo conijci potest, quo illam ingenuè & publicè professi sunt. Non deest ergo sua benedictione Deus ijs, qui in vocatione sua strenuè laborant, nec aliquorum incredulitas & pertinacia dei fidem irritam facere potest, vt alibi Paulus monet. Rom.2. Debent hinc consolationem & confirmationem petere quicunq; boftes graues & incurabiles sentiunt. Porrò sequitur memorabilis locus, qui Paulum, dum haec agerentur, diuina consolatione sustentatum fuisse docet: vbi primò quidem ipsius Pauli persona, deinde verò Deus, qui illum consolatione sua confirmauit, consyderandus erit.
units.tr: Yet Paul's zeal was not without fruit. For Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, came to believe from among the Jews, and he wrote in his earlier letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 1) that he had baptized him. At the same time, many of the Corinthians also believed, who a little before might have seemed utterly immersed in sins and destruction. That their faith was not feigned can be inferred from their baptism, by which they openly and sincerely professed it. God therefore does not withhold his blessing from those who labour earnestly in their calling, and the unbelief and obstinacy of some cannot make God's faithfulness void, as Paul warns elsewhere (Rom. 2). Those who feel that their hearers are serious and incurable should take comfort and encouragement from this. Next follows a memorable passage, which teaches that Paul, while these things were going on, was sustained by divine consolation. Here we must consider first the person of Paul himself, and then God, who strengthened him with his consolation.

units.la: Et Paulum quidè aliquid humani passum fuisse ac timuisse, ex dei consolatione patet. Quin multa quotidie illi ob oculos versata sunt, quae illum terrere potuerunt. Nota illi siquidem erat incurabilis aduersus Christi doctrinam Iudaeorum rabies. Recens adhuc erat periculorum, quae ijsdem authoribus ipsi multis in locis concitata erant, memoria. Nec magnam illi profectus ipsem facere potuerat immanis & publicis prouerbijs notata vrbis corruptio. Accesserunt falsorum fratrum & impostorum doli, de quibus non semel in suis epistolis conqueritur. Imò se cum multo timore & tremore Corinthi versatum fuisse, ingenuè fatetur. 1.Corinth.2. Et quantum ex dei verbis conijcere licet, de deferenda vrbe Paulus cogitauit, quae adeò exiguam de se spem praebere videbatur. Docemur exemplo hoc, sanctos quoq; dei cultores affectibus obnoxios esse, & imprimis quidem timore ita interdum concuti, vt officij sui non satis memores videri possint. Quod enim Paulo Corinthi accidit, hoc ipsum non pauci maiori cum lapsu experti sunt. Abraham credentium pater, postquam relictio patrio solo incomparabile fidei documentum dedit, timore superatus famam suam turpi mendacio polluit, & vxorem praesenti periculo implicat. Iacobus post toties perspectam Dei opem Esau fratris occursum expauescit. Moses Pharaonis tyrannidem veritus in Madian confugit, vixq; Deo vocante adduci potest, vt in Aegyptum redeat. Iosue, bellator fortissimus, vnica populi clade consternatus, fletu & ciulatu parum virili timorem animo conceptum testatur. Dauidem, qui puer adhuc Goliam deuicerat, iam virum & multoties victorem, non semel Saulis minas & conatus timuisse legimus. Helias, qui nec Achabi praesentia & tyrannide, nec populi furoribus absterreri potuerat, quò minus Baalis sacerdotes trucidaret, vnius mulierculae lefabelis minis territus fugit & mori exoptat. Quid de Petro dicam, qui cum armatam cohortem non exhorruisset, mox ancillula voce examinatus, Christum abnegauit? Poterant infinita alia huius generis exempla recenseri, quae non ideo commemoramus, quod sanctorum vitia traducere volupe sit, sed quod horum consyderatio nostra instititioni non parum seruiat. Nam & nostram infirmitatem inde agnoscimus, cuius cognitio confidentiae medetur: & charitatis admonemur, ne temerario iudicio viros alioqui bene meritos damnemus, si quid praeter officium faciunt. Vult enim in illis quoq; communis infirmitatis vestigia extare Deus, ne illis plus aequo addictis, diuinae gratiae obliuiscamur, quae per ipsos praeclara opera edidit. Interim precibus nostris iuuandi sunt, vt vel lapsum cauere, vel ab illo gratiae Dei beneficio quàm ocyfsime resurgere possint. Id enim officij Christum discipulis praestitisse, euangelica historia docet. Luc. 22. Iohan. 17. &c.
units.tr: That Paul suffered and feared something human is clear from God's consolation. Indeed, many things that could terrify him presented themselves to his eyes every day. He knew well the incurable rage of the Jews against the doctrine of Christ. The memory was still fresh of the dangers that these same men had stirred up against him in many places. Nor could the monstrous corruption of the city, notorious for its public proverbs, have given him much encouragement. Add to this the deceits of false brothers and impostors, about which he complains more than once in his letters. Indeed, he frankly confesses that he was at Corinth in much fear and trembling (1 Cor. 2). And, as far as we may gather from God's words, Paul thought of leaving the city, which seemed to offer him such slight hope. We are taught by this example that even the holy worshippers of God are subject to the passions, and above all that they are sometimes so shaken by fear that they may seem not sufficiently mindful of their duty. What happened to Paul at Corinth, not a few have experienced with a greater fall. Abraham, the father of believers, after he had given an incomparable proof of faith by leaving his native soil, was overcome by fear, stained his reputation with a shameful lie, and exposed his wife to present danger. Jacob, after so many clear experiences of God's help, trembled at the approach of his brother Esau. Moses, fearing the tyranny of Pharaoh, fled into Midian, and was scarcely brought, by God's call, to return to Egypt. Joshua, a most valiant warrior, dismayed by one defeat of the people, bore witness with weeping and wailing, hardly manly, to the fear that had taken hold of his mind. We read that David, who as a boy had already conquered Goliath, and now a man and often a victor, more than once feared the threats and attempts of Saul. Elijah, who had not been frightened by the presence and tyranny of Ahab, nor by the rage of the people, so that he failed to slay the priests of Baal, was terrified by the threats of a single frail woman, fled, and longed to die. What shall I say of Peter, who had not shrunk from an armed cohort, but soon, questioned by the voice of a servant girl, denied Christ? Countless other examples of this kind could be recounted. We mention them not because it is pleasant to expose the faults of the saints, but because the consideration of them greatly serves our instruction. For we recognise from them our own weakness, and the knowledge of this cures overconfidence; and we are reminded of charity, so that we do not rashly condemn men otherwise well deserving if they do something beyond their duty. For God wills that traces of common weakness remain in them too, lest, being too much devoted to them, we forget the grace of God, which worked such splendid deeds through them. Meanwhile they must be helped by our prayers, that they may either guard against a fall or rise again from it, by God's grace, as quickly as possible. For the gospel history teaches that Christ performed this duty for his disciples (Luke 22; John 17, etc.).

units.la: Sed dei personam inspiciamus, qui timentem & trepidum illico consolatur, licet nulla invocatio-
units.tr: But let us look at the person of God, who immediately comforts the fearful and trembling man, although no mention of prayer is made

units.la: nis mentio fiat. Nec enim eos duntaxat exaudit Deus, qui clamoribus vota animi sui exponunt, sed latentes animorum gemitus & fluctuantes in illis curas videns, consolationem & opem afferre solet. Id vero fieri cumprimis necesse est, quando frequenter fit, ut undiq; prementibus nos malis circum-
units.tr: For God does not listen only to those who pour out the desires of their souls in cries, but when he sees the hidden groanings of minds and the anxieties tossing within them, he is accustomed to bring consolation and help. This must especially happen when it often happens that, surrounded by evils pressing on us from every side, we do not know how to express the longings of our minds in words.

units.la: uenti, animi desyderia verbis exponere nesciamus. Tunc ergo impletur, quod apud Isaiam Cap. 65. promittit Deus: Futurum est, ut priusquam invocent, ego respondeam: et adhuc illis loquentibus, ego exaudiam. Ita Mosi ad mare rubrum stanti dicit dominus: Quid clamas? cum vocem nullam edidisse legatur. Est autem hoc ingens diuinae bonitatis argumentum. Ut enim novit Deus quibus rebus nobis opus sit, ita illas in tempore largiri consuevit, et licet tentationes immittat, quae nostrae nos infirmitatis admoneant & ad pietatis studium ardentius inflamment, simul tamen consolationem quoq; pro harum ratione temperat, ne toti absorbeamur. Nemo igitur desperet facile, cum infinita passim media Deus habeat, quibus nos consolari & iuuare possit. Et hoc quidem loco visione simul & oraculo uti voluit, quae duo cumprimis idonea erant, quando neminem ex hominibus consolatorem habebat Paulus, & multa occurrebant, quae deo nullum in corruptissima urbe locum esse, suadere poterant. Sunt autem diuinae huius orationis partes tres, de quibus singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Then, therefore, what God promises through Isaiah in chapter 65 is fulfilled: "It shall come to pass that before they call, I will answer; and while they are still speaking, I will hear." So the Lord said to Moses standing at the Red Sea: "Why do you cry out to me?" when it is read that he had uttered no voice. This is a great proof of divine goodness. For as God knows what things we need, so he is accustomed to bestow them in due time; and although he sends temptations, which remind us of our weakness and kindle us more ardently to the zeal of piety, at the same time he tempers consolation to match them, so that we are not wholly swallowed up. Let no one therefore despair readily, since God has countless means everywhere by which he can comfort and help us. And in this place he chose to use both a vision and an oracle, two things especially suitable, since Paul had no human comforter and many things came to mind that could persuade him that there was no place for God in that most corrupt city. There are three parts to this divine address, and we shall speak of each in order.

units.la: Prima causae omnis mali medetur, dum timere vetat. Est autem frequens admodum eiusdem praecepti mentio in sacris literis. Ita enim Mosi, ad Balaam regis occursum consternato, dicitur. Deuteronom. 3. Iosue quoq; cum quinq; regibus congressurus, audit: Ne timeas ab eis, &c. Iosh. 10. Et Jeremiae ad docendi munus vocato, dicit dominus: Ne timeas a conspectu illorum, &c. Ierem. 2. Apostolus quoq; Christus praecipit, ne eos metuant, qui corpus quidem occidere possunt, in animam vero nihil iuris habent. Matth. 10. Omitto multa alia huius generis loca. Tam frequenter vero suos timere vetat Deus, quia nihil efficacius ad retrahendum ab officio homines est, quam timor. Ut primum enim hoc correpti fuerint animi, rationis lux impeditur, ut quid facto opus sit, videre non queat, nec ulla magis incerta sunt consilia, quam quae a timidis & metu perplexis iniri solent. Quod si vero in universum praevaleat timor, pudorem quoq; excutit, ut praesentis vitae aut etiam opum metu indignissimaq; faciant homines, nec raro maius periculum incurrant, dum praesens vitare volunt. Id quia priuatis hominibus accidit, quanto maior necessitas est, ut praesenti animo et a metu alienissimo sint, qui publica officia sustinent? Isti enim non sibi ipsis tantum, verumetiam alijs peccant, quos ipsorum fidei commisit dominus. Quae causa est, quod a iudicibus quoq; animi fortitudinem prudentissimus vir Iethro requirit. Exod. 18. Et recte hinc consolationis initium hic quoq; Deus sumpsit.
units.tr: The first remedies the cause of all evil, while it forbids fear. The command is mentioned very often in the sacred letters. Thus Moses, dismayed at the approach of Balaam's king, is told (Deut. 3). Joshua also, about to engage five kings, hears: "Do not fear them" (Josh. 10). And to Jeremiah, called to the office of teaching, the Lord says: "Do not be afraid of their faces" (Jer. 1). Christ also commands the apostles not to fear those who can kill the body but have no power over the soul (Matt. 10). I pass over many other passages of this kind. God forbids his people to fear so often because nothing is more effective than fear in turning men back from their duty. For as soon as minds are seized by it, the light of reason is blocked, so that they cannot see what needs to be done, and no plans are more uncertain than those undertaken by the timid and perplexed by dread. But if fear prevails in general, it also shakes off shame, so that men, out of fear of present life or even of their wealth, act most unworthily, and not infrequently run into greater danger while wishing to avoid the present one. If this happens to private persons, how much greater is the need that those who bear public offices should have a calm mind and be most free from fear? For they sin not only against themselves but against others too, whom the Lord has entrusted to their faith. This is why the most prudent man Jethro also requires courage of judges (Exod. 18). And rightly, God here too began his consolation from this point.

units.la: Secunda parte, quid faciat, praecipit. Loquere (inquit) & ne taceas. Ubi nemo Pleonasmo aut superuacaneus verbum Deum vsum esse, putare debet. Duo enim ista coniungit, quia multi loquuntur simul & tacent: dum videlicet ea quidem loquuntur, quibus neminem offendi posse existimant, inte- rim vero multa alia tacent, quae illos ex Dei mandato dicere oportebat. Sensus ergo praecepti est, ut diserte euangelium praedicet, nec quicquam eorum dissimulet aut taceat, quae illo comprehenduntur, vtcunq; aliquos indigne laturos esse experiatur. Hinc vero discant ministri omnes, nequaquam ipsos suo officio defunctos esse, si Dei verbum praedicent, nisi totum praedicent, idq; diserte, adeoq; doctrinam singulis applicent, ut sibi ista dici intelligant. Ut enim malae fidei legatus fuerit, qui nihil quidem aliud loquatur quam quod in mandatis accepit, interim non omnia illa proferat, sed in quorundam gratiam multa dissimulet: ita fidelis Christi minister censeri non debet, quicunq; vel minimam euangelicae praedicationis portiunculam dissimulauerit, ut hominibus placere queat. Vide quae in hanc sententiam dicuntur, Ierem. 1. Ezech. 3. & 33. Matth. 28. &c.
units.tr: Second, he instructs what Paul is to do: "Speak," he says, "and do not keep silent." Here no one should think that God uses a pleonasm or a superfluous word. For he joins these two because many people speak and keep silent at the same time: they say those things by which they think no one can be offended, while meanwhile they pass over many other things which they ought to have said by God's command. The sense of the precept, then, is that he should preach the gospel plainly, and conceal or omit nothing of those things it contains, however much he may find that some will take them badly. From this all ministers should learn that they have by no means discharged their office merely by preaching God's Word, unless they preach all of it, and preach it plainly, and apply the teaching to each of their hearers so that they understand it is said to them. For just as a envoy would be acting in bad faith if he said nothing but what he had received in his instructions, yet did not deliver all of it, but concealed much to gain the favour of some, so a minister of Christ ought not to be regarded as faithful if he has suppressed even the smallest portion of evangelical preaching in order to be able to please men. See what is said to this effect in Jeremiah 1, Ezekiel 3 and 33, Matthew 28, etc.

units.la: Tertia parte rationes adhibet graues simul & efficaces: in quarum numero prima est: Quia ego tecum sum. Debebat vna haec aduersus quauis pericula sufficere. Cum enim omnipotens sit Deus, aliquid ijs deesse non poteit, quibus ille praesens adest. Quid enim aduersus Deum creaturae faciant, quae sine hoc ne subsistere quidem possunt? Recte ergo Dauid colligit, dicens: Dominus mihi adiutor, non timebo quid faciat mihi homo. Psal. 118. Quia autem generalis haec promissio est, ad omnes eos virtutem, qui in dei vocatione ambulant, singuli eam ad se transferre, & hac freti omnes mundi infultus intrepidi sustinere debent. Secunda ratio est: Nemo insurget contra te, ut noceat tibi. Irri​tos fore dicit hostium conatus. Eftq; hæc specialis promissio, quæ non semper locum habet. Frequen​ter enim fit, ut grauissimis periculis pij implicentur, & Paulo iam non semel manus iniectas fuisse audiuimus, imo idem postea captus per terras & maria Romam deducitur, vbi gladio vitam fini​uit. Licet vero ista fiant, firma tamen manet primæ promissionis veritas, & ex morte etiam suos sal​vat Dominus, nec illis vllam dee​st. Quare per ferrum & ignes in Dei vocatione ambulandum & strenuè pergendum est. Tertia ratio est, quòd fe multum Corinthi populum habere dicit. Ita ve​rò non infrugiferum fore docet laborem, quando Dei verbum in electis & prædestinatis ad salutem semper efficax esse solet, vt supra cap. 14. dictum est. Memorabile vero hoc est, quòd in corruptiffi​ma vrbe multum populum habet Deus, & plures quidem quàm Athenis, quæ sapientiæ & virtutis titulum præ aliis ciuitatibus sibi vendicabat. Vnde colligimus eos, qui peccatis palàm immersi sunt, ad percipiendum dei regnum magis idoneos esse, quàm iuftitiarios & fanctulos, qui iusti et boni omni​bus videntur. Eadem enim hic ratio est, quæ in corporum morbis. Vt enim qui morbis apertis labo​rant, medicos facilius admittunt, quàm qui occultioribus vexantur, quorū illos pudet, quosq; aliqua ratione dissimulare possunt: Ita palàm flagitiosi salutis doctrinam citius recipiunt, quàm hypocrita, qui suæ iustitiæ fiducia inflati, fe nulla alia opus habere arbitrantur. Nam quia fe peccatores esse ne​gare non possunt, de salutis ratione necessario cogitant, & hanc extra fe quærere coguntur. Quæ cau​fa est, quòd publicani & meretrices pharifæis in dei regno præferuntur. Matth.21. Et Christus àpu​catorum redargutione euangelij doctrinam inchoari vult, vt depresso propriæ iustitiæ supercilio, ad dei gratiam confugere discamus. Interim non parum nos consolatur, quòd in deploratiffima gente multos habet dominus æternæ salutis hæredes. Inde enim constat, deo nunquam non esse sua septem millia, etiamsi omnes perditi videantur. Vide 1. Reg. 19. Ea quippe est electionis & prædestinationis dei certitudo, vt pro dei electis censeantur, qui ab æterno in librum vitæ inscripti sunt, etiamsi adhuc peccatis immersi hæreant. Ita Christus suas oues esse dicit, quos nec externa prædicatione adhuc vo​carat, nec interna spiritus operatione traxerat, sibi vero àpatre datos esse nouerat, priusquam mundi huius fundamenta iacerentur. Vide Iohan. 10. Ephes. 1. Eftq; hæc omnium efficacissima consolatio, quòd ne peccatis quidem nostris dei electionem impediri posse constat. Quos enim ille prædestinauit, eos suo tempore vocat & trahit, filijq; fui imagini conformes reddit, nec vllis rebus à sua dilectione separari patitur. Rom. 8.
units.tr: Third, he adduces reasons that are at once weighty and effective. The first of these is: "For I am with you." This one reason alone ought to be sufficient against any dangers whatever. For since God is almighty, nothing can be lacking to those with whom he is present. For what can creatures do against God, who cannot even subsist without him? Rightly, then, David concludes, saying: "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me" (Ps. 118). But since this promise is general, applying to all who walk in the vocation of God, each one ought to appropriate it to himself, and, relying on this, all should bear with fearless hearts the assaults of the world. The second reason is: "No one shall rise up against you to harm you." He says that the attempts of enemies will come to nothing. And this is a special promise, which does not always hold good. For it often happens that the godly are entangled in the gravest dangers, and we have heard that hands were laid on Paul more than once; indeed, afterwards he was taken, carried by land and sea to Rome, where he ended his life by the sword. Yet although these things happen, the truth of the first promise remains firm, and the Lord saves his people even from death, nor is anything lacking to them. Wherefore we must walk through iron and fire in the vocation of God and press on vigorously. The third reason is that he says he has many people in Corinth. He teaches that labour will not be unfruitful, since the Word of God is always wont to be effective in the elect and predestined to salvation, as was said above in chapter 14. Yet this is worth noting: that in the most corrupt city God has many people, and more indeed than at Athens, which claimed for itself the title of wisdom and virtue above other cities. From this we gather that those who are openly immersed in sins are more fit to receive the kingdom of God than the self-righteous and the pious, who seem just and good to everyone. For here the reasoning is the same as in bodily diseases. For as those who suffer from open illnesses readily admit doctors more than those who are troubled by hidden ones, which they are ashamed of and can in some way conceal, so openly wicked men receive the doctrine of salvation more quickly than hypocrites, who, puffed up with confidence in their own righteousness, think they have no need of anything else. For since they cannot deny that they are sinners, they necessarily think about the way of salvation and are compelled to seek it outside themselves. This is why tax collectors and harlots are preferred to the Pharisees in the kingdom of God (Matt. 21). And Christ wills that the teaching of the gospel should begin with the rebuke of sinners, so that, with the pride of our own righteousness brought low, we may learn to flee to the grace of God.
