Meanwhile it comforts us not a little that the Lord has many heirs of eternal salvation among a most desperate people. For from this it is clear that God never lacks his seven thousand, even when all seem lost (see 1 Kings 19). Indeed, such is the certainty of God's election and predestination that those are counted among God's elect who have been written in the book of life from eternity, even though they still cling to their sins. Thus Christ says that those are his sheep whom he had not yet called by external preaching nor drawn by the inward working of the Spirit, yet whom he knew to have been given to him by the Father before the foundations of this world were laid (see John 10; Eph. 1). And this is the most effective of all consolations: that it is certain the election of God cannot be impeded even by our sins. For those whom he has predestined, he calls and draws at his appointed time, and makes them conformed to the image of his Son, nor does he allow them to be separated from his love by any things (Rom. 8).

units.la: Porrò quanta diuinæ consolationis vis fuerit in Paulo docetur, qui totum annum & menses sex Corinthi mansit, & dei verbum prædicauit. Vbi cum Dei fide & potentia, qui ferum suum in vrbe nefaria tam diu incolumem seruauit, Pauli quoq; patientia nobis confyderanda venit, qui in​ter superbos & ingratiffimos homines tanto tempore mansit, vt deo adduceret, quos ab illo electos esse audiuerat. Qua enim ferocia & improbitate aduersus Paulum vsi interea fuerint, ex eiusdem epi​stolis facile liquet. Arguuntur Pauli exemplo, qui ecclesias temere deferunt, vt primum non pro voto succedunt omnia. Admonemur præterea quanti laboris res fit ecclesiæ ædificatio, quando Paulum Corinthi tam diu laborauisse audimus, vbi tamen fe plantauisse duntaxat, ipsemet fatetur. 1. Cor. 3. Imò iugi postea studio & cura opus fuisse, epistolæ ipsius abunde docent. Detestabilis ergo est mini​ftrorum quorundam ignauia, qui ardentiore zelum in ecclesiæ ædificatione superuacaneum esse exi​ftimant. Imitentur singuli Pauli studium, vt fidei quotidiano exercitio electionem & vocationem no​ftram certam faciamus, & cœlestis regni hereditatem adeamus cum Iesu Christo, Domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, we are taught how great was the power of divine consolation in Paul, who remained at Corinth a whole year and six months and preached the Word of God. Here, along with the faithfulness and power of God, who kept his people safe for so long in a wicked city, we must also consider the patience of Paul, who stayed among proud and most ungrateful men for so long a time, so that he might bring to God those whom he had heard were chosen by him. How fierce and wicked the Corinthians were in the meantime towards Paul is easily made clear from his epistles. By Paul's example those are rebuked who rashly abandon churches when not all things succeed as they wish at first. We are also reminded how great a labour the building up of the church is, when we hear that Paul laboured so long at Corinth, where yet he himself confesses that he had only planted (1 Cor. 3). Indeed, that constant study and care were needed afterwards, his epistles abundantly teach. Detestable, therefore, is the idleness of certain ministers, who think that greater zeal in building up the church is superfluous. Let each one imitate Paul's diligence, so that by the daily exercise of faith we may make our election and calling sure, and attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom with Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXII.

units.la: Porrò cum Gallio Achaiæ proconsulem ageret, insurrexerunt vno animo Iudæi in Paulum, & adduxerunt eum ad tribunal, dicentes: Contra legem hic suadet hominibus colere Deum. Cum autem Paulus iam pararet aperire os, dixit Gallio ad Iudæos: Si qua iniuria effet aut facinus malum, ô Iudæi, merito vos sustinerem. Si vero quæstio est de sermone mône & nominibus & lege vestrate, vos ipsi videritis. Iudex enim horum nolo esse. Et abegit eos à tribunali. Apprehensum verò omnes Græci Softhenem, principem Synagogæ, percutiebant ante tribunal: neque quicquam eorum Gallioni curæ erat.
units.tr: Moreover, while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up with one accord against Paul, brought him before the tribunal, and said: "This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law." When Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews: "If there had been some wrong or wicked crime, O Jews, I would rightly hear you out. But if the question concerns a word, names and your own law, you yourselves must see to it, for I do not wish to be a judge of such things." And he drove them away from the tribunal. Then all the Greeks seized Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal; but Gallio cared nothing for any of this.

units.la: QVàmuis Deus verbi sui ministros tanquam oues in medium luporum emittat, eosdem tamen suo fauore & patrocinio protegit, ne quiduis in illos pro sua libidine impij veritatis hostes possint. Id tum sæpè aliàs, tum Corinthi maximè Paulus expertus est. Nam inter maxima pericula cum timore & tremore versantem, iamque metu tantum non absorptum, consolatione sua Deus prævenit, nec securitatem modò, verumetiam haud vulgarem sui laboris & studij fructum pollicetur. Et quod pollicitus est, summa fide præstat, quemadmodum præsens hic locus docet. Orto enim tumultu & horrendum in modum insanientibus Iudæis, cum nulla in humanis auxilijs spes affulgeret, mirabiliter tamen illum occultasua virtute seruat & liberat, ne quid mali patiatur. Et quia hoc peculiare & cumprimis memorabile est diuinæ protectionis exemplum, non inutile fuerit singulas historiæ huius circunstantias excutere.
units.tr: Although God sends the ministers of his Word out like sheep into the midst of wolves, he nevertheless protects them with his favour and patronage, so that the wicked enemies of the truth cannot do whatever they like to them. Paul experienced this often elsewhere, and especially at Corinth. For while he was living amid the greatest dangers, in fear and trembling, and almost overwhelmed by terror, God anticipated him with consolation, and promised not only safety but also a considerable fruit of his labour and zeal. And what he promised he performs with the utmost faithfulness, as this passage shows. For when the tumult arose and the Jews raged in a dreadful manner, and no hope of human help appeared, yet God wonderfully preserved and freed him by his hidden power, so that he suffered no harm. And since this is a singular and especially memorable example of divine protection, it will not be unprofitable to examine the individual circumstances of this history.

units.la: Et primò quidem turbarum authores producuntur, Iudæi nimirum, de quibus cum sæpe iam dictum sit, plura addere non est opus. Hi cum aliquandiu quieuissent, nimirum Dei virtute repressi, nunc Gallione novo Achaiæ Proconsule Corinthi agente, vnanimi consensu aduersus Paulum insurgunt, captumque in forum ad Proconsulis tribunal trahunt. Quo exemplo docemur diuinas promissiones non ita intelligendas esse, quasi extra omne periculum teíque iactum (vt aiunt) nos consistere velit Deus. Quin potius ille suos exerceri vult, quia ita carnis nostræ ingenium & salutis ratio exigit. Quæ causa est, quòd iuxta Dauidis dictum, multæ sunt tribulationes piorum, sed ex omnibus illos Dominus liberat. Psal 34. Huc referri debent omnium illorum exempla, qui pofst amplissimas promissiones à Deo acceptas, grauissimis periculis tentati sunt. Abrahamo dicitur: Benedicam tibi & magnificabo nomen tuum. Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, maledicentibus vero tibi maledicam. Genef. 12. At idem ille postea ob Saram vxorem periclitatur, belli fortuna exercetur & infinitas exilij molestias sustinet. Nec ideo mendax est Deus, cuius veritas eo luculentior est, quod ex tot tantisque periculis illum liberat. Idem de Mose, Dauide, Ieremia, apostolis deniq; omnibus dici poterat, nisi breuitati studeremus. Vehementer ergo falluntur, qui euangelij promissiones ita exponunt, vt huius ministros illicò mendacij arguant, vt primum crux aliqua oboritur. Memi-nerimus Christum eorum, quæ propter ipsius nomen amittimus, retributionem cum persecutionibus nobis polliceri, & iuxta huius exemplum ferendam esse crucem omnibus ijs, qui post ipsum venire voluerint. Marc. 10. Luc. 9.
units.tr: And first, the authors of the disturbance are named: the Jews, namely, about whom, since it has often been said already, there is no need to add more. These men, after being quiet for some time, restrained no doubt by the power of God, now rise up with one consent against Paul, while Gallio is the new proconsul of Achaia governing at Corinth; they seize him and drag him to the proconsul's tribunal in the forum. From this example we are taught that the divine promises are not to be understood as if God wished us to stand outside all danger, as they say, with the die already cast. Rather, he wills that his people be exercised, as the nature of our flesh and the reason of our salvation require. This is why, according to the saying of David, "many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers them out of them all" (Ps. 34). To this should be referred all the examples of those who, though they had received the most ample promises from God, were tested by the gravest dangers. To Abraham it is said: "I will bless you and make your name great; I will bless those who bless you, and curse him who curses you" (Gen. 12). Yet that same man was afterwards endangered on account of his wife Sarah, was harassed by the fortunes of war, and endured endless troubles of exile. Nor is God therefore false, whose truth is all the more evident because he frees him from so many and such great dangers. The same could be said of Moses, David, Jeremiah, and finally of all the apostles, were we not aiming at brevity. Those therefore greatly err who so expound the promises of the gospel that they at once accuse its ministers of lying as soon as some cross arises. Let us remember that Christ promises those who lose anything for his name a recompense together with persecutions, and that, following his example, every one who wishes to come after him must bear the cross (Mark 10; Luke 9).

units.la: Præterea hostium veritatis mores & artes hoc loco obseruemus, vt facilius à nobis caueri possint. Primò quidem Iudæos astutè nocendi occasionem quæsiuisse videmus, cum hucusque pacati & sopiti fuisse videri potuerint. Nam toto ferè se squianno nihil aduersus Paulum ab illis tentatum est. Sed nouo dato Proconsule insurgunt, vel quòd hominem à religione simul & iustitia alienum, & proinde illorum studijs mirè idoneum fore sperarent: vel quòd nouis rebus turbissimè studere posse crederent sub nouo magistratu, cui Corinthiorum res nondum satis cognitæ esse poterant. In illis ergo prudentia elucet, quia filios huius seculi filijs lucis superiores esse, Christus fatetur. Luc. 6. Vsus vero horum est, ne securi dormiamus, si quando quiescere videntur veritatis hostes, & qui nobiscum aliquando propter hanc inimiciciam exercuerunt. Quin potius serpentina prudentia illorum dolos & conatus obseruemus, qui prima quaque occasione oblata erumpent. Quare huc cumprimis illud Ecclesiastici pertinet: Inimico tuo non credas, &c. Deinde verò vnanimiter aduersus Paulum Iudæi insurgunt. Quæ altera est impiorum proprietas. Cum enim propter affectus diuersos ferè semper dissentiant, in solo Christo & verbo eius oppugnando consentire solent, eò quòd illud omnes ex æquo oderunt. Ita Pharisæi cum Sadducæis & Herodianis conueniunt, cum de Christo oppri-mendo agitur. Et Pilatum Herodi reconciliatum fuisse scimus, cum illi Christum illudendum trans-misset. Nemo igitur impiorum dissidijs confidat, sed in Christo, veræ vnitatis & consensionis au-ctore, spem omnem repositam habeat.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us observe here the manners and arts of the enemies of the truth, so that they may more easily be guarded against. First, we see the Jews cunningly seeking an opportunity to do harm, when until now they might have seemed peaceful and quiet. For almost the whole of the previous year nothing had been attempted by them against Paul. But with a new proconsul in office they rise up, either because they hoped that a man alien to religion and to justice would be wonderfully suited to their purposes, or because they believed they could stir up the greatest trouble with new affairs under a new magistrate, to whom the affairs of the Corinthians were not yet well known. In them, therefore, prudence shines forth, since Christ confesses that the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light (Luke 16). The use of this for us is that we should not sleep securely if at any time the enemies of the truth, and those who have sometimes harassed us on account of this enmity, seem to be at rest. Rather, we should observe with serpentine prudence their tricks and attempts, which will break out at the first opportunity. Hence especially applies that saying of Ecclesiasticus: "Do not trust your enemy," etc. Next, the Jews rise up against Paul with one accord. This is the second characteristic of the impious. For though, because of their differing passions, they almost always disagree, they are accustomed to agree in attacking Christ alone and his word, because all hate it equally. So the Pharisees join with the Sadducees and Herodians when it is a question of crushing Christ. And we know that Pilate was reconciled with Herod when he sent Christ to him to be mocked. Let no one therefore trust in the divisions of the impious, but let him place all his hope in Christ, the author of true unity and agreement.

units.la: Sed accusationis caput audiamus, quo Paulum ad Proconsulem Iudæi vrgent. Hic (inquiunt) contra legem suadet hominibus colere Deum. Sensus est, quòd nouos & legi Dei contrarios cultus inuebat. Erat autem exosa apud Romanos omnis religionis innouatio. Nec dubium est, quin crimen illud mirificè amplificarint, & Romanas quoq; leges in medium adduxerint, quod Philippis & Thessalonicæ antea factum fuisse audiuimus. Falsum verò fuisse crimen hoc, vel vno hoc argumento colligitur, quòd Christum prædicabat Paulus, qui legis finis est, & in quo impleta sunt, quæcunque in Mosis & prophetarum libris continentur. Interim videmus hoc nomine semper ferè accusari pios Dei cultores, quòd religionem prophanent, cuius non alij seueriores sunt assertores & vindices. Atqui hic religionis patrocinium mirificè & plenis buccis iactitant, qui ab omni religione sunt alienissimi, quemadmodum legem Iudæi prætexunt, cum tamen illam iampridem humanis traditionibus totam euertissent. Ita hodie Diuos & Diuorum imagines contra nos in ore habent prophani veritatis hostes, cum illos nec Diuos nec imagines multum curare constet. Si enim Diuorum honorem assertum volunt, cur non illorum fidem imitantur? cur illorum doctrinam & scripta ferro & igne persequuntur? cur hæreticos dicunt eos, qui Diuorum vestigijs insistere cupiunt? Si tanta apud illos est imaginum religio, cur vivas Dei imagines negligunt? cur pauperes spoliant, vt saxa & lapides vestire possint? cur homines Christianos, in quibus sanguinis sui precio Dei imaginem Christus instaurauit, propter Christi doctrinam & fidem exurunt? Quid ergo aliud isti homines faciunt, quàm quòd Iudæorum exemplo sub plausibili religionis prætextu religionem & veritatem omnem semel extinctam cupiunt?
units.tr: But let us hear the head of the accusation, by which the Jews press Paul before the proconsul. "This man," they say, "persuades people to worship God contrary to the law." The sense is that he was introducing new forms of worship contrary to the law of God. Now every innovation in religion was hated among the Romans. Nor is there doubt that they greatly magnified this charge and brought Roman laws into the matter too, as we heard had been done before at Philippi and Thessalonica. That the charge was false is gathered from this one argument alone: Paul preached Christ, who is the end of the law, and in whom all things contained in the books of Moses and the prophets are fulfilled. Meanwhile we see that godly worshippers of God are almost always accused under this name, of profaning religion, when no others are stricter defenders and avengers of it. And yet those who are most alien to all religion boast loudly and with full mouths of its protection here, just as the Jews pretended to defend the law, though they had long since utterly overturned it by human traditions. So today the profane enemies of the truth have on their lips the saints and the images of the saints against us, though it is well known that they care little for either saints or images. For if they want the honour of the saints upheld, why do they not imitate their faith? Why do they pursue their teaching and writings with sword and fire? Why do they call heretics those who wish to tread in the footsteps of the saints? If there is such great reverence for images among them, why do they neglect the living images of God? Why do they strip the poor so that they can clothe stones and blocks of wood? Why do they burn Christian men, in whom Christ restored the image of God at the price of his own blood, on account of Christ's doctrine and faith? What else, then, do these men do, but, after the example of the Jews, under the plausible pretext of religion, wish all religion and truth utterly extinguished?

units.la: Quid autem in tumultu hoc facit Gallio? Num Paulum causam dicere iuber, & dicentem audit? Nequaquam. Imò cum iam dicere vellet, sermonem eius interrumpit. Quod tamen tolerabile videri potuit, cum nullam quoque aduersus illum ferat indicta causa sententiam. Quin omnem causa huius cognitionem abse reijcit, eamque ad se pertinere negat. Contemptissimè autem de Iudaica religione loquitur, quasi illa in nudis verbis & incertis quibusdam nominibus consisteret. Ita verò loquens ab ipsis Iudæis occasionem sumpsisse videtur, qui ineptis logomachijs siue verborum contentionibus & genealogijs omnem suam religionem gentium ludibrio & risui exponebant. Quodipsum hodie in Papatu fit, cuius ineptissimæ præstigiæ & fabulosissima dogmata totum Christianum nomen Turcis & Iudæis deridendum propinant. Et vtinam non inter euangelij professores reperiretur, qui nouis & inauditis antea quæstionibus totum fidei Christianæ mysterium impiorum sannis & ludibrijs exponunt. Sed quo ad Gallionem, tumultuantes Iudæos tandem facessere iubet, & à tribunali abigit. Atqui in hoc quædam probanda, quædam improbanda veniunt. Probandum est, quòd religionem, quam ignorabat, temere damnare non vult. Eo enim factō multis nostri seculi magistratibus modestior & æquior est, qui cum omnis religionis egregiè ignari sint, immanitatem arrogantia huius cognitionem sibi solis vendicant. Quæ professo malorum non postrema causa est, quæ hodie orbem terrarum perturbant. Rursum nullo modo probari potest, quòd Religionem Gallio in vniuersum negligit, & eius cognitionem nihil ad se pertinere arbitratur. Deus enim regem assidua & diligenti legis lectione exerceri vult, & magistratus veræ religionis seueros & studiosissimos vindices constituit. Vide Deuteronom. 13. & 17. Nec exempla desunt sanctissimorum regum, qui in scriptura sacra potissimam laudem eo nomine meruerunt, quòd superstitionibus sublatâ religionem veram reduxerunt. Intolerabilis ergo illorum hodie error est, qui magistratibus persuadere conantur, ne in alicuius religionem inquirant, sed cuius liberam diuini cultus rationem permittant. Sed reuera illi ingens monstrum alunt. Sperant enim se effecturos vt principes Gallionis exemplum imitati, ipsis quæuis figmenta in ecclesiam inuehendi copiam faciant. Non minor quoque principum & magistratuum quorundam error est, qui cum Christiani dici & haberi velint, tamen religionis causam sui fori esse negant, & illam auaris Monachis & indoctis fastuque turgentibus Episcopis committentes, Christi oues ineptissimorum hominum libidini subijciunt, imò lupis dilaniandas exponunt. Ita verò se excusari putant principes. Quæ spes illos vehementer fallet: quia ex ipsorum manibus olim Deus requiret populum, quem illorum fidei commisit, & eo ipso argumento malæ fidei serui fuisse conuincentur, quòd religionis causam ad se pertinere negauerunt, quæ illis commendatissima esse debebat. Porrò exitum Tragœdiæ spectare libet, in quo diuinæ promissionis veritas clarissimè cernitur. Postquam enim Græci causam hanc Gallioni minimè cordi esse viderent, arreptum Synagogæ principem Sosthenem indignis modis verberant. Id verò Iudæis impulsoribus factum fuisse credibile est. Fuit enim Sosthenes fidelis Pauli collega, cuius opera illum in euangelij propagatione vsum fuisse, ex inscriptione priorum ad Corinthios facile patet. At miraculo simile est, quòd cũ ad manus res deuenerit, Paulus tamen, aduersus quem omnes illi insurrexerant, intactus & illasus discedat, imò ne cogatur quidem vrbe discedere: nam aliquot adhuc diebus eum illic moram traxisse audiemus. Quid verò causæ fuisse dicemus, ob quam illi Paulo pepercerint? Num illius eloquentia & apologia persuasi ab illo manus abstinuerunt? Atqui illum ne audire quidem Proconsul dignatus fuit. Num verò illum Proconsulis authoritas defendit? Atqui non curæ erant Iudæorum res homini prophano & palàm impio. Num alius illi patronus fuit? At quænam alterius tanta authoritas esse poterat, vt se furentibus opponeret, maximè cessante ab officio Proconsule, cui soli in ea vrbe mandandi ius erat? Restat ergo, vt solius Dei protectione occulta Paulum seruatum fuisse dicamus, vt promissio impleretur, iuxta quam nemo illi nocere debebat. Ita patriarchas olim inter Chananaeos seruatos fuisse legimus, domino illorum auribus & cordibus intonante: Nolite tangere Christos meos, &c. Psal. 105. Ita Christus vno verbo discipulos liberat, licet hostium rabiem stricto gladio & vulnerato Pontificis seruo Petrus irritauisset. Ex his nos consolationem petere decet, quando eam Dei in promissis fidem & in afferendis suis potentiam esse videmus, vt tunc quoq; incolumes euadant, quando inter medios hostium furores versari videntur.
units.tr: But what does Gallio do in this uproar? Does he order Paul to plead his case and listen to him? By no means. Rather, when Paul was about to speak, Gallio cut short his speech. This might still have seemed tolerable, since he pronounced no sentence against Paul before the case was heard. Indeed, he refuses to take cognizance of the matter at all and denies that it concerns him. He speaks most contemptuously of the Jewish religion, as if it consisted of mere words and certain obscure names. In speaking this way he seems to have taken his cue from the Jews themselves, who, by their silly verbal quarrels and genealogies, exposed their whole religion to the mockery and laughter of the Gentiles. This is what happens today in Papacy, whose most absurd tricks and fabulous dogmas offer the whole Christian name to be mocked by Turks and Jews. And would that there were not found among the professors of the gospel those who expose the whole mystery of the Christian faith to the jeers and ridicule of the impious, with questions new and never heard before. As for Gallio, he orders the tumultuous Jews to depart at last and drives them from the tribunal. Yet in this some things are to be commended and some to be condemned. What is to be commended is that he does not rashly wish to condemn a religion he did not know. In this he is more moderate and fairer than many magistrates of our age, who, though utterly ignorant of all religion, arrogantly claim this inquiry for themselves alone. This is certainly no small cause of the evils that now disturb the world. Again, it cannot in any way be approved that Gallio altogether neglects religion and judges that its knowledge does not concern him. For God wills that the king be exercised by diligent and constant reading of the law, and he appoints magistrates as strict and most zealous avengers of true religion. See Deuteronomy 13 and 17. Nor are examples lacking of the most holy kings, who earned the chief praise in Holy Scripture for this, that they removed superstitions and restored true religion. Therefore the error of those today is intolerable who try to persuade magistrates not to inquire into anyone's religion, but to allow each person a free manner of divine worship. In truth, they are nourishing a huge monster. For they hope that princes, imitating Gallio's example, will give them free rein to introduce whatever fictions they like into the Church. No less is the error of certain princes and magistrates who, while wanting to be called and considered Christians, nevertheless deny that religion is a matter for their jurisdiction. Committing its cause to greedy monks and unlearned bishops swollen with pride, they subject Christ's sheep to the lust of the most foolish men, indeed they expose them to be torn apart by wolves. Princes think they are thus excused. This hope will greatly deceive them, because God will one day require from their hands the people committed to their faith, and they will be convicted of bad faith by this very argument: that they denied the cause of religion pertained to them, when it should have been most commended to them. Furthermore, let us look at the outcome of the tragedy, in which the truth of the divine promise is most clearly seen. For after the Greeks saw that this cause was in no way dear to Gallio, they seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him shamefully. It is credible that this was done at the instigation of the Jews. For Sosthenes was a faithful colleague of Paul, and from the inscription of the former letter to the Corinthians it is easy to see that Paul made use of his work in spreading the gospel. But it is like a miracle that when matters came to blows, Paul, against whom all of them had risen up, departed untouched and unharmed; indeed he was not even compelled to leave the city, for we shall hear that he stayed there some days longer. What cause shall we say there was for which they spared Paul? Was it that they were persuaded by his eloquence and defence and kept their hands off him? But the proconsul did not even deign to hear him. Did the authority of the proconsul defend him? But the affairs of the Jews were of no concern to a profane man who was openly impious. Did he have some other patron? But what authority of another could there be, able to oppose the raging mob, especially since the proconsul, the only one in that city with the right to command, was idle? It remains, then, that we say Paul was preserved by the hidden protection of God alone, so that the promise might be fulfilled, according to which no one ought to harm him. Thus we read that the patriarchs were preserved of old among the Canaanites, their Lord thundering in their ears and hearts: "Touch not my anointed ones," etc. Psalm 105. So Christ with a single word freed his disciples, although Peter had provoked the rage of the enemies by drawing his sword and wounding the servant of the high priest. From these things we ought to draw consolation, when we see that God is faithful in his promises and powerful in carrying them out, so that his people come through unharmed even when they seem to be in the midst of the enemies' raging fury.

units.la: III. Exitus Tragœdiæ felix.
units.tr: III. A Happy Outcome to the Tragedy.

units.la: Sed ad Gallionem nobis reuertendum est, in quo magistratus impij & à religione alieni typum spiritus sanctus proponit. Is enim religionis causam ad suum forum pertinere, paulò ante diserte negauit. Simul verò ipse confessus est, sui officij esse iniurias ab innocentibus propulsare & scelera punire. At idem ille Sosthenem in conspectu suo indignis modis tractari patitur, nec id facit, quod modò sui officij esse testatus est. Tales hodie multi sunt, qui dum modestiæ causa religionis cognitionem abs se reijcere videntur, mox se & à religione & à iustitia alienissimos esse produnt, dum ne à ciuilibus quidem, imò notorijs iniurijs Dei cultores vindicat. Nec est, quòd iustitiæ assertores vnquam fore putemus eos, qui religionis curam & studium semel abiecerunt. Quî enim fieri potest, vt hominibus in iure suo vindicando fideliter adsit, qui in Deum iniustus est, nec sui officij esse putat, vt huius honorem & gloriam afferat? Multos ergo hodie, proh dolor, Galliones passim videre est, nec alia est maior publicæ iniustitiæ causa, quàm quòd religionis sensum omnem plerique principum exuerunt. Sed quanto grauius eos peccare dicemus, qui cum Christiano nomine glorientur, tamen Christi fideles in suo conspectu indignissimè tractari patiuntur, & quos sua authoritate atq; gladij iure tueri debebant, in hominum gratiam suo consensu hostium arbitrio & libidini adiudicant? quod hodie tam frequens est, vt exemplis illustrari non opus habeat.
units.tr: But we must return to Gallio, in whom the Holy Spirit sets before us an unjust magistrate, one estranged from religion. For a little before he plainly denied that the cause of religion belonged to his tribunal. Yet at the same time he confessed that it was his duty to repel wrongs done to the innocent and to punish crimes. But this same man allows Sosthenes to be handled in an outrageous manner in his presence, and does not do what he had just declared to be his duty. There are many like him today who, while they seem to put aside the knowledge of religion out of a pretence of moderation, soon show themselves utterly alien both to religion and to justice, since they do not defend the worshippers of God even against civil and notorious wrongs. Nor should we suppose that those who have once cast off all care and zeal for religion will ever become defenders of justice. For how can he faithfully help men to vindicate their rights who is unjust toward God, and does not think it his duty to uphold God's honour and glory? Therefore, alas, one may see many Gallios everywhere today, and the greatest cause of public injustice is nothing other than that most rulers have stripped off all sense of religion. But how much more grievously must we say that they sin who boast of the Christian name, and yet allow the faithful of Christ to be treated most shamefully in their sight, and, to win the favour of men, by their consent hand over to the will and lust of enemies those whom they ought to have protected by their authority and the right of the sword? This is so common today that it needs no illustration by examples.

units.la: Populi olim liberi conditio qualis sub tyrannide.
units.tr: What the condition of a free people is like under a tyrant.

units.la: Postremò consyderandum venit, quàm misera sit illorum conditio, qui libertate sua amissa alienis dominis subesse coguntur. Tales enim Iudæi fuerunt, quos à Pompeij Magni temporibus Romano Imperio subditos & per omne illius ditionem dispersos fuisse scimus. Tales quoq; Corinthij erant, quos L. Mummio duce ab ijsdem Romanis debellatos & subactos fuisse, historiæ testantur. Nec dubium est vtrosq; ob peccata sua iusto Dei iudicio fuisse punitos. Sed quanta vel ex hoc vno facto illorum miseria cernitur? Iudæi toto terrarum orbe diuisi, & simul omnibus inuisi sunt. Religionem verò suam ab ijs cotumeliosissimè notari audiunt, quos principes suos agnoscere coguntur. Corinthij autem, licet cum Romanis in religione consentiant, eum tamen proconsulem acceperunt, qui ne publicas quidem iniurias curæ habet, sed ad aperta flagitia turpissimè conniuet. Horum meminerint, quibus libertatis donum diuinitus datum est. Vtantur illo ad Dei gloriam, ne simile Dei iudicium experti alijs exemplo sint, quin potius corporum simul & animarum libertate ornati Deo seruiant cumq; illo in cœlis viuant per Christum Iesum vnicum verae libertatis vindicem: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, we must consider how wretched is the condition of those who, having lost their liberty, are compelled to be subject to foreign masters. Such were the Jews, whom we know were subject to the Roman Empire from the time of Pompey the Great and were scattered throughout all its dominions. Such too were the Corinthians, whom histories record were conquered and subdued by the same Romans under the leadership of Lucius Mummius. Nor is there doubt that both peoples were punished for their sins by the just judgment of God. But how great is their misery, seen from this one fact alone? The Jews, scattered over the whole earth, are at the same time hated by all. They hear their religion most contemptuously disparaged by those whom they are compelled to acknowledge as their rulers. The Corinthians, although they agree with the Romans in religion, nevertheless received a proconsul who does not even care about public wrongs, but most shamefully winks at open crimes. Let those remember these things to whom the gift of liberty has been given from heaven. Let them use it for the glory of God, lest, having experienced a like judgment of God, they become an example to others; rather, let them, adorned with liberty of both body and soul, serve God, and live with him in heaven through Jesus Christ, the only true vindicator of liberty, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXIII.

units.la: Paulus verò deinde cõmoratus dies multos, valedicto fratribus abnauigauit in Syriam, comitantibus eum Priscilla & Aquila, cùm sibi totondissent caput in Cenchreis. Habebat enim votū. Deuenitq; Ephesum, & illos ibi reliquit. Ipse vero ingressus Synagogam disputabat cum Iudeis. Rogantibus autem illis, vt plus temporis maneret apud eos, non annuit, sed valedixit illis, dicens: Oportet me omnino festum, quod instat, agere Hierosolymis: sed iterum reuertar ad vos, Deo volente. Et soluit Epheso, cumq; deuenisset Cesaream, ascendit & salutata ecclesia descendit Antiochiam. Et commoratus illic aliquantum temporis, profectus est, perambulans ex ordine Galaticam regionem ac Phrygiam, confirmans omnes discipulos.
units.tr: Paul, after staying many more days, bade the brothers farewell and sailed away to Syria, accompanied by Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had his head shaved, for he was under a vow. He came to Ephesus and left them there. He himself entered the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay longer with them, he did not consent but bade them farewell, saying: "I must by all means keep the coming feast in Jerusalem, but I will return to you again, God willing." He sailed from Ephesus, and when he had landed at Caesarea, he went up, greeted the church, and went down to Antioch. After spending some time there, he departed and travelled in order through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.

units.la: VT Paulus nuspiam locorum cum maiori timore & tremore quàm Corinthi versatus esset: non alibi Deum magis praesentem sensit. Primò enim per visionem illi opem & gratiam suam pol licitus est. Deinde ab Iudaeis captum & ad Proconsulem tractum mirabiliter liberauit, etiam ad manus res deueniret, & indignis modis tractaretur Sosthenes. Est vero (vt nuper monuimus) omnia horum vsus, vt communi piorum consolationi seruiant. Poterit enim hos quoq; simili ratione liberare Deus, nec de eius voluntate nobis dubitare licet, quando illum veracem esse constat, quare etiam promissionibus suis deesse non poterit. Quia tamen de his in praecedenti Sermone satis dictum est, historiae contextum secuti, quid post turbas Corinthi aduersus Paulum excitatas, factum sit, videamus.
units.tr: That Paul was never in any place with greater fear and trembling than at Corinth, and that he never felt God more present elsewhere. For first, in a vision, God promised him his help and grace. Then, when he had been seized by the Jews and dragged before the proconsul, God wonderfully freed him, even though matters came to blows and Sosthenes was treated shamefully. Indeed, as we noted recently, all these things are recorded so that they may serve the common comfort of the godly. For God can likewise deliver these others too, and we may not doubt his will, since it is certain that he is true, and therefore he cannot fail in his promises. Yet since enough has been said about these matters in the previous sermon, let us follow the thread of the history and see what happened after the disturbances raised against Paul at Corinth.

units.la: Occurrit hic primum quod de Paulo narratur, illum videlicet post tanti periculi terrores Corinthi non paucis diebus mansisse: deinde vero cum ecclesia recens constituta valedixisset, comitantibus illum Aquila & Priscilla, profectionem in Syriam, adeoq; Hierosolymas vsq; instituisse: raso tamen prius in Cenchreis capite propter votum, cui antea obstrictus fuerat. Quo in loco haud vulgaris laudem meretur Pauli constantia & fortitudo, qua animatus omnes periculorum terrores vincit, & inter acerrimos hostes, cum nulla ex magistratu aut aliis hominibus auxilij spes affulgeret, Corinthi manet: nimirum propter rudes & infirmos discipulos, quos confortatione opus habere videbat, ne tenella adhuc illorum fides in herba (quod aiunt) intercideret. Ita vero boni pastoris officio fungitur, quem dominus ad lupi conspectum nequaquam fugere, sed vitam suam pro ovium salute exponere docet. Iohan.10. Simul autem vniuersalis hinc doctrina peti debet, vt qui Dei opem semel experti sunt, in vocatione sua eo constantiori & fortiori animo pergant, nec (vt quidam praepostere sapientes solent) ideo sese liberatos arbitrentur, vt in posterum quasi omni officio suo defuncti, labores & pericula subire detrectent. NON minus vero Aquila & Priscilla, sanctissimi coniuges, nobis obstruandi veniunt, qui exilij molestias semel & iterum experti, rursum sedes mutant, & Paulum per terras & maria comitantur. Quàm vero id periculosum fuerit (vt de sumptibus & laboribus nihil dicamus) ex vno hoc aestimare licet, quòd in Pauli exitium tota Iudaeorum gens obstinatissimis animis conspirauisse videbatur. Paulus certè cum ob comitatum hunc, tum ob alias causas, eam illis laudem tribuit, quòd ceruices suas pro ipsius anima supposuerint. Qua re vt illo tempore apud omnes ecclesias magnam gratiam inierunt, ita immortalem sibi ipsis pararuerunt nominis gloriam, quae in hunc vsq; diem durat, & in finem seculi vsq; duratura est. Vide Rom.16. Horum exemplo nos quoq; excitari conuenit, vt pro Christi gloria, pro euangelio & ministris huius aliquid audeamus: quando vniuersales promissiones extant, quae certam mercedem illi quoque pollicentur, qui poculum frigidae aquae apostolo Christi nomine dederit. Eadem ratio reliquos etiam indigos nobis commendare debet, quos ita nobis commendauit dominus, vt sibi factum esse in die iudicij reputaturus sit, quicquid in illos collatum fuerit. Est quidem pudenda omnino & detestabilis illorum opinio, qui exulantium fratrum multitudinem publico onerari exististimant cum tales ferè Dei gratiam vrbibus concilient. Vnus Lot bello vitos & captos Sodomarum ciues in libertate asserit. Gen.14. Quòd si decem Loti similes vrbs eadem ciues aut incolas habuisset, ex horribili caelestis ignis supplicio per hos eripi poterat, vt videre est Gen.18. cap. Possent multa alia huius generis exempla commemorari, nisi nos alio vocaret temporis angustia, & praesentis loci contextus.
units.tr: Here we first meet what is told of Paul: that after the terrors of so great a danger at Corinth, he remained there not a few days; then, when he had bidden farewell to the newly founded church, Aquila and Priscilla accompanying him, he set out for Syria and so as far as Jerusalem; but first, at Cenchreae, he had his head shaved on account of a vow he had earlier bound himself to. In this place Paul's constancy and courage deserve no small praise: though inspired, he overcomes all the terrors of dangers, and he remains at Corinth among the bitterest enemies, when no hope of help from the magistrate or from other men shone forth. Surely he did so on account of the rude and weak disciples, whom he saw needed strengthening, lest their still tender faith should perish, as they say, in the blade. Thus he discharges the duty of a good shepherd, whom the Lord teaches not to flee at the sight of the wolf, but to expose his life for the safety of the sheep. John 10. At the same time, a general teaching should be drawn from this: that those who have once experienced God's help should press on in their calling with a steadier and braver spirit, and should not (as certain men who are foolishly wise are wont to do) think themselves freed for this reason, so that in future, as if they had completed all their duty, they shrink from undergoing labours and dangers. Nor are Aquila and Priscilla, most holy spouses, less worthy of imitation for us, who, having once and again experienced the troubles of exile, change their dwelling again and accompany Paul over lands and seas. How dangerous this was (not to say anything of the expenses and labours) may be judged from this one fact: that the whole nation of the Jews seemed to have conspired with most obstinate minds for Paul's destruction. Paul, certainly, both on account of this companionship and for other reasons, gives them this praise: that they laid down their necks for his life. Wherefore, as they gained great favour with all the churches at that time, so they obtained for themselves an immortal glory of name, which lasts to this day and will last to the end of the age. See Rom. 16. We ought to be stirred up by their example, to dare something for Christ's glory, for the gospel and for its ministers; since there are universal promises which also promise a sure reward to him who gives a cup of cold water in the name of Christ's apostle. The same reasoning ought to commend to us the other needy persons too, whom the Lord has so commended to us that he will count as done to himself on the day of judgement whatever has been bestowed on them. Truly shameful and detestable is the opinion of those who think that a multitude of exiled brethren is a burden to the public purse, since such people generally win God's favour for cities. Lot alone, when the Sodomites had been conquered and taken in war, secured their citizens' liberty. Gen. 14. But if the same city had had ten citizens or inhabitants like Lot, it could have been rescued by these from the dreadful punishment of heavenly fire, as may be seen in Gen. 18. Many other examples of this kind might be recalled, were we not called elsewhere by the shortness of time and by the context of the present passage.

units.la: Nouum enim & in noui Testamenti libris inauditum est, quòd Paulus propter votum caput rasisse dicitur: non poterit autem de alio, quàm Nazaraeorum voto, locus intelligi, nisi Paulum humanis traditionibus obstrictum fuisse dicamus, qui alibi ne diuinae quidem legis Ceremonijs fideles gravar
units.tr: For it is new and unheard of in the books of the New Testament that Paul is said to have shaved his head on account of a vow. But the passage cannot be understood of any vow other than that of the Nazirites, unless we say that Paul was bound by human traditions, he who elsewhere insists that the faithful ought not to be burdened even with the ceremonies of the divine law.

units.la: Votum Pauli. grauari debere contendit. De Nazaræis autem copiose Moses scribit in libro Numerorum Cap. 6. Quo loco facile patet liberam vnicuiuis fuisse eam vitæ rationem, ad quam illi voto ad tempus aliquod certum aut præfinitum astringebantur. Nam quòd Samsonem & Samuelem ( qui ab vtero matris ad maiora quaedam segregati fuerant ) toto vitæ curriculo Nazaræorum leges obseruauisse legimus, nequaquam in generale exemplum trahi debet. Obstringebant autem sese voto hoc sua sponte, quorum mentem propior religionis sensus commouerat, vt ardentius solito rebus diuinis vacare vellent. Quare vino in vniuersum abstinebant, eò quòd religioni & ebrietati nullo modo conuenire posset. Cum vino reliquas quoque voluptates, licitas alioqui vitabant. Praeterea funeribus minimè intererant, ne cognatorum quidem aut parentum, quia Deo vere addictos nullus affectus abripere debet, quando Christus quoque mortuorum curam ad eos potius pertinere ait, qui & ipsi mundo potius immori, quàm cum illo ad coelestis vitæ consortium aspirare volunt. Luc. 9. Adhæc toto voti tempore comam nutriebant Nazaræi, vt ita sese non sui iuris, sed peculiari voto obstrictos esse testarentur. Capitis enim velamen subiectionis symbolum esse, ipse Paulus docet, quando virum quidem aperto, mulierem verò tecto aut velato capite orare iubet, eò quòd ille liber, haec autem sub viri potestate fit, quem caput suum agnoscere debeat. 1. Cor. 11. Quae causa fuit, quòd euoluto voti tempore solenni quadam Ceremonia Nazaræi radebantur, vt pristinae libertati sese restitutos voto, solutos esse scirent. Videtur autem Paulus propter Iudæos votum hoc suscepisse, qui illum prophanum & impium Legis contemptorem esse putabant, quo facilius illos ad audiendum euangelium adductos Christo lucrifaceret. Tale quid enim ipse fateri videtur, quando se Iudæis Iudæum, & ijs qui sub lege sunt legi obnoxium factum fuisse scribit, &c. 1. Cor. 9. Alioqui minimè ignorabat Christianæ libertatis ius, quod nullis ceremonijs violari debere, passim docet. Vide Col. 2. Gal. 4. Ineptissimè ergo faciunt, qui Pauli exemplo, vt Monastici vótis patrocinium præbeant, abutuntur. Dei enim lege votum hoc nitebatur, quæ licet cum ceremonijs in Christi morte abrogata esset, tamen propter veterem dignitatem & infirmiores aliquot paulatim & cum honore sepelienda erat. At monachorum vota ex humanis traditionibus pendere constat, quarum nulla debet esse in religione authoritas. Deinde Deo vouebat Nazaræi, cum potissima monasticorum votorum pars creaturis nuncupari soleat. Rursum Nazaræorum votis nec vitæ conditio mutabatur, nec scindebatur ecclesiæ vnitas. Sed monastica vota vt omnes alias vitæ conditiones tollunt, ita sectas in ecclesiam infinitas inuehunt. Nazaræi ea vouebant, quæ ab homine præstari poterant. Monachi castitatem vouent, cuius donum non omnibus datum esse omnis scriptura docet. Nazaræi nemini graues erant voto suo. At monachi, du voluntariam paupertatem vouent, otiosi ventres aliorum laboribus pasci volunt. Nazaræos voti religio non impediebat, quo minus & magistratibus & parentibus reliquisque omnibus parerent, quibus nos naturae lex obstrictos reddit. Monastica autem vota obedientiam omnem turbant, & solis Abbatibus eos obstringunt, quos magistratus & parentum imperio subesse oportebat. Praeterea à Nazaræis procul aberat proprij meriti fiducia. Nam & se peccatores & omnis boni authorem Deum esse fatebantur, cum voto soluerentur. Monasticis autem votis humanae iustitiae & meritorum nostrorum fiduciam quàm maximè stabiliri constat. Quare si non alia esset, certè haec vna causa illis damnandis & explo dendis sufficeret, &c.
units.tr: The vow of Paul. Moses writes at length about the Nazirites in the book of Numbers, chapter 6. In that place it is easily seen that the manner of life to which those bound by such a vow were confined, for some set or fixed time, was free to anyone. For although we read that Samson and Samuel (who had been set apart from their mother's womb for greater things) observed the laws of the Nazirites through their whole course of life, this must by no means be drawn into a general example. Those who bound themselves by this vow did so of their own accord, whose minds a closer sense of religion had moved to wish to devote themselves to divine things more eagerly than usual. Therefore they abstained from wine altogether, because it could by no means agree with religion and drunkenness. Along with wine they also avoided other pleasures, otherwise lawful. Moreover, they did not attend funerals, not even those of kinsmen or parents, because no affection ought to draw away those truly devoted to God, since Christ also says that the care of the dead belongs rather to those who wish themselves to die to the world and to aspire with him to fellowship in the heavenly life. Luke 9. Besides, during the whole time of the vow the Nazirites let their hair grow, so as to attest that they were not their own masters but bound by a peculiar vow. For Paul himself teaches that a covering of the head is a symbol of subjection, since he bids men pray with the head uncovered but women with the head covered or veiled, because the man is free, while the woman is under the power of a husband, whom she ought to acknowledge as her head. 1 Cor. 11. This was the reason why, when the period of the vow was completed, the Nazirites were shaved by a certain solemn ceremony, so that they might know that, released from the vow, they had been restored to their former liberty. Paul seems to have undertaken this vow on account of the Jews, who thought him a profane and impious despiser of the Law, so that by this means he might more easily win over to Christ those who were drawn to hear the gospel. For he himself seems to confess something of this kind when he writes that he became to the Jews a Jew, and to those who are under the law as one under the law, etc. 1 Cor. 9. Yet he was by no means ignorant of the right of Christian liberty, which he teaches everywhere ought not to be violated by any ceremonies. See Col. 2; Gal. 4. Those therefore act most absurdly who abuse Paul's example to lend patronage to monastic vows. For this vow rested on the law of God, which, although it was abrogated along with the ceremonies at Christ's death, nevertheless, on account of its former dignity and of some weaker brethren, was gradually and honourably to be buried. But it is clear that the vows of monks depend on human traditions, and no authority in religion ought to belong to these. Moreover, the Nazirites vowed to God, whereas the chief part of monastic vows is usually addressed to creatures. Again, by the vows of the Nazirites the condition of life was not changed, nor was the unity of the church torn apart. But monastic vows, as they abolish all other conditions of life, so they introduce countless sects into the church. The Nazirites vowed those things which could be performed by a man. Monks vow chastity, a gift which all Scripture teaches is not given to everyone. The Nazirites were a burden to no one by their vow. But monks vow voluntary poverty, and, idle bellies, want to be fed by the labours of others. The religion of the vow did not hinder the Nazirites from obeying magistrates, parents and all others to whom the law of nature binds us. But monastic vows disturb all obedience, and bind men to abbots alone, whom it was fitting to be subject to the authority of magistrates and parents. Besides, confidence in one's own merit was far removed from the Nazirites. For they confessed themselves sinners and God the author of every good, when they were released by their vow. But it is established that monastic vows very greatly strengthen confidence in human righteousness and in our merits. Therefore, if there were no other cause, this one alone would certainly be sufficient for condemning and rejecting them, etc.

units.la: Caterum omissa hac superstitionis sententia ad Paulum reuertamur, qui ex Achaia in Asiam mi norem traijciens Ephesum deuenit, vbi quatuor nobis ex ordine consyderanda veniunt. Primò sy- nagogam ingressus cum Iudæis disputat. Rursum ergo illius amor erga suam gentem elucet, quam (vt alias monuimus ) multas ob causas odisse non poterat, licet tam semel & iterum in illos pluerem excusisset. Docet autem Pauli exemplum, Dei iram & iudicium ita impijs proponi debere, vt conuersis integra semper maneat diuinae gratiae & veniae spes. Dei enim vox est: Nolo mortem peccatoris, sed potius vt conuertatur & viuat. Ezech. 18. Quare simul omni studio imuigilandam est, si quì forte per nos domino lucrifieri possint. Secundò non irrita esse sanctorum studia Ephesiorum exemplum docet. Quia enim Paulum diutius secum manere cupiunt, facile patet, ipsos non parum profecisse. Nec enim fieri potest, vt ministrorum conuersatione delectentur, qui euangelicae doctrinae gustum nondum perceperunt. Nec etiam euangelij amantes censeri debent, quicunque buius ministros tdisse, illorum labores maligne taxare, ac eorundem comercia fastidiose fugere solent. Tertiò obsernemus, quod Paulus pium officium petentibus obsequi nequit. Ait enim: Oportet me omnino festum, quod instat, agere Hierosolymis. Unde vero illa necessitas Paulo incubuit? Num festi religionem, lum coactum fuisse dicemus? Minime gentium. Noverat enim dies festos vna cum reliquis ceremoniis abolitos esse, nec aliqua vrgebat causa, quae illum propter infirmos Iudaeos Hierosolymam ascendere cogeret, quando multi per omnes vrbes, Iudaicis superstitionibus adhuc immersi, inveniebantur, qui eo non ascendebant. Quare vt aliás spiritum sanctum Paulo rerum agendarum ducem fuisse audiimus: ita verisimile est, ipsum occulitori spiritus impulsu ad illam profectionem fuisse inflatum, quamuis causa non exprimatur, nec etiam eorum commemoratio fiat, quae tunc Hierosolymis gesserit, nisi quod ecclesiam salutauisse dicitur. Certe non potuit infrugiferum esse Pauli studium in ea vrbe, ad quam ex omnibus nationibus festi tempore ingens cum Iudaeorum tum gentium multitudo confluebat. Ita enim vno quasi momento euangelij doctrina in multas gentes simul propagari poterat. Interim admiratione dignum est, quod ab illis tam cito diuellitur Paulus, qui tantam profectus euangelici spem exhibebant, & quos deferere parum ciuile & pium videri poterat, si carnis ratio nem audias. Sed certa Deo constat iudiciorum suorum ratio. Et praecipuus eiusmodi exemplorum vsus est, vt voluntatem nostram & consilia omnia, quamuis in speciem pia & sancta, Dei arbitrio subiicere discamus. Quarto, vt Epheso Paulus discesserit, videamus. Valedicit illis, quod gratitudinis & amici animi significationem habet. Nimis enim turpis est illorum inciuilitas, qui insalutatis hospitibus discedunt, postquam beneficijs ornati sunt. Deinde apud illos Aquilam relinquit, ne omnino de statuti viderentur. Praeterea reditum pollicetur, siquidem ita velit dominus. Ex quibus facile erat colligere, ipsum non iniquo in illos animo esse, sed grauioribus causis ad discessum vrgeri & compelli. Hic vero imitanda venit Pauli religio, qui in re omnium sanctissima nihil temere praesumit, sed conatus & instituta sua omnia ex Dei prouidentia pendere intelligens, ad huius voluntatem omnia illa refert. Tritum enim est illud Solomonis, hominem quidem proponere, Deum vero disponere. Provb.16. Quanta ergo eorum temeritas est, qui in prophanis rebus tantum sibi tribuunt, vt perinde de suis negotiis constituant, ac si ipsi Deo leges praescribere possint? Vide Iac.4. Luc.12.
units.tr: But leaving aside this superstitious opinion, let us return to Paul, who, crossing from Achaia into Asia Minor, came to Ephesus, where four things come up for our consideration in order. First, entering the synagogue, he disputes with the Jews. Here again his love for his own nation shines forth, which (as we have said elsewhere) he could not hate for many reasons, although he had more than once and again stirred up trouble against them. Paul's example teaches that the wrath and judgment of God ought to be set before the wicked in such a way that for those who are converted the hope of divine grace and pardon always remains whole. For the voice of God is: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live" (Ezek. 18). Therefore we must watch over them with all diligence, if perhaps through us they can be won for the Lord. Second, the example of the Ephesians shows that the holy efforts of those who are zealous are not in vain. For since they wish Paul to stay with them longer, it is easy to see that they had made no small progress. For it cannot be that those delight in the company of ministers who have not yet tasted the doctrine of the gospel. Nor should those be considered lovers of the gospel who are accustomed to despise its ministers, to criticise their labours maliciously, and to shun their company with disdain. Third, let us observe that Paul could not comply with the pious request of those who asked him. For he says: "I must by all means keep the feast that is coming up at Jerusalem." But whence did that necessity press upon Paul? Shall we say that he was compelled by the religious observance of the feast? By no means. For he knew that the feast days had been abolished along with the other ceremonies, nor was there any pressing reason that would compel him to go up to Jerusalem for the sake of the weak Jews, since many throughout all the cities, still immersed in Jewish superstitions, were found who did not go up there. Therefore, just as we have heard elsewhere that the Holy Spirit was the guide of Paul's affairs, so it is likely that he was secretly impelled by the Spirit to that journey, although the cause is not stated, nor is there any mention of what he did then at Jerusalem, except that he is said to have greeted the church. Certainly Paul's zeal in that city could not have been fruitless, to which at festival time a huge crowd of both Jews and Gentiles from all nations flocked. For in this way, as if in a single moment, the doctrine of the gospel could be spread abroad among many nations at once. Meanwhile it is worthy of wonder that Paul is so quickly torn away from those who showed such hope of gospel progress, and whom it might seem uncivil and unkind to desert, if you listen to the reasoning of the flesh. But the reason of God's judgments is certain to him. And the chief use of such examples is that we learn to subject our will and all our plans, however pious and holy they may appear, to the decision of God. Fourth, let us see how Paul departed from Ephesus. He bids them farewell, which is a sign of gratitude and friendly feeling. For it is very rude of those who depart without greeting their hosts after they have been loaded with kindnesses. Then he leaves Aquila there, lest they should seem to be altogether dismissed. Besides, he promises a return, if the Lord so wills. From these things it was easy to gather that he was not ill-disposed towards them, but that he was urged and compelled to leave by weightier causes. Here indeed Paul's scrupulousness is to be imitated, who in the most holy matter presumes nothing rashly, but, understanding that all his undertakings and plans depend on God's providence, refers all of them to his will. Well known is that saying of Solomon: "Man proposes, but God disposes" (Prov. 16). How great, then, is the rashness of those who claim so much for themselves in worldly affairs that they settle their business as if they could prescribe laws to God himself? See James 4; Luke 12.

units.la: Caeterum Epheso digressus Paulus Caesaream Palaestinae contendit, inde Hierosolymam ascendens. Ibi vero salutata ecclesia & perattis omnibus, quorum gratia eo profectus erat, Antiochiam venit, quam commune quoddam piorum asylum fuisse, supra audiuimus. Inde Galatas & Phrygas obambulans, paßim fratres in fide confirmauit, eo quod satanae artes & improbos conatus minime ignoraret, quibus ille piorum saluti insidiari consueuit. Paucis vero Lucas immensos Pauli labores, indefessam curam & admirabilem industriam comprehendit, qua in ecclesia Christi gubernatione vsus est. Quod si cum his nostri seculi episcopos conferas, qui & Pauli & Petri titulo superbiunt, Deum immortalem, quam nihil in illis inuenies quod aliquam apostolici pastorum scintillam referat? Agnoscamus interim Dei fidem, qui ecclesiae tam fidis & selectis organis prosperum esse voluit, illumque oremus, vt hodie etiam operarios fidos in messem suam extrudere velit, quorum industria ecclesiae limites propagentur, vt per omnes gentes regnum obtineat dominus & saluator noster Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, having departed from Ephesus, Paul hastened to Caesarea in Palestine, and from there went up to Jerusalem. There, having greeted the church and fulfilled all the vows for whose sake he had gone, he came to Antioch, which, as we heard above, was a common sanctuary of the godly. From there, travelling through Galatia and Phrygia, he strengthened the brothers in the faith everywhere, because he was by no means ignorant of the arts of Satan and of the wicked attempts with which he is accustomed to lie in wait for the salvation of the godly. Luke briefly comprehends Paul's immense labours, his untiring care and his admirable diligence, with which he exercised the government of the church of Christ. But if you compare with these the bishops of our age, who take pride in the titles of Paul and Peter, immortal God, how little will you find in them that bears any spark of apostolic pastoring! Let us acknowledge meanwhile the faithfulness of God, who willed that the church should prosper through such trustworthy and chosen instruments, and let us pray to him that today also he will thrust out faithful workers into his harvest, through whose diligence the borders of the church may be extended, so that the Lord and Saviour our Jesus Christ may obtain his kingdom among all nations: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 124.

units.la: Iudaeus autem quidam Apollos nomine, Alexandrinus genere, vir eloquens, deuenit Ephesum, potens in scripturis. Hic erat instructus in via domini, & feruens spiritu loquebatur, & docebat diligenter ea quae sunt domini: sciens tantum baptisma Iohannis. Atqz hic coepit libere loqui in synagoga. Quem cum audissent Priscilla & Aquila, assumpserunt illum, & exactius ei expos-uerunt viam Dei. Cum autem vellet ire in Achaiam, exhortati fratres scripserunt discipulis, vt suscipieret illum. Qui cum venisset, contulit multum iis, qui crediderant, per gratiam. Vehementer enim Iudaeos reuincebat publice, ostendens per scripturas Iesum esse Christum.
units.tr: A certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures, came to Ephesus. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught carefully the things of the Lord, though he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and expounded to him the way of God more accurately. When he wished to go into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace. For he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

units.la: Rerum à Divo Paulo Corinthi & Ephesi gestarum narrationi Lucas percommode historiam hanc de Apollo, Judæo Alexandrino, interserit. Primò enim ad pleniorem eorum explicationem facit, quæ apud Corinthios gesta sunt, cùm paulò post ad hos quoq; Apollos profectus, ecclesiam Pauli ministerio non infeliciter plantatam rigaverit, & fidelis agricolæ instar ad maturionem fructum perduxerit, quod ipsum in priori ad Corinth. 3. cap. apostolus fatetur. Deinde mira Dei bonitas elucet, quia ille ecclesijs suis prospicere solet. Audiuimus enim in præcedenti Sermone, Paulum occulto spiritus sancti motu ab Ephesijs, qui euangelij amore inflammati, ipsum apud se aliquandiu retinere cupiebant, auulsum fuisse. Ne quis ergo salutis cupidos à domino indignis modis neglectos putaret, adeoq; de Dei in hos malignitate quærendi occasionem arriperet, Apollos surrogatur, qui Pauli absentiam suo studio & industria farciret. Nec enim aliquos veritatis studio ardentes negligit dominus, qui ipse passim homines ad se inuitat, & renitentes quoq; expansis manibus (ut propheta ait) allicit. Non parum ergo ad ecclesiæ consolationem facit ista historia, quæ simul fidelis & absoluti ministri exemplum continet, vnà cum multis alijs, quæ nostræ ædificationi seruire poterunt: quare singulas eius partes excutere non infrugiferum fuerit.
units.tr: Luke very fittingly inserts this account of Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew, into his narrative of what Paul did at Corinth and Ephesus. First, it serves to explain more fully what took place among the Corinthians, since shortly afterwards Apollos came to them too and watered the church that Paul had planted by his ministry, and as a faithful farmer brought it to a riper fruit. The apostle himself confesses this in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3. Next, the wonderful goodness of God shines forth, because he is accustomed to look after his churches. For we heard in the previous sermon that Paul was drawn away by a hidden movement of the Holy Spirit from the Ephesians, who, inflamed with love of the gospel, wished to keep him with them for some time. Lest anyone therefore think that those who desire salvation are neglected by the Lord in unworthy ways, and so seize on an occasion to complain of God's ill will towards them, Apollos is put in Paul's place, to supply by his zeal and diligence what Paul's absence lacked. For the Lord does not neglect those who burn with love of the truth; he himself invites people everywhere, and draws even the unwilling with outstretched hands, as the prophet says. This history therefore brings no small comfort to the church, since it contains at once the example of a faithful and accomplished minister, together with many other things that can serve our edification. It will not be unprofitable, therefore, to examine its individual parts.

units.la: Commodissimè autem à persona descriptione Lucas orditur, primò Iudæum fuisse dicens, quo par tim immensa Dei bonitas declaratur, qui ex infestissima gente & ad interitum ruente nouos quotidie filij sui cultores, & ministros elegit: parrim inexcusabilis redditur Iudæorum malitia, quæ nec fidelis apostolorum cura, nec quotidianis ipsq; domesticis exemplis superari potuit. Deinde patria Alexandrinum fuisse indicatur, in quo loco celeberrimam ecclesiam simul & scholam ipsis apostolorum temporibus constitutam fuisse, historiæ produnt & præsens hic locus non obscurè innuit. Inde enim prodit omniuarijs donis instructissimus Apollos, cuius tam fidelis postea claruit in ecclesiæ ædificatione industria. Paucis verò verbis maximas illius viri dotes Lucas comprehendit, dum eloquentiam illi tribuit, id est, aptè & rite de re quauis differendi facultatem: potentiam item in scripturis, id est, has tradendi dexteritatem non otiosam, vt pote cum illas non nudæ duntaxat ostentationis causa didicisset. Præterea in via domini institutum fuisse testatur, ita illi Christi cognitionem tribuens: in qua tamen illi adhuc aliquid defuisse monet, dum illum duntaxat Iohannis baptismum sciuisse ait. Ita verò prima Christianismi rudimenta nominat, baptismi vocabulo omnem Iohannis doctrinam, adeoq; totum illud negotium, cuius ille minister fuit, comprehendens: quo sensu Christus quoq; de Iohannis baptismo scribas interrogat, Matth. 21. Non tamen ita accipi debet locus hic, quasi Iohannes à Christi cognitione alienus fuerit, aut quicquam ab hac diuersum suis discipulis tradiderit. Vna enim & eadem fuit Iohannis & Christi doctrina. Vt enim hic apostolos pœnitentiam & peccatorum remissionem in suo nomine prædicare iubet: ita Iohannem ad pœnitentiam auditores suos inuitauisse, & ijsdem Dei gratiam & salutem in vno Christo monstrauisse legimus. Nam summa doctrinæ ipsius fuit: Respicite, appropinquat enim regnum Dei. Ecce agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccatum mundi. Pater diligit filium, & omnia dedit illi in manum, vt omnis qui credit in filium, habeat vitam æternam. Vide Luc. 3. Iohan. 1. & 3. cap. Quia verò Iohannes, inter prophetas & Christum medius, Messiæ promissi præcursor tantummodo esse debuit, qui populum ad excipiendum Saluatorem præpararet, sufficiebat illum summariam salutis & Christi cognitionem tradere, vt nimirum intelligerent omnes in hoc vno peccatorum remissionem & vitam inueniri. Interim occultiora mortis Christi & resurrectionis Ascensionisq; mysteria, adeoq; totum nostræ redemptionis modu nusquam disertis verbis ab illo traditum fuisse constat. Horum enim perfecta cognitio in aliud tempus reseruabatur. Imò ipsos Christi apostolos, licet de his frequenter Christus dissereret, rudiores fuisse legimus, quàm vt ista intelligere potuerint, donec post Ascensionem demum missó spiritu sancto totis animis illuminati sunt, quem admodum Christus fore promiserat. Apollos ergo licet in via domini institutus esset, Christumq; agno seret humani generis saluatorem esse, multa tamen adhuc ignorabat, quæ ad modum nostræ redemptionis spectant, de quibus plenius edocendus erat, vt paulo post sequetur. Interim duo nobis in persona huius descriptione obseruanda veniunt. Primum ordo & concatenatio donorum est, quibus Apollon Deus ornare voluit. Inter hæc primus locus Eloquentiæ tribuitur, quam omnibus cùm in ecclesia tum in republica versari volentibus cumprimis necessariam esse, vsus quotidianus docet. Num verò huius donum ex natura homini obtingat, aut arte & industria sine studio paretur, iam
units.tr: Luke begins most fittingly with a description of the man, first saying that he was a Jew. By this, on the one hand, the immeasurable goodness of God is declared, who chose new worshippers and ministers of his Son every day from a most hostile nation hastening to its ruin. On the other hand, the wickedness of the Jews is shown to be inexcusable, since it could be overcome neither by the faithful care of the apostles nor by the daily examples set in their own homes. Next, he is said to have been an Alexandrian by country. Histories report, and this passage hints at it clearly, that in that place a most famous church and at the same time a school was established in the very times of the apostles. From there Apollos came forth most richly furnished with all kinds of gifts, and afterwards his diligence in building up the church shone forth so faithfully. Luke sums up the great endowments of this man in a few words, when he ascribes to him eloquence, that is, the ability to discuss any subject aptly and properly; also power in the Scriptures, that is, skill in teaching them, not idle, since he had learned them not merely for the sake of display. Besides, he attests that Apollos was instructed in the way of the Lord, thus attributing to him knowledge of Christ. Yet he notes that something was still lacking in him, since he says that he knew only the baptism of John. He calls the first rudiments of Christianity by the word "baptism," comprehending in it all the teaching of John and that whole work of which John was the minister. In this sense Christ too asks the scribes about the baptism of John, Matthew 21. Yet this passage should not be understood as if John were ignorant of Christ, or had taught his disciples anything different from this knowledge. For the teaching of John and of Christ was one and the same. Just as here Christ commands the apostles to preach repentance and the forgiveness of sins in his name, so we read that John invited his hearers to repentance and showed them the grace and salvation of God in Christ alone. For the sum of his teaching was this: "Repent, for the kingdom of God is at hand. Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand, so that everyone who believes in the Son may have eternal life." See Luke 3, and John 1 and chapter 3. But since John, standing between the prophets and Christ, was to be only the forerunner of the promised Messiah, preparing the people to receive the Saviour, it was enough for him to deliver a summary knowledge of salvation and of Christ, so that all might understand that forgiveness of sins and life are to be found in this one. Meanwhile it is certain that he never set out in plain words the more hidden mysteries of the death, resurrection and ascension of Christ, nor the whole manner of our redemption. For their full knowledge was reserved for another time. Indeed, we read that the apostles of Christ themselves, although Christ often discoursed to them about these things, were too rude to understand them, until after the ascension, when the Holy Spirit was sent and they were enlightened in their whole minds, as Christ had promised. Apollos, therefore, although he had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and although he taught that Christ is the Saviour of mankind, was still ignorant of many things that pertain to the manner of our redemption, about which he had to be taught more fully, as will follow shortly. Meanwhile, two things come to be noted in this description of the man. The first is the order and chain of the gifts with which God willed to adorn Apollos. Among these, the first place is given to eloquence, which daily experience shows to be especially necessary for all who wish to be active both in the church and in the commonwealth. Whether the gift of this comes to a man from nature, or is acquired by art and industry without study, we know that was long disputed among the most acute orators and philosophers. But we, following the judgement of the apostles, count the power of speaking among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12. By his breath, we say, Apollos too was endowed with this. Second, Luke writes that he was mighty in handling the Scriptures and endowed with an effective skill. Thus the holy eloquence of this man is distinguished from the profane. For unless the matter of speech is taken from the holy Scriptures, and so from the mouth of God, there can be no virtue of eloquence, since it will be concerned with trifles and display rather than with things necessary to know and do. Indeed, those orators of the Gentiles ought not truly to be called eloquent, who speak magnificently and elegantly, but only about things that by no means pertain to living a blessed life. What else, then, shall we say they did, than that they were empty words, putting on, as the saying goes, Hercules' buskins on a boy? Very vain men admire the power of these men in speaking, and they are not much unlike them. But how much more rightly did that Laconian answer the sophist who promised a long and extemporaneous speech on any subject: "Indeed, I would not even approve a cobbler who put a large shoe on a small foot." Apollos therefore joined eloquence to a holy and zealous knowledge of the Scriptures. But since many also study the Scriptures for empty glory and display (as the Lord reproaches the scribes of the Jews), the third point is that Apollos is said to have been instructed in the way of the Lord, that is, to have held the knowledge of Christ. Luke uses the word "way" so as to teach that he was not occupied in this knowledge idly, but rather applied himself to it, so that by following the rule of Christ he ordered his whole manner of life according to it. This is the crowning point of all the gifts. For since the sum of our salvation is contained in Christ alone, the display of all other things will be empty and unfruitful unless people join the knowledge of him to their other studies. And that this is the aim we ought to set before us in searching the Scriptures, Christ himself plainly warns in John 5. Why did Paul count all things that are prized in the world as refuse, so that he might apprehend Christ? Philippians 3. The same Paul attests that Christ has been made wisdom to us by God, and he desires to know nothing else than Jesus Christ, and him crucified, 1 Corinthians 1 and 2. Would that those who in the schools of Christians waste their youth on empty philosophy, but who far away from them banish the knowledge of Christ, as if it pertained only to the ragged theologians (as they themselves put it), would take note of these things! The second thing to be observed in Apollos is that something was still lacking in so great a man, in those matters whose knowledge is necessary for us all. From this we gather that not all things are given to all, and that gifts are increased, since no one on earth attains the full and perfect knowledge of the mysteries of the kingdom of God, which Paul says will come to us only in the other age, when we are carried up into heaven and see God face to face, as we ought, just as he is, 1 Corinthians 13. Yet from this no one will conclude that everything handed down about religion in this age is uncertain. For since God himself reveals its reason to us through his Word in the Scriptures, whatever is delivered from it cannot be uncertain. Meanwhile, since the perfection of knowledge of God is granted only in heaven, we can make progress every day while we are here at work. We must therefore never rest, but must keep watch over the knowledge of divine things, so that even in this age, as far as it is possible, we may taste something of this perfection. Here, then, are rebuked the idle drones, who think that all the zeal spent on divine things is superfluous and useless, thereby plainly showing that they have not even tasted them with the tips of their lips. For such is the sweetness of these things that they allow people who have been, as it were, enticed by them never to be torn away. Also rebuked are those proud and self-confident men, who, as though nothing remained for them to learn, with huge disdain spurn all study of the divine Word. It is clear that they are so far from that perfection which they promise themselves that they do not even know themselves properly.

units.la: Apollos quis & qualis fuerit.
units.tr: Who and what sort of man Apollos was.

units.la: Baptismus Iohannis.
units.tr: The baptism of John.

units.la: Dona quibus Apollos instructus fuit. olim inter acutissimos Oratores & Philosophos disputatum esse scimus. At nos apostoli sententiam secuti, dicendi facultatem inter spiritus sancti dona recensemus. 1. Corinth. 12. Cuius afflatu Apollo quoq; hac donatum fuisse dicimus. Secundo in scripturis tractandis potentem & efficaci dexteritate praditum fuisse Lucas scribit. Ita vero sanctam huius viri eloquentiam a prophana distingui t. Nisi enim ex scripturis sacris, adeoq; Dei ore dicendi materia petatur, nulla esse poterit eloquentia virtutas, utpote quae circa nugas & ostentationem potius quam res cognitu & factu necessarias versabitur. Nec revera eloquentes dici debent gentium Oratores, qui magnifice quidem & ornate differunt, sed de iis tantum quae ad vitam beate transigendam minime pertinent. Quid ergo aliud illos fecisse dicemus, quam quod inania verba fuerunt, puero (ut dici solet) Herculis cothurnos induentes? Admirantur quidem horum in dicendo vim homines vanissimi, nec illis multum dissimiles. Sed quanto rectius Laconi lle, qui Sophistae prolixam eam q; extemporariam orationem de re quavis pollicenti, respondit: Ego vero ne sutorem quidem probauerim, qui paruo pedi magnum calceum induxerit. Sancto ergo & veili studio scripturae cognitionem eloquentiae Apollos coniunxit. At quia in scripturis quoque non pauci inani gloriae & ostentationi student (quemadmodum Iudaeorum scribae dominus exprobrat) tertio loco Apollos in via domini institutus fuisse, id est, Christi cognitionem tenuisse dicitur. Via autem vocabulum usurpat Lucas, ut illum non otiose in hac cognitione versatum fuisse, sed in hoc potius incubuisse doceat, ut Christi regulam sequendo, secundum hanc vitae suae conuersationem omnem instituerit. Est hic omnium donorum Colophon. Quia enim in uno Christo salutis nostrae ratio continetur, inanis & infrugifera erit omnium aliarum rerum ostentatio, nisi huius cognitionem reliquis studiis homines coniunxerint. Et hunc quidem scopum nobis in scrutandis scripturis propositum esse debere, ipse Christus diserte monet apud Ioban. 5. cap.
