Quae causa est, quod Paulus omnia, quae in pretio apud mundum existunt, pro excrementis duxit, ut Christum apprehenderet. Phil. 3. Idem Christum nobis a Deo sapientiam factum esse testatur, nec aliud scire affectat, quam Iesum Christum, & hunc quidem crucifixum. 1. Cor. 1. & 2. Vtinam observarent hac, qui in Christianorum scholis iuuenes inani quidem philosophia dementant, Christi vero cognitionem, quasi ad pannosos (ut ipsi loquuntur) duntaxat Theologos pertinentem, procul inde relegant. Alterum in Apollo obseruandum venit, quod tanto viro in iis adhuc aliquid defit, quorum cognitio omnibus nobis est necessaria. Vnde colligimus non omnibus data esse omnia, & incrementa donorum esse, quando nemini in terris plena & perfecta mysteriorum regni Dei cognitio contingit, quam in altero demum seculo nobis obuenturam Paulus dicit, quando nimirum in coelos translati, Deum facie ad faciem vt debimus sicuti est. 1. Cor. 13. Vnde tamen nemo colliget, incerta esse quae in hoc seculo de religione traduntur omnia. Quia enim huius rationem ipse Deus per Verbum suum in scripturis nobis reuelat, in certum esse non potest, quicquid illo traditur. Interim quia perfectio scientiae Dei in coelis demum obtingit, quotidie dum hic agimus proficere possumus. Nunquam ergo nobis quiescendum est, sed inuigilandum rerum diuinarum cognitioni, vt in hoc etiam seculo, quoad eius fieri potest, aliquem perfectionis huius gustum percipiamus. Arguuntur ergo hic otiosi fuci, qui omne, quod diuinis rebus impenditur, studium supervacaneum & inutile esse arbitrantur, ita nimirum significantes, se illas nec primis labijs degustauisse. Ea enim harum dulcedo est, ut inescatos quodammodo homines absque nunquam diuelli patiantur. Arguuntur item superbi & confidentes illi, qui quasi nihil illis discendum superfit, immani fastidio Verbi diuini studium omne aspernantur. Quos adeo a perfectione illa, quam sibi ipsis pollicentur, abesse constat, ut nec seipsos quidem adhuc probe nouerint.

units.la: Porrò vt ad Lucam reuertamur, persona descriptioni res gestas subijciens, vt Apollos donum sibi diuinitus collatis vsus sit, docet. Feruens spiritu (inquit) loquebatur & docebat diligenter ea quae sunt domini. Item, coepit libere loqui in Synagoga. Ergo ad domini gloriam illustrandam donis suis vsus est, suo exemplo docens, illum demum legitimum donorum vsum esse, si per ea domini nomen celebretur, a quo illa nobis data sunt. Id vero gratitudinis lex iubet, quam natura omnibus creaturis infulpsit. Peccant ergo quicunq; ociosi dona, quibus illos Deus exornauit, sepeliunt, de quibus sub feruine quam parabola dominus agit. Matth. 25. Grauior tamen multo illorum culpa est, qui donis suis pro sua libidine & diuini nominis contumelia abutuntur, id quod hodie vulgo fit, siue animi, siue corporis bonae spectes. At grauissimam Deo rationem olim reddent, quicunq; hoc scelere se polluerint. net simul exemplum hoc, quae docendi ratio in ecclesia teneri debeat. Primum zelo opus est & spiritus feruore, vt ex animo rem geri omnibus constet. Nisi enim is adsit, non nisi ostentationi doctrina seruiet. Ita Christum zelo flagrauisse, ardens & indefessum docendi studium, & feruidus ille in templo reformando spiritus abunde declarant. Nec vnquam illi probari poterunt tepidi doctores, quando nec priuatos homines Christus in religionis causa tepere vult. Vide Apocal. 3. Deinde diligentiam adhiberi necesse est, cum propter ingenij nostri tarditatem, quod diuina non capit, tum propter corruptionem naturae nostrae, quae Dei praeceptis semper reluctari consueuit. Accedit & satanae, communis hostis, improbitas, cuius insidijs fideles ministros dies & noctes irrequieta industria occurrere oportet. Ideo Paulus Timotheum, quem a pueris in scriptura studio enutritum esse sciebat, lectioni intendere iubet. 1. Tim. 4. Idemq; infra Ephesiorum pastores ad vigilantiam & diligentiam gravissimis argumentis hortabitur. Tertio docendi libertate ministros praeditos esse conuenit, ne quid vel metu vel fauore decepti dissimulent. Sed de eo supra diximus, vbi Paulus loqui, & non tacere, iubetur. At quae verbi ministris iniunguntur, ea omnibus, qui in publica aliqua functione versantur praestitu necessaria esse, passim scripturae docent. Imo priuatim haec singuli ad se transferant, siquidem in vocatione sua Deo probari volunt. Quia enim exigit Dominus, vt totus animus illi seruiamus, non possunt non in rebus suis diligentes simul & ingenui esse, adhaec feruere etiam, qui se illi totos, vt par est, consecrauerunt.
units.tr: Let us return to Luke. In describing the events, he shows how Apollos used the gifts divinely bestowed on him. "Being fervent in spirit," he says, "he spoke and taught diligently the things of the Lord." Likewise, "he began to speak boldly in the synagogue." So Apollos used his gifts to bring glory to the Lord, and by his example he teaches that the gifts are lawfully used only when, through them, the name of the Lord, from whom they were given to us, is honoured. Gratitude requires this, and nature has engraved this law on all creatures. Therefore those who sit idle and bury the gifts with which God has adorned them sin, and the Lord speaks of such people in the parable of Matth. 25. Yet the guilt of those is far greater who abuse their gifts for their own lust and to the insult of God's name, as is commonly done today, whether the gifts be of mind or of body. But those who have polluted themselves with this crime will one day render the gravest account to God. This example also shows how teaching ought to be carried on in the Church. First there must be zeal and fervour of spirit, so that all may see the work is done from the heart. Without this, teaching will serve only display. This is what Christ's burning and tireless eagerness to teach, and the fervent spirit with which he cleansed the temple, abundantly declare. Lukewarm teachers will never be approved, since Christ does not want even private persons to be lukewarm in the cause of religion. See Apoc. 3. Next, diligence must be applied, both because of the dullness of our wit, which does not grasp divine things, and because of the corruption of our nature, which always tends to resist God's precepts. Add also the malice of Satan, our common enemy, against whose snares faithful ministers must meet us day and night with restless industry. Therefore Paul bids Timothy, whom he knew to have been nurtured in the study of Scripture from boyhood, to give himself to reading. 1 Tim. 4. Likewise, later on, he urges the elders of Ephesus to watchfulness and diligence with the weightiest arguments. Thirdly, ministers ought to be endowed with freedom of teaching, so that they do not, deceived by fear or favour, hold anything back. But we have said this above, where Paul is bidden to speak and not to be silent. Moreover, what is enjoined on the ministers of the Word is everywhere taught in Scripture as necessary for all who hold any public office. Indeed, individuals should apply these things privately to themselves, if they wish to be approved by God in their calling. For since the Lord requires that we serve him with our whole mind, those who have wholly consecrated themselves to him, as is fitting, cannot fail to be diligent and openhearted in their affairs, and also to be fervent.

units.la: Caeterum describit Lucas, vt in Christi & salutis cognitione Apollos profecerit, dum huius gloriam prouebere & aliorum salutem propagare studet. Ait enim: Hunc cum audissent Priscilla & Aquila, assumpserunt illum, & exactius ei exposuerunt viam Dei. Et heic quidem ante omnia promissionis a Christo factae veritas elucet. Omni habenti (inquit) dabitur, & abundabit. Matth. 25. Habere autem dicuntur, qui dona sibi collata agnoscunt, & ijsdem sedulo ad Dei gloriam vtuntur, vt cum rationem ab illis Dominus exigit, illa cum foenore accipiat. Id quia Apollos summa fide & studio (vt modo diximus praestitit) non deest promissioni suae Dominus, sed mox fideles ministros excitat, qui illum in Christi cognitione plenius & perfectè instituant. Debet id communi omnium institutioni seruire, vt intelligant quasuis Dei dotes nulla re felicius quam fideli studio augeri. Ita sapientiae donum indies augeri sentiunt, quicunque illo ad diuinae gloriae propagationem vti consueuerunt. Eadem eruditionis, honorum, opum, omnium deniq; aliarum rerum ratio est: nec exempla desunt, quibus id probari potest. Rursum no alia maior causa est, ob quam dona Dei magis extingui solent, quam si suae potius ignauiae & ocio, quam gloriae Dei homines studeant. Hic vero multas ob causas tum Aquila & Priscilla, tum Apollos nobis consyderandi veniunt. In illis enim paucis verbis eximiam pietatem & virtutes maximas euangelista comprehendit. Pietatis ingens argumentum est, quod Apollon dicentem audiunt, cum ipsi tantam haberent mysteriorum Christi cognitionem, vt alios instituere possent. Est haec vera filiorum Dei nota, quibus hoc proprium esse Christus ait, quod verbum suum crebro & libenter audiant. Ioban. 8. Arguuntur autem hoc exemplo, qui sese in salutis negotio eo vsq; profecisse putant, vt institutione ipsis amplius non sit opus, & proinde nec scripturas domi legunt, nec sacros coetus ingrediuntur, vt concionibus intersint. Ita vero dum se plus satis profecisse arbitrantur, palam produnt, se adhuc ignorare, quae praecipua filiorum Dei nota sit. Hi enim quia regnum Dei no in nuda cognitione consistere norunt, sed hoc potius requiri, vt vita iuxta verbi Dei regulam instituamus, audiendo satiari non possunt, cum in eo quod praecipuum est, subinde sibi quam plurimum deesse sentiant. Deinde ardens gloriae Dei studium prae se ferunt sanctissimi isti concuges, dum eum sibi instituendum sumunt, quem ecclesia Christi plurimum prodesse posse videbant. Adhaec charitatis verè Christianae & ab omni inuidia alienissimae argumentum est, quod priuatim illum instituunt, nec illi gloriam hanc inuident, quam bucusq; fideli studio sibi pepererat, imò iuuant potius, vt & ipse plenius instruatur, & plures per hunc lucrifieri possint. Hoc si cum nostri seculi moribus conferas, Deum immortalem, quam exigua adeoq; nulla tam Christiani pectoris argumenta apud eos quoq; inuenies, qui sanctissimi simul & euangelicae lucis instauratores videri volunt. Vt primum enim alicuius authoritatem crescere sentiunt, mox ambitionis spiritu exagitati inuident, simulq; anxiè quaerunt, si qua sese offerat occasio, qua illum vel contemptum vel inuisum reddant, quasi vero suo honori non nisi per aliorum infamiam consulere possint. At quomodo fidem habere possunt, qui honoris humani vel mundani tam cupidi sunt? Ioan. 5. Caini certè hic spiritus est, quem non aliam ob causam contra fratrem insurrexisse legimus, quàm quòd illum se praestantiorem Deo magis acceptum videret. Ut verò in religionis causa & ecclesiae ministerio malum hoc vitare conue nit, ita etiam in priuatis negotijs omnes inuidiae & odij occasiones summo studio subterfugere decet, siquidem germani Dei filij dici volumus. Caeterum vt in Aquila & Priscilla virtutes istae elucent, ita in Apollo admirabilis ac fere exemplo carens modestia & tractabilitas cernitur. Qui enim eloquentia insignis, & proinde in omni disciplinarum genere instructissimus erat, ab opifice manuario & muliere ijsq; ignotis antehac & peregrinis, doceri fuistinet. Verum enim est illud Pauli, qui prophetarum spiritus prophetis subijci scribit. 1. Cor. 14. Confer autem cum Apollo hoc illorum arrogantiam, qui ne à Symmystis quidem admoneri siue corrigi volunt, quorum hodie nimis magnus numerus est. Sed vt olim talium insolentia ecclesijs multum nocuit, sic hodie haec praecipua causa est, quod inte stinis contentionibus misere laniantur, dum vbiq; locorum reperiuntur, qui dictaturam in hac affectantes, fratres & Symmystas suos vix canum aut porcorum loco habent.
units.tr: Luke goes on to describe how Apollos advanced in the knowledge of Christ while he strove to promote Christ's glory and spread the salvation of others. For he says: "When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him and expounded to him the way of God more accurately." Here above all the truth of the promise made by Christ shines forth: "To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound" (Matth. 25.). Now people are said to "have" when they acknowledge the gifts bestowed on them and diligently use them for God's glory, so that when the Lord demands an account of them, he receives them back with interest. Because Apollos, as we have just said, showed the greatest faith and zeal, the Lord does not fail his promise, but immediately raises up faithful ministers who instruct him more fully and perfectly in the knowledge of Christ. This instruction ought to serve the common good of all, so that they understand that whatever gifts of God are increased by no means more happily than by faithful zeal. Thus those who have been accustomed to use the gift of wisdom for the spreading of the divine glory feel it growing day by day. The same reasoning applies to learning, honours, wealth, and indeed to all other things; nor are there lacking examples by which this can be proved. Again, there is no greater cause for which the gifts of God are usually extinguished than when men strive for their own sloth and idleness rather than for the glory of God. Here, for many reasons, Aquila and Priscilla, and Apollos too, deserve our consideration. For in those few words the evangelist sets forth their outstanding piety and very great virtues. It is a strong proof of piety that they listened to Apollos speaking, although they themselves had such a great knowledge of the mysteries of Christ that they could instruct others. This is the true mark of the sons of God, of whom Christ says it is their peculiar trait that they hear his word often and gladly (John 8.). But those are rebuked by this example who think they have advanced so far in the business of salvation that they no longer need instruction, and therefore neither read Scripture at home nor enter the sacred assemblies to be present at sermons. While they think they have progressed more than enough, they plainly show that they are still ignorant of what is the chief mark of the sons of God. For these people, since they know that the kingdom of God does not consist in bare knowledge, but that what is required is rather that we order our lives according to the rule of God's word, cannot be satisfied with hearing, since they constantly feel themselves lacking in very much of what is most important. Next, those most holy spouses display an ardent zeal for God's glory, in that they take up the instruction of a man whom they saw could be of great benefit to the Church of Christ. Moreover, this is the proof of truly Christian charity, which is most remote from all envy: they instruct him privately, and do not begrudge him the glory he had won by his faithful labour until then, but rather help him, so that he may be more fully equipped and more people may be won through him. If you compare this with the manners of our own age, immortal God, how small, indeed how nonexistent, you will find such marks of a Christian heart even among those who wish to be seen as the most holy and the restorers of the light of the gospel. As soon as they feel the authority of someone growing, straightway, goaded by the spirit of ambition, they envy him, and they anxiously seek, if any occasion presents itself, to make him either despised or hated, as though they could look after their own honour only by the infamy of others. But how can those have faith who are so greedy for human or worldly honour? (John 5.) This is surely the spirit of Cain, who, we read, rose up against his brother for no other reason than that he saw his brother more acceptable to God. And just as in the cause of religion and the ministry of the Church this evil must be avoided, so also in private affairs everyone ought with the utmost care to shun all occasions of envy and hatred, since we wish to be called true sons of God. Moreover, as those virtues shine in Aquila and Priscilla, so in Apollos is seen a wonderful modesty and docility, almost without parallel. For though he was distinguished in eloquence, and therefore thoroughly trained in every kind of learning, he did not disdain to be taught by a manual craftsman and a woman, who until then were unknown and foreign to him. Paul's words are true, who writes that the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets (1 Cor. 14.). Compare with Apollos the arrogance of those who will not even be admonished or corrected by their fellow-workers, of whom there is today a very great number. But just as the insolence of such people did much harm to the churches in former times, so today this is the chief cause why they are miserably torn apart by internal quarrels, while everywhere there are those who, aspiring to domineer in this matter, scarcely count their brothers and fellow-workers as worth more than dogs or pigs.

units.la: Accedit porrò prioribus aliud argumentum, quo ardens propagandi regni Dei studium Apollos declarat. Postquam enim se in Christi cognitione abunde instructum esse sentit, in Achaiam profecta instituit, Corinthum videlicet, eò quòd eam ecclesiam opera sua non parum indigere videret. Ut enim strenui milites ea loca sponte sibi deligunt, in quibus plurimum laboris & periculi esse noverunt: ita qui in Christi & ecclesiae militia cum laude & fructu versari volunt, diligenter observant quibus in locis ipsorum opera cumprimis requiratur, eoq; promptis animis festinant, ne quid ipsorum negligentia regno Dei decedat. HIC vero Ephesiorum quoq; fratrum fides & induistria observanda venit, qui fidelissimum Christi ministrum, & de sua ecclesia optime meritum virum, non sine publico virtutis testimonio abs se dimittunt: imò Corinthijs ita illum commendant, vt hortentur etiam, vt illi in sua ecclesia docendi locum concedant. Ut enim verbi ministrum exterorum quoq; testimonij probari necesse est, ne in laqueum calumniatoris incidat, ita minimè negari debet virtutis testimonium ijs, qui ecclesijs fidem suam non obscuris argumentis probauerunt. Nam qui tales ad ecclesiae ministerium proueehunt, non paruam in regno Dei gloriam merentur. Rursum in ipsam ecclesiam & Christum impij merito censentur, quicunq; prauis affectibus excaecati obstant, quò minus ad ecclesiae ministerium admittantur, qui eo munere digni sunt. Videndum tamen iuxta Pauli praeceptum, ne temerè cuius manus imponendo, peccatis alienis communicemus. 1. Tim. 5. Et quod de ecclesiae ministris dicitur, idipsum in omnibus aliis officijs siue muneribus publicis observandum est, vt nimirum digni proueehantur, arceantur autem, quoad per nos fieri potest, inepti & indigni homines, ne illos commendando communi reipub. damnum demus. Porrò quoad Apollon, curauit is, vt fratrum testimonio & commendationi responderet, ne indignum alienae ecclesiae obtrusisse videri possent. Multum enim contulit Corinthijs fratribus, qui crediderant, per gratiam. Sive verò gratia vocabulum ad Apollon, siue ad Corinthios referat, in idem sensus recidet. Docet enim nihil hic humanae induistriae tribuendum, sed Deum omnis boni authorem agnoscendum esse, qui incrementum dare dignatus fuerit, qua de re multis Paulus in priori ad Cor. 3. cap. disputat. Et sanè si vnum hoc probè considerarent Corinthij, nunquam ijs locum dedissent, qui factiosis Paulinorum, Cephistarum & Apollonistarum nominibus illorum ecclesiam postea turbauerunt. SED modum quoq; & rationem indicat Lucas, qua fratribus multum Apollos contulerit, nimirum Iudaeos publicè confutando, & ex scripturis probando quòd Iesus sit Christus, id est, promissus ille humani generis saluator. Qui locus de multis obseruatu necessarijs nos admonet. Primò enim docemur in ecclesia nō modò institutione, verumetiam aduersariorum confutatione opus esse. Nec enim fieri potest, vt multum prosint ecclesijs, qui falsa dogmata non summo studio extirpare nituntur, vt nec agricultura frugifera esse possit, quae fructices & lolium infelix succrescere patitur. Ideo Ieremias euellere & extirpare, deinde vero aedificare & plantare iubetur. Et Paulus episcopum talem esse vult, qui contradicentes quoq; convincere queat. Tit. 1. Quod autem de falsis doctoribus dicitur, quos omnino cofutari oportet, hoc ipsum de palam flagitiosis & sceleratis debet intelligi, qui infirmis offendiculo esse solent. Nam hos quoque gladio spiritus oppugnare debent fideles ministri, nisi ecclesiam lupis dilaniandam exponere velint. Vehementer itaq; errant, qui hodie euangelium ita praedicari volunt, vt nec impijs doctrinis nec corruptis ruptis moribus resistatur. Praeterea admonemur, quibus armis in ecclesia pugnari oporteat: Scripturis nimirum, quas diuinitus inspiratas, & ad docendum, arguendum, hortandum & increpandum vtiles esse, alibi Paulus docet. 2. Tim. 3. Turpissime ergo falluntur, qui cum haereticis per scripturas agi debere negant, eo quod obscuriores illae sint, quam vt his commincendis sufficiant. Quare ad Ecclesiae & Conciliorum determinationem confugiunt. Sed id perinde esse, ac si quis iam pugnam inituro militi gladium ferreum eripiat, & plumbeo illum accingat. Quasi vero maior authoritas esse queat humanarum constitutionum quam spiritus sancti, qui in scripturis loquitur. Postremo quod saepe monuimus, hic quoq; inculcatur, euangelicae praedicationis hunc finem esse, vt credamus Iesum esse Christum, Dominum & saluatorem nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, there is another argument added to the foregoing, by which Apollos shows his ardent zeal for spreading the kingdom of God. For after he perceived that he was amply instructed in the knowledge of Christ, he resolved to set out for Achaia, namely for Corinth, because he saw that this church greatly needed his labour. For just as brave soldiers choose for themselves of their own accord those places in which they know there is the greatest toil and danger, so those who wish to serve in the warfare of Christ and of the Church with praise and profit carefully observe in which places their work is especially needed, and with eager minds they hasten there, lest anything be lost to the kingdom of God through their negligence. Here also the faith and diligence of the Ephesian brethren deserve notice, who dismissed from their midst a most faithful minister of Christ and a man who had deserved very well of their church, not without a public testimony to his virtue. Indeed, they so commended him to the Corinthians that they even urged them to grant him a place of teaching in their church. For just as the minister of the Word must be proved even by the testimony of outsiders, lest he fall into the snare of a slanderer, so the testimony of virtue ought by no means to be withheld from those who have proved their faith to the churches by clear evidence. For those who advance such men to the ministry of the Church earn no small glory in the kingdom of God. On the other hand, those who, blinded by depraved affections, stand in the way so that men worthy of that office are not admitted to the ministry of the Church, are rightly judged impious against the Church and against Christ. Yet, according to Paul's precept, we must take care not to lay hands rashly on anyone, lest we share in the sins of others (1 Tim. 5). And what is said of the ministers of the Church must be observed in all other offices and public functions as well: namely, that the worthy be advanced and that, as far as we can manage it, the unfit and unworthy be kept out, lest by recommending them we cause loss to the common state. As for Apollos, he took care to answer to the testimony and commendation of the brethren, so that they could not seem to have foisted an unworthy man on another's church. For he greatly benefited the Corinthian brethren who had believed through grace. Whether the word "grace" refers to Apollos or to the Corinthians, it comes down to the same sense. For it teaches that nothing here is to be attributed to human industry, but that God, the author of every good, must be acknowledged, who has deigned to give the increase; on this matter Paul disputes at length in the earlier letter to the Corinthians, chapter 3. And indeed, if the Corinthians had carefully considered this one point, they would never have given a place to those who later disturbed their church with the factious names of Paulines, Cephasites and Apollonians. But Luke also indicates the manner and method by which Apollos greatly benefited the brethren, namely by publicly refuting the Jews and proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ, that is, that promised saviour of the human race. This passage admonishes us of many things that must be observed. For first we are taught that in the Church there is need not only of instruction but also of refutation of opponents. For those who do not strive with the greatest zeal to root out false doctrines cannot really benefit the churches, just as no field can be fruitful that allows brambles and the baneful darnel to grow up. Therefore Jeremiah is commanded to pluck up and root out, and then to build and plant (Jer. 1). And Paul wills that a bishop be such a man as can also convince those who contradict (Tit. 1). What is said of false teachers, whom it is necessary altogether to refute, ought also to be understood of openly wicked and criminal men, who are wont to be a stumbling block to the weak. For faithful ministers must assail these too with the sword of the Spirit, unless they wish to expose the Church to be torn apart by wolves. Therefore those greatly err who today want the gospel to be preached in such a way that neither impious doctrines nor corrupt morals are resisted. Furthermore, we are admonished with what weapons one must fight in the Church: namely the Scriptures, which Paul teaches elsewhere are divinely inspired and useful for teaching, convicting, exhorting and rebuking (2 Tim. 3). Those therefore are most shamefully mistaken who deny that one must deal with heretics by means of the Scriptures, on the ground that they are too obscure to be sufficient for refuting them. Hence they flee to the determination of the Church and of Councils. But this is just as if someone were to snatch the iron sword from a soldier about to join battle and gird him with a leaden one. As if, indeed, the authority of human constitutions could be greater than that of the Holy Spirit, who speaks in the Scriptures. Finally, what we have often admonished, is also here impressed upon us: that the end of evangelical preaching is this, that we believe Jesus to be the Christ, our Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XIX. HOMILIA CXXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 19. HOMILY 125.

units.la: FACtum est autem cum Apollos esset Corinthi, vt Paulus peragratis superioribus partibus veniret Ephesum: & repertis quibusdam discipulis, dicit ad eos: An spiritum sanctum accepistis postquam credidistis? At illi dixerunt ad eum: Imo, neque an sit spiritus sanctus, audiimus. Et ait illis: In quid igitur baptizati estis? Illi vero dixerunt: In Iohannis baptismum. Dixit autem Paulus: Iohannes quidem baptizauit baptismo poenitentiae, populo loquens in eum qui venturus esset post ipsum, vt crederent, hoc est, in Christum Iesum. His auditis, baptizati sunt in nomen Domini Iesu. Et cum imposuisset illis manus Paulus, venit spiritus sanctus super eos, & loquebantur linguis & prophetabant. Erant autem omnes viri fere duodecim.
units.tr: Now it happened, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the upper parts, came to Ephesus. There he found certain disciples, and said to them: Have you received the Holy Spirit since you believed? They answered him: Nay, we have not so much as heard whether there is any Holy Spirit. And he said to them: Into what, then, were you baptized? They said: Into John's baptism. Then Paul said: John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Christ Jesus. When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke with tongues and prophesied. And there were about twelve men in all.

units.la: QVONIAM de Ephesinae ecclesiae primordijs in praecedenti Cap. Lucas agere coepit, huius historiam deinceps hoc Capite absoluit, docens vt Paulus Ephesum, sicuti se facturum promiserat, reuersus, ecclesiam prius illic inchoatam feliciter absoluerit. Vt vero diuinae gratiae per euangelij praedicationem sese exerentis vis clarius elucescat, ante omnia Ephesus nobis consyderanda erit, quam Asiae vrbium celeberrimam fuisse scriptores tradiderunt. Propter situm enim emporijs & circumiacentis agri fertilitate claritissima opibus in immensum creuerat. Accedebat falsae religionis celebritas, quae ex omnibus nationibus hospites eo vocabat. Illic enim Dianae templum erat, quo nullum in orbe sumptuosius & augustius extructum fuit, cum in eius aedificatione totam Asiam annis circiter ducentis & viginti laborauisse constet, vt non temere inter mundi miracula numeraretur. Regnabant igitur in ea vrbe luxus & superstitio, quae curiosas & Magicas artes fere comites & pedisequas habere solet, quarum studiosissimos quoque Ephesios fuisse, suo loco videbimus. Eam tamen Paulus apostolus intra biennij spatium ita conuertit, vt nobilissima illic constituta fuerit ecclesia, cui haud vulgarem laudem in sua reuelatione Christus post tribuit. Apocal. 2. Quo loco partim Dei gratia obseruanda venit, quam Paulus postea Ephesijs hoc domestico ipsorum exemplo commendauit, vt in vius ad hos Epistola cap. 2. videre licet: partim euangelij ministerij vis elucet, cui nec veteris superstitionis authoritas, nec mundi fastus & gloria obstare potest, quo minus Christi regnum exurgat, vbicunq; illud admissum fuerit. Porro rerum a Paulo Ephesi gestarum narrationem Lucas contexturus, ab eo orditur, vt quosdam euangelij nomine glorientes, nondum autem plene institutos & formatos absoluerit, & spiritus sancti donis ecclesiam illam nobilitarit. Quae historia vt nostrae institutioni plurimum seruit: ita vel hoc nomine diligenti consyderatione digna est, quod olim quidam huius exempli authoritate pugnarunt, qui ab haereticis baptizatos denuo baptizandos esse contendebant: hodie vero eadem Anabaptistae abutuntur, furiosum & mire pertinax hominum genus, qui paruulos a baptismo arcendos, nec nisi adultos iam & plene institutos baptismo tingi debere clamant. Sed tam hos, quam veteres falsos fuisse, ut ipso contextu facile patebit, quo euincetur nihil minus Paulo cordi fuisse cum haec ageret, quam quod illi hinc elicere conantur.
units.tr: Since Luke began to speak of the beginnings of the church at Ephesus in the preceding chapter, he now completes its history in this chapter, teaching that Paul, returning to Ephesus as he had promised, successfully finished the church he had begun there. But so that the power of divine grace, as it makes itself known through the preaching of the gospel, may shine more clearly, we must first consider Ephesus, which the writers tell us was the most famous city of Asia. It had grown immensely rich, being very prosperous because of its position for trade and the fertility of the surrounding countryside. Added to this was the fame of its false religion, which drew visitors to it from every nation. For there stood the temple of Diana, than which no more costly or magnificent building was ever erected in the world; it is recorded that the whole of Asia laboured for about two hundred and twenty years on its construction, so that it was not without reason counted among the wonders of the world. Luxury and superstition therefore reigned in that city, and these are usually accompanied and followed by curious and magical arts, of which we shall see in its place that the Ephesians were also most devoted practitioners. Yet the apostle Paul converted it within the space of two years, so that a most noble church was established there, to which Christ afterwards gave no small praise in his revelation (Rev. 2). In this passage the grace of God is to be observed, which Paul later commended to the Ephesians by this very example of their own household, as may be seen in his epistle to them, chapter 2. And partly the power of the ministry of the gospel is made clear, which neither the authority of ancient superstition nor the pomp and glory of the world can hinder, so that the kingdom of Christ rises up wherever it is admitted. Moreover, Luke, about to weave together the narrative of what Paul did at Ephesus, begins with this, so that he might show that the church there, whose members were boasting in the name of the gospel but were not yet fully instructed and formed, was ennobled by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. This history serves our instruction greatly, and it is also worthy of careful consideration on this account: some men of old fought by the authority of this example, contending that those baptized by heretics must be baptized again; and today the Anabaptists, a furious and wonderfully stubborn race of men, abuse the same passage, crying out that infants must be kept from baptism and that only adults, already fully instructed, may be baptized. But, as the context itself will readily make plain, both these men and the ancient ones were mistaken, and it will be shown that Paul had nothing less at heart in this matter than what they try to draw from it.

units.la: Principio enim Paulum quorundam discipulorum examen instituisse dicitur, in quos Ephe- sum reuersus incidit. At minime credibile est, solos hos Christo nomen dedisse, cum maiorem euan- gelij profectum apud Ephesios ex ijs conijcere liceat, quae in fine cap. 18. audiuimus. Quod autem bos sibi prae alijs examinandos sumit Paulus, in causa fuisse videtur, quod Christiani nominis professioni minus responderent. Verisimile enim est hoc ipsum Ephesi accidisse, quod passim fere accidere solet, quando primum praedicatur veritas, nondum tamen ecclesiae disciplina solide constituta est. Tunc enim multos inuenire licet, qui veteris conditionis odio potius quam veritatis amore, euangelicos se profitentur, dum sub euangelij praetextu maiorem sibi licentiam promittunt. Tales quia hos esse videbat Paulus, ut ad meliorem frugem adeo, maturitatem perducerentur, nec illorum instar perirent, qui euangelij semen in petricosam terram exceperunt, illorum fidem examinare, sicque illis quam procul adhuc a meta absint, ob oculos ponere instituit. Quaerit ergo, an spiritum sanctum acceperint? Debet autem de spiritus sancti donis, quae illo tempore credentibus conferri solebant, quaestio ista intelligi, nimirum linguarum cognitione et prophetia, de quibus iam saepe dictum est. Docet interim locus iste, quo indicio veri Christiani a fucatis siue falsis dignosci queant. Licet enim specialia illa spiritus dona, quae miraculose olim conferebantur, hodie cessarint, rata tamen manet Christi Iesu promissio, qua suis spiritum suum pollicitus est. Et ut alibi Paulus monet, qui spiritum Christi non habent, eiusdem membra esse non possunt. Rom. 8. Nec minus necessarij sunt hodie reliqui spiritus sancti effectus, quam olim linguarum cognitio et prophetia fuerint: quales sunt, veteris hominis mortificatio, regeneratio et innouatio mentis nostrae, purificatio, sanctificatio et si quae alia sunt huius generis. Quotquot ergo istis omnibus carent, bos falso Christi nomine et fide gloriari, certum est, nisi otiosum et inertem dicere libeat Christi spiritum.
units.tr: For, to begin with, it is said that Paul examined certain disciples whom he met on returning to Ephesus. Yet it is hardly credible that these alone had given their names to Christ, since from what we heard at the end of chapter 18 we may conjecture that the gospel had made greater progress among the Ephesians. But the reason Paul chose these men above others for examination seems to have been that they did not live up to their profession of the Christian name. For it is likely that what happened at Ephesus happens nearly everywhere when the truth is first preached but the discipline of the church is not yet firmly established. For then one may find many who profess themselves evangelical, not from a love of the truth but from hatred of their former condition, while under the pretext of the gospel they promise themselves greater freedom. Since Paul saw that such men were in this state, he set about examining their faith and placing before their eyes how far they still were from the goal, so that they might be brought to better fruit and to maturity, and not perish like those who received the seed of the gospel on stony ground. He asks therefore: Have you received the Holy Spirit? This question must be understood of those gifts of the Holy Spirit which were then commonly bestowed on believers, namely the knowledge of tongues and prophecy, of which we have often spoken already. Meanwhile this passage teaches by what sign true Christians may be distinguished from the counterfeit or false. For although those special gifts of the Spirit which were once conferred miraculously have now ceased, the promise of Christ Jesus, by which he promised his own his Spirit, nevertheless remains firm. And as Paul warns elsewhere, those who do not have the Spirit of Christ cannot be his members (Rom. 8). The remaining effects of the Holy Spirit are no less necessary today than the knowledge of tongues and prophecy were once: such as the mortification of the old man, the regeneration and renewal of our mind, purification, sanctification, and whatever other things are of this kind. Therefore, unless one is willing to call the Spirit of Christ idle and inactive, it is certain that all who lack all these things boast falsely of the name and faith of Christ.

units.la: Sed responsionem horum audiamus, quos Paulus examinare statuit, qua crassam omnino et nimis barbaram ignorantiam testantur, dicentes: Imo, neque an sit spiritus sanctus audiuimus. At quomodo spiritum sanctum esse ignorabant, qui toties huius mentionem fieri in lege et prophetis non- uerant? Iudaeos enim hos fuisse non dubium est, cum Iohannis baptismo initiati fuerint. An ergo illud Moysis ignorabant, qui suae historiae initio, spiritum Dei aquis incubuisse scribit? Velnum Dauid dictum nunquam audiuerant? Verbo Domini caeli facti sunt, et spiritu oris eius omnis exercitus eorum. Psal. 33. Item: Spiritum tuum sanctum ne a me auferas. Psalm. 51. Adhaec Messia vocem in propheta loquentis nouisse poterant: Spiritus Domini Dei super me est, &c. Isa. 61. Quomodo ergo se vnquam, an spiritus sanctus sit, audiuisse negant? Sed facilis est solutio. Vt enim de spiritus sancti effectus interrogauit Paulus, ita de ijsdem illi respondent, quasi dicant: Nos ijs, quae hucusque didicimus, contenti, nihil vltra quaerimus, nec curamus sit ne vel minus spiritus aliquis sanctus, qui peculiaria quaedam in hominum animis operetur: eo quod horum cognitionem supra nos esse, nec quicquam ad nos pertinere putamus. Ita vero carnalium hominum typus sunt isti, qui cum veritatem ore profiteantur, eius tamen vim (ut Paulus ait) abnegauerunt, et factis negant quod ore fateri solent. 2. Tim. 3. Tit. 1. Ingens horum numerus hodie passim inuenitur, qui nudum Christi nomen ad beatitudinem sufficere persuasi, spiritus sancti dona, carnis nimirum mortificationem, innouationem mentis, regenerationem, sanctificationem et alia huius generis quam minime curant. Et horum quidem culpa fere fieri solet, ut euangelij doctrina in mundo pessime audiat. Minime ergo tales ferendi sunt, sed argui et in lucem protrahi debet illorum fucus, ut et ipsi se errare intelligant, et alios minus offendant.
units.tr: But let us hear the answer of these men whom Paul determined to examine, which shows a crude and altogether too barbarous ignorance, when they say: Nay, we have not so much as heard whether there is any Holy Spirit. But how could they not know that there is a Holy Spirit, when mention of him is made so often in the law and the prophets? For there is no doubt that these men were Jews, since they had been initiated into John's baptism. Did they then not know that saying of Moses, who at the beginning of his history writes that the Spirit of God moved upon the waters? Or had they never heard what David said: By the word of the Lord were the heavens made, and all their host by the breath of his mouth (Ps. 33)? Likewise: Take not your holy Spirit from me (Ps. 51). Moreover, they could have known the voice of the Messiah speaking in the prophet: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, etc. (Isa. 61). How, then, do they deny that they have ever heard whether the Holy Spirit exists? But the solution is easy. For just as Paul asked about the effects of the Holy Spirit, so they answer him about the same things, as if they were saying: We are content with what we have learned so far; we seek nothing further, nor do we care whether there is any Spirit, holy or otherwise, who works special things in the minds of men, since we think the knowledge of these things is beyond us and has nothing to do with us. Indeed these men are a type of the carnal, who, while they profess the truth with their mouth, have nevertheless denied its power (as Paul says) and by their deeds deny what they are accustomed to confess with their lips (2 Tim. 3; Tit. 1). A vast number of such people is found everywhere today, persuaded that the bare name of Christ is sufficient for blessedness, and caring very little for the gifts of the Holy Spirit: that is, the mortification of the flesh, the renewal of the mind, regeneration, sanctification, and other things of this kind. And it is largely through the fault of such people that the doctrine of the gospel is so badly received in the world. Such men, then, must not be tolerated; their pretence must be exposed and brought into the light, so that they may understand that they are in error and offend others less.

units.la: Facit hoc ipsum in praesenti Paulus. Propius enim cum his pedem conferens, vrget illos, ut ex ipsorum ore couincat, eos nondum veram Christianismi metam attigisse. Ait enim: In quid ergo baptizati estis? Id est, quae vestra fuit professio, cum primum euangelio nomen daretis, ecclesiae Christi vos coniungentes? Respondent, se in Iohannis baptismum fuisse baptizatos: sicque testantur, se in eam doctrinam et religionem concessisse, cuius minister et doctor Iohannes fuerit, nec obscure innuunt, se praeter hanc non quicquam amplius curare. Hic vero captos arctissime constringens Paulus, inquit: Iohannes quidem baptizauit baptismo poenitentiae, populo loquens in eum qui venturus erat post. possit ipsum, ut crederent, hoc esset, in Iesum Christum. Ita vero docet, Iohannem longe aliud quàm nudam nominis sui & euangelii professionem, à suis discipulis requisiuisse. Primò enim poenitentiam praescripsit, ad quam magno spirio omnes ordines hortatus est, ut patet Luc.3. Nec tamen nudam poenitentiam exegit, sed simul peccatorum remissionem monstrauit, Christum Iesum praedicans, cuius ille praecursor à Deo erat constitutus. Hunc vero fide amplecti, hunc sequi, huic sese homines totos consecrare docuit: eò quòd in hoc solo ea inueniri possint, quae externo baptismo figurantur. Quis vero illa absque spiritus sancti operatione praestabit? Adeò ergo non sufficit inanis illa Iohannis vestri doctoris gloriatio, ut huius potius doctrina & baptismus, quo tincti estis, vos vlterius progredi compellant, & eò animiti, ut Christo viua fide insiti, & illius spiritu animati, ipsis spiritus sancti effectus, vos vere Christianos esse testemini. Et hunc quidem simplicissimum ac minimè coactum esse verborum Pauli sensum totus historiae contextus probat. Quare ridiculus illorum error est, qui ex hoc loco euincere conati sunt, non vnum & eundem, sed longè diuersum, Iohannis & Christi baptismum esse. Tam enim illud à Pauli mente alienum est, ut potius euincat, homines baptismo aquae, cuius minister Iohannes fuit, ad Christum relegari, in quo solo ea apprehendi possint, quorum symbola nobis baptismus offerre consueuit. Simul vero generale dogma hic stabilitur, minimè ferendum esse, ut homines authoritati insistant, qui Dei cultores haberi volunt, sed vrgeri debere quòsq; ut Christo totis animis consecrentur, & in illo viuant ipsius spiritu animati, ne dum hunc ore profitentur, se ab eodem alienissimos esse, factis testentur.
units.tr: Paul does this very thing in the present passage. Coming closer to these men, he presses them to prove from their own mouths that they have not yet reached the true goal of Christianity. For he says: "Into what then were you baptized?" That is, what was your profession when you first gave your name to the gospel and joined yourselves to the Church of Christ? They reply that they were baptized into John's baptism, and so they testify that they had given themselves to the teaching and religion whose minister and teacher John had been, and they clearly hint that they cared for nothing beyond this. But Paul, binding these captives tightly, says: "John indeed baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus Christ. Thus he teaches that John demanded from his disciples something far different from a bare profession of his name and of the gospel. For first he prescribed repentance, to which he urged all orders of people with great earnestness, as is clear from Luke 3. Yet he did not require bare repentance, but at the same time showed the forgiveness of sins, preaching Christ Jesus, whose forerunner he had been appointed by God. He taught them to embrace this one in faith, to follow him, and to devote themselves wholly to him, because in him alone could be found those things which the outward baptism signifies. Who, however, will supply those things without the working of the Holy Spirit? So that empty boasting of John, your teacher, is by no means enough; rather, let his teaching and the baptism with which you were washed urge you to advance further, and to be engrafted into Christ by living faith, and, animated by his Spirit, made partakers of the effects of the Holy Spirit, so that you may witness that you are truly Christians." The whole context of the history proves that this is the simplest meaning of Paul's words, and one that is not forced in any way. So ridiculous is the error of those who have tried to prove from this passage that the baptism of John and the baptism of Christ are not one and the same but wholly different. For that idea is so alien to Paul's mind that it rather proves that people are sent, by the water baptism whose minister John was, to Christ, in whom alone those things can be grasped which baptism usually offers us as signs. At the same time a general doctrine is established here: men who want to be regarded as worshippers of God must not be tolerated in relying on authority, but must be urged, every one of them, to devote themselves wholly to Christ, and to live in him animated by his Spirit, so that they show by their deeds that they are most alien from him, if they only profess him with their mouths.

units.la: Porrò historia huius finem latissimum Lucas subiungit. Cesserunt enim viri illi, nimirum Pauli rationibus & occulta spiritus suggestione in suis conscientiis conuicti. Et baptizati sunt in nomen Domini Iesu. Non autem de aquae baptismo verba ista exponi debent, quasi illum iterauerint. Ita enim sequeretur, Iohannis baptismum non legitimum fuisse, nec suffecisse hominibus Deo consecrandis. Id vero absurdum esse dicitur cum Christi exemplum docet, qui ab Iohanne baptizari, sicq; nostrae communionis socius fieri voluit: tum illud conuincit, quòd nusquam rebaptizatos fuisse legimus eos, quos Iohannes baptizauerat. Quare de ignis baptismo locus intelligi debet, cuius ministrum vel authorem Christum fore Iohannes antea praedixerat. Nam sub ignis specie spiritus sanctus conferri solebat, de quo Cap.2.huius libri diximus. Et baptizandi verbum frequenter pro spiritus sancti & donorum ipsius collatione vsurpari constat. Ita enim hoc ipse Iohannes vtitur, cum de Christo loquens ait: Ipse vos baptizabit spiritu sancto & igne. Eodem sensu Christus, iam coelos conscensu rus, ait: Baptizabimini spiritu sancto post dies hosce non multos. Cuius dicti rationem hoc ipso sensu Petrus reddit, coram ecclesia de Cornelij conuersione differens. Actor.11. Ita vero in praesenti quoque Baptizandi verbum accipi debere, Lucas docet, dum expositionis loco subiungit: Et cum Paulus illis imposuisset manus, venit spiritus sanctus super eos, & loquebantur linguis & prophetabant. Manuum ergo impositione Christo penitus consecrati sunt, quam spiritus sanctus pro more illico secutus est, quemadmodum Samaria quoq; factum fuisse audiuimus. Vnde veteres loco hoc abusos fuisse constat, dum huius authoritate rebaptizandos esse contenderunt, qui ab haereticis baptizati fuerant. Fefellit hos, quòd aquae baptismum Iohannis & Christi diuersum esse putarunt. Nec minor Anabaptistarum ignorantia est, qui ad aquae baptismum transferunt, quod de ignis baptismo, id est spiritus sancti collatione & dono, debebat intelligi. Nobis vero ante omnia miraculi finis & vsus obseruandus est, quòd nimirum hoc Deus euangelij sui authoritatem apud gentes quoq; confirmare & nobilitare voluit, ut iam saepe diximus. Credamus igitur euangelio, cuius fides & veritas tam multis tamq; magnificis signis asserta est. Fidei autem professioni vita respondeamus, ut spiritus Christi animati in illo viuamus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, Luke adds the widest outcome of this history. For those men gave way, convinced in their consciences by Paul's arguments and by the hidden prompting of the Spirit. "And they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus." These words ought not to be explained as if they had been baptized again with water. For then it would follow that John's baptism was not lawful, nor sufficient for people to be consecrated to God. This is said to be absurd, since the example of Christ teaches otherwise: he wished to be baptized by John, and so to become a sharer in our fellowship. Then, too, it is proved by the fact that we never read that those whom John had baptized were baptized again. Therefore the place must be understood of the baptism of fire, whose minister or author John had earlier foretold would be Christ. For the Holy Spirit was commonly conferred under the appearance of fire, of which we spoke in chapter 2 of this book. And it is established that the word "to baptize" is often used for the conferring of the Holy Spirit and of his gifts. For John himself uses it this way when, speaking of Christ, he says: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire." In the same sense Christ, about to ascend into heaven, says: "You shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence." Peter gives the reason for this saying in the same sense, when he speaks before the Church about the conversion of Cornelius, Acts 11. But that the word "baptize" should be taken in the same way here too, Luke teaches, when by way of explanation he adds: "And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke with tongues and prophesied." Therefore they were wholly consecrated to Christ by the laying on of hands, and the Holy Spirit immediately followed, as we have heard was also the case in Samaria. Hence it is evident that the ancients abused this passage when they contended, on its authority, that those who had been baptized by heretics must be baptized again. They were misled because they thought the water baptism of John and of Christ were different. The ignorance of the Anabaptists is no less, who apply to water baptism what ought to be understood of the baptism of fire, that is, of the conferring and gift of the Holy Spirit. But for us, above all, the purpose and use of the miracle must be observed: namely, that God wished to confirm and ennoble the authority of his gospel among the Gentiles also, as we have often said. Let us therefore believe the gospel, whose faith and truth have been asserted by so many and such great signs. And let us answer the profession of faith with a life, so that, animated by the Spirit of Christ, we live in him, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY 126.

units.la: Introgressus autem Synagogam liber loquebatur ad tres menses, disputans & suadens de regno Dei. Cum autem quidam indurarentur, nec crederent, male loquentes de via coram multitudine, digressus ab illis, segregauit discipulos, quotidie disputans in schola Tyranni cuiusdam. dam. Hoc autem factum est per biennium, ita vt omnes qui habitabant in Asia, audirent sermonem Domini Iesu: Iudæi simul & Græci. Virtutes non vulgares edebat Dominus per manus Pauli, ita vt etiam super infirmos deferrentur à corpore eius sudaria & semicincta, & recederent ab eis morbi, & spiritus mali egrederentur.
units.tr: He entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading concerning the kingdom of God. But when some were hardened and would not believe, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he withdrew from them, separated the disciples, and reasoned daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus. This went on for two years, so that all who dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks. God worked no ordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.

units.la: POstquam Diuus Lucas exposuit, vt Ephesi Paulus duodecim viros, Christiani nominis professioni non probè respondentes, plenè instituerit: narrat deinceps, vt eiusdem Pauli ministerio regnum Dei apud Ephesios totamq; finitimam regionem Asiæ longè lateq; propagatum fit. Et quidem summam huius historiæ praesens hic locus completitur, in cuius consyderatione eò diligentius nos versari conuenit, quòd singulis partibus multa insunt, quæ communi omnium nostrum institutioni seruiunt. Primò enim de doctrina Pauli agitur. Deinde quid cum reprobis & incredulis actum sit narratur. Tertiò apostolici studij haud vulgaris profectus describitur.
units.tr: After Saint Luke had explained how Paul thoroughly instructed the twelve men at Ephesus, who did not live up well to their profession of the Christian name, he goes on to tell how, through Paul's ministry, the kingdom of God was spread far and wide among the Ephesians and the whole neighbouring region of Asia. This present passage sums up the whole of this history, and it is well worth our while to dwell on it carefully, because each of its parts contains much that serves the common instruction of us all. First, the teaching of Paul is treated. Next, what happened with the reprobate and unbelieving is related. Third, the not inconsiderable progress of the apostolic work is described.

units.la: Principiò vniuersam doctrinæ Pauli rationem paucis Euangelista comprehendit, quando illum Synagogam ingressum esse, & illic per menses tres magna cum libertate disputauisse & dereno Dei suasisse dicit. Vt ergo alibi, ita hic quoq; Iudæis primùs prædicat. Patet ex eo partim ineffabilis Dei bonitas erga gentem rebellem & contumacissimam, partim ardentissimus ac minimè fructus in Paulo charitatis affectus, qui tot tamen atrocibus iniurijs extingui non potuit: quem nisi induant ecclesiarum ministri, nunquam cum fructu aliquo commissum sibi munus obire poterunt. Quia tamen de his iam aliquoties dictum est, omissis his videamus quam docendi rationem apud Ephesios Paulus obseruarit, ad quam tria pertinent, de quibus Lucas disserit. Primò locum nominat, & in Synagoga publica ipsum docuisse scribit. Quod ergo alibi sedulò obseruauit Paulus, idipsum Ephesi quoq; obseruandum esse putauit, nimirum vt publico & certo loco doceret, quàmuis non ignoraret Iudæorum mores; qui eo in loco imperium obtinebant. Vnde discimus certum esse debere locum doctrinæ, nec illum temere debere deseri. Facit enim hoc non parum ad retinendam saniorum doctrinam & impostores cohercendos, qui palàm obrepere & incautos seducere consueuerunt. Qua causa est, quòd Christus quoq; in templo & Synagogis publicis plerunq; docuit, ne suo exemplo ijs petrocinaretur, qui vel cætus publicos temere deserunt, vel in angulis falsa dogmata spargunt, quod vtrunq; nostro seculo Anabaptistæ nimis licenter faciunt. Secundò modus, quem in docendo Paulus obseruauit, exprimitur. Liberè & ingenuè egit, nihil nimirum dissimulans. Et primò quidem disputauit, Iudæorum errores confutans, quibus illi simplex alioqui salutis negotium confundebant. Deinde suadere cœpit & hortari, vt veritati cedere dignarentur. Est hic optimus docendi modus, in quo duo hæc necessario adhiberi oportet, vt & aduersariorum argumenta confutentur, & efficacibus rationibus vrgeantur aduersarij vt veritatem apprehendant & sedulò sectentur. Vt enim veritatis locus non erit, quoad mendacia & errores regnum obtinet: ita inanis & superuacanea erit veritatis cognitio, nisi serio illam amplexetur homines & in illam transformari studeant. Ideo Paulus verbi ministrum non modò docere, verumetiam hortari, increpare, imò opportunè simul & importunè instare iubet. 2. Tim. 4. Et Christus inuitatos compelli vult, vt ad nuptias cœlestis regni ingrediatur. Quare turpissimus illorum error est, qui nudam & literalem scripturæ tractationem in ecclesia suffi-cere clamant, nec permittunt, vt singulorum ædificationi adhibeantur, quæ in illa continentur: quasi vero in nuda contemplatione salutis negotium consistat. Tertiò argumentum & materiam doctrinæ Pauli exprimit Lucas, quando illum de regno Dei disseruisse ait. Ita verò dicitur nostræ redemptionis & salutis negotium, cuius administratorem & executorem Messiam fore, olim prophetæ prædixerant. Atqui de hoc non falsas modò, sed nimium quoq; carnales crassasq; opiniones Iudæi concepe-rant ex perperam intellectis prophetarum oraculis. Nam Messiæ regnum terrenum somniabant, aureumq; sub hoc seculum fore sperabant, quale olim sub Salomone fuisset. Quo errore apostoli quoq; seducti eximios honores & principatus sibi pollicebatur, vt ex illorum contentionibus facile colligitur. Quòd si qui inter Iudæos de salutis ratione potius quàm terreno illo regno cogitarent, hanc tamen in frigidis potius ceremonijs quàm Christi merito collocabant. Diligenter ergo Paulus veritate regni Dei Iudæis exposuit, docens nimirum illud spirituale, non terrenum esse, nec in ceremoniarum inani ob-seruatione.
units.tr: At the outset the Evangelist sums up the whole method of Paul's teaching in a few words, when he says that Paul entered the synagogue and there, for three months, disputed with great freedom and persuaded them concerning the kingdom of God. So, as elsewhere, so here too he preached to the Jews first. From this appears, partly, the ineffable goodness of God towards a rebellious and most stubborn people, and partly the most ardent and yet least fruitful affection of charity in Paul, which nonetheless could not be quenched by so many savage injuries. Unless the ministers of the churches clothe themselves with this, they will never be able to discharge the office committed to them with any fruit. Yet because these things have been said many times already, let us pass them by and look at the method of teaching that Paul observed among the Ephesians, to which three things pertain, which Luke discusses. First, he names the place, and writes that Paul taught in the public synagogue. Paul's careful practice elsewhere, therefore, he thought should be observed at Ephesus too, namely that he should teach in a public and certain place, although he was not unaware of the customs of the Jews, who held authority in that place. From this we learn that a place for teaching ought to be fixed, and that it should not be lightly abandoned. For this contributes not a little to keeping sounder doctrine intact and to restraining impostors, who are accustomed to creep in openly and seduce the unwary. For this reason Christ too taught for the most part in the temple and public synagogues, lest by his example he should lend support to those who either rashly desert public assemblies or spread false doctrines in corners, both of which the Anabaptists in our own age do all too freely. Second, the manner that Paul observed in teaching is set out. He acted freely and frankly, concealing nothing. And indeed at first he disputed, refuting the errors of the Jews, by which they otherwise confused the simple business of salvation. Then he began to persuade and exhort them to deign to yield to the truth. This is the best method of teaching, in which two things must necessarily be employed: that the arguments of opponents be refuted, and that opponents be pressed with effective reasons to grasp the truth and diligently pursue it. For just as the place of truth will not exist while lies and errors hold sway, so the knowledge of truth will be empty and superfluous unless men earnestly embrace it and strive to be transformed into it. Therefore Paul bids the minister of the Word not only to teach but also to exhort, rebuke, and indeed to press on in season and out of season. 2 Tim. 4. And Christ wishes that those who are invited be compelled to enter the wedding of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore the most shameful error is that of those who cry out that a bare and literal handling of Scripture suffices in the church, and do not allow what is contained in it to be applied to the building up of individuals, as if the business of salvation consisted in bare contemplation. Third, Luke sets out the subject and matter of Paul's teaching, when he says that Paul discoursed concerning the kingdom of God. This is the name for the business of our redemption and salvation, whose administrator and executor the prophets had long ago foretold would be the Messiah. Yet the Jews had conceived of this not only false but also excessively carnal and gross opinions, from misunderstood oracles of the prophets. For they dreamed of an earthly kingdom of the Messiah and hoped that under it there would be a golden age, such as once had been under Solomon. Led astray by this error, even the apostles promised themselves distinguished honours and principalities, as is easily gathered from their contentions. But if some among the Jews thought about the way of salvation rather than that earthly kingdom, they nonetheless placed it in cold ceremonies rather than in Christ's merit. Paul therefore diligently set out for the Jews the truth of the kingdom of God, teaching, of course, that it is spiritual, not earthly, nor in the empty observance of ceremonies, but rests on the merit of Christ and on the faith by which we are brought into it.

units.la: Paulus Iudæis prædicat in Synagoga.
units.tr: Paul preaches to the Jews in the synagogue.

units.la: Locus doctrinæ publicus fit.
units.tr: The place of teaching becomes public.

units.la: Modus docendi.
units.tr: The manner of teaching.

units.la: Argumentum doctrinæ apostolicæ. feruatione, sed Christi merito & fide, qua illi inferimur consistere. Habetur hæc Pauli doctrina tum in Sermonibus, quos in hoc libro Lucas descripsit, tum in epistolis ipsius, unde ea peti poterit, ut pro lixiori illius enumeratione no sit opus. Obseruemus tamen regnū Dei in scripturis dici nostræ redemptionis & salutis negotiū. Ita enim finis huius exprimitur, qui est, ut pulso satana & deuicto mudo, deus in nobis regnū obtineat, quod & inter orandū petimus, dicentes: Adueniat regnum tuum. Quamobrem pseudochristiani sunt, quotquot Christi nomine gloriantes, diabolo sese regendos præbent, cui nulla potest esse cum Christo Iesu comunio. Nec enim Christiani esse possunt, qui extra Dei regnum constituti sunt, cum no nisi huius instaurandi gratia Christus in mundū venerit. At quomodo in Dei regno esse poterunt, qui diaboli spiritu se se gubernari patiuntur, illiq; per omnia obtemperant?
units.tr: The subject of apostolic doctrine. It rests not on observance but on the merit of Christ and on faith, by which we are brought in. This doctrine of Paul is found both in the sermons that Luke recorded in this book and in his epistles, from which it can be drawn, so that there is no need for a longer enumeration of it. We should observe, however, that the kingdom of God is called in Scripture the business of our redemption and salvation. For this states its end, which is that, with Satan driven out and the world conquered, God may hold sway in us. We ask for this also in prayer, saying: Thy kingdom come. Therefore those are pseudo-Christians, however much they boast in the name of Christ, who submit themselves to be ruled by the devil, with whom there can be no communion with Christ Jesus. For those who stand outside the kingdom of God cannot be Christians, since Christ came into the world for no other purpose than to restore this kingdom. But how can those be in the kingdom of God who allow themselves to be governed by the spirit of the devil and obey him in all things?

units.la: Quia vero nunquam tam feliciter Christus prædicari potest, quin reprobi plures contra eius doctrinā insurgant, quid cum illis Paulus egerit indicatur, ita tamen ut quid ipsi priores fecerint, primum Lucas commemoret. Indurati fuisse dicuntur Pauli doctrina. Est hoc proprium impijs, ut quo magis vrgentur verbo dei, eo magis indurescant, non quidem verbi dei vitio, sed propria ipsorū culpa. Quia enim semen filiorum Dei in se non habent, verbum & vocem eius agnoscere non possunt, eoq; ferociores insurgunt, quo fortius in ordinem illos cogit spiritus sanctus. Exempla in Caino, Pharaone, Saule, Iuda & multis aliis extant, quibus vtinam non noua indies accederent. Indurationē sequitur quod credere & obedire nolunt. Abijciunt ergo Dei verbum quasi vanū & nihil ad se pertinens. Accedit tamen quod longe pessimū est, calumniandi videlicet & maledicendi studiū, quo viam hanc, id est, Christi doctrinam & religionem apud vulgus quoq; suspectā & inuisam reddere conantur. Diaboli enim ingenium secuti, quam plurimos suæ perditionis socios habere cupiunt. Et hū quidem gradibus procedit impietas, donec in summum euectā ad interitum ruit. Quid vero cum talibus Paulus agit? Discedit primo ab illis, ne vel illos magis inflammaret, vel noxijs contentionibus occasionem præberet: idq; iuxta Christi præceptum facit, qui canibus & porcis margaritas prosternere vetuit, & aduersus improbe rebelles pedum puluerem excutere iussit. Matth. 7. & 10. Deinde discipulos quoq;, qui saniore doctrinam amplexi fuerant, ab ijsdem segregat: boni nimirū pastoris officio fungens, cuius hæc non postrema cura esse debet, ne morbidorum contagio sanū pecus inficiatur. Nec ideo schismaticus dici debet Paulus, licet ecclesiæ & populi Dei titulū sibi vendicarent, à quibus ille suos segregatos esse voluit. Imo necesse est, ut impiorū comercia pij deuitent, cum & illi in his indurentur, & bi pœnarū consortes cū impijs plerunq; fieri soleat. Vide Apoc. 18. Tertiò quotidie in schola Tyranni cuiusdā docet Paulus: quæ qualis fuerit, & vnde loco nomen obtigerit, non multum refert, locū certè publicum & prædicationi comodum fuisse credibile est. Pauli potius inductria obseruemus, qui malorū improbitate se ab officio reuocari minimè patitur, quin eò studiosius docet, quò magis illi insaniunt. Imitentur exemplū hoc quicunq; vel in repub. vel in ecclesiæ ministerio versantur. Et hæc quidem veteris ecclesiæ exercitia fuerunt, quam Dei verbo maximè occupatā fuisse legimus, quod hodie non ab alijs magis quàm ab ijs negligitur, qui apostolorū successores dici & haberi volūt.
units.tr: But because Christ is never preached so happily that many reprobate do not rise up against his teaching, what Paul did with them is indicated, though Luke first recalls what they themselves did before. They are said to have been hardened against Paul's teaching. It is characteristic of the wicked that the more they are pressed by the Word of God, the more they harden themselves, not indeed through any fault of the Word of God, but through their own guilt. For since they do not have the seed of the children of God in them, they cannot recognise his word and voice, and so they rise up the more fiercely the more strongly the Holy Spirit tries to bring them into order. Examples exist in Cain, Pharaoh, Saul, Judas and many others, and would that new ones did not daily join them. Hardening is followed by their refusal to believe and obey. Therefore they cast away God's word as empty and having nothing to do with them. Yet there is added something far worse, namely the zeal for slander and abuse, by which they try to make this way, that is, the doctrine and religion of Christ, suspect and hateful even among the common people. For following the nature of the devil, they desire to have as many companions of their ruin as possible. And impiety proceeds by these steps until, raised to its height, it rushes to destruction. What, then, does Paul do with such people? He first withdraws from them, lest he either inflame them further or give occasion for harmful contentions. He does this in accordance with the precept of Christ, who forbade casting pearls before dogs and swine, and bade us shake off the dust of our feet against those who are wickedly rebellious. Matt. 7. and 10. Then he also separates from them the disciples who had embraced the sounder doctrine, performing the duty of a good shepherd, whose chief care ought to be this, that the healthy flock not be infected by the contagion of the diseased. Nor for this reason should Paul be called a schismatic, although those from whom he wished his people to be separated claimed for themselves the title of the church and people of God. Indeed, it is necessary that the godly avoid the company of the impious, since they are hardened in these things, and the godly usually become partners in punishment with the impious. See Rev. 18. Third, Paul teaches daily in the school of a certain Tyrannus. What kind of school it was, and whence the place got its name, does not matter much; it is certainly credible that it was a public place suitable for preaching. Rather, let us observe the diligence of Paul, who does not allow himself to be called back from his office by the wickedness of evil men, but teaches all the more zealously the more they rage. Let all who are engaged either in the commonwealth or in the ministry of the church imitate this example. These were the practices of the ancient church, which we read was greatly occupied with the Word of God, a thing that today is neglected no less by those who wish to be called and considered the successors of the apostles.

units.la: Porro profectum studij apostolici videamus, qui multiplex fuit. Primò per totam Asiam inter Iudæos simul & Græcos verbum Dei diuulgatur. Solet id fere fieri, ut fama euangelij eorum quoq; mentes moueantur, ad quos vox ministri nondum peruenit. Nec parum momenti affert ad eam rem magnarum & celebrium ciuitatum exemplum, ad cuius imitationem finitimi quiq; facile excitantur. Deinde ipse deus Paulo cooperatur, & per miracula haud vulgaria doctrinæ ipsius testimonium fert. Nam sudaria & semicinctia ad absentes delata, morbos pellunt & dæmones fugant. Nemo tamen sudarijs & semicinctijs vim diuinam tribuat, ut ij solent, qui superstitiosum reliquiarū cultum ecclesijs obtruserunt. Diserte enim hoc loco miraculorum author Deus designatur, Paulo autem nihil præter ministerium tribuitur. Et sane ridiculum foret, Pauli sudarijs maiorem virtutem quàm Christi tunicæ tribuere, ad cuius contactum hæmorrhæusa conualuit, non quidem tunicæ operatione, sed Christi virtute, quam is ex se prodijsse ibidem testatur. Vide Marc. 5. Finis potius miraculorū inspiciendus est, quòd nimirum Pauli doctrinam commendare debuerunt, ut alibi quoq; monuimus. Simul hic tertius fructus latet, quòd agroti curantur & dæmoniaci liberantur. Euangelio enim animarum salus affertur, & diaboli regnum destruitur, eò quòd Iesus Christus benedictum illud mulieris semen est, quod serpentis caput contriuit. Hunc ergo vera fide amplexi, illi toti vniamur, ut ipsius merito ex diaboli tyrannide asserti salutem veram assequamur, cum illo olim in coelis regnaturi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now look at the progress of the apostolic work, which was manifold. First, the word of God was spread throughout all Asia, among Jews and Greeks alike. This usually happens in such a way that the report of the gospel stirs up the minds of those also to whom the minister's voice has not yet come. And the example of great and famous cities contributes no little weight to this matter, since neighbouring peoples are easily roused to imitate them. Next, God himself cooperated with Paul and bore witness to his teaching by no ordinary miracles. For handkerchiefs and aprons carried to those who were absent drove out diseases and put demons to flight. Yet no one should attribute divine power to handkerchiefs and aprons, as those do who have forced the superstitious cult of relics upon the churches. For in this place the author of the miracles is clearly named as God, while nothing is ascribed to Paul except the ministry. And indeed it would be ridiculous to ascribe greater power to Paul's handkerchiefs than to Christ's garment, by whose touch the woman with the issue of blood was made well, not by the working of the garment but by the power of Christ, which the same passage testifies went out from him. See Mark 5. Rather, the purpose of the miracles is what should be examined: namely, that they were meant to commend Paul's teaching, as we have noted elsewhere. At the same time a third fruit lies hidden here, that the sick are cured and the demoniacs set free. For salvation of souls is brought by the gospel, and the kingdom of the devil is destroyed, because Jesus Christ is that blessed seed of the woman which crushed the serpent's head. Let us therefore embrace him with true faith and cling wholly to him, so that, having been rescued by his merit from the tyranny of the devil, we may obtain true salvation, to reign with him one day in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXVII.

units.la: Tentauerunt autem quidam e circumeuntibus Iudeis Exorcistis invocare super eos, qui habebant spiritus malos, nomen domini Iesu, dicentes: Adiuramus vos per Iesum, quem Paulus praedicat. Erant autem quidam filij Sceuae Iudaei principis sacerdotum septem, qui hoc faciebant. Respondens autem spiritus malus, dixit: Iesum noui, & Paulum scio, vos autem qui estis? Et insiliens in eos homo, in quo erat daemonium malum, & dominatus eis, inualuit contra eos, ita ut nudi & vulnerati effugerent de domo illa. Hoc autem innotuit omnibus Iudaeis simul & Graecis, qui habitabat Ephesi. Et incidit timor super omnes illos, & magnificabatur nome Domini Iesu. Multique ex iis qui crediderant veniebant, confitentes & annuntiantes facta sua. Multi vero ex iis, qui curiosas artes exercuerant, comportatos libros exufflerunt coram omnibus, & supputatis pretiis illorum, reperierunt pecuniae quinquaginta millia. Ita potenter crescebat sermo domini, & confirmabatur.
units.tr: Some of the wandering Jewish exorcists tried to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying: "We adjure you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches." There were seven sons of Sceva, a Jew and chief priest, who did this. But the evil spirit answered and said: "I know Jesus, and I know Paul, but who are you?" Then the man in whom the evil spirit was leapt upon them, overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled naked and wounded from that house. This became known to all the Jews and Greeks who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. Many of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds. Many of those who had practised curious arts brought their books together and burned them publicly, and when the price of them was reckoned, they found fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed.

units.la: Audiuimus heri, ut Pauli apostolatum & euangelicae doctrinae authoritatem Deus multis signis & inauditis hucusque miraculis apud Ephesios confirmauerit. Sequitur modo, ut eandem haud vulgari seueritatis exemplo contra illos asseruerit, qui Iesu Christi nomine, per Paulum praedicato, ex satanae instinctu ad quaestum suum abuti, sicque euangelij authoritatem suspectam reddere conati sunt. Cuius historiae hic praecipuus usus est, ut Deum suorum curam habere intelligamus, nec impune laturos esse, quotquot vel illorum authoritati improbe derogare, aut Christi nomine pro suo arbitrio, aut libidine potius abuti audent. Caeterum ut uberior ex his ad nos fructus redeat, singulas historiae partes eo, quo a Luca recensentur, ordine inspiciamus.
units.tr: Yesterday we heard how God confirmed the apostleship of Paul and the authority of the gospel doctrine among the Ephesians by many signs and by miracles unheard of until then. Now follows how He asserted the same authority with an example of no ordinary severity against those who, under the name of Jesus Christ as preached by Paul, were moved by Satan's prompting to abuse it for their own gain, and so tried to make the authority of the gospel suspect. The principal use of this history here is that we understand God has a care for His own, and that all who dare either to derogate wrongfully from the authority of His apostles, or to abuse the name of Christ at their own discretion or rather for their lust, will not go unpunished. But that more abundant fruit may return to us from these things, let us look at the parts of the history one by one, in the order in which Luke recounts them.

units.la: Prima personarum descriptionem habet, & quid illi fecerint commemorat. Iudaei fuerunt, necociscuri nominis, sed Sceuae principis sacerdotum filij. Deinde Exorcistae dicuntur, unde hanc illorum professionem fuisse constat, quod exorcismis & adiurationibus spirituum quaestum facerent, cuius rei gratia hinc inde vagari solebant. Hi ergo cum apostolum daemonibus per Christi Iesu nomen potenter praecipere, & miracula nunquam antehac visa edere viderent, uberioris quaestus spe illecti, nouam exorcismi formulam fingere, & huic Iesu Christi nomen interserere ausi sunt. Praestat autem diligentius Paulo inspicere, unde hoc hominum genus apud Iudaeos primum exortum sit. Licet enim Moses Leuitarum omnium officia per multos variosque ordines distribuat, nullam tamen ab illo Exorcistarum mentionem fieri videmus. Humani ergo ingenij inuentum fuit, & proinde fallax ac diuinis legibus contrarium. Initium vero ex veteri fabula traxisse videtur, qua Solomonem diuino instinctu adiurandi artem & exorcismos aduersus daemones & morbos omnis generis, inuenisse feratur. Ita vero satan prophetarum miraculis fidem derogare voluit, quasi illa quoque Magicis incantationibus potius quam peculiari diuinae virtutis operatione ad doctrinam illorum confirmandam ederentur. Tandem stulta & impia aemulatione accensus mirifica quaedam de ineffabilis nominis Dei vi suggerere coepit, & exorcismos fingere docuit, quibus inepti homines regnum ipsius fla-bilirent, & plurimorum mentes a Dei cultu & invocatione auocarent. Extant adhuc hodie veterum impietatis vestigia in Iudaeorum fabulis, quas illi de suo illo Schem Hamphoras confinxerunt, & frequens etiam apud illos in medicina exorcismorum usus est, quos inter Christianos quoque paulatim non sine graui verae pietatis iactura obrepsisse constat. Ex horum igitur ordine fuerunt septem isti Sceuae Summi sacerdotis filij.
