Nec leue hoc summae corruptionis argumentum est, quod Pontificum filij impijs & diabolicis impostoris opera dederunt, & quaestu ex ea arte venati sunt, qua cum dei legibus palam pugnabat. Docet tamen exemplum hoc, quam nullius errorum finis sit, ut primum extra Dei verbum homines vagari incipiunt. Quod enim apud Iudaeos euenit, hoc ipsum in Papatu accidisse
units.tr: First he describes the persons and recounts what they did. They were Jews, men of no good name, yet sons of Sceva, a chief priest. Then they are called exorcists, from which it is clear that this was their profession, since they made gain by exorcisms and adjurations of spirits, and for this purpose they were accustomed to wander hither and thither. These men, then, seeing the apostles command demons powerfully in the name of Jesus Christ, and perform miracles never seen before, were enticed by the hope of greater gain and dared to devise a new formula of exorcism and to insert into it the name of Jesus Christ. It is worth looking more carefully, as Paul does, at where this class of men first arose among the Jews. For although Moses distributes the duties of all the Levites through many and various orders, we see no mention of exorcists in him. It was therefore an invention of human ingenuity, and consequently false and contrary to the divine laws. Its origin seems to have come from an old fable, according to which Solomon, by divine instinct, is said to have discovered the art of adjuration and exorcisms against demons and diseases of every kind. Thus Satan wished to take away faith from the miracles of the prophets, as if those too were wrought by magical incantations rather than by a special operation of divine power to confirm their teaching. At last, kindled by a foolish and impious rivalry, he began to suggest wonderful things about the power of the ineffable name of God, and taught men to devise exorcisms by which foolish people would establish his kingdom and draw the minds of many away from the worship and invocation of God. Traces of this ancient impiety still survive today in the Jewish fables which they have fabricated about that Schem Hamphoras of theirs, and the use of exorcisms in medicine is common among them; and it is clear that these have also crept in little by little among Christians, not without grievous loss of true piety. From this order, then, came those seven sons of Sceva, the chief priest. And this is no slight proof of extreme corruption, that the sons of the high priests gave themselves to the impious and diabolical deceptions of an impostor, and sought gain from that art which openly fought against the laws of God. Yet this example teaches how there is no limit to errors, as soon as men begin to wander outside the Word of God. For what happened among the Jews, we see the same thing has happened under the Papacy.

units.la: Exorcistae Iudaeorum
units.tr: The exorcists of the Jews.

units.la: Ioseph. Antiq. lib.8.cap.2. accidisse cernimus. Ne quis enim veterû ecclesiæ ordo deesse videretur, Exorcistæ etiam instituti sunt, qui licet fere inani titulo superbirent, inuenti tamen sunt, quorû audacia eò vsque progressa est, vt dæmones quoq; & defunctorum animas adiurarent, qua in re non postremum Antichristianæ tyrannidis præsidium situm fuit: vt interim de eo nihil dicamus, quòd exorcismis suis plané impijs Baptismum & vniuersum cultum dei improbè conspurcarunt. Quid quòd ea occasione factum est, vt nullus hominum ordo plures haberet Necromantiæ & Magiæ studiosos, quàm Monachorû & Sacrificulorum, quodq; ne summi quidem Pontifices tanti sceleris immunes fuerunt? Nota enim sunt Syluestri Secundi, Gregorij Septimi, Alexandri Sexti & plurium aliorum historiæ. Simul admonemur, quid de ijs iudicari debeat, qui sacris & conceptis verbis diuinam virtutem tribuunt, quasi his vel mali spiritus fugari vel morbi ab hominum pecorumue corporibus propulsari possint: vel qui diuinationibus, quas humani ingenij curiositas inuenit, operam nauare solent, vt per has quid futurum sit intelligant. Est hæc Iudaica superstitio, imo gentilis siue ethnica, nec temere diuinis legibus damnata. Primò enim inani verborum sono, characteribus mutis & horrore plenis ceremonijs iuuandi vis tribuitur, quod haud vulgare in primum Decalogi præceptum peccatum est. Illo enim solum deum auxiliatorem agnoscere, in illo solo spem repositam habere, & ab vno hoc opem petere iubemur. Deinde à vera dei inuocatione ad impias artes relegantur homines, quasi illis deus vel inuitus ad opem ferendam cogi possit. Adhæc non alia re diaboli regnum magis stabilitur, qui hoc vnum quærit sedulò, vt homines extra deum consilium & auxilium quærant: eò quòd hæc illi sit commodissima fallendi & seducendi ratio. Non temere ergo cum diuinis tûm Cæsareis legibus artes hasce olim proscriptas esse legimus. Quin etiam in Pontificio iure Canones ex vetustissimis Conciliis & patribus excerpti extant, qui artibus his deditos à fidelium communione arcendos esse monent. Neq; hic illorum obiectionēs audiri debent, qui ab euentu & verborum sanctitate argumenta petunt, quibus superstitionem impiâ defendant. Multos enim his medijs curatos esse; & quotidie ijs dem res alioqui factu impossibiles fieri clamitant. Deinde peccatum his nullum subesse putant, quòd exorcismi feré sacrosancti dei nominibus aut nobilissimis scripturæ sanctæ sententijs constent. Facilis autem est ad vtrunq; responsio. Scimus enim stupenda omnino opera posse satanam efficere, non tamen absque dei permissione. Nota sunt, quæ per Ægypti Magos olim fecit, vt cælitus immissò igne Iobi pecora & seruos exusserit. Sed & D. Augustinus illum mirifica quædam posse testatur, cum sese etiam in lucis angelum transfigurare queat. Sed num propterea vel ipsius suggestionibus fidem habere, vel eiusdem opera Christianos homines vti conuenit? Quin potius dei consilium respicia mus, qui ista permittit satanæ, quòd vel suorum fidem probare, vel exitium meritis efficacem illusionem immittere instituit. Stemus ergo firmi in fide, ne ab hac deficientes, toti satanæ ludibrio permittamur. Rursum de verborum sanctitate non disputamus, sed eò execrabiliorem abusum esse dicimus, quò illa sanctiora sunt. Nec enim is vel nominum diuinorum vel verborum dei vsus est, vt Magici susurris feriant, & inani sono vel morbos vel dæmones fugent: sed vt dei naturam & voluntatem nobis cognoscendam proponant. Quòd si verborum sanctitas Magos & incantatores excusâ uerit, similiter excusatione merebuntur, quotquot alijs sanctissimis saluberrimisq; dei creaturis abuti consueuerunt. Sed quàm friuola sit horum excusatio, formula, qua nostri illi Exorcistæ vsi sunt, abunde docet. Quid enim in hac reprehendas? Adiurandi verbo iuxta sanctissimorum hominum exemplum utuntur. Deinde per nomen Iesu adiurant, nëue fictitium aliquem Iesum intelligere videantur, diserte eum exprimunt, quem Paulus prædicabat. Nihilominus impietatis accusantur, quod sacris verbis improbè & abfq; fide adsuum quæstum abuterentur. Facessant ergo quicunq; Iudaicis & gentilitijs superstitionibus prætextus inanes quærunt, nec ijs fidem habeamus, qui dei & Christi eius nominibus abuti audent.
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities, book 8, chapter 2. We see it has happened. For lest the church should seem to lack any order of the ancient Church, exorcists too were instituted, who, although they took pride in an almost empty title, were nevertheless found whose audacity went so far that they adjured even demons and the souls of the dead; in this matter no small support of Antichristian tyranny lay. To say nothing for now of the fact that by their utterly impious exorcisms they wickedly defiled baptism and the whole worship of God. What of the fact that, on this occasion, no order of men had more devotees of necromancy and magic than the monks and sacrificing priests, and that not even the highest pontiffs were free of such a great crime? For the histories of Silvester II, Gregory VII, Alexander VI and of many others are well known. At the same time we are reminded what ought to be judged of those who attribute divine power to sacred words and set formulas, as if by these evil spirits could be driven out or diseases expelled from the bodies of men or beasts; or of those who are accustomed to labour at divinations which the curiosity of the human mind has devised, so that by these they may understand what is to come. This is Jewish superstition, indeed pagan or heathen, and not rashly condemned by the divine laws. For first, the power of helping is attributed to an empty sound of words, to mute characters and to ceremonies full of horror, which is no slight sin against the first commandment of the Decalogue. For we are commanded to acknowledge God alone as helper, to place hope in Him alone, and to seek help from Him alone. Next, men are led away from the true invocation of God to impious arts, as if God could be compelled, even against His will, to bring aid. Moreover, the kingdom of the devil is strengthened by nothing more than this, that he diligently seeks to make men look for counsel and help outside God; for this is his most convenient method of deceiving and seducing. Not rashly, therefore, do we read that these arts were long ago proscribed both by divine and by imperial laws. Indeed, in the Papal law there are also canons, excerpted from the most ancient councils and fathers, which warn that those given to these arts must be kept away from the fellowship of the faithful. Nor should the objections of those be heard here who seek from the outcome and the holiness of the words arguments with which to defend impious superstition. For they cry out that many have been cured by these means, and that daily the same things, otherwise impossible to do, are done by them. Then they think there is no sin in them, because the exorcisms consist almost entirely of the most sacred names of God or the most noble sentences of Holy Scripture. But the answer to both is easy. For we know that Satan can perform truly stupendous works, yet not without God's permission. Well known are the things he once did through the magicians of Egypt, when by fire sent from heaven he destroyed the flocks and servants of Job. And Saint Augustine too bears witness that he can do certain marvellous things, since he is able even to transform himself into an angel of light. But is it therefore fitting for us either to give credence to his suggestions, or for Christians to use his works? Rather let us look to the counsel of God, who permits these things to Satan, either to test the faith of His own, or to send a delusion that is effective for the destruction of the deserving. Let us therefore stand firm in the faith, lest, falling away from it, we be given over wholly to the mockery of Satan. Again, we are not disputing about the holiness of the words, but we say that the abuse is all the more execrable the holier those words are. For it is not the use of divine names or of God's words to strike with magical whispers and drive away diseases or demons by an empty sound; rather they set forth the nature and will of God for us to know. But if the holiness of the words were to excuse magicians and enchanters, they would deserve the same excuse, as many as are accustomed to abuse other most holy and most wholesome creatures of God. But how frivolous this excuse is, the formula used by those exorcists of ours sufficiently shows. For what can you find to blame in it? They use the word "adjure" in accordance with the example of the most holy men. Then they adjure by the name of Jesus, and lest they should seem to mean some fictitious Jesus, they expressly name Him whom Paul preached. Nevertheless they are accused of impiety, because they wickedly and without faith abused sacred words for their own gain. Let those, then, who seek empty pretexts for Jewish and heathen superstitions be gone, and let us not give credence to those who dare to abuse the names of God and of His Christ.

units.la: Sed euentum huius conatus videamus impiæ istorum audaciæ pulchrè respondentem. Exorcistis enim illis respondens malus spiritus, ait: Iesum noui, & Paulum scio, vos autem qui estis? Nec mora, hominem quem obsidebat aduersus illos extimulans, facit vt in ipsos ruens, immani robore omnibus istis præualeat, nudosq; & malè multatos domo exigat. Quo argumento euidentissimè cernitur, nullam sacris verbis per se vim inesse, qua vel dæmones vel alia mala arceri possint, sed effectus omnes ex dei consilio pendere: qui interdum per infideles quoq; miracula edit, si quando borum
units.tr: But let us look at the outcome of this attempt, which answers their impious boldness splendidly. The evil spirit replied to those exorcists: "Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?" Without delay, the man he possessed turned on them, stirred them up against themselves, and with great force overpowered all of them, driving them out of the house naked and badly mauled. This event shows most clearly that there is no power in sacred words by themselves to ward off demons or other evils; all effects depend on God's counsel, who sometimes works miracles even through unbelievers when it pleases him.

units.la: Cod. lib. 9. Tit. 18. 26. quæst. 5. & 7. Aug. de doct. Christ. lib. 2. Cap. 22. De Trin. lib. 4. Cap. 11. Euentus Exorcistarum funesti operam regni & gloriæ suæ propagationi seruire videt. Docet autem exemplum hoc, quid omnes illi expectent, qui Christi nomine & institutis ad suum quæstum abuti solent. Est hoc nimis vulgare hodie. Quid enim aliud Papa facit, quando Christi nomine palliatus in ecclesia sibi primatum vendicat? Quid aliud Missatores sacrificuli faciunt, quando peruerso Cœnæ ritu & ordine Elicium nobis Christum fingunt, & Cœnæ verba in exorcismis commutant, cuius virtute panis & vinum in Christi corpus & sanguinem transubstantientur? Quid de Clauibus dicam, quarum prætextu in hominum conscientias penetrarunt, satisfactiones & expiationes peccatorum instituerunt, nihil aut parum ab illis differentes, quibus olim ethnicos vsos fuisse legimus? Omitto infinita alia, quorum pœnas etsi non subito Deus exigat, quemadmodum Sceuæ filijs euenisse cernimus, non dormitat tamen (ut Petrus ait) iudicium domini, quo iam olim illis dignæ pœnæ constitutæ sunt. 2. Pet. 2. Admonemur præterea hoc loco, quanta sit Christi Iesu saluatoris nostri potentia, cum is diabolo quoque, quantumuis inuito & renitente, ad sui regni propagationem uti queat. Quis enim huic volentem Iesu Christo eiusque seruo Paulo testimonium tulisse, suis vero organis & mancipiis nocuisse credat? Cogitur tamen utrunque facere, quia sic domino visum est, ad cuius confessum & nutum diabolos etiam contremiscere apostolus scribit. Iacob. 2. Quid ergo satanæ insidias aut vires timemus, cuius opera Christi iam potenter pro suo arbitrio uti cernimus? Iam olim regno male vsurpato princeps huius mundi esse, nec difficile est illis eum vincere, qui Christo per fidem insiti fuerint.
units.tr: Cod. lib. 9. Tit. 18. 26. quæst. 5. & 7. Aug. de doct. Christ. lib. 2. Cap. 22. De Trin. lib. 4. Cap. 11. The disastrous outcome for the exorcists shows that it serves the work of God's kingdom and the spreading of his glory. This example also teaches what all those can expect who are accustomed to abuse the name and institutions of Christ for their own gain, and this is far too common today. For what else does the Pope do when, cloaked in the name of Christ, he claims primacy for himself in the Church? What else do the mass-mongering little priests do when, by a perverted rite and order of the Supper, they fashion a Christ for us out of nothing and change the words of the Supper into exorcisms, by whose power bread and wine are supposedly transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ? What shall I say of the Keys, under whose pretext they have penetrated men's consciences, instituted satisfactions and expiations for sins, differing little or not at all from those by which we read the heathens once acted? I pass over countless other examples. Although God does not immediately exact their punishments, as we see happened to the sons of Sceva, nevertheless, as Peter says, the judgment of the Lord does not sleep, by which worthy punishments were long ago appointed for them. 2 Pet. 2. Moreover, we are reminded here how great is the power of Christ Jesus our Saviour, since he can use even the devil, however unwilling and resisting, to extend his kingdom. For who would believe that the devil, who bore witness to Jesus Christ and his servant Paul against his will, yet harmed his own instruments and slaves? Yet he is compelled to do both, because it seemed good to the Lord, before whose assembly and nod the apostle writes that even the devils tremble. James 2. Why then do we fear the snares or strength of Satan, whose works we see Christ already using powerfully at his own will? Long ago the prince of this world, having wrongly seized a kingdom, was to be overcome, and it is not difficult for those to conquer him who have been grafted into Christ by faith.

units.la: Transeamus autem ad vltimam huius loci partem, quæ multiplicem historiæ fructum continet. Primo enim omnibus Ephesijs factum illud innotuit, qui omnes insolito Dei timore perculsi sunt, quem filij & nominis sui abusum tam seuere vltum fuisse viderunt. Est hic legitimus iudiciorum Dei vsus, vt religionis sensum animis nostris incutiat. Sed o miseros nos, qui toti obsurduisse videmur, possumus, quādo nullis exemplis mouemur, quæ quotidie in blasphemos verbi & nominis sui contemptores Deus edit. Deinde multi ex ijs, qui crediderant, sponte veniunt & facta sua publice confitentur. Est hoc euidens mortificatæ carnis argumentum, quæ alioqui sui honoris & exaltationis sui diosissima, agre adduci potest, vt se errasse fateatur. Sed omnem carnis affectum in credentibus vincit veritatis & gloriæ Dei studium. Patet autem hoc loco, qualem a nobis peccatorum confessionem scripturæ exigant. Publicam nimirum, quæ gloriæ Dei propaganda & multorum emendationi seruiat. Nimis ergo crassa illorum ignorantia est, qui exemplo hoc auricularem confessionem stabiliri putant, cui nihil cum ea simile est, quam hic Lucas describit. Sponte enim Ephesij ipsi veniunt & vt teres errores fatentur, Deo nimirum gratias agentes, qui ipsos liberare dignatus erat. At Papa inuitos cogit occulta quoque fateri, quæ omnes hucusque latuerunt. Illi semel tantum confessi legantur, cum Papa confessionem multoties iterare iubeat. Illi publice fatentur, & quidem coram omnibus. At Papa in sacrificuli foliis aurę peccata demurmurare docet. Illi confitendo non aliud quam Dei gloriam quærunt. Papa autem a sacrificulo peccatorum remissionem & satisfactionem petere præcipit. Quid multis? quo diligentius huius facti circumstantias examinauerunt, eo luculentius pateat, illius exemplo auricularem confessionem euerti magis quam stabiliri. Sed ad Ephesios redeamus, quorum multi curiosis artibus hucusque dediti fuerant, nunc autem propiori numinis afflatu tacti, libros publice congestos exurunt. Vbi non Magicos modo libros intelligimus, sed omnes alios quoque, quotquot inutilibus & offendiculi plenis studijs potius quam pietati seruiunt: quales sunt Astrologici, Geomantici, fatidici, amatorij, & si qui alij sunt huius generis. Indicatur vero librorum precium, quod si ad Germanicæ monetæ rationem supputes, ad summam florenorum sex millium, sexcentorum & sexaginta sex ascendet. Ita vero sanctissimi homines tum sibi ipsis tum alijs in posterum peccandi occasionem eripere voluerunt. Est hoc proprium eorum, qui vere pœnitent, quod cum peccatis illorum quoque instrumenta odisse solent, nec illos piget quantumuis pretiosissimarum rerum iacturam facere, quas sibi aliquando offendiculo fuisse norunt. Quare nec peccatorum atrocitatem intelligere, nec vere pœnitere putandi sunt, quotquot scelerum instrumenta sedulo adhuc seruare & retinere solent, qualia fere nostro sæculo habentur imagines, superstitiosi templorum ornatus, libri superstitionum magistri, amatoria scripta, lasciuæ vestes, & alia huius generis infinita. Postremo Dei verbum potenter creuisse & in discipulorum mentibus confirmatum fuisse, Lucas scribit: quæ priora studij effectus fuit. Solet enim mirum in modum fructificare Dei verbum, si remore quibusdam illud illud impediri potest, è medio tollantur. Imitemur ergo celeberrima ecclesiæ exemplum, vt nouis indies fidei professibus austi tandem viri perfecti reddamur in Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now pass to the last part of this passage, which contains the manifold fruit of the history. First, that deed became known to all the Ephesians, who were all struck with an unaccustomed fear of God, seeing how severely he had avenged the abuse of his own name. This is the lawful way in which God's judgments work, to strike a sense of religion into our minds. But woe to us, who seem wholly deafened, since we are moved by no examples, which God displays daily against blasphemers and despisers of his Word and name. Next, many of those who had believed came of their own accord and publicly confessed their deeds. This is clear evidence of a mortified flesh, which otherwise, most prone to its own honour and exaltation, can hardly be brought to admit that it has erred. But the zeal for truth and the glory of God overcomes every affection of the flesh in believers. Moreover, what kind of confession of sins the Scriptures demand from us is plain from this passage: namely a public one, which serves to spread the glory of God and the amendment of many. Therefore the gross ignorance of those is great who think that auricular confession is established by this example, to which nothing is so unlike as what Luke describes here. For the Ephesians came of their own accord and confessed their errors, which were really their own, giving thanks to God, who had deigned to free them. But the Pope forces unwilling people to confess even secret things, which have lain hidden from everyone until now. Those people are read to have confessed only once, whereas the Pope orders confession to be repeated many times. They confessed publicly, and indeed before everyone; but the Pope teaches people to mutter their sins in the ear of a little priest. They confessed for no other purpose than the glory of God; but the Pope commands that forgiveness of sins and satisfaction be sought from the little priest. What more need be said? The more carefully we examine the circumstances of this deed, the more clearly it appears that by this example auricular confession is overthrown rather than established. But let us return to the Ephesians, many of whom had until then been devoted to curious arts, but now, touched by a closer breath of the divine power, publicly burned the books they had gathered together. Here we understand not only magical books but all others as well, however many serve useless and stumbling-block-filled studies rather than piety: such as those of astrology, geomancy, fortune-telling, love-charms, and whatever others there are of this kind. The value of the books is stated, which, if you reckon it by the currency of Germany, amounts to a sum of six thousand six hundred and sixty-six florins. Thus those most holy men wished to take away from themselves and others the occasion of sinning in future. It is characteristic of those who truly repent that, together with their sins, they are accustomed to hate the instruments of them as well, nor do they grieve to suffer the loss of however precious things they know once were a stumbling-block to them. Therefore those who still carefully keep and retain the instruments of their wickedness, of which kind nearly every age has such things as images, superstitious temple ornaments, books that teach superstitions, amatory writings, wanton garments, and countless others of this kind, are not to be thought either to understand the atrocity of their sins or to repent truly. Lastly, Luke writes that the Word of God grew mightily and was strengthened in the minds of the disciples: which was the first result of their zeal. For the Word of God is wont to bear fruit wonderfully when certain hindrances are removed from the midst. Let us therefore imitate the most famous example of the Church, so that, enriched daily with new professions of faith, we may at last be made perfect men in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 128.

units.la: His autem expletis, proposuit Paulus in spiritu, transita Macedonia & Achaia ire Hierosolymam, dicens: Postquam fuero ibi, oportet me & Romam videre. Missis autem in Macedoniam duobus qui ministrabant sibi, videlicet Timotheo & Erasto, ipse remansit ad tempus in Asia. Ortus est autem illo tempore tumultus non exiguus de illa via. Nam quidam nomine Demetrius, faber argentarius, qui faciebat delubra argentea Dianæ, præstabat artificibus non exiguum quæstum. Quibus conuocatis, & his qui similium rerum erant opifices, dixit: Viri, scitis quod ex hoc opificio quæstus nobis est, & videtis & auditis, quod non solum Ephesi, sed pene per totam Asiam Paulus hic persuasit, & auertit multam turbam, dicens, quod non sint Dii qui manibus fiant. Non solum autem hæc pars nobis in periculum venit, ne reprobetur: verum etiam ne magnæ Deæ Dianæ templum pro nihilo habeatur, futurumque sit, vt etiam destruatur maiestas eius, quam tota Asia & orbis colit.
units.tr: Having finished these things, Paul resolved in the Spirit, after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, to go to Jerusalem, saying: "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." Then, having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself remained for a time in Asia. But at that time no small tumult arose concerning the Way. For a certain man named Demetrius, a silversmith who made silver shrines of Diana, provided no small profit to the craftsmen. He called them together, along with the workmen in similar trades, and said: "Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this trade, and you see and hear that not only at Ephesus but almost throughout all Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great crowd, saying that gods are not those made with hands. Not only is this part of our business in danger of being discredited, but also the temple of the great goddess Diana may be regarded as nothing, and her majesty, which all Asia and the world worships, may be brought to destruction."

units.la: Quoniam non vnius modo gentis doctorem se à domino constitutum esse Paulus nouerat, non vni modo genti, sed passim omnibus per euangelij prædicationem inseruire voluit; imo sibi præcipue omnium ecclesiarum curam incumbere putauit, quemadmodum in posteriori ad Corinthios epistola testatur. Quæ causa est, quod non contentus ecclesias hinc inde collegisse, colleētas iam & bene constitutas inuisit, ne quid vel hominum securitate, vel diaboli improbitate & astutia rursum collabatur. Exempla huius studij non pauca hucusque vidimus, quibus hoc etiam adnumerari debet, quod huius loci initio Lucas commemorat, cui nouam de seditione aduersus Paulum excitata historiam subijcit, qua ad tempus consilium illud de inuisendis ecclesijs impeditum fuit.
units.tr: Since Paul knew that he had been appointed by the Lord as teacher not of one nation only, he wished to serve not just one people but all people everywhere through the preaching of the gospel. Indeed, he thought that the care of all the churches lay especially upon himself, as he testifies in his later letter to the Corinthians. For this reason, not content with having gathered churches here and there, he visited them once they were gathered and well established, so that nothing might again collapse either through people's carelessness or through the wickedness and cunning of the devil. We have seen not a few examples of this concern so far, and to these must be added what Luke records at the beginning of this passage, followed by a new story of the uprising stirred up against Paul, by which for a time that plan of visiting the churches was hindered.

units.la: Porrò consilij author indicatur spiritus, cuius auspicijs & ductu Paulum omnia sua fecisse & instituisse, iam sæpe diximus. Statuit autem in Macedonia & Achaiam redire, nimirum vt ecclesias Philippensium, Thessalonicensium & Corinthiorum inuiseret ac confirmaret, tum quoque vt in illis colleētam eleemosynam ad egenos Syriæ fratres deferret, sicuti ex illius ad Corinth. epistolis nō obscurè colligi potest. Qua profeētione perfeēta, Romam concedere voluit, vt illius quoque loci fidelibus aliquod donum spirituale conferret, mutuamque ex illorum fide consolationem caperet. Rom. 1. Ne quid tamen inconsultò agere videretur, ex familiaribus suis Timotheum & Erastum premisit, ipse non multò post secuturus, nisi exortus Ephesi tumultus per aliquot dies obstitisset. Iterum autem hoc exemplo patet, quanta in conseruandis ecclesijs cura opus sit, quando exercitatissimus apostolus, cui tot agenda restabant, iam ante constitutas toties inuisit & confirmat. Produnt ergo turpissimam oscitantiā suam cum immani & impia arrogantia, quicunque zelum, quem nostro seculo ea in re ministri adhibent, inutilem aut superuacaneum esse putant. Elucet præterea in Paulo verę fidei ingenium, quod hæc nimirum nequaquam ineris aut otiosa est, sed industrios in sua vocatione homines reddit. Quia enim gloriæ Dei zelo & proximi amore flagrat, fieri nequit vt torpida & segnis ociętur: imo nullis neque laboribus neque periculis sese fatigari sinit: quod vnò Pauli exemplo manifestius est, quam vt multis probari debeat. Transferant hoc potius ad se singand illud imitati, saltem se fidem habere testentur. Interim circumspeētam quoque esse fidem patet, quando Paulus, qui spiritu duce in omnibus vtebatur, præmittit tamē quos sibi fidos esse nouerat. Vt enim qui vere fideles sunt, vbi Dei expressum mandatum habent, illud absque omni tergiuersatione sequuntur, licet multa secus moneat carnis ratio: ita in reliquis, quæ nullo certo Dei præcepto continentur, prudenter & circumspeētè agunt omnia, ne sua temeritate Dei gloriam obscurent & infirmis aliquam offendiculi occasionem præbeant. Et hæc quidem tutissima est in rebus agendis regula, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, the author of the plan is shown to be the Spirit, under whose guidance and direction, as we have often said, Paul did and arranged all his affairs. He decided to return to Macedonia and Achaia, namely to visit and strengthen the churches of the Philippians, the Thessalonians and the Corinthians, and also to deliver in those places the alms collected for the needy brothers in Syria, as can be clearly gathered from his letters to the Corinthians. Once that journey was completed, he wished to go on to Rome, so that he might also impart some spiritual gift to the faithful of that place and receive mutual consolation from their faith (Rom. 1.). Yet so that he might not seem to act without deliberation, he sent ahead Timothy and Erastus, his close companions, while he himself was to follow not long after, had the tumult at Ephesus not held him back for some days. Again, this example makes clear how much care is needed in preserving the churches, when the most experienced apostle, who had so much still to do, visits and strengthens churches already founded so many times. Therefore, all those who think the zeal which ministers in our age apply in this matter useless or superfluous reveal their own shameful sloth together with a monstrous and impious arrogance. Moreover, the character of true faith shines forth in Paul, for it is by no means idle or inactive, but makes people diligent in their calling. Since he burned with zeal for the glory of God and love for his neighbour, it cannot be that such a man should lie idle and sluggish; indeed, he does not allow himself to be worn out by any labours or dangers, which is clearer from Paul's example alone than it needs to be proved by many arguments. Let them rather transfer this to themselves, imitating it, or at least let them testify that they have faith. Meanwhile, it is also plain that faith is circumspect, since Paul, who in all things was led by the Spirit, nevertheless sent ahead those whom he knew to be trustworthy. For those who are truly faithful, when they have God's express command, follow it without any evasion, even though human reason in the flesh advises otherwise; so in other matters, which are not contained under any certain precept of God, they act prudently and cautiously in everything, lest by their rashness they obscure God's glory and give the weak an occasion of stumbling. And indeed this is the safest rule in acting, etc.

units.la: Ceterum quamuis Paulus vix vspiam alibi maiori animorum promptitudine exceptus fuerit, quàm apud Ephesios, illicq; toto biennio cum fructu docuerit, vt nō ex plebe modò multi crederent, verumetiam non paucos Asiæ principum amicos haberet, vt infra patebit, hoc ipsum tamen experi-tur tandem, quod alibi sæpe iam expertum fuisse audiuimus, turbas nimirum & publicam seditio-nem, qua ita exagitatus fuit, vt quod Ephesi subijt periculum, inter grauissima, quæ illi vnquā ac-ciderunt, ipse numeret. Nam se illic cum bestijs pugnauisse, deq; vita iam desperauisse scribit. 1.Cor. 15. 2.Cor.1.&c. Describit autem historiam hanc omnē mira diligentia Lucas, eò quòd in ea hostium veritatis ingenium & mores, artes & arma ceu in speculo conspicienda proponuntur: simulq; pates vt Deus suos simul & veritatis causam fidelissimè asserere soleat. In præsenti verò primò quidem summam rei proponit, deinde seditionis authores commemorat vnà cum Demetrij, qui Tragœdia totius causa & actor fuit, oratione, quæ suorum animos aduersus Paulum extimulauit.
units.tr: Yet although Paul was received with greater readiness of minds almost nowhere else than among the Ephesians, and although he taught there for two years with fruit, so that not only many of the common people believed, but he also had not a few friends among the leaders of Asia (as will appear below), nevertheless at last he experienced this very thing which we have heard he had often experienced elsewhere: namely, disturbances and public sedition, by which he was so harassed that he counts what he suffered at Ephesus among the most grievous things that ever befell him. For he writes that he fought there with beasts and had despaired of life (1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 1, etc.). Luke describes this whole story with wonderful care, because in it the character and customs, the arts and weapons of the enemies of the truth are set forth to be seen as in a mirror, and at the same time it shows how God is accustomed to defend faithfully both his own people and the cause of the truth. Here, then, he first sets out the sum of the matter, and then he records the authors of the sedition, together with the speech of Demetrius, who was the principal agent and instigator of the whole tragedy, a speech which stirred up the minds of his men against Paul.

units.la: Ortus est (inquit) illo tempore tumultus non exiguus de illa via. Viam verò vocat Christianam sectam siue religionem, quam aduersarij oppressam voluerunt. Est autem cumprimis obseruanda temporis notatio, quæ tumultum & seditionem tunc excitatam fuisse docet, quando Paulus quasi optimè compositis Ephesiorum rebus, profectionem ad Macedones & Corinthios instituerat, iamq; duos ex suis familiaribus præmiserat, qui res ipsi necessarias præparårent. Quo exemplo admonemur, semper quidem nobis vigilandum, maximè tamen, quando res in portu & extra omne periculum constituta esse videtur. Nunquam enim quiescit satan, & expulsus redire satagit, quemadmodū Christus monet. Matth.12. Nec exempla desunt illorum, qui subita Cruce grauissime offensi, à fide exciderunt. Consoletur tamen nos, quòd vt vt improbus ille hostis nostr furat & tumultuetur, nihil tamen vel in Christum vel in illos iuris habet, qui Christo per fidem sunt insiti. Iohan.14. Imò iam olim deiectus, tanquam è pelui fulgurat, & inania præliorum simulachra ciet, quibus rudes & infirmos animos exterreat.
units.tr: "A no small tumult arose at that time," he says, "concerning the Way." By "the Way" he means the Christian sect or religion, which its opponents wished to crush. We must especially note the indication of time, which shows that the tumult and sedition were stirred up at the moment when Paul, as if the affairs of the Ephesians were very well settled, had decided to set out for the Macedonians and Corinthians, and had already sent ahead two of his companions to prepare what was necessary for him. From this example we are warned that we must always be watchful, and most of all when affairs seem to be placed in harbour and beyond all danger. For Satan never rests, and when driven out he strives to return, as Christ warns (Matt. 12.). Nor are there lacking examples of those who, struck hard by sudden adversity, fell away from the faith. Yet this comforts us, that however much that wicked enemy of ours rages and stirs up tumult, he has no right either over Christ or over those who are engrafted into Christ through faith (John 14.). Indeed, cast down long ago, he flashes like lightning from a pit, and raises empty images of battles, by which he may terrify rude and weak minds.

units.la: Sed tumultus authorum & ministros videamus. Princeps horum Demetrius fuit argentarius, homo dives, qui delubra siue ædiculas capsulasue argenteas, & si quæ alia erant superstitionis instrumenta, in Dianæ honorem faciebat, simulq; omnibus sui ordinis opificibus quæstum ingentem exhibebat. Colebatur enim apud Ephesios (vt supra quoque monuimus) Diana, sub ποληµάδς siue Multimammiæ titulo, quam gentili superstitione seductì omnium animantium nutricem esse credebant. Templum huius toto terrarum orbe celeberrimum & sumptuosissimum erat, ad quod peregrinationes ex totius Asiæ & finitimarum, imò etiam remotissimarum regionum locis instituebantur. Quæ causa erat, vt ex peregrinis ingentem quæstum quotidie haberent, quicunque superstitionis organa fabricabant. Non poterant ergo Pauli doctrinam ferre, quæ vnà cum superstitione omnè quo-que spem lucri euertebat. Conuocati ergo Demetrio authore, Paulum, quem rationibus nullis absq; conuincì posse nouerant, seditione populari opprimere conantur. HIC ergo luce clarius patet, euan-gelio & huius ministris seditionum causas minimè adscribi debere. Nam vt fides, quæ ab his prædicatur, nos Deo vnitas hæc ipsa charitatem & concordiam quàm maximè commendat. Et hic qui-dem diserte Demetrius seditionis author producitur, non Paulus, qui per biennium hucusq; ita docuit, vt nullum prorsus ediderit seditiosi hominis specimen. Et huius generis exempla non pauca tum in hoc libro, tum alijs historijs extant. Unde discimus, non temere illis credendum esse, qui euan-gelium & huius prædicōnes seditionis accusant, sed altius rei veritatem inuestigemus, & patebit ferè bos ipsos seditionum primos authores esse, qui crimen istud in alios deriuare volunt. Et talesferè sunt, quotquot Demetrij & suorum complicū instar, ex rebus à deo prohibitis vel viuunt, vel etiam quæstum siue voluptatem venantur. Primas inter hos tenet Romanus Pontifex cum suis Creatu-ris, Cardinalibus nimirum, Episcopis, Monachis, sacrificulis. Ad hunc enim maxima quæstus & di-gnitatis pars ex superstitione redit. Idem suis istis creaturis quæstum quoq; haud vulgarem præstat, dum suo charactere insignitis vendendi & emendi, id est, negotiandi & sacra cauponandi poteflate facit. At omnibus istis intolerabilis videtur euangelij Veritas, quæ grauissimi flagelli instar Christi manu & spiritu vibrata mercaturam omnem templo Dei eijcit, & numulariorum mensas euer-tit. Proximi ab his sunt principes & tota illa nobilium huius seculi cohors. Nam etiam his cum primis quæstuosa est superstitio, eò quòd huius prætextu liberorum multitudini prospicere, & suam dignitatem tueri possunt,dum illos sua authoritate in Episcopatus, Abbatias & Cardinalatus in- trudunt,qui fortassis vel ad mercaturam vel etiam ad manuarium laborem (quod illis indignis- mum facinus videtur) relegandi erant: Vtrunq; vero genus sordidiores ex vulgo iuuant,qui vel ex Monachis & sacrificulis, vel ex nobilibus victum sibi parant. Hi enim seruili ingenio prediti fa- mũq; metu perculsi,à Demetrijs istis sibi quiduis persuaderi sinunt. Accedunt omnibus istis, qui vel morum licentiam effræni libidine sectantur, vel alioqui ex sceleribus quæstum & voluptates quæ- runt: quales fere vsurarij sunt,scortatores,ebriosi, mercenarij milites, & si qui alij sunt huius fari- na. Isti enim opera sua,quia mala sunt, argui non volunt, & proinde euangelij lucem, qua illa ar- guuntur,quàm ocyssime extinctam volunt. Hi (inquam) seditionum contra euangelium authores sunt,quod nemo negabit,quisquis nostri seculi mores paulò diligentius inspexerit,&c.
units.tr: But let us look at the authors and ministers of this tumult. The chief of them was Demetrius the silversmith, a rich man, who made silver shrines or small temples or caskets, and whatever other instruments of superstition there were, in honour of Diana, and at the same time he provided great profit for all the craftsmen of his guild. For Diana was worshipped among the Ephesians (as we also noted above) under the title of Polymammia or "many-breasted," whom people seduced by pagan superstition believed to be the nurse of all living things. Her temple was the most famous and most splendid in the whole world, and to it pilgrimages were made from all parts of Asia and the neighbouring, indeed even the most remote, regions. This was the reason why those who fabricated the instruments of superstition made a huge profit every day from the pilgrims. They therefore could not bear Paul's teaching, which together with superstition overturned all hope of gain. Called together at the instigation of Demetrius, they tried to crush Paul, whom they knew could not be refuted by any arguments, by a popular uprising. Here, then, it is clearer than light that the causes of sedition must in no way be ascribed to the gospel and its ministers. For the faith which they preach unites us to God, and this very unity commends charity and concord above all things. And here indeed Demetrius is openly produced as the author of the sedition, not Paul, who for two years until now had taught in such a way that he had shown no example at all of a seditious man. Examples of this kind are not few, both in this book and in other histories. From this we learn that we should not rashly believe those who accuse the gospel and its preaching of sedition, but investigate the truth of the matter more deeply, and it will appear that almost always they themselves are the first authors of sedition, who want to shift this charge onto others. And almost all who are like Demetrius and his accomplices either live from things forbidden by God, or seek gain or pleasure from them. Foremost among these stands the Roman Pontiff with his creatures, namely the Cardinals, Bishops, Monks and little priests. For to him the greatest part of profit and dignity comes from superstition. The same man also provides no small profit to these creatures of his, while by giving to those marked with his character the power of selling and buying, that is, of trading and peddling sacred things. But to all these the truth of the gospel seems intolerable, which, brandished like a most severe whip by the hand and Spirit of Christ, drives out all the merchandise from God's temple and overturns the tables of the money-changers. Next after these are the princes and that whole band of nobles of this age. For superstition is especially profitable to them too, since under its pretext they can provide for a multitude of children and maintain their dignity, while they thrust them by their authority into bishoprics, abbeys and cardinalates, who perhaps ought to have been sent into trade or even manual labour (which seems to them an unworthy deed). Both kinds of superstition help the more sordid of the common people, who make their living either from monks and little priests or from the nobles. For these, endowed with a servile disposition and struck with fear of ruin, let themselves be persuaded of whatever such Demetriuses wish. To all these are added those who either pursue licence of morals with unbridled lust, or otherwise seek gain and pleasures from crimes: such as usurers, whoremongers, drunkards, mercenary soldiers, and whoever else is of this sort. For they do not want their works, because they are evil, to be reproved, and therefore they want the light of the gospel, by which those works are reproved, extinguished as quickly as possible. These (I say) are the authors of sedition against the gospel, as no one will deny who examines the manners of our age a little more carefully, etc.

units.la: Est autem memorabilis maximè Demetrij oratio,cuius propositio siue status est, non ferendum esse Paulum,qui doctrina sua à veteri religione abducat homines. Firmatur illa tribus rationibus, quarum maxima solet esse in genere deliberatiuo authoritas. Prima ab vtili est,cuius potissimam rationem apud homines sordidos & famelicos esse nouerat. Scitis (inquit) quòd ex hoc opificio quæ- stus nobis est. Quid ergo restabit,quàm vt fame pereatis,si Pauli doctrina opificium hoc vestrum tueri patiamini? Secunda à necessario sumitur. Videtis & auditis,quòd non solum Ephesi,sed pe- nè per totam Asiam Paulus hic persuasit, &c. Ergo diutius res hæc dissimulari aut ferri non po- test,sed necesse est in tempore remedium afferre. Tertium ab honesto petit,dicens: Non solum hæc pars nobis in periculum venit,ne reprobetur: verumetiam ne magnæ Dea Dianæ templum pro ni- hilo habeatur,futurumq;sit vt etiam destruatur maiestas eius,quam tota Asia & orbis colit. Quasi dicat, Quantam nobis ô viri infamiam contrahemus, si intra nostros parietes eam religionem in- tercidere patiamur, cuius tanta est tot iam seculis in toto terrarum orbe authoritas? Elucent au- tem in oratione hac impiorum artes & mores, qui cum solius priuati commodi cupiditate extimu- lentur, reipub. tamen & religionis defensores haberi volunt. Talem Caiaphan describit spiritus sanctus,Ioan.11. Tales hodie Monachorum adeoq; omnium illorum sermones sunt,qui Papatum saluum & incolumem vellent, inter quos vix vnum tam ingenuum reperias, quàm Demetrius hic fuit, qui priuati commodi rationem apud se potissimam esse non dissimulat. Discamus nos illorum clamores suspectos habere,& penitius,quò tendant inspicere. Patet præterea hoc loco,quibus argu- mentis fere superstitionem impij tueantur. Nimirum stolidæ multitudinis consensu,regum & prin- cipum authoritate,externæ religionis splendore,temporis diuturnitate, in primis autè priuati com- modi prætextu. Vulgaria hæc sunt hodie,si aduersariorum nostrorum sermones excutias. Sed turpe est, Christianos homines ethnicorum argumentis in religionis causa vti, quam ex scripturis solis diiudicare oportebat. Postremò ex Demetrij ore,quanta euangelij vis & potentia sit,colligi potest. Fatetur enim Pauli doctrina intra biennium celeberrimum illud Dianæ templum in periculum ad- ductum esse, in quo extruendo tota Asia (vt nuper diximus) circiter CCXX. laborauerat, & cui Persico bello pepercerant Barbari, qui omnibus alijs templis flammas intulerant. Idem omnium fere animos à Dianæ cultu auersos fuisse queritur. Atqui hæc nulla hominum vi & authoritate perfici potuisse constat. Simul verò docemur, tum demum ex euangelio verè profecisse homines, quando totus animus à superstitione & idololatria abalienantur. Quoad enim circa hanc suspensi hæ- rent, veritatis lucem animis illorum nondum irradiauisse certum est. Ad hanc ergo regulam nosmet ipsos examinemus, omni superstitione abiectâ totos nos fide ardenti conuertamus ad Christum Ie- sum dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor,gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Demetrius's speech is especially worth noting. Its proposition, or thesis, is that Paul must not be tolerated, since by his teaching he draws people away from the old religion. The case rests on three arguments, of which the strongest in deliberative oratory is usually authority. The first is drawn from advantage, which he knew was the most powerful argument among base and hungry men. "You know," he says, "that our livelihood comes from this trade. What then will remain for us but to starve, if you allow Paul's teaching to ruin this trade of yours?" The second is drawn from necessity. "You see and hear that this Paul has persuaded people not only at Ephesus but almost through all of Asia. Therefore this matter cannot be overlooked or tolerated any longer, but a remedy must be applied in time." The third appeals to honour. "Not only is this part of ours in danger of being discredited, but also the temple of the great goddess Diana may be counted as nothing, and her majesty, which all Asia and the world worships, may be destroyed." As if he were saying: "How much infamy, men, shall we incur if we allow that religion to be cut off within our walls, whose authority has held such sway over the whole world for so many centuries?" Moreover, the tricks and character of the ungodly stand out clearly in this speech. Though driven only by greed for private gain, they nevertheless want to be considered defenders of the commonwealth and of religion. The Holy Spirit describes Caiaphas in this way, John 11. Such are the words today of the monks, and of all those who wish the Papacy to remain safe and sound, among whom you will scarcely find one as frank as this Demetrius, who does not hide that private gain is his chief consideration. Let us learn to regard their outcries with suspicion, and to examine more closely where they tend. It is also clear from this passage what arguments the ungodly usually use to defend superstition: the agreement of a foolish multitude, the authority of kings and princes, the splendour of an outward religion, the long duration of time, and above all the pretext of private gain. These commonplaces are used today too, if you examine the arguments of our opponents. But it is shameful for Christians to use the arguments of the heathen in a matter of religion, which ought to be decided from Scripture alone. Finally, from Demetrius's own mouth one can gather how great the power and strength of the gospel is. For he admits that within two years Paul's teaching had brought into danger that most famous temple of Diana, on whose building all Asia had laboured for about 220 years (as we said recently), and which the barbarians had spared in the Persian war, though they had set fire to all the other temples. He complains that Paul had turned almost everyone's minds away from the worship of Diana. Yet it is established that such a thing could not have been accomplished by any power or authority of men. At the same time we are taught that people have truly profited from the gospel only when their whole mind is turned away from superstition and idolatry. For as long as they cling to these, it is certain that the light of truth has not yet shone into their minds. Let us therefore examine ourselves by this rule: with all superstition cast aside, let us turn ourselves wholly, with burning faith, to Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXIX.

units.la: His auditis repleti sunt ira, & exclamauerunt dicentes: Magna Diana Ephesiorum. Et impleta est ciuitas tota confusione. Et impetum fecerunt vno animo in theatrum, correpto Gaío & Aristarcho Mace- donibus, comitibus Pauli. Paulo autem volente intrare ad populum, non permiserunt discipuli. Quidam autem & ex Asiæ primoribus qui erant amici eius, miserunt ad eum, rogantes ne se daret in theatrum. Alij quidē igitur aliud clamabant. Erat enim concio confusa, & plerique nescirent, qua ex causa conuenissent. De turba autem protraxerunt Alexandrum, propellentibus eum Iudæis. Alexander autem manu silentio postulato, volebat rationem reddere populo. Quem vt cognoue-runt Iudæum esse, vox orta est vna omnium fermè ad duas horas clamantium: Magna Diana Ephesiorum.
units.tr: When they heard this, they were filled with anger and cried out, saying: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians." And the whole city was filled with confusion. They rushed with one accord into the theatre, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians, companions of Paul. When Paul wished to go in among the people, the disciples would not allow it. Some of the chief men of Asia, who were his friends, also sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theatre. Some therefore cried one thing and some another, for the assembly was confused, and most did not know why they had come together. Then they drew Alexander out of the crowd, the Jews pushing him forward. Alexander motioned with his hand for silence, wishing to make a defence to the people. But when they realised he was a Jew, one voice arose from almost all of them, shouting for about two hours: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians."

units.la: DIuus Lucas hoc libro ex spiritus sancti suggestione non modò persecutiones legitimè a magistratibus contra apostolos institutas, verumetiam insanas furentis vulgi seditiones, quibus exagitati fuerunt, commemorat: inter quas facilè primum locum meretur præsens hæc, quæ apud Ephesios Demetrio authore aduersus Paulum excitata fuit. Est vero tum huius, tum omnium aliarum, duplexferè vsus. Primò ministrorum institutioni seruiunt, ne vulgi seditiosi motibus, tam quam re noua & insolita offendantur, nec iflarum metu officium suum intermittant. Quin potius cogitent, ecclesiam in mundo hoc nauiculæ instar esse, quæ ventis & vndis agitatur, & cuius gubernator Christus interdum dormire videtur, quemadmodum euangelica historia adumbrat. Marc. 4. cap. Meminerint præterea vix fieri posse, vt seditiones omninò caueantur, quando tam multi passim inueniuntur, qui euangelij doctrinam nullo modo ferre possunt, eò quòd hæc illorum vel quæstui, vel dignitati, vel etiam licentiæ officit. Et Christus dominus non ciues modò, verumetiam eusdem familiæ domesticos inter-stinis diuisidijs & simultatibus scindendos fore prædixit. Sufficiat ergo ministris, si ipsi nullam seditionis tumultuandi causam præbeant: quòd si vero hanc ipsi, improbo affectu impulsi, arripuerint, euentum deo committant, interim autem stationem suam constanter tueantur: quando iuxta D. Ambrosij dictum, nostrum est non excitare populum, excitatum vero mitigare in solius domini manu est. Deinde ad communem omnium hominum doctrinam seditionum iflarum descriptiones faciunt. Docent enim, ne quis temere euangelio & illius ministris seditionum causas adscribat, quod vulgò fieri consueuit: sed penitius rem ipsam excutiant singuli, & illi tumultuum authores esse facilè deprehendentur, qui euangelio coherceri nolunt. Et talem quidem Demetrium fuisse audiuimus, cuius imitatores reuera sunt, quotquot hodie contra euangelium tumultuari solent. Sed quia de his nuper abunde dictum est, in præsenti ipsam seditionem, & qualem se in ea Paulus gesserit, videamus.
units.tr: St Luke, moved by the Holy Spirit, records in this book not only the persecutions lawfully instituted against the apostles by the magistrates, but also the mad uproars of the raging crowd by which they were harassed. Among these, this present one, stirred up at Ephesus against Paul at the instigation of Demetrius, rightly holds the first place. Now this incident, like all the others, serves a twofold purpose. First, it instructs ministers, so that they are not disturbed by the tumults of a seditious crowd, as if by something new and unusual, nor abandon their duty through fear of them. Rather, let them consider that the Church in this world is like a little ship, tossed by winds and waves, whose helmsman, Christ, sometimes seems to be asleep, as the gospel story depicts (Mark 4). Let them also remember that it is hardly possible for seditions to be avoided altogether, when so many people are found everywhere who cannot bear the doctrine of the gospel at all, because it stands in the way of their profit, their dignity, or even their licence. Christ the Lord foretold that not only citizens but the members of one's own household would be torn apart by civil divisions and quarrels. It is enough for ministers if they themselves give no cause for seditious tumult. But if, driven by wicked desire, others seize upon such a pretext, let them commit the outcome to God, meanwhile holding their post steadfastly. For, as St Ambrose said, it is ours not to stir up the people, but once stirred, to calm them is in the hand of the Lord alone. Second, these descriptions of seditions teach everyone in general that one should not rashly ascribe the causes of sedition to the gospel and its ministers, as is commonly done. Rather, let each person examine the matter more closely, and those who are unwilling to be restrained by the gospel will easily be found to be the authors of the tumults. We have heard that Demetrius was such a man, and truly, all who today are accustomed to stir up tumult against the gospel are his imitators. But since this has recently been discussed at length, let us now look at the sedition itself and how Paul conducted himself in it.

units.la: Describit hanc mira diligentia Lucas, singulas eius partes commemorans. ET primò quidem à causa exorsus, omnes ira repletos fuisse scribit, quæ vt pessimus in rebus agendis consultor est, ita Iacobo apostolo teste, nihil iusti vel recti operatur. Iræ vero causa ipsis fuit quæstus periculum, quod ex Pauli doctrina ipsis imminere Demetrius modò dixerat, & singuli fortasse iam priuatim fe-tire cœperant. Nec enim quicquam indignius fert mundus, quàm si quæstum suum interuerti aut imminui sentiat. Nec hodie alia causa est tumultuum, quibus euangelij doctrina oppugnatur. Irascuntur Pontifices & Episcopi, quòd sua dignitati plurimum derogari videant. Irascuntur sacrificuli & Monachi, quòd sacrorum nundinatione euersa, culina ipsorum friget. Irascuntur principes & nobiles, quòd ecclesiasticorum bonorum possessione deturbantur ipsorum liberi, qui ex illis bactenus deliciabantur. Irascuntur sordidiores quique ex vulgo, qui sacrificulis & nobilibus adulari solebant. Irascuntur moriones, mimi, lenones, cupediarij, scorta, agasones, spadones, cynedi, & tota ista turpissimorum nebulonum sex, quibus patres illi, si Dijs placet, sanctissimi quæstum hucusque præbuerunt. Et omnes isti ira frementes ad Comitia concurrunt, consultaturi qua ratione Christi vincula disrumpant, & disciplinæ ipsius iugum abijciant, sicuti Psal. 2. scribitur. Quid ergo ex horum Comitijs boni speres, in quibus ira præsidet, consultor cæcus & improbus? Deinde ad insanos clamores conuersi vociferantur: Magna Diana Ephesiorum. Qua voce se Dianæ cultum etiam vitæ periculo & sanguine asserturos esse testantur. Callidè vero religione ventri & quæstui suo prætexunt. Et borum imitatores sunt, qui hodie non magis sobrij aduersus nos Diuos & in primis Virginem Mariam tonant, cuius honorem & cultum sese defensuros esse pollicentur. Quanquam maior nostrorum impudentia est. Nec enim temere sic clamant Ephesij, quando Dianæ cultum palam Paulus oppugnabat, adeoque illius hostis erat publicus. Quis vero ex nobis Diuos negat? Quis debitum Mariæ cultum euertit? Quis illius honori & dignitati derogat? Fatemur hanc filij Dei matrem esse. Fatemur illius virginitatem illæsam & intemeratam esse. Fatemur Diuos electa fuisse dei organa, & nunc in cœlis beatos viuere. Inuocationem verò & diuinos cultus vni Deo impendi debere dicimus. Quæ verò hæc iniuria est, si hoc ipsum docemus, quod illi olim docuerūt, & cuius gratia mortem subeundam esse putauerunt? Manifesta ergo calumnia est, quòd illi nos Diuorum hostes esse vociferantur. Tertiò tota ciuitas confusione repleta fuisse dicitur. Eius verò vnicus author fuit Demetrius. Quo exemplo admonemur, quantum mali subitò ex paucis seditiosis enasci soleat. Vt enim exigua scintilla totam domum incendit, cuius flammæ vento dissectæ vicinia totam vno quasi momento corripiunt: ita seditio paucis authoribus & ex contemptis initijs orta, vel sola fama latissime spargitur, totasq; respub. non sine præsenti fortunarum omnium periculo inuoluit. Exempla in Core, Abfolonis, Sabæ & aliorum historijs sacra scriptura nobis exhibet. Similia quoq; in gentium historijs extant, inter quæ cumprimis memorabile est Catilinæ facinus, qui Rom. rempub. eo tempore, quo maximè florebat, seditiosis suis conatibus in extremum periculum adduxit. Discant hinc magistratus in tempore illis obstare, quos aliquando seditiosos fore credibile est, quales ferè sunt luxu perditi, & quotquot religionem pro quæstu ducunt. Qui nisi legum seueritate coherceantur, tandem cum publico malo virus illud suum pestiferum effundunt. Quartò, impetu in theatrum facto locum publicum violenter occupant, quo mox etiam Caium & Aristarchum, Pauli comites, abripiunt. Vt ergo res agitur, & in innocentium capita maximè sæuitur. Licet enim seditionum tempestas frequenter bonos quoq; viros inuoluat, qui inuiti partibus se iungere coguntur, plerunq; tamen maior malorum numerus est: quò fit, vt bonis & insontibus seditiones cumprimis exitiales sint. Quare stultissimi sunt, quicunque ex seditionibus boni aliquid sperant, quibus summo studio mederi decet eos, qui respub. saluas & incolumes esse volunt.
units.tr: Luke describes it with remarkable care, recounting its individual parts. First, beginning with its cause, he writes that all were filled with anger. Anger, as James the apostle attests, is the worst counsellor in matters of action and never works what is just and right. The cause of their anger was the danger to their profit, which Demetrius had just said was threatening them from Paul's teaching, and which perhaps each of them had already begun to feel privately. Indeed, the world takes nothing more ill than to perceive that its gain is being overturned or diminished. Nor is there any other cause today for the tumults by which the doctrine of the gospel is attacked. The pontiffs and bishops are angry because they see their dignity greatly diminished. The little priests and monks are angry because, with the trade in sacred things overturned, their kitchens grow cold. The princes and nobles are angry because their children, who have hitherto lived in luxury on church property, are being thrown out of possession of it. The lowest sort of the common people are angry, those who were accustomed to flatter the priests and nobles. Buffoons, mimes, pimps, pastry-cooks, prostitutes, muleteers, eunuchs, sodomites, and that whole crew of most shameful scoundrels, by whom those holy fathers, if it please the gods, have hitherto made their living, are angry too. All these, raging with anger, flock to the assembly, intending to consult how they may break the chains of Christ and cast off the yoke of his discipline, as is written in Psalm 2. What good, then, can you hope for from the deliberations of such men, in which anger presides as a blind and wicked counsellor? Next, turning to frenzied shouts, they cry: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians." By this cry they declare that they will defend the worship of Diana even at the risk of their lives and with their blood. Yet they cunningly pretend that it is religion they serve, when in fact they are serving their bellies and their profit. And there are those today who are imitators of these men, who thunder against us no less wildly on behalf of the saints, and especially the Virgin Mary, promising to defend her honour and worship. Yet the shamelessness of our opponents is greater. For the Ephesians did not shout thus without reason, since Paul was openly attacking the worship of Diana and was thus her public enemy. But who among us denies the saints? Who overturns the due worship of Mary? Who detracts from her honour and dignity? We confess that she is the mother of the Son of God. We confess that her virginity was unharmed and undefiled. We confess that the saints were chosen instruments of God and now live blessed in heaven. But we say that invocation and divine worship are to be offered to the one God alone. What injury is this, then, if we teach the very thing that they taught long ago, and for which they thought they must undergo death? Therefore it is a plain calumny when they cry out that we are enemies of the saints. Third, the whole city is said to have been filled with confusion. Yet the sole author of this was Demetrius. By this example we are warned how much evil can suddenly arise from a few seditious men. For just as a small spark sets a whole house on fire, and its flames, driven by the wind, seize the neighbourhood almost in an instant, so sedition, begun by a few authors and from despised beginnings, is spread widely even by rumour alone, and draws the whole commonwealth into danger to the fortunes of all. Sacred Scripture sets before us examples in the histories of Korah, Absalom, Sheba, and others. Similar things are also found in the histories of the nations, among which the deed of Catiline is especially memorable, who brought the Roman commonwealth, when it was flourishing most, into the greatest danger by his seditious attempts. Let magistrates learn from this to resist such men in time, men who may at some point be expected to become seditious, such as those who are generally abandoned to luxury, and all who make religion a source of profit. Unless these are restrained by the severity of the laws, they will at last pour out their pestilential poison to the public ruin. Fourth, by making a violent rush into the theatre, they seize a public place, whence they soon drag off Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's companions. Thus the matter proceeds, and the fury falls chiefly on the heads of the innocent. For although the storm of sedition often sweeps up good men too, who are forced against their will to join the factions, yet the greater number is usually of the wicked. Hence it comes about that seditions are especially ruinous to the good and the innocent. Therefore they are most foolish who hope for anything good from seditions, when those who wish the commonwealth to remain safe and sound ought to cure them with the utmost diligence.

units.la: Quid verò Paulus feruente iam seditione egit? In publicum prodire & cœtum illorum ingredi voluit, nimirum vt furentes mitigaret, ne quid mali paterentur ipsius comites, quos iam abreptos fuisse audiuimus. Sed non permittunt hoc discipuli, maximè quos ex Asiæ magnatibus amicos habebat, quibus populi ingenium melius erat perspectum. Atqui hoc loco præclarissimarum virtutum chorum in Paulo videre licet. Est enim singulare fidei & syncerae amicitiæ exemplum, quòd comites periclitantes minimè deserendos esse putat. Quòd si verò duos ex amicorum numero tanti fecit Paulus, vt pro illis mortis periculum subire voluerit, quàm illi curæ fuisse putabimus ecclesias totas, quas Christi sanguine redemptas esse nouerat? Deinde constantia & fortitudo admirabilis in eo elucet, quòd furenti vulgo se credere voluit. Quid enim hoc aliud erat, quàm insani maris fluctibus, aut etiam incendio se committere? At Christi promissiones respexit, quibus animatus, nullo periculo abster reri poterat, vt officium negligeret. Simul verò eximiæ modestiæ specimen est, quòd sanioribus consilijs cedit, nec pertinaciter illud vrget, quod periculosum quidem, sed nullo cum fructu coniunctum esse videbat. Imitentur exemplum hoc singuli, quando constat maxima quoq; ingenia in propriis periculis ferè omni consilio & rationis vsu destitui. EST præterea obseruatione dignum, quòd magnates quoque amicos habet Paulus. Tales Christo aliquot fuisse legimus, inter quos Nicodemus & Iosephus præcipui nominantur. Iohan. 3.12. Matth. 27. Arguitur hic Anabaptistarum error, qui Christianum, magistratum gerere posse negant. Cumprimis verò docemur, quàm vana sint mundi præsidia, quando borum authoritas obstare non potuit, quò minus seditionis periculo Paulus inuoluretur. In vno igitur Deo nos spem & fiduciam omnem collocata habere decet, nec principibus aut filijs hominum fidere, in quibus non est salus, Psalm. 146. Atq; hunc ipsum præsentis exempli vsum Paulus ipse tradit in posteriori ad Cor. 1. cap.
units.tr: What, however, did Paul do while the sedition was already raging? He wished to come forward into the public place and enter their assembly, evidently to calm the furious people, so that his companions, whom we have heard were already seized, would suffer no harm. But the disciples did not allow it, especially those among the great men of Asia whom he had as friends, and who knew the temper of the people better. And here we may see a whole chorus of most excellent virtues in Paul. For it is a singular example of faith and sincere friendship that he does not think companions in danger should be abandoned. And if Paul held two of his friends in such esteem that he was willing to face the peril of death for them, how dear, do we suppose, must the whole churches have been to him, which he knew had been redeemed with the blood of Christ? Next, an admirable steadfastness and courage shine forth in him, in that he was willing to trust himself to the raging crowd. For what else was this than to commit himself to the waves of a raging sea, or even to a fire? But he looked to the promises of Christ, and, encouraged by them, he could not be deterred by any danger from neglecting his duty. At the same time it is a specimen of remarkable modesty that he yields to wiser counsels and does not insist stubbornly on what he saw to be dangerous and joined with no fruit. Let each of us imitate this example, since it is established that even the greatest minds are for the most part deprived of all counsel and the use of reason in their own dangers. It is also worth noting that Paul had friends among the great men too. We read that Christ had some such, among whom Nicodemus and Joseph are named as the chief (John 3; Matt. 27). Here the error of the Anabaptists is refuted, who deny that a Christian can hold the office of magistrate. Above all, we are taught how vain the protections of the world are, since the authority of these men could not prevent Paul from being drawn into the danger of sedition. In the one God alone, therefore, we ought to place all our hope and trust, and not to trust in princes or the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation (Psalm 146). Paul himself hands down this very use of the present example in his later letter to the Corinthians, chapter 1.

units.la: Porrò ad seditiosos redit Lucas, de quibus duo adhuc commemorat. Primò, alij (inquit) aliud clamabant, & plerique cur conuenissent, ignorabant. Est hoc proprium seditionibus, quòd plures rerum plane ignaros, multos quoq; ex bonis inuitos abripiunt, inundantis torrentis instar. Quare easdem consilio potius & ratione, quàm vi, sedari oportet. Si enim hæc adhibeatur, ferè innocentium sanguine litatur, dum astute elabuntur authores improbi: cuius rei nimis funestum exemplum vidit Germania, cum anno M. D. XXV. horribiles sanguinis rusticorum riui totam quasi inundarunt. Meminerint potius principes propheticî illius, quo subditorum suorum sanguinem in summo precio babere iubentur. Psal.71. Deinde Iudæis propellentibus è turba protraxere Alexandrũ quendam, quem Pauli amicum fuisse, verisimile est, quando Iudæi illum periculo obijcere voluerunt. Voluit ú postulato silentio, omnium quæ circa religionem tentata fuerant, ratione reddere. Ast vbi Iudæum, & proinde gentilitiæ superstitionis hostem esse intelligunt, ad furiosos clamores denuò conuersi, per duas horas suam illam Dianam tonant. Vt enim venter auribus caret, ita surdi ferè sunt, nec vllas rationes admittunt, qui ventris gratia tumultuantur. Et impiorũ perpetuus hic mos est, quòd insa-nis clamoribus veritati obstrepunt, quam alioqui inuistam esse nouerunt. Arguitur autem interea multorum languor, qui cum Veritatem cognitam habeant, in eius tamen confessione toti frigent, nec impiorum zelo mouentur, quos in superstitionibus tuendis tam animosos esse vident. Discamus ergo quæ veritatis in hoc mundo sors sit, & fidei constantia armati fortiter excipiamus quicquid deus de-crit, vt omni fortuna superiores simus in Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lucas now returns to the rioters, and mentions two things about them. First, he says, some cried one thing and others another, and most did not even know why they had come together. This is characteristic of sedition: it sweeps away many who know nothing of the matter, and many good people against their will too, like a flooding torrent. Such uprisings should therefore be calmed by counsel and reason rather than by force. For if force is applied, innocent blood is generally poured out, while the wicked instigators slip away craftily. Germany saw a most grievous example of this in the year 1525, when rivers of peasants' blood flooded almost the whole land. Rulers should rather remember that prophetic saying, in which they are commanded to hold the blood of their subjects in highest value (Psalm 72). Then, when the Jews pushed forward and dragged out of the crowd a certain Alexander, who was probably a friend of Paul, since the Jews wanted to expose him to danger, he wished, once silence was called, to give an account of everything that had been attempted concerning the religion. But when they understood that he was a Jew, and therefore an enemy of the Gentile superstition, they turned again to furious shouting and for two hours bellowed out their great Diana. For just as the belly has no ears, so those who riot for the sake of their bellies are almost deaf and admit no reasons at all. This is the constant custom of the impious: they drown out the truth with insane shouting, because they know it is otherwise hateful to them. Meanwhile the lethargy of many is also exposed, who, though they have the truth known to them, nevertheless grow cold in confessing it, and are not stirred by the zeal of the impious, whom they see to be so spirited in defending their superstitions. Let us learn therefore what lot the truth has in this world, and armed with constancy of faith, let us bravely receive whatever God decrees, so that we may be superior to every fortune in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXX.
units.tr: HOMILY 130.

units.la: Cum autem sedasset scriba turbam, dixit: Viri Ephesij, quis enim est hominum, qui nesciat Ephesiorum ciuitatem cultricem esse magnæ Deæ Dianæ, & à Ioue delapsi simulachri? Cum autem hæc sint extra controuersiam, oportet vos sedatos esse, & nihil præcipitanter agere. Adduxistis enim homines istos, neq; sacrilegos, neq; contumelilosos in deam vestram. Quòd si Demetrius, & qui cum eo sunt artifices, habent aduersus aliquem causam, conuentus forenses aguntur, & Proconsu-les sunt: accusent inuicem. Si quid autem de rebus alijs quæritis, in le-gitima concione dirimetur. Nam periculum est, ne seditionis hodiernæ rei fiamus, cum nulla subsit causa, vnde poteriḿus reddere rationem concursus istius. Et cum hæc dixisset, dimisit concionem.
units.tr: When the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said: "Men of Ephesus, who is there among men who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the guardian of the great goddess Diana, and of the image that fell down from Jupiter? Since these things are beyond dispute, you ought to be calm and not act rashly. For you have brought these men here, who are neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers of your goddess. But if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another. If you seek anything further, it will be settled in a lawful assembly. For we are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause by which we could give an account of this gathering." And when he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.

units.la: VIdimus nuper à Luca descriptam seditionem, quæ Demetrio authore aduersus Paulum excitata fuit: in qua præter furentis vulgi ingenium, Paulus maximè nobis spectandus venit. Is primò quidem intrepidus & constans animi cætum populi ingredi & suæ cùm fidei tum doctrinæ rationem publicè reddere statuit. Vbi verò hoc illi facere non licet, inter amicos sese continens, Deo rei totius euentum permittit, ita tamen, vt à Veritatis confessione non latum vnguem discedat, nec quicquam ignauo metu dissimulet. Quo exemplo admonemur, quales nos in simili casu, vel etiam in aperta persecutione esse conueniat. Ante omnia quidem nos iuxta Petri apostoli præceptum para-tos esse decet ad reddendam rationem cuius petenti. 1. Pet. 3. Vbi verò ea fuerit hostium rabies, vt nullus Veritati eiuśq; confessioni locus supersit, prudenter & caute agendum, ne temere & citra Dei vocationem nos periculis obijcientes, deum tentare videamur. Interim constantes in Veritatis agni-tione, dominum expectemus, qui in se sperantes nunquam deseret, quiq; sua sapientia simul & poten-tia sæuissimas quoq; tempestates facile sedabit. Exemplum buius præsens quoq; historia exhibet, in qua seditionem, extrema quæq; Paulo minantem, vnius scribæ opera Deus cohercet, & eius quidem, quem à religione Christiana alienioremfuisse, tota orationis series euidentissimè probat. Quò illu-strior elucet dei potentia, quando reprobis quoq; & illorum opera in suis asserendis vti consueuit. Vi-deamus autem per singulas partes scribæ orationem, cuius hic potissimus status est, vt seditiosos su-rentis populi motus reprimat, cum interim de causa religionis non admodum solicitus fuerit.
units.tr: We recently saw the sedition described by Luke, which was stirred up against Paul at the instigation of Demetrius. In it, apart from the crowd's frenzied temper, Paul is the one we must chiefly observe. At first he resolved, fearless and steadfast in mind, to enter the assembly of the people and openly give an account both of his faith and of his teaching. But when he was not allowed to do this, he restrained himself among his friends and left the outcome of the whole affair to God, yet without retreating a hair's breadth from his confession of the truth or concealing anything out of cowardly fear. By this example we are admonished how we ought to behave in a similar case, or even in open persecution. Above all, we should, according to the precept of the apostle Peter, be ready to give an account to anyone who asks (1 Pet. 3). But when the enemies' rage is such that there is no room left for the truth and its confession, we must act prudently and cautiously, so that we do not seem to tempt God by rashly exposing ourselves to dangers without a call from God. Meanwhile, let us remain steadfast in the knowledge of the truth and wait for the Lord, who never forsakes those who hope in him, and who by his wisdom and power will easily calm even the most savage storms. The present history also sets forth an example of this: God restrains, through the work of a single town clerk, a sedition that threatened Paul with the worst, and this man, as the whole course of his speech most clearly proves, was rather alien to the Christian religion. How much more brightly the power of God shines forth, since he is accustomed to use even the reprobate and their works to vindicate his own cause. Let us look at the clerk's speech part by part. His main aim was to check the seditious movements of the furious people, while he himself was not greatly concerned about the cause of religion.

units.la: Orditur autem ab eo, quod seditiosos maximè exasperabat. Dianæ suæ cumprimis timebant, & ob hanc vociferabantur, vt nuper audiuimus, eò quòd huius cultu sublato, de quastu etiam suo actum esse viderent.
