At negat scriba, hanc ipsis iustam & sufficiente tumultuandi causam esse. Quis est bominum (inquit) qui nesciat Ephesiorum ciuitatem cultricem esse magnæ Deæ Dianæ, & à Ioue delapsi simulachri? Quasi dicat: Quorsum attinet Dianæ nomen furiosis vociferationibus identidem ingeminare? Quis verò negat vos huius cultores esse? Quis Dianæ simulachrum cœlitus delapsum esse ignorat? Aut quis prohibet, quò minus à patribus traditam religionem constanter retineatis? Hæc
units.tr: He begins with what chiefly inflamed the rioters. They were especially afraid for their Diana, and it was for her sake that they shouted, as we heard recently, because they saw that once her worship was abolished, their own profit would also be at an end. But the clerk denies that this gives them a just and sufficient reason for rioting. "Who is there among men," he says, "who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the guardian of the great goddess Diana, and of the image that fell down from Jupiter?" It is as if he said: "Why is it necessary to keep repeating Diana's name in frenzied shouts? Who denies that you are her worshippers? Who does not know that her image fell from heaven? Or who prevents you from steadfastly keeping the religion handed down by your fathers? These things..."

units.la: {y} Nota. Hæc (inquam) cum extra omnem controuersiam sint, conuenit vos quieti studere, nec quicquam temere aut inconsulto agere. Atqui non poterat ignorare scriba, Paulum Dianæ cultum doctrina sua oppugnauisse. Sed ciuili prudentia hoc omne dissimulat, hoc illis compescendis satis fore putans, si intelligant se nulla publica authoritate vrgeri aut compelli, vt à veteri religione discedant. Et vt modò monuimus, hoc vnum quærit homo ciuili prudentia instructus, vt seditionem semel coerceat, quam plus satis efferbuisse videbat: id quod callida dissimulatione commodius, quàm disputatione, fieri posse arbitratur, quam seditiosi difficulter admisissent. Hic vero minimè prætereundum est, quod de simulachro cœlitus delapso dicit. Hinc enim liquet vulgò receptam fuisse apud Ephesios opinionem, qua Dianæ simulachrum è cœlis allatum esse credebant. Etenim postquam prestigijs suis gentes dementauit satan, vt immortalis Dei gloriam mortalium creaturarum formis mutare auderent, nouis indies commentis miseros decepit, quo firmiores essent regni sui vires. Hinc Palladium cœlo lapsum esse, & in huius tutela victoriam consistere persuasit. Ita Ancile, imperij pignus, è cœlo Romanos sub Numa rege accepisse creditum fuit. Quibus merito quod de Ephesia Dianæ simulachro scriba ille commemorat, adnumerari debet. Sed tolerabile videri poterat, si olim duntaxat gentes eiusmodi prestigijs decepisset dæmon, nisi inter Christianos similia extarent. Quis enim nescit Lauretani sacelli, trans mare miraculose allati, fabulam? Quis sacella quædam ab ipso Deo & angelis consecrata ignorat? Offenduntur etiam non paucæ Virginis matris imagines, quas à Luca depictas esse, Monachi impudentissime affirmauerunt, cum illum non pictorem, sed medicum fuisse, historiæ prodant. Quò simul referri debent quæcunque in Monachorum libris narrantur imaginum miracula, quarum aliæ loco motæ esse, aliæ immobiles consistere, aliæ fleuisse, aliæ oracula edidisse, aliæ aliis signis celebres fuisse dicuntur. Ex quibus haud obscurè colligitur, quàm fecunda errorum messis ex imaginibus enasci soleat, vbi illarum vsus & cultus semel receptus fuerit: vt non temere Lactantius dixerit, religionem omnino nullam esse, vbicunque simulachrum habetur. Quæ etiam præcipua causa est, quòd in illis oppugnandis tanto studio & zelo omnis scriptura versatur: vt mirum sit tam multos nostro seculo illarum propugnatores inueniri, quando tot tamen infelicia superstitionis exempla passim omnium oculis incurrunt.
units.tr: {y} Note. "These things," I say, since they are beyond all dispute, it is fitting that you should be calm and do nothing rashly or without deliberation. Yet the clerk could not have been ignorant that Paul had attacked the worship of Diana by his teaching. But with civil prudence he passes over all this, thinking it will be enough to restrain them if they understand that they are not being pressed or compelled by any public authority to abandon the old religion. And as we have just observed, the only thing a man trained in civil prudence seeks is to check a sedition once, which he saw had boiled over more than enough. He judges that this can be done more conveniently by a cunning pretence than by argument, which the seditious would have found hard to accept. Here we must not pass over what he says about the image that fell from heaven. For it is clear from this that the opinion was commonly held among the Ephesians that the image of Diana had been brought down from the heavens. Indeed, after Satan had driven the nations out of their minds by his illusions, so that they dared to change the immortal glory of God into the forms of mortal creatures, he deceived the wretched people with new inventions every day, so that the strength of his kingdom would be more secure. From this he persuaded them that the Palladium had fallen from heaven and that victory depended on its protection. Likewise, it was believed that the Ancile, the pledge of empire, had been received from heaven by the Romans under King Numa. What that clerk mentions about the Ephesian image of Diana must rightly be counted among these. But it might seem tolerable if the demon had deceived only the nations of old with such illusions, were it not that similar things also exist among Christians. For who does not know the tale of the sanctuary of Loreto, miraculously carried across the sea? Who is unaware of certain shrines said to have been consecrated by God himself and the angels? Many images of the Virgin Mother also cause offence, which the monks most shamelessly affirmed were painted by Luke, although the histories show that he was not a painter but a physician. To these must be added whatever miracles of images are narrated in the books of the monks, some of which are said to have moved from their place, others to have stood immovable, others to have wept, others to have uttered oracles, and others to have become famous for other signs. From these things it is not obscurely gathered how rich a harvest of errors usually springs up from images, once their use and worship have been received. Hence Lactantius rightly said that there is no religion at all wherever an image is kept. This is also the principal reason why all writing is so much occupied, with such zeal and eagerness, in attacking them. It is therefore remarkable that so many defenders of them are found in our age, when so many unhappy examples of superstition meet everyone's eyes everywhere.

units.la: His vero præmissis, quibus furentes animos iam nonnihil mitigatos esse putabat, illos non obscurè reprehendit scriba & temeritatis nimiæ accusat, quòd Caium & Aristarchum, homines peregrinos, indicta causa ceperint. Adduxistis (inquit) homines istos, neque sacrilegos, neque blasphemos aut contumeliosos in Deam veslram. Id vero de illis fortasse verè dicit potuit, eò quòd isti non docuerant. At in Paulo hoc ipsum non habuisset locum, qui Dianæ cultum omnemque idololatriam sedulò oppugnabat, quemadmodum ex ijs, quæ Athenis gesserit, abunde colligitur. Nec credibile est dissimulaturum fuisse hanc defensionem scribæ, si præsens affuisset. Nam zelo Dei flagrans intolerabile esse censuit, quicquid veri Dei gloriæ & cultui quicquam derogaret. Interim docent scribæ verba, quibus criminibusferè veritatis ministri grauntur. Sacrilegij nimirum, & quòd in Deos Diuosq; blasphemi sint. Audiuntur hæc vulgò hodie, nec alijs nominibus siue titulis exornamur ab illis, qui euangelium ex professo oppugnant. At si causam ipsam inspicias, vtrunque falsum est. Sacrilegi enim sunt, qui opes deo & ecclesiæ sacras vel furtim surripiunt, vel violenter sibi vendicant, & in vsus propha nos conuertunt. Quis vero hoc impudentius facit, quàm Pontifices, Episcopi, Monachi, sacrificuli, & quicunq; alij sunt huius farinæ? Vt enim de eo nihil dicamus, quòd cognatus suus fere ex ecclesiæ bonis proficiunt, familias saltem horum inspiciamus, & patebit maximam ecclesiasticorum reddituum partem in scorta, aleam, equos, canes & inutile seruorum agmen insumi. Imò non alia de causa nobis grauius indignantur, quàm quòd per euangelij doctrinam ecclesiæ & Christo opes suas vendicare satagimus. Minimè enim illis patrocinamur, qui sub euangelij prætextu suæ auaritiæ ex ecclesiarum bonis consulunt. Rursum blasphemi sunt in Deum & Diuos, qui Dei nomine abutuntur, quiq; Diuos debito honore spoliant. Vtrunque ab ipsis potius quàm nobis fieri luce clarius patet. Ipsi enim Dei verbo & Christi nomine abutuntur, vt idololatriam suam & tyrannidem stabiliant. Ipsi honorem Deo debitum in creaturas transferunt. Ipsi Diuorum fidem & doctrinam hæresfeos accusant, & in illorum libros simul & seductores ferro & igne grassantur. Interim nos sacrilegij & bla
units.tr: Having premised these things, by which he thought the furious minds were now somewhat softened, the clerk openly rebukes them and accuses them of excessive rashness, because they had seized Gaius and Aristarchus, foreigners, without a hearing. "You have brought these men here," he says, "who are neither temple-robbers, nor blasphemers, nor revilers of your goddess." This he may perhaps have said truly of them, since these men had not taught against her. But the same could not have applied to Paul, who diligently attacked the worship of Diana and all idolatry, as is abundantly clear from what he did at Athens. Nor is it credible that the clerk would have kept up this defence had he been present. For, burning with zeal for God, he judged it intolerable whatever detracted in any way from the glory and worship of the true God. Meanwhile, the clerk's words show the charges with which the ministers of the truth are usually burdened: namely, sacrilege, and that they are blasphemers against gods and divinities. These charges are commonly heard today, and those who openly attack the gospel adorn us with no other names or titles. But if you look at the cause itself, both are false. For those are sacrilegious who either secretly steal, or violently claim for themselves, the wealth consecrated to God and the Church, and turn it to profane uses. Who does this more shamelessly than the Pontiffs, bishops, monks, little priests, and all others of that stripe? For, to say nothing of the fact that their relatives mostly profit from the goods of the Church, let us at least look at the households of these men, and it will be plain that the greatest part of the ecclesiastical revenues is spent on harlots, dice, horses, dogs, and a useless crowd of servants. Indeed, they are angry with us for no other reason than that we strive, through the doctrine of the gospel, to claim back the wealth of the Church and of Christ. For we do not defend those who, under the pretext of the gospel, provide for their own greed from the goods of the churches. Again, they are blasphemers against God and the divinities who abuse the name of God and strip the divinities of the honour due to them. It is clearer than light that both are done by them rather than by us. For they abuse the word of God and the name of Christ in order to establish their idolatry and tyranny. They transfer the honour due to God to creatures. They accuse the faith and teaching of the saints of heresy, and they rage with sword and fire against their books and their very persons as seducers. Meanwhile we are charged with sacrilege and blasphemy

units.la: Diane simulachrum cœlitus delapsum.
units.tr: The image of Diana that fell from heaven.

units.la: Euangelij ministri ac sacrilegi nec blasphemi sunt. phemiæ criminibus infames facere conantur. Sed ō tempori̇ nostrorum iniquitatem. Apud Ephe·sios gentilis homo inuenitur, qui innocentibus patrocinetur. At hodie inter Christiani nominis professores fere nulli sunt, qui Christi ministrūs innocentiæ testimonium ferant. Obseruemus præterea, quòd hos sacrilegos & blasphemos esse negat scriba, utique pœna dignos iudicaturus, si tales fuissent. Licet enim in fide & religione turpissimè aberrarint olim gentes, rata tamen apud illos mansit naturæ lex, quæ sacrilegos & blasphemos pœnis cohercere docet. At hodie ita languent omnia, ut euangelij fidei cultoribus plus periculi sit, quàm ijs, qui ecclesiam publicis sacrilegijs & atrocissimis blasphemijs prophanant.
units.tr: The ministers of the gospel are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemous, yet they try to brand them with the infamy of sacrilege and blasphemy. But oh, the wickedness of our times! Among the Ephesians a Gentile is found who defends the innocent. Today, among those who profess the Christian name, there are almost none who would bear witness to the innocence of Christ's ministers. Notice also that the town clerk says these men are not sacrilegious or blasphemous, and he would surely have judged them worthy of punishment if they had been. For although the nations of old went most shamefully astray in faith and religion, the law of nature remained valid among them, teaching that sacrilege and blasphemy are to be restrained by punishment. But today everything is so weakened that those who cultivate the faith of the gospel are in more danger than those who profane the Church with public sacrileges and most atrocious blasphemies.

units.la: Cæterum postremam orationis huius partem vidsamus, qua modum & rationem, quam in causis tum priuatis tum publicis sequuntur, præscribit, dicens: Quòd si Demetrius & qui cum eo sunt artifices, habent aduersus aliquem causam, conuentus forenses aguntur, & Proconsules sunt, accusent inuicem. Ita verò simul ipsos iniquitatis accusat, quòd ex priuata causa, ad paucos duntaxat homines pertinente, publicam faciant, seq; omnes simul liti alienæ implicent. Deinde alterum membrum subiungens, ait: Si quid autem de rebus alijs quæritis, legitima concione dirimetur. Quibus verbis admonet, ne publicam quidem causam hoc modo agi debuisse, simulq; periculum ob oculos ponit, quod ex seditione temere concitata immineat à Romanis, qui suo Imperio subiectos populos cumprimi tranquillos & quietos esse volebant. Docet autem locus hic, quæ olim reru̅pub.forma sub Romanis fuerit, quando iustitiæ & æquitatis adhuc obseruantes fuerunt. Erant hinc inde constituti Proconsules & magistratus certi, qui forenses conuentus agebant, nec aliquem indicta causa & nondum legitimè conuictum à quoquam lædi sinebant. Publicæ verò causæ legitimis quoq; & publicis comitijs, non seditiosis tumultibus componebantur. Probauit hanc reipub.formam ipse dominus, quando Iudices in populo suo constituit, quos causas omnes diligenter audire & æquum iudicare iubet. Neminem verò suæ causæ iudicem esse vult. Seruetur mos hic inter Christianos homines, quòs turpe est ab ethnicis vinci. In primis verò à seditionibus abhorreant, quibus & magistratuum authoritatim minui, & totus rerumpub.status conuelli solet.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us look at the last part of this speech, in which he lays down the manner and method that they should follow in both private and public cases, saying: "If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges against one another. But if you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in a lawful assembly." By these words he accuses them at once of wrongdoing, because they have turned a private dispute, touching only a few people, into a public matter and have dragged everyone into another man's quarrel. Then, adding the second part, he says: "If you seek anything about other matters, it will be settled in a lawful assembly." With these words he warns that not even a public cause ought to be pursued in this way, and at the same time he sets before their eyes the danger that threatens from the Romans, who wanted the peoples under their rule to be kept quiet and peaceable, if a sedition were rashly stirred up. This passage also shows what form of commonwealth existed under the Romans in the days when they still kept to justice and equity. Proconsuls and fixed magistrates were appointed in various places, who held the courts and did not allow anyone to be harmed by anyone else without a charge being laid and without a lawful conviction. Public causes were settled in lawful and public assemblies, not in seditious tumults. The Lord himself approved this form of commonwealth when he appointed judges among his people, whom he commands to hear all causes diligently and to judge fairly. Yet he does not want anyone to be judge in his own cause. Let this custom be kept among Christians, who are shamed to be surpassed by the heathen. Above all let them shun seditions, by which the authority of magistrates is diminished and the whole state of the commonwealth is usually overthrown.

units.la: Subiungit autem orationis huius effectum Lucas, dum concionem, quæ paulò ante confusissima erat, placidè dimissam fuisse scribit. Vt enim facilè commouetur vulgus, ita facilè etiam cicuratur, si rationem potius et consilium quàm vim adhibeas. Elucet autem hoc loco fidelis dei cura, quæ suos asserit & tuetur. Vt enim idem ille maris fluctus subitis ventorum flatibus attollere, & eosdem repente deponere & sedare consueuit: ita horrendis interdum periculorum procellis suos tentat, quàm ipsi visum fuerit, absque omni periculo componere nouit. Huius ergo bonitate & potentia freti stationem nostram constanter tueamur, certi nos quoque omnibus impiorum conatibus superiores fore per Christum Iesum, dominum & vindicem nostrum fidelißimum inuictissimumq; : cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke then adds the outcome of this speech, when he writes that the assembly, which a little before had been in utter confusion, was calmly dismissed. For just as a crowd is easily stirred up, so it is also easily calmed, if you apply reason and counsel rather than force. In this passage the faithful care of God is evident, which protects and defends his own. Just as the same sea's waves are wont to rise by sudden gusts of wind, and again to subside and be calmed at once, so God sometimes tries his people with dreadful storms of danger, yet he knows how to quiet them, whenever it pleases him, without any peril. Relying therefore on his goodness and power, let us hold our position steadfastly, certain that we shall also prevail over all the attempts of the impious through Jesus Christ, our Lord and most faithful and unconquered avenger, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXI.

units.la: POstquam autem cessauit tumultus, vocatis ad se Paulus discipulis, complexusq; illos, profectus est vt iret in Macedoniam. Cum autem perambulasset partes illas, & exhortatus eos fuisset multo sermone, venit in Græciam. Et ibi peractis mensibus tribus, cum essent illi structæ insidiæ à Iudæis soluturo in Syriam, habebat in animo vt reuerteretur per Macedoniam. Comitatus est autem eum vsq; ad Asiam Sopater Berrhœensis, Thessalonicensium verò Aristarchus, & Secundus, & Caius Derbæus, & Timotheus. Asiani verò Tychicus & Trophimus. Hi cum præcessissent, expectarunt nos Troade. Nos verò abnauigauimus post dies azymorū à Philippis, & venimus ad eos Troadem intra dies quinque: vbi demorati sumus diebus septem.
units.tr: When the uproar had ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, embraced them, and set out to go into Macedonia. When he had travelled through those regions and encouraged the believers with much teaching, he came into Greece. There he stayed three months, and when the Jews laid a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. Sopater of Berea, the son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him as far as Asia, and of the Thessalonians Aristarchus and Secundus, and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and from Asia Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and waited for us at Troas. But we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and within five days we joined them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.

units.la: VONIAM Paulum electum suum organum dixit dominus noster Iesus Christus, non temere fit, quòd res per illum gestas tanta diligentia Lucas commemorat. Ita enim testimonij, quod de illo Christus tulit, veritas asseritur, & exemplum generale proponitur, quod omnes imitentur, qui Deo organa electa esse & haberi volunt. Porrò in rerum Pauli commemoratione eo modo Euangelista procedit, vt interdum integras historias per singulas partes siue circumstantias commemoret, eas nimirum, in quarum singulis partibus multa, quae nostrae institutioni seruire possunt, continentur, quales sunt quas Philippis, Corinthi, Athenis, & nuper Ephesi vidimus: interdum vero multa simul comprehendit, & longissimas periculosissimasq; peregrinationes, quae vix multis mensibus confici potuerunt, paucis verbis complectitur, quò euidentius pateat, quanta illius viri in obeundo suo munere industria, quanta fides, & quàm incredibilis laborum tolerantia inq; subeundis periculis animi fortitudo fuerit. Vtrunq; vero hoc capite obseruat. Primò enim summatim narrat profectionem, qua Macedoniam & Achaiam inuisit, de cuius consilio supra dictum fuit. Deinde peculiaria quaedam recenset, nempe miraculum Troadis editum, quo Eutychus resuscitatus est, & Mileti coactam Ephesiorum pastorum Synodum. Nos verò in praesenti peregrinationem Pauli inspiciemus, cuius narratio ita contexitur, vt quid Paulus, quid item alij fecerint, commemoretur.
units.tr: Since our Lord Jesus Christ called Paul his chosen instrument, it is not by chance that Luke recounts the things done through him with such care. For in this way the truth of the testimony that Christ gave concerning him is confirmed, and a general example is set before all who wish to be, and to be regarded as, chosen instruments of God. In recounting Paul's deeds, the Evangelist proceeds in such a way that at times he relates whole episodes part by part, with their circumstances, namely those episodes in whose individual parts there is much that can serve our instruction, such as those we saw at Philippi, Corinth, Athens, and recently at Ephesus. At other times he embraces many things at once and sums up in a few words very long and perilous journeys, which could scarcely have been completed in many months, so that it may appear more clearly how great was that man's diligence in discharging his office, how great his faith, how incredible his endurance of toils, and the courage of his spirit in facing dangers. In this chapter he observes both methods. First he briefly describes the journey by which he visited Macedonia and Achaia, of which the plan was mentioned above. Then he recounts certain particular events, namely the miracle at Troas, by which Eutychus was raised, and the assembly of the elders of Ephesus, convened at Miletus. For the present we shall consider Paul's journey itself, whose narrative is so woven that both what Paul did and what the others did are recorded.

units.la: Atqui in ipsam peregrinationem tria incidunt, ad Paulum maximè spectantia. Primò enim narratur, quomodo ab Ephesijs discesserit. Postquam cessauit tumultus (inquit) vocatis ad se discipulis, complexusq; illos, vel illis salutatis, profectus est. Non ergo antea eam ecclesiam deseruit, quàm omni tumultu sedato illam extra periculum constitutam esse videret. Bonus ergo pastor est Paulus, non mercenarius, qui fere lupo visto fugit, vt suis rebus consulat. Iohan.10. Deinde ne tunc quidem clàm sese subducit, sed conuocata ecclesia publicè illis valedicit, simul de singulis illos admonens, quae ipsis cognitu & obseruatu necessaria erant. Id vt animi bene sibi conscij argumentum est, ita fidelis curae significationem habet, quòd nec absens quidem illorum memoriam & curam deponere velit. Vnde postea ad illos scribens, se ipsorum indefinentem mentionem in precibus suis facere testatur. Ephes.1. Et alibi omnium ecclesiarum curam humeris suis incumbere scribit. 2. Cor.11. Imitentur exemplum hoc omnes, quorum fidei vel ecclesiae vel respub. commissae sunt, ne vel suis duntaxat rebus consulat dum publica instant pericula, vel alioqui nulla aut perquam exigua & leui illorum cura tangantur, de quibus rationem olim domino reddere cogentur. Deinde quò nam abierit, indicatur. In Macedoniam nimirum, & inde Graeciam, quibus in locis mensis tres exegit, omne illud tempus visendis & confirmandis ecclesijs impendens. Hoc ipsum alias quoq; ab illo factitatum fuisse cap.14. & 15. audiuimus. Vnde colligimus, hunc apostolus visitatum morem fuisse, vt ecclesias non modo plantarent, sed easdem postea denuo inuisentes in fide confirmarent, & errores, si qui obrepserant, corrigerent. Admonemur illorum exemplo, minimè securos esse debere, qui ecclesias & respub. semel bene constitutas habent, sed vigilandum esse, ne (quod Christus monet) dormientibus nobis infelix lolium satan aspergat. Solet is ecclesijs quàm maximè insidias struere, vt à Christo abducat, quos illi fidelis sponsae instar adhaerere oportebat. 2. Cor.11. Idem bonas leges varie oppugnat, eò quòd his euersis suum regnum paruo negotio stabiliri posse intelligit. Necfruftranei semper illius conatus sunt, quàn do pauci sunt, qui Pauli fidem, industriam, tolerantiam & studium imitentur. Tertiò diferè quid in ecclesijs istis Paulus egerit exprimitur. Exhortatus est illos sermone multo, nimirum ad perseue-rantiam in fide, sine qua nemo saluatur. Exhortationibus autem crebrùs cùm propter nos opus est, qui natura ad lapsum procliues sumus, tum propter diabolum, qui nunquam non rugientis leonis instar obambulat, & quaerit quem deuoret. Minimè ergo illorum sententia admitti debet, qui curam banc superuacaneam esse putant. Interim admonemur, ecclesias nihil praestantius habere verbo Dei, e quo quotidianae institutiones, exhortationes & correctiones peti debent. Quibus ita fluduerunt apostoli, vt reliqua omnia prae hoc facile neglexerint, vt cap.6. vidimus. Parum ergo apostolici sunt, qui negligo verbi ministerio & docendi officio, circa frigidas ceremonias, aut etiam terrenarum ditionum administrationem occupantur.
units.tr: Now three things concerning Paul himself fall within this journey. First, it is related how he departed from Ephesus. "When the uproar had ceased," he says, "he sent for the disciples, embraced them," or, having greeted them, he set out. He therefore did not leave that church before he saw that, with all the tumult quelled, it had been placed beyond danger. Paul is therefore a good shepherd, not a hired hand, who almost at the sight of the wolf flees to look after his own affairs (John 10). Then, not even at that point does he slip away secretly, but, having called the church together, he bids them farewell publicly, at the same time admonishing each of them about what they needed to know and to observe. As this is a sign of a conscience conscious of its own integrity, so it also shows faithful care, in that even when absent he does not wish to let go of their memory and concern. Hence later, writing to them, he testifies that he makes unceasing mention of them in his prayers (Ephesians 1). And elsewhere he writes that the care of all the churches rests upon his shoulders (2 Corinthians 11). Let all those imitate this example to whom the faith or the churches or the commonwealth have been entrusted, so that they do not look only to their own affairs while public dangers press, nor are otherwise touched by no care, or by a very slight and superficial care, for those for whose account they will one day be compelled to render an answer to the Lord. Next, the place to which he went is indicated: namely Macedonia, and from there Greece, where he spent three months, devoting all that time to visiting and strengthening the churches. We have heard that he had done this also at other times, in chapters 14 and 15. Hence we gather that it was the apostle's customary practice not only to plant churches but also, by visiting them again afterwards, to confirm them in the faith and to correct any errors that had crept in. We are admonished by their example that those who have churches and commonwealths once well established must not be entirely secure, but must be watchful, lest (as Christ warns) while we sleep the unhappy tares of Satan be sown. He is wont to lay the most cunning snares for the churches, so as to draw away from Christ those whom they ought to cling to like a faithful bride (2 Corinthians 11). He likewise assails good laws in various ways, because he understands that when these are overthrown his kingdom can be established with little effort. Nor are his efforts always in vain, when there are few who imitate Paul's faith, diligence, endurance and zeal. Thirdly, what Paul did in these churches is summarily expressed. He encouraged them with much teaching, namely toward perseverance in the faith, without which no one is saved. Frequent exhortations are necessary both on account of ourselves, who are by nature prone to fall, and on account of the devil, who never ceases to prowl like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Therefore the opinion of those who think this care superfluous must by no means be admitted. Meanwhile we are reminded that churches have nothing more excellent than the Word of God, from which daily instruction, exhortation and correction ought to be sought. The apostles were so devoted to this that they readily neglected all other things in comparison with it, as we saw in chapter 6. Therefore those are little like the apostles who neglect the ministry of the Word and the office of teaching, and busy themselves with cold ceremonies or even with the administration of earthly dominions.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reuersi, quid in sua hac peregrinatione passus sit videamus. Insidiae illi in Syriam navigaturo à Iudaeis structae sunt, qui ipsum e medio sublatum volebant. Prudenter tamen has fidiantur. ille declinat, dū mutato consilio pedestri itinere per Macedoniam in Syriam contendit. Docet locus hic, quæ gratia veritatis ministris in mundo referatur. Pessima nimirum, dum illi hos perditos volunt, quorum saluti maximè inuigilant. Paulum enim pro Iudæis perquàm solicitum fuisse tum totus ille laborum ipsius cursus, tum eiusdem epistolæ testantur, cumprimis quæ ad Rom.cap.9. & 10. scribit. At non alios infensiores sibi hostes sensit. Hoc ipsum Mosen quoq; & prophetas, & cum hiu Dei filium, Iesum Christum, expertos fuisse, alibi diximus. Nemo igitur hodie offendatur, si quando similia contingant, quando ea mundi natura est, ut in piorum interitu suam felicitatem sitam esse existimet. Quo tamen iudicio infelicissimè fallitur. Itaenim seipsum salutari precum præsidio spoliat, quas pij pro inimicis etiam fundere consueuerunt. At quid (inquis) faciendum erit, si quando simili casu ipsi quoq; tentemur? Paulum imitare, in quo duo potissimum obseruabis. Nam & vocationem suam constantissimè tuetur, & simul periculum prudenter amolitur. Ita nos quoq; vocationis nostræ ante omnia meminisse oportet, ne ab hac propter mundi ingratitudinem nos dimoueri patiamur. Cur enim huius obliti, eos imitemur, quorum impios mores detestari consueuimus? Interim circumspe&i simus, & iuxta Christi consilium caueamus nobis ab hominibus, ne temere nos periculis obijcientes, Deum tentare dicamur. Vide Matth.10.
units.tr: But returning to Paul, let us see what he suffered on this journey. The Jews laid a plot against him as he was about to sail for Syria, since they wished him removed from the midst. Nevertheless he wisely evaded these snares: he changed his plan and, by making his way on foot through Macedonia, went on to Syria. This passage teaches what thanks ministers of the truth receive in the world. Clearly it is a very wicked return, when those men wish these men to perish, whose salvation they most diligently watch over. For that Paul was very anxious for the Jews is attested both by the whole course of his labours and by his letters, especially what he writes in Romans chapters 9 and 10. Yet he felt that no enemies were more hostile to him. That Moses also, and the prophets, and the Son of God himself, Jesus Christ, experienced this very thing, we have said elsewhere. Let no one therefore take offence today if similar things happen, since such is the nature of the world that it thinks its happiness lies in the destruction of the godly. Yet in this judgment it is most unhappily mistaken. For it deprives itself of the protection of prayers, which the godly are accustomed to pour out even for their enemies. But what (you may ask) must be done if at some time we ourselves are tested by a similar case? Imitate Paul, in whom you will observe two things above all. For he most steadfastly maintains his calling, and at the same time prudently averts the danger. So we too must above all remember our calling, and not allow ourselves to be moved from it on account of the ingratitude of the world. For why, forgetful of this, should we imitate those whose wicked ways we are accustomed to detest? Meanwhile let us be circumspect, and according to Christ's counsel beware of men, lest by rashly exposing ourselves to dangers we be said to tempt God (see Matthew 10).

units.la: Quid verò Deus interea rerum agit? Num periclitantem seruum suum negligit? Minimè gentium. Imò cùm illi à cognatis Iudæis simul & falsis fratribus (ut ipse alibi conqueritur, 2. Cor. 11.) insidiæ struerentur, Deus eidem fidos laborum & periculorum socios atq; comites adiungit, qui periclitantem suo tum consilio tum auxilio iuuarent. Numerantur autem septem præstantissimi ex diuersis ecclesijs viri, quorum multa fit in Paulinis epistolis mentio. Accessit his octauus Lucas præsentis historiæ scriptor. Et horum quidem alij precedunt, nimirum ut exploratis rebus omnibus tuta Paulo hospitia præparet, alij verò ipsi indiuulse adhærent, ut sua præsentia illum consolentur, ac necessarijs officijs subleuent. Est hic diligenti obseruatione digna Dei fides & bonitas, qua suis periclitantibus adesse, & ijs qui pro sui nominis gloria aliquid audent, fidos laborum & periculorum socios adiungere consueuit. Ita Iofepho Christi corpus ad sepulturam poscenti Nicodemus additur, qui & sumptuum & laboris periculi, partem cum illo sustineat. At hodie de aliorum quidem socordia vel perfidia querimur, nosq; solos causæ Christi pondus ferre posse negamus, ipsi interea non minus socordes & ignaui. Quòd si officium facere libeat, mox aliorum quoq; corda diminitus tangi videbimus. Habemus præterea in Pauli comitibus insigne pietatis & gratitudinis exemplum. Quanti laboris enim & periculi res fuerit Paulum per terras & maria comitari, quem tot vndiq; hostes premebant, cuius conijcere promptum est. At omnibus istis ab illo diuelli nequeunt, qui fidei donum, quod Paulo doctore ipsis obtigerat, rectè æstimabant. Nec carent isti suo præmio in terris, quando illorum nomina Deus æternæ memoriæ consecrare voluit, quorum animæ nunc procul dubio in cœlis cum Christo gaudent, cuius ministrum tam officiose deduxerunt. Prædicat hoc pij animi officium in Galatis quoq; apostolus, quos nec oculis quidem parsuros fuisse scribit, si illis opus habuisset. Sed ò tur-pem nostri seculi ingratitudinem, quæ eòusq; progressa est, ut qui fide gloriantur, illorum nomina fe-dis conuiciis lacerent, quorum opera & ministerio sidem primùm didicerunt. Soletur tamen nos Dei fides & bonitas, qui suo præsidio nunquam eos destituet, quos ad vitæ cœlestis hæreditatem adoptauit in filio suo Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But what, meanwhile, is God doing? Does he neglect his servant in peril? By no means. Indeed, when snares were being laid for him both by his kinsmen the Jews and by false brethren (as he himself complains elsewhere, 2 Corinthians 11), God attached to him faithful companions in toils and dangers, who might help the one in peril both by their counsel and by their assistance. Seven outstanding men from various churches are enumerated, of whom there is much mention in Paul's letters. To these an eighth was added, Luke, the writer of the present history. Some of them went ahead, namely to prepare safe lodgings for Paul once all matters had been explored; others attached themselves to him inseparably, so that by their presence they might console him and relieve him by necessary services. Here is the faith and goodness of God, worthy of careful observation, by which he is accustomed to be present with his people in peril, and to join faithful companions in labours and dangers to those who venture something for the glory of his name. So Nicodemus was added to Joseph when he asked for Christ's body for burial, to bear with him a share of the expense, the labour and the danger. Yet today we complain of the sloth or treachery of others, and deny that we alone can bear the weight of Christ's cause, while we ourselves are no less slothful and idle. But if we are willing to perform our duty, we shall soon see the hearts of others also touched by God. Moreover we have among Paul's companions a notable example of piety and gratitude. How great a matter of labour and danger it was to accompany Paul over lands and seas, whom so many enemies pressed on every side, is easy to conjecture. Yet they could not be torn away from him by any of these things, since they rightly valued the gift of faith that they had received through Paul as teacher. Nor do they lack their reward on earth, since God has willed to consecrate their names to eternal memory, while their souls now without doubt rejoice in heaven with Christ, whose minister they so dutifully escorted. The apostle also commends this dutiful spirit among the Galatians, to whom he writes that they would not have spared even their eyes, had he needed them (Galatians 4). But alas for the shameful ingratitude of our age, which has advanced so far that those who boast of their faith tear to pieces with foul abuse the names of those through whose labour and ministry they first learned the faith. Yet the faith and goodness of God comfort us, who will never abandon with his protection those whom he has adopted into the inheritance of heavenly life in his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXII.
units.tr: HOMILY 132.

units.la: Vno autem die sabbatorum, cùm conuenirent discipuli ad frangen-dum panem, Paulus disserebat eis, profecturus postridie, protraxitq; sermonem vsq; ad mediam noctem. Erant autem lucernæ multæ in cœnaculo, vbi erant congregati. Sedens autem quidam adolescens, nomine Eutychus, in fenestra, cùm degrauaretur somno profundo, disserente diu Paulo, magis depressus somno decidit ex tertio cœnaculo deorsum, & sublatus est mortuus. Cùm descendisset autem Paulus, incubuit super eum, & complexus dixit: Ne turbemini, anima enim eius in ipso est. Cùm verò ascendisseт, fregisseтq panem & degustasset, diu collocutus vsq; ad diluculum, ita profectus est. Adduxerunt autem puerum viuentem, & refocillati sunt non mediocriter. Nos autem conscensa nauí soluimus Asson, inde excepturi Paulum: sic enim ordinauerat, ipse per terram iter facturus. Cùm autem conuenissemus Asson, recepto eo venimus in Mitylenem, & inde nauigantes sequenti die venimus contra Chium. Postridie verò appulimus Samum, & commorati Trogylij proximo die venimus Miletum. Propositum enim erat Paulus praeternauigare Ephesum, ne tempus tereret in Asia. Festinabat enim, si possibile sibi esset, vt diem Pentecostes ageret Hierosolymis.
units.tr: On the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached to them, since he was to leave the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where they were gathered. A young man named Eutychus was sitting in a window, and as he sank into a deep sleep while Paul talked on and on, he fell from the third storey to the ground and was picked up dead. Paul went down, threw himself upon him, embraced him and said: "Do not be troubled, for his life is in him." Then he went back up, broke the bread, ate, and talked with them until dawn, and so he departed. They brought the boy home alive, and they were not a little comforted. We went on board the ship and sailed to Assos, intending to take Paul on board there, for he had so arranged it, intending to go by land himself. When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene, and from there, sailing on the next day, we came opposite Chios. On the following day we put in at Samos, and after staying at Trogyllium, on the next day we came to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so as not to waste time in Asia, for he was hurrying, if it were possible for him, to keep the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem.

units.la: Postquàm Diuus Paulus Ephesi omnia ea confecit, quae ad ecclesiae illius constitutionem faciebant, ante conceptum animo suo peregrinationis consilium executus est, in qua Macedoniae & Graciae ecclesias inuisit, & eosdem in vera fide confirmauit. Vidimus illic praeclara apostolicae fidei & industriae argumenta, quando Paulus nullos labores & nulla pericula subterfugit, vt ecclesias vel acquirere, vel acquisitas feruare posset. Tandem verò Troadem delatus est, vbi peculiaria quaedam acciderunt, in quorum descriptione diligenter admodum Lucas versatur. Et primò quidem ecclesiastici coetus exemplum, deinde verò miraculum, quo Pauli ministerium Deus illic loci graues haud dubiè ob causas exornare & commendare voluit, commemorat.
units.tr: After the divine Paul had completed at Ephesus everything that contributed to the establishing of that church, he carried out the plan for a journey he had conceived in his mind, in which he visited the churches of Macedonia and Greece and confirmed them in the true faith. We have seen there clear proofs of apostolic faith and diligence, since Paul shrank from no labours and no dangers, so that he might either gain churches or keep those he had gained. At last he was brought to Troas, where certain particular things happened, in describing which Luke is very careful. First he records an example of the church assembly, and then a miracle, by which God, for weighty reasons no doubt, wished to adorn and commend Paul's ministry in that place.

units.la: Ecclesiasticum coetum cum omnibus illius circumstantijs diligentissimè describit: Et à tempore quidem exorsus, hunc sabbati die conuenisse dicit, qui nimirum propter veterem morem tunc temporis adhuc celebrior habebatur. Postea verò, vbi magis auctae fuerunt ecclesiae, proximus à sabbato dies rebus sacris destinatus, & ob dominicae resurrectionis memoriam Dominicus dictus est. Admonemur autem hoc loco, minimè negligi debere à Christianis hominibus dies ab ipso Deo religioni destinatos. Nec enim propter externum modo cultum hic opus est, verumetiam propter internum, qui corpore & animo à prophanis negotijs vacante, in diuini verbi studio & beneficiorum Dei diligenti meditatione cumprimis consistit. Quae causa est, quòd sabbati prophanatores capitis poena Deus coercere iussit. Vide Num.15. Et quòd eiusdem prophanatio apud prophetas inter grauissima scelera, adeoque inter captiuitatis Babylonicae causas numeratur. Vt non temere huius religiosam observationem tam serio Nehemias sibi tuendam esse putauerit, cùm è Babylone redijssent. Nehem.13. Quo etiam Christi exemplum pertinet, qui ve sabbatis synagogas frequenter ingressus est, ita non semel de vero illius diei vsu summa diligentia disseruit, vt illum à superstitione simul & prophano contemptu vindicaret. Deinde locum quoq; indicat, vbi coetus iste coiuerit. Fuit is Coenaculum quodam in priuatâ fidelis alicuius domo, qui hoc ecclesiae dicatum esse voluit, cùm ab idololatrarum templis Christiani meritò abhorrerent, interim illius publicus locus negaretur, dominantibus passim Romanorum praesidibus, qui à religione Christiana vel alieni, vel aperti illius hostes erant. Lucernas verò plurimas in Coenaculo illo accensas fuisse dicit, nimirum vt noctis tenebrae discuterentur, nec aliqua daretur turpitudinis suspicio. Ridiculus ergo illorum error est, qui κακοζηλίᾳ seu stulta aemulatione decepti inter cultus diuini officia referunt, quod olim necessitati seruiuit, & Deum qui lux aeterna est, lucernis sebaceis aut ceraeis coli putant, & ad sui figmenti defensionem tum hoc loco tum Mosaicae legis exemplo abutuntur. Hic enim diserte exprimitur nocturnum tempus, quo lucernas accendi opus est. Et eandem ob causam posteà quoq; lucernis in suis coetibus vsi sunt Christiani, cùm illis propter insidias hostium non nisi aucte lucanis horis conuenire liceret, sicuti ex Plinij Secundi epistolis & scriptoribus ecclesiasticis colligere licet. Quae causa cùm sublata fit, stultum fuerit diurnam lucem adiuuare velle lucernis arte factis. Longè aliam verò candelabri Leuitici rationem fuisse constat. Vt enim omnes eius sacerdotij ceremoniae typos rerum, quas Christus perficere debebat, gesserunt, & ad solum correctionis tempus fuerunt instituta: ita candelabrum quoq; Christi typus fuit, qui vera & aeterna mundi lux est, quiq; per euangelij ministerium ecclesiam suam illuminat, qua ratione apostoli, & qui legitimi veriq; horum successores sunt, lux mundi dicuntur. Matth.5. Interim docemur, ad externum cultum coetusq; sacros certis locis opus esse, quales in veteri Testamento templum & synagogæ fuerunt: qualia item post apostolorum tempora, stabilitiùs iam aliquantulum ecclesiæ ri‑bus Oratoria extrui cæperunt. In his verò honestati & religioni omnia seruire debent, nec aliquid fe‑rendum, quod vel superstitionem, vel luxum nimium, vel apertam prophanationem referat. Tertiò conuentus huius causam exprimit, dum illos ad frangendum panem conuenisse scribit. Intelligitur autem sancta domini Cœna, quam panis fractionem olim vocarunt, quòd in ea panis ex domini insti‑tuto frangitur, tum vt nos peccatores & Christi mortis reos esse confiteamur, tum vt Christi meri‑tum in nos distribui, & ad omnes credentes ex æquo pertinere intelligamus. Est autem obseruatione dignissimus ritus & ordo Cœnæ, quo veteres apostolorum tempore vsos fuisse hoc loco docemur. Pri‑mò omnium concionem sacram Paulus habuit, vt sequentia docent, quando post refusitatum Eutychum demum Cœna perasta est. Quare finita demum concione sacra hanc celebrarunt, & quidem in publico cœtu, loco & tempore sacris destinato, nec alio ritu, quàm qui à domino traditus fuerat. Illum enim per omnia seruatum fuisse, tum fractionis panis vocabulum, tum Pauli exemplum docet, qui Corinthios tam anxiè ad formam Cœnæ à Christo traditam, reuocauit. Ita verò Christum quoq; do‑ctrinam Cœnæ præmisisse constat, nec quicquam tradidisse, quod superstitioni potius quàm religioni seruiat. Videant ergo quibus vel rationibus vel exemplis Missam suam Papistæ tueantur, in qua doctrina verbi planè silet, lingua peregrina agitur omnia, populus præter frigidas & ineptas ge‑sticulationes & theatricam saltationem nihil habet quod suspiciat vel meditetur: vt interim de eo nihil dicamus, quòd per hanc Christi sacrificium euacuatur, eiusdem merito derogatur, & tota Chri‑sti religio atq; fides ab ipsis fundamentis euertitur. Sed ita seduci oportet eos, qui suæ potius rationi figmenta sequi, quàm Christi institutionem retinere volunt. Porrò ad cœtus ecclesiastici descriptio‑nem concionandi quoq; modus, à Paulo obseruatus, pertinet, quem ex tempore conijcere licet. Primò enim ad mediam noctem vsq; sermonem protraxisse, inde Cœna perasta, ad diluculum vsque de rebus pietati seruientibus disseruisse dicitur. Non ergo perfunctorie & quasi aliud agens, sed magno cum zelo & diligentia docuit. Quia enim de ministerio suo rectè iudicabat, seq; Christi nomine à Deo lega‑tum misum esse nouerat (sicuti in posteriori ad Corinth. 5. cap. testatur) non potuit non ardenti zelo flagrare, ne male fidei legatus apud Deum haberetur. Simul verò auditores quoq; tam de Pauli mi‑nisterio quàm de doctrina eiusdem rectè iudicauisse constat, quando tam patienter tota nocte docen‑tem audire dignati sunt. Arguitur exemplo hoc nostri seculi vecordia & immanis verbi Dei contem‑ptus. Nec enim in ministris zeli illius apostolici vestigia apparent, quando plerique inanibus potius fa‑dijs, quàm verbi Dei meditatione occupantur, & tunc sese suo officio probè functos esse existimant, si semel aut iterum in septimana quàm frigidissimè concionati fuerint. Rursum populus quoque au‑diendi impatiens, omnem moram nimiam putat, quæcunq; verbo Dei impenditur, cùm interim in le‑uissimis, imò turpissimis studijs, nullius illum vel temporis vel sumptus & laboris pigeat. Hinc fit, quòd & collapsa iacet ministerij authoritas, & verbum Dei à multis aufertur. Vide quid de vtroq; malo dominus dicat apud Malachiam 2. cap. & Amos 3. &c.
units.tr: Luke describes the church assembly with all its circumstances most carefully. Beginning with the time, he says that they met on the day of the Sabbath, which, of course, because of the old custom, was then still held in greater honour. Later, when the churches had grown, the day next after the Sabbath was set apart for sacred purposes and, in memory of the Lord's resurrection, was called the Lord's Day. We are reminded here that Christians ought by no means to neglect the days that God himself has set apart for worship. For there is need not only of outward worship but also of inward, which chiefly consists, with body and mind free from secular business, in the study of the divine word and the diligent meditation on God's benefits. This is why God commanded that those who profaned the Sabbath be punished with death; see Num. 15. And why the profaning of it is counted among the gravest sins by the prophets, and so among the causes of the Babylonian captivity. So Nehemiah thought it must be guarded so seriously with religious observance once they had returned from Babylon; Nehem. 13. To this also belongs the example of Christ, who often entered the synagogues on the Sabbaths, and who more than once expounded with the greatest care the true use of that day, so as to defend it from superstition and at the same time from profane contempt. Next he also indicates the place where that assembly met. It was an upper room in the private house of a certain believer, who wished it to be dedicated to the church, since Christians rightly shrank from the temples of idolaters, while a public place was refused them, because the Roman governors, who were either strangers or open enemies of the Christian religion, held sway everywhere. He says that very many lamps were lit in that upper room, namely so that the darkness of the night might be dispelled and no suspicion of shameful conduct might arise. Ridiculous, therefore, is the error of those who, deceived by foolish zeal [κακοζηλίᾳ], count among the rites of divine worship what once served a need, and think that God, who is eternal light, is honoured with tallow or wax lamps, and who abuse both this place and the example of the Mosaic law to defend their invention. For here it is plainly stated that it was night-time, when lamps must be lit. And for the same reason Christians afterwards also used lamps in their assemblies, since, because of the plots of their enemies, they could meet only in the late hours, as may be gathered from the letters of Pliny the Younger and from the ecclesiastical writers. When that reason has been removed, it would be foolish to want to help the daylight with lamps made by art. It is clear that the reason for the Levitical candlestick was quite different. For just as all the ceremonies of that priesthood bore the types of the things that Christ was to accomplish, and were instituted only for the time of correction, so the candlestick was also a type of Christ, who is the true and eternal light of the world, and who illumines his church through the ministry of the gospel; in this way the apostles, and those who are their lawful and true successors, are called the light of the world; Matth. 5. Meanwhile we are taught that for outward worship and sacred assemblies there is need of fixed places, such as the temple and the synagogues were in the Old Testament, and such as, after the times of the apostles, buildings for the church began to be erected more firmly, and so oratories. In these places everything ought to serve honesty and religion, and nothing is to be tolerated that smacks of superstition, excessive luxury, or open profanation. Thirdly, he states the purpose of this gathering, when he writes that they came together to break bread. By this is meant the holy Supper of the Lord, which they once called the breaking of bread, because in it the bread is broken according to the Lord's institution, both so that we may confess that we are sinners and guilty of Christ's death, and so that we may understand that the merit of Christ is distributed to us and pertains equally to all believers. The rite and order of the Supper, which we are taught the ancients used in the time of the apostles here, is most worthy of observation. First of all Paul gave the sacred sermon, as what follows shows, since the Supper was finished only after Eutychus was restored to life. Therefore, when the sacred sermon was finished, they celebrated it, and indeed in a public assembly, at a place and time set apart for sacred use, and not by any other rite than that which had been handed down by the Lord. For that it was kept in every respect is shown both by the name "breaking of bread" and by the example of Paul, who so anxiously recalled the Corinthians to the form of the Supper delivered by Christ. Thus it is clear that Christ also set the teaching about the Supper before it, and handed down nothing that serves superstition rather than religion. Let those, then, consider with what reasons or examples the Papists defend their Mass, in which the word of doctrine is entirely silent, everything is done in a foreign tongue, and the people have nothing to look up to or ponder, except cold and silly gestures and theatrical dancing; to say nothing for the moment of the fact that through it the sacrifice of Christ is made void, his merit is detracted from, and the whole religion and faith of Christ is overturned from its foundations. But those ought to be led astray who want to follow their own reasoning in inventions rather than keep the institution of Christ. Moreover, to the description of the ecclesiastical assembly pertains also the manner of preaching observed by Paul, which may be conjectured from the time. For he is said first to have prolonged the sermon until midnight, then, after the Supper was finished, to have discoursed until dawn on matters serving piety. He therefore taught not carelessly and as if doing something else, but with great zeal and diligence. For since he judged rightly about his ministry, and knew that he had been sent by God as an ambassador in the name of Christ (as he testifies in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 5), he could not but burn with ardent zeal, lest he be held by God as an ambassador who had been unfaithful. At the same time it is clear that the hearers also judged rightly both about Paul's ministry and about his doctrine, since they deigned to listen so patiently to him teaching all night. By this example is shown the madness and monstrous contempt of God's word in our age. For traces of that apostolic zeal do not appear in ministers, since most of them are occupied with empty fables rather than with meditation on God's word, and think they have discharged their office well if they have preached, once or twice a week, as coldly as possible. Again the people, impatient of hearing, think every delay too long that is spent on God's word, while in the lightest, indeed the most shameful, pursuits, none of them is troubled by any expense of time, money or labour. Hence it comes about that the authority of the ministry lies fallen and the word of God is taken away from many. See what the Lord says about both evils in Malachi chapter 2 and Amos chapter 3, etc.

units.la: Sequitur miraculum, quo Deus Pauli ministerium approbare, simulq; omnes homines ad diligen‑tem apostolicæ doctrinæ considerationem excitare voluit. In cuius prima parte Eutychus considera‑tur, in cuius persona editum fuit. Is concionante Paulo in fenestra considerat dicitur, vel quòd tanta tamq; conferta esset auditorum multitudo, vt sedes nulla alia vacaret, vel quòd somnum, quò‑se oppugnari sentiebat, ita vitare & superare voluit. Attamen tandem superatus decidit, & ex ca‑su moritur. Quòd si verò hoc illi euenit, cuius somnolentia multis rationibus excusari potest, quid il‑lis euenturum putamus, qui verbum contemptim audiunt, & dum illud audire videntur, vel data opera sese ad somnum componunt, vel poculis & crapula obruti dormire coguntur? Hi enim vt sua salutis negligentes sunt, ita Dei maiestatem non magni faciunt. Quare fieri non potest, quin ad mo‑tem illis cedat euangelij prædicatio, quæ attentis & credentibus salutis ministra est. Simul autem docemur hoc loco, permittere aliquando Deum, vt triflissimis casibus sui tententur. Quid enim obsecro accidere poterat, quod Pauli doctrinam magis suspectam redderet, quando illius studium tam trifli casu turbatur? Quanta item apostolo inuidia conflari potuit, vt qui sermonis prolixitate tanti mali author fuerit? Sed non deest suis dominus, quin mox insigni miraculo docet, euangelio salutem offerri, sic vt huic confirmando seruiat, quod illi omnino aduersum videri poterat. Discamus ergo re‑ac in‑ Ite iudicare de omnibus aduersis, quae incidunt. Immittit ea, ut terreat Deus, & ut potentiam suam exercendi occasione habeat. Patiêter ergo feramus omnia, nec de agnita Veritate dubitemus. Ita enim fiet, ut lætissimus illorum exitus sit, quorum initium nimis funestum & infelix videbatur, id quod alterà huius miraculi pars evidentissime docebit, ut reliqua exempla omittamus, quae induci poterant.
units.tr: Next comes the miracle, by which God wished both to approve Paul's ministry and to stir all people to a diligent consideration of apostolic doctrine. The first part of it concerns Eutychus, in whose person it was performed. He is said to have been sitting in the window while Paul preached, either because the crowd of hearers was so large and packed that no other seat was free, or because he wanted to fend off and overcome the sleep by which he felt himself attacked. Yet at last, overcome, he fell and died from the fall. But if this happened to him, whose drowsiness can be excused on many grounds, what do we think will happen to those who hear the Word with contempt, and who, while they seem to be listening, either deliberately settle themselves to sleep or are forced to sleep, overwhelmed by drink and gluttony? For just as they are careless of their own salvation, so they do not hold the majesty of God in high regard. Therefore it cannot be that the preaching of the gospel, which is a minister of salvation to the attentive and believing, turns out to their death. At the same time we are taught in this place that God sometimes allows his own to be tried by the most grievous misfortunes. For what, I beg you, could have happened that would make Paul's doctrine more suspect, when his work is disturbed by so sad an accident? How much hatred could be stirred up against the apostle, who through the length of his speech had been the author of so great an evil? But the Lord does not abandon his own; soon, by a remarkable miracle, he shows that salvation is offered by the gospel, so that the very thing which seemed wholly adverse serves to confirm it. Let us therefore learn to judge rightly about all the adversities that befall us. God sends them to terrify us, and to have an occasion of exercising his power. Let us therefore bear everything patiently, and not doubt the truth we have recognised. For so it will happen that the most joyful outcome belongs to those whose beginning seemed too deadly and unhappy, as the second part of this miracle will most clearly teach, to leave aside the other examples that could be brought forward.

units.la: Describit enim deinceps miraculosam Eutychi resuscitationem Lucas, in qua singula, quae Paulus fecit, ordine consideranda sunt. Primò mox, re cognita, descendit ut periclitanti opem ferat, nec quicquam vel sabbati vel Coenae religionem causatur. Minime ergo superstitiosus est, sed Christi doctrinae memor, sabbatum propter hominem institutum esse, & externa omnia charitati cedere debere intelligit. Ineptè ergo, imò impiè superstitiosi sunt, qui in simili necessitate hominum traditiones violare nefas esse ducunt: ut qui monasticis regulis ita astricti sunt, ut ne parentibus quidem periclitantibus opem ferant, quiq; nullam causam satis iustam esse putant, ut Missae sacrificium interturbetur. Deinde super puerum prostratus, illum complectitur, non quòd sui corporis contactu illum vitae restituì posse putaret, sed quòd Christi nomine & virtute, cuius ipse legatum agebat, omne hoc confici oportere sciret. Quare salutis nostrae mysterium hic Pauli gestus continet. Ex superbo enim Adami lapsu in omnes nos peccati noxa & per hanc mors deriuata est. At in Christo nobis per euangelium vita salusq; offertur, cuius consortes erunt, quotquot apostolorum doctrina, quasi vinis attracti per fidem in Christi consortium transeunt. Praeterea trepidantes amicè consolatur. Nè urbemini, inquit. Nec enim temere metuebat (ut supra monuimus) ne infirmorum fides hoc casu graviter concuteretur. Quare mox addit: Anima enim eius in ipso est. Quibus verbis non negat miraculum, sed modestè de illo pronunciat, ne quid sibi ipsi tribuere videatur, neue aliis supra id quàm decet de se sentiendi occasionem praberet. Inde verò mox in Coenaculum reuersus, intermissam Coenae actionem absoluit, & nouum sermonem instituens, ad diluculum usque concionatur, quo orto iter inggreditur. His autem admiranda Pauli sedulitas commendatur, qui tanto edito miraculo adhuc in vocatione sua pergit, nec se iam officio suo per omnia defunctum esse arbitratur, ut ignaui quidam, sed nimium magnifici suorum laborum & operum aestimatores facere consueuerunt. Imitemur nos Pauli studium, eoq; plura nos Deo debere sentiamus, quò maiora virtutis & gratiae ipsius indicia videmus. Subijcit autem miraculo insignem studij huius fructum Lucas. Puerum enim adduxerunt viuentem. Perfecta enim sunt Dei opera, nec quenquam praestigiosis miraculis, ut circulatores solent, luserunt apostoli. Deinde non parum refocillati sunt fideles, non modò ob vitam pueri restitutam, sed quòd tam luculentum diuinae gratiae testimonium sibi propositum viderent. Admirantur autem nobis hoc loco fructus, qui euangelij studium perpetuò comitari solent. Nam & vitam nobis affert, eò quòd euangelium potentia Dei fit ad salutem omni credenti: & animos solido gaudio recreat, dum patrem nobis in filio reconciliatum esse docet. Quod gaudium ut verè solidum est, ita illud nemo nobis aufert repotes. Iohan. 16.
units.tr: Luke then describes the miraculous restoration of Eutychus, in which each thing Paul did must be considered in order. First, as soon as he learned of the accident, he went down at once to bring help to the one in danger, and pleaded nothing about the sabbath or the scruples of the Lord's Supper. He is therefore not superstitious, but mindful of Christ's teaching, he understands that the sabbath was instituted for man, and that all outward things ought to give way to charity. Those therefore are foolish, or rather impiously superstitious, who think it wrong to break human traditions in a similar necessity: such as those bound so tightly by monastic rules that they do not bring help even to their parents when they are in danger, and who think no cause sufficiently just to disturb the sacrifice of the Mass. Then, throwing himself upon the boy, he embraces him, not because he thought that by contact with his body he could restore him to life, but because he knew that all this had to be done in the name and power of Christ, whose envoy he was. Therefore this gesture of Paul contains the mystery of our salvation. For from Adam's proud fall, the harm of sin, and death derived through sin, has come upon all of us. But in Christ life and salvation are offered to us through the gospel, and all who, drawn as if by cords through faith, pass into fellowship with Christ by the doctrine of the apostles will be partakers of it. Moreover, he consoles the trembling kindly: "Do not be troubled," he says. For he was not rashly afraid (as we noted above) that the faith of the weak might be gravely shaken by this accident. Therefore he immediately adds: "For his soul is in him." By these words he does not deny the miracle, but speaks modestly about it, lest he seem to attribute something to himself, or give others occasion to think of him more highly than is fitting. Then, returning at once to the upper room, he finished the interrupted celebration of the Supper, and beginning a new sermon, he preached until daybreak, and when dawn came he set out on his journey. Here Paul's remarkable diligence is commended, for after so great a miracle he still persists in his calling, and does not think that he has now discharged his duty in every respect, as some idle yet excessively self-important judges of their own labours and works are accustomed to do. Let us imitate Paul's zeal, and let us feel that we owe God all the more, the more great signs of his virtue and grace we see. Luke then attaches to the miracle a notable fruit of this zeal: "They brought the boy alive." For the works of God are perfect, nor did the apostles mock anyone with showy miracles, as jugglers are wont to do. Then the faithful were not a little refreshed, not only because the boy's life was restored, but because they saw set before them so brilliant a testimony of divine grace. The fruits which usually accompany the study of the gospel are admirable here. For it both brings us life, since the gospel is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, and it refreshes our souls with solid joy, while it teaches that the Father has been reconciled to us in the Son. As this joy is truly solid, so no one takes it from us, as is said in Iohan. 16.

units.la: Porrò redit ad Pauli professionem describendam Euangelista, ordine vrbes & locos recensens, quos vel praeteruectus fuerunt, vel in quibus moram traxerunt aliquam. Quorum situm si quis scire cupit, Geographorum libros & tabulas consulat. Ex Troade verò Paulus Assos usque per terras iter fecisse dicitur, nauigio praemissis suis comitibus. Ipse enim vel ecclesias in transitu videre, vel nauigandi fastidium vitare voluit. Vbi tamen humanitas eius laudem meretur, quòd suos labore leuat, nec illorum induistria abutitur. Tandem Ephesum quoque praeterueetus Miletum venit, quò Asiae ministros ad Synodum euocauit. Summam verò festinationis rationem illum habuisse scribitur, eò quòd Pentecosten Hierosolymis agere cuperet, non quidem Iudaico ritu, sed propter hominum frequentiam, in qua se cum magno fructu praedicaturum sperabat. E S Tautem memorabilis omnino locus hic, qui Pauli labores & pericula continet. Quibus admonemur quàm ardua res sit, Deo ritè seruire, qui nihil minus quàm otiosos & ignauos cultores ferre potest. Ita enim Abraham, Isaacum, Iacobum, Mosen, prophetas, & postea hos ipsum Christum assiduis laboribus & periculis fatigatos esse legimus. Ad labores ergo & pericula ipsi quoq; praeparemur, ne ex improuiso iruentibus offendamur. Admonet praeterea locus hic, quanta apud nos esse debeat euangelij auctoritas, quod tantis laboribus tantoq; sanguine propagatum esse constat. Propter hoc enim laborarunt omnes apostoli, & ante hos prophetae, & ipse Dei filius, qui se ad euangelizandum quoq; venisse testatur. tur. Marc.1 .Luc.4. Execrabilis ergo illorum ignauia est, qui thesaurum tantum sibi tam facile eripi patiuntur. Præpostera item est illorum religio, qui cùm Diuos & horum cultum nunquam non in ore habeant, interim euangelij doctrinam fastidiunt, cuius nomine Dei omnes tot labores suffere, tot pericula subire, & tandem vitam & sanguinem profundere voluerunt. Recte ergo æstimemus Thesaurum hunc ô fratres, in quo solo salus offertur, cuius nobis author est Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next the evangelist returns to describing Paul's journey, listing in order the cities and places which they either passed by or where they stayed for some time. If anyone wishes to know their location, let him consult the books and maps of the geographers. From Troas, Paul is said to have made the journey to Assos on foot, his companions having been sent ahead by ship. For he wished either to visit the churches on the way, or to avoid the weariness of sailing. Here, however, his kindness deserves praise, in that he relieves his companions' labour and does not take advantage of their diligence. At last, passing by Ephesus as well, he came to Miletus, where he summoned the ministers of Asia to a synod. It is written that he had a most serious reason for haste: he wished to keep Pentecost at Jerusalem, not indeed in the Jewish manner, but because of the crowd of people, among whom he hoped to preach with great fruit. This place is altogether memorable, for it contains Paul's labours and dangers. By these we are admonished how hard a thing it is to serve God rightly, since he can bear nothing less than idle and lazy worshippers. For thus we read that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the prophets, and afterwards Christ himself, were worn out by constant labours and dangers. Let us therefore prepare ourselves also for labours and dangers, lest we be offended when they fall upon us unexpectedly. This place further admonishes us how great the authority of the gospel ought to be among us, since, as is well known, it was spread abroad with such labours and such blood. For this all the apostles laboured, and before them the prophets, and the Son of God himself, who testifies that he came also to preach the gospel: Marc. 1. Luc. 4. Therefore the sloth of those is detestable who suffer such a treasure to be so easily snatched from them. Perverse too is the religion of those who, while always having the saints and their worship on their lips, meanwhile despise the doctrine of the gospel, for whose sake all those men wished to endure so many labours, undergo so many dangers, and at last pour out their life and blood. Let us therefore rightly value this treasure, brothers, in which alone salvation is offered, and of which Jesus Christ is the author, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 133.

units.la: A Mileto autem missis Ephesum nuntijs, accersiuit Seniores ecclesiæ. Qui cùm peruenirent ad ipsum, dixit eis: Vos scitis à primo die, quo ingressus sum Asiam, quomodo vobiscum per omne tempus fuerim, seruiens domino cum omni animi humilitate, cumq; multis lachrymis & tentationibus, quæ mihi acciderunt ex insidijs Iudæorum: vt nihil suffugerim eorum, quæ essent in rem vestram, quin vobis annuntiarem & docerem vos publicè & per singulas domos, testificans Iudæis simul & Græcis eam quæ erga Deum est pœnitentiam, & fidem quæ est in dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Sending from Miletus to Ephesus, he called the elders of the church to him. When they had come to him, he said to them: "You know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you the whole time, serving the Lord with all humility of mind, with many tears and trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews; how I kept back nothing that was profitable to you, but declared it to you and taught you publicly and from house to house, testifying to both Jews and Greeks repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: Apostolorum domini Iesu Christi res gestas summa diligentia per Lucam diuinum scriptorem spiritus sanctus commemorat. partim quidem, vt exemplar habeant omnes ministri quod imitentur: partim verò vt omnes intelligant quanta merito apud nos esse debeat euangelij authoritas, quod illi tot tantisq; laboribus propagauerunt. Et huc quidem præsens etiam Pauli apostoli actio referri debet, qui licet Hierosolymam quàm maximè festinaret, nec tempus vellet terere in Asia, nihil tamen eorum intermisit, quæ ad ecclesiarum Asiæ salutem faciebant. Ad se enim Miletum vsq; Ephesiorum & vicinarum vrbium Seniores siue antistites euocat, & in generali Synodo cum illis de rebus maximis transigit. Quo exemplo vt Pauli fides & industria elucet: ita admonemur necessarios omnino esse ministrorum cœtus, in quibus ecclesiæ res communibus omnium suffragijs tractentur. Facit hoc ad retinendam ecclesiarum disciplinam, ad cohercendam ambitionem antistiium, ad seruandum in vera doctrina consensum, & ad reprimendas hæreses, quæ frequenter (nisi suas operas ministri fidelissimè coniungant) obrepere consueuerunt. Ideò supra quoque eorum error, qui legis operâ cum fide in Christum miscebant, generali Synodo explosus, & eiusdem authoritate veritas asserta est. Quò respexisse videtur pijssimus idemq; prudentissimus Imperator Constantinus Magnus, dum episcoporum Synodos frequenter conuocauit, quibus è contra acerrimè obstitit fidei Christiane publicus hostis Licinius, quem publicis edictis cauisse Eusebius tradit, ne ecclesiarum ministri aliquos conuentus agerent. Videbat enim astutissimus nequam, ministrorum consensu ecclesias & fidei verae professionem quàm maximè seruari, illum verò Synodorum authoritate cumprimis retineri. Nec minori astutia Antichristus Synodorum authoritatem omnem penes se esse voluit, ne legitimè congregatis Synodis ipsius tyrannis cohercari posset. Simul verò in Asiæ ministris præclarum modestiæ exemplum proponitur, qui licet plures essent numero, vnius tamen Pauli imperium minimè detrectant, qui primus in illis locis Christum prædicarat, quemq; selectum Christi organum esse multis indicijs compertum habebant. Licet enim vna eademq; sit omnium ministrorum ecclesiæ dignitas, nec quisquam in alios sibi imperium siue tyrannidem vendicare debeat, necessarius tamen in ecclesia ordo est, qui nisi inter se humilitate & modestia ministri certent, nunquam conseruari potest. Nec ideò Asianos hosce ad se Paulus euocauit, quòd sibi in illos priuatam aliquam authoritatem siue imperium vendicaret, sed quia illos de rebus maximis admoneri totius ecclesiæ interest, quaiure suum officium illis negare noluit, cùm se (vt alibi fatetur) omnibus, tum Iudæis tum gentibus, debitorem esse sciret. Rom.1.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit, through Luke the divine writer, records with the greatest care the deeds of the apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ: partly so that all ministers may have an example to imitate, and partly so that all may understand how great the authority of the gospel ought rightly to be among us, since the apostles spread it with so many and such great labours. This present action of the apostle Paul should also be referred to this purpose. Although he was in the greatest haste to reach Jerusalem and did not want to waste time in Asia, he still omitted none of the things that served the welfare of the churches of Asia. For he summoned to himself at Miletus the elders, or bishops, of Ephesus and of the neighbouring cities, and in a general synod dealt with them on the most important matters. By this example, as Paul's faith and diligence shine forth, so we are reminded that assemblies of ministers are absolutely necessary, in which the affairs of the church are handled by the common vote of all. This serves to maintain church discipline, to restrain the ambition of bishops, to preserve agreement in true doctrine, and to suppress heresies, which usually creep in unless ministers faithfully join their labours. Therefore also above, the error of those who mixed the works of the law with faith in Christ was driven out by a general synod, and the truth was affirmed by its authority. To this the most pious and at the same time most prudent emperor Constantine the Great seems to have looked, when he frequently convened synods of bishops, against which the public enemy of the Christian faith, Licinius, most fiercely set himself. Eusebius reports that Licinius guarded by public edicts against the ministers of the churches holding any assemblies. For that most crafty wretch saw that the churches and the profession of the true faith would be kept most effectively by the agreement of ministers, and that he himself would be especially hindered by the authority of synods. With no less cunning, Antichrist wanted all the authority of synods to be in his own hands, so that his tyranny could not be checked by synods lawfully gathered. At the same time, a notable example of modesty is set before the ministers of Asia: although they were more in number, they did not refuse the rule of Paul alone, who had first preached Christ in those places and whom they knew, by many signs, to be the chosen instrument of Christ. For although the dignity of all ministers of the church is one and the same, and no one ought to claim for himself dominion or tyranny over others, yet there is a necessary order in the church, which can never be maintained unless the ministers vie with one another in humility and modesty. Nor did Paul summon these men of Asia because he claimed for himself some private authority or dominion over them, but because it concerned the whole church that they be warned about the most important matters; and he was unwilling to deny them his duty, since he knew himself to be a debtor (as he confesses elsewhere) to all, both Jews and Gentiles. Rom. 1.

units.la: Porrò Pauli orationem videamus, quæ causas conuocatæ Synodi continet. Habet enim exhortationem grauem & vehementem, vt quando ipsum non amplius visuri sint, exemplum ipsius imitentur,
units.tr: Let us now look at Paul's address, which contains the reasons for the synod that was convened. For it contains a grave and vehement exhortation: that, since they were not going to see him again, they should imitate his example,

units.la: Argumentum Orationis Pauli Synodicæ. tentur, & abs se traditam doctrinam constanter retineant, pro ecclesiarum salute sedulò inuigilent, & hæreticis (qui plurimi simul & nocentissimi oriturí sint) fortiter resistant. Suo autem exemplo illos liberius hortatur & vrget, quia vt ipse sibi bene conscius erat, ita apud eos sermonem habebat, quibus sua fides & industria erat compertissima. Et initiò quidem paucis tum vitæ suæ exemplum tum doctrinæ suæ summam comprehendit.
units.tr: Argument of Paul's synodal address. ...and hold fast to the doctrine delivered by him, watch diligently for the welfare of the churches, and resist bravely the heretics (who were going to arise in great numbers and be most harmful at the same time). He urges and presses them more freely by his own example, because, as he was well aware of himself, so he spoke to those whose faith and diligence were best known to him. And at the beginning he briefly sums up both the example of his life and the substance of his teaching.

units.la: De vita sua hæc dicit: Vos scitis à primo die, quo ingressus sum Asiam, quomodo vobiscum per omne tempus fuerim, seruiens Domino cum omni animi humilitate, cumq; multis lachrymis & tentationibus quæ mihi acciderunt ex insidijs Iudæorum. Vt verò illos ipsos testes statuit, ita omne tempus suæ inter ipsos conuersationis allegat, ne quis ipsum breui tantummodo tempore pietatis studium simulauisse putaret, quod multi facere consueuerunt, qui vbi egregia virtutis simulatione sese hominum animos insinuauerunt, tandem occultatam aliquandiu animi nequitiam impudentissimè produnt. Nec enim apud improbos diuturna esse potest virtutis simulatio.
