At quia Paulus se totum Christo & pietati consecrauerat, eadem & sibi semper constans fuit vitæ ipsius conuersatio, idemq; semper in obeundo ministerio suo studium. De hoc autem intelligi debet, quod se Domino seruiuisse dicit: vbi tria potissimum allegat, Humilitatem animi, lachrymas quas publicæ salutis studium sibi extorserit, & tentationes graues, quibus tamen nunquam sese ab officio reuocari passus sit. EX his verò discant ecclesiarum ministri, quales ipsos in ecclesiæ ministerio esse conueniat. Et primò quidem bomilitati studeant, ne vel diuina sibi impudenter vendicent (quod Antichristi est.2. Thessal.2.) vel quenquam præ se fastidiant, & Symmystis suis superbè dominentur, de quo Petrus quoq; illos in priori epistola Cap.5. admonet. Decet enim, vt qui Christi ministri esse volunt, Christi exemplu imitentur, qui vt Dei patris gloriæ nihil derogat, ita neminè vnquam fastidiuit, adeò vt peccatoribus quoq; & publicanis familiarissimè conuixerit, & discipulis quoq; pedes abluere dignatus sit, ita extremum illis humilitatis exemplum relicturus, ne aliquod officium detrectare vellent. Humilitati verò publicæ salutis studium accedere debet, quam illos summo animi ardore, imò cum lachrymis quoq; quaerere decet. Nam huius etiam exemplum in Christo habetur, quem totis animi visceribbus comotum fuisse Matth.cap.9. tradit, quando Iudaicum populum instar dispersi gregis & pastore destituti obErrare vidit. Et alibi illum ad ingratæ & sanguinariæ Hierosolymæ conspectum illachrymatuisse legimus, cum illam ob enormia scelera & poenitere nescias metes breui corruituram esse sciret. Luc.19. Eundem charitatis affectum in Mose videmus, qui de libro vitæ potius deleri vult, quam suæ gentis excidium cernere. Exod.32. Eodem Samuel propheta flagrauit, qui cum Saulem à Domino reprobatum esse audiret, seipsum animo excrucians non antea, quàm à Domino corriperetur, lugere destitit. 1. Sam.15. & 16. Nec insolenter hoc ipso affectu Paulum gloriari tum illius fidelis & indefessa in propaganda publica salute industria probat, tum illud conuincit, quòd pro Iudæorum, acerrimorum hostium suorum salute, anathema fieri cupit. Et sanè affectu hoc carere non possunt, quicunq; sui ministerij rationem probè perspectam habent. Quia enim ministerio suo homines regenerari audiunt, filiorum loco habent quoscunq; Christo adduxerunt, & paterno plane affectu illos complecti confuerunt: quo quicunq; carent, nae illi abunde testantur, se ministerij quoq; sui dignitatem ignorare. SED tertium quoq; accedat oporteat, ne videlicet tentationibus succumbant, aut metu superati in persecutionibus ecclesias deferant. Id enim mercenariorum esse, Christus ait. Iohan.10. Imò tunc maximè suæ fidem & constantiam requiri intelligant, quando tum seipsos tum omnes Christi grauissimè tentari vident. Quòd si verò cum Pauli exemplo eos conferas, qui huius successores hodie dici volunt, facilè patebit quàm nihil in illis Paulini pectoris sit, quando immani fastu Barbaros quoq; satrapas superant, bellis omnia miscent, nulla omnium pereuntium miseria tanguntur, deq; vno hoc soliciti sunt, vt sibi suisq; cum publico aliorum malo consulant.
units.tr: Of his life he says this: "You know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you the whole time, serving the Lord with all humility of mind, with many tears and trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews." Just as he makes these men themselves his witnesses, so he claims his whole course of life among them, lest anyone think he had only pretended to zeal for piety for a short time, as many are accustomed to do, who, once they have insinuated themselves into people's minds by a splendid show of virtue, at last shamelessly reveal the wickedness they had hidden for some time. For pretence of virtue cannot last long among the wicked. But because Paul had devoted himself wholly to Christ and to piety, his manner of life was always consistent with itself, and so was his zeal in discharging his ministry at all times. Now this must be understood of what he says, that he served the Lord; where he mentions three things especially: humility of mind, the tears that zeal for the public welfare wrung from him, and the grievous trials by which he nevertheless never allowed himself to be called away from his duty. From these things let the ministers of the churches learn what kind of men they ought to be in the ministry of the church. And first let them strive for humility, so that they do not shamelessly claim divine honours for themselves (which belongs to Antichrist, 2 Thess. 2.), nor despise anyone, nor lord it proudly over their fellow ministers, a matter about which Peter also admonishes them in his first epistle, chapter 5. For those who wish to be ministers of Christ ought to imitate the example of Christ, who, while he detracted nothing from the glory of God the Father, never despised anyone, so that he lived on very familiar terms even with sinners and tax collectors, and deigned even to wash the feet of his disciples, leaving them this supreme example of humility, so that they would not be unwilling to undertake any duty. To humility there ought to be added zeal for the public welfare, which they should seek with the greatest ardour of mind, indeed even with tears. For an example of this too is found in Christ, who, as Matthew chapter 9 tells, was moved in the depths of his heart when he saw the Jewish people wandering like a scattered flock without a shepherd. And elsewhere we read that he wept at the sight of ungrateful and bloodthirsty Jerusalem, since he knew that it would soon fall because of its enormous crimes, which it would not repent of. Luke 19. We see the same affection of love in Moses, who would rather be blotted out of the book of life than see the destruction of his people. Exod. 32. The prophet Samuel burned with the same feeling, who, when he heard that Saul had been rejected by the Lord, tormented himself in mind and did not cease to mourn until he was rebuked by the Lord. 1 Sam. 15 and 16. Nor does Paul boast in this affection without reason: his faithful and tireless diligence in promoting the public welfare proves it, and it is proved also by his wish to be made accursed for the salvation of the Jews, his fiercest enemies. Indeed, those who have a properly clear understanding of their ministry cannot be without this affection. For since they hear that men are regenerated through their ministry, they regard as sons all whom they have brought to Christ, and are accustomed to embrace them with a truly fatherly affection. Those who lack this plainly testify that they do not know the dignity of their own ministry. BUT a third thing must also be added, namely that they must not yield to temptations, or, overcome by fear, desert the churches in persecutions. For Christ says that this is the mark of hired men. John 10. Indeed, they should understand that courage and constancy are required then most of all, when they see both themselves and all Christians most grievously tempted. But if you compare these men with the example of Paul, those who today wish to be called his successors, it will readily appear how little of Paul's spirit is in them: when with monstrous pride they surpass even barbarian satraps, stir up everything with wars, are moved by no misery of all who perish, and are anxious only about this, that they may provide for themselves and their own people at the public expense of others.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui doctrinæ etiam suæ rationem reddens, perfectum huius exemplar non Ephesijs modò & Asianis, sed omnibus omnium locorum & temporum ministris proponit. ET primo quidem, se bona fide cum illis egisse dicit. Nihil(inquit) suffugi eorum, quæ in rem vestram effent, quin vobis annunciarem, &c. Sensus est, se nihil eorum celauisse, quæ ipsis cognitu necessaria erant. Idè verò ab omnibus ministris exigitur, nempe vt salutis doctrinam perfecte tradant, nec quicquam celent in mundi gratiam. Imò quo magis ille furit, eò magis instare oportet verbi huc cinam, ne mundi furoribus Veritatem vinci & opprimi patiantur. Quo loco illorum error arguitur, qui hostibus veritatis aliquid dandum esse existimant, ne ingenua docendi libertate magis exarcentur: quasi vero illi ministrorum ignauia non ferociores fiant, dum sese timeri, illos autem sibi male conscios esse putant. Cumprimis autem obseruandum est hoc loco, apostolos plene & perfecte omnia tradidisse, quae ad hominum salutem faciunt, nec ullis additionibus opus esse, quibus illorum doctrina farciatur. Constat enim Christum nihil hos celauisse, qui eo argumento se illos amicorum loco habuisse probat, quod omnia reuelarit, quae a patre acceperat. Iohan. 15. Idem spiritum suum illis promisit, qui omnia suggereret, quem illos accepisse, supra vidimus. Iam vero Paulus publice fatetur, se nihil eorum celauisse, quae ipsis utilia & necessaria esse sciret. Plena ergo & perfecta apostolorum doctrina est, qua illi ecclesijs vnum Iesum Christum tradiderunt, quemadmodum ipsorum Epistolae & Sermones abunde testantur. Magnam ergo tum Christo tum apostolis iniuriam faciut, quicunque nouos fidei articulos condere, & ecclesijs multa, quae apostolorum doctrinae ex diametro repugnant, obtrudere audent.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, giving an account of his teaching too, sets forth a perfect model of it not only for the Ephesians and Asians but for all ministers in all places and times. First, he says that he dealt with them in good faith. "I kept back nothing," he says, "of those things which were profitable to you, but declared them to you," etc. The meaning is that he concealed nothing of what was necessary for them to know. And this is required of all ministers: namely, that they hand on the doctrine of salvation perfectly, and conceal nothing to win the favour of the world. Indeed, the more the world rages, the more ministers ought to press the Word of truth, so that they do not allow the truth to be conquered and crushed by the rages of the world. Here the error of those is refuted who think that something must be granted to the enemies of the truth, lest they be provoked more by a free manner of teaching; as if the cowardice of ministers did not make them fiercer, since they think that men fear them while they themselves are conscious of guilt. Above all, it must be observed in this place that the apostles delivered fully and perfectly everything that pertains to the salvation of men, and that there is no need of any additions with which their teaching should be stuffed. For it is certain that Christ concealed nothing from them, and he proves that he held them as friends by this argument, that he revealed all things which he had received from the Father (John 15). He also promised them his Spirit, who would bring all things to their minds, which we have seen above that they received. Now Paul openly confesses that he concealed nothing of those things which he knew to be useful and necessary for them. The teaching of the apostles, therefore, is full and perfect, by which they handed to the churches the one Jesus Christ, as their own Epistles and Sermons abundantly testify. Those, then, do great wrong both to Christ and to the apostles, whoever dare to frame new articles of faith and to impose on the churches many things which are wholly contrary to the doctrine of the apostles.

units.la: Deinde modum quoque, quem in docendo secutus sit, attingit, dum se publice simul & priuatim per singulas domos docuisse, & Iudaeis pariter ac gentibus testificatum fuisse dicit. Exprimunt haec indefessum apostoli studium, quo accensus vt omnibus salutis doctrinam propositu, ita nihil eorum omisit, quae ad plurimorum salutem facere poterant. Simul vero discimus quis verus & optimus docendi ordo sit. Primo enim in genere, & publice quidem, tradi debent quae salutaria sunt, sic vt omnes, quid ipsos facere quidue omittere conueniat, intelligant. Quia vero non omnes sponte obtemperant, interim tamen securitate potius quam malitia peccant, absque aliorum offendiculo, priuatas quoque admonitiones, hortationes & increpationes accedere oportet. Si enim cuiusque Christiani est, proximum admonere & errantem in viam reducere, quanto magis hoc ministrum facere conuenit, a quo Christus olim commissi muneris rationem exiget? At testificandi verbo ferium & liberum dicendi fludium notatur, quod nisi adhibeatur, frigebunt reliqua omnia. Est autem obseruatione dignum, quantum ministro in sua fidei commissas oues iuris sit, quando non publice modo, verumetiam priuatim per singulas domos docere & admonere debet. Vnde simul colligitur, quo loco habendi sint, qui nec publice nec priuatim a ministris admoneri & corrigi volunt. Cur enim oues Christi censeantur, qui pastoris vocem superbe & improbe fastidiunt?
units.tr: Next, he also touches on the manner which he followed in teaching, when he says that he taught publicly and at the same time privately, from house to house, and bore witness both to Jews and to Gentiles. These words express the apostle's tireless zeal, by which, being fired, he set the doctrine of salvation before all, and omitted nothing of those things which could serve the salvation of very many. At the same time we learn what the true and best order of teaching is. For first, in general terms and publicly, those things which are salutary ought to be delivered, so that all may understand what it becomes them to do and what to leave undone. But because not all obey willingly, yet sin more through carelessness than through malice, and that without offence to others, private admonitions, exhortations and rebukes ought to be added as well. For if it is the duty of every Christian to admonish his neighbour and to lead back one who has gone astray, how much more does this befit the minister, from whom Christ will one day demand an account of the office committed to him? Yet the wording of testifying notes an earnest and free zeal for speaking, which, unless it is applied, all the rest will grow cold. It is worth observing, moreover, how much authority the minister has over the sheep committed to his faith, since he must teach and admonish them not only publicly but also privately, from house to house. From this it is also gathered in what place those are to be held who will be neither admonished nor corrected by the ministers, neither publicly nor privately. For why should they be counted as Christ's sheep who proudly and wickedly despise the voice of the shepherd?

units.la: Postremo summam doctrinae suae comprehendit, duo illius capita statuens, nimirum poenitentiam in Deum, & fidem in Iesum Christum. Conueniunt haec cum Christi mandato, qui apostolos in suo nomine poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum praedicare iussit. Luc. 24. Vnde constat verum euangelium a Paulo praedicatum fuisse, simulque patet, qualis doctrina praedicari debeat. Et hic quidem primus locus poenitentiae tribuitur, quam alibi conuersionem ad Deum definiimus: cui definitioni Paulus subscribit, dum se poenitentiam erga Deum docuisse ait, id est, eam qua ad Deum homines couertuntur. Hinc vero exordiuntur ex Christi mandato apostoli, quia omnes defleximus & natura corrupti sumus. Quia autem iuxta Adami exemplum Dei conspectum borremus, fidem in Christum simul praedicari oportet, quae nos patri per filium reconciliatos esse docet, & per quam ex immortali Dei verbo regeniti, filij Dei efficimur. Noxius ergo valde & pudendus illorum error est, qui poenitentiam quidem multi vrgent, fidem vero interea negligunt, sine qua poenitentia subsistere nullo modo potest. Quomodo enim ad Deum conuertetur, qui Christum non habet, qui solus est via, lux & veritas, & sine quo ad patrem nemo venire potest? Iohan. 14. At quia de his alibi copiosius egimus, paucula haec modo sufficiant. Discat autem singuli ex Pauli exemplo de doctrinis iudicare, nec vllam sibi obtrudi patiantur, quam quae veram tradit conuersionem ad Deum & fidem in Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, he sums up the substance of his teaching, laying down its two heads, namely repentance toward God and faith in Jesus Christ. These agree with Christ's command, who bade the apostles preach repentance and remission of sins in his name (Luke 24). Hence it is clear that the true gospel was preached by Paul, and at the same time it is evident what kind of teaching ought to be preached. And here indeed repentance is given the first place, which elsewhere we have defined as conversion to God. Paul agrees with this definition when he says that he taught repentance toward God, that is, that by which men are turned to God. Now the apostles, following Christ's command, begin here, because we have all turned aside and are corrupt by nature. But since, following Adam's example, we dread the sight of God, faith in Christ must be preached at the same time, which teaches that we are reconciled to the Father through the Son, and through which, born again of the immortal Word of God, we become sons of God. Very harmful and shameful, therefore, is the error of those who indeed urge repentance much, yet meanwhile neglect faith, without which repentance can by no means stand. For how will he be converted to God who does not have Christ, who alone is the way, the light and the truth, and without whom no one can come to the Father? (John 14). But since we have treated these things more fully elsewhere, let these few points suffice for now. Let each one learn from Paul's example to judge doctrines, and let no one suffer any doctrine to be forced upon him except that which delivers true conversion to God and faith in Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 134.

units.la: Et nunc ecce ego alligatus spiritu proficiscor Hierosolymam, quae in ea obuentura sint mihi ignorans: nisi quod Spiritus sanctus per singulas vrbes testificatur, dicens quod vincula & afflictiones me manent. Verum nihil mihi curae est, nec vita ipsa preciosa est mihi ipsi, vt absolu-uam uam cursum meum cum gaudio, & ministerium quod accepi à Domino Iesu ad testificandum Euangelium gratiæ Dei. Et nunc ecce ego scio, quòd posthac non videbitis faciem meam vos omnes, per quos transiui prædicans regnum Dei. Quapropter contestor vos hodierno die, quòd mundus ego sum à sanguine omnium. Non enim subterfugi, quò minus annunciarim omne consilium Dei vobis.
units.tr: "And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will befall me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions await me. But none of these things moves me, nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my course with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God. And now, behold, I know that you will no longer see my face, all of you among whom I have gone about preaching the kingdom of God. Therefore I call you to witness this day that I am clean from the blood of all men. For I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God."

units.la: Quamuis Dei filius Iesus Christus, cum in hoc mundo ageret, suos nunquam non mirificè dilexerit, omnium tamen clarissima suæ dilectionis indicia tam discessurus edidit, quemadmodum graues illæ & salutares admonitiones, quibus in vltima Cœna illos instruxit, abunde testantur. Huius exemplum Paulus imitatus, non præsens modò ecclesiarum saluti consuluit, sed discessurus ab his, imò absens, luculentius multò declarauit, quàm illi omnium illarum incolumitas cordi fuerit. Patet id passim in Epistolis ipsius, cumprimis autem in Oratione hac, quam in Miletana Synodo coram Asianis ministris siue pastoribus habuit. Quia enim se nunquam ad Asiæ ecclesias rediturum esse præuidebat, simulque pericula ex falsis doctoribus post illius obitum oritura nouerat, illos summa qua potuit fide & diligentia de suo officio simul & aliis rebus ad salutem ipsorum necessarijs admonet. Ante omnia verò suum exemplum illis ob oculos statuit, quò maior sit suæ admonitionis authoritas: de quo cum heri copiosè satis dictum sit, modò ad præsentis loci explicationem accedamus.
units.tr: Although the Son of God, Jesus Christ, while he was in this world, always loved his own with wonderful love, yet he gave the clearest evidence of that love when he was about to depart, as those weighty and salutary admonitions with which he instructed them at the last supper abundantly testify. Paul, imitating this example, cared for the salvation of the churches not only while present but also when he was about to leave them, or rather while absent, and declared far more clearly how much their safety lay close to his heart. This appears everywhere in his Epistles, and especially in this speech which he delivered before the Asian ministers, or pastors, at the synod of Miletus. For since he foresaw that he would never return to the churches of Asia, and knew that dangers would arise from false teachers after his death, he admonishes them with the greatest faith and diligence he could muster, both about their office and about other things necessary for their salvation. Above all, he sets his own example before their eyes, so that the authority of his admonition may be greater. Since this was discussed at length yesterday, let us now turn to the explanation of the present passage.

units.la: Sequitur enim Causæ redditio, qua cur suum exemplum tam serio vrgeat, docet: nimirum quia iam iam discessurus, nec vnquam posthac ad illos reuersurus sit. Inde enim colligit, ipsos apostoli & doctoris sui exemplum sequi & ecclesiæ curam summo animorum studio suscipere debere, ne quod ille tot tantisq; laboribus acquisiuit, sua socordia aut negligentia denuo amittant. Et hæc quidem totius loci summa est. Præstat autem singula eo, quo dicuntur, ordine inspicere, adeoq; quæ in singulis versibus latent mysteria inuestigare.
units.tr: For there follows the reason why he presses his own example so earnestly: namely, because he is about to depart and will never return to them. From this he concludes that they ought to follow the example of the apostle and of their teacher, and take up the care of the church with the utmost zeal of mind, lest through their sloth or negligence they lose again what he gained with so many and so great labours. This is the sum of the whole passage. It is best, however, to examine each part in the order in which it is stated, and so to investigate the mysteries hidden in the individual verses.

units.la: Primò, Et nunc ecce (ait) ego alligatus spiritu proficiscor Hierosolymam. Quibus verbis occultum spiritus sancti motum intelligit, quem ipsi rerum agendarum ducem semper fuisse, iam sæpe vidimus. Cui licet volens obedire (vt sequentia docent) se tamen alligatum esse, & quodammodo vinctum duci testatur, ne vel leuis nimium, vel temerarius Dei tentator putaretur, qui sese præter causam in aperta pericula conjiceret. Docet ergo se aliter facere non posse, nisi cum Dei spiritu contumaciter luctari velit. Admonet autem nos Pauli locutio, quo loco apud nos esse debeant cum occulta spiritus sancti suggestiones, tum aperta siue diserta illius oracula. Vinculorum instar sint, quibus inuitam & reluctantem carnem in fidei obedientiam pertrahamus: & sponte quidem, ne magno nostro malo Dei potentis manum experiamur, qui vel inuitos quò vult rapit eos, qui carnis sensum potius sequi, quàm ipsius vocationi obedire volunt. Ita illum Mosi, officium detrectanti, iratum fuisse legimus. Exod. 4. Et Ieremiæ idem facienti, & ætatem alleganti, quasi indignabundus ait: Ne dicas, Puer sum ego. Quia ad omnia ad quæ te mitto, ibis: & quæcunq; mandauero tibi, loqueris, &c. Ierem. 1. Quid verò Ionæ euenerit, Dei vocationem declinare volenti, notius est quàm vt multis commemorari debeat.
units.tr: First, he says: "And now, behold, I go bound in the spirit to Jerusalem." By these words he signals the hidden movement of the Holy Spirit, which, as we have often seen, had always been the guide of his affairs. Though he is willing to obey it (as what follows shows), he nevertheless testifies that he is bound and, in a sense, led as a captive, lest he be thought either too light or a rash tempter of God, who throws himself without cause into obvious dangers. He teaches, therefore, that he cannot act otherwise unless he wishes to struggle stubbornly against the Spirit of God. Paul's words also remind us what place the secret promptings of the Holy Spirit, and likewise his open and plain oracles, ought to have among us. They should be like bonds by which we draw our unwilling and resisting flesh into obedience to faith, and that willingly, lest to our great harm we experience the hand of the mighty God, who drags even the unwilling wherever he wills, those who prefer to follow the sense of the flesh rather than to obey his calling. So we read that God was angry with Moses when he refused the office (Exod. 4.). And to Jeremiah, who did the same and pleaded his youth, he said, as one indignant: "Do not say, I am a child. For you shall go to all to whom I send you, and whatever I command you, you shall speak, etc." (Jer. 1.) What befell Jonah, who wished to decline God's calling, is too well known to need recounting to many.

units.la: Hinc verò sensim ad institutum delabitur, cum addit: Ignoro quidem, quæ mihi Hierosolymis euentura sint, quaq; potissima causa sit, quòd ita me vrget ad istam profectionem spiritus, hoc autem scio me passim eiusdem spiritus instinctu admoneri, quòd me illic vincula & afflictiones maneant, id quod constanter per omnes ecclesias sancti prophetæ testari solent. Pergendum tamen est per quæuis pericula, adeoq; per mortem ipsam, quando sic Deo videtur, penes quem solùm vita tum necessarium est. Est autem diligenti obseruatione dignus locus hic, eò quòd nostræ institutioni & consolationi plurimùm seruire poterit. Primò enim fidelem Dei curam exprimit, qua vt suos tueri & illis prospicere consueuit. Nam cum illos extremè diligat, eosdem negligere nullo modo potest, & in tempore de omnibus, quæ ipsis euentura sunt, admonet. Cur enim cultores suos negligeret, qui impijs quoq; pœnas prædicit, nec malùm aliquod infert, nisi per prophetas prius præmonitis? Deinde vt suos Deus admonere soleat, videmus. Afflictiones quidem & vincula sibi Hierosolymis parata esse, Paulus intellexit. Quis vero omnium euentus futurus esset, non reuelarat adhuc spiritus sanctus. In genere ergo suos plerunque Deus admonet, quamuis non omnia per singulas species exprimat. Nam quantum illos scire opus est, tantum reuelat, ut ad crucem ferendam praeparentur quidem, euentum vero omnem Deo permittant. Itaque nos quoque generales praedictiones habemus, quibus crucem & aduersa nos in mundo manere, docemur. Quarum vsus potissimus est, ut ad illa ferenda praeparemur, ne dum inopinantibus accidunt, grauis offendiculi causa sint. Tertio Dei consilium obseruare conuenit, quo ille erga cultores suos mirifice vti solet. Antea quidem non semel a fratribus admonitus Paulus, vel fuga sibi consuluit, vel insidias hostiles prudenter elusit. Nunc vero de vinculis & afflictionibus admonetur quidem, sed tamen a Dei spiritu vrgetur & impellitur, ut inuitis & multum dissuadentibus fratribus sibi in medias tribulationes pergendum esse intelligat. Ita Christum quoque alias quidem hostium suorum conatus & insidias eluisse legimus, tandem vero illis obuius procedit, cum nimirum horam suam iam aduenisse videret, sicque postularet aeternum patris caelestis consilium. Docet haec, pericula non semper iusta & sufficientem fugae causam esse. Quando enim Dei vocatione certa vrgemur, nec ferro, nec flammis, imo nec obiectus Oceani fluctibus (vt olim ad mare rubrum factum fuit) nos reuocari patiamur, quo minus officium nostrum faciamus, cui nos diuinitus destinatos esse intelligimus.
units.tr: From here he gradually comes to his purpose, when he adds: "I indeed do not know what will befall me at Jerusalem, and what is the chief reason why the Spirit so urges me to this journey. But this I know, that I am everywhere warned by the impulse of the same Spirit that bonds and afflictions await me there, as the holy prophets have constantly testified through all the churches." Yet one must press on through every danger, even through death itself, when it so seems good to God, in whose hand alone lies the life that is then necessary. This passage deserves careful observation, because it can greatly serve our instruction and consolation. For first it expresses God's faithful care, by which he is accustomed to protect his people and provide for them. For since he loves them exceedingly, he cannot in any way neglect them, and he warns them in good time about all that is to befall them. For why would he neglect his worshippers, when he foretells punishments even to the wicked, and inflicts no evil unless it has first been announced through the prophets? Next, we see that God is accustomed to admonish his people. Paul understood that bonds and afflictions were prepared for him at Jerusalem. But the Holy Spirit had not yet revealed what the outcome of everything would be. So in general God usually admonishes his people, though he does not set out every detail one by one. For he reveals as much as they need to know, so that they may be prepared to bear the cross, but leaves the whole outcome to God. Thus we too have general predictions, by which we are taught that the cross and adversity remain for us in the world. Their chief use is that we may be prepared to bear them, so that when they come upon us unexpectedly they may not be a cause of grievous stumbling. Thirdly, it is fitting to observe God's counsel, by which he is wont to deal wonderfully with his worshippers. Earlier, Paul, though admonished more than once by the brothers, either looked to his safety by flight or prudently eluded the plots of his enemies. But now he is indeed warned of bonds and afflictions, yet he is urged and impelled by the Spirit of God, so that, though the brothers are unwilling and strongly dissuade him, he understands that he must press on into the midst of tribulations. So we read that Christ too, though he had at other times evaded the attempts and plots of his enemies, at last went forth to meet them, when he saw that his hour had now come, and thus sought the eternal counsel of his heavenly Father. This teaches that dangers are not always a just and sufficient reason for flight. For when we are urged by a certain calling of God, we must not allow ourselves to be called back by sword or flames, nor even by the waves of the ocean thrown in our path (as once happened at the Red Sea), so that we fail to do our duty, to which we understand we have been destined by God.

units.la: Caeterum ne vinculorum mentione amicos & fratres nimium perterrefaceret, consolationem adhibet vere apostolicam & Christianam. Nihil (inquit) horum mihi curae est. Quasi diceret: Nolite mea causa discruciari. Cur enim vobis dolorem mouerent, quae mihi quam minimum cura sunt? Ergone spiritus sancti oracula, & pias fratrum admonitiones contemnis Paule? Nequaquam. Sed ideo parui facio, quae de periculis imminentibus dicuntur, quia vita mea minime mihi ipsi pretiosa est: id est, non maioris vitam hanc temporariam facio, quam vocationem meam, cui me Dominus destinauit. Imo cupio cursum meum cum gaudio absoluere, & ministerio meo probe defungi, testificando passim euangelium gratiae Dei. Si ergo vitam iam olim Christo deuoui, vincula & afflictiones me nullo modo terrere possunt. Docemur autem Pauli exemplo, quales se in aduersis pij gerere debeant. Primum est, ne illa sic curent, vt horum vitandorum gratia aliquid se indignum faciant. Alioqui minime nos Stoica indolentia praeditos esse vult Deus, sed ne nostri maiorem quam suae voluntatis rationem habeamus. Nulla vero in his efficacior esse poterit consolatio, quam si in diuina prouidentia consyderatione frequenter versemur, quam apostolis quoque suis Christus ob oculos statuit, & Dauid hoc sibi praesidium vnicum & asylum tutissimum facit, quod fugas suas apud Deum numeratas esse, suasque lachrymas in Dei lagenulam colligi credit. Matth. 10. Psal. 56. Deinde curent, ne temporalem hanc vitam aeternae praeferant. Cogitent potius ideo nos vita hac donari, vt Deo viuamus, cui etiam (si ita necessitas ferat) nos mori conueniat. Et quia semel moriendum est, nunquam felicius, quam in Dei vocatione, mori poterimus. Ita enim illud Dauidis in nos quadrabit: Pretiosa in oculis Domini mors sanctorum ipsius. Psalm. 116. Quod si vero vitam hanc aeternae praeferre nefas est, quanto minus opes, honores, voluptates & si quae alia huius mundi bona sunt, huic praeferre decebit? Quid enim lucrabitur homo, si totum mundum quidem acquisierit, suae vero animae iacturam fecerit? Aut quae res tanti precij est, vt ad vnius animae redemptionem sufficiat? Vide Matth. 16. Luc. 9. Tandem in hoc omni studio pios incumbere decet, vt per omnia aduersa cum gaudio enitantur, & cursum suum, id est, iniunctum sibi a Deo munus, feliciter absoluant. Nec enim recte coepisse sufficit, sed perseuerantia opus est, vt iam saepe monuimus. Meminerint ergo singuli vitam hanc instar stadij nobis esse, cuius meta mors fit, quae felicissime ab illis attingitur, qui in finem suum officium faciunt.
units.tr: Moreover, lest he frighten his friends and brothers too much by mention of bonds, he offers a consolation that is truly apostolic and Christian. "None of these things," he says, "is of concern to me." As if he said: "Do not be tormented on my account. For why should they cause you grief, when they matter very little to me? Do you then despise the oracles of the Holy Spirit and the godly admonitions of the brothers, Paul?" By no means. But I make little of what is said about impending dangers, because my life is by no means precious to me myself: that is, I do not value this temporal life more than my calling, to which the Lord has destined me. Indeed, I desire to finish my course with joy and to discharge my ministry well, by testifying everywhere to the gospel of the grace of God. If, then, I have long since devoted my life to Christ, bonds and afflictions cannot in any way terrify me. We are taught by Paul's example how the godly ought to conduct themselves in adversity. First, they should not so care for these things that for the sake of avoiding them they do anything unworthy. For God does not wish us to be endowed with Stoic indifference, but only that we should not take more account of ourselves than of his will. Yet there can be no more effective consolation in these matters than to dwell frequently on the consideration of divine providence, which Christ set before his apostles, and which David makes his one defence and most secure refuge, when he believes that his flights are counted before God and his tears gathered into God's flask (Matt. 10.; Ps. 56.). Next, they should take care not to prefer this temporal life to the eternal. Let them rather consider that we are given this life so that we may live to God, to whom, if necessity so requires, it is also fitting that we die. And since we must die once, we can never die more happily than in the calling of God. For so David's words will fit us: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints" (Ps. 116.). But if it is wrong to prefer this life to the eternal, how much less fitting is it to prefer to it riches, honours, pleasures, and whatever other goods this world has? For what will a man gain if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what thing is of such worth as to suffice for the redemption of a single soul? (Matt. 16.; Luke 9.) Finally, the godly should strive in all this effort to press on through all adversity with joy, and to finish their course, that is, the task laid upon them by God, happily. For it is not enough to have begun well, but perseverance is needed, as we have often warned. Let each therefore remember that this life is like a race-course for us, whose goal is death, which is reached most happily by those who perform their duty to the end.

units.la: Sed priusquam longius progrediamur, videndum est vt de euangelio simul & huius ministerio Paulus loquatur. Euangelium gratiae Dei vocat: ab effectu nimirum, quia Dei gratiam nobis offert, nos Deo Patri per filium Iesum Christum reconciliatos esse docet. Patet hinc, quam execranda sit illorum impietas, qui euangelium improbe fastidiunt & aspernantur. Similes enim seditiosis sunt, quibus non satis videtur seditiones & turbas aduersus magistratum concitauisse, nisi etiam sponte oblatam magistratus gratiam scurriliter eludant, & huius internuncios contumeliose lacerent. Nos enim omnes defectionis & seditionis contra Deum reos esse, & interim meruisse constat. At condo- nat nat culpam omnem Deus ob filij sui meritum, illamq; gratiam nobis per euangelium denunciat. Quod quicunq; vespuunt, nae illi sese in posterum omnino inexcusabiles & venia indignos esse produnt. Rursum de ministerio suo loquens, testificandi verbo utitur, quo ingenuam, liberam & seriam praedicationem intelligi, iam sæpe dictum est. Euangelium enim non simplex rei gestæ narratio, sed testimonium est de Iesu Christo. Et apostolos suos testes ipse Christus vocat. Ioan. 15. Actor. 1. Serio ergo Christum praedicauerunt, imò hunc mundi saluatorem esse, non verbis modò & factis, verumetiam morte & sanguine testati sunt, qua de causa vulgò martyres dicuntur. Quod verò apostolos fecisse diximus, idipsum singulos Christianos facere decet. Vult enim Christus ut illum confiteamur coram mundo hoc, nec pro cultoribus suis agnoscit, quoscunq; sui & euangelij sui coram mundo degenere & corrupto puduerit. Vide Marc. 8. Caeterum quoad Paulum, quò maior esset apud illos suæ adhortationis authoritas, breui Anacephalæosi vel Recapitulatione, quæ hucusq; dicta sunt, repetit, & in quem finem dicta sint inculcat.
units.tr: But before we go further, we must see how Paul speaks of the gospel and of his ministry at the same time. He calls it the gospel of the grace of God: clearly from its effect, because it offers us God's grace, and it teaches that we have been reconciled to God the Father through his Son Jesus Christ. From this it is plain how detestable is the impiety of those who wantonly scorn and despise the gospel. They are like seditious men, who think it is not enough to have stirred up rebellion and tumult against the magistrate, unless they also mock with buffoonery the grace the magistrate has freely offered and insult its messengers. For it is certain that we are all guilty of rebellion and sedition against God, and have deserved to be so. But God pardons every fault for the merit of his Son, and proclaims this grace to us through the gospel. Whoever spits on it shows that in future they are wholly inexcusable and unworthy of pardon. Again, speaking of his ministry, he uses the word "testify," by which we have often said that a sincere, free and earnest preaching is meant. For the gospel is not a simple narrative of events, but a testimony concerning Jesus Christ. Christ himself calls his apostles witnesses (John 15; Acts 1). The apostles, then, preached Christ earnestly, and that he is the Saviour of the world; they bore witness to it not only in words and deeds but also by death and blood, for which reason they are commonly called martyrs. And what we have said the apostles did, every Christian ought to do as well. For Christ wishes us to confess him before this world, and he does not acknowledge as his worshippers those whom shame of him and of his gospel has seized before a degenerate and corrupt world. See Mark 8. As for Paul, so that his exhortation might carry greater authority with them, he repeats in brief recapitulation what has been said so far, and presses home the purpose for which it was said.

units.la: Primò autem sui discessus mentionem denuo facit, nec hunc modò allegat, verumetiam quòd illum posthac nunquam amplius visuri sint, diserte testatur. Nunc ecce (inquit) ego scio, quòd posthac non videbitis faciem meam vos omnes, per quos transiui praedicans regnum Dei. Imitatur verò iam moriturus parentes, qui similia nouissimus suis admonitionibus frequenter interserunt, ut sic acriores stimulos in filiorum animis relinquant. E S T autem obseruatione simul & quauis laude dignissimus Pauli animus, cuius mira & inuicta constantia in paucis hisce verbis elucet. Licet enim hunc sibi vltimum cum his congressum fore sciat, & proinde nihil aliud quàm mortem sperare possit, non tamen muliebri fletu suum discessum deplorat, nec vllum edit vel eriflitia vel priuati doloris indicium, sed de sola ecclesiarum salute solicitus est, & huius curam illis vnicè commendat. Quo exemplo docemur, vt nos quoq; in mortis consyderatione, aut cum illa iam instat, affectos esse oporteat. Cauenda hic est muliebris illa pusillanimitas, qua multi suam sortem ita deplorant, quasi solis ipsis moriendi legem Deus impo suerit: & à suis non aliter cum summo luctu diuelluntur, quasi nemo in orbe restet, sub cuius prouidentia illi ipsis sublatis tutò agere possint. Atqui cogitandum erat, hanc vniuersæ terræ viam esse, sicuti Iosue & Dauid testantur. Ios. 24. 1. Reg. 2. Quæ ergo nobis iniuria fit, si à communi omnium sorte non eximimur? Quoad verò amicos, vxores, liberos, hos quoq; in morte nō amittimus, sed vel præmittimus ipsi mox secuturi, vel secuturos præcedimus in eum locum, vbi patriam nobis Christus parauit, & vbi omnes omnium nationum fideles cum Abrahamo, Isaaco & Iacobo discum bent. Matth. 8. Eorum autem, quos hic relinquimus, tutor & patronus Deus est, quem viduarum & peregrinorum protectorem, orphanorum verò patrem scripturæ vocant. Psalm. 68. Huius ergo curæ commendari debent, nos verò inuicta fidei constantia viam hanc, qua per Christum ad cœlos tenditur, ingredi debemus, &c.
units.tr: First, he makes mention again of his departure, and not only alludes to it but plainly testifies that they will never see him again. "Now, behold," he says, "I know that from now on you will not see my face, all of you, among whom I have passed preaching the kingdom of God." Indeed, a man about to die imitates parents who, in their final admonitions, often insert such words, so as to leave sharper goads in the minds of their children. The mind of Paul is worthy of observation and of every praise, and his remarkable and unconquered constancy shines out in these few words. For although he knows that this will be his last meeting with them, and therefore can expect nothing but death, he does not lament his departure with womanish tears, nor does he show any sign either of anxiety or of private grief, but he is anxious only for the salvation of the churches, and he commends their care to them alone. By this example we are taught that we too ought to be disposed in this way when we consider death, or when it is now at hand. We must avoid that womanish faint-heartedness with which many lament their lot as if God had laid the law of dying on them alone, and are torn from their own people with the greatest grief, as if no one remained in the world under whose providence they could safely act once they themselves were taken away. Yet it ought to have been considered that this is the way of all the earth, as Joshua and David testify (Josh. 24; 1 Kings 2). What injury, then, is done to us if we are not exempted from the common lot of all? As for friends, wives and children, we do not lose them in death either; rather we send them ahead, to follow us soon, or we go before those who will follow, into that place where Christ has prepared a homeland for us, and where all the faithful of every nation sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matt. 8). God is the guardian and protector of those whom we leave behind here, whom the Scriptures call the protector of widows and strangers, and the father of orphans (Ps. 68). They ought therefore to be commended to his care, and we ought, with unconquered constancy of faith, to enter upon this way by which we press through Christ to heaven, etc.

units.la: Postremò protestationem grauissimam Paulus adhibet, qua omnem perditionis culpam in ipsorum capita reijcit, si ecclesias suæ fidei comissas negligant, & à fide deficere patiantur. Contestor verò (inquit) hodierno die, quòd mundus ego sim à sanguine omnium. Causa: Quia non subterfugi, quò minus annunciarem vobis omne consilium Dei. Haud dubiè verò ad Dei verba respicit, quæ Ezechielis 3. & 33. cap. leguntur, quibus pereuntium sanguis verbi ministro imputatur, nisi diserte illos monuerit, idem verò omni culpa liberatur, si officio suo fideliter defunctus fuerit. Id quia Paulus fecerat, tanquam bene sibi conscius, ista dicit. Simul autem maximorum virorum exempla imitari videtur, Mosis nimirum & Iosuæ, quos non multum dissimilibus protestationibus iam morituros vsos fuisse legimus. Vide Deut. 30. Ios. 24. Docet autem Pauli exemplum, coram Deo excusatos esse qui suum officium faciunt, licet nibil aut parum apud suæ curæ commissos homines proficiant. In ijs enim hæret interitus culpa, qui incurabiles esse pergunt. Nec ad solos verbi ministros, verumetiam ad omnes alios ordines doctrina hæc referri debet. Et in magistratibus quidem hanc locum habere, Iosiæ exemplum docet, quem spiritus sanctus egregiè commendat, licet multos haberet in regno, imò etiam in aula sua, parum syncerōs, multos etiam palàm impios & incurabiles, quemadmodum Sophoniæ prophetæ Sermones testantur. Eadem parentum ratio est. Frequenter enim fieri solet, vt degeneres liberos habeant piissimi parentes, quibus tamen illorum improbitas fraudi non est, quando suo erga hos officio non desunt. Exempla in Iacobi patriarchæ & Dauidis aliorumq; similium filijs habentur. Quòd si vero vel magistratus vel parentes, officij sui immemores, nimia indulgentia aut etiam prauo exemplo suae fidei creditos corruperint, iam in ipsos quoque diuini iudicij seuerita, redundat, cuius exemplum in Heli scriptura proponit. 1. Sam. 2. 3. & 4. cap. Habes ergo quod illi respondeas, qui cessandum putant, vbi nulla profectus spes apparet. Obijcitur hoc hodie tum ministrorum magistratibus, & hoc ipso argumento ignaui sibijpsis blandiri solent. At cogitabis, tuam quoq; animam periclitari, quae non aliter quàm fideli industria liberari poterit: quam si liberauerit, nec tein cassum laborauisse nequaquam putare debes. Patet praeterea ex hoc loco, quàm infelix illorum sors sit, qui cum officio suo probè functi sint antecessores, ipsi vel ignaui relabuntur, velctiam aperta ma- litia corrumpunt quae ab illis bene constituta fuerunt. In his enim omnis interitus culpa haeret, nec vllam coram Deo excusationem habent, quando ab ipsorum sanguine mundi sunt, qui illorum cu- ram ante gesserunt. Debet hoc in ecclesijs nostro seculo per Dei verbum reformatis obseruari. Con- stitit in his reformatio magnis laboribus simul & periculis. Quam ergo excusationem habebunt le- ues apostatae, quando vel solus ministrorum pulus illis conuincendis sufficit, vt alibi monuimus? Idem in repub. obseruari necesse est. Habemus in Heluetia libertatem maiorum sanguine redem- ptam. Conditae sunt ex euangelij doctrina bonae leges, & morum disciplina non sine laboribus insti- tuta. O miseros ergo nos & quaui poena dignos, si vel ignauo metu superati, vel leuitate & malitia circumuenti, illa nobis eripi patiamur, ex quibus publica salus dependet. Ita liberos inexcusabiles reddit fidelis & industria parentum cura, si illi huic minus respondeant. Deniq; omnium est hac ob- seruare, ne dum sibijpsis blandiuntur, in alios culpam transferant, quae in illis tenaciter haeret. Est praeterea obseruatione dignum, quod Paulus omne Dei consilium annunciauit, nimirum quoad no- strae redemptionis & salutis negotium. Scimus alioqui multa esse in Dei prouidentia, quae nos scru- tari non licet, nec linguis enunciari possunt, qualia se in tertio caelo Paulus audiuisse testatur. 2. Cor. 12. At eorum, quae saluti nostrae seruiunt, nihil omisit: quando huius causas simul & rationem, de- inde eorum etiam qui saluantur officia fidelissimè tradidit. Vnde rursum colligimus, apostolorum do- strinam, quae scripturis continetur, perfectam & omnibus numeris absolutam esse. Quare nimis te- meraria est illorum vanitas, qui hominum traditiones ecclesiae obtrudunt, quarum maxima pars cum apostolorum doctrina aperte pugnat, qui vnum Christum nobis saluatorem tradiderunt. Nec enim fieri potest, vt eundem authorem habeant Dei spiritum, quae tam aperte inter se mutuò dif- sident. Postremò obseruabis, quòd licet omne Dei consilium Paulus Ephesijs coram annunciarit, po- stea tamen ad eosdem epistolam scripsit, qua hoc ipsum denuo exponit. Docemur illo exemplo, quanta à ministris ecclesiarum publicae salutis ratio & cura haberi debeat, & quàm parum apostolici sint, qui ecclesias tam facile negligunt. Discamus interim Dei consilium, quod in Christo Iesu per apostolos nobis reuelatum est, vera fide & obedientia amplesti, vt illud secuti salutem veram assequamur, per eundem Iesum Christum, Dominum & saluatorem nostrum vnicum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Last, Paul brings forward a most solemn protestation, by which he casts the whole guilt of perdition upon their own heads if they neglect the churches committed to their faith and allow them to fall away from the faith. "I call you to witness this day," he says, "that I am clean of the blood of all men. Because I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God." Without doubt he is looking to the words of God found in Ezekiel chapters 3 and 33, in which the blood of those who perish is imputed to the minister of the Word unless he has clearly warned them; but he is freed from all guilt if he has faithfully discharged his duty. Because Paul had done this, he says these things as one well aware of his own conscience. At the same time he seems to imitate the examples of the greatest men, namely Moses and Joshua, whom we read, on the point of death, used protestations not very unlike this one. See Deut. 30; Josh. 24. Paul's example teaches, moreover, that those who do their duty are excused before God, even though they accomplish nothing, or little, among the men committed to their care. For the guilt of ruin clings to those who persist in being incurable. Nor should this teaching be referred only to the ministers of the Word, but to all other orders as well. That it holds good for magistrates the example of Josiah shows, which the Holy Spirit commends outstandingly, although he had in his kingdom, indeed even in his own court, many who were little sincere and many who were openly impious and incurable, as the sermons of the prophet Zephaniah bear witness. The same reasoning applies to parents. For it often happens that most pious parents have degenerate children, yet their children's wickedness does not harm them, when they are not lacking in their duty towards them. Examples are found in the sons of the patriarch Jacob, and of David, and of others like them. But if magistrates or parents, forgetful of their duty, have corrupted those entrusted to their faith by excessive indulgence or even by bad example, then the severity of divine judgment falls upon them too, of which Scripture sets out an example in Eli (1 Sam. 2, 3 and 4). You have, then, what to answer to those who think one should cease when no hope of progress appears. This is objected today to ministers of the Word and to magistrates, and idle men are wont to flatter themselves with this very argument. But you should consider that your own soul too is in danger, which can be freed only by faithful diligence; and when you have freed it, you ought by no means to think that your labour has been in vain. Moreover, it is plain from this passage how unhappy is the lot of those who, when their predecessors have performed their duty well, either relapse into idleness themselves or even with open malice corrupt what those predecessors had well established. For the guilt of every ruin clings to these men, and they have no excuse before God, since they are not free of the blood of those who went before them in caring for these things. This ought to be observed in the churches of our own age, which have been reformed through the Word of God. That reformation was established with great labours and at the same time with dangers. What excuse, then, will light-minded apostates have, when the single example of ministers is enough to convict them, as we have warned elsewhere? The same must be observed in the commonwealth. We have in Helvetia a liberty redeemed by the blood of our ancestors. Good laws have been founded from the doctrine of the gospel, and the discipline of morals has been instituted not without labour. O wretched are we, then, and worthy of any punishment, if we, overcome by idle fear or deceived by levity and malice, allow those things to be snatched from us on which public safety depends. Thus the faithful and diligent care of parents makes children inexcusable if they do not answer to it. Finally, it is the duty of all to observe this, that while they flatter themselves they do not shift the blame onto others, when that blame clings stubbornly to themselves. It is also worthy of observation that Paul announced the whole counsel of God, namely as regards the business of our redemption and salvation. For we know that there are many things in God's providence which we are not permitted to search out, nor can they be spoken in human tongues, such as Paul testifies he heard in the third heaven (2 Cor. 12). But of those things which serve our salvation he omitted nothing, since he handed down most faithfully both their causes and their reasons, and then also the duties of those who are saved. Whence again we gather that the doctrine of the apostles, which is contained in the Scriptures, is perfect and absolute in every respect. Therefore the vanity of those is rash beyond measure who thrust upon the churches the traditions of men, most of which plainly fight against the doctrine of the apostles, who handed down to us Christ alone as Saviour. For it cannot be that the Spirit of God, which dissents so openly from itself, has the same author. Lastly, you will observe that although Paul announced the whole counsel of God to the Ephesians in person, he afterwards wrote an epistle to the same people in which he expounds this very thing again. We are taught by that example how great an account and care of public salvation ought to be taken by the ministers of the churches, and how little they are apostolic who so easily neglect the churches. Meanwhile let us learn to embrace with true faith and obedience the counsel of God, which has been revealed to us in Christ Jesus through the apostles, so that, following it, we may attain true salvation through the same Jesus Christ, our only Lord and Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXV.
units.tr: HOMILY 135.

units.la: Attendite ergo vobisipsis & cuncto gregi, in quo vos spiritus san- ctus posuit Episcopos, ad pascendam ecclesiam Dei, quā acquisiuit san- guine suo. Ego enim hoc noui, quòd ingressuri sint post discessum meum lupi graues in vos, non parcentes gregi. Et ex vobisipsis emer- gent viri loquentes peruersa, vt abducant discipulos post se. Propter quod vigilate, memores, quòd per triennium nocte & die non cessaue- rim cum lachrymis monere vnumquemq;. Et nunc commendo vos fra- tres Deo, & sermoni gratiae ipsius, qui potens est superstruere, & dare vobis haereditatem inter sanctificatos omnes.
units.tr: Take heed therefore to yourselves and to all the flock, over which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood. For I know this, that after my departure grievous wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock. And from among yourselves will arise men speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore watch, remembering that for three years I did not cease night and day to admonish each one of you with tears. And now I commend you, brethren, to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all the sanctified.

units.la: CVm Deo nihil charius & praestantius sit Ecclesia, quam Christi sanguine acquisiuit, eiusdem conseruationi omnes homines studere decet, quotquot Dei cultores & amici haberi volunt: cum primis tamen ad verbi ministros ea cura pertinet, eò quòd hos ecclesiae suae peculiari ordinatione deus praefecit, prafecit, & ab ijsdem olim sua dispensationis rationem exiget. Qua causa est, ob quam Paulus apo ftolus, Asiam reliEturus, ecclesiarum ministros conuocauit, & in horum publico conuentu diligentis- sime de omnibus disseruit, quae ad munerit ipsis commissi administrationem pertinebant. Et primò quidem suum exemplum illis ob oculos posuit, deq; suo discessu cum grauissima protestatione locutus est, vt sibi posthac solis omnem ecclefiarū curam incumbere scirent, & proinde maiori studio & zelo flagrarent. Porrò præmissis istis propius accedit, apertius illos sui officij admonens, rationibus simul grauissimis in medium adductis, quibus illos magis extimuler.
units.tr: Since nothing is dearer or more excellent to God than the Church, which he purchased with the blood of Christ, all men who wish to be counted worshippers and friends of God ought to labour for its preservation. Yet this care belongs above all to the ministers of the Word, because God has set them over his Church by a special ordination, and will one day demand from them an account of their stewardship. This is the reason why the apostle Paul, about to leave Asia, called together the ministers of the churches and, in their public assembly, discoursed most diligently on everything that pertained to the administration of the office committed to them. First he set his own example before their eyes, and spoke of his departure with the most solemn protestation, so that they might know that from now on the whole care of the churches rested on them alone, and so might burn with all the greater zeal and earnestness. Then, after these preliminaries, he comes closer, warning them more plainly of their office, and at the same time bringing forward the most weighty reasons by which he might stir them up the more.

units.la: Principio autem paucis summam rei proponens, ait: Attendite vobisipsis & cunctogregi. At tendendi autem voce summum studium illi commendat, ne se in suo munere obiter & quasi aliud agentes versari posse existiment, sed cura & circumspectione sibi opus esse intelligant. Et quidem duo proponit, quibus intenti esse debeant. Primum, Attendite vobisipsis, inquit. Illud vero iubet, ne seipsos exemptos putarent, sed hic non minus propriam ipsorum, quam aliorum salutem periclitari intelligerent. Et vt vix credibile est, eos aliorum salutem serio curaturos esse, qui propriæ negligen- tes fuerint: ita extra periculum esse non possunt, quicunq; in sublimi gradu constituti, omnium alio- rum vitam & mores & studia inspicere ac gubernare debent. Nam aut gloriæ studio elati exorbi- tabunt & in præceps ruent, aut iniquis de se hominum iudicijs offensi abripientur. Non temere er- go, vt sibijpsis attendant, monet. Æquibic quidem duorum maximè curam pastores habere conue- nit. Alterum doctrina est, in qua absq; manifesto damno errari non poterit. Vt ergo illa vera sit, ex Dei ore petatur, qui per scripturas nobis loqui solet, & eandem prudenter secando præsentibus locis & temporibus rite accommodent, vt ædificationi omnia seruiant. Id vero quia non parui momenti negotium est, indefesso scripturæ sacræ studio & lectione assidua opus erit, vt alibi idem Paulus mo- net. 1. Timoth. 4. 2. Timoth. 3. Alterum vitæ ratio est, quam in ministris optimè institutam, adeo ut irreprehensibilem esse oportet, ne quod doctrina ædificatur, malo exemplo destruat, neue propter ipsos doctrina simul & religio vilescat, quemadmodū olim sub filijs Heli & improbis sacerdotibus è Ba- bylone reuersis, accidisse legimus. 1. Sam. 2. Malach. 1. & 2. Ne quid vero tale fiat, non suarum mo- do personarum, sed totius etiam familiæ rationem ministros habere necesse est. Quomodo enim eccle- siam Dei administrabit, qui propriæ domui præesse nequit? 1. Timoth. 3. Tit. 1. Deinde secundo loco totius gregis curam ipsis commendat, in qua parte multis insistit, vt audiemus. Gregis autem voca- bulo ecclesiam designat, prophetas nimirum & ipsum Christum imitatus, qui eadem allegoria non raro vsi sunt. Estq; peropportunus huius vocabuli vsus, eò quòd omnes omnium ordinum homines significanter comprehendit, vt domus & familiæ voces, quibus alibi ecclesia designari consueuit. Nam ministros simul & populum sui officij istæ voces admonent. Discunt enim illi, ad se omnium homi- num curam pertinere, nec licere sibi vt quenquam negligant, siue ille doctus siue indoctus, nobilis aut obscurus, diues aut pauper, herus aut seruus fuerit: quin cogitandum illis esse in magna domo varia & diuersa vasa esse, quorum omnium legitimam & conuenientem curam à famulis geri vult pater- familias. Rursum auditores discunt, omnes in vniuersum homines, cuiuscunque loci siue ordinis fue- rint, verbi ministerio & disciplinæ subiectos esse debere, nec immunem esse aliquem, qui saltem inter diuini gregis oues & Dei domesticos censeri voluerit. Notum enim est illud, quod Ieremiæ dicit do- minus: Ecce ego facio te ciuitatem munitam, columnam ferream & murum æneum contra omnem terram, contra reges Iuda, contra principes eius, contra sacerdotes, & contra vniuersum populum terræ. Ierem. 1. Non temere ergo omnium ordinum homines olim prophetæ sibi reprehendendos & admonendos esse putauerunt, vt illorum sermones testantur. Quos Iohannes Baptista imitatus, non modo ignobile vulgus, sed simul etiam publicanos, milites, scribas, sacerdotes sui officij grauissimè admonuit, imò Herodi regi dicere audus est: Non licet tibi vxorem fratris tui habere. Fecit hoc ipsum Christus, mansuetissimus alioqui mortalium, quiq; inter fratres hereditatem diuidere noluit, ne quid à suo officio alienum faceret. Idem apostoli fecerunt & horum successores, quorum labores & studium hodie adhuc ecclesia veneratur. Nimis ergo crassa illorum stoliditas est, nimiumq; effrae- nis contumax q; rebellio, qui immunitatem quandam sibijpsis vendicantes, rerum suarum curam ad verbi ministros pertinere negant.
units.tr: At the outset, setting out the substance of the matter briefly, he says: "Take heed to yourselves and to all the flock." By the words "take heed" he commends to them the highest diligence, so that they may not think they can carry out their office casually, as if they were busy with something else, but understand that care and watchfulness are needed. He sets before them two things to which they must attend. The first is: "Take heed to yourselves." He orders this so that they would not think themselves exempt, but understand that their own salvation is at no less risk than that of others. Just as it is scarcely credible that those who neglect their own salvation will seriously care for the salvation of others, so those cannot be out of danger who, placed on a high rung, must watch over and govern the lives, morals and pursuits of all the rest. For either, elated by the desire for glory, they will go astray and rush headlong, or, offended by the unjust judgments of men about themselves, they will be carried away. Not without reason, then, he warns them to take heed to themselves. Indeed, pastors especially ought to attend to two things. The first is doctrine, in which one cannot err without manifest harm. So that it may be true, it must be sought from the mouth of God, who is accustomed to speak to us through the Scriptures; and they must apply it prudently, fitting it rightly to present places and times, so that all things serve edification. Since this is a matter of no small weight, it will require tireless study of holy Scripture and constant reading, as Paul admonishes elsewhere (1 Tim. 4; 2 Tim. 3). The second is the manner of life, which in ministers must be most well ordered, indeed so blameless that their example does not destroy by bad conduct what their doctrine builds up, nor doctrine and religion become cheap on account of the men themselves, as we read happened under the sons of Eli and the wicked priests who returned from Babylon (1 Sam. 2; Mal. 1 and 2). That nothing of this kind happens, ministers must have regard not only for their own persons but for the whole household as well. For how will he govern the Church of God who cannot preside over his own house? (1 Tim. 3; Tit. 1). Then, secondly, he entrusts to them the care of the whole flock, a point on which he dwells at length, as we shall hear. By the word "flock" he designates the Church, imitating the prophets and Christ himself, who used this allegory not rarely. The use of this word is very apt, since it meaningfully embraces all men of every rank, as do the words "house" and "family", by which the Church is elsewhere usually designated. For these words remind ministers and people alike of their duty. The ministers learn that the care of all men belongs to them, and that it is not lawful to neglect anyone, whether he be learned or unlearned, noble or obscure, rich or poor, master or servant; indeed they must reflect that in a great house there are various and diverse vessels, all of which the father of the household wishes to be lawfully and properly cared for by the servants. Again, the hearers learn that all men in general, of whatever place or rank, ought to be subject to the ministry of the Word and to discipline, and that no one is exempt who wishes at least to be counted among the sheep of God's flock and his household. For that saying of the Lord to Jeremiah is well known: "Behold, I make you a fortified city, an iron pillar and a bronze wall against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests and all the people of the land" (Jer. 1). Not without reason, then, the prophets of old thought that men of every order were to be rebuked and admonished by them, as their sermons attest. John the Baptist imitated them, and admonished not only the common people but also the tax collectors, soldiers, scribes and priests most gravely in their duty; indeed he dared to say to King Herod: "It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife." Christ himself did the same, most gentle as he was otherwise among mortals, and he refused to divide an inheritance among brothers, lest he do anything foreign to his office. The apostles did the same, and so did their successors, whose labours and zeal the Church still venerates today. Therefore the stupidity of those is too gross, and their unbridled and obstinate rebellion too great, who, claiming some immunity for themselves, deny that the care of their property belongs to the ministers of the Word.

units.la: Quia autem in difficilibus & periculosis funčtionibus carnem cunctatrice rationibus vrgeri ne esse est, illas quoque Paulus adhibet, & initio quidem multas simul paucis verbis complectitur. Nam attendite (inquit) gregi, in quo vos spiritus sanctus posuit Episcopos, ad pascendum ecclesiam Dei, quam acquisiuit sanguine suo. Primo ministerij sui authorem Deum allegat, ut doceat ipsos non sui iuris esse, sed in Dei negotio versari, cui aliquando rationem reddituri sint, quemadmodum in talentorum & dispensatoris parabolis Christus docet. Matth.25. Luc.16. Spiritus sanctus vero nominatim meminit, quia per hunc ecclesiam suam Christus potissimum administrat, sicut primo & secundo huius libri cap. vidimus. Est hæc grauis omnino ratio, si cogitemus nos ei rationem reddituros esse, quem nihil latere potest, & qui quo animo & qua fide singula à nobis fiant, intuetur: quia non iudex modo, verum etiam testis velox erit aduersus omnes qui excusso eius timore officium negligunt: sicut ipse apud prophetam minatur. Malach.3. Nec solos verbi ministros, verum etiam omnes alios, qui sua vocationis & conditionis authorem Deum habent, hæc ipsa ratio extimulare debet. Meminerint magistratus, se à Deo in sublimem illum eminentiæ gradum subuectos esse, & hunc in illorum consessu assistere, nec impune laturos, si officium suum negligant. Psal.82. Meminerint heri & domini se quoque in cœlis herum habere, cui rationem reddere cogentur. Ephes.6. Meminerint coniuges sui ordinis authorem esse Deum, qui vt coniugalem torum honorificum fecit, ita adulteros & scortatores graui iudicio punire solet. Hebr.13. Ita parentes cogitent à Deo sibi demandatam esse liberorum suorum curam, & proinde hos abs manifesto perfidiæ crimine negligi non posse. Ita serui & subditi quiuis suis heris & principibus non modo poenæ metu, sed propter conscientiam obedire discant, eò quòd Deus ipsos horum imperio subiecerit, cuius oculos nunquam fallent, licet homines fallant.
units.tr: But because the flesh is wont to be urged by hesitant reasons in difficult and dangerous functions, Paul also brings these forward, and at the start gathers many of them together in a few words. For he says: "Take heed to the flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood." First he appeals to God as the author of their ministry, to teach them that they are not their own masters but are engaged in God's business, and that one day they will have to render an account of it, as Christ teaches in the parables of the talents and of the steward (Matt. 25; Luke 16). He names the Holy Spirit specifically because it is chiefly through him that Christ governs his Church, as we saw in the first and second chapters of this book. This reason is altogether weighty if we consider that we shall render an account to him from whom nothing can be hidden, and who sees with what mind and what faith each thing is done by us; for he will be not only a judge but also a swift witness against all who, having cast off fear of him, neglect their office, as he himself threatens through the prophet (Mal. 3). This same reason ought to stir up not only the ministers of the Word but all others who have God as the author of their calling and station. Let magistrates remember that God has raised them to that lofty height of eminence, and that they stand in his assembly, and that they will not go unpunished if they neglect their office (Ps. 82). Let masters and lords remember that they too have a Lord in heaven, to whom they will be compelled to render an account (Eph. 6). Let spouses remember that God is the author of their order, who, as he has made the marriage bed honourable, so he is accustomed to punish adulterers and fornicators with severe judgment (Heb. 13). Thus let parents think that the care of their children has been entrusted to them by God, and that therefore it cannot be neglected without the manifest crime of faithlessness. Thus let servants and all subjects learn to obey their masters and rulers not only from fear of punishment but out of conscience, because God has subjected them to that authority, and his eyes they will never deceive, even if they deceive men.

units.la: Hinc verò sui officij fine illis ob oculos statuit, dum ipsos à spiritu sancto Episcopos positos esse dicit, ad pascendum Dei ecclesiam. Alludit autem ad Ezech.3. & 33. cap. vbi prophetæ Episcopi Speculatores dicuntur. Ne verò in nuda & inani speculatione suum officium consistere putarent, pascendi verbo vsitur, vt se pastores esse meminerint, & proinde pastorum officijs fungantur. Exprimuntur hæc partim ab ipso Christo apud Iohannem 10. cap. partim Ezech.34. Bonus enim pastor in pascua læta oues deducit, illas fidi ducis instar præcedit, perditas quærit, propulsatam reducit, contritam animo & conscientia obligat, infirmam roborat, pinguedine nimia ferocientes coercet, lupos fortiter oppugnat, atque omnia hæc cum iudicio & circumspectè agit. Horum omnium Ephesios siue Asianos ministros Paulus admonet, dum illos ad pascendum constitutos esse ait. Vtinam verò horum meminissent nostri sæculi episcopi, qui cum nihil horum, omnia verò his contraria faciant, impudenti tamen insolentia non episcoporum modo titulos, verumetiam manifestam in ecclesiam tyrannidem sibi vendicant, & contra Christi præceptum instar mundi huius principum regnum obtinent. Sed quid illos manet, vide Ezech.34. & Zach.11. cap.
units.tr: Then, by naming the Holy Spirit as the one who placed them as bishops to feed the Church of God, he sets before them the end of their office. He alludes to Ezekiel 3 and 33, where the prophets are called watchmen. But lest they think their office consists in bare and empty watching, he uses the word "feed," so that they remember they are shepherds and carry out the duties of shepherds. These duties are set out partly by Christ himself in John 10 and partly in Ezekiel 34. For the good shepherd leads the sheep into rich pastures, goes before them like a faithful leader, seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds up the broken in heart and conscience, strengthens the weak, restrains the overfed and fierce, boldly attacks the wolves, and does all this with judgment and circumspection. Paul admonishes the Ephesian, or Asian, ministers of all these things when he says they have been appointed to feed. Would that the bishops of our own age remembered them! Yet they do none of these things, but everything contrary to them. With shameless arrogance they claim not only the titles of bishops but also a manifest tyranny over the Church, and against Christ's command they hold a kingdom like that of the princes of this world. But see what awaits them: Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 11.

units.la: Tertia ratio ab ecclesiæ dignitate sumitur, quæ in eo elucet, quòd illam Deus suo sanguine acquisiuit. Deo autem sanguinem tribuit per idiomatum communicationem: eò quòd qui ab æterno Deus est, Christus Iesus, præfinito tempore homo factus, ecclesiam sui sanguinis pretio redemit. Non potest ergo illi non charissima esse, & sanguinis Christi reatu sese polluunt, quicunque ecclesiam negligentes huius fructum vel ipsi abolent, vel saltem perire & intercidere patiuntur. Obseruabis autem, ecclesiam non alicuius hominis, sed Dei esse, qui suo sanguine acquisitam & mundatam sibi ipsi despondit. Vide Ephes.5. Vt ergo nemo sibi ipsi temere in Dei sponsam dominium vendicare debet: ita singuli, qui huius membra esse volunt, curandum est, vt soli Deo consecrati, in nullius creaturæ verba iurent, ne execrabilis fornicationis poenas luant. Simul verò hoc ipsum consolationi seruire debet, quia illos à Deo negligi impossibile est, quos tanto pretio redemptos voluit. Vide 1.Pet.1. Eandem autem omnium Christianorum rationem coram Deo esse intelligas. Vt enim singuli horum ad Dei imaginem creati, ita filij Dei sanguine redempti & acquisiti sunt. Num ergo te impune laturum putas, si quem illorum conuiciaris, iniuria afficis, violenter laedis, contumeliose fastidis, aut etiam in religione sine vitæ conuersatione offendis? Lege quæ ad hunc locum mirifice pertinent à Paulo tractata ad Rom.14. & in priori ad Corinth.8.cap.
units.tr: The third reason is taken from the dignity of the Church, which shines forth in that God acquired it with his own blood. Blood is attributed to God through the communication of properties, since Christ Jesus, who is God from eternity, was made man at a set time and redeemed the Church with the price of his blood. It cannot therefore be other than most dear to him. Whoever neglect the Church, either destroying its fruit themselves or allowing it to perish and fall away, pollute themselves with the guilt of Christ's blood. Observe, moreover, that the Church belongs not to any man but to God, who betrothed it to himself, acquired and cleansed by his own blood. See Ephesians 5. Therefore, just as no one should rashly claim lordship over God's bride for himself, so each of those who wish to be her members must take care to be consecrated to God alone and to swear by the words of no creature, lest they pay the penalty of execrable fornication. At the same time this should serve for consolation, because it is impossible for God to neglect those whom he willed to redeem at so great a price. See 1 Peter 1. Understand also that all Christians stand in the same position before God. For just as each of them was created in the image of God, so the children of God have been redeemed and acquired by his blood. Do you think, then, that you will go unpunished if you revile any of them, wrong them, violently harm them, scorn them with insults, or even give offence in religion or in the conduct of life? Read what Paul treats so admirably on this point in Romans 14 and in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 8.

units.la: Quarta ratio necessitatis est. Docet enim necessariam omnino fore diligentiorē ecclesiæ Christi curam, eò quòd horrenda ex lupis siue falsis doctoribus pericula immineant. Licet enim pastori interdum terdum somnus & otium concedatur, quando nimirum nulla periculi suspicio subesse, nullus tamen vel otio vel somno locus est reliquus, ubi luporum vlulatus exaudiri & illorum agmina conspici incipiunt. At ego noui (inquit Paulus) post meum discessum graues lupos exorituros, qui nulla gregis misericordia tangentur: imo ex vobis ipsis prodibunt, qui simplicem veritatis doctrinam misere pervertent, in hoc potius intenti, ut sibi ipsis discipulos colligant, quam Christo, cuius gloria soli studere debebant. Nouerat autem tales exorituroc esse Paulus, nimirum peculiari spiritus revelatione admonitus. Nam alibi de falsis doctoribus vaticinaturus spiritum oraculi authorem facit. 1 Tim. 4.
units.tr: The fourth reason is one of necessity. For it teaches that a more diligent care of Christ's Church will be altogether necessary, because dreadful dangers from wolves, that is, false teachers, are looming. For although the shepherd may sometimes be granted sleep and leisure, namely when no suspicion of danger lies beneath, there is no room left for leisure or sleep once the howling of wolves begins to be heard and their packs to be seen. "But I know," says Paul, "that after my departure grievous wolves will arise, who will be moved by no pity for the flock. Indeed, from among you yourselves will come men who will miserably pervert the plain doctrine of truth, intent rather on gathering disciples for themselves than on Christ, to whose glory alone they ought to have devoted themselves." Paul knew that such men would arise, having been warned by a special revelation of the Spirit. For elsewhere, when he is about to prophesy concerning false teachers, he makes the Spirit the author of the oracle (1 Timothy 4).

units.la: Caeterum obseruemus hoc loco Dei fidelem curam, qua is ecclesiae suae rebus prospicere consuevit. Versatur hac ceu grex inermis in medio luporum. Sed ita Deo cura est, ut non de praesentibus modo, verum etiam futuris periculis illam diligenter admoneat. Extant enim prophetarum de Antichristo & Antichristianis doctoribus oracula. Christus quoque de nouissimis temporibus differens, eosdem ita describit, ut sciens volens pereat, quisquis illis fidem habet. Apostolorum vero scripta eiusmodi praemonitionibus passim plena sunt, quas brevitatis causa omittimus. Interim tamen docemur, quam delirent, qui hodie nudam veritatis doctrinam simpliciter tradi volunt, interim vero ecclesiam de imminentibus periculis admoneri, & lupos argui non volunt, eo quod hos pastorum clamoribus magis irritari & ferociores reddi videant. Quasi vero lupos vicurare aut si nemo illis negotium faciat, naturam mutare possibile sit, & non hic potius finis pastoribus propositus sit, ut oues a luporum insidijs sibi cauere discant? Quam vero ridiculum fuerit, apostolos de venturis lupis nos admonuisse, si hodie in ecclesia grassantes nemo arguere debet? Deinde obseruemus, quod lupos hos post suum discessum demum venturos dicit.
