Solent enim fidelium ministrorum praesentia terreri, & eorundem cura & inducтria coerceri, quo minus irruptionem faciant. At quia hanc mundus ingratus fere indigne aestimat, permittit Deus, ut fidelibus ministris sublatis, lupi effraenum equorum instar ingregem totum effundantur. Nec exempla desunt, quibus hoc abunde probari poterat. Discamus igitur, quanti a nobis fieri debeant fideles & industrij cum ecclesiarum tum rerumpub. antistites, quorum obitus fere ingentium malorum & publicarum calamitatum sunt praesagia. Tertio falsorum doctorum descriptionem, & quae horum omnino ratio sit, videamus. Lupos vocat apostolus, idque iuxta Christi exemplum, quem eodem nomine illos appellauisse constat. Matth. 7. Ioan. 10. Ita vero dicuntur, tum quod natiuo odio gregis Christi laborant, tum quod insatiabili auaritia & rapacitate ecclesiam dissipare solent. Inde autem vnde tales emergant, docet. Ex vobisipsis (inquit) prodibunt. Ita Iohannes ait: Ex nobis egressi sunt, &c. 1. Iohan. 2. Et Paulus Antichristi sedem in ipsa ecclesia nobis monstrat. 2. Thess. 2. Prodesse hoc diligenter obseruauisse, ne leuissimorum hominum apostasia offendamur, quando repente veritatis hostes fieri conspicimus, qui paulo ante huius propugnatores strenuissimi videbantur. Quid enim hoc novi est, quando Iudas quoque inter apostolos aliquandiu locum habuit, & Paulus ex illis ipsis lupos emersuros esse nouit, quibus ecclesiam tanta fide commendat? Simul autem confutatur hic stolida & inepta Romanorum Pontificum gloriatio, qua hodie maxime nituntur. Nam fieri non posse putant, ut eius ecclesiae antistites errent, quorum continua ab ipsis apostolorum temporibus successio numeratur. Ut enim hoc illis demus, Petrum & Paulum Romanos episcopos fuisse (quod tamen nunquam probabunt) num vero illorum successores errare potuisse negabunt? Atqui Pauli successores apud Ephesios fuerunt lupi isti graues, a quibus cauendum esse monet. Sed ut merito laruis Papatus consistit, ita laruatis quoq; argumentis illius maiestatem breui ruituram defendi oportet. Praeterea doctrinam horum attingit, dum illos peruersa & distorta locuturos dicit. Est enim simplex & recta veritatis oratio, quam falsi doctores suis figmentis peruertere, intricare & ita agendo omnia incerta reddere consueuerunt. Porro finis horum est, ut post se discipulos abducant. Sectis ergo ecclesiam scindunt, quod fore Petrus quoq; praedicit, 2. Pet. 2. Atqui non frustra haec Paulum monuisse, historiae testantur. Nota enim sunt haereticorum agmina, quae ecclesias per totum orbem miserrime turbauerunt. Etsi haec ipsa cum nostris temporibus conferas, non minus necessariam nobis hodie esse patebit Pauli admonitionem, quam olim fuerit. Ex ecclesia enim quotidie prodeunt graues illi lupi, qui eo impudentiae iam progressi sunt, ut non amplius ouium pellibus se velare studeant, quin potius purpureo colore sanguinis Christiani fictum, & satellitum armorumq; strepitu tyrannidem publice profitentur. Per hos infinitis erroribus & Labyrinthis intricata & quasi sepulta iacet veritatis doctrina. Et ijdem in sectas sexcentas ecclesiam, quae vnica esse debebat, sciderunt, quarum singulae propriam fidem & religionem nomine, habitu, ceremonijs & ritibus teguntur. Expergiscamur ergo o fratres, & lupis istis obuiam progressi cauea‐mus, ne mercenarij potius quam veri pastores esse deprehendamur.
units.tr: Moreover, let us observe here God's faithful care, by which he is accustomed to provide for his Church. It lives in the midst of wolves like an unarmed flock. Yet God so cares for it that he diligently warns it not only of present dangers but also of future ones. For there are prophetic oracles concerning Antichrist and the Antichristian teachers. Christ too, speaking of the last times, describes them in such a way that whoever believes them knowingly and willingly perishes. The writings of the apostles are everywhere full of such warnings, which for brevity we omit. Meanwhile we are taught how foolish are those who today want the bare doctrine of truth simply taught, yet do not want the Church warned of impending dangers or the wolves accused, because they see that the wolves are roused and made fiercer by the shepherds' cries. As if it were possible to conquer wolves, or to change their nature, if no one troubled them, and the aim set for shepherds were not rather that the sheep should learn to beware of the wolves' snares! How ridiculous it would be for the apostles to have warned us of coming wolves if no one today ought to refute those raging in the Church! Next, let us observe that he says these wolves will come only after his departure. For the presence of faithful ministers usually terrifies them, and their care and diligence restrain them from attacking. But because the ungrateful world almost unworthily values this, God permits, once the faithful ministers are removed, the wolves to pour out over the whole flock like unbridled horses. Nor are examples lacking by which this could amply be proved. Let us learn, then, how highly we should value faithful and diligent leaders, both of the churches and of the commonwealths, whose deaths are almost the forerunners of great evils and public calamities. Third, let us look at the description of false teachers and the reason behind all of them. The apostle calls them wolves, following Christ's example, who is known to have called them by the same name (Matthew 7; John 10). They are so called both because they labour under a natural hatred of Christ's flock and because they are accustomed to destroy the Church with insatiable greed and rapacity. He teaches where such men arise: "From among you yourselves," he says. So John says, "They went out from us," etc. (1 John 2), and Paul shows us the seat of Antichrist within the Church itself (2 Thessalonians 2). It is useful to observe this carefully, so that we are not offended by the apostasy of very light men when we suddenly see those become enemies of the truth who a little before seemed its most vigorous defenders. For what is new in this? Judas too held a place among the apostles for some time, and Paul knew that wolves would emerge from the very men to whom he commends the Church with such faith. At the same time, the foolish and silly boasting of the Roman pontiffs, on which they chiefly rely today, is refuted here. For they think it impossible that the bishops of that church should err, whose continuous succession is counted from the very times of the apostles. Grant them that Peter and Paul were bishops of Rome (which they will never prove); will they deny that their successors could err? Yet Paul's successors among the Ephesians were those grievous wolves against whom he warns. But just as the Papacy rests on masks, so its majesty, which will soon fall, must be defended with masked arguments too. Besides, he touches on their doctrine when he says they will speak perverse and distorted things. For the simple and right word of truth is what false teachers are accustomed to pervert and entangle with their fictions, and in so doing render everything uncertain. Moreover, the aim of these men is to draw disciples away after themselves. Therefore they split the Church into sects, which Peter also foretells (2 Peter 2). Yet histories bear witness that Paul's warning was not given in vain, for the hordes of heretics that most wretchedly troubled churches throughout the whole world are well known. And if you compare these very things with our own times, it will be clear that Paul's admonition is no less necessary for us today than it was then. For those grievous wolves come forth from the Church every day. They have now advanced to such impudence that they no longer seek to cover themselves with sheep's skins; rather, dyed in the purple colour of Christian blood, they openly profess tyranny with the clatter of guards and arms. Through these men the doctrine of truth lies entangled, and as if buried, in countless errors and labyrinths; and they have split the Church, which ought to have been one, into six hundred sects, each of which covers its own faith and religion with a name, dress, ceremonies and rites. Let us therefore awake, brothers, and go out to meet these wolves, and take care that we are not found to be hirelings rather than true shepherds.

units.la: Sed Paulum audiamus, qui suum exemplum denuo inculcans (quod quintum argumentum est) illos grauissime hortatur, dicens: Quapropter vigilate, memores, quod per triennium noctes & dies non cessauerim cum lachrymis monere vnumquenq. Triennij vero meminit, ne ipsi sese longo & continuo labore defatigari patiantur. Turpe enim foret labores & pericula subire nolle, quae tantus Christi apostolus subire non recusauit. Nec leuis illorum culpa esse poterit, qui apostolorum laboribus & sanguine collectas ecclesias sua negligentia dissipant. Porro vt ministros apostolorum exemplum imitari decet, ita eorundem vestigijs singuli Christiani insistere debent, quatenus illi Christi imitatores fuerunt, sicuti ipse Paulus admonet, cum ait: Imitatores mei estote, sicuti ego Christi sum. 1.Cor.11. Atqui hic demum legitimus Diuorum cultus est, non ille, qui in adoratione & inuocatione consistit, quam vni Deo deberi omnis scriptura docet.
units.tr: But let us hear Paul, who, repeating his own example once more (this is the fifth argument), urges them very earnestly, saying: "Therefore watch, remembering that for three years I did not cease night and day to warn every one of you with tears." He mentions the three years so that they may not allow themselves to be worn out by long and continual toil. For it would be shameful to be unwilling to undergo labours and dangers which so great an apostle of Christ did not refuse to undergo. Nor can the fault of those be small who through their negligence scatter the churches gathered by the labours and blood of the apostles. Moreover, just as it becomes ministers to imitate the example of the apostles, so each Christian ought to follow in their footsteps, inasmuch as they were imitators of Christ, as Paul himself admonishes when he says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ." 1 Cor. 11. Indeed, this is the lawful worship of the saints, not that which consists in adoration and invocation, which all Scripture teaches is owed to the one God alone.

units.la: Sexto a facili & utili argumentatur, vt ijs occurrat, qui muneris difficultate & vndiq; immi‐nentibus periculis abster rebantur. Et vt magis pathetica sit oratio, Imprecationis forma vtitur, cum ait: Et nunc comendo vos fratres Deo, & sermoni gratiae ipsius, qui potens est superstruere, &c. Quasi dicat: Scio ardui laboris opus esse quod exigo, & humanis viribus impar. Atqui non illud humana virtute confici oportet. Dei haec agricolatio, Dei hoc opus est. Ille fundamentum iecit. Idem ergo superstruere poterit, nec illi difficile erit vestra ad eam rem opera vti. Illo igitur auxiliante facile omnia superabitis. Aderit is suo spiritu, & verbo gratiae sua, quod licet in speciem vile sit, penetrat tamen, & quouis gladio ancipiti acutius ferit. Idem ille Deus digna tantis laboribus & pericu‐lis praemia iam praeparauit, hereditatem nimirum regni sui, in qua inter sanctificatos eius instar astrorum & firmamenti fulgebitis. Vide Dan.12. Sunt haec inimis animis recondenda, o fratres. Vt enim mirifice consolantur, ita docent, quae ministrorum ecclesiae arma & vires sint. Arma militiae nostrae spiritualia sunt, inquit Paulus. 2.Corinth.10. Sunt haec Dei spiritus & verbum, adeo, ipse Deus. Quem ergo timeant? Aut quis se illis opponere poterit? His armis potius pugnemus, quam mundi amicitijs, foederibus & carnis prudentia, quorum omnium nullus, aut perquam exiguus in regno Dei prouebendo vsus est. Discimus praeterea, ad sanctificatos solos regni caelestis haereditatem pertinere. Sunt hi, quorum corda fides mundauit, & quos Christus sui sanguinis precio patri Deo consecrauit. Iidem spiritu Dei animati officium suum sedulo faciunt, & per quaeuis pericula ad haereditatem illam acerrime contendunt, cuius spem inuictam & infallibilem esse norunt, eo quod Dei filio nitatur, domino nostro Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Sixthly, he argues from what is easy and useful, to meet those who were shrinking back because of the difficulty of the office and the dangers hanging over them on every side. And to make his speech more moving, he uses the form of a prayer, saying: "And now I commend you, brothers, to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up," etc. As if he were saying: "I know that the task I demand is a work of arduous labour and beyond human strength. But it must not be accomplished by human virtue. This tillage is God's, this work is God's. He laid the foundation; the same one will be able to build upon it, nor will it be hard for him to use your labour for that purpose. Therefore, with him helping, you will overcome all things easily. He will be present with his Spirit and with his word of grace, which, although it seems in appearance a worthless thing, nevertheless penetrates and strikes more keenly than any two-edged sword. That same God has already prepared rewards worthy of such labours and dangers, namely the inheritance of his kingdom, in which among his sanctified ones you will shine like the stars and the firmament. See Dan. 12. These things, brothers, must be stored deep in our minds. For as they comfort us wonderfully, so they teach what the arms and strength of the ministers of the Church are. 'The weapons of our warfare are spiritual,' says Paul, 2 Cor. 10. These are the Spirit and the word of God, indeed God himself. Whom then should they fear? Or who will be able to set himself against them? Let us fight with these weapons rather than with the friendships, alliances and worldly prudence of the flesh, of which none, or very little, has been of use in advancing the kingdom of God. We learn also that the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom belongs to the sanctified alone. These are those whose hearts faith has cleansed, and whom Christ has consecrated to the Father God at the price of his own blood. Animated by the Spirit of God, they faithfully perform their duty, and through whatever dangers they strive most eagerly for that inheritance, whose hope they know to be invincible and infallible, because it rests upon the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen."

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVI.
units.tr: HOMILIA CXXXVI.

units.la: Argentum & aurum, aut vestem nullius concupiui. Imo ipsi scitis, quod vsibus meis, & ijs qui mecum sunt, suppeditauerunt manus haec. Omnia ostendi vobis, quod sic laborantes oportet suscipere infirmos, ac meminisse verborum domini Iesu: quoniam ipse dixit: Beatum est dare potius quam accipere. Et cum haec dixisset, positis genibus suis, orauit cum omnibus illis. Magnus autem fletus coortus est omnium: & ruentes in collum Pauli, osculabantur eum, dolentes maxime ob sermonem, quem dixerat, quod amplius faciem eius non essent visuri. Et deduxerunt eum ad nauem.
units.tr: "I have coveted no one's silver, gold or clothing. Indeed, you yourselves know that these hands supplied my own needs and those of my companions. In every way I have shown you that by such labour we must help the weak, and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, who himself said: It is more blessed to give than to receive." When he had said this, he knelt down and prayed with them all. Then everyone wept loudly, and they threw themselves on Paul's neck and kissed him, grieving most of all at the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they escorted him to the ship.

units.la: Quoniam Paulus Apostolus in celebri ministrorum Asiae conuentu de ecclesiae administratione differens, ex illis ipsis, quibus cum agebat, graues lupos exorituros esse praedixit, qui peruersis doctrinis gregem Christi misere turbent, commode simul & prudenter vltima suae oratio‐nis parte docet, quid potissimum cauere debeant, si in eiusmodi lupos degenerare nolint. Solam verò anaritiam auaritiam illis fugiendam esse monet, eo quod haec omnium malorum radix est, nec quicquam integrum esse patitur, si antistitum animos semel obsederit. Nam religionem quaestum ducens, facit ut illis sacra omnia venalia sint, quae simul causa est, quod verbi doctrinam humanis traditionibus ut tiant, mundi favorem & amicitiam venantur, ad scelera publica conniveant, & omni denique corruptioni fenestram aperiunt. Exemplo nobis esse possunt Iudaeorum sacerdotes, in quibus hunc omnis corruptionis fontem Christus maxime reprehendit. Non temere ergo Paulus alibi monet, ne turpis lucri amantes sint episcopi, & in praesenti de hoc malo gravissime disserit. Ut enim maior esset sua admonitionis authoritas, suo exemplo illos urget, docens quid ipse in Asia versans egerit, & sui facti causas ac rationes gravissimas allegat.
units.tr: When Paul the Apostle, speaking at the famous assembly of the ministers of Asia about the government of the Church, foretold that fierce wolves would arise from among those very men he was dealing with, who would wretchedly trouble Christ's flock with perverse teachings, he taught, both wisely and fittingly, in the final part of his speech what they should above all guard against if they did not want to degenerate into such wolves. He warns them above all to shun covetousness, because it is the root of all evils, and it allows nothing to remain sound once it has taken hold of the minds of leaders. For, treating religion as a source of gain, it makes all sacred things saleable. This is also why they teach human traditions in place of the doctrine of the Word, hunt after the favour and friendship of the world, connive at public crimes, and in short open a window to every kind of corruption. The priests of the Jews can serve us as an example, in whom Christ rebukes most sharply this fountain of all corruption. Paul therefore is not without reason elsewhere warns that bishops must not be lovers of shameful gain, and here he treats this evil very seriously. To give greater authority to his admonition, he presses them with his own example, showing what he himself did while living in Asia, and offering the most weighty reasons and grounds for his conduct.

units.la: Aurum & argentum, aut vestem nullius concupiui, inquit. Quibus verbis testatur, se nequaquam studuisse, ut ex illis diteseceret, quando quae illi ad viuendum necessaria erant, nec cupierit quidem ex illis habere, ne dum acceperit. Ita vero docet, ecclesiarum ministros a cupiditate etiam opum coaceruandarum alienissimos esse debere, eo quod qui ditescere volunt, diaboli & tentationum laqueos nunquam effugient. 1 Timoth. 6. At ne quis exciperet: Unde ergo tibi vestis obtigit, o Paule? Mox subiungit: Ipsi scitis, quod vsibus meis, & iis qui mecum sunt, suppeditauerunt manus haec. Tentoriorum enim textor erat, quo artificio illum Corinthi quoque sibi vitam parauisse, supra audiimus. Obseruabis autem hoc loco apostolorum modestiam, qui suo potius iure cedere, quam alicui onerosi esse voluerunt. Qua de re plura in posteriori ad Thess. cap. 3. & secunda ad Corinth. cap. 11. esse videre. Eiusdem modestiae exemplum in Samuele etiam habetur, qui in frequentissimo totius populi comitiis de hoc ipso gloriari audet, cuius hic Paulus meminit. 1 Samuel 12. Docent autem exempla haec, quo spiritu agantur, quicunque vel in ecclesia vel repub. suis duntaxat commodis inuigilant, nec contenti necessariis, ex egentium sudore delitias quoque & voluptates quaerunt.
units.tr: "I have coveted no one's gold or silver or clothing," he says. By these words he testifies that he never strove to grow rich from them, since he neither desired to have from them even what was needed for living, much less to receive more. He teaches in this way that ministers of the churches ought to be most distant from the desire even to heap up wealth, because those who want to become rich never escape the snares of the devil and of temptations. 1 Timothy 6. But lest someone should object: "Where then did you get your clothing, Paul?" he immediately adds: "You yourselves know that these hands supplied my own needs and those of my companions." For he was a maker of tents, by which craft, as we heard above, he also earned his living at Corinth. Here you will notice the modesty of the apostles, who preferred to give up their own right rather than be a burden to anyone. On this matter you may see more in the later letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 3, and in the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 11. An example of the same modesty is also found in Samuel, who in the most crowded assembly of the whole people dares to boast of this very thing which Paul here mentions. 1 Samuel 12. These examples teach by what spirit those are driven who, whether in the Church or in the commonwealth, watch only over their own advantage, and who, not content with necessities, seek luxuries and pleasures too from the sweat of the needy.

units.la: Porro causas sui facti diligentius reddit, ne suum exemplum communi & publico ministrorum iuri praeiudicaret siue officeret. Nec eam Paulo mentem fuisse satis constat, ut nefas esse putaret, quod ipse Christus instituit, ut nimirum ex euangelio viuant, qui euangelio seruiunt: imo hoc quam maxime licere, cum scripturae authoritate tum rationibus e naturae lege petitis alibi copiose probat. 1 Corinth. 9. Adhaec se a Macedonibus pecunias accepisse fatetur, ut Corinthijs gratis inseruire posset. 2 Corinth. 11. Longe alia ergo Paulini consilij ratio fuit, ea nimirum, quod infirmos assumere, id est, illis indulgere voluit, & reliquos omnes docere, ne religionem quaestum ducentes, illa suspectam facerent, quin potius gratuito ministerio & omni officiorum genere se suam, quod doctrinam passim omnibus commendarent. Ineptissime ergo Pauli exemplum ad generalem doctrinam hodie detorquent quidam male feriati homines, qui verbi ministros non ad textoriam modo, verumetiam ad sinuam & porcos vsq; ablegatos volunt: quando satis constat, apostolos suo iure liberè vsos fuisse, vbi nulla metuenda fuit offendiculi occasio. Quod si autem Paulum Ephesi & Corinthi stipendio ecclesiastico ideo abstinuisse dicunt, quod illud exigere simpliciter nefas & iniquum sit, respondeant velim, quo iure idem Paulus a Philippensibus stipendium, imo pecuniarium subsidium sumpserit, quando non ipsis, sed Corinthijs praedicabat? Quod si illorum liberalitate vti ipsi licuit, quanto aequius erat ab illis stipendium sumere, quibus assidua doctrina seruiebat? Constat ergo, Paulum suo iure cessisse, ne vel infirmis offendiculum, vel improbis calumniandi occasionem praeberet. Et ut laudem meretur Pauli modestia: ita acri reprehensione digna est tum Ephesiorum tum Corinthiorum ingratitudo, qui apostolum manuum suarum labore vitare passi sunt, qui se fuosq; labores omnes solis ipsis impendebat.
units.tr: Moreover, he gives the reasons for his conduct more carefully, so that his own example would not prejudice or hinder the common and public right of ministers. It is quite clear that Paul did not think it wrong for those who serve the gospel to live from the gospel, which Christ himself instituted. Indeed, he proves elsewhere at length that this is most fully permitted, both by the authority of Scripture and by reasons drawn from the law of nature. 1 Corinthians 9. Besides, he confesses that he received money from the Macedonians so that he could serve the Corinthians without charge. 2 Corinthians 11. The reason for Paul's plan was therefore quite different: namely, that he wished to take up the weak, that is, to indulge them, and to teach all the others not to make religion a source of gain and so make it suspect, but rather to commend their doctrine everywhere by free ministry and every kind of service. So some foolish men, who are badly at ease, absurdly twist Paul's example today into a general doctrine, and want ministers of the Word sent away not only to the weaving loom but even to the sewing needle and the pigs. When it is clear that the apostles used their right freely where there was no fear of giving offence. But if they say that Paul abstained from ecclesiastical stipend at Ephesus and Corinth because demanding it is simply wrong and unjust, I would like them to answer by what right the same Paul took a stipend, indeed financial help, from the Philippians, since he was not preaching to them but to the Corinthians. If he was allowed to use their generosity, how much fairer was it to take a stipend from those whom he served with constant teaching? It is clear, then, that Paul gave up his right so that he might not offer a stumbling block to the weak or an occasion for slander to the wicked. And just as Paul's modesty deserves praise, so the ingratitude of the Ephesians and Corinthians, who allowed the apostle to bear the labour of his own hands, while he was spending all his labours solely on them, deserves sharp rebuke.

units.la: Caeterum ut maior esset sui exempli authoritas, & inde simul generalis doctrina decerpi posset, Christi dictum allegat: Beatum est dare potius quam accipere. Atqui non extant in euangelistarum scriptis huius sententiae verba, extant tamen similes multae, ex quibus ista clarissime colligi potest, quando passim nos ad charitatis officia Christus hortatur & ad conferenda potius alijs quam recipienda beneficia suos paratos esse vult. Deinde satis constat, non omnia tum dicta tum facta Christi literis mandata fuisse, sed ex multis ea, quae ad nostrae fidei institutionem & salutis rationem nobis abunde sufficere poterant. Est autem altius nobis inquirenda huius dicti ratio, nec in nudo cortice haerendum, ut ideo beatius nobis videatur dare quam accipere, quod dando tum fortuna
units.tr: But so that the authority of his example might be greater, and at the same time a general doctrine could be drawn from it, he cites the saying of Christ: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." Yet the words of this saying are not found in the writings of the evangelists, though many similar sayings are, from which this one can very clearly be inferred, since Christ everywhere urges us to acts of love and wants his people to be ready to confer benefits on others rather than to receive them. Furthermore, it is quite clear that not all the words and deeds of Christ were committed to writing, but only those that could sufficiently serve for the instruction of our faith and the manner of our salvation. We must, however, inquire more deeply into the reason for this saying, and not stop at the bare bark, as if giving seemed to us more blessed than receiving only because by giving we bear witness, with praise, both to the abundance of our means and to the generosity of our mind, and make others indebted to us.

units.la: Ab auaritia suo exemplo debortatur.
units.tr: He dissuades from covetousness by his own example.

units.la: Quare debitum sibi stipendium Paulus non exegerit?
units.tr: Why did Paul not demand the stipend owed to him?

units.la: Beatius est dare quam accipere. rum nostrarum & facultatum abundantiam, tum animi liberalitatem cum laude testemur, & alios nobis obstrictos reddamus. Istæ enim rationes humanæ gloriæ studium & culinæ nidore sapiunt, quibus ethnicos quoque olim ad beneficentiæ studium accensos fuisse legimus. Christianus vero homi-nibus longe alijs rationibus beneficentiam tantopere Christus commendat. Primo enim beatius est dare quàm accipere, quia qui id faciunt fideles bonorum, quæ illis Deus credidit, œconomi siue dispen-satores sunt. Constat enim Deum inæqualitatem fortunarum non temere hominibus imposuisse, sed ideò alios alijs opulentiores facere, vt locum habeant charitatis officia, adeoq; diuites egenos quasi patronos & tutores datos esse, qui illos sua beneficentia adiuuent. At quomodo non potest non beatus censeri, qui in munere sibi diuinitus commisso fideliS fuerit? Deinde iuxta Solomonis dictum Deo fœnerantur, qui egenis benefaciunt. Proverb. 19. Is enim sibi datum iudicat quicquid in illos confertur, & remunerator est fidelis simul & liberalis. Quare fieri non potest, quin promissis stet, quibus ad beneficentiæ studium homines inuitat. Quales sunt: Beatus vir, qui spargit, & dat pau-peribus. Huius iustitia manet in æternum, & cornu eius exaltabitur cum gloria. Psal. 112. Frange, esurienti panem tuum, afflictos, extorres & egenos introduc in domum tuam, si videris nudum tege eum, & à carne tua ne te abscondas. Tunc erumpet velut aurora lux tua, & diuturnitas tua proti-nus germinabit, iustitia anteibit faciem tuam, & gloria domini colliget te. Tunc inuocabis, & do-minus exaudiet: clamabis, & dicet: En me tibi, &c. Isa. 58. Postremò quia nihil tam diuinum est quàm benefacere, non alia re ad Dei naturam & similitudinem propius accedunt homines quàm be-nefaciendo quàm plurimùm. Vt verò solus Deus per se beatus est, ita non alia beatitudinis ratio certior est, quàm Deo simillimum fieri, id quod beneficentiæ Christianæ studium quàm maximè præ-stat. Quare et si nulla in hoc mundo siat beneficiorum compensatio, reuera tamen beatius multò est dare quàm accipere. H Æ C si propius inspiciamus, patebit quàm aliena à Christi doctrina sit om-nis Monachorum religio, qui in accipiendo felicitatem omnem collocant, dum ijs, quæ vel legitima hæreditate vel iustis medijs obtigerunt, renuntiantes, voluntariam paupertatē vouent, & aliorum laboribus viuunt, qui potius alijs victū & amictum subministrare debebant: ficq; sub plausibili vo-luntariæ paupertatis prætextu securé delitiantur, nullis quodammodo, vt reliqui mortales, fortunæ casibus obnoxij.
units.tr: It is more blessed to give than to receive. For those reasons savour of the desire for human glory and of the smell of the kitchen, and by such reasons we read that the heathen too were once fired with zeal for beneficence. But the Christian man is moved by quite different reasons, which is why Christ so greatly commends beneficence. First, it is more blessed to give than to receive, because those who give are faithful stewards, or dispensers, of the goods that God has entrusted to them. For it is clear that God did not inflict inequality of fortunes on men at random, but made some richer than others so that there would be room for acts of charity, and so that the rich are given to the poor as, so to speak, patrons and guardians, to help them by their beneficence. But how can he not be counted blessed who has been faithful in the office divinely committed to him? Next, according to the saying of Solomon, those who do good to the poor lend to God. Proverbs 19. For he judges whatever is bestowed on them as given to himself, and he is both a faithful and a generous repayer. So it cannot be that he fails to keep the promises by which he invites men to the zeal of beneficence. Such are these: "Blessed is the man who scatters and gives to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever, and his horn shall be exalted with glory." Psalm 112. "Break your bread for the hungry, bring the afflicted and the homeless poor into your house; if you see the naked, cover him, and do not hide yourself from your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up quickly, your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you in. Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry, and he will say: Here I am, etc." Isaiah 58. Lastly, because nothing is so godlike as doing good, men draw nearer to the nature and likeness of God by no other means than by doing good very often. And just as God alone is blessed in himself, so there is no surer way to blessedness than to become most like God, which the zeal of Christian beneficence especially brings about. Therefore, even if no repayment of benefits takes place in this world, it is nevertheless truly far more blessed to give than to receive. If we look more closely at this, it will be clear how far the whole religion of the monks, who place all happiness in receiving, is alien to the doctrine of Christ. They renounce what came to them by lawful inheritance or by just means, and vow voluntary poverty, and live by the labours of others, when they ought rather to supply food and clothing to others. And so, under the plausible pretext of voluntary poverty, they live in luxury in safety, not exposed in any way, as other mortals are, to the chances of fortune.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui Synodicam concionem precibus publicis concludit. Mox enim positis genibus suis orauit cum omnibus illis. Quia enim à solo Deo incrementū dari nouerat (quem-admodum alibi monet) precum obliuisci non potuit, maximè in causa tam graui, ex qua ecclesiæ sa-lus omnis dependebat. Atqui hinc vetus ille & celebris mos ecclesiæ fluxit, quo sacræ concionis à precibus inchoari & ijsdem finiri consueuerunt, quas quicunq; negligunt, abundè testantur, se ad con-ciones curiositate potius quàm vel gloriæ Dei vel propriæ salutis studio confluere, quales sunt quorū descriptio apud Ezechielem cap. 33. ponitur. V T verò exemplum hoc preces commendat, & qui-dem publicas maximè, quas ardenti mentis deuotione fieri oportet: ita in ijsdem gestuum quoque piam modestiam, qua animi sensus testemur, obseruare docet. Inter hos vetustissimus habetur, quòd aut genibus positis aut toto corpore humi prostrato sanctii orant, ita sese ad humilitatem componen-tes. Idem manus ferè in cœlum expandere solent, vt & animi desyderium ardens exprimant, & fi-dem testentur, quase petita acceptuKos esse firmiter credunt. Cauendum tamen, ne inani gesticula-tione animos prophanos tegamus, vel ne manus sanguine pollutas eleuemus. De vtroque vitio vide Isa. 1. & 29. cap.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who closes the sermon with public prayers. For immediately he knelt down with all of them and prayed. Since he knew that the increase comes from God alone (as he elsewhere reminds us), he could not neglect prayer, especially in a matter so serious, on which the whole salvation of the Church depended. From this came that ancient and well-known custom of the Church, by which sacred sermons were begun with prayers and ended with them. Those who neglect these prayers clearly show that they come to sermons out of curiosity rather than from zeal for the glory of God or for their own salvation. Ezekiel 33 describes such people. Paul's example commends prayer, especially public prayer, which ought to be offered with a burning devotion of mind. It also teaches us to observe a devout modesty of gesture in them, by which we show the feelings of our heart. Among these gestures the most ancient is to pray holy prayers either kneeling or with the whole body stretched on the ground, thereby humbling ourselves. Likewise they usually stretch their hands towards heaven, both to express an ardent longing of mind and to bear witness to their faith, since they firmly believe that what they ask will be granted. We must take care, however, that we do not cover up unholy minds with empty gesturing, or lift up hands polluted with blood. On both faults see Isaiah 1 and 29.

units.la: Omnibus verò istis Pauli ab Asia discessum Lucas subijcit, in quem duo potissimùm incidunt. Primò fletum magnum exortum fuisse, ait, & quidem inter illos, quos non omnino occulte Paulus perstrinxerat. Sed non quid priuatim vnumquenq; mordere possit, sed publicam ecclesiarum salutem respiciunt. Dolent ergo ecclesiam tanto organo priuari, & dolorem sletu, complexu & sculis testan-tur. Est verò perquàm iucundum hoc mutuæ charitatis exemplum, qua ministros & ecclesias simul certare conuenit. Amauit hos Paulus mirum in modū, vt tota eius vita testatur. Vicissim ergo illi suum apostolū vt patrem amant atq; venerantur. Vbi mutuus hic affectus regnat, feliciter cedunt o-mnia. At qui suos antistites odio habent, ferè infelissimi sunt, vt in Israelitis Mosen & Aaronem odio persequentibus, euidentissimè cernitur. Simul autem hoc loco Stoicorum indolentia damnatur. Nefas
units.tr: After all these things, Luke adds Paul's departure from Asia, and two things mainly occur in it. First, he says, a great weeping arose, and indeed among those whom Paul had not entirely spared in his rebuke. Yet they did not look to what might bite each one privately, but to the public salvation of the churches. So they grieve that the Church is deprived of such a instrument, and they bear witness to their grief by weeping, embracing and kissing. This is a most delightful example of mutual love, by which ministers and churches ought to vie with each other. Paul loved them in a remarkable way, as his whole life bears witness. In turn, they loved and revered their apostle as a father. Where this mutual affection reigns, all things turn out well. But those who hate their leaders are for the most part very unhappy, as is most clearly seen in the Israelites, who persecuted Moses and Aaron with hatred. At the same time, in this place the insensibility of the Stoics is condemned.

units.la: Monachismus cœrtitur.
units.tr: Monasticism is challenged.

units.la: Paulus concionem precibus claudit.
units.tr: Paul closes the sermon with prayer.

units.la: Pij discessu Pauli dolent.
units.tr: The godly grieve at Paul's departure.

units.la: Contra Stoicos. Nefas illi putant, si quis affectus alicuius indicium edat. Quasi vero affectus per se mali & non potius nobis ex natura insiti sint, & non nostro demum vitio mali fiant, si quando excessus admittitur. Moderationem animi a nobis Deus requirit, non autem homines in truncos aut lapides degenerare vult. Postremo ad nauem usq; ab illis Paulus deducitur, quod honoris officium est, & ex charitate plerunq; emanat. Docemur hic honore dignos esse, qui in Dei gloria proouehenda strenua operam nauant, vel alioqui officio suo probe funguntur. Rursum admonemur, Deum nunquam permittere, ut inglorij viuant quicunq; tales sunt. Eius enim promissio est: Honorantes me honorificabo. 1. Sam. 2. Meminerint horum cum ecclesiarum ministri tum magistratus, ut suam authoritatem similibus stu dijs conseruare & propagare discant. Nos vero mutuas operas ad ecclesiae conseruationem confera- mus, caelestis honoris olim consortes futuri cum Christo Iesu domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Against the Stoics. They think it wicked if anyone shows some sign of feeling, as though feelings were evil in themselves, and not rather implanted in us by nature, and made evil only by our own fault when some excess is admitted. God requires moderation of mind from us; he does not want men to degenerate into tree trunks or stones. Lastly, Paul is escorted by them all the way to the ship, which is an act of honour and usually springs from love. We are taught here that those are worthy of honour who work strenuously to advance the glory of God, or who otherwise discharge their duty well. Again we are reminded that God never allows those who are like this to live without glory, for his promise is: "Those who honour me I will honour" (1 Sam. 2). Let both the ministers of the churches and the magistrates remember this, so that they learn to preserve and extend their authority by similar zeal. As for us, let us contribute mutual labours to the preservation of the Church, so that we may one day become sharers in heavenly honour with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXXXVII.

units.la: CVm autem factum esset, ut soluissemus auulsi ab eis, recto cursu venimus Coum, & sequenti die Rhodum, & inde Pataram. Et nacti nauem, quę traijciebat in Phœnicen, ea conscensa soluimus. Cum autem coepissiet apparere nobis Cyprus, relicta ea ad sinistram, nauigauimus in Syriam, ac venimus Tyrum: nam huc nauis exponebat onus. Repertisq; discipulis mansimus ibidem diebus septem. Qui Paulo dicebant per spiritum sanctum, ne ascenderet Hierosolymam. Et expletis diebus, profecti ibamus, deducentibus nos omnibus, una cum uxoribus & liberis extra ciuitatem vsque: & positis genibus in littore precati sumus. Et cum inuicem vale dixissemus, conscendimus nauem: illi autem redierunt ad sua. Nos vero nauigatione explicita a Tyro descendimus Ptolemaidem, & salutatis fratribus mansimus diem vnum cum illis.
units.tr: When we had torn ourselves away from them, we sailed on a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. There we found a ship bound for Phoenicia, went on board, and set sail. When Cyprus came into view, we left it on our left and sailed on to Syria, and landed at Tyre, for the ship was to unload its cargo there. We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. They told Paul through the Holy Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem. When those days were over, we set out, and all of them, with their wives and children, escorted us out of the city. On the shore we knelt down and prayed. After we had said farewell to one another, we went on board the ship, and they returned home. We finished our voyage from Tyre, came down to Ptolemais, greeted the brothers, and stayed with them one day.

units.la: Spiritus sanctus Apostolorum peregrinationes, laborum & periculi plenas, magna dilirgentia commemorat, ut ex his immensam erga nos Dei bonitatem agnoscamus, qui electa sua organa & fidelissimos ministros nostrae salutis ergo tot laboribus atque periculis diu xari voluit, & ut Euangelij doctrinam, quam tot laboribus propagari oportuit, eo ardentiori studio complectamur. Atqui ad hunc finem huius etiam Capitis narratio referri debet, qua docetur, ut Paulus multa maria emensus per mille discrimina in Syriam, & inde Hierosolymam peruenerit, vbi a pijs quidem humanissime exceptus, a seditiosis autem proditus & captus in Romani Tribuni siue Praesidis potestatem deuenit: quae singula suo loco & tempore videbimus. Habet autem in primis praesens hic locus multa, quae ad eius (quod modo diximus) illustrationem multum faciunt. Quare aliquanto diligentius excutienda erunt, quae primo intuitu nimis sterilia videntur.
units.tr: The Holy Spirit records the journeys of the Apostles, full of toils and dangers, with great care, so that from them we may recognise God's immense goodness towards us, who wished his chosen instruments and most faithful ministers to be long tried by so many labours and perils for the sake of our salvation, and so that we may embrace the doctrine of the Gospel, which had to be spread through so many labours, with all the more eager zeal. And indeed this account of the chapter must be referred to this purpose too, for it teaches how Paul, after crossing many seas and passing through a thousand dangers, came into Syria, and from there reached Jerusalem, where the godly received him most kindly, but the seditious betrayed him and seized him and handed him over to the power of the Roman tribune, or governor. We shall see each of these matters in its own place and time. Moreover, this present passage contains in the first place many things that contribute greatly to illustrating what we have just said. Therefore those things which at first sight seem all too barren must be examined rather carefully.

units.la: Primo autem, quo animo Paulus cum suis ab Asia discesserit, narratur. Soluimus (inquit) auulsi ab eis. Ita Christus ad montem oliuarum a discipulis auulsus fuisse dicitur. Luc. 22. Quo vero ingens animi dolor, ex discessu obortus, exprimitur. Et sane nec pauca nec leues doloris huius causa erant. Amorem enim mutuum totius triennij conuersatio inter illos pepererat. Amoris argumenta non pauca extabant, quae omnia recentes lachrymae & communis ille omnium luctus in memoriam reuocauerant. Sciebat praeterea Paulus se ad illos nunquam reuersurum, a quibus tantopere amabatur. In primis vero animum ipsius angebat, quod lupis turbandas relinqueret ecclesias, tot abs se periculis & laboribus conflictatas. Haec (inquam) omnia ferreos quoq; animos mouere potuissent. Ita enim parentes dolere videmus, quando morte a liberis diuelluntur, quos sibi ipsis per aetatem
units.tr: First, the state of mind in which Paul departed from Asia with his companions is described. "We tore ourselves away from them," he says. So Christ is said to have been torn away from his disciples at the Mount of Olives (Luke 22). The great anguish of mind that arose from the parting is expressed here as well. And indeed the causes of this grief were neither few nor slight. For the intimacy of three years had produced mutual love between them. There were not a few tokens of that love, all of which their recent tears and the common lamentation of them all had brought back to memory. Paul also knew that he would never return to those by whom he was so greatly loved. Above all, what troubled his spirit was that he was leaving the churches, which had been battered by so many dangers and labours on his account, to be disturbed by wolves. All of this (I say) could have moved even hearts of iron. For we see parents grieve when death tears from them children whom they cannot yet, by reason of their age, see able to look after themselves.

units.la: Paulus ab Asia auulsus. nondum consulere posse vident. Superat tamen dolorem animi omnem Paulus, ut divinae vocationi quae illum Hierosolymam trahebat, obtemperet. Quo exemplo admonemur, Dei vocationem & voluntatem omnibus affectibus anteponi debere. Nam ut affectibus per omnia careamus, quoad in carne hac viuimus, impossibile est, & hos in pijs quoq; locum habere constat. Sed moderatio adhibe- ri debet, qua illos fidei obedientiae subijciamus. Et id quidem in omni casu obseruari debet, maxime quando per mortem a nostris diuellimur, vel a nobis diuelluntur, quorum consilio & ope plurimum iuuari poteramus. Cogitemus tunc nos Dei vocatione vrgeri, cui contradicere & reluctari ut nimis temerarium, ita stultum & periculosum fuerit.
units.tr: Paul torn away from Asia. Yet Paul overcame all the grief of his spirit so that he might obey the divine calling that drew him to Jerusalem. By this example we are reminded that God's calling and will ought to be placed above all the affections. For it is impossible for us to be entirely free of the affections as long as we live in this flesh, and it is agreed that they have a place even in the godly. But moderation must be applied, by which we subject them to faithful obedience. And this ought to be observed in every case, above all when we are torn away by death from those, or they are torn away from us, by whose counsel and help we might have been greatly aided. Let us then think that we are being urged by God's calling, to resist and struggle against which would be as rash as it would be foolish and dangerous.

units.la: Secundo nauigationem Pauli longam Lucas describit, quam periculi & molestiae plenam fuisse nemo dubitare potest. Locorum autem descriptioni non immoramur, quia haec a Geographis petenda erit. Quia vero tot nominantur loci, quos praeternauigans Paulus nulla in his mora tractauit, argumento est, illum summam festinationis rationem habuisse, ut Pentecosten Hierosolymis agere posset. HIC tamen obseruandum venit ardens Pauli in commisso sibi munere studium & inuicta fides. Poterat enim in mundo (quemadmodum ipse fatetur ad Philippen. scribens) quietum & in honore viuere, & non paruam eius inter Iudaeos authoritatem fuisse, prior vitae ipsius conditio abunde docet. Videbat praeterea sibi Christum sequenti perpetuum laborum telam texendam, & noua quotidie pericula subeunda esse. Hoc tame vitae genus, vocante & sic volente Deo, amplexu, per omnia pericula constanti cursu euasit, & quaecunq; in hoc seculo vel lucrosa vel gloriosa ipsi esse poterant, pro damnis & reiectamentis duxit, tantummodo ut Christum lucrifaceret. Philip. 3. Quain re illum spe caelestis illius coronae, quam sibi & omnibus pijs repositam esse nouerat, non mediocriter adiutum fuisse ipse testatur. 2. Tim. 4. Imitemur nos tanti apostoli exemplum, ne vel laboribus & periculis frangamur, vel mundi illecebris capti a Christo praescriptum vocationis nostrae cursum omittamus. Quid enim in mundo hoc stabile & perpetuum? Quid quod animi & carnis desyderia satiare possit? Vnus Deus omnisufficiens & summum bonum est, qui bonorum omnium thesaurum in Christo filio exposuit, in quo solo mentes hominum quiescere possunt. Qui ex hoc fonte biberit, non sitiet in aeternum. Iohan. 4. Felices ego & beati sunt, qui mundi vmbratilem felicitatem cum hac aeternae beatitudinis fonte permutare norunt.
units.tr: Second, Luke describes Paul's long voyage, which no one can doubt was full of danger and hardship. We will not linger over the description of the places, since that must be sought from the geographers. But because so many places are named which Paul sailed past without any delay, this is evidence that he had the greatest haste, so that he could keep Pentecost at Jerusalem. Here, however, we must notice Paul's ardent zeal for the office committed to him and his unconquered faith. For he could (as he himself confesses in writing to the Philippians) have lived quietly and in honour in the world, and his earlier condition of life teaches abundantly that he had no small authority among the Jews. Moreover, he saw that for Christ a continuous web of labours was to be woven for him, and that new dangers had to be faced every day. Yet he embraced this manner of life, since God called him and so willed it, and he got through all dangers with a steady course; and whatever in this age could be gainful or glorious for him, he counted as loss and refuse, only so that he might gain Christ (Phil. 3). And he himself testifies that he was not a little helped in this by the hope of that heavenly crown which he knew was laid up for himself and for all the godly (2 Tim. 4). Let us imitate the example of so great an apostle, so that we are neither broken by labours and dangers, nor, captured by the allurements of the world, abandon the course of our calling as prescribed by Christ. For what in this world is stable and lasting? What is there that can satisfy the desires of the spirit and of the flesh? The one God is all-sufficient and the supreme good, who has set forth the treasure of all goods in Christ the Son, in whom alone the minds of men can find rest. Whoever drinks from this fountain will never thirst (John 4). Happy and blessed are those who know how to exchange the shadowy happiness of the world for this fountain of eternal blessedness.

units.la: Tertio illos tandem Tyrum appulisse narratur, vbi multa nobis ordine consyderanda veniunt. Inter quae primum habetur, quod Tyri discipulos, id est, Christianos aliquot fratres inueniunt, & tales quidem, qui fidei & charitatis officijs reliquos omnes, quorum butusq; meutio facta est, superauisse videntur. Quod mirum videri potest, si veterem Tyriae vrbis conditionem, luxu, fastu, auaritia & libidine infamem, cum diris & horrendis contra hanc prophetarum oraculis consyderes. Quid? quod Christus dominus vrbium Galilaeae ingratitudinem deuouens, illas cum Tyro & Sidone confert, in quas olim seuera admodum fuit iusticiae exempla Deus ediderat. Matth. 11. Attamen in ea quoq; vrbe euangelij lux fulsit, & ibi ecclesiam insignibus donis celebrem Christus constitui voluit. Elucet ineo Dei veritas, & eiusdem erga peccatores ad se conuersos bonitas. Ita enim euenturu olim per Isaiam praedixerat: Exactis septuaginta annis visitabit dominus Tyrum, reuertetur, ad mercedem suam, & exercebit commercia cum omnibus regnis. Attamen negotiatio eius & merces eius sacrosanctae erunt domino, &c. Isa. 23. Et Psalmo 45. ecclesiae dicitur: Filia quoq; Tyri cum munere, & quiq; opulentiores populi faciem tuam precabuntur. Haec (inquam) impleta fuisse praesens hic locus docet, quando illic Christianos fide & charitate ex animo flagrantes, Paulus inuenit. Estq; hoc memorabile bonitatis Dei exemplum, quo docemur, ut nec de nobis ipsis, nec de alijs hominibus temere desperemus, quando in ea vrbe ecclesiam sibi constituere voluit Deus, in qua cumprimis atrox iustitiae sua exemplum ob peccata olim editum fuerat.
units.tr: Third, we are told that they at last landed at Tyre, where many things come to be considered by us in order. Among these, first, is that at Tyre they found disciples, that is, some Christian brothers, and indeed such as seem to have surpassed all the rest, whose names have been mentioned, in the offices of faith and love. This may seem strange, if you consider the old condition of the city of Tyre, notorious for luxury, pride, avarice and lust, together with the dreadful and horrifying oracles of the prophets against it. What of the fact that Christ the Lord, condemning the ingratitude of the cities of Galilee, compares them with Tyre and Sidon, on which God had once displayed severe examples of justice (Matt. 11)? Yet even in that city the light of the Gospel shone, and there Christ wished a church famous for its outstanding gifts to be established. The truth of God shines in this, and his goodness towards sinners who turn to him. For Isaiah had foretold that this would happen one day: "After seventy years the Lord will visit Tyre, and it will return to its wages, and will carry on trade with all the kingdoms. Yet its merchandise and its wages will be holy to the Lord," etc. (Isa. 23). And in Psalm 45 it is said to the Church: "The daughter of Tyre also, with a gift, and the richer peoples will entreat your face." That these things were fulfilled (I say) the present passage teaches, when Paul found there Christians burning with faith and love from their hearts. And this is a memorable example of God's goodness, by which we are taught not to despair rashly either of ourselves or of other men, since God wished to establish a church in that city in which, above all, a dreadful example of his justice had once been displayed on account of sins.

units.la: Deinde Paulum a Tyrijs fratribus per spiritum sanctum admonitum fuisse Lucas scribit, ut Hierosolymam ascenderet. Videtur id cum eo pugnare, quod Paulus in Miletana Synodo se spiritu alligatum eo profecturum dixit. Sed facilis est locorum conciliatio, si Synecdochen, scripturis sacris familiarissimam spectes: qua tota discipulorum borum oratio spiritui sancto tribuitur, qui tamen vnius duntaxat partis reuera author erat. Ex spiritus suggestione enim Paulum de vinculis & afflictionibus, quae ipsum Hierosolymis manebant, admonuerunt. Consilium vero de suo addiderunt, ut eo ne eò ascenderet, quòd illi pio affectu consultum cuperent, Dei autem consilium ignorarent. Frequen- ter enim fieri solet, vt prophetæ Deo reuelante quid futurum sit intelligant, interim tamen consilium Dei & eius finem prorsus ignorent, quæ causa est, quòd interdum suis consilijs aberret, dum Dei reue- latione non contenti, simul carnis quoque prudentiam adhibent, cuius rei exempla in Iona & alijs quibusdã habentur. Interim obserua quàm variè Deus Paulum tentari voluerit. Spiritu alligatum Hierosolymam trahit. Per singulas vrbes & ecclesias ipsum vinctū & captum iri prædicit. Et iam accedunt, qui vaticinandi spiritu prædití, ipsum ne eò proficiscatur, monent. Quorsum verò ista omnia? Voluit nimirum Deus apostolum suum diutina meditatione ad crucem præparari, ne furentis populi clamoribus & multiuarijs hostium insidijs territus deficeret. Simul verò nobis Christianæ constantiæ & obedientiæ exemplum proponit, cuius studium tantum tamen firmum esse debet, vt ne ijs quidem obsecundemus, in quibus non vulgaria spiritus sancti indicia apparent, si illos aliquid à Dei voluntate & iussu alienum monere audiamus. Refer huc infelicem prophetæ casum, qui ab alio propheta sub diuini oraculi prætextu seductus, contra Dei mandatum in Bethel cibum sumpsit, & à Leone discerptus est. 1. Reg. 13. Hinc simul de spirituum apparitionibus iudicare discito, quarum authoritate ferè Monachi sua de Purgatorio & reliquis superstitionibus figmenta probant, quæ nul lis scripturis probari posse intelligunt, &c.
units.tr: Next, Luke writes that Paul was warned by the Tyrian brothers through the Holy Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem. This seems to conflict with what Paul said at Miletus, that he was going there bound by the Spirit. But the reconciliation of the passages is easy if you look at synecdoche, a figure most familiar in the sacred Scriptures, by which the whole speech of these disciples is attributed to the Holy Spirit, who was in truth the author of only one part of it. For by the prompting of the Spirit they warned Paul about the chains and afflictions that awaited him at Jerusalem. But they added their own counsel, that he should not go up there, because they wished to provide for him out of pious feeling, yet did not know God's plan. For it often happens that prophets, with God revealing it, understand what is to come, yet at the same time are entirely ignorant of God's purpose and its end; and this is the reason why they sometimes go astray in their own counsels, while not content with God's revelation they also apply the wisdom of the flesh at the same time. Examples of this are found in Jonah and in some others. Meanwhile observe how variously God wished Paul to be tested. He draws him to Jerusalem, bound by the Spirit. He foretells in each city and church that he will be bound and seized. And now there come those who, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, advise him not to set out there. But why all this? Doubtless God wished his apostle to be prepared for the cross by long meditation, so that he would not be dismayed and give way at the shouts of a raging people and the many snares of enemies. At the same time he sets before us an example of Christian constancy and obedience, a zeal which must be so firm that we do not even obey those in whom no ordinary signs of the Holy Spirit appear, if we hear them advising something alien to God's will and command. Refer here the unhappy fate of the prophet who, misled by another prophet under the pretext of a divine oracle, ate food at Bethel against God's command, and was torn apart by a lion (1 Kings 13). From this learn at the same time to judge the appearances of spirits, by whose authority the Monks largely support their fictions about Purgatory and the other superstitions, which they understand cannot be proved by any Scripture, etc.

units.la: Porrò vbi Paulus Dei vocationem potius, quàm illorum consilium secutus, in cæpto itinere per- git, ipsi quoque dei voluntati sponte cedentes, illum vnà cum vxoribus & liberis extra vrbem vsq; co- mitantur & honorificè deducunt. Quo in loco & nouum Christiana charitatis argumentū elucet, & promissionum Christi Veritas cernitur, quæ Mar. 10. cap. in hæc verba habetur: Amen dico vobis, Quisquis relinquit domum, aut fratres aut sorores, aut patrem, aut matrem, aut vxorem, aut liberos, aut agros meæ causa et euangelij, is recipiet centupla nunc in tempore hoc, cū persecutionibus, ac in seculo venturo vitā æternā, &c. Paulū enim omnia hæc Christi causa reliquisse scimus. At idem passim fratres et sorores inuenit, qui ipsi tum opibus & fortunis, tū corporibus suis ministrare cupiunt, imò vxores et liberos ad præstanda illi pietatis officia paratos habet. Docet præterea locus hic, Christianorū esse, vt omnia sua ad dei cultum destinent, simulq; curent, vt non ipsi modò in pios Christi cultores officiosi sint, sed familiā quoq; omnē ad pia officia assuefaciant. Requirit hoc alibi in vidua ecclesiastica Paulus 1. Tim. 5. Et quod viduas facere decet, id maiori iure à reliquis exigi poterit. Sed ô detestabile nostri seculi socordiā, qua pleriq; patresfamiliās ita suos instituunt, vt peregrinos vexare potius, contemnere et odisse, quàm humanitatis officijs prosequi soleant. Meminerint illi quid pueris, Heliseo calui-tiū exprobrantibus, euenerit, quos ab vrsis laniatos fuisse, scriptura docet. 2. Reg. 2. cap.
units.tr: Moreover, when Paul followed God's calling rather than their advice and continued on his journey, they too, yielding willingly to God's will, accompanied him outside the city with their wives and children and escorted him with honour. Here the new evidence of Christian love shines forth, and the truth of Christ's promises is seen, which Mark 10 states in these words: "Verily I say unto you, there is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, but he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life, etc." For we know that Paul left all these things for Christ's sake. Yet he finds everywhere brothers and sisters who desire to minister to him with their goods and fortunes and their own bodies, and he even has wives and children ready to perform these duties of piety for him. This passage also teaches that it is the duty of Christians to dedicate all their possessions to the worship of God, and at the same time to take care not only that they themselves be dutiful worshippers of Christ, but that they also train their whole household for pious duties. Paul requires this elsewhere of the widows of the Church, 1 Tim. 5. And what it becomes widows to do may be demanded with even greater right from the rest. But, alas, the detestable carelessness of our age, by which many heads of households bring up their people so that they are accustomed to harass, despise and hate strangers rather than to show them the duties of humanity! Let them remember what befell the boys who mocked Elisha for his baldness; Scripture tells us they were torn to pieces by bears, 2 Kings 2.

units.la: Postremò Tyrij fratres in littore positis genibus orauerunt. Vbi rursum preces nobis commen- dari videmus, quibus in arduis & publicis negotijs cumprimis opus est. At quia de his alibi diximus, in præsenti hoc maximè obseruemus, quòd publice in aperto littore fideles orant, id quod sine arbitris fieri non poterat, quibus fortassis ridicula videri potuit ista religio. At non pudet suæ vel fidei vel re- ligionis eos, qui Christo verè insiti sunt. Norunt enim quæ gloria eos maneat, qui Christum coram mundo hoc confitentur: quæ item confusio & ignominia ijs destinata sit, quos Christi coram mundo hoc adultero & prauo pudet. Vide Marc. 8. Vtinam verò horum memores execrabili illa ignauia & pestifero metu nos quàm primùm liberaremus, quo hodie in hominum gratiam quiduis simulare & dissimulare consueuimus, &c.
units.tr: Finally, the brothers of Tyre knelt down on the shore and prayed. Here again we see that prayers are commended to us, which are especially needed in difficult and public affairs. But since we have spoken of these matters elsewhere, let us here observe chiefly that the faithful pray publicly on the open shore, something that could not be done without witnesses, and to whom perhaps this religion may have seemed ridiculous. But those who are truly grafted into Christ are not ashamed of their faith or their religion. For they know what glory awaits those who confess Christ before the world, and likewise what shame and disgrace are destined for those who are ashamed of Christ before this adulterous and perverse world. See Mark 8. Would that, mindful of these things, we might as soon as possible free ourselves from that accursed cowardice and deadly fear by which today we are accustomed to pretend and to dissemble for the sake of men's favour, etc.

units.la: Quarto & vltimo loco Ptolemaidem Paulus cum suis appulit, vbi rursus vnius diei moram tra- xit cum fratribus. Ergo illic quoq; ecclesiam constitutā fuisse patet. Et sanè dignū obseruatione est, quòd paucorū annorum spatio euangelij doctrina tam longè lateq; vulgata tot Christo ecclesias con- stituit. Si enim historiæ seriem expendas, circa annum Conuersionis Pauli vigesimum tertium hæc contigisse, verisimile est. Quare intra viginti tres annos per Asiam & Europam euangelij vox au- dita fuit, & passim fructum post se reliquit vberrimum. Ita verò olim à prophetis prædictum fuisse legimus. Docent hæc quàm feliciter succedant, quæcunq; Deo auspice & duce instituuntur, vt tut con- tra huius consilium tumultuetur mundus hic. Stulti ergo, qui huius minas atq; conatus formidant. Meditemur hæc nostro seculo, et constanti fide armati, Christi Iesu regnū propagare studeamus, cum todem ipsi quoq; olim regnaturi. Ipsi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: In the fourth and last place, Paul and his companions put in at Ptolemais, where he again stayed one day with the brothers. There, then, it is clear that a church was also established. And it is indeed worth noting that within a space of a few years the teaching of the gospel, spread so widely, established so many churches for Christ. For if you consider the sequence of the history, it is likely that these things happened about the twenty-third year after Paul's conversion. Therefore, within twenty-three years the voice of the gospel was heard throughout Asia and Europe, and everywhere left behind a most abundant fruit. We read that this had been foretold long ago by the prophets. These things teach how happily succeed all the undertakings that are begun under God's guidance and leadership, however the world may rage against this counsel. Foolish, then, are those who fear its threats and efforts. Let us consider these things in our age, and, armed with a steadfast faith, let us labour to spread the kingdom of Jesus Christ, since we also shall one day reign with him. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: Postridie vero qui cum Paulo erant, profecti venerunt Caesaream. Et ingressi domum Philippi euangelistae, qui erat unus e septem, manserunt apud eum. Huic autem erant filiae virgines quatuor prophetantes. Et cum permaneremus dies complures, aduenit quidam a Iudaea Propheta, nomine Agabus. Is cum venisset ad nos, tulit cingulum Pauli, et alligans sibi pedes ac manus dixit: Haec dicit spiritus sanctus, Virum, cuius est cingulum hoc, sic alligabunt Hierosolymae Iudaei, tradentque in manus gentium. Cum autem audissemus haec, rogabamus et nos et caeteri, qui loci illius erant, ne ascenderet Hierosolymam. Tunc respondit Paulus, ac dixit: Quid facitis flentes et affligentes cor meum? Ego vero non solum vinciri, sed et mori paratus sum Hierosolymis pro nomine domini Iesu. Cum vero non persuaderetur illi, acquieuimus, dicentes: Domini voluntas fiat. Post dies autem istos sublatis sarcinis conscendimus Hierosolymam. Venerunt autem una quidam discipulorum ex Caesarea nobiscum, adducentes secum, apud quem hospitaremur, Mnasonem quendam Cyprium, antiquum discipulum. Et cum venissemus Hierosolymam, libenter exceperunt nos fratres.
units.tr: On the next day we who were with Paul departed and came to Caesarea. And entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him. Now he had four virgin daughters, who prophesied. And as we stayed there many days, there came down from Judea a certain prophet named Agabus. When he came to us, he took Paul's girdle, and binding his own feet and hands, said: "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles." When we heard these things, both we and those of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered and said: "What mean ye to weep and to break my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying: "The will of the Lord be done." After those days, we took up our baggage and went up to Jerusalem. Some of the disciples also came with us from Caesarea, bringing with them one Mnason, a Cypriot, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge. And when we came to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.

units.la: Vt Deus euangelium filii sui Iesu Christi per Pauli vincula illustrare voluit, ita ut Paulus ad vincula festinauerit, per Lucam diligentissime describi curauit. Ita enim vniuersale constantis fidei simul et fidelis obedientiae exemplum omnibus nobis imitandum proponere voluit. Nam per terras et maria, adeoque per mille discrimina rerum Hierosolymam, ubi se capiendum fore nuntiarat, illum contendisse, bucusque audiuimus, nec vllas prophetarum praedictiones admisisse, quibus ab eo revocabatur, ad quod se a deo vocari nouerat. Porro incaepsam narrationem Lucas persequens, in praesenti quid Caesarea (quae ultima apostoli intra profectionem statio fuit) factum sit, deinde ut Hierosolymam tandem peruenerit, narrat.
units.tr: Just as God willed to illustrate the gospel of his Son Jesus Christ through Paul's bonds, so Luke took the greatest care to describe in detail how Paul hastened toward his chains. For in this way God willed to set before all of us a universal example of steadfast faith and at the same time of faithful obedience to be imitated. For we have heard thus far how, through lands and seas, and through a thousand dangers, he pressed on to Jerusalem, where he had announced he would be seized, and that he admitted no predictions of the prophets by which he was called back from that to which he knew God had called him. Now, following up the narrative he had begun, Luke relates what happened at Caesarea (which was the last stopping place of the apostle before his journey), and then how at length he arrived at Jerusalem.

units.la: RES Caesareae gestas ab hospitis descriptione orditur, quem Philippum fuisse dicit, vnumex septem illorum numero, quos ecclesiasticarum opum administrationi et egenis a primitiua ecclesia praefectos fuisse, supra Cap. 6. vidimus. Grassante autem Hierosolymis persecutione, in qua Pauli crudelitas maxime emicuit, ecclesia hinc inde dispersa fuit, et Philippus Samariam delatus illic regni dei semina iecit. Nunc autem Caesareae egit, et ecclesiae Christi, quae illic erat, minister siue antistes fuisse videtur. Estque hoc haud vulgare dei iudicium, vt eo hospite nunc vtatur Paulus, quem olim Hierosolymae abire et sua relinquere cogerat. Caeterum proponit in Philippo egregium veri pastoris typum Lucas, paucis omnia ea comprehendens, quae ab episcopo Paulus in priori ad Timoth. 3. et ad Titum 1. cap. requirit.
units.tr: Luke begins his account of events at Caesarea with the description of the host, whom he says was Philip, one of those seven whom we saw above, in chapter 6, appointed from the early Church to the administration of the Church's resources and to the care of the poor. But when a persecution raged at Jerusalem, in which Paul's cruelty especially flared up, the Church was scattered here and there, and Philip, carried to Samaria, sowed there the seeds of the kingdom of God. Now, however, he was at Caesarea, and seems to have been a minister or leader of the Church of Christ that was there. And it is no common judgement of God that Paul now makes use of that host whom he once compelled at Jerusalem to depart and leave his own possessions behind. Moreover, Luke presents in Philip an outstanding type of a true minister, comprehending in a few words all those qualities which Paul requires of a bishop in his first letter to Timothy, chapter 3, and in his letter to Titus, chapter 1.

units.la: Primo enim euangelistam fuisse ait: Fuit ergo ad docendum idoneus, quae prima et maxime necessaria ministri virtus est. Fuit autem euangelistarum gradus inter apostolos et pastores medius, vt ex Paulo Ephes. 4. cap. colligi potest. Nam certis quidem in locis consistebant, non tamen ita illis alligati erant, quin ad vicinos simul et remotiores locos, si quando vrgebat necessitas, excurrerent. Nomine autem suo officij admonebantur, quod illis cum apostolis simul et pastoribus, quoad doctrinam, commune erat, nimirum vt euangelij praedicationi incumberent, et illius doctrina homines erudirent. Nec enim liberum esse voluit apostolis suis Christus, vt pro suo arbitrio quiduis docerent, sed abs se traditam doctrinam praedicare iussit, quae hodie etiam sola ecclesiis proponi debet.
units.tr: For first he says that Philip was an evangelist: "He was therefore fit to teach," which is the first and most necessary virtue of a minister. Now the rank of evangelist was between that of the apostles and that of the pastors, as may be gathered from Paul, Ephesians 4. For they indeed remained in certain places, yet they were not so bound to them that they could not run out to nearby and more distant places, if necessity pressed. They were reminded of their office by its name, which was common to them with the apostles and the pastors as far as teaching went, namely that they should devote themselves to the preaching of the gospel and instruct people in its doctrine. For Christ did not want his apostles to be free to teach whatever they pleased at their own discretion, but commanded them to preach the doctrine handed down by him, which alone ought to be set before the churches even today.

units.la: Deinde domum habuit Philippus et facultates, quae tum suis vsibus, tum exercendae hospitalitati (quam ipsam quoque Paulus in ministro requirit) sufficerent. Paulum enim cum numeroso comitatu ad se recepit, et diebus aliquot benigne tractat, id quod abs se, sumptu, saltem mediocri, fieri non potuit. Non ergo vel mendicus vel erronis instar fuit, quales hodie quidem iniquissimi muneris ecclesiastici censores ministros verbi esse vellent, quos vel inuidia fascinat, vel ignorantia decipit, qua inter apostolos et pastores non distinguunt. Et hospitalem cumprimis fuisse oportet, qui Paulum cum tanto comitatu benigne excipit, qui ipsi exilij author fuerat, vt paulo ante diximus. PraePraeterea filias habuisse dicitur. Ergo & vxorem, nisi (quod vel cogitatu nefandum foret) scortatorem dicere velimus, quod fortasse aequius ferrent impuri caelibatus defensores, quem Papatus ecclesiae obtrusit. Conuincuntur autem tam hoc quam aliorum apostolorum exemplo, quos vxores secum circunduxisse Paulus diserte fatetur. 1. Cor. 9. Idem episcopum vnius vxoris maritum, id est, coniugio legitimo iuxta primam domini institutionem astrictum esse iubet. 1. Tim. 3. Et vanissimum est illorum commentum, qui matrimonio & vxoris conuersatione ecclesiasticum ministerium pollui putant, cum illud a Deo institutum & per se sanctum atque impollutum esse constet. Heb. 13. Vere ergo diabolicam doctrinam Paulus vocat, quae coniugij vsum prohibet: quia diaboli proprium est, Dei constitutiones vel impuras, vel inutiles & perniciosas dicere. Vide 1. Tim. 4. Sed & caelibatus Papistici fructus doctrinae huius authorem egregie arguunt, cum ex eo stupra, adulteria, incestus & horrendum Sodomiae scelus frequenter emanare soleat. Postremo quales Philippi filiae fuerint, indicatur: Prophetantes nimirum. Scimus autem, prophetandi verbo nonnunquam simpliciter diuini verbi & scripturae sacrae studium significari. Ita enim prophetare dicuntur Paulo, qui scripturas in ecclesia exponunt, & ad huius aedificationem, institutionem & consolationem omnia referunt. 1. Corinth. 14. Idem feminas prophetantes vocat, quae verbum dei publice audiunt, quas in ecclesia velatis capitibus sedere iubet. 1. Cor. 11. At quia singulare quid de Philippi filiabus Lucas narrare voluit, de peculiari spiritus sancti dono locus hic exponi debet, quo illas dominus ornare voluit. Quid enim opus erat hoc annotauisse, quod omnibus Christianis, doctis pariter & indoctis, omni deniq; aetati & sexui commune est? Et quis obsecro alios, quam verbi Dei studiosos, cogitaret fidelis euangelistae liberos? Sed singulare vaticinandi donum intelligitur, quo foemineum quoq; sexum, iuxta Ioelis prophetiam, Christi tempore insigniri Deus voluit, vt attentiores essent ad audiendam euangelij doctrinam homines, & Christi meritum ad mulieres quoq; pertinere, omnibus constaret. Interim patet, Philippum educationis & institutionis liberorum praecipuam rationem habuisse, id quod iuxta Pauli doctrinam cumprimis necessarium est, cum propter exemplum publicum, tum quod vix credibile est, ecclesiam ab eo regi posse, qui domui suae praefuit non nouit. 1. Timoth. 3. Et Heli sacerdotis exemplum docet, quam indignetur Deus ecclesiae ministris, qui liberorum petulantiam non seueriùs coherceant. Vide 1. Sam. 2. 3. 4. cap. &c.
units.tr: Next, Philip had a house and means sufficient both for his own use and for the exercise of hospitality (which Paul also requires in a minister). For he received Paul with his numerous company, and treated him kindly for several days, something which could not have been done by him without considerable, at least moderate, expense. He was therefore neither a beggar nor a vagabond, as those most unjust censors of the ecclesiastical office, who would have the ministers of the Word to be such, wish them to be, men whom envy bewitches or ignorance deceives, since they do not distinguish between apostles and pastors. And he must have been especially hospitable who kindly received Paul with so great a company, he who had himself been the cause of exile, as we said a little before. Besides, he is said to have had daughters. Therefore he had a wife as well, unless we are willing to call him a fornicator (which even to think of would be wicked), something the defenders of impure celibacy, which the Papacy has forced upon the Church, would perhaps more fairly bear. This is refuted both by this example and by that of the other apostles, whom Paul plainly admits to have led about with them as wives, 1 Cor. 9. He likewise orders a bishop to be the husband of one wife, that is, bound by lawful marriage according to the Lord's first institution, 1 Tim. 3. And vain is the invention of those who think the ecclesiastical ministry is polluted by marriage and the company of a wife, since it is established that marriage was instituted by God and is holy and undefiled in itself, Heb. 13. Rightly, then, does Paul call that a diabolical doctrine which forbids the use of marriage, because it is the devil's proper work to call God's ordinances either impure, or useless and pernicious, see 1 Tim. 4. But the fruits of Papistical celibacy also clearly prove the author of this doctrine, since from it fornication, adultery, incest and the horrible crime of sodomy commonly spring. Finally, we are told what sort of daughters Philip had: prophesying, that is. We know, however, that the word "prophesy" sometimes simply signifies the study of the divine Word and of Holy Scripture. For in this sense those are said by Paul to prophesy who expound the Scriptures in the Church and refer all things to its edification, instruction and consolation, 1 Cor. 14. The same Paul calls women who publicly hear the word of God prophesying, and he orders them to sit in the Church with their heads covered, 1 Cor. 11. But since Luke wished to relate something singular about Philip's daughters, the passage must be explained concerning the peculiar gift of the Holy Spirit with which the Lord willed to adorn them. For what need was there to note this, which is common to all Christians, learned and unlearned alike, to every age and sex? And who, I beg you, would think that a faithful evangelist's daughters were anything other than lovers of the Word of God? But a singular gift of prophecy is meant, by which God willed that the female sex also, according to the prophecy of Joel, should be distinguished in Christ's time, so that men might be more attentive to hearing the doctrine of the gospel, and it might be clear to all that Christ's merit pertains to women too. Meanwhile it is evident that Philip took especially careful account of the education and training of his children, which, according to Paul's teaching, is especially necessary, both because of the public example and because it is hardly credible that a church can be ruled by one who does not know how to rule his own household, 1 Tim. 3.
