And the example of Eli the priest shows how greatly God is angered with ministers of the Church who do not restrain the wantonness of their children more severely, see 1 Sam. 2, 3, 4, etc.

units.la: Porrò apud Philippum agente Paulo, Hierosolymis vel ex Iudaea superuenit Agabus propheta, qui illum denuo de vinculis admonet, nec id verbis modo, sed veterum prophetarum more chriam adhibet, qua rem omnem quasi oculis spectandam exhibere voluit. Nam Pauli cingulo sibijpsi manus & pedes alligat. Addit autem facti sui expositionem, dicens: Virum, cuius est cingulum hoc, sic alligabunt Hierosolymis Iudaei. Saepius vero Paulum admoneri voluit Deus, partim quidem vt illustrior esset illius constantia & fides (vt iam alibi docuimus) partim vero, vt exemplo hoc discamus, pericula praesentia non semper iustam fugae causam esse, cum illa nonnunquam, non vt ea deuitemus, praedicat Deus, sed vt ad illa ferenda & subeunda praeparemur.
units.tr: Meanwhile, while Paul was staying with Philip, there came down from Judea, from Jerusalem, a prophet named Agabus, who warned him again about his chains. He did this not only in words but, after the manner of the ancient prophets, by a visual sign (chria), by which he wished the whole matter to be set before their eyes, as it were, to be looked at. For he bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, and he added an explanation of his action, saying: "The man whose belt this is, the Jews in Jerusalem will bind in this way." God wished Paul to be warned more than once, partly so that his constancy and faith might shine more clearly (as we have already taught elsewhere), and partly so that we might learn from this example that present dangers are not always a just reason for flight, since God sometimes foretells them not so that we may avoid them, but so that we may be prepared to bear and undergo them.

units.la: Hic vero cumprimis obseruari debet, quid in praesenti & aperto periculo cum ipse Paulus, tum illius comites fecerint. Et hi quidem (vt ex Pauli verbis colligitur) fleuisse, & cum lachrymis illum rogauisse dicuntur, ne Hierosolymam ascenderet. Nec paucas rationes habuerunt, quibus id sua-dere poterant. Nam & Deum tentare videbatur, & non tam suam quam ecclesiae salutem neglige-re, quam suo ministerio spoliabat. Sed zelus est hic, bonus quidem, non tamen secundum scientiam: qualem in Petro Christus grauissime reprehendit, cum is quoque ipsum a cruce ferenda dehortaretur. Matth. 16. Interim laudem meretur pietas, qua Paulo consultum cupiunt: longe dissimiles ijs, qui nostro seculo ministros periculis temere obijciunt, & se probe officio functos putant, si horum capitibus & sanguine mundi pacem ad tempus redimant. Caterum acerrime illis contradicit Paulus, deq; illis conqueritur, quod fletu suo plus se quam periculi recordatione commoueant. Non ergo ferreus fuit Paulus, qualem suum virum bonum & beatum Stoici fingunt. Ingenue autem fatetur, Dei vocationem sibi suo corpore simul & vita potiorem esse. Huius exemplum ministris omnibus imo Christianis singulis, imitandum proponit spiritus sanctus. Nisi enim nobis quoq; idem animus fuerit, in Christi causa nihil aut parum proficiemus, quando vndiq; pericula imminent ijs, qui Christo seruire voluerint. 2. Tim. 3. Nec hoc graue est vere pijs, si rem ipsam probe aestimant. Quae enim vitæ huius momentaneæ corporis alioqui in terram reuersuri vtilior iactura fieri potest, quàm vt Christo impendatur, quem ideo mortuum & resuscitatum esse scimus, vt siue nos viuimus siue morimur, ipsum dominum & protectorem habeamus? Rom.14. Quæ causa est, quòd Christus quoq; eos timere vetat, qui corpus quidem occidere possunt, nihil verò in animâ, quæ potior hominis pars est, iuris habent. Matth.10. Atqui his rationibus Pauli etiam comites acquieuscunt. Vbi enim illum non temere tanta constantia pergere vident, Fiat (inquiunt) voluntas domini. Diuina vocatione ipsum vrgeri, iam demum sentiunt. Ne ergo huic relu&tari videantur, se totos & negotium hoc omne illi committunt, Christi nimirum & exemplum & præceptum secuti. Et sane non alius tutior portus est, in quem pij inter graues huius mundi æstus se recipiant, quàm Dei voluntas. Hæc quia & suaue & salutaris est, animos æstuantes sua consyderatione efficacissimè recreare & consolari poterit. Horum igitur exemplo in hanc vnà respicientes, forti animo, quicquid dominus dederit, subeamus, qui cum fidelis sit, nos vltra vires tentari non patietur, imò vnà cum tentatione euentum quoque facier, quò sufferre possimus, &c. 1. Cor. 10.
units.tr: Here we must especially observe what both Paul himself and his companions did in a present and open danger. These men (as is gathered from Paul's own words) are said to have wept and to have begged him with tears not to go up to Jerusalem. And they had not a few reasons by which they could persuade him to this. For he seemed to be tempting God, and to be neglecting not so much his own safety as that of the Church, which he was depriving of his ministry. But this is zeal, good indeed, yet not according to knowledge: the kind of zeal that Christ rebuked most severely in Peter, when Peter too urged him to turn back from bearing the cross. Matt. 16. Meanwhile their piety deserves praise, since they are anxious for Paul's welfare; they are very unlike those in our own age who rashly expose ministers to dangers, and think they have done their duty well if they buy peace for the world for a time with the heads and blood of these men. Yet Paul argues fiercely against them, and complains of them, that they move him by their weeping more than by a recollection of the danger. Paul, then, was not made of iron, such as the Stoics imagine their good and blessed man to be. Yet he frankly confesses that God's calling is dearer to him than his body and even his life. The Holy Spirit sets this example before all ministers, indeed before each individual Christian, for imitation. For unless we have the same spirit, we will make little or no progress in Christ's cause, since dangers hang on every side over those who wish to serve Christ. 2 Tim. 3. Nor is this hard for those who are truly godly, if they rightly weigh the matter. For what loss of this fleeting life could be more useful than to be spent on Christ, whom we know to have died and been raised again so that, whether we live or die, we may have him as Lord and protector? Rom. 14. This is why Christ also forbids us to fear those who can kill the body but have no power over the soul, which is the better part of man. Matt. 10. And indeed Paul's companions also yielded to these reasons of Paul. When they see that he does not go on so steadfastly without cause, they say: "The will of the Lord be done." Only now do they perceive that he is driven by a divine calling. So, lest they seem to resist it, they commit themselves and the whole matter entirely to him, following the example and precept of Christ. And indeed there is no safer harbour into which the godly may retreat amid the stormy waves of this world than the will of God. Since this is both sweet and salutary, its contemplation can most effectively refresh and console troubled minds. Therefore, looking to the example of these men and to this alone, let us with a brave spirit undergo whatever the Lord has given, for he is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond our strength, but will even make the outcome with the temptation, so that we may be able to bear it, etc. 1 Cor. 10.

units.la: Sequitur Pauli aduentus in Hierosolymorum vrbem, in quem tria incidunt. Primum comitantur illum amici, qui hucusque illi comites fuerunt, & insuper noui amici ex Cæsarienfibus accedunt. Quo loco Dei fides cernitur, qui pro suo nomine periclitantibus laborum socios adiungere solet, sicut alibi quoque monuimus. Simul verò præclarum in his elucet fidei & constantiæ exemplum. Nam quid Paulo euenturum esset, non ignorabant. Nec parua causa erat, quæ vt sibi quoq; timerent, monebat. Non deserunt tamen eum, quem Christi causam agere nouerant, nec aduerse fortunæ fluctibus se ab illo diuelli patiuntur. Obseruent exemplum hoc ollæ amici, qui dum læta fortuna arridet, huius se comites præbere solent: vt primum vero illa tonat, amicitiæ & beneficiorum obliti, terga vertunt. Alterum est, quòd de hospite commodo fideles illius loci Paulo prospiciunt. Licet enim semel periclitandum sit, locum tamen habet prudentia religioni coniunctA, sicuti Christus monet, dum nos serpentum instar esse vult in periculis. Matth. 10. Hospes autem Mnasonfuit, Cyprius natione, & vetus discipulus. Eo autem nomine perseuerantia notatur, quam in fide seruanda adhibuit. Fidem vero charitas comitatur, cuius argumentum cumprimis euidens est, quòd Paulum & huius comites, quos periculo proximos esse nouerat, hospitio excipit. Est autem hoc fidei vera ingenium, vt eo feruentior eluceat, quò propius & vehementius periculo vrgetur. Dignus igitur vituperio languor hic noster, qui in periculis & fidem dissimulamus, & charitatis officium pla-ne negligimus. Postremò, Hierosolymitani fratres Paulum libenter excipiunt. Atqui sinistros rumores de hoc iam sparsos fuisse, infrà audiemus. Illum tamen causa inaudita damnare nolunt. Sunt autem imitatione dignissimi, & suo exemplo docent, ne temere fidem illis adhibeamus, qui de fratribus crimina spargunt. Sunt enim hi fere sectæ diaboli organa, qui ecclesias nulla re efficacius & gravius, quàm fratrum dissidijs, turbari nouit. Charitatis ergo memores simus, quæ à suspicionibus quàm maxime abhorret, & in hoc toti simus, vt ecclesiarum vnitatem illæsam seruemus in Iesu Christo domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows Paul's arrival in the city of Jerusalem, in which three things occur. First, his friends who had been his companions up to this point accompany him, and in addition new friends join them from Caesarea. Here the faithfulness of God is seen, who is accustomed to join fellow workers to those in danger for his name, as we have also pointed out elsewhere. At the same time, a remarkable example of faith and constancy shines forth in these men. For they did not fail to know what would happen to Paul, and the reason he gave for fear for themselves was no small one. Yet they do not desert him whom they knew to be engaged in Christ's cause, nor do they allow themselves to be torn away from him by the waves of adverse fortune. Let those friends who are usually companions of prosperity when fortune smiles observe this example: as soon as it thunders, they forget friendship and benefits and turn their backs. The second thing is that the faithful of that place provide Paul with a convenient host. For although one must face danger once, prudence still has its place joined with religion, as Christ advises when he wills us to be like serpents in dangers. Matt. 10. The host was Mnason, a Cypriot by birth and an old disciple. By this name his perseverance is noted, which he showed in keeping the faith. Charity accompanies faith, and its proof is especially clear in that he receives Paul and his companions into his hospitality, knowing they were nearest to danger. This is indeed the true nature of faith, that it shines all the more warmly the more closely and violently it is pressed by danger. Therefore this sluggishness of ours is worthy of reproach, since in dangers we both dissemble our faith and plainly neglect the duty of charity. Lastly, the Jerusalem brethren receive Paul gladly. Yet we shall hear below that unfavourable rumours about him had already been spread; still, they are unwilling to condemn him without a hearing. They are most worthy of imitation, and by their example they teach us not to lend ready belief to those who spread accusations against brethren. For such men are almost instruments of the devil's sect, and the devil knows how to disturb the churches by nothing more effectively and gravely than by dissensions among brethren. Let us therefore be mindful of charity, which shrinks most of all from suspicions, and let us be intent on this: to keep the unity of the churches unharmed in Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXXXIX.
units.tr: HOMILY 139.

units.la: Postero autem die introiuit nobiscum Paulus ad Iacobum, omnesque adfuerunt Seniores. Quibus salutatis narrauit per singula, quæ Deus fecisset inter gentes per ministerium ipsius. At illi cum audissent, glorificabant dominum, dixeruntq; ei: Vides frater, quot millia sunt Iudæorum, qui crediderunt, & omnes sunt studiosi legis. Audiuerunt autem de te, quòd defectionem doceas à Mose omnes, qui inter gentes sunt Iudæos, dicens non debere eos circuncidere filios, nec secundùm instituta viuere. Quid est ergo? Omnino oportet conuenire multitudinem: audient enim te venisse. Hoc ergo fac quod tibi dicimus. Sunt nobis viri quatuor, votum habentes super se. His assumptis purifica te cum illis, & impende super eos vt radant caput: & sciant, quòd quæ de te audierunt te audiuerunt, nihil sunt: sed ambulas & ipse custodiens legem. De his autem qui crediderunt ex gentibus, nos scripsimus, decernentes, ne quid eiusmodi observent, nisi vt caueant ab his, quae sunt idolis immolata, & a sanguine, & suffocato, & scortatione.
units.tr: On the next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. After greeting them, he related one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. When they heard it, they glorified the Lord and said to him: "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. But they have heard about you, that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to fall away from Moses, telling them they ought not to circumcise their children or live according to the customs. What then is to be done? The multitude will certainly have to come together, for they will hear that you have come. So do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow. Take them, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are nothing, and that you yourself also walk keeping the law. As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have written to them, decreeing that they should observe nothing of this kind, except that they abstain from what is offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication."

units.la: QVamuis de electo Iesu Christi organo, apostolo Paulo, multi rumores sinistri sparsi essent, quibus illius tum fama tum doctrina ab aduersarijs acerrime petebatur, eundem tamen ab Hierosolymitanis fratribus amice & benigne exceptum fuisse Lucas scribit, ita docens, illos maiorem charitatis, quam paucorum hominum odio contabescentium rationem habuisse, & horum exemplum omnibus nobis imitandum proponit, quod nisi fiat, prauis suspicionibus omnis inter homines charitas turbari solet. Sequitur autem in praesenti narratione, quid inter Paulum & Hierosolymitanos fratres factum sit, qui locus propter multa, quae ex hoc nostrae institutioni seruire possunt, diligenti & attenta consyderatione dignus est.
units.tr: Although many malicious rumours had been spread about Jesus Christ's chosen instrument, the apostle Paul, and his adversaries attacked both his reputation and his teaching most fiercely, Luke writes that the brethren of Jerusalem nevertheless received him kindly and warmly. In this way he teaches that they paid greater regard to charity than to the hatred of a few men who were consumed by envy, and he sets this example before all of us to imitate. Unless this is done, all charity among men is usually disturbed by wicked suspicions. The present narrative goes on to tell what took place between Paul and the brethren of Jerusalem. Because this passage can serve our instruction in many ways, it deserves careful and attentive consideration.

units.la: Principio Paulus vna cum suis comitibus ad Iacobum apostolum, qui tunc temporis in vrbe agebat, accessit, & illic in Seniorum coetu rerum abs se gestarum rationem reddidit, singula quae per ipsius ministerium Deus hucusque gesserat, ordine recensens. Quo loco primum admonemur, in ecclesia or dine certo opus esse, ne quidus cuiuis vbique liceat. Fuit Paulus electum Christi organum, & plus omnibus alijs apostolis laborauit. Nihil tamen priuata authoritate agit in aliena ecclesia, sed priusquam aliquid tentet, loci illius ministros & antistites accedit, & illis honorifice salutatis sui ministerij rationem reddit. Sufficit vnum hoc exemplum ad confutandam Romanorum Pontificum insolentiam, qui in omnes ecclesias sibi primatum & dominium vendicant. Eodem etiam Anabaptistae turbatores confutantur, qui cum nullas ecclesias vspiam plantent, alioru labore & periculo plantatas turbant, hoc vno sibi laudem eximiam vendicantes, si pijs ministris insana sua & mordaci garrulita te negotium faciant, eosq; odio & inuidia apud quosuis aggrauent. Deinde Pauli modestia in eo etiam elucet, quod ita rerum abs se gestarum narrationem contexit, vt omnium authorem Deum faciat, sibi vero nihil praeter ministerium tribuat. Nouerat enim frustra ab hominibus plantari & rigari, nisi Deus incrementum dederit. 1. Cor. 3. Ita alibi cum se plus omnibus alijs apostolis laborauisse dixisset, mox addit: Non tamen ego, sed gratia Dei, quae mihi adest. 1. Cor. 15. Hoc ipsum in omni vocatione obseruandum esse, alibi monuimus. Nisi enim dominum aedificauerit Deus, frustra laborabunt, qui illi aedificandae studient. Psal. 127. Nisi respub. suo fauore Deus protegat, inanes erunt magistratuum curae & consilia. Nisi studijs nostris idem suo spiritu adsit, & ingenij vires acuat, nihil vel legendo vel scribendo proficitur. Horum ergo memores humiliter de nobis ipsis sentire discamus, studijsq; nostris omnibus preces frequentes interponamus, quibus Deus rogari & dona sua impetrari vult. Porro de Senioribus additur, quod auditus Pauli laboribus dominum glorificauerint. Est hoc haud vulgare charitatis argumentum, quod Symmystae laudibus non inuident, nec quicquam amarulenter oggannunt, quod fere faciunt, qui charitatis omnis expertes priuatae potius gloriae quam diuinae student. Vt autem Paulus rerum abs se praeclare gestarum authorem Deum fecerat, ita ipsi quoq; non Paulum fictitijs laudibus inebriant, sed illi congratulantes Deum glorificare studient. Docent autem suo exemplo, vt nos de sanctorum laboribus & virtutibus iudicare conueniat. Homines fuisse sciamus, humanis affectibus & casibus obnoxios. Si quid ergo ab illis plus quam humanum factum est, Dei opus hoc esse agnoscamus, qui ex mera gratia illorum ministerio vti voluit. Illis ergo eam felicitate gratulemur: obedientiam, qua Dei organa sese praebuerunt, imitemur: facti vero laudem omnem Deo tribuamus. Ita & illos imitando vere honorabimus, & sua Deo gloria integra manebit, quam impro be violant, quicunq; sanctis inhaerentes, illos bonorum authores & largitores faciunt, ita vt ab illis opem & auxilium petendum esse existiment. Vide supra cap. 3. & 14.
units.tr: First, Paul, together with his companions, went to the apostle James, who was then in the city, and there, before the assembly of the elders, he gave an account of his doings, recounting in order each thing that God had done through his ministry up to that point. Here we are first reminded that in the Church there must be a fixed order, so that not just anyone may do whatever he likes anywhere. Paul was the chosen instrument of Christ and laboured more than all the other apostles, yet he does nothing on his own authority in another man's church. Before he attempts anything, he approaches the ministers and leaders of that place, greets them with honour, and gives an account of his ministry. This one example is enough to refute the arrogance of the Roman pontiffs, who claim for themselves primacy and lordship over all churches. It also refutes the Anabaptist troublemakers, who plant no churches anywhere but disturb those planted by the labour and danger of others. They claim for themselves this one notable glory: that they can harass godly ministers with their mad and biting chatter and stir up hatred and envy against them among everyone. Next, Paul's modesty shines forth in the way he frames his account so that he makes God the author of everything, while attributing nothing to himself beyond the ministry. He knew that men plant and water in vain unless God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3). So, when he had said that he had laboured more than all the other apostles, he immediately added: "Yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me" (1 Cor. 15). We have noted elsewhere that this must be observed in every calling. Unless God builds the house, those who labour to build it labour in vain (Psalm 127). Unless God protects the commonwealth by his favour, the cares and counsels of magistrates are empty. Unless the same God is present with our studies and sharpens the powers of our minds by his Spirit, nothing is gained by reading or writing. Let us therefore remember these things, learn to think humbly of ourselves, and join frequent prayers to all our studies, by which God wishes to be asked and his gifts obtained. Further, it is added concerning the elders that, having heard of Paul's labours, they glorified the Lord. This is no common proof of charity: they do not begrudge their fellow believer his praise, nor do they mutter bitter sneers, as those do who, lacking all charity, seek private glory rather than the glory of God. Just as Paul had made God the author of the excellent things he had done, so they too do not puff Paul up with fictitious praises, but rejoice with him and seek to glorify God. By their example they also teach us how we ought to judge the labours and virtues of the saints. Let us remember that they were men, subject to human feelings and misfortunes. So if anything more than human was done by them, let us acknowledge it as God's work, since out of pure grace he chose to use their ministry. Let us therefore congratulate them on this happiness, imitate the obedience by which they made themselves instruments of God, and give all the praise for the deed to God. In this way we shall truly honour them by imitating them, and God's glory will remain intact. Those who cling to the saints and make them authors and givers of good things, so that they think help and aid must be sought from them, violate that glory wickedly. See above, chapters 3 and 14.

units.la: Sequitur autem actio perquam memorabilis, cuius primarij authores suo consilio Seniores Hierosolymitani fuerunt. Suadent enim, vt Nazarei votum Paulus suscipiat, & illius tempore tuolato iuxta legem sese in templo purificari aut a voto expiari patiatur. Quae res impijs hostibus contra Paulum tumultuandi occasionem praebuit, qua tandem comprehensus & vinctus est. Quia vero actioni huic quaedam vtcunq; tolerabilia insunt, quaedam vix vlla ratione excusari possunt, pe
units.tr: Next follows a very memorable action, whose chief authors were the elders of Jerusalem by their counsel. For they urge that Paul take up the Nazirite vow, and that, when the days of the vow were complete, he allow himself to be purified in the temple according to the law, or be released from the vow. This gave the impious enemies an occasion to stir up tumult against Paul, and in the end he was seized and bound. But since this action has some elements that are in some measure tolerable and others that can scarcely be excused by any reasoning, it must be examined more carefully

units.la: T nitius nobis excutienda erit. Quare vt rectius intelligantur singula, paulo altius controuersiam hanc omnem repetemus. Docebat Paulus, mera Dei gratia per Iesum Christum homines fide iustificari: quam doctrinam vnanimi apostolorum consensu approbatam fuisse, supra cap.15. vidimus. Quia autem Paulo, inter gentes praedicanti, multa lis erat cum ijs, qui legem euangelio miscere, & gentes ad circuncisionis & aliarum ceremoniarum observationem cogere nitebantur: de Legis fine & vsu illi diligentius disputandum erat, & singula ad viuum (vt dicitur) resecare cogebatur. Quare ingenue docebat, legem & huius ceremonias ad iustificationem nihil conferre, eo quod illi nemo mortalium satis facere posset: datam autem a Deo, vt nostram corruptionem arguat, conuictos peccati ad Christum deducat, in quo vno huius completio habeatur. Addebat simul, illorum opinione Christum euanescari, qui legi iustificationis meritum tribuunt, & eosdem non posse non damnari, quando ipsi sibi ipsi legis maledictionem accersant. Hinc illae locutiones: Lex iram operatur: Viuente mandato, peccatum reuixit: Potentia peccati, lex. Item: Quotquot ex operibus legis sunt, execrationi sunt obnoxij, &c. Videbantur haec duriuscula illis, qui legi a teneris assueuerant, illamque diuinitus per Mosen tam esse sciebant. Et qui Paulo plus satis infensi erant, inde calumniandi occasione arrepta, illum legis diuinae prophanum contemptorem & euersorem clamabant, quasi hanc simpliciter damnaret, cum non illam, sed illorum potius errorem impugnaret, qui alium legis finem & vsum commenti, huius observatione iustificari & saluari volebant. Omnibus ergo inuisus Paulus erat, perinde vt nostro seculo bonorum operum hostes esse dicimur, quando illa ad iustificandum & saluandum nihil conferre dicimus, cum interim suum illis locum relinquamus, & debita officia esse doceamus, quae homines necessario Deo praestare debeant. Caeterum his praemissis, facile patebit, quorsum sua oratione Seniores tendant, quis illis totius actionis scopus fuerit. Quare ipsam orationem per singulas ipsius partes modo inspiciemus. Seniorum oratio. Primo, nomen & famam Pauli apud omnes laborare, ingenue ipsi indicant. Nam fertur de te (inquiunt) quod defectionem a Mose doceas, &c. Est hoc in illis vehementer probandum, quod nihil dissimulant. Praestat enim ingenue cum fratribus & amicis agere, vt si quid peccauerunt, emendari possit, & culpa liberentur, si falsis criminibus suspecti sunt. Nec leue illorum peccatum est, qui cum absentes accusent, ijsdem praesentibus adulantur: qui item fratres ab alijs traduci patiuntur, nec illos a quibus sibi cauere debeant, admonent. Ita enim fit, vt obtrectandi libido passim amicitias violet, & pleriq; quid ipsis maxime cauendum sit ignorent. Simul vero vt se publice purget consulunt, & sui consilij rationes adducunt minime leues. Nam primo multitudinem credentium allegant, qui omnes sinistra de ipso suspicionem conceperint. Dicunt enim: Vides frater, quot millia sunt Iudaeorum qui crediderunt, & hi omnes zelo legis feruent. Diserte vero credentes nominant, ne quis ipsos praefractis & contumacibus patrocinari velle putaret. Et multa millia horum esse dicunt, vt ostendant, tot simul hominum salutem minime negligi oportere. Et sane verisimile est, hac ratione cumprimis motum fuisse Paulum, qui gentis suae tanto studio ardebat, vt pro illis anathema quoq; fieri optaret. Sed & zelum legis allegant, vt constet, aliquid illis adhuc concedendum esse, cum in zeli huius ardore violentis remedijs nihil profici possit. Praeterea a necessario argumentantur, cum dicunt: Oportet omnino conuenire multitudinem. Quia enim te vt niisse omnes norunt, res amplius dissimulari non potest. Purgatione ergo omnino opus erit. Quia vt rò apud eos, qui inueterata suspicione toti tenentur, verbis nihil aut parum proficies, publico aliquo facto te hucusq; immerito traductum fuisse, testeris oportet. Atqui non parui momenti erant rationes ha, nisi causa eiusmodi fuisset, quae non tam studiosos legis lucrifacere, quam superstitiosos & contumaces huius observatores in errore confirmare potuisset, vt moxaudiemus. Sequitur enim consilium ipsum, quo Paulum suae famae & nomini prospicere posse putant. Sunt (inquiunt) nobis viri quatuor, votum habentes super se, Nazaraeorum nimirum, de quo cap.decimo octauo ex libri Numerorum cap.6. diximus. His te coniungito, & communibus sumptibus te cum illis iuxta legem radi & purificari curato publice. Quod vt factu leue fuerit, ita ex eo omnibus constabit, te hucusque falsa suspicione grauatum fuisse, nec te legis prophanum contemptorem censeri debere, cum in illa mandatas Ceremonias ipse obserues. Hoc illud Seniorum Hierosolymitanae ecclesiae consilium est, quod in speciem quidem tolerabile videtur, & idem cum eo, quod Paulus in Cenchreis Rom.3. Galat.3. Rom.7. 1.Cor.15. Galat.3. Consilium Seniorum excusatur. Cenchreis antea fecerat. Sed rem exactius perpendenti magnum inter haec discrimen apparebit, nec debuisse illorum consilio cessisse apostolum, qui in aliis leviorum momenti fidei professionem & Christianam libertatem acerrime asseruerat. Primo enim Nazarei voto apud Corinthios sese obstrinxerat, quod ea re infirmos aliquos lucrifieri posse sciebat, sicut ipse testatur 1.Corinth.9. Nec quicquam per hoc fidei professioni derogabatur, cum sola capitis rasura illum voto liberaret. Hic vero sacrificium accedit, quod revera locum nullum habebat amplius, cum iam olim in Christi morte velum templi scissum, & sacrificia in universum abrogata essent. Deinde quod in Cenchreis fecerat, solis infirmis dabatur, nec in exemplum aut legalium ceremoniarum confirmationem trahi poterat. At huius factis id esse, ut Paulus testetur, sibi universam legem cum suis ceremoniis minime displicere. Quid vero hinc aliud oriri poterat, quam quod Iudaei in errore confirmarentur, & qui in Christo converterant ut legi renuntiassent, ad eius observationem revocarentur? Praeterea si primis nascentis ecclesiae annis id factum fuisset, merito hoc infirmis datum videri poterat. At cum iam annis totis viginti tribus euangelium in toto orbe praedicatum esset, nimia profecto haec fuit indulgentia, qua contumaciissimae gentis superstitio fovebatur.
units.tr: More carefully must we examine it. To understand each point properly, we shall go back a little further and trace this whole controversy from its beginning. Paul taught that people are justified by faith through Jesus Christ, by grace alone and with no merit of their own. We saw above, at chapter 15, that the apostles unanimously approved this teaching. Since Paul, preaching among the Gentiles, had a long dispute with those who tried to mix the Gospel with the Law and to compel the Gentiles to observe circumcision and the other ceremonies, he had to discuss the purpose and use of the Law more thoroughly and to cut away every point to the quick, as the saying goes. So he taught plainly that the Law and its ceremonies contribute nothing to justification, because no mortal could satisfy it. It was given by God, however, to expose our corruption, to lead those convicted of sin to Christ, in whom alone its fulfilment is found. At the same time he added that those who ascribe justification to the Law make Christ of no effect, and that they cannot avoid condemnation, since they bring the Law's curse upon themselves. Hence his expressions: "The Law works wrath"; "When the commandment came, sin revived"; "The power of sin is the Law"; and likewise: "As many as are of the works of the Law are under the curse," and so on. These statements seemed rather harsh to those who had been brought up on the Law from childhood and knew that it had been given by God through Moses. Those who were very hostile to Paul seized on this as an occasion for slander and cried out that he was a profane despiser and destroyer of the divine Law, as if he condemned the Law outright. Yet he was attacking not the Law but the error of those who, inventing another purpose and use for it, wanted people to be justified and saved by observing it. So Paul was hated by all, just as in our own age we are called enemies of good works when we say that good works contribute nothing to justifying and saving us, while nevertheless we assign them their place and teach that they are the duties which people must necessarily render to God. But with these things laid down beforehand, it will be easy to see where the elders' speech is heading and what the whole aim of the action was for them. Let us therefore look at the speech itself part by part. The speech of the elders. First, they openly show that Paul's name and reputation are under attack among everyone. For, they say, it is reported about you that you teach defection from Moses, and so on. In this they deserve great praise, that they conceal nothing. For it is better to deal openly with brothers and friends, so that if they have done wrong it can be corrected, and if they are suspected of false charges they may be cleared of blame. Those who accuse people in their absence and flatter them to their faces commit no small sin; so too do those who allow brothers to be slandered by others and do not warn them of the people they should be on guard against. In this way the lust for detraction violates friendships everywhere, and most people do not know what they most need to beware of. At the same time, they advise him to clear himself publicly, and they offer reasons of no small weight for their counsel. First, they point to the multitude of believers, all of whom have formed a bad suspicion of him. For they say: "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who have believed, and all of them are zealous for the Law." They name the believers expressly, lest anyone think they wished to defend the stubborn and obstinate. They say there are many thousands of them, to show that the salvation of so many people must not be neglected. And it is indeed likely that Paul was moved chiefly by this consideration, since he burned with such zeal for his own people that he even wished to be made an anathema for them. They also appeal to zeal for the Law, to show that some concession must still be made to them, since violent remedies can do nothing against the heat of this zeal. Furthermore, they argue from necessity when they say: "The multitude must by all means be brought together. Since everyone knows you have come, the matter cannot be concealed any longer. Purification will therefore be altogether necessary. For you will accomplish little by words among those who are held fast by an long-standing suspicion; you must bear witness by some public act that you have hitherto been unjustly slandered." Yet these reasons would not have been of slight weight, had the case not been of a kind that could confirm in error the superstitious and obstinate observers of the Law, rather than win over the zealous adherents of the Law, as we shall hear presently. For next comes the counsel itself, by which they think Paul can provide for his reputation and name. "There are with us," they say, "four men who have a vow upon them, namely of the Nazirites, concerning which we spoke at chapter 18, from Numbers chapter 6. Join yourself to them, and see that at common expense you are shaved and purified with them publicly, according to the Law. Just as this is a small matter to do, so by it all will know that you have until now been burdened by a false suspicion, and that you ought not to be counted a profane despiser of the Law, since you yourself keep the ceremonies commanded in it." This is the counsel of the elders of the church at Jerusalem, which in appearance seems tolerable enough, and it is the same as what Paul had earlier done at Cenchreae (Rom. 3; Gal. 3; Rom. 7; 1 Cor. 15; Gal. 3). The counsel of the elders is defended. Cenchreae is where he had done it before. But anyone who weighs the matter more exactly will see a great difference between these things, and the apostle ought not to have yielded to their counsel, when he had so sharply asserted the profession of faith and Christian liberty in matters of less weight. For first, he had bound himself by a Nazirite vow among the Corinthians, because he knew that some weak people could thereby be won, as he himself testifies (1 Cor. 9). Nor was the profession of faith in any way diminished by this, since merely shaving his head released him from the vow. Here, however, a sacrifice is added, which in truth had no place any longer, since long ago at Christ's death the veil of the temple had been torn and sacrifices had been abolished altogether. Moreover, what he did at Cenchreae was given only to the weak, and it could not be drawn into an example or a confirmation of the legal ceremonies. But by this act he would show, as Paul would be seen to do, that the whole Law with its ceremonies did not displease him at all. What else could arise from this, but that the Jews would be confirmed in their error, and that those who had been converted in Christ, who had renounced the Law, would be called back to its observance? Besides, if this had been done in the first years of the newly born church, it might rightly have been seen as a concession to the weak. But when the Gospel had already been preached throughout the whole world for twenty-three full years, this indulgence was surely excessive, by which the superstition of a most stubborn nation was fostered.

units.la: Quid quod Deus suo iudicio sibi ista displicere docuit? Ut enim de eo omittamus dicere, quod infeliciter Paulo cessit illud consilium, Deus certe plurimus post annos unam cum templo, superstitionis officina, funditus evertit, cum non antea legalis cultus finem vel levi facere. Nimio igitur gentis suae studio seniores decepti, ista consulunt, & nimia facilitate illis Paulus acquiescit, qui ea potius libertate uti debebat, qua in Titi causa & contra Petrum antea vi-sus fuerat. Galat.2. Longe ergo falluntur, qui exemplo hoc ipsis patrocinantur, qui in hominum gratiam quidvis admittendum putant. Id quidem in ipsis locum habere scimus, quae nec confessioni, nec Christianae libertati derogant. At ubi ista in periculum veniunt, ne latum unquam nobis a veritatis via discedendum est. Quare maximorum & sanctissimorum virorum error non in exemplum trahi debet, sed potius cautiores reddere, ne similli modo nos quoque abduci patiamur.
units.tr: Why, moreover, did God teach that these things displease him by his own judgment? For, to leave aside that the counsel turned out unhappily for Paul, God certainly, many years later, utterly destroyed the temple together with it, the workshop of superstition, though before this they had not made even a slight end of the legal worship. The elders, therefore, deceived by excessive zeal for their nation, gave this counsel, and Paul yielded to it with too much readiness, when he ought rather to have used that liberty which he had shown earlier in the case of Titus and against Peter (Gal. 2). Those therefore are far wrong who defend the elders by this example, who think anything should be admitted for the sake of men's goodwill. We know this may have a place in matters that do not derogate from the confession or from Christian liberty. But when such things endanger the truth, we must never depart from the way of the truth, not even a little. Hence the error of the greatest and most holy men ought not to be drawn into an example, but rather should make us more cautious, lest we too allow ourselves to be led astray in the same way.

units.la: Porro ultima parte quod de gentibus obici poterat, praeoccupant. Illis enim Pauli exemplum praeiudicare, & illorum sententiae subscribere videbatur, qui gentibus circumcisionem & reliquas caeremonias obtrudere nitebatur. Illud ergo negant, dicentes: His autem, qui ex gentibus crediderunt, iam ante scripsimus, illos ab omni legalium caeremoniarum observatione liberos esse iussimus, modo a palam prophanis abstineant, & inter libertatis suae usum charitatis non obliuiscantur, ne vel idolorum communione & fornicatione sese polluant, aut suffocati & sanguinis esu intempestivo (quo abstinere nec difficile nec incommodum est) quemquam offendant. Vide de his Actio. 15. Elucet autem in tota hac actione Iudaicae gentis peruicacia, & quam parum praerogativae habeat in religione mundi huius dignitas, quando non alibi maior infirmitas & imperfectio fidei apostolorum temporibus inventa est, quam in Hierosolymitana ecclesia, quae & urbis celebritate, & Christi concionibus, & nascentis euangelij primitijs gloriari poterat. Docemur item quantum euangelio incommodent superstitiosi illi ceremoniarum magistri, qui infirmitatem fidei harum diuturniori conseruatione fouent, & sua indulgentia ardentioribus ministris remoras obiiciunt. Abiectis ergo infirmis bisce carnis vacillantis & haesitabundae praesidijs, fidei veritatem impollutam teneamus, & libertatis Christianae memores, constanter huius authorem celebremus, qui est unigenitus Dei filius, dominus & saluator noster Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Next, they anticipate the last point that could be raised about the Gentiles. For Paul's example seemed to prejudge the matter and to lend support to those who tried to force circumcision and the other ceremonies on the Gentiles. They deny this, saying: "As for those of the Gentiles who have believed, we have already written to them and ordered that they be free from all observance of the legal ceremonies, provided only that they abstain from openly profane things, and that in using their liberty they do not forget charity, lest they defile themselves either by communion with idols and fornication, or give offence by eating what has been strangled and blood at an unseasonable time (from which abstaining is neither difficult nor burdensome)." See Acts 15 on these matters. Yet throughout this whole transaction the obstinacy of the Jewish nation shines forth, and how little prerogative the dignity of this world has in religion. For in the time of the apostles no greater weakness and imperfection of faith was found anywhere than in the church of Jerusalem, which could boast of the fame of its city, of Christ's sermons, and of the first fruits of the nascent gospel. We are also taught how greatly those superstitious masters of ceremonies harm the gospel: they nourish the weakness of faith by keeping these things in place for longer, and by their indulgence they put obstacles in the way of the more fervent ministers. Let us therefore cast off these supports of a wavering and hesitant flesh, hold fast to the unpolluted truth of the faith, and, mindful of Christian liberty, constantly celebrate its author, who is the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXL.
units.tr: HOMILY CXL.

units.la: Tunc Paulus assumptis viris, postero die purificatus cum illis intrauit in templum, annuntians expletionem dierum purificationis, donec offerretur pro unoquoque eorum oblatio. Cum autem septem dies iam pene essent expleti, qui ex Asia erant Iudaei, cum vidissent eum in templo, conturbarunt totum populum, & iniecerunt ei manus, clamantes: Viri Israelitae, succurrite. Hic est ille homo, qui aduersus populum, & legem, & locum hunc omnes ubique docet. Insuper & Graecos induxit in templum, & prophanauit sanctum locum hunc. Viderant enim Trophimum Ephesium in ciuitate cum ipso: quem existimauerunt quòd in templum introduxisset Paulus. Commotaq; est ciuitas tota, & factus est concursus populi, & apprehensum Paulum trahebant è templo: statimq; clausæ sunt fores. Quærentibus autem illis eum occidere, nuntiatum est Tribuno cohortis, quòd tota conturbata esset Hierosolyma. Qui statim assumptis militibus & Centurionibus, decurrit ad illos. At illi cùm vidissent Tribunum & milites, cessauerunt percutere Paulum.
units.tr: Then Paul took the men, and the next day, having been purified, went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfilling of the days of purification, until an offering should be made for each one of them. When the seven days were now almost over, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd, laid hands on him, and cried out: "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law and this place. Moreover, he has brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place." For they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then the whole city was stirred, and the people came running together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut. As they were trying to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in an uproar. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

units.la: QVoniam Paulus apostolus propter suam de lege doctrinam apud Hierosolymitanos pessimè audiebat, quasi illam cum suis præceptis & ceremonijs simpliciter & absolutè, vt perseme-lam & noxiam damnaret, ecclesiæ illius Seniores, vt se palàm omni suspicione liberet, consulunt. Et probandum quidem in illis esse, quòd tanti viri famæ consultum volunt: improbandum verò, quòd eiusmodi consilium præbent, quod cum ingenua fidei simul & libertatis Christianæ professione pugna-bat. Hæc enim legales cultus & Ceremonias per Christum abrogatas, & proinde nullum posthac illarum in religione vsum esse docet. Cur enim posse Christum inter ea, quæ ad Dei cultum faciunt, numerarentur, quando ne olim quidem Deus illis coli voluit, sed vt rerum futurarum, & promissæ redemptionis typi essent, instituit? Proponit autem exemplum hoc Spiritus sanctus, non vt imitemur, nec etiam vt vel Pauli vel Seniorum, & inter hos Iacobi cumprimis, authoritatem labefactet: sed vt discamus carnis prudentiam in salutis negotio & religionis causa suspectam habere, & à Dei verbo nelarium vnguem discedere. Id verò rei totius exitus plenius docebit, quem modò maximæ parte inspiciemus.
units.tr: Because the apostle Paul was being very badly spoken of among the Jerusalemites on account of his teaching about the law, as if he condemned it, together with its precepts and ceremonies, simply and absolutely, as something pernicious and harmful, the elders of that church advised him, so that he might clear himself openly of all suspicion. We must approve, indeed, that such great men wanted to protect his reputation; but the advice they gave is to be disapproved, for it fought against the open profession of both the Christian faith and Christian liberty. For Christ teaches that the legal worship and ceremonies have been abrogated through him, and that therefore no use of them in religion remains from now on. For why should Christ allow them to be counted among those things that serve the worship of God, when God did not even want them to be worshipped in former times, but instituted them only as types and figures of things to come and of the promised redemption? The Holy Spirit sets down this example, however, not that we should imitate it, nor that he should weaken the authority of Paul or of the elders, especially James among them; but that we might learn to regard human prudence with suspicion in the matter of salvation and of religion, and not to depart from the word of God by so much as a fingernail's breadth. The outcome of the whole affair will teach this more fully, and we shall look at it in large part shortly.

units.la: Obtemperat enim Seniorum consilio Paulus, qui haud leuem cum illis expostulandi causam habebat, qui manifestos errores & superstitionem hucusq; tulerant. Modestè tamen & amicè illis cedit, cùm ne contumax & præfractus habeatur, tum quòd ea ratione se apud Iudæos quoque liberius decendi occasionem inuenturum putabat. Quare templum vnà cum quatuor illis voti suscepti socijs ingreditur, purificationis tempus publicè annuntiat, curat deniq; vt pro singulis sacrificiū pro more offeratur. Quis verò hic non manifestum errorem videat? Cur enim non idem facit quod olim, quando ne minimam quidem simulationem in Petro ferre voluit? Cur non gentium rationem habet, quæ hoc illius facto non leuiter offendi poterant? An verò nullos Hierosolymis falsos fratres esse credit, qui clanculum Christianorum libertatem explorent? Cæterum docet exemplum hoc, quantum in religione aberretur, si nimiam facilitatem cum carnis prudentia in consilium adhibeas. Hac enim deceptus Paulus à solita simplicitate recedit, & ijs quidem, qui ex gentibus crediderant, offendiculi occasionem præbet, apud Iudæos verò nihil omnino proficit. Quos enim diuini verbi authoritas non monet, eos frustra vel lenitate vel carnis consilio flectere instituas. Tutissimum ergo est, vt religionis cau-sam omnem ad solum Deum pertinere, nec quicquam in illa nostri iuris esse agnoscamus. Ita fiet, vt nihil nobis in ea permittamus, sed Dei verbum vnicè sectemur, quod ille nobis tum fidei & religionis tum totius vitæ nostræ regulam esse voluit. Vide Num. decimo quinto. Deut. 4. & 12. cap.
units.tr: For Paul yields to the advice of the elders, although he had no slight cause to protest against them, since they had tolerated manifest errors and superstition up to that point. Nevertheless he gives way to them modestly and kindly, both so that he would not be thought obstinate and stubborn, and because he thought that by this method he would find an opportunity to speak more freely among the Jews as well. So he enters the temple together with the four companions of his vow, publicly announces the time of purification, and finally sees to it that a sacrifice is offered for each one, as is the custom. But who does not see the obvious error here? Why does he not do what he did before, when he would not tolerate even the slightest pretence in Peter? Why does he not take account of the Gentiles, who could easily be offended by this action of his? Or does he really believe there were no false brothers in Jerusalem, who secretly spied on the liberty of the Christians? Moreover, this example shows how far one can go astray in religion if one admits too much readiness and human prudence into one's counsel. For Paul, deceived by this, departs from his usual simplicity, and gives an occasion of stumbling indeed to those of the Gentiles who had believed, while among the Jews he accomplishes nothing at all. For those whom the authority of the divine word does not move, you attempt in vain to bend by gentleness or by human counsel. It is therefore safest to acknowledge that the whole cause of religion belongs to God alone, and that we have no right in it at all. Thus it will come about that we permit nothing to ourselves in it, but follow the word of God alone, which he willed to be for us the rule of faith and religion and of our whole life. See Numbers 15, Deuteronomy 4 and chapter 12.

units.la: Sed videamus tandem quis consilij huius & facti finis fuerit. Videtur quidè initiò successurum negotium, cum totis fere septem diebus nullum vspiam periculum appareat. Sed ecce, cùm iam sini proximus esset Paulus, iamq; se in portum recipere videtur, vndiq; fluctus & procellæ insurgunt, & præsens vitæ periculum imminet, vt nunquam aliàs. Nam paucorum aliquot improbitate tota Hierosolymorum ciuitas commouetur, & à seditiosis Paulus comprehensus haud dubiè perijsset, nisi singulari Dei consilio excitatus Tribunus, illum furentium manibus ereripuisset. Sed singula ordine vidi-mus, vt plus inde ad nos institutionis redeat.
units.tr: But let us at last see what the end of this counsel and this deed was. At first the matter seems to be going well, since for almost the whole seven days no danger appears anywhere. But behold, when Paul was now nearly at the end and seemed already to be entering harbour, waves and storms rise up on every side, and a danger to his life hangs over him as never before. For through the wickedness of a few men the whole city of Jerusalem is stirred up, and Paul, seized by the seditious, would certainly have perished, had the tribune not been roused by a singular counsel of God and snatched him from the hands of the raging men. But let us look at each thing in order, so that more instruction may come to us from it.

units.la: Primò authores totius Tragœdiæ indicantur, Iudæi, qui ab Asia aduenerant. Illi ipsi ergo sunt, quos implacabili Pauli odio iam diu laborauisse, & ipsum per multas vrbes insecutos fuisse, supra non semel vidimus. Nec enim vnquam, nisi his authoribus, persecutionem Paulus aliquam sustinuit. Cernitur in his incurabilis gentis illius cæcitas, quam ipse Paulus in priori ad Thess. 2. cap. deplorat, & quæ tandem iusto Dei iudicio grauissimè punita fuit. Interim obseruabis quàm laboriosos & audaces reddat veritatis odium. Nam & Paulum vbiq; insequuntur, & in aliena vrbe seditionem concitant, id quod absque euidenti periculo fieri non posse, satis intelligebant. Sed vtinam huius rei exempla non passim nostro etiam seculo ederentur.
units.tr: First, the authors of the whole tragedy are pointed out: the Jews who had come from Asia. These are the very men whom, as we have seen above more than once, had long suffered from an implacable hatred of Paul and had pursued him through many cities. Indeed Paul never endured any persecution except at their instigation. In them is seen the incurable blindness of that nation, which Paul himself laments in his first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 2, and which at last was most severely punished by the just judgement of God. Meanwhile you will observe how laborious and bold the hatred of the truth makes men. For they pursue Paul everywhere and stir up sedition in a foreign city, which they well understood could not be done without obvious danger. Would that examples of this were not published everywhere in our own age too.

units.la: Deinde opportunitatem aliquam nacti totum populum conturbant, & quasi ad commune incendium reflinguendum excitant. Nam iniectis in Paulum manibus, clamant: Viri Israelitæ, succurrite, &c. Quid vero ope & auxilio opus erat aduersus illum, qui nec occultas seditiones, nec apertam vim alicui parabat? Vides ergo, qui fere seditionum authores sint. Impingitur fere crimine hoc Verbi ministris, vt passim videmus. Sed si rem omnem penitius inspiciamus, non aliunde quam ab horum oribus & inimicis seditionis initium sumere patebit. Quia enim Veritatis lucem ferre non possunt, hanc si non alia ratione licet, saltem publica ruina (vt olim Catilina dicebat) extinguere conantur. Refer huc, quæ Cap. 14. 16. 17. 18. & 19. vidimus.
units.tr: Then, having found some opportunity, they throw the whole people into confusion and stir them up as if to put out a common fire. For, laying hands on Paul, they cry: "Men of Israel, help!" and so on. But what need was there of help and aid against a man who was preparing neither secret sedition nor open violence against anyone? You see therefore who are almost always the authors of seditions. This charge is commonly brought against the ministers of the Word, as we see everywhere. But if we examine the whole matter more closely, it will be plain that the beginning of sedition comes from none other than the enemies and haters of these men. For since they cannot bear the light of the truth, they try to extinguish it, if by no other means is permitted, at least by public ruin (as Catiline once put it). Refer here to what we saw in chapters 14, 16, 17, 18 and 19.

units.la: At ne temere tumultuari videantur, clamoribus seditiosis accusationis capita intermiscent. Et primo quidem doctrinam accusant, quod ea & populo Dei, & Legi, & Templo noxia siue damnosa sit. Id vero inde sumpsisse videntur, quod Paulus in Iudæis inanem suæ gentis & patrum fiduciam coerceret, ostendens, veros Israelitas non ex carne nasci, sed ex spiritu, nec omnes in Dei populo statim conseri qui ex Abrahamo secundum carnem nati sunt, nisi iuxta Abrahami exemplum in Christum credant. Item quod de vero legis vsu differens, huic iustificationem minime tribui debere doceret, vt in præcedenti Sermone vidimus, & quod legales cultus Christi aduentu & mortis ipsius merito abrogatos esse diceret. Ne tamen verbis inanibus illorum accusatio nici videretur, de facto etiá Pauli, & quidem recenti conqueruntur, nimirum quod homines ethnicos in templum introduxerit, & per hoc locum sanctissimum prophanarit. Atqui salsissima simul & impudentissima hæc erat calumnia, quæ tamen apud omnes fidem inueniebat, quod inter Pauli comites Trophimum Ephesium in vrbe conspexissent. Ita enim hunc in templum quoq; ab illo introductum fuisse suspicantur. Rursum vero admonet locus hic, quibus fere criminibus grauentur Veritatis ministri: nimirum quod in electum Dei populum, in dilectam eius sponsam, ecclesiam, peccent improbè: quod leges & traditiones ecclesiæ impudenter damnent, & quod templa simul & cultus veteres impiè euertant. Ita Christum accusatum fuisse legimus. Et hæc ipsa aduersus Stephanum Veritatis hostes protulerunt. Et hæc quidem nobis etiam hodie quidam obijciunt, quos nec vllus ecclesiæ Dei respectus, nec diuinæ legis authoritas, nec veræ religionis cura aut studium mouet. Interim ea Veritatis fors est, vt calumnia aduersus nullos alios & impudentius & efficacius, quàm huius ministros, stringi soleat. Quia enim mundo inuisi, & quodammodo communi omnium præiudicio damnati sunt, quiduis aduersus illos facilè omnes admittunt & recipiunt, nec quenquam suæ leuitatis pudet. Sed patienter feramus quæ non prophetas modò & apostolos, sed ipsum quoq; Dei filium tulisse scimus.
units.tr: But so that they may not seem to riot rashly, they mix accusations into their seditious clamours. And first they accuse the teaching, saying that it is harmful or damaging both to the people of God, to the law and to the temple. They seem to have taken this from the fact that Paul restrained the empty confidence of the Jews in their nation and their fathers, showing that true Israelites are not born of the flesh but of the Spirit, and that not all who are born of Abraham according to the flesh are at once counted among the people of God, unless they believe in Christ after the example of Abraham. Likewise, because in discussing the true use of the law he taught that justification must not be ascribed to it at all, as we saw in the preceding sermon, and because he said that the legal worship had been abrogated by the coming of Christ and the merit of his death. Yet, lest their accusation seem to rest on empty words, they also complain of Paul's deed, and a recent one at that, namely that he brought Gentiles into the temple and so defiled that most holy place. Yet this calumny was most absurd and at the same time most shameless, and yet it found belief among everyone, because they had seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city among Paul's companions. For they suspect that he too had been brought into the temple by Paul. Again, this passage warns us what charges the ministers of the truth are commonly burdened with: namely that they sin shamelessly against the chosen people of God, against his beloved spouse, the Church; that they impudently condemn the laws and traditions of the Church; and that they impiously overthrow both temples and the old worship. So we read that Christ was accused, and the enemies of the truth brought these same charges against Stephen. And some men even today throw these same things at us, men whom no regard for the Church of God, no authority of the divine law, and no care or zeal for true religion moves. Meanwhile it is the lot of the truth that calumny is usually levelled against no others more shamelessly and more effectively than against its ministers. For since they are hated by the world and in a sense condemned by the common prejudice of all, everyone readily admits and accepts whatever is alleged against them, and no one is ashamed of his own levity. But let us bear patiently what we know was borne not only by the prophets and apostles but by the Son of God himself.

units.la: Porrò non contenti comprehendisse hominem & falsis criminibus obruisse, simul apertam quoq; vim illi inferunt. Nam è templo protrahunt, verberibus indesinenter multant, imò eundem indignis modis trucidare conantur, prius tamen occlusis Templi foribus, nimirum quod de illius pollutione anxiè timerent. Quo exemplo docemur quousq; tandem impietas & Verbi Dei odium progrediatur. Licet enim diu occultum lateat, oblata tamen occasione erumpit, nec aliud quàm sanguinem ministrorum sitit, quo vno Veritatis hostes satiari & placari possunt. Exempla huius rei plura sunt passim, quàm vt longa demonstratione opus sit. In primis autem egregiam (si Dijs placet) istorum hominum sanctimoniam obseruat, qui pro focis & aris pugnare videri volunt. Nam de templo solicitine illud sanguine polluatur, confestim occludunt. Interim vero manus suas feq; totos innocenti sanguine polluere non verentur. Similia hic in euangelio Christus exprobrat, quando illos culicem colare, camelum vero deglutire dicit. Ita prætorium ingredi nolunt. Sacerdotes, ne in diem festum polluantur, qui interea innocentem Pilato tradunt, & illius sanguinem summa iniquitate simul & impor tunitate postulant. Quàm vero fucus iste Deo placuerit, ex eo patet, quod paucis post annis elapsis, sanguinarios hypocritas, vnà cum templo & vrbe infelici per Romanos excindi curauit.
units.tr: Moreover, not content with having seized the man and overwhelmed him with false charges, they also inflict open violence on him at the same time. They drag him out of the temple, beat him without ceasing, and even try to slaughter him by unworthy means, though first they shut the doors of the temple, obviously because they anxiously feared pollution from his blood. By this example we are taught how far impiety and hatred of God's Word will advance. For although it lies hidden for a long time, when an opportunity is offered it bursts out, and it thirsts for nothing but the blood of the ministers, by which alone the enemies of the truth can be satisfied and appeased. Examples of this are many and everywhere, more than need a long demonstration. Above all, they display (if the gods are pleased) an outstanding holiness, these men who want to seem to fight for hearths and altars. For they shut the temple at once, lest it be polluted by blood. Meanwhile they do not hesitate to pollute their own hands and themselves wholly with innocent blood. Christ rebukes similar conduct here in the Gospel, when he says they strain out a gnat but swallow a camel. So they are unwilling to enter the praetorium. The priests, lest they be defiled on the festival day, meanwhile hand the innocent man over to Pilate and demand his blood with the utmost iniquity and at the same time importunity. How much this pretence pleased God is clear from the fact that a few years later he saw to it that these bloody hypocrites were destroyed by the Romans, together with the temple and the unhappy city.

units.la: Cæterum non deest periclitanti apostolo dominus, qui cùm iam de illo prorsus actum esse videretur, liberatorem & vindicem, quem minimè sperauisset, excitat. Tribunus enim clamore vulgi & seditionis fama excitatus, mox cum parata militum manu aduolat, & Paulum ex furentis populi manibus eripit. Et hic quidem magistratus officio probè fungitur, quod nimium ofcitanter negligit, qui insontes audacissimorum hominum improbitate violenter opprimi patiuntur. Obseruabis autem Dei fidem & paternā curam, quā suis nunquam deest, licet illos aliquando negligere videatur. Nec illi hos liberare graue est, quādo per eos quoq; id facere potest, qui à fide & religione vera alieni sunt. Hic enim per Romanos milites Paulus asseritur, & Ieremiam olim per Nabuzardan, publicumpopuli Dei hostem, seruatum fuisse constat. Ierem. 39. & 40. Possent huius generis exempla multa referri, quorum omnium finis est, ne in Cruce & periculis desperemus, nec ad media illicita confugiamus, sed omni cura & fiducia animi in Deum collocata, illius manū expectemus. Sentit hanc in praesentie ficacissimam Paulus. Seditiosi enim, quos ab immanissimo scelere nec Dei timor, nec pudor reuocarit poterant, mox conspecto Tribuno & militibus manus abstinent, & Paulum percutere desinunt. Est hoc proprium impijs omnibus quod hominum magis metu quam Dei coercentur: & ideo magistratu opus est, qui illorum improbitati metam & fines statuat. Nos autem Dei potius timore perfusi, illi studia nostra omnia approbemus, qui non modo ex impiorum manibus suos eripere potest, sed eosdem ex mortis quoq; & inferni faucibus asserit per filium suum Iesum Christum, dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Yet the Lord is not lacking to the apostle in his peril. When it seemed altogether over for him, he raises up a deliverer and avenger whom Paul least expected. For the tribune, roused by the clamour of the crowd and the report of the sedition, soon flies in with a ready band of soldiers and snatches Paul from the hands of the raging people. And this man indeed discharges the duty of a magistrate well, which others too carelessly neglect: who allow the innocent to be violently oppressed by the wickedness of the most audacious men. You will observe God's faithfulness and fatherly care, which never fails his own, although he may sometimes seem to neglect them. Nor is it hard for him to free them, since he can do so even through those who are alien from the true faith and religion. For through the Roman soldiers Paul is defended, and it is well known that Jeremiah was once preserved through Nebuzaradan, the public enemy of the people of God. Jer. 39 and 40. Many examples of this kind could be related, and the aim of all of them is that we should not despair in the cross and in dangers, nor flee to unlawful means, but, with all our care and trust placed in God, await his hand. Paul feels this most effectively in the present case. For the seditious men, whom neither fear of God nor shame could restrain from such an outrageous crime, as soon as they see the tribune and soldiers, refrain their hands and cease to strike Paul. It is characteristic of all the impious that they are restrained more by fear of men than by fear of God; and therefore there is need of a magistrate who sets a limit and bounds to their wickedness. But let us, rather filled with fear of God, commit all our concerns to him, who can not only snatch his own from the hands of the impious, but also rescue those same people from the jaws of death and hell through his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLI.
units.tr: HOMILY 141.

units.la: Tunc accedens Tribunus apprehendit eum, & iussit alligari catenis duabus, & interrogauit quis nam esset, & quid fecisset. Alij autem aliud clamabant in turba. Et cùm non posset certum cognoscere prę tumultu, iussit eum duci in castra. Cùm autem venisset ad gradus, contigit vt portaretur à militibus, propter violentiam turbę. Sequebatur enim multitudo populi, clamans: Tolle eum. Et cùm coepisset induci in castra, Paulus dicit Tribuno: Licet ne mihi loqui ad te? Qui dixit: Graece nosti? Nonne tu ille es Aegyptius, qui ante hos dies tumultum concitasti, & induxisti in desertum quatuor millia virorum sicariorum? Dixit autem Paulus: Ego quidem homo sum Iudaeus, Tharsensis, non obscurae Ciliciū ciuitatis ciuis. Rogo autem te, permitte mihi loqui ad populum. Et cùm ille permisisset, Paulus stans in gradibus annuit manu ad plebem. Et magno silentio facto, allocutus est lingua Hebraea dicens:
units.tr: Then the tribune came up, seized him, and ordered him bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done. The crowd was shouting different things, and since he could not learn the truth because of the uproar, he ordered Paul taken into the barracks. When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because of the violence of the crowd. For the mass of people followed, shouting, "Away with him!" As they began to lead him into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune, "May I say something to you?" He replied, "Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian who some days ago stirred up a revolt and led four thousand assassins out into the wilderness?" Paul answered, "I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, let me speak to the people." When the tribune allowed it, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the crowd. When there was great silence, he addressed them in the Hebrew tongue, saying:

units.la: Quod Dauid, vir secundum cor Dei, dicit multas esse tribulationes iustorum, ex quibus omnibus tamē illos liberet dominus: hoc ipsum in praesenti historia verissime dictum esse apparet. Audiuimus enim Paulum a furentibus Iudaeorum multitudine captum, verberibus contusum, iam morti vicinum fuisse, cùm illum occidere statuissent, qui veteri odio Paulini nominis inflammati, nihil perinde vt illius sanguinem sitiebant. Sed ecce ex improuiso vindicem & assertorem excitat domi nus, & apostolum suum per eos liberat, qui & ipsi à fide & religione erant alienissimi. Quia verò de horum fine & visu in praecedenti Sermone diximus, in praesenti liberationis huius historia inspiciendā erit, quam per singulas circumstantias diligentissime Lucas describit.
units.tr: That David, a man after God's own heart, says there are many afflictions of the righteous, yet the Lord delivers them from all of them, is shown to be most truly said in the present story. For we have heard that Paul was seized by the raging crowd of Jews, beaten, and was already near death, when they had resolved to kill him. Inflamed with old hatred against the name of Paul, they thirsted for his blood above all else. But see, the Lord unexpectedly raises up an avenger and defender, and frees his apostle through men who were themselves most alien from the faith and religion. Since we spoke of the end and the outcome of these men in the previous sermon, we must now examine this story of deliverance, which Luke describes most carefully in each detail.

units.la: Primò quid Tribunus militum fecerit, commemorat. Is ante omnia Paulum furentium manibus ereptum, duabus catenis vinciri iussit: nec id temerè vel praecipiti ira superatus fecisse videtur, cùm tota actio moderati animi haud obscura argumenta habeat. Sed facit hoc partim, quòd hominem maleficum putaret, cum in illius caput omnes vnanimiter fauirent: partim verò quòd furentem turbam non alia ratione commodius sedari posse videret, quām si ipsem faceret, illum dignas meritis suis poenas breui exoluturum. Interim verò officij sui haudquaquam immemor, diligenter quis fit quidue fecerit, interrogat. Est enim hoc magistratus officium, ne quid temere aut praecipitanter agat. Nec enim aliquis excusationi locus superest, si iam iniuriam passus fit, qui illius authoritate defendi debebat. Ideò Moses Iudices tam paruum quàm magnum, adeoq; causarum circumstantias omnes audire & inquirere iubet, ne quid vel ignorantia vel caeco carnis affectu peccent. Inter im hoc loco liberationis modus probè obseruandus erit. Eripitur quidem praesenti vitae periculo, quod ab Iudaeis imminebat Paulus, idem verò catenis duabus instar facinorosi alicuius constringitur. Atque Atqui illum omnino liberare poterat Dominus. Id vero quia non facit, certè est, catenas has Paulo salutariores fuisse, & illius captiuitatem ad propagandum Christi regnum plus momenti habuisse. Estq; hic perpetuus Dei mos, qui beneficia sua temperare solet, maximè quando nobis adhuc capistro opus esse intelligit. Experimur hoc frequenter in morbis & reliquis tribulationibus, in quibus quicquid Dominus dederit, nos patienter ferre decet, quando & illius voluntas bona est, & nullis aduersis à diuinæ prouidentiæ cura & protectione separari possumus.
units.tr: First, he recounts what the tribune of the soldiers did. Before anything else, he ordered Paul, snatched from the hands of the rioters, to be bound with two chains. He does not seem to have done this rashly or carried away by hasty anger, since the whole action shows clear signs of a restrained mind. He did it partly because he thought the man was a criminal, since everyone was unanimously shouting against him, and partly because he saw that the raging crowd could not be calmed more suitably in any other way than by doing this himself, so that the man would shortly pay the punishment his deserts merited. Meanwhile, by no means forgetful of his office, he carefully asks who he is and what he has done. For this is the duty of a magistrate: not to act rashly or hastily. Nor is there any room for excuse if a man has already suffered an injury that it was the magistrate's duty to prevent by his authority. Therefore Moses orders judges to hear and inquire into every circumstance of a case, small and great alike, so that they do not sin through ignorance or the blind affection of the flesh. Meanwhile, in this place, the manner of the deliverance must be carefully observed. Paul is indeed rescued from the danger to his life that was hanging over him from the Jews, yet he is bound with two chains like some criminal. Yet the Lord could certainly have freed him altogether. That he did not do so means these chains were more beneficial to Paul, and his captivity had greater weight for spreading the kingdom of Christ. This is the constant custom of God, who is wont to temper his benefits, especially when he understands that we still need a bridle. We experience this often in sicknesses and other afflictions, in which we ought to bear patiently whatever the Lord has given, since both his will is good and we cannot be separated from the care and protection of divine providence by any adversities.

units.la: Quid vero interea populus agit? Primum confusis & incertis clamoribus miscet omnia, vt nihil certò cognosci aut intelligi possit: quod proprium esse seditionibus Cap. 19. dictum est. Deinde cum vinctum in castra abduci iussisset, vt illic causam cognosceret, impudenter omnes sequuntur, & ea violentia irruunt, vt milites illum gestare cogantur, ne quid à seditiosis mali patiatur. Tandem in hoc vno omnes consentiunt, quòd hominem è viuis tollendum esse clamant. In quibus vt viuam sedi tionis imaginem Lucas proponit, ita docet locus hic, nullos grauiores veritatis & piorum hostes esse, quàm qui pietatis zelum suis conatibus prætexunt. Hîc enim maiorem multò cùm æquitatem tum humanitatem in barbaris militibus, quàm in Iudæis, qui pro templo & religione pugnare videri vo lebant, cernere licet. Hi indicta causa occidere volunt, in cuius causam Tribunus diligenter inquirit. Hi clamoribus incertis & horrendis omnia turbant, cum Tribunus animo sedato & tranquillo agat omnia. Hi conculcant impudenter, quem manibus & humeris milites gestare dignantur.
units.tr: But what did the people do meanwhile? First, with confused and uncertain shouts they threw everything into confusion, so that nothing could be known or understood clearly. This is said to be the mark of rebellions (chap. 19). Then, when the tribune had ordered him led away in chains to the barracks, so that he could examine the case there, they follow shamelessly, and they rush on with such violence that the soldiers are forced to carry him, lest he suffer any harm from the seditious. Finally, they all agree on this one thing, that they shout that the man must be taken from the living. In these events, Luke sets before us a living image of sedition, and this passage teaches that there are no more serious enemies of truth and of the godly than those who cover their zeal for piety with their own efforts. Here one may see far greater fairness and humanity in the barbarous soldiers than in the Jews, who wanted to seem to be fighting for the temple and religion. These want to kill him without a hearing, and the tribune inquires carefully into the cause. These throw everything into turmoil with uncertain and horrible shouts, while the tribune acts with a calm and tranquil mind. These trample shamelessly on the man whom the soldiers deign to carry on their hands and shoulders.

units.la: Quid multùs? nec veritatem inquiri, nec causam cognosci, sed hominem illico occidi volunt, vt innocentis sanguinis conspectu nefarios oculos faciant. Simile exemplum in Christi passione contigisse legimus. Nam & illic maior in Pilato & Herode æquitas, quàm in Sacerdotibus & Scribis elucet. Et in Crucem suspensum Sacerdotes impiè deludunt, cui barbari milites propter visa signa innocentiæ testimonium deferunt. Hodie non desunt exempla, quando multos ob Veritatis confessionem à Turcis æquius & humanius tractari constat, quàm à Monachis & Episcopis, qui pietatis zelo toti ardere videri volunt. Sed hæc diaboli, sub pietatis velo sæuissimè grassantis, viua imago est. Admonemur autem exemplis istis, minimè excusari eos, qui huius zeli prætextu Christi fidelibus iniuriam faciunt. Hoc enim fore, Christus olim prædixit. Et Paulum zelo patriæ legis flagrauisse constat, quando ecclesiam persequebatur. Sed idem eam ob causam se primum & maximum inter peccatores esse fatetur. 1. Timot. 1. Nec enim nostro nos zelo ferri vult Deus, sed scientiam requirit, vt verbi sui cognitione illustrati, quod ille iubet & præcipit, faciamus. Vide Num. 15. cap.
units.tr: In short, they do not want the truth investigated or the cause known, but want the man killed at once, so that they may feast their wicked eyes on the sight of innocent blood. We read that a similar example happened at Christ's passion. For there too greater fairness shines forth in Pilate and Herod than in the priests and scribes. And the priests impiously mock him hanging on the cross, while the barbarous soldiers, because of the signs they saw, bear witness to his innocence. Today there are no lack of examples, since it is well known that many for the confession of the truth are treated more justly and humanely by the Turks than by monks and bishops, who want to seem to burn with zeal for piety. But these things are a living image of the devil, who rages most cruelly under the veil of piety. We are warned by these examples that those are by no means excused who do injury to Christ's faithful under the pretext of this zeal. For Christ foretold long ago that this would happen. And it is established that Paul too blazed with zeal for the law of his fathers when he persecuted the Church. Yet for this very reason he confesses that he is the first and greatest of sinners (1 Tim. 1). For God does not want us to be carried along by our own zeal, but requires knowledge, so that, enlightened by the knowledge of his word, we may do what he commands and prescribes. See Num. 15.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reu ersi, quod is tot vndiq; periculis circumuentus fecerit videamus. Vnum vero de hoc Lucas commemorat, ex quo tum fidei ipsius inuistam constantiam, tum animi magnitudinem æstimare licet. Nam in tanto populi furore & confusis clamoribus excusationem meditatur: partim quidem quòd summo suæ gentis studio teneretur, & illam lucrifacere cuperet: partim verò, quòd Christi causam, cuius minister erat, suspicione liberatam velleret. Estq; Pauli exemplum omnibus ministris imitandum, vt in priuatis periculis cùm aliorum hominum salutem, tum Christi gloriam vnicè quærant. Sed præstat singulas huius actionis partes inspicere. Primò non temere ad dicendum prorumpit, quod seditiosorum est, sed honorificè & modestè à Tribuno dicendi copiam petit. Nec illum quia miles erat contemnit: sed potius, quia legitimum imperium & magistratum gerebat, veneratur. Quo exemplo tum Pontifices tum Anabaptistæ arguuntur, quorum hi quidem magistratus omnes simpliciter damnant, illi verò eosdem pedum osculis subijciunt, imò improbè conculcant. Porrò Tribunus, quàmuis latronem arbitretur, amicè respondet, & num Ægyptius ille fit rogat, qui paucis antequam hæc gererentur diebus, ad res nouas populum excitarat, & cum dispersis sui exercitus reliquis hinc inde latrocinia exercebat. Ita enim fieri oportebat, vt qui verũ Messiam amplecti noluerant, ab impostoribus miserè deluderentur, vt alibi monuimus. Docet autem Tribuni exemplum, amicè cum captiuis agendum esse.
