Quia enim vinculorum finis est, vt malefici coerceantur, ne nocere possint, vtq; alijs exemplo sint, inhumanum simul & iniquum est, vltra hos fines in eum sæuire, cuius nos potius propter communem humanitatis sensum misereri oportebat. Vides rursum in Tribuni quæstione quàm horrendis criminibus seruos suos grauari & suspectos fieri Deus patiatur, qui tamen eorundem memoriam afferere & seruare consueuit. Psalm. 34. Quare non est, vt illa nos moueant, sed Paulum imitemur, qui indigna hac quæstione nihil cômotus, amicè & modestè. quis sit, indicat, eaq; modestia (ita negotium omne moderante Deo) dicendi copiam à Tribuno impetrat. Quòd si verò cum Tribuno hoc nostri seculi Monachos & haereticae prauitatis Inquisitores conferas, qui Martyrum Christi linguas erui curant, ne dum ducuntur, populo loqui possint, facile patebit quanto maior sit illorum cùm impietas tum truculentia. Caeterum Paulus impetrata à Tribuno dicendi copia, populo mox manu annuens, ab illo quoq; silentium impetrat, & ex tempore orationem accuratam, & non leue animi praesentis indicium, instituit. Quo loco Dei tum potentia tum Veritas nobis obseruanda venit. Illa enim in eo elucet, quòd furentis populi animos momento cicurare potuit, ut illi aures praebeant, quem modò ad mortem deposcebant. Huius autem argumentum haud vulgare est, quòd Paulo clamoribus seditiosorum obturbato & verberibus misere contuso animum praesentem & verba suggerit, quibus causam suam coram saeuissimis hostibus intrepidè simul & artificiose agat. Ita enim impletur, quod Christus dixerat: In illa hora dabitur vobis, quod loquamini, &c. Matth. 10. Marc. 13. Confer cum Paulo hoc catenato Romanae eloquentiae parentem Cicero nem, & intelliges quantis interuallis Christi spiritus omnem humani ingenij industriam & longum dicendi vsum superet. Is enim cum olim lectica in forum delatus, Milonis causam agere deberet, vi fis Pompei armis toto foro coruscantibus, faucibus metu interclusis vix singultire potuit. At Paulus catenis vinctus, & recentium adhuc verberum dolorem sentiens, inter militum arma, astante simul Tribuno, proprij capitis causam constanti ore & animo agit, nimirum Christi spiritu animatus, quem ille suis paracletum & aduocatum promiserat. Horum meditatione ipsi quoq; animemur, ut intrepidè coram mundo hoc salutis & fidei causam agamus, nec enim nos quoq; suo spiritu & fauore destituet is, cui credidimus, qui est Dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But returning to Paul, let us see what he did, though surrounded on every side by so many dangers. Luke mentions one thing about this, from which we may judge both the unconquered constancy of his faith and the greatness of his spirit. For amid such great fury of the people and confused shouts, he plans his defence: partly because he was held by the highest zeal for his nation and wished to win it over, and partly because he wanted the cause of Christ, whose minister he was, freed from suspicion. Paul's example is to be imitated by all ministers, so that in private dangers they seek both the salvation of other men and the glory of Christ alone. But it is better to examine the individual parts of this action. First, he does not rush rashly into speaking, which is the mark of seditious men, but honourably and modestly asks the tribune for permission to speak. He does not despise him because he was a soldier, but rather reveres him because he held lawful authority and magistracy. By this example both the Papists and the Anabaptists are rebuked: the latter simply condemn all magistrates, while the former subject them to kissing of their feet, and even shamefully trample on them. Furthermore, the tribune, although he thinks him a robber, answers kindly, and asks whether he is that Egyptian who a few days before these events stirred the people to revolution and carried on robberies here and there with the scattered remnants of his army. For it had to happen that those who had refused to embrace the true Messiah were wretchedly deluded by impostors, as we have noted elsewhere. The tribune's example teaches, moreover, that captives must be treated kindly. For since the purpose of chains is that criminals be restrained, so that they cannot harm and so that they may serve as examples to others, it is both inhumane and unjust to rage against a man beyond these limits; rather, we ought to pity him out of our common human feeling. You see again, in the tribune's question, with what dreadful accusations God allows his servants to be burdened and made suspect, though he is accustomed to vindicate and preserve their good name (Ps. 34). Therefore these things ought not to move us; rather, let us imitate Paul, who, unmoved by this unworthy question, indicates kindly and modestly who he is, and by this modesty (God so guiding the whole affair) obtains from the tribune permission to speak. But if you compare with this tribune the monks of our age and the inquisitors of heretical depravity, who take care to tear out the tongues of Christ's martyrs, so that they cannot speak to the people even while being led away, it will be easily evident how much greater is their impiety and their savagery. Moreover, Paul, having obtained from the tribune permission to speak, soon motions with his hand to the people, and obtains silence from them too, and begins an accurate speech on the spur of the moment, a no small sign of a present mind. Here we must observe God's power and truth. For his power shines forth in this, that he was able in a moment to tame the minds of a raging people, so that they lend their ears to the man whom only a moment before they demanded for death. And this is no small proof of it: though Paul was disturbed by the shouts of the seditious and cruelly bruised by the blows, God supplies him with a present mind and words, by which he pleads his cause boldly and skilfully before the most savage enemies. For thus what Christ had said was fulfilled: "In that hour it will be given you what to say," etc. (Matt. 10; Mark 13). Compare with this chained Paul Cicero, the father of Roman eloquence, and you will understand by what great intervals Christ's Spirit surpasses all human ingenuity and long practice in speaking. For when Cicero, once carried to the forum in a litter, was to plead the cause of Milo, with Pompey's armed men glittering throughout the forum, his throat, shut in by fear, could scarcely gasp. But Paul, bound with chains and feeling the pain of fresh blows, pleads the cause of his own life with a steady voice and mind, amid the weapons of soldiers, with the tribune standing by, and this surely by the Spirit of Christ, who had promised him as his Paraclete and advocate. Let us be encouraged by meditating on these things, so that we too may plead the cause of salvation and faith fearlessly before this world. For he in whom we have believed, who is our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, will not forsake us either, with his Spirit and favour. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXII. HOMILIA CXLII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 22. HOMILY 142.

units.la: Viri fratres & patres, audite meam, qua nunc apud vos vtor excusatione. Cum autem audissent, quòd Hebraea lingua ipsis loqueretur, magis praestiterunt silentium. Et dicit: Ego quidem sum vir Iudaeus, natus in Tharso Ciliciae, educatus autem in hac vrbe ad pedes Gamalielis, institutus accurate in Lege patria, studiosus Dei, sicut & vos omnes estis hodie: qui hanc viam persecutus sum vsq; ad mortem, alligàs ac tradens in carceres tam viros quam mulieres: sicut & Princeps sacerdotum mihi testis est, & totus Seniorum ordo. A quibus etiam acceptis ad fratres epistolis Damascum pergebam, adducturus & illos, qui illic essent, vinctos Hierosolymam, vt punirentur.
units.tr: Brothers and fathers, hear my defence, which I now make before you. And when they heard that he was speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they kept all the more silent. And he said: I am indeed a Jewish man, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, carefully instructed in the law of our fathers, zealous for God, as all of you are today; I persecuted this way even to death, binding and delivering to prisons both men and women. As the high priest also bears me witness, and the whole order of the elders. From them I received letters to the brothers and was travelling to Damascus, intending to bring back to Jerusalem, bound, those who were there, so that they might be punished.

units.la: Vamuis Saluator noster, Iesus Christus, discipulos suos in ferendis conuitiis & calumnijs patientes esse velit, hoc ipsum tamen non obstat, quò minus suam innocentiam publicè simul & constanter afferant. Imò hoc illos facere non raro necessitas iubet, ne propter ipsum Christus tum fides Christiana male audiant. Prudenter ergo hoc in praesenti actione Paulus obseruat. A Iudaeis enim hunc, vt publicum populi Dei, Legis diuinae & templi hostem accusatum fuisse audiuimus. Accesserit his sinistra Tribuni suspicio, qui eundem Aegyptium & sicariorum duce esse putabat. Quae omnia cum non tam Paulo quàm Christianae religioni & vniuersae causae Veritatis fraudi esse possent, non secures negligit, nec trunci instar tacet, sed in hoc diligentissimus est, vt se purgandi copiam à Tribuno impetret: qua impetrata, nihil eorum intermittit, quae causam ipsius iuuare poterant. Diligenti enim & longa narratione rerum abs se gestarum seriem contexit, vt omnium illarum ratio toti populo pateat, ne quid vel turpi leuitate, vel impia audacia fecisse vi deatur. Proderit autem, eximium Christi apostolum è vinculis concionantem diligenter audire, & singulas orationis ipsius partes inspicere.
units.tr: Although our Saviour Jesus Christ wants his disciples to be patient in bearing reproaches and slanders, this does not prevent them from openly and steadily affirming their innocence. Indeed, necessity often requires them to do so, lest Christ himself, and the Christian faith for his sake, be ill spoken of. Paul therefore observes this prudently in the present action. For we have heard that the Jews accused him of being a public enemy of the people of God, of the divine Law and of the temple. To these charges was added the Tribune's unfavourable suspicion, since he thought Paul was that Egyptian and leader of the assassins. Since all these things could bring discredit not so much on Paul as on the Christian religion and the whole cause of the truth, he neither neglects them carelessly nor keeps silent like a stump, but is most diligent in obtaining from the Tribune the opportunity to clear himself. Having obtained it, he omits nothing that could help his cause. For in a careful and lengthy narrative he sets out the sequence of what he had done, so that the reason for all of it lies open to the whole people, and he may not seem to have acted through shameful levity or impious audacity. It will be profitable, however, to listen carefully to this outstanding apostle of Christ preaching from his chains, and to examine each part of his speech.

units.la: Principio Exordium & Propositionem paucis simul comprehendit. Nam fratres & patres vo cat, quod benevolentiae conciliandae seruiebat. Quo etiam facit, quod lingua Hebraea vtitur, qua il- los cumprimis delectari nouerat. Mox vero excusationem praemittit, vt se innocentem esse intel- ligant. ES T autem diligenti obseruatione digna modestia, qua apertos hostes & tot modis in se iniurios, fratres & patres appellare dignatur. Nec enim adulandi causa, aut periculi metu su- peratus id facit, sed partim quod se ex populi numero esse agnoscit, partim vero quod spes erat, in tanta multitudine saltem aliquos bonos inueniri, aut per verbi doctrinam conuerti & lucrifieri posse. Arguuntur itaque Pauli exemplo, qui legitimos & receptos honorum titulos damnant, quos alibi idem apostolus obseruare praecipit, cum iubet vt nos mutuo honore praeueniamus. Quamus non probemus eos, qui in his inepta adulatione modum omnem excedunt, dum non tam aliorum bono- ri & famae quam suis commodis consulere studeant. Interim officij admonemur, ne propter paucos, qui in nos iniurij sunt, totam aliquam gentem damnemus. Qua enim atrociores iniuria excogitari possunt, quam quas a Iudaeis Paulus sustinuit? Memoria repete qua hoc libro a Luca expo- ni audiuisti, qui tamen singula non commemorauit, ijs nimirum contentus, sine quibus historiae se- ries constare non poterat. Illos tamen amat Paulus, & honorifice compellat. Eosdem saluos cupit, & illorum salutem animae propriae iactura redemptam vellet. Imo recenti adhuc verberum dolo- re excruciatus & vinctus fratres patresq; suos agnoscit. Examinent sese ad huius exempli regu- lam, qui praecipiti ira excaecati, ob leuiculam iniuriam, a vilissimo homuncione illatam, totas natio- nes conuitijs obruunt & diris devouent, quum Christiano homini ne contra hostem quidem vindi- kam persequi fas sit. Quae ergo vaesania est, vnius hominis improbitatem toti nationi aut genti ac- ceptam ferre?
units.tr: First, he briefly comprehends the exordium and the proposition together. For he calls them brothers and fathers, which served to win their goodwill. He also does this by using the Hebrew language, which he knew they especially delighted in. Soon, however, he prefaces an apology, so that they may understand he is innocent. There is a modesty worthy of careful observation, by which he deigns to call brothers and fathers those who were open enemies and had wronged him in so many ways. For he does this not for the sake of flattery, nor overcome by fear of danger, but partly because he acknowledges that he is one of the people, and partly because he hoped that among so great a multitude at least some good men could be found, or could be converted and won over through the teaching of the Word. They are therefore reproved by Paul's example, who condemn the legitimate and customary titles of honour, which the same apostle elsewhere commands us to observe when he bids us go before one another in honour. Yet we do not approve of those who go beyond every measure in such foolish flattery, since they strive to serve their own advantage rather than the good name and reputation of others. Meanwhile we are reminded of our duty not to condemn a whole nation because of a few who have wronged us. For what more atrocious injuries can be imagined than those Paul suffered from the Jews? Recall from this book, which you have heard Luke expound, what he endured; yet Luke did not record each thing, being content with those without which the sequence of the history could not stand. Still, Paul loves them and addresses them honourably. He desires their salvation, and would have wished it bought even at the cost of his own soul. Indeed, though still tormented by the recent pain of the blows and bound, he acknowledges them as his brothers and fathers. Let those examine themselves by the rule of this example who, blinded by headlong anger, overwhelm whole nations with insults and curse them with dire imprecations because of a slight wrong inflicted by some most worthless little man, whereas it is not even lawful for a Christian to pursue vengeance against an enemy. What madness, then, is it to lay the wickedness of one man at the door of a whole nation or people?

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reuertamur, qui breui hoc Exordio praemisso, Narrationem rerum suarum o- mnium instituit: non quidem vt gloriosulus suas virtutes iactet, sed quod illud res ipsa postulaaret. Primo enim a natalibus suis exorsus, Tribunum sinistra suspicione liberat, qui ipsum licariorum du- cem Aegyptium esse suspicabatur. Deinde Iudaeis respondet, qui partim religionis aui ta mutatio- nem indigne ferebant, partim succensebant quod euangelium inter gentes praedicaret. Summa vero sive scopus totius narrationis est, se nihil priuato consilio aut arbitrio, sed omnia ex Dei iussu & vocatione fecisse. Caeterum ita narrando progreditur, vt omnibus sinistris suspicionibus occurrat, ne vel inscitia & ignorantia, vel prophano omnis religionis contemptu, vel turpi leuitate ad Christi fi- dem & apostolatum transfuisse videatur. Et haec quidem singula ordine videamus.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, after this brief exordium, sets out the full narrative of his affairs. He does this not so that he might boast of his virtues in a vainglorious way, but because the matter itself demanded it. For, beginning first from his birth, he frees the Tribune from the unfavourable suspicion which had taken him to be that Egyptian leader of the assassins. Then he answers the Jews, who were partly indignant at the change of their ancestral religion, and partly angry that he preached the gospel among the Gentiles. The sum or aim of the whole narrative, however, is that he did nothing by private counsel or judgement, but did everything by God's command and calling. Moreover, he proceeds in his narrative in such a way as to meet every unfavourable suspicion, lest he seem to have passed over to the faith and apostleship of Christ through ignorance and lack of knowledge, or through contempt for all religion, or through shameful levity. Let us now look at each of these points in order.

units.la: Primo sunt, quos inscitia & ruditas in religione leues reddit, dum rerum ignari quouis doctri- ne vento se agitari patiuntur. Ne quis ergo illum ex horum numero putaret, a prima institutione orditur. Educatus sum (inquit) in hac vrbe ad pedes Gamalielis, institutus accurate in lege patria. Nontemere autem tum vrbis Hierosolymorum, tum praeceptoris sui meminit: quia in illa schola erat totius gentis celeberrima, huius autem praecipua erat inter doctores siue legisperitos authoritas, vt supra Cap. 5. audiuimus. Fieri ergo non poterat, vt religionis & scripturae sacra rudis & ignarus esset, qui a pueris in illa vrbe, inter media sacra educatus, & a tanto viro institutus fuerat. Porro omnium nostrum institutioni pulchre seruit Pauli exemplum, qui religionis & fidei causam actu- rus, primo omnium inscitiae & ruditatis crimen amolitur. Docet enim neminem in religione rudem & ignorantem esse debere, nec eorum sententiam probari, qui simpliciter credendum esse docent, nec permittunt, vt in religionis causa diligentius examen & iudicium maturum exhibeas. Vult enim nos a tenera institui Deus, vt videre est. Exod. 13. Deuter. 6. Psalm. 78. Nec alia de causa magis laudatur Abraham, quam quod in posteritate sua religiose instituenda diligentissimus fuit. Gen. 18. Habent ergo quod hoc loco obseruent parentes, qui nisi teneris puerorum animis religionem instilla- uerint, eosdem vbi cum aetate induruerunt, nunquam tractabiles habebunt. Quod enim in plantis, equis, canibus & aliis brutis experimur, hoc ipsum in puerorum educatione fieri consueuit. Sed o no- stram socordiam & impietatem, qui canes quidem & equos magno labore instituimus, liberos vero indomitos & effrenes negligimus, &c. ES T praeterea non paruum modestiae simul & pietatis argu- mentum, quod praeceptoris sui, Gamalielis, honorificam mentionem facit, quem tamen in multis er- rauisse nouerat, & ex cuius traditione praepostrum legis zelum hauserat. Gratiam tamen se illi debere agnoscit, cuius labore saltem bonas literas didicerat. Quanto maiorem ergo illis praeceptoribus gratiam debemus, qui cum bonis literis pietatem quoq; & veram salutis rationem tradunt? Refer huc Dei praeceptum, quod de parentibus honorandis in Decalogo habetur.
units.tr: First, there are those whom ignorance and rawness make light in religion, since, ignorant of things, they allow themselves to be tossed about by any wind of doctrine. Lest anyone therefore think him one of their number, he begins from his early upbringing. "I was brought up," he says, "in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, carefully instructed in the law of our fathers." Nor without reason does he mention both the city of Jerusalem and his teacher, because that school was the most celebrated in the whole nation, and the authority of this man was outstanding among the teachers, or legal experts, as we heard above in chapter 5. It could not therefore be that he was rough and ignorant of sacred religion and Scripture, having been brought up from boyhood in that city amid its holy things, and instructed by so great a man. Moreover, Paul's example serves the instruction of us all admirably: about to plead the cause of religion and faith, he first of all removes the charge of ignorance and rawness. For he teaches that no one ought to be rude and ignorant in religion, nor does he approve the view of those who teach that one must simply believe, and do not allow that a more careful examination and mature judgement be applied in the cause of religion. For God wills that we be trained from tender years, as can be seen at Exod. 13, Deut. 6, Ps. 78. Nor is Abraham praised for any other reason than that he was most diligent in religiously instructing his posterity. Gen. 18. Parents therefore have something to observe here: unless they instil religion into the tender minds of their children, they will never have them tractable once they have hardened with age. For what we experience in plants, horses, dogs and other brute beasts is customarily done also in the education of children. But O our sloth and impiety, who train dogs and horses with great labour, yet neglect our children, who are untamed and unbridled, etc. Moreover, it is no small evidence of modesty and piety at once that he makes honourable mention of his teacher Gamaliel, whom he knew had erred in many things, and from whose tradition he had drawn a perverse zeal for the law. Nevertheless, he acknowledges that he owes thanks to him, through whose labour at least he had learned good letters. How much greater thanks, then, do we owe to those teachers who pass on with good letters also piety and the true way of salvation? Refer here the command of God concerning the honouring of parents, which is found in the Decalogue.

units.la: Sed vt in Pauli narratione pergamus, sunt rursum alij, qui prophano contemptu ad alienas religiones transeunt, dum in quauis homines salvari posse sibi persuasum habet. Hi dum omnes religiones probare videntur, religionem omnem simpliciter euertunt, & Deum quendam stultè ambitiosum fingunt, quem varia & diuersa historionum genera delectent. Ne quis ergo Paulum istis adnumeret, si non absq; zelo veteri Iudaeorum religioni operam dedisse dicit. Nam studiosus Dei (inquit) fui, sicut & omnes vos. Alibi se supra omnes suos coaetaneos profecisse scribit. Quo exemplo, in religione zelum requiri docemur. Licet enim zelo suo Paulus grauissimè peccarit, non tamen simpliciter illæ damnari meretur. Nam totos nos sibi Deus vendicat, dum toto corde, tota anima & cunctis viribus à nobis amari, timeri & coli vult. Minimè ergo probari debent, qui stultum & ineptum arbitrantur, si quis cum quoquam in religionis causa contendat. Quasi verò in vtrunq; latus claudicare, imò quotidie religiones moneta instar, permutare liceat. Sed sunt isti homines ex eorum numero, quos ob teporem ignauum Deus se euomiturum minatur. Apoc. 3.
units.tr: But to press on with Paul's narrative: there are again others who, out of profane contempt, pass over to alien religions, persuaded that people can be saved in any religion whatever. While these seem to approve of all religions, they in fact simply overturn every religion, and they imagine a certain God who is foolishly ambitious, delighted by all sorts of varied and diverse performances. Let no one therefore count Paul among these, if I say that he did not devote himself to the religion of the Jews without a zeal of the old kind. For he says: "I was zealous for God, as all of you are." Elsewhere he writes that he had advanced beyond all his contemporaries. From this example we are taught that zeal is required in religion. For although Paul sinned very gravely through his zeal, yet that zeal does not deserve to be condemned outright. God claims us entirely for himself, since he wills to be loved, feared and worshipped by us with the whole heart, the whole soul and all our strength. Those therefore deserve no approval at all who think it foolish and silly if someone contends with anyone over a matter of religion, as though it were permissible to limp on both sides, or to exchange religions day by day like coins. But such men belong to the number of those whom God threatens to spit out for their lazy lukewarmness. Rev. 3.

units.la: Tertiò alij inueniuntur, qui cum natura ad res nouas proclives sint, leuissima quaq; priuati commodi spe & occasione impulsi, quidui sibi persuaderi patiuntur, aut etiam nemine suadente recipiunt. Quod vt turpissimum hominum genus est, ita ab hoc quoq; se alienissimum esse Paulus diligenter probat, cum ait: Hanc viam persecutus sum vsq; ad mortem, alligans ac tradens in carceres tam viros quàm mulieres. Nec contentus eos vinxisse, qui in vrbe hac Christo nomen dederant, publicarum literarum authoritate instructus, Damascum vsq; excurri, vt illic quoq; credentibus negotium facerem. Et huius quidem facti testes sistit ipsum Pontificem & Seniores, ne quis dubitaret. Hinc docere vult, tantum zeli feruorem, non nisi diuina virtute subitò mutari potuisse, adeoq; se diuinitus vocatum, imò coaetum ad Christi fidem transfuisse, quemadmodum in sequentibus clarius docebit. Admonet autem Pauli exemplum, in religione cumprimis cauendum esse, ne carnis affectus in consilium admittendo nostra quaeramus. Qui enim id faciunt, quouis vento circunferuntur, & licet veram religionem aliquando apprehendant, mox tamen ab ea quoq; resiliunt, vt primum illam suis affectibus minus respondere senserint. Abiecto igitur caeca carnis & mundi studio, Dei vocem audiamus, quam secuti Christum amplectamur, vt huic superaedificati aduersus omnes procellas immoti stemus, ac in illo adolescamus, cum eodem olim in coelis regnaturi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Thirdly, there are others who, since by nature they are inclined to novelties, and are moved by the slightest hope and occasion of private advantage, allow themselves to be persuaded of anything whatever, or even accept it when no one is persuading them. As this is the most shameful kind of people, so Paul carefully proves that he was most remote from it, when he says: "I persecuted this way even to death, binding and delivering into prisons both men and women." Not content to have bound those who in this city had given their names to Christ, armed with the authority of public letters, he hurried all the way to Damascus, so that he might do the same business there with those who believed. He even brings forward the High Priest and the elders as witnesses of this deed, lest anyone should doubt it. Here he wishes to teach that such a fervour of zeal could not have been changed suddenly except by divine power, and that he had been called by God, indeed compelled, to pass over to the faith of Christ, as he will show more clearly in what follows. The example of Paul, however, warns that in religion above all we must take care not to seek our own ends, admitting the desires of the flesh into our counsel. For those who do this are carried about by every wind, and although they sometimes grasp the true religion, they soon fall away from it as soon as they perceive that it does not answer to their passions. Therefore, casting aside the blind pursuit of the flesh and the world, let us hear the voice of God, and following it let us embrace Christ, so that, built upon him, we may stand immovable against all storms, and grow up in him, to reign with him one day in heaven: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLIII.

units.la: Accidit autem mihi iter facienti, & appropinquanti Damasco, citciter meridiem, vt subitò de coelo circumfulgurauerit me lux multa, cecidiq; in terram, & audiui vocem dicentem mihi: Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris? Ego verò respondi: Quis es Domine? Dixitq; ad me: Ego sum Iesus ille Nazarenus, quem tu persequeris. Et qui mecum erant, lumen quidem viderunt, & exterriti sunt: vocem autem non audierunt eius, qui mecum loquebatur. Tunc dixi: Quid faciā Domine? Dominus autem dixit mihi: Surge & vade Damascum, & illic tibi dicetur de omnibus, quae ordinata sunt tibi vt facias. Et cum non viderem praegloria luminis illius, per manum deductus à comitibus, qui erant mecum, veni Damascum.
units.tr: "As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon, suddenly a great light from heaven shone around me. I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' And I answered, 'Who are you, Lord?' He said to me, 'I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.' Those who were with me saw the light but did not hear the voice of him who spoke to me. Then I said, 'What shall I do, Lord?' The Lord said to me, 'Get up and go to Damascus, and there you will be told about everything that has been appointed for you to do.' Since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by my companions and came to Damascus."

units.la: Dluus Paulus, coram Iudaeis è vinculis verba faciens, diligentem rerum suarum narrationem contexit, non quidem vt inani ambitione suarum virtutum praeconem agat, sed vt sinistris suis spicionibus occurrat, notumq; fiat omnibus, se ex Dei iussu & vocatione, non temere aut priuato consilio ad Christi fidem transfuisse, & eandem praedicauisse gentibus. Et huc quidem cumprimis referri debent, quae in besternis de sua educatione, de suo item in legis disciplina profectu, de Iudaicis religionis zelo, & ecclesiæ Christi persecutione dixit. Ex illis enim cuius facile fuit cõijcere tantum tamq; feruentem Iudaismi propugnatorem & Christianismi hostem, non nisi diuina virtute tam subito mutari potuisse. Id vero in præsenti euidentius docet, dum suæ Conuersionis historiam ordine cũ omnibus circunstantijs commemorat. Quæ cum alibi copiosius tractata sit, modò ea duntaxat attingemus, quæ ad præsentis causæ statum faciunt, vnà cum paucis alijs, quorum repetitio minimè super vacanea esse videtur, & in quorum consyderatione nos frequentius versari decet.
units.tr: Blessed Paul, speaking from his chains before the Jews, gave a careful account of his affairs. He did not do this to boast of his own virtues out of empty ambition, but to meet the suspicions against him and to make known to all that he had gone over to faith in Christ, and preached that same faith to the Gentiles, by God's command and calling, and not rashly or on his own private decision. Above all, what he said yesterday about his upbringing, his progress in the discipline of the law, his zeal for Jewish religion, and his persecution of the Church of Christ should be referred to here. From those things it was easy to infer that such a great and fervent champion of Judaism and enemy of Christianity could not have been changed so suddenly except by divine power. He teaches this more clearly now, as he recounts the history of his conversion in order, with all its circumstances. Since this has been treated more fully elsewhere, we shall touch only on those points that bear on the present case, together with a few others whose repetition does not seem superfluous and on which we ought to dwell more often.

units.la: Et primò quidem obseruandum venit, quòd Paulus suum à Iudaismo ad Christi fidem transitũ hoc vno argumento excusat, quòd huius authorem & suasorem habuerit Deum. Vnde colligimus, minimè reprehendi debere eos, qui Deo vocante veteres superstitiones deserunt, & veram religionem amplectuntur, quando constat, Deum non nisi quod rectum & salutare esse iubere, nos̄ illi simpliciter debere obedientiam. Nisi enim hoc statuamus, leuitatis & inconstantiæ culpa nec Paulum nec apostolos liberare poterimus, qui omnes Dei filium secuti, religione in qua nati & enutriti fuerant, mutauerunt. Docent hæc, quàm iniquè ab aduersarijs nostris accusemur ob desertam à nobis Romanam ecclesiam, cum idem illis respondere possimus, quod in præsenti Paulus Iudæus respondit: Nihil nimirum à nobis priuato consilio factitatum esse, sed nos ex Christi iussu & mandato religionem mutauisse. Licet enim non eodem modo & ratione nobiscum Christus egerit, qua olim Paulum aggressus est, eiusdem tamen vocem in euangelio sonantem, audiuimus & secuti sumus. Clamat ille: Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego requiem vobis præstabo. Matth. 11. Si quis sitit veniat ad me & bibat, &c. Iohan. 7. Ego sum lux mundi. Qui me sequitur, non ambulat in tenebris. Iohan. 8. Ego sum ostium. Per me si quis introierit, seruabitur, & ingredietur & egredietur, & pascua inueniet. Qui non intrat per ostium, sed ascendit aliunde, ille fur est & latro. Iohan. 10. Item, Ego sum via, lux & veritas. Nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me, Iohan. 14. Accedunt his apostolorum voces, qui Christi spiritu extimulati, in hoc vno & solo salutem haberi & inueniri, vno ore clamant. Quis ergo cordatus nobis vitio vertat, quòd viuam Christi vocem secuti, Romanam sedem deseruimus, quæ nobis extra hunc infinitas salutis rationes monstrabat, imò suis traditionibus salutis omnino incertos reddebat? Quanto magis reprehendi debent, qui Christum expansis brachijs & clara voce ad se inuitantem improbè aspernantur, ingratis illis & pertinacibus similes, de quibus apud Isaiam conqueritur? Quòd si quis excusationem nostram non admiserit, nec is abunde probat, se eodem cum impijs Iudæis spiritu agitari, qui & ipsi Paulum hac ipsa ratione sese excusantem audire dedignati sunt, &c.
units.tr: And first we must observe that Paul excuses his passage from Judaism to faith in Christ on this one ground: that God was the author and persuader of it. From this we gather that those who abandon old superstitions at God's calling and embrace the true religion are not to be blamed at all, since it is clear that God commands only what is right and salutary, and we owe him simple obedience. For unless we hold this, we cannot free Paul or the apostles from the charge of levity and inconstancy, since all of them followed the Son of God and changed the religion in which they had been born and brought up. These things show how unjustly our opponents accuse us for having deserted the Roman Church, since we can give them the same answer that Paul the Jew gives here: that we did nothing on our own private counsel, but changed our religion by Christ's command and mandate. For although Christ has not dealt with us in the same way and manner as he once dealt with Paul, we have heard his voice sounding in the gospel and have followed it. He cries out: "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11). "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink," etc. (John 7). "I am the light of the world; he who follows me does not walk in darkness" (John 8). "I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture. He who does not enter by the door but climbs in another way is a thief and a robber" (John 10). Likewise: "I am the way, the light and the truth. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14). To these are added the voices of the apostles, who, stirred by the Spirit of Christ, cry with one mouth that salvation is had and found in this one thing alone. Who then of sound mind could find fault with us because, following the living voice of Christ, we abandoned the Roman see, which showed us countless ways of salvation apart from him, and indeed by its traditions made us utterly uncertain of salvation? How much more ought those to be blamed who wickedly spurn Christ, who invites them with outstretched arms and a clear voice, being like those ungrateful and stubborn people of whom he complains in Isaiah? But if anyone does not admit our excuse, he at least proves abundantly that he is driven by the same spirit as the impious Jews, who also refused to hear Paul excusing himself on this very ground, etc.

units.la: Secundò elucent hic mirabilis Christi potentia & modus, quo ille in hostibus suis oppugnandis uti consueuit. Vbi tria consyderanda veniunt. Primum est, quòd Paulum Damasco appropinquare pateretur, priusquam aliquod suæ iræ & iudicij specimen edat. Nec dubium est, quin in conspectu habens vrbem, quam credentium asylum esse putabat, totus rabie exarserit, miserè interim in vrbe trepidantibus pijs, ad quos accelerantis lupi fama peruenerat. Sed iam iam voraturo obiectum bolum occurrit Dominus. Est enim hoc Dei ingenium, vt multa impijs indulgeat, & ad illorum conatus aliquandiu conniueat, vt dum suos illorum opera castigat, ipsis interea paretur fouea, & gloriosior fiat suorum liberatio. Vide Psal. 94. Deinde facillimè & sine negotio sternit tyrannum, qui & animi viribus minax & publica authoritate instructus veniebat. Fulgure enim totum quasi exanimat. At quid Deo tam facile, quàm fulgura eiaculari cœlitus? Mox verò cadit furibundus ille Encelados, quem nec comites itineris, nec Pontificum literæ contra Christi iram defendere possunt. Nec mora, mitis iam & placidus, quis ille antagonista tam potens fit, interrogat, seque illi ad omne obsequium obedientem & facilem offert. Accedit, quòd non corpore modo debilitatus, verumetiam oculis captus in eam vrbem manibus aliorum ducitur, è qua Christianos vinctos eduscturus aduenerat. Ita solet mirificè Deus suorum hostium conatus eludere, vt omnium ludibrio exponantur, qui modò inuincti esse, & cœlis etiam leges ponere videbantur. Exempla huius rei plura alibi produximus, quorum omnium hic finis esse debet, ne hostium potentia terreamur, sed in Deo spem fixam habeamus, cui tam facile est suos ex illorum manu afferere.
units.tr: Second, the wonderful power of Christ shines forth here, and the manner in which he is accustomed to deal with his enemies. Three things are to be considered. The first is that he allowed Paul to approach Damascus before he showed any sign of his anger and judgment. There is no doubt that, with the city in view, which he thought a refuge for believers, he blazed with rage, while the godly in the city, to whom the report of the approaching wolf had come, trembled in the meantime. But the Lord meets the devouring wolf with a morsel put in his way. For it is God's way to indulge the wicked for a while and to overlook their efforts, so that while he chastises his own by their works, a pit is meanwhile prepared for them, and the deliverance of his people becomes more glorious. See Psalm 94. Then he very easily and without effort lays low the tyrant, who came threatening in spirit and armed with public authority. For with a flash of lightning he almost killed him outright. But what is so easy for God as to hurl lightning from heaven? Soon that raging Enceladus falls, whom neither his travelling companions nor the letters of the high priests can defend against the wrath of Christ. Without delay he, now gentle and calm, asks who this so powerful opponent is, and offers himself to him as obedient and ready for every service. Moreover, not only weakened in body but also blinded in his eyes, he is led by the hands of others into the city from which he had come to bring Christians back in chains. So God is wont to wonderfully mock the attempts of his enemies, so that those who seemed invincible and even seemed to make laws for heaven are exposed to the derision of all. We have brought forward many examples of this elsewhere, and the end of them all here ought to be that we should not be terrified by the power of enemies, but keep our hope fixed in God, for whom it is so easy to snatch his own from their hand.

units.la: Et huc cum primis faciunt (quod tertium huius tractationis caput est) Christi verba dicentis: Saul, Saul, cur me persequeris? Item: Ego sum Iesus ille Nazarenus, quem tu persequeris. His enim ad se pertinere fatetur, quacunq; contra fideles ipsius hucusq; gesta fuerant. Ea enim inter nos & Christum coniunctio est, quae inter caput & membra esse consueuit. Quis vero ecclesiam Christi curae esse putauisset, quando Stephanus lapidum acervo obrutus indignamorte peribat? Vel cum Saulus domos piorum effringens, viros & mulieres in vincula trahebat? At qui ista non modo vidit tum Christus, nec modo suorum cladibus doluit, sed ita illis affectus est, ac si vincula & flagrain proprio corpore sustineret. Huc pertinet quod apud prophetam ait: Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Zach.2. Haec vero ut piorum consolationi seruiunt, ita omnes eos terrere debent, quibus viculū videtur, Christi membra vel fidei & religionis ergo persequi, vel alioqui iniurijs afficere, vel vsuris aut vi iniusta opprimere. Audit enim suorum clamores, & vindicem agit potentissimū. Interim docet Christi exemplum, qualis συμπάθεια inter nos quoq; esse debeat, qui cum Christo capiti gloriamur, vnius & eiusdem corporis membra nos esse profitemur. Gaudeamus ergo cum gaudentibus, & ploremus cum plorantibus. Vide 1.Cor.12.Rom.12.&c.
units.tr: And here, as the third head of this discussion, the words of Christ are especially relevant: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" and again, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting." For by these words he confesses that whatever had been done until now against his faithful ones was done against himself. For there is that union between us and Christ which is customary between the head and the members. Who would have thought that the Church of Christ was a concern to him when Stephen perished unworthily, buried under a heap of stones? Or when Saul, breaking into the houses of the godly, dragged men and women to prison? Yet Christ not only saw these things at that time and not only grieved at the losses of his people, but was so affected by them as if he himself bore the chains and the scourges in his own body. To this belongs what he says through the prophet: "He who touches you touches the apple of my eye" (Zech. 2). These things serve for the comfort of the godly, and they ought to terrify all those who think that it is a small matter to persecute Christ's members for faith and religion, or otherwise to wrong them, or to oppress them by usury or unjust force. For he hears the cries of his people and takes up the cause as a most powerful avenger. Meanwhile the example of Christ teaches what kind of sympathy [συμπάθεια] ought to be among us also, who glory that we are joined to Christ as our head, and profess that we are members of one and the same body. Let us therefore rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. See 1 Cor. 12; Rom. 12, etc.

units.la: Postremo memorabile conuersionis verae exemplum hic proponitur, cuius singulas circumstantias insspexisse multum proderit. Initio autem ipse Paulus consyderandus erit, quem priusquam converteretur, lupi instar fuisse constat, qualem fore Iacob patriarcha praedixerat. Et rabie totus flagrans ad dissipandum Christi ovile pergit, nihil interim de conuersione suijpsius ad Christum cogitans. Ad interitum ergo ruit insano ardore, & periisset haud dubie, nisi caelitus extensa manu illum retraxisset Dominus. Vnde discimus, Conuersionis initium ex Deo esse. Eadem quippe omnium nostrum conditio est, quae Pauli fuit. Natura corrupti, caecos carnis affectus sequimur, & quia peccatorum blanditijs fascinamur, adeoq; inter peccandum nobisipsis placemus, de emendatione nunquam cogitamus, nisi quid tale bonus Dei spiritus nobis suggerat. Quid enim hic faceremus, qui ex nobis ipsis non sumus idonei ne ad cogitandum quidem? 2.Cor.3. Recte ergo propheta clamat: Convertite nos, & convertemur. Ier.31. Thren.5. Et Paulus Deum in nobis tum velle tum facere operari testatur, pro bona sua voluntate. Phil.2. Possset pars haec quam plurimis exemplis illustrari, sed quia scripturas legenti passim occurrunt, breuitati studemus. Conuincuntur autem hic liberi arbitrij asserentes, qui hominem propria sua voluntate ad poenitentiam converti posse docent. At si Conuersionis initium ex nobis est, vtiq; operi nostro aliqua meriti laus tribui debet, quod tamen absq; Christi contumelia fieri non potest. Quod si vero initium boni ex vno Deo est, quid obsecro superba liberi arbitrij gloriatione efferimur, quando ea in renullus illius vsus est, in qua nobis illo cumprimus opus erat, iuxta illorum hominum sententiam? Sed omissis hic modum Conuersionis videamus, qui quaedam externa, quaedam interna habet. Ad illa pertinet, quod fulgure consternatur Paulus & ex equo deijcitur, & quod verbo suo peccati atrocitatem Christus arguit. Interius autem spiritu suo operatur, & animum illius tractabilem reddit. Est hic solennis & communis modus, quo in conuertendis peccatoribus Deus vtitur, & quem nostrae naturae corruptio plane requirit. Quia enim securi in peccatis voluptuamur, insolita aliqua clade nos expergefieri oportet: & in eum finem varias castigationes Deus immittit, quales sunt, Morbi, egestas, sterilitas, fames, bella, & quaecunq; huius generis ad uersa vel publice vel priuatim accidunt. Rursum quia de peccato nunquam vere iudicat carnis sensus, Dei verbo illius atrocitatem reuelari necesse est, quod etiam Christus innuit, de spiritu suo dicens, quod mundum de peccato arguat. Ioban.16. Accedunt externis his occultae spiritus suggestiones, quibus animae aures nobis vellicat deus, & excitat, vt de poenitentia serio agenda cogitemus. Atqui but Dei ordinem, ab ipsa seculi origine obseruatum, facile in semetipso deprehendet, quisquis non omnem humanitatis sensum exuit. Quid vero nos facere coneniat, cum istis medijs a Deo inuitamur, Pauli exemplum docet. Apparet quidem in hoc carnalis socordiae vestigium, quando prostratus adhuc Dominum ignorat. At laude dignum est, quod Domini voce edoctus, mox quid vs fieri velit, interrogat. Ea enim animi vere humiliati vox est qua se totum diuinae voluntati obedienter subijcit. Imitemur ergo exemplum hoc, quod vt nostrae institutioni seruiret, literis mandari voluit spiritus sanctus. Et castigati quidem, nos a Domino castigari cogitemus, qui poenitentiam flagitet. Hanc vero non ex nostro cerebro, prout nobis bonum videtur, sed iuxta Dei placitum, quod ex verbo ipsius discitur, instituamus. Ita enim aduersa quoq; emendationi nostrae seruient, nostra vero emendatio sive conuersio Deo approbari poterit. At si haec cum nostri seculi moribus conferas, videbis quam varie pecctur.
units.tr: Lastly, a memorable example of true conversion is set before us here, and it will be very profitable to examine each of its circumstances. First, however, Paul himself must be considered: before his conversion he was, as is well known, like a wolf, just as the patriarch Jacob had foretold he would be. Burning wholly with rage, he set out to scatter Christ's flock, thinking nothing in the meantime about his own conversion to Christ. He was rushing headlong to ruin with a mad zeal, and undoubtedly would have perished, had the Lord not drawn him back with a hand stretched out from heaven. From this we learn that the beginning of conversion comes from God. For the condition of all of us is the same as Paul's was. Corrupt by nature, we follow the blind desires of the flesh, and because we are bewitched by the enticements of sin, and so are pleased with ourselves while we sin, we never think of amendment unless the good Spirit of God suggests something of the kind to us. For what would we do here, we who of ourselves are not even fit to think? 2 Cor. 3. Rightly therefore the prophet cries: Turn us, and we shall be turned. Jer. 31; Lam. 5. And Paul testifies that God works in us both to will and to do, according to his good pleasure. Phil. 2. This point could be illustrated by very many examples, but since they occur everywhere to anyone who reads Scripture, we aim at brevity. Here, however, those who assert free will are refuted, those who teach that a man can be turned to repentance by his own will. But if the beginning of conversion is from us, then surely some merit ought to be ascribed to our work, which yet cannot happen without dishonour to Christ. But if the beginning of good comes from God alone, why, I ask, are we puffed up with the proud boasting of free will, since, according to the opinion of those men, it has had no use in that very thing in which it was most needed by us? But, setting these aside, let us look at the manner of conversion, which has some external and some internal features. To the external belong the fact that Paul is struck down by a flash of lightning and thrown from his horse, and that Christ rebukes the atrocity of his sin by his word. Inwardly, however, he works by his Spirit, and makes his mind pliable. This is the usual and common manner by which God deals in converting sinners, and which the corruption of our nature plainly requires. For since we take pleasure in our sins while we are secure, we must be roused by some unusual blow; and to this end God sends various chastisements, such as diseases, want, barrenness, famine, wars, and whatever adversities of this kind happen either publicly or privately. Again, because the sense of the flesh never truly judges sin, its atrocity must be revealed by God's word, which Christ also hints at when, speaking of his Spirit, he says that he will convict the world of sin. John 16. To these external means are added the hidden promptings of the Spirit, by which God tickles the ears of our soul and stirs us to think seriously about repentance. Indeed, whoever has not stripped off all human feeling will easily discover in himself this order of God, observed from the very beginning of the world. What we ought to do when God invites us by these means, the example of Paul teaches. There is indeed in him a trace of carnal sluggishness, when, though prostrate, he still does not know the Lord. But it is worthy of praise that, taught by the Lord's voice, he immediately asks what he wishes him to do. For that is the voice of a truly humbled mind, by which it submits itself wholly and obediently to the divine will. Let us therefore imitate this example, which the Holy Spirit wished to be committed to writing for our instruction. And let us, when chastised, consider that we are being chastised by the Lord, who calls for repentance. And let us establish this repentance not from our own brain, as seems good to us, but according to God's pleasure, which is learned from his word. For in this way adversities too will serve our amendment, and our amendment or conversion may be approved by God. But if you compare these things with the manners of our age, you will see how variously people sin.

units.la: Conuersionis verae exemplum. tur. Paucos enim inuenias, qui castigati, eius rei authorem agnoscant Deum; sed plerique sua infortunia alijs causis accepta ferunt. Quòd si quos aliquis religionis sensus tangit, vt Dei manu agnoscere cogantur, ille vel perexiguus & momentaneus est, vel cum superstitione coniunctus, qua decepti, falsam & momentaneam poenitentiam instituunt, qualem Israeli apud prophetam Deus expro-brat. Vide Hos.6. Atqui hæc præcipua tot tamen pertinacium nostri seculi calamitatum causa est, quam nisi tollamus, meliorem sortem nunquam sperare licebit. Postremum in hac tractatione habetur, quòd in vrbem ad Ananiam relegatur Paulus, à quo pleniorem institutionem petat. Huius præcepti sive facti causas supra expo-suimus, vnde eas petere licebit. Nos pauli exemplum imitari decet, vt diuinæ vocationi nos accommodantes, à superstitione & reliquis peccatis ad Deum conuer-tamur, ab illius ore toti pendeamus, & vitæ nostræ conuersationem voluntati illius conformemus. Ita enim vitam hanc feliciter emensi, in cœlo coharedes erimus Iesu Christi, filij Dei æterni: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: An example of true conversion. For you will find few who, when chastised, acknowledge God as the author of the thing; but most attribute their misfortunes to other causes. And if some sense of religion touches anyone so that they are compelled to recognise God's hand, that sense is either very slight and momentary, or joined with superstition, by which, deceived, they institute a false and momentary repentance, such as God rebukes in Israel through the prophet. See Hos. 6. Yet this is the chief cause of the many calamities of our obstinate age, and unless we remove it, we shall never be able to hope for a better lot. Last in this passage is the fact that Paul is sent back into the city to Ananias, from whom he is to seek fuller instruction. The reasons for this precept or action we have set out above, from which they may be sought. It is fitting for us to imitate Paul's example, so that, accommodating ourselves to the divine calling, we may turn to God from superstition and the other sins, depend wholly on his mouth, and conform the conduct of our life to his will. For thus, having completed this life happily, we shall be co-heirs of Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLIIII.

units.la: Ananias autem quidam, vir pius secundum legem, testimonio probatus omnium illic habitantium Iudæorum, veniens ad me, & astans, dixit mihi: Saul frater, recipe visum. Et ego eadem hora recepto visu vidi illum. At ille dixit: Deus patrum nostrorum præparauit te, vt cognoscere voluntatem suam, & videres iustum, & audires vocem ex ore eius: quia eris testis illi apud omnes homines eorum quæ vidisti & audiuisti. Et nunc quid cunctaris? Exurge, & baptizare, & ablue peccata tua, invocato nomine domini.
units.tr: "Then a certain Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, came to me, stood by me, and said to me: 'Brother Saul, receive your sight.' And at that same hour I regained my sight and saw him. He said: 'The God of our fathers has appointed you to know his will, to see the Just One, and to hear a voice from his mouth. For you will be his witness before all men of what you have seen and heard. And now, why do you delay? Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord.'"

units.la: QVoniam omnis mutatio religionis odiosa est, vt quæ leuem & inconstantem animum arguat, Paulus non temere suum è Iudaismo transitum tanta diligentia excusat. Et primò quidem, se in illo non obiter aut perfunctorie, sed magno cum zelo, versatum fuisse docuit, ne quis ipsum vel insciitia lapsum, vel disciplinæ odio extimulatum, vel propbana animi leuitate impulsum, fidei professionem mutauisse diceret. Inde verò suæ vocationis historiam contexuit, vt se non tam à Deo vocatum, quàm coactum hoc fecisse, intelligerent. Istius in præsenti subijcit, vt ad apostolicæ functionis munus legitimè per Ananiæ ministerium ordinatus fit, quem etiam cœlestis visionis & oraculi à Deo destinatum interpretem habuerit. Loci verò huius principalis finis est, vt illis occurrat, qui vocationis suæ historiam suspectam habebant, & Paulum inani phantasia delusum fuisse calumniabantur.
units.tr: Since every change of religion is hateful, as it suggests a light and inconstant mind, Paul does not lightly excuse his passage out of Judaism with such great care. First, he shows that he was not casually or superficially involved in it, but had been engaged in it with great zeal, so that no one could say that he had abandoned his profession of faith through ignorance, or was driven by hatred of the discipline, or was moved by a profane levity of mind. Then he weaves together the history of his calling, so that they might understand that he did this not so much because he was called by God as because he was compelled. Here he goes on to show how he was lawfully ordained to the office of apostolic work through the ministry of Ananias, whom God had also appointed as the interpreter of the heavenly vision and oracle. The main purpose of this passage is to meet those who regarded the account of his calling with suspicion, and who charged that Paul had been deceived by an empty fantasy.

units.la: Commodè verò à personæ descriptione orditur, ne quis ipsum homini leui credidisse suspicaretur. Et quia apostatæ testimonium Iudæi minimè admisissent, ante omnia à diligenti legis obseruatione Ananiam commendat, dum illum virum pium secundum legem fuisse dicit. Addit huic elogio publicum Iudæorum omnium, qui Damasci illo tempore habitarunt, testimonium. Accedit his restituti visus miraculum, cuius hunc præcipuum vsum videri vult, vt Paulus Ananiam diuinitus ad se missum esse agnosceret. Quis verò vanitatis eum accusat, qui cælesti oraculo admonitus, imò totus consteruatus, & tantum oraculi interpretem secutus, religionem mutauit? Atqui docet Pauli exemplum, in religionis causa cumprimis leuitatem fugi debere, ne temere cuius fidem habeamus. Vt enim in hac nostræ salutis summa consistit, ita omnibus seculis impostores fuisse constat, qui simplicium animos errorum laqueos tetenderunt, & tales in posterum quoq; exorituros esse, tum Christus apostoli abundè testantur. Deploranda ergo est nostri seculi hominum socordia, qui in clarissima euangelij luce, contra Iohannis apostoli præceptum, cuiuis spiritui credunt: imò eos demum pro vere apostolicis habent, qui scurrili maledicentia & verbi ministros & magistratus clanculò profindunt: cùm interim nec eruditionis laude, nec morum grauitate commendentur. Simul autem obseruemus, quæ vera sit ministrorum commendatio, adeò omnium, qui in publico aliquo munere versantur. Primum hic locum habet, Pietas, quando ea iuxta legem, id est, Dei præscriptum instituta furit. Nec enim sufficit pium esse simpliciter, nisi in Dei verbum respiciatur. Alioqui enim zelus erit sine scientia, quali Iudaei simul & Paulus olim decepti fuerunt. Deinde bonum testimonium habeant ab ijs, quibus cum versantur, tum ab exteris quoque, ne propter ipsos euangelium male audiat. Vide de hoc Paulum in priori ad Timoth. 3. cap. His vero legitimam vocationem accedere oportet, cuius nisi fibijpsis probe conscij fuerint, nec fortiter, nec cum fructu aliquo munus suum obibunt. Atqui tales omnino esse constat, quibus credimus, prophetas nimirum & apostolos. Nam Dei verbum in omnibus secuti, ab illo ne latum vnguem sibi discedendum esse putauerunt. Ea vero fuit vita illorum integritas, vt hodie etiam inter Turcas & Papistas sancta habeatur nominis ipsorum memoria. De vocatione eorundem nemo dubitare potest, quando tot eius in scripturis sacrum testimonia extant. Minime ergo vanitatis accusari debent, qui his crediderunt. Quin potius fidem ab ipsis traditam constanter retineamus, vt quae sola salutem afferre poterit.
units.tr: He fittingly begins with a description of the man, so that no one may suspect that he believed a light-minded person. And since the Jews would never have admitted the testimony of an apostate, he first commends Ananias for his careful observance of the law, when he says that he was a devout man according to the law. To this praise he adds the public testimony of all the Jews who lived at Damascus at that time. To these is added the miracle of the restored sight, whose chief use he wishes us to see as this: that Paul would recognise that Ananias had been sent to him by God. But who can accuse of vanity the man who, admonished by a heavenly oracle, and indeed utterly dismayed, followed only the interpreter of the oracle and changed his religion? Yet Paul's example teaches that in matters of religion above all, levity must be avoided, so that we do not believe anyone rashly. For just as the sum of our salvation depends on this, so it is well established that in every age there have been impostors who have spread snares of error for the minds of simple people; and Christ and the apostles bear abundant witness that such men will also arise in the future. So we must lament the sloth of the people of our own age, who, in the clearest light of the gospel, contrary to the precept of the apostle John, believe every spirit. Indeed, they regard as truly apostolic those who with buffoonish slander secretly tear apart both the ministers of the Word and the magistrates, although such men are commended neither for learning nor for the gravity of their conduct. At the same time, let us observe what the true commendation of ministers is, indeed of all who hold any public office. First, piety has a place here, when it is exercised according to the law, that is, according to what God has prescribed. For it is not enough simply to be pious unless one looks to the Word of God; otherwise there will be zeal without knowledge, such as the Jews and Paul himself once had when they were deceived. Next, they should have a good testimony from those among whom they live, and also from outsiders, so that the gospel is not badly spoken of because of them. See on this matter Paul in his first letter to Timothy, chapter 3. To these must be added a lawful calling, and unless men are well aware of this in themselves, they will neither perform their office bravely nor with any fruit. Indeed, it is clear that such are the men whom we believe, namely the prophets and the apostles. For, following the Word of God in all things, they thought they must not depart from it by so much as a hair's breadth. Their integrity of life was such that even today the memory of their names is held sacred among Turks and Papists. No one can doubt their calling, since so many sacred testimonies to it exist in the Scriptures. Therefore those who believed them ought by no means to be accused of vanity. Rather, let us constantly hold fast to the faith handed down by them, since it alone can bring salvation.

units.la: Porro vbi Ananiae personam describit Paulus, illius quoque orationem verbotim commemorat, eo quod singula, quae in hac habentur, causae ipsius egregie seruiebant. Nam & totius negotij auctorem vnicum Deum esse docet, & vocationis finem indicat, ac postremo ad baptismum capessendum hortatur. Ad primum caput pertinet quod dicit: Deus patrum nostrorum praeparauit te. Hinc nimirum Paulus de sua vocatione ita certus fuit, vt postea se ab vtero matris ad euangelizandi munus praeparatum fuisse dicere ausit. Galat. 1. Diserte autem Deum patrum nominat, vt ita se neque quam a veri Dei cultu defecisse testetur. Caeterum, vt haec Pauli e Iudaismo transitum excusant, & eiusdem doctrinae fidem faciunt: ita eundem nullo suo merito, sed mera Dei gratia vocatum fuisse dicent. Quid enim in Paulo, acerrimo Christi hoste & protomartyrus Stephani sanguine madente, ipse potuit, cuius gratia vocaretur? Ipse certe se inter peccatores principem constituit, & meras bonitatis Dei beneficium fuisse fatetur, quod Christi minister & apostolus sit factus. 1. Timoth. 1. At quod de Paulo dicimus, de omnibus nobis debet intelligi. Eadem enim omnium nostrum conditio est, vt nisi sua bonitate nos Deus praeueniat, nos ex nobis ipsis ne ad cogitandum quidem idonei simus: quae re alibi copiosius diximus.
units.tr: Moreover, when Paul describes the person of Ananias, he also recounts his speech word for word, because each of the things contained in it served his cause admirably. For he teaches that the sole author of the whole matter is God, he indicates the end of the calling, and finally he urges him to take up baptism. The first point pertains to the words: "The God of our fathers has appointed you." From this, no doubt, Paul was so certain of his calling that he later dared to say that he had been set apart for the office of preaching the gospel from his mother's womb (Galatians 1). He clearly names the God of the fathers so that he may testify that he had not departed from the worship of the true God. Moreover, just as these things excuse Paul's passage out of Judaism and establish trust in his teaching, so they also show that he was called not by any merit of his own, but by the sheer grace of God. For what could Paul, the fiercest enemy of Christ, whose hands were dripping with the blood of Stephen the first martyr, have done to deserve being called? He himself certainly calls himself the foremost of sinners, and confesses that it was a mere gift of God's goodness that he became a minister and apostle of Christ (1 Timothy 1). But what we say of Paul ought to be understood of all of us. For the condition of all of us is the same: unless God anticipates us by his goodness, we are not even fit to think from ourselves. We have said more fully elsewhere about this matter.

units.la: Audiamus modo, in quem finem Deus Paulum praeparauerit, vbi multa nobis consideranda sunt. Primum est: Vt cognosceret voluntatem suam. Hinc autem ordiatur, quia hoc initio verbi ministris opus est: quia nisi ipsi voluntate Dei intelligant, hanc alios docere nunquam poterunt. Licet vero in lege a pueris institutus esset Paulus, Dei tamen voluntatem, quae ibi sub inuolucris continetur, bucusque ignorauerat. Lege enim homines iustificari & saluari putabat, eius voluntatis plane ignarus, quae est, vt omnis qui videt filium, & credit in eum, a quo ille missus est, non pereat in peccatis, sed filij meritô iustificatus habeat vitam aeternam. Iohan. 6. Hanc ergo illi reuelari oportuit, ne in legalibus vmbris, salutis suae incertus oberraret. Porro quia Dei salutifera voluntas in vno Christo continetur & addiscitur, huius quoque cognitionem mox subijcit Ananias, Paulum ad hoc praeparatum esse dicens, vt videret Iustum. Ita vero Christum nominat, tum quod ipse iustus & inculpatus est, tum quod iustos reddit in se credentes. Vnde hoc illi nomen fore propheta praedixit, Dominus iustitia nostra. Ierem. 23. At cum Dei opus fuerit, quod Christum agnouit Paulus, conflat in eiusdem cognitione neminem peruenire, nisi Deus illam manifestare dignetur. Nam etiam Christo teste, nemo videt filium, nisi pater, & cui is reuelare dignabitur. Matthaei vndecimo. Vnde rursus salutem nostram gratuitam esse constat. Tertiò in hoc praeparatum esse docet, vt audiret vocem ex ore Dei, adeoque praeter vulgarem morem diuinitus edoceretur, id quod alibi Paulum praecipue inculcat contra eos, qui ministerij sui authoritatem eleuare conabantur. Galat. primo & secundo. Est vero hoc admirabile Dei beneficium, & tale omnino apparebit, si Paulum Dei hostem fuisse cogitemus, quem tamen ille amico & salutari alloquio dignatus est. Agnoscamus & nos Dei bonitatem, qui alloqui quotidie eos dignatur, quos hostium loco censere & persequi optimo iure poterat. Interim hic officij sui omnes ministri admonentur, vt nimirum ex Dei ore, scripturis videlicet, dolorinam suam hauriant, nec sibi liberum esse putent, pro suo arbitrio noua decreta ecclesijs obtrudere. Vide quae in hanc sententiam alibi diximus. Postremo officium, ad quod a domino destinatus erat, diserte exprimit, ideo illi Dei voluntatem, Christi cognitionem simul & vocem innotuisse dicens, quod Christo testis futurus sit apud omnes homines, auritus nimirum & oculatus. Ita vero reliquum apostolus parem factum fuisse constat, quando illis quoque non aliud iniunctum fuit, quam vt de Christi
units.tr: Let us now hear for what end God prepared Paul, where we have many things to consider. The first is: "that he should know his will." This is where we must begin, since this is the first requirement of ministers of the Word: unless they themselves understand the will of God, they will never be able to teach it to others. Although Paul had been brought up in the law from boyhood, until then he had not known the will of God, which is contained there under veils. For he thought that men were justified and saved by the law, being entirely ignorant of that will which is that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him whom he has sent should not perish in sins, but, justified by the Son, have eternal life (John 6). So this had to be revealed to him, lest he wander uncertain of his salvation amid the legal shadows. Moreover, because God's saving will is contained and learned in Christ alone, Ananias immediately adds the knowledge of this too, saying that Paul had been prepared to "see the Just One." Christ is named "the Just One" both because he himself is just and blameless, and because he makes just those who believe in him. Hence the prophet foretold that this would be his name: "The Lord our righteousness" (Jeremiah 23). But since it was the work of God that Paul knew Christ, it is clear that no one comes to the knowledge of him unless God deigns to reveal it. For, as Christ himself witnesses, no one knows the Son except the Father, and to whomever the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11). Hence again it is clear that our salvation is free. Third, he shows that Paul was prepared to "hear a voice from the mouth of God," and so was taught by God in an unusual manner, which the apostle especially presses elsewhere against those who tried to diminish the authority of his ministry (Galatians 1 and 2). This, however, is a remarkable benefit of God, and it will appear altogether such if we consider that Paul was an enemy of God, yet God deigned to address him with a friendly and saving word. Let us also acknowledge the goodness of God, who deigns daily to speak to those whom he could rightly have regarded as enemies and pursued. Meanwhile, all ministers are admonished of their duty here: namely, that they should draw their doctrine from the mouth of God, that is, from the Scriptures, and not think it lawful for them, at their own discretion, to impose new decrees on the churches. See what we have said elsewhere to this effect. Finally, he clearly expresses the office to which he had been appointed by the Lord, saying that the will of God, the knowledge of Christ, and his voice were made known to him at the same time, because he was to be a witness to Christ before all men, namely, one who had both heard and seen. And indeed the apostle is known to have become equal to the rest, since they too were charged with nothing other than to bear witness of Christ...

units.la: Ananiae oratio. Christi vita & morte, & doctrina item & miraculis, tandemq; de eiusdem resurrectione & ascensione testimonium ferrent. Comprehendit autem testis nomen universum apostoli & cuiusuis ministri officium, ut supra capite primo diximus, unde peti debent, quae hic brevitatis studio omittuntur. Diserte vero omnium hominum meminit, ut illis respondeat, quibus indignum & iniquum videbatur, quod Christi euangelium gentibus incircuncisis praedicauisset. Simul vero generalis doctrina hinc de cerpi potest, quae officij admonet omnes eos, quos Deus suae voluntatis & filij sui cognitione illustrat. Est hoc, ut eandem cognitionem longe lateq; propagent, & de Dei gratia passim testentur. Iubet hoc partim gratitudinis lex, ut Dei gloriam prouehant, cuius salutarem manum senserunt: partim charitas fraterna, ut aliorum salutem, non minus quam nostram nobis commendatam habeamus. Quibus rationibus simul & expresso Dei mandato Paulum quoq; extimulatum fuisse constat, ut officium suum, quantumuis indignantibus Iudaeis, intermittere non potuerit.
units.tr: The speech of Ananias. They were to bear witness to Christ's life and death, and likewise to his teaching and miracles, and finally to his resurrection and ascension. The word "witness" embraces the whole office of an apostle and of any minister, as we said in the first chapter, from which passages should be sought, which are omitted here for the sake of brevity. He expressly mentions all men, so as to answer those to whom it seemed unworthy and unjust that he had preached the gospel of Christ to uncircumcised Gentiles. At the same time, a general teaching can be drawn from this, which reminds all those whom God illumines with the knowledge of his will and of his Son that this is their duty: to spread that same knowledge far and wide, and to bear witness everywhere to the grace of God. The law of gratitude requires this in part, so that they may advance the glory of God, whose saving hand they have felt; and brotherly love requires it in part, so that we hold the salvation of others no less commended to us than our own. It is clear that by these reasons, and by the express command of God, Paul too was spurred on, so that he could not abandon his office, however much the Jews resented it.

units.la: Restat ultima orationis Ananiae pars, qua illum ad baptismum suscipiendum hortatur, ut iuxta Christi institutum publice etiam ipsi nomen det, & ecclesiae suae inseratur. Id vero magna gratitate urget. Quid cunctaris? inquit: non quod Paulus tergiuersari voluerit, sed ut illi adhuc metu perculso & ob scelerus conscientiam trepidanti acriores stimulos adhiberet. Quare addit: Surge, baptizare, & ablue peccata tua, invocato nomine domini. Est autem observanda nobis sacramentalis locutio, quae baptismi rationem & dignitatem exprimit. Nec enim ea Ananiae mens fuit, quod aquae elemento peccata ablui putauerit, quae solius Christi sanguine ablui & expiari scriptura ubique docet. Sed quia ablutio, quae Christi sanguine fit, per baptismum extrinsecus quoq; figuratur & obsignatur, communi scripturae more fit, ut baptismo peccata ablui dicantur. Et sane, ne Paulus duriuscu-lum putaret dictum hoc, mox addit: Invocato nomine domini. His enim verbis ad Christum relegatur, qui fide apprehensus & invocatus, ea nobis salutis dona communicat, quae sacramentis figurari & obsignari solent. Ut vero in Sacramentorum usu Christum nos respicere conuenit, si illa nobis salutaria esse volumus: ita haec minime superuacanea esse, nec ullo modo negligi debere admonemur. Nec enim quicquam sine graui ratione Deus instituit, qui ecclesiam suam minime grauari vult. Ideo Aethiopem quoq; post perfectam fidei confessionem Philippus baptizat. Et Petrus Cornelij familiam, post acceptum spiritum sanctum, baptizandam esse censet. Imo ad baptismum suscipiendum hoc loco Paulus urgetur, quem tot tantisq; elogijs spiritus sanctus modo dignatus fuerat. Arguunt hae exempla Sacramentorum contemptores, qui dum nimium spirituales videri volunt, Dei instituta improbe conculcant. In primis autem nobis Paulus observandus erit, ut illius exemplum secuti, in religionis causa nihil temere aut leuiter agamus, de veritate autem probe edocti, illam constanter tenere studeamus. Ita enim per labores & pericula huius seculi ad aeterna vitae haereditatem penetrabimus, quam nobis ab aeterno destinauit Deus pater misericordiae, in filio suo Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There remains the last part of Ananias's speech, in which he urges Paul to receive baptism, so that, according to Christ's institution, he might also publicly give his name and be incorporated into his church. He presses this with great earnestness. "Why do you delay?" he says. This is not because Paul wished to shirk it, but so that he might apply sharper goads to him, still struck with fear and trembling from the burden of his guilty conscience. Therefore he adds: "Arise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on the name of the Lord." We must observe here the sacramental manner of speaking, which expresses the nature and dignity of baptism. For Ananias did not mean that sins are washed away by the element of water, since Scripture everywhere teaches that they are washed away and expiated by the blood of Christ alone. But because the washing that is effected by the blood of Christ is also figured and sealed outwardly through baptism, it is the common manner of Scripture that sins are said to be washed away by baptism. And indeed, lest Paul think this saying too harsh, he adds at once: "calling on the name of the Lord." For by these words he is referred back to Christ, who, grasped and called upon in faith, communicates to us those gifts of salvation which are usually figured and sealed by the sacraments. And just as it is fitting that in the use of the sacraments we look to Christ if we wish them to be salutary for us, so we are reminded that these are by no means superfluous and must in no way be neglected. For God instituted nothing without a weighty reason, since he does not wish his church to be burdened. Thus Philip also baptized the Ethiopian after the complete confession of faith. And Peter judged that the household of Cornelius, after receiving the Holy Spirit, was to be baptized. Indeed, here Paul is urged to receive baptism, he whom the Holy Spirit had only just honored with so many and such great commendations. These examples refute those despisers of the sacraments who, while wishing to appear too spiritual, wickedly trample underfoot the institutions of God. Above all, we must observe Paul, so that, following his example, we do nothing rashly or lightly in the cause of religion, but, once rightly taught in the truth, we strive to hold to it constantly. For thus, through the labors and dangers of this age, we shall attain to the inheritance of eternal life, which God the Father of mercies has destined for us from eternity in his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honor, glory and power forever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLV.
units.tr: HOMILY 145.

units.la: Factum est autem cum essem reuersus Hierosolymam, & orarem in templo, ut raperer extra me, ac viderem eum, dicentem mihi: Festina, & exi velociter Hierosolyma: quoniam non recipient testimonium tuum de me. Tum ego dixi: Domine, ipsi sciunt, quod ego coniiciebam in carceres, & caedebam in singulis Synagogis eos, qui credebant in te. Et cum funderetur sanguis Stephani testis tui, ego quoq; astabam, & consentiebam morti eius, & custodiebam vestes interficientium ipsum. Et dixit mihi: Vade, quoniam ego ad gentes procul mittam te. Audiebant autem eum usq; ad hoc verbum. Et sublatis vocibus suis dixerunt: Tolle de terra hominem talem: non enim conuenit eum viuere.
units.tr: It happened, when I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I was caught up out of myself and saw him saying to me: "Hurry, and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me." Then I said: "Lord, they themselves know that I used to throw into prison, and beat in every synagogue, those who believed in you. And when the blood of Stephen your witness was poured out, I too was standing by, and consented to his death, and guarded the garments of those who killed him." And he said to me: "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles." Now they listened to him up to this word; then they raised their voices and said: "Take such a man from the earth, for it is not right that he should live."

units.la: Paulus apostolus (sicuti iam saepe dictum est) diligenti hac & prolixa rerum suarum narratione sinistris Iudaeorum suspicionibus & hostium calumniis, quibus grauabatur, mederi instituit. Erant autem duo potissimùm, quæ vulgi animos aduersus ipsum irritabant: nimirum quòd è Iu-daismo ad Christi fidem transfuissent, & quòd euangelium salutis gentibus incircuncisis prædicans, illas Iudæis æquaret. Ex his enim colligebant, ipsum populi Dei hostem, legis totiusq; cultus Leui-tici prophanum & impium contemptorem esse. Ad primum caput respondit hactenus, vnum hoc vr-gens, quòd nihil temerè aut priuato cõsilio, sed omnia ex Dei iussu & vocatione fecerit: ita suo exem-plo docens quid nos quoq; in religione vel mutanda vel defendenda obseruare conueniat. Nunc ve-rò ad alterum caput descendit, in quo idem argumentũ adducit, à Deo nimirum se euocatum fuisse docens, vt gentibus prædicaret, nec tamen se vnquam sui populi studium depositisse: id quod ex singu-lis eius historiæ, quam hîc commemorat, partibus clarissimè patebit.
units.tr: Paul the apostle (as has often been said already) set about remedying, by this careful and lengthy account of his affairs, the hostile suspicions of the Jews and the slanders of his enemies, by which he was burdened.
