There were two things in particular that roused the minds of the crowd against him: namely, that he had passed over from Judaism to the faith of Christ, and that by preaching the gospel of salvation to the uncircumcised Gentiles he put them on the same level as the Jews. For from these they concluded that he was an enemy of the people of God, and a profane and impious despiser of the law and of the whole Levitical worship. To the first charge he has so far replied, urging this one point: that he did nothing rashly or on his own private counsel, but everything by God's command and calling; thus by his own example teaching what we too ought to observe in changing or defending religion. Now he comes to the second charge, in which he brings forward the same argument, showing that he had been summoned by God to preach to the Gentiles, and yet had never laid aside his zeal for his own people; this will be made quite clear from the individual parts of the history he recounts here.

units.la: Primò enim se Hierosolymam reuersum esse dicit: nimirum vt ijs suam operam locaret, ex qui-bus prognatus, & à quibus enutritus simul & institutus fuerat. Nec enim aliam ob causam huius profectionis meminit, quàm vt probet, per se nõ fletisse, quò minus suæ gentis hominibus salutis nun-tium afferret. Porrò profectionem hanc in quartum conuersionis Pauli annum incidere, supra capi-te nono ex ipsius ad Galatas epistola docuimus. Quare omissa temporis supputatione, Pauli exem-plum consyderemus, quo ministri admonentur, se licet omnibus hominibus debitores sint, suæ tamen gentis & patriæ præcipuam curam gerere debere. Siquidem ea naturæ lex est, vt ijs præ cæteris ob-strictî simus, quibus natales nostros omnemq; à pueris institutionem debemus. Obseruauit hanc Chri-stus quoq;, quando Nazarethanis suis salutis doctrinam ab initio statim obtulit, quorum tamen in-gratitudinem ignorare non poterat. Quod autem ministris dicitur, idipsum singulis obseruandum venit, vt patriam gentem sibi commendatissimam habeant. Qua in re Mosen illos sequi decet, qui aulæ opes & delitias potius, quàm fratres suos tyrannide oppressos derelinquere voluit. Agnoscant hinc suam improbitatem, qui eò impudentiæ processerunt, vt patriæ libertatem, iura & leges, omnia deniq; venalia habeant, modò priuatis commodis possint consulere.
units.tr: First, he says that he returned to Jerusalem: clearly so that he might offer his labour to those from whom he was born, and by whom he had been nourished and at the same time instructed. For he mentions this journey for no other reason than to prove that it was not through any fault of his own that he failed to bring the message of salvation to the men of his own nation. Moreover, we showed from the ninth chapter, from Paul's own letter to the Galatians, that this journey fell in the fourth year after his conversion. Therefore, leaving aside the reckoning of time, let us consider Paul's example, by which ministers are reminded that, although they are debtors to all men, they ought nevertheless to take special care of their own nation and country. For this is the law of nature: that we are bound more closely to those to whom we owe our birth and all our instruction from childhood. Christ also observed this, when from the very beginning he offered the teaching of salvation to his own Nazarenes, although he could not be ignorant of their ingratitude. What is said to ministers applies equally to each individual: that they should hold their native nation as most deserving of their care. In this matter they ought to follow Moses, who chose rather to forsake the riches and delights of the court than to abandon his brothers oppressed by tyranny. Let those who have gone so far in shamelessness that they hold their country's liberty, its rights and laws, and in the end everything, as things for sale, so long as they can serve their private advantage, recognise their own wickedness.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum redeamus, qui in vrbem reuersus, in templo orauit. Templi verò meminit, partim ne quis illum clàm latuisse diceret, partim vt templi prophanati suspicionem declinet, quam multorum animis iam insedisse nouerat. Quid verò orarit, ex Romanorum decimo capite facile colligi potest, vbi se pro Iudæis frequenter deprecari dicit, vt salutem consequantur. Nec alium huius quoque precationis scopum fuisse, ex sequenti colloquio, quod illi de Iudæis cum Christo in-terceßit, palàm videbimus. Rursum verò hic officij sui admonentur ministri: vt nimirum populi salutem assiduis precibus iuuare & promouere studeant. Vt enim hoc charitatis & fidei lex iubet, qua gregi sibi commissa obstricti sunt: ita hoc ipsum necessitas quoq; postulat, quando constat, vanos & irritos ipsorum labores fore, nisi Deus incrementum dederit. Viderunt hoc veteres etiā pro-phetæ, quorum non paucæ pro populo preces extant. Idipsum verò magistratus quoq; obseruare de-cet, quando nec hi quicquam absq; Dei ope efficient, cuius spiritu ipsos duci & regi necesse est. Ex-empla habent etiam hi, quæ imitentur, Mosis nimirum, Dauidis, Solomonis, Ezechiæ, vt de innu-meris aliis taceam.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul, who, returning to the city, prayed in the temple. He mentions the temple partly so that no one might say he had lurked there in secret, and partly so that he might avoid the suspicion of a profaned temple, which he knew had already settled in the minds of many. What he prayed for can easily be gathered from the tenth chapter of Romans, where he says that he often pleads for the Jews, that they may obtain salvation. And that this was also the aim of this prayer, we shall clearly see from the following conversation which he had with Christ about the Jews. Here again ministers are reminded of their duty: that they should strive to help and advance the salvation of the people by constant prayers. For just as the law of love and faith requires this, by which they are bound to the flock committed to them, so also necessity demands it, since it is certain that their labours will be empty and futile unless God gives the increase. The ancient prophets also saw this, many of whose prayers for the people survive. Magistrates too ought to observe the same, since they can accomplish nothing without God's help, by whose Spirit they must necessarily be led and ruled. These also have examples to imitate: namely Moses, David, Solomon, Hezekiah, not to mention countless others.

units.la: Tandem verò oraculum exponit Paulus, quo ad gentes proficisci iussus fuit. Se verò in ecstasi fuisse dicit, vt maior oraculi fides esset & authoritas. Diligenter autem suum cum Christo collo-quium narrat, cuius singulas personas consyderare oportet. Primò Christus illi apparens, festinan-ter ipsum Hierosolymis discedere iubet. Mandati verò sui rationem subijcit: Quia non recipient testimonium de me. At si hæc cum Pauli vocatione conferas, haud leuiter illum tentari po-tuisse patebit. Audiuerat enim, se electum Christi organum, & eiusdem testem fore apud omnes ho-mines. Nec dubium est, quin de suæ gentis conuersione præcipuam spem conceperit, cuius tanto stu-dio & amore flagrabat. Nunc verò se omni spe frustrari audit. Sed ita suorum fidem exercet domi-nus, quando sanctißimis illorum votis & conatibus euentus non semper respondet. Ita Moses dum suis liberator & assertor esse incipit, se ab illis ipsis impiè repelli sensit. Sic Helias, cùm post superatos & occisos Baalitas omnia sibi tuta pollicetur, nouis Iesabelis minis & diris conatibus terretur. His & similibus exemplis edocti, non succumbamus, sed stationem tenemus firmiter, nec deerit tandem occasio, qua vtile Deo obsequium præstemus. SED Paulum audiamus, qui quasi cum Deo disputaturus tergiuersari videtur. Priorem enim conditionem repetens, putat fieri non posse, quin repentina sua mutatione commoueantur, & euangelio credant. Est autem hoc frequens in scriptu-ris, quòd cum Deo contendere videntur sancti, non quidem contumaci animo & rebelli, sed quòd diuersarum rationum examine fidem suâ confirmari sentiunt. Quæ causa est, quòd id illis amicè permittit Deus, qui filius suum persequi velit, ne alloquio quidem suo nos dignaretur. Sternitur hic illorum superstitio, qui Diuis intercessoribus opus esse putant, eò quòd nobis peccatoribus in Dei conspectum venire non liceat: cùm non preces modò suorum, verumetiam contrarias suis mandatis rationes, quas illi attulerunt, clementer audiat. Curandum tamen nobis, ne Dei clementia abusi, contendendo ad murmura vsq; & contumacem inobedientiam progrediamur: quin potius Deo nos totos submittamus, cui rationes nostras omnes cedere conuenit. Nec enim ille, quasi per nos edoctus, sententiam mutat vnquam, cùm illius consilium in æternum maneat. Experitur hoc ipsum Paulus in præsenti. Vrget enim mandatum suum dominus, & diserte ad gentes illum ablegat, nihil interim de euangelij profectu inter illas pollicens: quia simpliciter nos sibi obedire vult.
units.tr: Finally, Paul sets forth the oracle by which he was ordered to go to the Gentiles. He says that he was in an ecstasy, so that the oracle might have greater credibility and authority. He carefully relates his conversation with Christ, and each of its persons ought to be considered. First, Christ, appearing to him, bids him quickly depart from Jerusalem. He adds the reason for his command: "Because they will not receive testimony concerning me." Yet if you compare this with Paul's calling, it will be plain that he could have been tempted not lightly. For he had heard that he was to be the chosen instrument of Christ and his witness before all men. Nor is there any doubt that he had conceived a chief hope of the conversion of his own nation, which he burned to achieve with such zeal and love. Now he hears that he is being robbed of every hope. But the Lord thus tests the faith of his own, when the outcome does not always answer to their most holy wishes and efforts. So Moses, when he began to be the liberator and champion of his own people, felt that he was impiously repulsed by those very people. So Elijah, when after the Baalites had been overcome and slain he promised himself that all was safe, was terrified by the fresh threats and dire plots of Jezebel. Taught by these and similar examples, let us not give way, but hold our post firmly, and an occasion will not be lacking at last on which we may render useful service to God. But let us hear Paul, who seems to argue with God as if he were about to dispute with him. For, repeating his former objection, he thinks it cannot be that men will be moved by his sudden change and believe the gospel. Now it is frequent in the Scriptures that the saints seem to contend with God, not indeed with a stubborn and rebellious spirit, but because they feel their faith confirmed by the testing of different arguments. This is why God allows it to them in a friendly way, when he would not even deign to speak with us who persecute his Son. Here the superstition of those is overthrown who think that the Divine intercessors are needed, because it is not allowed for us sinners to come into the sight of God: since he hears mercifully not only the prayers of his own people but also the reasons brought against his commands which they have offered. We must take care, however, that we do not abuse God's clemency, by pressing our murmurings and stubborn disobedience too far; rather let us submit ourselves wholly to God, to whom all our reasons ought to yield. For he, as though taught by us, never changes his decree, since his counsel remains for ever. Paul experiences this very thing at present. For the Lord presses his command and plainly sends him away to the Gentiles, promising nothing for the time about the progress of the gospel among them, because he wishes us simply to obey him.

units.la: Porrò plura dicturo Paulo, & haud dubiè doctrinæ suæ rationem redditurò, Iudæi insanis clamoribus obstrepunt, imò ad necem illum deposcunt. Gentium enim mentione audita, nullum amplius vel patientiæ vel modestiæ locum superesse putant. Huius verò importunitatis causa est, infelices suiipsius fiducia. Quia enim sibi solis populi Dei titulum vendicabant, & legalis cultus merito nitebantur, indignum & iniquissimum facinus esse credebant, si quis gentes incircumcisas, nulla adhuc legis disciplina cicuratas, ipsis in salutis causa pares faceret. Adeò ferox & insolens est hypocrisis malum. Ita Christo olim Pharisæos infensos fuisse scimus, quòd publicanis salutè prædicaret. Ita hodie Monachis & horum sectatoribus intolerabilis videtur euangelij doctrina, quòd peccatoribus salutem in Christo nuntiat, eosq; sola fide iustificari docet. Ita enim sua figmenta æterni videntur, quibus totis animis confidunt. Nos verò Dei bonitate agnoscamus, nec nos salutis socios habere pigeat peccatores ad fidem conuersos, quando inter latrones suspendi, & illic peccata totius mundi exspiare voluit vnigenitus Dei filius, & saluator noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, when Paul was about to say more, and no doubt to give an account of his teaching, the Jews drown him out with mad shouts, and even demand his death. For as soon as the mention of the Gentiles is heard, they think there is no longer any room for patience or moderation. The cause of this unreasonable behaviour is their own unhappy self-confidence. For since they claimed for themselves alone the title of the people of God and relied on the merit of legal worship, they believed it an unworthy and most unjust crime if anyone made the uncircumcised Gentiles, not yet tamed by any discipline of the law, equal to themselves in the cause of salvation. So fierce and insolent is the evil of hypocrisy. Thus we know that the Pharisees were once hostile to Christ because he preached salvation to the publicans. Thus today the teaching of the gospel seems intolerable to the Monks and their followers, because it announces salvation in Christ to sinners and teaches that they are justified by faith alone. For they seem to themselves to have eternal stability in their own fictions, in which they trust with their whole souls. But let us acknowledge God's goodness, and let us not be ashamed to have as partners in salvation sinners converted to the faith, since the only-begotten Son of God and our Saviour, Jesus Christ, chose to be hanged among thieves and there to expiate the sins of the whole world: to whom belongs blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLVI.

units.la: Vociferantibus autè eis, & proiicientibus vestimenta, & pulverem iactantibus in aerem, iussit Tribunus eum induci in castra, & imperauit eum flagris examinari, vt sciret propter quam causam sic acclamarent ei. Et cùm astrinxisset eum loris, dixit astanti sibi Centurioni Paulus: Num hominem Romanum & indemnatum licet vobis flagellare? Quo audito, Centurio accessit ad Tribunum, & nuntiauit ei, dicens: Quid facturus es? hic enim homo Romanus est. Accedens autem Tribunus dixit illi: Dic mihi, num tu Romanus es? At ille dixit: Etiam. Et respondit Tribunus: Ego multa summa ciuitatē istam comparaui. Paulus verò dixit: Ego autem etiam natus sum. Protinus ergo discesserunt ab illo, qui illū examinaturi fuerant. Tribunus quoq; timuit, postquam resciuit quòd Romanus esset, & quòd vinxisset eum. Postero autē die volens scire certum, qua de causa accusaretur à Iudæis, soluit eum à vinculis, & iussit principes Sacerdotum conuenire totumq; concilium, & deductum Paulum stetit coram illis.
units.tr: While they were shouting, throwing off their clothes and tossing dust into the air, the tribune ordered him to be taken into the barracks, and commanded that he be examined under the lash, so that he might learn why they cried out against him like this. But when they had stretched him out with thongs, Paul said to the centurion who stood by: "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen, and one who has not been condemned?" When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and reported it, saying: "What are you going to do? For this man is a Roman." So the tribune came up and said to him: "Tell me, are you a Roman?" And he said: "Yes." The tribune answered: "I acquired this citizenship for a large sum." But Paul said: "Yet I was born to it." Immediately those who were about to examine him withdrew from him. The tribune also was afraid, after he learned that he was a Roman and that he had bound him. On the next day, wishing to know for certain why he was being accused by the Jews, he released him from his chains, ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble, and brought Paul down and set him before them.

units.la: Ettsi Paulus apostolus ad accusationis capita, quibus illum aduersarij petebant, ita respondebit, vt pijs omnibus satisfacere potuerit, vtpote cùm Dei mandatum & imperium in omnibus allegarit: Iudæis tamen adeò non satisfecit, vt illum ne audire quidem dignati sint amplius. Indignationis verò huius causa vnica fuit, quòd se diuinitus ad gentes ablegatum fuisse diceret. Ita enim se tanquam salute indignos reiicit, & gentes ipsis præferri sentiebant, id quòd ipsis indignissimum facinus videbatur, eò quòd Iudæorum populus iam ante Dei peculiū, gentes verò pro immundis & alienos à regno Dei habitæ fuissent. Est enim hoc omnibus hypocritis proprium, quòd peccatores in salute tis consortio ferre non possunt, vt nuper audinimus. Caeterum coeptam historiam persequens Lucas, quid porrò factum sit narrat. Vbi singula personae nobis considerandae veniunt.
units.tr: Although the apostle Paul answered the heads of the accusation, with which his adversaries assailed him, in such a way that he could satisfy all the godly, since he had appealed in all things to the command and authority of God, nevertheless he did not satisfy the Jews so completely that they deigned to hear him any further. The sole cause of their indignation was that he said he had been sent by divine command to the Gentiles. For in this way he seemed to cast himself off as unworthy of salvation, and they felt that the Gentiles were being preferred to them, which seemed to them the most outrageous thing, since the Jewish people had already been God's peculiar possession, while the Gentiles had been regarded as unclean and strangers to the kingdom of God. For it is characteristic of all hypocrites that they cannot bear sinners as partners in salvation, as we heard recently. But Luke, pursuing the history he has begun, tells what was afterwards done. Here the individual persons come before us for consideration.

units.la: Et primò quidem de Iudaeis dicendum, qui Paulum vasanis clamoribus ad necem poscunt, priusquam perorauerit. Quod eo indignius fit, quòd suae gentis hominem, prophani ethnici & militis libidini (quantum in ipsis est) excruciandum propinant. Accedit etiam, quòd nullis vel argumentis, vel aliqua saltem honesti specie, sed clamoribus, vestium abiectione, pulueris iactatione, aliisque gestibus furiosis causam hanc agunt, qui insanis & mente captis in vsu esse consueuerunt. Quo exemplo admonemur, quantum possit Veritatis odium, dum eos, quorum mentes occupauit, omnis tum modestiae, tum aequitatis & charitatis obliuisci facit. Quod enim aduersus Paulum hic fit, id antea coram Pilato in Christi causa factitatum scimus. Nec exempla desunt, quibus probari possit, hodie etiam ab impiis hoc ipsum vsurpari. Docet praeterea locus hic, quibus argumentis fere Christi cultores oppugnentur, si quando illorum simul et fidei causa agitur. Clamoribus nimirum, minis, supplicijs, ferro, igne, &c. Pugnatum bis armis ab ipsa rerum origine, & ijsdem hodie etiam pugnatur. Estque haec deploranda mundi caecitas, siue peruersitas, quòd cum in prophanis negotijs maturam deliberationem omnes laudent, in religionis negotio & communi aeternae salutis causa plerique improbis clamoribus & vasanis tumultibus rem transfigendam esse existiment.
units.tr: And first we must speak of the Jews, who with savage outcries demand Paul's death before he has even finished speaking. This is the more outrageous because they hand over a man of their own nation to be tortured at the lust of a profane heathen soldier (so far as lies in them). Add to this that they carry on this case not with any arguments, or at least some appearance of honesty, but with shouting, stripping off their garments, throwing dust, and other frenzied gestures, the behaviour of madmen and people out of their minds. From this example we are warned how much the hatred of the truth can do, when it makes those whose minds it has seized forget all moderation, all fairness and all charity. For what is done here against Paul, we know was previously practised before Pilate in the cause of Christ. Nor are there lacking examples by which it could be shown that today also the ungodly use this very method. This passage also teaches with what arguments the worshippers of Christ are usually assailed, whenever their cause is brought into question: namely with outcries, threats, punishments, the sword, fire, and so on. From the very beginning of the world there has been fighting with arms, and the same fighting goes on today. And this is the lamentable blindness or perversity of the world: that, while everyone praises mature deliberation in profane affairs, in the matter of religion and the common cause of eternal salvation, most men think the matter must be settled by wicked clamour and violent tumults.

units.la: Quid autem in tanto Iudaeorum furore Tribunus agit? Primò Paulum in castra abducere iubet: quod prudenter ab illo factum fuit, eo quòd non aliud erat efficacius sedandi populi medium, quàm e conspectu eum subducere, aduersus quem tanta ira & odio exarserant. Mox autem iniustitia peccat, dum flagris eum examinari iubet pro veteri more, in quo nulla adhuc satis firma criminis suspicio haerebat. Nihil enim aduersus illum Iudaei probauerant. Et Paulum cordatissime illorum calumniis respondisse audierat. At excusatione dignus esse videtur, quòd verisimile erat, non extra culpam eum esse, qui communibus populi suffragijs ad necem postulabatur. Caeterum si hoc demus, quis obsecro innocens sit? Quis non seditiosis clamoribus obruetur? Graue ergo hoc Tribuni peccatum est. Et ex eo discant quicunque in magistratu versantur, ne in tormentis siue quaestionibus nimium vel praecipites vel crudeles sint. Vt enim grauis culpa est, innocentem infamibus tormentis subijcere: ita non raro fit, vt dolore superati homines, ea se fecisse fateantur, quae ne cogitarunt quidem. Interim vero impiorum magistratuum mores obseruabis. Prudentia quidem in rebus ciuilibus mirificè pollent, & ea fere filios lucis superant. Interea autem non veram iustitiam, sed huius inanem duntaxat speciem habent, qua palliati, iudicia pro suo arbitrio & commodo versare solent. Exemplum huius in Pilato quoque habetur: & multa eius generis per omnes historias extant. At infelix fere iudiciorum eiusmodi exitus est, vt paulò post videbimus. Iustitiae ergo veraeque deant quicunque in magistratu versantur, quando Dei iudicia illis credita sunt, & suorum sanguinem aliquando de ipsorum manibus dominus requiret. Docemur item exemplo hoc, quae nam in hoc munere sanctorum fors sit. Cum facinorosis deputantur, & mortalium vilissimi habentur, in quorum coporibus & vita cuiuis pro suo arbitrio impunè ludere liceat. Experti sunt hoc olim prophetae. Sensit idem Christus, cui hoc euenturum esse propheta praedixerat. Isa. 53. Luc. 22. Et eiusdem praecursorem Iohannem indigna sua morte incestae Herodis & Herodiadis libidini seruire oportuit. Horum ergo catalogo nos quoque adnumerari non pigeat, nec iniquis mundi iudicijs offendamur, quando constat, Deum suorum memoriam afferre, nec diu latitare posse calumniis oppressam innocentium famam. Vide Psal. 34. Luc. 12.
units.tr: But what does the tribune do amid such frenzy of the Jews? First he orders Paul to be led into the barracks; and this he did wisely, because there was no more effective means of calming the people than to remove from their sight the man against whom they had blazed up with such anger and hatred. Soon after, however, he sins by injustice, when he orders him to be examined with the lash according to the old custom, although as yet no sufficiently firm suspicion of crime clung to him. For the Jews had proved nothing against him, and he had heard Paul answer their calumnies most wisely. Yet he seems deserving of excuse, because it was likely that the man who was being demanded for death by the common votes of the people was not free from blame. Still, if we grant this, who, I beg you, is innocent? Who would not be overwhelmed by seditious shouts? This is therefore a grave sin of the tribune. Let all who hold office learn from it not to be either too hasty or too cruel in torments or examinations. For just as it is a grave fault to subject an innocent man to infamous torments, so it often happens that men overcome by pain confess to things they never even thought of. Meanwhile, observe the character of ungodly magistrates. They are indeed remarkably strong in prudence in civil affairs, and in this they mostly surpass the sons of light. Yet they have not true justice but only an empty appearance of it, under which, cloaked, they are accustomed to bend judgments to their own will and advantage. An example of this is found in Pilate too, and many things of this kind exist throughout all histories. But the outcome of such judgments is almost always unhappy, as we shall soon see. Let all who hold office, therefore, cultivate justice and true uprightness, since the judgments of God have been entrusted to them, and the Lord will at some time require the blood of his people at their hands. We are taught also by this example what the lot of the saints in this office may be: they are counted among criminals and held the most worthless of mortals, on whose bodies and lives anyone may freely sport at his own pleasure. The prophets once experienced this. Christ too felt it, though the prophet had foretold that this would happen to him (Isa. 53; Luke 22). And his forerunner John had to suffer an unworthy death, to serve the incestuous lust of Herod and Herodias. Let us therefore not be ashamed to be numbered among this catalogue, nor be offended by the unjust judgments of the world, since it is certain that God brings the memory of his own to light, and that the good name of the innocent, crushed by calumny, cannot lie hidden for long. See Ps. 34; Luke 12.

units.la: Sed Paulum videamus, de cuius capite hic agitur. Numquid trunci instar tacet? Minimè. Imò ad Leges recurrit, & Rom. ciuitatis ius allegat, quo etiam defenditur & liberatur. Vt primum enim Romanum ciuem esse Tribunus audit, illum vinculis solui iubet, nec tormentis in illum vtitur. Sanctorum ergo patientia non ignauia quaedam aut belluina stupiditas est, qualem multi imaginantur. Parati quidem sunt pro Christo quiduis ferre. Interim legitimam defensionem, quae cum fide non pugnat, minimè negligunt. Vt enim alijs Dei creaturis vti licet, ita legibus quoque, quando harum authoritas à Deo maximè dependet, à quo magistratus instituti esse constat. At quanto iniquior (prob dolor) hodie sanctorum fors est? Licet enim religionis causam hic agi Tribunus sciret, Paulum tamen Romanis priuilegijs gaudere patitur. At hodie leges simul & publica iura silent, fi quando de religione controuersia est. Id vero omne Pontificibus debemus, qui de hæresi suspectis da tam quoq; fidem fallere, licitum esse docent. Plura, quæ in hunc locum dici poterant, ex Cap. XVI. petantur, vbi quid Philippus Paulus simili omnino ratione egerit, describitur.
units.tr: But let us look at Paul, whose case is under discussion here. Does he keep silent like a stump? By no means. Rather he has recourse to the laws, and appeals to the right of Roman citizenship, by which he is also defended and set free. For as soon as the tribune hears that he is a Roman citizen, he orders him to be released from his chains, and does not use torments against him. The patience of the saints, therefore, is not a kind of cowardice or bestial stupidity, as many imagine. They are indeed ready to bear anything whatever for Christ; yet meanwhile they by no means neglect lawful defence, which does not conflict with faith. For just as it is lawful to use other creatures of God, so also to use the laws, since their authority depends greatly on God, by whom magistrates are known to have been appointed. But how much more unjust (alas!) is the lot of the saints today? For although the tribune knew that the cause of religion was being argued here, he still allowed Paul to enjoy the privileges of a Roman. Today, however, the laws and public rights fall silent whenever there is controversy about religion. We owe all this to the Papists, who teach that it is lawful to break faith even with those suspected of heresy. More things that could be said on this passage may be sought in chapter 16, where it is described how Paul and Silas acted in a quite similar manner.

units.la: Sequitur tandem primi actus huius Tragœdiæ exitus. Timet Tribunus, non quidem Deum, sed Romanarum legum seueritatem. Est hic omnium impiorum mos, vt præpostero metu territi, homines magis quam Deum timeant. Interim errorem commissum emendare, & causam omnem certius cognoscere volens, crastino Paulum in Concilium producit, de cuius integritate & sanctitate nimirum sibi multa promittebat. Ex eorum enim numero Tribunus hic est, qui hodie quoq; de Concilijs nihil non boni sperant, cum illa iam multis seculis omnium piorum spem fefellisse constet: quando ab illis & connocantur & reguntur, quibus sacra omnia venalia sunt, quorumq; tyrannide orbis Christianus premitur. Obseruemus autem, quam prosit publicas Leges seueriter custodire. Licet enim infamis bestia Claudius Cæsar fuerit, quo regnante hæc gesta sunt, quia tamen Legum authoritas adhuc viguit, aliqua superfuit bonus defensio. Ast vbi eadem extincta iacet, respub. diu stare impossibile est. Admonet præterea Tribuni exemplum, quid eos maneat, qui iudicia in hominum gratiam præcipitare solent: Metus nimirum, infamis trepidatio, & pudenda rerum omnium confusio. Horum itaq; memores, quicunq; magistratus gerunt, mature iudicia administrent. Interim consolationem hinc petant pij, quando impios persecutores tam facile terrefieri posse vident Christi virtute: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: At last comes the outcome of the first act of this tragedy. The tribune is afraid, not indeed of God, but of the severity of the Roman laws. This is the custom of all the ungodly: terrified by a perverted fear, they fear men rather than God. Meanwhile, wishing to correct the error committed and to learn the whole cause more certainly, he brings Paul before the council on the next day, from whose integrity and holiness he evidently expected much. For the tribune belongs to that number who today too hope for nothing but good from councils, although it is certain that for many centuries they have disappointed the hopes of all the godly, since they are convened and governed by men for whom all sacred things are for sale, and by whose tyranny the Christian world is oppressed. Let us observe, moreover, how useful it is to keep public laws strictly. For although Claudius Caesar, under whose reign these things were done, was an infamous beast, yet because the authority of the laws still flourished, some good defence survived. But where that authority lies extinguished, it is impossible for a commonwealth to stand long. The example of the tribune also warns what awaits those who are accustomed to rush judgments to win men's favour: namely fear, shameful trembling, and utter confusion of all things. Let all who hold magistracy therefore keep these things in mind, and administer judgments without delay. Meanwhile the godly may draw comfort from this, since they see that the ungodly persecutors can so easily be terrified by the power of Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVII.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLVII.

units.la: INtentis autem oculis in Concilium Paulus ait: Viri fratres, Ego omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum coram deo vsq; in hodiernũ diem. Princeps autem sacerdotum Ananias præcepit astantibus sibi, vt percuterent os eius. Tunc Paulus dixit ad eum: Percussurus est te Deus, paries dealbate. Et tu sedes iudicans secundum Legem, & contra Legem me iubes percuti? Qui vero astabant, dixerunt: Summo sacerdoti Dei maledicis? Dixit autem Paulus: Nesciebam fratres, quod Pontifex esset. Scriptum est enim: Principi populi tui non maledices.
units.tr: Fixing his eyes on the council, Paul said: "Brothers, I have lived before God in all good conscience up to this day." But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike his mouth. Then Paul said to him: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! Do you sit to judge me according to the Law, and yet order me to be struck contrary to the Law?" But those who stood by said: "Do you revile God's high priest?" Paul replied: "I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. For it is written: 'You shall not curse the ruler of your people.'"

units.la: VT Paulum electum sibi organum esse voluit Christus dominus: ita eiusdem exemplo omnes nos docet, quid fideles suos in hoc mundo maneat, quodq; illorum sit in ferendis aduersis officium. Paulus enim, vt primum Christo nomen dedit, eos acerrimos hostes sensit, pro quorum salute dies & noctes excubabat: Iudæos nimirum, in quorum gratiam anathema quoque fieri optauit. Eousque vero illorum rabies processit, vt Romanos Tribunos (quos alioqui cane & angue peius oderant) aduersus ipsum armauerint. Est hæc omnium piorum sors, vt domesticos suos & intimos quosque sibi hostiliter aduersari sentiant, quorum odium plerunque ita exardescit, vt ab hostibus quoq; contra fratres Christianos auxilia postulare non vereantur. Sed constans animi Paulus & ad quosuis aduersariorum conatus imperterritus, solo dei verbo & iussu se & causam suam tuetur: cuius exemplum nos quoq; cum simili casus vrget, imitari conuenit. Porro in tota hac actione cum primis admirandum est & consolationis plenum, quod maiorem æquitatem in Tribuno, ethnico & militari homine, Paulus inuenit, quam apud suæ gentis primates, qui & pietatis & eruditionis titulum sibi vendicabant. Illeenim apertam vim prohibet, & furentium manibus de vita periclitantem eripit. Deinde Leges inuocantem audit, illumq; Romanis priuilegijs gaudere patitur. Tandem cum causam hanc circa religionem maxime versari videret, nihil temere sibi amplius permittendum putans, adeos rem omnem refert, qui huius professione gloriabantur. Connocato enim Sacerdotum & Scribarum Concilio, in hoc Paulum sistit, vt legitima & feria fiat in illius causam, inquisitio. Prudenter quidem hoc nec iniquè, quoad ethnicum hominem, sed (vt heri monuimus) eo fallitur, quòd de Concilij sanctitate plus sibi pollicetur, quàm deberet. Docet hoc abunde sequens actio, quæ Sacerdotes hosce summam tum audaciam tum improbitatem cum hypocrisi coniunxisse testatur. Sed singulas eius partes ordine videamus.
units.tr: Just as the Lord Christ wished Paul to be his chosen instrument, so through Paul's example he teaches all of us what awaits his faithful people in this world, and what their duty is in bearing adversity. For when Paul first gave his name to Christ, he found those as his most bitter enemies for whose salvation he had watched day and night, namely the Jews, for whose sake he even wished to be made anathema. Their rage went so far that they armed the Roman tribunes against him, men whom they otherwise hated worse than dog and snake. This is the lot of all the godly: they find that their own household and closest intimates oppose them as enemies, and their hatred often blazes up so fiercely that they do not hesitate to seek help from enemies against Christian brothers. But Paul, steadfast in spirit and undaunted by any attempt of his opponents, defends himself and his cause by the word and command of God alone. When a similar case presses on us, it is fitting that we imitate his example. Moreover, in this whole action the most remarkable and comforting thing is that Paul found greater fairness in the tribune, a heathen and a military man, than among the leading men of his own nation, who claimed for themselves the title of both piety and learning. For the tribune forbids open violence and snatches him from the hands of the raging men, when his life was in danger. Then he hears Paul appealing to the laws, and allows him to enjoy the privileges of a Roman. At last, seeing that this cause concerned religion above all, and thinking he should not presume to do anything more on his own, he refers the whole matter to those who boasted of their profession of it. For, having summoned the council of priests and scribes, he sets Paul before them, so that a lawful and proper inquiry may be made into his case. This was wise and not unjust, so far as a heathen man could judge, but (as we noted yesterday) he was deceived in this, that he expected more from the holiness of the council than he should have. The following account teaches this amply, showing that these priests combined the greatest audacity and wickedness with hypocrisy. But let us look at each part of it in order.

units.la: A Paulo enim exorsus Lucas, quomodo se in Concilio hoc gesserit, docet. Et primò quidem gestum corporis & vultum denotans, ipsum intentis oculis totum illum confessum inspexisse dicit. Fuit hoc præsentis & constantis animi argumentum, quo cumprimis armatos esse conuenit, qui Veritatis causam agunt: ne metu superati & hanc perfidè deserant, & animum addant impijs Christi hostibus, qui plerunq; ex piorum ignauia vires colligunt. Interim apparet hic promissionum Christi veritas. Pollicetur is suis spiritum aduocatum, qui illos confortaturus simul & consilia suggestu-rus sit, si quando in frequenti procerum consessu fidei suæ rationem reddere cogantur. Promissionis ergo suæ memor in tanto tamq; præsenti periculo apostolum suum minimè deserit, sed eundem inuicta animi constantia armat. At cum generales sint promissiones hæ, nos quoque ex his consolatio-ne petere decet.
units.tr: Luke begins with Paul and shows how he conducted himself in this council. First, noting his bodily bearing and countenance, he says that Paul looked with fixed eyes upon the whole assembly. This was a sign of a present and steadfast spirit, with which those who contend for the cause of truth ought above all to be armed, so that they are not overcome by fear and basely desert it, and so that they do not give courage to Christ's impious enemies, who usually gather their strength from the cowardice of the godly. Here too the truth of Christ's promises appears. He promised his people the Spirit as Advocate, who would both strengthen them and suggest counsel when they are compelled to give an account of their faith before a crowded assembly of the leading men. Mindful of his promise, then, in so great and so present a danger, he does not desert his apostle, but arms him with unconquered constancy of spirit. And since these promises are general, it is fitting that we too seek comfort from them.

units.la: INDE vero dicendi Exordium faciens Paulus, de innocentia sua confidenter pronunciat. Ego (inquit) omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum coram Deo usque in hodiernum diem. Quæ verba non ita accipi debent, quasi se omnis peccati immunem esse, & coram Dei tribunali propria iustitia consistere posse glorietur, sed ad præsentem causam respicit. Accusabant enim illum aduersarij turpis ab avita religione defectionis, impietatis item, & quòd instar publici hostis Legem & templum totumq; cultum Leuiticum improbè violauisset, & impuras gentes impio ausu in populi Dei consortium intrudere conatus esset. Ne qui ergo初 sinistris suspicionibus præuenti, aures ipsi negarent, se initio statim omnicul-pa liberat, dum se, quoad apostolicum munus, bona conscientia omnia egisse dicit, adeò vt suæ integritatis testem Deum citare possit. Alioqui se peccatorem esse, & Christi gratia ac merito indigere passim fatetur. Ita frequenter sanctii in priuatis causis aduersus calumniatores suam innocentiam allegant, qui interim se in Dei conspectu immundos & peccatores esse, humiliter agnoscunt: cuius rei exempla in Dauide, Mose & innumeris alijs exstant.
units.tr: Then, beginning his speech, Paul confidently declares his innocence. "I," he says, "have lived before God in all good conscience up to this day." These words should not be taken as though he boasted that he was free from all sin and could stand before God's tribunal by his own righteousness. Rather he looks to the present case. For his adversaries accused him of shameful defection from the faith of his fathers, and also of impiety, and of having, like a public enemy, wickedly violated the Law, the temple, and the whole Levitical worship, and of having impiously tried to thrust unclean Gentiles into the fellowship of God's people. Lest, therefore, he be prejudiced by these sinister suspicions and the ears of his hearers be closed to him, he at once frees himself from all blame, saying that in the apostolic office he has done everything with a good conscience, so much so that he can call God to witness his integrity. Otherwise he freely confesses everywhere that he is a sinner and needs the grace and merit of Christ. So the saints often plead their innocence in private causes against slanderers, while at the same time they humbly acknowledge that they are unclean and sinners in the sight of God. Examples of this are found in David, Moses, and countless others.

units.la: DOCET autem hoc Pauli Exordium, in religionis causa cumprimis conscientiæ rationem habendam esse, ne quid dolo malo aut per hypocrisim fiat. Quia enim hic cum Deo nobis res est, qui corda renes-q; scrutatur, nullus dolo aut simulationi locus esse poterit. Licebit autem nobis de conscientiæ integritate gloriari, si religionem non pro nostri ingenij arbitrio, sed iuxta Dei verbum instituamus, & in Dei vocatione diligenter ambulemus. Quod si fiat, quotidianos vitæ lapsus, qui ex carnis infirmitate accidunt, clementer condonat Deus, eò quòd ad Christum conuersi, in illo pœnitentiam iugem agimus.
units.tr: This exordium of Paul teaches that, in matters of religion above all, account must be taken of conscience, so that nothing is done with evil intent or by hypocrisy. For since we have to do here with God, who searches hearts and reins, there can be no room for deceit or pretence. We may glory in the integrity of our conscience if we set up religion not according to the judgement of our own wit but according to God's Word, and walk carefully in the calling of God. If this is done, God mercifully pardons the daily slips of life that arise from the weakness of the flesh, because we have turned to Christ and in him live in continual repentance.

units.la: Porro cum dicendi initium Paulus fecisset, Ananias qui Concilio præsidebat, illius os percuteri iussit: Vel quòd nondum requisitus cœpisset causam dicere: Vel etiam quòd insolentes illos & superbos titulos, quibus iam ante assueuerant, omisisset. Est enim cumprimis irritabile hoc hominum genus, maximè quando æstimationem suam labefactari putant, quam ipsi cum gloria Dei, tum publica hominum salutì longè præferunt. Obseruemus autem hoc loco, qualia ferè esse soleant impiorum antistitum Concilia. Calumnijs ante grauatus fuit Paulus, quibus totius gentis odium illi conciliare studuerunt. His cum in frequenti totius populi concione responderet, furiosis clamoribus disturbarunt: nunc denuò excusationem paranti aperta vi resistunt, idq; in loco iustitiæ sacro, cuius studiosissimi videri volebant. Talè omnino Concilium fuit, in quo Christus, Caiapha præsidente damnatus fuit. Nec multum dissimile vidimus illud, quo Stephanus oppressus est. Talia item iam multis seculis fuerunt Pontificum Concilia, quod vel vno Constantiensi probari poterat, in quo ijsdem armis sanctissimos Christi martyres, Iohannem Huffum & Hieronymum Pragensem damnatos fuisse legimus. Quid vero de nostri seculi Concilijs sperari debeat, ex ipsis Indictionibus siue Bullis abunde patet: quarum fraudem & impudentiam qui non animaduertunt, nè illi communi sensu carere censendi sunt, &c.
units.tr: Moreover, when Paul had made the beginning of his speech, Ananias, who presided over the council, ordered his mouth to be struck. Perhaps he did so because Paul had begun to speak before being questioned, or perhaps because Paul had omitted those insolent and proud titles to which they had been accustomed before. For this kind of men is especially irritable, most of all when they think their own esteem, which they put far above both the glory of God and the public salvation of men, is being weakened. Let us observe here what sort of councils the impious bishops are usually accustomed to hold. Paul had already been burdened by slanders, by which they had tried to make the whole nation hate him. When he answered these in the crowded assembly of the whole people, they disturbed him with furious shouts; now, when he prepares to defend himself again, they resist him by open force, and that in a place of justice, sacred to it, of which they wished to appear the most zealous guardians. Such indeed was the council in which Christ was condemned, with Caiaphas presiding. Nor did we see anything very different in that by which Stephen was overwhelmed. Such councils of the Popes have existed for many centuries, as the single Council of Constance could prove, in which, with the same weapons, the most holy martyrs of Christ, John Hus and Jerome of Prague, were condemned, as we read. What may be hoped for from the councils of our own age is clear enough from their very indictments or bulls. Those who do not notice their deceit and shamelessness must be judged to lack common sense, etc.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum reuersi, vt is facinus hoc acceperit, videamus. Percutiet te (inquit) Deus, paries dealbate, &c. Quibus verbis nonnulli contra Christi præceptum peccare visus est, quo percutienti nos in vnam maxillam, alteram obuertere iubemur. At culpa facilè liberabitur, si tum verba cum batum personam eius inspiciamus. Nec enim quicquam illi prauo affectu imprecatur, sed pro apostoli officio peccatum arguit, & poenam à Deo paratam denunciat. Et primò quidem parietem dealbatum vocat, nimirum Christi exemplum secutus, qui totum illum ordinem sepulchris dealbatis similem esse dixit. Mox verò sui dicti rationem reddit, addens: Tu sedes me secundum legem iudicaturus, id est, legis praetextu superbus, iudicandi potestatem tibi vendicas, interim verò contra legem me percuti iubes. Minimè ergo iudicis titulo & personae respondes, sed sub hoc involucro animum veritatis impatientem & sanguinis sitientem improbè celas. Ideo te Deus percussurus est, licet nemo sit mortalium, qui tibi vindices manus iniicere ausit. Haec (inquam) non conuiciandi studio, sed pro ministri officio Paulus loquitur: nec dubium est, ipsum ad Christi exemplum respexisse, qui percutienti se Pontificis seruo, non alteram maxillam obuertit, sed illius proteruiam seuerè corripuit. Atqui hoc etiam loco docemur, patientiam, quam sacrae litterae praecipiunt, non stoicordiâ quandam esse, quae impijs quiduis faciendi copiam faciat. Licet enim patienter ferre inbeamur quicquid dominus dederit: minimè tamen impijs blandiri aut Dei iudicia dissimulare debemus. Simul verò generalis doctrina ijs, qui in magistratu versantur, hinc petenda est. Quod enim Ananiae Paulus minatur, non multo post accidit, quando circa initia belli Iudaici à Manaimo rebellium Iudaeorum duce crudeliter occisus est: dignus vt à talibus occideretur, qui Deo rebellare non verebatur. Nec vnquam Dei vindicis manum subterfugient, quicunq; hunc imitati, Deo aduersantur, et innocentes violenter opprimunt, vel ab alijs opprimi patiuntur. Percutiet illos dominus, quem solum verum iudiciorum praesidem & vindicem esse scriptura passim docent. Et licet homines terrere possint, Dei tamen manus nunquam euadent. Exempla sunt in Pharaone, Saulo, Achabo & multis alijs, quorum prophanae historiae mentionem faciunt.
units.tr: But let us return to Paul and see how he took this outrage. "God will strike you," he says, "you whitewashed wall, etc." By these words some seem to have sinned against Christ's command, by which we are bidden, when someone strikes us on one cheek, to turn the other. But the charge will easily be cleared if we look at both the words and the person of the speaker. For he does not invoke anything upon him out of ill feeling, but as an apostle's duty he rebukes the sin and declares the punishment prepared by God. First he calls him a whitewashed wall, following without doubt Christ's example, who said that that whole order was like whitewashed sepulchres. Then he gives the reason for his words, adding: "You sit to judge me according to the Law," that is, under the pretext of the Law you claim for yourself the power of judging, and meanwhile you order me to be struck contrary to the Law. Therefore you are not answering to the title and character of a judge, but under this cover you wickedly hide a mind impatient of the truth and thirsting for blood. Therefore God will strike you, although there is no mortal who dares to lay violent hands on you as an avenger. I say that Paul speaks these things not from a desire to revile, but from the duty of a minister; and there is no doubt that he looked to Christ's example, who, when struck by the servant of the high priest, did not turn the other cheek, but sharply rebuked his insolence. Indeed we are taught here too that the patience which the Holy Scriptures command is not a kind of stoic insensibility that gives the wicked free rein to do whatever they please. For although we are bidden to bear patiently whatever the Lord has given, yet we must by no means flatter the impious or dissemble the judgements of God. At the same time, a general teaching for those who hold office should be drawn from this. For what Paul threatens Ananias came to pass not long after, when, at the beginning of the Jewish war, he was cruelly killed by Manaem, leader of the rebellious Jews, being worthy to be slain by such men as he, who did not fear to rebel against God. Nor will any of those who imitate him, who oppose God and violently oppress the innocent or allow them to be oppressed by others, ever escape the hand of God the avenger. The Lord will strike them, he who alone the Scriptures everywhere teach is the true judge and avenger of judgements. And although men can terrify, they will never escape the hands of God. Examples are found in Pharaoh, Saul, Ahab and many others, whom profane histories also mention.

units.la: At Paulo haec dicente, mox prodeunt, qui illum corripiant, cum nemo interim Ananiae iniustam vim reprehenderit. Vt enim tyranni sibijpsis quiduis faciendi potestate faciunt, ita adulatores quoq; facile inueniunt, qui illorum authoritatem aduersus quosuis tueantur. Quo fit, vt cum omnibus fere iniurias inferant intolerabiles, nemo tamen de illis conqueri audeat. Similis in ecclesia iam multis annis Cleri tyrannis grassata est. Cū enim libidine sua omnibus molesti fuerint Monachi & Sacrificuli, sacrosancti tamen habiti fuerunt, illosque vel dicto lacessere fuit periculosissimum. Caeterum Paulus elegantì Ironia hypocrisim tyrannicam arguit, dicens: Nescieba fratres, quòd Pontifex esset. Quasi diceret: Quis verò pro Pontifice eum agnoscat, in quo nihil ipso nomine & titulo dignum cernitur? Si enim Pontifex est, cur non causas pacato animo & aequis auribus percipit? Cur causam dicenti impudenter obstrepit? Cur indemnatum percutere iubet? Alioqui non ignoro Lege Dei cautum esse, ne quis legitimis magistratibus maledicat. Vide Deutero. 22. & Exod. 22. Admonentur autem Pauli Ironia magistratus, tunc ipsis suam authoritatem integram & saluam fore, si officium faciant, & tales se praebeant, vt illos honore dignos esse cordati quiuis iudicare possint. Nisi enim Dei gloriam prouehant, vim prohibeant, leges bonas tueantur, exemplo vitae honesto praeeant, idem illis dici poterit, quod Ananiae Paulus hoc loco obijcit. Quis enim blasphemos homines, sanguinarios opprefores, Legum dissipatores, ebrios, adulteros, aleatores, scurras & alios similis farinae homines Senatorum & Principum loco habeat? Scimus equidem tales aliquando iusto Dei iudicio ordinari, quorum intemperiem in prophanis negotijs pij patienter ferunt. At si ijsdem non suus honos habeatur, mirari desinant, & culpam suam agnoscant simul & emendent. Ita enim fiet, vt authoritatis suae vindicem habituri sint regem Regum & dominum dominantium, Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But while Paul was saying these things, men soon came forward to rebuke him, though meanwhile no one censured Ananias for his unjust violence. For just as tyrants make their own power the measure of whatever they please to do, so flatterers readily find people to defend their authority against anyone at all. The result is that, although they inflict almost every kind of unbearable wrong, no one dares to complain about them. In the Church, a similar tyranny of the clergy has run rampant for many years now. For when monks and little priests had been troublesome to everyone at their own whim, they were nevertheless regarded as sacrosanct, and to challenge them even with a word was most dangerous. Paul, however, with elegant irony, exposes this tyrannical hypocrisy, saying: "I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest." As if he were saying: "Who could acknowledge him as a high priest, when nothing worthy of the name and title is to be seen in him? For if he is high priest, why does he not hear the causes with a calm mind and an impartial ear? Why does he shamelessly shout down the man who is pleading his case? Why does he order an uncondemned man to be struck? Otherwise, I am not unaware that the law of God forbids anyone to curse the lawful magistrates. See Deut. 22 and Exod. 22." But by Paul's irony the magistrates are admonished that their authority will remain whole and safe for them only if they perform their duty and show themselves such that all sensible people can judge them worthy of honour. For unless they promote the glory of God, restrain violence, uphold good laws, and lead the way with an honourable example of life, the same may be said of them as Paul here throws at Ananias. For who would count as senators and princes men who are blasphemers, bloody oppressors, destroyers of the laws, drunkards, adulterers, gamblers, buffoons, and others of the same stripe? We know indeed that such men are sometimes appointed by the just judgment of God, and the godly patiently bear their excesses in secular affairs. But if they are not accorded their proper honour, let them cease to wonder, and let them at once acknowledge and amend their own fault. For in this way they will have as the avenger of their authority the King of kings and Lord of lords, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 148.

units.la: Sciens autem Paulus, quòd vna pars esset Sadducaeorum, & altera Pharisaeorum, exclamauit in Concilio: Viri fratres, ego Pharisaeus sum, filius Pharisaei: de spe & resurrectione mortuorum ego iudicor. Et cum hoc dixisset, facta est seditio inter Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos, & scissa est multitudo. Nam Sadducaei quidem dicunt non esse resurrectionem, neque angelum, neque spiritum. Pharisaei autem vtraque confitentur. Fa
units.tr: When Paul knew that one part of the council were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council: "Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee; I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead." And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess all of these. Fa

units.la: Tyrannorum patroni adulatores.
units.tr: The flatterers are the patrons of tyrants.

units.la: Magistratuum authoritas quo modo seruetur. ctus est autem clamor magnus, & surgentes scribae de secta Pharisaeo-rum pugnabant, dicentes: Nihil mali invenimus in homine isto. Quòd si spiritus locutus est ei aut Angelus, ne repugnemus Deo. Et cum ma-gna seditio cohorta esset, veritus Tribunus, ne discerperetur Paulus ab ipsis, iussit milites descendere, & rapere eum de medio illorum, ac de-ducere eum in castra.
units.tr: How the authority of magistrates is to be preserved. ctus. And there was a great clamour, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and contended, saying: "We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, let us not fight against God." And when a great dissension had arisen, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, ordered the soldiers to go down, snatch him from the midst of them, and bring him into the camp.

units.la: VArijs quidem & grauissimis tribulationibus Deus electos suos exercere solet: at idem variis quoq; & nonnunquam inspera-tis medijs eosdem liberat. Exempla utriusq; rei passim extant. Sed inter haec cumprimis memorabile est, quod in Paulo, electo organo Christi, spiritus sanctus per Lucam proponit. Illum enim Iudaeorum insidijs multiuariam petitum fuisse, & aliquoties vitae pe-riculum subiuisse, audiuimus. Sed noua quoque auxilia subinde Deus excitauit, quae eiusmodi fere fuerunt, ut de ijs Paulus ne cogitare quidem, nedum illa petere siue optare potuerit. Primò enim per Tribunum & milites furentium Iudaeorum manibus eripitur. Mox, cum causam dicere-ne-quicquam tentauisset, Romanae ciuitatis priuilegio à flagris defenditur. Tandem cum illius cau-sam simul & vitam Tribunus iniquissimis iudicibus commisisset, ipsos Pauli hostes inter sese plu-rimos tuebantur. ...
units.tr: God is accustomed to exercise his elect with various and very grievous tribulations, but he also delivers the same with various means, and often unexpected ones. Examples of both are found everywhere. But among these, the thing especially worth remembering is what the Holy Spirit sets forth through Luke in Paul, the chosen instrument of Christ. For we have heard that he was sought in many ways by the snares of the Jews, and several times underwent danger to his life. But God also raised up new helps from time to time, and these were of such a kind that Paul could not even have thought of them, much less asked for or wished for them. First, he is snatched from the hands of the raging Jews through the tribune and the soldiers. Soon after, when he had attempted nothing to plead his cause, he is defended from scourging by the privilege of Roman citizenship. Finally, when the tribune had committed both his cause and his life to most unjust judges, many of Paul's own enemies protected him among themselves. ...

units.la: Principio autem causam dissensionis penitius excutere oportet, quam sectarum diuersitatem fuisse Lucas tradit. Aduersariorum enim alij quidem Pharisaei, alij vero Sadducaei erant. Atqui de Iudaeorum sectis multa apud Iosephum extant, qui illarum originem fere ad Machabaeorum tem-pora vsq; extendit. Et sub Ioanne Hircano primo illas coepisse, authores probatissimi testantur. Cū enim Sacerdotes regni potius quàm sacrorum curis & negotijs vacarent, diuersae circa religionem sententiae oriri coeperunt, cessante nimirum verbi dei doctrina, quam in suo populo Deus assiduè esse voluerat. Tres ergo sectae exortae, ecclesiae & populi Dei vnitatem sciderunt. Prima Pharisaeorum fuit, qui Lege non contenti, traditiones sectabantur, & operibus iustitiam ac salutem acquiri posse credebant. Adhaec astris & Astrologiae deditifatum docebant, ea re non multum à Stoicis differen-tes. Et hi quidem externa operum specie velati, pro sanctissimis haberi solebant. Secunda Saddu-caeos habuit, qui fato res hominum regi negantes, liberum arbitrium homini tribuebant. Et quamuis virtutis studium anxiè commendare viderentur, Epicuro tamen & peccandi licentiae fenestram ape-riebant, cum spiritus simul & animarum immortalitatem, deniq; & corporum resurrectionem nega-rent. Fuit ea potentissima omnium, ut alibi vidimus, eò quòd Pharisaeorum traditiones auferiores laxaret, & proinde plerisq; grata esset. Tertiam sectam Esseni constituerunt, qui cum Pharisaeos & Sadducaeos virtutem verbis duntaxat metiri dicerent, ipsi eam factis expressuri, caelibes viue-bant, seruis carebant, bona sua habebant communia, manuum labore victum parabant, sacra quoq; publica non adibant, ne aliorum hominum conuersatione polluerentur. Et quia hi pauci erant nume-ro, nec rempub. affectabant, ad loca hortorum balsami secessserunt, vbi et hortos plantabant & rei me-dicae operam dabant, qua cum multis prodesset, eximiam virtutis exist imationem apud omnes sustinebant. Horum mores fere nostri i seculi Anabaptistae referunt, nisi quod nostri illi & religio magis turbant, & professioni suae minus fideliter respondent, quando in omne libidinis genus proclives ruunt, & belluinis odij inuidiaq; affectibus miserrime ringuntur. Quia tamen auferior fuit Essenorum regula, pauciores quoq; (vt diximus) sectatores habuit. Quae causa est, quòd priorum duntaxat mentionem faciunt scriptores euangelici. Nobis vero obseruandum venit, quantum mali antistitum auaritia, & quae ex hac nascitur discordia, parere soleat: quando hae pestes in veteri ecclesia tam deformem tetramq; faciem induxerunt. Perpetuum enim hunc illarum effectum esse Monachorum ordines, in Papatu eadem origine exorti, abunde docent. Quò magis hodie aduigilandum nobis erit, ne quid simile aut etiā perniciosius accidat. Simul vero Dei bonitas praedicanda est, qui in tam foeda gregis
units.tr: First of all, we must examine more closely the cause of the dissension, which Luke relates to be the diversity of sects. For some of his adversaries were Pharisees, and others Sadducees. Yet much about the Jewish sects is found in Josephus, who traces their origin almost to the times of the Maccabees. And the most approved authors testify that they began under John Hyrcanus the first. For when the priests were concerned more with the affairs and business of the kingdom than with the sacred things, diverse opinions about religion began to arise, doubtless because the teaching of the Word of God had ceased, which God had wished to be constantly present among his people. Three sects therefore arose and split the unity of the Church and people of God. The first was that of the Pharisees, who, not content with the Law, followed traditions, and believed that righteousness and salvation could be obtained by works. Besides this, they were devoted to the stars and astrology, teaching fate, in which respect they did not differ much from the Stoics. And these, veiled in the outward appearance of works, were accustomed to be regarded as most holy. The second was that of the Sadducees, who, denying that human affairs are ruled by fate, attributed free will to man. And although they seemed to recommend the pursuit of virtue earnestly, nevertheless they opened a window to Epicurus and to licence in sinning, since they denied spirits and the immortality of souls, and finally the resurrection of bodies. This sect was the most powerful of all, as we have seen elsewhere, because it loosened the stricter traditions of the Pharisees, and therefore was pleasing to most. The Essenes established the third sect, who, while they said that the Pharisees and Sadducees measured virtue by words only, wished to express it by deeds themselves. They lived as celibates, had no slaves, held their goods in common, and procured their food by the labour of their hands. They also did not attend the public sacred rites, lest they be polluted by the company of other men. And because they were few in number and did not aspire to public office, they withdrew to places of balsam gardens, where they planted gardens and devoted themselves to the medical art, by which they were of benefit to many and enjoyed an outstanding reputation for virtue among all. Their manners are very much like those of our own Anabaptists of this age, except that those men disturb both religion and the state more, and respond less faithfully to their profession, since they rush headlong into every kind of lust, and are most miserably tormented by brutish hatreds and envious passions. Yet because the rule of the Essenes was stricter, they also had fewer followers, as we have said. This is why the evangelical writers mention only the former. For us, however, it is to be noted how much harm the greed of the leaders, and the discord that arises from it, is accustomed to bring forth, since these plagues in the ancient Church introduced so deformed and foul a face. For the orders of monks, arising from the same origin in the Papacy, abundantly teach that this is their perpetual effect. Therefore we must be all the more watchful today, lest something similar, or even more pernicious, happen. At the same time, the goodness of God is to be proclaimed, who, in so foul a dispersion of his flock,

units.la: [Remainder of text illegible at the lower right margin.] gregis sui dissipatione, ecclesia sua reliquias seruauit, ex quibus illa tandem renasci posset. Id quod in Papatu quoque Monachis longe lateque dominantibus, accidisse constat. Vbique enim locorum omnibus seculis inuenti sunt, qui illorum dolos & hypocrisim publicè insectari ausi fuerunt, vt interim de illis nihil dicamus, qui domi latentes, illorum superstitionibus communicare, ingens nefas duxerunt. Habes igitur hoc loco quod aduersarijs nostris respondeas, rogantibus, an nulla ante natos Lutherum & Zuinglium ecclesia fuerit? Fuisse enim hanc scimus, sed tantum non obrutam & sepultam, qualem ante Christi tempora inter Iudaeos fuisse legimus: & qualis Eliae temporibus fuit, quando septem millia hominum Deus superesse dixit, qui genua sua Baali nunquam flexerant, quamuis ne vnus quidem illorum Eliae notus esset. Porro quoad praesentem historiam, docemur, impios licet varie tum moribus tum in religione scindantur, contra Christum tamen & Veritatem facile conuenire. Quia enim vni & eidem principi militant, diabolo, non possunt non omnes eum pro hoste habere, cuius regnum ille cumprimis oppugnat. Vtinam vero in horum consyderatione diligentius versarentur, qui ex differentionibus & pugnis, quas contra Christi ministros, pessimis affectibus consultoribus suscipiunt, praecipuam laudem & gloriam quaerunt. Ita vero animos addunt impijs Christi hostibus, quibus facillimum videtur eos vincere, quos tam acriter dissidere vident. Sed de his alibi commodior erit dicendi locus.
units.tr: [Remainder of text illegible at the lower right margin.] preserved from it the remnants of his Church, from which it might at last be born again. This is known to have happened in the Papacy too, when the monks held sway far and wide. For everywhere and in all ages there have been found those who dared to attack openly their deceits and hypocrisy, not to mention those who, remaining hidden at home, thought it a great wickedness to share in their superstitions. You have here, therefore, something to answer to our adversaries when they ask whether there was no Church before Luther and Zwingli were born? For we know that there was, but almost buried and entombed, like that which we read existed among the Jews before the time of Christ, and like that which existed in the times of Elijah, when God said that seven thousand men remained, who had never bowed their knees to Baal, although not even one of them was known to Elijah. Moreover, as to the present history, we are taught that the impious, though divided in various ways both in morals and in religion, nevertheless readily agree against Christ and the Truth. For since they serve one and the same prince, the devil, they cannot all but regard as enemy the one whose kingdom he especially attacks. Would that those who seek their chief praise and glory in the differences and quarrels they undertake against the ministers of Christ, under the worst affections as their advisers, would consider these matters more diligently! For they thus add courage to the enemies of Christ, who think it very easy to conquer those whom they see disagreeing so bitterly. But a more suitable place for speaking of these things will come elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc Paulum videamus, qui cum ex diuersis sectis aduersariorum suorum cohortem confluxisse sciret, ex tempore de illis inter se committendis consilium capiens, exclamat: Viri fratres, ego Pharisaeus sum, filius Pharisaei, de spe & resurrectione mortuorum ego iudicor. Videtur autem vel dolo malo, vel etiam fidei suae & Christi abnegatione peccasse Paulus, quando se ex eorum ordine esse profitetur, quos acerrimos Christi hostes esse constabat. Sed facile excusari potest. Primo enim effugium tale quaerere cogitur, quando sibi omnem dicendi copiam negari & aperta tyrannide rem agi videbat. Maluisset vtiq; fidem suam ingenuè profiteri, & eius rationem reddere, quod & facere coeperat. Sed interturbatus, nouum consilium capit. Deinde non simpliciter totum Pharisaismum confitetur & probat, sed in solo resurrectionis articulo, quem illi orthodoxè tenebant, illorum partibus se adversus Sadducaeos coniungit. Quid vero de reliquis Pharisaeorum dogmatibus, & in primis operum fiducia, qua illi turgebant, senserit, Epistolae ipsius abunde declarant. Minime ergo illis patrocinatur Pauli exemplum, qui vt vitae & existimationi suae consulant, in fidei causa callide ter giuerfantur, & cum fide Christiana palam pugnantes articulos recipiunt atque probant. Docemur tamen, licere pijs, vt iniquis iudicijs circumuenti effugia quaerant, quatenus illa fine Veritatis iactura inuenire possunt: ne temerè periclitando Veritatem quoque secum in periculum adducant. In primis vero obserua, quod se de mortuorum resurrectione iudicari, dicit Paulus. Atqui longè aliter sonabant accusationis capita. Sed resurrectionem allegat, eò quod circa hanc totum fidei & religionis negotium versatur, quemadmodum ipse in priori ad Corinth.cap.15.docet. Et quia in eadem omnis sanctorum spes consistit, de spe quoque se iudicari dicit. Nam si resurrectionem tollas, quid habebunt quod sperent praeterea fideles, quando in mundo nil praeter crucem sibi propositam esse vident? Hinc patet, quo loco habendi sint, qui resurrectionem negant. Nam & fidei Christianae fundamenta conuellunt, & improbae mox licentiae fenestras aperiunt.
units.tr: Now let us look at Paul, who, knowing that a band from the various sects of his adversaries had gathered together, took counsel on the spur of the moment to set them against one another, and cries out: "Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee; I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead." Yet Paul seems to have sinned either by deceit, or even by a denial of his faith and of Christ, when he professes himself to belong to the order of those who were manifestly the bitterest enemies of Christ. But it can easily be excused. For first, he was compelled to seek such an escape when he saw that every opportunity of speaking was denied him and the matter was being carried on with open tyranny. He would certainly have preferred to profess his faith openly and give an account of it, which he had indeed begun to do. But, thrown into confusion, he adopted a new plan. Then, he does not simply confess and approve the whole of Pharisaism, but joins himself to their side against the Sadducees only in the single article of the resurrection, which they held in an orthodox way. What he thought of the remaining doctrines of the Pharisees, and above all of the confidence in works in which they were puffed up, his Epistles declare abundantly. Therefore the example of Paul gives no support to those who, in order to look after their life and reputation, cunningly twist themselves in a matter of faith, and openly accept and approve articles fighting against the Christian faith. We are taught, however, that it is lawful for the godly, when caught in unjust trials, to seek escapes, so far as they can find them without loss of the Truth, lest by rashly risking danger they also bring the Truth into danger with them. Above all, observe that Paul says he is being judged concerning the resurrection of the dead. Yet the heads of the accusation sounded quite different. But he alleges the resurrection because the whole business of faith and religion turns upon it, as he himself teaches in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 15. And because all the hope of the saints rests upon it, he says that he is also being judged concerning hope. For if you take away the resurrection, what will the faithful have left to hope for, when they see nothing in the world but the cross set before them? Hence it is clear in what place those are to be held who deny the resurrection. For they both overturn the foundations of the Christian faith and immediately open windows to shameless licence.

units.la: Caeterum egregiè Paulo suus conatus succedit. Mox enim Pharisaei illius causam contra Sadducaeos suflinent, & seditiosis vtrinq; clamoribus exortis, pro illo pugnantes, clamant: Nihil malii inuenimus in homine isto. Quod si spiritus locutus est ei, aut angelus, ne repugnemus Deo. Et haec quidem pijssimè simul & verissimè dicunt, nullam tamen apud Deum laudem merentur, quia non Veritatis aut iustitiae studium, sed prauus affectus hanc illis confessionem extorsit. Estque hoc memorabile exemplum, quantum possint partium studia, quando hi abrepti, mox Pauli defensores fiunt, qui paulo ante illius sanguinem sitiebant. Solet hoc frequenter tum in religione, tum in reliquis controuersijs accidere. At quia plerunque in deteriorem partem eiusmodi iudicia inclinant, diligenter ea vitari conuenit. Sunt praeterea & alia duo, quae obseruauisse prodest. Primum, impiorum consensum non posse diuturnum esse. Vt enim affectibus incertis, Euripi instar, hinc inde rapiuntur: ita illorum consilia Deus ex alto irridere & dissipare consueuit, idq; ea dexteritate faciens potest, vt interdum hostium impijssimorum opera in saluandis suis abutatur. Sic Philistaeorum
units.tr: But Paul's attempt succeeds admirably. For straightaway the Pharisees take up that man's cause against the Sadducees, and with seditious shouting breaking out on both sides, they fight for him and cry: "We find no evil in this man. But if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, let us not fight against God." And indeed they say these things most piously and most truly, yet they deserve no praise from God, because it was not a zeal for truth or justice but a perverse emotion that extorted this confession from them. And this is a memorable example of how much the zeal of parties can do, when these men, carried away, straightaway become the defenders of Paul, who a little before were thirsting for his blood. This tends to happen frequently, both in religion and in other controversies. But since such judgments for the most part lean toward the worse side, it is right to avoid them carefully. There are also two other points worth noting. First, that the agreement of the wicked cannot last long. For as they are tossed hither and thither by uncertain passions, like the Euripus, so God is accustomed to mock and scatter their plans from on high, and he can do this with such skill that he sometimes makes use of the works of most impious enemies for saving his own people. Thus the incursions of the Philistines profited David, while they drew Saul away from his persecution of him. And in our own age we have seen Turkish wars more than once give peace to the Church. Let no one, therefore, be dismayed by the conspiracies of the wicked, but let us keep our hope of salvation firmly fixed in God. The second point is that those who attack the doctrine revealed by God are fighting against God. This is a horrible crime, yet all too frequent today. For in assailing the gospel, princes and bishops of the churches labour most of all, although the Son of God himself deigned first to reveal it to the world with his own mouth. But in the end, to their great cost, those giants will feel how much more powerful God is than they, and how dreadful it is to fall into his hands.

units.la: {a} incursiones Dauidi profuêre, dum ab eius persecutione Saulum retraxerunt. Et nostro seculo Turcica bella non semel ecclesiae pacem dedisse vidimus. Neminem ergo impiorum conspirationes offendant, sed in Deo salutis spem firmissimè fixam habeamus. Alterum est, Deo illos repugnare, qui doctrinam diuinitus reuelatam oppugnant. Horrendum hoc facinus, sed nimiù frequens hodie. Nam in euangelio oppugnando cùm principes tumantiftites ecclesiarum maximè laborant, cum illud Dei filius suo ore mundo primùm reuelare dignatus sit. Sed tandem magno suo malo gigantes illi sentient, quanto illis potentior Deus sit, quamq; horrendum sit in illius manus incidere.
units.tr: the raids of the Philistines benefited David, inasmuch as they drew Saul away from pursuing him. And in our own age we have seen the Turkish wars more than once give peace to the Church. Let no one, then, be troubled by the plots of the wicked, but let us place our hope of salvation firmly in God. The second point is that God sets himself against those who attack the doctrine revealed by God. This is a horrible crime, yet one all too common today. For in assaulting the gospel, princes and bishops of the churches labour most of all, although it was the Son of God himself who deigned first to reveal it to the world with his own mouth. But in the end those giants will feel to their great cost how much more powerful God is than they, and how dreadful it is to fall into his hands.

units.la: Porrò in apertam seditionē clamores isti vtring, exorti vergunt, eoq; res progreditur, vt rursus Tribuni & militum opera Paulum liberari & in castra reduci oporteat. Quos, vt ante etiam, diuinitus ad hoc excitatos fuisse, nemo dubitare potest. Imitentur autem Tribuni exemplum magistratus omnes, & sui officij esse meminerint, bonos tueri atq; defendere. Detestabilis enim illorum factio est, qui bonos vel ignaui negligunt, vel etiam in hominum gratiam excruciandos tradunt, quae in re Pilatum peccauisse constat. Obseruent item, quid expectent, si quando veritatis ministros Antichristianus Concilijs committant. Hos enim aut turpiter deferere, aut si saluos velint, maiori periculo ex illorum manibus liberare cogentur, quibus iusus locus videtur iura publica simul & datam fidem impie violare. Exemplum huius in Sigismundo Imperatore, Constantiensis Concilij dolo & tyrannide circunuento, extat: quando Iohannem Hussium Imperatoria fide è Bohemia euocatum, ex illorum manibus eripere nequiuit. Porrò vt tum humana omnia cedant, Paulum imitati, veritatem causam constanter tueamur, nec suis deerit saluator & redemptor noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the outcries raised on both sides tend towards open sedition, and matters have advanced so far that once again the tribune and the soldiers must be employed to free Paul and bring him back into the barracks. That these men, as before, were roused up for this purpose by God, no one can doubt. Let all magistrates imitate the tribune's example, and let them remember that it is their office to protect and defend the good. Detestable indeed is the faction of those who either neglect the good through indolence, or even hand them over to be tortured to please men, a thing in which it is plain that Pilate sinned.
