Let them also observe what they may expect if they ever hand the ministers of the truth over to the Antichristian councils. For they will either be forced to desert them shamefully or, if they wish to save them, to rescue them from those men's hands at greater peril, since those men think they have license to violate public right and their given faith together with impunity. An example of this is found in the Emperor Sigismund, who, outwitted by the trickery and tyranny of the Council of Constance, could not snatch John Hus from their hands, though he had summoned him from Bohemia under imperial safe-conduct. Finally, whatever human affairs may do, let us, following Paul, defend the cause of truth steadfastly, and our Saviour and Redeemer, Jesus Christ, will not fail his own, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CXLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CXLIX.

units.la: Sequenti autem nocte assistens ei dominus ait: Bono animo esto Paule. Vt enim testificatus es de me Hierosolymis, sic te oportet & Romae testari. Orto autem die collegerunt se quidam ex Iudaeis, & devoverunt se, dicentes, neque esuros neque bibituros se, donec occiderent Paulum. Erant autem plures quàm quadraginta viri, qui hanc coniurationem fecerant. Qui accesserunt ad Summos Sacerdotes & Seniores, & dixerunt: Deuotione devouimus nos ipsos, nihil gustaturos, donec occidamus Paulum. Nunc ergo vos significate Tribuno & concilio, vt eras producat illum ad vos, tanquam aliquid certius cognitoros de eo. Nos verò priusquam appropinquet, parati sumus interficere illum. Cum autem audisset filius sororis Pauli insidias, venit & intrauit in castra, nunciauitq; Paulo.
units.tr: And the following night the Lord stood by him and said: "Be of good cheer, Paul; for as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome." When day came, some of the Jews formed a plot and bound themselves under an oath, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. There were more than forty men who had made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and the elders and said: "We have bound ourselves under a solemn vow to taste nothing until we have killed Paul. Now therefore you, together with the council, request the tribune to bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you intended to examine his case more carefully; and we, before he comes near, are ready to kill him." But when Paul's sister's son heard of the ambush, he came and entered the barracks and told Paul.

units.la: PAulus apostolus in posteriori ad Corinth. 1. cap. ait: Sicut abundant afflictiones Christi in nobis: ita per Christum abundat consolatio nostra. Est hac memorabilis simul & plena consolationis sententia, vt quae multis exemplis ab ipsa rerum origine confirmata sit. Quibus praesens hoc, quod de Paulo narratur, merito adnumerari debet. Illum enim hucusq; variis & grauissimis periculis exagitatum fuisse, audiuimus. Nec pauca acciderunt; quae illum ad desperationem impellerant, cum se à Romanis militibus vinctum, vnanimi Iudaeorum consensu ad mortem postulari videret, nec aliud habebat auxilium apparuisse, quàm quod milites tulerant, homines à religione alienissimi. Sed non deest periclitanti apostolo suo dominus, qui variis curis aestuantem amicissime consolatur, & quod verbis pollicetur, mox ipsa praestat, dum illum immanissimorum latronum manibus miraculose eripit. Quia verò haec, vt omnium institutioni et consolationi seruiant, scripta sunt, singulas partes ordine inspiciemus.
units.tr: The apostle Paul says in his second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 1: "As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds." This is a memorable saying, and at the same time full of comfort, and it has been confirmed by many examples from the very beginning of things. To these the present account of Paul rightly ought to be added. For we have heard that until now he had been harassed by various and most grievous dangers. Not a few things had happened which drove him to despair, when he saw himself bound by Roman soldiers and, by the unanimous consent of the Jews, sought for death; and it seemed that he had no other help than that which the soldiers gave, men most alien to his religion. But the Lord, who is not lacking to his apostle in danger, comforts him most kindly as he is troubled by various cares; and what he promises in words he soon bestows in deed, while he miraculously snatches him from the hands of most savage robbers. Since these things were written to serve the instruction and comfort of all, we shall examine the individual parts in order.

units.la: Primum in hus locum Consolatio habet, qua Pauli animus confirmatur. Nocte enim illi astitit dominus, nimirum per angelum suum, vt verum esse doceat, quod se nobiscum fore dixit vsque ad consummationem seculi. Iubet autem bono & praesenti animo esse Paulum, qui fortasse de Dei ergâ se cura & bonitate dubitare incipiebat. Causam verò subijcit, quod ipsum Romae etiam de Christo testifitestificari oporteat. Hinc vero euidentissimè patet, Deum non negligere res hominum, étiamsi illorum aliquando oblitus esse videatur. Quomodo enim homines negligeret, apud quem ne passerculos quidem in obliuione esse Christus testatur? Luc. 12. Videri quidem poterat Deo nequaquam curæ esse Paulus, in quem orbis terrarum coniurauisse videbatur. At cùm illi in custodia agenti dominus assistat, facilè patet nihil illi bucusq; vel inscio vel inuito Deo accidisse. Cæterum quia huius generis exempla passim extant, in præsenti ipsam Consolatione videamus. Cuius si nuda verba ad humanæ rationis captum examines, Deus minari potius aut terrere videbitur. Ait enim: Bono animo esto Paule. Vt enim testificatus es de me Hierosolymis, sic te oportet & Romæ testari. Ergo nouos labores & noua certamina prædicit dominus, perinde ac si ægroto medicus dicat: Confortare ô bone, nam noui te morbi manent, & nouis doloribus non multò post excruciaberis. Vel si quis recenti pugna dessum militem ad grauius quoddam certamen prouocet. Quis verò hanc consolationem esse diceret? Atqui tale quid est quod Paulo in præsenti dicitur. Nam vnius Romæ mentio illi itinerum molestias, nauigationum pericula & multiuarias immanissimasq; supplicitorum species, in mentem reuocare poterat, cùm illic rerum potiretur Claudius, vecors & crudelis homo, & ad supplicia innoxijs ferenda promptissimus. Sed si rem ipsam penitius inspiciamus, duo fuisse patebit, quæ Paulum baud mediocriter consolarentur. Alterum, quòd se Deo curæ esse videret. Alterum, quòd se organu & vas gloriæ futurum audiret, cuius opera apud Romanos quoq; rerum dominos, nomē Christi innotescere deberet. Admonemur igitur hoc loco, vnde nobis in aduersis Consolationes petendæ sint. Non veiq; ex lato rerū successu, aut ignaui otij spe, sed ex Dei prouidentia, & ex eo quòd nos suæ gloriæ vasa & organa Deus facere dignatur. Et huius quidem Christus nos admonet, quando discipulis nō quidem latos conatuum suorū euentus pollicetur, sed illis nihil absq; diuina prouidentiæ consilio euenturum dicit. Rursum docemur, Deum dum liberat & consolatur, nos non ad ocium, sed ad mai ora certamina præparare. Ideò enim suæ veritatis & promissionum gustu nos recreat, vt alacriores ad opus redeamus, id quod sanctos omnes sedulò facere videmus. Pudendus ergo illorum error est, qui diuinam opem experti, immunitatem quandam à periculis & laboribus sibi vendicant, aut etiam totos sese carnis libidini dedunt, & effrænem quiduis audendi & faciendi licentiam sectantur, &c.
units.tr: First, there is a consolation here, by which Paul's spirit is strengthened. For the Lord stood by him in the night, doubtless through his angel, so that he might teach that what he said is true, that he would be with us even to the end of the age. He bids Paul to be of good and present courage, though perhaps he had begun to doubt God's care and goodness towards him. He adds the reason: that he must bear witness of Christ also at Rome. From this it is most evidently clear that God does not neglect the affairs of men, even though he may sometimes seem to have forgotten them. For how would he neglect men, in whose remembrance not even the sparrows are, as Christ testifies? Luke 12. Indeed it might seem that Paul was in no way an object of God's care, against whom the whole world seemed to have conspired. But since the Lord stands by him while he is in custody, it is easily seen that nothing has happened to him until now, either without God's knowledge or against his will. Moreover, since examples of this kind are found everywhere, let us look at the consolation itself here. If you examine its bare words by the measure of human reason, God will seem rather to threaten or to terrify. For he says: "Be of good cheer, Paul; for as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome." Therefore the Lord foretells new labours and new contests, just as if a doctor said to a sick man: "Take heart, my good fellow, for new diseases remain for you, and before long you will be racked with new pains"; or as if someone, to a soldier wearied by a recent battle, were to challenge him to a more severe contest. Who would call this a consolation? Yet something of this kind is said to Paul at present. For the mere mention of Rome could bring back to his mind the troubles of journeys, the dangers of voyages, and many most savage forms of punishment, since Claudius, a mad and cruel man, ready to inflict punishment on the innocent, held power there. But if we look at the matter more closely, it will be clear that there were two things which greatly comforted Paul. The first, that he saw himself to be a care to God. The second, that he heard he would be a vessel and instrument of God's glory, by whose work the name of Christ ought to become known even among the Roman masters of the world. We are reminded therefore in this place where we should seek consolations in adversity: not from the happy outcome of affairs, nor from the hope of idle leisure, but from God's providence, and from the fact that God deigns to make us vessels and instruments of his glory. Christ reminds us of this when he promises his disciples not indeed happy outcomes of their undertakings, but tells them that nothing will happen to them except by the counsel of divine providence. Again we are taught that God, while he frees and consoles us, prepares us not for idleness but for greater struggles. For he refreshes us with a taste of his truth and promises so that we may return more eager to the work, which we see all the saints diligently doing. Shameful, therefore, is the error of those who, having experienced divine help, claim for themselves a certain immunity from dangers and labours, or even give themselves wholly to the lust of the flesh and pursue an unbridled licence to dare and do whatever they like, and so on.

units.la: Porrò quia multis præterea periculis vexandus erat apostolus, priusquam Romam veniret, recentem consolationem nouo statim beneficio confirmat, dum è summo & improuiso periculo illum eripit. Conspirauerunt enim in illius necem quadraginta viri, seq; devouerunt nec esuros nec bibituros, donec Paulum occidissent. In quorum facinore non immeritò dubites, audaciámne aut sanguinarios animos magis admireris. Nam præter id, quòd insonti necem parant, contra Dei legem sese devouent etiam, immemores quòd multa incidere possint, quæ illorum conatus impediant. Sed illorum exemplo de impiorum audacia iudicare discimus, deque omnibus illis, qui religionem quam profitentur, armis potius quàm scripturis defendendam esse putant. Sed ad nostros hosce redeamus, qui sanguinarium consilium ad Sacerdotes referunt, magnam nimirum apud illos gratiam inituri, eosq; facinoris socios expetunt. Vos (inquit) significate Tribuno & Concilio, vt cras producat illum ad vos, tanquam aliquid cogniturus de eo. Nos verò priusquam appropinquet, parati sumus interficere illum. Elucent hic impiorum artes, & quousque progrediatur veritatis odium. Zelum auitæ religionis profitentur illi, & iustitiam mirificè simulare possunt, cùm interim facinus ab omni tum religione tum iustitia alienissimum animo conceperint. Atqui ad posteros quoque stratagema hoc satan propagauit, & constat non semel ad disputationem euocatos Christi ministros, carnificum manibus occurrisse. Nec desunt nostri seculi exempla, quæ eiusmodi artes hodie etiam pertimescendas esse docent. Simul verò quanta illo tempore in Iudaica gente corruptio fuerit consydera, quando nefarium illud scelus sacerdotibus & Senioribus communicare audent, quos baud dubiè socios fore sciebant. Digni ergo fuerunt, qui simul omnes miserè perirent. Quod ipsum sibi euenturum sciant, quicunque hodie etiam innocentis sanguinis effusione & piorum proscriptionibus Antichristianis sacerdotibus seruire student. Quàm tamen irriti ferè illorum conatus sint, sequens historia docet. Resciscit enim impium consilium Pauli nepos, puer quidem, sed ad illud turbandum (ita moderante Deo) aptissimus. Is enim rem omnem Paulo nuntiat, qui illum ad
units.tr: Furthermore, since the apostle was to be harassed by many other dangers before he came to Rome, he confirms the recent consolation at once with a new benefit, while he rescues him from a great and unforeseen danger. For forty men conspired for his death, and bound themselves by an oath that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul. In such a deed you may well wonder whether to admire more their audacity or their bloodthirsty minds. For besides the fact that they prepare the death of an innocent man, they also bind themselves against God's law, forgetful that many things could happen to hinder their attempts. But from their example we learn to judge the boldness of the wicked, and of all those who think that the religion they profess should be defended by arms rather than by Scriptures. But let us return to these men of ours, who report their bloody plan to the priests, clearly intending to gain great favour with them, and they seek them as partners in the crime. "You," they say, "request the tribune and the council to bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you intended to examine his case more carefully; and we, before he comes near, are ready to kill him." Here the arts of the wicked shine forth, and how far their hatred of the truth will go. They profess zeal for their ancestral religion, and they can admirably counterfeit justice, while meanwhile they have conceived a crime most alien from all religion and all justice. Yet Satan has spread this stratagem to later times as well, and it is well known that more than once the ministers of Christ, summoned to a disputation, have met the hands of executioners. Nor are there lacking examples from our own age which teach that such arts are to be feared even today. At the same time, consider how great the corruption of the Jewish nation was at that time, when they dared to share this wicked crime with the priests and elders, whom they knew without doubt would be their accomplices. Therefore they deserved to perish miserably all together. And those who today also strive to serve Antichristian priests by the shedding of innocent blood and the proscription of the pious may know that the same will befall them. How much their attempts were nonetheless brought to nothing, the following story shows. For Paul's nephew, a boy indeed, but most fit (God so directing) to disturb that plot, learns of the wicked design. He reports the whole matter to Paul, who sends him to the tribune

units.la: X Tribunum ablegat, cuius studio & industria sanguinarius ille conatus ( vt alias audiemus) interturbatur. Ita vero Deus recenti promissioni fidem facere, nosq; omnes docere voluit, quàm illi facile sit impiorum consilia turbare. Quid enim aduersus illum impij hostes possent, qui nihil non videt, & infirma quoque aduersus illos armare potest? Ita per infantem expositicium Mosen, impiam Pharaonis tyrannidem destruit. Ita foeminis occidendos praebuit Sisaram & Holofernem, duces reimilitaris peritissimos fortissimosq;. Ita pueri Danielis folertia impuram senum libidinem arguit, & Susannae pudicitiae vitaeq; patrocinatur. Et in praesenti pueri opera consilium turbat, quod vix ulla ratione turbari posse videbatur, cum ab audacissimis hominibus susceptum, & voti religione confirmatum, Sacerdotum etiam & Seniorum authoritate confirmaretur. Extant huius generis exempla in omnibus historijs. Ex illis vero nos Dei potentiam agnoscere conuenit, qua confisi impiorum tyrannidem minus formidemus, & in veritatis causa strenui spem & fiduciam omnem in vno Deo repositam habeamus, per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: X to the tribune, through whose zeal and diligence that bloody attempt is thwarted (as we shall hear elsewhere). Thus God wished to make good his recent promise and to teach us all how easily he can overturn the counsels of the wicked. For what could the impious enemies do against him who sees all things and can arm even the weak against them? Thus through the infant Moses, exposed, he destroyed the impious tyranny of Pharaoh. Thus he delivered Sisera and Holofernes, most skilled and most brave leaders of the army, into the hands of women to be slain. Thus the cleverness of the boy Daniel exposed the foul lust of the old men and defended the chastity and life of Susanna. And in the present case a boy's work upsets a plan which seemed scarcely capable of being upset by any means, since it had been undertaken by the most daring men, confirmed by the religion of a vow, and strengthened by the authority of the priests and elders as well. Examples of this kind are found in all histories. From them we ought to recognise the power of God, by which, trusting in it, we may fear the tyranny of the wicked less, and in the cause of truth be vigorous, having all our hope and confidence placed in the one God, through Jesus Christ our Lord: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CL.
units.tr: HOMILY CL.

units.la: Accersito autem Paulus ad se vno ex Centurionibus, ait: Adolescentem hunc adduc ad Tribunum: habet enim quod renuntiet ei. Et ille quidem assumens eum duxit ad Tribunum, & ait: Vinctus Paulus accersitum me rogauit, vt hunc adolescentem perducerem ad te, habentem aliquid, quod loquatur tibi. Apprehensa autem manu illius Tribunus secessit cum eo seorsum, & percunctatus est illum: Quid est quod habes significandum mihi? Ille autem dixit: Iudaei conspirauerunt vt rogarent te, vt crastino die educas Paulum in Concilium, quasi aliquid certius inquisituri sint de illo. Tu vero ne morem gesseris illis. Insidiantur enim ei ex ipsis viri plures quadraginta, qui seipsos devouerunt, ne vel edant vel bibant, donec interfecerint eum. Et nunc parati sunt, exspectantes vt promittas. Tribunus igitur dimisit adolescentem, praecepitq; ei: Ne cui effutias, quòd haec indicaueris mihi. Et accersitis duobus Centurionibus, dixit: Parate milites ducentos, vt eant Caesaream, & equites septuaginta & lancearios ducentos, a tertia hora noctis, & iumenta parate, vt impositum Paulum saluum perducant ad Felicem Praesidem.
units.tr: Then Paul called one of the centurions to him and said, "Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him." So the centurion took him and brought him to the tribune and said, "The prisoner Paul called me to him and asked me to bring this young man to you, since he has something to tell you." The tribune took him by the hand, drew him aside, and asked him privately, "What is it you have to report to me?" He answered, "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if they intended to make some more exact inquiry into him. But do not give in to them. More than forty of their men are lying in wait for him; they have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor to drink until they have killed him. They are ready now and are waiting for your promise." So the tribune dismissed the young man and charged him, "Tell no one that you have informed me of this." Then he called two of the centurions and said, "Get ready two hundred soldiers to go to Caesarea, together with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen, leaving at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts, so that they may set Paul on one and bring him safely to the governor Felix."

units.la: Quamuis Deus electos suos nunquam deserat, sed illis iuxta promissiones suas semper & ubique fideliter adsit: idem tamen secundus aduersa & tristia subinde intermisceat, eo quòd illos ita in officio retineri & ipsorum fidem exerceri plurimum prodest, vt nimirum ab vno Deo pendere & euentus laetos rerum vni illi tribuere discant. Exempla huius multa passim extant, maximè in Mosis, Dauidis, & aliorum historijs: quibus praesens hoc, quod de Paulo commemoratur, merito adnumerari debet. Huic enim graviter simul & multiariam tentato dominum apparuisse, & efficacem consolationem adhibuisse audiimus, dum illum non modò Iudaeorum manus euasurum, sed Romae etiam de se testificaturum esse pollicetur. Sed ecce vix dum exorto die quadraginta viri in illum nefarium conspirant, & Sacerdotibus simul atq; Senioribus in consilium adhibitis, ita rem omnem instituunt, vt vix saluari posse videatur. Id vero cum Dei promissione ex diametro pugnare videbatur. Quia tamen Dei morem Paulus non ignorat, nec ipse improuisi periculi mentione terretur, nec suae promissis Deus deest: imò unde minimè speraret, illi opem & auxilium offert, sicuti modò videbimus. Visus vero omnium horum est, vt hinc in aduersis fidei confirmationem petamus, nec ideò spem omnem abijciamus, si quando rerum progressus cum Dei promissionibus minus conuenire videamus. Nam etiamsi cunctetur dominus, non tamen in perpetuum nostri obliuisci poterit. Sed vt plus hinc ad nos utilitatis redeat, singulae personae nobis considerandae erunt.
units.tr: Although God never forsakes his chosen ones, but is always and everywhere faithfully present with them according to his promises, he nevertheless from time to time mingles adversity and sorrow with their lot. This is greatly to their benefit, since it keeps them in their duty and exercises their faith, so that they may learn to depend on the one God alone and to ascribe all happy outcomes to him alone. Many examples of this appear everywhere, above all in the histories of Moses, David and others, and the present story about Paul rightly belongs among them. We hear that the Lord appeared to Paul when he was sorely tried on many fronts and gave him effective comfort, promising that he would not only escape the hands of the Jews but would also bear witness to himself at Rome. Yet see: scarcely has the day dawned when forty men conspire against him in their wicked plot, and, having taken counsel with the priests and elders, they arrange the whole affair so that his rescue scarcely seems possible. This seemed utterly at odds with God's promise. Yet Paul did not forget God's way of acting, nor was he terrified by the mention of an unforeseen danger, and God does not fail his promises. Rather, from where he would least expect it, God offers him help and aid, as we shall presently see. The purpose of all this is that we may seek from adversity a strengthening of faith, and that we do not abandon all hope whenever we see the course of events not agreeing well with God's promises. For even if the Lord delays, he cannot forget us for ever. But so that more benefit may come to us from this, each person in the story must be considered by us.

units.la: Primus hic omnium Paulus prodit, qui licet oraculo confirmatus esset, nō tamen vel promissionem vel prouidentiam Dei stulte iactat, nec periculum securus negligit: sed quod vnum reliquum erat in humanis medium, & quo salua religione & fide Christiana vti poterat, prudenter apprehendit, curans nimirum, vt Tribunus per nepotem suum rem omnem intelligat, & officij admonitus ipsum sanguinarijs coniuratorum manibus subducat. Et ne res leuis momenti videatur, aut ob pueri aetatem suspecta sit, Centurionem intercessorem illi addit. Quo exemplo primum admonemur, vt nos Dei promissionibus & prouidentia in aduersis vti conueniat. Minimè enim dubitandum est, Deum aeterno suae prouidentiae consilio res omnes mortalium administrare, nec illud vllis hostium ipsius conatibus vel dissipari vel saltem impediri posse. Ipse enim gentium consilia dissipare solet, at illius consilium (vt Dauid testatur) manet in aeternum. Psal. 33. Rursus idem ille se suis affuturum, & illos in aduersis asserturum esse pollicetur: cuius promissionibus nos sancte credere decet. Interim media, quae & per se licita sunt, & diuinitus offeruntur, nullo modo contemni aut negligi debent, ne temere nos in pericula coniiciendo Deum tentare videamur. Hoc ipsum enim in omnibus negotijs, quod in agricultura obseruari debet. Nam licet in illa quoq; omne incrementum solius Dei sit, hanc tamen absq; insigni diuinae ordinationis contemptu nemo negligere poterit. Ita Dauidem nunc fugā, nunc alijs medijs à Deo oblatis, religiose vsum fuisse legimus, quamuis de Dei veritate, qui regnum illi pollicitus erat, minimè dubitaret. Idem Ezechiam obseruauisse constat. Imò Christus à fuga non abhorruit, cùm horam suam nondum venisse sciret: nec etiam satana suasore e templi pinna se precipitare voluit, quamuis ille Dei promissionem allegaret, cuius authoritas illi sanctissima erat. Quid quòd idem discipulos quidem amplissimis promissionibus instruit, sed eosdem vt sibi ab hominibus caveant, diligenter admonet? Matth. 10. Turpis ergo & impius illorum error est, qui Dei prouidentia ad temeritatem suam & quiduis audendi licentiam abutuntur, & huius praetextu non prudentiam modò, sed etiam diuinitus oblata media improbe contemnunt. Diffidentiae potius malum nos vitare conuenit, ne hoc superati ad illicita media impie conuertamur: interim licitis & diuinitus oblatis religiose vtentes, euentum omnem bona & sanctae Dei voluntati committamus. Ita enim media via tutissimi ibimus, quando & diffidentiam & cofidentiam vitare studebimus: id quod Paulus hoc loco prudenter simul & pie facit, Deum q; sui consilij approbatorem habet. Docemur praeterea huius exemplo, licere pijs & Christianis hominibus vt magistratus opem implorent, & armatam quoq; (si ita necessitas iubeat) defensionem postulent. Neque hic audiendi sunt, qui Christi regnum armis propagari negant, & ab illo nobis mandatum esse clamant, ne malo resistamus. Nec enim legitimam à magistratu defensionem postulamus, quòd Christi regnum armis propagare in animo sit: sed officium petimus, quod magistratus, si bonus esse velit, negare non poterit; & quo pijs salua fide & religione vti licet. Constat enim à Deo constitutos esse magistratus, & quidem in bonum, nec illis frustra gladium esse à Deo creditum. Vide Rom. 13. Et reges ecclesiae nutritios fore per Isaiam Deus promisit. Quoad verò Christi praeceptum, quo malo resistere prohibemur, illo nequaquam legitimam magistratus functionem abrogare, sed priuatis hominibus immanem vindictae cupiditatem extorquere voluit, quae & leges publicas, & amicitias pacemq; omnem turbare solet. Rectè ergo Paulus à Tribuno defendi cupit, nec militum arma aspernatur, quibus coniuratorum insidias reprimi posse videbat. Nec etiam illi imputandum erat, etiamsi cum militum equitumq; manu coniurati illi commissi eadem vtrinq; commisissent: sed in impijs illis omnis potius culpa haesisset, qui nefarij conatus authores fuerant. At si Paulo Romanorum militum praesidio vti licuit, nam illi nimium sueri fidei censores sunt, qui hodie verbi ministris vitio vertunt, si Christianorum magistratuum opem implorent, & ab illis hoc ipsum officij postulent, quod ethnicus Tribunus Christi apostolo minimè denegandum esse putauit.
units.tr: Here first of all comes Paul, who, although he had been confirmed by an oracle, neither foolishly boasts of God's promise and providence nor carelessly neglects the danger. Rather, he wisely grasps the one remaining human means, which he could use without harming religion and the Christian faith, namely, arranging for the tribune to learn the whole matter through his nephew, so that, being warned of his duty, the tribune might snatch him from the bloodthirsty hands of the conspirators. And so that the matter should not seem trivial, or be suspect because of the boy's age, he adds a centurion as guarantor. From this example we are first admonished that it is fitting for us to use God's promises and providence in adversity. For there is no doubt that God administers all the affairs of mortals by the eternal counsel of his providence, and that this counsel cannot be scattered or at least hindered by any attempts of his enemies. For he is accustomed to scatter the counsels of the nations, but his counsel (as David bears witness) stands for ever (Ps. 33). Again, the same God promises that he will be present with his people and will defend them in adversity, and it is right for us to believe his promises devoutly. Meanwhile, the means that are lawful in themselves and are offered by God must in no way be despised or neglected, lest we seem to tempt God by rashly exposing ourselves to danger. For this must be observed in all undertakings, as it is in farming. For although in farming too all the increase belongs to God alone, yet no one can neglect this without a clear contempt for God's ordinance. Thus we read that David used flight, and other means offered by God, in a godly way, although he never doubted the truth of God, who had promised him the kingdom. It is evident that Ezekiel also observed this. Indeed, Christ did not shrink from flight when he knew that his hour had not yet come; nor did he wish, at the urging of Satan, to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple, although Satan cited God's promise, whose authority was most sacred to him. What more? Christ indeed instructed his disciples with the most generous promises, yet he also carefully warned them to beware of men (Matt. 10). Therefore the error of those is shameful and impious who abuse God's providence as a cover for their rashness and a licence to dare anything, and under this pretext not only disregard prudence but also wickedly despise the means offered by God. Rather, we ought to avoid the evil of distrust, lest, overcome by it, we impiously turn to unlawful means; meanwhile, using lawful means offered by God in a godly way, we should commit the whole outcome to the good and holy will of God. For thus we shall walk the safest middle way, when we strive to avoid both distrust and presumption. This is what Paul does here, wisely and piously at once, and he has God as the approver of his plan. We are further taught by this example that it is lawful for godly and Christian people to seek the help of the magistrate, and, if necessity so requires, to ask for armed defence. Nor should those be listened to who deny that the kingdom of Christ is spread by arms, and cry out that he commanded us not to resist evil. For we do not ask for lawful defence from the magistrate because we intend to spread Christ's kingdom by arms; rather, we seek a service which the magistrate, if he wishes to be good, cannot refuse, and which godly people may use without harm to faith and religion. For it is established that magistrates have been appointed by God, and indeed for good, and that the sword has not been entrusted to them by God in vain (see Rom. 13). And God promised through Isaiah that kings would be nursing fathers of the Church. As for Christ's precept by which we are forbidden to resist evil, he by no means meant to abolish the lawful office of the magistrate by it, but to strip private persons of a savage lust for revenge, which is accustomed to disturb public laws, friendships and all peace. Rightly, therefore, Paul desires to be defended by the tribune, and he does not scorn the weapons of the soldiers, by which he saw that the plots of the conspirators could be checked. Nor was he to blame for this, even if the conspirators had committed themselves with the band of soldiers and horsemen to the same thing on both sides; rather, all the guilt would have rested on those impious men who had been the authors of the wicked attempt. But if Paul was allowed to use the protection of the Roman soldiers, then those are excessively severe censors of faith who today find fault with ministers of the Word if they seek the help of Christian magistrates and ask of them that very service which the heathen tribune thought should not be denied to the apostle of Christ.

units.la: Sed omisso Paulo ad Centurionem transeamus, quo internuntio ille vsus est. Vocatum enim adse rogat, vt adolescentem ad Tribunum abducat: in quo officio praestando admodum facilem & promptum sese praeber. Solet enim suis apud exteros quoque gratiam conciliare Deus, & occulta quadam vi hominum animos illis deuincire. Ita Iosephus olim singulari gratia apud Potipharem pollebat, & Israelitas ab Aegyptijs preciosissima quaeque facile impetrauisse legimus, eò quòd dominus his illos gratiosos & amabiles reddidisset. Debent haec nobis pietatis studium commendare, quando videmus tunc demum nos hominibus quoq; facillimis & beneuolentissimis vsuros esse, quando Deum nobis obstrinxerimus: cui hominum animos pro suo arbitrio inclinare facillimum est. Simul autem imitandus est nobis Centurio hic, vt illius exemplo afflictis & calamitosis libenter inseruiamus: quando sibi collatum Christus putat, quicquid in illos collatum fuerit. Vide Matth.25. Sed o enormem nostri seculi improbitatem, quo eo impietatis progressi sunt homines, vt a Christianis difficulter impetres, quod a milite ethnico Paulus tam facile impetrare potuit. Plerosque enim captiuorum Christi hodie pudet, eosq; vel hoc vno nomine negligunt, ne dum horum causam agunt, ipsi quoque suspecti fiant.
units.tr: But let us pass over Paul and turn to the centurion, through whom the tribune acted as go-between. For when called to him, he asks that the young man be led to the tribune, and in performing this duty he shows himself very easy and ready. For God is accustomed to win favour for his people even among foreigners, and by some hidden power to bind men's minds to them. Thus Joseph once had singular favour with Potiphar, and we read that the Israelites easily obtained from the Egyptians all their most precious things, because the Lord had made them gracious and lovable in their eyes. These things ought to commend to us the zeal for godliness, since we see that we shall then at last have men also most ready and most kindly disposed to us, when we have bound God to ourselves, for it is very easy for him to incline men's minds as he pleases. At the same time this centurion is to be imitated by us, so that by his example we may gladly serve the afflicted and the distressed, since Christ counts whatever is done for them as done to himself (see Matt. 25). But see the monstrous wickedness of our age, to which men have advanced in impiety, so that it is hard to obtain from Christians what Paul was able to obtain so easily from a heathen soldier. For today many are ashamed of Christ's captives, and they neglect them on this ground alone, lest, while they plead their cause, they themselves also become suspect.

units.la: Caeterum qualis in Pauli causa Tribunus ipse fuerit videamus: vbi in ethnico homine maximarum virtutum specimina elucent, nimirum huius quoque animum Deo impellente, qui apostolum suum impiis coniuratorum insidijs subducere voluit. Primo enim singularem humanitatem exercet, dum ad se venientem puerum non fastidit, nec captiui nomine audito toruus aspernatur, sed manu prehensa seorsum abducit, & amice qua de causa venerit, interrogat. Quod exemplum omnes eos, qui in magistratu versantur imitari conuenit, cum hac non postrema illorum virtus sit, vt facilem ad se qui bus aditum praebeant, & subditorum causas clementer & patienter audiant. Ita enim Dei ingenium referunt, qui etiam sponte nos inuitat, aureisq; suas afflictorum precibus semper patere vult. Et sane cum multos vel pudor, vel metus impediat, quo minus animi concepta coram magistratibus eloqui possint, humanitatis & beneuolentiae significatione illis animum addere conuenit, ne praeposterus ille vel pudor vel metus illis fraudi sit. Deinde humanitati prudentiam coniungit Tribunus, quae ex eo colligitur, quod puero non difficulter fidem adhibet, quamuis multa essent, quae narrationem possent suspectam facere. Sed cum Iudaicae gentis malitiam iam ante non semel perspexisset, & ex prioribus actionibus facile intellexisset, quam iniquo quamque hostili in illum animo essent, tales omnino inter illos inueniri arbitratur, quales a puero describebantur: imo quae illius est humanitas, non iniquae fert, a puero sibi consilium dari, qui ne Paulum ad illos produceret, monebat. Habent ergo hic quoque, quod imitentur, principes. Nam vt nimia credulitas, quae leuitatis speciem habet, vitari debet: ita ad credendum difficiliores esse minime conuenit, maximae si rationes probabiles afferri audiant. Quin prudentes praesenti animo in omnem euentum aduigilent, ne (quod saepe accidit) nimia difficultate vel rempublicas totas, vel viros bonos in periculum adducant. Postremo summam in Tribuno hoc industriam videre licet: quando nihil eorum intermittit, quae praesenti negotio seruire poterant. Nam a puero silentij fidem prudenter exigit, ne res patefacta noui consilij occasionem coniuratoribus praebeat. Deinde accersitis duobus Centurionibus militum manum, quanta sufficere poterat, huic negotio destinat. Praeterea iumenta quoque parari iubet, quibus Paulus deuehi possit. Adhaec nolem obseruat, ne quis tumultus temere excitetur. Addit quoque commendatitias literas ad Felicem Praesidem. Quae omnia absque labore & absque sumptibus fieri nullo modo potuerunt. Sed officij sui memor, nec laboribus nec sumptibus sibi parcendum esse putat, vt captiuum hominem, & nullius ad hunc scelerisconuictum, ex latronum manibus liberet. Simili industria Christianos magistratus in bonis defendendis vti decet, quando in hunc finem illos praecipue instituitos fuisse constat. Sed ethnici hominis exemplo multorum tum negligentia tum nequitia arguitur, qui centum potius verbi ministros hostibus laniandos tradere, quam illorum causa tantos labores sumptusq; facere vellent. Neminem tamen seculi nostri ingratitudo abstreat, quo minus officio suo fideliter fungatur. Etsi enim cessent homines officium facere, nec vlla apud ipsos auxilij spes affulgeat, nunquam tamen promissis suis Deus deerit, qui cultores suos inter mille pericula inopinis medijs seruare tandemque ad coelestis regni hereditatem transferre consueuit, per Iesum Christum filium suum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Let us now see what sort of man the tribune himself was in Paul's case. In this heathen man there shine forth specimens of the greatest virtues, no doubt because God, who wished to rescue his apostle from the impious snares of the conspirators, moved his mind too. First, he shows remarkable kindness: he does not disdain the boy who came to him, nor does he scornfully spurn him when he hears the word "prisoner", but takes him by the hand, leads him aside, and kindly asks why he has come. This example ought all who hold office to imitate, since it is no small part of their virtue to offer ready access to themselves and to hear the causes of their subjects with mercy and patience. For in this way they reflect the character of God, who even invites us of his own accord and always wishes his ears to be open to the prayers of the afflicted. And indeed, since shame or fear often prevents many from being able to set out what they have conceived before magistrates, it is fitting to encourage them by a sign of kindness and goodwill, so that that misplaced shame or fear does not work to their harm. Next, the tribune joins prudence to kindness, which is seen in the fact that he does not find it hard to give credit to the boy, although there were many things that could make the account seem suspect. But since he had already more than once seen the malice of the Jewish nation, and had easily understood from their earlier actions how hostile and ill-disposed their minds were towards Paul, he judges that such men as the boy described are certainly to be found among them. Indeed, his very kindness does not bear it ill that the boy, who warned him not to bring Paul out to them, gives him counsel. Rulers, then, have here too something to imitate. For just as excessive credulity, which has the appearance of levity, ought to be avoided, so it is by no means fitting to be too hard to believe when they hear that there are probable reasons. Indeed, the prudent ought to keep watch with a ready mind against every outcome, lest (as often happens) through excessive difficulty they bring into danger either whole commonwealths or good men. Lastly, in this tribune one may see great diligence, since he omits nothing of those things that could serve the present business. For prudently he requires of the boy a promise of silence, lest the matter, once disclosed, give the conspirators an opportunity for a new plan. Then, having summoned two centurions, he assigns to this business a band of soldiers as large as could suffice. Besides, he orders that mounts also be made ready, on which Paul might be conveyed. Moreover, he observes the night, so that no tumult be rashly stirred up. He adds also letters of recommendation to the governor Felix. None of these things could by any means have been done without labour and without expense. But mindful of his duty, he thinks that neither labour nor expense should be spared, so that he might free from the hands of robbers a captive man, one convicted of no crime. Christian magistrates ought to use a similar diligence in defending good men, since it is clear that they were appointed chiefly for this end. But by the example of this heathen man, the negligence and the wickedness of many is rebuked, who would rather hand over a hundred ministers of the Word to be torn apart by enemies than undertake such labours and expenses on their behalf. Yet the ingratitude of our age should not turn anyone aside from faithfully performing his duty. For even if men cease to do their duty, and no hope of help shines forth from them, God will never fail in his promises; he is accustomed to preserve his worshippers amid a thousand dangers by unexpected means, and at last to transfer them to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, through Jesus Christ his Son, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLI.
units.tr: Homily 151.

units.la: Scripsit Tribunus literas in hanc formam: Claudius Lysias praestantissimo Praesidi Felici salutem. Virum hunc comprehensum a Iudaeis, cum iam prope esset interficiendus, superueniens cum militibus eripui, cognito quòd Romanus effet. Volensq; scire causam, ob quam accusa-rent illum, deduxi in concilium eorum. Quem comperi accusari de quæ-stionibus legis ipsorum, nullum dignum morte aut vinculis habentem crimen. Et cùm indicatum effet mihi de insidijs, quæ homini à Iudæis ini-minebant, protinus eum misi ad te, denuntians etiam accusatoribus vt quæ habent aduersus eum, dicat apud te. Vale. Milites verò iuxta quod sibi iniunctum erat, assumptum Paulum duxerunt per noctem Antipa-tridem. Postridie autem dimissis equitibus, vt cum eo irent, reuersi sunt in castra. Qui cùm venissent Cæsaream, ac tradidissent epistolam Præsi-di, statuerunt etiam Paulum coram ipso. Quum legisset autem Præses, & interrogauisset, ex qua esset prouincia, & cognouisset, quòd ex Cilicia, Audiam te (inquit) cùm accusatores quoq; tui aduenerint. Iussitq; in prę-torio Herodis custo diri eum.
units.tr: The tribune wrote a letter in this form: "Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix, greeting. When this man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed, I came upon them with soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman. Wishing to know the charge on which they accused him, I brought him before their council. I found that he was accused concerning questions of their law, and that he had no charge worthy of death or chains. And when it was reported to me that the Jews were plotting against the man, I immediately sent him to you, and I also ordered his accusers to state before you what they have against him. Farewell." The soldiers, as they had been ordered, took Paul by night to Antipatris. The next day they dismissed the horsemen to go on with him, and themselves returned to the camp. When the horsemen came to Caesarea and handed over the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul before him. When the governor had read the letter and asked what province he came from, and learned that he was from Cilicia, he said: "I will hear you when your accusers have also arrived." And he ordered him to be kept under guard in Herod's praetorium.

units.la: Vperuacanea alicui videri poterat Lucæ euangelistæ diligentia, qua vt Paulus Romanorum militum ope insidias, quas ipsi latrones quidam coniurati struxerant, effugerit, commemorat, eaq; commemoratione minutissima quæq; tantumnon ad nauseam vsq; inculcat. At quia ex spiritus san-cti suggestione illum scripsisse constat, nihil quod illo authore traditur, nobis superuacaneum videri debet. Ita enim infallibilem Dei fidem siue Veritatem & eiusdem inuictam potentiam, quæ in suis asse-rendis vtitur, nobis ob oculos statuit. Nec enim vulgari modo im piorum latronum conatus eludit, Paulumq; iuxta promissionem suam liberat, sed ita negotium omne instituit & administrat, vt illo-rum potissimum opera conficiatur, à quibus nihil tale sperauissent pij, cùm etiam ipsi Christianæ fidei hostes, & fortasse ab omni religione alienissimi essent. At quia Veritas ipsa Deus est, promissa sal-lere non potest: & quia hominum corda mentesq; sua manu versat, facillimum illi est hostium quo-que opera in ijs perficiendis vti, quæ fieri decreuit. Huius ergo virtuti tribuenda erit cùm Tribu-nitum militum induistria, quæ talis describitur, vt omnes hosce in Pauli obsequium perinde coniura-uisse putes, vt alteri in eiusdem necem conspirauerant. Omnium verò horum consyderatio (vt sæpè monuimus) fidei nostræ confirmandæ seruire debet: quam cùm propter quotidianas tentationes cre-bris consolationibus fulciri oporteat, diligentius aliquanto, vt Paulus Cæsaream ad Iudæa Præ-fidem perductus fit, videamus, quando in singulis multa deprehendes, quæ fidem nutantem erigere & sustentare possunt.
units.tr: Someone might think that the care the evangelist Luke takes is superfluous, since he records in such fine detail how Paul escaped the plots that certain robbers had conspired to lay, with the help of the Roman soldiers, and he presses home nearly every small point to the point of weariness. But since it is certain that he wrote under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, nothing that is handed down by such an author should seem superfluous to us. For it sets before our eyes the infallible faith, or truth, of God, and his unconquered power, which he uses in carrying out what he has asserted. He does not merely frustrate the attempts of wicked robbers and free Paul in accordance with his promise; he so arranges and manages the whole affair that it is accomplished chiefly through the agency of those from whom the godly would have hoped for nothing of the kind, since they were enemies of the Christian faith and perhaps utterly alien to all religion. But because truth itself is God, he cannot deceive in his promises; and because he turns the hearts and minds of men in his hand, it is very easy for him to use even the works of enemies to bring about what he has decided shall happen. Therefore the cunning of the tribune and the soldiers, which is described in such a way that you would think they had all conspired in Paul's service just as the others had conspired for his death, must be credited to his power. The consideration of all these things (as we have often warned) ought to serve to confirm our faith. Since, on account of our daily temptations, it must be strengthened by frequent consolations, let us look a little more carefully at how Paul was led to Caesarea, to the governor of Judaea, for in each detail you will find much that can raise up and sustain a wavering faith.

units.la: Initiò autem exemplum epistolæ, qua Paulum Felici Lysias Tribunus commendauit, ponitur. Docet hæc præter multa alia, qua breuitate veteres in rebus grauissimis vsi sunt, cùm bodie in leuis-simis rebus immodica verborum copia adhiberi soleat, cuius non alia causa adduci potest, quàm quòd fides omnis extincta est, cuius loco mendacium & vana simulatio passim dominantur. Habet autem epistola hæc suas partes, inter quas primum locum Inscriptio obtinet. Exprimit hæc cùm authoris nomen, tum eius ad quem scribitur, & quis nam illo tempore Iudæs Præses fuerit, docet: Felix ni-mirum, cuius multa apud exteros quoq; historicos mentio fieri solet. Hunc Claudij Cæsaris libertum fuisse, & principis stoliditate in tantum fastigium ascendisse tradunt, vt summos honores Roma-nis ciuibus & patritijs facile præriperet. Retinuit tamen seruile ingenium, cum libidine, stuprís & cede passim omnia fœdarit. Nam trium reginarum maritum fuisse Suetonius scribit, quas illum partim Claudij authoritate, partim denocinio infami in coniugium pellexisse constat. Drusillam cer-te Herodis filiam (eius, inquam, quem ab angelo percussum fuisse Cap. 12. audiuimus) Aziazo Ai-maforum regi Cyprij cuiusdam Magi arte & opera eripuit. Idem Ionathæ Pontifici latrones sub-misit, qui nihil tale cogitantem in templo crudeliter trucidarent. Quæ omnia in eum finem dicun-tur, vt Pauli fortem agnoscas, quem tam nefarij hominis potestati Deus permisit, simul verò eundem defendit, ne quid ab illo mali pateretur. Stultè ergo hominum potentiam & libidinem metuimus, quando leoninos quoq; animos cicurare Deus nouit, vt præter ingenium & morem suis parcant. Si-mul verò apparet hoc loco, quis populi status fit, qui aliquando libertatis dono abusus, Dei iram in se provocauit. Tales enim Iudæos fuisse constat, quos nō libertate modò Deus donauerat, verumetiam
units.tr: First, the copy of the letter by which the tribune Lysias commended Paul to Felix is set down. Among other things, this shows the brevity the ancients used even in the most serious matters, whereas today an excessive abundance of words is commonly used even in the most trivial matters. No other cause can be given for this than that all good faith has been extinguished, and in its place lies and empty pretence hold sway everywhere. This letter has its parts, of which the first place belongs to the inscription. It states both the name of the writer and of the one to whom he writes, and it tells who the Roman governor of Judaea was at that time: Felix, of course, whose name is often mentioned even by foreign historians. They report that he was a freedman of the emperor Claudius, and that by the dullness of his prince he rose to such a height that he could easily snatch away the highest honours from Roman citizens and patricians. Yet he kept a servile disposition, and with lust, adultery and slaughter he defiled everything everywhere. Suetonius writes that he was the husband of three queens, whom it is certain he enticed into marriage partly by the authority of Claudius and partly by infamous deceit. Drusilla, the daughter of Herod (of that Herod whom we heard in chapter 12 was struck down by an angel), he snatched from Aziz, king of the Emesenes, by the art and work of a certain Cypriot magician. He also sent robbers against the high priest Jonathan, who cruelly slaughtered him in the temple while he was thinking of nothing of the kind. All these things are told with this end in view: that you may recognise the strength of Paul, whom God allowed to be in the power of such a wicked man, and yet at the same time defended him, so that he suffered no harm at his hands. Therefore we foolishly fear the power and lust of men, when God knows how to tame even lion-like spirits, so that they spare his people beyond their own nature and custom. At the same time it appears in this place what the condition of a people is which, having once abused the gift of liberty, has provoked the wrath of God against itself. For it is certain that the Jews were such a people, to whom God had given not only liberty

units.la: Epistola Tri-buni, Cl. Lysiæ.
units.tr: The letter of the tribune Claudius Lysias.

units.la: Felix quis.
units.tr: Who Felix was.

units.la: Iosephus Antiq. lib. 20. cap. 9. & 11. sibi foli consecratos fuumq; peculium inter omnes gentes esse voluerat. At quia nec sanctis Dei legi-bus parere, nec prophetarum & Christi monitis corrigi voluerunt, & libertatis dono impie abusi sunt, illo spoliati Praesides tales ferre coguntur, quos nec generis nobilitas, nec virtutum gloria, sed infatuata libido & belluina crudelitas famosos reddebat. Cum, nec istis malis emendarentur, tandem repudium passi, & a Dei regno prorsus exclusi sunt. In quorum consyderatione eos frequentius versari oportebat, qui hodie etiam libertatis praerogativa licentiosius abuntur, eamq; in effrenem quidus audendi & faciendi licentiam converterunt, &c.
units.tr: Josephus, Antiquities, book 20, chapters 9 and 11. They had wanted to be consecrated to God alone and to be his own special people among all nations. But because they were unwilling to obey the holy laws of God, nor to be corrected by the admonitions of the prophets and of Christ, and impiously abused the gift of liberty, they were deprived of it, and were compelled to endure governors such as were made notorious not by the nobility of their family or the glory of their virtues, but by their infatuated lust and brutal cruelty. Since they were not reformed even by these evils, at last they suffered rejection and were utterly excluded from the kingdom of God. It would be right for us to dwell more often on the consideration of these people, who today also abuse the privilege of liberty more licentiously, and have turned it into an unbridled licence to dare and to do whatever they please, etc.

units.la: Sed ad Lysiae Tribuni epistolam reuertamur, qui post Inscriptionem a Narratione orditur, qua Paulum non vulgariter commendat. Illum enim nulla sua culpa aut merito, sed Iudaeorum improbitate captum esse testatur. Deinde Romanum civem esse fatetur. Tandem innocentiae etiam testimonium fert, dum in illo nullum crimen morte aut saltem vinculis dignum haerere scribit, nec ipsos Iudaeos aliam ob causam, quam propter ipsorum Legem & religionem aduersus illum tumultuari. Est hoc quidem praeclarum testimonium, sed cogitandum est, haec militis verba esse, & illum pro communi Romanorum more loquii. Hi enim cum Iudaicam religionem omnino abolitam cuperent, illam a suis Praesidibus minime defendi volebant. Quare illos religionis controversias nequaquam curauisse, passim videmus. At longe aliud Deus iubet, qui magistratus primam religionis curam habere precipit. Nec enim decet, ut Dei cultum vel negligant, vel prophanari patiantur, qui in summum huius dignitatis gradum Dei beneficio collocati sunt. Interim filiorum huius saeculi astutia in Tribuno eluceat, qui suum errorem, quem in vinciendo & adflagra relegando Romano civi commiserat, tam egregie dissimulat, ea modo scribens, quae sibi laudem & fauorem conciliare poterant. Cum primis vero obseruandum venit, quam Deo curae sint veri cultores, quando illorum innocentiam hostium quoq; testimonio asserit. Exemplum huius hodie passim cernitur, quando apostolorum & prophetarum laudes magnifice ij praedicant, quos eorundem doctrinam & fidem plusquam hostiliter persequi videmus. Quid ergo hostium calumnias aut mundi infamiam metuimus?
units.tr: But let us return to the letter of the tribune Lysias, which, after the inscription, begins with a narrative in which he does not commend Paul in a common way. For he testifies that Paul was seized not through any fault or merit of his own, but through the wickedness of the Jews. Then he confesses that Paul is a Roman citizen. Finally he also bears witness to his innocence, when he writes that no crime worthy of death or at least of chains clings to him, and that the Jews rage against him for no other cause than their own law and religion. This is indeed an excellent testimony, but we must bear in mind that these are the words of a soldier, and that he speaks in the usual manner of the Romans. For they, wishing the Jewish religion to be wholly abolished, were by no means willing for it to be defended by their governors. That is why we see everywhere that they never troubled themselves about disputes over religion. But God commands something far different, who orders that magistrates have the first care of religion. For it is not fitting that those who have been placed by God's benefit in the highest degree of this dignity should either neglect the worship of God or allow it to be profaned. Meanwhile the cunning of the children of this age shines forth in the tribune, who so skilfully conceals the mistake he had made in binding and beating a Roman citizen, writing only those things that could win him praise and favour. Above all, we should observe how much God cares for true worshippers, since he vindicates their innocence even by the testimony of their enemies. An example of this is seen everywhere today, when those men magnificently praise the apostles and prophets, while we see them persecuting the doctrine and faith of the same men more than hostilely. Why then should we fear the calumnies of enemies or the infamy of the world?

units.la: Restat vltima epistolae pars, quae praeoccupatione constat. Ne enim Felix indigne ferret, hominem innocentem non dimissum, sed potius tanto sumptu ad se ablegatum esse, huius quoque institutiones ratio reddit ur. Propter insidias enim a Iudaeis structas hoc factum esse scribit, quas dimissus Paulus nunquam effugere potuisset. Ita ergo cum innocentis hominis saluti, tum publicae paci consultum oportuit. VBI rursum Tribuni exemplo magistratus officij admonentur, ut curent nimirum, ne quis vim patiatur, quando in hunc finem ipsos potissimum instituto esse constat, ne boni malorum libidine & insolentia opprimantur. Vide Psal.72. Rom.13.
units.tr: There remains the last part of the letter, which consists of anticipation. For lest Felix take it ill that an innocent man was not dismissed but rather sent to him at such expense, the reason for this measure is also given. He writes that this was done on account of the plots laid by the Jews, which Paul, if dismissed, could never have escaped. Thus care had to be taken both for the safety of an innocent man and for the public peace. Here again, by the example of the tribune, magistrates are reminded of their duty, namely to take care that no one suffers violence, since it is certain that they have been appointed for this very purpose, so that good people are not overwhelmed by the lust and insolence of the wicked. See Psalm 72; Romans 13.

units.la: Sequitur quem euentum res ista habuerit, felicissimum nempe, ita moderante domino. Milites enim iniunctum sibi munus fidelissime exequuntur, & Paulum saluum coram Felice praeside statuunt. Hic vero, quasi naturam exuerit, praeter morem humanus & affabilis, illum cuias sit interrogat. Quo cognito, causae cognitionem in accusatorum aduentum vsque suspendit. Docet enim naturae lex, vtrangue partem audiendam esse, priusquam sententiam feras. Meminerimus autem omnia haec, Deo sic administrante euenisse. Huius enim opus est, quod milites absq; murmure Paulo insferuiunt, quod pro eius salute quidus facere parati sunt, quod Felix solito humanior illum amice excipit, & in Herodis praetorio non illiberali custodia asseruari curat. Vsus horum est, ut hominum conatus non multum moremur, sed vni Deo placere studeamus, qui barbaras mentes mansuefacere, mores efferos cicurare, & hostes quoq; in nostri amorem convertere potest. Amen ment hac nos, vt inuicta fidei constantia mundi tyrannidem vincamus, aeternum olim in caelis victuri cum Iesu Christo saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: What followed was the outcome of the affair, a most fortunate one, as the Lord directed it. The soldiers faithfully carry out the task laid upon them and bring Paul safe before the governor Felix. Felix, as if he had put off his nature, contrary to his custom, is kind and courteous, and asks him of what province he is. When he learned this, he deferred hearing the case until his accusers arrived. For the law of nature teaches that both parties ought to be heard before one passes judgment. Let us remember, moreover, that all these things came about with God so governing. For it is his doing that the soldiers serve Paul without grumbling, that they are ready to do whatever they can for his safety, and that Felix, more humane than usual, receives him kindly and takes care that he is kept in Herod's palace under no harsh custody. The purpose of these things is that we should not dwell long on men's efforts but strive to please the one God, who can tame barbarous minds, civilise savage manners, and turn even enemies to love of us. May he grant us this, that by the unconquered constancy of faith we may overcome the tyranny of the world, and one day live forever in heaven with Jesus Christ our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CLII.
units.tr: SERMON CLII.

units.la: POst quinque autem dies descendit Princeps Sacerdotum Ananias cum Senioribus & Tertullo quodam oratore, qui comparuerunt coram Praeside contra Paulum. Et citato Paulo coepit accusare Tertullus, dicens: Nos per te tuæq̄ prudentiæ egregia in hac gente facinora multam pacem consecutos esse, & prorsus & vbiq̄ agnoscimus, praestantissime Felix, cum omni gratiarum actione. Sed ne diutius te detineam, oro te vt audias nos paucis pro tua humanitate. Nacti enim sumus virum hunc pestiferum & concitantem seditionem omnibus Iudaeis in vniuerso orbe, & principem sectae Nazarenorum, qui etiam templum prophanare conatus est. Quem & apprehensum voluimus secundum Legem nostram iudicare. Sed superveniens Tribunus Lysias, cum magna vi eripuit eum e manibus nostris, iubens accusatores eius ad te venire: ex quo poteris ipse inquisitione facta de omnibus istis cognoscere, de quibus nos accusamus eum: Adiecerunt autem & Iudaei, dicentes haec ita habere.
units.tr: Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with the elders and a certain orator, Tertullus, who appeared before the governor against Paul. When Paul was summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: "Since through you and your outstanding prudence we have enjoyed great peace, and since by your foresight reforms are being made for this nation in every way and everywhere, we acknowledge this with all thankfulness, most excellent Felix. But so that I do not detain you longer, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. For we have found this man to be a pestilent fellow, who stirs up sedition among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, who even tried to profane the temple. We seized him and wished to judge him according to our law. But the tribune Lysias came up and with great violence took him out of our hands, ordering his accusers to come to you. From him you yourself can learn, by examining him, all those things of which we accuse him." The Jews also joined in, saying that these things were so.

units.la: Arrat hoc Capite Lucas quid Paulo apostolo apud Felicem praesidem euenerit, ad quem illum à Tribuno, qui Hierosolymis in praesidio erat, transmissum fuisse audiuimus. In qua narratione primum locum actio capitalis habet, quam contra apostolum Pontifices & Seniores instituerunt. Quamuis vero ita ille causam suam agat, vt nullum in eo crimen capitale Felix deprehendere posset, toto tamen biennio in vinculis detinet, & vt aliquam apud Iudaeos gratiam ineat, eundem provincia decedens successori suo Portio Festo, captum vinctumq̄ relinquit. Porro in eum finem ista describuntur, vt inde discamus, quae semper piorum in hoc mundo sors futura sit, & quam pertinaci odio illos mundus hic persequi soleat: quando Iudaeos nullis vel sumptibus vel laboribus pepercisse videmus, vt Paulum diuini verbi fidelissimum praeconem opprimere possent. Sed vt haec sint euentura esse Christus praedixit, ita quod praedixerat apostolorum exemplis illustrari & probari voluit, quo minus offenderemur, si quando nobis etiam similia acciderent. Nam vt aduersa quaeque & persecutiones grauissimas apostoli sustinuerunt: ita suo etiam exemplo docent, quid nos cum persecutionibus & aduersis tentamur, facere conueniat. Et hic quidem praecipuus praesentis quoq̄ loci, imò totius sequentis historiae vsus est. At in praesenti prima pars actionis contra Paulum institua commemoratur, cuius singulas partes modò excutiemus.
units.tr: In this chapter Luke relates what happened to the apostle Paul before the governor Felix, to whom, as we have heard, he was sent by the tribune who was in charge of the garrison at Jerusalem. In this narrative the first place is held by the capital prosecution which the high priests and elders brought against the apostle. Although Paul so conducted his case that Felix could find no capital crime in him, Felix nevertheless kept him in chains for the whole two years; and, in order to win some favour with the Jews, he left him bound and imprisoned to his successor Porcius Festus when he left the province. Moreover, these things are described to the end that we may learn from them what the lot of the pious in this world will always be, and with what stubborn hatred this world is accustomed to persecute them. For we see the Jews sparing neither expense nor labour, so that they might crush Paul, the most faithful herald of the divine word. But just as Christ foretold that these things would happen, so he wanted what he had foretold to be illustrated and confirmed by the examples of the apostles, so that we might be less offended if similar things should happen to us too. For just as the apostles endured all adversities and the most severe persecutions, so by their example they teach what we ought to do when we are tried by persecutions and adversities. This is indeed the principal use of the present passage, and indeed of the whole following history. But in the present passage the first part of the action brought against Paul is recorded, and we shall now examine its individual parts.

units.la: Orditur autem à descriptione partium, quae coram Felice praeside comparuerunt. Et ab vna quidem parte steterunt Pontifex Ananias, Seniores, & cum his Tertullus Rhetor celeberrimus & longo dicendi vsu instructus. Altera vero pars solum Paulum habet, & hunc quidem vinctum, multiq̄ nominibus iam ante suspectum. Patet rursum hoc loco (quod iam saepe aliàs diximus) qui fere praecipui Veritatis & huius ministrorum hostes sint, quibusq̄ armis pugnent. Hi nimirum, qui cum religionis tum rerumpub. fortissimi assertores videri volunt: & inter hos cumprimis ij, qui religionem quaestum fecerunt. Tales enim in praesenti Pauli aduersarios fuisse, passim euangelica historia abunde testatur. Atqui eiusmodi hominess plerunq̄ rerum vsu, prudentia, dicendi facultate, potentia item & authoritate praestare solent: quae causa est, quòd sectatores & fautores habeant quàm plurimos. E contra vero veritatis ministri, vt numero pauci, ita fere ignobiles & obscuri sunt, adhaec omnibus velinuisi vel contempti, vt qui animi amarulentia potius aut insciti a, quàm publicae salutis studio, mundi studijs sese opponere videntur. Atqui perpetuam hanc in mundo hoc piorum conditionem fuisse, vt nimirum pauci & contempti cum multis authoritate & potentia instructissimis pugnare coacti sint, omnium seculorum exempla docent: Ita enim Moses & Aaron cum Magis Aegyptijs committuntur, quos Regis fauor totiusq̄ Aegypti nobilitas tuebatur. Ita vnus Elias cum Baalis sacerdotibus quadringentis & quinquaginta, totidemq̄ fere lucorum prophetis coram Achabo, iniquissimo iudice, congreditur. Et Micheam paulò post cum quadringentis pseudoprophetis commis- sum fuisse legimus. Possent etiam aliorum prophetarum & apostolorum, adeoq; ipsius Christi bistoria allegari, quas breuitatis studio omittimus, cum scripturas legentibus passim occurrat. Nobis potius vsus borum obseruandus erit, è quo fructus haud exiguus ad nos redit. Primùm enim communi omnium institutioni seruiunt, ne videlicet de religione aut fide ex sectatorum multitudine siue authoritate iudicemus, id quod vulgò etiam hodie fieri consueuit. At si hoc admittamus, iam non Paulus modò causa cadet, qui solus & ignobilis à Pontificibus & toto Senatorio ordine accusatur, verum etiam prophetæ omnes vnà cū Christo & apostolis reliquis periclitabuntur. Imò Turcas Christianis præferemus, qui & amplissimis regnorum finibus, & hominum multitudine, victorijs item & secundis rerum successibus nos longè superant. Quare Christum potius audire decet, qui gregem suorum fidelium pusillum vocat, & per angustam vitæ portam paucissimos ingredi, multos autem perlatiorem viam ad interitum cateruatim ruere, ait. Luc.12. Matth.7. Deinde consolationem quoque haud vulgarem horum consyderatio nobis affert: ne videlicet terreamur, etiamsi nobis quoq; aliquando solis standum sit aduersus multos potentia, gloria & authoritate insignes. Qui enim Paulo in præsenti affuit, hic ipse nos quoq; in simili causa periclitantes minimè deseret. Extant enim promissiones amplissimæ, quibus spiritus sui suggestionem, os & sapientiam nobis pollicetur, cui nulli aduersarij possint resistere. Vide Luc.12. & 21. Matth.10. Marc.13. &c.
units.tr: The account begins with a description of the parties who appeared before the governor Felix. On one side stood the high priest Ananias, the elders, and with them Tertullus, a most celebrated rhetorician, well trained by long practice in speaking. The other side had only Paul, and him in chains, already long under suspicion on many counts. Here again (as we have often said elsewhere) it becomes clear who are generally the chief enemies of the Truth and of its ministers, and with what weapons they fight. These are, without doubt, men who want to seem the most valiant defenders both of religion and of the commonwealth; and among them especially those who have made religion a source of gain. For that such men were Paul's adversaries in this case, the evangelical history abundantly testifies throughout. Yet such men usually surpass others in experience of affairs, in prudence, in skill in speaking, and likewise in power and authority, and this is why they have very many followers and supporters. On the contrary, the ministers of the truth, being few in number, are generally also of low birth and obscure, and moreover are either hated or despised by everyone, since they seem to oppose the ways of the world out of bitterness of spirit or ill will rather than out of zeal for the public good. Yet all the ages teach that this has always been the lot of the pious in the world: that the few and despised are compelled to fight against many who are most richly endowed with authority and power. Thus Moses and Aaron came into conflict with the Egyptian magicians, whom the king's favour and the whole nobility of Egypt protected. So Elijah alone encountered the four hundred and fifty priests of Baal, and almost as many prophets of the groves, before Ahab, a most unjust judge. And we read that Micaiah, a little later, had to contend with four hundred false prophets. The examples of other prophets and apostles, and indeed of Christ himself, could also be cited, but for the sake of brevity we omit them, since they occur everywhere in the Scriptures for those who read them. Rather, we should observe the use of these examples, from which no small fruit comes back to us. First, they serve the common instruction of all, so that we do not judge concerning religion or faith by the multitude or authority of its followers, which is commonly done even today. But if we admitted this, not only would Paul's cause fall, he who alone and of low birth is accused by the high priests and the whole senatorial order, but all the prophets together with Christ and the remaining apostles would also be put in danger. Indeed, we would prefer the Turks to Christians, who far surpass us in the vast extent of their kingdoms, in the multitude of their people, and likewise in victories and prosperous successes. Therefore it is fitting rather to hear Christ, who calls his flock of faithful ones a little flock, and says that few enter by the narrow gate of life, while many rush in crowds by the broad and easy way to destruction. Luke 12; Matthew 7. Secondly, the consideration of these things brings us no ordinary consolation: that we should not be terrified even if sometimes we too must stand alone against many who are distinguished by power, glory and authority. For he who was present with Paul in this case will by no means desert us when we are in peril in a similar cause. For there are most ample promises by which he pledges to us the prompting of his Spirit, a mouth and wisdom, which no adversaries can resist. See Luke 12 and 21; Matthew 10; Mark 13, etc.

units.la: Sed Tertullum Rhetorem audiamus, cuius oratio tribus potissimum partibus constat. Prima exordium habet, quo non tam artificiose quàm subdola & impudenti adulatione beneuolentiam captat, partim ab ipsius Felicis, partim à propria ipsorum persona. Illius enim beneficium esse dicunt, quòd pace læta fruantur, & multa indies ipsius cura & prouidentia in melius restituantur. Rursum ab ipsis beneficium hoc agnosci & cum gratiarum actione suscipi fatentur. At vtrinq; splendidè mentiuntur. Felicem enim pessimè prouinciam administrauisse, multa truculenter & inustè fecisse, omnia denique immoderata libidine, stuprís & cædibus fœdauisse, supra audiuimus, & ethnici eius seculi scriptores abunde testantur. Deinde Iudæos quoq; illis temporibus, indefinentibus & perpetuis seditionibus contra Romanos tumultuatos esse, omnes nouerunt, quibus vel mediocris est historiarum cognitio. Attamen non pudet vanissimos homines impudenter mentiri, & tyrannum laudando publicam totius gentis causam, quæ ipsis commendatissima esse debebat, turpiter prodere. Sed ideo pacem & tranquillitatem publicam falsis laudibus euehunt, vt Paulum Felici inuisum reddant, quasi seditiosum huius turbatorem. ET in his quidem, quanta odij aduersus veritatem concepti virulentia sit, facilè elucet. Quia enim mundo nihil tam inuisum est, quàm Veritas, eò quòd huius luce illius opera mala arguuntur, acerrimos & immanissimos hostes potius, quàm hanc ferre & amare consueuit, & tolerabiles omnino tyranni videntur, modò suam in opprimenda Veritate operam conferant. Ita Tiberium Cæsarem, libidine & tyrannide infamem, Christo saluatori præferunt, quando se alium regem, præter Cæsarem habere negant. Imò Barrabam latronem & seditionis nefaria authorem Christo præferre non puduit. Nec noua est in mundo ista iudicij peruersitas. Hac ipsa enim Mosi olim in deserto Israelitas obstrepuisse, legimus, dum Ægyptiacam seruitutem propter pepones, cepas, allia, carnes & alia eius generis mirificè laudant, eam verò conditionem, quæ in singulas boras noua diuinæ beneficentiæ exempla exhibebat, ceu infelicissimam & miserrimam detestantur. Vide Num.11.cap. Atqui vtinam non hodiè etiam similia exempla extarent, quando multi pacem publicam, quæ sub Papatu floruit, magnificè prædicant, eamq; euangelij prædicatione turbatam esse quiritantur, interim verò funestissima bella callidè dissimulant, quorum Romani Pontifices iam se- culis aliquot authores fuerunt, nec aliquam faciunt eorum grauaminum mentionem, quæ cùm fortunas tum conscientias hominum miserrimè attriuerunt. Quid quod eò vsq; quorundam dementia pro greditur, vt cum acerrimis & inueteratis hostibus potius colludere, quàm euangelicæ veritatis lucem ferre velint? Sed idem aliquando isti homines experientur, quod à Romanis infelix Iudæorum gens non multis post eiectos apostolos annis perpessa est.
units.tr: But let us hear the rhetorician Tertullus, whose speech consists chiefly of three parts. The first is the exordium, in which he seeks goodwill, not so much by skilful art as by a sly and shameless flattery, partly from Felix himself and partly from the persons of the accusers. For they say that it is Felix's benefit that they enjoy happy peace, and that through his constant care and foresight many things are being set right day by day. Again, they confess that they acknowledge this benefit and receive it with thanksgiving. But on both counts they lie most splendidly. For we have heard above that Felix administered the province most wickedly, did many things savagely and cruelly, and in short polluted everything with unbridled lust, debauchery and murders, as the pagan writers of that age also abundantly testify. Next, everyone who has even a moderate knowledge of history knows that the Jews too in those times kept rising in tumult against the Romans in unceasing and perpetual seditions. Yet these most vain men are not ashamed to lie shamelessly, and by praising the tyrant they basely betray the public cause of the whole nation, which ought to have been most dear to them. But they extol public peace and tranquillity with false praises so that they may make Paul hateful to Felix, as if he were a seditious disturber of it. And in this one can readily see how great is the virulence of the hatred conceived against the truth. For since nothing is so hateful to the world as the Truth, because by its light the evil works of the world are exposed, the world is accustomed to prefer the most bitter and savage enemies to bearing and loving it, and tyrants seem altogether tolerable provided they devote their efforts to suppressing the Truth. Thus they prefer Tiberius Caesar, infamous for lust and tyranny, to Christ the Saviour, when they deny that they have any king other than Caesar. Indeed they were not ashamed to prefer Barabbas, a robber and the wicked author of sedition, to Christ. Nor is this perversity of judgment new in the world. For we read that the Israelites once in the desert also railed against Moses in this same way, while they extolled the Egyptian servitude for its melons, onions, garlic, meats and other things of that kind, and detested as most wretched and miserable that condition which displayed new examples of divine kindness every hour. See Numbers 11. Would that similar examples did not exist even today, when many loudly proclaim the public peace which flourished under the Papacy, and complain that it has been disturbed by the preaching of the gospel, while meanwhile they cunningly conceal the most deadly wars, of which the Roman Pontiffs have been the authors for several centuries, and make no mention of those burdens which have most wretchedly worn down both the fortunes and the consciences of men. And what of the fact that the madness of some goes so far that they would rather collude with the most bitter and long-standing enemies than bring the light of evangelical truth? But these same men will one day experience what the unhappy nation of the Jews suffered at the hands of the Romans not many years after the apostles were cast out.

units.la: Porrò ad Tertullum redeamus, qui secunda orationis suæ parte accusationem aduersus Paulum grauissimam instituit, quæ tribus capitibus continetur. Primò seditiosum dicit, imò ipsissimam pestem vocat, eò quòd passim in toto orbe Iudæos seditiose turbet. Ita autem in Paulum transferc crimen, cuius ipsi praecipui authores erant.
