Iudaeorum enim opera hactenus seditiones aduersus Paulum & illius collegas excitatas fuisse, tota huius libri series docuit. Nam huc referri possunt, quae de Corintho, Thessalonica, Epheso, Antiochia, Iconio, Lystris, & infinitis aliis ciuitatibus, per hos turbatis, audiuimus. Deinde propugnatorem sectae Nazarenorum vocant. Schismatis ergo & haereseos accusant, quod crimen omnibus seculis in ecclesia grauissimum habitum fuit. Videtur autem Tertullus Christianos per contemptum Nazarenos dicere, vtpote qui obscuram & ignobilem suae sectae originem haberent. Nazareth enim oppidulum nullius fere pretij fuisse, ex Iohannis cap. 1. patet, vbi Philippo Iesum Nazarenum nunciante, Nathanael respondet: A Nazareth potest ne aliquid boni esse? Estq; hoc vetus diaboli stratagema, quod veram religionem ignobilitatis nomine suspectam reddit. Cuius impulsu olim quoq; Iulianus apostata Christum Galilaeum, & Christianos Galilaeos nominauit. Tertio templi prophanati accusant, & templi nomine vniuersum cultum externum comprehendunt. Sunt haec nobis hodie eo diligentius obseruanda, vt intelligamus, quibus crimini bus fere grauetur Veritas, & ne offendamur, si quando nos quoq; seditiosi, schismatici, haeretici, templorum & imaginum prophanatores, sacrilegi deniq; & religionis auitae euersores dicimur. Haec ipsa enim crimina sunt, quae & prophetis & ipsi Christo maxime obiecerunt impij hostes. Vt vero illa nos non offendere debent, ita nec illis statim fidem habere debemus, qui insontes & pios viros istis criminibus impudenter grauant.
units.tr: But let us return to Tertullus, who in the second part of his speech brought a very grave accusation against Paul, contained under three heads. First, he calls him seditious, indeed a very plague, because he stirs up the Jews to sedition everywhere throughout the world. But in this way he transfers the crime of which they themselves were the chief authors. For the whole course of this book has shown that the seditions raised against Paul and his colleagues until now were the work of the Jews. What we have heard about Corinth, Thessalonica, Ephesus, Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and countless other cities disturbed by these men can all be referred here. Next, they call him a champion of the sect of the Nazarenes. So they accuse him of schism and heresy, a crime which in every age has been regarded as the gravest in the Church. Tertullus seems to call the Christians Nazarenes out of contempt, as people whose sect had an obscure and ignoble origin. For that Nazareth was a little town of almost no worth is clear from John chapter 1, where, when Philip announces Jesus of Nazareth, Nathanael replies: "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" This is an old stratagem of the devil, which makes the true religion suspect by the name of lowliness. At whose prompting Julian the Apostate also once called Christ the Galilean and the Christians Galileans. Third, they accuse him of profaning the temple, and by "temple" they mean the whole external worship. These charges are to be observed by us today all the more carefully, so that we may understand with what crimes the truth is commonly burdened, and so that we are not offended if we too are at any time called seditious, schismatic, heretical, profaners of temples and images, sacrilegious, and finally overthrowers of the religion of our fathers. For these are the very accusations which the impious enemies levelled most of all at the prophets and at Christ himself. But just as these charges ought not to offend us, so we ought not immediately to believe those who shamelessly burden innocent and godly men with such crimes.

units.la: Atque falsis criminibus Paulum vrgere viderentur, testes sistunt: Primo quidem ipsum Tribunum, quem tamen obiter accusant, vt qui nimium importunus iam iam poenas secundum legem daturum eripuerit. Deinde vero omnes vnanimi consensu Tertulli verbis astipulantur. Quo loco effrenis audaciae simul & impudentiae exemplum proponitur. Nam Tribunum accusare audent, & sibi sanguinis fundendi occasionem ereptam esse quiritantur per hunc, qui eo nomine maximam laudem merebatur. Adeo non piget scelerum impios, vt eos perpetuo oderint, qui illorum improbis conatibus obstant. Praeterea cum primo quidem accusatores, deinde iudices huius causae fuerint, nunc testes quoq; sunt, adeoq; quiduis sibi credi volunt, nec Dei iudicium verentur, qui falsos testes maxime exosos habet, & eosdem talionis poena coerceri iubet. Prouerb. 9. Deut. 19. Nobis vero haec non parum conducunt. Nam & eos suspectos habere discimus, qui hodie horum similes sunt, & minus offendimur, si quid tale nobis etiam accidit. Viuit enim & regnat Christus Iesus, qui similibus praeiudicijs oppressus, omnem inferorum potestatem vicit, & in coelos euectus, hostium suorum consilia ridet, suorum vero causam fidelissime tuetur. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: And so that they might seem to press false charges against Paul, they bring forward witnesses: first the tribune himself, whom they nonetheless accuse in passing, as one who, being too importunate, snatched away the man who was about to pay the penalty prescribed by law. Then all of them, with one accord, agree with the words of Tertullus. Here is set before us an example of unbridled audacity and shamelessness at the same time. For they dare to accuse the tribune, and complain that the chance of shedding blood was snatched from them by the very man who for that reason deserved the highest praise. So little do the wicked grieve over their crimes that they always hate those who stand in the way of their wicked attempts. Moreover, since they were first the accusers and then the judges of this cause, they are now witnesses as well, and so they want to be believed in anything whatever, and do not fear the judgment of God, who utterly abhors false witnesses and commands that they be restrained by the penalty of retaliation. Prouerb. 9. Deut. 19. For us, however, these things are of no small use. For we learn to regard with suspicion those who today are like them, and we are less offended if anything of the sort happens to us as well. For Christ Jesus lives and reigns, who, though oppressed by similar prejudgments, conquered all the power of the underworld, and, carried up into the heavens, laughs at the plans of his enemies and most faithfully defends the cause of his own. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 153.

units.la: Respondit autem Paulus, cum annuisset ipsi Praeses vt diceret: Aequiore animo pro meipso causam dico, cum sciam te a multis iam annis fuisse iudicem genti huic: qui possis cognoscere, quod non plures sunt mihi dies quam duodecim, ex quo ascendi adoraturus Hierosolymam. Et neq; in templo inuenerunt me cum aliquo disputantem, aut concursum turbae facientem, neq; in Synagogis, neq; in vrbe, neq; probare possunt ea, de quibus me accusant. Confiteor autem hoc tibi, quod iuxta viam, quam vocant haeresim, sic colo patrium Deum, credens omnibus quae in Lege & Prophetis scripta sunt, spem habens in Deum fore quam & hi ipsi expectant, resurrectionem mortuorum, iustorum simul & iniustorum. In hoc autem ipse studeo, sine offendiculo conscientiam habere erga Deum & erga homines semper.
units.tr: Then Paul, when the governor had nodded to him to speak, answered: "I make my defence the more willingly, since I know that you have been a judge over this nation for many years. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship. Neither in the temple did they find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, nor in the synagogues, nor in the city, and they cannot prove the things of which they accuse me. But this I confess to you: that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of my fathers, believing everything written in the Law and the Prophets, and having the same hope in God that these men themselves hold, that there will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous. In this I also take pains always to have a conscience without offence towards God and towards men."

units.la: Audiuimus heri grauissimae accusationis, aduersus Paulum institutae, capita, quae ex Tertulli ore spiritus sanctus diligentissime conscribi voluit, partim quidem vt apostolicae historiae veritas nobis minus suspecta esset, quando hostium quoque verba bona fide recenseri videmus: partim vero vt minus offendamur, si quando nobis aut aliis verae fidei sectatoribus similia obijci audimus. Porrò audiamus nunc Paulum apostolum, qui innuente sibi Felice præside omnia ista constan- ter simul & verè diluit. Priusquam tamen apostoli verba aggrediamur, duo nobis observuanda ve- niunt. Alterum, Felicis exemplum est, quo admonemur in iudicijs vtranq; partem audiri debere. Nisi enim id fiat, partialis erit iudex, nec vnquam causæ veritatem cognoscere poterit. Alterum in Pauli exemplo proponitur, qui grauissimus conuitijs petitus, non tamen impudenter ad dicen- dum prorumpit, nec impotenti iræ affectu abripitur, vt conuitia conuitijs diluat: sed expectata di- cendi copia & præsidis permissione, modestè & prudenter causam suam agit. Imitentur hunc pij om- nes, ne animi impotentia & conuitiandi libidine veritatis causam, quam tuentur, suspectam red- dant: quod non raro ab ijs fieri solet, qui suis potius affectibus indulgere, quàm rationis dictata sequi volunt.
units.tr: We heard yesterday the heads of the most serious accusation brought against Paul, which the Holy Spirit wished to have recorded most carefully from the mouth of Tertullus. This was partly so that the truth of the apostolic history might be less open to suspicion, since we see that the words of the enemies too are recounted in good faith, and partly so that we may be less offended when we hear similar charges brought against us or other followers of the true faith. Next, let us now hear the apostle Paul, who, at the invitation of the governor Felix, answers all those charges calmly and truthfully. Before we take up the apostle's words, two things come to our attention that we must observe. The first is the example of Felix, which reminds us that in trials both sides ought to be heard. If this is not done, the judge will be partial and will never be able to learn the truth of the case. The second is set before us in the example of Paul, who, though he was grievously assailed with insults, did not rush impudently into speech, nor was he swept away by an unbridled passion so as to answer insults with insults. Instead, having waited for his opportunity to speak and for the governor's permission, he pleads his cause modestly and wisely. Let all the godly imitate him, lest by lack of self-control and a lust for abuse they make the cause of truth, which they defend, suspect. This is something that is not infrequently done by those who want to indulge their own passions rather than follow the dictates of reason.

units.la: His præmissis ad Pauli responsionem accedamus, quæ Exordio & obiectorum criminum con- futatione constat. Et Exordio quidem ipse quoque à Felicis persona benevolentiam captat, sic tamen vt citra ineptam & mendacem adulationem aduersarios occultè perstringat. Nam eo æquiori ani- mo se coram Felice causam dicere ait, quòd multis iam annis genti huic præfuerit, & proinde eius mores probè cognitos habeat. Est enim hoc cumprimis optandum reo, vt iudicem peritum & gna- rum habeat, quando non raro fit, vt ignorantia peccent, qui alias iustitiæ vehementer studiosi sunt. Quo periculo se liberum esse Paulus fatetur, nec timendum esse, vt Felix sibi à Iudæis imponi patia- tur, quorum impudentiam & seditiosos spiritus multorum annorum experientia cognouerat. Hinc vero vniuersalis doctrina peti debet, à magistratibus diligentiam requiri in causarum cognitione, eò quòd ignorantiæ excusatio apud illos nulla est, si hæc voluntaria aut crassa fuerit. Cur enim rerum ignarus sit, qui Dei vices gerens, illius iudicia sibi concredita habet? Memores ergo, Dei iudicium esse, populi sui mores, ingenia & facta diligenter obseruent, causarum quoq; circunstantias probè exa- minent. Ita enim fiet, vt aut ignorantia peccare nequeant, aut excusabilis illorum error erit, si quem non turpi desidia, sed aliorum fallacijs decepti commiserint. Sed vtinam in horum confydina- tione frequentius versarentur, qui hodie honorum titulis & imperij fastu turgidi, ocio turpi & co- messationibus, choreis item & venationibus se totos dedunt, adeò vt ferarum lustra & quæuis libidi- nis instrumenta melius quàm populi sui conditionem, mores & ingenia perspecta habeant. Porrò priusquam hinc discedamus, illud quoq; obseruandum erit, quòd Felicem, turpissimum tyrannum, an- nis aliquot in sua gente præsidere Deus voluit. Id enim mirum alicui videri poterat. Sed merebatur hoc gentis illius ingratitudo planè incurabilis. Cum enim duces & pastores optimos illis impositos Dominus, illos adeò dedignati sunt, vt ne Christum quidem æternum Dei filium audire voluerint. Patiuntur ergo quod sæpe minatus fuerat Deus: vt huius præsidio nudati eiusmodi præsides habeat, qui suæ potius libidini & auaritiæ, quàm publicæ gentis saluti consultum cuperent. Possunt hæc do- cere, quid omnibus illis expectandum sit, qui vel libertatis donum, vel pios magistratus & fidos ver- bi ministros Iudaica planè ingratitudine & improbitate aspernantur.
units.tr: With these things premised, let us turn to Paul's reply, which consists of an exordium and a refutation of the charges made against him. In the exordium he too seeks goodwill from the person of Felix, yet in such a way that, without fawning and lying flattery, he subtly criticises his opponents. For he says that he is pleading his cause before Felix with the more willing mind because Felix has for many years presided over this nation and therefore knows its customs well. Indeed, this is especially to be wished for by an accused person: that he have a judge who is experienced and knowledgeable, since it not infrequently happens that people who are otherwise keen on justice go wrong through ignorance. Paul confesses that he is free from this danger, and that there is no need to fear that Felix will allow himself to be imposed upon by the Jews, whose impudence and seditious spirit he had come to know through many years' experience. From this, a general teaching ought to be drawn: that magistrates should be required to be diligent in investigating cases, since there is no excuse for ignorance before them if it was wilful or gross. For why should someone be ignorant of affairs who, acting in God's place, holds God's judgements committed to him? Let them therefore remember that judgement belongs to God, and let them carefully observe the morals, dispositions and deeds of their people, and examine closely the circumstances of cases. For in this way they will either be unable to err through ignorance, or their error will be excusable if they have been deceived by the trickery of others and not committed it through shameful sloth. But would that those who today, puffed up with the titles of honour and the arrogance of power, give themselves wholly to idleness, base pleasures, drinking parties, dances and hunting, would more often occupy themselves with these matters! As it is, they know the dens of wild beasts and every instrument of lust better than the condition, morals and dispositions of their own people. Before we leave this point, we must also observe that God willed Felix, a most vile tyrant, to preside for some years over this nation. This might seem strange to someone. But the utterly incurable ingratitude of that nation deserved it. For when the Lord had set over them excellent leaders and ministers, they so disdained them that they would not even listen to Christ, the eternal Son of God. So they suffer what God had often threatened: that, stripped of his protection, they should have rulers of this kind, who care more for their own lust and greed than for the public welfare of the nation. These things can teach what is to be expected by all those who spurn either the gift of liberty or pious magistrates and faithful ministers of the Word, with a thoroughly Jewish ingratitude and wickedness.

units.la: Pauli apologia
units.tr: Paul's apology

units.la: Sed in Pauli responsione progressi, quomodo obiecta crimina diluat, videamus. Inter hæc primùm est, quòd seditionum authorem dixerant, cui etiam violati templi crimen coniungit, eò quòd huius gratia cumprimis tumultuati fuerant. Est vero in istis diluendis valde diligens. Primò enim à tem- pore argumentum ducens, impossibile esse dicit, abs se seditionem commotam fuisse, cum duodecimus demum dies agatur, ex quo Hierosolymas venerit. A quo dierum numero si eos subtrahas, quos in vinculis iam egerat, vix vnus aut alter reliquus erit. Quis vero repente adueniens intra bidui aut tridui spacium vrbem populosissimam vniuersali seditione turbaret? Deinde non veni (inquit) vt turbas darem, sed vt adorarem, & (vt postea sequetur) vt eleemosyna inter gentes collecta huius po- puli inopiæ subuenirem. Falsum ergo est, quod illi de templi prophanatione dicunt. Tertiò nusquam me tale quid molientem inuenerunt. Nec enim vel in templo vel in Synagogis docui, nec aliquem fe- ci populi concursum. Deniq; nunquam probabunt ea, quæ de me dixerunt. Id quod grauiss. dicit. Ita enim illos non mendacij modò, sed falsi testimonij insimulat. At non repugnat Christiana patientia ratio, quò minus cum aduersariorum ignominia obiecta crimina diluamus, quando non tam no- stram existimationem, quàm veritatis causam periclitari videmus. Cæterùm institutioni seruit, quòd à seditionis crimine tam diligenter sese purgat Paulus. Inde enim discunt ministri, sibi maximè ca- uendum
units.tr: But let us see how Paul, in his reply, answers the charges brought against him. First among them, they said he was the author of the sedition, and they add the charge of profaning the temple, because it was on account of him that they had especially stirred up the tumult. Paul refutes these charges with great care. First, he argues from the time: it was impossible for him to have stirred up the sedition, since it was now only the twelfth day since he came to Jerusalem. If you subtract from this number of days those he had already spent in chains, hardly one or two will be left. Who, arriving suddenly, could throw a very populous city into general sedition within the space of two or three days? Second, he says, "I did not come to create disturbances, but to worship," and (as he goes on to say) to bring alms collected among the Gentiles to relieve the poverty of this people. So what they say about the profanation of the temple is false. Third, they never found me engaged in any such thing. For I neither taught in the temple nor in the synagogues, nor did I gather any crowd of people. Finally, they will never prove the things they have said about me. He says this most seriously, for he accuses them not merely of lying but of false witness. Yet Christian patience does not forbid us to refute the charges brought against us, even to the shame of our opponents, when we see that not so much our own reputation as the cause of truth is in danger. Moreover, Paul's clearing himself of the charge of sedition so carefully serves our instruction. For ministers learn from it that they must take the greatest care not to disturb the commonwealth by seditious conduct, since nothing is more destructive to it, and God especially delights in concord and unity. But if, through the preaching of the Word and without their fault, seditions are stirred up by the wicked, or arise from some uncertain authority, then that saying of Ambrose holds: it is within our right not to stir up the people, but it is in God's hand to calm them once they are stirred up.

units.la: Seditionis crimen diluit. uendum esse, ne respub. seditiose turbent, quando illis nihil exitiale est, & Deus concordia ac vnitate cumprimis delectatur. Quod si vero ad verbi praedicationem citra illorum culpam seditiones ab impijs excitantur, vel incerto authoritate oriuntur, tum illud Ambrosianum locum habet, In nostro iure esse ne excitemus populum, in Dei manu autem esse concitatum mitigare.
units.tr: Paul clears himself of the charge of sedition. They must be warned to take the greatest care not to disturb the commonwealth with seditious acts, since nothing is more ruinous to them, and God especially delights in harmony and unity. But if, through the preaching of the Word and without any fault on their part, the impious stir up sedition, or if it arises from an uncertain authority, then that saying of Ambrose applies: it is in our power not to stir up the people, but in God's hand to calm them once they are stirred up.

units.la: Deinde ad haereseos crimen Paulus transit. Fateor (inquit) me Deum colere iuxta eam viam & rationem, quam illi haeresim vocant. Interim me propterea haereticum aut schismaticum esse, pernego. Nam Deum patrium colo, & scripturis credo, &c. Quo loco multa nobis observanda veniunt.
units.tr: Next Paul turns to the charge of heresy. "I confess," he says, "that I worship the God of our fathers according to that way which they call a heresy. Yet I utterly deny that I am on that account a heretic or a schismatic. For I worship the God of my fathers and believe all things written in the Scriptures," and so on. Many things here deserve our notice.

units.la: Primùm, quòd fidem, de qua accusatus fuit, ingenuè fatetur, & quidem coram ethnico iudice. A fide ergo confessionem separare nefas est, nec sufficit vt corde credas, id est, opinionem quandam penes te animo concipias, sed coram hominibus fidem in Christum confitearis oportet. Nec enim eiusmodi cultores fert Christus, quos sui pudeat, vt saepe iam dictum est. Deinde fidem suam quatuor articulis comprehendit, quibus omnes alij continentur.
units.tr: First, that he frankly confesses the faith for which he was accused, and that before a heathen judge. Therefore it is wrong to separate faith from confession, and it is not enough for you to believe in your heart, that is, to hold some opinion in your mind; you ought to confess your faith in Christ before men. For Christ does not bear with worshippers of this kind, whom he is ashamed of, as has often been said already. Next, he sums up his faith in four articles, which contain all the others.

units.la: Primo patrium Deum se colere ait, eum intelligens, qui cum patribus egit, & quem illi coluerunt. Est hic praecipuus fidei articulus, vt uno vero Deo contenti, nullos nobis vel nouos vel alienos deos faciamus. Est autem verus Deus, qui cum patribus olim agens, filium promisit, & in hoc salutem hominibus contulit. Unde constat nec Iudaeos nec Turcas hodie veri Dei cultores esse, quando Deum sine filio sibi imaginantur. Secundo formam & modum sui cultus exprimit, dum se credere dicit omnibus quae in Lege & prophetis scripta sunt. Atqui omnium horum finis Christus est, de quo Mosem & prophetas testatos fuisse constat. Fide ergo in Christum Paulus Deum coluit. Vbi iam omnes fidei nostrae articuli, qui de Christo sunt, comprehenduntur. Nec sanè alius cultus Deo placere potest, quando in solo illo hic nobis placatus est. Nec patrem honorat, qui quis filium non honorauerit. Iohan. 5. cap. Simul vero Pauli exemplum monet, Dei cultum iuxta scripturas, non iuxta hominum traditiones instituti debere, quando illum his frustra coli, paßim docemur. Vide Isa. 29. Matth. 15. Tertiò resurrectionem mortuorum fatetur, quam ideo nominatim allegat, quia in illa omnis nostrae salutis ratio consistit, vt ipse in priori ad Corinth. cap. 15. docuit. Vniuersalem vero resurrectionem agnoscit, non vt fanatici quidam, qui hanc ad solos pios restringunt. Vt enim hos pietatis praemia in nouissimo die accipere oportet, ita impios aeternis poenis subijci iustum est. Quartò se huius fidei ductu in hoc vnum incumbere dicit, vt conscientiam tum coram Deo tum coram hominibus integram seruet. Qui germanus fidei fructus est. Haec enim iustificat homines: at qui iusti sunt, iustitiam operantur. 1. Iohan. 3. cap. Necesse fieri potest, vt conscientiam suam scelerum foeditate polluant, quicunque resurrectionem fore ex animo credunt. Ex his vero, quae Pauli fides fuerit, patet. Atqui hi probat, se pro haeretico haberi non posse. Quotquot ergo Paulum imitati, Deum patrium iuxta scripturas vera in Christum fide colunt, resurrectionis spem retinent, & conscientiae puritati erga Deum & homines pro virili studeant, hi vere Paulini & apostolici, imò Christiani & orthodoxi sunt, vt vt in illos infelix mundus desaeuiat. Teneamus ergo fidem hanc, ô fratres, & inuictam futurae resurrectionis spe per omnes tribulationes fortiter eluctemur, aeternum olim praemium habituri cum Christo Iesu, saluatore nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: First, he says that he worships the God of his fathers, meaning the God who made covenant with the fathers and whom they worshipped. This is the chief article of faith: content with the one true God, we make for ourselves no new or foreign gods. The true God is the one who, dealing with the fathers of old, promised a Son and in him brought salvation to men. It is therefore clear that neither the Jews nor the Turks today are worshippers of the true God, since they imagine God without the Son. Second, he states the form and manner of his worship, when he says that he believes everything written in the Law and the prophets. But the aim of all these writings is Christ, to whom Moses and the prophets are known to have borne witness. Paul, then, worshipped God by faith in Christ. In this all the articles of our faith that concern Christ are comprehended. Nor indeed can any other worship please God, since in Christ alone he has been appeased toward us. "He who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father" (John 5). At the same time, Paul's example warns that the worship of God ought to be instituted according to the Scriptures, not according to the traditions of men, since we are taught on every side that he is worshipped in vain by these. See Isa. 29; Matt. 15. Third, he confesses the resurrection of the dead, which he names expressly because the whole reason of our salvation rests on it, as he taught in his former letter to the Corinthians, chapter 15. He acknowledges a universal resurrection, not as certain fanatics do, who restrict it to the godly alone. For just as the godly must receive the rewards of piety on the last day, so it is right that the wicked be subjected to eternal punishments. Fourth, he says that, guided by this faith, he devotes himself to this one thing: to keep his conscience whole, both before God and before men. This is the true fruit of faith. For it is these who are justified, and those who are righteous practise righteousness (1 John 3). It can happen that those who sincerely believe in a resurrection to come nonetheless pollute their conscience with the foulness of their sins. From these things it is clear what Paul's faith was. But this proves that he cannot be regarded as a heretic. Therefore, all who imitate Paul, who worship the God of their fathers according to the Scriptures in true faith in Christ, who keep the hope of resurrection, and who strive earnestly to keep their conscience pure before God and men, these are truly Pauline and apostolic, indeed Christian and orthodox, however wretchedly the unhappy world may rage against them. Let us hold fast to this faith, brethren, and with the hope of the future resurrection unconquered, let us struggle bravely through all tribulations, that we may one day obtain the eternal reward with Christ Jesus our Saviour, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 154.

units.la: Post annos autem plures accessi, eleemosynas exhibiturus in gentem meam, & oblationes: in quibus comperarunt me purificatum in templo, haud cum turba neque tumultu. Quidam autem ex Asia Iudaei, quos oportebat apud te praesto esse, & accusare si quid haberent aduersum me: aut hipsi dicant, si quid deprehenderunt in me iniquitatis, cum steti in Concilio: nisi de vna hac voce, qua clamaui inter eos stans: De resurrectione mortuorum ego iudicor hodie à vobis. Auditis autem his Felix distulit illos, certò sciens quae ad eam viam attinebant, dicens: Cum Tribunus Lysias descenderit, pernoscam causam vestram. Iussitque Centurioni, vt custodiret Paulum, sineretque illum relaxari: & ne quem ex illius familiaribus vetaret subministrare ei, aut adire eum.
units.tr: "After many years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings. In these they found me purified in the temple, not with a crowd or with tumult. But certain Jews from Asia, who ought to have been here before you and to accuse me if they had anything against me; or let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found in me when I stood before the council, except this one word which I called out as I stood among them: 'I am judged by you today concerning the resurrection of the dead.'" When Felix heard these things, he put them off, knowing well what pertained to that way, and saying: "When the tribune Lysias comes down, I will examine your case." And he ordered the centurion to keep Paul in custody but to allow him some freedom, and not to forbid any of his friends to minister to him or to visit him.

units.la: Quemadmodum accusationem à Iudæis aduersus Paulum institutam spiritus sanctus diligentissimè describi voluit, vt ex ea discamus, de quibus fideles Christi ministros mundus hic semper accusaturus sit: ita non minori studio Pauli apologiam recenset, qua docemur, vt nos in simili casu gerere debeamus. Primò autem ad seditionis crimen constantissimè simul & diligentissimè respondit, suo exemplo docens, Christi ministros ab hoc alienissimos esse debere. Quoad fidem vero, cuius nomine illum hæreseos & schismatis accusarunt, illam ingenuè confessus est, ac eius ratio-nem paucis quidem, sed dilucidè reddidit. Vnde colligimus, fidei confessionem Christi ministros cum primis decere, quam tamen ita fieri conuenit, vt eiusdem ratio omnibus constare possit, qui aliquo minus sensu tanguntur.
units.tr: Just as the Holy Spirit wished the accusation brought by the Jews against Paul to be described with the greatest care, so that from it we might learn what things this world will always accuse the faithful ministers of Christ of, so with no less zeal he recounts Paul's defence, from which we are taught how we ought to act in a similar case. First, he answered most steadfastly and at the same time most carefully the charge of sedition, teaching by his own example that the ministers of Christ ought to be most remote from this. As for the faith, on whose account they accused him of heresy and schism, he openly confessed it and gave its reason in few words, but clearly. From this we gather that the confession of faith especially befits the ministers of Christ; yet it ought to be made in such a way that its reasoning can be understood by all who are touched by even a little sense.

units.la: Sequitur in præsenti loco violati templi crimen, in quo diluendo mirè diligens est Paulus, cum templi vsum & maiestatem, Christi aduentu & morte, maxima ex parte abolitam esse, non ignoraret. Nec verò hoc illum Iudæis dare putabimus, qui templum adhuc superstitiosius obseruabant, sed ad verum templorum vsum respicit, quo nec Christiani homines carere possunt. Licet enim nec Dei maiestas templis includi aut circunscribi possit, nec ijsdem cultus Dei alligari debeat, externa tamen religio locum certum postulat, in quo sacri cætus colligi, verbum prædicari, & sacramenta administrari possint. Atqui communis sensus dictat, locos hisce tantùm, rebus sacris ab omni profanatione diligenter custodiendos esse: quando Christum olim prohibuisse legimus, ne quis vas ad quod per templum gestaret. Marc. 11. Nec credibile est illum aliquo religionis sensu affici, qui huiusmodi consecratos locos improbè contemnit & profanat. Quæ potissima causa fuisse videtur, propter quam Paulus in hoc crimine diluendo tantum laborare voluit. Quo exemplo simul admonemur, bodie quoque Christianorum templa siue Oratoria ab omni contemptu & profanatione fortiter asseri ac vindicari debere, id quod Constantinus Magnum olim & alios huius similes magna cum laude fecisse, historici tradunt.
units.tr: In this passage follows the charge of violating the temple, in dispelling which Paul is remarkably careful, since he was not ignorant that the use and majesty of the temple had for the most part been abolished by the coming and death of Christ. Nor shall we think he is granting this to the Jews, who still observed the temple more superstitiously, but he looks to the true use of temples, which Christian people also cannot do without. For although neither the majesty of God can be enclosed or circumscribed in temples, nor should the worship of God be tied to them, nevertheless external religion requires a fixed place in which sacred assemblies may be gathered, the Word preached, and the sacraments administered. Indeed common sense dictates that these places, set apart for sacred things, must be carefully guarded from every profanation, since we read that Christ once forbade anyone to carry a vessel through the temple (Mark 11). Nor is it credible that a man is touched by any sense of religion who shamelessly despises and profanes such consecrated places. This seems to have been the chief reason why Paul wished to labour so hard in refuting this charge. By this example we are also admonished that today the temples or oratories of Christians too must be bravely defended and vindicated from all contempt and profanation, which historians report Constantine the Great and others like him once did with great praise.

units.la: Sed Pauli apologiam videamus, qui primùm argumento à tempore ducto se excusat. Nam multis annis se Hierosolymis abfuisse, ait. Vnde liquidò patet, nihil abs se contra templum tentari potuisse. Deinde causam aduentus sui allegat, quem non templi gratia instituerit, sed vt eleemosynam inter gentes collectam, egenis Syriæ fratribus afferret. Vide de hac, quæ in epistolis ad Corinthios habentur, in primis posterioris epistolæ Cap. 8. & 9. Obiter verò illos inhumanitatis & ingratitudinis accusat, qui optimè de tota gente meritum, & nouum beneficium offerentem, tam indignis modis exceperint. Nobis autem hoc loco, præter Christianæ beneficentiæ exemplum, de quo circa finem Cap. vndecimi diximus, mundi huius ingratitudo obseruanda venit, qua Christi ministros prosequi consueuit. Tanta hæc est, vt perditos velit, qui pro communi omnium salute dies & noctes inuigilant. Ita Lotum Sodomis inuisum fuisse legimus, cuius gratia ab hostibus captos Abraham asseruerat. Et Mosem ab Israelitis nihil præter conuitia & minas retulisse constat, propter quos aulicæ vita delitias & Ægypti thesauros reliquerat. Quid propheta euenerit, & pos bos Christo Domino, notius est, quàm vt multis exponi oporteat. Sed cum primis memorabile est, quod Paulo hic accidit, qui post multorum annorum labores, tot vigilatas noctes & vndiq; conquisitam eleemosynam, qua pauperum egestati subuenirent, hanc vnam mercedem retulit, quod ab illis ipsis verberibus, vinculis & quouis alio contumeliarum genere multatus est, quorum saluti vnice studebat, imò pro quibus anathema fieri optabat. Quid ergo mundi ingratitudine offendimur, qui cum totus in malo constitutus sit, meliorem gratiam salutis suæ authoribus referre nescit? Sed ad Pauli argumenta reuertamur, qui tertio loco, se in templo purificatum & fine turba atq; tumultu versatum fuisse dicit. Vnde rursum constat, templum abs se minimè prophanatum fuisse. At si vera est Pauli argumentatio (quod nemo Christianus negauerit) simul verum est, templa abijs, qui purificati sunt, violari non posse. Tales verò sunt quotquot in Christum credunt, cum hos à peccatis expiatos suo sanguine Christus sanctificet. Vide 1. Cor. 5. & 6. Cur ergo bodie templorum profanatores dicimur, qui & Christum saluatorem ex animo agnoscimus, & veterem templorum vsum pro virili asserimus, qui est, vt precibus, verbi doctrinæ & Sacramentorum administrationi seruiant? Quanto verius ijs hoc nomen conueniet, qui in templis sacra nundinantur, idola prostituunt, & infinita alia exercent, quibus Deum omnibus seculis offensum fuisse constat? Quarto in Asianos Iudæi Iudæos crime hoc transfert, quos tumultus omnis authores fuisse supra audiuimus, eos vero iam ab-esse conqueritur. Est enim hic perpetuus seditiosorum omnium mos, vt postquam turbas concitarunt, in quibus fere boni periclitantur, ipsi sese occulte subducant, & rei euentum securi expectent. Vtinam huius meminisset semper infelix vulgus hominum, quando illius intemperie & præcipiti audacia ne bulones eiusmodi ad res suas conficiendas abuti volunt.
units.tr: But let us look at Paul's defence, who first excuses himself by an argument from time. For he says that he had been absent from Jerusalem for many years. Whence it is clear that nothing could have been attempted by him against the temple. Next he states the reason for his coming, which he undertook not for the sake of the temple but to bring the alms collected among the Gentiles to the needy brothers of Syria. See about this what is found in the epistles to the Corinthians, especially in chapters 8 and 9 of the second epistle. In passing, he accuses of inhumanity and ingratitude those who received so roughly a man who had deserved so well of the whole nation and who was offering a new benefit. For us in this place, apart from the example of Christian beneficence, of which we spoke near the end of the eleventh chapter, the ingratitude of this world is to be noted, with which it is accustomed to pursue the ministers of Christ. It is so great that it wishes ruin upon those who keep watch day and night for the common salvation of all. Thus we read that Lot was hated by the Sodomites, on whose behalf Abraham had rescued him when he had been taken captive by enemies. And it is established that Moses received from the Israelites nothing but abuse and threats, for whose sake he had left the delights of court life and the treasures of Egypt. What happened to the prophets, and afterwards to Christ the Lord, is too well known to need explaining at length. But what happened to Paul here is especially memorable: after many years of labour, many sleepless nights, and alms gathered from every side to relieve the poverty of the needy, he received this one reward, that he was punished with beatings, chains and every other kind of insult from those very people for whose salvation alone he laboured, and for whom he even wished to become a curse. Why then are we surprised at the ingratitude of the world, which, since it is wholly placed in evil, does not know how to repay better favour to those who are the authors of its salvation? But let us return to Paul's arguments. In the third place he says that he was purified in the temple and was present there without crowd or tumult. Whence again it is established that the temple was by no means profaned by him. But if Paul's argument is true (which no Christian would deny), it is at the same time true that temples cannot be violated by those who are purified. Such are all who believe in Christ, since Christ sanctifies them, cleansed from their sins by his blood (see 1 Cor. 5 and 6). Why then are we today called profaners of temples, when we both acknowledge Christ as Saviour from the heart and defend, so far as we can, the ancient use of temples, which is that they should serve prayers, the teaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments? How much more truly would this name belong to those who trade in sacred things in temples, prostitute idols, and carry on countless other things by which God is known to have been offended in every age! Fourthly, the Jews transfer this crime to the Asians, whom we have heard above to have been the authors of every tumult, but he complains that they are now absent. For this is the constant custom of all seditious men: after they have stirred up disorders, in which good men are nearly always endangered, they secretly withdraw themselves and wait securely for the outcome of the affair. Would that the unhappy common crowd of men always remembered this, when they wish such scoundrels to be used for their own purposes, through the recklessness and headlong daring of these people.

units.la: Porro post criminum confutationem, ipsos aduersarios confidenter Paulus prouocat. Si isti (inquit) Asianorum illorum causam agere volunt, agedum dicant quid in me sceleris deprehenderint. Scio illos nihil habere, nisi forte tumultum in ipsorum Concilio propter liberam resurrectionis mortuorum confessionem obortum, mihi imputare velint. At qua fronte id facient, qui resurrectionem ipsi quoq; fateri cogentur, nisi palàm impij esse velint? Est autem obseruatione digna Pauli fiducia & dicendi libertas, quæ non obscurum innocentiæ illius argumentum præbet. Huc Christi ministros omnes studere conuenit, vt certi sint, se propter solam veritatem mundo inuisos esse. Hoc enim vere intrepidos & aduersus quæuis pericula constantes reddit. Vide Petrum in priori epist. 3. & 4. cap.
units.tr: Furthermore, after the refutation of the charges, Paul confidently challenges the adversaries themselves. "If these men," he says, "wish to plead the cause of those Asians, let them say what wrongdoing they have found in me. I know they have nothing, unless perhaps they wish to impute to me the tumult that arose in their own council on account of my free confession of the resurrection of the dead. But with what face will they do this, who will themselves be compelled to confess the resurrection, unless they wish openly to be impious?" Paul's confidence and freedom of speech are worthy of observation, for they offer no obscure proof of his innocence. To this all the ministers of Christ ought to strive, so that they may be certain that they are hated by the world for the sake of the truth alone. For this is what truly makes them fearless and steadfast against any dangers. See Peter in the first epistle, chapters 3 and 4.

units.la: Restat actionis huius exitus, longe alius quam Iudæi sperarint. Felix enim causam omnem in-Lysia tribuni aduentu differt, tum quòd non ignoraret quæ ad vitā hanc pertinebant, nempe pertinaces de fide & religione controuersias, vnà cum Iudæorum indomitis moribus: tum quòd ipsi in Lysiæ testimonio accusationem totam fundauerant. Interim Pauli rationem habet, cuius innocentiam haud obscure videbat. Illum enim relaxari iubet, eiusq; familiaribus libera facit ipsum accedendi eiq; ministrandi copiam. Perseuerarunt enim cum Paulo captiuo familiares quidam, e quorum numero Lucam quoq; fuisse constat: quorum exemplo docemur, non deserendos esse eos, qui pro Christi nomine periclitantur, quando vt sibi factum reputabit, quicquid officij in illos contulerus. Rursum Felicis exemplo magistratus discunt, cauendum esse, ne in hominum gratiam iudicia præcipitent. Dei enim est iudicium, cuius se ministros esse meminisse debent. Illius ergo æquitatem longanimitate temperatam imitentur. Interim captiuos non inhumaniter tractent, quando facinorosis etiam propter communem humanitatis sensum aliquâ misericordia debetur. Ante omnia vero Dei fidem erga suos cultores, & eiusdem in hostes suos potentiam in istis obseruemus. Huius enim opus est, quod Felix præter ingenium suum (de quo sæpe iam diximus) in Paulum humanus & facilis est. Nec difficile est Deo fores animos mollire, & suis apud hostes quoq; gratiâ conciliare, cum illi libera in omnes creaturas, adeoq; hominum corda etiam potestas sit. Nemo igitur nostrum homines timere in animum inducat, nec in illorum gratiam aliquid præter officium faciat. Quin potius Deo nos & studia nostra approbemus, qui in medio hostium suos tueri, hostium animos flectere, & tandem omnibus angustijs ereptos in regnum suum transferre potest, cuius hereditatem omnibus sui nominis cultoribus præparauit, per Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: The outcome of this proceeding remains, far different from what the Jews had hoped. For Felix postpones the whole cause until the arrival of the tribune Lysias, both because he did not ignore what pertained to this affair, namely the stubborn controversies about faith and religion, together with the unruly habits of the Jews, and because they had based the whole accusation on the testimony of Lysias. Meanwhile he takes account of Paul, whose innocence he saw clearly enough. For he orders him to be released, and he gives his friends the free right to approach him and to minister to him. For some of his friends remained with Paul in captivity, and it is known that Luke was among their number. By their example we are taught not to desert those who are in danger for the name of Christ, since he will count as done to himself whatever duty we have performed towards them. Again, from Felix's example magistrates learn to take care not to rush their judgements to win the favour of men. For judgement belongs to God, and they ought to remember that they are his ministers. Let them therefore imitate his justice, tempered by long-suffering. Meanwhile let them not treat prisoners inhumanely, since even to wrongdoers some mercy is owed on account of the common sense of humanity. Above all, let us observe in these events God's faithfulness towards his worshippers and his power against their enemies. For it is his work that Felix, beyond his own disposition (of which we have often spoken already), is humane and kind towards Paul. Nor is it difficult for God to soften hard hearts and to win favour for his own people even among their enemies, since he has free power over all creatures, and indeed over the hearts of men. Let none of us therefore bring himself to fear men, nor do anything beyond duty to win their favour. Rather let us commend ourselves and our endeavours to God, who can protect his own in the midst of enemies, bend the minds of enemies, and at last, snatching them from all distress, transfer them into his kingdom, the inheritance of which he has prepared for all who worship his name, through Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLV.
units.tr: Homily 155.

units.la: Postaliquot autem dies, cùm aduenisset Felix cum Drusilla vxore sua, quæ erat Iudæa, accersiuit Paulum, & audiuit eum de fide, quæ est in Christum. Disputante autem illo de iustitia & temperantia, & de iudicio futuro, tremefactus Felix respondit: In præsentia abi, cæterū opportunitatem nactus, accersam te. Simul & illud sperans fore, vt pecunia sibi daretur à Paulo, vt soluerer ipsum. Propter quod & frequenter accersens eum, loquebatur cum ipso. Biennio autem expleto, accepit successorem Felix Portium Festum. Volens autem gratiam præstare Iudæis Felix, reliquit Paulum vinctum.
units.tr: After some days, when Felix arrived with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jewess, he sent for Paul and heard him concerning faith in Christ. But as Paul discoursed about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come, Felix became frightened and answered, "Go away for now; when I find an opportunity, I will send for you." At the same time he hoped that money would be given to him by Paul, so that he might be released. For this reason he often sent for him and talked with him. But after two years had passed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. Wishing to do the Jews a favour, Felix left Paul in chains.

units.la: Perquam memorabile & præclarum diuinæ tum bonitatis tum potentiæ exemplum fuit, quòd Paulus Felice Præside humano & facili vsus est, cuius tyrannidem iniquissimam ethnici quoq; scriptores literis prodiderunt. At longè præclarius est, quod in præsenti Lucas commemorat. Nec enim tutus modo sub Felice agit Paulus, verumetiam coram illo concionandi occasionem inuenit. Vnde Paulini illius dicti veritas omnibus patet, Dei verbum videlicet vinciri non posse, licet eius. ministri interdum vinculis & carceribus constringantur. Nam quod Paulo euenit, idin multi Christi martyribus hodie etiam euenire solet, vt qui vinći ad rogos ducuntur, Dei verbum adim- piorum terrorem, piorum verò consolationem libere prædicent. Sed in præsenti singula huius loci or- dine videamus.
units.tr: It was a most memorable and splendid example of both God's goodness and his power that Paul, under the governor Felix, a man who was humane and easy-going, was able to make use of him, though the Gentile writers too have recorded the most unjust tyranny of Felix in their books. But what Luke records in the present passage is far more remarkable. For Paul not only lives safely under Felix, but also finds an opportunity to preach before him. Hence the truth of that saying of Paul's is plain to everyone: the word of God cannot be bound, although its ministers are sometimes bound with chains and imprisoned. For what happened to Paul is what usually happens today to many martyrs of Christ, who, when they are led in chains to the stake, freely proclaim the word of God, to the terror of the wicked and the comfort of the godly. But let us look at the individual points of this passage in their order.

units.la: Principiò auditores Pauli describuntur, quos si penitius inspiciamus, haud obscurù argumen- tis, quæ Paulo habenda concionis occasio fuerit, colligere poterimus. Felix enim, qui Cæsarea per aliquot dies abfuerat, illuc cum Drufilla vxore reuersus fuisse dicitur, quam ego potissimam con- cionis huius causam fuisse crediderim. Iudæa enim fuit, Herodis Agrippæ filia, qui post occisum la- cobum apostolum, ab angelo percussus impietatis & tyrannidis graues pœnas dedit. Primum verò Antiocho Epiphani desponsata, non autem coniunćta fuit, eò quòd Iudaicis ceremonijs ille initiari nollet. Inde Aziazo Amazorum regi nupsit, à quo per Felicem Præsidem magnificus promissiū & Cyprij cuiusdam Magi artibus abductam fuisse supra diximus. Quare non turpis modo adulterata, verumetiam Dei legem & patrum religionem impiè transgressa, homini incircuncifo conuixit. Quæ omnia licet ab illa indignißime facta sint, verisimile tamen est, aliquem in illa reliquum fuisse puriorĭs religionis sensum, cui à teneris assueuerat. Quæ causa fuisse videtur, quòd Paulum cuius doctrinam ab omnibus prædicari audiebat, concionantem audire voluerit, id quod à Felice marito sui amantissimo, non difficulter impetrare poterat. Hic verò in transitu videre est, quid fere eos ma neat, qui cum impijs & alienis à vera religione coniugia faciunt. Licet illi vel libidinis astro exca- cati, vel opum & honorum splendore fascinati, omnem religionis sensum exuere conentur, redit ta- men conscientiæ scrupulus, & accenditur rursus fidei male deserta & negata desyderium, quo surē frustra exagitantur, qui tam paruam Dei simul & salutis propria rationem habuerunt. Quare non temere factum putabimus, quòd suis coniugijs infidelium Deus per Mosen abstinere iussit, cum hinc certum saluti nostræ periculum oboriri posse non ignoraret. Qua de causa Paulus quoq; veterem le- gem ratam esse volens, cum incredulis iugum ducere vetat. 2. Corinth. 6. Simul verò Dei bonitatem nos obseruare conuenit, qui tam sæda libidine pollutis euangelij verbum prædicari passus est, quo salus & vita mortalibus offerri solet. Verè ergo is est Deus, qui homines saluos fieri cupit, nec vult mortem peccatoris, sed potius vt resipiscat & viuat. Pertinent huc multa euangelicæ historiæ exem- pla, in quibus Christum publicanis & meretricibus singulari quadam gratia atq; familiaritate sa- lutem obtulisse legimus. Quod vt consolationi seruire debet, quando tentationibus satanicis vexa- mur, quibus salutis nostræ certitudo in dubium vocatur: ita officij quoq; admoneat, ne Dei gratiam quam is tam amicè nobis offert, improbè aspernemur. Vt enim euangelij prædicatio salutis causa est credentibus & pœnitentiam agentibus: ita inexcusabiles coram Deo fiunt, qui pœnitere nescij obla- tam impiè contemnunt. è quorum numero Felicem quoq; fuisse, postea audiemus.
units.tr: First, the hearers of Paul are described. If we examine them more closely, we shall be able to gather, without any great difficulty, what the occasion for Paul's sermon was. Felix, who had been absent from Caesarea for some days, is said to have returned there with his wife Drusilla, and I believe she was the chief reason for this sermon. For she was the daughter of Herod Agrippa, who, after the apostle James was put to death, was struck down by an angel and paid heavy penalties for his impiety and tyranny. She was first betrothed to Antiochus Epiphanes, but was not married to him, because he was unwilling to be initiated into Jewish ceremonies. Afterwards she married Azizus, king of the Emesenes, a man of great wealth, and, as we said above, she was lured away from him by the arts of a certain Cypriot magician, through the agency of Felix the governor. Therefore she was not only an adulteress of the basest kind, but also had impiously broken God's law and the religion of her fathers, and lived with an uncircumcised man. Although she did all these things most shamelessly, it is nevertheless likely that some remnant of a purer religion remained in her, which she had been accustomed to from childhood. This seems to have been the reason why she wished to hear Paul, whose teaching she heard was proclaimed by everyone, and her husband Felix, who loved her dearly, could easily obtain this for her. Here, in passing, we can see what usually awaits those who make marriages with the ungodly and with people alien to the true religion. Although such people, either blinded by the star of lust or dazzled by the splendour of wealth and honours, try to cast off all sense of religion, the sting of conscience returns, and there is kindled again a longing for the faith they have abandoned and denied, by which they are tormented in vain, since they took so little account of God and of their own salvation. Therefore we shall not think it was by chance that God, through Moses, commanded his people to abstain from marriages with unbelievers, since he knew that a certain danger to our salvation could arise from them. For this reason Paul also, wishing the old law to remain in force, forbids yoking oneself with unbelievers (2 Corinthians 6). At the same time, we ought to notice the goodness of God, who allowed the word of the gospel, by which salvation and life are usually offered to mortals, to be preached before a woman so polluted by such shameful lust. Truly, then, he is the God who desires that men be saved, and does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he repent and live. To this belong many examples from the gospel history, in which we read that Christ offered salvation to tax collectors and prostitutes with a singular grace and familiarity. As this ought to serve for our comfort when we are troubled by satanic temptations, by which the certainty of our salvation is called into doubt, so it also warns us of our duty not to scorn wickedly the grace of God, which he so kindly offers us. For just as the preaching of the gospel is the cause of salvation for those who believe and repent, so those who do not know how to repent, and wickedly despise the grace offered to them, become inexcusable before God. We shall hear later that Felix too was one of their number.

units.la: Veruntamen Pauli concionem videamus, quam non quidem verbotim Lucas recenset, prima verò capita commemorat, ex quibus quid dixerit, facile colligitur. Sunt ea tria numero. Primò de fide in Christum differentem audiuit Felix. Porrò vt Christus semper sibijpsi constat, atq; vnus & idem est heri, hodie & in æternum: ita vna & eadem semper est fidei in Christum ratio, quæ mu- tari nequit. Quare non alia Paulum in præsenti dixisse putabimus, quàm quæ alibi in eius tum con- cionibus cum epistolis continentur. Quorum omnium summa est, Sola fide in Christum, absque legis operibus, homines gratis iustificari & salutem consequi. Et vt Iudæos à legalium operum fiducia ad Christum abducere studuit: ita verisimile est, illum coram Felice multa de moralibus virtutibus dixisse, quòd nimirum illæ ad iustitiam veram in Dei conspeċtu nihil conferant, sed propter solam fi- dem in Christum Deo acceptæ & gratæ fiant. At quia de his dicendi locus passim occurrit, non est quòd illis in præsenti diutius immoremur. Illud verò obseruabis, fidem in Christum non in angulis modò, aut vbi nullus periculi metus est, prædicari debere: sed tum demum illius confessionem libe- ram & ingenuam requiri, quando propter illam mundum nobis infestum esse sentimus. Minimè er- go audiendi sunt, qui fidei confessionem inter adiaphora numerant. Ita enim dementiæ accusant apo- stolos & sanctos Christi martyres, qui nuspiam in fide asserenda ferventiores fuere, quàm vbi illam sæuissimè oppugnari viderunt. Simul verò Anabaptistæ Pauli exemplo arguuntur, qui à magistra- tibus comprehensi, vix vnquam adduci possunt, vt fidei suæ rationem reddant, & plerunque nec ipsi sua dosua dogmata argumentis confirmare, nec ad obiecta argumenta respondere volunt. Atqui Petrus Christianos paratos esse iubet ad reddendam fidei sue rationem cuiuis exigenti. 1.Pet.3. Et Paulum sue cum fidei tum doctrinæ adeo non puduit, ut ex vinculis quoq; coram ethnico tyranno & turpi adultera illam prædicare dignetur.
units.tr: However, let us look at Paul's sermon, which Luke does not indeed record word for word, but mentions its main heads, from which it is easy to gather what he said. There are three of them. First, Felix heard a discourse on faith in Christ. Moreover, just as Christ is always consistent with himself, and is one and the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the way of faith in Christ is always one and the same, and cannot be changed. Therefore we shall think that Paul in the present case said nothing other than what is contained elsewhere in his sermons and his letters. The sum of all these is that men are justified freely, and obtain salvation, by faith in Christ alone, apart from the works of the law. And just as he tried to lead the Jews away from confidence in legal works to Christ, so it is likely that he said much to Felix about the moral virtues, namely that these contribute nothing to true righteousness in the sight of God, but become acceptable and pleasing to God only on account of faith in Christ alone. But since there is an opportunity to speak of these matters everywhere, there is no need for us to dwell on them longer at present. You should, however, note this: faith in Christ ought to be preached not only in corners, or where there is no fear of danger, but then especially is its free and open confession required, when we feel that the world is hostile to us because of it. Therefore those who count the confession of faith among things indifferent must by no means be listened to. For in this way they accuse of madness the apostles and the holy martyrs of Christ, who were nowhere more fervent in asserting the faith than where they saw it most fiercely attacked. At the same time, the Anabaptists are refuted by Paul's example. When they are seized by the magistrates, they can hardly ever be brought to give an account of their faith, and for the most part they neither wish to confirm their own doctrines by arguments, nor to answer the arguments put to them. Yet Peter bids Christians be ready to give an account of their faith to anyone who asks (1 Peter 3). And Paul was not ashamed of his faith and his doctrine to such an extent that he deigned to proclaim it, even from his chains, before a heathen tyrant and a shameful adulteress.

units.la: Secundo de iustitia & temperantia disseruisse dicitur Paulus. At sub hisce duabus virtutibus germani fidei iustificantis fructus comprehenduntur, & iustitiam quidem in præsenti intelligimus, quæ suum cuique tribuit, & proinde omnes in se virtutes complectitur. Commendat hanc Christus, quando quæ Dei sunt Deo, & Cæsari quæ sunt Cæsaris reddere iubet. Et ad eandem referri debet, quod Paulus alibi scribit: Reddite omnibus quod debetur: cui tributum, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timorem, timorem: cui honorem, honorem, &c. Romanorum decimo tertio. Temperantia vero illicitis desiderijs obstat & voluptates refrenant, ne harum illecebris abrepti contra Deum & iustitiam peccemus. Quicquid ergo de virtutum studio & bonis operibus dici potuit, duabus hisce speciebus, Iustitia nimirum & Temperantia Paulus complexus est. Atqui hæc fidei doctrinæ necessario subijci oportet, tum quod huius germani fructus sunt (ut modo diximus) ex quibus illa dignoscitur, tum ne quis fidei prætextu ad effrenem carnis licentiam abutatur: contra quam multa passim in apostolorum scriptis leguntur. Porro obseruanda hic venit Pauli prudentia cum ingenua dicendi libertate coniuncta. De iis enim fidei verae fructibus maxime disserit, qui in auditoribus præcipue desiderabantur. Felicem enim in provincia administratione multa tyrannice egisse supra diximus, & maiorem quæstus sui quam iustitiæ rationem habuisse. Drusilla vero turpis adultera præter legem Dei incircuncisio nupserat. Hæc ergo illis ob oculos ponenda erant, ut quantum a salutis ratione abessent, liquido intelligerent. Docemur exemplo hoc quid & quomodo prædicari oporteat. Vel lent quidem pleriq; solam Dei gratiam & fidem iustificantem prædicari. At longe aliud requirit muri di huius & nostri seculi nequitia, qua in omne scelus passim omnes ruere videmus. Argui ergo illa oportet, ne frustra Dei gratiam illis prædicemus, qui sibi illa opus esse nondum intelligunt. Nec quid mundus velit videndum est, sed quid Christus iubeat, qui in nomine suo pœnitentiam primum, deinde vero peccatorum remissionem prædicari voluit. Luc.24. Parum ergo pie nec prudenter agunt, qui dum coram mundo pœnitere nescio solam Dei gratiam & fidem iustificantem docent, peccandi licentiam plantant, & hominibus pestilentissimæ securitatis authores sunt. Quin potius duo hæc coniungantur, ut scelerum conuicti homines pœniteant, & remissione peccatorum in sola Dei gratia per fidem in Iesum Christum quærere discant.
units.tr: Secondly, we are told that Paul discoursed about righteousness and self-control. Yet under these two virtues the genuine fruits of justifying faith are included. By righteousness we understand here that which gives each his due, and therefore embraces all the virtues within itself. Christ commends this when he bids us render to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's. And to the same head should be referred what Paul writes elsewhere: "Render to all what is owed: tribute to whom tribute is owed, custom to whom custom, fear to whom fear, honour to whom honour," and so on (Romans 13). Self-control, on the other hand, opposes unlawful desires and restrains pleasures, so that, carried away by their allurements, we do not sin against God and righteousness. Whatever can be said about the pursuit of virtue and good works, Paul has comprehended under these two kinds, namely righteousness and self-control. Moreover, these must necessarily be subjected to the doctrine of faith, both because they are its genuine fruits (as we have just said), by which it is recognised, and so that no one may abuse faith as a pretext for unbridled licence of the flesh, against which many things are read everywhere in the writings of the apostles. Furthermore, here we must observe Paul's prudence, joined with a frank freedom of speech. For he speaks chiefly about those true fruits of faith which were especially lacking in his hearers. We said above that Felix had acted tyrannically in many things in the administration of his province, and had been more concerned for his own gain than for justice. Drusilla, moreover, a shameless adulteress, had married against the law of God, being uncircumcised. These things, therefore, had to be placed before their eyes, so that they might clearly understand how far they were from the way of salvation. From this example we are taught what and how things ought to be preached. Many would indeed like only God's grace and justifying faith to be preached. But the wickedness of this and our age, in which we see everyone rushing headlong into every crime, demands something quite different. Those sins must therefore be rebuked, lest we preach the grace of God in vain to those who do not yet understand that they need it. Nor must we consider what the world wishes, but what Christ commands, who wished that repentance be preached first in his name, and then the remission of sins (Luke 24). Those therefore act neither piously nor prudently who, while not knowing how to make men repent before the world, teach only God's grace and justifying faith, and so plant licence to sin and become the authors of the most pestilent security among men. Rather, these two things should be joined together, so that men convicted of their crimes may repent, and learn to seek the remission of sins in God's grace alone, through faith in Jesus Christ.

units.la: Tertio de extremo iudicio disputat Paulus, nimirum ut eum errorem confutaret, quo gentes mundum hunc æternum fore credendo maxime decepti & securi facti sunt. Inde enim Epicureismus prodijt, qui Deum terrena curare negabat. Quare de fine mundi & nouissimo Christi ad iudicium aduentu omnino dicendum fuit, ne ludicra & friuola putarentur quæ de iustitia & temperantia dixerat. Admonemur autem obseruatu dignissimum esse hunc fidei articulum, quo Christum iudicem viuorum & mortuorum venturum esse credimus. Nam infirmis medetur, quos mundi huius facies offendit, dum impios lætis rerum successibus frui, pios autem affligi vident. Nam vicissitudinem aliquando fore discunt, cuius gratia Christus suum illum aduentu nostræ redemptionis diem vocat. Luc.21. Rursum non alia efficacior ratio est commouendi homines, ut officium faciant & a peccatis abstineant, quam cum ille dies & seuerus iudicis conspectus illis ob oculos ponitur. Quæ causa est, quod Christum frequenter huius mentionem facere audimus, & apostoli hinc fere adhortationum & dehortationum argumenta petunt.
units.tr: Thirdly, Paul discusses the last judgment, namely to refute that error by which the Gentiles, believing this world to be eternal, were chiefly deceived and made secure. For from this came Epicureanism, which denied that God cares for earthly things. Therefore it was necessary to speak fully about the end of the world and Christ's final coming to judgment, lest what he had said about righteousness and temperance be thought playful and frivolous. We are reminded that this article of faith, by which we believe that Christ will come as judge of the living and the dead, is most worthy of notice. For it heals the weak, whom the appearance of this world offends when they see the impious enjoying happy successes and the pious afflicted. For they learn that there will at some time be a reversal, for the sake of which Christ calls that day of his coming the day of our redemption. Luke 21. Again, there is no more effective way of moving men to do their duty and abstain from sins than when that day and the stern sight of the judge are set before their eyes. This is why we hear Christ often making mention of it, and the apostles draw almost all their arguments for exhortation and dissuasion from it.

units.la: Restat modo, ut Paulinæ concionis effectum videamus, qui quoad Felicem plane irritus fuit. Primo enim terretur quidem horum mentione, sed nihil de emendatione cogitat. Paulum enim abs se ablegat, quasi illum diutius audire, ipsi minus commodum sit. Sunt autem isti impiorum mores, qui interdum curiositate adducti verbum audiunt, eoq; nonnihil afficiuntur, adeo ut conscientijs territi contremiscant. Sed nondum hæc melioris naturæ indicia sunt, quando hoc ipsum diabolos solere, apostolus testatur. Iacob.2. Nam ut primum Dei verbum votis suis minus respondere sentiunt, illud amplius audire dedignantur. Ita Achab Micheam odit, quod nunquam placentia loquatur. Porro, alio rursum argumento reprobam mentem Felix prodit. Pecuniam enim captat a Paulo, & quem iure dimittendu esse noterat, non nisi pecunia accepta dimittere statuit. Venale ergo ius habet, cuius vitij causa fuit auaritia, quam in Romanis vt insatiabilem exteri quiq; taxauerunt. Discant aute tam fœdo exemplo magistratus, vt in iudicijs munerū corruptelam caueant, quæ Deo teste sapientū corda excæcare & vias iustorum peruertere consueuit. Exod.13. Deut.16. Perdidit eadem respub. florentissimas, & quantum hodie vbiq; noceat, quotidiana exempla abundè docent. At ne hic quidē peccandi finem Felix facit. Sed quia Paulu (qui nimirum nec fratribus oneri esse, nec mali exempli author fieri voluit) ad numerandam pecuniam tardiorem esse videt, aliud ex innocenti commodum venatur. Misso enim successore Festo, prouincia decedens, Paulum in vinculis relinquit, vt vel hoc pacto apud Iudæos gratiam ineat, quos multis indignis modis offenderat. Vbi sanctorum fortem videre licet, quorum patientia impij pro ludibrio abutuntur, & ex illis sibi inuicem gratificandi materiam sumunt. Ita in Christo impie diuexando Pilatus & Herodes conuenerunt. Ita Drusilla pater Iacobum gladio ferit, & vbi id Iudæis placuisse videt, in eorundem gratiam Petro quoq; necem molitur. Attamen non semper votorū impij compotes fiunt, quos etsi tardior sequatur Dei vindicta, tarditatem tamen supplicij grauitate compensat. Nostrum est, Pauli exemplo fidei constantiam & in afflictionibus diuturnis patientiam discere, vt tandem omnibus malis superiores triumphemus in Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: It remains only to see the effect of Paul's sermon, which with Felix was wholly fruitless. For at first he is indeed terrified by the mention of these things, but he does not think at all about amendment. He dismisses Paul, as if it were less convenient for him to hear him any longer. Such is the manner of the wicked, who sometimes, drawn by curiosity, hear the word and are somewhat moved by it, so that, terrified in their consciences, they tremble. But these are not yet signs of a better nature, since the apostle testifies that even the devils do this very thing. James 2. For as soon as they perceive that God's word does not answer to their desires, they disdain to hear it any more. So Ahab hated Micaiah, because he never spoke what pleased him. Furthermore, Felix again reveals a reprobate mind by another argument. For he hopes to get money from Paul, and he resolves to release, only on receipt of money, the man whom he knew ought rightly to be released. He therefore has a venal justice, whose cause of vice was avarice, which other foreigners have censured in the Romans as insatiable. Let magistrates learn from so shameful an example to guard against the corruption of bribes in judgments, which, as God is witness, is accustomed to blind the hearts of the wise and pervert the ways of the righteous. Exod. 13. Deut. 16. The same commonwealth destroyed its most flourishing things, and daily examples abundantly teach how much this harms everywhere even today. But not even here does Felix make an end of sinning. Yet since Paul (who, of course, did not want to be a burden to the brethren nor become an author of bad example) is seen to be slower in counting out the money, he hunts for another advantage from the innocent man. For, when his successor Festus had been sent, Felix, leaving the province, leaves Paul in chains, so that by this means at least he might win favour with the Jews, whom he had offended with many unworthy outrages. Here one may see the lot of the saints, whose patience the impious abuse for mockery, and from it they take matter for gratifying one another. So in harassing Christ impiously Pilate and Herod came together. So Drusilla's father struck James with the sword, and when he saw this had pleased the Jews, he also undertook the death of Peter to win their favour. Yet the impious do not always obtain their desires; though God's vengeance may follow them slowly, they make up for the slowness by the severity of the punishment. It is our part, by the example of Paul, to learn constancy of faith and patience in long afflictions, so that at last we may triumph over all evils, being more than conquerors in Christ Jesus, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: HOMILIA CLVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLVI.

units.la: FEstus ergo suscepta prouincia, post triduum ascendit Hierosolymam ab vrbe Cæsarea. Significaruntq; illi principes Sacerdotum ac primores Iudæorum de Paulo, & rogabant eum, postulantes fauorem aduersus eum, vt accerseret eum Hierosolymam, insidias tendentes vt interficerent eum in via. Festus autem respondit, vt seruaretur quidē Paulus Cæsareæ, se verò breui illò profecturum. Qui ergo inter vos, inquit, potentes sunt, vnà descendant, & si quid est in hoc viro crimen, accusent eum. Demoratus autem inter eos diebus amplius quàm decem, descendit Cæsaream: ac postero die sedit pro tribunali, iussitq; Paulum adduci. Qui cum perductus esset, circumsteterunt eum qui ab Hierosolymis descenderant Iudæi, multa & grauia crimina proferentes aduersus Paulum, quæ non poterant probare, ipso excusante, quòd neq; in legem Iudæorum, neq; in templum, neq; in Cæsarem quicquam peccasset.
units.tr: Festus, therefore, having taken over the province, went up to Jerusalem three days after arriving from the city of Caesarea. The chief priests and the leading men of the Jews reported to him about Paul, and they asked him for a favour against Paul: that he would summon Paul to Jerusalem, while they laid ambushes to kill him on the way. Festus replied that Paul should indeed be kept at Caesarea, and that he himself would be leaving there shortly. "Let those among you who are powerful," he said, "go down with me, and if there is any crime in this man, let them accuse him." After staying among them not more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea. On the next day he sat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought in. When Paul had been brought, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges against Paul, which they could not prove, since Paul himself denied that he had sinned in any way against the law of the Jews, the temple, or Caesar.

units.la: DEscribuntur hoc vigesimo quinto & sequenti cap. duæ grauissimæ Pauli apostoli actiones, quarum alteram coram Festo Præside nouo sustinuit, altera verò coram Agrippa & Bernice regina fidei causam dixit. Eo autem nomine prior actio potissimum memorabilis est, quòd illius prætextu ingens periculum Paulo Iudæi struxerunt, quod tamen Dei beneficio euasit, qui illum saluum fore promiserat, vt Romæ etiam apud Cæsarem de Christo Iesu testari posset, sicuti supra cap.23. dictum fuit. Porrò præcipuus omnium horum finis est, vt Deum suum rum esse habere discamus, & permittere quidem vt varie tententur, eosdem tamen ex omni tentatione fideliter afferere, quando sua vocationis memores, in ipso spem & fiduciam omnem collocatam habent. Quare fidei nostræ cōfirmandæ hæc potissimum seruire debent: quod vt maiori cum fructu fiat, singula ordine consyderabimus.
units.tr: In this twenty-fifth chapter and the one following, two very weighty deeds of the apostle Paul are described. He defended himself in the first before Festus, the new governor, and in the second he pleaded the cause of the faith before Agrippa and Queen Bernice. The first of these is especially memorable, because under its pretext the Jews prepared a great danger for Paul. Yet by God's favour he escaped it, for God had promised that he would be safe, so that he might also bear witness to Christ Jesus at Rome, before Caesar himself, as was said above in chapter 23. Moreover, the chief purpose of all these things is that we learn to have our God as our own, and to let ourselves be tested in various ways, yet be faithfully preserved by him from every temptation, when, mindful of their calling, we have placed all our hope and confidence in him. Therefore these things ought chiefly to serve to strengthen our faith. So that this may be done with greater profit, we shall consider the individual parts in order.

units.la: Primò enim nouus Iudæorum conatus narratur, quo Paulum opprimere tentarunt. Nam cum Festus Hierosolymam profectus esset, nimirum vt eius loci cives & incolas fide publicè data sibi obstringeret, illico ad ipsum Sacerdotes & reliqui primates confluunt, Paulum quem in vinculis Festus reliquerat accusant, & eam sibi à nouo Præside gratiam concedi petunt, vt Hierosolymam abducum, duƈtum, iudicio sistat, ut aduersus illum iuxta suæ gentis leges procedere possint. Interim illum iter facientem insidijs excipere & occidere statuerunt. Quo loco videre licet, quàm inquieti sint impiorum animi, postquam veritatis odio semel exarserunt. Quia enim huius luce ipsorum prava opera nunquam non arguuntur, fieri non potest, ut semel conceptum odium facile deponant. Quin potius in cordibus suis Euripi instar fremunt & æstuant, in omnem occasionem totis animis intenti, qua inuisam sibi veritatis lucem extinguere possint. Et tantæ fere huius odij vires sunt, ut posthabitis interdum priuatis commodis, hoc unum quærant & cupiant, ut è medio tollantur veritatis ministri, quorum doctrina sese excruciari sentiunt. Utrumque in præsenti exemplo cernitur. Nam toto biennio Paulum captum fuisse audiuimus. At nec temporis diuturnitas, nec infelix vinctorum sors, illorum animos mitigare potuit, qui quiduis potius quàm veritatis doctrinam, ferendum esse putabant. Quare omnem occasionem diligentissimè venantur, nec ullis vel laboribus vel sumptibus parcunt, ut tandem voti compotes fiant. Deinde apud novum Præsidem primas preces contra Paulum insumunt, quas reipublicæ potius debebant, cuius nomine ea petenda fuissent, quæ ad commune omnium salutem pertinerent. Sed hoc quasi præiudicio Paulum grauari voluerunt, ut publicum patriæ & gentis totius hostem esse suspicaretur Præses, pro quo puniendo illi cumprimis laborabant.
units.tr: First, a new attempt of the Jews is narrated, by which they tried to crush Paul. When Festus had gone up to Jerusalem, no doubt to bind the citizens and residents of that place to himself by a public pledge, the priests and the other leading men immediately flocked to him. They accused Paul, whom Festus had left in chains, and asked the new governor to grant them the favour that Paul be led away to Jerusalem and brought before a court, so that they could proceed against him according to the laws of their nation. Meanwhile they resolved to lie in wait for him on the journey and kill him. Here we can see how restless the minds of the impious are once they have flared up in hatred of the truth. For since their wicked works are always exposed by the light of this truth, it cannot be that they easily lay aside a hatred once conceived. Rather, they rage and seethe in their hearts like the Euripus, intent with their whole minds on every opportunity by which they might extinguish the light of truth, which they hate. And the strength of this hatred is almost so great that, sometimes setting aside private advantages, they seek and desire this one thing: that the ministers of the truth, whose teaching they feel tormenting them, be removed from the midst. Both are seen in the present example. For we have heard that Paul had been held captive for the whole two years. Yet neither the length of time nor the wretched lot of the prisoner could soften the minds of those who thought anything should be endured rather than the doctrine of truth. So they hunt every opportunity most diligently and spare no labour or expense, so that at last they may get what they wish.
