Then they first lay their prayers against Paul before the new governor, which they ought rather to have offered to the commonwealth, in whose name those things should have been sought that pertain to the common salvation of all. But by this kind of prejudice they wished Paul to be burdened, so that the governor would suspect him of being a public enemy of the fatherland and of the whole nation, for whose punishment they laboured especially.

units.la: Nec verò in istis solùs tantas odij contra veritatem vires fuisse putabimus. Est enim hoc commune impijs omnibus, ut si optionem rerum maximarum illis offeras, ipsis nihil antiquius sit, quàm ut ij occidantur, quos suæ impietati & libidini aduersari nouerunt. Pertinet huc quod de Herodiade Euangelistæ scribunt: quæ cum filiæ ab Herode dimidiam regni partem oblatam audiret, vnius tamen Iohannis caput sibi dari postulauit, eò quòd hoc viuente & docente, non regnum modò, verumetiam vitam omnem sibi amaram esse putabat. Possent huius generis multa commemorari, & quidem nostri seculi exempla, sed quia passim obuia sunt, breuitati studendum arbitramur. Vsum potius horum obseruemus, qui est, ne fidamus iis temere, quos semel in veritatem coniurauisse constat. Licet enim huius odium interdum egregiè dissimulare possint, manet tamen alta mente repositum illud propheta locum habet, qui cor hominis prauum & inscrutabile esse dixit. Ieremiæ decimo septimo. Rursum verò, quæ impiorum arma sint apparet. Primò iuris speciem simulant, quando illum Hierosolymis in iudicio sisti postulant: id quod æquissimum videri poterat, tum quòd in ea vrbe turba hæc omnis primùm exorta fuisset, tum quòd ipsos qui & numero & authoritate valebant, vnius hominis causa ingentes sumptus & itinerum molestias sustinere parum æquum esse videretur. Interim sub plausibili iuris prætextu horrendum facinus & sanguinarium occultant, vt modò dictum est. Discamus autem hoc loco de iis iudicare, qui hodie similia faciunt, quos plures passim inuenire licet, quàm Christianæ reipublicæ conducat. Christus certè tales potestate tenebrarum pugnare ait, & proinde diaboli ministros esse, qui & mendax & homicida fuit ab initio. Lucæ vigesimo secundo. Iohannis octauo. Et Paulus Antichristum mendacijs præcipuè & aperta vi regnaturum prædicit. Quotquot ergo proditoriis artibus & violenter veritati eius, ministris negotium faciunt, eos sub Antichristi signis diabolo militare constat, cum quo (nisi in tempore resipiscat) æternæ damnationis stipendia olim recipient.
units.tr: Nor should we think that such great strength of hatred against the truth was present only in these men. For it is common to all the impious that, if you offer them the choice of the greatest things, nothing is more important to them than that those be killed whom they know to oppose their impiety and lust. This applies to what the Evangelists write about Herodias: when she heard that half the kingdom had been offered by Herod to her daughter, she nevertheless asked that the head of John alone be given to her, because, while he lived and taught, she thought not only her kingdom but her whole life was bitter to her. Many examples of this kind could be recounted, indeed examples from our own age, but since they are found everywhere, we think we should aim at brevity. Let us rather observe the use of these things, which is that we should not rashly trust those whom we know have once conspired against the truth. For although they can sometimes skilfully conceal their hatred, that prophetic saying remains fixed deep in their minds, which declared that the heart of man is wicked and unsearchable (Jeremiah 17). Again, what the weapons of the impious are becomes apparent. First, they put on a semblance of justice, when they demand that Paul be brought to trial at Jerusalem. This might have seemed most fair, both because this whole tumult first arose in that city, and because it would seem hardly fair that those who were powerful in both number and authority should bear great expense and the trouble of travel for the sake of one man. Meanwhile, under the plausible pretext of law, they conceal the horrible and bloody deed, as has just been said. But let us learn here to judge those who today do similar things, of whom many can be found everywhere, more than is good for the Christian commonwealth. Christ certainly says that such men fight by the power of darkness, and therefore are ministers of the devil, who was a liar and a murderer from the beginning (Luke 22; John 8). And Paul foretells that Antichrist will reign chiefly by lies and open violence. Whoever therefore by treacherous arts and violence harasses the ministers of his truth is clearly serving the devil under the signs of Antichrist, and with him (unless he repents in time) will one day receive the wages of eternal damnation.

units.la: Porrò, ut Deus sanguinaria hostium suorum consilia eluserit, videamus. Huius enim opus fuit, quòd Festus Iudæorum precibus & postulationi non consensit, quorum tamen gratiam illum non parui fecisse, postea patebit. Et sanè non leues causæ erant, quæ illum, ut Iudæis morem gereret, moue poterant. Nam & merito apud illum suspectus esse poterat Paulus, quem prouincia decedens Felix vinctum reliquerat: & minimè reijcienda videbantur preces, quas omnes gentis Iudaicæ pro ceres offerebant: & parum prudens videri poterat, qui circa initium gubernationis totius gentis odium propter vnicum hominem, & illum quidem captiuum & nullius authoritatis, in sese deriuaret. At Dei occulta suggestione fit, ut maiorem Legum Romanarum & iustitiæ, quàm Iudaicæ gentis rationem Festus habeat. Quare Paulum Cæsareæ seruandum esse censet, interim Iudæis contra hunc iure agendi copiam facit. Voluit autem ethnici exemplo omnes, qui in magistratu versantur, tradere dominus, quid ipsos facere oporteat. Ne quid videlicet in hominum gratiam, aut priuati studij, iniuriam, aut tumultu, molumenti respectu faciant, sed iura legesque sequantur, absque quarum obseruatione respub. saluas mantine.
units.tr: Furthermore, let us see how God frustrated the bloody plans of his enemies. It was his doing that Festus did not consent to the prayers and request of the Jews, although it will later become clear that he did not think lightly of their favour. And indeed there were no slight reasons that could move him to gratify the Jews. For Paul might rightly be suspected by him, since Felix had left him in chains when he departed the province. The prayers that the whole Jewish nation offered on behalf of this request also seemed not to be lightly rejected. And he might seem not very prudent who, near the beginning of his government, drew upon himself the hatred of a whole nation on account of a single man, and he a captive and of no authority. But by God's secret prompting, it comes about that Festus takes greater account of Roman law and justice than of the reasoning of the Jewish nation. Therefore he judges that Paul should be kept at Caesarea, while in the meantime he gives the Jews the opportunity to proceed against him by law. Moreover, the Lord wished, through the example of a heathen, to teach all who hold office what they ought to do: namely, that they should not do any wrong for the sake of men's favour, or of private partiality, or out of regard for advantage amid tumult, but should follow rights and laws, without whose observance the commonwealth cannot remain safe.

units.la: Deus hostium suorum consilia dissipat. nere, impossibile est. Pudeat ergo suae cum leuitatis tum iniustitiae Christianae professionis Regu & principes, qui euangelicae veritatis & fidei studiosos hodie in Pontificum & episcoporum gratiam fere inauditos damnant, imo ut satis religiosi videantur, illis omnem in Christi fideles potestatem permittunt, itanimirum omnes lupis committentes. Sentient illi aliquando magno suo malo quid faciant, quando & Pontifices sanguinarij poenas dabunt, & ex Regum manibus populum suum, ipsorum fidei commissum, Christus Iudex requiret. Praecipue vero omnium horum author, Deus nobis obseruandus erit, cuius omne hoc opus fuisse, paulo ante diximus. Is enim, cum Pauli Romae etiam apud Caesarem de Christo testificaturum esse dixisset, promissa praestare voluit. Cuius consilia cum nulla hominum astutia euerti possint, facile illi fuit Iudaeorum conatus frangere. Et cum illi in animos quoq; hominum ius sit, eam nunc Festo voluntatem suggerit, ut Paulo potius, quam Iudaeorum commodo consulium velit. Postea vero, cum Iudaeis gratificari cupit, alio medio obstat quo minus id facere possit. Hinc autem haud vulgaris consolatio peti potest, quando impios quoq; & mundo addictos homines Dei imperio subiectos esse videmus, adeo ut illi integra in illorum animos & corpora potestas sit. Quid ergo illorum consilijs terremur? quid potentiam formidamus? Quin potius Deo securi confidimus, qui nouas illorum animis voluntates suggerere, vel etiam manus potenter constringere poterit? Sed ad Iudaeos reuertamur, qui ex Praesidis mandato rursus Caesaream profecti, actionem gravissimam aduersus Paulum instituunt, in cuius descriptione breuior est Lucas, eo quod ea ferent currant, de quibus iam ante non semel dictum fuit. Nobis tamen Iudai actores inspiciendi veniunt. Qui primo Paulum, in forum productum, circumstetisse dicuntur: quod praeter communem iudicium morem factum fuit, nimirum ut & ipsum externa specie perterrefacerent, & sua authoritate Festum mouerent. Deinde vetera accusationis capita denuo proferunt, ut ex Pauli responsione videre licet. Cum primus tamen seditionis crimen illos vrsisse apparet, quasi per hoc in ipsam Caesaris maiestatem peccarit. At quamuis multa dicant, nihil tamen probare possunt, Paulo ita causam dicente, ut se neque in Legem Dei, neque in templum & externa sacra, neque in Caesarem aliquid peccasse, omnibus liquido constarer. Quibus vero argumentis vtrinq; pugnatum fit, ex praemissis actionibus quinis facile colliget. HIC autem quanta hostium Veritatis impudentia atq; audacia sit, obseruandum est. Quid enim ab ipsis impudentius fieri poterat, quam quod abfq; argumentis & testimonijs ea denuo proferunt, ad quae non semel Paulus responderat? Interim cum se & argumentis & testibus deficiant sciant, ea tamen confidentia Paulum circumstant, quasi sola ipsorum authoritas in capitis causa valere debeat. Est hoc proprium impijs, ut nullis responsionibus sibi satisfieri patiantur, sed ad calumnias veteres semper recurrant. Experimur illud hodie, quando tot argumentis, imo tot iam annorum experientia conuicti aduersarij, adhuc tamen nobis seductionis, seditionis, blasphemiae & infinita alia huius generis crimina impudenter intentant. Cur enim illos coram hominibus mendacij puderet, quos Deo contradicere non pudet? Caeterum in Pauli responsione obseruatu dignum est, quod se in Caesarem quoq; peccasse negat. Atqui Deum praedicabat Christum & nouae fidei suscipienda author erat populus Romano Imperio subiectus, id quod per leges Rom. nemini licuisse, Tertullianus docet. Quomodo ergo Paulus se nihil in Caesare peccasse ait? Hic tenendum est fratres, religionem nec Caesari nec vlli magistratui ita subiectam esse, ut illis pro suo arbitrio quidquid in ea statuere liceat. Ad Deum enim illa pertinet, & iuxta Dei verbum atq; praescriptum debit institui. Et ut Caesari, quae Caesaris sunt, dare iubet Christus: ita Deo quoq; integrum seruari uult, quod illi debetur. Quare in magistratum non peccat, qui abfq; tumultuandi studio verū Dei cultum asserit, licet id magistratus fieri prohibeat. Fines enim suos cum transgrediatur magistratus eius modi, et in dei pomaeria vsq; regnū suum extendat, minime audiri debet. Imo tunc Petri regula valet, qui Deo magis, quam hominibus obediendum esse monet. HABES ergo quod ijs respondeas, qui nos quoq; contra Caesarum edicta seditiose multa innouare clamant, & regibus in religionis quoq; causa simpliciter obediendum esse contendunt. Quorum sententia fi audiatur, non nos modo, verum etiam prophetae omnes, & cum his Christus atq; apostoli damnabuntur, quos contra magistratuum edicta Dei verbum praedicauisse, superstitiones oppugnauisse, & fidem veram plantauisse constat. Non est ergo quod calumnias eiusmodi moremur. Quin potius bene nobis conscij, in fide vera pergamus, & pura mente seruiamus saluatori nostro: Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: God scatters the counsels of his enemies. (The rest of the paragraph is hard to follow in the scan, but the sense is clear.) It is impossible otherwise. Let the kings and princes be ashamed, then, both of their own fickleness and of their injustice in professing the Christian faith. They condemn today those who zealously pursue the truth and faith of the gospel, nearly unheard of, to win the favour of the Popes and bishops; indeed, so that they may seem sufficiently pious, they grant those men all power over the faithful of Christ, thus committing all of them to wolves. They will one day feel, to their great cost, what they are doing, when the bloody Popes pay their penalties and Christ the Judge requires from the hands of kings his people, entrusted to them. Above all, God, the author of all this, must be kept in view, whose work all this was, as we said a little while ago. For when he had said that Paul would bear witness to Christ at Rome, even before Caesar, he wished to fulfil his promises. Since his counsels can be overturned by no cunning of men, it was easy for him to thwart the efforts of the Jews. And although he has power over men's minds too, he now suggests to Festus a disposition to favour Paul rather than the convenience of the Jews. Afterwards, however, when he wishes to gratify the Jews, he places another obstacle in the way, so that he cannot do so. From this we may draw no ordinary consolation, since we see that even impious men and those given over to the world are subject to the command of God, so that he has complete power over their minds and bodies. Why, then, are we terrified by their plans? Why do we fear their power? Rather, why do we not confidently trust in God, who can suggest new wills to their minds, or even powerfully bind their hands? But let us return to the Jews, who, by the governor's order, went down again to Caesarea and brought a very grave charge against Paul. Luke is brief in describing this, because these things were of the kind about which we have already spoken more than once. Yet the Jewish accusers deserve to be examined by us. They are said first to have stood around Paul, who had been brought into the court, which was done contrary to the common custom of judgment, namely so that they might terrify him by his outward appearance and move Festus by their authority. Then they again put forward the old heads of accusation, as can be seen from Paul's reply. The first charge that they seem to have raised was sedition, as if by this he had offended against the very majesty of Caesar. But although they say many things, they can prove nothing, since Paul pleaded his case in such a way that it was clear to all that he had committed no offence against the law of God, nor against the temple and external worship, nor against Caesar. From the preceding acts one may easily gather with what arguments each side fought. Here we must observe how great is the shamelessness and audacity of the enemies of the truth. For what could be more shameless on their part than that they should again bring forward, without arguments and witnesses, the very things to which Paul had more than once replied? Yet, though they know that they are failing both in arguments and in witnesses, they nevertheless surround Paul with such confidence as if their authority alone ought to count in a capital case. It is characteristic of the impious that they allow themselves to be satisfied by no answers, but always return to their old calumnies. We experience this today, when our adversaries, convicted by so many arguments and indeed by so many years of experience, still shamelessly charge us with the crimes of seduction, sedition, blasphemy and countless others of this kind. For why should they be ashamed before men of lying, who are not ashamed to speak against God? Moreover, in Paul's reply it is worthy of note that he denies having offended against Caesar either. And yet he was preaching Christ and was the author of a new faith to be embraced by a people subject to the Roman Empire, which Tertullian teaches was permitted to no one under the Roman laws. How, then, does Paul say that he has done nothing wrong against Caesar? Here, brethren, we must hold that religion is subject neither to Caesar nor to any magistrate in such a way that it is lawful for them to decide whatever they please in it at their own discretion. For religion belongs to God, and must be established according to the word and prescription of God. And just as Christ bids us give to Caesar what is Caesar's, so he also wills that what is owed to God be kept whole for him. Therefore he does not offend against the magistrate who, without any zeal for stirring up tumult, asserts the true worship of God, even though the magistrate forbids it. For when a magistrate of this kind oversteps his bounds and extends his kingdom even into the territory of God, he ought in no way to be heard. Indeed, then the rule of Peter holds, who warns that God must be obeyed rather than men. You have, therefore, what you may answer to those who cry out that we too stir up many seditious innovations against the edicts of Caesars, and contend that kings must be obeyed simply, even in matters of religion. If their opinion were heard, not only we but all the prophets, and with them Christ and the apostles, would be condemned, since it is plain that they preached the word of God against the edicts of magistrates, attacked superstitions, and planted the true faith. There is therefore no reason for us to dwell upon calumnies of this kind. Rather, conscious of our good conscience, let us persevere in the true faith and serve our Saviour Jesus Christ with a pure mind, to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLVII.
units.tr: Homily 157.

units.la: Festus autem volens gratificari Iudaeis, respondens Paulo, dixit: Vis Hierosolymam ascendere, & ibi de his iudicari apud me? Dixit autem Paulus: Ad tribunal Caesaris sto, vbi oportet me iudicari. Iudaeis nullam iniuriam feci, sicuti & tu melius nosti. Si enim iniuste quid facio, vel dignum aliquid morte commisi, non recuso mori. Si vero nihil est eorum, de quibus me isti accusant, nemo potest me illis donare. Caesarem appello. Tunc Festus cum Concilio collocutus, respondit: Caesarem appellasti? ad Caesarem ibis.
units.tr: Festus, wishing to gain the favour of the Jews, answered Paul and said: "Will you go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me on these charges?" But Paul said: "I am standing at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If I have done anything unjust, or committed anything deserving of death, I do not refuse to die. But if none of those things is true of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar." Then Festus conferred with the council and answered: "You have appealed to Caesar? To Caesar you shall go."

units.la: QVod Paulus apostolus apud Corinthios de suis afflictionibus loquens, se mundo & angelis atque hominibus spectaculum fuisse ait, id ex iis potissimum cernitur, quae illi in captiuitate sua postrema acciderunt. Iam enim quarto sistitur, capitis causam dicturus, cum primam actionem coram Hierosolymitana plebe in castrorum gradibus, secundam coram Concilio Sacerdotum, tertiam apud Felicem praesidem habuisset. Quas modo noua haec apud nouum praesidem, Festum, subsecuta est. Singulae vero periculis grauissimis insignes fuerunt, vt suis locis vidimus, quae tamen omnia dei virtute adiutus effugit. Docent haec, quantum impijs quoque in electos suos deus permittat, quos tamen pro sua fide ex omnibus tribulationibus potentissima manu asserit. Quare nos minime offendi decet, si quid huius generis nobis quoque euenire sentiamus. Et hic quidem praecipuus huius loci vsus est, quo docetur, vt nouum periculum, cuius ipse praeses author fuit, Paulus effugerit: ne quis illum antehac hominum potius beneficio & praesidum virtute, quam Dei gratia, liberatum putaret. Singula igitur ordine videamus.
units.tr: That the apostle Paul, speaking to the Corinthians about his afflictions, says that he has been made a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men, is seen most clearly in the events that befell him last during his imprisonment. For now he is brought before the court for the fourth time, to plead his case on a capital charge: he had already had a first hearing before the people of Jerusalem on the steps of the barracks, a second before the council of priests, and a third before the governor Felix. Now this new hearing has followed before the new governor, Festus. Each of these was attended by the gravest dangers, as we have seen in their places, yet from all of them he escaped, aided by the power of God. These events teach us how far God permits even the wicked to act against his chosen people, and yet with his mighty hand he rescues them for their faith out of all their tribulations. Therefore we ought not to be dismayed if we feel that something of this kind happens to us as well. This is the chief use of this passage: it teaches that Paul escaped the new danger, of which the governor himself was the author, so that no one should think he had previously been freed more by the kindness of men and the power of governors than by the grace of God. Let us, then, look at each matter in order.

units.la: Primus autem Festus nobis consyderandus venit, qui cum Iudaeos meris calumniis causam egere, & Paulum innocentem esse comperisset, nihilominus tamen illis gratificari statuit. Vnde facile coniicitur, illum vel muneribus vel magnificis promissis ab illis corruptum fuisse, quando sententiam tam subito mutauit. Siue vero de insidijs Paulo structis intellexerit, siue minus, iniquissime tamen illum fecisse constat. Interim mira astutia iniquitatem tegit. Ne quid enim praeter officium Iudaeis dare videatur, Paulum num Hierosolymam ascendere velit, interrogat, & se illic etiam huius causa iudicem fore spondet: hoc vnum quaerens nimirum, vt apud Iudaeos gratiam ineat, & inuidiam omnem declinet. Docemur exemplo hoc, quam facile corrumpantur, qui Dei cognitione & timore carent. Quia enim natura ad malum procliues sumus, quauis occasione impellimur, nisi Dei timore, ceu freno cohibeamur. Exemplum huius cumprimis euidens est Festus hic, qui ita repente spem omnem, quam de se optimam fecerat, fefellit. Minime ergo talibus fides haberi debet. Nam licet aliquando non obscurum de se praebeant virtutis specimen, mox tamen ad ingenium redeunt. Quod enim in Festo hic cernitur, idipsum de Pharaone, Saule, Achabo & alijs impijs scriptura tradunt. Admonet praeterea locus hic quanta iudiciorum pestis est, personarum respectus, quo apud homines gratiam venamur. Hoc enim Felix omnem priorem laudem obscurat, & ex iustissimo iudice, qui paulo ante videbatur, immanissimus latro efficitur, quando illis gratificari cupit, qui innocentis hominis eadem iam animo conceperant. Extant huius generis exempla in omnium gentium historijs. Non temere ergo cum diuinae leges, tum publica gentium iura personarum respectum a iudicibus alienissimum esse volunt. Et sane conueniens est, vt qui Dei vices obeunt, dei mores referant, quem personas nequaquam respicere omnes scripturae vnanimi consensu testantur. Rom.2. Ephes.6. Actorum 10. &c.
units.tr: First, Festus comes before us for consideration. Although the Jews had pleaded their case on pure calumnies, and he had found Paul to be innocent, he nevertheless resolved to gratify them. From this it is easily conjectured that he had been corrupted by them, either with bribes or with splendid promises, since he changed his verdict so suddenly. Whether he understood that a plot had been laid against Paul, or did not, it is clear that he acted most unjustly. Meanwhile, with remarkable cunning, he conceals his injustice. So that he may not seem to give the Jews anything beyond his duty, he asks Paul whether he is willing to go up to Jerusalem, and promises that he will himself be the judge there in this matter. He was seeking only this, of course: that he might win favour with the Jews and avoid all their ill will. We are taught by this example how easily those are corrupted who lack the knowledge and fear of God. For since we are naturally inclined to evil, we are driven by any occasion, unless we are restrained by the fear of God as by a bridle. The most striking example of this is this Festus, who so suddenly disappointed all the good hope he had given of himself. Therefore such men ought never to be trusted. For although at times they show some clear sign of virtue, they soon return to their nature. What is seen in Festus here, the Scriptures also record of Pharaoh, Saul, Ahab and other wicked men. This passage also warns us what a deadly plague in judgments is the respect of persons, by which we hunt for favour among men. For Felix too obscured all his earlier praise, and from a most just judge, as he seemed a little before, he became a most savage robber, when he desired to gratify those who had already conceived in their minds the same design against an innocent man. Examples of this kind are found in the histories of all nations. Therefore it is not without reason that both the divine laws and the public laws of nations wish judges to be most remote from respect of persons. And indeed it is fitting that those who discharge the office of God should reflect the character of God, whom all the Scriptures with one voice testify does not regard persons. Rom. 2; Eph. 6; Acts 10; etc.

units.la: Quid vero Paulus, qui periculum vix iam euasurus videtur? Sentit ille quorsum res tendat, nimirum ex spiritus reuelatione, quem suis aduocatum fore, Christus promisit. Liberè ergo agit, & validissimis rationibus iniquam Festi postulationem reijcit. Primò, ad Caesaris tribunal sto, ait. Ibi ergo me iudicari conuenit. Ita vero ad ipsum Caesarem iniuriam redundaturam innuit, si ab ipsius tribunali aulsus, Iudæis iudicandus subijciatur. Est boc oportuerit deducendum prouinciarum præfectis & quotquot magistratus inferiores gerunt: vt intelligant delicta, quæ ab ipsis præter ius & æquum committuntur, in eos redundare, à quibus illi suum gradum obtinuerunt, & proinde dignos esse, qui illis graues pœnas exoluant. Hinc illa apud veteres Romanos censuræ seueritas, qua magistratuum licentiam coercendam putarunt. Cuius memorabile exemplum Porcius Cato edidit in L. Flaminium, quem é numero Senatorum sustulit, quòd in prouincia quendam damnatu secuti percusserat, tempore supplicij ad arbitrium muliercula, quam amabat, delecto. Nolebant enim grauissimi & sapientissimi viri sui imperij maiestatem hominum leuissimorum licentia prostitui. Hodie quia admnia conniuent principes, tyrannis vbiq; regnat, & summorum magistratuū authoritas vbiq; colla-bitur. Sed de his aliàs, nunc in Pauli responsione pergamus, qui secundo loco ait: Iudæis nullam iniuriam feci. Vnde colligit, non æquum fore, vt secundum illorum Leges & priuilegia iudicetur. Innocentiæ verò suæ testem citat ipsum præsidem, qui hanc ex ipsius apologia facile intellexisse poterat. Tertiò dilemmate pugnat validiùs. Si mortem merui, non recusò mori: sin minus, nemini tanta potestas erit, vt innocentem me hostium arbitrio tradat. Atqui his rationibus præmissis ad Cæsarem prouocat, tum quòd nulla amplius de Festo spes esse poterat, tum quòd oraculo admonitus sciebat, Dei Consilium esse, vt apud Cæsarem quoq; de Christo testificaretur. Quo exemplo primum admonemur, pios Christianæ patientiæ legibus minimè cogi, vt se temerè impiorum libidini subijciant: imò licere potius illis, vt pericula aperta declinent, siquidem illud falsa fidei confessione & obedientia, quam Christo debent, facere possunt. Ita enim flagella illaturos antea legitimè à se depulit, & latrones coniuratos Tribuni auxilio elusit. Ridiculus ergo illorum error est, qui Petri verbu abusi (quibus ille nos paratos esse iubet ad reddendam cuiuis petenti fidei rationem) verbi ministros Pontificios Concilijs obijciendos esse censent, vt ibi fidei ratione reddant, vbi nulla ratio admittitur, sed mera tyrannis regnat. Quorum sententia si admittatur, iniquè Paulus fecisse dicetur, qui Romæ potius quàm Hierosolymis fidei causam agere voluit. Sed pie & prudenter fecit, Dei nimirum oraculum secutus, quem etiam rectissimè ex veteribus imitati sunt Athanasius & Ambrosius, quorum hic quidem Mediolani tantummodo de se iudicium ferri voluit, vbi docuerat: ille verò vt causam suam Concilijs suspectis committeret, nunquam adduci potuit, fugam sibi tutiorem & laudabiliorem putans, quàm eorum cœtus, quos iam ante contra Veritatem conspirasse nouerat. Deinde illud quoque obseruandum venit, quòd ita periculum declinat Paulus, vt diligentem habeat suæ innocentiæ rationem. Imitentur hoc pij omnes, in primis autem qui euangelij ministri sunt, ne dum vitæ suæ nimis imprudenter consulunt, famam suam in periculum adducant, sicq; fiat, vt propter ipsos euangelium male audiat. Tertiò quod sæpe dictum est, nouo exemplo probatur, licere nimirum Christianis ab minibus iudicio contendere, & ad regum præsidia confugere, quando nimirum ita necessitas postulat. Paulus enim, qui Romanæ ciuitatis priuilegium antea contra apertam vim opposuit, nunc prouocatione etiam vtitur, quod rarissimè absque iudicis contumelia fieri potest, nedum partis aduersaria. Abutuntur ergo Christi & Pauli verbis, quæ Matth.5. & in priori ad Corinth.6.cap.legum tur, phanatici quidam, quando illic non legitimus iudiciorum vsus improbatur, sed priuatæ & illegitimæ vindictæ cupiditas, & insatiabilis litigandi libido cohercetur, quæ & bonis alienis inhiat, & charitatem omnem turbat. Postremò generalem doctrinam, ad magistratus maximè pertinentem, Pauli verba continent: Nemini vid licet licere, vt innocentem aliorum libidini donet, eius sanguine illorum gratiam redimat. Dei enim ministri sunt, quicunque in magistratu versantur, vt innocentes defendant, malos autem & iniquos puniant. Quotquot ergo secus agunt, diaboli ministri fiunt, & Pilati atq; Herodis socij, quorum ille Christum Iudæis crucifigendum tradidit, hic vero in scorti gratiam Iohannem Baptistam decollauit.
units.tr: But what of Paul, who seems scarcely about to escape the danger? He perceives where the matter is tending, namely by a revelation of the Spirit, whom Christ promised would be his advocate. He therefore speaks freely, and rejects Festus's unjust demand with very strong arguments. First, he says, "I stand at Caesar's judgment seat. There, then, I ought to be judged." By this he indicates that an injury would redound to Caesar himself if, having been removed from his tribunal, he were handed over to be judged by the Jews. This should be brought home to the governors of provinces and to all who hold lower magistracies, so that they may understand that the wrongs committed by them beyond right and equity fall back upon those from whom they obtained their rank, and that they therefore deserve to pay heavy penalties to them. Hence that severity of censorship among the ancient Romans, by which they thought the licence of magistrates should be restrained. Porcius Cato gave a memorable example of this against Lucius Flaminius, whom he removed from the number of the senators, because in a province he had struck a certain condemned man at the time of his execution, at the pleasure of a little woman whom he loved. For those most grave and wise men did not want the majesty of their office to be prostituted to the licence of the most worthless men. Today, since the princes everywhere connive at everything, tyranny reigns everywhere, and the authority of the highest magistrates everywhere collapses. But of these matters elsewhere; now let us go on with Paul's reply, which in the second place says: "I have done no wrong to the Jews." From this he infers that it would not be fair for him to be judged according to their laws and privileges. He calls the governor himself as a witness to his innocence, who could easily have understood this from his defence. Thirdly, he argues more forcefully with a dilemma: "If I have deserved death, I do not refuse to die; but if not, no one will have such power as to hand me over, an innocent man, to the will of my enemies." Having set forth these reasons, he appeals to Caesar, both because no further hope could be had from Festus, and because, admonished by an oracle, he knew it was God's counsel that he should also bear witness to Christ before Caesar. From this example we are first admonished that the pious are by no means bound by the laws of Christian patience to subject themselves rashly to the lust of the wicked; rather, it is lawful for them to avoid open dangers, since they can do this without a false profession of faith and without the obedience they owe to Christ. For thus, when the Jews were already plotting to flog him, he legitimately turned them away, and with the help of the tribune he evaded the conspirators. Therefore the error of those is ridiculous who, abusing Peter's words (in which he bids us be ready to give an account of our faith to anyone who asks), think that the Papist ministers of the Word should be subjected to councils, so that they may give an account of their faith where no reason is admitted, but mere tyranny reigns. If their opinion were accepted, Paul would be said to have acted unjustly in wishing to plead the cause of the faith at Rome rather than at Jerusalem. But he acted piously and prudently, following, of course, God's oracle; and Athanasius and Ambrose rightly imitated him among the ancients. Of these, Ambrose wished that judgment on himself be passed only at Milan, where he had taught; but Athanasius could never be brought to commit his cause to suspect councils, thinking flight safer and more praiseworthy for himself than the assemblies of men whom he knew had already conspired against the truth. Next, this also must be noted: Paul avoids the danger in such a way that he keeps a careful account of his innocence. Let all the pious imitate this, and especially those who are ministers of the gospel, so that while they too imprudently consult for their own lives they do not bring their reputation into danger, and so the gospel itself come to be ill spoken of on account of them. Thirdly, what has often been said is proved by a new example: namely, that it is lawful for Christians to contend in court against men and to take refuge in the protection of kings, when necessity so requires. For Paul, who previously opposed open violence by the privilege of Roman citizenship, now also uses an appeal, which can very rarely be made without insult to the judge, let alone to the opposing party. Therefore certain fanatics misuse the words of Christ and Paul, which are read in Matthew 5 and in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 6, where the lawful use of courts is not condemned, but the desire for private and illegitimate vengeance, and the insatiable lust for litigation, which both covets the goods of others and disturbs all charity, is restrained. Finally, the words of Paul contain a general doctrine, pertaining chiefly to magistrates: no one may be permitted to hand over an innocent man to the lust of others, or to buy their favour with his blood. For all who hold office are ministers of God, to defend the innocent and to punish the wicked and unjust. Therefore whoever acts otherwise becomes a minister of the devil, and a companion of Pilate and Herod: the former handed Christ over to the Jews to be crucified, the latter beheaded John the Baptist to gratify a harlot.

units.la: Sed ad Festum redeamus, qui inspirata Pauli prouocatione attonitus, cum se ipse frustratum vi-deret, cum assessoribus re deliberata, tandem non sine stomacho respondet: Cæsarem appellasti? Quasi dicat: Itane confidens es, vt Cæsarem potius quàm me iudicem habere velis? Agedum, ad Cæsarem ibis. Egregiè verò impiorum mores exprimit, qui cum suæ iniquitatis sibi probè sint conscij, indigni fimè tamè ferunt, si quis illam vel leuiter suggillet, vel remoram illorum decretis obijciat. Attamen melior multò est plerisq; nostri sæculi principibus Festus hic, qui nimirum Christi fideles nullo legum aut publici iuris præsidio gaudere patiuntur. Et sanè memorabilis est hæc Romanorum in iure administrando seueritas, qua ita vsi sunt, vt Festus in vilissimum quoq; hominem, post factam prouocationem, nihil sibi amplius licere intelligat. Quo neruo rempub. multis alioqui vitiis labefactatam, diu seruatam fuisse constat. Eadem seueritate hodie etiam præsides coherceri oportebat (vt Paulò ante monuimus) quam si summi magistratus adhiberent, & ipsi minori inuidia grauarentur, & plus præsidij passim haberet innocentia. In primis tamen Dei potentiam ac fidem obseruemus, quae suos aduersus hostium conatus tuetur. Hac freti veritatem totis animis complectamur, semelq; apprehensam teneamus firmiter, nec vllis minis nos abstrahi patiamur à saluatore nostro vnico, Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: But let us return to Festus, who, astonished by Paul's unexpected appeal and seeing that he himself had been thwarted, after consulting with his assessors, finally answers, not without irritation: "You have appealed to Caesar? As if to say: Are you so confident that you would rather have Caesar as your judge than me? Very well, then, you shall go to Caesar." This truly expresses the character of the impious, who, though they are well aware of their own wickedness, take it very badly indeed if anyone so much as lightly censures it or places an obstacle in the way of their decrees. Yet this Festus is far better than most of the princes of our age, who will not allow the faithful of Christ to enjoy any protection of law or public right. And certainly this severity of the Romans in administering justice is worth remembering, since they practised it in such a way that Festus understood that, once an appeal had been made, he was no longer permitted to do anything further even to the most lowly man. It is well established that the commonwealth, otherwise weakened by many vices, was preserved for a long time by this sinew. With the same severity, governors ought today to be restrained (as we admonished a little earlier), since if the highest magistrates applied it, they themselves would be burdened with less odium, and innocence would everywhere have more protection. Above all, however, let us observe the power and faithfulness of God, who guards his people against the attempts of their enemies. Relying on this, let us embrace the truth with all our hearts, hold it firmly once grasped, and not allow ourselves to be drawn away by any threats from our one Saviour, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLVIII.
units.tr: HOMILY 158.

units.la: Et cum dies aliquot transfacti essent, Agrippa Rex & Bernice descenderunt Cæsaream, salutaturi Festum. Et cum dies complures ibi commorarentur, Festus regi retulit causam Pauli, dicens: Vir quidam est relictus à Felice vinctus, de quo cum venissem Hierosolymam, significarunt mihi principes Sacerdotum & Seniores Iudæorum, postulantes aduersus eum iudicium. Quibus respondi: Non est Romanis consuetudo, ob gratiam donare aliquem hominem vt pereat, priusquam is qui accusatur, præsentes habeat accusatores, & locum defensionis accipiat de crimine. Cū ergo huc conuenissent, sine vlla dilatione, sequenti die sedens pro tribunali iussi adduci virum. De quo cum stetissent accusatores, nullum crimen obiiciebant super hisce rebus, de quibus ego suspicabar: sed quæstiones quasdam de sua superstitione habebant aduersus eum, & de quodam Iesu defuncto, quem affirmabat Paulus viuere. Hæsitans autem ego de hac quæstione, rogaui num vellet ire Hierosolymam, & illic iudicari super istis. Cum autem Paulus appellasset, vt seruaretur Augusti cognitioni, iussi seruari eum, donec mitterem ad Cæsarem. Agrippa autem dixit ad Festum: Volebam & ipse hominem audire. Cras (inquit) audies eum.
units.tr: When several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice went down to Caesarea to greet Festus. As they stayed there for many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying: "There is a certain man left in prison by Felix. When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me about him and asked for a judgment against him. To them I replied that it is not the Roman custom to hand anyone over to die before the accused has his accusers face to face and has an opportunity to defend himself against the charge. So when they had come here, without any delay, on the next day I took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought in. When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge of the kind I had been expecting, but they had certain disputes with him about their own superstition and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. Being uncertain about this question, I asked whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there on these matters. But when Paul appealed that he be kept for the decision of the Emperor, I ordered him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar." Then Agrippa said to Festus: "I would like to hear the man myself." "Tomorrow," he said, "you shall hear him."

units.la: Multis quidem & variis tribulationibus suos in hoc mundo Deus exercere consueuit, sed pro sua sapientia & bonitate eadem ad sui nominis gloriam & illorum salutem dirigit. Exemplum huius cumprimis euidens in præsenti hac Pauli historia proponitur. Ex quo enim Hierosolymis captus fuit, nouam indies prædicandi occasionem habuit. Et primò quidem in vrbe ex castrorum gradibus ad populum vniuersum concionari potuit, quod illi alias nunquam facere licuisset. Deinde in Sacerdotum & Seniorum consilio fidem suam profitetur, qui ipsum alioqui nunquam dignari fuisset audire. Tertiò coram Felice præside prolixam de sua vocatione & officio orationem habuit, & ab illo sæpius accersitus, frequenter cum illo collocutus est. Tandem apud Festum quoq; fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem reddidit, vt nuper audiuimus. Ita vero causam suam vbiq; egit, vt & præsides Romani & barbari milites illius innocentiam non obscurè deprehenderent, id quod ad euangelii propagationem non parum facere potuit, et haud dubie in multorum animis fidei semina sparsa sunt, quæ aliquanto post fructus haud vulgares protulerunt: quando Dei verbum (sicuti Isaias testatur) nunquam frustra prædicari solet. Porrò ad id quod modò diximus sequentia quoque referri debent, quibus narrabitur, vt Paulo coram Agrippa rege & Bernice totaq; gentis illius nobilitate concionandi occasio oblata fuit. Et quia rari exempli res fuit, reges è vinculis conciona​ntem audire, nihil eorum, quæ hic acciderunt, Lucas silentio prætereundum esse putauit.
units.tr: God is accustomed to exercise his people with many and various afflictions in this world, but by his wisdom and goodness he directs these same afflictions to the glory of his name and to their salvation. An outstanding example of this is set before us in the present history of Paul. From the time he was seized in Jerusalem, he had a new opportunity to preach every day. First, in the city, he was able to address the whole people from the steps of the barracks, which otherwise they would never have allowed him to do. Then, before the council of the chief priests and elders, he professed his faith, men who otherwise would never have deigned to hear him. Thirdly, before the governor Felix he delivered a lengthy speech about his calling and his office, and since Felix summoned him often, he frequently conversed with him. Finally, before Festus too he gave an account of his faith and teaching, as we heard recently. He pleaded his cause everywhere in such a way that both the Roman governors and the barbarian soldiers clearly perceived his innocence. This could not but contribute not a little to the spread of the gospel, and without doubt seeds of faith were sown in the minds of many, which some time later bore no ordinary fruit, since the word of God (as Isaiah testifies) is never preached in vain. Moreover, what we have just said should be connected with what follows, in which we will be told how Paul was given an opportunity to preach before King Agrippa and Bernice and the whole nobility of that nation. And since it was a rare thing for kings to hear a preacher from prison, Luke thought that none of the things that happened here should be passed over in silence.

units.la: Principio autem totius negotij occasione præmittit, quæ fuit, quòd Agrippa Rex vnà cum Bernice Cæsaream descendit, vt Festum, qui nuper Româ aduenerat, salutaret. Nec mirum fuit hoc ofＦ Regem præsidi exhibuisse, quando illum à Cæsaribus regnum ex gratia consecutum fuisse, & ita obtinuisse constat, vt Romanos rerum dominos agnoscere cogeretur. Fuit autem Agrippa his
units.tr: At the outset Luke sets down the occasion of the whole affair, which was that King Agrippa came down to Caesarea together with Bernice, to greet Festus, who had recently arrived from Rome. Nor is it surprising that the king paid this courtesy to the governor, since it is well known that he had obtained his kingdom from the Caesars as a favour, and had held it in such a way that he was compelled to acknowledge the Romans as masters of affairs. Agrippa was, however, [...]

units.la: Agrippa & Bernice. Herodis Agrippa, de cuius tyrannide simul & horrenda morte Cap.12. dictum est, filius. Bernice vero soror erat, quam vulgo suspectam fuisse, Iosephus tradit, quasi cum fratre stupri consuetudinem haberet. Quare vitandae suspicionis causa, Polemoni Lyciorum regi nupsit, cum quo tamen paulo post diuortio facto, ad fratrem redijt, qui Romanorum amicitia & potentia fretus, vulgi sermones facile contemnebat. EST vero hoc haud vulgare diuinae bonitatis exemplum, quae salutem in Christo partam duobus hisce, ex nefaria familia ortis, & incestu pollutis, per Paulum annunciari voluit. Proauus enim horum Herodes Magnus fuit, qui Christo recens nato insidias struxit, & infantes Bethlehemiticos inaudita crudelitate trucidari curauit. Aui vero Aristobuli (siue Alexandri, vt quidam volunt) frater, Herodes Antipas, ipse quoque incestu infamis, Iohannem Baptistam decollari iussit, & Christo vincto fuerunt illusit. De patre Agrippa modo diximus, qui Iacobum necauit, & Petrum apostolum in carcerem coniecit, illum quoque occisurus, nisi angeli ope liberatus fuisset. His (inquam) progenitoribus orti, Agrippa & Bernice, ex Paulo euangelium salutis audiunt. Unde facile constat, Deum non ita morosum aut vindictam auidum esse, vt patrum scelera filij luere cogantur: imo illius gratiam omnibus patere, quicunque ad ipsum conuerti & poenitere voluerint. Vide de hoc, quae Ezechielis 18. Cap. ipse dicit. Quo etiam referri debet, quod ad illos Christum peculiariter missum fuisse scimus, quorum maiores, multis nominibus in Deum ingrati, prophetas ad se missos occiderant. Et hodie multi, qui horribiliter peccauere, gratiam Dei & Christi meritum bene dignissime offerri videmus. Hinc ergo consolationem petant, quos satan de Dei clementia dubitare docet, quasi haec nostra peccata superari possit. Simul etiam institutioni haec seruiant, neque temere propter maiores suos damnemus, quando in Christi Iesu genealogia multi sceleribus infames numerantur, vt illum ad peccatores cumprimis pertinere, nemo dubitare posset.
units.tr: Agrippa and Bernice. Bernice was the sister of Agrippa, son of Herod Agrippa, of whose tyranny and dreadful death we have spoken in chapter 12. Josephus relates that she was commonly suspected of having a sexual relationship with her brother. For this reason, to avoid the suspicion, she married Polemon, king of the Lycians, but after a divorce shortly afterwards she returned to her brother, who, relying on the friendship and power of the Romans, easily despised the gossip of the common people. Now this is no ordinary example of divine goodness, that God willed salvation won in Christ to be proclaimed through Paul to these two, sprung from a wicked family and polluted by incest. For the great-grandfather of these two was Herod the Great, who laid snares for the newborn Christ and had the infants of Bethlehem slaughtered with unheard-of cruelty. Their grandfather's brother, Herod Antipas, (the brother of Aristobulus, or of Alexander, as some hold), also notorious for incest, ordered John the Baptist to be beheaded, and mocked Christ when he was bound. We have just spoken of their father Agrippa, who put James to death and threw the apostle Peter into prison, intending to kill him too, had he not been freed by the help of an angel. Agrippa and Bernice, I say, born of these forebears, hear the gospel of salvation from Paul. From this it is easy to see that God is not so peevish or greedy for vengeance that children are forced to pay for their fathers' crimes; rather, his grace lies open to all who wish to turn to him and repent. On this, see what Ezekiel says in chapter 18. To this also should be referred the fact that we know Christ was sent in a special way to those whose ancestors, ungrateful to God in many respects, had killed the prophets sent to them. And today we see many who have sinned dreadfully being offered the grace of God and the merit of Christ very graciously indeed. Let those whom Satan teaches to doubt God's mercy, as if our sins could not be overcome, take comfort from this. At the same time, let these things serve for instruction: let us not rashly condemn people on account of their ancestors, since in the genealogy of Jesus Christ many infamous sinners are listed, so that no one could doubt that he belongs especially to sinners.

units.la: Sed ad institutum reuersi videamus, qua occasione Agrippa Paulum videre & audire cupierit. Id vero post multos demum dies (quos in delitijs & ludis transactos fuisse, credibile est) factum fuisse dicitur. Nec enim regibus & magnatibus multum curae sunt captiui & vincti homines. Festus vero apud Agrippam Pauli mentionem fecisse credederim, quod illius consilio se in causa admodum difficili & molesta iuuari posse putaret. Narrationem ergo totius rei instituit, sed subdolam plane & vafram, dum suam iniquitatem, qua Iudaeis gratificari voluit, callide dissimulat, vt suo loco videbimus. Sunt enim orationis partes tres, quas ordine executiemus.
units.tr: But returning to our purpose, let us see on what occasion Agrippa desired to see and hear Paul. It is said that this happened only after many days had passed (days which were, it is likely, spent in pleasures and games). For captives and prisoners are of little concern to kings and great men. I would believe that Festus mentioned Paul to Agrippa because he thought he could be greatly helped by his counsel in a very difficult and troublesome case. So he began the narration of the whole matter, but a plainly crafty and cunning one, while he cleverly conceals his injustice, by which he wished to gratify the Jews, as we shall see in its place. For the speech has three parts, which we will go through in order.

units.la: Prima parte, quis Paulus sit, quid in eius causa Iudaei postulauerint, quidque ipse illis responderit, commemorat. Et Paulum quidem ex captiuis esse, & a Felice in vinculis relictum fuisse, ait. Quod ideo praemittere videtur, ne Agrippa abs se captum putaret. Iudaei vero (inquit) per suos seniores & Pontifices, vt in illum capitis sententiam ferre, postulauerunt. Quod abs me illis negatum est. Nam Romanorum consuetudinem allegauit, quibus moris est, neminem in hominum gratiam morti dare, sed legitima inquisitione vti, sic vt accusatores coram accusent, & reus (sese defendendi locum tempusque) habeat. Est autem memorabilis omnino consuetudo haec, quam Festus allegat, quia omnes magistratus docentur, ne quid in alicuius hominis gratiam faciant legibus & iustitiae contrarium. Nam magna licet sic humanitatis laus, iudices tamen primam semper iustitiae rationem habere decet, quod tum dei leges, tum publica omnium gentium iura diserte monent. Solomon certe deo non minus exosum esse dicit eum, qui scelerato parcit, quam qui insontem occidit. Proverb. 17. At deploranda omnino est nostri temporis peruersitas, qua fit vt inter Christianos vix locum inueniat, quod Romanis in vsu fuisse, Festus testatur. Frequenter enim videmus, vt Christi fideles in Pontificum gratiam, indicta causa, diris supplicijs e medio tollantur. Quotquot ergo ex magistratibus officio suo probe defungi voluerint, legitimos iudiciorum processus obseruari curent. In his ante omnia requiritur, vt praesentes sint accusatores, ne calumnijs & obtrectationibus locus detur, quae non raro innocentibus periculum struxisse constat. Inde vero reis quoque defensionis legitimae copia fiat, & cogicent iudices, binas ideo sibi aures datas esse, vt altera quidem actores, altera vero reos audiant. In primis autem valeat regula haec, in nullius hominis gratiam iura legesque publicas violare debere. Quia enim communem personam iudices sustinent, singulis hominibus ex aequo se obstringere esse sciant. Porro vt laudem meretur Romanorum legum aequitas, ita detestabilis omnino fuit haec Iudaicorum Sacerdotum impudentia, qua illud petere ausi sunt, quod ethnicus homo iniquum & inu-
units.tr: In the first part he recounts who Paul is, what the Jews demanded in his case, and what Paul himself answered them. He says that Paul was one of the prisoners, and had been left in chains by Felix. This he seems to mention first so that Agrippa would not think he had been seized by him. The Jews, he says, through their elders and high priests, demanded that sentence of death be pronounced against him. This I refused them. For I cited the custom of the Romans, among whom it is the rule that no one is handed over to death to gratify men, but that a lawful inquiry is used, so that the accusers accuse face to face and the accused has a place and time to defend himself. This custom which Festus cites is altogether worth remembering, because all magistrates are taught not to do anything against the laws and justice for the sake of any man's favour. For although such a show of kindness is a great praise, judges should always give the first consideration to justice, as both the laws of God and the public laws of all nations plainly warn. Solomon certainly says that God abhors no less the one who spares the wicked than the one who kills the innocent (Prov. 17). But the perversity of our own time is utterly deplorable, by which it comes about that among Christians there is hardly any place for what Festus testifies was in use among the Romans. For we often see the faithful of Christ, to gratify the Papists, removed from the midst with dreadful punishments without any cause being heard. Therefore, however many of the magistrates wish to discharge their office properly, let them take care that lawful processes of judgment are observed. In these, above all, it is required that the accusers be present, so that no room is given to calumnies and slanders, which, as is well known, have not infrequently laid a trap for the innocent. Then the accused too should be given a lawful opportunity of defence, and judges should consider that they have been given two ears so that they may hear the plaintiffs with one and the defendants with the other. Above all, let this rule hold: that public rights and laws must never be violated for the favour of any man. For since judges bear a common character, they should know that they are bound equally to each individual. But just as the fairness of the Roman laws deserves praise, so the impudence of the Jewish high priests was altogether detestable, in that they dared to ask for what even a heathen man understood to be unjust and wrong. Since those who wished to seem the most holy and the pillars of the Church of God did this, should not their religion also rightly have been suspected by the nations? Would that today too the impudence of the monks and bishops were not similar...

units.la: Festi de Paulo ad Agrippam oratio. & iniustum esse intellexit. Id quia fecerunt, qui sanctissimi adeoq; ecclesiæ Dei columnæ videri volu-erunt, nonne merito gentibus ipsorum religio quoque suspecta fuit? Atqui vtinam non hodie quoque similis esset Monachorum & Episcoporum impudentia, qui in regum aulis iniquissima de-creta facere, & principum indulgentia ad suam tyrannidem stabiliendam contra Christi cultores abuti consueuerunt.
units.tr: The speech of Festus about Paul to Agrippa. and understood it to be unjust. Since those men did this, men who wished to be seen as the most holy and as the pillars of God's Church, was not their religion also rightly suspected by the Gentiles? And yet would that the shamelessness of monks and bishops were not similar even today, who are accustomed to make the most unjust decrees in royal courts and, through the indulgence of princes, to abuse that power to establish their own tyranny against the worshippers of Christ.

units.la: Altera parte, quomodo causam hanc egerit Festus, narratur. Vt primum huc venerunt (inquit) absque dilatione illos audiui. Mox vero innocentem esse comperi. Nec enim quicquam eorum pro-ferebant, quæ expectabam. Sed quæstiones aliquot ad ipsorum superstitionem pertinentes, in me-dium adduxerunt, & causam Iesu cuiusdam tractauerunt, quem Paulus à mortuis resuscitatum di-cebat. Ita vero contemptissimè de priori religione homo prophanus loquitur, quam tamen Pau-lum multis & diligenter tractauisse, ex ipsius Festi sermone colligitur. In hoc autem exemplum om-nium eorum proponitur, qui verbi Dei mysteria, & in primis resurrectione contemnunt atq; ridentes. In quibus erudiendis etsi parum proficiamus, nemo tamen offendi debet, quando Festum eorum, quæ à Paulo grauissimè dicta fuerunt, tam paruam rationem habuisse videmus. Interim aliud in ethni-co homine obseruare licet iudicibus, nimirum, vt absque dilatione causas audiant: quando iniquis procrastinationibus multos circumueniri constat, qui quod sumptibus non sufficiunt, ius suum per-sequi nō possunt. In primis vero Pauli innocentiam multiplici testimonio approbatam obseruemus. Huius enim testem initio Lysiam Trib. habuimus. Postea Felicem. Nunc Festum. Paulo post ve-ro Agrippa quoq; istius acceder. Et licet in accusando pergant impij Pontifices, Pauli tamen inno-centiam magis confirmant, dum nihil eorum, quæ aduersus illum proferunt, probare possunt. Eandem aliorum quoq; apostolorum rationem fuisse, iam sæpè vidimus. Ita Christum à Pilato simul & Herode innocentiæ testimonium habuisse, euangelistæ tradunt. Facit hoc ad commendandam Chri-stiana fidei & doctrinæ dignitatem. Quam qui hodie calumniantur, se gentibus deteriores esse pa-lam produnt. Patet præterea hoc loco, quàm infelix Iudæorum sors fuerit illo tempore, quando om-nis religionis contemptor inter ipsos summum ius atque potestatem obtinet, & coram illo religionis causas agere coguntur. Atqui hoc impijs sacerdotibus & impiæ ingratitudini debebant, qua Chri-stum regem & saluatorem coram Pilato abnegauerant. Similis hodie multorum sub Turcarum tyrannide conditio est: quorum exemplo nisi in tempore resipiscamus, periculum est, ne eandem for-tem aliquando subeant omnes, qui hodie Dei verbum audire dedignantur, & spiritus sancti de reli-gione ac fide iudicium detrectant.
units.tr: On the other side, we are told how Festus conducted this case. As soon as they came here, he says, I heard them without delay. But I soon found him innocent. For they brought forward none of those things which I expected, but raised some questions concerning their own superstition and dealt with the cause of a certain Jesus, whom Paul said had been raised from the dead. Thus the profane man speaks with the utmost contempt of the former religion, which nevertheless, from Festus's own words, we gather Paul had discussed at length and with care. In this man is set forth an example of all those who scorn the mysteries of God's Word, and above all the resurrection, and mock them. In instructing such people, although we make little progress, no one should be offended, since we see that Festus gave so little weight to what was said by Paul in the most serious terms. Meanwhile, judges may observe another thing in this pagan man, namely that they should hear cases without delay, since it is clear that many are worn down by unjust procrastination, and because they cannot afford the expense, they cannot pursue their right. Above all, let us note Paul's innocence, approved by manifold testimony. For at first we had Lysias the tribune as a witness of this. Afterwards Felix. Now Festus. Soon after, Agrippa also comes to the same verdict. And although the impious chief priests persist in their accusations, they nonetheless confirm Paul's innocence more firmly, since they can prove nothing of what they bring against him. That the other apostles had the same lot we have often seen. Thus the evangelists relate that Christ had the testimony of innocence from Pilate and likewise from Herod. This serves to commend the dignity of the Christian faith and doctrine. Those who today slander it openly show themselves worse than the Gentiles. It is also plain from this place how unhappy the lot of the Jews was at that time, when every despiser of religion holds the highest right and power among them, and they are compelled to plead the causes of religion before him. Yet they owed this to their impious priests and to their impious ingratitude, by which they had denied Christ as king and saviour before Pilate. A similar condition exists today for many under the tyranny of the Turks. Unless we repent in time, taking warning from their example, there is danger that all who now disdain to hear God's Word and refuse to judge matters of religion and faith by the Spirit may someday undergo the same fate.

units.la: Postremò, cur in vinculis adhuc detineat innocentem, docet: nimirum quòd ad Cæsarem prouo-cauerit. Ibi vero astutè suum sceleus dissimulat, quod tamen non aliter potest, quàm quòd sese prodit, dum se innoxium eò compullisse non obscurè fatetur, vt ad Cæsarem prouocandum fuerit. Nisi enim Iudæus cum Pauli periculo gratificari voluisset, nunquam is ad Cæsarem prouocare in animum in-duxisset. At vulgare nimis hoc est inter principes, vt flagitia sua artificiosè tegant, & tunc sibi ma-ximam iustitiæ opinionem apud homines vendicent, quando omnes iustitiæ & æquitatis metas lon-gissimè transiliunt. Porrò hac occasione factum est, vt Agrippa Paulum videre & audire cuperet, quæ res celeberrimæ concioni, quà sequenti Cap. describet Lucas, causam prabuit. Ita vero Dei pro-uidentiam videre licet, quia fit, vt quæ minime putares illius regnum prouehant. Quid ergo nostrũ ipsorum consilijs anxij tumultuamur? Quin potius in Deum reiecta omni cura, officium singulì fa-cimus? Ita enim fiet, vt passim sese Deo seruiendi occasio nobis offerat, & in periculis vindice & tu-tore vtamur Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, he shows why he still keeps the innocent man in chains: namely, because Paul appealed to Caesar. There, indeed, Festus cunningly conceals his own crime, which he cannot do except by betraying himself, since he does not obscurely confess that he was driven to this, so that Paul had to appeal to Caesar, though innocent. For unless the Jews had wished to gratify their own people at Paul's peril, he would never have brought himself to appeal to Caesar. But it is all too common among princes to cunningly hide their wicked deeds and then claim for themselves the greatest reputation for justice among men, when they most grossly overstep every limit of justice and equity. Moreover, by this occasion it came about that Agrippa wished to see and hear Paul, which matter gave rise to the most famous assembly, which Luke describes in the following chapter. Thus indeed we may see God's providence, for it happens that things you would least expect advance his kingdom. Why then do we anxiously stir ourselves up with our own plans? Rather, having cast all care upon God, let each of us perform his duty. For so it will come about that everywhere the opportunity to serve God presents itself to us, and in dangers we have Jesus Christ as our avenger and protector, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLIX.
units.tr: HOMILY CLIX.

units.la: Postero autem die cum venisset Agrippa & Bernice cum multo ap-paratu, & introisset in auditorium cum Tribunis & viris principalibus ciuitatis: iubente Festo adductus est Paulus. Et dicit Festus: Agrippa Rex, & omnes qui simul adestis nobiscũ viri, videtis hunc hominem, de quo omnis multitudo Iudæorum interpellauit me & Hierosolymis & hic, acclamantes, non oportere eum viuere amplius. Ego vero comperi, nihil dignum morte eum admisisse. Caeterum quia is ipse appella-uit Augustum, statui mittere eum. De quo quid certum scribam domi-no, non habeo. Quare produxi eum ad vos, & maxime ad te Rex A-grippa, vt examinatione facta habeam quod scribam. Absurdum enim mihi videtur mittere vinctum, & crimina de quibus accusatur, non indicare.
units.tr: The next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had arrived with a great retinue and had entered the hall with the tribunes and the leading men of the city, Paul was brought in at Festus's command. Festus says: "King Agrippa, and all you men who are present with us, you see this man, about whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought no longer to live. But I found that he had done nothing worthy of death. However, since he himself appealed to the Emperor, I have decided to send him. I have nothing certain to write to the lord about him. So I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after an examination I may have something to write. For it seems absurd to me to send a prisoner without stating the charges against him."

units.la: Quamuis mortalibus nihil vel praestantius vel salutarius a Deo datum sit, quam euangelij verbum, quo ille inexhaustos suae gratiae thesauros & veram salutis rationem nobis offert: ea tamen est infelicis mundi peruersitas, vt nihil perinde, atq; verbum hoc, inuisum & exosum habeat. Qua causa est, quod huius ministri variis subinde afflictionibus exercentur, & quasi publica quaedam sunt mundi catharmata. Caeterum ne ipsis offenderemur nos, in quos fines seculorum incidunt, quando mundum Antichristo duce cum primis seuiturum conflat, Deus nos partim oraculis, partim exemplis instrui voluit, quibus discereremus, nihil noui nobis contingere, sed hanc ipsam omnibus seculis in mundo hoc cum verbi tum ministrorum eius fortem fuisse: nec tamen illud vllis vnquam hostium conatibus potuisse extingui. Nam & in aeternum manet, & legitimos fructus quovis tempore profert, vt passim scripturae docent. Exempla huius multa extant, sed inter haec memorabile cumprimis est, quod in Paulo apostolo Lucas proponit. Is enim licet in vinculis vitae degat, & cum hostium improbitate, tum praesidis iniquitate ad Caesarem provocare coactus sit, tamen coram Agrippa rege, coram Tribunis, coram Caesarea primatibus, tota deniq; gentis illius nobilitate, Christi causam sic agit, vt & innocentiam suam omnibus probet, & non obscuros verbi Dei aculeos in admonitorum animis relinquat. SED praestat singula suo, quo dicuntur, ordine inspicere.
units.tr: Although God has given mortals nothing more excellent or more healthful than the word of the gospel, by which he offers us the inexhaustible treasures of his grace and the true way of salvation, yet such is the perversity of this unhappy world that it hates and loathes nothing as much as this word. For this reason the ministers of the word are repeatedly harassed with various afflictions, and they are, as it were, the public scapegoats of the world. But lest we be offended by these things, we who live at the end of the ages, when it is clear that the world under Antichrist as its leader will rage most fiercely, God has wanted us to be taught partly by his oracles and partly by examples, so that we might learn that nothing new happens to us, but that this same lot has fallen to the word and to its ministers in this world in every age, and that it has never been possible for it to be extinguished by any efforts of its enemies. For it remains forever, and at all times it brings forth its lawful fruits, as the Scriptures teach everywhere. There are many examples of this, but among them the one Luke sets before us in the apostle Paul is especially memorable. For although he lives in chains, and has been compelled to appeal to Caesar both by the wickedness of his enemies and by the injustice of the governor, nevertheless, before King Agrippa, before the tribunes, before the leading men of Caesarea, and indeed before the whole nobility of that nation, he so pleads the cause of Christ that he proves his innocence to all and leaves the sharp goads of God's word, not dulled, in the minds of his hearers. But it is better to look at each detail in the order in which it is told.

units.la: Orditur autem a Pauli auditoribus narrationem hanc euangelista. Inter quos primi numerantur Agrippa & Bernice soror, quos cum multo apparatu & plane regio fastu auditorium ingressos fuisse dicit. Comitantur hos Tribuni militum, nobiles item aulici, & quicunq; in vrbe dignitatem obtinebant. Quos nimirum actioni huic Festus interesse voluit, vt quocunq; tandem res exiret, ipse invidiam apud Iudaeos facilius subterfugeret. In primis vero Agrippa nobis consyderandus, quem audiendi Pauli cupidum fuisse, supra dictum est. Desyderium enim hoc non tam veritatis & salutis studium, quam curiositas quaedam & animi vanitas, excitauit. Vnde aui sui fratrem Herodem Antipam refert, qui & ipse Christi videndi desyderio tenetur, sed eam duntaxat ob causam, quod illius miracula a multis praedicari audiuisset. Eius animi indicium est, quod noster hic, non discipuli instar ad Pauli concionem accedit, nec quicquam ex regio fastu praetermittit, sed illum totum magna cum ostentatione in auditorium affert. At isto exemplo docemur, quomodo erga Dei verbum mundus hic affici soleat. Illud certe natura vel odit, vel saltem contemnit, vt qui eius luce arguntur, & terrena caelestibus praeferre solet. Fit tamen interea, vt frequenter aliqui ad illud audiendum accedant, non quidem salutis studio, sed carnis affectibus ducti, curiositate nimirum, vel privati alicuius commodi spe, vel Papisticae disciplinae odio, vel ne toti ecclesiae et omnis religionis hostes esse putentur. At quia tales, non vt discipuli, sed vt censores & iudices veniunt, & ante concepta praeiudicia secum afferunt, fieri nequit, vt in illis erudiendis aliquid proficiat euangelium, cuius finem hunc esse Paulus docet, vt tota carnis ratio, seu captiua, sub fidei obedientiam redigatur. Humiles ergo & honestos atq; discendi cupidos animos afferamus oportet, siquidem aliquid proficere volumus. Vide de Luc.8. Rursum monemur exemplo hoc, quales censeri debeant, qui luxum & fastum templis sacris concionibus inferunt. Sunt hi Agrippae & Bernicis similes, nec leue illorum peccatum est. Primo enim leuitatis magnae argumentum est, quod nec se luctuum esse meminerunt, nec vestium origine ex peccato prodijsse cogitant, adeo vt illis nos humiliari potius quam superbire conueniat. Accedit & offendiculi scelus, dum alijs vel stultae imitationis, vel libidinosarum cogitationum, vel etiam tenuioris fortunae hominibus impatientiae et murmuris contra Deum authores sumus. In horribilem ergo Christi sententiam incurrimus, qua Vae illud horrendum iis imprecatur, qui alijs scandalum praebuerint. Adhaec belluinae cuiusdam stupiditatis & animi plus satis perversi indicium est, si in Dei conspectu superbiamus, vbi nos cumprimis humiliari oportebat. Quis enim non dementem dicet eum, qui coram Rege delictorum veniam postulaturus, insolenti vestitu & procaci vultu prodiret? Et nos, vt peccatorum poenas deprecemur & salutis verbum audiamus, immani luxu & Sybaritico fastu templa accedimus? Christus certè nos de necessario quoq; vestitu solicitos esse vetat. Qua fronte ergo nos vestes ad luxum & libidinem indefessa cura & solicitudine componimus? Vide quae de hoc peccato multis apud Isaiam Cap.3.dicuntur.
units.tr: The evangelist begins this narrative with Paul's hearers. Among them the first to be named are Agrippa and his sister Bernice, who, as he says, entered the hall with a great retinue and a truly royal display. They are accompanied by the military tribunes, the noblemen of the court, and whoever held rank in the city. Festus, of course, wished these men to be present at this proceeding so that, whatever the outcome, he himself might more easily escape the hatred of the Jews. Agrippa deserves our particular attention here, since, as has been said above, he was eager to hear Paul. This desire was stirred not so much by a zeal for truth and salvation as by a certain curiosity and vanity of mind. Hence Luke recalls Agrippa's great-uncle Herod Antipas, who was also seized with a desire to see Christ, but only for the reason that he had heard many people proclaim his miracles. The sign of his state of mind is that our man here does not approach Paul's sermon like a disciple, but brings all his royal pomp into the hall with great show. From this example we are taught how this world is usually affected toward the word of God. By nature it certainly hates it, or at least despises it, since it is convicted by its light, and it is accustomed to prefer earthly things to heavenly. Nevertheless it happens that many people come to hear it, not indeed out of zeal for salvation, but driven by the affections of the flesh: namely, curiosity, or the hope of some private advantage, or hatred of Papist discipline, or the fear of being thought enemies of the whole Church and of all religion. But because such people come not as disciples but as critics and judges, and bring with them prejudices formed beforehand, it cannot be that the gospel makes any progress in instructing them. Its aim, as Paul teaches, is that the whole reasoning of the flesh, even when captive, should be brought under the obedience of faith. Therefore, if we want to make any progress, we must bring humble, honest minds that are eager to learn. See on Luke 8. Again, this example warns us what sort of people should be judged to be those who bring luxury and display into sacred assemblies. They are like Agrippa and Bernice, and their sin is no light one. First, it is a great sign of levity that they do not remember that they are mourners, nor think that the origin of clothing came from sin, so that it is fitting for us to be humbled by these things rather than to be proud. There is also the crime of giving offence, since we become the authors, for others, either of foolish imitation, or of lustful thoughts, or even of impatience and murmuring against God among people of more modest means. We therefore fall under Christ's dreadful sentence, by which he pronounces that dreadful Woe on those who give offence to others. Moreover, it is a sign of a certain bestial stupidity and of a mind more than perverse if we take pride in the sight of God, when we most of all ought to be humbled. For who would not call mad the man who came into the presence of a king, who was about to ask for pardon for his offences, dressed in an insolent manner and with a bold face? And do we approach the temple, to beg for the punishment of our sins and to hear the word of salvation, with monstrous luxury and Sybaritic display? Christ certainly forbids us to be anxious even about necessary clothing. With what face, then, do we arrange our clothes for luxury and lust with tireless care and anxiety? See what is said about this sin at many places in Isaiah, chapter 3.

units.la: Sed Paulum quoq; videamus, qui Festo iubente pri lucitur, & quidem catenis vinctus, vt ex ipsius sermone patebit: non tamen iam vt reus ad iudices, sed vt doctor & ecclesiastes. Elucet autem in hoc spectaculo admirabile Dei consilium, quo fit, vt praestantissimorum hominum confessus, totus auro & ostro fulgens, Paulum carceris situ squalidum & manibus vincula trahentem, audiendi cupidus expectet. Imo offert Deus in vinculis agenti praeclaram pro suo nomine fortiter agendi occasionem. Unde patet, quam nihil suis consiliis & conatibus impii proficiant. Quid enim aliud hucusq; quaesiuerunt Iudaei, quam vt Paulo omnem praedicandi occasionem praeriperent, adeoq; illius doctrinam omnem extinguerent? Id vero adeo non assequuntur, vt potius in celeberrimos coetus ipsorum opera producatur, in quibus illi vix unquam alias dicendi copia facta fuisset. Seruiant haec consolationi nostrae in terrificis mundi conatibus. Cur enim mundum posthac timeamus, quando eadem hodie quoq; est Dei in suis afferendis & prouehendo verbi sui cursu potentia? Praecipuè vero Paulus hoc loco obseruandus erit, quem praesenti omnino & forti animo fuisse, sequentia docebunt. Nec enim Regis aspectu & nobilium corona mouetur. Sed intrepido ore causam suam sic agit, vt ipse vinctus non paruum auditoribus terrorem incutiat, ipsumq; Regem mediocriter commoueat. Quod ipsum supra Felici quoq; euenisse vidimus. Docent haec, Dei verbum minimè vinciri, licet ipsius ministri vinculis & carceribus constringantur. Nec enim ex hominibus illius vel authoritas vel effectus dependet. Nam vbi ipse vult spirat Dei spiritus, nec hominum vanissimorum arbitrio subiacet. Admonemur praeterea, quid nobis quoq; in simili casu agendum sit. Intrepidi Christi causam agamus, nec vnius assis faciamus mundi huius authoritatem siue tyrannidem. Causa enim, quam agimus, iusta & bona est, & ex illa vniuersa salutis nostrae ratio dependet. Eadem non nostra, sed Dei est, cui illam afferere no difficile fuerit. Nec nos illam agimus, sed Dei spiritus, qui in nobis agit & loquitur, iuxta Christi promissionem. Quis ergo Dei spiritum oppugnet? Quis illi praevalebit? Aut quis illo confortatus & adiutus, ignauo metu sese corripi patiatur?
units.tr: But let us also look at Paul, who is brought forward at Festus's command, and indeed in chains, as will be clear from his own speech; yet not now as a defendant before judges, but as a teacher and preacher. In this spectacle there shines forth God's wonderful plan, by which it happens that the most distinguished men, all gleaming with gold and purple, wait eagerly to hear Paul, squalid from the prison and dragging his chains in his hands. Indeed, God offers to a man in chains a splendid opportunity to act boldly for his name. From this it is plain how little the wicked accomplish by their plans and efforts. For what else have the Jews sought up to now, than to snatch from Paul every opportunity of preaching and so to extinguish all his teaching? But they do not achieve this at all; rather, his work is brought forward into the most crowded assemblies of their own, where they would hardly ever otherwise have had such an opportunity to speak. Let these things serve for our comfort amid the frightening efforts of the world. For why should we fear the world from now on, since the same power of God is still present today in bringing forward his own and in advancing the course of his word? Paul must be observed especially in this place, since the following shows that he was entirely present and brave in spirit. For he is not moved by the king's presence or by the crowd of nobles.
