Rather, he pleads his cause with such a fearless voice that, though himself in chains, he strikes no small terror into his hearers and moves the king not a little. We have seen this also happen before with Felix. These things teach that the word of God is not bound at all, even when its ministers are bound with chains and imprisoned. For its authority and its effect do not depend on men. For the Spirit of God breathes where he wills, and is not subject to the judgment of the most worthless of men. We are also reminded what we too must do in a similar case. Let us plead the cause of Christ fearlessly, and let us not value the authority or tyranny of this world at a single farthing. For the cause we plead is just and good, and our whole salvation depends on it. It is not ours but God's, and it will not be difficult to assert it before him. Nor do we plead it, but the Spirit of God, who acts and speaks in us, according to Christ's promise. Who then will oppose the Spirit of God? Who will prevail against him? Or who, strengthened and aided by him, would allow himself to be seized by cowardly fear?

units.la: Postremò Festus Paulum Agrippae & reliquis auditoribus sistit, eiusq; causam & praesentis actionis finem paucis repetit. Hunc enim illum esse ait, quem omnes Iudaei ad mortem deposcant, qui tamen, se iudice, nullum morte dignum scelus admiserit. Quia vero ad Caesarem prouocarit, cupere se, vt illum attenti audiant, & singulorum examinationem faciant, vt certum quid de illo ad Caesarem perscribi possit. Ita vero attentionem Paulo Praeses Romanus conciliat, quod ipsum non sine numine factum fuisse satis constat. Interim nouum habemus innocentiae Pauli testimonium, quam multoties asseri oportuit: cum doctrinae ipsius acerrimos hostes omnibus seculis passim fore, Deus praeuideret. Simul vero incurabilis elucet Iudaeorum malitia, qui innocentem ad supplicium poscere non destiterunt. Ita enim patrum vestigiis pertinaciter insistunt, quos simili impudentia Dei filium, etiam multum reclamante Pilato, ad mortem postulauisse legimus. Iusto ergo Dei iudicio funditus excisi, & commune exemplum facti sunt, quod illis euenturum esse, Christus non semel praedixerat. Esse praeterea obseruanda nobis Festi sententia, qui absurdum esse dicit, captiuum mittere, nec significare de quibus ille accusetur, & quare in vincula coniectus sit. Docet haec, ita cum captiuis agendum esse, vt omnium ratio certa nobis constare possit. Nec enim in hominis vita temerè ludendum est. Hoc cum Ethnicus homo viderit, quid eos magistratus decebit; qui Christi nomine & verbo gloriantur? Qua deniq; animi moderatione singulos nos captiuos tractare conuenit, qui in his ipsi Christo beneficium conferre, aut iniuriam fieri sciimus? Atqui vtinam hac aequitate in Christi cultores hodie aduersarij nostri vterentur, quibus leuiculum videtur absque causa omni inhumanitatis genere in nos saeuire. Minimè tamen nos illa offendant, quando Christum quoq; iniquissimè tractatum fuisse nouimus. Cur enim discipuli fors potior esset quam praeceptoris? Quin volupe fit, pro veritatis causa quiduis malorum subire. Haec enim proxima ad coelos via est, in quibus aeterna regni hereditas nos manet, vt illam possideamus cum capite nostro Iesu Christo: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, Festus presents Paul to Agrippa and the other hearers, and briefly recounts his case and the outcome of the present proceedings. He says this is the man whom all the Jews demand to be put to death, though in his judgment he has committed no crime deserving of death. But since Paul has appealed to Caesar, Festus wishes that they listen to him attentively and examine each of them, so that something definite may be written to Caesar about him. In this way the Roman governor wins Paul a hearing, which is clearly not done without the divine will. Meanwhile we have a fresh testimony to Paul's innocence, which had to be asserted many times over, since God foresaw that the most bitter enemies of his teaching would appear everywhere in every age. At the same time, the incurable malice of the Jews shines forth, for they did not cease to demand the death of an innocent man. They persistently follow in the footsteps of their fathers, who, with the same shamelessness, we read, demanded the death of the Son of God, even though Pilate strongly objected. Therefore, by the just judgment of God they have been utterly cut off and have become a common example of what Christ had foretold more than once would happen to them. Furthermore, we should observe the opinion of Festus, who says it is absurd to send a prisoner without indicating the charges against him and why he has been put in chains. This teaches that prisoners must be treated in such a way that a clear account of everyone's case can be known to us. For one must not play carelessly with a person's life. If a heathen man has seen this, how much more should magistrates who glory in the name and word of Christ do so? And finally, with what restraint of spirit ought we to treat each prisoner, since we know that whatever benefit or injury is done to such people is done to Christ himself? Would that our adversaries today used this fairness toward the worshippers of Christ, who think it a trifling matter to rage against us with every kind of inhumanity, without any cause. Yet let us not be troubled by this, since we know that Christ himself was treated most unjustly. For why should the disciple fare better than the teacher? Indeed, it is a joy to undergo any kind of evil for the sake of the truth. For this is the nearest way to heaven, where the eternal inheritance of the kingdom awaits us, so that we may possess it together with our head, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXVI. HOMILIA CLX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI. HOMILY CLX.

units.la: AGrippa vero ad Paulum ait: Permittitur tibi loqui pro temetipso. Tunc Paulus extenta manu pro se dicebat: Super omnibus, de quibus accusor a Iudaeis, Rex Agrippa, existimo me beatum, qui causam dicturus sum apud te hodie: cum tu maxime sis gnarus earum quae apud Iudaeos sunt & consuetudinum & quaestionum. Quapropter oro te ut patienter me audias. Itaque vitam quidem meam, quam egi ab adolescentia, quae ab initio fuit in gente mea Hierosolymis, noverunt omnes Iudaei, qui prius noverant me ab initio, si velint testimonium ferre, quod secundum exquisitissimam sectam nostrae religionis vixerim Pharisaeus.
units.tr: Then Agrippa said to Paul: "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul, stretching out his hand, spoke in his own defence: "King Agrippa, I count myself happy that I am to make my defence before you today, concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, since you are especially acquainted with all the customs and questions that are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently. My manner of life from my youth, which was from the beginning among my own nation at Jerusalem, is known to all the Jews, who have known me from the beginning, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest sect of our religion I lived as a Pharisee."

units.la: DOminus & salvator noster, Iesus Christus, de Paulo & ministerio illius cum Anania colloquens, inter alia dicit: Organum electum est mihi iste, ut portet nomen meum coram gentibus, & regibus, & filiis Israel. Quae verba ut Pauli ministerium magnifice commendant, itanos quoque excitare debent ad diligentem omnium eorum consyderationem, quae in ministerio suo ille vel fecit vel passus est: quando in his nihil illi absque singulari divinae providentiae consilio accidisse constat. Observandum hoc cumprimis in praesenti actione, qua coram Agrippa rege, coram nobilibus aulicis, & praecipue eius gentis proceribus fidem & doctrinam sua ea dexteritate simul & constantia defendit, ut & auditores ipsos no mediocriter commouerit, & suo exemplo docuerit quanta cum vera Dei tum fidei vera virtus sit atque efficacia. Quod evidentius patebit, si singula ordine videamus.
units.tr: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, speaking with Ananias about Paul and his ministry, says among other things: "This man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the sons of Israel." Just as these words commend Paul's ministry magnificently, so they ought also to stir us to a careful consideration of all the things that he either did or suffered in his ministry, since it is clear that nothing happened to him in these apart from the singular counsel of divine providence. This is to be observed especially in the present action, in which, before King Agrippa and the noble courtiers, and above all the leaders of that nation, he defended his faith and doctrine with such skill and steadfastness that he moved his hearers no little, and by his example taught how great the true power and efficacy of true faith in God is. This will appear more clearly if we look at the individual parts in order.

units.la: Primo autem Agrippa proponitur, qui prior Paulum compellans, liberam illi pro se ipso dicendi copiam facit. Id vero Dei consilio factum fuisse nemini dubium est, qui hac occasione istis hominibus euangelium praedicari voluit. Quia enim (ut Paulus alibi testatur) vult omnes homines salvos fieri, simul etiam salutis verbum omnibus revelari & praedicari vult. Atque tam firmum & stabile est hoc illius decretum, ut nullis unquam mundi huius & tyrannorum conatibus impediri potuerit. Cuius rei tum testimonia tum exempla passim in scripturis occurrunt, quibus nos fidem nutantem in adversis confirmare decet. Ac quia de hoc iam saepe dictum est, modo equitatis & iustitiae exemplum observemus, quod in Agrippa, quantumvis fastuoso & impuro homine, spiritus sanctus proponit. Is enim Paulum a tota Iudaeorum gente ad mortem postulari audierat, nec in illo quicquam videbat, quod ipsi aliquam vel quaestus vel honoris spem facere posset. Minime tamen totius gentis praeiudicio movetur, nec suijpsius potius quam iustitiae plublicae rationem habendam esse putat: sed ipsum quoque Paulum coram audire instituit, adeoque illum prior ad dicendum provocat. Imitentur exemplum hoc quicunque in magistratu versantur, & quo plures adversus aliquem conspirauisse vident, eo maiori studio & diligentia causam illius inspiciant, ne sua vel indulgentia vel officiantia aliorum improbitatem adiuvent. Est autem hoc (proh dolor) nimis vulgare hodie, & frequenter fieri consueuit, ut regum & principum aures Christi fidelibus minime pateant, eo quod illi episcopis potius & borum affectus morem gerendum esse existiment, & praeiudicio corrupti non omnino extra culpam esse eos putent, quos ab illis tanto zelo & studio oppugnari sentiunt.
units.tr: First, Agrippa is introduced, who, addressing Paul first, gives him free opportunity to speak for himself. That this came about by the counsel of God no one doubts, who wished the gospel to be preached to these men on this occasion. For since (as Paul elsewhere testifies) he wants all men to be saved, so he also wants the word of salvation to be revealed and preached to all. And this decree of his is so firm and stable that it could never be hindered by any attempts of this world or of tyrants. Testimonies and examples of this thing occur everywhere in the Scriptures, by which it is fitting that we confirm a wavering faith in adversity. And since this has already often been said, let us observe the pattern of fairness and justice which the Holy Spirit sets before us in Agrippa, however proud and impure a man he was. For he had heard that Paul was being demanded for death by the whole nation of the Jews, and he saw nothing in him that could give him any hope of gain or honour. Yet he is not moved by the prejudice of the whole nation, nor does he think that he should consider his own advantage rather than public justice; instead he resolves to hear Paul himself in person, and so he first calls him to speak. Let all who hold public office imitate this example: the more people they see conspiring against someone, the more carefully and diligently they should examine his cause, lest by their favour or by the complaisance towards others they aid the wickedness of others. But (alas!) it is now all too common, and it has often come about, that the ears of kings and princes are scarcely open to the faithful of Christ, because they think they must rather humour the bishops and their feelings, and, corrupted by prejudice, they think that those whom they feel are attacked by the bishops with such zeal and eagerness are not altogether free of blame.

units.la: Sed ad Paulum transeamus, qui licet ex improviso coram tam illustri consessu causam ex vinculis dicere cogatur, mox tamen extenta manu sermonem orditur, qui ut omnia complectitur, quae ad causam hanc pertinebant, ita nullum habet animi consternati aut dubii indicium. Quo loco veritatem simul & effectum promissionum Christi videre licet. Habuit enim Paulus cum generales promissiones, tum peculiarem illam, cuius initio meminimus, fore nimirum, ut Christi nomen coram regibus quoque & magnatibus praedicaret. In his ergo respiciens, pericula quaevis facile contemnit, cum non ignoraret, maiorem multo Christi potentiam esse, quam quae mundi conatibus impediri aut superari possit. Caeterum nos quoque, ex huius exemplo consolationem petere convenit: eo quod omnibus piis suum spiritum Christus pollicitus est, qui corda & ora nostra regat, si quando fidei nostrae rationem reddere cogimur. Porro quoad orationem Pauli, tota narratione argumentosa & ad sui defensionem egregia egregiè accomodata constat. Narrat enim, quam vitæ rationem à puero secutus sit, & quàm nulla abs se vnquam data sit vel leuitatis vel impietatis suspicio. Quomodo item ad fidem Christianam & apostolatum vocatus, nihil scripturis contrarium docuerit vel fecerit. Quibus probare vult, se immerentem tam pertinaci Iudaicæ gentis odio grauari.
units.tr: But let us pass on to Paul, who, although he is compelled unexpectedly to plead his cause from his chains before so distinguished an assembly, nevertheless, stretching out his hand, begins his speech; and this speech, as it embraces everything that pertained to this cause, so it shows no sign of a dismayed or doubting mind. Here we can see both the truth and the effect of the promises of Christ. For Paul had both the general promises and that particular one, of which we recalled the beginning: namely, that he would preach the name of Christ also before kings and great men. Relying on these, he easily despised any dangers, since he knew that the power of Christ is far greater than can be hindered or overcome by the attempts of the world. Moreover, it is fitting that we too seek comfort from his example, since Christ has promised to all the godly his Spirit, who will rule our hearts and mouths whenever we are compelled to give an account of our faith. Further, as to Paul's speech, the whole narrative is argumentative and, for his defence, admirably suited to its purpose. For he relates what manner of life he followed from boyhood, and how no suspicion of levity or impiety was ever given by him. Likewise, how, when he was called to the Christian faith and the apostleship, he taught or did nothing contrary to the Scriptures. By these things he wishes to prove that he, undeserving, is burdened with the stubborn hatred of the Jewish nation.

units.la: Præmittitur autem narrationi breue exordium, quo à Regis persona beneuolentiam captat, dum se beatum dicit, quòd causam hanc coram ipso agere debeat, qui ritus & quæstiones Iudaeorum non ignoret. Nouerat enim Paulus, frustra apud eos de rebus grauibus disputari, quos insciitia & ignorantia totos occupauit. Quare vt iustitiæ studio iudicet flagrare conueniit, ita ijsdem prudentia cum rerum experientia coniuncta cumprimis necessaria est. Nec verò politica duntaxat illos nouisse conuenit, verumetiam ea quæ ad fidem & religionem spectant, cuius curam & studium magistratibus scriptura passim commendat. Quia enim à Deo illi ordinati sunt, qui ipsos authoritate simul & potestate exornauit, ipsa naturæ lege monentur, vt vicissim pro Dei gloria & cultu afferendo adiuuent. Ideò Legis librum Regibus familiarissimum esse voluit Deus, & idem sanctissimorum regum exemplis magistratus omnes ad studium illud excitare confuerunt. Quos non inepte Agrippa hic imitatus, religionis negotium cognitum & perspectum habuit. At nostro seculo eò stoliditatis deuentum est, vt Reges tum demum sibi religionis laudem vendicet, si illius causam nec intelligant, nec quicquam ad se pertinere dicant. Debemus hoc Pontificum tyrannidi, qui in regum ignorantia suæ potentiæ vires maxima ex parte confiltere viderunt.
units.tr: A brief introduction is placed before the narrative, by which he wins the goodwill of the king, saying that he counts himself happy that he must plead this cause before him, who is not ignorant of the rites and questions of the Jews. For Paul knew that it is in vain to dispute about weighty matters before those whom ignorance and lack of knowledge have wholly possessed. Therefore, just as it is fitting that they should be aflame with zeal for justice, so prudence joined with experience of affairs is especially necessary for them. Nor is it fitting that they know only political matters, but also those things which pertain to faith and religion; the Scriptures everywhere commend this care and zeal to magistrates. For since they have been appointed by God, who has adorned them with authority and power at the same time, the law of nature itself warns them to help in turn in asserting the glory and worship of God. Therefore God wished the book of the Law to be most familiar to kings, and the examples of the most holy kings have usually stirred all magistrates to that study. Agrippa, imitating them not foolishly here, had a knowledge and clear understanding of the business of religion. But in our age things have come to such stupidity that kings then claim for themselves the praise of religion only if they neither understand its cause nor say that it has anything to do with them. We owe this to the tyranny of the Popes, who, in the ignorance of kings, have seen that the greatest part of their own power consists.

units.la: Porrò narrationem, cuius argumentum modò exposuimus, ab ipsa pueritia vel vitæ anteacta primordijs orditur, ipsos Iudaeos testes citans, quàm sanctè pieq; illam transfegerit. Quia enim alibi episcopum ab exteris quoq; testimonium bonum habere debere scribit, ipse vel hostium testimonio suam innocentiam probare conatur. Ne verò in obscuro vitam duxisse putaretur, se Hierosolymis educatum fuisse ait, vbi religionis sedes erat, & schola totius gentis celeberrima florebat. Illic se laudatissimum vitæ genus iam statim ab initio secutum fuisse dicit, nimirum Pharisaeorum sectam. Iure enim hæc aliis omnibus præferri debuit, cùm & scripturas in maximo honore haberent Pharisæi, & vitæ honestati præ cæteris studerent. Præcipuus verò illorum error in eo consistebat, quòd suorum operum iustitiam & meritum statuebant. Caeterum finis & scopus Pauli est, vt Agrippæ persuadeat, se nihil vel impio vel leui & vago animo temere facere potuisse, cùm ab ipsa pueritia religioni & omnium se veris simæ sectæ assueuerit. Non temere autem pueritiam abs se pie transactam fuisse commemorat. Ita enim docet, in publicis personis multum referre, qualis quis à pueris fuerit. Quamuis enim minimè reijci debeant, qui in fera demum senecta conuertuntur, longè tamen præferendi sunt alteri illi, quos nulla vitæ anteactæ macula infames reddit. Tales enim in assueto virtutum studio constatius pergunt, & maiori cum authoritate improborum conatibus se opponere possunt: cùm alteri non raro ad intermissa vitia reuertuntur, & improborum exprobrationibus atq; calumniis expositi, authoritatem omnem paulatim amittunt. Quid, quòd boni quoq; illorum consilia, honesta licet & sancta, ferè suspecta sunt, dum illos vel animi leuitate, vel quouis alio affectu duci metuunt? Magnam igitur & diligentem educationis curam habere eos conuenit, qui liberos suos vel ecclesiæ vel reipub. destinauerunt. Et hic quidem duo hæc cumprimis necessaria sunt, quæ de seipso Paulus commemorat. Alterum videlicet, vt in ijs locis educentur, vbi religio maximè floret, vt cum literis & rerum experientia huius quoq; gustum imbibant. Alterum verò, vt ab initio statim tale vitæ genus deligant, in quo minima vitiorum occasio occurrat. Quia enim iuuentus ex innata corruptione ad peccandi licentiam proclivis est, mali occasiones vitandæ & arcendæ potius, quàm captandæ sunt. Hæc vtinam obserua rent nostri seculi homines, qui liberos suos plerunq; inter eos educari curat, quos à Christi cognitione & religione vera alienissimos esse constat: nec vlla religionis cura tanguntur, sed solius quæstus rationem habere solent. Ex eiusmodi ergo scholis illud hominum genus prodit, quod religionem hominum amicitia & quæstu metitur, quodq; sublatis veræ pietatis repagulis, in omne scelus præceps devolui tur, nec sibi ipsi modò, verumetiam ecclesijs & reipub. exitiale est. Docent hoc exempla tum vetera tum recentia, quibus nos excitari conuenit, vt liberos nostros deo consecratos ita à pueris instituì cure mus, vt tum sibi ipsis tum ecclesijs & reipub. utiles, tandem cœlestis regni hæreditatem adeant cum Christo Iesu, domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, the narrative, whose subject we have just set out, begins from his very boyhood or the first beginnings of his earlier life, citing the Jews themselves as witnesses of how holily and piously he conducted it. For since in another place he writes that a bishop ought to have a good testimony even from outsiders, he himself tries to prove his innocence by the testimony of his enemies. But lest he be thought to have lived in obscurity, he says that he was brought up at Jerusalem, where the seat of religion was, and where the most celebrated school of the whole nation flourished. There he says that from the very beginning he followed the most commended manner of life, namely the sect of the Pharisees. For indeed this sect rightly ought to be preferred to all others, since the Pharisees both held the Scriptures in the highest honour and studied the honesty of life above others. But their chief error consisted in this, that they set up the righteousness and merit of their own works. Yet the aim and purpose of Paul is to persuade Agrippa that he could not have done anything rashly, either wickedly or with a light and wandering mind, since from boyhood he had been accustomed to religion and to the strictest of all sects. He does not mention without reason that his boyhood was spent piously. For he teaches that in public persons it matters much what sort of person someone was from boyhood. For although those who are converted only in late and advanced old age ought by no means to be rejected, yet they must be preferred far less than those whom no stain of a previous life makes infamous. For such men continue more steadily in the habitual pursuit of virtue, and can oppose the attempts of the wicked with greater authority; whereas the others not rarely return to vices they had given up, and, exposed to the reproaches and slanders of the wicked, gradually lose all authority. What is more, even their good counsels, though honest and holy, are almost always suspected, while men fear that they are driven by levity of mind or by some other passion. Therefore those who have destined their children for the Church or the commonwealth ought to take great and careful care of their upbringing. And indeed these two things, which Paul mentions about himself, are especially necessary here: the first, namely that they be brought up in those places where religion flourishes most, so that they may imbibe along with letters a taste also of this and of experience of affairs; the second, that from the very beginning they choose such a manner of life in which there is the least occasion for vices. For since youth, from innate corruption, is prone to the licence of sinning, the occasions of evil ought to be avoided and kept off rather than sought out. Would that the men of our age observed these things, who commonly take care to have their children educated among those who are known to be most alien to the knowledge of Christ and to true religion, and are moved by no concern for religion but are wont to consider only the reckoning of gain. From such schools therefore comes that kind of men who measure religion by friendship and profit, and who, with the barriers of true piety removed, rush headlong into every crime, and are destructive not only to themselves but also to the churches and the commonwealth. Examples both ancient and recent teach this, by which we ought to be stirred, so that we take care to bring up our children, consecrated to God, from boyhood in such a way that, useful both to themselves and to the churches and the commonwealth, they may at last attain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom with Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII. HOMILIA CLXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. HOMILY CLXI.

units.la: Et nunc ob spem repromissionis, quæ ad Patres nostros facta est à Deo, sto iudicio subiectus: ad quam duodecim tribus nostræ instanter nocte & die colentes Deum sperant se peruenturas. De qua spe accusor, Rex Agrippa, à Iudæis. Cur incredibile iudicatur apud vos, si Deus mortuos suscitat?
units.tr: "And now I stand on trial for the hope of the promise that God made to our fathers, the hope that our twelve tribes, serving God earnestly night and day, expect to attain. It is concerning this hope that I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa. Why is it thought incredible among you that God raises the dead?"

units.la: Fidei & doctrinæ suæ rationem redditurus Paulus apostolus, in hoc maximè incumbit, vt nihil abs se impia animi leuitate aut temeritate factum esse euincat. In quem finem suæ etiam puericiæ mentionem fecit, ita se à pueris & institutum esse, & vitam duxisse probans, vt nulla in ipsum temeritatis aut leuitatis suspicio circa religionem merito cadere debeat. Quo exemplo inter alia ad monemur, ita nobis in religione versandum esse, vt quales in ea fuerimus à teneris annis, rationem cuius reddere possimus. Vt enim omnis ætatis tutor & assertor est Deus, ita omnem quoque ætatem huic consecratam esse conuenit: & ipsum hoc non semel postulare legimus, vt pueri quoque in ipsius lege & cultu à primis annis instituantur. Quo loco pudendus illorum error arguitur, qui religionis cautam grauiorem perplexioremq; esse clamant, quàm vt eam laici tractare debeant, cùm in illa tenera quoq; ætatem Deus exerceri velit, nec quicquam ita ex æquo ad omnes homines pertineat, vt religio, ad quam illos ab initio statim creatos fuisse scriptura docet. At quia de his alibi diximus, modò in Pauli oratione pergendum erit.
units.tr: When Paul the apostle is about to give an account of his faith and teaching, he labours above all to prove that he has done nothing in impetuousness or rashness of mind. To this end he also mentions his boyhood, showing that he was taught and lived from childhood in such a way that no suspicion of rashness or levity can rightly fall upon him in matters of religion. From this example, among other things, we are reminded that we must so conduct ourselves in religion that we can give an account of what we were in it from our tender years. For just as God is the guardian and defender of every age, so every age ought to be dedicated to him. We read that he himself has demanded this more than once: that children too be instructed in his law and worship from their earliest years. Here the shameful error of those is exposed who cry out that the matter of religion is too deep and too intricate for laymen to handle. God wishes to be served even in that tender age, and nothing pertains so equally to all people as religion, for which Scripture teaches that they were created from the beginning. But since we have spoken of these things elsewhere, we must now go on with Paul's speech.

units.la: Is verò cœptam paulò ante narrationem nonnihil interrumpens, statum totius controuersiæ, quæ sibi cum aduersarijs Iudæis intercedat, exponit. Se enim accusari dicit propter spem promissionis, quæ patribus olim à Deo facta sit, & ad quam duodecim tribus, id est, tota Iudæorum gens, assiduo Dei cultu se se peruenturas esse sperent. Nec id semel dixisse contentus, mox denuo repetit quod dixerat: De hac (inquiens) spe accusor, Rex Agrippa. Quæ verba aliquam præ se ferunt indignationis speciem, qua rei indignitatem exprimere voluit. Quasi diceret: Quis non videat, quæ & quanta sit aduersariorum meorum iniquitas, quando me capitis accersunt, & schismatis accusant, cuius doctrina simul & fides circa veterem illam Dei promissionem versatur, in qua patres omnes olim spem omnem collocatam habuerunt, & cuius consortes esse cupiunt quotquot in Israele veri Dei cultores sunt, vt qui non alium sui cultus & totius religionis scopum habeant? Caeterum spes illa promissionis, de qua loquitur, Dei filius est, Iesus Christus, in quo vno Deus ab ipso mundi exordio patribus, per Adami peccatum in exitium prolapsis, vitam & salutem pollicitus fuit, vt paulò post pluribus dicetur. Nō obscurè autem illorum tum ignorantiam tum præposteram suæ religionis fiduciam perstringit, qui fœdere quidem & promissionibus Dei gloriétur, & populus Dei omnino censeri velint, interim verò Christum reijciant, cuius merito & intercessione promissiones illæ ratæ sunt, quarum nullus omnino fructus foret, nisi ille fœderis vindex esset & assertor. Quia verò tam diuina potentia Christi, quàm eiusdem officium, cui illum pater destinauit, in resurrectione ex mortuis potissimum elucet (sicuti alibi Paulus testatur) omissis modò reliquis articulis, resurrectionem solam tractandam sibi sumit: id quod ad præsentem quoque controuersiam cumprimis faciebat. Ita enim & Christum Iesum vitæ ac salutis authorem esse patebat, qui è mortuis resurrexerat, & simul Sadducæorum error confutabatur, qui resurrectionem in vniuersum negabant. Nam verisimile est, illorum sectam apud plerosque tunc temporis prævaluisse, adeoq; ex Pauli auditoribus non paucos illa fuisse infectos. Nisi enim hoc demus, importunior planè videri poterit Paulus, qui non sine stomacho quærit, cur ipsis incredibile videatur, quòd Deus mortuos resuscitare dicitur? Nec dubium esse potest, omnia hæc fusius à Paulo tractata & scripturarum testimonijs confirmata fuisse. At Lucas summa tantùm rerum capita perstringere voluit, vt nobis de singulis cogitandi occasionem præberet. Et sanè planissimus erit locus hic, quem breuitas obscuriore reddidit, si propositiones Pauli ex eo elicias, quas illum tractauisse constat. Ex his prima erit: De spe promissionis patribus à Deo factæ, adeoq; de tota salutis ratione, controuersia nobis est: Secunda: Hanc ego in vno Christo Iesu sitam esse doceo, quod illi constanter negant. Tertia: In Christo vitæ & salutis rationem omnem consistere, resurrectione illius probo, quæ illum & Dei filium & vitæ authorem esse declarauit. Quarta: Nec incredibilis cuiquam videri
units.tr: Paul, interrupting the narrative he had begun a little earlier, sets out the state of the whole controversy that he has with his Jewish adversaries. He says that he is accused on account of the hope of the promise that God once made to the fathers, and which the twelve tribes, that is, the whole Jewish nation, hope to attain by constant worship of God. Not content to have said this once, he soon repeats what he had said: "It is concerning this hope that I am accused, King Agrippa." These words carry a certain appearance of indignation, by which he wished to express the outrageousness of the matter, as if he were saying: Who does not see how great the injustice of my adversaries is, when they summon me to a capital charge and accuse me of schism, when my teaching and my faith turn on that ancient promise of God, in which all the fathers once placed all their hope, and of which all who are true worshippers of the God of Israel wish to be partakers, since they have no other aim of their worship and of their whole religion? Moreover, that hope of the promise of which he speaks is the Son of God, Jesus Christ, in whom alone God, from the very beginning of the world, promised life and salvation to the fathers who had fallen into ruin through the sin of Adam, as will be said more fully a little later. Nor does he obscurely censure the ignorance and the perverse confidence in their own religion of those who glory in the covenant and promises of God, and who wish to be counted as the people of God altogether, yet meanwhile reject Christ, by whose merit and intercession those promises were ratified. Those promises would have no fruit at all unless he were the guarantor and defender of the covenant. But since the divine power of Christ, as well as the office for which the Father appointed him, shines forth above all in his resurrection from the dead (as Paul elsewhere testifies), he takes upon himself to treat the resurrection alone, leaving aside the other articles. This was especially relevant to the present controversy. For it made clear both that Christ Jesus is the author of life and salvation, since he rose from the dead, and at the same time it refuted the error of the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection altogether. For it is likely that their sect had then gained great strength among most people, and that not a few of Paul's hearers had been infected by it. Unless we grant this, Paul may seem rather too importunate, asking with some irritation why it seems incredible to them that God is said to raise the dead. Nor can there be any doubt that Paul treated all these things at greater length and confirmed them with testimonies of Scripture. But Luke meant only to touch on the chief heads of the matter, so as to give us an occasion to think about each of them. And this passage, which brevity has made obscure, will certainly be quite plain if you draw out of it the propositions which Paul is known to have treated. The first of these is: we have a controversy about the hope of the promise made by God to the fathers, and so about the whole manner of salvation. The second: I teach that this hope is located in the one Christ Jesus, which they firmly deny. The third: I prove by his resurrection, which declared him both the Son of God and the author of life, that the whole manner of life and salvation consists in Christ. The fourth: nor should the resurrection of Christ seem incredible to anyone, since it is very easy for God to raise all the dead at the end of the world, which Scripture teaches all will be done.

units.la: Summa et ordo præsentis loci. videri debet resurrectio Christi, cum Deo facillimum sit in fine mundi omnes mortuos resuscitare, quod illum facturum esse, scriptura omnes docent. Hic mihi tractationis Paulinae ordo, omniumque quae hoc loco dicta fuerunt, summa esse videtur, quam si observemus, facillimum erit singula fusius explicare. Ita vero attentos quoque facere voluit auditores rerum maximarum enumeratione, ne sibi (quod Festus ante dixerat) cum Iudaeis de re nihili controversiam esse putarent. Interim nobis loci quidam communes, qui hic incidunt, consyderandi erunt.
units.tr: Summary and order of the present passage. This, it seems to me, is the summary of Paul's treatment and of everything that has been said in this place, the order of which, if we observe it, will make it very easy to explain each point more fully. Luke wished, moreover, to make his hearers attentive by the enumeration of the greatest matters, so that they would not think (as Festus had said earlier) that the controversy with the Jews was about some trifling matter. Meanwhile, certain common topics that arise here must be considered by us.

units.la: Et primo quidem, quae omnium sanctorum, adeoque totius ecclesiae Dei omnibus saeculis fides atque spes fuerit, admonemur. Ea nimirum, quae Christo Dei filio pro nobis incarnato nititur, et in vno hoc vitam atq; salutem omne sitam esse credit. Hanc enim in praesenti Paulus spem promissionis, patribus olim factae, nominat. Atqui in Christo promissiones omnes ratas esse, fides catholica dicit, et ipse Paulus ubiq; fatetur, maxime in posteriori ad Corinth. primo cap. et in priori ad eosdem Corinth. cap. 10. ubi eandem patrum in veteri Testamento conditionem nobiscum fuisse scribit, sic ut nostra quoq; Sacramenta, Baptismum et Coenam, illis accommodet, sicut alibi nobis pascha et circumcisionem spiritualem tribuit. 1. Cor. 5. Colof. 2. Clarius tamen patebit haec, si promissiones Dei, quas ille patribus olim fecit, consyderemus. In his primus merito Adam numeratur, cui cum ex Paradiso in hanc lachrymarum vallem extruderetur, non alia salutis spes a Deo facta fuit, quam quae in vno Christo reperitur. Promittitur enim illi semen mulieris, cuius calcaneo quidem insidietur serpens, sed frustra, cum illud huius caput sit conteriturum. At mulieris semen solus Christus dici potest, qui nulla interveniente virilis seminis commixtione ex virgine Maria carnem assumpsit. Huius calcaneo, humanae nimirum naturae, improbe insidiatus est vetus ille serpens diabolus, perq; sua organa, ut in cruce occideretur, effecit: id autem magno suo malo. Ita enim factum est, ut moriens Christus suae mortis merito diaboli caput, id est, principatum et tyrannidem conculcaret, ipsumq; ex armatum plane e regno suo eiiceret. At quia promissioni huic Adamum credidisse, minime dubium est, cum ideo uxoris quoq; nomine mutato, illam Hevam, utpote quae viuentes paritura esset, dixerit, omnem illius spem atque fiduciam in uno Iesu Christo, promisso illo mulieris semine, collocatam fuisse constat. Christianus ergo fuit Adam, et se solius Christi merito e diaboli tyrannide cum posteris suis liberari et saluari credidit. Eandem Abelis quoq;, Henochi, Noe et aliorum patrum, quotquot ante diluvium Deo placuerunt, fidem fuisse, Paulus ad Hebraeos undecimo capite luculentissime probat. Post diluvium vero Abraham praecipue inspiciendus erit, cum quo foedus suum Deus in staurare dignatus est, et quem omnium credentium patrem scriptura vocat. Illum Deo credidisse, eamq; fidem illi ad iustitiam imputatam fuisse, Moses et Paulus testantur. Gen. 12. Rom. 4. Quid vero crediderit, omnibus notum est, Dei nimirum promissionem ratam fore, quae in ipsius semine omnes gentes benedictionem et salutem consecuturas esse, aiebat. Atqui semen illum Christum fuisse tum Paulus ad Galat. 3. tum Christus ipse testatur. Hic enim inquit: Abraham exultavit ut videret diem meum, et vidit, atq; gaudisse est. Ioannis octavo. Id vero de sola fidei contemplatione intelligi potest. Unde colligimus, Abrahamum quoq; sola fide in Christum sustentatum et tandem salvatum fuisse. De huius posteris, Isaaco et Iacobo, quid dicere attinet, quando promissiones patri factae multoties apud illos repetitae fuisse constat? Quid, quod moriturus Iacob filiis suis de promisso salvatore concionatur, et illius aduentum haud obscure designat? Quodsi Moysen videamus, hunc quoq; in Christum unum respicere patebit. Ad hunc Israelis populum relegat, quando magnum illum propheta promittit, quem omnes audire debeant, ut supra ex Stephani et Petri verbis intelleximus. Deinde legis ceremonias omnes, totumq; cultum illum Leviticum ipsius Christi et rerum illius umbras fuisse, vel unica ad Hebraeos epistola docere potest. Prophetarum testimonia breuitatis causa omittimus. Sufficiat pro omnibus istis, quod Christus suae cum mortis tum resurrectionis mysteria iam ante per Moysen, prophetas et Psalmorum authores praedicta fuisse docet. Luc. 24. Rectissime ergo Paulus se non aliam fidem aut spem salutis docere profitetur, quam quae patrum olim fuerit, qui promissionibus a Deo factis crediderunt.
units.tr: And first, we are reminded of the faith and hope that all the saints, and indeed the whole Church of God, have had in all ages. This faith rests on Christ the Son of God, incarnate for us, and believes that life and salvation are placed in him alone. For Paul calls this hope "the hope of the promise made to the fathers" in the present passage. Now the Catholic faith says that all the promises are confirmed in Christ, and Paul himself affirms this everywhere, especially in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 1, and in his earlier letter to the same Corinthians, chapter 10, where he writes that the fathers under the Old Testament were in the same condition as we are, so that he applies to them our sacraments, Baptism and the Supper, just as elsewhere he attributes to us the Passover and spiritual circumcision. 1 Cor. 5. Col. 2. But this will be clearer if we consider the promises of God that he made to the fathers long ago. Among these, Adam is rightly counted first. When he was thrust out of Paradise into this vale of tears, no other hope of salvation was given him by God than that which is found in Christ alone. For the promise made to him was of the seed of the woman, whose heel the serpent would indeed lie in wait for, but in vain, since this seed would crush his head. Now only Christ can be called the seed of the woman, who took on flesh from the virgin Mary without any intervening union of male seed. The old serpent, the devil, wickedly lay in wait for his heel, that is, human nature, and brought it about that he should be killed on the cross; but this was to his own great harm. For it came about that Christ, dying, by the merit of his death trampled on the devil's head, that is, his rule and tyranny, and utterly cast him, now disarmed, out of his kingdom. And since it is beyond doubt that Adam believed this promise, (for he changed his wife's name and called her Eve, as she was to be the mother of the living), it is plain that all his hope and trust was placed in the one Jesus Christ, the promised seed of the woman. Adam therefore was a Christian, and he believed that he and his posterity would be freed and saved from the devil's tyranny by the merit of Christ alone. Paul, in Hebrews chapter 11, most clearly proves that the same faith belonged to Abel, Enoch, Noah and the other fathers who pleased God before the flood. After the flood, Abraham must be especially looked at, with whom God condescended to renew his covenant, and whom Scripture calls the father of all believers. Moses and Paul testify that he believed God, and that this faith was imputed to him for righteousness. Gen. 12. Rom. 4. What he believed is known to all: namely, that God's promise would be fulfilled, which said that in his seed all nations would obtain blessing and salvation. Now that this seed was Christ, both Paul in Galatians 3 and Christ himself bear witness. For he says: "Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day, and he saw it, and was glad." John 8. This can be understood only of the contemplation of faith. From this we gather that Abraham too was sustained by faith alone in Christ and at last saved. What need is there to speak of his posterity, Isaac and Jacob, since it is plain that the promises made to their father were often repeated to them? And what of Jacob, who, about to die, preached to his sons of the promised Saviour and clearly pointed to his coming? If we look at Moses, it will be plain that he too looked to Christ alone. He refers the people of Israel to him when he promises that great prophet whom all must hear, as we understood above from the words of Stephen and Peter. Then the whole of the ceremonies of the law and all that Levitical worship were shadows of Christ himself and of his things, as the letter to the Hebrews alone can teach. We omit the testimonies of the prophets for the sake of brevity. It is enough for all these that Christ teaches that the mysteries both of his death and of his resurrection were foretold beforehand through Moses, the prophets and the authors of the Psalms. Luke 24. Rightly, then, Paul professes that he teaches no other faith or hope of salvation than that which the fathers of old had, who believed the promises made by God.

units.la: Simul vero observemus, quod de hac ipsa fide se accusari queritur, et quidem apud Iudaeos, qui et patribus et promissionibus maxime gloriabantur. Docet hoc, quae veritatis in hoc mundo fors fit: eanimirum, ut non modo ab apertis hostibus petatur, sed verumetiam ijs, qui huius sectatores strenuissimi videri volunt. Hoc quidem olim prophetarum tempore factum fuisse legimus. Et Christo docente prophetarum sepulchra ab illis colebantur, qui eorundem doctrinam cane & angue peius oderant. Ita cum ad eos veniret Christus, qui oraculis freti ipsum indies expectabant, ab ijsdem tamen nec agnitus nec receptus fuit. Hoc ipsum nostro etiam seculo fieri videmus. Qui enim Christi nomine gloriantur, qui Christi matrem Virginem & Diuos vna cum illorum reliquijs propter Christi nomen super stitiosius colunt, hi ipsi veram Christi fidem & apostolorum doctrinam hoc ipso nomine persequuntur, quod vni Christo omnem nostrae redemptionis & salutis gloriam vendicat. Et passim hodie inter Christianos impietatis & haereseos accusantur, qui vni Christo fidendum, & penes hunc vnum salutem omnem quaerendam esse docent. Non minor ergo nobis etiam hodie quiritandi occasio datur, quam Paulo, cui indignum visum fuit, se a Iudaeis propter spem promissionis patribus olim factae accusari. Sed haec est mundi huius peruersitas, qua nos minime offendi decet, cum & vetus sit, & omnium seculorum exempla doceant, perpetuam semper cum hac veris Dei cultoribus luctam fuisse.
units.tr: Let us note at the same time that Paul complains of being accused of this very faith, and indeed by the Jews, who prided themselves most of all on the fathers and the promises. This is what the way of the world is, that the truth is attacked not only by open enemies but also by those who want to appear the most zealous followers of it. We read that this happened in the time of the prophets of old. And when Christ was teaching, the tombs of the prophets were honoured by those who hated their teaching worse than dog or snake; so when Christ came to them, those who relied on the oracles and daily awaited him were yet neither recognised nor received by them. We see this same thing happening in our own age. For those who glory in the name of Christ, who worship with superstitious devotion the Virgin mother of Christ and the saints together with their relics for the sake of Christ's name, these very people persecute the true faith of Christ and the doctrine of the apostles under that same name, because it claims for Christ alone all the glory of our redemption and salvation. And everywhere today among Christians those are accused of impiety and heresy who teach that we must trust in Christ alone and seek all salvation in him alone. So we have no less occasion for complaint today than Paul had, who thought it unworthy that he should be accused by the Jews for the hope of the promise made long ago to the fathers. But this is the perversity of this world, and we ought in no way to be offended by it, since it is old, and the examples of all ages teach that there has always been a perpetual struggle between this and the true worshippers of God.

units.la: Obseruemus praeterea, quo ordine & qua ratione suam tum fidem tum doctrinam Paulus asse- rat. Primo Dei promissionem siue verbum allegat, & huic deinde totius ecclesiae consensum subijcit. Duodecim enim tribus simul nominat, ita ingenue declarans, se non quid pauci quidam Sacerdotes sentiant, sed quid omnibus seculis vniuersus cultorum Dei coetus iuxta Dei verbum crediderit, respicere. EST haec optima fidei afferendae & defendendae ratio. Quia enim nulla est apud Deum humanarum traditionum authoritas, Dei verbum ante omnia produci, & ex hoc dogmatum omnium ratio reddi debet. Quo fundamento iacto, ecclesiam quoq; obseruare licet, non quidem paucorum quorundam chorum, qui hunc sibi titulum vendicant, sed vniuersalem illum cultorum Dei coetum, quem continuo ordine ab ipso mundi exordio fuisse scimus: licet interdum rarior & obscurior, interdum frequentior & illustrior fuerit, prout illi visum fuit, qui nos in filio suo priusquam mundi fundamenta iacerent, elegit. EST ergo enormis & absurdus plane nostri seculi error: quo nonnulli primo statim loco ecclesiae consensum allegant, hanc vero ex coniuratis quibusdam laruis, vnctis nimirum & rasis Antichristi creaturis constituunt, quibus & Dei verbum eius q; interpretationem subijciunt, & quidus in fide decernendi potestatem faciunt. Quos si ad veteris ecclesiae notas examines, ne pro membris quidem ecclesiae, vedum eius proceribus haberi merebuntur.
units.tr: Let us observe further the order and the reason by which Paul asserts both his faith and his doctrine. First he cites the promise or word of God, and then he adds the agreement of the whole Church. For he names the twelve tribes together, thus openly declaring that he looks not to what a few priests think, but to what the whole assembly of God's worshippers has believed in all ages according to the word of God. This is the best way of setting forth and defending the faith. For since no human tradition has any authority before God, the word of God must be brought forward before all else, and the reason for all doctrines must be given from it. With this foundation laid, we may also observe the Church: not the church of some small band who claim this title for themselves, but that universal assembly of God's worshippers which we know has existed in continuous succession from the very beginning of the world, sometimes rarer and more obscure, sometimes more numerous and more illustrious, as it pleased him who chose us in his Son before the foundations of the world were laid. Therefore the error of our own age is enormous and plainly absurd: some men at the very first point allege the consent of the Church, yet they constitute this Church out of certain conspiring phantoms, anointed and shaven creatures of Antichrist, to whom they subject both the word of God and its interpretation, and to whom they grant the power of deciding in matters of faith. If you examine them by the marks of the ancient Church, they will not deserve to be regarded even as members of the Church, much less as its leaders.

units.la: Postremo certum & indubitatum esse debere videmus inter Christianos resurrectionis articulum, quando illum Paulus, non sine indignationis specie, contra eos, qui de hoc dubitabant, allegat, cum inquit: Cur vobis incredibile videtur, si Deus mortuos suscitat? Ac si diceret: Mirum est de hoc aliquem dubitare, cuius tot passim argumenta extant? Nam vt scripturas omittamus, diuinae iustitia ratio exigit, vt mortui resurgant, eorumq; quae hic fecere retributionem accipiant, quando in hoc seculo plerunq; impios feliciter, pios autem infeliciter agere videmus. Extant praeterea exempla, quae quotannis in plantis, arboribus adeoq; tota rerum natura apparent. Quid quod primum hominem ex terra creatum, & nonnullos per prophetas, & tandem per ipsum Christum, miraculose resuscitatos fuisse legimus? Sed omissis argumentis hisce Paulus ad solius potentiae Dei consyderationem auditores relegat: nimirum vt huic morbo occurreret, quo fidei mysteria iuxta nostrae rationis captum metimur. Est vero ridiculus error, Deo quoq; impossibile putare, cuius rationem nos non statim videre possumus. Nec in solo resurrectionis articulo id obseruandum erit, verum etiam omnibus alijs, vt nimirum nostrae rationis captum sub fidei obedientiam cogamus. Minime tamen (vt quidam solent) sub omnipotentiae Dei praetextu dogmata noua & absurda inuehere debemus. Vbi enim de Dei voluntate ex ipsius verbo constat, ibi demum ab omnipotentia eiusdem argumentari licebit: quod frustra facies, nisi prius Deum hoc, quod intendis, velle probaueris. Porro quod praecipuum huius loci caput est teneamus, vt ipsi veterum promissionum freti, dies & noctes Deum colamus, qui vitam & salutem aeternam nobis aperuit in promisso semine, Iesu Christo, domino nostro: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, we ought to see that the article of the resurrection must be certain and beyond doubt among Christians, since Paul, not without a show of indignation, appeals to it against those who doubted it, when he says: Why does it seem incredible to you, if God raises the dead? As if he said: is it a wonder that anyone doubts this, for which so many proofs exist everywhere? For, to leave the Scriptures aside, the reason of God's justice demands that the dead rise and receive recompense for what they have done here, since in this age we often see the wicked prosper and the godly suffer. There are besides examples which appear every year in plants, trees and indeed in the whole of nature. What of the fact that we read of the first man created from earth, and of some raised up miraculously by the prophets, and finally by Christ himself? But, setting these arguments aside, Paul refers his hearers to the consideration of God's power alone, namely to meet this disease by which we measure the mysteries of faith by the measure of our reason. Indeed it is a ridiculous error to think that anything is impossible for God, merely because we cannot at once see how it is done. Nor is this to be observed in the article of the resurrection alone, but in all the others also, so that we bring the measure of our reason under the obedience of faith. Yet we ought by no means (as some are wont to do) to introduce new and absurd doctrines under the pretext of God's omnipotence. For where the will of God is established from his own word, there at last it will be permitted to argue from his omnipotence; and this you will do in vain unless you first prove that God wills what you intend. Moreover, let us hold fast to what is the chief point of this passage: that, relying on the promises of old, we worship God day and night, who has opened to us life and eternal salvation in the promised seed, Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXII.
units.tr: HOMILY 162.

units.la: Et ego quidem existimabam me aduersus nomen Iesu Nazareni multa oportere repugnando facere. Quod & feci Hierosolymis, & multos tos sanctorum ego carceribus inclusi, à principibus Sacerdotum potestate accepta: & cum occiderentur, detuli sententiam. Et per omnes Synagogas frequenter puniens eos, compellebam blasphemare. Et amplius insaniens in eos, persequebar etiam in exteras vsq; ciuitates. Quarum rerum studio cum irem Damascum cum authoritate & permissu principum Sacerdotum, die medio, Rex, in via vidi e coelo supra splendorem Solis lumen me circumfulgens, & eos qui mecum faciebant iter. Cum autem omnes nos decidissemus in terram, audiui vocem loquentem ad me, & dicentem Hebraica lingua: Saul, Saul, quid me persequeris? Durum est tibi contra stimulos calcitrare. Ego autem dixi: Quis es domine? At ille dixit: Ego sum Iesus, quem tu persequeris.
units.tr: I myself thought that I ought to do many things in opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth. This I also did at Jerusalem: I shut up many of the saints in prison, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them. In all the synagogues I often punished them and forced them to blaspheme, and in my extreme fury against them I pursued them even to foreign cities. While I was on such a mission, going to Damascus with the authority and permission of the chief priests, at midday, O king, I saw on the road a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining round me and those who were travelling with me. When we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me and saying in the Hebrew language: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads." And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" He said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."

units.la: Dluus Paulus totius controuersiae, quae ipsi cum Iudaeis erat, statum in bellernis exposuit, docens, non de re leuicula, sed vniuersa salutis ratione contendi: vbi simul nihil aliud abs se tum credi, tum doceri probauit, quàm quod olim patribus Deus promiserit, & in quo omnibus seculis Israelitica ecclesiae spes vnica collocata fuerit. Quo loco didicimus, Christiana fidem & vetustissimam & vnicam esse, per quam patres olim omnes saluati sint. Porrò quia initio narrationis suae Paulus se Pharisaeum fuisse dixerat, commodè nunc ad intermissam narrationem reuersus, sua conuersionis historiam contexit: cuius hic vnicus finis & scopus est, vt leuitatis crimen excuseat, quando se à Deo vocatum, imò praeter animi sui voluntatem coactum fuisse docet.
units.tr: Saint Paul set out the state of the whole controversy he had with the Jews in a few words, showing that the dispute was not over some trivial matter but over the entire way of salvation. At the same time he proved that he was then believing and teaching nothing other than what God had long ago promised the fathers, and in which the one hope of the Israelite Church had been placed in every age. From this place we learn that the Christian faith is both the most ancient and the only faith through which all the fathers were saved. Moreover, since at the start of his narrative Paul had said that he was a Pharisee, he now conveniently returns to the interrupted story and weaves together the account of his conversion. Its one aim and purpose here is to excuse the charge of lightness, since he shows that he was called by God, and indeed was compelled against the will of his own mind.

units.la: Vt vero plus ponderis haberet narratio, ante omnia quali erga fidem Christianam animo fuerit, commemorat, & id quidem diligentissime, sic vt nihil eorum praetermittat, quae abs se contra Christum tentata fuerant. Primò enim omnium causam praemittit, dicens: Et mihi quidem olim idem animi fuit quod meus aduersarijs. Omnino enim mihi ipsi persuaseram, oportere me aduersus nomen Iesu Christi multa facere. Vnde vero ista persuasio exorta fuerat? Nimirum ex zelo carnis caeco & praecipiti, quem alibi Iudaeis omnibus tribuit. Nec tamen, vt peccatum suum vel excuseret vel extenuet, huius meminit: sed vt suo exemplo doceat, quousq; homines delabantur, nisi Dei verbo studia sua dirigant. Nam alibi se maximum peccatorem fuisse, nec apostoli nomine dignum fatetur. 1 Tim. 1. cap. & 1. Corinth. 15. Vnde liquet, quanto gravius ab illis peccetur, qui non zelo Dei, aut bona (vt dicunt) animi intentione, sed prauissimis affectibus abrepti, Christum & verbum eius persequuntur. Interim obseruabis, bellium ecclesiae conatus meram opinionem esse, & vanos caecae mentis conceptus, qui vtut initio procedere videantur, finem tamen suum nunquam attingunt. Nam vt Psaltes inquit, molestiam quidem & afflictionem bonorum concipiunt, parturiunt vero vanitatem, & mendacium pariunt. Psalm. 7. Id autem de se occultius fatetur Paulus, vt simul suo exemplo auditores admoneat, quid ipsis expectandum sit, si contra Christum grassari incipiant, aut etiam pergant. Quid enim proficiant, quorum consilia & conatus Deus e coelo ridet & dissipat? Vide Psalm. 2. & 33.
units.tr: In order to give the narrative more weight, he first recounts with great care what his attitude towards the Christian faith had been, and he leaves out nothing of what he had attempted against Christ. For first of all he states the cause, saying: "I too once had the same mind as my adversaries. For I had persuaded myself that I ought to do many things against the name of Jesus Christ." Where had this persuasion come from? Surely from a blind and headlong zeal of the flesh, which he elsewhere attributes to all Jews. Yet he does not mention this in order to excuse or minimise his sin, but to teach by his own example how far men fall unless they direct their zeal by the Word of God. For elsewhere he confesses that he was the greatest of sinners and not worthy of the name of apostle (1 Tim. 1; 1 Cor. 15). From this it is clear how much more gravely those sin who, carried away not by zeal for God or by a good intention (as they say), but by the most wicked passions, persecute Christ and his word. Meanwhile you will observe that the undertakings of the Church's enemies are mere opinion and the empty notions of a blinded mind, which, however well they seem to begin, never reach their goal. For, as the Psalmist says, they conceive trouble and affliction for the good, but they bring forth emptiness and bear lies (Ps. 7). Paul confesses this about himself somewhat more obscurely, so that by his own example he may warn his hearers what they should expect if they begin, or go on, to rage against Christ. For what will they achieve whose counsels and efforts God laughs at from heaven and scatters? See Ps. 2 and 33.

units.la: Caeterum ne quis Paulum Thrasonice potius quàm vere & serio loqui putaret, facta quoq; sua recenset, quibus ecclesiae Christi negotium fecerit. Multos sanctorum carceribus inclusi, inquit, potestate a Sacerdotibus accepta, quam illi nunquam mihi commisissent, nisi me serio vidissent ipsorum negotium agere. Sanctos autem vocat Christianos, eò quòd Christi sanguine & merito sanctificati sunt. 1. Cor. 5. Deinde cùm occiderentur, ipse quoq; in illos mortis sententiam tuli, & aliorum suffragia collegi. Adhaec, in Synagogis flagris & omni tormentorum genere excruciatos coegi blasphemare, Christum videlicet abnegando & recantando quae antea bene pieq; dixerant. Vnde colligitur, nunquam tam bene constitutam fuisse Christi ecclesiam, quin suas quoq; palmas habuerit, quae persecutionis ventilabro excussae defecerunt. Deniq;, ne quid insaniae omitterem, in exteras quoq; ciuitates excurrere coepi, ne quem Christianis locum tutum relinquerem. ET in his quidem tum persecutorum Christi imago euidens, tum piorum & fidelium fors siue conditio, quam in hoc mundo sustinent, proponitur. Hi enim potentissimis mundi fere inuisi & exosi sunt: maximè verò ijs, qui religio nis titulo & ecclesiae primatu celebres, to praetextu priuata tantummodo gloriae & quaestui studeant. Habent isti pofIea idoneos scelerum suorum ministros,qui vt dominis suis gratificentur,nullam oc-cafionem oppugnandæ ecclesiæ præterlabi sinunt,nec vllis parcunt laboribus. Hinc ergo enafci solent incarcerationes,condemnationes, tormenta omnis generis,exilia,cædes,blasphemia & infinita alia, quæ contra pios crudeles isti carnifices excogitare consueuerunt. Quos interim obseruare conuenie-bat,quid faciant quando ob Christi fidem pios persequuntur. Nimirum blasphemare cogunt infir-mos,dum reclamante conscientia fidem abnegant,seq; errauisse impio & infelici metu fatentur. Idenim Christus inter species peccati & blasphemiæ in spiritum sanctum connumerat.Luc.12. Et Paulus differte blasphemiam vocat fidei verae abnegationem,ad quam ipse credentes coegerat. Quid ergo persecutores illos aliud maneat,quàm horrendum illud Væ, quod scandalorum authoribus Christus minatur? Quod enim gravius & perniciosius scandalum poni potest,quàm illud,quo vt in spiritum sanctum peccent,homines adiguntur? Sentient itaq; grauem Domini manum,quibus hoc hodie leui-culum omnino esse videtur. Porrò vt in prislinis Pauli conatibus insani tyranni imago elucet:itain eorundem confessione pertus vere Christianum & totum gloriæ Dei studio flagrans cernitur. Quoe-nim alio consilio sua illa facinora commemorat, quàm quod illud ad Dei gloriam facere nouerat? Ita enim & ministerij sui authoritas afferebatur, & immensa commendabatur Dei bonitas, qua illein Christo Iesu peccatores maximos,imò hostes quoq;,complectitur. Vide 1. Timot.1. Atqui hæc præci-pua causa est, ob quam sanctii in peccatorum suorum confessione frequenter versari consueuerunt, quemadmodum in Dauide & multis aliis cernimus. Turpissima ergo est illorum ambitio,qui vt suæ gloriæ consulant, peccata sua & errores grauissimos vel nunquam confiteri volunt, vel saltem mirificè extenuant.
units.tr: But lest anyone think that Paul spoke in a boastful, Thrasonical manner rather than truly and seriously, he also recounts his own deeds by which he harassed the Church of Christ. "I shut up many of the saints in prison," he says, "with authority received from the priests, which they would never have committed to me unless they had seen me seriously doing their business." He calls the Christians "saints" because they have been sanctified by the blood and merit of Christ (1 Cor. 5). Then, when they were being put to death, I too pronounced the sentence of death against them and gathered the votes of others. Besides this, in the synagogues I forced those tortured with whips and every kind of torment to blaspheme, that is, to deny Christ and to retract what they had previously said well and piously. From this it is gathered that the Church of Christ was never so well established that it did not also have its chaff, which was driven off by the winnowing fan of persecution and fell away. Finally, so that I might leave no madness undone, I began to run out into foreign cities too, so that I might leave the Christians no safe place. In these things is set before us both the plain image of the persecutors of Christ and the lot or condition which the pious and faithful endure in this world. For they are almost always hated and detested by the most powerful of the world, and especially by those who are famous for the title of religion and the primacy of the Church, yet who under this pretext pursue only private glory and gain. Such men afterwards have suitable ministers of their crimes, who, to please their masters, let no opportunity of attacking the Church slip by and spare no labour. From this there usually arise imprisonments, condemnations, tortures of every kind, exiles, murders, blasphemies, and countless other things which these cruel executioners are accustomed to devise against the godly. Meanwhile we ought to observe what they do when they persecute the pious for the sake of Christ's faith. Clearly they force the weak to blaspheme: while their conscience protests, they deny the faith and confess with impious and wretched fear that they have been mistaken. For Christ counts this among the kinds of sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Luke 12). And Paul calls the compelled denial of the true faith blasphemy, to which he himself had forced believers. What, then, remains for those persecutors except that dreadful woe which Christ threatens against the authors of offences? For what more grievous and destructive offence can be imagined than that by which men are driven to sin against the Holy Spirit? They will therefore feel the heavy hand of the Lord, though to them this may seem to be a very trivial matter today. Moreover, just as the image of a mad tyrant shines through Paul's earlier efforts, so by his own confession he is seen to be a truly Christian man, burning with zeal for the glory of God. For why else does he recount those crimes except because he knew that he was doing them for God's glory? In this way the authority of his ministry was asserted, and the immense goodness of God was extolled, by which he embraced in Christ Jesus the greatest sinners, indeed even enemies (1 Tim. 1). Yet this is the chief reason why the saints have so often been accustomed to dwell on the confession of their sins, as we see in David and many others. Therefore the ambition of those is most shameful who, to look after their own glory, either never want to confess their sins and gravest errors, or at least greatly minimise them.

units.la: Porrò suis contra Christum conatibus conuersionis historiam opponit, vt ex ista collatione pa-teat, se non animi leuitate sed diuina virtute compulsum,ad Christi fidem transfuisse. Et huc cum-primis diligens omnium circunstantiarum expositio referri debet. Nam & loci,& tempus,& Chri-sti colloquium, & comites testes allegat, ne quis ipsum inani spectro aut mentis alienatione delusum putaret. At quia alibi de conuersione ad Deum & conuersorum officio diximus,eadem in præsentiri petere opus non est. Finem modò omnium horum obseruemus,qui est, vt suam vocationem afferat. Non temere tamen Christi verba, quibus ille ipsius temeritatem corripuit, tam diligenter commemorat.Illis enim docere vult audientes,ipsis quoq; non cum mortali homine rem fore,si euangelij doctrinam oppugnent,sed cum Dei filio,qui audaciam illam magno ipsorum malo puniturus sit.Debent autem hæc nostræ consolationi seruire, vt in vera fide constantes, inter omnes mundi conatus vni Deo firmiter hæreamus,qui omnibus cultoribus suis cœlestis regni hæreditatem pollicitus est in fi-lio suo Iesu Christo:cui debetur benedictio,honor,gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, he sets the history of his conversion against his efforts against Christ, so that from this comparison it may be clear that he was driven over to the faith of Christ not by lightness of mind but by divine power. Here especially a careful account of all the circumstances ought to be referred to: for he names the place, the time, the conversation with Christ, and his companions as witnesses, so that no one might think he had been deceived by an empty apparition or a derangement of his mind. But since we have spoken elsewhere about conversion to God and the duty of the converted, there is no need to seek those things again here. Let us only observe the purpose of all these details, which is to set forth his calling. Nor does he rashly recall so carefully the words of Christ by which Christ rebuked his recklessness. For by these words he wants his hearers to learn that they too will not be dealing with a mere mortal if they attack the doctrine of the gospel, but with the Son of God, who will punish that audacity to their great harm. These things ought to serve our consolation, so that, constant in true faith, we may cling firmly to the one God amid all the efforts of the world, who has promised to all his worshippers the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom in his Son Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXIII.

units.la: Sed exurge & sta super pedes tuos. Ad hoc enim apparui tibi, vt constituam te ministrum ac testem & eorum quæ vidisti, & eorum in quibus apparebo tibi:eripiens te à populo & gentibus,in quas nunc te mitto,vt aperias oculos earum,vt conuertantur à tenebris ad lucem,& à potestate satanæ ad Deum,vt accipiant remissionem peccatorum & sortem inter sanctificatos,per fidem,quæ est in me.
units.tr: "But rise and stand upon your feet. For I have appeared to you for this purpose: to make you a minister and a witness both of the things you have seen and of those things in which I will appear to you; delivering you from the people and the Gentiles, to whom I now send you, to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified, through faith that is in me."

units.la: QVoniam Paulus se à Iudæis de duobus potissimum accusari nouerat:quòd nimirum à Iudaismo ad Christi fidem transfuisset,& quòd euangelium inter gentes prædicando, has Iudæis a-quaret:non temere conuersionis suæ historiam diligentissimè narrat,quando sola hæc ad vtriusq; criminis dilutionem sufficiebat. Ad primum enim pertinent,quæ hucusq; dicta sunt,quibus,si non leui inconstantia religionem mutauisse,sed cum Christi hostis esset,diuinæ vocationi coactum cessisse proba-uit. Alterum præsenti hoc loco diluetur,quo ipsius Christi verbis totius ministerij sui ratione reddit, quod ea conditione sibi creditum fuisse docet,vt non Iudæis modò,verumetiam gentibus euangelium prædicaret. Quia verò hæc non tam ad Pauli defensionem,quàm ad nostram institutionem faciunt, qui inde cùm ministerij ecclesiastici,tum omnem salutis nostræ rationem discere possumus, singula ordine consyderanda erunt.
units.tr: Since Paul knew that he was chiefly accused by the Jews on two counts, namely that he had passed over from Judaism to the faith of Christ, and that by preaching the gospel among the Gentiles he was winning them away from the Jews, he narrates the history of his conversion with great care, and not without reason, since these things alone sufficed to clear him of both charges. To the first charge belongs what has been said so far, which shows that he did not change his religion through light inconstancy, but, though he had been an enemy of Christ, yielded under compulsion to the divine calling. The second charge will be cleared up in the present passage, where, in Christ's own words, he gives an account of his whole ministry and teaches that it was entrusted to him on the condition that he should preach the gospel not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles. Since these things serve not so much to defend Paul as to instruct us, from whom we can learn both the nature of the ecclesiastical ministry and the whole basis of our salvation, they must be considered one by one in order.

units.la: Primo autem loco occurrit, quòd Christus Paulum, quem modò vt hostem & persecutorem suum horribiliter prostrauerat, nunc amicè surgere & pedibus insistere iubet. Id verò non antea fa-ctum fuisse, alibi audiuimus, quam cum animo deiectus de voluntate Christi humiliter interroga-uit, & hunc suum agnouit dominum. Quod ipsum tamen nunquam fecisset, nisi efficacem sensisset in animo suo spiritus Christi operationem. EST verò hoc insigne diuinæ bonitatis exemplum, quæ tunc quoq; sese haud obscurè profert, quando irasci videtur Deus. Nec enim in perpetuum nobiscum altercatur, sed quia saluos vult fieri homines, hunc quoq; in iudiciis suis finem & scopū obseruat, vt illis ad salutem erudiantur potius homines, quàm perdantur. Nec prius flagella exerit, quàm vbi se verbo suo minus proficere videt. Nec tamen aliter flagellat, quàm vt ad se conuersis certam semper relinquat salutis spem: cuius rei cum testimonia tum exempla passim in scripturis extant: quibus nos in omnibus aduersis contra fidei nutantis lapsum confirmari oportet.
units.tr: In the first place, we meet with the fact that Christ bids Paul, whom he had just struck down terribly as his enemy and persecutor, now rise up kindly and stand upon his feet. We have heard elsewhere that this had not been done before, namely until Paul, cast down in spirit, humbly asked about the will of Christ and acknowledged him as his Lord. Yet he would never have done even this unless he had felt the effective working of Christ's Spirit in his mind. This is a notable example of divine goodness, which shows itself plainly even when God seems to be angry. For he does not contend with us forever, but since he wishes men to be saved, he keeps this end and aim in his judgments, that men may be instructed to salvation rather than destroyed. Nor does he stretch out the scourges before he sees that he is accomplishing less by his word. Nor does he scourge otherwise than so that for those who turn to him a sure hope of salvation always remains. Testimonies and examples of this are found everywhere in the Scriptures, and by them we ought to be confirmed in every adversity against the fall of a wavering faith.

units.la: Caterum quàmuis magnum sit, quòd acerrimo hosti surgendi copiam Christus facit, maius ta-men est, & stupendum plane, quòd eundem apostolatus muneri destinat, quo nullum in orbe est tum honorificentius tum salutarius. Imò in hunc finem se ipsi apparuisse testatur, vt illum minis-trum & testem constitueret omnium quæ iam viderat & posteà visurus erat. Hic verò duplex vo-cabulus vniuersum antistitum ecclesiæ munus siue officium comprehendit. Primò ministrum fore dicit Paulum, non dominum & principem. Itaverò passim nominantur apostoli, & tales quidem, qui in animarum cibo apponendo & curandis salutis humanæ negotiis toti ecclesiæ publicè seruire debeant. Vide Matth.20. & 24. Luc.12. Quò Paulus respexisse videtur, quando se omnibus hominibus, Iudæis & Græcis, doctis & indoctis, debitorem esse fatetur. Rom.1. Excluditur hic dominandi libido, contra quam multa sape coram apostolis Christus disseruit, cùm non ignoraret ventu-ros olim, qui sub ministerij huius prætextu in ecclesia tyrannidem affectarent. Deinde testem fore dicit, quo nomine apostolos quoque appellatos fuisse Capite primo vidimus. Ita verò ministerij rationem apertius definire voluit, cum simul exponat, de quibus ipsum testificari oporteat: ijs ni-mirum quæ viderat, & quæ posteà ipsi reuelaturus erat. Viderat autem Paulus, nec viderat modò, sed vere expertus erat, Christum viuere & regnare, suiq; populi vindicem esse acerrimum. Ex qui-bus facilè colligere poterat, eundem humani generis redemptorem, nec nudum hominem modò, sed Deum quoque esse, qualem ab apostolis prædicari cognouerat. Debis ergo illum testificari oporte-bat. Patet autem ex hoc loco (quod etiam alibi monuimus) quàm certa & infallibilis haberi debeat apostolicæ doctrinæ authoritas, quando qui hanc vulgauerunt, non circumforanei quidam præ-cones, sed Iesu Christi iurati testes fuerunt, quorum vocatio infinitis quoque miraculis confirmata fuit. Simul verò omnes ministri se testes esse meminerint, & proinde nequaquam pro suo arbitrio noua dogmata prædicent, sed quæ ex sacris literis certò comperta habent, liberè proferant, ne quis illos falsi accusare possit.
units.tr: However, although it is a great thing that Christ gives the most bitter enemy the opportunity to rise, it is greater, and plainly amazing, that he appoints the same man to the office of the apostleship, than which there is none in the world more honourable or more beneficial. Indeed, he testifies that he appeared to him for this very end, namely to make him a minister and a witness of all the things he had already seen and would afterwards see. Here the twofold word comprehends the whole office or function of the leaders of the Church. First, he says that Paul will be a minister, not a lord and ruler. The apostles are everywhere named thus, and indeed as those who ought to serve the whole Church publicly in setting out the food of souls and in attending to the affairs of human salvation. See Matt. 20 and 24; Luke 12. To these passages Paul seems to have looked when he confesses that he is a debtor to all men, both Jews and Greeks, both wise and unwise (Rom. 1). The lust for domination is excluded here, against which Christ often argued in the presence of the apostles, since he was not ignorant that there would one day come those who, under the pretext of this ministry, would aim at tyranny in the Church. Next, he says that Paul will be a witness, a name by which we saw in the first chapter that the apostles too were called. Thus he wished to define more plainly the nature of the ministry, while at the same time setting out about what things he ought to bear witness: namely those things which he had seen and which Christ would afterwards reveal to him. Paul had seen, and not only seen but had truly experienced, that Christ lives and reigns and is a fierce avenger of his people. From these things he could easily gather that the same one is the Redeemer of the human race, and not merely a bare man but also God, as he had learned that the apostles preached him to be. Therefore he had to bear witness to him. It is clear from this passage (as we have also noted elsewhere) how certain and infallible the authority of apostolic doctrine ought to be held, since those who spread it were not wandering heralds but sworn witnesses of Jesus Christ, whose calling was also confirmed by countless miracles. At the same time, let all ministers remember that they are witnesses, and therefore by no means should they preach new doctrines at their own pleasure, but freely set forth those things which they hold as certainly learned from the sacred letters, so that no one can accuse them falsely.
