units.la: At graue videri poterat Paulo, ad illud munus se destinari, quod periculis infinitis obnoxium esse, vel ex ijs solis nouisse poterat, quæ ipse paulo ante fuerat conatus. Commodè ergo consolatio-nem intermisceet Dominus, qua se illum ex populi Iudaici simul & gentium manibus ereptum esse pollicetur. Ita verò quasi aliud agens ostendit, se ad gentes quoq; missum fuisse, vt etiam illas ad ec-clesiæ communionem adduceret. Interim docet locus iste, ministros in hoc mundo odia, persecutiones & omnis generis aduersa manere. Nisi enim hæc illorum fors esset, nec consolationibus nec promissio-nibus Christi toties repetitis illos confirmari oporteret. Sunt autem diligenter obseruandæ promis-siones hæ, quibus docemur, Christum suos in tribulationibus nunquam deserere. Nec tamen ita illæ intelligi debent, quasi ex omnibus aduersis liberatos in otium tutum collocet, aut eosdem, quoad cor-pus, nunquam interire patiatur. Nam & Paulum postremò à Nerone obtruncatum, & apostolos crudeliter occisos fuisse legimus. Sed liberare dicitur Dominus, quando in præsenti seculo spiritu suo nobis adest, animi constantiam, dexteritatem agendi, os deniq; & sapientiam largitur, cui hostes nul-lis idoneis rationibus possunt resistere. Quando item inter supplicia consolationibus erigit, & corpo-ris ergastulo liberatos in regni sui possessionem transfert, deniq; apud posteros quoq; nostram famam & memoriam tuetur. Ita illum sanctos martyres liberauisse scimus, quorum hodie etiam inter fidei hostes sacrosancta memoria floret. Quæ promissiones cum & generales & semper verè sint, non es[?] quòd vllis huius mundi conatibus nos terreri aut superari patiamur. Quis enim nos separabit à dilectione Dei? &c. Vide locum Rom.8.cap.
units.tr: Yet the charge laid upon Paul might have seemed heavy, since it was subject to countless dangers, as he could know from those things alone which he had himself attempted a little before. So the Lord fittingly mingles in consolation, promising that he will be rescued from the hands both of the Jewish people and of the Gentiles. In this way, as if doing something else, he shows that he was also sent to the Gentiles, so that he might bring them too into fellowship with the Church. Meanwhile this passage teaches that ministers in this world remain subject to hatred, persecutions and adversities of every kind. For if this were not their lot, there would be no need for them to be strengthened by the consolations and promises of Christ so often repeated. These promises, by which we are taught that Christ never forsakes his people in tribulations, must be carefully observed. Yet they ought not to be understood as if he placed them, freed from all adversities, in a safe leisure, or as if he never allowed them to perish in body. For we read that Paul was finally beheaded by Nero, and that the apostles were cruelly put to death. But the Lord is said to deliver when, in the present age, he is with us by his Spirit, bestows constancy of mind, skill in acting, and finally speech and wisdom, against which enemies cannot resist with any suitable arguments. Likewise, when among tortures he raises us up with consolations, and, once delivered from the prison of the body, carries us into possession of his kingdom, and finally guards our name and memory among posterity as well. Thus we know that he delivered the holy martyrs, whose most sacred memory even today flourishes among the enemies of the faith. Since these promises are both general and always true, there is no reason why we should allow ourselves to be terrified or overcome by any efforts of this world. "For who will separate us from the love of God?" etc. See Rom. 8.

units.la: Postremo omnium finem subijcit, qui est, vt Pauli ministerio oculi caecorum aperiantur, vt illuminati convertantur à tenebris ad lucem, & ex satanae potestate asserti Deo reconcilientur, in quo peccatorum remissionem & haereditatem regni coelestis per fidem percipiant cum omnibus ijs, quos sibijpsi Deus elegerit. Continent haec ministrorum verbi officium & verum euangelij vsum. Propter hoc enim ministris tribuitur, quod proprie solius Dei opus est, vt 1.Cor.3. multis docetur. Per euangelium ergo aperiuntur hominum oculi, vt Deum & salutis viam videant. Per euangelium à tenebris ad lucem convertuntur homines, vt iam lucis opera faciant, qui tenebrarum operibus antea assueuerunt. Nec enim in inani speculatione Christiana philosophia consistit, sed praxin habet per omnes vitae partes sese extendentem. Euangelio item ex Satanae potestate ad Deum homines transferuntur, vt illi obtemperent & seruiant. Euangelium deniq; peccatorum remissionem & regni coelorum haereditatem nobis offert. Nec vero ista per inanem vocis sonum nobis obtingere putabimus, sed quia Christus per euangelium praedicatur, qui horum vnicus author est, euangelij praedicationi haec vere tribuuntur, quando ipsa non inanis, sed vera est. Summum ergo adeo, vnicum salutis thesaurum illa continet. Et hunc sibi scopum huius ministri praefixum habere debent, vt in horum communionem adducantur homines, nec illos inani dumtaxat & theatrico concionandi apparatu ludificatos circunducant. Habemus praeterea hic omnem nostrae salutis rationem comprehensam. Quia enim haec nobis diuinitus offeruntur, nos bonis istis naturaliter carere constat. Natura igitur in diuinis percipiendis caeci sumus, & ex ingenita corruptione sub Satanae tyrannide gemere meremur. Dei vero bonitate factum est, quod per Christum illuminati, & ex mortis ac tenebrarum potestate in regnum ipsius translati sumus. Huius enim merito sanctificati & iustificati, aeternae vitae regnum adimus. At omnia ista (vt modo diximus) per euangelium nobis fide percipienda Deus offert: quasi de nos & purificari & iustificari scriptura docet, quod sola hac Christum & bona ipsius nobis amplexi & percipere datur. Poterant haec fusissime diduci, & simul eorum exponi officia, quos Christus in patris sui regnum translulit. Sed quia de ijsdem saepe iam dictum est, summa rerum capita tantum demonstrauisse sufficiat. Interim deploranda hoc loco venit ingrata & infelix mundi caecitas, qui contempta hac tam simplici salutis ratione, ad labyrinthos inextricabiles & aeternae damnationis praecipitia conuerticur. Nostrum est Deo nos gratos praebere, & constanti fide retinere bonorum istorum vnicum authorem, qui est Dominus & saluator noster, Iesus Christus: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, he adds the end of all, which is that through Paul's ministry the eyes of the blind may be opened, so that, enlightened, they may turn from darkness to light, and, rescued from the power of Satan, be reconciled to God, in whom they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance of the heavenly kingdom through faith, together with all those whom God has chosen for himself. These words contain the office of the ministers of the Word and the true use of the gospel. For it is for this reason that the work is attributed to the ministers which is properly the work of God alone, as is taught in many places in 1 Cor. 3. Through the gospel, therefore, the eyes of men are opened, so that they may see God and the way of salvation. Through the gospel men are turned from darkness to light, so that they now do the works of light, who were formerly accustomed to the works of darkness. For Christian philosophy does not consist in empty speculation, but has a practice extending through all parts of life. Likewise, through the gospel men are transferred from the power of Satan to God, so that they may obey and serve him. Finally, the gospel offers us forgiveness of sins and the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. Nor should we think that these things come to us by the empty sound of a voice, but because Christ, the sole author of these things, is preached through the gospel, these things are truly attributed to the preaching of the gospel, when that preaching is not empty but true. Therefore it contains the supreme and only treasure of salvation. And ministers ought to set before themselves this aim, that men may be brought into fellowship with these things, and not that they should mock them with an empty and theatrical display of preaching. Moreover, we have here the whole basis of our salvation comprehended. For since these things are offered to us from God, it is plain that by nature we lack these goods. By nature, therefore, we are blind in receiving divine things, and by our inborn corruption we deserve to groan under the tyranny of Satan. But by the goodness of God it has come about that through Christ we have been enlightened and transferred from the power of death and darkness into his kingdom. For by his merit we are sanctified and justified, and we attain the kingdom of eternal life. Yet all these things (as we have just said) God offers to be received by us through faith in the gospel; just as Scripture teaches that we are both cleansed and justified, in that by faith alone we are given to embrace and receive Christ and his goods. These things could have been unfolded at great length, and the offices of those whom Christ has transferred into his Father's kingdom could have been set out at the same time. But since these matters have often been spoken of already, it is enough to have shown the chief heads of the matter. Meanwhile, here we must lament the ungrateful and unhappy blindness of the world, which, despising this so simple way of salvation, turns aside to inextricable labyrinths and the precipices of eternal damnation. It is our task to show ourselves grateful to God, and to hold fast by constant faith to the sole author of these goods, who is our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXIIII.

units.la: Vnde, Rex Agrippa, non fui inobediens coelesti visioni: sed his qui sunt Damasci primum & Hierosolymis, & per omnem regionem Iudaeae, deinde & gentibus annunciaui vt resipiscerent & conuerterentur ad Deum, opera facientes digna poenitentiae. Horum causa Iudaei me in templo comprehensum tentarunt interficere. Auxilium igitur nactus à Deo, vsque in praesentem diem sto, testificans tum paruo, tum magno, nihil aliud dicens, quàm ea quae Prophetae praedixerant futura esse, & Moses: an passurus fuerit Christus, an primus ex resurrectione mortuorum lumen annunciaturus sit populo & gentibus.
units.tr: Wherefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those at Damascus and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the region of Judaea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance. For these reasons the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. Therefore, having obtained help from God, I stand to this day, testifying both to small and to great, saying nothing other than what the prophets and Moses foretold would come: whether Christ would suffer, and whether, being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles.

units.la: Conuersionis suae historiam diligenter admodum Paulus coram Agrippa narrat, eò quòd per illam luculenter probare poterat, se nec leui animo ad Christi fidem transiisse, nec temerario ausu euangelium praedicauisse gentibus, sed omnium, quae hucusque fecerit, authorem habere Deum, qui & longè aliud animo versantem converterit, & gentibus quoque euangelium praedicare iusserit. ISTIS vero praemissis, in praesenti quid porrò fecerit ipse, quidq; sibi euenerit, narrat, & inde ijs qui tum aderant praedicandi occasionem arripit. Primò obedientiam, quam cœlesti visioni præstiterit, ingenuè fatetur. Id quod probè observandum est. Nam si Dei præceptum cum Sacerdotum mandato, quod ab illis Paulus acceperat, conferas, illa inter se plurimum dissidere videbis. Hi enim cum publicis literis Damascum miserunt, ut Christi fideles, qui illic erant, captos vinctosq; adducerent, Deus verò illum non modò à cœptis desistere, verumetiam euangelium prædicare iussit. Hic ergo se Dei vocationi obediuisse dicit, absque omni mora & tergiversatione: nec hoc ipsum fateri pudet coram iis, apud quos maiorem multò Sacerdotum, quàm suam, authoritatem esse noverat. Suo igitur exemplo docet, Deo potius quàm hominibus obediendum esse, nec vllam admitti debere tergiversandi causam, ut primum de huius voluntate nobis constat. Quam regulam qui sequuntur, maxima seipsos molestia & anxietate liberant, & minimum peccare possunt. Simul verò modus obedientiæ huius consyderandus erit, quem exijs, quæ se fecisse dicit Paulus, deprehendere licebit. Fecit enim quæ illum facere Deus iusserat, & sicut iusserat, tum gentibus tum Iudæis euangelium prædicans. Ea itaque demum vera obedientia est, quando absque omni exceptione Dei mandata exequimur. Sunt enim qui etiam ipsi Deo obediunt, sed ex parte duntaxat, & quatenus ipsis commodum esse videtur: cuius rei exempla in Saule sacra scriptura proponit. 1. Sam. 13. & 15. cap. At longè alia Dei mens est, qui nos nec ad dextram nec ad sinistram à verbo suo deflectere, nec illi quicquam nos adimere vel addere iubet. Rectè ergo Paulus absque vlla ampliori deliberatione à Deo sibi iniunctum negotium capessit, & quod iussus erat ad diuini præcepti normam exequitur. Porrò dum quid ipse fecerit narrat, docet simul quid per euangelium prædicari, & quo ordine illud proponi debeat. Primò in hoc incumbendum est, ut homines resipiscant, quando omnes nos peccatores & ira Dei obnoxios esse constat. Hinc Baptistam cœpisse legimus, & Christum deinceps, qui inde apostolos quoque exordiri docuit. Matth. 10. Luc. 24. cap. Unde constat parum euangelicos hodie esse, qui istud principium omittere vellent. Deinde resipiscentiæ veræ modus exprimitur, qui est ut ad Deum convertamur. Ut enim à Deo auersi peccamus & perimus: ita in hoc ferè tum pœnitentia tum salus nostra consistit, ut ad Deum reuersi, eidem reconciliemur. Id verò per solum Christum fit, qui & pœnitentiam veram suo spiritu in nobis operatur, & deleto peccati ac legis chirographo nos patri reconciliat. Quare Petrus alibi illum à Deo missum esse dicit, ut Israeli pœnitentiam simul & peccatorum remissionem confer at. Act. 5. cap. Vbi illorum error confutatur, qui pœnitentiam absque Christo prædicantes, hominem ad sua ipsius opera & merita ablegant. Tertium doctrinæ Pauli caput fuit, ut homines digna pœnitentia opera faciant. Quæ Iohannem quoque magna cum seueritate requisiuisse, & scripturas omnes passim exigere constat. Quia enim nos minimè hypocritas esse vult Deus, & totos nos sibi vendicat, necesse omnino fuerit, ut operibus & vitæ totius conuersatione nos ad Deum vere conuersos esse probemus. Id verò fiet, si depositis prioribus studijs, nouum vitæ genus, diuinis legibus conueniens instituamus, de qua re multa passim in Pauli epistolis leguntur. Ita verò docemur, bona opera non ut meriti loco sint, sed ut debita Deo officia, à nobis requiri: quando illa à nobis nunquam præstari poterunt, nisi Christi spiritu & merito regenerati ad Deum prius conuersi fuerimus. Et licet faciamus quæcunq; nos facere oportet, serui tamen sumus inutiles, quemadmodum Christus ipse admonet. Luc. 17. Ita verò tribus capitibus euangelium totum Paulus comprehendit, sicq; illud hoc ordine prædicare docet. His verò, quid sibi in isto munere versanti contigerit, narrat, ut inde cuius facile probet, quàm iniquè cum illo Iudæi egerint. Horum causa (inquit) quòd nimirum Deo obedire studui, Iudæi me in ipso templo captum occidere voluerunt, quod & fecissent, nisi repentino Dei auxilio fuissem liberatus. Templi verò & cædis iam imminentis meminit, ut illos cæco potius affectu abreptos, quàm iusta aliqua causa commotos fuisse probet: quando illos nec templi religio, nec publica iura & leges retinuerunt, ut modestius agerent. DOCET autem locus iste, obedientiam, quam Deo sancti præstare studeant, præcipuam persecutionum causam esse. Nec enim alias ob causas & prophetæ & apostoli mundo inuisi fuere, quàm quòd Dei verbum prædicando homines Deo adducere studuerunt. Et hodie Christi cultores hanc vnam ob causam persecutionibus subiacent, quòd vni Deo per Christum fidere, vnum illum colere, vnum illum timere, & illi vni seruire instituunt, quemadmodum ille iubet. Sed eò maior est huius rei indignitas, quòd tam malam gratiam reportant, qui omnium saluti publice & priuatim student. Interim soletur nos, quòd Paulum diuino auxilio subleuatum & latronum impijssimorum manibus ereptum fuisse audimus. Est enim hoc generale, & passim promissiones extant, quibus docemur, Deum suos ex tentationibus eripere, nec permittere vt vltra vires tententur. 2. Pet. 2. 1. Cor. 10. Psalm. 34. &c.
units.tr: Paul tells the story of his conversion in detail before Agrippa, because by it he could clearly show that he had not passed over to faith in Christ in a light-minded way, nor preached the gospel to the Gentiles out of rash daring, but that God was the author of all he had done so far, God who had converted him when his mind was set on something quite different and had also commanded him to preach the gospel to the Gentiles. Having said these things beforehand, he now tells what he himself did in the present matter and what happened to him, and from this he seizes the opportunity to preach to those who were present. First, he frankly confesses the obedience he rendered to the heavenly vision. This must be carefully noted. For if you compare God's command with the order of the priests, which Paul had received from them, you will see that the two differ greatly. For those men sent letters to Damascus that the faithful of Christ who were there should be seized, bound and brought back, whereas God ordered him not only to stop what he had begun but also to preach the gospel. Here, then, he says he obeyed God's calling without any delay or shifting, and he is not ashamed to admit this even before those whom he knew held far greater authority than himself. By his own example, therefore, he teaches that we must obey God rather than men, and that no excuse for delay should be admitted, as soon as we are clear about his will. Those who follow this rule free themselves from great trouble and anxiety, and are able to sin very little. At the same time, the manner of this obedience should be considered, which can be grasped from what Paul says he did. For he did what God had commanded him to do, and just as he had been commanded, preaching the gospel both to the Gentiles and to the Jews. True obedience is that which carries out God's commands without any exception. For there are those who do obey God, but only in part, and so far as it seems convenient to them; Scripture sets examples of this in Saul: 1 Sam. 13 and 15. But God's mind is quite different, for he bids us not to turn aside from his word either to the right or to the left, nor to take anything from it or add anything to it. Rightly, then, Paul took up the task laid on him by God without any further deliberation, and carried out what he had been commanded according to the rule of the divine precept. Moreover, while he tells what he himself did, he also teaches what should be preached in the gospel and in what order it ought to be set forth. First, one must press home that men repent, since it is certain that all of us are sinners and subject to the wrath of God. Hence we read that the Baptist began, and then Christ, who afterwards taught the apostles also to begin from this: Matt. 10; Luke 24. Hence it is clear that those today are little evangelical who would wish to leave out this beginning. Next, the manner of true repentance is expressed, which is that we be converted to God. For just as we sin and perish by turning away from God, so our repentance and our salvation consist chiefly in this: that, turning back to God, we are reconciled to him. This is accomplished through Christ alone, who both works true repentance in us by his Spirit and, having blotted out the handwriting of sin and of the law, reconciles us to the Father. Therefore Peter elsewhere says that he was sent by God to give Israel repentance and also the forgiveness of sins: Acts 5. Here the error of those is refuted who preach repentance without Christ and send a man away to his own works and merits. The third head of Paul's teaching was that men should do works worthy of repentance. It is clear that John too demanded this with great severity, and that all the Scriptures everywhere require it. For since God does not want us to be hypocrites, and claims us entirely for himself, it is absolutely necessary that we prove by our works and by the whole course of our life that we have truly been converted to God. This will happen if, having laid aside our former pursuits, we institute a new way of life agreeable to the divine laws, about which much is read everywhere in Paul's epistles. We are taught in this way that good works are not required of us as if they were a ground of merit, but as duties owed to God, since they could never be performed by us unless we had first been converted to God, regenerated by the Spirit and merit of Christ. And although we do all the things we ought to do, we are still unprofitable servants, as Christ himself warns: Luke 17. In this way Paul comprehends the whole gospel under three heads, and teaches that it is to be preached in this order. Then he tells what happened to him while he was engaged in this office, so that from this one may easily prove how unjustly the Jews dealt with him. "For these reasons," he says, namely because I sought to obey God, the Jews wanted to kill me when I had been seized in the very temple, and they would have done so had I not been freed by a sudden help of God. He mentions the temple and the slaughter now at hand, to show that they were carried away by a blind passion rather than moved by any just cause, since neither reverence for the temple nor public laws and rights restrained them from behaving more moderately. This passage also teaches that the obedience which the saints strive to render to God is the chief cause of persecutions. For the prophets and apostles were hated by the world for no other reason than that, by preaching God's word, they sought to bring men to God. And today the worshippers of Christ are subject to persecutions for this one cause: that they resolve to trust in the one God through Christ, to worship him alone, to fear him alone and to serve him alone, as he commands. But the indignity of this matter is all the greater, in that those who labour for the salvation of all, both publicly and privately, win such ill will in return. Meanwhile we may be comforted by hearing that Paul was lifted up by divine help and snatched from the hands of most wicked robbers. For this is a general truth, and everywhere there are promises by which we are taught that God rescues his people from temptations and does not allow them to be tempted beyond their strength: 2 Pet. 2; 1 Cor. 10; Ps. 34, etc.

units.la: Caterum postquam Paulus se innocentem & immerentem in vincula coniectum esse, abunde probauit, inde ad Agrippam regem & alios auditores conuersus, illis quoq; summa cum libertate dicendi concionari incipit. Et quia mirum alicui videri poterat, ipsum in eo munere obeundo tam constantem esse, in quo aduersam fortunam & hostium insidias toties expertus erat, eius rei rationem primo omnium reddit: quae est, se Dei auxilio liberatum esse, & proinde officio suo nequaquam defesse debere. Ita vero Deo tribuit liberationis beneficium, cuius author Tribunus fuisse videbatur: to quòd hunc illius manu & spiritu ductum fuisse sciret. Interim docet Pauli exemplum, eos qui Dei opem semel & iterum senserunt, ad maiorem industriam accendi debere, non (vt quidam solent) negligentiores fieri, quasi iam suo officio defuncti sint. Praeter id enim quòd omne officium Deo debemus, nouam fidem & industriam gratitudinis lex requirit, ne benefactori Deo parum grati esse videamur. Deinde ne parum opportunus videretur, qui ipsis iam concionari vellet, id quoq; se ex officio facere docet. Se enim omnibus hominibus, tum magnis tum paruis, debitorem esse. Ita vero illorum quoq; animos excitat, ne euangelium nihil ad se pertinere arbitrentur. Est autem diligenti obserua-tione dignum, quòd euangelium ex Dei mandato omnis loci & ordinis hominibus praedicari audimus. Ita enim discimus, personarum respectum apud Deum nullum esse, imò velle hunc, vt omnium conditionum homines saluentur. Ideo verbi ministros toti familiae suae Oeconomos & dispensatores constituit. Soletur hoc in tentationibus constitutos, simulq; officij tum ministros tum auditores admoneat, ne vel illi paucos modò aliquot discipulos pro suo arbitrio sibi deligant, aut bi se immunes esse, nec ad euangelij regulam astringi debere, existiment. Tandem quid doceat repetit: non aliud nisi mirum quàm quod Prophetae & Moses olim praedixerint. Totam vero doctrinam tribus Capitibus completitur, de quibus tunc maxime certatum fuisse constat. Primum est, Christum siue propofsum Saluatorem pati & mori debuisse. Id enim Iudaeis omnibus in primis absurdum visum fuisse, illorum verba, quae Iohan. 12. leguntur, abunde docent. Alterum est, eundem ex mortuis debuisse resurgere, & primum quidem, non ordine (nam plures alios ante Christū resuscitatos fuisse legimus) sed dignitate & potentia, vtpote resurrectionis & vitae omnium authorem. Tertium, quòd non Iudaeos modò, verumetiam gentes omnes verbo & spiritu suo illuminare debuerit. Haec vero Paulum plurimis scripturae locis demonstrauisse, vel sola Festi exclamatio postea docebit. Et sane passim extant tum Mosis tum prophetarum testimonia, quibus omnia haec probari possunt. Vnde rursum colligimus, euangelij doctrinam non nouam & paucorum hominum, sed vetustissimam esse, & omnium seculorum consensu approbatam. Adhaec scripturis contineri quaecunq; ad credendum necessaria sunt, quando ex his Paulus vniuersa fidei Christianae mysteria probare potuit. His ergo solis contenti, fidem quae istis traditur, constanter teneamus, vt iuxta has vitam asequamur sempiternam per Iesum Christum, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen. ses & Bernice, & qui assidebat eis. Et cùm secèssissent, loquebantur inter se, dicètes: Nihil morte aut vinculis dignū facit homo iste. Agrippa autem Festo dixit: Dimitti poterat homo hic, si non appellasset Cæsarē.
units.tr: Moreover, after Paul had amply shown that he had been thrown into chains innocent and undeserving, he turned to King Agrippa and the other hearers and began to preach to them also with great freedom of speech. And because it might seem strange to someone that he was so steadfast in discharging that office, in which he had so often experienced adverse fortune and the plots of enemies, he first of all gives the reason for this: that he had been freed by the help of God, and therefore ought by no means to grow weary of his duty. In this way he ascribes the benefit of his deliverance to God, although the tribune seemed to be its author, because he knew that he had been led by God's hand and Spirit. Meanwhile, Paul's example teaches that those who have felt God's help once or twice should be stirred up to greater diligence, and not (as some are wont to do) become more negligent, as if they had already done their duty. For besides the fact that we owe every duty to God, the law of gratitude requires a fresh zeal and diligence, lest we appear to be little grateful to a benefactor, God. Next, lest he should seem ill-timed in wanting to preach to them, he teaches that he is doing this too as a matter of duty. For he says he is a debtor to all men, both great and small. In this way he also stirs up their minds, so that they do not think the gospel has nothing to do with them. It is worthy of careful observation that we hear the gospel must, by God's command, be preached to people of every place and rank. For we learn from this that there is no respect of persons with God, but rather that he wills all people of every condition to be saved. Therefore he appoints ministers of the Word as stewards and dispensers to his whole household. This comforts those placed in temptations, and at the same time admonishes both ministers and hearers of their duties: that the former should not choose for themselves a few disciples at their own pleasure, nor should the latter think that they themselves are exempt and need not be bound by the rule of the gospel. Finally, he repeats what he teaches: nothing other than what the prophets and Moses long ago foretold. He completes the whole doctrine under three heads, on which it is clear that the greatest dispute then arose. The first is that Christ, as the promised Saviour, had to suffer and die. For this seemed absurd to all the Jews above all, as their words, which are read in John 12, abundantly show. The second is that he had to rise from the dead, and first indeed not in order (for we read that several others were raised before Christ) but in dignity and power, as the author of resurrection and life of all. The third is that he had to enlighten not only the Jews but all the Gentiles by his word and Spirit. That Paul proved these things from many passages of Scripture, the exclamation of Festus alone will later show. And indeed the testimonies of Moses and the prophets are found everywhere, by which all these things can be proved. From this we again conclude that the doctrine of the gospel is not new and belongs to a few people, but is most ancient and approved by the consent of all ages. Besides, whatever is necessary to believe is contained in the Scriptures, since from them Paul could prove all the mysteries of the Christian faith. Being content with these alone, therefore, let us hold firmly to the faith handed down in them, so that by following it we may attain eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. ...and Bernice, and those who sat with them. And when they had withdrawn, they spoke among themselves, saying: "This man does nothing worthy of death or chains." But Agrippa said to Festus: "This man could have been released, if he had not appealed to Caesar."

units.la: Postquàm Pauli orationem Lucas exposuit, deinceps quis huius apud auditores effectus fuerit, commemorat. Estq; memorabilis valde locus hic, eò quòd duobus exemplis duo hominū genera describit, quibus frustra Dei verbum prædicatur. Finis verò & vsus omnium est, vt cùm ministri discant quid cum talibus agendum sit, tum alij omnes intelligant, quid ipsos cauere oporteat, si Dei verbum non sine fructu audire velint.
units.tr: After Luke has set out Paul's speech, he next records what effect it had on the hearers. This is a very memorable passage, because in two examples it describes two kinds of men to whom the Word of God is preached in vain. The purpose and use of the whole is that ministers may learn how they ought to deal with such people, and that all others may understand what they must beware of, if they wish to hear the Word of God not without profit.

units.la: Primum genus in Festi Præsidis exemplo proponitur, qui hominum prophanorum & eorum, qui nullam in vniuersum rerum diuinarum notitiam siue gustum habent, typum gerit. Vbi primò quidem ipse Festus, deinde verò Paulus consyderandus erit. Audiuit ille Paulum visiones narrantem, & scripturarum testimonijs vniuersa humanæ salutis & Christianæ fidei mysteria explicantem, de quibus nihil vnquam audiuerat, vtpote homo ethnicus, qui maiorem fortassis rei militaris quàm religionis notitiam habebat. Quare Paulum de tam profundis & abstrusis rebus agentem insanire, & illorum instar, qui mania correpti mirifica quædam sibijpsis imaginari solent, hæc præter omnem rationem proferre putat, & dicentem admodum importune interpellat. In vno hoc tamen nō iniquus omnino, quòd mentis defectum, quo illum laborare arbitrabatur, nimio literarum studio tribuit, non alium aliquem affectū illi exprobrans, vt hodie plerique solent. Docet verò exemplum hoc, Dei verbo nihil apud eos profici, qui humana modò ratione ducuntur. Proprium enim illis est, vt quicquid rationis ipsorum captum & vires superat, pro delirio habeant: cùm interim nihil minus capiant, quàm ea quæ sunt spiritus Dei 1. Cor. 2. Fieri ergo non potest, quin euangelium de Iesu Christo crucifixo illis summa stulticia putetur, quando nihil tam absurdum & alienum à ratione videri potest, quàm ab eo salutem sperare & petere, qui in crucem suspensus inter latrones expirauit. Quà propter quod Paulo apud Festum concionanti euenit, hoc ipsum Prophetis antea, & deinceps apostolorum quoq; successoribus euenisse legimus, vt pro hominibus fanaticis haberentur. Quid, quòd ipse Christus à Pilato irrisus fuit, cùm se veritatis præconem in mundum venisse fateretur? Ita enim Pilatus ex eorum numero ipsum esse putat, qui in veritate inuestigANDA multùm frustra laborent, cùm inter homines omnia incerta sint & dubia. Quid ergo offendimur, si hodie etiā euangelij prædicatione parum proficiatur, quando magna passim hominum turba est, qui carnis rationibus excæcati, totúq; animis distracti, semen verbi in viam excipiunt, quod infernales graculi, affectus nimirum & satanicæ suggestiones, illicò absorbent?
units.tr: The first kind is set forth in the example of Festus the governor, who represents profane men, and those who have no knowledge or taste of divine things at all. Here we must consider first Festus himself, and then Paul. Festus heard Paul recounting visions and, by the testimonies of the Scriptures, explaining the whole mystery of human salvation and the Christian faith, things of which he had never heard anything, being a heathen man who perhaps had more knowledge of military affairs than of religion. Therefore he thinks that Paul, in speaking of such profound and abstruse matters, is out of his mind, and that, like those seized by madness who are wont to imagine marvellous things for themselves, he utters these things contrary to all reason; and he interrupts the speaker quite rudely. In this one thing, however, he is not wholly unfair, that he attributes the defect of mind which he believed Paul to suffer from to too much devotion to learning, and does not charge him with any other failing, as many do today. This example teaches, however, that nothing is achieved by the Word of God among those who are led only by human reason. For it is characteristic of them to regard as delirium whatever exceeds the grasp and powers of their reason, while in fact they grasp nothing less than the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). It cannot but be that the gospel of Jesus Christ crucified seems to them the greatest folly, since nothing can appear so absurd and so alien to reason as to hope for and seek salvation from one who was hanged on a cross and died between thieves. Therefore, what happened to Paul preaching before Festus, we read happened also to the Prophets before him, and afterwards to the successors of the apostles, that they were held to be fanatics. What of the fact that Christ himself was mocked by Pilate, when he confessed that he had come into the world as a herald of the truth? For Pilate thinks him to be one of those who labour in vain in seeking out the truth, since among men all things are uncertain and doubtful. Why then are we offended if today too little is achieved by the preaching of the gospel, when there is everywhere a great crowd of men who, blinded by the reasonings of the flesh and their minds wholly distracted, receive the seed of the Word on the path, which the infernal crows, namely the affections and satanic suggestions, at once devour?

units.la: Quid verò Paulus? Num Festi importuna interpellatione territus conticescit, vt sinistram de se alienatæ mentis suspicionem silentio suo confirmet? Minimè. Imò cùm ministerij sui tum euangelij authoritatem constanter asserit. Non insanio (inquit) præstantissime Feste, sed veritatis & sobrietatis verba eloquor. Conuicium ergo liberè reijcit, modestè tamen & cùm reuerentia, quæ magistratibus debetur, ne impatienti ira abreptus conuiciumq; referens, se mente captum esse testaretur. Itaque cordatè omnino se insanire negat: ea verò quæ Festo insanientis verba esse videbantur, verissima esse, nec abs se curiosius, sed summā quà fieri potest sobrietate exponi testatur. Id verò testibus fide dignissimis probat. Inter quos primo loco Regem sistit, qui nihil eorum, quæ hucusq; de Christo dicta erant, ignorare possit: eò quòd nihil horum in angulo & occultè, sed in celeberrima totius gentis vrbe, & in festo omnium frequentissimo omnia ista contigissent. Deinde prophetas simul omnes testes sistit, qui hæc ita euentura prædixerunt, sicut paulò ante susius demonstrauerat. Et ne ponderè careret oratio, prophetarum authoritatem liberè & fortiter asserit. Ad regem enim conuersus, Credis ne (ait) Rex Agrippa prophetis? Nec ipsius expectans responsum, ipse præueniit, addens: Scio quòd credis. Nouerat enim in quàmuis corruptissima Iudæorum gente eam tamen adhuc superesse scripturæ propheticæ maiestatem & fidem, vt illam nemo absque publica impietatis nota in dubium vocare auderet. Et credibile est pluribus adhuc causam hanc à Paulo tractatam fuisse, cùm Agrippa mox fateatur, se nō mediocriter illius verbis commotum esse. Cæterum occurrunt hic quædam diligentius nobis obseruanda, cùm ad communem omnium institutionem non parum faci
units.tr: But what did Paul do? Was he frightened by Festus's rude interruption and fall silent, so as to confirm by his silence the suspicion of a disordered mind? By no means. Rather, he constantly asserts both the authority of his ministry and of the gospel. "I am not mad," he says, "most excellent Festus, but I utter words of truth and soberness." He therefore freely rejects the insult, yet modestly and with the reverence due to magistrates, lest, carried away by impatient anger and returning insult for insult, he should prove himself out of his mind. So he flatly denies that he is mad, and testifies that what seemed to Festus to be the words of a madman are most true, and that they are set forth by him not with excessive curiosity but with the greatest soberness possible. He proves this by witnesses most worthy of trust. Among them, first in place, he calls the King, who could not be ignorant of any of the things so far said about Christ, because none of these things happened in a corner or in secret, but in the most famous city of the whole nation, and at the most crowded festival of all. Then he calls all the prophets together as witnesses, who foretold that these things would come to pass just as he had shown at length a little before. And so that his speech might not lack weight, he asserts the authority of the prophets freely and boldly. For turning to the king he says, "Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa?" And without waiting for his answer, he himself anticipates it, adding: "I know that you believe." For he knew that even in the most corrupt nation of the Jews the majesty and credibility of prophetic Scripture still survived, so that no one would dare to call it into doubt without a public mark of impiety. And it is credible that this cause had been handled by Paul at greater length to many others, since Agrippa soon confesses that he was not a little moved by his words. Moreover, there are some things here which we must observe more carefully, since they are not a little useful for the common instruction of all...

units.la: Festus eorū typa pus qui prophana mente veram bum audiunt.
units.tr: Festus, a type of those who hear the true Word with a profane mind.

units.la: Paulus ministe rium suum constanter & modestè asserit.
units.tr: Paul constantly and modestly asserts his ministry.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: ciant. Primùm docet locus hic, optimam docendi rationem esse, quam Paulus abs se hucusq; observa tam fuisse profitetur, quando se veritatis & sobrietatis verba loqui ait. Ante omnia enim veritatis ratio habenda est ministrus, ne sub divini nominis praetextu mendacium vendant, cuius patrem diabolum esse, Christus docet. In veritatis autem mysteriis tractandis sobrietatem piam & sanctam adhibeant, ijs duntaxat intenti, quae ad pietatem homines aedificare possunt: ne dum curiositati carnis indulgent, quaestionibus inutilibus & noxijs tum seipsos implicent, tum etiam rudiores & infirmiores offendant. Meminerint ergo, nos ex parte tantummodo cognoscere, & ex parte prophetare. Olim demum fore diem istum, quando omni sublato obstaculo coram in dei facie vniuersa regni caelorum mysteria speculabimur. Deinde docent Pauli verba, nostrae salutis & Christianae religionis negotium certum esse, nec quicquam vel obscuri vel suspecti habere. Vt enim nihil eorum in angulo gestum est, quae Christo acciderunt: ita publicè & apertè cum patribus quoque olim gesta sunt, quae Christum & in hoc salutis rationem adumbrauerunt. Nec enim obscuri aut malae notae homines fuerunt Patriarchae, ad quos primae promissiones delatae sunt. Nota quoque gentibus fuit Israelitici populi liberatio ex Aegypto. Clara & miraculis celebris fuit legis promulgatio, quae omnia Christi mysteria figurabat. De prophetis nemo bonus vnquam aliquid siniistri suspicari potuit. Quid, quod omnibus Monarchijs, Assyriae nimirum, Persica, Graeca & Romana, cum gente Iudaica res fuit, in qua salutis negotium docebatur? Apostolorum verò voces magna cum libertate orbem terrarum personuerunt, adeò vt omnibus nota essent quae ab illis fiebant simul & tradebantur. Est hac magna fidei nostrae dignitas, quae in nulla alia religione inuenitur. Eadem verò illorum impudentiam arguit, qui hodie illam in dubium vocare audent. Postremò admonet locus hic, scripturae sacrae auctoritatem & fidem certam esse, nec vlli permittendum, vt in controuersiam trahatur. Quia enim diuinitus inspirata est, nefas fuerit de illa dubitare. Quae causa est, quòd illud extra controuersiam ponit Paulus, Agrippam Prophetis credere. Et Christus cum Iudaeorum scribis agens, hoc illustrio buius, quòd in scripturis vitae aeternae rationem contineri firmiter credant. Iohan. 5. Quanto igitur execrabilior est nostri seculi impudentia, quo alij quidem scripturas impia scurrilitate cauillantur, alij verò illarum authoritatem mirificè imminuunt, dum illas hominum iudicio approbari & confirmari oportere contendunt?
units.tr: First, this passage teaches that the best method of teaching is the one Paul professes to have followed up to this point, when he says that he speaks words of truth and soberness. Above all, ministers must attend to truth, lest under the pretext of the divine name they sell lies, whose father Christ teaches the devil to be. In handling the mysteries of truth they should use a pious and holy soberness, intent only on those things that can build people up in godliness. They must not, while indulging the curiosity of the flesh, entangle both themselves and the cruder and weaker ones in useless and harmful questions. Let them remember, then, that we know only in part and prophesy only in part. The day will come at last when, every obstacle removed, we shall behold face to face in God's presence all the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Next, Paul's words teach that the matter of our salvation and of the Christian religion is certain and contains nothing obscure or suspect. Just as nothing that happened to Christ was done in a corner, so the things done long ago with the fathers, which foreshadowed Christ and the way of salvation in him, were also done publicly and openly. The patriarchs, to whom the first promises were delivered, were not obscure or disreputable men. The deliverance of the Israelite people from Egypt was known to the nations. The promulgation of the law was clear and famous for its miracles, and it all prefigured the mysteries of Christ. No good man has ever been able to suspect anything sinister about the prophets. What of the fact that all the monarchies, the Assyrian, Persian, Greek and Roman, had dealings with the Jewish nation, in which the matter of salvation was taught? The voices of the apostles, moreover, resounded through the world with great boldness, so that what they did was known to all and handed on at the same time. This is the great dignity of our faith, which is found in no other religion. The same dignity exposes the impudence of those who today dare to call it into doubt. Finally, this passage admonishes that the authority and certain trustworthiness of Holy Scripture must be upheld, and that no one may be allowed to drag it into controversy. For since it was divinely inspired, it would be wicked to doubt it. This is why Paul puts beyond dispute that Agrippa believes the Prophets. And Christ, when dealing with the scribes of the Jews, commends this in them, that they firmly believe the way of eternal life is contained in the Scriptures (John 5). How much more execrable, then, is the impudence of our age, when some mock the Scriptures with impious buffoonery, while others greatly diminish their authority, contending that they must be approved and confirmed by human judgment?

units.la: Porrò alterum auditorum verbi genus videamus, quorum typus in Agrippa Rege proponitur, & eorum est, qui mundo addicti, huius curis & studio verbi semen suffocari patiuntur. Nec enim scripturas negare audet, quarum authoritatem diuinam & infallibilem esse noverat. Illis praeterea conuenire videt, ea, quae à Paulo dicebantur. Sentit item non obscuros animi motus, quibus vt in Christi partes transfiret, solicitabatur. Nec id dissimulat, quando se nonnihil persuasum esse, palàm fatetur. Quid ergo obstat quo minus non vltra progressus Christo publicè nomen det? Nimirum infelix mundi studium, cuius amicitia & gloria illi multò praestantior videtur, quàm vt hac neglecta ad illos transfire debeat, quos plerique exosos & inuisos habebat, alij verò insanire iudicabant. Atqui vtinam vnus Agrippa huius rei nobis exemplum esset, & non hodie passim illorum voces audiretur, qui cum euangelio praeclarum testimonium ferant, Antichristi tamen doctrinam sibi potius sectandam esse censent, ne vel opum vel honorum iacturam faciant, aut etiam de vita periclitari cogantur. Interim elucet in illis hominibus diuina & mirifica euangelij vis, quae inuitis quoque & repugnantibus veri confessionem extorquet: illis tamen minimè salutarem, quando spiritui sancto fieri opponere non verentur.
units.tr: Next, let us consider the other kind of hearers, whose type is set forth in King Agrippa. These are men given over to the world, who allow the seed of the word to be choked by its cares and its pursuits. Agrippa does not dare to deny the Scriptures, whose divine and infallible authority he knew. Moreover, he sees that what Paul was saying agrees with them. He likewise perceives the not obscure stirrings of mind by which he was urged to pass over to Christ's side, and he does not conceal this, since he openly confesses that he is somewhat persuaded. What, then, stands in the way of his not going further and publicly giving his name to Christ? Plainly, it is the unhappy devotion to the world, whose friendship and glory seemed far more excellent to him than that he should neglect them and pass over to those whom most people hated and held in contempt, and whom others judged to be madmen. And yet would that Agrippa were the only example of this for us, and that the voices of those were not heard everywhere today, who, while bearing a splendid testimony to the gospel, nonetheless think they should rather follow the teaching of Antichrist, lest they suffer loss of wealth or honours, or be forced to risk their lives. Meanwhile, in these men shines the divine and wonderful power of the gospel, which wrings a confession of the truth even from those who are unwilling and resisting; yet this confession is in no way saving for them, since they do not hesitate to oppose the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Caeterum vt Festo prudenter admodum & fortiter Paulus respondit: ita Agrippae verbis vetum vere Christianum & charitatis ardore flagrans (quando aliud non potest) opponit. Optarim (inquit) à Deo, non solum modica in parte, verumetiam magna, nō te modò, sed omnes etiam quotquot audiunt hodie, esse tales, qualis ego sum, exceptis vinculis hijs. Nec dubium est ex animo ista optauisse Paulum, qui aliàs dies & noctes pro Iudaeis deprecabatur, & pro ijsdem anathema fieri cupiebat. Interim docemur non sufficere, vt ex parte credamus, sed fidei incrementa requiri, vt tandem in virum perfectum adolescamus in Christo Iesu. Nec illorum sententia admitti debet, qui vnum et alterum articulum ad salutem satis esse arbitrantur. Ita enim reliqui inutiles & superuacanei essent, id quod diuinae cùm sapientiae tum bonitati non parum derogaret. Docet praeterea Pauli votum nostros niftros nihil in animos hominum iuris vel potestatis habere, sed in illis solum Dei spiritum efficaciter operari. Cur enim inanibus votis seipsum discruciaret Paulus, si ipse Agrippae mentem flectere poterat? Sed vide quae cum ab ipso Paulo tum a Christo in hanc sententiam dicuntur. 1. Cor. 3. Ioban. 6. Matth. 11. &c. Nec omittendum est, quod vincula sua Paulus excipit. Quamvis enim haec sibi minime molesta essent, & in illis praecipuam sui ministerij gloriam sitam esse sciret, aliorum tamen otio & paci consultum esse optavit, quatenus id fidei & salutis nostrae ratio patitur. Ita vero omnes decet, suam quidem crucem patienter ferre, interim tamen aliorum commodis & tranquillitati pro virili consulere. Unde patet, quo spiritu agantur, qui omnium felicitati invident, vel qui praecipiti iudicio mox tanquam parum Christianos damnant, si quos Paulo commodius vitam ducere conspexerint.
units.tr: Moreover, just as Paul answered Festus with great prudence and courage, so he answers Agrippa's words with the warmth of charity, the wish of a true Christian, since he cannot do anything else. "I would pray to God," he says, "that not only in a small part but also in a great, not only you but all who hear me today might become such as I am, apart from these chains." There is no doubt that Paul wished this from his heart, he who at other times prayed day and night for the Jews and wished himself to be made accursed for them. Meanwhile we are taught that it is not enough to believe only in part, but that growth in faith is required, so that at last we grow into a perfect man in Christ Jesus. Nor should the opinion of those be admitted who think that one or two articles are enough for salvation. For the rest would then be useless and superfluous, which would greatly detract from the divine wisdom as well as from the divine goodness. This passage also teaches that the wish of Paul shows that our ministers have no right or power over people's minds, but that God's Spirit alone works effectually within them. For why would Paul torment himself with empty wishes if he himself could bend Agrippa's mind? But see what both Paul himself and Christ say to this effect: 1 Cor. 3; John 6; Matt. 11, etc. Nor must we pass over the fact that Paul excepts his chains. Although he knew that these were by no means troublesome to him, and that the chief glory of his ministry lay in them, he nevertheless wished that the ease and peace of others be consulted, so far as the reason of faith and salvation allows. Thus indeed all ought to bear their own cross patiently, while at the same time striving, as far as they can, for the advantage and tranquillity of others. From this it is plain by what spirit those are moved who envy the happiness of all, or who, with hasty judgment, straightway condemn as scarcely Christian those whom they see living more comfortably than Paul did.

units.la: Hus vero actionis totius finem Lucas subijcit, qui fuit, quod omnes soluto coetu & consessu exierunt, nihilo nimirum meliores factis, cum causis, quas supra commemoravimus, impedirentur. Memorabile tamen hic est, quod rursum omnium consensu Paulus absoluitur, quem tamen non ideo liberum dimittunt: unde patet, quam parum mundo curae sit piorum conditio, quos praeter meritum affligi videt. Plurimum vero facit ad commendandam Christianae fidei dignitatem totties iam probata Pauli innocentia: quae illorum quoque temeritatem arguit, qui euangelij doctrinam hodie seditiosam esse clamant, cum a seditionis crimine acerrimus euangelij praeco, Paulus, coram ethnicis & prophanis iudicibus sese toties purgare potuerit. Nemine ergo mundi huius calumnias moveant, sed in vera fidei doctrina constantes, deo libere serviamus, qui cultores suos inter mundi procellas asserit, & regni sui haereditate donat, per Iesum Christum dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Luke adds the end of the whole action: everyone left the assembly and the gathering, having become, of course, no better, since the causes we mentioned above had hindered them. It is memorable here, however, that once again by the consent of all Paul is acquitted, and yet they do not on that account set him free. From this it is plain how little concern the world has for the condition of the godly, whom it sees afflicted though they do not deserve it. Paul's innocence, so often now proved, contributes greatly to commending the dignity of the Christian faith, and it also exposes the rashness of those who today cry out that the doctrine of the gospel is seditious, when Paul, the most fierce herald of the gospel, was able so often to clear himself of the charge of sedition before heathen and profane judges. Let no one, therefore, be moved by the slanders of this world, but, steadfast in the true doctrine of the faith, let us serve God freely, who preserves his worshippers amid the storms of the world and grants them the inheritance of his kingdom, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPVT XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXVI.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXVI.

units.la: POstquam autem decretum est, ut nos navigaremus in Italiam, tradiderunt & Paulum & quosdam alios vinctos Centurioni, nomine Iulio, cohortis Augustae. Conscensa autem navi Adramyttina, navigaturi iuxta loca Asiae solvimus, perseverante nobiscum Aristarcho Macedone Thessalonicense. Sequenti autem die appulimus Sidonem. Et Iulius humaniter tractato Paulo, permisit ut ad amicos profectus, ab illis curaretur. Et inde cum solvissemus, subnavigavimus iuxta Cyprum, propterea quod essent venti contrarij. Et pelagus, quod est contra Ciliciam & Pamphyliam emensi, pervenimus Myram, quae est Lyciae. Et ibi nactus Centurio navem Alexandrinam navigantem in Italiam, imposuit nos in eam. Et cum multis diebus tarde navigaremus, vixque devenissemus contra Cnidū, prohibente nos vento, adnavigavimus Cretae iuxta Salmonem: & vix praeterlegentes eam, pervenimus in locum quendam, qui vocatur Pulchri portus, cui vicina erat civitas Lasea.
units.tr: When it had been decided that we should sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort. We boarded an Adramyttian ship that was about to sail along the coasts of Asia, and put out to sea, with Aristarchus the Macedonian from Thessalonica travelling with us. The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends and be cared for by them. From there we put out to sea again and sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. We crossed the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra in Lycia. There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board. We made slow progress for many days and had difficulty reaching the region of Cnidus, and since the wind did not allow us to go on, we sailed under the lee of Crete, off Salmone. Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

units.la: Iui Pauli apostoli navigationem, laboris & periculi plenam, qua Romam usque, ut illic Caesari sisteretur, delatus fuit, hoc capite Lucas describit. Et quidem superuacanea vi detur primo intuitu tam operosa spiritus sancti diligentia: at si penitius singula inspicias, multa occurrent, cognitu & consyderatu dignissima. Docet enim historia haec, quae sanctorum in hoc mundo fors sit. Et eadem in Paulo patientiae & constantiae exempla proponit. Adhaec infallibilem esse docet promissionum Dei fidem. Licet enim ipsa rerum natura Paulo adversari videatur, quo minus Romam perveniat, perrumpit tamen omnia adversa Dei veritas, quae ipsum Caesari quoque sistendum esse promiserat. Insunt etiam praeter haec multa alia, consolationis & institutionis plena; quae suis locis videbimus.
units.tr: Luke describes in this chapter the voyage of the apostle Paul, a voyage full of toil and danger, by which he was carried to Rome to be presented there to Caesar. At first sight the Holy Spirit's great care in recounting it may seem superfluous. But if you examine each detail more closely, many things will present themselves that are most worth knowing and considering. For this history teaches what the lot of the saints in this world is. It also sets before us, in Paul, examples of patience and steadfastness. Furthermore, it teaches that the faithfulness of God's promises cannot fail. For although the very nature of things seems to be against Paul, so that he should not reach Rome, the truth of God breaks through all obstacles, since God had promised that he would stand before Caesar. Besides these there are many other things, full of comfort and instruction, which we shall see in their places.

units.la: Argumentum capitis.
units.tr: The argument of the chapter.

units.la: Primò autem quomodo Romam dimissus sit apostolus narratur. Vbi Centurionis cuiusdam mentio fit, cui ipsum vnà cum alijs vinctis deducendum Festus tradidit. Vbi haud vulgaris officij currit Romanorum in administrando iure diligentia, quando illos in captiuis transmittendis tantos sumptus simul atq; labores sustinuisse videmus. Extant huius alia quoq; exempla, quae illis non paruam laudem & gloriam pepererunt. Imò hac potissimum ratione illos ad tantam imperij gloriam ascendisse constat. Nec aliam commodiorem esse cum dilatandi tum conseruandi imperii rationem, scriptura cum alibi, tum in Psal.72. clarissimè docet. Nam quod Romanis felicissimè cesserit, id ipsum multis alijs ad potentiam & gloriam adiumento fuisse legimus. Rursum florentissima regna subito corruisse scimus, vt primùm iusticiæ neruo laxato publica iura & legum disciplina neglegi ceperunt. In primis verò piorum fortem nos obseruare conuenit. Reliquis enim vinctis Paulus adiungitur, quos maxima ex parte facinorosos & sceleribus infames fuisse, nemini dubium esse potest. Ita Christum cum flagitiosis reputatus fuisse scriptura docet: quod etiā Martyribus frequenter accidit, quorum exemplis nos hodie animari oportet, ne iniquissimis mundi huius iudicijs offendamur. Simul verò in indigna Pauli sorte bonitatis diuinæ præclarum specimen elucet, quæ factum est, vt misera vinctorum turba talem tantumque consolatorem simul & consultorem haberet, cuius opera illos omnes tandem seruatos fuisse audiemus. Nec dubium est, Paulum in ijsdem infliguendis & tradendis fidei Christianæ mysterijs nullam occasionem neglexisse, quem semper hominum salutem ardentissimis votis quæsiuisse, hucusq; vidimus. Ita verò Deus tum quoq; præclaras bene agendi occasiones offert, quando nostri curam penitus depositurus videtur.
units.tr: First, the chapter tells how the apostle was sent on to Rome. Here mention is made of a certain centurion, to whom Festus handed Paul over, together with the other prisoners, to be taken there. Here we see the diligence of the Romans in administering justice, which is no ordinary office, since they undertook such great expense and labour in transporting prisoners. Other examples of this survive, which brought them no small praise and glory. Indeed, it is evident that they rose to such great imperial glory chiefly by this method. Scripture, both elsewhere and most clearly in Psalm 72, teaches that there is no more suitable method of both extending and preserving an empire. For we read that what turned out most happily for the Romans was likewise a help to many others in gaining power and glory. Conversely, we know that flourishing kingdoms have suddenly collapsed as soon as, with the sinews of justice relaxed, public laws and the discipline of the laws began to be neglected. Above all, it is fitting for us to observe the lot of the pious. For Paul is joined to the other prisoners, who for the most part were undoubtedly criminals and notorious for their crimes. Scripture teaches that Christ was reckoned among the wicked, and this often happened to the martyrs too; we ought to take courage from their examples today, so that we are not offended by the most unjust judgments of this world. At the same time, in Paul's undeserved lot a remarkable display of divine goodness shines forth: the wretched company of prisoners had such a comforter and counsellor, through whose work, as we shall hear, they were all at last saved. And there is no doubt that Paul did not neglect any opportunity of teaching the mysteries of the Christian faith to those in chains, since we have seen up to now that he always sought the salvation of men with the most fervent prayers. So too God offers excellent opportunities for doing good, even when he seems about to abandon our care altogether.

units.la: Huc verò sequentia quoq; pertinent, quibus Deum inter tanta pericula Pauli curā cumprimis habuisse docetur. Primò enim comites illi adiunxit fidelissimos, quorum præsentia & ministerio subleuaretur. Fuit inter hos Lucas huius historiæ scriptor, sicuti ex toto contextu patet. Deinde Aristarchus Macedo, vir haud dubiedus, qui tantis sumptibus sufficere potuerit. Cum Paulo enim ex Gracia Hierosolymam ascendit: & quamuis ab Iudæis captum videret, non tamen illum reliquit, sed toto biennio & amplius illi fidelem operam nauauit. Nunc eundem Romam usq; deducit. Ita verò Deus suis adesse solet, ne vltra vires tentetur, & ab hominibus quoq; omnino derelictos suo patrocinio tueatur. Est autem memorabile omnino Aristarchi exemplum, quo ollæ amici & molliculi quidam arguuntur, qui amicitias vtilitate metiri solent, quiq; nihil pro veritate pati instituerunt, adeò vt illos martyrum Christi pudeat. Sed Deum remuneratorem spectare oportebat, qui Aristarchi fidem immortali gloria & cœlestis regni hereditate compensauit. Alterum verò diuinæ bonitatis & curæ argumentum est, quòd Centurionem quoque Paulo amicissimum fuisse audimus. Nam & humaniter illum tractat, & vbi Sidonem ventum est, illi amicos inuisendi copiam facit, vt ab illis curari possit. Similia de Lysia Tribuno & Felice præside supra vidimus. Ita olim Abdias propheta protector datus fuit, nec Ieremiæ amici defuerunt, qui captum auxilio simul & consilio iuuarent. Vide 1. Reg. 18. Ierem. 38. &c. Ex his verò nos quoq; consolationem petere conuenit, ne tyrannorum conatibus cedamus, sed vni Deo nos & nostra omnia approbemus. Cæterum hoc loco Paulus consyderandus venit, qui cum in vrbe maritima & frequenti admodum facilè vel occultari vel elabi potuisset, omnem tamen occasionem illam neglexit. Causa fuerunt, tum quòd Centurioni optimè de se merito periculum conflare iniquissimum fuisset: tum quòd se Romam proficisci debere, oraculo didicerat. Docemur autem exemplo hoc, neminem sibi ipsi illicitis medijs consulere debere. Nam si nulla in periculis effugij via patet, nisi quæ cum charitate aut fidei & iustitiæ legibus pugnet, certum est, aliud de nobis esse Dei consilium, cuius voluntati nos cedere conuenit, ne dum corpori aut fortunis consulimus, animæ iacturam faciamus.
units.tr: What follows also pertains to this, in which we are taught that God took especial care of Paul amid such great dangers. For first he gave him most faithful companions, by whose presence and service he might be sustained. Among these was Luke, the writer of this history, as is clear from the whole context. Then there was Aristarchus the Macedonian, a man of no doubtful character, who could bear such expenses. For he had gone up with Paul from Greece to Jerusalem, and although he saw him seized by the Jews, he did not desert him but served him faithfully for two years and more. Now he leads him on to Rome. So God is accustomed to be present with his own, so that they are not tempted beyond their strength, and to protect with his patronage those who have been utterly forsaken by men too. Aristarchus's example is truly memorable, for it condemns those effeminate and soft-living friends who are accustomed to measure friendships by usefulness, and who have resolved to suffer nothing for the truth, so much so that they are ashamed of the martyrs of Christ. But we ought to look to God, the rewarder, who repaid Aristarchus's faithfulness with immortal glory and the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. The second proof of divine goodness and care is that we hear the centurion, too, was most friendly to Paul. For he treats him kindly, and when they came to Sidon he gave him the opportunity to visit his friends, so that he might be cared for by them. We saw similar things above concerning the tribune Lysias and the governor Felix. So of old the prophet Obadiah was given as a protector, and Jeremiah's friends did not fail, who helped him when he was taken, with both aid and counsel. See 1 Kings 18; Jeremiah 38, etc. We ought to draw comfort from these things too, so that we do not yield to the attempts of tyrants, but commit ourselves and all that is ours to God alone. But here Paul is to be considered, who, though in a busy maritime city he could easily have either hidden himself or slipped away, nevertheless neglected every such opportunity. The reasons were, first, that it would have been most unjust to bring danger upon the centurion, who had deserved so well of him; and second, that he had learned by an oracle that he must travel to Rome. We are taught by this example that no one ought to seek his own safety by unlawful means. For if no way of escape from dangers is open except one that conflicts with love, or with the laws of faith and justice, it is certain that God's counsel concerning us is otherwise, and we ought to yield to his will, lest while we look after our body or fortunes we suffer the loss of our soul.

units.la: Sequitur diligens & prolixa nauigationis descriptio, cuius cursum ex Geographorum tabulis petant, qui singula noiisse cupiunt. Nobis obseruandum est, molestam & periculi plenam fuisse, quādo ventos aduersos fuisse diserte dicitur. Atqui facilè huic malo mederi poterat Deus, qui multis exemplis, se maris quoq; dominum & rectorem esse declarauit. Ita verò eleētum organum suū exerceri voluit, vt euidentior esset sua cum veritatis tum potentiæ gloria. Interim, quæ vita nostræ conditio sit elucet. Ærumnosa nimirum & instar peregrinationis, in qua noui indies labores & noua pericula occurrunt. In primis autem in piorum vita icтud cernitur, quam noua semper molestiæ & curæ cura infestant. Exemplum huius in Christo, capite nostro habetur, qui recens natus hostes habuit, quorum insidia totum vitae cursum amarū & periculosum reddiderunt. Experitur hoc ipsum Paulus quoq;, qui cum Iudaeorum artibus & insidijs diu conflictatus, nunc tandem elemento omnium immanissimo, mari nimirum committitur, cuius pericula antea quoq; senserat, ut ex posteriori ad Corinth. ii. patet. Poterant infinita alia huius generis recenseri, si ita opus foret. Nos vsum potius horum obseruemus, qui est, ut forti fidei constantia armati, quaeuis aduersa superemus, quando constat nobis in caelis aeternae quietis praemia parata esse, quibus olim fruamur cum Christo Iesu: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows a careful and lengthy description of the voyage, whose course those who wish to know each detail may seek from the maps of the geographers. For us the point to note is that it was troublesome and full of danger, since the text expressly says that the winds were contrary. Yet God could easily have remedied this evil, he who has shown by many examples that he is also lord and governor of the sea. But he willed that his chosen instrument should be exercised in this way, so that the glory of his truth and of his power might be more evident. Meanwhile, what the condition of our life is becomes clear: it is indeed full of hardship and is like a pilgrimage, in which new labours and new dangers meet us every day. Above all, this is seen in the life of the godly, whom new troubles and cares always harass. An example of this is found in Christ, our head, who, though newly born, had enemies, whose plots made his whole course of life bitter and dangerous. Paul too experiences this, who, after long struggling with the schemes and plots of the Jews, is now at last committed to the most savage of all elements, the sea, whose perils he had felt before, as is clear from the second letter to the Corinthians, chapter 11. Countless other things of this kind could be listed if need required. Rather let us observe the use of these things, which is that, armed with a strong constancy of faith, we may overcome whatever adversities arise, since it is certain that rewards of eternal rest are prepared for us in heaven, to be enjoyed one day with Christ Jesus: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXVII.
units.tr: HOMILY 167.

units.la: Multo autem tempore peracto, & cum iam esset periculosa navigatio, quod iam ieiunium quoq; praeterierat: admonebat eos Paulus, dicens eis: Viri, video quod cum iniuria multoq; damno non solum oneris & navis, sed etiam animarum nostrarum futura sit navigatio. Centurio autem gubernatori & nauclero magis credebat, quam his quae a Paulo dicebantur. Et cum portus ineptus esset ad hybernandum, complures coeperunt consilium illinc soluendi, si quo modo possent perue nire Phoenicen, & illic hybernare. Is est portus Cretae spectans ad Africum & ad Corum. Aspirante autem Austro, rati se propositi compotes, cum soluissent, propius praeteriegebant Cretam. Sed non multo post coortus est contra ipsam ventus Typhonicus, qui vocatur Euroclydon. Cumq; correpta esset navis, nec posset obniti vento, data flatibus naue ferebantur. In insulam autem quandam deuecti, quae vocatur Clauda, vix potuimus obtinere schapha: qua sublata, adiutoriis vtebantur, sub cingentes nauem, timentesq; ne in Syrtim inciderent, demisso vase sic ferebantur. Cum autem vehementi tempestate iactaremur, sequenti die iactum fecerunt: ac tertio die nostris manibus armamenta nauis proiecimus. Sed neq; Sole neq; syderibus apparentibus ad complures dies, & tempestate non exigua imminente, iam ablata erat spes omnis salutis nostrae.
units.tr: After much time had passed, and the voyage was already dangerous because the fast had also gone by, Paul warned them and said: "Men, I see that the voyage will be with injury and great loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives." The centurion, however, put more trust in the pilot and the master of the ship than in what Paul said. Since the harbour was unsuitable for wintering, most of them decided to put to sea from there, if somehow they could reach Phoenix and winter there. This is a harbour of Crete facing south-west and north-west. When a south wind began to blow, thinking they had achieved their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed close along Crete. But before long a typhoon-like wind, called Euroclydon, rose against the island. When the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way and were driven before it. Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we could scarcely secure the skiff. Once it was hoisted aboard, they used helps, passing ropes under the ship to brace it, and, fearing they would run onto the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and were carried along in this way. As we were tossed by a violent storm, on the next day they threw out the cargo, and on the third day we threw the ship's tackle overboard with our own hands. Yet for many days neither sun nor stars appeared, a great storm was pressing on us, and now all hope of our being saved had been taken away.

units.la: Quod Dei filio & saluatori nostro Iesu Christo, in terris agenti euenit, vt variis & quotidianis afflictionibus exerceretur, id ipsum omnes eos manere, qui illius vestigia sequi instituerunt, cum alibi disertis verbis, tum in praesenti exemplo suo Paulus docet. Qui enim toto biennio vincula & carceris molestias pertulerat, & nouas indies senserat hostium insidias, nunc demum immanissimo quoq; elemento obijcitur, vt nimirum maris tempestates periculosissimas & tandem infelicis etiam naufragij incommoda sentiat. Dictum enim est, in iis quae proxime praecesserunt, vt aduersis ventis & difficili admodum navigatione ex Syria ad Cretam vsq; insulam peruenerit. Sed longe maioris periculi descriptio sequitur, quod tandem in naufragium desijsse audiemus, cuius ordinem & progressus summa fide & diligentia Lucas commemorat, eo quod in narratione hac, quae sterilis primo intuitu videtur, multa occurrunt, quae nostrae cum institutioni tum consolationi seruiunt.
units.tr: That the Son of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, while he lived on earth, was exercised by various and daily afflictions, this same thing, Paul teaches, awaits all who have set out to follow his footsteps, both in plain words elsewhere and by his own example in the present case. For he who had endured chains and the troubles of prison for two whole years, and had daily felt new snares of enemies, is now at last exposed to the most savage of all the elements, so that he may experience the most dangerous storms at sea and finally the misfortunes of a shipwreck. For it was said in what immediately preceded that he came from Syria to the island of Crete with adverse winds and very difficult sailing. But a description of a far greater danger follows, which we shall hear ended in shipwreck; Luke relates its order and progress with the greatest faithfulness and care, because in this narrative, which seems barren at first sight, many things occur which serve both our instruction and our consolation.

units.la: Inter quae facile primum locum obtinet, quod milites simul & nautas de periculo mature Deus admonuit. Cum enim multo tempore in Pulchroportu prope Lasaeam haesissent, iamq; hyemis instaret, praeterito nimirum ieiunij Iudaici tempore, quod septimo mense (qui nobis partim in Septembrem partim in Octobrem incidit) peragi solebat, Paulus vt navigatione differant, diligenter suadet. Quod ipsum non sine spiritus revelatione fecisse, vel ex eo patet, quod pericula, quae post secuta sunt aperte praedicit. Et hic quidem Deus nobis maxime spectandus est, qui suos nunquam negligit. Quia enim saluos vult homines, de periculis in tempore monet, vt sibi cauere & effugij viam circumspicere possint. Varie autem admonitiones suas attemperat. Aliquando enim per prophetas & verbi sui praecones monet, quae etiam illi omnium tritissima ratio est, & praecipuum sua erga nos benevolentiae argumentum, de quo vide Amos prophetae capite tertio. Interdum privatim per amicos & familiares, quo in periculo versemur revelat. Habet enim signa omnis generis, quae iram suam peccantibus portendunt. Adhaec per occultas spiritus sui & conscientiarum suggestiones auram nobis vellicat. Et quosdam angelorum ministerio admonitos fuisse legimus, Quae omnia adeo vulgaria sunt, ut illa exemplis illustrare minime opus sit. Discamus saltem Dei bonitatem agnoscere, nec contemnere fidas & salutares admonitiones, ne interitus proprij nobisipsis authores simus. Id enim contumaces fere manere, horum quoque exemplum postea docebit. Priusquam vero illud tractemus, de Paulo quaedam dicenda erunt. Illum enim coelesti oraculo admonitum fuisse supra audiimus, quod Romam venturus esset, cui illum firmiter credidisse certum est. Non tamen in eum finem oraculo abutitur, ut praeter causam sese periculo praesenti committere & ita Deum tentare inst-ituat. Quin potius noua revelatione de periculo admonitus, huic quoque credit, simulque alios, ut sibi ipsis caveant admonet. Unde patet, fidei & providentiae Dei doctrinam non temerarios reddere hominess & Dei tentatores. Ut enim prudentiam a suis Christus exigit, ita quandocunque Deus legitima & liciti effugij media nobis offert, certum est, illum nequaquam velle ut periclitemur. Illis ergo nos pie & religiose uti convenit.
units.tr: Among these, what first deserves to be noticed is that God timely warned both the soldiers and the sailors of the danger. For when they had remained a long time at Fair Havens near Lasea, and winter was already coming on, the Jewish fast having passed (which was customarily kept in the seventh month, which fell for us partly in September and partly in October), Paul diligently advised them not to set sail. That he did this not without a revelation of the Spirit is clear even from the fact that he plainly foretold the dangers which followed afterwards. And here God is especially to be regarded by us, for he never neglects his own. For because he wants men to be saved, he warns them of dangers in good time, so that they may take care for themselves and look about for a way of escape. He adapts his warnings in various ways. For sometimes he warns through the prophets and the heralds of his word, which is also the most common way of all and the chief proof of his goodwill toward us; on this see the prophet Amos, chapter three. At other times he reveals privately, through friends and family, what danger we are in. For he has signs of every kind which foretell his anger to sinners. Besides, through the secret promptings of his Spirit and of our consciences he stirs us. And we read that some were warned by the ministry of angels. All these things are so commonplace that there is scarcely any need to illustrate them with examples. Let us at least learn to recognise God's goodness, and not to despise faithful and salutary warnings, lest we become the authors of our own destruction. For that the stubborn usually remain so, the example of these men will also teach us later. Before we deal with that, some things must be said about Paul. For we have heard above that he was warned by a heavenly oracle that he was to go to Rome, and it is certain that he firmly believed this. Yet he does not abuse the oracle to that end, so as to expose himself to present danger without cause and so set about tempting God. Rather, when he is warned of the danger by a new revelation, he believes this too, and at the same time he advises the others to take care of themselves. From this it is clear that the doctrine of faith and of God's providence does not make men rash and testers of God. For just as Christ requires prudence from his own, so whenever God offers us lawful and legitimate means of escape, it is certain that he by no means wants us to be put in danger. We should therefore use these means devoutly and religiously.

units.la: Porrò non admittitur salutare Pauli consilium, sed magno omnium malo contemnitur. Vbi totius negotij progressum videre oportet, ut ex eo discamus quibus fere causis fiat, ut multi spretis sapientioribus consilijs, sibi ipsis malum & nonnunquam interitum concilient. Prima causa in praesenti adducitur, quod Centurio gubernatori potius & nauclero, quàm Paulo credendum esse putauit. Et id quidem, si carnis rationem audias, prudenter admodum facere videtur. Errat tamen, & Iupiter quidem, quod consilia non ex causis, sed hominum authoritate aestimat. Alioqui facile videret, non absque ratione esse, quod Paulus hyeme imminente navigationem periculosam fore dicebat.
