Est vero frequens admodum error hic, maximè si per verbi sui ministros consilium det dominus. Illos enim audire, multis non graue modo, verumetiam piaculum videtur. Et paßim hodie Achabi & Zedechiae sunt, qui nec Michaeas nec Ieremias audire dignantur, sed ipsi sibi optimi consultores videntur, vel alios sibi consultores adhibent, quos suis ingeniis & moribus melius convenire putant. Hinc fere fit, quod in bellorum periculis ad barbaros & sanguinarios milites, ad regum fabricas & munitiones: in morbis ad medicos solos: in vegetate & inopia ad illicitas artes confugimus, eosque solos audimus, qui similes conatus sibi aliquando successisse arbitrantur. Ita vero infinitis malis intricantur homines, quibus facile carere poterant, si solius Dei verbum, & ex hoc desumpta consilia admitterent. Altera, quae Pauli consilium contemnere suasit, causa fuit, quod portus illis ad hybernandum incommodus videtur: ideo illinc soluunt commodiorem quaesituri. Eadem vero causa maltis sanioribus consilijs viam obstruit, quod nimirum praesentibus bonis non contenti, aliena & nostro iudicio meliora affectamus. Ita enim fit, ut insatiabiles & caecos carnis affectus secuti, peccatorum laqueis intricemur, & maximorum malorum ipsi nobis authores simus. Accidit hoc isti militibus & nautis, qui cum portum, quem Deus dederat aspernantur, tandem naufragi omnium bonorum iacturam faciunt, & vitas quoque suas in discrimen adducunt. Extant huius generis exempla passim in stiftorijs. Inter quae praeclarum est omnino, quod de Israelitis legitur, qui praesentis fortis pertaesi regem sibi ipsis imposuerunt, nec vllis rationibus per Samuelem adductis, sese moueri passi sunt, ut à Deo traditam politiam retinerent. Simile quid de maioribus nostris, Heluetiis incolis, Caesar scribit, qui patrij soli fastidio correpti in Galliam suas sedes transferre magno suo malo conati sunt. Omnium vero horum vsus est, ut praesenti forte, quam Deus offert contenti, nihil vltra appetamus. Ita enim carnis affectus frenare, & nosipsos in officio retinere poterimus. Vide de hac, quam Paulus tradidit 1. Timoth. 6. SED ut ad nostros illos redeamus, tertium accessit, quod illos in suo proposito tenendo pertinaces fecit, quod austro aspirante navigationem feliciter exorsi esse videbantur. Nec dubium est, quin multorum ludibrio Paulus expositus fuerit, ut qui consilio suo successum hunc impeditur ut erat, si quidem illum audiuissent. At mox inobedientia sua graues poenas luunt. Est vero hoc infigne omnino diaboli stratagema, qui peccatorum principia fere facilia & felicia in speciem facere cogunt, ut nos successus ipse pelliciat. Vt enim peccatum corrupta nostra natura blanditur, itaque circa initium illius progressus videtur: quo fit, ut fortuna ebrij, admonitiones fanas improbe spernamus.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul's salutary counsel is not accepted, but to the great harm of all it is scorned. Here we must see the course of the whole affair, so that from it we may learn for what causes it generally happens that many, having spurned the wiser counsels, bring ruin and sometimes destruction upon themselves. The first cause mentioned in this passage is that the centurion thought he should trust the helmsman and the master of the ship rather than Paul. And indeed, if you listen to the reasoning of the flesh, he seems to have acted very prudently. Yet he is mistaken, and he judges counsels not by their reasons but by the authority of men. Otherwise he would easily have seen that there was good reason for Paul's saying that the voyage would be dangerous with winter coming on. This error is indeed very frequent, especially when the Lord gives counsel through the ministers of his word. For to hear them seems to many not only burdensome but even a sin. And everywhere today there are Ahabs and Zedekiahs, who do not deign to hear either Micaiah or Jeremiah, but seem to themselves the best advisers, or take other advisers whom they think better suited to their own talents and manners. Hence it generally happens that in dangers of war we flee to barbarous and bloody soldiers, to the works and fortifications of kings; in diseases, to physicians alone; in sickness and want, to unlawful arts; and we listen only to those who think that similar attempts have sometimes succeeded for them. And so men are entangled in endless evils, which they could easily have avoided if they had admitted the Word of God alone and the counsels drawn from it. The second cause which persuaded them to despise Paul's counsel was that the harbour seemed unsuitable to them for wintering; therefore they sail from it, seeking a more convenient one. But this same cause blocks the way to many far wiser counsels, namely that, not content with present goods, we desire what is other people's and, in our judgment, better. For thus it happens that, following the insatiable and blind affections of the flesh, we are entangled in the snares of sins, and become ourselves the authors of the greatest evils. This happened to those soldiers and sailors who, when they scorned the harbour which God had given, at last suffered shipwreck, the loss of all their goods, and also brought their own lives into peril. Examples of this kind are found everywhere in histories. Among these, what is truly outstanding is what is read about the Israelites, who, weary of the present condition, set up a king for themselves, and, though many reasons were brought forward through Samuel, they allowed themselves to be moved by no reasons to keep the polity handed down by God. Caesar writes something similar about our forebears, the Helvetian inhabitants, who, seized with disgust for their native soil, tried to move their dwellings into Gaul, to their great harm. The use of all these examples is that we should be content with the present lot which God offers and desire nothing beyond it. For in this way we shall be able to restrain the affections of the flesh and keep ourselves in our duty. See on this what Paul handed down in 1 Timothy 6. But to return to our men: a third thing was added which made them obstinate in holding to their purpose, namely that they seemed to have begun the voyage successfully with the south wind blowing. And there is no doubt that Paul was exposed to the mockery of many, since this success seemed to refute his counsel, had they listened to him. But soon they pay severe penalties for their disobedience. This is truly an outstanding stratagem of the devil, who makes the beginnings of sins seem easy and happy, so that success itself may entice us. For just as sin flatters our corrupt nature, so it appears at the beginning of its course; hence it happens that, drunk with good fortune, we wickedly scorn sound warnings

units.la: Psalm.36. namus, & cum risu sæpe exibilemus. Exempla huius passim sunt obuia, nec illis diu immorari opus est. Ita enim adulteris, ebriosis, vsurarijs, militibus, facinorosis deniq; omnibus mirificam læti successum spem faciunt, quæ paulò post magnæ calamitatis causa sunt. Id quod Paulini quoque consilij contemptores experti sunt, vt modò sequetur.
units.tr: Psalm. 36. We mock them, and often hiss them down with laughter. Examples of this are everywhere, and there is no need to linger over them. For they hold out to adulterers, drunkards, usurers, soldiers and, in short, all criminals the wonderful hope of a happy outcome, which a little later becomes the cause of great calamity. The same thing has been experienced by those who scorned Paul's counsel, as will soon follow.

units.la: Nam non multò post contra illos oritur ventus Typhonicus vel Euroclydon, quem alij Cæciam vocant, veteri quoq; prouerbio celebris, qui nauim totam insano turbine rotatam hinc inde rapit. Suo malo experiuntur, non posse diuturnos esse illorum successus, qui contra Dei voluntate aliquid instituunt. Fere enim fieri consueuit, vt quando sibi ipsis felicissimi videntur, subita aliqua & improuisa calamitas illos obruat. Cuius rei exempla quotidie occurrunt in adulteris, raptoribus, auaris, militibus mercenarijs, omnibus denique impijs, quos non dimidiare dies suos, propheta testatur. Nec in priuatis modo hominibus ista videre licet, verumetiam regnis & respub. quæ per vim & iniustitiam contra diuinas leges propagantur. Nam & illas fere infelix ruina subito sternit, quando rebus suis optime confultum, adeoque inuictas illarum vires esse, omnes suspicantur. Docent hoc Assyriorum & Babyloniorum occasus, Persarum clades, Græcorum interitus, & quæ præter totius mundi expectationem incidit Romani Imperij ruina. Non est ergo, vt vel nostris ipsorum successibus efferamur, vel alienis offendamur. Quin potius studiorum omnium regula nobis sit Dei verbum, cuius dum sum secuti, nec à vero aberrabimus, nec Dei iram in nos prouocabimus.
units.tr: For not long afterwards there rises against them a Typhonic wind, or Euroclydon, which others call Caecias and which is famous from an old proverb. It seizes the whole ship, spinning it in a mad whirlwind this way and that. They learn to their cost that the successes of those who undertake something against God's will cannot last long. For it usually happens that, just when they seem most fortunate, some sudden and unforeseen calamity overwhelms them. Examples of this occur daily among adulterers, robbers, misers, mercenary soldiers and, in short, all the wicked, whom the prophet testifies do not live out half their days. Such things can be seen not only in private individuals but also in kingdoms and commonwealths that are expanded by violence and injustice against the divine laws. For a sudden, unhappy ruin usually overthrows these as well, just when everyone supposes that their affairs are best managed and their strength invincible. The fall of the Assyrians and Babylonians, the defeat of the Persians, the destruction of the Greeks and the collapse of the Roman Empire, which came about beyond the expectation of the whole world, teach this. Therefore we should not be elated by our own successes or troubled by those of others. Rather, let the word of God be the rule of all our pursuits. As long as we follow it, we shall neither go astray from the truth nor provoke God's wrath against us.

units.la: Sequitur autem diligentior periculi, quod isti sibi ipsis conflauerunt, descriptio. Nauem enim ventí procella tanto impetu abripuit, vt illi resistere non possent, quare vento & undis illam comitantes incertis vicibus iactati sunt. Et quàmuis ad insulam Claudam delati, ipsem aliquam tenere potuerunt, mox tamen illa quoq; fructrati, de scapha simul & naui tota periclitari cæperunt. Quo exemplo docemur, vanas omnino illorum vires esse, quos diuina vltio persequitur. Quia enim Deus exercituum Dominus est, minutissima quæq; contra hostes suos armare poterit, vt illis domandis & coercendis sufficiant. Ita ventus, quo nihil vanius est & instabilius, si ita Deus velit, omnia turbat & subuertit. Et in Ægypto olim fornacis fuligine, ranas, pediculos, cimices, muscas & minutissima infecta, Pharaonis vitiores fuisse legimus. Nemo igitur vel suis viribus confidat, vel Deo scelerum pœnas exigenti reluctetur. Licet enim interdum contumacibus aliqua salutis spes affulgeat, clauda tamen vere & fallax illa est, & frivola sunt quæcunq; ex carne quæruntur præsidia. Vnica autem & certa salutis ratio est, si ad Deum conuersi, cum illo in gratiam redeamus.
units.tr: Next comes a more careful description of the danger these men brought upon themselves. For the storm wind seized the ship with such force that they could not resist it. So, accompanied by wind and waves, they were tossed about by uncertain turns. And although they were carried to the island of Clauda, they could hardly hold on to it there. Soon, however, they were also frustrated there, and they began to be in danger, both from the boat and from the whole ship. From this example we are taught that the strength of those whom divine vengeance pursues is altogether empty. For because God is the Lord of hosts, he can arm even the smallest things against his enemies, so that they suffice to tame and restrain them. Thus the wind, than which nothing is more empty and unstable, if God so wills, disturbs and overturns all things. We read that in Egypt of old, Pharaoh was vexed by soot from the furnace, by frogs, lice, gnats, flies and the tiniest insects. Therefore let no one trust in his own strength, or struggle against God when he exacts the punishment of sins. For although some hope of salvation sometimes gleams for the stubborn, that hope is in truth lame and deceptive, and whatever protections are sought from the flesh are frivolous. There is only one sure way of salvation: to turn to God and be reconciled with him.

units.la: Porrò accedit malis istis, quòd ipsi suis manibus iactum facere coguntur. In tantum modò animis mutati sunt, vt necessaria quoque ipsi sua sponte abijciant, qui paulò ante iuxta Lasæam aliquanto incommodius hybernare noluerunt: & nunc de vita soliciti sunt, qui autea delitias & summam rerum omnium commoditatem vnicè quærebant. Est hæc fere omnium illorum fors, qui vt Deo obediant, vilil omnino ferre, nec quicquam amittere volunt, etiam ex ijs quæ luxui duntaxat & voluptati seruiunt. Tandem enim ipsi omnia erogare & abijcere coguntur, & ea quoq; amittunt, sine quibus vita sustentari nequit. Nam tritum & verum est dictum illud, Quod non capit Christus, rapit fiscus. Et fere tyrannis excedendi propinantur, qui in fide & religionis causa de fortunis suis periclitari noluerunt. Similiter medicus excruciandi traduntur, qui gulæ & libidini suæ, Deo monente, frænum inijcere dedignantur. Quid, quòd tales plerunque conscientijs suis ita anguntur, vt illarum tranquillitatem omnibus fortunis & opibus suis (modò id fieri posset) libenter redimerent? Quin ergo nos nostraq; omnia Christo consecramus, qui retributionem liberalem & amplam omnibus ijs pollicetur, qui propter nomen suum rerum terrenarum & vitæ huius iacturam faciunt. Vide Matth.19. Marc.10. Abijciamus simul omnes salutis remoras, quando illam, si semel amissa fuerit, nunquam recuperari posse, scimus.
units.tr: Moreover, to these evils is added this, that they are compelled to make the jettison with their own hands. They are so changed in mind that they willingly throw away even necessities, those who a little before, near Lasaea, were unwilling to winter somewhat less comfortably. Now they are anxious about their lives, those who previously sought only luxury and the greatest comfort in all things. This is almost always the lot of all those who, when they are told to obey God, will bear nothing and want to lose nothing, not even those things that serve only luxury and pleasure. For in the end they are compelled to spend and throw away everything, and they lose even those things without which life cannot be sustained. The old and true saying is indeed: what Christ does not take, the treasury seizes. Those who would not risk their fortunes for faith and the cause of religion are often handed over to tyrants for exile. Likewise, those who, though God admonishes them, disdain to bridle their gluttony and lust are handed over to the torturers. What of the fact that such men are usually so tormented in their consciences that they would gladly buy back its peace with all their fortunes and wealth, if that could be done? Therefore let us consecrate ourselves and all that we have to Christ, who promises a generous and ample reward to all who, for his name's sake, suffer the loss of earthly things and of this life. See Matt. 19 and Mark 10. Let us all cast off together the hindrances to salvation, since we know that once it is lost it can never be recovered.

units.la: Postremò per multos dies nec Sol nec sydera lucent, & tandem vniuersa salutis spes intercidit. Et hoc quidem perpetuum est, vt mortiferis & exitialibus tenebris inuoluantur, qui in verbi diuini luce ambulare nolunt. Nec enim aliud nobis sydus datum est, cuius ductu per tempestuosum huius mundi æquor viam rectam tutamq; tenere possimus. Obseruandum verò hic venit, quòd cum immorigeris illis Paulum quoq; periclitari, & grauissimè tentari Deus patitur, ita vt ad preces conuersus diuina consolatione opus habuerit, vt sequentia docebunt. Est hæc piorum in hoc mundo fors, quæ multos offendit, quando hos vnà cum palàm impijs periclitari vident. Longè tamen alia est illorum ratio. Nam omnia ipsis in bonum cooperantur, & in medijs periculis bene sibi conscij, precibus suis Dei aures patere sciunt, eiusq; promissionibus freti, ab illo vires simul, quæ ferendo oneri sufficiant, & oportunam liberationem expectant. Cùm interim impios mens male sibi conscia infestet, & pericula illorum fere interitu ipso finiantur. Pauli ergo exemplum secuti, diuini verbi Cynosurâ obseruemus, vt si omnino nos quoque cum infelici mundo periclitari contingat, firmam tamen & ratam salutis spem in Deo repositam habeamus, qui suos non vltra vires tentari finit, & euentum felicem largitur, vt periculis omnibus erepti, transferantur tandem in regnum filij sui, Iesu Christi: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Finally, for many days neither sun nor stars shine, and at last all hope of salvation perishes. This indeed is the perpetual lot of those who refuse to walk in the light of the divine word: they are wrapped in deadly and destructive darkness. For no other star has been given to us by whose guidance we might keep a straight and safe course across the stormy sea of this world. Here it must be observed that God allowed Paul too to be in danger along with those unruly men and to be sorely tried, so that, turning to prayer, he needed divine consolation, as what follows will show. This is the lot of the godly in this world, which offends many, when they see them in danger together with the openly wicked. Yet their situation is very different. For all things work together for good for them, and, conscious of their good conduct even in the midst of dangers, they know that God's ears are open to their prayers. Relying on his promises, they expect from him both the strength to bear their burden and a timely deliverance. Meanwhile, a guilty conscience troubles the wicked, and their dangers usually end in destruction itself. Therefore, following the example of Paul, let us observe the guiding star of the divine word, so that if it should happen that we too are in danger along with this unhappy world, we may still have a firm and sure hope of salvation placed in God. He does not allow his people to be tried beyond their strength, and he grants a happy outcome, so that, delivered from all dangers, they may at last be transferred into the kingdom of his Son, Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXVIII.
units.tr: Homily 168.

units.la: Cum autem multa iam essent inedia, tunc stans Paulus in medio eorum, dixit: Oportebat quidem, o viri, mihi obtemperando, non soluere à Creta, nec accersere nobis iniuriam hanc & iacturam. Et nunc hortor, vt bono animo sitis. Iactura enim animæ nulla erit ex vobis, sed tantum nauis. Astitit enim mihi hac nocte Angelus Dei, cuius sum ego, quem & colo, dicens: Ne timeas Paule, Cæsari te oportet sisti. Et ecce donauit tibi Deus omnes, qui nauigant tecum. Propter quod bono animo estote viri. Credo enim Deo, quòd sic erit, quemadmodum dictum est mihi. In insulam autem quandam oportet nos exponi.
units.tr: When they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said: "Sirs, you ought indeed to have listened to me and not to have sailed from Crete, and so to have spared yourselves this injury and loss. But now I urge you to take courage. There will be no loss of life among you, only of the ship. For an angel of God stood by me last night, the one to whom I belong and whom I serve, and said: 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And see, God has given you all who sail with you.' So take courage, sirs. For I believe God, that it will be just as it was told me. But we must be cast up on a certain island."

units.la: Expositimus nuper tempestatem horrendam, qua Paulus simul & illius comites iactati fuerunt, quam Lucas tandem ita inualuisse dixit, vt nulla ipsis salutis spes reliqua fuerit. Atqui miretur hic aliquis, qualem se interea Paulus gesserit, tum erga Deum, cuius promissiones intercidere videbantur, tum erga socios, qui sua temeritate & inobedientia malum hoc sibijpsis conflauerant. Id verò omne ipsius oratio euidenter docet, quam in præsenti Euangelista commemorat, & quæ multas ob causas singularem consyderationem meretur.
units.tr: We recently described the dreadful storm by which Paul and his companions were tossed, which Luke said at last grew so strong that they had no hope of being saved. Someone here may well wonder how Paul conducted himself meanwhile, both toward God, whose promises seemed to be failing, and toward his companions, who by their rashness and disobedience had brought this evil upon themselves. All of this his speech clearly shows, the speech the evangelist now records, and it deserves special attention for many reasons.

units.la: Principio autem tempus notatur, & quæ rerum conditio fuerit, quando concionem hanc Paulus habuit. Quando nimirum inter pericula, quæ hucusq; descripta sunt, fames quoque prævalere incipiebat. Nec id temere factum fuit, quòd non ante ad concionandum prodijt, quando omnibus tumultuantibus dicendi locum non habuisset. Nunc verò cum animis simul & corporibus defessi, & amissâ omni salutis spe confidunt, consolationem simul & consilium opportunè profert. Vnde colligitur, illum inter pericula non ignauo metu superatum desperauisse, sed per preces ad Deum confugisse, qui illum ita confortauit, vt alijs quoque confirmandis & subleuandis sufficeret. Quo exemplo docemur in periculis non statim desperandum esse, sed in Deo spem & fiduciam habere debere, qui suos nunquam derelinquit, sicuti cum promissiones ipsius, tum exempla multorum abundè testantur. Pudendus ergo illorum error est, qui vt primum nulla in humanis spes superest, vel omnino desperant, vel ad Diuos aut alia illicita media conuersi, ex ijs auxilium & salutem quærunt. SED ipsam Pauli orationem videamus, breuem quidem pro temporis ratione, sed quæ res multas consyderatu dignissimas comprehendit.
units.tr: First, the time is noted, and the state of affairs when Paul gave this address. Clearly, this was when hunger too was beginning to prevail among the dangers described so far. Nor was it by chance that he did not come forward to speak before, when everyone was in an uproar and he would have had no chance to be heard. Now, when they were worn out in both mind and body and had lost all hope of being saved, he opportunely offers both comfort and counsel. From this we gather that Paul, though he was not overcome by cowardly fear amid the dangers, had despaired of nothing, but had fled to God in prayer, and God so strengthened him that he was able to encourage and support others. By this example we are taught that in dangers we must not despair at once, but must place our hope and trust in God, who never forsakes his own, as both his promises and the examples of many abundantly attest. Shameful, then, is the error of those who, as soon as no hope remains in human affairs, either despair altogether or, turning to the saints or other unlawful means, seek help and salvation from them. But let us look at Paul's speech itself, brief indeed for the occasion, yet containing many matters most worthy of consideration.

units.la: Primò inobedientiam, quia sibijpsis tanti periculi authores fuerint, exprobrat. Inde verò ordiatur, partim vt causam totius mali, peccatum videlicet suum agnoscant: partim vt recenti malo edocti, ipsum æquiori animo audiant. Interim modestissimè hoc agit, vt potius officij admonere, quàm miseris insultare videatur. Docemur hoc loco, argui quidem debere temeritatem & inobedientiam illorum, qui sibijpsis mala conciliant, non tamen insultandum esse amarulentius ijs, qui iam ante plus satis miseri & afflicti sunt, ne alioqui dolentibus dolorem acerbiorem addamus. Et sanè gra- uiter omnino peccant, qui cum rebus adhuc integris nihil potuerint consulendo præstare, in aduersis aliorum consilia nimis improbè & amarulenter exagitant. Qui vt aliorum iniqui iudices sunt, ita calamitosis calamitatem addunt, quod à Christiana charitate alienissimum est. Simul verò illos quoque suo exemplo Paulus arguit, qui si semel non audiantur, in posterum quoq; à consulendo in vniuersum abstinent, nec quicquam cum illis commercij amplius habere volunt, quibus antea nequicquam consuluerunt.
units.tr: First, he reproaches their disobedience, because they had been the authors of so great a danger to themselves. He begins there, partly so that they might recognise the cause of the whole evil, namely their own sin, and partly so that, taught by the recent calamity, they might hear him with a calmer mind. Meanwhile he does this very modestly, so that he seems to be giving a reminder of duty rather than mocking the wretched. We are taught here that the rashness and disobedience of those who bring evils upon themselves ought indeed to be rebuked, yet we must not insult with more bitterness those who are already more than miserable and afflicted, lest we add a sharper pain to those who are suffering. And truly they sin gravely who, when they could do nothing helpful by advising while things were still intact, in adversity criticise the counsels of others too wickedly and bitterly. Such people are unjust judges of others, and so they add calamity to the calamitous, which is most alien to Christian charity. At the same time Paul rebukes by his own example those who, if they are not heard once, thereafter refrain altogether from giving counsel and no longer wish to have any dealings with those whom they advised in vain before.

units.la: Deinde magna animi fiducia illos Paulus consolatur. Hortor (inquit) vt bono animo sitis. Ratio, Quia nullius animæ iactura erit ex vobis, sed tantummodo nauis. Vbi cumprimis spectanda est Pauli dignitas, qua vinctus licet reliquos omnes excelluit. Nam qui omnium miserrimus videbatur, solus in rebus deploratissimis consolationem simul & consilium afferre potest. Et hoc quidem proprium Christi opus est, quòd in suis ministris, quando contemptissimi omnium putantur gloriosissimè triumphat. Docent hoc martyrum exempla, qui inter medios ignes & horribiles cruciatus tum voce tum exemplo spectatores partim terrefaciunt, partim ad similem fidei constantiam excitant. Quò & illud referri debet, quòd hodie etiam mundo & peccatis per omnia deditos, si quando aut morbis aut aliis periculis præueniuntur, apud solos verbi ministros consilium & auxilium quærere videmus, quos alioqui cane & angue peius odisse consueuerunt.
units.tr: Next, Paul comforts them with great confidence of spirit. "I urge you," he says, "to take courage." The reason follows: "There will be no loss of any life among you, but only of the ship." Here especially we must consider Paul's dignity, by which, though a prisoner, he surpassed all the rest. For he who seemed the most wretched of all alone can bring comfort and counsel in the most desperate situations. This is indeed the proper work of Christ, that he triumphs most gloriously in his ministers when they seem most despised of all. The examples of the martyrs teach this, who in the midst of fires and dreadful tortures, by voice and example, partly terrified the onlookers and partly stirred them to a like constancy of faith. To this should also be referred the fact that today we see even those who are wholly given over to the world and sin, if at any time they are overtaken by sickness or other dangers, seeking counsel and help from ministers of the Word alone, whom otherwise they are wont to hate worse than dog or snake.

units.la: Porrò, ne vanus quidam ardelio Paulus videretur, oraculum allegat, dicens: Astitit enim mihi hac nocte angelus Dei, cuius sum ego, quem & colo, dicens: Ne timeas Paule, Cæsari te oportet stisti. Et ecce donauit tibi Deus omnes, qui navigant tecum, &c. Habent hic singula verba pondus suum, & de multis obseruatu dignissimis admonent. Primò enim bonitatem suam nobis Deus declarat, quæ tanta est, vt huius etiam dum nos pro meritis castigat, obliuisci non possit. Nec enim perpetuò irascitur, sed inter medias afflictiones consolatur & consilio nos subleuat, ne vltra quàm vires ferre possint, tentemur. Et ita quidem nos curat, vt angelos quoq; nostræ salutis causa occupatos esse velit, cuius rei non pauca exempla hucusq; vidimus. Deinde autem Pauli ingenuitas consideranda venit, qua ille circa religionem & fidem vtitur. Propter hanc enim vinctum fuisse scimus. Eandem tamen ingenuè & liberè fatetur, vt non modò se Dei esse, verumetiam illum abs se coli audacter pronunciat. Tale quid Christus à nobis exigit dum iubet, vt se coram hominibus confiteamur. Et Pauli exemplum Martyres quoq; imitatos fuisse legimus, qui fidem suam in Christum ne dissimulare quidem, nedum diserte negare voluerunt. Docent præterea Pauli verba, non sufficere, vt nos Dei esse dicamus: quando diabolos quoq; huius imperio subijci constat. Sed cultum & obsequium omne à nobis exigit Deus, quod nisi præstemus, Christiani nominis professio nostra damnationi potius quàm saluti seruiet. Adhæc docet locus iste, quàm prosit sanctis Dei cultoribus cohabitare. Vt enim Pauló omnium animas, qui cum ipso vehebantur, Deus donauit: ita illum frequenter propter paucos bonos multis, qui excidiũ meriti erant, pepercisse constat. Nota enim sunt, quæ de Noe, Loto, Mose & infinitis aliis scriptura tradunt. Nec tamen eò rapi debent exempla ista, vt Dium cultum diuinum tribuamus, & ab illis petamus, quæ dare solius Dei est. Nam longe alius illorum vsus est. Partim enim impios quoq; suis cultoribus Deus obstringere vult, quò tutius & commodius inter illos agere possint: partim ipsorum fide & religionem testimonijs eiusmodi commendat. Vt verò pij conuictori bus suis prodesse solent: ita vicissim pauci impij, si qui illos impunè grassari patiantur, totius rebus publicam afferre consueuerunt, vt in Ionæ exemplo cernitur, propter quam nauseas simul & vecto res omnes periclitatos fuisse legimus, &c. Quæ si ab omnibus obseruarentur, maiori in precio boni haberentur, & inuisa magis esset impiorum hominum societas.
units.tr: Furthermore, lest Paul seem a vain busybody, he cites an oracle, saying: "For an angel of God stood by me last night, the one to whom I belong and whom I serve, and said: 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And see, God has given you all who sail with you,' etc. Each of these words carries its weight and warns us of many things most worthy of notice. First, God declares to us his goodness, which is so great that even when he chastises us for our deserts, he cannot forget it. For he is not angry forever, but in the midst of afflictions he comforts us and supports us with counsel, so that we are not tempted beyond what we can bear. And he cares for us to such a degree that he wills even the angels to be busied for the sake of our salvation, of which we have seen not a few examples up to now. Next, we must consider the frankness of Paul, with which he acts in matters of religion and faith. For we know he was imprisoned on account of this very thing. Yet he confesses it frankly and freely, so that he boldly declares not only that he belongs to God, but also that he is served by him. Christ requires something of this kind from us when he commands that we confess him before men. And we read that the martyrs also imitated Paul's example, who did not wish even to dissemble their faith in Christ, much less to deny it openly. Paul's words also teach that it is not enough for us to say that we belong to God, since it is agreed that even the devils are subject to his command. Rather, God requires of us all worship and obedience, and unless we render these, our profession of the Christian name will serve our condemnation rather than our salvation. Moreover, this passage teaches how useful it is for the saints, the worshippers of God, to live together. For just as God granted Paul the lives of all who were carried with him, so it is well known that he has often spared many wicked people for the sake of a few good ones who deserved destruction. For the things Scripture relates about Noah, Lot, Moses and countless others are well known. Yet these examples must not be carried so far that we attribute divine worship to them and ask from them what belongs to God alone. For their use is quite different. Partly God wishes to bind even the wicked to his worshippers, so that they may live among them more safely and comfortably; partly he commends the faith and religion of his people by such testimonies. But just as the godly are wont to benefit their companions, so conversely, when a few wicked people are allowed to rage unpunished, they are accustomed to bring ruin upon the whole commonwealth, as is seen in the example of Jonah, on whose account, we read, the sailors and all the passengers were endangered, etc. If these things were observed by all, good people would be held in greater esteem, and the company of wicked men would be more hated.

units.la: Postremò orationem suam concludens Paulus, denuò illos bono animo esse iubet. Addit præterea: Credo enim quòd sic erit, quemadmodum dictum est mihi. Quoq; minus dubitarent, modum effugij exprimit, dum ipsos in insulam quandam exponi oportere dicit. Vbi admonemur, Dei promissiones fide recipiendas esse, eò quòd ita rita fiant: non quòd ex nobis dependeat Dei veritas, sed quòd ea conditione opem suam & salutem Deus pollicetur, quòd ea solis credentibus obtingere debeat. Exempla huius generis in euangelio passim extant. Vbi tamen consolationis plenum est, quòd licet pauciss mi credant, illos tamen ab impijs Deus facilè discernit, & suorum rationem habet, quod in Iosue & Chaleb olim accidisse scriptura docet, quos solos in terram promissam Deus deduxit, cum soli ipsius promissis credidissent. Versemur ergo in horum meditatione diligenter, & cum hodie quoq; consolationes simul & consilia salutis Deus offerat, ampletamur ea fide constanti. Ita enim fiet, vt vitæ hu ius pelagus tempestuosissimum emensi, ad æterni salutis portum deferamur, per Iesum Christum, Dominum nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen. Sed postquam quartadecima nox superuenit, nauigantibus nobis in Adria, circa medium noctis, suspicabantur nautæ apparere sibi aliquam regionem. Qui & demissa bolide repererunt passus viginti. Ac pusillum inde digressi, rursum demissa bolide repererunt passus quindecim. Timentesque ne in asperalocain inciderent, de puppi iactis ancoris quatuor, optabant diem oriri. Nautis vero quærentibus fugere e naui, cum demisissent scapham in mare, sub prætextu velut e prora ancoras extensuri, dixit Paulus Centurioni & militibus: Nisi hi in naui manserint vos salui fieri non potestis. Tunc abscinderunt milites funes scaphæ, & passi sunt eam excidere. Et cum dies inciperet apparere hortabatur Paulus omnes sumere cibū, dicens: Dies hic decimus quartus est, quod expectantes ieiuni permanetis, nihil accipientes. Propter quod hortor vos, ut sumatis cibum. Hoc enim ad salutem vestram pertinet: quia nullius vestrum capillus de capite cadet. Et cum hæc dixisset sumpto pane gratias egit Deo in conspectu omnium. Et cum fregisset, coepit edere. Porro animis iam recreati omnes, sumpserunt & ipsi cibum.
units.tr: Finally, concluding his speech, Paul again bids them take courage. He adds: "For I believe it will be just as it was told to me." So that they might doubt less, he names the manner of their escape, saying they must be put ashore on a certain island. Here we are reminded that God's promises must be received by faith, not because God's truth depends on us, but because God promises his help and salvation on the condition that it comes only to believers. Examples of this kind appear throughout the gospel. Yet there is something full of consolation here: although very few believe, God nevertheless easily distinguishes them from the ungodly and takes account of his own. Scripture teaches that this happened long ago with Joshua and Caleb, whom God alone led into the promised land, since only they had believed his promises. Let us therefore dwell diligently on the meditation of these things, and since God today also offers consolations and counsels of salvation, let us embrace them with steadfast faith. For so it will come about that, having sailed the most stormy sea of this life, we are brought to the harbour of eternal salvation, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen. But when the fourteenth night came, while we were sailing in the Adriatic, about midnight the sailors suspected that some land was appearing to them. Letting down the lead, they found twenty fathoms. Moving a little farther on and letting down the lead again, they found fifteen fathoms. Fearing lest they run onto rocky ground, they cast four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to dawn. But when the sailors, seeking to escape from the ship, had let the boat down into the sea, under the pretext of putting out anchors from the prow, Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers: "Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved." Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away. And as day was beginning to dawn, Paul urged them all to take food, saying: "This is the fourteenth day you have waited on, remaining fasting and taking nothing. Therefore I urge you to take food, for this pertains to your salvation; not a hair of your head will fall." When he had said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the sight of all, broke it, and began to eat. Then all of them, now refreshed in spirit, also took food.

units.la: Vamuis Deus cultores suos varie tentari patiatur, ijsdem tamen (ut sæpe monuimus) cum filio simul & consolatione semper adest, ne tentationibus succumbant. Exemplum eius rei cum primis euidens in præsenti historia habemus. Cum enim eousque inualuisset tempestas, ut nulla salutis spes in humanis reliqua esset, angelum suum Paulo transmisit Deus, qui illi veterem promissionem renouaret, qua denuo confirmatus alios quoque confirmare & consolari posset. Nec tantum inanibus verbis miseros lactauit Deus, sed promissam opem fidelissime præstitit, ut suo loco videbimus. Priusquam enim eousque perueniat Lucas, quid interea factum sit, & ut alij quidem diuinæ promissioni crediderint, alij vero minus, commemorat: de quibus singulis ordine dicemus.
units.tr: Although God allows his worshippers to be tried in various ways, he is nevertheless always present with them, as we have often reminded you, with a remedy alongside the trial and with consolation, so that they do not succumb to temptations. We have a most evident example of this in the present history. For when the storm had so grown that no hope of salvation remained among men, God sent his angel to Paul, who would renew for him the old promise, so that, strengthened again by it, he might also be able to strengthen and console others. Nor did God merely raise up the wretched with empty words, but most faithfully provided the promised help, as we shall see in its place. For before Luke tells what happened in the meantime, and how some indeed believed the divine promise while others believed less, he recounts these things, and we shall speak of each of them in order.

units.la: Et quidem primi omnium nautæ producuntur, qui cum in Adriatico mari ex signis quibusdam terram non procul abesse putarent, mox omnem diligentiam adhibent, ut littus attingant. Bolide enim (qua massa plumbea est ex fune dependens) maris profunditatem metiuntur, & reliqua etiam pro tempore necessaria haud dubie præparant. Id quod fidei opus videri poterat, dum itase diuinæ promissioni accommodant. Caeterum vbi iterum demissa bolide maris profunditatem vehementer decrescere sentiunt, nouo timore perculsi & promissionis oraculi, diuini immemores, turpissimæ fugam, summæ & detestabili perfidiæ coniunctam, moliuntur. Nam scapha demissa, in illam descendere parant, quasi ancoras ex prora extensuri, cum interim sibi ipsis consulere & periclitantes vt flores omni auxilio destituere in animo habeant. Elucet hic quod carnis ingenium sit, adeoque omnes qui carnis rationem sequi sibi ipsis propo suerunt. Deluduntur hi primum Dei promissionibus, & illis se accommodant: quando nimirum rei euentus hos conuenire videtur, & successum sibi ipsis polliceri possunt. Mox vero, cum noua periculorum facies oboritur, quæ successus spem euerit, fidei plane renunciant, & ad carnis consilia reuerti seipsos cum erga Deum tum erga homines turpissimos dare consueuerunt. Quod enim nautæ isti fecerunt, hoc ipsum in Israelitis quoque videmus. Qui cum primo liberationem sibi diuinitus promissi audirent, magna cum reuerentia Dei consilium amplexantur. Vt primum vero Pharao Mosis & Aaronis postulatione irritatus seruitutem illis aggrauaret, diuinæ promissionis oblitì, in conuitia erumpunt, clamantes: Videat Dominus super vos, & iudicet, qui fœtere fecistis odorem nostrum coram Pharaone & coram seruis eius, dando scilicet gladium in manus eorum, vt nos interficiant, &c. Exod. 5. cap. Idem, cum auro & pretiosa suppellectile onustis ex Ægypto migrandum esset, alacres iter capessunt, vbi vero ad mare rubrum consistentes, hostium turmas sibi a tergo imminere vident, mox Mosem & Aaronem, fidelissimos Dei seruos, proditionis & latrocinij insimulant. Exodi decimoquarto capite. Rursum periculo illo miraculose erepti, mentis lætitiam cantu quoque testantur. Verum illico ad murmur & querelas redeunt, quando cibi & potus inopia premuntur. Sed quid hæc de Israelitis dicere opus est, cum hodie huius generis exempla passim
units.tr: And first of all the sailors are brought forward, who, supposing from certain signs that land was not far off in the Adriatic Sea, soon apply all diligence to reach the shore. For with the lead (a leaden weight hanging from a rope) they measure the depth of the sea, and undoubtedly also prepare the other things needed for the moment. This could have seemed an act of faith, so long as they were adapting themselves to the divine promise. But when, after letting the lead down again, they perceive that the depth of the sea is greatly decreasing, struck with a new fear and mindful neither of the promise nor of the oracle of God, they plot a most shameful flight, joined with the greatest and most detestable faithlessness. For, letting down the boat, they prepare to climb into it, as though about to put out anchors from the prow, while in fact they intend to look to themselves and to abandon, as though they were dead, the people in peril and destitute of all help. Here is revealed what the nature of the flesh is, and so are all those who have chosen to follow the reasoning of the flesh. At first they are deluded by God's promises and accommodate themselves to them, since indeed the outcome of the matter seems to agree with them, and they can promise themselves success. But soon, when a new face of dangers appears that overturns the hope of success, they utterly renounce faith and are accustomed to turn back to the counsels of the flesh, giving themselves over to the most shameful conduct both towards God and towards men. For what those sailors did, we see the same thing in the Israelites too. When they first heard the deliverance promised to them by God, they embraced the plan with great reverence for God. But as soon as Pharaoh, provoked by the demand of Moses and Aaron, made their servitude heavier, forgetting the divine promise, they burst out into reproaches, crying: "The Lord look upon you and judge, you who have made our odour to stink before Pharaoh and before his servants, putting a sword into their hands to kill us," and so on. Exodus, chapter 5. Again, when they were to migrate out of Egypt laden with gold and precious household goods, they set out on the journey eagerly; but when they stood by the Red Sea and saw the troops of their enemies bearing down upon them from behind, at once they accused Moses and Aaron, the most faithful servants of God, of treachery and robbery. Exodus, chapter 14. Again, miraculously snatched from that peril, they bore witness to their joy of mind even with song. Yet straightway they returned to murmuring and complaints, when they were pressed by a lack of food and drink. But why is it necessary to speak of the Israelites in this way, when examples of this kind are found everywhere today,

units.la: Nautarum incredulitas & perfidia.
units.tr: The unbelief and treachery of the sailors.

units.la: Carnis ingenium in periculis. passim extent, & hæc ferè potissima causa fit, propter quam à fide homines deficiunt, et præceptorum Dei immemores officium negligunt? Discamus itaq; carnis ratione à verbo Dei longè remouendam esse, & in tentationibus ad hoc solum, non ad illam respici debere. Hæc enim, quia nihil præter præsentem rerum conditionem videre potest, facilè omni spe deijcitur. At vera fides in Dei solius verbū intenta labi nescit, cum omnipotentē illum esse sciat, de cuius voluntate per verbum certior facta est. Vide de hoc Abrahami exemplum, quod Paulus ad Roman. cap. 4. diligenter & pulchè tractat. Rursum in nautis istis videre licet, quo ferè ingenio prædití sint confidentes isti, qui & saniora consilia spernunt & admonitiones pias fidasq; auersantur. Hoc enim illos fecisse supra vidimus, dum Centurioni persuadent, ut contra Pauli consilium è Creta soluat. At ijdem vbi & se & alios in periculum adduxerunt, nunc ignauo metu superati, socios turpiter deserere statuerunt. Est hoc proprium omnibus ijs, quos suæ sapientiæ fiducia inebriat. Hoc ipsum sediticosi quoq; in rebuspub. turbarum auctores facere consueuerunt, ut nimirum vndiq; ingruescentibus periculis, ipsi sese subducere curent. Ita Core, cum totis castris tumultum concitauisset, ipse in tentorio suo animi securus considet. Num. 16. Et Absalon dum à suis pugnatur, mulieribus insidet, in communi omnium periculo suæ adhuc mollitiei & voluptati consulens. Docent exempla hæc, ut tales suspectos habeamus, nec aspernemur sobriorum hominum saniora consilia, quæ cum Dei verbo congruere sentimus.
units.tr: The nature of the flesh in dangers. and is this not almost the chief cause for which men fall away from faith and, forgetful of God's precepts, neglect their duty? Let us learn, then, that the reasoning of the flesh must be kept far from the Word of God, and that in temptations we ought to look to this alone and not to that. For the flesh, since it can see nothing beyond the present state of affairs, is easily cast down from all hope. But true faith, fixed on the Word of God alone, knows not how to slip, since it knows that he is almighty, of whose will it has been made certain through the Word. See on this the example of Abraham, which Paul handles diligently and beautifully in Romans, chapter 4. Again, in these sailors we may see what sort of disposition these self-confident men had, who both spurn the wiser counsels and turn away from pious and faithful admonitions. For we saw above that they did this when they persuaded the centurion to set sail from Crete against Paul's advice. But these same men, once they had led both themselves and others into danger, now overcome by cowardly fear, have decided to desert their companions shamefully. This is characteristic of all those whom confidence in their own wisdom intoxicates. Seditious men too are accustomed to do this in commonwealths, as authors of disturbances, namely that, when perils press in from every side, they take care to withdraw themselves. So Korah, when he had stirred up a tumult throughout the camp, sat himself carefree in his own tent. Numbers 16. And Absalom, while his men were fighting, sat among the women, looking after his own softness and pleasure in the common peril of all. These examples teach us to regard such men with suspicion, and not to despise the wiser counsels of sober men, which we perceive to agree with the Word of God.

units.la: Porrò ad Paulum transeamus, qui occulta spiritus sancti suggestione nautarum consilium animaduertens, Centurionem & milites admonet, ut illud prohibeant. Hic verò Pauli verba in primis consyderanda veniunt. Nisi hi (inquit) in naui manserint, vos salui fieri non poteritis. At qui incolumitatem iam antè omnibus promiserat Deus, cuius consilia irrita fieri non possunt. Quomodo igitur, nisi nautæ in naui manserint, euadere non possunt? Ergòne à nautis perfidis pendebat diuinæ promissionis veritas? At non de Dei potentia absoluta hoc loco Paulus disputat, cui facile fuisset absque nautarum simul & nauis præsidio omnes periculo subducere. At quia de miraculosa liberatione certam promissionem non habebat, imò omnes ipsos in insulam quandam exponi oportere didicerat, naturæ ordinem & quæ ad manum erant media, haudquaquam contemnenda esse putauit, ne promissionis diuinæ fiducia in confidentiam erumpens Dei tentatores faceret. Quo exemplo admonemur, Dei prouidentiam & fidem quæ huic nititur, non obstare, quò minus licitis & ordinarijs medijs pij legitimè vtantur. Vult enim abs se institutum ordine seruari Deus, quod multis exemplis doceri potest. In frugum prouentu certè absq; Dei incremento nihil succedere, scriptura docet. At eadem hunc ordinem nobis à Deo traditum esse testatur, ut nostris laboribus terra exculta, cœlestem benedictionem suscipiat, & frugibus proferendis idonea fiat. Ita in Oeconomia studium omne superuacaneum esse scimus, nisi dominus domum adificauerit. Laudantur tamen in scriptura industrij patresfamiliās, & in cantandis frugi matronæ laudibus nimius fere videri poterat spiritus sanctus. Prouerbiorum tricesimo primo cap. Recte ergo Paulus, nautas minimè dimittendos esse censet, quàmuis de dei promissione nihil dubitaret: Christi nimirum exemplum secutus, qui cum se angelorum ministerio & tutelæ commendatum esse certò sciret, nunquam tamen adduci potuit, ut è templi pinna sese præcipitando deum tentaret. Videndum tamen, ne dum medijs legitimè vti volumus, ijsdem nimium tribuendo à fidei meta exorbitemus, quæ nos in vnum deum intentos esse docet.
units.tr: Let us turn next to Paul, who, perceiving by a secret prompting of the Holy Spirit the plan of the sailors, admonishes the centurion and the soldiers to prevent it. Here above all Paul's words deserve consideration. "Unless these," he says, "remain in the ship, you cannot be saved." Yet God had already promised all of them safety, and his counsels cannot be made void. How then can they not escape, unless the sailors remain in the ship? Did the truth of the divine promise depend on faithless sailors? But Paul is not disputing here about God's absolute power, by which it would have been easy to bring everyone out of danger without the help of sailors and ship alike. Rather, since he had no certain promise of a miraculous deliverance, and indeed had learned that all of them must be cast up on some island, he judged that the order of nature and the means at hand were by no means to be despised, lest trust in the divine promise should break out into presumption and make them tempters of God. From this example we are taught that God's providence, and the faith that rests upon it, do not stand in the way of the godly making proper and lawful use of ordinary and lawful means. For God wills that the order he has established be kept, as can be shown by many examples. Scripture certainly teaches that nothing prospers in the yield of the fields without God's blessing. Yet the same Scripture testifies that this order was handed down to us by God, that the land, tilled by our labours, may receive heavenly blessing and become fit to bring forth fruits. So in household management we know that all effort is in vain unless the Lord builds the house. Yet in Scripture diligent householders are praised, and in the praise of the thrifty wife the Holy Spirit may seem almost excessive, in Proverbs chapter 31. Rightly, therefore, Paul judges that the sailors must by no means be dismissed, although he had no doubt about God's promise: following, of course, the example of Christ, who, although he knew for certain that he was commended to the ministry and protection of the angels, could never be brought to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple and tempt God. Yet we must take care that, while we wish to use means lawfully, we do not, by attributing too much to them, wander beyond the goal of faith, which teaches us to be fixed upon the one God.

units.la: Sed postquam hos Centurionem quoque & milites videamus, qui Pauli verbis obtemperantes, illico funes scapha abscinderunt, & illam in mare excidere passi sunt. Est hoc ingens fidei argumentum. Ita enim scapha seipsos spoliant, cuius in imminenti naufragii periculo maximus vsus esse poterat. Sed malo suo edocti, nullum tutius salutis præsidium fore intelligunt, quàm quod illis in deo Paulus monstrabat. Huic ergo obtemperandum esse censent, vt res omnis cadat. Imitemur nos horum exemplum, ut si non in initio statim, saltem periculis edomiti, dei verbo credamus, & huic nos moriges præbeamus.
units.tr: But let us now see the centurion and the soldiers also, who, obeying Paul's words, at once cut the ropes of the boat and allowed it to fall into the sea. This is a great proof of faith. For by it they deprive themselves of the boat, whose very great use they might have had in the imminent danger of shipwreck. But taught by their own harm, they understand that there will be no safer means of salvation than what Paul showed them in God. They therefore judge that they must obey this, so that everything else may fall away. Let us imitate the example of these men, so that, if not at the very beginning, at least when subdued by dangers, we may believe the word of God and yield ourselves obedient to it.

units.la: Cæterum rursus Paulum Lucas in medium adducit, qui denuo illos consolatus, quid porrò faciant, consulit. Nam ut cibum sumant, hortatur, & eius mandati rationes grauissimas allegat. Prima, à tempore sumitur. Dies hic (inquit) decimus quartus est, quòd ieiuni permanetis, nec quicquam sumpsistis. Ita verò periculi magnitudo exprimitur, qua impediti de cibo sumendo vix cogitarunt, certè toto illo tempore nulla ordinaria peregerunt conuiuia. Alter à necessario est. Hoc enim ad salutem vestram pertinet. Alioqui ex naufragio elapsi, inedia peribitis. Tertiò Dei promissionem magna cum fiducia repetit: Non cadet alicuius capillus de capite. Et sic illis occurrit, qui cibi vsum iam iam periturus & moriturus inutilem fore dicere poterant. Tandem suo exemplo illos excitat. His enim dicens, panem sumit, & in omnium conspectu gratias agens Deo frangit & edere cœpit, non aliquod videns animi timidi aut parum præsentis argumentum. Ita vero omnium animos recreat, ut & ipsi nova salutis spe concepta cibum sumant, ut imminentibus laboribus posse sufficere. Et in his quidem vera fidei ingenium cernitur. Quo propius enim instat naufragij periculum, quo minus spei apparet, eò considentior est Pauli animus, ut solus aliis quoq; animum et vires addat. Vbi simul patet, non sibi ipsis modo, verumetiam omnibus aliis utiles esse eos, qui vera fide præditi sunt: quando vnum Paulum omnia gubernare, omnibus consolatorem simul & consultorem adesse videmus. Tales ergo in precio habere discamus, quando illos contemptisse multis exitio fuit, ut omnium gentium historiæ testantur. Insuper vero obseruatione dignissimum est, quòd in tanto periculo cibum festinanter sumpturus Paulus, gratiarum actionis non obliuiscitur, sed illam in omnium conspectu adhibet. Decet hæc pios, imò ab omnibus iure exigitur, quando nos quotidiano pane diuinitus ali inter orandum confitemur, nec salutaris esse poterit cibus, nisi Dei benedictio accesserit. Qua causa est, quòd Christus quoq; morem hunc suo exemplo nobis frequenter commendat. Pudeat ergo sibi cum ingratitudinis tum impietatis porcos istos, qui nulla vel cum reverentia vel gratiarum actione mensas adeunt, nec non scurriliter illis nimiam superstitionè exprobrant, quos Christi & apostolorum exempla imitari vident. Dabunt isti aliquando sua proteruia graues pœnas. Nos vero diuinæ bonitatis memores, tam secundis quàm aduersis rebus officium præstemus, nec nobis sua ope deus deerit, qui nos filiorum loco adoptatos regni sui cœlestis hæredes fecit per filium suum Iesum Christum, redemptorem nostrum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Furthermore, Luke again brings Paul forward, who, consoling them once more, asks what they should do next. For he urges them to take food, and sets out the most weighty reasons for this command. The first is taken from the time. "This is the fourteenth day," he says, "that you have remained fasting and have taken nothing." Thus the magnitude of the danger is expressed, by which, hindered, they scarcely thought of taking food, and certainly through all that time they had held no ordinary feast. The second is drawn from what is necessary: "For this pertains to your safety. Otherwise, having escaped the shipwreck, you will perish from hunger." Thirdly, he repeats the promise of God with great confidence: "Not a hair of anyone's head will fall." And so he meets those who might say that the use of food would be useless, since they were about to perish and die at once. Lastly, he rouses them by his own example. For, saying this to them, he takes bread, and giving thanks to God in the sight of all, he breaks it and began to eat, showing no sign of a timid spirit or of one little present to himself. Thus he so restores the minds of all that they too, having conceived a new hope of salvation, take food, so that they may be able to suffice for the labours at hand. And in this is seen the true nature of faith. For the nearer the danger of shipwreck presses, and the less hope appears, the more confident is Paul's spirit, so that he alone adds courage and strength to the others also. Here it is plain that those who are endowed with true faith are useful not only to themselves but also to all others: since we see that Paul alone steers everything, and is at hand for all as both comforter and counsellor. Let us learn therefore to hold such men in esteem, since despising them has been the ruin of many, as the histories of all nations bear witness. Moreover, it is most worthy of observation that Paul, about to take food hastily in so great a danger, does not forget thanksgiving, but offers it in the sight of all. This becomes the godly, indeed it is rightly demanded of all of us, since in prayer we confess that we are fed daily with bread by God's gift, and food cannot be wholesome unless God's blessing is added. For this reason Christ too commends this custom to us often by his example. Let those swine be ashamed, then, both of their ingratitude and of their impiety, who approach their tables with no reverence or thanksgiving, and who also mockingly reproach with excessive superstition those who see that the examples of Christ and the apostles are to be imitated. Some of them will one day pay heavy penalties for their insolence. But we, mindful of the divine goodness, should discharge our duty in prosperity as well as in adversity, nor will God, who has made us adopted as sons and heirs of his heavenly kingdom through his Son Jesus Christ our redeemer, be lacking to us with his help: to whom be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXX.
units.tr: Homily 170.

units.la: Eramus vero vniuersæ animæ in naui ducentæ septuaginta sex. Et satiati cibo, alleuabant nauem, eiicientes triticum in mare. Cum autem dies esset, terram non agnoscebant: sinum vero quendam animaduerterunt habentem littus, in quod cogitabant appellere nauem. Et cum anchoras sustulissent, committebant se mari, simul laxatis iuncturis gubernaculorum, & sublato artemone ad aurae flatum, tendebant ad litus. Cum vero incidissent in locum bimarem, impegerunt nauem. Ac prora quidem infixa manebat immobilis, puppis vero solvebatur a vi undarum. Porro militum consilium erat, ut vinctos occiderent, ne quis postquam enatasset, aufugeret. At Centurio volens seruare Paulum, prohibuit eos a consilio, iussitque ut qui possent natare, abiicerent se primos, & in terram euaderent: caeteri-que partim in tabulis, partim in quibusdam fragmentis nauis. Et sic factum est, ut omnes incolumes euaderent in terram.
units.tr: Now we were in all in the ship two hundred and seventy-six souls. And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, casting out the wheat into the sea. When it was day, they did not recognise the land, but they perceived a certain bay with a shore, into which they planned to run the ship aground. So when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves to the sea, loosing the ropes of the rudders at the same time and hoisting the foresail to the breeze, and they made for the shore. But when they had fallen into a place where two seas met, they drove the ship aground. The prow stuck fast and remained immovable, but the stern was broken up by the force of the waves. Now the soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any of them, after swimming ashore, should escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from this plan, and ordered that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first and make for land, and the rest should follow, some on planks, some on pieces of the ship. And so it came about that all of them got safely to land.

units.la: Fidelis quidem & verax est Deus in promissionibus suis, idem tamen suorum fidem multiuariam exercere solet, non quod ex nostris miseriis & querelis voluptatem capiat, sed quod illud fidei nostrae confirmandae vehementer feruit, quando veritatem Dei per omnia aduersa victricem eniti, nec vllis rebus impediri posse videmus. Et hoc quidem præsens quoque historia referri debet, in qua Paulum cum suis ex naufragio saluauit quidem Deus, sicuti se factsurum esse promiserat, interim vero ipsorum fidem nouis subinde insultibus exercuit. Id vero euidentissime patebit, si singula huius loci ordine consyderemus.
units.tr: God is faithful and true in his promises, yet he is accustomed to test the faith of his people in many ways. He does not take pleasure in our miseries and complaints, but he strongly desires to confirm our faith, when we see that the truth of God strives on victoriously through all adversities and cannot be hindered by anything. This present history must also be related for this purpose, in which God indeed saved Paul and his companions from shipwreck, as he had promised he would, but meanwhile he tested their faith with new assaults from time to time. This will be most clearly seen if we consider the individual parts of this passage in order.

units.la: Et primò quidem numerus omnium, qui in eadem naui cum Paulo fuerunt, indicatur, quifuit animarum ducentarum & septuaginta sex. Voluit vero numerum istum diserte exprimi spiritus sanctus,
units.tr: And first, the number of all who were in the same ship with Paul is given, which was two hundred and seventy-six souls. The Holy Spirit wished this number to be stated expressly,

units.la: {y} Numerus navium fragorum. sanctus, partim quidem, ut ex illo certius nobis de Dei veritate constaret: partim vero ut evidentius esset liberationis illius miraculum. Quia enim certus erat hominum numerus, nemo illorum clam & insciis aliis desyderari poterat. Et cum in naufragij periculo pauci quoque sese invicem impedire soleant, dum quisq; etiam cum alterius periculo, propriae saluti consulit, haud obscurè suam manum Deus exeruit, quando tam multos simul salvos & incolumes in littus eduxit. Hinc vero colligere licet, Deo perinde esse vel multos vel paucos salvare. Ut enim omnia in numerato habet, & ad capillos quoq; & passerculos illius providentia extenditur: ita immensa & infinita est illius potentia, nec vel multitudine illorum, qui ope ipsius indigent, vel periculorum magnitudine superari potest. Ita olim omnes Israelitas simul per rubrum mare incolumes traduxit, quod illi facere tam proclive fuit, quàm vnius Mosis in Nilum expositi liberatio. Eadem ratione Israelem totum quadraginta annis in deserto miraculose aluit, non maiori negotio aut molestia, quàm postea Eliam coruorum ministerio pascere potuit. Quo Asa rex respexisse videtur, quando cum innumerabili Aethiopum multitudine congressurus, ita suam ad Deum orationem instituit: Domine, nihil refert apud te, ut auxilium feras vel multùm, vel his quibus non est robur, & c. secundo Paralipomenon decimo quarto. Multùm vero refert talem Deum agnoscere. Ita enim nec nostra ipsorum impotentia & miseria, nec periculorum multitudine terreri, aut ad desperationem adduci poterimus.
units.tr: {y} The number of those in the wreck. partly indeed so that from it we might be more certain of the truth of God, and partly so that the miracle of that deliverance might be more evident. For since the number of men was certain, none of them could be missing without the others knowing it. And although in a shipwreck danger even a few are wont to hinder one another, while each one looks to his own safety even at another's peril, God plainly put forth his hand, when he brought so many safe and sound to land together. From this it may be gathered that it is equally easy for God to save many or few. For just as he has all things numbered, and his providence extends even to the hairs of our head and the sparrows, so his power is immense and infinite, and it can be overcome neither by the multitude of those who need his help nor by the greatness of the dangers. So once he brought all the Israelites through the Red Sea safe together, which was as easy for him as the rescue of Moses alone when he was exposed on the Nile. For the same reason he miraculously fed Israel for forty years in the wilderness, with no greater effort or trouble than he afterwards had in feeding Elijah by the ministry of the ravens. Asa the king seems to have had this in view, when he was about to engage the innumerable multitude of the Ethiopians, and began his prayer to God thus: "Lord, it makes no difference to you whether you bring help to many or to those who have no strength," and so on, 2 Chronicles 14. But it matters greatly that we acknowledge such a God. For in this way we shall be terrified neither by our own weakness and misery, nor by the multitude of dangers, nor be driven to despair.

units.la: Porrò vbi Paulo hortante cibum sumpserunt quotquot in naui erant, nauem per omnia alleuauerunt, sic vt triticum quoq; in mare abijcerent. Merciû enim & armamentorum nauis iactu antea factum fuisse audiuimus. Et eò quidem delicatulos illos necessitas adigit, qui contra Dei voluntatem portum commodiorem quaerere, nec praesentibus bonis contenti esse voluerunt. Interim haud vulgare fidei argumentum est, quòd triticum quoque effuderunt. Nisi enim certò credidissent, Deum ipsos seruaturum, nunquam hoc sibi persuaderi passi fuissent, vt quod vnicum reliquum erat vitae praesidium abijcerent. At nobis imitandum proponitur exemplum hoc, vt nimirum ipsi quoque, quando ita Deus iubet, ea etiam sponte relinquamus, sine quibus vita nostra seruari non posse videtur. Hoc ipsum Abrahamum, apostolos item & multos alios olim fecisse videmus, quorum fidem in scripturis spiritus sanctus commendat.
units.tr: Next, when at Paul's urging all who were in the ship had taken food, they lightened the ship entirely, so that they even cast the wheat into the sea. For we have heard that before this the cargo and tackle of the ship had been thrown overboard. Necessity compels these pampered men, who against God's will wanted to seek a more convenient harbour and were not content with the goods they had. Meanwhile, the fact that they also poured out the wheat is no ordinary proof of faith. For unless they had firmly believed that God would save them, they would never have allowed themselves to be persuaded to throw away the only remaining means of sustaining life. And this example is set before us for imitation, so that we too, when God so commands, should willingly give up even those things without which our life seems unable to be preserved. We see that Abraham, the apostles too, and many others did this in former times, and the Holy Spirit commends their faith in the Scriptures.

units.la: Sequitur ipsius naufragij descriptio, breuis quidem, sed quae multa simul concurrisse docet, quae & Pauli & aliorum fidem labefactare potuissent, si carnis potius rationem, quàm Dei promissa audire voluissent. Primò enim, licet terram eminus comparere videant, littus tamen ignorant. Nesciunt ergo an ad amicos vel inimicos peruenturi sint, cum non raro fieri soleat, vt qui ex naufragijs elabuntur, in inhospitas terras incidant, vbi à barbaris hominibus plus mali quàm ex mari, elemento alioqui truculentissimo, patiuntur. Quare eminus sese ostendens salutis spes, haud paruum simul terrorem admixtum habuit. Deinde, cum omni conatu ad littus contendunt, in locum bimarem nauim impingunt, vbi prora in fabulo haerente, puppis vi vndarum & fluctuum dissoluitur. Et hic quidem diuini oraculi veritas sese exerit, quo nauim periturum esse praedictum fuerat, quae iam salua & integra in littus peruentura videbatur. Atqui illorum typus nauis hac dici potest, qui contra Dei verbum in sceleribus suis felices esse, nec vnquam scelerum poenas daturi videntur. Nam illis quoque fere, dum omne periculum euasisse videntur, repentinus imminet interitus, quemadmodum multa eius generis hominum exempla testantur. Vide de his, quae Psalmo 37. & 73. scribuntur.
units.tr: Next follows the description of the shipwreck itself, brief indeed, but showing that many things came together at once, which could have shaken the faith both of Paul and of the others, if they had been willing to heed the reasoning of the flesh rather than God's promises. First, although they see the land from afar, they do not know the shore. So they do not know whether they will reach friends or enemies, since it often happens that those who escape from shipwrecks fall into inhospitable lands, where they suffer more harm from barbarous men than from the sea, which is otherwise most savage. Therefore the hope of safety, showing itself from afar, had a considerable mixture of fear with it. Then, as they strive with all their effort towards the shore, they run the ship aground in a place where two seas meet, where the prow sticks fast in the mud and the stern is broken apart by the force of the waves and surges. And here indeed the truth of the divine oracle shows itself, by which it had been foretold that the ship would perish, though it now seemed about to reach land safe and whole. Yet this ship may be called a type of those who, against the word of God, seem happy in their sins and never likely to pay the penalties of their crimes. For to them too, just when they seem to have escaped every danger, sudden destruction is generally at hand, as many examples of this kind of men bear witness. See on these things what is written in Psalms 37 and 73.

units.la: Tertiò milites de captiuis occidendis consilium ineunt, ne quis vbi natando littus contigisset, fugam caperet. Nec dubium est, illos legum seueritate ad sanguinarium istud consilium capessendum impulsos fuisse, cuius exemplum supra in Herodianis militibus habuimus, quorum manus Petrus, angelo duce, effugerat. Alterum decimo. Interim iniquitas haec summa est, quòd ne Paulum quidem excipiunt, vt vel huius vitae consultum cupiant, cuius consilio & precibus se vitam debere intelligebant. Sed hoc mundi simul & omnium, qui mundo seruiunt, ingenii est, quòd beneficiorum facile obliuiscuntur, & ea fere atrocissimis iniurijs compensare solent. Stulti ergo reuera sunt, qui mundo studia sua approbare volunt, & non potius in Deum respiciunt, quem remuneratorem vnicum & fidelissimum esse constat. Porrò quoad militum consilium, ipso naufragio grauius fuit periculum, quod iam Pauli simul & aliorum capitibus imminebat, vt iam plane deplorata videri posset omnium captiuorum sors, & vana censeri Dei promissio, qui salutem omnibus pollicitus erat. Sed huic quoque malo in tempore dominus medetur. Centurio enim Paulo consulcum volens, militum consilio obstat, quo minus illud exequantur. Simul vero iubet, ut quotquot natare possint, primi sese mari committant, & illos reliqui tabulis & nauis fragmentis adiuti sequantur: prudenter nimirum cauens, ne temere tumultuantes se inuicem impedirent. Et ita quidem factum fuit, ut simul omnes viui & incolumes in litus euaderent, sicuti fore Deus promiserat. HIC vero spectabilis omnino est diuinarum promissionum veritas, quam nullis aduersis impediri posse videmus. Hactenus certe omnia simul in Pauli necem coniurauisse videri potuerunt. Saeuit enim indomita fluctuum vi mare. Ventus aerem quoque in illorum interitum armauit. Terra nauim impulsam & infixam detinuit. Caelestes ignes & sydera suum fulgorem miseris negauerunt. Nautae perfidi fugam, milites vero truculentissimi sanguinarias caedes iam animo conceperunt. At omnibus istis superior fuit Dei veritas, qui saluos esse voluit. Debent ergo haec nobis quoque consolationem afferre inter mundi huius pericula. Hunc enim turbulentissimi maris instar esse experientia docet. At Dei promissiones habemus, qui suis se semper affuturum esse, per filium suum pollicitus est. Si ergo Deus nobiscum est, quis contra nos? Huius certe protectione tuti, per omnes aerumnas & undique orientia pericula in aeternae beatitudinis portum feliciter euademus, vbi nobis nunquam intermoritura regni caelestis hereditas destinata & praeparata est per Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: Third, the soldiers form a plan to kill the captives, lest any of them, when he reached the shore by swimming, should take to flight. There is no doubt that they were driven to this bloodthirsty plan by the severity of the laws; we have had an example of this above in the soldiers of Herod, whose hands Peter had escaped, with an angel as his guide. See chapter 12. Yet this iniquity is great, in that they do not even spare Paul, so that they do not even care for his life, though they understood that they owed their lives to his counsel and prayers. But this is the nature of the world and of all who serve the world, that they readily forget benefits, and are generally accustomed to repay them with the most atrocious injuries. Those therefore are truly foolish who want to win the approval of the world for their own pursuits, and do not rather look to God, who is known to be the one and most faithful rewarder. Moreover, as for the soldiers' plan, the danger that now hung over the heads of Paul and the others was graver than the shipwreck itself, so that the fate of all the prisoners might seem already utterly hopeless, and God's promise, which had pledged salvation to all, might be judged empty. But the Lord also remedies this evil in time. For the centurion, wishing to look after Paul, opposes the plan of the soldiers, so that they cannot carry it out. At the same time he orders that all who can swim should first commit themselves to the sea, and that the rest should follow them, helped by planks and pieces of the ship; prudently taking care, of course, that they should not hinder one another by rushing about rashly. And so it came about that all of them, alive and unharmed, got safely to land, just as God had promised. Here indeed the truth of the divine promises is plainly remarkable, which we see cannot be hindered by any adversity. Up to this point, certainly, everything seemed to have conspired together for Paul's death. The raging force of the waves in the sea was violent. The wind too armed the air for their destruction. The land held the ship fast when it was driven on and stuck. The heavenly fires and stars denied their light to the wretched men. The treacherous sailors already planned flight in their minds, and the most savage soldiers planned bloody slaughter. But the truth of God, who willed that they be saved, was superior to all these things. These things ought therefore to bring us comfort too amid the dangers of this world. For experience teaches that this world is like a most turbulent sea. But we have the promises of God, who has promised through his Son that he will always be with his own. If God is with us, who can be against us? Surely, protected by his care, we shall safely pass through all troubles and dangers arising on every side into the harbour of eternal blessedness, where the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, which can never perish, has been destined and prepared for us through Jesus Christ, to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: CAPUT XXVIII.
units.tr: CAPUT XXVIII.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXI.
units.tr: HOMILIA CLXXI.

units.la: ET cùm euasissent, tunc cognouerunt quòd Melite insula vocaretur. Barbari vero praestabant non vulgarem humanitatem nobis. Accensa enim pyra recipiebant nos omnes propter imbrem, qui immine-bat, & propter frigus. Cùm congregasset autem Paulus sarmentorum multitudinem, & impositet in ignem, vipera e calore prorepens, inuasit manum eius. Vt vero viderunt Barbari pendentem bestiam de manu eius, inter se dicebant: Omnino homicida est homo hic, quem seruatum e mari, vltio non sinit viuere. Et ille quidem excussa vipera in ignem, mali nihil passus est. At illi existimabant futurum, vt incenderetur, ac concideret repente mortuus. Diu autem illis expectantibus & intuentibus nihil mali illi accidere, mutata mente dicebant illum esse Deum.
units.tr: And when they had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Melita. The barbarians showed us no ordinary kindness: for they kindled a fire and received us all, because of the rain that was coming on and because of the cold. But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper, creeping out of the heat, fastened on his hand. When the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand, they said to one another: "Surely this man is a murderer, whom, though he was saved from the sea, Justice does not allow to live." He, however, shook off the viper into the fire and suffered no harm. But they expected that he would swell up or suddenly fall dead. When they had waited a long time and saw nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.

units.la: Ilum est hucusq;, vt inter maris & tempestatis pericula Pauli & suorum curam Deus habuerit, quemadmodum illi pollicitus erat. Sequitur, vt e naufragio liberatos deinceps quo que seruarit, & Paulo apud Melitenses primùm, deinde verò apud Romanos euangelij praedicandi occasionem praebuerit. Quibus docemur, Dei opera perfecta esse, & licet nouis quotidie periculis tentemur, non tamen ideò spem omnem abijci, sed noua quotidie à Deo beneficia expectari debere, qui aduersa secundis temperare, & labefactatos animos efficaci consolatione erigere consueuit. Praestat autem singula suo, quo descripta sunt ordine, consyderare.
units.tr: So far it has been shown how God, amid the dangers of the sea and the storm, took care of Paul and his companions, just as he had promised. It follows that he also kept them safe after the shipwreck, and gave Paul the occasion of preaching the gospel first among the Melitans and then among the Romans. From this we are taught that the works of God are perfect, and that although we are tested daily by new dangers, we must not therefore abandon all hope, but daily expect new benefits from God, who is accustomed to temper adversity with prosperity and to raise up downcast spirits with effective consolation. It is worthwhile, however, to consider each thing in the order in which it is described.
