units.la: Principio in quam insulam iecti, & quomodo ab insulanis excepti fuerint, narratur. Melite fuit insula, quae hodie Maltha est, Iohannitarum militum sedes, inter Siciliam & Africam iacens. Singularem verò Melitensium humanitatem commendat Lucas, qua illos exceperunt, & omni officiorum genere prosecuti sunt, prout loci & temporis ratio postulabat. Ita verò haud vulgare charitatis & hospitalitatis exemplum, quod imitemur, proponitur. Ignotos enim Melitensibus fuisse naufragos illos, nemini dubium esse potest, nec ab illis, quos omnibus fortunis spoliatos esse videbant, aliqua merces aut remuneratio sperari poterat. Quia tamen miseros esse videns suæ opû indigos,hæc illis officia præstant. Atqui hoc illud est, quod in Samaritani parabola Christus docet, Lucæ decimo. Ita vero omnes nos facere conuenit, vt nullo vel personarum vel futuræ retributionis respectu habito, charitatem in eos exerceamus, quos nobis subleuandos & iuuandos Deus offert. Et in primis erga peregrinos hospitalitatis nos meminisse decet, cùm quòd illi pluribus indigent, tum quòd hanc multis felicißimè cessisse apostolus testatur, qui angelos interdum sub hominum specie exceptos fuisse scribit. Hebr. decimo tertio. Maius tamen est & salutarius, quòd ipsum Christum excipi & foueri scimus ab iis, qui peregrinos in domus suas colligere non dedignantur. Et sanè temporarijs quoq; præmijs illa officia Deus remunerari consueuit. Propter Lotum ex nim Sodomarum ciuis, cum bello victi & capti præda ab hostibus traberentur, per Abrahamum liberati sunt. Et paulò post Melitenses hac ipsa occasione euangelij doctrina illuminatos fuisse audiemus, quòd naufragos tanta humanitate exceperunt. De maioribus nostris modò nihil dicam, qui hospitalitatis studio Heluetia apud omnes nationes summam laudem pepererunt. Quorum vestigia si sectemur, nobis quoq; laudem & fructum haud vulgarem parabimus. Simul vero hinc consolationem petant, qui exilium propter religionem sustinent. Nam qui Melitensium animos Paulo & reliquis naufragis conciliare & deuincire potuit, idem nobis quoq; vbiq; locorum amicos facere poterit, cum omnium hominum animos manu sua teneat, & totus terrarū orbis ipsius imperio pareat. Passim ergo impleri oportet Christi promissionem, qui decuplam retributionem ijs pollicitus est, qui pro pter ipsum & euangelium ipsius vel domus vel fratres & sorores, vel agros, vel amicos reliquerint, &c. Marc. 10.
units.tr: First it is told into what island they were cast, and how they were received by the islanders. Melita was the island that is today called Malta, the seat of the Knights of St John, lying between Sicily and Africa. Luke commends the remarkable kindness of the Melitans, with which they received them and attended to them with every kind of service, as the circumstances of place and time required. Thus an uncommon example of charity and hospitality is set before us for us to imitate. For there can be no doubt that those shipwrecked men were unknown to the Melitans, nor could any reward or repayment be hoped for from those whom they saw stripped of all their goods. Yet, seeing them to be wretched and in need of help, they gave them these services. And this is precisely what Christ teaches in the parable of the Good Samaritan, in Luke chapter ten. In this way all of us ought to act, so that, with no regard either to persons or to future repayment, we exercise charity toward those whom God offers us to relieve and help. And above all we should remember to show hospitality to strangers, both because they are in greater need, and because the apostle testifies that by it many have fared most happily, he who writes that angels have sometimes been received in the form of men. Hebrews chapter thirteen. Yet it is greater and more wholesome that we know Christ himself is received and cherished by those who do not disdain to take strangers into their houses. And indeed God is accustomed to reward these services even with temporal recompenses. For on account of Lot, a citizen of Sodom, when he had been defeated in war and taken, and was being dragged away as booty by the enemies, he was freed through Abraham. And a little later we shall hear that the Melitans were enlightened by the teaching of the gospel on this very occasion, because they received the shipwrecked men with such kindness. I will say nothing for now of our own forefathers, who by their zeal for hospitality won the highest praise among all nations in Helvetia. If we follow their footsteps, we too shall win no ordinary praise and fruit. At the same time let those who endure exile for religion take comfort from this. For he who was able to win over and bind to Paul and the other shipwrecked men the hearts of the Melitans, the same will be able to make friends for us also in every place, since he holds the minds of all men in his hand, and the whole orb of the earth obeys his command. Therefore Christ's promise must be fulfilled everywhere, who promised a hundredfold return to those who for his sake and the gospel's have left house, or brothers and sisters, or fields, or friends, etc. Mark 10.

units.la: At non diu apud Melitenses Paulum latere voluit Deus, sed mox illum insigni miraculo nobili tauit, quo ipsius apostolatum sanciuit, & eidem præclaram prædicandi occasionem obtulit. Huius verò singulas partes excutere proderit. Inter quas primo loco Paulus occurrit, quem sarmenta colligisse scribitur: Atqui hic Paulum seruilia opera facientem consydera, qui & vinculis & recenti tempestatis atq; naufragij periculo defatigatus, non contemnendam otiandi aut feriandi causam habere videbatur. At nouerat, in publicis necessitatibus neminem suo otio consulere, sed omnes simul quod possunt, in commune conferre debere. Arguuntur ergo illius exemplo ignaui illi sponsi Penelopes, qui cum nemini vel priuatim vel publicè vtiles sint, ex aliorum tamen laboribus viuere, imò voluptuari instituunt. Qui licet Pauli nomine & successione glorientur, adeò tamen nihil Paulini perstoris sua vel doctrina vel vita referunt, vt mirum sit, illos vel Pauli nomen ferre posse, à cuius imitatione tam alieni sunt. Caeterum Paulo sarmenta colligente, vipera, quæ in illis gelu torpida deliuisse videtur, calore animata exilijt, & illius manum mordicus inuasit. Erat hoc nouum & inspe-ratum planè vitæ periculum, quo & Paulus non mediocriter terreri potuit, & quod Melitensibus de illo pessimè suspicandi occasionem præbuit. Mox enim homicida esse suspicantur, quem vltio Dei persequatur, & illum è naufragio elapsum novo atq; haud vulgari exemplo punire instituerit: Fingebant enim gentes, δίκη, quam nos Vltionem dicimus, Ioui assidere, & scelerum pœnas ab hominibus exigere: nimirum quòd lege naturæ edocti, peccata à Deo puniri scirent. Quia verò inter peccata ab ipsa mundi origine atrocissimum semper iudicatum fuit homicidium, Paulum in quem singulare & insolitum exemplum edi putabant, homicidij potius, quàm aliciuis vulgaris peccati insimulant. Pudeat verò hic suæ truculentiæ Christianos homines, qui militiam mercenariam colunt, & fundendi sanguinis innoxij studium laudi ducunt, cùm præter naturæ legem Dei oracula habeamus, qui maledictioni subiectos esse docet, quotquot pretio conducti sanguinem funduñt, & terras homicidijs pollutas non aliter quàm homicidarum quoque sanguine effuso expiari posse affirmat. Deut. 17. Num. 34. Interim obseruemus hoc loco admirabilem Dei in rebus gubernandis prouidentiam, qua fit vt suam simul & suorum gloriam per ea maximè illustret, quæ huic cumprimis officere videntur. Ex eo enim Christum prædicandi occasionem Paulus habuit, quod illi atrocissimam infamiæ notam iam inussisse videbatur. Ita Mosen prius exponi & ex Regis aula in exilium eijci oportuit, quàm populi vindex constitueretur. Cuius generis multa alia exempla extant: quorum vsus est, partim ne quem temerè propter afflictiones, quas sustinet damnemus: partim, ne ijs, quæ noxiis aduersa incidunt, facilè offendamur, quando diligentibus Deum omnia in bonum cooperantur. Et hoc quidem Paulo quoque euenisse sequentia docent. Nihil enim casu repentino perterritus, vi[?]
units.tr: But God did not want Paul to stay hidden among the Melitans for long. He soon made him known through a notable miracle, by which he confirmed Paul's apostleship and gave him an excellent opportunity to preach. It will be useful to examine its individual parts. Among them, Paul first comes into view, the one who is written to have gathered sticks. Consider here Paul doing servile work. Though he was worn out by his chains, by the recent storm and by the danger of shipwreck, he might seem to have a fair reason to rest and take his ease. But he knew that in public emergencies no one should consult his own leisure, and that everyone ought to contribute to the common good whatever he can. So by his example are condemned those idle suitors of Penelope, who, though useful to no one either privately or publicly, nevertheless choose to live by the labours of others, indeed to live in luxury. Although they boast of Paul's name and succession, they show so little of Paul's zeal, either in doctrine or in life, that it is remarkable they can even bear his name, from whose imitation they are so far removed. Meanwhile, as Paul was gathering the sticks, a viper, which seemed to have been numbed by the cold among them, came to life in the heat, leapt out and sank its teeth into his hand. This was a new and wholly unexpected danger to life, which could well have terrified Paul not a little, and which gave the Melitans an occasion to form a very bad opinion of him. For they soon suspected him of being a murderer, whom the vengeance of God was pursuing, and who had decided to punish him, having escaped from the shipwreck, by a new and unusual example. For the heathen imagined that Justice [δίκη], which we call Vengeance, sat beside Jove and exacted the penalties of crimes from men, since, taught by the law of nature, they knew that sins are punished by God. But because murder has always been judged the most atrocious of sins from the very beginning of the world, they accused Paul of murder rather than of some ordinary sin, since they thought he was the subject of a singular and unusual example of punishment. Here Christians should be ashamed of their own savagery, those who practise mercenary soldiering and count it a glory to shed innocent blood. For we have the oracles of God, beyond the law of nature. He teaches that all who shed blood for hire are subject to the curse, and he affirms that lands polluted by murders cannot be cleansed except by the blood of the murderers being poured out too. Deut. 17. Num. 35. Meanwhile let us observe here God's wonderful providence in governing things, by which he displays his own glory and that of his people most brightly through those very things which seem most to hinder them. For Paul had his opportunity to preach Christ from the very thing which seemed to have branded him with the most atrocious mark of infamy. So Moses too had first to be exposed and cast out into exile from the royal court, before he was appointed the avenger of the people. Many other examples of this kind exist. We use them partly so that we do not rashly condemn anyone because of the afflictions he endures, and partly so that we are not easily offended by adversity that befalls the wicked, since for those who love God all things work together for good. The following passage shows that this also happened to Paul. For, not at all terrified by the sudden accident, he shook the vi-

units.la: Paulus mirâculo apud Melitenses innotescit.
units.tr: Paul becomes known among the Melitans through a miracle.

units.la: Paulus à vipera mordetur. peram in ignem excuti, nec aliquid mali patitur: imò sic veram experitur Christi promissionem, quæ futuram dicit, ut qui credunt serpentes tollant, & à poculis toxico infectis salui & incolumes discedant. Marc. 16. Generalis quoque binc doctrina colligitur, veteri nimirum serpenti in Christi cultores virus inspiret, lethaliter tamen mordere non poterit, eò quòd Christi liuore sanati sumus, qui suæ mortis merito & resurrectionis maiestate caput illius contriuit. Sed ad Melitenses reuertamur, qui cum Paulum præter opinionem suam nihil mali pati vident, cum viperæ morsu præsentissimum venenum inspirari sciret, mox mutata mente, illum ex deorum numero esse censent: nimirum gentilitio errore seducti, quo nouorum beneficiorum authores & insolitis miraculis rerum euentibus celebres pro diis habere solebant. Ita enim illos in proximis causis considerandis satan detinuit, ne altius ascendendo in veri Dei cognitionem peruenirent. Eodem igitur figmento Melitensium animos præoccupare voluit, & Paulum diuinis quoque honoribus illustrem facere, modo Christi fidem, quam renuum suum in primis oppugnari nouerat, impediret. Quoties enim mortalium pro Diis coli & adorari potius admittit satan, quàm verum Deum, cui soli honor ille debetur. Causa est, quòd qui circa alios occupantur, manifestum salutis periculum subeunt. At qui vnum Deum colunt, excusso iugo diaboli, salutem veram inueniunt. Nemini ergo mirum videatur in Papatu falsis signis & diabolicis præstigiis cultum Diuorum stabiliri, quos olim Dei organa selecta fuisse scimus. Nec enim illos adorari & inuocari molestum est satanæ, modò doctrinam ipsorum vilipendi videat, quæ solius Dei cultores & vitæ hæredes facit. Et sanè profunda nimis est satanæ astutia, qui licet Pauli seculo ceteris coactus sit, postea tamen Melitensium superstitiosam de Paulo sententiam longè latéq; diffudit, per eos, qui Pauli nomine & familia gloriantes in tollendis & permulcendis serpentibus præstigiosa multa faciunt. Sed facilè hoc vno argumento illorum impietas arguitur, quòd serpentibus tantopere delectantur, quos primum ad seducendos homines diaboli instrumentum fuisse constat. Obseruemus autem hot loco vulgi inconstantiam, cuius simile exemplum, sed diuersi ordinis, supra in Lystrensibus vidimus. Illi enim, quem primò Deum esse dicunt, mox pro facinorosò habent & lapidibus obruunt. At isti, quem modò latronem dixere, nunc inter Deos numerant. Extant huius generis multa, & quotidie fiunt, quæ varium & mutabile semper vulgi ingenium esse docent. Stulti ergo & miseri sunt, qui huic fidendum esse arbitrantur, & non potius in vno Deo sperant, qui vindicem nobis constituit omnis mali acerrimum, filium suum Iesum Christum: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: Paul is bitten by a viper. ...shook it off into the fire and suffers no harm at all. Indeed, he thus experiences the true promise of Christ, which says that those who believe will take up serpents, and will leave unharmed and safe after drinking poisoned cups. Mark 16. A general doctrine is also drawn from this: the old serpent may breathe his venom into the worshippers of Christ, but he will not be able to bite them to death, because we have been healed by the bruising of Christ, who by the merit of his death and the majesty of his resurrection crushed the serpent's head. But let us return to the Melitans. When they see that Paul, contrary to their expectation, suffers no harm, although they knew that the most immediate poison is breathed in by the bite of a viper, they quickly change their minds and judge him to be one of the gods. Doubtless they were led astray by heathen error, by which they were accustomed to regard as gods the authors of new benefits and those made famous by unusual miracles. For Satan held them back in this way from weighing the nearer causes, so that they would not rise higher and reach the knowledge of the true God. So by this fiction he wanted to forestall the minds of the Melitans, and to make Paul illustrious with divine honours too, in order to hinder the faith of Christ, which he knew was to be attacked above all among his own. For how often Satan permits mortals to be worshipped and adored as gods rather than the true God, to whom alone that honour is owed. The reason is that those who are busied with others face a plain danger to salvation, whereas those who worship the one God, having shaken off the yoke of the devil, find true salvation. Therefore let no one think it strange that in the Papacy the cult of the saints is established by false signs and diabolical deceptions, though we know they were once chosen instruments of God. For it does not trouble Satan that they are invoked and called upon, provided he sees their teaching despised, which makes worshippers of the one God alone and heirs of life. And indeed the cunning of Satan is too profound, for although in Paul's time he was compelled to let the others go, he afterwards spread far and wide the superstitious opinion of the Melitans about Paul, through those who, boasting of Paul's name and family, do many deceitful things in removing and soothing serpents. But this impiety of theirs is easily proved by one argument: they delight so much in serpents, which are known first to have been the instrument of the devil for seducing men. Let us observe here, moreover, the inconstancy of the crowd, of which we saw a similar example, though of a different kind, above among the Lystrans. For they first called him a god and soon afterwards regarded him as a criminal and stoned him. But these now count among the gods the man whom they had just called a robber. Many examples of this kind exist, and they happen every day, teaching that the nature of the crowd is always varied and changeable. Foolish and wretched, then, are those who think that one should trust in it, and who do not rather hope in the one God, who has appointed for us his Son Jesus Christ, the most keen avenger of every evil. To him be blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXII.
units.tr: Homily 172.

units.la: In illis autem locis erant prædia primati insulæ, nomine Publio, qui nos exceptos triduo benigné tractauit hospitio. Contigit autem patrem Publij febribus ac dysenteria vexatum decumbere. Ad quem Paulus intrauit, & cum orasset impositis ei manus, sanauit eum. Hoc igitur facto, cæteri quoque qui habebant infirmitates in insula, accedebant & sanabantur. Qui etiam multis honoribus nos honorauerunt, & soluentibus impositurunt quæ necessaria erant. Post menses autem tres nauigauimus in naui Alaxandrina, quæ in insula hyemauerat, cui erat insigne Castor & Pollux. Et cùm venissemus Syracusas, mansimus triduo. Inde circumlegentes deuenimus Rhegium. Et post vnum diem, afflante Austro, postridie venimus Puteolos: vbi repertis fratribus rogati sumus manere apud eos dies septem; & sic venimus Romam.
units.tr: Now there were estates in that region belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us kindly and entertained us hospitably for three days. It happened that Publius's father lay sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him. When this had been done, the others on the island who had diseases also came and were healed. They honoured us with many gifts, and when we sailed they put on board whatever we needed. After three months we sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island, whose figurehead was Castor and Pollux. We put in at Syracuse and stayed three days. From there we sailed round the coast and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind blew up, and on the next day we came to Puteoli. There we found brothers, and at their request we stayed with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.

units.la: Celebris plane & consolationis plena est sententia Iesu Christi, dicentis: Nullus est, qui reliquit domum, aut fratres, aut sorores, aut parentes, aut uxorem, aut liberos, aut agros, meâ causa & euangelij, quin recipiat centupla, nunc in tempore hoc cum persecutionibus, & in seculo futuro vitam æternam. Marci decimo. Et huius quidem rei exemplum euidens in præsenti historia Lucas proponit. Paulus enim, qui Propter Christum & euangelium omnibus, quae in mun-do praeclara & vtilia habentur, renunciauerat, nunc vero naufragus quoq; in Melitam enatauerat, mox innumeros fratres, sorores, parentes & amicos fidelissimos inuenit, qui & domus & agros, bona denique omnia cum illo communia habent. Imo qui propter vincula omnium in eo naufragio miserrimus videri poterat, tanta apud Melitenses authoritatis est, vt propter ipsum alijs quoq; omnibus, tum nautis, tum militibus & captiuis in Pauli comitatu benefaciant. Id vero in ijs, quae modo sequuntur, plenius patebit.
units.tr: The saying of Jesus Christ is famous and full of comfort: "There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or parents, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake and the gospel's, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life" (Mark 10). In the present story Luke sets out a clear example of this. Paul, who for Christ and the gospel had renounced everything in the world that is esteemed excellent and useful, and who, now shipwrecked, had also swum ashore on Malta, soon found countless brothers, sisters, parents and most faithful friends, who held their houses, lands and all their goods in common with him. Indeed, though in that shipwreck he might seem the most wretched of all because of his chains, he had such authority among the Maltese that for his sake they showed kindness to all the others in Paul's company, sailors, soldiers and prisoners alike. This will become clearer in what follows.

units.la: Nouum enim hospitalitatis exemplum in Publio, qui Insulae primas siue Praetor fuit, proponitur. Is enim in praediis suis, quae in proximo erant, exceptos toto triduo benignissimè tractauit. Et eò memorabilior est eius humanitas, quòd & princeps & dives existens, ignotos tamen & multis modis afflictos non aspernatur, vt fere diuitum vulgus, qui aliorum infortunia nihil ad se pertinere putant. Tum quòd sine delectu omnes simul excipit, id quod absq; molestia & sumptu maximo fieri non poterat. Nam ducentos septuaginta sex in ea navi fuisse, & omnes in litus incolumes euasisse, audiuimus. Discant hinc officium suum diuites & magnates, ne scilicet sibi solis à Deo data existimēt tanta dona, sed se dispensatores constitutos esse meminerint. Quare in egenos benefici sint, vt ipsorum copia illorum inopiae subueniat. Et sanè ingens illorum peccatum est, qui sui officij immemores, nemini condolent, & surdis auribus pauperum clamores negligunt. Qui tandem iuxta Solomonis dictum, Dei quoq; aures ad suas preces occludi experiuntur. Imò in nouissimo die Christum accusatorem suum habebunt. Vide Matth.25.
units.tr: For a new example of hospitality is set before us in Publius, who was the chief or governor of the island. He received those who had been brought ashore on his estates nearby and treated them most kindly for the whole three days. His kindness is all the more remarkable because, though he was both a leader and a rich man, he did not scorn strangers who were afflicted in many ways, as the rich generally do, who think the misfortunes of others no concern of theirs. Moreover, he received them all together without distinction, which could not be done without trouble and very great expense. For we have heard that there were two hundred and seventy-six people in that ship, and that all of them reached the shore safe. Let the rich and the great learn their duty from this. They should not think that such gifts have been given them by God for themselves alone, but remember that they have been set up as stewards. Let them therefore be generous to the needy, so that their abundance may relieve the poverty of others. Truly the sin of those is great who, forgetful of their duty, feel for no one and close their ears to the cries of the poor. In the end, as Solomon says, they find that God also shuts his ears to their prayers. Indeed, on the last day they will have Christ as their accuser. See Matthew 25.

units.la: Porrò hospitalitatis suae haud poenitenda praemia Melitenses recipiunt, idq; per Pauli ministerium, vt doceremur, neminem tam vilem esse, qui non magni alicuius boni nobis author esse possit, si beneficos nos illi praebeamus. Potest enim per quemuis mortalium nobis gratiam referre Deus: nec illorum merces intercidere solet, quicunq; alicui hominum propter Deum aut Christum benefaciunt. In praesenti autem duo narrantur praemia, quae ex ipso Paulo ipsi retulerunt. Primum Publij pater recepit, qui cum febribus & dysenteria, morbo prorsus incurabili, laboraret, Pauli ministerio sanatus est. Id vero ingens bonum fuisse, si vel corpus solum spectetur, nemo negauerit: vt interim de eo nihil dicamus, quòd hac occasione ad fidem adduci potuit. Vbi obseruare decet, quòd in ea curatione modum & ordinem à Christo praescriptum Paulus obseruat. Nam & preces adhibet, & aegrotanti manus imponit. Quo docemur non Pauli, sed Dei virtute miraculum hoc editum fuisse, qui sic filium suum, Iesum Christum (sicuti supra Petrus & Iohannes dixerunt) illustrare voluit. Longè enim aliter miracula ediderant apostoli, quàm Christus, qui absoluta & libera potestate vtens, solo verbo pronunciato, morbos & daemones pepulit. Apostoli vero & sancti Christi cultores inuocato Christi nomine hoc ipsum praestiterunt. Vbi illorum error confutatur, qui propter edita miracula illos inuocandos esse putant, & non potius ad miraculorum authorem, Deum, respiciunt, cuius honorem & gloriam illi praecipuè quaesiuerunt. Vide plura capite tertio & decimo quarto. Alterum praemium ad plures pertinuit. Nam curati Publij patris fama alios quoq; excitauit, qui & ipsi à diuersis morbis liberati sunt. Omnium vero hic finis & vsus fuit, vt Paulum Christi ministrum esse intelligerent, qui ab omni cum corporis tum animae infirmitate liberat, & proinde in illius merito salutem omnem quarerent. At quia de his saepè alias diximus, paucis haec perstrinxisse, modò sufficiat.
units.tr: Moreover, the Maltese received rewards for their hospitality, which they need not regret, and these came through Paul's ministry. We are taught by this that no one is so humble that he cannot become the means of some great good for us, if we show ourselves kind to him. For God can repay us through any mortal whatever, and the reward of those who do good to any man for God's or Christ's sake is not usually lost. In the present passage two rewards are recorded, which they received through Paul himself. First, the father of Publius was healed through Paul's ministry, for he was suffering from fever and dysentery, a disease wholly incurable. If we consider the body alone, no one could deny that this was a great benefit, to say nothing yet of the fact that it may have led him to faith. Here it is fitting to notice that in this cure Paul followed the method and order prescribed by Christ. For he both offers prayer and lays his hands on the sick man. By this we are taught that the miracle was wrought not by Paul's power but by God's, who wished in this way to honour his Son, Jesus Christ, as Peter and John had said above. For the apostles worked miracles quite differently from Christ, who, using his absolute and free power, drove out diseases and demons by a word alone. The apostles and the saints who worship Christ did such things by invoking the name of Christ. Here the error of those is refuted who think that the apostles should be invoked because of the miracles they worked, and do not rather look to God, the author of miracles, whose honour and glory they above all sought. See more in chapters three and fourteen. The second reward concerned many people. For the fame of the healing of Publius's father stirred up others too, who were also freed from various diseases. The purpose and use of all this was that they might understand Paul to be Christ's minister, who frees from every infirmity, both of body and of soul, and that they should therefore seek all salvation through his merit. But since we have often spoken of these things elsewhere, it is enough to have touched on them briefly here.

units.la: Caeterum Melitenses videamus, quos pro tantis beneficijs summam gratitudinem retulisse, Lucas scribit. Nam & honoribus maximis illos omnes prosecuti sunt, & discessuris, quaecunque ad profectionem necessaria erant, imposuerunt. Sunt isti non obscuri fidei fructus, quibus simul admonemur, quid ijs debeamus, per quos Christus & euangelij lux nobis innotescit. Quia enim illi nobis parentum loco sunt, cum illorum ministerio regeneremur, honorem merentur: non quidem diuinum, sed qualem parentibus debemus, & hominem ab homine recipere fas est. Et sanè Paulus presbyteros, qui bene praesunt, duplici honore dignos esse scribit. Prima Timoth.quinto. Vide ergo quàm egregiè, si dijs placet, euangelici sint, qui hoc nomine potissimum sibi placent, quòd ministrorum famam dicterijs & scommatis lacessere nouerunt. Vt vero parentibus non honore modò, verumetiam necessaria ad victum liberi debent: ita ministrū illa ab auditoribus conferri aequum est. Iussit hoc olim in veteri Testamento deus, vt videre est Numeri decimo octauo & Deutero. vigesimo quinto. Et Christus apostolos pecunias & commeatum secum gestare prohibet, eò quòd aliorum operarios rum instar ex verbi ministerio victuri sint. Matthaei decimo. Lucae nono & decimo. Quod nisi fas & æquum fuisset, peccassent vtiq; qui illa receperunt apostoli. Sed plura de his vide in priori ad Corinthios nono capite. Magna ergo illorum hominum ingratitudo est hodie (ne quid gravius dicam) qui cum ipsi nihil conferant ministris, simul ea quoq; inuidcnt & maligne interuertunt, quae ab alijs iam olim collata sunt, &c.
units.tr: Let us now look at the Maltese, whom Luke writes returned the greatest gratitude for such great benefits. For they honoured all of them very greatly, and when they were about to leave, they put on board whatever was needed for the voyage. These are not obscure fruits of faith, and they remind us at the same time what we owe to those through whom Christ and the light of the gospel become known to us. For since they stand to us in the place of parents, since we are born again through their ministry, they deserve honour, not indeed divine honour, but such as we owe to parents, and it is right for one man to receive it from another. Indeed Paul writes that elders who rule well are worthy of double honour (1 Tim. 5). See, then, how splendidly evangelical those people are, if we may say so, who especially take pleasure in this, that they know how to assail the reputation of ministers with insults and jeers. Just as children owe parents not only honour but also what is necessary for life, so it is fair that such things be given to ministers by their hearers. God commanded this of old in the Old Testament, as may be seen in Numbers 18 and Deuteronomy 25. And Christ forbids the apostles to carry money or provisions with them, because they were to live by the ministry of the Word, as workers do from their labour (Matthew 10; Luke 9 and 10). Unless this were right and fair, those apostles who received such things would certainly have sinned. But see more on this in the first epistle to the Corinthians, chapter nine. Therefore the ingratitude of those men today is great (not to say anything harsher), who, though they contribute nothing to the ministers, at the same time envy and maliciously twist what others have long since given, and so on.

units.la: Sed euoluto trium mensium spatio ad navigationem redeunt, cuius cursum ex Geographicis tabulis petant, qui de singulis accuratius edoceri volunt. Nobis in his duo observanda veniunt. Alterum est, quòd nauem Alexandrinam Paulus cum suis conscendit, quae sub Castoris & Pollucis tutela esse, gentilitio errore credebatur. Quo exemplo multi idololatriam & superstitionem quamuis inter indifferentia numerant, quasi Christianus illis absque Dei offensa, quoad externam conuersationem, communicare possit. Sed simul cogitandum erat, Paulum hoc non sua sponte, sed coactum fecisse, nec etiam consensisse impiae superstitioni, vel aliquid dissimulauisse in hominum gratiam. Minimè ergo ignauis illis Pauli exemplum patrocinabitur, qui prout tempora postulare videntur, quidius in religione vel simulare vel dissimulare consueuerunt. Alterum est, quòd longum maris ambitum emensi, tandem ex Syracusis, Siciliae oppido, in Italiam traiciunt, & Puteolis fratres siue Christianos inueniunt, apud quos, ita ipsis rogantibus, dies septem commorantur. Vbi & fratrum illorum charitas conspicitur, qui peregrinos tanto tempore non sine maximis impensis fouere dignati sunt: & Centurionis militumq; humanitas, qui in hominis captiui gratiam tot diebus substiterunt. Ita verò & Dei manus elucet, qui suos acceptos atque gratiosos facere solet, & sanctorum maiestas, quae in Cruce & afflictionibus maximè triumphat. Iam enim Paulus, vinctus licet, Imperatoris & Regis instar militès ad suum nutum obedientes habet. Similia prius quoque non semel vidimus. Et Baptistam Herodi metum attulisse, euangelistae docent. Quid ergo afflictionibus & Cruce offendimur? Quin vocationem nostram constanter tuemur, quando inter medios hostes Dei manus nos tueri potest, & in coelis retributionem expectamus, quam suo merito nobis acquisiuit Iesus Christus, dominus noster: cui debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in aeternum. Amen.
units.tr: But after three months had passed, they return to their voyage, whose course those who wish to be taught more exactly about each detail may seek in the geographical charts. For us two things here are to be observed. The first is that Paul boarded the Alexandrian ship with his companions, which, by pagan error, was believed to be under the protection of Castor and Pollux. From this example many count idolatry and superstition among indifferent matters, as if a Christian could have dealings with such people, so far as outward conduct goes, without offence to God. But at the same time we must consider that Paul did this not of his own accord but under compulsion, and that he did not consent to impious superstition or conceal anything to win men's favour. Therefore Paul's example will by no means defend those cowards who are accustomed, as times seem to require, to pretend or to dissemble in matters of religion. The second is that, after a long voyage round the sea, they at last cross from Syracuse, a town in Sicily, into Italy, and at Puteoli they find brothers, that is, Christians, with whom, at their request, they stay seven days. Here we see the love of those brothers, who thought it worth spending great sums to care for strangers for so long, and the kindness of the centurion and soldiers, who remained so many days for the sake of a captive man. Here too the hand of God shines out, who is accustomed to make his own acceptable and pleasing, and the majesty of the saints, which triumphs most of all in the cross and in afflictions. For already Paul, though bound, has soldiers obedient to his nod, as if he were an emperor or a king. We have seen similar things before, more than once. And the evangelists teach that John the Baptist struck fear into Herod. Why then are we offended by afflictions and the cross? Rather, let us hold fast constantly to our calling, since God's hand can protect us even among our enemies, and let us look for the reward in heaven, which Jesus Christ our Lord has won for us by his merit: to whom belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIII.

units.la: Et inde cum audiuissent fratres de nobis, prodierūt in occursum nobis vsque ad Appij forum ac tres Tabernas. Quos cum vidisset Paulus, gratias actis Deo sumpsit fiduciam. Cum autem venissemus Romā, Centurio tradidit vinctos Principi exercitus. Permissum autè est Paulo, vt maneret solus cum custodiente se milite. Post tertium autè diem, conuocauit Paulus primarios ex Iudæis, cumq; venissent dixit eis: Ego, viri fratres, cum nihil fecerim aduersus plebem aut instituta maiorum, vinctus Hierosolymis traditus sum in manus Romanorum. Qui cum examinauissent, voluerunt me dimittere, eo quòd nulla esset causa mortis in me. Sed contradicentibus Iudaeis, coactus sum appellare Caesarem: non quasi habeam, de quo gentem meam accusem. Propter hanc igitur causam aduocaui vos, vt viderem & alloquerer. Propter spem enim Israelis catena hac circundatus sum. At illi dixerunt ad eum: Nos neque literas accepimus de te a Iudaea, neque aduenientis aliquis fratrum nunciauit aut locutus est aliquid de te malì. Volumus autem ex te audire quae sentias. Nam de secta ista notum est nobis, quòd vbique ei contradicitur.
units.tr: And from there the brothers, when they heard about us, came out to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. When we came to Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the captain of the guard. Paul was permitted to live by himself, with the soldier who guarded him. After three days Paul called together the leading men of the Jews, and when they had come he said to them: "Brothers, though I have done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over into the hands of the Romans. When they had examined me, they wanted to release me, because there was no cause for death in me. But when the Jews objected, I was forced to appeal to Caesar, not as though I had any charge to bring against my nation. For this reason, then, I have asked you to come, so that I might see you and speak with you. For it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain." They said to him: "We have received no letters about you from Judea, and none of the brothers who have arrived has reported or said anything bad about you. But we want to hear from you what you think, for we know that this sect is spoken against everywhere."

units.la: Memorabiles quidem & multis nominibus praeclarae sunt res Pauli omnes, quas in suo apostolatu gesserit: inter illas tamen facilè primatum obtinet, quòd ex Iudaea Romam vsque tanto cum apparatu deductus fuit, vt illic coram Cæsare Christi & fidei Christianæ causam ageret. Quàm enim istud nouum & insolens totius mundi iudicio fuerit, facilè patebit, si quis Pauli personam, vilem & ignobilem, adhæc omnibus pene inuisam & exosam, cum Cæsaris & totius Imperij Romani maiestate, quam omnes populi & nationes pertimescebant, conferat. Nec enim vllis hominum rationibus effici potuisset, vt aut Præsides Romani eiusmodi hominis causa tantum laboris suscipere, aut Cæsar Nero, totus libidine & tyrannide ardens, talem in conspectum admittere & audire voluisset, nisi suam manum potenter exeruisset Deus, cuius totum istud negotium agebatur. Quæ causa est, quòd profectionem hanc omnem tanta diligentia Lucas describat, quam multis modis illustrem esse voluit Dominus, vt famæ nuncio præcurrente Romanorum animi ad excipiendum & audiendum Paulum excitarentur. Nec inanem aut irritum fuisse diuini consilij euentum, præsens hic locus abunde docet, in quo simul multa alia concurrunt, quorum consyderatio haud vulgariter nos erudire & consolari potest.
units.tr: All the deeds of Paul are memorable and famous in many ways, which he performed in his apostleship; yet among them the first place is easily held by the fact that he was brought from Judea to Rome with such a display, so that there he might plead the cause of Christ and the Christian faith before Caesar. How new and unusual this was in the judgment of the whole world will be easily seen if someone compares the person of Paul, lowly and obscure, and moreover almost hated and detested by all, with the majesty of Caesar and of the whole Roman Empire, which all peoples and nations dreaded. For by no human reasoning could it have been brought about that the Roman governors would take on so much trouble for the sake of such a man, or that Caesar Nero, wholly burning with lust and tyranny, would have wished to admit and hear such a man in his presence, unless God, whose whole cause this was, had powerfully stretched out his hand. This is why Luke describes this whole journey with such great care: the Lord wished it to be made famous in many ways, so that, with the news of it running ahead, the minds of the Romans would be stirred to receive and hear Paul. That the outcome of the divine plan was neither empty nor fruitless, this present passage amply teaches, in which many other things come together at once, the consideration of which can teach and comfort us in no common way.

units.la: Nam fratres è Roma vsq; ad Forappij & tres Tabernas Paulo occurrisse, Lucas scribit, quibus visis ille Deo gratias egit, & maiorem concepit animi fiduciam. Quo loco ante omnia Deus obser uandus venit, cuius dispensatione omnia hæc contigisse certum est. Is enim fratrum occursu seruum suum confirmari voluit, vt maiori cum fiducia deinceps Christi causam ageret. Quo etiam referri debet, quod nuper de Puteolanis fratribus audiuimus. Licet enim fortissimus esset Paulus, nec vincula modò, verumetiam mortem pro Christi nomine subire paratus esset, homo tamen erat, nec suis quoq; carebat tentationibus. Et sanè timere poterat, frustra se in ea vrbe pro Christi causa laboraturum esse, in qua impietas & tyrannis dominabantur. Vt ergo hac illum cura Deus liberet, fratres in illius occursum excitat, vt videret nō defuturos, quos & suæ constantiæ exemplo confirmaret, & qui ipsum certantem precibus suis iuuarent. Hoc igitur exemplo animati vocationem nostram constanter tueamur. Nam nec fructu carebit pium verbi Dei studium, nec Deus ipse deerit, cui facillimum est vbiuis locorum nobis laborum & periculorum socios adiungere. Deinde ipsi quoq; fratres Romani nobis consyderandi veniunt. Ad hos enim Paulum, priusquam hæc fierent, scripsisse scimus, in qua epistola & sui animi voluntatem erga ipsos abunde declarat, & se ad ipsos venturum esse pollicetur. Pro illo igitur officio gratos se illi præbent, licet multa ipsos afterrere possent. Primò enim non magnifico apparatu splendidus aduenit, sed facinorosi instar cum alijs captiuis vinctus adducitur. Quem verò nō eiusmodi hominis pudeat? Vel quis non ex illius comercio periculum metuat? Deinde per se periculosum erat inter Romanos Christi fidem & religionem profiteri, quæ Tiberio adhuc regnante (vt Tertullianus scribit) publico Senatusconsulto damnata erat. Adhæc non de illis modò, qui occurrebant, sed tota ecclesia, quæ Romæ erat, agebatur, in quam hac occasione diligentior & seueriorinquisitio instituì poterat. Sed vtut ista habeant, pietatis officium tanto apostolo, pro communi causa laboranti, negare ipsis nefas esse videtur, & proinde quodus periculum subire, quàm suo officio deesse malunt. Docent hæc quid Christi ministris debeamus, qui suo ministerio nobis salutis authores sunt, si quando illos propter doctrinam & fidem periclitari contingat. Non pudeat nos vinctorum, quando & Christum vinctum fuisse, & Dei verbum vinculis nullis constrictum posse scimus. Idem verò in se collatum olim putabit, quod in ipsos collatum fuerit. TANDEM ipsum quoq; Paulum inspicere conuenit, de quo duo dicuntur. Primum, Deo gratias egit. Quod non ita accipi debet, quasi prætéritis omnino fratribus illos ne allocutus quidem sit. Nam quia nō potuit non illi gratum esse illorum officium, ipsis quoq; illum gratias egisse, minimè dubium est. Præcipuè tamen Dei opus agnoscit, qui illos, vt tantum auderent, excitauerat. Id ipsum nos quoq; facere decet, vt hominibus quidem gratias agamus & referamus etiam pro viris, sic tamen ne nos Dei obliuio capiat, cui nos omne bonum acceptum ferre conuenit. Alterum est, quòd noua fiducia sumpta, magis confirmatur Paulus, cum vt det quales certaminis quod ipsum manebat, spectatores habituri sit. Vnde patet, sanctos etiam confirmatione opus habere, quemadmodum Petri & reliquorum discipulorum exemplo Christus docet. Cum enim se pro Petro orasse dicit, mox addit: Et tu conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Similiter doctrina etiam & admonitione, hortatione item & increpatione opus habent, qui perfectissimi videntur. Magna igitur illorum inscitia est & intolerabilis confidentia, qui se homines esse obliti, omnem doctrinam & correctionem magno cum fastidio respuunt.
units.tr: For Luke writes that the brothers came from Rome as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet Paul; when he saw them he gave thanks to God and took on greater courage of spirit. In this place, above all, God must be observed, for it is certain that all these things happened by his arrangement. For by the meeting of the brothers he willed his servant to be strengthened, so that from then on he might plead Christ's cause with greater confidence. To this also should be referred what we heard recently about the brothers of Puteoli. For although Paul was most brave, and was ready to undergo not only chains but even death for the name of Christ, he was nonetheless a man, and was not free from his own temptations. And indeed he could fear that he would labor in vain for the cause of Christ in that city, where impiety and tyranny held sway. So, to free him from this anxiety, God stirred up brothers to meet him, so that he might see that there would not be lacking those whom he could strengthen by the example of his own steadfastness, and who would help him by their prayers while he struggled. Let us therefore, encouraged by this example, hold fast to our calling. For devout zeal for the Word of God will not go unrewarded, and God himself will not fail us, for it is very easy for him to join us as companions in labors and dangers in any place whatever. Next, the Roman brothers themselves come to be considered by us. For we know that Paul had written to them before these things happened; in that letter he makes clear enough his own good will towards them, and promises that he will come to them. For that kindness, then, they show themselves grateful to him, although they could have been frightened by many things. First, he did not arrive in splendid array with great pomp, but was brought in chains with other captives, like a criminal. And who would not be ashamed of such a man? Or who would not fear danger from association with him? Next, it was in itself dangerous among the Romans to profess the faith and religion of Christ, which under Tiberius (as Tertullian writes) had been condemned by a public decree of the Senate. Moreover, the question concerned not only those who came out to meet him but the whole Church that was at Rome, against which a more diligent and severe inquiry could be set on foot on this occasion. But however these things stand, it seems to be a wicked thing to deny the duty of kindness to so great an apostle, who was labouring for our common cause; and therefore they preferred to undergo whatever danger rather than to be wanting in their duty. These things teach us what we owe to the ministers of Christ, who are the authors of our salvation through their ministry, if ever it should happen that they are put in peril for the sake of doctrine and faith. Let us not be ashamed of prisoners, since we know both that Christ was bound and that the Word of God cannot be restrained by any chains. Whoever shows such kindness will think that what was shown to them has been shown to himself. FINALLY, it is fitting to look at Paul himself, about whom two things are said. First, he gave thanks to God. This should not be understood as though he did not even speak to the brothers who had come before him. For since their service could not but be pleasing to him, it is quite certain that he also thanked them. Yet he acknowledges above all the work of God, who had stirred them up to dare so much. We too ought to do the same: to give thanks to men and to repay them, even for their kindness, but in such a way that the forgetfulness of God does not take hold of us, to whom we ought to ascribe every good thing. The other thing is that Paul, having taken on new confidence, is strengthened more, since he is going to have spectators of the struggle that awaited him. From this it is clear that even saints need strengthening, just as Christ teaches by the example of Peter and the other disciples. For when he says that he has prayed for Peter, he immediately adds: "And you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers." In the same way, even those who seem most perfect need teaching and admonition, exhortation as well as rebuke. Great, therefore, is the folly and intolerable the presumption of those who, forgetting that they are men, reject all teaching and correction with great disdain.

units.la: Romani fratres Paulo occurrunt.
units.tr: The Roman brothers meet Paul.

units.la: Fratrum Rom. gratitudo.
units.tr: The gratitude of the Roman brothers.

units.la: Paulus occursu fratrum confirmatur.
units.tr: Paul is strengthened by the coming of the brothers.

units.la: Porrò vbi Romam ventum est, Paulus à Centurione cum reliquis vinctis exercitus Praefecto traditur, sed longè dispari conditione. Nec enim in carcerem detruditur, sed illi liberum est, vt ab vno duntaxat milite custoditus in domo priuata, quam ipse sibi conduxerat, versetur. Vbi Centurionis commendatione aliquid tribuere fas est, quem erga Paulum optimè affectum fuisse, bucusq; vidimus. In primis tamen Deum spectare decet, qui Praefecti animum, vt antea Lysiæ Tribuni, Felicis, Festi & aliorum, illi obstrinxit. EST autem hic obseruatu dignissima sanctorum fors. Illos enim in mundo fere cum iniquis reputari videmus, quod etiam Christo contigit. Interim ita illorum curam gerit Christus, vt nihil eorum ipsis defit, quæ tum ipsorum saluti, tum illustrandæ gloriæ Dei seruiunt. Hoc enim facit, quod Paulo & domus priuata conceditur, & vnus duntaxat miles adhibetur, qui illi non tam custos quàm fidus defensor fuit. Vnde simul nihil eorum, quæ ad vinctum pertinebant, illi defuisse videmus. Adhæc illi liberum fuit, vt & exteras ecclesias epistolis consolaretur, & ad se quosuis vocaret, adeoq; in suo hospitio ecclesiam colligeret, quemadmodum ex ijs, quæ modò sequuntur, euidentissimè patebit.
units.tr: Moreover, when they had come to Rome, Paul was handed over by the centurion, with the other prisoners, to the prefect of the army, but on a far different footing. For he is not thrust into prison, but is allowed to live in a private house, which he had rented for himself, guarded by a single soldier. Here it is right to grant something to the centurion's recommendation, who, as we have seen up to now, was very well disposed towards Paul. Yet above all we ought to look to God, who bound the mind of the prefect to him, as before he had bound that of the tribune Lysias, of Felix, of Festus and of others. Now this is a most noteworthy lot of the saints. For we see that they are generally counted among the wicked in the world, as also happened to Christ. Meanwhile Christ so cares for them that nothing is lacking to them of those things which serve both their salvation and the glory of God. For he arranges that Paul is given a private house and only one soldier is assigned to him, who was less a jailer than a faithful defender. Hence at the same time we see that nothing was lacking to him of what pertained to a prisoner. Besides, it was free for him both to comfort the churches abroad by letters and to call to himself whomever he wished, and so to gather a church in his lodging, as will be most clearly seen from what follows.

units.la: Postq; triduum enim primarios ex Iudæis ad se vocans suæ cùm captiuitatis tum prouocationis rationem illis reddit, quæ occasio fuit, vt deinceps plures ad illum quotidie confluerent, quibus euangelium prædicabat. Est autem singulare mansuetudinis & charitatis exemplum, quod in Paulo proponitur. Quot enim quamq; atrocibus iniurijs à Iudæis affectus fuerit, satis notum est. Idem etiam vinculorum, quæ gestabat, foli authores erant. Adhuc tamen pro illorum salute solicitus, illos conuocare & ijsdem rerum suarum rationem reddere dignatur. Verissimum ergo est, quòd se pro illis assiduè orare, adeoq; anathema à Christo fieri velle scribit, modò ipsi saluaretur. Rom.9. & 10. Imitemur tam pij pectoris affectum, & ipsi quoq; iuxta Christi regulam inimicos diligere & illorum salutem summo studio prouebere discamus. Matth.5.
units.tr: For after three days, summoning the leading men among the Jews to himself, he gives them an account both of his captivity and of his appeal; this was the occasion for more and more people to come to him daily, to whom he preached the gospel. Moreover, the example of gentleness and charity set before us in Paul is singular. It is well known how many and how atrocious the injuries he suffered from the Jews were. He was also the sole cause of the chains he bore. Yet, still anxious for their salvation, he deigns to call them together and to give them an account of his affairs. Therefore it is most true that he writes that he prays for them without ceasing, and even that he wishes to be made an anathema from Christ, provided that they might be saved. Rom. 9 and 10. Let us imitate the feeling of so pious a heart, and let us learn also to love our enemies according to Christ's rule, and to promote their salvation with the greatest zeal. Matth. 5.

units.la: I. Suspicionibus sinistris medetur.
units.tr: I. He remedies sinister suspicions.

units.la: Cæterum quoad Pauli orationem, suis illa partibus conflat, quas ordine videbimus. Prima sinistris suspicionibus medetur, quibus se grauari nouerat, quasi & publicam gentis Iudaicæ pacem seditiose turbaret, & auitam patrum religionem impie conuelleret. Vtrunque verò constantissimè negat, dum se nihil vel aduersus plebem, vel aduersus maiorum instituta fecisse dicit. Ita autem suo exemplo docet, licere Christianis hominibus, vt aduersus maledicos causam & famam suam tueantur, ne forte propter ipsos euangelij doctrina male audiat. SIMVL illud quoque obseruandum venit, Christi ministros, nec in publicam pacem, nec in patrum religionem peccare, dum superstitiosam ceremoniarum operumq; fiduciam oppugnant, & veram religionem fideliter tradunt. Nec enim legitima scelerum reprehensione, sed ipsis scelerib. pax publica turbari solet, vt passim prophetæ docent. Deinde fidem, quæ vno Christo nititur omnium vetustissimam esse constat. Falso igitur nouitatis accusantur, qui illam reducere & à superstitiosis hominum traditionibus repurgare studeant.
units.tr: For the rest, as to Paul's speech, it is made up of its parts, which we shall see in order. The first part remedies the sinister suspicions by which he knew himself to be burdened, as if he were seditiously disturbing the public peace of the Jewish nation and impiously tearing up the religion of their fathers. He denies both most firmly, saying that he has done nothing either against the common people or against the institutions of their ancestors. And by his own example he teaches that Christians may defend their cause and reputation against slanderers, lest perhaps the doctrine of the gospel be ill spoken of because of them. At the same time it must also be observed that Christ's ministers sin neither against the public peace nor against the religion of the fathers when they attack superstitious trust in ceremonies and works and faithfully hand down the true religion. For public peace is not usually disturbed by the lawful rebuke of sins, but by the sins themselves, as the prophets teach everywhere. Next, faith, which rests on Christ alone, is agreed to be the most ancient of all. Therefore those who strive to restore it and to cleanse it of human superstitious traditions are falsely accused of novelty.

units.la: II. Prouocationē excusat.
units.tr: II. He excuses his appeal.

units.la: Secunda parte suæ ad Cæsarem prouocationis rationem reddit, quæ ipsi graue apud Iudæos odium conflare poterat. Partim enim contra gentis libertatem Romanæ tyrannidi subscribere vi debantur qui prouocabant: partim per se ignominiosum & cum Iudicis contumelia coniunctum esse videtur, si quis ad alium prouocet. Ne quid ergo de se tale suspicarentur, se id coactum fecisse dicit, non vt Iudaicam gentem apud Cæsarem accusaret, sed vt vitæ suæ consuleret, cui illi contra omne ius & æquum insidiabantur. Vbi rursum admonemur, ciuiles defensiones Christianis hominibus minimè negatas esse, quàmuis Christus nos malo resistere prohibeat. Nam de priuata vindicta illud intelligi debet, quam licet persequi vetemur, legum tamen & legitimorum iudiciorum vsus omnibus à Deo conceditur, quem qui tollunt, magistratum quoq; in vniuersum tollant & abrogent necesse est.
units.tr: In the second part he gives the reason for his appeal to Caesar, which could stir up serious hatred against him among the Jews. For those who appealed seemed partly to submit the liberty of the nation to Roman tyranny, and partly to appeal to another is in itself shameful and joined with an insult to the judge. So that they might not suspect anything of the sort about him, he says that he did it under compulsion, not to accuse the Jewish nation before Caesar, but to look after his own life, which they were plotting against contrary to all law and right. Here again we are reminded that civil defences are by no means denied to Christians, although Christ forbids us to resist evil. For this must be understood of private vengeance, which we are forbidden to pursue; but the use of laws and lawful judgments is granted to all by God, and those who take it away must necessarily take away and abolish the magistracy in general as well.

units.la: III. Statum totius controuersiæ explicat.
units.tr: III. He explains the state of the whole controversy.

units.la: Tertia pars statum totius causæ, de qua illi cum Iudæis lis erat, comprehendit. Propter spem Israelis (inquit) hac catena circundatus sum. Ita verò Christum appellat, in quo Iudæi regnum & libertatem sperabant, quàmuis illum non rectè agnoscerent, dum terrenum regnum & carnis licentiam ex prophetijs perperam intelligebant. Quæ causa erat, quòd quem venturum sperabant, exhibitum persequebantur. Hoc ipsum verò frequens admodum est in salutis negotio, vt qui Christi nomine gloriantur, eundem tamen improbè fastidiant, maximè quando vel quæstiuo suo aliquid derògari, vel carni frænum inijci sentiunt. Admonet interim Pauli locutio, non aliam hominibus salutis spem datam esse, quàm quæ in Christo Iesu habetur. In hoc enim promissiones omnes impletæ & exhibitæ sunt. Hunc vnum patres expectarunt. Eundem Moses & prophetæ monstrant. Nec alium saluatorem nouerunt apostoli. In quo si & nos spem repositam habuerimus, minime fallemur.
units.tr: The third part comprises the state of the whole cause, over which he had a dispute with the Jews. "Because of the hope of Israel," he says, "I am bound with this chain." He calls Christ thus, in whom the Jews hoped for a kingdom and liberty, although they did not rightly acknowledge him, since they misunderstood the earthly kingdom and licence of the flesh from the prophecies. This was the cause why they persecuted him whom they hoped would come, once he was shown. Indeed this very thing is very frequent in the business of salvation: those who glory in the name of Christ nevertheless wickedly despise him, especially when they feel that something of their gain is taken away or a bridle put on the flesh. Meanwhile Paul's expression warns that no other hope of salvation is given to men than that which is held in Christ Jesus. For in him all the promises have been fulfilled and exhibited. The fathers waited for him alone. Moses and the prophets point to him alone. The apostles know no other saviour. If we too have placed our hope in him, we shall by no means be deceived.

units.la: Sequitur Iudæorum responsio, quæ duabus partibus absoluitur. Primò enim luculentum Paulo innocentiæ testimonium ferunt, quando se nec literas à quoquam accepisse, nec etiam vllius relatione quicquam de illo audiisse dicunt. Quid enim de Paulo scriberent Sacerdotes, qui illius innocentiam omnibus perspectam esse nouerant? Interim hic sanctorum fors elucet, qui quàmuis innocentissimi sint, hostes tamen facilè inueniunt, quibus authoribus vel in carceres abducuntur, vel in exilium relegantur. Verum vero horum fiat, hostes postea securi, illorum causam negligunt, nec quisquam est, qui illorum curam ad se pertinere putet. Tandem, vbi nouas odij flammas hostes concipiunt, necem quoq; insontibus machinantur. Altera vero parte Iudæi Pauli de fide & religione Christiana sententiam audire cupiunt, quàmuis illi passim ab omnibus contradici scirent. Et sanè magna laude dignum est, quòd aliorum præiudicijs non ita excæcantur, vt omnem de fide relationem fastidiant. Quod hodie multi faciunt, qui serpentum instar aures obturant, & ita sibi ipsis ostium regni cœlorum præclu- dunt. Quos si non alia ratio mouet, saltem pudeat ipsos, quòd Iudæos huius causæ æquiores iudices fuisse videmus. Cumprimis vero euangelij fors nobis hoc loco confyderanda venit, cui omnibus sectiis passim contradictum fuit. Nec enim Christi doctrinam ferre potest princeps huius mundi diabolus, quum Christus illius regnum potentissimè euertat. Similiter lucem hanc flagitiosi quoq; & scelerati aspernantur, eò quòd per hanc opera sua mala argui nouerunt. Et eandem iustitiarij quoq; hypocritæ subterfugiunt, vt quæ ingenitam nobis corruptionem manifestat, & omne humanæ iustitiæ fiduciam euertit. Quare fieri non potest, quin hostes vndiq; insurgant. Id vero tum institutioni tum consolationi nostræ seruit. Excitat enim nos vt ad certamen præparemur, nec ocium ignauum nobis promittamus. Deinde inuictam & diuinam plane docet esse euangelij potentiam, quæ tot seculis mundi & principis huius conatibus resistere potuit. Nam si alias religiones, quotquot vnquam in mundo fuere, omnes inspicias, sua sponte illas corruisse adeo; in ventum abiisse videbis, licet illas nemo armata manu oppugnauerit. At Christiana religio, quæ ex euangelio hauritur, cum omnibus seculis hostes habuerit acerrimos, qui illam ferro simul & igne persecuti sunt, durat tamen in hunc vsq; diem, & in nouissimum vsq; diem durabit, quo Christus ad iudicium venturus est, vt suorum afflictiones æterno gaudio compensat, hostibus vero dignas sceleribus suis poenas retribuat. Neminem ergo vel contradicentium contumacia, vel persecutorum rabies offendat. Viuit enim & regnat ecclesiæ sponsus, Iesus Christus, cui illam ex hostium manibus afferre facillimum fuerit. Illi debetur benedictio, honor, gloria & potestas in æternum. Amen.
units.tr: There follows the Jews' reply, which is completed in two parts. First, they bear Paul a splendid testimony of innocence, when they say that they neither received letters about him from anyone nor heard anything about him from any report. For what would the priests write about Paul, who knew that his innocence was seen by all? Meanwhile here shines forth the lot of the saints, who, however innocent they are, easily find enemies, by whose instigation they are either led off to prisons or banished into exile. But whatever happens to these men, the enemies afterwards, feeling secure, neglect their cause, and there is no one who thinks their care belongs to him. At last, when the enemies conceive new flames of hatred, they also plot death against the innocent. On the other side, the Jews wish to hear Paul's opinion about faith and the Christian religion, although they knew that he was everywhere contradicted by all. And indeed it is worthy of great praise that they are not so blinded by the prejudices of others that they scorn every account of the faith. Many do the opposite today, who stop their ears like serpents, and thus shut for themselves the door of the kingdom of heaven. If reason does not move them, at least let them be ashamed that we see the Jews to have been fairer judges of this cause. Above all, the lot of the gospel must be considered here, which has been contradicted everywhere by all sects. For the prince of this world, the devil, cannot bear the doctrine of Christ, since Christ most powerfully overthrows his kingdom. Likewise the wicked and the criminal also spurn this light, because they know that their evil works are exposed by it. And the justiciaries and hypocrites also flee from it, since it reveals our innate corruption and overthrows all trust in human righteousness. Therefore it cannot be but that enemies rise up on every side. This serves both our instruction and our consolation. For it stirs us to prepare for the struggle, and not to promise ourselves idle ease. Next, it clearly teaches that the power of the gospel is invincible and divine, since it has been able to resist the attempts of the world and of this prince through so many ages. For if you inspect all the other religions, as many as have ever existed in the world, you will see that they collapsed of their own accord and came to nothing, although no one attacked them with armed hand. But the Christian religion, which is drawn from the gospel, although it has had the fiercest enemies in all ages, who persecuted it with sword and fire at once, nevertheless endures to this day, and will endure to the last day, on which Christ is to come to judgment, when he will compensate his people's afflictions with eternal joy and will repay the enemies with punishments worthy of their crimes. Let no one therefore be offended either by the obstinacy of those who contradict or by the rage of persecutors. For the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ, lives and reigns, and he will most easily bring her from the hands of her enemies. To him belong blessing, honour, glory and power for ever. Amen.

units.la: HOMILIA CLXXIIII.
units.tr: HOMILY CLXXIIII.

units.la: Cùm autem constituissent illi diem, venerunt ad eum in hospitium complures, quibus exponebat testificans regnum Dei, suadensq; eis de Iesu ex Lege Moisis & Prophetis, à mane vsque ad vesperam. Et quidam credebant his quæ dicebantur, quidam vero non credebant. Cumq; inter se essent discordes, discesserunt, postquàm dixisset Paulus verbum vnum: Bene spiritus sanctus locutus est per Isaiam Prophetam ad patres nostros, dicens: Vade ad populum istum, & dic: Auribus audietis, & non intelligetis: & videntes videbitis, & non perspicietis. Incrassatum est enim cor populi huius, & auribus grauiter audierunt, & oculos suos compresserunt, ne quando videant oculis, & auribus audiant, & corde intelligant, & conuertantur, & sanem eos. Notum ergo sit hoc vobis, quòd Gentibus missum est hoc salutare Dei, & ipsi audient. Cùm hæc dixisset, exiuerunt ab eo Iudæi, multam habentes inter se disceptationem.
units.tr: When they had appointed him a day, many came to him at his lodging, and he expounded to them, testifying of the kingdom of God and persuading them concerning Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, from morning until evening. Some were persuaded by what was said, but others did not believe. Since they disagreed among themselves, they departed, after Paul had said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and not understand; you will see with your eyes and not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them. Let it be known therefore to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will hear it." When he had said these things, the Jews departed, having much dispute among themselves.

units.la: QVamuis ministri Iesu Christi & euangelij praecones variis persecutionibus exerceantur, & interdum carceres & vincula sustineant, tamen Dei verbum vinciri sine concludi non potest, eò quòd spiritus Christi ubi voluerit spirat, nec hominum arbitrio & libidini subijcitur. Imò ut Christi morte latius propagari coepit euangelij doctrina, sicuti ille fore praedixerat: ita ministrorum quoque afflictionibus & supplicijs auxit. Exemplum huius rei euidens in Pauli historia proponitur. Nam licet ille antehac euangelium longe lateque praedicarit per orbem, maius tamen ostium illi capto & catenato apertum fuit: quando in urbe Romana, ceu in frequentissimo totius mundi theatro, liberè omnibus praedicare poterat, & eo quidem successu, ut in Caesaris quoque familiam doctrina haec penetret, quemadmodum ex salutationibus ad Philippen. scriptis conijcere licet. Phil 4. Mira profectò & stupore digna res, in qua Christi prouidentiam & potentiam agnoscere licet, nisi quis in ipsa luce caecutire velit. Porrò, qua ratione istud factum sit, Lucas commemorat, & quidem ex multis concionibus vnam deligit, ex qua alias omnes iudicemus. Nobis verò de singulis circumstantijs ordine dicendum erit.
units.tr: Although the ministers of Jesus Christ and the heralds of the gospel are harassed by various persecutions, and at times endure prisons and chains, yet the Word of God cannot be bound or shut up, because the Spirit of Christ breathes where he wills and is not subject to the judgment and lust of men. Indeed, just as the teaching of the gospel began to spread more widely through the death of Christ, as he had foretold, so it has also been increased by the afflictions and sufferings of the ministers. A clear example of this is set before us in the history of Paul. For although he had earlier preached the gospel far and wide throughout the world, a greater door was opened to him when he was held captive and in chains, since in the city of Rome, as in the most crowded theatre of the whole world, he could preach freely to everyone, and with such success that this doctrine even penetrated into the household of Caesar, as may be gathered from the greetings written to the Philippians (Phil. 4). This is truly a wonderful thing, worthy of amazement, in which the providence and power of Christ may be recognised, unless someone wishes to be blind in the very light. Moreover, Luke relates by what means this happened, and he selects one of the many sermons, from which we may judge all the others. But we shall have to speak in order about each of the circumstances.

units.la: Primò locum & tempus notat Euangelista, quando illos constituto die in hospitium Pauli conuenisse dicit. Nondum enim illo seculo templa habere licebat Christianis: nec si habuissent, Paulo liberum fuisset in illis docere, cum captiuus detineretur. Quare vt alibi in priuatis aedibus apostoli praedicarunt, ita hic quoque in domo conductitia coetus sacros cogit. VNDE colligimus, Dei cultum & doctrinam non ita debere locis certis alligari, quasi illi ad salutem aliquid momenti conferant. Constat enim, Dei verbum ex semetipso authoritatem habere. Preces verò vbique locorum exaudit Deus, modò ex fide oremus & manus puras ad illum attollamus. Quare si ita necessitas urgeat, non est quòd de loco aut tempore soliciti simus. Caeterum vbi pace fruimur & magistratus Christianus regnat, ordini studendum erit, qui & locum & tempus certum requirit. Minimè ergo Anabaptistarum furiosis clamoribus primitiuae ecclesiae exempla patrocinantur, quando olim necessitas in coetibus sacris cogendis multa secus facere coegit.
units.tr: First, the evangelist notes the place and the time, when he says that they gathered at Paul's lodging on an appointed day. For in that age Christians were not yet permitted to have churches, and even if they had them, it would not have been lawful for Paul to teach in them, since he was held prisoner. Therefore, as the apostles elsewhere preached in private houses, so here too he gathers the holy assembly in a rented house. FROM THIS we gather that the worship and teaching of God ought not to be tied to fixed places, as if they contributed anything of weight to salvation. For it is agreed that the Word of God has authority from itself. God hears prayers in every place, provided we pray in faith and lift up pure hands to him. Therefore, if necessity so urges, we need not be anxious about place or time. But where we enjoy peace and a Christian magistrate reigns, care must be taken for order, which requires both a place and a fixed time. Therefore the frenzied clamours of the Anabaptists do not at all find support in the examples of the primitive Church, since at that time necessity compelled them to do many things otherwise in gathering sacred assemblies.

units.la: Secundò argumentum concionis Paulinae vnà cum modo seu ratione docendi, qua ille vsus est, exprimitur. Nam regnum Dei expositi, testificans simul & suadens de Iesu Christo. At sub regno Dei euangelium intelligi, iam saepe diximus. De hoc autem commodè dicere non potuit Paulus, nisi simul Iudaeorum errores confutaret, qui ex prophetijs male intellectis terrenum Messiae regnum somniabant. Quare docendi erant spirituale esse regnum illud, cuius initium in hoc seculo sit totius hominis regeneratio & vitae nouitas, finis autem & scopus aeterna felicitas, quae in coelis nobis praeparata est. Quia verò regni huius authorem Iudaei ignorabant, hunc docuit Christum Iesum esse, cui pro apostoli officio testimonium diserte tulit, simulque omnes, vt illum excipiant, hortatus est. Obseruemus autem, euangelij doctrinam regnum Dei dici: ab effectu nimirum & fine. Nam & Deiregnum siue felicitatem veram nobis offert, & nos totos Deo regendos subijcit, dum rationem & intellectum omnem cogit sub fidei obedientiam. Hic autem officij admonentur quotquot euangelij nomine gloriari solent. Meminerint illo Dei regnum praedicari, & proinde curent, vt in ipsis Deus regnet, aboleatur autem diaboli regnum, cuius destruendi causa Christum in carnem venisse scimus. Rursum ministri quoque de vera euangelij praedicandi ratione admonentur, ad quam tria haec necessaria sunt. Primùm exponant huius regni mysteria, ne falsis imaginationibus simplices seducantur. Deinde de Christo Iesu testentur, vt hunc regni & felicitatis verae authorem esse omnes intelligant. Tandem verò suadendo & hortando instent, ne oblatam in Christo salutem hominess aspernentur.
units.tr: Second, the subject of Paul's sermon is set forth together with the manner or method of teaching which he used. For he expounded the kingdom of God, testifying and at the same time persuading concerning Jesus Christ. But we have often said already that under the kingdom of God the gospel is understood. Paul could not speak of this suitably without at the same time refuting the errors of the Jews, who, from the prophecies badly understood, dreamed of an earthly kingdom of the Messiah. Therefore it had to be taught that that kingdom is spiritual, whose beginning in this age is the regeneration of the whole man and the newness of life, and whose end and goal is eternal happiness, which is prepared for us in heaven. But since the Jews did not know the author of this kingdom, he taught that it was Jesus Christ, to whom he bore clear testimony as part of his office as apostle, and at the same time exhorted all to receive him. Let us observe, moreover, that the teaching of the gospel is called the kingdom of God, plainly from its effect and end. For God both offers us the true kingdom or happiness and subjects us wholly to be ruled by him, while he compels every reason and understanding into the obedience of faith. Here, however, all those who are accustomed to glory in the name of the gospel are reminded of their duty. Let them remember that the kingdom of God is preached there, and therefore let them take care that God may reign in them, and that the kingdom of the devil, for whose destruction we know Christ came into the flesh, may be abolished. Again, the ministers too are reminded of the true method of preaching the gospel, for which three things are necessary. First, they should set out the mysteries of this kingdom, lest the simple be led astray by false imaginations. Then they should bear witness concerning Christ Jesus, so that everyone may understand that he is the author of this kingdom and of true happiness. Finally, by persuading and exhorting, they should press on, so that men do not scorn the salvation offered in Christ.

units.la: Tertiò fons doctrinae huius indicatur. Nam ex lege Mosis & prophetis de Christo Paulus disseruit, in hoc nimirum impleta esse probans, quaecunque illi de promisso humani generis saluatore praedixerunt. Ita verò ipsius Christi exemplum secutus est, qui eorundem testimonijs frequenter vti consueuit. Docet locus hic, in ecclesia non hominum figmenta, sed Dei verbū, quod scripturis sacris comprehensum est, praedicari debere. Quia enim Dei domus est ecclesia, aliam quàm patrisfamilias vocem in illa audiri nefas fuerit. Quae causa est, quòd huic praecepto omnes tum prophetae tum apostoli astringuntur, sicuti alias monuimus. Quare haud leuiter peccant, qui vel ipsi aliam doctrinam tradunt, vel aliam audiunt & sequuntur, quando haec demum vera ecclesiae nota est, quòd solius Ipsius fui voce delectatur. Vide Psal. 45. Iohan. 10. Praeterea veteris & noui Testamenti consensum obseruemus, ne illud (vt fanatici quidam) nihil ad nos pertinere dicamus: quando vtrinque vnum & eundem Christum, vnam & eandem salutis rationem tradi constat, nec quicquam in novo implerum & exhibitum esse doceatur, quàm quod in veteri promissum esse scimus. Vnde simul constat, fidem in Christum omnium vetustissimam, adeoque vnicam esse, per quam electi omnes ab ipsa mundi origine saluati sint. Quia tamen de his saepè aliàs diximus, haec in praesenti breuius seu digito notauisse sufficiat.
units.tr: Third, the source of this teaching is indicated. For Paul discoursed concerning Christ from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, proving that in him were fulfilled all the things which they had foretold concerning the Saviour of mankind who was promised. In this way he followed the example of Christ himself, who was accustomed to use their testimonies frequently. This passage teaches that in the Church not the inventions of men but the Word of God, which is contained in the holy Scriptures, ought to be preached. For since the Church is the house of God, it would be wrong for any voice other than that of the householder to be heard in it. This is the reason why all, both prophets and apostles, are bound by this precept, as we have pointed out elsewhere. Therefore those sin no little who either themselves teach another doctrine, or hear and follow another, since this is in the end the true mark of the Church: that it delights in his own voice alone. See Ps. 45; John 10. Moreover, let us observe the agreement of the Old and New Testaments, so that we do not say (like certain fanatics) that the Old has nothing to do with us, since it is plain that on both sides the same one Christ and the same one way of salvation are delivered, and it is taught that nothing has been fulfilled and exhibited in the New except what we know was promised in the Old. From this it is also plain that faith in Christ is the most ancient of all, and therefore the only faith, through which all the elect have been saved from the very beginning of the world. Yet since we have often spoken of these things elsewhere, it will be enough in the present place to have noted them more briefly, as it were with a finger.

units.la: Quarto quàm diu Paulus praedicarit, Lucas docet. A matutino nimirum tempore ad vesperam vsque. Vnde coniicere possumus, inter ipsos disputatum quoque fuisse, & illorum argumentis Paulum respondisse. Nec enim verisimile est, eos qui Christum adhuc prorsus ignorabant, tanta patientia Paulum audire potuisse, vt non aliquando dicentem suis obiectionibus interrumperent. Interim ardens cum Pauli tum auditorum ipsius studium exprimitur, cuius simile exemplum supra cap. vigesimo habuimus. Arguitur hic nostri seculi ignauia, qua & ministri aliquot verbi & auditores laborare solent, quibus nimium videtur omne studium, quod sacris concionibus impenditur. Sed orietur aliquando fames illa verbi, de qua apud prophetam legimus, &c. Amos 8. capite.
units.tr: Fourth, Luke teaches how long Paul preached: namely from morning until evening.
